ALG:010117.title: Strict greater-than keeps equal tagged keys in order; eight comparisons and six shifts sort the five-record array
ALG:010117.objective: Prove the sorted-stable-prefix invariant of insertion sort under a strict > test, execute the tagged trace to [1d,2b,3e,4a,4c] with exactly eight key comparisons and six shifts, and reject both a non-strict test that swaps 4a with 4c and a comparison count that drops the terminating failed tests.
ALG:010117.statement:
Fix a totally ordered key type and write records as tagged pairs $\mathit{key}\mathit{tag}$. Two records compare only by key: $\mathit{tag}$ is an identity witness and is never part of the comparison. Consider 1-based insertion sort on an array $A[1..n]$:
\begin{align*}
&\textbf{for } i=2\textbf{ to }n\textbf{ do}\\
&\quad \mathit{key}\leftarrow A[i];\quad j\leftarrow i-1\\
&\quad \textbf{while } j\ge 1\textbf{ and } A[j]>\mathit{key}\textbf{ do}\\
&\quad\quad A[j+1]\leftarrow A[j];\quad j\leftarrow j-1\\
&\quad A[j+1]\leftarrow \mathit{key}.
\end{align*}
A \emph{key comparison} is one evaluation of the predicate $A[j]>\mathit{key}$. The guard $j\ge 1$ is an index test, not a key comparison. A \emph{shift} is one assignment $A[j+1]\leftarrow A[j]$. The terminal write $A[j+1]\leftarrow\mathit{key}$ is a placement, not a shift. The algorithm is required to be stable: records of equal key must retain their original relative order.

1. State a loop invariant for the outer index $i$ that records both sortedness of a prefix and stability of that prefix relative to the original input. Prove initialization at $i=2$ (before the first insertion), maintenance across one insertion, and that termination at $i=n+1$ yields a stable sort of $A[1..n]$. Identify exactly where the proof uses the strict test $>$ rather than $\ge$.

2. Execute the algorithm on the five-record input
   \[
   A=[4a,2b,4c,1d,3e].
   \]
   After each outer iteration record the array, the number of key comparisons performed in that iteration, and the number of shifts. Prove that the terminal array is $[1d,2b,3e,4a,4c]$ and that the four iterations perform $1+1+3+3=8$ key comparisons and $1+0+3+2=6$ shifts.

3. Prove that the worst-case number of key comparisons on $n$ records with distinct keys is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, attained on a strictly decreasing array, and conclude that the worst-case running time is $\Theta(n^2)$ in the standard comparison model with constant-time assignments.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “replacing $>$ by $\ge$ is harmless because equal keys may be swapped”; (ii) “only comparisons that trigger a shift count, so the last insertion of $3e$ contributes two comparisons rather than three.”

Do not replace insertion sort by half-open binary search, and do not analyze an unequal-split divide-and-conquer recurrence.
permittedResults: If a prefix $A[1..i-1]$ is sorted and the inner loop shifts only records strictly larger than $\mathit{key}=A[i]$, then $A[1..i]$ is sorted after the placement and every equal-key pair in that prefix retains its former order.
On a strictly decreasing array of $n$ distinct keys, the $i$th insertion performs exactly $i-1$ successful key comparisons and $i-1$ shifts, for a total of $\sum_{i=2}^{n}(i-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Maintain the stable prefix explicitly, then fill a four-row trace table that records every true and every false key test before summing.
First exhibit the >= swap of 4a with 4c and the dropped failed test against 2b, then justify the strict predicate and the comparison model from those two defects.

milestones.criterion: Proves the stable sorted-prefix invariant and identifies the strict > test as the stability obligation.
Traces the five-record input to [1d,2b,3e,4a,4c] with exactly 8 key comparisons and 6 shifts.
Derives the quadratic worst-case comparison count and rejects both a non-strict test and a count that omits terminating failed comparisons.

commonErrors.description: Uses A[j] >= key instead of A[j] > key, so 4a shifts past 4c and the equal-key pair reverses.
commonErrors.consequence: The output may still be sorted by key but is no longer a stable permutation of the tagged input.

commonErrors.description: Counts only comparisons that trigger a shift, or drops the terminating failed test of the last insertion, reporting 6 or 7 key comparisons instead of 8.
commonErrors.consequence: The two failed tests (inserting 4c, then 2b > 3e) are invisible, so the comparison model is not the one stated.

hintTree.content: The inner loop on $4c$ stops immediately because $4a>4c$ is false. That failed test is still a key comparison, and it is what keeps $4a$ to the left of $4c$.
When $3e$ is inserted into $[1d,2b,4a,4c]$, the tests are $4c>3e$ (true), $4a>3e$ (true), and $2b>3e$ (false). Two shifts move $4c$ and $4a$; the failed test against $2b$ still counts.
If the inner predicate is $A[j]\ge\mathit{key}$, the insertion of $4c$ treats $4a$ as movable, so the equal-key pair reverses. The sorted-prefix invariant can survive, but stability does not.

ALG:010117.canonicalSolution:
Write $A^{(1)}$ for the input. For the outer index $i$ just before the insertion of $A[i]$, maintain
\[
(\mathrm{I})\quad
A[1..i-1]\text{ is a stably sorted permutation of }A^{(1)}[1..i-1].
\]
When $i=2$ the prefix has length one, so $(\mathrm{I})$ holds. Suppose $(\mathrm{I})$ holds and $\mathit{key}=A[i]$. The inner loop examines $A[i-1],A[i-2],\ldots$ and shifts a record one cell right only when that record is strictly larger than $\mathit{key}$. Thus every shifted record is $> \mathit{key}$, every unexamined record in the prefix is $\le\mathit{key}$, and the first failed test (or the index failure $j=0$) identifies the unique hole at which $\mathit{key}$ may be placed so that $A[1..i]$ is sorted. Records equal to $\mathit{key}$ are not shifted, so they remain to the left of the newly placed record; together with $(\mathrm{I})$ this preserves stability on $A^{(1)}[1..i]$. After the last insertion one has $i=n+1$, so $A[1..n]$ is a stable sort of the input.
\[
\boxed{\text{stable sorted prefix; strict > never moves an equal key}}.
\]
The strictness of $>$ is used only for stability: sortedness of the prefix would still hold under $\ge$, but an equal key already in the prefix would be treated as larger and would move to the right of $\mathit{key}$.

Now trace $A=[4a,2b,4c,1d,3e]$.

$i=2$, $\mathit{key}=2b$. One test $4a>2b$ succeeds, one shift writes $4a$ into position $2$, and $2b$ is placed at index $1$. State $[2b,4a,4c,1d,3e]$; comparisons $1$, shifts $1$.

$i=3$, $\mathit{key}=4c$. One test $4a>4c$ fails, so there is no shift and $4c$ is replaced in position $3$. State $[2b,4a,4c,1d,3e]$; comparisons $1$, shifts $0$. The failed test is required both for the count and to leave $4a$ left of $4c$.

$i=4$, $\mathit{key}=1d$. Three successful tests $4c>1d$, $4a>1d$, $2b>1d$ produce three shifts, then $1d$ is placed at index $1$. State $[1d,2b,4a,4c,3e]$; comparisons $3$, shifts $3$.

$i=5$, $\mathit{key}=3e$. Tests $4c>3e$ and $4a>3e$ succeed and shift those two records right; the next test $2b>3e$ fails, so $3e$ is placed at index $3$. State $[1d,2b,3e,4a,4c]$; comparisons $3$, shifts $2$.

The four iterations contribute $1+1+3+3=8$ key comparisons and $1+0+3+2=6$ shifts. The equal-key pair $4a,4c$ retains input order.
\[
\boxed{[1d,2b,3e,4a,4c];\ 8\text{ comparisons},\ 6\text{ shifts}}.
\]

If every key is distinct and the input is strictly decreasing, the $i$th insertion finds $\mathit{key}$ smaller than all $i-1$ preceding records, so it performs $i-1$ successful comparisons and $i-1$ shifts and never a failed key test (it stops on $j=0$). Summing $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)$ gives $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons and the same number of shifts. The quantity is $\Theta(n^2)$, and each iteration does $O(n)$ other constant-time work, so the worst-case running time is $\Theta(n^2)$. (Already-sorted distinct input is the matching linear best case: each insertion performs exactly one failed comparison.)

Sentence (i) is false on this input: $\ge$ makes the test $4a\ge 4c$ succeed, shifts $4a$ past $4c$, and yields a prefix $[2b,4c,4a,\ldots]$. Sortedness survives, stability does not. Sentence (ii) drops the two failed tests (the insertion of $4c$, and the terminating test $2b>3e$). Counting only shift-triggering comparisons reports $6$ rather than $8$; dropping only the last failed test reports $7$. Both counts are wrong under the stated model.

The argument never searches a half-open interval and never unfolds a divide-and-conquer recurrence.

graderFixtures.proofText: The strict test leaves $4a$ left of $4c$. The trace ends at $[1d,2b,3e,4a,4c]$ after $1+1+3+3=8$ key comparisons and $1+0+3+2=6$ shifts. The last insertion performs two successful tests and one failed test against $2b$. Replacing $>$ by $\ge$ reverses $4a$ and $4c$. Omitting failed tests undercounts.

Equal keys may be swapped, so I use A[j] >= key. Inserting 4c shifts 4a one cell right and the array becomes [2b,4c,4a,1d,3e] before the later insertions. The final order has 4c before 4a, which is still sorted by key.

A comparison counts only when it moves a record. The four insertions therefore contribute 1+0+3+2=6 comparisons, matching the six shifts. The last insertion of 3e does two comparisons, not three, because 2b > 3e fails and does no work.

ALG:010218.title: A merge counts every leftover left key, so the seven-key array has thirteen inversions, not three
ALG:010218.objective: Count inversions of [7,3,5,1,6,2,4] by merge-sort cross contributions, prove the leftover-left increment and the O(n log n) bound, and reject both an adjacent-only count and a merge that adds one per right take.
ALG:010218.statement:
An inversion of an array $A[1..n]$ of distinct keys is a pair of indices $i<j$ with $A[i]>A[j]$. Consider the standard merge-sort inversion counter: recursively count inversions in the left half and in the right half, then merge the two sorted halves while adding, each time a key is taken from the right half, the number of still-unconsumed keys in the left half.

1. Prove that this increment is exactly the number of inversions with one endpoint in the left half and one endpoint in the right half, and that the three contributions (left, right, cross) are pairwise disjoint and exhaustive.

2. Execute the algorithm on
   \[
   A=[7,3,5,1,6,2,4],
   \]
   splitting always into a left floor-half and a right ceiling-half (so the first split is $[7,3,5,1]$ and $[6,2,4]$). Record every merge, every right-take increment, and the three subproblem totals. Prove that the inversion count is $13$.

3. Bound the running time by $O(n\log n)$ in the standard RAM model. Identify the recurrence and why the combine step is linear.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “only adjacent descents are inversions, so the count is $3$”; (ii) “each right-take contributes $1$, because that one right key forms one inversion.”

Do not replace the count by an unequal-split recurrence-tree analysis, and do not treat the problem as interval scheduling.
permittedResults: Every inversion is confined to the left half, confined to the right half, or straddles the split. After the halves are sorted, the straddling inversions are exactly the leftover-left increments paid during the merge.
The merge-sort recurrence $T(n)=T(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)+T(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$ solves to $T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Unfold the merge tree, record every leftover-left payment, then confirm the total by enumerating inversions from each left endpoint.
First compute the inversion number by brute-force pairs to lock 13, then replay the merges only to exhibit the cross-count mechanism and the two named defects.

milestones.criterion: Proves that a right-take while r left keys remain contributes exactly those r crossing inversions.
Executes the prescribed merges and obtains left 5, right 2, cross 6, and total 13.
Gives the Theta(n log n) merge-sort bound and rejects both an adjacent-only count and a unit right-take increment.

commonErrors.description: Counts only adjacent descents (7,3), (5,1), (6,2) and reports 3 inversions.
commonErrors.consequence: Every non-adjacent inversion is discarded, so the merge-sort counter is replaced by a single-pass descent count.

commonErrors.description: Adds 1 for each right-take instead of the number of remaining left keys, typically reporting 9 rather than 13.
commonErrors.consequence: The final merge pays 3 instead of 6, and the left-half merge of 1 into [3,7] pays 1 instead of 2.

hintTree.content: The left half $[7,3,5,1]$ contributes $5$ inversions and the right half $[6,2,4]$ contributes $2$. The remaining $6$ inversions are created while merging $[1,3,5,7]$ with $[2,4,6]$.
When $2$ is taken from the right, the three leftover left keys $3,5,7$ each invert with $2$. Adding $1$ here is the leftover-left error.
Adjacent descents of $A$ are only $(7,3)$, $(5,1)$, and $(6,2)$. The pairs $(7,1)$ and $(5,2)$ are inversions that are not adjacent.

ALG:010218.canonicalSolution:
Split $A$ into left and right contiguous halves. An inversion has both endpoints on the left, both on the right, or one on each side. The first two classes are counted recursively. For the third class, after each half is sorted increasing, a merge that always emits the smaller current head is correct as a sort. If it emits a right key $y$ while $r\ge 1$ left keys remain, each remaining left key $x$ satisfies $x>y$ (because the left run is sorted and its head is already $>y$) and originally stood to the left of $y$. Those $r$ pairs are precisely the still-unpaid crossing inversions that involve $y$. Emitting a left key pays nothing more: every smaller right key that could invert with it has already been emitted and paid. The three classes partition the inversion set, so the algorithm returns the inversion number.

Execute the prescribed splits.

Left $[7,3,5,1]$ splits into $[7,3]$ and $[5,1]$.
Merging $[7]$ with $[3]$ emits $3$ and pays $1$, then emits $7$. Subtotal $1$.
Merging $[5]$ with $[1]$ emits $1$ and pays $1$, then emits $5$. Subtotal $1$.
Merging $[3,7]$ with $[1,5]$:
emit $1$ (pay $2$, leftover $3,7$); emit $3$ (left take); emit $5$ (pay $1$, leftover $7$); emit $7$.
Cross $2+1=3$. Left total $1+1+3=5$. Direct check: the five inversions of $[7,3,5,1]$ are $(7,3)$, $(7,5)$, $(7,1)$, $(3,1)$, $(5,1)$.

Right $[6,2,4]$ splits into $[6]$ and $[2,4]$. The pair $[2,4]$ is already sorted and pays $0$. Merging $[6]$ with $[2,4]$ emits $2$ (pay $1$), emits $4$ (pay $1$), then emits $6$. Right total $2$. Direct check: $(6,2)$, $(6,4)$.

Merge $[1,3,5,7]$ with $[2,4,6]$:
emit $1$ (left); emit $2$ (pay $3$, leftover $3,5,7$); emit $3$ (left); emit $4$ (pay $2$, leftover $5,7$); emit $5$ (left); emit $6$ (pay $1$, leftover $7$); emit $7$.
Cross $3+2+1=6$. Grand total $5+2+6=13$.
Direct check by left endpoints:
$7$ forms $6$ inversions; $3$ forms $2$; $5$ forms $3$; $6$ forms $2$; and $1,2,4$ form none. Sum $13$.
\[
\boxed{13}.
\]

Each merge of two runs whose lengths sum to $m$ performs $\Theta(m)$ work. The recursion tree therefore satisfies $T(n)=T(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)+T(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$, which is $\Theta(n\log n)$. The algorithm never enumerates pairs.

Sentence (i) counts only the adjacent descents $(7,3)$, $(5,1)$, $(6,2)$ and reports $3$, omitting every non-adjacent inversion. Sentence (ii) replaces the leftover-left increment $r$ by $1$. On this input that error pays $1$ instead of $2$ when $1$ is taken in the left-half merge, and pays $1+1+1$ instead of $3+2+1$ in the final merge, returning $9$ rather than $13$.

The argument never appeals to an unequal-split Master shortcut and never schedules intervals.

graderFixtures.proofText: Left $[7,3,5,1]$ contributes $5$, right $[6,2,4]$ contributes $2$, and merging $[1,3,5,7]$ with $[2,4,6]$ pays $3+2+1=6$. The inversion number is $13$. Adjacent descents give only $3$. A unit right-take increment underpays the leftover left keys.
The only inversions are the adjacent descents 7>3, 5>1, and 6>2. The array therefore has 3 inversions, and merge-sort is unnecessary.

Each time I take a key from the right I add 1, because that right key forms one inversion. The final merge takes 2,4,6 from the right and adds 3; together with left 5 and right 2 the total is 10, or 9 if the left-half take of 1 is likewise charged 1 instead of 2.

ALG:010219.title: Quickselect on the nine-key array uses pivot 5 then pivot 7, compares eleven times, and returns 6
ALG:010219.objective: Run deterministic Quickselect for the sixth smallest of [9,1,8,2,7,3,6,4,5] with prescribed pivots 5 then 7, count exactly 8+3 pivot comparisons, recurse only into the target side, and reject both a full sort and returning the second pivot 7.
ALG:010219.statement:
Let $A=[9,1,8,2,7,3,6,4,5]$. The task is to return the sixth smallest key (1-based order statistic). Use deterministic Quickselect with the following partition contract. In a subarray of length $m$, a designated pivot is compared once to each of the other $m-1$ keys; those $m-1$ tests are the only \emph{pivot comparisons} charged. After the partition, every strictly smaller key occupies a left block, the pivot occupies a single middle slot of well-defined rank, and every strictly larger key occupies a right block. Internal orders of the two blocks are irrelevant. Recurse into at most one block: the unique block that still contains the desired order statistic. If the pivot itself has the desired rank, stop and return it.

1. First designate pivot $5$ on the whole array. Record the two blocks, the rank of $5$, and the number of pivot comparisons. Decide which single side (if any) still contains the sixth smallest, and state the residual order-statistic index on that side.

2. On the residual side designate pivot $7$. Record the blocks, the rank of $7$ inside that side and inside the original array, the additional pivot comparisons, and the next residual (if any). Prove that the algorithm returns $6$ after exactly $8+3=11$ pivot comparisons and that the opposite block is never partitioned.

3. Prove partial correctness of the rank arithmetic: if a left block has size $L$ and the desired 1-based index is $k$, then the pivot has rank $L+1$; one recurses left with the same $k$ when $k\le L$, returns the pivot when $k=L+1$, and recurses right with index $k-L-1$ when $k>L+1$. Explain why both children are never explored.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Quickselect must sort both sides, or must recurse into both blocks, before the sixth smallest is known”; (ii) “after the second partition the pivot $7$ has residual rank $2$, so it is the sixth smallest.”

Do not replace the selection by a merge-sort inversion count, and do not treat the problem as a Karatsuba product.
permittedResults: After a correct partition the pivot is the $(L+1)$-st smallest key of the current subarray, where $L$ is the number of strictly smaller keys.
Quickselect examines only the unique child that can contain the desired order statistic, so it is not a sorting algorithm and does not establish order among discarded keys.

acceptableStrategies.description: Run the two prescribed partitions, update k by subtracting L+1, and stop at the singleton 6 before discussing discarded blocks.

First name the sorted order 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 only as an independent check that the sixth key is 6, then show that Quickselect discovers that key from the two pivots without producing the sorted array.

milestones.criterion: Partitions around 5, records rank 5, and recurses only into the right block for residual index 1.
Partitions around 7, returns 6, and charges exactly 8+3=11 pivot comparisons.
Proves the L+1 rank rule and rejects both a both-sides recursion and returning the second pivot 7.

commonErrors.description: Recurses into both blocks after a partition, or fully sorts the nine keys, instead of following only the target side.
commonErrors.consequence: The algorithm is no longer Quickselect; the 8+3 comparison contract is abandoned and discarded keys are ordered for no reason.

commonErrors.description: Returns 7, typically by computing the residual index as 6-4=2 and treating the second pivot as the sixth smallest.
commonErrors.consequence: The first pivot's rank is not subtracted, so the seventh-smallest key is reported as the sixth.

hintTree.content: The first partition compares all eight other keys to $5$. Four keys are smaller, so $5$ is the fifth smallest and the sixth smallest lives in the right block as that block's first smallest.
Among $\{6,7,8,9\}$ the pivot $7$ is compared to $6,8,9$. One key is smaller, so $7$ is the second smallest of the block and the first smallest is the leftover singleton $6$.
Returning $7$ is the rank error $k\leftarrow 6-4$ that forgets to subtract the first pivot as well. The correct residual index is $6-4-1=1$.

ALG:010219.canonicalSolution:
Designate $5$ as pivot of the nine-key array. The other eight keys are compared to $5$ once each:
\[
9>5,\ 1<5,\ 8>5,\ 2<5,\ 7>5,\ 3<5,\ 6>5,\ 4<5.
\]
The left block is $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and the right block is $\{6,7,8,9\}$, each in any internal order. Thus $L=4$ and the pivot $5$ has rank $5$. The desired index is $k=6>5$, so the algorithm discards the left block and the pivot and recurses into the right block for residual index $6-4-1=1$. Opposite-side work is illegal.

On $\{6,7,8,9\}$ designate $7$ as pivot. The three comparisons are $6<7$, $8>7$, $9>7$. The left block is $\{6\}$ and the right block is $\{8,9\}$. Here $L=1$, so $7$ has rank $2$ inside the residual array, hence rank $5+2=7$ in the original array. The desired residual index is $1<2$, so the algorithm discards $7$ and the right block and recurses into the singleton $\{6\}$. A singleton is returned with no further comparison.

The returned key is $6$. Pivot comparisons total $8+3=11$.
\[
\boxed{6\text{ after }8+3=11\text{ pivot comparisons}}.
\]

In general, a correct partition of a subarray places exactly $L$ keys below the pivot, so the pivot's 1-based rank in that subarray is $L+1$. If $k\le L$ the $k$th smallest cannot lie at or to the right of the pivot. If $k=L+1$ the pivot is the answer. If $k>L+1$ exactly $L+1$ keys have been eliminated from the bottom of the order, so the residual index on the right is $k-L-1$. In every case at most one recursive call is made. Exploring both children would sort (or at least heap-select) information that the rank arithmetic has already declared irrelevant; the comparison bound $8+3$ would be lost.

Sentence (i) is the full-sort confusion: after the first partition one already knows that every left-block key is among the first four order statistics and cannot be the sixth. Sentence (ii) computes the residual index as $6-4=2$, forgets to charge the first pivot, and therefore treats $7$ as the answer. That key is the seventh smallest.

The argument never counts inversions and never multiplies large integers.

graderFixtures.proofText: Pivot $5$ has rank $5$ after $8$ comparisons. The residual task is the first smallest of $\{6,7,8,9\}$. Pivot $7$ has residual rank $2$ after $3$ comparisons and is discarded. The singleton $6$ is returned. Total $11$. Both-sides recursion and returning $7$ are rank errors.

After splitting around 5 I still have to sort the left block and the right block, or recurse into both, because only a complete order tells me which key is sixth. Quickselect is just Quicksort stopped late.

Four keys are smaller than 5, so I want the second smallest of the right block. Partitioning that block around 7 puts one key on its left, so 7 has residual rank 2 and is the sixth smallest. The answer is 7.

ALG:010220.title: Karatsuba multiplies 1234 by 5678 with three base-100 products; 6164 is not the middle coefficient
ALG:010220.objective: Evaluate 1234*5678 by the Karatsuba identity at base 100, obtain z2=672, z0=2652, z1=2840 and product 7006652 from three recursive multiplications, and reject treating the unreduced 46*134=6164 as the cross term.
ALG:010220.statement:
Write $x=1234$ and $y=5678$ in base $B=100$:
\[
x=x_1 B+x_0=12\cdot 100+34,\qquad
y=y_1 B+y_0=56\cdot 100+78.
\]
Karatsuba computes the three products
\begin{align*}
z_2&=x_1 y_1,\\
z_0&=x_0 y_0,\\
z_1&=(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)-z_2-z_0
\end{align*}
and returns $z_2 B^2+z_1 B+z_0$. Each of $z_2$, $z_0$, and $(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)$ is a single recursive multiplication. Additions, subtractions, and multiplications by powers of $B$ are not recursive multiplications.

1. Compute $z_2$, $z_0$, and $(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)$ by hand. Then form $z_1$ by subtracting $z_2$ and $z_0$. Prove that $z_1$ equals the schoolbook cross term $x_1 y_0+x_0 y_1$, and that this identity uses three multiplications rather than four.

2. Assemble $z_2 B^2+z_1 B+z_0$ and prove that the product is $7{,}006{,}652$. Independently confirm the same integer by expanding $1234\cdot 5678$ in place values.

3. Write the Karatsuba recurrence $T(n)=3T(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$ for $n$-digit inputs and the schoolbook recurrence $T_{\mathrm{sb}}(n)=4T_{\mathrm{sb}}(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$. State the resulting asymptotic exponents and why the subtraction of $z_2$ and $z_0$ is essential to the three-multiplication claim.

4. Audit the sentence: “the middle coefficient is $46\cdot 134=6164$, so the product is $672\cdot 10000+6164\cdot 100+2652$.”

Do not replace the product by a selection algorithm, and do not treat the problem as inversion counting.
permittedResults: The recurrences $T(n)=3T(n/2)+\Theta(n)$ and $T(n)=4T(n/2)+\Theta(n)$ solve to $\Theta(n^{\log_2 3})$ and $\Theta(n^2)$ respectively.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the three prescribed products, subtract to form z1, then assemble place values and only afterwards expand 1234*5678 as a check.
First expand the schoolbook cross term 12*78+34*56=2840 to lock z1, then show that Karatsuba recovers the same 2840 from 6164-672-2652 with one fewer multiplication.

milestones.criterion: Computes z2=672, z0=2652, and z1=2840 from 46*134-672-2652, and proves z1 equals the two-term cross product.
Assembles 672*10000+2840*100+2652=7006652 and confirms the integer independently.

commonErrors.consequence: The middle place double-counts z2 and z0, so the returned integer is not the product.

commonErrors.description: Computes x1 y0 and x0 y1 as two extra multiplications and claims the four-product schoolbook recurrence is already Karatsuba.
commonErrors.consequence: The 3T(n/2) saving is lost; the algorithm is schoolbook multiplication written in base 100.

hintTree.content: $12\cdot 56=672$ and $34\cdot 78=2652$. The third product is $46\cdot 134=6164$, but that value still contains $z_2$ and $z_0$.
Using $6164$ as the middle coefficient double-counts $z_2$ and $z_0$ in the $B$ place and produces $7{,}339{,}052$ rather than $7{,}006{,}652$.

ALG:010220.canonicalSolution:
Compute the three products:
\begin{align*}
z_2&=12\cdot 56=672,\\
z_0&=34\cdot 78=34\cdot 80-34\cdot 2=2720-68=2652,\\
(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)&=46\cdot 134=46\cdot 100+46\cdot 30+46\cdot 4=4600+1380+184=6164.
\end{align*}
The middle coefficient is
\[
z_1=6164-672-2652=6164-3324=2840.
\]
Algebraically,
\[
(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)-x_1 y_1-x_0 y_0
=x_1 y_0+x_0 y_1,
\]
so $z_1$ is exactly the schoolbook cross term. The identity uses the three products $x_1 y_1$, $x_0 y_0$, and $(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0)$ and does not form $x_1 y_0$ or $x_0 y_1$ separately. The schoolbook expansion uses those two additional products and therefore four multiplications.

Assemble
\begin{align*}
z_2 B^2+z_1 B+z_0
&=672\cdot 10000+2840\cdot 100+2652\\
&=6{,}720{,}000+284{,}000+2{,}652
=7{,}006{,}652.
\end{align*}
Independent expansion:
\begin{align*}
1234\cdot 5000&=6{,}170{,}000,\\
1234\cdot 600&=740{,}400,\\
1234\cdot 70&=86{,}380,\\
1234\cdot 8&=9{,}872,
\end{align*}
and $6{,}170{,}000+740{,}400+86{,}380+9{,}872=7{,}006{,}652$. As a further check, $x_1 y_0+x_0 y_1=12\cdot 78+34\cdot 56=936+1904=2840$, which matches $z_1$ and uses two extra multiplications.
\[
\boxed{z_2=672,\ z_0=2652,\ z_1=2840,\ xy=7{,}006{,}652}.
\]

Each $n$-digit factor is split into two $\lceil n/2\rceil$-digit halves, so Karatsuba satisfies $T(n)=3T(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$ and runs in $\Theta(n^{\log_2 3})$ arithmetic operations on digits, whereas schoolbook satisfies $T_{\mathrm{sb}}(n)=4T_{\mathrm{sb}}(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$ and is $\Theta(n^2)$. If the unreduced product $6164$ is left in the middle place, the algorithm still performs three multiplications numerically on this instance, but it computes a different polynomial and therefore a different integer; the identity that licenses dropping from four products to three has been discarded.

The audited sentence sets the middle coefficient to $6164$ and assembles
\[
672\cdot 10000+6164\cdot 100+2652=6{,}720{,}000+616{,}400+2{,}652=7{,}339{,}052.
\]
That integer equals $xy+z_2 B+z_0 B$ and is not the product. The same sentence is also the claim that the third multiplication is already $z_1$.

The argument never selects an order statistic and never counts inversions.

graderFixtures.proofText: $z_2=672$, $z_0=2652$, $46\cdot 134=6164$, and $z_1=6164-672-2652=2840$. Assembly gives $7{,}006{,}652$. The value $6164$ is not $z_1$. Four schoolbook products are not Karatsuba.
The middle coefficient is the third product 46*134=6164. Therefore 1234*5678=672*10000+6164*100+2652=7339052.

Karatsuba still forms 12*56, 12*78, 34*56, and 34*78, then adds the two cross products. That is four recursive multiplications, so the recurrence is T(n)=4T(n/2)+O(n) and there is no improvement over schoolbook.

ALG:010221.title: The unique maximum subarray of the nine-key instance is the block 2 through 7 and sums to 11
ALG:010221.objective: Identify the unique nonempty maximum subarray of [-4,3,-2,5,-1,2,4,-10,6] as 1-based indices 2..7 with sum 11, justify it by a crossing split or an ending-here invariant, and reject both an empty-sum default and a local-greedy reset that restarts at every negative.
ALG:010221.statement:
Let $A[1..9]=[-4,3,-2,5,-1,2,4,-10,6]$. A feasible answer is a nonempty contiguous block $A[\ell..r]$ with $1\le\ell\le r\le 9$; its value is the sum $S(\ell,r)=\sum_{t=\ell}^{r}A[t]$. The empty block is illegal even if one assigns it sum $0$. The task is to return every optimal pair $(\ell,r)$ together with the optimal sum.

1. Either execute the divide-and-conquer algorithm that returns the best wholly-left block, the best wholly-right block, and the best block that crosses a chosen midpoint, or execute the linear ending-here recurrence
   \[
   E(1)=A[1],\qquad
   E(i)=\max\bigl(A[i],\,E(i-1)+A[i]\bigr)\quad(i\ge 2),
   \]
   with $\mathit{best}(i)=\max\{\mathit{best}(i-1),E(i)\}$ and an explicit start index for the block realizing $E(i)$. In the divide-and-conquer route take the split after index $5$, so the left half is $A[1..5]$ and the right half is $A[6..9]$. Prove that the chosen reasoning identifies a unique optimum.

2. Prove that the unique maximum block is $(\ell,r)=(2,7)$ with sum $11$. Give the crossing suffix-plus-prefix calculation or the ending-here table that isolates this pair, and give an independent prefix-sum check
   \[
   S(\ell,r)=P[r]-P[\ell-1],\qquad P[0]=0,\quad P[i]=\sum_{t=1}^{i}A[t].
   \]

3. State the all-negative convention: if every entry of an array is negative, the unique optimum is a single occurrence of the largest (least negative) entry, not the empty block. Explain why the empty default $0$ is illegal under the nonempty contract, even though $0$ exceeds every negative entry.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the empty subarray is always available and has sum $0$, so a negative prefix may be discarded in favour of emptiness”; (ii) “any negative entry resets the live block, so the candidates are $[3]$, $[5]$, $[2,4]$, and $[6]$ and the maximum is $6$.”

Do not replace the problem by Karatsuba multiplication, and do not treat it as earliest-finish interval scheduling.
permittedResults: Every nonempty block is wholly left of the split, wholly right of the split, or crossing. The three-way maximum is therefore the global maximum.

The quantity $E(i)$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty block that ends at $i$. Hence $\max_i E(i)$ is the maximum nonempty-block sum, and the maximizing $i$ together with the start index of that $E(i)$ recover the block.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split after index 5, compute the unique best left suffix and right prefix, then compare that crossing sum with the two one-sided maxima.
Fill the ending-here table with start indices, then use prefix sums only to prove that no other pair attains 11.

milestones.criterion: Justifies the optimum by a crossing suffix-plus-prefix calculation or by the ending-here recurrence, including the all-negative nonempty convention.
Identifies the unique 1-based block 2..7 with sum 11 and confirms it by prefix sums.
Rejects the empty-sum default and the local-greedy reset that reports 6.

commonErrors.description: Allows the empty block with sum 0, or treats a negative prefix as licence to return emptiness rather than a nonempty block.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasible set is changed. On an all-negative input the reported value is 0 instead of the largest entry, and the required indices disappear.

commonErrors.description: Restarts the live block at every negative entry, so the only candidates are [3], [5], [2,4], and [6], and the reported maximum is 6.
commonErrors.consequence: Positive prefixes are discarded at -2 and at -1, and the unique block 2..7 is never formed.

hintTree.content: The best suffix of $A[1..5]$ is $A[2..5]$ with sum $5$. The best prefix of $A[6..9]$ is $A[6..7]$ with sum $6$. Their join is $A[2..7]$ with sum $11$.
Prefix sums are $P=(0,-4,-1,-3,2,1,3,7,-3,3)$. The unique pair with $P[r]-P[\ell-1]=11$ is $r=7$, $\ell-1=1$.
Resetting at every negative entry never carries $3$ across $-2$ or $5$ across $-1$, so it never builds $11$ and reports $6$.

ALG:010221.canonicalSolution:
Split after index $5$. The left half is $[-4,3,-2,5,-1]$ and the right half is $[2,4,-10,6]$.

Maximum suffix of the left half, ending at index $5$:
\[
-1,\quad 5-1=4,\quad -2+5-1=2,\quad 3-2+5-1=5,\quad -4+3-2+5-1=1.
\]
The unique best left suffix is $A[2..5]$ with sum $5$.

Maximum prefix of the right half, starting at index $6$:
\[
2,\quad 2+4=6,\quad 2+4-10=-4,\quad 2+4-10+6=2.
\]
The unique best right prefix is $A[6..7]$ with sum $6$.

The unique best crossing block is therefore $A[2..7]$ with sum $5+6=11$.

A direct scan of left-only blocks gives maximum $3-2+5=6$ on $A[2..4]$. A direct scan of right-only blocks gives maximum $6$, attained both on $A[6..7]$ and on $A[9]$. The three-way maximum is $11$, attained only on the crossing block $A[2..7]$.

The same block is recovered by the ending-here recurrence. Writing $E(i)$ and a start index $s(i)$:
\begin{align*}
i=1&:\ E=-4,\ s=1,\ \mathit{best}=-4,\\
i=2&:\ E=\max(3,-4+3)=3,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=3,\\
i=3&:\ E=\max(-2,3-2)=1,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=3,\\
i=4&:\ E=\max(5,1+5)=6,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=6,\\
i=5&:\ E=\max(-1,6-1)=5,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=6,\\
i=6&:\ E=\max(2,5+2)=7,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=7,\\
i=7&:\ E=\max(4,7+4)=11,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=11,\\
i=8&:\ E=\max(-10,11-10)=1,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=11,\\
i=9&:\ E=\max(6,1+6)=7,\ s=2,\ \mathit{best}=11.
\end{align*}
The unique maximizing pair is $E(7)=11$ with start $2$.

Prefix sums $P[0..9]=(0,-4,-1,-3,2,1,3,7,-3,3)$ satisfy $S(2,7)=P[7]-P[1]=7-(-4)=11$. For each $r$ the best block ending at $r$ is $P[r]-\min_{0\le k<r}P[k]$. The running minima of $P$ begin at $0$ and then drop to $-4$ at index $1$ and never decrease again, so every $r\ge 2$ has best start $2$. The values are $3,1,6,5,7,11,1,7$; the unique maximum is $11$ at $r=7$.
\[
\boxed{\text{unique }(2,7)\text{ with sum }11}.
\]

If every entry were negative, every nonempty block would have negative sum, and the maximum would be the largest single entry (the longest block cannot help). The empty block is excluded by the feasible-set definition, so the default $0$ is not an admissible value. On the present instance emptiness is also suboptimal because $11>0$, but the convention is still required for the all-negative boundary.

Sentence (i) admits the empty block and would, on an all-negative input, return sum $0$ with no indices. Sentence (ii) restarts whenever $A[i]<0$, producing the disjoint positive clumps $[3]$, $[5]$, $[2,4]$, and $[6]$ whose maximum is $6$. That local reset refuses to carry a positive prefix across a later-compensated negative, so it never forms $A[2..7]$.

The argument never multiplies large integers and never selects compatible intervals.

graderFixtures.proofText: The unique nonempty maximum is $A[2..7]$ with sum $11$, as the crossing $5+6$ after index $5$ or as $E(7)=11$ with start $2$. Emptiness is illegal. Resetting at each negative reports $6$ and misses the block.
The empty subarray is always feasible and has sum 0. A negative prefix such as -4 can be discarded in favour of emptiness, and if every entry were negative I would return 0 with no indices.
Whenever I see a negative entry I start a new block. The candidates are therefore [3], [5], [2,4], and [6], and the maximum subarray sum is 6 on indices 6..7 (or on the last 6).

ALG:010322.title: Huffman merges the two lightest trees; largest-first and raw depth are not WPL
ALG:010322.objective: Execute Huffman on weights 2, 3, 7, 9, 18, obtain code lengths 4, 4, 3, 2, 1 and weighted path length 77, and prove the merge by the sibling property or an exchange.
ALG:010322.statement:
A binary prefix code for five symbols with positive frequencies
\[
w=(w_a,w_b,w_c,w_d,w_e)=(2,3,7,9,18)
\]
is represented by a full binary tree: every internal node has exactly two children, and the code length of a symbol is the number of edges from the root to its leaf. The weighted path length is
\[
\mathrm{WPL}(T)=\sum_{\ell} w_{\ell}\cdot d_T(\ell),
\]
where the sum is over leaves and $d_T(\ell)$ is the depth of leaf $\ell$. An equivalent identity, which you may use after proving it, is that $\mathrm{WPL}(T)$ equals the sum of the weights of all internal nodes when each internal node is labelled by the sum of its two children.

Huffman’s algorithm maintains a forest of trees, initially five single-node trees with the given weights. While two or more trees remain, it merges two trees of currently smallest root weight, creating a new parent whose weight is the sum. Ties do not occur on this instance.

1. Trace every merge. Report the four parent weights in the order they are created and the final tree. Read off the five leaf depths in the weight order $2,3,7,9,18$, and compute $\mathrm{WPL}$ both from the depth definition and from the internal-node sum.

2. Prove that there exists an optimal prefix-code tree in which the two lightest symbols are siblings (the sibling property). Then prove, by induction on the number of symbols, that each Huffman merge is a safe greedy contraction: replacing those two siblings by a single super-symbol of weight equal to their sum preserves optimality of the remaining tree.

3. Audit these claims: (i) one should repeatedly merge the two currently heaviest trees, because large weights should sit near the root only after they have been combined; (ii) the quality of the code is the unweighted height of the tree, or the unweighted sum of leaf depths, so the answer is $4$ or $14$. Do not replace the exercise by earliest-finish interval scheduling, and do not invoke a Master-theorem recurrence.

State that the code is a full binary prefix tree and that $\mathrm{WPL}$ is the objective.
permittedResults: In a full binary tree whose internal nodes store child-weight sums, $\mathrm{WPL}$ equals the sum of the internal-node labels: each leaf weight is charged once on every ancestor edge.

If $T$ is optimal and $a,b$ are sibling leaves, the tree obtained by replacing the parent of $a,b$ by a leaf of weight $w_a+w_b$ is optimal for the contracted instance, and conversely every optimal contracted tree expands to an optimal tree for the original instance.

acceptableStrategies.description: Run the lightest-pair forest, read depths, then prove optimality by a deepest-leaf exchange followed by inductive contraction.
Use the internal-node-sum identity as an independent checksum on WPL, and argue that any tree in which a heavier leaf sits strictly deeper than a lighter unused sibling can be improved by a swap.

milestones.criterion: Traces the four Huffman merges and reports depths 4,4,3,2,1 with WPL 77 from both identities.
Proves the sibling property and the contraction that makes each lightest-pair merge safe.
Rejects merging the heaviest pair first and rejects unweighted height or depth-sum as the objective.

commonErrors.description: Repeatedly merges the two currently heaviest roots, or otherwise places 18 and 9 at maximum depth, obtaining WPL 137 or code lengths 1,2,3,4,4 on the light-to-heavy order.
commonErrors.consequence: The constructed tree is not a Huffman tree and is not optimal for the stated WPL objective.

commonErrors.description: Reports the tree height 4, the unweighted depth sum 14, or another depth count that ignores leaf weights, as if that quantity were WPL.
commonErrors.consequence: The objective has been replaced by an unweighted shape statistic, so the required value 77 is never obtained.

hintTree.content: The two lightest roots begin at $2$ and $3$. After that parent of weight $5$ is created, compare $5$ with the unused $7$, not with $18$.

A leaf at maximum depth in an optimal tree may be swapped with a lighter leaf that sits higher: the change in $\mathrm{WPL}$ is nonpositive because the depth difference is nonnegative and the weight difference is nonpositive.
Merging $18$ with $9$ first produces depths that put the heavy leaves deepest. The unweighted height is only the longest code, not $\mathrm{WPL}$.

ALG:010322.canonicalSolution:
The initial forest is five leaves of weights $2,3,7,9,18$.

The unique pair of lightest roots is $2$ and $3$. Merge them to a parent of weight $5$. The forest is $5,7,9,18$.

The unique lightest pair is now $5$ and $7$. Merge them to a parent of weight $12$. The forest is $9,12,18$.

The unique lightest pair is $9$ and $12$. Merge them to a parent of weight $21$. The forest is $18,21$.

The last merge creates the root of weight $39$. The tree, up to left/right swap of any sibling pair, is
\[
\begin{array}{c}
39\\
/\qquad\backslash\\
18\qquad 21\\
\qquad /\quad\backslash\\
\quad 9\qquad 12\\
\qquad\quad /\quad\backslash\\
\qquad 5\qquad 7\\
\qquad /\backslash\\
\quad 2\qquad 3.
\end{array}
\]
Leaf depths in weight order $2,3,7,9,18$ are $4,4,3,2,1$. Therefore
\[
\mathrm{WPL}=2\cdot 4+3\cdot 4+7\cdot 3+9\cdot 2+18\cdot 1=8+12+21+18+18=77.
\]
The internal-node labels are $5,12,21,39$, and $5+12+21+39=77$, matching the depth definition because each leaf weight is added once for every ancestor edge.
\[
\boxed{2+3=5,\ 5+7=12,\ 9+12=21,\ 18+21=39;\ \text{lengths }4,4,3,2,1;\ \mathrm{WPL}=77}.
\]

Sibling property. Let $T^*$ be any optimal full binary prefix tree, and let $d$ be its maximum leaf depth. Because the tree is full, some internal node has two leaf children $u,v$ at depth $d$. Let $a,b$ be the two lightest symbols, with $w_a\le w_b$. Exchange $a$ with $u$ if they differ. The change in $\mathrm{WPL}$ is
\[
\bigl(d-d_{T^*}(a)\bigr)\,(w_a-w_u)\le 0,
\]
since $d\ge d_{T^*}(a)$ and $w_a\le w_u$. The tree remains optimal. A second exchange places $b$ opposite $a$ at depth $d$. Thus some optimal tree has the two lightest symbols as siblings.

Safe contraction. In that tree, replace the common parent of $a$ and $b$ by a single leaf $\sigma$ of weight $w_a+w_b$. Every remaining leaf keeps its depth, and
\[
\mathrm{WPL}(T)=\mathrm{WPL}(T')+w_a+w_b,
\]
where $T'$ is the contracted tree: the parent of $a,b$ contributes exactly $w_a+w_b$ to the internal-node sum, and that quantity is independent of $T'$. Therefore $T$ is optimal if and only if $T'$ is optimal for the contracted weights. Huffman’s first merge is exactly this contraction. By induction on the number of symbols, the algorithm returns an optimal tree. The inductive step uses that the two lightest current roots are a lightest pair in the contracted instance.

Claim (i) merges $18+9=27$, then $27+7=34$, then $34+3=37$, then $37+2=39$. The resulting depths are $4,4,3,2,1$ on weights $18,9,7,3,2$, so
\[
\mathrm{WPL}=18\cdot 4+9\cdot 4+7\cdot 3+3\cdot 2+2\cdot 1=72+36+21+6+2=137.
\]
The heavy symbols have been pushed to maximum depth, which is the opposite of the sibling-exchange direction. Claim (ii) reports the height $4$, or the unweighted depth sum $4+4+3+2+1=14$. Neither quantity is $\mathrm{WPL}$; weighting by frequency is the entire objective. This argument is a Huffman exchange, not an earliest-finish interval exchange and not a recurrence-tree bound.

graderFixtures.proofText: Huffman merges $2+3=5$, then $5+7=12$, then $9+12=21$, then $18+21=39$. The leaf depths on weights $2,3,7,9,18$ are $4,4,3,2,1$, so $\mathrm{WPL}=8+12+21+18+18=77$, matching the internal sum $5+12+21+39$. Some optimum has the two lightest leaves as siblings; contracting them adds a constant $w_a+w_b$ and reduces to a smaller optimal instance. Merging $18$ with $9$ first yields WPL $137$. Height $4$ and depth-sum $14$ are not WPL.

Combine the heaviest pair at every step: 18+9=27, 27+7=34, 34+3=37, 37+2=39. The large weights then sit near the root after they have been absorbed, which is the natural greedy rule. The resulting WPL is 137.
The Huffman tree has height 4 and unweighted leaf-depth sum 4+4+3+2+1=14. Those two shape numbers are the quality of the code, so the answer is 14.

ALG:010323.title: Kruskal accepts a lightest cut edge and rejects every intra-component edge
ALG:010323.objective: Trace Kruskal on the six-vertex graph with the given ten edges, select AB, CD, BC, EF, DE of total weight 13, and justify every acceptance by the cut property and every rejection by a cycle.
ALG:010323.statement:
Let $G$ be the undirected connected graph with vertices $\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}$ and exactly the ten weighted edges
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccccc}
e & AB & CD & BC & EF & DE & BD & AC & CE & BF & AF\\ \hline
w(e) & 1 & 2 & 3 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9.
\end{array}
\]
Kruskal’s algorithm sorts edges by nondecreasing weight, breaking the unique remaining tie $w(BC)=w(EF)=3$ by lexicographic endpoint order, so $BC$ precedes $EF$. It maintains the partition of vertices into forest components, initially six singletons. An edge is accepted if and only if its endpoints currently lie in distinct components; otherwise it is rejected. The output is required to be a minimum spanning tree.

1. Execute the scan. After each accepted edge, list the current disjoint components. After each rejected edge, name a simple cycle in the accepted forest plus that edge. Report the accepted edge set in scan order and the total weight.

2. For every accepted edge $e=uv$, exhibit the cut $\bigl(K(u),\,V\setminus K(u)\bigr)$ given by the component $K(u)$ of $u$ immediately before $e$ is considered, and prove that $e$ is a lightest edge crossing that cut. Invoke the cut property to conclude that $e$ is safe. Do not replace this justification by an earliest-finish interval-scheduling exchange.

3. Prove that the five accepted edges form a spanning tree: they are acyclic, they meet every vertex, and they have cardinality $|V|-1$. Combined with safety of each accepted edge, conclude that the tree is a minimum spanning tree.

4. Audit these claims: (i) after $AB,CD,BC$ have built the component $\{A,B,C,D\}$, the next light edge $EF$ may be discarded because it does not touch that component, so the algorithm should wait for an edge out of $\{A,B,C,D\}$; (ii) $BD$ has weight only $5$ and should be kept as a backup spanning edge, giving total weight $18$.

State the cut property and that components are the Kruskal forest, not a Prim growth from a single root.
permittedResults: A connected graph on $n$ vertices has a spanning tree if and only if it has an acyclic set of $n-1$ edges. Adding an edge whose ends lie in the same tree creates a unique simple cycle.
If every accepted Kruskal edge is safe for the component-cut at the moment it is accepted, the final spanning tree is a minimum spanning tree.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sort by weight, maintain the disjoint-component partition, and apply the cut property to the component of one endpoint at the moment an edge is accepted.
Run a union-find scan for the accepted set, then independently certify each accepted edge as a minimum outgoing edge of its pre-merge block and each rejected edge by an explicit fundamental cycle.

milestones.criterion: Traces components through AB, CD, BC, EF, DE, rejects the five cycle edges, and reports MST weight 13.
Identifies the component cut before each acceptance and proves the accepted edge is a lightest crossing edge.
Proves the output is a spanning tree of safe edges and rejects discarding EF or retaining BD.

commonErrors.description: Discards EF because it does not touch the component {A,B,C,D}, confusing Kruskal with Prim growth from a single tree.
commonErrors.consequence: The safe weight-3 edge is lost and a later edge such as BF is taken, so the spanning weight is 18 rather than 13.

commonErrors.description: Accepts BD after A,B,C,D are already connected, or otherwise keeps an intra-component edge as a backup and reports weight 18.
commonErrors.consequence: The accepted set is cyclic or is not a tree of weight 13.

hintTree.content: After $AB$ and $CD$ the components are $\{A,B\}$, $\{C,D\}$, $\{E\}$, $\{F\}$. The edge $BC$ joins the first two blocks. The edge $EF$ joins two still-untouched singletons.
Just before $BC$ is scanned, every cheaper edge is $AB$ or $CD$, and both of those lie inside a current block, so $BC$ is a lightest edge out of $\{A,B\}$.
Discarding $EF$ because it misses $\{A,B,C,D\}$ is a Prim-style restriction. Kruskal is allowed to grow several trees. The later edge $BD$ has both ends in $\{A,B,C,D\}$.

ALG:010323.canonicalSolution:
Sort the edges as $AB,CD,BC,EF,DE,BD,AC,CE,BF,AF$. Start with components $\{A\},\{B\},\{C\},\{D\},\{E\},\{F\}$.

Accept $AB$ of weight $1$. Components become $\{A,B\},\{C\},\{D\},\{E\},\{F\}$.

Accept $CD$ of weight $2$. Components become $\{A,B\},\{C,D\},\{E\},\{F\}$.

Accept $BC$ of weight $3$. The ends $B$ and $C$ lie in distinct blocks, so the blocks merge: $\{A,B,C,D\},\{E\},\{F\}$.

Accept $EF$ of weight $3$. Components become $\{A,B,C,D\},\{E,F\}$.

Accept $DE$ of weight $4$. The ends $D$ and $E$ lie in distinct blocks, so the forest becomes the single component $\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}$.

Reject $BD$: $B$ and $D$ already lie in the same tree, and $B{-}C{-}D{-}B$ is a cycle. Reject $AC$ by the cycle $A{-}B{-}C{-}A$. Reject $CE$ by the cycle $C{-}D{-}E{-}C$ (using the just-accepted $DE$). Reject $BF$ by a path $B{-}C{-}D{-}E{-}F$. Reject $AF$ by a path $A{-}B{-}C{-}D{-}E{-}F$.

The accepted set in scan order is $AB,CD,BC,EF,DE$, with weight
\[
1+2+3+3+4=13.
\]
\[
\boxed{AB,CD,BC,EF,DE;\ \mathrm{MST\ weight}=13}.
\]

Cut-property justifications, using the component $K(u)$ of the first endpoint immediately before the edge is scanned.

- For $AB$, $K(A)=\{A\}$. Edges leaving $\{A\}$ are $AB,AC,AF$ with weights $1,6,9$. The lightest is $AB$.
- For $CD$, $K(C)=\{C\}$. Edges leaving $\{C\}$ are $CD,BC,AC,CE$ with weights $2,3,6,7$. The lightest is $CD$.
- For $BC$, $K(B)=\{A,B\}$. Edges leaving $\{A,B\}$ are $BC,BD,AC,BF,AF$ with weights $3,5,6,8,9$. Every cheaper edge in the whole graph is $AB$ or $CD$, and neither crosses this cut, so $BC$ is a lightest crossing edge.
- For $EF$, $K(E)=\{E\}$. Edges leaving $\{E\}$ are $EF,DE,CE$ with weights $3,4,7$. The lightest is $EF$. Kruskal does not require this edge to touch $\{A,B,C,D\}$.
- For $DE$, $K(D)=\{A,B,C,D\}$. Edges leaving that block are $DE,CE,BF,AF$ with weights $4,7,8,9$ (and $EF$ is already accepted inside the other block). The lightest crossing edge is $DE$.

Each displayed component cut respects the previously accepted forest: accepted edges lie wholly inside its current components. Starting from the empty forest, the cut property therefore proves inductively that after every acceptance the whole accepted set is contained in one minimum spanning tree. The five accepted edges meet every vertex, form no cycle because Kruskal never closed one, and number $|V|-1=5$, so they themselves form that minimum spanning tree.

Claim (i) imposes a Prim-style restriction that the next edge must touch the already-grown block $\{A,B,C,D\}$. That discards the safe edge $EF$. The scan would then take $DE$ (merging $E$ only) and later $BF$, producing
\[
\{AB,CD,BC,DE,BF\}
\]
of weight $1+2+3+4+8=18$. Claim (ii) keeps the cycle edge $BD$ after the spanning tree is already connected, again producing weight $18$ and destroying acyclicity. Neither claim is Kruskal, and neither is an interval-scheduling exchange.

graderFixtures.proofText: Kruskal accepts $AB,CD,BC,EF,DE$ in that order and rejects $BD,AC,CE,BF,AF$ as cycle edges. The components after the five acceptances are $\{A,B\}$, then $\{A,B\},\{C,D\}$, then $\{A,B,C,D\}$, then $\{A,B,C,D\},\{E,F\}$, then one block. Each accepted edge is a lightest edge out of the component of one endpoint. The spanning weight is $13$. $EF$ is legal even though it misses $\{A,B,C,D\}$. $BD$ is a cycle edge.
After AB, CD, and BC the algorithm has a block {A,B,C,D}. EF does not touch that block, so it is ignored. The next accepted edges are DE and BF, and the spanning weight is 18.
BD has weight only 5 and connects B to D, so it should be kept as a backup spanning edge even after BC and CD. The accepted weight is then 18.

ALG:010424.title: Weighted half-open intervals need a predecessor DP, not a cardinality exchange
ALG:010424.objective: Build the finish-sorted predecessor array for the seven weighted half-open intervals, compute the recurrence through value 24, and reconstruct the unique optimum A,C,E,G.
ALG:010424.statement:
Seven requests occupy half-open intervals and carry nonnegative values
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
\mathrm{id} & A & B & C & D & E & F & G\\ \hline
[s,f) & [1,3) & [1,5) & [3,5) & [4,7) & [5,7) & [6,10) & [7,10)\\
v & 5 & 10 & 6 & 9 & 4 & 12 & 9.
\end{array}
\]
Two requests are compatible exactly when their intervals are disjoint. In particular a request that finishes at time $t$ is compatible with a request that starts at time $t$. The objective is to select a compatible subset of maximum total value, not of maximum cardinality.

Sort the requests by nondecreasing finish time, breaking remaining ties by identifier, obtaining the order $A,B,C,D,E,F,G$. Index them as $j=1,\ldots,7$ in that order. Let $p(j)$ be the rightmost index $i<j$ such that $f_i\le s_j$, or $p(j)=0$ if no such $i$ exists. Let $\mathrm{OPT}(0)=0$ and
\[
\mathrm{OPT}(j)=\max\bigl(v_j+\mathrm{OPT}(p(j)),\ \mathrm{OPT}(j-1)\bigr)\qquad(j=1,\ldots,7).
\]
A request $j$ is taken in the first branch and skipped in the second.

1. Compute the seven predecessor values $p(j)$. Justify each comparison with the half-open convention.

2. Fill $\mathrm{OPT}(1),\ldots,\mathrm{OPT}(7)$. At each $j$ record which branch attains the maximum. Reconstruct the taken set from $j=7$ backward. Report the set and its value.

3. Prove that the recurrence is exhaustive: after sorting by finish time, an optimal subset either excludes request $j$ or includes it together with an optimal subset of the requests that finish at or before $s_j$. Explain why a one-for-one earliest-finish exchange does not prove this weighted instance, even if that scan happens to return the same set.

4. Audit these three compatible sets as claimed optima: $B,E,G$ of value $23$; $A,D,G$ of value $23$; and $A,C,F$ of value $23$. Also audit the closed-endpoint predecessor that treats $f_i=s_j$ as a conflict, so that $A$ is declared incompatible with $C$. Do not replace the state by affine-gap alignment modes, and do not solve the unweighted cardinality problem in place of this one.

State the half-open compatibility rule and that the DP stores prefix optima after finish-sorting.
permittedResults: If request $j$ is taken, every other taken request that finishes before $j$ must finish at or before $s_j$, hence lies among the first $p(j)$ requests. Replacing that prefix by a better compatible prefix would improve the whole subset.
A one-for-one exchange that preserves cardinality need not preserve total value, so earliest-finish optimality for the unweighted problem does not transfer to arbitrary weights.

acceptableStrategies.description: Finish-sort, binary-search or scan for each predecessor, fill the take/skip table, and walk the recorded branches backward from n.
Build an explicit compatibility DAG on the seven requests with edges from j to compatible earlier i, then compute a maximum-weight path, using the predecessor array as the compact form of that DAG.

milestones.criterion: Computes the half-open predecessor array p=(0,0,A,A,C,C,E) from the finish-sorted order.
Fills OPT through 24 and reconstructs the unique set A,C,E,G.
Proves the take/skip recurrence, shows that the three value-23 sets are suboptimal, and rejects closed endpoints and a cardinality exchange as a weighted proof.

commonErrors.description: Treats a finish time equal to a later start time as a conflict, sets p(C)=0, and thereby declares A,C incompatible.
commonErrors.consequence: The chain A,C,E,G is excluded and the value 24 cannot appear.

commonErrors.description: Reports B,E,G or A,D,G or A,C,F, each of value 23, as an optimum, or stops at OPT(F)=23 without the last take-branch.
commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but strictly worse subset is substituted for the unique optimum of value 24.

hintTree.content: Half-open endpoints give $f_A=3\le s_C=3$ and $f_C=5\le s_E=5$ and $f_E=7\le s_G=7$. The predecessor of $D$ is still $A$, because $B$ and $C$ finish at $5>4$.
At $j=C$ compare $6+\mathrm{OPT}(A)=11$ with $\mathrm{OPT}(B)=10$. At $j=G$ compare $9+\mathrm{OPT}(E)$ with $\mathrm{OPT}(F)$.
Each of $BEG$, $ADG$, and $ACF$ totals $23$. Reconstruction from the last maximizing branch is what selects $ACEG$ of value $24$.

ALG:010424.canonicalSolution:
The finish-sorted order is $A,B,C,D,E,F,G$. Compatibility uses $f_i\le s_j$.

\[
\begin{aligned}
p(A)&=0 &&\text{no earlier request},\\
p(B)&=0 &&f_A=3>s_B=1,\\
p(C)&=A &&f_A=3\le 3,\ \text{and }A\text{ is the only earlier request that works},\\
p(D)&=A &&f_A=3\le 4,\ \text{while }f_B=f_C=5>4,\\
p(E)&=C &&f_A,f_B,f_C\le 5\text{ and }C\text{ is the rightmost},\\
p(F)&=C &&f_C=5\le 6,\ \text{while }f_D=f_E=7>6,\\
p(G)&=E &&f_E=7\le 7,\ \text{and }E\text{ is later than }D.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now the prefix table, recording the maximizing branch.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{OPT}(A)&=\max(5+0,\,0)=5 &&\text{take }A,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(B)&=\max(10+0,\,5)=10 &&\text{take }B,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(C)&=\max(6+5,\,10)=11 &&\text{take }A,C,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(D)&=\max(9+5,\,11)=14 &&\text{take }A,D,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(E)&=\max(4+11,\,14)=15 &&\text{take }A,C,E,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(F)&=\max(12+11,\,15)=23 &&\text{take }A,C,F,\\
\mathrm{OPT}(G)&=\max(9+15,\,23)=24 &&\text{take }G\text{ with the }E\text{-prefix}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Reconstruction from $G$: the take-branch wins, so include $G$ and jump to $p(G)=E$. At $E$ the take-branch wins, so include $E$ and jump to $C$. At $C$ the take-branch wins, so include $C$ and jump to $A$. At $A$ the take-branch wins. The recovered set is $\{A,C,E,G\}$ of value $5+6+4+9=24$. The intervals $[1,3),[3,5),[5,7),[7,10)$ are pairwise touching at endpoints and therefore compatible.
\[
\boxed{A,C,E,G\text{ with value }24}.
\]

Correctness. After finish-sorting, consider an optimal subset $S$ of the first $j$ requests. If $j\notin S$, then $S$ is optimal among the first $j-1$ requests, giving $\mathrm{OPT}(j-1)$. If $j\in S$, no other member of $S$ can finish after $s_j$ and still be compatible with $j$; every other member therefore lies among the first $p(j)$ requests, and the remainder $S\setminus\{j\}$ is optimal for that prefix, giving $v_j+\mathrm{OPT}(p(j))$. Both branches are feasible by construction of $p(j)$. Induction on $j$ proves the table.

The three listed sets are feasible and have value $23$:
\[
v(B)+v(E)+v(G)=10+4+9=23,\quad
v(A)+v(D)+v(G)=5+9+9=23,\quad
v(A)+v(C)+v(F)=5+6+12=23.
\]
Each is a feasible but strictly suboptimal witness; they appear as intermediate prefix values $\mathrm{OPT}(F)=23$ and as the skip-branch at $G$. They are not optima.

A closed-endpoint rule would treat $f_A=s_C$ as a conflict and set $p(C)=0$. Then $\mathrm{OPT}(C)=\max(6,10)=10$ and the chain $A,C,E,G$ is declared infeasible, so the value $24$ is lost.

Earliest-finish cardinality scan happens to accept $A,C,E,G$ on this particular instance, but that fact is not a weighted proof. The cardinality exchange replaces one request by one request and therefore preserves count, not value. The set $B$ alone already shows that a locally early request can carry a different value from $A$. The argument required here is the predecessor recurrence, not an exchange and not an affine-gap alignment state.

graderFixtures.proofText: Finish order $A,B,C,D,E,F,G$ has predecessors $0,0,A,A,C,C,E$ because touching half-open endpoints are compatible. The OPT row is $5,10,11,14,15,23,24$. Backward reconstruction takes $G$ with $E$, $E$ with $C$, $C$ with $A$, giving $\{A,C,E,G\}$ of value $24$. The sets of value $23$ are feasible and strictly worse. A closed-endpoint rule that conflicts $A$ with $C$ is wrong. Cardinality exchange is not a weighted proof.
A finishes at 3 and C starts at 3, so the intervals share an endpoint and conflict. Thus p(C)=0 and A cannot appear with C. The best remaining sets have value 23.
The compatible set B,E,G has value 10+4+9=23, and A,C,F has value 23 as well. Either set is optimal.

ALG:010425.title: The capacity-8 knapsack optimum is items 2 and 4; fractions and off-by-one cells are not 0/1
ALG:010425.objective: Fill the 0/1 knapsack table for capacity 8, reconstruct the unique optimum items 2+4 of value 12, and reject fractional reuse and a capacity-index error.
ALG:010425.statement:
Four items may be taken at most once:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
i & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \hline
w_i & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\
v_i & 3 & 5 & 6 & 7.
\end{array}
\]
The knapsack has integer capacity $W=8$. A feasible packing is a subset $S\subseteq\{1,2,3,4\}$ with $\sum_{i\in S}w_i\le 8$. The objective is maximum total value. Fractions of an item are illegal, and no item may be packed more than once.

Let $K[i][c]$ be the maximum value obtainable from the first $i$ items with capacity exactly at most $c$, for $i=0,\ldots,4$ and $c=0,\ldots,8$. The recurrence is $K[0][c]=K[i][0]=0$ and, for $i\ge 1$,
\[
K[i][c]=
\begin{cases}
K[i-1][c] & \text{if }w_i>c,\\
\max\bigl(K[i-1][c],\ v_i+K[i-1][c-w_i]\bigr) & \text{if }w_i\le c.
\end{cases}
\]

1. Fill the entire $5\times 9$ table, including the zero row and zero column. At every cell with $w_i\le c$, record whether the take-branch or the skip-branch wins.

2. Read $K[4][8]$. Reconstruct the unique maximizing subset by walking backward from that cell. Report the items, their total weight, and their total value. Prove uniqueness by listing every feasible subset and its value, or by showing that every other take/skip path is strictly worse.

3. Justify the recurrence: after deciding whether item $i$ is taken, the residual instance uses only items $1,\ldots,i-1$ and residual capacity $c$ or $c-w_i$. Explain why a one-dimensional left-to-right overwrite of the same row would permit an item to be reused.

4. Audit these claims: (i) item $2$ may be packed twice, or a fractional packing may take items $2$ and $1$ and three-quarters of item $3$, because density $v_i/w_i$ is the right greedy key; (ii) the useful capacities are the eight indices $0,\ldots,7$, so the answer is the cell $K[4][7]=11$. Do not replace the table by an affine-gap alignment state.

State that the model is 0/1, that $c$ runs through $0,\ldots,8$, and that reconstruction follows the recorded take/skip bits.
permittedResults: Every feasible 0/1 packing of the first $i$ items either excludes item $i$ or includes it and packs a feasible subset of the first $i-1$ items into the residual capacity. Both options are represented by the displayed recurrence.

If a one-dimensional array is updated left-to-right for increasing capacities, the take-branch may read a value that already includes the current item, which is the unbounded-knapsack recurrence rather than 0/1.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fill the two-dimensional table by increasing i then c, store a take bit in each cell, and walk those bits backward from (4,8).
Enumerate the ten feasible subsets as an independent checksum on uniqueness, then match the maximizing subset to the DP reconstruction.

milestones.criterion: Fills the 0/1 table through K[4][8]=12 with the correct take/skip choices.
Reconstructs the unique set {2,4} of weight 8 and value 12.
Justifies the previous-row residual recurrence and rejects fractional/unbounded reuse and the capacity-7 cell.

commonErrors.description: Allows a fraction of an item, or packs the same item more than once, for example taking item 2 twice or reporting the density packing of value 12.5.
commonErrors.consequence: The solved problem is fractional or unbounded knapsack, not the stated 0/1 instance.

commonErrors.description: Treats the eight indices 0 through 7 as the full budget and reports K[4][7]=11, or otherwise drops the capacity-8 column.
commonErrors.consequence: The cell for W=8 is never read, so the unique value-12 packing is missed.

hintTree.content: After item $2$ the row is $0,0,3,5,5,8,8,8,8$. Item $3$ then raises the capacities $4,6,7,8$ to $6,9,11,11$.
The cell $K[4][8]$ compares $11$ against $7+K[3][3]$. The cell $K[3][3]$ cannot hold item $3$, so it still equals $K[2][3]=5$.
Density order packs item $2$, then item $1$, then a fraction of item $3$, which is a different problem. The cell $K[4][7]$ is the capacity-$7$ subproblem and equals $11$.

ALG:010425.canonicalSolution:
Rows are items $0$ through $4$; columns are capacities $0$ through $8$.

The zero row and zero column are entirely $0$. After item $1$ of weight $2$ and value $3$,
\[
K[1]=[0,0,3,3,3,3,3,3,3],
\]
with the take-branch used on every $c\ge 2$.

After item $2$ of weight $3$ and value $5$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
K[2][2]&=3,\\
K[2][3]&=\max(3,5+0)=5,\\
K[2][4]&=\max(3,5+0)=5,\\
K[2][5]&=\max(3,5+3)=8,
\end{aligned}
\]
and $K[2][c]=8$ for $c=6,7,8$. Thus
\[
K[2]=[0,0,3,5,5,8,8,8,8].
\]

After item $3$ of weight $4$ and value $6$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
K[3][4]&=\max(5,6+0)=6,\\
K[3][5]&=\max(8,6+0)=8,\\
K[3][6]&=\max(8,6+3)=9,\\
K[3][7]&=\max(8,6+5)=11,\\
K[3][8]&=\max(8,6+5)=11,
\end{aligned}
\]
and the smaller capacities copy row $2$. Thus
\[
K[3]=[0,0,3,5,6,8,9,11,11].
\]

After item $4$ of weight $5$ and value $7$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
K[4][5]&=\max(8,7+0)=8,\\
K[4][6]&=\max(9,7+0)=9,\\
K[4][7]&=\max(11,7+3)=11,\\
K[4][8]&=\max(11,7+5)=12.
\end{aligned}
\]
So $K[4][8]=12$, and the take-branch of item $4$ wins.
\[
\boxed{K[4][8]=12}.
\]

For completeness, the take/skip decisions at every cell where the current item fits are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
i & \text{decisions as }c\text{ increases from }w_i\text{ through }8\\ \hline
1 & \text{take at }c=2,3,4,5,6,7,8,\\
2 & \text{take at }c=3,4,5,6,7,8,\\
3 & \text{take at }c=4,\ \text{skip at }c=5,\ \text{take at }c=6,7,8,\\
4 & \text{skip at }c=5,6,7,\ \text{take at }c=8.
\end{array}
\]

Reconstruction. From $(4,8)$ the take-branch was used, so item $4$ is included and the residual cell is $(3,3)$. Item $3$ has weight $4>3$, so it is skipped and the cell is $(2,3)$. From $(2,3)$ the take-branch was used, so item $2$ is included and the residual cell is $(1,0)$. Capacity $0$ forces item $1$ to be skipped. The set is $\{2,4\}$, with weight $3+5=8$ and value $5+7=12$.

Every feasible subset and its value:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varnothing\mapsto 0,\quad
\{1\}\mapsto 3,\quad
\{2\}\mapsto 5,\quad
\{3\}\mapsto 6,\quad
\{4\}\mapsto 7,\\
&\{1,2\}\mapsto 8,\quad
\{1,3\}\mapsto 9,\quad
\{1,4\}\mapsto 10,\quad
\{2,3\}\mapsto 11,\quad
\{2,4\}\mapsto 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
The sets $\{3,4\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{1,2,4\}$, $\{1,3,4\}$, $\{2,3,4\}$, and $\{1,2,3,4\}$ all exceed weight $8$. The unique maximum is therefore $\{2,4\}$.

The recurrence is exhaustive because a 0/1 packing of the first $i$ items either excludes $i$ or includes it once and then packs a subset of $\{1,\ldots,i-1\}$ into $c-w_i$. Using the previous row (or a right-to-left one-dimensional overwrite) prevents the current item from being read after it has already been taken. A left-to-right overwrite of a single row would let $K[c-w_i]$ already contain item $i$, which is unbounded knapsack.

Claim (i) is not 0/1. Taking item $2$ twice with item $1$ uses weights $3+3+2=8$ and value $13$, which reuses item $2$. The fractional packing of items $2$ and $1$ together with $3/4$ of item $3$ has value $5+3+4.5=12.5$, which is the fractional knapsack and is illegal here. Claim (ii) reads the capacity-$7$ cell $K[4][7]=11$, which is the optimum for a different budget; the instance asks for $W=8$. Neither audit is an alignment DP.

graderFixtures.proofText: The table ends at $K[4][8]=12$. Walking the take bits includes item $4$ and then item $2$, and skips items $3$ and $1$. The packing $\{2,4\}$ has weight $8$ and value $12$, and every other feasible subset is worth at most $11$. A fractional density packing of value $12.5$, or using item $2$ twice, is illegal. The cell $K[4][7]=11$ is a different capacity.

Sort by density v/w. Take all of item 2, all of item 1, and three-quarters of item 3 to fill the remaining capacity 3. The value is 5+3+4.5=12.5. Alternatively pack item 2 twice with item 1 for value 13.
Capacity runs through the eight indices 0,1,...,7. The bottom-right cell is K[4][7]=11, attained by items 2 and 3, so the optimum is 11.

ALG:010426.title: The unique minimum four-matrix product is (A1 A2)(A3 A4) at cost 405
ALG:010426.objective: Fill the matrix-chain table for dimensions 5x10, 10x3, 3x12, 12x5, reconstruct the unique order (A1 A2)(A3 A4) of cost 405, and reject a greedy adjacent product and a dropped last multiply.
ALG:010426.statement:
Four matrices are to be multiplied in the fixed order $A_1 A_2 A_3 A_4$, with dimensions
\[
A_1\text{ is }5\times 10,\quad
A_2\text{ is }10\times 3,\quad
A_3\text{ is }3\times 12,\quad
A_4\text{ is }12\times 5.
\]
Write $p=(p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)=(5,10,3,12,5)$, so $A_i$ is $p_{i-1}\times p_i$. The only legal rearrangements are parenthesizations of this product. The cost of multiplying an $r\times s$ matrix by an $s\times t$ matrix is the scalar product count $rst$. Let $m[i,j]$ be the minimum cost of computing $A_i\cdots A_j$, and let $s[i,j]$ be a minimizing split. Then $m[i,i]=0$ and, for $j>i$,
\[
m[i,j]=\min_{i\le k<j}\Bigl(m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+p_{i-1}\,p_k\,p_j\Bigr),
\]
with $s[i,j]$ recording a minimizing $k$.

1. Compute every $m[i,j]$ for $1\le i\le j\le 4$, including the three adjacent products, the two length-$3$ products, and $m[1,4]$. Record the minimizing $k$ at each cell.

2. Reconstruct the unique optimal parenthesization from the split table. Expand every full parenthesization of four matrices and give its exact cost. In particular account for the five values $405$, $630$, $1260$, $580$, and $1210$.

3. Prove that the recurrence enumerates every last multiplication $ (A_i\cdots A_k)\,(A_{k+1}\cdots A_j) $ and charges the final product $p_{i-1}p_k p_j$. Explain why an optimal last split uses optimal factors.

4. Audit these claims: (i) one should always multiply the currently cheapest adjacent pair, so the first product is $A_1 A_2$ at cost $150$ and the finished association is $((A_1 A_2)A_3)A_4$ of cost $630$; (ii) after computing $A_1 A_2$ at cost $150$ and $A_3 A_4$ at cost $180$, the work is already $330$, so that is the answer. Do not replace the table by an affine-gap alignment state.

State the dimension vector $p$ and that the last multiplication is part of the cost.
permittedResults: Matrix multiplication is associative, so every full parenthesization computes the same matrix, but the scalar multiplication counts generally differ.

If a last split $k$ is optimal for $A_i\cdots A_j$, then each factor $A_i\cdots A_k$ and $A_{k+1}\cdots A_j$ may be replaced by an optimal parenthesization of that factor without increasing the total cost.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fill m by increasing subchain length, store each minimizing k, and expand s[1,4] into a parenthesization.
Enumerate the five Catalan parenthesizations of four matrices as an independent checksum, then match the unique minimum 405 to the split k=2 in the table.

milestones.criterion: Fills the chain table through m[1,4]=405 with the listed length-2 and length-3 entries and the unique split k=2.
Reconstructs (A1 A2)(A3 A4) and accounts for the four strictly worse full costs 630, 1260, 580, and 1210.
Proves last-split exhaustiveness and rejects cheapest-adjacent greedy 630 and the dropped last product 330.

commonErrors.description: Always multiplies a currently cheapest adjacent pair and reports ((A1 A2)A3)A4 of cost 630 as the optimum.
commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but strictly worse association is substituted for the unique minimum of cost 405.

commonErrors.description: Adds the factor costs 150+180=330 and stops, omitting the last 5*3*5 product that turns those factors into a single matrix.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported cost is not the cost of any complete parenthesization of A1 A2 A3 A4.

hintTree.content: Adjacent costs are $5\cdot 10\cdot 3=150$, $10\cdot 3\cdot 12=360$, and $3\cdot 12\cdot 5=180$. The length-$3$ cell $m[1,3]$ prefers the split after $A_2$.
For $m[1,4]$ the three candidate totals are $330+5\cdot 10\cdot 5$, $150+180+5\cdot 3\cdot 5$, and $330+5\cdot 12\cdot 5$.
Greedy cheapest-adjacent can finish as $((A_1 A_2)A_3)A_4=630$. Stopping at $150+180$ forgets the last $5\cdot 3\cdot 5$ product.

ALG:010426.canonicalSolution:
The dimension vector is $p=(5,10,3,12,5)$. Diagonal entries vanish: $m[1,1]=m[2,2]=m[3,3]=m[4,4]=0$.

Length $2$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m[1,2]&=5\cdot 10\cdot 3=150,&&s[1,2]=1,\\
m[2,3]&=10\cdot 3\cdot 12=360,&&s[2,3]=2,\\
m[3,4]&=3\cdot 12\cdot 5=180,&&s[3,4]=3.
\end{aligned}
\]

Length $3$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m[1,3]&=\min(0+360+5\cdot 10\cdot 12,\ 150+0+5\cdot 3\cdot 12)\\
&=\min(360+600,\ 150+180)=\min(960,330)=330,
\end{aligned}
\]
so $s[1,3]=2$, corresponding to $(A_1 A_2)A_3$. Next
\[
\begin{aligned}
m[2,4]&=\min(0+180+10\cdot 3\cdot 5,\ 360+0+10\cdot 12\cdot 5)\\
&=\min(180+150,\ 360+600)=\min(330,960)=330,
\end{aligned}
\]
so $s[2,4]=2$, corresponding to $A_2(A_3 A_4)$.

Length $4$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1&\colon m[1,1]+m[2,4]+5\cdot 10\cdot 5=330+250=580,\\
k=2&\colon m[1,2]+m[3,4]+5\cdot 3\cdot 5=150+180+75=405,\\
k=3&\colon m[1,3]+m[4,4]+5\cdot 12\cdot 5=330+300=630.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $m[1,4]=405$ with unique minimizer $s[1,4]=2$.
\[
\boxed{m[1,4]=405,\ s[1,4]=2}.
\]

Reconstruction. The last split of $A_1\cdots A_4$ is after $A_2$, so the factors are $A_1 A_2$ and $A_3 A_4$. Each factor is already a single adjacent product. The parenthesization is $(A_1 A_2)(A_3 A_4)$.

The five full parenthesizations and their costs are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A_1 A_2)(A_3 A_4)&=150+180+5\cdot 3\cdot 5=405,\\
((A_1 A_2)A_3)A_4&=150+5\cdot 3\cdot 12+5\cdot 12\cdot 5=150+180+300=630,\\
(A_1(A_2 A_3))A_4&=360+5\cdot 10\cdot 12+5\cdot 12\cdot 5=360+600+300=1260,\\
A_1(A_2(A_3 A_4))&=180+10\cdot 3\cdot 5+5\cdot 10\cdot 5=180+150+250=580,\\
A_1((A_2 A_3)A_4)&=360+10\cdot 12\cdot 5+5\cdot 10\cdot 5=360+600+250=1210.
\end{aligned}
\]
The unique minimum is $405$.

The recurrence is exhaustive because any parenthesization of $A_i\cdots A_j$ has a last multiplication at a unique split $k$, the two factors are themselves parenthesizations, and the last product always costs $p_{i-1}p_k p_j$. If a factor were suboptimal it could be replaced by a cheaper parenthesization of the same dimensions, contradicting optimality of the whole. Filling by increasing chain length therefore computes every $m[i,j]$.

Claim (i) always multiplies a cheapest adjacent pair. The adjacent costs begin at $150,360,180$, so it forms $A_1 A_2$ first. The remaining chain has dimensions $5\times 3$, $3\times 12$, $12\times 5$, whose adjacent products both cost $180$. One legal continuation is $((A_1 A_2)A_3)A_4$, whose total is $630$, which the table already marked as a strictly worse split $k=3$. Claim (ii) adds the two factor costs $150+180=330$ and stops. That number is $m[1,2]+m[3,4]$ before the last multiplication $5\cdot 3\cdot 5=75$; it is not $m[1,4]$. Both claims compute a quantity other than the stated minimum chain cost. The table is a chain-split DP, not an alignment DP.

graderFixtures.proofText: Adjacent costs are $150,360,180$. Length-$3$ costs are $m[1,3]=m[2,4]=330$. The three splits of the full chain cost $580$, $405$, and $630$, so $m[1,4]=405$ at $k=2$. Reconstruction is $(A_1 A_2)(A_3 A_4)$. The other complete associations cost $630$, $1260$, $580$, and $1210$. Cheapest-adjacent greedy can finish at $630$. Stopping at $150+180=330$ drops the last multiply.
The cheapest adjacent product is A1 A2 at cost 150. The remaining cheapest product is then (A1 A2)A3 at cost 180, and the last multiply by A4 costs 300. The greedy total 630 is optimal.
Compute A1 A2 for 150 and A3 A4 for 180. Those are the two blocks of the balanced split, so the chain cost is 150+180=330.
