ALG:010527.title: A DAG longest s-t path is a topological max-DP with minus-infinity unreachable labels
ALG:010527.objective: Compute the unique longest s-t path in a given DAG by topological dynamic programming, reconstruct it from predecessors, initialize unreachable vertices to minus infinity, and reject Dijkstra or min-relaxation and a zero initialization of non-sources.
ALG:010527.statement:
Let $G$ be the directed acyclic graph with vertex set $\{s,a,b,c,t\}$ and exactly the seven weighted edges
\[
s\to a\ (2),\quad s\to b\ (4),\quad a\to c\ (3),\quad a\to t\ (4),\quad b\to c\ (5),\quad b\to t\ (2),\quad c\to t\ (2).
\]
A path weight is the sum of its edge weights. The task is the longest $s$-$t$ path: a directed $s$-$t$ path of maximum weight, together with that weight.

Process vertices in the topological order $s,a,b,c,t$. Maintain a label $L[v]$ intended to be the maximum weight of a directed $s$-$v$ path, or $-\infty$ if no such path exists, and a predecessor $\mathrm{pred}[v]$ for reconstruction. Initialize $L[s]=0$ and $L[v]=-\infty$ for every $v\ne s$. When a vertex $u$ is processed, replace $L[v]$ by $L[u]+w(u,v)$ for each outgoing edge $u\to v$ whenever $L[u]$ is finite and $L[u]+w(u,v)$ is strictly larger than the current $L[v]$, and then set $\mathrm{pred}[v]=u$.

1. Execute the algorithm. Record $L$ and $\mathrm{pred}$ after every vertex is processed. Reconstruct the unique longest $s$-$t$ path from $\mathrm{pred}[t]$ and prove that its weight is $11$. Enumerate every simple $s$-$t$ path and confirm that none is heavier.

2. Prove that after all vertices are processed, $L[v]$ equals the maximum $s$-$v$ path weight (or $-\infty$ if $v$ is unreachable from $s$). Identify the DAG hypothesis used: why a longest path is well-defined here, and why the same recurrence is not a polynomial algorithm on a general directed graph.

3. Explain why the initialization $L[v]=-\infty$ for $v\ne s$ is required. In particular, consider a colleague who adds an unreachable vertex $u$ with a single extra edge $u\to t$ of weight $100$ and initializes every label, including $L[u]$ and $L[t]$, to $0$. Show that their $t$-label is then at least $100$ even though no $s$-$t$ path through $u$ exists.

4. Audit these claims: (i) Dijkstra from $s$, or the same topological recurrence with $\min$ in place of $\max$, computes the longest path because all weights are positive; (ii) unreachable vertices may be initialized to $0$ because they contribute nothing; (iii) the point of the exercise is a negative-edge shortest-path counterexample to settled-vertex Dijkstra. Do not replace the longest-path computation by Bellman-Ford, potential reweighting, or a negative-cycle test.
permittedResults: On a DAG every walk is simple, so a longest $s$-$v$ path exists whenever $v$ is reachable from $s$. Dynamic programming in topological order computes it in $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ time.
Longest path is NP-hard on general directed graphs. Nonnegative Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford compute shortest paths, not longest paths.

acceptableStrategies.description: Relax outgoing edges once per vertex in topological order, storing a predecessor on every strict improvement, then walk pred from t.
Enumerate the four simple s-t paths to identify the unique maximum, then verify that the same path is recovered by the DP labels.

milestones.criterion: Executes the topological max-DP in order s,a,b,c,t, records labels (0,2,4,9,11) and reconstructs s-b-c-t of weight 11.
Proves the DAG optimal-substructure recurrence and the -infinity initialization, including the unreachable-tail pollution example.
Rejects Dijkstra or min-relaxation as a longest-path method and refuses a negative-edge shortest-path substitution.

commonErrors.description: Runs Dijkstra from s, or replaces max by min in the topological recurrence, and reports a shortest-path weight 6 as the longest-path answer.
commonErrors.consequence: The maximization objective is replaced by a shortest-path computation, so the unique optimum s-b-c-t of weight 11 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Initializes every non-source label to 0, or treats an unreachable vertex as having an empty s-path of weight 0.
commonErrors.consequence: A fictional path through an unreachable tail can improve t, so L[t] is no longer a true s-t path weight.

hintTree.content: After processing $s$ the labels are $L[a]=2$ and $L[b]=4$. The edge $b\to c$ then competes with $a\to c$.
The last improvement into $t$ should come from $c$, because $9+2$ beats both $2+4$ and $4+2$.
Zero at an unreachable tail is treated as a legitimate empty $s$-path of weight $0$, so a fictional edge out of that tail pollutes $t$.

ALG:010527.canonicalSolution:
Initialize $L[s]=0$ and $L[a]=L[b]=L[c]=L[t]=-\infty$, with every predecessor undefined.

Process $s$. The outgoing relaxations give $L[a]=2$ with $\mathrm{pred}[a]=s$ and $L[b]=4$ with $\mathrm{pred}[b]=s$.

Process $a$. Then $L[c]=\max(-\infty,2+3)=5$ with $\mathrm{pred}[c]=a$, and $L[t]=\max(-\infty,2+4)=6$ with $\mathrm{pred}[t]=a$.

Process $b$. Then $L[c]=\max(5,4+5)=9$ with $\mathrm{pred}[c]=b$, while $L[t]=\max(6,4+2)=6$ is unchanged.

Process $c$. Then $L[t]=\max(6,9+2)=11$ with $\mathrm{pred}[t]=c$.

Process $t$. There are no outgoing edges. The final labels and predecessors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
L[s]&=0, & L[a]&=2, & L[b]&=4, & L[c]&=9, & L[t]&=11,\\
\mathrm{pred}[a]&=s, & \mathrm{pred}[b]&=s, & \mathrm{pred}[c]&=b, & \mathrm{pred}[t]&=c.
\end{aligned}
\]
Walking predecessors from $t$ yields $t\leftarrow c\leftarrow b\leftarrow s$, hence the path
\[
s\to b\to c\to t
\]
of weight $4+5+2=11$.
\[
\boxed{s\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}t\text{ weight }11}.
\]
The complete list of simple $s$-$t$ paths is $s\text{-}a\text{-}t$ of weight $6$, $s\text{-}a\text{-}c\text{-}t$ of weight $7$, $s\text{-}b\text{-}t$ of weight $6$, and $s\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}t$ of weight $11$. The reconstructed path is therefore the unique longest $s$-$t$ path.

For correctness, proceed by induction on the topological prefix. The claim holds at $s$ because the empty path has weight $0$ and every other $s$-$s$ walk would repeat $s$, which a DAG forbids. When $v$ is processed, every incoming neighbor $u$ has already been processed, so $L[u]$ is the true longest $s$-$u$ weight (or $-\infty$). Any $s$-$v$ path is $P\cdot(u,v)$ for a unique last edge, and $P$ is a longest $s$-$u$ path without loss of optimality. The displayed relaxation therefore records the maximum. Unreachable vertices keep $-\infty$ because no incoming improvement is ever finite.

The DAG hypothesis is used twice: it supplies a topological order, and it forbids positive-length cycles, so a longest walk exists and is a simple path. On a general directed graph the same recurrence is not a polynomial algorithm: longest path is NP-hard, and a positive cycle reachable from $s$ makes the longest-walk value $+\infty$.

If an unreachable vertex $u$ with extra edge $u\to t$ of weight $100$ is added and every label is initialized to $0$, then $L[u]=0$ is treated as a real $s$-$u$ path of weight $0$. Processing $u$ writes $L[t]\ge 100$, which is not the weight of any $s$-$t$ path. The $-\infty$ initialization is exactly what blocks that fictional empty path.

Claim (i) is false. Dijkstra and the min-recurrence both compute shortest paths. On the given nonnegative instance they return weight $6$ (via $s\text{-}a\text{-}t$ or $s\text{-}b\text{-}t$), not $11$. Claim (ii) is the zero-initialization error just exhibited. Claim (iii) is the held negative-edge shortest-path packet: every weight here is positive, the objective is maximization, and no Bellman-Ford vector or negative-cycle test is asked.

graderFixtures.proofText: Initialize L[s]=0 and all other labels to -infinity. In order s,a,b,c,t the labels become 0,2,4,9,11 with pred t<-c<-b<-s, recovering s-b-c-t of weight 11. The other s-t paths weigh 6, 7, and 6. Dijkstra or a min-recurrence returns 6 and is the wrong objective. Zero-initializing an unreachable u with edge u->t of weight 100 writes L[t]>=100, which is not an s-t path. This is a DAG longest-path DP, not a negative-edge shortest-path audit.

All weights are positive, so Dijkstra from s is valid. It settles s, then a at 2, then b at 4, then t at 6 via a->t or b->t. The longest s-t path therefore has weight 6. The same number is obtained by replacing max with min in the topological recurrence.
Unreachable vertices contribute nothing, so every label may start at 0. If u has a single edge u->t of weight 100, that edge is a legitimate candidate and L[t] is at least 100.

ALG:010528.title: Strong connectivity is mutual reachability: the SCCs of a chain of cycles form a path DAG
ALG:010528.objective: Trace Kosaraju or Tarjan on a specified digraph, obtain the four SCCs {a,b,c}, {d,e}, {f,g}, {h} and a chain condensation, and reject treating one-way reachability as strong connectivity.
ALG:010528.statement:
Let $G$ be the directed graph on vertices $\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\}$ with exactly the edges
\[
a\to b,\ b\to c,\ c\to a,\quad d\to e,\ e\to d,\quad f\to g,\ g\to f,\quad c\to d,\ e\to f,\ g\to h.
\]
Write adjacency lists in alphabetical order:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a&:b, & b&:c, & c&:a,d, & d&:e,\\
e&:d,f, & f&:g, & g&:f,h, & h&:(\text{none}).
\end{aligned}
\]
A strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal vertex set in which every ordered pair is mutually reachable by directed walks. The condensation of $G$ has one vertex per SCC and a directed edge $A\to B$ whenever $G$ has an edge from $A$ to $B$ and $A\ne B$.

1. Trace Kosaraju's algorithm. In the first depth-first search, start new trees at unvisited vertices in alphabetical order and, at each vertex, scan the alphabetical adjacency list. Record every finish time. Then run depth-first search on the transpose $G^{T}$ in decreasing finish-time order, again scanning alphabetical in-neighbor lists, and record the vertex set of each second-pass tree. (A complete Tarjan trace that uses the same adjacency order, records every index and low-link value, and pops the same four components is an acceptable substitute.)

2. Prove that the SCCs are exactly $\{a,b,c\}$, $\{d,e\}$, $\{f,g\}$, and $\{h\}$. Prove that the condensation is the chain DAG
\[
\{a,b,c\}\to\{d,e\}\to\{f,g\}\to\{h\}.
\]

3. Exhibit a directed walk from $a$ to $h$ and prove that $h$ cannot reach $a$. Conclude that one-way reachability does not place $a$ and $h$ in the same SCC, and that the underlying undirected connectivity of $G$ is irrelevant to the SCC partition.

4. Audit these claims: (i) because $a$ reaches every other vertex, $G$ has a single SCC; (ii) the edge $g\to h$ places $h$ in the same SCC as $f$ and $g$; (iii) the second Kosaraju pass may be run on $G$ rather than $G^{T}$. Do not replace the SCC computation by a shortest-path label or a negative-cycle test.
permittedResults: Kosaraju: the second depth-first search, run on $G^{T}$ in decreasing $G$-finish-time order, yields the SCCs as its search trees.
Tarjan: a vertex $v$ is the root of an SCC exactly when $\mathrm{low}[v]=\mathrm{index}[v]$; the SCC is then the stack suffix popped down through $v$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Run Kosaraju with alphabetical adjacency and alphabetical first-pass starts, then read SCCs from the G^T trees in decreasing finish order.
Run Tarjan with the same adjacency order, popping a component whenever low[v]=index[v], and then contract the four blocks.

milestones.criterion: Traces Kosaraju or Tarjan and obtains exactly the SCCs {a,b,c}, {d,e}, {f,g}, {h}.
Proves the condensation is the chain DAG ABC->DE->FG->H and that a reaches h one-way.
Rejects one-way reachability as strong connectivity and rejects running the second Kosaraju pass on G rather than G^T.

commonErrors.description: Declares a and h, or the whole vertex set, or {f,g,h}, to be a single SCC because a directed walk exists in one direction.
commonErrors.consequence: Strong connectivity is replaced by ordinary reachability, so the condensation is no longer the required chain of four blocks.

commonErrors.description: Runs the second Kosaraju depth-first search on G rather than on G^T, or ignores finish-time order.
commonErrors.consequence: The search trees are not guaranteed to be the SCCs, so the partition is unproved.

hintTree.content: The first DFS from $a$ reaches every vertex. The finish order, earliest to latest, is $h,g,f,e,d,c,b,a$.
On $G^{T}$ the first unused vertex in decreasing finish order is $a$, and $a,c,b$ form one tree because $a\leftarrow c\leftarrow b\leftarrow a$.
$g$ reaches $h$, but $h$ has out-degree zero, so $h$ is a singleton SCC.

ALG:010528.canonicalSolution:
First Kosaraju pass. The only start vertex is $a$, which reaches the whole graph. The recursive visit order is
\[
a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h.
\]
With the conventional DFS clock incremented on each discovery and finish, the discovery times of $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ are $1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$, and the finish times are
\[
f(h)=9,\ f(g)=10,\ f(f)=11,\ f(e)=12,\ f(d)=13,\ f(c)=14,\ f(b)=15,\ f(a)=16.
\]
Thus $h$ finishes first, then $g,f,e,d,c,b,a$. Decreasing finish order is
\[
a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h.
\]
The transpose has alphabetical lists $a:c$, $b:a$, $c:b$, $d:c,e$, $e:d$, $f:e,g$, $g:f$, $h:g$.

Second pass on $G^{T}$:
- Start at $a$. Then $a\to c\to b$, and $b\to a$ is a back edge. The tree is $\{a,b,c\}$.
- Next unused vertex is $d$. Then $d\to e$, and $e\to d$ is a back edge, while $d\to c$ is already visited. The tree is $\{d,e\}$.
- Next unused vertex is $f$. Then $f\to g$, and $g\to f$ is a back edge, while $f\to e$ is already visited. The tree is $\{f,g\}$.
- Next unused vertex is $h$. Then $h\to g$ is already visited. The tree is $\{h\}$.

The four SCCs are therefore $\{a,b,c\}$, $\{d,e\}$, $\{f,g\}$, and $\{h\}$.

The same partition is recovered by Tarjan with the same adjacency order. Indices and low-links along the unique first-search spine $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{index}(h)&=\mathrm{low}(h)=8 &&\text{pop }\{h\},\\
\mathrm{low}(g)&=6=\mathrm{index}(f) &&\text{pop }\{g,f\}\text{ at }f,\\
\mathrm{low}(e)&=4=\mathrm{index}(d) &&\text{pop }\{e,d\}\text{ at }d,\\
\mathrm{low}(a)&=1=\mathrm{index}(a) &&\text{pop }\{c,b,a\}\text{ at }a.
\end{aligned}
\]

Mutual reachability inside each block is immediate: $\{a,b,c\}$ is a directed $3$-cycle, $\{d,e\}$ and $\{f,g\}$ are directed $2$-cycles, and $\{h\}$ is a singleton. No larger set works. The only edges that leave a block are $c\to d$, $e\to f$, and $g\to h$, so the condensation is the chain
\[
\{a,b,c\}\to\{d,e\}\to\{f,g\}\to\{h\}.
\]
A condensation is always a DAG; here it is a path.

The walk $a\to b\to c\to d\to e\to f\to g\to h$ shows that $a$ reaches $h$. Vertex $h$ has out-degree zero, so $h$ reaches only itself. Thus $a$ and $h$ are not strongly connected, even though they lie in the same weakly connected undirected component.

Claim (i) confuses one-way reachability from $a$ with mutual reachability. Claim (ii) makes the same error on the single edge $g\to h$. Claim (iii) is a wrong Kosaraju implementation: the second pass must use $G^{T}$ (equivalently, decreasing finish times as sources on $G$ is not the same search). This packet is an SCC partition, not a shortest-path or negative-cycle computation.
\[
\boxed{\{a,b,c\},\{d,e\},\{f,g\},\{h\}\text{ chain condensation}}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: First DFS from a finishes h,g,f,e,d,c,b,a. Second DFS on G^T in decreasing finish order yields trees {a,b,c}, {d,e}, {f,g}, {h}. The condensation is the chain ABC->DE->FG->H. The walk a-b-c-d-e-f-g-h is one-way: h has out-degree 0, so a and h are not strongly connected. Tarjan with the same adjacency order pops the same four sets. Running the second pass on G, or merging vertices that merely have a one-way walk, is incorrect.

Vertex a reaches every other vertex by a directed walk, and the underlying undirected graph is connected, so G has a single strongly connected component. In particular a and h are strongly connected, and g->h places h in the same SCC as f and g.
After recording finish times I rerun DFS on G itself, starting at a again. The single tree is the whole vertex set, which I report as the SCC partition.

ALG:010529.title: A feasible flow of 14 and the source cut of capacity 14 certify the max-flow min-cut value
ALG:010529.objective: Exhibit a feasible s-t flow of value 14, the residual augmentations that produce it, conservation at a and b, and the cut {s} of capacity 14, and reject summing every capacity or omitting reverse residual edges.
ALG:010529.statement:
Consider the directed $s$-$t$ network with vertices $\{s,a,b,t\}$ and capacities
\[
s\to a\ 8,\quad s\to b\ 6,\quad a\to b\ 2,\quad a\to t\ 6,\quad b\to t\ 8.
\]
A feasible flow assigns a number $f(e)$ to each edge with $0\le f(e)\le c(e)$, with conservation at $a$ and at $b$. The value is the net flow out of $s$. For a partition $(S,T)$ with $s\in S$ and $t\in T$, the cut capacity is the total capacity of edges from $S$ to $T$.

The residual graph of a feasible flow has, for every original edge $u\to v$, a forward residual capacity $c(u,v)-f(u,v)$ and a reverse residual capacity $f(u,v)$ on $v\to u$. An augmenting path is a directed $s$-$t$ path in the residual graph; its bottleneck is the minimum residual capacity along the path.

1. Starting from the zero flow, exhibit a sequence of residual augmentations that reaches a feasible flow of value $14$. After each augmentation, list every positive residual capacity, including reverse edges. Verify conservation at $a$ and at $b$ for the final flow, and verify that the residual graph then has no $s$-$t$ path.

2. Compute the capacity of the cut $S=\{s\}$, $T=\{a,b,t\}$. Combine the exhibited flow of value $14$ with this cut to prove that the maximum flow and the minimum cut both equal $14$.

3. Prove the weak inequality that every feasible flow value is at most every $s$-$t$ cut capacity, so the matching pair is optimal. (You need not reprove the full max-flow min-cut theorem beyond this certificate.)

4. Audit these claims: (i) the maximum flow is the sum $8+6+2+6+8=30$ of all listed capacities; (ii) residual graphs need only unused forward capacity, so reverse edges may be omitted; (iii) the exercise is a negative-edge shortest-path computation on the same four vertices. Do not replace the flow by Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford labels.
permittedResults: Weak duality: the value of every feasible $s$-$t$ flow is at most the capacity of every $s$-$t$ cut, because every unit of flow that leaves $S$ must use a forward cut edge.
Ford-Fulkerson: a feasible flow is maximum if and only if its residual graph has no $s$-$t$ path. Reverse residual edges are part of that residual graph.

acceptableStrategies.description: Run Ford-Fulkerson from the zero flow, recording forward and reverse residuals after each bottleneck push, then certify with the source cut.
Write down any feasible flow of value 14 by inspection (saturate every edge leaving s) and independently compute cut {s}, then exhibit one residual sequence that reaches that flow.

milestones.criterion: Exhibits a feasible flow of value 14 with conservation at a and b and a residual sequence that includes reverse edges.
Computes cut {s} capacity 14 and invokes weak duality to certify that 14 is the max-flow min-cut value.
Rejects summing all capacities as a flow value and rejects a residual graph that omits reverse edges.

commonErrors.description: Reports 8+6+2+6+8=30, or any other sum of capacities that is not the value of a feasible flow, as the maximum flow.
commonErrors.consequence: A capacity total is not a conserved s-t flow and already exceeds the source cut of capacity 14.

commonErrors.description: Defines the residual graph using only unused forward capacity and never records a reverse residual edge for used capacity.
commonErrors.consequence: Cancellation is impossible and the Ford-Fulkerson residual characterization is no longer the residual graph of the theorem.

hintTree.content: One sequence is $s\text{-}a\text{-}t$ of bottleneck $6$, then $s\text{-}b\text{-}t$ of bottleneck $6$, then $s\text{-}a\text{-}b\text{-}t$ of bottleneck $2$.
The cut $\{s\}$ has only the two edges $s\to a$ and $s\to b$, of capacities $8$ and $6$.
After the first augmentation the residual graph contains the reverse edge $t\to a$ of capacity $6$, even if a later path does not use it.

ALG:010529.canonicalSolution:
Start with the zero flow. All residual capacities equal the original capacities.

Augment $P_1=s\to a\to t$ with bottleneck $\min(8,6)=6$. The flow is now $f(s,a)=6$, $f(a,t)=6$, value $6$. The positive residual capacities are $s\to a:2$, $a\to s:6$, $t\to a:6$, $s\to b:6$, $a\to b:2$, and $b\to t:8$.

Augment $P_2=s\to b\to t$ with bottleneck $\min(6,8)=6$. The flow is now also $f(s,b)=6$, $f(b,t)=6$, value $12$. The positive residual capacities are $s\to a:2$, $a\to s:6$, $t\to a:6$, $a\to b:2$, $b\to t:2$, $b\to s:6$, and $t\to b:6$.

Augment $P_3=s\to a\to b\to t$ with bottleneck $\min(2,2,2)=2$. The final flow is
\[
f(s,a)=8,\quad f(s,b)=6,\quad f(a,b)=2,\quad f(a,t)=6,\quad f(b,t)=8,
\]
of value $8+6=14$. Residual: every original forward edge is saturated except that several are already listed as zero; reverse edges $a\to s$ of $8$, $b\to s$ of $6$, $b\to a$ of $2$, $t\to a$ of $6$, and $t\to b$ of $8$ are present. There is no residual $s$-$t$ path: $s$ has no unused outgoing residual edge.

Conservation at $a$: inflow $8$ on $s\to a$, outflow $6+2$ on $a\to t$ and $a\to b$. Conservation at $b$: inflow $6+2$ on $s\to b$ and $a\to b$, outflow $8$ on $b\to t$. Capacities are respected. Thus the assignment is a feasible flow of value $14$.
\[
\boxed{\text{flow value }14}.
\]

The cut $S=\{s\}$, $T=\{a,b,t\}$ has forward edges $s\to a$ and $s\to b$ only, of total capacity $8+6=14$.
\[
\boxed{\text{cut }\{s\}\text{ capacity }14}.
\]
Weak duality says that every feasible flow value is at most every cut capacity: each unit of net flow from $S$ to $T$ uses at least one unit of forward cut capacity, and reverse flow from $T$ to $S$ can only decrease the recorded value. Therefore no flow exceeds $14$ and no cut is smaller than $14$. The exhibited pair is optimal, and the max-flow min-cut value is $14$.

Claim (i) is not a flow. The number $30$ ignores capacities as a cut, ignores conservation, and is larger than the source cut. Claim (ii) omits reverse residual edges. After $P_1$ the reverse edge $t\to a$ of capacity $6$ is required by the definition of the residual graph; without reverse edges Ford-Fulkerson is incomplete, because a later augmentation may need to cancel flow. (On this particular instance the displayed sequence happens to use only forward residual edges after the first two steps, which does not license dropping reverse edges from the residual.) Claim (iii) is the held negative-edge shortest-path packet and is not asked: capacities are not shortest-path weights.

graderFixtures.proofText: Augment s-a-t by 6, s-b-t by 6, and s-a-b-t by 2. The final flow is f(s,a)=8, f(s,b)=6, f(a,b)=2, f(a,t)=6, f(b,t)=8, value 14, with conservation 8=6+2 at a and 6+2=8 at b. After the first push the residual already contains t->a of capacity 6; after the last push every reverse of a used edge is present and no s-t residual path remains. Cut {s} has capacity 8+6=14, so max flow = min cut = 14. The sum 30 is not a flow. Omitting reverse residual edges is a wrong residual graph.
The network has total capacity 8+6+2+6+8=30, so the maximum flow is 30. The source cut is irrelevant because flow can also use a->b.
After each augmentation I update only leftover forward capacity. Reverse edges are bookkeeping and may be omitted because the three forward paths s-a-t, s-b-t, and s-a-b-t already reach 14.

ALG:010630.title: 3SAT reduces to Independent Set by clause triangles and complementary conflict edges
ALG:010630.objective: Build the standard 3SAT-to-Independent-Set graph on three clauses, count nine vertices, nine triangle edges, and exactly five complementary conflicts, exhibit an independent set of size 3, and prove the yes-instance equivalence both ways.
ALG:010630.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the $3$-CNF formula with clauses
\[
C_1=(x\lor y\lor z),\qquad C_2=(\lnot x\lor\lnot y\lor w),\qquad C_3=(\lnot x\lor\lnot z\lor\lnot w).
\]
Construct the standard undirected graph $G_{\varphi}$ for the polynomial reduction from $3$-SAT to Independent Set, as follows.

- Create one vertex for each literal occurrence, nine vertices in all. Write $x_1,y_1,z_1$ for the occurrences in $C_1$, $\lnot x_2,\lnot y_2,w_2$ for the occurrences in $C_2$, and $\lnot x_3,\lnot z_3,\lnot w_3$ for the occurrences in $C_3$.
- Place a triangle on the three occurrences of each clause (nine within-clause edges).
- Place a complementary conflict edge between two occurrences that lie in different clauses and are a variable and its negation. Do not join two occurrences of the same polarity.

An independent set is a vertex subset containing no edge. The Independent Set decision problem asks whether $G$ has an independent set of size at least a given integer $k$.

1. List every complementary conflict edge and prove that there are exactly five of them. Conclude that $G_{\varphi}$ has nine vertices and fourteen edges.

2. Exhibit the independent set $\{y_1,w_2,\lnot x_3\}$ and prove that it is independent of size $3$. Translate it into a satisfying assignment of $\varphi$ and verify all three clauses.

3. Prove the general equivalence for this construction, specialized to $m=3$ clauses: $\varphi$ is satisfiable if and only if $G_{\varphi}$ has an independent set of size $3$. Both directions are required. In the forward direction, explain why a satisfying assignment cannot select both endpoints of a conflict edge. In the reverse direction, explain why an independent set of size $3$ selects exactly one vertex per triangle and defines a consistent truth assignment.

4. Audit these claims: (i) $\lnot x_2$ and $\lnot x_3$ must be joined because they mention the same variable; (ii) it is enough to prove that a satisfying assignment yields an independent set, because hardness reductions need only one direction; (iii) the exercise is a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover many-one reduction. Do not replace the construction by an incidence set system for vertex cover.
permittedResults: A triangle has independence number $1$, so an independent set meets each clause gadget in at most one vertex.
If a known NP-hard problem $A$ satisfies $A\le_p B$, then $B$ is NP-hard. The map must send yes-instances to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances.

acceptableStrategies.description: Name every occurrence, draw the three triangles, then add one conflict per complementary pair and test the displayed size-3 set.
Start from the assignment x false, y true, w true, pick one true literal per clause, then reverse the argument from an arbitrary size-3 independent set.

milestones.criterion: Lists nine vertices, nine triangle edges, and exactly five complementary conflict edges, excluding same-polarity ~x2--~x3.
Exhibits the independent set {y1, w2, ~x3} of size 3 and proves both directions of the satisfiability equivalence.
Rejects joining same-polarity occurrences, a one-sided reduction, and a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover substitution.

commonErrors.description: Joins ~x2 to ~x3, omits one of the five complementary edges, or reports a conflict count other than 5.
commonErrors.consequence: The constructed graph is not the standard 3SAT-to-Independent-Set image, so the size-3 equivalence need not hold.

commonErrors.description: Proves only that a satisfying assignment yields an independent set, or only that the displayed set is independent, and treats the converse as unnecessary.
commonErrors.consequence: A many-one reduction requires yes-iff-yes; a one-sided map can send no-instances to yes-instances.

hintTree.content: The complementary pairs are $x$ against the two $\lnot x$ occurrences, $y$ against $\lnot y$, $z$ against $\lnot z$, and $w$ against $\lnot w$. Same-polarity $\lnot x_2$ and $\lnot x_3$ are not a pair.
The set $\{y_1,w_2,\lnot x_3\}$ picks one vertex from each triangle and never a variable together with its negation.
An independent set of size $3$ cannot pick two vertices from one triangle, so it picks exactly one occurrence per clause.

ALG:010630.canonicalSolution:
The nine vertices are $x_1,y_1,z_1,\lnot x_2,\lnot y_2,w_2,\lnot x_3,\lnot z_3,\lnot w_3$. The nine triangle edges are
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1&: x_1y_1,\ y_1z_1,\ z_1x_1,\\
C_2&: \lnot x_2\lnot y_2,\ \lnot y_2w_2,\ w_2\lnot x_2,\\
C_3&: \lnot x_3\lnot z_3,\ \lnot z_3\lnot w_3,\ \lnot w_3\lnot x_3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Complementary conflicts, by variable:
- $x$ occurs positively once and negatively twice, giving $x_1\text{--}\lnot x_2$ and $x_1\text{--}\lnot x_3$;
- $y$ gives $y_1\text{--}\lnot y_2$;
- $z$ gives $z_1\text{--}\lnot z_3$;
- $w$ gives $w_2\text{--}\lnot w_3$.

There is no edge $\lnot x_2\text{--}\lnot x_3$, because those occurrences have the same polarity. The conflict list has exactly five edges. Hence $G_{\varphi}$ has nine vertices and $9+5=14$ edges.
\[
\boxed{9\text{ vertices, }9\text{ triangle edges, }5\text{ conflicts}}.
\]

The set $I=\{y_1,w_2,\lnot x_3\}$ has size $3$. No two lie in the same clause triangle. The only conflict edges incident to these vertices are $y_1\text{--}\lnot y_2$, $w_2\text{--}\lnot w_3$, and $x_1\text{--}\lnot x_3$; the other listed endpoints are not in $I$. Thus $I$ is independent. Setting $y$ true, $w$ true, and $x$ false (from $\lnot x$) satisfies
\[
C_1\text{ by }y,\qquad C_2\text{ by }w,\qquad C_3\text{ by }\lnot x,
\]
with $z$ arbitrary. So $\varphi$ is satisfiable.
\[
\boxed{\{y_1,w_2,\lnot x_3\}\text{ and }x=\bot,\,y=\top,\,w=\top}.
\]

General equivalence, $m=3$. If $\tau$ satisfies $\varphi$, choose one true literal occurrence in each clause. The three vertices lie in distinct triangles, so they use none of the nine triangle edges. They use no conflict edge either: a conflict edge joins a variable to its negation, which $\tau$ cannot make simultaneously true. The chosen set is therefore an independent set of size $3$.

Conversely, let $J$ be an independent set of size $3$. Each triangle contributes at most one vertex, and there are three triangles, so $J$ contains exactly one occurrence from each clause. Define $\tau$ by setting each selected literal true. This assignment is consistent: $J$ contains no conflict edge, so it never contains both a variable and its negation. Each clause has a selected true literal, so $\tau$ satisfies $\varphi$. Unmentioned variables may be set arbitrarily.

Thus $\varphi$ is satisfiable if and only if $\alpha(G_{\varphi})\ge 3$. The construction is polynomial: for $N$ literal occurrences it has $N$ vertices, $O(N)$ clause edges, and at most $O(N^2)$ complementary-conflict edges. Combined with Independent Set $\in$ NP, this is the standard many-one reduction used to prove Independent Set NP-hard from $3$-SAT.

Claim (i) misreads complementarity: same polarity is not a conflict. Claim (ii) drops the no-instance direction, which a many-one reduction requires. Claim (iii) is the held Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover packet: the present source problem is $3$-SAT, the target is Independent Set, and no set system on edges of a vertex-cover instance is constructed.

graderFixtures.proofText: Nine vertices, nine triangle edges, and the five conflicts x1--~x2, x1--~x3, y1--~y2, z1--~z3, w2--~w3; no ~x2--~x3 edge. The set {y1, w2, ~x3} meets each triangle once and uses no conflict, so it is an independent set of size 3, corresponding to x false, y true, w true. Satisfying assignments pick one true literal per clause and cannot pick a complementary pair; an independent set of size 3 picks exactly one vertex per triangle and defines a consistent assignment. Both directions are required. This is not a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover reduction.
Occurrences of the same variable must be adjacent, so ~x2 is joined to ~x3. That gives six conflict edges, or else I drop x1--~x3 and keep only four.
A satisfying assignment selects one true literal per clause and those three vertices are independent. That direction alone proves the reduction. The converse is unnecessary for NP-hardness.

ALG:010631.title: Both endpoints of a maximal matching 2-approximate Vertex Cover, tightly on a star
ALG:010631.objective: Prove that the endpoints of any maximal matching form a vertex cover of size at most twice the optimum, exhibit tightness on K_{1,4}, distinguish maximal from maximum, and reject taking only one endpoint or claiming that a maximal matching is maximum.
ALG:010631.statement:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph with no isolated-edge-free pathology: $E$ may be empty. A matching is a subset of edges with no two sharing a vertex. A matching $M$ is maximal if no unused edge is disjoint from every edge of $M$ (equivalently, $M$ is not a proper subset of another matching). A matching is maximum if it has the largest possible cardinality among all matchings. These are different predicates.

The endpoint algorithm returns $C(M)=\{\,v\in V:v\text{ is incident to some edge of }M\,\}$, the set of both endpoints of every edge of a maximal matching $M$. The Vertex Cover minimization problem asks for a smallest $C\subseteq V$ that meets every edge.

1. Prove that if $M$ is a maximal matching, then $C(M)$ is a vertex cover. The argument must use maximality, not maximum cardinality.

2. Prove that $|C(M)|=2|M|\le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the size of a minimum vertex cover. Identify the disjoint-edge lower bound $\mathrm{OPT}\ge|M|$.

3. Execute the algorithm on the star $K_{1,4}$, whose center $r$ is joined to four leaves $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$ and which has no other edges. Show that every maximal matching consists of a single edge, that $C(M)$ then has size $2$, and that $\{r\}$ is a vertex cover of size $1$. Conclude that the approximation ratio $2$ is tight on this instance.

4. Distinguish maximal from maximum. Give a graph on which some maximal matching is not maximum (a four-vertex path suffices). Explain why the algorithm does not require a maximum matching. Audit these claims: (i) it is enough to return one endpoint of each matching edge; (ii) every maximal matching is maximum, so the algorithm may as well compute a maximum matching; (iii) the exercise is a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover Karp reduction. Do not construct a set system on edges, and do not claim NP-hardness of Vertex Cover here.
permittedResults: Any vertex cover must include at least one endpoint of every edge of a matching, and those edges are vertex-disjoint, so $\mathrm{OPT}\ge|M|$ for every matching $M$.
A maximum matching is maximal, but a maximal matching need not be maximum. A greedy scan that adds any unused disjoint edge produces a maximal matching in linear time.

acceptableStrategies.description: Prove the cover property from maximality, prove OPT>=|M| from disjoint edges, then evaluate both quantities on the star.
Start from the tight star example to read off |C|=2 and OPT=1, then write the same two inequalities that make the example a 2-approximation in general.

milestones.criterion: Proves that both endpoints of a maximal matching form a vertex cover of size at most twice OPT, using maximality and the matching lower bound.
Executes the algorithm on K_{1,4}, obtaining cover size 2 against OPT=1, and distinguishes maximal from maximum.
Rejects returning only one endpoint, rejects identifying maximal with maximum, and refuses a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover substitution.

commonErrors.description: Returns only one endpoint of each matching edge, for example only the leaf of the chosen star edge, and claims the result is a vertex cover.
commonErrors.consequence: On K_{1,4} the three unused star edges remain uncovered, so the output is not a feasible vertex cover.

commonErrors.description: Claims that every maximal matching is maximum, or that the algorithm is incorrect unless M is a maximum matching.
commonErrors.consequence: The cover proof uses maximality only. Identifying the two predicates is false on a four-vertex path and misstates the algorithm.

hintTree.content: If some edge $uv$ missed $C(M)$, then both $u$ and $v$ would be free and $M\cup\{uv\}$ would still be a matching.
On $K_{1,4}$ every pair of edges shares the center, so a matching has size at most one, and any one edge is already maximal.
On the path $a\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}d$ the middle edge is a maximal matching of size $1$, while the two end edges form a matching of size $2$.

ALG:010631.canonicalSolution:
Let $M$ be a maximal matching and let $C=C(M)$ be its endpoint set. Suppose some edge $uv\in E$ has both ends outside $C$. Then neither $u$ nor $v$ meets any edge of $M$, so $M\cup\{uv\}$ is a matching strictly larger than $M$, contradicting maximality. Therefore every edge meets $C$, and $C$ is a vertex cover. The argument used only that no unused edge is disjoint from $M$. It did not use $|M|$ being maximum.

The set $C$ contains two distinct vertices per matching edge and those vertex pairs are disjoint, so $|C|=2|M|$. Any vertex cover, in particular a minimum one, must include at least one endpoint of each edge of $M$, and those edges share no vertices, so
\[
\mathrm{OPT}\ge|M|.
\]
Hence $|C|=2|M|\le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}$. The algorithm is a $2$-approximation. It returns a feasible cover after a single greedy scan that builds any maximal matching.

Now take $G=K_{1,4}$ with center $r$ and leaves $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$. Every edge is incident to $r$, so a matching contains at most one edge. Any single edge, say $r\ell_1$, is already a matching that meets every other edge at $r$, hence is maximal (and, on this graph, also maximum). Its endpoint set is $\{r,\ell_1\}$, of size $2$. The singleton $\{r\}$ meets every edge, so $\mathrm{OPT}=1$. The returned cover has size $2=2\cdot\mathrm{OPT}$. The ratio $2$ is therefore tight.
\[
\boxed{K_{1,4}:\ |C(M)|=2,\ \mathrm{OPT}=1}.
\]

Maximal is not maximum. On the path $a\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}d$, the singleton matching $\{bc\}$ is maximal, because $ab$ meets $b$ and $cd$ meets $c$, but $\{ab,cd\}$ is a matching of size $2$. The approximation proof never needed $|M|$ to be maximum: a smaller maximal matching only makes the $2|M|$ upper bound easier to satisfy, while maximality is what makes $C(M)$ a cover. Computing a maximum matching is unnecessary and, on general graphs, is a heavier algorithm than a greedy maximal scan.

Claim (i) is false on $K_{1,4}$. Returning only the leaf $\ell_1$ of $M=\{r\ell_1\}$ leaves the three edges $r\ell_2,r\ell_3,r\ell_4$ uncovered. (Returning only the center happens to be optimal on this star, which does not make the one-endpoint rule correct in general.) Claim (ii) is false by the path example: maximality is not maximum cardinality. Claim (iii) is the held Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover packet. The present argument is an approximation algorithm, not a many-one reduction, and it constructs no set system.

graderFixtures.proofText: If uv missed both endpoints of a maximal matching M, then M union {uv} would still be a matching. Thus C(M) is a cover, |C(M)|=2|M|, and OPT>=|M| because a cover hits every matching edge, so |C|<=2 OPT. On K_{1,4} any one edge is a maximal matching, C has size 2, and the center alone is an optimum of size 1, so the ratio 2 is tight. On the path a-b-c-d the middle edge is maximal but not maximum. Taking only one endpoint fails on the star. This is not a Vertex-Cover-to-Set-Cover reduction.
It is enough to keep one endpoint of each matching edge. On K_{1,4} I keep the leaf of the chosen edge. Every matching edge is then hit, so the unused star edges are automatically covered.

A matching that cannot be extended is a maximum matching, so the algorithm is really the endpoints of a maximum matching. If M is only maximal and not maximum, C(M) need not be a cover and the factor 2 fails.

CALC1:010117.title: Evaluate a radical limit by exposing the cancelling factor
CALC1:010117.objective: Evaluate a finite limit whose direct substitution gives 0/0, and justify every cancellation on a punctured neighborhood rather than at the excluded point.
CALC1:010117.statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to4}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}$. Explain why multiplying by a conjugate is valid here and why cancelling $x-4$ does not assert that the original quotient is defined at $x=4$.
permittedResults: If two functions agree on a deleted neighborhood of a point, then they have the same limit there.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the stated governing definition or theorem, showing its hypotheses and the requested algebraic or calculus steps.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the quotient with the conjugate and simplifies correctly for $x\ne4$.

commonErrors.description: Expands $(\sqrt{x+5}-3)(\sqrt{x+5}+3)$ incorrectly.
commonErrors.consequence: The simplification and final limit are unsupported.

commonErrors.consequence: This erases the hole that produced the indeterminate form.

CALC1:010117.canonicalSolution:
Direct substitution gives $0/0$, so rewrite the numerator using its conjugate:
\[\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x+5}+3}{\sqrt{x+5}+3}=\frac{x+5-9}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x+5}+3)}=\frac1{\sqrt{x+5}+3}\]
for $x\ne4$. The last expression is continuous at $4$, so the limit is $1/(3+3)=\boxed{1/6}$. The conjugate is nonzero near $4$ because $\sqrt{x+5}+3>0$. Cancellation is made only after restricting to $x\ne4$; the original quotient still has no value at $4$.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $x\ne4$ the quotient equals $1/(\sqrt{x+5}+3)$, so the limit is $1/6$; the original formula remains undefined at 4.
The numerator becomes $x+14$, so the limit is infinite.
Cancel $x-4$ and conclude the original quotient has value $1/6$ at $x=4$.

CALC1:010118.title: Classify the discontinuities and asymptotes of a rational function
CALC1:010118.objective: Use factoring and one-sided limits to distinguish a removable discontinuity from a vertical asymptote, then determine horizontal end behavior.
CALC1:010118.statement: For $g(x)=\displaystyle\frac{2x^2-5x-3}{x^2-x-2}$, identify the domain, every discontinuity, every vertical asymptote, any removable discontinuity (including its missing $y$-value), and the horizontal asymptote. Justify the classification with limits rather than only a cancelled formula.
permittedResults: A zero of a denominator that remains after simplification can produce a vertical asymptote when the one-sided function values are unbounded.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the stated governing definition or theorem, showing its hypotheses and the requested algebraic or calculus steps.
Use an algebraically equivalent setup that preserves the domain, sign, and limiting or extremum conditions, then verify the final result.

milestones.criterion: Factors numerator and denominator and states the domain $\mathbb R\setminus\{-1,2\}$.
Uses nonzero numerators and unbounded one-sided behavior to classify both $x=-1$ and $x=2$ as vertical asymptotes.
Correctly rules out a removable discontinuity and obtains horizontal asymptote $y=2$ from leading behavior.

commonErrors.description: Factors $2x^2-5x-3$ or $x^2-x-2$ incorrectly.
commonErrors.consequence: The discontinuity classification is based on the wrong function.

commonErrors.description: Calls an uncancelled denominator zero a removable discontinuity.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonzero numerator at that point gives unbounded behavior instead.

hintTree.content: Name the mathematical object that changes or is sought, and record the domain before doing algebra or calculus.
A zero of a denominator that remains after simplification can produce a vertical asymptote when the one-sided function values are unbounded.
Carry out the central transformation symbolically, then check it against the original conditions and requested units or interpretation.

CALC1:010118.canonicalSolution:
Factor both polynomials:
\[g(x)=\frac{(2x+1)(x-3)}{(x-2)(x+1)}.\]
No factor cancels, so the domain excludes $x=-1$ and $x=2$. At $x=-1$, the numerator is $(-1)(-4)=4\ne0$ while the denominator changes sign through zero, so the one-sided values are unbounded; $x=-1$ is a vertical asymptote. At $x=2$, the numerator is $(5)(-1)=-5\ne0$ and again the denominator changes sign through zero, so $x=2$ is a vertical asymptote. Since neither denominator factor cancels, there is no removable discontinuity and hence no missing finite $y$-value. The numerator and denominator have equal degree, so dividing leading terms gives $\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}g(x)=2$; thus the horizontal asymptote is $\boxed{y=2}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The factors are $(2x+1)(x-3)/[(x-2)(x+1)]$; -1 and 2 are vertical asymptotes, there is no hole, and the horizontal asymptote is y=2.
I factor $2x^2-5x-3$ as $(2x-3)(x+1)$ and therefore report a numerator zero at $x=-1$.
Because the denominator is zero at $x=-1$, that point is automatically a removable discontinuity even though the numerator is nonzero there.

CALC1:010119.title: Choose a parameter that joins two formulas continuously
CALC1:010119.objective: Compute the two one-sided limits of a parameterized piecewise function, enforce their equality with the actual function value, and distinguish continuity from merely having finite one-sided limits.
CALC1:010119.statement:
For a real parameter $a$, define
\[
f_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
ax+1, & x<2,\\
x^2-a, & x\ge 2.
\end{cases}
\]
Find the unique value of $a$ for which $f_a$ is continuous at $x=2$. Compute $f_a(2)$ for that value and explicitly identify the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value used in the continuity test.
permittedResults: For a piecewise function, the left branch determines the left-hand limit and the right branch determines both the right-hand limit and the value when its condition includes the joining point.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate each branch limit separately and solve the resulting linear matching equation.
Use a continuity table with columns for the left limit, right limit, and defined value, then require all three entries to match.

milestones.criterion: Computes the left-hand limit from the $x<2$ branch and the right-hand limit and function value from the $x\ge2$ branch.
Imposes the full continuity equality and solves it to obtain $a=1$.
Reports the common value $3$ and explains why finite but unequal one-sided limits would not be continuity.

commonErrors.description: Uses the $x\ge2$ formula to compute the left-hand limit or the $x<2$ formula to compute $f_a(2)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The continuity equation is built from the wrong branch data.

commonErrors.description: Claims that finite one-sided limits establish continuity without requiring them to agree with each other and with $f_a(2)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining condition for continuity is not applied.

hintTree.content: Approach $2$ separately from the left and the right before substituting the branch that contains equality.
Continuity requires $\lim_{x\to2^-}f_a(x)=f_a(2)=\lim_{x\to2^+}f_a(x)$.
Set $2a+1$ equal to $4-a$, solve for $a$, and then evaluate the branch containing $x=2$.

CALC1:010119.canonicalSolution:
The branch for $x<2$ gives
\[
\lim_{x\to2^-}f_a(x)=2a+1.
\]
The branch for $x\ge2$ is continuous as a polynomial and contains the joining point, so
\[
\lim_{x\to2^+}f_a(x)=4-a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f_a(2)=4-a.
\]
Continuity requires $2a+1=4-a$, hence $3a=3$ and
\[
\boxed{a=1}.
\]
For this value, both one-sided limits and the function value equal
\[
2(1)+1=4-1=\boxed{3}.
\]
Finite one-sided limits alone would not suffice: they must agree with each other and with the value at the joining point.

graderFixtures.proofText: The left limit is $2a+1$, while the right limit and $f_a(2)$ are $4-a$. Equating them gives $a=1$ and common value $3$.
Because the second branch includes $x=2$, I use $4-a$ for the left-hand limit as well as the right-hand limit and conclude every $a$ works.
Both branch formulas have finite limits at $2$, so the function is continuous there for every $a$ even when the two limits differ.

CALC1:010120.title: Control an oscillating factor with the Squeeze Theorem
CALC1:010120.objective: Prove a limit for an oscillatory product by an absolute-value bound and use the result to decide continuity of a piecewise extension.
CALC1:010120.statement:
Define
\[
q(x)=
\begin{cases}
x^2\sin(3/x), & x\ne0,\\
0, & x=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Prove that $\lim_{x\to0}q(x)=0$ using an explicit inequality and the Squeeze Theorem. Then decide whether $q$ is continuous at $0$. Explain why the failure of $\sin(3/x)$ to have a limit does not prevent the product from having one.
permittedResults: For every real $u$, $|\sin u|\le1$.
If $|f(x)|\le g(x)$ and $g(x)\to0$, then $f(x)\to0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Work with absolute values and invoke the zero-bound form of the Squeeze Theorem.
Write the two-sided inequality $-x^2\le q(x)\le x^2$ and squeeze directly.

milestones.criterion: Uses $|\sin(3/x)|\le1$ to derive $|q(x)|\le x^2$ for $x\ne0$.
Applies the Squeeze Theorem to prove the limit is zero.
Concludes continuity from $q(0)=0$ and explains how the shrinking factor controls oscillation.

commonErrors.description: Treats $\sin(3/x)$ as unbounded merely because its input $3/x$ is unbounded.
commonErrors.consequence: The controlling inequality is false.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that the product has no limit solely because the sine factor has no limit, despite the factor $x^2$ shrinking to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The Squeeze Theorem evidence is ignored.

hintTree.content: Do not try to assign a limit to the sine factor by itself; bound its absolute value.
Multiply $|\sin(3/x)|\le1$ by the nonnegative quantity $x^2$.
Compare $|q(x)|$ with $x^2$, then compare the resulting limit with the defined value $q(0)$.

CALC1:010120.canonicalSolution:
For $x\ne0$, the boundedness of sine gives
\[
|q(x)|=x^2|\sin(3/x)|\le x^2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
-x^2\le x^2\sin(3/x)\le x^2.
\]
Both outer functions tend to $0$ as $x\to0$, so the Squeeze Theorem yields
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}q(x)=0}.
\]
Because $q(0)=0$, the limit equals the function value; therefore $q$ is continuous at $0$.

The input $3/x$ becomes unbounded and $\sin(3/x)$ oscillates without approaching one number, but the sine values remain between $-1$ and $1$. Multiplication by $x^2\to0$ forces the entire product into an interval whose width tends to zero.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since $|x^2\sin(3/x)|\le x^2\to0$, the product tends to $0$. This equals $q(0)$, so $q$ is continuous at zero.
Because $3/x$ is unbounded near zero, $\sin(3/x)$ is unbounded, so no finite squeeze can be used.
The factor $\sin(3/x)$ has no limit, so the product $x^2\sin(3/x)$ automatically has no limit as well.

CALC1:010121.title: Bracket a root and separate existence from uniqueness
CALC1:010121.objective: Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem with an explicit continuity audit, refine a sign-change interval numerically, and use a separate algebraic argument to establish uniqueness.
CALC1:010121.statement: Let $p(x)=x^3+x-1$. Prove that $p$ has a zero in $(0,1)$, then sharpen the location to the interval $(0.68,0.69)$. State every hypothesis used in the Intermediate Value Theorem. Finally, determine whether the zero is unique by an argument that does not incorrectly attribute uniqueness to the theorem.
permittedResults: Every polynomial is continuous on the real line.
For $y>x$, strict positivity of $p(y)-p(x)$ proves that $p$ is strictly increasing.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use IVT twice for the two brackets, then compare values of the polynomial at two arbitrary ordered inputs.
Use continuity and signs for existence, then prove injectivity by factoring the difference of two function values.

milestones.criterion: Verifies continuity and the endpoint sign change needed for a zero in the original interval.
Computes both decimal endpoint values accurately and applies IVT on the refined interval.
Distinguishes existence from uniqueness and proves strict increase through a valid positive-factor argument.

commonErrors.description: Infers a root from opposite endpoint signs without verifying continuity on the closed interval.
commonErrors.consequence: The theorem is invoked without a required hypothesis.

commonErrors.description: Claims the Intermediate Value Theorem itself guarantees exactly one root from a sign change.
commonErrors.consequence: Existence is incorrectly strengthened to uniqueness.

hintTree.content: Evaluate the polynomial at both endpoints before invoking a continuity theorem.
Compute the signs at 0.68 and 0.69 without rounding them to the same displayed value.
For uniqueness, factor $p(y)-p(x)$ when $y>x$ and show the remaining factor is positive.

CALC1:010121.canonicalSolution:
Because $p$ is a polynomial, it is continuous on every closed interval. At the first pair of endpoints,
\[
p(0)=-1<0,
\qquad
p(1)=1>0.
\]
Thus $0$ lies between $p(0)$ and $p(1)$, so the Intermediate Value Theorem gives at least one $c\in(0,1)$ with $p(c)=0$.

For the sharper bracket, direct evaluation gives
\[
p(0.68)=0.68^3+0.68-1=-0.005568<0
\]
and
\[
p(0.69)=0.69^3+0.69-1=0.018509>0.
\]
Continuity on $[0.68,0.69]$ therefore places a zero in $(0.68,0.69)$.

The Intermediate Value Theorem proves existence, not uniqueness. For a separate uniqueness argument, let $y>x$. Then
\[
p(y)-p(x)
=(y^3-x^3)+(y-x)
=(y-x)(y^2+xy+x^2+1).
\]
The first factor is positive. The second is positive because
\[
y^2+xy+x^2+1
=\left(y+\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+\frac{3x^2}{4}+1>0.
\]
Hence $p(y)>p(x)$ whenever $y>x$, so $p$ is strictly increasing and can have at most one zero. Combined with existence, the bracketed zero is unique.

graderFixtures.proofText: The polynomial is continuous, its values change sign on both stated intervals, and IVT gives existence. Separately, the factored difference is positive for ordered inputs, so the root is unique.
The endpoint values have opposite signs, and that alone guarantees a root even if the function is not continuous between the endpoints.
Since the Intermediate Value Theorem finds a zero between 0.68 and 0.69, the theorem also guarantees that there cannot be any other zero.

CALC1:010122.title: Build an epsilon-delta proof with a controlled factor
CALC1:010122.objective: Construct a delta that depends only on epsilon, bound the non-small factor in a difference of squares, and verify the limit definition with strict inequalities.
CALC1:010122.statement:
Prove directly from the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition that
\[
\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4.
\]
Your proof must give an explicit formula for $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$, explain why $|x+2|$ has a fixed numerical bound, and explain why choosing $\delta=\varepsilon/|x+2|$ would not be a valid advance choice.
permittedResults: The identity $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$ isolates the factor that tends to zero from the factor that must first be bounded.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a unit neighborhood to control the growing factor, then allocate epsilon to the remaining distance factor.
Work backward from the factored error, replace its variable coefficient by a local constant, and formalize the resulting minimum choice.

milestones.criterion: Factors the error and introduces a valid fixed bound for the non-small factor.
Chooses $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/5\}$ and carries the strict inequality chain through to $\varepsilon$.
Explains the quantifier order and why a proposed delta containing the later variable x is invalid.

commonErrors.description: Defines delta using the input x whose closeness is supposed to be controlled by that delta.
commonErrors.consequence: The existential delta is placed after, rather than before, the quantified input.

commonErrors.description: Uses an unjustified bound such as $|x+2|<4$ near $x=2$ or omits the neighborhood restriction needed for a fixed bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The central error estimate is false or unsupported.

hintTree.content: Start with $|x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|$.
Impose $\delta\le1$ so that $|x-2|<1$ forces $1<x<3$.
After obtaining $|x+2|<5$, choose $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/5\}$.

CALC1:010122.canonicalSolution:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ be arbitrary and choose
\[
\delta=\min\left\{1,\frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right\}.
\]
Suppose that $0<|x-2|<\delta$. Since $\delta\le1$, we have
\[
|x-2|<1,
\]
so $1<x<3$. Consequently $3<x+2<5$, and in particular $|x+2|<5$. Factoring the target difference now gives
\[
|x^2-4|
=|x-2||x+2|
<5|x-2|
<5\delta
\le\varepsilon.
\]
This proves from the definition that $\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4$.

The proposed choice $\delta=\varepsilon/|x+2|$ is not a valid advance choice because $\delta$ in the definition must be selected from $\varepsilon$ and fixed data before the subsequently quantified value of $x$ is known. Bounding $|x+2|$ by $5$ removes that forbidden dependence. The auxiliary restriction $\delta\le1$ is what justifies the bound; using only $\varepsilon/5$ would leave that justification unavailable for large $\varepsilon$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/5\}$. Then $|x-2|<\delta$ makes $|x+2|<5$, so $|x^2-4|<5\delta\le\varepsilon$.
I choose $\delta=\varepsilon/|x+2|$; then $|x-2|<\delta$ immediately gives the result, even though this delta changes with the later input $x$.
Because $x$ is near $2$, I use $|x+2|<4$ and take $\delta=\varepsilon/4$, without imposing any separate neighborhood bound.

CALC1:010123.title: Intersect logarithmic and radical restrictions before taking limits
CALC1:010123.objective: Determine the exact real domain of a composite quotient, justify continuity only on that domain, and evaluate the meaningful one-sided limits at both excluded endpoints.
CALC1:010123.statement:
Define
\[
g(x)=\frac{\ln(4-x^2)}{\sqrt{x-1}}.
\]
Find the exact real domain of $g$ and the maximal interval or intervals on which it is continuous. Then evaluate
\[
\lim_{x\to1^+}g(x)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lim_{x\to2^-}g(x).
\]
Explain why these are one-sided limits and why neither endpoint belongs to the domain.

A quotient of continuous functions is continuous wherever both functions are defined and its denominator is nonzero.

commonErrors.description: Treats the logarithm of an argument approaching zero from above as approaching zero rather than negative infinity.

hintTree.content: Solve $4-x^2>0$ and $x-1>0$ separately, then intersect the resulting sets.

As $x\to2^-$, the logarithm's argument approaches $0^+$ while the square-root denominator approaches $1$.

The logarithm requires
\[
4-x^2>0,
\]
which is equivalent to $-2<x<2$. Because the square root occurs in the denominator, we need
\[
x-1>0,
\]
not merely $x-1\ge0$. Intersecting the restrictions gives
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{dom}(g)=(1,2)}.
\]
The numerator and denominator are continuous there and the denominator is positive, so $g$ is continuous on the single interval $(1,2)$.

At the left endpoint,
\[
\ln(4-x^2)\longrightarrow\ln3>0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sqrt{x-1}\longrightarrow0^+.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to1^+}g(x)=+\infty}.
\]
At the right endpoint, $4-x^2\to0^+$, so $\ln(4-x^2)\to-\infty$, while $\sqrt{x-1}\to1$. Hence
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to2^-}g(x)=-\infty}.
\]
Only the indicated sides contain domain points near the endpoints. The point $1$ is excluded by a zero denominator, and $2$ is excluded because $\ln0$ is undefined.

As $x\to2^-$, the logarithm's argument tends to zero, so I replace the numerator by $0$ and conclude that the limit is $0$.

CALC1:010124.title: Expose every scale factor in a cosine limit
CALC1:010124.objective: Transform a cosine difference with a half-angle identity, apply the standard sine limit in radians, and track the inner-variable scaling without direct substitution into an indeterminate form.
CALC1:010124.statement:
Evaluate
\[
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos(5x)}{x^2}
\]
using the identity $1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ and the standard limit $\lim_{u\to0}\sin u/u=1$. Display the substitution and every numerical scale factor. State why angle measure in radians matters.
permittedResults: The half-angle identity $1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ converts the numerator into a square of a standard-limit form.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the half-angle identity and reduce directly to the standard sine limit.
First derive the general formula $\lim_{x\to0}(1-\cos(ax))/x^2=a^2/2$, then substitute $a=5$.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the numerator correctly and rewrites the quotient as a squared sine ratio.
Introduces the scaled variable and preserves every factor through the standard limit.
Reports the exact result and explains the indeterminate-form and radian-measure conditions.

commonErrors.description: Applies the standard sine limit without converting the denominator x to the inner variable $5x/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor $(5/2)^2$ is lost and the numerical limit is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Treats the direct-substitution expression $0/0$ as either zero or a defined quotient.
commonErrors.consequence: No valid limit argument is supplied.

Rewrite $\sin(5x/2)/x$ as $(5/2)[\sin u/u]$.
Square the full scaled ratio before multiplying by the leading factor two.

For $x\ne0$, the half-angle identity gives
\[
\frac{1-\cos(5x)}{x^2}
=2\left(\frac{\sin(5x/2)}{x}\right)^2.
\]
Let $u=5x/2$. Then $u\to0$ with $x\to0$, and
\[
\frac{\sin(5x/2)}{x}
=\frac52\frac{\sin u}{u}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos(5x)}{x^2}
&=2\left(\frac52\right)^2
\left(\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}\right)^2\\
&=2\cdot\frac{25}{4}\cdot1
=\boxed{\frac{25}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct substitution produces $0/0$, which is an indeterminate form rather than a value. The standard sine limit equals one specifically in radian measure; a degree-based input would introduce a conversion factor and would not justify this computation as written.

graderFixtures.proofText: Using $u=5x/2$, the quotient is $2[(5/2)(\sin u/u)]^2$, so its limit is $2(25/4)=25/2$ in radians.
I replace $\sin(5x/2)/(5x/2)$ by $1$ but ignore the conversion from $x$ to $5x/2$, obtaining the limit $2$.
Substitution gives $(1-\cos0)/0^2=0/0$, and I interpret that quotient as $0$, so the limit is $0$.

CALC1:010125.title: Keep the absolute-value sign when rationalizing at negative infinity
CALC1:010125.objective: Evaluate a radical limit at negative infinity by conjugate rationalization, justify the relevant domain tail, and account explicitly for the sign hidden in the square root of a square.
CALC1:010125.statement:
Evaluate
\[
\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^2+6x}+x\right).
\]
First identify a left-hand tail on which the expression is real. Then rationalize and show how the fact that $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|=-x$ for negative $x$ affects the calculation. A numerical approximation alone is not sufficient.
permittedResults: Multiplying by the conjugate converts $\sqrt{x^2+6x}+x$ into a quotient with numerator $6x$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rationalize first, then factor the dominant absolute value from the remaining radical.
Set $t=-x$ so that $t\to\infty$, rewrite the expression in $t$, and rationalize there.

milestones.criterion: Identifies that the expression is real for all sufficiently negative inputs and rationalizes correctly.
Factors the radical using absolute value and preserves the negative-tail sign through cancellation.
Takes the resulting continuous limit and reports negative three with an explicit sign explanation.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the principal square root of x squared by x on a negative tail.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign of the limiting value is reversed or the cancellation is invalid.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts or combines the two unbounded terms informally without resolving the infinity-minus-infinity form.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed finite value has no valid limiting derivation.

hintTree.content: Factor the radicand as $x(x+6)$ to see that all $x\le-6$ lie in the real domain.
Multiply and divide by $\sqrt{x^2+6x}-x$.
On the negative tail, write $\sqrt{x^2+6x}=(-x)\sqrt{1+6/x}$ before cancelling.

CALC1:010125.canonicalSolution:
The radicand satisfies
\[
x^2+6x=x(x+6)\ge0
\]
when $x\le-6$ or $x\ge0$. Thus the expression is real on an entire tail approaching $-\infty$.

For $x\le-6$, rationalization gives
\[
\sqrt{x^2+6x}+x
=\frac{(x^2+6x)-x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+6x}-x}
=\frac{6x}{\sqrt{x^2+6x}-x}.
\]
Because $x<0$ on this tail, $|x|=-x$, so
\[
\sqrt{x^2+6x}=|x|\sqrt{1+\frac6x}
=(-x)\sqrt{1+\frac6x}.
\]
Substituting this form and factoring $-x$ from the denominator yields
\[
\frac{6x}{(-x)\sqrt{1+6/x}-x}
=\frac{6x}{(-x)(\sqrt{1+6/x}+1)}
=\frac{-6}{\sqrt{1+6/x}+1}.
\]
Now $6/x\to0$, and the square-root function is continuous at $1$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to-\infty}(\sqrt{x^2+6x}+x)=-3}.
\]
The negative sign is essential: replacing $\sqrt{x^2}$ by $x$ would be invalid along this negative tail.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $x<0$, $\sqrt{x^2+6x}=(-x)\sqrt{1+6/x}$. Rationalization therefore gives $-6/(\sqrt{1+6/x}+1)\to-3$.
I use $\sqrt{x^2}=x$ as $x\to-\infty$, divide by $x$, and obtain $6/(1+1)=3$.
The radical and $-x$ are both infinite in magnitude, so I cancel the infinity-minus-infinity expression and state that the answer is $0$ without rationalizing.

CALC1:010126.title: Map an affine input through the principal inverse cosine
CALC1:010126.objective: Solve the exact domain restriction for an inverse-trigonometric composite, determine its range and continuity interval, and evaluate only the endpoint limits supported by nearby domain points.
CALC1:010126.statement:
Let
\[
h(x)=\arccos\!\left(\frac{x-1}{2}\right),
\]
where $\arccos$ denotes the principal inverse cosine with values in $[0,\pi]$. Find the exact real domain and range of $h$, state where it is continuous, and evaluate
\[
\lim_{x\to-1^+}h(x),\qquad \lim_{x\to3^-}h(x).
\]
Explain why the opposite one-sided limits are not real-domain limits of this function.
permittedResults: A composition of continuous functions is continuous at every input where the inner output belongs to the outer function's domain.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the inverse-cosine domain as an outer-function constraint, then map interval endpoints.
Make an input-output table at the two endpoints and use monotonicity to infer the full range.

milestones.criterion: Solves the full inverse-cosine input inequality and obtains the exact closed domain.
Uses monotonic endpoint mapping to obtain the exact range and continuity statement.
Evaluates both supported one-sided limits and rejects the opposite approaches for the correct domain reason.

commonErrors.description: Allows the affine input of inverse cosine to exceed the interval from negative one to one.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated domain includes real inputs for which the composite is undefined.

commonErrors.description: Claims a real one-sided endpoint limit from a side containing no points of the function's domain.
commonErrors.consequence: The limiting approach is not defined relative to the real domain.

hintTree.content: Solve the compound inequality $-1\le(x-1)/2\le1$.
Track what the increasing affine inner function does at the two domain endpoints.
Use $\arccos(-1)=\pi$ and $\arccos(1)=0$, and inspect which side of each endpoint contains domain points.

CALC1:010126.canonicalSolution:
The inverse cosine requires its input to lie in $[-1,1]$. Thus
\[
-1\le\frac{x-1}{2}\le1.
\]
Multiplying by $2$ and adding $1$ gives
\[
-1\le x\le3,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{dom}(h)=[-1,3]}.
\]
The affine input $(x-1)/2$ increases from $-1$ to $1$ as $x$ increases from $-1$ to $3$. Since principal $\arccos$ decreases continuously from $\pi$ to $0$, the composite is continuous on its whole closed domain and has
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{range}(h)=[0,\pi]}.
\]
Continuity from within the domain gives
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to-1^+}h(x)=\arccos(-1)=\pi},
\qquad
\boxed{\lim_{x\to3^-}h(x)=\arccos(1)=0}.
\]
There are no domain points immediately to the left of $-1$ or to the right of $3$. Consequently $x\to-1^-$ and $x\to3^+$ are not real-domain one-sided approaches for this $h$; inserting out-of-range inner values into $\arccos$ would leave the real setting.

graderFixtures.proofText: The condition $-1\le(x-1)/2\le1$ gives domain $[-1,3]$. The range is $[0,\pi]$, with limits $\pi$ at $-1^+$ and $0$ at $3^-$.
Because $\arccos$ is a familiar trigonometric operation, I allow every real $x$ and declare the domain to be $(-\infty,\infty)$ even when $(x-1)/2>1$.
I report $\lim_{x\to3^+}h(x)=0$ by direct substitution, although every sufficiently close $x>3$ makes the real inverse-cosine input greater than $1$.

CALC1:010127.title: Control a reciprocal denominator before choosing delta
CALC1:010127.objective: Construct a complete epsilon-delta proof for a reciprocal limit by imposing a preliminary neighborhood bound, deriving a usable error estimate, and choosing a delta that satisfies both constraints.
CALC1:010127.statement:
Prove directly from the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition that
\[
\lim_{x\to2}\frac1x=\frac12.
\]
Your proof must work for every $\varepsilon>0$, explicitly keep $x$ away from zero, give a concrete formula for $\delta$, and show the full chain from $0<|x-2|<\delta$ to $|1/x-1/2|<\varepsilon$.
permittedResults: If $|x-2|<1$, then $1<x<3$, so $|x|>1$ and the reciprocal denominator has a fixed positive lower bound.

acceptableStrategies.description: Work backward from the reciprocal error, introduce a convenient unit neighborhood, and then take the minimum of the resulting constraints.
Use the reverse triangle inequality to obtain $|x|\ge2-|x-2|$ and choose a neighborhood that makes this lower bound simple.

milestones.criterion: Rewrites the error correctly and establishes a fixed lower bound for the variable denominator.
Chooses a positive delta satisfying both neighborhood and epsilon constraints and uses each part of the minimum.
Completes the quantified implication and states the claimed limit without circular appeal to limit laws.

commonErrors.description: Bounds the reciprocal error by replacing the variable denominator with a constant without first proving a lower bound for its magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The key inequality may fail near a zero denominator and the proof is incomplete.

commonErrors.description: Chooses delta using the variable x or selects a value that does not shrink with epsilon.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed delta is not a valid function of epsilon alone and cannot prove arbitrary accuracy.

hintTree.content: First require $|x-2|<1$ so that $|x|>1$.
Under that restriction the error is less than $|x-2|/2$; combine the neighborhood and epsilon requirements with a minimum.

CALC1:010127.canonicalSolution:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ be arbitrary. The difficulty is that
\[
\left|\frac1x-\frac12\right|
=\frac{|x-2|}{2|x|}
\]
contains the variable denominator $|x|$. We first control it. If $|x-2|<1$, then
\[
1<x<3,
\]
so $|x|>1$. This gives
\[
\frac{|x-2|}{2|x|}<\frac{|x-2|}{2}.
\]
Choose
\[
\boxed{\delta=\min\{1,2\varepsilon\}}.
\]
This number is positive. Suppose
\[
0<|x-2|<\delta.
\]
Because $\delta\le1$, the denominator control above applies. Because $\delta\le2\varepsilon$, we also have $|x-2|<2\varepsilon$. Therefore
\[
\left|\frac1x-\frac12\right|
=\frac{|x-2|}{2|x|}
<\frac{|x-2|}{2}
<\frac{2\varepsilon}{2}
=\varepsilon.
\]
This verifies the definition for every $\varepsilon>0$, and hence
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to2}\frac1x=\frac12}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta=\min\{1,2\varepsilon\}$. Then $|x-2|<1$ gives $|x|>1$, so $|1/x-1/2|=|x-2|/(2|x|)<|x-2|/2<\varepsilon$.
I write $|x-2|/(2|x|)\le |x-2|/2$ immediately, but never restrict $x$ or prove that $|x|\ge1$ in the neighborhood I use.
I choose $\delta=\varepsilon|x|$, which depends on the same variable $x$ being quantified, and claim this is a single delta chosen before x is given.

CALC1:010128.objective: Reduce an exponential difference quotient to the standard exponential limit, track the inner scaling factor exactly, and explain why direct substitution identifies an indeterminate form rather than a value.
CALC1:010128.statement:
Let $L$ denote the requested limit. Using only the standard limit
\[
\lim_{u\to0}\frac{e^u-1}{u}=1,
\]
evaluate
\[
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{3x}-1}{x}.
\]
Display the change of variable and every scale factor. Also explain what direct substitution produces and why that expression is not itself the value of the limit.

Use the change of variables $u=3x$ and replace $x$ by $u/3$ throughout the quotient.

\[
\frac{e^0-1}{0}=\frac00,

\[
\frac{e^{3x}-1}{x}
=3\frac{e^{3x}-1}{3x}
=3\frac{e^u-1}{u}.
\]
The standard exponential limit now applies, so
\[
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{3x}-1}{x}
=3\lim_{u\to0}\frac{e^u-1}{u}
=3\cdot1
=\boxed{3}.

CALC1:010131.title: Track the floor function from both sides of every integer
CALC1:010131.objective: Use the defining integer intervals of the floor function to compute directional limits of the fractional-part function, distinguish its value from its left-hand behavior, and classify all points of continuity and discontinuity.
CALC1:010131.statement:
Define the fractional-part function
\[
f(x)=x-\lfloor x\rfloor,
\]
where $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. For an arbitrary integer $m$, compute $f(m)$, $\lim_{x\to m^-}f(x)$, and $\lim_{x\to m^+}f(x)$. Classify the discontinuity at $m$, then prove that $f$ is continuous at every noninteger and state the intervals on which its formula is linear.
permittedResults: A finite jump discontinuity occurs when both finite one-sided limits exist but are unequal.

acceptableStrategies.description: Translate the floor definition into separate formulas on adjacent unit intervals.
Write x equals m plus h and analyze negative and positive h separately.

milestones.criterion: Uses the correct floor value on each side of an arbitrary integer.
Computes the unequal one-sided limits and classifies the jump.
Proves local linearity and continuity at every noninteger.

commonErrors.description: Uses floor x equals m on the left side of m and therefore reports the left-hand limit as zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The floor value on the interval immediately left of the integer is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims that f of m equals the right-hand limit zero makes the function continuous without comparing the left-hand limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The unequal left-hand limit and jump are ignored.

hintTree.content: At $x=m$, $\lfloor m\rfloor=m$.
Immediately left of $m$, the floor is $m-1$; immediately right, it is $m$.
Near a noninteger $x_0$, choose a neighborhood that does not cross an integer, so the floor is constant there.

CALC1:010131.canonicalSolution:
Because $m$ is an integer,
\[
f(m)=m-\lfloor m\rfloor=m-m=\boxed0.
\]
For $x$ immediately to the right of $m$, we have $m<x<m+1$, so $\lfloor x\rfloor=m$ and
\[
f(x)=x-m\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to m^+}f(x)=0}.
\]
For $x$ immediately to the left, $m-1<x<m$, so $\lfloor x\rfloor=m-1$ and
\[
f(x)=x-(m-1)\longrightarrow1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to m^-}f(x)=1}.
\]
The finite one-sided limits are unequal, so the two-sided limit does not exist and $f$ has a jump discontinuity of size $1$ at every integer $m$.

Now let $x_0$ be noninteger. It lies in a unique interval $(j,j+1)$ for some integer $j$. A sufficiently small open neighborhood of $x_0$ stays inside that interval, where
\[
f(x)=x-j.
\]
This linear formula is continuous, so $f$ is continuous at every noninteger. In summary, $f$ is linear with formula $x-j$ on each $(j,j+1)$ and discontinuous exactly at the integers.

graderFixtures.proofText: At an integer $m$, $f(m)=0$. To the left, $\lfloor x\rfloor=m-1$ and $f(x)\to1$; to the right, $\lfloor x\rfloor=m$ and $f(x)\to0$. Hence every integer is a jump, while on $(j,j+1)$ the formula $f(x)=x-j$ is continuous.
I use $\lfloor x\rfloor=m$ for points just left of $m$, so I incorrectly obtain a left-hand limit of $0$ instead of accounting for the branch $m-1$.
Since $f(m)=0$ agrees with the right-hand limit, I call $f$ continuous at $m$ without comparing the left-hand limit, which is $1$.

CALC1:010132.title: Keep the sign that survives a radical rationalization
CALC1:010132.objective: Rationalize a radical difference over an absolute-value denominator, preserve the directional sign of x over absolute x, and use unequal one-sided limits to decide a two-sided limit.
CALC1:010132.statement:
Evaluate, or prove that it does not exist,
\[
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{|x|}.
\]
Check that the expression has real domain points on both sides of zero. Rationalize the numerator, compute the left- and right-hand limits separately, and explain why canceling $x$ against $|x|$ as though their quotient were always $1$ is invalid.
permittedResults: A two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits both exist and are equal.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rationalize first and then use the piecewise definition of absolute value.
Compute the original quotient numerically from each side to predict the sign, then prove it by conjugation.

milestones.criterion: Rationalizes the radical expression without losing the absolute value.
Computes both directional limits with their correct signs.
Applies the equality criterion for a two-sided limit and explains the failed cancellation.

commonErrors.description: Cancels x with absolute x as one on both sides of zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign change that distinguishes the one-sided limits is erased.

commonErrors.description: Reports one fourth as the two-sided limit after checking only positive x.
commonErrors.consequence: The unequal negative-side behavior is omitted.

hintTree.content: Multiply by $(\sqrt{4+x}+2)/(\sqrt{4+x}+2)$.
The result contains $x/|x|$ rather than complete cancellation.
The radical sum approaches four from either side.

CALC1:010132.canonicalSolution:
The radicand $4+x$ is positive on an open interval about zero, so both one-sided approaches use real domain points. For $x\ne0$, rationalization gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{|x|}
=\frac{(4+x)-4}{|x|(\sqrt{4+x}+2)}
=\frac{x/|x|}{\sqrt{4+x}+2}.
\]
If $x\to0^+$, then $x/|x|=1$ and the radical sum tends to $4$, so
\[
\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{|x|}=\frac14.
\]
If $x\to0^-$, then $x/|x|=-1$, while the same denominator tends to $4$. Hence
\[
\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{|x|}=-\frac14.
\]
The one-sided limits are finite but unequal. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{4+x}-2}{|x|}\text{ does not exist}}.
\]
The distinction is not caused by the square root's domain; it is caused by the sign retained in $x/|x|$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Conjugation gives $(x/|x|)/(\sqrt{4+x}+2)$. The right-hand limit is $1/4$ and the left-hand limit is $-1/4$, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
After rationalizing I cancel $x/|x|$ to $1$ for every nonzero $x$, including negative $x$, and conclude that the limit is $1/4$.
I approach only through $x>0$, obtain $1/4$, and report it as the two-sided limit without evaluating the left-hand limit.
