CALC1:010425.title: Partition an absolute-value integral at every sign change
CALC1:010425.objective: Factor a polynomial to locate sign changes, convert an absolute-value definite integral into correctly signed pieces, and evaluate the exact nonnegative total with a transparent antiderivative audit.
CALC1:010425.statement:
Evaluate the absolute-value integral exactly:
\[
\int_{-2}^{3}|x^2-x-2|\,dx.
\]
Factor the polynomial $x^2-x-2$, make its sign pattern explicit, split the integral at every relevant zero, and show the signed antiderivative calculations. Include a brief check explaining why the final answer must be nonnegative.
permittedResults: A definite integral is additive across any finite set of partition points in its interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a sign chart first, then integrate the resulting piecewise polynomial.
Interpret the answer as total unsigned area: compute the signed integral over each lobe and take each lobe's positive magnitude.

milestones.criterion: Factors the polynomial and partitions the interval at both sign-changing roots.
Removes the absolute value with correct signs and evaluates every piece accurately.
Combines the pieces to forty-nine sixths and checks consistency with nonnegativity.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the original polynomial across the whole interval without reversing its negative middle lobe.
commonErrors.consequence: The computation gives signed net area rather than the requested integral of an absolute value.

commonErrors.description: Splits at only one zero or uses a single sign across an interval containing the other zero.
commonErrors.consequence: At least one subinterval uses the wrong formula for the absolute value.

hintTree.content: Factor $x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)$ and mark $-1$ and $2$.
The upward-opening quadratic is positive outside its two roots and negative between them.
Use $F(x)=x^3/3-x^2/2-2x$ for the polynomial, reversing the middle contribution.

CALC1:010425.canonicalSolution:
Factor the expression inside the absolute value:
\[
x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1).
\]
It is nonnegative on $[-2,-1]$ and $[2,3]$, and nonpositive on $[-1,2]$. Therefore
\[
\int_{-2}^{3}|x^2-x-2|\,dx
=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^2-x-2)\,dx
-\int_{-1}^{2}(x^2-x-2)\,dx
+\int_{2}^{3}(x^2-x-2)\,dx.
\]
An antiderivative is
\[
F(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}-2x.
\]
The needed values are
\[
F(-2)=-\frac23,\quad F(-1)=\frac76,
\quad F(2)=-\frac{10}{3},\quad F(3)=-\frac32.
\]
Thus the three nonnegative contributions are
\[
F(-1)-F(-2)=\frac{11}{6},
\]
\[
-\bigl(F(2)-F(-1)\bigr)=\frac92,
\]
and
\[
F(3)-F(2)=\frac{11}{6}.
\]
Adding them gives
\[
\boxed{\int_{-2}^{3}|x^2-x-2|\,dx
=\frac{11}{6}+\frac{27}{6}+\frac{11}{6}
=\frac{49}{6}}.
\]
The value is positive, as required because the integrand is nonnegative and is positive except at two isolated points.

graderFixtures.proofText: The roots are $-1$ and $2$, with the quadratic negative between them. Splitting into three pieces and reversing the middle one gives $11/6+9/2+11/6=49/6$.
I ignore the absolute value and compute only $F(3)-F(-2)=-5/6$, treating cancellation of positive and negative lobes as the requested answer.
I notice the root $x=2$ but miss $x=-1$, so I keep the same sign on all of $[-2,2]$ even though the polynomial changes sign inside that interval.

CALC1:010426.title: Divide before integrating a rational function
CALC1:010426.objective: Rewrite an improper-looking rational expression by exact polynomial division, integrate the polynomial and reciprocal pieces, and verify the logarithmic definite evaluation without losing the remainder.
CALC1:010426.statement:
Evaluate the rational-function integral exactly:
\[
\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{x+1}\,dx.
\]
Use polynomial division to rewrite the integrand $x^2/(x+1)$, display an antiderivative, evaluate the bounds, and differentiate your antiderivative as a check. Explain why no improper-integral issue occurs on the stated interval.
permittedResults: On an interval where $x+1>0$, an antiderivative of $1/(x+1)$ is $\ln(x+1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use long division before applying basic antiderivative rules.
Substitute $u=x+1$, expand $(u-1)^2/u$, and integrate the equivalent expression in $u$.

milestones.criterion: Performs exact polynomial division and retains the reciprocal remainder term.
Integrates each term and evaluates both bounds to obtain the correct exact value.
Differentiates the antiderivative to verify it and explains why the definite integral is proper.

commonErrors.description: Writes the quotient as x minus one but discards the nonzero remainder term.
commonErrors.consequence: The logarithmic contribution disappears and the definite value is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Evaluates the logarithmic term with the original x rather than x plus one at a bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculation introduces an undefined logarithm or an incorrect endpoint contribution.

hintTree.content: Integrate $x-1+1/(x+1)$ term by term.
At the bounds, use $\ln1=0$ and keep the polynomial contribution $1/2-1$.

CALC1:010426.canonicalSolution:
Polynomial division is exact because
\[
x^2=(x+1)(x-1)+1.
\]
Hence, for $x\ne-1$,
\[
\frac{x^2}{x+1}=x-1+\frac1{x+1}.
\]
The denominator is positive throughout $[0,1]$, so the original integrand is continuous there and the integral is proper. An antiderivative on this interval is
\[
A(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}-x+\ln(x+1).
\]
Indeed,
\[
A'(x)=x-1+\frac1{x+1}
=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)+1}{x+1}
=\frac{x^2}{x+1},
\]
which verifies the division and integration.

Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{x+1}\,dx
&=A(1)-A(0)\\
&=\left(\frac12-1+\ln2\right)
-\left(0-0+\ln1\right)\\
&=\boxed{\ln2-\frac12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is positive, consistent with the positive integrand; numerically it is about $0.1931$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since $x^2/(x+1)=x-1+1/(x+1)$, an antiderivative is $x^2/2-x+\ln(x+1)$. Evaluating from zero to one gives $\ln2-1/2$.
I divide $x^2$ by $x+1$, keep only the quotient $x-1$, throw away the remainder $1$, and conclude that the integral equals $-1/2$.
Using $\ln x$ for the reciprocal term, I evaluate at the lower bound as $\ln0$ and call the original proper integral divergent.

CALC1:010427.title: Differentiate an accumulation with two moving bounds
CALC1:010427.objective: Apply the Fundamental Theorem and chain rule to both endpoints of an integral, find and classify all critical points, and distinguish local from global extrema using an exact closed form.
CALC1:010427.statement:
Define
\[
F(x)=\int_x^{x^2}t\,dt
\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).
\]
Differentiate $F$ using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with both bounds treated as functions of $x$. Find and classify every critical point, and identify any global extrema on $\mathbb R$. Verify the classification by also evaluating the integral explicitly.
permittedResults: The signed integral automatically handles cases in which the upper numerical endpoint $x^2$ lies below the lower endpoint $x$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the two-endpoint FTC rule first, then use a first-derivative sign chart.
Evaluate the integral into a quartic at the outset and independently differentiate that expression as a verification route.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates both moving endpoints correctly and factors the resulting derivative.
Finds all critical points and classifies them from a valid sign chart.
Uses the explicit integral and end behavior to identify the global minima and absence of a global maximum.

commonErrors.description: Adds the lower-endpoint derivative contribution instead of subtracting it.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative and all subsequent critical points are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses the integrand value at x squared but omits the derivative two x of the upper endpoint.
commonErrors.consequence: The Fundamental Theorem is applied without the required chain rule.

hintTree.content: With $f(t)=t$, the upper contribution is $(x^2)(2x)$ and the lower contribution is $x(1)$.
Factor $F'(x)=x(2x^2-1)$ and make a sign chart around $-1/\sqrt2$, $0$, and $1/\sqrt2$.
Direct integration gives $F(x)=(x^4-x^2)/2$, whose end behavior decides globality.

CALC1:010427.canonicalSolution:
The integrand $f(t)=t$ is continuous for all real $t$. Applying the endpoint form of the Fundamental Theorem,
\[
F'(x)=f(x^2)(2x)-f(x)(1)
=(x^2)(2x)-x
=2x^3-x
=x(2x^2-1).
\]
Thus the critical points are
\[
x=-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad x=0,
\qquad x=\frac1{\sqrt2}.
\]
The derivative signs, from left to right, are
\[
-,\quad +,\quad -,\quad +.
\]
Therefore $x=\pm1/\sqrt2$ are local minima, while $x=0$ is a local maximum.

Direct evaluation confirms the structure:
\[
F(x)=\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_x^{x^2}
=\frac{x^4-x^2}{2}.
\]
At the two minima, $x^2=1/2$, so
\[
F\left(\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
=\frac{1/4-1/2}{2}
=-\frac18.
\]
At the local maximum, $F(0)=0$. Since $F(x)\to+\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, the two local minima are also equal global minima:
\[
\boxed{F_{\min}=-\frac18
\text{ at }x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}}.
\]
There is no global maximum because $F$ is unbounded above; $x=0$ is only a local maximum.

graderFixtures.proofText: FTC gives $F'=(x^2)(2x)-x=x(2x^2-1)$. Its sign chart makes $\pm1/\sqrt2$ global minima with value $-1/8$, while $0$ is only a local maximum and there is no global maximum.
I use $F'(x)=(x^2)(2x)+x$, adding the lower contribution instead of subtracting it, and obtain the wrong critical equation.
I write $F'(x)=x^2-x$, evaluating at the upper bound but omitting the chain factor $d(x^2)/dx=2x$.

CALC1:010428.title: Recover a continuous function from an integral equation
CALC1:010428.objective: Differentiate an integral equation where the unknown appears both inside and outside an accumulation, solve on the punctured real line, use continuity and initial data to join constants, and verify the result in the original equation.
CALC1:010428.statement:
Suppose $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable for $x\ne0$, satisfies $f(0)=3$, and obeys
\[
\int_0^x f(t)\,dt=x f(x)-x^2

for every real $x$. Determine $f(x)$ for all real $x$. Differentiate where justified, explain why division by $x$ must exclude zero, use continuity to join the two sides, and verify your answer in the original equation.

Because $f$ is continuous, the Fundamental Theorem gives
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x f(t)\,dt=f(x).
\]
For $x\ne0$, differentiate the right-hand side using the product rule:
\[
f(x)=f(x)+xf'(x)-2x.
\]
Canceling $f(x)$ gives
\[
x(f'(x)-2)=0.
\]
Only for $x\ne0$ may we divide by $x$, obtaining
\[
f'(x)=2.
\]
Therefore there are initially two possible integration constants:
\[
f(x)=2x+C_-\quad(x<0),
\qquad
f(x)=2x+C_+\quad(x>0).
\]
Continuity at zero and $f(0)=3$ force
\[
C_-=\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=3,
\qquad
C_+=\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=3.
\]
Together with the value at zero,
\[
\boxed{f(x)=2x+3\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R}.
\]
Finally, verify in the original equation:
\[
\int_0^x(2t+3)\,dt=x^2+3x,
\]
while
\[
x(2x+3)-x^2=x^2+3x.
\]
Both sides agree for every real $x$, including zero.

CALC1:010429.title: See what fails when the FTC integrand jumps
CALC1:010429.objective: Evaluate an accumulation built from a step function, identify its absolute-value cusp, and connect failed differentiability to the missing continuity hypothesis in the Fundamental Theorem.
CALC1:010429.statement:
Define
\[
q(t)=\begin{cases}-1,&t<0,\\0,&t=0,\\1,&t>0,\end{cases}
\qquad F(x)=\int_0^xq(t)\,dt.
\]
Find a closed formula for $F$ on the real line, determine its derivative away from zero, and decide whether $F'(0)$ exists. Explain why FTC does not guarantee $F'(0)=q(0)$ here.
permittedResults: FTC Part I identifies an accumulation derivative with the integrand at points where the integrand is continuous.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the signed integral piecewise.
Use geometric signed area, then differentiate the resulting absolute value.

milestones.criterion: Computes the accumulation correctly on both sides.
Identifies the cusp and all derivative behavior.
Explains why discontinuity blocks the pointwise FTC conclusion.

commonErrors.description: For negative x, forgets the sign from reversing the integration limits.
commonErrors.consequence: The accumulation is reported as x instead of negative x on the left.

commonErrors.description: Declares F-prime of zero equal to q of zero despite the jump.
commonErrors.consequence: FTC is invoked without its continuity hypothesis.

hintTree.content: Compute positive and negative inputs separately.
For $x<0$, account for reversed limits; the answer is $|x|$.
Compare the two one-sided difference quotients at zero.

CALC1:010429.canonicalSolution:
For $x>0$, $q(t)=1$ except at one irrelevant point, so
\[
F(x)=\int_0^x1\,dt=x.
\]
For $x<0$,
\[
F(x)=-\int_x^0(-1)\,dt=-x.
\]
Also $F(0)=0$, hence
\[
\boxed{F(x)=|x|}.
\]
Consequently $F'(x)=-1$ for $x<0$ and $F'(x)=1$ for $x>0$. At zero,
\[
\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{F(h)-F(0)}h=1,
\qquad
\lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{F(h)-F(0)}h=-1.
\]
The one-sided derivatives disagree, so $\boxed{F'(0)\text{ does not exist}}$. The assigned value $q(0)=0$ does not remove the jump. Since q is discontinuous at zero, the pointwise continuity hypothesis for the FTC derivative conclusion fails there.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $x>0$, $F=x$; for $x<0$, reversing limits gives $F=-x$. Thus $F=|x|$, whose one-sided derivatives at zero are $1$ and $-1$; q is discontinuous there.
For $x<0$ I forget the reversed orientation and state $F(x)=x$ on both sides.
Since $q(0)=0$, I quote FTC to claim $F'(0)=0$ without checking the discontinuity.

CALC1:010430.objective: Evaluate an exponential-trigonometric definite integral by integrating by parts twice, retain all frequency and boundary factors, solve the recurring-integral equation, and verify the exact result by differentiation.
CALC1:010430.statement:
Let
\[
I=\int_0^{\pi/3}e^{2x}\cos(3x)\,dx.
\]
Evaluate $I$ without quoting a memorized exponential-trigonometric antiderivative. Integrate by parts twice until $I$ reappears, show both definite boundary terms, and solve the resulting linear equation. Then construct an antiderivative and differentiate it to verify the answer.

Use two integrations by parts on an indefinite integral, solve for the antiderivative, then apply the definite endpoints.

commonErrors.consequence: The linear equation has five ninths instead of thirteen ninths and yields a wrong value.

hintTree.content: Introduce $J=\int_0^{\pi/3}e^{2x}\sin(3x)\,dx$ after the first integration by parts.

Substitute the equation for $J$ into $I=-(2/3)J$ and collect every $I$ term on one side.

CALC1:010430.canonicalSolution:
Set
\[
J=\int_0^{\pi/3}e^{2x}\sin(3x)\,dx.
\]
In $I$, integrate the cosine factor. Since $d(e^{2x})=2e^{2x}\,dx$,
\[
I=\left[\frac{e^{2x}\sin(3x)}3\right]_0^{\pi/3}
-\frac23J=-\frac23J,
\]
because the sine boundary term is zero at both endpoints. Next integrate the sine factor in $J$:
\[
J=\left[-\frac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}3\right]_0^{\pi/3}
+\frac23I
=\frac{e^{2\pi/3}+1}{3}+\frac23I.
\]
Substitution into the first equation gives
\[
I=-\frac23\left(\frac{e^{2\pi/3}+1}{3}+\frac23I\right)
=-\frac{2(e^{2\pi/3}+1)}9-\frac49I.
\]
Therefore $(13/9)I=-2(e^{2\pi/3}+1)/9$, so
\[
\boxed{I=-\frac{2(e^{2\pi/3}+1)}{13}}.
\]
For an independent check, define
\[
A(x)=\frac{e^{2x}}{13}\bigl(2\cos(3x)+3\sin(3x)\bigr).
\]
The product and chain rules give $A'(x)=e^{2x}\cos(3x)$. Also
\[
A(\pi/3)-A(0)
=-\frac{2e^{2\pi/3}}{13}-\frac2{13},
\]
which reproduces the boxed result.

CALC1:010431.title: Resolve a definite rational integral into two logarithms
CALC1:010431.objective: Factor a rational denominator, solve a nontrivial partial-fraction coefficient system, integrate with correct logarithmic bounds, and combine the exact result while respecting the integrand's domain.
CALC1:010431.statement:
Evaluate exactly
\[
\int_0^1\frac{5x+7}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx.
\]
Factor the denominator, derive the partial-fraction coefficients rather than guessing them, apply the bounds to each logarithm, and give both a sum-of-logs form and a single-log form. Briefly justify why no absolute-value sign issue arises on $[0,1]$.
permittedResults: On an interval where $x+c>0$, $\int dx/(x+c)=\ln(x+c)+C$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match coefficients after clearing denominators.
Find A and B by substituting x equals negative one and negative two into the cleared identity.

milestones.criterion: Factors and decomposes the rational function with correct coefficients.
Integrates each fraction and applies both bounds correctly.
Combines the logarithms and checks positivity and continuity on the interval.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the coefficients and claims the decomposition is three over x plus one plus two over x plus two.
commonErrors.consequence: That decomposition has numerator five x plus eight, not five x plus seven.

commonErrors.description: Evaluates each logarithm only at the upper endpoint and omits the lower-endpoint subtraction.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting definite integral contains an extra three log two.

hintTree.content: The equations are $A+B=5$ and $2A+B=7$.

CALC1:010431.canonicalSolution:
Factor the denominator:
\[
x^2+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2).
\]
Write
\[
\frac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+2}.
\]
Equating numerators gives
\[
5x+7=A(x+2)+B(x+1)=(A+B)x+(2A+B).
\]
Thus $A+B=5$ and $2A+B=7$, so $A=2$ and $B=3$. Since both $x+1$ and $x+2$ are positive on $[0,1]$, the integrand is continuous there and the logarithms have positive arguments. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1\frac{5x+7}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx
&=\left[2\ln(x+1)+3\ln(x+2)\right]_0^1\\
&=2\ln2+3(\ln3-\ln2)\\
&=3\ln3-\ln2
=\boxed{\ln\!\left(\frac{27}{2}\right)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The equivalent sum form is $\boxed{2\ln2+3\ln(3/2)}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Matching $5x+7=A(x+2)+B(x+1)$ gives $A=2$, $B=3$. The integral is $[2\ln(x+1)+3\ln(x+2)]_0^1=3\ln3-\ln2=\ln(27/2)$.
I swap the solved coefficients and use $3/(x+1)+2/(x+2)$, even though clearing denominators gives $5x+8$ rather than $5x+7$.
I plug in only $x=1$ and report $2\ln2+3\ln3$, omitting the lower-bound value $3\ln2$ from the antiderivative.

CALC1:010432.title: Complete the square before scaling to arctangent
CALC1:010432.objective: Convert an irreducible quadratic denominator to shifted-square form, scale it to the standard arctangent antiderivative with the correct constant factor, and exploit symmetric transformed bounds.
CALC1:010432.statement:
Evaluate exactly
\[
\int_0^2\frac{dx}{x^2-2x+5}.
\]
Complete the square, make a substitution that produces the standard integral $\int du/(1+u^2)$, track the differential and constant factor, and show how the transformed endpoint symmetry simplifies the answer.
permittedResults: The identity $x^2-2x+5=(x-1)^2+4$ places the denominator in the form $v^2+a^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Scale directly to the standard inverse-tangent integral.
Use the formula $\int dv/(v^2+a^2)=(1/a)\arctan(v/a)+C$ with $v=x-1$ and $a=2$.

milestones.criterion: Completes the square and rescales the denominator correctly.
Transforms the differential and both definite bounds with the correct factor.
Evaluates the arctangent difference and uses oddness to simplify exactly.

commonErrors.description: Writes x squared minus two x plus five as x minus one squared plus five.
commonErrors.consequence: The denominator is changed by one and the antiderivative is for the wrong function.

commonErrors.consequence: The definite integral is doubled.

The new bounds are $-1/2$ and $1/2$, and arctangent is odd.

CALC1:010432.canonicalSolution:
Completing the square gives
\[
x^2-2x+5=(x-1)^2+4.
\]
Let
\[
u=\frac{x-1}{2},\qquad dx=2\,du.
\]
Then $(x-1)^2+4=4(u^2+1)$. The original endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ become $u=-1/2$ and $u=1/2$, respectively. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^2\frac{dx}{x^2-2x+5}
&=\frac12\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{du}{1+u^2}\\
&=\frac12\left[\arctan u\right]_{-1/2}^{1/2}\\
&=\frac12\left(\arctan\frac12-\arctan\left(-\frac12\right)\right)\\
&=\boxed{\arctan\frac12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor one half comes from combining $dx=2\,du$ with the denominator factor four. The final simplification uses the oddness of arctangent.

graderFixtures.proofText: I complete the square as $(x-1)^2+5$, which expands to $x^2-2x+6$, and integrate that different denominator.

CALC1:010433.title: Derive a reduction formula for sine-power integrals
CALC1:010433.objective: Use integration by parts with endpoint control to derive a recurrence for a family of definite integrals, then apply separate even and odd base cases to compute exact examples.
CALC1:010433.statement:
For integers $n\ge0$, define
\[
I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dx.
\]
For $n\ge2$, derive the reduction formula
\[
I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}
\]
by integration by parts; do not quote it. State why the boundary term vanishes. Then use $I_0=\pi/2$ and $I_1=1$ to compute $I_5$ and $I_6$ exactly.
permittedResults: Integration by parts gives $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use sine to the n minus one as u and one remaining sine as dv.
Alternatively integrate a cosine-power analogue first and translate by the substitution x maps to pi over two minus x.

milestones.criterion: Carries out integration by parts and verifies the boundary term at both endpoints.
Rewrites cosine squared and solves the recurrence equation without dropping I n.
Uses the correct parity base cases to compute both exact integrals.

commonErrors.description: Declares the boundary contribution equal to one or keeps a nonzero endpoint term.
commonErrors.consequence: The recurrence acquires a spurious additive constant.

commonErrors.description: From I n equals n minus one times the difference I n minus two minus I n, drops the I n term on the right.
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient n in the denominator is lost.

hintTree.content: Write $I_n=\int\sin^{n-1}x\sin x\,dx$ and take $dv=\sin x\,dx$.
After integration by parts, replace $\cos^2x$ by $1-\sin^2x$.
The resulting equation contains $I_n$ on both sides; collect those terms before dividing.

CALC1:010433.canonicalSolution:
For $n\ge2$, write
\[
I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-1}x\sin x\,dx.
\]
Choose
\[
u=\sin^{n-1}x,
\quad dv=\sin x\,dx,
\quad du=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx,
\quad v=-\cos x.
\]
Integration by parts gives
\[
I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}
+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx.
\]
The boundary term is zero: at $\pi/2$ the cosine factor is zero, and at $0$ the positive power $\sin^{n-1}0$ is zero. Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$,
\[
I_n=(n-1)(I_{n-2}-I_n).
\]
Therefore $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ and
\[
\boxed{I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}}.
\]
For the odd case,
\[
I_5=\frac45I_3=\frac45\frac23I_1
=\boxed{\frac8{15}}.
\]
For the even case,
\[
I_6=\frac56I_4=\frac56\frac34I_2
=\frac56\frac34\frac12I_0
=\boxed{\frac{5\pi}{32}}.
\]
The two parity chains end at different base cases, which explains the presence of $\pi$ only in the even answer.

I evaluate the product $-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x$ as $1$ at an endpoint and carry that nonzero boundary constant into every recurrence step.
After obtaining $I_n=(n-1)(I_{n-2}-I_n)$, I erase the final $I_n$ and state $I_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ without collecting terms.

CALC1:010434.objective: Rewrite a composite-power factor to complete a substitution, transform definite bounds, apply integration by parts in the new variable, and verify the exact value with an antiderivative derivative check.
CALC1:010434.statement:
Evaluate exactly
\[
\int_0^1 x^3e^{x^2}\,dx.
\]
Use the substitution $u=x^2$, explicitly showing how $x^3\,dx$ is converted and how the bounds change. Finish the resulting integral by integration by parts. Then give an antiderivative in $x$ and differentiate it to verify the original integrand.
permittedResults: An antiderivative of $ue^u$ is $(u-1)e^u$, as direct differentiation confirms.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute x squared first and then integrate u e to u by parts.
Guess an antiderivative of the form (a x squared plus b)e to x squared, solve for coefficients by differentiation, and still audit the definite endpoints.

milestones.criterion: Completes the substitution with no leftover x and changes the bounds explicitly.
Applies integration by parts with the correct sign and evaluates the endpoints.
Provides and differentiates a valid antiderivative of the original integrand.

commonErrors.description: Sets x cubed dx equal to u du and omits the factor one half.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed integral and final value are doubled.

commonErrors.description: Uses (u plus one)e to u as an antiderivative or subtracts the endpoint values in reverse order.
commonErrors.consequence: The integration-by-parts evaluation has the wrong sign or value.

hintTree.content: Separate $x^3\,dx$ as $x^2(x\,dx)$.
The transformed interval is still from $0$ to $1$, but for reasons that should be stated.
For $\int ue^u\,du$, take the algebraic factor as the integration-by-parts $u$-choice.

CALC1:010434.canonicalSolution:
Let $u=x^2$. Then $du=2x\,dx$, and
\[
x^3\,dx=x^2(x\,dx)=u\frac{du}{2}.
\]
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=1$, $u=1$. Therefore
\[
\int_0^1x^3e^{x^2}\,dx
=\frac12\int_0^1ue^u\,du.
\]
Integration by parts, with algebraic factor $u$ and $dv=e^u\,du$, gives
\[
\int ue^u\,du=ue^u-\int e^u\,du=(u-1)e^u+C.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac12\left[(u-1)e^u\right]_0^1
=\frac12\left(0-(-1)\right)
=\boxed{\frac12}.
\]
Returning to $x$, one antiderivative is
\[
A(x)=\frac12(x^2-1)e^{x^2}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
A'(x)=\frac12\left(2xe^{x^2}+(x^2-1)2xe^{x^2}\right)
=xe^{x^2}[1+x^2-1]
=x^3e^{x^2}.
\]
This derivative check confirms both the substitution factor and the integration-by-parts sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $u=x^2$, $x^3dx=u\,du/2$ and the bounds remain $0,1$. Hence the integral is $(1/2)[(u-1)e^u]_0^1=1/2$. Also $[(x^2-1)e^{x^2}/2]'=x^3e^{x^2}$.
I write $du=2x\,dx$ but then replace $x^3\,dx$ by $u\,du$, losing the factor $1/2$, so my final integral is twice as large.
I claim $\int ue^u\,du=(u+1)e^u$ and also reverse the upper-minus-lower endpoint order, so the parts step does not differentiate back correctly.

CALC1:010435.title: Analyze an accumulation function with a reversing upper limit
CALC1:010435.objective: Differentiate an integral with a sine upper limit, use monotonicity of the underlying integral to find exact zeros and extrema, and respect the reversal of orientation.
CALC1:010435.statement:
For $0\le x\le2\pi$, define
$$
G(x)=\int_0^{\sin x}\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt.
$$
Find $G'(x)$ and every critical number. Determine all zeros of $G$, the absolute maximum and minimum values and where they occur, and the intervals on which $G$ increases and decreases. You may denote
$$
I=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt
$$
without trying to find an elementary antiderivative, but every sign and extremum claim must be justified.
permittedResults: If $H(u)=\int_0^u f(t)\,dt$ with continuous $f$, then $H'(u)=f(u)$; composition with $u=\sin x$ also requires the chain rule.

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate the accumulation map H from the sine composition, then analyze each one's monotonicity.
Use positivity to order values by the upper limit and cosine signs to verify the same extrema.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the variable-upper-limit integral with the full chain factor.
Uses the derivative sign to find all critical numbers and monotonicity intervals.
Uses positivity, oddness, and orientation to identify every zero and both global extrema.

commonErrors.description: Writes G prime as the integrand evaluated at sine x but omits multiplication by cosine x.
commonErrors.consequence: The critical numbers and monotonicity conclusions no longer follow from the derivative.

commonErrors.description: Treats the integral from zero to negative one as positive I by ignoring orientation.
commonErrors.consequence: The absolute minimum value and its sign are wrong.

hintTree.content: The integrand is strictly positive, so $H(u)=\int_0^u\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt$ is strictly increasing and odd.
The factor $\sqrt{1+\sin^4x}$ in $G'$ is never zero.
Compare the values corresponding to $\sin x=1,-1,0$.

CALC1:010435.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$
H(u)=\int_0^u\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt.
$$
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule,
$$
G'(x)=H'(\sin x)\cos x
=\boxed{\sqrt{1+\sin^4x}\cos x}.
$$
The square-root factor is strictly positive, so $G'(x)=0$ exactly when $\cos x=0$. The critical numbers in the open interval are
$$
\boxed{x=\pi/2,\ 3\pi/2}.
$$
The sign of $G'$ is the sign of $\cos x$. Thus $G$ increases on
$$
(0,\pi/2)\quad\text{and}\quad(3\pi/2,2\pi),
$$
and decreases on
$$
(\pi/2,3\pi/2).
$$

Because the integrand is positive, $H$ is strictly increasing and $H(u)=0$ only for $u=0$. Hence $G(x)=0$ exactly when $\sin x=0$:
$$
\boxed{x=0,\pi,2\pi}.
$$
The integrand is even, so $H$ is odd. With
$$
I=H(1)=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt>0,
$$
we have
$$
G(\pi/2)=H(1)=I,\qquad
G(3\pi/2)=H(-1)=-I,
$$
while all other values use $-1\le\sin x\le1$ and the increasing function $H$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\max_{[0,2\pi]}G=I\text{ at }x=\pi/2},
\qquad
\boxed{\min_{[0,2\pi]}G=-I\text{ at }x=3\pi/2}.
$$
The negative minimum is a consequence of the oriented integral when the upper limit is negative.

graderFixtures.proofText: Writing $H(u)=\int_0^u\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt$, $G'=H'(\sin x)\cos x=\sqrt{1+\sin^4x}\cos x$. Thus the critical numbers are $\pi/2,3\pi/2$; the zeros are $0,\pi,2\pi$; and since $H$ is increasing and odd, the maximum is $I$ and the minimum is $-I$.
By the FTC I write $G'(x)=\sqrt{1+\sin^4x}$, omitting the derivative $\cos x$ of the upper limit, and conclude that G has no critical numbers.
At $x=3\pi/2$ the upper limit is $-1$, but I say $G=\int_0^{-1}\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt=I>0$, reversing no sign.

CALC1:010436.title: Trap arctangent between two elementary integral bounds
CALC1:010436.objective: Derive sharp elementary bounds for arctangent from its defining integral, track strictness and signs correctly, and specialize them to a two-sided numerical interval for pi.
CALC1:010436.statement:
Using only
$$
\arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}
$$
and elementary comparisons, prove that for every $x\ge0$,
$$
\frac{x}{1+x^2}\le\arctan x\le x,
$$
with equality in either bound exactly when $x=0$. Then take $x=1/\sqrt3$, use the exact special-angle value $\arctan(1/\sqrt3)=\pi/6$, and derive explicit strict lower and upper bounds for $\pi$. State the width of the resulting interval. Explain why multiplying or dividing the inequality preserves its direction at every step.
permittedResults: For $0\le t\le x$, $1/(1+x^2)\le1/(1+t^2)\le1$; the inequalities are strict on a subinterval of positive length when $x>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Bound the integrand by its endpoint values on the positive interval, then integrate.
Interpret arctangent as area under a decreasing positive curve and use lower and upper rectangles.

milestones.criterion: Builds and integrates the correct two-sided comparison for the arctangent integrand.
Handles equality and strictness accurately for zero versus positive x.
Specializes and simplifies to the exact pi interval and its width while tracking inequality direction.

commonErrors.description: From one plus t squared at most one plus x squared, claims its reciprocal is also at most the reciprocal of one plus x squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The lower bound is reversed because all positive reciprocals reverse order.

commonErrors.description: Carries weak inequalities into the positive special-angle case and reports endpoints that pi might equal.
commonErrors.consequence: For positive x both integral comparisons are strict on sets of positive length.

hintTree.content: Integrate the constant lower and upper bounds over $0\le t\le x$.
At $x=1/\sqrt3$, simplify $x/(1+x^2)$ before inserting $\pi/6$.
All scale factors used to isolate $\pi$ are positive.

CALC1:010436.canonicalSolution:
Fix $x\ge0$. For $0\le t\le x$, we have
$$
1\le1+t^2\le1+x^2.
$$
All quantities are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the order:
$$
\frac1{1+x^2}\le\frac1{1+t^2}\le1.
$$
Integrating from $0$ to $x$ gives
$$
\frac{x}{1+x^2}
\le\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}
\le x,
$$
or
$$
\boxed{\frac{x}{1+x^2}\le\arctan x\le x}.
$$
At $x=0$, both are equalities. If $x>0$, the integrand is strictly less than $1$ for every $t>0$, and it is strictly greater than $1/(1+x^2)$ for every $0\le t<x$. Each strict set has positive length, so both integrated inequalities are strict.

Now let $x=1/\sqrt3>0$. The lower comparison becomes
$$
\frac{x}{1+x^2}
=\frac{1/\sqrt3}{1+1/3}
=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.
$$
Using $\arctan(1/\sqrt3)=\pi/6$, strictness gives
$$
\frac{\sqrt3}{4}<\frac\pi6<\frac1{\sqrt3}.
$$
Multiplying all three parts by $6>0$ preserves direction:
$$
\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}<\pi<\frac6{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}<\pi<2\sqrt3}.
$$
The interval width is
$$
2\sqrt3-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}
=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}.
$$
All divisions used positive denominators, reciprocal reversal was explicitly accounted for, and the final scaling factor was positive.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $0\le t\le x$, $1/(1+x^2)\le1/(1+t^2)\le1$, so integration gives $x/(1+x^2)\le\arctan x\le x$, strictly for $x>0$. At $x=1/\sqrt3$, $\sqrt3/4<\pi/6<1/\sqrt3$, hence $3\sqrt3/2<\pi<2\sqrt3$, with width $\sqrt3/2$.
Because $1+t^2\le1+x^2$, I keep the same direction and write $1/(1+t^2)\le1/(1+x^2)$, so my supposed lower and upper bounds are interchanged.
I obtain $\sqrt3/4\le\pi/6\le1/\sqrt3$ at the positive value $x=1/\sqrt3$ and never prove strictness, so I allow equality with both proposed endpoints.

CALC1:010437.title: Move a cusp through an integral
CALC1:010437.objective: Evaluate an absolute-value integral for every real parameter, analyze differentiability at the transition parameters, and determine its global minimum.
CALC1:010437.statement:
For every real number \(a\), define
$$
F(a)=\int_0^2 |x-a|\,dx.
$$
Find one formula for \(F(a)\) on each necessary parameter interval. Determine whether \(F\) is differentiable at \(a=0\) and \(a=2\), give a complete formula for \(F'(a)\), and identify the global minimum of \(F\) on \(\mathbb R\). Justify all parameter cases rather than assuming \(a\in[0,2]\).
permittedResults: A piecewise-defined function can be differentiable at a join even when the integrand used to define it has a cusp; the one-sided derivatives of the resulting parameter function must be compared.

acceptableStrategies.description: Locate the cusp x equals a relative to the fixed interval before removing the absolute value.
Complete the square in the middle piece and use the exterior slopes for the global conclusion.

milestones.criterion: Handles the two exterior parameter regions and the interior moving sign change correctly.
Differentiates the resulting function and explicitly checks both join parameters.
Uses the complete global formula to prove the unique minimum and its value.

commonErrors.description: Splits at \(x=a\) and uses the middle quadratic for every real \(a\), including when \(a\) lies outside \([0,2]\).
commonErrors.consequence: An integral may be split at a as an internal sign change only when a belongs to the integration interval.

commonErrors.description: Declares \(F\) nondifferentiable at \(a=0\) and \(a=2\) solely because \(|x-a|\) has a cusp.
commonErrors.consequence: Integration smooths the parameter function here; the one-sided derivative formulas agree at both joins.

hintTree.content: Separate the cases \(a\le0\), \(0\le a\le2\), and \(a\ge2\).
Only in the middle case should the integral be split at \(x=a\).
After differentiating the three formulas, compare their values at the two joins.

CALC1:010437.canonicalSolution:
If \(a\le0\), then \(x-a\ge0\) throughout \(0\le x\le2\), so
$$
F(a)=\int_0^2(x-a)\,dx=2-2a.
$$
If \(0\le a\le2\), the sign changes at \(x=a\), and
$$
\begin{aligned}
F(a)
&=\int_0^a(a-x)\,dx+\int_a^2(x-a)\,dx\\
&=\frac{a^2}{2}+\left(2-2a+\frac{a^2}{2}\right)\\
&=a^2-2a+2=(a-1)^2+1.
\end{aligned}
$$
If \(a\ge2\), then \(a-x\ge0\) throughout the interval, so
$$
F(a)=\int_0^2(a-x)\,dx=2a-2.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{
F(a)=
\begin{cases}
2-2a,&a\le0,\\
a^2-2a+2,&0\le a\le2,\\
2a-2,&a\ge2.
\end{cases}}
$$
The values agree at both joins. Differentiating within the pieces gives
$$
\boxed{
F'(a)=
\begin{cases}
-2,&a<0,\\
2a-2,&0<a<2,\\
2,&a>2.
\end{cases}}
$$
At \(a=0\), both one-sided derivative formulas give \(-2\); at \(a=2\), both give \(2\). Therefore \(F\) is differentiable at both joins, and the derivative formula extends there as \(F'(0)=-2\) and \(F'(2)=2\). In fact \(F'\) is continuous on all of \(\mathbb R\).

Outside \([0,2]\), the linear pieces increase without bound as \(a\) moves away from the interval. Inside, the completed square gives
$$
F(a)=(a-1)^2+1\ge1.
$$
Consequently the unique global minimum is
$$
\boxed{F(1)=1}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: The cusp lies left of the interval for \(a\le0\), inside for \(0\le a\le2\), and right for \(a\ge2\). Hence \(F=2-2a\), \(a^2-2a+2\), and \(2a-2\), respectively. The derivative pieces match at \(0\) and \(2\), so \(F\) is differentiable there. The middle formula is \((a-1)^2+1\), and the exterior pieces rise away, giving the unique global minimum \(F(1)=1\).
I split at \(x=a\) for every real \(a\) and report \(F(a)=a^2-2a+2\) even for \(a=5\), without checking whether the sign change lies inside \([0,2]\).
Because the absolute value integrand has a cusp when \(x=a\), I declare \(F\) nondifferentiable at \(a=0\) and \(a=2\) without comparing the one-sided derivatives, which actually agree.

CALC1:010438.title: Measure the area under an inverse without solving for it
CALC1:010438.objective: Derive the inverse-function integral identity by substitution and integration by parts, then evaluate a non-elementary inverse integral exactly.
CALC1:010438.statement:
Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on \([a,b]\) with \(f'(x)>0\) there. Prove
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}f^{-1}(y)\,dy
=b f(b)-a f(a).
$$
Then apply the identity to \(f(x)=x^3+x\) on \([0,1]\) to evaluate
$$
\int_0^2 f^{-1}(y)\,dy
$$
exactly, without finding a radical formula for \(f^{-1}\). State why all inverse-function and substitution steps are licensed.
permittedResults: If \(y=f(x)\) and \(f'(x)>0\), then \(dy=f'(x)\,dx\) carries \([a,b]\) to \([f(a),f(b)]\) without reversing orientation.
Integration by parts gives \(\int_a^b x f'(x)\,dx=[x f(x)]_a^b-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the inverse integral back to the original variable before attempting any antiderivative.
Interpret the identity as complementary areas in a rectangle, but prove it analytically with substitution and parts.

milestones.criterion: Licenses the inverse and substitution from the hypotheses and transforms the inverse integral correctly.
Uses integration by parts to derive the stated identity with all boundary terms.
Applies the identity to the cubic-plus-linear map and obtains five fourths without solving the cubic.

commonErrors.description: Writes \(y=f(x)\) but replaces \(dy\) by \(dx\), turning the inverse integral into \(\int_a^b x\,dx\).
commonErrors.consequence: The factor f prime is essential and is what makes integration by parts produce the boundary rectangle.

commonErrors.description: Attempts a cubic radical formula or uses \(0\) and \(1\) as the inverse integral's \(y\)-bounds.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity uses the image bounds f of zero equals zero and f of one equals two; explicit inversion is unnecessary.

hintTree.content: In the inverse integral, substitute \(y=f(x)\); then \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\).
The transformed inverse integral is \(\int_a^b x f'(x)\,dx\).
For the application, compute only \(f(0)\), \(f(1)\), and \(\int_0^1(x^3+x)\,dx\).

CALC1:010438.canonicalSolution:
Because \(f'(x)>0\), the function \(f\) is strictly increasing on \([a,b]\). It therefore maps that interval bijectively onto \([f(a),f(b)]\), with a continuous inverse. In the inverse integral, set \(y=f(x)\). The endpoints become \(x=a\) and \(x=b\), the orientation is preserved, and \(dy=f'(x)\,dx\). Hence
$$
\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}f^{-1}(y)\,dy
=\int_a^b f^{-1}(f(x))f'(x)\,dx
=\int_a^b x f'(x)\,dx.
$$
Integration by parts now yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}f^{-1}(y)\,dy
&=[x f(x)]_a^b-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\\
&=b f(b)-a f(a)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
$$
Rearranging proves
$$
\boxed{\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}f^{-1}(y)\,dy
=b f(b)-a f(a)}.
$$

For \(f(x)=x^3+x\) on \([0,1]\),
$$
f'(x)=3x^2+1>0,
\qquad
f(0)=0,
\qquad
f(1)=2.
$$
Thus the hypotheses hold and the requested inverse integral has the correct bounds. Also
$$
\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx
=\int_0^1(x^3+x)\,dx
=\frac14+\frac12
=\frac34.
$$
The identity gives
$$
\frac34+\int_0^2f^{-1}(y)\,dy
=1\cdot2-0\cdot0=2,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\int_0^2f^{-1}(y)\,dy=\frac54}.
$$
No explicit cubic inverse is needed.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since \(f'>0\), substitute \(y=f(x)\) in the inverse integral to get \(\int_a^b x f'(x)\,dx\). Integration by parts makes this \(b f(b)-a f(a)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), proving the identity. For \(x^3+x\) on \([0,1]\), the image is \([0,2]\) and the direct integral is \(3/4\), so the inverse integral is \(2-3/4=5/4\).
With \(y=f(x)\), I replace \(dy\) by \(dx\) and claim the inverse integral is \(\int_a^b x\,dx\), omitting the required Jacobian \(f'(x)\).
I keep \(0\) and \(1\) as the inverse integral bounds and start solving \(x^3+x=y\) by radicals, ignoring that the image endpoints are \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=2\).

CALC1:010439.title: Read monotonicity from an accumulation derivative
CALC1:010439.objective: Use the FTC to classify an accumulation function rather than differentiating an integral with moving endpoints.
CALC1:010439.statement: Let $$F(x)=\int_0^x(t^2-4t+3)\,dt.$$ Find a formula for $F$, determine where $F$ increases and decreases, and find its local extrema.
permittedResults: A sign change of $F'$ from positive to negative marks a local maximum, and the reverse marks a local minimum.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use FTC then a sign chart.
Differentiate the polynomial antiderivative as a check.

milestones.criterion: Gives the explicit accumulation polynomial.
Uses the factor sign chart correctly.
Reports both locations and function values of extrema.

commonErrors.description: Lists $1,3$ without checking derivative signs.
commonErrors.consequence: The local-extremum conclusion is unsupported.

commonErrors.description: Reports $F'(1)$ and $F'(3)$ as extremal values.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested values are values of $F$.

hintTree.content: Compute an antiderivative for the requested formula.
Factor the FTC derivative before making a sign chart.
Evaluate $F$, not $F'$, at extrema.

CALC1:010439.canonicalSolution: An antiderivative is $t^3/3-2t^2+3t$, so $$F(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+3x.$$ By the FTC, $F'(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$. Thus $F'>0$ on $( -\infty,1)$ and $(3,\infty)$, while $F'<0$ on $(1,3)$. Therefore $F$ has a local maximum at $x=1$, with $F(1)=4/3$, and a local minimum at $x=3$, with $F(3)=0$.

graderFixtures.proofText: $F=x^3/3-2x^2+3x$ and $F'=(x-1)(x-3)$. Thus it increases before $1$, decreases on $(1,3)$, then increases; $F(1)=4/3$ is a local maximum and $F(3)=0$ a local minimum.
The critical points are $1$ and $3$, so both are local maxima.
The local maximum value is $F'(1)=0$ and the local minimum value is $F'(3)=0$.

CALC1:010440.title: Locate where a function equals its average
CALC1:010440.objective: Compute an average and solve the resulting value equation rather than use symmetric cancellation.
CALC1:010440.statement: Find the average value of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,4]$. Then find the unique $c\in[0,4]$ for which $f(c)$ equals that average.
permittedResults: A continuous function attains its average value; strict monotonicity makes the location unique.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate and solve the average-value equation.
Use monotonicity to prove uniqueness.

milestones.criterion: Computes the average $4/3$.
Solves for $c=16/9$.
Justifies uniqueness and interval membership.

commonErrors.description: Reports $16/3$ as the average.
commonErrors.consequence: It is the integral, not the average.

commonErrors.description: States that a mean-value point exists but gives no $c$.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested explicit location is missing.

hintTree.content: Keep the interval length $4$ in the denominator.
Evaluate $4^{3/2}$ as $8$.
Square only after isolating the nonnegative square root.

CALC1:010440.canonicalSolution: The average value is $$\frac1{4-0}\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\,dx=\frac14\left[\frac23x^{3/2}\right]_0^4=\frac43.$$ Since $\sqrt{x}$ is strictly increasing on $[0,4]$, there can be at most one such point. Solving $\sqrt c=4/3$ gives $$\boxed{c=\frac{16}{9}}.$$ It lies in $[0,4]$, so it is the required unique point.

graderFixtures.proofText: The average is $\frac14\cdot\frac23\cdot8=4/3$. Solving $\sqrt c=4/3$ gives $c=16/9$; strict increase makes it unique.

CALC1:010441.objective: Translate a specified sampling rule into a definite integral and independently compute the limiting sum.
CALC1:010441.statement: Evaluate $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac2n\sum_{k=1}^n\left(1+\frac{2k-1}{n}\right)^2. $$ Identify the interval and sample points represented by the sum.

CALC1:010442.title: Separate a definite integral from total area
CALC1:010442.objective: Partition at zeros before converting signed accumulation into geometric area.
CALC1:010442.statement: For $$q(x)=x^2-4x+3,$$ compute both $$\int_0^4q(x)\,dx$$ and the total area between the graph and the $x$-axis on $[0,4]$.

Integrate $|q(x)|$ after writing its correct piecewise formula.

commonErrors.description: Adds $Q(3)-Q(1)$ as a positive area even though it is negative.
commonErrors.consequence: That integral is below the axis and must be negated for total area.

commonErrors.description: Factors $q$ as $(x-2)^2+1$ and concludes that it has no zeros.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign in the completed-square form is wrong: $q=(x-2)^2-1$, so the zeros are $1,3$.

CALC1:010443.title: Integrate an arctangent moment
CALC1:010443.objective: Choose integration-by-parts roles that leave a rational integral and evaluate the definite boundary term exactly.
CALC1:010443.statement: Evaluate $$\int_0^1 x\arctan x\,dx.$$ Show the integration-by-parts setup and simplify the remaining rational integral.
permittedResults: The identity $x^2/(1+x^2)=1-1/(1+x^2)$ reduces the rational remainder to elementary antiderivatives.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use integration by parts followed by rational division.
Use the substitution $x=\tan\theta$ and then integrate $\theta\tan\theta\sec^2\theta$ by parts.

milestones.criterion: Sets integration by parts with the correct differential and antiderivative.
Simplifies the rational remainder as $1-1/(1+x^2)$.
Obtains $\pi/4-1/2$.

commonErrors.description: Evaluates the boundary product at $x=1$ as $\pi/4$ rather than $\pi/8$.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor $x^2/2$ remains in the boundary term.
The recombined numerator would be $x^2+2$, not $x^2$.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $\arctan x$ and integrate $x$.
Keep the boundary evaluation attached to the product term.
Rewrite $x^2/(1+x^2)$ before integrating.

Then $du=dx/(1+x^2)$ and $v=x^2/2$, so $$\int_0^1x\arctan x\,dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\arctan x\right]_0^1-\frac12\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}\,dx.$$ Since $$\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=1-\frac1{1+x^2},$$ the remaining integral is $[x-\arctan x]_0^1=1-\pi/4$. The boundary term is $(1/2)(\pi/4)=\pi/8$. Therefore $$\frac\pi8-\frac12\left(1-\frac\pi4\right)=\boxed{\frac\pi4-\frac12}.$$

With $u=\arctan x$ and $dv=x\,dx$, I get the remainder $-(1/2)\int_0^1x^2/(1+x^2)dx$. I evaluate the boundary product as $(1)(\pi/4)=\pi/4$ and correctly compute the remaining integral as $1-\pi/4$, giving $3\pi/8-1/2$.

CALC1:010444.title: Evaluate an improper rational integral
CALC1:010444.objective: Introduce a finite cutoff, use partial fractions without splitting into divergent improper pieces, and compute the exact remaining tail.
CALC1:010444.statement: Evaluate the improper integral $$\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}.$$ Define it through a finite cutoff. Also find the exact tail $$R(B)=\int_B^\infty\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}$$ for $B\ge1$.
permittedResults: Partial fractions may be integrated at a common finite cutoff even when the separate improper integrals would diverge.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a common-cutoff partial fraction calculation.
Substitute $u=1/x$ to transform the full integral to $\int_0^1du/(1+u)$, while still deriving the requested tail.

milestones.criterion: Defines the improper integral using finite cutoffs.
Finds the value $\ln2$.
Derives $R(B)=\ln(1+1/B)$ and notes its decay.

commonErrors.description: Writes $\int_1^\infty dx/x-\int_1^\infty dx/(x+1)$ and cancels the two infinities.
commonErrors.consequence: The two divergent improper integrals are not finite quantities that may be subtracted.

commonErrors.description: Reports $R(B)=\ln[B/(B+1)]$.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed tail is negative even though the integrand is positive.

hintTree.content: Keep one common upper cutoff for both logarithms.
Compute the tail with the same cutoff before taking its limit.

CALC1:010444.canonicalSolution: For a finite cutoff $M>1$, use $$\frac1{x(x+1)}=\frac1x-\frac1{x+1}.$$ Then $$\int_1^M\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}=\left[\ln x-\ln(x+1)\right]_1^M=\ln\!\left(\frac{2M}{M+1}\right).$$ Taking $M\to\infty$ gives $$\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}=\boxed{\ln2}.$$ Similarly, for $M>B$, $$\int_B^M\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}=\ln\!\left(\frac{M(B+1)}{B(M+1)}\right),$$ so $$\boxed{R(B)=\ln\!\left(1+\frac1B\right)}.$$ This tends to zero, directly certifying convergence.

I split the full integral as $\int_1^\infty dx/x-\int_1^\infty dx/(x+1)=\infty-\infty=0$. Similarly, $R(B)=\int_B^\infty dx/x-\int_B^\infty dx/(x+1)=\infty-\infty=0$.
With a common cutoff $M$, the full integral is $\ln[2M/(M+1)]\to\ln2$. Starting at $B$, I reverse the terminal logarithm ratio and obtain $R(B)=\ln[B/(B+1)]$, which tends to zero.

CALC1:010445.title: Evaluate the classical improper log-sine integral
CALC1:010445.objective: Establish endpoint convergence before using symmetry, a product identity, and a change of variables to solve for an improper integral.
CALC1:010445.statement: Prove that the improper integral converges and evaluate $$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\,dx.$$
permittedResults: The identities $\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x$ and $\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x$ remain valid inside truncated integrals, after which limits may be taken using the established convergence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use symmetry and the sine double-angle identity.
Regularize with $I_\varepsilon=\int_\varepsilon^{\pi/2-\varepsilon}\ln(\sin x)\,dx$, perform the identities, and pass to the limit.

milestones.criterion: Justifies convergence at the logarithmic endpoint.
Uses the cosine symmetry and retains the factor $1/2$ from the double-angle identity.
Correctly relates the $[0,\pi]$ integral to $2I$ and obtains $-(\pi/2)\ln2$.

commonErrors.description: Identifies $\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin u)\,du$ with $I$ instead of $2I$.
commonErrors.consequence: The rescaled integral and resulting linear equation for $I$ have the wrong factor.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\ln(\sin x\cos x)=\ln(\sin2x)$ and omits $-\ln2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The constant term that determines the nonzero value of the integral is lost.

hintTree.content: First compare $-\ln(\sin x)$ with a constant plus $-\ln x$ near zero.
Replace $x$ by $\pi/2-x$ to obtain an equal cosine integral.
After adding, substitute $u=2x$ and use symmetry on $[0,\pi]$.

CALC1:010445.canonicalSolution: Near zero, $2x/\pi\le\sin x\le1$ on $(0,\pi/2]$. Hence $$0\le-\ln(\sin x)\le-\ln(2x/\pi),$$ and the right side is integrable at zero because $\int_0^a-\ln x\,dx$ is finite. Thus $I$ converges. Substituting $u=\pi/2-x$ shows $$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos x)\,dx.$$ Adding these forms and using $\sin x\cos x=\tfrac12\sin(2x)$ gives $$2I=-\frac\pi2\ln2+\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin2x)\,dx.$$ With $u=2x$, the remaining integral is $$\frac12\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin u)\,du=I,$$ because symmetry about $\pi/2$ makes the full integral equal to $2I$. Therefore $2I=-(\pi/2)\ln2+I$, and $$\boxed{I=-\frac\pi2\ln2}.$$

graderFixtures.proofText: Comparison with $-\ln(2x/\pi)$ proves convergence. Symmetry gives $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos x)dx$, so $2I=-(\pi/2)\ln2+(1/2)\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin u)du=-(\pi/2)\ln2+I$. Hence $I=-(\pi/2)\ln2$.

The logarithmic endpoint is integrable by comparison. Symmetry and the double-angle identity give $2I=-(\pi/2)\ln2+(1/2)\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin u)du$. I identify the full integral with $I$, so $2I=-(\pi/2)\ln2+I/2$ and obtain $I=-(\pi/3)\ln2$.
After verifying convergence, I add the sine and cosine forms but use $\ln(\sin x\cos x)=\ln(\sin2x)$. The substitution $u=2x$ and symmetry then give $2I=I$, so $I=0$.

CALC1:010519.title: Find an average value and its guaranteed witness point
CALC1:010519.objective: Compute the average value of a continuous function with the correct interval-length normalization and locate a point whose function value equals that average.
CALC1:010519.statement: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[1,4]$, find the average value $f_{\mathrm{avg}}$. Then find every $c\in[1,4]$ satisfying $f(c)=f_{\mathrm{avg}}$ and explain why the Integral Mean Value Theorem guarantees that at least one such point exists.
permittedResults: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, some $c\in[a,b]$ satisfies $f(c)=(1/(b-a))\int_a^bf(x)dx$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the average-value formula and solve the resulting level equation.
Interpret the integral as rectangle area $(b-a)f_{\mathrm{avg}}$, then locate where the continuous graph reaches that height.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the definite integral and normalizes by the correct interval length.
Obtains average value $7$ and solves $c^2=7$.
Retains only $\sqrt7$ in $[1,4]$ and verifies the theorem's continuity hypothesis.

commonErrors.description: Divides the integral by the upper endpoint instead of by the interval length $b-a$.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed average height is incorrect.

commonErrors.description: Keeps an algebraic solution that lies outside $[1,4]$ as a theorem witness.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed point does not belong to the interval in the theorem.

hintTree.content: The interval length is $4-1$, not the upper endpoint $4$.
Evaluate $\int_1^4x^2dx$ and divide by $3$.
Solve $c^2=f_{\mathrm{avg}}$ and retain only solutions in the stated interval.

CALC1:010519.canonicalSolution:
The interval length is $4-1=3$, and
\[
\int_1^4x^2\,dx=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4
=\frac{64-1}{3}=21.
\]
Thus
\[
f_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac1{3}(21)=\boxed{7}.
\]
Solving $f(c)=7$ gives $c^2=7$, hence $c=\pm\sqrt7$. Only
\[
\boxed{c=\sqrt7}
\]
lies in $[1,4]$. Since $x^2$ is continuous on the entire closed interval, the Integral Mean Value Theorem applies and guarantees a witness; the direct calculation identifies the unique one in the interval.

graderFixtures.proofText: The integral is $21$ and the interval length is $3$, so the average is $7$. Solving $c^2=7$ leaves only $c=\sqrt7$ in $[1,4]$.
I divide the integral $21$ by the upper endpoint $4$, obtaining the average value $21/4$.
The equation $c^2=7$ has two solutions, so both $c=\sqrt7$ and $c=-\sqrt7$ are witnesses in $[1,4]$.

CALC1:010520.title: Locate the center of mass of a nonuniform rod
CALC1:010520.objective: Translate a linear density into mass and first-moment integrals, retain physical units, and audit that the resulting center lies within the rod.
CALC1:010520.statement:
A thin rod occupies $0\le x\le3$ meters, where $x$ denotes the numerical meter-coordinate, and has linear density
\[
\lambda(x)=2+x\quad\text{kg/m}.
\]
Find the rod's total mass, its first moment about the origin, and its center of mass $\bar x$. Include units at every stage and check that the final location is physically plausible.
permittedResults: A positive density produces a center of mass within the interval supporting the rod.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the continuous mass and first-moment definitions directly.
Treat a small element as $dm=\lambda(x)dx$, integrate $dm$ and $x\,dm$, then form their ratio.

milestones.criterion: Constructs and evaluates the density integral for total mass with units.
Constructs and evaluates the first-moment integral $\int x\lambda(x)dx$ with units.
Computes $\bar x=Q/M=12/7$ m and checks its position against the rod and increasing density.

commonErrors.description: Uses $x\lambda(x)$ for total mass or treats one pointwise density value as the rod's mass.
commonErrors.consequence: Mass and moment are conflated and the units are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Computes the center of mass as $M/Q$ rather than $Q/M$.
commonErrors.consequence: The result has reciprocal-length units and is not a location.

hintTree.content: Integrate density alone for mass; multiply by position only for the first moment.
Compute $M=\int_0^3(2+x)dx$ and $Q=\int_0^3x(2+x)dx$.
Divide moment by mass, then verify the resulting length is between $0$ and $3$.

CALC1:010520.canonicalSolution:
The total mass is
\[
M=\int_0^3(2+x)\,dx
=\left[2x+\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^3
=6+\frac92
=\boxed{\frac{21}{2}\text{ kg}}.
\]
The first moment about the origin is
\[
Q=\int_0^3x(2+x)\,dx
=\int_0^3(2x+x^2)\,dx
=\left[x^2+\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3
=9+9
=\boxed{18\text{ kg m}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\bar x=\frac QM
=\frac{18}{21/2}
=\boxed{\frac{12}{7}\text{ m}}
\approx1.714286\text{ m}.
\]
This lies in $[0,3]$. It is to the right of the midpoint $1.5$ m, which is plausible because the density increases with $x$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Mass is $\int_0^3(2+x)dx=21/2$ kg and moment is $\int_0^3x(2+x)dx=18$ kg m, so $\bar x=18/(21/2)=12/7$ m.
I use $\int_0^3x(2+x)dx=18$ as the total mass, even though that integrand computes a first moment.
The center is mass divided by moment, $(21/2)/18=7/12$, which I report as a position in meters.

CALC1:010521.title: Construct a shell volume from radius and height geometry
CALC1:010521.objective: Model a solid of revolution with cylindrical shells, distinguish distance to the axis from vertical shell height, and cross-check the result with an independent washer setup.
CALC1:010521.statement: Let $R$ be the first-quadrant region bounded by $y=4-x^2$, the $x$-axis, and the $y$-axis. Rotate $R$ about the $y$-axis. Use cylindrical shells to set up and evaluate the volume. Identify the shell radius, height, and thickness with units. Then give a washer integral in $y$ as an independent check.
permittedResults: A correct shell model and a correct washer model of the same solid must yield the same volume even though their slicing variables differ.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use vertical shells for the requested primary method and horizontal disks for verification.
Sketch a representative strip, label its distance and length, and only then translate the geometry into both integrals.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the correct shell geometry and horizontal bounds with the required differential factor.
Evaluates the shell integral exactly and reports cubic units.
Builds an independent washer integral in y and verifies the same volume.

commonErrors.description: Uses distance to the boundary x=2 instead of distance to the rotation axis x=0 as the shell radius.
commonErrors.consequence: The constructed shells model a different geometry.

commonErrors.description: Treats the vertical shell height as a disk radius and applies a disk-area formula with dx.
commonErrors.consequence: The slice orientation and volume element are incompatible.

hintTree.content: Find where the parabola meets the x-axis to determine the horizontal bounds.
The shell radius is horizontal distance from x to the y-axis; the height is top minus bottom.
For the washer check, solve $y=4-x^2$ for the nonnegative radius $x$ and integrate from $y=0$ to $y=4$.

CALC1:010521.canonicalSolution:
The parabola meets the $x$-axis at $x=2$ in the first quadrant. A vertical strip at coordinate $x$ has shell radius
\[
r(x)=x,
\]
shell height
\[
h(x)=(4-x^2)-0=4-x^2,
\]
and thickness $dx$. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
V
&=2\pi\int_0^2x(4-x^2)\,dx\\
&=2\pi\left[2x^2-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2\\
&=2\pi(8-4)
=\boxed{8\pi\text{ cubic units}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For a washer check, a horizontal slice at height $y$ has radius
\[
x=\sqrt{4-y}.
\]
It rotates into a disk of area $\pi(4-y)$, so
\[
V=\pi\int_0^4(4-y)\,dy
=\pi\left[4y-\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^4
=8\pi.
\]
The agreement confirms that the shell radius was distance to the actual axis $x=0$, not distance to the edge $x=2$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Vertical shells have radius $x$ and height $4-x^2$, so $V=2\pi\int_0^2x(4-x^2)dx=8\pi$. Horizontal disks give $\pi\int_0^4(4-y)dy=8\pi$.
The shell radius is the distance to the right edge, $2-x$, so I use $2\pi\int_0^2(2-x)(4-x^2)\,dx$.
I treat $4-x^2$ as a disk radius for each vertical strip and write $V=\pi\int_0^2(4-x^2)^2\,dx$.

CALC1:010522.title: Accumulate pumping work with a height-dependent lift
CALC1:010522.objective: Translate fluid slices into force and work, derive the lift distance from a physical coordinate system, and preserve dimensional units through an exact and numerical evaluation.
CALC1:010522.statement: A vertical cylindrical tank has radius $2$ m and height $3$ m. It contains water to a depth of $2$ m. Water is pumped through an outlet located $1$ m above the top of the tank. Using water's weight density $9800\ \mathrm{N/m^3}$, find the work required to empty the tank. Define a vertical coordinate, derive the slice volume and lift distance, and give both an exact answer and a decimal audit.
permittedResults: A cylinder of radius $r$ has constant horizontal cross-sectional area $\pi r^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a bottom-based coordinate and integrate horizontal slice weight times remaining vertical travel.
Use a surface-based coordinate only if all bounds and the outlet distance are transformed consistently, then verify against the bottom-based result.

milestones.criterion: Defines the coordinate and derives the water bounds and outlet-based lift distance correctly.
Constructs the slice volume and force using the cylindrical cross-section and given weight density.
Evaluates the work exactly and numerically and completes a valid dimensional audit.

commonErrors.description: Uses the slice height itself or the distance only to the tank top instead of the distance to the outlet one meter above it.
commonErrors.consequence: Every slice is assigned the wrong travel distance.

commonErrors.description: Uses the weight density without multiplying by the cylindrical slice volume, including its cross-sectional area.
commonErrors.consequence: The integrand lacks the force of the actual water slice and has inconsistent units.

hintTree.content: Measure y upward from the tank bottom; locate both the water interval and the outlet in this coordinate.
A slice of thickness $dy$ has volume $\pi(2)^2dy=4\pi\,dy$.
The outlet is at height $4$ m, so a slice at height $y$ travels $4-y$ meters.

CALC1:010522.canonicalSolution:
Let $y$ measure height in meters from the tank bottom. The water occupies $0\le y\le2$. The tank top is at $y=3$, so the outlet one meter above it is at $y=4$.

A horizontal slice of thickness $dy$ has volume
\[
dV=\pi(2)^2\,dy=4\pi\,dy\quad\text{m}^3.
\]
Using the given weight density, its weight is
\[
dF=9800(4\pi\,dy)=39200\pi\,dy\quad\text{N}.
\]
The slice must be lifted $4-y$ meters. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
W
&=\int_0^2 39200\pi(4-y)\,dy\\
&=39200\pi\left[4y-\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^2\\
&=39200\pi(8-2)
=\boxed{235200\pi\text{ J}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Numerically,
\[
W\approx\boxed{738902.592\text{ J}}.
\]
The units are consistent: newtons per cubic meter times cubic meters gives newtons, and multiplying by meters of lift gives newton-meters, or joules.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $y$ from the bottom, a slice has volume $4\pi dy$ and travels $4-y$ meters. Thus $W=39200\pi\int_0^2(4-y)dy=235200\pi\approx738902.592$ J.
A slice at height $y$ is lifted only $3-y$ meters to the tank top, so I ignore the outlet located one additional meter above it.
I use $dW=9800(4-y)\,dy$ directly, omitting the slice volume $4\pi\,dy$ and its cross-sectional area.

CALC1:010523.title: Build a solid from square cross-sections over a curved base
CALC1:010523.objective: Find the base-region intersection bounds, convert vertical separation into the side length of a square cross-section, square that length to obtain area, and integrate the resulting volume exactly.
CALC1:010523.statement:
A solid has base in the $xy$-plane equal to the region bounded by
\[
y=x^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y=2x.
\]
Cross-sections perpendicular to the $x$-axis are squares. Find the volume of the solid. Derive the intersection bounds, identify top minus bottom on that interval, and distinguish square side length from square area.
permittedResults: The area of a square is the square of its side length, not the side length itself.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve for the base interval, write the square area, expand, and integrate term by term.
Keep the cross-sectional area factored during setup, expand only for evaluation, and check that it vanishes at both endpoints.

milestones.criterion: Finds both curve intersections and verifies the top and bottom functions on the resulting interval.
Converts the vertical separation into a square side and then into the correctly squared area function.
Evaluates the volume integral exactly and reports the proper dimensional interpretation.

commonErrors.description: Uses the vertical separation directly as the cross-sectional area instead of squaring the side length.
commonErrors.consequence: The integral computes base area rather than solid volume.

commonErrors.description: Uses only one intersection or an interval not bounded by both curves, such as zero to one.
commonErrors.consequence: The integral omits part of the solid or includes a different base.

hintTree.content: Solve $x^2=2x$ to locate both ends of the base.
On the interval between intersections, $2x$ is above $x^2$.
The square side is $s(x)=2x-x^2$, so the cross-sectional area is $[s(x)]^2$.

CALC1:010523.canonicalSolution:
The curves intersect when
\[
x^2=2x,
\qquad
x(x-2)=0,
\]
so the base extends from $x=0$ to $x=2$. On this interval, the line is above the parabola because $2x-x^2=x(2-x)\ge0$. The vertical separation, and hence the square side length, is
\[
s(x)=2x-x^2.
\]
Therefore the cross-sectional area is
\[
A(x)=[2x-x^2]^2
=4x^2-4x^3+x^4.
\]
The volume is
\[
\begin{aligned}
V
&=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)^2\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{4x^3}{3}-x^4+\frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2\\
&=\frac{32}{3}-16+\frac{32}{5}
=\boxed{\frac{16}{15}\text{ cubic units}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using $2x-x^2$ itself as $A(x)$ would integrate the base-region area, not the volume of square slices.

graderFixtures.proofText: The curves meet at $0$ and $2$, and the square side is $2x-x^2$. Thus $V=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)^2dx=16/15$ cubic units.
The vertical separation is $2x-x^2$, so I use it directly as the square area and compute $\int_0^2(2x-x^2)dx$.
I find only the intersection $x=0$, guess the other bound is $1$, and integrate the square cross-sections only from $0$ to $1$.

CALC1:010524.title: Normalize a continuous density before computing probability and mean
CALC1:010524.objective: Use a definite integral to normalize a nonnegative density, compute an interval probability, and distinguish the density integral from the extra position factor required for an expected value.
CALC1:010524.statement:
A random variable $X$ has proposed density
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
kx(1-x),&0\le x\le1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $k$ is a constant. Find $k$, compute $P(X\le1/2)$, and compute the mean $E[X]$. Verify nonnegativity and explain why the expectation integral has an additional factor of $x$.
permittedResults: On $[0,1]$, both $x$ and $1-x$ are nonnegative, so a positive normalization constant preserves nonnegativity.

acceptableStrategies.description: Normalize first, then compute probability and expectation as three distinct definite integrals.
Use symmetry about one half as an audit for the probability and mean after deriving both by integration.

milestones.criterion: Normalizes the proposed density correctly and verifies its nonnegativity and support.
Computes the requested cumulative probability from the normalized density with correct bounds.
Builds and evaluates the expectation integral with the necessary position weight and interprets the result.

commonErrors.description: Treats the constant k itself as a probability or fails to impose total integral one.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed function is not established as a probability density.

commonErrors.description: Computes the mean by integrating $f(x)$ again without multiplying by the position x.
commonErrors.consequence: Total probability is mislabeled as expected value.

hintTree.content: First impose $\int_0^1kx(1-x)dx=1$.
For $P(X\le1/2)$, integrate the normalized density only from $0$ to $1/2$.
For the mean, integrate $x f(x)$ across the full support rather than integrating $f$ again.

CALC1:010524.canonicalSolution:
Normalization requires
\[
1=\int_0^1kx(1-x)\,dx
=k\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1
=k\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)
=\frac{k}{6}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{k=6}.
\]
This is positive, and $x(1-x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$, so the normalized function is nonnegative.

The requested probability is
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(X\le1/2)
&=\int_0^{1/2}6x(1-x)\,dx\\
&=\left[3x^2-2x^3\right]_0^{1/2}
=\frac34-\frac14
=\boxed{\frac12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The mean weights each probability contribution by its location:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[X]
&=\int_0^1x\,f(x)\,dx
=6\int_0^1x^2(1-x)\,dx\\
&=6\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1
=6\left(\frac13-\frac14\right)
=\boxed{\frac12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Integrating $f$ without the additional factor $x$ would return total probability one, not the average location.

graderFixtures.proofText: Normalization gives $k/6=1$, so $k=6$. Then $P(X\le1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}6x(1-x)dx=1/2$ and $E[X]=\int_0^1x\,6x(1-x)dx=1/2$.
I choose $k=1$ because a probability density must be at most one, without checking whether the total integral equals one.
For the mean I compute $\int_0^1f(x)dx=1$ with no extra factor of $x$, so I report $E[X]=1$.

CALC1:010525.title: Choose a curve whose arc-length radical simplifies
CALC1:010525.objective: Apply the graph arc-length formula on a closed interval, differentiate a fractional-power curve including its endpoint behavior, and evaluate the resulting exact integral with correct geometric units.
CALC1:010525.statement:
Find the exact length of the curve $y=f(x)$ defined by
\[
y=\frac23x^{3/2},\qquad 0\le x\le3.
\]
State the arc-length formula, compute the derivative, justify its use at the left endpoint, evaluate the integral exactly, and distinguish curve length from vertical change or area under the curve.
permittedResults: For $x\ge0$, the derivative of $(2/3)x^{3/2}$ is $\sqrt{x}$, with right-hand derivative value $0$ at the left endpoint $x=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate first and look for a perfect simplification inside the arc-length square root.
Parameterize the graph by x and compute the speed magnitude from the horizontal and vertical component derivatives.

milestones.criterion: States and correctly specializes the arc-length formula using the derivative of the curve.
Evaluates the simplified definite integral exactly to fourteen thirds.
Justifies endpoint regularity and interprets the result as geometric length.

commonErrors.description: Uses the integral of the derivative or the integral of the function instead of the square root of one plus derivative squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed quantity is net rise or area, not curve length.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates x to the three-halves power with the wrong exponent or coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The arc-length integrand no longer simplifies correctly and the final length is wrong.

hintTree.content: Differentiate to obtain $y'=\sqrt{x}$.
Then $1+(y')^2=1+x$, so the arc-length integrand has no nested square remaining.
Use the antiderivative $(2/3)(1+x)^{3/2}$ and evaluate it at $0$ and $3$.

CALC1:010525.canonicalSolution:
For a graph with continuous derivative, arc length is
\[
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2}\,dx.
\]
Here
\[
f'(x)=\frac23\cdot\frac32x^{1/2}=\sqrt{x}.
\]
This derivative extends continuously to the left endpoint from the right, with $f'(0)=0$, so the formula applies on $[0,3]$. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
L
&=\int_0^3\sqrt{1+(\sqrt{x})^2}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^3\sqrt{1+x}\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac23(1+x)^{3/2}\right]_0^3\\
&=\frac23\left(4^{3/2}-1^{3/2}\right)\\
&=\frac23(8-1)
=\boxed{\frac{14}{3}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This value is measured in length units. It is neither the vertical change $f(3)-f(0)=2\sqrt3$ nor the area $\int_0^3f(x)\,dx$; the factor $\sqrt{1+(f')^2}$ accounts for both horizontal and vertical motion along the curve.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since $y'=\sqrt{x}$, the length is $\int_0^3\sqrt{1+x}\,dx=(2/3)[(4)^{3/2}-1]=14/3$ length units.
I calculate $\int_0^3 y\,dx$ and label that area value as the curve length, never using the factor $\sqrt{1+(y')^2}$.
I differentiate $x^{3/2}$ as $(3/2)x^{3/2}$ without reducing the exponent, so I use the wrong derivative and obtain a different arc-length integral.

CALC1:010526.title: Integrate pressure across a narrowing triangular plate
CALC1:010526.objective: Build a hydrostatic-force integral from depth-dependent pressure and a linearly varying plate width, then compute the exact force with consistent SI units and geometry.
CALC1:010526.statement: A vertical triangular plate is submerged in fresh water with its horizontal top edge at the water surface. The top edge is $6$ meters wide, the plate is $4$ meters tall, and its opposite vertex points straight down. Use water's weight density $9800\ \mathrm{N/m^3}$. Derive and evaluate the hydrostatic force on one face of the plate. Define your depth coordinate, derive the strip width by similar triangles, and include units.
permittedResults: For this downward-pointing triangle, width decreases linearly from $6$ at $y=0$ to $0$ at $y=4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Model a representative horizontal strip and multiply its local pressure by its local width and thickness.
Use the centroid depth shortcut only as an independent check after deriving the integral, not as a replacement for the requested model.

milestones.criterion: Defines depth and derives both the pressure and linearly decreasing width functions.

\[

\[

\[
\begin{aligned}

&=9800(48-32)\\

\end{aligned}

\[
\begin{aligned}

&=\int_{0.04}^{0.12}300x\,dx\\
&=150\left[x^2\right]_{0.04}^{0.12}\\
&=150\bigl((0.12)^2-(0.04)^2\bigr)\\
&=150(0.0144-0.0016)\\
&=150(0.0128)
=1.92\ \mathrm J.
\end{aligned}

\[

\[
dW_{\text{cable}}=6y\,dy.
\]
Therefore the work to lift the cable is
\[
W_{\text{cable}}
=\int_0^{10}6y\,dy
=\left[3y^2\right]_0^{10}
=300\ \mathrm J.
\]
The $20$-newton tool is a point load at depth $10$ meters, so it moves the full $10$ meters:
\[

\]
The total work is
\[
\boxed{W_{\text{total}}=300+200=500\ \mathrm J}.
\]
As a check, after pulling up a distance $s$, the hanging cable length is $10-s$ and the moving force is $6(10-s)+20$. Thus
\[

\]

\[

&=\frac{512}{15}.
\end{aligned}

=\frac{512/15}{64/3}
=\boxed{\frac85}.
\]
Thus
\[

\]
The factor one half comes from the centroid height of each vertical strip, which lies halfway from zero to $f(x)$.

CALC1:010530.title: Compute the effective value of a sinusoidal current
CALC1:010530.objective: Apply the root-mean-square definition over one period, integrate a squared sinusoid, and distinguish RMS from signed average and peak amplitude.
CALC1:010530.statement:
An alternating current is $I(t)=10\sin(120\pi t)$ amperes with period $T=1/60$ second. Compute
\[
I_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{\frac1T\int_0^T[I(t)]^2dt}.
\]
Give an exact value and explain why zero signed average does not imply zero RMS.
permittedResults: The identity $\sin^2u=(1-\cos2u)/2$ shows that sine squared averages to $1/2$ over a complete period.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the half-angle identity.
Change variables to phase and average sine squared over complete cycles.

commonErrors.consequence: The operations do not match RMS.

commonErrors.description: Reports fifty as RMS after computing mean square.
commonErrors.consequence: The required root is omitted.

The mean square is
\[
I_{\rm rms}^2=\frac{100}{T}\int_0^T\sin^2(120\pi t)dt.
\]
Using $\sin^2u=(1-\cos2u)/2$, the constant part integrates to $T/2$ and the cosine part completes whole cycles and integrates to zero. Hence
\[
I_{\rm rms}^2=\frac{100}{T}\frac T2=50.
\]
Taking the nonnegative square root,
\[
\boxed{I_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2\ {\rm A}}.
\]
The signed current averages to zero because positive and negative half-cycles cancel. RMS squares before averaging, so those signs do not cancel.

I find the mean square $50$ but call $50$ amperes the RMS without taking a square root.
