CALC1:010531.title: Resolve endpoint slopes in a spherical surface integral
CALC1:010531.objective: Set up a surface-of-revolution integral for a semicircle, simplify the coupled radius and arc-length factors on the open interval, and justify the finite result despite vertical endpoint tangents.
CALC1:010531.statement:
The upper semicircle
\[
y=\sqrt{9-x^2},\qquad -3\le x\le3,
\]
is revolved about the $x$-axis. Use the surface-area formula
\[
S=2\pi\int_a^b y\sqrt{1+(y')^2}\,dx
\]
to compute the exact surface area. Because $y'$ is undefined at $x=\pm3$, interpret the integral through interior truncations and explain why the endpoint behavior is nevertheless integrable.
permittedResults: An integrand that simplifies on the open interval to a constant with a finite endpoint extension has a finite improper integral over the closed interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Simplify the full product before evaluating the improper endpoints.
Parameterize the semicircle and recover the same area from a smooth angular surface integral.

milestones.criterion: Builds the surface-area integrand and differentiates the semicircle correctly.
Simplifies the radius times arc-length factor to the constant three.
Handles the endpoint vertical tangents through a limit and obtains thirty-six pi.

commonErrors.description: Uses only two pi times y and omits the square-root arc-length factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed integral is not surface area and gives the wrong value.

commonErrors.description: Declares the surface formula unusable and the area divergent solely because y-prime is undefined at the two endpoints.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores the finite simplified integrand and the proper limiting interpretation.

hintTree.content: Multiply the square-root arc-length factor by y before discussing the endpoints.

CALC1:010531.canonicalSolution:
For $-3<x<3$,
\[
y'=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
1+(y')^2
=1+\frac{x^2}{9-x^2}
=\frac9{9-x^2},
\]
and, because $y=\sqrt{9-x^2}>0$ in the interior,
\[
y\sqrt{1+(y')^2}
=\sqrt{9-x^2}\sqrt{\frac9{9-x^2}}
=3.
\]
For $0<r<3$, apply the formula on $[-r,r]$ and then let $r\to3^-$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S
&=\lim_{r\to3^-}2\pi\int_{-r}^{r}3\,dx\\
&=\lim_{r\to3^-}12\pi r
=\boxed{36\pi}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Although $y'$ becomes unbounded at the endpoints, the product in the surface integrand is exactly $3$ throughout the interior and extends continuously by the value $3$. Thus the vertical tangents do not make the surface area diverge. The result agrees with the area $4\pi(3)^2$ of a radius-three sphere.

graderFixtures.proofText: Inside the interval, $y'=-x/\sqrt{9-x^2}$ and $y\sqrt{1+(y')^2}=3$. Integrating on $[-r,r]$ and taking $r\to3^-$ gives $S=36\pi$; the endpoint vertical tangents are harmless.
I integrate only $2\pi y\,dx$ and omit the factor $\sqrt{1+(y')^2}$ from the surface strip, obtaining an unrelated quantity.
Since $y'$ is undefined at $x=\pm3$, I immediately call the area divergent without simplifying the full integrand or taking the interior limit.

\[
p(q)=100-q^2

\[
CS=\int_0^{q_*}\bigl(p(q)-p(q_*)\bigr)\,dq.
\]

\[
p(q_*)=p(6)=100-6^2=\boxed{64\text{ dollars per unit}}.
\]

\[
p(q)-64=36-q^2\ge0.
\]
Thus consumer surplus is the region between $p=100-q^2$ above and $p=64$ below, from $q=0$ to $q=6$. Its signed area is
\[
\begin{aligned}
CS
&=\int_0^6\bigl[(100-q^2)-64\bigr]\,dq\\
&=\int_0^6(36-q^2)\,dq\\
&=\left[36q-\frac{q^3}{3}\right]_0^6\\
&=216-72=\boxed{144}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because $q$ is measured in hundreds of units, the area unit is one hundred dollars. Therefore the monetary consumer surplus is
\[
\boxed{144\text{ hundred dollars}=14{,}400\text{ dollars}}.
\]
Subtracting the demand curve from the price line would give the negative of the geometric area and would not represent surplus.

CALC1:010533.title: Normalize the area between a Lorenz curve and equality
CALC1:010533.objective: Interpret a Lorenz curve, integrate the gap from perfect equality, normalize by the full comparison triangle, and connect the resulting Gini coefficient with a concrete population-share reading.
CALC1:010533.statement:
An idealized income distribution has Lorenz curve
\[
L(p)=p^3,\qquad 0\le p\le1,
\]
where $L(p)$ is the fraction of total income held by the bottom fraction $p$ of the population. Compute the income share of the bottom half. Then compute the area between the line of perfect equality $L=p$ and the Lorenz curve, and use
\[
G=\frac{\text{area between the curves}}{\text{area under }L=p}
\]
to find the Gini coefficient. Explain the orientation and normalization rather than quoting $G=1-2\int_0^1L(p)\,dp$.
permittedResults: On $0\le p\le1$, $p^3\le p$, so the equality line is the upper curve.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the vertical gap and divide by the half-unit comparison triangle.
Compute twice the area between the curves after independently establishing which curve is above.

milestones.criterion: Interprets and evaluates the cumulative share at one half.
Sets up and evaluates the correctly oriented area between curves.
Normalizes by the equality triangle and distinguishes area from coefficient.

commonErrors.description: Integrates p cubed minus p and reports a negative inequality measure.
commonErrors.consequence: The upper and lower curves are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Reports the raw gap area one fourth as the Gini coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The required normalization by the area one half is omitted.

hintTree.content: Evaluate $L(1/2)$ before integrating.
The gap height is $p-p^3$, not its negative.
The comparison triangle under $L=p$ has area $1/2$.

CALC1:010533.canonicalSolution:
The bottom half corresponds to $p=1/2$, so its modeled income share is
\[
L(1/2)=\left(\frac12\right)^3=\boxed{\frac18=12.5\%}.
\]
For $0\le p\le1$, we have $p^3\le p$, so the line of equality lies above the Lorenz curve. The area between them is
\[
A=\int_0^1(p-p^3)\,dp
=\left[\frac{p^2}{2}-\frac{p^4}{4}\right]_0^1
=\frac12-\frac14
=\boxed{\frac14}.
\]
The total comparison area under the equality line is
\[
\int_0^1p\,dp=\frac12.
\]
Therefore the normalized coefficient is
\[
\boxed{G=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac12}.
\]
The division by $1/2$ scales the gap relative to the largest available triangle in the unit square; the unnormalized area $1/4$ is not itself the Gini coefficient. Equivalently, this derivation yields $G=1-2\int_0^1L(p)\,dp$, but the geometric normalization explains the factor $2$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The bottom half receives $L(1/2)=1/8$. Since $p\ge p^3$, the gap area is $\int_0^1(p-p^3)dp=1/4$. Dividing by the area $1/2$ under the equality line gives $G=1/2$.
I integrate $p^3-p$ even though the Lorenz curve lies below equality, obtain $-1/4$, and accept a negative Gini coefficient.
I correctly find the area between the curves is $1/4$ but call that number the Gini coefficient without dividing by the equality triangle's area $1/2$.

CALC1:010534.title: Discount a growing continuous income stream
CALC1:010534.objective: Translate a time-varying income rate and continuous discount force into a present-value integral, evaluate it by integration by parts, and audit the result against the undiscounted total.
CALC1:010534.statement:
An income stream pays at the continuous rate
\[
R(t)=12000+800t
\]
dollars per year for $0\le t\le5$, where $t$ is measured in years. Money received at time $t$ has present-value factor $e^{-0.04t}$. Set up and evaluate the present value
\[
\operatorname{PV}=\int_0^5R(t)e^{-0.04t}\,dt
\]
exactly in terms of $e^{-0.2}$ and numerically to the nearest dollar. Compute the undiscounted total and use it as a reasonableness check.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the integral and apply parts only to the t exponential term.
Find one antiderivative of the complete linear-times-exponential integrand by solving for coefficients in (at plus b)e to the negative point zero four t.

milestones.criterion: Builds the present-value integral with correct units and discount sign.
Evaluates the constant and linear terms and combines them exactly.
Produces the numerical value and validates it against the undiscounted total.

commonErrors.description: Uses e to the positive point zero four t as the present-value factor.
commonErrors.consequence: Future payments are inflated instead of discounted, violating the stated model and reasonableness bound.

commonErrors.description: Treats the integral of t times the discount exponential as t times an exponential antiderivative and omits the remaining integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The linear income contribution and exact present value are wrong.

hintTree.content: Split the integral into a constant-rate part and a linear-in-time part.
Because $0<e^{-0.04t}\le1$, the present value must be below the undiscounted total.

CALC1:010534.canonicalSolution:
The present-value model is
\[
\operatorname{PV}=\int_0^5(12000+800t)e^{-0.04t}\,dt.
\]
For the constant part,
\[
12000\int_0^5e^{-0.04t}\,dt
=300000(1-e^{-0.2}).
\]
For the linear part, integration by parts gives
\[
\int_0^5te^{-0.04t}\,dt
=\frac1{0.04^2}-\left(\frac5{0.04}+\frac1{0.04^2}\right)e^{-0.2}
=625-750e^{-0.2}.
\]
Multiplying by $800$ and combining,
\[
\operatorname{PV}=300000(1-e^{-0.2})+500000-600000e^{-0.2},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{PV}=800000-900000e^{-0.2}\text{ dollars}}.
\]
Numerically this is approximately
\[
\boxed{63{,}142\text{ dollars}}.
\]
Without discounting, the total is
\[
\int_0^5(12000+800t)\,dt
=60000+10000
=\boxed{70{,}000\text{ dollars}}.
\]
The present value is positive and below $70{,}000$, as required because every future-payment factor is positive and at most one.

graderFixtures.proofText: PV is $\int_0^5(12000+800t)e^{-0.04t}dt$. The two pieces give $300000(1-e^{-0.2})$ and $500000-600000e^{-0.2}$, so PV is $800000-900000e^{-0.2}\approx63{,}142$ dollars, below the undiscounted $70{,}000$ dollars.
I use $e^{+0.04t}$ because I think future money should grow, so my alleged present value exceeds the undiscounted $70{,}000$.
For $\int te^{-0.04t}dt$ I write only $-25te^{-0.04t}$ and omit the remaining integration-by-parts integral, producing an incomplete linear contribution.

CALC1:010535.title: Show why a drilled sphere's remaining volume knows only its height
CALC1:010535.objective: Model a sphere with a centered cylindrical hole using washers, eliminate the unknown sphere and drill radii, and prove the resulting volume depends only on the remaining height.
CALC1:010535.statement: A cylindrical hole of radius $a$ is drilled through the center of a sphere of radius $R>a$, along a diameter. The remaining solid has total height $h$, measured along the drill axis from its lowest remaining point to its highest. Using washers perpendicular to the drill axis, derive the remaining volume solely in terms of $h$; your final formula must contain neither $R$ nor $a$. Explain the geometric relation that makes this elimination possible. Then find the exact and approximate volume when $h=6$ cm.
permittedResults: A sphere centered at the origin satisfies $x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2$, so its cross-sectional radius at axial coordinate $z$ is $\sqrt{R^2-z^2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Choose the drill axis as a coordinate axis and convert every cross-section into outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
Use symmetry to integrate twice from zero to h over two after eliminating the radii.

milestones.criterion: Builds the correct washer cross-section and identifies the axial endpoints.
Eliminates both original radii using the total-height relation and evaluates the integral.
States the invariance conclusion and computes the exact and decimal six-centimeter volume with units.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full sphere disk area pi times R squared minus z squared and never subtracts the cylindrical hole.
commonErrors.consequence: The integral computes the original sphere or a spherical segment, not the drilled remainder.

commonErrors.description: Sets the sphere radius R equal to h over two even when the drilled hole has positive radius.
commonErrors.consequence: The remaining height gives square root of R squared minus a squared, not R itself.

hintTree.content: The remaining solid exists where the sphere's cross-sectional radius is at least $a$, so its endpoints satisfy $R^2-z^2=a^2$.
Show that $R^2-a^2=h^2/4$.
The washer area becomes $\pi(h^2/4-z^2)$ on $[-h/2,h/2]$.

CALC1:010535.canonicalSolution:
Place the sphere at the origin and align the hole with the $z$-axis. At height $z$, the sphere's outer cross-sectional radius is
$$
r_o(z)=\sqrt{R^2-z^2},
$$
while the drilled cylindrical hole has inner radius $r_i=a$. The remaining washer exists when $R^2-z^2\ge a^2$. Its axial endpoints satisfy
$$
z=\pm\sqrt{R^2-a^2}.
$$
Since the total remaining height is $h$,
$$
\frac h2=\sqrt{R^2-a^2},
\qquad
\boxed{R^2-a^2=\frac{h^2}{4}}.
$$
This relation is exactly what removes the two original radii.

The washer area is
$$
\pi\left[(R^2-z^2)-a^2\right]
=\pi\left(\frac{h^2}{4}-z^2\right).
$$
Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
V
&=\int_{-h/2}^{h/2}\pi\left(\frac{h^2}{4}-z^2\right)\,dz\\
&=\pi\left[\frac{h^2z}{4}-\frac{z^3}{3}\right]_{-h/2}^{h/2}\\
&=\pi\left(\frac{h^3}{4}-\frac{h^3}{12}\right)
=\boxed{\frac{\pi h^3}{6}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The formula depends only on the remaining height, not separately on the original sphere or drill radius.

For $h=6$ cm,
$$
\boxed{V=\frac{\pi(6)^3}{6}=36\pi\ {\rm cm}^3
\approx113.097\ {\rm cm}^3}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: At axial coordinate $z$, the washer area is $\pi[(R^2-z^2)-a^2]$. Since $h/2=\sqrt{R^2-a^2}$, this is $\pi(h^2/4-z^2)$ for $-h/2\le z\le h/2$. Integration gives $V=\pi h^3/6$; at $h=6$, $V=36\pi\approx113.097\ {\rm cm}^3$.
I integrate $\pi(R^2-z^2)$ as solid disks and omit the inner radius $a$, so the cylindrical material that was drilled away remains in my volume.
Because the remaining height is $h$, I set $R=h/2$ despite $a>0$, rather than using $R^2-a^2=h^2/4$.

CALC1:010536.title: Integrate a piston force and audit two constant-pressure shortcuts
CALC1:010536.objective: Convert a position-dependent pressure into force and work, verify the result through average pressure and volume change, and quantify signed endpoint-approximation errors.
CALC1:010536.statement:
A cylindrical piston has radius $0.10$ m. As its position $x$, measured in meters, moves quasistatically from $x=0.20$ to $x=0.80$, the pressure pushing it is
$$
p(x)=30000+20000x\quad\text{pascals}.
$$
Assume the opposing pressure has already been subtracted, so $p(x)$ is the net pressure. Derive and evaluate the exact work done by this pressure. Verify the same result using average pressure times volume change. Then approximate the work once using the initial pressure throughout and once using the final pressure throughout; for each shortcut give the signed percent error relative to the exact work and identify it as an underestimate or overestimate.
permittedResults: A linear function's average value on an interval is the arithmetic mean of its endpoint values.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the linear pressure against the constant piston area, then use average value as a check.
Treat each shortcut as a rectangle under the pressure-position graph and compare its signed area error.

milestones.criterion: Builds the pressure-force-work integral with correct piston area and units.
Evaluates the exact work and independently verifies it using average pressure and volume change.
Computes both endpoint approximations and their signed percent errors with correct underestimate and overestimate labels.

commonErrors.description: Integrates pressure directly over displacement without multiplying by the piston face area.
commonErrors.consequence: Pascals times meters are not joules, and the numerical work is missing the area factor.

commonErrors.description: Divides each approximation difference by the approximate work rather than by the exact work.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported signed percentages are not errors relative to the exact result requested.

hintTree.content: The piston area is $A=\pi(0.10)^2=0.01\pi$ square meters.
Compute $\int_{0.2}^{0.8}(30000+20000x)\,dx$ before multiplying by area.
Signed percent error is $100(W_{\rm approx}-W_{\rm exact})/W_{\rm exact}$.

CALC1:010536.canonicalSolution:
The piston face area is
$$
A=\pi(0.10)^2=0.01\pi\ {\rm m}^2.
$$
Pressure times area gives force, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
W
&=\int_{0.20}^{0.80}p(x)A\,dx\\
&=0.01\pi\int_{0.20}^{0.80}(30000+20000x)\,dx\\
&=0.01\pi[30000x+10000x^2]_{0.20}^{0.80}\\
&=0.01\pi(18000+6000)\\
&=\boxed{240\pi\ {\rm J}\approx753.982\ {\rm J}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The units are $ {\rm Pa}\,{\rm m}^2\,{\rm m}={\rm N\,m}={\rm J}$.

For an independent check, the endpoint pressures are
$$
p_i=p(0.20)=34000\ {\rm Pa},\qquad
p_f=p(0.80)=46000\ {\rm Pa}.
$$
Because pressure is linear, its average is $40000$ Pa. The volume change is
$$
\Delta V=A(0.80-0.20)=0.006\pi\ {\rm m}^3.
$$
Thus
$$
p_{\rm avg}\Delta V=(40000)(0.006\pi)=240\pi\ {\rm J},
$$
confirming the integral.

The initial-pressure shortcut gives
$$
W_i=(34000)(0.006\pi)=204\pi\ {\rm J}.
$$
Its signed percent error is
$$
100\frac{204\pi-240\pi}{240\pi}
=\boxed{-15\%},
$$
so it underestimates. The final-pressure shortcut gives
$$
W_f=(46000)(0.006\pi)=276\pi\ {\rm J},
\qquad
100\frac{276\pi-240\pi}{240\pi}
=\boxed{+15\%},
$$
so it overestimates. The symmetric errors reflect the linear pressure and equally spaced endpoint values around the average.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $A=0.01\pi$, $W=A\int_{0.2}^{0.8}(30000+20000x)\,dx=240\pi\approx753.982$ J. Also $p_{\rm avg}=40000$ Pa and $\Delta V=0.006\pi$, giving the same work. Initial and final shortcuts are $204\pi$ and $276\pi$, with signed errors $-15\%$ and $+15\%$.
I compute $\int_{0.2}^{0.8}p(x)\,dx$ and call that joules, never multiplying by the piston area $0.01\pi\ {\rm m}^2$.
For the initial shortcut I calculate $100(204\pi-240\pi)/(204\pi)$, using the approximate value as denominator even though error relative to exact work was requested.

CALC1:010537.title: Build a torus from offset washers
CALC1:010537.objective: Derive the volume of a torus directly from horizontal washer radii and verify the geometry and units numerically.
CALC1:010537.statement:
Let \(R>r>0\). The disk
$$
(x-R)^2+y^2\le r^2
$$
is revolved about the \(y\)-axis. Using horizontal washers—not a memorized torus formula—derive the volume of the resulting solid. Clearly identify the inner and outer radii, the integration bounds, and why the cross-sections are washers rather than disks. Then evaluate the volume for \(R=5\) and \(r=2\), both exactly and to three decimal places.
permittedResults: The upper semicircle integral satisfies \(\int_{-r}^{r}\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\,dy=\pi r^2/2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the circle equation for the two horizontal endpoints before rotating.
Recognize the remaining integral as the area of a semicircle.

milestones.criterion: Extracts the horizontal interval and correctly identifies both washer radii and bounds.
Simplifies and integrates the washer area to derive the torus volume from first principles.
Evaluates the specified case exactly and numerically with cubic units and a valid check.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the outer radius \(R+\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\) and writes \(\pi(R+\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2\) for every cross-section.
commonErrors.consequence: The generating interval never reaches the axis because R exceeds r; rotation leaves an inner hole that must be subtracted.

commonErrors.description: Integrates from \(-R\) to \(R\) or puts \(\sqrt{R^2-y^2}\) in the slice formula.
commonErrors.consequence: The vertical bounds and circular half-width come from the generating disk's radius r, while R is its horizontal offset from the axis.

hintTree.content: At height \(y\), set \(s=\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\); the disk runs from \(x=R-s\) to \(x=R+s\).
Because \(R>r\), both horizontal endpoints remain positive, leaving a nonzero inner radius after rotation.
Simplify \((R+s)^2-(R-s)^2\) before integrating.

CALC1:010537.canonicalSolution:
The disk has vertical extent \(-r\le y\le r\). For a fixed such \(y\), let
$$
s(y)=\sqrt{r^2-y^2}.
$$
Solving the circle equation for \(x\) shows that the horizontal slice runs from
$$
x=R-s(y)
\quad\text{to}\quad
x=R+s(y).
$$
Since \(R>r\ge s(y)\), its left endpoint is positive. Rotation about the \(y\)-axis therefore leaves a hole: the outer radius is \(R+s(y)\) and the inner radius is \(R-s(y)\). The washer area is
$$
\begin{aligned}
A(y)
&=\pi\left[(R+s)^2-(R-s)^2\right]\\
&=4\pi R\,s\\
&=4\pi R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Consequently
$$
\begin{aligned}
V
&=\int_{-r}^{r}4\pi R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\,dy\\
&=4\pi R\left(\frac{\pi r^2}{2}\right)\\
&=\boxed{2\pi^2Rr^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The semicircle-area integral supplies the factor \(\pi r^2/2\). As an independent geometric check, the result is the area \(\pi r^2\) of the generating disk times the distance \(2\pi R\) traveled by its center.

For \(R=5\) and \(r=2\),
$$
\boxed{V=2\pi^2(5)(2^2)=40\pi^2\approx394.784}
$$
cubic units.

graderFixtures.proofText: For \(-r\le y\le r\), put \(s=\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\). The washer radii are \(R+s\) and \(R-s\), so its area is \(4\pi R s\). Integrating and using the semicircle area gives \(V=4\pi R(\pi r^2/2)=2\pi^2Rr^2\). At \(R=5,r=2\), this is \(40\pi^2\approx394.784\) cubic units.
I rotate the right endpoint alone and use disk area \(\pi(R+\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2\), never subtracting the inner radius even though \(R>r\) keeps the slice away from the axis.
I use bounds \(-R\le y\le R\) and the half-width \(\sqrt{R^2-y^2}\), treating the offset R as the generating circle's radius instead of using r.

CALC1:010538.title: Turn a changing arrival rate into queue and waiting time
CALC1:010538.objective: Integrate competing arrival and service rates to recover a fluid queue, certify its busy interval and maximum, and use area under the queue to compute an average waiting time.
CALC1:010538.statement:
A ticket line is modeled as a continuous fluid queue. It is empty at \(t=0\). During the next \(12\) minutes, people arrive at rate
$$
a(t)=120-10t
$$
people per minute. One bank of scanners can process \(60\) people per minute whenever anyone is waiting; after \(t=12\), arrivals stop, and the scanners would continue until the line cleared.

Let \(Q(t)\) be the number of people waiting, not including anyone already processed. Determine \(Q(t)\) through the time the line clears, verify that your formula is consistent with the scanners being busy, and find the clearing time and the maximum queue. Compute the total number of arrivals and the total person-minutes spent waiting. Finally use
$$
\text{average waiting time}
=\frac{\text{total person-minutes waiting}}{\text{total arrivals}}
$$
to find the average waiting time per person. Include units and explain why queue area, rather than maximum queue size, is used in the average.
permittedResults: Summing each person's waiting duration is equivalent to integrating the number still waiting over time; therefore total waiting time is the area under the queue-length graph.

acceptableStrategies.description: Construct cumulative arrivals and departures separately, then subtract them to obtain the queue.
Work directly with the net rate for queue shape, then use a second integral for aggregate waiting time.

milestones.criterion: Builds and integrates the correct net-rate balance and verifies the resulting busy interval and clearing time.
Finds the global maximum queue and checks total arrivals against processed volume.
Integrates queue length to person-minutes and computes and interprets the average wait with correct units.

commonErrors.description: Uses \(Q'(t)=60-a(t)\), obtains \(Q(t)=5t^2-60t<0\) just after opening, and still calls it a physical queue.
commonErrors.consequence: Departures were subtracted in the wrong order; a negative number of waiting people contradicts the model and reverses the maximum analysis.

commonErrors.description: Divides the peak queue \(180\) by the \(720\) arrivals and reports \(0.25\) minutes as the average wait, without integrating \(Q(t)\).
commonErrors.consequence: Peak people divided by total people is dimensionless and does not sum individual waiting durations; the queue-area integral is required.

hintTree.content: Assume the scanners are busy just after \(t=0\), integrate \(a(t)-60\), and then check that the resulting \(Q(t)\) stays positive until it returns to zero.
The queue maximum occurs when the net rate \(a(t)-60\) changes from positive to negative.
Integrate \(Q(t)\), with units people times minutes, before dividing by the dimensionless count of arrivals.

CALC1:010538.canonicalSolution:
While the line is nonempty, departures occur at the full service rate, so the net rate is
$$
Q'(t)=a(t)-60=(120-10t)-60=60-10t.
$$
At the single initial instant the line is empty, but \(a(0)=120>60\), so its right-hand net rate is positive and a queue forms immediately; whether one assigns service at that one instant does not change any integral.

Using \(Q(0)=0\), integration gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
Q(t)
&=\int_0^t(60-10u)\,du\\
&=60t-5t^2\\
&=5t(12-t).
\end{aligned}
$$
This candidate is positive for \(0<t<12\) and zero at \(t=0,12\). Thus the scanners really are busy throughout the open interval on which the full-service calculation was used, and the formula is self-consistent. The line clears at
$$
\boxed{t=12\ \text{minutes}}.
$$
After that, arrivals have stopped and the queue remains zero.

The queue grows while \(Q'(t)>0\), until \(t=6\), and shrinks while \(Q'(t)<0\), from \(6\) to \(12\). Hence
$$
\boxed{Q_{\max}=Q(6)=60(6)-5(6)^2=180\ \text{people}}.
$$

The total number of arrivals is
$$
\begin{aligned}
A
&=\int_0^{12}(120-10t)\,dt\\
&=\left[120t-5t^2\right]_0^{12}\\
&=\boxed{720\ \text{people}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
As a conservation check, the busy scanners process \(60(12)=720\) people by the clearing time.

The total person-minutes waiting is the area under \(Q\):
$$
\begin{aligned}
W
&=\int_0^{12}(60t-5t^2)\,dt\\
&=\left[30t^2-\frac53t^3\right]_0^{12}\\
&=4320-2880\\
&=\boxed{1440\ \text{person-minutes}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\text{average waiting time}=\frac{1440}{720}=2\ \text{minutes per person}}.
$$
At each instant, \(Q(t)\) counts how many individual waiting clocks are running. Integrating that count sums their durations. The peak value \(180\) describes only one instant and cannot replace this time accumulation.

graderFixtures.proofText: While busy, \(Q'=a-60=60-10t\), so \(Q=60t-5t^2=5t(12-t)\). It is positive on \((0,12)\), clears at \(12\), and peaks at \(Q(6)=180\). \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}
\]
converges and, if so, find its exact sum. Derive a formula for the $N$th partial sum by partial fractions and display enough terms to make the cancellation pattern and surviving endpoints explicit.

Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}
=\frac1{n+2}-\frac1{n+3}.
\]
Thus the $N$th partial sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N
&=\left(\frac13-\frac14\right)
+\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{N+2}-\frac1{N+3}\right)\\
&=\frac13-\frac1{N+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All middle terms cancel, but the first positive term and final negative term survive. Therefore
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}
=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N
=\frac13-0
=\boxed{\frac13}.
\]
The finite partial-sum formula is essential: “everything cancels” would incorrectly discard the boundary term $1/3$.

CALC1:010621.title: Prove a recursive sequence converges before solving its limit
CALC1:010621.objective: Establish invariant bounds and monotonicity for a nonlinear recursion, invoke the monotone convergence theorem, and reject an extraneous fixed point using the sequence's range.
CALC1:010621.statement:
Let $a_1=1$ and
\[
a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_n}\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
Prove that $(a_n)$ converges and find its limit. Your argument must establish a useful bound and monotonicity before passing to a limit in the recursion, and it must explain why every algebraic solution of the resulting fixed-point equation is not automatically a possible limit.
permittedResults: Continuity of the square-root function permits passing from $a_n\to L$ to $\sqrt{2+a_n}\to\sqrt{2+L}$ after convergence is known.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build an invariant interval, prove increase by comparing squares within it, and then solve the limiting recursion.
Study the update map on [1,2], use its order relation against the diagonal along the sequence, and apply monotone convergence.

milestones.criterion: Proves a uniform upper bound and nonnegative lower bound by induction.
Establishes monotonicity with a correctly signed comparison and invokes the convergence theorem.
Passes to the fixed-point equation only afterward and selects the unique range-compatible limit.

commonErrors.description: Solves the fixed-point equation and declares convergence without first proving that the sequence has a limit.
commonErrors.consequence: A necessary condition for a possible limit is mistaken for a convergence proof.

commonErrors.description: Accepts the negative algebraic root as a possible limit despite every sequence term being positive and at least one.
commonErrors.consequence: The fixed-point equation is used without respecting the sequence's invariant range.

hintTree.content: Use induction to show $1\le a_n<2$.
Compare squares and factor $a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2=2+a_n-a_n^2=(2-a_n)(a_n+1)$.
After convergence is established, solve $L=\sqrt{2+L}$ and use the nonnegative range to select a root.

CALC1:010621.canonicalSolution:
We first prove by induction that
\[
1\le a_n<2
\]
for every $n$. The claim holds for $a_1=1$. If $1\le a_n<2$, then
\[
a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_n}\ge\sqrt3>1
\]
and
\[
a_{n+1}<\sqrt4=2.
\]
Thus the interval is invariant, and in particular the sequence is bounded above by $2$.

For monotonicity, the bound gives
\[
a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2
=2+a_n-a_n^2
=(2-a_n)(a_n+1)>0.
\]
Both $a_{n+1}$ and $a_n$ are nonnegative, so the strict inequality between their squares implies $a_{n+1}>a_n$. Hence the sequence is increasing and bounded above. The monotone convergence theorem now guarantees a finite limit $L$.

Only after establishing convergence do we pass to the limit in the continuous recursion:
\[
L=\sqrt{2+L}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
L^2-L-2=0,
\qquad
(L-2)(L+1)=0.
\]
The candidates are $2$ and $-1$, but every term is at least $1$, so a limit cannot be negative. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=2}.
\]
Solving the fixed-point equation alone would identify possible limits, not prove that the sequence actually converges.

I solve $L=\sqrt{2+L}$ and get $L=2$, so this equation by itself proves that the original sequence converges to $2$.
The fixed-point equation has roots $2$ and $-1$, so the positive recursive sequence can converge to either one depending on later terms.

\]

\[
2^{j+1}-(2^j+1)+1=2^j

\[
\sum_{n=2^j+1}^{2^{j+1}}\frac1n

\]

\[

For large $n$, derive two-sided constant multiples of $1/n^2$ and use direct comparison as an alternative check.

Computes the comparison ratio limit exactly as two and applies the theorem correctly.

CALC1:010625.canonicalSolution:
The terms are positive for every $n\ge1$. Their dominant-power behavior is
\[
\frac{2n+1}{n^3+4}\sim\frac{2n}{n^3}=\frac2{n^2},
\]
so choose
\[
b_n=\frac1{n^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{(2n+1)/(n^3+4)}{1/n^2}\\
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^3+n^2}{n^3+4}\\
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2+1/n}{1+4/n^3}\\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This limit is finite and strictly positive. Since
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}
\]
is a convergent $p$-series with $p=2$, the Limit Comparison Test gives
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2n+1}{n^3+4}\text{ converges}}.
\]
It is true that $a_n\to0$, but that fact alone is only a necessary condition. The harmonic series also has terms tending to zero and nevertheless diverges, so the comparison argument is the step that proves convergence here.

CALC1:010626.title: Trap a factorial sequence beneath a geometric sequence
CALC1:010626.objective: Compute a consecutive-term ratio for a factorial sequence, prove a uniform one-half bound using the binomial theorem, and use induction plus squeezing to establish convergence without asymptotic formulas.
CALC1:010626.statement:
For $n\ge1$, let
\[
a_n=\frac{n!}{n^n}.
\]
Prove that $a_n\to0$ without using Stirling's formula or quoting a ratio test for series. Compute $a_{n+1}/a_n$, prove it is at most $1/2$, deduce an explicit geometric upper bound for $a_n$, and finish with the Squeeze Theorem.
permittedResults: The binomial theorem gives $(1+1/n)^n\ge1+n(1/n)=2$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Control each successive term by a fixed fraction of the previous term, then compare to a geometric sequence.
Alternatively expand $a_n=\prod_{k=1}^n(k/n)$ and group factors to seek a vanishing exponential bound, while retaining a rigorous inequality.

milestones.criterion: Computes the consecutive-term ratio exactly and rewrites it in a form suitable for bounding.
Proves the one-half ratio bound and iterates it to an explicit geometric upper bound.
Applies positivity and the Squeeze Theorem to conclude the sequence limit is zero.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the factorials or powers incorrectly and obtains a ratio such as one over n plus one.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed geometric control does not follow from the actual sequence.

commonErrors.description: From a denominator at least two, concludes its positive reciprocal is at least one half.
commonErrors.consequence: The inequality direction is reversed, destroying the upper bound needed for squeezing.

hintTree.content: Cancel factorials and powers carefully in $a_{n+1}/a_n$.
Rewrite the ratio as $1/(1+1/n)^n$ and use only the first two nonnegative binomial terms.
Starting from $a_1=1$, iterate $a_{n+1}\le a_n/2$ to prove $a_n\le2^{-(n-1)}$.

CALC1:010626.canonicalSolution:
Every $a_n$ is positive. Its consecutive-term ratio is
\[
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}
=\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+1)^{n+1}}\frac{n^n}{n!}
=\frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n}
=\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n
=\frac1{(1+1/n)^n}.
\]
By the binomial theorem, all omitted terms below are nonnegative and
\[
\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n
=1+n\left(\frac1n\right)+\cdots\ge2.
\]
Taking positive reciprocals reverses the inequality, so
\[
0<\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\le\frac12.
\]
Thus $a_{n+1}\le a_n/2$. Since $a_1=1$, induction gives
\[
0<a_n\le\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}
\]
for every $n\ge1$: the base case is equality, and multiplying the inductive bound by at most one half proves the next case.

Finally,
\[
\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The Squeeze Theorem therefore yields
\[
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n!}{n^n}=0}.
\]
No series ratio test is being invoked; the computed ratio supplies a direct geometric bound on the sequence itself.

graderFixtures.proofText: The ratio is $(n/(n+1))^n=1/(1+1/n)^n\le1/2$ because the binomial denominator is at least $2$. Hence $0<a_n\le(1/2)^{n-1}\to0$.
I cancel $(n+1)!/n!$ against all of $(n+1)^{n+1}$ and claim $a_{n+1}/a_n=1/(n+1)$, so my subsequent bound is based on the wrong ratio.
Since $(1+1/n)^n\ge2$, I say its reciprocal is also at least $1/2$ and use that lower bound as though it forced $a_n$ down to zero.

CALC1:010627.title: Let geometric decay dominate a polynomial factor
CALC1:010627.objective: Apply the Ratio Test to a positive polynomial-over-geometric series, simplify the consecutive-term quotient, compute its limit, and separate convergence of the series from the limit of its terms.
CALC1:010627.statement:
Determine whether
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{3^n}
\]
converges or diverges. Use the Ratio Test, simplify $a_{n+1}/a_n$ completely, state the test's conclusion from the limiting ratio, and explain why merely observing $a_n\to0$ would not by itself prove convergence. Do not compute the sum.
permittedResults: The elementary limit $(n+1)/n=1+1/n\to1$ controls the polynomial part of the ratio.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the Ratio Test and let the exponential cancellation expose a fixed factor one third.
As an alternative check, bound $n^2$ by a slower geometric factor for sufficiently large $n$ and compare with a convergent geometric series.

milestones.criterion: Forms and simplifies the consecutive-term quotient without losing the geometric factor.
Computes the limiting ratio as one third and invokes the correct branch of the Ratio Test.
States absolute convergence and distinguishes that proof from the insufficient term limit alone.

commonErrors.description: Cancels three to the n plus one against three to the n without retaining the factor one third.
commonErrors.consequence: The limiting ratio is computed as one instead of one third and the test is misapplied.

commonErrors.description: Concludes convergence solely from the fact that n squared over three to the n approaches zero.
commonErrors.consequence: A necessary condition is falsely treated as sufficient.

hintTree.content: Cancel the powers of three to obtain $(1/3)((n+1)/n)^2$.
Compare the limiting ratio with one, then state exactly what the Ratio Test proves.

CALC1:010627.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
a_n=\frac{n^2}{3^n}>0.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}
&=\frac{(n+1)^2}{3^{n+1}}\frac{3^n}{n^2}\\
&=\frac13\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^2\\
&=\frac13\left(1+\frac1n\right)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|
=\frac13(1)^2
=\frac13<1.
\]
By the Ratio Test,
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{3^n}
\text{ converges absolutely}}.
\]
The individual terms do tend to zero, but that is only a necessary condition for series convergence. For example, harmonic-series terms also tend to zero. Here the limiting ratio $L=1/3<1$ supplies the sufficient convergence argument.

I cancel $3^{n+1}$ with $3^n$ completely and lose the remaining factor $1/3$, so I get ratio limit $1$ rather than $1/3$.
I note that $n^2/3^n\to0$ and immediately declare the series convergent, using the converse of the nth-term divergence test.

CALC1:010628.title: Bracket a positive-series tail with two improper integrals
CALC1:010628.objective: Verify Integral Test hypotheses for a rational positive series, prove convergence, derive the two-sided remainder estimate with correct shifted index, and evaluate exact bounds for a specified partial sum.
CALC1:010628.statement:
Consider
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2+1}.
\]
Use the Integral Test to prove convergence. If $S_{10}$ is the sum through $n=10$ and $R_{10}$ is the remaining tail, use the Integral Test remainder theorem to give exact lower and upper bounds for $R_{10}$. State the positivity, continuity, and monotonicity checks for the comparison function and keep the lower-bound index shift correct.
permittedResults: An antiderivative of $1/(1+x^2)$ is $\arctan x$, and $\lim_{x\to\infty}\arctan x=\pi/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the decreasing-rectangle geometry behind the Integral Test to bracket the tail by adjacent integrals.
Quote the remainder theorem after verifying its hypotheses, then evaluate both arctangent improper integrals exactly.

milestones.criterion: Verifies every Integral Test hypothesis and evaluates the convergence integral correctly.
States the two-sided remainder theorem with the correct N plus one lower endpoint and N upper endpoint.
Evaluates exact bounds for the tenth remainder and reports correct orientation and optional decimals.

commonErrors.description: Uses the integral starting at N for the lower bound or starts both bounds at the same index.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed interval need not bracket the discrete remainder.

commonErrors.description: Claims the comparison function is increasing or computes its derivative with the wrong sign while invoking a decreasing-function theorem.
commonErrors.consequence: A required Integral Test and remainder hypothesis is not established.

hintTree.content: Use $f(x)=1/(x^2+1)$ for $x\ge1$ and compute $f'(x)$.
Convergence follows from $\int_1^{\infty}f(x)dx=\pi/4$.
For $N=10$, the lower integral starts at $11$ and the upper integral starts at $10$.

CALC1:010628.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac1{x^2+1},\qquad x\ge1.
\]
This function is continuous and positive on $[1,\infty)$. Moreover,
\[
f'(x)=-\frac{2x}{(x^2+1)^2}<0
\qquad(x\ge1),
\]
so it is decreasing. Its improper integral converges:
\[
\int_1^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+1}
=\lim_{b\to\infty}[\arctan x]_1^b
=\frac\pi2-\frac\pi4
=\frac\pi4.
\]
The Integral Test therefore proves that the series converges.

For the remainder
\[
R_{10}=\sum_{n=11}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2+1},
\]
the remainder theorem gives
\[
\int_{11}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+1}
\le R_{10}\le
\int_{10}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+1}.
\]
Evaluating the integrals,
\[
\boxed{
\frac\pi2-\arctan(11)
\le R_{10}\le
\frac\pi2-\arctan(10)}.
\]
Equivalently, because the arguments are positive,
\[
\boxed{\arctan\!\left(\frac1{11}\right)
\le R_{10}\le
\arctan\!\left(\frac1{10}\right)}.
\]
Numerically, this is approximately
\[
0.09066\le R_{10}\le0.09967.
\]
The shift to $11=N+1$ belongs to the lower integral; using $10$ for both sides would not bracket the discrete tail correctly.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $f(x)=1/(x^2+1)$, $f'<0$ and $\int_1^\infty f=\pi/4$, so the series converges. The tail satisfies $\pi/2-\arctan11\le R_{10}\le\pi/2-\arctan10$.
I use $\int_{10}^{\infty}f$ as the lower bound and also as the upper bound, omitting the required lower-bound shift to $N+1=11$.
I compute $f'(x)=2x/(x^2+1)^2>0$ and call the function increasing, yet still invoke the Integral Test remainder theorem that requires a decreasing function.

CALC1:010629.title: Find the full interval and sum of a shifted geometric series
CALC1:010629.objective: Identify a shifted geometric ratio, solve its strict convergence inequality, test both endpoints, and derive the sum function on the valid interval.
CALC1:010629.statement:
Analyze
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{x-2}{5}\right)^n.
\]
Let $r$ denote the geometric ratio. Find the exact interval of convergence, test both endpoints explicitly, and simplify the sum on that interval. Explain why a non-strict ratio inequality gives the wrong endpoints.
permittedResults: Ratios one and negative one both produce term sequences that fail to approach zero.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the geometric theorem and audit endpoints.
Solve in the ratio variable before mapping back to x.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the ratio and strict interval.
Tests both endpoints by their terms.
Simplifies the sum and states its domain.

commonErrors.description: Includes endpoints because the ratio magnitude is at most one.
commonErrors.consequence: The interval contains divergent endpoint series.

commonErrors.description: Simplifies one over one minus r with the wrong sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The sum function is incorrect.

hintTree.content: Solve $|r|<1$.
Write the actual series at each endpoint.

CALC1:010629.canonicalSolution:
The ratio is $r=(x-2)/5$. Convergence requires
\[
\left|\frac{x-2}{5}\right|<1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\boxed{-3<x<7}.
\]
At $x=7$, $r=1$ and the terms remain one. At $x=-3$, $r=-1$ and the terms alternate between one and negative one. Neither endpoint series has terms tending to zero, so both diverge.

Inside the interval,
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty r^n
=\frac1{1-r}
=\boxed{\frac5{7-x}}.
\]
Magnitude must be strictly below one; equality produces the two divergent endpoints just checked.

graderFixtures.proofText: The ratio $(x-2)/5$ has magnitude below $1$ exactly for $-3<x<7$. Both endpoints diverge at ratios $-1$ and $1$, and the sum inside is $5/(7-x)$.
I use $|r|\le1$ and include both endpoints even though their terms are $(-1)^n$ and $1$.
I simplify $1/[1-(x-2)/5]$ as $5/(x+3)$, using the wrong sign.

CALC1:010631.title: Locate the largest term of an nth-root sequence
CALC1:010631.objective: Analyze a discrete sequence through a logarithmic continuous extension, distinguish a real-variable critical point from neighboring integer indices, prove the largest term by an exact comparison, and classify an exact threshold set.
CALC1:010631.statement:
For positive integers $n$, let
\[
a_n=n^{1/n}.
\]
Find the largest term of the sequence and prove that it is largest. Use the continuous logarithmic extension to locate the only real-variable turning point, but explicitly compare the relevant neighboring integer terms rather than rounding the critical point. Then determine exactly which positive integers satisfy
\[
a_n\ge\sqrt2.
\]
Justify both the included indices and the exclusion of every later index.
permittedResults: The derivative $g'(x)=(1-\ln x)/x^2$ is positive for $0<x<e$ and negative for $x>e$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Analyze log x divided by x and then return to the discrete indices.
Compare the neighboring integer candidates exactly, then use monotonicity on $x>e$ to classify the threshold tail.

milestones.criterion: Uses the logarithmic continuous extension and derives its monotonicity intervals.
Reduces to and exactly compares the neighboring maximum candidates.
Checks the threshold boundary indices and uses tail monotonicity to classify exactly two, three, and four.

commonErrors.description: Rounds the real maximizer e to three and declares the discrete maximum without comparing the neighboring integer terms.
commonErrors.consequence: A continuous critical point alone does not decide which adjacent integer term is larger.

commonErrors.description: Assumes a larger integer base always produces a larger nth-root term and includes every n at least two in the threshold set.
commonErrors.consequence: The continuous extension is decreasing after e, so the claimed tail classification is false.

hintTree.content: Study $g(x)=\ln x/x$ instead of differentiating $x^{1/x}$ directly.
Since $2<e<3$, monotonicity leaves $n=2$ and $n=3$ as the only neighboring maximum candidates.
For the threshold, compute $a_2$, $a_3$, and $a_4$, then use decrease on $x>e$ to control all $n\ge5$.

CALC1:010631.canonicalSolution:
For $x>0$, define
\[
g(x)=\ln(x^{1/x})=\frac{\ln x}{x}.
\]
Because the exponential is strictly increasing, $x^{1/x}$ and $g(x)$ have the same order. Differentiate:
\[
g'(x)=\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}.
\]
Thus $g$ increases on $(0,e)$ and decreases on $(e,\infty)$. Since $2<e<3$, the largest integer-indexed term must be either $a_2$ or $a_3$; one may not simply round $e$ without comparing them. Both values are positive, and
\[
(a_2)^6=(\sqrt2)^6=8,
\qquad
(a_3)^6=(\sqrt[3]3)^6=9.
\]
Hence $a_3>a_2$. Also $a_1=1<a_3$, and monotonic decrease for real $x>e$ gives $a_n<a_3$ for every integer $n\ge4$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{a_3=\sqrt[3]3\text{ is the largest term}}.
\]

For the threshold, direct evaluation gives
\[
a_1=1<\sqrt2,\qquad
a_2=\sqrt2,\qquad
a_4=\sqrt[4]4=\sqrt2.
\]
The sixth-power comparison above shows $a_3>\sqrt2$. Finally, every integer $n\ge5$ lies to the right of $4>e$, where the continuous extension is strictly decreasing, so
\[
a_n<a_4=\sqrt2\qquad(n\ge5).
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{a_n\ge\sqrt2\text{ exactly for }n\in\{2,3,4\}}.
\]
The derivative locates the real turning point, but exact comparisons and integer-index reasoning are what settle both discrete claims.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $g(x)=\ln x/x$, $g'=(1-\ln x)/x^2$, so only $n=2,3$ need comparison for the maximum; sixth powers $8<9$ make $a_3$ largest. Also $a_2=a_4=\sqrt2$, $a_3>\sqrt2$, and decrease after $e$ excludes $n\ge5$, giving exactly $\{2,3,4\}$.
The continuous maximum occurs at $x=e$, so I round $e$ to $3$ and call $a_3$ largest without comparing the adjacent integer terms $a_2$ and $a_3$.
Because the base $n$ grows, I claim $n^{1/n}$ grows too and include every $n\ge2$ in the set where $a_n\ge\sqrt2$, ignoring the derivative's decreasing tail after $e$.

CALC1:010632.objective: Factor every term of a finite product, split it into two telescoping products with correct endpoints, derive a closed formula for the partial-product sequence, and use that formula to prove monotonicity and convergence.
CALC1:010632.statement:
For integers $n\ge2$, define the finite-product sequence
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=2}^{n}\left(1-\frac1{k^2}\right).
\]
Factor each term and derive a closed formula for $P_n$ by displaying both telescoping products and their uncanceled endpoints. Then prove that $(P_n)$ is strictly decreasing and bounded below, and find its limit. Explain why the fact that each individual factor tends to $1$ does not by itself determine the product limit.
permittedResults: A decreasing sequence bounded below converges; an explicit closed formula may then identify its limit.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the difference-of-squares factorization into two telescoping chains.
Prove the closed form by induction from $P_{n+1}=P_n[1-1/(n+1)^2]$, then analyze it.

milestones.criterion: Factors each term and splits the product without losing an endpoint factor.
Telescopes both products to the correct closed formula.
Uses the formula to prove monotonicity, boundedness, and the exact limit.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the second telescoping product to n plus one instead of n plus one over two, losing its initial denominator two.
commonErrors.consequence: The closed formula and limit are doubled.

commonErrors.description: Says every factor tends to one, so the growing finite product sequence must tend to one.
commonErrors.consequence: A limit law for a fixed number of factors is misapplied to products whose length grows.

hintTree.content: Split the product into $\prod_{k=2}^n(k-1)/k$ and $\prod_{k=2}^n(k+1)/k$.
The first product is $1/n$ and the second is $(n+1)/2$.

CALC1:010632.canonicalSolution:
For every $k\ge2$,
\[
1-\frac1{k^2}
=\frac{(k-1)(k+1)}{k^2}
=\frac{k-1}{k}\frac{k+1}{k}.
\]
Thus
\[
P_n=\left(\prod_{k=2}^{n}\frac{k-1}{k}\right)
\left(\prod_{k=2}^{n}\frac{k+1}{k}\right).
\]
Writing the endpoints makes the cancellations unambiguous:
\[
\prod_{k=2}^{n}\frac{k-1}{k}
=\frac12\frac23\cdots\frac{n-1}{n}=\frac1n,
\]
whereas
\[
\prod_{k=2}^{n}\frac{k+1}{k}
=\frac32\frac43\cdots\frac{n+1}{n}=\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{P_n=\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac12+\frac1{2n}}.
\]
This formula shows directly that $P_{n+1}<P_n$ for every $n\ge2$ and that $P_n>1/2$, so the sequence is strictly decreasing and bounded below. It also gives
\[
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n=\frac12}.
\]
Although each new factor tends to $1$, the number of factors grows with $n$. Limits of individual factors therefore cannot simply be multiplied as though the product had a fixed finite length; the telescoping calculation controls the whole sequence.

graderFixtures.proofText: Factoring gives $P_n=[(1/2)(2/3)\cdots((n-1)/n)][(3/2)(4/3)\cdots((n+1)/n)]=(1/n)((n+1)/2)=(n+1)/(2n)$. Hence it decreases to $1/2$.
I telescope the second chain $(3/2)(4/3)\cdots((n+1)/n)$ to $n+1$, dropping the uncanceled initial denominator $2$, so my formula is twice too large.
Since each factor $1-1/k^2$ tends to $1$, I claim the product sequence also tends to $1$ without controlling the growing number of factors.

CALC1:010633.title: Discover and prove the exact form of a reciprocal recurrence
CALC1:010633.objective: Generate initial terms of a rational recurrence, formulate an exact closed form, prove it by induction while controlling reciprocals, and derive monotonicity and convergence from the formula rather than a fixed-point guess.
CALC1:010633.statement:
Let
\[
a_1=2,
\qquad
a_{n+1}=2-\frac1{a_n}\quad(n\ge1).
\]
Compute the first four terms, conjecture a formula for $a_n$, and prove it by induction. Use the proved formula to show that the recurrence is well-defined for every $n$, determine whether the sequence is increasing or decreasing, and find its limit. A fixed-point equation by itself does not count as a convergence proof.
permittedResults: A proved identity $a_n=1+1/n$ immediately supplies positivity, monotonicity, and the limit through elementary sequence laws.

acceptableStrategies.description: Guess from initial terms and prove the rational formula directly by induction.
After verifying denominators, set $b_n=1/(a_n-1)$, derive a simple linear recurrence for $b_n$, and translate back.

milestones.criterion: Computes the pattern and states the correct indexed closed form.
Proves the formula by induction with correct reciprocal algebra and well-definedness.
Uses the formula to establish strict decrease and convergence to one.

commonErrors.description: Inverts (n plus one) over n as itself instead of n over n plus one in the induction step.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed formula is not preserved by the recurrence.

commonErrors.description: Solves the limiting fixed-point equation and declares convergence without proving a formula or another convergence criterion.
commonErrors.consequence: A necessary equation for a hypothetical limit is mistaken for an existence proof.

hintTree.content: The first terms are $2,3/2,4/3,5/4$.
Assume $a_n=(n+1)/n$ and invert that fraction carefully.
Compare $1+1/(n+1)$ with $1+1/n$.

CALC1:010633.canonicalSolution:
The recurrence gives
\[
a_1=2,
\qquad
a_2=2-\frac12=\frac32,
\qquad
a_3=2-\frac{2}{3}=\frac43,
\qquad
a_4=2-\frac34=\frac54.
\]
This suggests
\[
\boxed{a_n=\frac{n+1}{n}=1+\frac1n}.
\]
We prove the formula by induction. It holds at $n=1$. Suppose it holds at an arbitrary positive integer $n$. Then $a_n=(n+1)/n$ is nonzero, and
\[
a_{n+1}=2-\frac1{a_n}
=2-\frac{n}{n+1}
=\frac{2n+2-n}{n+1}
=\frac{n+2}{n+1}.
\]
This is exactly the proposed formula with $n+1$ in place of $n$. Induction proves it for every $n\ge1$. The same proof also confirms at each stage that the denominator in the recurrence is nonzero; indeed $a_n>1$.

Because
\[
a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac1{n+1}-\frac1n=-\frac1{n(n+1)}<0,
\]
the sequence is strictly decreasing. Finally,
\[
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac1n\right)=1}.
\]
Solving $L=2-1/L$ only identifies $L=1$ as a possible limit; the exact formula supplies the missing existence proof.

graderFixtures.proofText: The terms $2,3/2,4/3,5/4$ suggest $a_n=(n+1)/n$. If true at $n$, then $a_{n+1}=2-n/(n+1)=(n+2)/(n+1)$, proving it. Hence $a_n>1$, decreases because $1/n$ decreases, and tends to $1$.
Assuming $a_n=(n+1)/n$, I also use $1/a_n=(n+1)/n$ instead of inverting it, so my induction update does not produce the next indexed fraction.
I solve $L=2-1/L$ to get $L=1$ and call that equation alone a proof that the recursively defined sequence converges.

CALC1:010634.title: Control an integral-defined sequence two different ways
CALC1:010634.objective: Use an integrand comparison to prove monotonicity and convergence of a sequence of integrals, derive an exact neighboring-term recurrence, and use that recurrence to compute early terms without evaluating each integral anew.
CALC1:010634.statement:
For integers $n\ge0$, define
\[
b_n=\int_0^1\frac{x^n}{1+x}\,dx.
\]
Prove that $(b_n)$ is positive and strictly decreasing. Establish a direct bound that determines $\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n$. Then prove
\[
b_n+b_{n+1}=\frac1{n+1}
\]
and use $b_0=\ln2$ to compute $b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ exactly. Do not justify the limit merely by interchanging a pointwise limit and an integral.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare and bound the integrands first, then add neighboring fractions to derive the recurrence.
Use polynomial division identities for finite n to compute individual terms, while still proving the general bound and recurrence.

milestones.criterion: Proves positivity and strict decrease by comparing integrands.
Uses a direct squeeze bound to establish the limit without an unjustified interchange.
Derives the recurrence and computes all three requested exact terms.

commonErrors.description: Adds b n and b n plus one but fails to cancel the common factor one plus x in the combined numerator.
commonErrors.consequence: The neighboring-term recurrence is wrong.

commonErrors.description: States that x to the n tends to zero pointwise and therefore the integrals tend to zero, with no bound or convergence theorem.
commonErrors.consequence: Pointwise convergence alone does not justify passage of a limit through an integral.

hintTree.content: Compare the integrands for consecutive indices on the open interval $(0,1)$.
Bound $1/(1+x)$ above by $1$ and integrate $x^n$.
Add the two neighboring integrands before integrating.

CALC1:010634.canonicalSolution:
For $0<x<1$, the integrand $x^n/(1+x)$ is positive, so $b_n>0$. Also
\[
\frac{x^{n+1}}{1+x}<\frac{x^n}{1+x}
\qquad(0<x<1).
\]
The strict inequality holds on an interval of positive length, so integration gives
\[
\boxed{b_{n+1}<b_n}.
\]
For a direct limit bound, use $1/(1+x)\le1$:
\[
0<b_n\le\int_0^1x^n\,dx=\frac1{n+1}.
\]
The squeeze theorem therefore gives
\[
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n=0}.
\]
This bound is a valid uniform integral estimate; no unsupported interchange of limit and integral is needed.

For the recurrence, add before integrating:
\[
b_n+b_{n+1}
=\int_0^1\frac{x^n+x^{n+1}}{1+x}\,dx
=\int_0^1x^n\,dx
=\boxed{\frac1{n+1}}.
\]
Since
\[
b_0=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x}=\ln2,
\]
successive recurrence steps yield
\[
b_1=1-b_0=\boxed{1-\ln2},
\]
\[
b_2=\frac12-b_1=\boxed{\ln2-\frac12},
\]
and
\[
b_3=\frac13-b_2=\boxed{\frac56-\ln2}.
\]
All three values are positive and decreasing, consistent with the comparison proof.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $(0,1)$ the next integrand is strictly smaller, and $0<b_n\le\int_0^1x^n dx=1/(n+1)$, so $b_n\downarrow0$. Adding gives $b_n+b_{n+1}=\int_0^1x^n dx=1/(n+1)$. Thus $b_1=1-\ln2$, $b_2=\ln2-1/2$, and $b_3=5/6-\ln2$.
I add the two fractions but keep an extra denominator $1+x$ instead of cancelling $x^n(1+x)/(1+x)$, so I do not obtain $1/(n+1)$.
Because $x^n\to0$ for each $x$ in $[0,1)$, I immediately move the limit through the integral and conclude $b_n\to0$ without supplying a bound or valid interchange theorem.

CALC1:010635.title: Make an arctangent series telescope without losing its branch
CALC1:010635.objective: Prove a branch-safe inverse-tangent difference identity, telescope the associated series exactly, and derive an explicit positive remainder and quantitative tail guarantee.
CALC1:010635.statement:
For $n\ge1$, consider
$$
a_n=\arctan\!\left(\frac1{n^2+n+1}\right).
$$
Prove carefully, including the inverse-tangent branch justification, that
$$
a_n=\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n.
$$
Use this identity to find the exact partial sum $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n$, the infinite sum, and an exact expression for the remainder $R_N=S-S_N$. Prove $0<R_N<1/(N+1)$, find the smallest integer $N$ for which this bound alone guarantees $R_N<0.01$, and give $S_4$ in exact telescoped form.
permittedResults: $\tan(A-B)=(\tan A-\tan B)/(1+\tan A\tan B)$, and $0<\arctan u<u$ for $u>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert each term to a difference of consecutive inverse tangents, then cancel adjacent terms.
Start from the proposed consecutive angles, compute their tangent difference, and use monotonicity to certify the branch.

milestones.criterion: Proves the arctangent difference identity with an explicit principal-branch argument.
Telescopes correctly to exact partial and infinite sums.
Derives the exact remainder, proves its bound, and applies that bound sharply to the tolerance and fourth partial sum.

commonErrors.description: Uses the tangent subtraction formula and immediately applies arctangent without proving the angle difference lies in the principal range.
commonErrors.consequence: Tangent identities determine angles only modulo pi unless the branch is controlled.

commonErrors.description: Writes the tail as arctangent of one over N rather than one over N plus one.
commonErrors.consequence: The remainder does not match the exact telescoped partial sum and gives the wrong tolerance index.

hintTree.content: Take $A=\arctan(n+1)$ and $B=\arctan n$.
Both angles lie in $(0,\pi/2)$, and their difference lies in $(0,\pi/2)$, so no multiple of $\pi$ is introduced.
Use $\pi/2-\arctan y=\arctan(1/y)$ for $y>0$ to express the remainder.

CALC1:010635.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$
A=\arctan(n+1),\qquad B=\arctan n.
$$
Since $n+1>n>0$, we have $0<B<A<\pi/2$, hence
$$
0<A-B<\pi/2.
$$
The tangent difference formula gives
$$
\tan(A-B)
=\frac{(n+1)-n}{1+n(n+1)}
=\frac1{n^2+n+1}.
$$
Because $A-B$ is already in the principal range of arctangent,
$$
\boxed{a_n=A-B=\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n}.
$$
The branch check rules out adding or subtracting $\pi$.

Now the partial sum telescopes:
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_N
&=\sum_{n=1}^N[\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n]\\
&=\arctan(N+1)-\arctan1\\
&=\boxed{\arctan(N+1)-\frac\pi4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
As $N\to\infty$, $\arctan(N+1)\to\pi/2$, so
$$
\boxed{S=\frac\pi4}.
$$
The remainder is
$$
R_N=S-S_N
=\frac\pi2-\arctan(N+1)
=\boxed{\arctan\!\left(\frac1{N+1}\right)}.
$$
The reciprocal identity is branch-safe because both sides lie in $(0,\pi/2)$. Since $0<\arctan u<u$ for $u>0$,
$$
\boxed{0<R_N<\frac1{N+1}}.
$$
For this bound alone to guarantee $R_N<0.01$, it is enough that
$$
\frac1{N+1}\le0.01,
$$
because the remainder inequality is already strict. This first occurs at
$$
\boxed{N=99}.
$$
Finally,
$$
\boxed{S_4=\arctan5-\frac\pi4}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: For $A=\arctan(n+1)>B=\arctan n$, $0<A-B<\pi/2$ and $\tan(A-B)=1/(n^2+n+1)$, so the identity is branch-safe. Thus $S_N=\arctan(N+1)-\pi/4$, $S=\pi/4$, and $R_N=\arctan(1/(N+1))<1/(N+1)$. The bound first guarantees $0.01$ at $N=99$, and $S_4=\arctan5-\pi/4$.
I apply arctangent to the tangent-difference equation and declare the angles equal without checking whether their difference is in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ or could differ by $\pi$.
After telescoping I write $R_N=\arctan(1/N)$, shifting the remaining endpoint from $N+1$ to $N$, and therefore choose the wrong cutoff.

CALC1:010636.title: Find the sharp parameter threshold for a cosine series
CALC1:010636.objective: Use a small-angle limit comparison to classify a positive parameter family, treat the boundary case explicitly, and derive a usable integral tail bound in the convergent regime.
CALC1:010636.statement:
For a real parameter $p>0$, study
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(1-\cos\frac1{n^p}\right).
$$
Determine exactly which $p$ make the series converge. Your proof must use a limit comparison and must discuss the threshold value separately rather than hiding it inside a general statement. For every convergent $p$, derive an explicit upper bound for
$$
R_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\left(1-\cos\frac1{n^p}\right)
$$
using $1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ and an integral comparison. State the bound with all constants, and specialize it to $p=1$.
permittedResults: $\lim_{u\to0}(1-\cos u)/u^2=1/2$, and $\sum n^{-q}$ converges exactly when $q>1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Translate the small cosine difference into a power term through its standard quadratic limit.
Use a global cosine upper inequality for the tail and then apply the decreasing-function integral estimate.

milestones.criterion: Performs the correct small-angle limit comparison and identifies the exact parameter threshold.
Treats the boundary p equals one half and the lower positive range explicitly.
Combines the cosine inequality and integral comparison to derive the complete constant-sensitive remainder bound.

commonErrors.description: Compares one minus cosine of n to the negative p with n to the negative p instead of its square.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting threshold p greater than one is not supported by the small-angle behavior.

commonErrors.description: Uses one minus cosine u at most u squared but then states the sharper bound as if the required factor one half were still present.
commonErrors.consequence: The displayed remainder constant does not follow from the inequality actually used and is numerically inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Compare the term with $n^{-2p}$.
At $p=1/2$, the comparison series is the harmonic series.
For $p>1/2$, bound $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty n^{-2p}$ by $\int_N^\infty x^{-2p}\,dx$.

CALC1:010636.canonicalSolution:
Set
$$
a_n=1-\cos(n^{-p}),\qquad b_n=n^{-2p}.
$$
Since $p>0$, $n^{-p}\to0$. With $u=n^{-p}$,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{1-\cos(n^{-p})}{(n^{-p})^2}
=\frac12.
$$
This is finite and strictly positive, so limit comparison shows that the given series has the same behavior as
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^{2p}}.
$$
The latter converges exactly when $2p>1$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\text{the cosine series converges exactly for }p>\frac12}.
$$
At the threshold $p=1/2$, the comparison is with $\sum1/n$, so the series diverges. For $0<p<1/2$, the comparison $p$-series also diverges.

Now suppose $p>1/2$. The inequality $1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ gives
$$
0<R_N
\le\frac12\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^{2p}}.
$$
Because $x^{-2p}$ is positive and decreasing,
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^{2p}}
\le\int_N^\infty x^{-2p}\,dx
=\frac{N^{1-2p}}{2p-1}.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{0<R_N\le
\frac{N^{1-2p}}{2(2p-1)}}.
$$
All constants are retained: the factor $1/2$ comes from the cosine inequality.

For $p=1$, this becomes
$$
\boxed{0<R_N\le\frac1{2N}}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: Since $[1-\cos(n^{-p})]/n^{-2p}\to1/2$, limit comparison gives convergence exactly when $2p>1$, namely $p>1/2$; at $p=1/2$ it diverges with the harmonic series. For $p>1/2$, $R_N\le\frac12\sum_{n>N}n^{-2p}\le N^{1-2p}/[2(2p-1)]$, which is $1/(2N)$ for $p=1$.
I compare $1-\cos(n^{-p})$ with $n^{-p}$ instead of $n^{-2p}$, so I announce the false threshold $p>1$.
I cite $1-\cos u\le u^2$ and then claim $R_N\le N^{1-2p}/[2(2p-1)]$, inserting a factor $1/2$ that my stated inequality did not provide.

CALC1:010637.title: Track the moving root of a power equation
CALC1:010637.objective: Define a sequence through unique nonlinear roots, compare successive defining functions, and prove a non-obvious limiting value without informal infinite exponents.
CALC1:010637.statement:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \(a_n\) be the solution in \((0,1)\) of
$$
a_n^n+a_n=1.
$$
First prove that this solution exists and is unique for every \(n\). Compute \(a_1\) and \(a_2\). Then prove that \((a_n)\) is strictly increasing and determine its limit. Your limit argument must control the varying powers \(a_n^n\); do not use the undefined expression \(L^\infty\).
permittedResults: A continuous strictly increasing function that changes sign across an interval has exactly one zero there.
Every increasing sequence bounded above converges.

acceptableStrategies.description: Turn the implicit definition into a family of increasing root functions.
After obtaining convergence, replace the varying base by one fixed number below one in the contradiction case.

milestones.criterion: Proves each defining equation has exactly one root in the required interval and computes the first two.
Compares successive defining functions at the prior root to prove strict increase.
Uses monotone convergence plus a fixed geometric bound to establish the limit rigorously.

commonErrors.description: Writes \(a_n^n\to L^\infty\) and declares this to be zero without any uniform bound on the changing bases.
commonErrors.consequence: The exponent and base vary together, so a fixed geometric comparison is required when testing a proposed limit below one.

commonErrors.description: Finds \(\phi_{n+1}(a_n)<0\) but concludes \(a_{n+1}<a_n\).
commonErrors.consequence: Because the defining function is increasing, a negative value lies to the left of its zero, so the new root is larger.

hintTree.content: Check \(\phi_n(0)\), \(\phi_n(1)\), and \(\phi_n'(x)\).
Evaluate \(\phi_{n+1}\) at the old root \(a_n\), then use the fact that \(\phi_{n+1}\) is increasing.
If the limit were below \(1\), bound all \(a_n\) by a fixed \(q<1\) and use \(1-a_n=a_n^n\).

CALC1:010637.canonicalSolution:
Fix \(n\ge1\) and set
$$
\phi_n(x)=x^n+x-1.
$$
This function is continuous on \([0,1]\), with
$$
\phi_n(0)=-1,
\qquad
\phi_n(1)=1.
$$
The Intermediate Value Theorem gives a zero in \((0,1)\). Moreover,
$$
\phi_n'(x)=nx^{n-1}+1>0
$$
there, so the zero is unique.

$$

$$
For \(n=2\), the positive root of \(x^2+x-1=0\) is
$$
\boxed{a_2=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}}.
$$

At the old root,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{n+1}(a_n)
&=\phi_n(a_n)+a_n^{n+1}-a_n^n\\
&=a_n^n(a_n-1)<0.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since \(\phi_{n+1}\) is strictly increasing and vanishes at \(a_{n+1}\), this negative value occurs to the left of its root. Therefore
$$
\boxed{a_{n+1}>a_n}.
$$
The sequence is strictly increasing and bounded above by \(1\), so it converges to some \(L\le1\).

Suppose for contradiction that \(L<1\). Choose a fixed number \(q\) with \(L<q<1\). Because \(a_n\le L<q\) for every \(n\), the defining equation gives
$$
0<1-a_n=a_n^n\le q^n\longrightarrow0.
$$
Taking limits would give \(1-L=0\), contradicting \(L<1\). Hence
$$
\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=1}.
$$

CALC1:010638.title: Squeeze an arithmetic-harmonic iteration to its invariant
CALC1:010638.objective: Analyze two coupled mean sequences using order, monotonicity, an invariant product, and a quantitative gap contraction.
CALC1:010638.statement:
Start with \(a_1=4\) and \(b_1=1\). For \(n\ge1\), define
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2},
\qquad
b_{n+1}=\frac{2a_nb_n}{a_n+b_n}.
$$
Compute \(a_2,b_2\). Prove that both sequences converge to the same limit, and find that limit. Your proof must establish positivity and order, monotonicity, a preserved product, and a quantitative bound for \(a_n-b_n\). Using your bound, give the first index \(n\) for which the bound itself guarantees \(a_n-b_n<0.01\).
permittedResults: For positive \(a\ge b\), the harmonic mean is at least \(b\), the arithmetic mean is at most \(a\), and the arithmetic mean is at least the harmonic mean.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the updates as the arithmetic and harmonic means of the current ordered pair.
Use the invariant to identify the common limit only after the shrinking gap proves the limits agree.

milestones.criterion: Establishes positivity, order, and the two monotonic directions by induction.
Finds the preserved product and proves the quantitative contraction bound for the gap.
Uses the vanishing gap and invariant to obtain the common positive limit and correctly solves the threshold guarantee.

commonErrors.description: Assumes \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) approach the same number merely because both converge, then uses the product to state the answer.
commonErrors.consequence: Separate monotone convergence does not force equal limits; the gap recurrence or another valid squeeze is essential.

commonErrors.description: Uses \(b_{n+1}=a_nb_n/(a_n+b_n)\), omitting the factor \(2\), and still claims \(a_{n+1}b_{n+1}=a_nb_n\).
commonErrors.consequence: The omitted factor destroys the stated recurrence and its product invariant, so every later limit calculation is unsupported.

hintTree.content: Multiply the two recurrence formulas to discover an exact invariant.
Assuming \(a_n\ge b_n>0\), compare each new mean with both old endpoints.
Subtract the recurrences and show \(a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}=(a_n-b_n)^2/[2(a_n+b_n)]\).

CALC1:010638.canonicalSolution:
The first update is
$$
\boxed{a_2=\frac{4+1}{2}=\frac52},
\qquad
\boxed{b_2=\frac{2(4)(1)}{4+1}=\frac85}.
$$
Suppose \(a_n\ge b_n>0\). Both new terms are positive. Also
$$
a_{n+1}-b_n=\frac{a_n-b_n}{2}\ge0,
$$
and
$$
b_{n+1}-b_n
=\frac{b_n(a_n-b_n)}{a_n+b_n}\ge0.
$$
Thus \(b_n\le b_{n+1}\). Similarly \(a_{n+1}\le a_n\). Finally,
$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}
&=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2}-\frac{2a_nb_n}{a_n+b_n}\\
&=\frac{(a_n-b_n)^2}{2(a_n+b_n)}\ge0.
\end{aligned}
$$
Induction therefore preserves
$$
0<b_n\le b_{n+1}\le a_{n+1}\le a_n.
$$
So \(a_n\) decreases and is bounded below, while \(b_n\) increases and is bounded above; both converge.

The product is exactly preserved:
$$
a_{n+1}b_{n+1}
=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2}\frac{2a_nb_n}{a_n+b_n}
=a_nb_n.
$$
Hence
$$
\boxed{a_nb_n=a_1b_1=4}
$$
for every \(n\).

Let \(d_n=a_n-b_n\ge0\). From the difference formula and positivity,
$$
d_{n+1}
=\frac{d_n^2}{2(a_n+b_n)}
\le\frac{d_n^2}{2d_n}
=\frac{d_n}{2}
$$
when \(d_n>0\), while the inequality is automatic if \(d_n=0\). Since \(d_1=3\), induction gives
$$
\boxed{0\le a_n-b_n\le\frac{3}{2^{n-1}}}.
$$
The gap tends to zero, so the two sequence limits are equal; call the common positive limit \(L\). Passing to the product invariant gives
$$
L^2=4,
$$
and positivity selects
$$
\boxed{L=2}.
$$

For the requested guarantee,
$$
\frac{3}{2^{n-1}}<0.01.
$$
At \(n=9\), the bound is \(3/256\approx0.0117188\), which is not small enough. At \(n=10\), it is \(3/512\approx0.00585938\). Thus the first index certified by this bound is
$$
\boxed{n=10}.
$$

Their product stays \(4\). The gap satisfies \(d_{n+1}=d_n^2/[2(a_n+b_n)]\le d_n/2\), so \(d_n\le3/2^{n-1}\to0\). The common positive limit has square \(4\), hence is \(2\). The bound is still above \(0.01\) at \(n=9\) and below it at \(n=10\).
Because both sequences are monotone and bounded, I assume without a gap argument that their two limits are equal, then jump directly from the product to \(L=2\).
I drop the factor two and iterate \(b_{n+1}=a_nb_n/(a_n+b_n)\), yet claim the product remains four even though multiplying my altered recurrences gives only half the old product.

CALC2:010117.title: Keep two divergent logarithms under one cutoff
CALC2:010117.objective: Evaluate a two-parameter improper integral with a common cutoff, handle the coincident-parameter case, and prove that the off-diagonal formula extends continuously to the diagonal.
CALC2:010117.statement:
For $a,b>0$, define
\[
J(a,b)=\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{(x+a)(x+b)}.
\]
First prove that the integral converges. For $a\ne b$, evaluate it by partial fractions, but keep both logarithmic terms under the same upper cutoff. Compute $J(a,a)$ directly. Finally prove that your formula for $a\ne b$ has limit $1/a$ as $b\to a$, and explain why writing it as a difference of two separately evaluated improper integrals is invalid.
permittedResults: If $a>0$, then $\int_0^\infty (x+a)^{-2}\,dx=1/a$.
The derivative of $\ln x$ at $a>0$ is $1/a$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a finite upper cutoff before partial-fraction cancellation.
Treat the diagonal first and then identify the off-diagonal expression as a divided difference of the logarithm.

milestones.criterion: Justifies convergence and evaluates the off-diagonal case with one cutoff.
Computes the diagonal integral and proves continuity in the parameters.
Explains why the separated improper integrals are not legitimate.

commonErrors.description: Assigns finite values to the two divergent logarithmic improper integrals separately and subtracts them.
commonErrors.consequence: The cancellation must occur before the common cutoff tends to infinity.

commonErrors.description: Uses ln(a/b)/(b-a), making the integral negative when b is greater than a.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerator and denominator signs no longer agree for a positive integrand.

hintTree.content: For $a\ne b$, use $\dfrac1{(x+a)(x+b)}=\dfrac1{b-a}\left(\dfrac1{x+a}-\dfrac1{x+b}\right)$.
Evaluate both logarithms from $0$ to the same $R$ before taking a limit.
For the diagonal limit, recognize a difference quotient for $\ln x$.

CALC2:010117.canonicalSolution:
The integrand is continuous at $x=0$ because $a,b>0$, and it is $O(x^{-2})$ as $x\to\infty$, so the improper integral converges.

For $a\ne b$ and a common cutoff $R$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
J_R(a,b)
&=\frac1{b-a}\int_0^R\left(\frac1{x+a}-\frac1{x+b}\right)dx\\
&=\frac1{b-a}\left[\ln(x+a)-\ln(x+b)\right]_0^R\\
&=\frac1{b-a}\ln\!\left(\frac{b(R+a)}{a(R+b)}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $(R+a)/(R+b)\to1$,
\[
\boxed{J(a,b)=\frac{\ln(b/a)}{b-a}\qquad(a\ne b)}.
\]
This quantity is positive: $\ln(b/a)$ and $b-a$ have the same sign.

On the diagonal,
\[
J(a,a)=\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{(x+a)^2}
=\left[-\frac1{x+a}\right]_0^\infty
=\boxed{\frac1a}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\lim_{b\to a}\frac{\ln b-\ln a}{b-a}=(\ln)'(a)=\frac1a,
\]
so the off-diagonal formula has exactly the direct diagonal value.

The two partial-fraction terms cannot be integrated to infinity separately: both $\int_0^\infty dx/(x+a)$ and $\int_0^\infty dx/(x+b)$ diverge. Only their common-cutoff difference has the cancellation that produces the finite logarithmic ratio.

graderFixtures.proofText: With one cutoff, $J_R=(b-a)^{-1}\ln\!\bigl(b(R+a)/(a(R+b))\bigr)$, so $J=\ln(b/a)/(b-a)$. Directly $J(a,a)=1/a$, also the $b\to a$ logarithmic difference-quotient limit. The separated logarithmic integrals each diverge.
I evaluate $\int_0^\infty dx/(x+a)$ and $\int_0^\infty dx/(x+b)$ as if each had a finite logarithmic value, then subtract them without a shared cutoff.
My partial fractions give $J=\ln(a/b)/(b-a)$, which is negative for $b>a$ even though the integrand is positive.

CALC2:010118.title: Turn a reciprocal quartic into one arctangent
CALC2:010118.objective: Use inversion symmetry to average an improper quartic integrand into the exact differential of a global substitution and evaluate the resulting Cauchy integral.
CALC2:010118.statement:
Evaluate
\[
I=\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{x^4+4x^2+1}.
\]
Prove convergence at both endpoints. Apply $x=1/t$ to obtain a second expression for the same $I$, average the two expressions, and then use $u=x-1/x$. Track the limits of $u$ on the full interval $(0,\infty)$.
permittedResults: For $c>0$, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{du}{u^2+c^2}=\pi/c$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Exploit invariance of the positive half-line under reciprocal substitution.
Search for x minus reciprocal x after seeing a reciprocal quartic.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the integral correctly under reciprocal substitution.
Averages the two forms and matches the complete differential for u.
Tracks the infinite limits and evaluates the final arctangent integral.

commonErrors.description: After x equals one over t, keeps the original numerator one instead of the required t squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The averaged numerator and the later differential are then wrong.

commonErrors.description: Maps u=x-1/x from zero to infinity instead of from negative infinity to positive infinity.
commonErrors.consequence: Half of the transformed integral is omitted.

hintTree.content: Inverting gives $I=\int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^2\,dx}{x^4+4x^2+1}$.
The denominator equals $x^2[(x-1/x)^2+6]$.
For $u=x-1/x$, $du=(1+1/x^2)dx$ and the new limits are $-\infty$ and $+\infty$.

CALC2:010118.canonicalSolution:
Near zero the integrand is bounded, and as $x\to\infty$ it is $O(x^{-4})$, so the integral converges.

Under $x=1/t$,
\[
I=\int_0^\infty\frac{t^2\,dt}{t^4+4t^2+1}.
\]
Renaming the variable and adding this to the original form gives
\[
2I=\int_0^\infty\frac{1+x^2}{x^4+4x^2+1}\,dx.
\]
Now
\[
x^4+4x^2+1=x^2\left[\left(x-\frac1x\right)^2+6\right]
\]
and, for $u=x-1/x$,
\[
du=\left(1+\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=\frac{1+x^2}{x^2}\,dx.
\]
Therefore
\[
2I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{du}{u^2+6}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt6}.
\]
The limit conversion is global: $u\to-\infty$ as $x\to0^+$, $u=0$ at $x=1$, and $u\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. Hence
\[
\boxed{I=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt6}}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: Reciprocal substitution gives the x-squared numerator form. Averaging yields $2I=\int_0^\infty(1+x^2)/(x^4+4x^2+1)dx$. With $u=x-1/x$, this is $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}du/(u^2+6)=\pi/\sqrt6$, so $I=\pi/(2\sqrt6)$.
When I set $x=1/t$, I forget the Jacobian and claim the transformed integrand still has numerator $1$, so the averaging step cannot produce $1+x^2$.
I take $u=x-1/x$ to run from $0$ to $\infty$ as $x$ runs from $0$ to $\infty$, losing the entire negative-u half.
