CALC2:010119.title: Move exponents across a beta-integral lattice
CALC2:010119.objective: Derive an integration-by-parts reduction for a two-index family, audit the endpoint term and base case, obtain a factorial formula, and use it to evaluate a nontrivial definite integral exactly.
CALC2:010119.statement:
For nonnegative integers $m,n$, define
$$
I_{m,n}=\int_0^1x^m(1-x)^n\,dx.
$$
For $m\ge1$, derive a recurrence that lowers $m$ by one and raises $n$ by one. Explain why its integration-by-parts boundary term vanishes and why the case $m=0$ must be handled as a base case rather than by blindly repeating the same argument. Deduce a closed factorial formula for $I_{m,n}$, verify its symmetry in $m,n$, and compute $I_{4,3}$ exactly.
permittedResults: Integration by parts gives $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$.
For a nonnegative integer $q$, $\int_0^1(1-x)^qdx=1/(q+1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Move one power from x into one plus the power of one minus x by integration by parts.
Use the substitution x equals one minus u to cross-check symmetry before numerical evaluation.

milestones.criterion: Derives the recurrence with a valid endpoint audit.
Iterates to the correct factorial formula and handles the base case.
Checks symmetry and evaluates the requested integral exactly.

commonErrors.description: Claims the integration-by-parts boundary term vanishes at zero even when m equals zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduction is justified only for m at least one, so the base case is lost.

commonErrors.description: Stops the denominator product at m plus n and omits the base-case factor m plus n plus one.
commonErrors.consequence: The closed form and the value of I four three are too large by a factor of m plus n plus one.

hintTree.content: Take $u=x^m$ and $dv=(1-x)^n dx$.
The antiderivative of $(1-x)^n$ is $-(1-x)^{n+1}/(n+1)$.
After $m$ reductions, the remaining integral is $I_{0,m+n}$.

CALC2:010119.canonicalSolution:
For $m\ge1$, choose $u=x^m$ and $dv=(1-x)^n dx$. Then $du=mx^{m-1}dx$ and $v=-(1-x)^{n+1}/(n+1)$. Hence
$$
I_{m,n}=\left[-\frac{x^m(1-x)^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_0^1
+\frac{m}{n+1}I_{m-1,n+1}.
$$
At $x=1$ the factor $(1-x)^{n+1}$ is zero; at $x=0$ the factor $x^m$ is zero because $m\ge1$. Thus
$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{m}{n+1}I_{m-1,n+1}.
$$
Iterating exactly $m$ times gives
$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{m!}{(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+m)}I_{0,n+m}.
$$
The base case is computed directly, $I_{0,n+m}=1/(n+m+1)$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{I_{m,n}=\frac{m!n!}{(m+n+1)!}}.
$$
The expression is symmetric in $m,n$, agreeing with the substitution $x=1-u$. Finally,
$$
I_{4,3}=\frac{4!3!}{8!}=\boxed{\frac1{280}}.
$$
When $m=0$, the lower-end boundary factor $x^m$ is one, so the preceding boundary-vanishing claim is unavailable; that is precisely why it is the separately evaluated base case.

I use the same vanishing boundary argument at $m=0$, even though $x^0=1$ at the lower endpoint, and never establish a valid base case.
After reducing m times I write $I_{m,n}=m!n!/(m+n)!$, omitting the final factor from $I_{0,m+n}$ and obtaining the wrong numerical value.

CALC2:010120.title: Turn an infinite logarithmic tail into an arctangent
CALC2:010120.objective: Evaluate an improper integral through a finite-cutoff logarithmic substitution, prove convergence, and derive both an exact truncation remainder and a simpler certified tail bound.
CALC2:010120.statement:
Evaluate
$$
I=\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x\bigl(4+(\ln x)^2\bigr)}.
$$
Carry out the substitution $u=\ln x$ first on $[1,R]$ and then pass to the improper limit. For $R>1$, derive the exact error made by replacing $I$ with the integral only up to $R$, and prove the simpler bound that this error is at most $1/\ln R$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the upper endpoint as a parameter before substitution.
Express the error as a transformed positive tail and compare its denominator with u squared.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the finite-cutoff integral with correct bounds.
Passes to the limit and obtains the exact value and exact tail.
Proves the stated elementary upper bound with its domain condition.

commonErrors.description: Uses u equals log x but omits dx over x and leaves an extra exponential factor or wrong measure.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed integral and its value are invalid.

commonErrors.description: Applies the one over log R bound at R equal to one or without requiring a positive lower tail limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The comparison integral is undefined at zero and does not certify that case.

hintTree.content: On $[1,R]$, $du=dx/x$ and the new upper limit is $\ln R$.
The exact tail is an arctangent complement.
For $u\ge\ln R>0$, use $1/(4+u^2)\le1/u^2$.

For a finite $R>1$, the substitution $u=\ln x$ is legitimate and gives
$$
\int_1^R\frac{dx}{x(4+(\ln x)^2)}
=\int_0^{\ln R}\frac{du}{4+u^2}
=\frac12\arctan\!\left(\frac{\ln R}{2}\right).
$$
As $R\to\infty$, the arctangent tends to $\pi/2$, proving convergence and
$$
\boxed{I=\frac\pi4}.
$$
The exact truncation error is
$$
E(R)=\int_R^\infty\frac{dx}{x(4+(\ln x)^2)}
=\frac\pi4-\frac12\arctan\!\left(\frac{\ln R}{2}\right).
$$
Equivalently, after the same substitution,
$$
E(R)=\int_{\ln R}^\infty\frac{du}{4+u^2}.
$$
Because $R>1$ makes $\ln R>0$ and $4+u^2\ge u^2$,
$$
0<E(R)\le\int_{\ln R}^\infty\frac{du}{u^2}
=\boxed{\frac1{\ln R}}.
$$
The substitution is performed before the limit so that both its interval and transformed endpoint are explicit.

I set $u=\ln x$ but treat $dx$ as $du$, so my transformed integrand retains the wrong factor and no longer matches the finite bounds.
I claim the tail is at most $1/\ln R$ for every $R\ge1$, including $R=1$ where the proposed bound and comparison integral are not finite.

CALC2:010121.title: Separate a rational integrand before evaluating its cancelled endpoint
CALC2:010121.objective: Decompose a rational function, use the decomposition to evaluate a definite integral, and distinguish a removable endpoint value from a genuine improper singularity.
CALC2:010121.statement:
Evaluate
$$
\int_0^1\frac{x^2+3x+2}{x^3+3x^2+2x}\,dx.
$$
First simplify or decompose the integrand on $(0,1]$. Decide whether the lower endpoint requires an improper limit, state the continuous extension if one exists, and give the exact value of the integral.
permittedResults: For a positive improper integral, divergence of the defining limit means there is no finite integral value or continuous endpoint extension.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use factorization to expose the local endpoint behavior before applying an antiderivative.
Treat the lower bound as a limiting parameter and test whether its logarithmic term has a finite limit.

milestones.criterion: Factors and cancels only on the stated punctured interval, identifying the remaining 1/x pole.
Sets up and evaluates lim_{a->0+} integral_a^1 dx/x with the correct logarithm sign.
Concludes divergence to +infinity and explains why no continuous extension exists.

commonErrors.description: Calls x=0 removable after cancelling factors, even though the simplified integrand is 1/x on the punctured interval.
commonErrors.consequence: This replaces a genuine pole by an invented endpoint value and incorrectly turns a divergent improper integral into a proper one.

commonErrors.description: Uses ln(a) as the value of integral_a^1 1/x dx without subtracting it from ln(1).
commonErrors.consequence: The sign error reverses the limiting behavior and obscures divergence to +infinity.

hintTree.content: Factor both polynomials before deciding what happens at x=0.
After cancellation on (0,1], ask whether 1/x stays bounded as x approaches 0 from the right.
Write the integral from a to 1 and take a down to 0; evaluate ln(1)-ln(a) with its sign intact.

CALC2:010121.canonicalSolution:
Factor the denominator as $x(x+1)(x+2)$ and the numerator as $(x+1)(x+2)$. For every $x>0$, cancellation gives exactly $1/x$. This simplification exposes a nonremovable pole at the excluded endpoint rather than creating a continuous extension there. The proper definition is
$$
\lim_{a\downarrow0}\int_a^1\frac{dx}{x}=\lim_{a\downarrow0}(-\ln a).
$$
Since $-\ln a\to\infty$, the integral diverges; there is no finite exact value and no continuous extension at $0$. The cancellation reveals, rather than removes, the pole. A finite antiderivative on $(0,1]$ does not license substitution of $x=0$. Therefore the correct conclusion is $\boxed{\text{the improper integral diverges to }+\infty}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: For x>0 the integrand is 1/x, so its value is defined by lim a->0+ integral_a^1 dx/x=-ln a=+infinity. The lower endpoint is a genuine pole; the integral diverges.
I cancel factors and call the value at x=0 equal to 1, then integrate from 0 to 1 as though the pole had become removable.
I write integral_a^1 1/x dx=ln a and conclude its limit as a goes to zero is finite or negative infinity without using ln 1-ln a.

CALC2:010122.title: Certify convergence of an exponential tail without finding an antiderivative
CALC2:010122.objective: Prove convergence of a positive improper integral by comparison and derive a concrete tail estimate that is valid for every stated cutoff.

For $R\ge1$, let
$$
T(R)=\int_R^\infty xe^{-x^2}\,dx.
$$
Evaluate $T(R)$ exactly by a finite-cutoff substitution, then use the result to prove that $T(R)\le e^{-R}$ for every $R\ge1$. Explain why the inequality does not require replacing the improper integral by a numerical approximation.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the tail exactly by recognizing x e^{-x^2} as a substitution derivative.
Use the cutoff assumption R>=1 to make a one-line exponential comparison after the limit.

milestones.criterion: Performs the substitution with endpoints R^2 and b^2 and obtains the finite-b expression.
Takes b->infinity to derive T(R)=e^{-R^2}/2.
Uses the correct monotonic direction to prove e^{-R^2}/2<=e^{-R} for R>=1.

commonErrors.consequence: The finite integral and hence its improper limit are no longer the requested Gaussian tail.

commonErrors.description: Claims e^{-R^2}>=e^{-R} from R^2>=R.
commonErrors.consequence: Because exp(-x) decreases, this reverses the tail certificate and fails to prove the required bound.

Use u=x^2 and remember that the transformed upper limit is b^2.
Let b tend to infinity, then compare e^{-R^2}/2 with e^{-R} using R^2>=R.

Work first on $[R,b]$ and set $u=x^2$, so $du=2x\,dx$. Then
$$
\int_R^b xe^{-x^2}\,dx=\frac12\int_{R^2}^{b^2}e^{-u}\,du
=\frac12(e^{-R^2}-e^{-b^2}).
$$
Letting $b\to\infty$ gives $T(R)=\frac12e^{-R^2}$, which is finite and positive. For $R\ge1$, $R^2\ge R$, hence $-R^2\le-R$ and $e^{-R^2}\le e^{-R}$. Therefore
$$
T(R)=\frac12e^{-R^2}\le\frac12e^{-R}\le e^{-R}.
$$
The limit is exact because the discarded term $e^{-b^2}$ tends to zero; no decimal quadrature is involved. In particular $\boxed{T(R)=e^{-R^2}/2\le e^{-R}}$ certifies both convergence and the advertised tail bound.

CALC2:010123.title: Carry a trigonometric substitution to a singular endpoint
CALC2:010123.objective: Evaluate an endpoint-singular integral by a finite-cutoff trigonometric substitution, distinguish an integrable square-root singularity from divergence, and report the exact limiting value.
CALC2:010123.statement:
Evaluate the improper integral
$$
I=\int_0^3\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\,dx.
$$
Work first with an upper cutoff $b<3$. Use a trigonometric substitution, transform both bounds, and then let $b\uparrow3$. Explain why the integrand being undefined at $x=3$ does not by itself make the integral divergent, and give the exact value of $I$.
permittedResults: For $0\le x<3$, the substitution $x=3\sin\theta$ uses $0\le\theta<\pi/2$, where $\sqrt{9-x^2}=3\cos\theta$ without an absolute-value sign change.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a cutoff-aware trigonometric substitution and evaluate the resulting elementary integral.
Alternatively differentiate the exact antiderivative (9/2)arcsin(x/3)-(x/2)sqrt(9-x^2), then apply the cutoff limit.

milestones.criterion: Defines the improper integral with an upper cutoff b<3 and uses x=3 sin(theta) on the correct angle range.
Transforms the integral to 9 times the integral of sin^2(theta) with upper bound arcsin(b/3).
Takes the endpoint limit to obtain 9pi/4 and explains why the singularity is integrable.

commonErrors.description: Treats x=3 as an ordinary endpoint during substitution and cancels a zero cosine without first using a cutoff.
commonErrors.consequence: The work never defines the improper integral and performs algebra at the point where the original integrand is undefined.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that the integral diverges merely because sqrt(9-x^2) vanishes at x=3.
commonErrors.consequence: An unbounded endpoint alone does not decide convergence; here the defining cutoff limit is finite and equals 9pi/4.

hintTree.content: Replace the endpoint 3 by a cutoff b and set x=3 sin(theta) only on the finite interval.
After cancellation, the transformed integrand is 9 sin^2(theta); the upper angle is arcsin(b/3).
Use the half-angle identity to integrate sin^2(theta), then take arcsin(b/3) up to pi/2.

CALC2:010123.canonicalSolution:
For $0<b<3$, define
$$
I(b)=\int_0^b\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\,dx.
$$
Put $x=3\sin\theta$. On the relevant interval, $dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{9-x^2}=3\cos\theta$, so
$$
I(b)=9\int_0^{\arcsin(b/3)}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=\frac92\left[\theta-\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\arcsin(b/3)}.
$$
As $b\uparrow3$, the upper angle tends to $\pi/2$ and its doubled-angle sine tends to $0$. Therefore
$$
I=\lim_{b\uparrow3}I(b)=\frac92\cdot\frac\pi2=\boxed{\frac{9\pi}{4}}.
$$
The integrand is undefined and unbounded at the single endpoint, so ordinary endpoint substitution is unavailable. Convergence is instead decided by the finite cutoff limit above, which exists. Thus this square-root singularity is improper but integrable.

I substitute x=3 sin(theta) using theta=pi/2 at once, cancel cos(theta) even at that endpoint, and call the resulting ordinary integral a complete treatment without any cutoff limit.
The denominator is zero at x=3, so I declare that the integral diverges without examining how rapidly 1/sqrt(9-x^2) grows or computing the one-sided defining limit.

CALC2:010124.title: Reserve one sine factor before substituting cosine
CALC2:010124.objective: Choose the appropriate odd-power trigonometric-integral strategy, convert the remaining sine power through the Pythagorean identity, and evaluate a definite integral exactly with transformed orientation.
CALC2:010124.statement:
Evaluate exactly
$$
J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5x\cos^2x\,dx.
$$
Your solution must explain why saving one factor of $\sin x$ is useful, carry out the substitution $u=\cos x$ with its transformed limits, and simplify the resulting polynomial integral. Include a brief sign or magnitude check on the final answer.
permittedResults: Under $u=\cos x$, $du=-\sin x\,dx$ and the bounds $x=0,\pi/2$ become $u=1,0$, so the negative differential reverses the orientation.

acceptableStrategies.description: Save one sine factor and substitute the cosine directly.
Use the beta-integral identity only after identifying its exponents and endpoint factor correctly.

milestones.criterion: Separates one sine factor and rewrites sin^4(x) as (1-cos^2(x))^2.
Transforms to the correctly oriented polynomial integral from 0 to 1.
Evaluates the polynomial exactly as 8/105 and gives a consistent positivity check.

commonErrors.description: Uses u=cos(x) but keeps both the negative differential and the bounds 0 to 1, or otherwise fails to reverse exactly once.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign of a nonnegative definite integral becomes negative, so the evaluated answer cannot be correct.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sin^4(x) by 1-cos^4(x) instead of (1-cos^2(x))^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The polynomial integrand changes and yields a value for a different trigonometric integral.

hintTree.content: Write sin^5(x) as (sin^2(x))^2 sin(x).
Replace sin^2(x) by 1-cos^2(x), then let u=cos(x) and reverse the bounds carefully.

CALC2:010124.canonicalSolution:
Because the sine exponent is odd, separate one sine factor:
$$
\sin^5x\cos^2x=(\sin^2x)^2\cos^2x\sin x
=(1-\cos^2x)^2\cos^2x\sin x.
$$
Let $u=\cos x$, so $du=-\sin x\,dx$. The limits $x=0$ and $x=\pi/2$ become $u=1$ and $u=0$. Hence
$$
J=-\int_1^0(1-u^2)^2u^2\,du
=\int_0^1(u^2-2u^4+u^6)\,du.
$$
Therefore
$$
J=\left[\frac{u^3}{3}-\frac{2u^5}{5}+\frac{u^7}{7}\right]_0^1
=\frac13-\frac25+\frac17
=\boxed{\frac8{105}}.
$$
The original integrand is nonnegative on $[0,\pi/2]$, and $8/105$ is positive and smaller than the interval length, so its sign and rough magnitude are consistent.

With u=cos x I write du=-sin x dx but integrate the positive polynomial from 1 to 0 without retaining the minus sign, obtaining -8/105 for an integrand that is nonnegative.
I replace sin^4 x by 1-cos^4 x, so my substituted integrand is u^2(1-u^4) rather than u^2(1-u^2)^2 and I evaluate the wrong integral.

CALC2:010125.title: Expose a rational remainder after integration by parts
CALC2:010125.objective: Evaluate a logarithmic definite integral by choosing integration by parts so that polynomial division finishes the remaining rational integral, then verify the exact result against positivity and a simple upper bound.
CALC2:010125.statement:
Evaluate exactly
$$
I=\int_0^1 x^2\ln(1+x)\,dx.
$$
Choose the parts explicitly, retain the endpoint term, and divide the polynomial in the remaining fraction before integrating. Simplify the answer to a linear combination of $\ln2$ and a rational number. Finally, use $0\leq\ln(1+x)\leq\ln2$ on $[0,1]$ to check the sign and size of your result.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use integration by parts followed by polynomial division, as requested.
As an independent check, expand ln(1+x) into its alternating power series and justify termwise integration on truncated intervals before taking the endpoint limit.

milestones.criterion: Sets u=ln(1+x), dv=x^2 dx and obtains the correct definite integration-by-parts identity including its endpoint term.
Divides x^3/(1+x) as x^2-x+1-1/(1+x) and evaluates that integral as 5/6-ln2.
Simplifies to (2/3)ln2-5/18 and supplies a valid positivity and magnitude check.

commonErrors.description: Writes only the remaining rational integral after integration by parts and omits the endpoint contribution ln(2)/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The missing boundary term changes both the logarithmic coefficient and the final value.

commonErrors.description: Uses x^3/(1+x)=x^2-x+1 with no remainder term.
commonErrors.consequence: Multiplying the claimed quotient by 1+x gives x^3+1, so the subsequent integral is for a different function.

The remaining integrand is x^3/(1+x). Divide it as x^2-x+1-1/(1+x).
Combine (ln 2)/3 with minus one third of the divided integral, then compare the result with 0 and (ln 2)/3.

I=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\ln(1+x)\right]_0^1-\frac{1}{3}\int_0^1\frac{x^3}{1+x}\,dx.
$$

$$
\frac{x^3}{1+x}=x^2-x+1-\frac{1}{1+x}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\int_0^1\frac{x^3}{1+x}\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}+x-\ln(1+x)\right]_0^1
=\frac{5}{6}-\ln2.

$$
I=\frac{\ln2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{5}{6}-\ln2\right)
=\boxed{\frac{2}{3}\ln2-\frac{5}{18}}.

CALC2:010126.title: Separate oscillatory convergence from absolute divergence
CALC2:010126.objective: Prove convergence of an oscillatory improper integral by integration by parts with an explicit tail estimate, then prove failure of absolute convergence using uniform lower bounds on selected subintervals.
CALC2:010126.statement:
Consider
$$
\int_1^\infty \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx.
$$
(a) Prove that the integral converges and show that every tail
$T(R)=\int_R^\infty \sin x/x\,dx$ satisfies $|T(R)|\leq2/R$ for $R\geq1$.
(b) Prove that the integral is not absolutely convergent. For this part, use intervals on which $|\sin x|\geq1/2$ and compare the resulting lower bound with a harmonic series. Do not use the numerical value of the sine integral.
permittedResults: If the tails $\int_R^B f$ approach a limit uniformly as $B\to\infty$ and then vanish as $R\to\infty$, the Cauchy criterion gives convergence; integration by parts can expose that tail decay.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use cutoff integration by parts for the signed tail and an interval-by-interval harmonic comparison for the absolute integral.
Alternatively invoke Dirichlet's test for convergence after separately deriving the demanded tail bound; the absolute-divergence interval argument is still required.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the finite tail by parts and justifies passage to infinity.
Derives the explicit estimate |T(R)|<=2/R and uses it to establish signed convergence.
Builds disjoint intervals with |sin x|>=1/2, obtains a divergent harmonic lower bound, and concludes conditional convergence.

commonErrors.description: Argues that |sin x|/x converges because it is at most 1/x.
commonErrors.consequence: Comparison with a divergent upper bound gives no convergence conclusion and misses the harmonic lower bound.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sin x by its absolute value when estimating the signed tail and then claims the resulting divergent bound proves divergence.
commonErrors.consequence: Absolute-value domination is too coarse here; cancellation exposed by integration by parts is precisely why the signed tail tends to zero.

hintTree.content: For finite B>R, integrate sin(x)/x by parts with dv=sin(x)dx and u=1/x, then let B go to infinity.
Bound the surviving endpoint cosine term by 1/R and the integral of 1/x^2 from R to infinity by another 1/R.
On Ik=[k pi+pi/6,k pi+5pi/6], lower-bound both |sin x| and 1/x, then compare the sum of the interval contributions to sum 1/(k+1).

CALC2:010126.canonicalSolution:
For $B>R\geq1$, integration by parts with $u=1/x$ and $dv=\sin x\,dx$ gives
$$
\int_R^B\frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx
=\left[-\frac{\cos x}{x}\right]_R^B-\int_R^B\frac{\cos x}{x^2}\,dx.
$$
As $B\to\infty$, the boundary term $-\cos B/B$ vanishes and the last integral converges absolutely. Thus
$$
T(R)=\frac{\cos R}{R}-\int_R^\infty\frac{\cos x}{x^2}\,dx,
\qquad
|T(R)|\leq\frac{1}{R}+\int_R^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2}=\frac{2}{R}.
$$
In particular $T(R)\to0$, proving convergence of the signed improper integral.

For absolute convergence, let
$I_k=[k\pi+\pi/6,k\pi+5\pi/6]$ for integers $k\geq1$. On $I_k$, $|\sin x|\geq1/2$, its length is $2\pi/3$, and $x\leq(k+1)\pi$. Hence
$$
\int_{I_k}\frac{|\sin x|}{x}\,dx
\geq \frac{1}{2}\frac{2\pi/3}{(k+1)\pi}
=\frac{1}{3(k+1)}.
$$
The intervals are disjoint, and $\sum_{k\geq1}1/[3(k+1)]$ diverges. Therefore $\int_1^\infty|\sin x|/x\,dx=\infty$. The original integral is consequently conditionally, not absolutely, convergent.

Because |sin x|/x <= 1/x and integral 1/x diverges, I say the absolute integral converges by comparison.
I take absolute values before exploiting cancellation, get integral_R^infinity 1/x, and conclude the signed sine integral diverges without integrating by parts.

CALC2:010127.title: Retain every term in a repeated-factor decomposition
CALC2:010127.objective: Evaluate a rational definite integral whose denominator has both a repeated linear factor and an irreducible quadratic, determine every partial-fraction coefficient, and verify the resulting antiderivative before using the endpoints.
CALC2:010127.statement:
Evaluate exactly
$$
I=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2(x^2+1)}.
$$
Write the complete real partial-fraction template before solving for its coefficients. Integrate the decomposition, simplify the endpoint value, and differentiate your antiderivative (or recombine the fractions) to verify that neither the repeated-factor term nor the quadratic numerator has been lost.
permittedResults: For $(x+1)^2(x^2+1)$ the real decomposition must have the form $A/(x+1)+B/(x+1)^2+(Cx+D)/(x^2+1)$, and equality is certified by matching the polynomial numerator after clearing denominators.

acceptableStrategies.description: Clear denominators and match polynomial coefficients, then integrate the resulting elementary fractions.
As a coefficient check, first substitute x=-1 to get B and then use three additional coefficient or sample-value equations; the full identity still must be verified.

milestones.criterion: Writes the complete repeated-linear and irreducible-quadratic template and derives all four coefficient equations correctly.
Obtains (A,B,C,D)=(1/2,1/2,-1/2,0) and integrates every decomposed term with the correct signs.
Evaluates the endpoints as (1+ln2)/4 and verifies the antiderivative or recombined rational function.

commonErrors.description: Uses only A/(x+1)+(Cx+D)/(x^2+1), omitting the B/(x+1)^2 term required by the repeated pole.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced template cannot reproduce the second-order behavior at x=-1, so any antiderivative obtained from it integrates a different rational function.

commonErrors.description: Places only a constant over x^2+1 and never permits the linear numerator needed to match the odd-power coefficients.
commonErrors.consequence: The missing Cx term removes the logarithmic derivative of x^2+1 and makes the cleared numerator identity inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Start with A/(x+1)+B/(x+1)^2+(Cx+D)/(x^2+1), multiply by the full denominator, and compare coefficients through degree three.
The coefficient equations give C=-A, D=0, and B=A; the constant equation then determines A.
Integrate the resulting pieces and evaluate the single antiderivative at 1 and 0 before combining its logarithms.

CALC2:010127.canonicalSolution:
Use the complete decomposition
$$
\frac1{(x+1)^2(x^2+1)}
=\frac A{x+1}+\frac B{(x+1)^2}+\frac{Cx+D}{x^2+1}.
$$
Clearing denominators gives
$$
1=A(x+1)(x^2+1)+B(x^2+1)+(Cx+D)(x+1)^2.
$$
Comparison of the cubic, quadratic, linear, and constant coefficients yields
$$
A+C=0,\quad A+B+2C+D=0,\quad A+C+2D=0,\quad A+B+D=1.
$$
Thus $D=0$, $C=-A$, $B=A$, and $2A=1$. Therefore
$$
\frac1{(x+1)^2(x^2+1)}
=\frac1{2(x+1)}+\frac1{2(x+1)^2}-\frac{x}{2(x^2+1)}.
$$
An antiderivative is
$$
F(x)=\frac12\ln(x+1)-\frac1{2(x+1)}-\frac14\ln(x^2+1).
$$
Differentiating $F$ reproduces the displayed decomposition, which recombines to the original integrand. Finally,
$$
I=F(1)-F(0)
=\left(\frac14\ln2-\frac14\right)-\left(-\frac12\right)
=\boxed{\frac{1+\ln2}{4}}.
$$
The answer is positive, as it must be because the integrand is positive on $[0,1]$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The full template gives (A,B,C,D)=(1/2,1/2,-1/2,0). Hence F=(1/2)ln(x+1)-1/[2(x+1)]-(1/4)ln(x^2+1), whose derivative recombines correctly, and I=(1+ln2)/4.
I decompose the integrand using only A/(x+1)+(Cx+D)/(x^2+1), so I omit the repeated-pole term B/(x+1)^2 and integrate a fraction with the wrong pole order.
I insist the x^2+1 numerator must be a constant, discard the possible Cx term, and therefore cannot match the cubic and linear coefficients after clearing denominators.

CALC2:010128.title: Move the convergence threshold into a logarithmic variable
CALC2:010128.objective: Classify a one-parameter family of logarithmically weighted improper integrals for every real parameter, compute the convergent value, and retain the exact finite-cutoff tail rather than citing a threshold without proof.
CALC2:010128.statement:
For real $p$, classify the improper integral
$$
I_p=\int_e^\infty\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p}.
$$
Use a finite upper cutoff before substituting. State exactly which $p$ give convergence, evaluate $I_p$ in that range, and for $p>1$ derive the exact remainder
$$
T_p(R)=\int_R^\infty\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p},\qquad R\geq e.
$$
Explain separately what happens at the threshold $p=1$.
permittedResults: The power integral $\int_1^\infty u^{-p}\,du$ converges exactly when $p>1$; at $p=1$ its cutoff antiderivative is $\ln u$, while for $p\ne1$ it is $u^{1-p}/(1-p)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the logarithmic substitution on a finite cutoff and apply the ordinary p-integral classification.
Alternatively differentiate the proposed cutoff antiderivatives in x, but still take their limits separately for p<1, p=1, and p>1.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the finite-cutoff integral exactly to an integral of u^(-p) from 1 to ln B.
Separates p=1 from p not equal to 1 and proves convergence exactly for p>1 with value 1/(p-1).
Derives the exact convergent tail (ln R)^(1-p)/(p-1) and explains why it vanishes.

commonErrors.description: After u=ln x, keeps the upper cutoff as B instead of changing it to ln B.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting limit and tail are for a different integral and erase the logarithmic rate requested in the problem.

commonErrors.description: States convergence for p greater than or equal to 1 or substitutes p=1 into 1/(p-1).
commonErrors.consequence: At p=1 the cutoff is ln(ln B), which diverges, and the claimed value is undefined.

hintTree.content: Write the integral from e to B and let u=ln x, so the transformed upper endpoint is ln B rather than B.
For p not equal to 1, inspect the limit of (ln B)^(1-p); handle p=1 with its logarithmic antiderivative.
For the convergent tail, transform R as well and integrate from ln R to infinity without replacing the exact logarithmic power by a rough bound.

CALC2:010128.canonicalSolution:
For a finite cutoff $B>e$, put $u=\ln x$. Since $du=dx/x$ and the bounds become $1$ and $\ln B$,
$$
\int_e^B\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p}=\int_1^{\ln B}u^{-p}\,du.
$$
If $p\ne1$, this equals
$$
\frac{(\ln B)^{1-p}-1}{1-p}.
$$
When $p>1$, the exponent $1-p$ is negative, so $(\ln B)^{1-p}\to0$ and
$$
I_p=\boxed{\frac1{p-1}}.
$$
When $p<1$, the positive power $(\ln B)^{1-p}$ tends to infinity, so the integral diverges. At the threshold $p=1$,
$$
\int_1^{\ln B}\frac{du}{u}=\ln(\ln B)\to\infty,
$$
so this case also diverges.

For $p>1$ and $R\ge e$, the same substitution gives
$$
T_p(R)=\int_{\ln R}^{\infty}u^{-p}\,du
=\boxed{\frac{(\ln R)^{1-p}}{p-1}}.
$$
This exact positive tail tends to zero precisely because $p>1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: With u=ln x, the cutoff integral is integral_1^{ln B} u^{-p}du. It converges iff p>1, then I_p=1/(p-1) and T_p(R)=(ln R)^(1-p)/(p-1); p=1 diverges as ln ln B.
I set u=ln x but write the transformed upper endpoint as B, so my remainder is a power of R instead of the required power of ln R.
I claim p=1 is included because the p-test converges for p>=1, even though the actual cutoff at p=1 is ln(ln B) and grows without bound.

CALC2:010129.title: Make the boundary term vanish before reducing a sine power
CALC2:010129.objective: Derive the Wallis reduction formula for definite sine-power integrals from integration by parts, state its valid range, and use the recurrence with its correct even base case to evaluate a concrete high power exactly.
CALC2:010129.statement:
For an integer $n\ge2$, let
$$I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dx.$$
Derive a recurrence for $I_n$ by integration by parts, including the endpoint term and the algebra that moves an $I_n$ term to the left. State $I_0$ and $I_1$, then evaluate $I_8$ exactly.
permittedResults: Integration by parts gives $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$; on $[0,\pi/2]$ the product $\sin^{n-1}x\cos x$ vanishes at both endpoints.

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the recurrence directly by integration by parts before substituting n=8.
A symmetry-based Wallis derivation is acceptable if it proves the same recurrence and retains the definite endpoint justification.

milestones.criterion: Performs integration by parts with the correct endpoint term and proves that term is zero.
Uses cos^2=1-sin^2 and solves for I_n=(n-1)I_(n-2)/n.
States both base cases and evaluates I_8 as 35pi/256 with a reasonableness check.

commonErrors.description: Replaces cos^2 by 1 and writes I_n=(n-1)I_(n-2), losing the subtractive I_n term.
commonErrors.consequence: The recurrence is missing its factor 1/n and produces values larger than the integral's basic bound.

commonErrors.description: Terminates the even recurrence at I_1=1 instead of I_0=pi/2.
commonErrors.consequence: Even and odd chains have different base cases, so the final value loses its factor of pi and is not I_8.

hintTree.content: Write one sine factor as sin x dx and choose u=sin^(n-1)x, dv=sin x dx.
Replace cos^2 x by 1-sin^2 x; the second resulting integral is I_n itself.
For n=8, apply I_n=(n-1)I_(n-2)/n four times and finish at I_0=pi/2.

CALC2:010129.canonicalSolution:
Take $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv=\sin x\,dx$, so $du=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx$ and $v=-\cos x$. Then
$$I_n=[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx.$$
The boundary term is zero. Since $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$,
$$I_n=(n-1)(I_{n-2}-I_n),$$
so $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ and
$$\boxed{I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}}\qquad(n\ge2).$$
The bases are $I_0=\pi/2$ and $I_1=1$. Therefore
$$I_8=\frac78\frac56\frac34\frac12\frac\pi2
=\boxed{\frac{35\pi}{256}}.$$
The value is positive and less than $I_0$, consistent with $0\le\sin^8x\le1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The boundary product -sin^(n-1)x cos x vanishes. Thus I_n=(n-1)(I_(n-2)-I_n), so I_n=(n-1)I_(n-2)/n. Using I_0=pi/2 gives I_8=(7/8)(5/6)(3/4)(1/2)(pi/2)=35pi/256.
I replace cos^2 x by 1 during integration by parts, drop the subtractive copy of I_n, and conclude I_n=(n-1)I_(n-2).
I apply the two-step recurrence for I_8 but terminate the even chain at I_1=1, producing a rational answer with no pi factor.

CALC2:010130.title: Resolve a removable endpoint before exchanging two integrals
CALC2:010130.objective: Evaluate an improper exponential-difference integral without splitting it into two divergent pieces, certify both improper endpoints, justify a parameter-integral exchange, and derive an explicit positive tail bound.
CALC2:010130.statement:
Evaluate
$$J=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-2x}-e^{-5x}}{x}\,dx.$$
Show that the apparent singularity at $0$ is removable, do not split $J$ into two integrals containing $1/x$, and use a parameter integral to find the exact value. For $R>0$, bound the tail from $R$ to infinity explicitly.
permittedResults: Because $\int_a^b e^{-tx}\,dt=(e^{-ax}-e^{-bx})/x$, Tonelli's theorem applies to the resulting nonnegative integrand on a finite parameter interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the nonnegative parameter integral and Tonelli, which simultaneously evaluates and certifies convergence.
Differentiation with respect to a decay parameter is acceptable if the integration constant and both improper endpoints are independently controlled.

milestones.criterion: Shows the quotient extends continuously to value 3 at zero and refuses an invalid divergent split.
Uses the parameter bridge and Tonelli to obtain integral_2^5 dt/t=ln(5/2).
Derives a positive exact tail representation and a bound that tends to zero.

commonErrors.description: Writes J as integral e^(-2x)/x minus integral e^(-5x)/x and assigns finite values to the pieces.
commonErrors.consequence: Each separated integral diverges at zero, so subtracting them after independent evaluation destroys the cancellation defining J.

commonErrors.description: Reports ln(2/5) after integrating 1/t from 2 to 5.
commonErrors.consequence: The original integrand is positive for x>0, so a negative logarithmic value has the wrong sign.

hintTree.content: Use first-order exponential expansions at zero to compute the limiting integrand value.
Write the quotient as integral_2^5 e^(-tx) dt and then exchange the nonnegative integrals.
For x>=R, integrate first in x to obtain an exact parameter representation of the tail and bound t below by 2.

CALC2:010130.canonicalSolution:
As $x\to0^+$, $e^{-2x}-e^{-5x}=3x+O(x^2)$, so the quotient tends to $3$ and the endpoint at zero is removable. For $x>0$,
$$\frac{e^{-2x}-e^{-5x}}x=\int_2^5e^{-tx}\,dt.$$
This integrand is nonnegative. Tonelli therefore gives
$$J=\int_2^5\int_0^\infty e^{-tx}\,dx\,dt
=\int_2^5\frac{dt}{t}=\boxed{\ln\frac52}.$$
This representation also proves convergence at infinity. More quantitatively,
$$T(R)=\int_R^\infty\frac{e^{-2x}-e^{-5x}}x\,dx
=\int_2^5\frac{e^{-tR}}t\,dt.$$
Thus $T(R)>0$ and, since $t\ge2$,
$$0<T(R)\le\int_2^5\frac{e^{-2R}}2\,dt
=\boxed{\frac32e^{-2R}},$$
which tends to zero. Cancellation was preserved throughout; the two separated $1/x$ integrals would each diverge at zero.

graderFixtures.proofText: The quotient tends to 3 at zero and equals integral_2^5 e^(-tx)dt. Tonelli yields J=integral_2^5 dt/t=ln(5/2). The tail is integral_2^5 e^(-tR)/t dt, hence 0<T(R)<=(3/2)e^(-2R).
I split J into the two integrals of e^(-2x)/x and e^(-5x)/x, treat both divergent pieces as finite, and subtract their assigned values.
After obtaining integral_2^5 dt/t, I reverse the endpoint ratio and report ln(2/5), even though the given integrand is positive.

CALC2:010131.title: Keep both logarithmic endpoints inside one convergent integral
CALC2:010131.objective: Audit both endpoints of a logarithm-product improper integral, use a nonnegative power-series expansion with a justified exchange, and reduce the resulting rational series to an exact value.
CALC2:010131.statement:
Evaluate
$$I=\int_0^1 \ln x\,\ln(1-x)\,dx.$$
First prove convergence at both endpoints. Then expand only one logarithm, justify exchanging the sum and integral without a purely formal termwise step, and reduce the answer to the Basel sum $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-2}=\pi^2/6$.
permittedResults: For $0<x<1$, $-\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n$ with nonnegative terms, so Tonelli or monotone convergence permits exchange after multiplying by $-\ln x\ge0$; also $\int_0^1x^n(-\ln x)\,dx=(n+1)^{-2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand -ln(1-x), use Tonelli, and evaluate the logarithmic moments by integration by parts.
Expanding -ln x after the substitution x to 1-x is equivalent if the endpoint cutoffs and nonnegative exchange are explicit.

milestones.criterion: Proves convergence at zero and one using correct local logarithmic behavior.
Uses the nonnegative logarithm series and Tonelli/monotone convergence to obtain sum 1/[n(n+1)^2].
Telescopes the decomposed series and obtains 2-pi^2/6 with a sign check.

commonErrors.description: Reports pi^2/6-2 after reversing the subtraction in the telescoped series.
commonErrors.consequence: That number is negative even though ln x and ln(1-x) have a positive product on (0,1).

commonErrors.description: Integrates the infinite logarithm series term by term without proving endpoint convergence or justifying the exchange.
commonErrors.consequence: The power series is only pointwise on the open interval, so endpoint and exchange control are essential to the improper integral.

hintTree.content: Near zero use -ln(1-x)~x; near one put u=1-x and use -ln x~u.
Write the positive product as (-ln x) sum_(n>=1) x^n/n and invoke a nonnegative exchange theorem.

CALC2:010131.canonicalSolution:
The integrand is positive. As $x\to0^+$, $\ln(1-x)=-x+O(x^2)$, so the product is $-x\ln x+O(x^2|\ln x|)$ and is integrable. With $u=1-x\to0^+$, $\ln x=\ln(1-u)=-u+O(u^2)$, so the product is $-u\ln u+O(u^2|\ln u|)$ and is also integrable.

For $0<x<1$,
$$(-\ln x)(-\ln(1-x))=(-\ln x)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n}.$$
Every summand is nonnegative. Tonelli (equivalently, monotone convergence) therefore gives
$$I=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\int_0^1x^n(-\ln x)\,dx
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n(n+1)^2}.$$
Integration by parts on a cutoff interval and passage to the limit gives
$\int_0^1x^n(-\ln x)dx=(n+1)^{-2}$. Now
$$\frac1{n(n+1)^2}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}.$$
Hence the first two terms telescope to $1$, while
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n+1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}-1.$$
Thus
$$\boxed{I=2-\frac{\pi^2}{6}}.$$
This is positive because $\pi^2<12$, agreeing with the sign of the original integrand.

graderFixtures.proofText: Both endpoints behave like -u ln u. Since (-ln x)x^n/n is nonnegative, Tonelli gives I=sum 1/[n(n+1)^2]. The decomposition 1/n-1/(n+1)-1/(n+1)^2 yields I=1-(pi^2/6-1)=2-pi^2/6>0.
The series reduces to 1-(1-pi^2/6), so I=pi^2/6-2 even though the integrand is positive.
I substitute the power series on (0,1), integrate it through both singular endpoints without a cutoff or exchange theorem, and call the formal sum the improper integral.

CALC2:010132.title: Scale an improper quadratic family before differentiating it
CALC2:010132.objective: Evaluate a parameterized improper integral by scaling and trigonometric substitution, derive an explicit tail certificate, and cross-check it by differentiating a simpler improper family under stated uniform domination conditions.
CALC2:010132.statement:
For $a>0$, define
$$J(a)=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)^2}.$$
(a) Evaluate $J(a)$ exactly by a change of scale followed by a trigonometric substitution.
(b) For $R>0$, give an explicit upper bound for the tail $\int_R^\infty (x^2+a^2)^{-2}dx$ that proves convergence.
(c) Cross-check the result from $K(a)=\int_0^\infty (x^2+a^2)^{-1}dx$ by differentiating with respect to $a$. State a compact $a$-interval and an integrable dominating function that justify moving the derivative through the improper integral.
permittedResults: If $a\in[a_0/2,3a_0/2]$, then $|\partial_a(x^2+a^2)^{-1}|=2a/(x^2+a^2)^2$ is bounded by an integrable piecewise function independent of a; dominated differentiation then gives $K'(a)=\int_0^\infty-2a(x^2+a^2)^{-2}dx$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use scaling and u=tan(theta) as the primary evaluation, then dominated parameter differentiation as a check.
A beta-integral evaluation is acceptable for the primary route, but the independent derivative cross-check must still state its hypotheses.

milestones.criterion: Scales by x=au and evaluates the dimensionless tangent-substitution integral correctly.
Produces an explicit tail bound tending to zero.
Differentiates K only after supplying local uniform domination and recovers the same J(a).

commonErrors.description: Reports an a^(-4) or a^(-2) scale after substituting x=au.
commonErrors.consequence: The differential contributes one factor of a, so a fourth-power denominator leaves the required a^(-3).

commonErrors.description: Differentiates K(a) under the infinite integral merely because the pointwise derivative exists.
commonErrors.consequence: Pointwise differentiability alone does not justify exchanging a parameter derivative with an improper integral.

hintTree.content: First set x=au; the remaining integral is dimensionless and the factor a^(-3) should be visible.
For u=tan theta, du=sec^2 theta dtheta and (1+u^2)^(-2) becomes cos^2 theta.
At a fixed a_0, bound the derivative separately on 0<=x<=1 and x>=1 while keeping a in [a_0/2,3a_0/2].

CALC2:010132.canonicalSolution:
Set $x=au$. Then
$$J(a)=\frac1{a^3}\int_0^\infty\frac{du}{(1+u^2)^2}.$$
With $u=\tan\theta$, $0\le\theta<\pi/2$, the integrand becomes $\cos^2\theta$, so
$$J(a)=\frac1{a^3}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{4a^3}}.$$
For every $R>0$,
$$0<\int_R^\infty\frac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)^2}
\le\int_R^\infty\frac{dx}{x^4}=\boxed{\frac1{3R^3}}.$$

For the cross-check, the same tangent substitution gives $K(a)=\pi/(2a)$. Fix $a_0>0$ and restrict $a$ to $[a_0/2,3a_0/2]$. On $0\le x\le1$,
$$\frac{2a}{(x^2+a^2)^2}\le\frac{3a_0}{(a_0/2)^4},$$
and on $x\ge1$ it is at most $3a_0/x^4$. These two bounds form an integrable function on $[0,\infty)$ independent of $a$ in that interval. Dominated differentiation is therefore valid and yields
$$-\frac{\pi}{2a^2}=K'(a)=-2aJ(a),$$
again giving $J(a)=\pi/(4a^3)$. The power $a^{-3}$ also has the required dimension of inverse length cubed.

graderFixtures.proofText: x=au gives J=a^(-3) integral_0^infinity (1+u^2)^(-2)du; u=tan theta makes this integral cos^2 theta=pi/4. The tail is at most 1/(3R^3). On a compact interval around a_0 the derivative is bounded on [0,1] and by C/x^4 for x>=1, so K'=-2aJ and J=pi/(4a^3).
After x=au I keep all four denominator powers but forget dx=a du, so I report J=pi/(4a^4).
Since the integrand has a pointwise a-derivative, I move that derivative through the improper integral without restricting a or giving any integrable uniform majorant.

CALC2:010133.title: Make both endpoints vote on a rational-power family
CALC2:010133.objective: Determine a complete two-parameter convergence region by deriving and intersecting independent power models at zero and infinity.
CALC2:010133.statement:
For real parameters $a$ and $b$, determine exactly when
$$I(a,b)=\int_0^\infty \frac{x^a}{(1+x)^b}\,dx$$
converges. Split the integral at $1$, use a limit comparison at each improper
endpoint, classify both equality boundaries, and state whether conditional
convergence is possible. Do not evaluate the integral with the beta function.
permittedResults: For real $r$, $\int_0^1x^r\,dx$ converges exactly when $r>-1$, while $\int_1^\infty x^r\,dx$ converges exactly when $r<-1$. A positive finite limit ratio transfers either conclusion.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use two limit comparisons against power integrals and intersect their parameter regions.
Use equivalent two-sided constant bounds near each endpoint, proving both directions.

milestones.criterion: Derives a>-1 at zero using a valid comparison.
Derives b>a+1 at infinity and intersects the endpoint conditions.
Rejects both equality lines and correctly rules out conditional convergence.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the infinity condition and never audits zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The lower cutoff can diverge when a<=-1 even if b>a+1.

commonErrors.description: Allows either equality boundary by using a non-strict power-test inequality.
commonErrors.consequence: Each equality gives a logarithmically divergent 1/x model.

hintTree.content: Near zero, compare the integrand with x^a.
At infinity, factor x^b from (1+x)^b and compare with x^(a-b).
Keep both inequalities strict: equality at either endpoint produces the model 1/x.

CALC2:010133.canonicalSolution:
Split at $1$. As $x\to0^+$,
$$\frac{x^a/(1+x)^b}{x^a}=(1+x)^{-b}\longrightarrow1,$$
so the lower part converges exactly when $a>-1$. As $x\to\infty$,
$$\frac{x^a/(1+x)^b}{x^{a-b}}=\left(\frac{x}{1+x}\right)^b\longrightarrow1,$$
so the tail converges exactly when $a-b<-1$, equivalently $b>a+1$. Both
conditions are necessary and sufficient:
$$\boxed{a>-1\quad\text{and}\quad b>a+1}.$$
If $a=-1$, the integrand is asymptotic to $1/x$ at zero. If $b=a+1$, it is
asymptotic to $1/x$ at infinity. Each boundary diverges logarithmically. The
integrand is nonnegative on $(0,\infty)$, so convergence in the displayed
region is absolute and there is no conditional case.

graderFixtures.proofText: Near zero the ratio to x^a tends to 1, giving a>-1. At infinity the ratio to x^(a-b) tends to 1, giving b>a+1. Equality at either boundary gives 1/x divergence, and positivity means convergence is absolute only.
At infinity I obtain b>a+1, so I give that as the whole answer without testing zero.
I report a>=-1 and b>=a+1, including both equality cases despite their 1/x behavior.

CALC2:010134.title: Resolve the power boundary before the logarithm
CALC2:010134.objective: Classify a power-log improper family whose lower endpoint and logarithmic tail impose different, interacting parameter inequalities.
CALC2:010134.statement:
For real parameters $p$ and $q$, classify convergence of
$$J(p,q)=\int_0^\infty \frac{[\ln(1+x)]^p}{x^q}\,dx.$$
Analyze $0$ and $\infty$ separately. At infinity treat all three cases $q>1$,
$q<1$, and $q=1$; in the boundary case use an explicit substitution rather
than merely saying that logarithms grow slowly. State the full intersection
of the endpoint conditions and then simplify it, explicitly explaining what
happens to the $q=1$ branch.
permittedResults: As $x\to0^+$, $\ln(1+x)\sim x$. At infinity, every fixed logarithmic power is dominated by every positive power of $x$, and $\int^\infty (\ln x)^p\,dx/x$ converges exactly when $p<-1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use asymptotic equivalence at zero, epsilon-power domination off the tail boundary, and u=ln x on q=1.
Use eventual two-sided inequalities for ln(1+x) and standard power-log comparison integrals.

milestones.criterion: Uses ln(1+x)~x to derive q<p+1 at zero.
Correctly classifies q>1, q<1, and q=1 at infinity with a valid logarithmic substitution on the boundary.
Intersects and simplifies the conditions to q>1 and p>q-1, explaining why q=1 is impossible for the full integral.

commonErrors.description: Treats [ln(1+x)]^p as a harmless constant near zero and tests only x^(-q).
commonErrors.consequence: The missing factor x^p changes the lower condition to q<p+1.

commonErrors.description: Lists q=1,p<-1 as convergent without intersecting it with the lower endpoint.
commonErrors.consequence: At zero, q=1 requires p>0, so the alleged boundary branch is empty.

hintTree.content: Near zero, ln(1+x) contributes the power x^p; the model is x^(p-q).
For q different from 1, bound the logarithmic factor above or below by a small power of x.
When q=1, set u=ln x, then intersect that tail result with the zero condition.

CALC2:010134.canonicalSolution:
As $x\to0^+$, $\ln(1+x)/x\to1$, so the integrand is
limit-comparable to $x^{p-q}$. The lower endpoint converges exactly when
$$p-q>-1,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad q<p+1.\tag{1}$$
At infinity, replacing $\ln(1+x)$ by $\ln x$ does not change convergence. If
$q>1$, choose $\varepsilon=(q-1)/2>0$. The logarithmic factor is eventually
at most a constant times $x^\varepsilon$, leaving an integrable power
$x^{-(q-\varepsilon)}$. If $q<1$, choose $\varepsilon=(1-q)/2>0$. A
reciprocal epsilon-power lower bound leaves a divergent comparison with
$x^{-(q+\varepsilon)}$, whose denominator exponent is less than $1$. Thus
the tail converges for every $p$ when $q>1$ and diverges for every $p$ when
$q<1$.

When $q=1$, set $u=\ln x$ on a sufficiently large tail:
$$\int^\infty\frac{(\ln x)^p}{x}\,dx=\int^\infty u^p\,du,$$
which converges exactly when $p<-1$. Therefore the unsimplified full condition
is
$$q<p+1\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(q>1\ \text{or}\ (q=1\text{ and }p<-1)\bigr).$$
On the $q=1$ branch, condition (1) requires $1<p+1$, hence $p>0$, which is
incompatible with $p<-1$. That branch is empty. Consequently
$$\boxed{q>1\quad\text{and}\quad q<p+1},$$
or equivalently $\boxed{q>1\text{ and }p>q-1}$. The integrand is positive,
so no conditional convergence occurs.

graderFixtures.proofText: Near zero the model is x^(p-q), so q<p+1. The tail converges for q>1, diverges for q<1, and at q=1 requires p<-1 after u=ln x. But q=1 also requires p>0 at zero, so the full region is exactly q>1 and p>q-1.
Near zero I ignore [ln(1+x)]^p and require only q<1.
I keep q=1,p<-1 in the final answer without noticing that the zero endpoint simultaneously requires p>0.

CALC2:010135.title: Let one logarithm change both endpoint tests
CALC2:010135.objective: Classify a three-parameter finite-interval family, including the logarithmic exception at zero and the coupled effective power at one.
CALC2:010135.statement:
For real parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$,
determine exactly when
$$K(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\int_0^1
x^\alpha(1-x)^\beta|\ln x|^\gamma\,dx$$
converges. Split the integral at $1/2$. Your proof must include the exceptional
logarithmic case when $\alpha=-1$, explain why the logarithm changes the
effective power at $1$, classify every equality boundary, and state whether
conditional convergence is possible.
permittedResults: As $x\to1^-$, $-\ln x\sim1-x$. Consequently $|\ln x|^\gamma/(1-x)^\gamma\to1$ for each fixed real $\gamma$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the standard power-log test at zero and a limit comparison with (1-x)^(beta+gamma) at one.
Use u=-ln x at zero and t=1-x at one to derive both model integrals directly.

milestones.criterion: Classifies the zero endpoint, including the exceptional alpha=-1,gamma<-1 case.
Uses -ln x~1-x to derive beta+gamma>-1 at the upper endpoint.
Intersects the conditions, rejects equality boundaries, and rules out conditional convergence.

commonErrors.description: Rejects every alpha=-1 case by applying only the ordinary power test.
commonErrors.consequence: The cases gamma<-1 converge after u=-ln x and belong in the exact region.

commonErrors.description: Tests beta alone at the upper endpoint and treats the logarithmic factor as constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Because -ln x~1-x, gamma contributes directly to the exponent beta+gamma.

hintTree.content: On (0,1/2], the factor (1-x)^beta stays between two positive constants.
When alpha=-1, set u=-ln x and test the resulting power tail in u.
Near one, combine beta with the power contributed by |ln x|^gamma.

CALC2:010135.canonicalSolution:
On $(0,1/2]$, $(1-x)^\beta$ is bounded above and below
by positive constants, so the lower endpoint has the same convergence as
$x^\alpha|\ln x|^\gamma$. If $\alpha>-1$, it converges for every real
$\gamma$; if $\alpha<-1$, it diverges for every $\gamma$. On the boundary
$\alpha=-1$, set $u=-\ln x$. Since $dx/x=-du$, the cutoff integral becomes a
tail $\int^\infty u^\gamma\,du$, which converges exactly when $\gamma<-1$.
Thus zero requires
$$\alpha>-1\quad\text{or}\quad
(\alpha=-1\text{ and }\gamma<-1).\tag{1}$$

At $x\to1^-$, $x^\alpha\to1$ and $|\ln x|\sim1-x$. The integrand is
therefore limit-comparable to
$$(1-x)^{\beta+\gamma},$$
so the upper endpoint converges exactly when
$$\beta+\gamma>-1.\tag{2}$$
Combining (1) and (2),
$$\boxed{\beta+\gamma>-1\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\alpha>-1\ \text{or}\ (\alpha=-1\text{ and }\gamma<-1)\bigr).}$$
The boundary $\beta+\gamma=-1$ gives a $1/(1-x)$ divergence. The corner
$\alpha=-1,\gamma=-1$ becomes $\int^\infty du/u$ and also diverges. Because
the integrand is nonnegative on $(0,1)$, convergence is absolute and there is
no conditional case.

graderFixtures.proofText: At zero the power-log test gives alpha>-1, or alpha=-1 with gamma<-1. At one, |ln x|~1-x gives beta+gamma>-1. The equality beta+gamma=-1 and the corner alpha=-1,gamma=-1 both diverge logarithmically.
I use only the ordinary x^alpha test and reject alpha=-1 even when gamma=-3.
Near one I require beta>-1 and ignore gamma, although |ln x|^gamma contributes (1-x)^gamma.

CALC2:010136.title: Let the second logarithm decide only the first boundary
CALC2:010136.objective: Classify an iterated-logarithm tail by nested substitutions, separating the dominant log-power cases from the single boundary where the second exponent matters.
CALC2:010136.statement:
For real parameters $p$ and $q$, determine exactly when
the tail integral
$$L(p,q)=\int_{e^e}^\infty
\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p(\ln\ln x)^q}$$
converges. Use explicit substitutions rather than quoting an unnamed test.
Explain why $q$ matters when $p=1$ but cannot rescue $p<1$ or destroy $p>1$,
and classify the equality case $q=1$. The lower limit $e^e$ is fixed so that
only the infinite tail is improper.
permittedResults: For real $r$, $\int_A^\infty u^{-r}\,du$ with $A>0$ converges exactly when $r>1$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, every fixed power of $\ln u$ is eventually bounded in magnitude by a constant times $u^\varepsilon$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use u=ln x, logarithm-versus-power comparison off the boundary, and v=ln u on p=1.
Apply the standard power-log tail test after deriving it from the two substitutions and epsilon-power bounds.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the original tail to integral_e^infinity du/[u^p(ln u)^q].
Correctly proves convergence for p>1 and divergence for p<1 without letting q reverse those cases.
Uses v=ln u on p=1 and obtains q>1, explicitly rejecting q=1.

commonErrors.description: Claims a sufficiently large q can make the integral converge when p<1, or a negative q can destroy convergence when p>1.
commonErrors.consequence: A logarithmic power cannot reverse a strict power-integral classification.

commonErrors.description: Includes p=1,q=1 as a convergent boundary case.
commonErrors.consequence: After both substitutions the integral is exactly the divergent harmonic tail integral dv/v.

hintTree.content: First set u=ln x; the lower limit becomes e and dx/x=du.
For p greater or less than 1, compare the logarithmic factor with a small power of u.
On the boundary p=1, set v=ln u and apply one final power test.

CALC2:010136.canonicalSolution:
Set $u=\ln x$. Since $dx/x=du$ and $x=e^e$ gives
$u=e$,
$$L(p,q)=\int_e^\infty\frac{du}{u^p(\ln u)^q}.$$
If $p>1$, choose $0<\varepsilon<p-1$. For every real $q$, the factor
$(\ln u)^{-q}$ is eventually at most a constant times $u^\varepsilon$, so
the integrand is bounded above by a constant times $u^{-(p-\varepsilon)}$,
an integrable power. If $p<1$, choose $0<\varepsilon<1-p$. The same
logarithm-versus-power fact supplies an eventual lower bound by a positive
constant times $u^{-(p+\varepsilon)}$, whose exponent is below $1$, so the
integral diverges. Thus $q$ cannot reverse either strict case.

When $p=1$, make the second substitution $v=\ln u$, for which $du/u=dv$ and
the lower limit is $1$:
$$L(1,q)=\int_1^\infty v^{-q}\,dv.$$
This converges exactly when $q>1$. At $q=1$ it is $\int_1^\infty dv/v$ and
diverges logarithmically. Therefore
$$\boxed{p>1\quad\text{or}\quad(p=1\text{ and }q>1)}.$$
The integrand is positive, so this is an absolute-convergence classification;
no conditional case exists.

graderFixtures.proofText: Set u=ln x to obtain integral_e^infinity du/[u^p(ln u)^q]. Strictly p>1 converges and p<1 diverges because logs cannot beat powers. If p=1, v=ln u gives integral_1^infinity v^(-q)dv, so q>1; q=1 diverges.
I claim p=0,q=100 converges because the second logarithm has a large exponent, even though logarithms cannot rescue a subcritical u power.
For p=1,q=1 I call the boundary convergent, but two substitutions give the divergent integral dv/v.

CALC2:010217.title: Find the loop hidden in two parameter values
CALC2:010217.objective: Solve a distinct-parameter self-intersection, compute both crossing tangents, identify orientation, and evaluate loop area directly from a parametric line integral.
CALC2:010217.statement:
Consider
\[
x(t)=t^2-1,\qquad y(t)=t^3-3t,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.
\]
Find every point reached by two distinct parameter values. At the self-intersection, find the two tangent slopes. Identify the parameter interval that traces the closed loop, determine its orientation, and compute the loop's exact area using a parametric area integral.
permittedResults: For a positively oriented simple closed parametric loop, $A=\oint x\,dy=\int x(t)y'(t)\,dt$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Exploit even x and odd y before solving simultaneous equations.
Plot only a few directional points to determine orientation, then use the exact line integral.

milestones.criterion: Solves the self-intersection as a two-parameter problem.
Finds both tangent branches and the loop orientation.
Sets up and evaluates the signed parametric area correctly.

commonErrors.description: Uses t=0 as a self-intersection without producing two distinct parameter values.
commonErrors.consequence: A single regular parameter value is not a self-intersection.

commonErrors.description: Takes an absolute value inside the x times y-prime integral and obtains a different area.
commonErrors.consequence: The loop is already positively oriented, so the signed integral should be evaluated as a whole.

hintTree.content: Equality of x-coordinates gives $s=\pm t$; the distinct case is $s=-t$.
Then equality of y-coordinates requires $y(t)=0$.
On the loop, integrate $3(t^2-1)^2$ from $-\sqrt3$ to $\sqrt3$.

CALC2:010217.canonicalSolution:
Suppose parameters $s\ne t$ give the same point. Equality of the x-coordinates gives $s^2=t^2$, so the distinct case is $s=-t$. Since $y$ is odd, equality $y(s)=y(t)$ becomes $-y(t)=y(t)$, hence
\[
t^3-3t=t(t^2-3)=0.
\]
The value $t=0$ does not produce two distinct parameters. Thus $t=\pm\sqrt3$, and both give
\[
(x,y)=(2,0).
\]
For $t\ne0$,
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2-3}{2t}.
\]
At $t=\sqrt3$ the slope is $\sqrt3$, while at $t=-\sqrt3$ it is $-\sqrt3$.

The loop is traced for $-\sqrt3\le t\le\sqrt3$. At its rightmost crossing, the velocity for $t=-\sqrt3$ points up and left, so the loop is counterclockwise. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}x(t)y'(t)\,dt\\
&=\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}(t^2-1)(3t^2-3)\,dt\\
&=3\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}(t^2-1)^2\,dt\\
&=6\left[\frac{t^5}{5}-\frac{2t^3}{3}+t\right]_0^{\sqrt3}
=\boxed{\frac{24\sqrt3}{5}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: Equal x-values force $s=-t$ in the distinct case; oddness of y then gives $t=\pm\sqrt3$, both at $(2,0)$. The slopes are $\mp\sqrt3$ on the two branches, the interval is $[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3]$ counterclockwise, and $\int x y' dt=24\sqrt3/5$.
Because $y(0)=0$, I call $t=0$ a self-intersection even though I never find a second distinct parameter with the same point.
I replace $x(t)y'(t)$ by its pointwise absolute value before integrating, although the closed loop already has a consistent counterclockwise orientation.

CALC2:010218.title: Separate the two loops before integrating the limacon
CALC2:010218.objective: Use zero-radius parameters and the geometric meaning of negative polar radius to isolate inner and outer traces and compute both loop areas without double counting.
CALC2:010218.statement:
For the polar curve
\[
r=1-2\sin\theta,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,
\]
find the parameter values where the curve passes through the pole. Explain which interval traces the inner loop and where that loop lies geometrically despite $r<0$. Compute the exact inner-loop area, total area swept over $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, and outer-loop area.
permittedResults: A polar trace from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ has signed geometric area $\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r(\theta)^2\,d\theta$ when that interval traces the region once.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use pole crossings to partition the parameter interval before any area calculation.
Compute the full squared-radius area and subtract the separately isolated inner loop.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the pole crossings and the one-time inner-loop trace.
Interprets negative radius geometrically rather than discarding it.
Computes inner, total, and outer areas without double counting.

commonErrors.description: Discards the interval where r is negative and therefore omits the inner loop.
commonErrors.consequence: Negative radius represents a valid point in the opposite direction.

commonErrors.description: Calls the full zero-to-two-pi integral the outer-loop area without subtracting the inner loop.
commonErrors.consequence: The full trace contains both loops once.

hintTree.content: Solve $1-2\sin\theta=0$.
Between the two zeros, $r<0$, so angles are represented on the opposite side of the pole.
Expand $(1-2\sin\theta)^2=3-4\sin\theta-2\cos2\theta$.

CALC2:010218.canonicalSolution:
The curve reaches the pole when
\[
1-2\sin\theta=0,
\]
so on $[0,2\pi]$ the zero parameters are
\[
\boxed{\theta=\frac\pi6,\ \frac{5\pi}6}.
\]

\[

&=\frac12\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}(1-2\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta\\
&=\frac12\left[3\theta+4\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\\
&=\boxed{\pi-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}.
\end{aligned}

Over a full $2\pi$ trace,
\[
A_{\rm total}=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(1-2\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta
=\frac12(2\pi+4\pi)=3\pi.
\]
The inner and outer loops are each traced once and meet only at the pole, hence
\[
\boxed{A_{\rm out}=A_{\rm total}-A_{\rm in}
=2\pi+\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}.
\]

I compute $\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}r^2d\theta=3\pi$ and label all of it outer-loop area, never removing the separately traced inner loop.

CALC2:010219.title: Measure an astroid without pretending its cusps are regular
CALC2:010219.objective: Analyze a closed parametric curve with four nonregular cusp parameters, determine its orientation, and compute its exact enclosed area and perimeter using symmetry and absolute speed.
CALC2:010219.statement:
The curve
$$
x(t)=2\cos^3t,\qquad y(t)=2\sin^3t,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi
$$
is an astroid. Identify every parameter at which the velocity vanishes and explain why these isolated cusps do not invalidate the piecewise arc-length and area calculations. Determine the orientation, then compute the exact perimeter and enclosed area.
permittedResults: Parametric length is $\int\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}\,dt$ on each smooth piece.
For a positively oriented simple closed parametric curve, area is $\oint x\,dy$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use quadrant symmetry after deriving the full derivative and sign behavior.
Compute both full-interval integrals and use absolute values only where the geometric formula requires them.

milestones.criterion: Locates and interprets every zero-velocity cusp.
Computes length piecewise with the correct absolute speed.
Computes signed area with the correct orientation and exact value.

commonErrors.description: Uses six sine t cosine t as the speed on the entire zero-to-two-pi interval.
commonErrors.consequence: Signed cancellations produce a false perimeter.

commonErrors.description: Rejects all length or area formulas merely because velocity is zero at four isolated parameters.
commonErrors.consequence: The curve is piecewise regular and the integrals remain valid across the finite partition.

hintTree.content: Differentiate both cubic trigonometric coordinates and locate their common zeros.
On the first quadrant the speed simplifies to $6\sin t\cos t$.
For area, integrate $xy'$ over the full interval or use fourfold symmetry carefully.

CALC2:010219.canonicalSolution:
Differentiation gives
$$
x'=-6\cos^2t\sin t,\qquad y'=6\sin^2t\cos t.
$$
Both vanish exactly at $t=0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2,2\pi$, with the first and last representing the same cusp. Between successive cusp parameters the curve is regular. It starts at $(2,0)$ and moves into the first quadrant, so the trace is counterclockwise.

The speed is
$$
\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}=6|\sin t\cos t|.
$$
One quadrant therefore has length
$$
\int_0^{\pi/2}6\sin t\cos t\,dt=3,
$$
so the perimeter is $\boxed{12}$.

For the area,
$$
A=\int_0^{2\pi}x(t)y'(t)dt
=12\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^4t\sin^2t\,dt.
$$
Using fourfold symmetry and
$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2t\cos^4t\,dt=\pi/32$ gives
$$
A=12\cdot4\cdot\frac\pi{32}=\boxed{\frac{3\pi}{2}}.
$$
The finite set of zero-speed cusp parameters has no effect on either integral; the formulas apply on the four regular arcs and their integrals add.

graderFixtures.proofText: The common derivative zeros occur at multiples of $\pi/2$. On each open quadrant arc the curve is regular and the trace is counterclockwise. Speed is $6|\sin t\cos t|$, giving perimeter $4(3)=12$; $∫xy'dt=12(4)(\pi/32)=3\pi/2$.
I integrate $6\sin t\cos t$ without absolute values from zero to two pi, get cancellation, and report zero perimeter.
Because the derivative vanishes at the axis points, I declare the parametric length and area formulas unusable everywhere and do not partition into regular arcs.

CALC2:010220.title: Close one spiral turn with its radial seam
CALC2:010220.objective: Interpret the orientation of a spiral-plus-segment boundary and compute both the swept polar area and the spiral arc length, including the logarithmic term from the exact antiderivative.
CALC2:010220.statement: Trace the Archimedean spiral $r=\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, then close the curve by following the positive $x$-axis from $(2\pi,0)$ back to the origin. Prove that this is a simple positively oriented boundary except for its shared endpoints. Compute the exact enclosed area and the length of the spiral portion. Do not include the closing segment in the requested spiral length.

Polar arc length is $\int\sqrt{r^2+(dr/d\theta)^2}\,d\theta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: View the boundary ray by ray to establish simplicity and area orientation.
Apply the polar length formula directly and evaluate the standard hyperbolic-type antiderivative.

milestones.criterion: Justifies the boundary and its orientation.
Computes the polar area exactly with no repeated tracing.
Computes the requested spiral length and excludes the seam.

commonErrors.description: Uses the integral of r squared without the polar factor one half.
commonErrors.consequence: The enclosed area is doubled.

commonErrors.description: Adds the radial closing segment to the requested length of the spiral portion.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported quantity does not match the requested curve segment.

hintTree.content: Every ray with angle strictly between zero and two pi meets the spiral once.
The area integrand is one half theta squared.

Each intermediate ray is met once, and the return segment lies only on the positive $x$-axis. Thus the spiral followed outward and the seam followed inward form a simple counterclockwise boundary.

The radial seam contributes no swept polar area. Hence
$$
A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\theta^2d\theta
=\boxed{\frac{4\pi^3}{3}}.
$$
For the spiral, $r'=1$, so
$$
L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\theta^2+1}\,d\theta.
$$
Using the stated antiderivative gives
$$
\boxed{L=\pi\sqrt{4\pi^2+1}
+\frac12\ln\!\left(2\pi+\sqrt{4\pi^2+1}\right)}.
$$
The seam itself has length $2\pi$, but it is excluded by the question. The area formula counts the region once because radius is single-valued on every interior angle.

CALC2:010221.objective: Differentiate a parametric curve, obtain its speed, and integrate the speed over exactly one arch without losing the absolute-value information at the cusps.
CALC2:010221.statement:
The cycloid
$$
x=t-\sin t,\qquad y=1-\cos t
$$
traces one arch for $0\le t\le2\pi$. Find the exact length of that arch. Identify the parameter values where the velocity vanishes and explain why the speed formula remains integrable there.

acceptableStrategies.description: Simplify the squared speed with 2-2cos(t)=4sin^2(t/2) before taking the square root.
Use the geometry of one arch to choose an interval on which the half-angle sine has known sign.

milestones.criterion: Computes dx/dt and dy/dt and simplifies the speed to 2|sin(t/2)|.
Uses the one-arch interval to justify removing the absolute value.
Evaluates the arc-length integral as 8 and relates the endpoint zeros to the cusps.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sqrt(4 sin^2(t/2)) by 2 sin(t/2) without recording an absolute value or checking the interval.
commonErrors.consequence: That simplification is not valid for arbitrary parameter intervals and hides the sign reasoning required by arc length.

commonErrors.description: Uses sqrt(2-2cos(t))=sin(t/2), omitting the factor 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The speed and the resulting length are cut in half, producing 4 instead of 8.

$$
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{(1-\cos t)^2+\sin^2t}
=\sqrt{2-2\cos t}=2|\sin(t/2)|.
$$
On $[0,2\pi]$, $t/2\in[0,\pi]$, so the sine is nonnegative and the speed is $2\sin(t/2)$. The velocity vanishes only at $t=0$ and $t=2\pi$, the cusp endpoints; a continuous nonnegative speed with isolated zeros is still integrable. Thus
$$
L=\int_0^{2\pi}2\sin(t/2)\,dt=[-4\cos(t/2)]_0^{2\pi}=8.
$$
The absolute value cannot be discarded before its sign is audited. The exact one-arch length is $\boxed{8}$.

I simplify sqrt(4sin^2(t/2)) to 2sin(t/2) without recording the absolute value or checking its sign on the chosen interval.

CALC2:010223.title: Recover a cardioid tangent when both derivatives vanish
CALC2:010223.objective: Convert a polar cardioid to parametric coordinates, distinguish a regular vertical tangent from a cusp with zero velocity, and use a limiting argument to identify the cusp tangent correctly.
CALC2:010223.statement:
Consider the cardioid
$$
r=1-\cos\theta,
\qquad
x=(1-\cos\theta)\cos\theta,
\quad
y=(1-\cos\theta)\sin\theta.
$$
Show that $\theta=0$ is a cusp at the pole and determine its tangent line using a limiting derivative or limiting secant argument; do not divide $dy/d\theta$ by $dx/d\theta$ by simply substituting $\theta=0$. Then show that the point at $\theta=\pi$ has a vertical tangent and state that tangent line.
permittedResults: For a regular parametric point, $dx/d\theta=0$ and $dy/d\theta\ne0$ give a vertical tangent; at a zero-velocity cusp, that test must be replaced by a limit.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the derivative ratio away from the cusp and then pass to its limit.
Use the polar secant identity y/x=tan(theta) at the cusp, then use coordinate derivatives at the regular point.

milestones.criterion: Computes the two coordinate derivatives and identifies the zero-velocity point at theta=0.
Uses a two-sided limiting slope or secant direction to obtain the cusp tangent y=0.
Evaluates the regular derivatives at theta=pi and gives the vertical tangent x=-2.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes theta=0 into dy/dtheta divided by dx/dtheta and declares the slope to be 0/0 or zero without a limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The ordinary derivative quotient is undefined at the cusp, so the claimed tangent has not been established.

commonErrors.description: Calls the tangent at theta=pi horizontal because dx/dtheta is zero.
commonErrors.consequence: A zero x-derivative with nonzero y-derivative gives a vertical tangent, here the line x=-2.

hintTree.content: Differentiate x(theta) and y(theta) before evaluating either special parameter.
Near theta=0, use dy/dx=(dy/dtheta)/(dx/dtheta) for theta not equal to 0 and take the limit, or use y/x=tan(theta).
At theta=pi, evaluate the two coordinate derivatives directly and identify the fixed x-coordinate of the tangent line.

CALC2:010223.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the displayed parameterization:
$$
\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1),
\qquad
\frac{dy}{d\theta}=(1-\cos\theta)(2\cos\theta+1).
$$
At $\theta=0$, both derivatives vanish and $(x,y)=(0,0)$, so direct substitution into $(dy/d\theta)/(dx/d\theta)$ gives only $0/0$. For nearby nonzero $\theta$,
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{(1-\cos\theta)(2\cos\theta+1)}{\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)}.
$$
Using $1-\cos\theta\sim\theta^2/2$ and $\sin\theta\sim\theta$, this ratio tends to $0$ from both sides. Equivalently, every nonzero nearby point satisfies $y/x=\tan\theta\to0$. Thus the two branches meet with the common horizontal cusp tangent
$$
\boxed{y=0}.
$$
At $\theta=\pi$, the point is $(-2,0)$ and
$$
\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0,
\qquad
\frac{dy}{d\theta}=(1-(-1))(2(-1)+1)=-2\ne0.
$$
This is a regular vertical tangent, namely
$$
\boxed{x=-2}.
$$

At theta=0 both derivatives are zero, so I cancel the zeros and state dy/dx=1; I do not take any nearby limit or inspect the secant direction at the cusp.
At theta=pi I see dx/dtheta=0 and conclude the tangent is horizontal y=0, ignoring that dy/dtheta=-2 is nonzero and therefore the tangent is vertical.

Use symmetry only to replace the full integral by twice the half-interval integral, not as an additional multiplier afterward.

milestones.criterion: Solves cos(theta)>=0 and identifies the intersection rays theta=plus or minus pi/2.
Sets up one half integral from -pi/2 to pi/2 of (2+cos(theta))^2-4.
Evaluates the area as 4+pi/4 and explains why no extra doubling is needed.

commonErrors.description: Integrates over the full interval 0 to 2pi without restricting to rays where the limacon is outside the circle.
commonErrors.consequence: On half of those rays the squared-radius subtraction has the wrong geometric order and does not represent the requested set.

commonErrors.description: Integrates from -pi/2 to pi/2 and then multiplies by two for symmetry.
commonErrors.consequence: That interval already contains both symmetric halves, so the extra factor doubles the true area.

hintTree.content: Compare the two radii before writing an area formula; they are equal when cos(theta)=0.
Use the interval [-pi/2,pi/2], on which the limacon is the outer curve and both radii are positive.
Expand (2+cos(theta))^2-4 and integrate the cosine and cosine-squared terms separately.

CALC2:010224.canonicalSolution:
The limacon is outside the circle exactly when
$$
2+\cos\theta\ge2,
$$
or $\cos\theta\ge0$. A single interval representing all such rays is $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. The curves meet on the endpoint rays, and both radii are positive throughout, so this interval traces the desired region once with the limacon outside. Its area is
$$
A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\left((2+\cos\theta)^2-2^2\right)d\theta.
$$
Expanding gives
$$
A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(4\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta)d\theta.
$$
Now
$$
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}4\cos\theta\,d\theta=8,
\qquad
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac\pi2.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{A=4+\frac\pi4}.
$$
No additional symmetry multiplier is needed because the chosen interval already includes both the upper and lower halves of the region.

graderFixtures.proofText: The limacon is outside r=2 when cos(theta)>=0, so I use [-pi/2,pi/2]. The area is one half integral of ((2+cos theta)^2-4), which is one half(8+pi/2)=4+pi/4, with no extra doubling.
I integrate ((2+cos theta)^2-4)/2 from 0 to 2pi, even though cos(theta)<0 on half that range and the limacon is then inside rather than outside the circle.
I correctly integrate from -pi/2 to pi/2 and obtain 4+pi/4, but then double it for upper-lower symmetry even though the chosen interval already covered both halves.
