CALC2:010225.title: Check endpoint regularity before revolving a parametric arc
CALC2:010225.objective: Compute the surface area generated by revolving a parametric curve about the x-axis, using the parameter speed correctly and distinguishing a zero x-derivative from a singular parameterization.
CALC2:010225.statement:
The curve
$$
x=t^2,\qquad y=t,\qquad 0\leq t\leq1
$$
is revolved about the $x$-axis. Find the exact lateral surface area. State why the endpoint $t=0$ is regular even though $dx/dt=0$ there, and explain why the surface-area integral has no improper singularity at that endpoint.
permittedResults: For a regular parametric arc with $y\geq0$, revolution about the $x$-axis has area $S=2\pi\int y(t)\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2}\,dt$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the parametric surface-area formula directly and use a linear substitution in t^2.
Eliminate the parameter to get y=sqrt(x), then use the graph surface formula with a cutoff; simplifying shows the same proper parametric integrand.

milestones.criterion: Computes the velocity and speed and correctly identifies t=0 as regular.
Sets up S=2pi integral_0^1 t sqrt(4t^2+1)dt with the correct radius.
Evaluates the integral exactly and explains continuity at the endpoint.

commonErrors.description: Uses ds=|dx/dt|dt=2t dt and omits the y-component of velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Arc length and surface area depend on the full speed, so the resulting area is too small and describes neither the given curve nor its surface.

commonErrors.description: Declares t=0 singular solely because x'(0)=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The velocity is <0,1>, so the curve is regular and the area integrand is continuous at the endpoint.

hintTree.content: Compute the full velocity <2t,1>, rather than judging regularity from dx/dt alone.
The radius is y=t and the speed is sqrt(4t^2+1).
Use u=4t^2+1 to evaluate 2pi integral_0^1 t sqrt(4t^2+1) dt.

CALC2:010225.canonicalSolution:
The velocity is
$$
\langle x'(t),y'(t)\rangle=\langle2t,1\rangle,
$$
so its speed is $\sqrt{4t^2+1}$. At $t=0$ the velocity is $\langle0,1\rangle$, not the zero vector. Thus the endpoint is regular despite $x'(0)=0$.

The distance to the $x$-axis is $y=t$, so the surface-area formula gives
$$
S=2\pi\int_0^1 t\sqrt{4t^2+1}\,dt.
$$
With $u=4t^2+1$ and $du=8t\,dt$,
$$
S=\frac{\pi}{4}\int_1^5u^{1/2}\,du
=\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\left(5^{3/2}-1\right)
=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{6}(5\sqrt5-1)}.
$$
The area integrand $2\pi t\sqrt{4t^2+1}$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and actually tends to $0$ at the left endpoint. Therefore no improper limit is needed there; a vertical tangent in the $xy$-plane does not create a singular surface-area integrand.

graderFixtures.proofText: Here r'(t)=<2t,1>, so r'(0)=<0,1> is nonzero. Thus S=2pi integral_0^1 t sqrt(4t^2+1)dt=pi(5sqrt5-1)/6, and the integrand is continuous at t=0.
I use ds=dx=2t dt, ignoring dy/dt=1, and integrate 2pi t(2t) instead of the full parametric speed.
Since dx/dt=0 at t=0, I call the parameterization singular and treat the surface integral as divergent without checking the velocity vector.

CALC2:010226.title: Deduplicate tangent lines at repeated pole crossings
CALC2:010226.objective: Analyze every parameter value at which a polar rose passes through the pole, derive the limiting tangent direction at a simple zero of the radius, and distinguish parameter crossings from geometrically distinct tangent lines.
CALC2:010226.statement:
For the polar curve
$$r=\sin(3\theta),\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi,$$
find every geometrically distinct tangent line at the pole. List the parameter values that produce pole crossings, derive the tangent direction from the Cartesian parameterization near a zero of $r$, and explain why the repeated crossings and negative-radius representation do not create six distinct lines.
permittedResults: Polar coordinate pairs $(r,\theta)$ and $(-r,\theta+\pi)$ represent the same point, while an unoriented line direction is unchanged when its angle is increased by $\pi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the first-order expansion at each simple zero of r.
Alternatively evaluate the limiting ratio dy/dx from the polar derivative formulas, while separately tracking vertical directions and deduplicating angles modulo pi.

milestones.criterion: Finds theta=kpi/3 for k=0,...,5 and verifies r' is nonzero at each crossing.
Derives the local tangent direction theta_k modulo pi from the Cartesian displacement.
Deduplicates the crossings and gives exactly y=0 and y=plus-or-minus sqrt(3)x.

commonErrors.description: Reports six different tangents by treating direction angles theta and theta+pi as different lines.
commonErrors.consequence: A tangent line is unoriented, so opposite direction vectors define the same geometric line and the answer must contain only three lines.

commonErrors.description: Claims every negative-radius portion creates an additional tangent direction at the pole.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing the sign of r reverses the representative direction but cannot change the span of the tangent vector.

hintTree.content: First solve sin(3theta)=0 on the half-open interval and check that r'=3cos(3theta) does not vanish there.
Expand x=r cos(theta) and y=r sin(theta) to first order about theta0; the scalar r'(theta0) may reverse orientation but not the line.
Reduce the six direction angles k pi/3 modulo pi before writing Cartesian equations.

CALC2:010226.canonicalSolution:
The pole occurs when
$$
\sin(3\theta)=0,
\quad\text{so}\quad
\theta_k=\frac{k\pi}{3},\qquad k=0,1,2,3,4,5.
$$
Moreover $r'(\theta_k)=3\cos(k\pi)=3(-1)^k\ne0$, so every zero is simple. Put $h=\theta-\theta_k$. Then
$$
r(\theta)=r'(\theta_k)h+o(h)
$$
and therefore
$$
(x,y)=r(\theta)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)
=r'(\theta_k)h(\cos\theta_k,\sin\theta_k)+o(h).
$$
Thus the tangent direction is $\theta_k$ modulo $\pi$; the sign of $r'(\theta_k)$ only reverses its orientation. The six parameter values consequently pair as $k$ and $k+3$, leaving the three line directions $0,\pi/3,2\pi/3$. Their equations are
$$
\boxed{y=0},\qquad
\boxed{y=\sqrt3\,x},\qquad
\boxed{y=-\sqrt3\,x}.
$$
Negative radius values change which parameter angle names a point, but they do not produce another geometric line. Hence there are six simple pole crossings in the parameter interval and exactly three distinct pole tangents.

graderFixtures.proofText: The pole crossings are theta=kpi/3, k=0,...,5, and r'=3(-1)^k is nonzero. Locally (x,y) is a scalar times <cos theta_k,sin theta_k>, so directions are modulo pi and the three lines are y=0 and y=plus-or-minus sqrt3 x.
I list six tangent rays for k=0 through 5 and count theta and theta+pi as separate tangent lines.
Whenever r is negative I add a new pole tangent, even though multiplying a direction vector by -1 leaves its line unchanged.

CALC2:010227.title: Read geometric information from a quadratic Bezier parameter
CALC2:010227.objective: Expand a quadratic Bezier curve into coordinates, certify its regularity and monotone horizontal trace, locate its unique horizontal tangent, and compute the exact area under the curve from a parametric line integral.
CALC2:010227.statement:
Let $P_0=(0,0)$, $P_1=(1,2)$, and $P_2=(3,0)$. The quadratic Bezier arc is
$$
\mathbf r(t)=(1-t)^2P_0+2(1-t)tP_1+t^2P_2,\qquad0\leq t\leq1.
$$
(a) Find its endpoint tangent lines and prove the parameterization is regular.
(b) Find the unique horizontal tangent and show it occurs at the maximum height.
(c) Prove that $x(t)$ is strictly increasing and compute the exact area between the arc and the $x$-axis using $\int y\,dx$.
permittedResults: If $x'(t)>0$ on $[a,b]$ and $y(t)\ge0$, the area under a parametric graph is $\int_{x(a)}^{x(b)}y\,dx=\int_a^b y(t)x'(t)\,dt$ without an absolute value or retracing factor.

acceptableStrategies.description: Work entirely parametrically, using velocity for tangents and the oriented line integral for area.
One may eliminate t after proving x is one-to-one, but the endpoint tangents and exact area are cleaner before elimination.

milestones.criterion: Expands the Bezier formula, computes r', gives y=2x and y=-x+3, and proves regularity.
Finds the unique horizontal tangent at t=1/2, point (5/4,1), and classifies it using y''=-8.
Uses x'>0 to justify a graph and evaluates integral_0^1 y(t)x'(t)dt as 2.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two line segments P0P1 and P1P2 as the Bezier arc and reports their slopes and triangular area.
commonErrors.consequence: The control polygon guides the curve but is not its parameterized trace, so its corner, height, and area do not answer the problem.

commonErrors.description: Computes the planar area as the integral of y(t) dt and omits the factor x'(t).
commonErrors.consequence: Area is accumulated with respect to horizontal displacement dx=x'(t)dt; dropping that factor changes the value and its geometric units.

hintTree.content: First expand the vector formula to x=2t+t^2 and y=4t-4t^2, then differentiate both coordinates.
Use the velocity at t=0 and t=1 for endpoint lines; solve y'=0 and use y'' to classify the interior tangent.
Because x'=2+2t stays positive, integrate (4t-4t^2)(2+2t) from 0 to 1 exactly once.

CALC2:010227.canonicalSolution:
Expanding the blend gives
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle2t+t^2,\,4t-4t^2\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle2+2t,\,4-8t\rangle.
$$
At $t=0$, the point is $(0,0)$ and the velocity is $(2,4)$, so the tangent line is $y=2x$. At $t=1$, the point is $(3,0)$ and the velocity is $(4,-4)$, so the other endpoint tangent is $y=-x+3$.

Because $x'(t)=2+2t>0$ throughout $[0,1]$, the velocity never vanishes; the parameterization is regular and the arc is a graph traced from left to right. A horizontal tangent requires
$$
y'(t)=4-8t=0,
$$
hence $t=1/2$. Its point is
$$
\left(2\cdot\frac12+\frac14,\,4\cdot\frac12-4\cdot\frac14\right)
=\left(\frac54,1\right).
$$
Since $y''=-8<0$, this is the unique maximum height.

Finally $y=4t(1-t)\ge0$ and $x'>0$, so
$$
A=\int_0^1y(t)x'(t)\,dt
=\int_0^1(4t-4t^2)(2+2t)\,dt
=\int_0^1(8t-8t^3)\,dt
=\boxed2.
$$
No symmetry multiplier is needed because the full arc is traced once while $x$ increases from $0$ to $3$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Expanding gives r=<2t+t^2,4t-4t^2> and r'=<2+2t,4-8t>. The endpoint tangents are y=2x and y=-x+3; t=1/2 gives the maximum (5/4,1), and integral y x' dt=2.
I replace the Bezier arc by the broken control polygon P0-P1-P2, so I use its corner at P1 and its triangular area instead of expanding the given parameterization.
I call integral_0^1 y(t)dt the area under the curve and obtain 2/3, never multiplying by x'(t) to convert dt into the required horizontal differential dx.

CALC2:010228.title: Derive polar curvature before using it
CALC2:010228.objective: Derive the curvature formula for a regular polar curve from its Cartesian velocity and acceleration, then apply it at a specified point while retaining the absolute value, tangent direction, and regularity check.
CALC2:010228.statement:
A twice differentiable polar curve is parameterized by
$$
x(\theta)=r(\theta)\cos\theta,\qquad y(\theta)=r(\theta)\sin\theta.
$$
(a) Starting from $\kappa=|x'y''-y'x''|/(x'^2+y'^2)^{3/2}$, derive the polar formula in terms of $r,r',r''$ wherever the curve is regular.
(b) For $r=2+\sin\theta$, find the point, tangent slope, and curvature at $\theta=0$. Explicitly verify that the velocity is nonzero there.
permittedResults: For any regular planar parameterization, unsigned curvature is $\kappa=|x'y''-y'x''|/(x'^2+y'^2)^{3/2}$; the numerator is the magnitude of the signed two-dimensional cross product of velocity and acceleration.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the Cartesian derivatives directly and simplify with sin^2(theta)+cos^2(theta)=1.
Alternatively use the moving polar basis e_r,e_theta with e_r'=e_theta and e_theta'=-e_r, then take the determinant in that oriented orthonormal basis.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the Cartesian polar parameterization and derives x'^2+y'^2=r^2+(r')^2.
Computes the second derivatives and reduces the curvature numerator to r^2+2(r')^2-r r'', retaining its absolute value.
At theta=0 obtains (2,0), velocity (1,2), slope 2, regularity, and curvature 6/(5sqrt5).

commonErrors.description: Uses |r^2+2(r')^2| in every case and omits the -r r'' contribution from the acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The formula then gives incorrect curvature whenever radial acceleration is nonzero and was not derived from x'y''-y'x''.

commonErrors.description: Calls r'(0)=1 the Cartesian tangent slope without computing dy/dx from x' and y'.
commonErrors.consequence: A radial derivative measures change of radius with angle, not slope in the xy-plane; the actual velocity (1,2) has slope 2.

hintTree.content: Differentiate x and y once, square and add, and use cancellation of the mixed sine-cosine terms to get r^2+(r')^2.
Differentiate again and expand x'y''-y'x''; group the rotational terms before taking the absolute value.
At theta=0, use r=2, r'=1, r''=0; compute x' and y' directly for the tangent slope as well as using the curvature formula.

CALC2:010228.canonicalSolution:
Differentiation gives
$$
x'=r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta,
\qquad
y'=r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta.
$$
Squaring and adding cancels the mixed terms:
$$x'^2+y'^2=r^2+(r')^2.$$
A second differentiation gives
$$
x''=(r''-r)\cos\theta-2r'\sin\theta,
\qquad
y''=(r''-r)\sin\theta+2r'\cos\theta.
$$
Expanding the signed numerator and collecting terms yields
$$
x'y''-y'x''=r^2+2(r')^2-r r''.
$$
Therefore, wherever $r^2+(r')^2>0$,
$$
\boxed{\kappa=
\frac{|r^2+2(r')^2-r r''|}{\bigl(r^2+(r')^2\bigr)^{3/2}}}.
$$

For $r=2+\sin\theta$, at $\theta=0$ we have $r=2$, $r'=\cos0=1$, and $r''=-\sin0=0$. The point is $(2,0)$. The velocity formulas give
$$
(x',y')=(1,2),
$$
which is nonzero, and hence the tangent slope is $dy/dx=2$. Finally,
$$
\kappa(0)=\frac{|2^2+2(1)^2-2(0)|}{(2^2+1^2)^{3/2}}
=\boxed{\frac6{5\sqrt5}}.
$$
The absolute value is harmless for this positive numerator but is essential in the general unsigned formula.

graderFixtures.proofText: The derivatives give speed squared r^2+(r')^2 and x'y''-y'x''=r^2+2(r')^2-r r'', so kappa is its absolute value over speed cubed. At theta=0 the point is (2,0), velocity (1,2), slope 2, and kappa=6/(5sqrt5).
I quote a polar curvature numerator r^2+2(r')^2 and drop the -r r'' term during the second differentiation, so my claimed general derivation fails when r'' is nonzero.
Because dr/dtheta=1 at theta=0, I report tangent slope 1 without forming x'=r'cos(theta)-r sin(theta) and y'=r'sin(theta)+r cos(theta).

CALC2:010229.title: Complete a rational circle trace through an improper parameter limit
CALC2:010229.objective: Analyze a rational parameterization of the unit circle, prove its regularity and exact coverage, identify the missing finite-parameter point and orientation, and recover the full circumference through an improper arc-length integral.
CALC2:010229.statement:
For $-\infty<t<\infty$, let
$$x(t)=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\qquad y(t)=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}.$$
Prove that the trace lies on the unit circle and is regular. Determine its orientation and the only circle point not attained at finite $t$. Then compute the total length of the completed trace using an improper integral.
permittedResults: A regular parametric curve has speed $\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}$; its length over the real parameter line is the limit of lengths on finite intervals when the improper integral converges.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the rational coordinates and evaluate the improper speed integral directly.
The substitution t=tan(theta/2) may identify the angular parameter, provided finite coverage and the improper endpoint are still justified.

milestones.criterion: Verifies x^2+y^2=1 and derives the strictly positive speed.
Identifies counterclockwise orientation and proves exactly (-1,0) is missed at finite parameter.
Evaluates the full improper arc-length integral as 2pi and explains the completed trace.

commonErrors.description: Claims some finite t attains (-1,0), usually by informally setting t=infinity.
commonErrors.consequence: Infinity is not a real parameter value; the coverage distinction and improper completion are then misstated.

commonErrors.description: Treats the limits t to plus and minus infinity as two separate circuits and reports length 4pi.
commonErrors.consequence: The real line traces the punctured circle once, with its two ends approaching the same missing point from opposite sides.

hintTree.content: Square the two rational coordinates over the common denominator.
Differentiate both coordinates and simplify the speed before checking regularity.
At t=0 the point is (1,0) and the velocity points upward; integrate 2/(1+t^2) from -infinity to infinity.

CALC2:010229.canonicalSolution:
Direct calculation gives
$$x^2+y^2=\frac{(1-t^2)^2+4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=1.$$
Moreover
$$x'=\frac{-4t}{(1+t^2)^2},\qquad y'=\frac{2(1-t^2)}{(1+t^2)^2},$$
so
$$\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}=\frac{2}{1+t^2}>0.$$
Thus the parameterization is regular for every finite $t$. At $t=0$ it passes through $(1,0)$ with velocity $(0,2)$, so it runs counterclockwise. Solving $x=-1$ would require $1-t^2=-(1+t^2)$, or $1=-1$, so $(-1,0)$ is not attained for finite $t$; it is approached as $t\to\pm\infty$. Finally,
$$L=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}
=2[\arctan t]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=\boxed{2\pi}.$$

CALC2:010230.title: Keep the polar sign consistent with a parabola's directrix
CALC2:010230.objective: Convert a polar conic into Cartesian form without losing its opening direction, identify its focus-directrix geometry and latus rectum, and compute a finite exact polar arc length with a half-angle substitution.
CALC2:010230.statement:
Consider
$$r=\frac{2}{1+\cos\theta},\qquad-\frac\pi2\le\theta\le\frac\pi2.$$
(a) Convert the full conic to Cartesian form and identify its vertex, focus, directrix, opening direction, and latus-rectum endpoints.
(b) Compute the exact length of the displayed finite arc.
permittedResults: For a polar curve, $ds=\sqrt{r^2+(dr/d\theta)^2}\,d\theta$; also $1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2(\theta/2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the polar arc-length formula followed by the half-angle identity.
After proving the Cartesian equation and matching endpoints, parameterize by y and integrate sqrt(1+(dx/dy)^2) as an independent route.

milestones.criterion: Converts the polar equation to y^2=4(1-x) without reversing the sign.
Correctly identifies all focus-directrix and latus-rectum data.
Derives the polar speed and evaluates the finite arc length exactly.

commonErrors.description: Converts the equation to y^2=4(x+1) or assigns directrix x=-2.
commonErrors.consequence: That parabola opens in the opposite direction and does not satisfy r(1+cos theta)=2.

commonErrors.description: Changes variables to u=theta/2 but omits dtheta=2du in the arc-length integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting length is exactly half of the displayed arc's length.

hintTree.content: Rewrite the polar equation as r+x=2 and isolate r before squaring.

$$x^2+y^2=(2-x)^2,$$
so
$$\boxed{y^2=4(1-x)}.$$
This parabola has vertex $(1,0)$, opens left, has focus $(0,0)$ (the pole), and directrix $x=2$. Its latus rectum is the line $x=0$, giving endpoints $(0,2)$ and $(0,-2)$.

Let $u=\theta/2$. Then $r=\sec^2u$ and
$$\frac{dr}{d\theta}=\sec^2u\tan u,$$
so the speed is $\sec^3u$ on the given interval. Therefore
$$L=2\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\sec^3u\,du
=\boxed{2\sqrt2+2\ln(1+\sqrt2)}.$$
The logarithm follows from the standard antiderivative of secant cubed and symmetry; the finite value also agrees with integrating the Cartesian arc from $y=-2$ to $y=2$.

I change r+x=2 into the opposite-opening parabola y^2=4(x+1) and report a negative directrix, reversing the polar sign.
I set u=theta/2 and integrate sec^3u but forget that dtheta=2du, obtaining exactly half the correct arc length.

CALC2:010231.title: Let a spiral accumulate finite sweep but infinite length
CALC2:010231.objective: Compare the accumulated polar sweep and arc length of a hyperbolic spiral, evaluate both finite-cutoff expressions exactly, and prove that their improper limits have different convergence behavior.

Consider the hyperbolic spiral
$$r(\theta)=\frac1\theta,\qquad 1\le\theta<\infty.$$
For $\Theta>1$, define the accumulated polar sweep with multiplicity by
$$A(\Theta)=\frac12\int_1^\Theta r(\theta)^2\,d\theta$$
and let $L(\Theta)$ be the arc length from $\theta=1$ to $\theta=\Theta$.
Find exact formulas for $A(\Theta)$ and $L(\Theta)$. Decide whether each has a finite limit as $\Theta\to\infty$, and explain why the finite sweep does not imply finite length.

A hyperbolic substitution may evaluate the arc-length integral if the cutoff and divergence conclusion remain explicit.

milestones.criterion: Computes A(Theta)=1/2(1-1/Theta) and its finite limit.
Derives the polar speed and an exact antiderivative for L(Theta).

commonErrors.description: Uses length integral integral r dtheta and concludes the length equals the finite area-scale integral.
commonErrors.consequence: Polar arc length requires sqrt(r^2+(r')^2), and the omitted derivative changes convergence from theta^(-2) to theta^(-1).

commonErrors.description: Calls A(infinity)=1/2 the ordinary geometric union area without addressing infinitely repeated angles.
commonErrors.consequence: The defined integral records accumulated sweep with multiplicity, so a simple-region interpretation needs a separate overlap analysis.

hintTree.content: The sweep is one-half the integral of theta^(-2).
The polar speed simplifies to sqrt(1+theta^2)/theta^2.

The sweep is
$$A(\Theta)=\frac12\int_1^\Theta\frac{d\theta}{\theta^2}
=\boxed{\frac12\left(1-\frac1\Theta\right)},$$
so $A(\Theta)\to1/2$.

Since $r'=-1/\theta^2$, the polar speed is
$$\sqrt{r^2+(r')^2}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\theta^2}}{\theta^2}.$$
Writing
$$F(\theta)=\operatorname{arsinh}\theta-\frac{\sqrt{1+\theta^2}}\theta,$$
direct differentiation gives $F'(\theta)=\sqrt{1+\theta^2}/\theta^2$. Therefore
$$L(\Theta)=\boxed{\operatorname{arsinh}\Theta-\frac{\sqrt{1+\Theta^2}}\Theta-\operatorname{arsinh}1+\sqrt2}.$$
Moreover $\sqrt{1+\theta^2}/\theta^2\ge1/\theta$, so $L(\Theta)\ge\ln\Theta$ and diverges. Area uses $r^2\asymp\theta^{-2}$, whereas length contains a radial/tangential speed of order $\theta^{-1}$; the two convergence tests are therefore different. The word “with multiplicity” prevents interpreting repeated turns as a simple-region area without further geometry.

I use L=integral r dtheta and therefore claim the finite area sweep forces a finite spiral length.
Because the polar sweep tends to 1/2, I call 1/2 the area of a simple region even though the angle repeats infinitely and the definition counts multiplicity.

CALC2:010232.title: Split a two-circle lens at the correct radial boundary
CALC2:010232.objective: Find polar intersections of two circles, compute their acute tangent-crossing angle from polar velocity vectors, and integrate the overlap area with the correct piecewise radial minimum.

The curves
$$C_1:r=1,\qquad C_2:r=2\cos\theta$$
are unit circles. Find their two intersection points. At each intersection, find the acute angle between their tangent lines. Then compute the area lying inside both circles using a polar integral whose radial upper bound is split where the two curves meet.

Cartesian circle geometry may check the angle and lens area, but the requested polar radial split must still be shown.

milestones.criterion: Finds both polar intersections and converts them correctly.
Computes the tangent-line angle from polar tangent vectors.
Splits the radial minimum correctly and evaluates the overlap area.

commonErrors.description: Uses max(1,2cos theta) as the overlap boundary.
commonErrors.consequence: The maximum describes points inside at least one circle, not points inside both; overlap requires the minimum radius.

commonErrors.description: Calls the intersection angle pi/3 merely because the polar coordinate theta equals pi/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerical equality is coincidental unless tangent directions are computed; polar position angle is not generally tangent angle.

hintTree.content: Solve 1=2cos theta and convert the two polar points to Cartesian coordinates.
At an intersection, C_1 has tangent e_theta; C_2 has tangent (-2sin theta)e_r+(2cos theta)e_theta.
On |theta|<=pi/3 the unit circle is the smaller radius; on pi/3<=|theta|<=pi/2 the shifted circle is smaller.

The equations agree when $1=2\cos\theta$, so $\theta=\pm\pi/3$. The points are
$$\boxed{\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),\quad
\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)}.$$
For $C_1$, a tangent vector is $\mathbf e_\theta$. For $C_2$, $r'=-2\sin\theta$, so at either intersection its tangent vector is
$$r'\mathbf e_r+r\mathbf e_\theta=\mp\sqrt3\,\mathbf e_r+\mathbf e_\theta,$$
with norm $2$. Its dot product with $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $1$, hence the acute angle $\alpha$ satisfies $\cos\alpha=1/2$ and
$$\boxed{\alpha=\pi/3}.$$

Both radii are nonnegative for $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$. The common radial bound is $1$ for $|\theta|\le\pi/3$ and $2\cos\theta$ on the two outer angular pieces. By symmetry,
$$A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}1\,d\theta
+2\left(\frac12\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}4\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\right).$$
Since $\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi/12-\sqrt3/8$,
$$\boxed{A=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}.$$
This agrees with the standard lens formula for two unit circles whose centers are one unit apart.

CALC2:010317.title: A harmonic series whose dyadic signs still do not settle
CALC2:010317.objective: Prove divergence of a signed harmonic series whose individual terms tend to zero by identifying dyadic blocks with asymptotically nonzero mass and applying the Cauchy criterion to carefully chosen partial sums.
CALC2:010317.statement:
For $n\ge1$, let $k(n)$ be the unique nonnegative integer such that
\[
k(n)\le\log_2n<k(n)+1.
\]
Determine whether
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k(n)}}n
\]
converges. With $B_k=\sum_{n=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1}1/n$, prove $B_k\to\ln2$ as a Riemann sum and use dyadic endpoint partial sums to prove divergence. Explain why pairing adjacent opposite-sign blocks cannot alone prove convergence of the original series.
permittedResults: A convergent series has partial-sum differences tending to zero along every pair of index sequences.
Riemann sums for a continuous function on the unit interval converge to its integral.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert the block mass to a Riemann sum.
Use the Cauchy criterion on two dyadic endpoint subsequences.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the block sign and mass.
Gets B sub k tending to ln two by a Riemann sum.
Uses dyadic endpoints to prove divergence in the original order.

commonErrors.description: Claims convergence solely because individual terms tend to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Term decay does not imply a series is Cauchy.

commonErrors.description: Treats convergence of paired blocks as convergence of all original partial sums.
commonErrors.consequence: Single-block endpoint jumps do not tend to zero.

hintTree.content: The sign is constant and equal to (-1) to the k on dyadic block k.
Rewrite B sub k after factoring out 2 to the negative k.
Compare the partial sums at the two endpoints of one dyadic block.

CALC2:010317.canonicalSolution:
The sign is $(-1)^k$ throughout block $[2^k,2^{k+1}-1]$. Its unsigned mass is
\[
B_k=\sum_{n=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1}\frac1n
=2^{-k}\sum_{j=0}^{2^k-1}\frac1{1+j/2^k}.
\]
This is a left Riemann sum for $1/(1+x)$ on $[0,1]$, so $B_k\to\ln2$.

For $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N(-1)^{k(n)}/n$,
\[
S_{2^{k+1}-1}-S_{2^k-1}=(-1)^kB_k.
\]
If the series converged, this partial-sum difference would tend to zero by the Cauchy criterion. Its absolute value instead tends to $\ln2>0$. Hence
\[
\boxed{\text{the series diverges}.}
\]
Pairing two consecutive blocks only controls selected grouped endpoints. It cannot establish convergence of the original order, whose single-block endpoint jumps have nonzero limiting magnitude.

graderFixtures.proofText: $B_k=2^{-k}\sum_{j=0}^{2^k-1}(1+j/2^k)^{-1}\to\ln2$, while $S_{2^{k+1}-1}-S_{2^k-1}=(-1)^kB_k$. The difference does not tend to zero, so the series diverges by Cauchy.
The terms $(-1)^{k(n)}/n$ tend to zero, so I conclude the series converges without checking its partial sums.
I pair positive and negative dyadic blocks and declare the original series convergent, without controlling the partial sums after a single block.

CALC2:010318.title: Expose exponential decay hidden in a changing power
CALC2:010318.objective: Use the root test to recognize exponential decay in a positive-term series with a varying base and exponent, and distinguish a successful convergence test from the merely necessary condition that terms vanish.
CALC2:010318.statement:
Determine whether the positive-term series
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac n{n+1}\right)^{n^2}
\]
converges. Apply the root test by computing the exact limit of the nth roots. State the standard exponential limit you use, and explain why observing only that the terms tend to zero would not settle the question.
permittedResults: The standard exponential limit is (one plus one over n) to the n tending to e.

Rewrite the base using one plus one over n and invoke its defining exponential limit.

Uses the exponential limit to get one over e.
Concludes convergence by the root test and states the term-test boundary.

commonErrors.description: Removes the whole n-squared exponent when taking nth roots and obtains only n divided by n plus one.
commonErrors.consequence: The root test is then applied to the wrong sequence.

commonErrors.description: Claims convergence solely because the terms tend to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Term decay alone does not prove series convergence.

hintTree.content: Take the nth root before estimating the n-squared exponent.
Write n divided by n plus one as the reciprocal of one plus one over n.
The root limit is one over e, which is below one.

Let $a_n=(n/(n+1))^{n^2}$. Taking nth roots gives
\[
\sqrt[n]{a_n}=\left(\frac n{n+1}\right)^n
=\left(1+\frac1n\right)^{-n}\longrightarrow e^{-1}<1.
\]
The last limit uses $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+1/n)^n=e$. The root test therefore proves
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac n{n+1}\right)^{n^2}\text{ converges}.}
\]
The terms do tend to zero, but that fact alone is only necessary: a harmonic series has vanishing terms and still diverges. The strict root-test bound below one is the decisive convergence argument.

CALC2:010319.title: Linearize a nonlinear recurrence around both fixed points
CALC2:010319.objective: Prove monotone bounded convergence of a fractional-linear recurrence, identify its positive fixed point, and derive an exact geometric error coordinate using both fixed points.
CALC2:010319.statement:
Let $a_1=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{2a_n+3}{a_n+2}\qquad(n\ge1).
$$
Prove that $1\le a_n<\sqrt3$ and that $(a_n)$ is increasing. Find its limit without assuming in advance that a fixed point must be reached. Then set
$$
q_n=\frac{\sqrt3-a_n}{\sqrt3+a_n}
$$
and derive an exact recurrence for $q_n$. Use it to give a closed formula for $q_n$ and an explicit expression for $a_n$.
permittedResults: Every increasing sequence bounded above converges.
A convergent recurrence may be passed to a continuous update map after convergence has independently been established.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use order identities first, then pass to the fixed-point equation only after convergence.
Exploit both fixed points of the Möbius update to find a multiplicative cross-ratio coordinate.

milestones.criterion: Proves the invariant interval and monotone convergence.
Identifies the limit without circular fixed-point reasoning.
Derives and solves the exact conjugated recurrence.

commonErrors.description: Solves the fixed-point equation and declares convergence without proving the sequence has a limit.
commonErrors.consequence: A possible fixed point does not establish convergence of the recurrence.

commonErrors.description: Uses the reciprocal multiplier greater than one for q sub n and concludes the error grows.
commonErrors.consequence: The factorization and closed formula contradict the proven convergence.

hintTree.content: Show the update sends the interval $[1,\sqrt3)$ into itself.
Factor the numerator and denominator of $(a_{n+1}-\sqrt3)/(a_{n+1}+\sqrt3)$.

CALC2:010319.canonicalSolution:
Let $T(x)=(2x+3)/(x+2)$. If $1\le x<\sqrt3$, then $x+2>0$ and
$$
T(x)-x=\frac{3-x^2}{x+2}>0.
$$
Also
$$
\sqrt3-T(x)=\frac{(2-\sqrt3)(\sqrt3-x)}{x+2}>0.
$$
Induction gives $1\le a_n<\sqrt3$, and the first identity makes the sequence increasing. It is therefore convergent. If $a_n\to L$, continuity gives $L=(2L+3)/(L+2)$, so $L^2=3$; the positive interval forces $\boxed{L=\sqrt3}$.

The two fixed points are $\pm\sqrt3$. Direct factorization yields
$$
\frac{T(x)-\sqrt3}{T(x)+\sqrt3}
=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{2+\sqrt3}\frac{x-\sqrt3}{x+\sqrt3}.
$$
Thus, with
$$
\lambda=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{2+\sqrt3},
$$
we have $q_{n+1}=\lambda q_n$ and
$$
q_n=\lambda^{n-1}\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}.
$$
Solving $q_n=(\sqrt3-a_n)/(\sqrt3+a_n)$ for $a_n$ gives
$$
\boxed{a_n=\sqrt3\,\frac{1-q_n}{1+q_n}}.
$$
This exact coordinate also certifies geometric decay of the transformed error.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $[1,\sqrt3)$, $T(x)-x=(3-x^2)/(x+2)>0$ and $T(x)<\sqrt3$, so $a_n\uparrow\sqrt3$. Moreover $q_{n+1}=((2-\sqrt3)/(2+\sqrt3))q_n$, hence $q_n=\lambda^{n-1}(\sqrt3-1)/(\sqrt3+1)$ and $a_n=\sqrt3(1-q_n)/(1+q_n)$.
I solve $L=(2L+3)/(L+2)$ and immediately announce convergence to $\sqrt3$, without proving monotonicity, boundedness, or even existence of a limit.
My factorization gives $q_{n+1}=((2+\sqrt3)/(2-\sqrt3))q_n$, so the positive error coordinate grows despite the sequence approaching its fixed point.

CALC2:010320.title: Make a harmonic subseries converge by forbidding one digit
CALC2:010320.objective: Partition a positive subseries by decimal length, count the permitted integers without admitting leading zeros, dominate every block by a geometric term, and extract an explicit truncation certificate.
CALC2:010320.statement:
Let $A$ be the set of positive integers whose usual base-ten expansion contains no digit $9$. Determine whether the positive subseries
$$
\sum_{\substack{n\ge1\\n\in A}}\frac1n
$$
converges. Give a proof by grouping permitted integers according to their number of digits; do not appeal only to the fact that $A$ is a subset of the positive integers. If $T_K$ denotes the part of the subseries contributed by permitted integers $n\ge10^K$, prove an explicit geometric upper bound for $T_K$. Find the smallest integer $K$ for which that bound alone guarantees $T_K<0.01$.
permittedResults: A positive series converges if its terms can be partitioned into finite blocks whose block sums are bounded by a convergent positive series.
For $0<r<1$, $\sum_{j=K}^{\infty}r^j=r^K/(1-r)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Partition by decimal length and count admissible strings before estimating any reciprocal.
Majorize the entire tail by the remaining terms of one geometric series.

milestones.criterion: Counts every digit-length block without leading-zero errors.
Uses the reciprocal inequality in the correct direction to prove convergence.
Derives the tail certificate and verifies the smallest certified exponent.

commonErrors.description: Claims the subseries diverges because it is contained in the divergent harmonic series.
commonErrors.consequence: A smaller positive series may converge, so this comparison direction proves nothing.

commonErrors.description: Uses n less than ten to the k to claim one over n is at most ten to the minus k.
commonErrors.consequence: The inequality is reversed and the geometric block majorant is invalid.

hintTree.content: A permitted k-digit integer has eight choices for its first digit and nine for each later digit.
Every k-digit integer is at least $10^{k-1}$, so bound its reciprocal in the direction needed for convergence.
The tail beginning at $10^K$ starts with the block of $(K+1)$-digit integers.

CALC2:010320.canonicalSolution:
For each $k\ge1$, consider the permitted integers with exactly $k$ digits. The first digit cannot be zero or nine, so it has $8$ choices. Each of the remaining $k-1$ digits may be any of $0,1,\ldots,8$, giving $9$ choices. Thus the block contains exactly
$$
8\cdot9^{k-1}
$$
integers. Every integer in it is at least $10^{k-1}$, so every reciprocal is at most $10^{-(k-1)}$. If $B_k$ is the kth block sum, then
$$
0<B_k\le 8\cdot9^{k-1}10^{-(k-1)}
=8\left(\frac9{10}\right)^{k-1}.
$$
The geometric majorant has sum $8/(1-9/10)=80$. Hence
$$
\boxed{\sum_{\substack{n\ge1\\n\in A}}\frac1n\text{ converges}}.
$$
This does not follow merely from containment in the harmonic series: comparison with a divergent larger series gives no convergence conclusion.

The condition $n\ge10^K$ begins with the $(K+1)$-digit block, so
$$
T_K\le\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}8\left(\frac9{10}\right)^{k-1}
=\boxed{80\left(\frac9{10}\right)^K}.
$$
Direct calculation gives
$$
80(0.9)^{85}=0.0103205\ldots>0.01,\qquad
80(0.9)^{86}=0.0092885\ldots<0.01.
$$
Therefore the smallest integer certified by this bound is $\boxed{K=86}$. Leading zeros were never allowed; admitting them would corrupt the exact block count.

graderFixtures.proofText: There are $8\cdot9^{k-1}$ permitted k-digit integers, each at least $10^{k-1}$, so the kth block is at most $8(9/10)^{k-1}$. The geometric majorant proves convergence and gives $T_K\le80(9/10)^K$. Since the bounds at K equal 85 and 86 straddle 0.01, the first certified K is 86.
The set is a subset of the harmonic-series indices, so I conclude its reciprocal subseries must diverge as well.
For k-digit n I use n less than $10^k$ to assert $1/n\le10^{-k}$, reversing the reciprocal inequality and underestimating every block.

CALC2:010321.title: Classify a logarithmically weighted positive series
CALC2:010321.objective: Apply limit comparison to a positive series with a logarithmic factor and make the comparison target explicit enough to determine convergence.
CALC2:010321.statement:
Determine whether
$$
\sum_{n=2}^\infty\frac{\ln n}{n^2+\ln n}
$$
converges. Use limit comparison with a standard benchmark, compute the limiting ratio, and explain why positivity permits the conclusion.
permittedResults: Eventually ln(n)<=sqrt(n), so ln(n)/n^2<=1/n^(3/2), a convergent p-series benchmark.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match the numerator exactly so the limit comparison reveals the dominant n^2 denominator.
Bound the remaining logarithm by a small power of n and finish with a p-series.

milestones.criterion: Selects b_n=(ln n)/n^2 and computes a_n/b_n=n^2/(n^2+ln n)->1.
Justifies convergence of the benchmark, for example through ln n<=sqrt n eventually.
Applies positive-term limit comparison to conclude that the given series converges.

commonErrors.description: Claims divergence by mentioning 1/n without establishing a valid lower comparison to the harmonic series.
commonErrors.consequence: The given terms are much smaller than a harmonic benchmark, so that argument cannot decide the series.

commonErrors.description: Inverts or fails to cancel the limit-comparison ratio and reports an infinite limit.
commonErrors.consequence: This destroys the positive finite-limit criterion that links the problem to its convergent benchmark.

hintTree.content: Choose b_n=(ln n)/n^2 so the logarithm in the numerator cancels in the ratio.
Simplify a_n/b_n before taking the limit; the ratio should approach a nonzero finite number.
Prove the benchmark converges by bounding ln n with sqrt n for sufficiently large n.

CALC2:010321.canonicalSolution:
The logarithm grows more slowly than $n$, so the natural benchmark is $b_n=(\ln n)/n^2$, not the harmonic series. Both terms are positive for $n\ge2$. Compute
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln n/(n^2+\ln n)}{(\ln n)/n^2}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2}{n^2+\ln n}=1.
$$
It remains to know that $\sum (\ln n)/n^2$ converges. For sufficiently large $n$, $\ln n\le\sqrt n$, so $(\ln n)/n^2\le n^{-3/2}$; the latter is a convergent $p$-series. Limit comparison now transfers convergence to the given positive series. Thus $\boxed{\sum_{n=2}^\infty\ln n/(n^2+\ln n)\text{ converges}}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The limit ratio with (ln n)/n^2 is n^2/(n^2+ln n)->1. Since ln n<=sqrt n eventually, the benchmark is bounded by n^(-3/2), so both positive series converge.
I compare ln n/(n^2+ln n) to 1/n and conclude divergence because the harmonic series diverges, without a valid lower comparison.
I compute the ratio with (ln n)/n^2 as (n^2+ln n)/n^2 and say it tends to infinity, instead of cancelling the numerator correctly.

CALC2:010322.title: Recover a series from its partial-sum sequence
CALC2:010322.objective: Recover individual terms from a prescribed partial-sum formula, handle the first index without inventing an invalid zeroth formula, and extract the exact sum and truncation tail.
CALC2:010322.statement:
A series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n$ has partial sums
$$
S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_k=\frac{3n+1}{n+2}\qquad(n\ge1).
$$
Find $a_1$ and a formula for $a_n$ when $n\ge2$. Determine whether the series converges and, if it does, find its exact sum. For
$$
R_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}a_n,
$$
derive an exact formula for $R_N$ and find the smallest positive integer $N$ for which $R_N<0.01$. Verify your recovered terms by summing them rather than relying only on the limit of $S_n$.
permittedResults: The supplied formula is valid only for n>=1, so the first term must be obtained from S_1-S_0 with S_0=0.

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate the exceptional first index before applying the telescoping difference identity.
Derive the remainder from 3-S_N rather than estimating the terms numerically.

milestones.criterion: Uses S_0=0 to find a_1=4/3 and derives a_n=5/((n+1)(n+2)) for n>=2.
Finds the infinite sum as lim S_n=3 and the exact tail R_N=5/(N+2).
Solves the strict error target and identifies N=499 as the smallest valid integer.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes n=0 into a formula stated only for n>=1 and uses S_0=1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: This contradicts the empty partial sum and gives the wrong first term 5/6 instead of 4/3.

commonErrors.description: Simplifies 3-S_N as 5/(N+1) rather than 5/(N+2).
commonErrors.consequence: The shifted remainder changes the threshold calculation and produces the wrong minimal cutoff.

hintTree.content: Compute a_1 directly from S_1, not by extending the displayed rational formula to zero.
For n>=2 subtract S_{n-1} from S_n and factor the rational difference.
Use lim S_n for the sum, then solve the strict inequality 5/(N+2)<0.01 carefully at the equality case.

CALC2:010322.canonicalSolution:
The empty partial sum is $S_0=0$; the displayed rational formula is asserted only for $n\ge1$. Hence
$$
a_1=S_1=\frac{4}{3}.
$$
For $n\ge2$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}
&=\frac{3n+1}{n+2}-\frac{3n-2}{n+1}\\
&=\frac5{(n+1)(n+2)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Because $S_n\to3$, the series converges to $\boxed{3}$. The recovered formula independently verifies this value:
$$
\begin{aligned}
a_1+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}a_n
&=\frac43+5\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right)\\
&=\frac43+\frac53=3.
\end{aligned}
$$
The exact tail follows directly from the partial sum:
$$
R_N=3-S_N=3-\frac{3N+1}{N+2}=\boxed{\frac5{N+2}}.
$$
Thus $R_N<0.01$ exactly when $5/(N+2)<1/100$, or $N>498$. The smallest positive integer is therefore $\boxed{N=499}$. In particular, $N=498$ gives equality $R_{498}=0.01$ and does not meet the strict target.

graderFixtures.proofText: Because S_0=0, a_1=S_1=4/3. For n>=2, a_n=S_n-S_(n-1)=5/((n+1)(n+2)). Thus the series sums to lim S_n=3, its exact tail is R_N=5/(N+2), and N=499 is the first index with R_N<0.01.
I extend the displayed formula to S_0=1/2 and report a_1=S_1-S_0=5/6, even though the empty partial sum is S_0=0 and the formula was stated only for n>=1.
I write R_N=5/(N+1) and choose N=500, shifting the exact tail by one even though 3-S_N simplifies to 5/(N+2).

CALC2:010323.title: Start an alternating test only after monotonicity begins
CALC2:010323.objective: Classify an alternating rational series by verifying eventual rather than global monotonicity, prove failure of absolute convergence through limit comparison, and give an exact alternating-remainder certificate.
CALC2:010323.statement:
Classify the series
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{n}{n^2+9}
$$
as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. Your argument must address the fact that $b_n=n/(n^2+9)$ is not decreasing from $n=1$, identify an index after which it is decreasing, and justify the absolute-series conclusion separately. Finally, bound the absolute error made by truncating after $n=20$.
permittedResults: The alternating-series test needs $b_n\to0$ and only eventual decrease; changing or discarding finitely many initial terms does not affect convergence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use continuous monotonicity on the positive real line to certify eventual decrease of the terms.
Use an algebraic consecutive-term comparison for the tail, then a harmonic limit comparison for absolute values.

milestones.criterion: Shows b_n tends to zero and is decreasing for n>=3 using a derivative or an exact difference.
Uses limit comparison with 1/n to prove that the absolute-value series diverges and concludes conditional convergence.
Applies the first omitted term at n=21 to obtain the bound 7/150.

commonErrors.description: States that n/(n^2+9) decreases from n=1 without checking the initial values or the derivative sign change at x=3.
commonErrors.consequence: The cited alternating-test hypothesis is false as stated, even though eventual decrease can correctly prove convergence.

commonErrors.description: Claims absolute convergence because n/(n^2+9) tends to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Vanishing terms are necessary but not sufficient; the absolute series is harmonic-sized and diverges by limit comparison.

hintTree.content: Study f(x)=x/(x^2+9) with a derivative to locate where its values begin decreasing.
For absolute convergence, compare n/(n^2+9) with 1/n by taking their ratio.
Once N=20 lies in the decreasing tail, the alternating remainder is at most b_21.

CALC2:010323.canonicalSolution:
Let $b_n=n/(n^2+9)$. Clearly $b_n>0$ and $b_n\to0$. For
$$
f(x)=\frac{x}{x^2+9},
\qquad
f'(x)=\frac{9-x^2}{(x^2+9)^2}.
$$
Thus $f$ is decreasing for $x>3$, so $(b_n)$ is decreasing from $n=3$ onward (with strict decrease after that index). The finitely many earlier terms do not matter, and the alternating-series test proves convergence of the signed series.

For absolute values, compare with the harmonic series:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n/(n^2+9)}{1/n}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2}{n^2+9}=1.
$$
Limit comparison shows that $\sum b_n$ diverges. Therefore the original series is
$$
\boxed{\text{conditionally convergent}}.
$$
Since the tail after $n=20$ is alternating with decreasing magnitudes, the first-omitted-term estimate gives
$$
|S-S_{20}|\le b_{21}=\frac{21}{21^2+9}
=\boxed{\frac7{150}}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: For f(x)=x/(x^2+9), f'(x)=(9-x^2)/(x^2+9)^2, so b_n decreases after n=3 and tends to zero. The signed series converges, while b_n/(1/n)->1 makes the absolute series diverge. It is conditional and |R_20|<=21/450=7/150.
I say b_n is decreasing for every n starting at 1 and invoke the alternating test, but b_1<b_2<b_3 and I never repair the argument by using eventual monotonicity.
Since n/(n^2+9) tends to zero, I call the series absolutely convergent and do not compare its absolute values with the divergent harmonic series.

CALC2:010324.title: Trap a radical recurrence and quantify its approach
CALC2:010324.objective: Prove convergence of a nonlinear recursively defined sequence using invariant bounds and monotonicity, identify the admissible fixed point, and derive a geometric error estimate by rationalizing the recurrence.
CALC2:010324.statement:
Let
$$
a_1=1,
\qquad
a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}\quad(n\ge1).
$$
Prove that $(a_n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $3$, and hence converges. Find its limit. Then rationalize $3-a_{n+1}$ to prove the explicit estimate
$$
0\le3-a_n\le\frac{2}{4^{n-1}}
\qquad(n\ge1).
$$
Every induction hypothesis and every choice between the two algebraic fixed points must be justified.
permittedResults: Every increasing sequence bounded above converges; its limit may then be substituted into a continuous recurrence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build an invariant interval first, then use factorization of 6+a-a^2 for monotonicity.
View the recurrence map as a contraction on the invariant interval after identifying its fixed point.

milestones.criterion: Proves the invariant bound 1<=a_n<3 and uses it to establish strict increase.
Applies monotone convergence and selects the positive fixed point L=3.
Rationalizes the error, proves the one-quarter contraction, and iterates it to the stated bound.

commonErrors.description: Solves the fixed-point equation and treats L=3 as proof that the sequence converges.
commonErrors.consequence: A fixed point is only a candidate limit; monotonicity and boundedness or another convergence argument are still required.

commonErrors.description: Retains L=-2 or treats both roots as possible limits despite every term being a positive square root.
commonErrors.consequence: The negative root is incompatible with the range of the recurrence and gives the wrong limit.

hintTree.content: Inductively keep 1<=a_n<3, then compare 6+a_n with a_n^2 to prove the next term is larger.
If the limit is L, solve L=sqrt(6+L) and use positivity to reject the negative root.
Write 3-a_{n+1}=(9-(6+a_n))/(3+a_{n+1}) and bound the denominator below by 4.

CALC2:010324.canonicalSolution:
We prove first that $1\le a_n<3$. This holds for $a_1=1$. If it holds for $a_n$, then
$$
a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}<\sqrt9=3
$$
and certainly $a_{n+1}>1$, so the interval is invariant. Within $1\le a_n<3$,
$$
6+a_n-a_n^2=(3-a_n)(a_n+2)>0.
$$
Both sides being nonnegative, this implies $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+a_n}>a_n$. Thus the sequence is increasing and bounded above by $3$, so it converges.

If $a_n\to L$, continuity gives $L=\sqrt{6+L}$, hence
$$
L^2-L-6=(L-3)(L+2)=0.
$$
All terms are positive, so $L=-2$ is impossible and $\boxed{L=3}$.

For the rate, rationalization yields
$$
3-a_{n+1}
=\frac{9-(6+a_n)}{3+\sqrt{6+a_n}}
=\frac{3-a_n}{3+a_{n+1}}.
$$
Since $a_{n+1}\ge1$, the denominator is at least $4$, so
$$
0\le3-a_{n+1}\le\frac14(3-a_n).
$$
Iterating and using $3-a_1=2$ gives
$$
\boxed{0\le3-a_n\le\frac{2}{4^{n-1}}}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: Induction gives 1<=a_n<3, and (3-a_n)(a_n+2)>0 gives a_(n+1)>a_n. Thus a_n converges to the positive fixed point 3. Also 3-a_(n+1)=(3-a_n)/(3+a_(n+1))<=(3-a_n)/4, so 3-a_n<=2/4^(n-1).
I solve L=sqrt(6+L) to get L=3 and announce convergence, but I provide no monotone, Cauchy, contraction, or other argument showing that the recursively defined sequence has a limit.
Squaring the fixed-point equation gives roots 3 and -2, so I list both as possible limits even though every a_n is a positive square root and the sequence is trapped above 1.

CALC2:010325.title: Reindex a weighted harmonic series and retain its tail
CALC2:010325.objective: Evaluate a series with harmonic-number coefficients by a justified nonnegative double-sum interchange, then derive an exact tail decomposition and sharp elementary two-sided bounds.
CALC2:010325.statement:
Let $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n1/k$.
(a) Evaluate exactly
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{H_n}{2^n}$$
by rewriting it as a double series and justifying the change in summation order.
(b) For $R_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}H_n/2^n$, prove
$$
\frac{H_N}{2^N}<R_N\leq\frac{H_N}{2^N}+\frac{2^{1-N}}{N+1}.
$$
Display the exact tail decomposition from which the bounds follow.
permittedResults: Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative series permits changing the order of summation without first knowing that the common sum is finite.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Tonelli reindexing twice: once for the full sum and once for the tail remainder.
Alternatively derive the generating function sum H_n x^n=-ln(1-x)/(1-x), then perform a separate coefficient-level tail decomposition for the requested bounds.

milestones.criterion: Expands the harmonic numbers, invokes nonnegativity, and changes the summation order correctly.
Evaluates the full series as 2ln2 using a geometric inner sum and the logarithmic series.
Derives the exact tail decomposition and proves both the strict lower and stated upper bounds.

commonErrors.description: After reversing order, starts the inner n-sum at n=k+1 instead of n=k.
commonErrors.consequence: Every diagonal term 1/(k2^k) is lost, changing the value and invalidating the tail identity.

commonErrors.description: States R_N=H_N/2^N and drops the positive contribution from new harmonic increments k>N.
commonErrors.consequence: The alleged equality is only a strict lower bound; it cannot imply the requested upper estimate.

hintTree.content: Expand H_n and interchange the nonnegative sums over n>=1 and 1<=k<=n.
For the tail, write H_n=H_N+sum_{k=N+1}^n 1/k before interchanging the remaining triangular sum.
Evaluate sum_{n=N+1}^infinity 2^{-n}, then bound 1/k by 1/(N+1) in the leftover weighted sum.

graderFixtures.proofText: Tonelli gives sum_n sum_{k<=n}1/(k2^n)=sum_k 2^{1-k}/k=2ln2. Also R_N=H_N/2^N+2 sum_{k>N}1/(k2^k), whose positive second term is at most 2^{1-N}/(N+1).
When I reverse the sums I start n at k+1, omit all diagonal terms, and therefore get the wrong logarithmic multiple.
I assert R_N=H_N/2^N exactly, ignoring every increment 1/k that appears in H_n after index N.

CALC2:010326.title: Control an arctangent series without inventing a closed form
CALC2:010326.objective: Prove convergence of a positive arctangent series through a pointwise comparison and obtain a certified truncation error bound using the integral estimate for a p-series.
CALC2:010326.statement:
Define
$$
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\arctan\!\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right),
\qquad
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\arctan\!\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right).
$$
Prove that $S$ converges and that
$$0<S-S_N\leq\frac{1}{N}.$$
Use this to state a sufficient value of $N$ for an error at most $10^{-3}$. No closed form for $S$ is requested; every inequality used should be justified.
permittedResults: For $u\geq0$, $0\leq\arctan u\leq u$ because $g(u)=u-\arctan u$ has derivative $u^2/(1+u^2)\geq0$; also $\sum_{n>N}n^{-2}\leq\int_N^\infty x^{-2}\,dx=1/N$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the derivative of u-arctan(u), followed by comparison and the integral tail estimate.
Use the geometric integral representation arctan(u)=integral_0^u 1/(1+t^2)dt to get arctan(u)<=u, then proceed with the same p-series bound.

milestones.criterion: Establishes 0<arctan(1/n^2)<=1/n^2 and applies comparison to prove convergence.
Writes the positive remainder and bounds it by the p-series tail and then by 1/N.
Chooses N=1000 as a sufficient cutoff for tolerance 10^-3 and interprets the inequality correctly.

commonErrors.description: Uses arctan(1/n^2)>=1/n^2 as an upper comparison for convergence.
commonErrors.consequence: The inequality points the wrong way and cannot bound the arctangent tail from above.

commonErrors.description: Writes S-S_N=1/N and presents the integral-test upper bound as the exact remainder.
commonErrors.consequence: The arctangent comparison and the discrete-to-integral step are inequalities, so equality is unsupported.

hintTree.content: Prove or cite the inequality arctan(u)<=u only for nonnegative u, then compare term by term with 1/n^2.
Write the error as the positive tail from n=N+1 and retain the same comparison.
Apply the decreasing-function integral bound to the p-series tail and solve 1/N<=10^{-3}.

CALC2:010326.canonicalSolution:
For $u\geq0$, let $g(u)=u-\arctan u$. Then $g(0)=0$ and
$$
g'(u)=1-\frac{1}{1+u^2}=\frac{u^2}{1+u^2}\geq0.
$$
Thus $0<\arctan(1/n^2)\leq1/n^2$. Since $\sum1/n^2$ converges, the comparison test proves that $S$ converges.

Because every omitted term is positive,
$$
0<S-S_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty\arctan\!\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)
\leq\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^2}.
$$
The function $x^{-2}$ is positive and decreasing, so
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^2}
\leq\int_N^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2}=\frac{1}{N}.
$$
Therefore $0<S-S_N\leq1/N$. To guarantee an error at most $10^{-3}$, it suffices that $1/N\leq10^{-3}$, so
$$
\boxed{N=1000}
$$
is sufficient (and every larger integer is as well). This is a certified sufficient cutoff, not a claim that the actual error equals $1/N$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since g(u)=u-arctan u has g'(u)>=0, arctan(1/n^2)<=1/n^2. Hence 0<S-S_N<=sum_{n>N}1/n^2<=integral_N^infinity x^-2 dx=1/N, so N=1000 is sufficient for 10^-3.
I claim arctan(1/n^2) is at least 1/n^2 and use that as an upper comparison to prove convergence.
I write the exact identity S-S_N=1/N, even though both the arctangent comparison and integral estimate supplied only upper bounds.

CALC2:010327.title: Rationalize past a vanishing term to expose harmonic mass
CALC2:010327.objective: Classify a series whose terms approach zero only after cancellation, rationalize the cancellation exactly, and use a signed limit comparison to prove the direction of divergence rather than stopping at the term test.
CALC2:010327.statement:
Determine whether
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n-\frac12\right)
$$
converges. First verify that the summand tends to zero, then rationalize it exactly and compute
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}n\left(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n-\frac12\right).
$$
Use that limit to prove not only divergence but also whether the partial sums tend to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$.
permittedResults: If $b_n>0$ and $a_n/b_n\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ have the same convergence behavior; applying this to $-a_n$ handles an eventually negative sequence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use exact conjugate rationalization followed by signed limit comparison with the harmonic series.
A second-order Taylor expansion of sqrt(1+x) may establish a_n=-1/(8n)+O(1/n^2), provided its remainder is justified and the negative divergence conclusion is explicit.

milestones.criterion: Shows a_n tends to zero and explains why this necessary condition does not decide convergence.
Derives a_n=-1/[4(sqrt(n^2+n)+n+1/2)] and computes n a_n tending to -1/8.
Compares -a_n with 1/n and concludes that the original partial sums tend to negative infinity.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that the series converges solely because its summand tends to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Term convergence is necessary but not sufficient; here the surviving terms are asymptotic to -1/(8n) and accumulate without bound.

commonErrors.description: Rationalizes sqrt(n^2+n)-n but then drops the remaining subtraction of 1/2 before analyzing the series.
commonErrors.consequence: That discarded half is exactly what cancels the leading limit, so the resulting comparison describes the wrong summand.

hintTree.content: Compare sqrt(n^2+n) with n+1/2, not just with n, and multiply their difference by the conjugate sum.
The numerator after rationalization is n^2+n-(n+1/2)^2=-1/4.
Divide the rationalized denominator by n to compute n a_n, then compare -a_n to 1/n to determine the direction of the partial sums.

CALC2:010327.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$a_n=\sqrt{n^2+n}-n-\frac12.$$
Factoring out $n$ and using the standard square-root limit shows $a_n\to0$, so the term test alone is inconclusive.

Rationalizing against the entire quantity $n+1/2$ gives the exact identity
$$
a_n=\frac{n^2+n-(n+1/2)^2}{\sqrt{n^2+n}+n+1/2}
=-\frac1{4\left(\sqrt{n^2+n}+n+1/2\right)}.
$$
Consequently
$$
n a_n=-\frac1{4\left(\sqrt{1+1/n}+1+1/(2n)\right)}
\longrightarrow\boxed{-\frac18}.
$$
In particular $a_n<0$, and
$$
\frac{-a_n}{1/n}=-n a_n\longrightarrow\frac18>0.
$$
The positive series $\sum(-a_n)$ therefore diverges by limit comparison with the harmonic series. Hence the original partial sums do not merely fail to converge: because every term is negative and their magnitudes have divergent sum,
$$
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^N a_n\longrightarrow-\infty}.
$$
The fact that $a_n\to0$ is fully consistent with this harmonic-scale accumulation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The summand tends to zero, but exact rationalization gives a_n=-1/[4(sqrt(n^2+n)+n+1/2)]. Thus n a_n tends to -1/8, so -a_n is limit-comparable to 1/n and the original partial sums tend to -infinity.
Since sqrt(n^2+n)-n-1/2 tends to zero, I immediately declare the infinite series convergent without making any comparison to the harmonic series.
I rationalize sqrt(n^2+n)-n, obtain a quantity tending to 1/2, and then ignore the separate -1/2 cancellation when classifying the requested summand.

CALC2:010328.title: Telescope arctangent terms without losing the branch
CALC2:010328.objective: Recognize an inverse-tangent subtraction hidden in a rational sequence, justify the principal-value branch of the identity, and derive both the exact infinite sum and an exact finite-partial-sum remainder.
CALC2:010328.statement:
Evaluate
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\arctan\!\left(\frac1{n^2+n+1}\right).
$$
Derive the telescoping identity from the tangent subtraction formula and justify why no integer multiple of $\pi$ is introduced for $n\geq1$. Find the exact $N$th partial sum and the exact remainder after $N$ terms; then use the remainder to prove convergence.
permittedResults: For angles whose difference lies in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, $\arctan a-\arctan b=\arctan((a-b)/(1+ab))$ when $1+ab>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the principal arctangent subtraction identity term by term and telescope the finite sum.
One may verify the candidate difference by applying tangent and checking its range, which is an equivalent branch-safe route before telescoping.

milestones.criterion: Derives the tangent subtraction quotient as 1/(n^2+n+1) and justifies the principal arctangent branch.
Telescopes to S_N=pi/4-arctan(1/(N+1)) with the correct endpoint index.
Reports sum pi/4 and exact remainder arctan(1/(N+1)), using its decay to prove convergence.

commonErrors.description: Uses equality of tangents to assert equality of inverse-tangent expressions without checking their ranges.
commonErrors.consequence: Tangent is periodic, so an unchecked identity can differ by a multiple of pi; the telescoping conclusion is unsupported until the branch is fixed.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the finite sum to pi/4-arctan(1/N) or gives arctan(1/N) as the exact remainder.
commonErrors.consequence: The final negative term comes from n=N and is arctan(1/(N+1)); the shifted expression fails even for N=1.

hintTree.content: Try a=1/n and b=1/(n+1), and simplify both a-b and 1+ab before applying arctan.
Both arctangents are positive and the first is larger, so their difference lies between 0 and pi/2; this settles the branch.
Write the first N differences in a row. Everything except arctan(1) and arctan(1/(N+1)) cancels.

CALC2:010328.canonicalSolution:
Set $a=1/n$ and $b=1/(n+1)$. Then
$$
\frac{a-b}{1+ab}
=\frac{\frac1{n(n+1)}}{1+\frac1{n(n+1)}}
=\frac1{n^2+n+1}.
$$
Moreover
$$0<\arctan(1/n)-\arctan(1/(n+1))<\frac\pi2,$$
so the principal-value subtraction formula introduces no added multiple of $\pi$. Hence
$$
\arctan\!\left(\frac1{n^2+n+1}\right)
=\arctan\!\left(\frac1n\right)-\arctan\!\left(\frac1{n+1}\right).
$$
The $N$th partial sum telescopes:
$$
S_N=\arctan(1)-\arctan\!\left(\frac1{N+1}\right)
=\frac\pi4-\arctan\!\left(\frac1{N+1}\right).
$$
Since the last arctangent tends to zero,
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\arctan\!\left(\frac1{n^2+n+1}\right)
=\boxed{\frac\pi4}.
$$
The exact positive remainder is
$$
R_N=\frac\pi4-S_N
=\boxed{\arctan\!\left(\frac1{N+1}\right)},
$$
which tends to zero (and is at most $1/(N+1)$), directly proving convergence.

graderFixtures.proofText: Because arctan(1/n)-arctan(1/(n+1)) lies in (0,pi/2), its tangent identity is branch-safe and equals the given term. Thus S_N=pi/4-arctan(1/(N+1)), the sum is pi/4, and R_N=arctan(1/(N+1)).
The tangents match, so I equate the arctangent expressions automatically and never check whether their difference lies in the principal interval or differs by pi.
After cancellation I write S_N=pi/4-arctan(1/N), so my remainder is arctan(1/N); this shifted endpoint already gives the wrong first partial sum.

CALC2:010329.title: Let condensation expose the second logarithmic threshold
CALC2:010329.objective: Classify a two-parameter positive series with nested logarithms, verify the hypotheses for Cauchy condensation, and distinguish the primary power threshold from the secondary logarithmic threshold.
CALC2:010329.statement:
For real $p,q$, classify
$$\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}\frac1{n(\ln n)^p(\ln\ln n)^q}.$$
Prove the terms are eventually positive and nonincreasing before using Cauchy condensation. Give the complete convergence region in the $(p,q)$-plane and address all boundary cases.
permittedResults: If $a_n\ge0$ is eventually nonincreasing, Cauchy condensation says $\sum a_n$ and $\sum 2^k a_{2^k}$ converge or diverge together; finite initial terms do not matter.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Cauchy condensation followed by the ordinary power/logarithmic integral test.
A direct integral test with substitutions u=ln x and v=ln u is acceptable if eventual monotonicity and every parameter boundary are explicit.

milestones.criterion: Proves eventual positivity and monotonicity rather than applying condensation without hypotheses.
Derives the condensed asymptotic series 1/[k^p(ln k)^q].
States and proves the full region p>1 or p=1,q>1, with all complements divergent.

commonErrors.description: Claims convergence exactly for p>1 and declares every p=1 case divergent.
commonErrors.consequence: At p=1 the remaining logarithmic power creates a genuine second threshold: q>1 converges.

commonErrors.description: Transforms ln ln(2^k) into ln ln k or treats it as a fixed constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The correct quantity is ln(k ln2), asymptotic to ln k, and it determines the q boundary.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the logarithm of the continuous term to see eventual decrease for every fixed p and q.
After n=2^k, ignore only fixed positive constants, not powers of k or ln k.
For p=1, condense or apply the integral test once more to the remaining series 1/[k(ln k)^q].

CALC2:010329.canonicalSolution:
The terms are positive for $n\ge3$. For $x$ sufficiently large, the logarithmic derivative of
$$f(x)=\frac1{x(\ln x)^p(\ln\ln x)^q}$$
is
$$\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=-\frac1x-\frac{p}{x\ln x}-\frac{q}{x\ln x\ln\ln x}<0,$$
because the first term dominates the other two for fixed $p,q$. Thus eventual condensation is valid. It gives
$$2^k f(2^k)=\frac1{(k\ln2)^p[\ln(k\ln2)]^q}.$$
Up to fixed asymptotic factors this is $1/[k^p(\ln k)^q]$. Hence it converges when $p>1$ and diverges when $p<1$, regardless of $q$. At $p=1$, the integral test with $u=\ln k$ gives
$$\sum\frac1{k(\ln k)^q}\quad\hbox{converges exactly when }q>1.$$
Therefore the original series converges exactly in
$$\boxed{p>1\quad\text{or}\quad(p=1\text{ and }q>1)},$$
and diverges for $p<1$, and for $p=1,q\le1$. Negative exponents cause no exception: powers of logarithms cannot overturn a strict power threshold in $k$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The log derivative is eventually negative, so condensation applies. The condensed term is 1/[(k ln2)^p(ln(k ln2))^q], asymptotic to 1/[k^p(ln k)^q]. Thus convergence holds for p>1, or p=1 and q>1; all other cases diverge.
I use only the first p-threshold and state that every p=1 case diverges, never testing the surviving series 1/[k(ln k)^q].
After condensation I treat ln ln(2^k) as a constant, deleting the factor asymptotic to (ln k)^q and losing the q boundary.

CALC2:010330.title: Telescope a product without confusing its logarithmic remainder
CALC2:010330.objective: Convert a logarithmic series into a finite telescoping product, compute its exact partial sums and infinite sum, prove absolute convergence independently, and retain the sign and index of its exact tail.
CALC2:010330.statement:
Evaluate
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ln\left(1-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right).$$
Find the exact $N$th partial sum, prove absolute convergence, and compute the exact tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}$, including its sign.
permittedResults: For $0\le u\le1/2$, $0\le-\ln(1-u)\le2u$; this comparison can certify absolute convergence when $u$ is summable.

acceptableStrategies.description: Exponentiate the finite logarithmic sum and telescope the product.
Split each logarithm into two adjacent log differences at the finite-sum level, then use a quadratic comparison for absolute convergence.

milestones.criterion: Factors each term and telescopes the finite product with correct endpoints.
Obtains S_N and limit -ln2 and proves absolute convergence independently.
Computes the exact negative tail with N+1 and N+2 in the correct order.

commonErrors.description: Attempts to cancel the rational quantities inside logarithms additively without first combining them as a product.
commonErrors.consequence: Logarithms turn products into sums, not sums into telescoping rational terms, so the partial sum is unsupported.

commonErrors.description: Reports the exact tail as ln((N+2)/(N+1)), which is positive.
commonErrors.consequence: Every omitted term is the logarithm of a number below one and is negative, so the tail sign is reversed.

hintTree.content: Separate the finite product into n/(n+1) and (n+2)/(n+1) products.
Subtract S_N from the limiting value carefully: every omitted logarithm is negative.

CALC2:010330.canonicalSolution:
Every factor is positive, and
$$1-\frac1{(n+1)^2}=\frac n{n+1}\frac{n+2}{n+1}.$$
Thus
$$S_N=\ln\prod_{n=1}^N\frac n{n+1}\frac{n+2}{n+1}
=\ln\left(\frac1{N+1}\frac{N+2}{2}\right)
=\boxed{\ln\frac{N+2}{2(N+1)}}.$$
Letting $N\to\infty$ gives
$$\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ln\left(1-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right)=-\ln2}.$$
For absolute convergence, $u_n=1/(n+1)^2\le1/4$, so
$$\left|\ln(1-u_n)\right|\le2u_n,$$
and comparison with $\sum1/(n+1)^2$ applies. Finally the exact tail is
$$R_N=-\ln2-S_N
=\boxed{\ln\frac{N+1}{N+2}}<0.$$
Its magnitude tends to zero, as required.

graderFixtures.proofText: The factor is [n/(n+1)][(n+2)/(n+1)], so S_N=ln((N+2)/(2(N+1))) and the sum is -ln2. Since |ln(1-u)|<=2u here, convergence is absolute. The exact tail is ln((N+1)/(N+2))<0.
I try to telescope the fractions inside the logarithms by additive cancellation, never converting the finite log sum into the product of positive factors.
I subtract in the wrong order and call ln((N+2)/(N+1)) the tail, even though all omitted logarithmic terms are negative.

CALC2:010331.title: Turn reciprocal central binomials into one rational integral
CALC2:010331.objective: Prove convergence of a reciprocal-binomial series, convert every coefficient through a beta integral, justify the nonnegative sum-integral exchange, and evaluate the resulting rational integral exactly.
CALC2:010331.statement:
Evaluate exactly
$$S=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac1{\binom{2n}{n}}.$$
First use the ratio test and give a geometric upper bound for the tail after the $N$th term. Then use
$$\int_0^1[x(1-x)]^n\,dx=\frac{(n!)^2}{(2n+1)!}$$
to convert the series to a single integral. Justify the exchange, sum the resulting power series, and evaluate the integral.
permittedResults: For $0\le z\le1/4$, $\sum_{n\ge0}(2n+1)z^n=(1+z)/(1-z)^2$; nonnegative summands permit Tonelli's theorem.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the beta integral and the derivative of a geometric series before completing the square.
An independent trigonometric evaluation of the final rational integral is acceptable if all series-exchange steps remain explicit.

milestones.criterion: Proves convergence and derives a quantitative geometric tail bound.
Uses the beta identity with the essential factor 2n+1 and justifies the exchange.
Sums and evaluates the rational integral to the exact closed form.

commonErrors.description: Equates the beta integral directly with 1/C(2n,n), omitting the factor 2n+1.
commonErrors.consequence: The beta integral is smaller by exactly 2n+1, so the generating function and final sum are for a different series.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sum (2n+1)z^n by 1/(1-z).
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient 2n+1 requires the differentiated geometric series and changes the rational integrand.

hintTree.content: The consecutive ratio is (n+1)/[2(2n+1)], at most 1/3 for n>=1.
Write 1/C(2n,n)=(2n+1) integral_0^1 [x(1-x)]^n dx.
After u=x-1/2, decompose (5/4-u^2)/(u^2+3/4)^2 into a derivative term plus 1/(u^2+3/4).

CALC2:010331.canonicalSolution:
Let $a_n=1/\binom{2n}{n}$. Then
$$\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{(n+1)^2}{(2n+2)(2n+1)}
=\frac{n+1}{2(2n+1)}\longrightarrow\frac14,$$
so the series converges. For $n\ge1$ this ratio is at most $1/3$, hence
$$0<\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}a_n\le\frac{a_{N+1}}{1-1/3}
=\boxed{\frac32a_{N+1}}\qquad(N\ge1).$$

The supplied beta identity gives
$$a_n=(2n+1)\int_0^1[x(1-x)]^n\,dx.$$
The integrands are nonnegative, so Tonelli yields, with $z=x(1-x)$,
$$S=\int_0^1\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(2n+1)z^n\,dx
=\int_0^1\frac{1+z}{(1-z)^2}\,dx
=\int_0^1\frac{1+x-x^2}{(1-x+x^2)^2}\,dx.$$
Put $u=x-1/2$ and $q=u^2+3/4$. Then
$$\frac{5/4-u^2}{q^2}
=\frac43\frac{3/4-u^2}{q^2}+\frac13\frac1q.$$
Thus
$$S=\left[\frac43\frac{u}{u^2+3/4}
+\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}\arctan\left(\frac{2u}{\sqrt3}\right)\right]_{-1/2}^{1/2}.$$
The first difference is $4/3$ and the arctangent difference is $2\pi/(9\sqrt3)$. Therefore
$$\boxed{S=\frac43+\frac{2\pi}{9\sqrt3}}.$$
The value is about $1.736$, consistent with the first terms $1+1/2+1/6+\cdots$.

graderFixtures.proofText: a_(n+1)/a_n=(n+1)/[2(2n+1)]<=1/3 for n>=1, so the tail is <=(3/2)a_(N+1). The beta identity gives a_n=(2n+1) integral [x(1-x)]^n. Tonelli and sum (2n+1)z^n=(1+z)/(1-z)^2 lead to S=4/3+2pi/(9sqrt3).
I use integral [x(1-x)]^n dx=1/C(2n,n), dropping the required factor 2n+1 from the beta integral.
After introducing z=x(1-x), I sum (2n+1)z^n as the plain geometric series 1/(1-z).

CALC2:010332.title: Trap the harmonic-logarithm gap between two monotone sequences
CALC2:010332.objective: Prove existence of the Euler-Mascheroni constant using paired monotone sequences, derive their directions from sharp logarithm inequalities, and retain an explicit computable gap around the common limit.
CALC2:010332.statement:
Let $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n1/k$ and define
$$a_n=H_n-\ln(n+1),\qquad b_n=H_n-\ln n.$$
Prove that $(a_n)$ is increasing and $(b_n)$ is decreasing. Show that they converge to the same limit $\gamma$, and prove the two-sided estimate
$$H_n-\ln(n+1)<\gamma<H_n-\ln n$$
with gap exactly $\ln(1+1/n)$. Your proof must derive the logarithm inequalities it uses rather than quoting monotonicity without calculation.
permittedResults: For $x>0$, $x/(1+x)<\ln(1+x)<x$; both inequalities follow by differentiating the difference functions from value zero at x=0.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use differentiated logarithm inequalities and the monotone convergence theorem.
Integral comparison on each interval [n,n+1] is acceptable if it yields both strict directions and the exact gap identity.

milestones.criterion: Derives x/(1+x)<ln(1+x)<x from difference functions.
Uses the inequalities to prove the correct monotonic direction of both sequences and their boundedness.
Proves a common limit and the strict enclosure with exact gap.

commonErrors.description: Claims a_n decreases or b_n increases after reversing a logarithm inequality.
commonErrors.consequence: The nested intervals and common-limit squeeze then fail in the direction required to define gamma.

commonErrors.description: Starts by citing the known existence of gamma and uses it to assert convergence of a_n and b_n.
commonErrors.consequence: The task is to prove existence from bounded monotonicity, so assuming the limit is circular.

hintTree.content: Compute a_(n+1)-a_n and apply ln(1+x)<x with x=1/(n+1).
Compute b_(n+1)-b_n and apply ln(1+x)>x/(1+x) with x=1/n.
The identity b_n-a_n=ln(1+1/n) both orders the sequences and forces equal limits.

CALC2:010332.canonicalSolution:
For $x>0$, let $f(x)=x-\ln(1+x)$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=x/(1+x)>0$, so $\ln(1+x)<x$. Also let $g(x)=\ln(1+x)-x/(1+x)$. Then $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=x/(1+x)^2>0$, so $\ln(1+x)>x/(1+x)$.

Now
$$a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac1{n+1}-\ln\left(1+\frac1{n+1}\right)>0,$$
so $a_n$ increases. Similarly,
$$b_{n+1}-b_n=\frac1{n+1}-\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)<0,$$
because $\ln(1+1/n)>1/(n+1)$. Thus $b_n$ decreases. Moreover
$$b_n-a_n=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)>0.$$
Therefore $a_n<b_n\le b_1=1$, so the increasing sequence $a_n$ is bounded above and converges. Likewise $b_n>a_n\ge a_1=1-\ln2>0$, so $b_n$ is bounded below and converges. Since their gap tends to zero, their limits agree; call the common value $\gamma$. Strict monotonicity gives
$$\boxed{H_n-\ln(n+1)<\gamma<H_n-\ln n},$$
and the enclosing interval has exact width
$$\boxed{b_n-a_n=\ln(1+1/n)}.$$
This also gives a direct stopping certificate for approximating $\gamma$.

graderFixtures.proofText: From derivatives, x/(1+x)<ln(1+x)<x. Hence a_(n+1)-a_n=1/(n+1)-ln(1+1/(n+1))>0, while b_(n+1)-b_n=1/(n+1)-ln(1+1/n)<0. Their gap ln(1+1/n) tends to zero, so both converge to gamma between them.
I use ln(1+x)>x to declare a_n decreasing and b_n increasing, reversing the valid logarithm bound.
Because the Euler-Mascheroni constant is known to exist, both sequences converge to it; I do not prove bounded monotonicity or the common limit.
