CALC2:010337.title: Measure the cubic defect hidden behind sine
CALC2:010337.objective: Use local Taylor behavior to classify a positive defect series, derive a rigorous tail certificate, and find the first index certified at a requested tolerance.
CALC2:010337.statement:
Consider
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac1n-\sin\frac1n\right).$$
Prove that its terms are positive and that the series converges by identifying
an asymptotically equivalent $p$-series term. If $R_N$ is the tail after the
first $N$ terms, prove
$$0<R_N\le\frac1{12N^2}.$$
Using this bound, find the smallest positive integer $N$ that guarantees
$R_N<10^{-6}$.
permittedResults: For $0<x\le1$, $0<x-\sin x\le x^3/6$ and $(x-\sin x)/x^3\to1/6$ as $x\to0^+$. Also $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}n^{-3}\le\int_N^{\infty}x^{-3}\,dx=1/(2N^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use alternating Taylor bounds for sine and then an integral estimate for the p-series tail.
Use Taylor's theorem with remainder for the defect; any equivalent rigorous comparison must retain the explicit constant needed for the tail certificate.

milestones.criterion: Proves positivity and computes the limit-comparison ratio 1/6 against 1/n^3.
Derives R_N<=1/(12N^2) with correct tail indexing.
Checks N=288 and N=289 exactly and concludes the smallest certified index is 289.

commonErrors.description: Treats 1/n and sin(1/n) as equal because their ratio tends to one, concluding the defect is zero or negligible without finding its order.
commonErrors.consequence: The cubic defect is precisely the summand's leading behavior and determines convergence.

commonErrors.description: Bounds the tail beginning at N+1 by an integral beginning at N+1 in the wrong inequality direction.
commonErrors.consequence: For a decreasing positive function, that integral is a lower bound for this tail, not the required upper certificate.

hintTree.content: Set x=1/n and use the first nonzero omitted term in the Taylor expansion of sine.
For the tail, combine 0<x-sin x<=x^3/6 with an integral bound for sum n^(-3).
Compare the certificate at N=288 and N=289 using exact integer squares.

CALC2:010337.canonicalSolution:
For $x>0$, $\sin x<x$, so every term is positive.
Moreover,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{1/n-\sin(1/n)}{1/n^3}
=\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{x-\sin x}{x^3}=\frac16.$$
Limit comparison with $\sum n^{-3}$ therefore proves convergence.

For $0<x\le1$, the alternating Taylor bounds give
$0<x-\sin x\le x^3/6$. Consequently,
$$\begin{aligned}
0<R_N
&=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\left(\frac1n-\sin\frac1n\right)\\
&\le\frac16\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^3}
\le\frac16\int_N^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^3}
=\boxed{\frac1{12N^2}}.
\end{aligned}$$
The displayed bound decreases with $N$. For $N=288$ its denominator is
$12\cdot288^2=995328<10^6$, so the bound is greater than $10^{-6}$. For
$N=289$, the denominator is $12\cdot289^2=1002252>10^6$, so the bound is
less than $10^{-6}$. Thus the smallest index certified by this bound is
$\boxed{N=289}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since x-sin x is positive and asymptotic to x^3/6, the summand is asymptotic to 1/(6n^3), so the series converges. Also x-sin x<=x^3/6 and sum_(n>N)n^-3<=1/(2N^2), giving R_N<=1/(12N^2). The bound fails at 288 and succeeds at 289.
Because sin(1/n) is asymptotic to 1/n, I subtract the equivalents and claim every summand is asymptotic to zero, without identifying the cubic leading defect.
I use integral_(N+1)^infinity x^-3 dx as an upper bound for sum_(n=N+1)^infinity n^-3; the monotone integral comparison points the other way.

CALC2:010338.title: Expose a harmonic tail inside a cosine defect
CALC2:010338.objective: Recognize that multiplying a quadratic trigonometric defect by n leaves a harmonic-scale term and prove positive divergence despite terms tending to zero.
CALC2:010338.statement:
Determine whether
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\left(1-\cos\frac1n\right)$$
converges or diverges. Your argument must compute an explicit limit-comparison
constant with the harmonic series. Also state what happens to the partial sums
and explain why the fact that the individual terms tend to zero does not settle
the question.
permittedResults: As $x\to0$, $(1-\cos x)/x^2\to1/2$. If positive sequences $a_n,b_n$ satisfy $a_n/b_n\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, their series have the same convergence behavior.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the standard cosine limit and limit comparison with the harmonic series.
Use rigorous two-sided Taylor bounds to sandwich the summand between positive constant multiples of 1/n for all sufficiently large n.

milestones.criterion: Chooses 1/n as the comparison and computes the finite positive ratio 1/2.
Invokes limit comparison to prove divergence and identifies partial sums tending to +infinity.
Distinguishes the necessary term-to-zero condition from sufficient convergence evidence.

commonErrors.description: Compares the summand with 1/n^2 after forgetting the exterior factor n.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual leading term is 1/(2n), so this incorrectly changes divergence into convergence.

commonErrors.description: Concludes the series converges solely because its terms tend to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The harmonic series also has terms tending to zero; the computed harmonic-scale comparison proves divergence.

hintTree.content: Compare the nth term with 1/n, not with 1/n^2.
After dividing by 1/n, rewrite the ratio using x=1/n.
Use nonnegativity to translate divergence of the series into a statement about its partial sums.

CALC2:010338.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$a_n=n\left(1-\cos\frac1n\right),\qquad b_n=\frac1n.$$
Both are positive, and
$$\frac{a_n}{b_n}
=n^2\left(1-\cos\frac1n\right)
=\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\bigg|_{x=1/n}
\longrightarrow\frac12.$$
The limit-comparison constant is therefore $\boxed{1/2}$. Since the harmonic
series $\sum b_n$ diverges, so does the given series. Every term is
nonnegative, so its partial sums form an increasing sequence; because the
series does not converge, those partial sums satisfy
$$\boxed{S_N\longrightarrow+\infty}.$$
At the same time, $a_n\sim1/(2n)$, so $a_n\to0$. This necessary condition for
convergence is not sufficient: harmonic-scale decay is still too slow.

graderFixtures.proofText: Divide a_n=n(1-cos(1/n)) by 1/n. The ratio is n^2(1-cos(1/n)) and tends to 1/2. Thus limit comparison with the harmonic series proves divergence. Since terms are nonnegative, partial sums tend to +infinity even though a_n tends to zero.
I use 1-cos(1/n)~1/(2n^2) but forget the multiplier n, so I compare the given summand with a convergent p-series.
The nth term tends to zero, therefore I say the series converges without applying any convergence test.

CALC2:010339.title: Control an alternating exponential defect before estimating its tail
CALC2:010339.objective: Prove monotonicity for a non-obvious alternating magnitude, classify convergence using its harmonic asymptotic, and state the signed remainder bound.
CALC2:010339.statement:
For $n\ge1$, define
$$d_n=n\left(e^{1/n}-1\right)-1.$$
Study the series
$$S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}d_n.$$
Prove that $d_n>0$, that $(d_n)$ decreases to zero, and that
$nd_n\to1/2$. Classify the series as absolutely convergent, conditionally
convergent, or divergent. Finally, if $S_N$ is its $N$th partial sum, give a
signed inequality for $S-S_N$ as well as an absolute error bound.
permittedResults: The expansion $e^t=1+t+t^2/2+O(t^3)$ holds as $t\to0$. If $b_n\downarrow0$, then the remainder of $\sum(-1)^{n+1}b_n$ has the sign of term $N+1$ and magnitude at most $b_{N+1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a continuous derivative argument for monotonicity and Taylor expansion for the harmonic asymptotic.
Use an integral representation of e^t-1-t to establish positivity, monotonicity, and asymptotics, then apply the alternating remainder theorem.

milestones.criterion: Proves d_n>0 and decreasing to zero rather than merely asserting numerical monotonicity.
Computes nd_n->1/2 and uses it to prove failure of absolute convergence while alternation gives convergence.
States 0<(-1)^N(S-S_N)<d_(N+1) and the corresponding absolute bound.

commonErrors.description: Uses the alternating-series test and labels the conclusion absolute convergence.
commonErrors.consequence: Since nd_n tends to 1/2, the magnitude series has harmonic behavior and diverges.

commonErrors.description: States that S-S_N has sign (-1)^(N+1), the sign of the last retained term.
commonErrors.consequence: An alternating remainder has the sign of the first omitted term, which here is (-1)^N.

hintTree.content: For positivity, use e^t>1+t. For monotonicity, extend d_n to g(x)=x(e^(1/x)-1)-1 and differentiate.
Write t=1/x in g'(x); the inequality e^t(1-t)<1 follows by differentiating that expression in t.
The next omitted term has sign (-1)^(N+2)=(-1)^N.

CALC2:010339.canonicalSolution:
Since $e^t>1+t$ for $t>0$,
$$d_n=n(e^{1/n}-1)-1>0.$$
Extend the formula to
$$g(x)=x(e^{1/x}-1)-1\qquad(x>0).$$
Then
$$g'(x)=e^{1/x}-1-\frac{e^{1/x}}x.$$
Writing $t=1/x>0$, this is $e^t(1-t)-1$. The function
$h(t)=e^t(1-t)$ satisfies $h(0)=1$ and $h'(t)=-te^t<0$, so $g'(x)<0$.
Hence $d_n=g(n)$ decreases strictly.

Taylor expansion at zero gives
$$d_n=n\left(\frac1n+\frac1{2n^2}+O(n^{-3})\right)-1
=\frac1{2n}+O(n^{-2}),$$
so $d_n\to0$ and
$$\boxed{nd_n\longrightarrow\frac12}.$$
The alternating-series test now proves convergence of $S$. On the other hand,
limit comparison with $1/n$ shows that $\sum d_n$ diverges, so $S$ is
$\boxed{\text{conditionally convergent}}$.

The first omitted term has sign $(-1)^{N+2}=(-1)^N$. The signed alternating
remainder theorem therefore yields
$$\boxed{0<(-1)^N(S-S_N)<d_{N+1}},$$
and in particular
$$\boxed{|S-S_N|<d_{N+1}}.$$
(Replacing the strict inequalities by non-strict ones is also a valid standard
error statement.)

graderFixtures.proofText: Positivity follows from e^t>1+t. For g(x)=x(e^(1/x)-1)-1, g'=e^t(1-t)-1<0, so d_n decreases. Taylor gives d_n=1/(2n)+O(n^-2), hence nd_n->1/2: the alternating series converges but not absolutely. Also 0<(-1)^N(S-S_N)<d_(N+1).
The signs alternate and d_n tends to zero, so I call the series absolutely convergent without checking sum d_n, which is harmonic-scale.
I assign the remainder the sign (-1)^(N+1) of the Nth term rather than the sign (-1)^N of term N+1.

CALC2:010340.title: Pair a parity-shifted series without rearranging it
CALC2:010340.objective: Use exact even and odd partial sums to evaluate a conditionally convergent rational series whose adjacent terms cancel while its absolute series remains harmonic.
CALC2:010340.statement:
Analyze the series
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\displaystyle n+\frac{1-(-1)^n}{2}}.$$
Prove convergence directly from its even and odd partial sums, find its exact
sum, and determine whether convergence is absolute or conditional. Explain why
canceling consecutive pairs here is legitimate and does not invoke an
unjustified rearrangement.
permittedResults: A sequence of partial sums converges to L if both its even and odd subsequences converge to L. Absolute convergence requires convergence of the series of term magnitudes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Calculate the even and odd partial sums explicitly from adjacent pairs.
Apply the alternating-series test to establish convergence, then use parity partial sums to obtain the exact sum and pair magnitudes to disprove absolute convergence.

milestones.criterion: Shows adjacent terms are exactly 1/(2k) and -1/(2k) and computes both parity partial sums.
Proves the original series converges to zero and the absolute series diverges like sum 1/k.
Correctly distinguishes consecutive grouping from rearrangement and classifies convergence as conditional.

commonErrors.description: Declares the sum zero only because every even partial sum is zero.
commonErrors.consequence: One convergent subsequence of partial sums is insufficient; the odd partial sums must also approach zero.

commonErrors.description: Claims exact pair cancellation makes the absolute series converge.
commonErrors.consequence: Absolute values remove the cancellation and contribute 1/k per pair, producing harmonic divergence.

hintTree.content: Write n=2k-1 and n=2k; simplify the parity correction in the denominator in each case.
Compute S_(2m) exactly, then obtain S_(2m-1) from the last missing even term.
For absolute convergence, add the two magnitudes in each consecutive pair and identify the resulting familiar series.

CALC2:010340.canonicalSolution:
For $n=2k-1$, the parity correction is $1$, so the
denominator is $2k$ and the term is $1/(2k)$. For $n=2k$, the correction is
$0$, so the denominator is again $2k$ and the term is $-1/(2k)$. Thus each
consecutive pair is
$$\frac1{2k}-\frac1{2k}=0.$$
It follows that $S_{2m}=0$. The odd partial sum stops after the positive member
of the $m$th pair, so
$$S_{2m-1}=\frac1{2m}\longrightarrow0.$$
Both parity subsequences of partial sums tend to zero; hence the original
series converges and its exact sum is $\boxed{0}$.

For absolute values, the $k$th pair contributes
$$\frac1{2k}+\frac1{2k}=\frac1k.$$
Therefore the absolute series diverges with the harmonic series, and the
given series is $\boxed{\text{conditionally convergent}}$.

No term has moved past another: we grouped positions $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots$.
More importantly, the explicit formulas for both even and odd partial sums
verify convergence of the original ordering, so the zero sum is not being
inferred from a forbidden rearrangement.

Every adjacent pair cancels, so I announce sum zero without checking the odd partial sums of the original series.
Because the signed pairs cancel, I also say the absolute series converges, forgetting that each absolute pair contributes 1/k.

CALC2:010341.title: Separate the term threshold from the series threshold
CALC2:010341.objective: Classify a power-scaled exponential defect for every real parameter and distinguish when its terms vanish from when their series converges.
CALC2:010341.statement:
For real $p$, consider
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^p\left(e^{1/n}-1-\frac1n\right).$$
Determine exactly for which $p$ the series converges. Treat the boundary
$p=1$ explicitly rather than quoting only an inequality. Separately classify
the limit of the individual term for all real $p$, and identify the parameter
range in which the terms tend to zero even though the series diverges.
permittedResults: As $x\to0$, $e^x-1-x\sim x^2/2$. For real $q$, the positive p-series $\sum n^{-q}$ converges exactly when $q>1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Taylor expansion and limit comparison with n^(p-2).
Use Taylor's theorem to obtain two-sided constant bounds on the exponential defect, then apply the p-series criterion and analyze the same bounds for term limits.

milestones.criterion: Computes n^2(e^(1/n)-1-1/n)->1/2 and obtains the correct p-series model.
Concludes convergence exactly for p<1 and explicitly proves divergence at p=1.
Classifies term limits at p<2, p=2, and p>2 and identifies the range 1<=p<2.

commonErrors.description: Claims convergence for every p<2 merely because the individual term tends to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: For 1<=p<2 the terms vanish but have a divergent p-series scale.

commonErrors.description: Includes p=1 in the convergence region by mishandling the strict p-series inequality.
commonErrors.consequence: At p=1 the summand is asymptotic to 1/(2n), so the series is harmonic and diverges.

hintTree.content: First prove n^2(e^(1/n)-1-1/n)->1/2.
Rewrite the nth term as n^(p-2) times a factor tending to 1/2, then compare with a p-series.
For the term limit, the sign of p-2 matters; for convergence of the series, compare 2-p with 1.

CALC2:010341.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$a_n(p)=n^p\left(e^{1/n}-1-\frac1n\right).$$
Taylor expansion gives
$$e^{1/n}-1-\frac1n=\frac1{2n^2}+O(n^{-3}),$$
so
$$\frac{a_n(p)}{n^{p-2}}
=n^2\left(e^{1/n}-1-\frac1n\right)\longrightarrow\frac12.$$
All terms are positive. Thus limit comparison reduces the series to
$$\sum n^{p-2}=\sum\frac1{n^{2-p}}.$$
It converges exactly when $2-p>1$, namely
$$\boxed{p<1}.$$
At the boundary $p=1$, $a_n(1)\sim1/(2n)$, so the series diverges by direct
limit comparison with the harmonic series.

The same asymptotic gives the individual-term regimes:
$$\boxed{a_n(p)\to
\begin{cases}
0,&p<2,\\
1/2,&p=2,\\
+\infty,&p>2.
\end{cases}}$$
Consequently, for $\boxed{1\le p<2}$ the terms do tend to zero, but the series
still diverges. At $p\ge2$ the term test already proves divergence, whereas at
$p<1$ the positive series converges.

graderFixtures.proofText: The defect is 1/(2n^2)+O(n^-3), so the summand is asymptotic to (1/2)n^(p-2). The associated p-series converges iff 2-p>1, hence p<1; p=1 is harmonic. Terms tend to zero for p<2, to 1/2 at p=2, and to infinity for p>2, so 1<=p<2 is the zero-term divergent range.
Since n^p(e^(1/n)-1-1/n) tends to zero whenever p<2, I call the entire series convergent for every p<2.
I solve 2-p>=1 and include p=1, overlooking that equality gives the divergent harmonic comparison.

CALC2:010344.title: Certify a six-decimal integral with a geometric tail
CALC2:010344.objective: Convert a positive integral to a convergent series, derive a rigorous truncation bound, and find the smallest truncation index certified by that bound.
CALC2:010344.statement:
Let
$$I=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{-\ln(1-x)}x\,dx,$$
where the integrand at $x=0$ is understood by its limiting value. Starting
from the geometric series, justify the identity
$$I=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{-n}}{n^2}.$$
For $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}2^{-n}/n^2$ and $R_N=I-S_N$, prove
$$0<R_N\le \frac{2^{-N}}{(N+1)^2}.$$
Using this displayed bound—not a calculator's decimal agreement—find the
smallest positive integer $N$ that guarantees $|I-S_N|<10^{-6}$.
permittedResults: For $0\le x\le1/2$, the series $\sum_{n\ge1}x^{n-1}/n$ converges uniformly by the Weierstrass M-test and equals $-\ln(1-x)/x$ after continuous extension at zero. Also $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}=2^{-N}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use uniform convergence on [0,1/2], then dominate the tail by a geometric series.
Use nonnegative partial sums and monotone convergence for the integral exchange, followed by the same geometric tail comparison.

milestones.criterion: Derives and justifies I=sum 2^(-n)/n^2 from the logarithmic power series.
Proves 0<R_N<=2^(-N)/(N+1)^2 by a valid tail comparison.
Checks N=12 and N=13 exactly and concludes that 13 is the smallest certified index.

commonErrors.description: Uses 1/N^2 for the denominator bound but also replaces the geometric tail by 2^(-N-1), mixing incompatible indices.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed error certificate need not bound every term of the actual tail beginning at N+1.

commonErrors.description: Declares N=12 sufficient from a computed decimal approximation rather than the required proved tail bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The displayed certificate at N=12 is larger than 10^(-6); the first index it certifies is 13.

hintTree.content: Integrate the geometric identity 1/(1-x)=sum x^k once to obtain -ln(1-x), then divide by x.
In the tail n is at least N+1, so replace 1/n^2 by one constant and sum the remaining geometric series.
Check the proved bound at N=12 and N=13, and use its monotone decrease to establish minimality.

CALC2:010344.canonicalSolution:
For $|x|<1$, integrating the geometric series from
$0$ to $x$ gives
$$-\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n}.$$
    After division by $x$, the terms are $x^{n-1}/n$ (with the first term
    giving the continuous value at zero). On $[0,1/2]$ they satisfy
    $|x^{n-1}/n|\le2^{-(n-1)}/n$, whose series converges. The Weierstrass
    M-test therefore gives uniform convergence of the divided series, so
    termwise integration is justified and
$$I=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\int_0^{1/2}x^{n-1}\,dx
=\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{-n}}{n^2}}.$$

All tail terms are positive. For $n\ge N+1$,
$1/n^2\le1/(N+1)^2$, so
$$0<R_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{-n}}{n^2}
\le\frac1{(N+1)^2}\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}
=\boxed{\frac{2^{-N}}{(N+1)^2}}.$$
The bound decreases strictly with $N$. At $N=12$ it equals
$$\frac1{2^{12}\cdot13^2}=\frac1{692224}>10^{-6},$$
because $692224<10^6$. At $N=13$ it equals
$$\frac1{2^{13}\cdot14^2}=\frac1{1605632}<10^{-6}.$$
Thus the smallest index certified by this bound is $\boxed{N=13}$. The fact
that the bound at $N=12$ exceeds the tolerance does not say its actual error
does; it says this requested certificate first succeeds at $13$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Termwise integration of -ln(1-x)/x=sum x^(n-1)/n gives I=sum 2^(-n)/n^2. For n>=N+1, 1/n^2<=1/(N+1)^2 and the geometric tail is 2^(-N), so R_N<=2^(-N)/(N+1)^2. This bound exceeds 10^-6 at N=12 and is below it at N=13, hence N=13.
I start the omitted tail at N+1 but pair the denominator 1/N^2 with a geometric sum beginning one index later, then state an unsupported sharper bound.
A decimal calculation of S_12 looks accurate, so I choose N=12 even though the required proved bound is 1/692224, which exceeds 10^-6.

CALC2:010417.title: Recover a power series from its second derivative
CALC2:010417.objective: Differentiate a power series to expose a geometric series, recover the original function using its initial data, and evaluate both boundary points without extending an interior identity unjustifiably.
CALC2:010417.statement:
Let
\[
S(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n+2}}{(n+1)(n+2)}.
\]
Find the radius of convergence. On the open interval of convergence, differentiate twice, then use $S(0)=S'(0)=0$ to derive a closed formula for $S(x)$. Finally decide convergence at $x=1$ and $x=-1$ and evaluate both endpoint sums. Justify the endpoint values independently rather than merely substituting into a formula first proved only for $|x|<1$.
permittedResults: A power series may be differentiated term by term at every point strictly inside its radius of convergence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate until the coefficient pattern becomes geometric, then integrate back with initial data.
Use partial fractions on the endpoint coefficients and recognize telescoping and alternating harmonic tails.

milestones.criterion: Finds the radius and derives the interior differential identity.
Uses both initial conditions to recover the unique closed formula.
Checks and evaluates each endpoint as a convergent series rather than assuming the interior formula applies there.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the geometric expression twice but sets the constants arbitrarily or omits the initial conditions.
commonErrors.consequence: The recovered function need not equal the given power series.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes x equal to plus or minus one into the interior formula without checking either endpoint series.
commonErrors.consequence: An identity established only for absolute x below one does not by itself settle boundary convergence.

hintTree.content: Two differentiations give $S''(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n$.
Integrate $1/(1-x)$ twice and determine both constants from $S'(0)$ and $S(0)$.
At $x=1$, telescope $1/[(n+1)(n+2)]$; at $x=-1$, split the same partial fraction into two alternating harmonic tails.

CALC2:010417.canonicalSolution:
The coefficient denominator is only polynomial in $n$, so the coefficient ratio tends to $1$; equivalently, differentiating twice exposes a geometric series. Thus the radius is
\[
\boxed{R=1}.
\]
For $|x|<1$, termwise differentiation gives
\[
S'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1},
\qquad
S''(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n=\frac1{1-x}.
\]
Because $S'(0)=0$, integration yields $S'(x)=-\ln(1-x)$. A second integration, now using $S(0)=0$, gives
\[
\boxed{S(x)=x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)\qquad(|x|<1)}.
\]

Both endpoint series converge absolutely because their absolute terms are bounded by a constant multiple of $1/n^2$. At $x=1$,
\[
S(1)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right)=\boxed1.
\]
At $x=-1$, use the same partial fraction and the alternating harmonic sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(-1)
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\left(\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right)\\
&=\ln2-(1-\ln2)
=\boxed{2\ln2-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These direct convergent-series calculations agree with the one-sided limits of the interior formula, but the endpoint checks are what license the values there. Hence the interval of convergence is $[-1,1]$.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $|x|<1$, $S''=1/(1-x)$, so $S'=-\ln(1-x)$ and the two zero initial values give $S=x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)$. The radius is $1$. Separately, the endpoint series converge absolutely; telescoping gives $S(1)=1$, and alternating harmonic tails give $S(-1)=2\ln2-1$.
I integrate $S''(x)=1/(1-x)$ twice and simply declare both constants zero, without using the given series values $S(0)$ and $S'(0)$.
Because $x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)$ works for $|x|<1$, I plug in $x=\pm1$ immediately and never test whether either endpoint series converges.

CALC2:010418.title: Integrate a Gaussian series with a certified error
CALC2:010418.objective: Build an integral approximation from a truncated Maclaurin series, integrate every coefficient correctly, and prove a numerical error bound from the first omitted alternating term.
CALC2:010418.statement:
Approximate
\[
G=\int_0^{0.4}e^{-x^2}\,dx
\]
by replacing $e^{-x^2}$ with $1-x^2+x^4/2-x^6/6$. Give both an exact expression and a decimal value for the approximation. Then use the alternating-series structure on $0\le x\le0.4$ to prove that the absolute error is at most
\[
\frac{0.4^9}{216}.
\]
State a decimal value for this bound and identify the first omitted term after integration.
permittedResults: For $x\ge0$, $e^{-x^2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n x^{2n}/n!$; on $0\le x\le0.4$ its term magnitudes decrease, so the alternating remainder is no larger than the first omitted term.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the Taylor polynomial as an ordinary polynomial before addressing error.
Bound the integrand remainder pointwise and then integrate that nonnegative bound.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the truncated Maclaurin polynomial and reports the exact and decimal approximation.
Verifies the alternating remainder hypotheses throughout the integration interval.
Integrates the first omitted term to obtain the requested certified error bound.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes 0.4 into the Taylor polynomial coefficients without dividing each monomial by its new exponent.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed integral approximation is instead a function-value approximation.

commonErrors.description: Uses x to the eighth over twenty-four as the final integral error without integrating it from zero to 0.4.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested 0.4 to the ninth over 216 bound is not obtained.

hintTree.content: Integrate $x^{2n}$ as $x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)$ before substituting $0.4$.
The first omitted integrand term is $x^8/24$.
Integrating the pointwise bound gives $\int_0^{0.4}x^8/24\,dx=0.4^9/(24\cdot9)$.

CALC2:010418.canonicalSolution:
Termwise integration of the stated polynomial gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
A
&=\int_0^{0.4}\left(1-x^2+\frac{x^4}{2}-\frac{x^6}{6}\right)dx\\
&=\boxed{0.4-\frac{0.4^3}{3}+\frac{0.4^5}{10}-\frac{0.4^7}{42}}\\
&\approx\boxed{0.379651657142857}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $0\le x\le0.4$, successive magnitudes in the series for $e^{-x^2}$ have ratio $x^2/(n+1)\le0.16/(n+1)<1$. The terms therefore decrease, and the first omitted term after $-x^6/6$ is $x^8/24$. The alternating remainder satisfies
\[
\left|e^{-x^2}-\left(1-x^2+\frac{x^4}{2}-\frac{x^6}{6}\right)\right|
\le\frac{x^8}{24}.
\]
Integrating this inequality gives
\[
|G-A|\le\int_0^{0.4}\frac{x^8}{24}\,dx
=\boxed{\frac{0.4^9}{216}}
\approx\boxed{1.21362963\times10^{-6}}.
\]
The denominator $216=24\cdot9$ includes both the factorial from the exponential series and the power-integration factor.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integrating the cubic-in-$x^2$ polynomial gives $A=0.4-0.4^3/3+0.4^5/10-0.4^7/42\approx0.3796516571$. On $[0,0.4]$ the alternating magnitudes decrease; the next integrand term is $x^8/24$, so $|G-A|\le\int_0^{0.4}x^8/24\,dx=0.4^9/216\approx1.21363\times10^{-6}$.
I evaluate $1-0.4^2+0.4^4/2-0.4^6/6$ and call that the integral approximation, never dividing powers by $1,3,5,7$.
The next function-series term is $x^8/24$, so I state that same expression at the endpoint as the final integral-error calculation without integrating it over $[0,0.4]$.

CALC2:010419.title: Build an even power series around a hidden center
CALC2:010419.objective: Convert a shifted rational function into an even geometric power series, determine its exact interval including endpoint failures, and integrate it to obtain a new convergent series identity.
CALC2:010419.statement:
Find a power series centered at $x=3$ for
$$
f(x)=\frac1{x^2-6x+13}.
$$
Determine the radius and full interval of convergence, checking both endpoints from the series terms. Integrate the series from $3$ to $x$ inside its interval and use $x=4$ to obtain an exact infinite-series identity involving $\arctan(1/2)$.
permittedResults: A power series may be integrated term by term on compact subintervals inside its radius.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expose a geometric series in the squared shifted variable.
Cross-check the integrated series against the elementary arctangent antiderivative.

milestones.criterion: Derives the centered even power series.
Determines radius and audits both endpoints.
Integrates inside the radius and obtains the exact identity.

commonErrors.description: Expands in powers of x rather than x minus three without performing a valid recentering.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated center and convergence interval are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Calls the endpoint series convergent merely because its terms alternate.
commonErrors.consequence: The endpoint terms have constant magnitude one fourth and fail the term test.

hintTree.content: Complete the square: $x^2-6x+13=(x-3)^2+4$.
The antiderivative from the center is $(1/2)\arctan((x-3)/2)$.

CALC2:010419.canonicalSolution:
Completing the square gives
$$
f(x)=\frac1{4+(x-3)^2}
=\frac14\frac1{1+(x-3)^2/4}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{(-1)^n(x-3)^{2n}}{4^{n+1}}}
$$
when $|(x-3)^2/4|<1$, equivalently $|x-3|<2$. At $x=1$ or $x=5$, the nth term is $(-1)^n/4$, which does not tend to zero. Both endpoints diverge, so the interval is $\boxed{(1,5)}$ and the radius is $2$.

For $|x-3|<2$, termwise integration gives
$$
\int_3^x f(t)dt
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n(x-3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)4^{n+1}}.
$$
Direct integration yields the same left side as
$$
\frac12\arctan\!\left(\frac{x-3}{2}\right).
$$
Substituting $x=4$, which lies strictly inside the interval, gives
$$
\boxed{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{(2n+1)4^{n+1}}
=\frac12\arctan\!\left(\frac12\right)}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: $f=(1/4)/(1+(x-3)^2/4)=\sum(-1)^n(x-3)^{2n}/4^{n+1}$ for $|x-3|<2$. At both endpoints terms equal $(-1)^n/4$, so the interval is $(1,5)$. Integration and $x=4$ give the stated arctangent identity.
I expand as a power series in x around zero and still claim it is centered at three, without any valid change of center.
At x equal one and five the terms alternate, so I declare convergence even though their magnitude stays one fourth and never approaches zero.

CALC2:010420.title: Certify a cube-root approximation on the whole interval
CALC2:010420.objective: Construct a quadratic Taylor approximation for a fractional power, locate the maximum third derivative on the relevant interval, and report a numerical approximation with a rigorous Lagrange error certificate.
CALC2:010420.statement: Use the degree-two Maclaurin polynomial for $f(x)=(1+x)^{1/3}$ to approximate $\sqrt[3]{1.08}$. Derive the polynomial from derivatives rather than quoting a binomial series. Then use the Lagrange remainder theorem on the entire interval $[0,0.08]$ to prove an explicit error bound and give both the approximation and bound as decimals.
permittedResults: A negative power of one plus x is decreasing on a nonnegative interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the fractional power three times and apply Taylor's theorem directly.
Use monotonicity of the third derivative magnitude to choose the smallest simple interval bound.

milestones.criterion: Builds the degree-two polynomial from derivatives.
Audits the next derivative on the entire interval.
Computes a consistent approximation and rigorous decimal error bound.

commonErrors.consequence: The approximation polynomial has twice the correct quadratic correction.

The third derivative is $(10/27)(1+x)^{-8/3}$.

The derivatives are
$$
f'(x)=\frac13(1+x)^{-2/3},\qquad
f''(x)=-\frac29(1+x)^{-5/3},
$$
so
$$
P_2(x)=1+\frac{x}{3}-\frac{x^2}{9}.
$$
At $x=0.08$,
$$
P_2(0.08)=1+\frac{0.08}{3}-\frac{0.08^2}{9}
=\boxed{1.025955555555\ldots}.
$$
Also
$$
f'''(x)=\frac{10}{27}(1+x)^{-8/3}.
$$
This is positive and decreasing on $[0,0.08]$, so its maximum is $M=10/27$, not its value only at the target. Taylor's theorem gives
$$
|R_2(0.08)|\le\frac{10}{27}\frac{0.08^3}{3!}
=\boxed{\frac{5(0.08)^3}{81}}
=\boxed{0.00003160493827\ldots}.
$$
Thus the displayed decimal approximation is certified to lie within about $3.161\times10^{-5}$ of $\sqrt[3]{1.08}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: I write the quadratic term as $-2x^2/9$, forgetting to divide the second derivative at zero by two factorial.

CALC2:010421.title: Differentiate a geometric series to represent a rational function
CALC2:010421.objective: Obtain a power series by differentiating a known geometric series and state the open interval on which termwise differentiation is justified.
CALC2:010421.statement:
Starting from $1/(1-x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n$, derive a power series centered at zero for
$$
\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}.
$$
State its interval of convergence and evaluate the resulting series at $x=1/3$ to obtain an exact sum.
permittedResults: Differentiating sum_{n=0}^infinity x^n gives sum_{n=1}^infinity n x^(n-1)=sum_{n=0}^infinity (n+1)x^n for |x|<1.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the familiar geometric identity and then reindex to make the constant term visible.
Separate the radius argument from the endpoint term tests.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the geometric series and writes sum_{n=0}^infinity(n+1)x^n for 1/(1-x)^2.
Checks both endpoints and states the interval of convergence (-1,1).
Evaluates the requested interior series at x=1/3 as 9/4.

commonErrors.description: Writes sum n x^n after differentiation and thereby removes the constant coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The index/exponent mismatch gives the wrong power series for 1/(1-x)^2.

commonErrors.description: Includes x=1 in the interval despite terms n+1 that do not approach zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Failure of the term test makes the endpoint series divergent, so the claimed interval is false.

hintTree.content: Differentiate both sides of the geometric-series identity before shifting any index.
Rewrite the differentiated sum so its exponent is x^n; inspect the constant coefficient after the shift.
Test x=1 and x=-1 with the term test before reporting the convergence interval, then substitute x=1/3.

CALC2:010421.canonicalSolution:
For $|x|<1$, the geometric series converges to $(1-x)^{-1}$ and may be differentiated term by term. Differentiating gives
$$
\frac1{(1-x)^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n x^{n-1}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)x^n.
$$
The radius is still one. At $x=1$ the terms $n+1$ do not approach zero; at $x=-1$ the terms $(n+1)(-1)^n$ also do not approach zero. Thus the interval is $\boxed{(-1,1)}$. Substituting $x=1/3$, which lies inside that interval, yields
$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{n+1}{3^n}=\frac1{(1-1/3)^2}=\boxed{\frac94}.
$$
The index shift is essential: the constant coefficient is $1$, not $0$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differentiating inside |x|<1 gives 1/(1-x)^2=sum_(n=0)^infinity (n+1)x^n. Both endpoints fail the term test, so the interval is (-1,1), and x=1/3 gives 9/4.
I differentiate sum x^n as sum n x^n and therefore omit the index shift, making the constant coefficient zero.
I include x=1 in the convergence interval even though the terms n+1 do not tend to zero there.

CALC2:010422.title: Approximate a logarithm with a signed Taylor remainder
CALC2:010422.objective: Use the Taylor series for a logarithm at a safe interior point and provide a numerical error certificate whose direction follows from alternation.
CALC2:010422.statement:
Use
$$
\ln(1+x)=x-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}-\cdots
$$
to approximate $\ln(1.2)$ with the first four nonzero terms. Give a rigorous bound for the absolute error and state whether the approximation is above or below the true value.
permittedResults: At x=1/5, the logarithm-series term magnitudes x^n/n decrease to zero, so the alternating remainder theorem applies.

acceptableStrategies.description: Keep exact fractions so the retained fourth-term sign cannot be lost.
Use the first omitted term, together with its sign, as the entire error certificate.

milestones.criterion: Computes P_4=1367/7500 with the fourth term subtracted.
Verifies the decreasing alternating-term conditions at x=1/5.
States that P_4 underestimates ln(1.2) and bounds the absolute error by 1/15625.

commonErrors.description: Adds the fourth logarithm term instead of subtracting it.
commonErrors.consequence: The partial sum is no longer P_4 for ln(1+x), so both the approximation and its remainder direction are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims a 1/100000 error bound merely because the series alternates.
commonErrors.consequence: Alternation supplies the first omitted-term bound 1/15625, and the asserted tighter number is false.

hintTree.content: Substitute x=1/5 through the fourth power and retain the alternating signs exactly.
Add the four rational terms before converting to a common denominator for P_4.
The fifth term is positive, so use its magnitude (1/5)^5/5 to identify both the direction and the error bound.

CALC2:010422.canonicalSolution:
Here $x=0.2=1/5$, so the first four terms give
$$
P_4=\frac15-\frac1{50}+\frac1{375}-\frac1{2500}
=\frac{1367}{7500}.
$$
The positive term magnitudes $(1/5)^n/n$ decrease to zero. Therefore the alternating-series remainder has the sign of the next term and magnitude at most its magnitude. The fifth term is positive, so $\ln(1.2)-P_4>0$ and
$$
0<\ln(1.2)-\frac{1367}{7500}<\frac{(1/5)^5}{5}=\frac1{15625}.
$$
Consequently $\boxed{P_4=1367/7500}$ is an underestimate, with absolute error less than $\boxed{1/15625}$. The bound uses the first omitted term, not the final term retained in the polynomial.

graderFixtures.proofText: At x=1/5, P4=1/5-1/50+1/375-1/2500=1367/7500. The next term is positive and has size 1/15625, so P4 underestimates ln(1.2) by less than 1/15625.
I add the fourth logarithm term instead of subtracting it, ignoring the alternating sign and changing the approximation.
I claim the absolute error is less than 1/100000 because the omitted terms alternate, but the actual error is about 0.00005489, which is larger than 0.00001.

CALC2:010423.title: Let a differential equation generate its own power series
CALC2:010423.objective: Substitute a formal power series into a differential equation, align coefficient indices without losing the constant equation, generate coefficients through a prescribed degree, and identify the resulting entire function.
CALC2:010423.statement:
Seek a power-series solution centered at zero for
$$
y'=2xy,
\qquad y(0)=1.
$$
Write $y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n$, derive equations for the constant coefficient and for general coefficients, and compute every coefficient through $x^8$. State the degree-eight Taylor polynomial. Then identify the familiar function represented by the full series and verify directly that it satisfies both the differential equation and initial condition.
permittedResults: Differentiating $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n$ gives $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+1)a_{n+1}x^n$ inside its radius of convergence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match coefficients after shifting the multiplied series by one power.
Derive the two parity chains from the recurrence and recognize the exponential factorial pattern.

milestones.criterion: Substitutes aligned series and obtains a_0=1, a_1=0, and a_(n+2)=2a_n/(n+2).
Computes all coefficients through degree eight and states P_8 correctly.
Identifies e^(x^2), verifies the ODE and initial condition, and notes its global convergence.

commonErrors.description: Applies the recurrence as though the right side had a constant coefficient and fails to derive a_1=0.
commonErrors.consequence: Spurious odd coefficients enter the series, so it no longer satisfies y'=2xy with the stated initial data.

commonErrors.description: Matches (n+1)a_(n+1) to 2a_n instead of the coefficient 2a_(n-1) of x^n.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting coefficients represent a different differential equation and do not produce e^(x^2).

hintTree.content: Write y' with powers x^n, but note that 2xy has no constant term.
For n>=1, match (n+1)a_(n+1) with 2a_(n-1), or shift this to a_(n+2)=2a_n/(n+2).
Use a_0=1 and a_1=0 to separate the even and odd coefficient chains.

CALC2:010423.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$
y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n,
\qquad
y'=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+1)a_{n+1}x^n.
$$
Meanwhile,
$$
2xy=2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^{n+1}.
$$
The right side has no constant term, so $a_1=0$. For $n\ge1$, matching the coefficient of $x^n$ gives
$$
(n+1)a_{n+1}=2a_{n-1}.
$$
Equivalently, for $n\ge0$,
$$
a_{n+2}=\frac{2a_n}{n+2}.
$$
The initial condition gives $a_0=1$. Hence all odd coefficients vanish, while
$$
a_2=1,\quad a_4=\frac12,\quad a_6=\frac16,\quad a_8=\frac1{24}.
$$
Thus the requested polynomial is
$$
\boxed{P_8(x)=1+x^2+\frac{x^4}{2}+\frac{x^6}{6}+\frac{x^8}{24}}.
$$
The full even series is
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2k}}{k!}=e^{x^2}.
$$
Indeed, $(e^{x^2})'=2xe^{x^2}$ and $e^0=1$, so the identified function satisfies both requirements and its series converges for every real $x$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Writing y'=sum_(n>=0)(n+1)a_(n+1)x^n and 2xy=2sum_(n>=0)a_n x^(n+1) gives a_1=0 and a_(n+2)=2a_n/(n+2). With a_0=1, P8=1+x^2+x^4/2+x^6/6+x^8/24, the truncation of e^(x^2).
I match every coefficient to 2a_n, including the constant term, so I set a_1=2a_0 and generate nonzero odd powers even though 2xy has no x^0 term.
I write (n+1)a_(n+1)=2a_n without accounting for the extra x multiplying y; my recurrence is shifted and the resulting polynomial fails direct substitution in y'=2xy.

CALC2:010424.title: Separate a logarithmic series radius from its endpoints
CALC2:010424.objective: Find the radius and full interval of convergence of a shifted logarithmic power series, test its two endpoints by different criteria, and identify its sum function without extending an interior identity blindly.
CALC2:010424.statement:
For the power series
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-2)^n}{n\,4^n},
$$
find its radius of convergence and its complete interval of convergence, with both endpoints tested explicitly. On the open interval, find a closed form for the sum by reducing to a standard logarithmic series. Finally, determine the sum at every convergent endpoint and explain why the divergent endpoint cannot be assigned the same way.
permittedResults: For $|z|<1$, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^n/n=-\ln(1-z)$; at $z=-1$ the alternating harmonic series converges to $-\ln2$, while at $z=1$ the harmonic series diverges.

acceptableStrategies.description: Normalize the shifted variable to a standard sum z^n/n and then audit each boundary.
Differentiate the series to a geometric series in the interior, integrate back using the value at z=0, and test endpoints afterward.

milestones.criterion: Reduces to z=(x-2)/4, finds radius 4, and solves the open convergence inequality.
Tests x=-2 and x=6 separately and reports the interval [-2,6).
Gives the logarithmic sum in the interior and the endpoint value -ln2 with a valid justification.

commonErrors.description: Includes x=6 because its distance from the center equals the radius, without testing the resulting harmonic series.
commonErrors.consequence: The endpoint terms form sum 1/n, so the claimed interval contains a divergent boundary point.

commonErrors.description: Excludes x=-2 solely because the ratio or root test is inconclusive when |z|=1.
commonErrors.consequence: A direct alternating-series test proves convergence there and changes the complete interval and endpoint sum.

hintTree.content: Set z=(x-2)/4 and first solve |z|<1.
At x=-2 the series is sum (-1)^n/n; at x=6 it is sum 1/n.
Use the standard logarithm identity only on |z|<1, then justify the left endpoint separately.

CALC2:010424.canonicalSolution:
Set
$$
z=\frac{x-2}{4}.
$$
The series becomes $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^n/n$, whose radius in $z$ is $1$. Thus
$$
\left|\frac{x-2}{4}\right|<1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-2<x<6,
$$
so the radius in $x$ is $\boxed{R=4}$.

At $x=-2$, $z=-1$ and the series is
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n},
$$
which converges by the alternating-series test and has sum $-\ln2$. At $x=6$, $z=1$ and the series is harmonic, so it diverges. Therefore the complete interval is
$$
\boxed{[-2,6)}.
$$
For $-2<x<6$, the logarithmic identity gives
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-2)^n}{n\,4^n}
=-\ln\left(1-\frac{x-2}{4}\right).
$$
At the convergent left endpoint the same expression has the continuous value $-\ln2$, consistent with the alternating harmonic sum. At the right endpoint it would require the logarithm of zero, matching divergence rather than a finite assigned value.

graderFixtures.proofText: With z=(x-2)/4 the series is sum z^n/n, so R=4. At x=-2 it is sum (-1)^n/n=-ln2; at x=6 it is harmonic and diverges. Thus the interval is [-2,6), and inside it the sum is -ln(1-(x-2)/4).
I solve |x-2|<=4 and include x=6 without testing it, even though substitution gives the divergent harmonic series sum 1/n at that endpoint.
The ratio test gives limit one at x=-2, so I declare divergence and report (-2,6), ignoring that the endpoint series is alternating harmonic and converges to -ln2.

CALC2:010425.title: Read coefficients and endpoints from an exponential-geometric product
CALC2:010425.objective: Use the Cauchy product to derive coefficients of a power series, determine its radius and endpoint behavior from those coefficients, and evaluate the series at an interior point without confusing the product function with its convergence interval.
CALC2:010425.statement:
Find the Maclaurin series
$$
\frac{e^x}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_nx^n
$$
by multiplying the standard series for its two factors. Give a closed formula for $c_n$, determine the radius and full interval of convergence (including separate endpoint tests), and evaluate $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n/2^n$ exactly. The power-series endpoints are $x=\pm1$: explain why the represented function being undefined at $x=1$ but finite at $x=-1$ is not a substitute for testing the two endpoint series, both of which fail the term test.
permittedResults: Inside the common radius, $(\sum_{k\geq0}a_kx^k)(\sum_{j\geq0}b_jx^j)=\sum_{n\geq0}(\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k})x^n$; endpoints must be tested in the resulting series.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply the exponential and geometric series coefficient by coefficient, then analyze c_n.
Differentiate or manipulate the proposed series to verify its product identity, while still deriving its coefficients and testing endpoints explicitly.

milestones.criterion: Uses the Cauchy product to derive the finite partial-exponential coefficient c_n.
Finds radius 1 and rejects both endpoints because the series terms do not tend to zero.
Evaluates the interior sum as 2sqrt(e) and distinguishes function domain from series convergence.

commonErrors.description: Calls the x=-1 series convergent merely because its signs alternate.
commonErrors.consequence: Its term magnitudes c_n approach e instead of zero, so the necessary term test fails before any alternating-series criterion applies.

commonErrors.description: Includes x=-1 because e^x/(1-x) is defined there, without testing the Maclaurin series.
commonErrors.consequence: A power series can diverge at a boundary point where an analytic continuation of its represented function is finite.

hintTree.content: Multiply sum x^k/k! by sum x^j and collect all pairs k+j=n.
Observe that c_n increases to e; use this both in a radius test and in the term test at x=1 and x=-1.
At x=1/2, either substitute into the product function within its convergence interval or sum the absolutely convergent double series.

CALC2:010425.canonicalSolution:
For $|x|<1$, both factor series converge absolutely:
$$
e^x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{x^k}{k!},
\qquad
\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{j=0}^\infty x^j.
$$
The Cauchy product therefore gives
$$
c_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{1}{k!},
\qquad
\frac{e^x}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{1}{k!}\right)x^n.
$$
Because $c_n\to e$, one has $\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}=1$, so the radius is $R=1$. At $x=1$, the terms are $c_n\to e\ne0$; at $x=-1$, the terms are $(-1)^nc_n$, whose magnitudes also tend to $e$. Both endpoints fail the term test. The interval of convergence is therefore
$$
\boxed{(-1,1)}.
$$
Since $1/2$ lies inside it, substituting into the represented function is valid:
$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{c_n}{2^n}
=\frac{e^{1/2}}{1-1/2}
=\boxed{2\sqrt e}.
$$
Endpoint behavior is a property of the series terms. In particular, even though the formula $e^x/(1-x)$ is finite at $x=-1$, its Maclaurin series still diverges there.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Cauchy coefficient is c_n=sum_{k=0}^n1/k!, so c_n tends to e and R=1. At plus or minus 1 the terms have magnitude tending to e, hence both diverge and the interval is (-1,1). At x=1/2 the sum is 2sqrt(e).
At x=-1 the signs alternate, so I invoke the alternating series test even though c_n tends to e rather than zero.
Because e^x/(1-x) is finite at x=-1, I include -1 in the convergence interval without inspecting the series terms.

CALC2:010426.title: Extract a periodic coefficient pattern from a cubic geometric series
CALC2:010426.objective: Rewrite a rational function to expose a sparse periodic Maclaurin series, identify its coefficients, and test boundary points directly even where the rational function itself remains finite.
CALC2:010426.statement:
Starting from a geometric series, derive the Maclaurin expansion of
$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{1+x+x^2}.
$$
Give a formula or period-three pattern for the coefficient of $x^n$, determine the radius and complete interval of convergence by testing $x=\pm1$, and use the series to evaluate its sum at $x=1/2$. Include an explanation of why a finite value of the rational function at a boundary point does not force its Maclaurin series to converge there.
permittedResults: The identity $1+x+x^2=(1-x^3)/(1-x)$ gives $1/(1+x+x^2)=(1-x)\sum_{k\geq0}x^{3k}$ for $|x|<1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the factorization of 1-x^3 and a geometric series in x^3.
Alternatively solve the coefficient recurrence a_n+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}=0 with a_0=1, then establish radius and endpoints separately.

milestones.criterion: Rewrites the function as (1-x)/(1-x^3) and derives the sparse geometric expansion.
Identifies coefficients 1,-1,0 by residue class and obtains interval (-1,1) by endpoint term tests.
Evaluates the x=1/2 sum as 4/7 and explains the boundary function-versus-series distinction.

commonErrors.description: Includes one or both endpoints solely because 1/(1+x+x^2) has finite values there.
commonErrors.consequence: The Maclaurin terms fail to approach zero at both endpoints, so those rational values are analytic continuations rather than boundary sums.

commonErrors.description: States the repeating coefficients are 1,0,-1 instead of 1,-1,0.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed pattern contradicts (1-x)sum x^(3k) and changes every nonconstant block of the series.

hintTree.content: Factor 1-x^3 and cancel 1-x algebraically before expanding 1/(1-x^3).
Write several terms: 1-x+x^3-x^4+x^6-x^7+... and read exponents modulo 3.
At each endpoint, inspect the individual terms a_n x^n; do not substitute only into the rational function.

CALC2:010426.canonicalSolution:
Since $1-x^3=(1-x)(1+x+x^2)$,
$$
\frac{1}{1+x+x^2}=\frac{1-x}{1-x^3}
=(1-x)\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^{3k}
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(x^{3k}-x^{3k+1}\right),
\qquad |x|<1.
$$
Thus the coefficient pattern is
$$
a_{3k}=1,\qquad a_{3k+1}=-1,\qquad a_{3k+2}=0.
$$
The geometric construction gives radius $R=1$ (the coefficient limsup also gives 1). At $x=1$, the terms $a_n$ do not tend to zero. At $x=-1$, the terms $a_n(-1)^n$ equal $(-1)^k$ at both indices $3k$ and $3k+1$, so their magnitudes repeatedly equal $1$ and they again do not tend to zero. Both endpoints diverge, and the interval is
$$
\boxed{(-1,1)}.
$$
At $x=1/2$, which is safely inside the interval,
$$
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(2^{-3k}-2^{-(3k+1)}\right)
=\frac{1-1/2}{1-1/8}=\boxed{\frac{4}{7}}.
$$
Although $f(1)=1/3$ and $f(-1)=1$, those finite rational-function values are not sums of this divergent boundary series.

graderFixtures.proofText: Because (1-x)/(1-x^3)=(1-x)sum x^(3k), the coefficients repeat 1,-1,0. At x=1 and -1 the terms do not go to zero, so the interval is (-1,1). Substitution x=1/2 gives (1/2)/(1-1/8)=4/7.
The rational function is finite at x=1 and x=-1, so I include both endpoints without applying the term test to the power series.
I read the block x^(3k)-x^(3k+1) as coefficients 1,0,-1, shifting the negative coefficient to the wrong residue class.

CALC2:010427.title: Let central binomial growth decide two different endpoints
CALC2:010427.objective: Derive the Maclaurin series for an inverse square root, find its radius by coefficient ratios, and classify its two endpoints using alternation and central-binomial asymptotics rather than the interior formula alone.
CALC2:010427.statement:
Starting from the generalized binomial theorem, derive
$$
\frac1{\sqrt{1+x}}
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}x^n.
$$
Determine the radius and full interval of convergence. At each endpoint, classify convergence as absolute, conditional, or divergent and justify the classification using the behavior of $\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$. Where the series converges, identify its sum.
permittedResults: The generalized binomial theorem gives $(1+x)^\alpha=\sum_{n\ge0}\binom{\alpha}{n}x^n$ for $|x|<1$, and $\binom{-1/2}{n}=(-1)^n\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$; moreover $\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\sim1/\sqrt{\pi n}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use generalized binomial coefficients, a ratio calculation for the radius, and central-binomial asymptotics at the endpoints.
Wallis-product upper and lower bounds may replace the asymptotic equivalence, provided they establish decrease to zero and divergence of the positive endpoint series.

milestones.criterion: Derives the coefficient (-1)^n binom(2n,n)/4^n and uses its ratio to obtain radius 1.
Classifies x=1 as conditionally convergent with sum 1/sqrt2, including failure of absolute convergence.
Shows x=-1 produces a positive n^(-1/2)-scale series and states the interval (-1,1].

commonErrors.description: Claims x=-1 is alternating and x=1 is positive by tracking only x^n and forgetting the coefficient sign (-1)^n.
commonErrors.consequence: The endpoint classifications are reversed: the two signs cancel at x=-1, while the coefficient alternation survives at x=1.

commonErrors.description: Includes both endpoints because the function 1/sqrt(1+x) is assigned a value or limiting interpretation there, without testing the coefficient series.
commonErrors.consequence: Power-series endpoints must be tested from their terms; at x=-1 the positive central-binomial series diverges.

hintTree.content: Use the identity for binom(-1/2,n), then compute the ratio of successive positive magnitudes a_n=binom(2n,n)/4^n.
At x=1 the signs still alternate and a_n decreases to zero; decide whether the absolute series resembles a p-series.
At x=-1 the two sign factors cancel, so every term is positive and has the same n^(-1/2) scale.

CALC2:010427.canonicalSolution:
The generalized binomial theorem with $\alpha=-1/2$ gives
$$
(1+x)^{-1/2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{-1/2}{n}x^n,
$$
and direct simplification of the falling product yields
$$
\binom{-1/2}{n}=(-1)^n\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}.
$$
Put $a_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$. Its ratio is
$$
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}
=\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{4(n+1)^2}
=\frac{2n+1}{2n+2}\longrightarrow1.
$$
Thus the power series has radius $R=1$.

At $x=1$ the series is $\sum(-1)^na_n$. The displayed ratio is less than one and $a_n\to0$, so the alternating-series test gives convergence. Since
$$a_n\sim\frac1{\sqrt{\pi n}},$$
the absolute series diverges like $\sum n^{-1/2}$; convergence at $x=1$ is conditional. Abel's endpoint theorem (or the standard endpoint form of the binomial series) then gives the sum $1/\sqrt2$.

At $x=-1$, the factors $(-1)^n$ and $x^n$ cancel, leaving $\sum a_n$. The same asymptotic comparison with $n^{-1/2}$ proves divergence. Therefore the full interval is
$$
\boxed{(-1,1]},
$$
with absolute convergence for $|x|<1$, conditional convergence at $x=1$, and divergence at $x=-1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Here a_n=C(2n,n)/4^n has a_(n+1)/a_n=(2n+1)/(2n+2) and a_n~1/sqrt(pi n), so R=1. At x=1 the alternating series is conditional and sums to 1/sqrt2; at x=-1 signs cancel and the positive series diverges. Interval (-1,1].
I say x=-1 gives an alternating series and x=1 gives all positive terms, because I track x^n but forget that each coefficient already contains (-1)^n.
The formula 1/sqrt(1+x) is meaningful on the real domain I want, so I include both power-series endpoints without testing the central-binomial coefficient series there.

CALC2:010428.title: Remove a denominator by integrating the exponential series
CALC2:010428.objective: Determine the radius of a factorially weighted power series, derive its removable closed form through termwise integration, evaluate it at positive and negative inputs, and provide a uniform truncation bound on a full interval.
CALC2:010428.statement:
Let
$$
F(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!(n+1)}.
$$
(a) Find its radius of convergence.
(b) Multiply by $x$ and use a termwise integral of the exponential series to obtain a closed form, including the value at $x=0$.
(c) Evaluate $F(1)$ and $F(-1)$.
(d) If $S_N(x)$ stops after $n=N$, prove a simple bound for $|F(x)-S_N(x)|$ that holds uniformly for $|x|\leq1$.
permittedResults: A power series may be integrated term by term on every closed interval inside its radius; the exponential series has infinite radius, and $\int_0^x e^t\,dt=e^x-1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the exponential series after multiplying F by x, then dominate the factorial tail geometrically.
A direct index shift of e^x-1 may replace the integral derivation, provided the x=0 extension and uniform remainder proof are still explicit.

milestones.criterion: Uses the factorial ratio to prove infinite radius of convergence.
Derives F(x)=(e^x-1)/x for x nonzero and supplies the removable value F(0)=1.
Computes F(1), F(-1), and proves the uniform bound 2/(N+2)! (or a sharper valid bound).

commonErrors.description: States F(x)=(e^x-1)/x for every real x and leaves F(0) undefined.
commonErrors.consequence: The original power series is entire and equals 1 at zero; failing to remove the quotient singularity contradicts the series itself.

commonErrors.description: Claims the positive tail is at most its first omitted term 1/(N+2)! without accounting for any later terms.
commonErrors.consequence: At x=1 every omitted term is positive, so the full tail is strictly larger than its first term and the claimed certificate is false.

hintTree.content: Observe that n!(n+1)=(n+1)!, then apply the ratio test to the terms for any fixed x.
After multiplying by x, reindex x^(n+1)/(n+1)! as the integrated exponential series from 0 to x.
For |x|<=1, dominate the omitted terms by sum from m=N+2 of 1/m!, and compare successive terms with a geometric ratio at most 1/(N+3).

CALC2:010428.canonicalSolution:
Because $n!(n+1)=(n+1)!$, the absolute-term ratio for fixed $x$ is
$$
\frac{|x|^{n+1}/(n+2)!}{|x|^n/(n+1)!}
=\frac{|x|}{n+2}\longrightarrow0.
$$
Thus $F$ has infinite radius of convergence.

Multiplying by $x$ and reindexing gives
$$
xF(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}
=\int_0^x\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^n}{n!}\,dt
=\int_0^x e^t\,dt=e^x-1.
$$
Consequently
$$
F(x)=\frac{e^x-1}{x}\quad(x\ne0).
$$
The original series gives $F(0)=1$, and the quotient has the same limit, so the singularity is removable. In particular,
$$
\boxed{F(1)=e-1},\qquad
\boxed{F(-1)=1-e^{-1}}.
$$

For $|x|\le1$,
$$
|F(x)-S_N(x)|
\leq\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n+1)!}
=\sum_{m=N+2}^{\infty}\frac1{m!}.
$$
After the first term, each successive ratio is at most $1/(N+3)\le1/3$. Hence
$$
|F(x)-S_N(x)|
\leq\frac{1}{(N+2)!}\frac1{1-1/(N+3)}
\leq\boxed{\frac{2}{(N+2)!}}.
$$
This bound is independent of $x$ on the stated interval.

graderFixtures.proofText: Since n!(n+1)=(n+1)!, the radius is infinite and xF=sum x^(n+1)/(n+1)!=e^x-1. Thus F(0)=1, F(1)=e-1, F(-1)=1-e^(-1), and for |x|<=1 the tail is at most 2/(N+2)!.
I write F=(e^x-1)/x for all x and conclude the function is undefined at x=0, ignoring that the original series has constant term 1 and removes the quotient singularity.
At x=1 I claim the entire positive remainder is at most its first omitted term 1/(N+2)!, ignoring all later positive factorial terms and having no alternating cancellation.

CALC2:010429.title: Integrate a central-binomial series all the way to both endpoints
CALC2:010429.objective: Derive the Maclaurin series for inverse sine by integrating a binomial series, determine its radius and full endpoint behavior, and justify the two endpoint sums through absolute convergence rather than formal substitution.
CALC2:010429.statement:
Starting from
$$\frac1{\sqrt{1-z}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}z^n\qquad(|z|<1),$$
derive a power series for $\arcsin x$. Determine its radius and interval of convergence, classify both endpoints, and evaluate the series at $x=1$ and $x=-1$.
permittedResults: The central-binomial coefficient satisfies $\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\sim1/\sqrt{\pi n}$; after division by $2n+1$, the endpoint magnitudes are therefore of order $n^{-3/2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the supplied binomial series and use central-binomial asymptotics at the endpoints.
A Wallis-bound proof may replace the asymptotic equivalence if it proves the endpoint terms are dominated by a convergent p-series.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact central-binomial arcsine coefficients with the integration constant fixed.
Establishes radius one and absolute convergence at both endpoints.
States interval [-1,1] and evaluates endpoint sums as pi/2 and -pi/2 with correct signs.

commonErrors.description: Integrates t^(2n) but omits division by 2n+1 in the arcsine coefficients.
commonErrors.consequence: Differentiating the proposed series does not recover (1-x^2)^(-1/2), and its endpoint behavior is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Classifies one or both endpoints as merely conditional based only on the sign of x^(2n+1).
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient magnitudes are order n^(-3/2), so their sum converges absolutely at both endpoints.

hintTree.content: Substitute z=t^2 in the given binomial series before integrating from 0 to x.
Integrate t^(2n) term by term and use arcsin(0)=0.
At |x|=1, compare binom(2n,n)/[4^n(2n+1)] with n^(-3/2).

CALC2:010429.canonicalSolution:
For $|t|<1$, substitute $z=t^2$:
$$\frac1{\sqrt{1-t^2}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}t^{2n}.$$
Termwise integration from $0$ to $x$ gives
$$\boxed{\arcsin x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n(2n+1)}x^{2n+1}}\qquad(|x|<1).$$
The coefficient ratio (or the singularities at $\pm1$ together with the ratio test) gives radius $R=1$. At either endpoint, the absolute term is
$$b_n=\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n(2n+1)}\sim\frac1{2\sqrt\pi\,n^{3/2}},$$
so both endpoint series converge absolutely. Continuity of the integrated series at the endpoints (or Abel's theorem) yields
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_n=\arcsin1=\boxed{\frac\pi2},$$
while every odd power changes sign at $x=-1$, giving
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}-b_n=\arcsin(-1)=\boxed{-\frac\pi2}.$$
Thus the interval is $\boxed{[-1,1]}$, with absolute convergence everywhere on it.

graderFixtures.proofText: Substitute z=t^2 and integrate: arcsin x=sum C(2n,n)x^(2n+1)/[4^n(2n+1)]. The radius is 1, and endpoint magnitudes are asymptotic to 1/(2sqrt(pi)n^(3/2)), so both endpoints converge absolutely to pi/2 and -pi/2.
I integrate t^(2n) without dividing by 2n+1, so my derivative and coefficients do not reproduce the given binomial series.
I label x=1 and x=-1 conditionally convergent just from their signs, never checking that the absolute coefficients decay like n^(-3/2).

CALC2:010430.title: Let a Cauchy product accumulate harmonic coefficients
CALC2:010430.objective: Multiply the logarithmic and geometric power series with a justified Cauchy product, derive the harmonic-number coefficient formula, and separate the interior closed form from two endpoint series that fail the term test.
CALC2:010430.statement:
Use the power series for $\ln(1+x)$ and $1/(1+x)$ to derive the Maclaurin series of
$$G(x)=\frac{\ln(1+x)}{1+x}.$$
Express the coefficient of $x^n$ using $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n1/k$. Find the radius and test both endpoints directly.
permittedResults: Inside a common radius of absolute convergence, the coefficient of $x^n$ in a product is the finite Cauchy sum of coefficient pairs whose indices add to n.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the Cauchy product and then the root behavior of harmonic numbers.
Differentiating a parameterized binomial series may recover the same coefficients, but endpoint series must still be written and term-tested.

milestones.criterion: Writes the two input series on their common disk and forms the correct finite Cauchy coefficient.
Simplifies the coefficient to (-1)^(n+1)H_n and obtains radius one.
Tests both endpoints from their terms and states interval (-1,1).

commonErrors.description: Simplifies the product coefficient to H_n with no factor (-1)^(n+1).
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting series has the wrong first coefficients and cannot equal ln(1+x)/(1+x).

commonErrors.description: Includes x=1 by invoking the alternating-series test despite terms of magnitude H_n.
commonErrors.consequence: A necessary condition fails because H_n does not tend to zero; alternation cannot rescue the endpoint.

hintTree.content: For fixed n, set j=n-k and factor the common sign out of the coefficient sum.
At x=±1, inspect the actual nth term involving H_n before applying any convergence test.

CALC2:010430.canonicalSolution:
For $|x|<1$,
$$\ln(1+x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k x^k,
\qquad\frac1{1+x}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-1)^j x^j.$$
Their absolutely convergent Cauchy product has, for $n\ge1$, coefficient
$$\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k(-1)^{n-k}
=(-1)^{n+1}\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k=(-1)^{n+1}H_n.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\frac{\ln(1+x)}{1+x}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}H_nx^n}\qquad(|x|<1).$$
Since $H_n^{1/n}\to1$, the radius is $R=1$. At $x=1$, the terms are $(-1)^{n+1}H_n$, which do not tend to zero. At $x=-1$, they are $-H_n$, which also do not tend to zero. Both endpoint series diverge. Hence the interval is
$$\boxed{(-1,1)}.$$
The pointwise function's behavior outside this interval does not replace endpoint testing of its Maclaurin series.

graderFixtures.proofText: The x^n Cauchy coefficient is sum_(k=1)^n (-1)^(k+1)(-1)^(n-k)/k=(-1)^(n+1)H_n. Thus G=sum (-1)^(n+1)H_n x^n with R=1. At x=1 terms are ±H_n and at x=-1 terms are -H_n, so both diverge.
I cancel all signs in the Cauchy coefficient and report H_n instead of (-1)^(n+1)H_n, which already gives the wrong coefficient of x^2.
I include x=1 by calling the series alternating, even though its term magnitudes H_n grow and fail to approach zero.

CALC2:010431.title: Turn an odd geometric series into a certified logarithm
CALC2:010431.objective: Derive the inverse-hyperbolic-tangent series from a geometric series, classify both endpoints, specialize it to a rapidly convergent logarithm series, and track indexing in a rigorous remainder certificate.
CALC2:010431.statement:
Starting from a geometric series, derive
$$\operatorname{artanh}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}$$
as a power series. Find its radius and test both endpoints directly. Then set $x=1/3$ to obtain a series for $\ln2$. If
$$S_N=2\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{1}{(2n+1)3^{2n+1}},$$
derive an explicit upper bound for $R_N=\ln2-S_N$ and find the least $N\ge0$ for which the error is below $10^{-6}$. Keep the first omitted exponent and denominator explicit.
permittedResults: For $|x|<1$, $1/(1-x^2)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^{2n}$ uniformly on compact subintervals, so integration from zero is termwise valid.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the even geometric series and bound the positive omitted terms geometrically.
An exact integral remainder is acceptable if it produces an equally explicit bound and proves minimality under the same S_N indexing.

milestones.criterion: Derives the artanh series and tests both endpoints directly.
Specializes x=1/3 with the correct factor and indexing.
Derives the geometric remainder bound and proves the least N is 5.

commonErrors.description: Uses exponent 2N+1 or denominator 2N+1 for the first term omitted from S_N.
commonErrors.consequence: Those belong to the last included term; the tail starts at n=N+1 with 2N+3.

commonErrors.description: Includes x=1 or x=-1 because the original rational derivative is considered away from the opposite endpoint.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual endpoint series has odd-harmonic terms and fails to converge.

hintTree.content: Integrate sum t^(2n) from 0 to x and keep the denominator 2n+1.
At x=±1, the terms form the positive or negative odd harmonic series.
For the remainder after n=N, replace every denominator by the first omitted one 2N+3 and sum a geometric tail of ratio 1/9.

CALC2:010431.canonicalSolution:
For $|t|<1$,
$$\frac1{1-t^2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^{2n}.$$
Integrating from $0$ to $x$ gives
$$\boxed{\operatorname{artanh}x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}},\qquad |x|<1.$$
The radius is $1$. At $x=1$ the odd harmonic series diverges, and at $x=-1$ its negative diverges, so the interval of convergence is $(-1,1)$.

Since $\operatorname{artanh}(1/3)=\frac12\ln2$,
$$\ln2=2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac1{(2n+1)3^{2n+1}}.$$
All terms are positive. For the tail after $n=N$, the first omitted index is $n=N+1$, with denominator $2N+3$ and exponent $2N+3$. Therefore
$$0<R_N\le\frac{2}{2N+3}\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}3^{-(2n+1)}
=\boxed{\frac{9}{4(2N+3)3^{2N+3}}}.$$
For $N=4$ this bound is about $1.15\times10^{-6}$, and the first omitted term alone is $2/(11\cdot3^{11})>10^{-6}$, so $N=4$ does not work. For $N=5$ the bound is about $1.09\times10^{-7}$. Hence the least index is
$$\boxed{N=5}.$$
This conclusion depends on the stated convention that $S_N$ includes terms $n=0$ through $n=N$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integrating 1/(1-t^2)=sum t^(2n) gives artanh x=sum x^(2n+1)/(2n+1), R=1, with both endpoints divergent. At x=1/3, ln2=2sum 1/[(2n+1)3^(2n+1)]. The first omitted data are 2N+3, and R_N<=9/[4(2N+3)3^(2N+3)], giving least N=5.
Because S_N ends at n=N, I say the first omitted term has denominator and exponent 2N+1, and my error bound is shifted by one term.
I include x=1 in the interval because 1/(1-x^2) only has a simple formula there by a limiting argument, ignoring divergence of the odd harmonic endpoint series.

CALC2:010432.title: Integrate a sine series whose phase has no elementary antiderivative
CALC2:010432.objective: Derive an entire power series for a Fresnel-type integral, prove its radius from coefficient growth, and use the alternating-series theorem with explicit inclusive indexing to certify a numerical value.
CALC2:010432.statement:
Define
$$F(x)=\int_0^x\sin(t^2)\,dt.$$
Derive the Maclaurin series for $F$ and prove that its radius of convergence is infinite. For
$$T_N=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{(-1)^n}{(2n+1)!(4n+3)},$$
use the alternating-series theorem to find the least $N\ge0$ for which that theorem certifies $|F(1)-T_N|<10^{-7}$. Give the resulting numerical approximation and keep the first omitted factorial and linear factor explicit.
permittedResults: The sine series converges absolutely for every complex input and uniformly on every bounded real interval, so substituting $t^2$ and integrating term by term is valid.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use uniform convergence of the entire sine series and the alternating remainder theorem at x=1.
Taylor's theorem applied directly to sin(t^2) is acceptable if it yields the same integrated coefficients and explicit first omitted bound.

milestones.criterion: Substitutes into the sine series and integrates to the correct coefficients.
Proves infinite radius using a ratio or equivalent factorial-growth argument.
Uses inclusive indexing to obtain the correct alternating bound, least N, and approximation.

commonErrors.description: Writes x^(4n+1) or divides by 4n+1 after integrating t^(4n+2).
commonErrors.consequence: The antiderivative of t^(4n+2) has exponent and divisor 4n+3.

commonErrors.description: Uses (2N+1)!(4N+3) as the error after T_N.
commonErrors.consequence: Those factors belong to the last included term; the first omitted term has (2N+3)!(4N+7).

hintTree.content: Substitute t^2 into sin z=sum (-1)^n z^(2n+1)/(2n+1)! before integrating.
The power after integration is 4n+3, not 4n+1.
After T_N the first omitted magnitude is 1/[(2N+3)!(4N+7)].

CALC2:010432.canonicalSolution:
Substituting $z=t^2$ into the sine series gives
$$\sin(t^2)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nt^{4n+2}}{(2n+1)!}.$$
Uniform convergence on bounded intervals permits integration, so
$$\boxed{F(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{(-1)^nx^{4n+3}}{(2n+1)!(4n+3)}}.$$
For any fixed $x$, the ratio of consecutive absolute terms tends to zero because the denominator gains the factors $(2n+2)(2n+3)$ while the numerator gains only $x^4$ and a bounded rational factor. Thus the radius is infinite.

At $x=1$, the positive magnitudes decrease to zero. Since $T_N$ includes $n=0,\ldots,N$, the first omitted term is $n=N+1$ and
$$|F(1)-T_N|\le\boxed{\frac1{(2N+3)!(4N+7)}}.$$
For $N=3$ this is $1/(9!\cdot19)\approx1.45\times10^{-7}$, so the alternating-series bound does not yet certify the target. For $N=4$ it is
$$\frac1{11!\cdot23}\approx1.09\times10^{-9}<10^{-7}.$$
Therefore the least index certified by this theorem is $\boxed{N=4}$. The approximation is
$$T_4=\frac13-\frac1{42}+\frac1{1320}-\frac1{75600}+\frac1{6894720}
\approx\boxed{0.310268303},$$
with the stated error below $10^{-7}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: sin(t^2)=sum (-1)^n t^(4n+2)/(2n+1)!, hence F=sum (-1)^n x^(4n+3)/[(2n+1)!(4n+3)] with infinite radius. After T_N the alternating bound is 1/[(2N+3)!(4N+7)]; it first certifies 10^-7 at N=4, giving T_4 about 0.310268303.
I integrate t^(4n+2) as x^(4n+1)/(4n+1), so every Fresnel-series coefficient is shifted.
My error estimate after T_N repeats the last included denominator (2N+1)!(4N+3) instead of the first omitted one.

CALC2:010442.title: Make a logarithm decide only one endpoint
CALC2:010442.objective: Determine a shifted power series' radius and full interval of convergence, distinguishing an absolute interior from one conditional and one divergent endpoint.
CALC2:010442.statement:
Determine the radius and exact interval of convergence of
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{(x-1)^n}{2^n n\ln n}.$$
Test both endpoints separately and classify every included endpoint as absolute or conditional. A ratio or root computation alone is not a complete answer.
permittedResults: The positive series $\sum_{n\ge2}1/(n\ln n)$ diverges, while $1/(n\ln n)$ decreases to zero, so its alternating version converges. For every $0\le r<1$, $\sum r^n/(n\ln n)$ converges absolutely.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the root test for the radius, then the integral and alternating-series tests at the endpoints.
Compare absolute terms to a geometric series in the interior, then audit the two boundary series directly.

milestones.criterion: Uses a valid root or ratio argument to obtain |x-1|<2 and radius 2.
Separately proves divergence at x=3 and conditional convergence at x=-1.
States [-1,3) and accurately labels the absolute and conditional regions.

commonErrors.description: Includes x=3 because it lies at the computed radius without testing the endpoint series.
commonErrors.consequence: At x=3 the series is sum 1/(n ln n), which diverges.

commonErrors.description: Calls convergence at x=-1 absolute after using only alternation.
commonErrors.consequence: The absolute series is sum 1/(n ln n), so the included left endpoint is only conditional.

hintTree.content: Apply the root test to the absolute term and use (n ln n)^(1/n) -> 1.
The boundary equation |x-1|=2 gives two different values of x; substitute each before choosing a test.
At x=3 the signs are positive, while at x=-1 the factor (x-1)^n/2^n is (-1)^n.

CALC2:010442.canonicalSolution:
For the absolute term,
$$\sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{(x-1)^n}{2^n n\ln n}\right|}
=\frac{|x-1|}{2(n\ln n)^{1/n}}\longrightarrow\frac{|x-1|}{2}.$$
Thus the series converges absolutely when $|x-1|<2$ and diverges when
$|x-1|>2$, so its radius is $\boxed{R=2}$.

At the right endpoint $x=3$, the series becomes
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac1{n\ln n},$$
which diverges, for example by the integral test. At the left endpoint
$x=-1$, it becomes
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n\ln n}.$$
The magnitudes decrease to zero, so the alternating-series test gives
convergence. Absolute convergence there would require the divergent positive
series just encountered, so convergence at $x=-1$ is conditional. Therefore
the exact interval is
$$\boxed{[-1,3)},$$
with absolute convergence on $(-1,3)$ and conditional convergence only at
$x=-1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The root limit is |x-1|/2, so R=2. At x=3 the series is sum 1/(n ln n) and diverges. At x=-1 it is alternating with decreasing magnitudes tending to zero, but its absolute series diverges. Hence the interval is [-1,3), conditional only at -1.
I get R=2 and immediately report [-1,3], never noticing that x=3 gives the divergent logarithmic harmonic series.
At x=-1 the signs alternate, so I call the series absolutely convergent without testing the magnitudes 1/(n ln n).
