CALC2:010443.title: Square a logarithm before auditing its asymmetric endpoints
CALC2:010443.objective: Derive a genuinely new harmonic-number coefficient identity by squaring a logarithmic series, prove different behavior at the two boundary points, and evaluate a nontrivial interior sum exactly.
CALC2:010443.statement:
Starting from the Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+x)$,
    use a Cauchy product to prove that
    $$[\ln(1+x)]^2
    =\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{2(-1)^nH_{n-1}}n x^n,
    \qquad H_m=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k,$$
    for $|x|<1$. Your derivation must simplify the finite convolution rather
    than merely quote the displayed coefficient. Determine the radius and full
    interval of convergence, classifying every included endpoint as absolute
    or conditional. Finally, evaluate
    $$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{2(-1)^nH_{n-1}}{n2^n}$$
    exactly.
permittedResults: Inside a common disk of absolute convergence, power series may be multiplied by the Cauchy rule. Also $H_m\le1+\ln m$, so $H_m/m\to0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Square the logarithmic series, simplify its finite convolution by partial fractions, and then test the two endpoints directly.
Derive the same coefficient identity from a parameterized convolution or integral, provided the finite coefficient and both endpoint tests are still explicit.

milestones.criterion: Derives 2(-1)^n H_(n-1)/n from the finite Cauchy convolution.
Obtains radius one and proves conditional convergence at x=1 but divergence at x=-1.
Substitutes x=1/2 and evaluates the requested sum as [ln(3/2)]^2.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the convolution sum by H_(n-1)/n and loses the factor 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The coefficient already fails at n=2, so the derived series and exact value are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims x=-1 is alternating and x=1 is positive by ignoring the existing coefficient sign (-1)^n.
commonErrors.consequence: This reverses the half-open interval; x=1 is conditional and x=-1 diverges.

hintTree.content: For n at least 2, collect the products whose exponents are k and n-k, with 1<=k<=n-1.
Use 1/[k(n-k)]=(1/n)(1/k+1/(n-k)) to simplify the coefficient, then analyze 2H_(n-1)/n at x=1 and x=-1.
The requested sum is the derived power series evaluated at the interior point x=1/2.

CALC2:010443.canonicalSolution:
For $|x|<1$ the logarithmic series is absolutely
    convergent, so its square is given by the Cauchy product
    $$\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k x^k\right)^2.$$
    For $n\ge2$, the coefficient of $x^n$ is
    $$\begin{aligned}
    \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k
      \frac{(-1)^{n-k+1}}{n-k}
    &=(-1)^n\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac1{k(n-k)}\\
    &=\frac{(-1)^n}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}
      \left(\frac1k+\frac1{n-k}\right)\\
    &=\frac{2(-1)^nH_{n-1}}n.
    \end{aligned}$$
    This proves the stated identity on $|x|<1$.

    Since $H_{n-1}$ grows subexponentially,
    $[2H_{n-1}/n]^{1/n}\to1$, so the radius is $\boxed{R=1}$. At $x=1$ the
    series is alternating with magnitude $b_n=2H_{n-1}/n$. The bound
    $H_{n-1}\le1+\ln(n-1)$ gives $b_n\to0$, and
    $$\frac{H_n}{n+1}<\frac{H_{n-1}}n\qquad(n\ge3)$$
    because this inequality is equivalent to $1<H_{n-1}$. Thus the series at
    $x=1$ converges by the alternating-series test. Its absolute series
    diverges because $2H_{n-1}/n\ge2/n$, so this endpoint is conditional.

    At $x=-1$, the factor $(-1)^nx^n$ equals $1$, leaving the positive series
    $\sum 2H_{n-1}/n$, which diverges by the same harmonic comparison. Hence
    the full interval is $\boxed{(-1,1]}$, with absolute convergence on
    $(-1,1)$ and conditional convergence only at $x=1$.

    Finally $x=1/2$ is an interior point, so direct substitution gives
    $$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{2(-1)^nH_{n-1}}{n2^n}
    =\boxed{\left(\ln\frac32\right)^2}.$$
    This evaluation uses the interior identity and needs no endpoint theorem.

graderFixtures.proofText: The x^n coefficient is (-1)^n sum_(k=1)^(n-1)1/[k(n-k)]=2(-1)^nH_(n-1)/n. Its radius is one. At x=1 the decreasing magnitudes tend to zero but their positive sum dominates the harmonic series, so convergence is conditional; x=-1 removes all signs and diverges. At x=1/2 the sum is [ln(3/2)]^2.
I use 1/[k(n-k)]=(1/n)(1/k) and get only (-1)^nH_(n-1)/n, omitting the symmetric second term and its factor 2.
At x=-1 I call the series alternating and include that endpoint, forgetting that (-1)^n from the coefficient times (-1)^n from x^n makes every term positive.

CALC2:010445.title: Trap the cosine fixed point with one-sided Taylor bounds
CALC2:010445.objective: Use rigorous alternating Taylor bounds rather than calculator values to isolate a transcendental root and certify a midpoint approximation.
CALC2:010445.statement:
Let $r$ be the solution in $[0,1]$ of
$$\cos r=r.$$
Using alternating Taylor bounds for cosine, prove
$$0.739<r<0.740.$$
You must give explicit one-sided polynomial estimates that certify the two
signs; unsupported decimal values of cosine do not count. Also prove that the
solution in $[0,1]$ is unique and show that $0.7395$ approximates $r$ with
absolute error less than $0.0005$.
permittedResults:
For $0\le x\le1$, the alternating cosine series has decreasing term magnitudes and gives
$$1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{24}-\frac{x^6}{720}\le\cos x\le1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{24}.$$

acceptableStrategies.description: Use alternating-series truncation bounds of opposite parity at the two endpoints.
Use Taylor's theorem with a signed remainder or a sufficiently sharp absolute remainder, provided both endpoint signs are rigorously certified.

milestones.criterion: Uses correctly oriented alternating Taylor bounds to prove f(0.739)>0 and f(0.740)<0.
Applies continuity and strict decrease to prove existence and uniqueness of the root in [0,1].
Derives |r-0.7395|<0.0005 from the certified bracket.

commonErrors.description: Uses the polynomial ending in -x^6/720 as an upper bound, or the one ending in +x^4/24 as a lower bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign certificates no longer follow because the alternating truncation inequalities are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Reports calculator values of cos(0.739) and cos(0.740) without bounding approximation error.
commonErrors.consequence: Uncertified rounded decimals cannot prove the strict signs required for the root bracket.

hintTree.content: Apply the lower Taylor bound at x=0.739 and the upper Taylor bound at x=0.740 to f(x)=cos x-x.
For the lower estimate, use 0.739^2=0.546121, 0.739^4=0.298248146641, and the safe bound 0.739^6<0.165.
Once the root lies in an interval of width 0.001, compare it with that interval's midpoint.

CALC2:010445.canonicalSolution:
Set $f(x)=\cos x-x$. It is continuous on $[0,1]$.
The alternating cosine bounds on this interval give
$$1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{24}-\frac{x^6}{720}
\le\cos x\le
1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{24}.$$
At $x=0.739$, use
$x^2=0.546121$, $x^4=0.298248146641$, and $x^6<0.165$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
f(0.739)&\ge1-0.739-\frac{0.546121}{2}
+\frac{0.298248146641}{24}-\frac{0.165}{720}\\
&>0.000137>0.
\end{aligned}$$
This is a lower bound, so it certifies the positive sign. At $x=0.740$,
$x^2=0.5476$ and $x^4=0.29986576$, so the upper Taylor bound gives
$$\begin{aligned}
f(0.740)&\le1-0.740-\frac{0.5476}{2}
+\frac{0.29986576}{24}\\
&=-0.00130559\ldots<0.
\end{aligned}$$
The intermediate value theorem therefore supplies a root
$r\in(0.739,0.740)$. Moreover,
$$f'(x)=-\sin x-1<0\qquad(0\le x\le1),$$
so $f$ is strictly decreasing there and the root is unique.

The midpoint of the certified interval is $0.7395$, and every point strictly
inside that interval is less than half its width from the midpoint. Hence
$$\boxed{|r-0.7395|<\frac{0.740-0.739}{2}=0.0005}.$$
No floating-point evaluation of cosine is needed.

graderFixtures.proofText: For f=cos x-x, the alternating lower polynomial through -x^6/720 is positive at 0.739, while the upper polynomial through +x^4/24 is negative at 0.740. IVT gives a root between them; f'=-sin x-1<0 makes it unique. The midpoint error is below half the 0.001 interval width, namely 0.0005.
I treat 1-x^2/2+x^4/24-x^6/720 as an upper bound for cosine and use it to claim the sign at 0.739, reversing the alternating inequality.
My calculator prints cos(0.739)>0.739 and cos(0.740)<0.740, so I declare the result proved without any rounding or Taylor remainder control.

CALC2:010446.title: Let the parameter flip a logarithmic interval
CALC2:010446.objective: Track how a signed scale reverses the endpoint behavior of a logarithmic power series and solve exactly when the origin remains in its convergence set.
CALC2:010446.statement:
For a real parameter $a$, consider
$$F_a(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{[a(x-1)]^n}{n}.$$
(a) For $a>0$ and $a<0$, determine the radius and full interval of convergence,
testing both endpoints and classifying them as absolute, conditional, or
divergent. Treat $a=0$ separately.

(b) Determine exactly for which $a$ the series converges at $x=0$. In every
convergent parameter case, classify convergence at $x=0$ and find the sum in
closed form. Treat the boundary values of $a$ separately.
permittedResults: For $|z|<1$, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^n/n=-\ln(1-z)$. At $z=-1$ the alternating harmonic series converges conditionally to $-\ln2$, while at $z=1$ the harmonic series diverges.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce to z=a(x-1), audit z=-1 and z=1, then map the endpoints back separately for each sign of a.
Analyze sum (-a)^n/n directly at x=0 and reconcile its parameter set with the translated full interval.

milestones.criterion: Finds R=1/|a| and correctly maps z=-1 and z=1 to x-endpoints for both signs of a, including a=0.
Uses z=-a at x=0 to obtain exactly -1<a<=1, with both boundary parameters checked.
Classifies absolute versus conditional convergence at x=0 and evaluates the sum as -ln(1+a).

commonErrors.description: Uses the a>0 half-open interval when a<0 without reversing which endpoint is included.
commonErrors.consequence: For negative a, z=-1 occurs at the right x-endpoint, so the correct interval is open-left and closed-right.

commonErrors.description: Reports only |a|<1 for convergence at x=0 and omits the a=1 boundary case.
commonErrors.consequence: At a=1 the origin is the included left endpoint and the series converges conditionally to -ln2.

hintTree.content: Apply the ratio or root test with z=a(x-1); for a nonzero parameter, solve |x-1|<1/|a|.
The z=-1 endpoint is conditional and the z=1 endpoint diverges; identify their x-order separately for a>0 and a<0.
Inside the radius substitute z=-a into -ln(1-z); the conditional boundary a=1 has the same value by the alternating harmonic identity.

CALC2:010446.canonicalSolution:
Put $z=a(x-1)$. The root test gives
$$\sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{z^n}{n}\right|}=\frac{|z|}{n^{1/n}}
\longrightarrow |z|.$$
For $a\ne0$, the radius as a power series centered at $1$ is
$\boxed{R=1/|a|}$. The value $z=-1$ gives the conditionally convergent series
$\sum(-1)^n/n$, while $z=1$ gives the divergent harmonic series.

If $a>0$, then $z=-1$ occurs at $x=1-1/a$ and $z=1$ at $x=1+1/a$; hence
$$\boxed{[1-1/a,\,1+1/a)}\qquad(a>0).$$
If $a<0$, multiplication by $a$ reverses the endpoint order: $z=1$ occurs
at the left endpoint $x=1+1/a$, and $z=-1$ at the right endpoint
$x=1-1/a$. Hence
$$\boxed{(1+1/a,\,1-1/a]}\qquad(a<0).$$
In both cases convergence is absolute in the open interior and conditional
only at the included endpoint. If $a=0$, every term is zero, so the series
converges absolutely for every real $x$ (equivalently, its radius is infinite).

At $x=0$, convergence is equivalent to
$$-a\in[-1,1),$$
that is, $a\le1$ and $a>-1$. Therefore
$$\boxed{-1<a\le1}.$$
If $-1<a<1$, then $|-a|<1$ and convergence is absolute. The logarithmic
identity gives
$$F_a(0)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-a)^n}{n}
=\boxed{-\ln(1+a)}.$$
At $a=1$, this is the conditionally convergent alternating harmonic series
$\sum(-1)^n/n=-\ln2$, agreeing with the same formula. At $a=-1$, the terms
are $1/n$ and the series diverges; this explains why the lower parameter
inequality is strict while the upper one is not.

graderFixtures.proofText: With z=a(x-1), R=1/|a| for a nonzero. Since z=-1 is conditional and z=1 diverges, the interval is [1-1/a,1+1/a) for a>0 and (1+1/a,1-1/a] for a<0; a=0 gives the zero series. At x=0, z=-a, so convergence is exactly -1<a<=1 and the sum is -ln(1+a).
For a<0 I copy the a>0 endpoint brackets, forgetting that multiplying by a reverses which x-endpoint gives the alternating z=-1 series.
At x=0 I solve |a|<1 and stop, so I miss a=1 even though it produces the convergent alternating harmonic series.

CALC2:010517.title: Stop the separable solution at its first blow-up
CALC2:010517.objective: Solve and verify a separable initial-value problem, then determine the maximal interval containing the initial point by locating the nearest singularities of the explicit solution.
CALC2:010517.statement:
Solve the initial-value problem
\[
y'=x(1+y^2),\qquad y(0)=0.
\]
Derive an explicit formula, verify it by differentiation and the initial condition, and find the maximal open interval containing $0$ on which this IVP solution is finite and differentiable. Explain why the antiderivative equation does not justify calling the resulting tangent formula a global real-valued solution.
permittedResults: The tangent function is finite and differentiable between consecutive zeros of cosine, and $\frac{d}{du}\tan u=\sec^2u=1+\tan^2u$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve implicitly first, then impose the initial condition before applying the inverse tangent relation.
Audit the domain of the explicit elementary function after the algebraic solution is obtained.

milestones.criterion: Separates, integrates, and applies the initial condition correctly.
Verifies both the differential equation and initial value from the explicit formula.
Locates the first blow-ups and states the maximal IVP interval with a valid connectedness explanation.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that y equals x squared over two from arctangent y equals x squared over two.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse trigonometric step is incorrect and the proposed function fails the differential equation.

commonErrors.description: Calls the tangent formula a global solution on all real x despite its poles at plus and minus root pi nearest the initial point.
commonErrors.consequence: A solution cannot remain finite or differentiable through those singularities.

hintTree.content: Separate as $dy/(1+y^2)=x\,dx$.
Use the initial condition after obtaining $\arctan y=x^2/2+C$.
The nearest poles occur when $x^2/2=\pi/2$.

CALC2:010517.canonicalSolution:
Since $1+y^2>0$ for real $y$, separation is legal:
\[
\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=x\,dx.
\]
Integration gives
\[
\arctan y=\frac{x^2}{2}+C.
\]
The condition $y(0)=0$ implies $C=0$, hence
\[
\boxed{y(x)=\tan\!\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right)}.
\]
Differentiating wherever the formula is finite,
\[
y'(x)=x\sec^2\!\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right)
=x\left(1+\tan^2\!\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right)\right)
=x(1+y^2),
\]
and $y(0)=\tan0=0$.

The nearest poles to the initial point occur when
\[
\frac{x^2}{2}=\frac\pi2,
\]
that is, at $x=\pm\sqrt\pi$. The maximal interval containing $0$ is therefore
\[
\boxed{(-\sqrt\pi,\sqrt\pi)}.
\]
Although the implicit antiderivative is valid during the separation step, applying tangent produces a function with vertical blow-ups. Other branches between later tangent poles do not connect through those singularities to the initial condition, so they cannot enlarge this IVP interval into a global solution.

graderFixtures.proofText: Separation gives $\arctan y=x^2/2+C$, and $y(0)=0$ makes $C=0$, so $y=\tan(x^2/2)$. Its derivative is $x\sec^2(x^2/2)=x(1+y^2)$. The nearest poles satisfy $x^2/2=\pi/2$, so the maximal IVP interval is $(-\sqrt\pi,\sqrt\pi)$, not all of $\mathbb R$.
From $\arctan y=x^2/2$ I simply erase the arctangent and write $y=x^2/2$, which does not satisfy $y'=x(1+y^2)$.
I obtain $y=\tan(x^2/2)$ and declare it a global real-valued solution, ignoring its vertical blow-ups at $x=\pm\sqrt\pi$.

CALC2:010518.title: Carry the temperature continuously through an ambient switch
CALC2:010518.objective: Solve Newton cooling on two time stages, transfer the first-stage terminal temperature as the second initial value, and distinguish continuity of temperature from a jump in its derivative.
CALC2:010518.statement:
An object has temperature $80^\circ\mathrm C$ at $t=0$. For $0\le t<10$ minutes it is in a $20^\circ\mathrm C$ room. At $t=10$ it is moved instantly to a $5^\circ\mathrm C$ room. In each room it obeys Newton's law
\[
T'=-k(T-T_{\rm ambient}),\qquad k=\frac{\ln2}{10}\ \mathrm{min}^{-1}.
\]
Find a continuous piecewise formula for $T(t)$. Determine the first time it reaches $20^\circ\mathrm C$, and compute the left- and right-hand derivatives at $t=10$.
permittedResults: For constant $A$, every solution of $T'=-k(T-A)$ has the form $T(t)=A+Ce^{-kt}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Track excess above the current ambient separately on each stage.
Treat the switch value as a fresh initial condition while retaining absolute clock time in the final answer.

milestones.criterion: Solves the first stage and transfers its terminal temperature correctly.
Builds the continuous second-stage model and solves the target-temperature equation.
Computes both one-sided derivatives and explains why only the derivative jumps.

commonErrors.description: Starts the second stage with the original 80-degree temperature instead of the 50-degree switch value.
commonErrors.consequence: The piecewise temperature becomes discontinuous and every later value is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Continues using the 20-degree ambient law after t equals ten.
commonErrors.consequence: The model never reflects the move to the colder room and cannot reach the requested temperature at the stated finite time.

hintTree.content: On the first stage, use $T(t)=20+60e^{-kt}$.
Evaluate the first formula at $t=10$ and use that value, not $80$, to initialize the second stage.
After the switch solve $20=5+45e^{-k(t-10)}$ and evaluate $-k(T-A)$ from each side at $t=10$.

CALC2:010518.canonicalSolution:
In the first room, the initial excess above ambient is $80-20=60$, so
\[
T(t)=20+60e^{-kt},\qquad 0\le t<10.
\]
Because $e^{-10k}=e^{-\ln2}=1/2$, the temperature at the switch is
\[
T(10)=20+60\left(\frac12\right)=50.
\]
The second-room excess is therefore $50-5=45$, which gives the continuous piecewise model
\[
\boxed{
T(t)=
\begin{cases}
20+60e^{-kt},&0\le t<10,\\
5+45e^{-k(t-10)},&t\ge10.
\end{cases}}
\]
To find when the object first reaches $20^\circ\mathrm C$ after the move, solve
\[
20=5+45e^{-k(t-10)}.
\]
Thus $e^{-k(t-10)}=1/3$, and
\[
\boxed{t=10+\frac{\ln3}{k}
=10+\frac{10\ln3}{\ln2}\ \text{minutes}}
\approx25.8496\ \text{minutes}.
\]
The temperature is continuous at the switch, but the ambient temperature jumps. Newton's law gives
\[
\boxed{T'(10^-)=-30k},
\qquad
\boxed{T'(10^+)=-45k}.
\]
Hence $T'$ has a downward jump even though $T$ itself does not jump.

graderFixtures.proofText: The first stage is $20+60e^{-kt}$ and gives $T(10)=50$. Thus the second is $5+45e^{-k(t-10)}$. Solving $20=5+45e^{-k(t-10)}$ gives $t=10+10\ln3/\ln2\approx25.8496$. Continuity holds, while $T'(10^-)=-30k$ and $T'(10^+)=-45k$.
At the room change I restart with $T(10)=80$, writing $5+75e^{-k(t-10)}$, so my two pieces disagree at $t=10$.
I keep the first formula $20+60e^{-kt}$ for every $t\ge0$, ignoring the new $5^\circ\mathrm C$ ambient temperature after ten minutes.

CALC2:010519.title: Solve the Euler iterates before measuring their error
CALC2:010519.objective: Solve a first-order linear initial-value problem exactly, derive and solve its fixed-step explicit Euler recurrence, and obtain an exact signed formula for every nodal discretization error.
CALC2:010519.statement:
Consider the linear initial-value problem and a fixed Euler grid
$$
y'=2x-y,\qquad y(0)=1,\qquad x_n=\frac n2.
$$
First solve the differential equation by an integrating factor. Then apply explicit Euler with step size $h=1/2$ and starting value $Y_0=1$: derive the recurrence for $Y_n$, solve that recurrence in closed form, and compare $Y_4$ with the exact value $y(2)$. Finally derive a closed formula for the nodal error $e_n=y(x_n)-Y_n$ and prove its sign for every integer $n\ge1$ without relying on decimal approximations.
permittedResults: An integrating factor converts a first-order linear equation into a product derivative; a constant-coefficient affine recurrence is solved by combining a particular sequence with its homogeneous geometric sequence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the differential equation and the affine difference equation independently, then subtract their closed forms.
Shift the Euler sequence by its affine particular solution so that the remaining recurrence is geometric.

milestones.criterion: Solves the continuous linear IVP exactly.
Derives and solves the explicit Euler recurrence with the stated step size.
Computes the exact nodal error and proves its sign for every positive node.

commonErrors.description: Uses the slope itself as the Euler increment and omits the step-size factor one half.
commonErrors.consequence: The recurrence, all iterates, and the error formula are then for a different numerical method.

commonErrors.description: Declares the Euler value above the exact solution or supports the sign only with rounded values at n equals four.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested all-node signed error conclusion has not been established.

hintTree.content: Multiplying by $e^x$ makes the left side $(e^xy)'$.
With $h=1/2$ and $x_n=n/2$, Euler gives $Y_{n+1}=\tfrac12Y_n+\tfrac n2$.
Try the affine particular sequence $n-2$, then use $Y_0=1$ to determine the geometric term.

CALC2:010519.canonicalSolution:
Writing the equation as $y'+y=2x$ and multiplying by $e^x$ gives
$$
(e^xy)'=2xe^x,\qquad y(x)=2x-2+Ce^{-x}.
$$
The initial value gives $C=3$, so the exact solution is $y(x)=2x-2+3e^{-x}$.

For explicit Euler, $2x_n=n$, and therefore
$$
Y_{n+1}=Y_n+\frac12(2x_n-Y_n)=\frac12Y_n+\frac n2,\qquad Y_0=1.
$$
The sequence $n-2$ is a particular solution of this recurrence, and the homogeneous recurrence contributes $C2^{-n}$. Applying $Y_0=1$ yields
$$
\boxed{Y_n=n-2+3\cdot2^{-n}}.
$$
At the grid point $x_4=2$ this gives
$$
Y_4=2+\frac3{16}=\frac{35}{16},\qquad y(2)=2+3e^{-2}.
$$
More generally, evaluating the exact solution at $x_n=n/2$ and subtracting the discrete formula gives
$$
\boxed{e_n=3\left(e^{-n/2}-2^{-n}\right)}.
$$
To determine the sign exactly, note that $\log2=\int_1^2dt/t>1/2$. Hence $e^{-1/2}>1/2$, so raising both positive quantities to the $n$th power proves $e^{-n/2}>2^{-n}$ for every $n\ge1$. Thus $e_n>0$: at each positive grid node the Euler value lies below the exact solution. In particular, the error at $x=2$ is $3(e^{-2}-1/16)>0$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The integrating factor gives $y=2x-2+3e^{-x}$. Euler gives $Y_{n+1}=Y_n/2+n/2$, whose solution is $Y_n=n-2+3\cdot2^{-n}$. Thus $Y_4=35/16$ and $e_n=3(e^{-n/2}-2^{-n})>0$ for $n\ge1$, since $\log2>1/2$.
Euler uses $Y_{n+1}=Y_n+(2x_n-Y_n)$, so I obtain a recurrence without multiplying the slope by the given step size one half.
At the fourth node my rounded Euler value looks a little larger, so I assert the error is negative for every n without deriving an exact error formula or proving its sign.

CALC2:010520.title: Read three equilibria from one autonomous phase line
CALC2:010520.objective: Analyze an autonomous cubic differential equation without solving it explicitly, classify all equilibria, use uniqueness as a no-crossing barrier, and determine long-time behavior for an entire interval of initial values.
CALC2:010520.statement:
Consider
$$
y'=y(y-1)(y-3).
$$
Find every equilibrium solution and draw the phase-line sign pattern. Classify each equilibrium as stable or unstable. Use uniqueness at every relevant equilibrium to prove that the intervals $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are invariant, and determine the limit as $t\to\infty$ for initial data in either interval.
permittedResults: For a continuously differentiable autonomous vector field, local uniqueness prevents a non-equilibrium solution from crossing an equilibrium solution.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the sign chart and monotone convergence rather than separating and integrating.
Treat equilibrium solutions as uniqueness barriers and identify the only possible limiting equilibrium.

milestones.criterion: Builds the correct phase line and stability classification.
Uses uniqueness to justify equilibrium barriers.
Proves the long-time limit for every initial value between zero and three.

commonErrors.description: Calls zero and three stable and one unstable after reversing the phase arrows.
commonErrors.consequence: The qualitative dynamics and all long-time conclusions are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Allows a nonconstant solution to pass through an equilibrium while retaining the same differentiable autonomous equation.
commonErrors.consequence: This violates uniqueness for the polynomial vector field.

hintTree.content: Make a sign chart on $(-\infty,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,3)$, and $(3,\infty)$.
Arrows point away from zero and three but toward one on both sides.
A bounded monotone solution has a limit, and any finite limit must be an equilibrium.

CALC2:010520.canonicalSolution:
The equilibria are the constant solutions $y\equiv0$, $y\equiv1$, and $y\equiv3$. The sign of $F(y)=y(y-1)(y-3)$ is
$$
F<0\text{ on }(-\infty,0),\quad
F>0\text{ on }(0,1),\quad
F<0\text{ on }(1,3),\quad
F>0\text{ on }(3,\infty).
$$
Thus arrows point away from $0$, toward $1$, and away from $3$: zero and three are unstable, while one is stable.

Because $F$ is a polynomial, uniqueness holds. If a nonconstant solution met $0$ or $3$, uniqueness at that meeting point would force it to coincide locally, hence globally on overlap, with the corresponding equilibrium; this contradicts its initial value. The identical uniqueness argument at the equilibrium $y=1$ shows that a solution starting strictly below or strictly above $1$ cannot meet or cross that level either. Consequently both $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are invariant.

If $0<y(0)<1$, then $y'>0$, so the solution increases and is bounded above by $1$. If $1<y(0)<3$, then $y'<0$, so it decreases and is bounded below by $1$. In either case it has a finite limit $L$. If $F(L)\ne0$, continuity would keep the derivative bounded away from zero eventually, contradicting convergence. Hence $F(L)=0$. The invariant subinterval leaves only
$$
\boxed{L=1}.
$$
The equilibrium initial value $y(0)=1$ is already constant.

graderFixtures.proofText: The signs are negative, positive, negative, positive across the four intervals, so zero and three repel and one attracts. Polynomial uniqueness at zero, one, and three makes every equilibrium level a barrier, so $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are invariant. Solutions in the first interval increase and those in the second decrease, each bounded by one, so the limit is one.
I reverse every arrow, label zero and three stable, and say solutions between zero and three move away from one.
I let a trajectory starting between zero and one cross y equals one and later cross y equals three, without addressing uniqueness at either equilibrium.

CALC2:010521.title: Cross a parabola family at right angles
CALC2:010521.objective: Eliminate a family parameter from its differential equation, replace its slope by the negative reciprocal on a controlled domain, and identify and verify one orthogonal trajectory.
CALC2:010521.statement:
In the first quadrant $x>0$, $y>0$, consider the one-parameter family of parabolas
$$
y=Cx^2,\qquad C>0.
$$
Find the family of orthogonal trajectories in this quadrant. Then find the member of the orthogonal family through $(2,1)$, identify the original parabola through that same point, and verify orthogonality there using the two slopes (or tangent vectors). State why the first-quadrant restriction makes the negative-reciprocal step legitimate.
permittedResults: For y=Cx^2 with C constant, y'=2Cx=2y/x; in the first quadrant x and y are nonzero, so its negative reciprocal is defined.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert the parameterized family into a differential equation before changing to the perpendicular slope.
Verify orthogonality numerically at the requested point after solving the separated equation.

milestones.criterion: Eliminates C to obtain the original family slope y'=2y/x.
Solves the orthogonal equation y'=-x/(2y) to obtain x^2+2y^2=K.
Uses (2,1) to get K=6 and verifies slopes 1 and -1 for perpendicular crossing.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates C as C'(x) even though C labels a fixed parabola in the family.
commonErrors.consequence: The result is not the slope field of y=Cx^2 and blocks correct parameter elimination.

commonErrors.description: Uses y'=2y/x again for the requested trajectories instead of -x/(2y).
commonErrors.consequence: This reproduces the original parabola family rather than curves that cross it at right angles.

hintTree.content: Differentiate y=Cx^2 while treating C as a constant, then eliminate C using y=Cx^2.
Replace 2y/x by its negative reciprocal before separating variables.
Choose the integration constant through (2,1), then compare the original and new slopes at that point.

CALC2:010521.canonicalSolution:
Along any one original parabola, $C$ is constant. Differentiation and elimination of $C=y/x^2$ give
$$
y'=2Cx=\frac{2y}{x}.
$$
In the first quadrant this slope is finite and nonzero. A perpendicular tangent therefore has negative-reciprocal slope, so the orthogonal family satisfies
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{2y}.
$$
Separating and integrating,
$$
2y\,dy=-x\,dx,
\qquad
y^2=-\frac{x^2}{2}+K_0.
$$
Equivalently, the orthogonal trajectories are the first-quadrant arcs
$$
\boxed{x^2+2y^2=K},\qquad K>0.
$$
The member through $(2,1)$ has $K=2^2+2(1)^2=6$, hence
$$
\boxed{x^2+2y^2=6}
$$
on its first-quadrant arc. The original parabola through $(2,1)$ has $C=1/4$, so its slope there is $2y/x=1$. The orthogonal trajectory has slope $-x/(2y)=-1$. Their product is $-1$; equivalently, tangent vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ have dot product zero. Positivity of $x$ and $y$ prevents division by zero and keeps both slopes finite at every point under discussion.

graderFixtures.proofText: For y=Cx^2, elimination of C gives y'=2y/x. Orthogonal slopes are therefore -x/(2y), so separation yields x^2+2y^2=K. The member through (2,1) has K=6; the original parabola has C=1/4, and the two slopes there are 1 and -1.
I differentiate y=Cx^2 as y'=C'x^2+2Cx, treating the family label C as a function of x, so I never obtain the family slope 2y/x.
I reuse y'=2y/x for the requested trajectories and obtain the same parabolas again, instead of taking the negative reciprocal slope -x/(2y).

CALC2:010522.title: Infer a cooling constant from two temperatures
CALC2:010522.objective: Solve a first-order linear model, determine its positive physical parameter from data, and make a later temperature prediction with units and sign conditions intact.
CALC2:010522.statement: A cup is in a room held at $20^\circ\mathrm C$ and obeys Newton's law $T'=-k(T-20)$. It has $T(0)=90$ and $T(10)=60$, where time is in minutes. Find $k$ exactly and express $T(25)$ exactly. Explain why the chosen value of $k$ is positive.
permittedResults: If 0<e^{-10k}=4/7<1, then k=ln(7/4)/10 is positive, consistent with decay toward the ambient temperature.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the homogeneous equation for the excess temperature u=T-20.
Use the 10-minute ratio of excess temperatures to predict the 25-minute value without decimal rounding.

milestones.criterion: Solves for T(t)=20+70e^{-kt} after shifting by the ambient temperature.
Derives k=ln(7/4)/10 and explains why it is positive.
Computes T(25)=20+70(4/7)^(5/2) degrees C exactly.

commonErrors.description: Models the data with T'=-kT and T=90e^{-kt}, omitting the 20-degree ambient temperature.
commonErrors.consequence: That model decays toward zero instead of the room temperature and fails the differential equation given.
This makes k negative, implying growth away from ambient despite a decreasing temperature difference.

hintTree.content: Shift the dependent variable by the 20-degree ambient temperature before solving the differential equation.
Use T(0)=90 to determine the coefficient of e^{-kt}, then use T(10)=60 to solve the exponential equation.
Rewrite e^{-25k} from e^{-10k}=4/7 and attach degrees Celsius to the prediction.

CALC2:010522.canonicalSolution:
Set $u=T-20$. Then $u'=-ku$, so $u(t)=Ce^{-kt}$ and the initial condition gives $C=70$. Hence
$$
T(t)=20+70e^{-kt}.
$$
Using $T(10)=60$ gives $40=70e^{-10k}$, so $e^{-10k}=4/7$ and
$$
k=\frac1{10}\ln\frac74>0.
$$
The positivity is forced because $7/4>1$: the temperature difference decays rather than grows. At twenty-five minutes,
$$
T(25)=20+70e^{-(5/2)\ln(7/4)}
=\boxed{20+70(4/7)^{5/2}}\ ^\circ\mathrm C.
$$
Keeping the ambient shift $T-20$ is what makes the exponential law apply to the temperature difference rather than to $T$ itself.

graderFixtures.proofText: I solve T'=-kT and write T=90e^(-kt), losing the ambient 20-degree shift and failing the room-temperature equilibrium.
I solve e^(-10k)=4/7 as k=ln(4/7)/10, which is negative even though the observed temperature difference decays.

CALC2:010523.title: Keep a tank volume constant while its salt approaches equilibrium
CALC2:010523.objective: Derive a constant-volume mixing differential equation from independent inflow and outflow rates, solve the initial-value problem exactly, and use monotonicity to identify a unique first threshold time with units.
CALC2:010523.statement:
A well-stirred tank initially contains $100$ liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.5$ grams of salt per liter enters at $3$ liters per minute, and the mixture leaves at the same rate. Let $A(t)$ be the grams of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes.

Derive the differential equation and initial condition for $A$. Solve for $A(t)$ exactly, identify the limiting salt amount, and find the first time at which the tank contains $40$ grams of salt. Explain why that time is unique and attach units to the parameter and answer.
permittedResults: Equal volume flow rates keep the volume at $100$ L, so the outgoing concentration is $A(t)/100$ grams per liter at every time.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the affine linear ODE by shifting to the equilibrium amount.
Use an integrating factor e^(0.03t), then solve the threshold equation and inspect the derivative sign.

milestones.criterion: Derives A'=1.5-0.03A with A(0)=0 from the two physical rates and constant volume.
Solves A(t)=50(1-e^(-3t/100)) and identifies the 50-gram equilibrium.
Finds (100/3)ln5 minutes and proves uniqueness from strict increase below equilibrium.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts 3A or a fixed 1.5 from the inflow without using the outgoing concentration A/100.
commonErrors.consequence: The units and model are wrong, so the equilibrium and every predicted amount change materially.

commonErrors.description: Lets the tank volume grow or shrink even though the inflow and outflow are both 3 liters per minute.
commonErrors.consequence: The outgoing concentration and resulting differential equation no longer describe the stated constant-volume tank.

hintTree.content: Compute grams per minute entering and leaving before writing the ODE.
The equation has equilibrium 50 grams; solve it as A'=0.03(50-A) with A(0)=0.
Set the exact solution equal to 40 and solve for the exponential; monotonicity follows from A'>0 below equilibrium.

CALC2:010523.canonicalSolution:
The incoming salt rate is
$$
(0.5\ \mathrm{g/L})(3\ \mathrm{L/min})=1.5\ \mathrm{g/min}.
$$
Because the volume remains $100$ L, the outgoing concentration is $A/100$ g/L and the outgoing salt rate is $3A/100=0.03A$ g/min. Hence
$$
A'=1.5-0.03A,
\qquad A(0)=0.
$$
The equilibrium is $A=50$, and solving the linear equation gives
$$
A(t)=50+Ce^{-0.03t}.
$$
The initial condition yields $C=-50$, so
$$
\boxed{A(t)=50(1-e^{-3t/100})\ \mathrm g}.
$$
Thus $A(t)\to50$ g. To reach $40$ g,
$$
40=50(1-e^{-3t/100})
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e^{-3t/100}=\frac15.
$$
Therefore the first-passage time is
$$
\boxed{t=\frac{100}{3}\ln5\ \mathrm{min}}.
$$
For every finite $t\ge0$, $A(t)<50$, so $A'=0.03(50-A)>0$. The amount is strictly increasing, which makes this threshold time unique.

graderFixtures.proofText: The input is 0.5*3=1.5 g/min and the output is (A/100)*3=0.03A, so A'=1.5-0.03A, A(0)=0. Thus A=50(1-e^(-3t/100)); A=40 first at t=(100/3)ln5 minutes, uniquely because A increases toward 50.
I write the outflow as 3A grams per minute, forgetting to divide the current amount by the 100-liter volume to obtain concentration, and my solution decays toward the wrong equilibrium.
I use a volume 100+3t because brine enters, but I ignore the simultaneous equal three-liter-per-minute outflow, so my changing-volume concentration does not match the tank described.

CALC2:010524.title: Square a positive solution to linearize its equation
CALC2:010524.objective: Reduce a nonlinear initial-value problem to a linear equation through a square substitution, recover the branch forced by the initial value, and establish the maximal real interval by proving the radicand stays positive.
CALC2:010524.statement:
Solve the initial-value problem
$$
y'+y=\frac{e^x}{y},
\qquad y(0)=1,
$$
under the requirement that the solution be real and differentiable wherever stated. Use $z=y^2$ to derive and solve a linear initial-value problem. Then recover $y$, verify the original equation, and determine the maximal interval containing $0$. Explain why the positive square-root branch is forced and why no zero of $y$ interrupts the interval.
permittedResults: A continuous real solution of an equation containing $1/y$ cannot cross $y=0$; its sign is fixed on any interval of existence.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply by y and use z=y^2 to obtain an ordinary first-order linear equation.
Recognize the equation as Bernoulli-type, make the equivalent square substitution, and audit sign after solving.

milestones.criterion: Transforms the equation to z'+2z=2e^x with z(0)=1.
Solves z=(2e^x+e^(-2x))/3 and selects the positive square root from the initial value.
Verifies the original equation and proves the maximal interval is all real numbers because z stays positive.

commonErrors.description: Uses z'=yy' rather than z'=2yy' when z=y^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed linear equation has incorrect coefficients and produces a function that fails the original ODE.

commonErrors.description: Reports both plus and minus square roots as solutions despite the initial condition y(0)=1.
commonErrors.consequence: The negative branch has y(0)=-1 and the ambiguous plus-or-minus expression is not a single differentiable IVP solution.

hintTree.content: Multiply the equation by y before setting z=y^2, and keep the factor z'=2yy'.
Solve z'+2z=2e^x with z(0)=1 using the integrating factor e^(2x).
Show the resulting z is strictly positive for every real x before taking the branch selected by y(0)=1.

CALC2:010524.canonicalSolution:
Multiplying by $y$ gives
$$
yy'+y^2=e^x.
$$
Set $z=y^2$, so $z'=2yy'$. Then
$$
\frac12z'+z=e^x,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
z'+2z=2e^x,
$$
with $z(0)=1$. The integrating factor is $e^{2x}$, so
$$
(e^{2x}z)'=2e^{3x}.
$$
Integration gives
$$
z=\frac23e^x+Ce^{-2x}.
$$
Using $z(0)=1$ yields $C=1/3$, hence
$$
y^2=z=\frac{2e^x+e^{-2x}}{3}.
$$
Both terms in the numerator are positive for every real $x$, so $z>0$ on all of $\mathbb R$. Since $y(0)=1>0$ and a solution cannot pass through zero, the required branch is
$$
\boxed{y(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2e^x+e^{-2x}}{3}}}.
$$
Differentiating $y^2=z$ gives $2yy'=z'=2e^x-2z$, hence $yy'=e^x-y^2$. Division by the everywhere-positive $y$ recovers $y'+y=e^x/y$. Thus the maximal interval containing $0$ is
$$
\boxed{(-\infty,\infty)}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: Multiplying by y and setting z=y^2 gives z'+2z=2e^x, z(0)=1. Thus z=(2e^x+e^(-2x))/3>0 for all x, so y is the positive square root. It verifies the ODE and exists on all real x.
I set z=y^2 but write z'=yy', obtaining z'+z=e^x; the missing factor two changes the linear equation and my recovered function does not satisfy the original differential equation.
After finding y^2=(2e^x+e^(-2x))/3, I report y=plus or minus the square root, even though the minus branch gives y(0)=-1 and violates the initial condition.

CALC2:010525.title: Recover an implicit integral curve and certify its local graph
CALC2:010525.objective: Verify that a differential equation is exact, reconstruct its potential without double-counting terms, impose an initial condition, and use the implicit-function condition to justify a local solution slope.
CALC2:010525.statement:
Solve the initial-value problem in implicit form:
$$
(2xy+1)\,dx+(x^2+\cos y)\,dy=0,
\qquad y(0)=0.
$$
Verify exactness, construct a potential $F(x,y)$, and determine the level constant. Then show that the level curve defines $y$ as a differentiable function of $x$ near $(0,0)$ and compute $y'(0)$ both from the differential equation and from your implicit answer.
permittedResults: If $F(x_0,y_0)=C$ and $F_y(x_0,y_0)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem gives a unique differentiable local graph $y(x)$ with slope $y'=-F_x/F_y$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate M with respect to x, determine the missing y-function from N, and apply the implicit function theorem.
Integrate N with respect to y first and recover the missing x-function from M; then perform the same level and slope checks.

milestones.criterion: Verifies exactness through M_y=N_x=2x and reconstructs the potential correctly.
Applies the initial condition to obtain x^2y+x+sin y=0.
Uses F_y(0,0)!=0 to justify a local graph and computes the consistent slope -1 in two ways.

commonErrors.description: Integrates M and N separately and adds both x^2y contributions to the potential.
commonErrors.consequence: A potential must match both partial derivatives; double-counting makes F_x and F_y differ from the original coefficients.

commonErrors.description: Claims the implicit level equation defines one global function y(x) because it passes through the initial point.
commonErrors.consequence: Only the local nonvanishing condition F_y(0,0)=1 has been established; global single-valuedness does not follow.

hintTree.content: Check M_y and N_x before integrating either component.
Integrate M=2xy+1 with respect to x, then determine the remaining function of y by matching N.
Evaluate F_y and -F_x/F_y at (0,0), and compare with solving M+Ny'=0 there.

CALC2:010525.canonicalSolution:
Here
$$M(x,y)=2xy+1,\qquad N(x,y)=x^2+\cos y,$$
and
$$M_y=2x=N_x,$$
so the equation is exact on $\mathbb R^2$. Integrating $F_x=M$ with respect to $x$ gives
$$
F(x,y)=x^2y+x+g(y).
$$
Matching $F_y=x^2+g'(y)$ with $N$ yields $g'(y)=\cos y$, so we may take $g(y)=\sin y$. Thus the integral curves satisfy
$$
x^2y+x+\sin y=C.
$$
The initial point gives $C=0$, and the implicit solution is
$$
\boxed{x^2y+x+\sin y=0}.
$$
At $(0,0)$,
$$F_y=x^2+\cos y=1\ne0,$$
so the implicit function theorem gives a differentiable local graph $y(x)$. Its slope is
$$
y'(0)=-\frac{F_x(0,0)}{F_y(0,0)}=-\frac{1}{1}=\boxed{-1}.
$$
Directly, $M+Ny'=0$ at the initial point becomes $1+y'(0)=0$, confirming the same value.

graderFixtures.proofText: M_y=N_x=2x. Integrating M gives F=x^2y+x+g(y), and matching N gives g=sin y. The initial level is F=0. Since F_y(0,0)=1, a local graph exists and y'(0)=-F_x/F_y=-1, also from M+Ny'=0.
I integrate both components and add x^2y twice, obtaining a potential whose partial derivatives no longer equal M and N.
The level curve goes through (0,0), so I declare it a single differentiable graph for every x without checking F_y or any global behavior.

CALC2:010526.title: Keep the maximal interval when dividing a linear equation
CALC2:010526.objective: Solve a first-order linear initial-value problem with a singular coefficient, determine its integration constant, verify the result in the undivided equation, and identify the maximal interval containing the initial point.
CALC2:010526.statement:
Solve
$$
xy'+2y=x^2,
\qquad y(1)=3.
$$
Use an integrating factor on an interval where the standard linear form is valid. Give the explicit solution, verify it in the original undivided equation, and state the maximal interval on which this IVP solution is defined. Explain specifically why the formula cannot be continued as a finite differentiable solution through $x=0$.
permittedResults: On $x>0$, dividing by $x$ gives $y'+(2/x)y=x$ with integrating factor $\mu(x)=e^{\int2/x\,dx}=x^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use standard linear form and an integrating factor on the positive coefficient interval.
Recognize directly that multiplying the undivided equation by x makes its left side (x^2y)', then use the initial condition and domain analysis.

milestones.criterion: Restricts to x>0, obtains integrating factor x^2, and integrates (x^2y)'=x^3.
Uses the initial condition to derive y=x^2/4+11/(4x^2) and verifies it.
Identifies (0,infinity) as the maximal interval and explains blow-up at zero.

commonErrors.description: Computes the integrating factor as x^{-2} instead of x^2 after integrating 2/x.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting product derivative does not equal the transformed left side and produces the wrong solution family.

commonErrors.description: Reports the maximal interval as all x not equal to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: That set is disconnected; the IVP at x=1 belongs only to its positive component, and the solution blows up at the separating point.

hintTree.content: Because the initial point is positive, work first on x>0 before dividing by x.
After multiplying by x^2, recognize (x^2 y)'=x^3 and integrate.
Use y(1)=3 to find C, then inspect both the original coefficient x and the C/x^2 term as x approaches zero from the right.

CALC2:010526.canonicalSolution:
The initial point lies in $x>0$. On that interval, division by $x$ gives
$$
y'+\frac{2}{x} y=x.
$$
An integrating factor is $\mu(x)=x^2$, and multiplication yields
$$
x^2y'+2xy=x^3,
\qquad
(x^2y)'=x^3.
$$
Therefore
$$
x^2y=\frac{x^4}{4}+C,
\qquad
y=\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{C}{x^2}.
$$
The condition $y(1)=3$ gives $3=1/4+C$, so $C=11/4$ and
$$
\boxed{y(x)=\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{11}{4x^2}}.
$$
Differentiating and substituting into the original equation gives
$$
xy'+2y=x\left(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{11}{2x^3}\right)
+2\left(\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{11}{4x^2}\right)=x^2,
$$
as required for $x\ne0$. The largest connected coefficient domain containing $1$ is $(0,\infty)$. Moreover $y(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\downarrow0$ because of $11/(4x^2)$, so this particular solution has no finite differentiable continuation through zero. Thus its maximal IVP interval is $\boxed{(0,\infty)}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: On x>0, y'+2y/x=x and mu=x^2, so (x^2y)'=x^3. Hence y=x^2/4+C/x^2, and y(1)=3 gives C=11/4. Direct substitution yields x^2. The maximal connected interval containing 1 is (0,infinity), with blow-up at 0.
I integrate 2/x but choose mu=x^-2, so my alleged product derivative does not reproduce y'+2y/x.
I state the maximal interval is (-infinity,0) union (0,infinity), even though an IVP interval must be connected and contain x=1.

CALC2:010527.title: Connect a logistic formula to its phase line and clock
CALC2:010527.objective: Solve a logistic initial-value problem, analyze both equilibrium solutions and their stability, prove monotone approach for the given trajectory, and compute its inflection time and a later first-passage time exactly.
CALC2:010527.statement:
A population $P(t)$ satisfies
$$
P'=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{500}\right),\qquad P(0)=50,
$$
where $t$ is measured in years.
(a) Find and classify all nonnegative equilibria.
(b) Solve the IVP and prove that this solution increases toward its limiting population.
(c) Find the time and population at the inflection point.
(d) Find the first time at which $P=400$. Give both times exactly and explain why each requested time is unique.
permittedResults: For the autonomous equation $P'=f(P)$, an equilibrium is locally stable when nearby phase-line arrows point toward it and unstable when they point away; for $r,K>0$, logistic data in $(0,K)$ produce a unique increasing solution that remains in that interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use phase-line signs for qualitative dynamics and separation of variables for the exact logistic trajectory.
The substitution Q=1/P converts the IVP to a linear equation; after solving it, use P'' or the logistic midpoint property for the event times.

milestones.criterion: Finds P=0 unstable and P=500 asymptotically stable from the signs of the autonomous field.
Derives P=500/(1+9e^(-0.4t)) and proves it increases to 500.
Obtains the unique inflection (5ln3,250) and first P=400 time 5ln6, with units.

commonErrors.description: Calls P=0 stable because it is an equilibrium without inspecting the positive vector field immediately to its right.
commonErrors.consequence: Small positive populations move away from zero, so the stated phase-line classification and qualitative dynamics are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses P=500/(1+e^(-0.4t)), the special solution starting at 250, instead of fitting the constant to P(0)=50.
commonErrors.consequence: The formula violates the initial condition and consequently gives both requested event times incorrectly.

hintTree.content: Factor the right side to find P=0 and P=500, then inspect its sign on the intervals separated by those levels.
Separate variables or use the standard logistic form P=K/(1+A e^(-rt)); determine A from P(0)=50.
Set the denominator equal to 2 for the inflection level 250 and equal to 5/4 for the threshold 400.

CALC2:010527.canonicalSolution:
The autonomous right side
$$f(P)=0.4P(1-P/500)$$
vanishes at $P=0$ and $P=500$. It is positive on $(0,500)$ and negative for $P>500$. Thus $P=0$ is unstable on the nonnegative phase line, while $P=500$ is asymptotically stable.

The separated logistic solution has the form
$$
P(t)=\frac{500}{1+A e^{-0.4t}}.
$$
The initial condition gives $50=500/(1+A)$, so $A=9$ and
$$
\boxed{P(t)=\frac{500}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}}.
$$
Its denominator decreases from $10$ toward $1$, so $P$ increases from $50$ toward $500$. Equivalently, the phase line gives $P'>0$ while the solution remains in $(0,500)$.

For a logistic trajectory,
$$
P''=0.4P'\left(1-\frac{2P}{500}\right),
$$
so its unique inflection occurs at $P=250$. In the explicit solution,
$$
250=\frac{500}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
9e^{-0.4t}=1,
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{t_{\mathrm{infl}}=5\ln3\ \text{years}},\qquad \boxed{P=250}.
$$
For $P=400$,
$$
1+9e^{-0.4t}=\frac54,\qquad e^{-0.4t}=\frac1{36},
$$
so the first threshold time is
$$
\boxed{t_{400}=5\ln6\ \text{years}}.
$$
Both times are unique because the IVP solution is strictly increasing.

graderFixtures.proofText: The phase line makes P=0 unstable and P=500 stable. Fitting P(0)=50 gives P=500/(1+9e^(-0.4t)), strictly increasing to 500. P=250 occurs at t=5ln3 and the unique first P=400 hit is t=5ln6 years.
I label P=0 stable merely because the derivative vanishes there, even though f(P)>0 for every small positive P and the phase-line arrows point away from zero.
I use the memorized formula 500/(1+e^(-0.4t)) without fitting its constant, so it starts at 250 instead of 50 and produces the wrong inflection and threshold times.

CALC2:010528.title: Keep both singular barriers after a ratio substitution
CALC2:010528.objective: Solve a first-order initial-value problem by the homogeneous ratio substitution, recover the explicit solution with the correct logarithm branch, verify it directly, and identify the connected maximal interval imposed by two different obstructions.
CALC2:010528.statement:
Solve the initial-value problem
$$
y'=\frac yx+x e^{y/x},\qquad y(1)=0.
$$
Use $v=y/x$ and show every algebraic step in the reduced equation. Recover $y(x)$, verify it in the original differential equation and initial condition, and determine the maximal real interval containing $x=1$. Explain separately why neither endpoint of that interval can be included.
permittedResults: An IVP solution must live on a connected interval containing its initial point on which the differential equation is defined and the recovered real expression remains finite.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the ratio substitution, separate the reduced equation, and impose the initial condition before choosing the logarithm branch.
One may set w=e^{-y/x} and differentiate it directly; the resulting linear relation w=2-x must still be translated back and domain-audited.

milestones.criterion: Performs v=y/x with the product rule and reduces the equation to v'=e^v.
Uses v(1)=0 to derive y=-x ln(2-x) and verifies the original equation.
Identifies maximal interval (0,2) and explains the separate barriers at x=0 and x=2.

commonErrors.description: Sets y=xv but writes y'=xv', omitting the product-rule term v.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced equation is then wrong, so its separation and recovered solution cannot satisfy the original IVP.

commonErrors.description: Reports the maximal interval as (-infinity,2) because the explicit logarithm is real there.
commonErrors.consequence: The original differential equation contains y/x and is undefined at x=0; an IVP interval containing 1 cannot cross that singular point.

hintTree.content: With y=xv, substitute y'=v+xv' and y/x=v; the v terms cancel and leave v'=e^v.
Integrate e^(-v)dv=dx and use v(1)=0 to obtain e^(-v)=2-x before taking logarithms.
The original equation excludes x=0, while the logarithm requires 2-x>0; choose the connected component containing 1 and verify the formula there.

CALC2:010528.canonicalSolution:
Set $v=y/x$, so $y=xv$ and
$$y'=v+xv'.$$
Substitution into the differential equation gives
$$
v+xv'=v+x e^v.
$$
On an interval where $x\ne0$, cancellation and division by $x$ yield
$$v'=e^v.$$
Separating gives $e^{-v}dv=dx$, hence
$$-e^{-v}=x+C.$$
The condition $y(1)=0$ means $v(1)=0$, so $-1=1+C$ and $C=-2$. Therefore
$$
e^{-v}=2-x,\qquad
v=-\ln(2-x),
$$
and the solution is
$$
\boxed{y(x)=-x\ln(2-x)}.
$$

Direct differentiation gives
$$
y'=-\ln(2-x)+\frac{x}{2-x}.
$$
On the other hand,
$$
\frac yx+x e^{y/x}
=-\ln(2-x)+x e^{-\ln(2-x)}
=-\ln(2-x)+\frac{x}{2-x},
$$
and $y(1)=0$, so both the equation and initial value are verified.

The logarithm requires $x<2$, and the original vector field contains $y/x$, so it is undefined at $x=0$. The connected component of these conditions containing $1$ is
$$
\boxed{(0,2)}.
$$
At $x=2$ the logarithm blows up, while at $x=0$ the differential equation itself is undefined even though the formula for $y$ has a finite limiting value. Neither endpoint can be appended.

graderFixtures.proofText: With y=xv, y'=v+xv' and cancellation gives v'=e^v. The IVP yields e^(-v)=2-x, so y=-x ln(2-x); substitution gives y'=-ln(2-x)+x/(2-x). The maximal interval containing 1 is (0,2).
After setting y=xv I write y'=xv' and omit the product-rule v term, so I reduce to an equation that does not reproduce the given right-hand side.
Because ln(2-x) is real for every x<2, I claim (-infinity,2) is the maximal interval and cross x=0 even though y/x makes the original ODE undefined there.

CALC2:010529.title: Find the harvest threshold before solving a surviving branch
CALC2:010529.objective: Analyze a harvested logistic equation across its saddle-node threshold, classify every nonnegative equilibrium by phase-line signs, and solve a selected subcritical initial-value problem with an exact first-passage time.
CALC2:010529.statement:
Consider
$$P'=P(1-P)-h,\qquad P\ge0,\quad h\ge0.$$
(a) Determine for which $h$ there are two, one, or no nonnegative equilibria and classify their stability, including the threshold case.
(b) For $h=3/16$ and $P(0)=1/2$, solve the IVP exactly, find its limiting population, and find the first time $P=2/3$.
permittedResults: For $P'=f(P)$, simple equilibria are stable when arrows point inward and unstable when arrows point outward; a repeated equilibrium must be classified from signs on its two sides rather than by the simple-root rule.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the phase line before separation, then partial fractions for the subcritical IVP.
A Riccati-to-linear fractional substitution is acceptable if the threshold, semistability, and fitted IVP constant are all explicit.

milestones.criterion: Derives the equilibrium discriminant and classifies every h regime, including h=0 and semistable h=1/4.
Factors and separates the h=3/16 IVP with the correct ratio constant.
Obtains the explicit solution, stable limit 3/4, and unique time 2ln5.

commonErrors.description: Sets the saddle-node threshold at h=1/2 by reading the midpoint as the parameter value.
commonErrors.consequence: The maximum of P(1-P) is 1/4, so the number of equilibria and all subsequent classifications are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Calls the h=1/4 equilibrium asymptotically stable from both sides.
commonErrors.consequence: The field is negative on both sides: solutions above approach it, while solutions below move away, making it semistable.

hintTree.content: Complete the square in P(1-P)-h or inspect the discriminant of P^2-P+h.
At h=3/16 factor P' as -(P-1/4)(P-3/4).
After separation, fit the ratio (P-3/4)/(P-1/4) to the initial value before solving for P.

CALC2:010529.canonicalSolution:
Equilibria solve $P^2-P+h=0$, so
$$P_\pm=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4h}}2.$$
For $0<h<1/4$, both are positive. Since
$$P'=-(P-P_-)(P-P_+),$$
the field is negative below $P_-$, positive between the roots, and negative above $P_+$. Thus $P_-$ is unstable and $P_+$ is asymptotically stable. At $h=0$, the equilibria are $0$ (unstable on the nonnegative phase line) and $1$ (stable). At $h=1/4$, the sole equilibrium $P=1/2$ is semistable: $P'=-(P-1/2)^2\le0$, so trajectories approach it from above and move away below. For $h>1/4$ there is no equilibrium and the field is negative everywhere.

For $h=3/16$, $P_-=1/4$ and $P_+=3/4$. Separation gives
$$\ln\left|\frac{P-3/4}{P-1/4}\right|=-\frac t2+C.$$
At $P(0)=1/2$, the ratio is $-1$, so
$$\frac{P-3/4}{P-1/4}=-e^{-t/2},\qquad
\boxed{P(t)=\frac{3+e^{-t/2}}{4(1+e^{-t/2})}}.$$
This solution increases toward the stable limit $3/4$. Setting $P=2/3$ gives $e^{-t/2}=1/5$, hence the unique first hit is
$$\boxed{t=2\ln5}.$$
Uniqueness follows from strict increase while $1/4<P<3/4$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The discriminant gives threshold h=1/4. For 0<h<1/4, P_- is unstable and P_+ stable; at h=1/4, P=1/2 is semistable. For h=3/16 and P(0)=1/2, (P-3/4)/(P-1/4)=-e^(-t/2), so P=(3+e^(-t/2))/(4(1+e^(-t/2))), limit 3/4, and P=2/3 at 2ln5.
I claim the two equilibria merge when h=1/2, confusing the equilibrium population 1/2 with the maximum harvest value 1/4.
At h=1/4 I call P=1/2 stable from both sides, ignoring that P'=-(P-1/2)^2 is negative below as well as above it.

CALC2:010530.title: Keep the zero solution when separation divides it away
CALC2:010530.objective: Exhibit and verify the complete forward family of solutions to a non-Lipschitz initial-value problem, explain the mechanism of delayed departure, and identify exactly why routine separation misses valid solutions.
CALC2:010530.statement:
On $t\ge0$, solve the initial-value problem
$$y'=3y^{2/3},\qquad y(0)=0,$$
where $y^{2/3}=(\sqrt[3]y)^2$. Find all $C^1$ forward solutions, verify the joining points, and explain why dividing by $y^{2/3}$ loses solutions and why the usual uniqueness theorem does not apply.
permittedResults: Picard-Lindelof uniqueness near an initial point requires local Lipschitz control in y; the derivative of $3y^{2/3}$ with respect to y is unbounded at y=0.

acceptableStrategies.description: Construct the delayed family and use monotonicity of every solution to prove completeness.
Transform through the real cube root only on connected positive components, then recover the allowed equilibrium waiting interval.

milestones.criterion: Constructs every delayed cubic solution including the perpetual zero solution.
Checks the ODE and C1 joining at t=c.
Proves completeness using monotonicity/separation and explains both lost division and uniqueness-theorem failure.

commonErrors.description: Reports only y=t^3 after dividing by y^(2/3).
commonErrors.consequence: The division excludes y=0 and misses infinitely many delayed solutions, including the equilibrium solution.

commonErrors.description: Joins zero to a shifted linear or quadratic branch whose derivative does not satisfy the ODE at departure.
commonErrors.consequence: A valid solution must be C1 and must match both value and zero derivative at the waiting-time endpoint.

hintTree.content: Away from y=0, set u=cuberoot(y); separation gives u=t-C.
For any c>=0, join y=0 before c to (t-c)^3 after c and check both one-sided derivatives at c.
Use monotonicity y'>=0 to show any solution's zero set is an initial interval, completing the family.

CALC2:010530.canonicalSolution:
For every $c\in[0,\infty)$ define
$$y_c(t)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le t\le c,\\(t-c)^3,&t\ge c.\end{cases}$$
Also allow $c=\infty$, meaning $y_\infty\equiv0$. For $t<c$ both sides of the ODE are zero. For $t>c$,
$$y_c'=3(t-c)^2=3[(t-c)^3]^{2/3}.$$
At $t=c$, both the function and derivative join at zero, so every $y_c$ is $C^1$ and satisfies the IVP.

These are all forward solutions. Since $y'=3y^{2/3}\ge0$, a solution is nondecreasing. Its zero set containing $0$ is therefore an initial interval $[0,c]$ (possibly all of $[0,\infty)$). On any later interval where $y>0$, separation gives
$$3y^{-2/3}dy=9dt,$$
or $y^{1/3}=t-c$, and hence $y=(t-c)^3$. Dividing by $y^{2/3}$ at the outset assumes $y\ne0$ and discards the arbitrary zero interval. Finally, $f_y(y)=2y^{-1/3}$ is unbounded at zero, so the standard local-Lipschitz uniqueness hypothesis fails.

graderFixtures.proofText: All forward solutions are y_c=0 on [0,c] and (t-c)^3 afterward, for c>=0, plus c=infinity for y=0 forever. Values and derivatives join at zero. Monotonicity makes the zero set initial, separation on y>0 proves completeness; dividing by y^(2/3) loses the waiting interval and f_y is unbounded at zero.
I divide by y^(2/3) immediately and report only y=t^3, thereby excluding the zero solution and every delayed departure y_c.
I join y=0 to y=(t-c)^2 after c; its derivative and 3y^(2/3) do not match near the joining point, so the piecewise function is not a solution.

CALC2:010531.title: Linearize Gompertz growth in the logarithmic distance from capacity
CALC2:010531.objective: Solve a positive Gompertz initial-value problem by a logarithmic substitution, analyze stability and concavity from the transformed variable, and compute exact inflection and first-passage times.
CALC2:010531.statement:
Let $r,K>0$ and consider the positive-population model
$$P'=rP\ln\frac KP,qquad P(0)=Ke^{-2}.$$
Solve the IVP for $t\ge0$ using $u=\ln(K/P)$. Prove that $K$ is asymptotically stable within the positive state space, find the limiting population, locate the inflection point and its time, and find the first time at which $P=K/2$.
permittedResults: For an autonomous scalar equation, the sign of the vector field on each side of an equilibrium determines local attraction; concavity along a solution follows from differentiating the differential equation.

acceptableStrategies.description: Linearize with u=ln(K/P), then read stability and event levels in u.
Direct separation is acceptable if it preserves positivity and independently derives the phase-line and concavity claims.

milestones.criterion: Performs the logarithmic substitution and solves the exact IVP.
Uses the phase-line sign to establish positive-state stability and the limit K.
Derives concavity and both exact event times with uniqueness.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Gompertz solution by a logistic rational exponential such as K/(1+Ce^(-rt)).
commonErrors.consequence: That formula solves a different per-capita growth law and does not satisfy u'=-ru.

commonErrors.description: Calls P=K/2 the inflection level by analogy with logistic growth.
commonErrors.consequence: For Gompertz growth P'' changes sign at u=1, hence P=K/e, not K/2.

hintTree.content: Differentiate u=ln K-ln P and substitute P'/P.
With u(0)=2, solve u'=-ru before returning to P.
Use P''=r^2 P u(u-1), and set u=ln 2 for the K/2 passage.

CALC2:010531.canonicalSolution:
Let $u=\ln(K/P)$. Since $P>0$,
$$u'=-\frac{P'}P=-r\ln\frac KP=-ru,qquad u(0)=2.$$
Thus $u(t)=2e^{-rt}$ and
$$\boxed{P(t)=K\exp(-2e^{-rt})}.$$
This remains positive and satisfies the initial value. If $0<P<K$, then $\ln(K/P)>0$ and $P'>0$; if $P>K$, then $P'<0$. Hence $P=K$ attracts positive states from both sides, and the displayed solution tends to $\boxed K$.

Because $P'=rPu$ and $u'=-ru$,
$$P''=r(P'u+Pu')=r^2Pu(u-1).$$
For this solution $u$ decreases from $2$ to $0$, so concavity changes exactly when $u=1$, equivalently $P=K/e$. The inflection time is
$$2e^{-rt}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{t_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{\ln2}{r}}.$$
For $P=K/2$, the transformed variable is $u=\ln2$, so
$$2e^{-rt}=\ln2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{t_{1/2}=\frac1r\ln\left(\frac2{\ln2}\right)}.$$
Strict increase below $K$ makes this the unique first passage.

graderFixtures.proofText: u=ln(K/P) obeys u'=-ru with u(0)=2, so P=K exp(-2e^(-rt)) and tends monotonically to stable K. Since P''=r^2 P u(u-1), inflection occurs at u=1, P=K/e, t=ln2/r. P=K/2 occurs at t=ln(2/ln2)/r.
I recognize growth toward K and insert the logistic formula K/(1+e^(-rt)), without checking the logarithmic per-capita rate.
Like the logistic model, I declare the Gompertz curve inflects at K/2 and use that as the inflection time.

CALC2:010532.title: Reach terminal speed through a hyperbolic tangent, not an exponential
CALC2:010532.objective: Solve the quadratic-drag falling-body equation, integrate velocity to obtain distance, identify terminal speed and time scale, and compute exact time and distance to a prescribed speed fraction.
CALC2:010532.statement:
Take downward as positive. A body released from rest obeys
$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-cv^2,qquad v(0)=0,$$
where $m,g,c>0$. Solve for $v(t)$ and the downward distance $s(t)$ with $s(0)=0$. Identify the terminal speed and a natural inverse-time scale. Then find the exact time and distance at which the body first reaches $90\%$ of terminal speed. Audit the physical dimensions of every logarithm argument and scale.
permittedResults: For $|z|<1$, $\int dz/(1-z^2)=\operatorname{artanh}z$ and $\int\tanh(\alpha t)dt=\alpha^{-1}\ln\cosh(\alpha t)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Normalize by terminal speed and integrate with artanh.
A direct exponential-fraction form equivalent to tanh is acceptable if the initial condition, terminal limit, distance, and event values are all correct.

milestones.criterion: Separates the velocity equation and obtains the tanh solution with correct scales.
Integrates velocity to the log-cosh distance formula.
Computes the exact 90-percent event values and verifies dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Uses v=V(1-e^(-kt)) as though the drag force were proportional to v.
commonErrors.consequence: The model contains cv squared, whose separated solution is hyperbolic tangent, not a single exponential.

commonErrors.description: Writes the distance as a logarithm of sinh(alpha t).
commonErrors.consequence: That expression is singular at release and differentiates to coth rather than the required tanh velocity.

hintTree.content: Set V=sqrt(mg/c) so the equation becomes v'=g(1-v^2/V^2).
The inverse-time scale is alpha=sqrt(gc/m)=g/V.
Use cosh(artanh q)=1/sqrt(1-q^2) when converting a speed fraction q into distance.

CALC2:010532.canonicalSolution:
Balancing $mg=cv^2$ gives terminal speed
$$V=\sqrt{\frac{mg}{c}},$$
and define
$$\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{gc}{m}}=\frac gV.$$
Then $v'=g(1-v^2/V^2)$. Separation with $v(0)=0$ gives
$$\operatorname{artanh}(v/V)=\alpha t,$$
so
$$\boxed{v(t)=V\tanh(\alpha t)}.$$
Integrating once more,
$$s(t)=\frac V\alpha\ln\cosh(\alpha t)
=\boxed{\frac mc\ln\cosh(\alpha t)}.$$

For a fraction $q\in(0,1)$ of terminal speed,
$$t_q=\frac1\alpha\operatorname{artanh}q,qquad
s_q=\frac mc\ln\cosh(\operatorname{artanh}q)
=-\frac m{2c}\ln(1-q^2).$$
At $q=0.9=9/10$,
$$\boxed{t_{90}=\frac1{2\alpha}\ln19},\qquad
\boxed{s_{90}=\frac m{2c}\ln\frac{100}{19}}.$$
The arguments of tanh, cosh, and logarithms are dimensionless. Since $c$ has units mass/length for a $cv^2$ force, $m/c$ has units of length; $\alpha$ has units inverse time and $V$ has units length/time.

graderFixtures.proofText: With V=sqrt(mg/c) and alpha=sqrt(gc/m), separation gives v=V tanh(alpha t). Thus s=(m/c)ln cosh(alpha t). At q=0.9, t=ln19/(2alpha) and s=(m/(2c))ln(100/19); all transcendental arguments are dimensionless.
I treat cv^2 as linear drag and use the exponential approach v=V(1-e^(-kt)), which does not satisfy the quadratic-drag equation.
I integrate tanh(alpha t) as ln sinh(alpha t), producing an infinite negative distance at t=0 and derivative coth instead of tanh.

CALC2:010617.title: Prove a twisted cubic crosses the plane only once
CALC2:010617.objective: Solve and certify a unique space-curve plane intersection, construct its tangent line, and compute the acute line-plane angle using the normal-component convention.
CALC2:010617.statement:
The space curve
\[
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2,t^3\rangle
\]
meets the plane $x+y+z=3$. Find every real intersection parameter and prove there are no others. At the intersection, write a vector equation of the tangent line. Then find the acute angle $\phi$ between that tangent line and the plane, clearly distinguishing it from the angle between the tangent direction and the plane's normal.
permittedResults: If $\alpha$ is the acute angle between a direction $\mathbf v$ and a normal $\mathbf n$, then the acute line-plane angle is $\phi=\pi/2-\alpha$ and $\sin\phi=|\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n|/(\|\mathbf v\|\|\mathbf n\|)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the geometric intersection to a polynomial and certify all of its real roots.
Compute the normal component of the tangent direction to obtain the sine of the line-plane angle.

milestones.criterion: Finds the real intersection and proves uniqueness rather than stopping after one root.
Computes the tangent direction and writes the line through the correct point.
Uses the correct line-plane angle convention and reports an exact angle expression.

commonErrors.description: Finds t equal to one by inspection but never rules out the remaining roots of the cubic.
commonErrors.consequence: The request for every real intersection has not been justified.

commonErrors.description: Uses arccos of six over root forty-two as the line-plane angle without taking the complement.
commonErrors.consequence: That arccosine is the angle between the tangent direction and the plane normal, not the plane.

hintTree.content: Substitution into the plane gives $t^3+t^2+t-3=0$.
Factor the cubic as $(t-1)(t^2+2t+3)$ and inspect the quadratic discriminant.
Use $\mathbf r'(1)=\langle1,2,3\rangle$ and plane normal $\langle1,1,1\rangle$.

CALC2:010617.canonicalSolution:
Substituting the curve into the plane equation gives
\[
t+t^2+t^3=3,
\]
or
\[
t^3+t^2+t-3=(t-1)(t^2+2t+3)=0.
\]
The quadratic factor has discriminant $2^2-4(1)(3)=-8<0$, so its roots are nonreal. Hence the unique real parameter is $t=1$, and the sole intersection point is
\[
\boxed{(1,1,1)}.
\]
The velocity is
\[
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle1,2t,3t^2\rangle,
\]
so a vector equation for the tangent line is
\[
\boxed{\boldsymbol\ell(u)=\langle1,1,1\rangle+u\langle1,2,3\rangle}.
\]
Let $\mathbf v=\langle1,2,3\rangle$ and let $\mathbf n=\langle1,1,1\rangle$ be a plane normal. The acute angle $\phi$ between the line and the plane satisfies
\[
\sin\phi
=\frac{|\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n|}{\|\mathbf v\|\|\mathbf n\|}
=\frac6{\sqrt{14}\sqrt3}
=\boxed{\frac6{\sqrt{42}}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\phi=\arcsin\!\left(\frac6{\sqrt{42}}\right)}
\approx67.79^\circ.
\]

The tangent is $\langle1,1,1\rangle+u\langle1,2,3\rangle$. With normal $\langle1,1,1\rangle$, $\sin\phi=6/\sqrt{42}$, so $\phi=\arcsin(6/\sqrt{42})$.
I notice that $t=1$ works and immediately call it the only intersection, without factoring the cubic or excluding other real roots.

CALC2:010618.title: Invert arc length past a zero-speed endpoint
CALC2:010618.objective: Compute and invert an arc-length function, write an explicit unit-speed reparameterization, and verify its interior and endpoint speeds without misusing the inverse-function chain rule where the original speed vanishes.
CALC2:010618.statement:
For $t\ge0$, let
\[
\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2,\frac23t^3,0\right\rangle.
\]
Measure arc length $s(t)$ from $t=0$, invert it to obtain $t=t(s)$, and write an explicit reparameterization $\mathbf R(s)=\mathbf r(t(s))$ for $s\ge0$. Prove that $\|\mathbf R'(s)\|=1$ for $s>0$. Because $\|\mathbf r'(0)\|=0$, analyze $s=0$ separately: state why the usual inverse-function chain-rule quotient is unavailable there and compute the one-sided derivative of the explicit $\mathbf R$.
permittedResults: For a regular curve with arc length $s(t)=\int_0^t\|\mathbf r'(u)\|du$, the interior reparameterization satisfies $d\mathbf r/ds=\mathbf r'(t)/\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate speed first and exploit monotonicity to choose the nonnegative inverse branch.
Rewrite the composite in terms of one auxiliary q function so endpoint differentiation does not depend on an invalid inverse quotient.

milestones.criterion: Computes and inverts the arc-length function on the specified nonnegative domain.
Builds the explicit reparameterization and verifies unit speed for positive arc length.
Handles the nonregular endpoint separately and computes the correct one-sided derivative.

commonErrors.description: Computes the speed as two root one plus t squared, omitting the factor t on the nonnegative domain.
commonErrors.consequence: The arc-length function, inverse, and all later formulas are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Divides r prime of zero by its zero norm and claims this undefined quotient verifies unit speed at s equal to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse-function chain rule is unavailable at the nonregular endpoint; the explicit right derivative must be used.

hintTree.content: For $t\ge0$, $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=2t\sqrt{1+t^2}$.
Solve $1+3s/2=(1+t^2)^{3/2}$ for the nonnegative $t$.
Set $q(s)=(1+3s/2)^{2/3}-1$; then $\mathbf R(s)=\langle q,(2/3)q^{3/2},0\rangle$ and can be differentiated directly at the endpoint.

CALC2:010618.canonicalSolution:
We have
\[
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle2t,2t^2,0\rangle,
\qquad
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=2t\sqrt{1+t^2}\qquad(t\ge0).
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(t)
&=\int_0^t2u\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du\\
&=\boxed{\frac23\left((1+t^2)^{3/2}-1\right)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Solving for the nonnegative parameter gives
\[
\boxed{t(s)=\sqrt{\left(1+\frac{3s}{2}\right)^{2/3}-1}}.
\]
Put
\[
q(s)=\left(1+\frac{3s}{2}\right)^{2/3}-1.
\]
Then an explicit arc-length reparameterization is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf R(s)=\left\langle q(s),\frac23q(s)^{3/2},0\right\rangle},
\qquad s\ge0.
\]
For $s>0$, $q>0$ and
\[
q'(s)=\left(1+\frac{3s}{2}\right)^{-1/3}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbf R'(s)=q'(s)\langle1,\sqrt q,0\rangle
\]
and
\[
\|\mathbf R'(s)\|
=q'(s)\sqrt{1+q(s)}
=\left(1+\frac{3s}{2}\right)^{-1/3}
 \left(1+\frac{3s}{2}\right)^{1/3}
=\boxed1.
\]
At $t=0$, $ds/dt=\|\mathbf r'(0)\|=0$, so $dt/ds$ is not supplied by the inverse-function theorem and the quotient $\mathbf r'(t)/\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is $0/0$. Nevertheless the explicit formula has $q(0)=0$ and right derivative
\[
\mathbf R'_+(0)
=\left\langle q'(0),\lim_{s\downarrow0}\sqrt{q(s)}q'(s),0\right\rangle
=\boxed{\langle1,0,0\rangle}.
\]
Its norm is one. So the reparameterized curve is unit speed on $(0,\infty)$ and has unit one-sided speed at the endpoint, even though the original parameterization is nonregular there.

graderFixtures.proofText: The speed is $2t\sqrt{1+t^2}$, so $s=(2/3)[(1+t^2)^{3/2}-1]$ and $t=\sqrt{(1+3s/2)^{2/3}-1}$. With $q=(1+3s/2)^{2/3}-1$, $\mathbf R=\langle q,(2/3)q^{3/2},0\rangle$ and $\|\mathbf R'\|=q'\sqrt{1+q}=1$ for $s>0$. At $s=0$ the inverse quotient is invalid, but directly $\mathbf R'_+(0)=\langle1,0,0\rangle$.
From $\mathbf r'(t)=\langle2t,2t^2,0\rangle$ I report speed $2\sqrt{1+t^2}$, dropping the factor $t$ before integrating.
At the endpoint I write $\mathbf R'(0)=\mathbf r'(0)/\|\mathbf r'(0)\|$ and call the resulting $0/0$ expression a unit vector, without differentiating the explicit reparameterization.
