CALC2:010619.title: Find the unique normal drop to a polynomial space curve
CALC2:010619.objective: Minimize squared distance to a space curve globally, factor the stationarity equation exactly, and interpret the minimizing radius vector as perpendicular to the curve tangent and lying in the normal plane.
CALC2:010619.statement:
For the space curve
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2,4-t\rangle,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty,
$$
find the point closest to the origin and prove it is the unique global minimizer. Compute the minimum distance and a unit tangent there. Verify directly that the radius vector to the closest point is perpendicular to the tangent, and write the normal plane at that point.
permittedResults: A closest point to the origin on a regular curve satisfies $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r'=0$.
A coercive continuous squared-distance function has a global minimum on the real line.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate squared distance and use its factored sign chart.
Use the general identity D prime equals twice r dot r prime as a geometric cross-check.

milestones.criterion: Proves the unique global distance minimum.
Computes the closest point, distance, and unit tangent.
Connects stationarity with orthogonality and the normal plane.

commonErrors.description: Finds t equals one from a derivative equation but gives no uniqueness or global-minimum argument.
commonErrors.consequence: A stationary point alone does not answer the closest-point question.

commonErrors.description: Uses the position vector as the plane normal instead of the tangent vector.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting plane is not the normal plane to the curve.

hintTree.content: Minimize $D(t)=\|\mathbf r(t)\|^2$ rather than its square root.
At $t=1$, use $\mathbf r'=\langle1,2,-1\rangle$.

CALC2:010619.canonicalSolution:
The squared distance is
$$
D(t)=t^2+t^4+(4-t)^2=t^4+2t^2-8t+16.
$$
It tends to infinity as $|t|\to\infty$, so a global minimum exists. Its derivative factors as
$$
D'(t)=4t^3+4t-8=4(t-1)(t^2+t+2).
$$
The quadratic factor is always positive because its discriminant is $-7$. Hence $D'<0$ for $t<1$ and $D'>0$ for $t>1$, proving a unique global minimum at $t=1$.

The closest point is
$$
\mathbf r(1)=\langle1,1,3\rangle,
\qquad d_{\min}=\boxed{\sqrt{11}}.
$$
Since $\mathbf r'(t)=\langle1,2t,-1\rangle$, a unit tangent at the point is
$$
\boxed{\mathbf T(1)=\frac1{\sqrt6}\langle1,2,-1\rangle}.
$$
The orthogonality check is
$$
\mathbf r(1)\cdot\mathbf r'(1)=1+2-3=0.
$$
Thus the radius vector lies in the normal plane. With normal vector $\langle1,2,-1\rangle$, the plane is
$$
(x-1)+2(y-1)-(z-3)=0,
$$
or $\boxed{x+2y-z=0}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: $D=t^4+2t^2-8t+16$ has $D'=4(t-1)(t^2+t+2)$, whose quadratic is positive, so t equals one is the unique global minimum. The point is $(1,1,3)$, distance $\sqrt{11}$, tangent $\langle1,2,-1\rangle/\sqrt6$, and the normal plane is $x+2y-z=0$.
I solve D prime equals zero at t equals one and call it the global minimum without checking the other factor, derivative signs, or behavior at infinity.
I use the radius vector $\langle1,1,3\rangle$ as the normal of the normal plane, instead of using the curve tangent $\langle1,2,-1\rangle$.

CALC2:010620.title: Follow an exponential spiral up a cone at constant slope
CALC2:010620.objective: Verify a nonplanar curve's cone constraint, compute its exact speed and arc length, find a unit tangent, and prove that its tangent maintains a constant angle with the vertical axis.
CALC2:010620.statement:
For
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle e^t\cos t,e^t\sin t,e^t\rangle,
\qquad 0\le t\le\ln2,
$$
show that the curve lies on the upper cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$. Compute its speed and exact arc length over the stated interval. Find the unit tangent at $t=0$, then prove that the tangent makes a constant angle with the positive $z$-axis and determine that angle.
permittedResults: Arc length is $\int_a^b\|\mathbf r'(t)\|dt$.
For unit vectors $\mathbf u,\mathbf v$, $\cos\alpha=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the coordinate constraint and trigonometric identities before differentiating.
Normalize the velocity symbolically so the constant vertical component becomes visible.

milestones.criterion: Verifies the cone geometry and differentiates the curve correctly.
Computes exact speed and arc length.
Finds the unit tangent and proves the constant-angle property.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates the trigonometric factors but omits the derivative of e to t.
commonErrors.consequence: The velocity, speed, and tangent direction are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses the raw vertical velocity component e to t as a cosine without dividing by speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The value is not dimensionless and falsely varies with t.

hintTree.content: Square the first two coordinates and use $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$.
Differentiate the exponential and trigonometric factors together.
The vertical component of the unit tangent is independent of t.

CALC2:010620.canonicalSolution:
The coordinates satisfy
$$
x^2+y^2=e^{2t}(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)=e^{2t}=z^2,
$$
and $z=e^t>0$, so the curve lies on the upper cone.

Its velocity is
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=e^t\langle\cos t-\sin t,\sin t+\cos t,1\rangle.
$$
The squared bracket norm is
$$
(\cos t-\sin t)^2+(\sin t+\cos t)^2+1=3,
$$
so the speed is $\sqrt3e^t$. Therefore
$$
L=\int_0^{\ln2}\sqrt3e^t dt
=\sqrt3(2-1)=\boxed{\sqrt3}.
$$
The unit tangent is
$$
\mathbf T(t)=\frac1{\sqrt3}
\langle\cos t-\sin t,\sin t+\cos t,1\rangle,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{\mathbf T(0)=\frac1{\sqrt3}\langle1,1,1\rangle}.
$$
With $\mathbf k=\langle0,0,1\rangle$,
$$
\mathbf T(t)\cdot\mathbf k=\frac1{\sqrt3}
$$
for every $t$. Thus the constant tangent-axis angle is
$$
\boxed{\alpha=\arccos(1/\sqrt3)}.
$$

graderFixtures.proofText: $x^2+y^2=e^{2t}=z^2$ with positive z. Differentiation gives $e^t\langle\cos t-\sin t,\sin t+\cos t,1\rangle$, whose norm is $\sqrt3e^t$. Thus length is $\sqrt3$, $T(0)=\langle1,1,1\rangle/\sqrt3$, and $T\cdot k=1/\sqrt3$ gives the constant angle.
I differentiate only cosine and sine and ignore the derivative of their common exponential factor, producing an incomplete velocity.
I call the vertical component $e^t$ the cosine of the tangent angle without normalizing the velocity by its speed.

CALC2:010621.title: Track a space curve through a cylindrical boundary
CALC2:010621.objective: Solve a geometric intersection condition for a vector-valued curve and compute velocity and speed at the selected parameter value.
CALC2:010621.statement:
Let
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,\ t^2-1,\ 2t+1\rangle.
$$
Find every point where the curve meets the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$. At the point with positive $x$-coordinate, compute the velocity vector and speed.
permittedResults: A point lies on x^2+y^2=1 exactly when its first two curve coordinates satisfy that equation; all real parameter roots must be checked before selecting the positive-x point.

acceptableStrategies.description: Turn the geometric boundary into a scalar polynomial condition in t.
Finish by separating position selection, derivative calculation, and norm calculation into distinct steps.

milestones.criterion: Solves t^2+(t^2-1)^2=1 to obtain t=-1,0,1 and all three points.
Selects t=1 from the positive-x condition and computes r'(1)=<1,2,2>.
Computes the speed ||r'(1)||=sqrt(1+4+4)=3.

commonErrors.description: Factors t^4-t^2 with an incorrect power and omits the root t=-1.
commonErrors.consequence: The response then fails the instruction to find every point where the curve meets the cylinder.

commonErrors.description: Reports 1+4+4=9 as the speed instead of taking the norm's square root.
commonErrors.consequence: Nine is the squared speed, whereas the requested speed is the nonnegative norm 3.

hintTree.content: Substitute x=t and y=t^2-1 into the cylinder equation before differentiating the curve.
Factor the resulting polynomial completely and list the point for each real root.
Only after selecting t=1, differentiate r(t) and take the norm of r'(1), not its squared norm.

CALC2:010621.canonicalSolution:
Along the curve, the cylinder condition is
$$
t^2+(t^2-1)^2=1.
$$
Expanding gives $t^4-t^2=0$, or $t^2(t^2-1)=0$. Thus $t=-1,0,1$. The corresponding points are $\langle-1,0,-1\rangle$, $\langle0,-1,1\rangle$, and $\langle1,0,3\rangle$. The one with positive $x$ is at $t=1$. Differentiate componentwise:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle1,2t,2\rangle,
\qquad \mathbf r'(1)=\langle1,2,2\rangle.
$$
Its speed is the norm, not the sum of components:
$$
\|\mathbf r'(1)\|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=\boxed3.
$$
Therefore the requested point is $\boxed{\langle1,0,3\rangle}$ with velocity $\boxed{\langle1,2,2\rangle}$ and speed $\boxed3$.

I factor t^4-t^2=0 as t^2(t-1)=0 and omit t=-1, so I do not list every cylinder intersection.

CALC2:010622.title: Compare a unit tangent before and after a monotone reparameterization
CALC2:010622.objective: Compute a unit tangent vector and explain precisely why a positive reparameterization preserves its direction at corresponding points.
CALC2:010622.statement:
For
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t,t\rangle,
$$
find $\mathbf T(0)$. Now reparameterize the same curve by $t=2s$ for $s\ge0$. Find the unit tangent at $s=0$ and explain why it agrees with the first answer.

acceptableStrategies.description: Find velocity and normalize it before discussing the reparameterized curve.
Use the chain rule as a scalar-multiple comparison, then let normalization remove the positive scalar.

milestones.criterion: Uses q'(s)=2r'(2s) to obtain q'(0)=2<0,1,1>.
Normalizes q'(0) and explains that the positive factor preserves the unit-tangent direction.

commonErrors.description: Normalizes r(0) instead of r'(0) to form a tangent vector.
commonErrors.consequence: The position vector points from the origin and is unrelated to the curve's instantaneous direction here.

commonErrors.description: Writes q'(s)=r'(2s) and omits the factor 2 from the chain rule.
commonErrors.consequence: Without the positive scalar, the claimed agreement of the normalized tangents lacks the required reparameterization justification.

hintTree.content: Differentiate r(t) first; the position r(0) is not a tangent vector.
Evaluate r'(0) and normalize it using its norm sqrt(2).
Apply the chain rule to q(s)=r(2s) and compare q'(0) with r'(0) before normalizing.

CALC2:010622.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the original curve:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle-\sin t,\cos t,1\rangle,
\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt2.
$$
Therefore $\mathbf T(0)=\langle0,1,1\rangle/\sqrt2$. Under $t=2s$, the reparameterized curve is $\mathbf q(s)=\mathbf r(2s)$, so by the chain rule
$$
\mathbf q'(s)=2\mathbf r'(2s).
$$
At $s=0$ this is $2\langle0,1,1\rangle$, whose norm is $2\sqrt2$. Normalizing cancels the positive factor two and gives
$$
\boxed{\mathbf T_q(0)=\langle0,1,1\rangle/\sqrt2=\mathbf T_r(0)}.
$$
More generally a positive derivative of the new parameter preserves tangent direction; a negative derivative would reverse it. The position vector is irrelevant to this calculation.

I normalize r(0)=<1,0,0> to obtain a tangent vector, using the position rather than the velocity.
I write q'(s)=r'(2s) and ignore the positive chain-rule factor 2, so I do not justify why normalization cancels it.

CALC2:010623.title: Separate a particle's traveled distance from its displacement
CALC2:010623.objective: Recover a vector-valued position from velocity and initial data, distinguish displacement magnitude from arc length, evaluate a nontrivial speed integral exactly, and verify the geometric distance inequality numerically.
CALC2:010623.statement:
A particle has velocity
$$
\mathbf v(t)=\langle1,2t,2\rangle
$$
and initial position $\mathbf r(0)=\langle0,0,0\rangle$. Find $\mathbf r(t)$. From $t=0$ to $t=1$, compute both the magnitude of the displacement and the total distance traveled. Give the distance in an exact logarithmic form, then provide a short numerical comparison confirming that distance traveled is at least displacement magnitude.
permittedResults: For $a>0$, $\int\sqrt{u^2+a^2}\,du=\tfrac12\bigl(u\sqrt{u^2+a^2}+a^2\ln(u+\sqrt{u^2+a^2})\bigr)+C$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Recover the trajectory first, then compute displacement from endpoints and distance from velocity norm independently.
Use the hyperbolic or logarithmic antiderivative for sqrt(u^2+5) after the scaling u=2t.

milestones.criterion: Integrates velocity with the initial condition to get r(t)=<t,t^2,2t> and displacement magnitude sqrt6.
Sets up the distance as integral_0^1 sqrt(4t^2+5)dt and evaluates it exactly.
Simplifies to 3/2+(5/8)ln5 and checks numerically that it exceeds sqrt6.

commonErrors.description: Calls ||r(1)-r(0)|| the total distance traveled without integrating the nonconstant speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The curve is not a straight constant-direction path, so displacement magnitude undercounts the traveled distance.

commonErrors.description: Evaluates the logarithmic antiderivative only at u=2 and drops its nonzero logarithm at u=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact distance gains an erroneous logarithmic constant and no longer matches the definite integral.

hintTree.content: Integrate each velocity component and use all three initial coordinates.
The displacement is r(1)-r(0), whereas distance is integral_0^1 ||v(t)||dt=integral_0^1 sqrt(4t^2+5)dt.
Use u=2t and evaluate the logarithm at u=2 and u=0 as a ratio before simplifying.

CALC2:010623.canonicalSolution:
Integrating componentwise gives
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2,2t\rangle+\mathbf C.
$$
The initial position makes $\mathbf C=\mathbf0$, so
$$
\boxed{\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2,2t\rangle}.
$$
The displacement on $[0,1]$ is $\langle1,1,2\rangle$, with magnitude
$$
\boxed{\|\Delta\mathbf r\|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6}.
$$
The speed is $\|\mathbf v(t)\|=\sqrt{1+4t^2+4}=\sqrt{4t^2+5}$. Thus, with $u=2t$,
$$
D=\int_0^1\sqrt{4t^2+5}\,dt
=\frac12\int_0^2\sqrt{u^2+5}\,du.
$$
Using the stated antiderivative,
$$
D=\frac14\left[u\sqrt{u^2+5}+5\ln(u+\sqrt{u^2+5})\right]_0^2.
$$
Since $\sqrt{2^2+5}=3$, this becomes
$$
D=\frac32+\frac54\ln\frac5{\sqrt5}
=\boxed{\frac32+\frac58\ln5}.
$$
Numerically, $D\approx2.5059$, while $\sqrt6\approx2.4495$, so $D>\|\Delta\mathbf r\|$, as required.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integrating v gives r=<t,t^2,2t>. The displacement magnitude is sqrt6. Distance is integral_0^1 sqrt(4t^2+5)dt; with u=2t it evaluates to 3/2+(5/8)ln5, about 2.5059, greater than sqrt6 about 2.4495.
The endpoint difference is <1,1,2>, so I report sqrt6 as both displacement and total distance without integrating ||v(t)||, even though the velocity direction changes with t.
I evaluate the arc-length antiderivative at u=2 but treat its u=0 value as zero, dropping the term 5 ln(sqrt5) and obtaining the wrong logarithmic constant.

CALC2:010624.title: Use curvature direction to locate an ellipse's osculating center
CALC2:010624.objective: Compute curvature of a planar ellipse using the vector cross-product formula, determine the principal-normal direction from velocity and acceleration, and locate the center of curvature with the reciprocal radius.
CALC2:010624.statement:
For the planar space curve
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle3\cos t,2\sin t,0\rangle,
$$
compute the curvature $\kappa$ at $t=0$. Determine the unit tangent and principal unit normal there, and then find the center of curvature
$$
\mathbf C=\mathbf r(0)+\frac1\kappa\mathbf N(0).
$$
Explain why choosing the opposite normal direction would place the center on the geometrically wrong side of the ellipse.
permittedResults: For a regular curve, $\kappa=\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|/\|\mathbf r'\|^3$; when acceleration is perpendicular to velocity, its direction is the principal-normal direction.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the vector curvature formula and use perpendicular acceleration to read the normal direction.
Differentiate the normalized tangent to obtain N, then move one reciprocal-curvature unit from the point.

milestones.criterion: Computes velocity, acceleration, cross-product magnitude 6, speed 2, and curvature 3/4.
Finds T(0)=<0,1,0> and the inward principal normal N(0)=<-1,0,0>.
Uses radius 4/3 to obtain center <5/3,0,0> and explains the normal orientation.

commonErrors.description: Divides the cross-product magnitude by ||r'||^2 instead of ||r'||^3.
commonErrors.consequence: The curvature becomes 3/2 rather than 3/4, halving the radius and moving the osculating center.

commonErrors.description: Uses <1,0,0> as the principal normal at the rightmost ellipse point.
commonErrors.consequence: That direction points away from the side toward which the curve bends and places the center of curvature outside at x=13/3.

hintTree.content: Compute r'(0), r''(0), their cross product magnitude, and the speed before forming curvature.
Normalize r'(0) for T(0); at this point r''(0) is already perpendicular to the velocity and points inward.
Use radius 1/kappa=4/3 and add that multiple of N(0) to r(0)=<3,0,0>.

CALC2:010624.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate twice:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle-3\sin t,2\cos t,0\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf r''(t)=\langle-3\cos t,-2\sin t,0\rangle.
$$
At $t=0$,
$$
\mathbf r'(0)=\langle0,2,0\rangle,
\quad
\mathbf r''(0)=\langle-3,0,0\rangle,
\quad
\|\mathbf r'(0)\|=2.
$$
The cross product has magnitude
$$
\|\mathbf r'(0)\times\mathbf r''(0)\|=6,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\kappa(0)=\frac6{2^3}=\frac34}.
$$
The unit tangent is
$$
\mathbf T(0)=\langle0,1,0\rangle.
$$
Because $\mathbf r''(0)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf r'(0)$ and points toward the ellipse's interior, the principal unit normal is
$$
\mathbf N(0)=\langle-1,0,0\rangle.
$$
The radius of curvature is $1/\kappa=4/3$. Therefore
$$
\mathbf C=\langle3,0,0\rangle+\frac43\langle-1,0,0\rangle
=\boxed{\left\langle\frac53,0,0\right\rangle}.
$$
The opposite normal would move outward to $x=13/3$, whereas the curve bends toward decreasing $x$ at its rightmost point.

graderFixtures.proofText: I compute the cross product magnitude 6 but divide by speed squared 4, reporting curvature 3/2 and therefore the wrong radius and center of curvature.
I use the outward normal <1,0,0>, so from <3,0,0> I place the center at <13/3,0,0>, even though the ellipse bends toward decreasing x at that point.

CALC2:010625.title: Match independent parameters before comparing tangent directions
CALC2:010625.objective: Find all intersections of two space curves by solving their coordinate equations with independent parameters, then compute the smaller nonobtuse angle between the corresponding tangent lines at each intersection.
CALC2:010625.statement:
Let
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2,t^3\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf q(s)=\langle s^2,s,s^3\rangle,
\qquad t,s\in\mathbb R.
$$
Find every point at which the two curves intersect. At each intersection, compute the smaller (nonobtuse) angle between their tangent lines. Your work must solve for the two parameters rather than assuming $t=s$ at the outset, and must identify which tangent vector belongs to which parameter value.
permittedResults: The smaller (nonobtuse) angle $\alpha$ between nonzero tangent lines with direction vectors $u,v$ satisfies $\cos\alpha=|u\cdot v|/(\|u\|\|v\|)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the injectivity of real cubing to relate the parameters, then solve the remaining algebra and differentiate.
Alternatively solve the first two equations by substitution and use the third to discard any extraneous parameter pairs before computing tangent angles.

milestones.criterion: Solves the independent-parameter intersection equations and obtains only (0,0,0) and (1,1,1).
Computes the correct tangent vectors for r and q at each parameter pair.
Finds angles pi/2 and arccos(13/14), using the smaller nonobtuse line-angle convention.

commonErrors.description: Sets t=s simply because the parameter letters play similar roles, without deriving it from equality of the third coordinates.
commonErrors.consequence: Independent parameterizations do not generally meet at equal parameter values; the intersection argument is unsupported without the coordinate equations.

commonErrors.description: Computes the angle between the position vectors of the intersection points instead of differentiating the curves.
commonErrors.consequence: A tangent-line angle is determined by velocity vectors; at the origin the position vector is zero and has no angle at all.

hintTree.content: Equate all three coordinates: t=s^2, t^2=s, and t^3=s^3. Use injectivity of the real cube function only after writing these equations.
Once t=s, combine it with t=t^2 to find all real parameter pairs and corresponding points.
Differentiate r with respect to t and q with respect to s, then evaluate both vectors at 0 and at 1 before taking dot products.

CALC2:010625.canonicalSolution:
At an intersection the coordinates satisfy
$$
t=s^2,\qquad t^2=s,\qquad t^3=s^3.
$$
Because the real cube function is one-to-one, the last equation implies $t=s$. Substituting into the first gives $t=t^2$, hence $t=s=0$ or $t=s=1$. The intersection points are therefore
$$
P_0=(0,0,0),\qquad P_1=(1,1,1).
$$
The tangent vectors are
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle1,2t,3t^2\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf q'(s)=\langle2s,1,3s^2\rangle.
$$
At $P_0$, these are $\langle1,0,0\rangle$ and $\langle0,1,0\rangle$, so their dot product is zero and the angle is
$$\boxed{\pi/2}.$$
At $P_1$, they are $u=\langle1,2,3\rangle$ and $v=\langle2,1,3\rangle$. Their dot product is $13$, while both norms equal $\sqrt{14}$. Consequently
$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{|13|}{14},
\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\arccos\!\left(\frac{13}{14}\right)}.
$$
Both vectors are nonzero, and the absolute-value convention indeed selects the smaller, nonobtuse tangent-line angle.

graderFixtures.proofText: Intersection requires t=s^2, t^2=s, t^3=s^3. Real cube injectivity gives t=s, then t=t^2, so parameters are 0 and 1. Tangents at 0 are <1,0,0>,<0,1,0>, angle pi/2; at 1 they are <1,2,3>,<2,1,3>, angle arccos(13/14).
I assume t=s before equating any coordinates because the two curves use analogous formulas, so I never justify that parameter relation.
At each intersection I use the point coordinates as direction vectors instead of r'(t) and q'(s); at the origin this even gives two zero vectors.

CALC2:010626.title: Differentiate through a removable vector singularity
CALC2:010626.objective: Extend a vector-valued curve through removable coordinate singularities, use local series to compute its derivatives, and derive the tangent line, unit tangent, and curvature at the added point.
CALC2:010626.statement:
For $t\ne0$, let
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle\frac{\sin t}{t},\frac{1-\cos t}{t},t\right\rangle.
$$
Extend $\mathbf r$ continuously to $t=0$. Using Taylor expansions with enough terms to justify the derivatives, find $\mathbf r'(0)$, the tangent line at the added point, the unit tangent $\mathbf T(0)$, and the curvature $\kappa(0)$. Do not substitute $t=0$ into quotient-rule expressions that are undefined there.
permittedResults: At a regular point, $\mathbf T=\mathbf r'/\|\mathbf r'\|$ and $\kappa=\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|/\|\mathbf r'\|^3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read the extension and derivatives directly from coordinate Taylor series, then apply the vector curvature formula.
Alternatively evaluate each derivative by limit identities or l'Hopital where justified, while avoiding undefined direct substitution and still computing r''(0).

milestones.criterion: Uses valid Taylor expansions to extend the curve and determine both first and second derivatives at zero.
Gives the tangent line and correctly normalized unit tangent at <1,0,0>.
Computes the cross-product magnitude, speed cube, and curvature 4/15.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes t=0 into quotient-rule formulas containing zero denominators and assigns values by cancellation without a limit or expansion.
commonErrors.consequence: Those formulas are undefined at the missing parameter, so the claimed derivatives have no valid basis.

commonErrors.description: Divides the cross-product magnitude by the speed or speed squared instead of by the speed cubed.
commonErrors.consequence: The space-curve curvature formula requires ||r'||^3; using another power changes 4/15 to an incorrect value.

hintTree.content: Expand sin(t)/t through t^2 and (1-cos t)/t through t^3 before reading derivative coefficients.
The constant, linear, and quadratic vector coefficients determine r(0), r'(0), and r''(0).
Compute the cross product of <0,1/2,1> and <-1/3,0,0>, then divide its magnitude by (sqrt(5)/2)^3.

CALC2:010626.canonicalSolution:
The coordinate expansions near zero are
$$
\frac{\sin t}{t}=1-\frac{t^2}{6}+\frac{t^4}{120}+O(t^6),
\qquad
\frac{1-\cos t}{t}=\frac{t}{2}-\frac{t^3}{24}+O(t^5).
$$
Thus the continuous extension is
$$\boxed{\mathbf r(0)=\langle1,0,0\rangle},$$
and coefficient differentiation gives
$$
\mathbf r'(0)=\left\langle0,\frac{1}{2},1\right\rangle,
\qquad
\mathbf r''(0)=\left\langle-\frac{1}{3},0,0\right\rangle.
$$
Since $\|\mathbf r'(0)\|=\sqrt5/2\ne0$, the point is regular. The tangent line is
$$
\boxed{\ell(s)=\langle1,0,0\rangle+s\left\langle0,\frac{1}{2},1\right\rangle},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{\mathbf T(0)=\left\langle0,\frac{1}{\sqrt5},\frac{2}{\sqrt5}\right\rangle}.
$$
Furthermore
$$
\mathbf r'(0)\times\mathbf r''(0)
=\left\langle0,-\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{6}\right\rangle,
\quad
\left\|\mathbf r'(0)\times\mathbf r''(0)\right\|=\frac{\sqrt5}{6}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\kappa(0)=\frac{\sqrt5/6}{(\sqrt5/2)^3}
=\boxed{\frac{4}{15}}.
$$
All derivatives were taken from the smooth local extension, not from undefined quotient formulas at the missing parameter.

graderFixtures.proofText: Series give r(0)=<1,0,0>, r'(0)=<0,1/2,1>, and r''(0)=<-1/3,0,0>. Thus the tangent line uses r'(0), T=<0,1/sqrt5,2/sqrt5>, the cross magnitude is sqrt5/6, and kappa=(sqrt5/6)/(sqrt5/2)^3=4/15.
I plug t=0 directly into quotient-rule derivatives with t^2 denominators and cancel zeros informally, without using the extended function or any limit.
I compute the cross product correctly but divide by ||r'||^2 rather than ||r'||^3, so my curvature does not equal 4/15.

CALC2:010627.title: Recover the base circle from curvature centers of its involute
CALC2:010627.objective: Analyze a planar vector curve with a nonregular starting parameter, compute its speed, arc length, Frenet data, and curvature for positive parameter values, and prove that all centers of curvature trace the underlying unit circle.
CALC2:010627.statement:
For $t\geq0$, consider the involute
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t+t\sin t,\ \sin t-t\cos t,\ 0\rangle.
$$
(a) Find the velocity and explain why $t=0$ is nonregular but every $t>0$ is regular.
(b) For $a>0$, find the arc length from $t=0$ to $t=a$.
(c) For $t>0$, compute $\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B$ and $\kappa$.
(d) Find the center of curvature $\mathbf C=\mathbf r+\kappa^{-1}\mathbf N$ and prove that it lies on the unit circle for every $t>0$.
permittedResults: For a regular curve, $\mathbf T=\mathbf r'/\|\mathbf r'\|$, $\kappa=\|d\mathbf T/ds\|=\|\mathbf T'(t)\|/\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$, and a consistent planar binormal is $\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Simplify the derivative into the moving radial basis, then use dT/ds for curvature and the normal.
The cross-product curvature formula may replace dT/ds, but the signed choice of N must still be checked before computing the curvature center.

milestones.criterion: Computes velocity and speed, distinguishes t=0 from t>0, and obtains arc length a^2/2.
For t>0 gives T, N, B with consistent orientation and curvature 1/t.
Uses radius t to derive C=<cos t,sin t,0> and verifies the unit-circle equation.

commonErrors.description: Defines T(0) by dividing r'(0) by its zero norm and treats the Frenet frame as regular at the starting parameter.
commonErrors.consequence: The normalization is undefined at t=0; the frame and curvature calculation are valid only for t>0.

commonErrors.description: Chooses N=<sin t,-cos t,0> while retaining positive curvature and then forms r+tN as the center.
commonErrors.consequence: That vector is opposite dT/ds, so it is not the principal normal and its offset does not recover the osculating-circle center.

hintTree.content: Differentiate both coordinates before simplifying; all non-t terms cancel and r'=t<cos t,sin t,0>.
For t>0 the speed is t, so T is the radial unit vector and T' is the perpendicular angular unit vector.
Use N=<-sin t,cos t,0> and 1/kappa=t; adding tN to r cancels the two terms proportional to t.

CALC2:010627.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating gives
$$
\mathbf r'(t)
=\langle-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t,\ \cos t-\cos t+t\sin t,\ 0\rangle
=t\langle\cos t,\sin t,0\rangle.
$$
Thus $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=t$ for $t\ge0$. The velocity vanishes at $t=0$, so that starting parameter is nonregular, while every $t>0$ is regular. For $a>0$, the arc length is nevertheless the proper integral
$$
L(0,a)=\int_0^a t\,dt=\boxed{\frac{a^2}{2}}.
$$

For $t>0$,
$$
\mathbf T=\langle\cos t,\sin t,0\rangle,\qquad
\mathbf T'=\langle-\sin t,\cos t,0\rangle.
$$
Since $\|\mathbf T'\|=1$ and $ds/dt=t$,
$$
\kappa=\frac1t,\qquad
\mathbf N=\langle-\sin t,\cos t,0\rangle.
$$
The compatible binormal is
$$
\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\langle0,0,1\rangle.
$$

The radius of curvature is $1/\kappa=t$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf C(t)
&=\mathbf r(t)+t\mathbf N(t)\\
&=\langle\cos t+t\sin t,\ \sin t-t\cos t,0\rangle
 +t\langle-\sin t,\cos t,0\rangle\\
&=\boxed{\langle\cos t,\sin t,0\rangle}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Consequently $C_x^2+C_y^2=1$ and $C_z=0$: every center of curvature lies on the base unit circle. The formulas are asserted only for $t>0$, where the Frenet frame is defined.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differentiation gives r'=t<cos t,sin t,0>, so t=0 is nonregular, speed=t, and L(0,a)=a^2/2. For t>0, T=<cos,sin,0>, N=<-sin,cos,0>, B=<0,0,1>, kappa=1/t, and C=r+tN=<cos,sin,0> lies on the unit circle.
I compute T(0)=r'(0)/||r'(0)|| even though both numerator and denominator vanish, and I claim the Frenet frame is regular at the starting parameter.
I take N=<sin t,-cos t,0>, opposite the direction of dT/ds, but still add tN to r and call the resulting off-circle point the center of curvature.

CALC2:010628.title: Turn one derivative triple into the full Frenet geometry
CALC2:010628.objective: Compute the Frenet frame, curvature, signed torsion, and three canonical planes of a nonplanar exponential space curve at one point, with consistent cross-product orientation and plane normals.
CALC2:010628.statement:
For
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,e^t,e^{-t}\rangle,
$$
compute at $t=0$:
(a) the point and unit vectors $\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B$;
(b) the curvature $\kappa$ and signed torsion
$$
\tau=\frac{(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''}{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2};
$$
(c) Cartesian equations of the normal, osculating, and rectifying planes. State which Frenet vector is normal to each plane and verify that all three equations pass through the curve point.
permittedResults: For $\mathbf v=\mathbf r'$ and $\mathbf a=\mathbf r''$, $\kappa=\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a\|/\|\mathbf v\|^3$, $\mathbf B=(\mathbf v\times\mathbf a)/\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a\|$, and $\mathbf N=\mathbf B\times\mathbf T$ for the right-handed frame $\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use v, a, and j at the specified parameter to build B from v cross a, N from B cross T, then apply the standard invariants and plane-normal rules.
Gram-Schmidt may construct N from the acceleration component orthogonal to T; orient B=T cross N and confirm the signed torsion before writing planes.

milestones.criterion: Computes the derivative vectors and obtains the consistently oriented orthonormal frame T, N, B.
Uses the speed cube and scalar triple product to obtain kappa=sqrt2/3 and signed tau=-1/3.
Gives normal plane x+y-z=0, osculating plane 2x-y+z=0, and rectifying plane y+z-2=0 with correct normal assignments.

commonErrors.description: Normalizes the acceleration vector and calls it B instead of forming the cross product of velocity and acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: At this point the acceleration direction is N, not B; the substitution swaps Frenet roles and produces the wrong osculating and rectifying planes.

commonErrors.description: Uses N as the osculating-plane normal or B as the normal-plane normal.
commonErrors.consequence: The three planes are defined by different spans: normal is perpendicular to T, osculating to B, and rectifying to N; permuting them gives different planes.

hintTree.content: At zero compute v=<1,1,-1>, a=<0,1,1>, and j=<0,1,-1>; their cross product v cross a is <2,-1,1>.
Normalize v for T and v cross a for B, then use N=B cross T rather than guessing a normal from acceleration.
Write each plane through P=(0,1,1) using normals T, B, and N respectively; scalar multiples clear the square roots.

CALC2:010628.canonicalSolution:
At $t=0$,
$$
\mathbf P=\mathbf r(0)=\langle0,1,1\rangle,
\quad
\mathbf v=\mathbf r'(0)=\langle1,1,-1\rangle,
\quad
\mathbf a=\mathbf r''(0)=\langle0,1,1\rangle,
\quad
\mathbf j=\mathbf r'''(0)=\langle0,1,-1\rangle.
$$
We have $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt3$ and
$$
\mathbf v\times\mathbf a=\langle2,-1,1\rangle,\qquad
\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a\|=\sqrt6.
$$
Therefore
$$
\mathbf T=\frac1{\sqrt3}\langle1,1,-1\rangle,\qquad
\mathbf B=\frac1{\sqrt6}\langle2,-1,1\rangle.
$$
Using $\mathbf N=\mathbf B\times\mathbf T$ gives
$$
\mathbf N=\frac1{\sqrt2}\langle0,1,1\rangle.
$$
These unit vectors are mutually orthogonal and satisfy $\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B$.

The curvature and signed torsion are
$$
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt6}{(\sqrt3)^3}
=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt2}{3}},
$$
and
$$
\tau=\frac{\langle2,-1,1\rangle\cdot\langle0,1,-1\rangle}{6}
=\frac{-2}{6}
=\boxed{-\frac13}.
$$

The normal plane has normal $\mathbf T$ (equivalently $\mathbf v$), so through $\mathbf P$ it is
$$\boxed{x+y-z=0}.$$
The osculating plane has normal $\mathbf B$ (equivalently $\langle2,-1,1\rangle$), so
$$\boxed{2x-y+z=0}.$$
The rectifying plane has normal $\mathbf N$ (equivalently $\langle0,1,1\rangle$), so
$$\boxed{y+z-2=0}.$$
Substitution of $(0,1,1)$ gives zero in each left-hand form, verifying that every plane passes through the required point.

graderFixtures.proofText: At t=0, P=<0,1,1>, v=<1,1,-1>, and v cross a=<2,-1,1>. Thus T=v/sqrt3, B=<2,-1,1>/sqrt6, N=<0,1,1>/sqrt2, kappa=sqrt2/3, tau=-1/3; the normal, osculating, rectifying planes are x+y-z=0, 2x-y+z=0, y+z-2=0.
I normalize a=<0,1,1> and call it the binormal B because it is the second derivative, never forming v cross a; this swaps the normal and binormal plane roles.
I assign N as the osculating-plane normal and B as the normal-plane normal, permuting the defining Frenet normals and writing equations for the wrong planes.

CALC2:010629.title: Exploit two matching perfect squares in a polynomial space curve
CALC2:010629.objective: Compute speed, arc length, the full Frenet frame, curvature, and signed torsion for a polynomial space curve whose velocity and cross-product norms simplify to the same perfect square.
CALC2:010629.statement:
For $t\ge0$, let
$$\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t,\frac{t^2}{2},\frac{t^3}{6}\right\rangle.$$
Find the arc length from $0$ to $a>0$. For general $t\ge0$, compute $\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B$, curvature $\kappa$, and signed torsion $\tau$. Prove the frame is right-handed and identify the relation between $\kappa$ and $\tau$.
permittedResults: For a regular curve, $\mathbf B=(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')/\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|$, $\mathbf T=\mathbf r'/\|\mathbf r'\|$, and $\mathbf N=\mathbf B\times\mathbf T$ gives $\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use cross-product Frenet formulas and exploit the common norm q.
Differentiate T with respect to arc length to construct N; B and the signed triple product must still be oriented consistently.

milestones.criterion: Finds the perfect-square speed and exact arc length.
Computes and normalizes r' cross r'', then derives N with consistent orientation.
Obtains kappa and signed tau, proves right-handedness, and states their equality.

commonErrors.description: Leaves the speed as sqrt(1+t^2+t^4/4) and then integrates it as if no perfect-square simplification exists.
commonErrors.consequence: The radicand equals (1+t^2/2)^2; missing this identity derails the exact arc length and later normalizations.

commonErrors.description: Uses r'' cross r' for B but retains the r' cross r'' torsion formula, reporting negative torsion.
commonErrors.consequence: Mixing cross-product orientations reverses B without consistently changing the signed triple product.

hintTree.content: Set q=1+t^2/2 and notice ||r'||^2=q^2.
Compute r' cross r''=<t^2/2,-t,1>; its norm is also q.
Use N=B cross T and the scalar triple product with r'''=<0,0,1>.

CALC2:010629.canonicalSolution:
Write $q=1+t^2/2$. Then
$$\mathbf r'=\langle1,t,t^2/2\rangle,\quad
\mathbf r''=\langle0,1,t\rangle,\quad
\mathbf r'''=\langle0,0,1\rangle.$$
Since $\|\mathbf r'\|^2=1+t^2+t^4/4=q^2$, the speed is $q$ and
$$L(0,a)=\int_0^a\left(1+\frac{t^2}{2}\right)dt
=\boxed{a+\frac{a^3}{6}}.$$
Also
$$\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''=\langle t^2/2,-t,1\rangle,$$
whose norm is again $q$. Hence
$$\mathbf T=\frac1q\langle1,t,t^2/2\rangle,\qquad
\mathbf B=\frac1q\langle t^2/2,-t,1\rangle,$$
and
$$\mathbf N=\mathbf B\times\mathbf T
=\frac1q\langle-t,1-t^2/2,t\rangle.$$
Thus $\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B$ and the three vectors are an orthonormal right-handed frame. Finally,
$$\kappa=\frac{q}{q^3}=\frac1{q^2},\qquad
\tau=\frac{(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''}{q^2}=\frac1{q^2}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\kappa(t)=\tau(t)=\frac1{(1+t^2/2)^2}}.$$
The positive torsion sign agrees with the specified cross-product convention.

graderFixtures.proofText: With q=1+t^2/2, ||r'||=q and L=a+a^3/6. Also r' cross r''=<t^2/2,-t,1> has norm q. Thus T=<1,t,t^2/2>/q, B=<t^2/2,-t,1>/q, N=<-t,1-t^2/2,t>/q, and kappa=tau=1/q^2 with T cross N=B.
I fail to recognize 1+t^2+t^4/4 as (1+t^2/2)^2 and treat the exact speed and arc length as an unrelated radical integral.
I construct B from r'' cross r' but use the unreversed signed-torsion numerator, so my frame convention and negative torsion contradict each other.

CALC2:010630.title: Solve for closest points before quoting the skew-line distance
CALC2:010630.objective: Find the unique closest pair on two skew lines by imposing two orthogonality equations, write their common perpendicular segment, and verify its length independently with the scalar triple-product distance formula.
CALC2:010630.statement:
Let
$$L_1:\ \mathbf r_1(s)=\langle0,0,0\rangle+s\langle1,0,1\rangle,$$
$$L_2:\ \mathbf r_2(t)=\langle0,1,0\rangle+t\langle0,1,1\rangle.$$
Show the lines are skew. Find the closest point on each line, give a parameterization of their common perpendicular segment, and compute the distance between the lines. Check the distance with a scalar triple product.
permittedResults: For skew lines through p and q with directions u and v, their distance is $|(q-p)\cdot(u\times v)|/\|u\times v\|$; solving connector orthogonality also identifies the actual closest points.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the two normal equations for the closest connector, then check with the invariant distance formula.
Minimize the squared distance as a quadratic in s,t; the gradient equations must be interpreted as the two orthogonality conditions.

milestones.criterion: Shows the lines are neither parallel nor intersecting.
Solves both connector orthogonality equations and finds the exact closest points.
Writes the common perpendicular segment and verifies distance 1/sqrt3 by a scalar triple product.

commonErrors.description: Makes the connector perpendicular to only one line and treats the resulting nonunique family as the closest pair.
commonErrors.consequence: A common perpendicular to skew lines must be orthogonal to both directions; one equation cannot determine two parameters.

commonErrors.description: Uses the signed scalar triple product as a negative geometric distance.
commonErrors.consequence: Distance is nonnegative and requires an absolute value before division by the cross-product norm.

hintTree.content: First verify u cross v is nonzero and that the lines have no intersection.
Let D=r_2(t)-r_1(s) and solve D dot u=0 and D dot v=0.
Compare the connector norm with |(q-p) dot (u cross v)|/||u cross v||.

CALC2:010630.canonicalSolution:
The directions are $\mathbf u=\langle1,0,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle0,1,1\rangle$, with
$$\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\langle-1,-1,1\rangle\ne0,$$
so the lines are not parallel. An intersection would require $s=0$ from the x-coordinate and $t=0$ from the z-coordinate, contradicting the y-coordinate $0=1$; hence they are skew.

The connector from $L_1$ to $L_2$ is
$$\mathbf D=\mathbf r_2(t)-\mathbf r_1(s)=\langle-s,1+t,t-s\rangle.$$
Orthogonality gives
$$\mathbf D\cdot\mathbf u=t-2s=0,\qquad
\mathbf D\cdot\mathbf v=1+2t-s=0.$$
Thus $s=-1/3$ and $t=-2/3$. The closest points are
$$A=\langle-1/3,0,-1/3\rangle,\qquad
B=\langle0,1/3,-2/3\rangle,$$
and $B-A=\langle1/3,1/3,-1/3\rangle$. The common perpendicular segment is
$$\boxed{\mathbf c(\lambda)=A+\lambda(B-A),\quad0\le\lambda\le1},$$
and its length is $\boxed{1/\sqrt3}$. Independently, with $q-p=\langle0,1,0\rangle$,
$$\frac{|(q-p)\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)|}{\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|}
=\frac{|-1|}{\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt3}.$$
The two computations agree.

graderFixtures.proofText: u cross v=<-1,-1,1> and the lines do not intersect. With D=<-s,1+t,t-s>, D dot u=t-2s and D dot v=1+2t-s, giving s=-1/3,t=-2/3. The connector <1/3,1/3,-1/3> has length 1/sqrt3, matching the absolute scalar-triple-product formula.
I impose D dot u=0 but never require D dot v=0, leaving a family of connectors and selecting an unsupported pair as closest.
My scalar triple product is -1, so I report the line distance as -1/sqrt3 without taking the absolute value required for geometric distance.

CALC2:010631.title: Make a sphere force curvature before identifying equality
CALC2:010631.objective: Derive orthogonality identities for a unit-speed spherical curve, prove the sharp lower curvature bound from its Frenet decomposition, and characterize interval-wide equality as a great circle.
CALC2:010631.statement:
Let $\mathbf r(s)$ be a $C^3$ unit-speed curve with curvature $\kappa(s)>0$ on an interval, and suppose
$$\|\mathbf r(s)\|=R$$
for a constant $R>0$. Using the Frenet frame, prove
$$\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf T=0,qquad
\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf N=-\frac1\kappa,$$
and deduce the sharp bound $\kappa\ge1/R$. Finally prove that equality $\kappa\equiv1/R$ throughout a subinterval holds exactly when that arc is part of a great circle. Explain why equality at one isolated point is not enough for the final characterization.
permittedResults: For unit speed, $\mathbf T=\mathbf r'$ and $\mathbf T'=\kappa\mathbf N$; the Frenet equations give $\mathbf N'=-\kappa\mathbf T+\tau\mathbf B$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Frenet components of the radius vector and then the Frenet equations in the equality case.
A normal-curvature decomposition is acceptable if it is derived in this setting and includes the interval-wide equality proof.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the sphere constraint to obtain the two Frenet dot-product identities.
Uses an orthonormal-frame decomposition to prove kappa>=1/R.
Proves both directions of the equality characterization and states why pointwise equality is insufficient.

commonErrors.description: Concludes kappa<=1/R from R^2>=1/kappa^2.
commonErrors.consequence: For positive quantities, that inequality rearranges to kappa>=1/R; the sphere imposes a minimum curvature.

commonErrors.description: Infers a whole great-circle arc from equality at one parameter value.
commonErrors.consequence: A single vanishing binormal component does not force zero torsion or a constant osculating plane on an interval.

hintTree.content: Differentiate r dot r=R^2 once and then differentiate r dot T=0.
Because r is perpendicular to T, decompose it only along N and B before comparing norms.
Under equality on an interval, show r=-RN, differentiate, and use the Frenet equation to force tau=0.

CALC2:010631.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r=R^2$ gives
$$2\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf T=0,$$
so $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf T=0$. Differentiating this identity and using unit speed gives
$$0=\mathbf T\cdot\mathbf T+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf T'
=1+\kappa\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf N,$$
hence
$$\boxed{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf N=-1/\kappa}.$$
Since $\mathbf r$ has no $\mathbf T$ component,
$$R^2=\|\mathbf r\|^2=(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf N)^2+(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf B)^2
\ge\frac1{\kappa^2}.$$
Thus $\boxed{\kappa\ge1/R}$.

If equality holds throughout a subinterval, then $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf B=0$ there and the negative normal component gives $\mathbf r=-R\mathbf N$. Differentiating and using $\kappa=1/R$,
$$\mathbf T=-R\mathbf N'=-R(-\kappa\mathbf T+\tau\mathbf B)
=\mathbf T-R\tau\mathbf B,$$
so $\tau=0$. Hence $\mathbf B$ is constant, $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf B=0$, and the arc lies in the fixed plane through the origin perpendicular to $\mathbf B$: it is a great-circle arc. Conversely, a great circle has curvature $1/R$. Equality at a single point only says the binormal component of $\mathbf r$ vanishes at that point; it does not make $\mathbf B$ constant on a neighborhood.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differentiate ||r||^2=R^2 to get r dot T=0, then differentiate again to get 1+kappa r dot N=0. Decomposing r along N,B gives R^2>=1/kappa^2, so kappa>=1/R. Equality on an interval gives r=-RN and then tau=0, hence a fixed plane through the origin and a great circle.
From R^2>=1/kappa^2 I invert both sides without reversing the relation and conclude kappa<=1/R.
At one point r dot B=0, so I immediately declare the entire curve a great circle without showing equality on an interval or tau=0.

CALC2:010632.title: Follow a parabola's osculating centers into a cusp
CALC2:010632.objective: Compute curvature and the oriented principal normal of a regular plane curve, derive its full locus of osculating centers, eliminate the parameter, and identify the cusp of the evolute.
CALC2:010632.statement:
For the parabola
$$\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,t^2\rangle,qquad -\infty<t<\infty,$$
compute its speed, unit tangent, principal unit normal, and curvature. Then find the center of curvature
$$\mathbf C(t)=\mathbf r(t)+\frac1{\kappa(t)}\mathbf N(t).$$
Eliminate $t$ to obtain a Cartesian equation for the evolute, identify its cusp, and check the center and radius of curvature at the vertex $t=0$.
permittedResults: For an oriented plane curve $(x(t),y(t))$, $\kappa=|x'y''-y'x''|/(x'^2+y'^2)^{3/2}$, and the principal normal is the unit vector in the direction of $d\mathbf T/ds$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the plane curvature formula and differentiate T to orient N before forming the evolute.
A graph-curvature formula is acceptable if the signed normal and center are verified rather than guessed from concavity alone.

milestones.criterion: Computes speed, T, the principal N, and curvature with consistent orientation.
Forms the center of curvature with the normalized normal and obtains C(t).
Eliminates the parameter, identifies the cusp, and checks the vertex osculating circle.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the radius 1/kappa by <-2t,1> without dividing that vector by its norm.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting point is not one radius of curvature from the parabola and gives the wrong evolute powers.

commonErrors.description: Eliminates t to obtain a cusp shifted to Y=-1/2 or uses Y+1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: At t=0 the osculating center is visibly above the vertex at (0,1/2), fixing the sign of the shift.

hintTree.content: Let q=sqrt(1+4t^2); differentiating T shows N=<-2t,1>/q.
Multiply N by 1/kappa before adding it to r; one factor q cancels.
From X=-4t^3 and Y-1/2=3t^2, square X and cube the shifted Y relation.

CALC2:010632.canonicalSolution:
We have
$$\mathbf r'=\langle1,2t\rangle,qquad
v=\|\mathbf r'\|=q=\sqrt{1+4t^2},qquad
\mathbf T=\frac1q\langle1,2t\rangle.$$
Differentiating $\mathbf T$ and dividing by $ds/dt=q$ shows that the principal normal points along $\langle-2t,1\rangle$, so
$$\mathbf N=\frac1q\langle-2t,1\rangle.$$
The plane-curve curvature formula gives
$$\kappa(t)=\frac2{(1+4t^2)^{3/2}}=\frac2{q^3}.$$
Therefore
$$\frac1\kappa\mathbf N=\frac{q^2}{2}\langle-2t,1\rangle
=\left\langle-t(1+4t^2),\frac{1+4t^2}{2}\right\rangle,$$
and
$$\boxed{\mathbf C(t)=\left\langle-4t^3,\frac12+3t^2\right\rangle}.$$
Writing $X=-4t^3$ and $Y-1/2=3t^2$ gives
$$\boxed{X^2=\frac{16}{27}\left(Y-\frac12\right)^3},qquad Y\ge\frac12.$$
This is a semicubical parabola with cusp at $\boxed{(0,1/2)}$; indeed $\mathbf C'(0)=0$. At the original vertex, $\kappa(0)=2$, so the radius is $1/2$, the principal normal is $\langle0,1\rangle$, and the center is $(0,1/2)$, matching the cusp.

graderFixtures.proofText: With q=sqrt(1+4t^2), T=<1,2t>/q, N=<-2t,1>/q, and kappa=2/q^3. Thus C=r+N/kappa=<-4t^3,1/2+3t^2>. Eliminating t gives X^2=(16/27)(Y-1/2)^3, Y>=1/2, with cusp and vertex curvature center (0,1/2).
I use <-2t,1> as if it were already a unit normal when multiplying by 1/kappa, producing the wrong center locus.
I write the evolute with Y+1/2 and place its cusp below the parabola, contradicting the upward principal normal and radius 1/2 at t=0.

CRE:010117.title: Initial rates (1,1,2),(2,1,8),(1,3,6): m=2, n=1, k=2; CB=2, CA 0.50 to 0.25 in 0.50 min
CRE:010117.objective: From the three initial-rate rows prove m=2, n=1 and k=2 L^2 mol^{-2} min^{-1}, then with CB held at 2 integrate 1/CA-1/CA0=4t to t=0.50 min for CA:0.50->0.25, and refuse a first-order log law or a wrong unit on k.
CRE:010117.statement:
The irreversible power-law rate
\[
r=k C_A^{m} C_B^{n}
\]
is to be identified from constant-volume initial-rate data. Concentrations are in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ and $r$ is in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
C_A & C_B & r \\
\hline
1 & 1 & 2 \\
2 & 1 & 8 \\
1 & 3 & 6
\end{array}
\]

1. Determine the integer orders $m$ and $n$, then the rate constant $k$ with units consistent with the stated litre, mole, and minute data.
2. A later constant-volume batch holds $C_B=2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ fixed (buffered $B$) and starts at $C_A=0.50\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$. Compute the time at which $C_A=0.25\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.
3. Write the integrated law used in part 2.
4. Audit the claims (i) that a first-order log plot $\ln(C_{A0}/C_A)=k't$ is the correct batch integrator, and (ii) that $k$ may be reported as $2\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$ or $2\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$.

Do not replace the power law by a QSSA or pre-equilibrium mechanism, and do not treat $B$ as a consumed stoichiometric partner in part 2.
permittedResults: From the table, doubling $C_A$ at fixed $C_B$ multiplies $r$ by $4$, so $m=2$; tripling $C_B$ at fixed $C_A$ multiplies $r$ by $3$, so $n=1$.
Then $k=r/(C_A^2 C_B)=2\,\mathrm{L^{2}\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$. With $C_B=2$ one has $-{\mathrm d}C_A/{\mathrm d}t=4 C_A^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Isolate each order by a single-concentration ratio, read k from any row, then integrate the constant-B second-order ODE.
First write the illegal ln(CA0/CA) clock and the illegal k=2 min^{-1}, then restore r=k CA^2 CB and the 1/CA integrator.

milestones.criterion: Extracts m=2, n=1 and k=2 L^2 mol^{-2} min^{-1} from the three initial-rate rows.
Integrates 1/CA-1/CA0=4t at fixed CB=2 and obtains t=0.50 min.
Rejects a first-order log integrator and a mis-unit on k.

commonErrors.description: Treats the buffered batch as first-order in A and integrates ln(CA0/CA)=k't instead of 1/CA-1/CA0=4t.
commonErrors.consequence: The time from CA=0.50 to CA=0.25 is not 0.50 min, and the C_A^2 dependence is discarded.

commonErrors.description: Reports k=2 min^{-1} or 2 L mol^{-1} min^{-1}, or misreads the table so that (m,n) is not (2,1).
commonErrors.consequence: The rate law does not match the three rows and the factor 4 in the batch integrator is lost.

hintTree.content: Compare row 1 to row 2 ($C_B$ fixed): $r$ scales as $C_A^2$. Compare row 1 to row 3 ($C_A$ fixed): $r$ scales as $C_B$. Then $k=2/(1^2\cdot 1)=2$.
Buffered $C_B=2$ gives $-{\mathrm d}C_A/{\mathrm d}t=2\cdot C_A^2\cdot 2=4 C_A^2$, hence $1/C_A-1/C_{A0}=4t$.
Insert $C_A=0.25$ and $C_{A0}=0.50$: $4-2=2=4t$, so $t=0.50\,\mathrm{min}$. A log-first-order law cannot produce this time.

CRE:010117.canonicalSolution:
Row 1 to row 2 holds $C_B=1$ and doubles $C_A$. The rate quadruples, $8/2=4=2^2$, so $m=2$. Row 1 to row 3 holds $C_A=1$ and triples $C_B$. The rate triples, $6/2=3=3^1$, so $n=1$.
\[
r=k C_A^2 C_B.
\]
Any row recovers the same constant:
\[
k=\frac{2}{1^2\cdot 1}=\frac{8}{2^2\cdot 1}=\frac{6}{1^2\cdot 3}=2\,\mathrm{L^{2}\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{m=2,\quad n=1,\quad k=2\,\mathrm{L^{2}\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}}.
\]
In the buffered batch $C_B=2$ is not a dynamical unknown, so
\[
-\frac{\mathrm d C_A}{\mathrm d t}=k C_B C_A^2=2\cdot 2\cdot C_A^2=4 C_A^2.
\]
Separation of variables on $C_A>0$ yields the second-order integrator
\[
\frac{1}{C_A}-\frac{1}{C_{A0}}=4t.
\]
With $C_{A0}=0.50$ and $C_A=0.25$,
\[
\frac{1}{0.25}-\frac{1}{0.50}=4-2=2=4t\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad t=\frac12=0.50\,\mathrm{min}.
\]
\[
\boxed{1/C_A-1/C_{A0}=4t,\quad t=0.50\,\mathrm{min}}.
\]
Claim (i) replaces the $C_A^2$ law by $\ln(C_{A0}/C_A)=k't$. That first-order log is dimensionally a different ODE and cannot return $t=0.50\,\mathrm{min}$ from the assigned $k C_B=4$. Claim (ii) strips two concentration factors from $k$ and reports $2\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$ or $2\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$. Either unit is inconsistent with $r=k C_A^2 C_B$ when $r$ is in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$.

The construction never invokes a QSSA or pre-equilibrium reduction, and it never ranks batch against CSTR or PFR.

graderFixtures.proofText: Table ratios give $m=2$, $n=1$, $k=2\,\mathrm{L^{2}\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$. With $C_B=2$, $1/C_A-1/C_{A0}=4t$ and $t=0.50\,\mathrm{min}$. Not $\ln(C_{A0}/C_A)$ and not $k=2\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
The batch with fixed CB is first-order in A, so ln(CA0/CA)=k' t is the integrator from 0.50 to 0.25.
I take k=2 min^{-1} or k=2 L mol^{-1} min^{-1}, or I read the table as first-order in A and second-order in B.

CRE:010118.title: Closed A<->B, CT=1.20, kf=0.30, kr=0.10: Aeq=0.30, A=0.30+0.90 e^{-0.40 t}
CRE:010118.objective: For closed A <-> B with CT=1.20, kf=0.30, kr=0.10 and A0=1.20, prove Keq=3, Aeq=0.30, Beq=0.90, A=0.30+0.90 e^{-0.40 t}, relaxation 2.5 min, A(2.5)=0.30+0.90/e, equilibrium rates 0.09, and initial net B 0.36, without QSSA.
CRE:010118.statement:
A constant-volume closed batch carries only the elementary pair
\[
A\underset{k_r}{\stackrel{k_f}{\rightleftharpoons}} B
\]
with
\[
k_f=0.30\,\mathrm{min^{-1}},\qquad k_r=0.10\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}.
\]
The conserved total is $C_T=C_A+C_B=1.20\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, and the charge is pure $A$:
\[
C_A(0)=1.20\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\qquad C_B(0)=0.
\]
The kinetics are exact first-order in each direction. Quasi-steady-state and pre-equilibrium reductions are not licensed.

1. Compute $K_{\mathrm{eq}}$, $C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}$ and $C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}$.
2. Integrate the linear balance and show
   \[
   C_A(t)=0.30+0.90\,e^{-0.40 t},\qquad C_B(t)=1.20-C_A(t)
   \]
   with $t$ in minutes. Identify the relaxation time.
3. Evaluate $C_A$ at $t=2.5\,\mathrm{min}$. At equilibrium, compute the forward rate and the reverse rate. At $t=0$, compute the net rate of formation of $B$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that a QSSA or pre-equilibrium closure may replace the two-rate linear ODE, and (ii) that $K_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_r/k_f$ or that the decay rate is $k_f$ alone.

Do not invoke QSSA, and do not drop the reverse reaction.
permittedResults: Elementary first-order equilibrium is $K_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_f/k_r$, so $C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}/C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=K_{\mathrm{eq}}$ on the line $C_A+C_B=C_T$.
The linear balance $\mathrm{d}C_A/\mathrm{d}t=-(k_f+k_r)C_A+k_r C_T$ integrates to $C_A(t)=C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}+(C_A(0)-C_{A,\mathrm{eq}})e^{-(k_f+k_r)t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read Keq=kf/kr, place the equilibrium on CA+CB=CT, then integrate the linear ODE at rate kf+kr.
First write the illegal QSSA closure and the illegal Keq=kr/kf, then restore the exact two-rate balance.

milestones.criterion: Computes Keq=3, Aeq=0.30 and Beq=0.90 from kf/kr and CT=1.20.
Rejects QSSA/pre-equilibrium, inverted Keq, and a one-way kf decay.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the elementary A <-> B pair by a QSSA or pre-equilibrium reduction on a fabricated intermediate.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact linear ODE, the factor e^{-0.40 t}, and the assigned relaxation time are never obtained.

commonErrors.description: Takes Keq=kr/kf=1/3, or decays A at rate kf only, so Aeq is not 0.30 or the exponential is not e^{-0.40 t}.
commonErrors.consequence: Equilibrium composition, relaxation time 2.5 min, and the t=2.5 value 0.30+0.90/e all fail.

hintTree.content: $K_{\mathrm{eq}}=0.30/0.10=3$. Then $C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=C_T/(1+K_{\mathrm{eq}})=1.20/4=0.30$ and $C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}=0.90$.
The decay rate is $k_f+k_r=0.40\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Excess $A$ starts at $0.90$, so $C_A=0.30+0.90 e^{-0.40 t}$. Relaxation time $1/0.40=2.5\,\mathrm{min}$.
At $t=2.5$, $e^{-1}=1/e$ gives $C_A=0.30+0.90/e$. Equilibrium rates are $k_f\cdot 0.30=k_r\cdot 0.90=0.09$. Initial net $B$ is $k_f\cdot 1.20=0.36$.

CRE:010118.canonicalSolution:
The equilibrium constant of the elementary pair is
\[
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{k_f}{k_r}=\frac{0.30}{0.10}=3.
\]
On $C_A+C_B=1.20$ one has $C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}=3 C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}$, hence
\[
C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{1.20}{4}=0.30\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},
\qquad
C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}=0.90\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{K_{\mathrm{eq}}=3,\quad C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=0.30,\quad C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}=0.90}.
\]
The exact $A$ balance, using $C_B=C_T-C_A$, is
\[
\frac{\mathrm d C_A}{\mathrm d t}=-k_f C_A+k_r(C_T-C_A)=-(k_f+k_r)C_A+k_r C_T.
\]
The unique equilibrium of that linear ODE is $C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=k_r C_T/(k_f+k_r)=0.10\cdot 1.20/0.40=0.30$, matching the algebraic $K_{\mathrm{eq}}$. The solution with $C_A(0)=1.20$ is
\[
C_A(t)=0.30+(1.20-0.30)e^{-0.40 t}=0.30+0.90\,e^{-0.40 t},
\]
and $C_B(t)=1.20-C_A(t)$. The relaxation time is
\[
\tau=\frac{1}{k_f+k_r}=\frac{1}{0.40}=2.5\,\mathrm{min}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_A=0.30+0.90 e^{-0.40 t},\quad \tau=2.5\,\mathrm{min}}.
\]
At $t=2.5\,\mathrm{min}$,
\[
C_A(2.5)=0.30+0.90\,e^{-1}=0.30+\frac{0.90}{e}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.
\]
At equilibrium the two one-way rates are equal:
\[
k_f C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}=0.30\cdot 0.30=0.09\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}},
\qquad
k_r C_{B,\mathrm{eq}}=0.10\cdot 0.90=0.09\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}.
\]
The initial net rate of formation of $B$ is
\[
\bigl(k_f C_A-k_r C_B\bigr)_{t=0}=0.30\cdot 1.20-0=0.36\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_A(2.5)=0.30+0.90/e,\quad r_{\mathrm{eq}}=0.09,\quad r_{B}(0)=0.36}.
\]
Claim (i) inserts a QSSA or pre-equilibrium on a nonexistent intermediate. There is no intermediate: the assigned ODE is already closed and linear. Claim (ii) inverts $K_{\mathrm{eq}}$ to $1/3$ (sending $C_{A,\mathrm{eq}}$ to $0.90$) or decays at rate $k_f=0.30$ only, which cannot produce $e^{-0.40 t}$ or $\tau=2.5\,\mathrm{min}$.

The construction is not a QSSA mechanism reduction and not an initial-rate table.

graderFixtures.proofText: I close the kinetics with a QSSA or pre-equilibrium on an intermediate instead of integrating the elementary two-rate ODE.
Keq=kr/kf=1/3 so Aeq=0.90, or A decays as e^{-0.30 t} using kf alone, so tau is not 2.5 min.

CRE:010219.title: Isobaric PFR A->2B, v0=10, k=0.20, X=0.50: kV/v0=2 ln 2-0.5, V=100 ln 2-25 L
CRE:010219.objective: For isothermal isobaric pure-A PFR A->2B with v0=10, k=0.20 and X=0.50, prove v/v0=1+X, CA=CA0(1-X)/(1+X), kV/v0=2 ln 2-0.5 and V=100 ln 2-25=44.314718 L, and refuse constant volumetric flow.
CRE:010219.statement:
An ideal PFR carries the gas-phase reaction
\[
A\to 2B
\]
which is first-order in $A$ with
\[
k=0.20\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}.
\]
The feed is pure $A$. The reactor is isothermal and isobaric, so the volumetric flow expands with conversion. The inlet volumetric flow is
\[
v_0=10\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}.
\]
The target exit conversion is $X=0.50$. Pressure drop is absent.

1. Write $v/v_0$ and $C_A/C_{A0}$ as functions of $X$.
2. Form the PFR design integral $kV/v_0=\int_0^{X}(1+x)/(1-x)\,\mathrm d x$ and evaluate it at $X=0.50$.
3. Compute the reactor volume $V$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the flow may be treated as constant-density so that $V=-(v_0/k)\ln(1-X)$, and (ii) that $\varepsilon=2$ or that $C_A=C_{A0}(1-X)$ with no expansion in the denominator.

Do not replace the expanding PFR by a constant-flow PFR, and do not rank this PFR against a batch or CSTR.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify epsilon=1, substitute CA into the PFR balance, integrate 2/(1-x)-1, then scale by v0/k=50.
First write the illegal constant-flow V=50 ln 2 and the illegal epsilon=2, then restore v=v0(1+X).

milestones.criterion: Writes v/v0=1+X and CA=CA0(1-X)/(1+X) for isothermal isobaric pure A->2B.
Evaluates kV/v0=2 ln 2-1/2 and V=100 ln 2-25=44.314718 L.
Rejects constant-flow design and a wrong expansion factor.

commonErrors.description: Drops gas expansion and uses V=-(v0/k) ln(1-X)=50 ln 2, as if volumetric flow were constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned integral 2 ln 2-1/2 and the volume 100 ln 2-25 L are never obtained.

commonErrors.description: Takes epsilon=2 from the product coefficient, or writes CA=CA0(1-X) with no (1+X) in the denominator.
commonErrors.consequence: The concentration law and the design integrand are those of a different stoichiometry.

hintTree.content: Pure $A\to 2B$ is $\varepsilon=1$, hence $v/v_0=1+X$ and $C_A=C_{A0}(1-X)/(1+X)$.
Rewrite $(1+x)/(1-x)=2/(1-x)-1$ and integrate from $0$ to $1/2$ to get $2\ln 2-1/2$.
$v_0/k=10/0.20=50$, so $V=50(2\ln 2-0.5)=100\ln 2-25=44.314718\,\mathrm{L}$. Constant flow would drop the $1+x$ factor.

CRE:010219.canonicalSolution:
The feed is pure $A$ and the stoichiometry is $A\to 2B$, so $\varepsilon=y_{A0}\delta=1\cdot 1=1$. Under the assigned isothermal isobaric conditions
\[
\frac{v}{v_0}=1+\varepsilon X=1+X,
\qquad
C_A=C_{A0}\frac{1-X}{1+\varepsilon X}=C_{A0}\frac{1-X}{1+X}.
\]
\[
\boxed{v/v_0=1+X,\quad C_A=C_{A0}(1-X)/(1+X)}.
\]
The PFR mole balance is $F_{A0}\,\mathrm d X=(-r_A)\,\mathrm d V$ with $-r_A=k C_A$ and $F_{A0}=C_{A0} v_0$, hence
\[
\frac{kV}{v_0}=\int_0^{X}\frac{1+x}{1-x}\,\mathrm d x.
\]
The integrand identity $(1+x)/(1-x)=2/(1-x)-1$ gives
\[
\int_0^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac{2}{1-x}-1\Bigr)\,\mathrm d x
=\bigl[-2\ln(1-x)-x\bigr]_0^{1/2}
=-2\ln\tfrac12-\tfrac12
=2\ln 2-\tfrac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{kV/v_0=2\ln 2-1/2}.
\]
With $v_0/k=10/0.20=50\,\mathrm{L}$,
\[
V=50\Bigl(2\ln 2-\frac12\Bigr)=100\ln 2-25.
\]
The decimal evaluation $\ln 2=0.69314718056$ produces
\[
V=69.314718056-25=44.314718\,\mathrm{L}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V=100\ln 2-25=44.314718\,\mathrm{L}}.
\]
Claim (i) freezes $v=v_0$, replacing the integrand by $1/(1-x)$ and yielding $V=-(v_0/k)\ln(1-X)=50\ln 2\approx 34.657\,\mathrm{L}$. That is a different reactor. Claim (ii) takes $\varepsilon=2$ from the product stoichiometric coefficient, or writes $C_A=C_{A0}(1-X)$ as if the density were constant. Either move changes both the concentration factor and the design integral.

The construction is not a CSTR, not a recycle PFR, and not a nonisothermal fold.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\varepsilon=1$, $v/v_0=1+X$, $C_A=C_{A0}(1-X)/(1+X)$, $kV/v_0=2\ln 2-1/2$, $V=100\ln 2-25=44.314718\,\mathrm{L}$. Not constant flow and not $\varepsilon=2$.
Density is constant so v=v0. The PFR volume is V=-(v0/k) ln(1-X)=50 ln 2 L.
A->2B means epsilon=2, or else CA=CA0(1-X) with no expansion in the denominator.

CRE:010220.title: Recycle PFR R=1, q=1/2: Cin=2, Cout=1, overall X=2/3, fresh removal 8 mol/min
CRE:010220.objective: For constant-density first-order recycle PFR with v0=4, C0=3, k=0.5, R=1 and V=16 ln 2, prove single-pass q=1/2, Cin=2, Cout=1, overall X=2/3, and fresh removal 8 mol/min equal to the reactor drop 8*(2-1).
CRE:010220.statement:
A constant-density liquid PFR is placed in a recycle loop of ratio $R=1$. The kinetics are irreversible first-order with
\[
k=0.5\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}.
\]
Fresh feed and reactor volume are
\[
v_0=4\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}},\qquad C_0=3\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\qquad V=16\ln 2\,\mathrm{L}.
\]
The loop mixer is perfect. Recycle is taken from the PFR exit and returned to the mixer; the product stream leaving the splitter has the PFR exit concentration $C_{\mathrm{out}}$.

1. Show that the single-pass remaining fraction $q=C_{\mathrm{out}}/C_{\mathrm{in}}$ equals $1/2$.
2. Close the mixer $C_{\mathrm{in}}=(C_0+R C_{\mathrm{out}})/(1+R)$ together with $C_{\mathrm{out}}=q C_{\mathrm{in}}$, and compute $C_{\mathrm{in}}$, $C_{\mathrm{out}}$, and the overall conversion $X=1-C_{\mathrm{out}}/C_0$.
3. Show that the fresh-feed molar removal $v_0(C_0-C_{\mathrm{out}})$ equals $8\,\mathrm{mol\,min^{-1}}$, and that this equals the reactor drop $v_0(1+R)(C_{\mathrm{in}}-C_{\mathrm{out}})$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the PFR may be sized on the fresh flow $v_0$ alone so that $q=e^{-kV/v_0}$, and (ii) that the overall conversion equals the single-pass conversion $1-q=1/2$.

Do not drop the mixer, and do not replace the recycle PFR by a single-pass PFR or a CSTR.
permittedResults: With $R=1$ one has $v_0(1+R)=8$ and $kV/(v_0(1+R))=\ln 2$, hence $q=1/2$.
$C_{\mathrm{out}}/C_0=q/(1+R(1-q))$. At $q=1/2$ and $R=1$ this is $1/3$, so $X=2/3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the in-tube space time first, read q, then solve the linear mixer/PFR pair for Cin and Cout.
First write the illegal q=e^{-kV/v0}=1/4 and the illegal X=1/2, then restore the flow v0(1+R) and the fresh-basis conversion.

milestones.criterion: Shows q=1/2 from kV/(v0(1+R))=ln 2 at R=1.
Closes the mixer to Cin=2, Cout=1, X=2/3, and matches the 8 mol/min ledgers.
Rejects a fresh-flow Damkohler number and the identification of overall X with 1-q.

commonErrors.description: Ignores recycle flow and sets q=exp(-kV/v0)=1/4, as if the PFR saw only the fresh stream.
commonErrors.consequence: Cin, Cout, and the assigned half-pass remaining fraction are those of a different loop.

commonErrors.description: Reports the plant conversion as the single-pass conversion 1-q=1/2 instead of 1-Cout/C0=2/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The fresh-basis conversion and the 8 mol/min product ledger are wrong.

hintTree.content: Reactor flow is $4\cdot 2=8$. Then $k\tau=0.5\cdot(16\ln 2)/8=\ln 2$, so $q=e^{-\ln 2}=1/2$.
$C_{\mathrm{in}}=(C_0+C_{\mathrm{out}})/2$ and $C_{\mathrm{out}}=(1/2)C_{\mathrm{in}}$ force $C_{\mathrm{out}}=C_0/3=1$ and $C_{\mathrm{in}}=2$. Overall $X=2/3$.
Fresh removal is $4\cdot(3-1)=8$. Reactor drop is $8\cdot(2-1)=8$. Sizing on $v_0$ alone would give the wrong $q$.

CRE:010220.canonicalSolution:
The volumetric flow through the PFR is $v_0(1+R)=4\cdot 2=8\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$. The single-pass Damkohler number is
\[
\frac{kV}{v_0(1+R)}=\frac{0.5\cdot 16\ln 2}{8}=\ln 2,
\]
so the remaining fraction is
\[
q=\frac{C_{\mathrm{out}}}{C_{\mathrm{in}}}=e^{-\ln 2}=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{q=1/2}.
\]
The mixer and the PFR close as
\[
C_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{C_0+R C_{\mathrm{out}}}{1+R}=\frac{C_0+C_{\mathrm{out}}}{2},
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac12 C_{\mathrm{in}}.
\]
Substitute the second into the first:
\[
C_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{C_0+(1/2)C_{\mathrm{in}}}{2}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
2 C_{\mathrm{in}}=C_0+\tfrac12 C_{\mathrm{in}}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\tfrac32 C_{\mathrm{in}}=C_0.
\]
With $C_0=3$,
\[
C_{\mathrm{in}}=2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{out}}=1\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},
\qquad
\frac{C_{\mathrm{out}}}{C_0}=\frac13,
\qquad
X=1-\frac13=\frac23.
\]
Equivalently $C_{\mathrm{out}}/C_0=q/(1+R(1-q))=(1/2)/(1+1\cdot 1/2)=1/3$.
\[
\boxed{C_{\mathrm{in}}=2,\quad C_{\mathrm{out}}=1,\quad X=2/3}.
\]
Fresh-feed molar removal is
\[
v_0(C_0-C_{\mathrm{out}})=4\cdot(3-1)=8\,\mathrm{mol\,min^{-1}}.
\]
The reactor itself sees flow $v_0(1+R)=8$ and a concentration drop $C_{\mathrm{in}}-C_{\mathrm{out}}=1$, so
\[
v_0(1+R)(C_{\mathrm{in}}-C_{\mathrm{out}})=8\cdot(2-1)=8\,\mathrm{mol\,min^{-1}}.
\]
The two ledgers match because the recycle stream is internal.
\[
\boxed{\text{fresh removal}=8\,\mathrm{mol\,min^{-1}}=\text{reactor drop}}.
\]
Claim (i) sizes the PFR on the fresh flow $v_0$, giving $kV/v_0=2\ln 2$ and $q=1/4$. That ignores the doubled flow through the tube. Claim (ii) reports the overall conversion as the single-pass conversion $1-q=1/2$. The product leaving the plant is at $C_{\mathrm{out}}=1$, so the fresh-basis conversion is $2/3$, not $1/2$.

The construction is not a gas-expansion PFR and not a CSTR.

CRE:010221.title: Inert-fed batch V=1+0.5t, nA=2 e^{-0.5 t}: at t=2, CA=1/e, reacted 1-e^{-1}, dCA/dt=-3/(4e)
CRE:010221.objective: For an inert-fed first-order semi-batch with V0=1, CA0=2, q=0.5, k=0.5 and no A in the feed, prove V=1+0.5t, nA=2 e^{-0.5 t}, CA=2 e^{-0.5 t}/(1+0.5t), and at t=2: V=2, nA=2/e, CA=1/e, reacted fraction 1-e^{-1}, dCA/dt=-3/(4e), separating dilution from conversion.
CRE:010221.statement:
A well-mixed semi-batch starts at
\[
V(0)=V_0=1\,\mathrm{L},\qquad C_A(0)=2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.
\]
An inert liquid is fed at the constant volumetric rate $q=0.5\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$ with no $A$ in the feed. The only reaction is irreversible first-order
\[
-r_A=k C_A,\qquad k=0.5\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}.
\]
Density is constant, so $V(t)=V_0+q t$. There is no outlet stream.

1. Integrate the mole balance for $n_A=C_A V$ and write $C_A(t)$.
2. At $t=2\,\mathrm{min}$ compute $V$, $n_A$, and $C_A$.
3. Compute the reacted mole fraction $1-n_A(t)/n_A(0)$ at that instant, and compute $\mathrm d C_A/\mathrm d t$ at $t=2\,\mathrm{min}$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the concentration ratio $C_A(t)/C_A(0)$ is the unreacted fraction, and (ii) that $\mathrm d C_A/\mathrm d t=-k C_A$ with no dilution term, or that $n_A$ itself is diluted by $V(t)/V_0$.

Do not identify concentration loss with conversion, and do not replace this semi-batch by a CSTR or a PFR.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the nA ODE first, divide by V(t), then form X from moles and dCA/dt from the quotient rule.
First write the illegal X=1-CA/CA0 and the illegal dCA/dt=-k CA, then restore the q/V dilution term.

milestones.criterion: Integrates nA=2 e^{-0.5 t} and CA=2 e^{-0.5 t}/(1+0.5 t) with V=1+0.5 t.
At t=2 obtains V=2, nA=2/e, CA=1/e, X=1-e^{-1}, and dCA/dt=-3/(4e).
Separates dilution from conversion and rejects CA/CA0 as the unreacted fraction.

commonErrors.description: Treats CA(t)/CA0 as the unreacted fraction, so the reacted fraction at t=2 is reported as 1-1/(2e) rather than 1-e^{-1}.
commonErrors.consequence: Dilution is billed as reaction and the mole ledger is abandoned.

commonErrors.description: Writes dCA/dt=-k CA with no q/V term, or lets nA itself fall as V0/V as if moles were diluted.
commonErrors.consequence: Neither dCA/dt=-3/(4e) nor nA=2 e^{-0.5 t} is obtained.

hintTree.content: The mole ODE $\mathrm{d}n_A/\mathrm{d}t=-k n_A$ is independent of $V$. With $n_{A0}=2$ one has $n_A=2 e^{-0.5 t}$ and $C_A=2 e^{-0.5 t}/(1+0.5 t)$.
Differentiate $C_A=n_A/V$ to get $\mathrm{d}C_A/\mathrm{d}t=-(k+q/V)C_A$. At $t=2$ this is $-(0.5+0.25)(1/e)=-3/(4e)$.

CRE:010221.canonicalSolution:
Constant density and a single inert feed give
\[
V(t)=V_0+q t=1+0.5 t.
\]
The mole balance on $A$ has no inlet and no outlet term:
\[
\frac{\mathrm d n_A}{\mathrm d t}=-k C_A V=-k n_A.
\]
With $n_A(0)=C_A(0)V_0=2$,
\[
n_A(t)=2 e^{-0.5 t}.
\]
Concentration is the quotient
\[
C_A(t)=\frac{n_A(t)}{V(t)}=\frac{2 e^{-0.5 t}}{1+0.5 t}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V=1+0.5 t,\quad n_A=2 e^{-0.5 t},\quad C_A=2 e^{-0.5 t}/(1+0.5 t)}.
\]
At $t=2\,\mathrm{min}$,
\[
V=1+1=2\,\mathrm{L},
\qquad
n_A=\frac{2}{e}\,\mathrm{mol},
\qquad
C_A=\frac{2/e}{2}=\frac{1}{e}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.
\]
The reacted mole fraction is
\[
X=1-\frac{n_A}{n_{A0}}=1-e^{-kt}=1-e^{-1}.
\]
Differentiating $C_A=n_A/V$ with $\dot n_A=-k n_A$ and $\dot V=q$ produces
\[
\frac{\mathrm d C_A}{\mathrm d t}
=\frac{V\dot n_A-n_A\dot V}{V^2}
=-\Bigl(k+\frac{q}{V}\Bigr)C_A.
\]
At $t=2$, $k+q/V=0.5+0.5/2=3/4$ and $C_A=1/e$, so
\[
\frac{\mathrm d C_A}{\mathrm d t}=-\frac{3}{4e}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V(2)=2,\quad n_A=2/e,\quad C_A=1/e,\quad X=1-e^{-1},\quad \dot C_A=-3/(4e)}.
\]
Claim (i) treats $C_A(t)/C_A(0)=(1/e)/2=1/(2e)$ as the unreacted fraction. That number mixes reaction with dilution: the true unreacted mole fraction is $e^{-1}$, not $1/(2e)$. Claim (ii) either writes $\dot C_A=-k C_A$ (omitting $q/V$) or lets $n_A$ itself fall as $V_0/V$ (as if moles were diluted). Moles of $A$ respond only to reaction; volume growth changes concentration, not $n_A$.

The construction is not a CSTR, not a PFR, and not a recycle loop.

graderFixtures.proofText: The unreacted fraction is CA(t)/CA0, so at t=2 the reacted fraction is 1-(1/e)/2=1-1/(2e) rather than 1-e^{-1}.
Concentration obeys dCA/dt=-k CA with no dilution term, or nA itself is diluted by V0/V.

CRE:010322.title: Linear-cooling batch: theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}), unique peak t=ln 2, T=325 K
CRE:010322.objective: On the constant-k first-order batch with CA/CA0=e^{-t}, beta=100, h=2, T0=Tamb=300 K, prove theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}), unique peak at t=ln 2 with X=1/2, theta=25 K, T=325 K, and generation=loss=50 K/min, and refuse a reduced nonisothermal CSTR-fold substitution.
CRE:010322.statement:
A constant-volume batch reactor carries out an irreversible first-order reaction with the assigned concentration history
\[
\frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}=e^{-t},
\]
where $t$ is in minutes (equivalently the rate constant is $k=1\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$). The reduced energy balance is linear in the excess temperature $\theta=T-T_0$:
\[
\theta'+2\theta=100\,e^{-t}.
\]
The numerical coefficients are the assigned generation strength $\beta=100\,\mathrm{K}$ and the assigned linear cooling coefficient $h=2\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$. The reactor and the coolant start together at
\[
T(0)=T_0=T_{\mathrm{amb}}=300\,\mathrm{K},
\]
so $\theta(0)=0$. Conversion is $X=1-C_A/C_{A0}$. This is a single well-mixed batch; it is not a CSTR.

1. Integrate the linear ODE and show that
   \[
   \theta(t)=100\bigl(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\bigr)\,\mathrm{K}.
   \]
2. Locate the unique interior maximum of $\theta$. Report $t$, $X$, $\theta$, and $T$ at that instant.
3. Show that, at the same instant, thermal generation equals linear cooling loss and that both equal $50\,\mathrm{K\,min^{-1}}$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the energy balance should be replaced by a reduced nonisothermal CSTR fold / multiplicity diagram, and (ii) that the cooling term may be dropped or that generation may be taken Arrhenius-nonlinear, so that a unique explicit peak at $t=\ln 2$ is lost.

Do not replace the linear-cooling batch by a CSTR fold, and do not change the assigned linear ODE.
permittedResults: The integrating factor $e^{2t}$ converts $\theta'+2\theta=100 e^{-t}$ into $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(\theta e^{2t})=100 e^{t}$. With $\theta(0)=0$ one obtains $\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$.
A critical point of $\theta$ satisfies $\theta'=0$, hence $2\theta=100 e^{-t}$ (generation equals loss). Differentiating $\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$ gives the unique root $t=\ln 2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the integrating factor e^{2t}, fit theta(0)=0, then set theta'=0 and read generation=loss from the ODE.
First write the illegal CSTR G=L fold and the illegal cooling-free theta=100(1-e^{-t}), then restore the linear 2 theta term that produces the e^{-2t} transient.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the linear ODE with theta(0)=0 to theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}).
Locates the unique peak t=ln 2 with X=1/2, theta=25 K, T=325 K, and gen=loss=50 K/min.
Rejects a CSTR-fold substitution and any change to the assigned linear generation-loss ODE.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the linear-cooling batch ODE by a reduced nonisothermal CSTR generation-loss fold or multiplicity diagram.
commonErrors.consequence: The explicit trajectory theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}) and the unique time t=ln 2 are never obtained.

commonErrors.description: Drops the linear cooling term 2 theta, or replaces 100 e^{-t} by an Arrhenius-nonlinear rate, so the assigned ODE is not solved.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique peak (t,X,theta,T)=(ln 2, 1/2, 25 K, 325 K) and the 50 K/min balance are lost.

hintTree.content: Multiply by $e^{2t}$ and integrate. The constant is fixed by $\theta(0)=0$, which forces $\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$.
At that instant $\theta=100(1/2-1/4)=25\,\mathrm{K}$, hence $T=325\,\mathrm{K}$ and $2\theta=50\,\mathrm{K\,min^{-1}}$ equals generation $100 e^{-t}$.

CRE:010322.canonicalSolution:
The integrating factor of $\theta'+2\theta=100 e^{-t}$ is $e^{2t}$:
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigl(\theta e^{2t}\bigr)=100 e^{t}.
\]
Integration produces $\theta e^{2t}=100 e^{t}+C$. The initial value $\theta(0)=0$ forces $C=-100$, so
\[
\theta(t)=100\bigl(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\bigr)\,\mathrm{K}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})\,\mathrm{K}}.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\theta'(t)=100\bigl(-e^{-t}+2e^{-2t}\bigr).
\]
The unique positive root of $\theta'=0$ is $2e^{-2t}=e^{-t}$, or $e^{-t}=1/2$, hence
\[
t=\ln 2\,\mathrm{min}.
\]
Then $X=1-e^{-t}=1/2$ and
\[
\theta(\ln 2)=100\Bigl(\frac12-\frac14\Bigr)=25\,\mathrm{K},\qquad T=T_0+\theta=325\,\mathrm{K}.
\]
The second-derivative test $\theta''(\ln 2)=100(e^{-\ln 2}-4e^{-2\ln 2})=100(1/2-1)=-50<0$ confirms a maximum. From the ODE, $\theta'=0$ is exactly generation $=$ loss:
\[
2\theta=2\cdot 25=50\,\mathrm{K\,min^{-1}}=100 e^{-\ln 2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=\ln 2,\ X=1/2,\ \theta=25\,\mathrm{K},\ T=325\,\mathrm{K},\ \mathrm{gen=loss}=50\,\mathrm{K\,min^{-1}}}.
\]
Claim (i) replaces the batch ODE by a reduced nonisothermal CSTR $G(T)=L(T)$ fold analysis. That algebraic multiplicity problem is a different reactor and cannot produce the explicit trajectory $\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$ or the unique time $t=\ln 2$. Claim (ii) drops the $2\theta$ cooling or replaces $100 e^{-t}$ by an Arrhenius factor. Either change destroys the linear ODE and the closed peak.

The construction is not a CSTR fold, not an adiabatic PFR, and not a consecutive-network exercise.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integrating factor $e^{2t}$ and $\theta(0)=0$ give $\theta=100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})$. Then $\theta'=0$ at $t=\ln 2$, $X=1/2$, $\theta=25\,\mathrm{K}$, $T=325\,\mathrm{K}$, and $2\theta=100 e^{-t}=50\,\mathrm{K\,min^{-1}}$. Not a CSTR fold.
The energy balance is a reduced nonisothermal CSTR. I set G(T)=L(T) and read folds or ignition-extinction points instead of integrating the batch ODE.
Cooling can be dropped, or generation is Arrhenius in T, so theta is not 100(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}) and there is no unique explicit peak at t=ln 2.
