CRE:010323.title: Adiabatic PFR, k=k0 T/T0: atanh X = k0 V/v0, X=0.60 gives V=20 ln 2, Tout=480 K
CRE:010323.objective: For a constant-density adiabatic PFR with T=300(1+X), declared k=k0 T/T0, k0=0.25, v0=5, prove k0 V/v0=atanh X, and at X=0.60 obtain atanh X=ln 2, Tout=480 K, V=20 ln 2=13.862944, and refuse an Arrhenius substitution.
CRE:010323.statement:
An irreversible first-order reaction is carried out in an adiabatic plug-flow reactor at constant density. The inlet temperature and the assigned adiabatic coupling are
\[
T_0=300\,\mathrm{K},\qquad T=T_0(1+X)=300(1+X)\,\mathrm{K}
\]
(equivalently the adiabatic rise parameter is $\beta=300\,\mathrm{K}$). The rate constant is the declared linear law
\[
k=k_0\frac{T}{T_0},\qquad k_0=0.25\,\mathrm{min^{-1}},
\]
not an Arrhenius factor. The inlet volumetric flow is $v_0=5\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$. With constant density the design equation is
\[
v_0\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dV}=k(1-X).
\]

1. Eliminate $T$ and show that
   \[
   \frac{k_0 V}{v_0}=\int_0^X\frac{\mathrm du}{(1-u)(1+u)}=\operatorname{atanh} X.
   \]
2. At the design conversion $X=0.60$, evaluate $\operatorname{atanh} X$, the outlet temperature $T_{\mathrm{out}}$, and the required volume $V$.
3. Report $V$ both as an exact multiple of $\ln 2$ and as the decimal $13.862944$ (six digits after the point).
4. Audit the claims (i) that $k$ must be replaced by an Arrhenius factor $k_0\exp(-E/RT)$ or by an isothermal $k=k_0$, and (ii) that the integral is $X/(1-X)$ or $-\ln(1-X)$ (a constant-volume second-order batch law or an isothermal first-order PFR law).

Do not substitute Arrhenius kinetics, and do not treat the reactor as a CSTR or as a cooled batch.
permittedResults: Partial fractions give $1/[(1-u)(1+u)]=(1/2)[1/(1-u)+1/(1+u)]$, whose definite integral from $0$ to $X$ is $\operatorname{atanh} X=(1/2)\ln((1+X)/(1-X))$.
The identity $\operatorname{atanh}(3/5)=(1/2)\ln 4=\ln 2$ converts $X=0.60$ into $k_0 V/v_0=\ln 2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate T algebraically, separate variables, recognize atanh, then evaluate X=3/5 as ln 2.
First write the illegal Arrhenius integral and the illegal -ln(1-X) volume, then restore k=k0(1+X) and the even kernel 1/(1-X^2).

milestones.criterion: Reduces the adiabatic constant-density PFR to k0 V/v0=atanh X using k=k0 T/T0.
At X=0.60 obtains atanh X=ln 2, Tout=480 K, and V=20 ln 2=13.862944.
Rejects Arrhenius replacement of the declared k(T) and the imported isothermal-PFR or second-order-batch integrals.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the declared k=k0 T/T0 by Arrhenius k0 exp(-E/RT) or by an isothermal k=k0.
commonErrors.consequence: The atanh quadrature is lost and V is not 20 ln 2.

commonErrors.description: Integrates as -ln(1-X) or imports the constant-volume second-order batch form X/(1-X), or treats the unit as a CSTR residual.
commonErrors.consequence: atanh(0.60)=ln 2 is never used, so V=13.862944 and Tout=480 K are not obtained together from the assigned law.

hintTree.content: Substitute $k=k_0(1+X)$ into $v_0\mathrm dX/\mathrm dV=k(1-X)$ and separate variables to get $k_0\mathrm dV/v_0=\mathrm dX/[(1-X)(1+X)]$.
The integral is $\operatorname{atanh} X$. At $X=0.60=3/5$ one has $(1+X)/(1-X)=4$, so $\operatorname{atanh} X=\ln 2$.

CRE:010323.canonicalSolution:
Constant density and the declared law $k=k_0 T/T_0$ together with $T=T_0(1+X)$ give $k=k_0(1+X)$. The PFR balance becomes
\[
v_0\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dV}=k_0(1+X)(1-X).
\]
Separating variables and integrating from the inlet $(V,X)=(0,0)$ produces
\[
\frac{k_0 V}{v_0}
=\int_0^X\frac{\mathrm du}{(1-u)(1+u)}
=\operatorname{atanh} X
=\frac12\ln\frac{1+X}{1-X}.
\]
\[
\boxed{k_0 V/v_0=\operatorname{atanh} X}.
\]
At the design conversion $X=0.60=3/5$,
\[
\operatorname{atanh}(0.60)
=\frac12\ln\frac{1.60}{0.40}
=\frac12\ln 4
=\ln 2.
\]
The adiabatic temperature is
\[
T_{\mathrm{out}}=300(1+0.60)=480\,\mathrm{K}.
\]
With $k_0=0.25\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and $v_0=5\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$,
\[
\frac{0.25\,V}{5}=\ln 2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{V}{20}=\ln 2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
V=20\ln 2=13.862944\,\mathrm{L}.
\]
(The decimal is $20\times 0.693147=13.86294$, reported to six digits after the point as assigned.)
\[
\boxed{X=0.60,\ \operatorname{atanh} X=\ln 2,\ T_{\mathrm{out}}=480\,\mathrm{K},\ V=20\ln 2=13.862944\,\mathrm{L}}.
\]
Claim (i) replaces $k=k_0 T/T_0$ by Arrhenius $k_0 e^{-E/RT}$ or by an isothermal $k=k_0$. Arrhenius makes the integral non-elementary in $X$; isothermal $k=k_0$ produces $-\ln(1-X)$ and the wrong $V$. Claim (ii) imports the constant-volume second-order batch integral $X/(1-X)$ or the isothermal first-order PFR integral $-\ln(1-X)$. Neither equals $\operatorname{atanh}(0.60)=\ln 2$, so $V$ is not $20\ln 2$.

The construction is not a cooled batch, not a CSTR fold, and not an Arrhenius nonisothermal PFR.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $k=k_0(1+X)$ one has $k_0 V/v_0=\operatorname{atanh} X$. At $X=0.60$, $\operatorname{atanh} X=\ln 2$, $T_{\mathrm{out}}=480\,\mathrm{K}$, and $V=20\ln 2=13.862944$. Not Arrhenius and not $-\ln(1-X)$.
The rate must be Arrhenius k=k0 exp(-E/RT), or else k is the isothermal k0, so the integral is not atanh X.
The PFR integral is -ln(1-X), or I import the constant-volume second-order batch law X/(1-X), so V is not 20 ln 2 at X=0.60.

CRE:010424.title: Consecutive A->B->C: B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}), peak t=2 ln 2, (A,B,C)=(1/4,1/2,1/4)
CRE:010424.objective: For A->B->C with k1=1, k2=1/2, A0=1, prove A=e^{-t}, B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}), C=1-A-B, and that B peaks at t=2 ln 2 with A=1/4, B=1/2, C=1/4 and r_form=r_consume=1/4, and refuse equal-k or parallel framing.
CRE:010424.statement:
An irreversible consecutive first-order network in a constant-volume batch is
\[
A\xrightarrow{k_1}B\xrightarrow{k_2}C,
\qquad k_1=1\,\mathrm{min^{-1}},\qquad
k_2=\frac12\,\mathrm{min^{-1}},
\]
with $t$ measured in minutes and concentrations measured in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$. The only nonzero initial charge is $A(0)=A_0=1\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, and $B(0)=C(0)=0$. The rates are $r_1=k_1 A$ and $r_2=k_2 B$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$. The network is consecutive, not parallel.

1. Integrate the linear system and show that
   \[
   A=e^{-t},\qquad
   B=2\bigl(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}\bigr),\qquad
   C=1-A-B.
   \]
2. Locate the unique positive time at which $B$ is maximized. Report $t$ and the triple $(A,B,C)$ at that instant.
3. Show that, at the same instant, the formation rate of $B$ equals its consumption rate, and that both equal $1/4\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that $k_1=k_2$ so $B=t e^{-t}$ (the equal-k formula), and (ii) that the network is the parallel pair $A\to B$, $A\to C$.

Do not replace the consecutive scheme by an equal-k reduction or by a parallel selectivity problem.
permittedResults: If $k_1\neq k_2$ and $B(0)=0$, then $B=A_0 k_1(e^{-k_2 t}-e^{-k_1 t})/(k_1-k_2)$. Here this collapses to $B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t})$.
The identity $k_1/k_2=2$ gives $t_{\max}=\ln 2/(1/2)=2\ln 2$, after which $A=e^{-2\ln 2}=1/4$ and $B=2(1/2-1/4)=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve A first, apply the integrating factor e^{t/2} to B, then set k1 A=k2 B.
First write the illegal equal-k B=t e^{-t} and the illegal parallel split, then restore k1=1, k2=1/2 and consumption of B.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the consecutive system to A=e^{-t}, B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}), C=1-A-B.
Locates the B maximum at t=2 ln 2 with (A,B,C)=(1/4,1/2,1/4) and equal rates 1/4.
Rejects the equal-k formula and a parallel-network substitution.

commonErrors.description: Sets k1=k2 and uses B=t e^{-t} (or the equal-k maximizer t=1/k) in place of the assigned k1=1, k2=1/2 solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The peak is not at t=2 ln 2 and (A,B,C) is not (1/4,1/2,1/4).

commonErrors.description: Replaces A->B->C by the parallel pair A->B and A->C, so B is never consumed and has no interior maximum from k2 B.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}) profile and the rate identity r_form=r_consume=1/4 are lost.

hintTree.content: $A=e^{-t}$ is immediate. The $B$ ODE is $\dot B+ (1/2)B=e^{-t}$; the integrating factor $e^{t/2}$ produces $B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t})$.
Set $\dot B=0$, or differentiate $B$ directly: $-e^{-t/2}+2e^{-t}=0$ forces $e^{-t/2}=1/2$, hence $t=2\ln 2$.
Then $A=1/4$, $B=1/2$, $C=1/4$, and $k_1 A=k_2 B=1/4$. The equal-k profile $t e^{-t}$ and a parallel $A$-split are different ODEs.

CRE:010424.canonicalSolution:
The $A$ equation is $\dot A=-k_1 A=-A$ with $A(0)=1$, so
\[
A(t)=e^{-t}.
\]
The $B$ equation is $\dot B=A-(1/2)B$, or
\[
\dot B+\frac12 B=e^{-t}.
\]
The integrating factor $e^{t/2}$ yields
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigl(B e^{t/2}\bigr)=e^{-t/2}.
\]
Integration and $B(0)=0$ give $B e^{t/2}=-2 e^{-t/2}+2$, hence
\[
B(t)=2\bigl(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}\bigr).
\]
Mole conservation closes $C=1-A-B$.
\[
\boxed{A=e^{-t},\ B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}),\ C=1-A-B}.
\]
Now $\dot B=2\bigl(-(1/2)e^{-t/2}+e^{-t}\bigr)=0$ becomes $2e^{-t}=e^{-t/2}$, or $e^{-t/2}=1/2$, so
\[
t=2\ln 2.
\]
Substitution produces
\[
A=e^{-2\ln 2}=\frac14,\qquad
B=2\Bigl(e^{-\ln 2}-e^{-2\ln 2}\Bigr)=2\Bigl(\frac12-\frac14\Bigr)=\frac12,\qquad
C=1-\frac14-\frac12=\frac14.
\]
Formation and consumption of $B$ are
\[
k_1 A=1\cdot\frac14=\frac14,\qquad k_2 B=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14.
\]
They match, as required by $\dot B=0$.
\[
\boxed{t=2\ln 2\,\mathrm{min},\ (A,B,C)=(1/4,1/2,1/4)\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\ r_{\mathrm{form}}=r_{\mathrm{consume}}=1/4\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}}.
\]
Claim (i) forces $k_1=k_2$ and writes $B=t e^{-t}$. That is a different ODE: the assigned ratio $k_1/k_2=2$ is lost, and the peak is not at $t=2\ln 2$. Claim (ii) redraws the network as the parallel pair $A\to B$, $A\to C$. Then $B$ is monotone (no interior maximum from consumption of $B$), and $C$ is not produced from $B$.

The construction is not a parallel selectivity problem, not an equal-k textbook special case, and not a stoichiometric-extent ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: $A=e^{-t}$ and $B=2(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t})$ peak at $t=2\ln 2$ with $(A,B,C)=(1/4,1/2,1/4)$ and $k_1 A=k_2 B=1/4$. Not $B=t e^{-t}$ and not a parallel $A$-split.
I take k1=k2 so the intermediate is B=t e^{-t} and the maximum is at t=1, not at t=2 ln 2.
The network is parallel A->B and A->C, so B is never consumed and the interior maximum from k2 B does not exist.

CRE:010425.title: Stoich left-null: A+C+D=2, B+C=3; extents (1.2,0.4) give (0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4)
CRE:010425.objective: For R1: A+B->C and R2: C->D+B, prove left-null invariants A+C+D and B+C, map initial (2,3,0,0) and extents (1.2,0.4) to (0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4) with invariants 2 and 3, identify 0<=xi1<=2 and 0<=xi2<=xi1, and refuse a right-null computation.
CRE:010425.statement:
A constant-volume batch is described by the two irreversible reactions
\[
\mathrm{R}_1:\ A+B\to C,\qquad \mathrm{R}_2:\ C\to D+B.
\]
Order the species as $(A,B,C,D)$. The stoichiometric matrix $N$ (species by reactions) has columns
\[
\nu^{(1)}=(-1,-1,1,0)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\nu^{(2)}=(0,1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Extents of reaction are $\xi=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$, so the composition is $c=c(0)+N\xi$. The initial composition is
\[
c(0)=(A,B,C,D)(0)=(2,3,0,0).
\]
A concrete extent pair is $(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(1.2,0.4)$. Invariants are left-null vectors $\ell^{\mathsf T}N=0$, not right-null vectors in $\ker N$.

1. Compute a basis of the left-nullspace of $N$ and show that $A+C+D$ and $B+C$ are independent invariants.
2. Evaluate the invariants on $c(0)$. Then compute $c$ at $\xi=(1.2,0.4)$ and re-evaluate the invariants.
3. Determine the closed extent region on which every concentration is nonnegative, starting from the given $c(0)$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that invariants are right-null vectors (reaction dependencies / cycles in $\ker N$), and (ii) that the extent region is unbounded or is the full rectangle $0\le\xi_1\le 2$, $0\le\xi_2\le 2$ with no $\xi_2\le\xi_1$ cut.

Do not compute right-null vectors in place of species invariants, and do not treat the network as a kinetic QSSA mechanism.
permittedResults: The two independent solutions of $\ell^{\mathsf T}N=0$ may be taken as $\ell^{(1)}=(1,0,1,1)$ and $\ell^{(2)}=(0,1,1,0)$, i.e. $A+C+D$ and $B+C$.
From $c(0)=(2,3,0,0)$ one has $A=2-\xi_1\ge 0$, $D=\xi_2\ge 0$, $C=\xi_1-\xi_2\ge 0$, and $B=3-\xi_1+\xi_2\ge 1$ on that set, so the region is $0\le\xi_1\le 2$, $0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve ell^T N=0 first, evaluate the two constants, then impose A,C,D>=0 on the extent chart.
First exhibit the illegal right-null (cycle) computation and the illegal rectangle 0<=xi_i<=2, then restore C=xi1-xi2>=0.

milestones.criterion: Computes the left-null invariants A+C+D and B+C and their values 2 and 3 on c(0).
Maps extents (1.2,0.4) to (0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4) and identifies the nonnegative triangle 0<=xi1<=2, 0<=xi2<=xi1.
Rejects a right-null computation and an unbounded or rectangular extent region.

commonErrors.description: Computes right-null vectors in ker N (reaction dependencies / cycles) and treats them as species invariants.
commonErrors.consequence: A+C+D and B+C are never obtained as conserved concentrations.

commonErrors.description: Reports an unbounded extent orthant, or the full rectangle 0<=xi1<=2, 0<=xi2<=2, omitting the cut xi2<=xi1 from C>=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonnegative composition set is wrong, even if the point (1.2,0.4) happens to be written down.

hintTree.content: Solve $\ell^{\mathsf T}\nu^{(1)}=\ell^{\mathsf T}\nu^{(2)}=0$. The independent solutions $(1,0,1,1)$ and $(0,1,1,0)$ are $A+C+D$ and $B+C$.
On $c(0)$ the invariants are $2$ and $3$. At $\xi=(1.2,0.4)$ the state is $(0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4)$ and the same two numbers return.
Nonnegativity is $A=2-\xi_1\ge 0$, $C=\xi_1-\xi_2\ge 0$, $D=\xi_2\ge 0$. The pair $(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ therefore lives in the triangle $0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1\le 2$, not in $\ker N$.

CRE:010425.canonicalSolution:
Write
\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&1\\1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A left-null vector $\ell=( \ell_A,\ell_B,\ell_C,\ell_D)$ satisfies
\[
-\ell_A-\ell_B+\ell_C=0,\qquad \ell_B-\ell_C+\ell_D=0.
\]
Two independent solutions are $\ell^{(1)}=(1,0,1,1)$ and $\ell^{(2)}=(0,1,1,0)$. Therefore
\[
A+C+D=\mathrm{const},\qquad B+C=\mathrm{const}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{invariants }A+C+D\text{ and }B+C}.
\]
On $c(0)=(2,3,0,0)$ the constants are
\[
A+C+D=2,\qquad B+C=3.
\]
The extent map is
\[
A=2-\xi_1,\quad
B=3-\xi_1+\xi_2,\quad
C=\xi_1-\xi_2,\quad
D=\xi_2.
\]
At $(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(1.2,0.4)$,
\[
c=(2-1.2,\ 3-1.2+0.4,\ 1.2-0.4,\ 0.4)=(0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4).
\]
Re-evaluation gives $0.8+0.8+0.4=2$ and $2.2+0.8=3$, matching the invariants.
\[
\boxed{c(1.2,0.4)=(0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4),\ \text{invariants }2\text{ and }3}.
\]
Nonnegativity of all four concentrations, starting from the given $c(0)$, is
\[
\xi_1\le 2,\qquad \xi_2\ge 0,\qquad \xi_1-\xi_2\ge 0,\qquad 3-\xi_1+\xi_2\ge 0.
\]
The last inequality is automatic on $0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1\le 2$ because $3-\xi_1+\xi_2\ge 3-2=1$. Hence the closed reachable extent set is the triangle
\[
0\le\xi_1\le 2,\qquad 0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1.
\]
\[
\boxed{0\le\xi_1\le 2,\ 0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1}.
\]
Claim (i) computes a right-null vector of $N$. Here $\ker N=\{0\}$ (the two columns are independent), so that computation returns only the zero cycle and no species invariant. Even in a dependent network, right-null vectors constrain extents, not conserved concentrations. Claim (ii) drops the $C=\xi_1-\xi_2\ge 0$ cut and reports an unbounded orthant or the rectangle $0\le\xi_i\le 2$. Either region contains points with $C<0$.

The construction is not a QSSA/pre-equilibrium mechanism reduction and not a kinetic integration.

graderFixtures.proofText: Left-null vectors give invariants $A+C+D=2$ and $B+C=3$. Extents $(1.2,0.4)$ map to $(0.8,2.2,0.8,0.4)$. The nonnegative region is $0\le\xi_1\le 2$, $0\le\xi_2\le\xi_1$. Not $\ker N$.
Invariants are right-null vectors of N, i.e. reaction cycles in ker N, so I never compute a left-null species combination A+C+D or B+C.
Any xi1,xi2>=0 with xi1<=2 and xi2<=2 is allowed, or the extent plane is unbounded, so I do not cut by xi2<=xi1.

CRE:010426.title: Autocatalytic A+B->2B: B=1/(1+9 e^{-2t}), B=1/2 at t=ln 3, max rate 1/2
CRE:010426.objective: For A+B->2B with CT=1, B0=0.10, A0=0.90, k=2, prove dB/dt=2B(1-B), B=1/(1+9 e^{-2t}), and that B=1/2 at t=ln 3 with A=1/2, max rate 1/2, and initial rate 0.18, and audit the B0 seed, positivity, and a pure-exponential substitution.
CRE:010426.statement:
An irreversible autocatalytic reaction in a constant-volume batch is
\[
A+B\to 2B
\]
with rate $r=k C_A C_B$, time measured in minutes, concentrations measured in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, and the assigned rate constant
\[
k=2\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,min^{-1}}.
\]
The total concentration is conserved,
\[
C_T=C_A+C_B=1\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},
\]
and the initial charge is
\[
B(0)=B_0=0.10\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}},\qquad
A(0)=A_0=0.90\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.
\]
Net production of $B$ is $+1$ mole per mole of reaction, so $\mathrm dB/\mathrm dt=k A B$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$. The seed $B_0>0$ is required.

1. Reduce the $B$ equation to the logistic ODE $\mathrm dB/\mathrm dt=2B(1-B)$ and integrate to
   \[
   B(t)=\frac{1}{1+9e^{-2t}}.
   \]
2. Find the unique time at which $B=1/2$. Report $A$ and the instantaneous rate $\mathrm dB/\mathrm dt$ at that instant.
3. Compute the initial rate $\mathrm dB/\mathrm dt$ at $t=0$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that $B_0$ may be taken as $0$ (or that a nonpositive seed is harmless), and (ii) that the solution is the pure exponential $B=B_0 e^{2t}$ (or $B=B_0 e^{kt}$) with no logistic saturation.

Do not drop the $B_0$ seed, and do not replace the logistic by an unconstrained exponential.
permittedResults: Separation of variables $\mathrm dB/(B(1-B))=2\,\mathrm dt$ and $B_0=1/10$ produce $B/(1-B)=(1/9)e^{2t}$, hence $B=1/(1+9e^{-2t})$.
The logistic $2B(1-B)$ on $(0,1)$ has a unique maximum $1/2$ at $B=1/2$. The assigned seed reaches $B=1/2$ at $t=\ln 3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use A=1-B, separate variables, fit B0=1/10, then maximize 2B(1-B).
First write the illegal B==0 equilibrium and the illegal 0.10 e^{2t}, then restore the (1-B) saturation and the positive seed.

milestones.criterion: Reduces the autocatalytic batch to dB/dt=2B(1-B) and integrates to B=1/(1+9 e^{-2t}).
Obtains t=ln 3 at B=A=1/2, max rate 1/2, and initial rate 0.18.
Rejects a zero/nonpositive seed and a pure-exponential replacement of the logistic.

commonErrors.description: Takes B0=0 or otherwise drops the positive seed, so B remains 0 and the factor 9 never appears.
commonErrors.consequence: The logistic trajectory B=1/(1+9 e^{-2t}) is not produced and no half-time exists.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the logistic by B=B0 e^{2t} (or B=B0 e^{kt}), ignoring A=1-B saturation.
commonErrors.consequence: B exceeds 1 at finite time; t=ln 3, the max rate 1/2, and the initial rate 0.18 are not obtained from the assigned ODE.

hintTree.content: Replace $A=1-B$ to get $\dot B=2B(1-B)$. Separate variables and use $B_0/(1-B_0)=1/9$.
The initial rate is $2\cdot 0.10\cdot 0.90=0.18$. A zero seed stays at $0$; a pure exponential $0.10 e^{2t}$ crosses $1$ and is not the solution.

CRE:010426.canonicalSolution:
Conservation $A+B=1$ and the assigned $k=2$ reduce the rate law to
\[
\frac{\mathrm dB}{\mathrm dt}=2B(1-B).
\]
\[
\boxed{\dot B=2B(1-B)}.
\]
For $0<B<1$ one has
\[
\int\frac{\mathrm dB}{B(1-B)}=2\int\mathrm dt.
\]
Partial fractions give $\ln(B/(1-B))=2t+C$. The seed $B_0=0.10$ fixes $B_0/(1-B_0)=1/9$, so
\[
\frac{B}{1-B}=\frac19 e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
B(t)=\frac{1}{1+9e^{-2t}}.
\]
Positivity of the seed keeps $0<B(t)<1$ for every finite $t$, with $B\uparrow 1$ only as $t\to\infty$.
\[
\boxed{B=1/(1+9e^{-2t})}.
\]
The level $B=1/2$ solves $1+9e^{-2t}=2$, or $e^{-2t}=1/9$, hence
\[
t=\ln 3.
\]
Then $A=1-B=1/2$ and the logistic rate is
\[
\dot B=2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac12,
\]
which is the unique maximum of $2B(1-B)$ on $[0,1]$. The initial rate is
\[
\dot B(0)=2\cdot 0.10\cdot 0.90=0.18.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=\ln 3,\ A=B=1/2,\ \dot B_{\max}=1/2,\ \dot B(0)=0.18}.
\]
Claim (i) sets $B_0=0$ or allows a nonpositive seed. Then $B(t)\equiv 0$ is the only solution, $A$ never reacts, and the logistic formula with a $9$ in the denominator is undefined as a trajectory from that seed. Claim (ii) writes $B=B_0 e^{2t}=0.10 e^{2t}$. That unconstrained exponential exceeds $C_T=1$ at finite time and solves $\dot B=2B$, not $\dot B=2B(1-B)$.

The construction is not an exponential RTD mixing problem, not a pellet-effectiveness computation, and not a parallel-selectivity network.

graderFixtures.proofText: The seed can be B0=0, or a nonpositive B0 is harmless, so B stays 0 and there is no logistic with a 9 in the denominator.
The solution is the exponential B=B0 e^{2t}=0.10 e^{2t} with no (1-B) saturation, so B is not 1/(1+9 e^{-2t}).

CRE:010527.title: Two equal tanks tau_s=2: E=t/4 e^{-t/2}, mean 4, var 8, first-order X=3/4
CRE:010527.objective: On two equal isothermal tanks with per-tank space time tau_s=2, prove E(t)=(t/4)exp(-t/2), F(t)=1-exp(-t/2)(1+t/2), moments (norm, mean, var, second)=(1,4,8,24), and first-order k=1/2 survival (1+k tau_s)^{-2}=1/4 so X=3/4, and refuse a single-tank or PFR substitution.
CRE:010527.statement:
A constant-density liquid flows through two equal, isothermal, perfectly mixed tanks in series. Each tank has space time
\[
\tau_s=2
\]
in the same time unit as $t$. There is no bypass, no dead volume, and no interstage volume. The vessel RTD is the $n=2$ tanks-in-series (gamma) density with that per-tank scale, not a single exponential of the total mean and not a pulse at the total mean.

An irreversible first-order reaction $A\to$ products has rate constant
\[
k=\frac12
\]
in reciprocal time units. Density and $k$ are constant.

1. Write $E(t)$ and $F(t)$ for $t\ge 0$. Show that $E$ is normalized to $1$.
2. Compute the mean residence time, the second moment, and the variance.
3. For the first-order reaction, compute the exit survival $\overline{C}/C_{\mathrm{in}}$ from the two-tank formula and the conversion $X$.

CRE:010528.title: Uniform window E=1/2 on [1,3]: mean 2, var 1/3, k=ln 2, X=0.72949468
CRE:010528.objective: For the compact uniform RTD E=1/2 on 1<=t<=3, prove the piecewise F, moments (mean, second, var)=(2, 13/3, 1/3), and first-order k=ln 2 survival (e^{-k}-e^{-3k})/(2k)=3/(16 ln 2)=0.27050532 so X=0.72949468, and refuse a mean-PFR or mean-CSTR substitution.
CRE:010528.statement:
A steady-flow vessel has the compact uniform residence-time density
\[
E(t)=\frac12\qquad\text{for }1\le t\le 3,
\]

An irreversible first-order reaction has
\[
k=\ln 2
\]
in reciprocal time units. For first order the exit survival is the Laplace transform of $E$ at $s=k$; micromixing need not be specified.

1. Write the cumulative $F(t)$ on the three intervals $t<1$, $1\le t\le 3$, and $t>3$.
2. Compute the mean residence time, the second moment, and the variance.
3. Compute the first-order survival $\overline{C}/C_{\mathrm{in}}=\int e^{-kt}E(t)\,\mathrm dt$ and the conversion $X$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the window may be replaced by a PFR at the mean $t=2$, and (ii) that the window may be replaced by a single CSTR at the mean $t=2$ (an exponential RTD).

Do not replace the uniform window by an exponential RTD, a segregation-versus-maximum-mixedness pair, or a two-tank gamma.

CRE:010528.canonicalSolution:
The density is already a probability:
\[
\int_1^3\frac12\,\mathrm dt=1.
\]
The cumulative is therefore
\[
F(t)=
\begin{cases}
0,& t<1,\\
(t-1)/2,& 1\le t\le 3,\\
1,& t>3.
\end{cases}
\]
\[
\boxed{F=0\text{ on }t<1,\ (t-1)/2\text{ on }[1,3],\ 1\text{ on }t>3}.
\]
The mean is the midpoint
\[
\langle t\rangle=\int_1^3 t\cdot\frac12\,\mathrm dt=\frac{t^2}{4}\Big|_1^3=\frac{9-1}{4}=2.
\]
The second moment is
\[
\langle t^2\rangle=\int_1^3 t^2\cdot\frac12\,\mathrm dt=\frac{t^3}{6}\Big|_1^3=\frac{27-1}{6}=\frac{13}{3}.
\]
The variance is
\[
\langle t^2\rangle-\langle t\rangle^2=\frac{13}{3}-4=\frac{13}{3}-\frac{12}{3}=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{mean}=2,\quad\langle t^2\rangle=13/3,\quad\mathrm{Var}=1/3}.
\]
First-order survival is
\[
\frac{\overline{C}}{C_{\mathrm{in}}}
=\int_1^3 e^{-kt}\cdot\frac12\,\mathrm dt
=\frac{e^{-k}-e^{-3k}}{2k}.
\]
With $k=\ln 2$, $e^{-k}=1/2$ and $e^{-3k}=1/8$, so
\[
\frac{1/2-1/8}{2\ln 2}=\frac{3/8}{2\ln 2}=\frac{3}{16\ln 2}=0.27050532.
\]
Conversion is
\[
X=1-\frac{3}{16\ln 2}=0.72949468.
\]
\[
\boxed{\overline{C}/C_{\mathrm{in}}=3/(16\ln 2)=0.27050532,\quad X=0.72949468}.
\]
Claim (i) replaces the window by a PFR at the mean, giving survival $e^{-2\ln 2}=1/4$, which is not $3/(16\ln 2)$. Claim (ii) replaces the window by a single CSTR at the mean, giving survival $1/(1+2\ln 2)$, an exponential-RTD formula excluded from this seed. Neither illegal model sees the compact support $[1,3]$.

The construction is not a two-tank gamma, not a Dirac-plus-exponential bypass, not a spherical pellet, and not a segregation-versus-max-mixedness comparison.

CRE:010529.title: Bypass 1/4 plus exp tau=4: E has a delta, mean 3, var 15, first-order X=1/2

CRE:010529.statement:
A steady-flow vessel has the mixed RTD
\[
E(t)=\frac14\,\delta(t)+\frac34\cdot\frac14\,e^{-t/4},\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
The first term is a Dirac atom of weight $1/4$ at $t=0$ (instantaneous bypass). The second term is an exponential of mean $4$ with flowing weight $3/4$. There is no dead-volume atom at infinity.

An irreversible first-order reaction has
\[
k=\frac12.
\]

1. Show that $E$ is normalized to $1$. Write $F(t)$ for $t>0$, including the jump at the origin.
2. Compute the mean residence time, the second moment, and the variance.
3. Compute the first-order survival, keeping the bypass contribution $1$, and the conversion $X$.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the Dirac bypass may be dropped (pure exponential of mean $4$, or the un-normalized tail $(1/4)e^{-t/4}$), and (ii) that the weights $1/4$ and $3/4$ may be swapped.

Do not omit the delta, do not treat the atom as dead volume, and do not replace the law by a uniform window or a two-tank gamma.

CRE:010529.canonicalSolution:
The Dirac atom has mass $1/4$. The absolutely continuous tail has mass
\[
\int_0^\infty\frac34\cdot\frac14 e^{-t/4}\,\mathrm dt=\frac34.
\]
Hence $\int E=1$. For $t>0$ the cumulative includes the origin jump:
\[
F(t)=\frac14+\frac34\bigl(1-e^{-t/4}\bigr)=1-\frac34 e^{-t/4}.
\]
At $t=0+$ one has $F=1/4$, which is the bypass atom.
\[
\boxed{\int E=1,\quad F(t)=1-(3/4)e^{-t/4}\ (t>0),\ \mathrm{jump}\ 1/4}.
\]
The atom contributes nothing to positive moments. The exponential of mean $4$ has mean $4$ and second moment $2\cdot 16=32$, so
\[
\langle t\rangle=\frac34\cdot 4=3,
\qquad
\langle t^2\rangle=\frac34\cdot 32=24,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}=24-9=15.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{mean}=3,\quad\langle t^2\rangle=24,\quad\mathrm{Var}=15}.
\]
First-order survival keeps a factor $1$ on the bypass and the CSTR factor on the tail:
\[
\frac{\overline{C}}{C_{\mathrm{in}}}
=\frac14+\frac34\cdot\frac{1}{1+k\cdot 4}
=\frac14+\frac34\cdot\frac{1}{1+2}
=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12.
\]
Hence $X=1/2$.
\[
\boxed{\overline{C}/C_{\mathrm{in}}=1/2,\quad X=1/2}.
\]
Claim (i) drops $\delta(t)$. A pure exponential of mean $4$ has survival $1/3$; the un-normalized tail $(1/4)e^{-t/4}$ is not even a probability. Claim (ii) swaps the weights, giving survival $3/4+(1/4)/(1+2)=5/6$ and a different $F$.

The construction is not a uniform window, not a two-tank gamma, not a segregation-versus-max-mixedness comparison on a pure exponential, and not a dead-volume atom at infinity.

CRE:010630.title: Symmetric slab phi=ln3/2: eta=1/ln3, C(0)/Cs=sqrt(3)/2, wall slope ln3/4
CRE:010630.objective: On a symmetric catalytic slab with De C''-kC=0, C'(0)=0, C(L)=Cs, and phi=ln3/2, prove C/Cs=cosh(phi x/L)/cosh phi, tanh phi=1/2, eta=1/ln3=0.91023923, C(0)/Cs=sqrt(3)/2, and the surface dimensionless slope ln3/4, and refuse a spherical substitution.
CRE:010630.statement:
A wide isothermal catalyst pellet is a symmetric slab of half-thickness $L$. Pore diffusion of reactant $A$ with effective diffusivity $D_e$ and a first-order consumption $kC$ reduce to
\[
D_e\frac{\mathrm d^2C}{\mathrm dx^2}-kC=0,\qquad 0<x<L,
\]
where $x=0$ is the midplane and $x=L$ is the exposed face. The boundary conditions are
\[
C'(0)=0,\qquad C(L)=C_s.
\]
The Thiele modulus is given as
\[
\phi=L\sqrt{\frac{k}{D_e}}=\frac{\ln 3}{2}.
\]
The geometry is a Cartesian slab, not a sphere and not a cylinder.

1. Solve for $C(x)/C_s$ and evaluate the midplane ratio $C(0)/C_s$.
2. Form the effectiveness factor
   \[
   \eta=\frac{1}{L C_s}\int_0^L C(x)\,\mathrm dx
   \]
   and show that $\eta=\tanh\phi/\phi$. Evaluate $\tanh\phi$ and $\eta$.
3. Compute the dimensionless surface slope
   \[
   \left.\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d(x/L)}\Bigl(\frac{C}{C_s}\Bigr)\right|_{x=L}.
   \]
4. Audit the claims (i) that the pellet may be replaced by a sphere of radius $L$ with the spherical effectiveness $(3/\phi)(\phi\coth\phi-1)/\phi$, and (ii) that $\eta=\tanh\phi$ with the factor $1/\phi$ omitted, or that the midplane condition is $C'(L)=0$.

Do not replace the slab by a sphere, and do not introduce an external film or a nonisothermal energy balance.
permittedResults: The unique bounded solution of $C''=(\phi/L)^2 C$ with $C'(0)=0$ and $C(L)=C_s$ is $C/C_s=\cosh(\phi x/L)/\cosh\phi$.
The identity $\tanh u=(e^{2u}-1)/(e^{2u}+1)$ at $u=(\ln 3)/2$ gives $\tanh\phi=1/2$, because $e^{2\phi}=3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the constant-coefficient ODE with an even cosh, then evaluate tanh at e^{2 phi}=3.
First write the illegal spherical eta and the illegal eta=tanh phi, then restore the slab identities eta=tanh phi/phi and C(0)/Cs=1/cosh phi.

milestones.criterion: Solves C/Cs=cosh(phi x/L)/cosh phi and C(0)/Cs=sqrt(3)/2 on the slab.
Obtains tanh phi=1/2, eta=1/ln 3=0.91023923, and surface slope (ln 3)/4.
Rejects a spherical Thiele substitution and an eta that drops the factor 1/phi.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the symmetric slab by a sphere of radius L and uses the spherical profile or eta=(3/phi)(1/tanh phi-1/phi).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned cosh field, eta=1/ln 3, and midplane ratio sqrt(3)/2 are never obtained.

commonErrors.description: Reports eta=tanh phi=1/2, omitting the factor 1/phi, or places C'=0 at x=L so the face is not Cs.
commonErrors.consequence: Neither eta=1/ln 3 nor the surface slope (ln 3)/4 survives.

hintTree.content: Even solutions of $C''=(\phi/L)^2 C$ are multiples of $\cosh(\phi x/L)$. The face value $C(L)=C_s$ fixes the factor $1/\cosh\phi$.
Differentiate: $d(C/C_s)/d(x/L)=\phi\sinh(\phi x/L)/\cosh\phi$. At $x=L$ this is $\phi\tanh\phi=(\ln 3)/4$. The sphere formula is a different geometry.

CRE:010630.canonicalSolution:
Set $\lambda=\phi/L=\sqrt{k/D_e}$. The general solution of $C''=\lambda^2 C$ is a linear combination of $\cosh(\lambda x)$ and $\sinh(\lambda x)$. The midplane condition $C'(0)=0$ kills $\sinh$, so
\[
\frac{C(x)}{C_s}=\frac{\cosh(\phi x/L)}{\cosh\phi}.
\]
At the midplane,
\[
\cosh\phi=\frac{e^{\phi}+e^{-\phi}}{2},\qquad
e^{\phi}=e^{(\ln 3)/2}=\sqrt{3},\qquad
e^{-\phi}=1/\sqrt{3},
\]
hence
\[
\cosh\phi=\frac{\sqrt{3}+1/\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},
\qquad
\frac{C(0)}{C_s}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C/C_s=\cosh(\phi x/L)/\cosh\phi,\quad C(0)/C_s=\sqrt{3}/2}.
\]
The effectiveness is
\[
\eta=\frac{1}{L}\int_0^L\frac{\cosh(\phi x/L)}{\cosh\phi}\,\mathrm dx
=\frac{\tanh\phi}{\phi}.
\]
The double-angle identity
\[
\tanh\phi=\frac{e^{2\phi}-1}{e^{2\phi}+1},\qquad e^{2\phi}=3
\]
gives $\tanh\phi=(3-1)/(3+1)=1/2$. Therefore
\[
\eta=\frac{1/2}{(\ln 3)/2}=\frac{1}{\ln 3}=0.91023923.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tanh\phi=1/2,\quad\eta=1/\ln 3=0.91023923}.
\]
The dimensionless slope is
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d(x/L)}\Bigl(\frac{C}{C_s}\Bigr)
=\phi\frac{\sinh(\phi x/L)}{\cosh\phi}.
\]
At $x=L$ this equals $\phi\tanh\phi=(\ln 3)/2\cdot(1/2)=(\ln 3)/4$.
\[
\boxed{\text{surface dimensionless slope}=(\ln 3)/4}.
\]
Claim (i) replaces the slab by a sphere. The spherical effectiveness $(3/\phi)(1/\tanh\phi-1/\phi)$ at this $\phi$ is not $1/\ln 3$, and the dimensionless spherical profile is $\sinh(\phi r/R)/[(r/R)\sinh\phi]$, not a cosh. Claim (ii) either reports $\eta=\tanh\phi=1/2$ (drops $1/\phi$) or places the insulation condition at $x=L$, destroying the assigned face value $C_s$.

The construction is not a spherical pellet, not an external-film problem, and not a nonisothermal balance.

graderFixtures.proofText: Slab field $C/C_s=\cosh(\phi x/L)/\cosh\phi$ with $\phi=(\ln 3)/2$. Then $\tanh\phi=1/2$, $\eta=1/\ln 3=0.91023923$, $C(0)/C_s=\sqrt{3}/2$, and the face slope is $(\ln 3)/4$. Not a sphere.
The pellet is a sphere of radius L, so C/Cs=sinh(phi r/R)/( (r/R) sinh phi ) and eta=(3/phi)(1/tanh phi-1/phi), not tanh phi/phi.
Effectiveness is tanh phi=1/2 without dividing by phi, or the insulated face is x=L so the midplane condition is applied at the exposed surface.

CRE:010631.title: Nonporous kg=3, ks=6: Cs/Cb=1/3, K=2, film drop 2 Cb/3, resistances 2/3 and 1/3
CRE:010631.objective: On a nonporous catalyst with kg=3 and ks=6, close kg(Cb-Cs)=ks Cs to prove Cs/Cb=1/3, K=kg ks/(kg+ks)=2, rate/area=2 Cb, film drop=2 Cb/3, and resistance shares 2/3 (film) and 1/3 (surface), and refuse a pore-diffusion or heat substitution.
CRE:010631.statement:
A nonporous solid catalyst particle has no internal pore volume. Reactant $A$ is transferred from the bulk liquid or gas at concentration $C_b$ through an external film and is consumed by an irreversible first-order surface reaction. The film coefficient and the surface rate constant are
\[
k_g=3\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}},\qquad k_s=6\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.
\]
Steady surface balance reads
\[
k_g(C_b-C_s)=k_s C_s.
\]
There is no intraparticle diffusion, no Thiele modulus, no effectiveness factor, and no energy balance.

1. Solve for the surface-to-bulk ratio $C_s/C_b$.
2. Form the overall first-order coefficient $K$ defined by $\mathrm{rate/area}=K C_b$, and show that
   \[
   \frac{1}{K}=\frac{1}{k_g}+\frac{1}{k_s}.
   \]
   Evaluate $K$ and the rate per unit area.
3. Compute the film drop $C_b-C_s$ and the fractional film and surface resistances.
4. Audit the claims (i) that the particle may be replaced by a porous pellet with a Thiele effectiveness (or a nonisothermal heat balance), and (ii) that the conductances add as $K=k_g+k_s$ or that $C_s/C_b=k_s/(k_g+k_s)$.

Do not introduce pore diffusion, a spherical effectiveness, or a heat substitution.
permittedResults: Solving the surface balance gives $C_s/C_b=k_g/(k_g+k_s)$ and $C_b-C_s=k_s C_b/(k_g+k_s)$.
Rate per area is $k_s C_s=K C_b$ with $K=k_g k_s/(k_g+k_s)$, not $k_g+k_s$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the two-flux balance for Cs, then read K as the series harmonic mean and split 1/K.
First write the illegal K=9 and the illegal Thiele eta, then restore the series identity 1/K=1/kg+1/ks.

milestones.criterion: Closes kg(Cb-Cs)=ks Cs to obtain Cs/Cb=1/3 and K=2 with rate/area=2 Cb.
Reports film drop (2/3)Cb and resistance shares film 2/3, surface 1/3 from 1/K=1/kg+1/ks.
Rejects a pore/heat substitution and a parallel sum K=kg+ks or inverted Cs/Cb.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the nonporous film-surface pair by a porous Thiele/effectiveness problem or a nonisothermal heat balance.
commonErrors.consequence: A different catalytic-diffusion family is graded, colliding with the excluded spherical-pellet seed or introducing heat.

commonErrors.description: Adds the conductances as K=kg+ks=9, or writes Cs/Cb=ks/(kg+ks)=2/3 instead of kg/(kg+ks)=1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: Neither K=2 nor the 2/3 film share is obtained.

hintTree.content: From $k_g(C_b-C_s)=k_s C_s$ one has $k_g C_b=(k_g+k_s)C_s$, so $C_s/C_b=3/(3+6)=1/3$.
$K=k_g k_s/(k_g+k_s)=18/9=2$. Rate per area is $2 C_b$. The film drop is $C_b-C_s=(2/3)C_b$.
$1/K=1/3+1/6=1/2$. Film share $(1/3)/(1/2)=2/3$ and surface share $(1/6)/(1/2)=1/3$. Adding $k_g+k_s$ or inserting a Thiele $\eta$ is illegal.

CRE:010631.canonicalSolution:
The surface balance $k_g(C_b-C_s)=k_s C_s$ rearranges to
\[
k_g C_b=(k_g+k_s)C_s
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{C_s}{C_b}=\frac{k_g}{k_g+k_s}=\frac{3}{9}=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_s/C_b=1/3}.
\]
The rate per unit area is $k_s C_s=k_s(k_g/(k_g+k_s))C_b$, so the overall coefficient is
\[
K=\frac{k_g k_s}{k_g+k_s}=\frac{3\cdot 6}{9}=2\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.
\]
Equivalently
\[
\frac{1}{K}=\frac{1}{k_g}+\frac{1}{k_s}=\frac13+\frac16=\frac12,
\]
which returns $K=2$. The rate per unit area is $K C_b=2 C_b$.
\[
\boxed{K=2\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}},\quad\mathrm{rate/area}=2C_b,\quad 1/K=1/k_g+1/k_s}.
\]
The film drop is
\[
C_b-C_s=C_b\Bigl(1-\frac13\Bigr)=\frac23 C_b.
\]
The resistance shares are
\[
\frac{1/k_g}{1/K}=\frac{1/3}{1/2}=\frac23
\qquad\text{(film)},
\qquad
\frac{1/k_s}{1/K}=\frac{1/6}{1/2}=\frac13
\qquad\text{(surface)}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_b-C_s=(2/3)C_b,\quad\text{film }2/3,\ \text{surface }1/3}.
\]
Claim (i) inserts a porous Thiele problem or a heat balance. Those models introduce $\eta(\phi)$ or an energy equation that the assigned nonporous isothermal film-surface pair does not have. Claim (ii) adds the conductances in parallel, $K=k_g+k_s=9$, or writes the inverted ratio $C_s/C_b=k_s/(k_g+k_s)=2/3$. Either move destroys $K=2$ and the $2/3$--$1/3$ split.

The construction is not a slab or spherical effectiveness, not a QSSA mechanism, and not a reactor-network ranking.

graderFixtures.proofText: From $k_g(C_b-C_s)=k_s C_s$ one has $C_s/C_b=1/3$, $K=2$, rate/area $=2C_b$, film drop $(2/3)C_b$, and shares $2/3$ (film), $1/3$ (surface). Not a pore/Thiele model and not $K=k_g+k_s$.
The particle is porous, so a Thiele modulus and spherical or slab effectiveness replace kg and ks, or a heat balance sets the surface rate.
The overall coefficient is K=kg+ks=9, or Cs/Cb=ks/(kg+ks)=2/3, so the film drop is not (2/3)Cb.

CIR:010117.title: The 3-2-6 ohm delta has wye legs 6/11, 18/11, 12/11 ohm and open-C voltage 9 V
CIR:010117.objective: Convert a numerical three-terminal delta to its wye, drive A relative to grounded B with C unloaded, recover the driving-point resistance and the open voltage at C from the wye, and audit the same operating point on the original delta without a Thevenin or Norton reduction.
CIR:010117.statement:
A purely resistive three-terminal network has accessible terminals $A$, $B$, and $C$. In the given delta (mesh) connection the three branch resistances are
\[
R_{AB}=3\ \Omega,\qquad R_{AC}=2\ \Omega,\qquad R_{CB}=6\ \Omega.
\]
The equivalent wye (star) has a common interior node $N$ and leg resistances $R_A$ from $A$ to $N$, $R_B$ from $B$ to $N$, and $R_C$ from $C$ to $N$.

1. Compute $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ from the standard delta-to-wye identities. Each numerator is the product of the two delta sides that meet at the corresponding terminal, and the common denominator is $R_{AB}+R_{AC}+R_{CB}$.

2. Attach an independent $12\ \mathrm V$ source from $A$ to $B$ with the positive terminal at $A$ and with $B$ grounded. Leave terminal $C$ open (unloaded: no external current at $C$). Using only the wye, compute the driving-point resistance $R_{\mathrm{eq},AB}$ seen by the source, the source current $I_s$ leaving the positive terminal, and the open-circuit voltage $v_C$.

3. Repeat the same excitation on the original delta. Compute the current $I_{AB}$ through $R_{AB}$ and the series current $I_{ACB}$ along the unique path $A\to C\to B$. Show that $I_s=I_{AB}+I_{ACB}$ and that the same $v_C$ appears at the unloaded node $C$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the wye leg at $A$ is the product of the two delta sides that do not touch $A$, divided by the sum”; (ii) “because $C$ is open, $v_C=0$.”

Do not form a one-port Thevenin or Norton equivalent, do not introduce a dependent source, and do not compute element power. The exercise is three-terminal resistive equivalence checked by a single unloaded-C operating point.
permittedResults: Two resistors in series add; two resistors in parallel satisfy $R_1\parallel R_2=R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2)$.
If no current leaves an unloaded terminal, every series pair that ends at that terminal carries a common current, and the open voltage is the voltage of the interior node of that pair.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert to the wye, collapse the unloaded RC, and read Is and vC from the series divider RA+RB.
Stay on the original delta: place 12 V across R_AB and across the series pair RAC+RCB, then match the source current and vC to the wye.

milestones.criterion: Converts the 3-2-6 ohm delta to the wye RA=6/11, RB=18/11, RC=12/11 ohm.
With VA=12 V, VB=0, and C open, obtains ReqAB=24/11 ohm, Is=11/2 A, and vC=9 V.
Recovers I_AB=4 A and I_ACB=3/2 A on the original delta and rejects a swapped wye numerator or the claim vC=0.

commonErrors.description: Uses the product of the two delta sides that do not touch A as the numerator of RA, obtaining RA=12/11 ohm instead of 6/11 ohm.
commonErrors.consequence: The wye legs are permuted, so both the driving-point resistance and the open voltage at C are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Treats the unloaded terminal C as a grounded node and reports vC=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The open-circuit potential of the three-terminal network is lost; only the current at C is zero.

hintTree.content: The common denominator is $3+2+6=11$, so $R_A=3\cdot 2/11=6/11\ \Omega$.
With $C$ open the wye reduces to $R_A+R_B$ between $A$ and $B$, and $v_C$ is the voltage of the star node.
On the original delta, $R_{AB}$ sits directly across $12\ \mathrm V$ while $R_{AC}$ and $R_{CB}$ form a series path from $A$ to $B$.

CIR:010117.canonicalSolution:
The sum of the delta sides is $\Sigma=3+2+6=11\ \Omega$. The wye legs are therefore
\[
R_A=\frac{3\cdot 2}{11}=\boxed{\frac{6}{11}\ \Omega},\qquad
R_B=\frac{3\cdot 6}{11}=\boxed{\frac{18}{11}\ \Omega},\qquad
R_C=\frac{2\cdot 6}{11}=\boxed{\frac{12}{11}\ \Omega}.
\]

With $C$ unloaded the current through $R_C$ is zero, so the source sees only the series pair $R_A+R_B$:
\[
R_{\mathrm{eq},AB}=\frac{6}{11}+\frac{18}{11}=\boxed{\frac{24}{11}\ \Omega}.
\]
The source current leaving the positive terminal at $A$ is
\[
I_s=\frac{12}{24/11}=\boxed{\frac{11}{2}\ \mathrm A}.
\]
The star-node voltage, measured from ground at $B$, is the drop across $R_B$:
\[
v_N=I_s R_B=\frac{11}{2}\cdot\frac{18}{11}=9\ \mathrm V.
\]
Because $R_C$ carries no current, $v_C=v_N$, hence
\[
\boxed{v_C=9\ \mathrm V}.
\]
Equivalently, $v_N=12-I_s R_A=12-(11/2)(6/11)=9\ \mathrm V$.

On the original delta the same excitation places $12\ \mathrm V$ directly across $R_{AB}$, so
\[
I_{AB}=\frac{12}{3}=\boxed{4\ \mathrm A}
\]
from $A$ to $B$. Terminal $C$ is unloaded, therefore $R_{AC}$ and $R_{CB}$ are in series from $A$ to $B$ and carry
\[
I_{ACB}=\frac{12}{2+6}=\boxed{\frac{3}{2}\ \mathrm A}
\]
along $A\to C\to B$. The source must supply both paths:
\[
I_s=4+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{11}{2}\ \mathrm A.
\]
The voltage at $C$ is the drop from $B$ through $R_{CB}$,
\[
v_C=I_{ACB}\cdot 6=\frac{3}{2}\cdot 6=9\ \mathrm V,
\]
or the divider $12\cdot 6/(2+6)=9\ \mathrm V$. The parallel check $3\parallel(2+6)=24/11\ \Omega$ recovers $R_{\mathrm{eq},AB}$.

Sentence (i) is false: the product of the two sides that do not touch $A$ is $R_{AC}R_{CB}=12$, which is the numerator of $R_C$, not of $R_A$. Using that numerator at $A$ would report $R_A=12/11\ \Omega$ and a wrong divider. Sentence (ii) is false: an open $C$ sets the current at $C$ to zero, not the potential; $v_C=9\ \mathrm V$.

No one-port equivalent is required. The two three-terminal networks agree at the driven port $AB$ and at the unloaded terminal $C$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The wye is $R_A=6/11\ \Omega$, $R_B=18/11\ \Omega$, $R_C=12/11\ \Omega$. With $C$ open, $R_{\mathrm{eq},AB}=24/11\ \Omega$, $I_s=11/2\ \mathrm A$, and $v_C=9\ \mathrm V$. The original delta carries $I_{AB}=4\ \mathrm A$ and $I_{ACB}=3/2\ \mathrm A$.
RA is the product of the sides that do not meet at A, so RA=RAC RCB/11=12/11 ohm. Then RB=6/11 ohm and the open voltage at C is 3 V.
Terminal C is open, therefore vC=0. The source still sees 24/11 ohm and Is=11/2 A.

CIR:010118.title: The 2-4 vs 3-6 bridge is balanced at 8 V; the 9 ohm load gives Ig=-12/115 A
CIR:010118.objective: Recognize the balance ratio of a four-arm resistive bridge, compute the open detector voltage after a single arm is changed, and solve the loaded two-node system for the galvanometer current.
CIR:010118.statement:
A Wheatstone bridge is driven by an independent $12\ \mathrm V$ source from the top node $A$ to the grounded bottom node $B$. The left arm is the series pair $2\ \Omega$ from $A$ to the left mid-node $L$ and $4\ \Omega$ from $L$ to $B$. The right arm is the series pair $3\ \Omega$ from $A$ to the right mid-node $R$ and $6\ \Omega$ from $R$ to $B$. A detector of resistance $6\ \Omega$ may be connected between $L$ and $R$; its current $I_g$ is referenced from $L$ to $R$.

1. With the detector connected, show that the bridge is balanced. Compute the mid-node voltages $v_L$ and $v_R$ and the detector current $I_g$.

2. Replace the lower-right resistor by $9\ \Omega$ and remove the detector, leaving $L$ and $R$ open with respect to each other. Compute the open voltage difference $v_L-v_R$.

3. Reconnect the $6\ \Omega$ detector between $L$ and $R$ after the lower-right change. Write KCL at $L$ and at $R$, show that the mid-node voltages satisfy
   \[
   11v_L-2v_R=72,\qquad -3v_L+11v_R=72,
   \]
   and solve for $v_L$, $v_R$, and $I_g=(v_L-v_R)/6$ exactly.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the original bridge is unbalanced because $2\neq 3$”; (ii) “after the lower-right change the loaded detector current is the open difference divided by $6\ \Omega$.”

Do not introduce an operational amplifier, a dependent source, or a Thevenin one-port of the whole bridge. The circuit is a resistive four-arm bridge with a single linear detector.
permittedResults: An unloaded series divider from a source $V_s$ to ground through $R_1$ then $R_2$ produces the mid-node voltage $V_s R_2/(R_1+R_2)$.
KCL at a resistive node is the sum of $(v-v_{\mathrm{far}})/R$ over every incident resistor, with the reference current leaving the node.

acceptableStrategies.description: Check the divider ratios first, then write two-node KCL after the arm change and solve the 2-by-2 system exactly.
After the arm change, convert each source-and-divider side to a Thevenin pair at L and at R and load those two ports by the 6 ohm detector, recovering the same Ig.

milestones.criterion: Shows the original 2/4=3/6 balance and reports vL=vR=8 V with Ig=0.
After the lower-right 9 ohm change, obtains the open difference -1 V and the loaded pair vL=936/115 V, vR=1008/115 V, Ig=-12/115 A.
Derives the nodal system 11vL-2vR=72, -3vL+11vR=72 and rejects a ratio-blind unbalance claim or an open-circuit detector current.

commonErrors.description: Declares the original bridge unbalanced because the two upper arms are 2 ohm and 3 ohm, and reports a nonzero detector current before any arm is changed.
commonErrors.consequence: The balance condition is misstated as an equality of like-positioned resistors rather than an equality of arm ratios.

commonErrors.description: After the lower-right change, divides the open voltage difference -1 V by the 6 ohm detector and reports Ig=-1/6 A.
commonErrors.consequence: The detector loading of both mid-nodes is ignored, so the current has the wrong exact value.

hintTree.content: The original ratios are $2/4=1/2$ and $3/6=1/2$, so the two dividers both give $8\ \mathrm V$.
After the lower-right change the open right divider is $12\cdot 9/(3+9)=9\ \mathrm V$.
Clear the loaded KCL equations by $12$ at $L$ and by $18$ at $R$ to obtain $11v_L-2v_R=72$ and $-3v_L+11v_R=72$.

CIR:010118.canonicalSolution:
The original arm ratios are
\[
\frac{2}{4}=\frac12=\frac{3}{6},
\]
so the bridge is balanced. Each divider is independent of the detector:
\[
v_L=12\cdot\frac{4}{2+4}=\boxed{8\ \mathrm V},\qquad
v_R=12\cdot\frac{6}{3+6}=\boxed{8\ \mathrm V}.
\]
Hence $I_g=(8-8)/6=\boxed{0}$.

After the lower-right resistor is changed to $9\ \Omega$ and the detector is removed,
\[
v_L=8\ \mathrm V,\qquad
v_R=12\cdot\frac{9}{3+9}=9\ \mathrm V,
\]
so the open difference is
\[
\boxed{v_L-v_R=-1\ \mathrm V}.
\]

With the $6\ \Omega$ detector restored, KCL at $L$ (currents leaving) is
\[
\frac{v_L-12}{2}+\frac{v_L}{4}+\frac{v_L-v_R}{6}=0.
\]
Multiplication by $12$ yields $6(v_L-12)+3v_L+2(v_L-v_R)=0$, hence
\[
11v_L-2v_R=72.
\]
KCL at $R$ is
\[
\frac{v_R-12}{3}+\frac{v_R}{9}+\frac{v_R-v_L}{6}=0.
\]
Multiplication by $18$ yields $6(v_R-12)+2v_R+3(v_R-v_L)=0$, hence
\[
-3v_L+11v_R=72.
\]
Solving, $11$ times the first equation plus $2$ times the second eliminates $v_R$:
\[
121v_L-6v_L=792+144\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 115v_L=936,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{v_L=\frac{936}{115}\ \mathrm V}.
\]
Likewise $3$ times the first plus $11$ times the second eliminates $v_L$ and gives
\[
\boxed{v_R=\frac{1008}{115}\ \mathrm V}.
\]
The detector current referenced from $L$ to $R$ is
\[
I_g=\frac{v_L-v_R}{6}
=\frac{936-1008}{115\cdot 6}
=\frac{-72}{690}
=\boxed{-\frac{12}{115}\ \mathrm A}.
\]
The negative sign means the detector current actually flows from $R$ to $L$.

Sentence (i) is false: balance is a ratio condition, not an equality of the two upper arms. Sentence (ii) is false: the open difference $-1\ \mathrm V$ divided by $6\ \Omega$ is $-1/6\ \mathrm A$, which is not the loaded value $-12/115\ \mathrm A$.

No amplifier model and no one-port reduction of the whole bridge is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Originally $v_L=v_R=8\ \mathrm V$ and $I_g=0$. After the lower-right change the open difference is $-1\ \mathrm V$. Loaded, $11v_L-2v_R=72$ and $-3v_L+11v_R=72$ give $v_L=936/115\ \mathrm V$, $v_R=1008/115\ \mathrm V$, and $I_g=-12/115\ \mathrm A$.
The upper arms are 2 ohm and 3 ohm, so the bridge is unbalanced even before any change. The detector must carry a nonzero current.
After changing the lower-right arm to 9 ohm I keep the open voltages 8 V and 9 V and set Ig=(8-9)/6=-1/6 A.

CIR:010132.title: The 6 ohm resistor cube between opposite corners has Req=5 ohm; 12 V draws 12/5 A with outer 4/5 A, middle 2/5 A, and power 144/5 W
CIR:010132.objective: Use opposite-corner equipotentials on a uniform resistor cube to collapse twelve 6 Ω edges to the three-layer chain 6/3+6/6+6/3, then recover the source current, the two distinct branch currents, and the total dissipation.
CIR:010132.statement:
Twelve identical $6\,\Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube. A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source is connected between a pair of opposite corners (a space diagonal), not between adjacent vertices and not between opposite corners of a single face. Every edge resistance is $6\,\Omega$. Do not replace any face by a delta-wye transformation, and do not treat the cube as a Wheatstone bridge.

1. Label the driven corner $A$ and the opposite corner $H$. The three vertices adjacent to $A$ are equipotential; the three vertices adjacent to $H$ are a second equipotential. Collapse the network to three successive layers: the three edges leaving $A$, the six middle edges that join the two equipotential sets, and the three edges entering $H$.

2. Write the series chain of those layer equivalents and show that
   \[
   R_\mathrm{eq}=\frac{6}{3}+\frac{6}{6}+\frac{6}{3}=5\,\Omega.
   \]

3. With the $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source applied, compute the total source current $I$. Then split $I$ equally among the three outer edges at $A$ and among the six middle edges. Report both branch currents.

4. Compute the total power delivered by the source (equivalently absorbed by the twelve resistors).

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the cube is three independent $18\,\Omega$ paths in parallel, so $R_\mathrm{eq}=6\,\Omega$”; (ii) “opposite corners of a face use the same $5\,\Omega$ formula.”

Do not invoke a delta-wye on any face, do not load a Wheatstone bridge, and do not introduce a controlled source, an op-amp, or a reactive element.
permittedResults: For a uniform cube of edge $R$ driven between opposite corners, $R_\mathrm{eq}=R/3+R/6+R/3=5R/6$. With $R=6\,\Omega$ this is exactly $5\,\Omega$.
Current leaving an equipotential node splits equally among equal resistors attached to that node. The three outer edges therefore each carry $I/3$ and the six middle edges each carry $I/6$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify the two equipotential sets first, replace each layer by R/n, and only then apply Ohm's law to the 12 V source.
After Req=5 ohm, split the source current equally among the three outer edges and check the middle current by KCL at a near-corner node.

milestones.criterion: Collapses the cube by opposite-corner equipotentials to the chain 6/3+6/6+6/3=5 ohm.
Reports I=12/5 A, outer 4/5 A, middle 2/5 A, and total power 144/5 W.
Rejects three independent series paths and rejects the face-diagonal pair.

commonErrors.description: Deletes the six middle cross-links and treats the cube as three independent 18 Ω series paths in parallel, obtaining Req=6 Ω and I=2 A.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported equivalent is 1 Ω high, so every current and the dissipation belong to a different network.

commonErrors.description: Applies the face-diagonal formula Req=3R/4=9/2 Ω to the space-diagonal pair and computes I=8/3 A.
commonErrors.consequence: The driven terminals are the wrong pair, so the layer count, the currents, and the power are all attached to a different experiment.

hintTree.content: The three edges at $A$ are in parallel, as are the six middle edges and the three edges at $H$. That is the chain $6/3+6/6+6/3$.
The series sum is $2+1+2=5\,\Omega$. A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source then draws $I=12/5\,\mathrm{A}$.
Each outer edge carries $(12/5)/3=4/5\,\mathrm{A}$ and each middle edge carries $(12/5)/6=2/5\,\mathrm{A}$. The source power is $12\cdot 12/5=144/5\,\mathrm{W}$.

CIR:010132.canonicalSolution:
Opposite-corner symmetry places the three neighbors of $A$ at one potential and the three neighbors of $H$ at another. The twelve edges therefore collapse to three successive parallel layers:
\[
\frac{6}{3}+\frac{6}{6}+\frac{6}{3}=2+1+2=\boxed{5\,\Omega}.
\]
The $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source then draws
\[
I=\frac{12}{5}=\boxed{\frac{12}{5}\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]
Equal splitting on the outer and middle layers gives
\[
I_\mathrm{outer}=\frac{12/5}{3}=\boxed{\frac{4}{5}\,\mathrm{A}},
\qquad
I_\mathrm{middle}=\frac{12/5}{6}=\boxed{\frac{2}{5}\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]
KCL at a near-corner node recovers the same middle current: $4/5=2\cdot I_\mathrm{middle}$. The source power, which equals the twelve-resistor dissipation, is
\[
P=12\cdot\frac{12}{5}=\boxed{\frac{144}{5}\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: three series paths of three edges would be correct only if the six middle cross-links were deleted. Those links force the two equipotential sets and reduce $R_\mathrm{eq}$ from $6\,\Omega$ to $5\,\Omega$. Sentence (ii) is false: opposite corners of a face are a different pair; that resistance is $3R/4=9/2\,\Omega$, not $5\,\Omega$. (The value $7R/12$ belongs instead to adjacent cube vertices.)

The reduction uses only resistive equipotentials and series-parallel combination. It is not a delta-wye on a face, not a Wheatstone balance, and not a power-balance hunt through twelve unreduced KCL equations.

graderFixtures.proofText: Opposite-corner symmetry gives the chain $6/3+6/6+6/3=5\,\Omega$. Then $I=12/5\,\mathrm{A}$, each outer edge carries $4/5\,\mathrm{A}$, each middle edge carries $2/5\,\mathrm{A}$, and the source delivers $144/5\,\mathrm{W}$.
I take three independent paths of three 6 ohm resistors, so each path is 18 ohm and Req=6 ohm. Then I=12/6=2 A and I never use the middle cross-links.
Opposite corners of the cube use the face formula Req=3R/4=9/2 ohm, so I=12/(9/2)=8/3 A.

CIR:010133.title: The infinite 1 ohm series-then-shunt ladder locks to phi=(1+sqrt5)/2; 10 V draws 5(sqrt5-1) A, first node 5(3-sqrt5) V, power 50(sqrt5-1)
CIR:010133.objective: Close the input resistance of an infinite 1 Ω series-then-shunt ladder on the positive fixed point of X=1+X/(1+X), reject the negative root, and recover the 10 V source current, the first-node voltage, and the delivered power.
CIR:010133.statement:
An infinite resistive ladder is built from identical cells. Each cell is a $1\,\Omega$ series resistor followed by a $1\,\Omega$ shunt to ground; after that shunt the remainder of the ladder is an identical copy of the whole network. Let $X$ be the input resistance seen by a $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source attached at the left. Do not reverse the cell into a shunt-then-series ladder, and do not replace the infinite tail by a finite $N$-section truncation.

1. Write the fixed-point equation
   \[
   X=1+\frac{X}{1+X}
   \]
   and clear it to a quadratic.

2. Solve the quadratic. Identify the unique positive root and show that it equals $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$. Explicitly reject the negative root.

3. With $10\,\mathrm{V}$ applied, compute the source current $I=10/X$. Rationalize the answer to a multiple of $\sqrt{5}-1$.

4. The first interior node is the node after the leading $1\,\Omega$ series resistor. Compute its voltage.

5. Compute the power delivered by the $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source.

6. Audit both sentences: (i) “both roots of the quadratic are admissible input resistances”; (ii) “the cell is a shunt $1\,\Omega$ followed by a series $1\,\Omega$, so $X=1\parallel(1+X)$.”

Do not introduce a capacitor or inductor, do not take a finite-section limit as the required method, and do not convert the ladder into a Wheatstone or delta-wye network.
permittedResults: Clearing $X=1+X/(1+X)$ produces $(X-1)(1+X)=X$, hence $X^2-X-1=0$.
If $X=\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$, then $1/X=\varphi-1=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$ and $10/X=5(\sqrt{5}-1)$. The first-node voltage is $10(1-1/X)=5(3-\sqrt{5})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the self-similar input resistance, discard the negative quadratic root, then apply Ohm's law to the 10 V source and the leading series drop.
Use 1/X=X-1 after selecting phi, so I=10/X and v1=10(1-1/X) become rationalizations in sqrt5 without a finite truncation.

milestones.criterion: Forms X=1+X/(1+X), reduces it to X^2-X-1=0, and keeps only phi=(1+sqrt5)/2.
Reports I=5(sqrt5-1) A, first-node voltage 5(3-sqrt5) V, and power 50(sqrt5-1) W.
Rejects the negative root and rejects reversing the series-then-shunt cell.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the negative root X=(1-sqrt5)/2 as an admissible input resistance and reports a negative source current -5(1+sqrt5) A.
commonErrors.consequence: A passive ladder is assigned a negative driving-point resistance, so the current, the first-node voltage, and the power all change sign.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the cell to a shunt 1 Ω followed by a series 1 Ω, writes X=1||(1+X), and uses the positive root (-1+sqrt5)/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The quadratic becomes X^2+X-1=0, so I=5(sqrt5+1) A belongs to a different infinite network.

hintTree.content: From $X=1+X/(1+X)$ one obtains $X^2-X-1=0$, so $X=(1\pm\sqrt{5})/2$.
Keep only $X=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$. Then $I=10/X=5(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{A}$.
The remaining resistance after the leading $1\,\Omega$ is $X-1$, so the first-node voltage is $10(X-1)/X=5(3-\sqrt{5})\,\mathrm{V}$. Power is $10I=50(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{W}$.

CIR:010133.canonicalSolution:
The series-then-shunt cell gives the fixed point
\[
X=1+\frac{X}{1+X}.
\]
Clearing the denominator,
\[
X-1=\frac{X}{1+X}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
(X-1)(1+X)=X
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
X^2-1=X
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
X^2-X-1=0.
\]
The roots are
\[
X=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}.
\]
A passive resistive input cannot be negative, so
\[
X=\varphi=\boxed{\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\,\Omega},
\]
and the root $(1-\sqrt{5})/2$ is rejected. The $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source then draws
\[
I=\frac{10}{\varphi}=10\cdot\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}}=5(\sqrt{5}-1)
=\boxed{5(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]
After the leading series resistor the remaining resistance is $X-1=1/X$, so the first-node voltage is
\[
v_1=10\cdot\frac{X-1}{X}=10\Bigl(1-\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\Bigr)
=\boxed{5(3-\sqrt{5})\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
The delivered power is
\[
P=10I=\boxed{50(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $(1-\sqrt{5})/2<0$ cannot be the driving-point resistance of a network of positive resistors; using it yields a negative source current. Sentence (ii) is false: a shunt-then-series cell produces the different quadratic $X^2+X-1=0$ and the different positive root $(-1+\sqrt{5})/2$.

The argument uses only a resistive fixed point and Ohm's law. It is not a finite-section limit, not a reactive transient, and not a delta-wye or Wheatstone reduction.

graderFixtures.proofText: The fixed point $X=1+X/(1+X)$ is $X^2-X-1=0$. The positive root is $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$; the negative root is rejected. Then $I=5(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{A}$, the first node is $5(3-\sqrt{5})\,\mathrm{V}$, and the source delivers $50(\sqrt{5}-1)\,\mathrm{W}$.
Both roots are fine. I take X=(1-sqrt5)/2 and I=10/X=-5(1+sqrt5) A, then proceed with that input resistance.
I model each cell as a 1 ohm shunt then a 1 ohm series into the tail, so X=1||(1+X) and X=(-1+sqrt5)/2. Then I=5(sqrt5+1) A.

CIR:010134.title: The 12 V, 6k/3k divider with a 6k meter reads 3 V; unloaded 4 V, currents 1.5/0.5/1 mA, error -1/4, meter 1.5 mW
CIR:010134.objective: Compare the unloaded 6 kΩ/3 kΩ divider with the same divider loaded by a 6 kΩ voltmeter across the lower branch, then report the reading, the three branch currents, the relative error, and the meter dissipation.
CIR:010134.statement:
A DC source $V_s=12\,\mathrm{V}$ drives a series divider: $R_1=6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ from the source to the output node and $R_2=3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ from that node to ground. A voltmeter of internal resistance $R_m=6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ is placed across $R_2$ (not across $R_1$, and not in series with the divider). Resistances are exact.

1. With the meter disconnected, compute the unloaded output $v_\mathrm{open}$.

2. With the meter attached, replace $R_2\parallel R_m$ by a single resistance and compute the loaded reading $v_\mathrm{read}$.

3. Compute the source current, the meter current, and the current in $R_2$. State the units in milliamperes.

4. Form the relative loading error $(v_\mathrm{read}-v_\mathrm{open})/v_\mathrm{open}$.

5. Compute the power absorbed by the meter.

6. Audit both sentences: (i) “a voltmeter does not load the divider, so the reading is the unloaded $4\,\mathrm{V}$”; (ii) “the meter belongs in series with $R_1$ and $R_2$, or else across $R_1$.”

Do not convert the divider into a Wheatstone bridge, do not introduce a delta-wye, and do not replace the DC source by a phasor or a transient.
permittedResults: $3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. The loaded divider is then $6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ over $2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, so $v_\mathrm{read}=12\cdot 2/8=3\,\mathrm{V}$.
Relative loading error is $(v_\mathrm{read}-v_\mathrm{open})/v_\mathrm{open}$. Here $(3-4)/4=-1/4$. Meter power is $v_\mathrm{read}^2/R_m=9/6000=1.5\,\mathrm{mW}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the open divider first, then replace R2 by R2||Rm and reread the same voltage-divider formula.
After v_read=3 V, obtain the three currents from Ohm's law and check KCL and meter power v^2/Rm.

milestones.criterion: Computes the unloaded divider 4 V and the parallel load 3k||6k=2k.
Reports the reading 3 V, currents 1.5/0.5/1 mA, error -1/4, and meter 1.5 mW.
Rejects an unloaded reading and rejects a series or upper-branch meter connection.

commonErrors.description: Treats the voltmeter as an open circuit and reports the unloaded 4 V as the instrument reading, with zero relative error.
commonErrors.consequence: The 25 percent loading drop is missed, so the reported reading, currents, and meter power are those of a different experiment.

commonErrors.description: Places the 6 kΩ meter in series with the 6 kΩ and 3 kΩ resistors and reports a 4.8 V drop across the meter, or else places the meter across the upper 6 kΩ.
commonErrors.consequence: The instrument is no longer a shunt on R2, so the reading is not the loaded divider voltage.

hintTree.content: Unloaded: $v_\mathrm{open}=12\cdot 3/(6+3)=4\,\mathrm{V}$. Loaded: $3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.
The loaded reading is $12\cdot 2/8=3\,\mathrm{V}$. Source current is $12/8\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{mA}$.
Meter current $3/6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=0.5\,\mathrm{mA}$, lower-branch current $3/3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=1\,\mathrm{mA}$, error $(3-4)/4=-1/4$, meter power $1.5\,\mathrm{mW}$.

CIR:010134.canonicalSolution:
Disconnected, the divider is
\[
v_\mathrm{open}=12\cdot\frac{3}{6+3}=\boxed{4\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
With the meter across $R_2$,
\[
R_2\parallel R_m=3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=\boxed{2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega},
\]
so the loaded reading is
\[
v_\mathrm{read}=12\cdot\frac{2}{6+2}=\boxed{3\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
The three currents are
\[
I_s=\frac{12}{8\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}=\boxed{1.5\,\mathrm{mA}},
\qquad
I_m=\frac{3}{6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}=\boxed{0.5\,\mathrm{mA}},
\qquad
I_2=\frac{3}{3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}=\boxed{1\,\mathrm{mA}}.
\]
They satisfy KCL at the output node: $1.5=0.5+1$. The relative error is
\[
\frac{3-4}{4}=\boxed{-\frac{1}{4}},
\]
and the meter dissipation is
\[
\frac{3^2}{6000}=\boxed{1.5\,\mathrm{mW}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $R_m$ is comparable to $R_2$, so the reading drops from $4\,\mathrm{V}$ to $3\,\mathrm{V}$. Sentence (ii) is false: a voltmeter is a shunt across the measured branch. Placing it in series, or across $R_1$, measures neither $v_\mathrm{open}$ nor $v_\mathrm{read}$.

The calculation is a loaded resistive divider. It is not a Wheatstone bridge, not a delta-wye, and not an AC or transient problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: Unloaded, $v_\mathrm{open}=4\,\mathrm{V}$. Then $3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and the meter reads $3\,\mathrm{V}$. The currents are $1.5\,\mathrm{mA}$, $0.5\,\mathrm{mA}$, and $1\,\mathrm{mA}$; the relative error is $-1/4$; the meter absorbs $1.5\,\mathrm{mW}$.
A voltmeter has huge resistance, so I report the unloaded divider 4 V as the reading. The error is zero and I do not form 3k||6k.
I put the 6 kΩ meter in series with the 6 kΩ and 3 kΩ, so the string is 15 kΩ and the meter drop is 12*(6/15)=4.8 V.

CIR:010219.title: The floating 10 V source and 3 A injection force va=56/5 V and vb=6/5 V
CIR:010219.objective: Write a supernode KCL equation around a floating independent voltage source, enforce the source constraint, solve the two node potentials, and recover the current through the voltage source.
CIR:010219.statement:
A connected resistive circuit has two nonreference nodes $a$ and $b$ and a grounded reference. The branches are:

- a $4\ \Omega$ resistor from $a$ to ground;
- a $6\ \Omega$ resistor from $b$ to ground;
- an independent $3\ \mathrm A$ current source directed from ground into node $a$;
- an independent $10\ \mathrm V$ voltage source connecting $a$ to $b$ with the constraint $v_a-v_b=10\ \mathrm V$ (positive terminal at $a$).

No other elements are present. In particular the $10\ \mathrm V$ source is floating: neither of its terminals is grounded.

1. Explain why $a$ and $b$ cannot be treated as independent KCL nodes, form the supernode that encloses both terminals of the voltage source, and write the single supernode current balance.

2. Adjoin the source constraint and solve for $v_a$ and $v_b$ exactly.

3. Let $i_{ab}$ be the current through the voltage source directed from $a$ to $b$. Compute $i_{ab}$ from KCL at $b$ (or at $a$) and substitute the solved potentials to check both node balances.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a $10\ \mathrm V$ source from $a$ to $b$ means $v_a=10\ \mathrm V$ and $v_b=0$”; (ii) “the supernode equation is $v_a/4+v_b/6=0$ because a voltage source supplies whatever current is required.”

Do not convert the circuit to a Thevenin or Norton one-port, do not introduce a dependent source, and do not use mesh analysis as the primary method. The exercise is a two-node supernode.
permittedResults: KCL on a supernode equates the algebraic sum of currents leaving through the cut resistors to the algebraic sum of independent currents entering the surface.
An independent voltage source $v_a-v_b=V_s$ does not by itself ground either terminal.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form the supernode, write one KCL equation plus the voltage constraint, then back-solve i_ab from KCL at b.
Keep i_ab as an explicit unknown and write ordinary KCL at a and at b together with va-vb=10, recovering the same three numbers.

milestones.criterion: Writes the supernode balance va/4+vb/6=3 together with va-vb=10.
Solves va=56/5 V, vb=6/5 V and recovers the voltage-source current i_ab=1/5 A.
Rejects treating the floating source as a grounded 10 V node and rejects dropping the 3 A injection from the supernode.

commonErrors.description: Sets va=10 V and vb=0 because the source is 10 V, as if terminal b were the reference.
commonErrors.consequence: The floating constraint is replaced by two absolute potentials, and both resistor currents are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Writes the supernode equation as va/4+vb/6=0, omitting the 3 A source that enters the surface.
commonErrors.consequence: The only consistent solution is the zero state, which ignores the independent injection.

hintTree.content: Currents leaving the supernode through the resistors are $v_a/4$ and $v_b/6$; the $3\ \mathrm A$ source enters the surface at $a$.
Substitute $v_a=v_b+10$ into $v_a/4+v_b/6=3$ and clear by $12$.
At node $b$ the only resistor current is $v_b/6$, so that current must be supplied by $i_{ab}$.

CIR:010219.canonicalSolution:
The $10\ \mathrm V$ source ties $v_a$ to $v_b$, so the two nodes are not independent KCL nodes. Enclose $a$, $b$, and the voltage source in a supernode. The currents leaving that surface through resistors are $v_a/4$ and $v_b/6$; the $3\ \mathrm A$ source enters the surface. Therefore
\[
\frac{v_a}{4}+\frac{v_b}{6}=3.
\]
The source constraint is $v_a-v_b=10$, or $v_a=v_b+10$. Substitution yields
\[
\frac{v_b+10}{4}+\frac{v_b}{6}=3.
\]
Multiplication by $12$ gives $3(v_b+10)+2v_b=36$, hence $5v_b+30=36$ and
\[
\boxed{v_b=\frac{6}{5}\ \mathrm V},\qquad
\boxed{v_a=\frac{56}{5}\ \mathrm V}.
\]

Let $i_{ab}$ be the voltage-source current from $a$ to $b$. KCL at $b$ (currents leaving) is
\[
\frac{v_b}{6}-i_{ab}=0,
\]
so
\[
i_{ab}=\frac{v_b}{6}=\frac{6/5}{6}=\boxed{\frac{1}{5}\ \mathrm A}.
\]
KCL at $a$ is the audit:
\[
\frac{v_a}{4}+i_{ab}-3
=\frac{56/5}{4}+\frac{1}{5}-3
=\frac{14}{5}+\frac{1}{5}-3
=3-3=0.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $v_a-v_b=10$ does not ground $b$. Setting $v_a=10$ and $v_b=0$ would violate the supernode balance $10/4+0=2.5\neq 3$. Sentence (ii) is false: the voltage source current is internal to the supernode and cancels; the independent $3\ \mathrm A$ injection is not internal and must appear on the right-hand side.

No one-port reduction is used. The two unknowns are the node potentials, closed by one supernode KCL equation and one source constraint.

graderFixtures.proofText: The supernode is $v_a/4+v_b/6=3$ with $v_a-v_b=10$. The solution is $v_a=56/5\ \mathrm V$, $v_b=6/5\ \mathrm V$, and the voltage-source current from $a$ to $b$ is $1/5\ \mathrm A$.
The 10 V source from a to b means va=10 V and vb=0. Then the 4 ohm carries 2.5 A and the 6 ohm carries nothing.
A voltage source is a short for KCL, so the supernode equation is va/4+vb/6=0. Combined with va-vb=10 this forces inconsistent or zero resistor currents.

CIR:010220.title: Clockwise supermesh currents 2/5 A and 7/5 A put 42/5 V on the 1 A source
CIR:010220.objective: Write a supermesh KVL equation around a shared independent current source, enforce the mesh-current constraint, solve both mesh currents, and audit the current-source voltage by nodal analysis.
CIR:010220.statement:
A planar circuit shares a grounded bottom rail. The elements, from left to right, are:

- an independent $10\ \mathrm V$ source from the bottom rail to a left-top node $P$, positive terminal at $P$;
- a $4\ \Omega$ resistor from $P$ to a top node $T$;
- an independent $1\ \mathrm A$ current source from the bottom rail upward to $T$;
- a $6\ \Omega$ resistor from $T$ to the bottom rail.

There are two windows. Let $i_1$ be the clockwise mesh current in the left window (the window that contains the $10\ \mathrm V$ source, the $4\ \Omega$ resistor, and the current source). Let $i_2$ be the clockwise mesh current in the right window (the window that contains the current source and the $6\ \Omega$ resistor). With these references the current source occupies the shared vertical branch and its upward current is $i_2-i_1$.

1. Write the current-source constraint on $i_1$ and $i_2$. Form the supermesh that excludes the shared current source and write KVL around the outer path through the $10\ \mathrm V$ source, the $4\ \Omega$ resistor, and the $6\ \Omega$ resistor.

2. Solve for $i_1$ and $i_2$ exactly.

3. Let $v_T$ be the voltage at $T$ relative to the bottom rail. Compute $v_T$ from the left drop $10-4i_1$ and confirm it from the right drop $6i_2$. This $v_T$ is the voltage across the current source, positive at the top.

4. Give an independent nodal audit at $T$: express the $4\ \Omega$ and $6\ \Omega$ currents from $v_T$ and check KCL against the $1\ \mathrm A$ injection.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “clockwise references make the shared constraint $i_1-i_2=1$”; (ii) “the top of the current source is held at $10\ \mathrm V$ by the left source.”

Do not introduce a dependent source, a supernode as the primary method, or a transient. The exercise is a two-mesh supermesh with a nodal voltage audit.
permittedResults: KVL on the supermesh through a source $V_s$ and resistors $R_1$, $R_2$ carrying the respective mesh currents is $R_1 i_1+R_2 i_2=V_s$ when the source rise equals those ohmic drops.
The voltage on an independent current source is not an independent datum; it is whatever KVL or a node potential requires.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the shared-current constraint, KVL on the outer supermesh, then read vT from either resistor drop.
Use a single unknown vT at the top of the current source, write KCL at T with the left node held at 10 V, and recover the same mesh currents as (10-vT)/4 and vT/6.

milestones.criterion: Writes i2-i1=1 and the supermesh KVL 4i1+6i2=10.
Solves i1=2/5 A, i2=7/5 A and reports the current-source top voltage 42/5 V.
Confirms the nodal audit at T and rejects a reversed mesh constraint or the claim that T is held at 10 V.

commonErrors.description: Writes the clockwise shared-branch law as i1-i2=1 instead of i2-i1=1.
commonErrors.consequence: Both mesh currents and the current-source voltage fail the nodal KCL audit at T.

commonErrors.description: Reports the voltage at the top of the current source as 10 V, identifying T with the left source node P.
commonErrors.consequence: The 4 ohm resistor is treated as having zero drop, which contradicts a nonzero i1.

hintTree.content: Clockwise $i_1$ goes down the shared branch and clockwise $i_2$ goes up it, so $i_2-i_1=1$.
The outer KVL is the $4\ \Omega$ drop plus the $6\ \Omega$ drop equal to $10\ \mathrm V$.
$v_T=10-4i_1$. After $i_1=2/5$ this is $42/5\ \mathrm V$, which must also equal $6i_2$.

CIR:010220.canonicalSolution:
With both meshes clockwise, $i_1$ descends the shared branch and $i_2$ ascends it. The upward $1\ \mathrm A$ source therefore enforces
\[
i_2-i_1=1.
\]
The supermesh excludes that shared branch. Traversing the outer path, the ohmic drops $4i_1$ and $6i_2$ absorb the $10\ \mathrm V$ rise, so
\[
4i_1+6i_2=10.
\]
Substitute $i_2=i_1+1$:
\[
4i_1+6(i_1+1)=10\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 10i_1+6=10\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{i_1=\frac{2}{5}\ \mathrm A}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{i_2=\frac{7}{5}\ \mathrm A}.
\]

The left-top node $P$ is held at $10\ \mathrm V$. The $4\ \Omega$ resistor carries $i_1$ from $P$ to $T$, so
\[
v_T=10-4\cdot\frac{2}{5}=10-\frac{8}{5}=\boxed{\frac{42}{5}\ \mathrm V}.
\]
The right check is $v_T=6i_2=6\cdot(7/5)=42/5\ \mathrm V$. This is the voltage across the current source, positive at $T$.

Nodal audit at $T$: the current arriving through the $4\ \Omega$ resistor is
\[
\frac{10-v_T}{4}=\frac{10-42/5}{4}=\frac{8/5}{4}=\frac{2}{5}\ \mathrm A=i_1,
\]
the current leaving through the $6\ \Omega$ resistor is
\[
\frac{v_T}{6}=\frac{42/5}{6}=\frac{7}{5}\ \mathrm A=i_2,
\]
and KCL at $T$ is $i_1+1=i_2$, or $2/5+1=7/5$.

Sentence (i) is false: $i_1-i_2=1$ reverses the shared-branch orientation and would produce $i_1=8/5\ \mathrm A$, $i_2=3/5\ \mathrm A$, and a current-source voltage $18/5\ \mathrm V$ that fails the nodal audit. Sentence (ii) is false: the $10\ \mathrm V$ source holds $P$, not $T$; the $4\ \Omega$ drop of $8/5\ \mathrm V$ separates them.

No dependent source and no transient model is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Clockwise references give $i_2-i_1=1$ and $4i_1+6i_2=10$, so $i_1=2/5\ \mathrm A$ and $i_2=7/5\ \mathrm A$. The current-source top voltage is $v_T=10-4i_1=6i_2=42/5\ \mathrm V$, and KCL at $T$ reads $2/5+1=7/5$.
I take the shared law as i1-i2=1. Then 4i1+6(i1-1)=10 gives i1=8/5 A and i2=3/5 A, so vT=6i2=18/5 V.
The left source fixes the entire top rail, so the current-source voltage is 10 V. The 4 ohm drop is ignored.
