CIR:020221.title: Z=(2s+1)/(s+1) is positive-real and is 1 ohm in series with 1 ohm || 1 H
CIR:020221.objective: Split Z=(2s+1)/(s+1) as 1+s/(s+1), synthesize the Foster RL network 1 ohm series with 1 ohm parallel to 1 H, prove Re Z(jw)=(1+2w^2)/(1+w^2)>0, and invert the 1 V step current 1-(1/2)e^{-t/2} with initial 1/2 A and final 1 A.
CIR:020221.statement:
A one-port has the driving-point impedance
\[
Z(s)=\frac{2s+1}{s+1}\ \Omega.
\]
The port voltage $v$ and port current $i$ obey the passive sign convention: $i$ enters the terminal at which $v$ is positive. In the sinusoidal steady state the same convention applies to the phasors $\mathbf V=Z(j\omega)\mathbf I$, whether both phasors are peak values or both are RMS values. The real part $\operatorname{Re}Z(j\omega)$ is therefore the ratio of average absorbed power to the associated mean-square current, and it must be compared with zero as a real number of ohms. Time-domain $v(t)$ and $i(t)$ below are instantaneous, not RMS.

1. Decompose $Z(s)=1+s/(s+1)$ and synthesize the interconnection of a $1\ \Omega$ resistor in series with the parallel combination of a $1\ \Omega$ resistor and a $1\ \mathrm H$ inductor.
2. Compute $\operatorname{Re}Z(j\omega)$ for real $\omega$ and show
   \[
   \operatorname{Re}Z(j\omega)=\frac{1+2\omega^2}{1+\omega^2}>0.
   \]
3. The port is driven by the voltage step $v(t)=u(t)$ volt, with zero inductor current at $t=0^-$. Find $i(t)$ for $t\ge0$. Confirm the initial value $1/2\ \mathrm A$ and the final value $1\ \mathrm A$ from the time-domain formula and from the initial- and final-value theorems applied to $I(s)$.
4. Audit the claim that $Z$ is a single $2\ \Omega$ resistor in series with $1\ \mathrm H$, and the claim that the step current is $1-\frac12 e^{-t}$ (using the pole of $Z$ rather than the pole of $Y=1/Z$).

This is a driving-point frequency-response and synthesis check. It is not a two-port conversion and not a transmission-line calculation.
permittedResults: If $Z(j\omega)=(1+2j\omega)/(1+j\omega)$, then $\operatorname{Re}Z=(1+2\omega^2)/(1+\omega^2)$.
The admittance $Y=(s+1)/(2s+1)$ has a single stable pole at $s=-1/2$. A $1/s$ voltage therefore produces a current with DC value $1$ and transient $e^{-t/2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Extract the series 1 ohm, recognize s/(s+1) as 1 ohm || 1 H, then invert Y(s)/s.
Evaluate Z at s=0 and s=infty to read the DC short and the t=0+ open inductor, then confirm with Re Z(jw) and the two limit theorems.

milestones.criterion: Splits Z=1+s/(s+1) and identifies the series 1 ohm with parallel 1 ohm and 1 H.
Proves Re Z(jw)=(1+2w^2)/(1+w^2)>0 for all real w.
Inverts the 1 V step to i=1-(1/2)e^{-t/2} with initial 1/2 A and final 1 A, and rejects both a series 2 ohm+1 H model and the pole of Z as the current rate.

commonErrors.description: Synthesizes Z as 2 ohm in series with 1 H, i.e. Z=2+s, and obtains a step current that settles to 1/2 A.
commonErrors.consequence: The DC resistance, the parallel resistor, and the final current of 1 A are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the pole s=-1 of Z as the current time constant and reports i=1-(1/2)e^{-t}.
commonErrors.consequence: The transient is that of Z rather than of Y=1/Z, so i'(0+) and the inductor time constant are wrong.

hintTree.content: $Z-1=(2s+1)/(s+1)-1=s/(s+1)$, which is $sL\parallel R$ with $L=R=1$.
Multiply $Z(j\omega)$ by $(1-j\omega)/(1-j\omega)$ and read the real part.

CIR:020221.canonicalSolution:
Algebraic splitting gives
\[
Z(s)=\frac{2s+1}{s+1}=1+\frac{s}{s+1}.
\]
The parallel combination of $R=1\ \Omega$ and $L=1\ \mathrm H$ has impedance
\[
\frac{s\cdot 1}{s+1}=\frac{s}{s+1}\ \Omega,
\]
so $Z$ is exactly a $1\ \Omega$ resistor in series with that parallel pair:
\[
\boxed{Z\equiv 1\ \Omega\ \text{series with}\ (1\ \Omega\parallel 1\ \mathrm H)}.
\]
On the imaginary axis,
\[
Z(j\omega)=\frac{1+2j\omega}{1+j\omega}\cdot\frac{1-j\omega}{1-j\omega}
=\frac{1+2\omega^2+j\omega}{1+\omega^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Re}Z(j\omega)=\frac{1+2\omega^2}{1+\omega^2}>0}
\]
for every real $\omega$. (In particular the value lies in $[1,2)$ for
finite real $\omega$, and tends to $2$ as $|\omega|\to\infty$.)

The $1\ \mathrm V$ step has transform $1/s$. The port current is
\[
I(s)=\frac{1}{sZ(s)}=\frac{s+1}{s(2s+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{2s+1}
=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1/2}{s+1/2}.
\]
Hence, for $t\ge0$,
\[
\boxed{i(t)=1-\tfrac12 e^{-t/2}\ \mathrm A}.
\]
Direct substitution gives $i(0^+)=1/2\ \mathrm A$ and $i(\infty)=1\ \mathrm A$. The transform checks are
\[
\lim_{s\to\infty}sI(s)=\frac12,\qquad\lim_{s\to0}sI(s)=1,
\]
and the only pole of $sI(s)$ is $s=-1/2$. These limits match the network: at $t=0^+$ the inductor is an open circuit, so $Z(\infty)=2\ \Omega$ and $i(0^+)=1/2\ \mathrm A$; at DC the inductor is a short, so $Z(0)=1\ \Omega$ and $i(\infty)=1\ \mathrm A$.

A series $2\ \Omega$+$1\ \mathrm H$ network would be $Z=2+s$, whose real part is the constant $2$ and whose step current tends to $1/2\ \mathrm A$, not $1\ \mathrm A$. Using the pole $s=-1$ of $Z$ in place of the pole of $Y$ produces the incorrect transient $e^{-t}$ and the wrong time constant.

graderFixtures.proofText: Z=1+s/(s+1) is $1\ \Omega$ in series with $1\ \Omega\parallel 1\ \mathrm H$. $\operatorname{Re}Z(j\omega)=(1+2\omega^2)/(1+\omega^2)>0$. The $1\ \mathrm V$ step produces $i=1-\frac12 e^{-t/2}$, from $1/2\ \mathrm A$ to $1\ \mathrm A$.
Z(infty)=2, so the network is 2 ohm in series with 1 H. Then I=1/[s(s+2)] and the current settles to 1/2 A.
Z has its pole at s=-1, so the step current is i=1-(1/2)e^{-t}. The initial value is still 1/2 A.

CIR:020322.title: A matched 1 ohm pair with a shunt series-LC is a notch, not a band-pass
CIR:020322.objective: Derive H(s)=(s²+1)/(2s²+s+2) for a 1 Ω source, 1 Ω load, and shunt series L=C=1, locate the notch and left-half poles, and compute the half-power frequencies relative to the common end-gain 1/2.
CIR:020322.statement:
An ideal voltage source $v_s$ drives a series source resistor
$R_S=1.00\ \Omega$. At the output node a load $R_L=1.00\ \Omega$ goes to
the common reference, and a series $L$-$C$ branch is connected in shunt
across that same node, with
\[
L=1.00\ \mathrm H,\qquad C=1.00\ \mathrm F.
\]
The output voltage $v_o$ is the voltage of that node. All elements are
ideal, lumped, linear, and time-invariant. The transfer function is the
Laplace voltage ratio
\[
H(s)=\frac{V_o(s)}{V_s(s)},
\]
and the frequency response is the substitution $s=j\omega$ with $\omega$
in radians per second. $|H(j\omega)|$ is a voltage ratio; it is not a
power ratio in dBm and it is not an RMS-to-peak conversion. Do not replace
the circuit by a series $R$-$L$-$C$ with the output taken across $R$, and
do not treat the source as ideal with $R_S=0$.

1. Write the shunt series-$LC$ impedance $Z_{LC}(s)$ and the parallel
   combination of $Z_{LC}$ with $R_L$. Then include $R_S$ by voltage
   division and obtain the rational function $H(s)$. Show that
   \[
   H(s)=\frac{s^2+1}{2s^2+s+2}.
   \]
2. Locate the finite zeros and the poles. Identify the notch angular
   frequency, the common DC and high-frequency voltage gains, and confirm
   that both poles lie in the open left half-plane.
3. Half-power frequencies are defined relative to the common end-gain
   $|H(0)|=|H(\infty)|=1/2$: they are the positive $\omega$ at which
   $|H(j\omega)|^2$ equals half of $(1/2)^2$, i.e.
   $|H|=(1/2)/\sqrt{2}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$. Do not take half-power to mean
   $|H|=1/2$ (that is the passband voltage ratio itself) and do not use a
   series-RLC $|H|=1/\sqrt{2}$ template. Derive the exact pair
   \[
   \omega_L=\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}{4},\qquad
   \omega_H=\frac{\sqrt{17}+1}{4},
   \]
   and compute the product $\omega_L\omega_H$ and the difference
   $\omega_H-\omega_L$.

Audit these claims: (i) because $L=C=1$, the network is a series-RLC
band-pass with peak gain $1$ and half-power points where $|H|=1/\sqrt{2}$;
(ii) $R_S$ may be omitted, giving $H=(s^2+1)/(s^2+s+1)$; (iii) the poles
are $[-1\pm j\sqrt{15}]/2$. Keep ohms, henries, farads, and rad/s
dimensionally distinct.
permittedResults: Voltage division through $R_S$ into a load $Z_p$ gives $H=Z_p/(R_S+Z_p)$. With $R_S=R_L=1$ and $Z_{LC}=(s^2+1)/s$, this collapses to $H=(s^2+1)/(2s^2+s+2)$.
If $2s^2+s+2=0$, then $s=[-1\pm j\sqrt{15}]/4$. Both real parts equal $-1/4<0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form Z_LC=(s²+1)/s, parallel it with 1 Ω, then voltage-divide through RS=1 Ω and read zeros, poles, and |H(jω)|².
Use H=Z_LC/(1+2 Z_LC) from the matched divider, then impose 4(1-ω²)²=ω² to split the half-power condition about the notch.

milestones.criterion: Derives H(s)=(s²+1)/(2s²+s+2) from the shunt series-LC, the 1 Ω load, and the 1 Ω source resistor.
Identifies the notch at ω=1, the end-gain 1/2, and the LHP poles (-1±j√15)/4.
Computes half-power frequencies relative to the end-gain 1/2, obtaining (√17±1)/4, product 1, and difference 1/2.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the shunt series-LC by a series-RLC band-pass, omits RS, or takes half-power as |H|=1/2 or |H|=1/√2 about a peak of 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned H=(s²+1)/(2s²+s+2) and the end-gain-relative pair (√17±1)/4 never appear.

commonErrors.description: Reports the poles as [-1±j√15]/2, or otherwise fails to divide the quadratic 2s²+s+2 by its leading coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The damping -1/4 and the imaginary part √15/4 are both wrong, so stability and the characteristic equation are misread.

hintTree.content: First form $Z_{LC}=s+1/s=(s^2+1)/s$. The loaded impedance is $Z_p=Z_{LC}\parallel 1$, and $H=Z_p/(1+Z_p)$.
The denominator $2s^2+s+2$ is a quadratic with discriminant $1-16=-15$. Divide by the leading $2$ when applying the quadratic formula.
Set $|H(j\omega)|^2=1/8$. The identity $4(1-\omega^2)^2=\omega^2$ splits into $2|1-\omega^2|=\omega$, which is one quadratic below the notch and one above it.

CIR:020322.canonicalSolution:
The shunt branch is a series inductor and capacitor, so
\[
Z_{LC}(s)=sL+\frac1{sC}=s+\frac1s=\frac{s^2+1}{s}.
\]
In parallel with the $1\ \Omega$ load,
\[
Z_p(s)
=\frac{Z_{LC}}{1+Z_{LC}}
=\frac{s^2+1}{s^2+s+1}.
\]
Including the $1\ \Omega$ source resistor by voltage division,
\[
H(s)
=\frac{Z_p}{1+Z_p}
=\frac{s^2+1}{s^2+s+1+s^2+1}
=\boxed{\frac{s^2+1}{2s^2+s+2}}.
\]
Equivalently, $H=Z_{LC}/(1+2Z_{LC})$ yields the same rational function.

Finite zeros lie where $s^2+1=0$, i.e. $s=\pm j$. Thus $H(j1)=0$: the
network is a notch at $\omega=1\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, where $Z_{LC}=0$ shorts
the output. The common end-gains are
\[
H(0)=\frac12,\qquad
\lim_{|s|\to\infty}H(s)=\frac12.
\]
The poles solve $2s^2+s+2=0$:
\[
s=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-16}}{4}
=\boxed{\frac{-1\pm j\sqrt{15}}{4}}.
\]
Each real part is $-1/4<0$, so both poles are strictly stable. The
quadratic formula must divide by the leading coefficient $2$; the roots
are not $[-1\pm j\sqrt{15}]/2$.

On the $j\omega$ axis,
\[
H(j\omega)
=\frac{1-\omega^2}{2-2\omega^2+j\omega},
\qquad
|H(j\omega)|^2
=\frac{(1-\omega^2)^2}{4(1-\omega^2)^2+\omega^2}.
\]
Half-power relative to the end-gain $1/2$ means $|H|^2=(1/4)/2=1/8$, or
$|H|=1/(2\sqrt{2})$. Then
\[
4(1-\omega^2)^2=\omega^2
\qquad(\omega>0)
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
2|1-\omega^2|=\omega.
\]
Below the notch, $2(1-\omega^2)=\omega$ rearranges to $2\omega^2+\omega-2=0$,
so
\[
\omega_L=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}{4}.
\]
Above the notch, $2(\omega^2-1)=\omega$ rearranges to $2\omega^2-\omega-2=0$,
so
\[
\omega_H=\frac{1+\sqrt{17}}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{17}+1}{4}.
\]
The product and difference are
\[
\omega_L\omega_H=\frac{17-1}{16}=1,
\qquad
\omega_H-\omega_L=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega_L=(\sqrt{17}-1)/4,\
\omega_H=(\sqrt{17}+1)/4,\
\omega_L\omega_H=1,\
\omega_H-\omega_L=1/2}.
\]
The geometric mean equals the notch frequency, as expected from the
$\omega\leftrightarrow 1/\omega$ reciprocity of this equal-$L$,$C$
normalized network.

Claim (i) describes a different topology (series RLC, output across $R$)
and a different half-power template $|H|=1/\sqrt{2}$ about a peak of $1$.
Claim (ii) drops $R_S$ and never produces the leading $2$ in the
denominator. Claim (iii) forgets to divide the quadratic formula by $2$.
None of those substitutions is the matched shunt-notch calculation.

graderFixtures.proofText: Voltage division through $R_S=1$ into $Z_{LC}\parallel 1$ gives $H=(s^2+1)/(2s^2+s+2)$. The notch is at $\omega=1$ with end-gain $1/2$, and the poles are $(-1\pm j\sqrt{15})/4$. Half-power relative to that end-gain is $|H|=1/(2\sqrt{2})$, hence $\omega_L=(\sqrt{17}-1)/4$, $\omega_H=(\sqrt{17}+1)/4$, product $1$, and difference $1/2$.
L=C=1 makes a series-RLC band-pass with H=s/(s^2+s+1). Peak gain is 1, so half-power is |H|=1/√2, and RS may be omitted because the source is ideal.
The characteristic equation 2s^2+s+2=0 has roots s=[-1±j√15]/2. Those poles already lie in the left half-plane, so the leading 2 can be ignored.

CIR:020323.title: A first-order low-pass cannot meet both specs; two buffered sections can
CIR:020323.objective: Show that no unity-DC first-order low-pass meets |H(j1)|≥1/√2 and |H(j10)|≤1/20, then verify that two identical buffered sections with ωc=2 give H=(1+s/2)^{-2}, passband 4/5, and stopband 1/26.
CIR:020323.statement:
Voltage transfer magnitudes below are ordinary $|H(j\omega)|$ ratios.
They are not converted to decibels except insofar as $1/\sqrt{2}$ is the
half-power voltage ratio, and they are not RMS-to-peak conversions.
Consider first the one-pole family
\[
H_1(s)=\frac{1}{1+s/\omega_c},
\qquad
|H_1(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_c)^2}},
\]
with $\omega_c>0$. The design specifications are
\[
|H(j1)|\ge\frac1{\sqrt{2}},
\qquad
|H(j10)|\le\frac1{20}.
\]

1. Translate the passband specification into a lower bound on $\omega_c$
   and the stopband specification into an upper bound on $\omega_c$. Show
   that a first-order section requires both
   \[
   \omega_c\ge 1
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \omega_c\le\frac{10}{\sqrt{399}},
   \]
   and that this interval is empty. Conclude that no filter of the stated
   first-order family meets both specifications.
2. Now cascade two identical first-order sections, each with $\omega_c=2$,
   through an explicit ideal unity-gain voltage buffer (infinite input
   impedance, zero output impedance). The buffer is part of the circuit:
   without it the second section loads the first and the transfer functions
   do not multiply. Derive
   \[
   H(s)=\bigl(1+\tfrac s2\bigr)^{-2}
   \]
   and evaluate $|H(j1)|$ and $|H(j10)|$ exactly. Confirm that these two
   numbers meet the specifications.

Audit these claims: (i) $\omega_c=1$ meets both bounds because a decade of
frequency already supplies a factor of $10$ in $|H|$; (ii) two RC sections
may be wired directly in cascade and the section transfers still multiply,
so the buffer is optional; (iii) a series-RLC band-pass should be used
instead, because this is a resonance-filters unit. Do not replace the
exercise by a component-sensitivity calculation or by an unbuffered ladder
whose denominator is $1+3(s/2)+(s/2)^2$.
permittedResults: $|H_1(j\omega)|\ge 1/\sqrt{2}$ if and only if $\omega\le\omega_c$. At $\omega=1$ this is $\omega_c\ge 1$.
For two identical isolated sections, $|H(j\omega)|=1/(1+(\omega/\omega_c)^2)$. At $\omega_c=2$ this is $4/5$ at $\omega=1$ and $1/26$ at $\omega=10$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert each |H| inequality into a bound on ωc, compare 10/√399 with 1, then square the isolated one-pole magnitude for ωc=2.
Read the required decade ratio 20/√2 against the one-pole maximum ratio 10, then realize the second-order product with an explicit buffer.

milestones.criterion: Shows that a first-order unity-DC low-pass needs both ωc≥1 and ωc≤10/√399, an empty interval.
Writes the buffered product H=(1+s/2)^{-2} and treats the buffer as what makes the sections multiply.
Evaluates |H(j1)|=4/5 and |H(j10)|=1/26 and checks both specifications.

commonErrors.description: Claims a first-order section meets both specifications, typically by taking ωc=1 and treating a decade of frequency as a factor of 20, or by ignoring the stopband bound 10/√399.
commonErrors.consequence: The empty feasibility interval is never established.

commonErrors.description: Cascades two RC sections without a buffer and still writes H=(1+s/2)^{-2}, or replaces the assigned sections by a series-RLC band-pass or an unbuffered ladder 1/(1+3(s/2)+(s/2)^2) presented as the required answer.
commonErrors.consequence: The isolated product, the passband 4/5, and the stopband 1/26 are lost or attributed to the wrong circuit.

hintTree.content: The stopband inequality $1/\sqrt{1+100/\omega_c^2}\le 1/20$ squares to $1+100/\omega_c^2\ge 400$, hence $\omega_c\le 10/\sqrt{399}$.
Compare $10/\sqrt{399}$ with $1$. Because $\sqrt{399}>\sqrt{100}=10$, the upper bound is strictly less than $1$, so it cannot meet $\omega_c\ge 1$.
With a buffer, $|H(j\omega)|=|H_1(j\omega)|^2=1/(1+(\omega/2)^2)$. Substitute $\omega=1$ and $\omega=10$ without converting to decibels.

CIR:020323.canonicalSolution:
For $H_1(s)=1/(1+s/\omega_c)$,
\[
|H_1(j1)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1/\omega_c^2}}\ge\frac1{\sqrt{2}}
\]
if and only if $1+1/\omega_c^2\le 2$, i.e. $\omega_c\ge 1$. The stopband
requirement
\[
|H_1(j10)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+100/\omega_c^2}}\le\frac1{20}
\]
squares to $1+100/\omega_c^2\ge 400$, hence
\[
\omega_c^2\le\frac{100}{399},
\qquad
\omega_c\le\frac{10}{\sqrt{399}}.
\]
Now $\sqrt{399}>\sqrt{100}=10$, so
\[
\frac{10}{\sqrt{399}}<\frac{10}{10}=1.
\]
The two inequalities $\omega_c\ge 1$ and $\omega_c\le 10/\sqrt{399}$
cannot hold together. No first-order section of the stated family meets
both specifications.
\[
\boxed{\omega_c\ge 1\text{ and }\omega_c\le 10/\sqrt{399}\text{ is empty}}.
\]

Place an ideal unity-gain buffer between two copies of $1/(1+s/2)$. The
buffer contributes voltage gain $1$ and prevents the second resistor-capacitor
pair from loading the first, so
\[
H(s)
=\frac{1}{1+s/2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+s/2}
=\boxed{\bigl(1+\tfrac s2\bigr)^{-2}}.
\]
The magnitude is the square of one section,
\[
|H(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{1+(\omega/2)^2}.
\]
At the two specification frequencies,
\[
|H(j1)|=\frac{1}{1+1/4}=\boxed{\frac45},
\qquad
|H(j10)|=\frac{1}{1+25}=\boxed{\frac1{26}}.
\]
Because $4/5=0.8>1/\sqrt{2}$ and $1/26<1/20$, both specifications hold.
The buffer is essential: an unbuffered cascade of two series-$R$, shunt-$C$
sections with the same $RC$ produces the loaded denominator
$1+3(s/2)+(s/2)^2$, not $(1+s/2)^2$.

Claim (i) confuses a decade of frequency with a factor-of-$20$ stopband
ratio; a first-order pole supplies at most a factor $10$ between $\omega=1$
and $\omega=10$, which is already short of $20/\sqrt{2}$. Claim (ii) drops
the isolation that makes the transfers multiply. Claim (iii) replaces the
assigned low-pass order question by the seed band-pass sensitivity
exercise.

graderFixtures.proofText: A first-order section needs $\omega_c\ge 1$ and $\omega_c\le 10/\sqrt{399}$ simultaneously, which is impossible. Two buffered copies of $1/(1+s/2)$ give $H=(1+s/2)^{-2}$, $|H(j1)|=4/5$, and $|H(j10)|=1/26$, both inside the specifications. The buffer is what lets the section transfers multiply.
Take ωc=1. Then |H(j1)|=1/√2 meets the passband with equality, and a decade later a first-order roll-off has already reached 1/10, which is better than 1/20. First order is therefore feasible.
Two RC sections with ωc=2 may be wired directly together. Loading is negligible, so H=(1+s/2)^{-2} still holds and the buffer can be omitted.

CIR:020424.title: Series-then-shunt is not shunt-then-series: cascade order changes Zin
CIR:020424.objective: Multiply the elementary ABCD blocks S=[[1,2],[0,1]] and P=[[1,0],[1/3,1]] in both orders, verify both determinants equal 1, and show that an RL=3 Ω termination produces Zin=7/2 versus Zin=15/8.
CIR:020424.statement:
Two elementary resistive two-ports are given in the transmission
(ABCD) convention
\[
\begin{bmatrix}V_1\\I_1\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_2\\-I_2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Port currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ both enter the two-port at the marked
positive voltage terminals. The minus sign is part of the definition:
$-I_2$ is the current delivered onward into the next network or into a
load. All voltages are in volts, currents in amperes, $B$ in ohms, and
$C$ in siemens. These are real DC (or RMS phasors at a shared phase
reference); no peak-phasor factor $1/2$ appears in any resistance ratio.

Let
\[
S=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
P=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1/3&1\end{bmatrix},
\]
so $S$ is a series $2\ \Omega$ element and $P$ is a shunt $3\ \Omega$
element. Compatible transmission matrices cascade by ordinary matrix
multiplication, left to right in the order source-side then load-side.

1. Compute the products $SP$ and $PS$ entrywise. Evaluate $\det S$,
   $\det P$, $\det(SP)$, and $\det(PS)$.
2. Terminate port 2 by $R_L=3.00\ \Omega$, using the load law
   $I_2=-V_2/R_L$ that follows from the entering-current convention.
   Derive
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_1}{I_1}=\frac{AR_L+B}{CR_L+D}
   \]
   and evaluate it for both cascade orders.
3. State, in one comparison, why $SP$ and $PS$ are not interchangeable
   even though each factor is reciprocal with determinant $1$.

Audit these claims: (i) matrix multiplication commutes for $2\times 2$
reciprocal matrices, so $SP=PS$ and both loaded input impedances equal
$7/2$; (ii) a passive load takes $I_2=+V_2/R_L$, which flips the $B$ and
$D$ placement; (iii) the calculation is the same as converting one
reciprocal $Z$-parameter matrix to $Y$ and $ABCD$ and then loading it.
Do not convert a $2\times 2$ impedance matrix and do not compute delivered
power.
permittedResults: $\det S=1$ and $\det P=1$. The determinant is multiplicative, so $\det(SP)=\det(PS)=1$.
Matrix multiplication of distinct $2\times 2$ elementary chain matrices is noncommutative: $SP\neq PS$ whenever the series and shunt elements occupy opposite ends of the cascade.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply the two elementary chain matrices both ways, then substitute -I2=V2/RL into each product.
Read S as a series 2 Ω and P as a shunt 3 Ω, draw the two ladder orders, and compute each Zin by series-parallel reduction as a check on the ABCD arithmetic.

milestones.criterion: Computes SP=[[5/3,2],[1/3,1]] and PS=[[1,2],[1/3,5/3]] and verifies every determinant equals 1.
Uses the entering-current load law I2=-V2/RL to obtain Zin=(A RL+B)/(C RL+D).
Evaluates Zin=7/2 Ω for SP and Zin=15/8 Ω for PS and states that cascade order is not commutative.

commonErrors.description: Treats SP and PS as equal, or reports a single loaded input impedance (typically 7/2 Ω) for both orders.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned distinction 7/2 versus 15/8 is erased.

commonErrors.description: Takes I2=+V2/RL under the entering-current convention, or otherwise replaces Zin=(A RL+B)/(C RL+D) by a sign-flipped placement of B and D.
commonErrors.consequence: Both numerical Zin values, or their derivation, become inconsistent with the declared port convention.

hintTree.content: The $(1,1)$ entry of $SP$ is $1\cdot 1+2\cdot(1/3)=5/3$. The $(2,2)$ entry of $PS$ is $(1/3)\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=5/3$.
Entering-current load law: current through $R_L$ leaves the two-port, so $I_2=-V_2/R_L$ and $-I_2=V_2/R_L$.
For $SP$ the loaded formula is $(5+2)/(1+1)=7/2$. For $PS$ it is $(3+2)/(1+5/3)=15/8$.

CIR:020424.canonicalSolution:
Ordinary matrix multiplication gives
\[
SP
=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1/3&1\end{bmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}5/3&2\\1/3&1\end{bmatrix}},
\]
\[
PS
=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1/3&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1/3&5/3\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
The determinants are
\[
\det S=1,\qquad
\det P=1,\qquad
\det(SP)=\frac53-\frac23=1,\qquad
\det(PS)=\frac53-\frac23=1.
\]
Each block is reciprocal in the stated $ABCD$ convention, and so is each
cascade, but $SP\neq PS$: the series $2\ \Omega$ and the shunt $3\ \Omega$
do not occupy the same place in the chain.

A passive load attached at port 2 draws current out of the two-port, so
$I_2=-V_2/R_L$ and $-I_2=V_2/R_L$. Substituting into the transmission
equations,
\[
V_1=\bigl(A+B/R_L\bigr)V_2,
\qquad
I_1=\bigl(C+D/R_L\bigr)V_2,
\]
hence
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{AR_L+B}{CR_L+D}.
\]
With $R_L=3\ \Omega$,
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}(SP)
=\frac{(5/3)\cdot 3+2}{(1/3)\cdot 3+1}
=\frac{7}{2}\ \Omega,
\]
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}(PS)
=\frac{1\cdot 3+2}{(1/3)\cdot 3+5/3}
=\frac{5}{8/3}
=\frac{15}{8}\ \Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(SP)=7/2\ \Omega,\qquad Z_{\mathrm{in}}(PS)=15/8\ \Omega}.
\]
The two numbers differ because a series resistor at the source end adds
directly to a loaded shunt, whereas a shunt at the source end first
divides the input current. Reciprocity of each factor ($\det=1$) does not
make multiplication commutative.

Claim (i) asserts $SP=PS$ and reports a single $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$. Claim
(ii) uses $I_2=+V_2/R_L$, which is the opposite of the entering-current
load law and scrambles $(A R_L+B)/(C R_L+D)$. Claim (iii) is the seed
conversion-and-loading exercise on one $Z$-parameter two-port; it is not
this cascade-order comparison.

graderFixtures.proofText: The products are $SP=[[5/3,2],[1/3,1]]$ and $PS=[[1,2],[1/3,5/3]]$, each of determinant $1$. With $I_2=-V_2/R_L$ and $R_L=3\ \Omega$, $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(SP)=7/2\ \Omega$ and $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(PS)=15/8\ \Omega$. Cascade order is not commutative.
Both matrices have determinant 1, so they commute: SP=PS=[[5/3,2],[1/3,1]]. The loaded input impedance is 7/2 Ω in either order.
A passive load current is positive, so I2=+V2/RL. Then Zin=(A RL-B)/(C RL-D), and the two cascade numbers are not 7/2 and 15/8.

CIR:020425.title: Even and odd currents see 4 Ω and 2 Ω; declare the RMS power convention
CIR:020425.objective: Read the even- and odd-mode impedances 4 Ω and 2 Ω of Z=[[3,1],[1,3]], then compute V and absorbed power for I=(2,-2) and I=(1,1) under an explicit DC/RMS convention that excludes the peak-phasor factor 1/2.
CIR:020425.statement:
A reciprocal resistive two-port has impedance parameters
\[
\begin{bmatrix}V_1\\V_2\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}I_1\\I_2\end{bmatrix},
\]
with every $z_{ij}$ in ohms. Both port currents enter the network at the
marked positive voltage terminals. The entries of $I$ and $V$ in this
problem are real: they may be read as DC values, or as RMS phasors at a
common frequency with a common phase reference of zero. In either reading
the average power absorbed by the two-port is
\[
P=V_1I_1+V_2I_2=I^{\mathsf T}ZI.
\]
This is not the peak-phasor convention $P=\tfrac12\mathrm{Re}(V_1I_1^*+V_2I_2^*)$.
Do not insert a factor $1/2$.

1. Define the even mode by $I_1=I_2$ and the odd mode by $I_1=-I_2$.
   Compute the modal driving-point impedances $Z_{\mathrm{even}}=V_1/I_1$
   and $Z_{\mathrm{odd}}=V_1/I_1$ and show that they equal $4\ \Omega$ and
   $2\ \Omega$ respectively.
2. Apply $I=(2,-2)\ \mathrm A$. Compute $V$ and the absorbed power $P$.
3. Apply $I=(1,1)\ \mathrm A$. Compute $V$ and the absorbed power $P$.
4. State which excitation is pure odd, which is pure even, and why the
   peak-phasor factor $1/2$ would be inconsistent with the declared
   convention.

Audit these claims: (i) the given amperes are peak phasors, so the powers
are $8\ \mathrm W$ and $4\ \mathrm W$; (ii) even and odd impedances are
$z_{11}\pm z_{12}$ with the $4\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$ assignments
reversed; (iii) the problem is a loaded $Z$-to-$ABCD$ conversion. Keep
volts, amperes, ohms, and watts distinct.
permittedResults: If $Z=[[z,m],[m,z]]$, then $Z_{\mathrm{even}}=z+m$ and $Z_{\mathrm{odd}}=z-m$. Here those values are $4\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$.
For real $I$, $P=I^{\mathsf T}ZI$. A pure odd pair $I=(I,-I)$ absorbs $2Z_{\mathrm{odd}}I^2$; a pure even pair $I=(I,I)$ absorbs $2Z_{\mathrm{even}}I^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate Z I for the two given current vectors and form V·I with the stated RMS/DC convention.
Decompose each excitation as pure even or pure odd and use P=2 Z_mode I^2 as an independent check.

milestones.criterion: Identifies Zeven=z11+z12=4 Ω and Zodd=z11-z12=2 Ω.
Computes V=(4,-4) V and P=16 W for I=(2,-2) A under P=V1 I1+V2 I2.
Computes P=8 W for I=(1,1) A and rejects the peak-phasor factor 1/2.

commonErrors.description: Treats the given real currents as peak phasors and reports absorbed powers 8 W and 4 W, inserting a factor 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: Both required watt values are halved and the declared RMS/DC convention is abandoned.

commonErrors.description: Assigns Zeven=2 Ω and Zodd=4 Ω, or otherwise uses z11∓z12 with the mode labels reversed.
commonErrors.consequence: The modal identification of I=(2,-2) and I=(1,1) is inverted even if a matrix product is later written.

hintTree.content: For $I=(2,-2)$, the matrix product is $V=(4,-4)$. Then $P=4\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot(-2)$.
For $I=(1,1)$, $V=(4,4)$ and $P=8\ \mathrm W$. A peak-phasor reading would halve both powers and is excluded by the problem statement.

CIR:020425.canonicalSolution:
Even mode: $I_1=I_2=I$ gives
\[
V_1=3I+I=4I=V_2,
\qquad
Z_{\mathrm{even}}=\frac{V_1}{I_1}=4\ \Omega.
\]
Odd mode: $I_1=-I_2=I$ gives
\[
V_1=3I+1(-I)=2I=-V_2,
\qquad
Z_{\mathrm{odd}}=\frac{V_1}{I_1}=2\ \Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{even}}=4\ \Omega,\qquad Z_{\mathrm{odd}}=2\ \Omega}.
\]

Now $I=(2,-2)\ \mathrm A$ is a pure odd excitation of amplitude $2\ \mathrm A$:
\[
V
=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}2\\-2\end{bmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}4\\-4\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm V}.
\]
Under the declared DC/RMS convention,
\[
P=V_1I_1+V_2I_2
=4\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot(-2)
=\boxed{16\ \mathrm W}.
\]
The same number is $2Z_{\mathrm{odd}}(2)^2=2\cdot 2\cdot 4=16\ \mathrm W$.
Each port absorbs $8\ \mathrm W$.

The pair $I=(1,1)\ \mathrm A$ is a pure even excitation of amplitude
$1\ \mathrm A$:
\[
V
=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}4\\4\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm V,
\qquad
P=4\cdot 1+4\cdot 1
=\boxed{8\ \mathrm W}.
\]
Equivalently $2Z_{\mathrm{even}}(1)^2=8\ \mathrm W$.

A peak-phasor convention would replace both powers by half of these
values ($8\ \mathrm W$ and $4\ \mathrm W$). That convention is excluded:
the currents and voltages are declared real DC or RMS, so $P=V^{\mathsf T}I$
already is the average power. Inserting $1/2$ would be a change of
definition, not a circuit calculation.

Claim (i) is exactly that forbidden peak-phasor reading. Claim (ii) swaps
the $4\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$ assignments. Claim (iii) is the seed
loaded-conversion exercise, which this modal power audit does not ask.

graderFixtures.proofText: Even mode sees $4\ \Omega$ and odd mode sees $2\ \Omega$. For $I=(2,-2)\ \mathrm A$ one has $V=(4,-4)\ \mathrm V$ and $P=16\ \mathrm W$; for $I=(1,1)\ \mathrm A$ one has $P=8\ \mathrm W$. Both powers use the declared DC/RMS law $P=V_1I_1+V_2I_2$, not a peak-phasor factor $1/2$.
The currents are AC peak phasors, so P=(1/2)(V1 I1+V2 I2). Then I=(2,-2) absorbs 8 W and I=(1,1) absorbs 4 W.
Even mode is I1=-I2 and sees z11-z12=2 Ω; odd mode is I1=I2 and sees 4 Ω. The pair (2,-2) is therefore even.

CIR:020426.title: A 6 ohm gyrator inverts 9 ohm to 4 ohm and stores no net port power
CIR:020426.objective: From the declared gyrator laws V1=6 I2 and V2=-6 I1, invert RL=9 Ω to Zin=4 Ω, then with a 10 V source and 1 Ω series resistor compute I1=2 A, V1=8 V, V2=-12 V, load power 16 W, and the identity V1 I1+V2 I2=0.
CIR:020426.statement:
An ideal gyrator is defined by the port laws
\[
V_1=6I_2,\qquad V_2=-6I_1,
\]
with $V$ in volts and $I$ in amperes. Both currents enter the gyrator at
the marked positive voltage terminals. The gyration resistance is
$R=6.00\ \Omega$. These signs are part of the device: $z_{12}=+6\ \Omega$
and $z_{21}=-6\ \Omega$, so the two-port is anti-reciprocal and cannot be
replaced by a reciprocal $R$, $L$, $C$ network. The voltages and currents
below are real DC (equivalently RMS at a shared phase). Average power
absorbed by any two-port is $P=V_1I_1+V_2I_2$; do not insert a peak-phasor
factor $1/2$.

1. Terminate port 2 by $R_L=9.00\ \Omega$. Using the entering-current load
   law $V_2=-I_2 R_L$, derive the input impedance $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=V_1/I_1$
   and show that it equals $4.00\ \Omega$. Identify the inversion
   $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=R^2/R_L$.
2. Drive port 1 by an ideal $10.0\ \mathrm V$ source in series with
   $1.00\ \Omega$. Solve for $I_1$, $V_1$, $I_2$, and $V_2$.
3. Compute the power absorbed by the $9\ \Omega$ load and the gyrator's
   own port power $V_1I_1+V_2I_2$. Confirm that the gyrator is lossless
   and that the load absorbs $16\ \mathrm W$.
4. State why $z_{12}\ne z_{21}$ forbids a reciprocal realization, and why
   $V_1$ is not equal to the $10\ \mathrm V$ source.

Audit these claims: (i) the gyrator is reciprocal, so $V_2=+6I_1$ and
$Z_{\mathrm{in}}=R_L$ or $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=-4\ \Omega$; (ii) the source
voltage is already $V_1=10\ \mathrm V$, hence $I_1=10/4$; (iii) the
gyrator absorbs the $16\ \mathrm W$ that the load is said to absorb.
Do not convert a reciprocal $Z$-parameter matrix and do not analyze a
transmission-line bounce.
permittedResults: Substituting $V_2=-R I_1=-I_2 R_L$ into $V_1=R I_2$ produces $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=R^2/R_L$. Here $36/9=4\ \Omega$.
For the ideal gyrator, $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=R I_2 I_1+(-R I_1)I_2=0$ identically, independent of the termination.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate I2 between V2=-6 I1 and V2=-9 I2 to read Zin, then close the source loop 10=I1+V1.
Write Z=[[0,6],[-6,0]], impose V2=-9 I2, compute the operating point, and check both the load power and the gyrator identity V·I=0.

milestones.criterion: Derives Zin=R²/RL=4 Ω from the declared signs V1=6 I2, V2=-6 I1 and the load law V2=-I2 RL.
Solves the 10 V, 1 Ω source loop to obtain I1=2 A, V1=8 V, V2=-12 V, and I2=4/3 A.
Shows the load absorbs 16 W while V1 I1+V2 I2=0, and states that the gyrator is lossless and nonreciprocal.

commonErrors.description: Replaces V2=-6 I1 by V2=+6 I1, or reports Zin=RL or Zin=-4 Ω as the terminated input impedance.
commonErrors.consequence: The inversion Zin=R²/RL=4 Ω is lost and the device is no longer the declared anti-reciprocal gyrator.

commonErrors.description: Sets V1=10 V, or assigns the 16 W dissipation to the gyrator instead of the load, contradicting V1 I1+V2 I2=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The operating point (I1,V1)=(2 A, 8 V) and the lossless power split are both wrong.

hintTree.content: The source loop is $10=1\cdot I_1+V_1=5I_1$, so $I_1=2\ \mathrm A$ and $V_1=8\ \mathrm V$, not $V_1=10\ \mathrm V$.

CIR:020426.canonicalSolution:
The declared signs are
\[
V_1=6I_2,\qquad V_2=-6I_1,
\]
or, as an impedance matrix,
\[
Z=\begin{bmatrix}0&6\\-6&0\end{bmatrix}\ \Omega.
\]
Because $z_{12}\ne z_{21}$, the two-port is not reciprocal.

The load law consistent with entering $I_2$ is $V_2=-I_2 R_L=-9I_2$.
Combined with $V_2=-6I_1$,
\[
-6I_1=-9I_2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
I_2=\frac23 I_1.
\]
Then
\[
V_1=6I_2=6\cdot\frac23 I_1=4I_1,
\qquad
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_1}{I_1}
=\boxed{4\ \Omega}
=\frac{R^2}{R_L}=\frac{36}{9}.
\]
A reciprocal sign $V_2=+6I_1$ would have produced a negative input
resistance and is not the stated device.

The source equation is $10=1\cdot I_1+V_1$. With $V_1=4I_1$,
\[
10=5I_1
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
I_1=\boxed{2\ \mathrm A},
\qquad
V_1=\boxed{8\ \mathrm V}.
\]
The gyrator laws then give
\[
V_2=-6I_1=\boxed{-12\ \mathrm V},
\qquad
I_2=\frac{V_1}{6}=\frac43\ \mathrm A.
\]
The $10\ \mathrm V$ source is not $V_1$; two volts are dropped on the
series $1\ \Omega$ resistor.

The current leaving the gyrator into the load is $-I_2=-4/3\ \mathrm A$,
so the load absorbs
\[
P_L=V_2(-I_2)=(-12)\Bigl(-\frac43\Bigr)
=\frac{V_2^2}{R_L}=\frac{144}{9}
=\boxed{16\ \mathrm W}.
\]
The gyrator's own absorbed port power is
\[
V_1I_1+V_2I_2
=8\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot\frac43
=16-16
=\boxed{0}.
\]
The identity $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=RI_2I_1+(-RI_1)I_2=0$ holds for any
termination: the ideal gyrator is lossless. The $16\ \mathrm W$ is
dissipated in $R_L$, not in the gyrator. The source delivers
$10\cdot 2=20\ \mathrm W$, of which $I_1^2\cdot 1=4\ \mathrm W$ is
dissipated in the $1\ \Omega$ resistor and $16\ \mathrm W$ in the load.

Claim (i) replaces the anti-reciprocal pair by a reciprocal (or sign-flipped)
law and loses $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=4\ \Omega$. Claim (ii) sets $V_1$ equal to
the source. Claim (iii) assigns the load dissipation to the gyrator and
contradicts $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=0$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The laws $V_1=6I_2$ and $V_2=-6I_1$ with $V_2=-9I_2$ give $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=4\ \Omega$. Then $10=I_1+V_1$ yields $I_1=2\ \mathrm A$, $V_1=8\ \mathrm V$, $V_2=-12\ \mathrm V$, and $I_2=4/3\ \mathrm A$. The load absorbs $16\ \mathrm W$ while $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=0$. The two-port is lossless and nonreciprocal.
A gyrator is reciprocal, so V2=+6 I1. Terminated by 9 Ω the input impedance is either 9 Ω or -4 Ω, not R^2/RL.
The source is 10 V, so V1=10 V and I1=10/4=2.5 A. The gyrator is the element that absorbs the 16 W.

CIR:020527.title: Common and difference RC modes, not a hidden pole, give the two-node step
CIR:020527.objective: Derive the two-node RC state model from declared KCL, diagonalize it into common and difference modes with poles -1 and -3, integrate the unit current step from rest, and reject both a mode swap and a substitution by the held minimal-state or hidden-cancellation packets.
CIR:020527.statement:
Two nodes have voltages $v_1(t)$ and $v_2(t)$ relative to a common ground. Each node has a $1.00\,\mathrm{F}$ capacitor to ground and a $1.00\,\mathrm{S}$ conductance to ground. A $1.00\,\mathrm{S}$ conductance joins the two nodes. An independent current source $i_s(t)$ injects current from ground into node $1$ only.

Passive sign convention: capacitor and conductance currents leave a node into the element whose voltage is the node-to-ground voltage. The source current is positive when it enters node $1$. There is no port-$2$ injection. The network is ideal, lumped, linear, and time-invariant. Both capacitors are initially uncharged:
\[
v_1(0^-)=v_2(0^-)=0.
\]
There is no impulsive current, so both capacitor voltages are continuous. For $t\ge0$ the source is the unit current step
\[
i_s(t)=u(t)\ \mathrm{A}.
\]
Write the state as $x=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T}$ in volts, with $u:=i_s$ in amperes.

1. Apply KCL at each node and prove that
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu,\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{F}^{-1}.
\]
Do not assign a single blanket unit to every matrix entry.

2. Introduce the common and difference coordinates $s:=v_1+v_2$ and $d:=v_1-v_2$. Derive the decoupled modal equations, identify the poles $-1$ and $-3$ with the common and difference modes respectively, and invert the transformation to recover $v_1=(s+d)/2$ and $v_2=(s-d)/2$.

3. Integrate the unit step from rest and prove
\[
v_1(t)=\frac23-\frac12 e^{-t}-\frac16 e^{-3t}\ \mathrm{V},
\qquad
v_2(t)=\frac13-\frac12 e^{-t}+\frac16 e^{-3t}\ \mathrm{V}
\]
for $t\ge0$. Check $t=0^+$, the DC KCL equilibrium, and that both modal poles appear in each voltage.

4. Audit these claims: (i) the common mode decays at $-3$ and the difference mode at $-1$, or equivalently the $e^{-3t}$ signs on $v_1$ and $v_2$ may be swapped; (ii) the exercise is to count independent energy coordinates of parallel capacitors, or to expose a hidden unstable cancellation; (iii) the total response requires a unilateral series-RLC energy audit. Do not replace the packet by a state-dimension count, a hidden-mode Bode argument, or a switched RLC energy balance.
permittedResults: KCL at a capacitive node with passive references reads $C\dot v+\sum G(v-v_{\mathrm{nbr}})=i_{\mathrm{inj}}$. With $C=1\,\mathrm{F}$ the current balance is already a state equation in $\mathrm{V/s}$.
If $s'= -s+u$ and $d'=-3d+u$ with zero initial data and $u\equiv 1$ for $t>0$, then $s=1-e^{-t}$ and $d=(1-e^{-3t})/3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the two KCL rows, add and subtract them to isolate s and d, then invert s=1-e^{-t} and d=(1-e^{-3t})/3.
Compute the DC solve A x_ss=-B to get (2/3,1/3), expand the zero-state transient in the eigenbasis of A, and match coefficients from x(0)=0.

milestones.criterion: Derives the declared KCL realization A=[[-2,1],[1,-2]], B=(1,0) with mixed units and the common/difference poles -1 and -3.
Integrates the unit step from rest to the boxed voltages and checks t=0 and the DC KCL pair (2/3,1/3).
Rejects a common/difference pole swap and refuses a minimal-state, hidden-cancellation, or unilateral-RLC substitution.

commonErrors.description: Assigns pole -3 to the common mode and -1 to the difference mode, or flips the e^{-3t} signs between v1 and v2.
commonErrors.consequence: The rest-to-step voltages miss the DC pair (2/3,1/3) and no longer satisfy both KCL rows.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the packet by a parallel-capacitor state-dimension count, a hidden unstable cancellation, or a unilateral series-RLC energy audit.
commonErrors.consequence: A different Circuits II seed family is substituted for a fully visible two-mode RC step.

hintTree.content: Node 1: $\dot v_1+v_1+(v_1-v_2)=i_s$. Node 2 has no source term.
Adding the state rows gives $\dot s=-s+u$. Subtracting them gives $\dot d=-3d+u$.

CIR:020527.canonicalSolution:
KCL at node $1$ with the declared passive references is
\[
C_1\dot v_1+G_1 v_1+G_{12}(v_1-v_2)=i_s.
\]
Every capacitance is $1\,\mathrm{F}$ and every conductance is $1\,\mathrm{S}$, so
\[
\dot v_1=-2v_1+v_2+i_s.
\]
KCL at node $2$ has no injected source:
\[
C_2\dot v_2+G_2 v_2+G_{12}(v_2-v_1)=0,
\]
hence
\[
\dot v_2=v_1-2v_2.
\]
In matrix form,
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu,\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{F}^{-1}.
\]
The $(1,1)$ and $(2,2)$ entries of $A$ are reciprocal seconds; $B$ converts amperes into volts per second. A blanket $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on $B$ is dimensionally false.

Set $s=v_1+v_2$ and $d=v_1-v_2$. Adding the state equations uses $u=i_s$ and gives
\[
\dot s=\dot v_1+\dot v_2=-v_1-v_2+u=-s+u.
\]
Subtracting them gives
\[
\dot d=\dot v_1-\dot v_2=-3v_1+3v_2+u=-3d+u.
\]
Thus the common mode has pole $-1$ and the difference mode has pole $-3$. The inverse change of coordinates is $v_1=(s+d)/2$ and $v_2=(s-d)/2$. The characteristic polynomial
\[
\det(sI-A)=(s+2)^2-1=(s+1)(s+3)
\]
confirms the same poles; both modes are controllable from $u$ because $B$ feeds the first row, so both appear in a generic zero-state response. Neither pole is cancelled and both eigenvalues lie in the open left half-plane.

From rest, $s(0)=d(0)=0$ and $u(t)=1$ for $t>0$. The forced equilibria are $s_{\mathrm{ss}}=1$ and $d_{\mathrm{ss}}=1/3$, so
\[
s(t)=1-e^{-t},\qquad d(t)=\frac13\bigl(1-e^{-3t}\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
v_1(t)&=\frac{s+d}{2}
=\frac{1-e^{-t}+\tfrac13-\tfrac13 e^{-3t}}{2}
=\frac23-\frac12 e^{-t}-\frac16 e^{-3t}\ \mathrm{V},\\
v_2(t)&=\frac{s-d}{2}
=\frac{1-e^{-t}-\tfrac13+\tfrac13 e^{-3t}}{2}
=\frac13-\frac12 e^{-t}+\frac16 e^{-3t}\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{v_1=\tfrac23-\tfrac12 e^{-t}-\tfrac16 e^{-3t},\
v_2=\tfrac13-\tfrac12 e^{-t}+\tfrac16 e^{-3t}}.
\]
At $t=0^+$ both voltages vanish, matching continuity from rest. As $t\to\infty$, $(v_1,v_2)\to(2/3,1/3)$. DC KCL at node $1$ is
\[
G_1\cdot\frac23+G_{12}\Bigl(\frac23-\frac13\Bigr)=1=i_s,
\]
and at node $2$
\[
G_2\cdot\frac13+G_{12}\Bigl(\frac13-\frac23\Bigr)=0.
\]
Each voltage contains both $e^{-t}$ and $e^{-3t}$, so both visible modes are present.

Claim (i) swaps the modal poles. That would replace $d$ by $1-e^{-t}$ and $s$ by $(1-e^{-3t})/3$, or equivalently flip the $e^{-3t}$ signs between $v_1$ and $v_2$, and would miss the DC pair $(2/3,1/3)$. Claim (ii) is the held minimal-state packet (parallel capacitors forced to share one voltage) or the held hidden-cancellation packet (an unstable cancelled eigenvalue). Here the two capacitors already have distinct nodes, both modes are stable and observable in both outputs, and no rank test is asked. Claim (iii) is the held unilateral series-RLC switching/energy packet: there is no inductor, no pre-switch stored energy, and no joule balance requested.

graderFixtures.proofText: KCL gives A=[[-2,1],[1,-2]] /s and B=(1,0) /F. Common mode s=v1+v2 obeys s'=-s+u (pole -1); difference d=v1-v2 obeys d'=-3d+u (pole -3). From rest, s=1-e^{-t} and d=(1-e^{-3t})/3, so v1=2/3-(1/2)e^{-t}-(1/6)e^{-3t} V and v2=1/3-(1/2)e^{-t}+(1/6)e^{-3t} V. Both vanish at 0+ and the DC pair (2/3,1/3) satisfies KCL. This is not a parallel-capacitor count, a hidden cancellation, or a unilateral RLC energy problem.

Adding the rows gives a pole at -3 and subtracting gives a pole at -1. From rest I therefore take s=(1-e^{-3t})/3 and d=1-e^{-t}, so v1=2/3-(1/2)e^{-t}+(1/6)e^{-3t} after swapping the fast-mode signs.

The two capacitors are energy-storage elements, so the point is to decide whether the state dimension is one or two, or else to cancel an unstable factor from a Bode plot. Equivalently this is a unilateral series-RLC switching energy balance.

CIR:020528.title: Discarding the fast balanced RC mode costs exactly twice its Hankel singular value
CIR:020528.objective: Compute the controllability and observability Gramians of the two-input two-output diagonal RC realization, read the Hankel singular values 1/2 and 1/8, delete the fast mode, and prove that the exact H-infinity error is 1/4=2 sigma_2 rather than sigma_2 itself.
CIR:020528.statement:
Two independent grounded capacitors, each $1.00\,\mathrm{F}$, are driven by two independent current sources $u=(u_1,u_2)^{\mathsf T}$ in amperes and observed by the two capacitor voltages $y=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T}$ in volts. The conductances to ground are $1.00\,\mathrm{S}$ at node $1$ and $4.00\,\mathrm{S}$ at node $2$. There is no coupling conductance.

Passive sign convention: each source current enters its node from ground; each conductance current leaves the node. The linear state model is already
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu,\qquad y=Cx,
\]
with $x=y=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T}$ and
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-4)\ \mathrm{s}^{-1},\qquad B=C=I_2
\]
in mixed units ($B$ in $\mathrm{F}^{-1}$, $C$ dimensionless). Both modes are stable, controllable, and observable. The realization is internally balanced when the controllability Gramian $W_c$ and the observability Gramian $W_o$ are equal and diagonal.

The infinite-horizon Gramians of a stable realization solve
\[
AW_c+W_c A^{\mathsf T}+BB^{\mathsf T}=0,
\qquad
A^{\mathsf T}W_o+W_o A+C^{\mathsf T}C=0.
\]
Hankel singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $W_c W_o$, written in decreasing order $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2>0$. Balanced truncation that deletes the fast (more heavily damped) state produces a reduced transfer $\widehat H$ from the slow mode alone.

1. Solve the two Lyapunov equations and prove that $W_c=W_o=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/8)$. Conclude that the realization is already balanced with
\[
\sigma_1=\frac12,\qquad \sigma_2=\frac18.
\]

2. Write the $2\times 2$ transfer $H(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B$ and the reduced transfer $\widehat H$ obtained by deleting the eigenvalue $-4$. Prove that the exact induced $L^2$ (equivalently $H^\infty$) error is
\[
\bigl\|H-\widehat H\bigr\|_\infty=\frac14=2\sigma_2.
\]
Identify the discarded channel that attains the essential supremum at $\omega=0$.

3. Explain why reporting $\sigma_2=1/8$ as the truncation error confuses the Hankel norm of the discarded system with the $H^\infty$ error, and why the Glover bound $2\sigma_2$ is sharp on this example.

4. Audit these claims: (i) the fast mode is the one with pole $-1$, so that mode should be deleted; (ii) the error equals $\sigma_2$ because the realization is balanced; (iii) the exercise is a circuit state-dimension count or a hidden unstable cancellation. Do not replace the packet by a rank/minimality argument or by an unstable cancelled pole.

Glover: deleting Hankel singular values $\sigma_{r+1},\ldots,\sigma_n$ from a balanced realization yields $\|H-\widehat H\|_\infty\le 2(\sigma_{r+1}+\cdots+\sigma_n)$. Equality can hold for a single discarded first-order mode.

hintTree.content: Because $A$ is diagonal and $BB^{\mathsf T}=I$, the Lyapunov equations decouple as $-2w_1+1=0$ and $-8w_2+1=0$.
$H(s)=\operatorname{diag}(1/(s+1),1/(s+4))$. Deleting the fast state leaves $\operatorname{diag}(1/(s+1),0)$.
$\sup_\omega |1/(j\omega+4)|=1/4$, and $2\sigma_2=2\cdot(1/8)=1/4$.

CIR:020528.canonicalSolution:
The two Lyapunov equations share the same data because $A=A^{\mathsf T}$ and $BB^{\mathsf T}=C^{\mathsf T}C=I_2$. With a diagonal unknown $W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,w_2)$ they reduce to the scalar balances
\[
-2w_1+1=0,\qquad -8w_2+1=0,
\]
so $w_1=1/2$ and $w_2=1/8$. Thus
\[
W_c=W_o=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\frac12,\frac18\Bigr).
\]
The realization is already balanced. The Hankel singular values are the diagonal entries themselves:
\[
\sigma_1=\frac12,\qquad \sigma_2=\frac18.
\]
\[
\boxed{W_c=W_o=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/8),\ \sigma=(1/2,1/8)}.
\]
(The product $W_c W_o$ has eigenvalues $1/4$ and $1/64$, whose square roots recover the same pair.)

The transfer is the ohm-valued diagonal matrix
\[
H(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\frac1{s+1},\frac1{s+4}\Bigr).
\]
Deleting the fast state $v_2$ (pole $-4$, singular value $\sigma_2$) retains only the slow channel and sets the second input-output path to zero:
\[
\widehat H(s)=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\frac1{s+1},0\Bigr).
\]
The error transfer is therefore
\[
H(s)-\widehat H(s)=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(0,\frac1{s+4}\Bigr).
\]
Its frequency-response largest singular value is
\[
\sigma_{\max}\bigl(H(j\omega)-\widehat H(j\omega)\bigr)
=\Bigl|\frac1{j\omega+4}\Bigr|=\frac1{\sqrt{\omega^2+16}},
\]
whose essential supremum is $1/4$, attained at $\omega=0$ on the discarded current-to-voltage channel. Hence
\[
\bigl\|H-\widehat H\bigr\|_\infty=\frac14=2\sigma_2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\|H-\widehat H\|_\infty=1/4=2\sigma_2}.
\]
The Hankel norm of the discarded first-order system $1/(s+4)$ is $\sigma_2=1/8$, half of its $H^\infty$ norm. Reporting $1/8$ as the truncation error therefore quotes the wrong induced norm. Glover's bound on a single discarded singular value is $2\sigma_2$; this diagonal RC pair saturates the bound, so the factor two is sharp and is not an artifact.

The fast mode is the more heavily damped pole $-4$, which carries the smaller singular value $\sigma_2$. Deleting the slow pole $-1$ would instead cost $2\sigma_1=1$, a different reduced model.

Claim (i) misidentifies which mode is fast. Claim (ii) replaces the $H^\infty$ error by the Hankel singular value. Claim (iii) is the held minimal-state packet or the held hidden-cancellation packet: both modes here are already independent, stable, controllable, and observable, and no cancelled unstable factor appears.

The error is 1/|j omega+4|, whose H-inf norm is 1/4=2 sigma_2, attained at DC. The Hankel norm of the discarded mode is 1/8 and is the wrong error. Both modes are already minimal and stable; this is not a hidden-cancellation or state-count packet.
The realization is balanced, so the truncation error equals the discarded Hankel singular value 1/8. Alternatively the pole -1 is the one I delete because it is listed first.

CIR:020629.title: A 50 ohm quarter-wave match is exact only at lambda/4; at lambda/8 the feed sees 40-j30
CIR:020629.objective: Design the real quarter-wave transformer that matches 100 ohm to 25 ohm, evaluate Zin at lambda/4 and at lambda/8, compute the 25 ohm feed-line |Gamma|=3/sqrt(41), and reject both a Zt-referenced reflection and a bounce-diagram substitution.
CIR:020629.statement:
A lossless TEM transformer of characteristic impedance $Z_t$ and length $\ell$ is inserted between a real load
\[
Z_L=100\ \Omega
\]
and a lossless feed line of characteristic impedance
\[
Z_0=25\ \Omega.
\]
The design goal is a match at the feed-transformer junction: the input impedance $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ looking into the transformer toward the load should equal $Z_0$ at the design frequency. Phasors use the $e^{j\omega t}$ convention. Impedances are ratios of RMS voltage phasors to RMS current phasors; the same ratios are obtained from peak phasors. On every lossless section the traveling-wave convention is
\[
V=V^++V^-,\qquad I=\frac{V^+-V^-}{Z},
\]
with $I$ positive toward the load.

The lossless input-impedance formula is
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\ell)=Z_t\frac{Z_L+j Z_t\tan\beta\ell}{Z_t+j Z_L\tan\beta\ell},
\]
where $\beta=2\pi/\lambda$.

1. Prove that the unique positive real $Z_t$ that matches $Z_L=100\,\Omega$ to $Z_0=25\,\Omega$ at $\ell=\lambda/4$ is $Z_t=50\,\Omega$. Then evaluate $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda/4)$ and show that it equals $25\,\Omega$.

2. Keep the same physical line and the same $Z_L$, but now operate at the frequency for which $\ell=\lambda/8$. Evaluate $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ and prove that
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(\lambda/8\bigr)=40-j30\ \Omega.
\]

3. On the $25\,\Omega$ feed, the junction reflection coefficient is
\[
\Gamma=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_0}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_0}.
\]
Prove that $\lvert\Gamma\rvert=3/\sqrt{41}$. Explain why referencing $\Gamma$ to $Z_t=50\,\Omega$ instead of to the feed $Z_0=25\,\Omega$ is the wrong port.

4. Audit these claims: (i) $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda/8)=40+j30\,\Omega$, or $\lvert\Gamma\rvert$ should be computed against $Z_t$ and equals $1/3$; (ii) the same numbers are a multiple-reflection bounce sequence on a mismatched lossless line; (iii) RMS versus peak phasors change $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$. Do not replace the frequency-domain transformer by a timed bounce diagram.
permittedResults: As $\beta\ell\to\pi/2$, $\tan\beta\ell\to\infty$ and $Z_{\mathrm{in}}\to Z_t^2/Z_L$, provided $Z_t$ is finite and nonzero.
At $\ell=\lambda/8$, $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ and $\tan\beta\ell=1$, so $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_t(Z_L+j Z_t)/(Z_t+j Z_L)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Set Zt=sqrt(Z0 ZL), then substitute tan(pi/4)=1 into the lossless Zin formula and rationalize.
Check the quarter-wave limit Zt^2/ZL first, then compute |Zin-Z0|/|Zin+Z0| with Z0=25 rather than Zt.

milestones.criterion: Designs Zt=50 ohm and recovers Zin=25 ohm at quarter-wave.
Evaluates Zin(lambda/8)=40-j30 ohm and |Gamma|=3/sqrt(41) on the 25 ohm feed.
Rejects a Zt-referenced |Gamma|=1/3 or +j30 reactance, and refuses a bounce-diagram substitution.

commonErrors.description: Reports Zin(lambda/8)=40+j30, or computes |Gamma|=1/3 by referencing the reflection to Zt=50 ohm instead of the 25 ohm feed.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the off-design reactance sign is wrong or the reflection is taken at the wrong port.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the single-frequency transformer calculation by a timed multiple-reflection bounce sequence.
commonErrors.consequence: The held line-bounce seed is substituted for an off-design quarter-wave impedance.

hintTree.content: Against $Z_0=25$, the numerator $15-j30$ and denominator $65-j30$ have modulus ratio $3/\sqrt{41}$.

CIR:020629.canonicalSolution:
At $\ell=\lambda/4$ one has $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ and
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_t^2}{Z_L}.
\]
Imposing $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_0=25\,\Omega$ with $Z_L=100\,\Omega$ gives the unique positive solution
\[
Z_t=\sqrt{Z_0 Z_L}=\sqrt{2500}=50\ \Omega.
\]
Then $Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda/4)=50^2/100=25\,\Omega$, so the $25\,\Omega$ feed is matched and the junction reflection vanishes.
\[
\boxed{Z_t=50\ \Omega,\quad Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda/4)=25\ \Omega}.
\]

At the same physical length but at the frequency for which $\ell=\lambda/8$, one has $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ and $\tan\beta\ell=1$. Therefore
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}
=50\cdot\frac{100+j50}{50+j100}
=50\cdot\frac{2+j}{1+j2}.
\]
Multiply numerator and denominator by $1-j2$:
\[
(2+j)(1-j2)=2-j4+j+2=4-j3,
\qquad
(1+j2)(1-j2)=1+4=5,
\]
so
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\cdot\frac{4-j3}{5}=40-j30\ \Omega.
\]
(The input is capacitive relative to the design match because the section is shorter than $\lambda/4$.)
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda/8)=40-j30\ \Omega}.
\]

On the feed,
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_0=15-j30,
\qquad
Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_0=65-j30,
\]
and
\[
\lvert\Gamma\rvert
=\frac{\lvert 15-j30\rvert}{\lvert 65-j30\rvert}
=\frac{\sqrt{225+900}}{\sqrt{4225+900}}
=\frac{\sqrt{1125}}{\sqrt{5125}}
=\sqrt{\frac{9}{41}}
=\frac{3}{\sqrt{41}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lvert\Gamma\rvert=3/\sqrt{41}}.
\]
Referencing $\Gamma$ to $Z_t=50\,\Omega$ would describe a fictional wave decomposition inside the transformer referred to the wrong characteristic impedance at the feed junction. That calculation yields
\[
\frac{\lvert 40-j30-50\rvert}{\lvert 40-j30+50\rvert}
=\frac{\lvert -10-j30\rvert}{\lvert 90-j30\rvert}
=\frac13,
\]
which is not the feed-line reflection asked for.

Impedance is a phasor ratio, so the RMS-versus-peak convention cancels and cannot change $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$. Claim (i) either flips the reactance sign or uses the wrong $\Gamma$ reference. Claim (ii) is the held bounce-diagram packet: the present computation is a single-frequency input impedance, not a timed sequence of source and load reflections.

graderFixtures.proofText: Zt=sqrt(25*100)=50 ohm and Zin(lambda/4)=50^2/100=25 ohm. At lambda/8, tan=1 gives Zin=50(100+j50)/(50+j100)=40-j30 ohm. On the 25 ohm feed, |15-j30|/|65-j30|=3/sqrt(41). Against Zt one would get 1/3, which is the wrong port. Impedance is a phasor ratio, so RMS versus peak does not change Zin. This is not a bounce diagram.
I obtain Zin=40+j30 at lambda/8. The reflection should be taken against the transformer, so |Gamma|=|40+j30-50|/|40+j30+50|=1/3.
The same 25 ohm, 50 ohm, and 100 ohm numbers are a bounce diagram: launch a step, reflect at the load with Gamma_L=(100-50)/(100+50), and sum the infinite voltage series.

CIR:020630.title: RMS standing-wave extrema and a lambda/8 voltage max recover ZL=30+j40
CIR:020630.objective: From RMS voltage max 12 V and min 4 V on a 50 ohm lossless line, recover |Gamma|=1/2, place Gamma_L=j/2 at the load using the declared nearest-max coordinate, obtain ZL=30+j40, and compute incident/reflected RMS 8 V / 4 V and delivered power 0.96 W.
CIR:020630.statement:
A lossless TEM line has characteristic impedance
\[
Z_0=50.0\ \Omega.
\]
In sinusoidal steady state the RMS voltage standing-wave extrema on the line are
\[
V_{\max}=12.0\ \mathrm{V_{rms}},\qquad V_{\min}=4.00\ \mathrm{V_{rms}}.
\]
These are root-mean-square magnitudes, not peak phasor magnitudes.

Coordinate convention. Place the load at $z=0$ and the generator at $z<0$. Distance from the load toward the generator is $d=-z\ge 0$. Traveling-wave phasors (RMS) obey
\[
V(z)=V^+e^{-j\beta z}+V^-e^{j\beta z},
\qquad
I(z)=\frac{V^+e^{-j\beta z}-V^-e^{j\beta z}}{Z_0},
\]
with $I$ positive in the $+z$ (toward-the-load) direction. The load is passive: the current entering $Z_L$ is $I(0)$. Write
\[
\Gamma_L:=\frac{V^-}{V^+}=\frac{Z_L-Z_0}{Z_L+Z_0}
\]
and $\Gamma(d)=\Gamma_L e^{-j2\beta d}$. A voltage maximum occurs where $\Gamma(d)$ is real and nonnegative, so that the incident and reflected RMS voltages add in phase.

The voltage maximum nearest the load occurs at $d=\lambda/8$.

1. Compute the voltage standing-wave ratio and prove that $\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert=1/2$.

2. Using the declared coordinate and the nearest-maximum location, prove that $\Gamma_L=j/2$. Then invert the bilinear map and prove
\[
Z_L=30+j40\ \Omega.
\]

3. Recover the incident and reflected RMS traveling-wave amplitudes $\lvert V^+\rvert=8.00\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$ and $\lvert V^-\rvert=4.00\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. Compute the time-average power delivered to the load,
\[
P=\frac{\lvert V^+\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}^2-\lvert V^-\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{Z_0},
\]
and show that $P=0.960\,\mathrm{W}$. Confirm the same wattage from $P=\lvert V_L\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\operatorname{Re}(1/Z_L)$.

4. Audit these claims: (i) the $12\,\mathrm{V}$ and $4\,\mathrm{V}$ figures are peak amplitudes, so a factor $1/2$ belongs in $P$, or else $\lvert\Gamma\rvert=V_{\min}/V_{\max}=1/3$; (ii) the nearest maximum at $\lambda/8$ implies $\Gamma_L=-j/2$ and $Z_L=30-j40\,\Omega$; (iii) the exercise is a multiple-reflection bounce construction. Do not replace standing-wave phasor recovery by a timed bounce diagram.
permittedResults: $\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert=(S-1)/(S+1)$ where $S=V_{\max}/V_{\min}$, for a lossless line.
If a voltage maximum occurs at $d=\lambda/8$, then $2\beta d=\pi/2$ and $\Gamma_L=j\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert$ when $\Gamma(d)$ is taken positive real.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert Vmax/Vmin to |Gamma|, rotate Gamma_L by +j from 2 beta d=pi/2, then apply Z=Z0(1+Gamma)/(1-Gamma).
Read |V+| and |V-| from the sum and difference of the RMS extrema and check P two ways, including Re(VL I_L*).

milestones.criterion: Recovers |Gamma|=1/2 from the RMS extrema and Gamma_L=j/2 from the nearest maximum at lambda/8.
Inverts to ZL=30+j40 ohm and computes |V+|=8 Vrms, |V-|=4 Vrms, P=0.96 W.
Rejects a peak-power factor or |Gamma|=1/3, a conjugate load from a reversed coordinate, and a bounce-diagram substitution.

commonErrors.description: Treats 12 V and 4 V as peak amplitudes and inserts a factor 1/2 into P, or reports |Gamma|=Vmin/Vmax=1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the delivered power is halved to 0.48 W or the reflection magnitude is not (S-1)/(S+1).

commonErrors.description: Takes Gamma_L=-j/2 and ZL=30-j40 from a reversed phase, or replaces the standing-wave recovery by a bounce diagram.
commonErrors.consequence: The declared coordinate is violated, or a different seed family is substituted.

hintTree.content: $\Gamma(\lambda/8)=\Gamma_L e^{-j\pi/2}=-j\Gamma_L$ equals $+1/2$, hence $\Gamma_L=j/2$.

CIR:020630.canonicalSolution:
The standing-wave ratio is
\[
S=\frac{V_{\max}}{V_{\min}}=\frac{12}{4}=3.
\]
On a lossless line,
\[
\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert=\frac{S-1}{S+1}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert=1/2}.
\]
(The incorrect ratio $V_{\min}/V_{\max}=1/3$ is not $\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert$.)

At $d=\lambda/8$,
\[
2\beta d=2\cdot\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{2},
\]
so
\[
\Gamma(d)=\Gamma_L e^{-j\pi/2}=-j\Gamma_L.
\]
A voltage maximum requires $\Gamma(d)$ real and nonnegative, hence $\Gamma(d)=+\lvert\Gamma_L\rvert=+1/2$. Therefore
\[
-j\Gamma_L=\frac12\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\Gamma_L=\frac{j}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Gamma_L=j/2}.
\]
Now
\[
Z_L=Z_0\frac{1+\Gamma_L}{1-\Gamma_L}
=50\cdot\frac{1+j/2}{1-j/2}.
\]
Multiply numerator and denominator by $1+j/2$:
\[
\bigl(1+\tfrac{j}{2}\bigr)^2=1+j-\tfrac14=\tfrac34+j,
\qquad
\bigl(1-\tfrac{j}{2}\bigr)\bigl(1+\tfrac{j}{2}\bigr)=\tfrac54,
\]
so
\[
\frac{1+\Gamma_L}{1-\Gamma_L}
=\frac{3/4+j}{5/4}
=\frac35+j\frac45
\]
and
\[
Z_L=50\Bigl(\frac35+j\frac45\Bigr)=30+j40\ \Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_L=30+j40\ \Omega}.
\]

The RMS traveling-wave amplitudes are
\[
\lvert V^+\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_{\max}+V_{\min}}{2}=8.00\ \mathrm{V_{rms}},
\qquad
\lvert V^-\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_{\max}-V_{\min}}{2}=4.00\ \mathrm{V_{rms}}.
\]
Time-average power on a real $Z_0$, with RMS traveling-wave voltages, is
\[
P=\frac{8^2-4^2}{50}=\frac{48}{50}=0.960\ \mathrm{W}.
\]
Independently, $V_L=V^+(1+\Gamma_L)$ has RMS magnitude
\[
\lvert V_L\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}=8\bigl\lvert 1+j/2\bigr\rvert=8\sqrt{5/4}=4\sqrt5\ \mathrm{V_{rms}},
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Re}\bigl(1/Z_L\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((30-j40)/2500\bigr)=\frac{30}{2500}=\frac{3}{250},
\]
so
\[
P=\lvert V_L\rvert_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\operatorname{Re}(1/Z_L)=80\cdot\frac{3}{250}=0.960\ \mathrm{W}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lvert V^+\rvert=8\ \mathrm{V_{rms}},\ \lvert V^-\rvert=4\ \mathrm{V_{rms}},\ P=0.960\ \mathrm{W}}.
\]
A peak-phasor power formula $P=(\lvert V^+\rvert^2-\lvert V^-\rvert^2)/(2Z_0)$ applied to these already-RMS numbers would produce $0.480\,\mathrm{W}$ and is inconsistent with the declared RMS convention.

Claim (i) either inserts a spurious factor $1/2$ or confuses $\lvert\Gamma\rvert$ with $V_{\min}/V_{\max}$. Claim (ii) reverses the $e^{-j2\beta d}$ phase under the declared $d=-z$ coordinate, producing the conjugate load. Claim (iii) is the held bounce-diagram packet: the present data are sinusoidal standing-wave extrema, not a transient lattice of discrete reflections.

graderFixtures.proofText: S=3 so |Gamma|=1/2. Nearest max at d=lambda/8 makes -j Gamma_L=+1/2, hence Gamma_L=j/2 and ZL=50(1+j/2)/(1-j/2)=30+j40 ohm. RMS traveling waves are 8 V and 4 V, and P=(64-16)/50=0.96 W, matching |VL|^2 Re(1/ZL). Peak formulas or |Gamma|=1/3 are inconsistent with the RMS statement. Gamma=-j/2 is the opposite coordinate. This is not a bounce diagram.
The 12 V and 4 V values are peak phasors, so P=(8^2-4^2)/(2*50)=0.48 W. Also |Gamma|=4/12=1/3.
A maximum at lambda/8 means Gamma_L e^{+j pi/2} is positive, so Gamma_L=-j/2 and ZL=30-j40. Alternatively the same extrema come from summing bounce-diagram wavefronts.

CIR:020631.title: On a lossless line the forward-wave power is the stored energy density times the phase speed
CIR:020631.objective: From L'=250 nH/m and C'=100 pF/m compute Z0=50 ohm and v=2e8 m/s, evaluate lambda, beta, the 0.75 m phase and delay at 100 MHz, and show that a 5 V RMS forward wave carries 0.50 W with 2.5 nJ/m average storage, hence P=v w.
CIR:020631.statement:
A lossless TEM line has distributed parameters
\[
L'=250\ \mathrm{nH/m}=2.50\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H/m},
\qquad
C'=100\ \mathrm{pF/m}=1.00\times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F/m}.
\]
There is no distributed resistance or conductance. The $+z$ direction runs from the generator toward a matched load, so only a forward wave exists. Traveling-wave convention:
\[
v(z,t)=v^+(t-z/v),\qquad
i(z,t)=\frac{v^+(t-z/v)}{Z_0},
\]
with current positive in the $+z$ direction. Sinusoidal calculations use RMS phasors and the $e^{j\omega t}$ convention; $5.00\,\mathrm{V}$ below is an RMS amplitude, not a peak amplitude.

The characteristic impedance and phase speed are
\[
Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{2.50\times 10^{-7}}{1.00\times 10^{-10}}}
=\sqrt{2500}=50.0\ \Omega
\]

\[

=\frac1{5.00\times 10^{-9}}

\]

At $f=100\,\mathrm{MHz}=1.00\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$,
\[
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{2.00\times 10^{8}}{1.00\times 10^{8}}=2.00\ \mathrm{m},
\qquad
\beta=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}=\pi\ \mathrm{rad/m}.
\]
For $\ell=0.750\,\mathrm{m}$,
\[
\beta\ell=\pi\cdot 0.750=\frac{3\pi}{4}\ \mathrm{rad},
\qquad
t_d=\frac{\ell}{v}=\frac{0.750}{2.00\times 10^{8}}=3.75\times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}=3.75\ \mathrm{ns}.
\]
The delay is a propagation time, not the RF period $1/f=10.0\,\mathrm{ns}$.
\[
\boxed{\lambda=2\ \mathrm{m},\ \beta=\pi\ \mathrm{rad/m},\ \beta\ell=3\pi/4,\ t_d=3.75\ \mathrm{ns}}.
\]

A purely forward RMS voltage $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=5.00\,\mathrm{V}$ produces
\[
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{5.00}{50.0}=0.100\ \mathrm{A_{rms}}
\]
and time-average power
\[
P=\frac{5.00^2}{50.0}=\frac{25.0}{50.0}=0.500\ \mathrm{W}.
\]
The time-average stored energy density is
\begin{align*}
w
&=\frac12 L'I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2+\frac12 C'V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\\
&=\frac12(2.50\times 10^{-7})(0.0100)
+\frac12(1.00\times 10^{-10})(25.0)\\
&=1.25\times 10^{-9}+1.25\times 10^{-9}
=2.50\times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{J/m}
=2.50\ \mathrm{nJ/m}.
\end{align*}
The two storage contributions are equal because $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=Z_0 I_{\mathrm{rms}}$ and $Z_0=\sqrt{L'/C'}$. The energy-velocity identity is then immediate:
\[
vw=(2.00\times 10^{8})(2.50\times 10^{-9})=0.500\ \mathrm{W}=P.
\]

\[
\boxed{P=0.500\ \mathrm{W},\ w=2.50\ \mathrm{nJ/m},\ P=vw}.
\]

CA:010121.title: Zeros can accumulate only by vanishing identically
CA:010121.objective: Prove the identity theorem from local zero factorization and connectedness, then apply it to a uniqueness interpolation and a contrasting essential-boundary example.
CA:010121.statement:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$ be open and connected, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega$. Prove that the zero set $f^{-1}(0)$ is either discrete in $\Omega$ or equal to $\Omega$. In the proof you must use a local factorization $f(z)=(z-a)^n g(z)$ with $g$ holomorphic and $g(a)\ne0$ at a non-identically-vanishing germ, and you must use connectedness of $\Omega$.

Apply the theorem in two ways. First: show there is at most one entire function $F$ satisfying $F(1/n)=e^{1/n}$ for every integer $n\ge1$, and exhibit that function. Second: explain why $\sin(\pi/z)$, which vanishes at every $1/n$, does not contradict the theorem. Finally, prove that if two holomorphic functions on $\Omega$ agree on a nonempty open subset, they agree on all of $\Omega$.
permittedResults: A holomorphic function on a disk is given by its Taylor series, so a nonvanishing jet at the center yields a nonvanishing holomorphic factor.
A nonempty proper clopen subset of a connected space cannot exist.
The function $e^z$ is entire and satisfies $e^{1/n}$ at $z=1/n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Analyze the set where the germ vanishes identically and use connectedness.
After isolating zeros, argue that a limit point of zeros in the domain forces the germ to vanish, then propagate by connectedness.

milestones.criterion: Sets the correct domain, regularity, and reconstruction or contour hypotheses and carries them through the argument.
Proves the identity theorem by isolated-zero factorization plus a clopen argument, then applies it to the entire interpolant $e^z$.
Completes every requested identification, uniqueness, period, estimate, or comparison check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that $\sin(\pi/z)\equiv0$, or that any sequence of zeros forces a holomorphic function to vanish identically, without requiring the limit point to lie in the domain.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity theorem is misstated and the contrasting example is mishandled.

commonErrors.description: Asserts the identity theorem without a local $(z-a)^n g$ factorization or without a connectedness/clopen step.
commonErrors.consequence: The two structural ingredients of the theorem are not established.

hintTree.content: If a germ is not identically zero, a finite-order zero is isolated because $g$ is continuous and $g(a)\ne0$.
The set of points at which $f$ vanishes identically on a neighborhood is open and closed in $\Omega$.
The points $1/n$ accumulate at $0$, which lies in the domain of an entire $F$ but not in the domain of $\sin(\pi/z)$.

CA:010121.canonicalSolution:
Fix $a\in\Omega$. If $f$ is not identically zero on any neighborhood of $a$, Taylor expansion supplies a finite order $n\ge0$ and a holomorphic $g$ with $g(a)\ne0$ and $f(z)=(z-a)^n g(z)$ near $a$. Continuity of $g$ then isolates the zero when $n\ge1$, and supplies no zero when $n=0$.

Let $E$ be the set of points at which $f$ vanishes on some neighborhood. Then $E$ is open. If $a_k\in E$ and $a_k\to a\in\Omega$, continuity gives $f(a)=0$; the isolated-zero alternative is then impossible, so the germ at $a$ vanishes identically and $a\in E$. Thus $E$ is also closed in $\Omega$. Connectedness forces $E=\emptyset$ or $E=\Omega$. In the first case every zero is isolated in $\Omega$; in the second, $f\equiv0$.

The entire function $F(z)=e^z$ satisfies $F(1/n)=e^{1/n}$. If $\widetilde F$ is another such entire function, then $\widetilde F-e^z$ vanishes on $\{1/n\}$, whose limit point $0$ lies in $\mathbb C$. The identity theorem yields $\widetilde F\equiv e^z$. Thus
$$
\boxed{F(z)=e^z}
$$
is the unique entire interpolant.

The function $\sin(\pi/z)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and vanishes at $1/n$, but the accumulation point $0$ is missing from the domain. There is therefore no contradiction, and indeed $\sin(\pi/z)\not\equiv0$.

If $f$ and $h$ are holomorphic on $\Omega$ and agree on a nonempty open $U\subset\Omega$, then $f-h$ vanishes on $U$, so the set $E$ above is nonempty and equals $\Omega$.

graderFixtures.proofText: A nonvanishing germ factors as (z-a)^n g with g(a)≠0, so zeros are isolated. The set where f vanishes identically is clopen, hence empty or all of connected Ω. Thus F(z)=e^z is the unique entire interpolant of e^{1/n}. sin(π/z) is safe because 0 is not in its domain. Agreement on a nonempty open set propagates to Ω.
sin(π/z) vanishes at 1/n and these points accumulate, so the identity theorem says sin(π/z) is identically zero on C\{0}.
Zeros of holomorphic functions are isolated because holomorphic functions are continuous. Connectedness and a local power-factorization are unnecessary.

CA:010222.title: Quadratic growth forces a quadratic polynomial
CA:010222.objective: Extract Cauchy estimates from the integral formula, classify entire functions of polynomial growth, run the standard Liouville proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra, and identify an explicit quadratic.
CA:010222.statement:
Let $f$ be entire. From Cauchy's integral formula, prove the estimates
$$
\bigl|f^{(n)}(a)\bigr|\le\frac{n!\,M_R}{R^n},
$$
where $M_R=\max_{|z-a|=R}|f(z)|$. Deduce Liouville's theorem: a bounded entire function is constant.

Now suppose $|f(z)|\le 3|z|^2+1$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$. Prove that $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$. If in addition $f(0)=2$, $f'(0)=0$, and $f''(0)=6$, identify $f$ exactly.

Finally prove the fundamental theorem of algebra: a nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a root in $\mathbb C$. Your proof must use Liouville on $1/p$ after checking that a rootless $p$ would make $1/p$ a bounded entire function.
permittedResults: The length of the circle $|z-a|=R$ is $2\pi R$, and $|z-a|^{n+1}=R^{n+1}$ there.
If every Taylor coefficient of order greater than $d$ vanishes, an entire function is a polynomial of degree at most $d$.
If $p$ is a polynomial of degree at least $1$, then $|p(z)|\to\infty$ as $|z|\to\infty$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Estimate Taylor coefficients on large circles and pass to the limit.
After the degree bound, match the three jet conditions to the three unknown coefficients.

milestones.criterion: Sets the correct domain, regularity, and reconstruction or contour hypotheses and carries them through the argument.
Uses Cauchy estimates to force degree at most two and identifies $f(z)=2+3z^2$, then proves FTA by Liouville.
Completes every requested identification, uniqueness, period, estimate, or comparison check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: Declares $f$ quadratic from the growth bound without showing that coefficients of order $n\ge3$ vanish by letting $R\to\infty$.
commonErrors.consequence: The classification of polynomial-growth entire functions is not established.

commonErrors.description: Misreads $f''(0)=6$ as $a_2=6$ or otherwise identifies a polynomial other than $2+3z^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique jet-matching quadratic is wrong.

hintTree.content: Bound the integrand of Cauchy's formula by $M_R/R^{n+1}$ and multiply by the length $2\pi R$.
For $|f|\le 3|z|^2+1$, take $a=0$ and let $R\to\infty$ in the $n\ge3$ estimates.
A rootless nonconstant polynomial $p$ would make $1/p$ entire and bounded, hence constant.

CA:010222.canonicalSolution:
Cauchy's formula and the ML-inequality give
$$
\bigl|f^{(n)}(a)\bigr|
\le\frac{n!}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{M_R}{R^{n+1}}\cdot 2\pi R
=\frac{n!\,M_R}{R^n}.
$$
If $|f|\le M$ on $\mathbb C$, then $|f'(a)|\le M/R$ for every $R$, so $f'(a)=0$. Thus $f$ is constant: Liouville's theorem.

Under the growth $|f(z)|\le 3|z|^2+1$ one has $M_R\le 3(R+|a|)^2+1$. For $a=0$ and $n\ge3$,
$$
|a_n|=\frac{|f^{(n)}(0)|}{n!}
\le\frac{3R^2+1}{R^n}\to0
\qquad(R\to\infty).
$$
Hence $a_n=0$ for $n\ge3$, and $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$:
$$
f(z)=a_0+a_1 z+a_2 z^2.
$$
The jet $f(0)=2$, $f'(0)=0$, $f''(0)=6$ forces $a_0=2$, $a_1=0$, $2a_2=6$, so
$$
\boxed{f(z)=2+3z^2}.
$$

If a nonconstant polynomial $p$ had no root, then $1/p$ would be entire. Since $|p(z)|\to\infty$ as $|z|\to\infty$, the function $1/p$ would be bounded, hence constant by Liouville, hence $p$ constant, a contradiction. Therefore $p$ has a root in $\mathbb C$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Cauchy plus ML gives |f^{(n)}(a)|≤n! M_R/R^n. Boundedness implies f'=0. From |f|≤3|z|^2+1 the coefficients a_n for n≥3 vanish as R→∞, so f is quadratic. The jet yields f(z)=2+3z^2. A rootless nonconstant polynomial would make 1/p a nonconstant bounded entire function, which Liouville forbids.
An entire function bounded by a quadratic is obviously a quadratic polynomial, so f(z)=2+3z^2 after matching the jet. I did not estimate a_n for n≥3.
Cauchy estimates give a polynomial of degree at most 2. Since f''(0)=6 I take f(z)=2+6z^2.
