CA:020327.title: For a=1/2 the disk Green function vanishes on the circle, is positive inside, and its negative outward normal derivative is the Poisson kernel with P_a(1)=3
CA:020327.objective: On the unit disk with pole a=1/2, prove that G(z,a)=log|(1-conj(a)z)/(z-a)| vanishes on the boundary, is positive inside, has local singularity -log|z-a|, and satisfies -Delta G=2pi delta_a; derive that the negative outward normal derivative -dG/dn equals P_a, and evaluate G(0)=log 2, G(-1/2)=log(5/4), P_a(1)=3, P_a(-1)=1/3, and integral P=2pi.
CA:020327.statement:
Let $\mathbb D=\{z:|z|<1\}$ and fix the interior pole
$a=1/2$. Define
\[
G(z,a)=\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{1-\overline a\,z}{z-a}\Bigr\rvert
\]
for $z\in\overline{\mathbb D}\setminus\{a\}$, and write $P_a$ for the
unnormalized Poisson kernel
\[
P_a(e^{i\theta})=\frac{1-|a|^2}{\lvert e^{i\theta}-a\rvert^2}.
\]
Do not replace the argument by a disk Poisson Dirichlet extension,
an approximate-identity uniqueness proof, or a Rouche annular count.

1. Prove that $G(\,\cdot\,,a)$ vanishes identically on
   $\partial\mathbb D$, that $G>0$ throughout $\mathbb D\setminus\{a\}$,
   and that
   \[
   G(z,a)=-\log|z-a|+\log|1-\overline a\,z|
   \]
   is harmonic on $\mathbb D\setminus\{a\}$ with local singularity
   $-\log|z-a|$.

2. Prove the distributional identity
   \[
   -\Delta G(\,\cdot\,,a)=2\pi\,\delta_a
   \]
   on $\mathbb D$.

3. On the unit circle, with outward unit normal, derive
   \[
   -\frac{\partial G}{\partial n}(e^{i\theta},a)=P_a(e^{i\theta}).
   \]
   Then evaluate the samples
   \[
   G(0,a)=\log 2,\qquad
   G\bigl(-\tfrac12,a\bigr)=\log\frac54,
   \]
   \[
   P_a(1)=3,\qquad
   P_a(-1)=\frac13,\qquad
   \int_0^{2\pi}P_a(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta=2\pi.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$G$ is already the Poisson integral of
   its boundary data, so the Dirichlet extension of a continuous
   $g$ is the object of the problem”; (ii) “the Green function is
   $\frac1{2\pi}\log|z-a|$ with no Blaschke correction, hence
   $G(0)=\log 2$ fails and $P_a$ cannot equal $-\partial G/\partial n$.”
permittedResults: If $|z|=1$, then $|1-\overline a z|=|z-a|$, so $G$ vanishes on the circle. The Blaschke factor satisfies $|B_a(z)|<1$ for $|z|<1$, hence $G>0$ inside.

Distributionally $\Delta\log|z-a|=2\pi\delta_a$. The correction $\log|1-\overline a z|$ is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{\mathbb D}$ because its singularity lies at $1/\overline a$ outside the closed disk.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify G as -log of the Blaschke factor, then split off -log|z-a| and apply the fundamental-solution Laplacian.
Differentiate radially on |z|=1 to recover P_a and evaluate the five assigned samples by direct substitution.

milestones.criterion: Proves boundary vanishing, interior positivity, the local singularity -log|z-a|, and -Delta G=2pi delta_a.
Derives -dG/dn=P_a and reports G(0)=log 2, G(-1/2)=log(5/4), P_a(1)=3, P_a(-1)=1/3, and integral P=2pi.
Rejects a reserved disk Poisson Dirichlet substitution and a Green function without the Blaschke correction.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Green-function / normal-derivative problem by a disk Poisson Dirichlet extension or approximate-identity uniqueness argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities -Delta G=2pi delta_a and -dG/dn=P_a are never proved.

commonErrors.description: Takes G to be a multiple of log|z-a| with no Blaschke correction, so G fails to vanish on the circle and the sample G(0)=log 2 is lost.
commonErrors.consequence: Boundary vanishing, positivity, and the Poisson normal derivative cannot hold simultaneously.

hintTree.content: On $|z|=1$ factor $|1-\overline a z|=|z|\,|\overline z-\overline a|=|z-a|$.
Near $z=a$ the term $\log|1-\overline a z|$ is $C^\infty$. The Laplacian identity is then the standard fundamental-solution identity for $-\log|z-a|$.

CA:020327.canonicalSolution:
Write $a=1/2$, so $\overline a=a$. For $|z|=1$ one has
$\overline z=1/z$, hence
\[
\bigl|1-\overline a\,z\bigr|
=\bigl|z\bigr|\,\bigl|\overline z-\overline a\bigr|
=\lvert z-a\rvert.
\]
Therefore $G(z,a)=\log 1=0$ at every boundary point.
\[
\boxed{G=0\text{ on }\partial\mathbb D}.
\]
The disk automorphism $B_a(z)=(z-a)/(1-\overline a z)$ sends
$\mathbb D$ into itself and vanishes only at $a$, so
$|B_a(z)|<1$ for $z\in\mathbb D\setminus\{a\}$. Equivalently
\[
G(z,a)=-\log\lvert B_a(z)\rvert>0
\qquad\text{on }\mathbb D\setminus\{a\}.
\]
Splitting the logarithm gives the local representation
\[
G(z,a)=-\log|z-a|+\log|1-\overline a\,z|.
\]
The second summand is harmonic on a neighborhood of
$\overline{\mathbb D}$ because $1-\overline a z=0$ only at
$z=1/\overline a=2\notin\overline{\mathbb D}$. Thus $G$ is
harmonic on $\mathbb D\setminus\{a\}$ with isolated singularity
$-\log|z-a|$.
\[
\boxed{G>0\text{ in }\mathbb D\setminus\{a\},\quad
G=-\log|z-a|+O(1)}.
\]

In the sense of distributions on $\mathbb D$,
$\Delta\log|z-a|=2\pi\delta_a$ and $\Delta\log|1-\overline a z|=0$.
Hence $\Delta G=-2\pi\delta_a$, or
\[
-\Delta G(\,\cdot\,,a)=2\pi\,\delta_a.
\]
\[
\boxed{-\Delta G=2\pi\delta_a}.
\]

On the unit circle the outward unit normal is the radial direction.
Put $c=\operatorname{Re}(\overline a e^{i\theta})$ and
$D=|e^{i\theta}-a|^2=1-2c+|a|^2$. Then
\[
G(re^{i\theta},a)
=\frac12\log\frac{1-2rc+|a|^2r^2}
{r^2-2rc+|a|^2}.
\]
Direct radial differentiation gives
\[
\left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial r}\right|_{r=1}
=\frac{|a|^2-c}{D}-\frac{1-c}{D}
=-\frac{1-|a|^2}{D}.
\]
Since $\partial/\partial n=\partial/\partial r$ at $r=1$, this is
exactly
\[
-\frac{\partial G}{\partial n}(e^{i\theta},a)
=\frac{1-|a|^2}{\lvert e^{i\theta}-a\rvert^2}
=P_a(e^{i\theta}).
\]
(The same formula is the Poisson kernel of harmonic measure for
the disk; it is recovered here as a normal derivative of $G$,
not as an approximate-identity Dirichlet solver.)

The assigned samples are elementary substitutions. At $z=0$,
\[
G(0,a)=\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{1}{0-1/2}\Bigr\rvert=\log 2.
\]
At $z=-1/2$,
\[
G\bigl(-\tfrac12,a\bigr)
=\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{1-(1/2)(-1/2)}{-1/2-1/2}\Bigr\rvert
=\log\frac{5/4}{1}
=\log\frac54.
\]
The Poisson values are
\[
P_a(1)
=\frac{1-1/4}{\lvert 1-1/2\rvert^2}
=\frac{3/4}{1/4}=3,
\]
\[
P_a(-1)
=\frac{3/4}{\lvert -1-1/2\rvert^2}
=\frac{3/4}{9/4}=\frac13.
\]
Mean-value / harmonic-measure normalization of the same kernel
gives
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}P_a(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta=2\pi.
\]
\[
\boxed{G(0)=\log 2,\ G(-1/2)=\log(5/4),\ P_a(1)=3,\ P_a(-1)=1/3,\ \int P=2\pi}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the Green-function / normal-derivative
audit by the reserved disk Poisson Dirichlet extension. Sentence
(ii) drops the Blaschke correction and cannot produce $G(0)=\log 2$
or the identity $-\partial G/\partial n=P_a$. The construction is
not a Rouche count and not a prescribed-pole series.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $|z|=1$ one has $|1-\overline a z|=|z-a|$, so $G=0$. Inside the disk $|B_a|<1$, hence $G>0$. The split $G=-\log|z-a|+\log|1-\overline a z|$ and $\Delta\log|z-a|=2\pi\delta_a$ give $-\Delta G=2\pi\delta_a$. Radial differentiation gives the negative outward normal derivative $-\partial_nG=P_a$, with samples $G(0)=\log 2$, $G(-1/2)=\log(5/4)$, $P_a(1)=3$, $P_a(-1)=1/3$, and $\int P=2\pi$.

G is already the Poisson integral of its boundary data, so the problem is the Dirichlet extension of a continuous g by the approximate-identity kernel. I do not prove -Delta G=2pi delta_a or -dG/dn=P_a.
The Green function is (1/2pi) log|z-a| with no Blaschke correction, so G(0)=log 2 fails and P_a cannot equal -dG/dn. I never accept G=0 on the circle together with G(0)=log 2.

CA:020422.title: The single-valued series F(z)=sum (-1)^n z^n/(2n)! is entire of order 1/2 and type 1, with F(0)=1, F'(0)=-1/2, and first positive zeros pi^2/4, 9pi^2/4, 25pi^2/4
CA:020422.objective: Define F by the power series sum_{n>=0}(-1)^n z^n/(2n)!, prove it is entire, evaluate F(0)=1 and F'(0)=-1/2, locate the first three positive zeros at pi^2/4, 9pi^2/4, 25pi^2/4 and prove they are simple, and prove that the maximum modulus is M(r)=cosh(sqrt(r)) so that F has order 1/2 and type 1. Treat cos(sqrt z) only as a mnemonic after the series is defined.
CA:020422.statement:
Define an entire candidate by the power series
\[
F(z)
:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{z^{n}}{(2n)!}.
\]
The notation $F(z)=\cos\sqrt{z}$ is permitted only as a mnemonic
after this series has been shown to be entire and single-valued; do
not take a branched square root as the definition of $F$. Do not
replace the growth computation by a Weierstrass or canonical-product
construction, and do not recast $F$ as a Mittag-Leffler partial-
fraction expansion or as a prescribed-pole interpolant.

1. Prove that the series has infinite radius of convergence, so $F$
   is entire, and evaluate
   \[
   F(0)=1,\qquad F'(0)=-\frac12.
   \]

2. For arbitrary $z\in\mathbb C$, choose either algebraic square root
   $w$ with $w^2=z$ and use the power series to exclude non-real
   zeros. Then use a locally holomorphic square root only near each
   listed positive point (never as a global branch) to prove that the
   zeros of $F$ are exactly the simple points
   \[
   z_{k}=\Bigl(\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2}\Bigr)^{2},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,
   \]
   and record the first three positive zeros
   \[
   \frac{\pi^{2}}{4},\qquad \frac{9\pi^{2}}{4},\qquad \frac{25\pi^{2}}{4}.
   \]

3. Let $M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|F(z)|$. Prove the matching bounds
   \[
   M(r)\le\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{r^{n}}{(2n)!}=\cosh\sqrt{r}
   \]
   and $M(r)\ge|F(-r)|=\cosh\sqrt{r}$, hence $M(r)=\cosh\sqrt{r}$.
   Deduce that $F$ has order $1/2$ and type $1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\sqrt{z}$ is branched at the origin,
   so $F$ itself has a branch point there and is not entire”;
   (ii) “$\log M(r)\sim\sqrt{r}$ means order $1$ and type $1/2$, or
   else $M(r)=|F(r)|=|\cos\sqrt{r}|$.”
permittedResults: The radius test $\lvert a_{n+1}/a_{n}\rvert=\lvert z\rvert/((2n+2)(2n+1))\to0$ gives infinite radius, so $F$ is entire. Termwise differentiation is legitimate and yields $F'(0)=-1/2! =-1/2$.

For every scalar $z\in\mathbb C$, either algebraic square root $w$ satisfies $F(z)=\cos w$ because $w^{2n}=z^n$ term by term. The zeros of complex cosine are exactly $w=(k+1/2)\pi$, so every zero of $F$ is one of the listed positive squares. On a neighbourhood of each such point, a holomorphic square root $s$ gives $F'(z)=-s'(z)\sin s(z)\neq0$, proving simplicity without choosing a global branch.

acceptableStrategies.description: Establish infinite radius from the consecutive-term ratio, read F(0) and F'(0), use an arbitrary algebraic square root to exclude non-real zeros, and use local holomorphic square roots only to prove simplicity.
Bound M(r) by the series of absolute values and match it from below by F(-r)=sum r^n/(2n)!, then extract order and type from log cosh(sqrt(r))~sqrt(r).

milestones.criterion: Defines F by the series, proves it is entire, and records F(0)=1 together with F'(0)=-1/2 and the first three positive simple zeros pi^2/4, 9pi^2/4, 25pi^2/4.
Proves M(r)=cosh(sqrt(r)) by matching the absolute-series upper bound with the lower bound F(-r), and concludes order 1/2 and type 1.
Rejects a branched-square-root denial of entire-ness or an order/type swap, and refuses reserved Weierstrass, Mittag-Leffler, or prescribed-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the mnemonic cos(sqrt(z)) as a globally branched square root and concludes that F has a branch point at 0, so F is not entire.
commonErrors.consequence: The required entire function of order 1/2, the value F(0)=1, and the simple zeros on the positive axis are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reads log M(r)~sqrt(r) as order 1 and type 1/2, or replaces M(r) by the oscillatory |F(r)|=|cos sqrt(r)|.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair (order, type)=(1/2, 1) and the identity M(r)=cosh(sqrt(r)) are never produced.

hintTree.content: The coefficients involve $(2n)!$ in the denominator, so the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $0$ for every fixed $z$. The constant term is $1$ and the linear term is $-z/2$.

For arbitrary $z$, choose a scalar $w$ with $w^2=z$; the series gives $F(z)=\cos w$, and $\cos w=0$ forces $w=(k+1/2)\pi$. After this global exclusion, use the positive local holomorphic square root near each listed point to prove simplicity.

Bound $|F(z)|$ on $|z|=r$ by the series of absolute values, which is $\cosh\sqrt{r}$. Evaluate the same series at $z=-r$ to match the lower bound, then read order and type from $\log\cosh\sqrt{r}\sim\sqrt{r}$.

CA:020422.canonicalSolution:
Write $a_{n}=(-1)^{n}/(2n)!$. For $z\neq0$,
\[
\Bigl\lvert\frac{a_{n+1}z^{n+1}}{a_{n}z^{n}}\Bigr\rvert
=\frac{\lvert z\rvert}{(2n+2)(2n+1)}\to0
\qquad(n\to\infty).
\]
The radius of convergence is therefore infinite, and $F$ is entire
(in particular holomorphic and single-valued at the origin). The
constant term is $1$, so $F(0)=1$. Termwise differentiation,
justified by the same radius, gives
\[
F'(z)
=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n}\frac{n\,z^{n-1}}{(2n)!},
\qquad
F'(0)=-\frac{1}{2!}=-\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{F\text{ entire},\quad F(0)=1,\quad F'(0)=-1/2}.
\]
The identity $\cos w=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^{n}w^{2n}/(2n)!$ shows that
the mnemonic $F(z)=\cos\sqrt{z}$ is simply the series for $\cos w$
rewritten in the variable $z=w^{2}$. No branched square root enters
the definition.

Now let $z\in\mathbb C$ be arbitrary and choose either scalar square
root $w$ of $z$. Term by term, $w^{2n}=z^n$, so the two entire
power series give
\[
F(z)=\cos w.
\]
The value is independent of the choice $w$ or $-w$ because cosine
is even. If $F(z)=0$, then $\cos w=0$. Equivalently
$e^{2iw}=-1$, so $w=(k+\tfrac12)\pi$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$.
Thus $w$ is real and
\[
z_{k}=\Bigl(\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]
The negative integers repeat the same positive points, and this
argument excludes every non-real zero. The first three distinct
zeros are
\[
z_{0}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{4},\qquad
z_{1}=\frac{9\pi^{2}}{4},\qquad
z_{2}=\frac{25\pi^{2}}{4}.
\]
To prove simplicity, fix one listed positive zero $x$ and choose the
positive holomorphic square root $s$ on a small disc about $x$.
There $F=\cos\circ s$ and
$F'(z)=-s'(z)\sin s(z)$, with $s'(z)=1/(2s(z))\neq0$ and
$\sin((2k+1)\pi/2)=(-1)^{k}\neq0$. Hence each zero is simple. The
origin is not a zero, since $F(0)=1$.
\[
\boxed{\text{simple zeros }\pi^{2}/4,\;9\pi^{2}/4,\;25\pi^{2}/4,\;\dots}.
\]

On the circle $|z|=r$,
\[
\lvert F(z)\rvert
\le\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{r^{n}}{(2n)!}.
\]
The right-hand side is the series for $\cosh w$ at $w^{2}=r$, hence
equals $\cosh\sqrt{r}$ (again a mnemonic for a single-valued series
in $r$). In the other direction the same series evaluated at the
negative point $-r$ is
\[
F(-r)
=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{r^{n}}{(2n)!}
=\cosh\sqrt{r},
\]
so $M(r)\ge|F(-r)|=\cosh\sqrt{r}$. The two bounds match:
\[
M(r)=\cosh\sqrt{r}.
\]
As $r\to\infty$ one has $\log M(r)=\log\cosh\sqrt{r}\sim\sqrt{r}$,
and therefore
\[
\frac{\log\log M(r)}{\log r}\to\frac12,
\qquad
\frac{\log M(r)}{r^{1/2}}\to1.
\]
Thus $F$ has order $1/2$ and type $1$.
\[
\boxed{M(r)=\cosh\sqrt{r},\quad\rho=1/2,\quad\tau=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses the mnemonic $\cos\sqrt{z}$ with the definition
of $F$: the series in integer powers of $z$ has no branch point.
Sentence (ii) misreads $\log M(r)\sim r^{1/2}$ as order $1$ (or
replaces $M(r)$ by the oscillatory $|F(r)|$). The argument never
constructs a Weierstrass product over the zeros $z_{k}$, never
writes a Mittag-Leffler expansion, and never interpolates prescribed
poles.

graderFixtures.proofText: The series $F(z)=\sum(-1)^{n}z^{n}/(2n)!$ is entire, with $F(0)=1$ and $F'(0)=-1/2$. For arbitrary $z$, choose a scalar $w$ with $w^2=z$; then $F(z)=\cos w$, so a zero forces $w=(k+1/2)\pi$ and excludes non-real zeros. Local holomorphic square roots prove the listed zeros simple. The first three are $\pi^{2}/4$, $9\pi^{2}/4$, and $25\pi^{2}/4$. The maximum modulus is $M(r)=\cosh\sqrt{r}$, so $F$ has order $1/2$ and type $1$.
The square root is branched at the origin, so F(z)=cos(sqrt(z)) has a branch point there and is not entire. I do not report that the series is entire or that F(0)=1 is an entire value.
Since log M(r)~sqrt(r), the order is 1 and the type is 1/2; equivalently M(r)=|F(r)|=|cos sqrt(r)|. I never accept order 1/2 with type 1, nor M(r)=cosh(sqrt(r)).

CA:020423.title: The rational R=z^2/((z-1)(z+2)(z-3)) has residues -1/6, 4/15, 9/10 at 1, -2, 3, finite sum 1, residue at infinity -1, and sphere total 0
CA:020423.objective: For R(z)=z^2/((z-1)(z+2)(z-3)) compute the three finite residues in two ways, compute the residue at infinity from the chart w=1/z and from the Laurent coefficient at infinity, and prove that the finite sum is 1, Res_infinity=-1, and the sphere total is 0.
CA:020423.statement:
Let
\[
R(z)
=\frac{z^{2}}{(z-1)(z+2)(z-3)}.
\]
Do not replace the computation by a prescribed-pole interpolating
rational function, and do not recast $R$ as a Mittag-Leffler sum
over infinitely many poles or as a canonical-product construction.

1. Compute the residues at the simple poles $z=1$, $z=-2$, and
   $z=3$ in two ways (the simple-pole product formula, and partial
   fractions / the large-circle $1/z$ coefficient) and prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Res}(R;1)=-\frac16,\qquad
   \operatorname{Res}(R;-2)=\frac{4}{15},\qquad
   \operatorname{Res}(R;3)=\frac{9}{10}.
   \]

2. Deduce that the sum of the finite residues is $1$.

3. Pass to the chart $w=1/z$ and the Laurent expansion of $R$ at
   infinity, and prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)=-1.
   \]
   Conclude that the sum of all residues on the Riemann sphere is
   $0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the residue at infinity is the
   coefficient of $1/z$ in the large-$z$ expansion, hence
   $+1$, and the sphere sum is $2$”; (ii) “$\operatorname{Res}(R;1)=+1/6$,
   so the finite residues cannot sum to $1$.”
permittedResults: At a simple pole $a$ of $R(z)=z^{2}/((z-1)(z+2)(z-3))$ one has $\operatorname{Res}(R;a)=a^{2}$ divided by the product of $(a-b)$ over the other two poles $b$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the simple-pole product formula at 1, -2, and 3, then confirm the same coefficients by partial fractions and by R(z)~1/z at infinity.
Change variables w=1/z to read Res(infinity)=-Res_0(R(1/w)/w^2), and add the finite sum to obtain the sphere identity 0.

milestones.criterion: Computes the three finite residues -1/6, 4/15, 9/10 in two ways and obtains finite sum 1.
Computes Res(R;infinity)=-1 from w=1/z / the Laurent coefficient at infinity, and concludes that the sphere sum is 0.
Rejects a dropped minus sign at infinity or a flipped residue at 1, and refuses reserved prescribed-pole or Mittag-Leffler substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the residue at infinity to be the large-z coefficient a_{-1}=+1 rather than -a_{-1}, and reports sphere sum 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Res(R;infinity)=-1 and the sphere total 0 are replaced by the inconsistent pair +1 and 2.

commonErrors.description: Flips the sign of Res(R;1) to +1/6 (or otherwise miscomputes a finite residue) so that the finite residues do not sum to 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required triple (-1/6, 4/15, 9/10) and the finite sum 1 are lost.

hintTree.content: For $\operatorname{Res}(R;1)$ evaluate $1^{2}/((1+2)(1-3))$. The other two finite residues are the same product formula at $-2$ and at $3$.
Add the three fractions $-1/6+4/15+9/10$ over the common denominator $30$. Independently, $R(z)\sim1/z$ at infinity forces the finite sum to equal $a_{-1}=1$.
In the chart $w=1/z$ one finds $R(1/w)/w^{2}=1/(w(1-w)(1+2w)(1-3w))$, whose residue at $w=0$ is $1$, hence $\operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)=-1$.

CA:020423.canonicalSolution:
The denominator has three distinct simple zeros, so every finite
pole of $R$ is simple. The product formula gives
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Res}(R;1)
&=\frac{1^{2}}{(1+2)(1-3)}
=\frac{1}{3\cdot(-2)}
=-\frac16,\\
\operatorname{Res}(R;-2)
&=\frac{(-2)^{2}}{(-2-1)(-2-3)}
=\frac{4}{(-3)(-5)}
=\frac{4}{15},\\
\operatorname{Res}(R;3)
&=\frac{3^{2}}{(3-1)(3+2)}
=\frac{9}{2\cdot5}
=\frac{9}{10}.
\end{align*}
The same numbers are the partial-fraction coefficients in
\[
R(z)
=\frac{A}{z-1}+\frac{B}{z+2}+\frac{C}{z-3},
\]
because $\deg(\text{numerator})<\deg(\text{denominator})$. As a
second computation of the finite sum, expand at infinity:
\[
R(z)
=\frac{z^{2}}{z^{3}(1-z^{-1})(1+2z^{-1})(1-3z^{-1})}
=\frac1z\cdot\frac{1}{(1-z^{-1})(1+2z^{-1})(1-3z^{-1})}
=\frac1z+O(z^{-2}).
\]
A large positively oriented circle therefore sees residue $a_{-1}=1$,
which equals the sum of the finite residues. Checking the arithmetic,
\[
-\frac16+\frac{4}{15}+\frac{9}{10}
=-\frac{5}{30}+\frac{8}{30}+\frac{27}{30}
=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Res}_{1}=-1/6,\;
\operatorname{Res}_{-2}=4/15,\;
\operatorname{Res}_{3}=9/10,\;
\text{finite sum }=1}.
\]

For the residue at infinity, set $z=1/w$. Then
\[
R\Bigl(\frac1w\Bigr)
=\frac{w^{-2}}{(w^{-1}-1)(w^{-1}+2)(w^{-1}-3)}
=\frac{w}{(1-w)(1+2w)(1-3w)},
\]
and
\[
\frac{1}{w^{2}}R\Bigl(\frac1w\Bigr)
=\frac{1}{w(1-w)(1+2w)(1-3w)}.
\]
The Laurent coefficient of $w^{-1}$ at $w=0$ is $1$, so
\[
\operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)
=-\operatorname{Res}_{w=0}\Bigl(R(1/w)\,w^{-2}\Bigr)
=-1.
\]
This matches the large-$z$ coefficient rule $\operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)=-a_{-1}=-1$.
Adding the finite sum,
\[
\Bigl(-\frac16+\frac{4}{15}+\frac{9}{10}\Bigr)+(-1)
=1-1=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)=-1,\quad
\text{sphere total }=0}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the minus sign in the definition of the residue
at infinity and reports sphere sum $2$. Sentence (ii) flips the sign
of $\operatorname{Res}(R;1)$ and destroys the finite sum $1$. The
ledger is a three-pole rational identity on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$;
it is not a prescribed-pole interpolation, not a Mittag-Leffler
series of infinitely many poles, and not a canonical product.

graderFixtures.proofText: The residues are $\operatorname{Res}(R;1)=-1/6$, $\operatorname{Res}(R;-2)=4/15$, and $\operatorname{Res}(R;3)=9/10$, with finite sum $1$. The chart $w=1/z$ (equivalently $R(z)=z^{-1}+O(z^{-2})$) gives $\operatorname{Res}(R;\infty)=-1$, so the sum on the Riemann sphere is $0$.
The residue at infinity is the coefficient of 1/z in the large-z expansion, hence +1, and the sphere sum is 2. I do not report Res(R;infinity)=-1 or sphere total 0.
Res(R;1)=+1/6, so the finite residues cannot sum to 1. I never accept Res(R;1)=-1/6 or finite sum 1.

CA:020525.title: The Laplace integral I_n=int_0^1 e^{-n x}(1+x) dx equals 1/n+1/n^2-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^2), with n I_n->1, n^2(I_n-1/n)->1, and I_2=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}
CA:020525.objective: For I_n=int_0^1 e^{-n x}(1+x) dx derive the exact antiderivative expression 1/n+1/n^2-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^2), identify the two algebraic Watson terms from the endpoint x=0 and the exponentially small far-end remainder, prove n I_n->1 and n^2(I_n-1/n)->1, evaluate I_2=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}, and reject an interior saddle.
CA:020525.statement:
For integers $n\ge1$ define
\[
I_{n}
=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-nx}(1+x)\,dx.
\]
Do not replace the endpoint analysis by a stationary-phase or
interior-saddle argument, and do not recast the integral as a
Mittag-Leffler expansion, a canonical product, or a prescribed-pole
construction.

1. Integrate by parts (or compute the elementary antiderivative)
   and prove the exact identity
   \[
   I_{n}
   =\frac1n+\frac1{n^{2}}-e^{-n}\Bigl(\frac2n+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr).
   \]

2. Identify $1/n+1/n^{2}$ as the two-term Watson expansion obtained
   by replacing the upper limit $1$ by $\infty$ and expanding
   $1+x$ at the endpoint $x=0$. Show that the remainder
   $-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^{2})$ is exponentially small. Explain why the
   phase $-nx$ has no interior critical point on $(0,1)$.

3. Deduce the limits
   \[
   nI_{n}\to1,
   \qquad
   n^{2}\Bigl(I_{n}-\frac1n\Bigr)\to1,
   \]
   and evaluate
   \[
   I_{2}
   =\frac34-\frac54\,e^{-2}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Watson’s lemma already gives the
   exact value, so $I_{n}=1/n+1/n^{2}$ with no remainder”;
   (ii) “the phase $-nx$ has an interior saddle on $(0,1)$, and
   the leading term comes from that saddle rather than from
   $x=0$.”
permittedResults: The elementary primitives $\int e^{-nx}\,dx=-e^{-nx}/n$ and $\int x e^{-nx}\,dx=-e^{-nx}(x/n+1/n^{2})$ produce the exact formula for $I_{n}$ after evaluating from $0$ to $1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the two elementary integrals exactly by parts, then recognise 1/n+1/n^2 as the Laplace transform of 1+x on the half-line.
Read the two limits from the exact formula after multiplying by n and by n^2, substitute n=2, and note that phi'(x)=-1 never vanishes.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact formula I_n=1/n+1/n^2-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^2) and identifies the two algebraic Watson terms together with the exponentially small remainder.
Proves n I_n->1 and n^2(I_n-1/n)->1, evaluates I_2=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}, and rejects an interior saddle.
Rejects an exact identification I_n=1/n+1/n^2 or an interior-saddle substitution, and refuses reserved Mittag-Leffler or prescribed-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that Watson's two terms are already exact and reports I_n=1/n+1/n^2, omitting -e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^2).
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact remainder, the value I_2=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}, and the distinction between algebraic and exponentially small terms are lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the endpoint Watson analysis by a stationary-phase or interior-saddle argument on (0,1).
commonErrors.consequence: The actual contributing endpoint x=0 is abandoned, and the required expansion 1/n+1/n^2 plus an exponentially small remainder is never justified.

hintTree.content: Split $I_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-nx}\,dx+\int_{0}^{1}x e^{-nx}\,dx$ and integrate the second term by parts.
The same two terms arise as $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-nx}(1+x)\,dx$. Everything left is the integral from $1$ to $\infty$, which is $e^{-n}$ times a rational function of $n$.
Multiply the exact formula by $n$ and by $n^{2}$ and send $n\to\infty$. Then substitute $n=2$.

CA:020525.canonicalSolution:
Write $I_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-nx}\,dx+\int_{0}^{1}xe^{-nx}\,dx$.
The first integral is
\[
\int_{0}^{1}e^{-nx}\,dx
=\Bigl[-\frac{e^{-nx}}{n}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}
=\frac{1-e^{-n}}{n}.
\]
For the second, integrate by parts with $u=x$ and
$dv=e^{-nx}\,dx$:
\[
\int xe^{-nx}\,dx
=-\frac{x e^{-nx}}{n}+\int\frac{e^{-nx}}{n}\,dx
=-e^{-nx}\Bigl(\frac{x}{n}+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr).
\]
Evaluating from $0$ to $1$ yields
\[
\int_{0}^{1}xe^{-nx}\,dx
=-e^{-n}\Bigl(\frac1n+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr)+\frac1{n^{2}}.
\]
Adding the two pieces,
\begin{align*}
I_{n}
&=\frac{1-e^{-n}}{n}+\frac1{n^{2}}-e^{-n}\Bigl(\frac1n+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr)
=\frac1n+\frac1{n^{2}}-e^{-n}\Bigl(\frac2n+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr).
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{I_{n}=1/n+1/n^{2}-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^{2})}.
\]

Watson's lemma at the endpoint $x=0$ replaces the cutoff $1$ by
$\infty$ and uses $f(x)=1+x$:
\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-nx}(1+x)\,dx
=\frac1n+\frac1{n^{2}}.
\]
Those are the two algebraic Watson terms. The exact remainder is
the negative of the tail
\[
\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-nx}(1+x)\,dx
=e^{-n}\Bigl(\frac2n+\frac1{n^{2}}\Bigr),
\]
which is exponentially small as $n\to\infty$. The phase $\phi(x)=-x$
satisfies $\phi'(x)=-1\neq0$ on $(0,1)$, so there is no interior
critical point and no saddle-point contribution.

From the exact formula,
\[
nI_{n}
=1+\frac1n-e^{-n}\Bigl(2+\frac1n\Bigr)\to1
\]
and
\[
n^{2}\Bigl(I_{n}-\frac1n\Bigr)
=1-e^{-n}(2n+1)\to1.
\]
At $n=2$,
\[
I_{2}
=\frac12+\frac14-e^{-2}\Bigl(1+\frac14\Bigr)
=\frac34-\frac54\,e^{-2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{nI_{n}\to1,\quad
n^{2}(I_{n}-1/n)\to1,\quad
I_{2}=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the far-end remainder and claims that the two
Watson terms are already exact. Sentence (ii) invents an interior
saddle for a strictly monotone phase. The argument is an endpoint
Laplace / Watson expansion with an exact remainder; it is not a
Mittag-Leffler series, not a canonical product, and not a
prescribed-pole construction.

graderFixtures.proofText: The exact value is $I_{n}=1/n+1/n^{2}-e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^{2})$. The terms $1/n+1/n^{2}$ are the Watson endpoint contributions and the remaining piece is exponentially small; there is no interior saddle. Consequently $nI_{n}\to1$, $n^{2}(I_{n}-1/n)\to1$, and $I_{2}=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}$.
Watson's lemma already gives the exact value, so I_n=1/n+1/n^2 with no remainder. I do not report -e^{-n}(2/n+1/n^2) or I_2=3/4-(5/4)e^{-2}.

The phase -nx has an interior saddle on (0,1), and the leading term comes from that saddle rather than from x=0. I never accept an endpoint Watson expansion or the statement that phi'(x)=-1 has no zero.

CA:020526.title: The generating function (1-z)^{-3/2} has coefficients a_n=Gamma(n+3/2)/(Gamma(3/2) n!)=(2n+1)C(2n,n)/4^n, with a0..a3=(1, 3/2, 15/8, 35/16), ratio (n+3/2)/(n+1), and Darboux expansion (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128 n^2)+O(n^{-3})]
CA:020526.objective: For (1-z)^{-3/2}=sum a_n z^n derive a_n=Gamma(n+3/2)/(Gamma(3/2) Gamma(n+1))=(2n+1)C(2n,n)/4^n, record a0 through a3 as 1, 3/2, 15/8, 35/16, prove the recurrence ratio (n+3/2)/(n+1), and obtain the Darboux/Stirling expansion (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128 n^2)+O(n^{-3})].
CA:020526.statement:
Expand
\[
(1-z)^{-3/2}
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}
\]
as a power series at the origin. Do not replace the coefficient
analysis by a Mittag-Leffler expansion, a Weierstrass / canonical
product, or a prescribed-pole construction, and do not substitute
the neighbouring generating function $(1-z)^{-1/2}$.

1. From the generalized binomial theorem (or from the Cauchy
   integral $a_{n}=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint(1-z)^{-3/2}z^{-n-1}\,dz$)
   prove
   \[
   a_{n}
   =\frac{\Gamma(n+3/2)}{\Gamma(3/2)\,\Gamma(n+1)}
   =\frac{(2n+1)}{4^{n}}\binom{2n}{n}.
   \]

2. Evaluate the first four coefficients
   \[
   a_{0}=1,\qquad
   a_{1}=\frac32,\qquad
   a_{2}=\frac{15}{8},\qquad
   a_{3}=\frac{35}{16},
   \]
   and prove the exact ratio
   \[
   \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}}
   =\frac{n+3/2}{n+1}.
   \]

3. By Darboux analysis at the singularity $z=1$, or by the Stirling
   expansion of the Gamma ratio, prove
   \[
   a_{n}
   =\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\,n^{1/2}
   \Bigl(1+\frac{3}{8n}-\frac{7}{128n^{2}}+O(n^{-3})\Bigr).
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the coefficients are those of
   $(1-z)^{-1/2}$, namely $a_{n}=\binom{2n}{n}/4^{n}$, so the
   factor $2n+1$ is omitted”; (ii) “the $n^{-2}$ Darboux coefficient
   is $+9/128$ (or $+1/128$ without the $2n+1$ factor), not
   $-7/128$.”
permittedResults: The Pochhammer identity $\Gamma(n+3/2)/\Gamma(3/2)=(3/2)(5/2)\cdots(n+1/2)$ and the duplication relation for central binomials yield $a_{n}=(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}4^{-n}$. Consecutive coefficients satisfy $a_{n+1}/a_{n}=(n+3/2)/(n+1)$.
The expansion $\Gamma(n+a)/\Gamma(n+b)=n^{a-b}\bigl(1+(a-b)(a+b-1)/(2n)+O(n^{-2})\bigr)$ at $a=3/2$, $b=1$ gives the first correction $3/(8n)$. The $n^{-2}$ term evaluates to $-7/128$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read a_n from the generalized binomial / Cauchy formula and match it to (2n+1)C(2n,n)/4^n via (1-4x)^{-3/2}; compute the first four terms and the consecutive ratio from the Pochhammer identity.
Transfer the algebraic singularity at z=1 by Stirling of Gamma(n+3/2)/Gamma(n+1), or multiply the three-term expansion of C(2n,n)/4^n by 2n+1, to obtain the coefficient -7/128.

milestones.criterion: Produces a_n=Gamma(n+3/2)/(Gamma(3/2) n!)=(2n+1)C(2n,n)/4^n together with a0..a3=(1, 3/2, 15/8, 35/16) and the ratio (n+3/2)/(n+1).
Derives the Darboux/Stirling expansion (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128 n^2)+O(n^{-3})].
Rejects the (1-z)^{-1/2} coefficients or a wrong n^{-2} Darboux coefficient, and refuses reserved Mittag-Leffler, canonical-product, or prescribed-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the coefficients of (1-z)^{-1/2}, namely a_n=C(2n,n)/4^n, and omits the factor 2n+1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required sequence 1, 3/2, 15/8, 35/16 and the prefactor (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2} are replaced by the neighbouring generating function.

commonErrors.description: Reports the n^{-2} Darboux coefficient as +9/128 or as +1/128 (the raw central-binomial term) instead of -7/128.
commonErrors.consequence: The required three-term expansion (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128 n^2)+O(n^{-3})] is not obtained.

hintTree.content: Write $a_{n}=\Gamma(n+3/2)/(\Gamma(3/2)n!)$ and check $n=0,1,2,3$ directly from $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$ with $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt{\pi}/2$.
The ratio of successive Gamma values is $a_{n+1}/a_{n}=(n+3/2)/(n+1)$. To match the central binomial, compare with the known generating function $(1-4x)^{-3/2}=\sum(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}x^{n}$.
Apply Stirling to $\Gamma(n+3/2)/\Gamma(n+1)$ (or multiply the expansion of $\binom{2n}{n}4^{-n}\sim(\pi n)^{-1/2}(1-1/(8n)+1/(128n^{2}))$ by $2n+1$). The $n^{-2}$ coefficient becomes $-7/128$.

CA:020526.canonicalSolution:
The generalized binomial series with exponent $-3/2$ reads
\[
(1-z)^{-3/2}
=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{\Gamma(n+3/2)}{\Gamma(3/2)\,\Gamma(n+1)}\,z^{n}
\]
in $|z|<1$, so
\[
a_{n}
=\frac{\Gamma(n+3/2)}{\Gamma(3/2)\,n!}.
\]
The same coefficient is the Cauchy integral of $(1-z)^{-3/2}z^{-n-1}$
about the origin. The generating function
$(1-4x)^{-3/2}=\sum_{n\ge0}(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}x^{n}$ with $x=z/4$
rewrites
\[
a_{n}
=\frac{2n+1}{4^{n}}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
\[
\boxed{a_{n}=\Gamma(n+3/2)/(\Gamma(3/2)n!)=(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}/4^{n}}.
\]

Using $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$ and $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt{\pi}/2$,
\begin{align*}
a_{0}&=1,\\
a_{1}&=\frac{\Gamma(5/2)}{\Gamma(3/2)}=\frac32,\\
a_{2}&=\frac{\Gamma(7/2)}{2\Gamma(3/2)}=\frac{(5/2)(3/2)}{2}=\frac{15}{8},\\
a_{3}&=\frac{\Gamma(9/2)}{6\Gamma(3/2)}=\frac{(7/2)(5/2)(3/2)}{6}=\frac{35}{16}.
\end{align*}
The same four values are $(1)\binom{0}{0}$, $3\binom{2}{1}/4$,
$5\binom{4}{2}/16$, and $7\binom{6}{3}/64$. The consecutive ratio is
\[
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}}
=\frac{\Gamma(n+5/2)}{\Gamma(n+3/2)}\cdot\frac{n!}{(n+1)!}
=\frac{n+3/2}{n+1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{a_{0}=1,\;a_{1}=3/2,\;a_{2}=15/8,\;a_{3}=35/16,\;
a_{n+1}/a_{n}=(n+3/2)/(n+1)}.
\]

For the Darboux / Stirling expansion, write
\[
\frac{\Gamma(n+3/2)}{\Gamma(n+1)}
=n^{1/2}
\Bigl(1+\frac{(1/2)(3/2)}{2n}+\frac{c_{2}}{n^{2}}+O(n^{-3})\Bigr)
\]
with the standard second-order coefficient of the Gamma ratio at
$(a,b)=(3/2,1)$. The linear correction is $3/(8n)$. The $n^{-2}$
coefficient, equivalently obtained by multiplying the expansion
\[
\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^{n}}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi n}}
\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{8n}+\frac{1}{128n^{2}}+O(n^{-3})\Bigr)
\]
by $2n+1=(2n)(1+1/(2n))$ and converting $1/\sqrt{\pi n}$ into
$(2/\sqrt{\pi})\,n^{1/2}$ times $1/(2n)$, is $-7/128$. Dividing by
$\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt{\pi}/2$ therefore yields
\[
a_{n}
=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\,n^{1/2}
\Bigl(1+\frac{3}{8n}-\frac{7}{128n^{2}}+O(n^{-3})\Bigr).
\]
(The same three terms are the Darboux transfer of the algebraic
singularity $(1-z)^{-3/2}$ at $z=1$.)
\[
\boxed{a_{n}=(2/\sqrt{\pi})n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128n^{2})+O(n^{-3})]}.
\]

Sentence (i) substitutes the coefficients of $(1-z)^{-1/2}$ and
drops the factor $2n+1$. Sentence (ii) keeps a raw central-binomial
$n^{-2}$ coefficient ($+9/128$ or $+1/128$) instead of the
transferred coefficient $-7/128$. The argument is singularity
analysis of one algebraic generating function; it is not a
Mittag-Leffler expansion, not a canonical product, and not a
prescribed-pole interpolant.

graderFixtures.proofText: The coefficients are those of (1-z)^{-1/2}, namely a_n=C(2n,n)/4^n, so the factor 2n+1 is omitted. I do not report a_n=(2n+1)C(2n,n)/4^n or the list (1, 3/2, 15/8, 35/16).
The n^{-2} Darboux coefficient is +9/128, or else +1/128 from the raw central binomial, not -7/128. I never accept the expansion (2/sqrt(pi)) n^{1/2}[1+3/(8n)-7/(128 n^2)+O(n^{-3})].

CA:020530.title: The endpoint integral of x e^{i lambda x} on [0,1] is exact of size O(lambda^{-1}) with no saddle, and |lambda J(2 pi n)|=1
CA:020530.objective: For J(lambda)=int_0^1 x e^{i lambda x} dx, derive the exact formula e^{i lambda}/(i lambda)+(e^{i lambda}-1)/lambda^2, prove the O(lambda^{-1}) size from both endpoints with no interior saddle, and evaluate J(2 pi n)=-i/(2 pi n), J(pi)=-2/pi^2+i/pi, and |lambda J(2 pi n)|=1.
CA:020530.statement:
For real $\lambda\neq 0$ define
\[
J(\lambda)=\int_0^1 x\,e^{i\lambda x}\,dx.
\]
Do not replace the endpoint calculation by a saddle deformation, a
steepest-descent contour shift, or a disk Poisson integral.

1. Integrate by parts (or evaluate the elementary antiderivative)
   and prove the exact formula
   \[
   J(\lambda)
   =\frac{e^{i\lambda}}{i\lambda}+\frac{e^{i\lambda}-1}{\lambda^2}.
   \]

2. Prove that $J(\lambda)=O(\lambda^{-1})$ as $|\lambda|\to\infty$,
   and that both endpoints of $[0,1]$ contribute to the exact
   formula. Show that the phase $\phi(x)=x$ has $\phi'\neq 0$ on
   $[0,1]$, so there is no interior stationary point and no saddle
   to deform through.

3. Specialize to the samples
   \[
   J(2\pi n)=-\frac{i}{2\pi n}
   \qquad(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}),
   \]
   \[
   J(\pi)=-\frac{2}{\pi^2}+\frac{i}{\pi},
   \]
   and
   \[
   \bigl|\lambda\,J(2\pi n)\bigr|=1.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the phase has a saddle on $[0,1]$, so
   the leading term is obtained by steepest descent through an
   interior critical point”; (ii) “only the endpoint $x=1$ appears,
   so $J(\pi)=e^{i\pi}/(i\pi)=-i/\pi$ with no $1/\pi^2$ term, and
   $|\lambda J(2\pi n)|$ is not $1$.”
permittedResults: Integration by parts with $u=x$ and $dv=e^{i\lambda x}\,dx$ is legitimate for every real $\lambda\neq 0$ and produces an exact closed form.
If $e^{i\lambda}=1$, the second summand of $J$ vanishes and $J(\lambda)=1/(i\lambda)$. This occurs precisely at $\lambda=2\pi n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate by parts once and rearrange 1/(i lambda)^2=-1/lambda^2 to obtain the exact closed form.
Specialize to e^{i lambda}=1 and e^{i lambda}=-1 for the two assigned samples, and note that phi'=1 has no zero.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact antiderivative identity J=e^{i lambda}/(i lambda)+(e^{i lambda}-1)/lambda^2.
Proves the O(lambda^{-1}) endpoint size with no saddle and reports J(2 pi n)=-i/(2 pi n), J(pi)=-2/pi^2+i/pi, and |lambda J(2 pi n)|=1.
Rejects a reserved saddle deformation and a one-endpoint formula missing the 1/lambda^2 term.

commonErrors.description: Claims an interior saddle on [0,1] and replaces the endpoint integral by a steepest-descent contour shift.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact closed form and the identity |lambda J(2 pi n)|=1 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only the x=1 term e^{i lambda}/(i lambda), so J(pi) is reported as -i/pi and the 1/lambda^2 contribution is lost.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned sample J(pi)=-2/pi^2+i/pi and the two-endpoint accounting both fail.

hintTree.content: Integrate by parts once: the boundary term at $x=1$ is $e^{i\lambda}/(i\lambda)$, and the remaining integral produces $(e^{i\lambda}-1)/\lambda^2$.
The phase derivative is identically $1$, so there is no interior critical point on $[0,1]$.
At $\lambda=2\pi n$ one has $e^{i\lambda}=1$. At $\lambda=\pi$ one has $e^{i\pi}=-1$.

CA:020530.canonicalSolution:
Fix $\lambda\neq 0$. Integrate by parts with $u=x$ and
$dv=e^{i\lambda x}\,dx$, so $du=dx$ and $v=e^{i\lambda x}/(i\lambda)$:
\[
J(\lambda)
=\Bigl[\frac{x e^{i\lambda x}}{i\lambda}\Bigr]_0^1
-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_0^1 e^{i\lambda x}\,dx
=\frac{e^{i\lambda}}{i\lambda}
-\frac1{i\lambda}\cdot\frac{e^{i\lambda}-1}{i\lambda}.
\]
Since $1/(i\lambda)^2=-1/\lambda^2$, this rearranges to
\[
J(\lambda)
=\frac{e^{i\lambda}}{i\lambda}+\frac{e^{i\lambda}-1}{\lambda^2}.
\]
Equivalently, the elementary antiderivative
$e^{i\lambda x}\bigl(x/(i\lambda)-1/(i\lambda)^2\bigr)$ evaluated
from $0$ to $1$ produces the same identity: the $x=1$ endpoint
contributes both $e^{i\lambda}/(i\lambda)$ and
$-e^{i\lambda}/(i\lambda)^2$, while the $x=0$ endpoint contributes
$+1/(i\lambda)^2$. Both endpoints therefore appear in the exact
formula.
\[
\boxed{J=e^{i\lambda}/(i\lambda)+(e^{i\lambda}-1)/\lambda^2}.
\]

The first summand is $O(\lambda^{-1})$ and the second is
$O(\lambda^{-2})$, so $J(\lambda)=O(\lambda^{-1})$ as
$|\lambda|\to\infty$. The phase $\phi(x)=x$ satisfies
$\phi'(x)=1\neq 0$ at every point of $[0,1]$. There is therefore
no interior stationary point and no saddle through which a contour
could be deformed. The size $O(\lambda^{-1})$ is a pure endpoint
/ nonstationary-phase statement.
\[
\boxed{J=O(\lambda^{-1}),\ \text{both endpoints},\ \text{no saddle}}.
\]

If $\lambda=2\pi n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, then
$e^{i\lambda}=1$ and the second summand vanishes:
\[
J(2\pi n)=\frac{1}{i\,2\pi n}=-\frac{i}{2\pi n}.
\]
Hence
\[
\bigl|\lambda\,J(2\pi n)\bigr|
=\bigl|2\pi n\bigr|\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi |n|}=1.
\]
If $\lambda=\pi$, then $e^{i\pi}=-1$ and
\[
J(\pi)
=\frac{-1}{i\pi}+\frac{-1-1}{\pi^2}
=\frac{i}{\pi}-\frac{2}{\pi^2}
=-\frac{2}{\pi^2}+\frac{i}{\pi}.
\]
\[
\boxed{J(2\pi n)=-i/(2\pi n),\ J(\pi)=-2/\pi^2+i/\pi,\
|\lambda J(2\pi n)|=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) invents an interior saddle and replaces the
calculation by the reserved steepest-descent deformation. Sentence
(ii) drops the $x=0$ endpoint and the $1/\lambda^2$ term, so the
sample $J(\pi)$ and the identity $|\lambda J(2\pi n)|=1$ both fail.
The integral is not a Poisson kernel and not a Green-function
normal derivative.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integration by parts yields $J=e^{i\lambda}/(i\lambda)+(e^{i\lambda}-1)/\lambda^2$. Both endpoints appear, $\phi'=1$ has no zero, and $J=O(\lambda^{-1})$ with no saddle. The samples are $J(2\pi n)=-i/(2\pi n)$, $J(\pi)=-2/\pi^2+i/\pi$, and $|\lambda J(2\pi n)|=1$.
The phase has a saddle on [0,1], so the leading term is obtained by steepest descent through an interior critical point. I do not report the exact endpoint formula or |lambda J(2 pi n)|=1.
Only the endpoint x=1 appears, so J(pi)=e^{i pi}/(i pi)=-i/pi with no 1/pi^2 term, and |lambda J(2 pi n)| is not 1. I never accept J(pi)=-2/pi^2+i/pi.

CA:020624.title: The rational h=(z-1)^2/(z^3(z+2)) has orders +2, -3, -1, +2 at 1, 0, -2, infinity, divisor degree 0, total zero/pole degree 4, and h(2)=1/32
CA:020624.objective: For h(z)=(z-1)^2/(z^3(z+2)) compute the local orders at 1, 0, -2, and infinity via w=1/z, form the divisor, prove that its degree is 0 and that the total zero degree and total pole degree are each 4, and evaluate h(2)=1/32.
CA:020624.statement:
Let
\[
h(z)
=\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{z^{3}(z+2)}
\]
be viewed as a meromorphic function on the Riemann sphere
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$. Do not replace the order computation by a
Weierstrass or canonical-product construction of a function with a
prescribed divisor, and do not recast $h$ as a Mittag-Leffler
expansion or as a prescribed-pole interpolant.

1. Compute the local orders
   \[
   \operatorname{ord}_{1}h=+2,\qquad
   \operatorname{ord}_{0}h=-3,\qquad
   \operatorname{ord}_{-2}h=-1,
   \]
   and, in the chart $w=1/z$,
   \[
   \operatorname{ord}_{\infty}h=+2.
   \]

2. Write the principal divisor $(h)$ and prove that
   $\deg(h)=0$. Record that the total degree of zeros and the total
   degree of poles are each $4$.

3. Evaluate the sample value at the nonsingular point $z=2$:
   $h(2)=1/32$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the order at infinity is
   $\deg(\text{numerator})-\deg(\text{denominator})=-2$, so the
   divisor has degree $-4$ or $-2$”; (ii) “orders are the negatives
   of those listed, so $\operatorname{ord}_{1}h=-2$ and
   $\operatorname{ord}_{0}h=+3$.”
permittedResults: A reduced rational function has $\operatorname{ord}_{a}h$ equal to the multiplicity of $(z-a)$ in the numerator minus its multiplicity in the denominator. In the chart $w=1/z$, $h(1/w)=w^{2}(1-w)^{2}/(1+2w)$ is holomorphic and has a zero of order $2$ at $w=0$.
On $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ one has $\deg(h)=0$ for every non-zero meromorphic $h$. Evaluating at a regular point does not change the divisor.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read finite orders from unreduced numerator and denominator factors, then substitute z=1/w and clear powers of w to obtain ord_infinity=+2.
Add the four orders to check deg(h)=0, compare total zeros against total poles, and evaluate h at the regular point 2.

milestones.criterion: Computes the four local orders +2, -3, -1, +2 at 1, 0, -2, and infinity, including the chart w=1/z.
Writes the divisor, proves degree 0 with total zero/pole degree 4, and evaluates h(2)=1/32.
Rejects a naive affine degree at infinity or a global sign flip of orders, and refuses reserved canonical-product or prescribed-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Sets ord_infinity h equal to deg(numerator)-deg(denominator)=-2 instead of reading the chart w=1/z, and reports a non-zero divisor degree.
commonErrors.consequence: The required ord_infinity=+2 and the identity deg(h)=0 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the negatives of the true local orders, in particular ord_1 h=-2 and ord_0 h=+3.
commonErrors.consequence: Zeros and poles are exchanged, so the divisor and the value bookkeeping are inconsistent with h=(z-1)^2/(z^3(z+2)).

hintTree.content: The factor $(z-1)^{2}$ is a zero of order $2$; $z^{3}$ is a pole of order $3$; $z+2$ is a simple pole. None of these three points is cancelled.
Substitute $z=1/w$ and clear negative powers: $h(1/w)=w^{2}(1-w)^{2}/(1+2w)$. The vanishing order at $w=0$ is $2$.
Add $+2-3-1+2$ to obtain divisor degree $0$. Then substitute $z=2$ into $h$ to obtain $1/32$.

CA:020624.canonicalSolution:
The numerator and denominator of $h$ share no common root. At
$z=1$ the numerator contributes a zero of multiplicity $2$ and the
denominator is $1^{3}\cdot3=3\neq0$, so $\operatorname{ord}_{1}h=+2$.
At $z=0$ the denominator contributes $z^{3}$ and the numerator is
$1\neq0$, so $\operatorname{ord}_{0}h=-3$. At $z=-2$ the factor
$z+2$ is simple and the numerator is $9\neq0$, so
$\operatorname{ord}_{-2}h=-1$.

In the chart $w=1/z$,
\begin{align*}
h\Bigl(\frac1w\Bigr)
&=\frac{(w^{-1}-1)^{2}}{w^{-3}(w^{-1}+2)}
=\frac{(1-w)^{2}/w^{2}}{w^{-3}\cdot(1+2w)/w}
=\frac{(1-w)^{2}}{w^{2}}\cdot\frac{w^{4}}{1+2w}
=\frac{w^{2}(1-w)^{2}}{1+2w}.
\end{align*}
The function $w\mapsto(1-w)^{2}/(1+2w)$ is holomorphic and non-zero
at $w=0$, so $\operatorname{ord}_{w=0}h(1/w)=+2$, i.e.
$\operatorname{ord}_{\infty}h=+2$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ord}_{1}=+2,\;
\operatorname{ord}_{0}=-3,\;
\operatorname{ord}_{-2}=-1,\;
\operatorname{ord}_{\infty}=+2}.
\]

The principal divisor is therefore
\[
(h)
=2[1]-3[0]-[-2]+2[\infty].
\]
Its degree is $2-3-1+2=0$. The zeros (positive orders) contribute
total degree $2+2=4$, and the poles contribute total degree
$3+1=4$. Equivalently $h$, as a holomorphic map
$\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, has degree
$\max(2,4)=4$.
\[
\boxed{\deg(h)=0,\quad
\text{zero degree }=\text{pole degree }=4}.
\]

The point $z=2$ is none of the support points, and
\[
h(2)
=\frac{(2-1)^{2}}{2^{3}(2+2)}
=\frac{1}{8\cdot4}
=\frac{1}{32}.
\]
\[
\boxed{h(2)=1/32}.
\]

Sentence (i) uses the affine degree difference
$\deg(\text{num})-\deg(\text{den})=-2$ as if it were
$\operatorname{ord}_{\infty}h$, which has the wrong sign relative to
the chart $w=1/z$ (the chart produces $w^{2}$ in the numerator).
Sentence (ii) flips every local sign and never writes the divisor
of a meromorphic function. The computation is local order
bookkeeping on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$; it does not construct $h$
from a prescribed divisor by a canonical product, and it does not
expand $h$ by Mittag-Leffler or interpolate prescribed poles.

graderFixtures.proofText: The local orders are $\operatorname{ord}_{1}h=+2$, $\operatorname{ord}_{0}h=-3$, $\operatorname{ord}_{-2}h=-1$, and $\operatorname{ord}_{\infty}h=+2$. The principal divisor has degree $0$, with total zero degree $4$ and total pole degree $4$. At the nonsingular sample point $z=2$, one has $h(2)=1/32$.
The order at infinity is deg(numerator)-deg(denominator)=-2, so the divisor has degree -2 (or -4) rather than 0. I do not report ord_infinity=+2 or deg(h)=0.

CA:020629.title: The degree-3 sphere map z^3-3z has ramification 1+1+2=4=2d-2, with simple fiber {0,±sqrt(3)} over 0
CA:020629.objective: For f(z)=z^3-3z as a degree-3 map of the Riemann sphere, prove that the finite critical points z=±1 have local degree 2 and values -2 and +2, that infinity has local degree 3, that the ramification ledger is 1+1+2=4=2d-2, and that the fiber over 0 is the simple triple {0,±sqrt(3)}.
CA:020629.statement:
View
\[
f(z)=z^3-3z
\]
as a holomorphic map $\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ of
the Riemann sphere. Do not replace the ramification ledger by a
two-sheet cover $w^2=z(z-1)$, by a cubic algebraic punctured
monodromy, or by a Mittag–Leffler pole construction.

1. Prove that $f$ has degree $3$. Locate the finite critical points,
   prove that each has local degree $2$, and evaluate
   \[
   f(1)=-2,\qquad f(-1)=+2.
   \]

2. In the chart $w=1/z$ at infinity, prove that $f$ has local
   degree $3$ at $\infty$.

3. Form the ramification ledger
   \[
   \sum_{p}(e_p-1)=1+1+2=4
   \]
   and reconcile it with Riemann–Hurwitz on the sphere:
   \[
   2d-2=4.
   \]

4. Determine the fiber $f^{-1}(0)$ and prove that it is the simple
   triple $\{0,\pm\sqrt{3}\}$. Audit both sentences: (i) “the map
   is a two-sheet cover ramified only over $0$ and $1$”; (ii) “the
   point at infinity is unramified of local degree $1$, so the
   ramification sum is $2$ rather than $4$.”
permittedResults: A nonconstant rational function of numerator/denominator degree $d$ is a degree-$d$ map of the sphere. Here $f$ is a polynomial of degree $3$.
A simple zero of $f'$ is a local-degree-$2$ critical point. A pole of order $3$ at infinity is a local-degree-$3$ point.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute f' to locate finite critical points, then invert the chart at infinity to read the order-3 pole.
Add the three ramification numbers and check Riemann–Hurwitz; factor z(z^2-3) for the fiber over 0.

milestones.criterion: Identifies degree 3, the critical points ±1 of local degree 2 with values -2 and +2, and local degree 3 at infinity.
Records the ramification ledger 1+1+2=4=2d-2 and the simple fiber {0,±sqrt(3)} over 0.
Rejects a reserved two-sheet-cover substitution and an unramified-infinity ledger.

commonErrors.description: Replaces f=z^3-3z by a two-sheet cover ramified only over 0 and 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The degree-3 ledger, the values ±2, and the simple triple fiber over 0 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Treats infinity as unramified of local degree 1, so the ramification sum is reported as 2 rather than 4.
commonErrors.consequence: Riemann–Hurwitz 2d-2=4 fails, and the local degree 3 at infinity is lost.

hintTree.content: Differentiate: $f'(z)=3z^2-3=3(z-1)(z+1)$. The zeros are simple.
In $w=1/z$ one has $f=w^{-3}(1-3w^2)$, so the inverted map begins with $w^3$.
Solve $z^3-3z=0$ as $z(z^2-3)=0$ and check $f'\neq 0$ on that fiber.

CA:020629.canonicalSolution:
The map $f(z)=z^3-3z$ is a polynomial of degree $3$, hence a
holomorphic map $\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ of
degree $d=3$. Differentiating,
\[
f'(z)=3z^2-3=3(z-1)(z+1).
\]
The finite critical points are therefore the simple zeros $z=\pm 1$.
A simple zero of $f'$ is a local-degree-$2$ point. The critical
values are
\[
f(1)=1-3=-2,\qquad
f(-1)=-1+3=+2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\deg f=3,\quad z=\pm 1\text{ have }e_p=2,\quad
f(1)=-2,\ f(-1)=+2}.
\]

At infinity use $w=1/z$. Then
\[
f\bigl(1/w\bigr)=w^{-3}-3w^{-1}=w^{-3}(1-3w^2).
\]
In the target chart $\zeta=1/f$ one obtains
\[
\zeta=\frac{w^3}{1-3w^2}=w^3+O(w^5),
\]
so $\infty$ is a single point of local degree $3$.
\[
\boxed{e_{\infty}=3}.
\]

The ramification numbers $e_p-1$ are therefore $1$ at $z=1$, $1$
at $z=-1$, and $2$ at $\infty$. There are no other critical
points, because $f'$ has no further zeros and the only point at
infinity has been accounted for. The ledger is
\[
\sum_p(e_p-1)=1+1+2=4.
\]
Riemann–Hurwitz on the sphere demands
\[
\sum_p(e_p-1)=2d-2=2\cdot 3-2=4,
\]
which matches exactly.
\[
\boxed{1+1+2=4=2d-2}.
\]

The fiber over $0$ solves $z^3-3z=0$, or $z(z^2-3)=0$, hence
\[
f^{-1}(0)=\bigl\{0,\sqrt{3},-\sqrt{3}\bigr\}.
\]
None of these is a critical point:
$f'(0)=-3\neq 0$ and $f'(\pm\sqrt{3})=3(3-1)=6\neq 0$. Each
preimage is therefore simple, and the three distinct points
account for the full degree.
\[
\boxed{f^{-1}(0)=\{0,\pm\sqrt{3}\}\text{, all simple}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the cubic sphere map by the reserved
two-sheet cover $w^2=z(z-1)$. Sentence (ii) declares infinity
unramified and cannot reach the Hurwitz number $4$. The
construction is a ramification ledger, not a prescribed-pole
series and not a cubic punctured monodromy.

graderFixtures.proofText: The map $z^3-3z$ has degree $3$. The finite critical points $z=\pm 1$ have local degree $2$ and values $-2$ and $+2$. Infinity has local degree $3$. The ramification ledger is $1+1+2=4=2d-2$. The fiber over $0$ is the simple triple $\{0,\pm\sqrt{3}\}$.
The map is a two-sheet cover ramified only over 0 and 1. I do not report degree 3, the values ±2, or the simple fiber {0,±sqrt(3)}.
The point at infinity is unramified of local degree 1, so the ramification sum is 2 rather than 4. I never accept 1+1+2=4=2d-2.

CA:020631.title: On C/(Z+iZ) the form dz descends with periods 1, i, and 1+i, has no global primitive, and induces area 1
CA:020631.objective: For the square torus X=C/(Z+iZ), prove that dz descends as a holomorphic one-form, that its periods on the standard cycles are a=1, b=i, and a+b=1+i spanning the lattice Z+iZ, that dz has no global primitive despite being holomorphic, that (i/2) dz wedge dbar z gives area 1, and that dz has no zeros.
CA:020631.statement:
Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$ and let
$X=\mathbb C/\Lambda$ be the square torus, with quotient projection
$\pi:\mathbb C\to X$. Write $a$, $b$, and $a+b$ for the standard
closed cycles on $X$ lifted to the segments $[0,1]$, $[0,i]$, and
$[0,1+i]$ in $\mathbb C$. Do not replace the quotient-torus
argument by a two-sheet algebraic cover, by a cubic sphere
ramification ledger, or by a punctured-log monodromy.

1. Prove that the holomorphic one-form $dz$ on $\mathbb C$ is
   $\Lambda$-invariant, hence descends to a holomorphic one-form
   on $X$, still written $dz$.

2. Compute the periods
   \[
   \int_a dz=1,\qquad
   \int_b dz=i,\qquad
   \int_{a+b} dz=1+i,
   \]
   and conclude that the period lattice is exactly $\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$.

3. Prove that $dz$ admits no global holomorphic primitive on $X$,
   even though $dz$ is holomorphic on the compact Riemann surface
   $X$.

4. Prove that the $(1,1)$-form $(i/2)\,dz\wedge d\overline z$
   pulls back to Euclidean area on $\mathbb C$ and that
   \[
   \int_X\frac{i}{2}\,dz\wedge d\overline z=1.
   \]
   Prove also that $dz$ has no zeros on $X$. Audit both sentences:
   (i) “$X$ is the two-sheet cover $w^2=z(z-1)$, so $dz$ does not
   descend from a lattice”; (ii) “holomorphic forms on a compact
   surface are exact, so $dz=dF$ globally and the $a$-period must
   vanish.”
permittedResults: A holomorphic function on a compact Riemann surface is constant. Consequently a nowhere-zero holomorphic one-form cannot be exact.
If a closed one-form is exact, every period vanishes. The $a$-period of $dz$ is $1\neq 0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use translation invariance to descend dz, then integrate along the three standard lattice segments.
Compare periods with exactness, and expand (i/2) dz wedge dbar z as Euclidean area on the unit square.

milestones.criterion: Proves that dz descends to the square torus and computes the periods 1, i, and 1+i spanning Z+iZ.
Shows that dz has no global primitive, that the area form integrates to 1, and that dz has no zeros.
Rejects a reserved two-sheet-cover substitution and a claim that holomorphic forms on X are exact.

commonErrors.description: Replaces X=C/(Z+iZ) by the two-sheet cover w^2=z(z-1), so dz is not treated as a lattice-invariant form.
commonErrors.consequence: The periods 1, i, 1+i and the area identity 1 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Claims that every holomorphic form on a compact surface is exact, so the a-period of dz must vanish.
commonErrors.consequence: The obstruction to a global primitive is erased and the period lattice is lost.

hintTree.content: Translations act by $z\mapsto z+\lambda$ with $d(z+\lambda)=dz$.
Integrate $dz$ along $[0,1]$, $[0,i]$, and $[0,1+i]$ by the fundamental theorem.
Expand $dz\wedge d\overline z=(dx+i\,dy)\wedge(dx-i\,dy)=-2i\,dx\wedge dy$.

CA:020631.canonicalSolution:
Lattice translations $\tau_\lambda(z)=z+\lambda$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$ satisfy
\[
\tau_\lambda^*(dz)=d(z+\lambda)=dz.
\]
Thus $dz$ is $\Lambda$-invariant and descends through the local
biholomorphisms of $\pi:\mathbb C\to X$ to a holomorphic one-form
on the compact quotient $X=\mathbb C/\Lambda$.
\[
\boxed{dz\text{ descends to }X=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)}.
\]

Lifting the standard cycles to the segments $[0,1]$, $[0,i]$, and
$[0,1+i]$,
\[
\int_a dz=\int_0^1 dt=1,
\qquad
\int_b dz=\int_0^1 i\,dt=i,
\qquad
\int_{a+b} dz=\int_0^1(1+i)\,dt=1+i.
\]
Every closed cycle on the torus has homology class $ma+nb$ for
unique integers $m,n$, and periods of the closed form $dz$ depend
only on homology. Thus every period is $m+ni\in\Lambda$. Conversely,
the cycles $ma+nb$ realize every $m+ni\in\Lambda$. Both containments
hold, so the period lattice of $dz$ is exactly
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$.
\[
\boxed{\text{periods }1,\ i,\ 1+i;\ \text{lattice }\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z}.
\]

Suppose a global holomorphic primitive $F$ on $X$ existed, so that
$dF=dz$. Then $F$ would be a holomorphic function on the compact
Riemann surface $X$, hence constant, forcing $dz=0$, a
contradiction. Equivalently, an exact form has vanishing periods,
yet the $a$-period equals $1\neq 0$. Holomorphicity of $dz$ on $X$
is therefore compatible with the failure of exactness: the
obstruction is topological (the homology of the torus), not a
failure of the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
\[
\boxed{dz\text{ is holomorphic and not exact on }X}.
\]

On $\mathbb C$,
\begin{align*}
dz\wedge d\overline z
&=(dx+i\,dy)\wedge(dx-i\,dy)
=-i\,dx\wedge dy+i\,dy\wedge dx
=-2i\,dx\wedge dy,
\end{align*}
hence
\[
\frac{i}{2}\,dz\wedge d\overline z
=\frac{i}{2}(-2i)\,dx\wedge dy
=dx\wedge dy.
\]
Integrating over the fundamental square $[0,1]\times[0,1]$ of
$\Lambda$ yields
\[
\int_X\frac{i}{2}\,dz\wedge d\overline z
=\int_0^1\int_0^1 dx\,dy=1.
\]
Finally $dz$ is nowhere zero on $\mathbb C$, and the local
trivializations of $\pi$ identify the descended form with $dz$ in
every chart, so $dz$ has no zeros on $X$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{area}(X)=1,\quad dz\text{ has no zeros}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the lattice quotient by the reserved
two-sheet cover. Sentence (ii) claims that every holomorphic form
on a compact surface is exact and cannot accommodate the period
$1$. The construction is not a cubic Riemann–Hurwitz ledger and
not a punctured logarithm.

graderFixtures.proofText: Translations preserve $dz$, so $dz$ descends to $X=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$. The periods are $1$, $i$, and $1+i$, spanning $\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$. A global primitive is impossible because the $a$-period is $1$. The form $(i/2)\,dz\wedge d\overline z$ is Euclidean area and integrates to $1$. The descended $dz$ has no zeros.
X is the two-sheet cover w^2=z(z-1), so dz does not descend from a lattice. I do not report periods 1, i, 1+i or area 1.
Holomorphic forms on a compact surface are exact, so dz=dF globally and the a-period must vanish. I never accept the period 1 or the missing primitive.

ARCH:010117.title: beq x5,x6,-16 encodes 0xFE6288E3; the B-type immediate is 0x1FF0 = -16 and the target from PC 0x1000 is 0x0FF0, not 0x0FF4
ARCH:010117.objective: Reconstruct the B-type immediate of a concrete RISC-V beq, sign-extend 0x1FF0 to -16, form the PC-relative target from the current PC, and reject both a PC+4 base and an unsigned reading of the packed immediate.
ARCH:010117.statement:
A RISC-V RV32I processor fetches the 32-bit instruction word
\[
\mathtt{0xFE6288E3}
\]
from architectural address $\mathit{PC}=\mathtt{0x1000}$. The next
sequential instruction therefore lives at $\mathtt{0x1004}$. The
instruction is a B-type branch whose fields occupy these bit
positions, with bit $31$ the most significant bit of the word:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c}
31&30{:}25&24{:}20&19{:}15&14{:}12&11{:}8&7&6{:}0\\ \hline
\mathrm{imm}[12]&\mathrm{imm}[10{:}5]&\mathit{rs2}&\mathit{rs1}&\mathit{funct3}&\mathrm{imm}[4{:}1]&\mathrm{imm}[11]&\mathit{opcode}.
\end{array}
\]
The B-type immediate is the 13-bit quantity
\[
\mathrm{imm}[12\mid 10{:}5\mid 4{:}1\mid 11\mid 0],
\]
where the least-significant bit $\mathrm{imm}[0]$ is identically $0$
(branches target even byte addresses). The architectural target is
\[
\mathit{PC}+\operatorname{sext}_{32}(\mathrm{imm}),
\]
using the PC of the branch itself, not $\mathit{PC}+4$. The recognized
encoding of $\mathrm{beq}\ \mathit{rs1},\mathit{rs2},\mathit{offset}$ has
$\mathit{opcode}=\mathtt{1100011}$ and $\mathit{funct3}=\mathtt{000}$.

1. Extract every field of $\mathtt{0xFE6288E3}$. Reconstruct the
   13-bit immediate in the order $\mathrm{imm}[12\mid 10{:}5\mid 4{:}1\mid 11\mid 0]$
   and show that the packed hex value is $\mathtt{0x1FF0}$. Identify
   $\mathit{rs1}$, $\mathit{rs2}$, $\mathit{funct3}$, and the opcode, and
   confirm that the word is $\mathrm{beq}\ x5,x6,-16$.

2. Sign-extend $\mathtt{0x1FF0}$ as a 13-bit two's-complement integer
   to a 32-bit architectural offset and prove the value is $-16$. Form
   the branch target from $\mathit{PC}=\mathtt{0x1000}$. Prove that the
   reachable B-type offsets are exactly the even integers in
   $[-4096,4094]$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the adder that computes the target
   starts from $\mathit{PC}+4$, so this branch lands at
   $\mathtt{0x0FF4}$”; (ii) “$\mathtt{0x1FF0}$ is a positive
   hexadecimal constant, so the offset is $+8176$ bytes.”

Do not replace the decode by a wrapping ADDU/ADD equivalence argument,
and do not treat the instruction as a J-type or I-type encoding.
permittedResults: A $k$-bit two's-complement string $b_{k-1}\cdots b_0$ represents $-b_{k-1}2^{k-1}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-2}b_i 2^i$. Equivalently, if $b_{k-1}=1$ the signed value is $U-2^k$ where $U$ is the unsigned interpretation.
Forcing the least-significant bit of a signed $13$-bit quantity to $0$ yields every even integer in $[-2^{12},2^{12}-2]=[-4096,4094]$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Dump the 32 bits, read each named field, concatenate in architectural immediate order, then sign-extend and add to the instruction PC.
Assemble beq x5,x6,-16 from the B-type layout as a check, then use the 13-bit two's-complement identity 8176-8192=-16 to recover the target.

milestones.criterion: Extracts the B-type fields of 0xFE6288E3 and reconstructs imm[12|10:5|4:1|11|0]=0x1FF0 as beq x5,x6,-16.
Sign-extends 0x1FF0 to -16, forms target 0x0FF0 from the current PC, and states the even range [-4096,4094].
Rejects a PC+4 base (0x0FF4) and an unsigned reading of 0x1FF0 as +8176.

commonErrors.description: Adds the sign-extended immediate to PC+4 and reports the target 0x0FF4, or treats the sequential successor as the architectural base of a taken B-type branch.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed landing address is four bytes too high and is not the RISC-V PC-relative rule.

commonErrors.description: Reads 0x1FF0 as the unsigned offset +8176, or concatenates instruction-word fields in layout order rather than imm[12|10:5|4:1|11|0], so the packed immediate is not 0x1FF0.
commonErrors.consequence: The decoded offset is not -16 and the claimed encoding is not beq x5,x6,-16.

hintTree.content: The reconstructed bits are $\mathrm{imm}[12]=1$, $\mathrm{imm}[11]=1$, $\mathrm{imm}[10{:}5]=111111$, $\mathrm{imm}[4{:}1]=1000$, $\mathrm{imm}[0]=0$, i.e. $1111111110000=\mathtt{0x1FF0}$.
$\mathtt{0x1FF0}$ as an unsigned $13$-bit integer is $8176=2^{13}-16$, so the signed value is $-16$. Adding that offset to $\mathtt{0x1000}$ yields $\mathtt{0x0FF0}$, not $\mathtt{0x0FF4}$.

ARCH:010117.canonicalSolution:
The word $\mathtt{0xFE6288E3}$ is
\[
11111110\ 01100010\ 10001000\ 11100011.
\]
Reading the declared fields,
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{imm}[12]&=\text{bit }31=1,\\
\mathrm{imm}[10{:}5]&=\text{bits }30{:}25=111111,\\
\mathit{rs2}&=\text{bits }24{:}20=00110=6,\\
\mathit{rs1}&=\text{bits }19{:}15=00101=5,\\
\mathit{funct3}&=\text{bits }14{:}12=000,\\
\mathrm{imm}[4{:}1]&=\text{bits }11{:}8=1000,\\
\mathrm{imm}[11]&=\text{bit }7=1,\\
\mathit{opcode}&=\text{bits }6{:}0=1100011.
\end{align*}
The opcode and $\mathit{funct3}$ are those of $\mathrm{beq}$, and the
registers are $x5$ and $x6$. Placing those fields into bit positions
$12$, $11$, $10{:}5$, $4{:}1$, and $0$ produces
\[
\mathrm{imm}[12]=1,\quad
\mathrm{imm}[11]=1,\quad
\mathrm{imm}[10{:}5]=111111,\quad
\mathrm{imm}[4{:}1]=1000,\quad
\mathrm{imm}[0]=0,
\]
i.e. the $13$-bit string $1111111110000=\mathtt{0x1FF0}$. Instruction-word
order $31,30{:}25,11{:}8,7$ is not that bit-position order.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{imm}=\mathtt{0x1FF0},\ \mathrm{beq}\ x5,x6,-16}.
\]

Interpret $\mathtt{0x1FF0}$ as a $13$-bit two's-complement integer.
The sign bit is $1$, and the unsigned value of the $13$-bit string is
$8176$. Therefore the signed offset is
\[
8176-2^{13}=8176-8192=-16.
\]
Sign-extending to $32$ bits yields $\mathtt{0xFFFFFFF0}$. The
architectural target uses the current PC:
\[
\mathtt{0x1000}+(-16)=\mathtt{0x0FF0}.
\]
A B-type offset is a signed $13$-bit quantity whose bit $0$ is forced
to $0$, so the legal offsets are the even integers from $-2^{12}=-4096$
to $2^{12}-2=4094$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{sext}(\mathtt{0x1FF0})=-16,\ \mathit{target}=\mathtt{0x0FF0}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the specified adder input $\mathit{PC}$ by the
sequential successor $\mathit{PC}+4$. That would land at
$\mathtt{0x1004}-16=\mathtt{0x0FF4}$, which is the address of a
different instruction and is not the RISC-V B-type rule. Sentence (ii)
reads $\mathtt{0x1FF0}$ as an unsigned (or $16$-bit non-negative)
constant. The packed hex is only a notation for the $13$-bit field;
its sign bit is set, so the architectural offset is $-16$, not
$+8176$. Adding $+8176$ to $\mathtt{0x1000}$ would leave the $12$-bit
page entirely.

The argument never rewrites two arithmetic sequences under modular
or trapping addition and never treats the word as J-type or I-type.

graderFixtures.proofText: Fields of $0xFE6288E3$ give $\mathrm{imm}[12\mid 10{:}5\mid 4{:}1\mid 11\mid 0]=0x1FF0=-16$, $\mathit{rs1}=x5$, $\mathit{rs2}=x6$. The target from $\mathit{PC}=0x1000$ is $0x0FF0$. Legal B-type offsets are the even integers in $[-4096,4094]$. $\mathit{PC}+4$ would land at $0x0FF4$; treating $0x1FF0$ as unsigned gives $+8176$.
RISC-V already incremented the PC in fetch, so the branch adder starts at PC+4=0x1004. Adding the offset -16 lands at 0x0FF4, which I report as the architectural target.
The packed immediate 0x1FF0 is a positive hex constant, so the offset is +8176 bytes. Alternatively I concatenate bits 31:25 with bits 11:7 and never force imm[0]=0, so I never obtain 0x1FF0 or -16.

ARCH:010118.title: sum_to(3) pushes four 16-byte frames 0x80000FF0,FE0,FD0,FC0, returns 0,1,3,6, and restores the original sp
ARCH:010118.objective: Trace an RV32 ABI recursion of sum_to(3) through four 16-byte frames, prove that each call must save the incoming a0 and ra, and reject both an unaligned 8-byte frame and a return sequence that forgets the original n.
ARCH:010118.statement:
Use the RV32 integer calling convention. Argument $n$ and the
integer return value travel in $a0$. A $\mathrm{jal}$ writes the
return address into $ra$. At every call site the stack pointer $sp$
must satisfy $sp\equiv 0\pmod{16}$. Consider the straightforward
recursive procedure
\begin{align*}
&\mathit{sum\_to}(n):\\
&\quad\textbf{if }n=0\textbf{ then return }0\\
&\quad\textbf{else return }n+\mathit{sum\_to}(n-1).
\end{align*}
Every activation, including the leaf, uses the same $16$-byte
prologue and epilogue. The prologue is
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{addi}\ \mathit{sp},\mathit{sp},-16\\
\mathrm{sw}\ \mathit{ra},12(\mathit{sp})\\
\mathrm{sw}\ \mathit{a0},8(\mathit{sp}),
\end{array}
\]
and the matching epilogue reloads $ra$ from $12(\mathit{sp})$ and
adds $16$ to $sp$ before $\mathrm{jalr}\ x0,0(\mathit{ra})$. A
non-leaf body, after the prologue, writes $a0\leftarrow n-1$,
issues $\mathrm{jal}\ \mathit{ra},\mathit{sum\_to}$, then reloads the
saved $n$ and adds it to the value the callee left in $a0$. The
leaf writes $a0\leftarrow 0$ and takes the epilogue. The initial
call is $\mathit{sum\_to}(3)$ with
\[
\mathit{sp}=\mathtt{0x80001000}.
\]
No other register is callee-saved in this fragment. Memory other
than the four frames is irrelevant.

1. Prove that each non-leaf activation must spill both the incoming
   $a0$ and the incoming $ra$ before the recursive $\mathrm{jal}$.
   Identify the two overwrites. Prove that every legal $sp$ value
   at a call site remains $0\pmod{16}$, and that a uniform
   $8$-byte frame would violate the ABI alignment obligation.

2. Starting from $\mathit{sp}=\mathtt{0x80001000}$, execute
   $\mathit{sum\_to}(3)$ through the leaf and back. Record the $sp$
   of each live frame after its prologue, the saved $(ra,a0)$ pair,
   and the value returned by $\mathit{sum\_to}(0)$,
   $\mathit{sum\_to}(1)$, $\mathit{sum\_to}(2)$, and
   $\mathit{sum\_to}(3)$. Prove that the original $sp$ is restored
   on the final return.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “after the recursive call $a0$ still
   holds $n$, so there is nothing to reload”; (ii) “three frames
   suffice because the leaf need not allocate, and $8$-byte frames
   at $\mathtt{0x80000FF8},\mathtt{0x80000FF0},\mathtt{0x80000FE8}$
   are still aligned.”

Do not replace the ABI trace by a wrapping opcode-equivalence proof,
and do not introduce pipeline forwarding or a cache model.
permittedResults: $\mathrm{jal}\ \mathit{rd},\mathit{target}$ writes $\mathit{PC}+4$ into $\mathit{rd}$ and then sets $\mathit{PC}$ to the target. A later $\mathrm{jal}$ to the same $\mathit{rd}$ overwrites that value.
If each activation subtracts $16$ on entry and adds $16$ on exit, the net change in $sp$ across a completed call is $0$, independently of the depth.

acceptableStrategies.description: Name the two overwrites, then walk the four prologues downward from 0x80001000 and add the spilled n values on the way back.
First compute the triangular numbers 0,1,3,6 and the four aligned addresses, then show that omitting either spill or shrinking the frame cannot produce both facts.

milestones.criterion: Proves that each non-leaf must spill incoming a0 and ra before jal, and that 16-byte frames preserve sp = 0 (mod 16).
Traces sum_to(3) through frames 0x80000FF0, FE0, FD0, FC0 with returns 0, 1, 3, 6 and restores the original sp.
Rejects an unsaved a0 after jal and an 8-byte or leaf-omitted frame that breaks ABI alignment or the four-address witness.

commonErrors.description: Leaves a0 or ra in registers across the recursive jal, so the addition after the call uses n-1 or the child's return twice, or the epilogue returns to the wrong continuation.
commonErrors.consequence: The returned sequence is not 0,1,3,6, or control never gets back to the original caller.

commonErrors.description: Allocates 8-byte frames (0x80000FF8 and friends), grows the stack upward, or omits the leaf frame, so the live addresses are not 0x80000FF0, FE0, FD0, FC0.
commonErrors.consequence: Call-site alignment or the required four-frame witness is lost, and the final sp need not be 0x80001000.

hintTree.content: The four post-prologue stack pointers are $\mathtt{0x80000FF0}$, $\mathtt{0x80000FE0}$, $\mathtt{0x80000FD0}$, and $\mathtt{0x80000FC0}$. Each ends in a $0$ and is $0\pmod{16}$.
The leaf returns $0$. Unwinding adds the spilled $n$ values $1$, then $2$, then $3$, producing $1$, $3$, and $6$.
If $a0$ is not spilled, the addition after $\mathrm{jal}$ uses the child's return value twice, or uses the already-decremented $n-1$. Either way the returns are not $0,1,3,6$.

ARCH:010118.canonicalSolution:
The recursive $\mathrm{jal}$ writes a new return address into $ra$,
so the incoming $ra$ (the caller's continuation) is lost unless it
was stored first. The same $\mathrm{jal}$ is preceded by
$a0\leftarrow n-1$ and is followed by the callee's return value in
$a0$, so the incoming $n$ is likewise lost unless it was stored.
Those two overwrites force the pair of stores in the prologue. The
leaf does not issue $\mathrm{jal}$, but a uniform prologue still
spills the incoming $ra$ so the epilogue can return, and still
allocates $16$ bytes so every call site sees an aligned $sp$.

The initial $sp=\mathtt{0x80001000}$ is $0\pmod{16}$. Each prologue
subtracts $16$, so every live frame pointer remains $0\pmod{16}$.
An $8$-byte prologue from the same start would produce
$\mathtt{0x80000FF8}\equiv 8\pmod{16}$, which is not a legal RV32
call-site alignment.
\[
\boxed{\text{save }(ra,a0)\text{; frames stay }0\bmod 16}.
\]

Execute $\mathit{sum\_to}(3)$ from $\mathit{sp}=\mathtt{0x80001000}$.
After the four prologues the live frames, from oldest to newest, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
n&\mathit{sp}\text{ after prologue}&\text{saved }a0&\text{role of saved }ra\\ \hline
3&\mathtt{0x80000FF0}&3&\text{return to the original caller}\\
2&\mathtt{0x80000FE0}&2&\text{return to }\mathit{sum\_to}(3)\\
1&\mathtt{0x80000FD0}&1&\text{return to }\mathit{sum\_to}(2)\\
0&\mathtt{0x80000FC0}&0&\text{return to }\mathit{sum\_to}(1).
\end{array}
\]
The leaf writes $a0\leftarrow 0$ and deallocates, restoring
$\mathit{sp}=\mathtt{0x80000FD0}$ and returning $0$. Then
\[
\begin{align*}
\mathit{sum\_to}(1)&:\ a0\leftarrow 0+1=1,\quad \mathit{sp}\leftarrow\mathtt{0x80000FE0},\\
\mathit{sum\_to}(2)&:\ a0\leftarrow 1+2=3,\quad \mathit{sp}\leftarrow\mathtt{0x80000FF0},\\
\mathit{sum\_to}(3)&:\ a0\leftarrow 3+3=6,\quad \mathit{sp}\leftarrow\mathtt{0x80001000}.
\end{align*}
\]
The four returned values are $0,1,3,6$. Each epilogue adds the same
$16$ that the matching prologue subtracted, so the original $sp$ is
restored exactly.
\[
\boxed{\mathit{sp}\in\{\mathtt{FF0},\mathtt{FE0},\mathtt{FD0},\mathtt{FC0}\};\ \text{returns }0,1,3,6}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: after $\mathrm{jal}$, $a0$ holds
$\mathit{sum\_to}(n-1)$, not $n$. Reloading the spilled $a0$ is
exactly the addition $n+\mathit{sum\_to}(n-1)$. Omitting that
reload yields $0+0$, then $0+0$, then $0+0$, i.e. a final $0$, or
else $2\cdot\mathit{sum\_to}(n-1)$ if $a0$ is doubled. Sentence (ii)
is false twice. The leaf still needs a $16$-byte frame under the
stated uniform prologue, and the four addresses above are required.
An $8$-byte frame starting at $\mathtt{0x80001000}$ produces
$\mathtt{0x80000FF8}\equiv 8\pmod{16}$ and is ABI-illegal. Growing
the stack toward $\mathtt{0x80001010}$ would also be the wrong
direction.

The argument never compares two wrapping instruction sequences and
never schedules a pipeline or a cache.

graderFixtures.proofText: Each activation spills $ra$ at $12(sp)$ and $a0$ at $8(sp)$ in a $16$-byte frame. The live pointers are $0x80000FF0$, $0x80000FE0$, $0x80000FD0$, $0x80000FC0$. Returns are $0,1,3,6$, and the original $sp=0x80001000$ is restored. An unsaved $a0$ cannot form $n+\mathit{sum\_to}(n-1)$. An $8$-byte frame is $8\bmod 16$.
After jal, a0 still holds n (or I just add a0 to itself). I never store a0, and I allow ra to be overwritten, so the returns are 0,0,0,0 or I return into the leaf.
The leaf needs no frame, so there are only three activations, and 8-byte frames at 0x80000FF8, 0x80000FF0, 0x80000FE8 are aligned enough. Alternatively I increment sp to 0x80001010.
