ARCH:010219.title: Unsigned shift-add of 13*11 holds P+M*Q=143 for eight iterations; Q=0 is not an early stop
ARCH:010219.objective: Execute the unsigned 8-bit shift-add of 13*11 with 16-bit M and P, prove the invariant P+M*Q, and reject both an early stop when Q hits 0 and an add-after-shift order that misses the required accumulator trace.
ARCH:010219.statement:
An unsigned integer multiplier uses three registers:
\[
P\in\{0,\ldots,2^{16}-1\},\qquad
M\in\{0,\ldots,2^{16}-1\},\qquad
Q\in\{0,\ldots,2^{8}-1\}.
\]
$P$ is the accumulator, $M$ is the multiplicand (zero-extended to
$16$ bits so left shifts do not wrap), and $Q$ is the $8$-bit
multiplier. Initialization for the product $13\times 11$ is
\[
P\leftarrow 0,\qquad M\leftarrow 13,\qquad Q\leftarrow 11.
\]
One iteration is exactly
\begin{align*}
&\textbf{if }Q\bmod 2=1\textbf{ then }P\leftarrow P+M;\\
&M\leftarrow 2M;\\
&Q\leftarrow\lfloor Q/2\rfloor.
\end{align*}
The datapath is hard-wired to eight iterations. There is no
comparator that stops when $Q=0$. Addition is unsigned and the
$16$-bit width is enough that $P$ and $M$ never wrap on this
instance.

1. Prove that every iteration preserves the quantity $P+M\cdot Q$.
   Deduce that after eight iterations one has $Q=0$ and
   $P=13\cdot 11$. Record the pair $(P,Q)$ after each of the first
   four iterations and confirm
   \[
   P:\ 0\to 13\to 39\to 39\to 143,\qquad
   Q:\ 11\to 5\to 2\to 1\to 0.
   \]

2. Continue through iterations $5$--$8$. State $P$, $M$, and $Q$
   after the eighth iteration. Explain why the hardware still
   performs those four iterations even though $Q$ is already $0$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “once $Q=0$ the remaining iterations
   are optional, so a four-iteration algorithm is the one specified”;
   (ii) “one should shift $M$ and $Q$ first and only then add, so
   the first nonzero accumulator value is $26$, not $13$.”

Do not replace the algorithm by a one-hot single-cycle control table
or by an LW datapath trace.
permittedResults: Any integer $Q$ satisfies $Q=2\lfloor Q/2\rfloor+(Q\bmod 2)$. Substituting this identity into $P+M\cdot Q$ after the stated update proves invariance in both the add and the skip cases.
Eight logical right shifts send every $8$-bit $Q$ to $0$, whether or not $Q$ hit $0$ earlier.

acceptableStrategies.description: Prove P+M*Q from Q=2*floor(Q/2)+Q0, then fill an eight-row table that records the optional add before each shift.
Check 13*11=143 first, replay the LSB sequence 1,1,0,1 of 11, and use the later zero-Q iterations only to exhibit the fixed-width controller.

milestones.criterion: Proves that every iteration preserves P+M*Q and concludes P=143 after eight steps.
Produces the traces P: 0,13,39,39,143 and Q: 11,5,2,1,0, and continues through iterations 5-8 with P unchanged.
Rejects an early stop when Q hits 0 and an add-after-shift order whose first add is 26.

commonErrors.description: Stops after the fourth iteration because Q is already 0, and treats the remaining four iterations as optional or unspecified.
commonErrors.consequence: The controller is no longer the stated fixed-width eight-step machine, even though P happens to be 143 already.

commonErrors.description: Shifts M and Q before adding, so the first nonzero accumulator value is 26 rather than 13 and the sequence 0,13,39,39,143 never appears.
commonErrors.consequence: The bit test no longer uses the pre-shift LSB, and the invariant is applied to the wrong state.

hintTree.content: Write $Q=2\lfloor Q/2\rfloor+Q_0$. After an add-and-shift, $(P+M)+(2M)\lfloor Q/2\rfloor=P+M(2\lfloor Q/2\rfloor+1)=P+MQ$.
The first four inspected bits of $11=1011_2$ (LSB first) are $1,1,0,1$, producing the adds $13$, $26$, none, $104$ and the running $P$ values $13,39,39,143$.
Iterations $5$--$8$ keep $P=143$ and $Q=0$ while $M$ continues to $416,832,1664,3328$. A four-iteration stop is a different controller.

ARCH:010219.canonicalSolution:
Write $Q_0=Q\bmod 2$, so $Q=2\lfloor Q/2\rfloor+Q_0$. After one
stated iteration the new registers $(P',M',Q')$ satisfy
$M'=2M$ and $Q'=\lfloor Q/2\rfloor$, while $P'=P+Q_0 M$. Therefore
\[
P'+M'\cdot Q'
=(P+Q_0 M)+(2M)\lfloor Q/2\rfloor
=P+M\bigl(Q_0+2\lfloor Q/2\rfloor\bigr)
=P+M\cdot Q.
\]
The identity holds whether $Q_0$ is $0$ or $1$. Initialization gives
$P+M\cdot Q=0+13\cdot 11=143$, so the quantity remains $143$ after
every later iteration. After eight right shifts of an $8$-bit $Q$
one has $Q=0$, hence $P=143$.

The first four iterations, inspecting $11=1011_2$ from the LSB, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i&Q_0&P\text{ after optional add}&M\text{ after shift}&Q\text{ after shift}\\ \hline
0&&0&13&11\\
1&1&13&26&5\\
2&1&39&52&2\\
3&0&39&104&1\\
4&1&143&208&0.
\end{array}
\]
Thus
\[
P:\ 0\to 13\to 39\to 39\to 143,\qquad
Q:\ 11\to 5\to 2\to 1\to 0,
\]
and $13+26\cdot 5=39+52\cdot 2=39+104\cdot 1=143+208\cdot 0=143$.
\[
\boxed{P+M\cdot Q=143;\ P:\ 0,13,39,39,143}.
\]

Iterations $5$--$8$ see $Q_0=0$, so $P$ stays $143$ and $Q$ stays
$0$ while $M$ becomes $416$, $832$, $1664$, then $3328$. The
controller is a fixed eight-step counter, not a $Q=0$ detector: the
datapath has no early-out. Those four extra iterations are required
by the specification even though they do not change $P$. The
$16$-bit width is used: already $M=416$ does not fit in eight bits.

Sentence (i) replaces the specified controller by a data-dependent
stop. The product happens to be ready after four iterations on this
particular $Q$, but that is an instance accident, not the algorithm.
Sentence (ii) samples $Q$ after the shift, or adds the already
doubled $M$. The first add would then write $26$ (or a later
shifted multiplicand) and the required trace $0\to 13\to 39\to 39\to 143$
would be lost.

The argument never builds a one-hot opcode decoder and never traces
an LW through a single-cycle datapath.

graderFixtures.proofText: Each step preserves $P+M\cdot Q=143$. The first four iterations give $P=0,13,39,39,143$ and $Q=11,5,2,1,0$. Iterations $5$--$8$ keep $P=143$ because the controller has no $Q=0$ stop. Shifting before adding would write $26$ first.
Q is already 0 after four iterations, so I halt there. The last four iterations are wasted and are not part of the algorithm. A Q=0 detector is implied.
I shift M and Q first, then add if the new LSB is 1. The first add uses M=26 and the accumulator begins 0,26,... rather than 0,13,39,39,143.

ARCH:010220.title: A 250ps multicycle clock does not beat a 750ps single-cycle clock on this mix: 75ns versus 101.25ns for 100 instructions
ARCH:010220.objective: Derive the single-cycle period 750ps and the multicycle period 250ps, compute CPI 4.05 on the stated mix, compare 75ns with 101.25ns for 100 instructions, and reject the claim that a shorter multicycle clock is automatically faster.
ARCH:010220.statement:
A pedagogical datapath is built from five combinational blocks whose
propagation delays are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{block}&\mathrm{IF}&\mathrm{ID}&\mathrm{EX}&\mathrm{MEM}&\mathrm{WB}\\ \hline
\text{delay (ps)}&200&100&150&250&50.
\end{array}
\]
A single-cycle implementation places every block in series on the
same clock and must complete the worst-case instruction (a load,
which uses all five blocks) in one period. A multicycle
implementation gives each block its own cycle, clocks at the delay
of the slowest block, and uses
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{class}&R\text{-type}&\text{load}&\text{store}&\text{branch}\\ \hline
\text{cycles}&4&5&4&3
\end{array}
\]
corresponding to $\mathrm{IF}$-$\mathrm{ID}$-$\mathrm{EX}$-$\mathrm{WB}$,
$\mathrm{IF}$-$\mathrm{ID}$-$\mathrm{EX}$-$\mathrm{MEM}$-$\mathrm{WB}$,
$\mathrm{IF}$-$\mathrm{ID}$-$\mathrm{EX}$-$\mathrm{MEM}$, and
$\mathrm{IF}$-$\mathrm{ID}$-$\mathrm{EX}$. A representative mix is
\[
40\%\ R\text{-type},\quad
25\%\ \text{load},\quad
15\%\ \text{store},\quad
20\%\ \text{branch}.
\]
There are no stalls, no cache misses, and no overlap between
instructions in either implementation.

1. Compute the single-cycle clock period and the multicycle clock
   period. Justify each from the block delays and from the load
   being the single-cycle critical path.

2. Compute the multicycle CPI on the given mix. Then compute the
   wall-clock time for $100$ instructions on each implementation,
   in nanoseconds. State which implementation is faster on this mix
   and by what factor.

3. Audit the claim that “multicycle is automatically faster because
   $250\,\mathrm{ps}<750\,\mathrm{ps}$.” Also audit the two
   companion mistakes of giving every instruction five multicycle
   beats, and of setting the single-cycle period to the maximum
   block delay $250\,\mathrm{ps}$.

Do not replace the timing comparison by a one-hot control-invariant
or LW mux-select trace.
permittedResults: CPU time $=(\text{instruction count})\times\mathrm{CPI}\times(\text{clock period})$. A shorter period can be cancelled by a larger CPI.
The single-cycle period is a path delay, not a per-block delay. The multicycle period is a per-block delay, not a path delay.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the five block delays for the single-cycle load path, take the max delay for the multicycle clock, then evaluate CPI times period on the mix.
Compare per-instruction times 750ps and 4.05*250ps=1012.5ps first, then scale by 100 and audit the period-only speedup claim.

milestones.criterion: Derives the single-cycle period 750ps from the load path and the multicycle period 250ps from the MEM block.
Computes CPI 4.05 and the 100-instruction times 75ns versus 101.25ns.
Rejects the claim that a shorter multicycle clock is automatically faster, and the companion 5-cycle or 250ps-single mistakes.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that multicycle is faster solely because 250ps < 750ps, or reports a speedup of 3 from the period ratio while ignoring CPI.
commonErrors.consequence: The comparison is of clocks, not of instruction times. On this mix single-cycle is faster.

commonErrors.description: Gives every instruction five multicycle beats (CPI=5, 125ns), or sets the single-cycle period to the max block delay 250ps.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the stated cycle allocation or the single-cycle critical-path rule is discarded.

hintTree.content: The load path is $200+100+150+250+50=750\,\mathrm{ps}$. The slowest block is MEM at $250\,\mathrm{ps}$.
One hundred instructions take $100\cdot 750\,\mathrm{ps}=75\,\mathrm{ns}$ single-cycle and $100\cdot 4.05\cdot 250\,\mathrm{ps}=101.25\,\mathrm{ns}$ multicycle.

ARCH:010220.canonicalSolution:
A single-cycle load traverses every block, so the period is
\[
200+100+150+250+50=750\,\mathrm{ps}.
\]
$R$-type, store, and branch paths are shorter ($500$, $700$, and
$450\,\mathrm{ps}$), but the clock cannot be faster than the worst
case. A multicycle implementation fires one block per cycle and
must therefore clock at
\[
\max\{200,100,150,250,50\}=250\,\mathrm{ps}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T_{\mathrm{single}}=750\,\mathrm{ps},\quad T_{\mathrm{multi}}=250\,\mathrm{ps}}.
\]

On the stated mix the multicycle CPI is
\[
0.40\cdot 4+0.25\cdot 5+0.15\cdot 4+0.20\cdot 3
=1.60+1.25+0.60+0.60=4.05.
\]
One hundred instructions then cost
\begin{align*}
\text{single-cycle }&=100\cdot 750\,\mathrm{ps}=75\,000\,\mathrm{ps}=75\,\mathrm{ns},\\
\text{multicycle }&=100\cdot 4.05\cdot 250\,\mathrm{ps}=101\,250\,\mathrm{ps}=101.25\,\mathrm{ns}.
\end{align*}
The single-cycle machine is faster. The ratio of wall times is
$101.25/75=1.35$, matching the per-instruction comparison
$4.05\cdot 250=1012.5\,\mathrm{ps}$ against $750\,\mathrm{ps}$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{CPI}=4.05;\ 75\,\mathrm{ns}\text{ vs }101.25\,\mathrm{ns}}.
\]

The claim that multicycle is automatically faster because
$250<750$ compares clock periods and ignores CPI. The product
$\mathrm{CPI}\times T_{\mathrm{clk}}$ is the quantity that decides
instruction throughput. Giving every instruction five multicycle
beats would invent $\mathrm{CPI}=5$ and $125\,\mathrm{ns}$, which
is not the stated cycle allocation. Setting the single-cycle period
to the max block delay $250\,\mathrm{ps}$ confuses the two
implementations: a single-cycle load still has to propagate through
MEM and then WB in the same tick.

The argument never decodes a one-hot controller and never traces
an LW through mux selects.

graderFixtures.proofText: Single-cycle period $750\,\mathrm{ps}$, multicycle period $250\,\mathrm{ps}$, $\mathrm{CPI}=4.05$. One hundred instructions take $75\,\mathrm{ns}$ versus $101.25\,\mathrm{ns}$, so single-cycle is faster. A shorter clock is not an automatic win. A uniform $5$-cycle model and a $250\,\mathrm{ps}$ single-cycle period are different machines.
Multicycle must be faster because 250ps is three times shorter than 750ps. I report a speedup of 3 and do not compute CPI or the 101.25ns figure.
Every instruction uses all five blocks, so CPI=5 and 100 instructions take 125ns. Alternatively the single-cycle clock is just the slowest block, 250ps.

ARCH:010321.title: From SN, TTTNTTTN misses four times and ends in WT; the second pass misses only on the taken-to-not exits
ARCH:010321.objective: Trace a two-bit saturating predictor from 00 on TTTNTTTN to four misses and final state 10, show that the repeated string misses only on the two N exits, and reject both a wrapping counter and a one-bit or low-bit predictor.
ARCH:010321.statement:
A two-bit saturating branch predictor has states
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{bits}&\text{name}&\text{prediction}\\ \hline
00&\mathrm{SN}&\mathrm{N}\\
01&\mathrm{WN}&\mathrm{N}\\
10&\mathrm{WT}&\mathrm{T}\\
11&\mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}.
\end{array}
\]
The prediction is the high bit: states $0b$ predict not-taken and
states $1b$ predict taken. An observed $\mathrm{T}$ increments the
two-bit state by one unless the state is already $11$; an observed
$\mathrm{N}$ decrements it by one unless the state is already $00$.
There is no wrap from $11$ to $00$ or from $00$ to $11$. The
predictor is a single counter attached to one static branch; this
problem is not a pipeline schedule and does not squash instructions.

Start in $00$ and present the eight-outcome string
\[
\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{N}.
\]

1. Tabulate, for each outcome, the state before the prediction, the
   predicted direction, whether the prediction misses, and the next
   state. Prove that the string produces exactly four misses and
   ends in state $10$.

2. Repeat the same eight outcomes starting from that final state
   $10$. Prove that the only misses are the two $\mathrm{N}$
   outcomes (the exits from a taken run) and that the counter again
   ends in $10$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the low bit is the prediction, or a
   one-bit predictor is equivalent, so the second pass still pays
   the two warmup misses”; (ii) “the counter is just $\bmod 4$,
   so $\mathrm{T}$ from $11$ wraps to $00$.”

Do not replace the counter by an in-order forwarding, load-use, or
branch-squash cycle chart.
permittedResults: After two consecutive taken outcomes from $00$ the state is $10$ and every further taken outcome stays in $\{10,11\}$. A single not-taken from $11$ returns to $10$, not to a not-taken prediction.
A one-bit predictor has no hysteresis: an isolated $\mathrm{N}$ in a taken run flips the prediction, so the next $\mathrm{T}$ misses.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fill the eight-row state table twice, once from 00 and once from 10, marking each high-bit prediction before updating.
First argue hysteresis: two T outcomes are needed to leave SN, and a single N from ST still predicts T, then confirm on the given string.

milestones.criterion: Traces TTTNTTTN from 00 with high-bit predictions and saturating updates to four misses and final state 10.
Shows that the second presentation misses only on the two N exits and again ends in 10.
Rejects a one-bit or low-bit predictor and a wrapping counter, and does not substitute a pipeline squash chart.

commonErrors.description: Predicts with the low bit, or replaces the automaton by a one-bit counter, so the second pass still misses a T after each N.
commonErrors.consequence: Hysteresis is lost. The second presentation is no longer exit-miss only.

commonErrors.description: Treats the state as an integer mod 4, so T from 11 wraps to 00 and a later T is predicted N.
commonErrors.consequence: The counter leaves the taken pair {10,11} on a taken outcome, and the required second-pass table is impossible.

hintTree.content: From $00$, the first two $\mathrm{T}$ outcomes are misses ($00\to 01\to 10$). The third $\mathrm{T}$ hits and reaches $11$. The following $\mathrm{N}$ misses and returns to $10$.
The second half $\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{N}$ from $10$ hits, hits, hits, then misses, ending again in $10$. That is already the steady pattern.
A wrapping $11+\mathrm{T}\mapsto 00$ would make a later $\mathrm{T}$ predict $\mathrm{N}$. A one-bit counter flips on each $\mathrm{N}$ and then misses the next $\mathrm{T}$.

ARCH:010321.canonicalSolution:
Start in $00$. The first presentation of $\mathrm{TTTNTTTN}$ is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i&\text{state}&\text{pred}&\text{actual}&\text{next}\\ \hline
1&00\ \mathrm{SN}&\mathrm{N}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{miss}&01\\
2&01\ \mathrm{WN}&\mathrm{N}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{miss}&10\\
3&10\ \mathrm{WT}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
4&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{N}\ \text{miss}&10\\
5&10\ \mathrm{WT}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
6&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
7&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
8&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{N}\ \text{miss}&10.
\end{array}
\]
The misses are steps $1,2,4,8$: four of them. The final state is
$10$. The first two misses are warmup from strongly-not-taken; the
other two are the $\mathrm{N}$ exits from a taken run.
\[
\boxed{\text{four misses, final }10}.
\]

Now repeat $\mathrm{TTTNTTTN}$ from $10$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i&\text{state}&\text{pred}&\text{actual}&\text{next}\\ \hline
1&10\ \mathrm{WT}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
2&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
3&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
4&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{N}\ \text{miss}&10\\
5&10\ \mathrm{WT}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
6&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
7&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{T}\ \text{hit}&11\\
8&11\ \mathrm{ST}&\mathrm{T}&\mathrm{N}\ \text{miss}&10.
\end{array}
\]
Every $\mathrm{T}$ is predicted taken. The only misses are the two
$\mathrm{N}$ outcomes, which are exactly the exits from a taken run.
The counter ends in $10$ again, so further repetitions are
identical.
\[
\boxed{\text{second pass: only the two N-exit misses}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false in both forms. Predicting with the low bit
makes $01$ predict $\mathrm{T}$ and $10$ predict $\mathrm{N}$, so
the second pass starting at $10$ already misses the first $\mathrm{T}$.
A one-bit predictor that starts taken after the first string flips
to not-taken on each $\mathrm{N}$ and then misses the following
$\mathrm{T}$; the second pass therefore pays two extra warmup
misses that hysteresis would have avoided. Sentence (ii) replaces
saturation by a wrap. From $11$, two more $\mathrm{T}$ outcomes
would walk $11\to 00\to 01$, after which a $\mathrm{T}$ is predicted
$\mathrm{N}$. The second-pass “only exit misses” property
disappears.

The table is a per-branch automaton. It is not a five-stage
forwarding diagram, not a load-use bubble, and not a branch-squash
cycle chart.

graderFixtures.proofText: From $00$, $\mathrm{TTTNTTTN}$ misses at steps $1,2,4,8$ and ends in $10$. The repeat, starting at $10$, misses only on the two $\mathrm{N}$ exits and ends in $10$ again. A one-bit or low-bit rule reintroduces warmup misses. Wrapping $11+\mathrm{T}$ to $00$ is not saturation.
I predict with the low bit, so 10 predicts N. Alternatively I use a one-bit predictor. On the second pass the T that follows each N is a miss, not only the N exits.
The two-bit state is just an integer mod 4. From 11 a taken outcome wraps to 00, so a later T is predicted N and the second pass cannot be exit-miss only.

ARCH:010322.title: T1 wakes the older add; it cannot restore the younger F2 map
ARCH:010322.objective: Rename a four-instruction Tomasulo fragment through tags T1 and T3, show that the DIV result wakes I2 but cannot overwrite the younger F2 mapping, and compute F6=8 with final F2=42 and F14=40 under explicit issue, FU, CDB, and ROB rules.
ARCH:010322.statement:
A Tomasulo machine with a reorder buffer (ROB) issues the following
program in order. Destination tags are fixed by the problem:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|l}
I_1&\mathrm{DIV}\ F2,F0,F4&\text{dest tag }T_1\\
I_2&\mathrm{ADD}\ F6,F2,F8&\text{dest tag }T_2\\
I_3&\mathrm{MUL}\ F2,F10,F12&\text{dest tag }T_3\\
I_4&\mathrm{SUB}\ F14,F2,F16&\text{dest tag }T_4.
\end{array}
\]
The architectural sources that are ready at cycle $0$ are
\[
F0=20,\quad F4=4,\quad F8=3,\quad F10=6,\quad F12=7,\quad F16=2.
\]
Every operation is exact on these integers: $20/4=5$, addition, multiplication,
and subtraction. There are no branches, no exceptions, and no memory
operations. Do not replace the exercise by an in-order five-stage forwarding
or branch-squash chart.

The machine rules are exact.

- Issue is in program order, one instruction per cycle. $I_1$ issues in
  cycle $1$.
- On issue, the destination architectural register is renamed to the
  instruction's dest tag in the register-alias table (RAT). A source that
  currently maps to a ready value is copied into the reservation station
  (RS). A source that currently maps to a tag records that tag.
- There is one non-pipelined DIV unit, one non-pipelined MUL unit, and one
  non-pipelined ADD/SUB unit.
- An instruction may occupy its functional unit on the first cycle that is
  strictly after its issue cycle, on which every operand is already in its
  RS, and on which the unit is free. Occupancy lasts $8$ cycles for DIV,
  $4$ cycles for MUL, and $2$ cycles for ADD or SUB. The result is produced
  at the end of the last occupancy cycle.
- There is one common data bus (CDB). The first eligible CDB cycle is the
  cycle immediately after occupancy ends. If two results are eligible in
  the same cycle, the program-older instruction takes the CDB and the
  younger waits. An RS waiting on tag $T_k$ captures the value in the CDB
  cycle and may begin execution on a later cycle.
- A CDB broadcast of tag $T_k$ with value $v$ updates $\mathrm{RAT}[r]$ to
  ready-$v$ only if $\mathrm{RAT}[r]$ still equals $T_k$. A later issue that
  rewrites the same architectural register therefore prevents an older tag
  from restoring that mapping.
- The ROB commits at most one instruction per cycle, in program order. An
  instruction may commit on the first cycle that is strictly after its CDB
  cycle and on which every older instruction has already committed.
  Architectural register-file writes occur only at commit.

1. After each issue, give $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]$, $\mathrm{RAT}[F6]$, and
   $\mathrm{RAT}[F14]$, and name the tag or ready value each source reads.
   In particular identify the sources of $I_2$ and $I_4$.
2. Under the stated issue, FU, CDB, and ROB rules, construct the unique
   cycle table of issue, execute occupancy, CDB, and commit for $I_1$
   through $I_4$. Show that $T_1$ becomes ready in time to wake $I_2$ and
   that this broadcast does not restore $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]$.
3. Compute every result tag and the committed architectural values of
   $F6$, $F2$, and $F14$ after $I_4$ commits.
4. Audit these claims: (i) $I_4$ must read $T_1$ because $I_1$ is the first
   writer of $F2$; (ii) when $T_1$ completes, the final architectural $F2$
   is $5$; (iii) $I_3$ cannot issue until $I_1$ commits, because otherwise
   $F2$ would have a write-after-write hazard. State that the schedule is
   specific to the stated FU/CDB/ROB model.

State the RAT rule and that in-order commit still writes $I_1$'s value into
the architectural file before $I_3$ overwrites it.
permittedResults: If $I_a$ and $I_b$ both write architectural $r$ and $I_a$ is older, then after $I_b$ issues one has $\mathrm{RAT}[r]=T_b$. A later broadcast of $T_a$ can wake consumers of $T_a$ but cannot set $\mathrm{RAT}[r]$ back to $T_a$.

In-order ROB commit writes the architectural register file in program order. An older writer of $r$ may therefore update the architectural file before a younger writer of $r$ commits; the final committed value of $r$ is the younger writer's result.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rewrite the RAT at each issue, then fill EX occupancy from the first legal start cycle and attach one CDB cycle after occupancy.
Compute the four tag values from the integer operations first, then place CDB events and check that T1's cycle is after I3 has already remapped F2.

milestones.criterion: Renames F2 to T1 then T3, has I2 read T1, and has I4 read T3.
Builds the unique issue/EX/CDB/commit table and the values T1=5, F6=8, T3=42, F14=40 with final F2=42.
Shows that the T1 broadcast wakes I2 without restoring RAT[F2], and rejects reading T1 for I4, taking 5 as final F2, and stalling I3 for WAW.

commonErrors.description: Lets the T1 broadcast restore RAT[F2], or has I4 read T1 because I1 was the first writer of F2.
commonErrors.consequence: The younger MUL mapping is discarded and I4 consumes the DIV result instead of the MUL result.

commonErrors.description: Reports final architectural F2=5, or F14=3 from subtracting 2 from the DIV result, or F6 from an unrenamed F2.
commonErrors.consequence: The committed register file is not the in-order Tomasulo result F6=8, F2=42, F14=40.

hintTree.content: After $I_1$ issues, $F2$ maps to $T_1$, so $I_2$ records source tag $T_1$. After $I_3$ issues, $F2$ maps to $T_3$, so $I_4$ records $T_3$, not $T_1$.

$I_1$ occupies DIV in cycles $2$ through $9$ and is first eligible for the CDB in cycle $10$. $I_3$ occupies MUL in cycles $4$ through $7$ and is first eligible in cycle $8$. Those CDB cycles do not collide.
The results are $T_1=20/4=5$ and $T_3=6\cdot 7=42$. Then $F6=5+3=8$ and $F14=42-2=40$. The final architectural $F2$ is the committed $T_3$, not $T_1$.

ARCH:010322.canonicalSolution:
Issue and rename. Cycle $1$ issues $I_1$. Both sources are ready, so the
DIV RS copies $F0=20$ and $F4=4$, and $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]\leftarrow T_1$.
Cycle $2$ issues $I_2$. $F2$ maps to $T_1$ and $F8$ is ready $3$, so the
ADD RS records tag $T_1$ and value $3$, and $\mathrm{RAT}[F6]\leftarrow T_2$.
Cycle $3$ issues $I_3$. Both MUL sources are ready $6$ and $7$, and
$\mathrm{RAT}[F2]\leftarrow T_3$. Cycle $4$ issues $I_4$. $F2$ now maps to
$T_3$ and $F16$ is ready $2$, so the SUB RS records tag $T_3$ and value
$2$, and $\mathrm{RAT}[F14]\leftarrow T_4$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|l}
\text{after issue}&\mathrm{RAT}[F2]&\mathrm{RAT}[F6]&\mathrm{RAT}[F14]&\text{new sources}\\ \hline
I_1&T_1&\text{ready}&\text{ready}&I_1\text{ reads }20,4\\
I_2&T_1&T_2&\text{ready}&I_2\text{ reads }T_1,3\\
I_3&T_3&T_2&\text{ready}&I_3\text{ reads }6,7\\
I_4&T_3&T_2&T_4&I_4\text{ reads }T_3,2.
\end{array}
\]
Thus $I_2$ is a consumer of $T_1$ and $I_4$ is a consumer of $T_3$.

Execute, CDB, and commit. $I_1$ may occupy DIV starting in cycle $2$. Eight
occupancy cycles are $2$ through $9$, so the first eligible CDB cycle is
$10$. $I_3$ may occupy MUL starting in cycle $4$. Four occupancy cycles are
$4$ through $7$, so the first eligible CDB cycle is $8$. Those eligible
cycles differ, so the older-first CDB rule is not invoked.
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
&IS&EX&CDB&COM\\ \hline
I_1&1&2\text{--}9&10&11\\
I_2&2&11\text{--}12&13&14\\
I_3&3&4\text{--}7&8&15\\
I_4&4&9\text{--}10&11&16.
\end{array}
\]
$I_3$ broadcasts $T_3=42$ in cycle $8$. $I_4$ captures $42$ in that cycle
and occupies ADD/SUB in cycles $9$ and $10$. $I_1$ broadcasts $T_1=5$ in
cycle $10$. $I_2$ captures $5$ then and occupies ADD/SUB in cycles $11$ and
$12$; the ADD/SUB unit is free because $I_4$ finished occupancy in cycle
$10$. Commit is in order: $I_1$ commits in $11$, $I_2$ in $14$ (the cycle
after its CDB), $I_3$ in $15$ (it has been CDB-ready since cycle $8$ but
cannot pass $I_2$), and $I_4$ in $16$.

Wakeup versus the younger map. The cycle-$10$ broadcast of $T_1=5$ wakes
the ADD RS of $I_2$. At that moment $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]=T_3\neq T_1$, so the
broadcast does not restore $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]$. $I_4$ never records $T_1$
and does not capture the DIV result.

Values. $T_1=20/4=5$, $T_2=5+3=8$, $T_3=6\cdot 7=42$, and
$T_4=42-2=40$. In-order commit writes architectural $F2\leftarrow 5$ when
$I_1$ commits and then $F2\leftarrow 42$ when $I_3$ commits, writes
$F6\leftarrow 8$ when $I_2$ commits, and writes $F14\leftarrow 40$ when
$I_4$ commits. After $I_4$ commits,
\[
\boxed{F6=8},\qquad
\boxed{F2=42},\qquad
\boxed{F14=40}.
\]

Claim (i) ignores the RAT rewrite at $I_3$: the source $F2$ of $I_4$ is
the youngest issued writer, $T_3$. Claim (ii) confuses the temporary
architectural write at $I_1$'s commit with the final committed value, which
is $I_3$'s $42$. Claim (iii) confuses a WAW dependence on an architectural
name with a resource constraint: renaming removes the WAW from the issue
rule, and $I_3$ issues in cycle $3$ while $I_1$ is still in DIV. The
schedule uses the stated occupancy, CDB, and ROB rules and does not
transfer to a different FU mix, a different CDB width, or an in-order
five-stage pipeline.

graderFixtures.proofText: After $I_1$, $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]=T_1$. After $I_3$, $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]=T_3$. $I_2$ reads $T_1$ and $I_4$ reads $T_3$. Cycles: $I_1$ IS $1$, EX $2$--$9$, CDB $10$, COM $11$; $I_2$ IS $2$, EX $11$--$12$, CDB $13$, COM $14$; $I_3$ IS $3$, EX $4$--$7$, CDB $8$, COM $15$; $I_4$ IS $4$, EX $9$--$10$, CDB $11$, COM $16$. $T_1=5$ wakes $I_2$ in cycle $10$ and does not restore $\mathrm{RAT}[F2]$. Committed values are $F6=8$, final $F2=42$, $F14=40$. $I_3$ issues in cycle $3$ without a WAW stall.
I4 reads F2, and I1 is the producer of F2, so I4 waits on T1. When T1 broadcasts 5 the RAT writes F2 ready-5, overwriting T3. I4 therefore computes 5-2=3.
I1 writes F2=5 and that is the last architectural value of F2 because I3 only writes a tag. F6 is 20+3=23 if renaming is ignored, and F14 is 5-2=3.

ARCH:010423.title: Two dirty evictions and three fills: eighty bytes, no trailing flush
ARCH:010423.objective: Trace W00, W04, R20, W20, R00 on a two-line write-back write-allocate direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks, count three misses, two hits, three fills and two dirty writebacks, and obtain 80 bytes of lower-level traffic with no final writeback absent a flush.
ARCH:010423.statement:
A data cache has exactly two lines, is direct-mapped, and uses $16$-byte
blocks. Byte addresses are split as
\[
\langle\text{tag},\ \text{index},\ \text{offset}\rangle
=\langle A[7:5],\ A[4],\ A[3:0]\rangle
\]
on the $8$-bit addresses below; equivalently, the block number is
$\lfloor A/16\rfloor$ and the set index is that block number modulo $2$.
The cache is write-back and write-allocate. On a write miss the controller
fills the entire $16$-byte block from the lower level, then applies the
store to the cached copy and marks the line dirty. On a dirty eviction the
controller writes the entire $16$-byte victim back to the lower level. A
clean eviction generates no writeback. Hits generate no lower-level
traffic. Each reference below is a single-byte access. Both lines begin
invalid and clean. There is no victim buffer, no write combining, and no
flush at the end of the trace. Do not replace the exercise by a three-C
classification or by a read-only AMAT calculation.

The reference trace is
\[
W(\mathtt{0x00}),\quad
W(\mathtt{0x04}),\quad
R(\mathtt{0x20}),\quad
W(\mathtt{0x20}),\quad
R(\mathtt{0x00}).
\]

1. For each address give block number, set index, tag, and offset. Identify
   which references share a line.
2. Trace valid/tag/dirty state of both sets after every reference. Classify
   each reference as a hit or a miss and name every fill and every dirty
   writeback.
3. Count misses, hits, fills, dirty writebacks, line transactions with the
   lower level, and total lower-level traffic in bytes. Determine whether
   a writeback of the final resident line is owed in the absence of a flush.
4. Audit these claims: (i) $\mathtt{0x00}$ and $\mathtt{0x20}$ occupy
   different sets because their high bits differ, so $R(\mathtt{0x00})$ is
   a hit; (ii) $W(\mathtt{0x04})$ is a miss because the address is not
   $\mathtt{0x00}$; (iii) the cache is write-through, or a trailing flush
   must be charged, so the traffic is $48$ or $96$ bytes. State that only
   full-line transactions are charged.

State write-allocate fill-then-store and that dirty writebacks occur only
on eviction.
permittedResults: With $16$-byte blocks the offset is $A[3:0]$. Two lines that are direct-mapped use a one-bit index $A[4]$, so addresses $A$ and $A+32$ share a set whenever they share $A[4]$.
Lower-level traffic under write-back write-allocate is $16$ bytes times (fills plus dirty writebacks). Hits and clean evictions contribute $0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Index by A[4], then update one set's valid/tag/dirty flags and charge 16 bytes on every fill and every dirty eviction.
Name the five line transactions in order (fill 0, writeback 0, fill 2, writeback 2, fill 0) and multiply by the block size.

milestones.criterion: Splits every address into block, set-0 index, and tag, and traces valid/tag/dirty after each reference.
Counts 3 misses, 2 hits, 3 fills, 2 dirty writebacks, 5 line transactions, and 80 bytes with no trailing flush.
Rejects a two-set split of 0x00 from 0x20, a W04 miss, write-through charging, and a forced final writeback.

commonErrors.description: Places 0x00 and 0x20 in different sets, or treats W04 as a miss because the byte address differs from 0x00.
commonErrors.consequence: The hit/miss string and the two dirty evictions are no longer the stated trace.

commonErrors.description: Charges only the three fills (48 bytes), invents a trailing flush (96 bytes), or switches the cache to write-through.
commonErrors.consequence: The lower-level traffic is no longer the five line transactions totalling 80 bytes.

hintTree.content: $\mathtt{0x00}$, $\mathtt{0x04}$, and $\mathtt{0x20}$ all have $A[4]=0$, so they share set $0$. Set $1$ stays empty.
$W(\mathtt{0x00})$ fills and dirties block $0$. $R(\mathtt{0x20})$ must write that dirty victim back before filling block $2$. $W(\mathtt{0x20})$ then dirties block $2$.
After $R(\mathtt{0x00})$ the resident line is a just-filled clean copy of block $0$. No flush is ordered, so there is no third writeback.

ARCH:010423.canonicalSolution:
Address fields. The offset is $A[3:0]$, the index is $A[4]$, and the tag
is $A[7:5]$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
A&\text{block}&\text{index}&\text{tag}&\text{offset}\\ \hline
\mathtt{0x00}&0&0&0&\mathtt{0x0}\\
\mathtt{0x04}&0&0&0&\mathtt{0x4}\\
\mathtt{0x20}&2&0&1&\mathtt{0x0}.
\end{array}
\]
$W(\mathtt{0x00})$ and $W(\mathtt{0x04})$ address the same block. All five
references map to set $0$; set $1$ remains invalid.

Trace, writing a line as $(\mathrm{tag},\mathrm{valid},\mathrm{dirty})$.
Both sets start $(\text{--},0,0)$.

- $W(\mathtt{0x00})$. Compulsory miss in set $0$. Fill block $0$
  ($16$ bytes), store offset $0$, mark dirty. Set $0$ becomes $(0,1,1)$.
- $W(\mathtt{0x04})$. Same tag and index: hit. Store offset $4$. Set $0$
  stays $(0,1,1)$.
- $R(\mathtt{0x20})$. Tag $1$ misses in set $0$. The victim is dirty, so
  write back block $0$ ($16$ bytes), then fill block $2$ ($16$ bytes) and
  read offset $0$. The fill is a read, so the line is clean: set $0$
  becomes $(1,1,0)$.
- $W(\mathtt{0x20})$. Hit in set $0$. Store offset $0$ and mark dirty:
  $(1,1,1)$.
- $R(\mathtt{0x00})$. Tag $0$ misses. The victim is dirty, so write back
  block $2$ ($16$ bytes), then fill block $0$ ($16$ bytes) and read. The
  line is clean: $(0,1,0)$.

Set $1$ is untouched. Hits are $W(\mathtt{0x04})$ and $W(\mathtt{0x20})$.
Misses are $W(\mathtt{0x00})$, $R(\mathtt{0x20})$, and $R(\mathtt{0x00})$.
Fills are the three misses. Dirty writebacks are the two evictions.

Counts. Three misses, two hits, three fills, two dirty writebacks, and
\[
3+2=5
\]
line transactions. Traffic is
\[
(3+2)\cdot 16=\boxed{80\text{ bytes}}.
\]
The final resident line is a clean copy of block $0$. No flush is ordered,
so there is no third writeback.

Claim (i) uses the wrong index bit. $A[4]=0$ for both $\mathtt{0x00}$ and
$\mathtt{0x20}$, so they collide in set $0$ and $R(\mathtt{0x00})$ misses.
Claim (ii) confuses a byte offset with a block identity: $\mathtt{0x04}$
is in the already-resident block $0$. Claim (iii) either drops the two
writebacks ($3\cdot 16=48$) or invents a trailing flush of a clean line,
or flushes an imagined dirty final line ($96$ bytes). Write-through would
send stores to the lower level on every write and is not the stated
policy. Only the five named full-line transactions are charged.

graderFixtures.proofText: Addresses $\mathtt{0x00}$ and $\mathtt{0x04}$ are block $0$ in set $0$; $\mathtt{0x20}$ is block $2$ in the same set. The trace is miss-fill-dirty, hit, miss-writeback-fill-clean, hit-dirty, miss-writeback-fill-clean. Counts: $3$ misses, $2$ hits, $3$ fills, $2$ dirty writebacks, $5$ line transactions, $80$ bytes. The final line is clean block $0$, so there is no flush writeback.
Bit 5 of 0x20 is 1, so 0x20 goes to set 1 and 0x00 stays in set 0. Then R00 hits. Separately, W04 is a different address from W00, so it misses and allocates again.

Only misses traffic the lower level, and each miss is one 16-byte fill, so the traffic is 48 bytes. At the end the cache must be flushed, adding one more 16-byte writeback for 64 or 96 bytes. A write-through cache would send every store as well.

ARCH:010424.title: A TLB miss walks; a page fault does not install
ARCH:010424.objective: Translate VA 0x12345ABC through VPN 0x12345 to PA 0x00ABCABC, trace a two-entry LRU TLB on A, B, A, invalid-C as miss, miss, hit, page fault, and show that the fault does not install while the 12-bit offset is copied unchanged.
ARCH:010424.statement:
A machine uses $32$-bit virtual addresses and $4\,\mathrm{KiB}$ pages, so
the page offset is the low $12$ bits and the virtual page number (VPN) is
the high $20$ bits. Physical addresses are also $32$ bits: a valid page-table
entry (PTE) supplies a $20$-bit physical page number (PPN), and the physical
address is that PPN concatenated with the same $12$-bit offset. The
hardware page-table contents that matter are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\mathrm{VPN}&\mathrm{valid}&\mathrm{PPN}\\ \hline
\mathtt{0x12345}&1&\mathtt{0x00ABC}\\
\mathtt{0x22222}&1&\mathtt{0x00DEF}\\
\mathtt{0x33333}&0&\text{--}.
\end{array}
\]
Every other VPN is invalid. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) has two
fully associative entries and true LRU replacement. It begins empty. A TLB
hit returns the stored PPN and does not consult the page table. A TLB miss
with a valid PTE installs that VPN$\mapsto$PPN in the TLB, updates LRU, and
then completes the translation. A TLB miss with an invalid PTE is a page
fault: the trap is taken, and the TLB is left unchanged. A page fault is
not a TLB fill. Do not replace the exercise by a cache three-C witness or
by a write-back traffic count.

The reference addresses, in order, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\mathtt{0x12345ABC},\\
B&=\mathtt{0x22222ABC},\\
A&=\mathtt{0x12345ABC},\\
C&=\mathtt{0x33333ABC}.
\end{aligned}
\]

1. Split each address into VPN and $12$-bit offset. Translate $A$ and $B$
   to physical addresses, showing that the offset is copied and that
   $A$ becomes $\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$.
2. Trace the two-entry LRU TLB (most-recent first) and classify each of
   the four references as TLB hit, TLB miss with fill, or page fault.
3. Prove that the faulting reference does not install $C$, and that a
   retry of $C$ still faults with the same TLB contents.
4. Audit these claims: (i) the offset is $16$ bits, so $A$ has VPN
   $\mathtt{0x1234}$ and cannot become $\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$; (ii) the
   first $A$ is a page fault because the TLB starts empty; (iii) after
   $B$ the TLB has forgotten $A$, so the second $A$ misses; (iv) the
   faulting $C$ should be cached as invalid so the next $C$ is a TLB hit.
   State that a TLB miss and a page fault are different events.

Preserve the $12$-bit offset and the no-install rule on faults.
permittedResults: If the page size is $2^{12}$ bytes, then $\mathrm{VA}=\mathrm{VPN}\cdot 2^{12}+\mathrm{offset}$ with $0\le\mathrm{offset}<2^{12}$, and a valid translation is $\mathrm{PA}=\mathrm{PPN}\cdot 2^{12}+\mathrm{offset}$.
A two-entry LRU TLB that has just installed $A$ then $B$ still contains $A$. The next reference to $A$ is a hit and makes $A$ most recent; it does not evict $A$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Peel the low three hex digits as the offset, concatenate the given PPN, then walk a two-slot LRU list by hand.
Classify each reference first as TLB hit or miss, and only on a miss read the PTE to decide fill versus fault.

milestones.criterion: Splits 12-bit offsets and translates A to 0x00ABCABC and B to 0x00DEFABC.
Traces two-entry LRU as miss, miss, hit, page fault and leaves the TLB unchanged on the fault.
Distinguishes TLB miss from page fault and rejects a 16-bit offset, a cold page-fault, a second-A miss, and an invalid install.

commonErrors.description: Takes a 16-bit offset, splits A as VPN 0x1234, or produces a physical address other than 0x00ABCABC for A.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity VPN 0x12345 with PPN 0x00ABC mapping VA 0x12345ABC to PA 0x00ABCABC is lost.

commonErrors.description: Calls the first A a page fault, misses the second A, or installs C (even as an invalid TLB row) on the fault.
commonErrors.consequence: TLB miss and page fault are no longer distinct, or a faulting VPN is cached.

hintTree.content: The low three hex digits of $\mathtt{0x12345ABC}$ are the $12$-bit offset $\mathtt{0xABC}$. Concatenate $\mathtt{0x00ABC}$ with $\mathtt{0xABC}$.
The TLB is empty, then $\{A\}$, then $\{B,A\}$. The second $A$ hits and yields $\{A,B\}$. $C$ is not in the page table.
An invalid PTE must not create a TLB entry. A later $C$ therefore misses again and faults again.

ARCH:010424.canonicalSolution:
Offsets and translations. A $4\,\mathrm{KiB}$ page uses a $12$-bit offset,
which is three hexadecimal digits.
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\mathrm{VA}&\mathrm{VPN}&\text{offset}\\ \hline
A=\mathtt{0x12345ABC}&\mathtt{0x12345}&\mathtt{0xABC}\\
B=\mathtt{0x22222ABC}&\mathtt{0x22222}&\mathtt{0xABC}\\
C=\mathtt{0x33333ABC}&\mathtt{0x33333}&\mathtt{0xABC}.
\end{array}
\]
The valid PTE for $A$ supplies PPN $\mathtt{0x00ABC}$, so
\[
\mathrm{PA}(A)=\mathtt{0x00ABC}\,\|\,\mathtt{0xABC}
=\boxed{\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}}.
\]
The valid PTE for $B$ supplies PPN $\mathtt{0x00DEF}$, so
\[
\mathrm{PA}(B)=\mathtt{0x00DEF}\,\|\,\mathtt{0xABC}
=\boxed{\mathtt{0x00DEFABC}}.
\]
$C$ has no valid PPN.

TLB trace, writing the LRU list as most-recent first.

- $A$. TLB empty: miss. PTE valid: install $\mathtt{0x12345}\mapsto
  \mathtt{0x00ABC}$. Translate to $\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$. TLB $[A]$.
- $B$. $B$ is absent: miss. PTE valid: install
  $\mathtt{0x22222}\mapsto\mathtt{0x00DEF}$. Translate to
  $\mathtt{0x00DEFABC}$. TLB $[B,A]$.
- $A$. $A$ is still present: hit. No page-table reference. Translate to
  $\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$. LRU becomes $[A,B]$.
- $C$. $C$ is absent: miss. PTE invalid: page fault. The TLB is not
  written, so it remains $[A,B]$.

The four-event string is therefore
\[
\boxed{\text{TLB miss},\ \text{TLB miss},\ \text{TLB hit},\ \text{page fault}}.
\]

No-install. The fault rule forbids allocating an entry for an invalid VPN.
A retry of $C$ again finds no TLB entry and again reads an invalid PTE, so
it faults again with TLB still $[A,B]$. The second $A$ never needed a fill.

Claim (i) uses a $64\,\mathrm{KiB}$ page. A $16$-bit offset would make the
VPN of $A$ equal to $\mathtt{0x1234}$ and would break the required identity
$\mathrm{PA}(A)=\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$. Claim (ii) conflates a cold TLB miss
with a page fault: $A$'s PTE is valid, so the first $A$ fills and
translates. Claim (iii) invents a one-entry TLB or FIFO eviction of $A$ at
$B$; two-entry LRU still holds $A$. Claim (iv) would cache a faulting VPN,
turning a later $C$ into a TLB hit and hiding the invalid PTE. The
architecture distinguishes a TLB miss (a cache of translations) from a
page fault (an invalid mapping).

graderFixtures.proofText: Offset $\mathtt{0xABC}$ on $A$, $B$, and $C$. $\mathrm{PA}(A)=\mathtt{0x00ABCABC}$ and $\mathrm{PA}(B)=\mathtt{0x00DEFABC}$. TLB walk: miss-fill $[A]$, miss-fill $[B,A]$, hit $[A,B]$, page fault with TLB still $[A,B]$. $C$ is not installed; a retry of $C$ faults again. The first $A$ is a TLB miss, not a page fault.
4 KiB is 16 bits of offset because 2^16=65536 is the usual software page. So A has VPN 0x1234 and offset 0x5ABC, and the PA cannot be 0x00ABCABC.
The TLB starts empty, so the first A is a page fault. After B there is room for only one VPN, so the second A misses. The faulting C should be inserted as invalid so the next C hits in the TLB.

ARCH:010425.title: FR-FCFS serves the open row first; aging must still free the closed one
ARCH:010425.objective: On one bank with row 0 open, schedule A(row 1), B(row 0), C(row 0) arriving at t=0 under FCFS and FR-FCFS, obtain completion times 30, 60, 70 versus 10, 20, 50 and averages 53 1/3 ns versus 26 2/3 ns, and show that pure row-hit priority needs aging.
ARCH:010425.statement:
A single DRAM bank has one open row, initially row $0$. The controller
serves at most one request at a time and is non-preemptive: once a request
starts, it occupies the bank until it completes. Already-folded command
timings are
\[
t_{\mathrm{hit}}=10\,\mathrm{ns}
\quad\text{if the request's row is the open row},
\]
\[
t_{\mathrm{conflict}}=30\,\mathrm{ns}
\quad\text{if the request's row differs from the open row}.
\]
After a request completes, the open row is the row just served. Three
requests are present at time $t=0$, with oldest-first arrival order
$A$, then $B$, then $C$:
\[
A\text{ wants row }1,\qquad
B\text{ wants row }0,\qquad
C\text{ wants row }0.
\]
No other request arrives unless a later part of the problem adds one. There
is no additional burst, refresh, or data-bus turnaround charge. Do not
replace the exercise by a cache three-C string or by an AMAT average.

Two schedulers are compared.

- FCFS starts the oldest not-yet-started request whenever the bank is free.
- FR-FCFS, among not-yet-started requests that would be row hits on the
  currently open row, starts the oldest such hit; if there is no pending
  hit, it starts the oldest request.

1. Under FCFS, give the service order, each request's service time, the
   three completion times, and the average completion time.
2. Under FR-FCFS, give the same four items.
3. Exhibit a continuation in which further row-$0$ requests keep arriving
   whenever the bank becomes free, and prove that pure row-hit priority
   then starves $A$. State a finite aging rule that eventually starts $A$.
4. Audit these claims: (i) FCFS should start $B$ first because row $0$ is
   already open; (ii) the average completion time is the completion time
   of the last request; (iii) FR-FCFS never needs aging because every
   finite request set drains. State that the numbers are bank-service
   completions, not cache AMAT.

Give mixed-number averages in nanoseconds.
permittedResults: If requests $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ occupy a single bank sequentially with service times $s_i$, the completion time of $X_k$ in that service order is $C_k=\sum_{i=1}^k s_i$, and the average completion time is $(C_1+\cdots+C_n)/n$.
A work-conserving priority that always prefers a nonempty class $H$ over a waiting job $J\notin H$ starves $J$ whenever arrivals can replenish $H$ whenever the server becomes free.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply each scheduler's selection rule at every free instant, accumulate service times, then average the three completion epochs.
Compare the two Gantt charts first, then reuse the hit-class replenishment argument for starvation.

milestones.criterion: Computes FCFS completions 30, 60, 70 and FR-FCFS completions 10, 20, 50.
Reports averages 53 1/3 ns and 26 2/3 ns from the sums 160/3 and 80/3.
Proves open-arrival starvation of A under pure hit priority, states a finite aging rule, and rejects an FCFS open-row start and a makespan-as-average.

commonErrors.description: Starts FCFS with B because row 0 is open, so FCFS is reported as identical to FR-FCFS.
commonErrors.consequence: The FCFS completions 30, 60, 70 and the contrast with FR-FCFS disappear.

commonErrors.description: Reports 70 ns or 50 ns as the average, swaps the two averages, or omits division by 3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair 53 1/3 ns versus 26 2/3 ns is not obtained.

hintTree.content: FCFS must start $A$ first even though $A$ is a conflict. After $A$ finishes, row $1$ is open, so both $B$ and $C$ are then conflicts until $B$ reopens row $0$.
At $t=0$ the pending hits are $B$ and $C$. FR-FCFS therefore starts $B$, then $C$, then the leftover conflict $A$.
Average FCFS completion is $(30+60+70)/3$. Average FR-FCFS completion is $(10+20+50)/3$. An infinite stream of new row-$0$ hits keeps $A$ off the bank.

ARCH:010425.canonicalSolution:
FCFS. The oldest request is $A$, a conflict on row $1$, so $A$ occupies
$[0,30]$ and completes at $30\,\mathrm{ns}$. The open row is now $1$.
$B$ is then a conflict on row $0$, occupies $[30,60]$, and completes at
$60\,\mathrm{ns}$. The open row is now $0$. $C$ is a hit, occupies
$[60,70]$, and completes at $70\,\mathrm{ns}$. The completion triple is
\[
\boxed{C_A=30,\ C_B=60,\ C_C=70},
\]
and the average is
\[
\frac{30+60+70}{3}=\frac{160}{3}=\boxed{53\tfrac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{ns}}.
\]

FR-FCFS. At $t=0$ the open row is $0$, so the pending hits are $B$ and
$C$. The oldest hit is $B$, which occupies $[0,10]$ and completes at
$10\,\mathrm{ns}$. Row $0$ stays open, so $C$ is still a hit, occupies
$[10,20]$, and completes at $20\,\mathrm{ns}$. The only remaining request
is $A$, a conflict, occupying $[20,50]$ and completing at $50\,\mathrm{ns}$.
The completion triple is
\[
\boxed{C_B=10,\ C_C=20,\ C_A=50},
\]
and the average is
\[
\frac{10+20+50}{3}=\frac{80}{3}=\boxed{26\tfrac{2}{3}\,\mathrm{ns}}.
\]
FR-FCFS therefore reduces average completion from $160/3$ to $80/3$ on
this instance by draining the open row before paying one conflict.

Starvation and aging. Keep $A$ pending after $t=20$ and, each time the
bank becomes free with row $0$ open, let a fresh row-$0$ request arrive
just then. Pure row-hit priority starts that new hit, row $0$ remains
open, and $A$ never begins. The waiting time of $A$ is unbounded. A
legal aging rule: every time a pending conflict is passed over in favour
of a hit, increment a skip count on the oldest conflict; when that count
reaches a finite threshold $K\ge 1$, the next scheduling decision must
start that conflict. After at most $K$ hits, $A$ starts. Any other finite
bound (a time quantum, a maximum hit run, or promoting $A$ to the hit
class after $K$ skips) likewise restores progress.

Claim (i) replaces FCFS by FR-FCFS: FCFS is arrival order, so it must
start $A$ and pay the first $30\,\mathrm{ns}$ conflict. Claim (ii)
confuses the makespan $70$ or $50$ with the average of the three
completion times. Claim (iii) is true of a closed finite instance but
false of an open arrival process; the aging requirement is exactly about
that open process. The averages are mean request-completion times at the
bank, not a cache AMAT.

graderFixtures.proofText: FCFS serves $A,B,C$ with completions $30,60,70$ and average $160/3=53\tfrac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{ns}$. FR-FCFS serves $B,C,A$ with completions $10,20,50$ and average $80/3=26\tfrac{2}{3}\,\mathrm{ns}$. An infinite stream of new row-$0$ hits starves $A$; a finite skip threshold forces $A$ onto the bank. FCFS may not start $B$ first, and $70$ is the FCFS makespan, not the average.
Row 0 is already open, so the oldest ready request is B even under FCFS. FCFS therefore also runs B, C, then A and matches FR-FCFS.
The average completion time is the time when the last request finishes, so FCFS averages 70 ns and FR-FCFS averages 50 ns. Alternatively the sums 160 and 80 are the averages.

ARCH:010526.title: Polling, interrupt, and DMA change winners with B; the unit is CPU cycles
ARCH:010526.objective: Compare CPU-cycle costs P=24B, I=180+12B, and D=780+2B, prove ties at B=15 and B=60, and identify polling cheapest on 1-14, interrupt strictly cheapest on 16-59, and DMA strictly cheapest on 61 and above, without treating the models as wall-clock transfer time.
ARCH:010526.statement:
A processor moves $B$ bytes, where $B$ is a positive integer, by one of
three programmed methods. The quantities below count CPU cycles during
which the processor is occupied by that transfer. They are not wall-clock
device or bus transfer times.
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{\mathrm{P}}(B)&=24B
&&\text{polling, $24$ cycles of spinning and a byte move per byte,}\\
C_{\mathrm{I}}(B)&=180+12B
&&\text{interrupt, one $180$-cycle handler prologue plus $12$ cycles per byte,}\\
C_{\mathrm{D}}(B)&=780+2B
&&\text{DMA, one $780$-cycle setup plus $2$ cycles of CPU involvement per byte.}
\end{aligned}
\]
The constants $180$ and $780$ are paid once per transfer. After the
programmed method is chosen, the CPU occupancy is exactly the displayed
function. Do not replace the exercise by a precise-interrupt retirement
trace or by an Amdahl speedup.

1. Solve $C_{\mathrm{P}}(B)=C_{\mathrm{I}}(B)$ and
   $C_{\mathrm{I}}(B)=C_{\mathrm{D}}(B)$ in positive real $B$, then
   evaluate all three functions at the adjacent integers. Identify every
   positive integer $B$ at which two methods tie for cheapest, and every
   interval on which one method is strictly cheapest.
2. Solve $C_{\mathrm{P}}(B)=C_{\mathrm{D}}(B)$ and show that this crossing
   is not a regime boundary among the three methods.
3. Explain why a larger $B$ can make DMA cheapest in CPU cycles even if
   the DMA engine's wall-clock bus transfer is slower than a programmed
   byte loop.
4. Audit these claims: (i) DMA always wins because the device runs in
   parallel with the CPU, so $C_{\mathrm{D}}$ is a wall-clock transfer
   time that is smaller for every $B$; (ii) polling costs $24+B$ or a
   flat $24$ cycles; (iii) interrupt strictly wins at $B=15$ and DMA
   strictly wins at $B=60$. State that the comparison is CPU occupancy.

Give the integer regimes $B\le 14$, $B=15$, $16\le B\le 59$, $B=60$, and
$B\ge 61$.
permittedResults: The unique positive root of $24B=180+12B$ is $B=15$. The unique positive root of $180+12B=780+2B$ is $B=60$. Because each pair of affine functions meets at most once, the cheapest method can change only at those roots or at the unused $C_{\mathrm{P}}=C_{\mathrm{D}}$ root.

If $C_{\mathrm{I}}(B)<C_{\mathrm{P}}(B)$ and $C_{\mathrm{I}}(B)<C_{\mathrm{D}}(B)$ on an interval, then a crossing of $C_{\mathrm{P}}$ with $C_{\mathrm{D}}$ inside that interval does not change the cheapest method.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve each adjacent pair of affine costs, tabulate the six neighbouring integers, and read off ties versus strict winners.
Plot the three lines against B and mark the two relevant intersections, then test the third intersection against the already-cheapest interrupt line.

milestones.criterion: Solves the ties B=15 and B=60 and lists the five integer regimes 1-14, 15, 16-59, 60, and 61+.
Shows that the polling-DMA crossing at 390/11 is not a cheapest-method boundary.
Keeps the comparison in CPU cycles and rejects wall-clock DMA-always-wins, a corrupted polling formula, and absorbing the tie integers into a strict regime.

commonErrors.description: Treats C_D or the other two models as wall-clock bus or device transfer time and concludes that DMA is cheapest for every B.
commonErrors.consequence: The CPU-cycle comparison, including polling's win on small B, is replaced by an unstated latency contest.

commonErrors.description: Uses a corrupted polling formula, takes 15 or 60 as a strict win, or uses the polling-DMA crossing as the DMA threshold.
commonErrors.consequence: The required ties at 15 and 60 and the interrupt window 16-59 are lost.

hintTree.content: $24B=180+12B$ rearranges to $12B=180$. $180+12B=780+2B$ rearranges to $10B=600$.
Check $B=14,15,16$ for polling versus interrupt and $B=59,60,61$ for interrupt versus DMA. Interrupt is already cheaper than both at $B=36$, where polling meets DMA.
DMA's $2B$ term is leftover CPU work, not the bus burst duration. A slow device can still free the processor.

ARCH:010526.canonicalSolution:
Pairwise roots. Setting $C_{\mathrm{P}}=C_{\mathrm{I}}$ gives
\[
24B=180+12B\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 12B=180\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad B=15.
\]
Setting $C_{\mathrm{I}}=C_{\mathrm{D}}$ gives
\[
180+12B=780+2B\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 10B=600\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad B=60.
\]
Adjacent integers:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
B&C_{\mathrm{P}}&C_{\mathrm{I}}&C_{\mathrm{D}}\\ \hline
14&336&348&808\\
15&360&360&810\\
16&384&372&812\\
59&1416&888&898\\
60&1440&900&900\\
61&1464&912&902.
\end{array}
\]
Thus polling is strictly cheapest for $1\le B\le 14$, polling and interrupt
tie at $B=15$ with cost $360$, interrupt is strictly cheapest for
$16\le B\le 59$, interrupt and DMA tie at $B=60$ with cost $900$, and DMA
is strictly cheapest for every integer $B\ge 61$. In short,
\[
\boxed{P=I\text{ at }15;\quad
I\text{ wins }16\text{--}59;\quad
I=D\text{ at }60;\quad
D\text{ wins }61+}.
\]

The unused crossing. Setting $C_{\mathrm{P}}=C_{\mathrm{D}}$ gives
\[
24B=780+2B\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 22B=780\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
B=\frac{390}{11}\approx 35.45.
\]
At the neighbouring integers,
\[
C_{\mathrm{I}}(35)=600<\min(840,850),\qquad
C_{\mathrm{I}}(36)=612<\min(864,852).
\]
Interrupt is already strictly cheaper than both, so the polling-DMA
crossing does not bound any cheapest-method regime.

Wall-clock versus occupancy. $C_{\mathrm{D}}(B)$ charges $780$ setup
cycles and $2$ cycles per byte of residual CPU work (for example
coherence or completion acknowledgement). The DMA engine may occupy the
bus for a longer wall-clock interval than a tight programmed loop. That
bus interval is not $C_{\mathrm{D}}$. For large $B$ the CPU is nonetheless
occupied for fewer cycles under DMA than under interrupt or polling, which
is why DMA wins the stated comparison for $B\ge 61$.

Claim (i) replaces CPU occupancy by an unstated wall-clock transfer time
and then concludes DMA wins for every $B$, contradicting the table at
$B\le 60$. Claim (ii) corrupts the polling model: the given occupancy is
$24B$, not $24+B$ and not a flat $24$. Claim (iii) moves the tie integers
into the neighbouring strict regimes. Equality at $15$ and at $60$ must
be reported as ties. The comparison never leaves the three CPU-cycle
formulae.

graderFixtures.proofText: $24B=180+12B$ at $B=15$ with cost $360$. $180+12B=780+2B$ at $B=60$ with cost $900$. Polling is strictly cheapest on $1\le B\le 14$, interrupt on $16\le B\le 59$, and DMA on $B\ge 61$. The polling-DMA root $390/11$ is unused because $C_{\mathrm{I}}$ is smaller there. The three formulae count CPU occupancy, not wall-clock bus time, so DMA is not automatically cheapest.
DMA runs the device in parallel with the CPU, so C_D is the wall-clock transfer time and is smaller than polling or interrupt for every B. The CPU is free after the 780-cycle setup.

Polling costs 24+B. Interrupt therefore beats polling as soon as B=15, and DMA beats interrupt as soon as B=60. Equivalently the DMA threshold is where polling meets DMA, B=390/11, so DMA wins for all B>=36.

ARCH:010527.title: A capacity-4 descriptor ring posts through wrap and publishes only after data
ARCH:010527.objective: Track monotonic producer and consumer indices on a four-slot descriptor ring, identify the leftover posted descriptor after a wrap-around post and a partial consume, and enforce descriptor/data release before doorbell together with completion release before CPU acquire.
ARCH:010527.statement:
A NIC and a CPU share a descriptor ring of capacity $N=4$. Producer and consumer indices $p$ and $c$ are unbounded monotonic integers. Slot $i\bmod 4$ holds the descriptor whose produce index is $i$. Occupancy is $p-c$. The ring is empty exactly when $p=c$ and full exactly when $p-c=4$. A post writes a new descriptor into slot $p\bmod 4$ and then increments $p$ by one. A consume reads the descriptor in slot $c\bmod 4$ and then increments $c$ by one. Descriptors are named by the produce index at the moment they are posted.

Initially $p=c=6$. The CPU then posts three descriptors and the device later consumes two of them.

Publication uses the following memory-order contract. Shared descriptor and payload memory is coherent after an explicit fence, and an MMIO doorbell is only a publication event, not a data path.

- CPU post: write the payload (if any), write the descriptor, issue a store-release or MMIO fence, then publish the new $p$ and/or ring the doorbell.
- Device consume: acquire-observe the published $p$ or doorbell, then read the descriptor and payload.
- Device complete: write completion status, issue a store-release, then publish the new $c$.
- CPU harvest: acquire-load the published $c$, then read the completion and reuse the slot.

1. Starting from $p=c=6$, execute the three posts. Report every slot written and the resulting $p$. Then execute the two consumes. Report the resulting $c$, the occupancy, and the unique leftover descriptor together with its slot.

2. Prove that the leftover descriptor is forced by the monotonic indices, not by wrapping $p$ and $c$ into $\{0,1,2,3\}$ as stored counters. In particular, show that reducing the initial pair modulo $4$ before posting would lose the identity of the leftover descriptor.

3. Suppose the CPU rings the doorbell after writing $p$ but before the descriptor and payload stores are visible to the device. Construct the stale-fetch failure. Then suppose the CPU reads a completion after seeing a new $c$ without an acquire. Construct the stale-completion failure.

4. Audit these claims: (i) any leftover after two consumes must sit in slot $2$ because that is where the first post went; (ii) a doorbell is itself a coherent copy of the descriptor; (iii) the point of the exercise is a precise interrupt retirement boundary in a five-stage pipeline. Do not replace the ring by a store-buffer squash or an $EPC$ restart argument.
permittedResults: If $p$ and $c$ increase by whole posts and consumes, the live produce indices are exactly $\{c,c+1,\dots,p-1\}$, and those descriptors occupy slots $c\bmod N,\dots,(p-1)\bmod N$.
A publication event does not transport data. Without a preceding release, an observer of the event may still read stale descriptor, payload, or completion state.

acceptableStrategies.description: List every live produce index after each post and consume, then map each index to a slot by i mod 4 only at the end.
Write the four-step post and complete protocols first, then break exactly one release or acquire to produce each stale-fetch witness.

milestones.criterion: Traces the three posts through slots 2,3,0 to p=9 and the two consumes to c=8 with descriptor 8 left in slot 0.
Keeps monotonic produce indices distinct from slot residues and exhibits both publish-before-release failures.
Rejects leftover-in-slot-2, doorbell-as-data, and precise-interrupt substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reduces p and c modulo 4 before naming descriptors, reports leftover descriptor 0, or claims the leftover sits in slot 2 because that was the first post.
commonErrors.consequence: The live produce index 8 is lost, so occupancy no longer identifies the posted work that the device has not consumed.

commonErrors.description: Rings the doorbell or publishes p before descriptor and payload are visible, or lets the CPU read a completion without acquiring the released c.
commonErrors.consequence: The device may fetch a stale descriptor, or the CPU may harvest a stale completion and reuse a still-live slot.

hintTree.content: The first free slot is $6\bmod 4=2$. Three posts therefore touch $2$, then $3$, then $0$, and leave $p=9$.
Two consumes advance $c$ from $6$ to $8$. The live produce indices are then $\{8\}$, so descriptor $8$ remains in slot $0$.
A doorbell seen before the descriptor stores is exactly a publish-before-release error; the device may fetch the previous occupant of that slot.

ARCH:010527.canonicalSolution:
Initially $p=c=6$, so the ring is empty and the next produce index is $6$. The three posts write
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{produce index}& \text{slot }i\bmod 4& p\text{ after post}\\ \hline
6&2&7\\
7&3&8\\
8&0&9.
\end{array}
\]
Thus the posts use slots $2,3,0$ and finish with $p=9$. Occupancy is $9-6=3$.

The two consumes read produce indices $6$ and $7$ from slots $2$ and $3$ and leave $c=8$. Occupancy is then $9-8=1$. The unique live produce index is $8$, which occupies slot $8\bmod 4=0$.
\[
\boxed{p=9,\ c=8,\ \text{descriptor }8\text{ in slot }0}.
\]

The leftover identity is the produce index $8$, not the residue $0$ alone. The live set is $\{c,\dots,p-1\}=\{8\}$ because $p$ and $c$ are monotonic. If the initial pair were first reduced modulo $4$ to $(p,c)=(2,2)$ and then treated as $2$-bit counters, three posts could be recorded as advancing a wrapped $p$ to $1$, two consumes as advancing a wrapped $c$ to $0$, and the leftover would be misnamed descriptor $0$ even though the architectural produce index is $8$. Slot arithmetic $i\bmod 4$ is only an addressing map; it does not replace the monotonic names.

If the CPU writes $p\leftarrow 9$ and rings the doorbell before the stores that fill descriptor $8$ and its payload are visible, the device may acquire the new $p$ and fetch slot $0$ while that slot still holds whatever previous descriptor or stale payload was last written there. The post has been published, but the posted work is not the work the CPU intended. If the device later writes completions for descriptors $6$ and $7$ and publishes $c\leftarrow 8$ without a release, or the CPU observes $c=8$ and reads those completions without an acquire, the CPU may harvest stale completion words and reuse slots $2$ and $3$ before the completion stores are visible. Slot $0$ remains occupied by live descriptor $8$ and is not made reusable by $c=8$.

Claim (i) confuses the first posted slot with the leftover live index: slots $2$ and $3$ were consumed. Claim (ii) treats a doorbell as a data copy; the doorbell is only a publication event after a release of descriptor and payload. Claim (iii) is the held precise-interrupt packet. The present state is a ring occupancy and fence order, not a five-stage retirement prefix, $EPC$, or store-buffer squash.

graderFixtures.proofText: From p=c=6 the three posts write produce indices 6,7,8 into slots 2,3,0 and leave p=9. Two consumes advance c to 8 and leave descriptor 8 in slot 0. Wrapping the indices into 2-bit counters before naming descriptors would mislabel that leftover as descriptor 0. Descriptor and payload stores must release before the doorbell; completion stores must release before the CPU acquires c. A doorbell is not a copy of the descriptor. This is not a precise-interrupt retirement exercise.

Reduce the initial pair modulo 4 to p=c=2. Three posts wrap p to 1 and two consumes wrap c to 0, so the leftover is descriptor 0. Alternatively the leftover must still be in slot 2 because that is where posting began.

The CPU may write p=9 and ring the doorbell immediately; the doorbell itself makes the new descriptors visible. The CPU may also read completions as soon as it sees a larger c, with no acquire, because coherent memory already contains the status.

ARCH:010528.title: A nonpreemptive round-robin bus grants M0 then M1 then M2 and needs bounded bursts
ARCH:010528.objective: Schedule one nonpreemptive round-robin grant sequence from M0, compute the three wait times and their average, and prove that three masters with a 3-cycle burst cap have next-grant wait at most 6, which fails if bursts are unbounded.
ARCH:010528.statement:
A shared bus has three masters $M_0,M_1,M_2$ and a nonpreemptive round-robin arbiter. A grant, once given, is held for the entire requested burst. The arbiter's pointer starts at $M_0$. All three masters request at time $0$ with burst lengths $3,2,1$ cycles respectively. Time is discrete and grants occupy half-open intervals of cycles.

1. Give the grant intervals. For each master report the wait from time $0$ until its grant begins. Compute the average wait.

2. Now consider the same three masters, still nonpreemptive and still round-robin, but every burst length is at most $3$ cycles. Prove that a master that has already requested has next-grant wait at most $6$ cycles, measured from the moment it is not the current grantee until its next grant begins.

3. Drop the burst bound, keeping nonpreemptive round-robin. Exhibit a finite request pattern in which some already-requesting master's next-grant wait exceeds $6$, and explain why no finite wait bound survives.

4. Audit these claims: (i) the arbiter should preempt after one cycle, so the grants are $M_0[0,1)$, $M_1[1,2)$, $M_2[2,3)$; (ii) the average wait is $3+2+1=6$; (iii) the point of the exercise is a precise interrupt retirement or a five-stage squash. Do not replace the bus schedule by an $EPC$ prefix.
permittedResults: Under round-robin, the masters other than a given requester are served at most once each before that requester's next grant.
A wait bound that is a multiple of a burst cap becomes false as soon as some burst is allowed to be arbitrarily long.

acceptableStrategies.description: Draw the occupied half-open intervals in pointer order, then read each wait as the start of that master's interval.
Bound a requester's wait by one pass over the other masters, then replace the burst cap by an arbitrary B to destroy the bound.

milestones.criterion: Reports grants M0[0,3), M1[3,5), M2[5,6), waits 0,3,5, and average 8/3.
Proves next-grant wait at most 6 from two other max-3 bursts, and exhibits unbounded wait without a burst cap.
Rejects preemptive slicing, burst-sum averages, and interrupt-retirement substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Preempts after one cycle, starts with a master other than M0, or reports grant intervals other than M0[0,3), M1[3,5), M2[5,6).
commonErrors.consequence: The nonpreemptive round-robin chart is replaced by a different arbiter, so the waits 0,3,5 and average 8/3 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims next-grant wait remains at most 6 even if bursts are unbounded, or treats the bound as a property of round-robin alone.
commonErrors.consequence: A single long nonpreemptive burst can stall the other masters for an arbitrary time, so the wait theorem is false.

hintTree.content: Start at $M_0$ and do not preempt: the first grant occupies three cycles, so $M_1$ cannot start before time $3$.
After $M_0$ and $M_1$ have each been served at most once, at most $3+3=6$ cycles have elapsed before $M_2$ can be granted.
If any burst may be $7$ cycles, the other masters already wait more than $6$ while that burst runs.

ARCH:010528.canonicalSolution:
All three request at time $0$ and the pointer starts at $M_0$. Because the grant is nonpreemptive, $M_0$ keeps the bus for its whole $3$-cycle burst:
\[
M_0\text{ holds }[0,3),\qquad M_1\text{ waits }3.
\]
The pointer then moves to $M_1$, which holds for $2$ cycles:
\[
M_1\text{ holds }[3,5),\qquad M_2\text{ waits }5.
\]
Finally $M_2$ holds its $1$-cycle burst:
\[
M_2\text{ holds }[5,6).
\]
The waits from time $0$ are $0,3,5$. Their average is
\[
\frac{0+3+5}{3}=\frac{8}{3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{M_0[0,3),\ M_1[3,5),\ M_2[5,6);\ \text{waits }0,3,5;\ \text{avg }8/3}.
\]

Now every burst is at most $3$ cycles. A requesting master $M$ that is not the current grantee waits only for the remaining current burst, if any, and then for each of the other masters that stand ahead of $M$ in the present round-robin order. There are only two other masters, and each is served at most once before $M$'s next grant, each for at most $3$ cycles. Hence the wait until $M$'s next grant begins is at most $3+3=6$. The bound is tight: if $M_0$ and $M_1$ each take a full $3$-cycle burst, then $M_2$'s next-grant wait is $6$.

If bursts are unbounded, let $M_0$ request a $7$-cycle burst at time $0$ while $M_1$ is already requesting. Nonpreemptive service gives $M_0$ the interval $[0,7)$, so $M_1$'s next-grant wait is $7>6$. The same construction with burst length $B$ yields wait $B$ for every other master. No finite wait bound exists without a burst cap.

Claim (i) replaces the stated nonpreemptive arbiter by a $1$-cycle time-slicer and is therefore a different schedule. Claim (ii) adds burst lengths instead of averaging the three waits. Claim (iii) is the held interrupt-retirement packet; the present object is a bus grant chart, not a precise $EPC$ prefix.

graderFixtures.proofText: Nonpreemptive RR from M0 grants M0[0,3), M1[3,5), M2[5,6). Waits are 0,3,5 and the average is 8/3. With three masters and a 3-cycle burst cap, a requester waits for at most the other two bursts, hence at most 6 cycles. A 7-cycle burst already forces some next-grant wait above 6, so the bound needs the burst cap. One-cycle preemption is a different arbiter. This is not a precise-interrupt retirement chart.

The arbiter should give each master one cycle at a time, so the grants are M0[0,1), M1[1,2), M2[2,3), then M0 again. Alternatively start with M1 because its burst is shorter. The waits are therefore 0,1,2.
Round-robin itself guarantees fairness, so next-grant wait is at most 6 even if some master holds the bus for 100 cycles. The burst cap is only a performance hint, not part of the wait proof.

ARCH:010629.title: Roofline time is the max of a compute ceiling and a bandwidth ceiling
ARCH:010629.objective: Compute the ridge point of a 200 GFLOP/s, 50 GB/s machine, classify intensities 0.5 and 6, and bound two kernel times by min attainable performance / max of the two ceilings, without mixing the bounds and without invoking Amdahl's serial fraction.
ARCH:010629.statement:
A machine has peak floating-point performance $\pi=200\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s}$ and peak DRAM bandwidth $\beta=50\ \mathrm{GB/s}$. Arithmetic intensity is $I=W/Q$ in $\mathrm{FLOP/B}$, where $W$ is work in floating-point operations and $Q$ is DRAM traffic in bytes. Attainable performance is
\[
P=\min(\pi,I\beta),
\]
and a lower bound on running time is
\[
T\ge\max\!\left(\frac{W}{\pi},\frac{Q}{\beta}\right)=\frac{W}{P}.
\]
The ridge point is $I_\star=\pi/\beta$. Use these two ceilings consistently: never add the two times, and never replace $P$ by $\max(\pi,I\beta)$.

1. Compute $I_\star$. For a kernel with $I=0.5\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}$, give $P$ and classify the kernel as compute-bound or memory-bound.

2. That same kernel performs $W=1\ \mathrm{GFLOP}$ of work and moves $Q=2\ \mathrm{GB}$. Bound its running time from below.

3. A second kernel performs the same $W=1\ \mathrm{GFLOP}$ at intensity $I=6\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}$. Classify it, give $P$, and bound its running time from below. Confirm that the two ceilings are consistent with the stated $P$.

4. Audit these claims: (i) $I=0.5$ still runs at $200\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s}$ because that is the peak; (ii) the two ceilings should be added, so the first kernel takes at least $45\ \mathrm{ms}$; (iii) the bound is Amdahl's law with the held serial fraction $1-p=0.08$ and coordination overhead $h(N)$. Do not rederive that Amdahl fraction, and do not convert the ridge into a speedup-versus-$N$ plot.
permittedResults: $W/\pi$ and $Q/\beta$ are simultaneously attainable only in the weak sense that hardware cannot beat either resource. The realized time is therefore at least their maximum, not their sum, unless both resources are fully consumed in disjoint phases by a stated schedule.
Arithmetic intensity is a property of a kernel's work-to-traffic ratio. It is not a parallel fraction and does not determine an Amdahl $N$-core speedup by itself.

acceptableStrategies.description: Locate I relative to the ridge first, read P from the nearer roof, then check T>=W/P against max(W/pi, Q/beta).
Keep a two-column table of compute time and memory time for each kernel and always take the larger entry.

milestones.criterion: Computes ridge 4 FLOP/B and the memory-bound cap 25 GFLOP/s at intensity 0.5.
Bounds the 1 GFLOP / 2 GB kernel by 40 ms and the intensity-6 kernel by 5 ms using min P / max time.
Rejects peak-for-memory-bound, added ceilings, and Amdahl-fraction substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Assigns 200 GFLOP/s to the I=0.5 kernel, or reports T>=5 ms for the 1 GFLOP / 2 GB kernel because that is W/pi.
commonErrors.consequence: The bandwidth roof is ignored, so a memory-bound kernel is treated as if it ran at peak.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two ceilings to get 45 ms, replaces min by max on performance, or imports the held Amdahl serial fraction 0.08 and overhead h(N).
commonErrors.consequence: The roofline bound is replaced by an undeclared sum or by a different performance law.

hintTree.content: $I_\star=200/50=4\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}$. Intensity $0.5$ lies below the ridge.
For $W=1\ \mathrm{GFLOP}$ and $Q=2\ \mathrm{GB}$, $Q/\beta=2/50=0.040\ \mathrm{s}$ while $W/\pi=5\ \mathrm{ms}$.
At $I=6>4$ the bandwidth ceiling is $W/(I\beta)=1/300\ \mathrm{s}<5\ \mathrm{ms}$, so the compute ceiling dominates.

ARCH:010629.canonicalSolution:
The ridge is
\[
I_\star=\frac{\pi}{\beta}=\frac{200}{50}=4\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}.
\]
For $I=0.5<4$,
\[
P=\min(200,0.5\cdot 50)=\min(200,25)=25\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s}.
\]
The kernel is memory-bound.
\[
\boxed{I_\star=4\ \mathrm{FLOP/B},\ P=25\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s}}.
\]

With $W=1\ \mathrm{GFLOP}$ and $Q=2\ \mathrm{GB}$ the two ceilings are
\[
\frac{W}{\pi}=\frac{1}{200}\ \mathrm{s}=5\ \mathrm{ms},\qquad
\frac{Q}{\beta}=\frac{2}{50}\ \mathrm{s}=40\ \mathrm{ms}.
\]
Hence
\[
T\ge\max(5,40)=40\ \mathrm{ms},
\]
which matches $W/P=1/25\ \mathrm{s}=40\ \mathrm{ms}$. Adding the ceilings would invent an undeclared two-phase schedule and is forbidden by the statement.
\[
\boxed{T\ge 40\ \mathrm{ms}}.
\]

For the second kernel, $I=6>4$, so it is compute-bound and $P=200\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s}$. The implied traffic is $Q=W/I=1/6\ \mathrm{GB}$. The ceilings are
\[
\frac{W}{\pi}=5\ \mathrm{ms},\qquad
\frac{Q}{\beta}=\frac{1/6}{50}\ \mathrm{s}=\frac{1}{300}\ \mathrm{s}\approx 3.333\ \mathrm{ms}.
\]
Thus $T\ge\max(5,3.333)=5\ \mathrm{ms}=W/P$.
\[
\boxed{I=6\text{ compute-bound},\ P=200\ \mathrm{GFLOP/s},\ T\ge 5\ \mathrm{ms}}.
\]

Claim (i) replaces $\min$ by the peak and would incorrectly report $T\ge 5\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the memory-bound kernel. Claim (ii) adds the ceilings. Claim (iii) is the held Amdahl packet: no serial fraction, coordination $h(N)$, or core count is supplied here, and none is to be imported.

graderFixtures.proofText: Ridge I*=200/50=4 FLOP/B. Intensity 0.5 is memory-bound with P=min(200,25)=25 GFLOP/s. For 1 GFLOP and 2 GB, T>=max(5 ms,40 ms)=40 ms=W/P. Intensity 6 is compute-bound at 200 GFLOP/s, and the same 1 GFLOP has T>=max(5 ms, 1/300 s)=5 ms. Do not add the ceilings and do not use the peak below the ridge. This is not the held Amdahl latency/throughput packet.
Peak is 200 GFLOP/s, so both kernels run at 200 GFLOP/s. The 1 GFLOP kernel therefore takes 1/200 s=5 ms even when it moves 2 GB, because bandwidth is a separate issue from performance.

A kernel must pay both ceilings, so T>=5 ms+40 ms=45 ms. Equivalently this is Amdahl with serial fraction 0.08 and the held coordination overhead h(N)=0.2(N-1) ms, which already supplies the true bound.
