ARCH:010630.title: False sharing ping-pongs one MESI line without being a data race
ARCH:010630.objective: Trace four alternating writes to two variables that share one MESI line, count BusUpgr, BusRdX, invalidations, and cache-to-cache line transfers, and separate false sharing from a race and from a compulsory-miss AMAT exercise.
ARCH:010630.statement:
Two processors $C_0$ and $C_1$ implement MESI on a single cache line that currently holds both variables $x$ and $y$. Initially both caches hold that line in state $S$. Writes use these bus transactions:

- a write by a cache that already has $S$ issues $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$; every other $S$ copy invalidates; the writer becomes $M$; no data are transferred;
- a write by a cache in $I$ issues $\mathrm{BusRdX}$; the current $M$ owner, if any, supplies the full line (cache-to-cache) and becomes $I$; the writer becomes $M$.

Memory is not the supplier whenever a cache holds $M$. Count one invalidation for each cache that leaves $S$ or $M$ for $I$ on a transaction.

The processors then perform four writes in this order, each to the named variable only:
\[
C_0{:}x,\quad C_1{:}y,\quad C_0{:}x,\quad C_1{:}y.
\]

1. For each write, give the transaction, the data-transfer count, the caches that invalidate, and the MESI pair $(C_0,C_1)$ immediately afterwards.

2. Total the $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$ count, the $\mathrm{BusRdX}$ count, the invalidations, and the full-line transfers. Report the final pair $(C_0,C_1)$.

3. Explain why padding $x$ and $y$ onto distinct lines removes the ping-pong. Explain why the original four writes are not a data race: each variable is written by only one processor, and the coherence problem is the shared line, not a conflicting access to one address.

4. Audit these claims: (i) the first write is already a $\mathrm{BusRdX}$ with a line transfer because a write always fetches; (ii) false sharing is a race, so the program is undefined; (iii) the point of the exercise is to classify compulsory, conflict, and capacity misses and compute a read-only AMAT. Do not replace the coherence trace by a three-C witness string.
permittedResults: In MESI, a writer that already holds S need not refetch the line; upgrade plus invalidation is enough.
A data race requires conflicting accesses to one memory location. Distinct locations in one line can still generate coherence traffic.

acceptableStrategies.description: Update a two-cache MESI pair after every write, issuing BusUpgr only from S and BusRdX only from I.
Count transactions, invalidations, and transfers in separate columns so an upgrade is not silently turned into a data fetch.

milestones.criterion: Traces the four writes as BusUpgr then three BusRdX with states (M,I), (I,M), (M,I), (I,M).
Totals 1 BusUpgr, 3 BusRdX, 4 invalidations, 3 transfers, and final C1 M / C0 I, and explains padding.
Rejects first-write-as-BusRdX, false-sharing-as-race, and three-C AMAT substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the first write as BusRdX, reports 4 BusRdX, or counts 4 full-line transfers because every write is assumed to fetch the line.
commonErrors.consequence: The Shared upgrade path is erased, so the transaction and transfer totals no longer match the stated MESI rules.

commonErrors.description: Calls the four writes a data race, claims the program is undefined, or says padding cannot remove the ping-pong because the accesses still conflict.
commonErrors.consequence: A line-granularity coherence cost is misidentified as a conflicting access to one variable.

hintTree.content: The first write is $C_0$ in $S$, so it is $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$ and $C_1$ goes $S\to I$.
Each later writer is in $I$ and the other cache holds $M$, so each of the last three writes is a cache-to-cache $\mathrm{BusRdX}$.
Padding puts $x$ and $y$ on different lines, so each cache can remain $M$ on its own line.

ARCH:010630.canonicalSolution:
Initially both caches are $S$.

Write $C_0{:}x$. $C_0$ has $S$, so the transaction is $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$. $C_1$ invalidates $S\to I$. No line is transferred. States become $(M,I)$.

Write $C_1{:}y$. $C_1$ has $I$, so the transaction is $\mathrm{BusRdX}$. $C_0$ owns $M$, supplies the full line, and goes to $I$. One transfer. States become $(I,M)$.

Write $C_0{:}x$. $C_0$ has $I$, so $\mathrm{BusRdX}$. $C_1$ supplies the line and goes to $I$. One transfer. States become $(M,I)$.

Write $C_1{:}y$. $C_1$ has $I$, so $\mathrm{BusRdX}$. $C_0$ supplies the line and goes to $I$. One transfer. States become $(I,M)$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{write}&\text{txn}&\text{xfers}&\text{inv.}&\text{states}\\ \hline
C_0{:}x&\mathrm{BusUpgr}&0&C_1&(M,I)\\
C_1{:}y&\mathrm{BusRdX}&1&C_0&(I,M)\\
C_0{:}x&\mathrm{BusRdX}&1&C_1&(M,I)\\
C_1{:}y&\mathrm{BusRdX}&1&C_0&(I,M).
\end{array}
\]
Totals: $1$ $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$, $3$ $\mathrm{BusRdX}$, $4$ invalidations, $3$ full-line transfers. Final pair is $C_1=M$, $C_0=I$.
\[
\boxed{1\ \mathrm{BusUpgr}+3\ \mathrm{BusRdX},\ 4\ \mathrm{inv.},\ 3\ \mathrm{xfers},\ (I,M)}.
\]

If $x$ and $y$ are padded onto distinct lines, $C_0$'s first write upgrades only the line that contains $x$, and $C_1$'s writes never touch that line. Each cache can remain $M$ on its own line; the three cache-to-cache transfers disappear.

The four writes are not a data race. $C_0$ writes only $x$ and $C_1$ writes only $y$. There is no pair of conflicting accesses to one address. The pathology is coherence traffic on a shared line.

Claim (i) erases $\mathrm{BusUpgr}$ and would invent a fourth transfer. Claim (ii) confuses false sharing with a race. Claim (iii) is the held three-C / AMAT packet; no compulsory/conflict/capacity string or read-only AMAT is asked.

graderFixtures.proofText: Start from (S,S). C0:x is BusUpgr, C1 invalidates, states (M,I), no transfer. Each later write is BusRdX from I against an M owner, so three cache-to-cache transfers and four invalidations in all. Totals: 1 BusUpgr, 3 BusRdX, final (I,M). Padding x and y onto different lines stops the ping-pong. The writes touch different addresses, so this is false sharing, not a race, and not a three-C AMAT witness.
Every write needs exclusive data, so the first write is already BusRdX and transfers the line from memory. The four writes therefore produce 4 BusRdX and 4 full-line transfers. BusUpgr is never used.
C0 and C1 both write the same cache line, so the program has a data race and is undefined. Padding cannot help because the two processors still race on the line.

ARCH:010631.title: A 1024-value binary reduction is span 10 but 36 cycles and memory bound
ARCH:010631.objective: Compute work and span of a 1024-input binary reduction, schedule it on 32 add-per-cycle workers by tree level, and compare 18 ns of compute at 2 GHz with 128.125 ns of traffic at 64 GB/s without importing the held Amdahl fraction.
ARCH:010631.statement:
A pairwise binary reduction sums $n=1024$ independent values. Each internal node is one addition. Unlimited parallelism would execute the tree by levels; the span is the number of levels. Work is the number of additions.

Thirty-two workers are available. Each worker performs at most one addition per cycle, and a value produced at one level is available only at the next level. Level $k$ therefore costs $\lceil a_k/32\rceil$ cycles, where $a_k$ is the number of additions at that level.

Traffic is $8200\ \mathrm{B}$: the $1024$ eight-byte inputs together with one eight-byte write of the result. Off-chip bandwidth is $64\ \mathrm{GB/s}$. The clock is $2\ \mathrm{GHz}$.

1. Compute the work and the span.

2. List the ten level costs under the $32$-worker constraint and sum them.

3. Convert the scheduled cycle count to a compute time at $2\ \mathrm{GHz}$. Convert the $8200\ \mathrm{B}$ traffic to a memory time at $64\ \mathrm{GB/s}$. Decide whether the reduction is compute-bound or memory-bound on this machine.

4. Audit these claims: (i) $32$ workers make the scheduled time equal to the span $10$; (ii) $T$ is the sum of compute time and memory time, or else compute dominates because $18\ \mathrm{ns}$ is the critical path; (iii) the bound is the held Amdahl law with serial fraction $0.08$ and overhead $h(N)=0.200(N-1)\ \mathrm{ms}$. Do not rederive that Amdahl fraction, and do not replace the tree schedule by a speedup-versus-$N$ plot.
permittedResults: Work$/P$ is only a lower bound. A level-synchronous reduction of $1024$ values still pays one cycle for every level that has fewer than $P$ additions.
A kernel is memory-bound when the traffic time at peak bandwidth exceeds the scheduled compute time at peak issue rate. That comparison is not an Amdahl serial-fraction argument.

acceptableStrategies.description: Halve the addition count at every level, take ceil(a/32), and add the ten integers before converting to nanoseconds.
Compare the two resource times directly and keep Amdahl's serial-fraction formula out of the argument.

milestones.criterion: Computes work 1023, span 10, and the ten level costs that sum to 36 cycles.
Converts 36 cycles to 18 ns and 8200 B at 64 GB/s to 128.125 ns, and concludes memory-bound.
Rejects span-as-schedule, compute-dominated or added-time substitutes, and the held Amdahl fraction.

commonErrors.description: Reports that 32 workers execute the reduction in 10 cycles because the span is 10, or omits the 16-cycle first level.
commonErrors.consequence: The width-limited prefix of the tree is ignored, so the cycle count is no longer 36 and the 18 ns compute time is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the reduction is compute-bound, adds 18 ns to 128.125 ns as a required sum, or imports the held Amdahl serial fraction 0.08 and overhead h(N).
commonErrors.consequence: The larger memory ceiling is discarded, or a different performance law is substituted for the traffic comparison.

hintTree.content: The first level has $512$ additions, so it costs $512/32=16$ cycles. The next three finite full-width levels cost $8,4,2$.
Once $a_k\le 32$, every remaining level costs $1$ cycle. There are six such levels.
$8200/64=128.125$, and a $2\ \mathrm{GHz}$ cycle is $0.5\ \mathrm{ns}$, so $36$ cycles are $18\ \mathrm{ns}$.

ARCH:010631.canonicalSolution:
A pairwise tree on $1024=2^{10}$ values has
\[
W=1023\text{ additions},\qquad D=\log_2 1024=10.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{work }1023,\ \text{span }10}.
\]

The level addition counts are $512,256,128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1$. With $P=32$,
\[
\left\lceil\frac{512}{32}\right\rceil=16,
8,\ 4,\ 2,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1.
\]
The scheduled time is
\[
16+8+4+2+1+1+1+1+1+1=36
\]
cycles. The last six levels each cost one cycle even though they underfill the $32$ workers; span $10$ is therefore not the scheduled time.

At $2\ \mathrm{GHz}$ one cycle is $0.5\ \mathrm{ns}$, so compute time is
\[
36\times 0.5\ \mathrm{ns}=18\ \mathrm{ns}.
\]
Traffic time is
\[
\frac{8200\ \mathrm{B}}{64\ \mathrm{GB/s}}
=\frac{8200}{64}\ \mathrm{ns}
=128.125\ \mathrm{ns}.
\]
Because $128.125>18$, the reduction is memory-bound.
\[
\boxed{36\text{ cycles},\ 18\ \mathrm{ns}\text{ compute},\ 128.125\ \mathrm{ns}\text{ memory}}.
\]

Claim (i) confuses span with a $P$-worker schedule. Claim (ii) either adds the two resource times without a stated two-phase occupancy or else ignores the larger memory ceiling. Claim (iii) is the held Amdahl packet. No serial fraction $0.08$, coordination $h(N)$, or core-count latency minimization is supplied or required.

graderFixtures.proofText: Work is 1023 adds and span is 10. With 32 workers the levels cost 16,8,4,2,1,1,1,1,1,1 cycles, totaling 36. At 2 GHz that is 18 ns. Traffic 8200 B at 64 GB/s is 128.125 ns, so the kernel is memory-bound. Span 10 is not the scheduled time. Do not import the held Amdahl fraction 0.08 or h(N).

The span is 10 and 32 workers exceed the width of every level after the first few, so the reduction finishes in 10 cycles. The 16-cycle accounting of the 512-add level is unnecessary because those adds are embarrassingly parallel.
Compute is the critical path, so the reduction is compute-bound at 18 ns. Alternatively T=18+128.125 ns, which is just Amdahl with serial fraction 0.08 and the held overhead h(N)=0.2(N-1) ms.

CONT:010117.title: Incompressible plane-strain annulus 1<=R<=2: r=sqrt(R^2+3), lambdas (R/r,r/R,1), J=1, radii 2 and sqrt(7), areas 3pi, rho=rho0
CONT:010117.objective: From the plane-strain map r=sqrt(R^2+3), Theta map, z=Z on the annulus 1<=R<=2, recover the principal stretches, the Jacobian J=1, the deformed radii 2 and sqrt(7), the endpoint stretch triples, the equal reference and deformed areas 3pi, and the density identity rho=rho0.
CONT:010117.statement:
A circular annulus occupies the reference region
\[
1\le R\le 2,\qquad 0\le\Theta<2\pi,\qquad Z\in\mathbb{R}
\]
in cylindrical coordinates $(R,\Theta,Z)$. The body is deformed by
the plane-strain inflation
\[
r=\sqrt{R^2+3},\qquad \theta=\Theta,\qquad z=Z.
\]

1. Compute the principal stretches $\lambda_r=\partial r/\partial R$,
   $\lambda_\theta=r/R$, and $\lambda_z=\partial z/\partial Z$. Prove
   that
   \[
   \lambda_r=\frac{R}{r},\qquad
   \lambda_\theta=\frac{r}{R},\qquad
   \lambda_z=1,
   \]
   and that the Jacobian is $J=\lambda_r\lambda_\theta\lambda_z=1$.

2. Evaluate the deformed inner and outer radii and the stretches at
   the two edges: prove $r(1)=2$ and $r(2)=\sqrt7$, and
   \[
   (\lambda_r,\lambda_\theta,\lambda_z)\Big|_{R=1}
   =\Bigl(\tfrac12,\,2,\,1\Bigr),\qquad
   (\lambda_r,\lambda_\theta,\lambda_z)\Big|_{R=2}
   =\Bigl(\tfrac{2}{\sqrt7},\,\tfrac{\sqrt7}{2},\,1\Bigr).
   \]

3. Compute the reference and deformed annular areas (per unit
   thickness) and prove that both equal $3\pi$. Using mass balance
   $\rho_0=\rho J$, deduce $\rho=\rho_0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $r>R$, every stretch is
   greater than $1$, so $\lambda_r=r/R$ and $J=r^2/R^2>1$”; (ii)
   “the deformed area is $\pi(7-1)=6\pi$, or density must drop
   because the outer radius grew, or this is a polar-decomposition /
   objective-strain exercise.”

Do not replace the calculation by a polar decomposition of $F$, an
objective strain measure, or a compressible radial map with $J\not=1$.
permittedResults: If $r=\sqrt{R^2+c}$ with constant $c$, then $\partial r/\partial R=R/r$ and $(R/r)(r/R)=1$. Plane strain forces $\lambda_z=1$, so $J=1$.
The area of an annulus of inner radius $a$ and outer radius $b$ is $\pi(b^2-a^2)$. Here $2^2-1^2=7-4=3$, so both configurations have area $3\pi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate r=sqrt(R^2+3) in the polar basis, multiply the three stretches, then evaluate at the two edges.
Check global area equality pi((R_out)^2-(R_in)^2)=pi((r_out)^2-(r_in)^2) as an independent confirmation of J=1, then read density from rho_0=rho J.

milestones.criterion: Computes the principal stretches (R/r, r/R, 1) and the Jacobian J=1.
Records the deformed radii 2 and sqrt(7), the two edge stretch triples, the common area 3pi, and rho=rho0.
Refuses the hoop-for-radial swap and does not replace the map by a polar-decomposition exercise.

commonErrors.description: Sets lambda_r=r/R because r>R, or reports J=r^2/R^2>1, treating every fibre as extended.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned incompressible product J=1 and the compressive radial stretch R/r are lost.

commonErrors.description: Computes the deformed area as pi(7-1)=6pi, or claims rho<rho0 because the outer radius grew.
commonErrors.consequence: The equal areas 3pi and the identity rho=rho0 are lost.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $r=(R^2+3)^{1/2}$ to get $\partial r/\partial R=R/r$. Circumferential stretch is the hoop ratio $r/R$, not $\partial r/\partial R$.
At $R=1$, $r=2$. At $R=2$, $r=\sqrt7$. The product of the first two stretches is identically $1$.
Reference area $\pi(4-1)=3\pi$. Deformed area $\pi(7-4)=3\pi$. Then $\rho=\rho_0/J=\rho_0$.

CONT:010117.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the assigned radial law:
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial R}
=\frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+3}}
=\frac{R}{r}.
\]
The hoop stretch of a circumferential fibre is the ratio of current
to reference radius, $r/R$. Plane strain gives $\partial z/\partial Z=1$.
Thus
\[
\lambda_r=\frac{R}{r},\qquad
\lambda_\theta=\frac{r}{R},\qquad
\lambda_z=1.
\]
The Jacobian in this orthonormal principal basis is the product
\[
J=\lambda_r\lambda_\theta\lambda_z
=\frac{R}{r}\cdot\frac{r}{R}\cdot 1
=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lambda_r=R/r,\quad\lambda_\theta=r/R,\quad\lambda_z=1,\quad J=1}.
\]

The deformed edges are
\[
r(1)=\sqrt{1+3}=2,\qquad r(2)=\sqrt{4+3}=\sqrt7.
\]
Substituting these radii,
\[
R=1:\quad
\Bigl(\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{2}{1},\,1\Bigr)
=\Bigl(\frac12,\,2,\,1\Bigr),
\]
\[
R=2:\quad
\Bigl(\frac{2}{\sqrt7},\,\frac{\sqrt7}{2},\,1\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{r(1)=2,\quad r(2)=\sqrt7}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R=1:\ (1/2,2,1);\quad R=2:\ (2/\sqrt7,\sqrt7/2,1)}.
\]

The reference annular area (per unit thickness) is
\[
\pi(2^2-1^2)=\pi(4-1)=3\pi.
\]
The deformed annular area is
\[
\pi\bigl((\sqrt7)^2-2^2\bigr)=\pi(7-4)=3\pi.
\]
Mass balance $\rho_0=\rho J$ with $J=1$ yields $\rho=\rho_0$ at every
particle. The common area $3\pi$ is the global counterpart of $J=1$.
\[
\boxed{\text{areas }=3\pi,\quad\rho=\rho_0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\lambda_r$ by the hoop stretch $r/R$. That
makes every stretch appear expansive, produces the false Jacobian
$J=r^2/R^2>1$, and contradicts both the chain rule and
incompressibility. Sentence (ii) computes a deformed area from the
wrong outer-minus-unit difference $7-1$, or claims that growth of
the outer radius forces a density drop, or else replaces the
exercise by a polar-decomposition / objective-strain argument,
which is not asked.

The argument never factors $F=RU$, never introduces an objective
rate, and never treats a compressible radial law.

graderFixtures.proofText: Stretches $\lambda_r=R/r$, $\lambda_\theta=r/R$, $\lambda_z=1$ and $J=1$. Deformed radii $2$ and $\sqrt7$. At $R=1$ the stretches are $(1/2,2,1)$; at $R=2$ they are $(2/\sqrt7,\sqrt7/2,1)$. Both areas equal $3\pi$ and $\rho=\rho_0$.
Because r>R every stretch is greater than 1, so I set lambda_r=r/R and conclude J=r^2/R^2>1.
The outer radius grew from 2 to sqrt(7), so the deformed area is pi(7-1)=6pi and the density must drop below rho0.

CONT:010118.title: Compatible F=[[1+2X1,2X2],[X2,X1+2]] on [0,1/2]^2: x=(X1+X1^2+X2^2,X1 X2+2X2), J>=3/2, at (1/2,1/2) x=(1,5/4) and J=9/2
CONT:010118.objective: Verify row-wise compatibility of the assigned F, integrate the motion through x(0)=0, prove J=(1+2X1)(X1+2)-2X2^2>=3/2 on the square, evaluate the motion and F at (1/2,1/2), and exhibit the unit incompatibility of the counterfeit entry F12=2X2+X1.
CONT:010118.statement:
On the closed square $\Omega=[0,1/2]^2$ a candidate deformation
gradient is prescribed in Cartesian components
\[
F
=\begin{pmatrix}
1+2X_1 & 2X_2 \\
X_2 & X_1+2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
together with the placement condition $x(0)=0$.

1. Check the two row-compatibility identities
   $\partial F_{11}/\partial X_2=\partial F_{12}/\partial X_1$ and
   $\partial F_{21}/\partial X_2=\partial F_{22}/\partial X_1$.
   Integrate $F=\mathrm{Grad}\,x$ with $x(0)=0$ and prove
   \[
   x=(X_1+X_1^2+X_2^2,\; X_1 X_2+2X_2).
   \]

2. Compute $J=\det F=(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)-2X_2^2$ and prove $J\ge 3/2$
   throughout $\Omega$.

3. Evaluate the motion and the tensor at the corner
   $(X_1,X_2)=(1/2,1/2)$ and prove
   \[
   x=(1,5/4),\qquad
   F=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1/2&5/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   J=9/2.
   \]

4. Now replace the $(1,2)$ entry by the counterfeit
   $F_{12}=2X_2+X_1$. Prove that the first-row compatibility defect
   equals $1$. Audit both sentences: (i) “any $C^1$ matrix field is
   a deformation gradient, so the counterfeit $F$ is equally
   admissible”; (ii) “the lower bound on $J$ is $2$, or this is a
   polar-decomposition / objective-strain calculation.”

Do not replace the compatibility test by a polar factorization, and
do not treat $F$ as an independent constitutive variable.
permittedResults: On a simply connected domain, a curl-free $C^1$ row integrates path-independently. The constant of integration is fixed by $x(0)=0$.
If the $(1,2)$ entry is replaced by $2X_2+X_1$, then $\partial F_{12}/\partial X_1-\partial F_{11}/\partial X_2=1$, so no $C^2$ placement exists.

acceptableStrategies.description: Check mixed partials row by row, then integrate from the origin and match the off-diagonal entries.
Bound (1+2X1)(X1+2) from below by 2 and 2X2^2 from above by 1/2, and evaluate the assigned corner by direct substitution.

milestones.criterion: Verifies row compatibility and reconstructs x=(X1+X1^2+X2^2, X1 X2+2X2).
Proves J>=3/2 on the square and evaluates x=(1,5/4), F=[[2,1],[1/2,5/2]], J=9/2 at (1/2,1/2).
Exhibits the unit defect of the counterfeit F12 and refuses a polar-decomposition reading.

commonErrors.description: Accepts F12=2X2+X1 as a deformation gradient, or claims every C^1 matrix field is Grad x.
commonErrors.consequence: The unit compatibility defect is ignored and no placement exists for the counterfeit tensor.

commonErrors.description: Reports min J=2, drops the -2X2^2 term, or reconstructs a placement missing X2^2 or the 2X2 term.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned bound 3/2 or the motion (X1+X1^2+X2^2, X1 X2+2X2) is lost.

hintTree.content: First row: $\partial(1+2X_1)/\partial X_2=0=\partial(2X_2)/\partial X_1$. Second row: both mixed derivatives equal $1$.
Integrate $F_{11}$ in $X_1$ to get $X_1+X_1^2+f(X_2)$, then match $\partial x_1/\partial X_2=2X_2$.
On $\Omega$, $(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)\ge 2$ and $2X_2^2\le 1/2$, so $J\ge 3/2$. The counterfeit mixed difference is $1$.

CONT:010118.canonicalSolution:
The mixed derivatives of the assigned rows are
\[
\frac{\partial F_{11}}{\partial X_2}=0
=\frac{\partial F_{12}}{\partial X_1},
\qquad
\frac{\partial F_{21}}{\partial X_2}=1
=\frac{\partial F_{22}}{\partial X_1}.
\]
Both rows are therefore curl-free. Integrating the first row from the
origin,
\[
x_1
=\int_0^{X_1}(1+2\xi)\,d\xi+f(X_2)
=X_1+X_1^2+f(X_2).
\]
Matching $F_{12}$ gives $f'(X_2)=2X_2$, so $f=X_2^2$ after
$x(0)=0$. Integrating the second row,
\[
x_2
=\int_0^{X_1}X_2\,d\xi+g(X_2)
=X_1 X_2+g(X_2),
\]
and $F_{22}=X_1+2$ forces $g'=2$, hence $g=2X_2$. Thus
\[
x=(X_1+X_1^2+X_2^2,\; X_1 X_2+2X_2).
\]
\[
\boxed{x=(X_1+X_1^2+X_2^2,\;X_1 X_2+2X_2)}.
\]

The Jacobian is
\[
J
=(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)-(2X_2)(X_2)
=(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)-2X_2^2.
\]
On $[0,1/2]$ one has $1+2X_1\ge 1$ and $X_1+2\ge 2$, so the product
is at least $2$, while $2X_2^2\le 2\cdot(1/4)=1/2$. Therefore
\[
J\ge 2-\frac12=\frac32.
\]
\[
\boxed{J=(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)-2X_2^2\ge 3/2}.
\]

At $(1/2,1/2)$,
\[
x
=\Bigl(\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac14,\;
\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12+2\cdot\tfrac12\Bigr)
=(1,5/4),
\]
\[
F
=\begin{pmatrix}1+1&1\\1/2&1/2+2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1/2&5/2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
J=2\cdot\frac52-\frac12=\frac92.
\]
\[
\boxed{x(1/2,1/2)=(1,5/4),\quad F=[[2,1],[1/2,5/2]],\quad J=9/2}.
\]

The counterfeit entry $F_{12}=2X_2+X_1$ produces the defect
\[
\frac{\partial F_{12}}{\partial X_1}
-\frac{\partial F_{11}}{\partial X_2}
=1-0=1.
\]
No $C^2$ placement can have that matrix as its gradient.

Sentence (i) drops the curl-free test and treats an arbitrary matrix
field as $\mathrm{Grad}\,x$. Sentence (ii) reports the unsubtracted
lower bound $2$ as the minimum of $J$, or else replaces the
compatibility calculation by a polar-decomposition /
objective-strain argument, which is not asked.

The argument never factors $F=RU$, never introduces an objective
rate, and never treats $F$ as a constitutive unknown.

graderFixtures.proofText: Row compatibility holds. The motion is $x=(X_1+X_1^2+X_2^2,\,X_1 X_2+2X_2)$ with $J=(1+2X_1)(X_1+2)-2X_2^2\ge 3/2$. At $(1/2,1/2)$ one has $x=(1,5/4)$, $F=[[2,1],[1/2,5/2]]$, $J=9/2$. The counterfeit $F_{12}=2X_2+X_1$ has compatibility defect $1$.
Any C^1 matrix field is a deformation gradient, so I accept the counterfeit F12=2X2+X1 as equally admissible and integrate it anyway.
I drop the subtracted term 2X2^2 and report the lower bound on J as 2 rather than 3/2.

CONT:010119.title: Constant L=[[1,2],[0,-1]]: F=[[e^t,2 sinh t],[0,e^{-t}]], J=1, v=(x1+2x2,-x2), D=[[1,1],[1,-1]], t=ln2 maps (1,2) to (5,1)
CONT:010119.objective: Integrate Fdot=L F with F(0)=I for the assigned constant L, using L^2=I, obtain F=[[e^t,2 sinh t],[0,e^{-t}]] and J=1, read the spatial velocity, stretching, spin, and vanishing divergence, and evaluate the flow at t=ln 2 on the particle X=(1,2).
CONT:010119.statement:
A homogeneous motion has the constant spatial velocity gradient
\[
L
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}.
\]
The deformation gradient obeys $\dot F=LF$ with $F(0)=I$. Direct
multiplication gives $L^2=I$.

1. Using $L^2=I$, or by solving the linear matrix ODE componentwise,
   prove
   \[
   F(t)
   =\begin{pmatrix}e^{t}&2\sinh t\\0&e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}
   \]
   and $J=\det F=1$.

2. Write the spatial velocity $v=Lx$, the stretching
   $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and the spin $W=(L-L^T)/2$. Prove
   \[
   v=(x_1+2x_2,\,-x_2),\qquad
   D=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   W=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
   \]
   and $\operatorname{div} v=\operatorname{tr} L=0$.

3. At the instant $t=\ln 2$, evaluate $F$ and the image of the
   particle $X=(1,2)$. Prove
   \[
   F(\ln 2)
   =\begin{pmatrix}2&3/2\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad
   x=F X=(5,1).
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $L$ is constant one may take
   $F=I+tL$, so the off-diagonal entry is $2t$ rather than
   $2\sinh t$”; (ii) “$D$ and $W$ may be swapped, or
   $\operatorname{div} v=1$, or this is a polar-decomposition /
   neo-Hookean tangent exercise.”

Do not replace the exponential flow by a small-strain increment, and
do not introduce a constitutive tangent.
permittedResults: If $L^2=I$, then $\exp(tL)=\cosh t\,I+\sinh t\,L$. The $(1,2)$ entry of that matrix is $2\sinh t$, not $2t$.
For a homogeneous motion $v=Lx$ one has $\operatorname{div} v=\operatorname{tr} L$. Here $\operatorname{tr} L=0$, which matches $J\equiv 1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce exp(tL) with L^2=I to cosh t I + sinh t L, then read D and W from the algebraic split of L.
Integrate the three scalar ODEs for F11, F22, and F12 with identity data, and evaluate sinh(ln 2) from (2-1/2)/2.

milestones.criterion: Integrates Fdot=LF to F=[[e^t,2 sinh t],[0,e^{-t}]] with J=1, using L^2=I.
Refuses the increment F=I+tL and does not swap D with W or replace the flow by a constitutive tangent.

commonErrors.description: Replaces F=exp(tL) by the increment I+tL, writing the off-diagonal as 2t rather than 2 sinh t.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned F(ln 2)=[[2,3/2],[0,1/2]] and the image (5,1) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the assigned D and W, or reports div v=1 from L11 alone.
commonErrors.consequence: The stretching/spin split or the incompressibility identity tr L=0 is erased.

hintTree.content: Write $\exp(tL)=\cosh t\,I+\sinh t\,L$ and add: the $(1,1)$ entry is $\cosh t+\sinh t=e^t$.

CONT:010119.canonicalSolution:
First confirm $L^2=I$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The exponential of a matrix with $L^2=I$ is
\[
\exp(tL)=\cosh t\,I+\sinh t\,L
=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh t+\sinh t&2\sinh t\\0&\cosh t-\sinh t\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}e^{t}&2\sinh t\\0&e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(The same formulae are recovered by integrating $\dot F_{11}=F_{11}$,
$\dot F_{22}=-F_{22}$, and $\dot F_{12}=F_{12}+2F_{22}$ with identity
initial data.) The determinant is $e^{t}e^{-t}=1$.
\[
\boxed{F=[[e^{t},2\sinh t],[0,e^{-t}]],\quad J=1}.
\]

The spatial velocity of the homogeneous motion is $v=Lx$, i.e.
\[
v=(x_1+2x_2,\,-x_2).
\]
The symmetric and skew parts are
\[
D
=\frac12\Bigl(
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}
\Bigr)
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
W
=\frac12\Bigl(
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
-
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}
\Bigr)
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The divergence is $\operatorname{tr} L=1-1=0$, consistent with $J\equiv 1$.
\[
\boxed{v=(x_1+2x_2,-x_2),\ D=[[1,1],[1,-1]],\ W=[[0,1],[-1,0]],\ \operatorname{div} v=0}.
\]

At $t=\ln 2$ one has $e^{t}=2$, $e^{-t}=1/2$, and
\[
2\sinh(\ln 2)=e^{\ln 2}-e^{-\ln 2}=2-\frac12=\frac32.
\]
Thus
\[
F(\ln 2)
=\begin{pmatrix}2&3/2\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The particle $X=(1,2)$ is sent to
\[
x
=\begin{pmatrix}2&3/2\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2+3\\1\end{pmatrix}
=(5,1).
\]
\[
\boxed{F(\ln 2)=[[2,3/2],[0,1/2]],\quad X=(1,2)\mapsto x=(5,1)}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the matrix exponential by the small-strain
increment $I+tL$. That produces the off-diagonal $2t$ instead of
$2\sinh t$ and, at $t=\ln 2$, the false entry $2\ln 2$ in place of
$3/2$. Sentence (ii) swaps the assigned $D$ and $W$, or reports
$\operatorname{div} v=1$ from the $(1,1)$ entry alone, or else
replaces the flow by a polar-decomposition or neo-Hookean tangent
calculation, which is not asked.

The argument never linearizes $F\approx I+tL$ as the exact solution,
never factors $F=RU$, and never introduces a constitutive modulus.

graderFixtures.proofText: L is constant, so I take F=I+tL and write the off-diagonal as 2t instead of 2 sinh t. At t=ln 2 I report F12=2 ln 2.
I swap the assigned D and W, or I read div v from the single entry L11=1 instead of tr L=0.

CONT:010220.title: Manufactured sigma=q[[2x+y,x-y],[x-y,3y]]: div=q(1,4), b=(-1,-4), at (1,2) traction (8/5,21/5), normal 108/25, shear 31/25
CONT:010220.objective: From the assigned Cauchy field with q=1 kPa/m and rho=1000 in static balance, compute div sigma, the body force, the stress at (1,2), and the traction, normal, and shear components on n=(3/5,4/5).
CONT:010220.statement:
A plane Cauchy stress is manufactured as
\[
\sigma
=q
\begin{pmatrix}
2x+y & x-y \\
x-y & 3y
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
q=1\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{m},
\]
in a continuum of density $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^3$.
The motion is static.

1. Compute $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ and prove
   \[
   \operatorname{div}\sigma
   =q(1,4)
   =(1000,4000)\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3.
   \]
   From static balance $\operatorname{div}\sigma+\rho b=0$, deduce
   \[
   b=(-1,-4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2.
   \]

2. Evaluate the stress at the point $(x,y)=(1,2)$ and prove
   \[
   \sigma(1,2)
   =\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kPa}.
   \]

3. On the unit normal $n=(3/5,4/5)$, compute the traction
   $t=\sigma n$ and its projections onto $n$ and onto the unit
   tangent $m=(-4/5,3/5)$. Prove
   \[
   t=\Bigl(\frac85,\,\frac{21}{5}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{kPa},\qquad
   t\cdot n=\frac{108}{25},\qquad
   t\cdot m=\frac{31}{25}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “static balance is
   $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\rho b$, so $b=(1,4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$”;
   (ii) “the normal component is $|t|$ or $t\cdot m$, or this is a
   Cauchy-tetrahedron / stress-symmetry derivation.”

Do not replace the manufactured field by a tetrahedron argument, and
do not drop the sign of the body-force balance.
permittedResults: In components, $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial\sigma_{ij}/\partial x_j$. For the assigned field this is $q(2-1,1+3)=q(1,4)$.
With $q=1\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{m}=1000\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3$ and $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^3$, the static body force is $b=-(1,4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate each row of sigma, convert q to N/m^3, and solve b=-(div sigma)/rho.
Substitute (1,2) into sigma, multiply by n=(3/5,4/5), then project onto n and onto the rotate m=(-4/5,3/5).

milestones.criterion: Computes div sigma=q(1,4)=(1000,4000) N/m^3 and the static body force b=(-1,-4) m/s^2.
Evaluates sigma(1,2)=[[4,-1],[-1,6]] kPa and the traction split t=(8/5,21/5), t·n=108/25, t·m=31/25.
Keeps the minus sign in static balance and refuses a Cauchy-tetrahedron substitution.

commonErrors.description: Writes static balance as div sigma = rho b and reports b=(1,4) m/s^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned body force (-1,-4) is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the normal component with |t| or with t·m, or reports the shear 31/25 as the normal 108/25.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned split t·n=108/25 and t·m=31/25 is lost.

hintTree.content: $\partial\sigma_{11}/\partial x=2q$ and $\partial\sigma_{12}/\partial y=-q$, so the first residual is $q$. The second residual is $q+3q=4q$.
Static balance forces $b=-(\operatorname{div}\sigma)/\rho=(-1,-4)$. At $(1,2)$ the matrix is $q[[4,-1],[-1,6]]$.

CONT:010220.canonicalSolution:
Write $\sigma_{11}=q(2x+y)$, $\sigma_{12}=\sigma_{21}=q(x-y)$,
$\sigma_{22}=3qy$. The Cartesian divergence is
\[
(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_1
=q\bigl(2+(-1)\bigr)=q,
\qquad
(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_2
=q\bigl(1+3\bigr)=4q.
\]
With $q=1\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{m}=1000\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3$,
\[
\operatorname{div}\sigma
=(1000,4000)\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3.
\]
Static balance $\operatorname{div}\sigma+\rho b=0$ and
$\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^3$ give
\[
b
=-\frac{(1000,4000)}{1000}
=(-1,-4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{div}\sigma=q(1,4)=(1000,4000)\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3,\quad b=(-1,-4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2}.
\]

At $(1,2)$,
\[
\sigma(1,2)
=q
\begin{pmatrix}2+2&1-2\\1-2&6\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kPa}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma(1,2)=[[4,-1],[-1,6]]\,\mathrm{kPa}}.
\]

On $n=(3/5,4/5)$,
\[
t
=\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}3/5\\4/5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}12/5-4/5\\-3/5+24/5\end{pmatrix}
=\Bigl(\frac85,\,\frac{21}{5}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{kPa}.
\]
The normal scalar is
\[
t\cdot n
=\frac85\cdot\frac35+\frac{21}{5}\cdot\frac45
=\frac{24}{25}+\frac{84}{25}
=\frac{108}{25},
\]
and the shear scalar on $m=(-4/5,3/5)$ is
\[
t\cdot m
=\frac85\cdot\Bigl(-\frac45\Bigr)+\frac{21}{5}\cdot\frac35
=-\frac{32}{25}+\frac{63}{25}
=\frac{31}{25}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=(8/5,21/5)\,\mathrm{kPa},\quad t\cdot n=108/25,\quad t\cdot m=31/25}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the minus sign in $\operatorname{div}\sigma+\rho b=0$
and reports $b=(1,4)$. Sentence (ii) identifies the normal component
with $|t|$ or with the shear $t\cdot m$, or else replaces the
manufactured evaluation by a Cauchy-tetrahedron derivation of
stress, which is not asked.

The argument never invokes a tetrahedron, never discusses couple
stresses, and never claims that all stresses are equal.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\operatorname{div}\sigma=q(1,4)=(1000,4000)\,\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^3$ and $b=(-1,-4)\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$. At $(1,2)$, $\sigma=[[4,-1],[-1,6]]\,\mathrm{kPa}$. On $n=(3/5,4/5)$ the traction is $(8/5,21/5)\,\mathrm{kPa}$ with $t\cdot n=108/25$ and $t\cdot m=31/25$.
Static balance is div sigma = rho b, so I report b=(1,4) m/s^2 instead of (-1,-4).
I identify the normal component with |t| or with the shear t·m, and I report 31/25 as the normal traction.

CONT:010221.title: Harmonic Airy phi=q(x^3 y-x y^3): sigma=[[-6qxy,3q(y^2-x^2)],[...]], residuals 0, at (1,2) principals +/-15 and t=(-12,9)
CONT:010221.objective: From the cubic Airy function phi=q(x^3 y-x y^3), prove it is harmonic and biharmonic, recover the plane stress, verify vanishing equilibrium residuals, and evaluate the tensor, principal stresses, and e1-traction at (1,2).
CONT:010221.statement:
In the plane, an Airy stress function is given by
\[
\phi=q(x^3 y-xy^3),\qquad q=1\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{m}^2.
\]
The standing sign convention (zero body force) is
\[
\sigma_{xx}=\partial_{yy}\phi,\qquad
\sigma_{yy}=\partial_{xx}\phi,\qquad
\sigma_{xy}=-\partial_{xy}\phi.
\]

1. Compute $\Delta\phi$ and $\Delta^2\phi$ and prove that both
   vanish, so $\phi$ is harmonic and therefore biharmonic.

2. Recover the Cauchy stress and prove
   \[
   \sigma_{xx}=-6qxy,\qquad
   \sigma_{yy}=6qxy,\qquad
   \sigma_{xy}=3q(y^2-x^2).
   \]
   Verify that the two equilibrium residuals
   $\partial_x\sigma_{xx}+\partial_y\sigma_{xy}$ and
   $\partial_x\sigma_{xy}+\partial_y\sigma_{yy}$ vanish identically.

3. Evaluate the stress at $(x,y)=(1,2)$ and prove
   \[
   \sigma(1,2)
   =\begin{pmatrix}-12&9\\9&12\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kPa}.
   \]
   Compute the principal stresses and the traction on $n=e_1$, and
   prove that the principals are $\pm 15\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and that
   $t=\sigma e_1=(-12,9)\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the shear convention is
   $\sigma_{xy}=+\partial_{xy}\phi$, so the off-diagonal at $(1,2)$
   is $-9$”; (ii) “a harmonic Airy function need not be biharmonic,
   or the equilibrium residuals are the nonzero body force, or this
   is an acoustic-tensor / ellipticity-loss calculation.”

Do not replace the Airy evaluation by a wave-propagation argument,
and do not flip the shear sign convention.
permittedResults: If $\Delta\phi=0$, then automatically $\Delta^2\phi=0$. A harmonic Airy function is biharmonic, and the associated stress satisfies both equilibrium residuals with zero body force.
For $\sigma=[[-12,9],[9,12]]$ one has $\operatorname{tr}\sigma=0$ and $\det\sigma=-144-81=-225$, so the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-225=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the four second derivatives of phi, read the Airy stress, and differentiate once more to check the residuals.
Substitute (1,2) into the stress formulae, form the characteristic polynomial lambda^2-225=0, and read the e1-traction from the first column.

milestones.criterion: Proves phi is harmonic (hence biharmonic) and recovers sigma=[[-6qxy, 3q(y^2-x^2)],[3q(y^2-x^2), 6qxy]] with zero residuals.
Evaluates sigma(1,2)=[[-12,9],[9,12]] kPa, principals +/-15 kPa, and t=(-12,9) kPa on n=e1.
Keeps the Airy shear sign sigma_xy=-phi_xy and refuses an acoustic-tensor reading.

commonErrors.description: Takes sigma_xy=+phi_xy instead of -phi_xy, or reports the (1,2) entry at (1,2) as -9 kPa.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned tensor [[-12,9],[9,12]] and the residual identities are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the equilibrium residuals are a nonzero body force, or reports principals other than +/-15.
commonErrors.consequence: The Airy self-equilibrium or the characteristic identity lambda^2-225=0 is denied.

hintTree.content: $\phi_{,x}=q(3x^2 y-y^3)$ and $\phi_{,xx}=6qxy$. Likewise $\phi_{,yy}=-6qxy$. Their sum is $0$.
$\phi_{,xy}=3q(x^2-y^2)$, so $\sigma_{xy}=-\phi_{,xy}=3q(y^2-x^2)$. Differentiate to check the residuals.

CONT:010221.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate
\[
\phi_{,x}=q(3x^2 y-y^3),\qquad
\phi_{,xx}=6qxy,
\]
\[
\phi_{,y}=q(x^3-3xy^2),\qquad
\phi_{,yy}=-6qxy.
\]
The Laplacian is
\[
\Delta\phi=\phi_{,xx}+\phi_{,yy}=6qxy-6qxy=0.
\]
Hence $\Delta^2\phi=\Delta(0)=0$: the function is harmonic and
therefore biharmonic.
\[
\boxed{\Delta\phi=0,\quad\Delta^2\phi=0}.
\]

The standing Airy convention then gives
\[
\sigma_{xx}=\phi_{,yy}=-6qxy,\qquad
\sigma_{yy}=\phi_{,xx}=6qxy,
\]
and, since $\phi_{,xy}=3q(x^2-y^2)$,
\[
\sigma_{xy}=-\phi_{,xy}=3q(y^2-x^2).
\]
The first equilibrium residual is
\[
\partial_x\sigma_{xx}+\partial_y\sigma_{xy}
=-6qy+6qy=0,
\]
and the second is
\[
\partial_x\sigma_{xy}+\partial_y\sigma_{yy}
=-6qx+6qx=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{xx}=-6qxy,\ \sigma_{yy}=6qxy,\ \sigma_{xy}=3q(y^2-x^2);\ \text{residuals }0}.
\]

At $(1,2)$ with $q=1\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{m}^2$,
\[
\sigma_{xx}=-12,\qquad
\sigma_{yy}=12,\qquad
\sigma_{xy}=3(4-1)=9,
\]
so
\[
\sigma(1,2)
=\begin{pmatrix}-12&9\\9&12\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kPa}.
\]
The characteristic polynomial is
\[
(-12-\lambda)(12-\lambda)-81
=\lambda^2-144-81
=\lambda^2-225,
\]
hence the principals are $\pm 15\,\mathrm{kPa}$. The traction on
$n=e_1$ is the first column,
\[
t=\sigma e_1=(-12,9)\,\mathrm{kPa}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma(1,2)=[[-12,9],[9,12]]\,\mathrm{kPa},\quad\text{principals }\pm 15,\quad t=(-12,9)}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the shear convention to $\sigma_{xy}=+\phi_{,xy}$
and therefore reports the off-diagonal $-9$ at $(1,2)$. That also
destroys the residual identities. Sentence (ii) denies that a
harmonic function is biharmonic, or treats the identically zero
residuals as a nonzero body force, or else replaces the Airy
evaluation by an acoustic-tensor / ellipticity-loss argument, which
is not asked.

The argument never forms an acoustic tensor, never discusses
loss of ellipticity, and never changes the Airy shear sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\Delta\phi=0$ (hence biharmonic). Stress $\sigma_{xx}=-6qxy$, $\sigma_{yy}=6qxy$, $\sigma_{xy}=3q(y^2-x^2)$ with vanishing residuals. At $(1,2)$, $\sigma=[[-12,9],[9,12]]\,\mathrm{kPa}$, principals $\pm 15\,\mathrm{kPa}$, and $t=\sigma e_1=(-12,9)\,\mathrm{kPa}$.
I take the shear convention sigma_xy=+phi_xy and therefore report the off-diagonal at (1,2) as -9 kPa.
A harmonic Airy function still leaves nonzero equilibrium residuals, which I treat as a body force, and I do not obtain principals +/-15.

CONT:010322.title: Orthotropic engineering Q=[[12,3,0],[3,8,0],[0,0,2]] MPa, e=(0.01,-0.005,0.02): sigma=(0.105,-0.01,0.04) MPa, W=0.00095 MPa; 90-degree material-axis swap gives (0.065,-0.03,0.04) and 0.0008 MPa
CONT:010322.objective: Evaluate the orthotropic engineering-shear law on the given strain, audit the three assigned positive-definiteness minors 12, 87, and 2, then rotate only the material axes by 90 degrees with the spatial frame and strain components held fixed, recovering the swapped-axis stress (0.065,-0.03,0.04) MPa and the new density 0.0008 MPa.
CONT:010322.statement:
A linearly elastic orthotropic sheet is described, in a fixed
spatial orthonormal frame, by the engineering-shear pairing
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{11}\\\sigma_{22}\\\tau_{12}\end{pmatrix}
=
Q
\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_{11}\\\varepsilon_{22}\\\gamma_{12}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q
=
\begin{pmatrix}12&3&0\\3&8&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{MPa},
\]
where $\gamma_{12}=2\varepsilon_{12}$ is the engineering shear strain
and the third row/column of $Q$ multiplies $\gamma_{12}$ to produce
$\tau_{12}$. The imposed engineering strain is
\[
e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12})=(0.01,-0.005,0.02).
\]
The matrix $Q$ is written in the material principal axes, which
initially coincide with the spatial axes.

1. Compute the engineering stress $\sigma=Qe$ and the stored-energy
   density $W=\tfrac12\sigma\cdot e$. Prove
   \[
   \sigma=(0.105,-0.01,0.04)\ \mathrm{MPa},
   \qquad
   W=0.00095\ \mathrm{MPa}=950\ \mathrm{J/m}^3.
   \]

2. Audit positive definiteness of $Q$ by the three assigned minors
   $Q_{11}=12$, $\det Q_{\mathrm{inplane}}=87$, and $Q_{33}=2$
   (all in consistent megapascal powers). Record that each is
   strictly positive, so $W>0$ for every $e\not=0$.

3. Now rotate the material principal axes by $90^\circ$ about the
   out-of-plane axis, keeping the spatial frame and the numerical
   strain components $e$ fixed. This interchange swaps the material
   normal stiffnesses $Q_{11}\leftrightarrow Q_{22}$ and leaves
   $Q_{12}$ and $Q_{33}$ unchanged, producing
   \[
   Q'
   =
   \begin{pmatrix}8&3&0\\3&12&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{MPa}.
   \]
   Recompute $\sigma'=Q'e$ and $W'=\tfrac12\sigma'\cdot e$ and prove
   \[
   \sigma'=(0.065,-0.03,0.04)\ \mathrm{MPa},
   \qquad
   W'=0.0008\ \mathrm{MPa}=800\ \mathrm{J/m}^3.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “engineering shear must be replaced by
   the tensor shear $\varepsilon_{12}=\gamma_{12}/2$ inside the same
   matrix $Q$, so the third stress is $2\cdot 0.01=0.02$ and $W$
   changes”; (ii) “material-frame indifference of an isotropic law,
   or an observer rotation of a finite-strain viscoelastic
   Clausius--Duhem model, forces $\sigma$ and $W$ to be numerically
   unchanged, so the $90^\circ$ material-axis swap is either
   forbidden or else is the polar-decomposition / hyperelastic-tangent
   / acoustic-tensor intake exercise.”

Do not replace the calculation by an observer-rotated finite-strain
viscoelastic law, a polar decomposition, a neo-Hookean tangent, or an
acoustic-tensor argument.
permittedResults: A symmetric $3\times 3$ block-diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(A,q)$ with $A$ a $2\times 2$ block is positive definite if and only if $A_{11}>0$, $\det A>0$, and $q>0$. Here those three minors are $12$, $87$, and $2$.

Material-frame indifference for an isotropic linear law would force the same $Q$ in every rotated spatial frame. The present $Q$ is orthotropic, so a material-axis rotation at fixed spatial strain is allowed to change both $\sigma$ and $W$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply Qe in the engineering basis, form W as one-half the engineering inner product, then swap only Q11 and Q22 and repeat.
Audit the three assigned principal minors of the block-diagonal Q first, then treat the axis rotation as a change of material orientation at fixed spatial strain components.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates sigma=(0.105,-0.01,0.04) MPa and W=0.00095 MPa with the engineering-shear pairing, and records the positive-definiteness minors 12, 87, and 2.
After the 90-degree material-axis swap at fixed spatial strain, obtains sigma'=(0.065,-0.03,0.04) MPa and W'=0.0008 MPa.
Distinguishes a material-axis rotation of an orthotropic linear law from an observer rotation or from the reserved finite-strain intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces gamma12 by the tensor shear eps12=gamma12/2 inside the same matrix Q, or reports tau12=0.02 MPa and a changed energy for the original Q.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned stress (0.105,-0.01,0.04) MPa and the density 0.00095 MPa are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that material-frame indifference, isotropy, or an observer rotation of a finite-strain viscoelastic law forces sigma and W to be unchanged after the material-axis swap, or replaces the exercise by a polar-decomposition / Clausius-Duhem / hyperelastic-tangent / acoustic-tensor argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The swapped-axis values (0.065,-0.03,0.04) MPa and 0.0008 MPa are denied, or a reserved intake family is substituted.

hintTree.content: The first row is $12\cdot 0.01+3\cdot(-0.005)=0.12-0.015=0.105$. The second row is $0.03-0.04=-0.01$. The shear row is $2\cdot 0.02=0.04$.
The in-plane minor is $12\cdot 8-3\cdot 3=96-9=87$. After the axis swap the first row becomes $8\cdot 0.01+3\cdot(-0.005)=0.065$.
Energy uses the engineering pairing: $\tfrac12\bigl(0.105\cdot 0.01+(-0.01)\cdot(-0.005)+0.04\cdot 0.02\bigr)=0.00095$. After the swap the same pairing yields $0.0008$.

CONT:010322.canonicalSolution:
Apply $Q$ to the given engineering strain:
\begin{align*}
\sigma_{11}
&=12\cdot 0.01+3\cdot(-0.005)+0
=0.12-0.015
=0.105\ \mathrm{MPa},\\
\sigma_{22}
&=3\cdot 0.01+8\cdot(-0.005)+0
=0.03-0.04
=-0.01\ \mathrm{MPa},\\
\tau_{12}
&=2\cdot 0.02
=0.04\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\end{align*}
The stored-energy density in the engineering pairing is
\[
W
=\frac12\bigl(
0.105\cdot 0.01
+(-0.01)\cdot(-0.005)
+0.04\cdot 0.02
\bigr)
=\frac12\bigl(0.00105+0.00005+0.0008\bigr)
=\frac12\cdot 0.0019
=0.00095\ \mathrm{MPa}
=950\ \mathrm{J/m}^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma=(0.105,-0.01,0.04)\ \mathrm{MPa},\quad W=0.00095\ \mathrm{MPa}}.
\]

The three assigned positive-definiteness minors are
\[
Q_{11}=12>0,
\qquad
\det\begin{pmatrix}12&3\\3&8\end{pmatrix}
=96-9=87>0,
\qquad
Q_{33}=2>0.
\]
(The full determinant is $174=2\cdot 87$, which is consistent with
the block-diagonal factorization but is not one of the three assigned
minors.) Every minor is strictly positive, so $Q$ is positive definite
and $W>0$ for every nonzero engineering strain.
\[
\boxed{\text{PD minors }12,\,87,\,2}.
\]

A $90^\circ$ material-axis rotation about the out-of-plane direction,
with the spatial frame and the components of $e$ held fixed, produces
$Q'$ with $Q_{11}$ and $Q_{22}$ swapped:
\[
\sigma'_{11}
=8\cdot 0.01+3\cdot(-0.005)
=0.08-0.015
=0.065\ \mathrm{MPa},
\]
\[
\sigma'_{22}
=3\cdot 0.01+12\cdot(-0.005)
=0.03-0.06
=-0.03\ \mathrm{MPa},
\]
\[
\tau'_{12}=0.04\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\]
The new energy density is
\[
W'
=\frac12\bigl(
0.065\cdot 0.01
+(-0.03)\cdot(-0.005)
+0.04\cdot 0.02
\bigr)
=\frac12\bigl(0.00065+0.00015+0.0008\bigr)
=\frac12\cdot 0.0016
=0.0008\ \mathrm{MPa}
=800\ \mathrm{J/m}^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma'=(0.065,-0.03,0.04)\ \mathrm{MPa},\quad W'=0.0008\ \mathrm{MPa}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\gamma_{12}$ by the tensor shear
$\varepsilon_{12}=0.01$ inside the same $Q$. That is a different
constitutive pairing: it would report $\tau_{12}=0.02$ and would
change $W$, contradicting the assigned engineering-shear convention.
Sentence (ii) confuses a material-axis rotation of an orthotropic
linear law at fixed spatial strain with an observer transformation of
an isotropic or finite-strain viscoelastic law. Material-frame
indifference does not freeze the numbers $(0.105,-0.01,0.04)$ after
the material axes have been rotated, and the calculation is not the
polar-decomposition, Clausius--Duhem, hyperelastic-tangent, or
acoustic-tensor intake exercise.

The argument never introduces a deformation gradient, never rotates
the observer, and never linearizes a finite-strain stored energy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Engineering pairing with $\gamma_{12}=2\varepsilon_{12}$. $\sigma=Qe=(0.105,-0.01,0.04)$ MPa and $W=\tfrac12\sigma\cdot e=0.00095$ MPa $=950$ J/m$^3$. Positive-definiteness minors $12$, $87$, $2$. After a $90^\circ$ material-axis rotation at fixed spatial $e$, $Q_{11}\leftrightarrow Q_{22}$ gives $\sigma'=(0.065,-0.03,0.04)$ MPa and $W'=0.0008$ MPa $=800$ J/m$^3$.
I treat the third strain as the tensor shear eps12=0.01 inside the same Q, so tau12=2*0.01=0.02 MPa and the energy is no longer 0.00095 MPa.

Material-frame indifference of the constitutive law forces the stress and energy to be numerically unchanged after any 90-degree rotation, so I refuse the swapped-axis values (0.065,-0.03,0.04) and 0.0008 MPa and treat the problem as an observer-rotated finite-strain Clausius-Duhem exercise.

CONT:010323.title: Maxwell E=6 MPa, tau=2 s, ramp eps=t/10 on [0,4] then hold 0.4: sigma=1.2(1-e^{-t/2}), sigma(4)=1.03759766 MPa, sigma(6)=0.381710847 MPa, W=0.27248047 MPa
CONT:010323.objective: Integrate the Maxwell law on a linear strain ramp followed by a hold, recover the closed ramp 1.2(1-e^{-t/2}) MPa and the hold decay from sigma(4), evaluate the corrected hold value sigma(6)=0.381710847 MPa, record the long-time limits 1.2 MPa on a never-held ramp and 0 on the hold, and compute the work density 0.27248047 MPa.
CONT:010323.statement:
A one-dimensional Maxwell element obeys
\[
\dot\sigma+\frac{\sigma}{\tau}=E\dot\varepsilon,
\qquad
E=6\ \mathrm{MPa},\qquad
\tau=2\ \mathrm{s},\qquad
\sigma(0)=0.
\]
The imposed strain history is the ramp-then-hold
\[
\varepsilon(t)
=
\begin{cases}
t/10,&0\le t\le 4\ \mathrm{s},\\
0.4,&t\ge 4\ \mathrm{s}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus $\dot\varepsilon=0.1\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on the open ramp and
$\dot\varepsilon=0$ on the hold.

1. On $0\le t\le 4$, solve the linear ODE and prove
   \[
   \sigma(t)=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-t/2}\bigr)\ \mathrm{MPa}.
   \]
   Evaluate the end-of-ramp value
   \[
   \sigma(4)=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-2}\bigr)=1.03759766\ \mathrm{MPa}.
   \]

2. On the hold $t\ge 4$, prove
   \[
   \sigma(t)=\sigma(4)\,e^{-(t-4)/2}.
   \]
   Evaluate the corrected mid-hold value
   \[
   \sigma(6)
   =1.2\bigl(e^{-1}-e^{-3}\bigr)
   =0.381710847\ \mathrm{MPa}.
   \]

3. Record the two long-time limits: if the ramp were continued
   forever then $\sigma\to 1.2$ MPa; on the actual hold,
   $\sigma\to 0$. Compute the work density
   $W=\int\sigma\,d\varepsilon$ and prove that it receives no
   contribution after $t=4$ and equals
   \[
   W=0.24\bigl(1+e^{-2}\bigr)=0.27248047\ \mathrm{MPa}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Maxwell is the same as a
   Kelvin--Voigt dashpot-spring, or the ramp is quasi-static so
   $\sigma=E\varepsilon=0.6t$ and $\sigma(4)=2.4$ MPa”; (ii) “the
   ramp formula continues past $t=4$, so $\sigma(6)=1.2(1-e^{-3})$,
   or else this is the finite-strain observer-rotated
   Clausius--Duhem viscoelastic intake exercise.”

Do not replace the Maxwell ODE by a Kelvin--Voigt law, a
quasi-static spring, or a finite-strain objectivity calculation.
permittedResults: For constant $\dot\varepsilon$ and $\sigma(0)=0$, the Maxwell solution is $\sigma(t)=E\tau\dot\varepsilon\,(1-e^{-t/\tau})$. Here $E\tau\dot\varepsilon=6\cdot 2\cdot 0.1=1.2$ MPa.

On a hold the Maxwell ODE reduces to $\dot\sigma+\sigma/\tau=0$, so $\sigma(t)=\sigma(t_{\mathrm{hold}})e^{-(t-t_{\mathrm{hold}})/\tau}$. Substituting $\sigma(4)=1.2(1-e^{-2})$ at $t=6$ produces the factored value $1.2(e^{-1}-e^{-3})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the integrating factor e^{t/tau} on the constant-rate ramp, then switch to homogeneous decay at t=4.
Compute work only on the interval where strain-rate is nonzero, and factor sigma(6) as 1.2(e^{-1}-e^{-3}).

milestones.criterion: Integrates the Maxwell ODE on the ramp to sigma(t)=1.2(1-e^{-t/2}) MPa and sigma(4)=1.03759766 MPa.
Applies hold decay to obtain sigma(6)=0.381710847 MPa, the limits 1.2 MPa and 0, and the work density 0.27248047 MPa.
Refuses Kelvin-Voigt / quasi-static spring substitutions and refuses to continue the ramp formula past t=4.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Maxwell ODE by a Kelvin-Voigt law or by the quasi-static spring sigma=E eps, for example reporting sigma(4)=2.4 MPa.
commonErrors.consequence: Relaxation is erased and the assigned ramp 1.2(1-e^{-t/2}) MPa is lost.

commonErrors.description: Continues sigma=1.2(1-e^{-t/2}) past t=4, reports sigma(6)=1.2(1-e^{-3}), or replaces the exercise by a finite-strain Clausius-Duhem viscoelastic argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The corrected hold value 0.381710847 MPa is lost, or a reserved intake family is substituted.

hintTree.content: The integrating factor is $e^{t/2}$. On the ramp, $\frac{d}{dt}(\sigma e^{t/2})=1.2 e^{t/2}$, so $\sigma=1.2(1-e^{-t/2})$.

CONT:010323.canonicalSolution:
On the ramp, $\dot\varepsilon=1/10$ is constant and $\sigma(0)=0$.
The Maxwell ODE is the linear first-order equation
\[
\dot\sigma+\frac12\sigma=6\cdot\frac1{10}=0.6\ \mathrm{MPa/s}.
\]
The integrating factor $e^{t/2}$ yields
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\sigma e^{t/2}\bigr)
=0.6\,e^{t/2},
\qquad
\sigma(t)e^{t/2}
=1.2\bigl(e^{t/2}-1\bigr),
\]
hence
\[
\sigma(t)=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-t/2}\bigr)\ \mathrm{MPa}
\qquad(0\le t\le 4).
\]
Equivalently, the constant-rate formula $\sigma=E\tau\dot\varepsilon(1-e^{-t/\tau})$
gives the same prefactor $E\tau\dot\varepsilon=6\cdot 2\cdot 0.1=1.2$ MPa.
At the end of the ramp,
\[
\sigma(4)
=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-2}\bigr)
=1.03759766\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{\mathrm{ramp}}(t)=1.2(1-e^{-t/2})\ \mathrm{MPa},\quad\sigma(4)=1.03759766\ \mathrm{MPa}}.
\]

On the hold, $\dot\varepsilon=0$, so $\dot\sigma+\sigma/2=0$ and
\[
\sigma(t)=\sigma(4)\,e^{-(t-4)/2}
=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-2}\bigr)e^{-(t-4)/2}\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\]
At $t=6$ the decay factor is $e^{-1}$, and
\[
\sigma(6)
=1.2\bigl(1-e^{-2}\bigr)e^{-1}
=1.2\bigl(e^{-1}-e^{-3}\bigr)
=0.381710847\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{\mathrm{hold}}(t)=\sigma(4)e^{-(t-4)/2},\quad\sigma(6)=0.381710847\ \mathrm{MPa}}.
\]

If the ramp were continued for all time, $\sigma(t)\to 1.2$ MPa.
On the actual hold, $\sigma(t)\to 0$. The work density receives a
contribution only while $\dot\varepsilon\not=0$:
\begin{align*}
W
&=\int_0^4\sigma(t)\cdot\frac1{10}\,dt
=0.12\int_0^4\bigl(1-e^{-t/2}\bigr)\,dt
=0.12\Bigl[t+2e^{-t/2}\Bigr]_0^4\\
&=0.12\bigl(4+2e^{-2}-2\bigr)
=0.12\cdot 2\bigl(1+e^{-2}\bigr)
=0.24\bigl(1+e^{-2}\bigr)
=0.27248047\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{W=0.24(1+e^{-2})=0.27248047\ \mathrm{MPa};\ \text{ramp }\infty\to 1.2,\ \text{hold }\infty\to 0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces Maxwell by Kelvin--Voigt or by the
quasi-static spring $\sigma=E\varepsilon$. The latter would give
$\sigma(4)=2.4$ MPa and would erase relaxation. Sentence (ii)
continues the ramp formula past $t=4$, producing the incorrect
value $1.2(1-e^{-3})$ at $t=6$, or else substitutes the reserved
finite-strain observer-rotated Clausius--Duhem intake exercise.

The argument never invokes a finite deformation gradient, never
rotates an observer, and never uses a parallel spring-dashpot.

Work $W=0.24(1+e^{-2})=0.27248047$ MPa, all accumulated on $[0,4]$.

CONT:010424.title: Prandtl ellipse a=2 m, b=1 m, G theta=3 MPa/m: C=12/5 MPa m, tau=(-24/5 y, 6/5 x), max 24/5 MPa, T=24 pi/5 MN m
CONT:010424.objective: Fit the quadratic Prandtl function on the ellipse, recover C=12/5 MPa m from Delta psi=-2 G theta, differentiate to the shear field tau_xz=-(24/5)y and tau_yz=(6/5)x, locate the maximum 24/5 MPa at (0,+/-1), and evaluate the torque T=pi a b C=24 pi/5 MN m.
CONT:010424.statement:
Saint-Venant torsion of a uniform isotropic cylinder is reduced to
a Prandtl stress function $\psi(x,y)$ on the elliptical cross-section
\[
\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1,
\qquad
a=2\ \mathrm{m},\qquad
b=1\ \mathrm{m}.
\]
The trial function vanishing on the boundary is
\[
\psi=C\Bigl(1-\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}\Bigr),
\]
and the standing Poisson problem and shear identifications are
\[
\Delta\psi=-2G\theta,
\qquad
\tau_{xz}=\partial_y\psi,
\qquad
\tau_{yz}=-\partial_x\psi,
\]
with the given product $G\theta=3$ MPa/m. The torque about the axis
is $T=2\iint\psi\,dA$, which on this ellipse reduces to
$T=\pi a b C$.

1. Compute $\Delta\psi$ and determine $C$. Prove $C=12/5$ MPa m.

2. Differentiate and prove
   \[
   \tau_{xz}=-\frac{24}{5}y\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
   \qquad
   \tau_{yz}=\frac65 x\ \mathrm{MPa/m}.
   \]
   Show that the maximum shear magnitude on the bar is $24/5$ MPa
   and is attained at the ends of the minor axis $(0,\pm 1)$.

3. Evaluate the torque and prove
   \[
   T=\pi a b C=\frac{24\pi}{5}\ \mathrm{MN\cdot m}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Prandtl identifications should be
   swapped or sign-flipped, $\tau_{xz}=-\partial_y\psi$ and
   $\tau_{yz}=\partial_x\psi$”; (ii) “the torque is $2\pi a b C$
   or $\pi a b C/2$, or the cross-section should be replaced by a
   circle and the warping function of Saint-Venant, or this is the
   acoustic-tensor / hyperelastic-tangent intake exercise.”

Do not replace the elliptical Prandtl calculation by a circular
Saint-Venant warping function or by a finite-strain tangent.
permittedResults: For $\psi=C(1-x^2/a^2-y^2/b^2)$ one has $\Delta\psi=-2C(1/a^2+1/b^2)$. The Poisson identity $\Delta\psi=-2G\theta$ therefore fixes $C(1/a^2+1/b^2)=G\theta$.

On the boundary $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1$, the squared shear magnitude is a linear function of $y^2$. Because $a>b$, it is maximized at the ends of the minor axis, where $|\tau_{xz}|=2C/b$ and $\tau_{yz}=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute Delta of the quadratic, solve C(1/a^2+1/b^2)=G theta, then differentiate for the shears.
Compare |tau| at the two axis ends to locate the maximum, and evaluate T as pi a b C after the unit-disk substitution.

milestones.criterion: Determines C=12/5 MPa m from the Poisson identity on the quadratic Prandtl function.
Recovers tau_xz=-(24/5)y and tau_yz=(6/5)x, the maximum 24/5 MPa at (0,+/-1), and T=24 pi/5 MN m.
Keeps the assigned Prandtl signs and torque identity and refuses a circular Saint-Venant or reserved-intake substitution.

commonErrors.description: Uses tau_xz=-psi_y or tau_yz=+psi_x, or otherwise swaps the two Prandtl identifications.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned field tau_xz=-(24/5)y, tau_yz=(6/5)x is lost and the traction-free identity is compromised.

commonErrors.description: Reports T=2 pi a b C or pi a b C/2, replaces the ellipse by a circular Saint-Venant warping function, or treats the exercise as an acoustic-tensor / hyperelastic-tangent packet.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned torque 24 pi/5 MN m is lost, or a reserved family is substituted.

hintTree.content: Then $\partial_y\psi=C(-2y/b^2)=-(24/5)y$ and $-\partial_x\psi=C(2x/a^2)=(6/5)x$.
At $(0,\pm 1)$ one has $|\tau|=24/5$. At $(\pm 2,0)$ one has $|\tau|=12/5$. The torque is $\pi\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 12/5=24\pi/5$.

CONT:010424.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the quadratic Prandtl function:
\[
\partial_{xx}\psi=-\frac{2C}{a^2},
\qquad
\partial_{yy}\psi=-\frac{2C}{b^2},
\qquad
\Delta\psi=-2C\Bigl(\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}\Bigr).
\]
The Poisson equation $\Delta\psi=-2G\theta$ therefore requires
\[
C\Bigl(\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}\Bigr)=G\theta.
\]
With $a=2$, $b=1$, and $G\theta=3$ MPa/m,
\[
C\Bigl(\frac14+1\Bigr)=3,
\qquad
C\cdot\frac54=3,
\qquad
C=\frac{12}{5}\ \mathrm{MPa\cdot m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C=12/5\ \mathrm{MPa\cdot m}}.
\]

The shears are
\[
\tau_{xz}
=\partial_y\psi
=C\Bigl(-\frac{2y}{b^2}\Bigr)
=\frac{12}{5}(-2y)
=-\frac{24}{5}y\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
\]
\[
\tau_{yz}
=-\partial_x\psi
=-C\Bigl(-\frac{2x}{a^2}\Bigr)
=\frac{12}{5}\cdot\frac{2x}{4}
=\frac65 x\ \mathrm{MPa/m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau_{xz}=-(24/5)y\ \mathrm{MPa/m},\quad\tau_{yz}=(6/5)x\ \mathrm{MPa/m}}.
\]
On the closed ellipse the shear is purely tangential. At the ends of
the minor axis $(0,\pm 1)$ one has
$|\tau_{xz}|=24/5$ MPa and $\tau_{yz}=0$. At the ends of the major
axis $(\pm 2,0)$ one has $|\tau_{yz}|=12/5$ MPa and $\tau_{xz}=0$.
On the boundary $x^2/4+y^2=1$,
\[
|\tau|^2=\frac{576}{25}y^2+\frac{36}{25}x^2
=\frac{144+432y^2}{25}.
\]
Thus the boundary maximum occurs at $y^2=1$, and radial scaling of
the linear stress field shows that no interior point can be larger.
The maximum is $24/5$ MPa, attained at $(0,\pm 1)$.
\[
\boxed{\max|\tau|=24/5\ \mathrm{MPa}\ \text{at }(0,\pm 1)}.
\]

For the torque, the change of variables $\xi=x/a$, $\eta=y/b$ maps
the ellipse onto the unit disk and gives $dA=ab\,d\xi\,d\eta$, so
\[
\iint_\Omega\psi\,dA
=C\,ab\iint_{D}
(1-\xi^2-\eta^2)\,d\xi\,d\eta
=C\,ab\cdot 2\pi\int_0^1(1-r^2)r\,dr
=C\,ab\cdot 2\pi\cdot\frac14
=\frac{\pi ab}{2}C.
\]
Hence $T=2\iint\psi\,dA=\pi ab C$. With the present numbers,
\[
T=\pi\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot\frac{12}{5}
=\frac{24\pi}{5}\ \mathrm{MN\cdot m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T=\pi ab C=24\pi/5\ \mathrm{MN\cdot m}}.
\]

Sentence (i) swaps or sign-flips the Prandtl identifications and
would replace $\tau_{xz}=-(24/5)y$ by $+(24/5)y$ (or would exchange
the two components), destroying both the field and the location of
the maximum. Sentence (ii) uses the wrong torque prefactor, replaces
the ellipse by a circular Saint-Venant warping calculation, or
substitutes a reserved acoustic-tensor / hyperelastic-tangent intake
exercise.

The argument never introduces a warping function $\varphi$, never
specializes to a circle, and never linearizes a finite-strain energy.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\Delta\psi=-2C(1/a^2+1/b^2)=-2G\theta$ gives $C=12/5$ MPa m. Shears $\tau_{xz}=\psi_y=-(24/5)y$ MPa/m and $\tau_{yz}=-\psi_x=(6/5)x$ MPa/m. Maximum $24/5$ MPa at $(0,\pm 1)$. Torque $T=2\iint\psi=\pi a b C=24\pi/5$ MN m.
I take the Prandtl identifications as tau_xz=-psi_y and tau_yz=+psi_x, so I report tau_xz=+(24/5)y and tau_yz=-(6/5)x.
I compute the torque as 2 pi a b C=48 pi/5 MN m, or else I replace the ellipse by the circular Saint-Venant warping function.

CONT:010425.title: Spherical cavity a=0.1 m, p=2 MPa, mu=5 MPa: A=1e-4 m^3, u(a)=0.01 m, at 2a stresses (-0.25,0.125,0.125) MPa, U=400 pi J
CONT:010425.objective: Use the decaying spherical field u=A/r^2 in an infinite isotropic linear elastic solid, recover the traceless strain and the mu-only stresses, fit A from sigma_rr(a)=-p, evaluate the cavity values and the field at r=2a, and identify the stored energy U=pi p^2 a^3/(2 mu) with half the pressure times the first-order cavity volume change.
CONT:010425.statement:
An infinite isotropic linearly elastic solid contains a spherical
cavity of radius $a$ subjected to internal pressure $p$. The remote
displacement tends to $0$. Restrict attention to a purely radial
field of the decaying spherical form
\[
u_r=u(r)=\frac{A}{r^2},\qquad u_\theta=u_\phi=0,
\]
and write the isotropic Hooke law
$\sigma=\lambda(\mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon)I+2\mu\varepsilon$.

1. Compute the spherical strain components and prove
   \[
   \varepsilon_{rr}=-\frac{2A}{r^3},
   \qquad
   \varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=\varepsilon_{\phi\phi}=\frac{A}{r^3},
   \qquad
   \mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon=0.
   \]
   Deduce that the stresses are independent of $\lambda$,
   \[
   \sigma_{rr}=-\frac{4\mu A}{r^3},
   \qquad
   \sigma_{\theta\theta}=\sigma_{\phi\phi}=\frac{2\mu A}{r^3}.
   \]

2. Impose the cavity traction $\sigma_{rr}(a)=-p$ and prove
   $A=pa^3/(4\mu)$ and $u(a)=pa/(4\mu)$. Rewrite the field as
   \[
   \sigma_{rr}=-p\Bigl(\frac{a}{r}\Bigr)^3,
   \qquad
   \sigma_{\theta\theta}=\sigma_{\phi\phi}
   =\frac p2\Bigl(\frac{a}{r}\Bigr)^3.
   \]
   At $r=2a$, prove $u(2a)=u(a)/4$, $\sigma_{rr}=-p/8$, and
   hoop stress $p/16$.

3. Show that the stored energy in the infinite exterior equals
   \[
   U=\frac{\pi p^2 a^3}{2\mu},
   \]
   and that this is half the pressure times the first-order cavity
   volume change $4\pi a^2 u(a)$. Then specialize to
   $a=0.1$ m, $p=2$ MPa, $\mu=5$ MPa and prove
   \[
   A=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^3,
   \quad
   u(a)=0.01\ \mathrm{m},
   \quad
   u(2a)=0.0025\ \mathrm{m},
   \]
   stresses $(-0.25,0.125,0.125)$ MPa at $r=2a$, and
   $U=400\pi\ \mathrm{J}=1256.637\ \mathrm{J}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the cavity is cylindrical, so the
   decaying field is $u=A/r$ and $\lambda$ must appear in the
   stresses”; (ii) “a nonzero volumetric strain is required, or
   the energy depends on $\lambda$, or this is the manufactured
   incompressible extensional-flow / acoustic-tensor intake
   exercise.”

Do not replace the spherical $1/r^2$ field by a cylindrical $1/r$
Lamé field, and do not introduce a $\lambda$-dependence into the
stresses or the energy.
permittedResults: Because $\mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon=0$, Hooke's law collapses to $\sigma=2\mu\varepsilon$. In particular $\sigma_{rr}=-4\mu A/r^3$ and the hoop stresses equal $2\mu A/r^3$, with no $\lambda$ dependence.

The cylindrical Lamé field $u=A/r$ (an ideal plane-strain cavity) produces $\varepsilon_{rr}=-A/r^2$ and $\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=A/r^2$. Its ideal plane-strain trace also vanishes, so $\lambda$ need not appear; it is a different problem because its displacement decays as $1/r$ and its stresses as $1/r^2$, rather than the spherical $1/r^2$ displacement and $1/r^3$ stresses assigned here.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate u=A/r^2 in spherical components, drop lambda because the trace vanishes, and fit A on the cavity.
Identify U with mu times the integrated strain energy, then match it to (1/2)p Delta V using Delta V=4 pi a^2 u(a).

milestones.criterion: Computes the traceless spherical strains and the mu-only stresses, and fits A=p a^3/(4 mu) from sigma_rr(a)=-p.
Evaluates u(a), the field at 2a including stresses (-0.25,0.125,0.125) MPa on the numerical data, and U=400 pi J as half p times the first-order cavity volume change.
Rejects a cylindrical 1/r field and any claim that the stresses or energy depend on lambda.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the spherical field by the cylindrical Lamé field u=A/r, or treats the cavity as a plane-strain annulus with a logarithmic potential.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned A=p a^3/(4 mu), the 1/r^3 stresses, and the energy 400 pi J are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims a nonzero volumetric strain, inserts lambda into the stresses or the energy, or replaces the exercise by a manufactured incompressible-flow / acoustic-tensor intake argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The mu-only spherical field and the identification U=pi p^2 a^3/(2 mu) are denied.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $A r^{-2}$ to get $u'=-2A r^{-3}$. The two hoop strains are $u/r=A r^{-3}$, so the trace is zero.
$\sigma_{rr}(a)=-4\mu A/a^3=-p$ fixes $A=pa^3/(4\mu)$. Then $\sigma_{rr}=-p(a/r)^3$ and the hoop is half as large with the opposite volumetric-looking sign.

CONT:010425.canonicalSolution:
For $u(r)=A/r^2$,
\[
\varepsilon_{rr}=u'(r)=-2A r^{-3},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=\varepsilon_{\phi\phi}=\frac{u}{r}=A r^{-3}.
\]
The trace is $-2A/r^3+A/r^3+A/r^3=0$. Hooke's law therefore
reduces to $\sigma=2\mu\varepsilon$, independently of $\lambda$:
\[
\sigma_{rr}=2\mu\varepsilon_{rr}=-\frac{4\mu A}{r^3},
\qquad
\sigma_{\theta\theta}=\sigma_{\phi\phi}=2\mu\cdot\frac{A}{r^3}=\frac{2\mu A}{r^3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon_{rr}=-2A/r^3,\ \varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=\varepsilon_{\phi\phi}=A/r^3,\ \mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon=0}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{rr}=-4\mu A/r^3,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{hoop}}=2\mu A/r^3}.
\]

The cavity traction $\sigma_{rr}(a)=-p$ gives $-4\mu A/a^3=-p$, so
\[
A=\frac{p a^3}{4\mu},
\qquad
u(a)=\frac{A}{a^2}=\frac{p a}{4\mu}.
\]
Substituting $A$ into the stresses produces
\[
\sigma_{rr}=-p\Bigl(\frac{a}{r}\Bigr)^3,
\qquad
\sigma_{\theta\theta}=\sigma_{\phi\phi}=\frac p2\Bigl(\frac{a}{r}\Bigr)^3.
\]
At $r=2a$,
\[
u(2a)=\frac{A}{4a^2}=\frac{u(a)}{4},
\qquad
\sigma_{rr}=-\frac p8,
\qquad
\sigma_{\mathrm{hoop}}=\frac p{16}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A=pa^3/(4\mu),\quad u(a)=pa/(4\mu),\quad\text{at }2a:\ u=u(a)/4,\ \sigma_{rr}=-p/8,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{hoop}}=p/16}.
\]

Because the strain is traceless, the stored energy is
$U=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3\setminus B_a}\mu\,\varepsilon:\varepsilon\,dV$.
Here $\varepsilon:\varepsilon=6A^2/r^6$ and $dV=4\pi r^2\,dr$, so
\[
U
=\mu\int_a^\infty 6A^2 r^{-6}\cdot 4\pi r^2\,dr
=24\pi\mu A^2\int_a^\infty r^{-4}\,dr
=\frac{8\pi\mu A^2}{a^3}.
\]
Insert $A=pa^3/(4\mu)$ to obtain $U=\pi p^2 a^3/(2\mu)$. The
first-order cavity volume change is $\Delta V=4\pi a^2 u(a)=\pi p a^3/\mu$,
and $\tfrac12 p\Delta V$ reproduces the same $U$.

Now $a=0.1$ m, $p=2$ MPa, $\mu=5$ MPa:
\[
A=\frac{2\cdot(0.1)^3}{4\cdot 5}
=\frac{0.002}{20}
=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^3,
\]
\[
u(a)=\frac{10^{-4}}{(0.1)^2}=0.01\ \mathrm{m},
\qquad
u(2a)=0.0025\ \mathrm{m}.
\]
At $r=2a$ the stresses are
$(-p/8,\,p/16,\,p/16)=(-0.25,\,0.125,\,0.125)$ MPa, and
\[
U
=\frac{\pi\cdot 4\cdot 10^{-3}}{10}
=4\cdot 10^{-4}\pi\ \mathrm{MJ}
=400\pi\ \mathrm{J}
=1256.637\ \mathrm{J}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^3,\ u(a)=0.01\ \mathrm{m},\ u(2a)=0.0025\ \mathrm{m}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma(2a)=(-0.25,0.125,0.125)\ \mathrm{MPa},\ U=400\pi\ \mathrm{J}=1256.637\ \mathrm{J}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the spherical field by the cylindrical Lamé
field $u=A/r$, which has different decay powers and stresses. The
ideal plane-strain cylindrical field can also be traceless, so the
geometry change—not a supposed mandatory $\lambda$ term—is the decisive
error. Sentence (ii) invents a
nonzero volumetric strain or a $\lambda$-dependence that the
traceless spherical field forbids, or else substitutes the reserved
manufactured incompressible-flow / acoustic-tensor intake exercise.

The argument never uses a logarithmic or $1/r$ cylindrical annulus,
never inserts $\lambda$ into $\sigma$ or $U$, and never treats the
solid as a fluid.

graderFixtures.proofText: Spherical $u=A/r^2$: $\varepsilon_{rr}=-2A/r^3$, $\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=\varepsilon_{\phi\phi}=A/r^3$, $\mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon=0$. Then $\sigma_{rr}=-4\mu A/r^3$, hoop $2\mu A/r^3$, $A=pa^3/(4\mu)$, $u(a)=pa/(4\mu)$. Field $\sigma_{rr}=-p(a/r)^3$, hoop $(p/2)(a/r)^3$. At $r=2a$: $u=u(a)/4$, $\sigma_{rr}=-p/8$, hoop $p/16$. Data $a=0.1$ m, $p=2$ MPa, $\mu=5$ MPa give $A=10^{-4}$ m$^3$, $u(a)=0.01$ m, $u(2a)=0.0025$ m, stresses $(-0.25,0.125,0.125)$ MPa, $U=400\pi$ J $=1256.637$ J. No $\lambda$ and no cylindrical $1/r$.
I treat the cavity as cylindrical and take u=A/r, so the strains are +/- A/r^2 and I fit A from a plane-strain Lamé reduction that involves lambda.
The volumetric strain cannot vanish in a compressible solid, so I insert lambda into sigma_rr and into the stored energy and refuse U=pi p^2 a^3/(2 mu).

CONT:010426.title: Plane strain u=(alpha x^2, beta x y), alpha=0.01 /m, beta=0.02 /m, lambda=2 MPa, mu=3 MPa: at (2,1) sigma=[[0.4,0.06],[0.06,0.4]] MPa, b=(-0.26,0), W=0.0166 MPa
CONT:010426.objective: From the manufactured plane-strain displacement, build the strain and the isotropic stress, compute the divergence and the balancing body force, and evaluate the field and stored-energy density at (2,1).
CONT:010426.statement:
Consider plane strain in the $(x,y)$-plane, with
\[
u_1=\alpha x^2,
\qquad
u_2=\beta x y,
\qquad
\alpha=0.01\ \mathrm{m}^{-1},
\qquad
\beta=0.02\ \mathrm{m}^{-1},
\]
and isotropic moduli $\lambda=2$ MPa, $\mu=3$ MPa. The out-of-plane
displacement vanishes, so $\varepsilon_{33}=0$. The strain is the
symmetric gradient and the stress is
$\sigma=\lambda(\mathrm{tr}\,\varepsilon)I+2\mu\varepsilon$.
Equilibrium is $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma+b=0$.

1. Compute the in-plane strain and prove
   \[
   \varepsilon_{11}=2\alpha x,
   \qquad
   \varepsilon_{22}=\beta x,
   \qquad
   \varepsilon_{12}=\frac12\beta y.
   \]
   Then form the in-plane stress and prove
   \[
   \sigma_{11}=0.20\,x\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
   \qquad
   \sigma_{22}=0.20\,x\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
   \qquad
   \sigma_{12}=0.06\,y\ \mathrm{MPa/m}.
   \]

2. Compute $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma$ and the body force required for
   equilibrium, and prove
   \[
   \mathrm{div}\,\sigma=(0.26,0)\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
   \qquad
   b=(-0.26,0)\ \mathrm{MN/m}^3.
   \]

3. Evaluate the field at the point $(x,y)=(2,1)$ and prove
   \[
   u=(0.04,0.04)\ \mathrm{m},
   \quad
   \varepsilon
   =
   \begin{pmatrix}0.04&0.01\\0.01&0.04\end{pmatrix},
   \quad
   \sigma
   =
   \begin{pmatrix}0.4&0.06\\0.06&0.4\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{MPa},
   \]
   together with the density
   \[
   W=\tfrac12\sigma:\varepsilon=0.0166\ \mathrm{MPa}=16.6\ \mathrm{kJ/m}^3.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$u_1=\alpha x_2$ is a simple shear, or
   the reduction is plane stress so $\lambda$ is replaced by the
   plane-stress modulus and $\sigma_{11}\not=0.20\,x$”; (ii) “the
   body force vanishes, or $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma$ has the opposite
   sign, or this is the manufactured incompressible extensional-flow
   / spherical-cavity / acoustic-tensor intake exercise.”

Do not replace $u_1=\alpha x^2$ by the shear field $\alpha x_2$,
and do not switch to plane stress or to a fluid manufactured field.
permittedResults: The in-plane trace is $(2\alpha+\beta)x=0.04\,x$. Then $\sigma_{11}=\lambda(0.04x)+2\mu(2\alpha x)=0.08x+0.12x=0.20x$ MPa/m, and $\sigma_{12}=2\mu\cdot(\beta y/2)=\mu\beta y=0.06y$ MPa/m.
The only nonzero contribution to $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma$ is $\partial_x\sigma_{11}+\partial_y\sigma_{12}=0.20+0.06=0.26$ MPa/m. Equilibrium therefore requires $b=(-0.26,0)$ MN/m$^3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the polynomial displacement, insert the in-plane trace into plane-strain Hooke, then take div sigma.
Evaluate every tensor at (2,1) last, forming W from the engineering inner product (1/2)(sigma11 eps11+sigma22 eps22+2 sigma12 eps12).

milestones.criterion: Builds eps11=2 alpha x, eps22=beta x, eps12=beta y/2 and the plane-strain stresses sigma11=sigma22=0.20 x MPa/m, sigma12=0.06 y MPa/m.
Computes div sigma=(0.26,0) MPa/m and b=(-0.26,0) MN/m^3, and evaluates the (2,1) field including W=0.0166 MPa.
Keeps plane strain with u1=alpha x^2 and refuses a plane-stress, simple-shear, or reserved-intake reading.

commonErrors.description: Reads u1 as the shear field alpha x_2, or replaces plane strain by plane stress so that the normal-stress coefficient is no longer 0.20.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned strain eps11=2 alpha x and the stresses 0.20 x are lost.

commonErrors.description: Sets b=0, flips the sign of div sigma, or replaces the exercise by a manufactured incompressible extensional flow or another reserved intake family.
commonErrors.consequence: The required body force (-0.26,0) MN/m^3 is lost, or a reserved family is substituted.

hintTree.content: $\partial_x u_1=2\alpha x$, $\partial_y u_2=\beta x$, and $\varepsilon_{12}=\tfrac12(\partial_y u_1+\partial_x u_2)=\tfrac12\beta y$.
The in-plane trace is $0.04x$. Plane-strain Hooke then gives both normal stresses equal to $0.20x$ and $\sigma_{12}=0.06y$.
At $(2,1)$, $\varepsilon_{11}=\varepsilon_{22}=0.04$ and $\varepsilon_{12}=0.01$. Then $W=\tfrac12(0.4\cdot 0.04+0.4\cdot 0.04+2\cdot 0.06\cdot 0.01)=0.0166$.

CONT:010426.canonicalSolution:
The in-plane displacement gradients are
\[
\partial_x u_1=2\alpha x,
\qquad
\partial_y u_1=0,
\qquad
\partial_x u_2=\beta y,
\qquad
\partial_y u_2=\beta x.
\]
Hence
\[
\varepsilon_{11}=2\alpha x,
\qquad
\varepsilon_{22}=\beta x,
\qquad
\varepsilon_{12}=\frac12\beta y,
\qquad
\varepsilon_{33}=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon_{11}=2\alpha x,\ \varepsilon_{22}=\beta x,\ \varepsilon_{12}=\beta y/2}.
\]
The in-plane trace is
\[
\varepsilon_{11}+\varepsilon_{22}=(2\alpha+\beta)x=(0.02+0.02)x=0.04\,x.
\]
Plane-strain Hooke with $\lambda=2$ MPa and $\mu=3$ MPa gives
\begin{align*}
\sigma_{11}
&=\lambda(0.04x)+2\mu(2\alpha x)
=0.08x+6\cdot 0.02x
=0.20\,x\ \mathrm{MPa/m},\\
\sigma_{22}
&=\lambda(0.04x)+2\mu(\beta x)
=0.08x+6\cdot 0.02x
=0.20\,x\ \mathrm{MPa/m},\\
\sigma_{12}
&=2\mu\cdot\frac12\beta y
=\mu\beta y
=0.06\,y\ \mathrm{MPa/m}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{22}=0.20\,x\ \mathrm{MPa/m},\ \sigma_{12}=0.06\,y\ \mathrm{MPa/m}}.
\]

The divergence is
\[
(\mathrm{div}\,\sigma)_1
=\partial_x\sigma_{11}+\partial_y\sigma_{12}
=0.20+0.06
=0.26\ \mathrm{MPa/m},
\]
\[
(\mathrm{div}\,\sigma)_2
=\partial_x\sigma_{12}+\partial_y\sigma_{22}
=0,
\]
so equilibrium $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma+b=0$ forces
$b=(-0.26,0)$ MN/m$^3$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{div}\,\sigma=(0.26,0)\ \mathrm{MPa/m},\quad b=(-0.26,0)\ \mathrm{MN/m}^3}.
\]

At $(x,y)=(2,1)$,
\[
u=(\alpha\cdot 4,\,\beta\cdot 2\cdot 1)=(0.04,0.04)\ \mathrm{m},
\]
\[
\varepsilon
=
\begin{pmatrix}2\alpha\cdot 2&\beta\cdot 1/2\\ \beta\cdot 1/2&\beta\cdot 2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}0.04&0.01\\0.01&0.04\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\sigma
=
\begin{pmatrix}0.20\cdot 2&0.06\cdot 1\\0.06\cdot 1&0.20\cdot 2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}0.4&0.06\\0.06&0.4\end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{MPa}.
\]
The stored-energy density is
\begin{align*}
W
&=\frac12\sigma:\varepsilon
=\frac12\bigl(
\sigma_{11}\varepsilon_{11}+\sigma_{22}\varepsilon_{22}+2\sigma_{12}\varepsilon_{12}
\bigr)\\
&=\frac12\bigl(0.4\cdot 0.04+0.4\cdot 0.04+2\cdot 0.06\cdot 0.01\bigr)
=\frac12\cdot 0.0332
=0.0166\ \mathrm{MPa}
=16.6\ \mathrm{kJ/m}^3.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{u(2,1)=(0.04,0.04),\ \varepsilon=[[0.04,0.01],[0.01,0.04]],\ \sigma=[[0.4,0.06],[0.06,0.4]]\ \mathrm{MPa}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{W=0.0166\ \mathrm{MPa}=16.6\ \mathrm{kJ/m}^3}.
\]

Sentence (i) misreads $u_1=\alpha x^2$ as the shear field
$u_1=\alpha x_2$, which would give $\varepsilon_{11}=0$, or else
switches to plane stress and changes the coefficient $0.20$.
Sentence (ii) drops the manufactured body force or flips its sign,
or substitutes the reserved manufactured incompressible-flow /
spherical-cavity / acoustic-tensor intake exercise.

The argument never treats the solid as a fluid, never uses plane
stress, and never interprets $x2$ as the second Cartesian
coordinate in $u_1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Plane strain $u=(\alpha x^2,\beta xy)$ with $\alpha=0.01$/m, $\beta=0.02$/m. $\varepsilon_{11}=2\alpha x$, $\varepsilon_{22}=\beta x$, $\varepsilon_{12}=\beta y/2$. $\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{22}=0.20x$ MPa/m, $\sigma_{12}=0.06y$ MPa/m. $\mathrm{div}\,\sigma=(0.26,0)$ MPa/m and $b=(-0.26,0)$ MN/m$^3$. At $(2,1)$: $u=(0.04,0.04)$, $\varepsilon=[[0.04,0.01],[0.01,0.04]]$, $\sigma=[[0.4,0.06],[0.06,0.4]]$ MPa, $W=0.0166$ MPa $=16.6$ kJ/m$^3$.
I read u1=alpha x2 as the simple shear u1=alpha x_2, so eps11=0, or else I use plane stress and replace the 0.20 x normal-stress coefficient.
Polynomial equilibrium should not need a body force, so I set b=0 instead of b=(-0.26,0) MN/m^3, or I flip the sign of div sigma.
