CONT:010527.title: Polynomial streamfunction ψ=UL(X²Y-Y³/3): v=(U(X²-Y²),-2UXY), D=(2U/L)[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]], flux -2UL/3
CONT:010527.objective: Recover the plane velocity from the cubic streamfunction ψ=UL(X²Y-Y³/3), prove that the motion is incompressible and irrotational, assemble the rate-of-deformation tensor, evaluate the local kinematics at (x,y)=(L/2,L/4), and match the flux across x=0 to the streamfunction endpoints.
CONT:010527.statement:
A plane incompressible motion is generated by the streamfunction
\[
\psi=UL\Bigl(X^{2}Y-\frac{Y^{3}}{3}\Bigr),\qquad
X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad Y=\frac{y}{L},
\]
with the standing 2-D convention
\[
v_{x}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad
v_{y}=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}.
\]
The data are $U=2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $L=1\,\mathrm{m}$.

1. Prove that the velocity field is
   \[
   \mathbf{v}=\bigl(U(X^{2}-Y^{2}),\,-2UXY\bigr).
   \]
   Compute $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v}$ and the out-of-plane vorticity
   $\omega_{z}=\partial v_{y}/\partial x-\partial v_{x}/\partial y$, and
   show that both vanish identically.

2. Form the velocity gradient and the rate-of-deformation tensor
   $\mathbf{D}=\tfrac12\bigl(\nabla\mathbf{v}+(\nabla\mathbf{v})^{T}\bigr)$.
   Prove
   \[
   \mathbf{D}=\frac{2U}{L}
   \begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\-Y&-X\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

3. At the physical point $(x,y)=(L/2,L/4)=(0.5,0.25)\,\mathrm{m}$,
   evaluate $\mathbf{v}$, the speed $|\mathbf{v}|$, the matrix of
   $\mathbf{D}$, and the invariant $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}$.

4. Compute the volume flux (per unit depth) of $\mathbf{v}$ across the
   segment $x=0$, $y\in[-L,L]$, taking the unit normal in the $+x$
   direction. Prove that the same flux equals
   $\psi(0,L)-\psi(0,-L)$. Audit both sentences: (i) “the 2-D
   streamfunction convention is $v_{x}=-\partial\psi/\partial y$, so
   the velocity components flip and the flux changes sign”; (ii) “this
   is a Hagen-Poiseuille duct profile or a finite-strain polar
   decomposition of a prescribed $\mathbf{F}$.”

Do not replace the streamfunction recovery by a Newtonian duct
solution, a polar decomposition, or a yield-surface audit.
permittedResults: If $\psi=UL(X^{2}Y-Y^{3}/3)$ with $X=x/L$ and $Y=y/L$, then $\partial\psi/\partial y=U(X^{2}-Y^{2})$ and $\partial\psi/\partial x=2UXY$. The standing convention therefore produces $\mathbf{v}=(U(X^{2}-Y^{2}),-2UXY)$.
A twice-differentiable streamfunction automatically satisfies $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v}=0$. Irrotationality is an extra condition on $\psi$ and must be checked by computing $\omega_z$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate psi with the scaled chain rule, read D from the already-symmetric velocity gradient, then integrate v_x on x=0.
Evaluate the local tensors at (X,Y)=(1/2,1/4) first, then confirm the flux identity psi(0,L)-psi(0,-L)=-2UL/3 as an independent check.

milestones.criterion: Recovers v=(U(X^2-Y^2),-2UXY) and proves div v=0 together with omega_z=0 and D=(2U/L)[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]].
Evaluates the point kinematics v=(3/8,-1/2), speed 5/8, D=[[2,-1],[-1,-2]], D:D=10, and the flux -2UL/3=-4/3 m^2/s matching the streamfunction endpoints.
Keeps the standing streamfunction sign convention and refuses a duct-flow or polar-decomposition substitution.

commonErrors.description: Takes v_x=-d psi/dy and v_y=+d psi/dx, or reports the flux across x=0 as +2UL/3.
commonErrors.consequence: Both velocity components flip, the assigned point values (3/8,-1/2) are lost, and the flux no longer matches psi(0,L)-psi(0,-L).

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor 2U/L in D, reports D:D as 5 instead of 10, or replaces the speed 5/8 by a single velocity component.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned local kinematics at (0.5,0.25) are lost.

hintTree.content: Chain-rule the scaled coordinates: $\partial/\partial y=(1/L)\partial/\partial Y$ and $\partial/\partial x=(1/L)\partial/\partial X$. Then $v_x=U(X^{2}-Y^{2})$ and $v_y=-2UXY$.
The velocity gradient is already symmetric: $\nabla\mathbf{v}=(2U/L)[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]]$, so $\mathbf{D}=\nabla\mathbf{v}$. At $(X,Y)=(1/2,1/4)$ one has $\mathbf{v}=(3/8,-1/2)$.
On $x=0$ one has $v_x=-UY^{2}$. Integrate $Y=y/L$ from $-L$ to $L$, or evaluate $\psi(0,L)-\psi(0,-L)=-2UL/3$.

CONT:010527.canonicalSolution:
Write $X=x/L$ and $Y=y/L$. Differentiating the given streamfunction,
\[
\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial Y}=UL(X^{2}-Y^{2}),\qquad
\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial X}=UL\cdot 2XY,
\]
and the chain rule supplies the extra factor $1/L$. The standing
convention therefore yields
\[
v_{x}=U(X^{2}-Y^{2}),\qquad
v_{y}=-2UXY.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{v}=(U(X^{2}-Y^{2}),-2UXY)}.
\]
The Cartesian derivatives are
\[
\frac{\partial v_{x}}{\partial x}=\frac{2UX}{L},\qquad
\frac{\partial v_{y}}{\partial y}=-\frac{2UX}{L},
\]
so $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v}=0$. Likewise
\[
\frac{\partial v_{y}}{\partial x}=-\frac{2UY}{L},\qquad
\frac{\partial v_{x}}{\partial y}=-\frac{2UY}{L},
\]
hence $\omega_{z}=0$. The motion is incompressible and irrotational.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v}=0,\quad\omega_{z}=0}.
\]

The velocity gradient is already symmetric:
\[
\nabla\mathbf{v}
=\frac{2U}{L}
\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\-Y&-X\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore $\mathbf{D}=\nabla\mathbf{v}$ has the same matrix.
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{D}=(2U/L)[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]]}.
\]

At $(x,y)=(1/2,1/4)$ one has $L=1$, $X=1/2$, $Y=1/4$, and $U=2$, so
\[
\mathbf{v}
=\bigl(2\bigl(\tfrac14-\tfrac1{16}\bigr),\,-2\cdot 2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14\bigr)
=\bigl(\tfrac38,\,-\tfrac12\bigr).
\]
The speed is
\[
|\mathbf{v}|
=\sqrt{\Bigl(\frac38\Bigr)^{2}+\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{2}}
=\sqrt{\frac{9+16}{64}}
=\frac58.
\]
The deformation-rate matrix collapses to
\[
\mathbf{D}
=4\begin{pmatrix}1/2&-1/4\\-1/4&-1/2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix},
\]
and $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=4+1+1+4=10$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{v}=(3/8,-1/2),\;|\mathbf{v}|=5/8,\;
\mathbf{D}=[[2,-1],[-1,-2]],\;\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=10}.
\]

On the segment $x=0$, $y\in[-L,L]$ the outward-to-the-right flux is
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}v_{x}(0,y)\,dy
=\int_{-L}^{L}-U\Bigl(\frac{y}{L}\Bigr)^{2}\,dy
=-\frac{U}{L^{2}}\cdot\frac{2L^{3}}{3}
=-\frac{2UL}{3}.
\]
With the assigned data this is $-4/3\,\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}$. The
same value is recovered from the streamfunction endpoints:
\[
\psi(0,L)-\psi(0,-L)
=UL\Bigl(-\frac13\Bigr)-UL\Bigl(\frac13\Bigr)
=-\frac{2UL}{3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{flux}=-2UL/3=-4/3\,\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}}.
\]

Sentence (i) reverses the streamfunction convention, flips both
velocity components, and changes the sign of the flux. Sentence (ii)
replaces the assigned polynomial kinematics by a Hagen-Poiseuille
duct profile or a finite-strain polar decomposition, neither of which
is asked.

The argument never introduces a viscosity, never decomposes a
deformation gradient, and never quotes a yield condition.

graderFixtures.proofText: Velocity $\mathbf{v}=(U(X^{2}-Y^{2}),-2UXY)$ with $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v}=0$ and $\omega_{z}=0$. Then $\mathbf{D}=(2U/L)[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]]$. At $(0.5,0.25)$ one has $\mathbf{v}=(3/8,-1/2)$, speed $5/8$, $\mathbf{D}=[[2,-1],[-1,-2]]$, and $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=10$. Flux across $x=0$ equals $\psi(0,L)-\psi(0,-L)=-2UL/3=-4/3\,\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}$.
I reverse the 2-D streamfunction convention and take v_x=-d psi/dy, so the flux across x=0 becomes +2UL/3 rather than -2UL/3.
I drop the prefactor 2U/L and report D=[[X,-Y],[-Y,-X]] at (0.5,0.25) as [[1/2,-1/4],[-1/4,-1/2]], so D:D becomes 5/8 instead of 10.

CONT:010528.title: Power-law η=m γeq^{n-1}: shear and planar extension share γeq=9, η=4/3, dissipation 108 W/m³
CONT:010528.objective: For the power-law fluid τ=2η_eff D with η_eff=m γ_eq^{n-1} and γ_eq=√(2D:D), evaluate the extra-stress and dissipation in simple shear of rate 9 s^{-1} and in planar extension with the same equivalent shear rate, and record that the two motions share η_eff and the dissipation.
CONT:010528.statement:
A generalized Newtonian fluid is defined by
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}=2\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}\mathbf{D},\qquad
\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=m\,\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}^{n-1},\qquad
\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sqrt{2\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}},
\]
with $m=4\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}^{1/2}$ and $n=1/2$. The extra-stress
dissipation (per unit volume) is $\boldsymbol{\tau}:\mathbf{D}$.

1. Simple shear of engineering shear rate $9\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ has
   the only nonzero strain-rate components $D_{12}=D_{21}=9/2=4.5$.
   Compute $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the shear
   stress $\tau_{12}$, and the dissipation.

2. Planar extension with
   \[
   \mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(4.5,-4.5)
   \]
   is a different motion. Compute the same four quantities and prove
   that $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and the
   dissipation are unchanged, while the extra-stress becomes
   $\boldsymbol{\tau}=\operatorname{diag}(12,-12)\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

3. Record the identity $\boldsymbol{\tau}:\mathbf{D}=\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}^{2}$
   and confirm it on both motions.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the equivalent shear rate is
   $\sqrt{\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}}$ rather than $\sqrt{2\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}}$,
   so $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is smaller by $\sqrt{2}$”; (ii) “this is
   a Hagen-Poiseuille Newtonian duct solution or an incompressible
   neo-Hookean pressure-multiplier exercise.”

Do not replace the power-law comparison by a Newtonian duct profile,
a hyperelastic pressure constraint, or a yield-surface calculation.
permittedResults: In simple shear with $D_{12}=D_{21}=\dot\gamma/2$ one has $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=\dot\gamma^{2}/2$, hence $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=\dot\gamma$. Here $\dot\gamma=9\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

Planar extension $\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\dot\varepsilon,-\dot\varepsilon)$ produces the same invariant $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=2\dot\varepsilon^{2}$. Taking $\dot\varepsilon=4.5$ therefore matches the simple-shear equivalent rate $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the invariant D:D once, read gamma_eq=sqrt(2 D:D), then reuse that scalar for both motions.
Compute tau=2 eta D componentwise and check the dissipation identity eta gamma_eq^2 against tau:D.

milestones.criterion: Computes the simple-shear values D12=4.5, gamma_eq=9, eta_eff=4/3, tau12=12 Pa, and dissipation 108 W/m^3.
Shows that planar extension D=diag(4.5,-4.5) shares gamma_eq, eta_eff, and dissipation 108, with tau=diag(12,-12) Pa.
Uses gamma_eq=sqrt(2 D:D) and refuses a Newtonian-duct or neo-Hookean substitution.

commonErrors.description: Defines gamma_eq as sqrt(D:D) instead of sqrt(2 D:D), or treats the engineering shear rate 9 as equal to D12.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned values gamma_eq=9, eta=4/3, tau12=12, and dissipation 108 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that planar extension has a different equivalent rate or a different dissipation from simple shear, or reports tau=diag(4.5,-4.5) without the factor 2 eta.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned common dissipation 108 and the extra-stress diag(12,-12) are lost.

hintTree.content: For $D_{12}=4.5$ one has $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=2\cdot(4.5)^{2}=40.5$, so $2\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=81$ and $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9$.
Then $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4\cdot 9^{-1/2}=4/3$ and $\tau_{12}=2\cdot(4/3)\cdot 4.5=12$. Dissipation is $(4/3)\cdot 81=108$.
Planar $\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(4.5,-4.5)$ has the same $\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=40.5$, hence the same $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and dissipation.

CONT:010528.canonicalSolution:
In simple shear the only nonzero entries of $\mathbf{D}$ are
$D_{12}=D_{21}=4.5$. Therefore
\[
\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=2\cdot(4.5)^{2}=40.5,\qquad
\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sqrt{2\cdot 40.5}=\sqrt{81}=9.
\]
The effective viscosity is
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}
=4\cdot 9^{1/2-1}
=4\cdot 9^{-1/2}
=\frac43\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}.
\]
The shear extra-stress is
\[
\tau_{12}
=2\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}D_{12}
=2\cdot\frac43\cdot 4.5
=12\,\mathrm{Pa},
\]
and the dissipation is
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}:\mathbf{D}
=\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}^{2}
=\frac43\cdot 81
=108\,\mathrm{W/m}^{3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{shear: }D_{12}=4.5,\;\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9,\;
\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4/3,\;\tau_{12}=12\,\mathrm{Pa},\;
\Phi=108\,\mathrm{W/m}^{3}}.
\]

Planar extension $\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(4.5,-4.5)$ has
\[
\mathbf{D}:\mathbf{D}=(4.5)^{2}+(-4.5)^{2}=40.5
\]
as well, so $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9$ and $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4/3$
are unchanged. The extra-stress is
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}
=2\cdot\frac43\cdot\operatorname{diag}(4.5,-4.5)
=\operatorname{diag}(12,-12)\,\mathrm{Pa},
\]
and the dissipation is again
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}^{2}=108\,\mathrm{W/m}^{3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{planar: }\boldsymbol{\tau}=\operatorname{diag}(12,-12),\;
\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9,\;\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4/3,\;
\Phi=108\,\mathrm{W/m}^{3}}.
\]
The identity $\boldsymbol{\tau}:\mathbf{D}=\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}^{2}$
holds for every traceless $\mathbf{D}$ and is verified on both
motions by the common product $(4/3)\cdot 81$.

Sentence (i) drops the factor $2$ inside $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$,
which replaces $9$ by $9/\sqrt{2}$ and destroys both $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$
and the dissipation $108$. Sentence (ii) replaces the power-law
comparison by a Hagen-Poiseuille Newtonian duct profile or by an
incompressible neo-Hookean pressure multiplier, neither of which is
asked.

The argument never introduces a yield surface, never solves a
duct-flow balance, and never treats a hyperelastic stored energy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Simple shear: $D_{12}=4.5$, $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=9$, $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4/3$, $\tau_{12}=12\,\mathrm{Pa}$, dissipation $108\,\mathrm{W/m}^{3}$. Planar extension $\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(4.5,-4.5)$ shares $\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and dissipation $108$, with $\boldsymbol{\tau}=\operatorname{diag}(12,-12)\,\mathrm{Pa}$.
I take gamma_eq=sqrt(D:D)=sqrt(40.5) instead of sqrt(2 D:D)=9, so eta_eff is no longer 4/3 and the dissipation is no longer 108.
Planar extension has a different equivalent shear rate from simple shear, so I report a different viscosity and a dissipation other than 108 W/m^3.

CONT:010629.title: Bar-wave interface Z1:Z2=1:3: Rv=-1/2, Tv=1/2, signed stresses -6,-3,-9 kPa, energy 1/4 and 3/4
CONT:010629.objective: On two equal-area bars with impedances Z1=2e6 and Z2=6e6, impose the tension-positive one-way laws, compute the velocity coefficients and the signed stresses for an incident particle velocity +3 mm/s, and recover the energy split 1/4 reflected and 3/4 transmitted.
CONT:010629.statement:
Two semi-infinite bars of equal cross-section meet at $x=0$, with
mechanical impedances $Z_{1}=2\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s/m}$ on
the left and $Z_{2}=6\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s/m}$ on the right.
A right-going incident wave occupies bar 1 and carries the particle
velocity $v_{i}=+3\,\mathrm{mm/s}=+3\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Standing sign convention (tension positive). For a right-going wave
$\sigma=-Zv$; for a left-going wave $\sigma=+Zv$. Consequently the
three waves obey
\[
\sigma_{i}=-Z_{1}v_{i},\qquad
\sigma_{r}=+Z_{1}v_{r},\qquad
\sigma_{t}=-Z_{2}v_{t}.
\]
Particle velocity and signed axial stress are continuous at $x=0$:
\[
v_{i}+v_{r}=v_{t},\qquad
\sigma_{i}+\sigma_{r}=\sigma_{t}.
\]
The magnitude of the one-way power flux of a simple wave is
$P=Zv^{2}=|\sigma v|$ (per unit area). Its signed flux in the $+x$
direction is positive for a right-going wave and negative for a
left-going wave.

1. Prove that the velocity reflection and transmission coefficients
   are $R_{v}=v_{r}/v_{i}=(Z_{1}-Z_{2})/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})=-1/2$ and
   $T_{v}=v_{t}/v_{i}=2Z_{1}/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})=1/2$. Deduce
   $v_{r}=-1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$ and $v_{t}=+1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$.

2. Evaluate the three signed stresses and prove that they equal
   $\sigma_{i}=-6\,\mathrm{kPa}$, $\sigma_{r}=-3\,\mathrm{kPa}$,
   and $\sigma_{t}=-9\,\mathrm{kPa}$. Confirm signed continuity
   $\sigma_{i}+\sigma_{r}=\sigma_{t}$. Record the three magnitudes
   $6$, $3$, and $9\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

3. Compute the three one-way power-flux magnitudes and the energy fractions
   $P_{r}/P_{i}$ and $P_{t}/P_{i}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $Z_{2}>Z_{1}$ one should take
   $R_{v}=+1/2$ (a free-end formula), or compression-positive signs
   may be mixed with the stated tension-positive laws”; (ii) “this
   is a linear acoustic gas Riemann problem or a Kelvin-Voigt
   dissipative-rod calculation.”

Do not replace the elastic impedance jump by a gas-acoustic Riemann
solver or by a viscoelastic decay estimate.
permittedResults: Eliminating the stresses from the two interface identities produces $R_{v}=(Z_{1}-Z_{2})/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})$ and $T_{v}=1+R_{v}=2Z_{1}/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})$. For $Z_{2}=3Z_{1}$ these are $-1/2$ and $1/2$.

A stiffer downstream bar reflects a right-going incident velocity with a negative $R_{v}$. The associated reflected stress is still compressive under the tension-positive convention whenever $v_{i}>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate stresses from the two interface identities to get Rv=(Z1-Z2)/(Z1+Z2), then evaluate the three one-way stresses.
Compute the three powers from Z v^2 and check both energy conservation and the identities Pr/Pi=Rv^2, Pt/Pi=(Z2/Z1)Tv^2.

milestones.criterion: Obtains Rv=-1/2, Tv=1/2, vr=-1.5 mm/s, and vt=+1.5 mm/s from the stated tension-positive interface laws.
Reports signed stresses -6, -3, -9 kPa with continuity, magnitudes 6, 3, 9 kPa, powers 18, 4.5, 13.5 W/m^2, and energy fractions 1/4 and 3/4.
Keeps the tension-positive one-way signs and refuses a gas-Riemann or viscoelastic substitution.

commonErrors.description: Takes Rv=+1/2 or Rv=(Z2-Z1)/(Z1+Z2), or reports vr=+1.5 mm/s for the assigned incident velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The stiffer-bar reflection is reversed and the assigned transmitted velocity +1.5 mm/s is lost.

commonErrors.description: Mixes compression-positive formulas with the stated tension-positive laws, reports tensile incident stress +6 kPa, or replaces the energy fractions 1/4 and 3/4 by 1/2 and 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: Signed stress continuity fails, or the assigned powers 18, 4.5, 13.5 W/m^2 are lost.

hintTree.content: Substitute $\sigma_{i}=-Z_{1}v_{i}$, $\sigma_{r}=+Z_{1}v_{r}$, $\sigma_{t}=-Z_{2}v_{t}$ into stress continuity and use $v_{t}=v_{i}+v_{r}$.
Then $v_{r}=-(1/2)v_{i}=-1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$ and $v_{t}=+(1/2)v_{i}=+1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$. Stresses: $\sigma_{i}=-Z_{1}v_{i}=-6\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

CONT:010629.canonicalSolution:
Insert the one-way laws into signed-stress continuity:
\[
-Z_{1}v_{i}+Z_{1}v_{r}=-Z_{2}(v_{i}+v_{r}).
\]
Rearrangement produces
\[
(Z_{1}+Z_{2})v_{r}=(Z_{1}-Z_{2})v_{i},
\]
hence
\[
R_{v}=\frac{Z_{1}-Z_{2}}{Z_{1}+Z_{2}}
=\frac{2-6}{2+6}
=-\frac12,\qquad
T_{v}=1+R_{v}=\frac12.
\]
With $v_{i}=+3\,\mathrm{mm/s}$,
\[
v_{r}=-1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s},\qquad
v_{t}=+1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_{v}=-1/2,\;T_{v}=1/2,\;
v_{r}=-1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s},\;v_{t}=+1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}}.
\]

The signed stresses under the stated convention are
\begin{align*}
\sigma_{i}&=-Z_{1}v_{i}
=-2\times 10^{6}\cdot 3\times 10^{-3}
=-6\,\mathrm{kPa},\\
\sigma_{r}&=+Z_{1}v_{r}
=2\times 10^{6}\cdot(-1.5\times 10^{-3})
=-3\,\mathrm{kPa},\\
\sigma_{t}&=-Z_{2}v_{t}
=-6\times 10^{6}\cdot 1.5\times 10^{-3}
=-9\,\mathrm{kPa}.
\end{align*}
Continuity holds: $-6+(-3)=-9$. The three magnitudes are $6$, $3$,
and $9\,\mathrm{kPa}$. All three stresses are compressive, which is
consistent with a positive incident particle velocity under
$\sigma=-Zv$ for right-going waves.
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{i}=-6\,\mathrm{kPa},\;
\sigma_{r}=-3\,\mathrm{kPa},\;
\sigma_{t}=-9\,\mathrm{kPa}}.
\]

The one-way power-flux magnitudes are
\begin{align*}
P_{i}&=Z_{1}v_{i}^{2}
=2\times 10^{6}\cdot(3\times 10^{-3})^{2}
=18\,\mathrm{W/m}^{2},\\
P_{r}&=Z_{1}v_{r}^{2}
=4.5\,\mathrm{W/m}^{2},\\
P_{t}&=Z_{2}v_{t}^{2}
=13.5\,\mathrm{W/m}^{2}.
\end{align*}
Energy is conserved: $18=4.5+13.5$. The fractions are
\[
\frac{P_{r}}{P_{i}}=R_{v}^{2}=\frac14,\qquad
\frac{P_{t}}{P_{i}}=\frac{Z_{2}}{Z_{1}}T_{v}^{2}=\frac34.
\]
Equivalently, using signed fluxes in the $+x$ direction gives
$18+(-4.5)=13.5$ W/m$^2$.
\[
\boxed{P_{i}=18,\;P_{r}=4.5,\;P_{t}=13.5\,\mathrm{W/m}^{2};
\text{ fractions }1/4\text{ and }3/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) either inserts the free-end coefficient $R_{v}=+1$, or
the rigid-end coefficient $R_{v}=-1$, or the swapped ratio
$(Z_{2}-Z_{1})/(Z_{1}+Z_{2})=+1/2$, or else mixes a
compression-positive table with the stated tension-positive laws.
Any of those choices flips $v_{r}$ or the signed stresses and
destroys continuity $\sigma_{i}+\sigma_{r}=\sigma_{t}$. Sentence
(ii) replaces the elastic bar jump by a gas-acoustic Riemann problem
or a Kelvin-Voigt decay estimate, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a gas equation of state, never adds
viscosity, and never treats an area change.

graderFixtures.proofText: Tension-positive laws $\sigma=-Zv$ (right-going) and $\sigma=+Zv$ (left-going) give $R_{v}=-1/2$, $T_{v}=1/2$, $v_{r}=-1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$, $v_{t}=+1.5\,\mathrm{mm/s}$. Signed stresses $\sigma_{i}=-6\,\mathrm{kPa}$, $\sigma_{r}=-3\,\mathrm{kPa}$, $\sigma_{t}=-9\,\mathrm{kPa}$ are continuous. Powers $18$, $4.5$, $13.5\,\mathrm{W/m}^{2}$ split as $1/4$ and $3/4$.
Because Z2>Z1 I take the free-end or swapped coefficient Rv=+1/2 and report vr=+1.5 mm/s instead of -1.5 mm/s.
I mix a compression-positive table with the stated tension-positive laws and report sigma_i=+6 kPa, breaking signed continuity with sigma_t.

CONT:010630.title: Strain-gradient rod ω²=c0²k²(1+l²k²): q=3/4 gives cp=2500, cg=3400, ω=62500, high-k cg/cp→2
CONT:010630.objective: From the strain-gradient rod equation u_tt=c0² u_xx-l² c0² u_xxxx, derive the dispersion relation and the phase/group speeds, evaluate them at c0=2000, l=0.03, k=25, and record the long-wave and high-k limits.
CONT:010630.statement:
A linear strain-gradient rod is governed by
\[
u_{tt}=c_{0}^{2}u_{xx}-l^{2}c_{0}^{2}u_{xxxx}.
\]
Seek real wave-numbers $k>0$ in the form $u=\operatorname{Re}e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$.

1. Prove the dispersion relation
   \[
   \omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}\bigl(1+l^{2}k^{2}\bigr).
   \]
   Writing $q=lk$, deduce the phase and group speeds
   \[
   c_{p}=\frac{\omega}{k}=c_{0}\sqrt{1+q^{2}},\qquad
   c_{g}=\frac{d\omega}{dk}
   =c_{0}\frac{1+2q^{2}}{\sqrt{1+q^{2}}}.
   \]

2. For $c_{0}=2000\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $l=0.03\,\mathrm{m}$, and
   $k=25\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, compute $q$, $c_{p}$, $c_{g}$,
   $\omega$, the wavelength $2\pi/k$, and the cyclic frequency
   $f=\omega/(2\pi)$. Report $f$ to two decimal places in hertz.

3. Prove the long-wave limits $c_{p}\to c_{0}$ and $c_{g}\to c_{0}$
   as $q\to 0$, and the high-wave-number ratio $c_{g}/c_{p}\to 2$ as
   $q\to\infty$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the fourth-order term is stabilizing
   in the sense of decreasing $c_{p}$ below $c_{0}$, so one should
   write $\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}(1-l^{2}k^{2})$”; (ii) “this is a
   Kelvin-Voigt dissipative-rod problem or a linear acoustic gas
   Riemann calculation.”

Do not replace the conservative strain-gradient dispersion by a
viscous decay rate or by a two-bar impedance jump.
permittedResults: Substituting $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ into the PDE produces $-\omega^{2}=-c_{0}^{2}k^{2}-l^{2}c_{0}^{2}k^{4}$, hence $\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}(1+l^{2}k^{2})$. Both signs of $\omega$ are admissible; speeds use $\omega>0$.
Differentiating $\omega=c_{0}k\sqrt{1+q^{2}}$ with $q=lk$ yields $c_{g}=c_{0}(1+2q^{2})/\sqrt{1+q^{2}}$. The high-$k$ ratio $c_{g}/c_{p}=(1+2q^{2})/(1+q^{2})$ tends to $2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert the complex exponential, collect omega^2, then differentiate omega=c0 k sqrt(1+q^2) with q=l k.
Evaluate the exact radicals at q=3/4 first (sqrt(25/16)=5/4), then convert omega to f=omega/(2pi).

milestones.criterion: Derives omega^2=c0^2 k^2(1+l^2 k^2) and the speeds cp=c0 sqrt(1+q^2), cg=c0(1+2q^2)/sqrt(1+q^2).
Evaluates q=3/4, cp=2500, cg=3400, omega=62500, lambda=2pi/25, f=9947.18 Hz, and the limits cp,cg->c0 and cg/cp->2.
Keeps the stabilizing +l^2 k^2 sign and refuses a Kelvin-Voigt or gas-Riemann reading.

commonErrors.description: Writes omega^2=c0^2 k^2(1-l^2 k^2), or claims that the strain-gradient term decreases cp below c0.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned branch cp=2500>c0 is lost, and short waves become Hadamard-unstable.

commonErrors.description: Reports cg=2500 or cg=cp, omits the 2q^2 numerator, or records f=62500 Hz instead of omega=62500 rad/s.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned values cg=3400 and f=9947.18 Hz are lost.

hintTree.content: $(ik)^{2}=-k^{2}$ and $(ik)^{4}=k^{4}$. The fourth-order term therefore adds $+l^{2}c_{0}^{2}k^{4}$ to $\omega^{2}$.

CONT:010630.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $u=e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ into the PDE:
\[
-\omega^{2}
=c_{0}^{2}(ik)^{2}-l^{2}c_{0}^{2}(ik)^{4}
=-c_{0}^{2}k^{2}-l^{2}c_{0}^{2}k^{4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}\bigl(1+l^{2}k^{2}\bigr).
\]
Taking the positive branch and writing $q=lk$,
\[
\omega=c_{0}k\sqrt{1+q^{2}},\qquad
c_{p}=c_{0}\sqrt{1+q^{2}}.
\]
Differentiating with respect to $k$,
\[
c_{g}
=c_{0}\sqrt{1+q^{2}}
+c_{0}k\cdot\frac{l^{2}k}{\sqrt{1+q^{2}}}
=c_{0}\frac{1+2q^{2}}{\sqrt{1+q^{2}}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}(1+l^{2}k^{2}),\;
c_{p}=c_{0}\sqrt{1+q^{2}},\;
c_{g}=c_{0}(1+2q^{2})/\sqrt{1+q^{2}}}.
\]

With $c_{0}=2000$, $l=0.03$, and $k=25$,
\[
q=lk=\frac{3}{4}.
\]
Then $1+q^{2}=1+9/16=25/16$ and $\sqrt{1+q^{2}}=5/4$, so
\[
c_{p}=2000\cdot\frac54=2500\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]
The group speed is
\[
c_{g}
=2000\cdot\frac{1+2\cdot 9/16}{5/4}
=2000\cdot\frac{17/8}{5/4}
=2000\cdot\frac{17}{10}
=3400\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]
The angular frequency is $\omega=c_{p}k=2500\cdot 25=62500\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
The wavelength is $2\pi/k=2\pi/25$. The cyclic frequency is
\[
f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{62500}{2\pi}=9947.18\,\mathrm{Hz}
\]
to two decimal places.
\[
\boxed{q=3/4,\;c_{p}=2500,\;c_{g}=3400,\;
\omega=62500,\;\lambda=2\pi/25,\;f=9947.18\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
\]

As $q\to 0$ both $c_{p}$ and $c_{g}$ tend to $c_{0}$. As $q\to\infty$,
\[
\frac{c_{g}}{c_{p}}=\frac{1+2q^{2}}{1+q^{2}}\to 2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{long-wave }c_{p},c_{g}\to c_{0};\quad
\text{high-}k\text{ }c_{g}/c_{p}\to 2}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the sign of the fourth-order term, producing a
Hadamard-unstable short-wave branch $\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}(1-l^{2}k^{2})$
and a phase speed below $c_{0}$. The assigned model is the opposite:
$c_{p}>c_{0}$. Sentence (ii) replaces the conservative dispersion
by a Kelvin-Voigt decay calculation or a gas-acoustic Riemann
problem, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces viscosity, never forms an impedance
jump, and never treats a complex temporal root.

graderFixtures.proofText: Dispersion $\omega^{2}=c_{0}^{2}k^{2}(1+l^{2}k^{2})$ with $c_{p}=c_{0}\sqrt{1+q^{2}}$ and $c_{g}=c_{0}(1+2q^{2})/\sqrt{1+q^{2}}$. At $q=3/4$ one has $c_{p}=2500$, $c_{g}=3400$, $\omega=62500\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $\lambda=2\pi/25$, $f=9947.18\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Long waves recover $c_{0}$; high-$k$ gives $c_{g}/c_{p}\to 2$.
I flip the fourth-order sign and write omega^2=c0^2 k^2(1-l^2 k^2), so the phase speed falls below c0.
I identify the group speed with the phase speed 2500, or I report the cyclic frequency as 62500 Hz instead of omega=62500 rad/s.

CONT:010631.title: Kelvin-Voigt rod: E'=-η∫uxt²≤0, kc=2, roots -1±i√3, double -4, -9±3√5 all Re<0
CONT:010631.objective: For the periodic Kelvin-Voigt rod ρ u_tt=μ u_xx+η u_xxt, derive the temporal characteristic polynomial and the energy dissipation identity, compute the critical wave-number, and classify the roots at k=1,2,3 as stable by strictly negative real part.
CONT:010631.statement:
A one-dimensional Kelvin-Voigt rod on the periodic interval is
governed by
\[
\rho u_{tt}=\mu u_{xx}+\eta u_{xxt},
\]
with $\rho=1$, $\mu=4\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\eta=2\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}$.
Modes $u=e^{st}e^{ikx}$ with real $k$ are admitted.

1. Derive the temporal characteristic equation
   \[
   \rho s^{2}+\eta k^{2}s+\mu k^{2}=0.
   \]

2. Define the mechanical energy
   \[
   E=\frac12\int\bigl(\rho u_{t}^{2}+\mu u_{x}^{2}\bigr)\,dx
   \]
   over one period. Prove $E'=-\eta\int u_{xt}^{2}\,dx\le 0$.

3. Show that the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial
   vanishes at the critical wave-number
   \[
   k_{c}=\frac{2\sqrt{\rho\mu}}{\eta}=2\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}.
   \]
   Compute the roots at $k=1$, $k=2$, and $k=3$, and prove that
   every root is stable in the sense that its real part is strictly
   negative. In particular the complex pair at $k=1$ is stable
   because $\operatorname{Re}s=-1<0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “complex roots are oscillatory and
   therefore neutrally stable, or the $k=3$ roots include a positive
   real root”; (ii) “this is a conservative strain-gradient
   dispersion relation or a two-bar elastic impedance jump.”

Do not replace the dissipative energy identity by a conservative
higher-gradient dispersion, and do not treat a complex root as
unstable merely because it is not real.
permittedResults: The quadratic $\rho s^{2}+(\eta k^{2})s+\mu k^{2}=0$ has discriminant $k^{2}(\eta^{2}k^{2}-4\rho\mu)$. The critical wave-number is therefore $k_{c}=2\sqrt{\rho\mu}/\eta$.
On a periodic interval, integration by parts with vanishing boundary terms converts $\int u_{t}u_{xx}\,dx$ into $-\int u_{xt}u_{x}\,dx$ and $\int u_{t}u_{xxt}\,dx$ into $-\int u_{xt}^{2}\,dx$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert e^{st+ikx} to get the quadratic, then integrate the energy identity by parts on the periodic interval.
Classify k against kc=2 and compute each discriminant separately, checking Re s<0 in every case (including the complex pair).

milestones.criterion: Derives rho s^2+eta k^2 s+mu k^2=0 and the energy identity E'=-eta int uxt^2<=0, with kc=2 m^{-1}.
Computes the roots -1+/-i sqrt(3), double -4, and -9+/-3 sqrt(5), and records that every real part is strictly negative.
Treats complex roots as stable by negative real part and refuses a conservative strain-gradient or impedance-jump reading.

commonErrors.description: Treats the pair -1+/-i sqrt(3) as neutrally stable because it is oscillatory, or claims that a complex root cannot be asymptotically stable.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned stability criterion Re s<0 is replaced by a demand that every root be real.

commonErrors.description: Reports kc other than 2, misses the double root -4, or claims that -9+3 sqrt(5) is positive.
commonErrors.consequence: The overdamped pair is misclassified as unstable, or the critical damping threshold is lost.

hintTree.content: Insert $e^{st+ikx}$: $\rho s^{2}=-\mu k^{2}-\eta k^{2}s$. Rearrange to $\rho s^{2}+\eta k^{2}s+\mu k^{2}=0$.
Differentiate $E$ under the integral, replace $\rho u_{tt}$ from the PDE, and integrate by parts. The $\mu$ terms cancel.
At $k=1$ the discriminant is $4-16=-12$, so $s=-1\pm i\sqrt{3}$. At $k=3$, $s=-9\pm 3\sqrt{5}$, both negative.

CONT:010631.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $u=e^{st}e^{ikx}$ into the PDE:
\[
\rho s^{2}
=\mu(ik)^{2}+\eta(ik)^{2}s
=-\mu k^{2}-\eta k^{2}s.
\]
Hence
\[
\rho s^{2}+\eta k^{2}s+\mu k^{2}=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\rho s^{2}+\eta k^{2}s+\mu k^{2}=0}.
\]

Differentiate the energy and insert the PDE:
\begin{align*}
E'
&=\int\bigl(\rho u_{t}u_{tt}+\mu u_{x}u_{xt}\bigr)\,dx\\
&=\int\bigl(u_{t}(\mu u_{xx}+\eta u_{xxt})+\mu u_{x}u_{xt}\bigr)\,dx.
\end{align*}
Periodicity permits integration by parts with no boundary terms,
\[
\int u_{t}u_{xx}\,dx=-\int u_{xt}u_{x}\,dx,\qquad
\int u_{t}u_{xxt}\,dx=-\int u_{xt}^{2}\,dx,
\]
so the $\mu$ contributions cancel and
\[
E'=-\eta\int u_{xt}^{2}\,dx\le 0.
\]
\[
\boxed{E=\tfrac12\int(\rho u_{t}^{2}+\mu u_{x}^{2}),\quad
E'=-\eta\int u_{xt}^{2}\le 0}.
\]

The discriminant of the temporal quadratic is
\[
\Delta=(\eta k^{2})^{2}-4\rho\mu k^{2}
=k^{2}(\eta^{2}k^{2}-4\rho\mu).
\]
It vanishes at
\[
k_{c}=\frac{2\sqrt{\rho\mu}}{\eta}
=\frac{2\sqrt{4}}{2}
=2\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{k_{c}=2\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}}.
\]

At $k=1<k_{c}$ one has $\eta k^{2}=2$ and $\mu k^{2}=4$, so
\[
s=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}
=-1\pm i\sqrt{3}.
\]
These roots are complex, but they are stable because the real part
is strictly negative: $\operatorname{Re}s=-1<0$. Oscillation does
not cancel dissipation.

At $k=2=k_{c}$ the discriminant vanishes and there is a double real
root
\[
s=-\frac{\eta k^{2}}{2\rho}=-4.
\]
The value $-4$ is strictly negative, hence stable.

At $k=3>k_{c}$ one has $\eta k^{2}=18$ and $\mu k^{2}=36$, so
\[
s=\frac{-18\pm\sqrt{324-144}}{2}
=\frac{-18\pm\sqrt{180}}{2}
=-9\pm 3\sqrt{5}.
\]
Because $3\sqrt{5}<9$, both real roots are strictly negative:
\[
-9+3\sqrt{5}<0,\qquad -9-3\sqrt{5}<0.
\]
Thus every assigned root is stable by negative real part.
\[
\boxed{k=1:\;-1\pm i\sqrt{3};\quad
k=2:\;-4,-4;\quad
k=3:\;-9\pm 3\sqrt{5};
\text{ all }\operatorname{Re}s<0}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats a complex root as neutrally stable, contradicting
$\operatorname{Re}s=-1<0$, or claims that $-9+3\sqrt{5}$ is positive,
contradicting $3\sqrt{5}<9$. Sentence (ii) replaces the dissipative
identity by a conservative strain-gradient dispersion or by a
two-bar elastic impedance jump, which is not asked.

The argument never drops the viscous term $\eta u_{xxt}$, never
claims a purely imaginary spectrum, and never introduces a
higher-gradient conservative correction.

graderFixtures.proofText: Characteristic law $\rho s^{2}+\eta k^{2}s+\mu k^{2}=0$. Energy $E=\tfrac12\int(\rho u_{t}^{2}+\mu u_{x}^{2})$ satisfies $E'=-\eta\int u_{xt}^{2}\le 0$. Then $k_{c}=2$. Roots: $k=1$ gives $-1\pm i\sqrt{3}$ with $\operatorname{Re}s=-1<0$; $k=2$ is the double root $-4$; $k=3$ gives $-9\pm 3\sqrt{5}$, both negative.
The k=1 roots are complex, so I call the mode neutrally stable and ignore Re s=-1<0.
I report that -9+3 sqrt(5) is a positive real root at k=3, or I take kc=1 instead of kc=2.

CTRL:010117.title: With P=2/(s+1) and C=3 the step finals through T, PS, and -T are 6/7, 2/7, and -6/7
CTRL:010117.objective: Form S=(s+1)/(s+7), T=6/(s+7), and PS=2/(s+7) for unity negative feedback, write y=Tr+PSd-Tn, and evaluate the three unit-step finals 6/7, 2/7, and -6/7.
CTRL:010117.statement:
A strictly proper plant and a constant controller are
\[
P(s)=\frac{2}{s+1},\qquad C(s)=3.
\]
They are placed in unity negative feedback with $C$ in the forward path.
The controller output is $u_c$. An actuator disturbance $d$ is added at
the plant input, so the plant sees $u_c+d$. The measured signal fed back
is $y_m=y+n$, where $n$ is additive measurement noise. The summing
junction implements $u_c=C(r-y_m)$. All signals are scalar Laplace
transforms of causal time functions; initial conditions are zero.

The sensitivity, complementary sensitivity, and input-disturbance maps
are the ordinary closed-loop transfers
\[
S=\frac{1}{1+CP},\qquad
T=\frac{CP}{1+CP},\qquad
PS=\frac{P}{1+CP}.
\]

1. Compute $S$, $T$, and $PS$ as reduced rational functions. Prove
   $S+T=1$ by direct addition, and prove $T=CP\,S$ and $PS=P\,S$.

2. Starting from $y=P\bigl(C(r-y-n)+d\bigr)$, solve for $y$ and obtain
   the three-path identity
   \[
   y=Tr+PSd-Tn.
   \]
   Identify which closed-loop map multiplies each exogenous input, and
   explain the minus sign on the noise path from the declared summing
   junction.

3. With the loop initially at rest, evaluate the three separate
   unit-step finals by the final-value theorem:
   (i) $r=1/s$, $d=n=0$;
   (ii) $d=1/s$, $r=n=0$;
   (iii) $n=1/s$, $r=d=0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “an actuator disturbance is an output
   disturbance, so its map is $S$ and the $d$-step final is $S(0)=1/7$”;
   (ii) “measurement noise enters with the same sign as the reference,
   so the $n$-step final is $+6/7$.”

Do not replace the loop by a biased-pendulum linearization, and do not
classify a hidden cancelled mode or a sampled alias.
permittedResults: If $1+CP$ is Hurwitz and each closed-loop map is strictly proper or has a finite DC gain, the final-value theorem gives $\lim_{t\to\infty}y(t)=\lim_{s\to 0}sY(s)$.
The algebraic identity $S+T=1$ holds whenever $T=CP/(1+CP)$ and $S=1/(1+CP)$, independently of the particular $C$ and $P$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form the loop gain 6/(s+1), invert 1+CP, then clear y from y=PC(r-y-n)+Pd and read each DC gain.
Write the three block-diagram paths (reference through T, actuator through P/(1+CP), noise back through -T) and apply the final-value theorem to each path separately.

milestones.criterion: Derives the reduced maps S=(s+1)/(s+7), T=6/(s+7), and PS=2/(s+7), with S+T=1.
Obtains y=Tr+PSd-Tn from the declared summing junction and reports the three unit-step finals 6/7, 2/7, and -6/7.
Rejects relocating d to the output and rejects a positive noise-to-output DC gain.

commonErrors.description: Writes y=Tr+PSd+Tn, or reports the unit-step noise final as +6/7 instead of -6/7.
commonErrors.consequence: The negative feedback of the measured signal is lost, and the noise experiment is scored with the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Treats the actuator disturbance as an output disturbance, so its map is S and the d-step final is S(0)=1/7, or drops C and uses P/(1+P).
commonErrors.consequence: The required map PS=2/(s+7) and the final 2/7 are replaced by a different exogenous channel.

hintTree.content: The loop gain is $CP=6/(s+1)$. Then $1+CP=(s+7)/(s+1)$, so $S=(s+1)/(s+7)$ and $T=6/(s+7)$.
Clearing $y$ from $y=PC(r-y-n)+Pd$ produces the factor $1+PC$ on the left and the three forcing terms $PCr$, $Pd$, and $-PCn$.
Each unit-step final is the DC gain of the corresponding map: $T(0)=6/7$, $PS(0)=2/7$, and $-T(0)=-6/7$.

CTRL:010117.canonicalSolution:
The loop gain is
\[
CP=\frac{6}{s+1}.
\]
Hence
\[
1+CP=\frac{s+1+6}{s+1}=\frac{s+7}{s+1},
\]
and the three reduced maps are
\[
S=\frac{s+1}{s+7},\qquad
T=\frac{6}{s+7},\qquad
PS=\frac{2}{s+7}.
\]
Adding the first two recovers the identity
\[
S+T=\frac{s+1+6}{s+7}=1.
\]
The remaining two identities are immediate:
$T=CP\cdot S=6/(s+7)$ and $PS=P\cdot S=2/(s+7)$.
\[
\boxed{S=(s+1)/(s+7),\quad T=6/(s+7),\quad PS=2/(s+7)}.
\]

Start from the declared interconnection
\[
y=P\bigl(C(r-y-n)+d\bigr)=PC(r-y-n)+Pd.
\]
Collect every occurrence of $y$:
\[
y+PCy=PCr+Pd-PCn,
\]
\[
y=\frac{PC}{1+PC}\,r+\frac{P}{1+PC}\,d-\frac{PC}{1+PC}\,n
=Tr+PSd-Tn.
\]
The minus sign is the negative feedback of $y_m=y+n$: noise is subtracted
from the reference before it is multiplied by $T$. The map from $d$ is
$PS$, not $S$, because $d$ enters at the plant input rather than at the
output.
\[
\boxed{y=Tr+PSd-Tn}.
\]

Each closed-loop map is analytic at $s=0$ (the unique closed-loop pole
is $s=-7$). The final-value theorem therefore applies to each unit step.

(i) $Y=T/s$, so $y(\infty)=T(0)=6/7$.

(ii) $Y=PS/s$, so $y(\infty)=PS(0)=2/7$.

(iii) $Y=-T/s$, so $y(\infty)=-T(0)=-6/7$.

The same numbers are the DC gains of $T$, $PS$, and $-T$.
\[
\boxed{\text{step finals }6/7,\ 2/7,\ -6/7}.
\]

Sentence (i) relocates $d$ to the plant output. An output disturbance
would indeed travel through $S$ and finish at $S(0)=1/7$, but that is a
different exogenous channel. Sentence (ii) reverses the summing-junction
sign and reports $+6/7$ for noise. Neither substitution is the declared
loop.

The argument never linearizes a biased pendulum and never introduces a
cancelled hidden mode or a sampled-data alias.

graderFixtures.proofText: Loop gain $CP=6/(s+1)$ gives $S=(s+1)/(s+7)$, $T=6/(s+7)$, and $PS=2/(s+7)$. Clearing $y=PC(r-y-n)+Pd$ produces $y=Tr+PSd-Tn$. The three unit-step finals are $T(0)=6/7$, $PS(0)=2/7$, and $-T(0)=-6/7$. An output-disturbance reading of $d$ and a positive noise sign are both wrong.
Noise is just another reference, so y=Tr+PSd+Tn. A unit step in n therefore finishes at T(0)=+6/7.
Every disturbance is an output disturbance. The map from d to y is S=(s+1)/(s+7), and a unit step in d finishes at S(0)=1/7.

CTRL:010118.title: The unity DC motor has Omega/V=1/(s^2+2s+2), poles -1±j, and step speed (1/2)[1-e^{-t}(cos t+sin t)]
CTRL:010118.objective: From J=b=L=R=Kt=Ke=1 derive Omega/V=1/(s^2+2s+2) and I/V=(s+1)/(s^2+2s+2), locate the poles at -1±j, invert the unit-step speed to (1/2)[1-e^{-t}(cos t+sin t)], and read the finals omega=i=1/2.
CTRL:010118.statement:
An armature-controlled DC motor is modeled by the pair
\[
J\dot\omega+b\omega=K_t i,\qquad
L\dot\imath+Ri=v-K_e\omega,
\]
with the normalized parameter values
\[
J=b=L=R=K_t=K_e=1.
\]
Here $\omega$ is shaft speed, $i$ is armature current, and $v$ is the
applied armature voltage. The second equation already includes the
back-EMF $K_e\omega$. Take zero initial conditions
$\omega(0^-)=i(0^-)=0$, and write $\Omega(s)$, $I(s)$, and $V(s)$ for
the unilateral Laplace transforms.

1. Eliminate the current between the transformed equations and obtain
   the reduced voltage-to-speed map $\Omega(s)/V(s)$. Then recover the
   voltage-to-current map $I(s)/V(s)$. State both as reduced rational
   functions.

2. Factor the common characteristic polynomial and locate its poles in
   the complex plane.

3. For the unit-step voltage $v(t)=u(t)$, invert $\Omega(s)$ and prove
   \[
   \omega(t)=\frac12\Bigl[1-e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)\Bigr],\qquad t\ge 0.
   \]
   Evaluate the steady speed and, from either the current transfer or
   the static torque balance $b\omega=K_t i$, the steady current.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “back-EMF may be dropped, so
   $\Omega/V=1/(s+1)^2$ with a repeated pole at $-1$”; (ii) “the
   underdamped speed step is $\tfrac12\bigl(1-e^{-t}\cos t\bigr)$, or
   else the finals are $\omega(\infty)=i(\infty)=1$ because $K_t=K_e=1$.”

Do not replace the motor by a biased pendulum, an unbuffered RC ladder,
or a series-resistor feedthrough circuit, and do not introduce a
sampled-data hold.
permittedResults: The quadratic $s^2+2s+2=(s+1)^2+1$ has roots $-1\pm j$.
If $F(s)=(as+b)/((s+\alpha)^2+\omega^2)$, then $f(t)=e^{-\alpha t}(A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t)$ with $A,B$ read from $a(s+\alpha)+(b-a\alpha)=A(s+\alpha)+B\omega$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform both first-order laws, substitute I=(s+1)Omega, then invert 1/[s(s^2+2s+2)] by completing the square.
First read the static balance omega=i=v/2 to lock the finals, then recover the same quadratic from the coupled ODEs and match the underdamped inverse Laplace.

milestones.criterion: Derives Omega/V=1/(s^2+2s+2) and I/V=(s+1)/(s^2+2s+2) and locates the poles at -1±j.
Inverts the unit-step speed to (1/2)[1-e^{-t}(cos t+sin t)] and reports the finals omega=i=1/2.
Rejects omitting back-EMF and rejects a sine-free step or unit finals.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Ke omega term and reports Omega/V=1/(s+1)^2 with a repeated pole at -1, or factors the electrical and mechanical lags as if they were independent.
commonErrors.consequence: The required quadratic s^2+2s+2, the poles -1±j, and the underdamped step are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes omega=(1/2)[1-e^{-t} cos t], or claims the steady speed or current is 1 rather than 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse Laplace of (s+2)/((s+1)^2+1) is incomplete, or the static torque balance is ignored.

hintTree.content: From $\Omega=(s+1)^{-1}I$ and $(s+1)I=V-\Omega$, substitute to get $((s+1)^2+1)\Omega=V$.
The unit-step transform is $1/[s(s^2+2s+2)]$. Partial fractions give $1/(2s)-(1/2)(s+2)/(s^2+2s+2)$.
Write $s+2=(s+1)+1$ over $(s+1)^2+1$ to produce $e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)$, then read $\omega(\infty)=i(\infty)=1/2$.

CTRL:010118.canonicalSolution:
With every coefficient equal to $1$ the time-domain pair is
\[
\dot\omega+\omega=i,\qquad \dot\imath+i=v-\omega.
\]
Zero-state transformation produces
\[
(s+1)\Omega=I,\qquad (s+1)I=V-\Omega.
\]
Substitute $I=(s+1)\Omega$ into the second equation:
\[
(s+1)^2\Omega+\Omega=V,
\qquad
\bigl(s^2+2s+1+1\bigr)\Omega=V.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{\Omega}{V}=\frac{1}{s^2+2s+2}.
\]
The current map follows at once from $I=(s+1)\Omega$:
\[
\frac{I}{V}=\frac{s+1}{s^2+2s+2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Omega/V=1/(s^2+2s+2),\quad I/V=(s+1)/(s^2+2s+2)}.
\]

The characteristic polynomial is $s^2+2s+2=(s+1)^2+1$, so the poles are
\[
s=-1\pm j.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{poles }-1\pm j}.
\]

For $V=1/s$ one has $\Omega(s)=1/[s(s^2+2s+2)]$. Decompose
\[
\frac{1}{s(s^2+2s+2)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{s^2+2s+2}.
\]
Clearing the denominator gives $1=A(s^2+2s+2)+(Bs+C)s$. The value
$s=0$ forces $A=1/2$. Equating the remaining coefficients then forces
$B=-1/2$ and $C=-1$, so
\[
\Omega(s)=\frac{1}{2s}-\frac12\cdot\frac{s+2}{s^2+2s+2}.
\]
Complete the square and split the numerator:
\[
s+2=(s+1)+1,
\qquad
\frac{s+2}{(s+1)^2+1}
=\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+1}+\frac{1}{(s+1)^2+1}.
\]
Inversion therefore yields
\[
\omega(t)=\frac12-\frac12 e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)
=\frac12\Bigl[1-e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)\Bigr],
\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega(t)=\tfrac12[1-e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)]}.
\]
The final-value theorem on $\Omega$ gives $\omega(\infty)=1/2$. For the
same unit step,
\[
I(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s^2+2s+2)},
\]
so the final-value theorem also gives $i(\infty)=1/2$.
Equivalently, the static balance $b\omega=K_t i$ with $b=K_t=1$ forces
$i(\infty)=\omega(\infty)=1/2$.
\[
\boxed{\omega(\infty)=i(\infty)=1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) deletes the back-EMF coupling. Without $K_e\omega$ the
electrical and mechanical first-order factors multiply, and one obtains
the false map $1/(s+1)^2$ with a repeated real pole. Sentence (ii)
either drops the sine term produced by the shift $s+2=(s+1)+1$, or
ignores viscous damping and claims that a unit voltage produces a unit
speed.

The argument never linearizes a pendulum, never writes KCL for an RC
ladder or a series-resistor feedthrough, and never introduces a hold.

graderFixtures.proofText: Coupling through the back-EMF produces $\Omega/V=1/(s^2+2s+2)$ and $I/V=(s+1)/(s^2+2s+2)$, with poles $-1\pm j$. The unit-step speed is $\tfrac12[1-e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)]$. Both $\omega$ and $i$ finish at $1/2$. Dropping $K_e\omega$ or omitting the sine term is incorrect.
Ignore back-EMF. Then Omega/V=Kt/[(Js+b)(Ls+R)]=1/(s+1)^2, and both poles sit at -1.
Completing the square I only keep the cosine, so omega=(1/2)(1-e^{-t} cos t). Because Kt=Ke=1 the motor eventually tracks the voltage and both finals equal 1.

CTRL:010219.title: The map 2(1-s)/[(s+1)(s+2)] undershoots to -1/3 at ln(3/2) before finishing at 1
CTRL:010219.objective: Invert the unit-step response of T=2(1-s)/[(s+1)(s+2)] to y=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}, prove the initial slope is negative, locate the unique minimum ymin=-1/3 at t=ln(3/2), and identify the RHP zero at +1.
CTRL:010219.statement:
A causal closed-loop complementary-sensitivity map is
\[
T(s)=\frac{2(1-s)}{(s+1)(s+2)}.
\]
The corresponding unit-step output is the causal inverse Laplace
transform of $Y(s)=T(s)/s$. All initial conditions are zero.

1. Decompose $Y(s)$ into partial fractions and invert to obtain an
   explicit formula for $y(t)$ on $t\ge 0$. Evaluate $y(0^+)$ and
   $\dot y(0^+)$, and prove that the first motion is opposite in sign
   to the eventual steady value (inverse response).

2. Solve $\dot y(t)=0$ for the unique positive critical time. Evaluate
   $y$ there, and use the second-derivative sign (or the first-derivative
   sign chart) to prove that the critical point is a minimum.

3. Compute the DC gain $T(0)$ and the right-half-plane zero of $T$.
   Confirm that the final value of the step equals $T(0)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the factor $(1-s)$ may be replaced by
   $(1+s)$ or $(s-1)$ without changing the undershoot, because only the
   pole locations matter”; (ii) “the minimum occurs at $t=\ln 2$ or at
   $t=1/2$, and its depth is $-1$ or $0$.”

Do not replace $T$ by a Signals two-exponential convolution kernel, a
resonant undamped oscillator, or an impulsively forced actuator, and do
not run a Routh array in place of the time-domain minimum.
permittedResults: The initial-value formulae are $y(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}sY(s)$ and $\dot y(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}s(sY(s)-y(0^+))$.
If $y(t)=1+Ae^{-\alpha t}+Be^{-\beta t}$ with $\alpha,\beta>0$, the unique positive critical point of a single-RHP-zero second-order step solves $\alpha|A|e^{-\alpha t}=\beta|B|e^{-\beta t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute residues at 0, -1, and -2, then solve 4e^{-t}=6e^{-2t} and substitute e^{-t}=2/3 into y.
Read the initial slope from lim s T(s) and the final value from T(0), then maximize the undershoot by a single critical-point calculation.

milestones.criterion: Inverts the unit step to y=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t} and shows y(0+)=0 with negative initial slope.
Locates the unique minimum ymin=-1/3 at t=ln(3/2) and identifies the RHP zero at +1 with final value 1.
Rejects a minimum-phase or sign-flipped zero and rejects an invented critical time or depth.

commonErrors.description: Replaces (1-s) by (1+s) or (s-1), producing a minimum-phase or negative-DC-gain map with no inverse undershoot to -1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The RHP zero at +1 is lost and the step either stays nonnegative or finishes at -1.

commonErrors.description: Reports the critical time as ln 2 or 1/2, or reports the minimum depth as 0 or -1 rather than -1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The stationarity condition e^{-t}=2/3 is not solved, and the required pair (ln(3/2),-1/3) is lost.

hintTree.content: Write $2(1-s)/[s(s+1)(s+2)]=A/s+B/(s+1)+C/(s+2)$. The residues are $A=1$, $B=-4$, and $C=3$.
Differentiate $y=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}$ to get $\dot y=4e^{-t}-6e^{-2t}$. The unique positive root is $e^{-t}=2/3$, hence $t=\ln(3/2)$.
Substitute $e^{-t}=2/3$ into $y$ to obtain $1-8/3+4/3=-1/3$. The zero of $1-s$ is $s=+1$.

CTRL:010219.canonicalSolution:
The step transform is
\[
Y(s)=\frac{2(1-s)}{s(s+1)(s+2)}.
\]
Partial fractions
\[
Y(s)=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+2}
\]
have residues
\begin{align*}
A&=\frac{2(1-0)}{(1)(2)}=1,\\
B&=\frac{2(1-(-1))}{(-1)(1)}=-4,\\
C&=\frac{2(1-(-2))}{(-2)(-1)}=3.
\end{align*}
Hence $Y(s)=1/s-4/(s+1)+3/(s+2)$, and
\[
y(t)=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t},\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
\[
\boxed{y(t)=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}}.
\]
Direct evaluation gives $y(0^+)=1-4+3=0$. The derivative is
\[
\dot y(t)=4e^{-t}-6e^{-2t},
\qquad
\dot y(0^+)=4-6=-2<0.
\]
The same initial slope is the high-frequency limit
$\lim_{s\to\infty}sT(s)=-2$. The response therefore leaves $0$ in the
negative direction, while
\[
y(\infty)=T(0)=\frac{2(1)}{(1)(2)}=1>0.
\]
This is inverse response.

Set $\dot y(t)=0$:
\[
4e^{-t}=6e^{-2t}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
e^{-t}=\frac23
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
t=\ln\frac32.
\]
The value there is
\[
y\Bigl(\ln\frac32\Bigr)
=1-4\cdot\frac23+3\cdot\frac49
=1-\frac83+\frac43
=-\frac13.
\]
The second derivative $\ddot y(t)=-4e^{-t}+12e^{-2t}$ equals
$-8/3+16/3=8/3>0$ at this instant, so the critical point is a minimum.
No other positive root of $\dot y=0$ exists, because $e^{-t}$ is
one-to-one.
\[
\boxed{y_{\min}=-1/3\text{ at }t=\ln(3/2),\quad y(\infty)=1}.
\]

The numerator $2(1-s)$ vanishes at $s=+1$, a real right-half-plane zero.
\[
\boxed{\text{RHP zero }+1}.
\]

Sentence (i) either replaces $T$ by the minimum-phase mate
$2(1+s)/[(s+1)(s+2)]$, which has no undershoot, or multiplies $T$ by
$-1$ via the factor $(s-1)$, which reverses the DC gain. In either
case the inverse-response picture is destroyed. Sentence (ii) invents
the critical time $\ln 2$ or $1/2$ and cannot recover the depth $-1/3$.

The calculation never convolves two causal exponentials as a Signals
kernel, never treats an undamped resonance or an impulsive actuator,
and never substitutes a Routh count for the time-domain minimum.

graderFixtures.proofText: Partial fractions give $y=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}$. Then $\dot y(0^+)=-2<0$, the unique minimum is $y=-1/3$ at $t=\ln(3/2)$, the final value is $T(0)=1$, and the RHP zero is $+1$. Flipping the zero or moving the critical time destroys the inverse-response numbers.
Only the poles matter, so I replace T by 2(1+s)/[(s+1)(s+2)]=2/(s+2). The step is 1-e^{-2t}, which never goes negative.
I set the two exponentials equal without the coefficients 4 and 6, so the critical time is ln 2. At that instant I evaluate y as -1, or I declare there is no undershoot and ymin=0.

CTRL:010220.title: L=K(s+2)/[s^2(s+5)] is type 2, stable iff K>0, and the t^2/2 error is 5/(2K)
CTRL:010220.objective: Form the characteristic polynomial s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K and prove Hurwitz stability iff K>0, classify the loop as type 2 with zero step and ramp errors, compute Ka=2K/5, and show the parabolic error 5/(2K) equals 1/2 at K=5.
CTRL:010220.statement:
A unity-negative-feedback loop has open-loop transfer
\[
L(s)=\frac{K(s+2)}{s^2(s+5)},\qquad K\in\mathbb R.
\]
The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is $1+L(s)=0$ after clearing
the open-loop denominator. The system type is the number of poles of
$L$ at $s=0$. The position, velocity, and acceleration error constants
are
\[
K_p=\lim_{s\to 0}L(s),\qquad
K_v=\lim_{s\to 0}sL(s),\qquad
K_a=\lim_{s\to 0}s^2L(s),
\]
when the limits exist in $[0,\infty]$. For a type-$2$ loop the unit-step
and unit-ramp errors vanish, and the error to the parabola $r(t)=t^2/2$
(for $t\ge 0$) is $1/K_a$ whenever $K_a\in(0,\infty)$ and the closed
loop is stable.

1. Clear the characteristic equation and obtain a monic cubic in $s$.
   Build the Routh array of that cubic (this is an ordinary array: no
   zero row and no zero leading entry for $K\ne 0$). Prove that every
   first-column entry is positive if and only if $K>0$.

2. Read the system type from $L$. Evaluate $K_p$, $K_v$, and $K_a$,
   and conclude the unit-step and unit-ramp errors.

3. For the reference $r(t)=t^2/2$ write the steady error in terms of
   $K$. Determine the unique positive gain at which that error equals
   $1/2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “there is only one free integrator after
   cancelling $s$ against $s+2$, so the loop is type $1$ and the ramp
   error is positive”; (ii) “$K_a=K$ or $K_a=K/5$, so the parabolic
   error equals $1/2$ at $K=1$ or at $K=5/2$.”

Do not replace the cubic by the exceptional fourth-order Routh pair
from the intake seed, and do not construct a root locus or a sampled
alias.
permittedResults: A cubic $s^3+a_2 s^2+a_1 s+a_0$ with real coefficients is Hurwitz if and only if $a_2>0$, $a_0>0$, and $a_2 a_1>a_0$.
For a stable type-$k$ loop the error to $t^m/m!$ vanishes when $m<k$ and equals $1/K_{m}$ (in the standard $K_p,K_v,K_a$ notation) when $m=k$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Clear 1+L to a cubic, run the four-row Routh array, then evaluate the three limits that define Kp, Kv, and Ka.
Apply the Hurwitz inequalities a2>0, a0>0, a2 a1>a0 to lock K>0, then read type and Ka directly from the two free integrators and the DC value of s^2 L.

milestones.criterion: Derives s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K and proves closed-loop stability if and only if K>0 by a regular Routh or Hurwitz test.
Classifies the loop as type 2, obtains Ka=2K/5, and shows the t^2/2 error is 5/(2K), equal to 1/2 at K=5.
Rejects counting the type as 1 and rejects an acceleration constant other than 2K/5.

commonErrors.description: Cancels one integrator against the zero at -2, declares the loop type 1, and reports a positive unit-ramp error.
commonErrors.consequence: The type-2 conclusions (zero ramp error, finite Ka, parabolic error 5/(2K)) are replaced by a type-1 story.

commonErrors.description: Computes Ka=K or Ka=K/5 (or 2K), so the parabolic error is not 5/(2K) and the gain that makes the error 1/2 is not K=5.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity Ka=2K/5 coming from lim K(s+2)/(s+5) is lost.

hintTree.content: Clearing $1+L=0$ produces $s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K=0$. The Routh $s^1$ entry is $3K/5$.
Two poles at the origin make the loop type $2$, so $K_p=K_v=\infty$ and both the step and the ramp errors vanish.
Then $K_a=\lim K(s+2)/(s+5)=2K/5$, and $5/(2K)=1/2$ forces $K=5$.

CTRL:010220.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic equation is
\[
1+\frac{K(s+2)}{s^2(s+5)}=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
s^2(s+5)+K(s+2)=0,
\]
hence the monic cubic
\[
s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K}.
\]
The Routh array (ordinary, for $K\ne 0$) is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
s^3&1&K\\
s^2&5&2K\\
s^1&3K/5&0\\
s^0&2K&
\end{array}
\]
because the $s^1$ entry is
\[
-\frac1{5}\det\begin{pmatrix}1&K\\5&2K\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{5K-2K}{5}=\frac{3K}{5}.
\]
The first column is $1$, $5$, $3K/5$, $2K$. Every entry is positive if
and only if $K>0$. Equivalently, the Hurwitz test on the cubic requires
$5>0$, $2K>0$, and $5\cdot K>2K$, all of which reduce to $K>0$. For
$K=0$ the polynomial is $s^2(s+5)$ and is not Hurwitz. For $K<0$ the
last two first-column entries are negative, and there is a single
right-half-plane root.
\[
\boxed{\text{stable iff }K>0}.
\]

The open-loop transfer has a double pole at $s=0$ and no cancellation
against the finite zero $s=-2$. The loop is therefore type $2$. The
error constants are
\[
K_p=\lim_{s\to 0}L(s)=\infty,
\qquad
K_v=\lim_{s\to 0}sL(s)=\infty,
\qquad
K_a=\lim_{s\to 0}s^2L(s)=\lim_{s\to 0}\frac{K(s+2)}{s+5}=\frac{2K}{5}.
\]
A stable type-$2$ loop then has vanishing unit-step and unit-ramp
errors.
\[
\boxed{\text{type }2,\quad K_a=2K/5,\quad e_{\mathrm{step}}=e_{\mathrm{ramp}}=0}.
\]

The reference $r(t)=t^2/2$ is the inverse Laplace of $1/s^3$. For
$K>0$ the parabolic error is
\[
e_{ss}=\frac{1}{K_a}=\frac{5}{2K}.
\]
The identity $5/(2K)=1/2$ forces $K=5$. At that gain one has
$K_a=2$ and $e_{ss}=1/2$, as required.
\[
\boxed{e_{ss}=5/(2K)\text{ for }r=t^2/2;\quad e_{ss}=1/2\text{ at }K=5}.
\]

Sentence (i) invents a cancellation of one integrator against the zero
at $-2$. That cancellation does not occur, the type is not $1$, and the
ramp error is not positive. Sentence (ii) drops either the numerator
value $2$ or the denominator value $5$ from $K_a$, and therefore
solves the wrong gain equation for the error $1/2$.

The cubic is regular: it is not the intake pair of exceptional
fourth-order Routh polynomials, and the argument never draws a root
locus or a sampled-data alias.

graderFixtures.proofText: The characteristic polynomial is $s^3+5s^2+Ks+2K$, stable iff $K>0$. The loop is type $2$, so step and ramp errors vanish. Then $K_a=2K/5$ and the error to $r=t^2/2$ is $5/(2K)$, which equals $1/2$ at $K=5$. A type-$1$ count or a wrong $K_a$ factor is incorrect.
Cancel one s against s+2 at DC. Only one integrator remains, so the loop is type 1 and a unit ramp has a positive finite error.
Ka is the DC value of L after removing s^2, but I drop the 2 and write Ka=K/5. Then 5/K=1/2 forces K=10, or I drop the 5 and write Ka=2K so K=1 makes the error 1/2.

CTRL:010221.title: P=I/2 solves the Lyapunov equation for A=[[-1,1],[-1,-1]] and the state norm decays as e^{-t}
CTRL:010221.objective: Verify that P=I/2 solves A^T P+PA=-I for the assigned A, identify V=||x||^2/2 and Vdot=-||x||^2=-2V, construct exp(At)=e^{-t}[[cos t, sin t],[-sin t, cos t]], and conclude ||x(t)||=e^{-t}||x(0)||.
CTRL:010221.statement:
Consider the planar linear system $\dot x=Ax$ with the assigned matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^2$. A symmetric
positive-definite matrix $P$ is said to solve the Lyapunov equation
for $Q=I$ when
\[
A^TP+PA=-I.
\]
The associated quadratic Lyapunov function is $V(x)=x^TPx$.

1. Take $P=I/2$. Compute $A^T+A$ and verify the Lyapunov identity
   $A^TP+PA=-I$. Write $V$ in terms of $\|x\|$, differentiate $V$
   along $\dot x=Ax$, and prove
   \[
   \dot V=-\|x\|^2=-2V.
   \]

2. Factor $A=-I+R$ with $R=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
   Using $R^2=-I$, compute the matrix exponential $e^{Rt}$ and hence
   $e^{At}$. Write the result as a scalar exponential times an explicit
   $2\times 2$ matrix of trigonometric functions.

3. Deduce the exact Euclidean-norm decay
   $\|x(t)\|=e^{-t}\|x(0)\|$. Reconcile this formula with the
   differential identity $\dot V=-2V$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$P=I$ already solves the Lyapunov
   equation, so $V=\|x\|^2$ and $\dot V=-\|x\|^2$ can be used
   interchangeably with $\dot V=-2V$”; (ii) “the rotation factor is
   the counterclockwise matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\ \sin t&\cos t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
   as in the planar linearization $x'=-x-y$, $y'=x-y$.”

Do not replace $A$ by that opposite-rotation linearization, by a
defective Jordan block, or by a nonlinear pair with the same
linearization and opposite stability, and do not run a Routh test in
place of the Lyapunov identity.
permittedResults: If $A=-I+R$ and $IR=RI$, then $e^{At}=e^{-t}e^{Rt}$.
A real $2\times 2$ rotation matrix is orthogonal, so it preserves the Euclidean norm.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the symmetric part A^T+A=-2I, scale by I/2, then exponentiate A=-I+R from the series for e^{Rt}.
Integrate Vdot=-2V to lock the norm decay e^{-t}, then identify the remaining orthogonal factor by solving the two scalar ODEs for the columns of exp(At).

milestones.criterion: Verifies that P=I/2 solves A^TP+PA=-I and obtains V=||x||^2/2 with Vdot=-||x||^2=-2V.
Constructs exp(At)=e^{-t}[[cos t, sin t],[-sin t, cos t]] and concludes ||x(t)||=e^{-t}||x(0)||.
Rejects taking P=I as the Lyapunov solution and rejects the opposite-rotation semigroup.

commonErrors.description: Claims that P=I solves A^TP+PA=-I, and treats V=||x||^2 with Vdot=-||x||^2 as interchangeable with Vdot=-2V.
commonErrors.consequence: The Lyapunov equation is off by a factor of 2, and the identities V=||x||^2/2 and Vdot=-2V are lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes exp(At)=e^{-t}[[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]], the counterclockwise factor belonging to [[-1,-1],[1,-1]] rather than to the assigned A.
commonErrors.consequence: The semigroup is that of a different matrix, and the assigned clockwise rotation is not obtained.

hintTree.content: The symmetric part is $A^T+A=-2I$. Multiplying by $P=I/2$ therefore yields $A^TP+PA=-I$.
Along the flow, $\dot V=x^T(A^TP+PA)x=-\|x\|^2$. But $V=\|x\|^2/2$, so $\dot V=-2V$.
The series for $e^{Rt}$ is $\cos t\,I+\sin t\,R$, hence $e^{At}=e^{-t}\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

CTRL:010221.canonicalSolution:
The transpose is
\[
A^T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
so the symmetric part is
\[
A^T+A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}=-2I.
\]
With $P=I/2$ one has $A^TP+PA=\tfrac12(A^T+A)=-I$, which is the
required Lyapunov identity.
\[
\boxed{P=I/2\text{ solves }A^TP+PA=-I}.
\]
The Lyapunov function is therefore
\[
V(x)=x^TPx=\frac12\|x\|^2.
\]
Differentiating along $\dot x=Ax$ gives
\[
\dot V=x^T(A^TP+PA)x=-\|x\|^2=-2V.
\]
\[
\boxed{V=\|x\|^2/2,\quad \dot V=-\|x\|^2=-2V}.
\]

Write $A=-I+R$ with
\[
R=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then $R^2=-I$, $R^3=-R$, and $R^4=I$. The exponential series collapses
to
\[
e^{Rt}
=\Bigl(\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{(-1)^k t^{2k}}{(2k)!}\Bigr)I
+\Bigl(\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{(-1)^k t^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\Bigr)R
=\cos t\,I+\sin t\,R
=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Because $-I$ commutes with $R$,
\[
e^{At}=e^{-t}e^{Rt}
=e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{e^{At}=e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
The trigonometric factor is orthogonal (its columns are orthonormal and
its determinant is $1$), so it preserves the Euclidean norm. Therefore
\[
\|x(t)\|=\bigl\|e^{At}x(0)\bigr\|=e^{-t}\|x(0)\|.
\]
The same decay follows from $\dot V=-2V$: separation of variables
yields $V(t)=V(0)e^{-2t}$, hence
$\|x(t)\|^2=\|x(0)\|^2 e^{-2t}$, and the nonnegative square root is
$\|x(t)\|=e^{-t}\|x(0)\|$.
\[
\boxed{\|x(t)\|=e^{-t}\|x(0)\|}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $P$ by $I$. Then $A^TI+IA=-2I$, not $-I$, so
$P=I$ does not solve the stated equation, and the identities
$\dot V=-\|x\|^2$ and $\dot V=-2V$ cannot hold simultaneously for
$V=\|x\|^2$. Sentence (ii) inserts the opposite rotation
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\ \sin t&\cos t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
which is $e^{tS}$ for $S=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
and belongs to the different matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
That matrix is the linearization of the unused DE intake pair; it is
not the assigned $A$.

The argument never passes to a defective Jordan form, never introduces
a nonlinear remainder, and never substitutes a Routh count for the
Lyapunov identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The symmetric part $A^T+A=-2I$ shows that $P=I/2$ solves $A^TP+PA=-I$. Then $V=\|x\|^2/2$ and $\dot V=-\|x\|^2=-2V$. Factoring $A=-I+R$ produces $e^{At}=e^{-t}[[\cos t,\sin t],[-\sin t,\cos t]]$ and $\|x(t)\|=e^{-t}\|x(0)\|$. Taking $P=I$ or flipping the rotation sense is incorrect.
P=I already works because A is Hurwitz, so V=||x||^2 and Vdot=-||x||^2. That is the same statement as Vdot=-2V.
Every planar focus rotates counterclockwise, so exp(At)=e^{-t}[[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]], the same semigroup as x'=-x-y, y'=x-y.

CTRL:010322.title: The K/[s(s+2)(s+4)] locus breaks away at -2+2sqrt(3)/3 and crosses at K=48
CTRL:010322.objective: Construct the positive-K Evans locus of K/[s(s+2)(s+4)]: real segments (-inf,-4) and (-2,0), centroid -2, asymptotes 60/180/300, the unique valid breakaway s=-2+2sqrt(3)/3 at K=16sqrt(3)/9, and the imaginary-axis crossing K=48 at ±j 2sqrt(2) with third pole -6.
CTRL:010322.statement:
Consider the negative-unity-feedback loop with open-loop transfer
\[
L(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s+4)},\qquad K>0.
\]
There are no finite zeros. The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is
\[
s(s+2)(s+4)+K=s^3+6s^2+8s+K.
\]
Work throughout with the standard Evans construction for a real
parameter $K>0$: a test point $s$ lies on the locus if and only if
$\angle L_0(s)=180^\circ$ (odd multiple), where $L_0(s)=1/(s(s+2)(s+4))$,
and the gain is $K=-1/L_0(s)$.

1. Mark the open-loop poles. Apply the real-axis rule and prove that the
   positive-$K$ real locus is exactly the union of the two open segments
   $(-\infty,-4)$ and $(-2,0)$. Identify the complementary intervals that
   are absent from the positive-$K$ locus.

2. Compute the centroid of the asymptotes and the three asymptote angles.
   Confirm that the large-$|s|$ branches depart at $60^\circ$, $180^\circ$,
   and $300^\circ$ from the centroid.

3. Stationarise $K(s)=-s(s+2)(s+4)$ (equivalently, impose
   $\sum 1/(s-p_i)=0$). Prove that the critical points are
   \[
   s=-2\pm\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}.
   \]
   Evaluate $K$ at both roots. Identify the unique valid positive-$K$
   breakaway, and explain why the other critical point is not a
   breakaway of this locus.

4. Substitute $s=j\omega$ into the characteristic polynomial and separate
   real and imaginary parts. Prove that the unique positive-frequency
   imaginary-axis crossing occurs at $K=48$, $\omega=\pm 2\sqrt2$. Factor
   the cubic at that gain and identify the third closed-loop pole.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “every real root of $dK/ds=0$ is a
   breakaway, so $s=-2-2\sqrt3/3$ is on the locus”; (ii) “the reduced
   cancelled hidden-mode locus of the intake seed is the same
   construction, so the unstable cancelled pole may be ignored.”

Do not replace the plant by a cancelled nonminimal realization, and do
not invoke an exceptional Routh array as a substitute for the Evans
geometry.
permittedResults: For $n$ poles, $m$ zeros and $n>m$, the $n-m$ asymptotes radiate from $\sigma_a=(\sum p_i-\sum z_j)/(n-m)$ at angles $(2q+1)180^\circ/(n-m)$, $q=0,\ldots,n-m-1$.
A purely imaginary root $s=j\omega$ of $s^3+6s^2+8s+K=0$ forces the pair of real equations $K-6\omega^2=0$ and $\omega(8-\omega^2)=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the real-axis odd-count rule and the centroid formula, then stationarise K(s)=-s(s+2)(s+4) and substitute s=j omega into the cubic.
Use the sum-of-reciprocals condition for breakaways and Routh on s^3+6s^2+8s+K only as a cross-check of the same imaginary-axis pair, keeping the Evans geometry primary.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the real locus (-inf,-4) union (-2,0), the centroid -2, and the asymptotes 60/180/300.
Produces the unique valid breakaway s=-2+2sqrt(3)/3 at K=16sqrt(3)/9 and the crossing K=48 at ±j 2sqrt(2) with third pole -6.
Rejects the off-locus critical point as a breakaway and refuses the cancelled hidden-mode seed.

commonErrors.description: Treats s=-2-2sqrt(3)/3 as a valid positive-K breakaway, or claims both roots of 3s^2+12s+8=0 lie on the locus.
commonErrors.consequence: A negative-K critical point in the even-count gap (-4,-2) is reported as a breakaway, and K=16sqrt(3)/9 is no longer attached to a unique real departure.

commonErrors.description: Misses K=48 at ±j 2sqrt(2), or reports the third pole as -2 or -4 instead of -6, or replaces the crossing by an exceptional Routh or hidden-mode construction.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique imaginary-axis event of the cubic is lost, and the factorisation (s^2+8)(s+6) is never produced.

hintTree.content: On the real axis, the odd-count rule keeps only $(-\infty,-4)$ and $(-2,0)$. The centroid of three poles and no zeros is $-2$.
The condition $1/s+1/(s+2)+1/(s+4)=0$ expands to $3s^2+12s+8=0$, whose roots are $-2\pm 2\sqrt3/3$. Only the root in $(-2,0)$ has $K>0$.
At $s=j\omega$ the imaginary part of the cubic is $\omega(8-\omega^2)$. The nonzero roots $\omega=\pm 2\sqrt2$ give $K=6\omega^2=48$, and the cubic is then $(s^2+8)(s+6)$.

CTRL:010322.canonicalSolution:
The open-loop poles are $0$, $-2$, and $-4$. There are no finite zeros.
A real test point $s$ lies on the positive-$K$ locus if and only if the
number of real poles strictly to its right is odd. That count is $3$ on
$(-\infty,-4)$, $2$ on $(-4,-2)$, $1$ on $(-2,0)$, and $0$ on $(0,\infty)$.
Hence the real locus is exactly
\[
(-\infty,-4)\cup(-2,0).
\]
The complementary intervals $(-4,-2)$ and $(0,\infty)$ are absent.

With $n=3$ and $m=0$ the centroid is
\[
\sigma_a=\frac{0+(-2)+(-4)}{3}=-2,
\]
and the asymptote angles are
\[
\frac{(2q+1)180^\circ}{3}=60^\circ,\;180^\circ,\;300^\circ
\quad(q=0,1,2).
\]
The $180^\circ$ asymptote is the negative real axis already identified.

Write $K(s)=-s(s+2)(s+4)$. Stationarity $K'(s)=0$ is equivalent to
\[
\frac1s+\frac1{s+2}+\frac1{s+4}=0,
\]
or $(s+2)(s+4)+s(s+4)+s(s+2)=0$, which expands to
\[
3s^2+12s+8=0.
\]
The discriminant is $144-96=48=16\cdot 3$, so
\[
s=\frac{-12\pm 4\sqrt3}{6}=-2\pm\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}.
\]
At $s_+=-2+2\sqrt3/3$ one has $s_+\in(-2,0)$, hence $s_+$ lies on the
locus. The three factors are $s_+=-2+a$, $s_++2=a$, $s_++4=2+a$ with
$a=2\sqrt3/3$ and $a^2=4/3$, so
\[
s_+(s_++2)(s_++4)=a(a^2-4)=a\Bigl(-\frac83\Bigr)=-\frac{16\sqrt3}{9},
\]
and therefore $K(s_+)=16\sqrt3/9>0$. This is the unique valid breakaway.

At $s_-=-2-2\sqrt3/3$ one has $s_-\in(-4,-2)$, which fails the real-axis
rule. The same algebra with $b=2\sqrt3/3$ gives
$s_-(s_-+2)(s_-+4)=b(4-b^2)=16\sqrt3/9$, hence $K(s_-)=-16\sqrt3/9<0$.
The point is a critical point of the complementary negative-$K$ locus,
not a breakaway of the problem.
\[
\boxed{s=-2+2\sqrt3/3,\quad K=16\sqrt3/9}.
\]

Now set $s=j\omega$ in $s^3+6s^2+8s+K=0$:
\[
-j\omega^3-6\omega^2+8j\omega+K=0,
\]
so
\[
K-6\omega^2=0,\qquad \omega(8-\omega^2)=0.
\]
The roots are $\omega=0$ (which recovers the pole at the origin, $K=0$)
and $\omega=\pm\sqrt8=\pm 2\sqrt2$. The latter give
\[
K=6\cdot 8=48.
\]
At this gain the cubic factors as $(s^2+8)(s+6)=s^3+6s^2+8s+48$, so the
third closed-loop pole is $-6$. The pair $\pm j 2\sqrt2$ is therefore the
unique positive-frequency imaginary-axis crossing.
\[
\boxed{K=48\text{ at }s=\pm j 2\sqrt2;\quad\text{third pole }-6}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats every critical point of $K$ as a breakaway. The root
$s_-$ has negative gain and fails the real-axis rule, so it is not on
this locus. Sentence (ii) replaces the present three-pole plant by the
intake cancelled hidden-mode realization; that seed has an unstable
unobservable pole and a different Evans diagram. No cancellation occurs
here, and no exceptional Routh construction is required.

The argument never introduces a nonminimal cancelled pole.

graderFixtures.proofText: Real loci $(-\infty,-4)$ and $(-2,0)$; centroid $-2$; asymptotes $60^\circ/180^\circ/300^\circ$. The only positive-$K$ breakaway is $s=-2+2\sqrt3/3$ at $K=16\sqrt3/9$. The $j\omega$ crossing is $K=48$ at $\pm j 2\sqrt2$, with third pole $-6$. The root $s=-2-2\sqrt3/3$ has $K<0$ and is off the locus.
Both roots of 3s^2+12s+8=0 are breakaways, including s=-2-2sqrt(3)/3 between the poles -4 and -2. I place a real departure there for K>0 and do not check the real-axis count or the sign of K.

The imaginary-axis test gives omega=sqrt(8) but I leave K unspecified, or I take the third pole to be the open-loop pole -2. Alternatively I replace the construction by the cancelled hidden-mode seed and ignore the unstable cancelled pole.

CTRL:010323.title: The lead of z=1/sqrt(3), p=sqrt(3) makes |L(j)|=1 with phase -105 and PM 75
CTRL:010323.objective: For P=1/[s(s+1)] and C=sqrt(2/3)(1+s/z)/(1+s/p) with z=1/sqrt(3), p=sqrt(3), evaluate the lead at omega=1 to magnitude sqrt(3) and phase 30, prove |L(j)|=1 with loop phase -105 and phase margin 75, and refuse a plant-only margin or a hidden-mode substitution.
CTRL:010323.statement:
Let the plant and the cascade lead be
\[
P(s)=\frac1{s(s+1)},\qquad
C(s)=\sqrt{\frac23}\,\frac{1+s/z}{1+s/p},
\]
with the exact zero-pole pair
\[
z=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad p=\sqrt3.
\]
The loop transfer is $L(s)=C(s)P(s)$. Frequencies are in radians per
second. No additional loop gain is present.

1. Evaluate the frequency-sensitive factor $(1+s/z)/(1+s/p)$ at
   $s=j$. Prove that its magnitude is $\sqrt3$ and its phase is
   $+30^\circ$. Then include the constant $\sqrt{2/3}$ and obtain
   $C(j)$.

2. Evaluate $P(j)$. Compute $|L(j)|$ and $\angle L(j)$. Conclude that
   $\omega=1$ is a gain crossover, and compute the phase margin.

3. Identify $\omega=1$ as the geometric mean $\sqrt{zp}$ of the lead
   corner frequencies, and record the lead ratio $\alpha=z/p=1/3$.
   Explain why the constant $\sqrt{2/3}$ is required if the midband
   frequency is to be an exact unity-gain crossover of $L$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the uncompensated plant already has
   $|P(j)|=1$, so the phase margin is $180^\circ-135^\circ=45^\circ$
   and the lead is only a phase decoration”; (ii) “the calculation is
   a hidden-mode or cancelled-locus exercise, so the compensator may
   be dropped.”

Do not replace $P$ by $K/[s(s+2)(s+4)]$, and do not invoke a Nyquist
encirclement count in place of the exact Bode arithmetic at $\omega=1$.
permittedResults: If $z=1/\sqrt3$ and $p=\sqrt3$, then $\sqrt{zp}=1$ and $p/z=3$, so the midband lead factor has magnitude $\sqrt3$ and phase $\arctan\sqrt3-\arctan(1/\sqrt3)=60^\circ-30^\circ=30^\circ$.
The identity $P(j)=1/(-1+j)$ gives $|P(j)|=1/\sqrt2$ and $\angle P(j)=-135^\circ$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate 1+j/z and 1+j/p in polar form, multiply by the prefactor, then add the plant polar form -1+j.
Recognise omega=1 as sqrt(zp), read midband lead as sqrt(p/z) angle +30, and choose the displayed constant so that |C P|=1 at that frequency.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the lead factor at omega=1 as magnitude sqrt(3) and phase +30, and includes the prefactor to obtain |C(j)|=sqrt(2).
Proves |L(j)|=1, loop phase -105 degrees, and phase margin 75 degrees.
Rejects a plant-only crossover claim and any hidden-mode or Evans substitution.

commonErrors.description: Omits the constant sqrt(2/3), reports the lead magnitude as 1 or as sqrt(2/3) rather than sqrt(3), or concludes |L(j)| is not 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The designed unity-gain crossover at omega=1 is lost, and the subsequent phase-margin statement is attached to the wrong frequency.

commonErrors.description: Uses only angle P=-135 and reports PM=45, or reports loop phase -150 or PM=105, or claims |P(j)|=1 so the lead does not change the crossover.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair (loop phase -105, PM 75) is never obtained.

hintTree.content: At $s=j$ one has $1+j/z=1+j\sqrt3$ (magnitude $2$, angle $60^\circ$) and $1+j/p=1+j/\sqrt3$ (magnitude $2/\sqrt3$, angle $30^\circ$).
The constant $\sqrt{2/3}$ times the midband factor $\sqrt3$ produces $|C(j)|=\sqrt2$. Combined with $|P(j)|=1/\sqrt2$ this forces $|L(j)|=1$.
Loop phase is $30^\circ-135^\circ=-105^\circ$, so the phase margin is $75^\circ$.

CTRL:010323.canonicalSolution:
The lead corners satisfy $\sqrt{zp}=\sqrt{1}=1$ and $p/z=3$. At
$s=j$,
\[
1+\frac{j}{z}=1+j\sqrt3,\qquad
\bigl|1+j\sqrt3\bigr|=2,\qquad
\angle(1+j\sqrt3)=60^\circ,
\]
\[
1+\frac{j}{p}=1+\frac{j}{\sqrt3},\qquad
\Bigl|1+\frac{j}{\sqrt3}\Bigr|=\sqrt{1+\frac13}=\frac2{\sqrt3},\qquad
\angle\Bigl(1+\frac{j}{\sqrt3}\Bigr)=30^\circ.
\]
The frequency-sensitive factor therefore has magnitude
$2/(2/\sqrt3)=\sqrt3$ and phase $60^\circ-30^\circ=+30^\circ$. Including
the constant,
\[
\bigl|C(j)\bigr|=\sqrt{\frac23}\cdot\sqrt3=\sqrt2,\qquad
\angle C(j)=+30^\circ.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{lead factor }\sqrt3\angle 30^\circ;\quad C(j)=\sqrt2\angle 30^\circ}.
\]

The plant at the same frequency is
\[
P(j)=\frac1{j(j+1)}=\frac1{-1+j}.
\]
Thus $|P(j)|=1/\sqrt2$ and $\angle P(j)=-135^\circ$. The loop is
\[
\bigl|L(j)\bigr|=\sqrt2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt2}=1,\qquad
\angle L(j)=30^\circ-135^\circ=-105^\circ.
\]
So $\omega=1$ is a gain crossover, and the phase margin is
\[
180^\circ+(-105^\circ)=75^\circ.
\]
\[
\boxed{|L(j)|=1,\quad\angle L(j)=-105^\circ,\quad\mathrm{PM}=75^\circ}.
\]

Without the prefactor $\sqrt{2/3}$, the midband lead magnitude $\sqrt3$
would give $|L(j)|=\sqrt3/\sqrt2\neq 1$. The constant is exactly the
number that converts the geometric-mean frequency into an exact
unity-gain crossover. Equivalently, $\alpha=z/p=1/3$ and
$\sin\phi_m=(1-\alpha)/(1+\alpha)=1/2$, recovering $\phi_m=30^\circ$.

Sentence (i) asserts $|P(j)|=1$. In fact $|P(j)|=1/\sqrt2$, so
$\omega=1$ is not an uncompensated gain crossover, and a plant-only
margin of $45^\circ$ is the wrong object. Sentence (ii) replaces the
compensated loop by the cancelled hidden-mode seed; no pole-zero
cancellation occurs in $C$ or $P$, and the numbers above are ordinary
Bode arithmetic.

The argument never forms a three-pole Evans diagram and never counts
Nyquist encirclements.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $\omega=1$ the lead factor has magnitude $\sqrt3$ and phase $+30^\circ$, so $C(j)=\sqrt2\angle 30^\circ$. Then $|P(j)|=1/\sqrt2$, $|L(j)|=1$, $\angle L(j)=-105^\circ$, and $\mathrm{PM}=75^\circ$. The prefactor $\sqrt{2/3}$ is required for an exact crossover; a plant-only $45^\circ$ margin is the wrong object.
I evaluate only (1+s/z)/(1+s/p) and ignore sqrt(2/3), or I treat that constant as the lead magnitude. Then |L(j)| is sqrt(3)/sqrt(2) or 1/sqrt(2), not 1, so omega=1 is not a gain crossover.
The plant already satisfies |P(j)|=1 with angle -135, so the phase margin is 45 degrees and the lead is optional decoration. I never add the lead phase to the plant phase.
