CTRL:010324.title: For L=K/[(s-1)(s+2)] the full Nyquist image encircles -1 once CCW when K>2
CTRL:010324.objective: Prove that the closed loop of L=K/[(s-1)(s+2)] is stable iff K>2, is marginal at K=2, and has one RHP pole for 0<K<2; then show that the full omega in (-inf,inf) Nyquist image gives one counterclockwise encirclement of -1 precisely when K>2, cancelling the single open-loop RHP pole.
CTRL:010324.statement:
Let the open-loop transfer of a negative-unity-feedback system be
\[
L(s)=\frac{K}{(s-1)(s+2)},\qquad K>0.
\]
The open-loop poles are $+1$ and $-2$, so the open loop is unstable.
The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is
\[
(s-1)(s+2)+K=s^2+s+(K-2).
\]
The standard Nyquist $D$-contour traverses the imaginary axis from
$-j\infty$ to $+j\infty$ and closes with a large clockwise semicircle
in the right half-plane. There are no open-loop poles on the imaginary
axis, so no indentation is required. Write $N_{\mathrm{ccw}}$ for the
number of counterclockwise encirclements of the point $-1$ by the image
of the full imaginary-axis traversal $\omega\in(-\infty,+\infty)$,
counting the large-arc image (which is the origin, since the relative
degree is two). The closed-loop right-half-plane count is
$Z=P-N_{\mathrm{ccw}}$, where $P$ is the number of open-loop
right-half-plane poles.

1. Apply the Routh–Hurwitz criterion (or the elementary conditions on
   a real quadratic) to $s^2+s+(K-2)$. Prove that the closed loop is
   asymptotically stable if and only if $K>2$, that $K=2$ is
   marginally stable, and that there is exactly one closed-loop
   right-half-plane pole when $0<K<2$.

2. Compute $L(j\omega)$ in real and imaginary parts. Show that
   $\operatorname{Re}L(j\omega)<0$ for every finite $\omega$, that the
   only real-axis meeting is $L(0)=-K/2$, and that the image for
   $\omega\in(-\infty,+\infty)$ is a simple oval in the closed left
   half-plane joining $0$ to $-K/2$.

3. Determine the orientation of that oval as $\omega$ increases, and
   decide for which $K>0$ the point $-1$ lies in its interior. Conclude
   that $N_{\mathrm{ccw}}=1$ if $K>2$ and $N_{\mathrm{ccw}}=0$ if
   $0<K<2$. Reconcile the count with $P=1$ and with part 1.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “an unstable open loop cannot be
   stabilised by constant gain, so the oval never encircles $-1$”;
   (ii) “clockwise and counterclockwise counts may be swapped, or the
   open-loop pole at $+1$ may be forgotten, so $Z=1$ whenever $K>2$.”

Do not replace the plant by $K/[s(s+2)(s+4)]$, and do not substitute
the exceptional-Routh intake polynomials.
permittedResults: The quadratic $s^2+a s+b$ with $a>0$ is Hurwitz if and only if $b>0$. Here $a=1$ and $b=K-2$.
If $L(j\omega)=K/[(-( \omega^2+2)+j\omega)]$, then $\operatorname{Re}L=-K(\omega^2+2)/D$ and $\operatorname{Im}L=-K\omega/D$ with $D=\omega^4+5\omega^2+4>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Decide stability from the quadratic s^2+s+(K-2), then plot L(j omega) from its real and imaginary parts and read the encirclement of -1 off the oval.
First compute L(0)=-K/2 to see when -1 is interior, then check orientation from the sign of Im L and reconcile Z=P-N_ccw with the quadratic.

milestones.criterion: Proves the closed loop is stable iff K>2, marginal at K=2, and has one RHP pole for 0<K<2.
Shows that the full imaginary-axis image is a left-half oval from 0 to -K/2, traversed CCW, encircling -1 exactly when K>2, so N_ccw=P=1.
Rejects the claim that an unstable open loop cannot be stabilised and rejects a reversed or P-omitted Nyquist count.

commonErrors.description: Claims that an unstable open loop cannot be stabilised by constant K, or that the oval never encircles -1.
commonErrors.consequence: The K>2 stability region and the required counterclockwise encirclement are both denied.

commonErrors.description: Counts a clockwise encirclement, or forgets the open-loop pole at +1, and therefore reports Z=1 or Z=2 for K>2.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity Z=P-N_ccw fails to recover closed-loop stability for K>2.

hintTree.content: The closed-loop polynomial is $s^2+s+(K-2)$. Both coefficients are positive precisely when $K>2$. At $K=2$ the roots are $0$ and $-1$.
$L(0)=-K/2$ and $L(j\omega)\to 0$ as $|\omega|\to\infty$. The imaginary part vanishes only at $\omega=0$, so the image is an oval on $[-K/2,0]$.
As $\omega$ runs from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ the oval is traversed counterclockwise. The point $-1$ is inside if and only if $K/2>1$.

CTRL:010324.canonicalSolution:
The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is
\[
s^2+s+(K-2).
\]
A real monic quadratic is Hurwitz if and only if every coefficient is
positive, hence if and only if $K-2>0$, that is $K>2$. At $K=2$ the
polynomial is $s(s+1)$, with a simple root at the origin, so the loop
is marginally stable. For $0<K<2$ the product of the roots is $K-2<0$,
so the roots are real and of opposite sign: exactly one lies in the
open right half-plane.
\[
\boxed{\text{stable iff }K>2;\quad\text{marginal at }K=2;\quad\text{one RHP for }0<K<2}.
\]

Now $L(j\omega)=K/[(j\omega-1)(j\omega+2)]$. The denominator is
\[
(j\omega-1)(j\omega+2)=-(\omega^2+2)+j\omega,
\]
with squared modulus $D=(\omega^2+2)^2+\omega^2=\omega^4+5\omega^2+4$.
Inversion gives
\[
L(j\omega)=K\frac{-(\omega^2+2)-j\omega}{D}.
\]
Thus $\operatorname{Re}L=-K(\omega^2+2)/D<0$ for every finite $\omega$,
and $\operatorname{Im}L=-K\omega/D$. The imaginary part vanishes only at
$\omega=0$, where $L(0)=-K/2$. As $|\omega|\to\infty$ one has $L\to 0$.
The image of $\omega\in(-\infty,+\infty)$ is therefore a simple oval in
the closed left half-plane whose real-axis span is the segment
$[-K/2,0]$. The large clockwise semicircle of the $D$-contour maps to
the origin and does not add an extra loop about $-1$.

Orientation: as $\omega\to-\infty$, $L$ approaches $0$ from the upper
half-plane; as $\omega$ increases toward $0$, the image travels leftward
along the upper half of the oval to $-K/2$; as $\omega$ continues through
positive values the image returns to $0$ along the lower half. The
interior of the oval therefore lies to the left of the direction of
travel, so the oval is traversed counterclockwise.

The point $-1$ lies in the interior if and only if $-K/2<-1<0$, that is
$K>2$. Hence
\[
N_{\mathrm{ccw}}=\begin{cases}
1,&K>2,\\
0,&0<K<2.
\end{cases}
\]
At $K=2$ the oval passes through $-1$ and the count is undefined
(marginal). The open loop contributes $P=1$. The Nyquist relation
$Z=P-N_{\mathrm{ccw}}$ therefore yields $Z=0$ for $K>2$ and $Z=1$ for
$0<K<2$, matching the quadratic analysis. The single counterclockwise
encirclement present when $K>2$ is exactly the encirclement needed to
cancel the open-loop right-half-plane pole.
\[
\boxed{N_{\mathrm{ccw}}=1\text{ for }K>2,\text{ cancelling }P=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses open-loop instability with closed-loop
impossibility. Constant gain can and does stabilise this plant once
$K>2$, and the oval then does encircle $-1$. Sentence (ii) either
reverses the orientation (reporting a clockwise encirclement, hence
$Z=2$) or forgets $P=1$ (reporting $Z=1$ for $K>2$). Both destroy the
reconciliation with the quadratic.

The argument never uses the three-pole Evans plant and never invokes
the exceptional-Routh intake polynomials.

graderFixtures.proofText: The polynomial $s^2+s+(K-2)$ is Hurwitz iff $K>2$, is marginal at $K=2$, and has one RHP root for $0<K<2$. The full $\omega\in(-\infty,+\infty)$ image is a left-half oval from $0$ to $-K/2$, traversed counterclockwise, so $N_{\mathrm{ccw}}=1$ for $K>2$. That single CCW encirclement cancels the open-loop pole at $+1$.
The open loop already has a pole at +1, so no constant gain can stabilise the closed loop. The Nyquist image stays to the right of -1 for every K, and I report no encirclement.
I count the oval as a clockwise loop about -1 when K>2, and I do not include the open-loop RHP pole in Z=P-N. I conclude the closed loop has one or two RHP poles whenever K>2.

CTRL:010425.title: The pair (A,B,C) is minimal with G=-s/[(s+1)(s+2)] and Rosenbrock kernel ((2,1),2)
CTRL:010425.objective: For A=diag(-1,-2), B=(1,1)^T, C=(1,-2), compute G=-s/[(s+1)(s+2)], prove controllability det=-1 and observability det=2 so the realization is minimal, locate the invariant zero at 0, and exhibit the Rosenbrock null vector (x,u)=((2,1)^T,2).
CTRL:010425.statement:
Consider the continuous-time SISO realization
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu,\qquad y=Cx,
\]
with
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
There is no feedthrough. The Rosenbrock system matrix at a complex
value $s$ is
\[
R(s)=\begin{pmatrix}sI-A&-B\\ C&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
An invariant zero is a number $z\in\mathbb C$ for which $R(z)$ drops
rank; equivalently, there exist $x\in\mathbb C^2$ and $u\in\mathbb C$,
not both zero, with $(sI-A)x=Bu$ and $Cx=0$ at $s=z$. (The input
column is written $-B$ so that $R(s)\begin{pmatrix}x\\ u\end{pmatrix}=0$
reproduces those two equations.)

1. Compute the transfer function $G(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B$ in unreduced
   form and simplify. Identify every finite transmission zero.

2. Form the controllability matrix $\mathcal C=[B\ AB]$ and the
   observability matrix $\mathcal O=\begin{pmatrix}C\\ CA\end{pmatrix}$.
   Compute both determinants and conclude that the realization is
   minimal. Explain why minimality implies that every invariant zero
   is a transmission zero of $G$, and conversely.

3. Solve $R(0)\begin{pmatrix}x\\ u\end{pmatrix}=0$ and exhibit a
   concrete nonzero kernel vector with $u=2$. Confirm that the same
   pair satisfies $Cx=0$ and $-Ax=Bu$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$G$ has a zero at the origin, so the
   realization is nonminimal and the mode at $0$ is a hidden
   cancellation as in the intake seed”; (ii) “controllability or
   observability fails because $A$ is diagonal, or the kernel of
   $R(0)$ is trivial.”

Do not replace $(A,B,C)$ by the intake hidden-mode triple
$\operatorname{diag}(-3,2)$, $(1,1)^T$, $(1,0)$, and do not treat the
problem as a reachable-subspace permutation audit.
permittedResults: If $A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-2)$, then $(sI-A)^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/(s+1),1/(s+2))$ and $G(s)=1/(s+1)-2/(s+2)$.
The two-by-two determinants $\det[B\ AB]=-1$ and $\det\begin{pmatrix}C\\ CA\end{pmatrix}=2$ are equivalent to controllability and observability of this pair.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form G from the resolvent, compute the two 2-by-2 determinants, then solve -A x = B u and C x = 0 at s=0 with the scale u=2.
First guess the transmission zero from the numerator of G, then construct the Rosenbrock kernel and only afterwards confirm controllability and observability.

milestones.criterion: Computes G=-s/[(s+1)(s+2)] and the determinants det[B AB]=-1, det[C; CA]=2, concluding minimality.
Locates the invariant zero at 0 and exhibits the Rosenbrock null vector (x,u)=((2,1)^T,2).
Rejects reading the zero as a hidden cancellation and refuses the intake hidden-mode or permutation-rank plants.

commonErrors.description: Treats the zero of G at the origin as a pole-zero cancellation, declares the realization nonminimal, or substitutes the intake hidden-mode triple.
commonErrors.consequence: A genuine transmission zero of a minimal pair is misread as a hidden mode, and the Rosenbrock kernel is never required.

commonErrors.description: Claims that R(0) has trivial kernel, or reports a kernel other than a scale of ((2,1)^T,2), or asserts that a diagonal A makes the pair uncontrollable or unobservable.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned null vector is lost, and the determinants -1 and 2 are contradicted.

hintTree.content: $AB=(-1,-2)^T$, hence $\det[B\ AB]=-2+1=-1$. Likewise $CA=(-1,4)$ and $\det\mathcal O=4-2=2$.
At $s=0$ the equation $-Ax=Bu$ is $(x_1,2x_2)=(u,u)$. Combined with $x_1-2x_2=0$ this forces $x=(2,1)^T$ when $u=2$.

CTRL:010425.canonicalSolution:
Because $A$ is diagonal,
\[
(sI-A)^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\frac1{s+1},\frac1{s+2}\Bigr),
\]
so
\[
(sI-A)^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}1/(s+1)\\ 1/(s+2)\end{pmatrix}
\]
and
\[
G(s)=\frac1{s+1}-\frac2{s+2}
=\frac{(s+2)-2(s+1)}{(s+1)(s+2)}
=\frac{-s}{(s+1)(s+2)}.
\]
The only finite transmission zero is $s=0$. The poles $-1$ and $-2$
remain, uncancelled.
\[
\boxed{G(s)=-s/[(s+1)(s+2)]}.
\]

The controllability matrix is
\[
\mathcal C=[B\ AB]=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\ 1&-2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det\mathcal C=-2-(-1)=-1\neq 0.
\]
The observability matrix is
\[
\mathcal O=\begin{pmatrix}C\\ CA\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\ -1&4\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det\mathcal O=4-2=2\neq 0.
\]
Thus the pair is controllable and observable, hence minimal. For a
minimal SISO realization there is no cancellation between $C(sI-A)^{-1}B$
and the characteristic polynomial, so the invariant zeros of $R$ are
exactly the finite zeros of $G$. In particular the zero at the origin
is a genuine transmission zero, not a cancelled hidden mode.
\[
\boxed{\det\mathcal C=-1,\quad\det\mathcal O=2;\quad\text{minimal}}.
\]

Now evaluate the Rosenbrock matrix at $s=0$:
\[
R(0)=\begin{pmatrix}-A&-B\\ C&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1\\ 0&2&-1\\ 1&-2&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The kernel equation is $-Ax=Bu$ together with $Cx=0$, that is
\[
x_1=u,\qquad 2x_2=u,\qquad x_1-2x_2=0.
\]
The third equation is dependent. Choosing the convenient scale $u=2$
gives $x_1=2$ and $x_2=1$. The nonzero vector
\[
\begin{pmatrix}x\\ u\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}
\]
therefore spans the kernel, and $R(0)$ is rank-deficient. Equivalently,
$Cx=2-2=0$ and $-Ax=(2,2)^T=B\cdot 2$.
\[
\boxed{\text{invariant zero }0;\quad (x,u)=\bigl((2,1)^T,2\bigr)}.
\]

Sentence (i) reads a transmission zero as a pole-zero cancellation.
The realization is minimal, $G$ still has poles at $-1$ and $-2$, and
the intake hidden-mode triple (unstable unobservable pole at $+2$) is
a different plant. Sentence (ii) claims a rank failure that the two
determinants contradict, or a trivial Rosenbrock kernel that the
explicit vector $(2,1,2)^T$ contradicts.

The argument never permutes a three-state reachable subspace.

graderFixtures.proofText: $G(s)=-s/[(s+1)(s+2)]$. Controllability $\det=-1$ and observability $\det=2$, so the realization is minimal. The invariant zero is $0$, with Rosenbrock kernel $(x,u)=((2,1)^T,2)$. The origin is a transmission zero, not a hidden cancellation.

G has a factor s in the numerator, so a pole is cancelled and the realization is nonminimal. This is the same hidden-mode phenomenon as the intake seed, and I replace (A,B,C) by diag(-3,2) with C=(1,0).
A is diagonal, so the pair cannot be controllable. I also find only the zero solution of R(0)v=0, or I report the kernel vector (1,1,1)^T, which does not satisfy C x=0.

CTRL:010526.title: The ARE 2P-P^2+1=0 has stabilizing root 1+sqrt(2), pole -sqrt(2), and J*=(1+sqrt(2)) x0^2
CTRL:010526.objective: For xdot=x+u and J=int(x^2+u^2), derive the ARE 2P-P^2+1=0, select the stabilizing root P=K=1+sqrt(2), obtain the closed-loop pole -sqrt(2) and the optimal cost (1+sqrt(2))x0^2, and reject the other root whose closed-loop pole is the unstable +sqrt(2).
CTRL:010526.statement:
Consider the scalar linear plant and the infinite-horizon quadratic
cost
\[
\dot x=x+u,\qquad
J=\int_0^\infty\bigl(x(t)^2+u(t)^2\bigr)\,dt,
\]
with free initial state $x(0)=x_0$ and with admissible inputs those
square-integrable feedbacks that render $x\in L^2[0,\infty)$. There is
no cross term in the integrand, the state weight is $Q=1$, and the
control weight is $R=1$. The associated algebraic Riccati equation
for a scalar decision variable $P$ is written in the sign convention
\[
A^\top P+PA-PBR^{-1}B^\top P+Q=0,
\]
which here reduces to a quadratic in $P$. The candidate linear law is
$u=-Kx$ with $K=R^{-1}B^\top P=P$.

1. Substitute $A=1$, $B=1$, $Q=1$, $R=1$ and derive the scalar ARE
   \[
   2P-P^2+1=0.
   \]
   Solve it and record both real roots.

2. For each root compute the gain $K=P$ and the closed-loop pole
   $A-BK=1-K$. Identify the unique stabilizing root, the associated
   gain, and the associated pole. Confirm that the other root produces
   the unstable pole $+\sqrt2$.

3. For the stabilizing $P$, evaluate the optimal cost $J^\star=Px_0^2$.
   Complete the square (or invoke the standard Riccati identity) to
   prove that this $P$ is indeed the cost-to-go of $u=-Px$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “both roots of the ARE are admissible
   costs, so $P=1-\sqrt2$ is an equally valid solution and the
   closed-loop pole $+\sqrt2$ may be kept”; (ii) “the problem is an
   observer-separation exercise, so an estimator pole must be placed
   and the ARE may be ignored.”

Do not introduce a full-order observer, and do not replace the scalar
plant by the two-state separation seed.
permittedResults: With $A=B=Q=R=1$ the ARE $2P-P^2+1=0$ is equivalent to $P^2-2P-1=0$, with roots $1\pm\sqrt2$.
Completing the square gives $x^2+u^2+\frac{d}{dt}(Px^2)=(u+Px)^2+(2P-P^2+1)x^2$. On the ARE the extra term vanishes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the general ARE, specialise to A=B=Q=R=1, then test each root by the sign of 1-P and complete the square for the stabilizing P.
Complete the square first to discover the quadratic 2P-P^2+1, then keep only the root that makes A-BK negative.

milestones.criterion: Derives the ARE 2P-P^2+1=0 and records both roots 1±sqrt(2).
Selects the stabilizing root P=K=1+sqrt(2), obtains the pole -sqrt(2) and the cost (1+sqrt(2)) x0^2, and identifies +sqrt(2) as the unstable companion.
Rejects the negative ARE root as a valid cost and refuses an observer-separation substitution.

commonErrors.description: Treats P=1-sqrt(2) as an admissible cost or stabilizing gain, or reports the closed-loop pole +sqrt(2) as the designed LQR pole.
commonErrors.consequence: The infinite-horizon problem is declared solved by an unstable feedback whose cost is infinite.

commonErrors.description: Writes the wrong scalar ARE (for example P^2-2P+1=0, giving P=1), or replaces the exercise by observer-controller pole separation.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair P=K=1+sqrt(2) and pole -sqrt(2) is never obtained.

hintTree.content: The general ARE collapses to $2P-P^2+1=0$. The quadratic formula produces $P=1\pm\sqrt2$.
Only $P=1+\sqrt2$ is positive. The law $u=-(1+\sqrt2)x$ places the pole at $1-(1+\sqrt2)=-\sqrt2$.
The other root $P=1-\sqrt2$ gives the pole $+\sqrt2$. Along $u=-(1+\sqrt2)x$ one has $J=Px_0^2$ after the square completion.

CTRL:010526.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $A=1$, $B=1$, $Q=1$, $R=1$ into
$A^\top P+PA-PBR^{-1}B^\top P+Q=0$:
\[
P+P-P\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot P+1=0,
\]
that is
\[
2P-P^2+1=0.
\]
Equivalently $P^2-2P-1=0$, so
\[
P=1\pm\sqrt2.
\]
\[
\boxed{2P-P^2+1=0;\quad P=1\pm\sqrt2}.
\]

The candidate gain is $K=P$ and the closed-loop vector field is
$1-K$. For $P_+=1+\sqrt2$ one has $K=1+\sqrt2>0$ and
\[
1-K=1-(1+\sqrt2)=-\sqrt2<0,
\]
so the closed loop is exponentially stable. For $P_-=1-\sqrt2<0$ one
has $K=1-\sqrt2$ and
\[
1-K=1-(1-\sqrt2)=+\sqrt2>0,
\]
so the closed loop is exponentially unstable. Only $P_+$ is a
stabilizing root. A negative cost-to-go is also incompatible with
$J=\int(x^2+u^2)\ge 0$.
\[
\boxed{P=K=1+\sqrt2,\quad\text{pole }-\sqrt2}.
\]

Along any trajectory of $\dot x=x+u$,
\begin{align*}
x^2+u^2+\frac{d}{dt}(Px^2)
&=x^2+u^2+2Px(x+u)\\
&=(u+Px)^2+(2P-P^2+1)x^2.
\end{align*}
On the ARE the second parenthesis vanishes, so
\[
x^2+u^2=\bigl(u+Px\bigr)^2-\frac{d}{dt}(Px^2).
\]
Integrate from $0$ to $T$ and let $T\to\infty$. For every admissible
input one has $x(T)\to 0$, hence
\[
J=Px_0^2+\int_0^\infty\bigl(u+Px\bigr)^2\,dt\ge Px_0^2,
\]
with equality if and only if $u=-Px$. Restricting to the stabilizing
root $P=1+\sqrt2$ therefore yields
\[
J^\star=(1+\sqrt2)\,x_0^2.
\]
The same identity with $P=1-\sqrt2$ cannot be used: the associated
closed-loop trajectory diverges, $x(T)\not\to 0$, and $J=\infty$.
\[
\boxed{J^\star=(1+\sqrt2)\,x_0^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats both ARE roots as costs. The root $1-\sqrt2$
produces the unstable pole $+\sqrt2$ and is not an admissible
infinite-horizon cost-to-go. Sentence (ii) replaces the problem by the
observer-controller separation seed; no estimator is present, and the
ARE is the object of the exercise.

The argument never places an observer pole.

graderFixtures.proofText: The ARE is $2P-P^2+1=0$, with roots $1\pm\sqrt2$. The stabilizing choice is $P=K=1+\sqrt2$, giving closed-loop pole $-\sqrt2$ and $J^\star=(1+\sqrt2)x_0^2$. The other root produces the unstable pole $+\sqrt2$ and is not an admissible cost.
Both roots of the ARE are valid. I use P=1-sqrt(2) as the cost-to-go, set K=1-sqrt(2), and keep the closed-loop pole +sqrt(2) as an acceptable LQR design.
I complete the square with the wrong sign and obtain (P-1)^2=0, so P=K=1 and the pole is 0. Alternatively I ignore the ARE and place an observer pole as in the separation seed.

CTRL:010527.title: Integral action holds x=r and rejects a constant d; the homogeneous poles are -2 and -3
CTRL:010527.objective: Close the scalar plant xdot=-x+u+d with zdot=r-y and u=-4x+6z, prove the homogeneous poles are -2 and -3, compute the unique constant equilibrium x=r, z=(5r-d)/6, u=r-d, and conclude exact zero tracking error for every constant pair (r,d) in the absence of saturation.
CTRL:010527.statement:
A scalar plant and a measured output are
\[
\dot x=-x+u+d,\qquad y=x,
\]
where the constant command $r$ and the constant load $d$ are unknown to the
designer except that they are constant. An integral state and a static
feedback are implemented exactly as
\[
\dot z=r-y,\qquad u=-4x+6z.
\]
There is no actuator saturation in the nominal algebra. Time is in seconds.
If $x$ and $r$ share one physical unit, then $z$ has that unit times
seconds, the coefficients multiplying $x$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$,
and the coefficient multiplying $z$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

1. Substitute the control into the plant and write the homogeneous
   $(r,d)=(0,0)$ dynamics in the coordinates $(x,z)$. Compute the
   characteristic polynomial and prove that the closed-loop poles are
   exactly $-2$ and $-3$.

2. For arbitrary constant $r$ and $d$, compute the unique constant
   equilibrium $(x,z,u)$. Prove that it satisfies $x=r$,
   $z=(5r-d)/6$, and $u=r-d$.

3. Conclude that the tracking error $e=r-y$ is identically zero at every
   such equilibrium, independently of the value of $d$. State the role of
   the integrator in making that cancellation algebraic rather than
   approximate.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because the homogeneous poles are Hurwitz,
   every trajectory tracks $r$ even if $u$ saturates”; (ii) “the same
   equilibrium is obtained from the unaugmented law $u=-4x$ by treating
   $d$ as a vanishing perturbation.”

Do not replace the problem by a full-order observer-controller separation
on $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}$, and do not linearize a
biased pendulum.
permittedResults: For $\dot\xi=A\xi$, the characteristic polynomial is $\det(sI-A)$. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-5&6\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det(sI-A)=s^2+5s+6=(s+2)(s+3)$.
A constant equilibrium of $\dot x=-x+u+d$, $\dot z=r-x$, $u=-4x+6z$ is a root of the three algebraic equations obtained by setting every derivative to zero.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute u=-4x+6z first, form sI-A, factor s^2+5s+6, then solve the three algebraic equilibrium equations.
Read x=r from zdot=0, recover u=r-d from the plant balance, and back-substitute into u=-4x+6z to get z.

milestones.criterion: Derives the homogeneous matrix [[-5,6],[-1,0]] and the poles -2,-3 from s^2+5s+6.
Computes the unique constant equilibrium x=r, z=(5r-d)/6, u=r-d and the exact zero tracking error.
Rejects a saturation-immunity reading of the Hurwitz poles and rejects dropping the integrator.

commonErrors.description: Computes poles from the unaugmented plant with u=-4x, or writes a wrong augmented matrix, and reports a set other than {-2,-3}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required factorization s^2+5s+6 is lost, and later equilibrium identities are attached to the wrong linearization.

commonErrors.description: Claims the equilibrium is x=0 or x=d/5, or writes z=r, or sets u=0, omitting x=r, z=(5r-d)/6, and u=r-d.
commonErrors.consequence: Exact constant-disturbance rejection and zero tracking error are no longer identities of the closed loop.

hintTree.content: After $u=-4x+6z$ the plant reads $\dot x=-5x+6z+d$. Together with $\dot z=r-x$ the unforced matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}-5&6\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
At a constant equilibrium one has $x=r$ from $\dot z=0$. The plant balance $0=-x+u+d$ then forces $u=r-d$.
Substitute $x=r$ into $0=-5r+6z+d$ to recover $z=(5r-d)/6$. Saturation would freeze $u$ and break both algebraic identities.

CTRL:010527.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $u=-4x+6z$ into the plant:
\[
\dot x=-x+(-4x+6z)+d=-5x+6z+d,\qquad \dot z=r-x.
\]
The homogeneous system $(r,d)=(0,0)$ is therefore
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\dot x\\ \dot z\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}-5&6\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\ z\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic polynomial is
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}s+5&-6\\1&s\end{pmatrix}
=s(s+5)+6=s^2+5s+6=(s+2)(s+3).
\]
The homogeneous poles are exactly $-2$ and $-3$.
\[
\boxed{\text{homogeneous poles }-2,-3}.
\]

Now restore constant $r$ and $d$ and set both derivatives to zero:
\[
0=-5x+6z+d,\qquad 0=r-x.
\]
The second equation forces $x=r$. The first then becomes
$0=-5r+6z+d$, so
\[
z=\frac{5r-d}{6}.
\]
The implemented control at this point is
\[
u=-4r+6\cdot\frac{5r-d}{6}=-4r+5r-d=r-d.
\]
The same $u$ is recovered from the plant balance $0=-x+u+d$. Uniqueness
follows because the homogeneous matrix is nonsingular (its determinant is
$6\neq 0$).
\[
\boxed{x=r,\quad z=(5r-d)/6,\quad u=r-d}.
\]

At this equilibrium $y=x=r$, so the tracking error $e=r-y$ is exactly
zero for every constant $d$. The integrator is what makes the identity
algebraic: $\dot z=0$ is possible only when $y=r$, and the two-dimensional
equilibrium map is solvable for a finite $z$ precisely because the
homogeneous matrix is invertible. No small-gain or high-gain approximation
is used.

Sentence (i) confuses Hurwitz transients of the unsaturated linear model
with behavior under a saturated $u$. If $u$ is frozen by a stop, $\dot z$
need not vanish at $y=r$ and the displayed equilibrium generally ceases to
exist. Sentence (ii) drops the integrator. The unaugmented law $u=-4x$
gives the forced equilibrium $0=-x-4x+d$, hence $x=d/5$, which equals $r$
only for the special pair $d=5r$. Constant-disturbance rejection is then
lost.

The argument never introduces a full-order observer, never uses the seed
pair $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}$, and never linearizes a
pendulum.

graderFixtures.proofText: The homogeneous matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}-5&6\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ with characteristic polynomial $s^2+5s+6$ and poles $-2,-3$. Every constant pair $(r,d)$ has the unique unsaturated equilibrium $x=r$, $z=(5r-d)/6$, $u=r-d$, hence $e=r-y=0$. Saturation would break the identities; $u=-4x$ alone cannot reject a generic constant $d$.
I close only the plant by u=-4x and ignore z. Then xdot=-5x+d, the only pole is -5, and I report the homogeneous poles as -5 and 0. The factor s^2+5s+6 never appears.
At equilibrium I set x=0 because the origin is the only rest point of a Hurwitz system, take z=r from the integrator command, and set u=0. The formulas x=r, z=(5r-d)/6, and u=r-d are not used.

CTRL:010528.title: The reduced-order observer with ell=3 runs on q=xhat2-3y and never differentiates y
CTRL:010528.objective: Build the reduced-order observer of x2 for x1dot=x2+u, x2dot=-2x2+u, y=x1 at gain ell=3, implement it as qdot=-5q-15y-2u with xhat2=q+3y, prove the estimation error is e0 e^{-5t}, and reject any implementation that differentiates y.
CTRL:010528.statement:
A second-order plant with a single measured coordinate is
\[
\dot x_1=x_2+u,\qquad \dot x_2=-2x_2+u,\qquad y=x_1.
\]
The input $u$ is known. Only $x_2$ must be reconstructed. Use the reduced-
order observer gain $\ell=3$ and the Gopinath coordinate
\[
q=\hat x_2-3y.
\]

1. Write the full-information identity $\dot y=x_2+u$ and the corresponding
   observer ODE that would involve $\dot y$. Then pass to $q$ and prove that
   the implemented dynamics are exactly
   \[
   \dot q=-5q-15y-2u,\qquad \hat x_2=q+3y.
   \]
   In particular, $\dot y$ is absent from the implemented equations.

2. Let $e=x_2-\hat x_2$. Derive $\dot e=-5e$ from the plant and the
   observer, without quoting a separation theorem, and conclude
   \[
   e(t)=e_0e^{-5t},\qquad e_0=e(0).
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “a reduced-order observer must differentiate
   the measured output, so the $q$-coordinate is optional cosmetics”;
   (ii) “the error decays as $e^{-3t}$ because the gain is $3$, or as
   $e^{-2t}$ because the $(2,2)$ plant entry is $-2$.”

Do not replace the problem by a full-order observer-controller separation
on $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}$ with controller poles
$-2,-5$ and observer poles $-6,-7$, and do not invoke a hidden-mode
realization.
permittedResults: If $\dot y=x_2+u$ and $\dot{\hat x}_2=(-2-\ell)\hat x_2+(1-\ell)u+\ell\dot y$, then $e=x_2-\hat x_2$ obeys $\dot e=-(2+\ell)e$.
The scalar ODE $\dot e=-5e$ has the unique solution $e(t)=e(0)e^{-5t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the raw reduced-order ODE, pass to q=xhat2-3y to cancel ydot, then subtract to get the error pole -5.
Form the error e=x2-xhat2 first from the innovation identity ydot-u-xhat2=e, then reconstruct the q-filter as an implementation identity.

milestones.criterion: Derives the implemented filter qdot=-5q-15y-2u with xhat2=q+3y and no y derivative.
Proves the error ODE edot=-5e and the solution e(t)=e0 e^{-5t} by subtracting plant from observer.
Rejects treating ydot as a required implementation signal and rejects the decay rates e^{-3t} or e^{-2t}.

commonErrors.description: Implements the estimator by forming ydot as a live signal, or treats the q-coordinate as optional cosmetics that do not cancel ydot.
commonErrors.consequence: The required implementation qdot=-5q-15y-2u is never obtained, and a differentiator is introduced that the problem forbids.

commonErrors.description: Reports e(t)=e0 e^{-3t} from the gain ell=3, or e(t)=e0 e^{-2t} from the plant entry -2, instead of e0 e^{-5t}.
commonErrors.consequence: The error pole -(2+ell)=-5 is lost, so the assigned transient is wrong.

hintTree.content: The raw observer is $\dot{\hat x}_2=-2\hat x_2+u+\ell(\dot y-u-\hat x_2)$. At $\ell=3$ this is $\dot{\hat x}_2=-5\hat x_2-2u+3\dot y$.
Set $q=\hat x_2-3y$. Differentiating and substituting the raw observer cancels $3\dot y$ and produces $\dot q=-5q-15y-2u$.
Subtract the implemented $\dot{\hat x}_2$ from $\dot x_2=-2x_2+u$ and replace $\dot y$ by $x_2+u$ to obtain $\dot e=-5e$.

CTRL:010528.canonicalSolution:
The measurement identity is $\dot y=x_2+u$. A reduced-order copy of the
$x_2$-equation that injects the innovation $\dot y-u-\hat x_2$ through
gain $\ell$ is
\[
\dot{\hat x}_2=-2\hat x_2+u+\ell\bigl(\dot y-u-\hat x_2\bigr)
=(-2-\ell)\hat x_2+(1-\ell)u+\ell\dot y.
\]
At the assigned gain $\ell=3$ this specializes to
\[
\dot{\hat x}_2=-5\hat x_2-2u+3\dot y.
\]
Define $q=\hat x_2-3y$, so $\hat x_2=q+3y$. Differentiating and
substituting the raw observer cancels the output derivative:
\begin{align*}
\dot q
&=\dot{\hat x}_2-3\dot y
=-5\hat x_2-2u+3\dot y-3\dot y
=-5(q+3y)-2u
=-5q-15y-2u.
\end{align*}
The pair
\[
\dot q=-5q-15y-2u,\qquad \hat x_2=q+3y
\]
is therefore an exact realization of the reduced-order observer, and it
uses only the measured $y$ and the known $u$.
\[
\boxed{\dot q=-5q-15y-2u,\quad\hat x_2=q+3y}.
\]

Let $e=x_2-\hat x_2$. From the plant, $\dot x_2=-2x_2+u$. From the raw
observer with a general gain,
\[
\dot{\hat x}_2=(-2-\ell)\hat x_2+(1-\ell)u+\ell\dot y,
\]
and $\dot y=x_2+u$, so
\begin{align*}
\dot e
&=-2x_2+u-(-2-\ell)\hat x_2-(1-\ell)u-\ell(x_2+u)\\
&=-(2+\ell)x_2+(2+\ell)\hat x_2
=-(2+\ell)e.
\end{align*}
The $u$ coefficients cancel: $1-(1-\ell)-\ell=0$. At $\ell=3$ one has
$\dot e=-5e$, hence
\[
e(t)=e_0e^{-5t},\qquad e_0=e(0).
\]
\[
\boxed{e(t)=e_0e^{-5t}}.
\]
No separation principle was cited: the error ODE was subtracted from the
plant.

Sentence (i) mistakes a cancelled intermediate $\dot y$ for a signal that
must be formed in hardware. The $q$-filter is the device that removes
that derivative. Sentence (ii) confuses the observer gain $\ell=3$ or the
open-loop entry $-2$ with the error pole $-(2+\ell)=-5$.

The argument never builds a full-order pair $(A-BK,A-LC)$ on the seed
matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix}$ and never discusses a
hidden mode of a nonminimal realization.

graderFixtures.proofText: The raw observer at $\ell=3$ is $\dot{\hat x}_2=-5\hat x_2-2u+3\dot y$. The coordinate $q=\hat x_2-3y$ cancels $\dot y$ and yields $\dot q=-5q-15y-2u$ with $\hat x_2=q+3y$. Subtracting from the plant gives $\dot e=-5e$, hence $e(t)=e_0e^{-5t}$. No output derivative is implemented.

I implement xhat2dot=-5 xhat2-2u+3 ydot by differentiating the measured y with a difference quotient. The q-coordinate is only a rewriting and is not needed. The filter qdot=-5q-15y-2u is never integrated.
The observer gain is 3, so the error should decay as e0 e^{-3t}. Alternatively the open-loop x2 pole is -2, so the error is e0 e^{-2t}. I never form the pole -(2+ell)=-5.

CTRL:010629.title: Exact ZOH of the double integrator at T=1 is Ad=[[1,1],[0,1]], Bd=(1/2,1), Gd=(z+1)/(2(z-1)^2)
CTRL:010629.objective: Discretize the double integrator by exact zero-order hold at T=1, obtain Ad=[[1,1],[0,1]] and Bd=(1/2,1)^T, prove controllability from det[Bd, Ad Bd]=-1, and derive the pulse transfer Gd=(z+1)/(2(z-1)^2) with a zero at -1.
CTRL:010629.statement:
A continuous double integrator in first-order form is
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A digital command is applied through an ideal zero-order hold of period
$T=1$, with no computational delay. Write $x_k=x(kT)$ and $u(t)=u_k$ for
$t\in[kT,(k+1)T)$.

1. Compute the exact discrete pair
   \[
   A_d=e^{AT},\qquad
   B_d=\int_0^T e^{A\tau}B\,d\tau
   \]
   at $T=1$. Record $A_d$ and $B_d$ as explicit matrices.

2. Form the controllability matrix $\begin{pmatrix}B_d&A_d B_d\end{pmatrix}$
   and prove that its determinant equals $-1$. Conclude discrete
   controllability.

3. Compute the pulse transfer function
   $G_d(z)=C(zI-A_d)^{-1}B_d$ in reduced form and locate its finite zero.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “forward Euler is exact on a double
   integrator, so $B_d=TB=(0,1)^T$”; (ii) “$G_d$ is $1/(z-1)^2$ because
   each integrator contributes a pole at $1$ and there is no discrete
   zero.”

Do not replace the problem by a first-order integrator sampled at $T=0.1$
with an intersample aliasing sinusoid, and do not construct continuous-
time sampling aliases of a cosine.
permittedResults: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, then $A^2=0$, so $e^{At}=I+At=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
A pair $(A_d,B_d)$ in $\mathbb R^{2\times 2}\times\mathbb R^2$ is controllable if and only if $\det\begin{pmatrix}B_d&A_d B_d\end{pmatrix}\ne 0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use nilpotence to write e^{At}=I+At, integrate e^{Aτ}B, then invert zI-Ad by the adjugate.
Integrate the double-integrator step response on one hold interval to read Bd and the discrete convolution that produces the zero at -1.

milestones.criterion: Computes the exact ZOH pair Ad=[[1,1],[0,1]] and Bd=(1/2,1)^T from e^{At}=I+At.
Proves det[Bd, Ad Bd]=-1 and derives Gd=(z+1)/(2(z-1)^2) with zero -1.
Rejects forward-Euler Bd=TB and the claim that Gd has no finite zero.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the exact hold integral by forward Euler and reports Bd=TB=(0,1)^T, or otherwise omits the 1/2 in Bd.
commonErrors.consequence: The controllability matrix and every subsequent pulse-transfer coefficient become wrong.

commonErrors.description: Reports Gd=1/(z-1)^2 or another zero-free form, missing the numerator z+1 and the zero at -1.
commonErrors.consequence: The averaging action of the hold is deleted, so the assigned discrete zero is lost.

hintTree.content: Because $A^2=0$, one has $A_d=I+A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ at $T=1$, and $e^{A\tau}B=(\tau,1)^T$.
Integrate $(\tau,1)^T$ from $0$ to $1$ to get $B_d=(1/2,1)^T$. Then $A_d B_d=(3/2,1)^T$.
$(zI-A_d)^{-1}=(z-1)^{-2}\begin{pmatrix}z-1&1\\0&z-1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplying by $C$ and $B_d$ produces $(z+1)/(2(z-1)^2)$.

CTRL:010629.canonicalSolution:
The nilpotence $A^2=0$ gives $e^{At}=I+At=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
At the assigned period $T=1$,
\[
A_d=e^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The integrand of $B_d$ is
\[
e^{A\tau}B=\begin{pmatrix}1&\tau\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\tau\\1\end{pmatrix},
\]
so
\[
B_d=\int_0^1\begin{pmatrix}\tau\\1\end{pmatrix}\,d\tau
=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A_d=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
B_d=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1\end{pmatrix}}.
\]

Next $A_d B_d=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3/2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, and
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}B_d&A_d B_d\end{pmatrix}
=\det\begin{pmatrix}1/2&3/2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\tfrac12-\tfrac32=-1.
\]
The determinant is nonzero, so $(A_d,B_d)$ is controllable.
\[
\boxed{\det\begin{pmatrix}B_d&A_d B_d\end{pmatrix}=-1}.
\]

For the pulse transfer,
\[
zI-A_d=\begin{pmatrix}z-1&-1\\0&z-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(zI-A_d)^{-1}
=\frac1{(z-1)^2}
\begin{pmatrix}z-1&1\\0&z-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
C(zI-A_d)^{-1}
=\frac1{(z-1)^2}\begin{pmatrix}z-1&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\begin{align*}
G_d(z)
&=\frac1{(z-1)^2}\Bigl((z-1)\cdot\tfrac12+1\Bigr)
=\frac{\tfrac12 z+\tfrac12}{(z-1)^2}
=\frac{z+1}{2(z-1)^2}.
\end{align*}
The unique finite zero is the root of $z+1=0$, namely $z=-1$.
\[
\boxed{G_d(z)=(z+1)/\bigl(2(z-1)^2\bigr),\quad\text{zero }-1}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the exact hold integral by a forward-Euler input
matrix $TB=(0,1)^T$. That approximation misses the $1/2$ that comes from
integrating the ramp $\tau$. Sentence (ii) keeps the double pole at $z=1$
but drops the averaging zero of the hold; the numerator $z+1$ is not
optional.

The argument never samples a first-order integrator at $T=0.1$ and never
constructs a continuous sinusoid that vanishes at the sample instants.

graderFixtures.proofText: Nilpotence gives $A_d=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B_d=(1/2,1)^T$. Then $\det[B_d,A_d B_d]=-1$. The pulse transfer is $G_d(z)=(z+1)/(2(z-1)^2)$ with finite zero $-1$. Forward Euler $B_d=(0,1)^T$ and the zero-free form $1/(z-1)^2$ are both false.
Forward Euler is exact on integrators, so Ad=I+AT=[[1,1],[0,1]] is fine but Bd=T B=(0,1)^T. I never integrate tau against the hold and the 1/2 never appears.
Each continuous integrator becomes a discrete pole at 1, so Gd(z)=1/(z-1)^2. A hold cannot create a finite zero. I never form C(zI-Ad)^{-1}Bd.

CTRL:010630.title: Jury on K(z+1/2)/((z-1)(z-1/2)) forces 0<K<1; the endpoints hit z=1 and a unit-circle conjugate pair
CTRL:010630.objective: Form the closed-loop polynomial z^2+(K-3/2)z+(1+K)/2, apply the three Jury inequalities to obtain K>0, K<6, and K<1, conclude 0<K<1, and identify the K=0 pole at 1 and the K=1 unit-circle conjugate pair.
CTRL:010630.statement:
A discrete plant under unity negative feedback with scalar gain $K$ has
open-loop transfer
\[
L(z)=\frac{K\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr)}{(z-1)\bigl(z-\tfrac12\bigr)}.
\]
The loop is well-defined for every real $K$. The value $K=0$ makes the
forward-path numerator zero but remains a meaningful boundary case for
the closed-loop characteristic polynomial.

1. Derive the closed-loop characteristic polynomial
   \[
   p(z)=z^2+\Bigl(K-\tfrac32\Bigr)z+\frac{1+K}{2}.
   \]

2. Apply the Jury criteria for a monic quadratic. Prove that they are
   equivalent to the three inequalities $K>0$, $K<6$, and $K<1$, and
   conclude that the open interval of Schur-stabilizing gains is
   $0<K<1$.

3. Evaluate the closed-loop poles at the two finite endpoints of that
   interval. Prove that $K=0$ produces a pole at $z=1$, and that $K=1$
   produces a complex-conjugate pair on the unit circle.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Routh’s criterion applied to $p(z)$ as if
   it were a continuous polynomial gives the same $K$-interval”;
   (ii) “Jury’s $|a_0|<1$ test may be dropped, so the stabilizing range
   is $0<K<6$.”

Do not replace the problem by a continuous Routh array with a zero row,
and do not construct a sampled-integrator alias at $T=0.1$.
permittedResults: A pair of complex conjugates has modulus $1$ if and only if it is a root of a monic real quadratic with constant term $1$ and discriminant negative.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand D+N, evaluate p(1), p(-1), and |a0|, then intersect the three inequalities.
Track the closed-loop roots as functions of K and locate the first unit-circle meeting at K=1, then confirm the same interval by Jury.

milestones.criterion: Derives p(z)=z^2+(K-3/2)z+(1+K)/2 from 1+L(z)=0.
Applies Jury to obtain K>0, K<6, and K<1, concludes 0<K<1, and identifies the K=0 pole at 1 and the K=1 unit-circle conjugates.
Rejects a continuous Routh reading of p(z) and rejects dropping |a0|<1.

commonErrors.description: Applies Routh’s criterion to p(z) as if z were a continuous Laplace variable, or otherwise replaces Jury by a continuous-time array.
commonErrors.consequence: The unit-circle crossing at K=1 is not detected as a sampled-data stability boundary.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only p(1)>0 and p(-1)>0 and reports the stabilizing range as 0<K<6, omitting |a0|<1.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned open interval 0<K<1 is replaced by a strictly larger set that already contains the K=1 unit-circle pair.

hintTree.content: Expand $(z-1)(z-1/2)=z^2-(3/2)z+1/2$ and add $Kz+K/2$ to obtain $p(z)$.
Compute $p(1)=(3/2)K$, $p(-1)=3-K/2$, and $a_0=(1+K)/2$. The Jury tests become $K>0$, $K<6$, and $|1+K|<2$.
Intersecting those inequalities with each other yields $0<K<1$. At $K=1$ one has $p(z)=z^2-(1/2)z+1$.

CTRL:010630.canonicalSolution:
The closed-loop characteristic equation is $1+L(z)=0$, or
\[
(z-1)\Bigl(z-\tfrac12\Bigr)+K\Bigl(z+\tfrac12\Bigr)=0.
\]
The first product is $z^2-(3/2)z+1/2$, so
\[
p(z)=z^2+\Bigl(K-\tfrac32\Bigr)z+\frac{1+K}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{p(z)=z^2+(K-3/2)z+(1+K)/2}.
\]

Write $a_1=K-3/2$ and $a_0=(1+K)/2$. The three Jury tests are
$p(1)>0$, $p(-1)>0$, and $|a_0|<1$. Direct evaluation gives
\begin{align*}
p(1)
&=1+\Bigl(K-\tfrac32\Bigr)+\frac{1+K}{2}
=\tfrac32 K,\\
p(-1)
&=1-\Bigl(K-\tfrac32\Bigr)+\frac{1+K}{2}
=3-\tfrac K2.
\end{align*}
Thus $p(1)>0$ if and only if $K>0$, and $p(-1)>0$ if and only if $K<6$.
The remaining inequality is
\[
\Bigl|\frac{1+K}{2}\Bigr|<1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad -3<K<1.
\]
Intersecting $K>0$, $K<6$, and $-3<K<1$ leaves only
\[
0<K<1.
\]
(The assignment’s compact listing $K>0$, $K<6$, $K<1$ is the three
Jury faces after $K>0$ has already discarded the left half of $|a_0|<1$.)
\[
\boxed{0<K<1}.
\]

At $K=0$,
\[
p(z)=z^2-\tfrac32 z+\tfrac12=(z-1)\Bigl(z-\tfrac12\Bigr),
\]
so one closed-loop pole sits at $z=1$ (the open-loop integrator is no
longer moved). At $K=1$,
\[
p(z)=z^2-\tfrac12 z+1.
\]
The discriminant is $1/4-4=-15/4<0$, and the constant term is $1$, so
the roots are a complex-conjugate pair of modulus $1$:
\[
z=\frac{1}{4}\pm j\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4},\qquad |z|=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{K=0\text{ pole }1;\quad K=1\text{ unit-circle conjugates}}.
\]

Sentence (i) applies a continuous-time test to a discrete polynomial.
Routh on $p(z)$ does not detect the unit-circle crossing at $K=1$ as a
stability boundary of the sampled loop. Sentence (ii) keeps only
$p(\pm 1)>0$ and reports the strictly larger interval $0<K<6$, which
already contains the unit-circle pair at $K=1$.

The argument never builds a Routh array with a zero row and never
samples a continuous integrator at $T=0.1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The characteristic polynomial is $p(z)=z^2+(K-3/2)z+(1+K)/2$. Jury gives $p(1)=(3/2)K>0$, $p(-1)=3-K/2>0$, and $|(1+K)/2|<1$, hence $K>0$, $K<6$, and $K<1$, so $0<K<1$. At $K=0$ there is a pole at $1$; at $K=1$ the roots are unit-circle conjugates. Routh on $p(z)$ and the range $0<K<6$ are both wrong.
I treat p(z) as a continuous characteristic polynomial and run Routh on s^2+(K-3/2)s+(1+K)/2. The Routh conditions are not the Jury tests, and I never mention a unit-circle pair at K=1.
Jury in degree two is just p(1)>0 and p(-1)>0, so K>0 and K<6. The constant-term test |a0|<1 is optional. The stabilizing range is therefore 0<K<6.

CTRL:010631.title: Additive small-gain on P0=1/(s+1), C=2 guarantees every stable Delta only for rho<1/2
CTRL:010631.objective: Compute S=(s+1)/(s+3), T=2/(s+3), and CS=2(s+1)/(s+3) with H-infinity norms 1, 2/3, and 2, and prove that every stable additive perturbation with ||Delta||_inf<=rho is strictly guaranteed to preserve internal stability whenever the small-gain radius satisfies rho<1/2.
CTRL:010631.statement:
A nominal loop is the stable pair
\[
P_0(s)=\frac1{s+1},\qquad C(s)=2,
\]
with negative unity feedback. Write
\[
S=\frac1{1+P_0 C},\qquad
T=\frac{P_0 C}{1+P_0 C},\qquad
CS=C S.
\]
An additive perturbation is a stable proper transfer function $\Delta$
placed as $P=P_0+\Delta$. The only robustness test authorized here is the
small-gain theorem applied to the $\Delta$-$CS$ interconnection.

1. Derive the three closed-loop maps $S$, $T$, and $CS$ as explicit
   rational functions.

2. Compute the three $H_\infty$ norms
   \[
   \|S\|_\infty,\qquad \|T\|_\infty,\qquad \|CS\|_\infty
   \]
   from $|F(j\omega)|$ on the extended imaginary axis. Record the
   frequencies at which each maximum is attained.

3. Apply the small-gain theorem to the additive interconnection and prove
   that every stable $\Delta$ with $\|\Delta\|_\infty\le\rho$ is strictly
   guaranteed to preserve internal stability whenever the sufficient
   radius satisfies $\rho<1/2$. (The bound is the small-gain guarantee,
   not a claim that $\rho=1/2$ is always destabilizing.)

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “additive uncertainty is limited by
   $\|T\|_\infty$ or $\|S\|_\infty$, so the guaranteed radius is $3/2$ or
   $1$”; (ii) “the closed inequality $\rho\le 1/2$ is already a strict
   small-gain certificate, or the same radius applies to multiplicative
   $P=P_0(1+\Delta)$.”

Do not replace the problem by the induced $L^2$ gain of the open plant
$1/(s+2)$, and do not compute an observability Gramian.
permittedResults: Small-gain: the $M$-$\Delta$ loop with stable $M$ and $\Delta$ is internally stable whenever $\|\Delta\|_\infty\|M\|_\infty<1$. Here $M=CS$ for additive $\Delta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form 1+P0 C first, read S, T, and CS, maximize each |F(jω)|, then apply small-gain to M=CS.
Identify the additive M-Delta map as CS by block-diagram algebra, compute ||CS||_inf from the high-frequency limit 2, and invert that gain.

milestones.criterion: Computes the three H-infinity norms 1, 2/3, and 2 and the strict additive guarantee rho<1/2 from ||CS||_inf=2.
Rejects an ||S|| or ||T|| additive test and rejects the closed certificate rho<=1/2.

commonErrors.description: Limits additive Delta by ||T||_inf=2/3 or ||S||_inf=1 and reports a guaranteed radius 3/2 or 1 instead of 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The map actually seen by an additive perturbation, namely CS, is replaced by a multiplicative or inverse-additive test.

commonErrors.description: Accepts rho<=1/2 as already a small-gain certificate, or transfers the same radius to multiplicative P=P0(1+Delta).
commonErrors.consequence: The required strict inequality rho<1/2, or the distinction between additive and multiplicative channels, is lost.

hintTree.content: $|S(j\omega)|=\sqrt{\omega^2+1}/\sqrt{\omega^2+9}$ increases to $1$; $|T(j\omega)|=2/\sqrt{\omega^2+9}$ decreases from $2/3$; $|CS(j\omega)|$ increases to $2$.
Additive small-gain is $\rho\|CS\|_\infty<1$. With $\|CS\|_\infty=2$ this is the strict radius $\rho<1/2$.

CTRL:010631.canonicalSolution:
The return difference is
\[
1+P_0 C=1+\frac{2}{s+1}=\frac{s+3}{s+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\frac{s+1}{s+3},\qquad
T=\frac{P_0 C}{1+P_0 C}=\frac{2}{s+3},\qquad
CS=\frac{2(s+1)}{s+3}.
\]
All three maps are stable.
\[
\boxed{S=(s+1)/(s+3),\quad T=2/(s+3),\quad CS=2(s+1)/(s+3)}.
\]

On the imaginary axis,
\begin{align*}
|S(j\omega)|
&=\frac{\sqrt{\omega^2+1}}{\sqrt{\omega^2+9}},&
|T(j\omega)|
&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\omega^2+9}},&
|CS(j\omega)|
&=\frac{2\sqrt{\omega^2+1}}{\sqrt{\omega^2+9}}.
\end{align*}
The first quotient is strictly increasing from $1/3$ to $1$, so
$\|S\|_\infty=1$, attained as $\omega\to\infty$. The second is strictly
decreasing from $2/3$ to $0$, so $\|T\|_\infty=2/3$, attained at
$\omega=0$. The third is strictly increasing from $2/3$ to $2$, so
$\|CS\|_\infty=2$, attained as $\omega\to\infty$.
\[
\boxed{\|S\|_\infty=1,\quad \|T\|_\infty=2/3,\quad \|CS\|_\infty=2}.
\]

For additive $\Delta$, the standard $M$-$\Delta$ map is $M=CS$ (up to
sign, which does not change the $H_\infty$ norm). Small-gain therefore
guarantees internal stability of every stable $\Delta$ with
$\|\Delta\|_\infty\le\rho$ once
\[
\rho\|CS\|_\infty<1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \rho\cdot 2<1
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \rho<\frac12.
\]
The inequality is strict: the theorem requires
$\|\Delta\,CS\|_\infty<1$. The closed bound $\rho\le 1/2$ is not a
small-gain certificate, even though some particular $\Delta$ of size
$1/2$ may remain stabilizing.
\[
\boxed{\text{strict additive guarantee }\rho<1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) applies the complementary-sensitivity test (multiplicative
uncertainty) or the sensitivity test (inverse-additive uncertainty) to an
additive $\Delta$. Those radii would be $1/\|T\|_\infty=3/2$ and
$1/\|S\|_\infty=1$, both strictly larger than $1/2$. Sentence (ii)
either closes the small-gain inequality or transfers the additive radius
to $P=P_0(1+\Delta)$.

The argument never computes the induced $L^2$ gain of $1/(s+2)$ as a
standalone open operator and never forms an observability Gramian.

graderFixtures.proofText: The maps are $S=(s+1)/(s+3)$, $T=2/(s+3)$, $CS=2(s+1)/(s+3)$ with $\|S\|_\infty=1$, $\|T\|_\infty=2/3$, and $\|CS\|_\infty=2$. Additive small-gain is $\rho\|CS\|_\infty<1$, hence every stable $\Delta$ with $\|\Delta\|_\infty\le\rho$ is strictly guaranteed only for $\rho<1/2$. Using $\|T\|$ or $\|S\|$, or closing the inequality, is wrong.
Robustness to additive Delta is a complementary-sensitivity test, so the radius is 1/||T||_inf=3/2. If I use sensitivity instead I get 1/||S||_inf=1. I never invert ||CS||_inf=2.
Small-gain allows ||Delta CS||_inf<=1, so rho<=1/2 is already guaranteed. The same number applies to multiplicative P=P0(1+Delta) because the loop is the same.

OPT:010117.title: The form e^x a^2+e^y b^2+e^{-x-y}(a+b)^2 is positive; AM-GM min 3 uniquely at 0; H(0) has eigs 1 and 3
OPT:010117.objective: Compute the gradient and Hessian of a smooth exponential sum, identify the Hessian quadratic form, prove strict positivity, locate the unique AM-GM minimizer, and read the spectrum of H at the origin.
OPT:010117.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be the $C^\infty$ function
\[
f(x,y)=e^{x}+e^{y}+e^{-x-y}.
\]
Do not pass to an epigraph, a perspective, or a conjugate.

1. Compute the gradient $\nabla f(x,y)$ exactly.

2. Compute the Hessian matrix $H(x,y)=\nabla^2 f(x,y)$. For an arbitrary vector $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$, expand the quadratic form $(a,b)\,H(x,y)\,(a,b)^\top$ and prove the identity
   \[
   (a,b)\,H(x,y)\,(a,b)^\top
   =e^{x}a^{2}+e^{y}b^{2}+e^{-x-y}(a+b)^{2}.
   \]
   Deduce that the right-hand side is strictly positive whenever $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and conclude that $H(x,y)$ is positive definite at every point.

3. Apply the AM-GM inequality to the three positive terms of $f$. Prove that
   \[
   f(x,y)\ge 3
   \]
   for every $(x,y)$, with equality if and only if $(x,y)=(0,0)$. In particular the unconstrained minimizer is unique.

4. Evaluate $H(0,0)$ and compute its two eigenvalues exactly.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the quadratic form vanishes along $a=-b$, so $H$ is only positive semidefinite”; (ii) “AM-GM equality holds on the whole line $x+y=0$.”

Do not replace $f$ by a perspective, do not form an epigraph argument, and do not introduce a Fenchel conjugate.
permittedResults: A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is strictly convex whenever its Hessian is positive definite at every point.
If $e^{x}=e^{y}=e^{-x-y}$, then necessarily $x=y=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the Hessian quadratic form by collecting the mixed partials into a perfect square, then apply AM-GM to the three exponential summands.
Read strict convexity from H>0, locate the critical point by setting the two gradient components equal, and confirm it is the unique AM-GM equality case before computing the spectrum at 0.

milestones.criterion: Computes the gradient and expands the Hessian quadratic form as e^x a^2+e^y b^2+e^{-x-y}(a+b)^2, proving it is strictly positive off the origin.
Obtains the AM-GM bound f>=3 with equality only at (0,0), and reports the eigenvalues of H(0,0) as 1 and 3.
Rejects both a vanishing-form claim along a=-b and an AM-GM equality claim on the line x+y=0.

commonErrors.description: Drops the mixed term 2ab e^{-x-y} and concludes that the Hessian quadratic form vanishes along a=-b, reporting only positive semidefiniteness.
commonErrors.consequence: Strict convexity is lost and the spectrum of H(0,0) is misread as containing a zero eigenvalue.

commonErrors.description: Applies AM-GM but claims equality throughout the line x+y=0, so the minimizer is reported as a whole affine line rather than the unique point (0,0).
commonErrors.consequence: The uniqueness half of AM-GM is discarded and the unconstrained minimizer is no longer a singleton.

hintTree.content: The mixed partial of $e^{-x-y}$ is itself, so the off-diagonal Hessian entries are $e^{-x-y}$ and the $(a+b)^2$ cross term is required.
The product of the three exponential terms is $e^{x+y+(-x-y)}=1$, so AM-GM yields the constant lower bound $3$.
At the origin the Hessian is $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Its characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$.

OPT:010117.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating termwise gives
\[
\nabla f(x,y)
=\bigl(e^{x}-e^{-x-y},\; e^{y}-e^{-x-y}\bigr).
\]
A second differentiation produces
\[
H(x,y)
=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{x}+e^{-x-y}&e^{-x-y}\\
e^{-x-y}&e^{y}+e^{-x-y}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The associated quadratic form expands as
\begin{align*}
(a,b)\,H(x,y)\,(a,b)^\top
&=a^{2}\bigl(e^{x}+e^{-x-y}\bigr)+2ab\,e^{-x-y}+b^{2}\bigl(e^{y}+e^{-x-y}\bigr)\\
&=e^{x}a^{2}+e^{y}b^{2}+e^{-x-y}\bigl(a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}\bigr)\\
&=\boxed{e^{x}a^{2}+e^{y}b^{2}+e^{-x-y}(a+b)^{2}}.
\end{align*}
Each exponential is positive. If $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, then either $a\ne 0$, or $b\ne 0$, or both; in every case at least one of $a^{2}$, $b^{2}$, and $(a+b)^{2}$ is positive (if $a=-b\ne 0$ the first two terms survive). Hence the quadratic form is strictly positive, $H(x,y)\succ 0$ everywhere, and $f$ is strictly convex.

AM-GM applied to the three positive summands yields
\[
f(x,y)
\ge 3\bigl(e^{x}\cdot e^{y}\cdot e^{-x-y}\bigr)^{1/3}
=3\bigl(e^{0}\bigr)^{1/3}
=\boxed{3},
\]
with equality if and only if $e^{x}=e^{y}=e^{-x-y}$. The first equality forces $x=y$; substituting into the second gives $x=-x-x$, hence $3x=0$. Thus equality holds if and only if
\[
\boxed{(x,y)=(0,0)}.
\]
The unconstrained minimum value is $3$ and is attained at a unique point.

At the origin,
\[
H(0,0)
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic polynomial is $(2-\lambda)^{2}-1=\lambda^{2}-4\lambda+3=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$, so the eigenvalues are
\[
\boxed{1\text{ and }3}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: along $a=-b\ne 0$ the form reduces to $(e^{x}+e^{y})a^{2}>0$. Sentence (ii) is false: $x+y=0$ makes the product of the three terms equal to $e^{x}\cdot e^{-x}\cdot 1=1$, but equality in AM-GM still requires the three terms themselves to coincide, which forces $x=y=0$.

The argument never uses an epigraph, a perspective construction, or a Fenchel conjugate.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Hessian form is $e^{x}a^{2}+e^{y}b^{2}+e^{-x-y}(a+b)^{2}>0$ off the origin. AM-GM gives $f\ge 3$ with equality only at $(0,0)$. The matrix $H(0,0)$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $3$.
I expand (a,b)H(a,b)^T as e^x a^2+e^y b^2+e^{-x-y}(a^2+b^2). Along a=-b the form is zero, so H is only positive semidefinite and H(0,0) has a zero eigenvalue.
AM-GM gives f>=3. Equality holds whenever the exponent sum x+y+(-x-y) vanishes, i.e. on the whole line x+y=0, so the minimizer is not unique.

OPT:010118.title: LSE on R^3 has gradient p and Hessian diag(p)-pp^T; at 0 the eigs are 0,1/3,1/3 and the plane min is log 3 uniquely at 0
OPT:010118.objective: Identify the softmax gradient of log-sum-exp on R^3, write the Hessian as a categorical variance, read its nullspace and the spectrum at the origin, record the shift identity, and minimize on the plane sum x_i=0.
OPT:010118.statement:
Let $\ell:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be the log-sum-exp function
\[
\ell(x)=\log\bigl(e^{x_1}+e^{x_2}+e^{x_3}\bigr).
\]
Write $s(x)=\sum_{i=1}^3 e^{x_i}$ and $p(x)\in\mathbb R^3$ for the softmax vector with coordinates
\[
p_i(x)=\frac{e^{x_i}}{s(x)},\qquad i=1,2,3.
\]
Thus $p(x)$ lies in the relative interior of the probability simplex. Do not introduce a Fenchel conjugate, an accelerated method, or a semidefinite relaxation.

1. Compute $\nabla\ell(x)$ and identify it with $p(x)$.

2. Compute the Hessian $H(x)=\nabla^2\ell(x)$ and prove
   \[
   H(x)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(p(x)\bigr)-p(x)p(x)^\top.
   \]
   For $v\in\mathbb R^3$, rewrite the quadratic form as a variance:
   \[
   v^\top H(x)\,v
   =\sum_{i=1}^3 p_i(x)\,v_i^2-\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^3 p_i(x)\,v_i\Bigr)^2.
   \]

3. Deduce that $\ker H(x)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}$ at every $x$, where $\mathbf 1=(1,1,1)$. Evaluate $H(0)$ and prove that its eigenvalues are $0$, $1/3$, and $1/3$.

4. Prove the shift identity $\ell(x+t\mathbf 1)=\ell(x)+t$ for every real $t$. Restricting to the plane $\sum_{i=1}^3 x_i=0$, prove that $\ell$ attains the minimum value $\log 3$ uniquely at the origin.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$H=\operatorname{diag}(p)$, so $H(0)$ has a triple eigenvalue $1/3$ and is invertible”; (ii) “$\ell$ itself is minimized at the origin with value $\log 3$, with no plane restriction.”

Do not form a conjugate, do not run a first-order algorithm, and do not recast the exercise as a semidefinite program.
permittedResults: The Hessian of log-sum-exp is $\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top$, with kernel equal to the constants on the support of $p$. For softmax the support is full, so the kernel is $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}$.
Log-sum-exp is translation-equivariant: $\ell(x+t\mathbf 1)=\ell(x)+t$. On the hyperplane $\mathbf 1^\top x=0$ Jensen gives $\ell(x)\ge\log n$, with equality only at the origin.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate log-sum-exp twice, recognize the categorical covariance, and read the spectrum of (1/3)I-(1/9)11^T by splitting along 1 and 1^perp.
Use the shift identity to reduce the plane problem to a mean-zero Jensen bound, then recover the Hessian kernel by differentiating the identity twice.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the gradient as the softmax vector and writes H=diag(p)-pp^T in variance form, with kernel span{1}.
Computes the eigenvalues 0, 1/3, 1/3 of H(0), records the shift identity, and proves that on sum x_i=0 the unique minimizer is 0 with value log 3.
Rejects both the diagonal-only Hessian and the claim that unconstrained LSE is minimized at the origin.

commonErrors.description: Writes H=diag(p) and omits the rank-one term -pp^T, so H(0) is reported as (1/3)I with a triple eigenvalue 1/3 and trivial kernel.
commonErrors.consequence: The variance structure, the nullspace span{1}, and the assigned spectrum 0,1/3,1/3 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that unconstrained log-sum-exp attains the value log 3 at the origin, ignoring the shift identity.
commonErrors.consequence: The function is treated as coercive when it is unbounded below along -1, and the plane restriction is dropped.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $\log s$ to obtain $p$. A further derivative of $p_i$ produces the rank-one update $-p_i p_k$.
At $x=0$ one has $p=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ and $H=(1/3)I-(1/9)\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top$. The all-ones vector is killed; on $\mathbf 1^\perp$ the eigenvalue is $1/3$.
On $\sum x_i=0$, Jensen or AM-GM yields $(e^{x_1}+e^{x_2}+e^{x_3})/3\ge 1$, hence $\ell(x)\ge\log 3$.

OPT:010118.canonicalSolution:
Write $s=\sum_{i=1}^3 e^{x_i}$. Then
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial x_j}
=\frac{e^{x_j}}{s}
=p_j,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\nabla\ell(x)=p(x)}.
\]
Differentiating $p_j$ gives
\[
\frac{\partial p_j}{\partial x_k}
=\delta_{jk}p_j-p_j p_k,
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{H(x)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(p(x)\bigr)-p(x)p(x)^\top}.
\]
The quadratic form is
\[
v^\top H v
=\sum_i p_i v_i^2-\Bigl(\sum_i p_i v_i\Bigr)^2,
\]
which is the variance of a random coordinate that takes the value $v_i$ with probability $p_i$. The variance vanishes if and only if $v$ is constant on the support of $p$. Every coordinate of $p$ is positive, so
\[
\boxed{\ker H(x)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}}.
\]
At the origin, $p(0)=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ and
\[
H(0)=\frac13 I-\frac19\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top.
\]
One has $H(0)\mathbf 1=0$. On the plane $\mathbf 1^\top v=0$ the rank-one term drops and $H(0)v=(1/3)v$. The spectrum is therefore
\[
\boxed{0,\;\tfrac13,\;\tfrac13}.
\]
The shift identity is
\[
\ell(x+t\mathbf 1)
=\log\Bigl(e^{t}\sum_i e^{x_i}\Bigr)
=\boxed{\ell(x)+t}.
\]
Differentiating twice in $t$ recovers $\mathbf 1^\top H(x)\mathbf 1=0$, consistent with the kernel computation.

On the plane $\sum_i x_i=0$, Jensen (or AM-GM) gives
\[
\frac1{3}\sum_{i=1}^3 e^{x_i}
\ge\exp\Bigl(\frac1{3}\sum_{i=1}^3 x_i\Bigr)
=1,
\]
so $\sum_i e^{x_i}\ge 3$ and
\[
\ell(x)\ge\boxed{\log 3},
\]
with equality if and only if $x_1=x_2=x_3$. Intersecting with the plane forces
\[
\boxed{x=0}.
\]
Thus the constrained minimum is $\log 3$, attained uniquely at the origin.

Sentence (i) is false: omitting $-pp^\top$ makes $H(0)$ a multiple of the identity and destroys both the kernel and the listed eigenvalues. Sentence (ii) is false: the shift identity shows $\ell(t\mathbf 1)=t+\log 3$, which is unbounded below as $t\to-\infty$, so $\ell$ has no unconstrained minimizer.

The calculation stays inside smooth convex analysis on $\mathbb R^3$. No conjugate, first-order iteration, or semidefinite certificate is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The gradient is $p$ and $H=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top$ with $\ker H=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}$. At $0$ the eigenvalues are $0,1/3,1/3$. The shift identity is $\ell(x+t\mathbf 1)=\ell(x)+t$. On $\sum x_i=0$ the unique minimizer is the origin with value $\log 3$.
I differentiate once to get p and stop. The Hessian is diag(p). At 0 this is (1/3)I, so the eigenvalues are 1/3,1/3,1/3 and H is invertible.
By AM-GM one has ell(x)>=log 3 with equality at 0, so the unconstrained minimizer of LSE on R^3 is the origin. I do not restrict to a plane.

OPT:010219.title: The subdifferential of max{x1,x2,0} at 0 is the triangle conv{e1,e2,0}; (0.4,0.3) is valid and (0.8,0.4) is not
OPT:010219.objective: Identify the max of three affine functions with the support of a triangle, compute the subdifferential at the origin and at (1,1), match the directional derivative to that support, and audit two candidate subgradients at 0.
OPT:010219.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be
\[
f(x)=\max\{x_1,x_2,0\}.
\]
Write $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$. Do not pass to a Fenchel conjugate of a quadratic kink, and do not introduce a proximal mapping.

1. Prove that $f$ is the support function of the triangle
   \[
   T:=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2,0\}
   =\bigl\{(s,t):s\ge 0,\; t\ge 0,\; s+t\le 1\bigr\}.
   \]

2. Compute the subdifferential $\partial f(0)$ by taking the convex hull of the gradients of the active pieces, and identify it with $T$. Prove that the directional derivative equals the support of that set:
   \[
   f'(0;d)=\max\{d_1,d_2,0\}=\sigma_{\partial f(0)}(d).
   \]

3. Compute $\partial f(1,1)$.

4. Decide, with an explicit convex-combination or supporting-inequality argument, whether each of the vectors $(0.4,0.3)$ and $(0.8,0.4)$ lies in $\partial f(0)$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “at the origin only $x_1$ and $x_2$ are active, so $\partial f(0)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2\}$ and $(0.4,0.3)$ is excluded”; (ii) “any vector with nonnegative coordinates at most $1$ is a subgradient at $0$, so $(0.8,0.4)$ is valid.”

Do not compute a conjugate of $\tfrac12 x^2+|x|$, and do not replace $f$ by a soft-thresholding proximal.
permittedResults: The support of $\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}$ is $\max_i v_i\cdot d$. In particular the support of $T=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2,0\}$ is $\max\{d_1,d_2,0\}$.
A vector $g$ lies in $\partial f(x)$ if and only if $f(y)\ge f(x)+g\cdot(y-x)$ for every $y$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read the active gradients at each point, form their convex hull, and test membership by barycentric coordinates in the triangle.
Use the support-function description of f and check the subgradient inequality directly at (1,1) for the exterior candidate.

milestones.criterion: Identifies f as the support of T=conv{e1,e2,0} and computes partial f(0)=T together with the directional formula max(d1,d2,0).
Computes partial f(1,1)=conv{e1,e2}, admits (0.4,0.3) at 0, and rejects (0.8,0.4) by a supporting-inequality or barycentric witness.
Rejects both dropping the origin from the active set and accepting (0.8,0.4) as a subgradient.

commonErrors.description: Treats only x1 and x2 as active at the origin, writes partial f(0)=conv{e1,e2}, and excludes (0.4,0.3) because the coordinates do not sum to 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The subdifferential is reduced to an edge of the triangle and a valid subgradient is rejected.

commonErrors.description: Accepts (0.8,0.4) as a subgradient at 0 because both coordinates are nonnegative and at most 1, ignoring the constraint s+t<=1.
commonErrors.consequence: A vector outside T is certified, and the subgradient inequality already fails at (1,1).

hintTree.content: At the origin all three pieces $x_1$, $x_2$, and the zero function are active, so the subdifferential is the full triangle, not just the opposite edge.
$(0.4,0.3)=0.4\,e_1+0.3\,e_2+0.3\cdot 0$ lies in $T$ because the weights are nonnegative and sum to $1$.
For $g=(0.8,0.4)$ test the point $(1,1)$: $f(1,1)=1$ but $g\cdot(1,1)=1.2$, which already violates the subgradient inequality.

OPT:010219.canonicalSolution:
Each of $x_1$, $x_2$, and $0$ is the support of a singleton $\{e_1\}$, $\{e_2\}$, or $\{0\}$. The pointwise maximum of supports is the support of the convex hull, so
\[
f(x)=\sigma_T(x),\qquad
T=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2,0\}.
\]
The same set is cut out by the three linear inequalities $s\ge 0$, $t\ge 0$, and $s+t\le 1$.

At the origin every piece is active. The gradients are $e_1$, $e_2$, and $0$, hence
\[
\boxed{\partial f(0)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2,0\}=T}.
\]
The directional derivative is
\[
f'(0;d)
=\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{\max\{td_1,td_2,0\}}{t}
=\boxed{\max\{d_1,d_2,0\}},
\]
which is exactly $\sigma_T(d)=\sigma_{\partial f(0)}(d)$.

At $(1,1)$ one has $f(1,1)=1$, and the active pieces are $x_1$ and $x_2$ (both strictly larger than $0$). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\partial f(1,1)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2\}}.
\]

The vector $(0.4,0.3)$ admits the convex combination
\[
(0.4,0.3)=0.4\,e_1+0.3\,e_2+0.3\cdot 0,
\]
with nonnegative weights summing to $1$. Equivalently $0.4\ge 0$, $0.3\ge 0$, and $0.4+0.3=0.7\le 1$. Hence
\[
\boxed{(0.4,0.3)\in\partial f(0)}.
\]
The subgradient inequality holds because $0.4 x_1+0.3 x_2$ is a convex combination of $x_1$, $x_2$, and $0$, and is therefore at most their maximum.

The vector $(0.8,0.4)$ satisfies $0.8+0.4=1.2>1$, so it lies outside $T$. Concretely, at $y=(1,1)$,
\[
f(y)=1<1.2=g\cdot y,
\]
which violates $f(y)\ge f(0)+g\cdot y$. Hence
\[
\boxed{(0.8,0.4)\notin\partial f(0)}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: the zero piece is active at the origin, so the subdifferential is the full triangle and $(0.4,0.3)$ is admitted. Sentence (ii) is false: nonnegativity of the coordinates is not enough; the sum must be at most $1$.

The argument uses only the finite-max subdifferential calculus and a support identification. No Fenchel conjugate of a quadratic kink and no proximal mapping appear.

graderFixtures.proofText: At the origin $\partial f(0)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2,0\}$ and $f'(0;d)=\max\{d_1,d_2,0\}$. At $(1,1)$ the subdifferential is $\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,e_2\}$. The vector $(0.4,0.3)$ lies in $\partial f(0)$; the vector $(0.8,0.4)$ does not.
At 0 the zero piece is inactive. So partial f(0)=conv{e1,e2}, which is the segment s+t=1, s,t>=0. Then (0.4,0.3) is not a subgradient because 0.4+0.3 is not 1.
Any g with 0<=g1<=1 and 0<=g2<=1 is a convex combination of e1, e2, and 0. Therefore (0.8,0.4) lies in partial f(0).

OPT:010220.title: The projection of (3,2) onto [-1,1]^2 is (1,1), distance sqrt(5); n=(2,1) supports at 3 and the midplane 11/2 is strict
OPT:010220.objective: Project an exterior point onto the square, form the outward normal, write the supporting inequality and the support value, evaluate the pairing against the exterior point, and prove strict separation by the midplane.
OPT:010220.statement:
Let $C=[-1,1]^2\subset\mathbb R^2$ and let $z=(3,2)$. Equip $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean inner product. Do not treat $C$ as a spectrahedron and do not pass through a Fenchel conjugate.

1. Compute the Euclidean projection $p=\Pi_C(z)$ by clipping each coordinate independently to $[-1,1]$. Compute the distance $\|z-p\|$ exactly.

2. Set $n=z-p$. Prove the variational inequality
   \[
   n\cdot(x-p)\le 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.
   \]

3. Compute the support value $\sigma_C(n)=\max_{x\in C}n\cdot x$ and the pairing $n\cdot z$.

4. Let $m=(p+z)/2$ be the midpoint of the segment from $p$ to $z$. Write the midplane $\{x:n\cdot x=n\cdot m\}$ and evaluate $n\cdot m$. Prove that this midplane strictly separates $C$ from $\{z\}$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $C$ is centered at the origin, the projection of $z$ is $0$”; (ii) “the support of $C$ in the direction $n$ is the pairing $n\cdot z$.”

Do not replace the square by a second-order cone or a semidefinite slice, and do not introduce a conjugate calculation.
permittedResults: A point $p\in C$ is the Euclidean projection of $z$ onto a closed convex set $C$ if and only if $(z-p)\cdot(x-p)\le 0$ for every $x\in C$.
If $p=\Pi_C(z)$ and $n=z-p\ne 0$, then $\sigma_C(n)=n\cdot p$, and the midplane $n\cdot x=n\cdot(p+z)/2$ strictly separates $C$ from $z$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Clip coordinates to obtain p, set n=z-p, read the support as n·p, and compare 3, 11/2, and 8.
Invoke the variational inequality characterizing Euclidean projection, then form the unique hyperplane orthogonal to n through the midpoint.

milestones.criterion: Computes the clipped projection p=(1,1), the distance sqrt(5), and the normal n=(2,1), and proves n·(x-p)<=0 on C.
Reports the support value 3 and the pairing n·z=8, and proves that the midplane at 11/2 strictly separates C from z.
Rejects both projecting z to the origin and identifying the support of C with the exterior pairing n·z.

commonErrors.description: Uses centering of the square to declare that the projection of z is the origin, so the normal is taken to be z itself.
commonErrors.consequence: The foot of the perpendicular is wrong, the distance is misreported as sqrt(13), and the supporting plane does not touch C at the true exposed point (1,1).

commonErrors.description: Reports the support of C in the direction n as the pairing n·z=8 rather than n·p=3.
commonErrors.consequence: The supporting value is taken on the wrong side of the midplane and strict separation is no longer witnessed by 3<11/2<8.

hintTree.content: Clipping $3$ and $2$ to $[-1,1]$ produces $p=(1,1)$. Then $n=(2,1)$ and $\|n\|=\sqrt{5}$.
On the square both $x_1-1\le 0$ and $x_2-1\le 0$, so $2(x_1-1)+(x_2-1)\le 0$. The support is $n\cdot p=3$.
The midpoint is $(2,3/2)$ and $n\cdot m=4+3/2=11/2$. Compare $3<11/2<8$.

OPT:010220.canonicalSolution:
Each coordinate of $z=(3,2)$ exceeds $1$, so clipping to $[-1,1]$ yields
\[
\boxed{p=(1,1)}.
\]
The residual is $n=z-p=(2,1)$ and
\[
\|z-p\|=\sqrt{4+1}=\boxed{\sqrt{5}}.
\]
For every $x=(x_1,x_2)\in C$ one has $x_1\le 1$ and $x_2\le 1$, hence
\[
n\cdot(x-p)
=2(x_1-1)+(x_2-1)
\le 0.
\]
This is the variational characterization of the Euclidean projection. The same inequality says that $n$ supports $C$ at $p$.

The support value is therefore attained at $p$:
\[
\sigma_C(n)
=\max_{x\in C}(2x_1+x_2)
=2\cdot 1+1
=\boxed{3}.
\]
The pairing against the exterior point is
\[
n\cdot z=2\cdot 3+1\cdot 2=\boxed{8}.
\]
The midpoint is $m=(p+z)/2=(2,3/2)$, and
\[
n\cdot m
=2\cdot 2+1\cdot\frac32
=\boxed{\frac{11}{2}}.
\]
The midplane is $\{x:n\cdot x=11/2\}$. For every $x\in C$ one has $n\cdot x\le 3<11/2$, while $n\cdot z=8>11/2$. Thus the midplane strictly separates $C$ from $\{z\}$.

Sentence (i) is false: centering of $C$ does not move the projection of an exterior point to the origin; $\Pi_C(z)=(1,1)$, not $(0,0)$. Sentence (ii) is false: $n\cdot z=8$ is the pairing against the exterior point, not the support of $C$.

The argument uses only Euclidean projection onto a product of intervals and a supporting/separating hyperplane. No conjugate and no semidefinite representation of the square is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The projection is $p=(1,1)$ with distance $\sqrt{5}$ and normal $n=(2,1)$. The supporting inequality is $n\cdot(x-p)\le 0$, the support is $3$, $n\cdot z=8$, and the midplane value $11/2$ strictly separates $C$ from $z$.
C is centered at 0, so the nearest point to z is the origin. I take p=(0,0), n=(3,2), and distance sqrt(13). Then n·x<=0 is the supporting inequality.
I correctly get p=(1,1) and n=(2,1). The support of C in the direction n is the pairing against the given point, so sigma_C(n)=n·z=8. The midplane value is then not needed.
