DLOG:010630.title: A registered ready/valid stage must hold when the consumer is not ready
DLOG:010630.objective: Write the next-state equations of a same-clock registered ready/valid stage, prove the backpressure hold invariant, complete a six-cycle fire trace, and reject an overwrite or a CDC-toggle substitute.
DLOG:010630.statement:
A single clock domain contains a producer, one registered pipeline stage, and a consumer. The stage stores a data word $D_s$ and a valid bit $v_s$. The producer presents $(v_p,D_p)$. The consumer presents a ready bit $r_c$. All signals are sampled on the rising edge. Implement the stage by
\[
r_p=\overline{v_s}+r_c
\]
and the synchronous update
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_s^+&=
\begin{cases}
0& \text{if reset},\\
v_p& \text{if }r_p=1,\\
v_s& \text{if }r_p=0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
D_s^+=
\begin{cases}
D_p& \text{if }r_p=1\text{ and }v_p=1,\\
D_s& \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
Define the producer fire $f_p=v_p r_p$ and the consumer fire $f_c=v_s r_c$. The producer is well-behaved: it holds $(v_p,D_p)$ until $f_p=1$, then it may change. Reset is released before cycle $0$, with $v_s=0$.

1. Prove the backpressure invariant: if $v_s=1$ and $r_c=0$, then $r_p=0$, $f_p=0$, $v_s^+=1$, and $D_s^+=D_s$. Conclude that a valid unread word cannot be overwritten.

2. Complete the six-cycle table for the inputs
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
\text{cycle}&0&1&2&3&4&5\\ \hline
v_p&1&1&1&1&0&0\\
D_p&A&B&B&B&{-}&{-}\\
r_c&1&0&0&1&1&1.
\end{array}
\]
For each cycle report $v_s$, $D_s$, $r_p$, $f_p$, and $f_c$ at the beginning of the cycle (after the previous edge). List the cycle of every consumer fire and the word transferred.

3. A proposed revision updates $D_s\leftarrow D_p$ whenever $v_p=1$, ignoring $r_p$. Show on this waveform that the unread word $A$ is lost. A second proposal replaces the stage by a two-flop toggle handshake between unrelated clocks. Explain why that proposal answers a different (CDC) question.

4. Do not assign analog metastability values, do not introduce a second clock, and do not claim that tying $r_p$ to $1$ is safe because the consumer will eventually catch up.
permittedResults: From $r_p=\overline{v_s}+r_c$ one has $v_s\overline{r_c}\Rightarrow r_p=0$. Combined with the synchronous update, $r_p=0$ freezes both $v_s$ and $D_s$.
A well-behaved producer may change $D_p$ only after $f_p=1$. Ignoring $r_p$ inside the stage is still unsafe, because the stage can then overwrite an unread $D_s$ even if the producer itself holds.

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive r_p=0 from the combinational identity under v_s AND NOT r_c, then fill the waveform from the reset state using only that identity and the synchronous update.
Mark producer and consumer fires first, then fill D_s by the rule that a fire_p loads a new word and a stalled valid copies the old word.

milestones.criterion: Proves that a valid unread stage forces r_p=0 and holds both v_s and D_s.
Completes the six-cycle fire table and reports consumer transfers of A at cycle 3 and B at cycle 4.
Shows that ignoring r_p loses A, and rejects a CDC toggle handshake or a tied-high ready as a repair.

commonErrors.description: Updates D_s whenever v_p is high, ties r_p to 1, or otherwise overwrites a valid unread stage while r_c=0, losing A on the assigned waveform.
commonErrors.consequence: The backpressure invariant fails and a transferred word is dropped.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the same-clock ready/valid stage by a two-flop synchronizer or a toggle handshake between unrelated clocks, or treats the problem as the held CDC-repair exercise.
commonErrors.consequence: The intra-domain stall equations are never written, and a different clock-crossing packet is substituted.

hintTree.content: At the start of cycle $0$, $v_s=0$, so $r_p=1$ regardless of $r_c$. The first rising edge captures $A$ but the consumer does not fire that cycle.
Cycles $1$ and $2$ have $v_s=1$ and $r_c=0$. The invariant forces $r_p=0$ and holds $A$.
The producer offers $B$ from cycle $1$, but $B$ can enter the stage only on the first later cycle with $r_p=1$, which is cycle $3$.

DLOG:010630.canonicalSolution:
Assume $v_s=1$ and $r_c=0$. The ready equation gives
\[
r_p=\overline{1}+0=0.
\]
Hence $f_p=v_pr_p=0$. The synchronous update with $r_p=0$ yields $v_s^+=v_s=1$ and $D_s^+=D_s$. Therefore a valid unread word is frozen, and no new producer beat is accepted.
\[
\boxed{v_s\overline{r_c}\Rightarrow r_p=f_p=0,\ v_s^+=1,\ D_s^+=D_s}.
\]

State at the beginning of each cycle:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{cycle}&v_s&D_s&r_p&f_p&f_c\\ \hline
0&0&{-}&1&1&0\\
1&1&A&0&0&0\\
2&1&A&0&0&0\\
3&1&A&1&1&1\\
4&1&B&1&0&1\\
5&0&{-}&1&0&0.
\end{array}
\]
Cycle $0$: $r_p=\overline{0}+1=1$, so $f_p=1$ captures $A$ and $f_c=0$. After the edge, $v_s=1$, $D_s=A$.
Cycles $1$--$2$: $v_s\overline{r_c}$ holds $A$ and refuses $B$.
Cycle $3$: $r_c=1$ so $r_p=1$, $f_c=1$ delivers $A$ to the consumer, and $f_p=1$ captures $B$.
Cycle $4$: $v_p=0$, $r_p=1$, $f_c=1$ delivers $B$, and $v_s$ clears.
Cycle $5$: idle.
Consumer fires: $A$ in cycle $3$, $B$ in cycle $4$.
\[
\boxed{f_c\text{ transfers }A\text{ at }3\text{ and }B\text{ at }4}.
\]

If the stage writes $D_s\leftarrow D_p$ whenever $v_p=1$, then in cycle $1$ the unread $A$ is replaced by $B$ while $r_c=0$. The later consumer fire in cycle $3$ then pops $B$, and $A$ is lost. That revision violates the invariant of part 1.

A two-flop toggle handshake between unrelated clocks is the held CDC packet. The present circuit has one clock; there is no metastability aperture to close and no pulse-stretching problem. Importing a CDC toggle answers a different question and does not implement $r_p=\overline{v_s}+r_c$.

Tying $r_p$ to $1$ likewise overwrites $D_s$ on every producer beat, including while $r_c=0$. Eventual later consumer readiness does not recover a discarded word.

graderFixtures.proofText: From r_p=NOT v_s OR r_c, a valid unread stage forces r_p=0 and freezes D_s. The table is (v_s,D_s,r_p,f_p,f_c): 0/- /1/1/0; 1/A/0/0/0; 1/A/0/0/0; 1/A/1/1/1; 1/B/1/0/1; 0/- /1/0/0. Consumer receives A at cycle 3 and B at cycle 4. Writing D_s on every v_p loses A at cycle 1. A CDC toggle handshake is a different, two-clock problem and is not a repair. Tying r_p high is also an overwrite.
Whenever v_p=1 I write D_s<=D_p, so in cycle 1 the stage data becomes B even though r_c=0. The consumer later pops B. Holding the old word is unnecessary because the producer already offered B.

This is a handshake, so I repair it with a toggle pulse and two flip-flop synchronizers between unrelated clocks A and B, as in the clock-domain-crossing exercise. Ready/valid on one clock is unnecessary.

DLOG:010631.title: Incomplete combinational assignment latches; an enabled flip-flop does not
DLOG:010631.objective: Diagnose latch inference, incomplete sensitivity, and blocking-assignment swap collapse, rewrite the fragments, and distinguish an enabled flip-flop from a level-sensitive latch.
permittedResults: If a combinational block's sensitivity list omits a right-hand-side source, event-driven simulation can skip an update that synthesized hardware still performs. That is a simulation/synthesis mismatch, not a latch.
On a clock edge, the sequential blocking pair $a=b;\,b=a;$ assigns both registers the old $b$. The NBA pair $a<=b;\,b<=a;$ exchanges them.

acceptableStrategies.description: Ask, for each fragment, whether the procedure is combinational or clocked, then whether every path assigns every output, then whether the sensitivity list names every source.
Execute X's two blocking statements in textual order from (1,0), then repeat the trace with both RHS values sampled before either update.

milestones.criterion: Classifies W, X, Y, and Z, including the incomplete-sensitivity mismatch in W and the latch in Z.
Simulates the blocking swap collapse (1,0)->(0,0) and gives a working NBA swap with trace (1,0)->(0,1)->(1,0).
Rewrites W and Z as a latch-free mux, states the combinational-versus-clocked incompleteness rule, and rejects 'Y is a latch' and 'blocking is always illegal'.

commonErrors.description: Calls fragment Y a latch because q is not assigned when en=0, or applies the combinational latch-inference rule to a posedge block.
commonErrors.consequence: An enabled flip-flop is misidentified as level-sensitive storage, so the clocked hold path is treated as a transparent latch.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a=b; b=a; on a clock edge swaps the two registers, or reports the two-edge trace from (1,0) as (1,0)->(0,1)->(1,0) for fragment X.
commonErrors.consequence: The sequential blocking collapse to (0,0) is missed, so the NBA repair is never motivated.

hintTree.content: Fragment W assigns $y$ on every path, so it is not a latch. Its sensitivity list still omits $b$.
In X the second statement sees the already-updated $a$. Start from $(1,0)$ and execute the two lines in order.
Y is missing an assignment only inside a clocked block. That held value is the $Q$ of an enabled flip-flop, not a transparent latch.

DLOG:010631.canonicalSolution:
Fragment W assigns $y$ on both the $\texttt{sel}$ and $\texttt{else}$ paths, so synthesis infers combinational mux logic, not a latch. The sensitivity list is $\texttt{(a or sel)}$ and omits $b$. If $b$ changes while $\texttt{sel}=0$, event-driven simulation does not re-evaluate $y$, while the synthesized mux does. That is a simulation/synthesis mismatch.

Fragment X is a pair of edge-triggered flip-flops written with blocking assignments. It is not a swap.

Fragment Y is an enabled flip-flop: $q$ updates on the rising edge only when $\texttt{en}=1$, and otherwise holds as ordinary clocked state. It is not a latch.

Fragment Z has a complete sensitivity list $\texttt{@(*)}$ but does not assign $y$ when $\texttt{sel}=0$. Synthesis therefore infers a level-sensitive latch with enable $\texttt{sel}$ and data $a$.
\[
\boxed{W:\text{combo mux + sim mismatch};\ X:\text{FF, not swap};\ Y:\text{enabled FF};\ Z:\text{latch}}.
\]

Simulate X from $(a,b)=(1,0)$. On the first rising edge, $a=b$ sets $a\leftarrow 0$; then $b=a$ sets $b\leftarrow 0$. The state is $(0,0)$. The second edge leaves $(0,0)$.
\[
\boxed{X\text{ from }(1,0)\to(0,0)\to(0,0)}.
\]
The NBA rewrite
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\texttt{always @(posedge clk) begin}\\
&\quad\texttt{a <= b;}\\
&\quad\texttt{b <= a;}\\
&\texttt{end}
\end{aligned}
\]
samples both right-hand sides at the edge, so $(1,0)\to(0,1)\to(1,0)$.
\[
\boxed{\text{NBA swap }(1,0)\to(0,1)\to(1,0)}.
\]

A repaired W (and a repaired Z) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\texttt{always @(*) begin}\\
&\quad\texttt{if (sel) y = a; else y = b;}\\
&\texttt{end}
\end{aligned}
\]
or the equivalent $\texttt{assign y = sel ? a : b;}$. Blocking assignment is legal in this combinational block. The distinguishing rule: incomplete assignment infers a latch only in a combinational always; the same incompleteness in $\texttt{always @(posedge clk)}$ infers an enabled flip-flop, which is fragment Y.

Claim (i) is false: Y is an enabled flip-flop. Claim (ii) is false: combinational blocks conventionally use blocking assignment; changing Z to NBA would not remove the latch. Claim (iii) is false: X collapses both registers to the old $b$. None of the fragments is a CDC synchronizer, and no second clock appears.

graderFixtures.proofText: W is a combinational mux with a simulation/synthesis mismatch from omitting b. X is two flip-flops whose blocking pair sends (1,0) to (0,0) and stays there; the NBA pair a<=b; b<=a; swaps (1,0) to (0,1) to (1,0). Y is an enabled flip-flop, not a latch. Z infers a latch because the combinational block does not assign y when sel=0. Repaired W and Z assign both mux paths under always @(*) (or an assign ternary). Incomplete assignment latches only in combinational always; the same gap in posedge infers an enabled FF.
Fragment Y does not assign q when en=0, so synthesis infers a level-sensitive latch for q. Clocked incomplete assignment is the same rule as combinational incomplete assignment.
In fragment X both a and b are assigned, so the pair swaps. From (1,0) the first clock gives (0,1) and the second gives (1,0). Nonblocking assignments are unnecessary.

DSP:010117.title: Aperiodic r[k] of (1,2,-1) is 6,0,-1 with |X|^2=6-2cos 2w and Parseval energy 6
DSP:010117.objective: Compute the aperiodic autocorrelation r[0]=6, r[±1]=0, r[±2]=-1 of x=(1,2,-1), identify |X|^2=6-2cos 2ω with range [4,8], confirm the Parseval integral equals 6, and distinguish the self-convolution (1,4,2,-4,1).
DSP:010117.statement:
Let $x$ be the finite real sequence with
\[
x[0]=1,\qquad x[1]=2,\qquad x[2]=-1,
\]
and $x[n]=0$ for every other integer $n$. The deterministic aperiodic
autocorrelation is
\[
r[k]=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}x[n]x[n-k],
\]
and the DTFT is
\[
X(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}x[n]e^{-j\omega n}.
\]
Parseval's identity is used in the standing convention
\[
\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|x[n]|^2
=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\bigl|X(e^{j\omega})\bigr|^2\,d\omega.
\]

1. Evaluate every nonzero lag of $r$. In particular prove
   $r[0]=6$, $r[\pm 1]=0$, and $r[\pm 2]=-1$, and confirm $r[-k]=r[k]$.

2. Write $X(e^{j\omega})=1+2e^{-j\omega}-e^{-j2\omega}$. Using either the
   Wiener--Khinchin sum $\sum_k r[k]e^{-j\omega k}$ or a direct expansion,
   prove
   \[
   \bigl|X(e^{j\omega})\bigr|^2=6-2\cos 2\omega.
   \]
   Determine the exact minimum and maximum of this nonnegative function
   on $[-\pi,\pi]$.

3. Evaluate both sides of Parseval's identity and prove that each equals
   $6$. Do not replace the $1/(2\pi)$ convention by an un-normalized
   integral of $|X|^2$.

4. Compute the linear self-convolution $(x*x)[n]=\sum_k x[k]x[n-k]$ and
   prove that the length-$5$ list starting at $n=0$ is $(1,4,2,-4,1)$.
   Audit both sentences: (i) “autocorrelation is the same operator as
   $x*x$, so $r$ equals $(1,4,2,-4,1)$”; (ii) “$|X|^2$ is the constant
   energy $6$, or else a min-phase / max-phase spectral factor of a
   periodogram.”

Do not replace the calculation by linear-versus-circular convolution of
two distinct sequences, and do not invoke coefficient quantization,
decimation, a rectangular window, or a periodogram variance identity.
permittedResults: Wiener--Khinchin for finite energy sequences: $|X(e^{j\omega})|^2=\sum_k r[k]e^{-j\omega k}$. Evenness of $r$ converts the sum into a real cosine polynomial.
The identity $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(m\omega)\,d\omega=0$ for every nonzero integer $m$ reduces the Parseval integral of a cosine polynomial to its constant term.

acceptableStrategies.description: Tabulate the five lags of r, convert the even list to 6-2cos 2ω, then compute x*x on {0,...,4} as a separate operator.
Expand |1+2e^{-jω}-e^{-j2ω}|^2 by conjugates to lock the cosine polynomial, then identify r as the inverse DTFT of that polynomial.

milestones.criterion: Computes the aperiodic lags r[0]=6, r[±1]=0, r[±2]=-1 and the DTFT energy density |X|^2=6-2cos 2ω with range [4,8].
Confirms the Parseval integral equals 6 and distinguishes the linear self-convolution (1,4,2,-4,1) from r.
Rejects a constant-|X|^2 or spectral-factor reading and refuses the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Reports r as the linear self-convolution (1,4,2,-4,1), or writes r[k]=sum x[k]x[n-k] without the lag-reversed factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The required even list 6,0,-1 is lost, so Wiener--Khinchin cannot produce 6-2cos 2ω.

commonErrors.description: Takes |X|^2 to be the constant 6, drops the double angle, reports min/max other than 4 and 8, or calls the un-normalized integral 12π the Parseval value 6.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy identity and the range [4,8] fail, or a spectral-factor / periodogram reading is imported.

hintTree.content: Only pairs with both samples nonzero contribute. The three products in $r[0]$ are $1$, $4$, and $1$. The lag-$1$ products are $2\cdot 1$ and $(-1)\cdot 2$.
Evenness gives $|X|^2=r[0]+2r[2]\cos 2\omega$ after the lag-$1$ terms cancel. The range of $\cos 2\omega$ is $[-1,1]$.
Self-convolution at index $2$ is $1\cdot(-1)+2\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 1=2$, which already differs from $r[2]=-1$.

DSP:010117.canonicalSolution:
The support of $x$ is $\{0,1,2\}$, so $r[k]$ can be nonzero only for
$|k|\le 2$. Direct expansion yields
\begin{align*}
r[0]
&=x[0]^2+x[1]^2+x[2]^2
=1+4+1=6,\\
r[1]
&=x[1]x[0]+x[2]x[1]
=2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 2=0,\\
r[2]
&=x[2]x[0]
=(-1)\cdot 1=-1.
\end{align*}
The sequence is real, so $r[-k]=r[k]$. In particular $r[\pm 1]=0$ and
$r[\pm 2]=-1$.
\[
\boxed{r[0]=6,\quad r[\pm 1]=0,\quad r[\pm 2]=-1}.
\]

The DTFT is the trigonometric polynomial
\[
X(e^{j\omega})=1+2e^{-j\omega}-e^{-j2\omega}.
\]
Wiener--Khinchin and evenness of $r$ give
\[
\bigl|X(e^{j\omega})\bigr|^2
=r[0]+2r[1]\cos\omega+2r[2]\cos 2\omega
=6-2\cos 2\omega.
\]
The same identity follows by multiplying $X$ by its conjugate
$1+2e^{j\omega}-e^{j2\omega}$ and collecting the constant and
double-angle terms. Because $\cos 2\omega$ ranges over $[-1,1]$,
\[
4\le 6-2\cos 2\omega\le 8,
\]
with the minimum $4$ at $2\omega\equiv 0\pmod{2\pi}$ and the maximum $8$
at $2\omega\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$.
\[
\boxed{|X|^2=6-2\cos 2\omega,\quad \min 4,\quad \max 8}.
\]

The left-hand side of Parseval is the energy already computed:
$\sum|x[n]|^2=r[0]=6$. The right-hand side is
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(6-2\cos 2\omega)\,d\omega
=\frac1{2\pi}\cdot 12\pi=6,
\]
because the cosine integrates to zero. Thus both sides equal $6$. An
un-normalized integral $\int|X|^2\,d\omega=12\pi$ is a different
convention and is not the Parseval integral of this packet.

Linear self-convolution has support $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ and samples
\begin{align*}
(x*x)[0]&=1,\\
(x*x)[1]&=1\cdot 2+2\cdot 1=4,\\
(x*x)[2]&=1\cdot(-1)+2\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 1=2,\\
(x*x)[3]&=2\cdot(-1)+(-1)\cdot 2=-4,\\
(x*x)[4]&=(-1)\cdot(-1)=1.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{x*x=(1,4,2,-4,1)}.
\]
This list is $x*x$, not $x*x^\vee$. In particular the middle sample
$2$ is not $r[2]=-1$, and the list is not even about the origin.

Sentence (i) therefore replaces autocorrelation by self-convolution.
Sentence (ii) either freezes $|X|^2$ at the energy $6$ or imports a
min-phase / max-phase spectral-factorization exercise (or a periodogram
bias identity) that is not asked. The present $|X|^2$ is a two-harmonic
cosine polynomial attached to a length-$3$ pulse, not a spectral factor.

The argument never compares linear convolution with circular wrap of two
distinct sequences, never quantizes a coefficient, never decimates, and
never windows a sinusoid.

graderFixtures.proofText: Aperiodic lags are $r[0]=6$, $r[\pm 1]=0$, $r[\pm 2]=-1$. Then $|X|^2=6-2\cos 2\omega$ ranges over $[4,8]$, and Parseval gives energy $6$. The self-convolution $x*x=(1,4,2,-4,1)$ is a different operator.
Autocorrelation is just convolution of x with itself, so r equals the length-5 list (1,4,2,-4,1). I do not reverse the second factor and I treat r[2]=2 as the energy-density coefficient.

|X|^2 equals the energy 6 for every ω, so there is no cosine and no min 4 or max 8. Alternatively I integrate |X|^2 without 1/2π and call 12π the Parseval integral 6, or I factor |X|^2 into min-phase and max-phase spectral factors.

DSP:010118.title: Hilbert of 1+(-1)^n+2cos(πn/3)+3sin(πn/2) is 2sin(πn/3)-3cos(πn/2)
DSP:010118.objective: Apply the discrete Hilbert transformer that is -j on (0,π), +j on (-π,0), and 0 at DC and Nyquist to obtain x̂=2sin(πn/3)-3cos(πn/2) and the analytic signal 1+(-1)^n+2e^{jπn/3}-3j e^{jπn/2}, doubling interior positives and leaving DC/Nyquist undoubled.
DSP:010118.statement:
Adopt the standing discrete-time Hilbert transformer
\[
H_d(e^{j\omega})=\begin{cases}
-j,&0<\omega<\pi,\\
+j,&-\pi<\omega<0,\\
0,&\omega=0\text{ or }\omega=\pm\pi,
\end{cases}
\]
with $2\pi$-periodic extension. The corresponding analytic filter is
$1+jH_d$, which equals $2$ on the open positive-frequency interval
$(0,\pi)$, equals $0$ on the open negative-frequency interval
$(-\pi,0)$, and equals $1$ at DC and at Nyquist. Let
\[
x[n]=1+(-1)^n+2\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)+3\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr).
\]

1. Identify the four signal components in $x$, list all of their
   discrete-time spectral locations, and classify each location as DC,
   Nyquist, strictly positive interior, or strictly negative interior.
   Apply $H_d$ tone by tone and prove
   \[
   \hat x[n]=2\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)-3\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr).
   \]

2. Form the analytic signal $x_a[n]=x[n]+j\hat x[n]$ and prove
   \[
   x_a[n]=1+(-1)^n+2e^{j\pi n/3}-3j\,e^{j\pi n/2}.
   \]
   Explain why the interior positive tones are doubled, the interior
   negative tones vanish, and the DC and Nyquist tones remain undoubled.

3. Confirm the two elementary rules used above: for $0<\omega_0<\pi$,
   the Hilbert transform of $\cos(\omega_0 n)$ is $\sin(\omega_0 n)$ and
   the Hilbert transform of $\sin(\omega_0 n)$ is $-\cos(\omega_0 n)$.
   Check that neither rule applies to $\omega_0=0$ or $\omega_0=\pi$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “DC and Nyquist are ordinary positive
   frequencies, so they are phase-shifted by $-90^\circ$ and doubled in
   $x_a$”; (ii) “the opposite convention $H_d=+j$ on $(0,\pi)$ is
   equivalent, or the calculation is a rectangular-window leakage /
   periodogram exercise.”

Do not replace the transformer by a linear-versus-circular convolution
identity, and do not invoke spectral factorization.
permittedResults: For $0<\omega_0<\pi$ one has $H_d\{\cos(\omega_0 n)\}=\sin(\omega_0 n)$ and $H_d\{\sin(\omega_0 n)\}=-\cos(\omega_0 n)$, because $e^{\pm j\omega_0 n}$ are multiplied by $\mp j$.
The complex tones $1$ and $(-1)^n=e^{j\pi n}$ are fixed by $1+jH_d$ rather than doubled, because $H_d$ vanishes at $0$ and $\pi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split every real tone into a complex conjugate pair, multiply by Hd, and reassemble the real and analytic combinations.
Use the interior rules Hd cos=sin and Hd sin=-cos, then handle the two real frequencies 0 and π separately as fixed points of 1+jHd.

milestones.criterion: Applies the stated Hd convention tone by tone to obtain x̂=2sin(πn/3)-3cos(πn/2), with DC and Nyquist annihilated.
Builds the analytic signal 1+(-1)^n+2e^{jπn/3}-3j e^{jπn/2} and explains doubling of interior positives versus undoubled DC/Nyquist.
Rejects a DC/Nyquist phase shift or doubling, the opposite Hd sign, and reserved intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Applies a -90° shift to 1 or to (-1)^n, or doubles those tones in xa, as if DC and Nyquist were ordinary frequencies in (0,π).
commonErrors.consequence: The required x̂ loses its vanishing DC/Nyquist part and xa is no longer 1+(-1)^n plus the two interior analytic tones.

commonErrors.description: Takes Hd=+j on (0,π) and -j on (-π,0), producing x̂=-2sin(πn/3)+3cos(πn/2) and conjugating the analytic tones.
commonErrors.consequence: The displayed Hilbert pair and the factor -3j e^{jπn/2} are replaced by their conjugates.

hintTree.content: The constant $1$ lives at $\omega=0$ and $(-1)^n$ lives at $\omega=\pi$. Both are killed by $H_d$.
The tone $2\cos(\pi n/3)$ is interior, so its Hilbert transform is $2\sin(\pi n/3)$. The tone $3\sin(\pi n/2)$ becomes $-3\cos(\pi n/2)$.
Adding $j\hat x$ converts $2\cos+j\cdot 2\sin$ into $2e^{j\pi n/3}$ and converts $3\sin+j\cdot(-3\cos)$ into $-3j e^{j\pi n/2}$.

DSP:010118.canonicalSolution:
Expand each real tone into complex exponentials. The constant $1$ is a
DC tone at $\omega=0$. The alternating sequence $(-1)^n=e^{j\pi n}$ is a
Nyquist tone at $\omega=\pi$. The cosine
$2\cos(\pi n/3)=e^{j\pi n/3}+e^{-j\pi n/3}$ occupies the interior pair
$\pm\pi/3$, and the sine
$3\sin(\pi n/2)=(3/(2j))(e^{j\pi n/2}-e^{-j\pi n/2})$ occupies the
interior pair $\pm\pi/2$.

The multiplier $H_d$ vanishes at $0$ and at $\pi$, so
\[
H_d\{1\}=0,\qquad H_d\{(-1)^n\}=0.
\]
On the open interval $(0,\pi)$ one has $H_d=-j$, and on $(-\pi,0)$ one
has $H_d=+j$. Therefore
\[
H_d\{e^{j\pi n/3}\}=-j\,e^{j\pi n/3},\qquad
H_d\{e^{-j\pi n/3}\}=+j\,e^{-j\pi n/3},
\]
which together send $2\cos(\pi n/3)$ to $2\sin(\pi n/3)$. The same signs
send $e^{j\pi n/2}$ to $-j e^{j\pi n/2}$ and $e^{-j\pi n/2}$ to
$+j e^{-j\pi n/2}$, hence
\[
H_d\bigl\{3\sin(\pi n/2)\bigr\}=-3\cos(\pi n/2).
\]
Adding these contributions,
\[
\boxed{\hat x[n]=2\sin(\pi n/3)-3\cos(\pi n/2)}.
\]
(The elementary rules $H_d\{\cos(\omega_0 n)\}=\sin(\omega_0 n)$ and
$H_d\{\sin(\omega_0 n)\}=-\cos(\omega_0 n)$ are valid only for
$0<\omega_0<\pi$; they fail at DC and at Nyquist, where $H_d=0$.)

The analytic signal is $x_a=x+j\hat x$. The DC and Nyquist terms are
copied:
\[
1+j\cdot 0=1,\qquad (-1)^n+j\cdot 0=(-1)^n.
\]
The cosine pair becomes
\[
2\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)+j\cdot 2\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)
=2e^{j\pi n/3},
\]
so the interior positive tone is doubled and the interior negative tone
is cancelled. The sine pair becomes
\begin{align*}
3\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr)+j\bigl(-3\cos(\pi n/2)\bigr)
&=-3j\Bigl(\cos\frac{\pi n}{2}+j\sin\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr)
=-3j\,e^{j\pi n/2},
\end{align*}
again doubling the positive frequency $\pi/2$ and annihilating
$-\pi/2$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{x_a[n]=1+(-1)^n+2e^{j\pi n/3}-3j\,e^{j\pi n/2}}.
\]
Equivalently, $1+jH_d$ equals $2$ on $(0,\pi)$, equals $0$ on $(-\pi,0)$,
and equals $1$ at $\omega=0$ and $\omega=\pi$.

Sentence (i) treats DC and Nyquist as ordinary interior positives. That
error phase-shifts $1$ and $(-1)^n$ and doubles them in $x_a$, destroying
both displayed formulas. Sentence (ii) reverses the sign of $H_d$ on
$(0,\pi)$, which negates $\hat x$, or else replaces the transformer by a
rectangular-window leakage or periodogram calculation that is not asked.

The argument never compares linear and circular convolution and never
factors a spectrum into min-phase and max-phase parts.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $H_d=-j$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $H_d=0$ at DC/Nyquist, $\hat x=2\sin(\pi n/3)-3\cos(\pi n/2)$ and $x_a=1+(-1)^n+2e^{j\pi n/3}-3j e^{j\pi n/2}$. Interior positives are doubled; DC and Nyquist are copied, not doubled.

The constant 1 and the Nyquist tone (-1)^n are positive-frequency tones, so I send them through -j and double them in xa. Then xa starts with 2+2(-1)^n rather than 1+(-1)^n, and x̂ contains a constant and an alternating term.

I take Hd=+j on (0,π), so the Hilbert transform of 2cos(πn/3) is -2sin(πn/3) and the Hilbert transform of 3sin(πn/2) is +3cos(πn/2). The analytic signal then uses e^{-jπn/3} and the conjugate of -3j e^{jπn/2}.

DSP:010219.title: The symmetric FIR (1,2,3,4,3,2,1) is e^{-j3w}(4+6cos w+4cos 2w+2cos 3w) and folds to y=11
DSP:010219.objective: Factor H(e^{jω})=e^{-j3ω}[4+6cos ω+4cos 2ω+2cos 3ω], identify the delay-3 real amplitude after the linear-phase factor is taken away, compare 4 folded multiplies with 7 direct multiplies, and evaluate the folded contributions 2,-6,15,0 giving y=11 on the register (1,-1,2,0,3,-2,1).
DSP:010219.statement:
Let $h$ be the real Type-I linear-phase FIR
\[
h[0]=1,\; h[1]=2,\; h[2]=3,\; h[3]=4,\; h[4]=3,\; h[5]=2,\; h[6]=1,
\]
so $h[n]=h[6-n]$ and $h[n]=0$ outside $\{0,\ldots,6\}$. The DTFT is
\[
H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{6}h[n]e^{-j\omega n}.
\]

1. Factor the bulk delay $e^{-j3\omega}$ away and prove
   \[
   H(e^{j\omega})
   =e^{-j3\omega}\bigl[4+6\cos\omega+4\cos 2\omega+2\cos 3\omega\bigr].
   \]
   Identify the group delay $3$ wherever $H(e^{j\omega})\ne 0$ and
   explain why the remaining amplitude is real and even. Locate the
   zeros of that real amplitude on $[0,\pi]$.

2. Draw (or describe) the folded direct-form arithmetic that pairs taps
   $n$ and $6-n$ before multiplying by the common coefficient. Count the
   multiplies: $4$ in the folded realization versus $7$ in the unfolded
   tap-by-tap sum.

3. Suppose the delay register, from the newest sample $x[n]$ down to
   $x[n-6]$, holds
   \[
   \bigl(1,-1,2,0,3,-2,1\bigr).
   \]
   Compute the four folded contributions
   $h[0](x[n]+x[n-6])$, $h[1](x[n-1]+x[n-5])$, $h[2](x[n-2]+x[n-4])$,
   and $h[3]x[n-3]$, and prove that they equal $2$, $-6$, $15$, and $0$.
   Conclude that the filter output is $y[n]=11$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “symmetry already absorbs the delay, so
   $H$ is the real amplitude $4+6\cos\omega+\cdots$ with group delay
   $0$”; (ii) “seven distinct coefficients must be multiplied, and the
   register output is the unfolded inner product written without pairing.”

Do not replace the structure by a coefficient-quantized pole, a
decimator, or a spectral-factor lattice.
permittedResults: The pairing $e^{-j\omega n}+e^{-j\omega(6-n)}=e^{-j3\omega}\cdot 2\cos((3-n)\omega)$ converts the seven-tap sum into $e^{-j3\omega}$ times a cosine polynomial.
Substituting $\cos 2\omega=2c^2-1$ and $\cos 3\omega=4c^3-3c$ with $c=\cos\omega$ factors the present amplitude as $A(\omega)=8\cos^2\omega\,(\cos\omega+1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor e^{-j3ω} first, read the four cosine coefficients from the symmetric pairs, then evaluate the folded sum on the given register.
Compute the seven-tap inner product 1-2+6+0+9-4+1=11 to lock the output, then regroup it as the four folded products.

milestones.criterion: Factors H(e^{jω})=e^{-j3ω}[4+6cos ω+4cos 2ω+2cos 3ω] and identifies the delay-3 real amplitude.
Counts 4 folded versus 7 unfolded multiplies and evaluates the contributions 2,-6,15,0 with y=11.
Rejects dropping the delay factor and refuses quantized-pole, decimation, or spectral-factor substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Writes H as the real amplitude 4+6cos ω+4cos 2ω+2cos 3ω with group delay 0, or treats symmetry as already absorbing e^{-j3ω}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required delay-3 factorization is lost, and ‘factor the delay away’ has nothing left to factor.

commonErrors.description: Insists on seven distinct multiplies, or evaluates the register without pairing and misses the contributions 2,-6,15,0 and the sum 11.
commonErrors.consequence: The folded arithmetic that the structure is meant to exhibit is never produced.

hintTree.content: Shift every exponential by $e^{-j3\omega}$. The center tap contributes $4$. The outermost pair contributes $2\cos 3\omega$.
Folding uses the four coefficients $1,2,3,4$ rather than all seven taps. Pair $1$ with $1$, $-1$ with $-2$, $2$ with $3$, and keep the center $0$.
The four products are $1\cdot 2$, $2\cdot(-3)$, $3\cdot 5$, and $4\cdot 0$. Their sum is $11$.

DSP:010219.canonicalSolution:
Write $H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{6}h[n]e^{-j\omega n}$ and factor
$e^{-j3\omega}$ from every term. The center tap $h[3]=4$ is already
aligned. Each symmetric pair contributes a real cosine:
\begin{align*}
h[2]e^{-j2\omega}+h[4]e^{-j4\omega}
&=e^{-j3\omega}\cdot 6\cos\omega,\\
h[1]e^{-j\omega}+h[5]e^{-j5\omega}
&=e^{-j3\omega}\cdot 4\cos 2\omega,\\
h[0]+h[6]e^{-j6\omega}
&=e^{-j3\omega}\cdot 2\cos 3\omega.
\end{align*}
Adding the center contribution $4e^{-j3\omega}$ produces
\[
\boxed{H(e^{j\omega})=e^{-j3\omega}\bigl[4+6\cos\omega+4\cos 2\omega+2\cos 3\omega\bigr]}.
\]
The factor $e^{-j3\omega}$ is the bulk delay of a length-$7$ Type-I
filter: on every frequency interval where $H(e^{j\omega})\ne0$, the
group delay is the constant $3$. At the response zeros the phase, and
hence the group delay, is undefined. After that delay is taken away, the amplitude
\[
A(\omega)=4+6\cos\omega+4\cos 2\omega+2\cos 3\omega
\]
is real and even. The trigonometric reduction
$A(\omega)=8\cos^2\omega\,(\cos\omega+1)$ shows that $A$ vanishes at
$\omega=\pi/2$, $\omega=\pi$, and (by evenness) $\omega=-\pi/2$, while
$A(0)=16\neq 0$. Those unit-circle zeros are properties of the real
amplitude, not a replacement for the delay factor.

Because $h[n]=h[6-n]$, the seven-tap inner product folds to four
multiplies:
\[
y[n]
=1\cdot\bigl(x[n]+x[n-6]\bigr)
+2\cdot\bigl(x[n-1]+x[n-5]\bigr)
+3\cdot\bigl(x[n-2]+x[n-4]\bigr)
+4\cdot x[n-3].
\]
The unfolded tap-by-tap form uses all seven coefficients as separate
multiplies. Symmetry therefore saves three multiplies.

On the given register $(x[n],\ldots,x[n-6])=(1,-1,2,0,3,-2,1)$ the
folded contributions are
\begin{align*}
1\cdot(1+1)&=2,\\
2\cdot(-1+(-2))&=-6,\\
3\cdot(2+3)&=15,\\
4\cdot 0&=0.
\end{align*}
Their sum is $2-6+15+0=11$.
\[
\boxed{\text{folded contributions }2,-6,15,0;\quad y[n]=11}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $e^{-j3\omega}$ and reports a zero-delay real
frequency response. That error loses both the group delay $3$ and the
meaning of “factor the delay away.” Sentence (ii) refuses the fold,
counts seven multiplies as mandatory, and never produces the four
contributions $2,-6,15,0$.

The argument never quantizes a coefficient, never decimates, and never
factors $H$ into min-phase and max-phase spectral factors.

graderFixtures.proofText: After factoring the delay $e^{-j3\omega}$ away one has $H=e^{-j3\omega}[4+6\cos\omega+4\cos 2\omega+2\cos 3\omega]$ with group delay $3$ wherever $H\ne0$; it is undefined at response zeros. Folding uses $4$ multiplies, not $7$. On the register $(1,-1,2,0,3,-2,1)$ the contributions are $2,-6,15,0$ and $y=11$.
A symmetric FIR is already zero-phase, so H is just the real function 4+6cos w+4cos 2w+2cos 3w. There is no factor e^{-j3w} and the group delay is 0.

Seven distinct coefficients must be multiplied, so the folded count 4 is wrong. I evaluate the register without pairing and list the seven products 1, -2, 6, 0, 9, -4, 1. I never form the folded contributions 2, -6, 15, 0.

DSP:010220.title: The moving sum 1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3} equals (1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1}) with removable value 4
DSP:010220.objective: Identify the removable value 4 in H=(1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1}), realize v[n]=v[n-1]+x[n] and y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4], compute the step responses y=1,2,3,4,4,... and v=n+1, and separate external FIR BIBO stability from internal canceled-state overflow risk.
DSP:010220.statement:
Consider the length-$4$ moving-sum FIR
\[
H(z)=1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3},
\]
initially at rest. The same rational function may be written
\[
H(z)=\frac{1-z^{-4}}{1-z^{-1}}
\]
at every $z$ where the denominator is nonzero.

1. Prove the polynomial identity
   $(1-z^{-1})(1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3})=1-z^{-4}$. Explain why $z=1$ is a
   removable discontinuity of the rational expression, and prove that the
   removable value is $H(1)=4$.

2. Realize the rational form by the pair of recurrences
   \[
   v[n]=v[n-1]+x[n],\qquad y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4],
   \]
   with rest initial conditions. Interpret $v$ as an accumulator and the
   second equation as a comb $1-z^{-4}$.

3. Let $x[n]=u[n]$ be the unit step. Compute $v[n]$ and $y[n]$ for
   $n\ge 0$ and prove that
   \[
   y[n]=\begin{cases}
   n+1,&0\le n\le 3,\\
   4,&n\ge 4,
   \end{cases}
   \qquad v[n]=n+1\quad(n\ge 0).
   \]
   In particular the output sequence begins $1,2,3,4,4,4,\ldots$ while
   the accumulator $v[n]=n+1$ is unbounded.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the pole at $z=1$ cancels, so the recursive
   realization is internally BIBO stable and $v$ remains bounded”;
   (ii) “the removable value is $0$, or the external FIR is unstable
   because an internal state grows.” Distinguish the external FIR (which
   is BIBO stable) from the canceled-state overflow risk of the recursive
   realization.

Do not replace the identity by a decimator aliasing calculation, and do
not quantize the canceled pole.
permittedResults: The finite geometric sum $1+r+r^2+r^3=(1-r^4)/(1-r)$ for $r\neq 1$, with continuous extension $4$ at $r=1$, is the present identity with $r=z^{-1}$.
Under rest initial conditions the accumulator $v[n]=\sum_{k\le n}x[k]$ realizes $1/(1-z^{-1})$, and the comb $1-z^{-4}$ applied to $v$ recovers the length-$4$ moving sum.

acceptableStrategies.description: Telescope the geometric product, evaluate H(1)=4 by continuity, then run the two recurrences on the step.
First write y as the explicit FIR moving sum of u to lock 1,2,3,4,4,..., then exhibit v as the unbounded partial-sum state that the comb differences.

milestones.criterion: Proves H=(1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1}) with removable value 4 and writes the accumulator/comb recurrences.
Computes the step responses y=1,2,3,4,4,... and v=n+1, and separates external FIR BIBO stability from internal overflow.
Rejects ‘canceled hence internally stable’ and refuses decimation or quantized-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the pole-zero cancellation as making the recursive realization internally BIBO stable, or claims that v remains bounded on the step.
commonErrors.consequence: The overflow risk of the accumulator v[n]=n+1 is denied, which is the point of the realization.

commonErrors.description: Leaves the removable value as 0, reports a step output other than 1,2,3,4,4,..., or calls the external FIR unstable because v grows.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the identity H(1)=4 is lost or external BIBO is confused with internal state growth.

hintTree.content: Multiply $1-z^{-1}$ through the moving-sum polynomial and telescope to $1-z^{-4}$. At $z=1$ the left FIR equals $4$.
With $x=u$ and $v[-1]=0$ the accumulator is the running count $v[n]=n+1$.
Then $y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4]$ equals $n+1$ before time $4$ and equals $(n+1)-(n-3)=4$ afterwards.

DSP:010220.canonicalSolution:
Expand the product
\[
(1-z^{-1})(1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3})
=1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3}-z^{-1}-z^{-2}-z^{-3}-z^{-4}
=1-z^{-4}.
\]
Thus the rational expression $(1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1})$ agrees with the FIR
$H(z)=1+z^{-1}+z^{-2}+z^{-3}$ wherever $z\neq 1$. At $z=1$ the rational
expression is the indeterminate form $0/0$, while the polynomial form is
$H(1)=4$. The singularity is therefore removable, and the removable
value is $4$.
\[
\boxed{H(z)=(1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1}),\quad\text{removable value }4}.
\]

The factorization $H(z)=(1-z^{-4})\cdot(1-z^{-1})^{-1}$ is realized by
an accumulator followed by a length-$4$ comb. Rest initial conditions
give
\[
v[n]=v[n-1]+x[n],\qquad y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4],
\]
which is the claimed pair.

Now take $x[n]=u[n]$ and $v[-1]=0$. Then $v[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}1=n+1$ for
every $n\ge 0$, which is unbounded. The comb produces
\[
y[0]=v[0]=1,\quad
y[1]=2,\quad
y[2]=3,\quad
y[3]=4,
\]
and, for $n\ge 4$,
\[
y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4]=(n+1)-(n-3)=4.
\]
So the output begins $1,2,3,4,4,4,\ldots$, which is exactly the FIR
moving sum of a step, while the internal state $v[n]=n+1$ grows without
bound.
\[
\boxed{y=1,2,3,4,4,\ldots;\quad v[n]=n+1}.
\]

The external operator $x\mapsto y$ is a length-$4$ FIR, hence BIBO
stable: every bounded input produces a bounded output (in particular
$|y[n]|\le 4\|x\|_\infty$). The recursive realization nevertheless
contains a canceled pole on the unit circle. That hidden accumulator
can overflow in finite precision even though the external map is
stable. Sentence (i) confuses cancellation on paper with internal BIBO
stability of the state. Sentence (ii) either leaves the removable value
as $0$ or condemns the external FIR because an internal state grows.

The identity is not a decimation aliasing calculation, and the canceled
pole is not a quantized-coefficient sensitivity example.

graderFixtures.proofText: The identity $H=(1-z^{-4})/(1-z^{-1})$ has removable value $4$. The realization $v[n]=v[n-1]+x[n]$, $y[n]=v[n]-v[n-4]$ produces $y=1,2,3,4,4,\ldots$ and $v[n]=n+1$ on a step. The FIR is externally BIBO stable; the canceled accumulator can overflow.
The pole at z=1 cancels the zero of 1-z^{-4}, so the recursive realization is internally BIBO stable. On a step the state v stays bounded because the canceled mode is unreachable.

At z=1 the rational form is 0/0, which I read as removable value 0. Because v[n]=n+1 grows, I also declare the external moving-sum FIR BIBO unstable, and I do not accept the step output 1,2,3,4,4,... as a stable response.

DSP:010221.title: The allpass (a+z^{-1})/(1+a z^{-1}) at a=1/2 has energy 1, τ(0)=1/3, and τ(π)=3
DSP:010221.objective: For A=(a+z^{-1})/(1+a z^{-1}) with a=1/2, locate the pole -1/2 and zero -2, prove unit magnitude, derive h[0]=1/2 and h[n]=(3/4)(-1/2)^{n-1}, confirm energy 1, and evaluate the group delay (1-a^2)/(1+a^2+2a cos ω) at 0 and π as 1/3 and 3.
DSP:010221.statement:
Let $a=1/2$ and consider the first-order real allpass
\[
A(z)=\frac{a+z^{-1}}{1+a z^{-1}}=\frac{\tfrac12+z^{-1}}{1+\tfrac12 z^{-1}},
\]
realized causally at rest. Group delay is
\[
\tau(\omega)=-\frac{d}{d\omega}\arg A(e^{j\omega}).
\]

1. Locate the pole and the zero. Prove that $|A(e^{j\omega})|=1$ for every
   real $\omega$ (so $A$ is allpass on the unit circle) while the pole
   lies strictly inside the unit circle. Write the input--output
   recurrence.

2. Compute the causal impulse response. Prove $h[0]=1/2$ and
   \[
   h[n]=\frac34\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)^{n-1},\qquad n\ge 1.
   \]
   Evaluate the energy $\sum_{n\ge 0}|h[n]|^2$ and prove that it equals
   $1$.

3. Using the standing closed form
   \[
   \tau(\omega)=\frac{1-a^2}{1+a^2+2a\cos\omega}
   \]
   (or an equivalent differentiation of $\arg A(e^{j\omega})$), compute
   $\tau(0)$ and $\tau(\pi)$ and prove that they equal $1/3$ and $3$
   respectively.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “unit magnitude means zero phase, or at
   least constant phase, so the group delay vanishes”; (ii) “the pole
   and zero are swapped, or coefficient quantization of the pole is the
   intended sensitivity calculation.”

Do not replace the allpass by a min-phase / max-phase spectral factor
pair, and do not invoke a periodogram.
permittedResults: On the unit circle, $|a+e^{-j\omega}|=|1+a e^{j\omega}|=|1+a e^{-j\omega}|$ whenever $a$ is real, so $|A(e^{j\omega})|=1$.
The causal impulse response of this allpass is $h[0]=a$ and $h[n]=(1-a^2)(-a)^{n-1}$ for $n\ge 1$. Its $\ell^2$ energy equals $1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read pole and zero from the rational form, iterate the rest-initial recurrence for h, then substitute a=1/2 into the standing τ formula.
Use Parseval and |A|=1 to lock energy 1 first, then compute h and τ(0), τ(π) as independent checks of the same allpass.

milestones.criterion: Locates pole -1/2 and zero -2, proves unit magnitude, and derives h[0]=1/2 with h[n]=(3/4)(-1/2)^{n-1} and energy 1.
Evaluates the group delay formula to τ(0)=1/3 and τ(π)=3.
Rejects reading unit magnitude as zero or constant phase, and refuses pole/zero swap or quantized-pole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Infers from |A|=1 that the phase is zero or constant, hence that the group delay vanishes, contradicting τ(0)=1/3 and τ(π)=3.
commonErrors.consequence: The frequency-dependent delay that distinguishes this allpass from a pure delay or a zero-phase filter is lost.

commonErrors.description: Places the pole at -2 and the zero at -1/2, or replaces the problem by coefficient-quantized sensitivity of the pole.
commonErrors.consequence: Causality/stability is lost, or a reserved intake family is imported in place of the allpass delay calculation.

hintTree.content: The denominator $1+a z^{-1}$ vanishes at $z=-a=-1/2$. The numerator vanishes at $z=-1/a=-2$.
The recurrence $y[n]=a x[n]+x[n-1]-a y[n-1]$ gives $h[0]=a$ and then $h[n]=-a h[n-1]$ for $n\ge 2$ after the single feed of $x[n-1]$ at time $1$.
Substitute $a=1/2$ into $\tau(\omega)=(1-a^2)/(1+a^2+2a\cos\omega)$. At $\omega=0$ the denominator is $9/4$; at $\omega=\pi$ it is $1/4$.

DSP:010221.canonicalSolution:
The denominator $1+a z^{-1}$ vanishes when $z=-a=-1/2$. The numerator
$a+z^{-1}$ vanishes when $z=-1/a=-2$. The pole therefore lies strictly
inside the unit circle and the zero is its reciprocal on the negative
real axis.
\[
\boxed{\text{pole }-1/2,\quad\text{zero }-2}.
\]
For real $a$ and $|z|=1$ the identity
$|a+z^{-1}|=|z|\,|az+1|/|z|=|1+a z|$ together with
$|1+a z^{-1}|=|1+a\overline{z}|$ (since $\overline{z}=z^{-1}$) shows
\[
\bigl|A(e^{j\omega})\bigr|=1.
\]
Causality and rest initial conditions give the recurrence
\[
y[n]=a\,x[n]+x[n-1]-a\,y[n-1],
\]
or, with $a=1/2$,
$y[n]=\tfrac12 x[n]+x[n-1]-\tfrac12 y[n-1]$.

Drive the recurrence with $x=\delta$. Then $h[0]=a=1/2$. At time $1$
the feedthrough of $x[n-1]$ contributes $1$, so
\[
h[1]=-a h[0]+1=1-a^2=\frac34.
\]
For every $n\ge 2$ one has $x[n]=x[n-1]=0$, hence $h[n]=-a h[n-1]$.
Iterating from $h[1]$ produces
\[
h[n]=(1-a^2)(-a)^{n-1}=\frac34\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)^{n-1},\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
\[
\boxed{h[0]=1/2,\quad h[n]=(3/4)(-1/2)^{n-1}\ (n\ge 1)}.
\]
The energy is
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n\ge 0}|h[n]|^2
&=h[0]^2+\sum_{n\ge 1}\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^{n-1}
=\frac14+\frac{9}{16}\sum_{k\ge 0}\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^k
=\frac14+\frac{9}{16}\cdot\frac{4}{3}
=1.
\end{align*}
The same value is Parseval's theorem: a stable causal allpass sends the
unit impulse to a unit-energy sequence because $|A|=1$ almost everywhere
on the circle.

The given group-delay formula with $a=1/2$ reads
\[
\tau(\omega)
=\frac{1-1/4}{1+1/4+\cos\omega}
=\frac{3/4}{5/4+\cos\omega}.
\]
Hence
\[
\tau(0)=\frac{3/4}{5/4+1}=\frac{3/4}{9/4}=\frac13,
\qquad
\tau(\pi)=\frac{3/4}{5/4-1}=\frac{3/4}{1/4}=3.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau(0)=1/3,\quad \tau(\pi)=3}.
\]
Unit magnitude constrains the modulus, not the argument. The phase of
$A(e^{j\omega})$ is a nontrivial decreasing function, and the group
delay is a positive frequency-dependent weight that is larger near the
pole angle $\omega=\pi$ than near $\omega=0$.

Sentence (i) reads “$|A|=1$” as zero phase or constant phase and
concludes $\tau\equiv 0$. That error contradicts both displayed values.
Sentence (ii) swaps the pole and zero (destroying causality or
stability) or replaces the exercise by coefficient-quantized pole
sensitivity, which is a reserved intake family.

The calculation never splits $A$ into min-phase and max-phase spectral
factors and never estimates a periodogram.

graderFixtures.proofText: Pole $-1/2$, zero $-2$, and $|A|=1$ on the circle. The impulse response has $h[0]=1/2$ and $h[n]=(3/4)(-1/2)^{n-1}$ for $n\ge 1$, with energy $1$. Group delay is $(1-a^2)/(1+a^2+2a\cos\omega)$, so $\tau(0)=1/3$ and $\tau(\pi)=3$. Unit magnitude is not zero phase.
Because |A(e^{jω})|=1, the filter is zero phase (or at least constant phase). Differentiating a constant argument gives τ(ω)=0, so the values 1/3 and 3 cannot occur.
I read A as having a pole at -2 and a zero at -1/2, or else I treat the exercise as coefficient quantization of the pole and discuss sensitivity instead of group delay.

DSP:010322.title: Upsampling cos(pi n/3) by 3 images at ±pi/9, ±5pi/9, ±7pi/9; gain-3 LPF recovers cos(pi m/9)
DSP:010322.objective: Prove that the L=3 expander of cos(pi n/3) has DTFT V(e^{j 3 omega}) with spectral lines at ±pi/9, ±5pi/9, ±7pi/9, that the ideal interpolator H=3 on |omega|<pi/3 keeps only ±pi/9 and yields y[m]=cos(pi m/9) with y[3n]=x[n], and that gain 1 leaves amplitude 1/3.
DSP:010322.statement:
Let $x[n]=\cos(\pi n/3)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$, and let $L=3$. The
expander (upsample-by-$L$ with zeros inserted) is
\[
v[m]=\begin{cases}
x[m/3],&3\mid m,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Work throughout with $2\pi$-periodic DTFTs on $(-\pi,\pi]$.

1. Write $V(e^{j\omega})$ in terms of $X(e^{j\omega})$. Locate every
   spectral line of $X$ in $(-\pi,\pi]$, then locate every spectral line
   of $V$ in $(-\pi,\pi]$. Prove that the six frequencies are
   $\pm\pi/9$, $\pm 5\pi/9$, and $\pm 7\pi/9$.

2. Let $H$ be the ideal lowpass interpolator of gain $L=3$ and cutoff
   $\pi/L=\pi/3$:
   \[
   H(e^{j\omega})=\begin{cases}
   3,&|\omega|<\pi/3,\\
   0,&\pi/3<|\omega|\le\pi.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   Determine which lines of $V$ survive, write the unique cosine
   $y[m]$ with those lines and the interpolating gain, and prove
   $y[3n]=x[n]$.

3. Repeat the filtering with the same cutoff but with gain $1$ in place
   of $3$. Prove that the output amplitude is $1/3$ of the gain-$3$
   interpolant.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “upsampling compresses the digital
   frequency by $3$, so $V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j\omega/3})$ and the only
   lines are $\pm\pi/9$”; (ii) “an ideal cutoff $\pi/3$ already
   reconstructs $x$ at the fine rate, so the passband gain may be $1$
   and $y[m]=\cos(\pi m/9)$ still holds.”

Do not replace the calculation by any of the six stated Digital Signal
Processing seed exercises.
permittedResults: The sequence $\cos(\omega_0 n)$ has DTFT lines at $\pm\omega_0$ in $(-\pi,\pi]$, extended $2\pi$-periodically. After the stretch $V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j L\omega})$, lines occur wherever $L\omega\equiv\pm\omega_0\pmod{2\pi}$.
If $Y(e^{j\omega})=L\,X(e^{j L\omega})$ on $|\omega|<\pi/L$ and $Y=0$ on the complementary Nyquist interval, then $y[\ell n]=x[n]$ for every $n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Start from the expander identity V(e^{j omega})=X(e^{j 3 omega}), pull back the 2pi-periodic lines of the cosine, then keep only the pair inside |omega|<pi/3 and restore gain 3.
Write v[m] in the time domain, recognize the images as the L-fold aliases of ±pi/3, and check y[3n]=x[n] before discussing the gain-1 amplitude 1/3.

milestones.criterion: Derives V=X(e^{j 3 omega}) and locates the six image lines ±pi/9, ±5pi/9, ±7pi/9.
Applies the gain-3 cutoff |omega|<pi/3 to obtain y[m]=cos(pi m/9) with y[3n]=x[n], and shows gain 1 leaves amplitude 1/3.
Rejects the inverse stretch V=X(e^{j omega/3}) and any reconstruction claim that drops the interpolating gain L=3.

commonErrors.description: Writes V(e^{j omega})=X(e^{j omega/3}) (or X(e^{j omega})) and reports only the baseband pair ±pi/9, or places images at ±pi/3 rather than at ±5pi/9 and ±7pi/9.
commonErrors.consequence: The four interpolation images are lost, so the role of the cutoff pi/3 cannot be checked.

commonErrors.description: Takes the ideal cutoff with gain 1 and still claims y[m]=cos(pi m/9), or treats the factor 3 as optional for sample recovery.
commonErrors.consequence: The recovered amplitude is silently 1/3 and y[3n]=x[n] fails.

hintTree.content: The original cosine has lines at $\pm\pi/3$. The identity $V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j 3\omega})$ pulls back every $2\pi$-periodic replica, not only the principal pair.
Solve $3\omega\equiv\pm\pi/3\pmod{2\pi}$ inside $(-\pi,\pi]$ to obtain the six image frequencies $\pm\pi/9,\pm 5\pi/9,\pm 7\pi/9$.
Only $\pm\pi/9$ lie in the ideal passband $|\omega|<\pi/3$. Gain $3$ restores amplitude $1$; gain $1$ leaves amplitude $1/3$.

DSP:010322.canonicalSolution:
The DTFT of $x[n]=\cos(\pi n/3)$ consists of a conjugate pair of lines at
$\omega=\pm\pi/3$ in $(-\pi,\pi]$, together with the $2\pi$-periodic
replicas of that pair. The expander identity is the pure frequency-axis
stretch
\[
V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j 3\omega}).
\]
There is no explicit factor $1/3$ in this functional identity. When the
DTFT is written as a sum of Dirac lines, however, pulling a line back
through $3\omega$ contributes the distributional scale factor $1/3$ to
each image. That line-weight reduction is why the interpolation filter
needs passband gain $3$ to recover unit amplitude.

A line of $V$ occurs wherever $3\omega\equiv\pm\pi/3\pmod{2\pi}$, that is
\[
\omega=\pm\frac{\pi}{9}+\frac{2\pi k}{3},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
The six representatives in $(-\pi,\pi]$ are
\begin{align*}
k=0&\colon &&\pm\pi/9,\\
k=1&\colon &&\pi/9+2\pi/3=7\pi/9,\qquad -\pi/9+2\pi/3=5\pi/9,\\
k=-1&\colon &&\pi/9-2\pi/3=-5\pi/9,\qquad -\pi/9-2\pi/3=-7\pi/9.
\end{align*}
Thus $V$ has lines exactly at $\pm\pi/9$, $\pm 5\pi/9$, and $\pm 7\pi/9$.
The last four are the spectral images created by the $2\pi$-periodicity
of $X$ under the stretch by $3$.
\[
\boxed{V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j 3\omega});\ \text{lines }\pm\pi/9,\pm 5\pi/9,\pm 7\pi/9}.
\]

The ideal interpolator $H$ of gain $3$ and cutoff $\pi/3$ annihilates
every line with $|\omega|>\pi/3$, hence kills $\pm 5\pi/9$ and
$\pm 7\pi/9$, and multiplies the surviving pair $\pm\pi/9$ by $3$. Those
are precisely the lines of $\cos(\pi m/9)$ after the interpolating gain
has restored unit amplitude, so
\[
y[m]=\cos(\pi m/9).
\]
Restricting to the coarse grid,
\[
y[3n]=\cos(\pi(3n)/9)=\cos(\pi n/3)=x[n].
\]
\[
\boxed{y[m]=\cos(\pi m/9),\qquad y[3n]=x[n]}.
\]

If the same cutoff is used with passband gain $1$, the surviving lines
are still $\pm\pi/9$ but they are not multiplied by $L=3$. Relative to
the gain-$3$ interpolant the amplitude is therefore $1/3$:
\[
y_{\mathrm{gain}\,1}[m]=\tfrac13\cos(\pi m/9).
\]
In particular $y_{\mathrm{gain}\,1}[3n]=x[n]/3$, so the original samples
are not recovered.

Sentence (i) writes the inverse stretch $X(e^{j\omega/3})$. That formula
is the DTFT of an $L$-fold compressor (or of an interpolant already
stripped of images), not of the zero-inserter. It hides the images at
$\pm 5\pi/9$ and $\pm 7\pi/9$. Sentence (ii) treats the cutoff as a
perfect reconstructor independently of gain. The cutoff selects the
correct pair of lines; the factor $L$ is what matches $y[3n]$ to $x[n]$.

The argument never substitutes any of the six stated seed exercises.

graderFixtures.proofText: The expander satisfies $V(e^{j\omega})=X(e^{j 3\omega})$ with lines at $\pm\pi/9,\pm 5\pi/9,\pm 7\pi/9$. Ideal $H=3$ on $|\omega|<\pi/3$ keeps $\pm\pi/9$ and yields $y[m]=\cos(\pi m/9)$ with $y[3n]=x[n]$. Gain $1$ leaves amplitude $1/3$.
Upsampling by 3 compresses digital frequency, so V(e^{j omega})=X(e^{j omega/3}). The only lines are therefore ±pi/9, and there are no images at ±5pi/9 or ±7pi/9 to reject.
The ideal cutoff |omega|<pi/3 already isolates the desired cosine, so I may take H=1. The output is still y[m]=cos(pi m/9) and the original samples are recovered.

DSP:010323.title: Type-I polyphase of (1,2,3,4,5,6) at M=3 gives y[2]=56 with 6 multiplies, not 18
DSP:010323.objective: Factor H(z)=E0(z^3)+z^{-1}E1(z^3)+z^{-2}E2(z^3) with E0=1+4z^{-1}, E1=2+5z^{-1}, E2=3+6z^{-1}, evaluate y[2]=18+20+18=56 on x[n]=n u[n], and qualify the 18-versus-6 multiply comparison as naive full-rate-then-discard versus polyphase.
DSP:010323.statement:
Let $h$ be the length-$6$ FIR
\[
h[0]=1,\ h[1]=2,\ h[2]=3,\ h[3]=4,\ h[4]=5,\ h[5]=6,
\]
and let $M=3$. Write $H(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{5}h[k]z^{-k}$. The Type-I
polyphase components of stride $M$ are the length-$2$ filters $E_r$
defined by $e_r[\ell]=h[M\ell+r]$ for $r=0,1,2$. Decimation by $M$
after filtering is
\[
y[m]=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}h[k]\,x[3m-k].
\]

1. Exhibit the identity
   \[
   H(z)=E_0(z^3)+z^{-1}E_1(z^3)+z^{-2}E_2(z^3)
   \]
   with the explicit polynomials $E_0(z)=1+4z^{-1}$,
   $E_1(z)=2+5z^{-1}$, and $E_2(z)=3+6z^{-1}$. Explain the noble
   identity that lets each $E_r$ run at the decimated rate.

2. Let $x[n]=n\,u[n]$, where $u$ is the unit step that is $1$ for
   $n\ge 0$ and $0$ otherwise. Compute $y[2]$ from the defining sum,
   then recompute it as the sum of the three polyphase inner products,
   and prove that both calculations give $18+20+18=56$.

3. Count coefficient-times-sample multiplies needed to produce one
   retained output, treating every tap of $h$ as a general nonzero
   coefficient (do not exploit that the taps are $1,\ldots,6$ or that
   $x$ is a ramp). Compare a naive full-rate FIR followed by keep-every-
   third-sample against the polyphase realization.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the three polyphase branches are the
   contiguous triples $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,5,6)$”; (ii) “every
   implementation of a decimator uses $18$ multiplies, or else the
   $18$-versus-$6$ comparison needs no hypothesis on what is being
   counted.”

Do not replace the calculation by any of the six stated Digital Signal
Processing seed exercises.
permittedResults: A length-$L$ FIR computed at the input rate and then decimated by $M$ spends $LM$ general multiplies per retained output. The equivalent polyphase bank spends $L$ multiplies per retained output.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read every third tap to form E0, E1, E2, expand the Type-I identity, then group the six products for y[2] by k mod 3.
First compute the six-term sum y[2]=56 to lock the number, then identify the same addends as the three polyphase branches and count discarded full-rate work.

milestones.criterion: Factors H as E0(z^3)+z^{-1}E1(z^3)+z^{-2}E2(z^3) with the three stated length-2 components and invokes the noble identity.
Evaluates y[2]=18+20+18=56 from the defining sum and from the three polyphase inner products.
Qualifies 18 versus 6 as naive full-rate-then-discard versus polyphase, counting general coefficient multiplies.

commonErrors.description: Takes the contiguous triples (1,2,3) and (4,5,6) as polyphase branches, or writes E0=1+2z^{-1}+3z^{-2} instead of stride-3 components.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity H=E0(z^3)+z^{-1}E1(z^3)+z^{-2}E2(z^3) fails and the grouping 18+20+18 is unavailable.

commonErrors.description: Claims naive full-rate-then-discard and polyphase use the same number of multiplies, or quotes 18 versus 6 without stating that the comparison is general-tap full-rate-then-discard versus polyphase.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor-M saving is either denied or left un-auditable.

hintTree.content: Stride-$3$ grouping of $h$ is every third tap: $(1,4)$, $(2,5)$, and $(3,6)$, not the contiguous blocks $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,5,6)$.
For $m=2$ the live products are $h[k]x[6-k]$. Grouping by $k\bmod 3$ produces $1\cdot 6+4\cdot 3=18$, $2\cdot 5+5\cdot 2=20$, and $3\cdot 4+6\cdot 1=18$.
Naive full-rate-then-discard computes three length-$6$ outputs to keep one of them ($18$ multiplies). Polyphase computes three length-$2$ outputs once ($6$ multiplies). Qualify both counts.

DSP:010323.canonicalSolution:
The Type-I components of stride $3$ read every third tap:
\begin{align*}
E_0(z)&=h[0]+h[3]z^{-1}=1+4z^{-1},\\
E_1(z)&=h[1]+h[4]z^{-1}=2+5z^{-1},\\
E_2(z)&=h[2]+h[5]z^{-1}=3+6z^{-1}.
\end{align*}
Substituting $z^3$ and reattaching the delays $z^{-r}$ rebuilds $H$:
\begin{align*}
E_0(z^3)+z^{-1}E_1(z^3)+z^{-2}E_2(z^3)
&=(1+4z^{-3})+z^{-1}(2+5z^{-3})+z^{-2}(3+6z^{-3})\\
&=1+2z^{-1}+3z^{-2}+4z^{-3}+5z^{-4}+6z^{-5}=H(z).
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{H(z)=E_0(z^3)+z^{-1}E_1(z^3)+z^{-2}E_2(z^3)}.
\]
The noble identity commutes each $E_r(z^3)$ past the compressor, so the
three length-$2$ filters run at the decimated rate on the commutated
subsequences $x[3m-r]$.

Now $x[n]=n\,u[n]$, so $x[n]=n$ for every $n\ge 0$ that appears below.
The defining sum at $m=2$ is
\[
y[2]=\sum_{k=0}^{5}h[k]x[6-k]
=1\cdot 6+2\cdot 5+3\cdot 4+4\cdot 3+5\cdot 2+6\cdot 1=56.
\]
The same six products grouped by residue $k\bmod 3$ are the three
polyphase inner products
\begin{align*}
E_0&\colon 1\cdot x[6]+4\cdot x[3]=6+12=18,\\
E_1&\colon 2\cdot x[5]+5\cdot x[2]=10+10=20,\\
E_2&\colon 3\cdot x[4]+6\cdot x[1]=12+6=18.
\end{align*}
Hence $y[2]=18+20+18=56$.
\[
\boxed{y[2]=18+20+18=56}.
\]

Multiply count, under the standing convention that every tap is a
general nonzero coefficient and that a multiply is one
coefficient-times-sample product: a naive full-rate length-$6$ FIR
computes an output at every input instant and then discards two of every
three outputs. Three full-rate outputs cost $3\times 6=18$ multiplies
for each retained sample. The polyphase bank computes only the retained
sample, as three length-$2$ inner products, hence $6$ multiplies. The
factor $M=3$ is exactly the discarded work.

The comparison is not a claim about every conceivable decimator. A
direct-form implementation that already evaluates $y[m]=\sum h[k]x[3m-k]$
and never forms the discarded instants also uses $6$ multiplies; that
arithmetic is the same as polyphase, merely not organized by noble
identities. The numbers $18$ versus $6$ compare naive
full-rate-then-discard against polyphase, and they count general
multiplies rather than the special arithmetic of the ramp $x[n]=n$ or
the integer taps $1,\ldots,6$.

Sentence (i) replaces stride-$M$ polyphase by a contiguous block
partition. Those blocks are not $E_0,E_1,E_2$, and they do not produce
the identity $H(z)=\sum z^{-r}E_r(z^M)$. Sentence (ii) either pretends
that every implementation pays the discarded work, or quotes $18$ versus
$6$ without the qualification above.

The argument never substitutes any of the six stated seed exercises.

graderFixtures.proofText: Type-I components are $E_0=1+4z^{-1}$, $E_1=2+5z^{-1}$, $E_2=3+6z^{-1}$, and $H=E_0(z^3)+z^{-1}E_1(z^3)+z^{-2}E_2(z^3)$. For $x[n]=n u[n]$ one has $y[2]=18+20+18=56$. Naive full-rate-then-discard spends $18$ general multiplies per retained output; polyphase spends $6$.
I split h into the contiguous triples (1,2,3) and (4,5,6) and call those the polyphase filters. Then H is not E0(z^3)+z^{-1}E1(z^3)+z^{-2}E2(z^3) with E0=1+4z^{-1}.

Both realizations compute the same y, so both use 18 multiplies per output, or else I quote 18 versus 6 without saying that the expensive side is naive full-rate-then-discard of a general length-6 FIR.

DSP:010424.title: Eight-point radix-2 DIT of (1,2,3,4,0,0,0,0) has X0=10, Parseval 240, and 12 butterflies
DSP:010424.objective: Bit-reverse the length-8 input to (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7), compute X0=10, X4=-2, X2=-2+2j and conjugate X6, the closed forms for X1,X7 and X3,X5, check Parseval sum|X|^2=240=8*30, and count 3 stages times 4 butterflies.
DSP:010424.statement:
Let $N=8$ and let
\[
x=(x[0],\ldots,x[7])=(1,2,3,4,0,0,0,0).
\]
The DFT is $X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{7}x[n]e^{-j 2\pi kn/8}$. A radix-$2$
decimation-in-time FFT takes its input in bit-reversed order and
produces $X$ in natural order.

1. List the bit-reversed index order of $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and confirm
   that it is $(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7)$. State how many stages and how many
   butterflies per stage the length-$8$ radix-$2$ flowgraph contains,
   and count the complex add/subtracts. Count the available twiddle
   slots and the genuinely nontrivial general complex multiplies in the
   standard radix-$2$ DIT flowgraph.

2. Compute $X[0]$, $X[4]$, $X[2]$, and $X[6]$ in closed form. Then
   compute
   \[
   X[1]=1-\sqrt{2}-j(3+3\sqrt{2}),\qquad
   X[3]=1+\sqrt{2}+j(3-3\sqrt{2}),
   \]
   and identify $X[7]$ and $X[5]$ by conjugate symmetry.

3. Verify Parseval's identity
   \[
   \sum_{k=0}^{7}|X[k]|^2=N\sum_{n=0}^{7}|x[n]|^2
   \]
   by evaluating both sides as $240=8\cdot 30$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “natural order is already bit-reversed, or
   the DIT input order is $0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7$”; (ii) “Parseval is
   $\sum|X|^2=\sum|x|^2$, so the right-hand side is $30$ rather than
   $240$.”

Do not replace the calculation by any of the six stated Digital Signal
Processing seed exercises.
permittedResults: A real sequence has $X[N-k]=\overline{X[k]}$. In particular $X[6]=\overline{X[2]}$, $X[7]=\overline{X[1]}$, and $X[5]=\overline{X[3]}$.
A radix-$2$ FFT of length $N$ has $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies. Each butterfly is two complex add/subtracts and at most one twiddle multiply; $W^0=1$ and $W^{N/4}=-j$ are trivial.

acceptableStrategies.description: Bit-reverse the three-bit indices, evaluate the four real/imaginary-axis bins by inspection, then expand X[1] and X[3] with the two octant roots and close Parseval from the time energy 30.
Use conjugate symmetry of the real input to cut the work in half, and treat the 12-butterfly count as a separate flowgraph audit from the bin values.

milestones.criterion: Lists the DIT bit-reversed order (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7) and counts 3 stages of 4 butterflies (24 complex add/subs, 12 twiddle slots, and 2 genuinely nontrivial general complex multiplies).
Computes X0=10, X4=-2, X2=-2+2j, X6 conjugate, the closed forms for X1 and X3, and their conjugates, and checks Parseval 240=8*30.
Rejects natural-order DIT input and any Parseval statement that drops the factor N.

commonErrors.description: Feeds the radix-2 DIT flowgraph in natural order (0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7) instead of the bit-reversed order (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7).
commonErrors.consequence: The stage-1 butterflies pair the wrong samples, so the DIT factorization is not the one asked for.

commonErrors.description: Claims sum_k |X[k]|^2 equals the time energy 30, omitting the unnormalized factor N=8 that produces 240.
commonErrors.consequence: The DFT convention is silently replaced by a unitary one, and the identity 240=8*30 fails.

hintTree.content: Three-bit reversal sends $001\mapsto 100$, $011\mapsto 110$, $101\mapsto 101$, giving the order $(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7)$.
$X[0]$ is the sum $10$ and $X[4]$ is the alternating sum $-2$. The bin $k=2$ is $\sum x[n](-j)^n=-2+2j$.
Expand $X[1]=\sum_{n=0}^{3}x[n]e^{-j\pi n/4}$ with $e^{-j\pi/4}=(\sqrt{2}/2)(1-j)$ and $e^{-j 3\pi/4}=(\sqrt{2}/2)(-1-j)$. Parseval multiplies the time energy $30$ by $N=8$.

DSP:010424.canonicalSolution:
Three-bit reversal of the indices $000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111$ is
$000,100,010,110,001,101,011,111$, hence
\[
(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7).
\]
A length-$8$ radix-$2$ flowgraph has $\log_2 8=3$ stages and $N/2=4$
butterflies in each stage, so $12$ butterflies in all. Each butterfly
performs two complex additions (or one add and one subtract), giving
$24$ complex add/subtracts. There are $12$ butterfly twiddle slots in
all. Seven use the unity twiddle and may be skipped; three use $-j$ and
need only a swap-and-sign. Only the stage-$3$ twiddles $W_8^1$ and
$W_8^3$ require general complex multiplication, so the standard
flowgraph has exactly $2$ genuinely nontrivial complex multiplies.
\[
\boxed{\text{bit-rev }(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7);\ 3\times 4=12\text{ butterflies}}.
\]

Because $x[n]=0$ for $n\ge 4$,
\[
X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{3}x[n]e^{-j\pi kn/4}.
\]
The DC and Nyquist bins are
\[
X[0]=1+2+3+4=10,\qquad
X[4]=1-2+3-4=-2.
\]
The quarter-rate bin uses $(-j)^n$:
\[
X[2]=1+2(-j)+3(-1)+4(j)=-2+2j,
\]
and reality of $x$ gives $X[6]=\overline{X[2]}=-2-2j$.

For $k=1$,
\begin{align*}
X[1]
&=1+2e^{-j\pi/4}+3e^{-j\pi/2}+4e^{-j 3\pi/4}\\
&=1+\sqrt{2}(1-j)-3j-2\sqrt{2}(1+j)\\
&=1-\sqrt{2}-j(3+3\sqrt{2}).
\end{align*}
Conjugate symmetry yields
$X[7]=\overline{X[1]}=1-\sqrt{2}+j(3+3\sqrt{2})$. For $k=3$,
\begin{align*}
X[3]
&=1+2e^{-j 3\pi/4}+3e^{-j 3\pi/2}+4e^{-j\pi/4}\\
&=1-\sqrt{2}(1+j)+3j+2\sqrt{2}(1-j)\\
&=1+\sqrt{2}+j(3-3\sqrt{2}),
\end{align*}
and $X[5]=\overline{X[3]}=1+\sqrt{2}-j(3-3\sqrt{2})$.
\[
\boxed{X[0]=10,\ X[4]=-2,\ X[2]=-2+2j,\ X[6]=\overline{X[2]}}.
\]

Time-domain energy is $1+4+9+16=30$. Parseval for the unnormalized DFT
therefore reads
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{7}|X[k]|^2=8\cdot 30=240.
\]
An independent check of the eight moduli squared is available but not
required once the identity and the time energy are both established.
\[
\boxed{\sum|X[k]|^2=240=8\cdot 30}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses natural order with bit-reversed order and would
feed the DIT flowgraph the wrong pairs. Sentence (ii) drops the factor
$N$ from Parseval, confusing the unnormalized DFT with a unitary one.

The argument never substitutes any of the six stated seed exercises.

graderFixtures.proofText: Bit-reversed DIT order is $(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7)$. $X[0]=10$, $X[4]=-2$, $X[2]=-2+2j$, $X[6]=\overline{X[2]}$, $X[1]=1-\sqrt{2}-j(3+3\sqrt{2})$, $X[3]=1+\sqrt{2}+j(3-3\sqrt{2})$, with $X[7],X[5]$ conjugate. Parseval is $240=8\cdot 30$. Three stages of four butterflies give $12$ butterflies, $24$ complex add/subs, $12$ twiddle slots, and only $2$ genuinely nontrivial general complex multiplies.
A radix-2 DIT FFT already takes x in natural order (0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7). I do not bit-reverse the input to (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7) before the first stage.
Parseval says the DFT preserves energy, so sum |X[k]|^2 equals sum |x[n]|^2=30. I do not multiply by N=8 and I never write 240.

DSP:010425.title: Goertzel at k=2 on the length-8 ramp pad gives G=2+2j and X2=e^{j omega}G=-2+2j
DSP:010425.objective: Run the Goertzel recurrence q[n]=x[n]-q[n-2] on the same N=8 input at k=2 to obtain (1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2), form G=q[7]-e^{-j omega}q[6]=2+2j=e^{j(N-1)omega}X[2], recover X[2]=e^{j omega}G=-2+2j, and show that omitting the phase keeps the magnitude but not the argument.
DSP:010425.statement:
Reuse the length-$8$ sequence $x=(1,2,3,4,0,0,0,0)$ of the previous
packet. Fix the DFT bin $k=2$, so the resonator frequency is
$\omega=2\pi k/N=\pi/2$. The Goertzel state is initialized by
$q[-2]=q[-1]=0$ and, because $2\cos\omega=0$, reduces to
\[
q[n]=x[n]-q[n-2],\qquad n=0,1,\ldots,7.
\]
Define the complex combination
\[
G=q[7]-e^{-j\omega}q[6].
\]

1. Compute the eight samples $q[0],\ldots,q[7]$ and prove that they are
   $(1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2)$.

2. Evaluate $G$ and prove $G=2+2j$. Using the already-known DFT value
   $X[2]=-2+2j$ from the eight-point transform, prove the phase
   identities
   \[
   G=e^{j(N-1)\omega}X[2]=e^{-j\omega}X[2]
   \]
   and therefore $X[2]=e^{j\omega}G$.

3. Compare $|G|$ with $|X[2]|$ and compare $\arg G$ with $\arg X[2]$.
   Conclude that omitting the phase factor $e^{j\omega}$ keeps the
   magnitude of the bin and destroys the phase.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the general Goertzel recurrence keeps the
   middle term $2\cos\omega\,q[n-1]$ even though $\omega=\pi/2$, or the
   state sequence is just $x$ itself”; (ii) “$G$ already equals $X[2]$,
   so no phase correction is required.”

Do not replace the calculation by any of the six stated Digital Signal
Processing seed exercises.
permittedResults: For $N=8$ and $k=2$ one has $(N-1)\omega=7\pi/2\equiv-\pi/2\pmod{2\pi}$, so $e^{j(N-1)\omega}=e^{-j\omega}=-j$.
The map $z\mapsto e^{j\omega}z$ is a rotation, hence $|e^{j\omega}G|=|G|$. Phase is not preserved: $\arg(e^{j\omega}G)=\arg G+\omega$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Specialize 2 cos omega=0, iterate the two-step recurrence, form G=q[7]+j q[6], then rotate by j to match the known bin X[2].
Start from the independently known X[2]=-2+2j, multiply by e^{j(N-1)omega}=-j to predict G=2+2j, then confirm by running the state.

milestones.criterion: Computes the specialized recurrence q[n]=x[n]-q[n-2] and obtains q=(1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2).
Evaluates G=2+2j, proves G=e^{j(N-1)omega}X[2], and recovers X[2]=e^{j omega}G=-2+2j.
States that omitting the phase factor preserves magnitude and destroys phase, and refuses G=X[2].

commonErrors.description: Keeps a nonzero 2 cos(omega) q[n-1] term even though omega=pi/2, or sets q=x, so the state is not (1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2).
commonErrors.consequence: The combination G=q[7]-e^{-j omega}q[6] cannot equal 2+2j.

commonErrors.description: Reports G=2+2j as the DFT bin X[2], omitting the identity X[2]=e^{j omega}G that produces -2+2j.
commonErrors.consequence: The magnitude 2 sqrt(2) is retained but the phase is pi/4 instead of 3pi/4.

hintTree.content: Both $G$ and $X[2]$ have modulus $2\sqrt{2}$, but $\arg G=\pi/4$ while $\arg X[2]=3\pi/4$.

DSP:010425.canonicalSolution:
Because $\omega=\pi/2$, the coefficient $2\cos\omega$ vanishes and the
resonator is the two-step recurrence $q[n]=x[n]-q[n-2]$ with zero
prehistory. Iterating on $x=(1,2,3,4,0,0,0,0)$ yields
\begin{align*}
q[0]&=1-0=1,\\
q[1]&=2-0=2,\\
q[2]&=3-1=2,\\
q[3]&=4-2=2,\\
q[4]&=0-2=-2,\\
q[5]&=0-2=-2,\\
q[6]&=0-(-2)=2,\\
q[7]&=0-(-2)=2.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{q=(1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2)}.
\]

Now $e^{-j\omega}=e^{-j\pi/2}=-j$, so
\[
G=q[7]-e^{-j\omega}q[6]=2-(-j)(2)=2+2j.
\]
For $N=8$ one has $(N-1)\omega=7\pi/2\equiv-\pi/2\pmod{2\pi}$, hence
$e^{j(N-1)\omega}=e^{-j\omega}=-j$. Multiplying the known bin
$X[2]=-2+2j$ by this factor recovers $G$:
\[
e^{j(N-1)\omega}X[2]=(-j)(-2+2j)=2+2j=G.
\]
Equivalently $G=e^{-j\omega}X[2]$, so
\[
X[2]=e^{j\omega}G=j(2+2j)=-2+2j,
\]
which matches the eight-point DFT computed independently.
\[
\boxed{G=2+2j=e^{j(N-1)\omega}X[2],\qquad X[2]=e^{j\omega}G=-2+2j}.
\]

The moduli agree:
\[
|G|=|2+2j|=2\sqrt{2}=|-2+2j|=|X[2]|.
\]
The arguments do not:
$\arg G=\pi/4$ while $\arg X[2]=3\pi/4$. Omitting the rotation
$e^{j\omega}$ (equivalently, reporting $G$ as if it were $X[2]$)
therefore preserves the magnitude of the bin and returns the wrong
phase.

Sentence (i) either retains a vanishing middle tap, which changes the
state, or skips the resonator and sets $q=x$. Sentence (ii) identifies
$G$ with $X[2]$ and so reports $2+2j$ as the DFT bin; that value has
the correct modulus and the wrong argument.

The argument never substitutes any of the six stated seed exercises.

graderFixtures.proofText: The specialized state is $q=(1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2)$. Then $G=q[7]-e^{-j\omega}q[6]=2+2j=e^{j(N-1)\omega}X[2]$, so $X[2]=e^{j\omega}G=-2+2j$. Omitting the phase keeps the magnitude $2\sqrt{2}$ and returns the wrong argument.
I keep the general middle tap 2 cos(omega) q[n-1] even at omega=pi/2, or I just set q[n]=x[n]. The eight-term state is then not (1,2,2,2,-2,-2,2,2).
The Goertzel combination is already the DFT bin, so X[2]=G=2+2j. I do not multiply by e^{j omega} and I treat the phase of G as the phase of X[2].

DSP:010426.title: Periodic Hann N=8 hop 4 is COLA-1; a second Hann is not square-COLA and needs normalization
DSP:010426.objective: Prove that the periodic Hann of length 8 at hop 4 satisfies w[n]+w[n+4]=1, hence analysis-window plus IDFT plus OLA is exact on a fully covered or padded region; show that a second Hann produces the hop-sum 0.5(1+cos^2(pi n/4)) with values 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.75, which is not constant and needs pointwise normalization; distinguish COLA from square-COLA.
DSP:010426.statement:
Let $N=8$ and let $w$ be the \emph{periodic} Hann window
\[
w[n]=\frac12\Bigl(1-\cos\frac{2\pi n}{N}\Bigr)
=\frac12\Bigl(1-\cos\frac{\pi n}{4}\Bigr),\qquad n=0,1,\ldots,7,
\]
extended by zero outside $\{0,\ldots,7\}$ when used as an analysis
window, or $N$-periodically when the complementarity identity is
written on one period. Let the hop be $R=4=N/2$.

1. Prove the constant-overlap-add identity $w[n]+w[n+4]=1$ for
   $n=0,1,2,3$ (and hence, by hopping, for every fully covered time
   index). Conclude that analysis-windowing, length-$N$ DFT/IDFT, and
   overlap-add reconstruct the input exactly on any fully covered or
   periodically padded region.

2. Now apply the same Hann a second time as a synthesis window (WOLA).
   Prove that the hop-sum of the squared window is
   \[
   w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2=\frac12\Bigl(1+\cos^2\frac{\pi n}{4}\Bigr)
   \]
   and that the four values on one hop are $1$, $3/4$, $1/2$, and
   $3/4$. In particular the sum is not constant.

3. State the pointwise normalization that restores perfect
   reconstruction for this WOLA, and distinguish COLA (sum of the
   windows constant) from square-COLA (sum of the squares constant).

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the symmetric Hann
   $\tfrac12\bigl(1-\cos(2\pi n/(N-1))\bigr)$ may be substituted, or
   $w[n]+w[n+4]$ need not be identically $1$”; (ii) “because the
   analysis hop-sum is already $1$, applying Hann again is still COLA,
   so no normalization is required.”

Do not replace the calculation by any of the six stated Digital Signal
Processing seed exercises.
permittedResults: The shift $n\mapsto n+N/2$ sends $\cos(\pi n/4)$ to $-\cos(\pi n/4)$, so the two periodic-Hann values on a hop are $\tfrac12(1-\cos\theta)$ and $\tfrac12(1+\cos\theta)$ and sum to $1$.

If $\sum_m w[n-mR]=1$ on a fully covered (or periodically padded) region, then analysis windowing, an invertible length-$N$ DFT/IDFT, and overlap-add reconstruct the input there. A non-constant sum of squares requires pointwise division by that sum.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use cos(theta+pi)=-cos(theta) to get the pair 1/2(1∓cos theta), add for COLA-1, square-and-add for the four WOLA weights, then normalize.
Evaluate the eight window samples first, add neighbors four apart to lock COLA-1, then square those samples to see 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.75 before identifying the closed form.

milestones.criterion: Proves that periodic Hann N=8 at hop 4 satisfies w[n]+w[n+4]=1 and that analysis-window+IDFT+OLA is exact on a fully covered or padded region.
Computes the squared hop-sum 0.5(1+cos^2(pi n/4)) with values 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.75 and states the pointwise WOLA normalization.
Distinguishes COLA from square-COLA and rejects treating a second Hann as already complementary.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the symmetric Hann 1/2(1-cos(2 pi n/(N-1))), or reports that w[n]+w[n+4] is not identically 1, so analysis OLA is no longer exact.
commonErrors.consequence: The COLA-1 identity and the exact analysis-window+IDFT+OLA claim are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats a second Hann as still COLA, claims the hop-sum of w^2 is constant, or omits the pointwise normalization required by the values 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.75.
commonErrors.consequence: WOLA is declared perfectly reconstructing when the effective window is not complementary.

hintTree.content: Write $w[n]=\tfrac12(1-\cos\theta)$ and $w[n+4]=\tfrac12(1-\cos(\theta+\pi))=\tfrac12(1+\cos\theta)$ with $\theta=\pi n/4$.
Square and add: $\tfrac14\bigl[(1-\cos\theta)^2+(1+\cos\theta)^2\bigr]=\tfrac12(1+\cos^2\theta)$. The hop values are $1,3/4,1/2,3/4$.
COLA is a statement about $\sum w$, not about $\sum w^2$. WOLA with a second Hann needs division by $w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2$.

DSP:010426.canonicalSolution:
Set $\theta=\pi n/4$. The periodic Hann and its hop-$4$ shift are
\[
w[n]=\frac12(1-\cos\theta),\qquad
w[n+4]=\frac12\bigl(1-\cos(\theta+\pi)\bigr)=\frac12(1+\cos\theta).
\]
Adding these identities gives
\[
w[n]+w[n+4]=1
\]
for $n=0,1,2,3$, and therefore at every time index that is covered by
exactly the two hops of a $50\%$ overlap (or by the periodic extension
of those hops). Explicit samples confirm the same constant:
$w[0]+w[4]=0+1=1$, $w[1]+w[5]=1$, $w[2]+w[6]=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$,
and $w[3]+w[7]=1$.

On any fully covered or periodically padded region the analysis windows
therefore form a partition of unity. Windowing, a length-$8$ DFT, the
inverse DFT, and overlap-add then reconstruct the input exactly: the
DFT/IDFT pair is invertible on each frame, and the overlapped windows
sum to $1$. Edge frames that are not fully overlapped are outside the
claim unless the signal is padded or periodized.
\[
\boxed{w[n]+w[n+4]=1\ \text{(COLA-$1$)}}.
\]

Applying the same Hann again after each IDFT produces the WOLA hop-sum
of squares
\begin{align*}
w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2
&=\frac14\Bigl[(1-\cos\theta)^2+(1+\cos\theta)^2\Bigr]
=\frac14\bigl(2+2\cos^2\theta\bigr)
=\frac12\Bigl(1+\cos^2\frac{\pi n}{4}\Bigr).
\end{align*}
The four values on one hop are
\[
n=0\mapsto 1,\qquad
n=1\mapsto \tfrac34,\qquad
n=2\mapsto \tfrac12,\qquad
n=3\mapsto \tfrac34.
\]
The sum is not constant, so the second Hann is not square-COLA at hop
$4$.
\[
\boxed{w^2\text{ hop-sum }=\tfrac12(1+\cos^2(\pi n/4))\in\{1,3/4,1/2,3/4\}}.
\]

Pointwise normalization restores perfect reconstruction for this WOLA:
divide the overlapped output at each $n$ by $w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2$ (on a
fully covered region this denominator is exactly the displayed
combination and is never zero). Equivalently, take the synthesis window
to be $w[n]/(w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2)$ on that region.

COLA is the statement that $\sum_m w[n-mR]$ is constant. Square-COLA is
the distinct statement that $\sum_m w[n-mR]^2$ is constant. Periodic
Hann at hop $N/2$ is COLA-$1$ and is not square-COLA; a second Hann
therefore needs the normalization above. Confusing the two notions is
what produces the false claim that WOLA is already perfect.

Sentence (i) replaces the periodic Hann by the symmetric endpoint
formula, which is not COLA-$1$ at hop $4$ for $N=8$, or else denies the
identity $w[n]+w[n+4]=1$. Sentence (ii) treats a second Hann as if it
were still a sum of unsquared windows.

The argument never substitutes any of the six stated seed exercises.

graderFixtures.proofText: Periodic Hann $N=8$ at hop $4$ satisfies $w[n]+w[n+4]=1$, so analysis-window+IDFT+OLA is exact on a fully covered or padded region. A second Hann produces $w[n]^2+w[n+4]^2=\tfrac12(1+\cos^2(\pi n/4))$ with values $1,3/4,1/2,3/4$, which is not square-COLA and needs pointwise normalization. COLA is not square-COLA.
I use the symmetric Hann 1/2(1-cos(2 pi n/(N-1))) in place of the periodic formula, and I do not obtain w[n]+w[n+4]=1. Analysis OLA is therefore not exact even on a fully covered region.
The analysis hop-sum is already 1, so applying Hann again is still COLA. The hop-sum of w^2 is constant and I do not divide by 1/2(1+cos^2(pi n/4)).
