DM:010519.title: Six-bead two-color bracelets split one chiral necklace pair
DM:010519.objective: Apply Burnside's lemma to the action of the dihedral group on two-colorings of a hexagon, separate the cyclic necklace count from the bracelet count, and audit both integers by a complete listing that isolates the unique chiral pair.
DM:010519.statement:
Six workshop stations sit at the vertices of a regular hexagon. Each station receives a red or blue status tag. Two taggings represent the same bracelet when one is obtained from the other by rotating the bench or flipping it over (the full dihedral group $D_6$ of order $12$). Two taggings represent the same necklace when only rotations (the cyclic group $C_6$) are allowed.

1. State Burnside's lemma for a finite group $G$ acting on a finite set $X$: the number of orbits is $\frac1{\lvert G\rvert}\sum_{g\in G}\operatorname{Fix}(g)$. Explain why, for $G$ acting on the set of functions from vertices to $\{$red, blue$\}$, a coloring is fixed by $g$ if and only if it is constant on every cycle of $g$.

2. For each of the six rotations, compute the cycle type on the six vertices and the number of fixed $2$-colorings. Deduce the number of necklaces under $C_6$.

3. The six reflections of a hexagon fall into two conjugacy classes: three axes through opposite vertices and three axes through midpoints of opposite edges. Compute the cycle type and the number of fixed colorings in each class. Deduce the number of bracelets under $D_6$.

4. Audit both integers by listing representatives. Classify colorings by the number $w$ of red tags, $w=0,\ldots,6$. For $w\le 3$ give a complete set of convenient dihedral representatives (binary words with $1=$red), and obtain $w\ge 4$ by complementation. Identify the unique pair of $C_6$-orbits that merge under a reflection, and name binary representatives of that chiral pair.

Do not replace $D_6$ by $C_6$ when counting bracelets, and do not assign every reflection the cycle type of a vertex axis.
permittedResults: Burnside: the number of $G$-orbits on $X$ is the average number of fixed points. A vertex-coloring is fixed by a permutation if and only if each cycle is monochromatic, so a permutation with $c$ cycles fixes $2^c$ binary colorings.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the Burnside averages for C_6 and D_6 from cycle types, then confirm 13 by a weight-by-weight listing.
List binary hexagons up to dihedral action first, then match the orbit counts against the two Burnside averages and isolate the mirrors 110100 and 110010.

milestones.criterion: Computes the cyclic necklace count 14 from the six rotation cycle types.
Separates the two reflection cycle types and obtains the bracelet count 13.
Lists the 13 dihedral classes and identifies the unique chiral necklace pair.

commonErrors.description: Treats all six reflections as having the same cycle type (usually two fixed vertices), assigning $2^4=16$ fixed colorings to every reflection.
commonErrors.consequence: The edge-midpoint axes are miscounted, so the dihedral average is not $13$.

commonErrors.description: Averages only over the six rotations and reports $14$ as the number of bracelets, or uses $\lvert D_6\rvert=6$.
commonErrors.consequence: Flips are never quotiented, so a chiral pair is counted twice for bracelets.

hintTree.content: Rotation by $k\cdot 60^\circ$ decomposes into $\gcd(k,6)$ cycles. In particular $180^\circ$ is three transpositions.
A vertex axis fixes two vertices and pairs the other four. An edge-midpoint axis is a product of three transpositions and fixes no vertex.
Among weight-$3$ binary hexagons, $111000$ and $101010$ are achiral, while $110100$ and $110010$ are mirrors that are not rotations of one another.

DM:010519.canonicalSolution:
Burnside's lemma says that if a finite group $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, then the number of orbits is
\[
\frac1{\lvert G\rvert}\sum_{g\in G}\lvert\{x\in X:gx=x\}\rvert.
\]
Here $X$ is the set of $2^6$ colorings of the six vertices. A group element, viewed as a permutation of vertices, fixes a coloring precisely when every cycle is monochromatic, hence fixes $2^{c(g)}$ colorings if it has $c(g)$ cycles.

Label vertices $0,1,2,3,4,5$ in cyclic order. The rotations and their fixed-coloring counts are
\begin{align*}
r^0=\mathrm{id}&: 6\text{ ones},\ 2^6=64,\\
r^{\pm1}&: \text{one $6$-cycle},\ 2^1=2\text{ each},\\
r^{\pm2}&: \text{two $3$-cycles }(0\,2\,4)(1\,3\,5),\ 2^2=4\text{ each},\\
r^{3}&: \text{three transpositions }(0\,3)(1\,4)(2\,5),\ 2^3=8.
\end{align*}
Averaging over $C_6$ gives
\[
\frac{64+2+4+8+4+2}{6}=\frac{84}{6}=14
\]
necklaces:
\[
\boxed{\text{14 necklaces}}.
\]

The three vertex axes (through $0$--$3$, $1$--$4$, $2$--$5$) each have cycle type $1+1+2+2$, so each fixes $2^4=16$ colorings. The three edge-midpoint axes (through the midpoints of $0$--$1$ and $3$--$4$, and the two rotates) each have cycle type $2+2+2$, so each fixes $2^3=8$ colorings. Averaging over all twelve dihedral elements gives
\[
\frac{84+3\cdot16+3\cdot8}{12}=\frac{84+48+24}{12}=\frac{156}{12}=13
\]
bracelets:
\[
\boxed{\text{13 bracelets}}.
\]

Dihedral representatives by red-weight $w$, written as binary words:
\begin{align*}
w=0&: 000000,\\
w=1&: 100000,\\
w=2&: 110000,\ 101000,\ 100100,\\
w=3&: 111000,\ 110100,\ 101010,\\
w=4&: 111100,\ 111010,\ 110110,\\
w=5&: 111110,\\
w=6&: 111111.
\end{align*}
That is $1+1+3+3+3+1+1=13$ bracelets. The $w=4,5,6$ rows are complements of $w=2,1,0$.

The $C_6$-orbits of $110100$ and $110010$ are distinct: the rotations of $110100$ are
\[
110100,\ 101001,\ 010011,\ 100110,\ 001101,\ 011010,
\]
which do not include $110010$. The reverse of $110100$ is $001011$, and rotating $001011$ by four positions produces $110010$. Thus those two necklaces form a single bracelet, which is why the cyclic count is $14$ and the dihedral count is $13$. The other listed representatives are achiral: each is dihedrally equivalent to its reverse.

Treating every reflection as a vertex axis would replace $3\cdot8$ by another $3\cdot16$ and produce $(84+96)/12=15$, which is not the bracelet count. Using only $C_6$ produces the necklace count $14$, not the bracelet count.

graderFixtures.proofText: Rotations fix $64,2,4,8,4,2$ colorings, so there are $84/6=14$ necklaces. Vertex reflections fix $16$ each and edge reflections fix $8$ each, so there are $(84+48+24)/12=13$ bracelets. The extra necklace is the chiral pair $110100$ and $110010$.
Every reflection of a hexagon fixes two opposite vertices and pairs the rest, so each of the six reflections fixes $16$ colorings. The bracelet count is $(84+96)/12=15$.
The symmetry group of the circular bench has order $6$. Burnside therefore gives $84/6=14$ bracelets; flipping the bench is the same as rotating it.

DM:010520.title: The sixth derangement number is 265 by two independent recurrences
DM:010520.objective: Derive the inclusion-exclusion formula for derangements, prove the two standard recurrences, and show that all three evaluations agree at n=6, including the exact integer rather than a rounded n!/e estimate.
DM:010520.statement:
Six guests check six distinct hats. A derangement of $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ with $\sigma(i)\ne i$ for every $i$. Write $!n$ for the number of derangements of $[n]$.

1. For each $i\in[n]$ let $A_i$ be the permutations that fix $i$. Apply inclusion-exclusion to prove
   \[
   !n=n!\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^i}{i!}.
   \]
   Explain why this is an integer even though it is written with denominators, and why replacing the finite sum by the nearest integer to $n!/e$ is a theorem about $!n$, not a definition.

2. Prove the adjacent recurrence
   \[
   !n=n\cdot!(n-1)+(-1)^n\qquad(n\ge 1),\qquad !0=1,
   \]
   directly from the inclusion-exclusion sums (do not quote it as a black box). Then deduce the two-step recurrence
   \[
   !n=(n-1)\bigl(!(n-1)+!(n-2)\bigr)\qquad(n\ge 2)
   \]
   from the adjacent recurrence. Give a combinatorial reading of the two-step relation by cases on whether $n$ and $\sigma(n)$ form a $2$-cycle.

3. Compute $!4$, $!5$, and $!6$ from inclusion-exclusion as exact integers (display every term of the $n=6$ sum). Recompute $!6$ from each recurrence, using the values $!4=9$ and $!5=44$.

4. A locker-room audit invokes $!6=\lfloor 720/e+1/2\rfloor$ without proving the nearest-integer theorem and therefore refuses to expand the inclusion-exclusion sum. Explain what that unsupported invocation leaves unproved and why, even after the theorem is established, it does not supply the exact derivation requested here. Another audit writes $!n=n\bigl(!(n-1)+!(n-2)\bigr)$ or $!n=n\cdot!(n-1)+(-1)^{n-1}$. Show that both recurrences fail already at $n=4$ or $n=6$.

Do not pass to exponential generating functions or to the Master theorem, and do not treat a rounded real as a replacement for the exact count.
permittedResults: Inclusion-exclusion on the sets of permutations that fix a prescribed point yields $!n=n!\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i/i!$. The same sequence obeys $!n=n\cdot!(n-1)+(-1)^n$ and $!n=(n-1)(!(n-1)+!(n-2))$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the n=6 inclusion-exclusion sum to the integer 265, then match both recurrences as a consistency check.
Compute the sequence up to !6 from !n=n*!(n-1)+(-1)^n and confirm the last value against the explicit six-term IE sum.

milestones.criterion: Derives the inclusion-exclusion formula and both recurrences, including the sign (-1)^n.
Evaluates !6=265 from the IE sum and from each recurrence, using !4=9 and !5=44.
Rejects a rounded n!/e substitute and exhibits the failure of the two mutated recurrences.

commonErrors.description: Reports $!6$ as $720/e$, or invokes $\lfloor720/e+1/2\rfloor$ without proving the nearest-integer theorem and without expanding inclusion-exclusion or running a proved recurrence.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested exact derivation is absent; in the floor version even the theorem connecting the rounded value to derangements is merely assumed.
The consistency check is performed against a false recurrence, so a wrong integer can appear internally consistent.

hintTree.content: A permutation that fixes a prescribed set of $i$ points may permute the rest arbitrarily, so those intersections have size $(n-i)!$.
Subtract $n\cdot!(n-1)$ from the IE formula: the two sums agree through $i=n-1$, and the last term is $(-1)^n$.
For the two-step relation, write $n= (n-1)+1$ in the adjacent recurrence and cancel the two copies of $(-1)^{n-1}$.

DM:010520.canonicalSolution:
Let $A_j\subseteq S_n$ be the permutations with $\sigma(j)=j$. If $I\subseteq[n]$ has size $i$, then $\lvert\bigcap_{j\in I}A_j\rvert=(n-i)!$. Inclusion-exclusion therefore gives
\[
!n
=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\binom{n}{i}(n-i)!
=n!\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^i}{i!}.
\]
Each summand $\binom{n}{i}(n-i)!$ is an integer, so $!n$ is an integer. The Taylor remainder for $e^{-1}$ implies that $!n$ is the integer nearest to $n!/e$ for $n\ge 1$, but that approximation is a consequence of the finite sum, not a substitute for computing the sum.

From the finite sums,
\begin{align*}
n\cdot!(n-1)
&=n\cdot(n-1)!\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^i}{i!}
=n!\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^i}{i!},\\
!n-n\cdot!(n-1)
&=n!\cdot\frac{(-1)^n}{n!}
=(-1)^n.
\end{align*}
Hence
\[
\boxed{!n=n\cdot!(n-1)+(-1)^n}.
\]
Now substitute $!(n-1)=(n-1)\cdot!(n-2)+(-1)^{n-1}$ and $n=(n-1)+1$:
\begin{align*}
!n
&=(n-1)\cdot!(n-1)+!(n-1)+(-1)^n\\
&=(n-1)\cdot!(n-1)+\bigl((n-1)\cdot!(n-2)+(-1)^{n-1}\bigr)+(-1)^n\\
&=(n-1)\bigl(!(n-1)+!(n-2)\bigr),
\end{align*}
because $(-1)^n+(-1)^{n-1}=0$. Combinatorially: there are $n-1$ choices for $\sigma(n)=k$. If $\sigma(k)=n$, the rest is a derangement of an $(n-2)$-set. If $\sigma(k)\ne n$, rename the hat $n$ as $k$ to obtain a derangement of an $(n-1)$-set.

The $n=6$ inclusion-exclusion expansion is
\[
720\Bigl(1-1+\frac12-\frac16+\frac1{24}-\frac1{120}+\frac1{720}\Bigr)
=720-720+360-120+30-6+1
=265.
\]
The same arithmetic gives $!4=9$ and $!5=44$. The recurrences recover
\[
!6=6\cdot44+(-1)^6=264+1=265
\]
and
\[
!6=5\bigl(44+9\bigr)=5\cdot53=265.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{!6=265}.
\]
The nearest-integer identity is a theorem, not the definition of $!n$.
Invoking it without proof leaves the link to derangements unjustified; after
it has been proved, it can correctly recover the integer, but it still does
not provide this packet's requested inclusion-exclusion or recurrence
derivation. The mutated recurrences fail immediately:
\[
4\bigl(!3+!2\bigr)=4(2+1)=12\ne9=!4,
\]
and
\[
6\cdot44+(-1)^{5}=264-1=263\ne265.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: IE gives $!6=720-720+360-120+30-6+1=265$. The adjacent recurrence is $!6=6\cdot44+1=265$ and the two-step recurrence is $!6=5(44+9)=265$. Both mutated recurrences already fail at $n=4$ or $n=6$.
Since $!n$ is the integer nearest to $n!/e$, I record $!6=\lfloor720/e+1/2\rfloor$ and do not expand $\sum (-1)^i/i!$.
There are $n$ choices for the image of $n$, so $!n=n(!(n-1)+!(n-2))$. In particular $!6=6(44+9)=318$, and the signed recurrence is $!6=6\cdot44-1=263$.

DM:010521.title: A first-touch reflection subtracts the lattice paths that cross the diagonal
DM:010521.objective: Count east-north lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,n) that never rise strictly above the diagonal by the reflection principle, identify the count with the Catalan number, and audit C_3 by listing and C_4 by both Catalan formulas.
DM:010521.statement:
A courier on the grid takes steps $E=(1,0)$ and $N=(0,1)$. A path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ is legal when it never enters the half-plane $y\ge x+1$: equivalently, in every prefix the number of $E$ steps is at least the number of $N$ steps. Let $C_n$ denote the number of legal paths.

1. The total number of unrestricted paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ is $\binom{2n}{n}$. A path is illegal when it first touches the barrier line $y=x+1$ at some point $P$. Reflect the initial segment from $(0,0)$ to $P$ across the line $y=x+1$, and prove that this reflection is a bijection between illegal paths to $(n,n)$ and all unrestricted paths from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$. Conclude that there are $\binom{2n}{n-1}$ illegal paths (equivalently $\binom{2n}{n+1}$) and therefore
   \[
   C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}.
   \]

2. Algebraically rewrite the difference to obtain the equivalent formula
   \[
   C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
   \]
   Record the convention $C_0=1$.

3. For $n=3$, list all five legal words in $E$ and $N$. For $n=4$, evaluate $C_4$ from both displayed formulas, showing the binomial arithmetic $\binom{8}{4}=70$ and $\binom{8}{3}=56$.

4. Audit two false shortcuts. (i) "Half of all paths stay on or below the diagonal, so $C_n=\tfrac12\binom{2n}{n}$." Check this against $n=3$ and $n=4$. (ii) "Reflect the whole path across $y=x$ to pair every illegal path with a legal one." Explain why reflection across the diagonal $y=x$ (rather than across the barrier $y=x+1$) does not produce the Catalan subtraction.

Do not replace the reflection argument by an unmarked binomial double count of the marked-subset type, and do not quote the Catalan generating function or a recursive decomposition as a substitute for the first-touch bijection.
permittedResults: Reflection principle: reflecting the prefix of an illegal path up to its first visit to $y=x+1$ sends $(0,0)$ to $(-1,1)$ and gives a bijection with all paths from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$. Hence $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Set up the first-touch bijection with the barrier y=x+1, subtract binom(2n,n-1), then audit C_3 by listing and C_4 by both formulas.
Start from the closed form (1/(n+1)) binom(2n,n), derive the binomial difference algebraically, and justify the subtracted term by the reflection bijection.

milestones.criterion: Carries out the first-touch reflection across y=x+1 and obtains C_n=binom(2n,n)-binom(2n,n-1).
Rewrites the difference as (1/(n+1)) binom(2n,n) and evaluates C_3=5 and C_4=14.
Lists the five n=3 legal words and refutes both the half-of-all-paths shortcut and reflection across y=x.

commonErrors.description: Reflects across $y=x$ rather than $y=x+1$, or claims that every path is paired with a distinct path so that $C_n=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The first-touch correspondence with paths from $(-1,1)$ is never established, so the subtracted binomial is unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that half of the unrestricted paths are legal and reports $C_3=10$ or $C_4=35$.
commonErrors.consequence: The two sides of the diagonal are not equinumerous among paths that are allowed to touch $y=x$, so the Catalan count is doubled.

hintTree.content: Reflection of a point $(a,b)$ across $y=x+1$ is $(b-1,a+1)$. In particular $(0,0)$ maps to $(-1,1)$.
A path from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ uses $n+1$ east steps and $n-1$ north steps, so there are $\binom{2n}{n-1}$ of them.
The five $n=3$ words are $EEENNN$, $EENENN$, $EENNEN$, $ENEENN$, and $ENENEN$.

DM:010521.canonicalSolution:
Any path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ has $n$ east steps and $n$ north steps, so there are $\binom{2n}{n}$ unrestricted paths. An illegal path has a first vertex $P$ on the line $y=x+1$. Reflection across $y=x+1$ is the isometry
\[
(a,b)\mapsto(b-1,a+1),
\]
which swaps the two sides of the barrier and fixes the barrier pointwise. The start $(0,0)$ is sent to $(-1,1)$, while $P$ and the suffix from $P$ to $(n,n)$ are unchanged. The inverse construction is the same reflection of the prefix up to the first visit to the barrier, which every path from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ must make because it starts on the illegal side. This is therefore a bijection between illegal paths to $(n,n)$ and all paths from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$.

A path from $(-1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ uses $(n-(-1))=n+1$ east steps and $(n-1)$ north steps, hence
\[
\binom{2n}{n+1}=\binom{2n}{n-1}
\]
illegal paths. Subtracting from the unrestricted total yields
\[
\boxed{C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}}.
\]
Algebraically,
\begin{align*}
\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}
&=\frac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}-\frac{(2n)!}{(n-1)!\,(n+1)!}\\
&=\frac{(2n)!}{n!\,(n+1)!}\bigl((n+1)-n\bigr)
=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n},
\end{align*}
so
\[
\boxed{C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}}.
\]
The $n=0$ path is empty and is legal, hence $C_0=1$.

For $n=3$ the legal words are exactly
\[
EEENNN,\quad EENENN,\quad EENNEN,\quad ENEENN,\quad ENENEN,
\]
five of them, and $C_3=\frac14\binom{6}{3}=5$. For $n=4$,
\[
\binom{8}{4}=70,\qquad\binom{8}{3}=56,\qquad70-56=14,
\]
and $\frac15\cdot70=14$, so
\[
\boxed{C_4=14}.
\]

The shortcut $C_n=\tfrac12\binom{2n}{n}$ fails: $\tfrac12\binom{6}{3}=10\ne5$ and $\tfrac12\binom{8}{4}=35\ne14$. Paths that touch the diagonal from below are not paired with paths that cross it; the two classes have different sizes. Reflection of an entire path across the diagonal $y=x$ merely swaps $E$ with $N$ and therefore swaps the region $y<x$ with $y>x$. It does not measure first contact with the barrier $y=x+1$: a path can cross the diagonal several times, and its whole reflection need not be legal when the original is illegal. Unlike the first-touch map, it keeps the start at $(0,0)$ rather than moving it to $(-1,1)$, so it supplies no bijection from the illegal class to the paths counted by $\binom{2n}{n-1}$. That involution therefore cannot justify the Catalan subtraction.

graderFixtures.proofText: First contact with $y=x+1$ reflects $(0,0)$ to $(-1,1)$, so there are $\binom{2n}{n-1}$ illegal paths and $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$. The five $n=3$ words give $C_3=5$, and $C_4=70-56=14=70/5$. Half of $\binom{2n}{n}$ is not Catalan.

Reflect every path across the diagonal $y=x$. This pairs east-heavy paths with north-heavy paths, so after identifying mirrors there are no leftover illegal paths and the count collapses, or at best one simply swaps $E$ and $N$ without a barrier argument.
By symmetry half the paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ stay on or below $y=x$. Thus $C_3=\binom{6}{3}/2=10$ and $C_4=\binom{8}{4}/2=35$.

DM:010525.title: Prefix residues force a consecutive block divisible by n
DM:010525.objective: Prove that every integer n-tuple has a nonempty consecutive block whose sum is divisible by n, by pigeonhole on n+1 prefix residues, and handle the zero-residue prefix case, the equal nonzero-prefix case, and a length-(n-1) counterexample separately.
DM:010525.statement:
Let $n\ge 2$ be an integer, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb Z$. Write $s_0=0$ and $s_k=a_1+\cdots+a_k$ for $1\le k\le n$.

1. Prove that there exist indices $0\le i<j\le n$ with $s_j\equiv s_i\pmod n$. Deduce that the nonempty consecutive block $a_{i+1}+\cdots+a_j$ is divisible by $n$. Your pigeonhole must use the $n+1$ prefixes $s_0,\ldots,s_n$ and the $n$ residues modulo $n$. Explain why $s_0=0$ is a legitimate pigeon even though the empty sum is not a legitimate block.

2. Split the argument into the two exhaustive cases: (i) $s_k\equiv 0\pmod n$ for some $k\ge 1$; (ii) no nonempty prefix is $0\bmod n$, so the collision is $s_i\equiv s_j\not\equiv 0$ for some $1\le i<j\le n$. Explain why a single term $a_r\equiv 0\pmod n$ is represented by the adjacent-prefix collision $s_{r-1}\equiv s_r$, and why that singleton can occur in either case rather than automatically forcing a zero prefix.

3. Take $n=6$. Exhibit an explicit block in each of the sequences
   \[
   (2,4,1,1,1,1),\qquad
   (1,1,1,1,1,2),\qquad
   (1,2,6,3,1,1),
   \]
   and state which of the two cases each sequence realises. For the middle sequence, prove that no nonempty prefix is $0\bmod 6$, so the zero residue of $s_0$ is not itself the witness.

4. Prove that $n$ terms are necessary in the worst case: the sequence of $n-1$ ones has no nonempty consecutive block sum divisible by $n$. Audit both sentences: (i) “the empty prefix $s_0=0$ is already a block sum divisible by $n$, so there is nothing to prove”; (ii) “among $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ there are $n$ terms and $n$ residues, so some $a_r\equiv 0\pmod n$.” The middle sequence of part 3 must serve as a counterexample to (ii).

Do not replace the prefix argument by an averaging argument, and do not count the empty block as a witness.
permittedResults: If $s_j\equiv s_i\pmod n$, then $n$ divides $s_j-s_i$. The difference is a nonempty block precisely when $j>i$.
A sequence of length $n-1$ need not have a consecutive block sum divisible by $n$; the $n+1$st prefix is essential to the counting.

acceptableStrategies.description: Place all prefixes into residue boxes first, then classify the colliding pair according to whether its common residue is 0.
Compute the six prefixes of each n=6 example before naming the block, so the case (i)/(ii) diagnosis is read off the residue list.

milestones.criterion: Applies pigeonhole to the n+1 prefixes and extracts a nonempty block s_j-s_i divisible by n, keeping s_0 as a pigeon rather than a witness.
Separates the zero-prefix case from the equal-nonzero-prefix case and identifies all three n=6 examples, including the interior block of (1,1,1,1,1,2).
Proves sharpness with n-1 ones and rejects both audited sentences.

commonErrors.description: Treats s_0=0 as an already-valid consecutive block, or declares the theorem vacuous because the empty sum is divisible by n.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonempty-block claim is never proved, and the pigeonhole on later prefixes is skipped.

commonErrors.description: Applies pigeonhole to the n terms a_1,...,a_n and concludes that some a_r ≡ 0 (mod n).
commonErrors.consequence: The conclusion is false for (1,1,1,1,1,2), which has a block sum 0 (mod 6) but no term 0 (mod 6).

hintTree.content: There are $n+1$ prefixes and only $n$ residues. The empty prefix occupies residue $0$, but the witness block is $s_j-s_i$ with $j>i$, never the empty prefix itself.
If every $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ avoids residue $0$, then those $n$ prefixes live in the $n-1$ nonzero residues, which already forces a collision without using $s_0$.
For $(1,1,1,1,1,2)$ the prefixes are $0,1,2,3,4,5,7\equiv 1$. The repeated residue is $1$, not $0$. Five ones have block sums $1,2,3,4,5$ only.

DM:010525.canonicalSolution:
The $n+1$ integers $s_0,s_1,\ldots,s_n$ take values in a set of $n$ residues. By the pigeonhole principle there exist $0\le i<j\le n$ with $s_j\equiv s_i\pmod n$. Then
\[
s_j-s_i=a_{i+1}+\cdots+a_j\equiv 0\pmod n.
\]
The inequality $j>i$ makes the block nonempty. The empty prefix $s_0$ is used only as a pigeon: if the other pigeon in its box is some $s_k$ with $k\ge 1$, the witness is the nonempty prefix $a_1+\cdots+a_k$, not the empty sum.
\[
\boxed{\exists\,0\le i<j\le n\text{ with }n\mid(s_j-s_i)}.
\]

Case (i): $s_k\equiv 0\pmod n$ for some $k\ge 1$. Then $i=0$, $j=k$ works, and the block is a nonempty prefix. Case (ii): $s_k\not\equiv 0$ for all $k\ge 1$. Then $s_0$ is the unique prefix in residue $0$, so the forced collision guaranteed by part 1 must be $s_i\equiv s_j\not\equiv 0$ for some $1\le i<j\le n$, and the witness is an interior block (or a suffix). These cases exhaust the possibilities. Independently, $a_r\equiv0\pmod n$ is exactly the adjacent collision $s_{r-1}\equiv s_r$. Its common residue may be zero or nonzero, so a divisible singleton need not belong specifically to case (i).

For $n=6$:
- $(2,4,1,1,1,1)$ has prefixes $0,2,6,7,8,9,10$, so $s_2\equiv 0$. Case (i), block $(2,4)$.
- $(1,1,1,1,1,2)$ has prefixes $0,1,2,3,4,5,7$. The nonempty prefixes occupy $1,2,3,4,5,1$ and never $0$. The collision is $s_1\equiv s_6\equiv 1$, so the block is $a_2+\cdots+a_6=1+1+1+1+2=6$. Case (ii).
- $(1,2,6,3,1,1)$ has prefix residues $0,1,3,3,0,1,2$. Thus the sequence is in case (i), witnessed by the prefix $(1,2,6,3)$ of sum $12$. It also has the singleton block $(6)$ from the adjacent nonzero collision $s_2\equiv s_3\equiv3$; this illustrates why the singleton mechanism is not the same thing as a zero-prefix witness.
\[
\boxed{(2,4);\ (1,1,1,1,2);\ (6)\text{ (with prefix }(1,2,6,3)\text{ also available)}}.
\]

For the sequence of $n-1$ ones, the nonempty block sums are the integers $1,2,\ldots,n-1$, none of which is $0\bmod n$. Thus length $n$ is sharp. Sentence (i) mistakes a pigeon for a witness: the empty sum is excluded by the claim, and $s_0$ is present only to create a collision with a later prefix. Sentence (ii) applies the pigeonhole principle to the $n$ terms rather than to the $n+1$ prefixes. The middle sequence of part 3 has no term $0\bmod 6$, yet it has a consecutive block sum $0\bmod 6$, so (ii) is false.

graderFixtures.proofText: The $n+1$ prefixes collide modulo $n$, so some $s_j-s_i$ with $j>i$ is $0\bmod n$. Either a nonempty prefix is $0\bmod n$, or two nonzero prefixes agree. For $n=6$ the blocks are $(2,4)$, the suffix $(1,1,1,1,2)$, and the singleton $(6)$; in the third sequence a zero prefix also occurs at $s_4$. A divisible singleton is an adjacent-prefix collision and need not itself force a zero prefix. Five ones have no such block.
s_0=0 is already divisible by n, and the empty consecutive block is allowed, so the statement is immediate and no pigeonhole is required.
There are n integers a_1,...,a_n and n residues modulo n, so some a_r ≡ 0 (mod n). That single term is the required block. In particular (1,1,1,1,1,2) must have a term divisible by 6.

DM:010727.title: A Prüfer word rebuilds its labeled tree and counts all of them
DM:010727.objective: Encode and decode explicit labeled trees by the Prüfer algorithm, recover vertex degrees from code multiplicities, and identify Cayley's count with the set of words of length n-2.
DM:010727.statement:
Work throughout with simple trees on the labeled vertex set $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, where $n\ge2$. The Prüfer code of such a tree is the word of length $n-2$ produced by the following encoding. While at least three vertices remain, delete the current leaf of smallest label and record the label of its unique neighbor. The two vertices that remain are discarded unrecorded.

1. Let $T$ be the tree on $[6]$ with edge set
   \[
   \{1{-}2,\ 2{-}3,\ 2{-}4,\ 4{-}5,\ 4{-}6\}.
   \]
   Run the encoding algorithm step by step, listing the deleted leaf and the recorded neighbor at each of the four deletions. Write the Prüfer code $\operatorname{Prufer}(T)$. Prove that the degree of each vertex equals one plus its multiplicity in that code.

2. Decode the word $(3,1,3,1)$ on $[6]$ by the inverse algorithm: initialize $\deg(v)=1+m(v)$ where $m(v)$ is the number of times $v$ appears in the remaining word, then for each successive letter $a$ join $a$ to the current smallest degree-$1$ label, decrease both degrees by $1$, and finally join the two leftover degree-$1$ vertices. List every edge. Re-encode the tree you obtain and prove that the original word is recovered.

3. Prove that Prüfer encoding and decoding are mutually inverse on every labeled tree on $[n]$ and every word in $[n]^{n-2}$. Conclude Cayley's formula: there are exactly $n^{n-2}$ distinct trees on the labeled set $[n]$. Evaluate the count at $n=6$.

4. A proposed shortcut reports $n^{n-1}$ by counting rooted labeled trees, or says that after fixing a root each other vertex may independently choose any parent. Explain the extra-root factor in the first count and the cyclic or disconnected parent assignments included in the second. Another shortcut counts unlabeled isomorphism types instead; identify the missing labels. Do not replace the Prüfer bijection by an unproved citation of Cayley's formula, and do not delete the largest remaining leaf.
permittedResults: In a tree on $n\ge 2$ vertices every degree is at least $1$, there are at least two leaves, and the sum of degrees is $2n-2$.
A vertex $v$ appears in $\operatorname{Prufer}(T)$ exactly $\deg(v)-1$ times, so the leaves of $T$ are precisely the labels absent from the code.

acceptableStrategies.description: Run the smallest-leaf encoder on the given tree, then run the degree-table decoder on the second word and check inversion by re-encoding.
Read degrees from code multiplicities first, reconstruct the unique tree with that degree sequence compatible with the word, and count words of length n-2.

milestones.criterion: Encodes the given six-vertex tree as (2,2,4,4) and matches every degree to one plus the code multiplicity.
Decodes (3,1,3,1) to the correct five-edge tree and re-encodes it to the same word.
Identifies Prüfer words with [n]^{n-2}, concludes the labeled count n^{n-2} (1296 at n=6), and rejects n^{n-1} and unlabeled-type counts.

commonErrors.description: Deletes the current largest leaf, or an arbitrary leaf, instead of the smallest-label leaf, and reports the resulting word as the Prüfer code.
commonErrors.consequence: The recorded word is not the Prüfer code of T, and decoding the assigned word will not invert.

commonErrors.description: Reports the rooted count n^{n-1} as unrooted, treats arbitrary parent-pointer assignments as trees, or counts unlabeled isomorphism types instead of labeled trees.
commonErrors.consequence: An extra root, invalid cyclic/disconnected assignments, or missing vertex labels replace the Cayley count attached to Prüfer words of length n-2.

hintTree.content: The initial leaves of $T$ are $1,3,5,6$. The algorithm is forced to delete $1$ first, then $3$.
For the word $(3,1,3,1)$ the initial degree sequence is $(3,1,3,1,1,1)$. The first leaf joined is therefore $2$, not $1$.

There are $n$ choices for each of the $n-2$ letters of a Prüfer word. Choosing one of $n$ roots after choosing an unrooted labeled tree gives the rooted count $n^{n-1}$; arbitrary parent pointers need not form a tree.

DM:010727.canonicalSolution:
The tree $T$ has degrees $\deg 1=1$, $\deg 2=3$, $\deg 3=1$, $\deg 4=3$, $\deg 5=1$, $\deg 6=1$. The leaves are therefore $1,3,5,6$.

Delete the smallest leaf $1$, whose neighbor is $2$, and record $2$. The remaining edges are $2{-}3$, $2{-}4$, $4{-}5$, $4{-}6$, with current leaves $3,5,6$. Delete $3$, record $2$. The remaining edges are $2{-}4$, $4{-}5$, $4{-}6$, with current leaves $2,5,6$. Delete $2$, record $4$. The remaining edges are $4{-}5$, $4{-}6$, with current leaves $5,6$. Delete $5$, record $4$. Two vertices $4,6$ remain, so the algorithm stops.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Prufer}(T)=(2,2,4,4)}.
\]
Vertex $2$ appears twice and vertex $4$ appears twice; every other label is absent. Adding one recovers the degree sequence $(1,3,1,3,1,1)$.
In general, each time $v$ is recorded, one incident edge is deleted while
$v$ remains. Its final incident edge is removed when $v$ itself becomes a
leaf, or is the unrecorded last edge if $v$ survives to the final pair.
Thus exactly one incident edge is unrecorded, proving that the code
multiplicity of $v$ is $\deg(v)-1$.

Now decode $w=(3,1,3,1)$ on $[6]$. The multiplicities are $m(1)=2$, $m(3)=2$, and $m(v)=0$ otherwise, so the initial degrees are
\[
(\deg 1,\ldots,\deg 6)=(3,1,3,1,1,1).
\]
The current degree-$1$ labels are $2,4,5,6$. The first letter is $3$, so join $2{-}3$ and decrease $\deg 2$ and $\deg 3$. The current degree-$1$ labels are $4,5,6$. The next letter is $1$, so join $4{-}1$. The current degree-$1$ labels are $5,6$. The next letter is $3$, so join $5{-}3$. The current degree-$1$ labels are $3,6$. The last letter is $1$, so join $3{-}1$. The leftover degree-$1$ vertices are $1$ and $6$; join $1{-}6$. The edge set is
\[
\boxed{\{2{-}3,\ 4{-}1,\ 5{-}3,\ 3{-}1,\ 1{-}6\}}.
\]
Re-encoding this tree: the leaves are $2,4,5,6$. Delete $2$ and record $3$; delete $4$ and record $1$; delete $5$ and record $3$; delete $3$ and record $1$. The leftover edge is $1{-}6$. The code is again $(3,1,3,1)$.

In general, a tree on $n$ vertices has at least two leaves, so the smallest-leaf deletion is always defined and produces a word of length $n-2$. Each deletion decreases the remaining order by $1$ and the remaining degree of the recorded neighbor by $1$, so the residual graph stays a tree. Decoding rebuilds those deleted edges in the same order: the current smallest unused leaf is exactly the leaf the encoder would have deleted, because a label remains a leaf in the residual tree if and only if it has not yet been recorded in the unread suffix. The final unused pair is the last residual edge. Thus encoding and decoding are mutually inverse, and the Prüfer map is a bijection
\[
\{\text{trees on }[n]\}\ \longleftrightarrow\ [n]^{n-2}.
\]
The right-hand side has cardinality $n^{n-2}$. At $n=6$ this is $6^4=1296$.
\[
\boxed{\text{there are }6^{4}=1296\text{ labeled trees on }[6]}.
\]
Choosing a distinguished root on each labeled tree multiplies Cayley's
unrooted count by $n$, giving $n\cdot n^{n-2}=n^{n-1}$ rooted labeled
trees. That is a different enumeration, not the size of the function set
$[n]^{[n]}$, which is $n^n$. Likewise, if a root is fixed and each other
vertex independently chooses a parent, many resulting directed graphs
contain cycles or fail to connect to the root, so those choices do not
form a tree bijection. Unlabeled isomorphism types are far fewer: already
at $n=6$ there are only six nonisomorphic trees. Neither shortcut equals
the labeled unrooted enumeration produced by Prüfer words.

graderFixtures.proofText: Smallest-leaf deletions on T record 2,2,4,4, and degrees match one plus those multiplicities. Decoding (3,1,3,1) produces edges 2-3, 1-4, 5-3, 1-3, 1-6, which re-encode to the same word. The Prüfer map is a bijection onto [n]^{n-2}, so there are n^{n-2} labeled trees and 1296 trees on [6]. Distinguishing a root gives the different count n^{n-1}; arbitrary parent functions also include non-trees.

The largest leaf of T is 6, adjacent to 4, so I delete 6 first and continue deleting largest remaining leaves. The Prüfer code is therefore a word beginning with 4, and I do not recompute from the smallest leaf.

There are 6^5 rooted labeled trees, so I report 6^5 as the unrooted count. Equivalently, after fixing a root I let every other vertex choose any parent and assume all 6^5 parent assignments are connected and acyclic. Alternatively only the six unlabeled shapes matter.

DM:010728.title: Hierholzer certifies an Euler trail that Hamiltonicity cannot replace
DM:010728.objective: Prove the exact Euler-trail degree-and-connectivity criterion, construct an explicit trail by a Hierholzer splice, and separate the certificate from Hamiltonian vertex-tour conditions.
DM:010728.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite undirected graph, loops forbidden, multiple edges permitted only if explicitly introduced. An Euler trail is a walk that uses every edge exactly once. An Euler circuit is a closed Euler trail.

1. Prove that $G$ has an Euler trail if and only if $G$ has exactly zero or two vertices of odd degree and every edge of $G$ lies in a single connected component. Identify the endpoints when there are two odd vertices. Deduce the Euler-circuit case as the substatement with zero odd vertices. Your necessity argument must use the handshaking lemma and the observation that an interior visit of a trail uses two incident edges.

2. Let $G_0$ have vertex set $\{u,v,x,y,z\}$ and edge set
   \[
   \{ux,\ uy,\ uz,\ vx,\ vy,\ vz,\ xy,\ yz,\ zx\}.
   \]
   Compute every degree, name the odd vertices, and decide whether $G_0$ has an Euler trail or an Euler circuit. Then execute the following Hierholzer audit. Start at $u$ and take the trail
   \[
   T_0:\quad u{-}x{-}v{-}y{-}u{-}z{-}v.
   \]
   List the unused edges, prove that $T_0$ is stuck, grow a closed trail of unused edges based at a $T_0$-vertex that still has unused incidence, and splice to produce an Euler trail of $G_0$. Write the spliced trail as an explicit nine-edge walk.

3. Let $H$ be the disjoint union of two triangles. Compute its degrees and the number of nontrivial components, and decide whether $H$ has an Euler circuit. Explain which hypothesis of part 1 fails.

4. A proposed argument says: '$G_0$ is connected and has minimum degree $3$, so Dirac's theorem supplies a Hamiltonian cycle, and that cycle is an Euler circuit.' Prove that this confuses vertex tours with edge tours. Exhibit a Hamiltonian cycle of $G_0$ that is not Eulerian, and exhibit the Euler trail of part 2, which repeats a vertex and therefore is not a Hamiltonian path. Do not treat Hamiltonian existence, Hall's theorem, or a vertex-cut obstruction as a substitute for the Euler criterion.
permittedResults: The handshaking lemma says that the number of odd-degree vertices is even, and that the sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges.
A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every degree is even, and an Euler trail if and only if it has exactly zero or two odd-degree vertices.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pair incidences along a hypothetical Euler trail for necessity, then run Hierholzer and the temporary-edge reduction for sufficiency, auditing T0 by listing unused edges.
First classify G0 by the degree criterion, construct any u-to-v Euler trail, and only afterwards match it to the prescribed splice of the unused triangle.

milestones.criterion: Proves the Euler-trail criterion in both directions, including the even-to-circuit reduction and the role of a single edge-component.
Computes the degrees of G0 and produces an explicit Hierholzer splice of T0 with the unused triangle, yielding a nine-edge u-to-v trail.
Shows that the two-triangle graph fails the criterion and that a Hamiltonian cycle of G0 is not an Euler tour.

commonErrors.description: Treats a Hamiltonian cycle or path as an Euler tour, or cites Dirac, Ore, Hall, or a vertex-cut obstruction in place of the Euler degree criterion.
commonErrors.consequence: A vertex-exhaustive tour is confused with an edge-exhaustive trail, which is the quantity the packet asks to certify.

commonErrors.description: Declares that zero or two odd vertices alone guarantee an Euler trail, or claims that the two-triangle graph H has an Euler circuit because every degree is even.
commonErrors.consequence: The single-edge-component hypothesis is dropped, so the criterion is applied to the wrong class of graphs.

hintTree.content: Inside an Euler trail every intermediate visit to a vertex pairs incoming and outgoing unused edges. Only the two endpoints can have leftover odd degree.
After $T_0$ the unused edges are exactly the triangle $xy,yz,zx$. Splice that triangle at $x$.
A Hamiltonian cycle in $G_0$ uses five edges and cannot be Eulerian. The Euler trail of part 2 revisits $x$.

DM:010728.canonicalSolution:
Necessity. Suppose $W$ is an Euler trail. Every edge lies on $W$, so the edges occupy a single connected component (isolated vertices elsewhere are harmless). At an interior occurrence of a vertex $a$ on $W$, the trail arrives on one unused edge and leaves on another, so those two incidences are paired. If $W$ is closed, every incidence is paired and every degree is even. If $W$ is open, the same pairing leaves exactly one unpaired incidence at each endpoint, so those two vertices are odd and every other vertex is even. Sufficiency. If every degree is even and all edges lie in one component $C$, start at any vertex of $C$ and grow a trail of unused edges until it is stuck. The stuck vertex must be the start: every other vertex of even degree can be left whenever it is entered. The resulting closed trail $T$ is an Euler circuit of $C$ once unused edges are exhausted; if some unused edge remains, connectivity of $C$ supplies a vertex of $T$ still incident to an unused edge, and a new unused closed trail based there may be spliced into $T$. Repeating yields an Euler circuit. If exactly two vertices $s,t$ are odd, add a temporary edge $st$, apply the even case, and delete $st$ from the resulting circuit to obtain an Euler trail from $s$ to $t$.
\[
\boxed{\text{Euler trail }\Leftrightarrow\text{ one edge-component and }0\text{ or }2\text{ odd vertices}}.
\]

In $G_0$ the degrees are $\deg u=\deg v=3$ and $\deg x=\deg y=\deg z=4$. Exactly two vertices are odd, namely $u$ and $v$, and $G_0$ is connected (every vertex meets $x$ or equals $x$). Hence $G_0$ has an Euler trail from $u$ to $v$ and no Euler circuit.

The prescribed trail $T_0=u{-}x{-}v{-}y{-}u{-}z{-}v$ uses the six edges $ux,xv,vy,yu,uz,zv$ and ends at $v$. The unused edges are $xy,yz,zx$. No unused edge is incident to $v$, so $T_0$ is stuck. Vertex $x$ lies on $T_0$ and is incident to the unused edges $xy$ and $zx$. The unused closed trail $x{-}y{-}z{-}x$ may therefore be spliced at the first visit to $x$, producing
\[
\boxed{u{-}x{-}y{-}z{-}x{-}v{-}y{-}u{-}z{-}v}.
\]
This walk uses each of the nine edges of $G_0$ once and runs from $u$ to $v$, as required.

The graph $H=C_3\cup C_3$ has six vertices of degree $2$ and two nontrivial components. Every degree is even, but the edges do not lie in one component, so $H$ has no Euler circuit (and no Euler trail). The failed hypothesis is the single-edge-component requirement.

Dirac's theorem, even if it applied, would produce a cycle through every vertex, not a trail through every edge. A Hamiltonian cycle of $G_0$ is
\[
u{-}x{-}v{-}y{-}z{-}u,
\]
which uses only five of the nine edges. The Euler trail displayed above revisits $x$ (and also $y,u,z$) and is therefore not a Hamiltonian path. Minimum degree $3$ on five vertices does meet Dirac's numerical hypothesis, which only underscores that a Hamiltonian certificate is the wrong kind of tour. Hall's theorem and vertex-cut obstructions likewise address matchings or spanning cycles, not edge-exhaustive trails.

graderFixtures.proofText: A graph has an Euler trail iff it has one edge-component and zero or two odd vertices. In G0 the degrees are 3,3,4,4,4, so a trail from u to v exists. After T0 the unused edges form the triangle on x,y,z; splicing x-y-z-x at x yields u-x-y-z-x-v-y-u-z-v. Two disjoint triangles have all even degrees but two edge-components, hence no Euler circuit. A five-cycle through the vertices of G0 uses only five edges.
G0 is connected with minimum degree 3, so Dirac's theorem gives a Hamiltonian cycle. That cycle visits every vertex and is therefore an Euler circuit. Hierholzer is unnecessary.
Every degree in H is even, so H has an Euler circuit. Connectedness is not required once the handshaking lemma is satisfied.

DM:010729.title: Four-sided faces make Euler's formula refuse a specified K_{3,3}
DM:010729.objective: Prove Euler's formula for connected plane graphs, derive the bipartite face-length bound, and use it to certify that a specified copy of K_{3,3} is nonplanar.
DM:010729.statement:
Let $K$ be the complete bipartite graph with parts
\[
A=\{a,b,c\},\qquad B=\{x,y,z\}
\]
and with all nine possible $A$--$B$ edges, and with no edge inside $A$ or inside $B$.

1. Prove Euler's formula for a connected plane graph: if $G$ is drawn in the plane without crossings, with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges, and $f$ faces including the unbounded face, then
   \[
   v-e+f=2.
   \]
   Induct on the number of faces. Identify the tree case $f=1$ as the base.

2. Suppose $G$ is a simple connected bipartite plane graph with at least three vertices. Prove that every facial walk has even length at least $4$, and deduce
   \[
   2e\ge 4f.
   \]
   Explain why the weaker simple-graph bound $2e\ge 3f$ is the one obtained from faces of length at least $3$, and why that weaker bound is the wrong hypothesis for a bipartite graph.

3. Compute $v$ and $e$ for the specified graph $K$. Assuming toward a contradiction that $K$ admits a plane embedding, compute the forced face count $f$ from Euler's formula and obtain a numerical contradiction with $2e\ge 4f$. Conclude that $K$ is nonplanar.

4. Show that the same arithmetic with $2e\ge 3f$ does not contradict Euler's count for this $K$. A drawing of $K$ in which some edges cross is not a plane embedding and cannot be used to compute $f$. Do not quote Kuratowski's theorem, and do not replace $K$ by $K_5$ or by an unspecified complete bipartite graph.
permittedResults: A tree on $v$ vertices has $v-1$ edges. A connected graph with $v$ vertices and $e$ edges has a cycle if and only if $e\ge v$.
Every cycle in a bipartite graph is even, so a bipartite graph contains no triangle.

acceptableStrategies.description: Induct on faces to get Euler, then handshake the facial walks at length 4 and plug in v=6, e=9.
Assume a plane embedding of the specified K, compute f from Euler first, and only then invoke the bipartite length hypothesis to reach 18>=20.

milestones.criterion: Proves Euler's formula for connected plane graphs by induction on faces, with the tree case f=1 as base.
Derives 2e>=4f from even facial walks of length at least 4 in a simple bipartite plane graph.
Computes f=5 for the specified K and obtains the 18>=20 contradiction, while recording that 2e>=3f does not obstruct.

commonErrors.description: Applies only the simple-graph inequality 2e>=3f to K, notes that 18>=15 is consistent, and either stops or incorrectly claims that this already proves nonplanarity.
commonErrors.consequence: The bipartite face-length hypothesis is never used, so the intended obstruction 18>=20 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Computes faces from a drawing of K that contains a crossing, or quotes Kuratowski's theorem, or replaces the specified K by K5, as a substitute for the Euler-and-bound arithmetic.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested plane-graph counting certificate for this K_{3,3} is never produced.

hintTree.content: If $f\ge 2$, some edge lies on the boundary of two faces. Delete it: $e$ and $f$ each drop by $1$, so $v-e+f$ is unchanged.
A simple bipartite facial walk cannot have length $1$ or $2$, and cannot have odd length, so its length is at least $4$. Summing over faces counts each edge twice.
For this $K$ one has $v=6$ and $e=9$, so Euler would force $f=5$. Then $4f=20$ exceeds $2e=18$.

DM:010729.canonicalSolution:
Let $G$ be a connected plane graph. Proceed by induction on $f$. If $f=1$, the complement of the drawing is connected, so $G$ contains no cycle and is therefore a tree. A tree satisfies $e=v-1$, hence $v-e+f=v-(v-1)+1=2$. Now suppose $f\ge 2$. Some edge $\varepsilon$ is incident to two distinct faces (otherwise the complement would be connected and $f$ would be $1$). The graph $G-\varepsilon$ is still connected and plane, with $e-1$ edges and $f-1$ faces. The inductive hypothesis gives $v-(e-1)+(f-1)=2$, which rearranges to $v-e+f=2$.
\[
\boxed{v-e+f=2\text{ for connected plane graphs}}.
\]

Now assume $G$ is additionally simple and bipartite, connected, and has
at least three vertices. A facial walk cannot have length $1$ because
there are no loops. A length-$2$ facial walk in a simple graph would have
to traverse the same bridge in both directions; for that to be the entire
facial boundary in a connected graph, both endpoints would have degree
$1$, forcing $G=K_2$, which the vertex hypothesis excludes. Thus every
facial walk has length at least $3$. Bipartiteness forces every closed
walk to have even length, so every facial walk has length at least $4$.
Summing face lengths therefore yields $\sum \ell(F)\ge 4f$. Each edge
contributes to exactly two face-ends (or twice to the same face), so
$\sum \ell(F)=2e$. Thus $2e\ge 4f$. The weaker inequality $2e\ge 3f$
is the same handshake under only the length-at-least-$3$ hypothesis; it
is valid here but strictly weaker than the available bipartite bound.

The specified graph $K$ has $v=|A|+|B|=6$ and $e=9$. If $K$ admitted a plane embedding, Euler would force
\[
f=e-v+2=9-6+2=5.
\]
The bipartite face bound would then require $2e\ge 4f$, i.e. $18\ge 20$, which is false. Therefore no plane embedding exists:
\[
\boxed{K\cong K_{3,3}\text{ is nonplanar}}.
\]
The weaker simple bound $2e\ge 3f$ would only claim $18\ge 15$, which is consistent with $f=5$ and supplies no contradiction. A drawing in which an $A$--$B$ edge crosses another is not a plane embedding: crossings are not vertices of $K$, and the complementary regions of such a drawing are not the faces of a plane graph isomorphic to $K$. Kuratowski's subdivision criterion is not needed; the Euler-and-face-count obstruction is self-contained for this specified $K$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Deleting a two-face edge preserves v-e+f, and a tree has f=1, so Euler gives v-e+f=2. Simple bipartite facial walks have even length at least 4, hence 2e>=4f. The specified K has v=6, e=9, so a plane embedding would force f=5 and 18>=20. The weaker 2e>=3f only yields 18>=15 and does not obstruct. A crossing is not a planar embedding.

K is simple, so 2e>=3f. With v=6 and e=9 Euler would give f=5 and 18>=15, which holds, and I conclude that the Euler method cannot prove nonplanarity. I do not use that every face would have to be even.

I draw K with one crossing in the middle and count six regions including the outer region. This drawing is a plane graph. Alternatively K contains a K_{3,3} subdivision so Kuratowski already finishes, or I switch to K5 where 2e>=3f works.

DM:010730.title: BFS two-coloring is the certificate that no odd cycle exists
DM:010730.objective: Prove that a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle, and produce an explicit BFS two-color certificate on a specified graph together with an odd-cycle obstruction on a specified non-bipartite graph.
DM:010730.statement:
A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be partitioned into two independent sets. Equivalently, the vertices admit a $2$-coloring in which every edge is bichromatic.

1. Prove that a graph $G$ is bipartite if and only if $G$ contains no odd cycle. For the forward direction, show that an odd cycle cannot be $2$-colored. For the converse, run breadth-first search independently in each connected component, color a vertex red or blue according to the parity of its BFS distance from the component root, and prove that a monochromatic edge would produce an odd closed walk and hence an odd cycle.

2. Let $G_0$ have vertex set $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$ and edge set
   \[
   \{1{-}2,\ 1{-}3,\ 2{-}4,\ 2{-}5,\ 3{-}5,\ 3{-}6,\ 4{-}7,\ 5{-}7,\ 6{-}7\}.
   \]
   Run BFS from vertex $1$. Record the layer of every vertex, the resulting $2$-coloring, and the two color classes. Verify every edge of $G_0$ against that coloring, and conclude that $G_0$ is bipartite. The certificate must be the BFS layering, not an unspecified greedy coloring.

3. Let $H$ be the $5$-cycle on vertices $\{p,q,r,s,t\}$ with edges $pq,qr,rs,st,tp$. Run BFS from $p$, record colors by layer parity, and exhibit the first monochromatic edge that BFS detects. Extract an explicit odd cycle (the whole vertex set of $H$ is acceptable) and conclude that $H$ is not bipartite.

4. Audit the claim '$G_0$ has no triangles, therefore $G_0$ is bipartite' and the claim '$H$ contains a cycle, therefore $H$ is not bipartite'. Identify the missing length hypothesis. Do not treat an even cycle as an obstruction, and do not replace the BFS certificate by a matching argument or by Hall's theorem.
permittedResults: A graph is bipartite if and only if it admits a $2$-coloring with no monochromatic edge, if and only if it contains no odd cycle.
In a BFS tree, every edge of the original graph joins vertices whose layers differ by at most $1$. A same-layer edge produces an odd closed walk through the rootward paths.

acceptableStrategies.description: Color each component by BFS parity and convert a monochromatic edge into an odd cycle through the two rootward paths.
Build the BFS tree of G0 first as a certificate, then treat H as a one-edge conflict in the same algorithm.

milestones.criterion: Proves that bipartiteness is equivalent to the absence of odd cycles, including the BFS-layer converse.
Produces the explicit BFS layers and color classes of G0 and checks every edge.
Exhibits the monochromatic BFS edge and the 5-cycle in H, and rejects triangle-freeness or mere cyclicity as characterizations.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that G0 is bipartite solely because it has no $3$-cycle, or states the characterization as 'bipartite iff triangle-free'.
commonErrors.consequence: Longer odd cycles are ignored, so the theorem and the H obstruction are both misstated.

commonErrors.description: Declares that the existence of any cycle, or of an even cycle, proves non-bipartiteness, or replaces the BFS certificate by Hall's theorem or a matching argument.
commonErrors.consequence: Even cycles, which are compatible with bipartiteness, are treated as obstructions, or the requested coloring certificate is never produced.

hintTree.content: If a monochromatic edge $ab$ appears in a BFS coloring, the two rootward paths plus $ab$ form a closed walk whose length is odd because $\operatorname{dist}(a)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(b)$ have the same parity.
From vertex $1$ the first layer of $G_0$ is $\{2,3\}$ and the second layer is $\{4,5,6\}$.
In $H$, BFS from $p$ colors $r$ and $s$ the same color, and $rs$ is an edge.

DM:010730.canonicalSolution:
If $G$ is bipartite with parts $X,Y$, then every edge runs between $X$ and $Y$, so every walk alternates parts. A cycle of odd length cannot return to its start after an odd number of steps, a contradiction. Thus a bipartite graph has no odd cycle.

Conversely, suppose $G$ has no odd cycle. It is enough to $2$-color each component. Fix a root $r$ in a component and color $v$ red or blue according as $\operatorname{dist}(r,v)$ is even or odd. Suppose an edge $ab$ is monochromatic. Then $\operatorname{dist}(r,a)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(r,b)$ have the same parity, so the closed walk that follows a shortest $r$--$a$ path, the edge $ab$, and a shortest $b$--$r$ path has odd length. A shortest odd closed walk is an odd cycle, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence the BFS coloring is proper and $G$ is bipartite.
\[
\boxed{G\text{ bipartite }\Leftrightarrow G\text{ has no odd cycle}}.
\]

BFS from $1$ in $G_0$ produces the layers
\[
L_0=\{1\},\qquad L_1=\{2,3\},\qquad L_2=\{4,5,6\},\qquad L_3=\{7\}.
\]
The coloring is red on even layers and blue on odd layers, so the color classes are
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Red}=\{1,4,5,6\},\qquad \operatorname{Blue}=\{2,3,7\}}.
\]
Checking edges: $1{-}2$, $1{-}3$ leave red for blue; $2{-}4$, $2{-}5$, $3{-}5$, $3{-}6$ leave blue for red; $4{-}7$, $5{-}7$, $6{-}7$ leave red for blue. There is no monochromatic edge, so $G_0$ is bipartite. (The same partition is the unique $2$-coloring up to swapping colors in this connected graph.)

BFS from $p$ in $H$ produces $L_0=\{p\}$, $L_1=\{q,t\}$, $L_2=\{r,s\}$. Thus $p$ is red, $q,t$ are blue, and $r,s$ are red. The edge $rs$ joins two red vertices. The closed walk $p{-}q{-}r{-}s{-}t{-}p$ has length $5$, and is already a cycle:
\[
\boxed{H\text{ has the odd cycle }pqrstp\text{ and is not bipartite}}.
\]

Absence of triangles in $G_0$ is true — every cycle of $G_0$ that one immediately writes has length $4$ or $6$ — but it is not a proof of bipartiteness: a graph can be triangle-free and still contain a $5$-cycle, as $H$ itself demonstrates. The correct length-free statement is that every cycle is even, equivalently that a BFS $2$-coloring exists. The mere existence of a cycle in $H$ is likewise insufficient: $G_0$ has even cycles and is bipartite. An even cycle is $2$-colorable. Hall's theorem certifies matchings, not bipartitions, and is not a substitute for the BFS certificate.

graderFixtures.proofText: BFS parity 2-colors a graph iff there is no odd cycle, because a monochromatic edge closes an odd walk. In G0 the layers from 1 are {1}, {2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7}, with red {1,4,5,6} and blue {2,3,7}, and every listed edge is bichromatic. In H the edge rs is monochromatic and pqrstp is a 5-cycle. Triangle-freeness is weaker than bipartiteness, and an even cycle is not an obstruction.

I checked that G0 has no 3-cycle. A graph with no triangles is bipartite, so G0 is bipartite and I do not need BFS layers. The same reasoning would say H is bipartite if I had not noticed its triangle, but H is a 5-cycle.

H has a cycle, so H is not bipartite. G0 also has cycles such as 1-2-5-3-1, so the same argument would say G0 is not bipartite. Alternatively Hall's theorem on some bipartition already decides the matter and BFS is unnecessary.

DM:010731.title: A Laplacian cofactor enumerates the weighted spanning trees
DM:010731.objective: Apply the Matrix-Tree theorem to an explicit four-vertex weighted graph, evaluate a Kirchhoff cofactor by determinant arithmetic, and independently list spanning trees with weight products that match the cofactor.
DM:010731.statement:
Let $W$ be the weighted graph with vertex set $\{a,b,c,d\}$ and with the five undirected edges
\[
ab\ \text{weight }2,\quad
ac\ \text{weight }1,\quad
bc\ \text{weight }3,\quad
bd\ \text{weight }1,\quad
cd\ \text{weight }2.
\]
There is no edge $ad$. The weight of a spanning tree is the product of the weights of its three edges. The Kirchhoff Laplacian $L$ is the $4\times 4$ matrix with $L_{ii}$ equal to the sum of weights incident to vertex $i$ and with $L_{ij}=-w_{ij}$ for $i\neq j$ (and $L_{ij}=0$ when $ij$ is not an edge).

1. Write $L$ explicitly, including the ordered basis $(a,b,c,d)$. Prove that every row of $L$ sums to $0$, and deduce $\det L=0$ without expanding a $4\times 4$ determinant.

2. Let $L^{(d)}$ be the principal minor obtained by deleting the row and column indexed by $d$. Compute $\det L^{(d)}$ by cofactor expansion (or by an equivalent $3\times 3$ method), recording every $2\times 2$ determinant that appears. State the Matrix-Tree theorem for weighted graphs and conclude the sum of spanning-tree weights of $W$.

3. Independently list every spanning tree of the underlying unweighted graph. There are $\binom{5}{3}=10$ three-edge subsets; exclude the two $3$-cycles. For each of the eight trees record the edge set and the weight product. Sum the eight products and confirm exact agreement with $\det L^{(d)}$.

4. Recompute any other principal $3\times 3$ cofactor, for example the minor deleting $a$, and verify that it equals the same integer. Do not replace $L$ by the adjacency matrix, do not report $\det L$ as the tree count, and do not report the unweighted enumeration $8$ as the value of the weighted Kirchhoff invariant.
permittedResults: Matrix-Tree theorem (weighted): every cofactor of $L$ equals $\sum_T\prod_{e\in T}w(e)$, the sum running over spanning trees $T$.
A connected graph on $4$ vertices has a spanning tree with exactly $3$ edges. A $3$-edge subgraph is a tree if and only if it is acyclic.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form L from weighted degrees, expand the d-minor by the first row, then classify the ten triples into two triangles and eight trees.
List the eight trees and sum their weight products first as a generating-function check, then confirm by an independent cofactor of L.

milestones.criterion: Writes the correct weighted Laplacian and explains det L=0 from the all-ones kernel.
Evaluates det L^{(d)}=39 by explicit 3x3 arithmetic and invokes the weighted Matrix-Tree theorem.
Lists the eight spanning trees with weight products summing to 39 and checks a second cofactor.

commonErrors.description: Computes the determinant of the adjacency matrix of W, or reports det L (which is zero) as the number or weight-sum of spanning trees.
commonErrors.consequence: The Kirchhoff cofactor is never evaluated, so the Matrix-Tree theorem is not applied.

commonErrors.description: Reports the unweighted enumeration 8 as the value of the weighted Kirchhoff invariant, or includes one or both triangles in the spanning-tree list and still claims agreement with the cofactor.
commonErrors.consequence: The weight products are discarded or a cyclic subgraph is treated as a tree, so the independent audit fails.

hintTree.content: The weighted degrees are $3,6,6,3$, and the only zero off-diagonal entries of $L$ are the $(a,d)$ and $(d,a)$ positions.
The minor deleting $d$ is $\begin{pmatrix}3&-2&-1\\-2&6&-3\\-1&-3&6\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant expands as $3\cdot 27+(-2)\cdot 15+(-1)\cdot 12$.
The two excluded triples are the triangle $abc$ and the triangle $bcd$. The eight remaining triples are the spanning trees.

DM:010731.canonicalSolution:
The incident weight sums are $\deg_w(a)=2+1=3$, $\deg_w(b)=2+3+1=6$, $\deg_w(c)=1+3+2=6$, and $\deg_w(d)=1+2=3$. Therefore
\[
L=\begin{pmatrix}
3&-2&-1&0\\
-2&6&-3&-1\\
-1&-3&6&-2\\
0&-1&-2&3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each row sums to $0$ because the diagonal records the total outgoing weight that the off-diagonal entries subtract. The all-ones vector is a kernel vector, so $\det L=0$.
\[
\boxed{L\text{ as displayed, }\det L=0}.
\]

Deleting the last row and column produces
\[
L^{(d)}=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2&-1\\-2&6&-3\\-1&-3&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding along the first row,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det\begin{pmatrix}6&-3\\-3&6\end{pmatrix}&=36-9=27,\\
\det\begin{pmatrix}-2&-3\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}&=-12-3=-15,\\
\det\begin{pmatrix}-2&6\\-1&-3\end{pmatrix}&=6+6=12,
\end{aligned}
\]
and the cofactors are $+27$, $-(-15)=15$, and $+12$. Hence
\[
\det L^{(d)}=3\cdot 27+(-2)\cdot 15+(-1)\cdot 12=81-30-12=39.
\]
The weighted Matrix-Tree theorem says that this cofactor equals the sum of spanning-tree weight products.
\[
\boxed{\det L^{(d)}=39}.
\]

The underlying simple graph has the five edges $ab,ac,bc,bd,cd$. The ten three-edge subsets include two cycles: $\{ab,ac,bc\}$ (triangle $abc$) and $\{bc,bd,cd\}$ (triangle $bcd$). The remaining eight subgraphs are spanning trees, with weight products
\begin{align*}
\{ab,ac,bd\}&=2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2,\\
\{ab,ac,cd\}&=2\cdot 1\cdot 2=4,\\
\{ab,bc,bd\}&=2\cdot 3\cdot 1=6,\\
\{ab,bc,cd\}&=2\cdot 3\cdot 2=12,\\
\{ab,bd,cd\}&=2\cdot 1\cdot 2=4,\\
\{ac,bc,bd\}&=1\cdot 3\cdot 1=3,\\
\{ac,bc,cd\}&=1\cdot 3\cdot 2=6,\\
\{ac,bd,cd\}&=1\cdot 1\cdot 2=2.
\end{align*}
The sum is $2+4+6+12+4+3+6+2=39$, matching the cofactor.

Deleting the first row and column instead produces
\[
L^{(a)}=\begin{pmatrix}6&-3&-1\\-3&6&-2\\-1&-2&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding along the first row,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det L^{(a)}
&=6\det\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}
-(-3)\det\begin{pmatrix}-3&-2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}
+(-1)\det\begin{pmatrix}-3&6\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}\\
&=6(18-4)+3\bigl((-9)-2\bigr)-1\bigl(6-(-6)\bigr)\\
&=6\cdot 14+3\cdot(-11)-12
=84-33-12=39.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two cofactors agree, as the theorem requires. The unweighted count of spanning trees is $8$, which would be the Kirchhoff number if every weight were $1$; it is not the value of $\det L^{(d)}$ for these weights. The adjacency determinant and $\det L=0$ are different invariants.

graderFixtures.proofText: L has diagonal 3,6,6,3 and row sums zero, so det L=0. The minor deleting d expands as 3*27-2*15-12=39. The eight trees have weight products 2,4,6,12,4,3,6,2, summing to 39, and the minor deleting a is also 39. The two excluded triples are the triangles abc and bcd.
The adjacency matrix of W has zeros on the diagonal and the five weights off-diagonal. Its determinant, or else det L=0, is the spanning-tree number. I do not form a principal minor of L.
There are eight spanning trees, so the Matrix-Tree value is 8. Weights may be ignored because they cancel in the ratio of cofactors, and I include {ab,ac,bc} as a spanning tree of weight 6.

DYN:010117.title: Cable x+2y=C with vx=3 and ax=-2 forces vy=-3/2 m/s and ay=1 m/s2
DYN:010117.objective: Differentiate an inextensible moving-pulley length constraint twice, preserve the signed sense of each coordinate, and recover the dependent velocity and acceleration of the movable block from the given free-end motion.
DYN:010117.statement:
An inextensible cable of fixed total length has one free end whose signed position is the coordinate $x$ and wraps a movable pulley whose signed position is the coordinate $y$. Both coordinates increase in the same absolute direction (downward from a fixed overhead support). The two vertical segments that support the movable pulley, together with the free end, give the holonomic constraint
\[
x+2y=C
\]
with $C$ a constant length. At the instant of interest
\[
v_x=\dot x=3\ \text{m/s},\qquad a_x=\ddot x=-2\ \text{m/s}^2.
\]
No polar basis, no contact-normal kinematics, and no rolling constraint is to be introduced.

1. Differentiate the length constraint once with respect to time. Solve for the signed velocity $v_y=\dot y$. State the units.

2. Differentiate a second time. Solve for the signed acceleration $a_y=\ddot y$. State the units.

3. Interpret both signs in the chosen coordinates: does the free end descend or ascend, and is the movable pulley rising or descending? Is the pulley speeding up or slowing down in that direction?

4. Show that the constant $C$ never appears in $\dot y$ or $\ddot y$, and that a first-derivative-only analysis cannot determine $a_y$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “two supporting segments imply $v_y=-2v_x$, so $v_y=-6$ m/s”; (ii) “the constraint fixes only the velocities, so the accelerations $a_x$ and $a_y$ may be assigned independently.”

Do not replace the cable by a polar-basis derivation, a curved-path contact condition, or an instantaneous center.
permittedResults: If $x+2y=C$ with $C$ constant, then $\dot x+2\dot y=0$ and $\ddot x+2\ddot y=0$ at every instant at which the coordinates are twice differentiable.
Signed differentiation preserves orientation: a positive $\dot x$ with $x+2y=C$ forces $\dot y=-\dot x/2$, so the movable pulley moves opposite the free end.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the stated length constraint once for velocity and once more for acceleration, then read the signs in the downward-positive frame.
Solve the linear relations vy=-vx/2 and ay=-ax/2 directly, then confirm that C is absent and that a first-derivative-only argument cannot produce ay.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates x+2y=C once and reports the signed velocity vy=-3/2 m/s.
Differentiates a second time and reports the signed acceleration ay=1 m/s2.
Interprets both signs and rejects an inverted segment count or independent accelerations.

commonErrors.description: Places the factor 2 on the free end, treating the constraint as 2x+y=C, and reports vy=-6 m/s and ay=4 m/s2.
commonErrors.consequence: The movable pulley is assigned four times the correct speed and the wrong acceleration, which is the kinematics of a different tackle arrangement.

commonErrors.description: Uses the first derivative to obtain a velocity but then treats ax and ay as unrelated, typically leaving ay undetermined or setting ay=ax=-2.
commonErrors.consequence: The second derivative of the length constraint is discarded, so the dependent acceleration of the pulley is lost.

hintTree.content: The factor $2$ multiplies $y$, not $x$. One time derivative is $\dot x+2\dot y=0$.
A second derivative is required for acceleration: $\ddot x+2\ddot y=0$, hence $a_y=-a_x/2$.
With $a_x=-2$ the second identity gives $a_y=1$. The first identity with $v_x=3$ gives $v_y=-3/2$.

DYN:010117.canonicalSolution:
The inextensible cable enforces
\[
x+2y=C
\]
at every instant. Differentiating once with respect to time yields
\[
\dot x+2\dot y=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
v_y=-\frac{v_x}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}\ \text{m/s}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{v_y=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
Differentiating a second time yields
\[
\ddot x+2\ddot y=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
a_y=-\frac{a_x}{2}=-\frac{-2}{2}=1\ \text{m/s}^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{a_y=1\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
In the chosen downward-positive coordinates, $v_x=3>0$ means the free end is descending, while $v_y=-3/2<0$ means the movable pulley is rising. The pulley’s upward velocity has magnitude $3/2$ m/s; $a_y=1>0$ is downward, so that upward motion is slowing. The constant $C$ cancels upon differentiation and cannot affect $\dot y$ or $\ddot y$. The numerical velocity equation at one instant does not determine $a_y$; differentiating the underlying position constraint a second time supplies the additional acceleration identity.

Sentence (i) is false: two supporting segments place the factor $2$ on $y$, so $v_y=-v_x/2=-3/2$, not $v_y=-2v_x=-6$. Sentence (ii) is false: the same constraint differentiated twice forces $a_y=-a_x/2$. The values $a_x=-2$ and $a_y=1$ are not independent.

No polar unit-vector derivation, no contact-normal $v\cdot n=0$ statement, and no instantaneous center is used. The only kinematic object is the twice-differentiated length constraint.

graderFixtures.proofText: From $x+2y=C$ I obtain $\dot x+2\dot y=0$ and $\ddot x+2\ddot y=0$. With $v_x=3$ and $a_x=-2$ this gives $v_y=-3/2$ m/s and $a_y=1$ m/s$^2$. The free end descends while the pulley rises and slows. The constant $C$ never enters.
Two segments support the pulley, so I write 2x+y=C. Then 2 vx+vy=0 and 2 ax+ay=0, hence vy=-6 m/s and ay=4 m/s2.
Differentiating once gives vy=-3/2 m/s. The constraint does not involve accelerations, so ay may be chosen freely; I take ay=ax=-2 m/s2.

DYN:010118.title: Collar absolute velocity is (5,0); five-term acceleration is (-1,17.5)
DYN:010118.objective: At the instant when a translating-and-rotating frame aligns with the fixed axes, assemble the three-term absolute velocity and the five-term absolute acceleration of a collar, naming every vector contribution and refusing a river-crossing reduction.
DYN:010118.statement:
A rigid frame with origin $O$ translates and rotates relative to a fixed Newtonian frame $XYZ$. A collar $P$ slides on a straight guide fixed in the moving frame. At one instant the moving unit vectors $(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$ coincide with $(\mathbf I,\mathbf J,\mathbf K)$, and the following quantities are known in those coinciding axes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v_O&=(1,-1,0)\ \text{m/s},&
\mathbf a_O&=(2,0,0)\ \text{m/s}^2,\\
\boldsymbol\omega&=2\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s},&
\boldsymbol\alpha&=3\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}^2,\\
\mathbf r_{P/O}&=\tfrac12\mathbf i\ \text{m},&
\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}&=4\mathbf i\ \text{m/s},&
\mathbf a_{\mathrm{rel}}&=-\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The relative velocity and acceleration are those of $P$ as observed in the moving frame.

1. Compute $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/O}$ and the absolute velocity
   \[
   \mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_O+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/O}+\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}.
   \]

2. Compute, as five separate vectors, the absolute-acceleration ingredients
   \[
   \mathbf a_O,\quad
   \boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/O},\quad
   \boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/O}),\quad
   2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}},\quad
   \mathbf a_{\mathrm{rel}}.
   \]
   Name them as the origin term, the angular-acceleration term, the centripetal term, the Coriolis term, and the relative term.

3. Sum the five vectors to obtain $\mathbf a_P$. Report components in m/s$^2$.

4. State why axis alignment at the instant permits componentwise addition, and why alignment does not drop the Coriolis or centripetal term.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “because the axes presently coincide, Coriolis acceleration vanishes”; (ii) “the motion is a river crossing, so $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_O+\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and the $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ term is omitted.”

Do not reduce the problem to a boat-and-current river crossing, do not derive a polar basis from $\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta$, and do not invoke an instantaneous center of zero velocity.
permittedResults: If $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r=r\mathbf i$, then $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=\omega r\mathbf j$ and $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)=-\omega^2 r\mathbf i$.

The Coriolis acceleration $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is present whenever the moving frame rotates and the particle has a nonzero velocity relative to that frame, including at an instant when the moving and fixed axes coincide.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the three-term velocity first, then compute the five acceleration cross products one at a time before adding.
Use the aligned-axis 2D rules omega k × (x i)=omega x j and k × j=-i to fill a term table, then sum columns.

milestones.criterion: Computes omega×r=(0,1) and the absolute velocity vP=(5,0) m/s.
Lists all five acceleration terms and sums them to aP=(-1,17.5) m/s2.
Keeps Coriolis and centripetal at the aligned instant and rejects a river-crossing two-term velocity.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Coriolis term 2 omega × v_rel because the moving and fixed axes coincide, reporting aP=(-1,1.5) m/s2.
commonErrors.consequence: The dominant 16 m/s2 contribution to a_y is lost, so the collar acceleration is wrong by (0,-16).

commonErrors.description: Treats the motion as a river crossing and writes vP=vO+v_rel=(5,-1) m/s, omitting omega × r.
commonErrors.consequence: The rotational transport of the position vector is discarded and the absolute velocity misses the +1 j contribution.

hintTree.content: $2\mathbf k\times\tfrac12\mathbf i=\mathbf j$, so $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=(0,1,0)$ and $\mathbf v_P=(1,-1,0)+(0,1,0)+(4,0,0)$.
$\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r=3\mathbf k\times\tfrac12\mathbf i=\tfrac32\mathbf j$. The centripetal term is $2\mathbf k\times\mathbf j=-2\mathbf i$.
Coriolis is $2\cdot 2\mathbf k\times 4\mathbf i=16\mathbf j$. Adding the five listed vectors produces $(-1,17.5,0)$.

DYN:010118.canonicalSolution:
At the given instant the moving and fixed axes coincide, so every listed vector may be added by components. The cross product is
\[
\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/O}
=2\mathbf k\times\tfrac12\mathbf i
=\mathbf j
=(0,1,0)\ \text{m/s}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbf v_P
=(1,-1,0)+(0,1,0)+(4,0,0)
=\boxed{(5,0,0)\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The five acceleration terms, all in m/s$^2$, are
\begin{align*}
\mathbf a_O&=(2,0,0),\\
\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/O}
&=3\mathbf k\times\tfrac12\mathbf i
=\tfrac32\mathbf j
=(0,1.5,0),\\
\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/O})
&=2\mathbf k\times\mathbf j
=-2\mathbf i
=(-2,0,0),\\
2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}
&=2\cdot 2\mathbf k\times 4\mathbf i
=16\mathbf j
=(0,16,0),\\
\mathbf a_{\mathrm{rel}}&=(-1,0,0).
\end{align*}
Their sum is
\[
\mathbf a_P
=(2-2-1,\ 0+1.5+16,\ 0)
=\boxed{(-1,17.5,0)\ \text{m/s}^2}
=\boxed{\Bigl(-1,\frac{35}{2},0\Bigr)\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
Axis alignment is only a convenience for reading components in a common basis. It does not set $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$ and does not set $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rel}}=\mathbf 0$, so neither the centripetal term nor the Coriolis term vanishes.

Sentence (i) is false: Coriolis is $16\mathbf j$ at this instant and is the dominant contribution to $a_y$. Sentence (ii) is false: a river-crossing superposition omits $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ and would report $\mathbf v_P=(5,-1,0)$ rather than $(5,0,0)$. The collar is not a boat in a current.

The calculation uses a translating-and-rotating rigid frame and a sliding collar. It does not derive $\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta$, does not use a contact normal, and does not locate an instantaneous center.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=(0,1)$ and $\mathbf v_P=(5,0)$ m/s. The five acceleration terms are $(2,0)$, $(0,1.5)$, $(-2,0)$, $(0,16)$, and $(-1,0)$, which sum to $\mathbf a_P=(-1,17.5)$ m/s$^2$. Alignment of axes does not drop Coriolis.
The axes coincide at this instant, so the Coriolis term is zero. The remaining terms (2,0)+(0,1.5)+(-2,0)+(-1,0) give aP=(-1,1.5) m/s2. Velocity is still (5,0).
This is a river-crossing superposition: vP=vO+v_rel=(1,-1)+(4,0)=(5,-1) m/s. I never form omega × r.
