DYN:010132.title: Helix r=(3cos2t,3sin2t,4t) has speed 2sqrt13; at t=0 the Frenet data are T=(0,3/sqrt13,2/sqrt13), N=(-1,0,0), B=(0,-2/sqrt13,3/sqrt13), kappa=3/13, tau=2/13, at=0, an=12
DYN:010132.objective: From a circular helix with a doubled angular argument, recover the constant speed, the Frenet triad at t=0, the curvature and torsion, and the tangential versus normal accelerations, without switching to a polar moving basis.
DYN:010132.statement:
A particle has the space curve
\[
\mathbf r(t)=\bigl(3\cos 2t,\ 3\sin 2t,\ 4t\bigr)\ \text{m},
\]
with $t$ in seconds. The path is a circular helix of cylinder radius $3$ m and constant rise rate $4$ m/s. Do not replace the parametrization by polar unit vectors $\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta$ in the $xy$-plane, and do not invoke an instantaneous center.

1. Differentiate once. Show that the speed is the constant $2\sqrt{13}$ m/s, keeping the chain-rule factor $2$ that multiplies the trigonometric terms.

2. At the instant $t=0$ form the unit tangent $\mathbf T=\dot{\mathbf r}/|\dot{\mathbf r}|$. Then form $\ddot{\mathbf r}$ and identify the principal normal $\mathbf N$ as the unit vector in the direction of $\ddot{\mathbf r}$ (the speed is constant). Complete the triad by $\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N$.

3. Compute the curvature $\kappa=|\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}|/|\dot{\mathbf r}|^3$ and the torsion $\tau=(\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r})\cdot\dddot{\mathbf r}/|\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}|^2$ at $t=0$.

4. Split the acceleration into tangential and normal parts $a_t=\mathrm{d}|\mathbf v|/\mathrm{d}t$ and $a_n=\kappa|\mathbf v|^2$. Report the units.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the angular argument is $t$, so $\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=(0,3,4)$ and the speed is $5$ m/s”; (ii) “$\mathbf N$ at $t=0$ is the cylindrical radial direction $+\mathbf i$, because that is the direction of $\mathbf r(0)$.”

Do not derive a polar basis from a rotating $\mathbf e_r$, do not treat the helix as a constrained curved-path contact problem, and do not locate an instantaneous center of zero velocity.
permittedResults: If $|\dot{\mathbf r}|$ is constant then the tangential acceleration vanishes and the normal acceleration equals $\kappa|\dot{\mathbf r}|^2$, which is also $|\ddot{\mathbf r}|$.
Differentiating $\cos 2t$ and $\sin 2t$ inserts a factor $2$ in the first derivative and a factor $4$ in the second; omitting that factor describes a different helix.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate three times, evaluate the speed as a constant, then insert t=0 into the Frenet and Serret formulae.
Use constancy of speed to read N from r̈ and a_t=0, compute κ from |r̈|/v², and finish τ from the scalar triple product.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the helix with the factor 2 and reports the constant speed 2sqrt13 m/s.
At t=0 reports T=(0,3/sqrt13,2/sqrt13), N=(-1,0,0), B=(0,-2/sqrt13,3/sqrt13), kappa=3/13, tau=2/13, at=0, and an=12.
Rejects a dropped chain-rule factor and rejects identifying N with the cylindrical radius +i.

commonErrors.description: Treats the angular argument as t rather than 2t, obtaining rdot(0)=(0,3,4), speed 5 m/s, and the inconsistent triad and curvature of that slower helix.
commonErrors.consequence: Every subsequent Frenet quantity belongs to a different curve; the reported speed, T, kappa, and an are all wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets N at t=0 equal to the cylindrical radius r/|r|=(+1,0,0) instead of the direction of r̈, and therefore reports B with the opposite sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The principal normal and binormal are reversed, so the oriented Frenet frame is left-handed relative to the acceleration.

hintTree.content: The first derivative is $\dot{\mathbf r}=(-6\sin 2t,\ 6\cos 2t,\ 4)$. Its Euclidean norm is $\sqrt{36+16}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}$.
At $t=0$, $\dot{\mathbf r}=(0,6,4)$ and $\ddot{\mathbf r}=(-12,0,0)$. The unit vectors are then immediate, and $\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N$.
The cross product $\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}$ at $t=0$ is $(0,-48,72)$. Its magnitude is $24\sqrt{13}$, so $\kappa=3/13$. One more derivative gives $\tau=2/13$.

DYN:010132.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the given helix, retaining the factor $2$ from the angular argument:
\[
\dot{\mathbf r}(t)=(-6\sin 2t,\ 6\cos 2t,\ 4)\ \text{m/s}.
\]
The speed is
\[
|\dot{\mathbf r}|=\sqrt{36\sin^2 2t+36\cos^2 2t+16}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}\ \text{m/s},
\]
a constant. Hence
\[
\boxed{|\mathbf v|=2\sqrt{13}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
A second derivative is
\[
\ddot{\mathbf r}(t)=(-12\cos 2t,\ -12\sin 2t,\ 0)\ \text{m/s}^2.
\]
At $t=0$,
\[
\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=(0,6,4),\qquad\ddot{\mathbf r}(0)=(-12,0,0).
\]
The Frenet vectors are
\[
\mathbf T=\frac{(0,6,4)}{2\sqrt{13}}=\boxed{\Bigl(0,\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\Bigr)},
\]
\[
\mathbf N=\frac{(-12,0,0)}{12}=\boxed{(-1,0,0)},
\]
\[
\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\boxed{\Bigl(0,-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\Bigr)}.
\]
The first cross product at this instant is
\[
\dot{\mathbf r}\times\ddot{\mathbf r}=(0,-48,72),
\]
with magnitude $24\sqrt{13}$. Therefore
\[
\kappa=\frac{24\sqrt{13}}{(2\sqrt{13})^3}=\frac{24\sqrt{13}}{104\sqrt{13}}=\boxed{\frac{3}{13}\ \text{m}^{-1}}.
\]
A third derivative is $\dddot{\mathbf r}=(24\sin 2t,\ -24\cos 2t,\ 0)$, so $\dddot{\mathbf r}(0)=(0,-24,0)$ and
\[
\tau=\frac{(0,-48,72)\cdot(0,-24,0)}{7488}=\frac{1152}{7488}=\boxed{\frac{2}{13}\ \text{m}^{-1}}.
\]
Because the speed is constant,
\[
a_t=\boxed{0},\qquad
a_n=\kappa|\mathbf v|^2=\frac{3}{13}\cdot 52=\boxed{12\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
The same $a_n$ equals $|\ddot{\mathbf r}(0)|=12$ m/s$^2$.

Sentence (i) is false: dropping the chain-rule factor $2$ produces $\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=(0,3,4)$ and speed $5$, which is a different curve. Sentence (ii) is false: $\mathbf r(0)=(3,0,0)$ points along $+\mathbf i$, but $\ddot{\mathbf r}(0)$ points along $-\mathbf i$, so $\mathbf N=(-1,0,0)$ and not $+\mathbf i$. Reversing $\mathbf N$ also reverses $\mathbf B$.

The calculation uses only the Frenet formulae of a space curve. It does not introduce $\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta$, a contact normal on a constraint, or an instantaneous center.

graderFixtures.proofText: From $\dot{\mathbf r}=(-6\sin 2t,6\cos 2t,4)$ the speed is the constant $2\sqrt{13}$ m/s. At $t=0$ I obtain $\mathbf T=(0,3/\sqrt{13},2/\sqrt{13})$, $\mathbf N=(-1,0,0)$, $\mathbf B=(0,-2/\sqrt{13},3/\sqrt{13})$, $\kappa=3/13$, $\tau=2/13$, $a_t=0$, and $a_n=12$ m/s$^2$.
I differentiate as if the angle were t, so rdot=( -3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4 ). At t=0 the speed is 5 m/s and T=(0,3/5,4/5). I keep N=(-1,0,0).
Speed 2sqrt13 is fine. At t=0 the position is (3,0,0), so N is the cylinder radius (+1,0,0) and B=T×N=(0,2/sqrt13,-3/sqrt13).

DYN:010133.title: Relative path (6-2t,-2+t) is closest at t=14/5 with offset (2/5,4/5), distance 2/sqrt5, and vanishing dot product
DYN:010133.objective: Form the relative position and the constant relative velocity of two particles on straight tracks, locate the unique closest-approach instant by orthogonality, and evaluate the minimum separation.
DYN:010133.statement:
Two particles move in the plane with the prescribed positions (meters, $t$ in seconds)
\[
\mathbf r_A(t)=(3t,\ t),\qquad
\mathbf r_B(t)=(6+t,\ -2+2t).
\]
Both paths are straight. The relative motion of $B$ as seen from $A$ is itself a straight line at constant velocity. Do not convert the problem into a river-crossing boat-and-current superposition, and do not introduce polar unit vectors.

1. Form the relative position $\mathbf r_{B/A}(t)=\mathbf r_B(t)-\mathbf r_A(t)$ and the relative velocity $\mathbf v_{B/A}=\dot{\mathbf r}_{B/A}$. Confirm that $\mathbf v_{B/A}$ is constant.

2. The closest approach occurs at the unique instant $t_*$ for which $\mathbf r_{B/A}(t_*)\cdot\mathbf v_{B/A}=0$ and $t_*$ is admitted by the motion (here every real $t$ is admitted). Solve for $t_*$.

3. Evaluate $\mathbf r_{B/A}(t_*)$ and the minimum distance $d_{\min}=|\mathbf r_{B/A}(t_*)|$. State the units.

4. Substitute $t_*$ back into the inner product and confirm that it is exactly zero.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “closest approach is the instant when the $x$-components coincide, so $6-2t=0$ and $t=3$”; (ii) “the particles meet if and only if each component of $\mathbf r_{B/A}$ can be set to zero separately.”

Do not reduce the geometry to a river-crossing relative-velocity diagram, do not use an instantaneous center, and do not replace the straight tracks by a constrained curved path.
permittedResults: For $\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf r_0+\mathbf v t$ with $\mathbf v$ constant and nonzero, the time of closest approach to the origin is $t_*=-(\mathbf r_0\cdot\mathbf v)/|\mathbf v|^2$.
Two particles on straight tracks need not collide: the componentwise system $\mathbf r_{B/A}(t)=\mathbf 0$ may be inconsistent even though a positive minimum distance exists.

acceptableStrategies.description: Subtract the two affine laws, impose orthogonality of relative position and relative velocity, then evaluate the remaining vector and its length.
Minimize |r_{B/A}|^2 by an ordinary derivative, which produces the same linear equation 5t=14, then back-substitute.

milestones.criterion: Forms the relative law (6-2t,-2+t) with constant velocity (-2,1) m/s.
Solves r·v=0 to t*=14/5 s and reports r(t*)=(2/5,4/5) m with dmin=2/sqrt5 m and a checked zero inner product.
Rejects a single-component zero at t=3 and rejects treating the inconsistent meeting system as a collision.

commonErrors.description: Declares closest approach when the relative x-component vanishes, taking t=3 s and reporting a minimum distance of 1 m.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported instant is not stationary for the separation, so both the time and the distance are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets both components of the relative position to zero, obtains the inconsistent pair t=3 and t=2, and concludes that the particles collide or that no closest-approach time exists.
commonErrors.consequence: A perfectly well-defined positive minimum distance is discarded because a collision was demanded.

hintTree.content: Subtract the position laws: $\mathbf r_{B/A}=(6-2t,\ -2+t)$ and $\mathbf v_{B/A}=(-2,1)$.
The orthogonality condition is $(6-2t)(-2)+(-2+t)(1)=0$, which simplifies to $5t=14$.
At $t=14/5$ the relative position is $(2/5,4/5)$ and its length is $2/\sqrt{5}$.

DYN:010133.canonicalSolution:
The relative position is
\[
\mathbf r_{B/A}(t)
=(6+t-3t,\ -2+2t-t)
=\boxed{(6-2t,\ -2+t)}\ \text{m}.
\]
Differentiating gives the constant relative velocity
\[
\mathbf v_{B/A}=\boxed{(-2,1)}\ \text{m/s}.
\]
Closest approach requires
\[
\mathbf r_{B/A}(t)\cdot\mathbf v_{B/A}=0,
\]
that is
\[
(6-2t)(-2)+(-2+t)(1)=0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
-12+4t-2+t=0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
5t=14.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{t_*=\dfrac{14}{5}\ \text{s}}.
\]
The relative position at that instant is
\[
\mathbf r_{B/A}\Bigl(\frac{14}{5}\Bigr)
=\Bigl(6-\frac{28}{5},\ -2+\frac{14}{5}\Bigr)
=\boxed{\Bigl(\frac{2}{5},\frac{4}{5}\Bigr)}\ \text{m},
\]
and the minimum distance is
\[
d_{\min}
=\sqrt{\frac{4}{25}+\frac{16}{25}}
=\sqrt{\frac{20}{25}}
=\boxed{\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\ \text{m}}.
\]
The inner product at $t_*$ is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{2}{5}\Bigr)(-2)+\Bigl(\frac{4}{5}\Bigr)(1)
=-\frac{4}{5}+\frac{4}{5}
=\boxed{0},
\]
which confirms orthogonality.

Sentence (i) is false: setting only the $x$-component to zero gives $t=3$, at which $\mathbf r_{B/A}=(0,1)$ and the inner product is $1\ne 0$, so the particles are still closing or opening. Sentence (ii) is false: the pair $6-2t=0$ and $-2+t=0$ demands $t=3$ and $t=2$ simultaneously and has no solution; the particles never meet.

The construction uses only the relative straight-line geometry of two particles. It is not a river-crossing current problem, not a polar-basis derivation, and not a constrained curved-path exercise.

graderFixtures.proofText: The relative position is $(6-2t,-2+t)$ with velocity $(-2,1)$. Orthogonality gives $t_*=14/5$ s, $\mathbf r=(2/5,4/5)$ m, $d_{\min}=2/\sqrt{5}$ m, and $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v=0$.
Closest approach is when the x-coordinates match, so 6-2t=0 and t=3 s. Then r_rel=(0,1) and dmin=1 m.
Set both components to zero: 6-2t=0 and -2+t=0. These require t=3 and t=2, so the particles collide at no consistent time and I report no closest-approach instant.

DYN:010134.title: Parabola r=(10t,10t-5t^2) reenters y=x/2 at (10,5); plane travel is 5sqrt5, v=(10,0) splits as 4sqrt5 and -2sqrt5 on (2,1)/sqrt5 and (-1,2)/sqrt5
DYN:010134.objective: Find the first positive intersection of a projectile parabola with the plane y=x/2, measure distance along that plane from the origin, and resolve the impact velocity onto the plane tangent and normal.
DYN:010134.statement:
A projectile leaves the origin with the Cartesian law (meters, $t$ in seconds)
\[
\mathbf r(t)=\bigl(10t,\ 10t-5t^2\bigr).
\]
A fixed plane through the origin has equation $y=x/2$. The particle starts on the plane at $t=0$ and later strikes the same plane again. Gravity is already built into the given parametrization; do not replace the flight by a particle constrained to a curved guide, and do not introduce polar unit vectors.

1. Impose $y(t)=x(t)/2$ and find every real root. Identify the first positive impact time $t_1$ and the impact point $\mathbf r(t_1)$.

2. The path distance of interest is the straight-line distance along the plane from the origin to $\mathbf r(t_1)$, not the arc length of the parabola. Compute that distance.

3. Differentiate to obtain $\mathbf v(t)$ and evaluate $\mathbf v(t_1)$. Confirm that its Euclidean speed is $10$ m/s.

4. An orthonormal pair adapted to the plane is
   \[
   \mathbf e_t=\frac{(2,1)}{\sqrt{5}},\qquad
   \mathbf e_n=\frac{(-1,2)}{\sqrt{5}},
   \]
   with $\mathbf e_t$ pointing up the plane and $\mathbf e_n$ pointing to the side of increasing $y-x/2$. Resolve $\mathbf v(t_1)$ onto this pair.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the particle hits the horizontal ground $y=0$ at $t=2$, so that is the reentry of interest”; (ii) “because $\mathbf v(t_1)$ is horizontal, the tangent and normal components on the plane are $10$ and $0$.”

Do not treat the plane as a constrained curved-path contact during the flight, do not invoke restitution or an impact law, and do not derive a polar basis.
permittedResults: Substituting a linear target $y=x/2$ into a quadratic flight law produces a quadratic in $t$ with a root at launch; the remaining positive root is the reentry time.
If $\mathbf v=(v,0)$ and $\mathbf e_t=(2,1)/\sqrt{5}$, $\mathbf e_n=(-1,2)/\sqrt{5}$, then $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_t=2v/\sqrt{5}$ and $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_n=-v/\sqrt{5}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the scalar plane condition first, then compute the chord along the plane and the two inner products at that instant.
Factor t out of the impact equation to separate launch from reentry, evaluate r and v at t=1, and project onto the supplied orthonormal pair.

milestones.criterion: Finds the positive plane intersection t1=1 s at the point (10,5) m and the along-plane distance 5sqrt5 m.
Reports v(1)=(10,0) m/s, speed 10 m/s, and the plane components 4sqrt5 and -2sqrt5 m/s.
Rejects replacing the plane by y=0 and rejects treating a horizontal velocity as purely tangential to y=x/2.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the target plane y=x/2 by the horizontal y=0, reports the later root t=2 s and the point (20,0), and measures distance 20 m.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported impact is not on the given plane, so the point, the path distance, and every subsequent component are attached to the wrong event.

commonErrors.description: Observes that v(1)=(10,0) is horizontal and assigns the full speed 10 m/s to the plane tangent with a zero normal component.
commonErrors.consequence: The decomposition ignores the slope of y=x/2, so both reported components are wrong by construction.

hintTree.content: The impact condition $10t-5t^2=(10t)/2$ rearranges to $5t-5t^2=0$, so $t=0$ or $t=1$.
At $t=1$ the point is $(10,5)$ and the planar distance from the origin is $\sqrt{100+25}=5\sqrt{5}$.
The velocity is $(10,10-10t)$, hence $(10,0)$ at $t=1$. Inner products against the given pair are $4\sqrt{5}$ and $-2\sqrt{5}$.

DYN:010134.canonicalSolution:
The plane condition is $10t-5t^2=5t$, or
\[
5t-5t^2=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 5t(1-t)=0.
\]
The roots are $t=0$ (launch) and the first positive reentry
\[
\boxed{t_1=1\ \text{s}}.
\]
The impact point is
\[
\mathbf r(1)=(10,\ 10-5)=\boxed{(10,5)\ \text{m}},
\]
which lies on $y=x/2$. Distance along the plane from the origin is the Euclidean length of that point,
\[
\boxed{5\sqrt{5}\ \text{m}}.
\]
The velocity is
\[
\mathbf v(t)=(10,\ 10-10t)\ \text{m/s},
\]
so
\[
\mathbf v(1)=\boxed{(10,0)\ \text{m/s}},\qquad
|\mathbf v(1)|=\boxed{10\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The given plane basis yields
\[
\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_t
=10\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}
=\boxed{4\sqrt{5}\ \text{m/s}},
\qquad
\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_n
=10\cdot\frac{-1}{\sqrt{5}}
=\boxed{-2\sqrt{5}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
These components reconstruct the speed:
\[
\bigl(4\sqrt{5}\bigr)^2+\bigl(-2\sqrt{5}\bigr)^2=80+20=100.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $y=0$ occurs at $t=2$ with point $(20,0)$, which is not on $y=x/2$ except at the origin. Sentence (ii) is false: a horizontal velocity is not aligned with $\mathbf e_t=(2,1)/\sqrt{5}$, so both plane components are nonzero.

The flight is an unconstrained parabola that merely intersects a line. No curved-guide constraint, no restitution, and no polar basis is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The plane condition gives $t_1=1$ s and the point $(10,5)$ m. Distance along the plane is $5\sqrt{5}$ m. Then $\mathbf v=(10,0)$ m/s, $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_t=4\sqrt{5}$ m/s, $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf e_n=-2\sqrt{5}$ m/s, and the speed is $10$ m/s.
Reentry means the projectile hits the ground y=0. Then 10t-5t^2=0 so t=2 s, the point is (20,0), and the travel is 20 m. I still write v=(10,0).
I agree the hit is t=1 at (10,5) with v=(10,0). Because that velocity is horizontal it is already tangent to the plane, so the components are 10 m/s and 0.

DYN:010219.title: B descends; a=g(2-sqrt3)/14 and T=3g(12+sqrt3)/14 after a motion audit
DYN:010219.objective: Write Newton’s laws for a hanging block connected to a kinetically sliding block on a 30-degree incline, audit which sense of motion is consistent with kinetic friction, and solve for the common acceleration and the cable tension.
DYN:010219.statement:
Block $A$ of mass $m_A=4$ kg is in contact with a fixed plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The connected assembly is released from rest. For this idealized onset problem there is no separate static-friction branch: as motion begins, the contact immediately follows the kinetic law with coefficient $\mu_k=1/4$. Determine which candidate onset direction is dynamically consistent. An inextensible cable, parallel to the plane at $A$, passes over a small ideal pulley and supports a hanging block $B$ of mass $m_B=3$ kg. The cable tension is $T$ and the common initial acceleration magnitude is $a\ge 0$. Take $g$ as a positive scalar and keep every answer exact in terms of $g$. Both blocks are particles; the pulley is massless and frictionless.

1. Draw the free-body diagram of $A$. Compute the exact normal $N_A$ and the kinetic friction magnitude $f_k=\mu_k N_A$.

2. Compare the hanging weight $m_B g$ with the downhill capacity $m_A g\sin 30^\circ+f_k$ of block $A$. Decide which block descends, and state the sense of $f_k$ on $A$.

3. Write Newton’s second law for each block in the consistent sense, solve for $a$ and $T$, and record the units implied by $g$.

4. Substitute the solved pair back into both block equations.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “assume $A$ slides down the plane; friction then acts up the plane, and that sense may be kept without a consistency check”; (ii) “the normal on $A$ is $m_A g$, so $f_k=g$.”

Do not treat the contact as a curved-path constraint, do not introduce a coefficient of restitution or an external impulse, and do not replace kinetic friction by a rolling-without-slip capacity.
permittedResults: Along an inextensible cable over an ideal pulley the two particles share one tension $T$ and one acceleration magnitude $a$.
If $m_B g>m_A g\sin\theta+\mu_k m_A g\cos\theta$, then $B$ descends and $A$ slides up the plane, so friction on $A$ acts down the plane.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare mB g with mA g sinθ+fk to fix the sense, then write the two Newton equations and add them to eliminate T.
Write both candidate orientations, keep only the one whose solved a is positive, and finish T from the hanging-block equation.

milestones.criterion: Computes NA=2sqrt(3) g and fk=sqrt(3) g/2 and audits that B descends.
Solves the consistent system to a=g(2-sqrt(3))/14 and T=3g(12+sqrt(3))/14.
Substitutes back and rejects both an unaudited A-down sense and a missing cosine in the normal.

commonErrors.description: Orients friction up the plane and writes the A-descends / B-ascends Newton pair without a consistency check, obtaining a negative acceleration while still claiming that A descends.
commonErrors.consequence: The kinetic-friction arrow is opposite the true slip, so both a and T belong to an impossible motion.

commonErrors.description: Takes the normal on A as mA g rather than mA g cos 30°, producing fk=g and then a=0, T=3g in the B-descends system.
commonErrors.consequence: The friction force is too large by the factor 2/sqrt(3), and the blocks are incorrectly predicted to remain at rest.

hintTree.content: $N_A=4g\cos 30^\circ=2\sqrt{3}\,g$ and $f_k=(1/4)N_A=\sqrt{3}\,g/2$.
$m_B g=3g$ exceeds $2g+\sqrt{3}\,g/2$, so $B$ descends and friction on $A$ acts down the plane.
The pair $3g-T=3a$ and $T-2g-\sqrt{3}\,g/2=4a$ adds to $g-\sqrt{3}\,g/2=7a$.

DYN:010219.canonicalSolution:
The acceleration of $A$ is parallel to the plane, so
\[
N_A=m_A g\cos 30^\circ=4g\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\boxed{2\sqrt{3}\,g},
\]
and
\[
f_k=\mu_k N_A=\frac14\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\,g=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,g}.
\]
The downhill resisting capacity of $A$ (weight component plus kinetic friction) is
\[
m_A g\sin 30^\circ+f_k=2g+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}g.
\]
Compare with the hanging weight:
\[
m_B g=3g
>2g+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}g,
\]
because $3>2+\sqrt{3}/2$. Therefore $B$ descends, $A$ slides up the plane, and $f_k$ on $A$ acts down the plane.

Newton’s laws in that consistent sense are
\begin{align*}
m_B g-T&=m_B a,\\
T-m_A g\sin 30^\circ-f_k&=m_A a,
\end{align*}
that is
\[
3g-T=3a,\qquad T-2g-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}g=4a.
\]
Adding eliminates $T$:
\[
g-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}g=7a
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
a=\frac{g\bigl(1-\sqrt{3}/2\bigr)}{7}
=\boxed{\frac{g(2-\sqrt{3})}{14}}.
\]
Then
\[
T=3g-3a
=3g\Bigl(1-\frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{14}\Bigr)
=3g\cdot\frac{12+\sqrt{3}}{14}
=\boxed{\frac{3g(12+\sqrt{3})}{14}}.
\]
Both $a$ and $T$ are positive. Substitution recovers the two left-hand sides: $3g-T=3a$ and $T-2g-\sqrt{3}\,g/2=4a$.

Sentence (i) is false. The $A$-descends orientation produces
\[
2g-T-f_k=4a,\qquad T-3g=3a,
\]
which collapses to $a=-g(2+\sqrt{3})/14<0$ and therefore rejects that sense. Sentence (ii) is false: omitting $\cos 30^\circ$ gives the wrong normal $N_A=4g$ and $f_k=g$, after which the consistent $B$-descends system forces $a=0$.

The model is two particles, an ideal cable, and kinetic Coulomb friction on a straight incline. It is not a curved-path contact problem, not an impact with restitution, and not a rolling-friction capacity check.

graderFixtures.proofText: The normal is $N_A=2\sqrt{3}\,g$ and $f_k=\sqrt{3}\,g/2$. Because $3g>2g+\sqrt{3}\,g/2$, block $B$ descends. The consistent solution is $a=g(2-\sqrt{3})/14$ and $T=3g(12+\sqrt{3})/14$.
I assume A slides down, so friction acts up the plane. Then 2g-T-fk=4a and T-3g=3a, which give a=-g(2+sqrt(3))/14. I still report that A descends.
I take NA=mA g=4g, so fk=g. With B descending, 3g-T=3a and T-2g-g=4a, hence a=0 and T=3g.

DYN:010220.title: At t=1 the polar force is -10 e_r+8 e_theta N; the slot supplies the 8 N
DYN:010220.objective: Evaluate prescribed polar kinematics of a particle in a smooth rotating slot, convert the radial and transverse accelerations into force components, and identify the transverse slot reaction versus the prescribed radial actuator.
DYN:010220.statement:
A particle of mass $m=2$ kg is guided in a smooth radial slot that rotates about a fixed origin in the plane. The prescribed motion, with $t$ in seconds, $r$ in meters, and $\theta$ in radians, is
\[
r(t)=1+\frac{t^2}{2},\qquad \theta(t)=2t.
\]
The polar acceleration formulae
\[
a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2,\qquad
a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta
\]
may be used as known identities; do not derive the polar basis.

1. At the instant $t=1$ s compute the exact values of $r$, $\dot r$, $\ddot r$, $\dot\theta$, and $\ddot\theta$. Confirm
   \[
   (r,\dot r,\ddot r)=\bigl(1.5,\ 1,\ 1\bigr)
   \]
   in SI units.

2. Evaluate $a_r$ and $a_\theta$ at $t=1$ s.

3. Form the force $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ in the polar basis $\{\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta\}$ and state the unit.

4. The slot is smooth, so it cannot exert a radial friction force. Identify which polar component is the transverse slot reaction and which is the prescribed radial actuator force.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$a_r$ is simply $\ddot r$, because $r(t)$ is prescribed”; (ii) “$a_\theta$ reduces to $r\ddot\theta$, so the transverse force vanishes when $\ddot\theta=0$.”

Do not derive $\mathbf e_r$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$ from scratch, do not replace the slot by a curved-path contact normal, and do not introduce restitution or an impulsive reaction.
permittedResults: Newton’s second law in a polar basis is $F_r=m a_r$ and $F_\theta=m a_\theta$, with the standard polar acceleration components.
If $\theta(t)=\omega_0 t$ with $\omega_0$ constant, then $\ddot\theta=0$ but $a_\theta=2\dot r\dot\theta$ remains in general nonzero (the Coriolis term).

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate r(t) and theta(t), substitute into the two polar acceleration identities, then multiply by m and split the components by the smooth-slot idealization.
Compute the four kinematic scalars (rdot, rddot, thetadot, thetaddot) first, fill a two-row table for (ar, atheta), and only then interpret Fr versus Ftheta.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the prescribed polar state (r,rdot,rddot)=(1.5,1,1) with thetadot=2 and thetaddot=0 at t=1.
Computes ar=-5, atheta=4, and F=-10 er+8 etheta N, identifying the 8 N slot reaction and the -10 N actuator.
Rejects dropping the centripetal term from ar and dropping the Coriolis term from atheta.

commonErrors.description: Takes ar as rddot=1 because r(t) is prescribed, omitting -r thetadot^2, and reports F=2 er+8 etheta N.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial actuator is assigned the wrong sign and the wrong magnitude; the particle would not follow r=1+t^2/2.

commonErrors.description: Takes atheta as r thetaddot=0 because thetaddot=0, omitting 2 rdot thetadot, and reports a vanishing slot reaction.
commonErrors.consequence: The transverse force required to rotate with the slot is lost, so the smooth-slot reaction is reported as 0 N instead of 8 N.

hintTree.content: At $t=1$, $r=1+1/2=3/2$, $\dot r=t=1$, $\ddot r=1$, $\dot\theta=2$, and $\ddot\theta=0$.
Multiply by $m=2$ to obtain $\mathbf F=-10\mathbf e_r+8\mathbf e_\theta$. The $8$ N is the smooth-slot reaction.

DYN:010220.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the prescriptions:
\[
\dot r=t,\qquad \ddot r=1,\qquad \dot\theta=2,\qquad \ddot\theta=0.
\]
At $t=1$ s,
\[
r=1+\frac12=\frac32,\qquad
\dot r=1,\qquad
\ddot r=1,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{(r,\dot r,\ddot r)=\bigl(1.5,\ 1,\ 1\bigr)}
\]
in meters and seconds, together with $\dot\theta=2$ rad/s and $\ddot\theta=0$. The polar accelerations are
\[
a_r
=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2
=1-\frac32\cdot 4
=1-6
=\boxed{-5\ \text{m/s}^2},
\]
\[
a_\theta
=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta
=0+2\cdot 1\cdot 2
=\boxed{4\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
Newton’s second law with $m=2$ kg then gives
\[
\mathbf F
=m(a_r\mathbf e_r+a_\theta\mathbf e_\theta)
=\boxed{-10\,\mathbf e_r+8\,\mathbf e_\theta\ \text{N}}.
\]
Because the slot is smooth and radial, it supplies only the transverse reaction
\[
N_\theta=F_\theta=\boxed{8\ \text{N}},
\]
while the prescribed radial motion is enforced by an actuator
\[
F_r^{\mathrm{act}}=\boxed{-10\ \text{N}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: the centripetal term $-r\dot\theta^2=-6$ m/s$^2$ is present even though $r(t)$ is prescribed, and dropping it yields the wrong radial force $+2$ N. Sentence (ii) is false: $\ddot\theta=0$ does not kill $a_\theta$; the Coriolis term $2\dot r\dot\theta=4$ m/s$^2$ remains, and the slot reaction is $8$ N, not $0$.

The polar identities are used, not re-derived. The particle is not on a curved constraint with a single contact normal, and no impulse appears.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $t=1$ I obtain $(r,\dot r,\ddot r)=(1.5,1,1)$, $a_r=-5$ m/s$^2$, $a_\theta=4$ m/s$^2$, and $\mathbf F=-10\mathbf e_r+8\mathbf e_\theta$ N. The smooth slot supplies the $8$ N transverse reaction; the radial actuator supplies $-10$ N.
Because r(t) is prescribed I take ar=rddot=1. Then F=2 er+8 etheta N, with the slot still supplying 8 N.
Because thetaddot=0 I take atheta=r thetaddot=0. Then F=-10 er and the smooth-slot reaction is 0 N. The actuator is still -10 N.

DYN:010235.title: Conical pendulum m=2, L=2, g=10, theta=60 deg has radius sqrt3, T=40 N, speed sqrt30, rate sqrt10, period 2pi/sqrt10
DYN:010235.objective: For a particle flying a horizontal circle at a fixed angle from the vertical, resolve the string tension into vertical support and inward centripetal force, then recover the speed, the angular rate, and the period.
DYN:010235.statement:
A particle of mass $m=2$ kg is attached to a light inextensible string of length $L=2$ m whose other end is fixed. The particle travels in a horizontal circle at a constant angle $\theta=60^\circ$ from the downward vertical. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The string remains taut. Do not replace the motion by a bead on a rotating hoop, do not introduce kinetic friction on an incline, and do not derive polar unit vectors from scratch.

1. Compute the radius of the horizontal circle from the fixed length and the given angle.

2. Resolve Newton’s second law in the vertical direction and in the horizontal inward direction. Solve for the string tension $T$.

3. From the horizontal law recover the orbital speed $v$ and the angular rate $\omega=v/r$. Then form the period $2\pi/\omega$.

4. Check that the three kinematic quantities are consistent with $v=\omega r$ and with the centripetal requirement $T\sin\theta=mv^2/r$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the vertical balance is $T\sin\theta=mg$ because $60^\circ$ is already a large angle”; (ii) “the circling radius is the full string length $L=2$ m.”

Do not treat the string as a rotating-slot constraint, do not introduce restitution, and do not convert the problem into a forced oscillator.
permittedResults: Vertical equilibrium of a conical pendulum is $T\cos\theta=mg$. The companion horizontal law is $T\sin\theta=mv^2/r=m\omega^2 r$.
Dividing the two Newton statements eliminates $T$ and yields $\omega^2=g\tan\theta/r\cdot\sin\theta=g/(L\cos\theta)$, hence $\omega=\sqrt{g/(L\cos\theta)}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the two Newton components with cosθ on the vertical, solve T first, then recover v from the horizontal statement.
Use ω=sqrt(g/(L cosθ)) after reading r=L sinθ, then form v=ωr and T=mg/cosθ.

milestones.criterion: Computes the circling radius r=L sinθ=sqrt3 m.
Solves T=40 N, v=sqrt30 m/s, omega=sqrt10 rad/s, and period 2pi/sqrt10 s.
Rejects writing T sinθ=mg and rejects taking the radius as L=2 m.

commonErrors.description: Writes the vertical balance as T sinθ=mg because the angle is 60° from the vertical, obtaining T=40/sqrt3 N and a correspondingly wrong speed.
commonErrors.consequence: Sine and cosine are assigned to the wrong directions, so the tension and every rate derived from it are inconsistent with zero vertical acceleration.

commonErrors.description: Takes the horizontal radius as the full string length L=2 m instead of L sinθ, then computes the speed from T sinθ=mv^2/L.
commonErrors.consequence: The centripetal term uses the wrong lever, so v and ω no longer match the cone geometry.

hintTree.content: The radius is $L\sin 60^\circ=2\cdot\sqrt{3}/2=\sqrt{3}$ m.
Vertical balance $T\cos 60^\circ=mg$ is $T/2=20$, so $T=40$ N.
Then $T\sin 60^\circ=20\sqrt{3}=2v^2/\sqrt{3}$ gives $v^2=30$. The rate is $v/r=\sqrt{10}$.

DYN:010235.canonicalSolution:
The horizontal radius is
\[
r=L\sin 60^\circ=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\boxed{\sqrt{3}\ \text{m}}.
\]
With upward positive, vanishing vertical acceleration gives
\[
T\cos 60^\circ=mg\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{T}{2}=2\cdot 10=20\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{T=40\ \text{N}}.
\]
The inward horizontal law is
\[
T\sin 60^\circ=\frac{mv^2}{r},
\]
so
\[
40\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{2v^2}{\sqrt{3}}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
20\sqrt{3}=\frac{2v^2}{\sqrt{3}}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
v^2=30.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{v=\sqrt{30}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The angular rate and period are
\[
\omega=\frac{v}{r}=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{3}}=\boxed{\sqrt{10}\ \text{rad/s}},
\qquad
\tau=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\boxed{\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{10}}\ \text{s}}.
\]
Consistency checks: $\omega r=\sqrt{10}\cdot\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{30}=v$, and $m\omega^2 r=2\cdot 10\cdot\sqrt{3}=20\sqrt{3}=T\sin 60^\circ$. The same rate follows from $\omega=\sqrt{g/(L\cos\theta)}=\sqrt{10/(2\cdot 1/2)}=\sqrt{10}$.

Sentence (i) is false: $\sin\theta$ multiplies the horizontal (centripetal) statement; using $T\sin\theta=mg$ yields $T=40/\sqrt{3}$ N and an inconsistent vertical residual. Sentence (ii) is false: the circling radius is $L\sin\theta=\sqrt{3}$ m, not the string length $2$ m. Using $r=2$ understates the centripetal acceleration and produces the wrong speed.

The model is a single taut string and a particle in uniform horizontal circular motion. It is not a hoop constraint, not an incline-friction pair, and not a polar-basis derivation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The radius is $L\sin 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ m. Vertical balance gives $T=40$ N. Then $v=\sqrt{30}$ m/s, $\omega=\sqrt{10}$ rad/s, and the period is $2\pi/\sqrt{10}$ s.
At 60 degrees from the vertical I write T sin60=mg, so T*sqrt3/2=20 and T=40/sqrt3 N. The radius is still sqrt3 m.
Tension is T=40 N from T cos60=mg. I take the circling radius as the string length 2 m, so 40*sqrt3/2=2 v^2/2 and v^2=20sqrt3.

DYN:010236.title: Hoop R=2, Omega=sqrt10, g=10 holds a bead at cosθ=1/2 from downward; radius sqrt3, centripetal 10sqrt3, reaction 20 from 10sqrt3 inward and 10 up
DYN:010236.objective: Locate the nontrivial relative equilibrium of a smooth bead on a hoop that spins about its vertical diameter, then assemble the inertial centripetal demand and the hoop reaction that meets both that demand and the particle weight.
DYN:010236.statement:
A smooth circular hoop of radius $R=2$ m rotates at the constant rate $\Omega=\sqrt{10}$ rad/s about its fixed vertical diameter. A bead of mass $m=1$ kg can slide without friction on the hoop. Measure the polar angle $\theta$ from the downward vertical (so $\theta=0$ is the bottom of the hoop). Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. Seek a relative equilibrium $\dot\theta=\ddot\theta=0$ with $\theta\in(0,\pi)$. Do not replace the hoop by a conical pendulum on a string, do not introduce rolling friction, and do not treat the motion as a free rigid disk.

1. In the rotating frame the effective potential of the bead is
   \[
   V(\theta)=-mgR\cos\theta-\tfrac12 m\Omega^2 R^2\sin^2\theta.
   \]
   Stationary points satisfy $V'(\theta)=0$. Show that either $\sin\theta=0$ or
   \[
   \cos\theta=\frac{g}{\Omega^2 R}.
   \]
   Evaluate the nontrivial cosine and the corresponding $\theta\in(0,\pi)$.

2. Compute the horizontal distance from the axis of rotation to the bead at that angle.

3. The inertial motion at relative rest is uniform circular motion of that horizontal radius at rate $\Omega$. Compute the inward centripetal acceleration $\Omega^2\rho$.

4. A smooth hoop can exert only a force along the hoop radius (from the bead toward the hoop center, or the opposite). Find the reaction components in the horizontal-inward and upward directions, then the magnitude of the reaction.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the equilibrium cosine is $\Omega^2 R/g$, so $\cos\theta=2$ and the only rest point is the bottom”; (ii) “the hoop reaction equals the centripetal requirement alone, so it is $10\sqrt{3}$ N inward with no vertical part.”

Do not convert the constraint into a taut string of fixed free length, do not apply an impact law, and do not analyze rolling of the hoop itself.
permittedResults: If $V(\theta)=-mgR\cos\theta-\frac12 m\Omega^2 R^2\sin^2\theta$, then $V'(\theta)=mgR\sin\theta-m\Omega^2 R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, so the interior equilibria obey $\cos\theta=g/(\Omega^2 R)$ whenever that value lies in $(-1,1)$.

At polar angle $\theta$ from the bottom, the unit vector from the bead toward the hoop center is $(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta)$ in a horizontal-outward / upward basis. A force of magnitude $S$ along that direction has inward horizontal part $S\sin\theta$ and upward part $S\cos\theta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Stationarize the given effective potential for θ, then reconstruct the inertial circular motion and the unique radial reaction that matches both Newton components.
Write Newton’s laws in the inertial description (known horizontal circle plus zero vertical acceleration) and enforce that the contact force lies along the hoop radius.

milestones.criterion: Obtains the interior equilibrium cosθ=1/2 and θ=π/3 from the downward vertical.
Reports horizontal radius sqrt3 m, inward centripetal demand 10sqrt3 N, and reaction components 10sqrt3 N inward plus 10 N up with magnitude 20 N.
Rejects the inverted cosine Ω²R/g and rejects dropping the vertical part of the reaction.

commonErrors.description: Writes the interior condition as cosθ=Ω²R/g=2, declares that no such angle exists, and keeps only the bottom rest point θ=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The nontrivial relative equilibrium at θ=π/3 is discarded, so the radius, centripetal demand, and reaction are never formed.

commonErrors.description: Takes the hoop reaction to be exactly the centripetal requirement 10sqrt3 N inward, with no upward component and with magnitude 10sqrt3 N.
commonErrors.consequence: The bead’s weight is left unbalanced, which is incompatible with a constant-height relative equilibrium.

hintTree.content: The interior stationarity condition is $\cos\theta=g/(\Omega^2 R)=10/(10\cdot 2)=1/2$, so $\theta=\pi/3$.
The horizontal radius is $R\sin\theta=2\cdot\sqrt{3}/2=\sqrt{3}$ m, and $\Omega^2\rho=10\sqrt{3}$ m/s$^2$.
A reaction of $20$ N toward the hoop center splits as $20\sin(\pi/3)=10\sqrt{3}$ N inward and $20\cos(\pi/3)=10$ N upward.

DYN:010236.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the stated effective potential:
\[
V'(\theta)=mgR\sin\theta-m\Omega^2 R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta
=mR\sin\theta\bigl(g-\Omega^2 R\cos\theta\bigr).
\]
Vanishing of the derivative gives $\sin\theta=0$ or
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{g}{\Omega^2 R}=\frac{10}{10\cdot 2}=\boxed{\dfrac12}.
\]
The interior angle in $(0,\pi)$ is
\[
\boxed{\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}}.
\]
The horizontal radius from the axis is
\[
\rho=R\sin\theta=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\boxed{\sqrt{3}\ \text{m}}.
\]
Uniform circular motion of that radius at rate $\Omega$ has inward centripetal acceleration
\[
\Omega^2\rho=10\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}^2,
\]
so the inward force demand on the unit mass is
\[
\boxed{10\sqrt{3}\ \text{N inward}}.
\]
Vertical acceleration is zero, so the hoop must also supply $mg=10$ N upward. The unique force along the hoop radius that meets both components is directed from the bead toward the hoop center. Its magnitude $S$ satisfies
\[
S\sin\theta=10\sqrt{3},\qquad S\cos\theta=10,
\]
and both statements give
\[
S=\boxed{20\ \text{N}}.
\]
The reaction components are therefore
\[
\boxed{10\sqrt{3}\ \text{N inward and }10\ \text{N upward}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: inverting the cosine formula produces $\Omega^2 R/g=2$, which is not a cosine and would incorrectly discard the interior rest point. Sentence (ii) is false: omitting the vertical support leaves an unbalanced weight, so the particle could not have $\ddot z=0$. The magnitude would then be $10\sqrt{3}$ N rather than $20$ N.

The model is a smooth particle constraint on a spinning wire. It is not a free string conical pendulum, not a rolling-friction capacity check, and not a free-disk kinetics problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: Stationarity gives $\cos\theta=1/2$ and $\theta=\pi/3$. The horizontal radius is $\sqrt{3}$ m and the inward centripetal demand is $10\sqrt{3}$ N. The hoop reaction is $10\sqrt{3}$ N inward and $10$ N upward, with magnitude $20$ N.
I set cosθ=Ω² R/g=2, which is impossible, so the only relative equilibrium is the bottom θ=0. There is no interior radius to report.
I agree θ=π/3 and the inward demand is 10sqrt3 N. The hoop reaction is that centripetal force alone, magnitude 10sqrt3 N, with no upward part.

DYN:010237.title: Frictionless bank tanθ=3/4 yields N=25 N and v=5sqrt6 m/s
DYN:010237.objective: Resolve the single contact normal on a frictionless banked horizontal circle, recover the unique design speed from the bank angle, and refuse both a rest-incline normal and a flat-curve speed.
DYN:010237.statement:
A particle of mass $m=2$ kg travels at constant speed on a fixed, frictionless track that is a horizontal circle of radius $R=20$ m. The track is banked at a constant angle $\theta$ satisfying
\[
\tan\theta=\frac34,
\]
so the associated right triangle has
\[
\sin\theta=\frac35,\qquad\cos\theta=\frac45.
\]
Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The only contact force is the normal $N$ directed up the bank, perpendicular to the track surface. There is no friction, no path-tangent drive, and no rolling contact.

1. Write Newton’s second law in the vertical direction and in the horizontal radial (centripetal) direction. Use $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ as given.

2. Solve the vertical statement for $N$. State the unit.

3. Substitute that $N$ into the radial statement and solve for $v^2$, then for the positive speed $v$. State the units.

4. Explain, from the two scalar equations, why a frictionless bank admits only this one speed: any other $v$ would require a second tangential-in-the-section force that is not present.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the particle sits on a plane of angle $\theta$, so $N=mg\cos\theta$ as in statics on a fixed incline”; (ii) “every frictionless circle has $v^2=gR$, bank or no bank.”

Do not replace the banked circle by a signed path-tangent and path-normal decomposition of a general space curve, do not introduce a kinetic-friction arrow, and do not convert the contact into a rolling-without-slip capacity check.
permittedResults: If a particle of mass $m$ moves at constant speed on a frictionless bank of angle $\theta$, then $N\cos\theta=mg$ and $N\sin\theta=mv^2/R$, hence $N=mg/\cos\theta$ and $v^2=Rg\tan\theta$.
The rest-incline identity $N=mg\cos\theta$ applies only when the acceleration has no component into the plane. It is not the normal law on a banked horizontal circle.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the vertical statement for N first, then feed that N into the radial statement for v^2.
Form tanθ=v^2/(Rg) directly from the two Newton components and insert R=20, g=10, tanθ=3/4, then recover N=mg/cosθ as a check.

milestones.criterion: Resolves N cosθ=mg and N sinθ=mv^2/R and reports N=25 N.
Reports v^2=150 and v=5sqrt6 m/s and states that this is the only frictionless speed.
Rejects the rest-incline normal N=mg cosθ and the unsupported bank-independent identity v^2=gR.

commonErrors.description: Takes the normal as the rest-incline value N=mg cosθ=16 N and then builds a speed from that wrong contact force.
commonErrors.consequence: The vertical balance N cosθ=mg is inverted, so both the contact force and the design speed belong to a different problem.

commonErrors.description: Ignores the bank and writes the unsupported claim v^2=gR=200, typically with N=mg=20 N.
commonErrors.consequence: The horizontal component of the normal is discarded, so the unique frictionless speed 5sqrt6 m/s is lost.

hintTree.content: Vertical: $N\cos\theta=mg$. With $\cos\theta=4/5$, $m=2$, and $g=10$ this fixes $N$ at once.
Radial: $N\sin\theta=mv^2/R$. Insert $N=25$ and $\sin\theta=3/5$ to obtain $v^2$.
$v^2=Rg\tan\theta=20\cdot 10\cdot 3/4=150$, so $v=5\sqrt{6}$. Only this speed keeps friction at zero.

DYN:010237.canonicalSolution:
The bank angle is given through the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle
\[
\sin\theta=\frac35,\qquad\cos\theta=\frac45,\qquad\tan\theta=\frac34.
\]
With no friction the free-body diagram contains only the weight $mg$ and the normal $N$. Vertical Newton is
\[
N\cos\theta=mg\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
N=\frac{mg}{\cos\theta}=\frac{2\cdot 10}{4/5}=20\cdot\frac54
=\boxed{25\ \text{N}}.
\]
Horizontal Newton, toward the center of the circle, is
\[
N\sin\theta=\frac{mv^2}{R}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
v^2=\frac{NR\sin\theta}{m}=\frac{25\cdot 20\cdot(3/5)}{2}=150.
\]
The same $v^2$ follows from the compact identity
\[
v^2=Rg\tan\theta=20\cdot 10\cdot\frac34=150.
\]
The positive speed is
\[
v=\sqrt{150}=\boxed{5\sqrt{6}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The two scalar statements determine the pair $(N,v)$ uniquely. If the speed differed from $5\sqrt{6}$ m/s, the required radial force would no longer match $N\sin\theta$ while $N$ was still fixed by the vertical balance, and a frictional component in the bank section would have to appear. That component is identically zero here, so this is the only admissible speed.

Sentence (i) is false: $N=mg\cos\theta=16$ N is the rest-incline formula and contradicts $N\cos\theta=mg$. Sentence (ii) is false: $v^2=gR=200$ is an unsupported bank-independent claim. It ignores $\tan\theta$ and fails the two component equations for this frictionless bank.

The model is a particle on a frictionless banked horizontal circle. It is not a general signed curved-path resolution, not a kinetic-friction incline, and not a rolling-contact capacity check.

graderFixtures.proofText: Vertical balance gives $N=mg/\cos\theta=25$ N. Then $v^2=Rg\tan\theta=150$ and $v=5\sqrt{6}$ m/s. A frictionless bank admits only this speed; any other $v$ would require a frictional component that is absent.
The surface is a plane at angle θ, so N=mg cosθ=16 N. Then N sinθ=mv^2/R gives v^2=96 and v=4sqrt6 m/s.
Frictionless circular motion always has v^2=gR=200, so v=10sqrt2 m/s. I take N=mg=20 N and never use tanθ.

DYN:010321.title: Elevator shaft output is 40.68 kW; supplied input at eta=0.8 is 50.85 kW
DYN:010321.objective: Obtain the cable tension of an upward-accelerating elevator from Newton’s law, convert tension and speed into mechanical shaft output power, and divide by the given efficiency to recover the supplied input power.
DYN:010321.statement:
A loaded elevator of mass $m=1200$ kg is being hoisted by a single vertical cable. At the instant of interest the elevator has upward velocity $v=3$ m/s and upward acceleration $a=1.5$ m/s$^2$. Take $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$. The hoisting machine has overall efficiency $\eta=0.8$, defined as the ratio of mechanical shaft output power to supplied input power. The cable, drum, and sheaves are otherwise ideal.

1. Write Newton’s second law for the elevator, with upward positive, and solve for the cable tension $T$.

2. The mechanical shaft output is the instantaneous power delivered by the tension through the cable speed, $P_{\mathrm{out}}=Tv$. Compute $P_{\mathrm{out}}$ in watts and in kilowatts.

3. The supplied input power is $P_{\mathrm{in}}=P_{\mathrm{out}}/\eta$. Compute $P_{\mathrm{in}}$ in watts and in kilowatts.

4. Distinguish, in one sentence each, the mechanical output $P_{\mathrm{out}}$ from the supplied input $P_{\mathrm{in}}$, and state why $P_{\mathrm{out}}$ is not equal to $mgv$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “power is weight times speed, so $P_{\mathrm{out}}=mgv$”; (ii) “efficiency multiplies the mechanical output, so $P_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta P_{\mathrm{out}}$.”

Do not replace the power balance by a forced-harmonic oscillator, do not introduce an impulsive tension, and do not treat the elevator as a rolling rigid body.
permittedResults: For a particle hoisted vertically with upward acceleration $a$, the tension satisfies $T-mg=ma$, hence $T=m(g+a)$.
If a force $\mathbf F$ acts on a particle of velocity $\mathbf v$, the instantaneous power of that force is $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve T=m(g+a) first, form P_out=T v, then divide by eta to recover the supplied input.
Keep symbolic T=m(g+a) through the power step, so P_out=m(g+a)v and P_in=m(g+a)v/eta, then insert the four numbers once.

milestones.criterion: Obtains the cable tension T=m(g+a)=13560 N from the upward Newton law.
Reports shaft output Tv=40680 W=40.68 kW and supplied input 50850 W=50.85 kW.
Distinguishes mechanical output from supplied input and rejects both P=mgv and P_in=eta P_out.

commonErrors.description: Takes mechanical output as the weight power mg v=35280 W, omitting the ma contribution to the tension.
commonErrors.consequence: The shaft output and the subsequent input are both too small, as if the elevator were not accelerating.

commonErrors.description: Forms the supplied input as eta times the mechanical output, reporting P_in=0.8*40680=32544 W.
commonErrors.consequence: The input is predicted to be smaller than the output, which inverts the definition of a lossy machine.

hintTree.content: Upward positive: $T-1200\cdot 9.8=1200\cdot 1.5$, so $T=1200\cdot 11.3$.
Mechanical output is $T v$, not $mgv$. With $T=13560$ N and $v=3$ m/s the product is $40680$ W.
Input is output divided by $\eta=0.8$, which is $50850$ W.

DYN:010321.canonicalSolution:
Upward is positive. Newton’s second law on the elevator is
\[
T-mg=ma\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
T=m(g+a)=1200(9.8+1.5)=1200\cdot 11.3
=\boxed{13560\ \text{N}}.
\]
The mechanical shaft output is the power of the tension at the present cable speed,
\[
P_{\mathrm{out}}=Tv=13560\cdot 3
=\boxed{40680\ \text{W}}
=\boxed{40.68\ \text{kW}}.
\]
The supplied input must cover that output at efficiency $\eta=0.8$,
\[
P_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{out}}}{\eta}
=\frac{40680}{0.8}
=\boxed{50850\ \text{W}}
=\boxed{50.85\ \text{kW}}.
\]
$P_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the mechanical power the drum must deliver to the cable. $P_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the larger power that must be supplied to the machine so that, after dissipative losses, the shaft still produces $P_{\mathrm{out}}$. The weight power $mgv$ equals $Tv$ only in the special case $a=0$; here $a=1.5$ m/s$^2$, so $T>mg$ and $P_{\mathrm{out}}>mgv$.

Sentence (i) is false: $mgv=1200\cdot 9.8\cdot 3=35280$ W is not the shaft output, because the cable must also produce the unbalanced force $ma$. Sentence (ii) is false: multiplying by $\eta$ would report an input $32544$ W smaller than the output, which inverts the definition of efficiency.

The balance is a particle Newton law plus an instantaneous power identity. It is not a forced harmonic oscillator, not an impact, and not a rolling-contact power loss.

graderFixtures.proofText: Newton gives $T=1200(9.8+1.5)=13560$ N. Shaft output is $Tv=40680$ W $=40.68$ kW. Supplied input is $40680/0.8=50850$ W $=50.85$ kW. Output is mechanical; input is the larger supplied power.
Power is weight times speed, so P_out=mg v=1200*9.8*3=35280 W=35.28 kW. Then P_in=35280/0.8=44100 W. I still take T=13560 N.
Tension and shaft output are T=13560 N and P_out=40680 W. Efficiency multiplies the output, so P_in=0.8*40680=32544 W=32.544 kW.

DYN:010322.title: The impulse (12,8) N s sends vf to (6,5/3) m/s and does 152/3 J of work
DYN:010322.objective: Integrate a polynomial force to a vector impulse, convert the impulse into final momentum and velocity, form the time-average force, and prove that the work equals the kinetic-energy change 152/3 J.
DYN:010322.statement:
A particle of mass $m=3$ kg moves in a fixed right-handed $xy$-frame. At the instant $t=0$ its velocity is
\[
\mathbf v_0=(2,-1)\ \text{m/s}.
\]
For $0\le t\le 2$ s the only force on the particle is the polynomial
\[
\mathbf F(t)=(6t,3t^2)\ \text{N}.
\]

1. Compute the linear impulse $\mathbf J=\int_0^2\mathbf F(t)\,dt$ exactly, with units.

2. Apply the linear impulse–momentum principle to obtain the final momentum $\mathbf p_f$ and the final velocity $\mathbf v_f$ at $t=2$ s.

3. Form the time-average force $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{avg}}=\mathbf J/\Delta t$ on the same interval.

4. Compute the initial and final kinetic energies $K_i$ and $K_f$. Prove that the work of $\mathbf F$ on $[0,2]$ equals $\Delta K=K_f-K_i$ in two ways: (i) by the work–energy principle, and (ii) by constructing $\mathbf v(t)$ from $\mathbf a=\mathbf F/m$ and evaluating $\int_0^2\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “impulse–momentum is $\mathbf v_f=\mathbf v_0+\mathbf J$, because mass appears only in the kinetic energy”; (ii) “the work done by $\mathbf F$ is the final kinetic energy $349/6$ J.”

Do not introduce a polar basis, a curved-path contact force, a coefficient of restitution, or a harmonic oscillator. The particle is free of impacts.
permittedResults: Linear impulse–momentum for a particle: $\mathbf J=\mathbf p_f-\mathbf p_i=m\mathbf v_f-m\mathbf v_i$.
Work–energy for a particle: $W=\Delta K=K_f-K_i$, where $K=\frac12 m\|\mathbf v\|^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate F first, add the impulse to m v0, then evaluate both kinetic energies and their difference.
Construct v(t) from a=F/m immediately, read vf at t=2, and obtain the work only as the definite integral of F·v.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the polynomial force to J=(12,8) N s and converts impulse–momentum into pf=(18,5) and vf=(6,5/3).
Reports Favg=(6,4) N, Ki=15/2 J, Kf=349/6 J, and W=DeltaK=152/3 J, confirmed by integrating F·v.
Rejects omitting the mass from impulse–momentum and rejects identifying work with the final kinetic energy.

commonErrors.description: Treats impulse–momentum as vf=v0+J, reporting vf=(14,7) m/s and a momentum that is not m vf.
commonErrors.consequence: The final state is dimensionally and numerically inconsistent with the integrated impulse of a 3 kg particle.

commonErrors.description: Reports the work of F as the final kinetic energy 349/6 J rather than the change Kf-Ki=152/3 J.
commonErrors.consequence: The work–energy principle is misstated and the numerical work is too large by the missing initial kinetic energy 15/2 J.

hintTree.content: Componentwise, $\int_0^2 6t\,dt=3t^2\big|_0^2=12$ and $\int_0^2 3t^2\,dt=t^3\big|_0^2=8$.
The initial momentum is $m\mathbf v_0=(6,-3)$. Adding $\mathbf J$ produces $\mathbf p_f$, then divide by $m=3$.
After $\mathbf a=(2t,t^2)$, integrate once: $\mathbf v(t)=(2+t^2,-1+t^3/3)$. Then $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=12t+6t^3-3t^2+t^5$.

DYN:010322.canonicalSolution:
The impulse is
\[
\mathbf J
=\int_0^2(6t,3t^2)\,dt
=\bigl(3t^2,t^3\bigr)\Big|_0^2
=\boxed{(12,8)\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}}.
\]
The initial momentum is $\mathbf p_i=m\mathbf v_0=3(2,-1)=(6,-3)$ kg m/s. Impulse–momentum gives
\[
\mathbf p_f=\mathbf p_i+\mathbf J=(6,-3)+(12,8)=\boxed{(18,5)\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}},
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbf v_f=\frac{\mathbf p_f}{m}=\boxed{\Bigl(6,\frac53\Bigr)\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The duration is $\Delta t=2$ s, so the time-average force is
\[
\mathbf F_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathbf J}{2}=\boxed{(6,4)\ \text{N}}.
\]
The kinetic energies are
\[
K_i=\frac12\cdot 3\cdot\bigl(2^2+(-1)^2\bigr)=\boxed{\frac{15}{2}\ \text{J}}
\]
and
\[
K_f=\frac12\cdot 3\cdot\Bigl(6^2+\Bigl(\frac53\Bigr)^2\Bigr)
=\frac32\Bigl(36+\frac{25}{9}\Bigr)
=\frac32\cdot\frac{349}{9}
=\boxed{\frac{349}{6}\ \text{J}}.
\]
Work–energy therefore yields
\[
W=\Delta K=\frac{349}{6}-\frac{15}{2}=\frac{349}{6}-\frac{45}{6}=\boxed{\frac{152}{3}\ \text{J}}.
\]
To confirm by a line integral, note $\mathbf a=\mathbf F/m=(2t,t^2)$, so
\[
\mathbf v(t)=\mathbf v_0+\int_0^t\mathbf a(s)\,ds=(2+t^2,-1+t^3/3).
\]
At $t=2$ this recovers $\mathbf v_f=(6,5/3)$. The integrand is
\[
\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=6t(2+t^2)+3t^2\bigl(-1+t^3/3\bigr)=12t+6t^3-3t^2+t^5,
\]
and
\[
\int_0^2(12t+6t^3-3t^2+t^5)\,dt
=\bigl(6t^2+\tfrac32 t^4-t^3+\tfrac16 t^6\bigr)\Big|_0^2
=24+24-8+\frac{32}{3}
=\frac{152}{3}\ \text{J}.
\]
The two computations of the work agree.

Sentence (i) is false: omitting the mass produces $\mathbf v_f=\mathbf v_0+\mathbf J=(14,7)$, which is not a velocity consistent with $\mathbf p_f=(18,5)$. Sentence (ii) is false: work equals the change $K_f-K_i$, not the final kinetic energy alone.

The construction never uses a polar basis, a contact normal, restitution, or a restoring oscillator.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\mathbf J=(12,8)$ N s, $\mathbf p_f=(18,5)$ kg m/s, $\mathbf v_f=(6,5/3)$ m/s, and $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{avg}}=(6,4)$ N. Then $K_i=15/2$ J, $K_f=349/6$ J, and $W=\Delta K=152/3$ J, matching $\int\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$.
Impulse–momentum is vf=v0+J, so vf=(2,-1)+(12,8)=(14,7) m/s. I treat that vector as the final velocity of the 3 kg particle.
I have J=(12,8), vf=(6,5/3), and Kf=349/6 J. The work done by F is the final kinetic energy, so W=349/6 J.

DYN:010323.title: The force 6x^2 does 16 J of work; the final power is 24sqrt17 W
DYN:010323.objective: Integrate a position-dependent force to obtain the work and the final speed, construct the potential with the datum U(0)=0, and evaluate the instantaneous power at the end of the interval.
DYN:010323.statement:
A particle of mass $m=2$ kg is constrained to the $x$-axis. It starts at $x=0$ with speed $v_0=1$ m/s in the positive $x$ direction. The only force in the $x$ direction is the position-dependent force
\[
F_x=6x^2\ \text{N},
\]
with $x$ measured in meters. The particle is observed from $x=0$ to $x=2$ m.

1. Compute the work $W=\int_0^2 F_x\,dx$ exactly.

2. Apply the work–energy principle to obtain the final kinetic energy $K_f$ and the final speed $v_f$. State the sign of $v_f$.

3. The force is conservative. Choosing the datum $U(0)=0$, determine the potential $U(x)$ and verify that $K+U$ is the same at the two endpoints.

4. Compute the instantaneous power $P=F_x v$ at $x=2$ m.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$F_x$ may be replaced by its terminal value $24$ N, so the work is $24\cdot 2=48$ J”; (ii) “because $F_x=6x^2$ is already written as a derivative, the potential with $U(0)=0$ is $U(x)=+2x^3$.”

The motion is rectilinear. Do not introduce a polar basis, an impact, or a time-harmonic forcing.
permittedResults: Work–energy on the line: $\int_{x_i}^{x_f}F_x\,dx=K_f-K_i$ with $K=\frac12 m v^2$.
If $F_x=-U'(x)$, then $K+U$ is constant. At a point, $P=F_x v$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate Fx dx first, convert the work into Kf and vf, then read U as the negative antiderivative with U(0)=0.
Build U(x)=-2x^3 immediately, conserve K+U from the initial state, and evaluate power as Fx v at the end.

milestones.criterion: Integrates Fx=6x^2 to W=16 J and obtains Kf=17 J with vf=+sqrt(17) m/s.
Constructs U(x)=-2x^3 from the datum U(0)=0, checks K+U, and reports P=24sqrt(17) W.
Rejects a terminal-value constant-force work and rejects the reversed potential +2x^3.

commonErrors.description: Replaces Fx by its terminal value 24 N and reports W=48 J, Kf=49 J, and vf=7 m/s.
commonErrors.consequence: The work integral is abandoned and every subsequent energy and speed is inconsistent with Fx=6x^2.

commonErrors.description: Takes U(x)=+2x^3 with U(0)=0, as if Fx were +U' rather than -U'.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential no longer generates the given force, and K+U is not conserved between the endpoints.

hintTree.content: $\int_0^2 6x^2\,dx=2x^3\big|_0^2=16$. The initial kinetic energy is $\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 1^2=1$.
At $x=2$, $F_x=24$ N and $v_f=\sqrt{17}$ m/s, both positive.

DYN:010323.canonicalSolution:
The work of the given force is
\[
W=\int_0^2 6x^2\,dx=2x^3\Big|_0^2=\boxed{16\ \text{J}}.
\]
The initial kinetic energy is $K_i=\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 1^2=1$ J. Work–energy gives
\[
K_f=K_i+W=\boxed{17\ \text{J}}.
\]
Then $K_f=\frac12 m v_f^2=v_f^2$, so
\[
v_f=\boxed{\sqrt{17}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The speed is taken positive because $v_0>0$ and $F_x\ge 0$ on $[0,2]$, so the particle never reverses.

The force is conservative. The potential satisfying $F_x=-U'(x)$ and $U(0)=0$ is
\[
U(x)=-\int_0^x 6s^2\,ds=\boxed{-2x^3}\ \text{J}.
\]
Mechanical energy at the start is $K_i+U(0)=1$. At $x=2$,
\[
K_f+U(2)=17+(-16)=1,
\]
so $K+U$ is conserved.

At $x=2$, $F_x=6\cdot 4=24$ N and $v=\sqrt{17}$ m/s, hence
\[
P=F_x v=\boxed{24\sqrt{17}\ \text{W}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: replacing $F_x$ by its terminal value $24$ N produces the spurious work $48$ J and the impossible final kinetic energy $49$ J. Sentence (ii) is false: $U=+2x^3$ would give $F_x=-6x^2$, the opposite force, and would not conserve $K+U$ with the computed $K_f$.

The exercise is rectilinear work, a potential datum, and a single power evaluation. It does not use polar coordinates, restitution, or a forced oscillator.

graderFixtures.proofText: The work is $W=16$ J, so $K_f=17$ J and $v_f=\sqrt{17}$ m/s. With $U(0)=0$ one has $U(x)=-2x^3$. The final power is $P=24\sqrt{17}$ W.
At x=2 the force is 24 N. Treating that value as constant on [0,2] gives W=48 J, Kf=49 J, and vf=7 m/s. I keep U=-2x^3.
I have W=16 J, Kf=17 J, and vf=sqrt(17). Because Fx=6x^2=d(2x^3)/dx, the potential with U(0)=0 is U(x)=+2x^3.

DYN:010338.title: Central pull keeps H=12, raises vθ from 3 to 6, and does 27 J
DYN:010338.objective: Conserve angular momentum of a particle drawn inward by a central string, convert the two circular stations into kinetic energies, and compute the positive work of the string while refusing the claim that zero torque implies zero work.
DYN:010338.statement:
A particle of mass $m=2$ kg slides on a smooth horizontal table. A light inextensible string fastened to the particle passes through a small hole in the table and is handled from below. At the first circular station the radius is $r_i=2$ m and the purely tangential speed is $v_{\theta i}=3$ m/s. The string is then shortened until a second circular station of radius $r_f=1$ m is reached. Gravity and the table normal do no work; the only horizontal force is the central string tension.

1. Compute the angular momentum $H$ of the particle about the hole at the initial station, and state why $H$ is the same at the final station. Include the unit.

2. Recover the final tangential speed $v_{\theta f}$ from conservation of $H$. Then form the two angular speeds $\omega_i=v_{\theta i}/r_i$ and $\omega_f=v_{\theta f}/r_f$.

3. Evaluate the kinetic energies $K_i$ and $K_f$ at the two circular stations (radial velocity is zero at each station). The work $W$ of the string equals $K_f-K_i$. Compute $W$.

4. In one sentence, distinguish the vanishing moment of the tension about the hole from the non-vanishing work of that same tension through the inward radial displacement.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the torque about the hole is zero, therefore the string does no work and $K$ is conserved”; (ii) “linear speed is conserved by the central force, so $v_{\theta f}=v_{\theta i}=3$ m/s.”

Do not replace the two circular stations by an impulsive jerk, do not introduce a coefficient of restitution, and do not treat the tension as a prescribed position-dependent force along a single straight line.
permittedResults: If the only horizontal force passes through a fixed hole, then $m r v_\theta$ is constant. In particular $v_{\theta f}=(r_i/r_f)v_{\theta i}$ when both stations are circular.
Vanishing torque about a point does not imply vanishing work: $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0$ can hold while $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r\neq 0$ along a radial pull.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form H=m r vθ at the first station, scale vθ by the inverse radius, then convert the two speeds into kinetic energies and subtract.
Keep H=m r^2 ω, read ωi=3/2 and ωf=6 from H=12, and evaluate K=(1/2) H ω at each station as a check that W=27 J.

milestones.criterion: Conserves H=m r vθ=12 and reports vθf=6 m/s together with ωi=3/2 and ωf=6 rad/s.
Reports Ki=9 J, Kf=36 J, and string work W=27 J.
Distinguishes vanishing torque from nonzero work and rejects both W=0 and conserved linear speed.

commonErrors.description: Infers from vanishing torque that the string does no work, reports W=0 and Kf=Ki=9 J, and keeps vθf=3 m/s.
commonErrors.consequence: Angular momentum at the inner station is halved, and the positive work of the inward pull is erased.

commonErrors.description: Treats the central force as conserving linear speed and sets vθf=vθi=3 m/s without using H=m r vθ.
commonErrors.consequence: The inner-circle kinetic energy is left at 9 J and the required string work 27 J never appears.

hintTree.content: $H=m r_i v_{\theta i}=2\cdot 2\cdot 3=12$. The central tension cannot change $H$.
At $r_f=1$, $v_{\theta f}=H/(m r_f)=6$. Then $\omega_i=3/2$ and $\omega_f=6$.
$K_i=\tfrac12 m v_{\theta i}^2=9$ J and $K_f=36$ J, so the string work is $27$ J.

DYN:010338.canonicalSolution:
At the initial circular station
\[
H=m r_i v_{\theta i}=2\cdot 2\cdot 3=\boxed{12\ \text{kg·m}^2\text{/s}}.
\]
The tension always points at the hole, so its moment about the hole is zero and $H$ is the same at the final station. Therefore
\[
v_{\theta f}=\frac{H}{m r_f}=\frac{12}{2\cdot 1}=\boxed{6\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The angular speeds are
\[
\omega_i=\frac{v_{\theta i}}{r_i}=\boxed{\frac32\ \text{rad/s}},\qquad
\omega_f=\frac{v_{\theta f}}{r_f}=\boxed{6\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
Radial velocity vanishes at each circular station, so
\[
K_i=\frac12 m v_{\theta i}^2=\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 9=\boxed{9\ \text{J}},
\qquad
K_f=\frac12 m v_{\theta f}^2=\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 36=\boxed{36\ \text{J}}.
\]
The work–energy statement for the string (the only working horizontal force) is
\[
W=K_f-K_i=\boxed{27\ \text{J}}.
\]
Zero moment about the hole is compatible with a nonzero radial displacement: the tension does $27$ J of work while leaving $H$ unchanged.

Sentence (i) is false: zero torque conserves $H$, not $K$. Setting $W=0$ would freeze $v_\theta$ at $3$ m/s and would violate $H=12$ at $r=1$ m. Sentence (ii) is false: a central force does not conserve the linear speed; $v_{\theta f}=3$ m/s would drop $H$ to $6$.

The balance is angular-momentum conservation plus work–energy between two circular stations. It is not an impact, not a restitution model, and not a straight-line position-force quadrature.

graderFixtures.proofText: Angular momentum about the hole is $H=12$ and is conserved, so $v_{\theta f}=6$ m/s with $\omega_i=3/2$ and $\omega_f=6$. Then $K_i=9$ J, $K_f=36$ J, and the string work is $27$ J. Zero torque does not mean zero work.
Torque about the hole is zero, so the string does no work. Kinetic energy is conserved: Ki=Kf=9 J and vθf=3 m/s. I still write H=12 at the start.
A central force cannot change the linear speed, so vθf=vθi=3 m/s. Then Kf=9 J and W=0. I do not form m r vθ.

DYN:010339.title: Inner-loop contact needs hmin=5R/2; at h=3R the top normal is mg
DYN:010339.objective: Combine energy with the inner-loop top normal law, obtain the leave-contact threshold from N=0, evaluate the finite normal at a higher release, and refuse both a weightless top balance and an energy statement that omits the top height.
DYN:010339.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ is released from rest on a smooth approach track at height $h$ above the lowest point of a fixed, smooth vertical circular loop of radius $R$. The approach track feeds the particle into the inner surface at the loop's lowest point, so $h$ may exceed the loop's diameter. Gravity is the only working force. Contact with the inner surface can transmit a nonnegative normal $N$ directed away from the surface (toward the center when the particle is at the top) and cannot pull.

1. At the top of the loop write Newton’s second law along the inward radius, including both $N$ and the weight. Set the leave-contact threshold $N=0$ and solve for $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2$.

2. Apply mechanical energy between the release point and the top, whose height above the bottom is $2R$. Insert the threshold $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2$ and solve for the least release height $h_{\min}$ that preserves contact through the top.

3. Now take the larger release $h=3R$. Compute $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2$ from energy, then recover the top normal $N$.

4. State why a release strictly below $h_{\min}$ cannot complete the loop while preserving contact. Distinguish $R<h<5R/2$, where $N$ reaches zero with positive speed before the top, from $0\le h<R$, where the particle turns back before the upper half while $N$ remains positive. Treat $h=R$ as the marginal zero-speed, zero-normal case at the side.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “at the top the normal alone supplies $mv^2/R$, so the threshold is $v_{\mathrm{top}}=0$ and $h_{\min}=2R$”; (ii) “energy ignores the $2R$ rise, so $h_{\min}=v_{\mathrm{top}}^2/(2g)=R/2$.”

Do not treat the particle as a bead on a two-sided wire, do not replace the energy statement by a signed path-tangent Newton law along a general curve, and do not introduce friction or restitution.
permittedResults: On a smooth inner loop, $N=0$ at the top forces $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=gR$. Energy from rest at height $h$ then gives $mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac12 m(gR)$, so $h_{\min}=5R/2$.
If the particle is released from rest at $h=3R$, energy yields $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=2gR$ and the top normal is $N=mg$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fix the threshold speed from N=0 at the top, then lift that speed through an energy statement that includes the 2R rise.
Keep energy symbolic in h, solve vtop^2=2g(h-2R), and impose vtop^2≥gR to read hmin=5R/2 before evaluating h=3R.

milestones.criterion: Writes N+mg=mvtop^2/R, sets N=0, and reports vtop^2=gR with hmin=5R/2.
At h=3R reports vtop^2=2gR and N=mg, and correctly distinguishes the below-threshold failure regimes.
Rejects both a weightless top threshold and an energy balance that omits the height 2R.

commonErrors.description: Writes only N=mvtop^2/R at the top, so the threshold N=0 forces vtop=0 and hmin=2R.
commonErrors.consequence: The weight contribution to the centripetal requirement is discarded and the particle is predicted to coast over the top with zero speed.

commonErrors.description: Applies energy as mgh=(1/2)m vtop^2 with no 2R potential rise, producing hmin=R/2 from vtop^2=gR.
commonErrors.consequence: The top is treated as if it were at the bottom height, so the threshold release is four-fifths too small.

hintTree.content: Inward at the top: $N+mg=mv_{\mathrm{top}}^2/R$. The threshold $N=0$ is $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=gR$.
Energy: $mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac12 mv_{\mathrm{top}}^2$. The threshold inserts to $h_{\min}=5R/2$.
At $h=3R$, $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=2gR$ and $N+mg=2mg$, so $N=mg$.

DYN:010339.canonicalSolution:
At the top of the inner surface the inward Newton statement is
\[
N+mg=\frac{m v_{\mathrm{top}}^2}{R}.
\]
The one-sided contact can vanish but cannot become negative. The leave-contact threshold is therefore $N=0$, which forces
\[
v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=\boxed{gR}.
\]
Mechanical energy from rest at height $h$ to the top at height $2R$ reads
\[
mgh=mg(2R)+\frac12 m v_{\mathrm{top}}^2.
\]
Inserting the threshold $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=gR$ produces
\[
h_{\min}=2R+\frac{R}{2}=\boxed{\frac{5R}{2}}.
\]
For the larger release $h=3R$,
\[
mg(3R)=mg(2R)+\frac12 m v_{\mathrm{top}}^2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=\boxed{2gR}.
\]
The top normal is then
\[
N+mg=\frac{m(2gR)}{R}=2mg\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
N=\boxed{mg}.
\]
For a precise below-threshold audit, let $\phi$ be the angle measured from the bottom. Energy and inward Newton give
\[
v^2=2g\bigl[h-R(1-\cos\phi)\bigr],\qquad
N=mg\left(\frac{2h}{R}-2+3\cos\phi\right).
\]
Thus every $h<5R/2$ fails to complete a full loop while maintaining contact, but the failure mode depends on $h$. If $R<h<5R/2$, $N$ reaches zero with positive speed before the top and the particle leaves the surface. If $0\le h<R$, the particle instead reaches $v=0$ at $\cos\phi=1-h/R$ and turns back with $N=mg(1-h/R)>0$. At $h=R$ it reaches the side with both $v=0$ and $N=0$, the marginal case. Merely extrapolating a negative top normal does not prove that every shorter release actually loses contact before reaching its turning point.

Sentence (i) is false: dropping the weight from the top balance makes the threshold $v_{\mathrm{top}}=0$ and $h_{\min}=2R$, which understates the speed needed to stay on a one-sided surface. Sentence (ii) is false: omitting the rise $2R$ produces the much smaller $h_{\min}=R/2$ and pretends the top is at the same height as the bottom.

The argument is energy plus a one-sided normal at one station. It is not a bead-on-a-wire two-sided constraint, not a general signed curved-path force resolution, and not an impact.

graderFixtures.proofText: At the top, $N+mg=mv^2/R$. The threshold $N=0$ is $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=gR$, and energy then gives $h_{\min}=5R/2$. For $h=3R$ I obtain $v_{\mathrm{top}}^2=2gR$ and $N=mg$. Every shorter release fails to complete the loop in contact: $R<h<5R/2$ loses contact with positive speed, while $0\le h<R$ turns back with positive normal and $h=R$ is marginal at the side.
At the top only the normal is centripetal, so N=m vtop^2/R. Threshold N=0 means vtop=0 and therefore hmin=2R. At h=3R I still get some leftover kinetic energy.
N=0 still gives vtop^2=gR, but energy is just mgh=(1/2)m vtop^2, so hmin=R/2. I never add the 2R rise to the top.

DYN:010424.title: Rigid kinematics give vB=(-2,2+3sqrt3) and aB=(1-9sqrt3,-6-2sqrt3)
DYN:010424.objective: Apply the rigid-body two-point formulae for velocity and acceleration, keeping the cross-product order, the angular-acceleration term, and the centripetal term all explicit.
DYN:010424.statement:
A rigid body moves in the $xy$-plane of a fixed right-handed frame. At a given instant the kinematics of a point $A$ of the body and the angular motion of the body are
\[
\mathbf v_A=(1,2)\ \text{m/s},\qquad
\mathbf a_A=(-1,3)\ \text{m/s}^2,\qquad
\boldsymbol\omega=3\,\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s},\qquad
\boldsymbol\alpha=-2\,\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}^2.
\]
A second point $B$ of the same rigid body has relative position
\[
\mathbf r_{B/A}=(\sqrt{3},1)\ \text{m}.
\]

1. Compute $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$ and the velocity $\mathbf v_B=\mathbf v_A+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$.

2. Compute the angular-acceleration term $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$ and the centripetal term $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A})$. Confirm the latter equals $-\omega^2\mathbf r_{B/A}$.

3. Form the acceleration $\mathbf a_B=\mathbf a_A+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A})$.

4. Record the intermediate vectors $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$ and the centripetal term exactly, in the order requested.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the relative velocity is $\mathbf r_{B/A}\times\boldsymbol\omega$, which is just as valid as $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$”; (ii) “because the formula already contains $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$, the centripetal term may be omitted.”

The body is rigid. Do not replace the two-point formulae by an instantaneous center, do not introduce rolling friction, and do not treat $B$ as a particle in polar coordinates.
permittedResults: If $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r=(x,y)$, then $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=(-\omega y,\omega x)$.
If $\boldsymbol\omega$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf r$, then $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)=-\omega^2\mathbf r$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the planar shortcuts ω×r=(-ωy,ωx) and -ω²r, then add vA and aA.
Expand both cross products in determinants, then check the centripetal term against -ω² r_B/A.

milestones.criterion: Computes ω×r_B/A=(-3,3√3) and vB=(-2,2+3√3) m/s with the right-handed order.
Records α×r=(2,-2√3) and the centripetal term (-9√3,-9), and sums to aB=(1-9√3,-6-2√3).
Rejects r×ω in place of ω×r and rejects dropping the centripetal acceleration.

commonErrors.description: Computes r_B/A cross ω instead of ω cross r_B/A, obtaining the relative velocity (3,-3√3) and vB=(4,2-3√3).
commonErrors.consequence: The right-hand rule is violated and every subsequent velocity component of B has the wrong sense.

commonErrors.description: Forms aB from aA+α×r alone, reporting aB=(1,3-2√3) and discarding (-9√3,-9).
commonErrors.consequence: A rigid point at finite distance from A is missing its entire normal acceleration ω² r.

hintTree.content: With $\omega=3$, $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A}=(-3,3\sqrt{3})$. Adding $\mathbf v_A$ produces the $x$ component $-2$.
With $\alpha=-2$, $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}=(2,-2\sqrt{3})$.
$\omega^2=9$, so the centripetal term is $-9(\sqrt{3},1)=(-9\sqrt{3},-9)$.

DYN:010424.canonicalSolution:
Here $\omega=3$ and $\mathbf r_{B/A}=(\sqrt{3},1)$, so
\[
\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A}
=(-3\cdot 1,\,3\cdot\sqrt{3})
=(-3,3\sqrt{3})\ \text{m/s}.
\]
The velocity of $B$ is
\[
\mathbf v_B=(1,2)+(-3,3\sqrt{3})
=\boxed{(-2,\,2+3\sqrt{3})\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The angular-acceleration term is
\[
\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}
=\bigl(-(-2)\cdot 1,\,(-2)\cdot\sqrt{3}\bigr)
=\boxed{(2,-2\sqrt{3})\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
The centripetal term may be evaluated as a double cross product,
\[
\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A})
=3\mathbf k\times(-3,3\sqrt{3})
=(-9\sqrt{3},-9)\ \text{m/s}^2,
\]
or as $-\omega^2\mathbf r_{B/A}=-9(\sqrt{3},1)$. The two expressions agree:
\[
\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{B/A})=(-9\sqrt{3},-9)\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
Adding the three acceleration contributions gives
\[
\mathbf a_B
=(-1,3)+(2,-2\sqrt{3})+(-9\sqrt{3},-9)
=\boxed{(1-9\sqrt{3},\,-6-2\sqrt{3})\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $\mathbf r_{B/A}\times\boldsymbol\omega=(3,-3\sqrt{3})$ is the opposite vector and yields $\mathbf v_B=(4,2-3\sqrt{3})$. Sentence (ii) is false: dropping the centripetal term produces $\mathbf a_B=(1,3-2\sqrt{3})$, which omits a contribution of magnitude $9\|\mathbf r_{B/A}\|=18$ m/s$^2$.

The calculation uses only the rigid two-point formulae. It does not locate an instantaneous center of zero velocity and does not introduce contact friction.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\mathbf v_B=(-2,2+3\sqrt{3})$ m/s, $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{B/A}=(2,-2\sqrt{3})$ m/s$^2$, centripetal term $(-9\sqrt{3},-9)$ m/s$^2$, and $\mathbf a_B=(1-9\sqrt{3},-6-2\sqrt{3})$ m/s$^2$.
The relative velocity is r_B/A cross omega=(3,-3sqrt(3)), so vB=(1,2)+(3,-3sqrt(3))=(4,2-3sqrt(3)) m/s. I keep the given acceleration formula.
vB=(-2,2+3sqrt(3)) is fine. Acceleration is aA+alpha×r=(-1,3)+(2,-2sqrt(3))=(1,3-2sqrt(3)) m/s^2. I do not add a centripetal term.
