DYN:010425.title: External gears send the top rack right at 0.4 m/s and 0.16 m/s^2
DYN:010425.objective: Convert an external gear pair into the signed angular motion of a coaxial pinion, match a translating top rack to the pinion’s tangential kinematics, and refuse a centripetal acceleration for the rack.
DYN:010425.statement:
Two circular gears mesh externally. Gear $A$ has pitch radius $r_A=0.20$ m and gear $B$ has pitch radius $r_B=0.50$ m. The shaft of $B$ also carries a coaxial pinion $C$ of pitch radius $r_C=0.10$ m. A straight rack meshes with $C$ along the top generator of $C$ (the contact point is directly above the center of $C$). The rack translates horizontally; it does not rotate.

Take counterclockwise rotations as positive and rack displacement to the right as positive. At the instant of interest
\[
\omega_A=10\ \text{rad/s (CCW)},\qquad
\alpha_A=4\ \text{rad/s}^2\text{ (CCW)}.
\]
The centers of $A$, $B$, and $C$ are fixed.

1. Write the external no-slip conditions relating $(\omega_A,\omega_B)$ and $(\alpha_A,\alpha_B)$. Solve for $\omega_B$ and $\alpha_B$.

2. Deduce $\omega_C$ and $\alpha_C$ from the common shaft.

3. Determine the velocity and acceleration of the rack. State both as signed scalars and as vectors in the $xy$-plane with $\mathbf i$ to the right and $\mathbf j$ upward.

4. Explain why the rack has no normal (centripetal) acceleration, even though a material point of pinion $C$ at the contact does.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “an external mesh behaves like an internal mesh, so $B$ turns in the same sense as $A$ and $\omega_B=+4$ rad/s”; (ii) “the rack must share the centripetal acceleration $\omega_C^2 r_C$ of the contact point of $C$.”

Do not invent a normal acceleration of the translating rack. Do not replace the gear ratio by an instantaneous-center construction, and do not introduce friction capacity or slip.
permittedResults: External rolling without slip: $r_A\omega_A+r_B\omega_B=0$ and $r_A\alpha_A+r_B\alpha_B=0$.

If a rack rides on the top of a pinion of radius $r$ with $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}}=r\mathbf j$, then $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rack}}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}}=-\omega r\,\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf a_{\mathrm{rack}}=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}}$ only. The rack does not inherit $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write rA ωA+rB ωB=0, copy the ratio onto the shaft of C, then take ωC×r_top and αC×r_top for the rack.
Convert the external pair into a signed speed ratio ωB/ωA=-rA/rB first, then treat the rack as a pitch line of radius infinity.

milestones.criterion: Applies the external no-slip ratio to obtain ωB=ωC=-4 rad/s and αB=αC=-8/5 rad/s².
Matches the top rack to the pinion tangent and reports vrack=0.4 m/s right and arack=0.16 m/s² right.
Rejects an internal-mesh same-sense rotation and rejects a centripetal acceleration of the translating rack.

commonErrors.description: Uses rA ωA=rB ωB with the same sign, reporting ωB=ωC=+4 rad/s and a leftward rack velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The external pair is assigned the wrong rotation sense and the rack travels in the opposite direction.

commonErrors.description: Gives the translating rack the pinion contact centripetal acceleration ωC² rC=1.6 m/s² downward in addition to the 0.16 m/s² tangent.
commonErrors.consequence: A purely translating body is assigned a normal acceleration that only a rotating pinion point possesses.

hintTree.content: $0.20\cdot 10+0.50\,\omega_B=0$ forces $\omega_B=-4$. The identical ratio on the accelerations gives $\alpha_B=-8/5$.
$C$ is keyed to the shaft of $B$, so $\omega_C=\omega_B$ and $\alpha_C=\alpha_B$.

With $\boldsymbol\omega_C=-4\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}}=0.10\,\mathbf j$, the cross product $\boldsymbol\omega_C\times\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}}=+0.40\,\mathbf i$. The term $\boldsymbol\omega_C\times(\boldsymbol\omega_C\times\mathbf r_{\mathrm{top}})$ belongs to $C$, not to the rack.

DYN:010425.canonicalSolution:
External no-slip at the $A$–$B$ pitch point is
\[
r_A\omega_A+r_B\omega_B=0,\qquad
r_A\alpha_A+r_B\alpha_B=0.
\]
Substituting the given data,
\[
0.20\cdot 10+0.50\,\omega_B=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\omega_B=-4\ \text{rad/s}},
\]
\[
0.20\cdot 4+0.50\,\alpha_B=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\alpha_B=-\frac85\ \text{rad/s}^2}.
\]
Pinion $C$ shares the shaft of $B$, therefore
\[
\boxed{\omega_C=\omega_B=-4\ \text{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha_C=\alpha_B=-\frac85\ \text{rad/s}^2}.
\]
The rack contacts $C$ at the top point $\mathbf r_{P/C}=0.10\,\mathbf j$. The velocity of that point of the pinion is
\[
\boldsymbol\omega_C\times\mathbf r_{P/C}
=(-4\mathbf k)\times(0.10\mathbf j)
=0.40\,\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}.
\]
The rack translates and remains in no-slip contact, so
\[
\mathbf v_{\mathrm{rack}}=\boxed{0.40\,\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}}
\quad(0.4\ \text{m/s to the right}).
\]
Its acceleration matches only the tangential acceleration of $P$,
\[
\boldsymbol\alpha_C\times\mathbf r_{P/C}
=\Bigl(-\frac85\mathbf k\Bigr)\times(0.10\mathbf j)
=0.16\,\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbf a_{\mathrm{rack}}=\boxed{0.16\,\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^2}
\quad(0.16\ \text{m/s}^2\text{ to the right, tangential}).
\]
A material point of the pinion at $P$ does have the centripetal acceleration
\[
\boldsymbol\omega_C\times(\boldsymbol\omega_C\times\mathbf r_{P/C})
=-16\cdot 0.10\,\mathbf j=-1.6\,\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}^2,
\]
but the rack is in pure translation: $\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{rack}}=\mathbf 0$, so that normal term is not an acceleration of the rack. Assigning $-1.6\,\mathbf j$ to the rack would claim that a translating body is turning.

Sentence (i) is false: an internal mesh would give $\omega_B=+4$, and the rack would then move to the left. Sentence (ii) is false: a translating rack has no centripetal acceleration.

The reduction uses only rolling-without-slip kinematics of gears and a rack. It does not locate an instantaneous center of the compound body and does not discuss friction capacity.

graderFixtures.proofText: External no-slip gives $\omega_B=\omega_C=-4$ rad/s and $\alpha_B=\alpha_C=-8/5$ rad/s$^2$. The top rack then has $\mathbf v=0.40\,\mathbf i$ m/s and $\mathbf a=0.16\,\mathbf i$ m/s$^2$, with no centripetal term.
I treat the A-B mesh as internal, so omegaB=omegaC=+4 rad/s and alphaB=alphaC=+8/5 rad/s^2. The top rack then moves left at 0.4 m/s.
omegaB=omegaC=-4 and the tangential rack motion 0.4 m/s, 0.16 m/s^2 to the right are correct, but the rack also has the contact centripetal acceleration 1.6 m/s^2 downward.

DYN:010440.title: Slider-crank at θ=π/2 has x=sqrt3, vx=-2, and ax=4/sqrt3
DYN:010440.objective: Differentiate the closed slider-crank position twice at the right-angle station, convert θ-derivatives into slider velocity and acceleration with constant crank rate, and refuse both a missing ω² factor and a frozen connecting-rod length.
DYN:010440.statement:
A planar slider-crank has crank length $1$ and connecting-rod length $2$. The slider coordinate $x$, measured from the crank pivot along the line of stroke, is the holonomic function
\[
x(\theta)=\cos\theta+\sqrt{4-\sin^2\theta}.
\]
The crank rate $\dot\theta=2$ rad/s is constant, so $\ddot\theta=0$. The station of interest is the right-angle configuration $\theta=\pi/2$ (crank perpendicular to the stroke; the colinear dead centers are not required here).

1. Evaluate $x$ at $\theta=\pi/2$.

2. Differentiate $x(\theta)$ once and evaluate $dx/d\theta$ at $\theta=\pi/2$. Convert to the slider velocity $v_x=(dx/d\theta)\dot\theta$.

3. Differentiate a second time and evaluate $d^2x/d\theta^2$ at $\theta=\pi/2$. Convert to the slider acceleration
   \[
   a_x=\frac{d^2x}{d\theta^2}\dot\theta^2+\frac{dx}{d\theta}\ddot\theta.
   \]

4. State why the factor $\dot\theta^2$, not $\dot\theta$, multiplies the second $\theta$-derivative when $\ddot\theta=0$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “acceleration is $(d^2x/d\theta^2)\dot\theta$ because $\dot\theta$ is the only time scale”; (ii) “the connecting-rod term is the constant $2$, so $x=\cos\theta+2$ and $a_x=-\cos\theta\cdot\dot\theta^2=0$ at $\theta=\pi/2$.”

Do not locate an instantaneous center, do not expand a rigid-point relative-acceleration formula at a second body point, and do not replace the linkage by a compound gear train.
permittedResults: At $\theta=\pi/2$, $\sin\theta=1$ and $\cos\theta=0$, so $x=\sqrt{3}$ and $x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta-(\sin\theta\cos\theta)/\sqrt{4-\sin^2\theta}=-1$.
The second derivative at that station reduces to $x''(\theta)=1/\sqrt{3}$. With $\dot\theta=2$ and $\ddot\theta=0$ one has $v_x=-2$ and $a_x=4/\sqrt{3}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the given x(θ) symbolically, substitute θ=π/2 after each derivative, then multiply by θdot and θdot^2.
At the right-angle station drop every factor of cosθ first, read x'=−1 and x''=1/sqrt3 from the surviving terms, and only then restore the time scale θdot=2.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates x=sqrt3 and dx/dθ=-1 at θ=π/2 and reports vx=-2.
Evaluates d2x/dθ2=1/sqrt3 and reports ax=4/sqrt3 with the θdot^2 factor.
Rejects replacing θdot^2 by θdot and rejects a frozen connecting-rod length that forces ax=0.

commonErrors.description: Forms ax as (d^2x/dθ^2)θdot=2/sqrt3 instead of (d^2x/dθ^2)θdot^2, while keeping vx=-2.
commonErrors.consequence: The slider acceleration is too small by a factor of the crank rate, so the mid-stroke peak is reported as 2/sqrt3 rather than 4/sqrt3.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sqrt(4-sin^2θ) by the constant 2, so x=cosθ+2, x''=-cosθ, and ax=0 at θ=π/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The entire connecting-rod contribution to acceleration is discarded and the slider is predicted to have zero acceleration at the assigned station.

hintTree.content: At $\theta=\pi/2$, $x=0+\sqrt{4-1}=\sqrt{3}$.
$x'=-\sin\theta-(\sin\theta\cos\theta)/\sqrt{4-\sin^2\theta}$ equals $-1$ when $\cos\theta=0$. Then $v_x=-2$.
The surviving second-derivative piece at $\theta=\pi/2$ is $1/\sqrt{3}$, and $a_x=(1/\sqrt{3})\cdot 4=4/\sqrt{3}$.

DYN:010440.canonicalSolution:
At $\theta=\pi/2$,
\[
\sin\theta=1,\qquad\cos\theta=0,\qquad
x=0+\sqrt{4-1}=\boxed{\sqrt{3}}.
\]
Differentiate the position:
\[
\frac{dx}{d\theta}
=-\sin\theta-\frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sqrt{4-\sin^2\theta}}.
\]
The second summand vanishes at $\theta=\pi/2$, leaving
\[
\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-1.
\]
With $\dot\theta=2$,
\[
v_x=\frac{dx}{d\theta}\dot\theta=\boxed{-2\ \text{m/s}}
\]
in the length units of the given $x$. A second differentiation produces
\[
\frac{d^2x}{d\theta^2}
=-\cos\theta-\frac{\cos 2\theta}{\sqrt{4-\sin^2\theta}}
-\frac{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{(4-\sin^2\theta)^{3/2}}.
\]
At $\theta=\pi/2$ one has $\cos\theta=0$, $\cos\pi=-1$, and $\cos\theta=0$ in the last term, so
\[
\frac{d^2x}{d\theta^2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
\]
Because $\ddot\theta=0$,
\[
a_x=\frac{d^2x}{d\theta^2}\dot\theta^2
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot 4
=\boxed{\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
The factor $\dot\theta^2$ is the chain-rule square of $d\theta/dt$. Replacing it by $\dot\theta$ would be dimensionally inconsistent with $x''(\theta)$ and would not be an acceleration.

Sentence (i) is false: $(d^2x/d\theta^2)\dot\theta=2/\sqrt{3}$ is not $a_x$. Sentence (ii) is false: freezing the rod projection at $2$ forces $x''=-\cos\theta=0$ and $a_x=0$, which erases the connecting-rod contribution that supplies the entire acceleration at this station.

The calculation uses only the holonomic slider coordinate and the chain rule. It does not invoke an instantaneous center, a two-point rigid-body acceleration expansion, or a gear train.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $\theta=\pi/2$ I obtain $x=\sqrt{3}$, $dx/d\theta=-1$, and $d^2x/d\theta^2=1/\sqrt{3}$. With $\dot\theta=2$ and $\ddot\theta=0$ this gives $v_x=-2$ and $a_x=4/\sqrt{3}$. The connecting-rod projection still depends on $\theta$.
I agree that d2x/dθ2=1/sqrt3 and vx=-2, but acceleration is just that second derivative times θdot, so ax=2/sqrt3.
The rod length is 2, so I write x=cosθ+2. Then dx/dθ=-sinθ=-1 and d2x/dθ2=-cosθ=0, hence ax=0 at θ=π/2. Velocity is still -2.

DYN:010441.title: Guided coupler gives vC=(8,0) and aC=(-154/3,0) by vector kinematics
DYN:010441.objective: Apply the rigid-body vector velocity and acceleration formulae to a crank-and-guided-coupler, enforce the horizontal constraint on C at both orders, and refuse both an instantaneous-center acceleration shortcut and a dropped coupler centripetal term.
DYN:010441.statement:
Link $AB$ has length $2$ and lies along the positive $x$-axis from a fixed pin $A$ to $B$. At the instant of interest
\[
\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}=3\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s (CCW)},\qquad
\boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}=\mathbf 0.
\]
A rigid coupler $BC$ has the present relative position
\[
\mathbf r_{C/B}=(3,4)\ \text{m},
\]
and the endpoint $C$ is confined to a fixed horizontal guide, so both $v_{C,y}$ and $a_{C,y}$ vanish. Use only the vector formulae
\[
\mathbf v_C=\mathbf v_B+\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B},
\qquad
\mathbf a_C=\mathbf a_B+\boldsymbol\alpha_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B}
+\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B}).
\]

1. Form $\mathbf v_B=\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A}$.

2. Write $\mathbf v_C$ with unknown $\omega_{BC}=\omega\mathbf k$. Enforce $v_{C,y}=0$, solve for $\omega$, and report $\mathbf v_C$.

3. Form $\mathbf a_B=\boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A}+\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A})$.

4. Write $\mathbf a_C$ with unknown $\alpha_{BC}=\alpha\mathbf k$. Enforce $a_{C,y}=0$, solve for $\alpha$, and report $\mathbf a_C$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “once the instantaneous center of $BC$ is known, $\mathbf a_C=\boldsymbol\alpha_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/\mathrm{IC}}$ and the centripetal construction may be skipped”; (ii) “because $\boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}=\mathbf 0$, the coupler centripetal term $\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B})$ may be dropped as well.”

Do not replace the acceleration analysis by an instantaneous-center argument, do not reduce the linkage to a single rigid-point relative pair without the guide constraint, and do not introduce gears.
permittedResults: If $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf r=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j$, then $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=-\omega y\mathbf i+\omega x\mathbf j$ and $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)=-\omega^2\mathbf r$.
A point confined to a fixed straight guide has vanishing acceleration into the forbidden direction. That scalar statement, not an instantaneous-center radius, fixes $\alpha$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build vC=vB+ω×r first, fix ω from the vanishing y-component, then repeat the pattern for aC including the centripetal term before fixing α.
Tabulate every cross product as a pair of components, write the two guide constraints as linear equations for (ω,α), and only then assemble vC and aC.

milestones.criterion: Computes vB=(0,6), enforces vC,y=0, and reports ωBC=-2 with vC=(8,0).
Computes aB=(-18,0), enforces aC,y=0, and reports αBC=16/3 with aC=(-154/3,0).
Requires the vector velocity and acceleration formulae and rejects both an IC acceleration shortcut and a dropped coupler centripetal term.

commonErrors.description: Locates an instantaneous center of BC from the velocity field and writes aC=α×r_C/IC, skipping ω×(ω×r) and failing to recover aC=(-154/3,0).
commonErrors.consequence: Acceleration is treated as a velocity-center construction, so the coupler centripetal contribution is lost and aC is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Drops ωBC×(ωBC×r_C/B) because αAB=0, leaving aC=(-18,0)+(-4α,3α). Then aC,y=0 forces α=0 and aC=(-18,0).
commonErrors.consequence: The −16 m/s^2 vertical centripetal piece is discarded, αBC is reported as 0 instead of 16/3, and aC,x stays at −18 instead of −154/3.

hintTree.content: $\mathbf v_B=3\mathbf k\times 2\mathbf i=(0,6)$. Then $\mathbf v_C=(-4\omega,\ 6+3\omega)$, so $\omega=-2$ and $\mathbf v_C=(8,0)$.
$\mathbf a_B=3\mathbf k\times(0,6)=(-18,0)$.
With $\omega=-2$ the coupler centripetal term is $(-12,-16)$. The $y$-statement $3\alpha-16=0$ gives $\alpha=16/3$ and $a_{C,x}=-154/3$.

DYN:010441.canonicalSolution:
The crank position is $\mathbf r_{B/A}=(2,0)$. The driving velocity is
\[
\mathbf v_B
=\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A}
=3\mathbf k\times 2\mathbf i
=\boxed{(0,6)\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
With $\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}=\omega\mathbf k$,
\[
\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B}
=\omega\mathbf k\times(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)
=(-4\omega,\ 3\omega),
\]
so
\[
\mathbf v_C=(0,6)+(-4\omega,\ 3\omega)=(-4\omega,\ 6+3\omega).
\]
The guide requires $v_{C,y}=0$, hence $6+3\omega=0$ and $\omega=-2$. Therefore
\[
\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}=\boxed{-2\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}},\qquad
\mathbf v_C=\boxed{(8,0)\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The driving acceleration, with $\boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}=\mathbf 0$, is the centripetal term of $AB$:
\[
\mathbf a_B
=\boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times\mathbf v_B
=3\mathbf k\times 6\mathbf j
=\boxed{(-18,0)\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
Now $\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}=-2\mathbf k$ and $\boldsymbol\alpha_{BC}=\alpha\mathbf k$. The coupler ingredients are
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol\alpha_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B}
&=(-4\alpha,\ 3\alpha),\\
\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{BC}\times\mathbf r_{C/B})
&=-(-2)^2(3,4)=(-12,-16).
\end{align*}
Adding,
\[
\mathbf a_C
=(-18,0)+(-4\alpha,\ 3\alpha)+(-12,-16)
=(-30-4\alpha,\ 3\alpha-16).
\]
The guide requires $a_{C,y}=0$, hence $3\alpha-16=0$ and $\alpha=16/3$. The remaining component is
\[
a_{C,x}=-30-4\cdot\frac{16}{3}=-30-\frac{64}{3}=-\frac{154}{3}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boldsymbol\alpha_{BC}=\boxed{\frac{16}{3}\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}^2},\qquad
\mathbf a_C=\boxed{\Bigl(-\frac{154}{3},\ 0\Bigr)\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: the instantaneous center of $BC$ is a velocity construction and does not replace $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)$ in the acceleration formula. Using $\mathbf a_C=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{C/\mathrm{IC}}$ drops the centripetal piece and cannot recover $-154/3$. Sentence (ii) is false: $\boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}=\mathbf 0$ does not cancel the coupler centripetal term. Dropping $(-12,-16)$ would force $\alpha=0$ and $\mathbf a_C=(-18,0)$.

The solution uses the two-term velocity formula and the three-term acceleration formula together with the guide constraints. It does not compute acceleration from an instantaneous center, and it does not introduce gears.

graderFixtures.proofText: Vector velocity gives $\mathbf v_B=(0,6)$, $\omega_{BC}=-2$, and $\mathbf v_C=(8,0)$. Vector acceleration then gives $\mathbf a_B=(-18,0)$, $\alpha_{BC}=16/3$, and $\mathbf a_C=(-154/3,0)$. The coupler centripetal term is required; an instantaneous center is not used for acceleration.
I get the velocities vB=(0,6), omegaBC=-2, vC=(8,0) from an instantaneous center of BC. Acceleration is then aC=alpha × r_C/IC. I never form omega × (omega × r) and I do not obtain aC=(-154/3,0).
Velocities are vB=(0,6), omegaBC=-2, vC=(8,0) and aB=(-18,0). Because alphaAB=0 I drop the coupler centripetal term. Then aC=(-18,0)+(-4α,3α) and aC,y=0 give α=0 and aC=(-18,0).

DYN:010442.title: Slot constraint at (3,4) forces ydot=-3/2 and yddot=-13/16; floor-angle omega=-1/2 and alpha=1/16
DYN:010442.objective: Differentiate the perpendicular-slot length identity twice, then recover the CCW-positive floor-angle rate and angular acceleration and close both endpoint accelerations from the same angle.
DYN:010442.statement:
A rigid rod of fixed length $5$ m has end $A$ constrained to the horizontal slot (the $x$-axis) and end $B$ constrained to the vertical slot (the $y$-axis). The slots meet at a fixed origin $O$, so the endpoint coordinates satisfy
\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=25
\]
with $A=(x,0)$ and $B=(0,y)$ and with $x>0$, $y>0$. At the instant of interest
\[
x=3\ \text{m},\qquad y=4\ \text{m},\qquad
\dot x=2\ \text{m/s},\qquad \ddot x=-1\ \text{m/s}^{2}.
\]
Define $\theta$ as the CCW-positive angle from the positive $x$-slot to the rod, so that
\[
x=5\cos\theta,\qquad y=5\sin\theta.
\]
Write $\omega:=\dot\theta$ and $\alpha:=\ddot\theta$. Do not locate an instantaneous center, and do not replace the rod by a particle on a curved guide.

1. Differentiate the slot identity once and solve for the signed velocity $\dot y$. State the unit.

2. Differentiate a second time and solve for the signed acceleration $\ddot y$. State the unit.

3. From $x=5\cos\theta$ obtain $\omega$ and then $\alpha$. Report both as CCW-positive scalars and name the clockwise or counterclockwise sense of each.

4. Close the endpoint accelerations as the second time derivatives of the position vectors $\mathbf r_A=x\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf r_B=y\mathbf j$ expressed through $\theta$. Confirm that the pair
   \[
   \ddot x=-x\omega^{2}-y\alpha,\qquad
   \ddot y=-y\omega^{2}+x\alpha
   \]
   recovers the given $\ddot x$ and the $\ddot y$ already obtained from the constraint.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the second derivative of $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ reduces to $x\ddot x+y\ddot y=0$, so $\ddot y=-x\ddot x/y$”; (ii) “$A$ is moving outward, therefore $\theta$ is increasing and $\omega=+1/2$.”

Do not invoke an instantaneous center of zero velocity, do not quote a prepackaged rigid-point formula for a third body point, and do not introduce kinetics.
permittedResults: If $x^{2}+y^{2}=L^{2}$ with $L$ constant, then $x\dot x+y\dot y=0$ and $\dot x^{2}+x\ddot x+\dot y^{2}+y\ddot y=0$ at every twice-differentiable instant.

If $x=L\cos\theta$ and $y=L\sin\theta$, then $\ddot x=-x\dot\theta^{2}-y\ddot\theta$ and $\ddot y=-y\dot\theta^{2}+x\ddot\theta$. These two scalar identities are the component form of differentiating $\mathbf r_A$ and $\mathbf r_B$ twice.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the circle identity once for ydot and once more for yddot, then read omega from x-dot=-y omega and alpha from x-ddot=-x omega^2-y alpha.
Parametrize both endpoint position vectors by the same floor angle, differentiate each vector twice, and use the given x-ddot as the closing check on alpha.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates x^2+y^2=25 twice and reports ydot=-3/2 m/s and yddot=-13/16 m/s2.
Obtains the CCW-positive floor-angle pair omega=-1/2 (clockwise) and alpha=1/16, and closes both endpoint accelerations.
Rejects dropping the quadratic velocity terms and rejects an unsigned claim that theta is increasing.

commonErrors.description: Reduces the second derivative of x^2+y^2=25 to x xddot+y yddot=0 and reports yddot=3/4 m/s2.
commonErrors.consequence: The squared slot speeds are discarded, so the dependent acceleration of B has the wrong magnitude and the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Takes outward motion of A as proof that theta is increasing and reports omega=+1/2 with the consistent but opposite alpha=-1/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The rod is assigned a counterclockwise spin even though the floor angle must decrease as A moves out and B descends.

hintTree.content: The first derivative is $x\dot x+y\dot y=0$. At $(3,4)$ with $\dot x=2$ this is $6+4\dot y=0$.
Keep the quadratic velocity terms in the second derivative: $4+3(-1)+(9/4)+4\ddot y=0$.
From $x=5\cos\theta$ one has $\dot x=-y\omega$. With $\dot x=2$ and $y=4$ this forces $\omega=-1/2$, after which $\ddot x=-x\omega^{2}-y\alpha$ yields $\alpha=1/16$.

DYN:010442.canonicalSolution:
The slot identity $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ differentiated once is
\[
x\dot x+y\dot y=0.
\]
At the given instant
\[
3\cdot 2+4\dot y=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\dot y=-\frac{3}{2}\ \text{m/s}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\dot y=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
A second differentiation produces
\[
\dot x^{2}+x\ddot x+\dot y^{2}+y\ddot y=0,
\]
so
\[
2^{2}+3(-1)+\Bigl(-\frac{3}{2}\Bigr)^{2}+4\ddot y=0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
4-3+\frac{9}{4}+4\ddot y=0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{13}{4}+4\ddot y=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\ddot y=-\frac{13}{16}\ \text{m/s}^{2},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\ddot y=-\dfrac{13}{16}\ \text{m/s}^{2}}.
\]
The CCW floor angle satisfies $x=5\cos\theta$, hence
\[
\dot x=-5\sin\theta\cdot\omega=-y\omega.
\]
With $\dot x=2$ and $y=4$,
\[
2=-4\omega\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\omega=-\frac12\ \text{rad/s}.
\]
The rate is negative, so $\theta$ is decreasing: the rod is rotating clockwise. Differentiating $\dot x=-y\omega$ once more, or using the ready identity $\ddot x=-x\omega^{2}-y\alpha$, gives
\[
-1=-3\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)^{2}-4\alpha
=-3\cdot\frac14-4\alpha
=-\frac34-4\alpha.
\]
Thus
\[
-1+\frac34=-4\alpha\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
-\frac14=-4\alpha\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha=\frac{1}{16}\ \text{rad/s}^{2}.
\]
The angular acceleration is positive, hence CCW: the clockwise spin is slowing. In boxed form
\[
\boxed{\omega=-\dfrac12\ \text{rad/s (clockwise)}},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\dfrac{1}{16}\ \text{rad/s}^{2}\text{ (CCW)}}.
\]
Vector closure from $\mathbf r_A=5\cos\theta\,\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf r_B=5\sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ is exactly
\[
\ddot x=-x\omega^{2}-y\alpha
=-3\cdot\frac14-4\cdot\frac{1}{16}
=-\frac34-\frac14=-1\ \text{m/s}^{2},
\]
\[
\ddot y=-y\omega^{2}+x\alpha
=-4\cdot\frac14+3\cdot\frac{1}{16}
=-1+\frac{3}{16}
=-\frac{13}{16}\ \text{m/s}^{2}.
\]
The first line recovers the given $\ddot x$; the second line recovers the constraint value of $\ddot y$. The two endpoint accelerations therefore close on the same $(\omega,\alpha)$.

Sentence (i) is false: dropping $\dot x^{2}+\dot y^{2}$ produces the spurious $\ddot y=3/4$ instead of $-13/16$. Sentence (ii) is false: outward motion of $A$ increases $x=5\cos\theta$ only if $\theta$ decreases, so $\omega=-1/2$, not $+1/2$.

No instantaneous center is introduced. The only kinematic objects are the twice-differentiated slot identity and the twice-differentiated floor-angle parametrization.

graderFixtures.proofText: From $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ I obtain $\dot y=-3/2$ m/s and $\ddot y=-13/16$ m/s$^{2}$. The floor angle with $x=5\cos\theta$ gives $\omega=-1/2$ (clockwise) and $\alpha=1/16$ (CCW). The closures $\ddot x=-x\omega^{2}-y\alpha$ and $\ddot y=-y\omega^{2}+x\alpha$ recover $-1$ and $-13/16$.
Differentiating twice I keep only x xddot+y yddot=0. Then yddot=-x xddot/y=3/4 m/s2. I still take ydot=-3/2 m/s.
A is moving outward, so theta increases. From |xdot|=y |omega| I take omega=+1/2 and then alpha=-1/16. I still report ydot=-3/2 and yddot=-13/16.

DYN:010526.title: A released pinned bar has alpha=-15/2 rad/s^2 and pin reaction (0,15) N
DYN:010526.objective: Form the end-pinned inertia of a uniform bar, convert the gravity moment into the angular acceleration at release, and recover the pin reaction from the mass-center acceleration.
DYN:010526.statement:
A uniform rigid bar of mass $m=6$ kg and length $L=2$ m is pinned at the end $O$ and is held at rest in the horizontal position. The pin is ideal. The bar is released from rest. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$, the $x$-axis along the bar from $O$ toward the free end, $y$ upward, and counterclockwise moments positive. Gravity acts in the $-\mathbf j$ direction.

1. Compute the moment of inertia $I_O$ of the bar about the fixed axis through $O$.

2. Compute the moment of gravity about $O$ at the instant of release, and solve $\sum M_O=I_O\alpha$ for the angular acceleration $\boldsymbol\alpha$.

3. At that same instant $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$. Determine the acceleration $\mathbf a_G$ of the mass center.

4. Write $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a_G$ and solve for the pin reaction $\mathbf O=(O_x,O_y)$ on the bar.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “moments about the pin may equally well use the centroidal inertia $I_G=\frac1{12}mL^2$”; (ii) “immediately after release the mass center is in free fall, so $\mathbf a_G=(0,-g)$ and the pin reaction vanishes.”

The bar is a single rigid body released from rest. Do not introduce rolling contact, friction capacity, or a prescribed harmonic torque.
permittedResults: Parallel-axis theorem: $I_O=I_G+md^2$ with $d=\|\mathbf r_{G/O}\|$.
At an instant when $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$, the centripetal term vanishes and $\mathbf a_G=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{G/O}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take moments about the pin to isolate α, then return to ΣF=m aG with aG=α×r_G.
Use the moment equation about G, bringing the unknown pin into ΣMG=IG α, and recover the same pair (α, O).

milestones.criterion: Computes IO=8 kg m^2 and the gravity moment -60 N m, and solves alpha=-15/2 rad/s^2.
Uses ω=0 to obtain aG=(0,-15/2) m/s^2 and the pin reaction (0,15) N.
Rejects writing ΣMO=IG α and rejects a free-fall mass center with a zero pin force.

commonErrors.description: Writes ΣMO=IG α with IG=2 kg m^2, obtaining α=-30 rad/s^2 at release.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular acceleration is four times too large because the parallel-axis shift m(L/2)^2 was discarded.

commonErrors.description: Sets aG=(0,-g)=(0,-10) m/s^2 as if the bar were unsupported, concluding that the pin reaction is (0,0).
commonErrors.consequence: The pin is removed from the kinetics and the kinematic link aG=α×r_G is abandoned.

hintTree.content: $I_O=\frac13\cdot 6\cdot 2^2=8$ kg m$^2$. Gravity $mg=60$ N acts at $G$, a distance $1$ m from $O$.
$\mathbf r_{G/O}\times(-60\mathbf j)=-60\mathbf k$, so $\sum M_O=-60=8\alpha$.
With $\omega=0$, $\mathbf a_G=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{G/O}=(0,-15/2)$. The $y$ force equation is $O_y-60=6\cdot(-15/2)$.

DYN:010526.canonicalSolution:
The end inertia is
\[
I_O=\frac13 mL^2=\frac13\cdot 6\cdot 4=\boxed{8\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}.
\]
Equivalently, $I_G=\frac1{12}mL^2=2$ and $I_O=I_G+m(L/2)^2=2+6\cdot 1=8$.

At the release instant the weight $\mathbf W=(0,-60)$ N acts at $G$, where $\mathbf r_{G/O}=(1,0)$ m. The gravity moment about $O$ is
\[
\mathbf r_{G/O}\times\mathbf W
=(1,0,0)\times(0,-60,0)
=\boxed{-60\,\mathbf k\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}}.
\]
The pin force contributes no moment about $O$. Euler’s law about the fixed axis therefore reads
\[
-60=8\alpha\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=-\frac{15}{2}\ \text{rad/s}^2},
\]
or $\boldsymbol\alpha=-(15/2)\mathbf k$. The sense is clockwise, as gravity demands.

The bar is released from rest, so $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$ and
\[
\mathbf a_G
=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{G/O}
=\Bigl(-\frac{15}{2}\mathbf k\Bigr)\times(1\,\mathbf i)
=\boxed{\bigl(0,-\tfrac{15}{2}\bigr)\ \text{m/s}^2}.
\]
Newton’s law for the mass center is $\mathbf O+\mathbf W=m\mathbf a_G$,
\begin{align*}
O_x&=6\cdot 0=0,\\
O_y-60&=6\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{15}{2}\Bigr)=-45.
\end{align*}
Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbf O=(0,15)\ \text{N}}.
\]
The pin pushes upward with $15$ N and supplies no horizontal force at the initial instant.

Sentence (i) is false: replacing $I_O$ by $I_G=2$ produces $\alpha=-30$ rad/s$^2$ and is not a valid moment equation about $O$. Sentence (ii) is false: free-fall $\mathbf a_G=(0,-10)$ would require a vanishing pin, but then $\sum M_O=-60$ could not equal $I_O\alpha$ with the kinematic $\mathbf a_G=\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{G/O}$.

The model is an ideal pin, a uniform rigid bar, and gravity. It does not use rolling contact or a time-varying applied couple.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $I_O=8$ kg m$^2$, gravity moment $-60$ N m, $\alpha=-15/2$ rad/s$^2$, $\mathbf a_G=(0,-15/2)$ m/s$^2$, and pin reaction $(0,15)$ N.
Moments about O use the centroidal inertia IG=2 kg m^2, so -60=2 alpha and alpha=-30 rad/s^2.
IO=8 and alpha=-15/2 are fine, but right after release G is in free fall, so aG=(0,-10) m/s^2 and the pin reaction is (0,0) N.

DYN:010527.title: Angular impulse 8 N m s takes the flywheel from 4 to 52/5 rad/s; the work is 288/5 J
DYN:010527.objective: For a fixed-axis solid disk driven by a linearly decaying shaft torque, form the polar mass moment, integrate the angular impulse, construct alpha(t) and omega(t), and prove that the rotational work equals the change in kinetic energy.
DYN:010527.statement:
A homogeneous solid circular disk of mass $m=10\ \text{kg}$ and radius $R=0.5\ \text{m}$ is keyed to a fixed frictionless shaft through its mass center, perpendicular to the plane of the disk. The disk therefore rotates as a rigid flywheel about that fixed axis. Its rotation is specified by the signed angular velocity $\omega(t)$ in $\text{rad/s}$. At $t=0$ the flywheel has
\[
\omega(0)=\omega_0=4\ \text{rad/s}.
\]
A single applied shaft torque, positive in the same sense as $\omega$, acts for two seconds:
\[
\tau(t)=6-2t\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m},\qquad 0\le t\le 2\ \text{s}.
\]
No other moment acts about the shaft.

1. Confirm that the mass moment of inertia about the fixed central axis is $I=\tfrac12 mR^2=5/4\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Compute the angular impulse $\displaystyle\int_0^2\tau(t)\,dt$.

2. Write Euler's law $I\alpha=\tau(t)$ and obtain the angular acceleration $\alpha(t)$. Integrate from the given initial spin to obtain $\omega(t)$ on $0\le t\le 2$.

3. Evaluate the terminal spin $\omega(2)$ and the angular displacement
   \[
   \Delta\theta=\int_0^2\omega(t)\,dt.
   \]

4. Compute the change in rotational kinetic energy $\Delta K=\tfrac12 I\bigl(\omega(2)^2-\omega_0^2\bigr)$ and the rotational work
   \[
   W=\int\tau\,d\theta=\int_0^2\tau(t)\,\omega(t)\,dt.
   \]
   Prove that $\Delta K=W$ and report the common exact value in joules.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the polar moment of a solid disk about its center is $I=mR^2$”; (ii) “the work of the torque equals the angular impulse $\int\tau\,dt$.”

The shaft is fixed. Do not introduce a translating mass center, a polar-coordinate particle basis, rolling contact, restitution, or an instantaneous center of zero velocity.
permittedResults: A homogeneous solid circular disk of mass $m$ and radius $R$ has $I=\tfrac12 mR^2$ about the central axis perpendicular to its plane.
Euler's law about a fixed central axis is $I\alpha=\tau$. If $\tau$ is integrable, $\omega(t)=\omega(0)+\int_0^t\alpha(s)\,ds$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate I alpha = 6-2t once for omega and again for theta, then evaluate both 1/2 I (omega_f^2-omega_0^2) and the time integral of tau omega.
Use angular impulse-momentum for omega(2) first, recover omega(t) by a single quadrature, and invoke work-energy rather than expanding tau omega.

milestones.criterion: Computes I=5/4 kg m^2 and the angular impulse 8 N m s, then integrates Euler's law to alpha=24/5-8t/5 and omega=4+24t/5-4t^2/5.
Reports omega(2)=52/5 rad/s, Delta theta=232/15 rad, and Delta K=W=288/5 J.
Rejects the ring inertia I=mR^2 and the claim that work equals the angular impulse.

commonErrors.description: Takes the polar moment as I=mR^2=5/2 kg m^2 instead of (1/2)mR^2=5/4, so alpha and every integrated spin are halved.
commonErrors.consequence: The terminal rate becomes 36/5 rad/s and the work-energy value is no longer 288/5 J.

commonErrors.description: Reports the work of the torque as the angular impulse integral 8 J rather than integral tau d theta.
commonErrors.consequence: Work is assigned the wrong dimension and the numerical value 8 fails to match Delta K.

hintTree.content: $\tfrac12\cdot 10\cdot(1/2)^2=5/4$. The impulse is $\int_0^2(6-2t)\,dt=[6t-t^2]_0^2=8$.
$\alpha=\tau/I=(6-2t)\cdot 4/5=24/5-8t/5$. One further quadrature produces $\omega$.
The product $\tau\omega$ is a cubic. Its definite integral on $[0,2]$ equals $(5/8)\bigl((52/5)^2-16\bigr)$.

DYN:010527.canonicalSolution:
The polar moment about the fixed shaft is
\[
I=\frac12 mR^2=\frac12\cdot 10\cdot\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2=\boxed{\frac54\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}.
\]
The angular impulse of the shaft torque is
\[
\int_0^2(6-2t)\,dt=\bigl[6t-t^2\bigr]_0^2=12-4=\boxed{8\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}}.
\]
Euler's law gives
\[
\alpha(t)=\frac{\tau(t)}{I}=\frac{6-2t}{5/4}=\boxed{\frac{24}{5}-\frac{8t}{5}\ \text{rad/s}^2}.
\]
Integrating from $\omega(0)=4$,
\[
\omega(t)=4+\int_0^t\Bigl(\frac{24}{5}-\frac{8s}{5}\Bigr)\,ds
=\boxed{4+\frac{24t}{5}-\frac{4t^2}{5}\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
The terminal spin is
\[
\omega(2)=4+\frac{48}{5}-\frac{16}{5}=4+\frac{32}{5}=\boxed{\frac{52}{5}\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
Angular impulse-momentum recovers the same value: $I\omega(2)-I\omega_0=8$ implies $\omega(2)=4+8/(5/4)=52/5$. The angular displacement is
\[
\Delta\theta=\int_0^2\Bigl(4+\frac{24t}{5}-\frac{4t^2}{5}\Bigr)\,dt
=\Bigl[4t+\frac{12t^2}{5}-\frac{4t^3}{15}\Bigr]_0^2
=8+\frac{48}{5}-\frac{32}{15}
=\boxed{\frac{232}{15}\ \text{rad}}.
\]
The kinetic-energy change is
\[
\Delta K=\frac12\cdot\frac54\Biggl(\Bigl(\frac{52}{5}\Bigr)^2-4^2\Biggr)
=\frac58\cdot\frac{2704-400}{25}
=\frac58\cdot\frac{2304}{25}
=\boxed{\frac{288}{5}\ \text{J}}.
\]
The rotational work is the time integral of $\tau\omega$. Expanding the cubic
\[
(6-2t)\Bigl(4+\frac{24t}{5}-\frac{4t^2}{5}\Bigr)
=24+\frac{104t}{5}-\frac{72t^2}{5}+\frac{8t^3}{5}
\]
and integrating on $[0,2]$ produces
\[
W=\Bigl[24t+\frac{52t^2}{5}-\frac{24t^3}{5}+\frac{2t^4}{5}\Bigr]_0^2
=48+\frac{208}{5}-\frac{192}{5}+\frac{32}{5}
=\frac{288}{5}\ \text{J}.
\]
Thus $\boxed{\Delta K=W=288/5\ \text{J}}$.

Sentence (i) is false: $I=mR^2=5/2$ is the moment of a thin ring (or of a particle at radius $R$), not of a solid disk, and halves every subsequent $\alpha$ and $\Delta\omega$. Sentence (ii) is false: $\int\tau\,dt=8$ has units of angular momentum, not work; the work is $\int\tau\,d\theta=288/5\ \text{J}$.

The model is a single rigid body on a fixed frictionless shaft. No polar-basis particle kinematics, no contact impulse, and no rolling constraint is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: I use $I=5/4$ kg m$^2$. The angular impulse is $8$ N m s, $\alpha=24/5-8t/5$, $\omega=4+24t/5-4t^2/5$, $\omega(2)=52/5$ rad/s, and $\Delta\theta=232/15$ rad. Work-energy gives $\Delta K=W=288/5$ J.
The polar moment of the disk is I=mR^2=5/2 kg m^2. Then alpha=(6-2t)/(5/2)=12/5-4t/5, omega=4+12t/5-2t^2/5, and omega(2)=36/5 rad/s. The impulse is still 8 N m s.
I obtain I=5/4, omega(2)=52/5 rad/s, and Delta theta=232/15 rad. The work of the torque is the angular impulse integral of 6-2t from 0 to 2, so W=8 J.

DYN:010528.title: The free disk reaches v=4 m/s and omega=12 rad/s; translational work 32 J and rotational work 36 J total 68 J
DYN:010528.objective: For an unconstrained disk on a frictionless plane, integrate the independent center-of-mass and Euler equations under a central force plus a couple, split the work and kinetic energy into translational and rotational parts, and refuse any rolling constraint.
DYN:010528.statement:
A homogeneous solid disk of mass $m=4\ \text{kg}$ and radius $R=0.5\ \text{m}$ lies on a horizontal frictionless plane. The disk is free: there is no friction, no rolling constraint, and no kinematic relation between the motion of the mass center $G$ and the spin about $G$. The central moment is
\[
I_G=\frac12 mR^2=0.5\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2.
\]
The disk is at rest at $t=0$. For $0\le t\le 2\ \text{s}$ two constant actions are applied simultaneously:
- a force $\mathbf F$ of magnitude $8\ \text{N}$ whose line of action passes through $G$,
- a couple of moment $M=3\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ about the axis through $G$ perpendicular to the plane.

After $t=2\ \text{s}$ both actions cease.

1. Explain why the force determines only the motion of $G$ and the couple determines only the spin about $G$. In particular, state why $a=R\alpha$ is not available.

2. Integrate $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a_G$ from rest to obtain the center-of-mass acceleration $a$, the speed $v(2)$, and the distance $s$ traveled by $G$ during the two seconds.

3. Integrate $M=I_G\alpha$ from rest to obtain $\alpha$, $\omega(2)$, and the angular displacement $\theta$ during the two seconds.

4. Compute the translational work and the translational kinetic energy, the rotational work and the rotational kinetic energy, and the totals. Confirm the two work-energy identities separately.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the disk must roll, so $a=R\alpha$ couples the force to the couple”; (ii) “a free couple does no work, so the only work is $F s$.”

Do not introduce friction, a no-slip constraint, an instantaneous center, or an impact.
permittedResults: If a constant force $F$ acts through $G$ on an initially resting mass $m$, then $a=F/m$, $v=at$, and $s=\tfrac12 at^2$.
If a constant couple $M$ acts on an initially resting rotor of inertia $I_G$, then $\alpha=M/I_G$, $\omega=\alpha t$, and $\theta=\tfrac12\alpha t^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the two Newton-Euler equations independently, then check F s against 1/2 m v^2 and M theta against 1/2 I omega^2.
Compute the two kinetic energies from the integrated rates and identify each with the corresponding work, never forming a rolling IC.

milestones.criterion: Decouples F=ma_G from M=I_G alpha and integrates to a=2, v=4, s=4 and alpha=6, omega=12, theta=12.
Splits work and kinetic energy as 32 J translational and 36 J rotational, totaling 68 J.
Rejects the rolling constraint a=R alpha and the claim that a free couple does no work.

commonErrors.description: Imposes the no-slip relation a=R alpha on the frictionless disk, coupling the 8 N force to the 3 N m couple.
commonErrors.consequence: Translation is no longer a=2 m/s^2 and the work split 32+36 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Counts only the translational work Fs=32 J and asserts that a free couple does no work.
commonErrors.consequence: The rotational 36 J is missing and the energy audit fails to reach 68 J.

hintTree.content: Friction is absent, so there is no tangential force at the rim and no reason to set $a=R\alpha$.
$8=4a$ gives $a=2$. Independently, $3=0.5\alpha$ gives $\alpha=6$.
Translational work is $8\cdot 4=32$ J. Rotational work is $3\cdot 12=36$ J.

DYN:010528.canonicalSolution:
Because the plane is frictionless, the only force in the plane is the applied $8\ \text{N}$ through $G$, and the only moment about $G$ is the applied couple $3\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. A force through $G$ has zero moment about $G$, and a couple is a pure moment, so the two equations
\[
F=ma_G,\qquad M=I_G\alpha
\]
decouple. The no-slip statement $a_G=R\alpha$ would require a frictional impulse or force at the contact point, which is identically zero. The disk therefore translates and spins independently.

Translation from rest:
\[
a=\frac{8}{4}=\boxed{2\ \text{m/s}^2},\qquad
v(2)=2\cdot 2=\boxed{4\ \text{m/s}},\qquad
s=\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 2^2=\boxed{4\ \text{m}}.
\]
Rotation from rest:
\[
\alpha=\frac{3}{0.5}=\boxed{6\ \text{rad/s}^2},\qquad
\omega(2)=6\cdot 2=\boxed{12\ \text{rad/s}},\qquad
\theta=\frac12\cdot 6\cdot 2^2=\boxed{12\ \text{rad}}.
\]
Translational work and kinetic energy agree:
\[
W_{\text{tr}}=Fs=8\cdot 4=\boxed{32\ \text{J}},\qquad
K_{\text{tr}}=\frac12 mv^2=\frac12\cdot 4\cdot 16=32\ \text{J}.
\]
Rotational work and kinetic energy agree:
\[
W_{\text{rot}}=M\theta=3\cdot 12=\boxed{36\ \text{J}},\qquad
K_{\text{rot}}=\frac12 I_G\omega^2=\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot 144=36\ \text{J}.
\]
The totals are
\[
\boxed{W=K=68\ \text{J}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: imposing $a=R\alpha$ invents a frictional constraint that the frictionless plane does not supply and ruins both the kinematics and the work split. Sentence (ii) is false: a couple does work $M\theta=36$ J through a finite rotation.

The calculation never uses rolling capacity, an instantaneous center, or an impact map.

graderFixtures.proofText: There is no friction, so $a=2$ m/s$^2$, $v=4$ m/s, $s=4$ m and, independently, $\alpha=6$ rad/s$^2$, $\omega=12$ rad/s, $\theta=12$ rad. Translational work/KE is $32$ J, rotational work/KE is $36$ J, and the total is $68$ J.
The disk rolls, so a=R alpha. From M=I alpha I get alpha=6 rad/s^2 and therefore a=3 m/s^2, v=6 m/s, s=6 m, with omega=12 rad/s and theta=12 rad. The works are 8*6+3*12=84 J.
I get a=2, v=4, s=4 and alpha=6, omega=12, theta=12. A free couple does no work, so the only work is Fs=32 J and the total kinetic energy is 32 J.

DYN:010543.title: A 12 N offset on the 6 kg square gives aG=2 i, M=-12 k, alpha=-3 k, and aP=5 i
DYN:010543.objective: Split an offset in-plane force into mass-center translation and a couple about G, then convert the initial angular acceleration into the acceleration of the loaded edge midpoint.
DYN:010543.statement:
A uniform square plate of mass $m=6$ kg and side $2$ m rests on a smooth horizontal plane and is initially at rest. The geometric center $G$ is the mass center. A single horizontal force
\[
\mathbf F=12\mathbf i\ \text{N}
\]
is applied at the midpoint $P$ of the top edge. In the body axes centered at $G$,
\[
\mathbf r_{P/G}=\mathbf j\ \text{m}.
\]
The centroidal inertia about the vertical axis is the lamina value
\[
I_G=\frac{m}{6}(2)^{2}=4\ \text{kg·m}^{2}.
\]
There is no friction. Gravity and the smooth-plane reaction cancel vertically and do no horizontal work.

1. Write $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a_G$ and solve for $\mathbf a_G$.

2. Form the moment $\mathbf M_G=\mathbf r_{P/G}\times\mathbf F$ and state its unit.

3. Integrate the moment equation $I_G\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf M_G$ for the angular acceleration $\boldsymbol\alpha$.

4. At the initial instant $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$. Compute the acceleration of the loaded point,
   \[
   \mathbf a_P=\mathbf a_G+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/G}.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the force line misses $G$, but $P$ is still a body point, so $\mathbf a_P=\mathbf a_G$”; (ii) “$\mathbf j\times\mathbf i=+\mathbf k$, therefore $\boldsymbol\alpha=+3\mathbf k$.”

Do not pin the plate, do not introduce rolling friction, and do not replace the offset force by a pure couple with $\mathbf a_G=\mathbf 0$.
permittedResults: If a rigid body has a unique external force $\mathbf F$ and mass $m$, then $\mathbf a_G=\mathbf F/m$.
At an instant when $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$, the acceleration of a body point $P$ reduces to $\mathbf a_P=\mathbf a_G+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/G}$; the centripetal term vanishes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve translation at G first, form the single couple r_P/G × F, then add alpha × r at the loaded point while omega is still zero.
Replace the offset force by a force at G plus a couple, integrate both rigid-body laws, and only then reconstruct a_P.

milestones.criterion: Reports aG=2 i m/s2 from the mass-center law and MG=-12 k N m from r×F.
Integrates IG alpha=MG to alpha=-3 k and evaluates the rest-start acceleration aP=5 i.
Rejects equating aP with aG and rejects the reversed planar cross product.

commonErrors.description: Sets aP=aG=2 i because P belongs to the plate, omitting alpha × r_P/G.
commonErrors.consequence: The loaded edge is assigned the mass-center acceleration, so the initial kinematics of P are short by 3 i.

commonErrors.description: Takes j × i = +k, reports M_G=+12 k and alpha=+3 k, and then aP=2 i-3 i=-i.
commonErrors.consequence: The plate is spun the wrong way and the loaded point is predicted to start opposite the applied force.

hintTree.content: Horizontal Newton at $G$ is $12\mathbf i=6\mathbf a_G$.
The planar cross product is $\mathbf j\times 12\mathbf i=-12\mathbf k$. Then $4\boldsymbol\alpha=-12\mathbf k$.
With $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$, $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf j=(-3\mathbf k)\times\mathbf j=3\mathbf i$, so $\mathbf a_P=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf i$.

DYN:010543.canonicalSolution:
The plane is smooth, so $\mathbf F$ is the only horizontal force. The mass-center law is
\[
12\mathbf i=6\mathbf a_G\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf a_G=\boxed{2\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^{2}}.
\]
The moment about $G$ is
\[
\mathbf M_G
=\mathbf j\times 12\mathbf i
=12(\mathbf j\times\mathbf i)
=12(-\mathbf k)
=\boxed{-12\mathbf k\ \text{N·m}}.
\]
The centroidal moment equation then yields
\[
I_G\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf M_G\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
4\boldsymbol\alpha=-12\mathbf k\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boldsymbol\alpha=\boxed{-3\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}^{2}}.
\]
Initially $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$, so
\[
\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/G}
=(-3\mathbf k)\times\mathbf j
=3\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^{2}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf a_P
=\mathbf a_G+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/G}
=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf i
=\boxed{5\mathbf i\ \text{m/s}^{2}}.
\]
The same split shows why an offset force cannot be replaced by a couple alone: $G$ still accelerates at $2\mathbf i$.

Sentence (i) is false: $P$ is a distinct body point, and the missing $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r_{P/G}$ term is $3\mathbf i$. Sentence (ii) is false: $\mathbf j\times\mathbf i=-\mathbf k$, not $+\mathbf k$; the reversed moment would send $\boldsymbol\alpha$ to $+3\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf a_P$ to $-\mathbf i$.

The plate is free and planar. No pin reaction, no rolling contact, and no energy integral is required.

graderFixtures.proofText: Newton at $G$ gives $\mathbf a_G=2\mathbf i$. The couple is $\mathbf j\times 12\mathbf i=-12\mathbf k$, so $\boldsymbol\alpha=-3\mathbf k$. At rest, $\mathbf a_P=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf i=5\mathbf i$.
aG=2 i and alpha=-3 k, but P is a point of the same rigid body so aP=aG=2 i. I never form alpha × r.
I take j × i = +k, so MG=+12 k and alpha=+3 k. Then aP=2 i + (3 k)×j=2 i-3 i=-i.

DYN:010544.title: Transverse impulse 6 N s at the rod end yields vG=2 j, omega=6 k, end speeds 8 and -4, KE=24 J
DYN:010544.objective: Convert a transverse end impulse on a free slender rod into the mass-center velocity and spin, then read both endpoint velocities and the split kinetic energy.
DYN:010544.statement:
A uniform slender rod of mass $m=3$ kg and length $L=2$ m lies at rest on a smooth horizontal plane, aligned with the $x$-axis. The mass center $G$ is at the origin, so the right end $R$ is at $\mathbf r_{R/G}=\mathbf i$ m and the left end $L$ is at $\mathbf r_{L/G}=-\mathbf i$ m. The centroidal inertia is
\[
I_G=\frac{mL^{2}}{12}=1\ \text{kg·m}^{2}.
\]
A single impulsive blow
\[
\mathbf J=6\mathbf j\ \text{N·s}
\]
acts at $R$. No other horizontal impulse acts.

1. Integrate the mass-center law through the blow and solve for $\mathbf v_G$ just afterward.

2. Form the angular impulse $\mathbf r_{R/G}\times\mathbf J$ about $G$ and solve $I_G\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf r_{R/G}\times\mathbf J$ for $\boldsymbol\omega$.

3. Compute the velocities of $R$ and $L$ from
   \[
   \mathbf v=\mathbf v_G+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{/G}.
   \]

4. Split the kinetic energy as $\tfrac12 m v_G^{2}+\tfrac12 I_G\omega^{2}$ and confirm the two summands $6$ J and $18$ J.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “an impulse determines only the motion of $G$, so every point of the rod has velocity $2\mathbf j$”; (ii) “angular impulse should be referred to an end, so $I=mL^{2}/3=4$ and $\omega=3/2$.”

Do not pin either end, do not introduce restitution or a second impacting body, and do not compute work as $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf v_G$ during the blow.
permittedResults: A transverse impulse $\mathbf J=J\mathbf j$ at $\mathbf r=r\mathbf i$ produces the central angular impulse $rJ\mathbf k$.

After the blow, the velocity field of a planar rigid body is $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_G+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{P/G}$, and the kinetic energy splits into translational and rotational summands about $G$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply linear impulse at G and angular impulse about G, then reconstruct the two ends from the rigid velocity field.
Keep IG=mL^2/12 through the spin step so the rotational energy is 18 J and the end formula uses omega=6 rather than a reduced rate.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the linear and central angular impulses to vG=2 j and omega=6 k.
Reports the end velocities 8 j and -4 j and the energy split 6 J+18 J=24 J.
Rejects a translation-only field and rejects using I=mL^2/3 about G.

commonErrors.description: Applies only the linear impulse and assigns every point the velocity 2 j, taking KE=6 J and omega=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The moment of the blow about G is discarded, so both ends are wrong and two-thirds of the kinetic energy is lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes the G-moment equation with I=mL^2/3=4 and reports omega=3/2 k, then vR=7/2 j and vL=1/2 j.
commonErrors.consequence: The spin is four times too small, so the end-velocity split and the rotational energy are those of a different inertia.

hintTree.content: $m\mathbf v_G=\mathbf J$ is $3\mathbf v_G=6\mathbf j$.
$\mathbf i\times 6\mathbf j=6\mathbf k$ and $I_G=1$, so $\boldsymbol\omega=6\mathbf k$.
Right-end addition is $6\mathbf k\times\mathbf i=6\mathbf j$; left-end addition is $6\mathbf k\times(-\mathbf i)=-6\mathbf j$. Energy is $6+18$.

DYN:010544.canonicalSolution:
The rod is free and initially at rest, so
\[
m\mathbf v_G=\mathbf J\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
3\mathbf v_G=6\mathbf j\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf v_G=\boxed{2\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The central angular impulse is
\[
\mathbf r_{R/G}\times\mathbf J
=\mathbf i\times 6\mathbf j
=6\mathbf k\ \text{N·m·s},
\]
and
\[
I_G\boldsymbol\omega=6\mathbf k\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boldsymbol\omega=\boxed{6\mathbf k\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
The endpoint velocities are therefore
\[
\mathbf v_R
=2\mathbf j+6\mathbf k\times\mathbf i
=2\mathbf j+6\mathbf j
=\boxed{8\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}},
\]
\[
\mathbf v_L
=2\mathbf j+6\mathbf k\times(-\mathbf i)
=2\mathbf j-6\mathbf j
=\boxed{-4\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The kinetic energy splits as
\[
\frac12 m v_G^{2}
=\frac12\cdot 3\cdot 4
=\boxed{6\ \text{J}},
\qquad
\frac12 I_G\omega^{2}
=\frac12\cdot 1\cdot 36
=\boxed{18\ \text{J}},
\]
and the total is
\[
\boxed{6+18=24\ \text{J}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: the same impulse has a moment about $G$, so the body field is not a pure translation at $2\mathbf j$. Sentence (ii) is false: the moment equation written about $G$ must use $I_G=mL^{2}/12=1$, not the end inertia $mL^{2}/3$. Using $I=4$ would give $\omega=3/2$ and destroy both end velocities and the $18$ J rotational energy.

The model is a single free rod and one external impulse. No pin, no coefficient of restitution, and no work identity through the blow is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Linear impulse gives $\mathbf v_G=2\mathbf j$. Central angular impulse $6\mathbf k$ with $I_G=1$ gives $\boldsymbol\omega=6\mathbf k$. Then $\mathbf v_R=8\mathbf j$, $\mathbf v_L=-4\mathbf j$, and $\mathrm{KE}=6+18=24$ J.
J=6 j so vG=2 j. I treat the rod as a particle: every point moves at 2 j, omega=0, and KE=6 J.
Angular impulse about G is 6 k but I take I=m L^2/3=4, so omega=3/2 k. Then vR=2j+(3/2)j=7/2 j and vL=2j-(3/2)j=1/2 j.

DYN:010629.title: Underdamped free decay has omega_d=4 and log decrement 3pi/2; same-phase peaks ratio e^{3pi/2}
DYN:010629.objective: Classify a viscously damped free SDOF oscillator as underdamped, fit the two free constants to a rest release, and extract the damped period, logarithmic decrement, and same-phase peak ratio.
DYN:010629.statement:
A linear single-degree-of-freedom oscillator has mass $m=1\ \text{kg}$, viscous damping $c=6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s/m}$, and stiffness $k=25\ \text{N/m}$. There is no external force. The free motion satisfies
\[
\ddot x+6\dot x+25x=0,
\]
with the rest-release data
\[
x(0)=0.1\ \text{m},\qquad \dot x(0)=0.
\]

1. Compute the undamped natural frequency $\omega_n$, the damping ratio $\zeta$, and the damped frequency $\omega_d$. Confirm that the motion is underdamped.

2. Write the underdamped free solution
   \[
   x(t)=e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\bigl(A\cos\omega_d t+B\sin\omega_d t\bigr)
   \]
   and determine $A$ and $B$ from the initial data. (A vanishing initial velocity does not force $B=0$.)

3. Compute the damped period $T_d=2\pi/\omega_d$ and the logarithmic decrement
   \[
   \delta=\ln\frac{x(t)}{x(t+T_d)}=\zeta\omega_n T_d
   \]
   evaluated on successive same-phase peaks.

4. Report the same-phase peak ratio $x(t)/x(t+T_d)$ as an exact exponential.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “because the mass is released from rest, the solution is a pure damped cosine, $B=0$”; (ii) “the logarithmic decrement is the decay constant $\zeta\omega_n$ itself.”

The oscillator is free. Do not introduce a harmonic forcing function, a particular solution, or a two-mass modal analysis.
permittedResults: If $x(t)=e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}(A\cos\omega_d t+B\sin\omega_d t)$, then $x(0)=A$ and $\dot x(0)=-\zeta\omega_n A+\omega_d B$.
Successive same-phase peaks of an underdamped free response stand in the exact ratio $e^{\zeta\omega_n T_d}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute zeta and omegad first, apply both initial conditions to A and B, then form delta = zeta omegan Td.
Write x(t)=D e^{-3t} cos(4t-phi), fit D and phi to the rest release, and read the peak ratio from the exponential envelope over one Td.

milestones.criterion: Classifies the oscillator as underdamped with omegan=5, zeta=3/5, and omegad=4, and fits A=0.1, B=0.075.
Reports Td=pi/2, log decrement 3pi/2, and same-phase peak ratio e^{3pi/2}.
Rejects the pure-damped-cosine shortcut from v(0)=0 and the identification of delta with zeta omegan.

commonErrors.description: Sets B=0 because the initial velocity vanishes, writing x=0.1 e^{-3t} cos 4t.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated motion has xdot(0)=-0.3 m/s and is not the rest release.

commonErrors.description: Reports the logarithmic decrement as the decay constant zeta omegan=3 rather than 3 Td = 3pi/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The same-phase peak ratio is written e^3 instead of e^{3pi/2}.

hintTree.content: $\omega_n=\sqrt{25}=5$ and $\zeta=6/(2\cdot 5)=3/5<1$, so $\omega_d=5\sqrt{1-9/25}=4$.
$\dot x(0)=-3A+4B=0$ with $A=0.1$ forces $B=0.075$, not $B=0$.
$T_d=\pi/2$, so $\delta=3\cdot\pi/2=3\pi/2$ and the peak ratio is $e^{3\pi/2}$.

DYN:010629.canonicalSolution:
The undamped frequency and damping ratio are
\[
\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\boxed{5\ \text{rad/s}},
\qquad
\zeta=\frac{c}{2m\omega_n}=\frac{6}{10}=\boxed{\frac35}.
\]
Because $0<\zeta<1$ the free motion is underdamped, with
\[
\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}=5\sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}}=5\cdot\frac45=\boxed{4\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
The decay constant is $\zeta\omega_n=3$. The general underdamped solution is
\[
x(t)=e^{-3t}\bigl(A\cos 4t+B\sin 4t\bigr).
\]
The initial displacement gives $A=x(0)=0.1$. Differentiating,
\[
\dot x(t)=-3e^{-3t}(A\cos 4t+B\sin 4t)+e^{-3t}(-4A\sin 4t+4B\cos 4t),
\]
so $\dot x(0)=-3A+4B=0$. Hence $4B=0.3$ and $B=0.075$. The free response is
\[
\boxed{x(t)=e^{-3t}\bigl[0.1\cos 4t+0.075\sin 4t\bigr]\ \text{m}}.
\]
The damped period is
\[
T_d=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_d}=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}\ \text{s}}.
\]
The logarithmic decrement is
\[
\delta=\zeta\omega_n T_d=3\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\boxed{\frac{3\pi}{2}},
\]
which matches $2\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}=2\pi\cdot(3/5)/(4/5)=3\pi/2$. Successive same-phase peaks therefore stand in the ratio
\[
\boxed{\frac{x(t)}{x(t+T_d)}=e^{3\pi/2}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $\dot x(0)=0$ constrains $-3A+4B=0$, not $B=0$. The pure-cosine choice $x=0.1e^{-3t}\cos 4t$ has $\dot x(0)=-0.3\neq 0$. Sentence (ii) is false: $\zeta\omega_n=3$ is the decay rate in inverse seconds, not the dimensionless decrement $\delta=3\pi/2$.

No forcing term is introduced. The oscillator remains a single viscously damped degree of freedom.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\omega_n=5$, $\zeta=3/5$, $\omega_d=4$, and $x=e^{-3t}[0.1\cos 4t+0.075\sin 4t]$. Then $T_d=\pi/2$, $\delta=3\pi/2$, and the same-phase peak ratio is $e^{3\pi/2}$.
Released from rest, so B=0 and x=0.1 e^{-3t} cos 4t. The period is still Td=pi/2 and the log decrement is 3pi/2.
The response is x=e^{-3t}[0.1 cos 4t + 0.075 sin 4t] with omegad=4. The logarithmic decrement is the decay constant itself, delta=3, so successive peaks ratio e^3.

DYN:010630.title: Coulomb half-cycle loss is 0.04 m; the mass sticks after 7 half-cycles at 7pi/10 s
DYN:010630.objective: Under ideal Coulomb damping, derive the constant amplitude drop per half-cycle from the shifted-equilibrium construction, list the turning-point amplitudes, and count the half-cycles to the stick threshold.
DYN:010630.statement:
A mass $m=1\ \text{kg}$ is attached to a linear spring of stiffness $k=100\ \text{N/m}$ and slides on a dry horizontal surface. The friction force has constant magnitude $F_c=2\ \text{N}$ whenever the mass is moving and opposes the velocity. Static and kinetic friction are equal (ideal Coulomb damping: no extra stiction, no viscous term, no dependence of $F_c$ on speed or on position except through the sign of $\dot x$). The undamped natural frequency is $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}=10\ \text{rad/s}$. The mass is released from rest at
\[
A_0=+0.30\ \text{m}.
\]

Ideal Coulomb motion between reversals is simple harmonic about the displaced equilibrium $x=\pm F_c/k$, and the half-period between consecutive turning points remains $\pi/\omega_n$ independently of amplitude.

1. State the ideal Coulomb assumptions just given, including the equal static and kinetic magnitudes. Derive the turning-point drop $2F_c/k$ per half-cycle and the full-cycle drop $4F_c/k$. Give both lengths in meters.

2. List the signed positions and magnitudes of the successive alternating turning points starting from $A_0=+0.30\ \text{m}$ until the remaining amplitude is no larger than the stick threshold.

3. The mass sticks at the first turning point that satisfies $|A|\le F_c/k$. Compute the stick threshold $F_c/k$, the number of half-cycles required to reach it, and the elapsed time. Count a half-cycle as one swing from one turning point to the next.

4. Confirm that after that many half-cycles the amplitude equals the stick threshold exactly, so the spring force no longer exceeds $F_c$ and the mass remains at rest.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “each half-cycle drops the amplitude by the full-cycle amount $4F_c/k=0.08\ \text{m}$”; (ii) “Coulomb friction cannot hold the mass at a nonzero displacement, so motion continues until the amplitude is zero.”

Do not replace Coulomb friction by a viscous dashpot, and do not treat the oscillator as forced.
permittedResults: Released from rest at $A_0>F_c/k$, the first half-cycle is harmonic about $+F_c/k$ with radius $A_0-F_c/k$, so the next turning point is at $-(A_0-2F_c/k)$. Each half-cycle therefore drops the extreme amplitude by $2F_c/k$.
The time between consecutive turning points is $\pi/\omega_n$, independent of the current amplitude.

acceptableStrategies.description: Shift the equilibrium by ±Fc/k on each half-cycle, read the 2Fc/k drop from the two radii, then decrement A0 until A<=Fc/k.
Use the standard memory rule (amplitude falls 2Fc/k per reversal, sticks at Fc/k) and multiply the half-count by pi/omegan.

milestones.criterion: States the ideal Coulomb assumptions and derives the half-cycle drop 0.04 m and full-cycle drop 0.08 m.
Lists the alternating signed turning positions and their magnitudes down to 0.02 m and concludes stick after 7 half-cycles at t=7pi/10 s.
Rejects treating 4Fc/k as a half-cycle drop and rejects continuing the motion until amplitude zero.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full-cycle drop 4Fc/k=0.08 m as the loss on each half-cycle.
commonErrors.consequence: The turning list becomes 0.30,0.22,0.14,0.06 and the stick time is no longer 7pi/10 s.

commonErrors.description: Continues the 0.04 m half-cycle drop past Fc/k=0.02 m down to amplitude zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The motion is given a non-physical extra half-swing and the reported duration is not 7pi/10 s.

hintTree.content: $2F_c/k=4/100=0.04\ \text{m}$ and $F_c/k=0.02\ \text{m}$. The full-cycle drop is twice the half-cycle drop.
After $7$ half-cycles the amplitude is exactly $0.02=F_c/k$. Each half-cycle lasts $\pi/10$ s.

DYN:010630.canonicalSolution:
Ideal Coulomb assumptions used here: the friction force has constant magnitude $F_c=2\ \text{N}$ and is opposite to the velocity whenever $\dot x\neq 0$; static and kinetic magnitudes are equal, so there is no extra stiction; there is no viscous term and $F_c$ does not depend on speed. Between reversals the signed equilibrium is the constant $x=\pm F_c/k$.

Released from rest at $A_0=+0.30\ \text{m}$, the first motion has $\dot x<0$, so friction equals $+F_c$. Newton's law is
\[
\ddot x+\omega_n^2\Bigl(x-\frac{F_c}{k}\Bigr)=0,
\]
simple harmonic motion about $x_c=+F_c/k$ with radius $A_0-F_c/k$. The next turning point is
\[
x_c-(A_0-F_c/k)=2F_c/k-A_0=-(A_0-2F_c/k).
\]
Thus each half-cycle drops the extreme amplitude by
\[
\frac{2F_c}{k}=\frac{4}{100}=\boxed{0.04\ \text{m}},
\]
and each full cycle drops it by
\[
\frac{4F_c}{k}=\boxed{0.08\ \text{m}}.
\]
The successive signed turning positions are
\[
+0.30,\;-0.26,\;+0.22,\;-0.18,\;+0.14,\;-0.10,\;+0.06,\;-0.02\ \text{m}.
\]
Their magnitudes are
\[
0.30,\;0.26,\;0.22,\;0.18,\;0.14,\;0.10,\;0.06,\;0.02.
\]
The stick threshold is
\[
\frac{F_c}{k}=\frac{2}{100}=\boxed{0.02\ \text{m}}.
\]
After $n$ half-cycles the amplitude is $0.30-n\cdot 0.04$. This first meets $0.02$ at $n=7$:
\[
0.30-7\cdot 0.04=0.02.
\]
A half-cycle lasts $\pi/\omega_n=\pi/10$ s, so the elapsed time is
\[
\boxed{7\text{ half-cycles at }t=7\pi/10\ \text{s}}.
\]
At that seventh turning point $kA=F_c$, so the available spring force no longer exceeds friction and the mass sticks. Counting is from turning point to turning point: seven such swings, not seven full periods, and not an extra half-cycle down to amplitude zero.

Sentence (i) is false: $4F_c/k$ is the drop per full cycle (two reversals). Using $0.08$ per half-cycle reaches the threshold after the wrong number of swings. Sentence (ii) is false: when $|A|\le F_c/k$ the spring cannot overcome $F_c$, so the mass sticks at $0.02\ \text{m}$ and never continues to zero.

The model is an unforced SDOF oscillator with ideal dry friction only.

graderFixtures.proofText: Ideal Coulomb friction drops the amplitude by $2F_c/k=0.04$ m each half-cycle ($0.08$ m per full cycle). The signed turning positions are $+0.30,-0.26,+0.22,-0.18,+0.14,-0.10,+0.06,-0.02$ m. The mass sticks at $F_c/k=0.02$ m after $7$ half-cycles, at $t=7\pi/10$ s.
Each half-cycle drops the amplitude by 4Fc/k=0.08 m. I solve 0.30-0.08n<=0.02, obtain n>=3.5, and round up to report 4 half-cycles at t=2pi/5 s.

The half-cycle drop is 0.04 m, but I ignore the stick threshold at the seventh turning point and extrapolate the linear amplitude envelope to zero halfway through the next nominal half-period. I therefore report 7.5 half-periods and t=3pi/4 s.

DYN:010631.title: Parallel torsional springs give omega_n=2sqrt2; amplitude sqrt6/20 rad and energy 3/25 J
DYN:010631.objective: Reduce two grounded torsional springs on a single rotor to one equivalent stiffness, solve the undamped SDOF free response from mixed initial data, and report the motion amplitude and the conserved mechanical energy.
DYN:010631.statement:
A single rigid rotor has mass moment of inertia $I=2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ about its fixed spin axis. Two linear torsional springs, of stiffnesses
\[
k_1=6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad},\qquad k_2=10\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad},
\]
are attached in parallel between the same rotor and a fixed frame: each spring sees the same rotation $\theta$ of the one rotor, and their restoring moments add. There is no damper and no second rotor. The free equation is therefore the single-degree-of-freedom statement
\[
I\ddot\theta+(k_1+k_2)\theta=0.
\]
The initial data are
\[
\theta(0)=0.1\ \text{rad},\qquad \dot\theta(0)=-0.2\ \text{rad/s}.
\]

1. Form the equivalent torsional stiffness $k_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and the undamped natural frequency $\omega_n=\sqrt{k_{\mathrm{eq}}/I}$.

2. Write $\theta(t)=A\cos\omega_n t+B\sin\omega_n t$ and apply both initial conditions. Record the exact coefficients.

3. Compute the motion amplitude $\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ in radians.

4. Compute the conserved mechanical energy
   \[
   E=\frac12 I\dot\theta(0)^2+\frac12 k_{\mathrm{eq}}\theta(0)^2
   \]
   and confirm that it equals $\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{eq}}$ times the squared amplitude.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the two springs are in series, so $k_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_1k_2/(k_1+k_2)$”; (ii) “two springs require two rotors and therefore two natural frequencies.”

Keep the model as one SDOF rotor. Do not introduce a two-mass (two-rotor) modal problem, and do not add damping or a prescribed harmonic torque.
permittedResults: If $\theta=A\cos\omega_n t+B\sin\omega_n t$, then $\theta(0)=A$ and $\dot\theta(0)=B\omega_n$.
For undamped free SDOF motion, $\tfrac12 I\dot\theta(0)^2+\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{eq}}\theta(0)^2=\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{eq}}(A^2+B^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the two grounded stiffnesses, solve the SDOF oscillator from the two initial conditions, and read amplitude and energy from A and B.
Compute energy directly from the initial data and recover the amplitude as sqrt(2E/keq), after checking keq=k1+k2.

milestones.criterion: Forms keq=16 and omegan=2 sqrt(2), then fits theta=0.1 cos(2sqrt2 t) - 1/(10 sqrt2) sin(2sqrt2 t).
Reports amplitude sqrt6/20 rad and conserved energy 3/25 J.
Rejects series stiffness 15/4 and any two-rotor / two-frequency reduction.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two grounded springs as series elements and sets keq=k1 k2/(k1+k2)=15/4 N m/rad.
commonErrors.consequence: The natural frequency becomes sqrt(15/8) and every subsequent coefficient is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Introduces a second rotor so that the two springs connect two inertias, and reports a pair of natural frequencies.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned hardware is a single SDOF rotor; the two-mass modes are not present.

hintTree.content: Both springs see the same $\theta$, so $k_{\mathrm{eq}}=6+10=16$ and $\omega_n=\sqrt{16/2}=2\sqrt{2}$.

DYN:010631.canonicalSolution:
The springs are parallel on a single rotor, so
\[
k_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_1+k_2=\boxed{16\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}}.
\]
The undamped frequency is
\[
\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{k_{\mathrm{eq}}}{I}}=\sqrt{\frac{16}{2}}=\sqrt{8}=\boxed{2\sqrt{2}\ \text{rad/s}}.
\]
The free solution $\theta(t)=A\cos(2\sqrt{2}\,t)+B\sin(2\sqrt{2}\,t)$ has $A=\theta(0)=0.1$ and
\[
B=\frac{\dot\theta(0)}{\omega_n}=\frac{-0.2}{2\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{1}{10\sqrt{2}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\theta(t)=0.1\cos(2\sqrt{2}\,t)-\frac{1}{10\sqrt{2}}\sin(2\sqrt{2}\,t)\ \text{rad}}.
\]
The amplitude is
\[
\sqrt{A^2+B^2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}+\frac{1}{200}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{200}}=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{6}}{20}\ \text{rad}}.
\]
The conserved energy from the initial data is
\[
E=\frac12\cdot 2\cdot(0.2)^2+\frac12\cdot 16\cdot(0.1)^2
=0.04+0.08
=\boxed{\frac{3}{25}\ \text{J}}.
\]
The same value is $\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{eq}}(A^2+B^2)=8\cdot(3/200)=3/25$ J. There is a single inertia and a single rotation, so there is only one natural frequency.

Sentence (i) is false: series reduction $k_{\mathrm{eq}}=60/16=15/4$ describes two springs sharing a torque through an intermediate angle, not two grounded springs on one rotor; it produces $\omega_n=\sqrt{15/8}$ and a different response. Sentence (ii) is false: two grounded springs on one rotor remain SDOF. A two-rotor model would invent a second inertia and a pair of modal frequencies that the hardware does not have.

No damper and no prescribed harmonic torque is introduced.

graderFixtures.proofText: Parallel reduction gives $k_{\mathrm{eq}}=16$ and $\omega_n=2\sqrt{2}$. The free response is $\theta=0.1\cos(2\sqrt{2}\,t)-1/(10\sqrt{2})\sin(2\sqrt{2}\,t)$, with amplitude $\sqrt{6}/20$ rad and energy $3/25$ J.
The springs act in series, so keq=6*10/16=15/4 N m/rad and omegan=sqrt(15/8). Then B=-0.2/omegan and the amplitude is no longer sqrt6/20.

Two springs require two rotors. I split I=2 into a pair of inertias joined by k1 and k2 and compute two modal frequencies. The motion is a linear combination of both modes, not a single 2 sqrt(2) oscillation.

DYN:010645.title: Gravity step from slack is x=(2/5)(1-cos 5t); vmax=2 at pi/10 and xmax=4/5 with spring 40 N
DYN:010645.objective: Shift a suddenly applied weight to the static sag of an initially slack spring, write the 1-cosine particular-plus-homogeneous response, and extract the first speed and stretch extrema together with the peak spring force.
DYN:010645.statement:
A linear spring of stiffness $k=50$ N/m hangs vertically and is initially unstretched. A particle of mass $m=2$ kg is attached at rest to the free end and released. Take $g=10$ m/s$^{2}$. Measure the downward displacement $x(t)$ from the unstretched position. The motion begins at
\[
x(0)=0,\qquad \dot x(0)=0,
\]
and thereafter obeys
\[
m\ddot x=-kx+mg.
\]
No damper is present.

1. Compute the undamped natural frequency $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}$ and the static sag $x_{\mathrm{eq}}=mg/k$.

2. Shift to $z=x-x_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and solve the release-from-slack problem. Show that
   \[
   x(t)=\frac25\bigl(1-\cos 5t\bigr).
   \]

3. Locate the first instant of maximum downward speed and report that speed.

4. Locate the first instant of maximum stretch and report $x_{\max}$. Then compute the maximum spring force $k x_{\max}$ and compare it with $2mg$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the mass simply settles at the sag $x_{\mathrm{eq}}=2/5$ m and remains there”; (ii) “measured from the unstretched end, the motion is $x=(2/5)\cos 5t$.”

Do not introduce viscous or Coulomb damping, do not replace the gravity step by a harmonic base motion, and do not treat the spring as torsional.
permittedResults: The equation $m\ddot x+kx=mg$ is equivalent to $\ddot z+\omega_n^{2}z=0$ with $z=x-mg/k$ and $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}$.
The unique solution with $x(0)=\dot x(0)=0$ is $x(t)=x_{\mathrm{eq}}(1-\cos\omega_n t)$. Its first speed maximum occurs at $\omega_n t=\pi/2$ and its first stretch maximum at $\omega_n t=\pi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Shift to the sag coordinate, fit z(0)=-xeq and zdot(0)=0, then translate back to x=xeq(1-cos omega t) before reading extrema.
Leave the equation as xddot+25x=10, add the particular solution 2/5, and fit the two rest conditions directly on x.

milestones.criterion: Reports omega_n=5 and xeq=2/5 m and constructs x=(2/5)(1-cos 5t) from the slack rest data.
Locates vmax=2 m/s at t=pi/10 and xmax=4/5 m at t=pi/5, with peak spring force 40 N=2mg.
Rejects a static sag-only settle and rejects a homogeneous cosine written from the unstretched origin.

commonErrors.description: Claims the mass translates to xeq=2/5 m and remains there, so vmax=0 and xmax=2/5 m.
commonErrors.consequence: The homogeneous oscillator about the sag is discarded, and both the dynamic overshoot and the 40 N peak force are lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes x=(2/5) cos 5t from the unstretched origin, missing the particular sag, and reports xmax=2/5 m.
commonErrors.consequence: The initial stretch is not zero and the motion never reaches 4/5 m, so the peak spring force is predicted as only mg.

hintTree.content: $\omega_n=\sqrt{50/2}=5$ and $x_{\mathrm{eq}}=20/50=2/5$.
$\dot x=2\sin 5t$ peaks at $t=\pi/10$; $x$ peaks at $t=\pi/5$ with value $4/5$, and $k x_{\max}=40$.

DYN:010645.canonicalSolution:
The undamped frequency and the sag are
\[
\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{50}{2}}=\boxed{5\ \text{rad/s}},
\qquad
x_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{mg}{k}=\frac{20}{50}=\boxed{\frac25\ \text{m}}.
\]
Set $z=x-2/5$. Then $\ddot z+25z=0$. The initial slack rest state is
\[
z(0)=-\frac25,\qquad \dot z(0)=0,
\]
so
\[
z(t)=-\frac25\cos 5t
\]
and
\[
x(t)=\frac25-\frac25\cos 5t
=\boxed{\dfrac25\bigl(1-\cos 5t\bigr)}.
\]
The velocity is
\[
\dot x(t)=2\sin 5t.
\]
The first positive peak of $\sin 5t$ occurs at $5t=\pi/2$, that is at
\[
t=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{10}\ \text{s}},
\]
and
\[
v_{\max}=\boxed{2\ \text{m/s}}.
\]
The first maximum of $1-\cos 5t$ occurs at $5t=\pi$, that is at
\[
t=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{5}\ \text{s}},
\]
where
\[
x_{\max}=\frac25\bigl(1-(-1)\bigr)=\boxed{\frac45\ \text{m}}.
\]
The corresponding spring force is
\[
k x_{\max}=50\cdot\frac45=\boxed{40\ \text{N}}=2mg,
\]
since $mg=20$ N. The extra $mg$ above the static load is the dynamic overshoot of an undamped step.

Sentence (i) is false: there is no damper, so the mass does not settle; it oscillates between $0$ and $4/5$ m. Sentence (ii) is false: $x=(2/5)\cos 5t$ misses the particular solution $x_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and never reaches $4/5$ m, nor does it satisfy $x(0)=0$.

The forcing is a constant gravity step, not a harmonic support motion and not a free decay about an already-loaded equilibrium.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\omega_n=5$ and $x_{\mathrm{eq}}=2/5$. The slack rest solution is $x=(2/5)(1-\cos 5t)$, with $v_{\max}=2$ m/s at $t=\pi/10$ and $x_{\max}=4/5$ m at $t=\pi/5$. The peak spring force is $40$ N $=2mg$.
The sag is xeq=2/5 m. After release the mass settles there and stays. So vmax=0, xmax=2/5 m, and the spring force is 20 N.
From the unstretched origin I write x=(2/5) cos 5t. Then xmax=2/5 m and the peak spring force is 20 N. I still take omega=5.
