DYN:010646.title: Critical release x=(1/10+t/5)e^{-2t} has no overshoot; peak speed 1/(5e) at t=1/2
DYN:010646.objective: Recognize a critically damped oscillator, fit the (A+Bt)e^{-ωt} release-from-rest solution, prove the coordinate never changes sign, and maximize the speed.
DYN:010646.statement:
A viscously damped oscillator has
\[
m=1\ \text{kg},\qquad
c=4\ \text{N·s/m},\qquad
k=4\ \text{N/m},
\]
and is released from
\[
x(0)=\frac{1}{10}\ \text{m},\qquad
\dot x(0)=0.
\]
The coordinate $x$ is already measured from the static equilibrium of any constant load.

1. Compute $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}$ and $\zeta=c/(2m\omega_n)$. Identify the damping case.

2. Write the critically damped family $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-\omega_n t}$ and fit $A$ and $B$ to the release data. Show that
   \[
   x(t)=\Bigl(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{t}{5}\Bigr)e^{-2t}.
   \]

3. Differentiate and show that
   \[
   \dot x(t)=-\frac25\, t\, e^{-2t}.
   \]
   Deduce that $x(t)$ never changes sign for $t\ge 0$.

4. Maximize the speed $|\dot x|$ for $t>0$. Report the maximizing time and the speed value.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\zeta=1$ still permits a damped sinusoid, so $x$ overshoots”; (ii) “critical damping has only one time factor, so $x=(1/10)e^{-2t}$ and the speed is largest at $t=0$.”

Do not replace the damper by Coulomb friction, do not switch to a torsional coordinate, and do not treat the case as a forced step.
permittedResults: If $\zeta=1$ and $\dot x(0)=0$, then $B=\omega_n A$ with $A=x(0)$, hence $x(t)=x(0)(1+\omega_n t)e^{-\omega_n t}$.
For $x(t)=x(0)(1+\omega_n t)e^{-\omega_n t}$ one has $\dot x(t)=-x(0)\omega_n^{2} t e^{-\omega_n t}$. The speed $|\dot x|$ on $t>0$ is maximized at $t=1/\omega_n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Classify zeta first, fit A and B to x(0) and v(0), then maximize t e^{-2t} by a single derivative.
Write the rest-release template x=x0(1+omega t)e^{-omega t} with omega=2, differentiate once, and read the critical point t=1/omega.

milestones.criterion: Identifies zeta=1 and fits x=(1/10+t/5)e^{-2t} to the rest data.
Produces v=-(2/5)t e^{-2t}, rules out overshoot, and reports the peak speed 1/(5e) at t=1/2.
Rejects an underdamped sinusoid and rejects a single-exponential critical solution.

commonErrors.description: Treats zeta=1 as still oscillatory, writes a damped sinusoid, and claims the mass overshoots the origin.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonexistent damped period is introduced, so both the sign of x and the peak-speed calculation belong to the wrong damping case.

commonErrors.description: Drops the t e^{-2t} term and writes x=(1/10)e^{-2t}, then claims the maximum speed is 1/5 m/s at t=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The rest condition v(0)=0 is lost, and the true interior peak 1/(5e) is replaced by the release value of a different solution.

hintTree.content: $\omega_n=\sqrt4=2$ and $\zeta=4/(2\cdot 1\cdot 2)=1$, so the case is critical.
$A=1/10$ and $\dot x(0)=B-2A=0$ force $B=1/5$. Differentiating the product yields $\dot x=-(2/5)t e^{-2t}$.
The speed $(2/5)t e^{-2t}$ has a critical point where $1-2t=0$, hence $t=1/2$ and $|\dot x|=1/(5e)$.

DYN:010646.canonicalSolution:
The natural frequency and damping ratio are
\[
\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{4}{1}}=\boxed{2\ \text{rad/s}},
\qquad
\zeta=\frac{4}{2\cdot 1\cdot 2}=\boxed{1}.
\]
The oscillator is therefore critically damped, and
\[
x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-2t}.
\]
The rest data give $A=1/10$ and
\[
\dot x(0)=B-2A=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad B=\frac15.
\]
Hence
\[
x(t)=\boxed{\Bigl(\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{t}{5}\Bigr)e^{-2t}}.
\]
Differentiating the product,
\begin{align*}
\dot x
&=\frac15 e^{-2t}+\Bigl(\frac{1}{10}+\frac t5\Bigr)(-2)e^{-2t}
=e^{-2t}\Bigl(\frac15-\frac15-\frac{2t}{5}\Bigr)
=\boxed{-\dfrac25\, t\, e^{-2t}}.
\end{align*}
For $t\ge 0$ the prefactor $1/10+t/5$ is positive and the exponential is positive, so $x(t)>0$. There is no overshoot. The velocity is nonpositive, and the speed is
\[
\bigl|\dot x(t)\bigr|=\frac25\, t\, e^{-2t}.
\]
Set the derivative of $t e^{-2t}$ to zero:
\[
e^{-2t}(1-2t)=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad t=\frac12\ \text{s}.
\]
The peak speed is
\[
\bigl|\dot x\bigr|_{\max}
=\frac25\cdot\frac12\cdot e^{-1}
=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{5e}\ \text{m/s}}
\quad\text{at}\quad
\boxed{t=\dfrac12\ \text{s}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $\zeta=1$ is not underdamped; there is no $\omega_d$ and no sinusoid, and $x$ stays positive. Sentence (ii) is false: a repeated root still supplies the independent factor $t e^{-\omega_n t}$. Dropping it makes the rest condition $\dot x(0)=0$ impossible unless $x(0)=0$, and it wrongly places the speed maximum at the release instant (where the true speed is $0$).

The damper is linear and viscous. The problem is free, not a forced step, and not a Coulomb or torsional oscillator.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\omega_n=2$ and $\zeta=1$. The rest fit is $x=(1/10+t/5)e^{-2t}$ with $\dot x=-(2/5)t e^{-2t}$. There is no overshoot. The speed peaks at $t=1/2$ with value $1/(5e)$.
zeta=1 but I still write a damped sinusoid x=e^{-2t}(A cos omega_d t+B sin omega_d t) and conclude that x overshoots. I never form (A+Bt)e^{-2t}.
Critical damping has only one exponential, so x=(1/10)e^{-2t}. Then v=-(1/5)e^{-2t}, which is largest at t=0 with speed 1/5 m/s.

ED:020117.title: Parallel static fields: energy density, vanishing Poynting flux, and the mixed-trace-free stress-energy tensor
ED:020117.objective: For E=3E0 ẑ and B=4E0/c ẑ in SI with metric signature +---, prove u=25 ε0 E0²/2, S=0, σ=diag(−u,−u,+u), T^{ij}=diag(+u,+u,−u), mixed trace T^μ_μ=0, and that the defined laboratory-slice field energy-momentum integral over a volume V has components P^μ=(U/c,0,0,0) and component quadratic P²=(U/c)², without treating the field-only integral as the conserved four-momentum of a closed system.
ED:020117.statement:
Work in SI units with the Minkowski metric of signature $(+,-,-,-)$.
A static electromagnetic field occupies a laboratory region and is
spatially uniform there:
\[
\mathbf{E}=3E_0\,\hat{\mathbf{z}},\qquad
\mathbf{B}=\frac{4E_0}{c}\,\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\]
with $E_0>0$. Adopt the dictionary
\[
T^{00}=u,\qquad
T^{0i}=\frac{S^i}{c},\qquad
T^{ij}=-\sigma^{ij},
\]
where $u$ is the field energy density, $\mathbf{S}$ is the Poynting
vector, and $\sigma^{ij}$ is the Maxwell stress tensor. Do not replace
this parallel-field stress-energy audit by a crossed-field Maxwell
tensor, a component / invariant catalogue of $\mathbf{E}\perp\mathbf{B}$,
or a covariant Lorentz-force / uniform-parallel-$E$ boost problem.

1. Compute the energy density and the Poynting vector, and prove
   \[
   u=\frac{25}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2,\qquad
   \mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}.
   \]

2. Evaluate the Maxwell stress tensor and the spatial block of
   $T^{\mu\nu}$, and prove
   \[
   \sigma^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(-u,-u,+u),\qquad
   T^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(+u,+u,-u).
   \]
   Show that the mixed trace vanishes: $T^\mu{}_\mu=0$.

3. Let $U=uV$ be the field energy stored in a laboratory volume $V$
   on which the fields are the given constants. Define the
   laboratory-slice field energy-momentum integral by
   $P^\mu=c^{-1}\int_V T^{0\mu}\,\mathrm dV$. Prove that its
   components are
   \[
   P^\mu=\Bigl(\frac{U}{c},0,0,0\Bigr)
   \]
   and that its assigned $+---$ component quadratic is
   $P^2=(U/c)^2$. A finite uniform static field requires material
   sources or boundary stresses, so do not claim that this field-only
   integral is by itself the conserved Lorentz four-momentum of a
   closed system.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the fields are crossed, so
   $\mathbf{S}\neq\mathbf{0}$ and $T^{0i}$ is nonzero”; (ii) “the
   spatial block is $T^{ij}=+\sigma^{ij}$, or the mixed trace equals
   $2u$ rather than $0$.”
permittedResults: $E^2=9E_0^2$ and $B^2=16E_0^2/c^2$, so $u=(9/2)\varepsilon_0 E_0^2+8\varepsilon_0 E_0^2=(25/2)\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$. Parallel fields force $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}$.
The transverse stresses equal $-u$ and the longitudinal stress equals $+u$. Then $T^{xx}=T^{yy}=+u$, $T^{zz}=-u$, $T^0{}_0=u$, $T^x{}_x=T^y{}_y=-u$, $T^z{}_z=+u$, and $T^\mu{}_\mu=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert B²/(2μ0) with 1/μ0=ε0 c², add the electric term, and read S=0 from E∥B before assembling σ^{ij}.
Set T^{ij}=−σ^{ij}, lower spatial indices with g_{ij}=−δ_{ij} to check T^μ_μ=0, then integrate u and S over the laboratory volume.

milestones.criterion: Produces u=25 ε0 E0²/2, S=0, σ=diag(−u,−u,+u), and T^{ij}=diag(+u,+u,−u).
Reports the mixed trace T^μ_μ=0 and the defined lab-slice field integral P^μ=(U/c,0,0,0) with component quadratic P²=(U/c)², without a false closed-system claim.
Rejects a crossed-field Poynting flux or a sign error that destroys the mixed trace, and refuses reserved crossed-tensor or covariant-force substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the given parallel fields as crossed, reports a nonzero Poynting vector, and takes T^{0i}≠0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required S=0, the lab-slice field integral P^μ=(U/c,0,0,0), and P²=(U/c)² are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes T^{ij}=+σ^{ij}, or reports σ=diag(+u,+u,−u), or claims that the mixed trace equals 2u rather than 0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required spatial block diag(+u,+u,−u) and the identity T^μ_μ=0 are replaced by inconsistent signs.

hintTree.content: Convert $B^2/(2\mu_0)$ with $1/\mu_0=\varepsilon_0 c^2$ before adding the electric term. The two contributions are $(9/2)\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$ and $8\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$.
Because $E_x=B_x=0$, the $xx$ (and $yy$) stress is just minus the isotropic field energy. The $zz$ stress keeps the full $E_z^2$ and $B_z^2$ and equals $+u$.
Lower the spatial indices with $g_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}$. The mixed spatial trace is $-T^{xx}-T^{yy}-T^{zz}=-u$, which cancels $T^0{}_0=u$.

ED:020117.canonicalSolution:
The squared field strengths are
\[
E^2=9E_0^2,\qquad
B^2=\frac{16E_0^2}{c^2}.
\]
The SI energy density is therefore
\begin{align*}
u
&=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2
=\frac{9}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2
+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\cdot\frac{16E_0^2}{c^2}.
\end{align*}
The vacuum identity $c^2=1/(\varepsilon_0\mu_0)$ rewrites
$1/\mu_0=\varepsilon_0 c^2$, so the magnetic term is
$8\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$ and
\[
u=\frac{9}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2+8\varepsilon_0 E_0^2
=\frac{25}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2.
\]
The two fields are parallel, so
\[
\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}.
\]
\[
\boxed{u=25\varepsilon_0 E_0^2/2,\;\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}}.
\]

The Maxwell stress tensor in SI is
\[
\sigma^{ij}
=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E^i E^j-\frac12\delta^{ij}E^2\Bigr)
+\frac1{\mu_0}\Bigl(B^i B^j-\frac12\delta^{ij}B^2\Bigr).
\]
The $x$ and $y$ diagonal entries have vanishing field components, so
each equals $-u$. The $z$ entry keeps the full longitudinal squares:
\begin{align*}
\sigma^{zz}
&=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(9E_0^2-\frac92 E_0^2\Bigr)
+\frac1{\mu_0}\Bigl(\frac{16E_0^2}{c^2}-\frac{8E_0^2}{c^2}\Bigr)
=\frac92\varepsilon_0 E_0^2+8\varepsilon_0 E_0^2
=u.
\end{align*}
Off-diagonal stresses vanish. Hence
\[
\sigma^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(-u,-u,+u).
\]
The assigned dictionary $T^{ij}=-\sigma^{ij}$ then gives the spatial
block
\[
T^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(+u,+u,-u).
\]
With $g_{00}=+1$ and $g_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}$,
\begin{align*}
T^0{}_0&=T^{00}=u,\\
T^x{}_x&=-T^{xx}=-u,\\
T^y{}_y&=-T^{yy}=-u,\\
T^z{}_z&=-T^{zz}=+u,
\end{align*}
so the mixed trace is
\[
T^\mu{}_\mu=u-u-u+u=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma=\operatorname{diag}(-u,-u,+u),\;
T^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(+u,+u,-u),\;
T^\mu{}_\mu=0}.
\]

On the specified laboratory slice define
$P^\mu=c^{-1}\int_VT^{0\mu}\,\mathrm dV$. The stored field energy is
$U=uV$. Because $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}$, the field momentum density
vanishes on that slice and
\[
P^\mu=\Bigl(\frac{U}{c},0,0,0\Bigr).
\]
The assigned $+---$ component quadratic is
\[
P^2=(P^0)^2-\mathbf{P}^2=\Bigl(\frac{U}{c}\Bigr)^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{P^\mu=(U/c,0,0,0),\;P^2=(U/c)^2}.
\]
These are the field contributions integrated over the stated
laboratory slice. A finite uniform static field needs material
sources or boundary stresses; without including their stress-energy,
the field-only integral is not asserted to be the conserved
four-momentum of a closed system.

Sentence (i) imports a crossed-field geometry that the given
$\mathbf{E}\parallel\mathbf{B}$ configuration does not possess, and
it invents a nonzero $T^{0i}$. Sentence (ii) drops the minus sign in
$T^{ij}=-\sigma^{ij}$ or fails to lower spatial indices, so the mixed
trace is no longer zero. The construction is a static parallel-field
stress-energy dictionary; it is not a crossed-field Maxwell-tensor
invariant catalogue and not a covariant Lorentz-force / parallel-$E$
boost problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: The energy density is $u=25\varepsilon_0 E_0^2/2$ and $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}$. The Maxwell stress is $\sigma=\operatorname{diag}(-u,-u,+u)$ and $T^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(+u,+u,-u)$. The mixed trace vanishes. For the defined laboratory-slice field integral, $P^\mu=(U/c,0,0,0)$ and its component quadratic is $P^2=(U/c)^2$; the field-only finite region is not asserted to be a closed conserved system.
The fields are crossed, so S is nonzero and T^{0i} is nonzero. I do not accept S=0 or P^μ=(U/c,0,0,0).
The spatial block is T^{ij}=+σ^{ij}, or the mixed trace equals 2u rather than 0. I never obtain T^{ij}=diag(+u,+u,−u) and T^μ_μ=0.

ED:020118.title: Boost a rest four-current: lab density, three-current, invariant square, and contracted volume
ED:020118.objective: For rest j'=(c ρ0,0,0,0) boosted with β=3/5 and γ=5/4, prove ρ=5ρ0/4, Jx=3c ρ0/4, J/(c ρ)=3/5, j_μ j^μ=c² ρ0², Vlab=4V0/5, and ρ Vlab=ρ0 V0.
ED:020118.statement:
A uniform comoving charge parcel is at rest in the frame $S'$. It has
constant proper density $\rho_0>0$ throughout a proper volume $V_0$;
one edge is parallel to the later boost and the transverse edges are
unchanged by it. Inside the parcel its four-current is the pure density
\[
j^{\prime\mu}=(c\rho_0,0,0,0),\qquad \rho_0>0.
\]
The frame $S'$ moves at constant velocity $\boldsymbol{\beta}c=\frac35 c\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}$
relative to the laboratory, so
\[
\gamma=\frac{5}{4}.
\]
Use the standard Lorentz boost of a four-vector and the Minkowski
metric of signature $(+,-,-,-)$. Do not replace this four-current
boost by a covariant Lorentz-force problem, a charge accelerating in
a uniform parallel electric field, or a crossed-field Maxwell-tensor
invariant audit.

1. Boost $j^{\prime\mu}$ to the laboratory and prove
   \[
   \rho=\frac{5\rho_0}{4},\qquad
   J^x=\frac{3c\rho_0}{4},\qquad
   \frac{|\mathbf{J}|}{c\rho}=\frac35.
   \]

2. Evaluate the Minkowski square and prove the invariant
   \[
   j_\mu j^\mu=c^2\rho_0^2.
   \]

3. Observe that parcel on a simultaneous laboratory slice. Prove the
   contracted volume and the charge
   identity
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\frac{4V_0}{5},\qquad
   \rho V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\rho_0 V_0.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “charge density is a scalar, so
   $\rho=\rho_0$ and $\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{0}$ in every frame”;
   (ii) “the laboratory volume is $V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\gamma V_0$, or
   $j_\mu j^\mu=0$ because the current is lightlike.”
permittedResults: $\rho=\gamma\rho_0=5\rho_0/4$ and $J^x=\gamma\beta c\rho_0=(5/4)(3/5)c\rho_0=3c\rho_0/4$, so $|\mathbf{J}|/(c\rho)=\beta=3/5$.
$j_\mu j^\mu=\gamma^2 c^2\rho_0^2(1-\beta^2)=c^2\rho_0^2$. Length contraction gives $V_{\mathrm{lab}}=V_0/\gamma=4V_0/5$, hence $\rho V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\rho_0 V_0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the standard x-boost to j'=(c ρ0,0,0,0) and read ρ=γ ρ0, J^x=γ β c ρ0, and |J|/(cρ)=β.
Factor γ²(1−β²)=1 from the Minkowski square, then contract only the boost-parallel edge of V0.

milestones.criterion: Reports ρ=5ρ0/4, J^x=3c ρ0/4, and |J|/(cρ)=3/5.
Proves j_μ j^μ=c²ρ0² together with V_lab=4V0/5 and ρ V_lab=ρ0 V0.
Rejects a scalar-density / missing-current reading or a γ-lengthened volume, and refuses reserved covariant-force or crossed-tensor substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats charge density as a Lorentz scalar, reports ρ=ρ0 in the laboratory, and takes J=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required ρ=5ρ0/4, J^x=3c ρ0/4, and |J|/(cρ)=3/5 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Writes V_lab=γ V0 rather than V0/γ, or claims that j_μ j^μ=0 because the current is lightlike.
commonErrors.consequence: The required V_lab=4V0/5, the charge identity ρ V_lab=ρ0 V0, and the invariant c²ρ0² are lost.

hintTree.content: The rest current has $j^{\prime x}=0$. The laboratory current is therefore just $\gamma\beta$ times the rest $j^{\prime 0}$.
Factor $\gamma^2 c^2\rho_0^2$ out of $j_\mu j^\mu$ and use $1-\beta^2=1/\gamma^2$.
Only the $x$-edge of the rest volume contracts. Charge is the product of the boosted density with the contracted volume.

ED:020118.canonicalSolution:
The laboratory four-current is the boost of the rest four-current.
With $j^{\prime x}=0$,
\begin{align*}
j^0
&=\gamma j^{\prime 0}
=\gamma c\rho_0
=\frac54 c\rho_0,\\
j^x
&=\gamma\beta j^{\prime 0}
=\gamma\beta c\rho_0
=\frac54\cdot\frac35\,c\rho_0
=\frac{3c\rho_0}{4},
\end{align*}
and $j^y=j^z=0$. Therefore
\[
\rho=\frac{j^0}{c}=\frac{5\rho_0}{4},\qquad
J^x=\frac{3c\rho_0}{4}.
\]
The three-velocity of the charge distribution is recovered as
\[
\frac{|\mathbf{J}|}{c\rho}
=\frac{3c\rho_0/4}{c\cdot(5\rho_0/4)}
=\frac35=\beta.
\]
\[
\boxed{\rho=5\rho_0/4,\;
J^x=3c\rho_0/4,\;
|\mathbf{J}|/(c\rho)=3/5}.
\]

The Minkowski square with signature $(+,-,-,-)$ is
\begin{align*}
j_\mu j^\mu
&=(j^0)^2-(J^x)^2
=\gamma^2 c^2\rho_0^2-\gamma^2\beta^2 c^2\rho_0^2
=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)c^2\rho_0^2
=c^2\rho_0^2.
\end{align*}
The four-current of a rest charge is timelike; it is not a null
vector.
\[
\boxed{j_\mu j^\mu=c^2\rho_0^2}.
\]

Only the boost-parallel edge of a rest-frame volume $V_0$ contracts,
so
\[
V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\frac{V_0}{\gamma}=\frac{4V_0}{5}.
\]
The laboratory charge contained in the image of that volume is
\[
\rho V_{\mathrm{lab}}
=\frac{5\rho_0}{4}\cdot\frac{4V_0}{5}
=\rho_0 V_0,
\]
which is the rest-frame charge. Charge is a Lorentz scalar.
\[
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{lab}}=4V_0/5,\;
\rho V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\rho_0 V_0}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats $\rho$ as a scalar and discards the entire
three-current. Sentence (ii) either lengthens the volume by $\gamma$
instead of contracting it, or declares a timelike four-current to be
null. The construction is a pure four-current boost of rest charge
density; it is not a covariant Lorentz-force / uniform-parallel-$E$
problem and not a crossed-field tensor audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The laboratory current is $\rho=5\rho_0/4$, $J^x=3c\rho_0/4$, and $|\mathbf{J}|/(c\rho)=3/5$. The invariant is $j_\mu j^\mu=c^2\rho_0^2$. The contracted volume is $V_{\mathrm{lab}}=4V_0/5$ and $\rho V_{\mathrm{lab}}=\rho_0 V_0$.
Charge density is a scalar, so ρ=ρ0 and J=0 in every frame. I do not accept ρ=5ρ0/4 or J^x=3c ρ0/4.
The laboratory volume is V_lab=γ V0, or j_μ j^μ=0 because the current is lightlike. I never obtain V_lab=4V0/5 or j_μ j^μ=c²ρ0².

ED:020219.title: Uniform-motion Liénard–Wiechert field: present-position and retarded evaluations agree at closest approach
ED:020219.objective: A charge q with β=3/5, γ=5/4 passes the origin at t=0. At the observer (0,b,0) and time t=0, prove t_r=−5b/(4c), source x=−3b/4, R=5b/4, and with E*=q/(4π ε0 b²) that E=(5/4)E* ŷ, B=(3/4)(E*/c) ẑ, S=(15/16) ε0 c E*² x̂, u=(17/16) ε0 E*², with present-position and retarded derivations in agreement.
ED:020219.statement:
A point charge $q$ moves on the laboratory $x$-axis at constant
velocity $\boldsymbol{\beta}c=\frac35 c\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, so $\gamma=5/4$.
The charge passes the origin at laboratory time $t=0$. An observer
sits at the fixed point $(0,b,0)$ with $b>0$. Write
\[
E_\ast=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 b^2}
\]
and work in SI units. Evaluate the electromagnetic field at the
observer at time $t=0$ in two ways: (i) the present-position formula
for uniform motion, and (ii) the $a=0$ Liénard–Wiechert formula at
the retarded time. The two evaluations must agree. Do not replace
this constant-velocity field by a retarded causal-cone / compact-pulse
problem, an advanced Green's function, or an electric-dipole near /
induction / radiation-zone decomposition.

1. Locate the retarded event that influences the observer at $t=0$,
   and prove
   \[
   t_r=-\frac{5b}{4c},\qquad
   x(t_r)=-\frac{3b}{4},\qquad
   R=c(0-t_r)=\frac{5b}{4}.
   \]

2. From the present-position formula (the charge is at the origin at
   $t=0$) prove
   \[
   \mathbf{E}=\frac54 E_\ast\,\hat{\mathbf{y}},\qquad
   \mathbf{B}=\frac34\frac{E_\ast}{c}\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}.
   \]
   Recover the same pair from the retarded Liénard–Wiechert formula
   \[
   \mathbf{E}=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
   \frac{(\hat{\mathbf{n}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})(1-\beta^2)}{\kappa^3 R^2},
   \qquad
   \kappa=1-\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\beta}.
   \]

3. Compute the Poynting vector and the energy density, and prove
   \[
   \mathbf{S}=\frac{15}{16}\varepsilon_0 c E_\ast^2\,\hat{\mathbf{x}},
   \qquad
   u=\frac{17}{16}\varepsilon_0 E_\ast^2.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “at closest approach the field is the
   Coulomb field $E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, with no $\gamma$”;
   (ii) “the retarded source is at the origin, or $\mathbf{S}$ points
   in the $-\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ direction.”
permittedResults: The light-delay identity $R=-c t_r$ with $x=\beta c t_r$ produces $t_r=-\gamma b/c=-5b/(4c)$, $x=-3b/4$, and $R=5b/4$.

At $\psi=\pi/2$ the present-position formula gives $\mathbf{E}=\gamma E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Retarded data $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=(3/5,4/5,0)$ and $\kappa=16/25$ reproduce the same $\mathbf{E}$. Then $\mathbf{B}=(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{E})/c$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the light-delay identity for t_r<0, then evaluate the present-position formula at ψ=π/2 to obtain E=γ E* ŷ.
Insert n̂=(3/5,4/5,0) and κ=16/25 into the a=0 Liénard–Wiechert formula and confirm the same E before forming S and u.

milestones.criterion: Locates the retarded event t_r=−5b/(4c), x=−3b/4, R=5b/4 and reports E=(5/4)E* ŷ, B=(3/4)(E*/c) ẑ from both evaluations.
Produces S=(15/16)ε0 c E*² x̂ and u=(17/16)ε0 E*², and records that the two derivations agree.
Rejects a Coulomb field without γ or a retarded source at the origin, and refuses reserved causal-cone / pulse / advanced or electric-dipole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the closest-approach electric field as the Coulomb value E* ŷ, omitting the factor γ=5/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The required E=(5/4)E* ŷ, B=(3/4)(E*/c) ẑ, and both energy quantities are rescaled.

commonErrors.description: Places the retarded source at the origin, or reports that S points in the −x̂ direction.
commonErrors.consequence: The required retarded data (t_r, x, R) and the Poynting vector (15/16)ε0 c E*² x̂ are lost.

hintTree.content: The retarded charge sits on the negative $x$-axis. Solve $(\beta c t_r)^2+b^2=c^2 t_r^2$ for $t_r<0$.
At closest approach the present-position formula reduces to $\mathbf{E}=\gamma E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Do not stop at the Coulomb value $E_\ast$.
From the retarded side, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is purely $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. The algebra $\kappa=16/25$ and $R=5b/4$ is arranged to cancel to $\gamma E_\ast$.

ED:020219.canonicalSolution:
At laboratory time $t=0$ the observer is at $(0,b,0)$ and the charge
is at the origin. The retarded event that influences this observation
satisfies $R=c(0-t_r)=-c t_r$ with $t_r<0$ and
$x(t_r)=\beta c t_r$. Then
\[
(\beta c t_r)^2+b^2=c^2 t_r^2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
b^2=c^2 t_r^2(1-\beta^2)=\frac{c^2 t_r^2}{\gamma^2},
\]
so
\[
t_r=-\frac{\gamma b}{c}=-\frac{5b}{4c}.
\]
The retarded source coordinate and the retarded distance are
\[
x(t_r)=\beta c t_r=\frac35 c\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{5b}{4c}\Bigr)=-\frac{3b}{4},
\qquad
R=-c t_r=\frac{5b}{4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t_r=-5b/(4c),\;x=-3b/4,\;R=5b/4}.
\]

Present-position evaluation. The vector from the present charge
position to the observer is $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{p}}=b\hat{\mathbf{y}}$,
so $\psi=\pi/2$ and $\sin\psi=1$. The uniform-motion formula collapses
to
\[
\mathbf{E}
=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
\frac{1-\beta^2}{b^2(1-\beta^2)^{3/2}}\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}
=\frac{\gamma q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 b^2}\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}
=\frac54 E_\ast\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}.
\]
The companion magnetic field is
\[
\mathbf{B}
=\frac{\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{E}}{c}
=\frac{\beta}{c}\cdot\frac54 E_\ast\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}
=\frac34\frac{E_\ast}{c}\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}.
\]

Retarded evaluation. The retarded separation is
$\mathbf{R}=(3b/4,b,0)$, so
\[
\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\Bigl(\frac35,\frac45,0\Bigr),\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\beta}=\frac{9}{25},\qquad
\kappa=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25},
\]
and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0,4/5,0)$. The $a=0$
Liénard–Wiechert electric field is
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{E}
&=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
\frac{(\hat{\mathbf{n}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})(1-\beta^2)}{\kappa^3 R^2}
=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
\frac{(4/5)\hat{\mathbf{y}}\cdot(16/25)}{(16/25)^3\,(5b/4)^2}.
\end{align*}
The prefactor simplifies as
\[
\frac{(4/5)(16/25)}{(4096/15625)\cdot(25b^2/16)}
=\frac{5}{4b^2},
\]
hence again $\mathbf{E}=(5/4)E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. The same
$\mathbf{B}=(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{E})/c$ follows. The two
derivations agree.
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{E}=(5/4)E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}},\;
\mathbf{B}=(3/4)(E_\ast/c)\hat{\mathbf{z}}}.
\]

The Poynting vector is
\[
\mathbf{S}
=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}
=\varepsilon_0 c^2\cdot\frac54 E_\ast\cdot\frac34\frac{E_\ast}{c}\,
\hat{\mathbf{x}}
=\frac{15}{16}\varepsilon_0 c E_\ast^2\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}.
\]
The energy density is
\begin{align*}
u
&=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2
=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\cdot\frac{25}{16}E_\ast^2
+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\cdot\frac{9}{16}E_\ast^2
=\frac{17}{16}\varepsilon_0 E_\ast^2.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{S}=(15/16)\varepsilon_0 c E_\ast^2\hat{\mathbf{x}},\;
u=(17/16)\varepsilon_0 E_\ast^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the $\gamma$ of the present-position formula and
never produces $(5/4)E_\ast$. Sentence (ii) places the retarded
source at the origin (so $R=b$ and $\kappa=1$) or reverses the
Poynting direction. The construction is the constant-velocity
Liénard–Wiechert field; it is not a causal-cone / compact-pulse /
advanced-Green problem and not an electric-dipole zone decomposition.

graderFixtures.proofText: The retarded event is $t_r=-5b/(4c)$, $x=-3b/4$, $R=5b/4$. Both the present-position and Liénard–Wiechert formulae give $\mathbf{E}=(5/4)E_\ast\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\mathbf{B}=(3/4)(E_\ast/c)\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. Then $\mathbf{S}=(15/16)\varepsilon_0 c E_\ast^2\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $u=(17/16)\varepsilon_0 E_\ast^2$.
At closest approach the field is the Coulomb field E* ŷ, with no γ. I do not accept E=(5/4)E* ŷ.
The retarded source is at the origin, or S points in the −x̂ direction. I never obtain t_r=−5b/(4c), x=−3b/4, R=5b/4, and S=(15/16)ε0 c E*² x̂.

ED:020320.title: Liénard power at fixed lab |a|: parallel versus perpendicular orientation, and the low-β limit
ED:020320.objective: For P=q² γ⁶[a²−(β×a)²]/(6π ε0 c³) at the same laboratory |a|=a0 and β=3/5, prove P_∥=(15625/4096) P0=3.814697265625 P0, P_⊥=(625/256) P0=2.44140625 P0, ratio P_∥/P_⊥=25/16, and that both tend to P0 as β→0.
ED:020320.statement:
A point charge $q$ has instantaneous laboratory velocity
$\boldsymbol{\beta}c$ with $\beta=3/5$ (hence $\gamma=5/4$) and
instantaneous laboratory acceleration of fixed magnitude
$|\mathbf{a}|=a_0>0$. The relativistic Liénard radiated power in SI
units is
\[
P=\frac{q^2\gamma^6}{6\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}
\Bigl[a^2-(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a})^2\Bigr].
\]
Write
\[
P_0=\frac{q^2 a_0^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}
\]
for the nonrelativistic Larmor power at the same $|\mathbf{a}|$.
Compare the two orientations $\mathbf{a}\parallel\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and
$\mathbf{a}\perp\boldsymbol{\beta}$. Do not replace this point-charge
Liénard orientation problem by an electric-dipole near / induction /
radiation-zone decomposition, a rectangular TE10 waveguide, or a
Cherenkov / medium problem.

1. For $\mathbf{a}\parallel\boldsymbol{\beta}$ prove
   \[
   P_\parallel
   =\gamma^6 P_0
   =\frac{15625}{4096}\,P_0
   =3.814697265625\,P_0.
   \]

2. For $\mathbf{a}\perp\boldsymbol{\beta}$ prove
   \[
   P_\perp
   =\gamma^4 P_0
   =\frac{625}{256}\,P_0
   =2.44140625\,P_0.
   \]

3. Form the orientation ratio and the low-velocity limit:
   \[
   \frac{P_\parallel}{P_\perp}=\frac{25}{16},
   \qquad
   \lim_{\beta\to 0}P_\parallel
   =\lim_{\beta\to 0}P_\perp
   =P_0.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “parallel radiation is the weaker
   channel, so $P_\parallel=\gamma^4 P_0$ and $P_\perp=\gamma^6 P_0$”;
   (ii) “the formula is just the Larmor power $P_0$ at any $\beta$,
   or the cross term $(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a})^2$ may be
   dropped in both orientations.”

acceptableStrategies.description: Set β×a=0 in the parallel channel to isolate γ⁶, then insert γ=5/4 as (5/4)⁶=15625/4096.
Factor 1−β²=1/γ² from the perpendicular bracket to obtain γ⁴, then form the ratio γ²=25/16 and take β→0.

commonErrors.description: Replaces both orientations by the Larmor power P0 at finite β, or drops (β×a)² so that P_⊥=P_∥=γ⁶ P0.

hintTree.content: If $\mathbf{a}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, the cross product vanishes and only $\gamma^6$ survives.
If $\mathbf{a}$ is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, factor $1-\beta^2=1/\gamma^2$ out of the bracket to drop two powers of $\gamma$.
$(5/4)^2=25/16$, $(5/4)^4=625/256$, and $(5/4)^6=15625/4096$. The two decimal expansions are exact dyadic values.

ED:020320.canonicalSolution:
The nonrelativistic reference power at the assigned laboratory
magnitude $a_0$ is
\[
P_0=\frac{q^2 a_0^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}.
\]
When $\mathbf{a}\parallel\boldsymbol{\beta}$ one has
$\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}$, so the Liénard formula
collapses to
\[
P_\parallel
=\frac{q^2\gamma^6 a_0^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}
=\gamma^6 P_0.
\]
With $\gamma=5/4$,
\[
\gamma^6=\Bigl(\frac54\Bigr)^6=\frac{15625}{4096}=3.814697265625,
\]
and therefore
\[
P_\parallel=\frac{15625}{4096}\,P_0=3.814697265625\,P_0.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_\parallel=(15625/4096)P_0=3.814697265625\,P_0}.
\]

When $\mathbf{a}\perp\boldsymbol{\beta}$ one has
$|\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a}|=\beta a_0$, so
\[
a^2-(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a})^2
=a_0^2(1-\beta^2)=\frac{a_0^2}{\gamma^2}.
\]
The Liénard formula then reduces by two powers of $\gamma$:
\[
P_\perp
=\gamma^6\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma^2}\,P_0
=\gamma^4 P_0.
\]
Now
\[
\gamma^4=\Bigl(\frac54\Bigr)^4=\frac{625}{256}=2.44140625,
\]
and therefore
\[
P_\perp=\frac{625}{256}\,P_0=2.44140625\,P_0.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_\perp=(625/256)P_0=2.44140625\,P_0}.
\]

The orientation ratio is
\[
\frac{P_\parallel}{P_\perp}
=\frac{\gamma^6}{\gamma^4}
=\gamma^2
=\frac{25}{16}.
\]
As $\beta\to 0$ one has $\gamma\to 1$, so both oriented powers tend
to the same Larmor value:
\[
\lim_{\beta\to 0}P_\parallel
=\lim_{\beta\to 0}P_\perp
=P_0.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_\parallel/P_\perp=25/16,\;
\text{both}\to P_0\text{ as }\beta\to 0}.
\]

Sentence (i) swaps the two $\gamma$ powers and makes the parallel
channel the weaker one. Sentence (ii) either drops the entire
relativistic structure or discards $(\boldsymbol{\beta}\times\mathbf{a})^2$
in the perpendicular case, forcing $P_\perp=P_\parallel$. The
construction is the point-charge Liénard formula at fixed laboratory
$|\mathbf{a}|$; it is not an electric-dipole zone decomposition, not
a rectangular TE10 waveguide, and not a Cherenkov problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $\beta=3/5$ one has $P_\parallel=(15625/4096)P_0=3.814697265625\,P_0$ and $P_\perp=(625/256)P_0=2.44140625\,P_0$. The ratio is $25/16$, and both powers tend to $P_0$ as $\beta\to 0$.
Parallel radiation is the weaker channel, so P_∥=γ⁴ P0 and P_⊥=γ⁶ P0. I do not accept P_∥=(15625/4096)P0 or P_⊥=(625/256)P0.
The formula is just the Larmor power P0 at any β, or the cross term (β×a)² may be dropped in both orientations. I never obtain the split γ⁶ versus γ⁴.

ED:020321.title: Cherenkov threshold and Frank–Tamm photon yield in a finite constant-n band
ED:020321.objective: In a transparent nonmagnetic constant-n band with β=4/5 and n=3/2, prove the threshold β_th=2/3, cos θ=5/6, sin²θ=11/36, θ=0.5856855434571508 rad, and that a unit charge yields d²N/(dx dω)=11α/(36c) inside the band and zero below threshold. Keep the finite-band hypothesis separate from Kramers–Kronig / Debye response.
ED:020321.statement:
A charge $q=e$ (unit charge in the sense of the fine-structure
prefactor $\alpha=e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c)$) moves at constant
speed $\beta=4/5$ through a linear medium that is transparent,
nonmagnetic, and of constant real refractive index $n=3/2$ throughout
a stated angular-frequency band $\omega\in(\omega_-,\omega_+)$.
Outside that band the medium is not asserted to be constant-$n$, and
no Kramers–Kronig or Debye model is to be used. The Cherenkov
condition and the Frank–Tamm photon yield apply only inside the
stated band. Do not replace this finite-band Cherenkov problem by a
Kramers–Kronig / Debye dielectric function, a rectangular TE10
waveguide, or an electric-dipole radiation-zone construction.

1. State the Cherenkov threshold in the band and prove
   \[
   \beta_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac1n=\frac23.
   \]
   Confirm that the assigned speed $\beta=4/5$ lies above threshold.

2. Inside the band, the Cherenkov opening angle satisfies
   $\cos\theta=1/(\beta n)$. Prove
   \[
   \cos\theta=\frac56,\qquad
   \sin^2\theta=\frac{11}{36},\qquad
   \theta=\arccos\Bigl(\frac56\Bigr)=0.5856855434571508\,\mathrm{rad}.
   \]

3. The Frank–Tamm photon number yield per path length per angular
   frequency, for unit charge, is
   \[
   \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 N}{\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\omega}
   =\frac{\alpha}{c}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\beta^2 n^2}\Bigr)
   \]
   inside the band, and vanishes below threshold. Prove that the
   in-band value is $11\alpha/(36c)$, and that the yield is $0$ if
   the same charge is imagined to travel at $\beta<\beta_{\mathrm{th}}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the threshold is $n$ itself, or
   $\cos\theta=\beta n$ rather than $1/(\beta n)$”; (ii) “the
   Frank–Tamm formula is an energy intensity rather than a photon
   yield, or the constant-$n$ band must be replaced by a
   Kramers–Kronig / Debye dielectric throughout all frequencies.”
permittedResults: $1/(\beta^2 n^2)=25/36$, hence $1-1/(\beta^2 n^2)=11/36$ and $\mathrm{d}^2 N/(\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\omega)=11\alpha/(36c)$. The same factor is $\sin^2\theta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare β=4/5 with 1/n=2/3, then evaluate cos θ=1/(β n)=5/6 and sin²θ=1−25/36.
Insert 1/(β² n²)=25/36 into the Frank–Tamm photon formula and refuse to continue the expression below threshold or to replace n by a Debye function.

milestones.criterion: Reports β_th=2/3, cos θ=5/6, sin²θ=11/36, and θ=arccos(5/6)=0.5856855434571508 rad.
Produces the in-band Frank–Tamm photon yield 11α/(36c) and the vanishing yield below threshold, keeping the finite-band hypothesis.
Rejects a threshold or cosine inversion or a KK/Debye replacement of the band, and refuses reserved TE10 or electric-dipole substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the Cherenkov threshold to be n itself, or writes cos θ=β n rather than 1/(β n).
commonErrors.consequence: The required β_th=2/3, cos θ=5/6, and θ=0.5856855434571508 rad are replaced by inverted kinematics.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Frank–Tamm photon yield by an energy intensity, or replaces the finite constant-n band by a Kramers–Kronig / Debye dielectric on all frequencies.
commonErrors.consequence: The required in-band yield 11α/(36c) and the finite-band validity statement are lost.

hintTree.content: The threshold is the reciprocal of the in-band index, not the index itself. Compare $4/5$ with $2/3$ before computing an angle.
$\cos\theta=1/(\beta n)=5/6$. Square this cosine and subtract from $1$ to obtain $\sin^2\theta=11/36$.
The Frank–Tamm photon prefactor is $\alpha/c$ times $\sin^2\theta$. Do not insert an extra $\hbar\omega$, and do not replace $n$ by a Debye function.

ED:020321.canonicalSolution:
Inside the stated transparent nonmagnetic band the refractive index
is the real constant $n=3/2$. Cherenkov radiation exists only when
the charge outruns the in-band phase speed $c/n$, i.e. only when
\[
\beta>\beta_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac1n=\frac23.
\]
The assigned speed $\beta=4/5=0.8$ lies strictly above $2/3\approx 0.667$.
\[
\boxed{\beta_{\mathrm{th}}=2/3,\;4/5>2/3}.
\]

The in-band Cherenkov opening angle is unique:
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\beta n}
=\frac{1}{(4/5)(3/2)}
=\frac{1}{6/5}
=\frac56.
\]
Then
\[
\sin^2\theta
=1-\cos^2\theta
=1-\frac{25}{36}
=\frac{11}{36},
\]
and
\[
\theta=\arccos\Bigl(\frac56\Bigr)=0.5856855434571508\,\mathrm{rad}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\cos\theta=5/6,\;
\sin^2\theta=11/36,\;
\theta=0.5856855434571508\,\mathrm{rad}}.
\]

The Frank–Tamm photon number yield for a unit charge, valid only
inside the constant-$n$ band, is
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 N}{\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\omega}
=\frac{\alpha}{c}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\beta^2 n^2}\Bigr).
\]
Now
\[
\beta^2 n^2=\frac{16}{25}\cdot\frac94=\frac{36}{25},
\qquad
\frac{1}{\beta^2 n^2}=\frac{25}{36},
\qquad
1-\frac{1}{\beta^2 n^2}=\frac{11}{36},
\]
so
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 N}{\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\omega}
=\frac{11\alpha}{36c}.
\]
The same numerical factor is $\sin^2\theta$. If instead
$\beta<\beta_{\mathrm{th}}$, the in-band phase velocity cannot be
overtaken and the yield is identically zero; one does not continue
the algebraic expression $1-1/(\beta^2 n^2)$ below threshold, where
it would become negative.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{d}^2 N/(\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\omega)=11\alpha/(36c)
\text{ in-band; }0\text{ below threshold}}.
\]

The constant-$n$ hypothesis is restricted to
$\omega\in(\omega_-,\omega_+)$. A Kramers–Kronig or Debye dielectric
would supply a complex, frequency-dependent $n(\omega)$ on the whole
real axis and is a different medium; it is not used to evaluate the
in-band cone or the in-band yield.

Sentence (i) either takes the threshold to be $n$ itself or inverts
the cosine formula. Sentence (ii) either replaces the photon yield
by an energy intensity $\propto\hbar\omega\sin^2\theta$ or exports
the problem into a Kramers–Kronig / Debye model. The construction is
a finite-band Cherenkov cone plus Frank–Tamm photon count; it is not
a KK/Debye response, not a rectangular TE10 waveguide, and not an
electric-dipole radiation field.

graderFixtures.proofText: The in-band threshold is $\beta_{\mathrm{th}}=2/3$, with $\cos\theta=5/6$, $\sin^2\theta=11/36$, and $\theta=0.5856855434571508\,\mathrm{rad}$. The unit-charge Frank–Tamm photon yield is $11\alpha/(36c)$ inside the band and $0$ below threshold.
The threshold is n itself, or cos θ=β n rather than 1/(β n). I do not accept β_th=2/3 or cos θ=5/6.

The Frank–Tamm formula is an energy intensity rather than a photon yield, or the constant-n band must be replaced by a Kramers–Kronig / Debye dielectric throughout all frequencies. I never report 11α/(36c) as an in-band photon yield.

ED:020422.title: A lossless coax TEM ledger with b/a=e^π: fields, C', L', Z0, matched power, and equal stored energies
ED:020422.objective: For a lossless coax with b/a=e^π prove Er=V0/(π r), Hφ=I0/(2π r), C'=2ε, L'=μ/2, Z0=η/2, v=1/√(με); on a match with peak phasors I0=2V0/η prove Pavg=V0²/η, equal time-average energies εV0²/2 per length, total εV0²=Pavg/v, and no cutoff.
ED:020422.statement:
A lossless coaxial line has inner radius $a>0$, outer radius $b=a e^{\pi}$,
and a homogeneous filling of permittivity $\varepsilon>0$ and permeability
$\mu>0$. The line supports a TEM wave. Peak phasors are used throughout:
the time average of a product of two harmonic fields is
$\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\,\cdot\,)$. Write $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$
and let $V_0$ be the peak phasor of the inner-to-outer voltage. Do not
replace the TEM coax by a rectangular TE$_{10}$ waveguide, a cutoff
wavenumber $\pi$ over a guide width, a Kramers–Kronig or Debye
dielectric, or a uniform electric field acting on a charged particle.

1. From $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=0$ in a transverse plane and the voltage
   integral, prove that the only nonzero electric peak phasor is
   \[
   E_r=\frac{V_0}{\pi r},\qquad a<r<b.
   \]
   From Ampère's law with peak current $I_0$ on the inner conductor,
   prove that the only nonzero magnetic peak phasor is
   \[
   H_\phi=\frac{I_0}{2\pi r}.
   \]

2. Compute the distributed parameters and the TEM speed, and prove
   \[
   C'=2\varepsilon,\qquad
   L'=\frac\mu2,\qquad
   Z_0=\frac\eta2,\qquad
   v=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}.
   \]

3. The line is matched, so the peak phasors satisfy $I_0=V_0/Z_0$.
   Prove $I_0=2V_0/\eta$ and
   \[
   P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{V_0^2}{\eta}.
   \]
   Prove that the time-average electric and magnetic energies stored
   per unit length are each $\varepsilon V_0^2/2$, that their sum
   equals $\varepsilon V_0^2=P_{\mathrm{avg}}/v$, and that the TEM
   mode has no cutoff.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the guide is a rectangular TE$_{10}$
   waveguide, so there is a cutoff $\omega_c=\pi/(a\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon})$
   and $E_r$ is not $V_0/(\pi r)$”; (ii) “peak phasors may be treated
   as RMS, so $P_{\mathrm{avg}}=V_0 I_0=2V_0^2/\eta$, or the magnetic
   stored energy differs from the electric stored energy.”
permittedResults: The radius ratio $b/a=e^{\pi}$ forces $\ln(b/a)=\pi$, hence $E_r=V_0/(\pi r)$, $C'=2\varepsilon$, $L'=\mu/2$, and $Z_0=\eta/2$.
On a match $I_0=2V_0/\eta$, so $P_{\mathrm{avg}}=V_0^2/\eta$. Then $U_E'=U_M'=\varepsilon V_0^2/2$ and $U_E'+U_M'=P_{\mathrm{avg}}/v$. A TEM mode has vanishing cutoff wavenumber.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert b/a=e^π into ln(b/a)=π, read Er and Hφ from the logarithmic potential and Ampère's law, then form C', L', Z0, and v.
Impose I0=V0/Z0 with peak-phasor power ½ V0 I0, evaluate UE' and UM' from C' and L', and compare their sum with Pavg/v.

milestones.criterion: Produces Er=V0/(π r), Hφ=I0/(2π r), C'=2ε, L'=μ/2, Z0=η/2, and v=1/√(με).
Reports matched I0=2V0/η, Pavg=V0²/η, equal stored energies εV0²/2 per length, total εV0²=Pavg/v, and no cutoff.
Rejects a TE10 cutoff substitution or an RMS/unequal-energy reading, and refuses reserved KK/Debye or uniform-E substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the lossless coaxial TEM ledger by a rectangular TE10 waveguide, reports a cutoff ωc=π/(a√(με)), and never accepts Er=V0/(π r) or the statement that there is no cutoff.
commonErrors.consequence: The required TEM fields, distributed parameters, and no-cutoff statement are replaced by a reserved TE10 cutoff exercise.

commonErrors.description: Treats the peak phasors as RMS and reports Pavg=V0 I0=2V0²/η, or claims that the time-average magnetic energy per length differs from the electric energy εV0²/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Pavg=V0²/η and the equal stored energies UE'=UM'=εV0²/2 are lost.

hintTree.content: The electrostatic potential in the annulus is logarithmic. The assigned ratio $b/a=e^{\pi}$ converts $\ln(b/a)$ into $\pi$.
Form $Z_0=\sqrt{L'/C'}$ before introducing $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$. The factor $1/2$ is $\sqrt{(\mu/2)/(2\varepsilon)}$.
Keep the peak-phasor factor $1/2$ in $P_{\mathrm{avg}}$. After $I_0=2V_0/\eta$ the two stored-energy formulae become identical.

ED:020422.canonicalSolution:
In a source-free transverse plane a TEM electric field is irrotational,
so $E_r=A/r$. The inner-to-outer voltage is
\[
V_0=\int_a^b E_r\,\mathrm{d}r=A\ln(b/a).
\]
The assigned ratio $b/a=e^{\pi}$ gives $\ln(b/a)=\pi$, hence $A=V_0/\pi$
and
\[
E_r=\frac{V_0}{\pi r}.
\]
Ampère's law on a circle of radius $r\in(a,b)$ yields
$2\pi r H_\phi=I_0$, so
\[
H_\phi=\frac{I_0}{2\pi r}.
\]
There is no longitudinal field.
\[
\boxed{E_r=V_0/(\pi r),\;H_\phi=I_0/(2\pi r)}.
\]

The capacitance and inductance per unit length are the standard coaxial
integrals
\[
C'=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\pi}=2\varepsilon,
\qquad
L'=\frac{\mu}{2\pi}\ln(b/a)=\frac{\mu}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac\mu2.
\]
Therefore
\[
Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu/2}{2\varepsilon}}=\frac12\sqrt{\frac\mu\varepsilon}=\frac\eta2
\]
and
\[
v=\frac1{\sqrt{L'C'}}=\frac1{\sqrt{(\mu/2)\cdot 2\varepsilon}}=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C'=2\varepsilon,\;L'=\mu/2,\;Z_0=\eta/2,\;v=1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}.
\]

A matched termination enforces $I_0=V_0/Z_0=2V_0/\eta$. Peak-phasor
power is
\[
P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac12 V_0 I_0=\frac12 V_0\cdot\frac{2V_0}{\eta}=\frac{V_0^2}{\eta}.
\]
The stored energies per unit length are
\begin{align*}
U_E'
&=\frac14 C'|V_0|^2
=\frac14\cdot 2\varepsilon\cdot V_0^2
=\frac{\varepsilon V_0^2}{2},\\
U_M'
&=\frac14 L'|I_0|^2
=\frac14\cdot\frac\mu2\cdot\frac{4V_0^2}{\eta^2}
=\frac{\mu V_0^2}{2}\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}
=\frac{\varepsilon V_0^2}{2}.
\end{align*}
(The cylindrical integrals of $(\varepsilon/4)|E_r|^2$ and
$(\mu/4)|H_\phi|^2$ reproduce the same pair, because
$\int_a^b\mathrm{d}r/r=\pi$.) Their sum is
\[
U_E'+U_M'=\varepsilon V_0^2
=\frac{V_0^2}{\eta}\cdot\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{avg}}}{v}.
\]
A TEM mode has vanishing cutoff wavenumber $k_c=0$ and the linear
dispersion $\omega=vk$; there is no cutoff frequency. The construction
is a coaxial TEM ledger, not a rectangular TE$_{10}$ guide.
\[
\boxed{I_0=2V_0/\eta,\;
P_{\mathrm{avg}}=V_0^2/\eta,\;
U_E'=U_M'=\varepsilon V_0^2/2,\;
U'=\varepsilon V_0^2=P_{\mathrm{avg}}/v,\;
\text{no cutoff}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the TEM coax by a reserved TE$_{10}$ cutoff
problem and destroys $E_r=V_0/(\pi r)$ together with the statement
that there is no cutoff. Sentence (ii) drops the peak-phasor factor
$1/2$ or unbalances the two stored energies, and never produces
$P_{\mathrm{avg}}=V_0^2/\eta$ with $U_E'=U_M'$. The exercise is not a
Kramers–Kronig or Debye dielectric and not a uniform-$E$ Lorentz-force
orbit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The TEM fields are $E_r=V_0/(\pi r)$ and $H_\phi=I_0/(2\pi r)$, with $C'=2\varepsilon$, $L'=\mu/2$, $Z_0=\eta/2$, and $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$. On a match $I_0=2V_0/\eta$ and $P_{\mathrm{avg}}=V_0^2/\eta$. The stored energies are each $\varepsilon V_0^2/2$ per length, their sum is $\varepsilon V_0^2=P_{\mathrm{avg}}/v$, and the TEM mode has no cutoff.
The guide is a rectangular TE10 waveguide, so there is a cutoff ωc=π/(a√(με)) and Er is not V0/(π r). I do not accept a TEM coax with no cutoff.
Peak phasors may be treated as RMS, so Pavg=V0 I0=2V0²/η, or the magnetic stored energy differs from εV0²/2. I never report Pavg=V0²/η with UE'=UM'.

ED:020423.title: A 50-to-200 Ω quarter-wave transformer: exact match at βℓ=π/2 and a single-frequency audit at βℓ=π/4
ED:020423.objective: For Z0=50 Ω, ZL=200 Ω, Zt=100 Ω prove that βℓ=π/2 gives Zin=50 Ω and Γ=0, while βℓ=π/4 gives Zin=80−60i Ω, Γ=(15−12i)/41, |Γ|²=9/41 and delivered fraction 32/41, and that the match is not broadband.
ED:020423.statement:
A lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance $Z_0=50\,\Omega$
is to be matched to a real load $Z_L=200\,\Omega$ by a single lossless
section of characteristic impedance $Z_t=100\,\Omega$ and length $\ell$.
The generator is matched to $Z_0$. Peak phasors and the ordinary
telegrapher input-impedance formula are used. Do not replace the
section by a rectangular TE$_{10}$ waveguide, a coaxial TEM field
ledger, a Kramers–Kronig or Debye dielectric, or a uniform electric
field.

1. At the design frequency one has $\beta\ell=\pi/2$. Prove
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_t^2}{Z_L}=50\,\Omega,\qquad \Gamma=0.
   \]

2. At the frequency for which $\beta\ell=\pi/4$, evaluate
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{in}}
   =Z_t\frac{Z_L+j Z_t\tan\beta\ell}{Z_t+j Z_L\tan\beta\ell}
   \]
   and prove
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{in}}=(80-60j)\,\Omega.
   \]
   Then prove
   \[
   \Gamma=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_0}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_0}
   =\frac{15}{41}-\frac{12}{41}j,
   \qquad
   |\Gamma|^2=\frac{9}{41},
   \qquad
   1-|\Gamma|^2=\frac{32}{41}.
   \]

3. Conclude that the delivered fraction of the incident power is
   $32/41$ at $\beta\ell=\pi/4$, and that the match $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_0$
   is not broadband: it holds at the isolated design frequency
   $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ and fails at $\beta\ell=\pi/4$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a quarter-wave transformer has
   $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_t$ or $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_L$, so $\Gamma\neq 0$
   already at $\beta\ell=\pi/2$”; (ii) “at $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ one has
   $|\Gamma|^2=9/25$, or $\Gamma$ is real, or the match remains exact
   at every frequency.”
permittedResults: $Z_t^2/Z_L=10000/200=50$, so $\Gamma=0$ at $\beta\ell=\pi/2$. At $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ one has $\tan\beta\ell=1$ and $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=100(200+100j)/(100+200j)=80-60j$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Collapse the input formula at βℓ=π/2 to Zt²/ZL, then evaluate the same formula at tan(π/4)=1 and rationalize.
Form Γ=(Zin−Z0)/(Zin+Z0), reduce (15−12j)/41, and convert |Γ|²=369/1681 into 9/41.

milestones.criterion: Reports Zin=50 Ω and Γ=0 at βℓ=π/2, together with Zin=80−60j Ω at βℓ=π/4.
Produces Γ=(15−12j)/41, |Γ|²=9/41, delivered fraction 32/41, and the statement that the match is not broadband.
Rejects Zin=Zt or Zin=ZL at design, or a corrupted |Γ|² / broadband claim, and refuses reserved TE10, KK/Debye, or uniform-E substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports Zin=Zt=100 Ω or Zin=ZL=200 Ω at βℓ=π/2 instead of Zin=Zt²/ZL=50 Ω, and never obtains Γ=0 at design.
commonErrors.consequence: The required matched design point Zin=50 Ω, Γ=0 is lost.

commonErrors.description: At βℓ=π/4 reports |Γ|²=9/25, takes Γ real, or claims that Zin remains equal to Z0 at every frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Γ=(15−12j)/41, |Γ|²=9/41, delivered fraction 32/41, and non-broadband conclusion are not produced.

hintTree.content: At $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ the tangent diverges and the input formula reduces to $Z_t^2/Z_L$. Check $100^2/200=50$.
At $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ rationalize $(20000+10000j)/(100+200j)$ against $100-200j$. The denominator is $50000$.
After $\Gamma=(15-12j)/41$, square the modulus over $41^2=1681$ and reduce $369/1681=9/41$.

ED:020423.canonicalSolution:
At the design electrical length $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ the lossless input
formula collapses to
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_t^2}{Z_L}=\frac{100^2}{200}=50\,\Omega=Z_0.
\]
The reflection coefficient on the $Z_0$ line therefore vanishes:
\[
\Gamma=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_0}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_0}=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\pi/2)=50\,\Omega,\;\Gamma=0}.
\]

At $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ one has $\tan\beta\ell=1$, so
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}
=100\cdot\frac{200+100j}{100+200j}
=\frac{20000+10000j}{100+200j}.
\]
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $100-200j$ produces
\[
(20000+10000j)(100-200j)
=2\,000\,000-4\,000\,000j+1\,000\,000j+2\,000\,000
=4\,000\,000-3\,000\,000j
\]
in the numerator and $100^2+200^2=50\,000$ in the denominator. Hence
\[
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{4\,000\,000-3\,000\,000j}{50\,000}=(80-60j)\,\Omega.
\]
The reflection coefficient is
\[
\Gamma
=\frac{(80-60j)-50}{(80-60j)+50}
=\frac{30-60j}{130-60j}.
\]
Multiplying by $130+60j$ gives numerator
\[
(30-60j)(130+60j)=3900+1800j-7800j+3600=7500-6000j
\]
and denominator $130^2+60^2=20\,500$, so
\[
\Gamma=\frac{7500-6000j}{20500}=\frac{15}{41}-\frac{12}{41}j.
\]
Then
\[
|\Gamma|^2
=\frac{15^2+12^2}{41^2}
=\frac{369}{1681}
=\frac{9}{41},
\qquad
1-|\Gamma|^2=\frac{32}{41}.
\]
Because the section is lossless, $32/41$ of the incident power is
delivered to the load.
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(\pi/4)=80-60j,\;
\Gamma=(15-12j)/41,\;
|\Gamma|^2=9/41,\;
\text{delivered }32/41}.
\]

The identity $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_0$ holds at $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ and fails
at $\beta\ell=\pi/4$. A single-section quarter-wave transformer is
therefore not a broadband match: it is exact only at isolated
frequencies.
\[
\boxed{\text{match not broadband}}.
\]

Sentence (i) refuses $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_t^2/Z_L$ and never produces a
vanishing $\Gamma$ at design. Sentence (ii) corrupts $|\Gamma|^2$ or
claims a frequency-independent match. The construction is a TEM
telegrapher section, not a TE$_{10}$ cutoff problem, not a coaxial
field ledger, and not a KK/Debye or uniform-$E$ exercise.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $\beta\ell=\pi/2$ one has $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\,\Omega$ and $\Gamma=0$. At $\beta\ell=\pi/4$ one has $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=(80-60j)\,\Omega$, $\Gamma=(15-12j)/41$, $|\Gamma|^2=9/41$, and delivered fraction $32/41$. The match is not broadband.
A quarter-wave transformer has Zin=Zt=100 Ω or Zin=ZL=200 Ω, so Γ≠0 already at βℓ=π/2. I do not accept Zin=50 Ω.
At βℓ=π/4 I take |Γ|²=9/25, or Γ is real, or the match remains exact at every frequency. I never report |Γ|²=9/41 and delivered 32/41 with a non-broadband match.

ED:020430.title: Symmetric lossless Fabry–Pérot: F=360, exact phase FWHM, and the 3π√10 approximation
ED:020430.objective: For a symmetric lossless cavity with R=0.9 prove F=4R/(1−R)²=360, T=1/[1+F sin²(δ/2)] with resonance 1 and antiresonance 1/361, exact phase FWHM=4 asin(1/(6√10)), and exact finesse π/[2 asin(1/(6√10))], distinguishing the standard 3π√10 approximation.
ED:020430.statement:
A symmetric lossless Fabry–Pérot resonator has power
reflectance $R=0.9$ at each mirror and no absorption. The Airy
coefficient of finesse and the intensity transmission are
\[
\mathcal F=\frac{4R}{(1-R)^2},\qquad
T=\frac{1}{1+\mathcal F\sin^2(\delta/2)},
\]
where $\delta$ is the round-trip phase. Do not replace the cavity
linewidth problem by a rectangular TE$_{10}$ waveguide cutoff, a
dispersive phase/group-velocity audit in a conducting pipe, or a
Kramers–Kronig integral.

1. Evaluate $\mathcal F$ and prove $\mathcal F=360$. Then read off
   the on-resonance and antiresonance transmissions
   \[
   T(0)=1,\qquad
   T(\pi)=\frac{1}{361}.
   \]

2. Define the exact intensity half-maximum by $T=1/2$. Prove that
   the full phase width between the two adjacent half-maxima about
   $\delta=0$ is
   \[
   \Delta\delta
   =4\arcsin\Bigl(\frac{1}{6\sqrt{10}}\Bigr)
   =0.21091623404379986\,\mathrm{rad}.
   \]

3. The free spectral range in the same phase variable is $2\pi$.
   Define the exact finesse by $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ex}}=2\pi/\Delta\delta$
   and prove
   \[
   \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ex}}
   =\frac{\pi}{2\arcsin\bigl(1/(6\sqrt{10})\bigr)}
   =29.7899558830298.
   \]
   Record that the standard high-finesse approximation
   $\pi\sqrt{\mathcal F}/2=3\pi\sqrt{10}=29.8037647973883$ is not
   equal to the exact value.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the coefficient of finesse
   $\mathcal F=360$ is the finesse”; (ii) “the exact finesse is
   $3\pi\sqrt{10}$, or the half-maximum condition is
   $\sin(\delta/2)=1/\mathcal F$ rather than $1/\sqrt{\mathcal F}$.”
permittedResults: At $R=0.9$ one has $1-R=0.1$ and $\mathcal F=3.6/0.01=360$. Then $1/\sqrt{360}=1/(6\sqrt{10})$. Resonance gives $T=1$; antiresonance gives $T=1/(1+360)=1/361$.

$\Delta\delta=4\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ex}}=\pi/(2\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10})))$. The approximation $3\pi\sqrt{10}$ is larger than the exact finesse and must be labelled as such.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute 4R/(1−R)², set 1+F sin²(δ/2)=2, and convert 1/√360 into 1/(6√10).
Form 2π/Δδ exactly, then compare with π√F/2=3π√10 without replacing one by the other.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates F=360 and the Airy transmissions T(0)=1 and T(π)=1/361, and derives the exact phase FWHM 4 asin(1/(6√10)).
Reports the exact finesse π/[2 asin(1/(6√10))] and distinguishes it from the approximation 3π√10.
Rejects identifying F with the finesse or promoting 3π√10 to an exact value, and refuses reserved TE10 substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the Airy coefficient of finesse F=360 with the cavity finesse, and never forms 2π/Δδ.
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact finesse 29.7899558830298 is replaced by the coefficient 360.

commonErrors.description: Quotes 3π√10 as the exact finesse, or sets the half-maximum condition to sin(δ/2)=1/F rather than 1/√F.
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact width 4 asin(1/(6√10)) and exact finesse π/[2 asin(1/(6√10))] are not produced.

hintTree.content: Compute $4R/(1-R)^2$ before touching the Airy function. $0.9$ and $0.1^2$ produce $360$ on the nose.
Set $1+\mathcal F\sin^2(\delta/2)=2$. The half-angle is $\arcsin(1/\sqrt{\mathcal F})$, and the full width doubles twice.
Finesse is FSR divided by FWHM, i.e. $2\pi/\Delta\delta$. Do not identify it with $\mathcal F$ or with $\pi\sqrt{\mathcal F}/2$.

ED:020430.canonicalSolution:
The coefficient of finesse is
\[
\mathcal F
=\frac{4\cdot 0.9}{(0.1)^2}
=\frac{3.6}{0.01}
=360.
\]
On resonance $\sin(\delta/2)=0$, so $T=1$. At antiresonance
$\delta=\pi$ and $\sin(\delta/2)=1$, so
\[
T=\frac{1}{1+360}=\frac{1}{361}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathcal F=360,\;T(0)=1,\;T(\pi)=1/361}.
\]

The half-maximum condition $T=1/2$ is
\[
1+\mathcal F\sin^2(\delta/2)=2
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\sin(\delta/2)=\frac1{\sqrt{\mathcal F}}
=\frac1{\sqrt{360}}
=\frac1{6\sqrt{10}}.
\]
The two adjacent roots about $\delta=0$ sit at
$\delta=\pm 2\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))$, so the full width is
\[
\Delta\delta
=4\arcsin\Bigl(\frac{1}{6\sqrt{10}}\Bigr)
=0.21091623404379986\,\mathrm{rad}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta\delta=4\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))
=0.21091623404379986\,\mathrm{rad}}.
\]

With free spectral range $2\pi$,
\[
\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ex}}
=\frac{2\pi}{\Delta\delta}
=\frac{\pi}{2\arcsin\bigl(1/(6\sqrt{10})\bigr)}
=29.7899558830298.
\]
The standard approximation is
\[
\frac{\pi\sqrt{\mathcal F}}{2}
=\frac{\pi\sqrt{360}}{2}
=3\pi\sqrt{10}
=29.8037647973883,
\]
which is not equal to the exact finesse.
\[
\boxed{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ex}}=\pi/[2\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))]
=29.7899558830298,\;
3\pi\sqrt{10}\text{ is approximate}}.
\]

Sentence (i) identifies the coefficient of finesse $360$ with the
finesse. Sentence (ii) promotes the $3\pi\sqrt{10}$ approximation
to an exact value, or uses $\sin(\delta/2)=1/\mathcal F$ and
destroys the half-maximum width. The resonator is a symmetric
lossless Fabry–Pérot; it is not a TE$_{10}$ waveguide cutoff.

graderFixtures.proofText: The coefficient of finesse is $\mathcal F=360$, with $T(0)=1$ and $T(\pi)=1/361$. The exact phase FWHM is $4\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))=0.21091623404379986$ rad and the exact finesse is $\pi/[2\arcsin(1/(6\sqrt{10}))]=29.7899558830298$. The value $3\pi\sqrt{10}=29.8037647973883$ is the high-finesse approximation, not the exact finesse.
The coefficient of finesse F=360 is the finesse. I do not form 2π/Δδ and I do not accept the exact value 29.7899558830298.
The exact finesse is 3π√10, or the half-maximum condition is sin(δ/2)=1/F rather than 1/√F. I never report 4 asin(1/(6√10)) or π/[2 asin(1/(6√10))].

ED:020524.title: Cold-plasma dispersion at ω=5ωp/3: index 4/5, vp vg=c², and an excess delay L/(4c)
ED:020524.objective: For a cold collisionless plasma with εr=1−ωp²/ω² and k=√(ω²−ωp²)/c, at ω=5ωp/3 prove n=4/5, k=4ωp/(3c), vp=5c/4, vg=4c/5, vp vg=c², excess group delay L/(4c) across thickness L, and evanescence below ωp.
ED:020524.statement:
A cold, collisionless, unmagnetized plasma has plasma frequency
$\omega_p>0$ and relative permittivity
\[
\varepsilon_r(\omega)=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}
\]
for a monochromatic wave $e^{i(kz-\omega t)}$ in free space with
$c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$. The dispersion relation above cutoff
is $k=\sqrt{\omega^2-\omega_p^2}/c$. Fix the operating frequency
\[
\omega=\frac{5\omega_p}{3}.
\]
Do not replace the cold-plasma law by a Kramers–Kronig integral, a
Debye relaxation $\varepsilon_r=\varepsilon_\infty+(\varepsilon_s-\varepsilon_\infty)/(1+i\omega\tau)$,
a rectangular TE$_{10}$ cutoff, or a uniform electric field.

1. Prove that the refractive index and the wavenumber are
   \[
   n=\frac45,\qquad
   k=\frac{4\omega_p}{3c}.
   \]

2. Prove that the phase and group velocities satisfy
   \[
   v_p=\frac{5c}{4},\qquad
   v_g=\frac{4c}{5},\qquad
   v_p v_g=c^2.
   \]

3. A narrow-band packet centered at this frequency traverses a
   uniform plasma slab of thickness $L$. Prove that the group transit
   time is $L/v_g=5L/(4c)$, so the excess delay relative to vacuum is
   \[
   \frac{L}{v_g}-\frac Lc=\frac{L}{4c}.
   \]
   State that for $\omega<\omega_p$ one has $\varepsilon_r<0$ and the
   wave is evanescent, with imaginary $k=i\sqrt{\omega_p^2-\omega^2}/c$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the plasma is a Debye dielectric (or
   must be reconstructed from a Kramers–Kronig integral), so
   $\varepsilon_r=1+\omega_p^2/\omega^2$ and $n>1$”; (ii) “the group
   velocity is $5c/4$ and the phase velocity is $4c/5$, or the excess
   delay is the vacuum transit $L/c$.”
permittedResults: At $\omega=5\omega_p/3$ one has $\omega_p^2/\omega^2=9/25$, so $n=\sqrt{1-9/25}=4/5$ and $k=(4/5)(5\omega_p/3)/c=4\omega_p/(3c)$.
Then $v_p=\omega/k=5c/4$ and $v_g=c^2/v_p=4c/5$. Excess delay: $5L/(4c)-L/c=L/(4c)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute ω=5ωp/3 into εr=1−ωp²/ω², take n=√εr, and read k=nω/c.
Use vp=ω/k and vg=c²/vp from ω²=ωp²+c²k², then subtract L/c from L/vg.

milestones.criterion: Produces n=4/5, k=4ωp/(3c), vp=5c/4, vg=4c/5, and vp vg=c².
Reports the excess group delay L/(4c) and evanescence for ω<ωp.
Rejects a KK/Debye or sign-flipped permittivity, or a vp↔vg / vacuum-delay error, and refuses reserved TE10 or uniform-E substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the cold-plasma law by a Kramers–Kronig reconstruction or a Debye dielectric, or writes εr=1+ωp²/ω² so that n>1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required index n=4/5 and every subsequent velocity and delay identity are lost.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the velocities to vg=5c/4 and vp=4c/5, or reports the excess delay as the vacuum transit L/c (or as the raw group time 5L/(4c)).
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair (vp,vg)=(5c/4,4c/5) and the excess delay L/(4c) are not produced.

hintTree.content: Substitute $\omega_p/\omega=3/5$ into $\varepsilon_r=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$ before taking the square root.
The identity $v_g=c^2/v_p$ follows from $\omega\,\mathrm{d}\omega=c^2 k\,\mathrm{d}k$ and does not require a fresh derivative of $n(\omega)$.
The excess delay subtracts the vacuum transit $L/c$ from $L/v_g=5L/(4c)$. Do not report $5L/(4c)$ as the excess.

ED:020524.canonicalSolution:
At the assigned frequency $\omega=5\omega_p/3$,
\[
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}=\frac{9}{25},
\qquad
\varepsilon_r=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25}.
\]
The refractive index (positive branch above cutoff) is
\[
n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}=\frac45.
\]
The wavenumber is
\[
k=\frac{n\omega}{c}=\frac45\cdot\frac{5\omega_p}{3c}=\frac{4\omega_p}{3c},
\]
which matches $k=\sqrt{\omega^2-\omega_p^2}/c=\sqrt{16\omega_p^2/9}/c$.
\[
\boxed{n=4/5,\;k=4\omega_p/(3c)}.
\]

The phase velocity is
\[
v_p=\frac\omega k=\frac{5\omega_p/3}{4\omega_p/(3c)}=\frac{5c}{4}.
\]
Differentiating $\omega^2=\omega_p^2+c^2 k^2$ produces
$2\omega\,\mathrm{d}\omega=2c^2 k\,\mathrm{d}k$, hence
\[
v_g=\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}=\frac{c^2 k}{\omega}=\frac{c^2}{v_p}=\frac{4c}{5}.
\]
The product identity is immediate:
\[
v_p v_g=\frac{5c}{4}\cdot\frac{4c}{5}=c^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{v_p=5c/4,\;v_g=4c/5,\;v_p v_g=c^2}.
\]

A packet centered at this frequency crosses a slab of thickness $L$ in
the group time $L/v_g=5L/(4c)$. The vacuum transit of the same
thickness is $L/c$, so the excess delay is
\[
\frac{L}{v_g}-\frac Lc=\frac{5L}{4c}-\frac Lc=\frac{L}{4c}.
\]
For $\omega<\omega_p$ one has $\varepsilon_r<0$ and
$k=i\sqrt{\omega_p^2-\omega^2}/c$: the wave is evanescent and does not
propagate. The law $\varepsilon_r=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$ is the cold
collisionless plasma response, not a Debye relaxation and not a
Kramers–Kronig reconstruction of a causal dielectric.
\[
\boxed{\text{excess delay }L/(4c),\;
\omega<\omega_p\text{ evanescent}}.
\]

Sentence (i) imports a reserved KK/Debye dielectric and flips the sign
in $\varepsilon_r$, destroying $n=4/5$. Sentence (ii) swaps $v_p$ with
$v_g$ or reports the vacuum transit as if it were the excess delay.
The construction is not a TE$_{10}$ cutoff problem and not a
uniform-$E$ Lorentz-force orbit.

ED:020525.title: Good-conductor skin depth in the e^{iωt} convention: γ=(1+i)/δ, Zs, and |H0|²/8 loss
ED:020525.objective: With e^{iωt} and e^{−γz}, prove γ=(1+i)/δ, δ=√(2/(μσω)), Zs=(1+i)√(ωμ/(2σ)); for μ=1, σ=8, ω=1 prove δ=1/2, γ=2+2i, Zs=(1+i)/4, amplitude e^{−1} and phase lag 1 at z=δ, and loss per area |H0|²/8.
ED:020525.statement:
A linear isotropic good conductor occupies the half-space $z>0$, with
permeability $\mu>0$, conductivity $\sigma>0$, and negligible
displacement current. Harmonic fields are written in the engineering
convention $e^{i\omega t}$, and a wave decaying into $z>0$ is written
$e^{-\gamma z}$. Peak phasors are used. Do not replace the
good-conductor limit by a Kramers–Kronig integral, a Debye relaxation,
a rectangular TE$_{10}$ cutoff, or a uniform electric field.

1. Starting from $\gamma^2=i\omega\mu\sigma$ in this time convention,
   prove
   \[
   \delta=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}},
   \qquad
   \gamma=\frac{1+i}{\delta},
   \qquad
   Z_s=(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu}{2\sigma}}.
   \]

2. Specialize to the normalized values $\mu=1$, $\sigma=8$,
   $\omega=1$ and prove
   \[
   \delta=\frac12,\qquad
   \gamma=2+2i,\qquad
   Z_s=\frac{1+i}{4}.
   \]

3. At the depth $z=\delta$, prove that the field amplitude is
   $e^{-1}$ times its surface value and that the phase lags the
   surface phase by $1$ radian. Prove that the time-average power
   absorbed per unit area is
   \[
   \frac12\operatorname{Re}(Z_s)\,|H_0|^2=\frac{|H_0|^2}{8}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the physics convention $e^{-i\omega t}$
   is being used, so $\gamma=(1-i)/\delta$ (or the wave grows as
   $e^{+\gamma z}$)”; (ii) “the absorbed power density is
   $\operatorname{Re}(Z_s)|H_0|^2=|H_0|^2/4$, or else $\delta=2$.”
permittedResults: The principal square root of $i$ is $(1+i)/\sqrt{2}$, so $\gamma=\sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma}\,(1+i)/\sqrt{2}=(1+i)/\delta$. Then $Z_s=i\omega\mu/\gamma=(1+i)/(\sigma\delta)$.
At $\mu=1$, $\sigma=8$, $\omega=1$ one has $\delta=1/2$, $\gamma=2+2i$, and $Z_s=(1+i)/4$. At $z=\delta$ the factor $e^{-\gamma z}=e^{-1}e^{-i}$. Loss: $\tfrac12\cdot(1/4)|H_0|^2=|H_0|^2/8$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take the first-quadrant square root of γ²=iωμσ to fix γ=(1+i)/δ, then form Zs=iωμ/γ.
Insert μ=1, σ=8, ω=1, evaluate e^{−γδ}=e^{−1}e^{−i}, and keep the factor 1/2 in ½ Re(Zs)|H0|².

milestones.criterion: Derives γ=(1+i)/δ, δ=√(2/(μσω)), and Zs=(1+i)√(ωμ/(2σ)), and evaluates δ=1/2, γ=2+2i, Zs=(1+i)/4.
Reports amplitude e^{−1} and phase lag 1 at z=δ, together with loss per area |H0|²/8.
Rejects a flipped time-convention γ=(1−i)/δ or a loss |H0|²/4, and refuses reserved KK/Debye, TE10, or uniform-E substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Imports the e^{−iωt} convention and reports γ=(1−i)/δ, or writes a wave that grows as e^{+γz} into the conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: The required γ=2+2i, the phase lag of +1 radian, and Zs=(1+i)/4 are replaced by the opposite imaginary part.

commonErrors.description: Reports the absorbed power per unit area as Re(Zs)|H0|²=|H0|²/4, dropping the peak-phasor factor 1/2, or inverts the skin depth to δ=2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required loss |H0|²/8 and the depth δ=1/2 are not produced.

hintTree.content: Write $i=e^{i\pi/2}$ and take the square root in the first quadrant: $\sqrt{i}=(1+i)/\sqrt{2}$. That fixes $\gamma=(1+i)/\delta$, not $(1-i)/\delta$.
The normalized arithmetic is $\delta=\sqrt{2/8}=1/2$ and $\gamma=(1+i)/(1/2)=2+2i$.
Keep the peak-phasor factor $1/2$ in the Poynting flux. $\operatorname{Re}(Z_s)=1/4$ is not itself the loss per area.

ED:020525.canonicalSolution:
In the convention $e^{i\omega t}$ Faraday's and Ampère's laws with
$\mathbf{J}=\sigma\mathbf{E}$ and negligible displacement current give
\[
\gamma^2=i\omega\mu\sigma.
\]
The square root of $i$ in the first quadrant is $(1+i)/\sqrt{2}$, so
the decaying root is
\[
\gamma=\sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma}\cdot\frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1+i}{\delta},
\qquad
\delta=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}}.
\]
The surface impedance is
\[
Z_s=\frac{i\omega\mu}{\gamma}
=\frac{i\omega\mu\,\delta}{1+i}
=(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu}{2\sigma}}.
\]
(Equivalently $Z_s=(1+i)/(\sigma\delta)$.)
\[
\boxed{\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)},\;
\gamma=(1+i)/\delta,\;
Z_s=(1+i)\sqrt{\omega\mu/(2\sigma)}}.
\]

With the normalized values $\mu=1$, $\sigma=8$, $\omega=1$,
\[
\delta=\sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}=\frac12,
\qquad
\gamma=\frac{1+i}{1/2}=2+2i,
\qquad
Z_s=(1+i)\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}}=\frac{1+i}{4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\delta=1/2,\;\gamma=2+2i,\;Z_s=(1+i)/4}.
\]

At $z=\delta=1/2$,
\[
e^{-\gamma z}=e^{-(2+2i)(1/2)}=e^{-(1+i)}=e^{-1}e^{-i}.
\]
The amplitude is therefore $e^{-1}$ times the surface amplitude. In
the convention $e^{i\omega t}$ the real field is proportional to
$\cos(\omega t-\beta z)$, so the phase at $z=\delta$ lags the surface
phase by $\beta\delta=1$ radian.

The time-average inward Poynting flux is
\[
\frac12\operatorname{Re}(Z_s)\,|H_0|^2
=\frac12\cdot\frac14\cdot|H_0|^2
=\frac{|H_0|^2}{8}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{at }z=\delta\text{: amplitude }e^{-1},\;
\text{phase lag }1,\;
\text{loss }|H_0|^2/8}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the time convention and produces $\gamma=(1-i)/\delta$
or a growing wave. Sentence (ii) drops the peak-phasor factor $1/2$
from the loss or inverts $\delta$. The construction is the
good-conductor skin-effect limit; it is not a Kramers–Kronig or Debye
dielectric, not a TE$_{10}$ cutoff, and not a uniform-$E$ orbit.

graderFixtures.proofText: In the $e^{i\omega t}$ convention one has $\gamma=(1+i)/\delta$ and $Z_s=(1+i)\sqrt{\omega\mu/(2\sigma)}$. For $\mu=1$, $\sigma=8$, $\omega=1$ one has $\delta=1/2$, $\gamma=2+2i$, and $Z_s=(1+i)/4$. At $z=\delta$ the amplitude is $e^{-1}$ and the phase lag is $1$ radian. The loss per unit area is $|H_0|^2/8$.
The physics convention e^{−iωt} is being used, so γ=(1−i)/δ, or the wave grows as e^{+γz}. I do not accept γ=2+2i.
The absorbed power density is Re(Zs)|H0|²=|H0|²/4, or else δ=2. I never report loss |H0|²/8 with δ=1/2.

ED:020529.title: Fizeau drag by velocity addition: exact w± for n=2, u=c/3, and the Fresnel first-order piece
ED:020529.objective: From the relativistic addition of ±c/n with a boost u prove w±=(±c/n+u)/(1±u/(nc)), evaluate n=2 and u=c/3 to w+=5c/7 and w−=−c/5, and recover the first-order co-moving law c/2+3u/4 with Fresnel coefficient 3/4.
ED:020529.statement:
Light travels at phase speed $c/n$ relative to a dielectric of
index $n>1$ that itself moves at laboratory speed $u$ with
$|u|<c$. Collinear addition of velocities, with the optical
velocity taken in the dielectric rest frame, gives the exact
laboratory speeds
\[
w_\pm=\frac{\pm c/n+u}{1\pm u/(nc)}.
\]
The upper sign is co-propagating ($+c/n$ with $+u$); the lower
sign is counter-propagating. Do not replace the addition formula
by a Kramers–Kronig integral, a Debye-model sum rule, a scalar
unmagnetized cold-plasma index $n^2=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$, or a
magnetoionic Faraday rotation.

1. Derive the displayed $w_\pm$ from the collinear Einstein
   addition of $\pm c/n$ with $u$. Confirm that the formula is
   exact in special relativity for a rest-frame phase speed $c/n$.

2. Specialize to $n=2$ and $u=c/3$. Prove
   \[
   w_+=\frac{5c}{7},\qquad w_-=-\frac c5.
   \]

3. Expand the co-propagating speed to first order in $u/c$ and
   prove
   \[
   w_+=\frac cn+u\Bigl(1-\frac1{n^2}\Bigr)+O(u^2/c).
   \]
   At $n=2$ this is $c/2+3u/4$. Identify $1-1/n^2=3/4$ as the
   Fresnel drag coefficient.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “laboratory speeds add Galileanly, so
   $w_+=c/2+c/3=5c/6$ and $w_-=-c/2+c/3=-c/6$”; (ii) “the exact
   co-propagating value is the first-order expression $c/2+3u/4$,
   or $|w_+|$ may exceed $c$.” Record that both exact roots are
   strictly subluminal.
permittedResults: $|5c/7|<c$ and $|-c/5|<c$. The first-order co-moving law is $c/2+(3/4)u$, whose numerical value $c/2+(3/4)(c/3)=3c/4$ is not $5c/7$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert v′=±c/n into the collinear Einstein addition formula and evaluate the two rational numbers at n=2, u=c/3.
Expand the co-moving root to first order in u/c to isolate 1−1/n²=3/4, then compare 3c/4 with the exact 5c/7.

milestones.criterion: Derives w±=(±c/n+u)/(1±u/(nc)) and evaluates n=2, u=c/3 to w+=5c/7 and w−=−c/5.
Recovers the first-order co-moving law c/2+3u/4 with Fresnel coefficient 3/4 and records that both exact roots are subluminal.
Rejects Galilean addition or first-order-as-exact, and refuses reserved Kramers–Kronig or scalar-cold-plasma substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Adds the rest-frame optical speeds Galileanly and reports w+=c/2+c/3=5c/6 and w−=−c/6.
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact values 5c/7 and −c/5, and every subsequent first-order comparison, are lost.

commonErrors.description: Quotes the first-order law c/2+3u/4 as the exact co-propagating speed, or claims that |w+| may exceed c.
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact pair (5c/7, −c/5) and the subluminal audit are not produced.

hintTree.content: The rest-frame optical speeds are $+c/n$ and $-c/n$, not $\pm c$. Insert them into $(v'+u)/(1+v'u/c^2)$.
For $n=2$ and $u=c/3$ the co-moving numerator is $5c/6$ and the denominator is $7/6$.
Expand $(c/n+u)(1-u/(nc)+O(u^2/c^2))$ and drop $u^2$. The coefficient of $u$ is $1-1/n^2$.

ED:020529.canonicalSolution:
In the dielectric rest frame the two collinear phase velocities
are $v'_\pm=\pm c/n$. Einstein addition with the laboratory boost
$u$ gives
\[
w_\pm=\frac{v'_\pm+u}{1+v'_\pm u/c^2}
=\frac{\pm c/n+u}{1\pm u/(nc)}.
\]
The identity is exact for those rest-frame speeds.
\[
\boxed{w_\pm=(\pm c/n+u)/(1\pm u/(nc))}.
\]

Now set $n=2$ and $u=c/3$. The co-propagating root is
\[
w_+
=\frac{c/2+c/3}{1+(c/3)/(2c)}
=\frac{5c/6}{1+1/6}
=\frac{5c/6}{7/6}
=\frac{5c}{7}.
\]
The counter-propagating root is
\[
w_-
=\frac{-c/2+c/3}{1-(c/3)/(2c)}
=\frac{-c/6}{1-1/6}
=\frac{-c/6}{5/6}
=-\frac c5.
\]
\[
\boxed{w_+=5c/7,\;w_-=-c/5}.
\]

For the first-order co-moving expansion,
\begin{align*}
w_+
&=\bigl(\tfrac cn+u\bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac{u}{nc}+O(u^2/c^2)\Bigr)
=\frac cn+u-\frac{u}{n^2}+O(u^2/c)\\
&=\frac cn+u\Bigl(1-\frac1{n^2}\Bigr)+O(u^2/c).
\end{align*}
At $n=2$ the Fresnel coefficient is $1-1/4=3/4$, so
\[
w_+=\frac c2+\frac{3u}{4}+O(u^2/c).
\]
Both exact roots are strictly subluminal:
$|5c/7|<c$ and $|-c/5|<c$. The first-order number
$c/2+(3/4)(c/3)=3c/4$ is not equal to the exact $5c/7$.
\[
\boxed{\text{first-order co }c/2+3u/4,\;
\text{Fresnel }3/4,\;
\text{exact subluminal}}.
\]

Sentence (i) uses Galilean addition and reports $5c/6$ and $-c/6$.
Sentence (ii) promotes the first-order Fresnel law to an exact
value, or permits a superluminal laboratory speed. The exercise is
pure velocity addition in a moving dielectric; it is not a
Kramers–Kronig integral and not a scalar cold-plasma index.

graderFixtures.proofText: The exact laboratory speeds are $w_+=(5c/7)$ and $w_-=(-c/5)$. The first-order co-moving law is $c/2+3u/4$ with Fresnel coefficient $3/4$. Both exact roots are strictly subluminal, and $3c/4$ is not equal to $5c/7$.
Laboratory speeds add Galileanly, so w+=c/2+c/3=5c/6 and w−=−c/2+c/3=−c/6. I do not accept w+=5c/7 or w−=−c/5.
The exact co-propagating value is the first-order expression c/2+3u/4, or |w+| may exceed c. I never distinguish 5c/7 from 3c/4.
