ED:020531.title: Magnetized-plasma Faraday rotation: n± at ω=3ωp, ωc=ωp, and a negative φ that flips with B
ED:020531.objective: With n+²=1−ωp²/[ω(ω−ωc)] and n−²=1−ωp²/[ω(ω+ωc)], and φ=(k+−k−)L/2, evaluate ω=3ωp, ωc=ωp, L=c/ωp to n+=√(5/6), n−=√(11/12), and φ=(3/2)(√(5/6)−√(11/12)), and record that reversing B flips the sign.
ED:020531.statement:
A cold magnetized electron plasma supports two circularly
polarized electromagnetic modes propagating parallel to a uniform
background field $\mathbf B_0$. Adopt the index convention
\[
n_+^2=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega-\omega_c)},\qquad
n_-^2=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega+\omega_c)},
\]
with plasma frequency $\omega_p>0$ and signed cyclotron frequency
$\omega_c=eB_0/m$ (so $\omega_c$ flips when $\mathbf B_0$ is
reversed). The Faraday rotation angle of a linearly polarized wave
that travels a distance $L$ is
\[
\phi=\frac{(k_+-k_-)L}{2},\qquad
k_\pm=n_\pm\frac{\omega}{c}.
\]
Do not replace the magnetized two-mode problem by the scalar
unmagnetized cold-plasma index $n^2=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$, a
Kramers–Kronig integral, or a Fizeau moving-dielectric addition.

1. Specialize to $\omega=3\omega_p$, $\omega_c=\omega_p$, and
   $L=c/\omega_p$. Prove
   \[
   n_+=\sqrt{\frac56},\qquad
   n_-=\sqrt{\frac{11}{12}}.
   \]

2. Insert $k_\pm=n_\pm\omega/c$ into the stated rotation convention
   and prove
   \[
   \phi
   =\frac32\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac56}-\sqrt{\frac{11}{12}}\Bigr)
   =-0.0668342678715918\,\mathrm{rad}.
   \]

3. Reverse $\mathbf B_0$, which sends $\omega_c\mapsto-\omega_c$
   and therefore swaps the two indices. Prove that $\phi$ changes
   sign and that $|\phi|$ is unchanged.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “magnetization does not matter, so
   both indices collapse to the scalar cold-plasma value
   $n=\sqrt{1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2}=\sqrt{8/9}$ and $\phi=0$”;
   (ii) “the rotation is $(k_--k_+)L/2$, or the factor $1/2$ may
   be dropped, so $\phi$ is positive (or twice as large).”
permittedResults: At $\omega=3\omega_p$ and $\omega_c=\omega_p$ one has $n_+^2=1-1/(3\cdot 2)=5/6$ and $n_-^2=1-1/(3\cdot 4)=11/12$.
Then $\phi=(3\omega_p/c)(n_+-n_-)(c/\omega_p)/2=(3/2)(n_+-n_-)$. Because $n_+<n_-$, the angle is negative. Reversing $B$ swaps the roots.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the two plasma denominators to 6ωp² and 12ωp², then take positive square roots of 5/6 and 11/12.
Form (k+−k−)L/2 with ωL/c=3 and keep the negative sign of n+−n−; reverse ωc to swap the roots.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates n+=√(5/6) and n−=√(11/12) from the stated magnetoionic indices at ω=3ωp, ωc=ωp.
Reports φ=(3/2)(√(5/6)−√(11/12))=−0.0668342678715918 rad and the sign reversal under B→−B.
Rejects a scalar cold-plasma collapse or a swapped/unsigned angle, and refuses reserved Kramers–Kronig or Fizeau substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the cyclotron splitting and uses the scalar unmagnetized index n²=1−ωp²/ω² for both modes, concluding φ=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair (√(5/6), √(11/12)) and the nonzero Faraday angle are replaced by the c14 cold-plasma collapse.

commonErrors.description: Writes φ=(k−−k+)L/2 or drops the factor 1/2, producing a positive angle or twice the stated magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The required signed value (3/2)(√(5/6)−√(11/12)) is not produced.

hintTree.content: Reduce the two plasma terms first: $\omega(\omega-\omega_c)=6\omega_p^2$ and $\omega(\omega+\omega_c)=12\omega_p^2$.
The prefactor is $(\omega L)/c=3$. Halving it produces the $3/2$ in front of $n_+-n_-$.
Keep the stated sign $\phi\propto(n_+-n_-)$. Do not import the scalar cold-plasma index, which erases Faraday rotation entirely.

ED:020531.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $\omega=3\omega_p$ and $\omega_c=\omega_p$ into the
stated indices:
\begin{align*}
n_+^2
&=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{3\omega_p\cdot(3\omega_p-\omega_p)}
=1-\frac{1}{6}
=\frac56,\\
n_-^2
&=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{3\omega_p\cdot(3\omega_p+\omega_p)}
=1-\frac{1}{12}
=\frac{11}{12}.
\end{align*}
Both values lie in $(0,1)$, so
\[
n_+=\sqrt{\frac56},\qquad
n_-=\sqrt{\frac{11}{12}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{n_+=\sqrt{5/6},\;n_-=\sqrt{11/12}}.
\]

With $k_\pm=n_\pm\omega/c$ and $L=c/\omega_p$,
\[
\phi
=\frac{(n_+-n_-)\omega L}{2c}
=\frac{(n_+-n_-)\cdot 3\omega_p\cdot(c/\omega_p)}{2c}
=\frac32\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac56}-\sqrt{\frac{11}{12}}\Bigr).
\]
Numerically
\[
\phi=-0.0668342678715918\,\mathrm{rad}.
\]
The sign is negative because $n_+<n_-$ in this convention.
\[
\boxed{\phi=(3/2)(\sqrt{5/6}-\sqrt{11/12})
=-0.0668342678715918\,\mathrm{rad}}.
\]

Reversing $\mathbf B_0$ sends $\omega_c\mapsto-\omega_c$, which
interchanges the two denominators and therefore swaps $n_+$ with
$n_-$. The combination $n_+-n_-$ changes sign while its modulus is
unchanged, so $\phi\mapsto-\phi$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbf B_0\to-\mathbf B_0\;\Rightarrow\;\phi\to-\phi}.
\]

Sentence (i) collapses both modes onto the scalar unmagnetized
index $\sqrt{1-1/9}=\sqrt{8/9}$ and forces $\phi=0$, which is the
c14 cold-plasma substitution this packet is written to forbid.
Sentence (ii) reverses the stated $(k_+-k_-)$ convention or drops
the factor $1/2$, producing the wrong sign or twice the angle.
The construction is a magnetized two-mode Faraday rotation; it is
not a Kramers–Kronig integral and not a Fizeau boost.

graderFixtures.proofText: The magnetoionic indices are $n_+=\sqrt{5/6}$ and $n_-=\sqrt{11/12}$. With $\phi=(k_+-k_-)L/2$ one has $\phi=(3/2)(\sqrt{5/6}-\sqrt{11/12})=-0.0668342678715918$ rad. Reversing $\mathbf B_0$ flips the sign of $\phi$ and leaves $|\phi|$ unchanged.

ED:020626.title: A relativistic cyclotron orbit at β=3/5: energy, gyro frequency, radius 3L/16, and clockwise sense
ED:020626.objective: For q>0, B along z, v along x, β=3/5, γ=5/4, and qB/m=4c/L prove that B does no work, E=5mc²/4, K=mc²/4, gyro angular frequency 16c/(5L), radius 3L/16, period 5πL/(8c), and clockwise sense viewed from +z.
ED:020626.statement:
A particle of charge $q>0$ and rest mass $m>0$ moves in a uniform
magnetic field $\mathbf{B}=B\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ with $B>0$ and no
electric field. At $t=0$ the velocity is $\mathbf{v}=v\hat{\mathbf{x}}$
with
\[
\beta=\frac vc=\frac35.
\]
The cyclotron scale is given as
\[
\frac{qB}{m}=\frac{4c}{L}
\]
for a fixed length $L>0$. Work in Minkowski kinematics with
$\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ and the Lorentz force
$q(\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})$. Do not replace the pure-$B$
orbit by a uniform electric field, a covariant Lorentz-force boost
along $\mathbf{E}$, a rectangular TE$_{10}$ cutoff, or a
Kramers–Kronig / Debye dielectric.

1. Prove $\gamma=5/4$. Show that the magnetic force does no work, and
   prove that the total energy and kinetic energy are
   \[
   \mathcal{E}=\frac54 mc^2,\qquad
   K=\frac14 mc^2.
   \]

2. Prove that the relativistic gyro angular frequency and the
   orbital radius are
   \[
   \omega=\frac{qB}{\gamma m}=\frac{16c}{5L},\qquad
   \rho=\frac{\gamma m v}{qB}=\frac{3L}{16}.
   \]
   Deduce the orbital period
   \[
   T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{5\pi L}{8c}.
   \]

3. Under the declared signs $q>0$, $\mathbf{B}=B\hat{\mathbf{z}}$,
   $\mathbf{v}(0)=v\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, prove that the initial force is
   $-qvB\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and that the orbit is clockwise when
   viewed from $+z$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the motion is nonrelativistic, so
   $\omega=qB/m=4c/L$ and $T=\pi L/(2c)$”; (ii) “viewed from $+z$ the
   orbit is counterclockwise, or the radius is $5L/16$ (or $3L/4$).”
permittedResults: $\beta=3/5$ gives $1-\beta^2=16/25$ and $\gamma=5/4$. Then $\mathcal{E}=\gamma mc^2=5mc^2/4$ and $K=(\gamma-1)mc^2=mc^2/4$.
$\omega=(qB/m)/\gamma=(4c/L)/(5/4)=16c/(5L)$ and $\rho=(\gamma\beta c)/(qB/m)=(3/4)c\cdot L/(4c)=3L/16$. Clockwise from $+z$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute γ from β=3/5, keep magnetic work at zero, and insert γ into ω=qB/(γm) and ρ=γmv/(qB).
Evaluate v×B=−vB ŷ with q>0 to name the +z clockwise sense, then convert T=2π/ω.

milestones.criterion: Reports γ=5/4, no magnetic work, E=5mc²/4, K=mc²/4, ω=16c/(5L), and ρ=3L/16.
Produces the period T=5πL/(8c) and the clockwise sense viewed from +z under the declared signs.
Rejects a nonrelativistic ω=qB/m or a counterclockwise / wrong-radius claim, and refuses reserved uniform-E, TE10, or KK/Debye substitutions.

hintTree.content: Compute $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-(3/5)^2}=5/4$ before any dynamical quantity. Magnetic forces never change $\gamma$.
The factor $\gamma$ belongs in the denominator of $\omega$ and in the numerator of $\rho$. Do not use the nonrelativistic pair $(qB/m,\,mv/qB)$.
Evaluate $\hat{\mathbf{x}}\times\hat{\mathbf{z}}=-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ with $q>0$ before naming the sense. Clockwise is the $+z$ view.

ED:020626.canonicalSolution:
The assigned speed is $\beta=3/5$, so
\[
1-\beta^2=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25},
\qquad
\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}=\frac54.
\]
There is no electric field. The magnetic force $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$
is orthogonal to $\mathbf{v}$, hence
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}}{\mathrm{d}t}=q\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{E}=0.
\]
The energy is therefore conserved at the initial value
\[
\mathcal{E}=\gamma mc^2=\frac54 mc^2,
\qquad
K=(\gamma-1)mc^2=\frac14 mc^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\gamma=5/4,\;
\text{no magnetic work},\;
\mathcal{E}=5mc^2/4,\;
K=mc^2/4}.
\]

The relativistic angular gyrofrequency uses the inertial mass
$\gamma m$:
\[
\omega=\frac{qB}{\gamma m}
=\frac{qB/m}{\gamma}
=\frac{4c/L}{5/4}
=\frac{16c}{5L}.
\]
The gyroradius is
\[
\rho
=\frac{\gamma m v}{qB}
=\frac{\gamma\beta c}{qB/m}
=\frac{(5/4)(3/5)c}{4c/L}
=\frac{3L}{16}.
\]
(The same radius is $v/\omega=(3c/5)/(16c/(5L))=3L/16$.) The period is
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
=2\pi\cdot\frac{5L}{16c}
=\frac{5\pi L}{8c}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega=16c/(5L),\;
\rho=3L/16,\;
T=5\pi L/(8c)}.
\]

Under the declared signs,
\[
\mathbf{v}(0)\times\mathbf{B}
=v\hat{\mathbf{x}}\times B\hat{\mathbf{z}}
=-vB\,\hat{\mathbf{y}},
\qquad
q(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})=-qvB\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}.
\]
A particle moving toward $+x$ is therefore accelerated toward $-y$.
On the standard right-handed screen viewed from $+z$ ($+x$ to the
right, $+y$ up) that is a clockwise turn. The construction is a
pure-$B$ relativistic gyro orbit; it is not a uniform-$E$ covariant
Lorentz-force boost.
\[
\boxed{\text{clockwise viewed from }+z}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $\gamma$ from $\omega$ and reports the
nonrelativistic pair $\omega=4c/L$, $T=\pi L/(2c)$. Sentence (ii)
reverses the sense or corrupts the radius. The exercise is not a
TE$_{10}$ cutoff and not a KK/Debye dielectric.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $\gamma=5/4$, no magnetic work, $\mathcal{E}=5mc^2/4$, and $K=mc^2/4$. The gyro angular frequency is $16c/(5L)$, the radius is $3L/16$, and the period is $5\pi L/(8c)$. Viewed from $+z$ the orbit is clockwise.
The motion is nonrelativistic, so ω=qB/m=4c/L and T=πL/(2c). I do not accept ω=16c/(5L) or T=5πL/(8c).
Viewed from +z the orbit is counterclockwise, or the radius is 5L/16 (or 3L/4). I never report clockwise sense with ρ=3L/16.

ED:020627.title: Abraham–Lorentz rectangular pulse: reject the runaway and keep the no-runaway preacceleration
ED:020627.objective: From ma=Fext+mτȧ write a−τȧ=F/m, discard the runaway Ce^{t/τ}, evaluate the no-runaway kernel on a rectangular pulse of height F0 and width T, and for T=τ ln 4 prove a(0)=3F0/(4m), a(T/2)=F0/(2m), and a(−τ ln 2)=3F0/(8m).
ED:020627.statement:
A nonrelativistic charge of inertial mass $m>0$ obeys the
Abraham–Lorentz equation
\[
m\mathbf a=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}+m\tau\dot{\mathbf a},
\]
with a fixed radiation-reaction time $\tau>0$. Restrict to
one-dimensional motion, write $a(t)$ and $F(t)$ for the parallel
components, and rearrange to
\[
a-\tau\dot a=\frac{F}{m}.
\]
Do not replace the radiation-reaction initial-value problem by a
covariant Lorentz-force rapidity integration, a mass-shell audit, a
tensor Maxwell component recovery, or an electric-dipole radiation
zone expansion.

1. The homogeneous equation $\dot a=a/\tau$ has the runaway family
   $a_{\mathrm{run}}(t)=C e^{t/\tau}$. Reject every such solution
   that grows as $t\to+\infty$. Show that the unique no-runaway
   particular solution bounded as $t\to+\infty$ is the advanced
   kernel
   \[
   a(t)=\frac1{m\tau}\int_t^{\infty}
   \exp\Bigl[-\frac{t'-t}{\tau}\Bigr]F(t')\,\mathrm{d}t'.
   \]

2. Let $F$ be the rectangular pulse of height $F_0>0$ on the open
   interval $0<t<T$ and zero otherwise. Evaluate the kernel in each
   of the three regions and prove
   \begin{align*}
   t<0&\colon&
   a(t)&=\frac{F_0}{m}\,e^{t/\tau}\bigl(1-e^{-T/\tau}\bigr),\\
   0\le t\le T&\colon&
   a(t)&=\frac{F_0}{m}\bigl(1-e^{-(T-t)/\tau}\bigr),\\
   t>T&\colon&
   a(t)&=0.
   \end{align*}

3. Specialize to the width $T=\tau\ln 4$. Prove the three sample
   values
   \[
   a(0)=\frac{3F_0}{4m},\qquad
   a\Bigl(\frac T2\Bigr)=\frac{F_0}{2m},\qquad
   a(-\tau\ln 2)=\frac{3F_0}{8m}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the physical solution is the runaway
   $C e^{t/\tau}$ fitted to $a(0)=F_0/m$”; (ii) “there is no
   acceleration for $t<0$, so $a(-\tau\ln 2)=0$, or the interior
   samples are $a(0)=F_0/m$ and $a(T/2)=F_0/m$.” Record that the
   no-runaway kernel preaccelerates, and that this is a pathology of
   the Abraham–Lorentz equation rather than a laboratory prediction
   to be trusted at the scale $\tau$.
permittedResults: On a rectangular pulse the future integral collapses to an interval of length at most $T$. For $t<0$ one integrates $t'\in(0,T)$ and obtains $(F_0/m)e^{t/\tau}(1-e^{-T/\tau})$. For $0\le t\le T$ the lower limit is $t$, giving $(F_0/m)(1-e^{-(T-t)/\tau})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate a−τȧ=F/m against e^{−t/τ} from t to +∞ and impose vanishing of the future boundary term.
Restrict the advanced integral to the pulse support, then insert e^{−T/τ}=1/4 and e^{−ln 2}=1/2.

milestones.criterion: Writes a−τȧ=F/m, discards the runaway Ce^{t/τ}, and produces the no-runaway advanced kernel together with the three-region rectangular-pulse acceleration.
Evaluates T=τ ln 4 to a(0)=3F0/(4m), a(T/2)=F0/(2m), and a(−τ ln 2)=3F0/(8m).
Rejects a runaway fit or a denial of preacceleration, and refuses reserved covariant-force or dipole-zone substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the physical solution to be the runaway C e^{t/τ} fitted at t=0, and never writes the no-runaway advanced kernel.
commonErrors.consequence: The required kernel, the vanishing post-pulse acceleration, and the three T=τ ln 4 samples are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Sets a(t)=0 for all t<0, or reports the interior samples a(0)=F0/m and a(T/2)=F0/m instead of 3F0/(4m) and F0/(2m).
commonErrors.consequence: The required preacceleration value 3F0/(8m) and the no-runaway interior samples are not produced.

hintTree.content: Integrate the first-order ODE against the integrating factor $e^{-t/\tau}$ from $t$ to $+\infty$, then impose vanishing of $e^{-t/\tau}a(t)$ at future infinity.
Split the $t'$ integral at the edges of the pulse. Outside the support of $F$ the integrand is identically zero.
With $T=\tau\ln 4$ the only numerical ingredients are $e^{-\ln 4}=1/4$ and $e^{-\ln 2}=1/2$. The preacceleration sample sits at $t=-\tau\ln 2<0$.

ED:020627.canonicalSolution:
Rewrite the Abraham–Lorentz law as the linear first-order equation
\[
\dot a-\frac1\tau a=-\frac{F}{m\tau}.
\]
The integrating factor is $e^{-t/\tau}$. Multiplying through and
integrating from $t$ to $+\infty$ produces
\[
\Bigl[e^{-t'/\tau}a(t')\Bigr]_t^{\infty}
=-\frac1{m\tau}\int_t^{\infty}e^{-t'/\tau}F(t')\,\mathrm{d}t'.
\]
The no-runaway condition forces the boundary term at $+\infty$ to
vanish, and the remaining term is the advanced kernel
\[
a(t)=\frac1{m\tau}\int_t^{\infty}
\exp\Bigl[-\frac{t'-t}{\tau}\Bigr]F(t')\,\mathrm{d}t'.
\]
Every homogeneous addend $C e^{t/\tau}$ with $C\ne 0$ violates that
future bound and is rejected.
\[
\boxed{a=(m\tau)^{-1}\textstyle\int_t^{\infty}e^{-(t'-t)/\tau}F(t')\,\mathrm{d}t',
\;\text{runaway discarded}}.
\]

On the rectangular pulse the integrand is supported only for
$0<t'<T$. If $t>T$ the integration range lies entirely to the right
of the pulse, so $a(t)=0$. If $0\le t\le T$ the range is $t<t'<T$:
\begin{align*}
a(t)
&=\frac{F_0}{m\tau}\,e^{t/\tau}\int_t^{T}e^{-t'/\tau}\,\mathrm{d}t'
=\frac{F_0}{m}\bigl(1-e^{-(T-t)/\tau}\bigr).
\end{align*}
If $t<0$ the range is the whole pulse:
\begin{align*}
a(t)
&=\frac{F_0}{m\tau}\,e^{t/\tau}\int_0^{T}e^{-t'/\tau}\,\mathrm{d}t'
=\frac{F_0}{m}\,e^{t/\tau}\bigl(1-e^{-T/\tau}\bigr).
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{t<0:\;(F_0/m)e^{t/\tau}(1-e^{-T/\tau});\;
0\le t\le T:\;(F_0/m)(1-e^{-(T-t)/\tau});\;
t>T:\;0}.
\]

Now set $T=\tau\ln 4$, so $e^{-T/\tau}=1/4$. Then
\[
a(0)=\frac{F_0}{m}\bigl(1-\tfrac14\bigr)=\frac{3F_0}{4m}.
\]
At the midpoint $T/2=(\tau\ln 4)/2=\tau\ln 2$ one has
$e^{-(T-T/2)/\tau}=e^{-\ln 2}=1/2$, hence
\[
a\Bigl(\frac T2\Bigr)=\frac{F_0}{m}\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac{F_0}{2m}.
\]
The preacceleration sample $t=-\tau\ln 2$ uses the $t<0$ formula:
\[
a(-\tau\ln 2)
=\frac{F_0}{m}\,e^{-\ln 2}\bigl(1-\tfrac14\bigr)
=\frac{F_0}{m}\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac34
=\frac{3F_0}{8m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{a(0)=3F_0/(4m),\;
a(T/2)=F_0/(2m),\;
a(-\tau\ln 2)=3F_0/(8m)}.
\]

Sentence (i) restores the runaway family and never produces the
advanced kernel or the three sample values. Sentence (ii) denies
preacceleration, or replaces the no-runaway interior values by the
bare $F_0/m$. The kernel is acausal on the scale $\tau$: the charge
accelerates before the pulse arrives. That preacceleration is a
known pathology of the Abraham–Lorentz equation, not a laboratory
signal and not a substitute for a covariant Lorentz-force or dipole
radiation calculation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The no-runaway acceleration is the advanced kernel $(m\tau)^{-1}\int_t^{\infty}e^{-(t'-t)/\tau}F(t')\,\mathrm{d}t'$. On the rectangular pulse, $a(t)=(F_0/m)e^{t/\tau}(1-e^{-T/\tau})$ for $t<0$, $a(t)=(F_0/m)(1-e^{-(T-t)/\tau})$ for $0\le t\le T$, and $a(t)=0$ for $t>T$. At $T=\tau\ln 4$ one has $a(0)=3F_0/(4m)$, $a(T/2)=F_0/(2m)$, and $a(-\tau\ln 2)=3F_0/(8m)$. The runaway $Ce^{t/\tau}$ is discarded.
The physical solution is the runaway C e^{t/τ} fitted to a(0)=F0/m. I do not write the no-runaway advanced kernel and I do not accept a(t)=0 for t>T.
There is no acceleration for t<0, so a(−τ ln 2)=0, or the interior samples are a(0)=F0/m and a(T/2)=F0/m. I never report 3F0/(4m), F0/(2m), and 3F0/(8m).

ED:020628.title: Adiabatic magnetic mirror: μ conserved, pitch at 2B0, and a mirror ratio of four
ED:020628.objective: From μ=p_perp²/(2mB) and conservation of p² prove sin²α/B constant, and for α0=30° obtain α=45° at 2B0 with p_perp=mv/√2 and |p_par|=mv/√2, together with the mirror field Bm=4B0.
ED:020628.statement:
A nonrelativistic charge of mass $m$ and speed $v$ moves in a
static, slowly varying magnetic bottle. The magnetic moment
\[
\mu=\frac{p_\perp^2}{2mB}
\]
is an adiabatic invariant, and the kinetic energy (equivalently the
total momentum squared $p^2=m^2v^2$) is conserved because a static
magnetic field does no work. The pitch angle $\alpha$ is defined by
$p_\perp=p\sin\alpha$ and $p_\parallel=p\cos\alpha$. Do not replace
the adiabatic-mirror problem by a covariant Lorentz-force rapidity
integration, a uniform crossed-field tensor audit, or an
Abraham–Lorentz radiation-reaction calculation.

1. Combine $\mu$ conservation with $p^2$ conservation and prove
   \[
   \frac{\sin^2\alpha}{B}=\text{constant}.
   \]

2. A particle is injected at $B=B_0$ with $\alpha_0=30^\circ$. At
   the location where the field has risen to $2B_0$, prove
   \[
   \alpha=45^\circ,\qquad
   p_\perp=\frac{mv}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
   |p_\parallel|=\frac{mv}{\sqrt{2}}.
   \]

3. The particle reflects where $\alpha$ reaches $90^\circ$. Prove
   that the mirror field for this injection pitch is
   \[
   B_m=4B_0.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the magnetic field removes kinetic
   energy, so $p$ decreases and the particle stops rather than
   reversing $p_\parallel$”; (ii) “$\sin\alpha/B$ is the invariant,
   so at $2B_0$ one has $\alpha=60^\circ$ and $B_m=2B_0$.” State
   the adiabaticity requirement $r_L/L_B\ll 1$, where $r_L$ is the
   local Larmor radius and $L_B=|\nabla_\parallel\ln B|^{-1}$ is the
   parallel field scale.
permittedResults: $\mu=p^2\sin^2\alpha/(2mB)$. With $p$ fixed, $\sin^2\alpha/B$ is constant. From $\alpha_0=30^\circ$ one has $\sin^2\alpha_0=1/4$, so at $B=2B_0$ one finds $\sin^2\alpha=1/2$ and $\alpha=45^\circ$.
Mirror: $1/B_m=\sin^2\alpha_0/B_0=(1/4)/B_0$, hence $B_m=4B_0$. At $45^\circ$ both $p_\perp$ and $|p_\parallel|$ equal $mv/\sqrt{2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute p_perp=p sinα into μ, cancel the conserved p², and transport sin²α/B from B0 to 2B0 and to the sinα=1 surface.
Read the turning point as a sign change of p_par at fixed p, and name the adiabaticity requirement rL/LB≪1.

milestones.criterion: Derives sin²α/B constant from μ and p² conservation, and reports α=45° at 2B0 with p_perp=|p_par|=mv/√2.
Obtains the mirror field Bm=4B0 and states that p_par reverses at fixed energy under rL/LB≪1.
Rejects an energy-loss reading or the invariant sinα/B, and refuses reserved covariant-force substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the magnetic field removes kinetic energy so the particle stops, rather than reversing p_par at fixed p.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pitch-angle kinematics, the samples at 2B0, and the elastic mirror reversal are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes sinα/B as the invariant, reports α=60° at 2B0, or quotes the mirror field as Bm=2B0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required station α=45° with p_perp=|p_par|=mv/√2 and the mirror ratio Bm=4B0 are not produced.

hintTree.content: Write $p_\perp=mv\sin\alpha$ before forming $\mu$. The $p^2$ in the numerator is the conserved kinetic datum.
$\sin 30^\circ=1/2$, so $\sin^2\alpha_0=1/4$. Doubling $B$ doubles $\sin^2\alpha$.
The loss-cone edge is $\sin\alpha=1$. Solving $1/B_m=(1/4)/B_0$ gives the factor of four, not two.

ED:020628.canonicalSolution:
A static magnetic field does no work, so the speed $v$ and the
momentum magnitude $p=mv$ are constant. The adiabatic invariant is
\[
\mu=\frac{p_\perp^2}{2mB}=\frac{p^2\sin^2\alpha}{2mB}.
\]
With $p$ and $m$ fixed, conservation of $\mu$ is exactly
\[
\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{B}=\text{constant}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sin^2\alpha/B=\mathrm{const}}.
\]

At injection, $\alpha_0=30^\circ$ and $B=B_0$, so
$\sin^2\alpha_0=1/4$ and the constant equals $1/(4B_0)$. At the
station $B=2B_0$,
\[
\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{2B_0}=\frac{1}{4B_0}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\sin^2\alpha=\frac12
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha=45^\circ
\]
in the first quadrant. Then
\[
p_\perp=mv\sin 45^\circ=\frac{mv}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
|p_\parallel|=mv\cos 45^\circ=\frac{mv}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\alpha(2B_0)=45^\circ,\;
p_\perp=|p_\parallel|=mv/\sqrt{2}}.
\]

Reflection occurs at $\alpha=90^\circ$, where $\sin^2\alpha=1$:
\[
\frac{1}{B_m}=\frac{\sin^2\alpha_0}{B_0}=\frac{1}{4B_0}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
B_m=4B_0.
\]
The parallel momentum reverses sign at that turning point; the
energy $p^2/(2m)$ is unchanged.
\[
\boxed{B_m=4B_0,\;p_\parallel\text{ reverses at fixed }p}.
\]

The invariant itself is controlled only in the adiabatic regime
$r_L/L_B\ll 1$. Sentence (i) invents a magnetic energy sink and
never produces a pitch-angle turning point. Sentence (ii) replaces
$\sin^2\alpha/B$ by $\sin\alpha/B$, which yields the wrong station
angle $60^\circ$ and the wrong mirror ratio $2$. The construction
is a guiding-center mirror; it is not a covariant Lorentz-force
rapidity problem and not a radiation-reaction pulse.

graderFixtures.proofText: The invariant is $\sin^2\alpha/B$. From $\alpha_0=30^\circ$ one has $\alpha=45^\circ$ at $B=2B_0$, with $p_\perp=|p_\parallel|=mv/\sqrt{2}$. The mirror field is $B_m=4B_0$. A static $\mathbf B$ reverses $p_\parallel$ at fixed energy, and the adiabaticity requirement is $r_L/L_B\ll 1$.
The magnetic field removes kinetic energy, so p decreases and the particle stops rather than reversing p_par. I do not accept an elastic pitch-angle turning point at fixed p.
sinα/B is the invariant, so at 2B0 one has α=60° and Bm=2B0. I never report α=45°, p_perp=|p_par|=mv/√2, or Bm=4B0.

ELEC:010117.title: The 5 V / 1 kOhm Shockley load line has a unique root VD=0.555374 V and 55.9331 microV ripple
ELEC:010117.objective: Prove the Shockley / 1 kOhm load-line equation has a unique root VD=0.555374038859 V, ID=4.444625961 mA, confirm three Newton iterates from 0.55 V, compute rd=5.624770276 Ohm and a 55.9331 microV diode ripple, and refuse a constant 0.7 V drop.
ELEC:010117.statement:
A silicon junction diode obeys the Shockley law
\[
i_D=I_S\bigl(e^{v_D/V_T}-1\bigr)
\]
with $I_S=1\times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{A}$ and $V_T=0.025\,\mathrm{V}$.
The diode is placed in series with $R=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ across a
dc source $V_S=5\,\mathrm{V}$, so Kirchhoff's voltage law is
$v_D+R i_D=5$. Equivalently the operating point is a root of
\[
I_S\bigl(e^{v/V_T}-1\bigr)=\frac{5-v}{1000}.
\]

1. Prove that this transcendental equation has exactly one real root
   $v=V_D$ in $(0,5)$. Identify the corresponding forward current $I_D$
   and prove
   \[
   V_D=0.555374038859\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   I_D=4.444625961\,\mathrm{mA}.
   \]

2. Starting from $v^{(0)}=0.55\,\mathrm{V}$, apply Newton's method to
   \[
   f(v)=I_S\bigl(e^{v/V_T}-1\bigr)-\frac{5-v}{1000}
   \]
   and prove that the first three iterates are
   $0.5559910529$, $0.5553815495$, and $0.5553740400$ (volts).

3. Linearize the diode about this $Q$-point. Prove that the incremental
   resistance is $r_d=V_T/(I_D+I_S)=5.624770276\,\Omega$, that
   $R\parallel r_d=5.593309197\,\Omega$, and that a $10\,\mathrm{mV}$
   supply ripple therefore appears across the diode as
   $55.9331\,\mu\mathrm{V}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a silicon diode is a $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$
   battery, so $I_D=4.3\,\mathrm{mA}$ and there is nothing unique to
   solve”; (ii) “the load line may cross the exponential more than
   once, or $r_d=V_T/I_D$ with the $10\,\mathrm{mV}$ ripple copied
   undivided onto the diode.”

Do not replace the calculation by a piecewise diode-region
current-direction test, and do not treat the $Q$-point as a headroom
certificate.
permittedResults: If $f'(v)=(I_S/V_T)e^{v/V_T}+1/R>0$ everywhere, then $f$ is strictly increasing and $f(v)=0$ has at most one root. Sign change of $f$ on $(0,5)$ produces existence.
Newton's update is $v\leftarrow v-f(v)/f'(v)$. About a root, $r_d=V_T/(I_D+I_S)$ and the diode ripple is $v_{d,\mathrm{ac}}=r_d/(R+r_d)$ times the source ripple.

acceptableStrategies.description: Show f'>0 and a sign change on (0,5), then run three Newton steps and linearize with rd=VT/(ID+Is).
Intersect the graphs of the exponential and the falling load line to lock uniqueness, then convert the source ripple through the r_d divider.

milestones.criterion: Proves uniqueness of the load-line root and reports VD=0.555374038859 V, ID=4.444625961 mA, and the three Newton iterates from 0.55 V.
Computes rd=5.624770276 Ohm including Is, R||rd=5.593309197 Ohm, and the 55.9331 microV diode ripple.
Rejects the constant 0.7 V drop and refuses reserved diode-region or Q-point-headroom substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Shockley law by a fixed 0.7 V battery, reports ID=4.3 mA, and never solves the transcendental load-line equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique root VD=0.555374038859 V, the Newton sequence, and the incremental resistance are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the exponential and the load line may meet more than once, drops Is from rd=VT/(ID+Is), or copies the 10 mV source ripple onto the diode without the divider rd/(R+rd).
commonErrors.consequence: Uniqueness fails, or the required rd=5.624770276 Ohm and 55.9331 microV ripple are not produced.

hintTree.content: Evaluate $f(0)=-5\,\mathrm{mA}<0$ and $f(5)>0$. The derivative $f'$ never vanishes, so the graph of $f$ crosses zero once.
From $v=0.55$ one has $e^{v/V_T}=e^{22}$. The first Newton correction is about $+6\,\mathrm{mV}$.
Keep $I_S$ in the denominator of $r_d$. The divider that multiplies the $10\,\mathrm{mV}$ source ripple is $r_d/(R+r_d)$, not $1$.

ELEC:010117.canonicalSolution:
Write
\[
f(v)=I_S\bigl(e^{v/V_T}-1\bigr)-\frac{5-v}{1000}.
\]
Then
\[
f'(v)=\frac{I_S}{V_T}e^{v/V_T}+\frac{1}{1000}>0
\]
for every real $v$, so $f$ is strictly increasing and has at most one
zero. Direct evaluation gives $f(0)=-0.005<0$ and $f(5)=I_S(e^{200}-1)>0$,
hence exactly one root $V_D\in(0,5)$. Graphically the Shockley curve is
strictly increasing and the load line $i=(5-v)/1000$ is strictly
decreasing, so they meet once.

The unique root and the matching current are
\[
\boxed{V_D=0.555374038859\,\mathrm{V},\quad
I_D=(5-V_D)/1000=4.444625961\,\mathrm{mA}}.
\]
(The current is recovered from the load line, which is exact once $V_D$
is known; it also equals $I_S(e^{V_D/V_T}-1)$.)

Newton uses the same $f$ and $f'$. Starting at $v^{(0)}=0.55$,
\[
e^{0.55/0.025}=e^{22},\qquad
f(0.55)=I_S(e^{22}-1)-0.00445,
\]
and $f'(0.55)=(I_S/V_T)e^{22}+0.001$ produce the update
\[
v^{(1)}=0.55-\frac{f(0.55)}{f'(0.55)}=0.5559910529.
\]
Repeating the same arithmetic at $v^{(1)}$ and then at $v^{(2)}$ yields
\[
v^{(2)}=0.5553815495,\qquad v^{(3)}=0.5553740400.
\]
The third iterate already agrees with $V_D$ to about $1\,\mathrm{nV}$.
\[
\boxed{0.5559910529,\;0.5553815495,\;0.5553740400}.
\]

The incremental conductance is $(I_D+I_S)/V_T$, so
\[
r_d=\frac{V_T}{I_D+I_S}
=\frac{0.025}{4.444625961\times 10^{-3}+10^{-12}}
=5.624770276\,\Omega.
\]
The parallel combination against the $1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ bias resistor
is
\[
R\parallel r_d
=\frac{1000\cdot 5.624770276}{1005.624770276}
=5.593309197\,\Omega.
\]
A source ripple $v_{s,\mathrm{ac}}=10\,\mathrm{mV}$ divides as
\[
v_{d,\mathrm{ac}}
=\frac{r_d}{R+r_d}\cdot 10\,\mathrm{mV}
=5.593309197\times 10^{-3}\cdot 10\,\mathrm{mV}
=55.9331\,\mu\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{r_d=5.624770276\,\Omega,\quad
R\parallel r_d=5.593309197\,\Omega,\quad
v_{d,\mathrm{ac}}=55.9331\,\mu\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the exponential by a constant $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$
drop. That model predicts $I_D=4.3\,\mathrm{mA}$ and never produces the
unique Shockley root, the Newton sequence, or a finite $r_d$. (As a
check, $I_S(e^{0.7/0.025}-1)\approx 1.45\,\mathrm{A}$, which is not the
load-line current at $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$.) Sentence (ii) either denies
uniqueness or drops $I_S$ from $r_d$ and copies the $10\,\mathrm{mV}$
ripple onto the diode undivided.

The argument never classifies piecewise diode regions by current
direction and never treats the numerical $Q$-point as a large-signal
headroom certificate.

graderFixtures.proofText: The map $f$ is strictly increasing and changes sign on $(0,5)$, so the load-line root is unique: $V_D=0.555374038859\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_D=4.444625961\,\mathrm{mA}$. Newton from $0.55\,\mathrm{V}$ yields $0.5559910529$, $0.5553815495$, $0.5553740400$. Then $r_d=V_T/(I_D+I_S)=5.624770276\,\Omega$, $R\parallel r_d=5.593309197\,\Omega$, and a $10\,\mathrm{mV}$ supply ripple becomes $55.9331\,\mu\mathrm{V}$ on the diode. A $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$ drop is a different model.
A silicon diode is a 0.7 V battery in forward bias, so ID=(5-0.7)/1000=4.3 mA. There is no transcendental root, no Newton iteration, and no incremental rd.
An exponential can cross a load line more than once, so uniqueness is not guaranteed. I take rd=VT/ID and I place the entire 10 mV supply ripple across the diode.

ELEC:010118.title: A 10 sin(theta) bridge with two 0.7 V drops conducts from 8.05 deg and has PIV 9.3 V
ELEC:010118.objective: For vs=10 sin(theta) into a full bridge with two 0.7 V drops and RL=1 kOhm, obtain vo=max(10|sin theta|-1.4,0), alpha=0.1404614147 rad, Vavg=5.028688967 V, Vrms=5.837496002 V, and PIV=9.3 V rather than 20 V.
ELEC:010118.statement:
A full-wave bridge is driven by $v_s=10\sin\theta$ (volts, $\theta$ in
radians) and feeds $R_L=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Each conducting path
contains two silicon drops of $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$, so the load voltage is
\[
v_o(\theta)=\max\bigl(10|\sin\theta|-1.4,\,0\bigr).
\]

1. Let $\alpha=\arcsin(0.14)$. Prove
   $\alpha=0.1404614147\,\mathrm{rad}=8.047846^{\circ}$ and that each
   half-cycle conducts on the interval $[\alpha,\pi-\alpha]$ (and is
   off on $[0,\alpha)\cup(\pi-\alpha,\pi]$). Identify the peak load
   voltage and current
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{pk}}=8.6\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   I_{\mathrm{pk}}=8.6\,\mathrm{mA}.
   \]

2. Averaging over a half-period of length $\pi$, prove
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{avg}}
   =\frac{20\cos\alpha-1.4(\pi-2\alpha)}{\pi}
   =5.028688967\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

3. Prove the mean-square identity
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
   =\frac1{\pi}\Bigl\{
   50\bigl(\pi-2\alpha+\sin 2\alpha\bigr)
   -56\cos\alpha
   +1.96(\pi-2\alpha)
   \Bigr\}
   \]
   and conclude $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=5.837496002\,\mathrm{V}$.

4. While one pair conducts, each reverse-biased diode sees
   $|v_s|-0.7$. Prove that the peak inverse voltage on each off diode
   is $9.3\,\mathrm{V}$. Audit both sentences: (i) “a full-wave
   rectifier has PIV $2V_m=20\,\mathrm{V}$”; (ii) “the two drops may
   be ignored, so conduction starts at $\theta=0$ and
   $V_{\mathrm{avg}}=2\cdot 10/\pi$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a piecewise region-direction test of
a single diode, and do not invoke Miller poles or cascade port
resistances.
permittedResults: On $[\alpha,\pi-\alpha]$ one has $\int(10\sin\theta-1.4)\,d\theta=-10\cos\theta-1.4\theta$, which evaluates to $20\cos\alpha-1.4(\pi-2\alpha)$.
Expanding $(10\sin\theta-1.4)^2=100\sin^2\theta-28\sin\theta+1.96$ and integrating with $\int\sin^2=(\theta/2-\sin(2\theta)/4)$ produces the displayed $V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$ formula.

acceptableStrategies.description: Locate alpha from 10 sin alpha=1.4, integrate the two-drop waveform over [alpha, pi-alpha], then read PIV from |vs|-0.7.
Expand (10 sin theta-1.4)^2 first to lock Vrms, then recover Vavg as the first moment on the same window and compare PIV with the center-tap 2 Vm myth.

milestones.criterion: Identifies alpha=0.1404614147 rad, the conduction window [alpha, pi-alpha], Vpk=8.6 V, and Ipk=8.6 mA.
Evaluates Vavg=5.028688967 V, the displayed Vrms^2 integral, Vrms=5.837496002 V, and PIV=9.3 V.
Rejects PIV=20 V and a drop-free 20/pi average, and refuses reserved region-direction or Miller substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports PIV=2 Vm=20 V, as if the circuit were a two-diode center-tap full-wave rectifier rather than a four-diode bridge.
commonErrors.consequence: The required off-diode reverse peak 9.3 V is replaced by a different topology's rating.

commonErrors.description: Sets both diode drops to zero, takes alpha=0, or writes Vavg=20/pi (or Vrms of a pure full-wave sine) instead of the two-drop window formulas.
commonErrors.consequence: The conduction angle, Vavg=5.028688967 V, and Vrms=5.837496002 V are all lost.

hintTree.content: Conduction begins when $10\sin\theta=1.4$, i.e. $\sin\theta=0.14$. The same threshold appears at $\pi-\alpha$.
The half-period average uses the interval of length $\pi-2\alpha$, not the full half-sine of length $\pi$.
An off diode has one end at the source crest and the other end one drop above the opposite source terminal, so PIV $=10-0.7$, not $20$.

ELEC:010118.canonicalSolution:
The load is nonzero only when $10|\sin\theta|\ge 1.4$, i.e. when
$|\sin\theta|\ge 0.14$. On $[0,\pi]$ this is the closed interval
$[\alpha,\pi-\alpha]$ with
\[
\alpha=\arcsin(0.14)=0.1404614147\,\mathrm{rad}
=8.047846^{\circ}.
\]
The complementary subintervals of the half-cycle are cutoff. The peak
source is $10\,\mathrm{V}$, so
\[
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{pk}}=10-1.4=8.6\,\mathrm{V},\quad
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=8.6/1000=8.6\,\mathrm{mA}}.
\]

Because $|v_s|$ already folds the negative half-cycle, it is enough to
average $v_o$ over $[0,\pi]$:
\begin{align*}
V_{\mathrm{avg}}
&=\frac1{\pi}\int_{\alpha}^{\pi-\alpha}(10\sin\theta-1.4)\,d\theta
=\frac1{\pi}\Bigl[-10\cos\theta-1.4\theta\Bigr]_{\alpha}^{\pi-\alpha}\\
&=\frac{20\cos\alpha-1.4(\pi-2\alpha)}{\pi}.
\end{align*}
(The cosine terms add because $\cos(\pi-\alpha)=-\cos\alpha$.)
Substituting the numerical $\alpha$ produces
\[
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{avg}}=5.028688967\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

The mean square on the same interval is
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
=\frac1{\pi}\int_{\alpha}^{\pi-\alpha}(10\sin\theta-1.4)^2\,d\theta.
\]
Expand the integrand as $100\sin^2\theta-28\sin\theta+1.96$. The
identities
\[
\int\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac\theta2-\frac{\sin 2\theta}4,\qquad
\int\sin\theta\,d\theta=-\cos\theta
\]
evaluate to
\[
\int_{\alpha}^{\pi-\alpha}100\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=50(\pi-2\alpha+\sin 2\alpha)
\]
and
\[
\int_{\alpha}^{\pi-\alpha}(-28\sin\theta)\,d\theta=-56\cos\alpha,
\]
while the constant term contributes $1.96(\pi-2\alpha)$. Therefore
\[
V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2
=\frac1{\pi}\Bigl\{
50(\pi-2\alpha+\sin 2\alpha)-56\cos\alpha+1.96(\pi-2\alpha)
\Bigr\},
\]
and the positive square root is
\[
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{rms}}=5.837496002\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Label the bridge nodes in the usual way: source terminals $A,B$ and
load terminals $+\,,-$. When $v_s=v_A-v_B>1.4$, the pair $A\to+$ and
$-\to B$ conducts. Each off diode then has reverse voltage
$|v_s|-0.7$, whose peak is $10-0.7=9.3\,\mathrm{V}$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{PIV}=9.3\,\mathrm{V}\text{ on each off diode}}.
\]
The figure $20\,\mathrm{V}=2V_m$ is the PIV of a two-diode center-tap
full-wave secondary, not of this four-diode bridge.

Sentence (i) imports that center-tap $2V_m$ bound. Sentence (ii)
drops both forward drops, so $\alpha=0$ and
$V_{\mathrm{avg}}=20/\pi$, destroying the conduction window and both
numerical averages.

The argument never classifies a single diode by piecewise current
direction, and it never mentions Miller two-node poles or cascade
port resistances.

graderFixtures.proofText: With two $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$ drops, $v_o=\max(10|\sin\theta|-1.4,0)$, $\alpha=\arcsin(0.14)=0.1404614147\,\mathrm{rad}=8.047846^{\circ}$, and conduction occupies $[\alpha,\pi-\alpha]$ each half-cycle. Then $V_{\mathrm{pk}}=8.6\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_{\mathrm{pk}}=8.6\,\mathrm{mA}$, $V_{\mathrm{avg}}=5.028688967\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=5.837496002\,\mathrm{V}$, and each off diode has $\mathrm{PIV}=9.3\,\mathrm{V}$, not $20\,\mathrm{V}$.
Any full-wave rectifier has PIV equal to twice the source peak, so each diode must block 20 V. I do not subtract the remaining 0.7 V drop and I do not accept 9.3 V.
The two 0.7 V drops are negligible, so vo=10|sin theta|, alpha=0, and Vavg=20/pi. I never form the window integrals that produce 5.028688967 V and 5.837496002 V.

ELEC:010219.title: Source-resistor NMOS bias keeps ID=1 mA from ID=(2-ID)^2 and rejects the 4 mA ghost root
ELEC:010219.objective: Solve ID=(2-ID)^2 for the VG=3 V, RS=1 kOhm, K=1 mA/V^2 NMOS, reject the 4 mA root because VOV=2-ID<0, and report the physical point ID=1 mA, VS=1 V, VD=8 V, VGS=2 V, VOV=1 V, VDS=7 V, saturation 7>=1, gm=2 mS, dissipation 7 mW.
ELEC:010219.statement:
An enhancement NMOS is biased from $V_{DD}=10\,\mathrm{V}$ with
$R_D=2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ in the drain and $R_S=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ in
the source. The gate is held at the dc value $V_G=3\,\mathrm{V}$. Device
parameters are $V_T=1\,\mathrm{V}$ and $K=1\,\mathrm{mA}/\mathrm{V}^2$,
and channel-length modulation is neglected. In saturation
\[
I_D=K(V_{GS}-V_T)^2.
\]
Take $I_D$ in milliamperes when a resistance in kilo-ohms multiplies it
to a voltage in volts.

1. Using $V_S=I_D R_S$ and $V_{GS}=V_G-V_S$, prove that saturation
   forces the quadratic
   \[
   I_D=(2-I_D)^2.
   \]
   Solve and show that the algebraic roots are $I_D=1\,\mathrm{mA}$ and
   $I_D=4\,\mathrm{mA}$.

2. Reject $I_D=4\,\mathrm{mA}$ by showing that it produces
   $V_{OV}=2-I_D<0$ (equivalently $V_{GS}<V_T$). Keep the physical root
   and compute
   \[
   V_S=1\,\mathrm{V},\;
   V_D=8\,\mathrm{V},\;
   V_{GS}=2\,\mathrm{V},\;
   V_{OV}=1\,\mathrm{V},\;
   V_{DS}=7\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

3. Confirm saturation by $V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}$, i.e. $7\ge 1$. Compute
   $g_m=2K V_{OV}=2\,\mathrm{mS}$ and the MOSFET dissipation
   $P_D=I_D V_{DS}=7\,\mathrm{mW}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “both roots of the quadratic are physical
   operating points”; (ii) “$V_{DS}=7\,\mathrm{V}$ is so large that the
   device must be in triode, or $g_m=2K V_{GS}$ rather than
   $2K V_{OV}$.” Also refuse to read the numerical $Q$-point as a
   headroom certificate for large-signal swing.

Do not replace the calculation by a finite-beta bipolar mirror, and do
not invoke a small-signal gain as a rail-crossing license.
permittedResults: With $I_D$ in milliamperes and $R_S=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, $V_S=I_D$ (volts) and $V_{OV}=V_G-V_T-I_D=2-I_D$. Saturation then reads $I_D=(2-I_D)^2$.
The saturation transconductance is $g_m=2K V_{OV}=2\sqrt{K I_D}$. MOSFET dissipation is $I_D V_{DS}$, not $I_D V_{DD}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Close the VG-RS loop to VOV=2-ID, square it, discard the negative-overdrive root, then check VDS>=VOV.
Test I_D=1 mA directly in KVL and the square law to lock the bias point, then show I_D=4 mA violates VGS>VT.

milestones.criterion: Forms ID=(2-ID)^2, lists both algebraic roots, and rejects 4 mA because VOV<0.
Reports the physical point ID=1 mA, VS=1 V, VD=8 V, VGS=2 V, VOV=1 V, VDS=7 V, saturation 7>=1, gm=2 mS, and PD=7 mW.
Rejects keeping both roots or a triode/gm misread, and refuses Q-point-headroom or rail-crossing substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Accepts ID=4 mA as a physical saturation solution, ignoring VOV=2-ID=-2 V and VGS<VT.
commonErrors.consequence: The circuit is assigned a non-physical bias with VS=4 V and a negative VDS, and the required 1 mA point is lost or duplicated.

commonErrors.description: Reads VDS=7 V as triode, or computes gm=2K VGS=4 mS instead of gm=2K VOV=2 mS, or replaces PD=ID VDS by ID VDD.
commonErrors.consequence: The saturation check 7>=1 and the required gm=2 mS, PD=7 mW fail.

hintTree.content: $V_{GS}=3-I_D$ and $V_{OV}=2-I_D$ when $I_D$ is in milliamperes. Square the overdrive and set it equal to $I_D$.
The roots of $x=(2-x)^2$ are $1$ and $4$. At $x=4$ the overdrive is $-2\,\mathrm{V}$.
With $I_D=1\,\mathrm{mA}$ one has $V_D=10-2=8$ and $V_{DS}=7$, which already exceeds $V_{OV}=1$.

ELEC:010219.canonicalSolution:
Let $I_D$ be measured in milliamperes. Then $V_S=I_D\cdot 1=I_D$
(volts) and
\[
V_{GS}=V_G-V_S=3-I_D,\qquad
V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T=2-I_D.
\]
Saturation with $K=1\,\mathrm{mA}/\mathrm{V}^2$ becomes
\[
I_D=(2-I_D)^2.
\]
Set $x=I_D$. Then $x=4-4x+x^2$, or $x^2-5x+4=0$, or
$(x-1)(x-4)=0$. The algebraic roots are therefore $1\,\mathrm{mA}$ and
$4\,\mathrm{mA}$.

The candidate $I_D=4\,\mathrm{mA}$ produces $V_{OV}=2-4=-2\,\mathrm{V}$
and $V_{GS}=-1\,\mathrm{V}<V_T$. An enhancement device is off, not in
saturation, so this root is extraneous. (It would also force
$V_S=4\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_D=10-8=2\,\mathrm{V}$, hence a negative
$V_{DS}$.) The only physical root is $I_D=1\,\mathrm{mA}$.

The corresponding node voltages are
\begin{align*}
V_S&=1\cdot 1=1\,\mathrm{V},\\
V_D&=10-1\cdot 2=8\,\mathrm{V},\\
V_{GS}&=3-1=2\,\mathrm{V},\\
V_{OV}&=1\,\mathrm{V},\\
V_{DS}&=8-1=7\,\mathrm{V}.
\end{align*}
Saturation holds because $V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}$, i.e. $7\ge 1$. The
transconductance and the device dissipation are
\[
g_m=2K V_{OV}=2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2\,\mathrm{mS},
\qquad
P_D=I_D V_{DS}=1\,\mathrm{mA}\cdot 7\,\mathrm{V}=7\,\mathrm{mW}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_D=1\,\mathrm{mA},\;V_S=1,\;V_D=8,\;V_{GS}=2,\;
V_{OV}=1,\;V_{DS}=7;\;7\ge 1;\;g_m=2\,\mathrm{mS};\;P_D=7\,\mathrm{mW}}.
\]

Sentence (i) keeps the ghost root $4\,\mathrm{mA}$ as a second
operating point. Sentence (ii) misreads a large $V_{DS}$ as triode
(triode would require $V_{DS}<V_{OV}$) or replaces $g_m=2K V_{OV}$ by
$2K V_{GS}=4\,\mathrm{mS}$. The numerical $Q$-point is a bias
calculation, not a certificate that some unspecified signal can swing
to the rails.

The argument never introduces a finite-$\beta$ bipolar mirror and never
treats a small-signal gain as a license to cross the supply rails.

graderFixtures.proofText: Saturation plus $V_{GS}=3-I_D$ yields $I_D=(2-I_D)^2$ with roots $1\,\mathrm{mA}$ and $4\,\mathrm{mA}$. The $4\,\mathrm{mA}$ root has $V_{OV}<0$ and is rejected. The physical point is $I_D=1\,\mathrm{mA}$, $V_S=1\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_D=8\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{GS}=2\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{OV}=1\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{DS}=7\,\mathrm{V}$, with $7\ge 1$, $g_m=2\,\mathrm{mS}$, and $P_D=7\,\mathrm{mW}$.
The quadratic ID=(2-ID)^2 has two roots, 1 mA and 4 mA, and both are valid saturation operating points. I keep ID=4 mA with VS=4 V and I do not reject VOV=-2 V.
VDS=7 V is far above threshold, so the MOSFET must be in triode. I also take gm=2 K VGS=4 mS and I report the dissipation as ID VDD=10 mW rather than 7 mW.

ELEC:010220.title: A beta=100 matched NPN mirror delivers 0.980392 mA and stays active only for RL<=4.386 kOhm
ELEC:010220.objective: For a matched NPN mirror with VCC=5 V, Rref=4.3 kOhm, VBE=0.7 V, and beta=100, obtain Iref=1 mA, Iout=0.9803921569 mA, IB=9.8039216 uA, RLmax=4.386 kOhm from Vout>=0.7 V, compare the 0.2 V sat-only bound 4.896 kOhm, and show that at 4 kOhm the output is still active while beta=infinity overpredicts the true current by 2%.
ELEC:010220.statement:
Two matched NPNs form a simple current mirror. The reference device is
diode-connected through $R_{\mathrm{ref}}=4.3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ to
$V_{CC}=5\,\mathrm{V}$. Emitters are grounded. The output collector
drives a load $R_L$ returned to $V_{CC}$. Take $V_{BE}=0.7\,\mathrm{V}$
on both devices when forward-active and $\beta=100$. Early effect is
neglected, so the collector currents match whenever the base--emitter
voltages match.

1. Compute $I_{\mathrm{ref}}=(V_{CC}-V_{BE})/R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and prove
   $I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\,\mathrm{mA}$. Using $I_{\mathrm{ref}}=I_C+2I_B$
   and $I_{\mathrm{out}}=I_C=\beta I_B$, prove
   \[
   I_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{ref}}}{1+2/\beta}
   =0.9803921569\,\mathrm{mA}
   \]
   and that each base current is $I_B=9.8039216\,\mu\mathrm{A}$.

2. Forward-active operation of the output device requires
   $V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge V_B=0.7\,\mathrm{V}$. With the load returned to
   $5\,\mathrm{V}$, prove that the largest $R_L$ that keeps the mirror
   active is
   \[
   R_{L,\max}=(5-0.7)/I_{\mathrm{out}}=4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
   \]
   Show that a saturation-only bound $V_{CE}\ge 0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ would
   instead give $4.896\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, which is not the
   forward-active limit.

3. At $R_L=4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ compute
   $V_{\mathrm{out}}=1.078431\,\mathrm{V}$ and
   $V_{CB}=0.378431\,\mathrm{V}$, and conclude the output remains
   forward-active. Compare the $\beta\to\infty$ prediction
   $I_{\mathrm{out}}=I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ with the true current and prove
   that infinite $\beta$ overpredicts the true $I_{\mathrm{out}}$ by
   $2\%$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “base currents are negligible at
   $\beta=100$, so $I_{\mathrm{out}}=1\,\mathrm{mA}$ exactly”; (ii)
   “the device stays active until $V_{CE}=0.2\,\mathrm{V}$, so
   $R_{L,\max}=4.896\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.” Do not treat this $R_{L,\max}$
   as a large-signal headroom certificate for an unspecified swing.

Do not replace the mirror by a MOSFET square-law source-resistor bias,
and do not invoke feedback DC accuracy versus a stability boundary.
permittedResults: With $V_{CC}=5\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{BE}=0.7\,\mathrm{V}$, and $R_{\mathrm{ref}}=4.3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, one has $I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\,\mathrm{mA}$ exactly.
At finite $\beta$, $I_{\mathrm{out}}/I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1/(1+2/\beta)$. For $\beta=100$ this ratio is $50/51$, so infinite $\beta$ overpredicts $I_{\mathrm{out}}$ by the factor $1.02$, i.e. by $2\%$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write KCL at the diode-connected node, divide by 1+2/beta, then convert Vout>=0.7 into RLmax.
First compute the infinite-beta current 1 mA as an upper bound, then insert the 2% correction and test VCB at 4 kOhm.

milestones.criterion: Derives Iref=1 mA, Iout=0.9803921569 mA, and each IB=9.8039216 uA from Iref=IC(1+2/beta).
Gives active RLmax=4.386 kOhm, distinguishes the 4.896 kOhm sat-only figure, and checks the 4 kOhm point with the 2% infinite-beta error.
Rejects neglecting base current or using the 0.2 V bound as the active limit, and refuses reserved headroom or feedback-stability substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes Iout=Iref=1 mA exactly at beta=100, as if both base currents vanished.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 0.9803921569 mA, the 9.8039216 uA bases, and the 2% infinite-beta overprediction all disappear.

commonErrors.description: Uses VCE>=0.2 V as the forward-active limit and reports RLmax=4.896 kOhm instead of 4.386 kOhm from Vout>=0.7 V.
commonErrors.consequence: A slice of the saturation region is mislabeled active, and the 4 kOhm VCB check is attached to the wrong bound.

hintTree.content: $(5-0.7)/4.3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=1\,\mathrm{mA}$. The two base currents add in the reference node.
$1+2/100=1.02$, so $I_{\mathrm{out}}=1/1.02\,\mathrm{mA}$. Each $I_B$ is that current over $100$.
Active means $V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0.7\,\mathrm{V}$, not $V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0.2\,\mathrm{V}$. At $4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ the drop is $3.921569\,\mathrm{V}$.

ELEC:010220.canonicalSolution:
The reference branch is a diode-connected VBE plus $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$:
\[
I_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{5-0.7}{4300}=1\,\mathrm{mA}.
\]
Let $I_C$ be the common collector current and $I_B=I_C/\beta$ each base
current. KCL at the diode-connected collector/base node reads
\[
I_{\mathrm{ref}}=I_C+I_B+I_B=I_C\Bigl(1+\frac2\beta\Bigr).
\]
The output current is that same $I_C$, so
\[
I_{\mathrm{out}}
=\frac{I_{\mathrm{ref}}}{1+2/\beta}
=\frac{1}{1.02}
=0.9803921569\,\mathrm{mA}.
\]
Each base current is
\[
I_B=\frac{I_{\mathrm{out}}}{100}=9.8039216\,\mu\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\,\mathrm{mA},\;
I_{\mathrm{out}}=0.9803921569\,\mathrm{mA},\;
I_B=9.8039216\,\mu\mathrm{A}}.
\]

The output base sits at $V_B=0.7\,\mathrm{V}$. Forward-active operation
requires $V_{CB}\ge 0$, hence $V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0.7\,\mathrm{V}$.
With $V_{\mathrm{out}}=5-I_{\mathrm{out}} R_L$ this is
\[
R_L\le\frac{5-0.7}{I_{\mathrm{out}}}
=\frac{4.3}{0.9803921569\times 10^{-3}}
=4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
A saturation-only convention $V_{CE}\ge 0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ would instead
give
\[
\frac{5-0.2}{I_{\mathrm{out}}}=4.896\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,
\]
which already includes a slice of the saturation region and is not the
active bound.

At $R_L=4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega<4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$,
\[
V_{\mathrm{out}}=5-4\cdot 0.9803921569=1.078431\,\mathrm{V},
\qquad
V_{CB}=1.078431-0.7=0.378431\,\mathrm{V}>0,
\]
so the output remains forward-active.
\[
\boxed{R_{L,\max}=4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\text{ (active)};\quad
4.896\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\text{ is sat-only};\quad
\text{at }4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\;V_{\mathrm{out}}=1.078431\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
If $\beta\to\infty$ then $I_{\mathrm{out}}=I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\,\mathrm{mA}$,
which exceeds the true $0.9803921569\,\mathrm{mA}$ by the factor
$1.02$. Infinite $\beta$ therefore overpredicts the true current by
$2\%$.

Sentence (i) drops the two base currents at $\beta=100$ and reports
$1\,\mathrm{mA}$ as exact. Sentence (ii) replaces the active bound
$V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0.7\,\mathrm{V}$ by a $0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ saturation
convention. The number $R_{L,\max}=4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ is a dc
region boundary, not a certificate that an unspecified waveform has
headroom.

The argument never solves a MOSFET square-law source-resistor quadratic
and never discusses loop-gain stability of a feedback amplifier.

graderFixtures.proofText: Matched KCL gives $I_{\mathrm{out}}=I_{\mathrm{ref}}/(1+2/\beta)=0.9803921569\,\mathrm{mA}$ from $I_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\,\mathrm{mA}$, with each $I_B=9.8039216\,\mu\mathrm{A}$. Forward-active operation needs $V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0.7\,\mathrm{V}$, so $R_{L,\max}=4.386\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$; the $0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ figure yields only a saturation-edge $4.896\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. At $4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, $V_{\mathrm{out}}=1.078431\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_{CB}=0.378431\,\mathrm{V}$ remain active. Infinite $\beta$ overpredicts the true current by $2\%$.
At beta=100 the base currents are negligible, so Iout=Iref=1 mA exactly. I do not divide by 1+2/beta and I do not report a 2% infinite-beta overprediction.
The output stays active until VCE=0.2 V, so RLmax=(5-0.2)/Iout=4.896 kOhm. I treat 4.386 kOhm as too conservative and I do not use Vout>=0.7 V.

ELEC:010321.title: Unbypassed RS=0.5 kOhm cuts the CS gain to -20/3 and splits vg into vs=2/3 and vgs=1/3
ELEC:010321.objective: For gm=4 mS, ro=infinity, RD=RL=10 kOhm, RS=0.5 kOhm, obtain RD'=5 kOhm, 1+gm RS=3, gm_eff=4/3 mS, vo/vg=-20/3, vs/vg=2/3, vgs/vg=1/3, and the 0.15 V peak excursion vs=0.10 V, vgs=0.05 V, id=0.20 mA, vo=-1.00 V, with Rin infinite, unloaded Rout=RD=10 kOhm, and loaded 5 kOhm.
ELEC:010321.statement:
A common-source MOSFET is degenerated by an unbypassed source resistor
$R_S=0.5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. The small-signal parameters are
$g_m=4\,\mathrm{mS}$ and $r_o=\infty$. The drain resistor is
$R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, and an external load $R_L=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$
is AC-coupled from the drain to ground. The signal $v_g$ is applied
directly at the gate.

1. Form $R_D'=R_D\parallel R_L$ and the degeneration factor
   $1+g_m R_S$. Prove
   \[
   R_D'=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\qquad
   1+g_m R_S=3,\qquad
   g_{m,\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{g_m}{1+g_m R_S}=\frac43\,\mathrm{mS}.
   \]
   Then prove the three transfer ratios
   \[
   \frac{v_o}{v_g}=-\frac{20}{3},\qquad
   \frac{v_s}{v_g}=\frac23,\qquad
   \frac{v_{gs}}{v_g}=\frac13.
   \]

2. A gate peak $v_{g,\mathrm{pk}}=0.15\,\mathrm{V}$ is applied. Prove
   that the corresponding peaks are
   $v_s=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$, $v_{gs}=0.05\,\mathrm{V}$,
   $i_d=0.20\,\mathrm{mA}$, and $v_o=-1.00\,\mathrm{V}$.

3. With an ideal gate, prove $R_{\mathrm{in}}=\infty$. Looking into the
   amplifier output with $R_L$ removed, prove that the unloaded output
   resistance is $R_{\mathrm{out}}=R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. With $R_L$
   attached, the effective load is $R_D'=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “degeneration may be ignored, so
   $v_o/v_g=-g_m R_D'=-20$ and $v_{gs}=v_g$”; (ii) “the gate input
   resistance is $R_S$, or the unloaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ is
   $R_D\parallel R_S$.” Do not read the gain $-20/3$ as a license to
   drive the drain across the rails, and do not replace $R_D\parallel R_L$
   by a cascade of finite port resistances or by a Miller two-node
   calculation.

Do not invoke feedback DC accuracy versus a stability boundary.
permittedResults: The three ratios follow from $v_s=g_m R_S\,v_{gs}$ and $v_g=v_{gs}+v_s$: $v_s/v_g=(g_m R_S)/(1+g_m R_S)$, $v_{gs}/v_g=1/(1+g_m R_S)$, and $v_o/v_g=-g_{m,\mathrm{eff}} R_D'$.
A peak $v_g$ scales every linear small-signal voltage and the controlled current $i_d=g_m v_{gs}$ by the same factor.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split vg=vgs+vs with id=gm vgs, form gm_eff and RD', then scale the three ratios by 0.15 V.
Compute id from the 0.15 V gate peak after the 1/3 vgs share, then recover vo=-id RD' and the two port resistances from ro=infinity.

milestones.criterion: Computes RD'=5 kOhm, 1+gm RS=3, gm_eff=4/3 mS, and the ratios vo/vg=-20/3, vs/vg=2/3, vgs/vg=1/3.
Evaluates the 0.15 V peaks vs=0.10 V, vgs=0.05 V, id=0.20 mA, vo=-1.00 V, and the ports Rin=infinity, unloaded Rout=10 kOhm, loaded 5 kOhm.
Rejects an undegenerated gain -20 or a misread Rin/Rout, and refuses rail-crossing, cascade-port, Miller, or feedback-stability substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Ignores RS in the controlled-source loop, reports vo/vg=-gm RD'=-20, and sets vgs=vg (so vs=0).
commonErrors.consequence: The required -20/3, 2/3, 1/3 split and the 0.15 V excursion (0.10 V, 0.05 V, 0.20 mA, -1.00 V) are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes the gate Rin to be RS, or takes the unloaded Rout to be RD||RS (or RD||RL) rather than RD=10 kOhm with loaded RD'=5 kOhm.
commonErrors.consequence: The ideal-gate infinite Rin and the ro=infinity identification Rout=RD are replaced by a source-resistor fiction.

hintTree.content: $R_D\parallel R_L=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $g_m R_S=4\,\mathrm{mS}\cdot 0.5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=2$, so the degeneration factor is $3$.
Then $g_{m,\mathrm{eff}}=(4/3)\,\mathrm{mS}$ and $v_o/v_g=-(4/3)\cdot 5=-20/3$. The source takes $2/3$ of $v_g$.
For $v_g=0.15\,\mathrm{V}$ one has $v_{gs}=0.05\,\mathrm{V}$ and $i_d=g_m v_{gs}=0.20\,\mathrm{mA}$, hence $v_o=-1.00\,\mathrm{V}$.

ELEC:010321.canonicalSolution:
The AC drain load is
\[
R_D'=R_D\parallel R_L=\frac{10\cdot 10}{20}=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
The loop $v_g=v_{gs}+i_d R_S$ with $i_d=g_m v_{gs}$ gives
\[
1+g_m R_S=1+4\times 10^{-3}\cdot 500=1+2=3,
\]
and therefore
\[
g_{m,\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{g_m}{1+g_m R_S}=\frac43\,\mathrm{mS}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_D'=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad 1+g_m R_S=3,\quad
g_{m,\mathrm{eff}}=4/3\,\mathrm{mS}}.
\]
The three transfer ratios are then
\begin{align*}
\frac{v_o}{v_g}
&=-g_{m,\mathrm{eff}} R_D'
=-\frac43\times 10^{-3}\cdot 5\times 10^{3}
=-\frac{20}{3},\\
\frac{v_s}{v_g}
&=\frac{g_m R_S}{1+g_m R_S}=\frac23,\\
\frac{v_{gs}}{v_g}
&=\frac{1}{1+g_m R_S}=\frac13.
\end{align*}
These add consistently: $v_{gs}+v_s=v_g$.
\[
\boxed{v_o/v_g=-20/3,\quad v_s/v_g=2/3,\quad v_{gs}/v_g=1/3}.
\]

Scale by the given gate peak $v_{g,\mathrm{pk}}=0.15\,\mathrm{V}$:
\begin{align*}
v_s&=\tfrac23\cdot 0.15=0.10\,\mathrm{V},\\
v_{gs}&=\tfrac13\cdot 0.15=0.05\,\mathrm{V},\\
i_d&=g_m v_{gs}=4\times 10^{-3}\cdot 0.05=0.20\,\mathrm{mA},\\
v_o&=-\tfrac{20}{3}\cdot 0.15=-1.00\,\mathrm{V}.
\end{align*}
The same $v_o$ is $-i_d R_D'=-0.20\,\mathrm{mA}\cdot 5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.
\[
\boxed{v_s=0.10\,\mathrm{V},\;v_{gs}=0.05\,\mathrm{V},\;
i_d=0.20\,\mathrm{mA},\;v_o=-1.00\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

An ideal MOSFET gate draws no current, so $R_{\mathrm{in}}=\infty$.
With $r_o=\infty$ the controlled source does not load the drain node
from inside the device, and the resistance looking into the MOSFET
drain is infinite. Removing $R_L$ therefore leaves
$R_{\mathrm{out}}=R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Reattaching $R_L$ makes
the effective load $5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$; that figure is $R_D'$, not a
second value of $R_{\mathrm{out}}$.
\[
\boxed{R_{\mathrm{in}}=\infty,\quad
R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad
R_D'=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}.
\]

Sentence (i) sets $g_m R_S=0$, producing $v_o/v_g=-20$ and
$v_{gs}=v_g$, which contradicts every displayed ratio and the
$0.15\,\mathrm{V}$ excursion. Sentence (ii) invents a finite gate
resistance $R_S$ or a source-resistor contribution to $R_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The gain $-20/3$ is a local small-signal derivative; it is not a
rail-crossing license. The parallel $R_D\parallel R_L$ is a single
drain load, not a cascade of finite port resistances and not a Miller
two-node network.

The argument never discusses feedback DC accuracy or a stability
boundary.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $R_D'=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $1+g_m R_S=3$ one has $g_{m,\mathrm{eff}}=4/3\,\mathrm{mS}$, $v_o/v_g=-20/3$, $v_s/v_g=2/3$, and $v_{gs}/v_g=1/3$. A $0.15\,\mathrm{V}$ gate peak gives $v_s=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$, $v_{gs}=0.05\,\mathrm{V}$, $i_d=0.20\,\mathrm{mA}$, $v_o=-1.00\,\mathrm{V}$. The gate $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ is infinite; unloaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}=R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$; the loaded drain node is $5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.
Source degeneration can be ignored at this gm, so vo/vg=-gm (RD||RL)=-20 and vgs=vg. I never form the factor 3 or the ratios -20/3, 2/3, 1/3.
The gate input resistance is the source resistor RS=0.5 kOhm, and the unloaded Rout is RD||RS. I do not accept Rin infinite or unloaded Rout=RD=10 kOhm.

ELEC:010322.title: Loaded emitter follower: RE||RL=500 ohm gives Rin=52.475k, ve/vsig=0.86994, Rout=69.551 ohm
ELEC:010322.objective: With beta=99, gm=40mS, rpi=2475 ohm, RE=RL=1k and Rs=5k, compute RE'=500, Rin_base=52.475k, ve/vb=0.9528346832, ve/vsig=0.8699434537 so 100mV yields 86.9943mV, and Rout=69.5510584 ohm after (rpi+Rs)/(beta+1)=74.75 ohm.
ELEC:010322.statement:
A discrete BJT emitter follower is biased in forward-active
operation. The hybrid-$\pi$ parameters at the given $Q$-point are
\[
\beta=99,\qquad g_m=40\,\mathrm{mS},\qquad r_\pi=2475\,\Omega,
\]
with Early effect neglected ($r_o=\infty$). The emitter resistor and
the external load are
\[
R_E=R_L=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,
\]
and the signal source $v_{\mathrm{sig}}$ drives the base through
$R_s=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. The collector is AC-grounded. Write
\[
R_E'=R_E\parallel R_L
\]
for the AC resistance attached to the emitter.

1. Evaluate $R_E'$ and the small-signal resistance looking into the
   base with the emitter attached to $R_E'$,
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=r_\pi+(\beta+1)R_E'.
   \]
   Prove $R_E'=500\,\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.

2. Prove the internal follower ratio
   \[
   \frac{v_e}{v_b}=\frac{(\beta+1)R_E'}{r_\pi+(\beta+1)R_E'}
   =\frac{50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}
   =0.9528346832.
   \]
   With the source resistance present, prove
   \[
   \frac{v_e}{v_{\mathrm{sig}}}
   =\frac{50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega+5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}
   =0.8699434537.
   \]
   Hence a $100\,\mathrm{mV}$ source amplitude produces
   $v_e=86.9943\,\mathrm{mV}$.

3. Remove $R_L$ and set $v_{\mathrm{sig}}=0$ (so $R_s$ remains from
   base to AC ground). Prove that the resistance looking into the
   emitter of the transistor is
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{look}}=\frac{r_\pi+R_s}{\beta+1}=74.75\,\Omega,
   \]
   and that the stage output resistance is
   $R_{\mathrm{out}}=R_{\mathrm{look}}\parallel R_E=69.5510584\,\Omega$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the load is $R_E=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$
   alone, or else this is a common-emitter inversion with gain
   $-g_m R_L$”; (ii) “$R_{\mathrm{out}}=1/g_m=25\,\Omega$, or
   $r_\pi/(\beta+1)$ with $R_s$ omitted.” Do not replace the
   calculation by a diode-region current-direction test, a $Q$-point
   headroom certificate, a rail-crossing reading of a local
   derivative, a cascade finite-port gain bite, a Miller two-node
   pole shortcut, or a feedback DC-accuracy versus stability claim.
permittedResults: Base input resistance of a follower: $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=r_\pi+(\beta+1)R_E'$. The internal voltage ratio is $v_e/v_b=(\beta+1)R_E'/(r_\pi+(\beta+1)R_E')$.
The identity $g_m=\beta/r_\pi$ is consistent with the given numbers ($99/2475=40\,\mathrm{mS}$) but does not license replacing $(\beta+1)$ by $\beta$ or replacing $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ by $1/g_m$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form RE'=RE||RL first, reflect (beta+1)RE' to the base to lock Rin and both voltage ratios, then recompute Rout with RL removed and Rs kept.
Use the exact hybrid-pi loop equations at the base and emitter nodes; cancel Rin in ve/vsig to see the 50k/(52.475k+5k) collapse.

milestones.criterion: Computes RE'=500 ohm and Rin_base=52.475k, then the ratios ve/vb=0.9528346832 and ve/vsig=0.8699434537 with the 86.9943mV amplitude.
Computes R_look=(rpi+Rs)/(beta+1)=74.75 ohm and Rout=R_look||RE=69.5510584 ohm after removing RL and killing the source.
Rejects an RE-only or common-emitter substitute, a 1/gm or Rs-free Rout, and the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Uses RE=1k as the sole emitter AC load, or replaces the follower by a common-emitter inversion -gm RL (or by the 20/21 beta-not-beta+1 ratio as if it were the required ve/vb).
commonErrors.consequence: Rin_base, ve/vb, and ve/vsig all move off 52.475k / 0.9528346832 / 0.8699434537, so the 86.9943mV amplitude is lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports Rout=1/gm=25 ohm, or (rpi)/(beta+1)=24.75 ohm, omitting Rs and/or the parallel RE after the load is removed.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 74.75 ohm looking-in resistance and the 69.5510584 ohm stage Rout never appear.

hintTree.content: Two $1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistors in parallel are $500\,\Omega$. Then $(\beta+1)R_E'=100\cdot 500=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.
After the $50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ piece is known, $v_e/v_{\mathrm{sig}}$ is that piece over $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}+R_s$, because the $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}$ factors cancel.
For $R_{\mathrm{out}}$, kill $v_{\mathrm{sig}}$ but keep $R_s$. Then $(2475+5000)/100=74.75\,\Omega$, and that value in parallel with $R_E$ is $69.5510584\,\Omega$.

ELEC:010322.canonicalSolution:
The two emitter-node resistors are equal, so
\[
R_E'=R_E\parallel R_L=\frac{1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{2}=500\,\Omega.
\]
With $\beta+1=100$,
\[
(\beta+1)R_E'=100\cdot 500=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,
\]
and therefore
\[
R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=r_\pi+(\beta+1)R_E'
=2475+50000=52475\,\Omega=52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_E'=500\,\Omega,\quad R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}.
\]
(The given $g_m=\beta/r_\pi=99/2475=40\,\mathrm{mS}$ is consistent and
is not needed as a separate datum.)

The internal follower ratio is the voltage divider between
$(\beta+1)R_E'$ and $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}$:
\[
\frac{v_e}{v_b}
=\frac{50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}
=\frac{50000}{52475}
=\frac{2000}{2099}
=0.9528346832.
\]
Attaching $R_s=5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ at the base gives
\[
\frac{v_b}{v_{\mathrm{sig}}}
=\frac{R_{\mathrm{in,base}}}{R_{\mathrm{in,base}}+R_s},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{v_e}{v_{\mathrm{sig}}}
=\frac{50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}{52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega+5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}
=\frac{50000}{57475}
=\frac{2000}{2299}
=0.8699434537.
\]
A source amplitude $v_{\mathrm{sig}}=100\,\mathrm{mV}$ therefore
produces
\[
v_e=100\cdot 0.8699434537\,\mathrm{mV}=86.9943\,\mathrm{mV}.
\]
\[
\boxed{v_e/v_b=0.9528346832,\quad v_e/v_{\mathrm{sig}}=0.8699434537,\quad
v_e=86.9943\,\mathrm{mV}}.
\]
The approximation $g_m R_E'/(1+g_m R_E')=20/21\approx 0.95238$ is a
different $(\beta$ versus $\beta+1)$ model and is not the required
ratio.

To obtain $R_{\mathrm{out}}$, remove $R_L$ and set $v_{\mathrm{sig}}=0$.
The base Thevenin resistance is then $R_s$, so the resistance looking
into the emitter of the transistor is
\[
R_{\mathrm{look}}=\frac{r_\pi+R_s}{\beta+1}
=\frac{2475+5000}{100}=74.75\,\Omega.
\]
Paralleling the standing emitter resistor,
\[
R_{\mathrm{out}}=74.75\parallel 1000
=\frac{74750}{1074.75}=69.5510584\,\Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_{\mathrm{look}}=74.75\,\Omega,\quad
R_{\mathrm{out}}=69.5510584\,\Omega}.
\]
Neither $1/g_m=25\,\Omega$ nor $r_\pi/(\beta+1)=24.75\,\Omega$ is
$R_{\mathrm{out}}$: both omit $R_s$ and the parallel $R_E$.

Sentence (i) either refuses to form $R_E'$ or replaces the follower
by a common-emitter inversion $-g_m R_L$. Sentence (ii) quotes a
source-free $1/g_m$ (or an $R_s$-free $r_\pi/(\beta+1)$) in place of
the loaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}$. The six reserved intake families
(diode-region tests, $Q$-point headroom, rail-crossing licenses,
cascade port-resistance bites, Miller two-node poles, and feedback
stability boundaries) are not asked and are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: RE'=500 $\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{in,base}}=52.475\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Then $v_e/v_b=0.9528346832$ and $v_e/v_{\mathrm{sig}}=0.8699434537$, so $100\,\mathrm{mV}$ yields $86.9943\,\mathrm{mV}$. With $R_L$ removed, $R_{\mathrm{look}}=74.75\,\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{out}}=69.5510584\,\Omega$.
The emitter sees RE=1k, not RE||RL. Alternatively this is just a common-emitter stage with gain -gm RL, so I never form RE'=500 or Rin=52.475k and I never obtain ve/vsig=0.8699434537.

Output resistance of a follower is 1/gm=25 ohm, or at best rpi/(beta+1)=24.75 ohm. I kill the source by shorting the base, drop Rs, and I do not parallel RE, so 74.75 ohm and 69.5510584 ohm never appear.

ELEC:010323.title: Matched MOS pair with ideal tail: vo1/vid=-10, vo2/vid=+10, vod/vid=-20, ACM=0
ELEC:010323.objective: For a matched MOS pair with ideal tail, gm=2mS each, ro=infinity, RD=10k each, and a split vid, show vs is AC 0, id1=gm vid/2, vo1/vid=-10, vo2/vid=+10, vod/vid=-20, a 20mV peak vid yields -0.2 V, +0.2 V, -0.4 V, and ACM=0 because the source follows vcm.
ELEC:010323.statement:
A matched NMOS differential pair is biased by an ideal tail current
source (infinite incremental resistance) attached to the common source
node. Each device has
\[
g_m=2\,\mathrm{mS},\qquad r_o=\infty,
\]
and each drain is loaded by $R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ to an AC ground.
The gates are driven in the pure split
\[
v_1=+\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2},\qquad v_2=-\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2}.
\]
Body terminals are AC-grounded and body effect is neglected.

1. Argue that the common source node is an incremental AC ground for
   this purely differential drive, and prove
   \[
   i_{d1}=g_m\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2},\qquad
   i_{d2}=-g_m\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2}.
   \]

2. Taking the polarity $v_{o1}=-i_{d1}R_D$ and
   $v_{o2}=-i_{d2}R_D$, prove
   \[
   \frac{v_{o1}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}=-10,\qquad
   \frac{v_{o2}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}=+10,\qquad
   \frac{v_{\mathrm{od}}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}
   =\frac{v_{o1}-v_{o2}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}=-20.
   \]
   For a peak differential input $v_{\mathrm{id,pk}}=20\,\mathrm{mV}$,
   report the three peak outputs
   $v_{o1}=-0.2\,\mathrm{V}$, $v_{o2}=+0.2\,\mathrm{V}$, and
   $v_{\mathrm{od}}=-0.4\,\mathrm{V}$.

3. Now drive both gates by the same common-mode increment $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$.
   Prove that the ideal tail forces the source node to follow
   $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$, so both $v_{\mathrm{gs}}$ increments vanish, both
   drain currents stay at their bias values, and the incremental
   common-mode gain from $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ to either drain (and to
   $v_{\mathrm{od}}$) is identically $0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “each single-ended gain is $-g_m R_D=-20$,
   because the whole $v_{\mathrm{id}}$ appears as $v_{\mathrm{gs}}$ of
   $M_1$”; (ii) “the tail is only moderately stiff, so
   $A_{\mathrm{cm}}=-R_D/(2R_{\mathrm{SS}})$ is nonzero.” Do not
   replace the calculation by a diode-region test, a $Q$-point
   headroom certificate, a rail-crossing license, a cascade
   port-resistance bite, a Miller two-node pole shortcut, or a
   feedback stability-boundary claim.
permittedResults: With the source increment equal to zero, $i_{d1}=g_m v_{\mathrm{gs}1}=g_m v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$ and $i_{d2}=-g_m v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$. Drain voltages are $v_{ok}=-i_{dk}R_D$ when $r_o=\infty$.
Differential output $v_{\mathrm{od}}=v_{o1}-v_{o2}$ then equals $-g_m R_D v_{\mathrm{id}}$. Single-ended gains from $v_{\mathrm{id}}$ are half of that value and opposite in sign.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use matching plus the ideal-tail current-sum constraint to force vs=0, then write each drain as -id RD.
Superpose a common-mode test: the only KCL-legal motion is vs=vcm, which zeros both vgs and both drain increments.

milestones.criterion: Establishes the differential virtual ground and the split currents, then the three gains -10, +10, and -20.
Converts the 20mV peak vid into the three peak voltages -0.2 V, +0.2 V, and -0.4 V, and proves ACM=0 from source-following.
Rejects a dropped half-vid single-ended gain of -20, a finite-tail ACM, and the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the whole vid to one vgs and reports vo1/vid=-gm RD=-20 (or flips the sign of vod to +20).
commonErrors.consequence: The required triple -10, +10, -20 and the 20mV peak voltages -0.2, +0.2, -0.4 V are lost.

commonErrors.description: Gives the pair a finite-RSS common-mode gain such as -RD/(2 RSS), or claims the source node is AC ground under vcm.
commonErrors.consequence: The ideal-tail identity ACM=0, which is the point of part 3, is replaced by a different circuit.

hintTree.content: Matched devices plus $i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$ incremental force $v_s=0$ under antisymmetric gate drive. Each $v_{\mathrm{gs}}$ is then $\pm v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$.
$g_m R_D=2\,\mathrm{mS}\cdot 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=20$. Half of that, with a minus sign at drain 1, is $-10$.
Under $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ the only motion compatible with a fixed tail current is $v_s=v_{\mathrm{cm}}$. Then both $v_{\mathrm{gs}}=0$.

ELEC:010323.canonicalSolution:
The tail is ideal, so the incremental sum $i_{d1}+i_{d2}$ is identically
zero. Matched devices under the antisymmetric drive
$v_1=+v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$, $v_2=-v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$ then force the
common source increment to vanish: any $v_s\neq 0$ would produce a
common $v_{\mathrm{gs}}$ error that a pair of equal $g_m$ values could
not cancel while keeping the current sum at zero. Thus the source node
is an incremental AC ground, and
\[
v_{\mathrm{gs}1}=\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2},\qquad
v_{\mathrm{gs}2}=-\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2}.
\]
With $r_o=\infty$,
\[
i_{d1}=g_m\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2},\qquad
i_{d2}=-g_m\frac{v_{\mathrm{id}}}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{i_{d1}=g_m v_{\mathrm{id}}/2,\quad i_{d2}=-g_m v_{\mathrm{id}}/2}.
\]

Each drain current through $R_D=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ produces
\[
\frac{v_{o1}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}
=-\,g_m R_D\cdot\frac12
=-\,0.002\cdot 10000\cdot\frac12=-10,
\]
\[
\frac{v_{o2}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}
=+\,g_m R_D\cdot\frac12=+10.
\]
The differential output therefore satisfies
\[
\frac{v_{\mathrm{od}}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}
=\frac{v_{o1}-v_{o2}}{v_{\mathrm{id}}}=-20.
\]
Equivalently $v_{\mathrm{od}}=-g_m R_D v_{\mathrm{id}}$. For
$v_{\mathrm{id,pk}}=20\,\mathrm{mV}=0.020\,\mathrm{V}$,
\[
v_{o1}=-0.2\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
v_{o2}=+0.2\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
v_{\mathrm{od}}=-0.4\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{v_{o1}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=-10,\quad v_{o2}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=+10,\quad
v_{\mathrm{od}}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=-20}.
\]
\[
\boxed{v_{\mathrm{id,pk}}=20\,\mathrm{mV}\Rightarrow
(-0.2,+0.2,-0.4)\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Under a common-mode increment $v_1=v_2=v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ the ideal tail
still forbids any incremental current sum. The unique solution is
$v_s=v_{\mathrm{cm}}$, hence $v_{\mathrm{gs}1}=v_{\mathrm{gs}2}=0$,
$i_{d1}=i_{d2}=0$, and $v_{o1}=v_{o2}=v_{\mathrm{od}}=0$. The
common-mode gain is identically zero. A formula such as
$-R_D/(2R_{\mathrm{SS}})$ would require a finite tail resistance,
which is not present.

Sentence (i) assigns the whole $v_{\mathrm{id}}$ to one $v_{\mathrm{gs}}$
and quotes the single-ended gain as $-20$. Sentence (ii) invents a
finite $R_{\mathrm{SS}}$ and a nonzero $A_{\mathrm{cm}}$. The six
reserved intake families are not asked and are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The source is AC ground for the split $v_{\mathrm{id}}$, so $i_{d1}=g_m v_{\mathrm{id}}/2$. Gains are $v_{o1}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=-10$, $v_{o2}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=+10$, $v_{\mathrm{od}}/v_{\mathrm{id}}=-20$. A $20\,\mathrm{mV}$ peak gives $-0.2$, $+0.2$, $-0.4\,\mathrm{V}$. Ideal-tail $A_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ because $v_s$ follows $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$.
M1 sees the whole vid as vgs, so vo1/vid=-gm RD=-20. I never split vid/2, and I am willing to flip vod to +20 as a polarity convention.
Even with an ideal tail I assign a finite RSS and write ACM=-RD/(2 RSS), or I ground the source under vcm and compute a nonzero common-mode drain swing.
