ELEC:010424.title: Body-effect source follower splits 100uA and -50uA so Av=5/7, not 5/6
ELEC:010424.objective: With gm=5mS, gmb=1mS, ro=infinity, RL=1k, and body/drain AC ground, prove Av=5/7, unloaded Rout=166.6667 ohm, loaded Rout=142.8571 ohm, and that vg,pk=70mV yields vs=50mV, vgs=20mV, vbs=-50mV with currents 100uA, -50uA, and 50uA. Omitting body effect gives 5/6.
ELEC:010424.statement:
An NMOS source follower has
\[
g_m=5\,\mathrm{mS},\qquad g_{mb}=1\,\mathrm{mS},\qquad r_o=\infty,
\]
and a load $R_L=1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ from source to AC ground. The
drain and the body are both tied to incremental AC ground, so the
bulk-source voltage is $v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-v_s$.

1. Write KCL at the source node and prove
   \[
   A_v=\frac{v_s}{v_g}
   =\frac{g_m}{g_m+g_{mb}+1/R_L}=\frac{5}{7}.
   \]
   Confirm that omitting $g_{mb}$ would produce the distinct and
   incorrect value $5/6$.

2. Prove that the unloaded output resistance (load removed, gate AC
   grounded) is
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}=\frac{1}{g_m+g_{mb}}=166.6667\,\Omega,
   \]
   and that reattaching $R_L$ gives the loaded resistance
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{out,loaded}}
   =\frac{1}{g_m+g_{mb}}\parallel R_L=142.8571\,\Omega.
   \]

3. Apply a peak gate increment $v_{g,\mathrm{pk}}=70\,\mathrm{mV}$.
   Prove
   \[
   v_s=50\,\mathrm{mV},\qquad
   v_{\mathrm{gs}}=20\,\mathrm{mV},\qquad
   v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-50\,\mathrm{mV},
   \]
   and that the controlled currents are
   $g_m v_{\mathrm{gs}}=100\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ into the source node,
   $g_{mb} v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ (body contribution out
   of the source node), hence a net $50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ through $R_L$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “body effect only shifts the threshold,
   so $A_v=g_m R_L/(1+g_m R_L)=5/6$”; (ii) “$v_{\mathrm{bs}}=+v_s$
   because the body sits at the source, or else
   $R_{\mathrm{out}}=1/g_m=200\,\Omega$.” Do not replace the
   calculation by a diode-region test, a $Q$-point headroom
   certificate, a rail-crossing license, a cascade port-resistance
   bite, a Miller two-node pole shortcut, or a feedback
   stability-boundary claim.
permittedResults: KCL at the source: $g_m(v_g-v_s)+g_{mb}(-v_s)-v_s/R_L=0$, hence $A_v=g_m/(g_m+g_{mb}+1/R_L)$.
The same small-signal conductances give $R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}=1/(g_m+g_{mb})$ and $R_{\mathrm{out,loaded}}=R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}\parallel R_L$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write source-node KCL with both controlled sources and RL, then reuse the same conductances for a gate-grounded Rout test.
Insert vg=70mV into Av=5/7 to lock vs, vgs, and vbs, and check KCL by evaluating the two controlled currents against vs/RL.

milestones.criterion: Derives Av=5/7 from source-node KCL and distinguishes the omitted-body value 5/6.
Computes unloaded 166.6667 ohm and loaded 142.8571 ohm, then the 70mV voltage triple and the 100uA / -50uA / 50uA current split.
Rejects a threshold-only body-effect reading, a flipped vbs or 1/gm Rout, and the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Omits gmb from the source-node KCL and reports Av=gm/(gm+1/RL)=5/6, treating body effect as a DC threshold shift only.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 5/7, the 50mV source amplitude, and the 100uA / -50uA split are replaced by a no-body-effect circuit.

commonErrors.description: Takes vbs=+vs (body sitting at the source), or reports Rout=1/gm=200 ohm without the gmb term and without paralleling RL.
commonErrors.consequence: The body current flips sign or the required 166.6667 ohm / 142.8571 ohm pair never appears.

hintTree.content: The three conductances leaving the source increment are $g_m$, $g_{mb}$, and $1/R_L=1\,\mathrm{mS}$. Their sum is $7\,\mathrm{mS}$, and $g_m$ is $5\,\mathrm{mS}$.
Unloaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ drops the $1\,\mathrm{mS}$ load, leaving $1/6\,\mathrm{mS}=166.6667\,\Omega$. Parallel $1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ is $1000/7\,\Omega$.
$70\cdot 5/7=50$. Then $v_{\mathrm{gs}}=20\,\mathrm{mV}$ and $v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-50\,\mathrm{mV}$ produce $+100\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ and $-50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$.

ELEC:010424.canonicalSolution:
KCL at the source node, with currents of $g_m v_{\mathrm{gs}}$ and
$g_{mb} v_{\mathrm{bs}}$ oriented drain-to-source and with $R_L$
leaving the source toward ground, reads
\[
g_m(v_g-v_s)+g_{mb}(-v_s)-\frac{v_s}{R_L}=0.
\]
Rearrangement produces
\[
A_v=\frac{v_s}{v_g}
=\frac{g_m}{g_m+g_{mb}+1/R_L}
=\frac{5\,\mathrm{mS}}{5\,\mathrm{mS}+1\,\mathrm{mS}+1\,\mathrm{mS}}
=\frac{5}{7}.
\]
Dropping $g_{mb}$ would leave
\[
\frac{g_m}{g_m+1/R_L}=\frac{5}{6},
\]
which is a different circuit. The value $5/6$ is recorded only as the
omitted-body error, not as $A_v$.
\[
\boxed{A_v=5/7}.
\]

With the gate incrementally grounded and $R_L$ removed, a test voltage
$v_x$ at the source produces $v_{\mathrm{gs}}=-v_x$ and
$v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-v_x$, hence a test current
$(g_m+g_{mb})v_x$. Therefore
\[
R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}=\frac{1}{g_m+g_{mb}}
=\frac{1}{6\,\mathrm{mS}}=\frac{500}{3}=166.6667\,\Omega.
\]
Reattaching $R_L$ parallels that resistance:
\[
R_{\mathrm{out,loaded}}
=\frac{500}{3}\parallel 1000
=\frac{1000}{7}=142.8571\,\Omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_{\mathrm{out,unloaded}}=166.6667\,\Omega,\quad
R_{\mathrm{out,loaded}}=142.8571\,\Omega}.
\]

A peak gate increment $v_g=70\,\mathrm{mV}$ produces
\[
v_s=\frac{5}{7}\cdot 70\,\mathrm{mV}=50\,\mathrm{mV},
\]
\[
v_{\mathrm{gs}}=v_g-v_s=20\,\mathrm{mV},\qquad
v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-v_s=-50\,\mathrm{mV}.
\]
The controlled currents are
\[
g_m v_{\mathrm{gs}}=5\,\mathrm{mS}\cdot 20\,\mathrm{mV}=100\,\mu\mathrm{A}
\]
into the source node, and
\[
g_{mb} v_{\mathrm{bs}}=1\,\mathrm{mS}\cdot(-50\,\mathrm{mV})
=-50\,\mu\mathrm{A}
\]
(body contribution leaving the source node). Their net is
$50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ through $R_L$, recovering
$50\,\mu\mathrm{A}\cdot 1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=50\,\mathrm{mV}$.
\[
\boxed{v_s=50\,\mathrm{mV},\; v_{\mathrm{gs}}=20\,\mathrm{mV},\;
v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-50\,\mathrm{mV}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{100\,\mu\mathrm{A},\;-50\,\mu\mathrm{A},\;\mathrm{net}\,50\,\mu\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats body effect as a DC threshold shift only and
quotes $A_v=5/6$. Sentence (ii) either flips the sign of
$v_{\mathrm{bs}}$ or quotes $R_{\mathrm{out}}=1/g_m=200\,\Omega$.
The six reserved intake families are not asked and are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Source-node KCL gives $A_v=5/7$, not $5/6$. Unloaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}=166.6667\,\Omega$ and loaded $R_{\mathrm{out}}=142.8571\,\Omega$. For $v_g=70\,\mathrm{mV}$ one has $v_s=50\,\mathrm{mV}$, $v_{\mathrm{gs}}=20\,\mathrm{mV}$, $v_{\mathrm{bs}}=-50\,\mathrm{mV}$, and currents $100\,\mu\mathrm{A}$, $-50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$, net $50\,\mu\mathrm{A}$.
Body effect only shifts Vth, so I drop gmb and write Av=gm RL/(1+gm RL)=5/6. I never produce 5/7 or the 100uA / -50uA split.
The body sits at the source, so vbs=+vs, or else Rout is just 1/gm=200 ohm. I do not form 1/(gm+gmb) or parallel RL, so 166.6667 ohm and 142.8571 ohm never appear.

ELEC:010425.title: Stacked NMOS Rout=5.10M; RD=100k loads it to 98.077k, enhancement 2.94 not 102
ELEC:010425.objective: For stacked NMOS with ro1=ro2=50k, gm2=2mS, gmb=0, prove exact Rout=5.10M (not only gm ro^2), Rout||RD=98.076923k, a 10uA test current gives |vo|=0.980769V, the single-device loaded resistance is 33.333k, and the loaded enhancement is 2.9423077 rather than the raw 102.
ELEC:010425.statement:
Two NMOS transistors are stacked as a cascode. Device $M_1$ is on
the bottom (source AC-grounded, gate AC-grounded) with
$r_{o1}=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Device $M_2$ sits on top with
\[
g_{m2}=2\,\mathrm{mS},\qquad g_{mb2}=0,\qquad r_{o2}=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
The resistance looking into the drain of $M_2$, with both gates
incrementally grounded, is denoted $R_{\mathrm{out}}$. A standing
drain resistor $R_D=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ may then be attached from
that drain to AC ground.

1. Derive the exact looking-in resistance
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{out}}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}
   \]
   and prove that its value is $5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$. Record that
   the truncated estimate $g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$
   is not the exact $R_{\mathrm{out}}$.

2. Attach $R_D=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and prove that the effective
   resistance at the output node is
   \[
   R_{\mathrm{eff}}=R_{\mathrm{out}}\parallel R_D=98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
   \]
   A defined $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ small-signal current pulled from that
   node therefore produces $|v_o|=0.980769\,\mathrm{V}$.

3. For comparison, a single device with $r_{o1}=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$
   loaded by the same $R_D$ presents
   $r_{o1}\parallel R_D=33.333\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Prove that the
   loaded enhancement is
   \[
   \frac{R_{\mathrm{eff}}}{r_{o1}\parallel R_D}=2.9423077,
   \]
   and that this is not the raw unloaded ratio
   $R_{\mathrm{out}}/r_{o1}=102$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “cascode $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ is
   $g_m r_o^2=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$, and the extra $r_{o1}+r_{o2}$
   may be dropped”; (ii) “the load does not matter, so the
   enhancement is the raw $102$.” Do not replace the calculation by
   a diode-region test, a $Q$-point headroom certificate, a
   rail-crossing license, a cascade finite-port gain bite, a Miller
   two-node pole shortcut, or a feedback stability-boundary claim.
permittedResults: Test-source analysis of the stack: the current through $r_{o1}$ is amplified by $(1+g_{m2} r_{o2})$ at the upper source, and $r_{o2}$ adds in series, giving $R_{\mathrm{out}}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}(1+g_{m2} r_{o1})$.
Parallel combination $R_a\parallel R_b=R_a R_b/(R_a+R_b)$ converts $5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega\parallel 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ into $98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the exact series/controlled-source expression first, add the 100k of ro1+ro2 to 5.00M, then parallel RD before any enhancement ratio.
Convert the 10uA test into |vo| from Reff, and form the enhancement only after both the cascode and the single device have been loaded by RD.

milestones.criterion: Derives exact Rout=ro1+ro2+gm2 ro1 ro2=5.10M and refuses the truncated 5.00M estimate as the answer.
Computes Reff=98.076923k, |vo|=0.980769V at 10uA, the single-device 33.333k, and the loaded enhancement 2.9423077.
Rejects quoting the raw unloaded 102 as the loaded enhancement and refuses the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Reports Rout=gm2 ro1 ro2=5.00M and drops the exact ro1+ro2 piece, or uses 2 gm ro^2 as a substitute.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 5.10M never appears, so Reff and the 0.980769V test voltage shift.

commonErrors.description: Compares unloaded Rout to ro1 and quotes the enhancement as 102, ignoring that both the cascode and the single device are loaded by RD=100k.
commonErrors.consequence: The loaded ratio 2.9423077, which is what multiplies the 10uA test against the single-device 33.333k, is replaced by an unloaded figure of merit.

hintTree.content: $g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}=0.002\cdot 50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\cdot 50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$. Adding $r_{o1}+r_{o2}=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ produces $5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$.
$5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega\parallel 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=5.10/5.20\cdot 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Times $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ is $0.980769\,\mathrm{V}$.

The single-device loaded resistance is $50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=100/3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$. The ratio of $98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ to that value is $2.9423077$, not $102$.

ELEC:010425.canonicalSolution:
Apply a test voltage $v_x$ at the drain of $M_2$ with both gates
incrementally grounded. The current through $r_{o1}$ is the source
current of $M_2$. With $g_{mb2}=0$ the upper device contributes the
series combination of $r_{o2}$ and the controlled source $g_{m2} v_{gs2}$,
and $v_{gs2}$ equals the negative of the voltage across $r_{o1}$.
Collecting terms yields the exact looking-in resistance
\[
R_{\mathrm{out}}
=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}
=r_{o1}+r_{o2}(1+g_{m2} r_{o1}).
\]
Numerically
\[
g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}
=0.002\cdot 50000\cdot 50000=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega,
\]
\[
r_{o1}+r_{o2}=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,
\]
so
\[
R_{\mathrm{out}}=5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega.
\]
The truncated estimate $g_m r_o^2=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$ omits
$r_{o1}+r_{o2}$ and is not the exact value.
\[
\boxed{R_{\mathrm{out}}=5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega}.
\]

Attaching $R_D=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$,
\[
R_{\mathrm{eff}}
=5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega\parallel 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega
=\frac{5.10\times 10^6\cdot 1.00\times 10^5}{5.20\times 10^6}
=98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
A defined $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ small-signal current pulled from the
output node therefore produces
\[
|v_o|=10\times 10^{-6}\cdot 98.076923\times 10^3
=0.980769\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_{\mathrm{eff}}=98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad
|v_o|=0.980769\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

A single device with $r_{o1}=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ loaded by the same
$R_D$ presents
\[
r_{o1}\parallel R_D
=50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega
=\frac{100}{3}\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=33.333\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
The loaded enhancement is
\[
\frac{98.076923}{100/3}=2.9423077.
\]
The raw unloaded ratio $R_{\mathrm{out}}/r_{o1}=5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega/50\,\mathrm{k}\Omega=102$
compares two different (unloaded) resistances and is not the
enhancement that multiplies the $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ test current.
\[
\boxed{\text{loaded enhancement }2.9423077,\text{ not raw }102}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $r_{o1}+r_{o2}$ and freezes $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ at
$5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$. Sentence (ii) quotes the raw $102$ as if
$R_D$ were absent. The six reserved intake families are not asked
and are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Exact $R_{\mathrm{out}}=5.10\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$, not $g_m r_o^2=5.00\,\mathrm{M}\Omega$. With $R_D=100\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ one has $R_{\mathrm{eff}}=98.076923\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $|v_o|=0.980769\,\mathrm{V}$ at $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$. The single-device loaded resistance is $33.333\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, so the loaded enhancement is $2.9423077$, not the raw $102$.
Cascode Rout is just gm ro^2=5.00M. I drop ro1+ro2 (or I double it to 2 gm ro^2) and I never write 5.10M.
The enhancement is Rout/ro1=102. The RD load is a side issue and I compare unloaded resistances, so 2.9423077 never appears.

ELEC:010426.title: Class-B at Vp=10, VCC=12: eta=5pi/24, PD peaks at 2VCC/pi not at full swing
ELEC:010426.objective: For ideal complementary class-B at +/-12V, RL=8 ohm, vo peak 10V, compute Ipk=1.25A, PL=6.25W, Pdc=30/pi=9.549296586W, eta=0.6544984695, total transistor dissipation 3.299296586W (each 1.649648293W), the PD(Vp) peak at 7.639437V of 3.647562611W (each 1.823781306W), and the ideal ceiling eta=pi/4 only at Vp=VCC.
ELEC:010426.statement:
An ideal complementary class-B push-pull stage is supplied from
$\pm V_{\mathrm{CC}}=\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$ and drives $R_L=8\,\Omega$.
Crossover is ideal (no dead zone, no standing bias current). The
sinusoidal output voltage has peak $V_p=10\,\mathrm{V}$.

1. Prove $I_{\mathrm{pk}}=V_p/R_L=1.25\,\mathrm{A}$ and
   \[
   P_L=\frac{V_p^2}{2R_L}=6.25\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]
   Each supply delivers the half-wave average $I_{\mathrm{pk}}/\pi$,
   so the total DC input power is
   \[
   P_{\mathrm{dc}}=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}} I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{\pi}
   =\frac{30}{\pi}=9.549296586\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   \eta=\frac{P_L}{P_{\mathrm{dc}}}=0.6544984695.
   \]
   Total transistor dissipation is $P_{\mathrm{dc}}-P_L=3.299296586\,\mathrm{W}$,
   or $1.649648293\,\mathrm{W}$ in each device.

2. For a general peak $V_p$ (still $V_p\le V_{\mathrm{CC}}$) derive
   \[
   P_D
   =\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}} V_p}{\pi R_L}-\frac{V_p^2}{2R_L}.
   \]
   Maximize with respect to $V_p$ and prove that the maximum occurs
   at
   \[
   V_p=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}}{\pi}=7.639437\,\mathrm{V},
   \]
   where the total dissipation is
   \[
   P_{D,\max}=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2}{\pi^2 R_L}=3.647562611\,\mathrm{W}
   \]
   ($1.823781306\,\mathrm{W}$ in each device). In particular the
   maximum is not at the present $V_p=10\,\mathrm{V}$ and is not at
   $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}$.

3. Confirm that the ideal efficiency ceiling
   $\eta=\pi/4$ is attained only at $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}$, and that
   the present operating point with $V_p=10\,\mathrm{V}$ is strictly
   below that ceiling.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “class-B efficiency is always
   $\pi/4$, so the $10\,\mathrm{V}$ swing already delivers $0.785$”;
   (ii) “transistor dissipation is largest at full swing
   $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}$, or else this is a class-A $V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2/R_L$
   calculation.” Do not replace the calculation by a diode-region
   test, a $Q$-point headroom certificate, a rail-crossing license
   for a small-signal gain, a cascade port-resistance bite, a Miller
   two-node pole shortcut, or a feedback stability-boundary claim.
permittedResults: Half-sine average: if $i(t)=I_{\mathrm{pk}}\sin(\omega t)$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $0$ on $(\pi,2\pi)$, then the average is $I_{\mathrm{pk}}/\pi$.
Differentiating $P_D(V_p)=2 V_{\mathrm{CC}} V_p/(\pi R_L)-V_p^2/(2 R_L)$ yields a unique critical point $V_p=2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}/\pi$, where $P_{D,\max}=2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2/(\pi^2 R_L)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute PL and the two half-sine supply averages first, then subtract to get PD at 10V; afterwards differentiate the general PD(Vp).
Write eta(Vp)=(pi/4)(Vp/VCC) to see that pi/4 is a ceiling, and use dPD/dVp=0 to place the dissipation peak inside the swing range.

milestones.criterion: Computes Ipk=1.25A, PL=6.25W, Pdc=30/pi W, eta=5pi/24, and the 3.299296586W / 1.649648293W dissipation split at Vp=10V.
Derives PD(Vp), locates the maximum at 2VCC/pi=7.639437V with PDmax=3.647562611W (each 1.823781306W), and reserves pi/4 for Vp=VCC only.
Rejects quoting pi/4 at the 10V swing, placing PDmax at full swing or substituting class-A, and the six reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Reports eta=pi/4 at Vp=10V, or uses a single-supply / class-A input power so that 5pi/24 never appears.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned efficiency 0.6544984695 and the associated Pdc=30/pi W are replaced by the full-swing ceiling or by a different class.

commonErrors.description: Claims transistor dissipation is largest at Vp=VCC=12V (or at the operating Vp=10V) instead of at 2VCC/pi=7.639437V.
commonErrors.consequence: The interior peak PDmax=3.647562611W is missed, and the 10V point is misread as a dissipation extreme.

hintTree.content: $I_{\mathrm{pk}}=10/8=1.25\,\mathrm{A}$ and $P_L=100/(16)=6.25\,\mathrm{W}$. Two supplies give $P_{\mathrm{dc}}=2\cdot 12\cdot 1.25/\pi=30/\pi$.
Efficiency is $6.25\cdot\pi/30=5\pi/24=0.6544984695$, which is strictly less than $\pi/4$.
Set $dP_D/dV_p=0$: $2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}/(\pi R_L)=V_p/R_L$ produces $V_p=2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}/\pi=24/\pi$, inside $(0,12)$.

ELEC:010426.canonicalSolution:
The load equation is $I_{\mathrm{pk}}=V_p/R_L=10/8=1.25\,\mathrm{A}$.
Average load power for a sinusoid is
\[
P_L=\frac{V_p^2}{2 R_L}=\frac{100}{16}=6.25\,\mathrm{W}
\]
(equivalently $\tfrac12 V_p I_{\mathrm{pk}}$). Each supply conducts a
half-sine, so its average current is $I_{\mathrm{pk}}/\pi$. The two
rails together consume
\[
P_{\mathrm{dc}}
=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}} I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{\pi}
=\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot 1.25}{\pi}
=\frac{30}{\pi}=9.549296586\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
Efficiency at this operating point is
\[
\eta=\frac{6.25}{30/\pi}=\frac{5\pi}{24}=0.6544984695.
\]
Total transistor dissipation is the difference
\[
P_D=P_{\mathrm{dc}}-P_L
=\frac{30}{\pi}-6.25=3.299296586\,\mathrm{W},
\]
split equally as $1.649648293\,\mathrm{W}$ in each device.
\[
\boxed{I_{\mathrm{pk}}=1.25\,\mathrm{A},\; P_L=6.25\,\mathrm{W},\;
P_{\mathrm{dc}}=30/\pi\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\eta=5\pi/24=0.6544984695,\;
P_D=3.299296586\,\mathrm{W}\;(1.649648293\,\mathrm{W\ each})}.
\]

For a general peak $V_p\le V_{\mathrm{CC}}$,
\[
P_D(V_p)
=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}} V_p}{\pi R_L}-\frac{V_p^2}{2 R_L}.
\]
Differentiating,
\[
\frac{dP_D}{dV_p}
=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}}{\pi R_L}-\frac{V_p}{R_L}.
\]
The unique critical point is
\[
V_p=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}}{\pi}=\frac{24}{\pi}=7.639437\,\mathrm{V},
\]
which lies in $(0,V_{\mathrm{CC}})$. The second derivative
$-1/R_L<0$ confirms a maximum. Substituting the critical peak gives
\[
P_{D,\max}
=\frac{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2}{\pi^2 R_L}
=\frac{2\cdot 144}{\pi^2\cdot 8}
=\frac{36}{\pi^2}=3.647562611\,\mathrm{W},
\]
or $1.823781306\,\mathrm{W}$ in each device. The present
$V_p=10\,\mathrm{V}$ is past this peak, and $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}=12\,\mathrm{V}$
is still farther past it.
\[
\boxed{P_D\text{ max at }V_p=2V_{\mathrm{CC}}/\pi=7.639437\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_{D,\max}=3.647562611\,\mathrm{W}\;(1.823781306\,\mathrm{W\ each})}.
\]

At $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}$ the efficiency becomes
\[
\eta=\frac{V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2/(2 R_L)}{2 V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2/(\pi R_L)}
=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
That ceiling is not available at $V_p=10\,\mathrm{V}<12\,\mathrm{V}$.
The number $\pi/4\approx 0.785398$ is therefore not the efficiency of
the assigned operating point.

Sentence (i) quotes $\pi/4$ at a partial swing. Sentence (ii) places
the dissipation maximum at full swing (or imports a class-A
$V_{\mathrm{CC}}^2/R_L$ budget). The six reserved intake families
are not asked and are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Ipk $=1.25\,\mathrm{A}$, $P_L=6.25\,\mathrm{W}$, $P_{\mathrm{dc}}=30/\pi\,\mathrm{W}$, $\eta=5\pi/24=0.6544984695$, and $P_D=3.299296586\,\mathrm{W}$ ($1.649648293\,\mathrm{W}$ each). The dissipation maximum is at $V_p=2V_{\mathrm{CC}}/\pi=7.639437\,\mathrm{V}$ with $P_{D,\max}=3.647562611\,\mathrm{W}$ ($1.823781306\,\mathrm{W}$ each). The ceiling $\pi/4$ holds only at $V_p=V_{\mathrm{CC}}$.
Class-B efficiency is always pi/4, so at Vp=10V I already have eta=0.785. I do not form 30/pi or 5pi/24, and I may also treat the input power as a class-A budget.
Devices burn the most power at full swing Vp=VCC=12V, or at the given 10V peak. I do not differentiate PD(Vp) and I never report the interior critical peak 2VCC/pi=7.639437V or PDmax=3.647562611W.

ELEC:010527.title: Equal coupling poles at 20 Hz give |H|=5 and a lower -3 dB at 31.075 Hz
ELEC:010527.objective: For H(s)=-10[s/(s+wL)]^2 with equal noninteracting coupling poles at fL=20 Hz, prove the relative magnitude f^2/(f^2+fL^2), evaluate |H|=5 and principal phase -90 deg at 20 Hz, locate the overall lower -3 dB at fL sqrt(1+sqrt(2))=31.07547948 Hz, and compute |H|=9.615384615 with principal phase -157.380135 deg at 100 Hz.
ELEC:010527.statement:
A midband-inverting amplifier is AC-coupled at two noninteracting
equal highpass nodes. The declared coupling poles coincide at
\[
f_L=20\,\mathrm{Hz},\qquad \omega_L=2\pi f_L,
\]
and the transfer is
\[
H(s)=-10\left(\frac{s}{s+\omega_L}\right)^2.
\]
The two poles do not interact: each coupling time constant is set by
its own series capacitor and the resistance it faces, and the second
node does not load the first.

1. On the $j\omega$ axis write the exact magnitude
   $|H(j2\pi f)|$ and prove that the midband-relative magnitude is
   \[
   \frac{|H(j2\pi f)|}{10}=\frac{f^2}{f^2+f_L^2}.
   \]
   Identify the midband gain as the constant $-10$.

2. At $f=f_L=20\,\mathrm{Hz}$ evaluate $|H|$ and the decibel drop from
   midband. Prove
   \[
   |H(j2\pi\cdot 20)|=5
   \]
   and that this is $-6.0206\,\mathrm{dB}$ from midband. Then prove that
   the principal argument is $-90^{\circ}$.

3. The overall lower $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ frequency $f_{-3}$ is defined by
   $|H(j2\pi f_{-3})|=10/\sqrt{2}$. Prove
   \[
   f_{-3}=f_L\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}=31.07547948\,\mathrm{Hz}.
   \]
   In particular $f_{-3}$ is not the single-pole location $f_L$.

4. At $f=100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ prove
   \[
   |H(j2\pi\cdot 100)|=9.615384615
   \]
   and that the principal phase is
   \[
   -180^{\circ}+2\arctan(0.2)=-157.380135^{\circ}.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) "two equal poles still give a single-pole
   highpass, so the lower $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ point is $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$,
   $|H(20)|=10/\sqrt{2}$, and the phase at $f_L$ is $-45^{\circ}$";
   (ii) "Miller's shortcut on a two-node $C_\pi,C_\mu$ pair already
   locates these coupling poles."

Do not replace the calculation by a diode-region test, a Q-point
headroom certificate, a small-signal rail-crossing license, or a
cascade port-resistance bite.
permittedResults: A real pole factor $s/(s+\omega_L)$ contributes magnitude $f/\sqrt{f^2+f_L^2}$ and argument $90^{\circ}-\arctan(f/f_L)$. Two equal factors square the magnitude and double the argument.
For $x>0$ one has $\arctan x+\arctan(1/x)=90^{\circ}$, so $-2\arctan(f/f_L)=-180^{\circ}+2\arctan(f_L/f)$ as principal values on $f>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Square the first-order highpass factor first, then evaluate the two spot frequencies and solve f^2/(f^2+fL^2)=1/sqrt(2).
Use arg(-1)+2 arg(j f/(j f+fL)) to lock the principal phase, then convert to -180 deg + 2 arctan(fL/f) at 100 Hz.

milestones.criterion: Derives |H|/10=f^2/(f^2+fL^2) and evaluates |H(20)|=5, -6.0206 dB from midband, and principal phase -90 deg.
Locates f-3=31.07547948 Hz and evaluates |H(100)|=9.615384615 with principal phase -157.380135 deg.
Rejects a single-pole-at-fL reading and refuses Miller two-node or reserved intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the pair as one highpass pole at fL, reporting a lower -3 dB of 20 Hz, |H(20)|=10/sqrt(2), and phase -45 deg.
commonErrors.consequence: The stacked 6 dB drop at fL and the shifted corner 31.07547948 Hz are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the first-order law f/sqrt(f^2+fL^2) for |H|/10, or computes a principal phase other than -90 deg at 20 Hz or -157.380135 deg at 100 Hz.
commonErrors.consequence: The required values |H(20)|=5 and |H(100)|=9.615384615 with the assigned principal phases fail.

hintTree.content: Midband is the $s\to\infty$ value $-10$. Each factor $j2\pi f/(j2\pi f+\omega_L)$ has magnitude $f/\sqrt{f^2+f_L^2}$.
At $f=f_L$ the relative magnitude is $1/2$, so $|H|=5$. The inversion contributes $-180^{\circ}$ and the two factors contribute $+90^{\circ}$ together.
Set $f^2/(f^2+f_L^2)=1/\sqrt{2}$ and solve $f=f_L\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}$. At $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ use $f_L/f=0.2$ in the complementary arctangent form.

ELEC:010527.canonicalSolution:
Write $s=j\omega=j2\pi f$. Then
\[
H(j2\pi f)
=-10\left(\frac{j2\pi f}{j2\pi f+\omega_L}\right)^2.
\]
Each first-order factor has magnitude $f/\sqrt{f^2+f_L^2}$, so
\[
|H(j2\pi f)|
=10\cdot\frac{f^2}{f^2+f_L^2}.
\]
The midband gain is the constant $H(\infty)=-10$, hence the
midband-relative magnitude is exactly $f^2/(f^2+f_L^2)$.
\[
\boxed{|H|/10=f^2/(f^2+f_L^2)}.
\]

At $f=f_L=20\,\mathrm{Hz}$ the relative factor is $1/2$, so
$|H|=5$. The drop from midband is
\[
20\log_{10}(1/2)=-6.020599913\,\mathrm{dB},
\]
which rounds to the assigned $-6.0206\,\mathrm{dB}$.

The argument is the sum of the inversion $-180^{\circ}$ and two copies
of $90^{\circ}-\arctan(f/f_L)$. At $f=f_L$ this is
\[
-180^{\circ}+2\bigl(90^{\circ}-45^{\circ}\bigr)=-90^{\circ}.
\]
Equivalently the principal value is $-2\arctan(f/f_L)=-90^{\circ}$.
\[
\boxed{|H(20\,\mathrm{Hz})|=5,\quad -6.0206\,\mathrm{dB},\quad -90^{\circ}}.
\]

The overall lower $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ frequency satisfies
$f^2/(f^2+f_L^2)=1/\sqrt{2}$. Rearrangement gives
\[
f^2=f_L^2(1+\sqrt{2}),
\]
so
\[
f_{-3}=f_L\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}.
\]
Numerically $\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}=1.553773974$ and
$20\times 1.553773974=31.07547948\,\mathrm{Hz}$. This is strictly
above the single-pole location $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$, as it must be: two
equal highpass poles have already cost $6\,\mathrm{dB}$ at $f_L$.
\[
\boxed{f_{-3}=31.07547948\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
\]

At $f=100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ one has $f^2=10^4$ and $f_L^2=400$, hence
\[
|H|=10\cdot\frac{10000}{10400}=\frac{125}{13}=9.615384615.
\]
The complementary-angle identity produces the principal phase
\[
-180^{\circ}+2\arctan(f_L/f)
=-180^{\circ}+2\arctan(0.2).
\]
Now $\arctan(0.2)=11.30993247^{\circ}$, so
$2\arctan(0.2)=22.61986495^{\circ}$ and the phase is
$-157.380135^{\circ}$. The same number is $-2\arctan(5)$.
\[
\boxed{|H(100\,\mathrm{Hz})|=9.615384615,\quad -157.380135^{\circ}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the stacked pair by a single pole at $f_L$. That
error reports $|H(20)|=10/\sqrt{2}$, a $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ frequency of
$20\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and a $-45^{\circ}$ phase, all of which contradict
the displayed values. Sentence (ii) imports the reserved Miller
two-node $C_\pi,C_\mu$ exercise; those poles are interacting device
capacitances, not the declared equal coupling poles.

The argument never tests a diode region, never certifies Q-point
headroom, never treats a small-signal gain as a rail-crossing license,
and never accounts cascade port-resistance bites.

graderFixtures.proofText: Relative magnitude $f^2/(f^2+f_L^2)$ gives $|H(20)|=5$ ($-6.0206\,\mathrm{dB}$) and principal phase $-90^{\circ}$. The overall lower $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ frequency is $f_L\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}=31.07547948\,\mathrm{Hz}$. At $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $|H|=9.615384615$ and the principal phase is $-180^{\circ}+2\arctan(0.2)=-157.380135^{\circ}$.
Two equal coupling poles are still a single-pole highpass at fL=20 Hz. The lower -3 dB frequency is therefore 20 Hz, |H(20)|=10/sqrt(2), and the phase at fL is -45 deg.

I take the relative magnitude to be the first-order law f/sqrt(f^2+fL^2), so |H(20)|=10/sqrt(2) and |H(100)| is not 9.615384615. I also report the 100 Hz principal phase as -2 arctan(0.2) or as -90 deg.

ELEC:010528.title: A 0.8 follower into 100 pF has fp=7.958 MHz and a 10-90 rise of tau ln 9
ELEC:010528.objective: For the follower H=0.8/(1+s Rout CL) with Rout=200 ohm and CL=100 pF, compute tau=20 ns, fp=7.957747155 MHz, the 5 MHz magnitude 0.677386413 and phase -32.141908 deg, the exact 10-90 rise tau ln 9=43.94449155 ns, and the exact doubling of rise (halving of fp) when CL doubles.
ELEC:010528.statement:
A voltage follower with finite DC gain $A_0=0.8$ and output resistance
$R_\mathrm{out}=200\,\Omega$ drives a capacitive load
$C_L=100\,\mathrm{pF}$. No other poles are declared. The loaded
transfer is
\[
H(s)=\frac{0.8}{1+s R_\mathrm{out}C_L}.
\]

1. Identify the time constant $\tau=R_\mathrm{out}C_L$ and the output
   pole $f_p=1/(2\pi\tau)$. Prove
   \[
   \tau=20\,\mathrm{ns},\qquad f_p=7.957747155\,\mathrm{MHz}.
   \]

2. At $f=5\,\mathrm{MHz}$ evaluate the magnitude and the principal
   phase of $H(j2\pi f)$. Prove
   \[
   |H|=0.677386413,\qquad \arg H=-32.141908^{\circ}.
   \]

3. Drive the follower with a step and measure the $10\%$ to $90\%$
   rise of the exponential $A_0(1-e^{-t/\tau})$. Prove that the exact
   rise time is
   \[
   t_{10-90}=\tau\ln 9=43.94449155\,\mathrm{ns}.
   \]
   Do not replace $\ln 9$ by the decimal slogan $2.2$.

4. Replace $C_L$ by $2C_L$ and prove that $f_p$ halves while
   $t_{10-90}$ doubles. The DC gain $A_0=0.8$ is unchanged.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) "the pole is $1/\tau=50\,\mathrm{MHz}$
   because frequency is the reciprocal of a time constant"; (ii) "the
   $10$--$90$ rise is $2.2\tau$ by definition, or doubling $C_L$ cannot
   change the rise because the follower GBW is fixed."

Do not replace the output pole by Miller's two-node calculation, and
do not treat $A_0=0.8$ as a rail-crossing license or a Q-point
headroom certificate.
permittedResults: On $s=j2\pi f$ one has $|H|=A_0/\sqrt{1+(f/f_p)^2}$ and $\arg H=-\arctan(f/f_p)$.
Both $f_p$ and $t_{10-90}$ are homogeneous of degree one in $\tau=R_\mathrm{out}C_L$, so doubling $C_L$ halves $f_p$ and doubles the rise.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form tau=Rout CL first, convert with 2 pi to fp, then reuse f/fp=pi/5 at 5 MHz.
Solve 1-e^{-t/tau}=0.1 and 0.9 exactly to lock ln 9, then scale both fp and the rise with tau.

milestones.criterion: Computes tau=20 ns and fp=7.957747155 MHz, then |H(5 MHz)|=0.677386413 with phase -32.141908 deg.
Proves t10-90=tau ln 9=43.94449155 ns and that doubling CL halves fp and doubles the rise.
Rejects fp=1/tau and a CL-invariant or slogan-only rise, and refuses reserved intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the output pole as 1/tau=50 MHz, omitting the conversion from rad/s to Hz.
commonErrors.consequence: The 5 MHz magnitude and phase, which depend on f/fp=pi/5, cannot be recovered.

commonErrors.description: Replaces t10-90 by an unexplained 2.2 tau as if that were exact, or claims doubling CL leaves the rise (or fp) unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact identity tau ln 9=43.94449155 ns and the homogeneous scaling in CL are lost.

hintTree.content: Compute $\tau=200\times 100\times 10^{-12}=20\,\mathrm{ns}$, then $f_p=1/(2\pi\tau)$.
The ratio $f/f_p$ at $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$ equals $\pi/5$. Use that exact ratio in the magnitude and arctangent.
The $10\%$ and $90\%$ times differ by $\tau(\ln 10-\ln(10/9))=\tau\ln 9$. Doubling $C_L$ doubles $\tau$.

ELEC:010528.canonicalSolution:
The product of the given output resistance and load is
\[
\tau=R_\mathrm{out}C_L=200\times 100\times 10^{-12}=20\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}.
\]
The pole in hertz is the reciprocal of $2\pi\tau$, not of $\tau$:
\[
f_p=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}=\frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 20\times 10^{-9}}
=7.957747155\,\mathrm{MHz}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau=20\,\mathrm{ns},\quad f_p=7.957747155\,\mathrm{MHz}}.
\]

At $f=5\,\mathrm{MHz}$ the normalized frequency is exact:
\[
\frac{f}{f_p}=5\times 10^6\cdot 2\pi\cdot 20\times 10^{-9}=\frac{\pi}{5}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|H|=\frac{0.8}{\sqrt{1+(\pi/5)^2}}=0.677386413
\]
and
\[
\arg H=-\arctan(\pi/5)=-32.141908^{\circ}.
\]
\[
\boxed{|H(5\,\mathrm{MHz})|=0.677386413,\quad -32.141908^{\circ}}.
\]

The step response is $0.8(1-e^{-t/\tau})$. Setting the normalized
exponential equal to $0.1$ and $0.9$ gives
\[
t_{10}=\tau\ln\frac{10}{9},\qquad t_{90}=\tau\ln 10,
\]
so
\[
t_{10-90}=\tau\ln 9=20\times 10^{-9}\cdot\ln 9=43.94449155\,\mathrm{ns}.
\]
The decimal $2.2\tau=44\,\mathrm{ns}$ is a rounded slogan, not the
exact rise required here.
\[
\boxed{t_{10-90}=\tau\ln 9=43.94449155\,\mathrm{ns}}.
\]

Doubling $C_L$ doubles $\tau$. Consequently $f_p=1/(2\pi\tau)$ halves
to $3.978873577\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and $t_{10-90}=\tau\ln 9$ doubles to
$87.88898310\,\mathrm{ns}$. The DC factor $0.8$ does not move.

Sentence (i) drops the $2\pi$ and reports a $50\,\mathrm{MHz}$ pole.
Sentence (ii) freezes the rise at the slogan $2.2\tau$ or denies the
linear scaling with $C_L$ by appealing to a fixed follower GBW that
is not the declared one-pole model.

The calculation is not a Miller two-node pole pair, not a Q-point
headroom certificate, and not a small-signal rail-crossing license.

graderFixtures.proofText: The loaded follower has $\tau=20\,\mathrm{ns}$ and $f_p=7.957747155\,\mathrm{MHz}$. At $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $|H|=0.677386413$ and the phase is $-32.141908^{\circ}$. The exact $10$--$90$ rise is $\tau\ln 9=43.94449155\,\mathrm{ns}$. Doubling $C_L$ halves $f_p$ and doubles the rise.
Frequency is the reciprocal of the time constant, so fp=1/tau=50 MHz. I never divide by 2 pi, and I evaluate the 5 MHz point against this 50 MHz pole.
The 10-90 rise of any first-order step is 2.2 tau by definition, and doubling CL cannot change that rise because the follower GBW is fixed. I do not accept tau ln 9 as the exact rise.

ELEC:010629.title: Finite A0=1e5 and fp=10 Hz close a noninverting loop to 10.9988 with fcl=90.92 kHz
ELEC:010629.objective: For A(s)=1e5/(1+s/wp) with fp=10 Hz and noninverting beta=1/11, compute DC closed gain 10.998790133 versus ideal 11, fractional error 1.099879e-4=0.01099879%, exact closed pole 90.9190909 kHz, one-pole 1% settling 8.06140483 us, and |Acl(fcl)|=T0/sqrt(2).
ELEC:010629.statement:
An internally compensated op-amp has the one-pole open-loop gain
\[
A(s)=\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_p},\qquad A_0=10^5,\qquad f_p=10\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]
It is placed in a purely resistive noninverting feedback network with
\[
\beta=\frac{1}{11}.
\]
No additional loop poles are declared. Write
\[
T_0:=\frac{A_0}{1+\beta A_0}
\]
for the DC closed-loop gain (the DC closed-loop transmission).

1. Prove that the DC closed-loop gain is
   \[
   A_\mathrm{cl}(0)=T_0=10.998790133
   \]
   while the ideal infinite-loop-gain closed-loop value is $1/\beta=11$.
   Prove that
   the fractional error relative to $11$ is
   \[
   \frac{1}{1+\beta A_0}=1.099879\times 10^{-4}=0.01099879\%.
   \]

2. Close the one-pole loop and prove that the exact closed-loop pole is
   \[
   f_\mathrm{cl}=f_p(1+\beta A_0)=90.9190909\,\mathrm{kHz}.
   \]

3. For this one-pole closed-loop response, the residual step error is
   $e^{-t/\tau_\mathrm{cl}}$ with $\tau_\mathrm{cl}=1/(2\pi f_\mathrm{cl})$.
   Prove that the time to $1\%$ residual is
   \[
   t_{1\%}=\frac{\ln 100}{2\pi f_\mathrm{cl}}=8.06140483\,\mu\mathrm{s}.
   \]

4. Prove that the closed-loop magnitude at $f=f_\mathrm{cl}$ is
   $T_0/\sqrt{2}$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) "finite $A_0$ is already infinite for
   engineering purposes, so $A_\mathrm{cl}(0)=11$ exactly and the
   fractional error is $1/A_0$"; (ii) "the closed pole is $f_p$ itself,
   or else the loop is a three-pole Routh problem and more feedback
   improves DC accuracy only up to a stability boundary."

Do not replace the one-pole close by a three-pole characteristic, and
do not invoke Miller two-node poles or a cascade port-resistance
identity.
permittedResults: The identity $1-T_0\beta=1/(1+\beta A_0)$ is the exact DC fractional error against the ideal gain $1/\beta$.
A one-pole step of time constant $1/\omega_\mathrm{cl}$ reaches residual $1/100$ at time $\ln 100/\omega_\mathrm{cl}$. On the $j\omega$ axis, $|A_\mathrm{cl}(j\omega_\mathrm{cl})|=T_0/\sqrt{2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form 1+beta A0=100011/11 first; every required scalar is a rational multiple of that factor.
Write Acl(s)=T0/(1+s/omega_cl) and read fcl, the 1% exponential time, and the j-axis factor 1+j from that one pole.

milestones.criterion: Computes T0=10.998790133, ideal 11, and fractional error 1.099879e-4=0.01099879%.
Locates fcl=90.9190909 kHz, t1%=8.06140483 us, and |Acl(fcl)|=T0/sqrt(2).
Rejects an ideal-11 or 1/A0 error and refuses three-pole/Routh or reserved intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Sets Acl(0)=11 exactly, or reports the fractional error as 1/A0=1e-5 instead of 1/(1+beta A0).
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-loop-gain correction 10.998790133 and the error 0.01099879% are discarded.

commonErrors.description: Leaves the closed pole at fp=10 Hz, uses a settling time other than ln 100/(2 pi fcl), or replaces the one-pole close by a three-pole Routh stability boundary.
commonErrors.consequence: The values 90.9190909 kHz and 8.06140483 us fail, or a reserved intake family is imported.

hintTree.content: The closed pole multiplies $f_p$ by that same factor $100011/11$, giving $1000110/11$ hertz.
One percent residual means $e^{-t/\tau}=1/100$, so $t=\tau\ln 100$ with $\tau=1/(2\pi f_\mathrm{cl})$.

ELEC:010629.canonicalSolution:
The DC loop gain is $\beta A_0=10^5/11$. Therefore
\[
1+\beta A_0=\frac{100011}{11},
\]
and the DC closed-loop gain is
\[
T_0=\frac{A_0}{1+\beta A_0}=\frac{10^5\cdot 11}{100011}=\frac{1100000}{100011}
=10.998790133.
\]
The ideal value is $1/\beta=11$. The fractional error against that ideal
is
\[
\frac{11-T_0}{11}=\frac{1}{1+\beta A_0}=\frac{11}{100011}
=1.099879\times 10^{-4}=0.01099879\%.
\]
\[
\boxed{T_0=10.998790133,\quad\text{ideal }11,\quad 0.01099879\%}.
\]

Substitute $A(s)$ into $A/(1+\beta A)$:
\[
A_\mathrm{cl}(s)
=\frac{A_0}{1+\beta A_0+s/\omega_p}
=\frac{T_0}{1+s/[\omega_p(1+\beta A_0)]}.
\]
The closed-loop pole in hertz is therefore
\[
f_\mathrm{cl}=f_p(1+\beta A_0)=10\cdot\frac{100011}{11}
=90.9190909\,\mathrm{kHz}.
\]
\[
\boxed{f_\mathrm{cl}=90.9190909\,\mathrm{kHz}}.
\]

The closed-loop time constant is $\tau_\mathrm{cl}=1/(2\pi f_\mathrm{cl})$.
A $1\%$ residual requires $e^{-t/\tau_\mathrm{cl}}=1/100$, hence
\[
t_{1\%}=\frac{\ln 100}{2\pi f_\mathrm{cl}}=8.06140483\,\mu\mathrm{s}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t_{1\%}=8.06140483\,\mu\mathrm{s}}.
\]
At $f=f_\mathrm{cl}$ the remaining denominator factor is $1+j$, so
\[
\bigl|A_\mathrm{cl}(j2\pi f_\mathrm{cl})\bigr|=\frac{T_0}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]

Sentence (i) sets $A_0=\infty$ after the fact and reports gain $11$
with error $1/A_0$. That estimate is wrong for this noise gain because
it omits the factor $1/\beta=11$:
$1/A_0=10^{-5}$ is not $1.099879\times 10^{-4}$. Sentence (ii) either
leaves the closed pole at the open-loop $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ or replaces
the declared one-pole loop by a three-pole Routh stability boundary,
which is the reserved three-pole Routh / feedback-stability-boundary
family.

The calculation never forms a three-pole characteristic polynomial,
never applies Routh--Hurwitz, never uses Miller's two-node shortcut,
and never accounts a cascade port resistance.

graderFixtures.proofText: DC closed gain $T_0=10.998790133$ versus ideal $11$, with fractional error $1.099879\times 10^{-4}=0.01099879\%$. The closed pole is $f_p(1+\beta A_0)=90.9190909\,\mathrm{kHz}$, the one-pole $1\%$ settling time is $8.06140483\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, and $|A_\mathrm{cl}(f_\mathrm{cl})|=T_0/\sqrt{2}$.
A0=1e5 is already infinite for engineering purposes, so the noninverting gain is exactly 11 and the fractional error is 1/A0=1e-5. I do not accept 10.998790133 or 0.01099879%.

The closed pole remains the open-loop 10 Hz pole, or else this is a three-pole Routh problem in which more feedback improves DC accuracy only up to a stability boundary. I do not use fcl=fp(1+beta A0) or ln 100/(2 pi fcl).

ELEC:010630.title: A 0.5 V/us follower with a 5 V sine has full-power bandwidth 15.915 kHz, not 1 MHz
ELEC:010630.objective: For a unity follower with 1 MHz small-signal BW, SR=0.5 V/us, and sine amplitude 5 V, compute fFP=15.91549431 kHz, compare required slopes 0.314159 V/us at 10 kHz (no slew) and 0.628319 V/us at 20 kHz (slew), find max undistorted Vp=0.795774715 V at 100 kHz, and keep the same 15.915 kHz large-signal limit when the small-signal BW is 100 kHz at gain 10.
ELEC:010630.statement:
A unity-gain follower has small-signal closed-loop bandwidth
$1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and a constant slew-rate limit
\[
\mathrm{SR}=0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}.
\]
The commanded output is the sinusoid $v(t)=V_p\sin(2\pi f t)$ with
$V_p=5\,\mathrm{V}$. Full-power bandwidth means the largest $f$ at
which the sine's peak slope still does not exceed $\mathrm{SR}$.

1. Prove that the full-power bandwidth at this amplitude is
   \[
   f_\mathrm{FP}=\frac{\mathrm{SR}}{2\pi V_p}=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}.
   \]
   In particular $f_\mathrm{FP}$ is not the small-signal $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

2. Evaluate the required peak slope $2\pi f V_p$ at $10\,\mathrm{kHz}$
   and at $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Prove
   \[
   2\pi\cdot 10^{4}\cdot 5=0.314159\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}
   \]
   (no slew) and
   \[
   2\pi\cdot 2\times 10^{4}\cdot 5=0.628319\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}
   \]
   (slew). Classify each frequency against the $0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}$
   budget.

3. At $f=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ compute the largest undistorted sine
   amplitude allowed by the same slope budget. Prove
   \[
   V_{p,\max}=\frac{\mathrm{SR}}{2\pi f}=0.795774715\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

4. The same op-amp is now closed at noise gain $10$. Its small-signal
   bandwidth becomes $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ if the unity GBW is
   $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$. Prove that a $5\,\mathrm{V}$ output sine is still
   slope-limited at $f_\mathrm{FP}=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The
   small-signal $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ number is not a large-signal
   certificate.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) "the $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ small-signal
   bandwidth is already the full-power bandwidth"; (ii) "once the
   amplifier slews, the output is exactly triangular, so the $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$
   waveform may be replaced by a triangle of amplitude $5\,\mathrm{V}$
   without a large-signal model."

Do not assert an exact triangular shape without a slew model. Do not
replace the slope budget by a three-pole Routh test, a Miller two-node
calculation, or a cascade port-resistance identity.
permittedResults: Differentiating $V_p\sin(2\pi f t)$ produces a peak value $2\pi f V_p$. Comparing that peak to $\mathrm{SR}$ is a pointwise slope test, not a small-signal Bode reading.

At fixed $\mathrm{SR}$ and fixed $V_p$, $f_\mathrm{FP}$ is independent of the small-signal closed-loop pole. At fixed $\mathrm{SR}$ and fixed $f$, the largest undistorted $V_p$ is $\mathrm{SR}/(2\pi f)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare 2 pi f Vp to SR at each requested frequency, then invert the same identity for Vp,max.
Compute fFP=SR/(2 pi Vp) once and reuse it for the gain-10 paragraph, stressing that SR does not track the small-signal pole.

milestones.criterion: Computes fFP=15.91549431 kHz and classifies the 10 kHz slope 0.314159 V/us as no slew and the 20 kHz slope 0.628319 V/us as slew.
Finds Vp,max=0.795774715 V at 100 kHz and keeps the 15.915 kHz large-signal limit at noise gain 10.
Rejects identifying fFP with small-signal BW and refuses an unmodeled triangular-output claim or reserved intake substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the 1 MHz unity small-signal bandwidth, or the 100 kHz gain-10 small-signal bandwidth, to be the full-power bandwidth at 5 V.
commonErrors.consequence: The slope-limited value 15.91549431 kHz is never produced.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the 10/20 kHz classification, computes a Vp,max other than 0.795774715 V, or asserts an exact 5 V triangular output at 20 kHz without a slew model.
commonErrors.consequence: The pointwise slope test is replaced by a wrong comparison or by an unsupported large-signal waveform.

hintTree.content: Convert $\mathrm{SR}=0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}$ to $5\times 10^5\,\mathrm{V/s}$ before dividing by $2\pi V_p$.
The $10\,\mathrm{kHz}$ slope is $\pi\times 10^5\,\mathrm{V/s}=0.314159\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}$. Double the frequency to double the slope.
At $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ invert the same identity: $V_{p,\max}=\mathrm{SR}/(2\pi f)=2.5/\pi$. Gain $10$ changes the small-signal pole, not $\mathrm{SR}$.

ELEC:010630.canonicalSolution:
The slew-rate budget is
\[
\mathrm{SR}=0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}=5\times 10^5\,\mathrm{V/s}.
\]
The peak slope of $5\sin(2\pi f t)$ equals this budget when
\[
f_\mathrm{FP}=\frac{5\times 10^5}{2\pi\cdot 5}=\frac{5\times 10^4}{\pi}
=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}.
\]
That number is nearly two orders of magnitude below the small-signal
$1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ pole.
\[
\boxed{f_\mathrm{FP}=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}}.
\]

At $10\,\mathrm{kHz}$ the required peak slope is
\[
2\pi\cdot 10^4\cdot 5=\pi\times 10^5\,\mathrm{V/s}
=0.314159\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}<0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s},
\]
so the sine stays inside the slew budget. At $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ the
required slope doubles to
\[
0.628319\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}>0.5\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s},
\]
so the stage slews.
\[
\boxed{10\,\mathrm{kHz}:\ 0.314159\text{ no slew};\ 20\,\mathrm{kHz}:\ 0.628319\text{ slew}}.
\]

At $f=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ invert the slope identity:
\[
V_{p,\max}=\frac{5\times 10^5}{2\pi\cdot 10^5}=\frac{2.5}{\pi}
=0.795774715\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
A $5\,\mathrm{V}$ command at $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ is far outside the
budget.
\[
\boxed{V_{p,\max}(100\,\mathrm{kHz})=0.795774715\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Closing the same amplifier at noise gain $10$ moves the small-signal
closed-loop pole to $\mathrm{GBW}/10=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The output
slope budget $\mathrm{SR}$ and the commanded $V_p=5\,\mathrm{V}$ are
unchanged, so the large-signal ceiling remains
$f_\mathrm{FP}=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$
figure is a linearized bandwidth, not a $5\,\mathrm{V}$ sine
certificate.

Sentence (i) identifies $f_\mathrm{FP}$ with the $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$
small-signal bandwidth and never produces $15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}$.
Sentence (ii) asserts an exact triangular $5\,\mathrm{V}$ waveform at
$20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ without a large-signal model (recovery from slew,
available current, and the linear region after the peak slope). The
present packet only classifies the slope budget; it does not claim a
triangle.

The argument never forms a Routh array, never uses Miller's two-node
shortcut, and never accounts a cascade port resistance.

graderFixtures.proofText: Full-power bandwidth at $V_p=5\,\mathrm{V}$ is $f_\mathrm{FP}=15.91549431\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The $10\,\mathrm{kHz}$ slope $0.314159\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}$ does not slew; the $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ slope $0.628319\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}$ does. At $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$, $V_{p,\max}=0.795774715\,\mathrm{V}$. Gain $10$ still slope-limits a $5\,\mathrm{V}$ output at $15.915\,\mathrm{kHz}$. No exact triangle is claimed.

The follower already has 1 MHz of small-signal bandwidth, so that is the full-power bandwidth for a 5 V sine. At gain 10 the small-signal 100 kHz pole is likewise the large-signal certificate. I do not compute SR/(2 pi Vp).

The 10 kHz sine already needs more than 0.5 V/us so it slews, while 20 kHz does not. Once it slews the output is exactly a 5 V triangle, so I replace the 20 kHz sinusoid by that triangle without a large-signal model.

ELEC:010631.title: Rf=30k and Rg=10k put an inverting Schmitt at +/-3 V with 50 percent high time on 5 sin theta
ELEC:010631.objective: For an inverting comparator with rails +/-12 V, Rf=30k from output to plus, and Rg=10k from plus to ground, compute beta=0.25, thresholds +/-3 V and width 6 V, identify the rising +3 and falling -3 trips, locate the 5 sin theta crossings at 36.869898 deg and 216.869898 deg, prove 50 percent high/low with average 0, and show +/-1 V noise about zero cannot flip the latch.
ELEC:010631.statement:
An inverting comparator is bounded by the rails $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$.
Positive feedback is a resistive divider from the output to the
noninverting pin:
\[
R_f=30\,\mathrm{k}\Omega
\quad\text{(output to plus)},\qquad
R_g=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega
\quad\text{(plus to ground)}.
\]
The signal $v_\mathrm{in}$ drives the inverting pin. The comparator
is otherwise ideal (infinite gain, instant switching, no input
current).

1. Identify the feedback fraction $\beta=R_g/(R_g+R_f)$ and the two
   thresholds $\pm\beta\cdot 12\,\mathrm{V}$. Prove
   \[
   \beta=0.25,\qquad V_\mathrm{TH}=\pm 3\,\mathrm{V},
   \]
   and that the hysteresis width is $6\,\mathrm{V}$.

2. With the output high at $+12\,\mathrm{V}$, the plus pin sits at
   $+3\,\mathrm{V}$. Prove that a rising $v_\mathrm{in}$ flips the
   output low when it crosses $+3\,\mathrm{V}$. With the output low at
   $-12\,\mathrm{V}$, prove that a falling $v_\mathrm{in}$ flips the
   output high when it crosses $-3\,\mathrm{V}$.

3. Let $v_\mathrm{in}=5\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians. Prove that
   the rising trip through $+3\,\mathrm{V}$ occurs at
   \[
   \theta=\arcsin(0.6)=0.643501109\,\mathrm{rad}=36.869898^{\circ}
   \]
   and that the falling trip through $-3\,\mathrm{V}$ occurs at
   \[
   \theta=\pi+\arcsin(0.6)=3.785093763\,\mathrm{rad}=216.869898^{\circ}.
   \]

4. Conclude that the output is high for half of each $2\pi$ period and
   low for the other half, so the duty cycle is symmetric $50\%$
   high / $50\%$ low and the average output is $0$. Then argue that a
   $\pm 1\,\mathrm{V}$ disturbance about $v_\mathrm{in}=0$ cannot cross
   either threshold and therefore cannot change the latch.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) "an inverting Schmitt with high output
   trips on a falling crossing of $-3\,\mathrm{V}$" (the trip
   directions reversed); (ii) "the thresholds are the rails
   $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$, or there is no memory, so $5\sin\theta$
   switches at every zero crossing and $\pm 1\,\mathrm{V}$ of noise
   chatters the output."

Do not replace the latch by a linear finite-gain one-pole close, a
slew-rate slope budget, or the reserved "more feedback / Routh
boundary" family.
permittedResults: For $v_\mathrm{in}=V\sin\theta$ the rising crossing of $+V_\mathrm{TH}$ on the first half-cycle is $\theta=\arcsin(V_\mathrm{TH}/V)$, and the later falling crossing of $-V_\mathrm{TH}$ is $\theta=\pi+\arcsin(V_\mathrm{TH}/V)$.
Those two angles differ by $\pi$, so a two-state $\pm V_\mathrm{sat}$ waveform that switches only there is high for half a period and low for half a period, hence has mean zero.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read beta from the divider, arm +/-3 V from the rails, then keep only the rising +3 and falling -3 roots of 5 sin theta = +/-3.
Track the latch state around one period of 5 sin theta to lock the pi-separated trips, the 50% duty, and the interior noise ball of radius 1 V.

milestones.criterion: Computes beta=0.25, thresholds +/-3 V, width 6 V, and the rising +3 / falling -3 trip law.
Locates the 5 sin theta crossings at 36.869898 deg and 216.869898 deg, proves 50% high/low with average 0, and shows +/-1 V about zero cannot flip the latch.
Rejects reversed trips, missing hysteresis, and reserved linear-opamp or Routh substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the inverting law, claiming a high output flips low on a falling crossing of -3 V, or a low output flips high on a rising crossing of +3 V.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned angle pair 36.869898 deg and 216.869898 deg, and the 50% high interval they bound, are lost.

commonErrors.description: Places the thresholds at the rails +/-12 V, or treats the stage as a memoryless comparator that switches at every zero crossing, so +/-1 V noise chatters the output.
commonErrors.consequence: The 6 V window and the noise-immunity claim about zero both fail.

hintTree.content: The divider is $\beta=10/(10+30)=1/4$, so the plus pin is $\pm 3\,\mathrm{V}$ when the output is $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$.
High output arms $+3\,\mathrm{V}$ on the plus pin; the minus pin must rise through that value to flip the comparator low.
Solve $5\sin\theta=\pm 3$ and keep the rising $+3$ root $\arcsin(0.6)$ together with the falling $-3$ root $\pi+\arcsin(0.6)$. Those roots are $\pi$ apart.

ELEC:010631.canonicalSolution:
The feedback fraction is
\[
\beta=\frac{R_g}{R_g+R_f}=\frac{10}{40}=0.25.
\]
The plus pin therefore sits at
\[
\beta\cdot(\pm 12)=\pm 3\,\mathrm{V}
\]
according to the present output rail. The hysteresis width is the
distance between those armed levels, $6\,\mathrm{V}$.
\[
\boxed{\beta=0.25,\quad V_\mathrm{TH}=\pm 3\,\mathrm{V},\quad\text{width }6\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

With the output high, the plus pin is $+3\,\mathrm{V}$. The comparator
stays high while $v_\mathrm{in}<+3\,\mathrm{V}$ and flips low when a
rising $v_\mathrm{in}$ crosses $+3\,\mathrm{V}$. With the output low,
the plus pin is $-3\,\mathrm{V}$. The comparator stays low while
$v_\mathrm{in}>-3\,\mathrm{V}$ and flips high when a falling
$v_\mathrm{in}$ crosses $-3\,\mathrm{V}$.
\[
\boxed{\text{rising }+3\text{ flips high}\to\text{low};\ \text{falling }-3\text{ flips low}\to\text{high}}.
\]

Now take $v_\mathrm{in}=5\sin\theta$. The rising $+3\,\mathrm{V}$
crossing on the first increasing half-cycle solves
$5\sin\theta=3$, so $\sin\theta=0.6$ and
\[
\theta=\arcsin(0.6)=0.643501109\,\mathrm{rad}=36.869898^{\circ}.
\]
The subsequent falling $-3\,\mathrm{V}$ crossing solves
$5\sin\theta=-3$ on the decreasing half-cycle after $\theta=\pi/2$,
which is
\[
\theta=\pi+\arcsin(0.6)=3.785093763\,\mathrm{rad}=216.869898^{\circ}.
\]
\[
\boxed{36.869898^{\circ}\text{ and }216.869898^{\circ}}.
\]

Those trip angles differ by $\pi$. Starting from a high output after
the falling $-3\,\mathrm{V}$ trip, the output remains high until the
next rising $+3\,\mathrm{V}$ trip, an interval of $\pi$ radians, and
then remains low until the next falling $-3\,\mathrm{V}$ trip, again
$\pi$ radians. The duty cycle is therefore $50\%$ high and $50\%$ low,
and the average of the $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$ waveform is $0$.

A $\pm 1\,\mathrm{V}$ disturbance about $v_\mathrm{in}=0$ remains inside
$(-1,1)\subset(-3,3)$. Neither armed threshold can be reached, so the
latch state cannot change.

Sentence (i) reverses the trip directions and would switch high-to-low
on a falling $-3\,\mathrm{V}$ crossing, destroying both the stated
switching law and the $5\sin\theta$ angle pair. Sentence (ii) either
moves the thresholds to the rails $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$ (which $5\sin\theta$
never reaches) or erases hysteresis, switching at every zero crossing
and allowing $\pm 1\,\mathrm{V}$ noise to chatter the output.

The latch is not a linear one-pole finite-gain close, not a slew-rate
full-power calculation, and not a three-pole Routh stability boundary.

graderFixtures.proofText: The divider gives $\beta=0.25$, so the thresholds are $\pm 3\,\mathrm{V}$ with width $6\,\mathrm{V}$. A high output flips low on a rising crossing of $+3\,\mathrm{V}$; a low output flips high on a falling crossing of $-3\,\mathrm{V}$. For $5\sin\theta$ those trips are $36.869898^{\circ}$ and $216.869898^{\circ}$, yielding $50\%$ high/low and average $0$. A $\pm 1\,\mathrm{V}$ disturbance about zero cannot flip the latch.

With the output high the stage trips low when vin falls through -3 V, and with the output low it trips high when vin rises through +3 V. I therefore use the opposite angle pair for 5 sin theta and I do not accept 36.869898 deg as the high-to-low trip.

The thresholds are the rails +/-12 V, or else there is no hysteresis and 5 sin theta switches at every zero crossing. In either reading a +/-1 V disturbance about zero chatters the output, and the width is not 6 V.

EMB:010117.title: Ideal 12-bit ADC over [0,3.3V] maps 2.2V to 2730, 1.65V to 2048, 3.3V to 4095; code 2730 occupies [9009/4096, 90123/40960)
EMB:010117.objective: Apply the saturating 12-bit floor quantizer q=min(4095,floor(V/Delta)) with Delta=33/40960 V, recover the three required codes, identify the half-open input bin of code 2730, and bound midpoint reconstruction error by Delta/2.
EMB:010117.statement:
An ideal uniform 12-bit analog-to-digital converter maps an analog
voltage $V$ on the closed interval $[0,3.3]$ volts onto the integer
codes $\{0,1,\ldots,4095\}$. The converter uses $4096$ equal steps of
width
\[
\Delta=\frac{3.3}{4096}=\frac{33}{40960}\ \mathrm{V}
\]
and the saturating floor rule
\[
q(V)=\min\bigl(4095,\lfloor V/\Delta\rfloor\bigr).
\]
Code $q$ therefore occupies the half-open analog bin
$[q\Delta,(q+1)\Delta)$ whenever $0\le q\le 4094$. Code $4095$
absorbs the remaining closed endpoint $V=3.3$, which would otherwise
be the fictitious code $4096$. Midpoint reconstruction of an interior
bin replaces every voltage in that bin by the bin midpoint; the
absolute reconstruction error is then at most $\Delta/2$.

1. Evaluate $q(2.2)$, $q(1.65)$, and $q(3.3)$. Show the exact
   rational arithmetic that produces each code, including the
   saturation step at full scale.

2. Identify the analog input bin of code $2730$ as a pair of
   rational voltages, written in lowest terms for the left endpoint
   and with denominator $40960$ for the right endpoint. Prove that
   midpoint reconstruction on that bin has absolute error at most
   $33/81920$ volts.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “full scale $3.3\,\mathrm{V}$ is
   exactly $4096\Delta$, so $q(3.3)=4096$”; (ii) “code $2730$
   occupies the closed interval $[2730\Delta,2731\Delta]$ and the
   worst-case error is a full step $\Delta$.”

Do not replace the specified floor quantizer by nearest-code
rounding, which would send $2.2\,\mathrm{V}$ to $2731$, and do not
treat the converter as $11$-bit.
permittedResults: An interval of length $\Delta$ reconstructed at its midpoint has uniform worst-case absolute error $\Delta/2$. Closing the right endpoint does not change the length, but it mis-assigns the next code's left edge.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert each voltage to an exact multiple of 1/Delta, take the floor, then clamp 4096 to 4095 and write the 2730 bin as consecutive multiples of Delta.
First check 1.65=2048 Delta and 3.3=4096 Delta, then recover 2.2 as 2730+22/33 steps and halve Delta for the midpoint bound.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates q(2.2)=2730, q(1.65)=2048, and the saturating full-scale code q(3.3)=4095 from Delta=33/40960.
Identifies the code-2730 bin [9009/4096, 90123/40960) and bounds midpoint error by 33/81920 V.
Rejects the fictitious code 4096 at full scale and a closed or full-step reading of the 2730 bin.

commonErrors.description: Reports q(3.3)=4096 because 3.3 is exactly 4096 Delta, or treats the converter as having 4096 as a legal output code.
commonErrors.consequence: The 12-bit range is abandoned. Full scale is no longer the saturating code 4095.

commonErrors.description: Closes the code-2730 bin on the right, writes a different pair of rationals, or bounds midpoint error by a full step Delta rather than Delta/2=33/81920.
commonErrors.consequence: The analog preimage of 2730 is not [9009/4096, 90123/40960), or the reconstruction guarantee is twice too large.

hintTree.content: $1.65=33/20$ yields $1.65/\Delta=2048$ exactly. Full scale is $3.3/\Delta=4096$, so saturation sends $q(3.3)$ to $4095$, not $4096$.

EMB:010117.canonicalSolution:
The step is $\Delta=3.3/4096=33/40960$ volts. For $V=2.2=11/5$,
\[
\frac{2.2}{\Delta}=\frac{11}{5}\cdot\frac{40960}{33}=\frac{90112}{33}.
\]
Division gives $33\cdot 2730=90090$ and remainder $22$, so
\[
\biggl\lfloor\frac{90112}{33}\biggr\rfloor=2730.
\]
The code is already in range, hence $q(2.2)=2730$. For
$V=1.65=33/20$,
\[
\frac{1.65}{\Delta}=\frac{33}{20}\cdot\frac{40960}{33}=2048,
\]
so $q(1.65)=2048$. For $V=3.3$,
\[
\frac{3.3}{\Delta}=\frac{33}{10}\cdot\frac{40960}{33}=4096,
\]
and the saturating rule yields
$q(3.3)=\min(4095,4096)=4095$.
\[
\boxed{q(2.2)=2730,\ q(1.65)=2048,\ q(3.3)=4095}.
\]

Code $2730$ is interior, so its analog bin is the half-open interval
\[
[2730\Delta,2731\Delta)
=\Bigl[\frac{2730\cdot 33}{40960},\frac{2731\cdot 33}{40960}\Bigr)
=\Bigl[\frac{90090}{40960},\frac{90123}{40960}\Bigr)
=\Bigl[\frac{9009}{4096},\frac{90123}{40960}\Bigr).
\]
Midpoint reconstruction uses $2730.5\cdot\Delta$. Every voltage in a
bin of length $\Delta$ then lies at most $\Delta/2$ from that
midpoint:
\[
\frac{\Delta}{2}=\frac{33}{81920}\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{bin }[9009/4096,90123/40960);\ \text{midpoint error }\le 33/81920}.
\]

Sentence (i) reports the fictitious code $4096$. The converter has
only $12$ bits, so the legal codes stop at $4095$ and the exact
full-scale voltage is clamped. Sentence (ii) closes the right
endpoint, which would steal the left edge of code $2731$, and

EMB:010118.title: Little-endian 30 0D encodes signed Q4 -45; A0 02 encodes 42; packed word 0x02A00D30; mean -3/2
EMB:010118.objective: Decode two little-endian halfwords as signed 12-bit Q4 samples, pack them into the 32-bit word 0x02A00D30, form the mean -3/2, and reject both an unsigned 12-bit reading and a big-endian or swapped-halfword pack.
EMB:010118.statement:
A microcontroller emits two successive $16$-bit samples on a
little-endian bus. Only the low $12$ bits of each halfword are
significant. Those $12$ bits are a two's-complement integer in
Q4 format: the signed integer $n$ represents the rational $n/16$.
The first sample arrives as the byte pair
\[
\mathtt{30}\ \mathtt{0D}
\]
in increasing address order (lowest address first). The second
sample arrives as
\[
\mathtt{A0}\ \mathtt{02}.
\]
The firmware then packs the two $16$-bit little-endian halfwords
into one $32$-bit word, first sample in the low halfword, second
sample in the high halfword.

1. Reconstruct the first $16$-bit halfword, extract the low $12$
   bits, convert that field from unsigned $0$--$4095$ to a signed
   $12$-bit integer, and apply the Q4 scale. Repeat for the second
   sample.

2. Form the packed $32$-bit word and the arithmetic mean of the two
   Q4 values.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the low $12$ bits $0xD30=3376$ are
   already the sample, so Q4 yields $3376/16=211$”; (ii) “the bus
   is most-significant-byte first, so the first sample is $0x300D$,
   or the packed word is $0x0D3002A0$.”

Do not replace the $12$-bit field by a $16$-bit signed decode of
the whole halfword, and do not treat the samples as unsigned Q4.
permittedResults: A $k$-bit two's-complement string with unsigned value $U$ represents $U-2^k$ when the sign bit is set. Here $k=12$ and $2^{12}=4096$, so $0xD30=3376$ represents $3376-4096=-720$.
Packing little-endian halfwords $h_0,h_1$ as first-in-low gives the word $h_0+2^{16}h_1$. For $h_0=0x0D30$ and $h_1=0x02A0$ this is $0x02A00D30$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Assemble each halfword low-byte first, mask 12 bits, subtract 4096 when bit 11 is set, then divide by 16 and pack first-in-low.
Check 0xD30-0x1000=-720 and 672/16=42 first, then form the 32-bit concatenation 0x02A00D30 and average.

milestones.criterion: Decodes little-endian 30 0D to signed 12-bit -720 and Q4 -45, and A0 02 to Q4 42.
Packs the halfwords as 0x02A00D30 and computes the mean -3/2.
Rejects an unsigned 12-bit Q4 reading and a big-endian or swapped-halfword pack.

commonErrors.description: Treats 0xD30=3376 as a non-negative Q4 value 211, or sign-extends the full 16-bit halfword instead of the low 12 bits.
commonErrors.consequence: The first sample is not -45 and the mean cannot be -3/2.

commonErrors.description: Reads the bytes most-significant first (0x300D / 0xA002) or packs the halfwords as 0x0D3002A0 rather than 0x02A00D30.
commonErrors.consequence: Either sample is the wrong 12-bit field, or the required packed word is lost.

hintTree.content: Bytes $30$ $0D$ are the halfword $0x0D30$. The low $12$ bits are $0xD30=3376$. The sign bit $0x800$ is set, so the signed value is $3376-4096=-720$ and Q4 yields $-45$.
Bytes $A0$ $02$ are $0x02A0$. The low $12$ bits $0x2A0=672$ are non-negative, so Q4 yields $42$.
Low halfword $0x0D30$ and high halfword $0x02A0$ pack as $0x02A00D30$. The mean is $(-45+42)/2=-3/2$.

EMB:010118.canonicalSolution:
The first byte pair is little-endian, so the halfword is
\[
\mathtt{0x30}+256\cdot\mathtt{0x0D}=\mathtt{0x0D30}.
\]
The low $12$ bits are $\mathtt{0xD30}=13\cdot 256+3\cdot 16=3376$.
Bit $11$ is set because $3376\ge 2048$, therefore the signed $12$-bit
value is
\[
3376-4096=-720.
\]
Q4 divides by $16$:
\[
-720/16=-45.
\]
The second byte pair is
\[
\mathtt{0xA0}+256\cdot\mathtt{0x02}=\mathtt{0x02A0},
\]
with low $12$ bits $\mathtt{0x2A0}=672$. This is strictly less than
$2048$, so the signed value is $+672$ and Q4 yields $672/16=42$.
\[
\boxed{0xD30\mapsto -45,\quad 0x2A0\mapsto 42}.
\]

Packing the first sample into the low halfword and the second into
the high halfword produces
\[
\mathtt{0x0D30}+2^{16}\cdot\mathtt{0x02A0}=\mathtt{0x02A00D30}.
\]
The arithmetic mean of the two Q4 values is
\[
\frac{-45+42}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{word }0x02A00D30;\ \text{mean }-3/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) skips the signed $12$-bit step. The bit pattern
$0xD30$ is a negative Q4 sample; treating $3376$ as already signed
yields $+211$, which is not $-45$. Sentence (ii) either reverses
each halfword (reading $0x300D$ and $0xA002$) or swaps the packed
halves to $0x0D3002A0$. Neither is the stated little-endian,
first-sample-low convention.

The argument never sign-extends the full $16$-bit halfword
$0x0D30=3376$ and never treats the field as unsigned Q4.

graderFixtures.proofText: Bytes $30$ $0D$ give $0x0D30$, low $12$ bits $0xD30=3376=-720$ in signed $12$-bit, Q4 $-45$. Bytes $A0$ $02$ give $0x2A0=672$ and Q4 $42$. The packed word is $0x02A00D30$ and the mean is $-3/2$. Unsigned $3376/16=211$ and the pack $0x0D3002A0$ are wrong.
The low 12 bits 0xD30 equal 3376, so the Q4 sample is 3376/16=211. I do not subtract 4096. Alternatively I sign-extend the whole 16-bit halfword 0x0D30.
The first byte is the high byte, so the first sample is 0x300D. Alternatively I pack first-sample-high and report the word 0x0D3002A0.

EMB:010219.title: Split-32 increment 0x0001FFFF to 0x00020000 can tear to 0x00010000; seqlock 10 to 11 to 12 yields only old or new
EMB:010219.objective: Exhibit the impossible torn reading 0x00010000 of a split 32-bit increment, show that a seqlock walking 10 to 11 to 12 accepts only equal even versions, and reject both treating the tear as legal and accepting an odd or unequal version.
EMB:010219.statement:
A $32$-bit monotonically increasing counter is stored as two
$16$-bit halves on a machine whose native accesses are $16$-bit.
A writer that increments the counter from
\[
\mathrm{old}=\mathtt{0x0001FFFF}
\quad\text{to}\quad
\mathrm{new}=\mathtt{0x00020000}
\]
must update the low half $\mathtt{0xFFFF}\to\mathtt{0x0000}$ and
the high half $\mathtt{0x0001}\to\mathtt{0x0002}$. Those two stores
are not atomic as a pair. A reader that loads the high half and
then the low half (or the reverse) may therefore observe a mixture
of the two sequential values. The only sequential values of the
counter on this transition are $\mathrm{old}$ and $\mathrm{new}$.

The same writer protects the pair of stores with a seqlock version
word. The version is even when the counter is stable and odd while
a write is in progress. On this transition the version walks
\[
10\ \to\ 11\ \to\ 12.
\]
A reader samples the version, then the two halves, then the version
again, and accepts the sample only when the two version reads are
equal and even.

1. Exhibit one interleaving that produces the $32$-bit reading
   $\mathtt{0x00010000}$. Prove that this bit pattern is not equal
   to $\mathrm{old}$ or $\mathrm{new}$, hence is not a sequential
   value of the counter.

2. List the accepted seqlock outcomes on the walk $10\to 11\to 12$.
   Prove that a reader who insists on equal even versions can
   obtain only $\mathrm{old}$ or $\mathrm{new}$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\mathtt{0x00010000}$ is just the
   previous high half with a cleared low half, so it is a legal
   intermediate count”; (ii) “a reader who sees version $11$ on
   either sample, or who sees $10$ then $12$, may still accept
   the payload.”

Do not replace the split counter by a software FIFO or by a
fixed-priority task set.
permittedResults: Incrementing $0x0001FFFF$ by one yields $0x00020000$ and changes both halves. Any mixed pair of halves is therefore not a sequential $32$-bit value.
While the version is odd the writer may be mid-update. Equal even versions sandwich a stable snapshot: version $10$ is the old counter, version $12$ is the new counter.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the old and new halfword pairs, mix high-old with low-new to form 0x00010000, then keep only equal even seqlock versions.
First name the two sequential 32-bit values, then argue that odd version 11 is exactly the torn window and must be dropped.

milestones.criterion: Exhibits the torn reading 0x00010000 and proves it is neither old 0x0001FFFF nor new 0x00020000.
Shows that seqlock versions 10 to 11 to 12 accept only equal even samples, hence only old or new.
Rejects treating the tear as a legal count and accepting an odd or unequal version.

commonErrors.description: Treats 0x00010000 as a legal intermediate counter value, or claims the only possible tear is 0x0002FFFF and that 0x00010000 cannot occur.
commonErrors.consequence: The required impossible-read witness is lost or is misclassified as sequential.

commonErrors.description: Accepts a payload when either version sample is 11, or when the samples are 10 then 12, dropping the equal-and-even rule.
commonErrors.consequence: A torn mixture can be published. The seqlock no longer yields only old or new.

hintTree.content: Old halves are $(\mathrm{hi},\mathrm{lo})=(0x0001,0xFFFF)$. New halves are $(0x0002,0x0000)$. Reading hi first then lo after the writer finishes yields $(0x0001,0x0000)=0x00010000$.
The other tear is $(0x0002,0xFFFF)=0x0002FFFF$. Neither tear equals old or new.
Version $10$ is even and stable at old; $11$ is odd (write in progress); $12$ is even and stable at new. Equal even pairs are only $(10,10)$ and $(12,12)$.

EMB:010219.canonicalSolution:
Write the two sequential states as halfword pairs
\[
\mathrm{old}=(h,l)=(\mathtt{0x0001},\mathtt{0xFFFF}),\qquad
\mathrm{new}=(\mathtt{0x0002},\mathtt{0x0000}).
\]
One concrete tear is: the reader loads the high half and obtains
$\mathtt{0x0001}$; the writer then commits both stores; the reader
loads the low half and obtains $\mathtt{0x0000}$. The assembled
word is
\[
\mathtt{0x00010000}.
\]
This equals neither $\mathtt{0x0001FFFF}$ nor $\mathtt{0x00020000}$.
It is therefore not a value the sequential counter ever held. (The
symmetric tear $\mathtt{0x0002FFFF}$ is likewise illegal; the
required witness is $\mathtt{0x00010000}$.)
\[
\boxed{\text{torn reading }0x00010000\text{ is not sequential}}.
\]

The seqlock version is even in a stable state and odd during the
write. The walk $10\to 11\to 12$ therefore means
\begin{align*}
\text{version }10&:\ \text{stable at }\mathrm{old},\\
\text{version }11&:\ \text{write in progress, halves may disagree},\\
\text{version }12&:\ \text{stable at }\mathrm{new}.
\end{align*}
A reader who samples the version, then the two halves, then the
version again, and who accepts only when the two version samples
are equal and even, can accept only the pairs $(10,10)$ and
$(12,12)$. The first pair yields $\mathrm{old}$; the second yields
$\mathrm{new}$. Any sample that sees $11$, or that sees $10$ then
$12$, is rejected, so a tear cannot be published.
\[
\boxed{\text{equal even versions yield only old or new}}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats the tear $\mathtt{0x00010000}$ as an
intermediate sequential count. The counter is specified to jump
from $\mathtt{0x0001FFFF}$ to $\mathtt{0x00020000}$; it never
stores $\mathtt{0x00010000}$. Sentence (ii) relaxes the accept
rule to odd or unequal versions. Version $11$ is exactly the
window in which the halves may be mixed, and $10$ then $12$ is
exactly an overlapping write.

The argument never substitutes a FIFO occupancy argument or a
fixed-priority schedule.

graderFixtures.proofText: The increment $0x0001FFFF\to 0x00020000$ can be read as $0x00010000$ by mixing the old high half with the new low half. That word is not sequential. Seqlock versions $10\to 11\to 12$ are accepted only when both samples are equal and even, so the reader obtains only old or new.
0x00010000 is just the old high half with a cleared low half, so it is a legal intermediate count. Alternatively I say the only tear is 0x0002FFFF and 0x00010000 cannot happen.
I accept the payload on version 11, or when I see 10 then 12. Equal even versions are optional. The reader may therefore publish a torn pair.

EMB:010220.title: L(C6) at t0, M(C4) at t1, H(C2) at t2 run L[0,1], M[1,2], H[2,4], M[4,7], L[7,12]; responses 12, 6, 2; nest 3
EMB:010220.objective: Trace the preemptive fixed-priority schedule of L, M, and H through the five execution intervals, compute response times 12, 6, and 2, record maximum nesting 3, and reject both a non-preemptive order and a leftover-time or finish-time response.
EMB:010220.statement:
Three tasks share a single processor under preemptive fixed
priorities $H>M>L$. Arrival times and worst-case execution times
are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{task}&L&M&H\\ \hline
C&6&4&2\\
\text{arrival}&t=0&t=1&t=2.
\end{array}
\]
A newly arrived higher-priority task preempts immediately. A
preempted task resumes with its remaining execution time and does
not restart. Response time is completion time minus arrival time.
Nesting depth at an instant is the number of tasks that have
started and not yet completed, including the running task.

1. Construct the unique execution calendar on $[0,12]$. Identify
   each occupied interval and the task that owns it.

2. Compute the three response times and the maximum nesting depth
   attained anywhere in the calendar.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “priorities are advisory, so $L$
   runs to completion on $[0,6]$ before $M$ and $H$ start”;
   (ii) “$M$ has only two units left after $t=2$, so $M$ occupies
   $[4,6]$, or response time is the completion instant itself.”

Do not replace the calendar by a seqlock argument or by a
producer-consumer FIFO.
permittedResults: Remaining time after a preemption is $C$ minus the units already executed. $M$ executes one unit on $[1,2]$, so three units remain after $H$ completes.
While $H$ runs on $[2,4]$, both $L$ and $M$ are started and incomplete, so the nesting depth is $3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Advance event by event, always running the highest arrived incomplete task, then subtract arrivals from completions.
First place H on [2,4], backfill M around that window with remaining time 3, then give L the leftover [0,1] and [7,12].

milestones.criterion: Traces the preemptive calendar L[0,1], M[1,2], H[2,4], M[4,7], L[7,12].
Computes response times 12, 6, 2 and maximum nesting 3.
Rejects a non-preemptive or wrong-priority order and a leftover-time or finish-time response.

commonErrors.description: Lets L run to completion on [0,6], or ignores H>M>L, so the five-interval calendar never appears.
commonErrors.consequence: The execution intervals and the response triple 12, 6, 2 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Resumes M with only two remaining units (M[4,6]), or reports response times as the completion instants 12, 7, 4 without subtracting arrivals.
commonErrors.consequence: Either M[4,7] and R_M=6 disappear, or the required responses 12, 6, 2 are replaced by finish times.

hintTree.content: $L$ is alone on $[0,1]$ and loses the processor at $t=1$. $M$ is then alone only until $t=2$.
$H$ occupies $[2,4]$ completely. $M$ still has $3$ units, so $M$ occupies $[4,7]$. $L$ still has $5$ units, so $L$ occupies $[7,12]$.
Responses are $12-0=12$, $7-1=6$, $4-2=2$. Nesting is $3$ throughout $[2,4]$.

EMB:010220.canonicalSolution:
At $t=0$ only $L$ is present, so $L$ runs on $[0,1]$ and consumes
one of its six units. At $t=1$ task $M$ arrives and preempts $L$.
$M$ runs on $[1,2]$ and consumes one of its four units. At $t=2$
task $H$ arrives and preempts $M$. $H$ needs two units and is
highest priority, so $H$ occupies $[2,4]$ and completes at $t=4$.
$M$ then resumes with $4-1=3$ units remaining and occupies
$[4,7]$, completing at $t=7$. $L$ resumes with $6-1=5$ units
remaining and occupies $[7,12]$, completing at $t=12$. The calendar
is therefore
\[
L[0,1],\quad M[1,2],\quad H[2,4],\quad M[4,7],\quad L[7,12].
\]
\[
\boxed{L[0,1],\ M[1,2],\ H[2,4],\ M[4,7],\ L[7,12]}.
\]

Response times are completion minus arrival:
\begin{align*}
R_L&=12-0=12,\\
R_M&=7-1=6,\\
R_H&=4-2=2.
\end{align*}
On $[2,4]$ the started-and-incomplete set is $\{L,M,H\}$, so the
nesting depth is $3$. No larger set of tasks exists, so the maximum
nesting is $3$.
\[
\boxed{R=(12,6,2);\ \text{max nesting }3}.
\]

Sentence (i) is a non-preemptive (or ignored-priority) schedule.
If $L$ ran to completion on $[0,6]$ the later intervals and the
response triple $12,6,2$ would both disappear. Sentence (ii)
either forgets that $M$ has three remaining units after one
consumed unit, finishing $M$ at $t=6$ instead of $t=7$, or reports
response times as the raw completion instants $12,7,4$. Either
mistake misses $R_M=6$ or the interval $M[4,7]$.

The argument never appeals to a seqlock version word and never
counts FIFO occupancy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Preemptive priorities $H>M>L$ produce $L[0,1]$, $M[1,2]$, $H[2,4]$, $M[4,7]$, $L[7,12]$. Responses are $12$, $6$, $2$. Maximum nesting is $3$ on $[2,4]$. A non-preemptive $L[0,6]$ run, leftover $M[4,6]$, and finish-time responses $12,7,4$ are all wrong.
Priorities are only advisory, so L runs to completion on [0,6] before M and H start. The calendar is L[0,6], M[6,10], H[10,12].
M has only two units left after t=2, so M occupies [4,6]. Alternatively I report response times as the finish instants 12, 7, 4 and never subtract arrivals.
