EMB:010221.title: FIFO cap 4, produce at 3k, consume at 5k, producer first on ties; first overflow at t=30 with 10 attempts, 9 successes, 6 consumed, occupancy 3
EMB:010221.objective: Simulate the capacity-4 FIFO under period-3 production and period-5 consumption with producer-first ties through the first overflow at t=30, report the four required counters, and reject both a consumer-first tie break and a timeline that stops without the t=30 consume.
EMB:010221.statement:
A single FIFO has capacity $4$. Occupancy starts at $0$ at time
$t=0$. A producer attempts an enqueue at every positive multiple
of $3$, i.e. at
\[
t=3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27,30,\ldots.
\]
A consumer attempts a dequeue at every positive multiple of $5$,
i.e. at
\[
t=5,10,15,20,25,30,\ldots.
\]
At a shared instant the producer is serviced first. An enqueue
into a full FIFO is an overflow: the attempt is counted, the write
is rejected, and occupancy does not increase. A dequeue from a
non-empty FIFO succeeds and decreases occupancy by one. Events at
the same integer time are otherwise instantaneous.

1. Trace occupancy through $t=30$. Identify the first overflow
   instant. Count producer attempts, successful enqueues, and
   successful dequeues on the closed interval $(0,30]$, and state
   the occupancy immediately after the $t=30$ consumer.

2. Compare the long-run attempt rates $1/3$ and $1/5$, and explain
   why the inequality forces an overflow at some finite time even
   without computing the first instant.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “on a tie the consumer should go
   first, so $t=30$ is still safe”; (ii) “overflow at $t=30$ ends
   the trace with occupancy $4$ and only five consumptions,
   because the consumer never runs after a rejected enqueue.”

Do not replace the occupancy trace by a seqlock version argument
or by a three-task priority calendar.
permittedResults: If $r_p>r_c$, the cumulative excess of offered enqueues over possible dequeues grows without bound. Because actual FIFO occupancy is capped by its finite capacity, some enqueue attempt must therefore be rejected after finite time.

On $(0,30]$ there are $\lfloor 30/3\rfloor=10$ producer attempts and $\lfloor 30/5\rfloor=6$ consumer attempts. Producer-first at $t=30$ with occupancy $4$ rejects the tenth enqueue and then admits the sixth dequeue.

acceptableStrategies.description: Walk every multiple of 3 or 5, service the producer first on ties, and keep a running occupancy through the t=30 consume.
Count 10 producer and 6 consumer attempts on (0,30] first, then fill the occupancy table only far enough to see the tenth enqueue hit a full buffer.

milestones.criterion: Traces producer-first occupancy to the first overflow at t=30 with 10 attempts, 9 successes, 6 consumed, and occupancy 3.
Uses 1/3>1/5 to conclude that a finite overflow is forced independently of the explicit first instant.
Rejects a consumer-first tie break and a trace that stops at the rejected enqueue without the t=30 consume.

commonErrors.description: Services the consumer before the producer at t=15 and t=30, so t=30 does not overflow and the four counters are not 10, 9, 6, 3.
commonErrors.consequence: The first overflow moves later and the required t=30 witness disappears.

commonErrors.description: Treats the rejected enqueue at t=30 as the end of the trace, reporting occupancy 4 and only five consumptions, or claims the finite buffer plus the rates never overflow.
commonErrors.consequence: The sixth consume and final occupancy 3 are lost, or the 1/3>1/5 forcing argument is denied.

hintTree.content: Occupancy after the non-tie events is $1,0,1,2,1,2$ at $t=3,5,6,9,10,12$. The first tie $t=15$ is produce-then-consume: $2\to 3\to 2$.
Continuing: $t=18\to 3$, $20\to 2$, $21\to 3$, $24\to 4$, $25\to 3$, $27\to 4$. At $t=30$ the producer faces occupancy $4$.
The tenth enqueue overflows; the $t=30$ consumer then leaves occupancy $3$. Rates $1/3>1/5$ already force some finite overflow.

EMB:010221.canonicalSolution:
Start at occupancy $0$. The discrete events through the first
overflow are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
t&\text{event}&\text{occupancy after}\\ \hline
3&\text{produce}&1\\
5&\text{consume}&0\\
6&\text{produce}&1\\
9&\text{produce}&2\\
10&\text{consume}&1\\
12&\text{produce}&2\\
15&\text{produce then consume}&3\text{ then }2\\
18&\text{produce}&3\\
20&\text{consume}&2\\
21&\text{produce}&3\\
24&\text{produce}&4\\
25&\text{consume}&3\\
27&\text{produce}&4\\
30&\text{produce (overflow) then consume}&4\text{ then }3.
\end{array}
\]
The first overflow is at $t=30$, when the producer faces a full

\[
\boxed{\text{overflow }t=30;\ 10\text{ attempts},\ 9\text{ ok},\ 6\text{ consumed},\ \mathrm{occ}=3}.
\]

The long-run attempt rates are $1/3$ and $1/5$. Because
\[
\frac13>\frac15,
\]
successful enqueues outpace dequeues whenever the buffer is not

and an overflow occurs. The explicit trace only identifies the

Sentence (i) reverses the tie break. With consumer-first service,

EMB:010322.title: 16-bit counter 65530 plus delay 20 wraps to target 14; elapsed 11,19,20; naive now>=14 fires now
EMB:010322.objective: Form the wrapping 16-bit deadline 14 from start 65530 and delay 20, compute modular elapsed 11, 19, and 20 at now 5, 13, and 14, justify the signed half-range due test, and reject the naive comparison now>=14.
EMB:010322.statement:
A free-running hardware counter is an unsigned $16$-bit register
that increments once per tick and wraps
\[
0,1,2,\ldots,65535,0,1,\ldots
\]
so all arithmetic on counter values is in $\mathbb{Z}/65536\mathbb{Z}$.
A one-shot software delay is armed at
\[
\mathit{start}=65530
\]
for a duration of
\[
\mathit{delay}=20
\]
ticks. The architectural deadline is the unique residue
\[
\mathit{target}=(\mathit{start}+\mathit{delay})\bmod 65536.
\]
At a later sample $\mathit{now}$, the modular elapsed time is
\[
e(\mathit{now})=(\mathit{now}-\mathit{start})\bmod 65536,
\]
and the delay is due exactly when $e(\mathit{now})\ge 20$. Samples
of interest are $\mathit{now}=5$, $\mathit{now}=13$, and
$\mathit{now}=14$.

Because $20<2^{15}=32768$, a signed half-range test is valid on
this instance: if $s$ denotes interpretation of a $16$-bit string
as a two's-complement integer in $[-32768,32767]$, then
\[
s\bigl((\mathit{now}-\mathit{target})\bmod 65536\bigr)\ge 0
\]
if and only if the delay is due, provided every sample occurs
while the true signed difference $\mathit{now}-\mathit{target}$
still lies in $[-32768,32767]$. There is no
wider signed test in this problem; the hardware counter itself
remains unsigned.

1. Compute $\mathit{target}$. Then evaluate $e(5)$, $e(13)$, and
   $e(14)$, and decide at each sample whether the delay is due.

2. Evaluate the signed half-range predicate at the same three
   samples and at the arming instant $\mathit{now}=65530$. Prove
   that the predicate agrees with $e(\mathit{now})\ge 20$ on this
   instance, and name the half-range hypothesis that makes the
   agreement legal.

3. Audit the sentence: “the deadline is the integer $14$, so the
   software may fire as soon as $\mathit{now}\ge 14$.” Also audit
   the companion mistake of reporting $65530+20=65550$ as a
   $16$-bit target, or of computing $5-65530$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ and
   calling the elapsed time negative.

Do not replace the wrap-safe delay by a PWM duty cycle, a capture
compare waveform, or a real-time scheduling admission test.
permittedResults: For $a,b\in\{0,\ldots,2^{16}-1\}$, the residue $(a-b)\bmod 2^{16}$ equals $a-b$ if $a\ge b$ and equals $a-b+2^{16}$ if $a<b$.
If $0\le e<2^{15}$ then the signed $16$-bit reading of $e$ is $e$ itself. If the remaining time $r$ satisfies $0<r\le 2^{15}$, the signed reading of $(-r)\bmod 2^{16}$ is $-r$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce start+delay modulo 65536 first, then evaluate (now-start) mod 65536 at the three samples before discussing the signed reading.
Compute remaining time 20,9,1,0 as a signed 16-bit quantity and only afterwards name the equivalent modular elapsed values.

milestones.criterion: Computes target 14 and the modular elapsed values 11, 19, and 20, marking due only at now=14.
Justifies the signed half-range due test from delay=20<32768 and shows it is false at 65530, 5, and 13 and true at 14.
Rejects the naive comparison now>=14, an unwrapped target 65550, and a negative elapsed computed in Z.

commonErrors.description: Treats the deadline as the integer comparison now>=14, which is already true at the arming value 65530, or otherwise ignores wrap when asking whether the delay has expired.
commonErrors.consequence: The one-shot fires immediately and never waits the required 20 ticks.

commonErrors.description: Reports the target 65550 as a 16-bit deadline, or computes elapsed times in Z so that now=5 yields a negative duration rather than 11.
commonErrors.consequence: The deadline is not a 16-bit residue and the required triple 11,19,20 never appears.

hintTree.content: $(65530+20)\bmod 65536=65550-65536=14$. The deadline is the residue $14$, not the integer $65550$.
At arming, $65530\ge 14$ is already true, so a naive $\mathit{now}\ge 14$ test fires immediately. The signed reading of $(65530-14)\bmod 65536=65516$ is $65516-65536=-20<0$.

EMB:010322.canonicalSolution:
The deadline is the residue of the ordinary sum:
\[
65530+20=65550=1\cdot 65536+14,
\]
hence
\[
\mathit{target}=(65530+20)\bmod 65536=14.
\]
Elapsed times use the same modulus. Because each listed sample is
numerically smaller than $\mathit{start}$, the subtraction in
$\mathbb{Z}$ is negative and one must add $65536$:
\begin{align*}
e(5)&=(5-65530)\bmod 65536=-65525+65536=11,\\
e(13)&=(13-65530)\bmod 65536=-65517+65536=19,\\
e(14)&=(14-65530)\bmod 65536=-65516+65536=20.
\end{align*}
The delay is due exactly when $e(\mathit{now})\ge 20$, so it is
not due at $\mathit{now}=5$ or $\mathit{now}=13$ and it becomes
due at $\mathit{now}=14$.
\[
\boxed{\mathit{target}=14;\ e(5)=11,\ e(13)=19,\ e(14)=20\text{ due}}.
\]

Write $s$ for signed $16$-bit interpretation. The three elapsed
values $11$, $19$, and $20$ all lie in $[0,32767]$, so $s$ of the
elapsed string equals the elapsed integer, and $s(e(\mathit{now}))\ge 20$
agrees with the unsigned test. Equivalently, the remaining times
at the four listed instants are $20$, $9$, $1$, and $0$, so every
true difference $\mathit{now}-\mathit{target}$ lies in the signed
range $[-32768,32767]$:
\begin{align*}
s((65530-14)\bmod 65536)&=s(65516)=-20<0,\\
s((5-14)\bmod 65536)&=s(65527)=-9<0,\\
s((13-14)\bmod 65536)&=s(65535)=-1<0,\\
s((14-14)\bmod 65536)&=s(0)=0.
\end{align*}
The half-range hypothesis used here is $0<\mathit{delay}=20<32768$
together with the stated guarantee that each sampled true difference
$\mathit{now}-\mathit{target}$ remains between $-32768$ and $32767$ ticks.
Under that hypothesis the signed predicate is valid, and it first
becomes true at $\mathit{now}=14$.
\[
\boxed{\text{signed half-range test valid; first true at }14}.
\]

The sentence “fire as soon as $\mathit{now}\ge 14$” compares two
unsigned residues as if they were integers on a line that does not
wrap. At the arming instant one already has $65530\ge 14$, so the
naive test fires immediately and the $20$-tick delay is discarded.
Reporting $65550$ as the target leaves the $16$-bit register
altogether. Computing $5-65530=-65525$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ and calling
that the elapsed time is the same wrap omission: the hardware
counter cannot hold a negative tick count.

The argument never introduces a PWM compare waveform and never
performs a processor-utilization or deadline-monotonic admission
test.

graderFixtures.proofText: $(65530+20)\bmod 65536=14$. Modular elapsed values are $e(5)=11$, $e(13)=19$, $e(14)=20$ (due). The signed half-range test is valid because $20<32768$ and first holds at $14$. The comparison $\mathit{now}\ge 14$ is already true at $65530$ and fires immediately.
The deadline is the integer 14, so I fire as soon as now>=14. At the arming instant now is already 65530, which is greater than 14, so the delay is due immediately.
65530+20=65550 is the target, and I never reduce modulo 65536. At now=5 the elapsed time is 5-65530=-65525, a negative integer, so I never report 11, 19, or 20.

EMB:010323.title: 10 MHz into exact-average 3 kHz uses 3333,3333,3334 with phase -1/3,-2/3,0 and 10000 clocks per 3 ticks
EMB:010323.objective: Realize an exact-average 3 kHz tick from a 10 MHz input by the cycle-count pattern 3333,3333,3334, record interval errors -1/3,-1/3,+2/3 and cumulative phase -1/3,-2/3,0, and reject any constant divider.
EMB:010323.statement:
A timer is clocked at a stable
\[
f_{\mathrm{in}}=10\,\mathrm{MHz}=10^{7}\,\mathrm{Hz}
\]
and must emit a software tick whose long-run average frequency is
exactly
\[
f_{\mathrm{out}}=3\,\mathrm{kHz}=3\cdot 10^{3}\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]
The ideal inter-tick interval, measured in input clocks, is the
ratio
\[
\frac{f_{\mathrm{in}}}{f_{\mathrm{out}}}=\frac{10^{7}}{3\cdot 10^{3}}=\frac{10000}{3}=3333+\frac{1}{3}.
\]
A hardware reload register can hold only an integer number of
input clocks, so a constant divider cannot hit $3\,\mathrm{kHz}$
exactly. The firmware instead uses a three-step cycle-count
pattern
\[
n_0=3333,\qquad n_1=3333,\qquad n_2=3334
\]
and then repeats. Interval $i$ lasts exactly $n_i$ input clocks.
The interval error and the cumulative phase after interval $i$
are
\begin{align*}
\varepsilon_i&=n_i-\frac{10000}{3},\\
\phi_{-1}&=0,\qquad
\phi_i=\phi_{i-1}+\varepsilon_i=\sum_{k=0}^{i}\varepsilon_k,
\end{align*}
measured in input clocks. The pattern is required to close: after
one period of three ticks the cumulative phase must return to $0$
and the number of consumed input clocks must be an integer.

1. Prove that the pattern $3333,3333,3334$ has exact long-run
   average $3\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Record the three interval errors
   $\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2$ and the three
   cumulative phases $\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2$.

2. Count the input clocks consumed by one period of three ticks.
   Prove that this count is exactly $10000$, and deduce that
   every later period is an exact time-shift of the first.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “reload $3333$ on every tick; the
   average is close enough”; (ii) “reload $3334$ on every tick,
   or use the single compromise $3333.3$ as if the hardware
   accepted a tenth of a clock.”

Do not replace the divider by a $16$-bit wrap deadline, a capture
waveform, or a processor-utilization test.
permittedResults: Three positive integers average to $10000/3$ if and only if they sum to $10000$. Equivalently, their errors against $10000/3$ sum to $0$.
A periodic phase that returns to $0$ after $p$ steps produces an exact average frequency $p\cdot f_{\mathrm{in}}/N$ whenever $N$ input clocks are consumed in those $p$ steps.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the three reloads to 10000 first, then subtract 10000/3 from each reload to read the errors and their running sum.
Translate exact 3 kHz into 3 ticks per millisecond at 10 MHz, hence 10000 clocks, and partition 10000 as 3333+3333+3334.

milestones.criterion: States the cycle-count pattern 3333,3333,3334 and the interval errors -1/3,-1/3,+2/3.
Records cumulative phase -1/3,-2/3,0 and the exact 10000 input clocks per 3 ticks that make the average 3 kHz.
Rejects a constant integer divider and a non-integral reload that the hardware cannot store.

commonErrors.description: Uses a constant reload 3333 or 3334, or pretends the timer can be programmed with 3333.3 clocks, and claims the long-run frequency is already exact.
commonErrors.consequence: The average is not 3 kHz, and the required three-step error triple never appears.

commonErrors.description: Reports interval errors other than (-1/3,-1/3,+2/3), or a cumulative phase that is not (-1/3,-2/3,0), or a three-tick clock count other than 10000.
commonErrors.consequence: The pattern is not shown to be exact-average, and later periods would accumulate phase.

hintTree.content: $3333+3333+3334=10000$. Three ticks in $10000$ input clocks at $10\,\mathrm{MHz}$ are exactly $3\,\mathrm{kHz}$.
A constant $3333$ consumes $9999$ clocks per three ticks and runs fast by one input clock every three ticks. A constant $3334$ runs slow by two clocks every three ticks.

EMB:010323.canonicalSolution:
The three reloads sum to
\[
3333+3333+3334=10000.
\]
Their mean is therefore $10000/3$, which is exactly the ideal
interval. Against that ideal the interval errors are
\begin{align*}
\varepsilon_0&=3333-\frac{10000}{3}=\frac{9999-10000}{3}=-\frac{1}{3},\\
\varepsilon_1&=3333-\frac{10000}{3}=-\frac{1}{3},\\
\varepsilon_2&=3334-\frac{10000}{3}=\frac{10002-10000}{3}=+\frac{2}{3}.
\end{align*}
The cumulative phases are the running sums
\begin{align*}
\phi_0&=-\frac{1}{3},\\
\phi_1&=-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=-\frac{2}{3},\\
\phi_2&=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=0.
\end{align*}
The pattern closes: after three ticks the phase residual is
identically $0$.
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon=(-1/3,-1/3,+2/3);\ \phi=(-1/3,-2/3,0)}.
\]

One period therefore consumes exactly $10000$ input clocks and
emits exactly $3$ ticks. The corresponding duration is
\[
\frac{10000}{10^{7}}\,\mathrm{s}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s},
\]
so the three ticks occupy one millisecond and the average
frequency is $3000\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Every later period is the same
triple of reloads, hence the same $10000$-clock block, so the
average remains exact for every complete period and the phase
never accumulates from period to period.
\[
\boxed{10000\text{ input clocks per }3\text{ ticks}}.
\]

Sentence (i) installs the constant divider $3333$. Three such
reloads consume $9999$ input clocks, one clock short of $10000$,
and the long-run frequency is $10^{7}\cdot 3/9999\neq 3000$.
Sentence (ii) is the opposite constant, $3334$, whose three-tick
block is $10002$ clocks and is likewise off, or else a
non-integral reload $3333.3$ that the integer timer cannot
store. Neither constant pattern produces the required error
triple or a vanishing third phase.

The argument never forms a wrap-around software deadline and
never computes a CPU utilization bound.

graderFixtures.proofText: The reloads $3333,3333,3334$ sum to $10000$ input clocks per $3$ ticks, hence exact-average $3\,\mathrm{kHz}$ from $10\,\mathrm{MHz}$. Interval errors are $-1/3,-1/3,+2/3$ and cumulative phase is $-1/3,-2/3,0$. A constant $3333$ or $3334$ divider is not exact.
I reload 3333 on every tick (or 3334, or the non-integral 3333.3). The average is close enough to 3 kHz and I never form the three-step pattern.
I keep a varying pattern but I report errors +1/3,+1/3,-2/3 or a cumulative phase that ends at 1, and I count 9999 or 10002 input clocks in three ticks.

EMB:010424.title: UART 8N1 at 115200 carries 11520 B/s; a 68-byte frame is 680 bits in 17/2880 s, 100 pkt/s uses 85/144, max 169
EMB:010424.objective: Count 10 bits per UART 8N1 byte at 115200 baud, time a 2+64+2 byte frame, obtain utilization 85/144 at 100 packet/s, and reject both a 9-bit frame and a non-integral 170 packet/s ceiling.
EMB:010424.statement:
An asynchronous serial link is configured as UART $8\mathrm{N}1$
at
\[
R=115200\text{ baud},
\]
meaning $115200$ line symbols per second and one symbol per bit.
Each data byte is framed as
\[
1\text{ start bit}+8\text{ data bits}+0\text{ parity bits}+1\text{ stop bit}=10\text{ bits}.
\]
There is no idle gap beyond the stop bit in the calculations
below: adjacent bytes on the wire are back-to-back. A firmware
datagram is laid out as
\[
2\text{ header bytes}+64\text{ payload bytes}+2\text{ CRC bytes}=68\text{ bytes}
\]
and is transmitted as $68$ consecutive UART characters.

1. Prove that the link carries exactly $11520$ data bytes per
   second when it is fully occupied. Then count the on-wire bits
   of one datagram and the exact transmission time of one
   datagram, in seconds, as a reduced rational.

2. A periodic sender emits $100$ datagrams per second, still
   with no inter-byte gap inside a datagram and with whatever
   idle line remains between datagrams. Compute the line
   utilization as a reduced rational. Then compute the largest
   integer $N$ such that $N$ whole datagrams can be sent
   back-to-back in one second.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$8\mathrm{N}1$ is eight data bits
   and one stop, so a byte is $9$ line bits, or else only the
   $64$-byte payload occupies the wire”; (ii) “the maximum rate
   is $115200/680\approx 169.41$, so $170$ whole packets fit in
   a second.” If utilization is first written as $68000/115200$,
   reduce that equivalent fraction to $85/144$ as requested.

Do not replace the UART accounting by a CAN arbitration trace or
by a sliding-window ARQ argument.
permittedResults: A fully occupied $8\mathrm{N}1$ link at baud $R$ delivers $R/10$ data bytes per second, because each byte consumes exactly ten line bits.
For positive integers $a,b$, the largest integer $N$ with $N\cdot a\le b$ is $\lfloor b/a\rfloor$. A non-integral quotient does not license rounding up.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert baud to a 10-bit character rate, multiply 68 by 10, then form the two rationals 680/115200 and 100*680/115200 and reduce.
Check 169*680=114920<=115200<115600=170*680 first, then recover the reduced time and utilization from the same 680-bit frame.

milestones.criterion: Counts 10 bits per 8N1 byte, 11520 B/s, 680 on-wire bits, and time 17/2880 s for the 68-byte datagram.
Computes utilization 85/144 at 100 packet/s and the largest whole back-to-back rate 169 packet/s.
Rejects a 9-bit character or payload-only bit count, and rejects rounding the max rate up to 170.

commonErrors.description: Frames an 8N1 byte as 9 line bits, or times only the 64-byte payload, so the datagram is not 680 bits and the byte rate is not 11520 B/s.
commonErrors.consequence: The required time 17/2880 s and utilization 85/144 cannot appear.

commonErrors.description: Reports a maximum whole rate of 170 packet/s from the fractional quotient 169.41, rather than taking the floor to obtain 169.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed whole-packet rate overfills the one-second bit budget.

hintTree.content: $115200/10=11520$ bytes per second. One datagram is $68\cdot 10=680$ bits.
$680/115200=17/2880$ seconds. One hundred datagrams use $68000/115200=85/144$ of the line.

EMB:010424.canonicalSolution:
Each UART character is $10$ line bits, so a saturated link
delivers
\[
\frac{115200}{10}=11520
\]
data bytes per second. One datagram is $2+64+2=68$ bytes and
therefore
\[
68\cdot 10=680
\]
line bits. Its transmission time is
\[
\frac{680}{115200}=\frac{17}{2880}\,\mathrm{s},
\]
where the reduction is division by $40$.
\[
\boxed{10\text{ bits/byte},\ 11520\,\mathrm{B/s},\ 680\text{ bits},\ 17/2880\,\mathrm{s}}.
\]

One hundred datagrams per second occupy
\[
100\cdot 680=68000
\]
line bits per second, hence utilization
\[
\frac{68000}{115200}=\frac{85}{144}.
\]
The largest integer number of whole back-to-back datagrams in
one second is
\[
\biggl\lfloor\frac{115200}{680}\biggr\rfloor
=\biggl\lfloor\frac{2880}{17}\biggr\rfloor
=\lfloor 169+7/17\rfloor=169,
\]
which is legal because $169\cdot 680=114920\le 115200$, while
$170\cdot 680=115600>115200$.
\[
\boxed{\text{utilization }85/144;\ \text{max whole rate }169}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the start bit, leaving a $9$-bit character
and a byte rate $12800$, or else times only the $64$-byte
payload and reports $640$ bits. Either choice destroys both
$17/2880$ and $85/144$. Sentence (ii) rounds the quotient
$169.41$ up to $170$, which overfills the second. The fraction
$68000/115200$ is mathematically the same utilization as $85/144$;
it is merely not reduced to the requested form.

The argument never inspects a multi-master arbitration field
and never discusses sequence-number windows.

graderFixtures.proofText: UART $8\mathrm{N}1$ is $10$ bits/byte, hence $11520\,\mathrm{B/s}$. The $68$-byte datagram is $680$ bits and lasts $17/2880\,\mathrm{s}$. At $100$ packet/s the utilization is $85/144$. The largest whole back-to-back rate is $169$ packet/s, since $170\cdot 680>115200$.
8N1 is eight data bits plus one stop, so a byte is 9 line bits, or I time only the 64-byte payload. I never obtain 680 bits or 11520 B/s.
115200/680 is about 169.41, so I round up and claim that 170 whole packets fit in a second, even though 170*680 exceeds 115200.

EMB:010425.title: Dominant-zero arbitration of 1011000 vs 1010000 differs at bit 4: bus 0, A loses, B wins with 1010000
EMB:010425.objective: Run bitwise dominant-zero arbitration on IDs A=1011000 and B=1010000, identify the first difference at the fourth bit, conclude that B wins with result 1010000, and reject a recessive-one or wrong-bit comparison.
EMB:010425.statement:
Two nodes share an abstract wired bus on which
\[
0\text{ is dominant and }1\text{ is recessive}.
\]
If any node drives $0$ during a bit slot, every node reads $0$.
A node that transmitted $1$ and reads $0$ has lost arbitration
and must stop driving for the remainder of the field. Nodes that
have not lost continue. The identifier that remains on the bus
is the identifier of the unique winner (the bus is assumed
collision-free once a single node remains).

Node $A$ and node $B$ begin simultaneously with the $7$-bit
identifiers, most-significant bit first,
\[
A=1011000,\qquad B=1010000.
\]
Bit positions are numbered $1$ through $7$ in transmission
order, so bit $1$ is the leading $1$ of each identifier.

1. Write the seven bit slots. Identify the first position at
   which $A$ and $B$ differ, the bit each node transmits there,
   and the bit that appears on the bus. Decide who loses and
   who wins.

2. State the $7$-bit string that remains on the bus after
   arbitration. Prove that it equals $B$'s identifier, and that
   $A$ is silent for every later slot.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$1$ is dominant, so $A$'s $1$ in
   the first differing slot wins and the result is $1011000$”;
   (ii) “the first difference is some other bit (the leading
   bit, the last bit, or a $0$-based index that points at a
   position where $A$ and $B$ still agree), so the loser is
   undecided or both nodes continue.”

Do not replace the abstract dominant-zero field by UART bit
accounting or by a sliding-window sequence-number argument.
permittedResults: Under dominant-zero arbitration the winner is the identifier that is numerically smallest when the bits are read as an unsigned integer transmitted MSB first. Equivalently, at the first differing bit the winner is the node that transmitted $0$.
After a node loses it contributes neither $0$ nor $1$ to later slots, so the remaining bus string equals the winner's identifier.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the two 7-bit strings in transmission order, walk until the first mismatch, and apply wired AND at that slot.
Treat dominant-zero arbitration as unsigned MSB-first minimum: 1010000<1011000, then confirm the fourth-bit witness.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the first difference at the fourth bit as A=1, B=0 with bus 0.
Concludes that A loses, B wins, and the bus result is 1010000.
Rejects a dominant-one rule that awards the bus to A, and a first-difference claimed at a bit where the IDs still agree.

commonErrors.description: Treats 1 as dominant, so A's 1 in the first differing slot wins and the reported bus result is 1011000.
commonErrors.consequence: The winner is reversed and the required result 1010000 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the first difference is the leading bit, the last bit, or another index at which A and B still agree, so the loser is not identified from A=1 versus B=0 at bit 4.
commonErrors.consequence: Arbitration is undecided or is decided by a bit that is not the first mismatch.

hintTree.content: The first three bits are $1,0,1$ on both IDs. The fourth bits are $A{:}1$ and $B{:}0$.
Dominant zero makes the fourth slot $0$. $A$ transmitted $1$ and therefore loses. $B$ continues and the bus holds $1010000$.
If $1$ were dominant, $A$ would win. The last bits are both $0$ and cannot decide the contest.

EMB:010425.canonicalSolution:
Transmission order, MSB first, is
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
\text{slot}&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
A&1&0&1&1&0&0&0\\
B&1&0&1&0&0&0&0\\
\text{bus}&1&0&1&0&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots
\end{array}
\]
Slots $1$--$3$ agree. The first difference is slot $4$: $A$
drives $1$ and $B$ drives $0$. Dominant zero forces the bus to
$0$. Node $A$ transmitted $1$ and samples $0$, so $A$ loses and
releases the bus. Node $B$ transmitted $0$ and samples $0$, so
$B$ continues as the unique remaining driver.
\[
\boxed{\text{first difference bit }4;\ A{=}1,\ B{=}0;\ \text{bus }0;\ A\text{ loses}}.
\]

From slot $5$ onward only $B$ drives, and $B$'s remaining bits
are $000$. The completed bus string is therefore
\[
1010000,
\]
which is exactly $B$'s identifier. $A$ drives nothing after the
loss, so $A$ cannot change any later slot.
\[
\boxed{B\text{ wins};\ \text{result }1010000}.
\]

Sentence (i) inverts the dominance rule. If $1$ were dominant
the fourth slot would be $1$, $B$ would lose, and the result
would be $A$'s identifier $1011000$. That is a different bus.
Sentence (ii) mis-identifies the first differing position. The
leading bits are equal, the trailing bits are equal, and any
index that still points at a $1$, $0$, or $1$ prefix has not
yet reached the decision bit. Without the fourth-bit witness
the loser is not determined.

The argument never counts UART start and stop bits and never
introduces sequence numbers.

graderFixtures.proofText: IDs $A=1011000$ and $B=1010000$ first differ at the fourth bit, $A{=}1$ and $B{=}0$. Dominant zero puts $0$ on the bus, so $A$ loses and $B$ wins with result $1010000$. A dominant-one rule would award $A$. A last-bit or leading-bit comparison is not the first difference.
1 is dominant on this bus, so A's 1 in the first differing slot wins. The result on the wire is 1011000 and B loses.
I compare the leading bits (both 1) or the last bits (both 0), or I use a 0-based index that still sits in the shared 101 prefix. I never name the fourth-bit pair A=1, B=0.

EMB:010426.title: Selective-repeat with 3-bit sequence numbers needs W<=4; W=5 makes the next window {5,6,7,0,1} overlap delayed 0,1
EMB:010426.objective: Prove that 3-bit selective-repeat requires W<=4 from N>=2W, exhibit the W=5 overlap of the next receive window {5,6,7,0,1} with delayed 0 and 1, and reject the go-back-N bound W<=7.
EMB:010426.statement:
A selective-repeat ARQ uses $3$-bit sequence numbers, so the
sequence-number space has cardinality
\[
N=2^{3}=8
\]
and the identifiers are the residues
\[
\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}=\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}.
\]
The sender window and the receiver window each have the same
width $W$. Under the declared bounded-lifetime model, a frame
(or its acknowledgment) may be delayed long enough to arrive
after the window has advanced, but not long enough for its
sequence number to be reused twice; stale frames from the
immediately previous occupancy of a sequence number are the
only ghosts that must be rejected. In that model the exact
safety condition is
\[
N\ge 2W,
\]
equivalently $W\le N/2$. Equality is permitted.

1. Specialize the bound to $N=8$ and state the largest safe
   $W$. Then consider the unsafe width $W=5$. After the
   receiver has accepted the initial window
   $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ in order, write the next receive window
   and prove that it contains both $0$ and $1$.

2. Explain why a delayed copy of the old frame $0$ or the old
   frame $1$ cannot be distinguished from a new legitimate
   frame once that next window is open. Conclude that $W=5$
   is unsafe, and that $N\ge 2W$ is exact (both necessary and
   sufficient) under the declared model.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “selective-repeat obeys the
   go-back-N rule $W\le N-1$, so $W=5$ is legal because
   $5\le 7$”; (ii) “$0$ and $1$ already arrived, so they
   cannot appear in a later window, and $\{5,6,7,0,1\}$ does
   not overlap the old frames.”

Do not replace the window-bound argument by UART bit
accounting or by a dominant-zero arbitration trace.
permittedResults: If the receiver just accepted $\{i,i+1,\ldots,i+W-1\}$ (residues mod $N$) in order, the next window is $\{i+W,\ldots,i+2W-1\}\bmod N$. This set meets $\{i,\ldots,i+W-1\}$ if and only if $2W>N$.
Go-back-N uses a receive window of width $1$ and may take a send window as large as $N-1$. That bound is not the selective-repeat bound.

acceptableStrategies.description: Specialize N>=2W to W<=4, then slide a width-5 window from {0,1,2,3,4} to {5,6,7,0,1} and inspect the intersection.
Contrast the safe W=4 partition {0,1,2,3} vs {4,5,6,7} with the W=5 wrap, then dismiss the go-back-N bound as a different receive-window width.

milestones.criterion: Derives W<=4 from N=8 and N>=2W, and writes the next receive window {5,6,7,0,1} after the initial window 0..4.
Shows that delayed old frames 0 and 1 overlap that next window, so W=5 is unsafe and N>=2W is exact under the declared model.
Rejects the go-back-N rule W<=N-1 and the claim that already-received 0 and 1 cannot occupy a later window.

commonErrors.description: Applies the go-back-N bound W<=N-1=7 and concludes that W=5 is safe for selective-repeat.
commonErrors.consequence: The half-modulus condition is discarded and the required overlap witness is never treated as fatal.

commonErrors.description: Claims that because 0 and 1 were already received they cannot appear in a later window, so {5,6,7,0,1} is treated as disjoint from the old frames.
commonErrors.consequence: The delayed-ghost ambiguity is denied and W=5 is incorrectly certified.

hintTree.content: $N=8$ forces $W\le 4$. The unsafe probe is $W=5$, which already violates $8\ge 10$.
After $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ the next receive window is $\{5,6,7,0,1\}$. It contains the old numbers $0$ and $1$.
Go-back-N would allow $W=7$, but that protocol has receive window $1$ and is not this problem.

EMB:010426.canonicalSolution:
The specialized bound is
\[
8\ge 2W\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad W\le 4.
\]
The largest safe window is therefore $W=4$, and $W=5$ is already
over the line because $2\cdot 5=10>8$. After the receiver
accepts the initial window $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ in order, the next
window is the next $W=5$ residues:
\[
\{5,6,7,8\bmod 8,9\bmod 8\}=\{5,6,7,0,1\}.
\]
It contains both $0$ and $1$.
\[
\boxed{W\le 4;\ \text{next window }\{5,6,7,0,1\}}.
\]

A delayed copy of the old frame $0$ (respectively $1$) still
carries sequence number $0$ (respectively $1$). Once the next
window is open those numbers are again legal receive numbers, so
the receiver must accept the ghost as if it were the new frame
$0$ or $1$ of the wrapped generation. That is precisely the
overlap forbidden by $N\ge 2W$. The same counting is tight:
when $W=4$ the next window after $\{0,1,2,3\}$ is $\{4,5,6,7\}$,
which is disjoint from $\{0,1,2,3\}$, so every still-legal ghost
falls outside the new window. Thus $N\ge 2W$ is necessary and
sufficient under the declared bounded-lifetime model, and
equality $N=2W$ is allowed.
\[
\boxed{W=5\text{ unsafe: delayed }0,1\text{ overlap};\ N\ge 2W\text{ exact}}.
\]

Sentence (i) quotes the go-back-N send-window bound $W\le N-1$.
That bound assumes a receive window of width $1$ and does not
apply to selective-repeat. Under that wrong rule $W=5$ would
look legal, and the overlap $\{5,6,7,0,1\}\cap\{0,1\}\neq\emptyset$
would be ignored. Sentence (ii) claims that a number, once
received, can never re-enter a later window. Sequence numbers
are residues modulo $8$; after a wrap they are reused, which is
exactly why the delayed old $0$ and $1$ become ambiguous.

The argument never counts UART framing bits and never compares
dominant and recessive identifiers.

graderFixtures.proofText: Selective-repeat with $N=8$ requires $W\le 4$ because $N\ge 2W$ is exact under the declared bounded-lifetime model. For $W=5$, after $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ the next receive window is $\{5,6,7,0,1\}$, which overlaps delayed old $0$ and $1$. The go-back-N bound $W\le 7$ is a different protocol.
Selective-repeat uses the go-back-N rule W<=N-1, so W=5 is legal because 5<=7. I never impose N>=2W.
0 and 1 already arrived, so they cannot appear in a later window. The set {5,6,7,0,1} does not overlap the old frames and W=5 is safe.

EMB:010527.title: A u8,u32,u16 record pads to offsets 0,4,8 and size 12; reordering to u32,u16,u8 yields 0,4,6 and size 8, saving 400 B over 100 records
EMB:010527.objective: Place a three-field C record under alignof 1/4/2, prove the original offsets 0,4,8 and size 12, prove the reordered offsets 0,4,6 and size 8, and reject both a packed no-pad layout and a missing tail-pad that cannot save 400 B over 100 records.
EMB:010527.statement:
A C compiler for a 32-bit little-endian microcontroller places
each field of a structure at the smallest offset that is a multiple
of that field's alignment, then rounds the whole structure size up
to a multiple of the structure alignment (the maximum field
alignment). No packed attribute is in force. The three scalar types
have
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{type}&\mathtt{uint8\_t}&\mathtt{uint32\_t}&\mathtt{uint16\_t}\\ \hline
\text{size (B)}&1&4&2\\
\text{alignment}&1&4&2.
\end{array}
\]
The original record is declared in source order
\[
\texttt{struct Rec \{ uint8\_t a; uint32\_t b; uint16\_t c; \}}.
\]
A proposed rewrite keeps the same three fields and only changes
declaration order to
\[
\texttt{struct Rec2 \{ uint32\_t b; uint16\_t c; uint8\_t a; \}}.
\]
A table of $100$ consecutive records of one type is stored in
internal SRAM. Padding bytes are not reused for any other object.

1. Compute the offset of each field of $\mathtt{Rec}$ and the
   $\mathtt{sizeof}$ of $\mathtt{Rec}$. Show the internal pad after
   $\mathtt{a}$ and the tail pad after $\mathtt{c}$. Prove that the
   structure alignment is $4$ and that the size is therefore $12$.

2. Repeat the placement for $\mathtt{Rec2}$. Prove that the field
   offsets are $0,4,6$ and that the size is $8$. Deduce the SRAM
   saved by storing $100$ records of $\mathtt{Rec2}$ instead of
   $100$ records of $\mathtt{Rec}$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “C packs scalars back-to-back, so
   $\mathtt{Rec}$ has offsets $0,1,5$ and size $7$ (or $8$)”;
   (ii) “the last field already ends at offset $10$ (or $7$), so
   there is no tail pad and one hundred records save something
   other than $400$ bytes.”

Do not replace the layout by a cache-line or DMA-burst argument,
and do not invoke a bit-field or packed-attribute ABI.
permittedResults: If every field offset and the structure size are multiples of the corresponding alignments, every array element remains correctly aligned. Rounding $\mathrm{sizeof}$ up to a multiple of $A$ is exactly what makes the next element's offset a multiple of $A$.
Reordering fields never changes any field's size or alignment, but it can shrink both internal padding and the tail pad. SRAM saved by $N$ records is $N$ times the per-record size difference.

acceptableStrategies.description: Walk each field to the next aligned offset, then round the used end up to the structure alignment, and multiply the size gap by 100.
First compute sizeof from max alignment, then confirm the reorder removes the three-byte hole after the u8 and shrinks the tail pad from 2 to 1.

milestones.criterion: Places Rec at offsets 0,4,8 with sizeof 12, naming the 3-byte internal pad and the 2-byte tail pad.
Places Rec2 at offsets 0,4,6 with sizeof 8 and computes a 400 B saving over 100 records.
Rejects a packed no-pad layout and a missing-tail-pad size that cannot save 400 B.

commonErrors.description: Places Rec back-to-back at offsets 0,1,5 (size 7 or 8), ignoring the 4-byte alignment of the u32.
commonErrors.consequence: The original record is no longer size 12, so the required 400 B comparison cannot arise.

commonErrors.description: Stops at the last field byte and reports sizeof(Rec)=10 or sizeof(Rec2)=7, or computes a 100-record saving other than 400 B.
commonErrors.consequence: Array elements are no longer 4-aligned, and the SRAM figure is not 400 B.

hintTree.content: In $\mathtt{Rec}$, $\mathtt{a}$ sits at $0$. The next multiple of $4$ after offset $1$ is $4$, so three pad bytes precede $\mathtt{b}$. Then $\mathtt{c}$ sits at $8$.

The last byte of $\mathtt{Rec}$ used by a field is offset $9$. Rounding $10$ up to a multiple of $4$ yields size $12$, so two tail-pad bytes exist. In $\mathtt{Rec2}$ the used end is $7$, which rounds to $8$.
One hundred copies save $100\cdot(12-8)=400$ bytes. A no-pad packing, or a size-$10$ / size-$7$ reading that drops the tail pad, cannot produce that figure.

EMB:010527.canonicalSolution:
Place $\mathtt{Rec}$ from offset $0$. The field $\mathtt{a}$ has
alignment $1$, so it occupies offset $0$ and ends at $1$. The field
$\mathtt{b}$ has alignment $4$; the least $o\ge 1$ with
$o\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ is $o=4$. Offsets $1,2,3$ are internal padding.
Then $\mathtt{b}$ occupies $[4,8)$ and $\mathtt{c}$ (alignment $2$)
may sit at $8$. The last field ends at $10$. The structure
alignment is $\max\{1,4,2\}=4$, so
\[
\mathrm{sizeof}(\mathtt{Rec})=4\bigl\lceil 10/4\bigr\rceil=12.
\]
Offsets $10$ and $11$ are tail padding. Every later array element
therefore starts at a multiple of $4$.
\[
\boxed{\mathtt{Rec}\text{ offsets }0,4,8;\ \mathrm{sizeof}=12}.
\]

Place $\mathtt{Rec2}$ from offset $0$. The field $\mathtt{b}$ occupies
$[0,4)$. The field $\mathtt{c}$ has alignment $2$ and sits at $4$,
occupying $[4,6)$. The field $\mathtt{a}$ has alignment $1$ and sits
at $6$, occupying $[6,7)$. The used end is $7$, and
\[
\mathrm{sizeof}(\mathtt{Rec2})=4\bigl\lceil 7/4\bigr\rceil=8.
\]
Offset $7$ is the single tail-pad byte. The offsets are $0,4,6$.
One hundred records then occupy $1200$ bytes as $\mathtt{Rec}$ and
$800$ bytes as $\mathtt{Rec2}$, so the SRAM saved is
\[
100\cdot(12-8)=400\text{ B}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathtt{Rec2}\text{ offsets }0,4,6;\ \mathrm{sizeof}=8;\ \text{save }400\text{ B}}.
\]

Sentence (i) discards natural alignment. Offsets $0,1,5$ would be
legal only under a packed attribute that this ABI does not grant.
That layout is not $\mathtt{Rec}$, and its size is not $12$.
Sentence (ii) stops at the last field byte and omits the mandated
round-up. A size-$10$ $\mathtt{Rec}$ (or a size-$7$ $\mathtt{Rec2}$)
would make an array element start at an offset not divisible by $4$,
and $100\cdot(10-7)=300$ or $100\cdot(10-8)=200$ is not the required
$400$ B saving.

The argument never invokes a cache line, a DMA burst, a bit-field,
or a packed attribute.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\mathtt{Rec}$ has offsets $0,4,8$ and size $12$ (pad $3$ after $\mathtt{a}$, tail pad $2$). $\mathtt{Rec2}$ has offsets $0,4,6$ and size $8$. One hundred records save $400$ B. Packed offsets $0,1,5$ and a size-$10$ or size-$7$ reading are not this ABI.
C packs the three scalars back-to-back, so Rec has offsets 0,1,5 and size 7. I never insert the three pad bytes before the u32.
The last field of Rec ends at offset 10, so sizeof is 10; Rec2 ends at 7, so sizeof is 7. One hundred records therefore save 300 B, not 400 B.

EMB:010528.title: Deepest stack is 32+48+16 plus 64 plus 40 = 200 B; from 0x20001000 the SP is 0x20000F38, a 256 B region leaves 56 B, and a 32 B reserve leaves 24 B
EMB:010528.objective: Sum the deepest foreground frames with a nested low then high ISR, prove the 200 B watermark and SP 0x20000F38 from top 0x20001000, and reject both an omitted nested ISR and a reserve that does not leave 24 B.
EMB:010528.statement:
A Cortex-M style microcontroller grows the Main stack downward
from the exclusive top address
\[
\mathit{SP}_{\mathrm{top}}=\mathtt{0x20001000}.
\]
The allocated stack region is $256$ bytes, occupying
$[\mathtt{0x20000F00},\mathtt{0x20001000})$. A context is live when
its frame has been pushed and has not yet been popped. The deepest
foreground call chain that can be preempted consists of three
frames of
\[
32\,\mathrm{B},\qquad 48\,\mathrm{B},\qquad 16\,\mathrm{B}
\]
from outermost to innermost. A low-priority ISR may preempt any
foreground context and pushes a $64$-byte exception frame. A
high-priority ISR may nest on that low-priority ISR and pushes a
$40$-byte exception frame. No other ISR can nest further. The
hardware does not switch stacks on exception entry. After the
worst-case watermark is known, the integrator requires a $32$-byte
emergency reserve that must remain unused by the watermark.

1. Compute the deepest foreground occupancy, then add the two
   exception frames in nesting order. Prove that the worst-case
   live stack is $200$ bytes. Deduce the remaining margin inside
   the $256$-byte region.

2. From $\mathit{SP}_{\mathrm{top}}=\mathtt{0x20001000}$, compute
   the stack pointer after that $200$-byte push. Prove that the
   address is $\mathtt{0x20000F38}$. Then apply the $32$-byte
   reserve to the remaining margin and state how many bytes are
   still free.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the high-priority ISR cannot nest,
   so the watermark is only $32+48+16+64=160$ bytes and the SP
   is $\mathtt{0x20000F60}$”; (ii) “the stack grows upward from
   $\mathtt{0x20001000}$, or the $32$-byte reserve is already
   included in the $200$, so $56$ bytes remain after the reserve.”

Do not replace the watermark by a heap-fragmentation or MPU-region
argument, and do not introduce a process swap to a PSP.
permittedResults: If frames of sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_k$ are simultaneously live, the occupancy is $\sum n_i$ and the pointer is $\mathit{SP}_{\mathrm{top}}-\sum n_i$, independently of push order.
A reserve of $r$ bytes that must stay unused by the watermark leaves $(\text{region size})-(\text{watermark})-r$ free, not $(\text{region size})-(\text{watermark})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Add frames in live-nesting order, subtract the total from the exclusive top, then take the reserve from the remaining margin.
First convert 200 to 0xC8 and check 0x1000-0xC8=0xF38, then audit the two ways of dropping either the 40 B nest or the 32 B reserve.

milestones.criterion: Sums 32+48+16+64+40 to a 200 B watermark and a 56 B margin in the 256 B region.
Computes deepest SP 0x20000F38 from top 0x20001000 and leaves 24 B after the 32 B reserve.
Rejects an omitted nested high ISR and a reserve or growth-direction error that leaves 56 B or the wrong SP.

commonErrors.description: Treats the high-priority ISR as unable to nest, so the watermark is only 32+48+16+64=160 B and the SP is 0x20000F60.
commonErrors.consequence: The worst-case live occupancy and the required pointer 0x20000F38 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Grows the stack upward from 0x20001000, or reports the post-reserve remainder as the pre-reserve margin 56 B.
commonErrors.consequence: The deepest pointer is not 0x20000F38, or the leftover after the 32 B reserve is not 24 B.

hintTree.content: Foreground $32+48+16=96$. Adding the low ISR gives $160$. The nested high ISR adds $40$, for $200$.
$\mathtt{0x20001000}-200=\mathtt{0x20001000}-\mathtt{0xC8}=\mathtt{0x20000F38}$. The $256$-byte region then has $56$ bytes left.
The $32$-byte reserve is taken from that $56$, leaving $24$. Omitting the $40$-byte nest, or treating $56$ as already post-reserve, misses both figures.

EMB:010528.canonicalSolution:
The three foreground frames are simultaneously live at the
preemption instant, so the foreground occupancy is
\[
32+48+16=96\,\mathrm{B}.
\]
The low-priority ISR may preempt that chain and pushes $64$ bytes,
producing $96+64=160$ bytes live. The high-priority ISR may nest
on that still-live low-priority frame and pushes $40$ more bytes.
The worst-case watermark is therefore
\[
96+64+40=200\,\mathrm{B}.
\]
The allocated region is $256$ bytes, so the unused margin is
$256-200=56$ bytes.
\[
\boxed{\text{watermark }200\,\mathrm{B},\ \text{margin }56\,\mathrm{B}}.
\]

The stack grows downward from the exclusive top. After a $200$-byte
push,
\[
\mathtt{0x20001000}-200=\mathtt{0x20001000}-\mathtt{0xC8}=\mathtt{0x20000F38}.
\]
That address lies $0xC8$ bytes below the top and $0x38$ bytes above
the region base $\mathtt{0x20000F00}$, matching the $56$-byte margin
($0x38=56$). The required $32$-byte reserve is unused stack, not
part of the $200$-byte watermark, so the still-free remainder is
\[
56-32=24\,\mathrm{B}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathit{SP}=\mathtt{0x20000F38};\ \text{after reserve }24\,\mathrm{B}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the nested high-priority frame. The resulting
$160$-byte watermark would leave $\mathit{SP}=\mathtt{0x20000F60}$
and a $96$-byte margin, which is not the specified nesting. Sentence
(ii) either grows the stack toward $\mathtt{0x200010C8}$ (the wrong
direction on this core) or treats the $32$-byte reserve as already
folded into the $200$, leaving the pre-reserve margin $56$ instead
of $24$.

The argument never fragments a heap, never programs an MPU region,
and never switches to a process stack pointer.

graderFixtures.proofText: Foreground $32+48+16=96$, plus low ISR $64$ and nested high ISR $40$, is $200$ B. From $0x20001000$ the deepest $\mathit{SP}$ is $0x20000F38$. The $256$ B region leaves $56$ B, and a $32$ B reserve leaves $24$ B. Omitting the nest or growing upward is not this core.
The high-priority ISR cannot nest on the low ISR, so the watermark is 32+48+16+64=160 B and the SP from 0x20001000 is 0x20000F60.
The stack grows upward, so the deepest pointer is 0x200010C8. Alternatively the 32 B reserve is already inside the 200 B, so 56 B still remain.

EMB:010529.title: One update a minute on 16 pages of endurance 1000 lasts 1000 min unleveled, 16000 min = 100/9 days leveled, and 14000 min = 175/18 days with two reserved pages
EMB:010529.objective: Convert single-page, perfectly leveled, and two-page-reserved flash lifetimes at one update per minute into 1000, 16000, and 14000 minutes and into 100/9 and 175/18 days, and reject both a 24-hour day conversion and a reserved-page bonus.
EMB:010529.statement:
A parameter block is stored in a small NOR-style flash of
\[
N=16
\]
erase pages. Each page survives at most
\[
E=1000
\]
erase/program cycles and then is retired. The application writes a
new parameter image once per minute and each image occupies exactly
one page. A page must be erased before it is rewritten. The clock
is a $24$-hour day, so one day is $1440$ minutes.

Three policies are compared.

- Single-page: every update erases and programs the same page.
- Perfect leveling: each update uses a still-living page of
  currently least cycle count, and all $16$ pages are in the pool.
- Reserved-page leveling: two pages are held out of the pool as
  factory spares and are never cycled; the remaining fourteen
  pages are perfectly leveled.

No read-disturb, no partial-page write, and no journal overhead
are present. Lifetimes are the minutes until the first in-pool
page would be asked to exceed $E$ cycles.

1. Compute the single-page lifetime in minutes. Then compute the
   perfectly leveled lifetime in minutes and in days, expressed
   as a reduced fraction of a day.

2. Compute the reserved-page lifetime in minutes and in days,
   again as a reduced fraction. Explain why holding two pages
   out of the pool shortens, rather than lengthens, the time
   until the first exhaustion.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$16000$ minutes is $16000/24$ hours
   counted as days, or $11$ days after dropping the fraction”;
   (ii) “reserved pages are extra endurance, so the pool has
   $18$ pages and lasts $18000$ minutes.”

Do not replace the wear model by a file-system journal or by an
ECC-correction-limit argument.
permittedResults: At a constant update rate of one page per minute, lifetime in days is $(\text{minutes})/1440$. The reduced form of $16000/1440$ is $100/9$ and of $14000/1440$ is $175/18$.
With perfect leveling the $pE$ updates are necessary and sufficient: after $pE$ updates every in-pool page has seen exactly $E$ cycles.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply in-pool page count by endurance, then divide by 1440 and reduce the fraction.
Compare the three pool sizes 1, 16, and 14 first, then audit the 24-hour mis-conversion and the 18-page bonus.

milestones.criterion: Computes 1000 min unleveled and 16000 min = 100/9 days under perfect leveling of all 16 pages.
Computes 14000 min = 175/18 days when two pages are reserved out of the pool.
Rejects a minutes-as-hours day conversion and a reserved-page bonus that enlarges the pool to 18.

commonErrors.description: Converts 16000 minutes by dividing by 24, or reports 11 days instead of the reduced fraction 100/9.
commonErrors.consequence: The leveled lifetime in days is not 100/9, so the reserved-page comparison 175/18 cannot be checked either.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two reserved pages as additional cycling capacity, so the pool has 18 pages and lasts 18000 minutes.
commonErrors.consequence: The reserved-page policy is inverted: lifetime grows instead of shrinking to 14000 minutes.

hintTree.content: Single-page uses $p=1$, so the lifetime is $1000$ minutes. Perfect leveling uses $p=16$, so $16\cdot 1000=16000$ minutes.
Dividing minutes by $24$ treats minutes as hours. Adding the two reserved pages into the pool invents $18$ pages that the policy does not cycle.

EMB:010529.canonicalSolution:
Under the single-page policy every update hits the same page.
That page reaches $E=1000$ cycles after $1000$ updates, hence after
$1000$ minutes. Perfect leveling spreads the same updates across
all $N=16$ pages. The pool budget is
\[
16\cdot 1000=16000
\]
updates, hence $16000$ minutes. Converting with a $1440$-minute day,
\[
\frac{16000}{1440}=\frac{1600}{144}=\frac{400}{36}=\frac{100}{9}
\]
days.
\[
\boxed{1000\text{ min unleveled};\ 16000\text{ min}=100/9\text{ days leveled}}.
\]

With two pages reserved the active pool has $16-2=14$ pages, so
the budget is
\[
14\cdot 1000=14000
\]
minutes. As a fraction of a day,
\[
\frac{14000}{1440}=\frac{1400}{144}=\frac{350}{36}=\frac{175}{18}
\]
days. The reserved pages are not cycled, so they contribute $0$
updates to the budget. Holding them out therefore shortens the
time until the first in-pool page is exhausted, from $16000$ to
$14000$ minutes. They would lengthen life only under a different
policy that brought them into the pool after a failure, which is
not the policy stated here.
\[
\boxed{14000\text{ min}=175/18\text{ days with }2\text{ reserved}}.
\]

Sentence (i) divides minutes by $24$, as if each minute were an
hour, or else rounds $100/9$ down to the integer $11$. Neither
equals $100/9$. Sentence (ii) treats the two reserved pages as
additional cycling pages, inventing a pool of $18$ and a lifetime
of $18000$ minutes. Under the stated policy those two pages are
absent from the pool, not added to it.

The argument never introduces a journal, a wear-leveling tree, or
an ECC correction limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: Single-page lifetime $1000$ min. Perfect leveling of $16$ pages lasts $16000$ min $=100/9$ days. Two reserved pages leave a $14$-page pool of $14000$ min $=175/18$ days. Dividing minutes by $24$, or adding reserved pages into the pool, is a different policy.
16000 minutes is 16000/24 = 666.7 days, or I drop the fraction and report 11 days instead of 100/9.
Reserved pages are extra endurance, so the device has 18 cycling pages and lasts 18000 minutes rather than 14000.

EMB:010630.title: Guarded two-door opens and closes preserve not(L&&R) by induction on {00,10,01}; non-atomic simultaneous opens from 00 reach 11
EMB:010630.objective: Prove by induction that guarded opens and closes keep the reachable set {00,10,01} and the invariant not(L&&R), and reject both a claim that 11 is reachable under the guards and a claim that simultaneous independent opens from 00 cannot produce 11.
EMB:010630.statement:
A two-door airlock is modelled by Boolean variables $L$ and $R$,
each $1$ when that door is open and $0$ when it is closed. Write a
state as the bit pair $LR$. The safety invariant is
\[
I:\quad \lnot(L\land R).
\]
The intended controller exposes four guarded commands, evaluated
against the current state and executed atomically:
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{openL}&:\ \textbf{if }R=0\textbf{ then }L\leftarrow 1,\\
\mathrm{openR}&:\ \textbf{if }L=0\textbf{ then }R\leftarrow 1,\\
\mathrm{closeL}&:\ L\leftarrow 0,\\
\mathrm{closeR}&:\ R\leftarrow 0.
\end{align*}
The system starts at $00$. A command whose guard fails is a no-op.

A proposed firmware defect implements $\mathrm{openL}$ and
$\mathrm{openR}$ as two independent check-then-write actions in the
same evaluation cycle. Both guards are evaluated against the same
\emph{pre-cycle} values of $L$ and $R$, and both passing writes commit.

1. Starting from $00$, enumerate every state reachable by a finite
   sequence of the four guarded commands. Prove that the reachable
   set is exactly $\{00,10,01\}$.

2. Prove $I$ by induction on guarded executions. Then exhibit one
   buggy simultaneous pair of independent opens from $00$ that
   reaches $11$, and confirm that $11$ falsifies $I$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$11$ is reachable under the guards,
   because one can open $L$ and then open $R$”; (ii) “even the
   non-atomic simultaneous pair cannot reach $11$, because one
   action must observe the sibling's committed post-state before
   evaluating its own guard.”

Do not replace the interlock by a watchdog, CRC, or lockstep-core
argument, and do not encode the doors as a continuous hybrid
automaton.
permittedResults: If $I$ holds, at most one of $L,R$ is $1$. A guarded open of the closed door is then enabled only when the other door is already $0$, so the post-state still satisfies $I$.
A pair of writes that both commit against the same pre-state $(0,0)$ produces $(1,1)$ regardless of any intended sequential order.

acceptableStrategies.description: Draw the three-state guarded graph, then check I on each edge, then evaluate both non-atomic check-then-write actions against the same pre-state 00.
First prove I by cases on which command fires, then use unreachability of 11 as the contrast that makes the race visible.

milestones.criterion: Enumerates the guarded reachable set as exactly {00,10,01}.
Proves not(L&&R) by induction on guarded commands and exhibits the buggy 00-to-11 simultaneous open.
Rejects a guarded path to 11 and a denial of the simultaneous independent-open race.

commonErrors.description: Claims that 11 is reachable by a guarded openL followed by a guarded openR, and includes 11 in the reachable set.
commonErrors.consequence: The inductive invariant not(L&&R) is abandoned and the guarded controller is treated as already unsafe.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that simultaneous check-then-write opens from 00 cannot produce 11, usually by serializing them through each other's post-state.
commonErrors.consequence: The firmware defect is declared impossible and the required 00-to-11 witness disappears.

hintTree.content: From $00$ the guarded opens reach $10$ and $01$. From $10$, $\mathrm{openR}$ is disabled and $\mathrm{closeL}$ returns to $00$. The symmetric statement holds at $01$.
Inductive step: a close can only clear a bit; a guarded open is enabled only when the opposite bit is already $0$. Neither produces $11$.
The buggy pair from $00$ lets both writes see the pre-state $00$ and commit, reaching $11$. That state is not in the guarded reachable set.

EMB:010630.canonicalSolution:
Begin at $00$. The enabled guarded commands and their successors
are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{state}&\mathrm{openL}&\mathrm{openR}&\mathrm{closeL}&\mathrm{closeR}\\ \hline
00&10&01&00&00\\
10&10&10&00&10\\
01&01&01&01&00
\end{array}
\]
No guarded command leaves $\{00,10,01\}$. Every state in that set
is reached in at most one step from $00$. Therefore the reachable
set is exactly $\{00,10,01\}$.
\[
\boxed{\text{reachable }\{00,10,01\}}.
\]

Invariant $I$ holds at $00$. Suppose $I$ holds at a reachable
state $s$. A close clears a bit and cannot establish $L\land R$.
A guarded $\mathrm{openL}$ fires only when $R=0$, so the post-state
has $R=0$ and $I$ holds; symmetrically for $\mathrm{openR}$. A
disabled open is a no-op and preserves $I$. By induction every
guarded execution satisfies $I$, and $11$ (which falsifies $I$) is
unreachable under the guards.

Now evaluate the two independent check-then-write opens in one cycle
from $00$. Each action checks the pre-cycle pair $(L,R)=(0,0)$:
$\mathrm{openL}$ sees $R=0$ and sets $L\leftarrow 1$;
$\mathrm{openR}$ sees $L=0$ and sets $R\leftarrow 1$. Both commits
produce $11$, and $1\land 1$ falsifies $I$.
\[
\boxed{I\text{ inductive under guards; buggy pair }00\Rightarrow 11}.
\]

Sentence (i) assumes that $\mathrm{openR}$ is enabled at $10$. The
guard $L=0$ fails there, so the second open is a no-op and $11$ is
not produced. Sentence (ii) pretends that the two writes are
serialized through each other's post-state. The defect is that they
sample the same pre-cycle $00$ and both commit, which is exactly
the transition to $11$.

The argument never invokes a watchdog, a CRC, a lockstep pair, or
a hybrid continuous model.

graderFixtures.proofText: Guarded commands reach exactly $\{00,10,01\}$ and preserve $\lnot(L\land R)$ by induction: a guarded open is enabled only when the opposite door is closed. Non-atomic simultaneous check-then-write opens from $00$ both sample $00$ and commit to $11$. A guarded path to $11$, or a denial of that race, is false.
From 00 I open L to reach 10, then I open R, so 11 is reachable under the guards and belongs in the reachable set.
Even if both opens are issued together, the second write sees the first door already open and refuses. Simultaneous independent opens from 00 cannot reach 11.

EMB:010631.title: Monitor OK-1->SUSPECT-1->SAFE, a match 0 resets SUSPECT, SAFE is absorbing with output 0; input 0,1,0,1,1 yields OK,SUSPECT,OK,SUSPECT,SAFE
EMB:010631.objective: Trace the two-mismatch monitor on 0,1,0,1,1 to OK,SUSPECT,OK,SUSPECT,SAFE, prove that only two consecutive mismatches enter SAFE, and reject both a first-mismatch trip and a non-absorbing SAFE or missing reset.
EMB:010631.statement:
A dual-channel comparison monitor has three control states
\[
\mathrm{OK},\qquad \mathrm{SUSPECT},\qquad \mathrm{SAFE}.
\]
Each sample is a bit $b\in\{0,1\}$, where $b=0$ is a match of the
two channels and $b=1$ is a mismatch. The transition rule is
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{OK}&\xrightarrow{\,1\,}\mathrm{SUSPECT},\\
\mathrm{SUSPECT}&\xrightarrow{\,1\,}\mathrm{SAFE},\\
\mathrm{SUSPECT}&\xrightarrow{\,0\,}\mathrm{OK},\\
\mathrm{OK}&\xrightarrow{\,0\,}\mathrm{OK},
\end{align*}
and $\mathrm{SAFE}$ is absorbing: both $0$ and $1$ leave the state
in $\mathrm{SAFE}$. The monitor output is $1$ in $\mathrm{OK}$ and
in $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$, and $0$ in $\mathrm{SAFE}$. The machine
starts in $\mathrm{OK}$. Isolated mismatches are required not to
trip the output; any two consecutive mismatches must trip on the
second sample.

1. Execute the five-sample input
   \[
   0,1,0,1,1
   \]
   from $\mathrm{OK}$. Record the state after each sample. Prove
   that the state sequence is
   \[
   \mathrm{OK},\ \mathrm{SUSPECT},\ \mathrm{OK},\ \mathrm{SUSPECT},\ \mathrm{SAFE}
   \]
   and that the output becomes $0$ only on the last sample.

2. Prove that an isolated mismatch (a $1$ whose neighbours are $0$,
   or a leading $1$ followed by $0$) never enters $\mathrm{SAFE}$,
   and that every occurrence of the consecutive pair $1,1$ enters
   $\mathrm{SAFE}$ on the second $1$. Confirm that once
   $\mathrm{SAFE}$ is entered, no later sample restores a nonzero
   output.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “a single mismatch already trips, so
   the second sample of $0,1,0,1,1$ is already $\mathrm{SAFE}$”;
   (ii) “a later match leaves $\mathrm{SAFE}$, or a match does not
   reset $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$, so the given sequence cannot be
   $\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{SAFE}$.”

Do not replace the monitor by a two-door interlock or by a CRC /
watchdog argument.
permittedResults: From $\mathrm{OK}$, a word matching $10$ returns to $\mathrm{OK}$ without visiting $\mathrm{SAFE}$. From $\mathrm{OK}$ or $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$, the word $11$ ends in $\mathrm{SAFE}$.
An absorbing state with output $0$ makes every extension of a tripped word also trip.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fill a five-row state table, then classify every 10 walk as a reset and every 11 walk as a trip.
First argue hysteresis: one 1 only raises suspicion, a following 0 clears it, a following 1 cuts the output, then confirm on the given word.

milestones.criterion: Traces 0,1,0,1,1 from OK to the post-sample states OK,SUSPECT,OK,SUSPECT,SAFE.
Proves isolated mismatches never enter SAFE, that 11 trips on the second 1, and that SAFE is absorbing with output 0.
Rejects a first-mismatch trip and a missing reset or non-absorbing SAFE that cannot produce the required sequence.

commonErrors.description: Enters SAFE on the first 1, so isolated mismatches trip and the second sample of 0,1,0,1,1 is already SAFE.
commonErrors.consequence: The required sequence is lost and the monitor no longer waits for two consecutive mismatches.

commonErrors.description: Lets a later match leave SAFE, or does not reset SUSPECT to OK on a match, so the third sample of 0,1,0,1,1 is not OK.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the cut-off is reversible or the required OK after the isolated mismatch never appears.

hintTree.content: Start in $\mathrm{OK}$. The first $0$ stays in $\mathrm{OK}$. The next $1$ enters $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$. The following $0$ resets to $\mathrm{OK}$.
The fourth sample $1$ returns to $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$. The fifth sample $1$ is the second consecutive mismatch and enters $\mathrm{SAFE}$.
A first-sample trip would already be in $\mathrm{SAFE}$ after the second bit. A missing reset would stay in $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$ after the third bit and skip the required $\mathrm{OK}$.

EMB:010631.canonicalSolution:
Start in $\mathrm{OK}$. The five samples update the state as
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
i&\text{input}&\text{state after}&\text{output}\\ \hline
1&0&\mathrm{OK}&1\\
2&1&\mathrm{SUSPECT}&1\\
3&0&\mathrm{OK}&1\\
4&1&\mathrm{SUSPECT}&1\\
5&1&\mathrm{SAFE}&0.
\end{array}
\]
The recorded state sequence is therefore
\[
\mathrm{OK},\ \mathrm{SUSPECT},\ \mathrm{OK},\ \mathrm{SUSPECT},\ \mathrm{SAFE}.
\]
The output is $1$ on the first four samples and becomes $0$ only
when $\mathrm{SAFE}$ is entered on the last sample.
\[
\boxed{0,1,0,1,1\mapsto\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{SAFE}}.
\]

An isolated mismatch is a $1$ that is not immediately followed by
another $1$ before a reset. From $\mathrm{OK}$ the word $10$ walks
$\mathrm{OK}\to\mathrm{SUSPECT}\to\mathrm{OK}$ and never visits
$\mathrm{SAFE}$. A leading $1$ followed by $0$ is the same walk.
Thus an isolated mismatch never trips. The consecutive pair $11$,
read from $\mathrm{OK}$, walks
$\mathrm{OK}\to\mathrm{SUSPECT}\to\mathrm{SAFE}$; read from
$\mathrm{SUSPECT}$, the first $1$ already enters $\mathrm{SAFE}$
and the second $1$ stays there. In every case the trip occurs on
the second consecutive mismatch. Because $\mathrm{SAFE}$ is
absorbing and is the unique state with output $0$, no later sample
restores a nonzero output.

Sentence (i) collapses $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$ into $\mathrm{SAFE}$.
The second sample of $0,1,0,1,1$ would then already be
$\mathrm{SAFE}$, isolated mismatches would trip, and the required
trace would be lost. Sentence (ii) either adds an edge
$\mathrm{SAFE}\xrightarrow{0}\mathrm{OK}$ or deletes the reset
$\mathrm{SUSPECT}\xrightarrow{0}\mathrm{OK}$. In the first case
$\mathrm{SAFE}$ is not absorbing; in the second the third sample
would remain $\mathrm{SUSPECT}$ and the sequence could not return
to $\mathrm{OK}$ before the final pair.

The monitor is not a two-door interlock and is not a CRC or
watchdog.

graderFixtures.proofText: Input $0,1,0,1,1$ yields post-sample states $\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{OK},\mathrm{SUSPECT},\mathrm{SAFE}$. Isolated mismatches reset; any two consecutive mismatches enter absorbing $\mathrm{SAFE}$ (output $0$) on the second $1$. A first-mismatch trip or a missing reset / non-absorbing $\mathrm{SAFE}$ is a different machine.
A single mismatch already trips. After the second sample of 0,1,0,1,1 I am already in SAFE, and an isolated 1 is enough to cut the output.
A later match leaves SAFE, or a match does not reset SUSPECT, so after 0,1,0 I remain in SUSPECT or I leave SAFE, and I never obtain OK,SUSPECT,OK,SUSPECT,SAFE.

ERAND:010117.title: Three iid Weibull lifetimes with S(t)=exp[-(t/10)^2] have series survival exp[-3(t/10)^2], hazard 3t/50, median 10 sqrt(ln 2 / 3), and mean 5 sqrt(pi/3)
ERAND:010117.objective: From three iid Weibull devices with S(t)=exp[-(t/10)^2], derive the series survival exp[-3(t/10)^2], series hazard 3t/50, series median 10 sqrt(ln 2 / 3), and series mean 5 sqrt(pi/3), and write the parallel survival 1-[1-exp(-(t/10)^2)]^3.
ERAND:010117.statement:
Three devices have independent identically distributed lifetimes $T_1,T_2,T_3$
with common survival function
\[
S(t)=\mathbb P(T_i>t)=\exp\bigl[-(t/10)^2\bigr],\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
(The common law is a Weibull law of shape $2$ and scale $10$.) Write $T_{\mathrm{ser}}=\min\{T_1,T_2,T_3\}$ for a series string that fails at the first device failure, and $T_{\mathrm{par}}=\max\{T_1,T_2,T_3\}$ for a parallel bank that fails only when every device has failed.

1. Derive the series survival $S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)=\mathbb P(T_{\mathrm{ser}}>t)$. Then compute the series hazard
   \[
   h_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\log S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)
   \]
   for $t>0$. Identify both formulas in closed form.

2. Solve $S_{\mathrm{ser}}(m)=1/2$ for the unique series median $m>0$. Then compute the series mean $\mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{ser}}]$ either as a Weibull mean $\lambda\Gamma(1+1/k)$ after reading off the series scale, or as the survival integral $\int_0^\infty S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)\,dt$.

3. Derive the parallel survival $S_{\mathrm{par}}(t)=\mathbb P(T_{\mathrm{par}}>t)$ in closed form.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a series of three independent devices has the same survival as one device run three times as long, or else the complementary parallel formula $1-[1-S(t)]^3$”; (ii) “the series hazard remains the single-device hazard $t/50$, or the mean is the single-device Weibull mean $5\sqrt{\pi}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a Poisson-process waiting time, and do not change the Weibull shape or the scale $10$.
permittedResults: Independence converts a minimum into a product of survivals and a maximum into a product of failure functions.
If $S(t)=\exp[-c(t/\lambda)^k]$ with $c>0$, the law is Weibull of the same shape and of scale $\lambda c^{-1/k}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Cube the common survival, differentiate the cumulative hazard, solve S_ser(m)=1/2, then read the series law as Weibull of scale 10/sqrt(3).
Compute the series mean as the Gaussian integral of exp[-3 t^2/100], then obtain the parallel survival from the complementary product of failure functions.

milestones.criterion: Derives the series survival exp[-3(t/10)^2] and the series hazard 3t/50 from independence and the cumulative hazard.
Computes the series median 10 sqrt(ln 2 / 3) and the series mean 5 sqrt(pi/3), and writes the parallel survival 1-[1-exp(-(t/10)^2)]^3.
Rejects a time-scaled single-device survival, a swapped parallel formula, an untripled hazard, and a mean that omits the series scale.

commonErrors.description: Writes the series survival as S(3t)=exp[-(3t/10)^2], as 3S(t), or as the parallel formula 1-[1-S(t)]^3.
commonErrors.consequence: The series hazard, median, and mean are computed from the wrong survival, so 3t/50, 10 sqrt(ln 2 / 3), and 5 sqrt(pi/3) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Leaves the series hazard as the single-device value t/50 (or as 3t/100), or reports the single-device mean 5 sqrt(pi) instead of 5 sqrt(pi/3).
commonErrors.consequence: The threefold superposition of independent Weibull hazards is omitted, and the required median or mean cannot occur.

hintTree.content: Independence gives $S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)=[S(t)]^3=\exp[-3(t/10)^2]$. Differentiating the cumulative hazard $3(t/10)^2$ produces the series hazard.
The equation $\exp[-3(m/10)^2]=1/2$ rearranges to $(m/10)^2=(\ln 2)/3$. The series law is Weibull of shape $2$ and scale $10/\sqrt{3}$.
A parallel bank fails only when all three devices have failed, so $S_{\mathrm{par}}(t)=1-\bigl[1-\exp(-(t/10)^2)\bigr]^3$.

ERAND:010117.canonicalSolution:
Independence of the three lifetimes yields
\[
S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)
=\mathbb P(T_1>t,\,T_2>t,\,T_3>t)
=[S(t)]^3
=\exp\bigl[-3(t/10)^2\bigr].
\]
The series cumulative hazard is therefore $3(t/10)^2$, and for $t>0$
\[
h_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)
=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[3t^2/100\bigr]
=\frac{6t}{100}
=\frac{3t}{50}.
\]
Equivalently, a single device has hazard $t/50$, and independent series superposition triples the hazard.
\[
\boxed{S_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)=\exp[-3(t/10)^2],\quad h_{\mathrm{ser}}(t)=3t/50}.
\]

The unique positive median solves $S_{\mathrm{ser}}(m)=1/2$:
\[
\exp\bigl[-3(m/10)^2\bigr]=\frac12
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
3(m/10)^2=\ln 2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
m=10\sqrt{\frac{\ln 2}{3}}.
\]
The series survival is Weibull of shape $2$ and scale $10/\sqrt{3}$. The mean of a shape-$2$ Weibull of scale $\lambda$ is $\lambda\Gamma(3/2)=\lambda\sqrt{\pi}/2$, so
\[
\mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{ser}}]
=\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}
=5\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}}.
\]
The same value is the survival integral. The substitution $u=t\sqrt{3}/10$ gives $dt=(10/\sqrt{3})\,du$ and
\[
\int_0^\infty\exp\bigl[-3t^2/100\bigr]\,dt
=\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du
=\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}
=5\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{m=10\sqrt{(\ln 2)/3},\quad \mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{ser}}]=5\sqrt{\pi/3}}.
\]

A parallel bank is still alive at time $t$ unless every device has failed:
\[
S_{\mathrm{par}}(t)
=1-\bigl[1-S(t)\bigr]^3
=1-\bigl[1-\exp\bigl(-(t/10)^2\bigr)\bigr]^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{S_{\mathrm{par}}(t)=1-\bigl[1-\exp(-(t/10)^2)\bigr]^3}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses a product of survivals with a time-scale of a single device, or else swaps the series formula for the complementary parallel formula. The identity $S(3t)=\exp[-(3t/10)^2]$ is not the series survival, and $1-[1-S(t)]^3$ is the parallel survival. Sentence (ii) leaves the single-device hazard $t/50$ untripled, or computes the single-device mean $10\cdot\sqrt{\pi}/2=5\sqrt{\pi}$ and never inserts the series scale $10/\sqrt{3}$.

The argument never replaces the Weibull string by a Poisson arrival and never changes the shape or the scale $10$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Series survival is $\exp[-3(t/10)^2]$ with hazard $3t/50$, median $10\sqrt{(\ln 2)/3}$, and mean $5\sqrt{\pi/3}$. Parallel survival is $1-\bigl[1-\exp(-(t/10)^2)\bigr]^3$. A time-scaled single device and an untripled hazard or mean are refused.
A series of three devices is the same as one device run three times as long, so S_ser(t)=S(3t)=exp[-(3t/10)^2]. Alternatively I use the complementary formula 1-[1-S(t)]^3 for the series string.
Each device already has hazard t/50, so the series hazard is t/50. The mean is the ordinary Weibull mean 10 Gamma(3/2)=5 sqrt(pi). I do not insert a factor 3 in the cumulative hazard.
