ERAND:010630.title: The BLUE of theta from Y=(theta+N1,theta+N2) with covariance [[4,1],[1,2]] uses weights (1/4,3/4), has variance 7/4, and reads 13 at (10,14)
ERAND:010630.objective: For the linear model Y1=theta+N1, Y2=theta+N2 with noise covariance [[4,1],[1,2]], derive the unbiased BLUE weights (1/4,3/4), prove that the minimum variance is 7/4, and evaluate the estimate 13 at the observation (10,14).
ERAND:010630.statement:
An unknown real level $\theta$ is observed through two noisy sensors
\[
Y_1=\theta+N_1,\qquad Y_2=\theta+N_2,
\]
where the noise pair $N=(N_1,N_2)$ has mean zero and covariance
\[
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\ 1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Consider linear estimators $\hat\theta=w_1 Y_1+w_2 Y_2$. Unbiasedness
for every $\theta$ is the constraint $w_1+w_2=1$. Among such weights
the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) minimises
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)=w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w$.

1. Invert $\Sigma$. Form $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1$ and normalise to obtain
   the unique BLUE weight vector. Record the two coordinates exactly.

2. Evaluate the minimum variance $w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w$, or
   equivalently $(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)^{-1}$.

3. At the observation $(Y_1,Y_2)=(10,14)$, compute the numerical BLUE
   $\hat\theta$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “unbiasedness forces equal weights
   $w=(1/2,1/2)$, so the estimate is the sample mean $12$”; (ii) “the
   off-diagonal covariance may be dropped, so each sensor is weighted
   by the reciprocal of its own variance only.”

Do not replace BLUE by a likelihood that assumes a Gaussian density
beyond second moments, and do not restate an intake-seed exercise in
place of this two-sensor covariance.
permittedResults: If $\Sigma=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&1\\ 1&2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ then $\det\Sigma=7$ and $\Sigma^{-1}=(1/7)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\ -1&4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
The Gauss–Markov minimum variance is $(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)^{-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Invert Sigma, form Sigma^{-1} 1, normalise, then evaluate both w^T Sigma w and the affine combination of (10,14).
Minimise w^T Sigma w subject to w1+w2=1 by a Lagrange multiplier, recover w=(1/4,3/4), and substitute the observation.

milestones.criterion: Inverts Sigma and derives the unbiased BLUE weights (1/4,3/4).
Computes the minimum variance 7/4 and evaluates theta-hat=13 at the observation (10,14).
Rejects equal weights / the sample mean 12 and a diagonal-only weighting that drops the covariance.

commonErrors.description: Takes unbiasedness to force w=(1/2,1/2), reports variance 2 instead of 7/4, and reads the estimate as the sample mean 12.
commonErrors.consequence: The BLUE weights (1/4,3/4) and the required value 13 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Inverts only the diagonal of Sigma, or otherwise ignores the covariance 1, and obtains weights other than (1/4,3/4).
commonErrors.consequence: The Gauss–Markov normal equations are not those of the given Sigma, so both the variance 7/4 and the estimate 13 fail.

hintTree.content: $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1=(1/7)(1,3)^{\mathsf T}$. Normalising the two coordinates $1$ and $3$ produces the weights $(1/4,3/4)$.
The information scalar is $\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1=4/7$, so the minimum variance is $7/4$. Directly, $\Sigma w=(7/4)\mathbf 1$ and $w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w=7/4$.
The numerical estimate is $(1/4)\cdot 10+(3/4)\cdot 14=13$.

ERAND:010630.canonicalSolution:
The determinant is $4\cdot 2-1\cdot 1=7$, so
\[
\Sigma^{-1}=\frac17\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\ -1&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Applying this matrix to the all-ones vector gives
\[
\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1=\frac17\begin{pmatrix}2-1\\ -1+4\end{pmatrix}
=\frac17\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The BLUE weights are the normalisation of that vector:
\[
\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1=\frac47,
\qquad
w
=(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1
=\frac74\cdot\frac17\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1/4\\ 3/4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first sensor is noisier ($4>2$) and is positively correlated with
the second, so it receives the smaller weight.
\[
\boxed{w=(1/4,3/4)}.
\]
The minimum variance is the reciprocal information scalar
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)
=(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)^{-1}
=\frac74.
\]
As a check, $\Sigma w=(7/4)\mathbf 1$, hence
$w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w=7/4$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)=7/4}.
\]
At the observation $(10,14)$,
\[
\hat\theta=\frac14\cdot 10+\frac34\cdot 14
=\frac{10+42}{4}
=13.
\]
\[
\boxed{\hat\theta=13}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the $\Sigma^{-1}$ inner product by the Euclidean
sample mean. Equal weights are unbiased but not optimal: their
variance is
\[
\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)\Sigma\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathsf T}
=2,
\]
which is strictly larger than $7/4$, and they would read $12$ rather
than $13$ at the given sample. Sentence (ii) drops the covariance $1$
and weights by $(1/4,1/2)$ before renormalising, which is a different
(diagonal-$\Sigma$) estimator.

The argument never invokes a Gaussian likelihood beyond second moments
and never restates an intake seed.

graderFixtures.proofText: BLUE weights are $w=(1/4,3/4)$ from $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1\propto(1,3)$. The minimum variance is $7/4$. At $(Y_1,Y_2)=(10,14)$ one has $\hat\theta=13$. Equal weights and a diagonal-only inverse are different estimators.
Unbiasedness is w1+w2=1 and I have no reason to prefer one sensor, so I take w=(1/2,1/2). The estimate is the sample mean (10+14)/2=12, and I do not invert Sigma.
I drop the off-diagonal 1 and invert diag(4,2). The un-normalised weights are (1/4,1/2), which I renormalise to (1/3,2/3). Neither coordinate is 1/4 or 3/4, and the estimate is not 13.

ERAND:010631.title: The exact 2-bit midrise quantizer of Unif[-1,1) has error variance 1/48, SQNR 16 (about 12.04 dB), and error independent of Q but not of X
ERAND:010631.objective: For the exact 2-bit midrise quantizer of X~Unif[-1,1) with step 1/2 and levels +/-1/4, +/-3/4, prove that e=Q-X is Unif[-1/4,1/4] of mean 0 and variance 1/48, compute Var Q=5/16 and Var X=1/3, evaluate SQNR=16 (about 12.04 dB), and show that e is independent of the bin index (hence of Q) but not of X.
ERAND:010631.statement:
Let $X$ be uniform on the half-open interval $[-1,1)$. A two-bit
midrise uniform quantizer of step $\Delta=1/2$ partitions $[-1,1)$
into the four bins
\[
[-1,-1/2),\quad[-1/2,0),\quad[0,1/2),\quad[1/2,1)
\]
and emits the corresponding reconstruction levels
\[
Q\in\bigl\{-3/4,-1/4,+1/4,+3/4\bigr\}.
\]
Define the quantization error by $e=Q-X$. The signal-to-quantization-
noise ratio is
\[
\operatorname{SQNR}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(e)}.
\]

1. Prove that $e$ is uniform on $[-1/4,1/4]$ (or the half-open
   counterpart $[-1/4,1/4)$). Compute $E[e]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(e)$.

2. Compute $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Q)$. Evaluate
   $\operatorname{SQNR}$ as an exact rational and as a decibel figure
   $10\log_{10}(\operatorname{SQNR})$ to two decimal places.

3. Let $B\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ be the output-bin index. Prove that $e$ is
   independent of $B$ and therefore independent of the reconstruction
   $Q$. Prove that $e$ is nevertheless not independent of $X$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\operatorname{SQNR}$ is
   $\operatorname{Var}(Q)/\operatorname{Var}(e)$, or else
   $\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{Var}(Q)$”; (ii) “the error is
   independent of the input $X$, or else the error law depends on the
   bin index.”

Do not replace the midrise grid by a midtread grid, and do not restate
an intake-seed exercise in place of this exact uniform calculation.
permittedResults: A uniform random variable on an interval of length $\ell$ has variance $\ell^2/12$. In particular $\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1)$ has variance $1/3$ and $\operatorname{Unif}[-1/4,1/4]$ has variance $1/48$.
If $X$ is uniform on a union of equal-length bins and $Q$ is the bin midpoint, then the error $Q-X$ is uniform on $[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2)$ and is independent of the bin index.

acceptableStrategies.description: Map each equal-length bin through e=Q-X to lock the uniform error, compute the three variances, then argue that the error law does not depend on the bin while e is a nonconstant function of X.
First compute SQNR=(1/3)/(1/48)=16 from the two variances, then use Var X=Var Q+Var e as a check that e is uncorrelated with Q, and finish with the functional dependence e=Q(X)-X.

milestones.criterion: Shows that e=Q-X is uniform on [-1/4,1/4] with mean 0 and variance 1/48, and computes Var Q=5/16 and Var X=1/3.
Evaluates SQNR=16 (about 12.04 dB) and proves that e is independent of the bin index and of Q but not of X.
Rejects an inverted SQNR ratio and the claim that the error is independent of X or depends on the bin index.

commonErrors.description: Defines SQNR as Var(Q)/Var(e)=15 or as Var(X)/Var(Q)=16/15, or otherwise fails to report the exact ratio 16 and the decibel figure 12.04 dB.
commonErrors.consequence: The required SQNR=16 is lost even if the three variances are individually available.

commonErrors.description: Claims that e is independent of X, or claims that the error law depends on the output-bin index (hence that e is not independent of Q).
commonErrors.consequence: The exact midrise independence structure — e independent of Q but not of X — is inverted or denied.

hintTree.content: On the bin $[k\Delta,(k+1)\Delta)$ one has $Q=(k+1/2)\Delta$, so $e=Q-X$ ranges over an interval of length $\Delta=1/2$ centred at $0$. Uniformity of $X$ makes $e$ uniform on $[-1/4,1/4)$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/3$ and $\operatorname{Var}(e)=1/48$, so $\operatorname{SQNR}=16$ and $10\log_{10}16\approx 12.04\,\mathrm{dB}$. The four values of $Q$ are equiprobable, and $E[Q^2]=5/16$.

The conditional law of $e$ given the bin index does not depend on the index, so $e$ is independent of $B$ and of $Q$. Given $X=x$ the error $e=Q(x)-x$ is deterministic, so $e$ is a function of $X$ and cannot be independent of $X$.

ERAND:010631.canonicalSolution:
On a generic bin $[k\Delta,(k+1)\Delta)$ the reconstruction is the
midpoint $Q=(k+1/2)\Delta$ and the error is
\[
e=Q-X\in\bigl(-\Delta/2,\Delta/2\bigr]=\bigl(-1/4,1/4\bigr]
\]
(or the half-open counterpart $[-1/4,1/4)$, according to the closed
end of the bin; the two versions agree almost surely). Because $X$ is
uniform and every bin has the same length $\Delta=1/2$, the image of
each bin under $x\mapsto Q-x$ is the same interval of length $1/2$,
and $e$ is uniform on that interval. In particular
\[
E[e]=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e)=\frac{(1/2)^2}{12}=\frac1{48}.
\]
\[
\boxed{e\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1/4,1/4],\quad E[e]=0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(e)=1/48}.
\]

The input $X\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1)$ is centred, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{2^2}{12}=\frac13.
\]
The reconstruction $Q$ takes each of the four midpoints with
probability $1/4$, and is centred, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Q)
=E[Q^2]
=\frac14\Bigl(2\cdot\frac{9}{16}+2\cdot\frac{1}{16}\Bigr)
=\frac{10}{32}
=\frac{5}{16}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{SQNR}
=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(e)}
=\frac{1/3}{1/48}
=16,
\qquad
10\log_{10}16=10\log_{10}(2^4)=40\log_{10}2\approx 12.04\,\mathrm{dB}.
\]
As a consistency check, independence of $e$ and $Q$ (proved next)
together with $X=Q-e$ would give
$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Q)+\operatorname{Var}(e)=5/16+1/48=1/3$,
which matches.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(Q)=5/16,\ \operatorname{Var}(X)=1/3,\ \operatorname{SQNR}=16\approx 12.04\,\mathrm{dB}}.
\]

Write $B$ for the bin index. The computation of the first part shows
that the conditional law of $e$ given $B=b$ is the same uniform law
on $[-1/4,1/4]$ for every $b$. Hence $e$ is independent of $B$. The
reconstruction $Q$ is a (deterministic) function of $B$, so $e$ is
independent of $Q$. On the other hand $e=Q(X)-X$ is a deterministic
function of $X$, and that function is nonconstant on $[-1,1)$. A
nonconstant function of $X$ cannot be independent of $X$. Equivalently,
the pair $(X,e)$ is supported on the four line segments
$e=q_b-x$ inside each bin, which is not a product set.

Sentence (i) replaces the definition $\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{Var}(e)$
by either $\operatorname{Var}(Q)/\operatorname{Var}(e)=15$ or
$\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{Var}(Q)=16/15$. Neither is the
required SQNR of $16$. Sentence (ii) either claims independence of
$e$ and $X$, contradicting $e=Q(X)-X$, or claims that the error law
depends on the bin, contradicting uniformity of $X$ across equal bins.

The argument never switches to a midtread grid and never restates an
intake seed.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $e=Q-X$ one has $e\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1/4,1/4]$, mean $0$, variance $1/48$. Also $\operatorname{Var}(Q)=5/16$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/3$, so $\operatorname{SQNR}=16\approx 12.04\,\mathrm{dB}$. The error is independent of the bin index and of $Q$, but is a nonconstant function of $X$.
I take SQNR to be Var(Q)/Var(e)=(5/16)/(1/48)=15, or alternatively Var(X)/Var(Q)=(1/3)/(5/16)=16/15. I never form Var(X)/Var(e)=16 and I do not report 12.04 dB.

Quantization error is an additive noise independent of the input, so e is independent of X. Alternatively the four bins sit at different amplitudes, so I claim the error law depends on the bin index and therefore e is not independent of Q.

FEM:010117.title: Two P1 elements for -u''+u=1 with Robin: free A [[13/3,-23/12],[-23/12,25/6]], u=(0,63/109,114/109), reaction -148/109
FEM:010117.objective: Assemble the Robin weak form of -u''+u=1, u(0)=0, u'(1)+2u(1)=3 on two uniform P1 elements, recover the stated local and free matrices and load, solve for the nodal vector, read the constrained-row residual -148/109, and record that uh need not satisfy the strong Robin identity pointwise.
FEM:010117.statement:
Consider the two-point boundary-value problem
\[
-u''+u=1\quad\text{on }(0,1),\qquad u(0)=0,\qquad u'(1)+2u(1)=3.
\]
Use two uniform linear (P1) elements of length $h=1/2$, with nodes
$x_0=0$, $x_1=1/2$, $x_2=1$. The trial and test spaces vanish at $x=0$.
The standing sign convention after integration by parts is
\[
\int_0^1 u'v'\,dx+\int_0^1 uv\,dx+2u(1)v(1)
=\int_0^1 v\,dx+3v(1)
\]
for every admissible $v$. In particular the Robin datum contributes
the boundary terms $+2u(1)v(1)$ on the left and $+3v(1)$ on the right.

1. On a single element of length $1/2$, form the local matrix of
   $\int u'v'+\int uv$ in the standard hat basis and prove that it
   equals
   \[
   A^{\mathrm{loc}}
   =\begin{pmatrix}13/6&-23/12\\-23/12&13/6\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

2. Assemble the two-element system, add the Robin term $+2$ on the
   $(x_2,x_2)$ entry, eliminate the homogeneous Dirichlet unknown at
   $x_0$, and prove that the free $2\times 2$ matrix and free load are
   \[
   A
   =\begin{pmatrix}13/3&-23/12\\-23/12&25/6\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   f=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\13/4\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

3. Solve $A(u_1,u_2)^T=f$ and prove that the nodal vector is
   \[
   (u_0,u_1,u_2)=\bigl(0,\,63/109,\,114/109\bigr).
   \]
   Evaluate the constrained row of the assembled (pre-elimination)
   residual and prove that this discrete reaction equals $-148/109$.

4. On the last element, compute $u_h'(1)+2u_h(1)$ and show that it
   is not equal to $3$. Audit both sentences: (i) “Robin is a natural
   Neumann condition $u'(1)=3$, so the $+2u(1)v(1)$ term is omitted”;
   (ii) “a conforming Galerkin method must satisfy the strong Robin
   identity pointwise, or else this is a variable-rigidity axial bar
   / three-element Dirichlet-elimination exercise.”

Do not replace the calculation by a variable-coefficient axial-bar
weak form, a natural traction without the reaction $+u$, or a
three-element nonzero Dirichlet elimination.
permittedResults: On an interval of length $h=1/2$, the P1 element matrix of $\int u'v'$ is $(1/h)[[1,-1],[-1,1]]=2[[1,-1],[-1,1]]$ and the element matrix of $\int uv$ is $(h/6)[[2,1],[1,2]]=(1/12)[[2,1],[1,2]]$.
A conforming Galerkin solution of a Robin problem lies in $H^1$ and need not satisfy $u_h'(1)+2u_h(1)=3$ pointwise. The Robin condition is built into the weak form, not into the nodal interpolation.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form each element's diffusion-plus-mass matrix, assemble, add the Robin rank-one terms at x=1, then eliminate u(0)=0.
Write the $3\times 3$ unconstrained system first, solve the free $2\times 2$ block, and read the discrete reaction from row 0 of $Au-f$.

milestones.criterion: Solves for the nodal vector (0,63/109,114/109) and reports the constrained-row residual -148/109.
Records that uh need not satisfy the strong Robin identity pointwise and refuses the reserved axial-bar substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Omits the bilinear term +2u(1)v(1), treats the end condition as the natural Neumann law u'(1)=3, or leaves the last diagonal at 13/6.
commonErrors.consequence: The free matrix is no longer [[13/3,-23/12],[-23/12,25/6]] and the nodal values 63/109 and 114/109 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that uh satisfies u'(1)+2u(1)=3 pointwise, or reports the constrained-row residual as +148/109.
commonErrors.consequence: The weak-versus-strong distinction is erased, or the assigned reaction sign is flipped.

hintTree.content: Add the local diffusion matrix $2[[1,-1],[-1,1]]$ to the local mass $(1/12)[[2,1],[1,2]]$. The $(1,2)$ entry is $-2+1/12=-23/12$.
Interior assembly doubles the middle diagonal $13/6+13/6=13/3$. Robin then replaces the last diagonal $13/6$ by $13/6+2=25/6$ and adds $3$ to the last load $1/4$.
The constrained residual is $A_{01}u_1-f_0=(-23/12)(63/109)-1/4$. The last-element slope is $2(u_2-u_1)=102/109$.

FEM:010117.canonicalSolution:
Each element has length $h=1/2$. In the standard two-node hat basis,
\[
\int u'v'
=\frac1h\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
=2\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\int uv
=\frac h6\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}
=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Adding these contributions,
\[
A^{\mathrm{loc}}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}1/6&1/12\\1/12&1/6\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}13/6&-23/12\\-23/12&13/6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A^{\mathrm{loc}}=[[13/6,-23/12],[-23/12,13/6]]}.
\]

Both elements contribute the same local matrix. Before Robin, the
global $3\times 3$ matrix on nodes $(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ therefore has
diagonal entries $13/6$, $13/3$, $13/6$ and off-diagonal entries
$-23/12$ on the two element couplings. The Robin term $+2u(1)v(1)$
adds $2$ to the $(x_2,x_2)$ entry, so that entry becomes
$13/6+2=25/6$. The source $f\equiv 1$ produces the element load
$(h/2)(1,1)=(1/4,1/4)$ on each element, hence the assembled load
$(1/4,1/2,1/4)$ before Robin. The Robin term $+3v(1)$ then replaces
the last load by $1/4+3=13/4$. Eliminating the homogeneous Dirichlet
unknown $u_0=0$ leaves the free system
\[
\begin{pmatrix}13/3&-23/12\\-23/12&25/6\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}u_1\\u_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\13/4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A=[[13/3,-23/12],[-23/12,25/6]],\quad f=[1/2,13/4]}.
\]

The determinant is
\[
\frac{13}{3}\cdot\frac{25}{6}-\Bigl(\frac{23}{12}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{325}{18}-\frac{529}{144}
=\frac{2071}{144}.
\]
Cramer's rule gives
\[
u_1
=\frac{(25/6)(1/2)+(23/12)(13/4)}{2071/144}
=\frac{399}{48}\cdot\frac{144}{2071}
=\frac{1197}{2071}
=\frac{63}{109},
\]
\[
u_2
=\frac{(13/3)(13/4)+(23/12)(1/2)}{2071/144}
=\frac{361}{24}\cdot\frac{144}{2071}
=\frac{2166}{2071}
=\frac{114}{109},
\]
after cancelling a common factor $19$. Thus
\[
\boxed{(u_0,u_1,u_2)=(0,63/109,114/109)}.
\]

The unconstrained assembled row at the Dirichlet node (no Robin
contribution lives there) applied to this vector is
\[
A_{00}u_0+A_{01}u_1-f_0
=\Bigl(-\frac{23}{12}\Bigr)\frac{63}{109}-\frac14
=-\frac{1449}{1308}-\frac{327}{1308}
=-\frac{1776}{1308}
=-\frac{148}{109}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{constrained-row residual }=-148/109}.
\]
This algebraic residual is the discrete reaction reported here. It is
not claimed to equal the point value $-u'(0)$, because the reaction
term $\int uv$ participates in row $0$.

On the last element the discrete slope is constant and equals
$(u_2-u_1)/h=2(114-63)/109=102/109$. Therefore
\[
u_h'(1)+2u_h(1)
=\frac{102}{109}+\frac{228}{109}
=\frac{330}{109}
\neq 3=\frac{327}{109}.
\]
The Galerkin solution satisfies the Robin condition weakly, not as a
pointwise identity on $u_h'$.

Sentence (i) drops $+2u(1)v(1)$ and treats the end condition as

and destroys both the free matrix and the nodal values. Sentence (ii)
demands that a conforming method reproduce $u'(1)+2u(1)=3$ pointwise,
which the explicit difference $330/109\neq 327/109$ refutes, or else
replaces the exercise by a variable-rigidity axial bar or a
three-element Dirichlet-elimination problem that is not asked.

The argument never introduces a variable axial rigidity, never treats
the right-hand end as a pure natural traction, and never uses three
elements or a nonzero Dirichlet value.

FEM:010118.title: One-mode Ritz for -u''=x: a=1/4, uh=x(1-x)/4, min J=-1/96, energy-error squared 1/720
FEM:010118.objective: Minimize the Dirichlet energy of -u''=x with homogeneous ends in the one-dimensional trial space spanned by phi=x(1-x), obtain a=1/4 and min J=-1/96, compute the squared energy error 1/720, confirm Galerkin orthogonality, and distinguish the calculation from collocation of the strong form.
FEM:010118.statement:
Let
\[
-u''=x\quad\text{on }(0,1),\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0.
\]
The exact solution is $u=(x-x^3)/6$. Restrict the trial space to the
single mode $u_h=a\,\phi$ with
\[
\phi(x)=x(1-x).
\]
The energy inner product and load are
\[
a(w,v)=\int_0^1 w'v'\,dx,\qquad \ell(v)=\int_0^1 xv\,dx,
\]
and the quadratic energy to be minimized is
\[
J(v)=\frac12 a(v,v)-\ell(v).
\]

1. Prove $(\phi',\phi')=1/3$ and $(x,\phi)=1/12$. Deduce that the
   Ritz / Galerkin condition $a(u_h,\phi)=\ell(\phi)$ gives $a=1/4$
   and therefore $u_h=x(1-x)/4$.

2. Evaluate $J(u_h)$ and prove that the minimum value on this line
   is $-1/96$.

3. Using Galerkin orthogonality $a(u-u_h,u_h)=0$, or by a direct
   integration, prove that the squared energy error is
   \[
   a(u-u_h,u-u_h)=\frac1{720}.
   \]
   Confirm $a(u-u_h,\phi)=0$ by expanding the integrand.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $-u_h''=2a$ is constant, one
   should collocate $-u_h''=x$ at a convenient node, and that is the
   same method as energy minimization”; (ii) “the squared energy
   error is $\|u\|_E^2=1/45$ or $\|u_h\|_E^2=1/48$, or the exercise
   is a Cea / uniform-P1 interpolation-error estimate for a quadratic
   exact solution on a mesh.”

Do not replace the one-mode calculation by a mesh interpolation
estimate, a residual-jump estimator, or a Cea lemma argument.
permittedResults: On a one-dimensional trial space the Ritz coefficient is the Rayleigh quotient $a=(f,\phi)/(\phi',\phi')$. Here that quotient is $(1/12)/(1/3)=1/4$.

Collocation of $-u_h''=x$ at a point $x_*$ would enforce the constant $2a=x_*$ and is a different method. Agreement at the midpoint $x_*=1/2$ is a coincidence and does not identify collocation with energy minimization.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the two scalar inner products, solve a/3=1/12, then get the energy error from ||u||_E^2-||uh||_E^2.
Expand J(a phi) as a quadratic in the coefficient a, complete the square to read the minimum -1/96, and check orthogonality by integrating (u-uh)' phi'.

milestones.criterion: Computes (phi',phi')=1/3 and (x,phi)=1/12 and obtains the Ritz coefficient a=1/4 with uh=x(1-x)/4.
Evaluates min J=-1/96 and the squared energy error 1/720, with Galerkin orthogonality a(u-uh,phi)=0.
Distinguishes energy minimization from collocation of the strong form and refuses a Cea / mesh-interpolation reading.

commonErrors.description: Determines a by collocating the constant -uh''=2a against x at a point, or treats that collocation as identical to energy minimization.
commonErrors.consequence: The variational characterization is lost, and a point other than the midpoint produces the wrong coefficient.

commonErrors.description: Reports the squared energy error as 1/45 or 1/48, skips the orthogonality subtraction, or claims a(u-uh,phi) is nonzero.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned value 1/720 is lost, or Galerkin orthogonality is denied.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $\phi=x-x^2$ to get $\phi'=1-2x$. Then $\int_0^1(1-2x)^2\,dx=1-2+4/3=1/3$.

FEM:010118.canonicalSolution:
Write $\phi=x-x^2$, so $\phi'=1-2x$. Then
\[
(\phi',\phi')
=\int_0^1(1-2x)^2\,dx
=\int_0^1(1-4x+4x^2)\,dx
=1-2+\frac43
=\frac13.
\]
The load against the same mode is
\[
(x,\phi)
=\int_0^1 x\cdot x(1-x)\,dx
=\int_0^1(x^2-x^3)\,dx
=\frac13-\frac14
=\frac1{12}.
\]
The Galerkin scalar equation $(\phi',\phi')a=(x,\phi)$ is therefore
$a/3=1/12$, hence $a=1/4$ and
\[
u_h=\frac14 x(1-x).
\]
\[
\boxed{(\phi',\phi')=1/3,\quad(x,\phi)=1/12,\quad a=1/4}.
\]

Substitute into the energy:
\[
J(u_h)
=\frac12 a^2(\phi',\phi')-a(x,\phi)
=\frac12\cdot\frac1{16}\cdot\frac13-\frac14\cdot\frac1{12}
=\frac1{96}-\frac1{48}
=-\frac1{96}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\min J=-1/96}.
\]

The exact derivative is $u'=(1-3x^2)/6$, so
\[
a(u,u)
=\int_0^1\Bigl(\frac{1-3x^2}{6}\Bigr)^2\,dx
=\frac1{36}\int_0^1(1-6x^2+9x^4)\,dx
=\frac1{36}\Bigl(1-2+\frac95\Bigr)
=\frac1{45}.
\]
The discrete energy is
\[
a(u_h,u_h)=a^2(\phi',\phi')=\frac1{16}\cdot\frac13=\frac1{48}.
\]
Galerkin orthogonality $a(u-u_h,u_h)=0$ therefore yields
\[
a(u-u_h,u-u_h)
=a(u,u)-a(u_h,u_h)
=\frac1{45}-\frac1{48}
=\frac1{720}.
\]
To see the orthogonality directly, note
\[
(u-u_h)'
=\frac{1-3x^2}{6}-\frac{1-2x}{4}
=\frac{-1+6x-6x^2}{12}.
\]
Then
\[
a(u-u_h,\phi)
=\int_0^1\frac{-1+6x-6x^2}{12}\,(1-2x)\,dx
=\frac1{12}\int_0^1(12x^3-18x^2+8x-1)\,dx
=0,
\]
because $3-6+4-1=0$.
\[
\boxed{a(u-u_h,u-u_h)=1/720,\quad a(u-u_h,\phi)=0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces energy stationarity by collocation of the
strong form. Here $-u_h''=2a$ is constant, so collocation at a point
$x_*$ would force $a=x_*/2$. That recovers $a=1/4$ only at the
midpoint $x_*=1/2$, and fails at every other node (for example
$x_*=1/3$ would give $a=1/6$). The residual $1/2-x$ is orthogonal to
$\phi$ but is not identically zero, so the methods are not the same.
Sentence (ii) reports $1/45$ or $1/48$ as the squared energy error,
dropping the orthogonality subtraction, or else replaces the
one-mode calculation by a Cea / uniform-P1 interpolation-error or
residual-jump argument on a mesh, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a mesh size $h$, never quotes Cea's
lemma, and never estimates interpolation error for a quadratic.

graderFixtures.proofText: Inner products $(\phi',\phi')=1/3$ and $(x,\phi)=1/12$ give $a=1/4$ and $u_h=x(1-x)/4$. Then $\min J=-1/96$, $a(u-u_h,u-u_h)=1/720$, and $a(u-u_h,\phi)=0$. Collocation of $-u_h''=x$ is a different method.
uh'' is the constant -2a, so I collocate -uh''=x at a convenient point and treat that as the Ritz method. Energy minimization is not used. At x=1/3 this gives a=1/6 rather than a=1/4.
I report the squared energy error as ||u||_E^2=1/45 and omit the Galerkin-orthogonality subtraction that gives 1/720.

FEM:010119.title: Symmetric Nitsche on one P1 interval: stiffness 3, load 6, uh=2(1-x), coercive here iff gamma>1
FEM:010119.objective: Impose u(0)=2 by symmetric Nitsche on a single P1 element with u(1)=0 strong, gamma=4 and h=1, obtain the scalar stiffness 3 and load 6, recover uh=2(1-x), record the one-mode coercivity threshold gamma>1, and contrast the penalty-only omission 5, 8, 8/5.
FEM:010119.statement:
On the unit interval take a single linear element and the
homogeneous condition $u(1)=0$ strongly, so the trial space is
spanned by $\phi(x)=1-x$. The remaining boundary condition $u(0)=g$
with $g=2$ is imposed by the symmetric Nitsche method with mesh size
$h=1$ and penalty parameter $\gamma=4$. The standing sign convention,
using the outward normal $n=-1$ at $x=0$, is
\[
a(w,v)
=\int_0^1 w'v'\,dx
+w'(0)v(0)
+v'(0)w(0)
+\gamma\,w(0)v(0),
\]
with matching load (for $-u''=0$)
\[
\ell(v)=g\,v'(0)+\gamma g\,v(0).
\]

1. Evaluate the scalar stiffness $a(\phi,\phi)$ and the scalar load
   $\ell(\phi)$ and prove that they equal $3$ and $6$ respectively.
   Deduce that the Nitsche coefficient is $2$ and that
   $u_h=2(1-x)$.

2. Restricting attention to this one-dimensional trial space, prove
   that $a(\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,)$ is coercive if and only if
   $\gamma>1$. Do not upgrade this one-mode threshold to a general
   mesh-independent Nitsche condition.

3. Now drop the two consistency terms $w'(0)v(0)$ and $v'(0)w(0)$,
   leaving a penalty-only method. Prove that the stiffness becomes
   $5$, the load becomes $8$, and the coefficient becomes $8/5$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the outward-normal sign should be
   flipped, or the consistency terms may be omitted without changing
   the method”; (ii) “the form is coercive for every $\gamma>0$, or
   this is a three-element strong Dirichlet elimination / axial-bar
   reaction exercise.”

Do not replace symmetric Nitsche by strong nodal elimination, and do
not invoke a variable-rigidity bar or a Cea interpolation argument.
permittedResults: On $\mathrm{span}\{\phi\}$ with $\phi=1-x$ one has $\phi'=-1$, $\phi(0)=1$, and $a(\phi,\phi)=\gamma-1$. Coercivity on this line is exactly the inequality $\gamma>1$. Equality $\gamma=1$ produces a vanishing energy and is not coercive.
The matching Nitsche load for $f=0$ and $u(0)=g$ is $\ell(v)=g v'(0)+\gamma g v(0)$. With $g=2$ and $\gamma=4$ this is $2v'(0)+8v(0)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert phi=1-x into the stated Nitsche form and load, then compare with the same integrals after dropping the consistency terms.
Read coercivity from the single Rayleigh value a(phi,phi)=gamma-1, and keep that threshold attached to this one-dimensional space only.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the symmetric Nitsche stiffness 3 and matching load 6 and obtains uh=2(1-x).
Proves coercivity on span{phi} iff gamma>1 and computes the penalty-only values 5, 8, 8/5.
Refuses a normal-sign flip or penalty-only identification and does not upgrade gamma>1 to a general-mesh theorem.

commonErrors.description: Flips the signs of w'(0)v(0) and v'(0)w(0), or drops those consistency terms and still reports stiffness 3, load 6, and coefficient 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned triple (3,6,2) is lost, or the penalty-only triple (5,8,8/5) is misidentified with symmetric Nitsche.

commonErrors.description: Claims the form is coercive for every gamma>0, includes the endpoint gamma=1, or upgrades gamma>1 to a mesh-independent theorem.
commonErrors.consequence: The one-mode identity a(phi,phi)=gamma-1 is contradicted, or a stronger statement than the calculation supports is asserted.

hintTree.content: For $\phi=1-x$ one has $\int(\phi')^2=1$, $\phi'(0)=-1$, and $\phi(0)=1$, so $a(\phi,\phi)=1-1-1+\gamma=\gamma-1$.
The load is $2\phi'(0)+8\phi(0)=-2+8=6$. Penalty-only drops the two $-1$ contributions and the $2\phi'(0)$ term.
Coercivity on this single ray is $a(\phi,\phi)>0$, i.e. $\gamma>1$. At $\gamma=1$ the form is only semidefinite.

FEM:010119.canonicalSolution:
The function $\phi=1-x$ satisfies $\phi(1)=0$, $\phi(0)=1$, and
$\phi'=-1$. With $\gamma=4$,
\begin{align*}
a(\phi,\phi)
&=\int_0^1(\phi')^2\,dx
+\phi'(0)\phi(0)
+\phi'(0)\phi(0)
+\gamma\phi(0)^2\\
&=1+(-1)+(-1)+4
=3.
\end{align*}
The matching load is
\[
\ell(\phi)
=2\phi'(0)+4\cdot 2\cdot\phi(0)
=2(-1)+8
=6.
\]
The Nitsche coefficient $\alpha$ on this line therefore solves
$3\alpha=6$, so $\alpha=2$ and
\[
u_h=2\phi=2(1-x).
\]
\[
\boxed{a(\phi,\phi)=3,\quad\ell(\phi)=6,\quad u_h=2(1-x)}.
\]
(The exact solution of $-u''=0$ with $u(0)=2$ and $u(1)=0$ is the
same line, so symmetric Nitsche is exact on this one-element space.
That exactness is special to the present data and is not claimed for
a general source or a general mesh.)

On $\mathrm{span}\{\phi\}$ one has $a(\phi,\phi)=\gamma-1$. The form
is coercive on this trial space if and only if $\gamma-1>0$, i.e.
\[
\gamma>1.
\]
At $\gamma=1$ one has $a(\phi,\phi)=0$ with $\phi\not=0$, so the form
is not coercive. This threshold is a one-mode calculation. It is not
a general statement about Nitsche on arbitrary meshes, where a trace
inverse inequality would produce a mesh-dependent lower bound.
\[
\boxed{\text{coercive on span}\{\phi\}\iff\gamma>1}.
\]

If the consistency terms $w'(0)v(0)$ and $v'(0)w(0)$ are dropped,
the remaining penalty-only stiffness is
\[
\int_0^1(\phi')^2+\gamma\phi(0)^2
=1+4=5,
\]
and the remaining load is $\gamma g\phi(0)=8$. The coefficient
becomes $8/5$, and the discrete solution $(8/5)(1-x)$ no longer
matches $2(1-x)$.
\[
\boxed{\text{penalty-only: stiffness }5,\text{ load }8,\text{ coefficient }8/5}.
\]

Sentence (i) either flips the outward-normal sign, which replaces
$+w'(0)v(0)$ by $-w'(0)v(0)$ and changes both $3$ and $6$, or else
treats the penalty-only omission as equivalent to symmetric Nitsche.
Sentence (ii) claims coercivity for every $\gamma>0$, contradicting
$a(\phi,\phi)=\gamma-1$, or else replaces the method by strong
Dirichlet elimination on a multi-element axial bar, which is not
asked.

The argument never eliminates a nodal Dirichlet unknown by deleting a
row, never introduces a variable rigidity, and never quotes Cea's
lemma.

graderFixtures.proofText: Symmetric Nitsche gives $a(\phi,\phi)=3$, $\ell(\phi)=6$, coefficient $2$, and $u_h=2(1-x)$. On $\mathrm{span}\{\phi\}$ the form is coercive iff $\gamma>1$. Penalty-only omission produces stiffness $5$, load $8$, and coefficient $8/5$.
I flip the stated outward-normal convention and write both consistency terms with minus signs, changing the assigned Nitsche stiffness and load.
The Nitsche form is coercive for every gamma>0, including gamma=1 where a(phi,phi)=0.

FEM:010220.title: P1 triangle (0,0),(2,0),(0,1) with k=3,q=6: K=[[15/4,-3/4,-3],[-3/4,3/4,0],[-3,0,3]], energy 39
FEM:010220.objective: On the triangle with vertices (0,0), (2,0), (0,1), assemble the P1 stiffness for conductivity k=3 and the load for source q=6, reproduce 1+2x+3y from the nodal values (1,5,4), evaluate the centroid value 10/3, gradient (2,3) and energy 39, and record that reversing local orientation flips the signed Jacobian but not the physical area or energy.
FEM:010220.statement:
Let $T$ be the triangle with vertices
\[
P_1=(0,0),\qquad P_2=(2,0),\qquad P_3=(0,1),
\]
oriented in that order. Let $k=3$ be a constant conductivity and
$q=6$ a constant source. Use the standard affine P1 hat basis on $T$,
mapped from the reference triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$,
$(0,1)$.

1. Prove that the physical area is $1$ and that $\det J=2$. Write the
   hats
   \[
   N=(1-x/2-y,\;x/2,\;y)
   \]
   and the constant gradients
   \[
   \nabla N_1=(-1/2,-1),\quad
   \nabla N_2=(1/2,0),\quad
   \nabla N_3=(0,1).
   \]

2. Form $K_{ij}=k\int_T\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j\,dA$ and the load
   $f_i=\int_T q N_i\,dA$, and prove
   \[
   K
   =\begin{pmatrix}15/4&-3/4&-3\\-3/4&3/4&0\\-3&0&3\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad
   f=(2,2,2).
   \]

3. Show that the nodal values $(1,5,4)$ reproduce the linear
   polynomial $1+2x+3y$. Evaluate this polynomial at the centroid,
   read off its gradient, and prove that the energy
   $k\int_T|\nabla u_h|^2\,dA$ equals $39$.

4. Reverse the local vertex order to $(P_1,P_3,P_2)$ and audit both
   sentences: (i) “the signed Jacobian flip changes the physical
   area and therefore flips the sign of the energy $39$”; (ii) “this
   is an oriented Q1 quadrilateral mapping / one-point rank audit, or
   a Cea interpolation argument.”

Do not replace the triangle by a bilinear quadrilateral, and do not
invoke a one-point rank-deficient quadrature on a quad.
permittedResults: For constant $k$ and constant gradients, $K_{ij}=k\,|T|\,\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j$. For constant $q$, each load entry is $q\,|T|/3$.
A linear polynomial is reproduced exactly by its P1 nodal interpolant. Consequently $\nabla(1+2x+3y)=(2,3)$ is recovered from the nodal triple $(1,5,4)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build J from the two edge columns, read the three constant gradients, and multiply each inner product by k|T|.
Interpolate the nodal triple, evaluate at the centroid, and compute k|grad|^2|T| directly from the recovered slope (2,3).

milestones.criterion: Computes area 1, det J=2, the stated hats and gradients, and the stiffness K together with the load f=(2,2,2).
Reproduces 1+2x+3y from (1,5,4) and obtains centroid 10/3, gradient (2,3), and energy 39.
Records that reversing orientation flips signed det J but not physical area or energy, and refuses a Q1 rank-audit reading.

commonErrors.description: Takes det J=1 in place of 2, writes the wrong hat gradients, or treats a reversed orientation as flipping the physical area and the energy 39.
commonErrors.consequence: The stiffness entries and the energy lose their assigned values, or orientation is confused with measure.

commonErrors.description: Reports the energy as 39/2, fails to reproduce 1+2x+3y from (1,5,4), or replaces the consistent load (2,2,2) by a lumped corner load.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned energy 39 or the nodal reproduction check is lost.

hintTree.content: The matrix with columns $P_2-P_1$ and $P_3-P_1$ is $\mathrm{diag}(2,1)$, so $\det J=2$ and $|T|=1$.
$\nabla N_1\cdot\nabla N_1=5/4$, so $K_{11}=3\cdot 5/4=15/4$. Each load is $6\cdot(1/3)=2$.
$1\cdot N_1+5\cdot N_2+4\cdot N_3=1+2x+3y$. Then $k|\nabla u_h|^2|T|=3\cdot 13\cdot 1=39$.

FEM:010220.canonicalSolution:
The Jacobian of the affine map from the reference triangle is the
matrix with columns $P_2-P_1=(2,0)$ and $P_3-P_1=(0,1)$, so
$\det J=2$. The physical area is $|\det J|/2=1$. The barycentric
coordinates on $T$ are
\[
N_1=1-\frac x2-y,\qquad N_2=\frac x2,\qquad N_3=y,
\]
with constant gradients
\[
\nabla N_1=\Bigl(-\frac12,-1\Bigr),\quad
\nabla N_2=\Bigl(\frac12,0\Bigr),\quad
\nabla N_3=(0,1).
\]
\[
\boxed{|T|=1,\quad\det J=2}.
\]

Because the gradients are constant and $|T|=1$,
\[
K_{ij}=k\,\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j.
\]
The six inner products are
\begin{align*}
\nabla N_1\cdot\nabla N_1&=\frac14+1=\frac54,\\
\nabla N_1\cdot\nabla N_2&=-\frac14,\\
\nabla N_1\cdot\nabla N_3&=-1,\\
\nabla N_2\cdot\nabla N_2&=\frac14,\\
\nabla N_2\cdot\nabla N_3&=0,\\
\nabla N_3\cdot\nabla N_3&=1,
\end{align*}
and multiplication by $k=3$ produces
\[
K
=\begin{pmatrix}15/4&-3/4&-3\\-3/4&3/4&0\\-3&0&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(The row sums vanish, as they must for a pure gradient form.) The
constant source $q=6$ loads each hat by $q|T|/3=2$, so $f=(2,2,2)$.
\[
\boxed{K=[[15/4,-3/4,-3],[-3/4,3/4,0],[-3,0,3]],\quad f=(2,2,2)}.
\]

The nodal combination $(1,5,4)$ expands as
\[
1\cdot N_1+5\cdot N_2+4\cdot N_3
=1-\frac x2-y+\frac{5x}2+4y
=1+2x+3y.
\]
The centroid is $((0+2+0)/3,(0+0+1)/3)=(2/3,1/3)$, and
\[
1+2\cdot\frac23+3\cdot\frac13
=\frac{10}3.
\]
The gradient is the constant $(2,3)$. The energy in the standing
convention $k\int_T|\nabla u_h|^2\,dA$ (no factor $1/2$) is
\[
k\,|(2,3)|^2\,|T|
=3\cdot 13\cdot 1
=39.
\]
\[
\boxed{1+2x+3y;\quad\text{centroid }10/3;\quad\nabla=(2,3);\quad\text{energy }39}.
\]

Reversing the local order to $(P_1,P_3,P_2)$ replaces $J$ by the
matrix with columns $(0,1)$ and $(2,0)$, whose determinant is $-2$.
The signed Jacobian flips. The geometric triangle, the physical area
$|\det J|/2=1$, the physical hat gradients, and the energy $39$ do
not flip.

Sentence (i) treats the signed determinant as the physical area and
therefore changes the sign of $K$ and of the energy. That confuses
orientation with measure. Sentence (ii) replaces the affine P1
triangle by an oriented Q1 quadrilateral mapping, a one-point rank
audit, or a Cea interpolation argument, none of which is asked.

The argument never introduces bilinear hats, never uses a one-point
quad rule, and never estimates interpolation error.

The values $(1,5,4)$ reproduce $1+2x+3y$, with centroid $10/3$, gradient $(2,3)$, and energy $39$. Reversing orientation flips signed $\det J$ only.

FEM:010221.title: Quadratic [0,1] Gauss: K exact at 2 pts, M2 singular on (2,-1,2), exact v^T M v=4/5
FEM:010221.objective: On a quadratic Lagrange element of [0,1] with reference nodes -1,0,1, record the exact stiffness, mass and unit load, show that two-point Gauss is exact for K and the load but produces the singular M2 with kernel (2,-1,2), compare with exact v^T M v=4/5, and conclude that three-point Gauss is required for the mass.
FEM:010221.statement:
Consider the quadratic Lagrange element on the physical interval
$[0,1]$ with nodes $0$, $1/2$, $1$, obtained from the reference
element on $[-1,1]$ with nodes $-1$, $0$, $1$ by $x=(\xi+1)/2$.
The exact element stiffness, consistent mass, and unit-source load
in the physical basis are
\begin{align*}
K&=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}7&-8&1\\-8&16&-8\\1&-8&7\end{pmatrix},\\
M&=\frac1{30}\begin{pmatrix}4&2&-1\\2&16&2\\-1&2&4\end{pmatrix},\\
f&=\bigl(1/6,\,2/3,\,1/6\bigr).
\end{align*}

1. Confirm these three exact arrays by integrating the standard
   quadratic hats (or by quoting a fully expanded antiderivative).
   In particular check that the stiffness row sums vanish and that
   the load entries are the integrals of the three hats.

2. Apply the two-point Gauss rule (reference nodes $\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$,
   weights $1,1$, pulled back by the Jacobian $1/2$). Prove that this
   rule is exact for $K$ and for $f$, but that the resulting mass is
   \[
   M_2
   =\frac1{18}\begin{pmatrix}2&2&-1\\2&8&2\\-1&2&2\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

3. Show that $v=(2,-1,2)$ lies in the kernel of $M_2$. Using the
   exact mass, prove that the same vector satisfies
   $v^TMv=4/5$. Conclude that two-point Gauss is not exact for $M$
   and that a three-point rule (exact for degree $5$, hence for the
   degree-$4$ mass integrands) is required to recover $M$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $M_2v=0$, the exact energy
   $v^TMv$ is also $0$, so two-point Gauss is good enough for the
   mass”; (ii) “three-point Gauss is required for $K$ as well, or
   this is a consistent-mass heat generalized eigenproblem /
   lumped-mass backward-Euler / Neumann-mode exercise.”

Do not replace the quadrature audit by a heat-spectrum calculation,
mass lumping in time, or an incompressible mixed method.
permittedResults: A two-point Gauss mass on this quadratic element admits the nontrivial kernel vector $(2,-1,2)$. The exact mass is positive definite on the same vector, with $v^TMv=4/5$.

Exactness of an $n$-point Gauss rule for degree $2n-1$ is the reason three points recover $M$ while two points already recover $K$ and $f$. This is a quadrature statement, not a spectral statement about a heat operator.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare polynomial degrees: N'N' and N are degree <=2, while N N is degree 4, then evaluate the two-point pullback only for M.
Multiply the stated M2 and M by v=(2,-1,2) to separate the discrete kernel from the exact energy 4/5.

milestones.criterion: Records the exact K, M, and unit load and shows that two-point Gauss reproduces K and the load.
Produces M2=(1/18)[[2,2,-1],[2,8,2],[-1,2,2]], exhibits the kernel vector (2,-1,2), and computes exact v^T M v=4/5.
Concludes that three-point Gauss is required for the mass and refuses a heat-spectrum or lumping substitution.

commonErrors.description: Claims that two-point Gauss integrates the degree-4 mass products exactly, or identifies M2 with the exact mass M.
commonErrors.consequence: The distinction between K (exact at two points) and M (not exact at two points) is erased.

commonErrors.description: Misses the kernel vector (2,-1,2) of M2, or concludes that exact v^T M v vanishes because M2 v=0, or says three-point Gauss is required for K.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned energy 4/5 is lost, or the degree count for stiffness versus mass is reversed.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $N_1=2x^2-3x+1$ to get $N_1'=4x-3$. Then $\int_0^1(4x-3)^2\,dx=7/3$, which is the $(1,1)$ entry of $K$.
Two-point pullback: $\hat N_2(\pm 1/\sqrt{3})=2/3$ and $\hat N_1(1/\sqrt{3})=((1/3)-1/\sqrt{3})/2$. The physical mass multiplies by the Jacobian $1/2$.
For $v=(2,-1,2)$, the exact product $Mv=(1/30)(4,-8,4)$ and $v^TMv=24/30=4/5$. Three-point Gauss integrates degree $5$.

FEM:010221.canonicalSolution:
The physical hats on $[0,1]$ are
\[
N_1=2x^2-3x+1,\qquad
N_2=4x(1-x),\qquad
N_3=2x^2-x,
\]
with derivatives $N_1'=4x-3$, $N_2'=4-8x$, $N_3'=4x-1$. Direct
integration produces
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1(N_1')^2&=\frac73,&
\int_0^1 N_1'N_2'&=-\frac83,&
\int_0^1 N_1'N_3'&=\frac13,\\
\int_0^1(N_2')^2&=\frac{16}3,&
\int_0^1 N_2'N_3'&=-\frac83,&
\int_0^1(N_3')^2&=\frac73,
\end{align*}
which is the stated stiffness $K$. The row sums of $K$ vanish, as
required for a pure derivative form. The mass integrals are the
standard quadratic formula
\[
M=\frac1{30}\begin{pmatrix}4&2&-1\\2&16&2\\-1&2&4\end{pmatrix},
\]
and the unit loads are
\[
\int_0^1 N_1=\frac16,\qquad
\int_0^1 N_2=\frac23,\qquad
\int_0^1 N_3=\frac16.
\]
\[
\boxed{K=(1/3)[[7,-8,1],[-8,16,-8],[1,-8,7]],\quad f=(1/6,2/3,1/6)}.
\]

Two-point Gauss on $[-1,1]$ uses nodes $\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$ and weights
$1,1$. After the affine pullback $dx=d\xi/2$, products of degree at
most $3$ are integrated exactly. Each $N_i'$ is linear, so each
product $N_i'N_j'$ has degree $2$; each hat $N_i$ has degree $2$.
Thus the two-point rule reproduces $K$ and $f$ exactly.

The mass integrands $N_i N_j$ have degree $4$ and are not exact at
two points. Evaluating the reference hats at $\xi=\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$ and
multiplying by the Jacobian $1/2$ produces
\[
M_2
=\frac1{18}\begin{pmatrix}2&2&-1\\2&8&2\\-1&2&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(For a check of the $(1,1)$ entry:
$\hat N_1(\pm 1/\sqrt{3})=(1/3\mp 1/\sqrt{3})/2$, and
$(1/2)\bigl(\hat N_1(a)^2+\hat N_1(-a)^2\bigr)=1/9=2/18$.)
\[
\boxed{M_2=(1/18)[[2,2,-1],[2,8,2],[-1,2,2]]}.
\]

For $v=(2,-1,2)$,
\[
M_2v
=\frac1{18}
\begin{pmatrix}4-2-2\\4-8+4\\-2-2+4\end{pmatrix}
=0.
\]
The same vector is not in the kernel of the exact mass:
\[
Mv
=\frac1{30}\begin{pmatrix}8-2-2\\4-16+4\\-2-2+8\end{pmatrix}
=\frac1{30}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-8\\4\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
v^TMv
=\frac{8+8+8}{30}
=\frac45.
\]
\[
\boxed{M_2v=0,\quad v^TMv=4/5}.
\]
A three-point Gauss rule is exact for degree $5$ and therefore
integrates every degree-$4$ mass product exactly. Two points do not
suffice for $M$; they already suffice for $K$ and for the unit load.

Sentence (i) transfers the kernel of $M_2$ to the exact mass and
concludes that two-point Gauss is acceptable. That claim contradicts
$v^TMv=4/5>0$. Sentence (ii) demands three points for the stiffness
as well, contradicting the degree count, or else replaces the
quadrature audit by a consistent-mass heat generalized eigenproblem,
a lumped-mass backward-Euler step, or a Neumann-mode calculation,
which is not asked.

The argument never forms a generalized spectrum $Kx=\lambda Mx$,
never lumps $M$, and never discusses incompressible mixed methods.

graderFixtures.proofText: Two-point Gauss is exact for every polynomial of degree 4 on this element, so M2 equals the exact mass M. I do not distinguish stiffness products from mass products.
Because M2 v=0 for v=(2,-1,2), I claim the exact energy v^T M v is also 0 instead of 4/5.

FEM:010222.title: Cubic Hermite cantilever L=2, EI=6, q=12 has tip (4,8/3), support residual (-24,-24), midpoint 4/3 not 17/12
FEM:010222.objective: Assemble the given cubic Hermite Euler-Bernoulli element, reduce the clamp at node 1, solve (w2,theta2)=(4,8/3), recover support residuals (-24,-24), and compare the FE midpoint 4/3 with the exact quartic value 17/12 without claiming pointwise exactness from a matching tip.
FEM:010222.statement:
Consider one Euler--Bernoulli beam element of length $L=2$ and
bending stiffness $EI=6$, with cubic Hermite interpolation of the
transverse displacement $w$. The four element degrees of freedom are
$(w_1,\theta_1,w_2,\theta_2)$, ordered from node 1 at $x=0$ to node 2
at $x=L$. Adopt the standing sign convention that $w$ is positive
downward and $\theta$ is the compatible rotation $\theta=dw/dx$. In
that convention the element stiffness is given as
\[
K=\begin{bmatrix}
9&9&-9&9\\
9&12&-9&6\\
-9&-9&9&-9\\
9&6&-9&12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
A uniform distributed load of intensity $q=12$ acts in the positive
$w$ direction. The consistent nodal load is
\[
f=(12,4,12,-4).
\]
Node 1 is clamped: $w_1=\theta_1=0$. Node 2 is free.

1. Extract the free $2\times 2$ block on $(w_2,\theta_2)$ and the
   corresponding load entries. Solve
   \[
   \begin{bmatrix}9&-9\\-9&12\end{bmatrix}
   \begin{bmatrix}w_2\\ \theta_2\end{bmatrix}
   =
   \begin{bmatrix}12\\ -4\end{bmatrix}
   \]
   and prove $(w_2,\theta_2)=(4,8/3)$.

2. Form the discrete residual $r=Ku-f$ on the full four-vector
   $u=(0,0,4,8/3)$. Prove that the free residuals vanish and that the
   support residual (shear, moment) at the clamp is $(-24,-24)$ in
   the same sign convention as the rows of $K$. Interpret the pair
   statically: the total load is $qL=24$ downward, so the support
   force in the $+w$ direction is $-24$; the load moment about the
   clamp tends to increase $\theta$, so the support moment in the
   $+\theta$ direction is $-24$. Do not replace this residual by a
   continuum identification $M=\pm EI w''$ that is not computed here.

3. On the element the cubic Hermite interpolant of these nodal values
   has midpoint value $w_{\mathrm{FE}}(1)=4/3$. The exact strong-form
   solution of $EI\,w''''=q$ with the same clamp and the same free-end
   conditions $w''(L)=w'''(L)=0$ is the quartic
   \[
   w_{\mathrm{ex}}(x)=\frac{x^4}{12}-\frac23 x^3+2x^2,
   \]
   which satisfies $w_{\mathrm{ex}}(2)=4$, $w_{\mathrm{ex}}'(2)=8/3$,
   and $w_{\mathrm{ex}}(1)=17/12$. Prove the midpoint comparison
   $4/3\neq 17/12$. Matching tip data therefore does not make the
   cubic field pointwise exact.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the consistent couple at node 2 may be
   dropped, or the load may be lumped as $(12,0,12,0)$, and the tip
   is then still $(4,8/3)$”; (ii) “because the tip matches the
   exact quartic, the cubic element is the exact solution everywhere,
   so the midpoint must be $17/12$.”

Do not replace the beam by a variable-rigidity axial bar, and do not
invoke a Q1 quadrilateral mapping or a Cea interpolation estimate.
permittedResults: Elimination of a homogeneous essential pair $(w_1,\theta_1)=(0,0)$ reduces $Ku=f$ to the trailing principal $2\times 2$ block acting on $(w_2,\theta_2)$.

A cubic polynomial that matches a genuine quartic at the two ends, including slopes, need not match the quartic at the midpoint. Nodal exactness of a computed tip is not pointwise exactness of the field.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate the clamped pair, solve the 2x2 by substitution, multiply Ku-f for the residual, then evaluate Hermite and the given quartic at x=1.
First check that the given K and f match EI/L^3 and qL/2 times the standard integer patterns, then run the same reduction and the midpoint comparison.

milestones.criterion: Reduces the clamp and solves the free block to (w2,theta2)=(4,8/3), then recovers the support residual (-24,-24) as the first two entries of Ku-f.
Evaluates the cubic Hermite midpoint 4/3, compares it with the exact quartic value 17/12, and refuses to read a matching tip as pointwise exactness.
Rejects lumped or couple-dropped loads and refuses reserved axial-bar, Q1-mapping, and Cea substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the consistent couples $\pm 4$, lumps the uniform load to $(12,0,12,0)$, or otherwise replaces $f_f=(12,-4)$ before solving the free block.
commonErrors.consequence: The tip $(4,8/3)$ and the support residual $(-24,-24)$ are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats the matching tip $(4,8/3)$ as proof that the cubic field equals the exact quartic, and reports the midpoint as $17/12$ rather than $4/3$.
commonErrors.consequence: The required distinction between nodal agreement and pointwise exactness disappears.

hintTree.content: The free block is the lower-right $2\times 2$ of $K$, namely $[[9,-9],[-9,12]]$, loaded by $(12,-4)$. The first row says $w_2-\theta_2=4/3$.
With $u=(0,0,4,8/3)$, the first row of $Ku$ is $-9\cdot 4+9\cdot(8/3)=-12$. Subtract $f_1=12$ to get residual $-24$.
Hermite evaluation at $\xi=x/L=1/2$ uses $N_3=1/2$ and $N_4=L(-1/8)=-1/4$, hence $w(1)=(1/2)\cdot 4+(-1/4)\cdot(8/3)=4/3$. The quartic at $x=1$ is $1/12-2/3+2=17/12$.

FEM:010222.canonicalSolution:
The given stiffness is the standard cubic Hermite Euler--Bernoulli
matrix in the downward-positive, $\theta=dw/dx$ convention:
$EI/L^3=6/8=3/4$, and $12\cdot(3/4)=9$, $6L\cdot(3/4)=9$,
$4L^2\cdot(3/4)=12$, $2L^2\cdot(3/4)=6$. The consistent load for
uniform $q=12$ is
\[
\frac{qL}{2}\Bigl(1,\frac L6,1,-\frac L6\Bigr)=(12,4,12,-4).
\]
Clamping node 1 sets $w_1=\theta_1=0$ and leaves the free block
\[
K_{\mathrm{ff}}=\begin{bmatrix}9&-9\\-9&12\end{bmatrix},\qquad
f_{\mathrm{f}}=(12,-4).
\]
The first equation is $9w_2-9\theta_2=12$, or $w_2-\theta_2=4/3$.
The second is $-9w_2+12\theta_2=-4$. Substitute $w_2=\theta_2+4/3$:
\[
-9\Bigl(\theta_2+\frac43\Bigr)+12\theta_2=-4
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
3\theta_2-12=-4
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\theta_2=\frac83,
\]
hence $w_2=8/3+4/3=4$.
\[
\boxed{(w_2,\theta_2)=(4,8/3)}.
\]

Now $u=(0,0,4,8/3)$. Direct multiplication gives
\begin{align*}
(Ku)_1&=-9\cdot 4+9\cdot(8/3)=-36+24=-12,\\
(Ku)_2&=-9\cdot 4+6\cdot(8/3)=-36+16=-20,\\
(Ku)_3&=9\cdot 4-9\cdot(8/3)=36-24=12,\\
(Ku)_4&=-9\cdot 4+12\cdot(8/3)=-36+32=-4.
\end{align*}
Subtracting $f=(12,4,12,-4)$ produces
\[
r=Ku-f=(-24,-24,0,0).
\]
The free residuals vanish, as required by the reduced solve. The
support residual in the convention of the rows of $K$ is therefore
the shear/moment pair $(-24,-24)$. Statically, $qL=24$ downward so
the clamp must supply force $-24$ in the $+w$ direction; the load
tends to increase $\theta$ with moment $qL^2/2=24$, so the clamp
must supply moment $-24$ in the $+\theta$ direction. This packet
does not identify those residuals with a continuum formula
$M=\pm EI w''$ beyond the discrete residual $Ku-f$.
\[
\boxed{r=(-24,-24,0,0)}.
\]

On $[0,L]$ the cubic Hermite field with vanishing left data is
$w(\xi)=N_3(\xi)w_2+N_4(\xi)\theta_2$, $\xi=x/L$,
$N_3=3\xi^2-2\xi^3$, $N_4=L(-\xi^2+\xi^3)$. At the midpoint
$\xi=1/2$ one has $N_3=1/2$ and $N_4=L(-1/8)=-1/4$, so
\[
w_{\mathrm{FE}}(1)=\frac12\cdot 4+\Bigl(-\frac14\Bigr)\cdot\frac83
=\frac43.
\]
The displayed quartic satisfies $EI w''''=6\cdot 2=12=q$,
$w(0)=w'(0)=0$, and $w''(2)=w'''(2)=0$. Its tip values are
$w(2)=4$ and $w'(2)=8/3$, matching the discrete tip, but
\[
w_{\mathrm{ex}}(1)=\frac1{12}-\frac23+2=\frac{17}{12}\neq\frac43.
\]
A cubic that matches a quartic at the endpoints, including slopes,
is not that quartic. Matching tip data is not pointwise exactness.
\[
\boxed{w_{\mathrm{FE}}(1)=4/3,\quad w_{\mathrm{ex}}(1)=17/12}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the consistent couples $\pm 4$ or lumps the load
to $(12,0,12,0)$. Either change replaces $f_{\mathrm{f}}$ by $(12,0)$
and destroys $(w_2,\theta_2)=(4,8/3)$. Sentence (ii) infers
pointwise exactness from the matching tip and reports the midpoint
$17/12$ as the FE value, contradicting the Hermite evaluation $4/3$.

The argument never replaces the beam by a variable-rigidity axial
bar, never maps a Q1 quadrilateral, and never quotes a Cea lemma.

graderFixtures.proofText: The free block $[[9,-9],[-9,12]]$ loaded by $(12,-4)$ yields $(w_2,\theta_2)=(4,8/3)$. Then $Ku-f=(-24,-24,0,0)$. The cubic Hermite midpoint is $4/3$, while the exact quartic has $w(1)=17/12$. A matching tip is not pointwise exactness.
Uniform load may be lumped to the translations, so I take f=(12,0,12,0) and drop the consistent couples. The free system is then [[9,-9],[-9,12]](w2,theta2)=(12,0), which I solve in place of (4,8/3).
The computed tip equals the exact quartic tip (4,8/3), therefore the cubic Hermite field is the exact solution at every x. In particular the midpoint is 17/12, not 4/3.

FEM:010323.title: Two CCW triangles on the unit square give K with free u2=u4=1/2 and reactions r1=-1/2, r3=1/2
FEM:010323.objective: Scatter two counterclockwise linear triangles on the unit square for unit diffusion, impose u1=0 and u3=1, solve the free pair u2=u4=1/2, and recover reactions r1=-1/2, r3=1/2 with vanishing free residuals and reaction sum 0.
FEM:010323.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,1)^2$ be the closed unit square with nodes
\[
x_1=(0,0),\quad x_2=(1,0),\quad x_3=(1,1),\quad x_4=(0,1).
\]
Split $\Omega$ into two linear triangles with counterclockwise
connectivity $T_1=(1,2,3)$ and $T_2=(1,3,4)$. The discrete problem is
unit diffusion (conductivity $1$) with zero source: the bilinear form
is $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$, and the load vector is $f=0$.
Essential data are $u_1=0$ and $u_3=1$. Nodes $2$ and $4$ are free
(homogeneous natural conditions in the discrete system).

1. On each triangle of area $A=1/2$, form the standard linear-element
   stiffness $K_{ij}^{(T)}=(1/(4A))(b_i b_j+c_i c_j)$ with
   $b_i=y_j-y_k$ and $c_i=x_k-x_j$ in cyclic order. Assemble by
   scatter in the given counterclockwise orientation and prove that
   the global matrix is
   \[
   K=\begin{bmatrix}
   1&-1/2&0&-1/2\\
   -1/2&1&-1/2&0\\
   0&-1/2&1&-1/2\\
   -1/2&0&-1/2&1
   \end{bmatrix}.
   \]

2. Impose $u_1=0$, $u_3=1$ and solve the free $2\times 2$ system for
   $(u_2,u_4)$. Prove $u_2=u_4=1/2$.

3. Compute the residual $r=Ku$ (since $f=0$). Prove $r_2=r_4=0$,
   $r_1=-1/2$, $r_3=1/2$, and $r_1+r_2+r_3+r_4=0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “orientation is cosmetic, so a clockwise
   listing of either triangle may be scattered without recomputing
   $(b_i,c_i)$, and $K_{13}$ need not be checked”; (ii) “after
   setting $u_1=0$ and $u_3=1$ one may delete those rows of $K$
   without moving the known columns to the right-hand side, or the
   reactions need not sum to zero because the mesh is only two
   triangles.”

Require an explicit local-to-global scatter. Do not replace the mesh
by a three-element axial bar, and do not invoke a Q1 quadrilateral
or an inf-sup checkerboard.
permittedResults: Each of the present right triangles has area $1/2$, so $1/(4A)=1/2$ and $K_{ij}=(1/2)(b_i b_j+c_i c_j)$.
A constant field has zero energy for pure diffusion, so $K\mathbf{1}=0$. Consequently the residual $Ku$ is orthogonal to $(1,1,1,1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute (b,c) on each CCW triangle, write the two local 3x3 matrices, scatter, then reduce the free rows with u1=0 and u3=1.
Use K 1=0 as a running checksum on the assembled matrix and on the residual, then evaluate the two free rows directly.

milestones.criterion: Builds both counterclockwise local stiffnesses and scatters them to the stated global K, including K_13=0.
Solves u2=u4=1/2 and recovers r=(-1/2,0,1/2,0) with vanishing free residuals and reaction sum 0.
Rejects orientation-free assembly and omitted column transfer, and refuses reserved axial-bar, Q1, and checkerboard substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats triangle orientation as cosmetic, scatters a clockwise listing with the counterclockwise $(b,c)$ table, or fails to check that $K_{13}$ remains $0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The assembled $K$ is no longer the required four-by-four matrix, so the later solve is not the assigned problem.

commonErrors.description: Deletes rows and columns of the essential nodes without transferring $K_{*3}u_3$ to the right-hand side, or reports reactions that do not sum to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The free solution $u_2=u_4=1/2$ and the reaction pair $r_1=-1/2$, $r_3=1/2$ are lost.

hintTree.content: After scatter, row 2 of $Ku=0$ with $u_1=0$ and $u_3=1$ collapses to $u_2-1/2=0$. Row 4 likewise gives $u_4=1/2$.
Then $(Ku)_1=-1/2$ and $(Ku)_3=1/2$. The four residuals sum to zero because $K$ annihilates constants.

FEM:010323.canonicalSolution:
Both triangles have area $A=1/2$, so $1/(4A)=1/2$.

On $T_1$ the vertices are $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$. Cyclic differences
give
\[
(b,c)_1=(-1,0),\quad (b,c)_2=(1,-1),\quad (b,c)_3=(0,1).
\]
Hence the local matrix in order $(1,2,3)$ is
\[
K^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}
1/2&-1/2&0\\
-1/2&1&-1/2\\
0&-1/2&1/2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
On $T_2$ the vertices are $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(0,1)$, and
\[
(b,c)_1=(0,-1),\quad (b,c)_3=(1,0),\quad (b,c)_4=(-1,1)
\]
in global labels, so the local matrix in order $(1,3,4)$ is
\[
K^{(2)}=\begin{bmatrix}
1/2&0&-1/2\\
0&1/2&-1/2\\
-1/2&-1/2&1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Scatter $K^{(1)}$ into indices $(1,2,3)$ and $K^{(2)}$ into
$(1,3,4)$. The diagonal becomes
$K_{11}=1/2+1/2=1$, $K_{22}=1$, $K_{33}=1/2+1/2=1$, $K_{44}=1$.
The only nonzero off-diagonal couplings are the four edge pairs
$(1,2)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,4)$, and $(4,1)$, each equal to $-1/2$, while
the diagonal $K_{13}$ receives $0+0=0$. The assembled matrix is
therefore the stated $K$.
\[
\boxed{K_{11}=K_{22}=K_{33}=K_{44}=1,\ K_{13}=K_{24}=0,\
\text{edge entries }-1/2}.
\]

Insert $u_1=0$, $u_3=1$, $f=0$. The free rows are
\begin{align*}
u_2-\tfrac12 u_3&=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad u_2=\tfrac12,\\
-\tfrac12 u_3+u_4&=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad u_4=\tfrac12.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{u=(0,1/2,1,1/2)}.
\]
The residual $r=Ku$ is
\begin{align*}
r_1&=-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=-\tfrac12,\\
r_2&=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cdot 1=0,\\
r_3&=-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12+1-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12,\\
r_4&=-\tfrac12\cdot 1+\tfrac12=0.
\end{align*}
Free residuals vanish. The reactions are $r_1=-1/2$ and $r_3=1/2$,
and $r_1+r_2+r_3+r_4=0$, as required by $K\mathbf{1}=0$.
\[
\boxed{r=(-1/2,0,1/2,0)}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats orientation as cosmetic. Reusing a
counterclockwise $(b,c)$ table on a clockwise listing flips the
area sign or permutes the local rows, and can pollute $K_{13}$.
The required matrix is the scatter of the two displayed local
blocks, not an orientation-free guess. Sentence (ii) deletes the
essential rows of $K$ without moving the known columns $K_{*3}u_3$
to the right-hand side, or denies $r_1+r_3=0$. Either mistake
loses $u_2=u_4=1/2$ or the reaction pair $(-1/2,1/2)$.

The mesh is not a three-element axial bar, not a single Q1
quadrilateral, and not a Stokes checkerboard.

graderFixtures.proofText: CCW scatter of $T_1=(1,2,3)$ and $T_2=(1,3,4)$ produces the stated $K$. With $u_1=0$ and $u_3=1$ one gets $u_2=u_4=1/2$ and $r=Ku=(-1/2,0,1/2,0)$. Free residuals vanish and the reactions sum to zero.
Orientation does not matter, so I scatter T1 as (1,3,2) with the same (b,c) numbers I computed for (1,2,3). I do not recompute area signs and I do not check that K_13 stays 0.
I delete the prescribed rows and columns but never move the nonzero Dirichlet column contribution onto the free right-hand side.

FEM:010324.title: MPC u3=u1+u2 with K=diag(2,3,4) reduces to q=(7/13,9/13) and lambda=-12/13
FEM:010324.objective: Apply the transformation T=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]] to K=diag(2,3,4) and f=(2,3,4), solve Kr q=fr for q=(7/13,9/13), recover u=(7/13,9/13,16/13), identify Ku-f=(12/13)C, and read lambda=-12/13 from the KKT stationarity condition.
FEM:010324.statement:
Consider three unconstrained degrees of freedom with
\[
K=\mathrm{diag}(2,3,4),\qquad f=(2,3,4)
\]
and the linear multipoint constraint $u_3=u_1+u_2$. Write the
constraint as $Cu=0$ with $C=(-1,-1,1)$. A basis for the admissible
displacements is the reduced coordinate $q=(q_1,q_2)$ through
\[
u=Tq,\qquad
T=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix},
\]
so that $u=(q_1,q_2,q_1+q_2)$.

1. Form the reduced operators $K_r=T^{\mathsf T}KT$ and
   $f_r=T^{\mathsf T}f$. Prove
   \[
   K_r=\begin{bmatrix}6&4\\ 4&7\end{bmatrix},\qquad f_r=(6,7).
   \]

2. Solve $K_r q=f_r$ and prove $q=(7/13,9/13)$. Recover
   \[
   u=Tq=\Bigl(\frac7{13},\frac9{13},\frac{16}{13}\Bigr).
   \]

3. Compute the unconstrained residual $Ku-f$ and prove
   \[
   Ku-f=\Bigl(-\frac{12}{13},-\frac{12}{13},\frac{12}{13}\Bigr)
   =\frac{12}{13}\,C^{\mathsf T}.
   \]
   The first-order KKT stationarity condition for minimizing
   $\tfrac12 u^{\mathsf T}Ku-f^{\mathsf T}u$ subject to $Cu=0$ is
   $Ku-f+C^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0$. Deduce $\lambda=-12/13$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the constraint $u_3=u_1+u_2$ is
   enforced by adding row 3 of $K$ into row 1 (or into row 2) and
   deleting row 3, without forming $T^{\mathsf T}KT$”; (ii) “the
   reduced load may be taken as the first two entries of $f$, so
   $f_r=(2,3)$, because the third force is already absorbed by the
   constraint.”

Do not replace the MPC by a pair of nonzero Dirichlet values, and do
not treat the Schur complement of an interior node as the same
reduction.
permittedResults: For diagonal $K=\mathrm{diag}(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ and the present $T$, one has $KT=[[k_1,0],[0,k_2],[k_3,k_3]]$ and $K_r=[[k_1+k_3,k_3],[k_3,k_2+k_3]]$.
The identity $T^{\mathsf T}C^{\mathsf T}=0$ forces the reduced residual $T^{\mathsf T}(Ku-f)$ to vanish whenever $u=Tq$ solves $K_r q=f_r$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply T^T K T and T^T f first, solve the 2x2, then identify Ku-f as a multiple of C^T.
Solve the KKT system (K, C^T; C, 0)(u,lambda)=(f,0) directly and check that u lies in the column space of T.

milestones.criterion: Forms Kr=[[6,4],[4,7]] and fr=(6,7), then solves q=(7/13,9/13) and recovers u=(7/13,9/13,16/13).
Shows Ku-f=(12/13)C^T and reads lambda=-12/13 from KKT stationarity.
Rejects illegal row merging and omitted load transformation, and refuses Dirichlet-elimination or condensation substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Enforces $u_3=u_1+u_2$ by adding row 3 of $K$ into another row and deleting row 3, instead of forming $T^{\mathsf T}KT$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced operator is not $[[6,4],[4,7]]$, so $q=(7/13,9/13)$ is not obtained.

commonErrors.description: Takes the reduced load to be the first two entries $(2,3)$ of $f$, omitting $f_r=T^{\mathsf T}f=(6,7)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced solve and the multiplier $\lambda=-12/13$ are lost.

hintTree.content: $KT=[[2,0],[0,3],[4,4]]$. Left-multiplying by $T^{\mathsf T}$ adds the third row of $KT$ into both reduced rows, giving $[[6,4],[4,7]]$.

FEM:010324.canonicalSolution:
Compute $KT=\mathrm{diag}(2,3,4)\,T=[[2,0],[0,3],[4,4]]$. Then
\[
K_r=T^{\mathsf T}(KT)
=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\ 0&1&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\\ 4&4\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}6&4\\ 4&7\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The load transform is
\[
f_r=T^{\mathsf T}f=(2+4,\,3+4)=(6,7).
\]
\[
\boxed{K_r=[[6,4],[4,7]],\quad f_r=(6,7)}.
\]
Solve $6q_1+4q_2=6$ and $4q_1+7q_2=7$. Multiplying the first
equation by $7$ and the second by $4$ and subtracting yields
$26q_1=14$, so $q_1=7/13$. Back-substitution gives
$4\cdot(7/13)+7q_2=7$, hence $7q_2=63/13$ and $q_2=9/13$. Then
$u_3=q_1+q_2=16/13$.
\[
\boxed{q=(7/13,9/13),\quad u=(7/13,9/13,16/13)}.
\]
The unconstrained residual is
\[
Ku-f=\Bigl(\frac{14}{13}-2,\,\frac{27}{13}-3,\,\frac{64}{13}-4\Bigr)
=\Bigl(-\frac{12}{13},-\frac{12}{13},\frac{12}{13}\Bigr)
=\frac{12}{13}\,C^{\mathsf T}.
\]
KKT stationarity $Ku-f+C^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0$ therefore forces
$(12/13)+\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=-12/13$. As a check,
$T^{\mathsf T}(Ku-f)=(0,0)$, which is the reduced equilibrium
$K_r q-f_r=0$.
\[
\boxed{Ku-f=(12/13)C^{\mathsf T},\quad\lambda=-12/13}.
\]

Sentence (i) is illegal row merging: adding row 3 of $K$ into row 1
and deleting row 3 produces a $2\times 3$ or inconsistently reduced
matrix that is not $T^{\mathsf T}KT$. Sentence (ii) omits the load
transform and takes $f_r=(2,3)$ instead of $T^{\mathsf T}f=(6,7)$.
Either error loses $q=(7/13,9/13)$ and the multiplier $-12/13$.

The constraint is not a pair of nonzero Dirichlet values, and $K_r$
is not the Schur complement of an interior unknown.

graderFixtures.proofText: I enforce u3=u1+u2 by adding row 3 of K into row 1 and deleting row 3. I never form T^T K T, and I treat that merged 2x3 (or 2x2) block as the reduced stiffness.
The third force is absorbed by the constraint, so I take fr=(2,3) from the first two entries of f and skip T^T f=(6,7). I solve Kr q=(2,3) instead of (6,7).

FEM:010325.title: Condensing internal dof 3 from the given 3x3 yields boundary (7/5,57/35) and internal 52/35
FEM:010325.objective: Form the Schur complement Kbar=[[16/5,-7/5],[-7/5,14/5]] and condensed load fbar=(11/5,13/5), solve the boundary pair (7/5,57/35), recover the internal value 52/35, confirm det Kbar=7 and a vanishing full residual, and record that condensation changes both matrix and load before recovery.
FEM:010325.statement:
Partition three degrees of freedom as boundary $(u_1,u_2)$ and
internal $u_3$, with
\[
K=\begin{bmatrix}
4&-1&-2\\
-1&3&-1\\
-2&-1&5
\end{bmatrix},\qquad
f=(1,2,3).
\]
No essential condition is imposed; the internal unknown is to be
eliminated by static condensation.

1. Write the block partition $K_{bb}$, $K_{bi}$, $K_{ib}$, $K_{ii}$
   with $K_{ii}=5$. Form the Schur complement
   $K_{\mathrm{bar}}=K_{bb}-K_{bi}K_{ii}^{-1}K_{ib}$ and the condensed
   load $f_{\mathrm{bar}}=f_b-K_{bi}K_{ii}^{-1}f_i$. Prove
   \[
   K_{\mathrm{bar}}=\begin{bmatrix}16/5&-7/5\\ -7/5&14/5\end{bmatrix},
   \qquad
   f_{\mathrm{bar}}=\Bigl(\frac{11}{5},\frac{13}{5}\Bigr),
   \]
   and $\det K_{\mathrm{bar}}=7$.

2. Solve $K_{\mathrm{bar}}u_b=f_{\mathrm{bar}}$ and prove
   $u_b=(7/5,57/35)$. Recover the internal value from
   $u_3=K_{ii}^{-1}(f_i-K_{ib}u_b)$ and prove $u_3=52/35$.

3. Substitute $u=(7/5,57/35,52/35)$ into the original residual
   $Ku-f$ and prove that it is the zero vector. Condensation
   therefore changes both the matrix and the load; the internal
   unknown is recovered afterwards from the condensed boundary
   solution, not by solving the original third row with the
   unreduced $f$ alone.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “it is enough to form $K_{\mathrm{bar}}$
   and keep the original $f_b=(1,2)$, because condensation is a
   matrix-only operation”; (ii) “after $u_b$ is known, $u_3$ may
   be read from the original third equation using the unreduced $f$
   but ignoring the coupling $K_{ib}u_b$, or the whole reduction is
   an inf-sup / locking Schur complement.”

Do not replace condensation by a multipoint constraint $u_3=u_1+u_2$,
and do not invoke a checkerboard or nonlinear tangent.
permittedResults: For a one-dimensional interior block $K_{ii}=5$, one has $K_{ii}^{-1}=1/5$ and $K_{bi}K_{ib}=[[4,2],[2,1]]$, so the rank-one update is $(1/5)[[4,2],[2,1]]$.
The identity $\det K_{\mathrm{bar}}=(16\cdot 14-7\cdot 7)/25=7$ is a scalar checksum on the condensed matrix before the $2\times 2$ solve.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the rank-one Schur update, condense the load with the same K_ii^{-1}, solve the 2x2, then recover u3 and check Ku=f.
Solve the original 3x3 as a checksum first, then reproduce the same triple by condensation plus recovery.

milestones.criterion: Forms Kbar=[[16/5,-7/5],[-7/5,14/5]] and fbar=(11/5,13/5), including the checksum det Kbar=7.
Solves ub=(7/5,57/35), recovers u3=52/35, and verifies that the original residual Ku-f vanishes.
Rejects a matrix-only condensation or an unreduced interior recovery, and refuses MPC, inf-sup, locking, and tangent substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Forms $K_{\mathrm{bar}}$ but keeps the original $f_b=(1,2)$, treating condensation as a matrix-only operation.
commonErrors.consequence: The boundary solve is not $(7/5,57/35)$ and the original residual cannot vanish.

commonErrors.description: After a boundary solve, sets $u_3=f_3/K_{33}=3/5$ while ignoring $K_{ib}u_b$, or relabels the reduction as an inf-sup / locking Schur complement.
commonErrors.consequence: The interior value $52/35$ is lost, or a reserved checkerboard/locking family is imported.

FEM:010325.canonicalSolution:
The blocks are $K_{bb}=[[4,-1],[-1,3]]$, $K_{bi}=(-2,-1)^{\mathsf T}$,
$K_{ib}=(-2,-1)$, and $K_{ii}=5$. Then
\[
K_{bi}K_{ib}=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
K_{\mathrm{bar}}
=\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\ -1&3\end{bmatrix}
-\frac15\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}16/5&-7/5\\ -7/5&14/5\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is
\[
\det K_{\mathrm{bar}}=\frac{16\cdot 14-49}{25}=\frac{175}{25}=7.
\]
The condensed load uses $K_{ii}^{-1}f_i=3/5$:
\[
K_{bi}\cdot\frac35=\Bigl(-\frac65,-\frac35\Bigr),
\qquad
f_{\mathrm{bar}}=(1,2)-\Bigl(-\frac65,-\frac35\Bigr)
=\Bigl(\frac{11}5,\frac{13}5\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{K_{\mathrm{bar}}=[[16/5,-7/5],[-7/5,14/5]],\quad
f_{\mathrm{bar}}=(11/5,13/5),\quad\det=7}.
\]
Clearing the common denominator $5$ produces the integer system
$16u_1-7u_2=11$, $-7u_1+14u_2=13$. From the second equation,
$u_1=2u_2-13/7$. Substitution into the first gives
$32u_2-208/7-7u_2=11$, hence $25u_2=285/7$ and $u_2=57/35$. Then
$u_1=114/35-65/35=49/35=7/5$. Recovery of the interior unknown is
\begin{align*}
u_3
&=\frac15\Bigl(3-(-2,-1)\cdot\Bigl(\frac75,\frac{57}{35}\Bigr)\Bigr)
=\frac15\Bigl(3+\frac{14}5+\frac{57}{35}\Bigr)
=\frac15\cdot\frac{52}7
=\frac{52}{35}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{u_b=(7/5,57/35),\quad u_3=52/35}.
\]
Direct multiplication confirms $Ku=f$:
\begin{align*}
4\cdot\frac75-\frac{57}{35}-2\cdot\frac{52}{35}
&=\frac{196-57-104}{35}=1,\\
-\frac75+3\cdot\frac{57}{35}-\frac{52}{35}
&=\frac{-49+171-52}{35}=2,\\
-2\cdot\frac75-\frac{57}{35}+5\cdot\frac{52}{35}
&=\frac{-98-57+260}{35}=3.
\end{align*}
The full residual is therefore $0$. Condensation changed both the
matrix ($K_{bb}$ became $K_{\mathrm{bar}}$) and the load ($f_b$
became $f_{\mathrm{bar}}$) before the interior value was recovered.

Sentence (i) keeps $f_b=(1,2)$ unreduced. Then the $2\times 2$ solve
is not $(7/5,57/35)$ and the later residual cannot vanish. Sentence
(ii) recovers $u_3$ from $f_3/K_{33}=3/5$ while ignoring $K_{ib}u_b$,
or else relabels the present algebraic Schur complement as an
inf-sup / locking argument. This $3\times 3$ is not a Stokes pair
and is not a nonlinear tangent.

The reduction is not the MPC $u_3=u_1+u_2$ of the previous packet.

graderFixtures.proofText: Static condensation produces $K_{\mathrm{bar}}=[[16/5,-7/5],[-7/5,14/5]]$ and $f_{\mathrm{bar}}=(11/5,13/5)$, with $\det K_{\mathrm{bar}}=7$. The boundary solve is $(7/5,57/35)$ and the recovered interior value is $52/35$. The original residual $Ku-f$ is zero. Both matrix and load change before recovery.
I form the Schur matrix Kbar but keep the original load fb=(1,2). Condensation is a matrix operation, so I solve Kbar ub=(1,2) and never build fbar=(11/5,13/5).
Once ub is known I recover the interior unknown as u3=f3/K33=3/5, ignoring the coupling term K_ib ub.
