FEM:010426.title: Qh=11/4,35/16,131/64 on h=1/2,1/4,1/8 has ratio 4, observed p=2, Richardson value 2, and C=3
FEM:010426.objective: From the three values Qh=11/4,35/16,131/64 fit Q+C h^p, compute successive differences 9/16 and 9/64, read ratio 4 and observed order p=2, form the Richardson value 131/64+(131/64-35/16)/3=2, recover C=3, and refuse to treat the fit as a Cea theorem.
FEM:010426.statement:
A scalar output $Q_h$ is tabulated on three nested mesh sizes:
\[
h=\frac12,\;\frac14,\;\frac18,
\qquad
Q_h=\frac{11}4,\;\frac{35}{16},\;\frac{131}{64}.
\]
Assume the exact three-term model $Q_h=Q+C h^p$ with the same $Q$,
$C$, and $p$ on all three grids (so the model is an ansatz, not a
theorem). The refinement ratio is $r=2$.

1. Form the successive differences
   \[
   Q_{1/2}-Q_{1/4}=\frac9{16},\qquad Q_{1/4}-Q_{1/8}=\frac9{64}.
   \]
   Prove that their ratio is $4$. Under the model $Q_h=Q+C h^p$ this
   ratio equals $r^p$. Deduce the observed order $p=2$, not $p=4$.

2. Apply one Richardson step from the finest pair,
   \[
   Q_{\mathrm{Rich}}=Q_{1/8}+\frac{Q_{1/8}-Q_{1/4}}{r^p-1}
   =\frac{131}{64}+\frac{1}{3}\Bigl(\frac{131}{64}-\frac{35}{16}\Bigr),
   \]
   and prove that the value is $2$. Then recover $C$ from
   $Q_{1/8}=Q+C(1/8)^p$ and prove $C=3$.

3. Verify the model on the two coarser grids:
   $2+3\cdot(1/2)^2=11/4$ and $2+3\cdot(1/4)^2=35/16$. The three
   given numbers therefore lie exactly on $Q+C h^2$ with
   $(Q,C)=(2,3)$. This is a completed fit of the standing ansatz,
   not an a priori error theorem.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the difference ratio is already the
   order, so $p=4$, or the Richardson correction should be added with
   the opposite sign $Q_{1/4}-Q_{1/8}$”; (ii) “observed order $p=2$
   on these three numbers is Cea's lemma, or is the interpolation
   theory of uniform $P_1$ elements for a quadratic, so the residual
   and jumps of a $P_1$ interpolant are being estimated.”

Do not replace the table by a residual-jump estimator, and do not
invoke a heat-mass spectrum.
permittedResults: For $r=2$ and $p=2$ one has $r^p-1=3$, so the displayed correction is exactly one-third of $Q_{1/8}-Q_{1/4}$.
The three-term model with $(Q,C,p)=(2,3,2)$ reproduces $2+3/4=11/4$, $2+3/16=35/16$, and $2+3/64=131/64$ exactly. No remainder is claimed beyond these three nodes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Tabulate the three Qh values, form the two differences, read 2^p from their ratio, then apply the one-third Richardson step and back out C.
Assume Q+C h^2 from the start, solve the 2x2 for (Q,C) on the finest pair, and check the coarsest value as a checksum.

milestones.criterion: Computes the differences 9/16 and 9/64, the ratio 4, and the observed order p=2 rather than p=4.
Forms the Richardson value 2 and recovers C=3, stating that the result is a fit of Q+C h^p and not a Cea or interpolation theorem.
Rejects a sign-reversed correction and refuses reserved Cea/P1 residual-jump and heat-spectrum substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Sets the observed order equal to the raw difference ratio $p=4$, or reverses the Richardson increment by using $Q_{1/4}-Q_{1/8}$ in place of $Q_{1/8}-Q_{1/4}$.
commonErrors.consequence: Either the order is wrong or the extrapolated value is not $2$.

commonErrors.description: Treats the three-value fit as Cea's lemma or as uniform-$P_1$ interpolation theory for a quadratic, including residual and jump identities.
commonErrors.consequence: An asymptotic model on three numbers is overclaimed as a theorem, and a reserved intake family is imported.

hintTree.content: The model says the ratio equals $2^p$, so $p=2$. It does not say that the order equals the ratio $4$.

FEM:010426.canonicalSolution:
The successive differences are
\[
\frac{11}4-\frac{35}{16}=\frac{44-35}{16}=\frac9{16},
\qquad
\frac{35}{16}-\frac{131}{64}=\frac{140-131}{64}=\frac9{64}.
\]
Their ratio is
\[
\frac{9/16}{9/64}=4.
\]
Under $Q_h=Q+C h^p$ with $r=2$ the same ratio equals $2^p$. Therefore
$2^p=4$ and the observed order is $p=2$. The raw ratio $4$ is
$r^p$, not $p$.
\[
\boxed{Q_{1/2}-Q_{1/4}=9/16,\quad Q_{1/4}-Q_{1/8}=9/64,\quad
\text{ratio }4,\quad p=2}.
\]
One Richardson step from the finest pair, using $r^p-1=3$, is
\[
Q_{\mathrm{Rich}}
=\frac{131}{64}+\frac13\Bigl(\frac{131}{64}-\frac{35}{16}\Bigr)
=\frac{131}{64}+\frac13\Bigl(-\frac9{64}\Bigr)
=\frac{131}{64}-\frac{3}{64}
=2.
\]
The model at $h=1/8$ then reads $131/64=2+C/64$, so $C=3$.
Checking the coarser nodes:
\[
2+3\cdot\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2=\frac{11}4,
\qquad
2+3\cdot\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^2=\frac{35}{16}.
\]
The three given values lie exactly on $Q+Ch^2$ with $(Q,C)=(2,3)$.
That statement is a completed algebraic fit of the standing ansatz
on three numbers. It is not a proof that a finite-element error
tends to zero at rate $2$, and it is not Cea's lemma.
\[
\boxed{Q_{\mathrm{Rich}}=2,\quad C=3}.
\]

Sentence (i) either sets $p$ equal to the difference ratio $4$, or
reverses the Richardson increment by using $Q_{1/4}-Q_{1/8}$ in
place of $Q_{1/8}-Q_{1/4}$. The first mistake reports the wrong
order; the second replaces $2$ by $131/64+(9/64)/3=134/64\neq 2$.
Sentence (ii) promotes the fit to Cea's lemma or to the
interpolation theory of uniform $P_1$ elements on a quadratic,
including residual and jump identities. Those are a reserved intake
family and are not implied by three tabulated numbers.

The table is not a residual-jump estimator and is not a generalized
eigenvalue of a heat-mass pair.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differences $9/16$ and $9/64$ have ratio $4$, so the observed order is $p=2$, not $4$. Richardson gives $131/64+(131/64-35/16)/3=2$ and $C=3$. The identity $Q_h=2+3h^2$ is a fit of the standing ansatz on these three grids, not a Cea or $P_1$ interpolation theorem.
The difference ratio is 4, so I report the observed order as p=4 instead of taking log base 2 and obtaining p=2.
I claim that observing p=2 in this three-value fit proves Cea's lemma, rather than treating it as a fit to the stated error model.

FEM:010427.title: Dorfler theta=0.70 on squared indicators (16,4,1,1) marks only {K1} with share 8/11
FEM:010427.objective: On four elements with squared indicators (16,4,1,1) and theta=0.70, prove the Dorfler bulk set of smallest cardinality is uniquely {K1} because 16>=15.4, record the marked share 8/11, and reject the unsquared list (4,2,1,1) that would mark K1+K2. Marking is an allocation, not a proof of exact error reduction.
FEM:010427.statement:
A residual-type estimator on a four-element mesh supplies the
squared local indicators
\[
\eta_{K_1}^2=16,\qquad
\eta_{K_2}^2=4,\qquad
\eta_{K_3}^2=1,\qquad
\eta_{K_4}^2=1.
\]
Write $\eta^2=\sum_{i=1}^4\eta_{K_i}^2$ and $\eta=\sqrt{\eta^2}$.
Dorfler bulk marking with parameter $\theta=0.70$ selects a subset
$\mathcal M$ of elements of smallest cardinality such that
\[
\sum_{K\in\mathcal M}\eta_K^2\ge\theta\,\eta^2.
\]
If several subsets attain that minimal cardinality, every such subset
must be identified.

1. Compute $\eta^2$, $\eta$, and the numerical threshold
   $\theta\eta^2$. Prove that the unique smallest-cardinality Dorfler
   set is $\mathcal M=\{K_1\}$, and that the marked share of the
   squared indicator is $16/22=8/11$.

2. Repeat the cardinality-minimizing construction on the unsquared
   list $(4,2,1,1)$ with the same $\theta=0.70$ (that is, pretend the
   given numbers are $\eta_K$ rather than $\eta_K^2$). Prove that this
   false convention demands the two-element set $\{K_1,K_2\}$.

3. State precisely what the marking decides and what it does not
   decide. In particular, do not claim that marking $\{K_1\}$ reduces
   the exact energy error by the factor $8/11$, and do not convert the
   exercise into a Cea-lemma plus uniform-P1 interpolation-error or
   residual/jump estimator rate proof.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) "because $\sqrt{16}+\sqrt{4}=6$ already
   exceeds $0.70$ times the unsquared total, the marked set must be
   $\{K_1,K_2\}$"; (ii) "Dorfler marking with share $8/11$ proves the
   exact error on the next mesh is at most $3/11$ of the present
   error."

Do not replace the calculation by a variable-rigidity axial-bar weak
form, a Q1 mapping rank audit, or Dirichlet elimination of reactions.
permittedResults: Any Dorfler set for a strictly positive threshold must contain every element whose squared indicator already meets the threshold by itself; a singleton $\{K\}$ is admissible precisely when $\eta_K^2\ge\theta\eta^2$.

If the largest squared indicator is the unique value that meets the threshold, then that singleton is the unique minimal-cardinality Dorfler set, because every set that omits that element has squared mass strictly below the threshold.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the four squared indicators, compare each singleton to 15.4, then prove every complementary set has mass at most 6.
Sort the squared list decreasingly and accumulate until the threshold; then rerun the same greedy pass on (4,2,1,1) as a diagnostic only.

milestones.criterion: Computes eta^2=22, eta=sqrt(22), threshold 15.4, and the unique smallest-cardinality Dorfler set {K1} with share 8/11.
Shows that the unsquared convention (4,2,1,1) spuriously marks {K1,K2}, and refuses to read the share as exact-error reduction.
Rejects Cea / P1 interpolation / residual-jump substitutions and the remaining reserved intake families.

commonErrors.description: Treats the data as unsquared indicators (4,2,1,1), or otherwise marks {K1,K2} as the Dorfler set of the given estimator.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique minimal set {K1} and the share 8/11 are lost, and a two-element refinement set is manufactured.

commonErrors.description: Claims that marking {K1} proves the exact energy error drops by 8/11, or replaces the packet by a Cea plus interpolation / residual-jump rate theorem.
commonErrors.consequence: An indicator allocation is misread as an exact a-posteriori contraction, which this calculation does not prove.

hintTree.content: The four squared indicators add to $22$, so $\eta=\sqrt{22}$ and the Dorfler threshold is $0.70\cdot 22=15.4$.
Compare $16$ with $15.4$. No other single element reaches $15.4$, and $4+1+1=6<15.4$.
On the unsquared list $(4,2,1,1)$ the total is $8$ and the false threshold is $5.6$. Then $4<5.6$ while $4+2=6\ge 5.6$.

FEM:010427.canonicalSolution:
The given data are already squared:
\[
\eta^2=16+4+1+1=22,\qquad\eta=\sqrt{22}.
\]
With $\theta=0.70$,
\[
\theta\eta^2=0.70\cdot 22=15.4.
\]
The singleton $\{K_1\}$ satisfies $16\ge 15.4$. Every other singleton
fails: $4<15.4$ and $1<15.4$. Moreover every set that omits $K_1$ has
squared mass at most $4+1+1=6<15.4$. Therefore every Dorfler set
contains $K_1$, and the unique smallest-cardinality Dorfler set is
\[
\boxed{\mathcal M=\{K_1\}}.
\]
The marked share is
\[
\frac{16}{22}=\frac{8}{11}.
\]
This is strictly larger than $\theta=0.70$, which is allowed: Dorfler
marking asks only for a lower bound on the captured squared mass.

If the same numbers are misread as unsquared indicators
$\eta_{K_1}=4$, $\eta_{K_2}=2$, $\eta_{K_3}=1$, $\eta_{K_4}=1$, the
false total is $8$ and the false threshold is $0.70\cdot 8=5.6$. Then
$4<5.6$, so $\{K_1\}$ is no longer admissible, while
$4+2=6\ge 5.6$. The false construction therefore demands
$\{K_1,K_2\}$. That two-element set is an artifact of dropping the
squares; it is not the Dorfler set of the given estimator.

Marking decides only which elements carry at least the fraction
$\theta$ of the present squared indicator. It does not identify the
exact energy error, does not prove a contraction
$\|u-u_h^{\mathrm{new}}\|\le(1-8/11)\|u-u_h\|$, and does not replace
a Cea argument or a residual/jump interpolation-error analysis. Those
are different theorems, and they are not asked. In particular the
share $8/11$ is not an exact-error reduction factor.

Sentence (i) replaces squared indicators by their square roots and
thereby manufactures the spurious mark $\{K_1,K_2\}$. Sentence (ii)
promotes a marking allocation into a theorem about the exact error on
a refined mesh. Both sentences are false for this packet.

The argument never writes a variable-rigidity axial weak form, never
maps a Q1 quadrilateral, and never eliminates Dirichlet dofs.

graderFixtures.proofText: Squared mass $22$, $\eta=\sqrt{22}$, threshold $15.4$. Unique smallest-cardinality Dorfler set $\{K_1\}$ because $16\ge 15.4$ and every set omitting $K_1$ has mass at most $6$. Marked share $8/11$. Unsquared $(4,2,1,1)$ would mark $\{K_1,K_2\}$ and is the wrong convention. The share is not an exact-error reduction factor.
I take the indicators as 4,2,1,1 without squaring. The total is 8 and 0.70 times 8 is 5.6, so K1 alone is not enough and the Dorfler set is {K1,K2}.
Because {K1} captures 8/11 of the estimator, I claim the exact energy error on the next mesh is at most 3/11 of the present error.

FEM:010528.title: Linearized buckling K phi = P G phi has Pcr=3-sqrt(3) and G-normalized low mode
FEM:010528.objective: For K=[[4,-2],[-2,4]] and G=diag(1,2), derive det(K-P G)=2(P^2-6P+6), loads 3+/-sqrt(3), critical load 3-sqrt(3), low-mode ratio (1+sqrt(3))/2, G-normalize by dividing (1,(1+sqrt(3))/2) by sqrt(3+sqrt(3)), and show the trial (1,1) Rayleigh quotient 4/3 is an upper bound. Audit the determinant sign and the larger root.
FEM:010528.statement:
A two-degree-of-freedom linearized buckling model is the generalized
eigenproblem
\[
K\phi=P\,G\phi,
\qquad
K=\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
G=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both $K$ and $G$ are symmetric positive definite. The physically
critical load is the smallest positive generalized eigenvalue.

1. Expand $\det(K-PG)$ and prove that the characteristic polynomial
   is exactly $2(P^2-6P+6)$. Solve for both loads and prove they are
   $3\pm\sqrt{3}$. Identify the critical load $P_{\mathrm{cr}}=3-\sqrt{3}$.

2. For the critical eigenpair, prove that the component ratio of a
   corresponding eigenvector is
   \[
   \frac{\phi_2}{\phi_1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}.
   \]
   $G$-normalize the representative $\bigl(1,(1+\sqrt{3})/2\bigr)$ by
   dividing it by $\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3}}$, and confirm
   $\phi^{\mathsf T}G\phi=1$ after that scaling.

3. Evaluate the Rayleigh quotient of the trial vector $(1,1)$ and
   prove that it equals $4/3$. Explain why $4/3$ is an upper bound for
   $P_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and is not equal to either exact load.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) "the critical load is the larger root
   $3+\sqrt{3}$, because a determinant computation with the opposite
   sign $\det(PG-K)$ flips which root is smallest"; (ii) "this is a
   consistent-mass heat eigenproblem, so the lowest mode is a Neumann
   constant and $G$ may be replaced by a lumped mass."

Do not replace $G$ by a heat consistent-mass matrix, and do not invoke
Newmark integration or a mixed incompressible tangent.
permittedResults: If $K$ and $G$ are SPD then every generalized eigenvalue is positive and the variational characterization $P_{\mathrm{cr}}=\min_{v\ne 0}(v^{\mathsf T}Kv)/(v^{\mathsf T}Gv)$ holds.
The two conventions $\det(K-PG)=0$ and $\det(PG-K)=0$ differ by a global sign and therefore have the same roots. They do not swap which numerical root is smaller.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand det(K-PG), solve the quadratic, then back-substitute Pcr into the first row and G-normalize.
Compute both Rayleigh extrema on a basis, then match the smaller stationary value to 3-sqrt(3) and the mode ratio to (1+sqrt(3))/2.

milestones.criterion: Derives det(K-PG)=2(P^2-6P+6), loads 3+/-sqrt(3), and critical load 3-sqrt(3).
Obtains the low-mode ratio (1+sqrt(3))/2, the G-normalized representative, and the trial quotient 4/3 as an upper bound.
Audits the determinant-sign / larger-root confusion and refuses heat-spectrum / lumping substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the critical load as 3+sqrt(3), or claims that writing det(PG-K) swaps which root is smallest.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical first-buckling load 3-sqrt(3) is replaced by the higher eigenload, and the low mode is lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces (K,G) by a consistent-mass heat eigenproblem, lumps G, takes a Neumann constant mode, or omits the G-normalization factor sqrt(3+sqrt(3)).
commonErrors.consequence: The geometric-stiffness pair and the normalized mode (1,(1+sqrt(3))/2)/sqrt(3+sqrt(3)) are abandoned.

hintTree.content: Write $K-PG=\bigl(4-P,-2;-2,4-2P\bigr)$. The determinant is $(4-P)(4-2P)-4$.
At $P=3-\sqrt{3}$ the first row gives $(1+\sqrt{3})\phi_1=2\phi_2$.
For $v=(1,1)$ one has $Kv=(2,2)$ so $v^{\mathsf T}Kv=4$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Gv=3$.

FEM:010528.canonicalSolution:
Form
\[
K-PG=\begin{pmatrix}4-P&-2\\-2&4-2P\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is
\begin{align*}
(4-P)(4-2P)-4
&=16-8P-4P+2P^2-4
=2P^2-12P+12
=2(P^2-6P+6).
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\det(K-PG)=2(P^2-6P+6)}.
\]
The quadratic $P^2-6P+6=0$ has discriminant $36-24=12$, so
\[
P=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}=\frac{6\pm 2\sqrt{3}}{2}=3\pm\sqrt{3}.
\]
Both roots are positive. The critical load is the smaller one:
\[
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{cr}}=3-\sqrt{3}}.
\]
The opposite determinant $\det(PG-K)$ equals $-2(P^2-6P+6)$ and has
the same two roots. A global sign change does not promote $3+\sqrt{3}$
into the critical value.

At $P=3-\sqrt{3}$ the $(1,1)$ entry is $4-P=1+\sqrt{3}$. The first
row of $(K-PG)\phi=0$ therefore reads
\[
(1+\sqrt{3})\phi_1-2\phi_2=0,
\qquad
\frac{\phi_2}{\phi_1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}.
\]
Take the representative $v=\bigl(1,(1+\sqrt{3})/2\bigr)$. Then
\begin{align*}
v^{\mathsf T}Gv
&=1\cdot 1^2+2\cdot\Bigl(\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}\Bigr)^2
=1+2\cdot\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2}
=1+2+\sqrt{3}
=3+\sqrt{3}.
\end{align*}
Dividing $v$ by $\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3}}$ produces a $G$-normalized critical
mode
\[
\boxed{\phi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3}}}\Bigl(1,\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}\Bigr)}.
\]

For the trial $w=(1,1)$,
\[
Kw=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
w^{\mathsf T}Kw=4,
\qquad
w^{\mathsf T}Gw=1+2=3,
\]
so the Rayleigh quotient is $4/3$. Because $K$ and $G$ are SPD,
\[
\frac43\ge P_{\mathrm{cr}}=3-\sqrt{3}.
\]
Numerically $4/3\approx 1.333$ and $3-\sqrt{3}\approx 1.268$, so the
trial is a strict upper bound and is not an exact eigenpair (the exact
low-mode ratio is not $1$).

Sentence (i) either selects the larger root or claims that flipping
the determinant sign swaps the identity of the smaller root. Both
readings are false. Sentence (ii) replaces geometric-stiffness
buckling by a consistent-mass heat spectrum, a lumped-mass backward-
Euler reduction, or a Neumann constant mode. Those are different
exercises and are not asked.

The argument never integrates a Newmark step and never forms a mixed
incompressible tangent.

graderFixtures.proofText: Characteristic polynomial $2(P^2-6P+6)$, loads $3\pm\sqrt{3}$, critical load $3-\sqrt{3}$. Low-mode ratio $(1+\sqrt{3})/2$. $G$-normalize by dividing $(1,(1+\sqrt{3})/2)$ by $\sqrt{3+\sqrt{3}}$. Trial $(1,1)$ has Rayleigh quotient $4/3$, a strict upper bound. The larger root is not critical, and $\det(PG-K)$ has the same roots.
I take the critical load to be the larger positive root 3+sqrt(3) instead of the smallest positive root 3-sqrt(3).
I normalize the low mode with its Euclidean norm instead of dividing by sqrt(3+sqrt(3)), so its G-norm is not one.

FEM:010529.title: One Newmark average-acceleration step on m=2,k=8 is u1=3/5 with energy 4
FEM:010529.objective: On the undamped SDOF m=2, k=8, dt=1/2, u0=1, v0=0, a0=-4, take one implicit Newmark step with beta=1/4 and gamma=1/2. Obtain u1=3/5, a1=-12/5, v1=-8/5 by solving equilibrium and the update simultaneously, and prove the discrete energy remains 4. Unconditional stability is not exactness of the trajectory.
FEM:010529.statement:
Consider the undamped free single-degree-of-freedom oscillator
\[
m\ddot u+ku=0,
\qquad m=2,\qquad k=8,
\]
with initial data $u(0)=1$, $\dot u(0)=0$. The consistent initial
acceleration is $a_0=-4$. Advance one step of size $\Delta t=1/2$ by
the implicit Newmark method with $\beta=1/4$ and $\gamma=1/2$
(constant average acceleration):
\begin{align*}
u_1
&=u_0+\Delta t\,v_0+\Delta t^2\bigl[(1/2-\beta)a_0+\beta a_1\bigr],\\
v_1
&=v_0+\Delta t\bigl[(1-\gamma)a_0+\gamma a_1\bigr],\\
m a_1+k u_1
&=0.
\end{align*}
The three update / equilibrium statements are to be solved
simultaneously.

1. Prove that the unique solution of the coupled system is
   $u_1=3/5$, $a_1=-12/5$, $v_1=-8/5$.

2. Define the discrete mechanical energy
   $E_n=\tfrac12 m v_n^2+\tfrac12 k u_n^2$. Prove $E_0=E_1=4$.

3. Explain why unconditional stability of this Newmark pair does not
   make the step exact. In particular, do not claim $u_1=\cos(1)$,
   and do not replace the integrator by a consistent-mass heat
   backward-Euler scheme, with or without mass lumping.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) "first insert $a_1=a_0$ into the
   displacement update, then recover a new $a_1$ from $a=-4u$, then
   update $v$; the implicit step does not need a simultaneous solve";
   (ii) "because the method is unconditionally stable, $u_1$ equals
   the exact value $u(\Delta t)$, or else the energy identity proves
   the whole trajectory is exact."

Do not replace the oscillator by a linearized buckling eigenproblem
and do not invoke mixed incompressible constraints.
permittedResults: On $m\ddot u+ku=0$ one has $a_n=-(k/m)u_n$ at every accepted Newmark state. Here $k/m=4$, so $a=-4u$ may be substituted into the displacement update before solving for $u_1$.

Constant-average-acceleration Newmark is unconditionally stable for linear undamped oscillators and conserves the discrete energy above. Stability and discrete energy conservation do not imply $u_1=u(\Delta t)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute a1=-4 u1 into the beta=1/4 displacement update and finish with the gamma=1/2 velocity update.
Form the effective stiffness m/(beta dt^2)+k=40 acting on the predictor 3/4, recover a1=-12/5, then update u and v.

milestones.criterion: Solves the coupled Newmark / equilibrium system to u1=3/5, a1=-12/5, v1=-8/5.
Proves E0=E1=4 and distinguishes discrete energy conservation from exactness of u(Delta t).
Rejects sequential frozen-a1 updates, stability-as-exactness, and heat / buckling substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Freezes a1=a0 (or otherwise predicts u1 from known data only) instead of solving equilibrium and the Newmark update simultaneously.
commonErrors.consequence: The implicit values u1=3/5, a1=-12/5, v1=-8/5 are replaced by an inconsistent predictor such as u1=1/2.

commonErrors.description: Claims that unconditional stability or the identity E1=E0 makes u1 equal to the exact sample cos(1), or replaces the step by heat BE / mass lumping.
commonErrors.consequence: A discrete conservation property is misread as exactness of the trajectory, or the oscillator is abandoned.

hintTree.content: With $\Delta t=1/2$ and $\beta=1/4$ the displacement update collapses to $u_1=3/4+a_1/16$. Equilibrium forces $a_1=-4u_1$.
Substitute to obtain $u_1=3/4-u_1/4$, hence $(5/4)u_1=3/4$.

FEM:010529.canonicalSolution:
The data $m=2$, $k=8$ give $a=-(k/m)u=-4u$, so the supplied
$a_0=-4$ is consistent with $u_0=1$. Insert $\Delta t=1/2$,
$\beta=1/4$, $v_0=0$, and $a_0=-4$ into the displacement update:
\begin{align*}
u_1
&=1+\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac12-\frac14\Bigr)(-4)+\frac14 a_1\Bigr]
=1+\frac14\Bigl(-1+\frac{a_1}{4}\Bigr)
=\frac34+\frac{a_1}{16}.
\end{align*}
Equilibrium at the new step is $2a_1+8u_1=0$, hence $a_1=-4u_1$.
Substitute:
\[
u_1=\frac34-\frac{u_1}{4},
\qquad
\frac54 u_1=\frac34,
\qquad
u_1=\frac35.
\]
Then $a_1=-4\cdot(3/5)=-12/5$. The velocity update with $\gamma=1/2$
is
\begin{align*}
v_1
&=\frac12\Bigl[\frac12(-4)+\frac12\Bigl(-\frac{12}{5}\Bigr)\Bigr]
=\frac12\Bigl(-2-\frac65\Bigr)
=\frac12\Bigl(-\frac{16}{5}\Bigr)
=-\frac85.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{u_1=3/5,\quad a_1=-12/5,\quad v_1=-8/5}.
\]
These three values satisfy displacement update, velocity update, and
equilibrium at once. A sequential substitute that first freezes
$a_1=a_0$ in the displacement formula produces $u_1=1/2$, which is
not the implicit step.

The energies are
\begin{align*}
E_0
&=\tfrac12\cdot 8\cdot 1^2=4,\\
E_1
&=\tfrac12\cdot 2\cdot\Bigl(-\frac85\Bigr)^2+\tfrac12\cdot 8\cdot\Bigl(\frac35\Bigr)^2
=\frac{64}{25}+\frac{36}{25}
=4.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{E_0=E_1=4}.
\]
Discrete energy conservation is a property of this Newmark pair on a
linear undamped oscillator. It is not a proof that $u_1$ equals the
exact sample $u(\Delta t)=\cos(\omega\Delta t)=\cos(1)$, since
$\omega=\sqrt{k/m}=2$ and $\cos(1)\ne 3/5$. Unconditional stability
likewise bounds the recurrence; it does not make one step exact.

Sentence (i) replaces the simultaneous implicit solve by a predictor
that freezes $a_1=a_0$. Sentence (ii) confuses stability (or discrete
energy conservation) with exactness of the trajectory. Both are
false for this packet.

The argument never replaces the oscillator by a consistent-mass heat
equation, never lumps a mass matrix, never forms a buckling pencil,
and never introduces a mixed incompressible constraint.

graderFixtures.proofText: Simultaneous Newmark / equilibrium solve gives $u_1=3/5$, $a_1=-12/5$, $v_1=-8/5$. Discrete energy $E_0=E_1=4$. Unconditional stability and energy conservation do not make $u_1=\cos(1)$. A frozen-$a_1$ predictor is not the implicit step.
I first set a1=a0=-4 in the displacement update and get u1=1/2. Then I recompute a1=-2 from equilibrium and finally update v. I do not solve the three Newmark statements as one system.
Average acceleration is unconditionally stable, so I claim u1 equals the exact value cos(1) instead of the computed value 3/5.

FEM:010630.title: Two consistent-tangent Newton steps from u0=1/2 give u2=536/511, not the root 1
FEM:010630.objective: For R(u)=u^3+u-2 with J=3u^2+1 and u0=1/2, compute R0=-11/8, J0=7/4, u1=9/7, then recompute R1=484/343, J1=292/49, u2=536/511, and R(u2)=27085850/133432831. The unique exact root is 1 because J>0. Audit increment sign, tangent recomputation, and premature convergence.
FEM:010630.statement:
A scalar residual and its consistent tangent are
\[
R(u)=u^3+u-2,
\qquad
J(u)=R'(u)=3u^2+1.
\]
Newton's method from a current state $u_n$ is the simultaneous linear
solve
\[
J(u_n)\,\Delta u_n=-R(u_n),
\qquad
u_{n+1}=u_n+\Delta u_n.
\]
Start at $u_0=1/2$ and take exactly two consistent-tangent steps
(recompute $J$ at every accepted state).

1. Prove $R(u_0)=-11/8$ and $J(u_0)=7/4$, and that the first update
   is $u_1=9/7$.

2. Recompute the tangent at $u_1$ and prove
   $R(u_1)=484/343$, $J(u_1)=292/49$, and
   $u_2=536/511$. Record the decimal checks
   $536/511\approx 1.0489236791$ and
   \[
   R(u_2)=\frac{27085850}{133432831}\approx 0.2029923955.
   \]

3. Prove that $R$ has a unique real root and that the root is exactly
   $1$. Use $J(u)>0$ for every real $u$. Do not claim that $u_1$ or
   $u_2$ is already that root.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) "the consistent update is
   $u\leftarrow u+R/J$, or else $J$ may be frozen at $7/4$ for the
   second step"; (ii) "two steps are enough to declare convergence to
   the unique root $1$, or the same tangent construction is the mixed
   incompressible consistent tangent for a checkerboard / locking
   element."

Do not replace the scalar residual by an inf-sup Schur complement,
and do not invoke Dorfler marking or Newmark integration.
permittedResults: The Newton increment is $\Delta u=-R(u)/J(u)$. The opposite sign $u\leftarrow u+R/J$ walks uphill on a strictly increasing residual and leaves the attraction basin of the unique root when started at $u_0=1/2$.
Reusing $J(u_0)$ at the second iteration is a frozen-tangent (modified Newton) step, not a consistent-tangent step. It produces a different $u_2$ from $536/511$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply Delta u=-R/J twice, recomputing J at 9/7, and keep every value as an exact rational.
Factor R(u)=(u-1)(u^2+u+2) to lock the unique real root, then run the same two consistent Newton steps as a residual reduction only.

milestones.criterion: Computes R0=-11/8, J0=7/4, u1=9/7 and the recomputed second step R1=484/343, J1=292/49, u2=536/511.
Evaluates R(u2)=27085850/133432831 and identifies the unique exact root 1 from J>0, without declaring u2 converged.
Audits increment sign / frozen tangent / premature convergence and refuses mixed incompressible substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Updates with the wrong sign u <- u+R/J, or reuses J0=7/4 at the second iteration instead of recomputing J(9/7)=292/49.
commonErrors.consequence: The consistent pair (u1,u2)=(9/7,536/511) is lost; a frozen or uphill step is not the requested tangent.

commonErrors.description: Declares u1 or u2 equal to the exact root 1, or replaces the scalar tangent by a mixed incompressible / checkerboard / locking tangent.
commonErrors.consequence: A still-nonzero residual is hidden, or an unrelated inf-sup exercise is imported.

FEM:010630.canonicalSolution:
Evaluate at the given start:
\[
R\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)
=\frac18+\frac12-2
=-\frac{11}{8},
\qquad
J\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)
=\frac34+1
=\frac74.
\]
The consistent increment is
\[
\Delta u_0
=-\frac{R(u_0)}{J(u_0)}
=\frac{11/8}{7/4}
=\frac{11}{14},
\qquad
u_1
=\frac12+\frac{11}{14}
=\frac97.
\]
\[
\boxed{R(u_0)=-11/8,\quad J(u_0)=7/4,\quad u_1=9/7}.
\]
The opposite sign $u_0+R(u_0)/J(u_0)$ would produce $-2/7$ and is not
Newton.

Recompute at $u_1=9/7$:
\begin{align*}
R\Bigl(\frac97\Bigr)
&=\frac{729}{343}+\frac97-2
=\frac{729+441-686}{343}
=\frac{484}{343},\\
J\Bigl(\frac97\Bigr)
&=3\cdot\frac{81}{49}+1
=\frac{292}{49}.
\end{align*}
The second consistent increment is
\[
\frac{R(u_1)}{J(u_1)}
=\frac{484}{343}\cdot\frac{49}{292}
=\frac{121}{511},
\]
hence
\[
u_2
=\frac97-\frac{121}{511}
=\frac{657-121}{511}
=\frac{536}{511}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R(u_1)=484/343,\quad J(u_1)=292/49,\quad u_2=536/511}.
\]
The requested decimal check is $536/511\approx 1.0489236791$. The
residual at this state has denominator $511^3=133432831$ and
numerator
\[
536^3+536\cdot 511^2-2\cdot 511^3=27085850,
\]
so
\[
R(u_2)=\frac{27085850}{133432831}\approx 0.2029923955.
\]
In particular $R(u_2)\ne 0$, so $u_2$ is not the root.

Finally $J(u)=3u^2+1\ge 1>0$ for every real $u$, so $R$ is strictly
increasing. Direct evaluation gives $R(1)=0$. Therefore $1$ is the
unique real root. Neither $u_1=9/7$ nor $u_2=536/511$ equals $1$,
and a nonzero residual at $u_2$ forbids a convergence declaration
after two steps.

Sentence (i) either flips the increment sign or freezes the tangent
at $J(u_0)=7/4$. Sentence (ii) either declares premature convergence
or imports a mixed incompressible consistent tangent, a checkerboard
mode, a Schur complement, or a locking argument. Those are different
exercises.

The argument never marks elements and never takes a Newmark step.

graderFixtures.proofText: First consistent step: $R_0=-11/8$, $J_0=7/4$, $u_1=9/7$. Recomputed second step: $R_1=484/343$, $J_1=292/49$, $u_2=536/511$. Then $R(u_2)=27085850/133432831\ne 0$. Unique exact root is $1$ because $J>0$ and $R(1)=0$. Increment sign and tangent recomputation are required; two steps are not a convergence proof.
I use the wrong Newton increment sign and update by u <- u+R/J instead of u <- u-R/J.
After two steps I declare u2=536/511 to be the exact root 1 even though the recomputed residual is nonzero.

FEM:010631.title: Active-set contact on K[[2,-1],[-1,2]] is u=(0,3/2), lambda=(1/2,0), energy -9/4
FEM:010631.objective: Minimize (1/2)u^T K u - f^T u with K=[[2,-1],[-1,2]], f=(-2,3), and u>=0. Show the unconstrained pair (-1/3,4/3) is infeasible, that the active-set KKT solution is u=(0,3/2), lambda=(1/2,0), energy -9/4, and that naive clipping to (0,4/3) leaves a free residual -1/3 and energy -20/9, so it is not a solve.
FEM:010631.statement:
Minimize the strictly convex quadratic
\[
I(u)=\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Ku-f^{\mathsf T}u,
\qquad
K=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
f=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\]
over the closed cone $u\ge 0$ (componentwise). The KKT system is
\begin{align*}
Ku-f-\lambda&=0,\\
u&\ge 0,\\
\lambda&\ge 0,\\
\lambda_i u_i&=0\quad(i=1,2).
\end{align*}

1. Solve the unconstrained stationarity condition $Ku=f$ and prove
   that the unique unconstrained minimizer is $(-1/3,4/3)$. Explain
   why it is infeasible for the contact problem.

2. Activate the first gap ($u_1=0$) and keep the second gap free
   ($\lambda_2=0$). Solve the resulting $2\times 2$ KKT block and
   prove that
   \[
   u=\bigl(0,3/2\bigr),
   \qquad
   \lambda=\bigl(1/2,0\bigr)
   \]
   is feasible and complementary. Evaluate $I(u)$ and prove that the
   energy equals $-9/4$.

3. Form the naive clip of the unconstrained minimizer onto $u\ge 0$,
   namely $(0,4/3)$. Compute $Ku-f$ at that point and prove that the
   free-node residual is $-1/3$. Evaluate the energy and prove that
   it equals $-20/9$. Conclude that the clip is not a KKT solution.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) "projecting the unconstrained minimizer
   onto $u\ge 0$ solves the contact problem, because the clip
   $(0,4/3)$ already has a nonnegative first component"; (ii) "the
   same saddle is an incompressible checkerboard / inf-sup / Schur /
   locking calculation, or a consistent tangent for a mixed
   nonlinear element."

Do not replace the inequality $u\ge 0$ by a Dirichlet elimination,
and do not invoke Dorfler marking or Newmark integration.
permittedResults: Because $K$ is SPD, $I$ is strictly convex, so the feasible KKT point is the unique global minimizer on $u\ge 0$.

If a candidate has a strictly negative residual on a strictly positive (free) component, it violates stationarity and cannot be a minimizer, regardless of how its energy compares to the unconstrained value.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve Ku=f, discard the infeasible point, then test the active set u1=0, lambda2=0 and verify complementarity.
Compare energies of the three candidates (unconstrained, clip, active-set) and keep only the feasible KKT point.

milestones.criterion: Computes the infeasible unconstrained point (-1/3,4/3) and the KKT pair u=(0,3/2), lambda=(1/2,0) with energy -9/4.
Shows that the clip (0,4/3) leaves free residual -1/3 and energy -20/9 and is not a contact solve.
Rejects clip-as-KKT and incompressible checkerboard / Schur / locking / mixed-tangent substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the contact solution as the clip (0,4/3) of the unconstrained minimizer, or treats a nonnegative projection as a KKT solve.
commonErrors.consequence: A free-node residual -1/3 remains, the energy is -20/9 rather than -9/4, and complementarity fails.

commonErrors.description: Accepts the unconstrained point (-1/3,4/3), or replaces the contact KKT system by a checkerboard / inf-sup / Schur / locking / mixed-tangent argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasible active-set solution is abandoned, or an unrelated incompressible exercise is imported.

hintTree.content: The unconstrained solve is $2u_1-u_2=-2$ and $-u_1+2u_2=3$, hence $(u_1,u_2)=(-1/3,4/3)$.
With $u_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=0$ the second row collapses to $2u_2=3$. The first row then yields $\lambda_1=1/2$.
At the clip $(0,4/3)$ one has $Ku-f=(2/3,-1/3)$. The second residual is the free-node defect $-1/3$.

FEM:010631.canonicalSolution:
Unconstrained stationarity $Ku=f$ is the pair
\[
2u_1-u_2=-2,
\qquad
-u_1+2u_2=3.
\]
The first equation gives $u_2=2u_1+2$. Substitute:
\[
-u_1+2(2u_1+2)=3,
\qquad
3u_1+4=3,
\qquad
u_1=-\frac13,
\qquad
u_2=\frac43.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{unconstrained }(-1/3,4/3)}.
\]
The first component is negative, so the point lies outside $u\ge 0$
and is not admissible.

Now activate $u_1=0$ and set $\lambda_2=0$. The second row of
$Ku-f=\lambda$ becomes
\[
-u_1+2u_2=3,
\qquad
2u_2=3,
\qquad
u_2=\frac32.
\]
The first row becomes
\[
2u_1-u_2+2=\lambda_1,
\qquad
-\frac32+2=\lambda_1,
\qquad
\lambda_1=\frac12.
\]
The pair
\[
\boxed{u=(0,3/2),\qquad\lambda=(1/2,0)}
\]
satisfies $u\ge 0$, $\lambda\ge 0$, and complementary slackness.
Because $K$ is SPD this KKT point is the unique minimizer. Its energy
is
\begin{align*}
Ku&=\begin{pmatrix}-3/2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u^{\mathsf T}Ku=\frac92,
\qquad
f^{\mathsf T}u=\frac92,\\
I(u)
&=\frac12\cdot\frac92-\frac92
=-\frac94.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{I(0,3/2)=-9/4}.
\]

The naive clip of the unconstrained minimizer is $(0,4/3)$. Then
\[
K\begin{pmatrix}0\\4/3\end{pmatrix}-f
=\begin{pmatrix}-4/3\\8/3\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2/3\\-1/3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The second component is free ($u_2=4/3>0$) yet carries residual
$-1/3\ne 0$, so complementarity / stationarity fails. The energy of
the clip is
\begin{align*}
u^{\mathsf T}Ku&=\frac{32}{9},
\qquad
f^{\mathsf T}u=4,\\
I(0,4/3)
&=\frac{16}{9}-4
=-\frac{20}{9}.
\end{align*}
Since $-20/9>-9/4$, the clip is also strictly worse as an energy.
It is not a solution of the contact problem.

Sentence (i) treats nonnegativity of the clipped displacement as a
substitute for the KKT system. Sentence (ii) replaces unilateral
contact by an incompressible checkerboard, an inf-sup or Schur
argument, a locking diagnosis, or a mixed nonlinear tangent. Those
are different exercises and are not asked.

The argument never eliminates a Dirichlet dof in place of the
inequality, never marks elements, and never takes a Newmark step.

graderFixtures.proofText: Unconstrained minimizer $(-1/3,4/3)$ is infeasible. Active-set KKT solution $u=(0,3/2)$, $\lambda=(1/2,0)$, energy $-9/4$. Naive clip $(0,4/3)$ leaves free residual $-1/3$ and energy $-20/9$ and is not a solve.
I clip the unconstrained minimizer to (0,4/3) and call that the contact solution because both components are now nonnegative. I do not check the free residual or complementarity.
I accept the unconstrained point (-1/3,4/3) as the contact minimizer even though its first component violates u>=0.

FLUID:010117.title: Three-fluid manometer: pA-pB=26487 Pa=26.487 kPa; if pB=101.325 kPa abs then pA=127.812 kPa
FLUID:010117.objective: Walk a three-fluid manometer from A to B by adding hydrostatic increments down a column and subtracting them up a column, isolate pA-pB, and convert the same difference into an absolute pressure at A when B is given.
FLUID:010117.statement:
A three-fluid manometer joins two vessels. Start at point $A$ on the left. The connecting path goes
\[
\text{down }0.30\ \text{m of water},\quad
\text{through mercury to a right-hand mercury interface }0.20\ \text{m higher},
\quad
\text{then up }0.35\ \text{m of oil to }B.
\]
The constant densities and gravity are
\[
\rho_w=1000\ \text{kg}/\text{m}^3,\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}=13600\ \text{kg}/\text{m}^3,\qquad
\rho_o=800\ \text{kg}/\text{m}^3,\qquad
g=9.81\ \text{m}/\text{s}^2.
\]
Hydrostatic increments are $\rho g h$ with $h$ the vertical travel. Pressure rises when the path goes down and falls when the path goes up.

1. Write the exact path identity relating $p_B$ to $p_A$ by adding the water column, subtracting the net mercury rise of $0.20$ m, and subtracting the oil column.

2. Rearrange to $p_A-p_B$. Evaluate the difference in pascals and in kilopascals. Keep every factor of $g=9.81$.

3. If $B$ is at $101.325$ kPa absolute, compute the absolute pressure at $A$ in kilopascals.

4. Confirm the arithmetic identity
   \[
   -1000\cdot 0.30+13600\cdot 0.20+800\cdot 0.35=2700
   \]
   and therefore $p_A-p_B=2700\,g$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the right mercury interface is higher, so mercury increases pressure from $A$ to $B$”; (ii) “the oil column may be dropped because oil is lighter than water.”

Do not introduce a velocity head, a Bernoulli term, or a capillary correction. The fluids are static.
permittedResults: If a manometer path descends a height $h_1$ in density $\rho_1$ and then ascends a height $h_2$ in density $\rho_2$, the net change is $\rho_1 g h_1-\rho_2 g h_2$.
A net rise $h$ through a single fluid of density $\rho$ contributes $-\rho g h$ regardless of any equal-and-opposite down-and-up pair inside that fluid.

acceptableStrategies.description: Walk the manometer from A to B with signed hydrostatic increments, factor 2700 g, then add the given absolute pressure at B.
Write pA-pB as the sum of column weights per unit area with opposite signs on the two rising legs, then convert pascals to kilopascals.

milestones.criterion: Writes the path identity pB=pA+rw g(0.30)-rHg g(0.20)-ro g(0.35) and isolates pA-pB=26487 Pa=26.487 kPa.
Converts the same difference to pA=127.812 kPa absolute when pB=101.325 kPa absolute.
Rejects a reversed mercury sign and an omitted oil column, and does not introduce a Bernoulli or capillary term.

hintTree.content: From $A$ to $B$ the signed vertical travels are $+0.30$ m in water, $-0.20$ m in mercury, and $-0.35$ m in oil.
Absolute pressure adds: $p_A=p_B+(p_A-p_B)$ with $p_B=101.325$ kPa and $p_A-p_B=26.487$ kPa.

FLUID:010117.canonicalSolution:
Travel from $A$ to $B$. Pressure rises through the $0.30$ m water column, falls through the net $0.20$ m mercury rise (the right interface is $0.20$ m higher than the left mercury interface), and falls through the $0.35$ m oil column:
\[
p_B=p_A+\rho_w g(0.30)-\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} g(0.20)-\rho_o g(0.35).
\]
Rearrangement gives
\[
p_A-p_B
=-\rho_w g(0.30)+\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} g(0.20)+\rho_o g(0.35)
=g\bigl(-1000\cdot 0.30+13600\cdot 0.20+800\cdot 0.35\bigr).
\]
The parenthesis is $-300+2720+280=2700$, so
\[
p_A-p_B=2700\cdot 9.81=\boxed{26487\ \text{Pa}}=\boxed{26.487\ \text{kPa}}.
\]
If $B$ is at $101.325$ kPa absolute, then
\[
p_A=101.325+26.487=\boxed{127.812\ \text{kPa absolute}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: a higher right mercury interface is an upward travel through mercury from $A$ toward $B$, so mercury decreases $p_B$ relative to $p_A$. Replacing the mercury sign produces
\[
p_A-p_B=g(-300-2720+280)=-2740\cdot 9.81=-26879.4\ \text{Pa}.
\]
Sentence (ii) is false: dropping the oil column omits $+800\cdot 0.35\cdot 9.81=+2746.8$ Pa and reports $p_A-p_B=23740.2$ Pa. Density ranking does not authorize omitting a column that is actually present.

No velocity head appears. The fluids are at rest, so the hydrostatic walk is the complete relation between $p_A$ and $p_B$.

FLUID:010118.title: Box barge GM=7/60>0; neutral KG=11/12 m; 5deg righting moment 6867 sin5≈598.50 N m
FLUID:010118.objective: Compute the displaced volume, waterplane inertia, KB, BM, and GM of a rectangular barge, locate the neutrally stable KG, and evaluate the small-angle righting moment at five degrees.
FLUID:010118.statement:
A rectangular barge floats upright in fresh water. The hull is a rectangular box of length $L=6$ m, beam $B=2$ m, and uniform draft $T=0.5$ m. The center of gravity is on the centerplane at $KG=0.8$ m above the keel. Take
\[
\rho=1000\ \text{kg}/\text{m}^3,\qquad g=9.81\ \text{m}/\text{s}^2.
\]
The waterplane is a rectangle $L\times B$. The submerged body is a rectangular prism. Small-angle hydrostatics applies.

1. Compute the displaced volume $\nabla=LBT$ and the transverse waterplane inertia $I_{wp}=LB^3/12$.

2. Locate the center of buoyancy $KB$ for the rectangular submerged prism, then form
   \[
   BM=\frac{I_{wp}}{\nabla},\qquad GM=KB+BM-KG.
   \]
   Show $GM=7/60$ m and $GM>0$.

3. The neutrally stable KG is the value that makes $GM=0$. Compute it.

4. The righting moment at a heel $\theta=5^\circ$ is $\rho g\nabla\,GM\sin\theta$. Evaluate the exact prefactor $\rho g\nabla\,GM$ and the numerical moment in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$KB$ equals the draft $T$ because buoyancy acts at the keel-to-waterline height”; (ii) “$I_{wp}=LB^2/12$ is the waterplane inertia for heel about the longitudinal axis.”

Do not invoke a free-surface correction, a longitudinal metacenter, or a large-angle $GZ$ curve. The barge is wall-sided at $5^\circ$.
permittedResults: The centroid of a rectangular submerged prism of draft $T$ lies at $KB=T/2$ above the keel.
The second moment of a rectangle of length $L$ and beam $B$ about its longitudinal centerline is $LB^3/12$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Assemble GM=KB+Iwp/V-KG from the rectangular identities, then multiply ρ g V GM by sin5°.
Keep every term as a rational (1/4, 2/3, 4/5) until GM=7/60 is in hand, then evaluate the single decimal 6867 sin5°.

milestones.criterion: Computes V=6 m^3, Iwp=LB^3/12=4 m^4, KB=0.25 m, BM=2/3 m, and GM=7/60 m>0.
Reports the neutrally stable KG=11/12 m and the 5° righting moment 6867 sin5≈598.50 N m.
Rejects KB=T and Iwp=LB^2/12, and does not introduce a free-surface or large-angle correction.

commonErrors.description: Sets KB=T=0.5 m instead of T/2, obtaining GM=11/30 m and a righting prefactor 21582 rather than 6867.
commonErrors.consequence: The buoyancy centroid is placed at the waterline, inflating GM and overstating the restoring moment by a factor of 11/3.5.

commonErrors.description: Uses Iwp=LB^2/12=2 m^4 instead of LB^3/12=4 m^4, obtaining BM=1/3 m and GM=-13/60 m<0.
commonErrors.consequence: A stable barge is declared unstable and the righting moment changes sign.

hintTree.content: $\rho g\nabla\,GM=1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 6\cdot(7/60)=6867$, and $6867\sin 5^\circ\approx 598.50$ N m.

FLUID:010118.canonicalSolution:
The displaced volume and waterplane inertia are
\[
\nabla=LBT=6\cdot 2\cdot 0.5=\boxed{6\ \text{m}^3},
\qquad
I_{wp}=\frac{LB^3}{12}=\frac{6\cdot 2^3}{12}=\boxed{4\ \text{m}^4}.
\]
The submerged prism is rectangular, so its centroid is at mid-draft:
\[
KB=\frac{T}{2}=\boxed{0.25\ \text{m}}.
\]
The metacentric radius is
\[
BM=\frac{I_{wp}}{\nabla}=\frac{4}{6}=\boxed{\frac23\ \text{m}}.
\]
Hence
\[
GM=KB+BM-KG=\frac14+\frac23-\frac45=\frac{15+40-48}{60}=\boxed{\frac{7}{60}\ \text{m}}>0.
\]
The barge is stable in the small-angle sense. Neutral stability occurs at
\[
KG_{\mathrm{n}}=KB+BM=\frac14+\frac23=\boxed{\frac{11}{12}\ \text{m}}.
\]
The $5^\circ$ righting moment has prefactor
\[
\rho g\nabla\,GM=1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 6\cdot\frac{7}{60}=6867\ \text{N},
\]
so
\[
\rho g\nabla\,GM\sin 5^\circ=\boxed{6867\sin 5^\circ\approx 598.50\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: buoyancy acts at the centroid of the submerged volume, so $KB=T/2=0.25$ m, not $T=0.5$ m. Using $KB=0.5$ produces $GM=0.5+2/3-0.8=11/30$ and a righting prefactor $1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 6\cdot(11/30)=21582$. Sentence (ii) is false: heel about the longitudinal axis uses the beam cubed, $LB^3/12=4$. The replacement $LB^2/12=2$ yields $BM=1/3$ and $GM=1/4+1/3-4/5=-13/60<0$, a spurious capsize prediction.

The calculation uses only wall-sided small-angle hydrostatics. No free-surface tank, no $I_L$, and no finite-angle $GZ$ integration appear.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\nabla=6$ m$^3$, $I_{wp}=4$ m$^4$, $KB=0.25$ m, $BM=2/3$ m, and $GM=7/60>0$. Neutral $KG=11/12$ m. The $5^\circ$ righting moment is $6867\sin 5^\circ\approx 598.50$ N m.
Buoyancy acts at the waterline, so KB=0.5 m. Then BM=4/6=2/3 and GM=0.5+2/3-0.8=11/30. The 5deg moment is 21582 sin5 N m.
I take Iwp=L B^2/12=6*4/12=2 m^4, so BM=2/6=1/3 and GM=0.25+1/3-0.8=-13/60<0. The barge is unstable.

FLUID:010219.title: psi=a(x^2 y-y^3/3) is incompressible and irrotational; at (2,1) the speed is 5 and the signed psi difference is 11/3
FLUID:010219.objective: Recover the Cartesian velocity from a given stream function, prove vanishing divergence and vorticity, construct the velocity potential, locate the only stagnation point, and evaluate a signed stream-function difference.
FLUID:010219.statement:
A steady plane flow has the stream function
\[
\psi=a\Bigl(x^2 y-\frac{y^3}{3}\Bigr),\qquad
a=1\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}.
\]
With $x,y$ in meters, this choice of $a$ gives $\psi$ dimensions $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.
The two-dimensional stream-function convention is
\[
u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}.
\]

1. Compute the velocity components $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$.

2. Show that $\partial u/\partial x+\partial v/\partial y=0$ and that the $z$-vorticity $\omega_z=\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y$ vanishes identically.

3. Because the flow is irrotational, a velocity potential $\phi$ with $u=\partial\phi/\partial x$ and $v=\partial\phi/\partial y$ exists. Construct $\phi$ up to a constant $C$.

4. Solve $u=v=0$ and prove that the only stagnation point is the origin. Evaluate $\mathbf V$ and $\|\mathbf V\|$ at $(x,y)=(2,1)$ m.

5. The signed volume flux per unit depth from $(1,0)$ to $(2,1)$ equals $\psi(2,1)-\psi(1,0)$. Compute it.

6. Audit both sentences: (i) “the stream-function definitions may be swapped to $u=\partial\psi/\partial x$ and $v=-\partial\psi/\partial y$”; (ii) “every point of the axes $x=0$ and $y=0$ is a stagnation point.”

Do not introduce viscosity, a Bernoulli constant along a streamline as a substitute for $\phi$, or a three-dimensional stream function.
permittedResults: A $C^2$ stream function automatically satisfies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf V=0$ when $\mathbf V=(\partial\psi/\partial y,-\partial\psi/\partial x)$.
If $\partial v/\partial x=\partial u/\partial y$, the line integral of $\mathbf V$ is path-independent in a simply connected plane domain and defines $\phi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate psi for (u,v), check the two first-order identities, then integrate u for phi and finish with the two algebraic stagnation equations.
Recognize psi/a as the imaginary part of z^3/3, read phi/a as the real part, and evaluate the same velocity and flux from that analytic function.

milestones.criterion: Recovers u=a(x^2-y^2), v=-2axy and proves div=0 together with omega_z=0.
Constructs phi=a(x^3/3-xy^2)+C, proves the only stagnation point is the origin, and reports V(2,1)=(3,-4), speed 5, and signed psi difference 11/3 m^2/s.
Rejects swapped stream-function derivatives and the claim that the coordinate axes are stagnation loci.

commonErrors.description: Takes u=∂ψ/∂x=2axy and v=-∂ψ/∂y=-a(x^2-y^2), obtaining V(2,1)=(4,-3) m/s and a nonzero divergence 4ay.
commonErrors.consequence: The recovered field is not the stream-function velocity, continuity fails, and the potential of the assigned flow is lost.

commonErrors.description: Concludes from v=-2axy=0 that every point of the axes x=0 and y=0 is a stagnation point.
commonErrors.consequence: The only true stagnation point (the origin) is missed as unique, and the velocity on the axes is incorrectly declared to vanish.

hintTree.content: $\partial\psi/\partial y=a(x^2-y^2)$ and $\partial\psi/\partial x=2axy$, so $v=-2axy$.
Integrate $u=a(x^2-y^2)$ in $x$ to get $\phi=a(x^3/3-xy^2)+f(y)$, then $f'(y)=0$ from $v$.
$v=-2axy=0$ forces $x=0$ or $y=0$; either case reduces $u=a(x^2-y^2)=0$ to the origin only.

FLUID:010219.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating the given stream function yields
\[
u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}=a(x^2-y^2),\qquad
v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}=-2axy.
\]
With $a=1/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s})$,
\[
\boxed{u=a(x^2-y^2)},\qquad\boxed{v=-2axy}.
\]
The divergence is
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=2ax+(-2ax)=0.
\]
The planar vorticity is
\[
\omega_z=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-2ay-(-2ay)=0.
\]
The flow is therefore incompressible and irrotational. Integrating $u=\partial\phi/\partial x$ gives
\[
\phi=a\Bigl(\frac{x^3}{3}-xy^2\Bigr)+f(y).
\]
The $y$-derivative is $a(-2xy)+f'(y)$, which must equal $v=-2axy$, so $f'=0$ and
\[
\boxed{\phi=a\Bigl(\frac{x^3}{3}-xy^2\Bigr)+C}.
\]
Stagnation requires $u=v=0$. From $v=-2axy=0$ either $x=0$ or $y=0$. If $x=0$ then $u=-a y^2=0$ forces $y=0$. If $y=0$ then $u=a x^2=0$ forces $x=0$. The only stagnation point is the origin.

At $(2,1)$ m,
\[
\mathbf V=\bigl(a(4-1),-2a\cdot 2\cdot 1\bigr)=\boxed{(3,-4)\ \text{m}/\text{s}},
\qquad
\|\mathbf V\|=\boxed{5\ \text{m}/\text{s}}.
\]
The signed stream-function difference is
\[
\psi(2,1)-\psi(1,0)
=a\Bigl(4\cdot 1-\frac13\Bigr)-a\Bigl(0-0\Bigr)
=a\cdot\frac{11}{3}
=\boxed{\frac{11}{3}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $u=\partial\psi/\partial x=2axy$ and $v=-\partial\psi/\partial y=-a(x^2-y^2)$ produce $\nabla\cdot\mathbf V=4ay\neq 0$ and $\mathbf V(2,1)=(4,-3)$ m/s. Sentence (ii) is false: on $x=0$ one has $u=-ay^2$, and on $y=0$ one has $u=ax^2$, both nonzero off the origin.

The construction stays two-dimensional and inviscid-kinematic. No Bernoulli constant is used as a substitute for $\phi$.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $u=a(x^2-y^2)$, $v=-2axy$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf V=0$, $\omega_z=0$, and $\phi=a(x^3/3-xy^2)+C$. The only stagnation point is the origin. At $(2,1)$, $\mathbf V=(3,-4)$ m/s with speed $5$. The signed difference is $\psi(2,1)-\psi(1,0)=11/3$ m$^2$/s.
I take u=dpsi/dx=2axy and v=-dpsi/dy=-a(x^2-y^2). Then at (2,1) I get V=(4,-3) m/s and speed 5. The signed psi difference is still 11/3.
v=-2axy=0 on the whole axes x=0 and y=0, so every point of both axes is a stagnation point. The origin is only one of them.

FLUID:010220.title: Rankine half-body U=2, m=4pi: stagnation at (-1,0); dividing psi=2pi; downstream halfwidth pi
FLUID:010220.objective: Superpose a uniform stream and a source, locate the Rankine-half-body stagnation point, identify the dividing stream function, and extract the body polar equation together with the downstream widths.
FLUID:010220.statement:
A Rankine half-body is the dividing streamline of the plane superposition of a uniform stream $U=2$ m/s in the $+x$ direction and a source of strength $m=4\pi$ m$^2$/s at the origin. Polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ are centered at the source, with $\theta=0$ downstream and $\theta=\pi$ upstream. The stream function, continuous with $\psi=0$ on the downstream ray through a vanishing source angle, is
\[
\psi=Ur\sin\theta+\frac{m}{2\pi}\theta.
\]

1. Write $\psi$ with the given numbers. Locate the stagnation point by setting the polar velocity components to zero, or equivalently by balancing the source speed $m/(2\pi r)$ against $U$ on $\theta=\pi$. Give its Cartesian coordinates.

2. Evaluate $\psi$ at that stagnation point. This is the dividing value $\psi_{\mathrm{body}}$.

3. Impose $\psi=\psi_{\mathrm{body}}$ and solve for the polar equation $r=r(\theta)$ of the half-body. Use the same continuous stream-function branch on $0<\theta<2\pi$: $0<\theta<\pi$ is the upper surface and $\pi<\theta<2\pi$ is the lower surface.

4. Compute the downstream half-width $\lim_{\theta\to 0^+} r\sin\theta$ and the full downstream width.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the body is the streamline $\psi=0$”; (ii) “the downstream half-width equals the stagnation radius $m/(2\pi U)=1$ m.”

Do not add a sink, a vortex, or a Rankine oval. The source remains at the origin.
permittedResults: On $\theta=\pi$ the uniform stream and the source are collinear and opposite. They cancel at $r=m/(2\pi U)$.
For $\psi=Ur\sin\theta+(m/2\pi)\theta$, the value at $\theta=\pi$, $r=m/(2\pi U)$ is $m/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Cancel U against m/(2πr) on θ=π to place the stagnation point, read psi=m/2 there, and rearrange the level set for r(θ) and the far-field height.
Use global volume flux: the source discharge m must escape between the body and the x-axis as 2U times the half-width, so the half-width is m/(2U)=π without taking a limit.

milestones.criterion: Writes psi=Ur sinθ+(m/2π)θ with U=2, m=4π and locates the stagnation point at (-1,0).
Identifies the dividing value psi=2π, the polar body r=(π-θ)/sinθ m, and the downstream halfwidth π (full width 2π).
Rejects the streamline psi=0 as the body and rejects equating the halfwidth to the stagnation radius.

commonErrors.description: Takes the body to be ψ=0 instead of ψ=m/2=2π, obtaining r=-θ/sinθ rather than r=(π-θ)/sinθ.
commonErrors.consequence: The dividing streamline and both downstream widths are those of the wrong level set, not the Rankine half-body through the stagnation point.

commonErrors.description: Reports the downstream half-width as the stagnation radius m/(2πU)=1 m instead of π m.
commonErrors.consequence: Mass conservation of the source discharge is violated: the far-field opening would pass only 2U·1=4 m^2/s rather than m=4π m^2/s.

hintTree.content: Stagnation radius $m/(2\pi U)=4\pi/(4\pi)=1$ m on $\theta=\pi$, hence the point $(-1,0)$.
$\psi(-1,0)=2\cdot 1\cdot\sin\pi+(4\pi/2\pi)\pi=0+2\pi=m/2$.
On the body, $2r\sin\theta+2\theta=2\pi$, so $r=(\pi-\theta)/\sin\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta\to\pi$ as $\theta\to 0$.

FLUID:010220.canonicalSolution:
With the assigned numbers
\[
\psi=2r\sin\theta+\frac{4\pi}{2\pi}\theta=2r\sin\theta+2\theta.
\]
On the upstream axis $\theta=\pi$ the radial source speed $m/(2\pi r)$ opposes $U$. They cancel at
\[
\frac{m}{2\pi r}=U\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad r=\frac{m}{2\pi U}=\frac{4\pi}{2\pi\cdot 2}=1\ \text{m}.
\]
The stagnation point is therefore
\[
\boxed{(-1,0)\ \text{m}}.
\]
The stream function there is
\[
\psi_{\mathrm{body}}=U\cdot 1\cdot\sin\pi+\frac{m}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac{m}{2}=\boxed{2\pi\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}}.
\]
The body is the level set $\psi=2\pi$:
\[
2r\sin\theta+2\theta=2\pi\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad r\sin\theta=\pi-\theta\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{r=\frac{\pi-\theta}{\sin\theta}\ \text{m}},
\]
for $0<\theta<\pi$ on the upper surface and $\pi<\theta<2\pi$ on the lower surface. Both numerator and denominator are negative on the lower branch, so $r$ remains positive. Downstream,
\[
\lim_{\theta\to 0^+}r\sin\theta=\pi\ \text{m},
\qquad
\lim_{\theta\to 2\pi^-}r\sin\theta=-\pi\ \text{m},
\]
so the downstream half-width is $\pi$ m and the full distance between the two surfaces is
\[
\boxed{2\pi\ \text{m}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $\psi=0$ is the downstream ray $\theta=0$ (and the continuation through the source), not the dividing streamline. Imposing $\psi=0$ yields $r=-\theta/\sin\theta$, which is not the Rankine half-body. Sentence (ii) is false: the stagnation radius is $1$ m, but the far downstream half-width is the mass-conservation height $m/(2U)=\pi$ m, not $1$ m.

No sink is introduced, so the body remains a half-body rather than a closed Rankine oval.

graderFixtures.proofText: The stream function is $\psi=2r\sin\theta+2\theta$. Stagnation is at $(-1,0)$, where $\psi=m/2=2\pi$. The body is $r=(\pi-\theta)/\sin\theta$ m. Downstream half-width $\pi$ m, full width $2\pi$ m.
The body is the streamline psi=0. Then 2 r sinθ + 2θ=0 so r=-θ/sinθ. I never use psi=2pi.
Stagnation is at r=m/(2πU)=1 m, and that same length is the downstream half-width. Full width 2 m.

FLUID:010321.title: Stationary vane: vane-on-fluid (-50,50sqrt3) N; fluid-on-vane (50,-50sqrt3) N of magnitude 100 N at -60 deg
FLUID:010321.objective: Apply the steady inertial control-volume momentum balance to a stationary turning vane, compute the force of the vane on the fluid and the equal-and-opposite force of the fluid on the vane, and report the magnitude and polar direction of the latter.
FLUID:010321.statement:
A stationary vane turns a liquid jet. The mass-flow rate is $\dot m=5$ kg/s. Atmospheric pressure surrounds the jet, so gage pressure is zero on every cut. Gravity and the weight of fluid inside the vane are neglected. The inlet and outlet velocities are
\[
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}=(20,0)\ \text{m}/\text{s},
\qquad
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}=20(\cos 60^\circ,\sin 60^\circ)=(10,10\sqrt{3})\ \text{m}/\text{s}.
\]
The vane does not move. The inertial $x,y$ frame is attached to the ground.

1. Confirm the listed outlet components from $20(\cos 60^\circ,\sin 60^\circ)$.

2. The force of the vane on the fluid is the external force required by the steady momentum balance
   \[
   \mathbf F_{\text{vane on fluid}}=\dot m\bigl(\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr).
   \]
   Compute $\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}$ and that force.

3. The force of the fluid on the vane is the reaction $-\mathbf F_{\text{vane on fluid}}$. Give its Cartesian components, its magnitude, and the polar angle of its direction measured from $+x$ toward $+y$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the momentum theorem already returns the force of the fluid on the vane, so no sign change is required”; (ii) “the specified outlet direction is $120^\circ$ from $+x$, therefore $\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}=20(\cos 120^\circ,\sin 120^\circ)$.”

Do not introduce vane motion, a relative-velocity frame, or a Bernoulli pressure recovery on the vane face. Atmospheric pressure contributes no net gage force on the cuts.
permittedResults: If $\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}=(-10,10\sqrt{3})$ m/s and $\dot m=5$ kg/s, then $\dot m\Delta\mathbf V=(-50,50\sqrt{3})$ N.
A vector $(F,-F\sqrt{3})$ has magnitude $2|F|$ and argument $-60^\circ$ when $F>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form ΔV in components, multiply by mdot for the force on the fluid, then reverse the vector and read magnitude and atan2.
Resolve inlet and outlet momenta ṁVin=(100,0) and ṁVout=(50,50√3), subtract for the force on the fluid, and react that difference onto the vane.

milestones.criterion: Computes Vout=(10,10sqrt3) and the vane-on-fluid force mdot(Vout-Vin)=(-50,50sqrt3) N.
Reports the fluid-on-vane reaction (50,-50sqrt3) N of magnitude 100 N at -60 deg.
Rejects dropping the action-reaction sign and rejects placing the outlet at 120 deg from +x.

commonErrors.description: Identifies mdot(Vout-Vin)=(-50,50sqrt3) N as the force of the fluid on the vane rather than the force of the vane on the fluid.
commonErrors.consequence: The load on the support is reversed: the reported direction is +120 deg instead of -60 deg.

commonErrors.description: Reads the explicitly specified outlet direction as 120 deg from +x, writing Vout=20(cos120,sin120)=(-10,10sqrt3) and a reaction of magnitude 100sqrt3 N.
commonErrors.consequence: Both momentum components are wrong, and the force magnitude is 100sqrt3 N rather than 100 N.

hintTree.content: $\cos 60^\circ=1/2$ and $\sin 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}/2$, so $\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}=(10,10\sqrt{3})$.
$\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}=(-10,10\sqrt{3})$. Multiply by $\dot m=5$.
The reaction is $(50,-50\sqrt{3})$. Its magnitude is $50\sqrt{1+3}=100$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(-50\sqrt{3},50)=-60^\circ$.

FLUID:010321.canonicalSolution:
The outlet direction is $60^\circ$ from $+x$, so
\[
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}=20\Bigl(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\Bigr)=\boxed{(10,10\sqrt{3})\ \text{m}/\text{s}}.
\]
The velocity change is
\[
\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf V_{\mathrm{in}}=(-10,10\sqrt{3})\ \text{m}/\text{s}.
\]
The force of the vane on the fluid is
\[
\mathbf F_{\text{vane on fluid}}
=5(-10,10\sqrt{3})
=\boxed{(-50,50\sqrt{3})\ \text{N}}.
\]
The force of the fluid on the vane is the reaction
\[
\mathbf F_{\text{fluid on vane}}
=\boxed{(50,-50\sqrt{3})\ \text{N}}.
\]
Its magnitude is
\[
\sqrt{50^2+(50\sqrt{3})^2}=\sqrt{2500+7500}=\boxed{100\ \text{N}},
\]
and its direction from $+x$ is
\[
\operatorname{atan2}(-50\sqrt{3},50)=\boxed{-60^\circ}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $\dot m\Delta\mathbf V$ is the force on the fluid. Omitting the sign change reports the load on the vane as $(-50,50\sqrt{3})$ N, which points $120^\circ$ rather than $-60^\circ$. Sentence (ii) is false: the assigned outlet direction is $60^\circ$ from $+x$, not $120^\circ$. That substitution gives $\mathbf V_{\mathrm{out}}=(-10,10\sqrt{3})$, $\dot m\Delta\mathbf V=(-150,50\sqrt{3})$ N, and a reaction of magnitude $50\sqrt{12}=100\sqrt{3}$ N.

The vane is stationary, so there is no relative-velocity correction and no moving-frame momentum flux.

FLUID:010322.title: The fluid force on the reducing elbow is (4500,-1000) N, of magnitude 500sqrt85 N at 12.53 deg below +x
FLUID:010322.objective: Apply steady mass and linear-momentum balances to a fixed reducing elbow, include the inlet gauge-pressure force, isolate the wall-on-fluid reaction, and reverse that reaction once to obtain the fluid force on the elbow.
FLUID:010322.statement:
Liquid water of constant density $\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ flows steadily through a fixed reducing elbow. A right-handed $xy$-frame is attached to the elbow. Inlet station $1$ has area $A_1=0.02\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and uniform velocity $\mathbf V_1=5\,\mathbf i\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Outlet station $2$ has area $A_2=0.01\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and uniform velocity $\mathbf V_2=10\,\mathbf j\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Gauge pressures are $p_1=200\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $p_2=0$. Atmospheric pressure acts on the exterior of the elbow and is already removed by the gauge convention. Body forces are negligible compared with the pressure and wall forces. The control volume is the interior of the elbow, fixed to the metal.

1. Compute the volume flow rate $Q$ at each station and the mass-flow rate $\dot m$. Confirm mass conservation.

2. Evaluate the steady momentum efflux $\dot m(\mathbf V_2-\mathbf V_1)$.

3. Write the inlet and outlet gauge-pressure forces on the fluid. Then write the $x$ and $y$ components of the wall-on-fluid force $\mathbf R$ from the linear-momentum equation.

4. Reverse the action–reaction pair once to obtain the force of the fluid on the elbow. Report that vector, its Euclidean magnitude exactly and to two decimals in newtons, and the angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $p_2=0$ there is no pressure force anywhere, so $\mathbf R$ equals the momentum efflux”; (ii) “the force the designer needs on the elbow is the same vector as the wall force on the fluid.”

Do not introduce a deforming control surface, a relative flux through a moving boundary, or an angular-momentum balance. The elbow is rigid and the stations are fixed.
permittedResults: Mass conservation for a steady incompressible stream is $Q=A_1V_1=A_2V_2$ and $\dot m=\rho Q$.
If body $\mathrm A$ exerts $\mathbf R$ on body $\mathrm B$, then body $\mathrm B$ exerts $-\mathbf R$ on body $\mathrm A$. The pair is reversed exactly once.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write sum F = mdot(V2-V1), insert the single inlet pressure force, solve for the wall-on-fluid reaction, then reverse that vector once.
Balance x and y separately: 4000+Rx=-500 and Ry=1000, then report the metal load as (-Rx,-Ry) with magnitude 500sqrt(85).

milestones.criterion: Computes Q=0.1 m^3/s, mdot=100 kg/s, and the momentum efflux (-500,1000) N.
Includes the inlet pressure force (4000,0) N and obtains wall-on-fluid (-4500,1000) N and fluid-on-elbow (4500,-1000) N of magnitude 500sqrt(85) N at 12.53 deg below +x.
Rejects dropping the inlet pressure force and rejects identifying the elbow load with the unreversed wall-on-fluid vector.

commonErrors.description: Drops the inlet gauge-pressure force because the outlet gauge pressure is zero, setting the wall-on-fluid force equal to the momentum efflux (-500,1000) N.
commonErrors.consequence: The 4000 N inlet push is missing, so both the wall reaction and the fluid-on-elbow load have the wrong x-component and the wrong magnitude.

commonErrors.description: Reports the force of the fluid on the elbow as the wall-on-fluid vector (-4500,1000) N rather than its reverse.
commonErrors.consequence: The design load on the metal points into the wrong quadrant and the 12.53 deg statement is measured from the wrong ray.

hintTree.content: $A_1V_1=0.02\cdot 5=0.1\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$ and $A_2V_2=0.01\cdot 10=0.1\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$. Then $\dot m=\rho Q=100\ \mathrm{kg/s}$.
The momentum efflux is $100\bigl((0,10)-(5,0)\bigr)=(-500,1000)\ \mathrm N$. The only nonzero pressure force is $p_1A_1=4000\,\mathbf i\ \mathrm N$.
If $\mathbf R$ is the wall-on-fluid force, then $(4000,0)+\mathbf R=(-500,1000)$. Reverse $\mathbf R$ once for the fluid-on-elbow force.

FLUID:010322.canonicalSolution:
The volume fluxes are
\[
Q_1=A_1V_1=0.02\cdot 5=0.10\ \mathrm{m^3/s},
\qquad
Q_2=A_2V_2=0.01\cdot 10=0.10\ \mathrm{m^3/s}.
\]
They agree, so
\[
\boxed{Q=0.1\ \mathrm{m^3/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\dot m=\rho Q=100\ \mathrm{kg/s}}.
\]
The steady momentum efflux of the fluid is
\[
\dot m(\mathbf V_2-\mathbf V_1)
=100\bigl((0,10)-(5,0)\bigr)
=\boxed{(-500,1000)\ \mathrm N}.
\]
The inlet gauge-pressure force on the fluid is directed into the volume along $+\mathbf i$:
\[
p_1A_1=(2.00\times 10^5)(0.02)=\boxed{(4000,0)\ \mathrm N}.
\]
The outlet gauge pressure vanishes, so that station contributes $\mathbf 0$. Body forces are neglected. The linear-momentum equation is therefore
\[
(4000,0)+\mathbf R=(-500,1000),
\]
and the wall-on-fluid force is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf R=(-4500,1000)\ \mathrm N}.
\]
The force of the fluid on the elbow is the single reversal
\[
\boxed{-\mathbf R=(4500,-1000)\ \mathrm N}.
\]
Its magnitude is
\[
\|-\mathbf R\|=\sqrt{4500^2+1000^2}=500\sqrt{85}\ \mathrm N
\approx\boxed{4609.77\ \mathrm N}.
\]
The vector $(4500,-1000)$ lies $12.53^\circ$ below the positive $x$-axis because
\[
\arctan\bigl(1000/4500\bigr)=\arctan(2/9)\approx 12.53^\circ.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $p_2=0$ removes only the outlet pressure force. Dropping the inlet force $4000\,\mathbf i$ reports $\mathbf R=(-500,1000)$ and a fluid-on-elbow force of the opposite sign and the wrong magnitude $500\sqrt{5}\ \mathrm N$. Sentence (ii) is false: the designer’s load on the metal is $-\mathbf R$, not $\mathbf R$. Leaving the pair unreversed points the $4500\ \mathrm N$ component the wrong way.

The control volume is fixed. No moving-boundary relative flux and no angular-momentum balance is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Mass conservation gives $Q=0.1$ m$^3$/s and $\dot m=100$ kg/s. Momentum efflux is $(-500,1000)$ N and the inlet pressure force is $(4000,0)$ N, so the wall-on-fluid force is $(-4500,1000)$ N. The fluid-on-elbow force is $(4500,-1000)$ N, of magnitude $500\sqrt{85}\approx 4609.77$ N, at $12.53^\circ$ below $+x$.
p2=0 so I drop every pressure force. Then R equals the momentum efflux (-500,1000) N and the fluid-on-elbow force is (500,-1000) N.
The force the elbow feels is the same as the wall force on the fluid, so I report (-4500,1000) N at arctan(1000/4500) above the negative x-axis.

FLUID:010323.title: Rotor-on-fluid torque is -105 N m; the extracted shaft power is 10.5 kW
FLUID:010323.objective: Evaluate the axial torque on a rotor from radius times signed absolute tangential velocity at two cylindrical stations, reverse the action–reaction pair exactly once to obtain the fluid-on-rotor torque, and convert that torque with the given shaft speed into extracted power.
FLUID:010323.statement:
A radial rotor turns at the constant angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega=100\,\mathbf k\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Steady incompressible flow crosses two cylindrical control stations fixed in the inertial laboratory frame. The mass-flow rate is $\dot m=20\ \mathrm{kg/s}$. At the outer station $r_1=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ the absolute tangential velocity is $V_{\theta 1}=+15\ \mathrm{m/s}$. At the inner station $r_2=0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ the absolute tangential velocity is $V_{\theta 2}=-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The sign convention is the right-handed $\theta$ sense about $+\mathbf k$. Radial and axial velocity contributions produce no $z$-moment about the shaft. Shaft bearings and the casing contribute no additional axial torque on the fluid inside the rotor passages.

The control volume is the fluid occupying the rotor passages. This is not a closed stirred tank: mass crosses both stations, and the angular-momentum flux is carried by the throughflow.

1. Form the products $r_1V_{\theta 1}$ and $r_2V_{\theta 2}$ with the given signed absolute tangential velocities. Do not replace $V_\theta$ by a relative blade speed $V_\theta-\omega r$ and do not replace either value by its absolute value.

2. The axial torque of the rotor on the fluid is
   \[
   T_{z,\text{rotor on fluid}}=\dot m\bigl(r_2V_{\theta 2}-r_1V_{\theta 1}\bigr).
   \]
   Evaluate the scalar and the vector $T_{z}\,\mathbf k$.

3. Reverse the action–reaction pair exactly once to obtain the axial torque of the fluid on the rotor.

4. The ideal extracted shaft power is the inner product of the fluid-on-rotor torque with $\boldsymbol\omega$. Compute that power in kilowatts and state the sign convention that makes “extracted” positive.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$V_{\theta 2}$ should enter as $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ because a speed is nonnegative”; (ii) “extracted power uses the rotor-on-fluid torque, or equivalently one may reverse the pair twice and still use $\boldsymbol\omega$.”

Do not replace the rotor by a closed stirred tank, do not write a linear-momentum elbow balance, and do not introduce a viscous couple on a tank wall.
permittedResults: For a steady rotor control volume with cylindrical stations, $T_{z,\text{on fluid}}=\dot m(r_2V_{\theta 2}-r_1V_{\theta 1})$ when $V_\theta$ is the signed absolute tangential velocity.

Action–reaction reverses a couple exactly once: $\mathbf T_{\text{fluid on rotor}}=-\mathbf T_{\text{rotor on fluid}}$. Power extracted by the shaft is $\mathbf T_{\text{fluid on rotor}}\cdot\boldsymbol\omega$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate mdot(r2 V_theta2-r1 V_theta1) with the given signs, reverse that scalar once, and multiply by +100 rad/s.
Track axial angular momentum per unit mass r V_theta through the two stations, then identify extraction with T_fluid-on-rotor · omega rather than with the rotor-on-fluid couple.

milestones.criterion: Forms r1 V_theta1=+4.5 m^2/s and r2 V_theta2=-0.75 m^2/s from signed absolute tangential velocities and obtains rotor-on-fluid torque -105 N m.
Reverses the pair exactly once to fluid-on-rotor +105 N m and reports extracted shaft power 10.5 kW.
Rejects dropping the sign of V_theta2 and rejects using the unreversed or twice-reversed couple in the power product.

commonErrors.description: Treats V_theta2 as the unsigned speed +5 m/s, so r2 V_theta2=+0.75 m^2/s and the rotor-on-fluid torque becomes -75 N m.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular-momentum change is understated by 30 N m and the extracted power is reported as 7.5 kW.

commonErrors.description: Pairs the rotor-on-fluid torque -105 N m directly with omega, or reverses the couple twice, and reports extracted power as -10.5 kW or as a shaft load of the wrong sense.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign of the shaft work is inverted: extraction from the fluid is misread as work input to the fluid.

hintTree.content: The difference is $-0.75-4.5=-5.25\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$, so $\dot m$ times that difference is $-105\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$.
Reverse once to $+105\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$ on the rotor. Then $(+105)(100)=1.05\times 10^4\ \mathrm W=10.5\ \mathrm{kW}$.

FLUID:010323.canonicalSolution:
The signed products are
\[
r_1V_{\theta 1}=0.30\cdot(+15)=+4.50\ \mathrm{m^2/s},
\qquad
r_2V_{\theta 2}=0.15\cdot(-5)=-0.75\ \mathrm{m^2/s}.
\]
The axial torque of the rotor on the fluid is
\[
T_{z,\text{rotor on fluid}}
=\dot m(r_2V_{\theta 2}-r_1V_{\theta 1})
=20\bigl(-0.75-4.50\bigr)
=\boxed{-105\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}},
\]
or $-105\,\mathbf k\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$. The fluid-on-rotor torque is the single reverse
\[
\boxed{T_{z,\text{fluid on rotor}}=+105\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}}.
\]
The shaft angular velocity is $+100\,\mathbf k\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, so the ideal extracted power is
\[
\mathbf T_{\text{fluid on rotor}}\cdot\boldsymbol\omega
=(105)(100)=1.05\times 10^4\ \mathrm W
=\boxed{10.5\ \mathrm{kW}}.
\]
The inner product is positive: the fluid loses angular momentum about $+\mathbf k$ and the shaft extracts work.

Sentence (i) is false: replacing $V_{\theta 2}$ by $+5$ produces $r_2V_{\theta 2}=+0.75$ and $T_{z,\text{on fluid}}=20(0.75-4.50)=-75\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$, then $7.5\ \mathrm{kW}$. Sentence (ii) is false: using the unreversed rotor-on-fluid torque with $\boldsymbol\omega$ reports $-10.5\ \mathrm{kW}$ as “extracted,” while reversing twice returns to the same wrong pairing.

The balance is an open rotor throughflow. No closed-tank viscous couple is introduced.

graderFixtures.proofText: Using signed absolute products $r_1V_{\theta 1}=+4.5$ and $r_2V_{\theta 2}=-0.75$, the rotor-on-fluid torque is $\dot m(r_2V_{\theta 2}-r_1V_{\theta 1})=-105$ N m. One reversal gives fluid-on-rotor $+105$ N m and extracted power $(105)(100)=10.5$ kW.
Tangential speed at station 2 is 5 m/s, so r2 V_theta2=0.75 m^2/s. Then T_rotor-on-fluid=20(0.75-4.5)=-75 N m, fluid-on-rotor=+75 N m, and power=7.5 kW.
Extracted power is the rotor-on-fluid torque times omega, so P=(-105)(100)=-10.5 kW. Reversing twice would give the same pairing.
