FLUID:010424.title: Free-vortex pressure rises 1500 Pa from r=1 m to r=2 m; circulation is 4pi and vorticity vanishes for r>0
FLUID:010424.objective: Integrate the radial Euler equation for a free vortex of strength K=2, recover the Bernoulli invariant, evaluate circulation on circles about the origin, and confirm that vorticity vanishes for every r>0 with the core excluded.
FLUID:010424.statement:
An incompressible inviscid liquid of density $\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ occupies the punctured plane $r>0$. The velocity field is the free vortex
\[
\mathbf v=\frac{K}{r}\,\mathbf e_\theta,\qquad K=2\ \mathrm{m^2/s},
\]
in polar coordinates, with no radial or axial motion. The origin $r=0$ is excluded: it is not part of the flow domain. Gravity is absent and the motion is steady.

1. Evaluate $v_\theta$ at $r_1=1\ \mathrm m$ and at $r_2=2\ \mathrm m$.

2. Reduce the radial Euler equation to $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr$ and show that
   \[
   \frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm dr}=\frac{\rho K^2}{r^3}.
   \]
   Integrate from $r_1$ to $r_2$ to obtain $p_2-p_1$.

3. Form the Bernoulli combination $p+\rho v_\theta^2/2$ at both radii and prove it is the same constant.

4. Compute the circulation $\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf v\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf l$ on every simple closed circle $C$ of radius $r>0$ centered at the origin. Then compute the vorticity $\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf v$ for $r>0$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “radial equilibrium is $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr=\rho v_\theta^2$, or equivalently $\rho K^2/r^2$, so $p_2-p_1=2000\ \mathrm{Pa}$”; (ii) “a free vortex is rotational with vorticity $2K/r^2$, and the circulation on a circle is $2\pi v_\theta$ rather than $2\pi K$.”

Do not fill in a forced-vortex core, do not restore viscosity, and do not replace the free vortex by a Couette or Poiseuille profile.
permittedResults: If $v_\theta=K/r$, then $p+\rho v_\theta^2/2=p+\rho K^2/(2r^2)$ is spatially constant wherever the motion is steady, inviscid, and of constant density.
In the punctured plane, $\nabla\times(K/r\,\mathbf e_\theta)=\mathbf 0$ for $r>0$, while $\oint_{r=\mathrm{const}}\mathbf v\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf l=2\pi K$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate rho K^2/r^3 from 1 m to 2 m, then check Bernoulli and evaluate 2pi K and the polar curl.
Convert the radial Euler integral into a Bernoulli difference rho(v1^2-v2^2)/2=1500 Pa, then treat circulation and vorticity as a separate Stokes-theorem audit on the punctured plane.

milestones.criterion: Obtains v1=2 m/s, v2=1 m/s, dp/dr=rho K^2/r^3, and p2-p1=1500 Pa.
Shows p+rho v^2/2 is constant, circulation is 4pi, and vorticity vanishes for every r>0.
Rejects the radial-Euler power error that yields 2000 Pa and rejects a rotational free-vortex claim.

commonErrors.description: Writes dp/dr=rho v_theta^2=rho K^2/r^2 instead of rho v_theta^2/r, and integrates to p2-p1=2000 Pa.
commonErrors.consequence: The pressure rise is overstated by 500 Pa and p+rho v^2/2 is no longer invariant.

commonErrors.description: Assigns vorticity 2K/r^2 to the free vortex and reports circulation 2pi v_theta=4pi/r, which changes with radius.
commonErrors.consequence: The flow is misclassified as rotational and Stokes’ theorem on the punctured plane is violated.

hintTree.content: $v_\theta(r_1)=2/1=2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_\theta(r_2)=2/2=1\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Then $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr=\rho(K/r)^2/r=\rho K^2/r^3$.
$\int_1^2\rho K^2 r^{-3}\,\mathrm dr=1000\cdot 4\cdot\bigl[-1/(2r^2)\bigr]_1^2=4000\cdot(3/8)=1500\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
Circulation is $v_\theta\cdot 2\pi r=2\pi K=4\pi$. The polar curl of $K/r\,\mathbf e_\theta$ is zero for $r>0$.

FLUID:010424.canonicalSolution:
The swirl speeds are
\[
\boxed{v_1=v_\theta(r_1)=2\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{v_2=v_\theta(r_2)=1\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Radial Euler with $v_r=0$ is $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr=\rho v_\theta^2/r$. Substituting $v_\theta=K/r$ gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm dr}=\frac{\rho K^2}{r^3}}.
\]
Integration from $r_1=1$ to $r_2=2$ produces
\[
p_2-p_1
=\rho K^2\int_1^2 r^{-3}\,\mathrm dr
=1000\cdot 4\Bigl[-\frac{1}{2r^2}\Bigr]_1^2
=4000\Bigl(-\frac18+\frac12\Bigr)
=\boxed{1500\ \mathrm{Pa}}.
\]
The Bernoulli combination is
\begin{align*}
p_1+\frac12\rho v_1^2
&=p_1+\frac12\cdot 1000\cdot 4=p_1+2000\ \mathrm{Pa},\\
p_2+\frac12\rho v_2^2
&=(p_1+1500)+\frac12\cdot 1000\cdot 1=p_1+2000\ \mathrm{Pa}.
\end{align*}
Thus $p+\rho v_\theta^2/2$ is the same constant at both stations.

On any origin-centered circle of radius $r>0$,
\[
\Gamma=\int_0^{2\pi}v_\theta\,r\,\mathrm d\theta=2\pi K=\boxed{4\pi\ \mathrm{m^2/s}}.
\]
In polar components, for $r>0$,
\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(rv_\theta)}{\partial r}=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial K}{\partial r}=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0\quad(r>0)}.
\]
The origin is excluded and is not assigned a vorticity value.

Sentence (i) is false: omitting the extra $1/r$ produces $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr=\rho K^2/r^2$ and $p_2-p_1=2000\ \mathrm{Pa}$, and it also breaks $p+\rho v^2/2$. Sentence (ii) is false: local vorticity vanishes on $r>0$; the nonzero circulation is $2\pi K=4\pi$, not $2\pi v_\theta=4\pi/r$.

The field is an inviscid free vortex on the punctured plane. No forced-vortex core and no viscous profile is introduced.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $v_1=2$ m/s, $v_2=1$ m/s, $\mathrm dp/\mathrm dr=\rho K^2/r^3$, and $p_2-p_1=1500$ Pa. Then $p+\rho v^2/2$ is constant, $\Gamma=4\pi$, and $\boldsymbol\omega=\mathbf 0$ for $r>0$ with the core excluded.
Radial equilibrium is dp/dr=rho v_theta^2=rho K^2/r^2. Integrating from 1 m to 2 m gives p2-p1=2000 Pa. Bernoulli with that rise is not constant.
A free vortex has vorticity 2K/r^2. Circulation on a circle is 2pi v_theta=4pi/r, which decreases as r increases.

FLUID:010425.title: Stokes wall traction magnitude is mu U/sqrt(pi nu t); u/U=0.1 at y=2.32617 sqrt(nu t)
FLUID:010425.objective: Use the complementary-error-function solution of Stokes’ first problem to evaluate wall shear, identify the positive plate-on-fluid traction, match the time derivative of fluid momentum per unit area to that traction, and locate the u/U=0.1 isosurface.
FLUID:010425.statement:
An infinite plate occupies $y=0$ and bounds the half-space $y>0$ of an incompressible Newtonian fluid of density $\rho$, viscosity $\mu$, and kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho$. For $t<0$ the fluid and plate are at rest. At $t=0$ the plate is impulsively set into motion with constant speed $U>0$ in the $+\mathbf i$ direction and thereafter remains at that speed. There is no imposed streamwise pressure gradient. The exact similarity solution of this Stokes first problem is
\[
\frac{u(y,t)}{U}=\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{y}{2\sqrt{\nu t}}\right),
\qquad t>0,\quad y\ge 0.
\]
The complementary error function satisfies $\operatorname{erfc}(0)=1$, $\operatorname{erfc}(\infty)=0$, and
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\eta}\operatorname{erfc}(\eta)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-\eta^2}.
\]

1. Compute the fluid shear stress $\tau_{xy}=\mu\partial u/\partial y$ and evaluate $\tau_{xy}(0,t)$.

2. The fluid occupies $y>0$, so the outward normal from the fluid at the plate is $-\mathbf j$. Deduce the $x$-component of the plate-on-fluid traction and confirm that its magnitude is positive.

3. Compute the $x$-momentum of the fluid per unit plate area,
   \[
   M'(t)=\int_0^\infty\rho u(y,t)\,\mathrm dy.
   \]
   Differentiate in $t$ and prove that $\mathrm dM'/\mathrm dt$ equals the plate-on-fluid traction.

4. Find the height $y$ at which $u/U=0.1$. Use $\operatorname{erfc}^{-1}(0.1)\approx 1.163087$ and report the coefficient of $\sqrt{\nu t}$ to five decimals.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\partial u/\partial y>0$ at the wall, so $\tau_{xy}(0,t)=+\mu U/\sqrt{\pi\nu t}$ is the fluid stress, and the plate-on-fluid traction is negative”; (ii) “the similarity variable is $y/\sqrt{\nu t}$ with no factor $2$, so $u/U=0.1$ occurs at $y\approx 1.16309\sqrt{\nu t}$ and $M'$ lacks the factor $2$.”

Do not replace the problem by a steady Couette or Poiseuille profile, and do not introduce a finite gap or a second moving wall.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the erfc profile at y=0, reverse the stress with the fluid outward normal, then integrate the profile for M' and differentiate under the integral.
Evaluate M' first by the substitution eta=y/(2 sqrt(nu t)), differentiate in t, and recover tau from the momentum theorem without recomputing du/dy.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates tau_xy(0,t)=-mu U/sqrt(pi nu t) from the erfc profile and identifies the positive plate-on-fluid traction magnitude.
Computes momentum per unit area 2 rho U sqrt(nu t/pi), matches its time derivative to the traction, and locates u/U=0.1 at y≈2.32617 sqrt(nu t).
Rejects a positive tau_xy(0,t) from the wrong wall slope and rejects a similarity variable missing the factor 2.

commonErrors.description: Takes du/dy>0 at the wall and reports tau_xy(0,t)=+mu U/sqrt(pi nu t) as the fluid stress, then a negative plate-on-fluid traction.
commonErrors.consequence: The plate is predicted to drag the fluid backward, contradicting the +x plate motion and the growth of M'.

commonErrors.description: Writes u/U=erfc(y/sqrt(nu t)) without the factor 2, so u/U=0.1 is placed at y≈1.16309 sqrt(nu t) and M' is halved.
commonErrors.consequence: The 10-percent thickness and the momentum inventory are both wrong by a factor of 2, and dM'/dt no longer matches the traction.

hintTree.content: At $y=0$, $\eta=0$ and $\partial u/\partial y=-U/\sqrt{\pi\nu t}$, hence $\tau_{xy}(0,t)=-\mu U/\sqrt{\pi\nu t}$.
Plate-on-fluid $x$-traction is $-\tau_{xy}(0,t)=+\mu U/\sqrt{\pi\nu t}$. Differentiating $2\rho U\sqrt{\nu t/\pi}$ recovers the same value.
$\operatorname{erfc}(\eta)=0.1$ at $\eta\approx 1.163087$, so $y=2\eta\sqrt{\nu t}\approx 2.32617\sqrt{\nu t}$.

FLUID:010425.canonicalSolution:
Set $\eta=y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})$. Then
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}
=U\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-\eta^2}\Bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\nu t}}
=-\frac{U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}}e^{-\eta^2}.
\]
The fluid shear stress is
\[
\tau_{xy}(y,t)=-\frac{\mu U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}}e^{-\eta^2},
\]
and the wall value is
\[
\boxed{\tau_{xy}(0,t)=-\frac{\mu U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}}}.
\]
The outward normal from the fluid at the plate is $-\mathbf j$, so the plate-on-fluid $x$-traction is
\[
-\tau_{xy}(0,t)=+\frac{\mu U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}}.
\]
Its magnitude
\[
\boxed{\frac{\mu U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}}}
\]
is positive and points in the direction of $U$.

The momentum per unit area is
\[
M'(t)
=\rho U\int_0^\infty\operatorname{erfc}\!\bigl(y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})\bigr)\,\mathrm dy
=\rho U\cdot 2\sqrt{\nu t}\int_0^\infty\operatorname{erfc}(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta.
\]
The remaining integral equals $1/\sqrt{\pi}$, therefore
\[
\boxed{M'(t)=2\rho U\sqrt{\frac{\nu t}{\pi}}}.
\]
Differentiating in time gives
\[
\frac{\mathrm dM'}{\mathrm dt}
=\rho U\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\pi t}}
=\frac{\mu U}{\sqrt{\pi\nu t}},
\]
which equals the plate-on-fluid traction.

The level set $u/U=0.1$ is $\operatorname{erfc}(\eta)=0.1$, so $\eta=\operatorname{erfc}^{-1}(0.1)\approx 1.163087$ and
\[
\boxed{y\approx 2.32617\sqrt{\nu t}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $u$ decreases with $y$, so $\partial u/\partial y<0$ and $\tau_{xy}(0,t)$ is negative. Sentence (ii) is false: dropping the factor $2$ in $\eta$ misplaces the $0.1$ contour at $1.16309\sqrt{\nu t}$ and halves $M'$.

The construction is the classical infinite-plate Stokes problem. No steady Couette gap is introduced.

graderFixtures.proofText: The wall slope is positive, so tau_xy(0,t)=+mu U/sqrt(pi nu t). The plate-on-fluid traction is then negative and M' would decrease.
I take eta=y/sqrt(nu t) with no factor 2. Then u/U=0.1 at y≈1.16309 sqrt(nu t) and M'=rho U sqrt(nu t/pi).

FLUID:010526.title: Droplet frequency is sqrt(sigma/(rho D^3)) F(Oh); halving D multiplies f by 2sqrt2
FLUID:010526.objective: Reduce the droplet list f, D, rho, sigma, mu to exactly two independent dimensionless groups, write the inviscid fixed-mode C scaling, and evaluate the exact factors for halving diameter and quadrupling density.
FLUID:010526.statement:
A small free droplet oscillates in a surrounding gas of negligible density. The oscillation frequency $f$ is assumed to depend only on
\[
f=\Phi(D,\rho,\sigma,\mu),
\]
where $D$ is a characteristic diameter, $\rho$ is the liquid density, $\sigma$ is the surface tension, and $\mu$ is the liquid viscosity. The dimensions are
\[
[f]=\mathrm T^{-1},\quad
[D]=\mathrm L,\quad
[\rho]=\mathrm M\mathrm L^{-3},\quad
[\sigma]=\mathrm M\mathrm T^{-2},\quad
[\mu]=\mathrm M\mathrm L^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}.
\]

1. Count the five quantities and the three independent dimensions, and conclude that exactly two independent dimensionless groups are required.

2. Construct the two groups
   \[
   \Pi_1=f\sqrt{\frac{\rho D^3}{\sigma}},
   \qquad
   \mathrm{Oh}=\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\rho\sigma D}}.
   \]
   Verify that each is dimensionless. Show that no other independent group can be formed from this list.

3. Invert the first group to obtain
   \[
   f=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho D^3}}\,F(\mathrm{Oh})
   \]
   for a function $F$ of a single variable.

4. In the inviscid fixed-mode limit $\mathrm{Oh}\to 0$, $F(\mathrm{Oh})$ approaches a positive constant $C$ that depends only on the mode. Write the resulting $C$-scaling for $f$. Then, holding $\sigma$ and the mode fixed, determine the exact factor by which $f$ changes if $D$ is halved, and the exact factor if $\rho$ is quadrupled.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\mu/\sqrt{\rho\sigma/D}$ is a valid dimensionless Ohnesorge number”; (ii) “frequency scales as $1/D$, so halving $D$ doubles $f$, and quadrupling $\rho$ leaves $f$ unchanged.”

Do not introduce gravity, a Reynolds–Froude pair, a pipe-loss factor, or any quantity outside $\{f,D,\rho,\sigma,\mu\}$.
permittedResults: Buckingham’s theorem: five quantities involving mass, length, and time reduce to $5-3=2$ independent dimensionless groups.
If $f=C\sqrt{\sigma/(\rho D^3)}$, then $f(D/2)/f(D)=2\sqrt{2}$ and $f(4\rho)/f(\rho)=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Nondimensionalize f by the inertio-capillary time sqrt(rho D^3/sigma), isolate Oh as the remaining viscosity group, then read the two scale factors from the C-prefactor.
Assign repeating variables rho, D, sigma, form Pi groups by exponents, then specialize F(0)=C and compare ratios at (D/2) and at (4 rho).

milestones.criterion: Constructs the two groups f sqrt(rho D^3/sigma) and Oh=mu/sqrt(rho sigma D) and writes f=sqrt(sigma/(rho D^3)) F(Oh).
States the inviscid fixed-mode C scaling and the exact factors 2sqrt(2) for halved D and 1/2 for quadrupled rho.
Rejects an Ohnesorge number with inverted diameter and rejects a linear 1/D frequency rule.

commonErrors.description: Writes Oh=mu/sqrt(rho sigma/D), which has dimensions of length rather than being dimensionless.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed quantity cannot be a Buckingham Pi group and carries the wrong diameter exponent, so viscous corrections scale incorrectly.

commonErrors.description: Takes f proportional to 1/D (or independent of rho), so halving D only doubles f and quadrupling rho is predicted to leave f unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: The inertio-capillary time scale D^{3/2} rho^{1/2} is lost and both required scale factors are wrong.

hintTree.content: $\sqrt{\rho D^3/\sigma}$ has dimension $\mathrm T$, so $\Pi_1$ is dimensionless. $\sqrt{\rho\sigma D}$ has the dimensions of $\mu$, so $\mathrm{Oh}$ is dimensionless.
Any third group built from the same list is a function of $\Pi_1$ and $\mathrm{Oh}$. The inversion $f=\sqrt{\sigma/(\rho D^3)}\,F(\mathrm{Oh})$ is then unique.
Halving $D$ multiplies $\sqrt{1/D^3}$ by $\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$. Quadrupling $\rho$ multiplies $\sqrt{1/\rho}$ by $1/2$.

FLUID:010526.canonicalSolution:
The list has five quantities and three independent dimensions, so exactly two independent groups exist. Direct substitution of the dimensions gives
\[
\Bigl[\sqrt{\frac{\rho D^3}{\sigma}}\Bigr]=\mathrm T,
\qquad
\bigl[\sqrt{\rho\sigma D}\bigr]=\mathrm M\mathrm L^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}=[\mu],
\]
hence both
\[
\boxed{\Pi_1=f\sqrt{\frac{\rho D^3}{\sigma}}}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\boxed{\mathrm{Oh}=\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\rho\sigma D}}}
\]
are dimensionless. Any other dimensionless combination is of the form $\Pi_1^a\mathrm{Oh}^b$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{f=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho D^3}}\,F(\mathrm{Oh})}.
\]
In the inviscid fixed-mode limit $\mathrm{Oh}\to 0$, $F\to C$ and
\[
\boxed{f=C\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\rho D^3}}}.
\]
Holding $\sigma$ and $C$ fixed,
\[
\frac{f(D/2)}{f(D)}
=\sqrt{\frac{D^3}{(D/2)^3}}
=\sqrt{8}
=\boxed{2\sqrt{2}},
\]
and
\[
\frac{f(4\rho)}{f(\rho)}
=\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{4\rho}}
=\boxed{\tfrac12}.
\]
Halving the diameter multiplies the frequency by $2\sqrt{2}$; quadrupling the density halves the frequency.

Sentence (i) is false: $\sqrt{\rho\sigma/D}$ has dimensions $\mathrm M\mathrm L^{-2}\mathrm T^{-1}$, so $\mu/\sqrt{\rho\sigma/D}$ has dimensions of length rather than unity. It also reverses the required diameter exponent and is not $\mathrm{Oh}$. Sentence (ii) is false: the capillary time is not linear in $D$. A $1/D$ rule would predict a factor $2$ on halving $D$ and no change on quadrupling $\rho$.

No gravitational acceleration and no Reynolds–Froude pair enters the list.

graderFixtures.proofText: The only independent groups are $f\sqrt{\rho D^3/\sigma}$ and $\mathrm{Oh}=\mu/\sqrt{\rho\sigma D}$, so $f=\sqrt{\sigma/(\rho D^3)}\,F(\mathrm{Oh})$. Inviscid fixed-mode scaling is $f=C\sqrt{\sigma/(\rho D^3)}$. Halving $D$ multiplies $f$ by $2\sqrt{2}$; quadrupling $\rho$ halves $f$.
I take Oh=mu/sqrt(rho sigma/D) and assume its units cancel. Then f=sqrt(sigma/(rho D^3)) F(Oh) uses that proposed viscosity argument.
Frequency scales as 1/D, so halving D doubles f. Density does not enter a 1/D rule, so quadrupling rho leaves f unchanged.

FLUID:010527.title: Similar pumps at N2/N1=3/2 and D2/D1=4/5 have Q2/Q1=96/125, H2/H1=36/25, P2/P1=3456/3125
FLUID:010527.objective: Form the three pump coefficients, impose complete similarity, and convert the given speed and diameter ratios into exact discharge, head, and power ratios.
FLUID:010527.statement:
Two geometrically similar pumps handle the same incompressible liquid of density $\rho$. At homologous operating points, use the standard discharge, head, and power coefficients
\[
\phi=\frac{Q}{ND^3},\qquad
\psi=\frac{gH}{N^2D^2},\qquad
\lambda=\frac{P}{\rho N^3D^5}.
\]
Pump 2 runs at speed and diameter ratios
\[
\frac{N_2}{N_1}=\frac32,\qquad
\frac{D_2}{D_1}=\frac45
\]
relative to a dynamically similar point of pump 1. Gravity $g$ is the same at both installations. Complete similarity means $\phi_2=\phi_1$, $\psi_2=\psi_1$, and $\lambda_2=\lambda_1$.

1. Starting from equal $\phi$, derive $Q_2/Q_1$ as a product of the given $N$ and $D$ ratios. Evaluate the exact rational value and the decimal $0.768$.

2. Starting from equal $\psi$, derive $H_2/H_1$. Evaluate the exact rational value and the decimal $1.44$.

3. Starting from equal $\lambda$ (or equivalently from $P\sim\rho gQH$ at equal efficiency), derive $P_2/P_1$. Evaluate the exact rational $3456/3125$ and the decimal $1.10592$.

4. Confirm that the three coefficients are dimensionless and that the same three ratios are recovered if one first scales $Q\sim ND^3$ and $H\sim N^2D^2/g$, then forms $P\sim\rho gQH$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “discharge scales with area, so $Q_2/Q_1=(N_2/N_1)(D_2/D_1)^2=24/25$”; (ii) “power uses the same diameter exponent as discharge, so $P_2/P_1=(N_2/N_1)^3(D_2/D_1)^3=1728/1000$.”

Do not introduce a Reynolds–Froude pair, a droplet Ohnesorge number, or a pipe-friction factor. Use only the three stated pump coefficients in this comparison.
permittedResults: If $\psi_2=\psi_1$ and $g$ is common, then $H_2/H_1=(N_2/N_1)^2(D_2/D_1)^2$. If also $\lambda_2=\lambda_1$, then $P_2/P_1=(N_2/N_1)^3(D_2/D_1)^5$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Invert each coefficient separately against the given N and D ratios, then cross-check P2/P1=(Q2/Q1)(H2/H1).
Write Q=phi N D^3, gH=psi N^2 D^2, P=lambda rho N^3 D^5 at common (phi,psi,lambda) and cancel the common factors.

milestones.criterion: States the three coefficients and obtains Q2/Q1=96/125=0.768 and H2/H1=36/25=1.44 from equal phi and psi.
Obtains P2/P1=3456/3125=1.10592 from equal lambda, equivalently from P~rho g Q H.
Rejects an area-based Q scaling and a D^3 power scaling.

commonErrors.description: Replaces ND^3 by an area rule ND^2, reporting Q2/Q1=(3/2)(16/25)=24/25=0.96.
commonErrors.consequence: The discharge ratio is 25 percent high and any power reconstructed from QH misses 3456/3125.

commonErrors.description: Gives the power coefficient the same diameter exponent as discharge, reporting P2/P1=(27/8)(64/125)=1.728.
commonErrors.consequence: The shaft-power ratio is overstated and is inconsistent with lambda=P/(rho N^3 D^5).

FLUID:010527.canonicalSolution:
Equal discharge coefficients give
\[
\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}
=\frac{N_2}{N_1}\Bigl(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\Bigr)^3
=\frac32\cdot\Bigl(\frac45\Bigr)^3
=\frac32\cdot\frac{64}{125}
=\boxed{\frac{96}{125}=0.768}.
\]
Equal head coefficients with common $g$ give
\[
\frac{H_2}{H_1}
=\Bigl(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\Bigr)^2
=\frac94\cdot\frac{16}{25}
=\frac{144}{100}
=\boxed{\frac{36}{25}=1.44}.
\]
Equal power coefficients give
\[
\frac{P_2}{P_1}
=\Bigl(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\Bigr)^3\Bigl(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\Bigr)^5
=\frac{27}{8}\cdot\frac{1024}{3125}
=\frac{27\cdot 128}{3125}
=\boxed{\frac{3456}{3125}=1.10592}.
\]
Each coefficient is dimensionless:
\[
[\phi]=1,\qquad [\psi]=1,\qquad [\lambda]=1.
\]
The same power ratio follows from $P\sim\rho gQH$ at equal efficiency:
\[
\frac{P_2}{P_1}
=\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\cdot\frac{H_2}{H_1}
=\frac{96}{125}\cdot\frac{36}{25}
=\frac{3456}{3125}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: replacing $D^3$ by an area factor $D^2$ yields $Q_2/Q_1=24/25=0.96$ and then a power ratio that cannot recover $3456/3125$. Sentence (ii) is false: $\lambda$ carries $D^5$, not $D^3$; the assignment $(27/8)(64/125)=1.728$ overstates the power ratio.

No Reynolds, Froude, or Ohnesorge group is required. The three pump coefficients already close the list.

graderFixtures.proofText: Discharge scales with area, so Q2/Q1=(3/2)(4/5)^2=24/25=0.96. Head is still 36/25.
Power uses the same D^3 as flow, so P2/P1=(3/2)^3 (4/5)^3=1728/1000=1.728.

FLUID:010528.title: A 1 mm wetting tube rises 0.0293578 m with Bo=0.13625; doubling D halves h and quadruples Bo
FLUID:010528.objective: Evaluate Jurin’s capillary rise and the Bond number for a fully wetting millimetre tube of water, then read the exact factors for doubled diameter.
FLUID:010528.statement:
A vertical circular glass tube of interior diameter $D=1\ \mathrm{mm}=0.001\ \mathrm{m}$ is dipped into a large reservoir of water. Use
\[
\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3},\qquad
\sigma=0.072\ \mathrm{N/m},\qquad
\theta=0,\qquad
g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.
\]
The contact angle $\theta=0$ is measured through the liquid (complete wetting). The reservoir free surface is the elevation datum.

1. Balance the vertical surface-tension force on the contact line against the weight of the risen column and obtain
   \[
   h=\frac{4\sigma\cos\theta}{\rho g D}.
   \]
   Evaluate $h$ for the stated data, and report $h/D$.

2. Form the Bond number $\mathrm{Bo}=\rho g D^2/\sigma$ and evaluate it exactly as a decimal.

3. Holding $\rho,\sigma,g,\theta$ fixed, determine the exact factors by which $h$ and $\mathrm{Bo}$ change if $D$ is doubled.

4. Interpret $\mathrm{Bo}\ll 1$ together with $h/D\gg 1$: the meniscus is capillary-dominated relative to the tube scale, while the risen column is many diameters tall.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the vertical force uses the radius, so $h=2\sigma/(\rho g D)$ and the rise is $0.0146789\ \mathrm{m}$”; (ii) “$\mathrm{Bo}=\rho g D/\sigma$, which is independent of a second length, so doubling $D$ doubles $\mathrm{Bo}$ and leaves $h$ unchanged.”

Do not introduce a pump coefficient, a droplet frequency, or a Reynolds–Froude pair. Gravity enters only through the column weight and $\mathrm{Bo}$.
permittedResults: If $\theta=0$, then $h=4\sigma/(\rho g D)$ and $h/D=4\sigma/(\rho g D^2)=4/\mathrm{Bo}$.
Under a diameter change at fixed $\rho,\sigma,g,\theta$, $h\propto D^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{Bo}\propto D^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Balance pi D sigma against rho g (pi D^2/4) h, then form Bo=rho g D^2/sigma and read h/D=4/Bo.
Nondimensionalize the rise by D first, obtain h/D=4/Bo, insert the numerical Bo=9.81/72, then scale in D.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates h=0.0293578 m from 4 sigma/(rho g D) and reports h/D=29.3578.
Evaluates Bo=0.13625 and the exact doubled-D factors: h halves, Bo quadruples.
Rejects a 2-sigma rise and a Bond number linear in D.

commonErrors.description: Writes the vertical capillary force as if D were already a radius, obtaining h=2 sigma/(rho g D)=0.0146789 m.
commonErrors.consequence: The rise and h/D are both half the Jurin values and no longer equal 4/Bo.

commonErrors.description: Defines Bo=rho g D/sigma, a quantity that is not the Bond number, and concludes that doubling D doubles Bo while h is unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: Both required diameter factors are wrong and Bo is no longer dimensionless against sigma/(rho g D^2).

hintTree.content: Doubling $D$ multiplies $h$ by $1/2$ and $\mathrm{Bo}$ by $4$.

FLUID:010528.canonicalSolution:
Complete wetting gives $\cos\theta=1$, so
\[
h=\frac{4\sigma}{\rho g D}
=\frac{4\cdot 0.072}{1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 0.001}
=\frac{0.288}{9.81}
=\boxed{0.0293578\ \mathrm{m}}.
\]
The aspect ratio is
\[
\boxed{\frac{h}{D}=29.3578}.
\]
The Bond number is
\[
\mathrm{Bo}
=\frac{\rho g D^2}{\sigma}
=\frac{1000\cdot 9.81\cdot(0.001)^2}{0.072}
=\frac{9.81}{72}
=\boxed{0.13625}.
\]
The identity $h/D=4/\mathrm{Bo}$ holds: $4/0.13625=29.3578$. Because $h\propto D^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{Bo}\propto D^2$, doubling the diameter
\[
\boxed{\text{halves }h}\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{\text{quadruples }\mathrm{Bo}}.
\]
The small Bond number and the large $h/D$ are consistent: gravity is weak on the millimetre scale, so the column climbs many diameters.

Sentence (i) is false: replacing the diameter by a single radius factor $2\sigma$ halves the rise to $0.0146789\ \mathrm{m}$ and breaks $h/D=4/\mathrm{Bo}$. Sentence (ii) is false: a linear Bond number $\rho g D/\sigma=136.25$ is not dimensionless in the same way, predicts the wrong $D$-scaling, and cannot leave $h$ invariant.

No pump affinity group and no droplet frequency is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $\theta=0$, $h=4\sigma/(\rho g D)=0.0293578$ m, $h/D=29.3578$, and $\mathrm{Bo}=\rho g D^2/\sigma=0.13625$. Doubling $D$ halves $h$ and quadruples $\mathrm{Bo}$.
The contact-line force uses the radius, so h=2 sigma/(rho g D)=0.0146789 m and h/D=14.6789.
I take Bo=rho g D/sigma=136.25. Doubling D then doubles Bo, and h does not depend on D once Bo is written that way.

FLUID:010629.title: The 1 mm, 30 deg film has q'=1.635e-5 m^2/s, Ubar=0.01635 m/s, us=0.024525 m/s, tauw=4.905 Pa
FLUID:010629.objective: Integrate the exact Nusselt falling-film balance, identify the surface and wall quantities, and evaluate the stated water–glycerin numbers.
FLUID:010629.statement:
A steady, fully developed liquid film of constant thickness $h$ drains down a wide plane inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The flow is unidirectional, $u=u(y)$ with $y$ measured normal to the wall from the wall toward the free surface. The liquid has constant $\rho$ and $\mu$. The free surface $y=h$ is stress-free and exposed to constant atmospheric pressure. There is no applied streamwise pressure gradient beyond hydrostatics; the driving body-force component is $\rho g\sin\theta$.

1. Reduce the streamwise momentum equation to $\mu u''+\rho g\sin\theta=0$. Integrate with $u(0)=0$ and $u'(h)=0$ to obtain
   \[
   u(y)=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta}{\mu}\Bigl(hy-\frac{y^2}{2}\Bigr).
   \]

2. Compute the volume flow rate per unit width $q'=\int_0^h u\,\mathrm dy$, the bulk speed $\bar U=q'/h$, the surface speed $u_s=u(h)$, and the wall shear $\tau_w=\mu u'(0)$. Show
   \[
   q'=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta\,h^3}{3\mu},\quad
   \bar U=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta\,h^2}{3\mu},\quad
   u_s=\frac32\bar U,\quad
   \tau_w=\rho g h\sin\theta.
   \]

3. Evaluate the four quantities for
   \[
   \rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3},\quad
   \mu=0.1\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s},\quad
   h=0.001\ \mathrm{m},\quad
   \theta=30^\circ,\quad
   g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.
   \]

4. Confirm $u_s=(3/2)\bar U$ from the profile, not from a Couette guess.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the plane is steep enough that $\sin\theta$ may be replaced by $1$, doubling every numerical value”; (ii) “a free surface behaves like a moving lid, so $u_s=2\bar U$ as in plane Couette flow.”

Do not replace the film by a pipe-loss problem, a Stokes sphere, or a boundary-layer integral.
permittedResults: The second integral of $u''=-(\rho g\sin\theta)/\mu$ with $u(0)=0$ and $u'(h)=0$ is $u=(\rho g\sin\theta/\mu)(hy-y^2/2)$.
Global streamwise balance on a slice of length $1$ equates wall shear to the downslope weight: $\tau_w=\rho g h\sin\theta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate u''=-(rho g sin theta)/mu with the two boundary conditions, then compute the four integral/wall quantities before inserting numbers.
Obtain tauw from a global downslope weight balance, recover Ubar from q'=Ubar h, and only then evaluate the 30-degree numbers.

milestones.criterion: Integrates the exact profile and the closed forms for q', Ubar, us=3 Ubar/2, and tauw.
Evaluates q'=1.635e-5 m^2/s, Ubar=0.01635 m/s, us=0.024525 m/s, and tauw=4.905 Pa.
Rejects replacing sin theta by 1 and rejects us=2 Ubar.

commonErrors.description: Replaces sin(30 deg) by 1, doubling q' to 3.27e-5 m^2/s, Ubar to 0.0327 m/s, us to 0.04905 m/s, and tauw to 9.81 Pa.
commonErrors.consequence: Every transport and stress number is too large by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Treats the free surface as a moving lid and sets us=2 Ubar=0.0327 m/s while keeping the correct Ubar.
commonErrors.consequence: The surface speed contradicts the stress-free parabola, which requires us=3 Ubar/2.

hintTree.content: $\bar U=q'/h=0.01635\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $u_s=(3/2)\bar U=0.024525\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
$\tau_w=\rho g h\sin\theta=1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 0.001\cdot(1/2)=4.905\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

FLUID:010629.canonicalSolution:
The fully developed balance is $\mu u''+\rho g\sin\theta=0$. One integration with $u'(h)=0$ gives
\[
u'(y)=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta}{\mu}(h-y).
\]
A second integration with $u(0)=0$ gives
\[
\boxed{u(y)=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta}{\mu}\Bigl(hy-\frac{y^2}{2}\Bigr)}.
\]
The volume flux per unit width is
\[
q'
=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta}{\mu}\int_0^h\Bigl(hy-\frac{y^2}{2}\Bigr)\,\mathrm dy
=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta}{\mu}\Bigl[\frac{h}{2}h^2-\frac16 h^3\Bigr]
=\boxed{\frac{\rho g\sin\theta\,h^3}{3\mu}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\bar U=\frac{q'}{h}=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta\,h^2}{3\mu}},
\qquad
u_s=u(h)=\frac{\rho g\sin\theta\,h^2}{2\mu}=\boxed{\frac32\bar U},
\]
and
\[
\tau_w=\mu u'(0)=\rho g h\sin\theta=\boxed{\rho gh\sin\theta}.
\]
With $\sin 30^\circ=1/2$ and $\rho g\sin\theta=4905\ \mathrm{N/m^3}$,
\begin{align*}
q'&=\frac{4905\cdot(0.001)^3}{3\cdot 0.1}
=\boxed{1.635\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}},\\
\bar U&=\frac{q'}{0.001}
=\boxed{0.01635\ \mathrm{m/s}},\\
u_s&=\frac32\cdot 0.01635
=\boxed{0.024525\ \mathrm{m/s}},\\
\tau_w&=1000\cdot 9.81\cdot 0.001\cdot\frac12
=\boxed{4.905\ \mathrm{Pa}}.
\end{align*}

Sentence (i) is false: replacing $\sin 30^\circ$ by $1$ doubles every number ($q'=3.27\times 10^{-5}$, $\tau_w=9.81$). Sentence (ii) is false: a stress-free surface is not a moving lid; the Couette factor $u_s=2\bar U$ would give $0.0327\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

The construction is an exact fully developed film. No pipe friction factor is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The exact film is $u=(\rho g\sin\theta/\mu)(hy-y^2/2)$. For the stated numbers, $q'=1.635\times 10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\bar U=0.01635$ m/s, $u_s=0.024525$ m/s, and $\tau_w=4.905$ Pa, with $u_s=(3/2)\bar U$.
I take the drain as vertical, sin theta=1. Then q'=3.27e-5 m^2/s, Ubar=0.0327 m/s, us=0.04905 m/s, and tauw=9.81 Pa.
The free surface is like a Couette lid, so us=2 Ubar=0.0327 m/s. The flux and wall shear are otherwise unchanged.

FLUID:010630.title: The quadratic profile has delta*=delta/3, theta=2 delta/15, H=5/2, and Cf=4/sqrt(30 Re_x)
FLUID:010630.objective: Check the quadratic boundary-layer profile, compute displacement, momentum, and wall quantities, close the von Kármán integral, and extract the local skin-friction law.
FLUID:010630.statement:
A steady zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer on a flat plate has free-stream speed $U$ and thickness $\delta(x)$. The assumed profile, written in $\eta=y/\delta$, is
\[
\frac{u}{U}=2\eta-\eta^2,\qquad 0\le\eta\le 1,
\]
and $u=U$ for $\eta>1$. The fluid has kinematic viscosity $\nu$ and dynamic viscosity $\mu=\rho\nu$.

1. Check the profile: $u(0)=0$, $u(\delta)=U$, and $\partial u/\partial y$ at $y=\delta$ vanishes. State why a linear profile would fail the last check.

2. Compute the displacement thickness $\delta^*=\int_0^\delta(1-u/U)\,\mathrm dy$ and the momentum thickness $\theta=\int_0^\delta(u/U)(1-u/U)\,\mathrm dy$. Form the shape factor $H=\delta^*/\theta$.

3. Evaluate the wall shear $\tau_w=\mu(\partial u/\partial y)_{y=0}$.

4. Close the von Kármán integral $d\theta/dx=\tau_w/(\rho U^2)$ with $\theta=2\delta/15$ and $\tau_w=2\mu U/\delta$. Integrate from a leading-edge state $\delta(0)=0$ to obtain $\delta=\sqrt{30\nu x/U}$. Then form the local skin-friction coefficient $C_f=\tau_w/(\tfrac12\rho U^2)$ and show
   \[
   C_f=\frac{4}{\sqrt{30\,\mathrm{Re}_x}},\qquad \mathrm{Re}_x=\frac{Ux}{\nu}.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “a linear profile is just as good, so $\delta^*=\delta/2$, $\theta=\delta/6$, and the $30$ is replaced by $12$”; (ii) “the Blasius local law $C_f=0.664/\sqrt{\mathrm{Re}_x}$ is the exact value of this integral model, so the factor $4/\sqrt{30}$ may be discarded.”

Do not replace the integral model by a pipe-friction chart or a falling-film exact solution.
permittedResults: If $u/U=2\eta-\eta^2$ on $0\le\eta\le 1$, then $\delta^*=\delta/3$, $\theta=2\delta/15$, $H=5/2$, and $\tau_w=2\mu U/\delta$.
The separable integral $\delta\,\mathrm d\delta=15\nu\,\mathrm dx/U$ with $\delta(0)=0$ integrates to $\delta=\sqrt{30\nu x/U}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the two definite integrals in eta, insert theta=2 delta/15 into d theta/dx=2 nu/(U delta), and integrate.
Check the three profile conditions first, then obtain Cf=4 nu/(U delta) and substitute the integrated delta.

milestones.criterion: Checks the quadratic profile and obtains delta*=delta/3, theta=2 delta/15, H=5/2, and tauw=2 mu U/delta.
Closes von Karman to delta=sqrt(30 nu x/U) and Cf=4/sqrt(30 Re_x).
Rejects a linear profile that fails the edge-slope check and rejects replacing 4/sqrt(30) by the Blasius 0.664.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the quadratic profile by u/U=eta, taking delta*=delta/2 and theta=delta/6 and integrating to delta=sqrt(12 nu x/U).
commonErrors.consequence: The edge shear does not vanish, H becomes 3 rather than 5/2, and Cf is no longer 4/sqrt(30 Re_x).

commonErrors.description: Discards 4/sqrt(30) and reports the Blasius local law Cf=0.664/sqrt(Re_x) as the result of this integral model.
commonErrors.consequence: The quadratic closure is abandoned and the factor 30 is never used.

hintTree.content: $\int_0^1(1-2\eta+\eta^2)\,\mathrm d\eta=1/3$ and $\int_0^1(2\eta-5\eta^2+4\eta^3-\eta^4)\,\mathrm d\eta=2/15$.
Wall slope $\partial u/\partial y=2U/\delta$, so $\tau_w=2\mu U/\delta$. Then $(2/15)\delta'=2\nu/(U\delta)$.
$\delta=\sqrt{30\nu x/U}$ into $C_f=4\nu/(U\delta)$ produces $4/\sqrt{30\,\mathrm{Re}_x}$.

FLUID:010630.canonicalSolution:
At $\eta=0$, $u/U=0$. At $\eta=1$, $u/U=2-1=1$. The wall-normal derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\frac{U}{\delta}(2-2\eta),
\]
which vanishes at $\eta=1$. A linear profile $u/U=\eta$ matches $u(0)$ and $u(\delta)$ but has $\partial u/\partial y=U/\delta\neq 0$ at the edge, so it cannot merge smoothly into the free stream.

The thicknesses are
\[
\delta^*
=\delta\int_0^1(1-2\eta+\eta^2)\,\mathrm d\eta
=\delta\Bigl[\eta-\eta^2+\frac{\eta^3}{3}\Bigr]_0^1
=\boxed{\frac{\delta}{3}},
\]
\[
\frac{u}{U}\Bigl(1-\frac{u}{U}\Bigr)
=(2\eta-\eta^2)(1-2\eta+\eta^2)
=2\eta-5\eta^2+4\eta^3-\eta^4,
\]
\[
\theta
=\delta\int_0^1(2\eta-5\eta^2+4\eta^3-\eta^4)\,\mathrm d\eta
=\delta\Bigl[1-\frac53+1-\frac15\Bigr]
=\boxed{\frac{2\delta}{15}}.
\]
The shape factor is
\[
H=\frac{\delta/3}{2\delta/15}=\boxed{\frac52}.
\]
Wall shear is
\[
\tau_w=\mu\cdot\frac{2U}{\delta}=\boxed{\frac{2\mu U}{\delta}}.
\]
The von Kármán statement becomes
\[
\frac{2}{15}\frac{\mathrm d\delta}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2\nu}{U\delta}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\delta\,\mathrm d\delta=\frac{15\nu}{U}\,\mathrm dx.
\]
Integration from $\delta(0)=0$ yields
\[
\frac{\delta^2}{2}=\frac{15\nu x}{U}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\delta=\sqrt{\frac{30\nu x}{U}}}.
\]
The local skin-friction coefficient is
\[
C_f
=\frac{2\mu U/\delta}{\tfrac12\rho U^2}
=\frac{4\nu}{U\delta}
=\frac{4\nu}{\sqrt{30\nu U x}}
=\boxed{\frac{4}{\sqrt{30\,\mathrm{Re}_x}}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: the linear profile fails the edge-slope check and replaces $30$ by $12$, giving $C_f=2/\sqrt{12\,\mathrm{Re}_x}=1/\sqrt{3\,\mathrm{Re}_x}$. Sentence (ii) is false: $4/\sqrt{30}\approx 0.730$ is the integral-model coefficient, not the Blasius $0.664$; the two closures are distinct.

The model is a single assumed profile plus the momentum integral. No pipe chart is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: The profile satisfies $u(0)=0$, $u(\delta)=U$, and $\partial u/\partial y|_ {\delta}=0$. Then $\delta^*=\delta/3$, $\theta=2\delta/15$, $H=5/2$, $\tau_w=2\mu U/\delta$, $\delta=\sqrt{30\nu x/U}$, and $C_f=4/\sqrt{30\,\mathrm{Re}_x}$.
A linear profile is just as good: delta*=delta/2, theta=delta/6, H=3, and delta=sqrt(12 nu x/U). I never enforce zero edge shear.
The exact local skin friction is the Blasius value Cf=0.664/sqrt(Re_x), so I discard 4/sqrt(30) and never integrate the 30.

FLUID:010631.title: The 1 mm sphere settles at 8.175e-4 m/s with Re=8.175e-4 and reaches 95 percent in 4.1607e-4 s
FLUID:010631.objective: Balance buoyant weight against Stokes drag, confirm the Reynolds number is small, integrate the linear transient, and evaluate the 95-percent time.
FLUID:010631.statement:
A smooth solid sphere of diameter $d=1\ \mathrm{mm}=0.001\ \mathrm{m}$ and density $\rho_p=2500\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is released from rest in an unbounded still liquid of density $\rho_f=1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and viscosity $\mu=1\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$. Gravity is $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Use the Stokes drag $3\pi\mu d V$ on the particle, omit added mass and Basset history, and take the particle inertia as $\rho_p\mathcal V$ with $\mathcal V=\pi d^3/6$.

1. Equate the submerged weight $(\rho_p-\rho_f)\mathcal V g$ to the Stokes drag and obtain the terminal speed
   \[
   V_t=\frac{(\rho_p-\rho_f)d^2 g}{18\mu}.
   \]
   Evaluate $V_t$.

2. Form the terminal Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=\rho_f V_t d/\mu$ and confirm that it is far below $1$, so the Stokes drag is consistent.

3. Write the linear momentum balance
   \[
   \rho_p\mathcal V\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dt}
   =(\rho_p-\rho_f)\mathcal V g-3\pi\mu d\,V
   \]
   and show that
   \[
   V(t)=V_t\bigl(1-e^{-t/\tau}\bigr),\qquad
   \tau=\frac{\rho_p d^2}{18\mu}.
   \]
   Evaluate $\tau$.

4. The time to $V=0.95V_t$ is $\tau\ln 20$. Evaluate that time.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “buoyancy may be dropped, so $V_t$ uses $\rho_p$ rather than $\rho_p-\rho_f$ and is $1.3625\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$”; (ii) “Stokes drag is $6\pi\mu d V$ if $d$ is the diameter, which replaces $18$ by $36$ in $V_t$ and $\tau$.”

Do not replace the sphere by a falling film or a flat-plate integral, and do not invoke a pipe-friction chart.
permittedResults: Terminal balance $(\rho_p-\rho_f)(\pi d^3/6)g=3\pi\mu d V_t$ rearranges to $V_t=(\rho_p-\rho_f)d^2 g/(18\mu)$.
The unique solution of $\tau\dot V+V=V_t$ with $V(0)=0$ is $V=V_t(1-e^{-t/\tau})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Cancel pi d between submerged weight and 3 pi mu d Vt, then read tau from rho_p Vol/(3 pi mu d) and multiply by ln 20.
Form the linear ODE tau V'+V=Vt from the start, identify Vt and tau by matching coefficients, then evaluate the two numbers.

milestones.criterion: Obtains Vt=8.175e-4 m/s from the buoyant Stokes balance and Re=8.175e-4.
Obtains tau=1.38889e-4 s, V(t)=Vt(1-e^{-t/tau}), and t_95=tau ln 20 ≈ 4.1607e-4 s.
Rejects dropping buoyancy and rejects the 6 pi mu d diameter-as-radius drag.

commonErrors.description: Omits the displaced-fluid weight and uses rho_p in place of rho_p-rho_f, reporting Vt=1.3625e-3 m/s and Re=1.3625e-3.
commonErrors.consequence: The terminal speed and Reynolds number are both 2500/1500 times too large.

commonErrors.description: Writes the Stokes drag as 6 pi mu d V with d the diameter, replacing 18 by 36 and halving Vt and tau.
commonErrors.consequence: Vt becomes 4.0875e-4 m/s and the 95-percent time is halved, corresponding to a sphere of twice the true radius.

hintTree.content: $\ln 20\approx 2.99573$, so $\tau\ln 20\approx 4.1607\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm s$.

FLUID:010631.canonicalSolution:
The terminal balance is
\[
(\rho_p-\rho_f)\frac{\pi d^3}{6}g=3\pi\mu d\,V_t,
\]
which rearranges to
\[
V_t
=\frac{(\rho_p-\rho_f)d^2 g}{18\mu}
=\frac{1500\cdot(0.001)^2\cdot 9.81}{18\cdot 1}
=\boxed{8.175\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The terminal Reynolds number is
\[
\mathrm{Re}
=\frac{\rho_f V_t d}{\mu}
=\frac{1000\cdot 8.175\times 10^{-4}\cdot 0.001}{1}
=\boxed{8.175\times 10^{-4}}\ll 1,
\]
so the Stokes drag is consistent. Particle inertia over the linear drag gives the time constant
\[
\tau
=\frac{\rho_p(\pi d^3/6)}{3\pi\mu d}
=\frac{\rho_p d^2}{18\mu}
=\frac{2500\cdot 10^{-6}}{18}
=\boxed{1.38889\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The solution released from rest is
\[
\boxed{V(t)=V_t\bigl(1-e^{-t/\tau}\bigr)}.
\]
The 95-percent time satisfies $e^{-t/\tau}=1/20$, hence
\[
t_{95}=\tau\ln 20
=\boxed{4.1607\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm s}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: dropping buoyancy replaces $1500$ by $2500$ and reports $V_t=1.3625\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, which is not the submerged weight. Sentence (ii) is false: $6\pi\mu d V$ is the radius formula written with the diameter, doubles the drag, and halves both $V_t$ and $\tau$.

The model is an unbounded Stokes sphere. No film profile and no pipe factor is used.

GA:010117.title: On the three-element chain, Yoneda gives one natural map Hom(-,1) to Hom(-,2) and none in reverse
GA:010117.objective: For the poset category P on 0<1<2, prove Nat(Hom(-,1),Hom(-,2)) has cardinality 1, the reverse set is empty, and the unique forward transformation is determined by sending id_1 to the unique arrow 1→2.
GA:010117.statement:
Let $P$ be the poset category with objects $\{0,1,2\}$ and a
unique morphism $i\to j$ if and only if $i\le j$. Write
$h_1=\operatorname{Hom}_P(-,1)$ and $h_2=\operatorname{Hom}_P(-,2)$
for the covariant representable functors $P^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$.

1. Compute every hom-set of $P$. Prove that
   \[
   \bigl\lvert\operatorname{Nat}(h_1,h_2)\bigr\rvert=1
   \]
   and that $\operatorname{Nat}(h_2,h_1)$ is empty.

2. Let $\eta:h_1\Rightarrow h_2$ be the unique natural
   transformation. Prove that $\eta$ is completely determined by
   the component $\eta_1$, and that
   \[
   \eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)
   \]
   is the unique arrow $1\to 2$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “there is no natural map $h_1\Rightarrow h_2$,
   or else there is a natural map $h_2\Rightarrow h_1$”; (ii) “the
   unique forward transformation, if it exists, may send
   $\mathrm{id}_1$ to $\mathrm{id}_1$ or to the unique arrow
   $0\to 2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $\mathbb{F}_5$ split
exact matrix ledger of this shard, by a Schreier basis, by a node
ring spectrum, or by an $\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{Z}/9\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3)$
count. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.
permittedResults: Yoneda's lemma specialises to $\operatorname{Nat}(h_A,h_B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$, via $\eta\mapsto\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$. In $P$ one has $\lvert\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)\rvert=1$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(2,1)=\emptyset$.

Naturality at $\mathrm{id}_A$ forces every component: if $f:X\to A$ then $\eta_X(f)=\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)\circ f$. Thus a natural transformation $h_A\Rightarrow h_B$ is determined by the single arrow $\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A):A\to B$.

acceptableStrategies.description: List every hom-set, then either assemble the unique family of component functions or quote Yoneda as Nat(h_A,h_B)≅Hom(A,B).
Use naturality at id_1 to recover every component from the single arrow 1→2.

milestones.criterion: Computes the hom-sets of P and proves |Nat(h1,h2)|=1 while Nat(h2,h1) is empty.
Shows the unique forward transformation is determined by eta_1(id_1), equal to the unique arrow 1→2.
Rejects reversing the two Yoneda counts and refuses a wrong image of id_1.

commonErrors.description: Claims that Nat(h1,h2) is empty, or that a natural transformation h2⇒h1 exists.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities |Nat(h1,h2)|=1 and Nat(h2,h1)=∅ are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Sends eta_1(id_1) to id_1 or to the unique arrow 0→2 instead of the unique arrow 1→2.
commonErrors.consequence: The unique forward transformation is no longer identified with the Yoneda correspondent of 1→2.

hintTree.content: List all nine hom-sets. Exactly six are nonempty; the three empty ones are $\operatorname{Hom}(2,0)$, $\operatorname{Hom}(2,1)$, and $\operatorname{Hom}(1,0)$.

A family $\eta_X:\operatorname{Hom}(X,1)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X,2)$ can exist only for $X=0,1$, because $\operatorname{Hom}(2,1)=\emptyset$ while $\operatorname{Hom}(2,2)$ is a singleton; the empty function $\emptyset\to\{\ast\}$ is unique, so the obstruction is in the reverse direction.
Yoneda (or naturality at $\mathrm{id}_1$) sends $\eta$ to $\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)\in\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)$, a singleton. The reverse would require an arrow $2\to 1$, which does not exist.

GA:010117.canonicalSolution:
The hom-sets of $P$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Hom}(0,0)&=\{\mathrm{id}_0\},&
\operatorname{Hom}(0,1)&=\{\,0\to 1\,\},&
\operatorname{Hom}(0,2)&=\{\,0\to 2\,\},\\
\operatorname{Hom}(1,0)&=\emptyset,&
\operatorname{Hom}(1,1)&=\{\mathrm{id}_1\},&
\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)&=\{\,1\to 2\,\},\\
\operatorname{Hom}(2,0)&=\emptyset,&
\operatorname{Hom}(2,1)&=\emptyset,&
\operatorname{Hom}(2,2)&=\{\mathrm{id}_2\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular $h_1(0)$ and $h_1(1)$ are singletons, $h_1(2)=\emptyset$,
and $h_2(X)$ is a singleton for every object $X$.

A natural transformation $\eta:h_1\Rightarrow h_2$ is a family of
functions
\[
\eta_0:\{\ast\}\to\{\ast\},\qquad
\eta_1:\{\ast\}\to\{\ast\},\qquad
\eta_2:\emptyset\to\{\ast\}.
\]
Each of these functions exists and is unique. Naturality squares
are automatic: whenever a hom-set on the $h_1$ side is nonempty,
both paths are maps between singletons. Thus there is exactly one
natural transformation $h_1\Rightarrow h_2$.
\[
\boxed{\lvert\operatorname{Nat}(h_1,h_2)\rvert=1}.
\]

In the reverse direction a component
$\theta_2:h_2(2)\to h_1(2)$ would be a function
$\{\mathrm{id}_2\}\to\emptyset$, which cannot exist. Hence
$\operatorname{Nat}(h_2,h_1)=\emptyset$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Nat}(h_2,h_1)=\emptyset}.
\]

Equivalently, Yoneda's lemma gives
$\operatorname{Nat}(h_A,h_B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ by
$\eta\mapsto\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$. Then
$\operatorname{Nat}(h_1,h_2)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)$ is a
singleton and $\operatorname{Nat}(h_2,h_1)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(2,1)$
is empty.

For the unique $\eta:h_1\Rightarrow h_2$, naturality at an arbitrary
arrow $f:X\to 1$ reads
\[
\eta_X(f)=\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)\circ f.
\]
Thus $\eta$ is determined by the single arrow
$\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)\in\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)$. That hom-set
contains only the unique morphism $1\to 2$, so
\[
\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)=(1\to 2).
\]
This arrow is not $\mathrm{id}_1$ (wrong target) and is not the
unique arrow $0\to 2$ (wrong source).
\[
\boxed{\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)=\text{the unique arrow }1\to 2}.
\]

Sentence (i) reverses the two Yoneda cardinalities. Sentence (ii)
sends $\mathrm{id}_1$ to an arrow that is not the unique element
of $\operatorname{Hom}(1,2)$.

The argument never replaces the three-chain Yoneda ledger by the
sibling $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a Schreier basis, by a
node ring spectrum, or by an endomorphism count, and it does not
open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The hom-sets of $P$ make $h_1(2)=\emptyset$ and $h_2$ pointwise a singleton, so there is a unique family $\eta:h_1\Rightarrow h_2$ and no family $h_2\Rightarrow h_1$. Yoneda identifies $\eta$ with $\eta_1(\mathrm{id}_1)$, which must be the unique arrow $1\to 2$.
There is no natural map h1⇒h2, and there is a natural map h2⇒h1. I do not accept |Nat(h1,h2)|=1 or an empty reverse set.
The unique forward transformation sends id_1 to id_1, or else to the unique arrow 0→2. I do not accept that eta_1(id_1) is the unique arrow 1→2.

GA:010118.title: Over F_5 the maps f(x,y)=(x,y,x+y) and g=a+b-c form a split exact rank 2/1 ledger
GA:010118.objective: Over F_5, prove that f(x,y)=(x,y,x+y) and g(a,b,c)=a+b-c give a short exact sequence of ranks 2 and 1, that im f=ker g=span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}, that s(t)=(t,0,0) is a section, that v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b), and evaluate the identity on (4,3,2).
GA:010118.statement:
Work throughout over the field $\mathbb{F}_5$. Define
\[
f:\mathbb{F}_5^2\to\mathbb{F}_5^3,\qquad
f(x,y)=(x,y,x+y),
\]
and
\[
g:\mathbb{F}_5^3\to\mathbb{F}_5,\qquad
g(a,b,c)=a+b-c.
\]

1. Prove that
   \[
   0\to\mathbb{F}_5^2\xrightarrow{f}\mathbb{F}_5^3\xrightarrow{g}\mathbb{F}_5\to 0
   \]
   is exact, that $\operatorname{rank}f=2$ and $\operatorname{rank}g=1$,
   and that
   \[
   \ker g=\operatorname{im}f=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}.
   \]

2. Let $s:\mathbb{F}_5\to\mathbb{F}_5^3$ be $s(t)=(t,0,0)$. Prove
   that $g\circ s=\mathrm{id}$ and that every
   $v=(a,b,c)$ satisfies
   \[
   v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b).
   \]
   Evaluate the identity on the sample vector $(4,3,2)$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\ker g$ is not $\operatorname{im}f$,
   or the ranks are not $2$ and $1$”; (ii) “both
   $t\mapsto(0,t,0)$ and $t\mapsto(0,0,t)$ fail to be sections.”
   Explain why the first alternate is a valid different section with
   a different complementary projection, while the second is not a
   section, and retain the assigned identity for $s(t)=(t,0,0)$.

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling three-chain Yoneda
ledger, by a Schreier basis, by a node ring spectrum, or by an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{Z}/9\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3)$ count. Do not
reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: If $g\circ f=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}f=\dim\ker g$, then $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$. Here $g(f(x,y))=x+y-(x+y)=0$ and both spaces are two-dimensional.
Given a section $s$, the identity $v=s(gv)+(v-s(gv))$ is the splitting of $v$. If $v-s(gv)$ lies in $\operatorname{im}f$ and $f$ is injective, the preimage is unique.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute g∘f=0, read the two columns of f, and compare dimensions of im f and ker g.
Insert s(t)=(t,0,0) into v-s(gv) and match the result to f(c-b,b); evaluate at (4,3,2) as a checksum.

milestones.criterion: Proves short exactness with rank f=2, rank g=1, and ker g=im f=span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}.
Checks that s(t)=(t,0,0) is a section, that v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b), and that the identity holds at (4,3,2).
Audits the alternate sections correctly: (0,t,0) is valid with a different projection, while (0,0,t) is not a section.

commonErrors.description: Claims that ker g is not im f, or that the ranks of f and g are not 2 and 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The short exact sequence of ranks 2/1 and the identification span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)} are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that t↦(0,t,0) is not a section or gives the assigned projection f(c-b,b), treats t↦(0,0,t) as a section, or denies the assigned identity v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b).
commonErrors.consequence: The alternate-section audit is false, or the assigned section (t,0,0) and its complementary identity on (a,b,c) and (4,3,2) fail.

hintTree.content: $g(f(x,y))=x+y-(x+y)=0$. The columns of $f$ are $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$, which are independent, so $\operatorname{rank}f=2$.
$\ker g=\{(a,b,c):c=a+b\}$ is spanned by the same two vectors, so $\operatorname{rank}g=1$ and $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$.
For $v=(a,b,c)$ one has $s(gv)=(a+b-c,0,0)$, hence $v-s(gv)=(c-b,b,c)=f(c-b,b)$. At $(4,3,2)$ one has $g=0$ in $\mathbb{F}_5$.

GA:010118.canonicalSolution:
Over $\mathbb{F}_5$,
\[
g\bigl(f(x,y)\bigr)=x+y-(x+y)=0,
\]
so $\operatorname{im}f\subseteq\ker g$. The matrix of $f$ has columns
$(1,0,1)^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $(0,1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}$. These are linearly
independent (a relation $\alpha(1,0,1)+\beta(0,1,1)=0$ forces
$\alpha=\beta=0$), so
\[
\operatorname{rank}f=2=\dim\mathbb{F}_5^2
\]
and $f$ is injective. The functional $g$ is $(1,1,-1)$, which is
nonzero, so $\operatorname{rank}g=1$ and $g$ is surjective. Then
\[
\dim\ker g=3-1=2=\operatorname{rank}f,
\]
hence $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$. Explicitly,
\[
\ker g=\{(a,b,c):c=a+b\}=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}=\operatorname{im}f.
\]
The sequence is therefore short exact of ranks $2$ and $1$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}f=2,\ \operatorname{rank}g=1,\ \ker g=\operatorname{im}f=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}}.
\]

The proposed section is $s(t)=(t,0,0)$. Then
\[
g\bigl(s(t)\bigr)=t+0-0=t,
\]
so $g\circ s=\mathrm{id}$. For $v=(a,b,c)$ one has $gv=a+b-c$ and
\[
v-s(gv)=(a,b,c)-(a+b-c,0,0)=(c-b,b,c).
\]
On the other hand
\[
f(c-b,b)=(c-b,b,(c-b)+b)=(c-b,b,c).
\]
Thus $v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b)$.
\[
\boxed{s(t)=(t,0,0),\quad v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b)}.
\]

On the sample $v=(4,3,2)$ one has
\[
gv=4+3-2=5\equiv 0\pmod{5},
\]
so $s(gv)=(0,0,0)$ and $v-s(gv)=(4,3,2)$. The claimed preimage is
$(c-b,b)=(2-3,3)=(-1,3)\equiv(4,3)$, and
\[
f(4,3)=(4,3,7)\equiv(4,3,2)\pmod{5}.
\]
\[
\boxed{(4,3,2)-s(g(4,3,2))=f(4,3)=(4,3,2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies exactness or the rank pair $2/1$. In sentence
(ii), the map $s_2(t)=(0,t,0)$ really is a section because
$g(0,t,0)=t$; it simply gives the different projection
\[
v-s_2(gv)=(a,c-a,c)=f(a,c-a).
\]
By contrast, $s_3(t)=(0,0,t)$ is not a section because
$g(0,0,t)=-t\ne t$ in general. Neither observation changes the
assigned section $s(t)=(t,0,0)$ or its identity
$v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b)$.

The argument never replaces the $\mathbb{F}_5$ ledger by the sibling
Yoneda count, by a Schreier basis, by a node ring spectrum, or by
an endomorphism count, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: Over $\mathbb{F}_5$ one has $g\circ f=0$, $\operatorname{rank}f=2$, $\operatorname{rank}g=1$, and $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}$. The map $s(t)=(t,0,0)$ is a section and $v-s(gv)=f(c-b,b)$, which holds at $(4,3,2)$.
ker g is not im f, and the ranks are not 2 and 1. I do not accept span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)} as both the image and the kernel.
Both t↦(0,t,0) and t↦(0,0,t) fail to be sections, so there is no alternate splitting to audit. I do not accept that g(0,t,0)=t.

GA:010127.title: Over F2 tensor-Hom currying has dimension 12 and cardinality 4096, with matrix [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]] and B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0)
GA:010127.objective: For U=F2^2, V=F2^3, W=F2^2, prove the currying isomorphism Hom(U tensor V, W) cong Hom(U, Hom(V,W)), both of dimension 12 and cardinality 4096. For B((a,b),(x,y,z))=(ax+by, bx+az), exhibit the curry matrix [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]] and verify B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0).
GA:010127.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_2$ be the field with two elements, and set
\[
U=\mathbb{F}_2^2,\qquad V=\mathbb{F}_2^3,\qquad W=\mathbb{F}_2^2
\]
with the standard ordered bases. Write $\otimes$ for the tensor
product of vector spaces over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

1. Prove that the currying (tensor--Hom adjunction) map
   \[
   \operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)
   \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
   \operatorname{Hom}\bigl(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\bigr)
   \]
   is a linear isomorphism. Compute both dimensions and both
   cardinalities, and prove they equal $12$ and $4096$.

2. Let $B:U\times V\to W$ be the bilinear map
   \[
   B\bigl((a,b),(x,y,z)\bigr)=(ax+by,\ bx+az).
   \]
   Write $\widetilde B:U\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ for the curry
   of $B$. Prove that, in the standard bases of $V$ and $W$,
   \[
   \widetilde B(a,b)
   =\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Evaluate the locked sample
   \[
   B\bigl((1,1),(1,0,1)\bigr)=(1,0).
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)$
   has dimension $6$ (or cardinality $12$), so the two sides are
   not both of dimension $12$ and cardinality $4096$”; (ii) “the
   curry matrix is not $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix}$,
   or $B((1,1),(1,0,1))$ is not $(1,0)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a product universal-property
uniqueness argument, by a Jordan--Hölder comparison, by a
localization construction, by Nakayama, by Maschke averaging, or
by a projective-lifting / split-epimorphism audit. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: $\dim(U\otimes V)=(\dim U)(\dim V)=6$ and $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)=(\dim X)(\dim Y)$, so both $\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W))$ have dimension $6\cdot 2=2\cdot 6=12$.
Evaluating $B((a,b),-)$ on the standard basis of $V$ produces the columns $(a,b)^\top$, $(b,0)^\top$, and $(0,a)^\top$, hence the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute dim(U tensor V)=6 and dim Hom(V,W)=6 first, then both Hom-spaces have dimension 12 and cardinality 2^12.
Read the three columns of the curry as B((a,b),e_i), then multiply the matrix at (a,b)=(1,1) by (1,0,1)^T.

milestones.criterion: Proves the currying isomorphism and computes both dimensions 12 and both cardinalities 4096.
Exhibits the curry matrix [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]] and evaluates B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0).
Rejects a dropped dim W (or dim/cardinality swap) and refuses a wrong curry matrix or wrong locked sample.

commonErrors.description: Reports dim Hom(U tensor V, W)=6 by dropping dim W=2, or reports cardinality 12 by confusing dimension with the F2-count, so the two sides are not both of dimension 12 and cardinality 4096.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities dim=12 and |Hom|=4096=2^12 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports a curry matrix other than [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]], or evaluates B((1,1),(1,0,1)) as a vector other than (1,0).
commonErrors.consequence: The required locked sample B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0) and the matrix [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]] fail.

hintTree.content: Count dimensions first: $\dim(U\otimes V)=2\cdot 3=6$, so $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)=6\cdot 2=12$. The other side is $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)=6$ and then $2\cdot 6=12$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the cardinality is $2^{12}=4096$.
The curry sends $u$ to the linear map $v\mapsto B(u,v)$. Expand $B((a,b),(x,y,z))=(ax+by,bx+az)$.

The three columns of $\widetilde B(a,b)$ are $B((a,b),e_1)$, $B((a,b),e_2)$, and $B((a,b),e_3)$. At $(a,b)=(1,1)$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which sends $(1,0,1)^\top$ to $(1,0)^\top$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

GA:010127.canonicalSolution:
Write $F=\mathbb{F}_2$. Then $\dim U=2$, $\dim V=3$, and $\dim W=2$, so
\[
\dim(U\otimes V)=2\cdot 3=6.
\]
Therefore
\[
\dim\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)=6\cdot 2=12.
\]
On the other side,
\[
\dim\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)=3\cdot 2=6,
\]
hence
\[
\dim\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\bigr)=2\cdot 6=12.
\]
The standard currying map
\[
\Phi:\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)\to
\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\bigr),
\qquad
(\Phi\varphi)(u)(v)=\varphi(u\otimes v)
\]
is $F$-linear. It is injective because if $\Phi\varphi=0$ then
$\varphi$ vanishes on every elementary tensor, hence $\varphi=0$.
Equal finite dimensions therefore force $\Phi$ to be an isomorphism.
Over $F$ one has
\[
\bigl\lvert\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)\bigr\rvert
=2^{12}=4096
=\bigl\lvert\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\bigr)\bigr\rvert.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Phi\text{ iso},\ \dim=12,\ \lvert\,\cdot\,\rvert=4096}.
\]

The assigned pairing is bilinear over $F$ (the two coordinates are
sums of monomials of bidegree $(1,1)$). Its curry is
\[
\widetilde B(a,b):(x,y,z)\mapsto(ax+by,\ bx+az).
\]
Evaluating on the standard basis of $V$ gives the three columns
\[
\widetilde B(a,b)(e_1)=(a,b),\quad
\widetilde B(a,b)(e_2)=(b,0),\quad
\widetilde B(a,b)(e_3)=(0,a),
\]
so
\[
\widetilde B(a,b)
=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At $(a,b)=(1,1)$ the curry matrix is
\[
\widetilde B(1,1)
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\ 1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Multiplying by $(1,0,1)^\top$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ gives
$(1,1+1)^\top=(1,0)^\top$, so
\[
B\bigl((1,1),(1,0,1)\bigr)=(1,0).
\]
\[
\boxed{\widetilde B(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix},\quad
B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $\dim W=2$ or confuses dimension with
cardinality, so it cannot recover $12$ and $4096$. Sentence (ii)
corrupts the curry matrix or the locked bilinear evaluation.

The argument never replaces the assigned tensor--Hom curry by a
product universal-property uniqueness argument, by a
Jordan--Hölder comparison, by a localization construction, by
Nakayama, by Maschke averaging, or by a projective-lifting audit,
and it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: Currying is the isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W))$. Both sides have dimension $12$ and cardinality $2^{12}=4096$. The assigned pairing has curry matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&0\\ b&0&a\end{pmatrix}$, and $B((1,1),(1,0,1))=(1,0)$.
Hom(U tensor V, W) has dimension 6, or else cardinality 12, so the two sides are not both of dimension 12 and cardinality 4096.
The curry matrix is not [[a,b,0],[b,0,a]], and B((1,1),(1,0,1)) is not (1,0).

GA:010219.title: A Schreier transversal {1,a,a²} for F(a,b) onto C_3 yields free generators b, aba^{-1}, a²ba^{-2}, a³
GA:010219.objective: For φ:F(a,b)→C_3 with a↦1 and b↦0, prove that {1,a,a²} is a Schreier transversal of H=ker φ, that the Schreier generators are b, aba^{-1}, a²ba^{-2}, a³, that H is free of rank 4, and that H^{ab}≅Z^4.
GA:010219.statement:
Let $F=F(a,b)$ be free of rank $2$, and let
$\varphi:F\to C_3$ be the homomorphism to the cyclic group of
order $3$ (written additively) determined by $\varphi(a)=1$ and
$\varphi(b)=0$. Write $H=\ker\varphi$.

1. Prove that $T=\{1,a,a^2\}$ is a Schreier transversal for the
   left cosets of $H$, and that the associated Schreier generators
   are
   \[
   b,\qquad aba^{-1},\qquad a^2ba^{-2},\qquad a^3.
   \]

2. Prove that these four elements freely generate $H$, so $H$ is
   free of rank $4$. Deduce that the abelianisation satisfies
   $H^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^4$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$a^3$ is omitted, or $H$ is free of
   rank $3$”; (ii) “the conjugates of $b$ are $bab^{-1}$ and
   $b^2ab^{-2}$, so the displayed Schreier basis is wrong.”

Do not replace the calculation by a three-chain Yoneda ledger, by
the sibling $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a node ring
spectrum, or by an $\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{Z}/9\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3)$
count. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.
permittedResults: Nielsen–Schreier: if $F$ is free of rank $r$ and $H$ has index $n$, then $H$ is free of rank $1+n(r-1)$. Here $r=2$ and $n=3$, so the rank is $1+3\cdot 1=4$.
The abelianisation of a free group of rank $k$ is $\mathbb{Z}^k$. Thus $H^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute φ on T to see the three cosets, then evaluate every s x (sx)bar^{-1} for x in {a,b}.
Quote Nielsen–Schreier for rank 1+3(2-1)=4, then abelianise a free group of that rank.

milestones.criterion: Identifies T={1,a,a^2} as a Schreier transversal and lists the generators b, aba^{-1}, a^2ba^{-2}, a^3.
Proves H is free of rank 4 and concludes H^{ab}≅Z^4.
Rejects omitting a^3 or rank 3 and refuses a wrong conjugate family.

commonErrors.description: Omits the generator a^3, or claims that H is free of rank 3 rather than rank 4.
commonErrors.consequence: The Schreier basis and the Nielsen–Schreier rank 1+3(2-1)=4 are lost, and H^{ab}≅Z^4 fails.

commonErrors.description: Replaces aba^{-1} and a^2ba^{-2} by bab^{-1} and b^2ab^{-2}, or otherwise changes the Schreier conjugates of b.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned basis b, aba^{-1}, a^2ba^{-2}, a^3 is no longer recovered from the transversal {1,a,a^2}.

hintTree.content: The map $\varphi$ is surjective because $\varphi(a)$ generates $C_3$, so $[F:H]=3$ and the cosets are $H$, $aH$, $a^2H$.
For $s\in T$ and the generator $a$, the elements $1\cdot a\cdot a^{-1}$ and $a\cdot a\cdot(a^2)^{-1}$ are trivial, while $a^2\cdot a\cdot\overline{a^3}^{-1}=a^3$.
For the generator $b$ one has $\overline{sb}=s$ because $\varphi(b)=0$, hence the three conjugates $b$, $aba^{-1}$, $a^2ba^{-2}$.

GA:010219.canonicalSolution:
The assignment $\varphi(a)=1$, $\varphi(b)=0$ extends uniquely to a
homomorphism $\varphi:F(a,b)\to C_3$. It is surjective because $1$
generates $C_3$, so $H=\ker\varphi$ has index $3$. The three left
cosets are $H$, $aH$, and $a^2H$, and these are distinct because
$\varphi(1)=0$, $\varphi(a)=1$, $\varphi(a^2)=2$. The set
$T=\{1,a,a^2\}$ is therefore a transversal. It is Schreier because
it is prefix-closed in the free generators: the only nonempty
prefixes of $a$ and $a^2$ already lie in $T$.

Write $\overline{w}$ for the unique element of $T$ with
$\overline{w}^{-1}w\in H$, equivalently $\varphi(\overline{w})=\varphi(w)$.
The Schreier generators are the non-identity elements
$s\,x\,\overline{sx}^{-1}$ for $s\in T$ and $x\in\{a,b\}$.

For $x=a$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1\cdot a\cdot\overline{a}^{-1}&=a\cdot a^{-1}=1,\\
a\cdot a\cdot\overline{a^2}^{-1}&=a^2\cdot(a^2)^{-1}=1,\\
a^2\cdot a\cdot\overline{a^3}^{-1}&=a^3\cdot 1^{-1}=a^3,
\end{aligned}
\]
because $\varphi(a^3)=0$, so $\overline{a^3}=1$. For $x=b$ one has
$\varphi(sb)=\varphi(s)$ for every $s$, hence $\overline{sb}=s$ and
\[
\begin{aligned}
1\cdot b\cdot\overline{b}^{-1}&=b,\\
a\cdot b\cdot\overline{ab}^{-1}&=aba^{-1},\\
a^2\cdot b\cdot\overline{a^2b}^{-1}&=a^2ba^{-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The non-identity Schreier generators are therefore
\[
b,\qquad aba^{-1},\qquad a^2ba^{-2},\qquad a^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{T=\{1,a,a^2\};\ \text{basis }b,\ aba^{-1},\ a^2ba^{-2},\ a^3}.
\]

These four elements freely generate $H$ by the Schreier method.
Independently, Nielsen–Schreier gives
\[
\operatorname{rank}H=1+[F:H]\bigl(\operatorname{rank}F-1\bigr)=1+3\cdot 1=4.
\]
A free group of rank $4$ has abelianisation $\mathbb{Z}^4$, so
$H^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^4$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}H=4,\qquad H^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^4}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the generator $a^3$ (the only Schreier generator
coming from $x=a$) and reports rank $3$. Sentence (ii) replaces the
$a$-conjugates of $b$ by $b$-conjugates of $a$, which are not the
Schreier generators of this transversal.

The argument never replaces the index-three Schreier basis by the
sibling Yoneda count, by the $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a
node ring spectrum, or by an endomorphism count, and it does not
open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The kernel of $\varphi:F(a,b)\to C_3$, $a\mapsto 1$, $b\mapsto 0$, has Schreier transversal $\{1,a,a^2\}$ and free generators $b$, $aba^{-1}$, $a^2ba^{-2}$, $a^3$. Thus $H$ has rank $4$ and $H^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^4$.
I omit a^3 from the generating set, so H is free of rank 3. I do not accept rank 4 or H^{ab}≅Z^4.
The conjugates of b are bab^{-1} and b^2ab^{-2}, so the displayed Schreier basis is wrong. I do not accept aba^{-1} and a^2ba^{-2}.

GA:010228.title: UT4(F2) has order 64, lower central series of class 3 with |gamma2|=8 on positions 13,14,24 and |gamma3|=2 on E14, center of order 2, and abelianization (C2)^3 of order 8
GA:010228.objective: For G=UT4(F2), prove |G|=64, gamma2 consists of the unipotent matrices with free positions (1,3),(1,4),(2,4) and has order 8, gamma3=<I+E14> has order 2, gamma4=1 so the class is 3, Z(G) has order 2, and G^ab cong (C2)^3 has order 8.
GA:010228.statement:
Let $G=\operatorname{UT}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ be the group of $4\times 4$
upper-triangular unipotent matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Write
$\gamma_1(G)=G$ and $\gamma_{k+1}(G)=[\gamma_k(G),G]$ for the
lower central series, and write $E_{ij}$ for the matrix unit.

1. Prove that a general element of $G$ has the shape
   \[
   \begin{pmatrix}
   1&a&b&c\\
   0&1&d&e\\
   0&0&1&f\\
   0&0&0&1
   \end{pmatrix},
   \qquad a,b,c,d,e,f\in\mathbb{F}_2,
   \]
   so $\lvert G\rvert=2^6=64$.

2. Prove that $\gamma_2(G)$ consists exactly of those matrices
   with $a=d=f=0$ and with free positions $(1,3)$, $(1,4)$,
   $(2,4)$, hence $\lvert\gamma_2(G)\rvert=8$; that
   $\gamma_3(G)=\{I,I+E_{14}\}$ has order $2$; and that
   $\gamma_4(G)=\{I\}$, so $G$ is nilpotent of class $3$.

3. Prove that the centre satisfies $\lvert Z(G)\rvert=2$ and that
   the abelianization is
   \[
   G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/\gamma_2(G)\cong (C_2)^3
   \]
   of order $8$, with coordinates $(a,d,f)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$G$ has class $2$, or
   $\lvert\gamma_2(G)\rvert$ is not $8$ on the three positions
   $13,14,24$”; (ii) “$Z(G)$ does not have order $2$, or
   $G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is not $(C_2)^3$ of order $8$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a Jordan--Hölder comparison of
maximal normal terms, by Maschke averaging, by a product
universal property, by a localization construction, or by a
projective-lifting audit. Do not reopen, import, or execute any
of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Commutators of elementary unipotent factors $I+E_{i,i+1}$ and $I+E_{j,j+1}$ produce the next superdiagonal: $[I+E_{12},I+E_{23}]=I+E_{13}$ and $[I+E_{23},I+E_{34}]=I+E_{24}$ in characteristic $2$, while $[\gamma_2,G]$ is generated by $I+E_{14}$.
The first superdiagonal coordinates $(a,d,f)$ descend to an isomorphism $G/\gamma_2(G)\cong(\mathbb{F}_2)^3\cong(C_2)^3$. The centre coincides with $\gamma_3(G)=\{I,I+E_{14}\}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Generate gamma2 from the three first-superdiagonal commutators, then commute once more to isolate E14.
Read the abelianization as the three first-superdiagonal coordinates and the centre as the last superdiagonal.

milestones.criterion: Computes |G|=64 and identifies gamma2 as the order-8 group on positions 13,14,24, gamma3=<I+E14>, gamma4=1, and class 3.
Proves |Z(G)|=2 and G^ab cong (C2)^3 of order 8.
Rejects class 2 or a wrong gamma2, and refuses a wrong centre or a wrong abelianization.

commonErrors.description: Claims that G has nilpotency class 2, or that gamma2 is not the order-8 subgroup on the three positions (1,3),(1,4),(2,4).
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities |gamma2|=8, gamma3=<I+E14>, gamma4=1, and class 3 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports a centre of order other than 2, or an abelianization other than (C2)^3 of order 8.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities |Z(G)|=2 and G^ab cong (C2)^3 of order 8 fail.

hintTree.content: Six free $\mathbb{F}_2$-entries give $\lvert G\rvert=64$. The first superdiagonal is spanned by $E_{12},E_{23},E_{34}$.
Compute $[I+E_{12},I+E_{23}]=I+E_{13}$ and $[I+E_{23},I+E_{34}]=I+E_{24}$. A further commutator with $I+E_{34}$ or $I+E_{12}$ produces $I+E_{14}$.
Once $\gamma_2$ is the three-parameter group on positions $13,14,24$, the quotient $G/\gamma_2$ is the three first-superdiagonal coordinates. The centre is the last superdiagonal $E_{14}$.

GA:010228.canonicalSolution:
A matrix in $G=\operatorname{UT}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ is determined by the
six strictly upper-triangular entries $a,b,c,d,e,f\in\mathbb{F}_2$,
so
\[
\lvert G\rvert=2^6=64.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lvert G\rvert=64}.
\]

Write $A=I+E_{12}$, $D=I+E_{23}$, and $F=I+E_{34}$ for the three
first-superdiagonal generators. In characteristic $2$ one has
$A^{-1}=A$ and $D^{-1}=D$, and the matrix product gives
\[
[A,D]=ADA D=I+E_{13}.
\]
Likewise $[D,F]=I+E_{24}$. Commuting $I+E_{13}$ with $F$ (or
$I+E_{24}$ with $A$) produces $I+E_{14}$. Thus $\gamma_2(G)$
contains every matrix with vanishing first superdiagonal and with
free positions $(1,3)$, $(1,4)$, $(2,4)$. Dimension counting in
the unipotent coordinates (or the standard filtration of
$\operatorname{UT}_4$ by superdiagonals) shows there are no further
commutators, so
\[
\gamma_2(G)=\bigl\{I+b E_{13}+c E_{14}+e E_{24}\bigr\},
\qquad\lvert\gamma_2(G)\rvert=2^3=8.
\]
A further commutator of this three-parameter group against $G$
retains only the last superdiagonal:
\[
\gamma_3(G)=\{I,I+E_{14}\},\qquad\lvert\gamma_3(G)\rvert=2,
\]
and $\gamma_4(G)=\{I\}$. Hence $G$ is nilpotent of class $3$.
\[
\boxed{\lvert\gamma_2\rvert=8\text{ on }13,14,24;\
\gamma_3=\langle I+E_{14}\rangle;\ \gamma_4=1;\ \text{class }3}.
\]

An element with a nonzero first-superdiagonal coordinate fails to
commute with one of $A,D,F$. An element with a nonzero
$(1,3)$ or $(2,4)$ entry likewise fails to be central. The
remaining one-parameter subgroup $\{I,I+E_{14}\}$ is central, so
\[
Z(G)=\gamma_3(G),\qquad\lvert Z(G)\rvert=2.
\]
The first-superdiagonal coordinates $(a,d,f)$ are group
homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb{F}_2$ vanishing on $\gamma_2(G)$, and
they assemble to
\[
G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/\gamma_2(G)\cong(\mathbb{F}_2)^3\cong(C_2)^3
\]
of order $64/8=8$.
\[
\boxed{\lvert Z(G)\rvert=2,\quad G^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong(C_2)^3,\
\lvert G^{\mathrm{ab}}\rvert=8}.
\]

Sentence (i) collapses the class to $2$ or corrupts the three
positions of $\gamma_2$. Sentence (ii) loses the centre of order
$2$ or replaces $(C_2)^3$ by a different group of order $8$ (or
the wrong order).

The argument never replaces the assigned $\operatorname{UT}_4$
lower-central-series ledger by a Jordan--Hölder comparison, by
Maschke averaging, by a product universal property, by a
localization construction, or by a projective-lifting audit, and
it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The group $G=\operatorname{UT}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ has order $64$. Its lower central series satisfies $\lvert\gamma_2(G)\rvert=8$ on positions $(1,3),(1,4),(2,4)$, $\gamma_3(G)=\langle I+E_{14}\rangle$ of order $2$, and $\gamma_4(G)=1$, so the class is $3$. The centre has order $2$ and $G^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong(C_2)^3$ has order $8$.
G has class 2, or else |gamma2| is not 8 on the three positions 13,14,24. I do not accept gamma3=<I+E14> or class 3.
The centre does not have order 2, and the abelianization is not (C2)^3 of order 8.
