GA:010320.title: The crossing k[x,y]/(xy) is reduced of dimension one, with components meeting at (x,y) and tangent dimension two
GA:010320.objective: For R=k[x,y]/(xy), prove that the minimal primes are (x) and (y), that their intersection is 0, that R is reduced of Krull dimension 1, that the components meet at (x,y), that the only idempotents are 0 and 1, and that the tangent dimension at (x,y) is 2.
GA:010320.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $R=k[x,y]/(xy)$. Write $\overline{x}$
and $\overline{y}$ for the images of $x$ and $y$ in $R$, and write
$(\overline{x})$, $(\overline{y})$, $(\overline{x},\overline{y})$
for the corresponding principal and maximal ideals (abbreviated
$(x)$, $(y)$, $(x,y)$ in $R$).

1. Prove that the minimal primes of $R$ are $(x)$ and $(y)$, that
   $(x)\cap(y)=(0)$, and that $R$ is reduced. Prove that the
   Krull dimension of $R$ is $1$.

2. Prove that the two irreducible components of $\operatorname{Spec}R$
   meet at the closed point $(x,y)$. Prove that the only
   idempotents of $R$ are $0$ and $1$. Prove that the tangent
   dimension $\dim_k\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$ at
   $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)$ is $2$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$R$ is a domain, or else it is not
   reduced, or it has a third minimal prime”; (ii) “$\operatorname{Spec}R$
   is disconnected, so there is a nontrivial idempotent, or else
   the tangent dimension at $(x,y)$ is $1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a three-chain Yoneda ledger, by
the sibling $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a Schreier basis, or
by an $\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{Z}/9\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3)$ count. Do
not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake
seeds.
permittedResults: The correspondence theorem identifies primes of $k[x,y]/(xy)$ with primes of $k[x,y]$ containing $(xy)$. The minimal such primes are $(x)$ and $(y)$, and $(x)\cap(y)=(xy)$.

The map $R\to k[t]\times k[t]$ given by $\overline{p}\mapsto\bigl(p(t,0),p(0,t)\bigr)$ is injective with image $\{(f,g):f(0)=g(0)\}$. Idempotents of the product that lie in the image are only $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Lift primes to k[x,y], use (x)∩(y)=(xy), and read dimension from the chains (x)⊂(x,y) and (y)⊂(x,y).
Embed R into k[t]×k[t] by restriction to the axes to control idempotents, then compare degrees in m/m^2.

milestones.criterion: Identifies minimal primes (x) and (y), proves their intersection is 0, and concludes R is reduced of dimension 1.
Shows the components meet at (x,y), that the only idempotents are 0 and 1, and that the tangent dimension is 2.
Rejects treating R as a domain or non-reduced ring and refuses a nontrivial idempotent or tangent dimension 1.

commonErrors.description: Claims that R is a domain, or that R is not reduced, or that R has a minimal prime other than (x) and (y).
commonErrors.consequence: The ledger Min(R)={(x),(y)}, (x)∩(y)=0, and reducedness of dimension 1 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that Spec R is disconnected or that R has a nontrivial idempotent, or that the tangent dimension at (x,y) is 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The meeting of components at (x,y), the idempotent set {0,1}, and tangent dimension 2 all fail.

hintTree.content: In $k[x,y]$ one has $(x)\cap(y)=(xy)$. Passing to the quotient gives $(x)\cap(y)=(0)$ in $R$, so the nilradical vanishes.
The chains $(x)\subset(x,y)$ and $(y)\subset(x,y)$ have length $1$, and no longer chain exists, so $\dim R=1$. The two generic points meet at $(x,y)$.

Embed $R$ into $k[t]\times k[t]$ by restriction to each axis. The image consists of pairs with equal constant terms, so the only idempotents are $0$ and $1$. The relation $xy=0$ is quadratic, so $x,y$ remain independent in $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$.

GA:010320.canonicalSolution:
Primes of $R=k[x,y]/(xy)$ correspond to primes of $k[x,y]$
containing $(xy)$. Since $xy\in\mathfrak{p}$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ is
prime, $x\in\mathfrak{p}$ or $y\in\mathfrak{p}$. The minimal such
primes are therefore $(x)$ and $(y)$, and their images in $R$ are
the distinct minimal primes of $R$. In $k[x,y]$ one has
$(x)\cap(y)=(xy)$, so in $R$
\[
(x)\cap(y)=(0).
\]
The nilradical is the intersection of the minimal primes, hence is
$(0)$, and $R$ is reduced.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Min}(R)=\{(x),(y)\},\quad(x)\cap(y)=(0),\quad R\text{ reduced}}.
\]

Every prime of $R$ contains $(x)$ or $(y)$. Primes containing $(x)$
correspond to primes of $R/(x)\cong k[y]$, and primes containing
$(y)$ correspond to primes of $R/(y)\cong k[x]$. Both polynomial
rings have dimension $1$, so every prime chain in either component
has length at most $1$. The chain $(x)\subset(x,y)$ has length $1$,
so the Krull dimension is exactly $1$.
\[
\boxed{\dim R=1}.
\]

The irreducible components of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ are
$V(x)\cong\operatorname{Spec}k[y]$ and
$V(y)\cong\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$. Their intersection is
$V(x,y)$, a single closed point. Hence the components meet at
$(x,y)$.

To identify idempotents, consider
\[
\iota:R\to k[t]\times k[t],\qquad
\overline{p}\mapsto\bigl(p(t,0),\,p(0,t)\bigr).
\]
If $p(t,0)=p(0,t)=0$ then every monomial in $p$ is divisible by
$xy$, so $\overline{p}=0$ and $\iota$ is injective. The image is
precisely the pairs $(f,g)$ with $f(0)=g(0)$. Idempotents of
$k[t]\times k[t]$ are $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,1)$; only
the first two have equal constant terms. Therefore the only
idempotents of $R$ are $0$ and $1$.
\[
\boxed{\text{components meet at }(x,y);\ \text{idempotents }\{0,1\}}.
\]

Let $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)$. Then $\mathfrak{m}^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)=(x^2,y^2)$
in $R$, because $xy=0$. The classes of $x$ and $y$ in
$\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$ are linearly independent over $k$: a
relation $\alpha x+\beta y\in\mathfrak{m}^2$ would make
$\alpha x+\beta y$ a combination of $x^2$ and $y^2$ in $R$, which
forces $\alpha=\beta=0$ by comparing degree $1$. Thus
\[
\dim_k\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2=2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{tangent dimension }2}.
\]

Sentence (i) claims $R$ is a domain (it is not: $\overline{x}\,\overline{y}=0$
with neither factor zero), or denies reducedness, or invents a
third minimal prime. Sentence (ii) disconnects $\operatorname{Spec}R$
or collapses the tangent space to dimension $1$.

The argument never replaces the node ring ledger by the sibling
Yoneda count, by the $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a Schreier
basis, or by an endomorphism count, and it does not open any of
the six existing intake seeds.

R is a domain, or else it is not reduced, or it has a third minimal prime. I do not accept Min(R)={(x),(y)} with intersection 0.

GA:010326.title: F3[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^3) has basis {1,x,y,y^2}, order 81, unique max ideal of order 27, layers of dimensions 1,2,1 and length 4, and socle span{x,y^2} of order 9
GA:010326.objective: For R=F3[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^3), record the basis {1,x,y,y^2} and |R|=81, prove R is local with unique maximal ideal m of order 27 and 54 units, compute m^2=(y^2) of order 3 and m^3=0, read the layers of dimensions 1,2,1 and length 4, and identify the socle as span{x,y^2} of dimension 2 and order 9.
GA:010326.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3$ be the field with three elements, and let
\[
R=\mathbb{F}_3[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^3).
\]

1. Prove that $\{1,x,y,y^2\}$ is an $\mathbb{F}_3$-basis of $R$,
   so $\lvert R\rvert=3^4=81$.

2. Let $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)$. Prove that $\mathfrak{m}$ is the
   unique maximal ideal, that $\lvert\mathfrak{m}\rvert=27$, and
   that $R$ has exactly $54$ units. Compute
   \[
   \mathfrak{m}^2=(y^2),\qquad \lvert\mathfrak{m}^2\rvert=3,
   \qquad\mathfrak{m}^3=0.
   \]

3. Read the associated-graded layers
   $R/\mathfrak{m}$, $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$,
   $\mathfrak{m}^2/\mathfrak{m}^3$ as having $\mathbb{F}_3$-dimensions
   $1,2,1$, and conclude that $R$ has composition length $4$ as a
   module over itself. Prove that the socle is
   \[
   \operatorname{soc}(R)=\operatorname{Ann}_R(\mathfrak{m})
   =\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_3}\{x,y^2\},
   \]
   of dimension $2$ and cardinality $9$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the monomials $xy$ or $y^3$ survive
   in $R$, so the basis is larger or smaller than
   $\{1,x,y,y^2\}$ and $\lvert R\rvert$ is $27$ or $243$ rather
   than $81$”; (ii) “the socle coincides with $\mathfrak{m}^2=(y^2)$
   or with $\mathfrak{m}$, so it does not have dimension $2$ and
   order $9$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $S_3$ or $C_4$
representation packets of this shard, or by a
$\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ or Baer packet. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds,
including a localization-with-zerodivisors construction or a
bare Nakayama statement without this explicit basis.

If $r=a+bx+cy+dy^2$, then $xr=ax$ and $yr=ay+cy^2$. Vanishing of both forces $a=c=0$, so $\operatorname{soc}(R)=\operatorname{span}\{x,y^2\}$.

hintTree.content: The relations kill $x^2$, $xy$, and $y^3$, so the only surviving monomials are $1,x,y,y^2$. Over $\mathbb{F}_3$ this gives $\lvert R\rvert=81$.
The non-units are those with zero constant term, forming $\mathfrak{m}=\operatorname{span}\{x,y,y^2\}$ of order $27$. Then $\mathfrak{m}^2=(y^2)$ and $\mathfrak{m}^3=0$.
The condition $xr=yr=0$ forces the constant term and the coefficient of $y$ to vanish, leaving $\operatorname{span}\{x,y^2\}$ of order $9$.

GA:010326.canonicalSolution:
The ideal $(x^2,xy,y^3)$ contains every monomial of
$x$-degree at least $2$, the mixed term $xy$, and $y^3$. The
surviving monomials are therefore $1$, $x$, $y$, and $y^2$,
and these are $\mathbb{F}_3$-linearly independent in the
quotient. Hence $\{1,x,y,y^2\}$ is a basis and
\[
\lvert R\rvert=3^4=81.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{basis }\{1,x,y,y^2\},\ \lvert R\rvert=81}.
\]

A general element is $a+bx+cy+dy^2$ with
$a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{F}_3$. The subset of elements with $a=0$
is the ideal $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)=\operatorname{span}\{x,y,y^2\}$,
of dimension $3$ and cardinality $27$. The complement consists
of the elements with $a\in\{1,2\}$, hence has cardinality
$2\cdot 27=54$. If $a\ne0$, write the element as $a(1+n)$ with
$n\in\mathfrak{m}$. Since $\mathfrak{m}^3=0$, also $n^3=0$, and
\[
(1+n)^{-1}=1-n+n^2.
\]
Thus every element with nonzero constant term is a unit. Every
element with zero constant term lies in the nilpotent ideal
$\mathfrak{m}$ and is a nonunit. Hence $\mathfrak{m}$ is precisely
the set of nonunits, so it is the unique maximal ideal and $R$ is
local. Next,
\[
\mathfrak{m}^2=(x,y)^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)=(y^2),
\]
so $\mathfrak{m}^2=\operatorname{span}\{y^2\}$ has order $3$, and
\[
\mathfrak{m}^3=(y^2)(x,y)=(xy^2,y^3)=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lvert\mathfrak{m}\rvert=27,\ \lvert R^\times\rvert=54,\
\mathfrak{m}^2=(y^2),\ \lvert\mathfrak{m}^2\rvert=3,\
\mathfrak{m}^3=0}.
\]

The associated-graded pieces are
\[
R/\mathfrak{m}\cong\mathbb{F}_3\quad(\dim 1),\qquad
\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2=\operatorname{span}\{\overline{x},\overline{y}\}
\quad(\dim 2),\qquad
\mathfrak{m}^2/\mathfrak{m}^3=\operatorname{span}\{y^2\}
\quad(\dim 1).
\]
The composition length of $R$ as a module over itself is
therefore $1+2+1=4$. For the socle, take
$r=a+bx+cy+dy^2$. Then
\[
xr=ax,\qquad yr=ay+cy^2,
\]
because $x^2=xy=xy^2=y^3=0$. The conditions $xr=yr=0$ force
$a=0$ and $c=0$, hence
\[
\operatorname{soc}(R)=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_3}\{x,y^2\},
\]
of dimension $2$ and cardinality $9$.
\[
\boxed{\text{layers }1,2,1;\ \text{length }4;\
\operatorname{soc}=\operatorname{span}\{x,y^2\},\ \dim 2,\
\lvert\operatorname{soc}\rvert=9}.
\]

Sentence (i) retains a killed monomial or drops $y^2$, so
$\lvert R\rvert$ is no longer $81$. Sentence (ii) confuses the
socle with $\mathfrak{m}^2$ or with $\mathfrak{m}$.

The argument never replaces the assigned Artinian ledger by an
$S_3$ or $C_4$ representation computation, or by a
$\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ or Baer packet, and it does not
open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The ring $R=\mathbb{F}_3[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^3)$ has basis $\{1,x,y,y^2\}$ and order $81$. The unique maximal ideal has order $27$ and there are $54$ units. One has $\mathfrak{m}^2=(y^2)$ of order $3$ and $\mathfrak{m}^3=0$. The layers have dimensions $1,2,1$ and length $4$, and $\operatorname{soc}(R)=\operatorname{span}\{x,y^2\}$ has dimension $2$ and order $9$.
The monomials xy or y^3 survive in R, so the basis is not {1,x,y,y^2} and |R| is 27 or 243 rather than 81. I do not accept |R|=81.
The socle coincides with m^2=(y^2) or with m, so it does not have dimension 2 and order 9. I do not accept soc=span{x,y^2}.

GA:010329.title: In k[x,y] the ideal (x^2,xy) equals (x) intersect (x^2,y), with associated primes (x) and embedded (x,y), radical (x) of dimension 1, and colons I:y=(x), I:x=(x,y)
GA:010329.objective: In k[x,y], prove I=(x^2,xy)=(x) intersect (x^2,y), radicals (x) and (x,y), Ass(R/I)={(x),(x,y)} with (x,y) embedded, rad(I)=(x) and dim R/I=1, and the colon identities I:y=(x), I:x=(x,y).
GA:010329.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $R=k[x,y]$. Set
\[
I=(x^2,xy)\subset R.
\]

1. Prove the primary decomposition
   \[
   I=(x)\cap(x^2,y),
   \]
   that $(x)$ is prime (hence primary), and that $(x^2,y)$ is
   $(x,y)$-primary.

2. Compute the radicals
   \[
   \sqrt{(x)}=(x),\qquad \sqrt{(x^2,y)}=(x,y),
   \]
   and prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Ass}(R/I)=\bigl\{(x),\ (x,y)\bigr\}
   \]
   with $(x,y)$ embedded. Conclude that $\sqrt{I}=(x)$ and that
   $\dim R/I=1$.

3. Prove the colon identities
   \[
   I:y=(x),\qquad I:x=(x,y).
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\operatorname{Ass}(R/I)$ is only
   $\{(x)\}$, or $(x,y)$ is isolated rather than embedded”;
   (ii) “the colons are swapped, so $I:y=(x,y)$ or $I:x=(x)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a localization-with-zero-divisors
universal-property construction, by Nakayama, by a product
universal property, by Maschke averaging, or by a
projective-lifting audit. Do not reopen, import, or execute any
of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: If $\sqrt Q$ is a maximal ideal, then $Q$ is primary: every class outside the unique maximal ideal of $R/Q$ is a unit. In $k[x,y]$ one has $\sqrt{(x^2,y)}=(x,y)$.
The isolated primes of $I$ are the minimal primes over $I$, and $\sqrt{I}$ is their intersection. Here the only isolated prime is $(x)$, so $\sqrt{I}=(x)$ and $\dim R/I=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Establish the intersection identity by a UFD divisibility argument, then read Ass from the two radicals.
Compute each colon from the generator identity x(x,y)=I and from y dividing a leftover x^2 term.

Computes the colon identities I:y=(x) and I:x=(x,y).
Rejects dropping the embedded prime and refuses swapped colons.

hintTree.content: The containment $I\subset(x)\cap(x^2,y)$ is immediate. For the reverse, write an element of the intersection as $xh=ax^2+by$ and use that $y$ is prime.
Associated primes are the radicals of the primary components. The containment $(x)\subset(x,y)$ makes $(x,y)$ embedded.
If $fy\in(x^2,xy)$ then $y$ divides a leftover $x^2$ term, forcing $f\in(x)$. If $fx\in I$ then $f\in(x,y)$ because $x(x,y)=I$.

GA:010329.canonicalSolution:
Write $R=k[x,y]$ and $I=(x^2,xy)$. The generator $x^2$ lies in
both $(x)$ and $(x^2,y)$. The generator $xy$ lies in $(x)$, and
$xy=x\cdot y$ lies in $(x^2,y)$ because
$xy=0\cdot x^2+x\cdot y$. Thus
\[
I\subset(x)\cap(x^2,y).
\]
Conversely, if $f\in(x)\cap(x^2,y)$ then $f=xh=ax^2+by$ for some
$h,a,b\in R$. Rearranging gives
\[
y b=x(h-ax),
\]
so $y$ divides $x(h-ax)$. Since $y$ is prime and does not divide
$x$, one has $y\mid(h-ax)$, hence $h=ax+yc$ and
\[
f=x(ax+yc)=ax^2+c\,xy\in I.
\]
Thus $I=(x)\cap(x^2,y)$. The ideal $(x)$ is prime, hence primary.
The radical computation
\[
\sqrt{(x^2,y)}=(x,y)
\]
exhibits a maximal ideal, so $(x^2,y)$ is $(x,y)$-primary.
The decomposition is irredundant because
$x\in(x)\setminus(x^2,y)$ and $y\in(x^2,y)\setminus(x)$.
\[
\boxed{I=(x)\cap(x^2,y)}.
\]

The radicals of the two components in this irredundant primary
decomposition are $(x)$ and $(x,y)$, so
\[
\operatorname{Ass}(R/I)=\bigl\{(x),\ (x,y)\bigr\}.
\]
The containment $(x)\subsetneq(x,y)$ makes $(x)$ the unique
minimal prime over $I$ and makes $(x,y)$ embedded. Therefore
\[
\sqrt{I}=(x).
\]
The closed set $V(I)=V(x)\subset\mathbb{A}^2$ is a line, so
$\dim R/I=1$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Ass}=\{(x),(x,y)\}\text{ with }(x,y)\text{ embedded};\
\sqrt{I}=(x);\ \dim=1}.
\]

For the colons: $x\cdot y=xy\in I$, so $(x)\subset I:y$. If
$fy\in I=(x^2,xy)$ then $fy=ax^2+bxy$, hence
$y(f-bx)=ax^2$. Thus $y$ divides $ax^2$, so $y$ divides $a$
(because $y$ does not divide $x$), and $f\in(x)$. Therefore
\[
I:y=(x).
\]
On the other side, $x\cdot(x,y)=(x^2,xy)=I$, so $(x,y)\subset I:x$.
If $fx\in I$ then $fx=ax^2+bxy$, hence $x(f-ax-by)=0$ in the
domain $R$, so $f\in(x,y)$. Therefore
\[
I:x=(x,y).
\]
\[
\boxed{I:y=(x),\quad I:x=(x,y)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the embedded prime or calls $(x,y)$ isolated.
Sentence (ii) swaps the two colons.

The argument never replaces the assigned embedded primary
decomposition by a localization-with-zero-divisors universal
property, by Nakayama, by a product universal property, by
Maschke averaging, or by a projective-lifting audit, and it does
not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

Ass(R/I) is only {(x)}, or else (x,y) is isolated rather than embedded. I do not accept both associated primes with (x,y) embedded.

GA:010421.title: Z-endomorphisms of Z/9 ⊕ Z/3 number 243, of which 108 are automorphisms and 135 are not
GA:010421.objective: Parametrize End(Z/9⊕Z/3) by (u,v)↦(au+3bv mod 9, cū+dv mod 3) with a in Z/9 and b,c,d in Z/3, prove |End|=243, prove Aut consists of those maps with a not divisible by 3 and d≠0 and therefore has order 108, and conclude there are 135 non-automorphisms.
GA:010421.statement:
Let $M=\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, viewed
as a module over $\mathbb{Z}$. Write $\overline{u}$ for the image
of $u\in\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$.

1. Prove that every $f\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)$ has the
   form
   \[
   f(u,v)=\bigl(au+3bv\bmod 9,\ \ c\,\overline{u}+dv\bmod 3\bigr)
   \]
   for a unique quadruple $(a,b,c,d)$ with $a\in\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$
   and $b,c,d\in\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. Deduce
   \[
   \bigl\lvert\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\bigr\rvert=243.
   \]

2. Prove that $f$ is an automorphism if and only if $a\not\equiv 0
   \pmod{3}$ and $d\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. Conclude
   \[
   \bigl\lvert\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\bigr\rvert=108
   \]
   and that there are $135$ endomorphisms that are not automorphisms.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the parameters are all in
   $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$, or all in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, so
   $\lvert\operatorname{End}\rvert$ is $81$ or $729$”; (ii) “$f$ is
   an automorphism as soon as $a\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$,
   so $\lvert\operatorname{Aut}\rvert$ is not $108$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a three-chain Yoneda ledger, by
the sibling $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a Schreier basis, or
by a node ring spectrum. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of

Because $M$ is finite, $f$ is an automorphism if and only if $\ker f=0$. This holds precisely when $a$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ and $d\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, giving $6\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 2=108$ automorphisms.

hintTree.content: The condition $3f(0,1)=0$ forces the first component of $f(0,1)$ to be a multiple of $3$ in $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$.
If $a\equiv 0\pmod{3}$ then $f(3,0)=(3a,0)=(0,0)$. If $d=0$ then the second row of $f$ does not constrain $v$ injectively.
Count: $9\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 3=243$ endomorphisms; $6\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 2=108$ automorphisms; the complement has $243-108=135$ elements.

GA:010421.canonicalSolution:
Let $f\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)$. Write
\[
f(1,0)=(a,\gamma)\in\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z},\qquad
f(0,1)=(\beta,\delta)\in\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}.
\]
The relation $9(1,0)=0$ imposes no condition. The relation
$3(0,1)=0$ forces $3(\beta,\delta)=0$, hence $3\beta=0$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ and $\delta$ is unrestricted in
$\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. Thus $\beta=3b$ for a unique
$b\in\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. Writing $c=\gamma$ and $d=\delta$,
one has
\[
f(u,v)=u(a,c)+v(3b,d)=\bigl(au+3bv,\ c\overline{u}+dv\bigr),
\]
and the quadruple $(a,b,c,d)$ is unique. The parameter space has
cardinality
\[
9\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 3=243,
\]
so $\lvert\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\rvert=243$.
\[
\boxed{f(u,v)=(au+3bv,\ c\overline{u}+dv),\quad\lvert\operatorname{End}\rvert=243}.
\]

The induced map on
\[
M/3M\cong(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^2
\]
has matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\overline a&0\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
An automorphism of $M$ must induce an automorphism of this quotient,
so necessarily $\overline a d\ne0$. Thus $a$ must be a unit modulo
$9$ and $d$ must be nonzero modulo $3$.

Conversely, suppose $a$ is a unit modulo $9$ and $d\ne0$. Given a
target $(r,s)\in M$, the second coordinate forces
\[
v=d^{-1}(s-c\overline u)\quad\text{in }\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Substitution in the first coordinate gives
\[
\bigl(a-3bd^{-1}c\bigr)u=r-3bd^{-1}s\quad\text{in }\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z},
\]
where $3\overline u=3u$ modulo $9$. The coefficient on the left is
congruent to $a$ modulo $3$, hence is a unit modulo $9$, so there is
a unique $u$ and then a unique $v$. Therefore $f$ is bijective.

The automorphisms are parametrized by $6$ choices of $a$ (the
units of $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$), $3$ choices of $b$, $3$ choices
of $c$, and $2$ choices of $d\neq 0$, hence
\[
6\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 2=108.
\]
The complementary count is $243-108=135$.
\[
\boxed{\lvert\operatorname{Aut}\rvert=108,\qquad\lvert\operatorname{End}\setminus\operatorname{Aut}\rvert=135}.
\]

Sentence (i) puts every parameter in a single cyclic group and
reports $\lvert\operatorname{End}\rvert=81$ or $729$. Sentence (ii)
treats $a=3$ and $a=6$ as admissible for automorphisms (they are
nonzero in $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ but divisible by $3$) and
destroys the count $108$.

The argument never replaces the endomorphism count by the sibling
Yoneda ledger, by the $\mathbb{F}_5$ matrix sequence, by a Schreier
basis, or by a node ring spectrum, and it does not open any of the
six existing intake seeds.

f is an automorphism as soon as a≠0 in Z/9, so |Aut| is not 108. I do not accept the criterion a not ≡0 mod 3 and d≠0.

GA:010431.title: The Prüfer 2-group Z[1/2]/Z has unique finite submodules P[2^n], is Artinian not Noetherian, divisible hence injective, and has essential socle P[2] with injective hull P
GA:010431.objective: For P=Z[1/2]/Z, prove the only finite submodules are the unique cyclic groups P[2^n], that the strict ascending chain shows P is not Noetherian while every descending chain stabilizes so P is Artinian, that P is divisible hence an injective Z-module, and that socle P[2] is essential with injective hull P.
GA:010431.statement:
Let
\[
P=\mathbb{Z}\bigl[\tfrac12\bigr]\big/\mathbb{Z}
=\bigl\{a/2^k+\mathbb{Z}:a\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\ge 0\bigr\}
\]
be the Prüfer $2$-group, viewed as a module over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Write $P[2^n]=\{x\in P:2^n x=0\}$.

1. Prove that the only finite submodules of $P$ are the cyclic
   groups $P[2^n]\cong\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$, and that they
   are unique of each finite order $2^n$. Exhibit the strict
   ascending chain
   \[
   0\subset P[2]\subset P[4]\subset P[8]\subset\cdots\subset P
   \]
   and conclude that $P$ is not Noetherian.

2. Prove that every descending chain of submodules stabilizes, so
   $P$ is Artinian. Prove that $P$ is divisible, hence injective
   as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module.

3. Prove that the socle is $\operatorname{soc}(P)=P[2]$, that
   this socle is essential, and that $P$ is the injective hull of
   $P[2]$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$P$ is Noetherian, or the chain
   $P[2^n]$ stabilizes”; (ii) “$P$ is not divisible/injective, or
   the socle $P[2]$ is not essential, or the injective hull of
   $P[2]$ is not $P$.”

Do not replace the calculation by Nakayama with finite-generation
and radical hypotheses, by a projective-lifting / split
epimorphism audit, by Maschke averaging, by a localization
construction, or by a product universal property. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Every proper submodule of $P$ is one of the finite cyclic groups $P[2^n]\cong\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$. Consequently the lattice of submodules is the single chain $0\subset P[2]\subset P[4]\subset\cdots\subset P$.
A divisible abelian group is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module. The injective hull of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is the Prüfer $2$-group $P$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Classify submodules as the single chain of cyclic 2-power torsion groups, then read both chain conditions from that lattice.
Check divisibility by odd units and by powers of 2 separately, then identify the unique simple submodule as an essential socle.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the unique finite submodules P[2^n], the strict ascending chain, and the failure of the Noetherian property, together with Artinian descending stabilization.
Proves P is divisible hence injective, that soc(P)=P[2] is essential, and that P is the injective hull of P[2].
Rejects a Noetherian claim and refuses a denial of injectivity or of the essential socle / hull.

hintTree.content: Any nonzero element of $P$ has the form $a/2^k+\mathbb{Z}$ with $a$ odd, and generates $P[2^k]$. Thus each finite order $2^n$ occurs exactly once.
The unique infinite ascending chain of finite submodules prevents the ascending-chain condition. Any descending chain in a single discrete chain must stabilize.
Divisibility by $2$ is division of the denominator exponent; divisibility by odd integers is invertible on $P$. The unique simple submodule $P[2]$ meets every nonzero submodule.

GA:010431.canonicalSolution:
Every nonzero element of
$P=\mathbb{Z}[1/2]/\mathbb{Z}$ has a reduced expression
$a/2^k+\mathbb{Z}$ with $a$ odd. Its numerator is therefore a unit
modulo $2^k$, so the element generates
\[
P[2^k]=\bigl\langle 1/2^k+\mathbb{Z}\bigr\rangle
\cong\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z}.
\]
If a nonzero submodule $N$ has bounded element orders, choose an
element of maximal order $2^n$. It generates $P[2^n]$, while every
element of $N$ lies in $P[2^n]$, so $N=P[2^n]$. If the element
orders in $N$ are unbounded, then $N$ contains $P[2^n]$ for
arbitrarily large $n$, hence contains their union $P$ and equals
$P$. Thus the proper nonzero submodules are exactly the unique
groups $P[2^n]$. They nest as
\[
0\subset P[2]\subset P[4]\subset P[8]\subset\cdots\subset P,
\]
a strictly ascending infinite chain, so $P$ is not Noetherian.
\[
\boxed{\text{unique }P[2^n];\ \text{strict ascending};\
\text{not Noetherian}}.
\]

The complete submodule lattice is this single chain together with
$P$ itself. In a descending chain, after a possible first step from
$P$ to some $P[2^n]$, the natural-number indices can decrease only
finitely many times. Hence every descending chain stabilizes and
$P$ is Artinian.

To see divisibility, take $x=a/2^k+\mathbb{Z}$ and $n\ge 1$. Write
$n=2^r m$ with $m$ odd. Multiplication by $m$ is invertible on
$P$ because $m$ is a unit modulo every $2$-power. Multiplication
by $2^r$ is surjective because
\[
2^r\cdot\bigl(a/2^{k+r}+\mathbb{Z}\bigr)=a/2^k+\mathbb{Z}.
\]
A divisible abelian group is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so
$P$ is injective.
\[
\boxed{\text{descending stabilizes / Artinian};\
\text{divisible / injective}}.
\]

The only simple submodule is $P[2]\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, so
\[
\operatorname{soc}(P)=P[2].
\]
Every nonzero submodule is some $P[2^n]$ or $P$ itself, and each
of these contains $P[2]$. Therefore $P[2]$ is essential in $P$.
An essential injective extension of $P[2]$ is an injective hull,
so $P$ is the injective hull of its socle.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{soc}(P)=P[2]\text{ essential};\
E(P[2])=P}.
\]

Sentence (i) claims the Noetherian property or a stabilizing
ascending chain. Sentence (ii) denies divisibility/injectivity,
essentiality of the socle, or the identification of the injective
hull.

The argument never replaces the assigned Prüfer two-chain ledger
by Nakayama with finite-generation and radical hypotheses, by a
projective-lifting / split-epimorphism audit, by Maschke
averaging, by a localization construction, or by a product
universal property, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The only finite submodules of $P=\mathbb{Z}[1/2]/\mathbb{Z}$ are the unique groups $P[2^n]$. The strict ascent $P[2^n]$ shows $P$ is not Noetherian, while every descending chain stabilizes, so $P$ is Artinian. The module is divisible, hence injective. Its socle $P[2]$ is essential, and $P$ is the injective hull of $P[2]$.
P is Noetherian, or else the chain P[2^n] stabilizes. I do not accept a strict infinite ascent or the failure of the Noetherian property.
P is not divisible/injective, or the socle P[2] is not essential, or the injective hull of P[2] is not P.

GA:010522.title: S3 permutation character (3,1,0) splits as triv+std with inner products (1,0,1) and averaging projector J/3 sending (1,2,4) to (7/3,7/3,7/3)
GA:010522.objective: For the permutation representation of S3 on C^3, record class sizes 1,3,2 and character values (3,1,0), compute inner products (1,0,1) against triv, sign, and std, identify the invariant line and the sum-zero complement, and apply the averaging projector J/3 to send (1,2,4) to (7/3,7/3,7/3).
GA:010522.statement:
Let $S_3$ act on $\mathbb{C}^3$ by permuting the standard basis
$\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}$ for the resulting
permutation character, and write $\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}=(1,1,1)$,
$\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}=(1,-1,1)$, and $\chi_{\mathrm{std}}=(2,0,-1)$
for the three irreducible characters, listed on the conjugacy
classes $\{e\}$, the three transpositions, and the two $3$-cycles.

1. Confirm the class equation sizes $1,3,2$ and prove
   \[
   \chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=(3,1,0).
   \]

2. With the standard inner product
   \[
   \langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\frac1{6}\bigl(\alpha(e)\overline{\beta(e)}
   +3\,\alpha(\tau)\overline{\beta(\tau)}
   +2\,\alpha(c)\overline{\beta(c)}\bigr),
   \]
   compute
   \[
   \bigl\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}\bigr\rangle=1,\qquad
   \bigl\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}\bigr\rangle=0,\qquad
   \bigl\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{std}}\bigr\rangle=1.
   \]
   Conclude that the permutation module itself splits as
   $\mathbb{C}^3\cong\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathrm{std}$.

3. Identify the $S_3$-invariant line as $\mathbb{C}(1,1,1)$ and the
   complementary sum-zero plane
   $\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0\}$. Prove that the averaging projector is
   $J/3$, where $J$ is the $3\times 3$ all-ones matrix, and evaluate
   \[
   \frac J3\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}
   =\begin{pmatrix}7/3\\7/3\\7/3\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the three conjugacy classes may be
   treated as singletons, so the inner products are not $(1,0,1)$
   and $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}$ is irreducible”; (ii) “the averaging
   operator is the un-normalized all-ones matrix $J$, so
   $(1,2,4)$ is sent to $(7,7,7)$ rather than to $(7/3,7/3,7/3)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $C_4$ regular Fourier
idempotent packet of this shard, by a $\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$
ledger, by a Baer-criterion extension count, or by an Artinian
socle ledger. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six
existing intake seeds, including Maschke averaging as a general
existence theorem without this $S_3$ character table.
permittedResults: The column orthogonality formula with class sizes $1,3,2$ yields $\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}\rangle=1$, $\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}\rangle=0$, and $\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{std}}\rangle=1$, so $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}+\chi_{\mathrm{std}}$.
The all-ones vector is fixed, and $J(1,2,4)^T=(7,7,7)^T$, hence $(J/3)(1,2,4)^T=(7/3,7/3,7/3)^T$. The complementary component is $(-4/3,-1/3,5/3)$, which sums to $0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Count fixed points on each class, then insert the class-size weights 1,3,2 into the inner-product formula against the three irreducibles.
Recognize the Reynolds operator as the coordinate-average projector J/3 and apply it directly to (1,2,4).

milestones.criterion: Records class sizes 1,3,2 and chi_perm=(3,1,0), then computes the three inner products (1,0,1) and the splitting triv+std.
Identifies the invariant line and sum-zero complement, proves the averaging projector is J/3, and evaluates J/3*(1,2,4)^T=(7/3,7/3,7/3)^T.
Rejects singleton class sizes and the un-normalized projector J.

commonErrors.consequence: The required splitting C^3=triv+std and the multiplicity 1 of the trivial summand are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the un-normalized all-ones matrix J instead of J/3, sending (1,2,4) to (7,7,7) rather than to (7/3,7/3,7/3).
commonErrors.consequence: The averaging projector is not a projector, and the required image (7/3,7/3,7/3) fails.

hintTree.content: Class sizes are $1$ (identity), $3$ (transpositions), $2$ (three-cycles). A transposition fixes one letter and a $3$-cycle fixes none, so $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=(3,1,0)$.
The inner-product weights are $1/6$, $3/6$, and $2/6$. Against triv this is $(3+3+0)/6=1$; against sign, $(3-3+0)/6=0$; against std, $(6+0+0)/6=1$.
The coordinate average of $(1,2,4)$ is $7/3$. The averaging projector therefore sends the vector to $(7/3,7/3,7/3)$, not to $(7,7,7)$.

GA:010522.canonicalSolution:
The conjugacy classes of $S_3$ are $\{e\}$ of size $1$, the three
transpositions of size $3$, and the two $3$-cycles of size $2$.
The permutation representation on $\mathbb{C}^3$ has
\[
\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(e)=3,\qquad
\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(\tau)=1,\qquad
\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}(c)=0,
\]
because the identity fixes three letters, a transposition fixes
one letter, and a $3$-cycle fixes none.
\[
\boxed{\text{class sizes }1,3,2;\quad \chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=(3,1,0)}.
\]

The standard inner product on class functions of $S_3$ is
\[
\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle
=\frac1{6}\bigl(\alpha(e)\overline{\beta(e)}
+3\,\alpha(\tau)\overline{\beta(\tau)}
+2\,\alpha(c)\overline{\beta(c)}\bigr).
\]
Against the three irreducibles one obtains
\begin{align*}
\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}\rangle
&=\frac{3\cdot 1+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\cdot 1}{6}=1,\\
\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{sgn}}\rangle
&=\frac{3\cdot 1+3\cdot 1\cdot(-1)+2\cdot 0\cdot 1}{6}=0,\\
\langle\chi_{\mathrm{perm}},\chi_{\mathrm{std}}\rangle
&=\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 0+2\cdot 0\cdot(-1)}{6}=1.
\end{align*}
Thus $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=\chi_{\mathrm{triv}}+\chi_{\mathrm{std}}$,
so the permutation module is
$\mathbb{C}^3\cong\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathrm{std}$.
\[
\boxed{\text{inner products }(1,0,1);\quad
\mathbb{C}^3=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathrm{std}}.
\]

The line $\mathbb{C}(1,1,1)$ is pointwise fixed. Its unique
$S_3$-stable complement in $\mathbb{C}^3$ is the sum-zero plane
$\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0\}$. The Reynolds operator equals $J/3$: each
matrix entry of $\sum_{\sigma\in S_3}\rho(\sigma)$ equals $2$, since
exactly two permutations send any fixed basis vector to any fixed
basis vector. Hence the sum is $2J$, and dividing by
$\lvert S_3\rvert=6$ yields $J/3$. Applying this
projector,
\[
\frac J3\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{1+2+4}{3}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}7/3\\7/3\\7/3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The complementary component is
$(1,2,4)-(7/3,7/3,7/3)=(-4/3,-1/3,5/3)$, which sums to $0$.
\[
\boxed{J/3\cdot(1,2,4)^T=(7/3,7/3,7/3)^T}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the class-size weights $3$ and $2$, so the
inner products are no longer $(1,0,1)$ and the permutation
character is incorrectly declared irreducible. Sentence (ii)
omits the factor $1/3$ and reports the un-normalized image
$(7,7,7)$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $S_3$ permutation
character by the sibling $C_4$ Fourier packet, by a
$\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ ledger, by a Baer extension count,
or by an Artinian socle computation, and it does not open any
of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: Class sizes of $S_3$ are $1,3,2$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{perm}}=(3,1,0)$. Inner products against triv, sign, and std are $(1,0,1)$, so the permutation module is $\mathbb{C}^3=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathrm{std}$. The invariant line is $\mathbb{C}(1,1,1)$ with sum-zero complement, the Reynolds sum is $2J$, the averaging projector is $J/3$, and $(J/3)(1,2,4)^T=(7/3,7/3,7/3)^T$.
I treat the three conjugacy classes as singletons, so the inner products are not (1,0,1) and I declare chi_perm irreducible. I do not accept the splitting triv+std.
The averaging operator is the un-normalized all-ones matrix J, so (1,2,4) is sent to (7,7,7) rather than to (7/3,7/3,7/3).

GA:010523.title: C4 Fourier idempotents e_j=(1/4)sum i^{-jr}g^r are orthogonal, sum to 1, satisfy g e_j=i^j e_j, and the regular character is (4,0,0,0) with det L_g=-1
GA:010523.objective: For C4=<g>, write the four Fourier idempotents e_j explicitly, prove they are orthogonal idempotents summing to 1 with g e_j=i^j e_j, record the regular character (4,0,0,0), and prove det of left multiplication by g equals -1.
GA:010523.statement:
Let $C_4=\langle g\rangle$ with $g^4=1$, and let $i\in\mathbb{C}$
be a fixed primitive fourth root of unity. The irreducible
characters are $\chi_j(g^r)=i^{jr}$ for $j=0,1,2,3$. Define
\[
e_j=\frac14\sum_{r=0}^{3} i^{-jr}\,g^r\in\mathbb{C}[C_4].
\]

1. Expand the four elements explicitly:
   \begin{align*}
   e_0&=\frac{1+g+g^2+g^3}{4},\\
   e_1&=\frac{1-ig-g^2+ig^3}{4},\\
   e_2&=\frac{1-g+g^2-g^3}{4},\\
   e_3&=\frac{1+ig-g^2-ig^3}{4}.
   \end{align*}

2. Prove that the $e_j$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
   summing to $1$, and that
   \[
   g\,e_j=i^j e_j\qquad(j=0,1,2,3).
   \]

3. Record the regular character of $C_4$ on the classes
   $\{1,g,g^2,g^3\}$ as $(4,0,0,0)$. Viewing left multiplication
   $L_g$ as a permutation of the basis $\{1,g,g^2,g^3\}$, prove
   that $L_g$ is a $4$-cycle and
   \[
   \det L_g=-1.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Fourier formula uses $i^{jr}$
   rather than $i^{-jr}$, so $e_1$ and $e_3$ are swapped and
   $g e_1=-i e_1$”; (ii) “the regular character is $(1,1,1,1)$
   or $(4,1,1,1)$, and a $4$-cycle is an even permutation, so
   $\det L_g=+1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $S_3$ permutation
character packet of this shard, by a $\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$
ledger, by a Baer-criterion extension count, or by an Artinian
socle ledger. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six
existing intake seeds.

A $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$, so a $4$-cycle is odd and $\det L_g=-1$. The regular character is $(4,0,0,0)$.

hintTree.content: Substitute $i^{-1}=-i$, $i^{-2}=-1$, and $i^{-3}=i$ into $e_j=\frac14\sum_r i^{-jr}g^r$ to obtain the four explicit formulae.
Character orthogonality gives $e_je_k=\delta_{jk}e_j$ and $\sum_je_j=1$. Multiplying the defining sum by $g$ replaces $r$ by $r-1$ and produces the factor $i^j$.
$L_g$ sends $1\mapsto g\mapsto g^2\mapsto g^3\mapsto 1$. The sign of a $4$-cycle is $-1$, so $\det L_g=-1$.

GA:010523.canonicalSolution:
Write $i^{-1}=-i$, $i^{-2}=-1$, and $i^{-3}=i$. Then
\begin{align*}
e_0&=\frac14(1+g+g^2+g^3),\\
e_1&=\frac14\bigl(1+i^{-1}g+i^{-2}g^2+i^{-3}g^3\bigr)
=\frac{1-ig-g^2+ig^3}{4},\\
e_2&=\frac14\bigl(1+i^{-2}g+i^{-4}g^2+i^{-6}g^3\bigr)
=\frac{1-g+g^2-g^3}{4},\\
e_3&=\frac14\bigl(1+i^{-3}g+i^{-6}g^2+i^{-9}g^3\bigr)
=\frac{1+ig-g^2-ig^3}{4}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3\text{ as displayed}}.
\]

Character orthogonality on $C_4$ yields
$e_je_k=\delta_{jk}e_j$ and $\sum_{j=0}^{3}e_j=1$. For the
eigenvalue identity, shift the summation index in
$g e_j=\frac14\sum_r i^{-jr}g^{r+1}$ by $s=r+1$:
\[
g e_j=\frac14\sum_s i^{-j(s-1)}g^s
=i^j\cdot\frac14\sum_s i^{-js}g^s=i^j e_j.
\]
Thus $g e_0=e_0$, $g e_1=i e_1$, $g e_2=-e_2$, and
$g e_3=-i e_3$.
\[
\boxed{e_je_k=\delta_{jk}e_j,\ \sum e_j=1,\ g e_j=i^j e_j}.
\]

The regular character counts fixed basis vectors of left
multiplication, hence equals $4$ at the identity and $0$ at
every non-identity element:
\[
\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}=(4,0,0,0).
\]
On the ordered basis $\{1,g,g^2,g^3\}$ the operator $L_g$ is
the permutation matrix of the $4$-cycle $(1\ g\ g^2\ g^3)$.
A $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$, so a $4$-cycle is odd and
\[
\det L_g=-1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}=(4,0,0,0),\ \det L_g=-1}.
\]

Sentence (i) inserts $i^{jr}$ in place of $i^{-jr}$, which
swaps $e_1$ with $e_3$ and replaces $g e_1=i e_1$ by
$g e_1=-i e_1$. Sentence (ii) misrecords the regular
character and treats a $4$-cycle as even.

The argument never replaces the assigned $C_4$ Fourier
computation by the sibling $S_3$ permutation character, by a
$\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ ledger, by a Baer extension count,
or by an Artinian socle computation, and it does not open any
of the six existing intake seeds.

GA:010624.title: Multiplication by 12 on Z/18 has kernel {0,3,6,9,12,15} and image {0,6,12}, so Hom(Z/12,Z/18) and Ext^1 are both Z/6 while Ext^{q>=2}=0
GA:010624.objective: From the resolution of Z/12 given by multiplication by 12, compute the kernel {0,3,6,9,12,15} and image {0,6,12} of ×12 on Z/18, and conclude Hom(Z/12,Z/18)≅Z/6, Ext^1(Z/12,Z/18)≅Z/6, and Ext^q=0 for q≥2.
GA:010624.statement:
Work throughout with abelian groups, equivalently with
$\mathbb{Z}$-modules. Start from the standard length-$1$ resolution
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times 12}\mathbb{Z}
\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow 0.
\]

1. Apply $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(-,\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})$ and
   identify the induced endomorphism of
   $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z}$
   with multiplication by $12$ on $\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z}$. Compute
   \[
   \ker(\times 12)=\{0,3,6,9,12,15\}\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z},
   \]
   \[
   \mathrm{im}(\times 12)=\{0,6,12\}.
   \]

2. Conclude
   \[
   \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})
   \cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z},
   \]
   \[
   \mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})
   \cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z},
   \]
   and $\mathrm{Ext}^q=0$ for every $q\ge 2$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/m)$
   is $\mathbb{Z}/n$ or $\mathbb{Z}/m$, so the Hom group is
   $\mathbb{Z}/12$ or $\mathbb{Z}/18$ rather than $\mathbb{Z}/6$”;
   (ii) “the kernel of $\times 12$ on $\mathbb{Z}/18$ is the image
   $\{0,6,12\}$, so Hom is $\mathbb{Z}/3$ and the Ext ledger is
   swapped.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling Baer-criterion
packet of this shard, by an $S_3$ or $C_4$ representation
packet, or by an Artinian socle ledger. Do not reopen, import,
or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.

A cyclic group has projective dimension $1$ over $\mathbb{Z}$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^q(\mathbb{Z}/12,-)=0$ for every $q\ge 2$.

The values $12\cdot 0,12\cdot 1,12\cdot 2$ are $0,12,6$, and then the list repeats, so the image is $\{0,6,12\}$.

GA:010624.canonicalSolution:
The standard resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$ is
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times 12}\mathbb{Z}
\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})$ and identifying
$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})$ with
$\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z}$ produces the endomorphism $\times 12$
on $\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z}$. The congruence $12k\equiv 0\pmod{18}$
is equivalent to $18\mid 12k$, or $3\mid 2k$. Since $2$ is a unit
modulo $3$, this is $3\mid k$, hence
\[
\ker(\times 12)=\{0,3,6,9,12,15\}\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Evaluating on residue representatives gives
$12\cdot 0=0$, $12\cdot 1=12$, $12\cdot 2=24\equiv 6$, and then
the values repeat, so
\[
\mathrm{im}(\times 12)=\{0,6,12\}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\ker=\{0,3,6,9,12,15\}\cong\mathbb{Z}/6,\quad
\mathrm{im}=\{0,6,12\}}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})
\cong\ker(\times 12)\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}
\]
and
\[
\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})
\cong\operatorname{coker}(\times 12)
\cong(\mathbb{Z}/18\mathbb{Z})/\{0,6,12\}
\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}.
\]
The same conclusions follow from the general identities
$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/m)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(n,m)$
and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z}/m)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(n,m)$
with $\gcd(12,18)=6$. Because the projective resolution has
length $1$, one has $\mathrm{Ext}^q=0$ for every $q\ge 2$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Hom}\cong\mathbb{Z}/6,\ \mathrm{Ext}^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/6,\
\mathrm{Ext}^{q\ge 2}=0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(12,18)$ by $\mathbb{Z}/12$
or $\mathbb{Z}/18$. Sentence (ii) swaps kernel and image, so Hom
is incorrectly reported as $\mathbb{Z}/3$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$
ledger by the sibling Baer packet, by an $S_3$ or $C_4$
representation computation, or by an Artinian socle ledger, and
it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

GA:010625.title: Q/Z is injective by divisibility and Baer, and the map 6Z→Q/Z with f(6)=1/4+Z has exactly six extensions β=1/24+k/6 for k=0..5
GA:010625.objective: Prove Q/Z is injective by checking divisibility and invoking Baer's criterion, then classify the extensions of f:6Z→Q/Z with f(6)=1/4+Z as the six maps determined by β(1)=1/24+k/6+Z for k=0,1,2,3,4,5.
GA:010625.statement:
Let $Q=\mathbb{Q}$ and write $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ for the
quotient group of rationals modulo integers.

1. Prove that $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is divisible: for every
   $x\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ and every integer $n\ge 1$ there
   exists $y$ with $ny=x$. Deduce from Baer's criterion that
   $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective abelian group.

2. Let $n=6$ and let $f:6\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ be
   the homomorphism determined by
   \[
   f(6)=\frac14+\mathbb{Z}.
   \]
   Prove that the extensions $\beta:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$
   of $f$ are precisely the six maps with
   \[
   \beta(1)=\frac1{24}+\frac k6+\mathbb{Z},\qquad k=0,1,2,3,4,5.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “divisibility of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$
   is not enough for Baer's criterion, so $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is
   not injective”; (ii) “the equation $6\xi=1/4+\mathbb{Z}$ has the
   unique solution $\xi=1/24+\mathbb{Z}$, or else twenty-four
   solutions indexed by a denominator $24$, so there are not
   exactly six extensions.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling
$\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ ledger of this shard, by an $S_3$
or $C_4$ representation packet, or by an Artinian socle ledger.
Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.

hintTree.content: For $x=a/b+\mathbb{Z}$ take $y=a/(nb)+\mathbb{Z}$. Baer's criterion then upgrades divisibility to injectivity.
An extension is a choice of $\xi=\beta(1)$ with $6\xi\equiv 1/4\pmod{\mathbb{Z}}$. One particular solution is $\xi=1/24$.
The general solution adds $\ker(\times 6$ on $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})=\frac16\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$, giving exactly the six classes $k=0,\ldots,5$.

GA:010625.canonicalSolution:
Write a general element of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ as
$x=a/b+\mathbb{Z}$ with $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $b\ge 1$. Given
$n\ge 1$, the element $y=a/(nb)+\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies
\[
ny=\frac ab+\mathbb{Z}=x.
\]
Thus $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is divisible. Baer's criterion
says that an abelian group is injective if and only if every
map $n\mathbb{Z}\to E$ extends to $\mathbb{Z}$, which is
precisely the statement that $E$ is divisible. Therefore
$\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is injective.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\text{ divisible}\Rightarrow\text{injective}}.
\]

Now take $n=6$ and $f(6)=1/4+\mathbb{Z}$. An extension
$\beta:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is determined by
$\xi=\beta(1)\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ subject to
$6\xi=f(6)=1/4+\mathbb{Z}$. One particular solution is
$\xi_0=1/24+\mathbb{Z}$, since $6\cdot(1/24)=1/4$. The
difference of two solutions lies in
\[
\{\eta\in\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}:6\eta=0\}
=\frac16\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}
=\bigl\{0,\tfrac16,\tfrac26,\tfrac36,\tfrac46,\tfrac56\bigr\}+\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Hence the complete list is
\[
\xi=\frac1{24}+\frac k6+\mathbb{Z},\qquad k=0,1,2,3,4,5.
\]
These six classes are distinct: $k/6$ runs through a complete
set of representatives of $\frac16\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$.
Explicitly they are
\[
\frac1{24},\ \frac5{24},\ \frac9{24},\ \frac{13}{24},\
\frac{17}{24},\ \frac{21}{24}
\]
modulo $\mathbb{Z}$. Each satisfies
$6\bigl(1/24+k/6\bigr)=1/4+k\equiv 1/4\pmod{\mathbb{Z}}$.
\[
\boxed{\beta(1)=1/24+k/6+\mathbb{Z},\ k=0,\ldots,5
\text{ (exactly six)}}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies that divisibility implies injectivity over
$\mathbb{Z}$ and so rejects Baer's criterion. Sentence (ii)
either drops the $\frac16\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$ ambiguity or
indexes solutions by a denominator $24$, and so misses the
count of exactly six.

The argument never replaces the assigned Baer count by the
sibling $\mathrm{Hom}/\mathrm{Ext}$ ledger, by an $S_3$ or
$C_4$ representation computation, or by an Artinian socle
ledger, and it does not open any of the six existing intake
seeds.

GA:010630.title: C2 with the sign action on Z has periodic cochains multiplication by -2,0,-2,0, vanishing even cohomology including H0, and H^odd = Z/2, with H0 through H3 exact
GA:010630.objective: For G=C2 acting on Z by the sign representation, prove the standard periodic cochain maps are multiplication by -2,0,-2,0, that H^{even} including H^0 vanishes, that H^{odd} cong Z/2, and that the values are H^0=0, H^1=Z/2, H^2=0, H^3=Z/2.
GA:010630.statement:
Let $G=C_2=\langle\sigma\mid\sigma^2=1\rangle$ act on the
coefficient module $M=\mathbb{Z}$ by the sign representation
$\sigma\cdot n=-n$. Let
\[
\cdots\to\mathbb{Z}[G]\xrightarrow{\ N\ }
\mathbb{Z}[G]\xrightarrow{\ \sigma-1\ }
\mathbb{Z}[G]\xrightarrow{\ N\ }
\mathbb{Z}[G]\xrightarrow{\ \sigma-1\ }
\mathbb{Z}[G]\to\mathbb{Z}\to 0
\]
be the standard periodic resolution of the trivial module
$\mathbb{Z}$, with norm $N=1+\sigma$.

1. Identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}G}(\mathbb{Z}[G],M)$
   with $M=\mathbb{Z}$ and prove that the induced cochain maps
   are multiplication by
   \[
   -2,\ 0,\ -2,\ 0
   \]
   in cohomological degrees $0,1,2,3$.

2. Compute
   \[
   H^0(G,M)=0,\qquad
   H^1(G,M)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2,\qquad
   H^2(G,M)=0,\qquad
   H^3(G,M)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2,
   \]
   and conclude that every even group (including $H^0$) vanishes
   while every odd group is $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the action is trivial, so the
   cochain maps are $0,-2,0,-2$ and the parity of vanishing is
   reversed”; (ii) “$H^0$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}/2$, so
   even cohomology (including $H^0$) does not vanish.”

Do not replace the calculation by a projective-lifting / split
epimorphism / free-summand audit, by Nakayama, by Maschke
averaging, by a product universal property, or by a localization
construction. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six
existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: On the sign module one has $(\sigma-1)n=-n-n=-2n$ and $Nn=n+(-n)=0$. Thus the cochain maps are $\times(-2)$, $\times 0$, $\times(-2)$, $\times 0$.

Therefore $H^0=\ker(\times(-2))=0$, while each positive even group is $\ker(\times(-2))/\operatorname{im}(\times 0)=0$ and each odd group is $\ker(\times 0)/\operatorname{im}(\times(-2))=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate sigma-1 and the norm on the sign module first, locking the four maps -2,0,-2,0.
Read H^0 as ker(x |-> -2x)=0 and each odd group as Z / 2Z, then fill H^2 from the same pattern.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the periodic cochain maps as multiplication by -2, 0, -2, 0 on the sign module.
Computes H^0=0, H^1=Z/2, H^2=0, H^3=Z/2, with all even groups vanishing and all odd groups Z/2.
Rejects the trivial-action parity swap and refuses a nonzero H^0 or nonzero even group.

hintTree.content: The even coboundary is $\sigma-1$. On the sign module this is multiplication by $-2$. The odd coboundary is the norm $1+\sigma$, which vanishes on the sign module.
$H^0$ is the kernel of $\times(-2)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, hence $0$. Invariants of the sign action on $\mathbb{Z}$ are likewise $0$.
Odd cohomology is $\mathbb{Z}/\operatorname{im}(\times(-2))\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$. Even positive cohomology has incoming map $0$ and outgoing map $\times(-2)$, hence vanishes.

GA:010630.canonicalSolution:
Identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}G}(\mathbb{Z}[G],M)$ with
$M=\mathbb{Z}$. Under the sign action $\sigma n=-n$ one has
\[
(\sigma-1)n=-n-n=-2n,\qquad
Nn=(1+\sigma)n=n-n=0.
\]
The standard periodic cochain complex is therefore
\[
0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times(-2)\ }
\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times 0\ }
\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times(-2)\ }
\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ \times 0\ }\cdots,
\]
i.e. the degree $0,1,2,3$ coboundaries are multiplication by
$-2,0,-2,0$.
\[
\boxed{\text{cochains }\times(-2),\,\times 0,\,\times(-2),\,\times 0}.
\]

Now compute the cohomology. In degree $0$,
\[
H^0(G,M)=\ker(\times(-2))=0.
\]
In odd degrees the incoming map is $\times(-2)$ and the outgoing
map is $\times 0$, so
\[
H^{2k+1}(G,M)=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}.
\]
In positive even degrees the incoming map is $\times 0$ and the
outgoing map is $\times(-2)$, so
\[
H^{2k}(G,M)=0\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]
In particular the first four groups are
\[
H^0=0,\qquad H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/2,\qquad
H^2=0,\qquad H^3\cong\mathbb{Z}/2.
\]
Thus every even group, including $H^0$, vanishes, and every odd
group is $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
\[
\boxed{H^{\mathrm{even}}=0\text{ (incl. }H^0{)},\quad
H^{\mathrm{odd}}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2;\quad
H^0..H^3=0,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z}/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the sign action by the trivial action and
reverses the parity. Sentence (ii) claims a nonzero even group,
in particular a nonzero $H^0$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $C_2$ sign-cohomology
parity ledger by a projective-lifting / split-epimorphism audit,
by Nakayama, by Maschke averaging, by a product universal
property, or by a localization construction, and it does not open
any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: On the sign module the periodic cochain maps are multiplication by $-2,0,-2,0$. Even cohomology, including $H^0$, vanishes, and odd cohomology is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. In particular $H^0=0$, $H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H^2=0$, and $H^3\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$.
The action is trivial, so the cochain maps are 0,-2,0,-2 and the parity of vanishing is reversed. I do not accept maps -2,0,-2,0.
H^0 is Z or Z/2, so even cohomology (including H^0) does not vanish. I do not accept H^0=0 or H^2=0.

GA:020117.title: X^2-3 is 3-Eisenstein, so Q_3(sqrt(3)) has uniformizer pi=sqrt(3), different (pi), and residue F_3
GA:020117.objective: For K=Q_3(sqrt(3)), prove X^2-3 is 3-Eisenstein, [K:Q_3]=2, O=Z_3[pi] with pi=sqrt(3) a uniformizer, e=2, f=1, residue F_3, Trace(pi)=0, Norm(pi)=-3, basis discriminant 12 with local discriminant ideal (3), (3)=(pi)^2, different=(2pi)=(pi), and different exponent 1.
GA:020117.statement:
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$ and write $\pi=\sqrt{3}$. Let
$\mathcal{O}$ be the valuation ring of $K$.

1. Prove that $X^2-3$ is $3$-Eisenstein, hence irreducible, that
   $[K:\mathbb{Q}_3]=2$, and that $\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{Z}_3[\pi]$
   with uniformizer $\pi$. Deduce $e=2$, $f=1$, and residue field
   $\mathbb{F}_3$. Record the ideal factorization $(3)=(\pi)^2$.

2. For the power basis $\{1,\pi\}$, prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}(\pi)=0,\qquad
   \operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}(\pi)=-3,
   \]
   and that the basis discriminant equals $12$, with local
   discriminant ideal in $\mathbb{Z}_3$ is $(12)=(3)$.

3. Prove that the different is
   \[
   \mathfrak{D}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}=(2\pi)=(\pi)
   \]
   and that the different exponent is $1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$X^2-3$ fails to be $3$-Eisenstein,
   so $e=1$ and $\pi$ is not a uniformizer”; (ii) “$2$ is not a
   $3$-adic unit, so $(2\pi)\ne(\pi)$ and the different exponent
   is not $1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling Gaussian splitting
ledger, by the fifth-cyclotomic lattice, by a cusp conductor, or
by a Hilbert–Samuel length. Do not reopen, import, or execute any
of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Eisenstein's criterion at $p=3$ applies to $X^2-3$: $3$ divides the constant term $3$ and $9$ does not. The unique extension of $\mathbb{Q}_3$ cut out by this polynomial therefore has degree $2$, ramification index $e=2$, and residue degree $f=1$.
For $f(X)=X^2-3$ one has $f'(\pi)=2\pi$. The element $2$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}_3$, so $(2\pi)=(\pi)$ and $v_K(\mathfrak{D})=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the Eisenstein test at 3, read e from v_K(pi^2)=2, and identify the residue field O/(pi).
Compute the different as (f'(pi))=(2pi) and use that 2 is a 3-adic unit to collapse the ideal and read exponent 1.

milestones.criterion: Proves X^2-3 is 3-Eisenstein, O=Z_3[pi], e=2, f=1, residue F_3, and (3)=(pi)^2.
Computes Trace(pi)=0, Norm(pi)=-3, disc=12 with local discriminant ideal (3), and different=(2pi)=(pi) of exponent 1.
Rejects a failed Eisenstein test and refuses to treat 2 as a nonunit in Z_3.

commonErrors.consequence: The required identities e=2, f=1, residue F_3, and (3)=(pi)^2 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats 2 as a nonunit of Z_3, so (2pi) is not collapsed to (pi) and the different exponent is not 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities different=(2pi)=(pi) and exponent 1 fail.

hintTree.content: Check the two Eisenstein divisibility conditions on $X^2-3$ at the prime $3$. Then $\pi^2=3$ forces $v_K(3)=2$ once $v_K(\pi)=1$.
The minimal polynomial is $X^2-3=X^2+0\cdot X-3$, so the trace is $0$ and the norm is $-3$. The power-basis discriminant is $\operatorname{N}(f'(\pi))$ up to sign, hence $12$.
Locally at $3$ the scalar $2$ is a unit, so the principal ideals $(2\pi)$ and $(\pi)$ coincide.

GA:020117.canonicalSolution:
The polynomial $f(X)=X^2-3\in\mathbb{Z}_3[X]$ is monic of degree $2$.
The linear coefficient is $0$, which is divisible by $3$, and the
constant term is $-3$, which is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$.
Thus $f$ is $3$-Eisenstein, hence irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}_3$.
Adjoining a root $\pi=\sqrt{3}$ therefore yields a quadratic
extension
\[
[K:\mathbb{Q}_3]=2.
\]
Eisenstein's lemma supplies the valuation ring and a uniformizer:
\[
\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{Z}_3[\pi],\qquad v_K(\pi)=1.
\]
From $\pi^2=3$ one obtains $v_K(3)=2$. The ramification index of
$K/\mathbb{Q}_3$ is therefore $e=v_K(3)=2$, the residue degree is
$f=[K:\mathbb{Q}_3]/e=1$, and the residue field is
$\mathcal{O}/(\pi)\cong\mathbb{F}_3$. Equivalently,
\[
(3)=(\pi)^2
\]
as ideals of $\mathcal{O}$.
\[
\boxed{[K:\mathbb{Q}_3]=2,\;\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{Z}_3[\pi],\;e=2,\;f=1,\;\kappa=\mathbb{F}_3}.
\]

The minimal polynomial of $\pi$ is $X^2-3=X^2-(\operatorname{Tr}\pi)X+\operatorname{N}\pi$
after rewriting $X^2+0\cdot X-3$, so
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}(\pi)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}(\pi)=-3.
\]
The discriminant of the power basis $\{1,\pi\}$ is
\[
\operatorname{disc}(1,\pi)
=\det\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Tr}(1)&\operatorname{Tr}(\pi)\\
\operatorname{Tr}(\pi)&\operatorname{Tr}(\pi^2)\end{pmatrix}
=\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}
=12.
\]
The same value is $-\operatorname{N}(f'(\pi))=-\operatorname{N}(2\pi)=-4\operatorname{N}(\pi)=12$.
Because $4$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_3$, the corresponding local
discriminant ideal is
\[
(12)=(3)\subset\mathbb{Z}_3.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Tr}\pi=0,\;\operatorname{N}\pi=-3,\;\operatorname{disc}(1,\pi)=12,\;(\operatorname{disc})=(3)}.
\]

Because $\mathcal{O}$ is monogenic on $\pi$, the different is the
principal ideal
\[
\mathfrak{D}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3}=(f'(\pi))=(2\pi).
\]
The prime $3$ does not divide $2$, so $2\in\mathbb{Z}_3^\times$ and
\[
(2\pi)=(\pi).
\]
The different exponent is therefore
\[
v_K(\mathfrak{D}_{K/\mathbb{Q}_3})=v_K(\pi)=1.
\]
This matches the tame formula $e-1=1$ (here $3\nmid e$).
\[
\boxed{\mathfrak{D}=(2\pi)=(\pi),\;\text{exponent }1}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies the Eisenstein criterion and loses both the
uniformizer and the pair $(e,f)=(2,1)$. Sentence (ii) treats $2$
as a nonunit in $\mathbb{Z}_3$ and cannot collapse $(2\pi)$ to
$(\pi)$.

The argument never replaces the assigned local ramification of
$\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$ by the sibling Gaussian splitting ledger,
by the fifth-cyclotomic lattice, by a cusp conductor, or by a
Hilbert–Samuel length, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The polynomial $X^2-3$ is $3$-Eisenstein, so $K=\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$ has degree $2$, valuation ring $\mathbb{Z}_3[\pi]$ with uniformizer $\pi=\sqrt{3}$, $e=2$, $f=1$, and residue $\mathbb{F}_3$. Then $\operatorname{Tr}\pi=0$, $\operatorname{N}\pi=-3$, the basis discriminant is $12$ with local discriminant ideal $(3)$, and $\mathfrak{D}=(2\pi)=(\pi)$ has exponent $1$.
X^2-3 is not 3-Eisenstein, so e=1 and pi=sqrt(3) is not a uniformizer of Z_3[pi]. I do not accept e=2, f=1, or residue F_3.
The scalar 2 is not a 3-adic unit, so (2pi) is not equal to (pi) and the different exponent is not 1.

GA:020118.title: In Q(i) the prime 2 ramifies as (1+i)^2, 3 is inert with residue F_9, and 5 splits, with Frob_3 conjugation
GA:020118.objective: In Q(i), prove (2)=-i(1+i)^2 with e=2,f=1,g=1; 3 is inert with e=1,f=2,g=1 and residue F_9; 5=(2+i)(2-i) splits; disc=-4; Frob_3 is conjugation; and Frob_5 is the identity.
GA:020118.statement:
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ with ring of integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.

1. Prove the exact factorization $(2)=-i(1+i)^2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$,
   and record the splitting type $e=2$, $f=1$, $g=1$ of the rational
   prime $2$.

2. Prove that $3$ is inert, with splitting type $e=1$, $f=2$,
   $g=1$ and residue field $\mathbb{F}_9$. Prove that $5$ splits as
   $5=(2+i)(2-i)$. Record that the field discriminant is $-4$.

3. Identify the Frobenius element of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ at
   $3$ with complex conjugation, and the Frobenius element at $5$
   with the identity.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$3$ splits or ramifies, or $2$ is
   inert, so the ledger of types is not $e_2=2,f_2=1,g_2=1$,
   $e_3=1,f_3=2,g_3=1$, and $5$ split”; (ii) “$\mathrm{Frob}_3$ is
   the identity, or $\mathrm{Frob}_5$ is conjugation.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling local ramification
of $\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the fifth-cyclotomic lattice, by a
cusp conductor, or by a Hilbert–Samuel length. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Dedekind–Kummer on $X^2+1$: the polynomial is a square modulo $2$, irreducible modulo $3$, and split modulo $5$. Correspondingly $2$ ramifies, $3$ is inert, and $5$ splits.
In an abelian extension the Frobenius at a split prime is the identity, while the Frobenius at an inert prime is the unique nontrivial element. Thus $\mathrm{Frob}_3=c$ and $\mathrm{Frob}_5=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor X^2+1 by Dedekind-Kummer at 2, 3, and 5, and expand (1+i)^2=2i for the unit-normalized identity at 2.
Read Frob_p from i |-> i^p in Gal(Q(i)/Q)={1, conjugation}.

milestones.criterion: Records (2)=-i(1+i)^2 with type (2,1,1), 3 inert of type (1,2,1) with residue F_9, and 5=(2+i)(2-i).
Computes disc=-4, Frob_3=conjugation, and Frob_5=identity.
Rejects a permuted splitting ledger and refuses swapped Frobenius elements.

commonErrors.description: Claims that 3 splits or ramifies, or that 2 is inert, or that 5 does not split as (2+i)(2-i).
commonErrors.consequence: The required ledger (2) ramified of type (2,1,1), 3 inert of type (1,2,1) with residue F_9, and 5 split is lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes Frob_3 to be the identity or Frob_5 to be complex conjugation.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities Frob_3=conjugation and Frob_5=identity fail.

hintTree.content: Expand $(1+i)^2=2i$ to obtain the unit-normalized identity $2=-i(1+i)^2$.
Modulo $3$ the values of $X^2+1$ are $1,2,2$, never $0$. Modulo $5$ one has $2^2\equiv-1$, so $5=(2+i)(2-i)$.
Check $i^3=-i$ and $i^5=i$ to read the two Frobenius elements.

GA:020118.canonicalSolution:
The ring of integers of $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, with
field discriminant
\[
\operatorname{disc}(K)=-4.
\]
Expand $(1+i)^2=1+2i-1=2i$. Multiplying by the unit $-i$ recovers
the rational prime:
\[
-i(1+i)^2=-i\cdot 2i=2.
\]
As ideals this is $(2)=(1+i)^2$, so $2$ is totally ramified:
\[
e=2,\qquad f=1,\qquad g=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{(2)=-i(1+i)^2,\;(e,f,g)=(2,1,1)}.
\]

Modulo $3$ the polynomial $X^2+1$ takes the values $1$, $2$, $2$
at $X=0,1,2$, none of which vanish. Thus $X^2+1$ is irreducible
over $\mathbb{F}_3$, the ideal $(3)$ remains prime in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$,
and
\[
e=1,\qquad f=2,\qquad g=1,\qquad
\mathbb{Z}[i]/(3)\cong\mathbb{F}_9.
\]
Modulo $5$ one has $2^2=4\equiv-1$, so $X^2+1=(X-2)(X+2)$ and
\[
5=(2+i)(2-i)
\]
is a product of two distinct principal primes (the factors are not
associates). Thus $5$ splits with $(e,f,g)=(1,1,2)$.
\[
\boxed{3\text{ inert }(e,f,g)=(1,2,1),\;\kappa=\mathbb{F}_9;\quad
5=(2+i)(2-i);\quad\operatorname{disc}=-4}.
\]

Galois conjugation $c$ is determined by $c(i)=-i$. At the inert
prime $3$ one has
\[
i^3=i^2\cdot i=-i=c(i),
\]
so $\mathrm{Frob}_3=c$. At the split prime $5$ one has
\[
i^5=(i^2)^2\cdot i=i,
\]
so $\mathrm{Frob}_5$ is the identity.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Frob}_3=c,\;\mathrm{Frob}_5=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) permutes the three splitting types and cannot keep
the ledger. Sentence (ii) swaps the two Frobenius elements.

The argument never replaces the assigned Gaussian ledger by the
sibling local ramification of $\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the
fifth-cyclotomic lattice, by a cusp conductor, or by a
Hilbert–Samuel length, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: In $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ one has $(2)=-i(1+i)^2$ of type $(e,f,g)=(2,1,1)$, while $3$ is inert of type $(1,2,1)$ with residue $\mathbb{F}_9$ and $5=(2+i)(2-i)$ splits. The discriminant is $-4$. Then $\mathrm{Frob}_3$ is conjugation and $\mathrm{Frob}_5$ is the identity.
The prime 3 splits or ramifies and 2 is inert, so I do not accept the ledger e2=2,f2=1,g2=1, e3=1,f3=2,g3=1, and 5=(2+i)(2-i).
Frob_3 is the identity and Frob_5 is complex conjugation. I do not accept Frob_3=conjugation or Frob_5=identity.

GA:020219.title: The extension Q(zeta_5)/Q is cyclic of degree 4 with unique quadratic Q(sqrt(5)), trace -1, and discriminant 125
GA:020219.objective: For K=Q(zeta_5), prove [K:Q]=4, Gal=C_4, unique order-2 element is conjugation with fixed field Q(sqrt(5)), u=zeta+zeta^{-1} satisfies u^2+u-1=0 with quadratic-field trace -1 and norm -1, while separately Trace_K/Q(zeta)=-1 and Norm_K/Q(zeta)=1; prove disc=125 and the exact three-level lattice Q subset Q(sqrt(5)) subset Q(zeta_5).
GA:020219.statement:
Let $\zeta=\zeta_5$ be a primitive fifth root of unity and write
$K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$.

1. Prove $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=4$ and
   $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})\cong C_4$. Identify the unique
   element of order $2$ with complex conjugation, and prove that
   its fixed field is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$.

2. Let $u=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$. Prove $u^2+u-1=0$ and compute
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1,\qquad
   \operatorname{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1.
   \]
   Separately compute in the full cyclotomic extension
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta)=-1,\qquad
   \operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta)=1,
   \]
   and prove that the field discriminant is $125$.

3. Record the exact three-level lattice of subfields
   \[
   \mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\subset\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)
   \]
   corresponding to $\{1\}\subset\langle c\rangle\subset C_4$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Galois group is not $C_4$, or
   there is more than one quadratic subfield”; (ii) “$u$ does not
   satisfy $u^2+u-1=0$, or its quadratic norm is $+1$ just like
   the full-field norm of $\zeta$, or the discriminant is not $125$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a local ramification of
$\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the Gaussian splitting ledger, by a
cusp conductor, or by a Hilbert–Samuel length. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: A cyclic group of order $4$ has a unique subgroup of each dividing order. Correspondingly $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$ has a unique quadratic subfield.

The polynomial $T^2+T-1$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1$ and $\operatorname{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1$. Separately, the trace and norm of $\zeta$ in the degree-$4$ field are the negated cubic coefficient and constant term of $\Phi_5$, hence $-1$ and $1$; the cyclotomic discriminant formula gives $125$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify Gal with (Z/5Z)^x = C_4 and match the unique order-2 class -1 with conjugation.
Divide Phi_5 by zeta^2 to lock u^2+u-1=0 and its quadratic norm -1, then separately read the full-field norm of zeta as +1 and evaluate 5^{3}=125.

milestones.criterion: Proves [K:Q]=4, Gal=C_4, unique order-2 conjugation, and fixed field Q(sqrt(5)).
Computes u^2+u-1=0 with quadratic Trace(u)=-1 and Norm(u)=-1, keeps the separate full-field Trace(zeta)=-1 and Norm(zeta)=1, and obtains disc=125 and the three-level lattice.
Rejects a non-C_4 Galois group or extra quadratic, and refuses a wrong u-relation or discriminant.

commonErrors.description: Takes Gal(Q(zeta_5)/Q) to be other than C_4, or claims there is more than one quadratic subfield, or denies that conjugation is the unique order-2 element.
commonErrors.consequence: The required unique three-level lattice Q subset Q(sqrt(5)) subset Q(zeta_5) is lost.

commonErrors.description: Denies that u=zeta+zeta^{-1} satisfies u^2+u-1=0, gives its quadratic-field norm as +1 rather than -1, reports a discriminant other than 125, or corrupts the separate full-field Trace(zeta)=-1 or Norm(zeta)=1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities u^2+u-1=0, Norm_Q(u)=-1, Norm_K(zeta)=1, and disc=125 fail.

hintTree.content: The group $(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})^\times=\{1,2,3,4\}$ is cyclic of order $4$, generated by $2$. The unique order-$2$ class is $4\equiv-1$, i.e. conjugation.
Divide $\Phi_5(\zeta)=0$ by $\zeta^2$ to obtain $u^2+u-1=0$ for $u=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; its linear and constant coefficients give quadratic trace $-1$ and norm $-1$.
Keep the fields separate: read the full-field values $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\zeta=-1$ and $\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\zeta=1$ from $\Phi_5$, and evaluate $p^{p-2}=125$.

GA:020219.canonicalSolution:
The fifth cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_5(X)=X^4+X^3+X^2+X+1$ is
irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, so
\[
[K:\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(5)=4.
\]
The extension is Galois, and
\[
\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})^\times
=\{1,2,3,4\}\cong C_4,
\]
generated by $\sigma_2:\zeta\mapsto\zeta^2$. The unique element of
order $2$ is $\sigma_4=\sigma_{-1}$, which is complex conjugation
$c(\zeta)=\zeta^{-1}=\zeta^4$. Its fixed field is the maximal real
subfield
\[
K^{\langle c\rangle}=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}).
\]
The standard evaluation $2\cos(2\pi/5)=(-1+\sqrt{5})/2$ identifies
this field with $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Because $C_4$ has a unique
subgroup of order $2$, this is the unique quadratic subfield.
\[
\boxed{[K:\mathbb{Q}]=4,\;\mathrm{Gal}\cong C_4,\;
K^{\langle c\rangle}=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})}.
\]

Let $u=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$. Dividing $\zeta^4+\zeta^3+\zeta^2+\zeta+1=0$
by $\zeta^2$ produces
\[
\zeta^2+\zeta+1+\zeta^{-1}+\zeta^{-2}=0.
\]
The identity $\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}=u^2-2$ rearranges this to
$u^2-2+u+1=0$, i.e.
\[
u^2+u-1=0.
\]
This is the minimal polynomial of $u$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, so its two
roots have sum $-1$ and product $-1$. Hence
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1,\qquad
\operatorname{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1.
\]
These quadratic-field invariants must not be confused with the
following full-field invariants of $\zeta$.
From $\Phi_5(X)=X^4+X^3+X^2+X+1$ one reads
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta)=-1,\qquad
\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta)=1.
\]
The cyclotomic discriminant formula gives
\[
\operatorname{disc}(K)=(-1)^{(5-1)/2}5^{5-2}=5^3=125.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}(u)=-1;\;
\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta)=1,\;\operatorname{disc}=125}.
\]

The subgroup lattice $\{1\}\subset\langle c\rangle\subset C_4$ is
the unique chain of length three. By Galois correspondence the
field lattice is exactly
\[
\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\subset\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\subset\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)}.
\]

Sentence (i) destroys uniqueness of the order-$2$ subgroup or the
identification $\mathrm{Gal}\cong C_4$. Sentence (ii) corrupts the
quadratic relation for $u$ or the discriminant $125$.

The argument never replaces the assigned fifth-cyclotomic lattice
by the sibling local ramification of $\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by
the Gaussian splitting ledger, by a cusp conductor, or by a
Hilbert–Samuel length, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$ has degree $4$ and Galois group $C_4$. The unique order-$2$ element is conjugation, with fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Then $u=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$ satisfies $u^2+u-1=0$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}u=-1$ and $\operatorname{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)/\mathbb{Q}}u=-1$. Separately $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\zeta=-1$ and $\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\zeta=1$. Also $\operatorname{disc}=125$, and the lattice is exactly $\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})\subset\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$.
The Galois group of Q(zeta_5)/Q is not C_4, and there is more than one quadratic subfield. I do not accept the unique three-level lattice Q subset Q(sqrt(5)) subset Q(zeta_5).
The element u=zeta+zeta^{-1} does not satisfy u^2+u-1=0, and its quadratic norm is +1 just like Norm(zeta). The discriminant is not 125.

GA:020227.title: Compatible 2-adic partial sums of (-2)^k invert 3 with residues 1,3,3,11,11,43 though the real series diverges
GA:020227.objective: For x_n=sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-2)^k, prove x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3, the system is compatible modulo 2^n, 3x_n=1 mod 2^n, the residues for n=1..6 are [1,3,3,11,11,43], and the inverse limit is 1/3 in Z_2 even though the real series diverges.
GA:020227.statement:
Let $x_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-2)^k\in\mathbb{Z}$ for each integer
$n\ge 1$. View $x_n$ as a class in $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$.

1. Sum the finite geometric series to prove
   \[
   x_n=\frac{1-(-2)^n}{3}.
   \]
   Deduce the compatibility $x_{n+1}\equiv x_n\pmod{2^n}$ and the
   inversion identity
   \[
   3x_n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}.
   \]

2. Compute the residues of $x_n$ in $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ for
   $n=1,\dots,6$ and prove they are
   \[
   1,\;3,\;3,\;11,\;11,\;43.
   \]

3. Prove that $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ is a Cauchy sequence in the $2$-adic
   metric, hence defines an element of $\mathbb{Z}_2$, and that this
   element is the multiplicative inverse of $3$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
   Contrast only the real series $\sum_{k\ge 0}(-2)^k$, which
   diverges in $\mathbb{R}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the real series $\sum(-2)^k$ diverges,
   so there is no $2$-adic limit and $3$ is not invertible in
   $\mathbb{Z}_2$”; (ii) “the residues for $n=1,\dots,6$ are not
   $1,3,3,11,11,43$, or else $3x_n\not\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling quadric-cone DVR, by
an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, by an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic
point count, or by a twisted-cubic Hilbert polynomial. Do not
reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The geometric sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}r^k=(1-r^n)/(1-r)$ with $r=-2$ yields $x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3$. Then $3x_n=1-(-2)^n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}$.

If $x_{n+1}-x_n=(-2)^n$, then $v_2(x_{n+1}-x_n)=n$, so $(x_n)$ is $2$-adic Cauchy and its limit $x$ satisfies $3x=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$. The real series $\sum(-2)^k$ diverges because $\lvert-2\rvert=2>1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the geometric series with ratio -2, then read compatibility and inversion from the closed form.
Reduce the closed form modulo 2^n for n=1..6, then pass 3x_n=1 to the inverse limit.

milestones.criterion: Derives x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3, compatibility modulo 2^n, and 3x_n=1 mod 2^n.
Computes residues [1,3,3,11,11,43] and identifies the limit as 1/3 in Z_2.
Rejects treating real divergence as a missing 2-adic limit and refuses a corrupted residue list.

commonErrors.description: Treats divergence of the real series sum (-2)^k as proving that (x_n) has no 2-adic limit and that 3 is not a unit in Z_2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required inverse-limit value 1/3 in Z_2 and the inversion 3x=1 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports a residue list other than [1,3,3,11,11,43] for n=1..6, or claims 3x_n is not congruent to 1 modulo 2^n.
commonErrors.consequence: The required compatible residues and the identity 3x_n=1 mod 2^n fail.

hintTree.content: The ratio is $r=-2$, so $1-r=3$ and $x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3$.
Then $x_{n+1}-x_n=(-2)^n$, which is divisible by $2^n$, and $3x_n-1=-(-2)^n$.
Reduce $(1-(-2)^n)/3$ modulo $2^n$ for $n=1,\dots,6$. The real series is a contrast only.

GA:020227.canonicalSolution:
The finite geometric series with ratio $r=-2$ is
\[
x_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-2)^k=\frac{1-(-2)^n}{1-(-2)}=\frac{1-(-2)^n}{3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3}.
\]
The next partial sum differs by one extra term:
\[
x_{n+1}-x_n=(-2)^n.
\]
In particular $2^n$ divides $x_{n+1}-x_n$, so
$x_{n+1}\equiv x_n\pmod{2^n}$. Multiplying the closed form by $3$
gives
\[
3x_n=1-(-2)^n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n},
\]
because $(-2)^n=(-1)^n 2^n$.
\[
\boxed{x_{n+1}\equiv x_n\pmod{2^n},\quad 3x_n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}}.
\]

The residues in $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ are the unique
representatives of $(1-(-2)^n)/3$ in $\{0,\dots,2^n-1\}$:
\begin{align*}
n=1&\colon (1+2)/3=1,\\
n=2&\colon (1-4)/3=-1\equiv 3\pmod{4},\\
n=3&\colon (1+8)/3=3,\\
n=4&\colon (1-16)/3=-5\equiv 11\pmod{16},\\
n=5&\colon (1+32)/3=11,\\
n=6&\colon (1-64)/3=-21\equiv 43\pmod{64}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{[1,3,3,11,11,43]}.
\]

Compatibility makes $(x_n)$ an element $x\in\mathbb{Z}_2$. The
identities $3x_n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}$ pass to the limit, so $3x=1$
in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $x=1/3$. Equivalently $v_2(x_{n+1}-x_n)=n\to\infty$,
so the sequence is $2$-adic Cauchy. The real series
$\sum_{k\ge 0}(-2)^k$ is a contrast only: $\lvert-2\rvert=2>1$, so
the real partial sums are unbounded and do not converge in
$\mathbb{R}$. Divergence in $\mathbb{R}$ does not obstruct
convergence in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
\[
\boxed{x=1/3\in\mathbb{Z}_2;\quad\sum(-2)^k\text{ diverges in }\mathbb{R}}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses real divergence with the absence of a
$2$-adic limit and loses $3^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_2$. Sentence (ii)
corrupts the residue list or the inversion $3x_n\equiv 1$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $2$-adic inverse by the
sibling quadric-cone DVR, by an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, by
an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic point count, or by a twisted-cubic
Hilbert polynomial, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The geometric sum is $x_n=(1-(-2)^n)/3$. Then $x_{n+1}-x_n=(-2)^n$, so the system is compatible, and $3x_n\equiv 1\pmod{2^n}$. The residues for $n=1,\dots,6$ are $1,3,3,11,11,43$. The inverse limit is $1/3$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Real divergence of $\sum(-2)^k$ is a contrast only.
The real series sum (-2)^k diverges, so there is no 2-adic limit and 3 is not invertible in Z_2. I do not accept the limit 1/3 in Z_2.
The residues for n=1..6 are not [1,3,3,11,11,43], and 3x_n is not congruent to 1 modulo 2^n.
