GA:020320.title: The cusp k[t^2,t^3] is not normal, has conductor t^2 k[t] and delta 1, and is singular of tangent dimension 2
GA:020320.objective: For A=k[t^2,t^3]=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3), prove Frac(A)=k(t), t is integral but not in A, the integral closure is k[t], the conductor is t^2 k[t]=(t^2,t^3), k[t]/A has basis {t} so delta=1, dim A=1, and the tangent space at m has dimension 2.
GA:020320.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and write
\[
A=k[t^2,t^3]\cong k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3).
\]
Let $\mathfrak{m}=(t^2,t^3)$ be the maximal ideal at the origin.

1. Prove $\operatorname{Frac}(A)=k(t)$, that $t$ is integral over
   $A$, and that $t\notin A$. Deduce that the integral closure of
   $A$ in its fraction field is $k[t]$.

2. Prove that the conductor of $k[t]$ into $A$ is
   \[
   \mathfrak{c}=t^2k[t]=(t^2,t^3).
   \]
   Prove that $k[t]/A$ is one-dimensional on the basis $\{t\}$,
   so the delta invariant is $1$.

3. Prove $\dim A=1$ and that the tangent space
   $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$ has dimension $2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$t$ already lies in $A$, or $k[t]$
   is not the integral closure”; (ii) “the conductor is not
   $t^2k[t]$, or $\delta\ne 1$, or the tangent dimension is $1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a local ramification of
$\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the Gaussian splitting ledger, by the
fifth-cyclotomic lattice, or by a Hilbert–Samuel length. Do not
reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Every polynomial in $k[t]$ is uniquely $a+bt$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in k$, because $A$ contains $1$ and every power $t^n$ for $n\ge 2$. Thus $\{t\}$ is a $k$-basis of $k[t]/A$.
The relation $y^2-x^3$ lies in $\mathfrak{m}^2$ and has no linear part, so the images of $x$ and $y$ remain linearly independent in $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Exhibit t=t^3/t^2 in the fraction field and the monic equation X^2-t^2, then name k[t] as the finite normal closure.
Read the conductor from the condition f*t in A, and read tangent dimension from the missing linear part of y^2-x^3.

milestones.criterion: Proves Frac(A)=k(t), t integral not in A, and integral closure k[t].
Computes conductor t^2 k[t]=(t^2,t^3), basis {t} with delta=1, dim A=1, and tangent dim 2.
Rejects t in A or a wrong closure, and refuses a wrong conductor, delta, or regular tangent space.

commonErrors.description: Claims that t already lies in A, or that the integral closure of A is not k[t].
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities t notin A and closure k[t] are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports a conductor other than t^2 k[t]=(t^2,t^3), or a delta other than 1, or a tangent dimension 1 at m.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities conductor=(t^2,t^3), delta=1, and tangent dim 2 fail.

hintTree.content: $t=t^3/t^2$ lies in $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, and $t$ satisfies the monic equation $X^2-t^2=0$ over $A$.
An element $f\in A$ satisfies $f\cdot t\in A$ if and only if $f\in t^2k[t]$. As an $A$-ideal this is $(t^2,t^3)$.
The only monomial missing from $A$ is $t$, so $\delta=1$. The cusp equation has no linear term, so the tangent space is $2$-dimensional.

GA:020320.canonicalSolution:
The $k$-algebra $A=k[t^2,t^3]$ is the image of
$k[x,y]\twoheadrightarrow k[t]$ along $x\mapsto t^2$, $y\mapsto t^3$,
with kernel $(y^2-x^3)$. In particular $t=t^3/t^2$ lies in
$\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, so
\[
\operatorname{Frac}(A)=k(t).
\]
The monic polynomial $X^2-t^2\in A[X]$ annihilates $t$, hence $t$
is integral over $A$. The $k$-basis of $A$ is
$\{1,t^2,t^3,t^4,\ldots\}$, so the monomial $t$ does not lie in
$A$. The polynomial ring $k[t]$ is integrally closed and finite
over $A$ (generated by the single integral element $t$), therefore
\[
\overline{A}=k[t].
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Frac}(A)=k(t),\;t\notin A,\;\overline{A}=k[t]}.
\]

Write $\mathfrak{c}=(A:k[t])=\{a\in A:a\cdot k[t]\subseteq A\}$.
Every element of $k[t]$ is uniquely $a+bt$ with $a\in A$ and
$b\in k$, so $f\in\mathfrak{c}$ if and only if $f\cdot t\in A$.
If $f=\sum_{n\ne 1}c_nt^n$, the product $ft$ introduces a $t^1$
coefficient precisely from the constant term of $f$. Thus $f$ must
be divisible by $t^2$, i.e.
\[
\mathfrak{c}=t^2k[t].
\]
As an ideal of $A$ (or of $k[t]$) one has $t^2k[t]=(t^2,t^3)$,
because $t^2\cdot t=t^3$. The same decomposition
$k[t]=A\oplus k\cdot t$ shows that $k[t]/A$ has $k$-basis $\{t\}$,
so the delta invariant is
\[
\delta=\dim_k k[t]/A=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathfrak{c}=t^2k[t]=(t^2,t^3),\;\delta=1}.
\]

The ring $A$ is a domain of Krull dimension $1$ (it is finite over
$k[t^2]\cong k[x]$). At the origin $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)=(t^2,t^3)$,
the relation $y^2-x^3$ has vanishing linear part, so the images of
$x$ and $y$ in $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$ remain linearly
independent and
\[
\dim_k\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2=2.
\]
In particular $A_{\mathfrak{m}}$ is not regular.
\[
\boxed{\dim A=1,\;\dim\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) either places $t$ in $A$ or names the wrong
normalization. Sentence (ii) corrupts the conductor, the value
$\delta=1$, or the tangent dimension.

The argument never replaces the assigned cusp conductor by the
sibling local ramification of $\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the
Gaussian splitting ledger, by the fifth-cyclotomic lattice, or by
a Hilbert–Samuel length, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The cusp $A=k[t^2,t^3]$ has fraction field $k(t)$. The parameter $t$ is integral and does not lie in $A$, so the integral closure is $k[t]$. The conductor is $t^2k[t]=(t^2,t^3)$, $k[t]/A$ has basis $\{t\}$ hence $\delta=1$, $\dim A=1$, and $\dim\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2=2$.
The parameter t already lies in A, and k[t] is not the integral closure. I do not accept t notin A or closure k[t].
The conductor is not t^2 k[t]=(t^2,t^3), delta is not 1, and the tangent dimension at m is 1.

GA:020421.title: The local ring k[x,y]_(x,y) has Hilbert-Samuel length n(n+1)/2, associated graded k[x,y], and multiplicity 1
GA:020421.objective: For R=k[x,y]_(x,y), prove length(R/m^n)=n(n+1)/2, dim m^n/m^{n+1}=n+1, gr_m(R)=k[x,y], dim R=2, multiplicity 1, and the sample values length(R/m^4)=10 and dim m^4/m^5=5.
GA:020421.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$, and let
$\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)R$.

1. Prove that
   \[
   \operatorname{length}_R(R/\mathfrak{m}^n)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
   \]
   and that
   \[
   \dim_k\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}=n+1.
   \]

2. Identify the associated graded ring $\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)$
   with $k[x,y]$, and deduce $\dim R=2$ with Hilbert–Samuel
   multiplicity $1$.

3. Evaluate the sample values
   \[
   \operatorname{length}_R(R/\mathfrak{m}^4)=10,\qquad
   \dim_k\mathfrak{m}^4/\mathfrak{m}^5=5.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the length is $n+1$ or $n^2$ rather
   than $n(n+1)/2$”; (ii) “the multiplicity is not $1$, or the
   sample values at $n=4$ are not $10$ and $5$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a local ramification of
$\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by the Gaussian splitting ledger, by the
fifth-cyclotomic lattice, or by a cusp conductor. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Localization at $(x,y)$ does not change associated graded pieces: $\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}$ has $k$-basis the monomials of degree $n$, hence dimension $n+1$. Summing $1+2+\cdots+n$ yields length $n(n+1)/2$.
The Hilbert–Samuel polynomial $n(n+1)/2=\frac12 n^2+\frac12 n$ has degree $2$ and leading coefficient $1/2=e/2!$, so $e=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Count monomials of degree less than n to lock the triangular length, then read the degree-n piece as dimension n+1.
Match the leading coefficient of n(n+1)/2 against e/2! and specialize at n=4.

milestones.criterion: Proves length(R/m^n)=n(n+1)/2, dim m^n/m^{n+1}=n+1, gr=k[x,y], dim R=2, and multiplicity 1.
Evaluates length(R/m^4)=10 and dim m^4/m^5=5.
Rejects a wrong length formula and refuses a multiplicity other than 1 or wrong n=4 samples.

commonErrors.description: Reports length(R/m^n) as n+1 or n^2 rather than n(n+1)/2, or reports dim m^n/m^{n+1} other than n+1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities length=n(n+1)/2 and dim m^n/m^{n+1}=n+1 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports a multiplicity other than 1, or evaluates length(R/m^4) other than 10, or dim m^4/m^5 other than 5.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities multiplicity 1, length(R/m^4)=10, and dim m^4/m^5=5 fail.

hintTree.content: A $k$-basis of $R/\mathfrak{m}^n$ is the monomials $x^ay^b$ with $a+b<n$. Count them by degree.
The degree-$n$ piece is spanned by $x^n,x^{n-1}y,\ldots,y^n$, hence has dimension $n+1$.
At $n=4$ one obtains $4\cdot 5/2=10$ and $4+1=5$. The leading term $\frac12 n^2$ forces multiplicity $1$.

GA:020421.canonicalSolution:
Write $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)R$. Localization at the maximal ideal
$(x,y)$ of $k[x,y]$ does not change the associated graded pieces of
the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic filtration, so
\[
R/\mathfrak{m}^n\cong_k k[x,y]/(x,y)^n
\]
has $k$-basis the monomials $x^ay^b$ of total degree strictly less
than $n$. Grouping by degree $d=0,1,\ldots,n-1$ produces $d+1$
monomials in each degree, hence
\[
\operatorname{length}_R(R/\mathfrak{m}^n)
=\sum_{d=0}^{n-1}(d+1)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\]
The successive quotient $\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}$ is
spanned by the degree-$n$ monomials $x^n,x^{n-1}y,\ldots,y^n$, so
\[
\dim_k\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}=n+1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{length}(R/\mathfrak{m}^n)=n(n+1)/2,\;
\dim\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}=n+1}.
\]

These graded pieces assemble as
\[
\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)
=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}
\cong k[x,y],
\]
the standard graded polynomial ring on two variables. In particular
$\dim R=\dim\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)=2$, and $x,y$ form a
regular system of parameters. The Hilbert–Samuel polynomial is
already equal to the function for every $n\ge 1$:
\[
\chi(n)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=\frac12 n^2+\frac12 n.
\]
The leading coefficient is $e(R)/2!$, so $e(R)=1$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)=k[x,y],\;\dim R=2,\;e(R)=1}.
\]

Specializing at $n=4$ gives
\[
\operatorname{length}_R(R/\mathfrak{m}^4)=\frac{4\cdot 5}{2}=10,
\qquad
\dim_k\mathfrak{m}^4/\mathfrak{m}^5=4+1=5.
\]
\[
\boxed{n=4:\;\operatorname{length}=10,\;\dim\mathfrak{m}^4/\mathfrak{m}^5=5}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the triangular count $n(n+1)/2$ by $n+1$ or
$n^2$. Sentence (ii) corrupts the multiplicity or the two sample
values at $n=4$.

The argument never replaces the assigned Hilbert–Samuel computation
by the sibling local ramification of $\mathbb{Q}_3(\sqrt{3})$, by
the Gaussian splitting ledger, by the fifth-cyclotomic lattice, or
by a cusp conductor, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: For $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ the monomial count gives $\operatorname{length}(R/\mathfrak{m}^n)=n(n+1)/2$ and $\dim\mathfrak{m}^n/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}=n+1$. The associated graded ring is $k[x,y]$, so $\dim R=2$ and the multiplicity is $1$. At $n=4$ the length is $10$ and $\dim\mathfrak{m}^4/\mathfrak{m}^5=5$.
The length of R/m^n is n+1 or n^2 rather than n(n+1)/2, and dim m^n/m^{n+1} is not n+1.
The multiplicity is not 1, length(R/m^4) is not 10, and dim m^4/m^5 is not 5.

GA:020422.title: In k[x,y]_(x,y) the pair (y),(y-x^2) has colength 2 on the basis 1,x while the transverse line x=0 has length 1
GA:020422.objective: In R=k[x,y]_(x,y), prove R/(y,y-x^2) isomorphic to k[x]_(x)/(x^2) with k-basis 1,x and length 2, and that the transverse pair (y),(x) has length 1.
GA:020422.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ be the localization
of the polynomial ring at the maximal ideal $(x,y)$. Write
$I=(y)$ and $J=(y-x^2)$ for the ideals of the $x$-axis and of the
parabola $y=x^2$.

1. Prove $I+J=(x^2,y)$ and construct a $k$-algebra isomorphism
   \[
   R/(I+J)\;\simeq\;k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2).
   \]

2. Prove that $k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$ has $k$-basis $\{1,x\}$, hence
   \[
   \operatorname{length}_R\bigl(R/(I+J)\bigr)=2.
   \]

3. Let $K=(x)$ be the ideal of the transverse line $x=0$. Prove
   $I+K=(x,y)$ and
   \[
   \operatorname{length}_R\bigl(R/(I+K)\bigr)=1.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the parabola is transverse to the
   $x$-axis, so the colength is $1$ and the quotient is $k$”;
   (ii) “after localizing at $(x,y)$ the quotient
   $k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$ acquires negative powers of $x$ and has
   infinite length.”

Do not replace the calculation by assembling projectivity from
local freeness and finite presentation, by a Tor computation, or
by a Nullstellensatz census. Do not reopen, import, or execute any
of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The relations $y\equiv 0$ and $y\equiv x^2$ force $x^2\equiv 0$, so $I+J=(x^2,y)$. Killing $y$ and then localizing at $(x)$ yields $R/(x^2,y)\simeq k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$.
Every element of $k[x]_{(x)}$ is a unit times a polynomial, and units of $k[x]_{(x)}$ are regular at $0$, so modulo $x^2$ one has a unique writing $a+bx$ with $a,b\in k$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce modulo y first, then modulo x^2, and compare the resulting artinian ring to k[x]_(x)/(x^2).
Read length as dim_k and test the transverse line x=0 as a one-dimensional contrast.

milestones.criterion: Identifies I+J=(x^2,y) and the isomorphism R/(I+J) isomorphic to k[x]_(x)/(x^2) with k-basis {1,x}.
Computes length 2 for the tangent pair and length 1 for the transverse pair (y),(x).
Rejects a transverse-length-1 reading of the parabola and refuses negative powers in the localized quotient.

commonErrors.description: Treats V(y-x^2) as transverse to the x-axis and reports colength 1 with quotient k.
commonErrors.consequence: The required isomorphism to k[x]_(x)/(x^2), the basis {1,x}, and length 2 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that localizing at (x,y) introduces negative powers of x into k[x]_(x)/(x^2), so the length is infinite.
commonErrors.consequence: The required finite basis {1,x} and the identity length=2 fail.

hintTree.content: From $y\in I+J$ and $y-x^2\in I+J$ one gets $x^2\in I+J$, hence $I+J=(x^2,y)$.
Any $f\in k[x,y]$ reduces modulo $(x^2,y)$ to $a+bx$. Localization at $(x,y)$ does not introduce $x^{-1}$, because $x$ is nilpotent in the quotient.
The transverse sum $(y)+(x)=(x,y)$ has residue field $k$, so length $1$.

GA:020422.canonicalSolution:
In $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ one has $y\in I$ and $y-x^2\in J$, so
\[
x^2=y-(y-x^2)\in I+J.
\]
Thus $(x^2,y)\subseteq I+J$. The reverse inclusion is immediate
because $y-x^2\in(x^2,y)$, so $I+J=(x^2,y)$.
The quotient $k[x,y]/(x^2,y)$ is $k[x]/(x^2)$. Localizing at the
image of $(x,y)$, which is the ideal $(x)$ of $k[x]/(x^2)$, gives
\[
R/(I+J)\;\simeq\;k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2).
\]
\[
\boxed{I+J=(x^2,y),\quad R/(I+J)\simeq k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)}.
\]

An arbitrary element of $k[x]_{(x)}$ has the form $f/u$ with
$f\in k[x]$ and $u(0)\ne 0$. Write
$f=a+bx+x^2g$ and $u=u_0+u_1x+x^2h$, where $u_0\ne0$. Modulo
$x^2$, the denominator has the explicit inverse
\[
u^{-1}\equiv u_0^{-1}-u_1u_0^{-2}x\pmod{x^2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac{f}{u}\equiv
au_0^{-1}+\bigl(bu_0^{-1}-au_1u_0^{-2}\bigr)x\pmod{x^2},
\]
so $\{1,x\}$ spans $k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$ over $k$. The two classes
are linearly independent because a relation $a+bx\in(x^2)$ in
$k[x]_{(x)}$ clears denominators to a polynomial identity
$v(a+bx)=x^2 h$ with $v(0)\ne 0$, forcing $a=b=0$. Therefore
\[
\dim_k k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)=2,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{length}_R\bigl(R/(I+J)\bigr)=2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{basis }\{1,x\},\quad\operatorname{length}=2}.
\]

For the transverse line $K=(x)$ one has $I+K=(x,y)$, so
$R/(I+K)$ is the residue field $k$ and
\[
\operatorname{length}_R\bigl(R/(I+K)\bigr)=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{transverse }x=0\text{ has length }1}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats the parabola as a transverse line and reports
the false colength $1$. Sentence (ii) confuses localization at
$(x)$ with passage to the fraction field and invents an infinite
basis of negative powers.

The argument never replaces the assigned colength computation by
a projectivity criterion from local freeness, by a Tor comparison,
or by a Nullstellensatz census, and it does not open any of the
six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: In $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ one has $I+J=(x^2,y)$ and $R/(I+J)\simeq k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$, with $k$-basis $\{1,x\}$ and length $2$. The transverse pair $(y),(x)$ has quotient $k$ and length $1$. Localization does not create negative powers.
The parabola is transverse to the x-axis, so the colength is 1 and the quotient is k. I do not accept length 2 or the basis 1,x.
After localizing at (x,y) the quotient k[x]_(x)/(x^2) acquires negative powers of x and has infinite length.

GA:020428.title: Localizing the quadric cone k[x,y,z]/(xz-y^2) at (x,y) is the DVR k(z)[y]_(y) with v(x)=2
GA:020428.objective: For A=k[x,y,z]/(xz-y^2) and p=(x,y), prove z is a unit at p, x=y^2/z in A_p, A_p=k(z)[y]_(y) is a DVR of dimension 1 with uniformizer y, residue field k(z), completion k(z)[[y]], valuations v(y)=1, v(x)=2, v(z)=0, and p A_p=(y).
GA:020428.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let
\[
A=k[x,y,z]/(xz-y^2),\qquad \mathfrak{p}=(x,y)\subset A.
\]

1. Prove that $z\notin\mathfrak{p}$, so $z$ is a unit in the local
   ring $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$, and that the cone relation rearranges to
   \[
   x=\frac{y^2}{z}\qquad\text{in }A_{\mathfrak{p}}.
   \]

2. Prove that there is a $k$-algebra identification
   \[
   A_{\mathfrak{p}}\cong k(z)[y]_{(y)}
   \]
   with a discrete valuation ring of Krull dimension $1$,
   uniformizer $y$, residue field $k(z)$, and completion
   $k(z)[\![y]\!]$.

3. Prove the valuations
   \[
   v(y)=1,\qquad v(x)=2,\qquad v(z)=0
   \]
   and the identity $\mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}}=(y)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\mathfrak{p}$ is not height one, or
   $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is not a DVR”; (ii) “the uniformizer is $x$
   rather than $y$, so $v(x)=1$ or $v(z)\ne 0$, and
   $\mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is not $(y)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $2$-adic inverse of
$3$, by an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, by an $\mathbb{F}_5$
elliptic point count, or by a twisted-cubic Hilbert polynomial.
Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake
seeds.
permittedResults: If $R=K[t]_{(t)}$ for a field $K$, then $R$ is a DVR of dimension $1$ with uniformizer $t$, residue field $K$, and completion $K[\![t]\!]$.
In $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ one has $(x,y)=(y^2 z^{-1},y)=(y)$ because $z$ is a unit, so $v(y)=1$, $v(x)=2$, and $v(z)=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Invert z first, substitute x=y^2/z, and recognize the localization of k(z)[y] at (y).
Read the maximal ideal as (y) and compute v(x)=v(y^2/z)=2 from the uniformizer.

milestones.criterion: Proves z is a unit at p, x=y^2/z, and A_p=k(z)[y]_(y) is a DVR of dimension 1.
Identifies uniformizer y, residue field k(z), completion k(z)[[y]], valuations v(y)=1, v(x)=2, v(z)=0, and p A_p=(y).
Rejects denying the DVR and refuses a wrong uniformizer or corrupted valuations.

commonErrors.description: Claims that p=(x,y) is not height one, or that A_p is not a discrete valuation ring of dimension 1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identification A_p=k(z)[y]_(y) as a DVR of dimension 1 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes the uniformizer to be x rather than y, reports v(x)=1 or v(z)≠0, or claims p A_p is not (y).
commonErrors.consequence: The required valuations v(y)=1, v(x)=2, v(z)=0 and the identity p A_p=(y) fail.

hintTree.content: $A/\mathfrak{p}\cong k[z]$, so $z\notin\mathfrak{p}$ and $z$ is a unit in $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$. Then $x=y^2 z^{-1}$.
Sending $y$ to the indeterminate of $k(z)[Y]$ induces $A_{\mathfrak{p}}\cong k(z)[Y]_{(Y)}$.
The maximal ideal is $(y)$, so $v(y)=1$ and $v(x)=v(y^2/z)=2$.

GA:020428.canonicalSolution:
The quotient by $\mathfrak{p}=(x,y)$ is
\[
A/\mathfrak{p}\cong k[z],
\]
a domain, so $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime and $z\notin\mathfrak{p}$.
Thus $z$ is a unit in $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$. The defining relation
$xz=y^2$ may be rewritten
\[
x=y^2 z^{-1}\qquad\text{in }A_{\mathfrak{p}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{z\in A_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times,\quad x=y^2/z}.
\]

Every element of $A$ is the class of a polynomial in $x,y,z$. After
localizing at $\mathfrak{p}$ one may invert every polynomial whose
image in $k[z]$ is nonzero, hence invert every nonzero element of
$k[z]$ and then pass to the fraction field $k(z)$. Substituting
$x=y^2 z^{-1}$ leaves only the coordinate $y$ over $k(z)$. The
elements of $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ are therefore rational functions in
$y$ with coefficients in $k(z)$ whose denominators are units at
$y=0$. This is the identification
\[
A_{\mathfrak{p}}\cong k(z)[y]_{(y)}.
\]
The ring $k(z)[y]_{(y)}$ is the localization of a PID at a
principal prime, hence a discrete valuation ring of Krull
dimension $1$, with uniformizer $y$, residue field $k(z)$, and
completion $k(z)[\![y]\!]$.
\[
\boxed{A_{\mathfrak{p}}\cong k(z)[y]_{(y)}\text{ DVR, dim }1,\ \widehat{A_{\mathfrak{p}}}=k(z)[\![y]\!]}.
\]

The maximal ideal is $(y)$. Because $z$ is a unit,
\[
\mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}}=(x,y)=(y^2 z^{-1},y)=(y).
\]
The discrete valuation therefore satisfies
\[
v(y)=1,\qquad v(x)=v(y^2 z^{-1})=2,\qquad v(z)=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{v(y)=1,\ v(x)=2,\ v(z)=0,\ \mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}}=(y)}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies that $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a height-one DVR.
Sentence (ii) takes $x$ as uniformizer or corrupts the valuations.

The argument never replaces the assigned quadric-cone localization
by the sibling $2$-adic inverse, by an $A_2$-quiver Ext
computation, by an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic point count, or by a
twisted-cubic Hilbert polynomial, and it does not open any of the
six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: In $A=k[x,y,z]/(xz-y^2)$ the prime $\mathfrak{p}=(x,y)$ does not contain $z$, so $x=y^2/z$ in $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ and $A_{\mathfrak{p}}\cong k(z)[y]_{(y)}$ is a DVR of dimension $1$ with uniformizer $y$, residue field $k(z)$, and completion $k(z)[\![y]\!]$. Then $v(y)=1$, $v(x)=2$, $v(z)=0$, and $\mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}}=(y)$.
The prime p=(x,y) is not height one, and A_p is not a DVR of dimension 1. I do not accept A_p=k(z)[y]_(y).
The uniformizer is x rather than y, so v(x)=1 or v(z) is not 0, and p A_p is not (y).

GA:020523.title: Koszul homology of (x,xy) on k[x,y] is H0=R/(x), H1=R/(x), H2=0, so the sequence is not regular
GA:020523.objective: For R=k[x,y] and the sequence (x,xy), compute the Koszul differentials, prove H0=R/(x), H2=0, cycles R(-y,1), boundaries xR(-y,1), H1=R/(x), and conclude the sequence is not regular.
GA:020523.statement:
Let $R=k[x,y]$ over a field $k$, and consider the length-two
sequence $(x,xy)$. Write $K_\bullet(x,xy)$ for the Koszul complex
\[
0\longrightarrow R\xrightarrow{d_2} R^{\oplus 2}\xrightarrow{d_1} R\longrightarrow 0
\]
with
\[
d_1(a,b)=ax+bxy,\qquad d_2(c)=(-xyc,\,xc).
\]

1. Check $d_1\circ d_2=0$. Identify
   \[
   H_0\bigl(K_\bullet(x,xy)\bigr)=R/(x)
   \]
   and prove $H_2=0$.

2. Prove that the $1$-cycles are the rank-one free module
   $R\cdot(-y,1)$ and that the $1$-boundaries are
   $xR\cdot(-y,1)$. Conclude
   \[
   H_1\bigl(K_\bullet(x,xy)\bigr)\;\simeq\;R/(x).
   \]

3. Deduce that $(x,xy)$ is not a regular sequence on $R$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$(x,xy)$ is regular, so Koszul
   homology vanishes in positive degrees”; (ii) “$H_0=0$, or the
   cycles are not the rank-one module $R\cdot(-y,1)$.”

From $ax+bxy=0$ factor $x(a+by)=0$. Since $R$ is a domain, $a=-by$.

GA:020523.canonicalSolution:
First,
\[
d_1\bigl(d_2(c)\bigr)=d_1(-xyc,\,xc)=-xyc\cdot x+xc\cdot xy=0,
\]
so $K_\bullet$ is a complex. The cokernel of $d_1$ is
$R/(x,xy)$. Since $xy\in(x)$ one has $(x,xy)=(x)$, hence
\[
H_0\bigl(K_\bullet(x,xy)\bigr)=R/(x).
\]
If $d_2(c)=0$ then $xc=0$ and $xyc=0$. The ring $R=k[x,y]$ is a
domain, so $c=0$. Thus $H_2=0$.
\[
\boxed{H_0=R/(x),\quad H_2=0}.
\]

A pair $(a,b)$ lies in $\ker d_1$ precisely when
$ax+bxy=0$, i.e. $x(a+by)=0$. Again $R$ is a domain, so
$a+by=0$ and $a=-by$. Therefore
\[
\ker d_1=\bigl\{(-by,b):b\in R\bigr\}=R\cdot(-y,1).
\]
The image of $d_2$ is
\[
\operatorname{im}d_2=\bigl\{(-xyc,xc):c\in R\bigr\}=xR\cdot(-y,1).
\]
The evident map $R\to\ker d_1$, $b\mapsto b(-y,1)$, is an
isomorphism sending $(x)$ onto the boundaries, so
\[
H_1\bigl(K_\bullet(x,xy)\bigr)\;\simeq\;R/(x).
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{cycles }R(-y,1),\ \text{boundaries }xR(-y,1),\ H_1=R/(x)}.
\]

The element $x$ is a nonzerodivisor on $R$. In the quotient
$R/(x)\simeq k[y]$ the image of $xy$ is zero, and $0$ is a
zerodivisor on a nonzero ring. Hence $(x,xy)$ is not a regular
sequence. Equivalently, $H_1\ne 0$ already forbids regularity.
\[
\boxed{(x,xy)\text{ is not regular}}.
\]

Sentence (i) declares the sequence regular and erases $H_1$.
Sentence (ii) corrupts $H_0$ or the cycle module $R\cdot(-y,1)$.

Tor comparison across two resolutions, by a tangent colength, or

existing intake seeds.

GA:020524.title: The Cech tail H^1_(x)(k[x])=R_x/R has basis x^{-1},x^{-2},... is not finitely generated, and x kills the first pole
GA:020524.objective: For R=k[x] and the Cech complex 0->R->R_x, prove H^0=0, H^1=R_x/R with basis x^{-1},x^{-2},..., graded 1 in negative degrees and 0 in nonnegative degrees, that x kills x^{-1} and shifts the tail, and that H^1 is not finitely generated.
GA:020524.statement:
Let $R=k[x]$ over a field $k$, graded by $\deg x=1$. Let
$R_x=k[x,x^{-1}]$ be the localization at the powers of $x$, and
consider the Cech complex of the ideal $(x)$
\[
0\longrightarrow R\longrightarrow R_x\longrightarrow 0.
\]

1. Prove $H^0_{(x)}(R)=0$ and
   \[
   H^1_{(x)}(R)=R_x/R,
   \]
   with $k$-basis $\{x^{-1},x^{-2},x^{-3},\ldots\}$.

2. Prove that the graded pieces satisfy
   $\dim_k H^1_{(x)}(R)_d=1$ for every $d<0$ and
   $H^1_{(x)}(R)_d=0$ for every $d\ge 0$.

3. Prove that multiplication by $x$ sends $x^{-1}$ to $0$ in
   $H^1$ and shifts the tail $x\cdot x^{-n}=x^{-n+1}$. Conclude
   that $H^1_{(x)}(R)$ is not a finitely generated $R$-module.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the map $R\to R_x$ fails to be
   injective, so $H^0\ne 0$, or else $H^1=0$”; (ii) “$H^1$ is
   generated by the single class of $x^{-1}$, hence finitely
   generated.”

Do not replace the calculation by a Tor comparison, by the sibling
Koszul computation of $(x,xy)$, or by a tangent colength. Do not
reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: A domain injects into every localization at a multiplicative set not containing $0$. Thus $H^0_{(x)}(R)=\ker(R\to R_x)=0$ and $H^1_{(x)}(R)=R_x/R$.
If a finitely generated graded $R$-module were spanned by finitely many negative powers $x^{-1},\ldots,x^{-N}$, multiplication by elements of $R$ could not produce $x^{-N-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare the Laurent and polynomial monomial bases, then read cohomology as the negative tail.
Use the shift x·x^{-n}=x^{-n+1} to show a finite set of poles cannot reach a deeper pole.

milestones.criterion: Proves H0=0 and H1=R_x/R with basis x^{-1},x^{-2},... and the graded vanishing in nonnegative degrees.
Shows that x kills x^{-1}, shifts the tail, and that H1 is not a finitely generated R-module.
Rejects a nonzero H0 or vanishing H1 and refuses finite generation by a single pole.

commonErrors.description: Claims the localization map R->R_x is not injective, so H0 is nonzero, or else claims H1=0.

commonErrors.description: Claims that H1 is generated by the single class of x^{-1}, hence is a finitely generated R-module.
commonErrors.consequence: The required infinite basis x^{-1},x^{-2},... and the non-finite-generation statement fail.

hintTree.content: $R=k[x]$ is a domain, so $R\to R_x$ is injective and $H^0=0$. The cokernel is $R_x/R$.
Laurent monomials of nonnegative degree lie in $R$. The remaining basis is $x^{-1},x^{-2},\ldots$.
$x\cdot x^{-1}=1\in R$, hence $0$ in the quotient. A finite set of poles cannot generate a deeper pole.

GA:020524.canonicalSolution:
The ring $R=k[x]$ is a domain and $x\ne 0$, so the canonical map
$R\to R_x$ is injective. Therefore
\[
H^0_{(x)}(R)=\ker(R\to R_x)=0
\]
and
\[
H^1_{(x)}(R)=\operatorname{coker}(R\to R_x)=R_x/R.
\]
As a $k$-vector space, $R_x=k[x,x^{-1}]$ has basis
$\{x^d:d\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ while $R$ is spanned by
$\{x^d:d\ge 0\}$. The classes of the negative powers are
linearly independent in the quotient, so
\[
\bigl\{x^{-1},x^{-2},x^{-3},\ldots\bigr\}
\]
is a $k$-basis of $H^1_{(x)}(R)$.
\[
\boxed{H^0=0,\quad H^1=R_x/R,\quad\text{basis }x^{-1},x^{-2},\ldots}.
\]

With $\deg x=1$, the degree-$d$ piece of $R_x/R$ is $k\cdot x^d$
when $d<0$ and is zero when $d\ge 0$. Thus
\[
\dim_k H^1_{(x)}(R)_d=
\begin{cases}
1&d<0,\\
0&d\ge 0.
\end{cases}
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{graded }1\text{ in negative degrees, }0\text{ in nonnegative degrees}}.
\]

Multiplication by $x$ sends $x^{-1}$ to $1\in R$, which is zero
in $R_x/R$, and sends $x^{-n}$ to $x^{-n+1}$. In particular $x$
kills the first pole and shifts the rest of the tail toward
degree $0$.

Suppose $H^1_{(x)}(R)$ were generated by finitely many elements.
Clearing denominators, those generators involve only finitely
many poles, say depths at most $N$. Every $R$-linear combination
is then a $k[x]$-combination of $x^{-1},\ldots,x^{-N}$, which
cannot produce the class of $x^{-N-1}$. Hence $H^1_{(x)}(R)$ is
not a finitely generated $R$-module.
\[
\boxed{x\text{ kills }x^{-1}\text{ and shifts the tail; not finitely generated}}.
\]

Sentence (i) corrupts injectivity of $R\to R_x$ or erases $H^1$.
Sentence (ii) claims that the single class $x^{-1}$ generates the
whole tail.

The argument never replaces the assigned Cech tail by a Tor
comparison, by the sibling Koszul complex of $(x,xy)$, or by a
tangent colength, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Cech complex $0\to R\to R_x$ has $H^0=0$ and $H^1=R_x/R$, with $k$-basis $x^{-1},x^{-2},\ldots$. Graded pieces are one-dimensional in every negative degree and zero in nonnegative degrees. Multiplication by $x$ kills $x^{-1}$ and shifts the tail, so $H^1$ is not finitely generated.
The map R->R_x fails to be injective, so H0 is nonzero, or else H1=0. I do not accept H0=0 and H1=R_x/R.
H1 is generated by the single class of x^{-1}, hence finitely generated. I do not accept the infinite tail x^{-1},x^{-2},....

GA:020529.title: The A2 quiver has Ext^1(S1,S2)=k nonsplit while Ext^1(S2,S1)=0 because S2 is projective
GA:020529.objective: For the quiver 1->2, identify simples and projectives P1=(k->k id) and P2=S2, resolve S1 by 0->P2->P1->S1, prove Ext^1(S1,S2)=k is nonsplit, Ext^1(S2,S1)=0, higher Ext vanish, cross Hom vanish, and End=k.
GA:020529.statement:
Let $Q$ be the $A_2$ quiver $1\to 2$ and let $k$ be a field.
Write $S_1,S_2$ for the simple representations supported at the
two vertices, and write $P_1,P_2$ for the indecomposable
projectives.

1. Prove $P_1=(k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}k)$ and $P_2=S_2$, and
   exhibit a short exact sequence
   \[
   0\to P_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0.
   \]

2. Prove $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)\cong k$ and that the
   displayed extension is nonsplit. Prove
   $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)=0$ because $S_2$ is projective,
   and that all higher $\operatorname{Ext}$ groups among
   $\{S_1,S_2\}$ vanish.

3. Prove the cross Hom-spaces vanish,
   $\operatorname{Hom}(S_1,S_2)=\operatorname{Hom}(S_2,S_1)=0$,
   while $\operatorname{End}(S_1)=\operatorname{End}(S_2)=k$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\operatorname{Ext}^1$ is symmetric,
   so $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)\cong\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)$,
   or both groups vanish”; (ii) “$S_2$ is not projective, or the
   extension $0\to S_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0$ splits.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $2$-adic inverse of
$3$, by a quadric-cone DVR, by an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic point
count, or by a twisted-cubic Hilbert polynomial. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,S_2)$ to $0\to P_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0$ yields $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_1,S_2)\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_2,S_2)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(P_1,S_2)=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(P_2,S_2)=k$, so $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)\cong k$.

A projective module has vanishing $\operatorname{Ext}^{i\ge 1}$. Here $S_2=P_2$ is projective, so $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)=0$. The displayed resolution also forces $\operatorname{Ext}^{i\ge 2}(S_1,-)=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the path-basis projectives, then take the kernel of P1->S1 to obtain the length-one resolution.
Compute Hom(P1,S2)=0 and Hom(P2,S2)=k, then invoke projectivity of S2=P2 for the opposite Ext.

milestones.criterion: Identifies P1=(k->k id), P2=S2, and the resolution 0->P2->P1->S1->0.
Proves Ext^1(S1,S2)=k nonsplit, Ext^1(S2,S1)=0, higher Ext vanish, cross Hom=0, and End=k.
Rejects Ext^1 symmetry and refuses a split extension or a non-projective S2.

commonErrors.description: Claims Ext^1(S1,S2) is isomorphic to Ext^1(S2,S1), or that both Ext^1 groups vanish.
commonErrors.consequence: The required asymmetry Ext^1(S1,S2)=k and Ext^1(S2,S1)=0 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Denies that S2 is projective, or claims that the extension 0->S2->P1->S1->0 splits.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities P2=S2, Ext^1(S2,S1)=0, and the nonsplit class generating Ext^1(S1,S2) fail.

hintTree.content: $P_1$ evaluated at the two vertices is $kQ e_1$, which is $k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}k$. The kernel of $P_1\to S_1$ is $S_2=P_2$.
A morphism $P_1\to S_2$ must vanish at vertex $1$, hence vanish at vertex $2$ by the identity arrow.
Cross Hom of distinct simples of a path algebra of type $A_2$ vanishes, and each endomorphism ring is $k$.

GA:020529.canonicalSolution:
A representation of $Q\colon 1\to 2$ is a single linear map
$V_1\to V_2$. The simples are $S_1=(k\to 0)$ and $S_2=(0\to k)$.
The indecomposable projective at vertex $1$ is the representation
on the incoming path basis,
\[
P_1=\bigl(k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}k\bigr),
\]
while the indecomposable projective at vertex $2$ is $P_2=S_2$.
The canonical surjection $P_1\to S_1$ is the identity on vertex
$1$ and zero on vertex $2$. Its kernel is $0\to k$, hence
\[
0\to P_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0
\]
is exact.
\[
\boxed{P_1=(k\to k,\ \mathrm{id}),\ P_2=S_2,\ 0\to P_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0}.
\]

Apply $\operatorname{Hom}(-,S_2)$. A morphism $P_1\to S_2$ must be
zero at vertex $1$ because the target there is $0$; commutativity
with the identity arrow then forces the map at vertex $2$ to
vanish, so $\operatorname{Hom}(P_1,S_2)=0$. Meanwhile
$\operatorname{Hom}(P_2,S_2)=\operatorname{End}(S_2)=k$. The
resulting long exact sequence therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)\cong k.
\]
The displayed extension is nonsplit: $P_1$ is indecomposable, so
$P_1\not\cong S_1\oplus S_2$. Because $S_2=P_2$ is projective,
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^i(S_2,-)=0\qquad(i\ge 1),
\]
and in particular $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)=0$. The same
short resolution of $S_1$ has length $1$, so
$\operatorname{Ext}^{i\ge 2}(S_1,-)=0$. Thus every higher Ext
among $\{S_1,S_2\}$ vanishes.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)=k\text{ nonsplit},\ \operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)=0,\ \operatorname{Ext}^{\ge 2}=0}.
\]

A morphism $S_1\to S_2$ or $S_2\to S_1$ must vanish at one vertex
and then, by support, vanish at the other, so the cross Hom-spaces
are zero. Each simple is one-dimensional over $k$ at its support,
so $\operatorname{End}(S_i)=k$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Hom}(S_1,S_2)=\operatorname{Hom}(S_2,S_1)=0,\ \operatorname{End}(S_i)=k}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces a false symmetry of $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ or
kills both groups. Sentence (ii) denies projectivity of $S_2$ or
splits the unique nonsplit class.

The argument never replaces the assigned $A_2$-quiver Ext
asymmetry by the sibling $2$-adic inverse, by a quadric-cone DVR,
by an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic point count, or by a twisted-cubic
Hilbert polynomial, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: On the quiver $1\to 2$ one has $P_1=(k\to k,\mathrm{id})$ and $P_2=S_2$, with resolution $0\to P_2\to P_1\to S_1\to 0$. Then $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_1,S_2)=k$ is nonsplit, $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S_2,S_1)=0$ because $S_2$ is projective, higher Ext vanish, the cross Hom-spaces are zero, and each endomorphism ring is $k$.
Ext^1 is symmetric, so Ext^1(S1,S2) is isomorphic to Ext^1(S2,S1), or else both groups vanish. I do not accept Ext^1(S1,S2)=k with Ext^1(S2,S1)=0.
S2 is not projective, and the extension 0->S2->P1->S1->0 splits.

GA:020625.title: The blowup of A^2 at the origin separates the lines y=0, y=x, and x=0 along the exceptional P^1 at [1:0],[1:1],[0:1]
GA:020625.objective: On Bl_0(A^2), identify charts Ux=Spec k[x,t] with y=xt and Uy=Spec k[s,y] with x=sy, prove t=s^{-1} on the overlap, identify the exceptional P^1 and the isomorphism off the origin, and show the strict transforms of y=0, y=x, x=0 meet E at [1:0], [1:1], [0:1].
GA:020625.statement:
Let $X=\operatorname{Bl}_0\mathbb{A}^2$ be the blowup of the
affine plane at the origin, realized as the closed subset
\[
X=\bigl\{\bigl((x,y),[u:v]\bigr)\in\mathbb{A}^2\times\mathbb{P}^1:xv=yu\bigr\}.
\]

1. On the chart $U_x=\{u\ne 0\}$ set $t=v/u$ and prove the
   coordinate ring is $k[x,t]$ with $y=xt$. On the chart
   $U_y=\{v\ne 0\}$ set $s=u/v$ and prove the coordinate ring is
   $k[s,y]$ with $x=sy$. On the overlap prove $t=s^{-1}$.

2. Identify the exceptional divisor $E$ with $\mathbb{P}^1$, and
   prove that the projection $X\setminus E\to\mathbb{A}^2\setminus\{0\}$
   is an isomorphism.

3. Compute the strict transforms of the three lines $y=0$,
   $y=x$, and $x=0$, and prove they meet $E$ at the three distinct
   points $[1:0]$, $[1:1]$, and $[0:1]$ respectively.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the three strict transforms still
   meet at a single point of $E$”; (ii) “the chart transition is
   $t=s$, or the incidence points are not $[1:0]$, $[1:1]$,
   $[0:1]$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a Nullstellensatz census of
points and radicals, by a tangent colength, or by a Koszul or
Cech computation. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the
six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: On $U_x\cap U_y$ one has $u\ne 0$ and $v\ne 0$, so $t=v/u$ and $s=u/v$ are reciprocal units. Away from $E$ the pair $(x,y)$ recovers $[u:v]$ as $[x:y]$.
In $U_x$ the equation $y=0$ becomes $xt=0$, so the strict transform is $t=0$ and meets $E=\{x=0\}$ at $t=0$, i.e. $[1:0]$. The diagonal gives $t=1$, and the $y$-axis is $s=0$ in $U_y$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the two standard charts from xv=yu and invert the slope coordinates on the overlap.
Split each total transform into E union a graph of constant slope, then read the slope as a point of P^1.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the two charts, the transition t=s^{-1}, the exceptional P^1, and the isomorphism off the origin.
Computes the three strict transforms and their distinct incidences [1:0], [1:1], [0:1] on E.
Rejects a single common meeting point on E and refuses a wrong chart transition or swapped incidences.

commonErrors.description: Claims the three strict transforms still meet at a single point of the exceptional divisor.
commonErrors.consequence: The required distinct incidences [1:0], [1:1], [0:1] and the separation statement are lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes the chart transition to be t=s, or attaches the strict transforms to points other than [1:0], [1:1], [0:1].
commonErrors.consequence: The required transition t=s^{-1} and the three incidence points fail.

hintTree.content: From $xv=yu$ and $u\ne 0$ one gets $y=x(v/u)=xt$. The symmetric chart is $x=sy$.
Off $E$ one has $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$, so $[u:v]=[x:y]$ is uniquely determined.
On $U_x$, $y=0$ forces $t=0$ off $E$; $y=x$ forces $t=1$. The line $x=0$ is $s=0$ on $U_y$, meeting $E$ at $[0:1]$.

GA:020625.canonicalSolution:
On $U_x=\{u\ne 0\}$ set $t=v/u\in\mathbb{A}^1$. The defining
equation $xv=yu$ becomes $x(tu)=y u$, hence $y=xt$ after
cancelling the unit $u$. The remaining coordinates are free, so
$U_x\simeq\operatorname{Spec} k[x,t]$. On $U_y=\{v\ne 0\}$ set
$s=u/v$. Then $x=sy$ and $U_y\simeq\operatorname{Spec} k[s,y]$.
On the overlap $u\ne 0$ and $v\ne 0$, so $s$ and $t$ are units
and $t=v/u=s^{-1}$.
\[
\boxed{U_x:k[x,t],\ y=xt;\quad U_y:k[s,y],\ x=sy;\quad t=s^{-1}}.
\]

The exceptional divisor is $E=\{x=y=0\}$. In $U_x$ this is the
line $x=0$ with free coordinate $t$, and in $U_y$ it is $y=0$
with free coordinate $s$. The identifications $[u:v]=[1:t]=[s:1]$
exhibit $E\simeq\mathbb{P}^1$. Off $E$ one has $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$,
and the relation $xv=yu$ forces $[u:v]=[x:y]$. Thus the
projection $X\setminus E\to\mathbb{A}^2\setminus\{0\}$ is a
bijection with set-theoretic inverse
$(x,y)\mapsto\bigl((x,y),[x:y]\bigr)$. This inverse is regular:
on the principal open $D(x)$ it is
$(x,y)\mapsto(x,t=y/x)$ in $U_x$, while on $D(y)$ it is
$(x,y)\mapsto(s=x/y,y)$ in $U_y$. The two regular formulas agree
on $D(xy)$, so they glue to a morphism. It is inverse to the
projection, proving the claimed isomorphism.
\[
\boxed{E\simeq\mathbb{P}^1,\quad X\setminus E\;\simeq\;\mathbb{A}^2\setminus\{0\}}.
\]

The line $y=0$ pulls back in $U_x$ to $xt=0$, the union of $E$
and $\{t=0\}$. The strict transform is $t=0$, which meets $E$ at
$(x,t)=(0,0)$, i.e. $[u:v]=[1:0]$.

The line $y=x$ pulls back in $U_x$ to $xt=x$, or $x(t-1)=0$. The
strict transform is $t=1$, which meets $E$ at $t=1$, i.e. $[1:1]$.

The line $x=0$ is not a graph in $U_x$. In $U_y$ it pulls back to
$sy=0$, the union of $E$ and $\{s=0\}$. The strict transform is
$s=0$, which meets $E$ at $s=0$, i.e. $[u:v]=[0:1]$.

The three points $[1:0]$, $[1:1]$, $[0:1]$ of $\mathbb{P}^1$ are
distinct, so the blowup separates the three lines.
\[
\boxed{\widetilde{y=0}\cap E=[1:0],\ \widetilde{y=x}\cap E=[1:1],\ \widetilde{x=0}\cap E=[0:1]}.
\]

Sentence (i) claims the three strict transforms still collide on
$E$. Sentence (ii) corrupts the transition $t=s^{-1}$ or the
three incidence points.

The argument never replaces the assigned blowup by a
Nullstellensatz census, by a tangent colength, or by a Koszul or
Cech computation, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

The exceptional divisor is $\mathbb{P}^1$, and the projection is an isomorphism off the origin. The strict transforms of $y=0$, $y=x$, and $x=0$ meet $E$ at $[1:0]$, $[1:1]$, and $[0:1]$.
The three strict transforms still meet at a single point of E. I do not accept distinct incidences [1:0], [1:1], [0:1].
The chart transition is t=s, and the incidence points are not [1:0], [1:1], [0:1].

GA:020626.title: The smooth conic x^2+y^2=z^2 over F_5 is parametrized bijectively by P^1(F_5) onto six explicit points
GA:020626.objective: Prove C: x^2+y^2=z^2 is smooth over F_5, that [s:t]|->[s^2-t^2:2st:s^2+t^2] is a bijection P^1(F_5)->C(F_5), and that the six points are [1:0:1], [0:1:1], [1:2:0], [1:3:0], [0:4:1], [4:0:1].
GA:020626.statement:
Let $k=\mathbb{F}_5$ and let $C\subset\mathbb{P}^2_k$ be the
projective curve $x^2+y^2=z^2$. Consider the morphism
\[
\varphi:\mathbb{P}^1\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^2,\qquad
[s:t]\longmapsto\bigl[s^2-t^2:2st:s^2+t^2\bigr].
\]

1. Prove that $C$ is smooth over $\mathbb{F}_5$.

2. Prove that $\varphi$ lands in $C$ and induces a bijection
   $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)\xrightarrow{\sim} C(\mathbb{F}_5)$.

3. Evaluate $\varphi$ on the six $\mathbb{F}_5$-points of
   $\mathbb{P}^1$ and prove that the image is exactly
   \[
   [1:0:1],\ [0:1:1],\ [1:2:0],\ [1:3:0],\ [0:4:1],\ [4:0:1].
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$C(\mathbb{F}_5)$ has five points,
   or $[1:0:0]$ lies on $C$”; (ii) “the parametrization misses a
   point, or the conic is singular in characteristic $5$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a Nullstellensatz census of
points, radicals, and nilpotents, by a blowup of three lines, or
by a local-cohomology tail. Do not reopen, import, or execute any
of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: A direct expansion gives $(s^2-t^2)^2+(2st)^2=(s^2+t^2)^2$, so $\varphi(\mathbb{P}^1)\subseteq C$. Over a finite field, an injective map between sets of equal cardinality is bijective.

The conic has the $\mathbb{F}_5$-point $[1:0:1]$. A smooth conic with a rational point is isomorphic over its base field to $\mathbb{P}^1$, so $C(\mathbb{F}_5)$ and $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)$ both have $q+1=6$ points.

acceptableStrategies.description: Check that 2 is invertible in F_5 so the gradient vanishes only at the origin, then expand the Pythagorean identity.
Evaluate phi on the six points of P^1(F_5) and compare cardinalities to lock bijectivity.

milestones.criterion: Proves C is smooth over F_5 and that phi lands on C.
Evaluates phi on P^1(F_5) and obtains exactly the six points [1:0:1], [0:1:1], [1:2:0], [1:3:0], [0:4:1], [4:0:1] as a bijection.
Rejects a five-point count or the illegal point [1:0:0], and refuses a singularity claim or a missed point.

hintTree.content: In characteristic not $2$, $\nabla(x^2+y^2-z^2)=0$ forces $x=y=z=0$, which is not projective. Thus $C$ is smooth.
Expand $(s^2-t^2)^2+4s^2t^2=(s^2+t^2)^2$. Then evaluate $\varphi$ on the six points of $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)$.
Use the rational point $[1:0:1]$ to justify $C\cong\mathbb{P}^1$ over $\mathbb{F}_5$, hence $\#C(\mathbb{F}_5)=6$. Then the six distinct values of $\varphi$ force the required bijection.

GA:020626.canonicalSolution:
Let $F=x^2+y^2-z^2$. Then
$\nabla F=(2x,2y,-2z)$. In $\mathbb{F}_5$ one has $2\ne 0$, so
$\nabla F=0$ if and only if $x=y=z=0$. That triple is not a
point of $\mathbb{P}^2$. Hence $C$ is smooth.
\[
\boxed{C\text{ is smooth over }\mathbb{F}_5}.
\]

The algebraic identity
\[
(s^2-t^2)^2+(2st)^2=(s^4-2s^2t^2+t^4)+4s^2t^2=(s^2+t^2)^2
\]
shows that $\varphi$ lands in $C$. The source
$\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)$ consists of the six points
$[1:0]$, $[0:1]$, $[1:1]$, $[1:2]$, $[1:3]$, $[1:4]$. Evaluating,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi([1:0])&=[1:0:1],\\
\varphi([0:1])&=[-1:0:1]=[4:0:1],\\
\varphi([1:1])&=[0:2:2]=[0:1:1],\\
\varphi([1:2])&=[1-4:4:1+4]=[2:4:0]=[1:2:0],\\
\varphi([1:3])&=[1-4:6:1+4]=[2:1:0]=[1:3:0],\\
\varphi([1:4])&=[1-1:8:1+16]=[0:3:2]=[0:4:1].
\end{aligned}
\]
(The last two scalings use $3\cdot[2:1:0]=[1:3:0]$ and
$3\cdot[0:3:2]=[0:4:1]$ in $\mathbb{F}_5$.) These six points are
distinct and each satisfies $x^2+y^2=z^2$:
\[
1+0=1,\quad 0+1=1,\quad 1+4=0,\quad 1+9=0,\quad 0+16=1,\quad 16+0=1.
\]
Thus $\varphi$ is injective on $\mathbb{F}_5$-points. The displayed
point $[1:0:1]$ is $\mathbb{F}_5$-rational, and a smooth conic with
a rational point is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^1$ over the base
field (for instance by projection from that point). Therefore
$\lvert C(\mathbb{F}_5)\rvert=6$; the six distinct image points force
\[
\varphi:\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)\xrightarrow{\sim} C(\mathbb{F}_5)
\]
with image exactly
\[
[1:0:1],\ [0:1:1],\ [1:2:0],\ [1:3:0],\ [0:4:1],\ [4:0:1].
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{six points }[1:0:1],\,[0:1:1],\,[1:2:0],\,[1:3:0],\,[0:4:1],\,[4:0:1]}.
\]

Sentence (i) undercounts $C(\mathbb{F}_5)$ or inserts the illegal
point $[1:0:0]$, which fails $1+0=0$. Sentence (ii) claims a
missed point or a singularity in characteristic $5$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $\mathbb{F}_5$ census by
a Nullstellensatz argument about radicals and nilpotents, by a
blowup of three lines, or by a local-cohomology tail, and it does
not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

C(F_5) has five points, or [1:0:0] lies on C. I do not accept the six-point list or the bijection with P^1(F_5).
The parametrization misses a point, or the conic is singular in characteristic 5. I do not accept smoothness or a bijection.

GA:020630.title: The curve y^2=x^3+x+1 over F5 has nine rational points and is cyclic of order 9 generated by (0,1)
GA:020630.objective: For E:y^2=x^3+x+1 over F5, prove the discriminant is nonzero, list the eight affine points (0,±1),(2,±1),(3,±1),(4,±2) plus O for a total of 9, deduce trace -3, compute P=(0,1), 2P=(4,2), 3P=(2,1), and conclude that P has order 9 so E(F5)=C9.
GA:020630.statement:
Let $E$ be the Weierstrass curve
\[
y^2=x^3+x+1
\]
over the field $\mathbb{F}_5$.

1. Prove that the discriminant is nonzero in $\mathbb{F}_5$, so $E$
   is an elliptic curve. Enumerate the affine $\mathbb{F}_5$-points
   \[
   (0,\pm 1),\quad (2,\pm 1),\quad (3,\pm 1),\quad (4,\pm 2)
   \]
   and conclude that together with the point at infinity $O$ one
   has $\#E(\mathbb{F}_5)=9$. Deduce that the trace of Frobenius
   is $-3$.

2. Let $P=(0,1)$. Using the chord-and-tangent group law, prove
   \[
   2P=(4,2),\qquad 3P=(2,1).
   \]

3. Prove that $P$ has order $9$ and therefore
   $E(\mathbb{F}_5)\cong C_9$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$E$ is singular, or the affine point
   count is not eight, so $\#E(\mathbb{F}_5)\ne 9$ and the group is
   not $C_9$”; (ii) “$2P$ is not $(4,2)$ or $3P$ is not $(2,1)$, so
   the order of $P$ divides $3$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $2$-adic inverse of
$3$, by a quadric-cone DVR, by an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, or
by a twisted-cubic Hilbert polynomial. Do not reopen, import, or
execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The quadratic residues modulo $5$ are $0,1,4$. Testing $x=0,1,2,3,4$ in $x^3+x+1$ yields the eight affine points $(0,\pm 1)$, $(2,\pm 1)$, $(3,\pm 1)$, $(4,\pm 2)$. With $O$ one has $\#E(\mathbb{F}_5)=5+1-t=9$, hence $t=-3$.
A group of order $9$ is $C_9$ or $C_3\times C_3$. The latter has exponent $3$. If $3P\ne O$ then $P$ cannot have order $1$ or $3$, so $P$ has order $9$ and $E(\mathbb{F}_5)\cong C_9$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Test the cubic at each of the five field elements against the squares 0,1,4, then apply q+1-t.
Double P with slope 1/2=3, add P with slope 1/4=4, and rule out C3xC3 by 3P≠O.

milestones.criterion: Proves Delta nonzero, lists the eight affine points plus O, and obtains #E(F5)=9 with trace -3.
Computes 2P=(4,2) and 3P=(2,1), then concludes ord(P)=9 and E(F5)=C9.
Rejects a singular or miscounted curve and refuses a wrong double, triple, or exponent-3 group.

commonErrors.description: Claims E is singular, or that the affine point count is not eight, so that #E(F5) is not 9 and the group is not C9.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities #E(F5)=9, trace -3, and E(F5)=C9 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Computes 2P other than (4,2) or 3P other than (2,1), or concludes that the order of P divides 3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required multiples 2P=(4,2), 3P=(2,1) and the generator of C9 fail.

hintTree.content: Squares in $\mathbb{F}_5$ are $0,1,4$. The values of $x^3+x+1$ are $1,3,1,1,4$ as $x$ runs through $0,1,2,3,4$.
Doubling $P=(0,1)$ uses $\lambda=(0+1)/2=1/2=3$. Adding $2P+P$ uses $\lambda=(1-2)/(0-4)=1/4=4$.
Order $9$ follows once $3P\ne O$, because $\lvert E(\mathbb{F}_5)\rvert=9$.

GA:020630.canonicalSolution:
For $y^2=x^3+Ax+B$ with $A=B=1$ the discriminant is
$\Delta=-16(4A^3+27B^2)$. Reducing modulo $5$ one has
$4+27\equiv 4+2=6\equiv 1\not\equiv 0$, and $-16\not\equiv 0$, so
$\Delta\not\equiv 0$. Thus $E$ is an elliptic curve over
$\mathbb{F}_5$.

The squares in $\mathbb{F}_5$ are $0,1,4$. Evaluating the cubic:
\begin{align*}
x=0&\colon 1=1^2,\quad y\equiv\pm 1,\\
x=1&\colon 1+1+1=3,\quad\text{nonsquare},\\
x=2&\colon 8+2+1\equiv 1,\quad y\equiv\pm 1,\\
x=3&\colon 27+3+1\equiv 1,\quad y\equiv\pm 1,\\
x=4&\colon 64+4+1\equiv 4,\quad y\equiv\pm 2.
\end{align*}
The eight affine points are therefore
$(0,\pm 1)$, $(2,\pm 1)$, $(3,\pm 1)$, $(4,\pm 2)$. Adjoining $O$
gives $\#E(\mathbb{F}_5)=9$. The trace of Frobenius satisfies
$\#E(\mathbb{F}_q)=q+1-t$, so $9=5+1-t$ and $t=-3$.
\[
\boxed{\Delta\ne 0,\ \#E(\mathbb{F}_5)=9,\ t=-3}.
\]

Let $P=(0,1)$. The doubling slope is
\[
\lambda=\frac{3\cdot 0+1}{2\cdot 1}=\frac12=3\in\mathbb{F}_5,
\]
because $2\cdot 3=6\equiv 1$. Then
\[
x(2P)=3^2-0-0=9\equiv 4,\qquad
y(2P)=3(0-4)-1=-12-1\equiv 2,
\]
so $2P=(4,2)$. Adding $2P+P=(4,2)+(0,1)$ uses
\[
\lambda=\frac{1-2}{0-4}=\frac{-1}{-4}=\frac14=4,
\]
because $4\cdot 4=16\equiv 1$. Then
\[
x(3P)=4^2-4-0=12\equiv 2,\qquad
y(3P)=4(4-2)-2=8-2\equiv 1,
\]
so $3P=(2,1)$.
\[
\boxed{P=(0,1),\ 2P=(4,2),\ 3P=(2,1)}.
\]

In particular $3P\ne O$, so the order of $P$ does not divide $3$.
The only groups of order $9$ are $C_9$ and $C_3\times C_3$, and
the latter has exponent $3$. Therefore $P$ has order $9$ and
$E(\mathbb{F}_5)=\langle P\rangle\cong C_9$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ord}(P)=9,\ E(\mathbb{F}_5)\cong C_9}.
\]

Sentence (i) claims $E$ is singular or miscounts the points.
Sentence (ii) corrupts $2P$ or $3P$ and forces order dividing $3$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic
count by the sibling $2$-adic inverse, by a quadric-cone DVR, by
an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, or by a twisted-cubic Hilbert
polynomial, and it does not open any of the six existing intake
seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The curve $y^2=x^3+x+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_5$ has nonzero discriminant. Its affine points are $(0,\pm 1)$, $(2,\pm 1)$, $(3,\pm 1)$, $(4,\pm 2)$, and with $O$ one has $\#E(\mathbb{F}_5)=9$ and trace $-3$. For $P=(0,1)$ one has $2P=(4,2)$ and $3P=(2,1)$, so $P$ has order $9$ and $E(\mathbb{F}_5)\cong C_9$.
E is singular, or the affine point count is not eight, so #E(F5) is not 9 and the group is not C9.
2P is not (4,2) or 3P is not (2,1), so the order of P divides 3. I do not accept E(F5)=C9 generated by (0,1).

GA:020631.title: The twisted cubic in P3 has Hilbert polynomial 3n+1, value 7 in degree 2, degree 3 and genus 0
GA:020631.objective: For the embedding P1->P3, [s:t]|->[s^3:s^2 t:s t^2:t^3], prove the homogeneous ideal is generated by the three quadrics x0 x2-x1^2, x0 x3-x1 x2, x1 x3-x2^2, identify the degree-n piece with binary forms of degree 3n, prove H(n)=3n+1 with H(2)=7, and conclude degree 3, genus 0, and that the map is an embedding.
GA:020631.statement:
Let $\nu\colon\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^3$ be the morphism
\[
[s:t]\longmapsto\bigl[s^3:s^2 t:s t^2:t^3\bigr],
\]
and write $C=\nu(\mathbb{P}^1)$ for the twisted cubic, with
homogeneous coordinates $[x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3]$ on $\mathbb{P}^3$.

1. Prove that the homogeneous ideal of $C$ is generated by the
   three quadrics
   \[
   x_0 x_2-x_1^2,\qquad x_0 x_3-x_1 x_2,\qquad x_1 x_3-x_2^2.
   \]

2. Prove that the degree-$n$ piece of the homogeneous coordinate
   ring of $C$ is canonically identified with the space of binary
   forms of degree $3n$, and therefore that the Hilbert function
   (equal already to the Hilbert polynomial) is
   \[
   H(n)=3n+1.
   \]
   Evaluate $H(2)=7$.

3. Conclude that $C$ has degree $3$ and arithmetic genus $0$, and
   that $\nu$ is a closed embedding.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Hilbert polynomial is $n+1$ or
   $3n+3$ rather than $3n+1$, so $H(2)$ is not $7$”; (ii) “$C$ has
   degree $1$, or the genus is not $0$, or $\nu$ is not an
   embedding.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling $2$-adic inverse of
$3$, by a quadric-cone DVR, by an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, or
by an $\mathbb{F}_5$ elliptic point count. Do not reopen, import,
or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: For graded reverse lexicographic order $x_0>x_1>x_2>x_3$, the three minors have leading monomials $x_1^2,x_1x_2,x_2^2$ and form a Grobner basis. Their degree-$n$ standard monomials number $(n+1)+n+n=3n+1$.
Pullback along $\nu$ identifies $H^0(\mathbb{P}^3,\mathcal{O}(n))\big/I(C)_n$ with $H^0(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathcal{O}(3n))$, a space of dimension $3n+1$. Thus $H(2)=7$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pull monomials back along [s^3:s^2 t:s t^2:t^3] and count binary forms of degree 3n.
Match H(n)=dn+(1-g) to 3n+1, then invoke the complete linear system O(3) to get the embedding.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the three quadric generators and the degree-n piece with binary forms of degree 3n, obtaining H(n)=3n+1 and H(2)=7.
Concludes degree 3, genus 0, and that the map is a closed embedding.
Rejects a wrong Hilbert polynomial and refuses degree 1, nonzero genus, or a non-embedding.

commonErrors.consequence: The required identities H(n)=3n+1 and H(2)=7 are lost.

commonErrors.consequence: The required conclusions deg=3, g=0, and that nu is a closed embedding fail.

hintTree.content: Substitute $x_0=s^3$, $x_1=s^2 t$, $x_2=s t^2$, $x_3=t^3$ into each minor to see vanishing, then compare dimensions.
A binary form of degree $3n$ is uniquely $s^{3n-i}t^i$ for $i=0,\dots,3n$, hence $3n+1$ dimensions.
A curve Hilbert polynomial $dn+(1-g)$ with $H=3n+1$ forces $d=3$ and $g=0$. Separating points and tangents shows $\nu$ is an embedding.

GA:020631.canonicalSolution:
Write $x_0=s^3$, $x_1=s^2 t$, $x_2=s t^2$, $x_3=t^3$. Each
$2\times 2$ minor of the catalecticant matrix vanishes identically:
\begin{align*}
x_0 x_2-x_1^2&=s^3\cdot s t^2-(s^2 t)^2=0,\\
x_0 x_3-x_1 x_2&=s^3\cdot t^3-(s^2 t)(s t^2)=0,\\
x_1 x_3-x_2^2&=(s^2 t)t^3-(s t^2)^2=0.
\end{align*}
Thus the three quadrics lie in $I(C)$. Let $J$ be the ideal they
generate. For graded reverse lexicographic order
$x_0>x_1>x_2>x_3$, their leading monomials are
$x_1^2,x_1x_2,x_2^2$. Buchberger's criterion applies: the two
adjacent $S$-polynomials reduce respectively to a multiple of the
third and first minor, and the remaining $S$-polynomial reduces to
zero using the same three relations. Hence the minors form a
Grobner basis. The degree-$n$ standard monomials are exactly
\[
x_0^a x_3^{n-a}\ (0\le a\le n),\quad
x_0^a x_1x_3^{n-1-a},\ x_0^a x_2x_3^{n-1-a}\ (0\le a<n),
\]
so $\dim_k(S/J)_n=(n+1)+n+n=3n+1$.

The parametrization induces a graded surjection
\[
S/J\longrightarrow k[s^3,s^2t,st^2,t^3].
\]
Every binary monomial of degree $3n$ is a product of $n$ of the
four displayed cubics, so the target's degree-$n$ piece also has
dimension $3n+1$. The surjection is therefore an isomorphism in
every degree. Consequently $J$ is the full homogeneous kernel,
and the three quadrics generate $I(C)$ scheme-theoretically.
\[
\boxed{I(C)=(x_0 x_2-x_1^2,\ x_0 x_3-x_1 x_2,\ x_1 x_3-x_2^2)}.
\]

The preceding kernel computation identifies the degree-$n$ piece
under pullback by $\nu$:
\[
\bigl(k[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]/I(C)\bigr)_n
\cong H^0\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathcal{O}(3n)\bigr).
\]
The latter space has basis $\{s^{3n-i}t^i:0\le i\le 3n\}$ and
therefore dimension $3n+1$. This is the Hilbert function for every
$n\ge 0$, hence also the Hilbert polynomial:
\[
H(n)=3n+1.
\]
In degree $2$ one has $H(2)=7$.
\[
\boxed{H(n)=3n+1,\quad H(2)=7}.
\]

A closed curve of degree $d$ and arithmetic genus $g$ has Hilbert
polynomial $dn+(1-g)$. Matching $3n+1$ gives $d=3$ and $g=0$.
The morphism $\nu$ is given by a complete linear system that
separates points and tangent vectors on $\mathbb{P}^1$, so $\nu$
is a closed embedding and $C\cong\mathbb{P}^1$.
\[
\boxed{\deg C=3,\ g=0,\ \nu\text{ is an embedding}}.
\]

Sentence (i) corrupts the Hilbert polynomial and loses $H(2)=7$.
Sentence (ii) claims degree $1$, a nonzero genus, or a
non-embedding.

The argument never replaces the assigned twisted-cubic Hilbert
polynomial by the sibling $2$-adic inverse, by a quadric-cone DVR,
by an $A_2$-quiver Ext computation, or by an $\mathbb{F}_5$
elliptic point count, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The twisted cubic is cut out by $x_0 x_2-x_1^2$, $x_0 x_3-x_1 x_2$, and $x_1 x_3-x_2^2$. Its degree-$n$ piece is the space of binary forms of degree $3n$, so $H(n)=3n+1$ and $H(2)=7$. Thus $C$ has degree $3$ and genus $0$, and $\nu$ is a closed embedding.
The Hilbert polynomial is n+1 or 3n+3 rather than 3n+1, so H(2) is not 7.
C has degree 1, or the genus is not 0, or nu is not an embedding.

GCM:010117.title: Cycloid through (πa,2a) has time π√(a/g); the straight chord takes √(π²+4)√(a/g)
GCM:010117.objective: With downward y positive, derive the cycloid element identities ds=2a sin(θ/2)dθ, v=√(2gy)=2√(ag)sin(θ/2), dt=√(a/g)dθ; at the θ=π endpoint (πa,2a) obtain T_cycloid=π√(a/g) and compare the constant-slope chord time √(π²+4)√(a/g); at a=g=1 report π versus √(π²+4).
GCM:010117.statement:
Work in the vertical plane with downward $y$ positive and
$g>0$. A particle starts from rest at the origin and slides
without friction to the endpoint $(\pi a,2a)$ with $a>0$. Do not
replace the cycloid-versus-chord endpoint comparison by a
magnetic momentum-map / gauge Noether identity, a central
power-law effective-potential stability calculation, or an
accelerating-frame canonical transform.

1. Using the Beltrami identity for the travel-time integrand
   (which does not depend explicitly on the horizontal
   coordinate), derive the cycloid
   \[
   x=a(\theta-\sin\theta),\qquad
   y=a(1-\cos\theta)
   \]
   as a stationary path, and prove the element identities
   \[
   ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta,\qquad
   v=\sqrt{2gy}=2\sqrt{ag}\,\sin(\theta/2),\qquad
   dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta.
   \]

2. Specialize to the endpoint $\theta_1=\pi$, which is the point
   $(\pi a,2a)$. Prove that the cycloid transit time is
   \[
   T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi\sqrt{a/g}.
   \]

3. For the straight constant-slope chord from the origin to
   $(\pi a,2a)$, prove that the transit time from rest is
   \[
   T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\,\sqrt{a/g}
   \]
   and that $T_{\mathrm{chord}}>T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}$. At the
   sample $a=g=1$, report the numerical pair
   \[
   T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi,\qquad
   T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the cycloid transit is a full $2\pi$
   generating period, so $T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=2\pi\sqrt{a/g}$
   rather than $\pi\sqrt{a/g}$”; (ii) “the chord time is
   $(\pi^2+4)^{1/4}\sqrt{a/g}$, so at $a=g=1$ one does not obtain
   $\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$.” Scope is the Beltrami derivation and this
   endpoint comparison only; do not claim global uniqueness over
   nonsmooth curves.
permittedResults: From $dx=a(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta$ and $dy=a\sin\theta\,d\theta$ one has $ds^2=2a^2(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta^2$, hence $ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta$. Then $v=\sqrt{2gy}=2\sqrt{ag}\sin(\theta/2)$ and $dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta$.

Integrating $dt$ from $0$ to $\pi$ gives $T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi\sqrt{a/g}$. The chord of length $a\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$ has along-path acceleration $2g/\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$, hence $T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\,\sqrt{a/g}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the Beltrami identity to the x-independent travel-time integrand and identify the downward cycloid of generating radius a.
Cancel the half-angle factors in ds/v to integrate dt, then compare with the constant-slope chord using s=(1/2)(g sin alpha)t^2.

milestones.criterion: Produces the Beltrami cycloid, the element identities ds, v, and dt, and the endpoint (pi a,2a) with T_cycloid=pi sqrt(a/g).
Reports T_chord=sqrt(pi^2+4)sqrt(a/g) and the sample pair pi versus sqrt(pi^2+4) at a=g=1.
Rejects a full-period 2pi cycloid time or a fourth-root chord time, and refuses reserved momentum-map, power-law, or accelerating-frame substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the cycloid transit as a full 2π generating period and reports T_cycloid=2π√(a/g) instead of π√(a/g).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned endpoint time π√(a/g) and the sample value π at a=g=1 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the chord time as (π²+4)^{1/4}√(a/g) instead of √(π²+4)√(a/g).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned straight-chord comparison and the sample value √(π²+4) are replaced by an inconsistent root.

hintTree.content: Write $T[y]=\int_0^{x_1}\sqrt{1+y'^2}/\sqrt{2gy}\,dx$ and apply Beltrami. The first integral rearranges to $y(1+y'^2)=$ constant, which is solved by the stated cycloid.
Compute $ds=\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$ from the parametric derivatives and use $1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)$. Cancel $\sin(\theta/2)$ against $v=\sqrt{2gy}$ to obtain $dt$.
For the chord, the slope angle $\alpha$ satisfies $\sin\alpha=2/\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$. Distance over $\tfrac12(\,g\sin\alpha\,)t^2$ produces $T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\,\sqrt{a/g}$.

GCM:010117.canonicalSolution:
With downward $y$ positive the travel time of a graph $y(x)$
from the origin to a prescribed endpoint is
\[
T[y]=\int_0^{x_1}\frac{\sqrt{1+y'^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}}\,dx.
\]
The integrand $L(y,y')$ does not depend on $x$, so Beltrami gives
\[
L-y'\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y'^2}\,\sqrt{2gy}}=C.
\]
Hence $y(1+y'^2)=k$ with $k=1/(2gC^2)$. The standard parametric
solution is the cycloid of generating radius $a=k/2$,
\[
x=a(\theta-\sin\theta),\qquad
y=a(1-\cos\theta).
\]
\[
\boxed{x=a(\theta-\sin\theta),\;y=a(1-\cos\theta)}.
\]

Differentiating,
\[
dx=a(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad
dy=a\sin\theta\,d\theta,
\]
so
\[
ds^2=a^2\bigl((1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta\bigr)\,d\theta^2
=2a^2(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta^2
=4a^2\sin^2(\theta/2)\,d\theta^2.
\]
For $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ one has $\sin(\theta/2)\ge 0$, hence
\[
ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta.
\]
Energy from rest at the origin gives
\[
v=\sqrt{2gy}
=\sqrt{2ga(1-\cos\theta)}
=2\sqrt{ag}\,\sin(\theta/2).
\]
The time element is therefore
\[
dt=\frac{ds}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\,d\theta.
\]
\[
\boxed{ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta,\;
v=2\sqrt{ag}\sin(\theta/2),\;
dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta}.
\]

At $\theta_1=\pi$ the endpoint is
\[
\bigl(a(\pi-0),\,a(1-(-1))\bigr)=(\pi a,2a).
\]
Integrating $dt$ from $0$ to $\pi$ produces
\[
T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi\sqrt{a/g}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi\sqrt{a/g}}.
\]

The straight chord from the origin to $(\pi a,2a)$ has length
$L=a\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$ and inclination $\alpha$ with
$\sin\alpha=2/\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$. The along-path acceleration from
rest is $g\sin\alpha$, so
\[
L=\frac12(g\sin\alpha)\,T_{\mathrm{chord}}^2
\]
and therefore
\[
T_{\mathrm{chord}}
=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{g\sin\alpha}}
=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\,\sqrt{a/g}.
\]
Since $\sqrt{\pi^2+4}>\pi$, one has
$T_{\mathrm{chord}}>T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}$. At $a=g=1$ the times
are $\pi$ and $\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$.
\[
\boxed{T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\sqrt{a/g};
\;a=g=1\Rightarrow\pi\text{ vs }\sqrt{\pi^2+4}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the half-generating-period integral
$[0,\pi]$ by a full $2\pi$ period and doubles the cycloid time.
Sentence (ii) takes a fourth root of $\pi^2+4$ and loses the
assigned chord time. The construction is a Beltrami derivation
together with an endpoint comparison against the straight chord;
it does not assert global uniqueness among nonsmooth curves, and
it is not a magnetic momentum-map, power-law effective-potential,
or accelerating-frame problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: The downward cycloid $x=a(\theta-\sin\theta)$, $y=a(1-\cos\theta)$ has $ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta$, $v=2\sqrt{ag}\sin(\theta/2)$, and $dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta$. At $\theta=\pi$ the endpoint is $(\pi a,2a)$ with $T_{\mathrm{cycloid}}=\pi\sqrt{a/g}$. The straight chord takes $T_{\mathrm{chord}}=\sqrt{\pi^2+4}\sqrt{a/g}$, hence $\pi$ versus $\sqrt{\pi^2+4}$ at $a=g=1$.
The cycloid transit is a full 2pi generating period, so T_cycloid=2pi sqrt(a/g). I do not report T_cycloid=pi sqrt(a/g).
The chord time is (pi^2+4)^{1/4} sqrt(a/g). I never obtain T_chord=sqrt(pi^2+4) sqrt(a/g) or the sample value sqrt(pi^2+4).

GCM:010131.title: Inverse-square conformal mechanics has sl(2) brackets and charges D-tH, K-2tD+t²H; at E=2,g=1,t0=0 one finds q_min=1/2 and at t=1/2 the ledger q=√5/2, p=4/√5, Casimir=1/4
GCM:010131.objective: For q>0 and H=(p²+g²/q²)/2 with D=qp/2 and K=q²/2, prove the sl(2) Poisson brackets {D,H}=H, {D,K}=-K, {H,K}=-2D and the Casimir HK-D²=g²/4, show that D and K are not themselves conserved (Ḋ=H, Ḱ=2D) while D-tH and K-2tD+t²H are conserved, derive the energy-E orbit q²=2E(t-t0)²+g²/(2E) with p=2E(t-t0)/q, and at E=2, g=1, t0=0 obtain q_min=1/2 and at t=1/2 the values q=√5/2, p=4/√5, D=1, K=5/8, H=2, Casimir=1/4.
GCM:010131.statement:
Work on the half-line $q>0$ with the inverse-square conformal
Hamiltonian
\[
H=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(p^2+\frac{g^2}{q^2}\Bigr)
\]
and the generators
\[
D=\frac{qp}{2},\qquad K=\frac{q^2}{2}.
\]
The Poisson bracket is the standard $\{q,p\}=1$. Do not replace
the conformal $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$ ledger by a magnetic
momentum-map / gauge Noether identity, a Dirac–Bergmann constraint
chain, a planar isotropic-oscillator Hamilton–Jacobi radial action,
a near-$1{:}1$ resonant averaging calculation, an Euler–Poincaré
free rigid body, or a standard-map fixed-point stability problem.

1. Prove the Poisson brackets
   \[
   \{D,H\}=H,\qquad \{D,K\}=-K,\qquad \{H,K\}=-2D
   \]
   and the Casimir identity
   \[
   HK-D^2=\frac{g^2}{4}.
   \]

2. Prove that $D$ and $K$ are not themselves conserved:
   $\dot D=H$ and $\dot K=2D$. Deduce that the actual conserved
   charges (for time-dependent conformal symmetries) are
   \[
   D-tH\qquad\text{and}\qquad K-2tD+t^2 H.
   \]

3. At energy $E>0$ derive the explicit orbit
   \[
   q^2=2E(t-t_0)^2+\frac{g^2}{2E},\qquad
   p=\frac{2E(t-t_0)}{q}.
   \]
   Specialize to $E=2$, $g=1$, $t_0=0$. Prove that the periapsis
   is $q_{\min}=1/2$, and that at $t=1/2$ one has
   \[
   q=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2},\qquad
   p=\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}},\qquad
   D=1,\qquad
   K=\frac58,\qquad
   H=2,\qquad
   HK-D^2=\frac14.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$D$ and $K$ are themselves first
   integrals, so there is no need for the time-dependent charges
   $D-tH$ and $K-2tD+t^2 H$”; (ii) “at $E=2$, $g=1$, $t_0=0$ and
   $t=1/2$ one has $q_{\min}=1$ (or $q=1$) rather than
   $q_{\min}=1/2$ and $q=\sqrt{5}/2$, so the Casimir is not
   $1/4$.”
permittedResults: With $\{q,p\}=1$ one computes $\{D,H\}=H$, $\{D,K\}=-K$, and $\{H,K\}=-2D$. Expanding $HK-D^2$ yields $g^2/4$.
Energy reduction gives $\dot q^2=2E-g^2/q^2$, hence $q^2=2E(t-t_0)^2+g^2/(2E)$. At $E=2$, $g=1$, $t_0=0$, $t=1/2$ one has $q=\sqrt{5}/2$, $p=4/\sqrt{5}$, $D=1$, $K=5/8$, and Casimir $1/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the three Poisson brackets from {q,p}=1 and expand the quadratic Casimir HK-D^2.
Integrate the energy identity for q^2 and evaluate the time-dependent charges and the numerical sample at E=2, g=1, t=1/2.

milestones.criterion: Produces the sl(2) brackets {D,H}=H, {D,K}=-K, {H,K}=-2D, the Casimir HK-D^2=g^2/4, and the non-conservation Ddot=H, Kdot=2D.
Reports conserved charges D-tH and K-2tD+t^2 H, the orbit q^2=2E(t-t0)^2+g^2/(2E), and the sample q_min=1/2 together with q=sqrt(5)/2, p=4/sqrt(5), D=1, K=5/8, H=2, Casimir=1/4.

Rejects treating D or K as first integrals or a wrong periapsis/sample ledger, and refuses reserved magnetic-Noether, Dirac, oscillator-HJ, 1:1-resonance, Euler-Poincare, or standard-map substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that D and K are themselves first integrals, denying Ddot=H, Kdot=2D and the time-dependent charges D-tH and K-2tD+t^2 H.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conformal charge ledger is replaced by a false conservation statement for D and K.

commonErrors.description: At E=2, g=1, t0=0 reports q_min=1 or q=1 at t=1/2, denying q_min=1/2, q=sqrt(5)/2, p=4/sqrt(5), and Casimir 1/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned numerical conformal ledger and the Casimir value 1/4 are lost.

hintTree.content: Compute $\{D,H\}=(\partial D/\partial q)(\partial H/\partial p)-(\partial D/\partial p)(\partial H/\partial q)$ with $\partial D/\partial q=p/2$ and $\partial H/\partial q=-g^2/q^3$.
Differentiate $D-tH$ along the flow: $\dot D-H-t\dot H=H-H=0$. The special-conformal combination is similar.
At periapsis $\dot q=0$ forces $q_{\min}^2=g^2/(2E)$. Insert $E=2$, $g=1$, $t=1/2$ into $q^2=2E t^2+g^2/(2E)$.

GCM:010131.canonicalSolution:
The canonical bracket is $\{q,p\}=1$. Then
\[
\frac{\partial D}{\partial q}=\frac p2,\quad
\frac{\partial D}{\partial p}=\frac q2,\quad
\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}=p,\quad
\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}=-\frac{g^2}{q^3},
\]
so
\[
\{D,H\}=\frac p2\cdot p-\frac q2\Bigl(-\frac{g^2}{q^3}\Bigr)
=\frac{p^2}{2}+\frac{g^2}{2q^2}=H.
\]
Likewise $\{D,K\}=-(q/2)\cdot q=-q^2/2=-K$ and
$\{H,K\}=-p\cdot q=-2D$. The Casimir expands as
\[
HK-D^2
=\frac{p^2+g^2/q^2}{2}\cdot\frac{q^2}{2}-\frac{q^2 p^2}{4}
=\frac{g^2}{4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\{D,H\}=H,\;\{D,K\}=-K,\;\{H,K\}=-2D,\;
HK-D^2=g^2/4}.
\]

Along the flow $\dot F=\{F,H\}$, so $\dot D=\{D,H\}=H$ and
$\dot K=\{K,H\}=-\{H,K\}=2D$. In particular $D$ and $K$ are not
conserved unless the motion is trivial. The time-dependent
combinations satisfy
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{dt}(D-tH)&=\dot D-H-t\dot H=H-H=0,\\
\frac{d}{dt}(K-2tD+t^2 H)
&=\dot K-2D-2t\dot D+2t H+t^2\dot H
=2D-2D-2t H+2t H=0.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\dot D=H,\;\dot K=2D;\;
D-tH\text{ and }K-2tD+t^2 H\text{ conserved}}.
\]

At energy $E>0$ one has $\dot q=p$ and
$\dot q^2=2E-g^2/q^2$. The even solution about a periapsis time
$t_0$ is
\[
q^2=2E(t-t_0)^2+\frac{g^2}{2E},
\]
and differentiating gives $p=2E(t-t_0)/q$. The periapsis value is
$q_{\min}=|g|/\sqrt{2E}$. For $E=2$, $g=1$, $t_0=0$ this is
$q_{\min}=1/2$. At $t=1/2$,
\[
q^2=2\cdot 2\cdot\frac14+\frac{1}{4}=\frac54,\qquad
q=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2},
\]
\[
p=\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot(1/2)}{q}=\frac{2}{q}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}.
\]
Then
\[
D=\frac{qp}{2}
=\frac{(\sqrt{5}/2)\cdot(4/\sqrt{5})}{2}=1,\qquad
K=\frac{q^2}{2}=\frac{5}{8},\qquad
H=2,
\]
and $HK-D^2=2\cdot(5/8)-1=1/4$.
\[
\boxed{q_{\min}=1/2;\;
t=1/2\Rightarrow
q=\sqrt{5}/2,\;p=4/\sqrt{5},\;
D=1,\;K=5/8,\;H=2,\;
HK-D^2=1/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats $D$ and $K$ as first integrals and discards
the time-dependent charges. Sentence (ii) reports the wrong
periapsis and the wrong sample $q$, so the Casimir $1/4$ is lost.
The construction is an inverse-square conformal $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$
audit; it is not a magnetic Noether identity, a Dirac constraint
chain, an oscillator Hamilton–Jacobi action, a $1{:}1$ resonant
average, an Euler–Poincaré rigid body, or a standard-map seed.

graderFixtures.proofText: The brackets are $\{D,H\}=H$, $\{D,K\}=-K$, $\{H,K\}=-2D$ with Casimir $HK-D^2=g^2/4$. Then $\dot D=H$ and $\dot K=2D$, while $D-tH$ and $K-2tD+t^2 H$ are conserved. GCM:010218.title: Rotating hoop at Ω=√2, m=R=g=1 has pitchfork angles ±π/3, frequency √(3/2), bottom growth 1
GCM:010218.objective: From L=(mR²/2)(θ̇²+Ω² sin²θ)+mgR cos θ with θ measured from the bottom, derive θ̈=sin θ(Ω² cos θ-g/R), identify Ω_c=√(g/R), and at m=R=g=1, Ω=√2 obtain θ0=±π/3, small frequency Ω sin θ0=√(3/2), and bottom growth √(Ω²-g/R)=1.
GCM:010218.statement:
A bead of mass $m$ slides without friction on a hoop of radius
$R$ that rotates with constant angular speed $\Omega$ about its
vertical diameter. Measure the polar angle $\theta$ from the
bottom. Do not replace the rotating-hoop pitchfork by an
Euler–Poincaré free rigid body, a Dirac–Bergmann constraint
chain, or a standard-map fixed-point stability calculation.

1. Starting from the Lagrangian
   \[
   L=\frac{mR^2}{2}\bigl(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)
   +mgR\cos\theta,
   \]
   derive the exact equation
   \[
   \ddot\theta=\sin\theta\bigl(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R\bigr).
   \]

2. Identify the relative equilibria and the critical speed
   $\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R}$. Prove that the bottom $\theta=0$ is
   linearly stable for $\Omega<\Omega_c$ and has exponential
   growth rate $\sqrt{\Omega^2-g/R}$ for $\Omega>\Omega_c$, and
   that the top $\theta=\pi$ is always linearly unstable.

3. For $\Omega>\Omega_c$ prove that the off-axis equilibria
   satisfy $\cos\theta_0=g/(R\Omega^2)$ and are linearly stable
   with small frequency $\Omega\sin\theta_0$.

4. Specialize to $m=R=g=1$ and $\Omega=\sqrt{2}$. Prove
   \[
   \theta_0=\pm\pi/3,\qquad
   \omega=\sqrt{3/2},\qquad
   \text{bottom growth rate }=1.
   \]
   Audit both sentences: (i) “$\cos\theta_0=1/2$ forces
   $\theta_0=\pm\pi/6$ rather than $\pm\pi/3$”; (ii) “the
   off-axis frequency is $\Omega\cos\theta_0=1/\sqrt{2}$ rather
   than $\Omega\sin\theta_0=\sqrt{3/2}$.”

At $m=R=g=1$, $\Omega=\sqrt{2}$ one has $\cos\theta_0=1/2$, hence $\theta_0=\pm\pi/3$, $\omega=\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{3}/2=\sqrt{3/2}$, and bottom growth $\sqrt{2-1}=1$.

milestones.criterion: Produces the exact equation, Omega_c=sqrt(g/R), the bottom/top linearizations, and the off-axis condition with frequency Omega sin theta0.

Rejects theta0=+-pi/6 or the frequency Omega cos theta0, and refuses reserved rigid-body, Dirac-Bergmann, or standard-map substitutions.

Near $\theta=0$ replace $\sin\theta$ by $\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ by $1$. Near an off-axis root, differentiate $\sin\theta(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R)$ and use $\Omega^2\cos\theta_0=g/R$.
Insert $\Omega=\sqrt{2}$ and $R=g=1$ into $\cos\theta_0=g/(R\Omega^2)$ and into $\omega=\Omega\sin\theta_0$.

GCM:010218.canonicalSolution:
The Euler–Lagrange derivative is
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta}
=mR^2\ddot\theta,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta}
=mR^2\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-mgR\sin\theta.
\]
Hence
\[
\ddot\theta
=\sin\theta\bigl(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R\bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\ddot\theta=\sin\theta(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R)}.
\]

Equilibria occur at $\sin\theta=0$ or
$\cos\theta=g/(R\Omega^2)$. Thus $\theta=0$ (bottom) and
$\theta=\pi$ (top) are always present, while off-axis roots exist
precisely when $\Omega>\Omega_c:=\sqrt{g/R}$. Linearizing at the
bottom gives
\[
\ddot\theta=(\Omega^2-g/R)\theta,
\]
so the bottom is oscillatory for $\Omega<\Omega_c$ and has
exponential growth rate $\sqrt{\Omega^2-g/R}$ for
$\Omega>\Omega_c$. At the top, $\phi:=\theta-\pi$ satisfies
\[
\ddot\phi=(\Omega^2+g/R)\phi,
\]
which is unstable for every $\Omega$.
\[
\boxed{\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R};\ \text{bottom growth }\sqrt{\Omega^2-g/R};\ \text{top always unstable}}.
\]

At an off-axis root $\Omega^2\cos\theta_0=g/R$, the derivative of
the right-hand side is $-\Omega^2\sin^2\theta_0$, so
\[
\ddot\delta=-(\Omega\sin\theta_0)^2\delta.
\]
The off-axis equilibria are linearly stable with small frequency
$\Omega\sin\theta_0$.
\[
\boxed{\cos\theta_0=g/(R\Omega^2),\ \omega=\Omega\sin\theta_0}.
\]

Now set $m=R=g=1$ and $\Omega=\sqrt{2}$. Then
$\cos\theta_0=1/2$, so $\theta_0=\pm\pi/3$, and
\[
\omega=\sqrt{2}\cdot\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
=\sqrt{3/2}.
\]
The bottom growth rate is $\sqrt{2-1}=1$.
\[
\boxed{\theta_0=\pm\pi/3,\;\omega=\sqrt{3/2},\;\text{bottom growth }=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) misreads $\cos^{-1}(1/2)$ as $\pi/6$. Sentence (ii)
replaces $\Omega\sin\theta_0$ by $\Omega\cos\theta_0$ and reports
$1/\sqrt{2}$ instead of $\sqrt{3/2}$. The construction is a
rotating-hoop pitchfork audit; it is not an Euler–Poincaré rigid
body, a Dirac–Bergmann chain, or a standard-map calculation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The equation is $\ddot\theta=\sin\theta(\Omega^2\cos\theta-g/R)$ with $\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/R}$. Off-axis roots have $\cos\theta_0=g/(R\Omega^2)$ and frequency $\Omega\sin\theta_0$. At $m=R=g=1$, $\Omega=\sqrt{2}$ one has $\theta_0=\pm\pi/3$, $\omega=\sqrt{3/2}$, and bottom growth $1$.
Because cos theta0=1/2 I take theta0=+-pi/6. I do not report theta0=+-pi/3.
The off-axis frequency is Omega cos theta0=1/sqrt(2). I never obtain Omega sin theta0=sqrt(3/2).
