GED:010626.title: Uniform-field hyperbolic motion from rest has γ=√(1+(t/τ)²) and proper time τ ln 2 at t=3τ/4
GED:010626.objective: For a charge qE>0 released from rest in a uniform electric field, prove τ=mc/qE, p=qEt, γ=√(1+(t/τ)²), β=t/√(t²+τ²), x=c(√(t²+τ²)-τ), proper acceleration qE/m, and that t=3τ/4 gives γ=5/4, β=3/5, x=cτ/4, and proper time τ ln 2.
GED:010626.statement:
A particle of charge $q$ and rest mass $m$ is released from rest
at the origin in a uniform electric field $\mathbf{E}=E\hat{\mathbf{x}}$
with $qE>0$. Radiation reaction is not included: the Minkowski
force is the Lorentz force alone.

1. Introduce the characteristic time $\tau=mc/qE$ and prove
   \[
   p=qEt,\qquad
   \gamma=\sqrt{1+(t/\tau)^2},\qquad
   \beta=\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}},
   \]
   \[
   x=c\bigl(\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}-\tau\bigr),
   \]
   together with the constant proper acceleration $qE/m$.

2. Specialize to the laboratory time $t=3\tau/4$ and prove
   \[
   \gamma=\frac54,\qquad
   \beta=\frac35,\qquad
   x=\frac{c\tau}{4},
   \]
   and that the elapsed proper time from release is $\tau\ln 2$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the motion is Newtonian, so
   $x=\frac12(qE/m)t^2$ and $\gamma$ is not $5/4$ at $t=3\tau/4$”;
   (ii) “this is the Abraham–Lorentz runaway or a future boundary
   condition, so the proper time is not $\tau\ln 2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by an Abraham–Lorentz runaway, by
a relativistic beaming-denominator radiation integral, by a
waveguide iris, by a Rayleigh sphere, by a Lorentz oscillator,
or by a negative-index wave. Do not reopen, import, or execute
any of the six existing intake seeds, and do not substitute an
undergraduate Electrodynamics 1 or Electrodynamics 2 constant-field
kinematics drill.
permittedResults: If $p=qEt$ then $\gamma\beta=t/\tau$. The identity $\gamma^2-\gamma^2\beta^2=1$ rearranges to $\gamma=\sqrt{1+(t/\tau)^2}$.
The proper-time integral $\int_0^{3\tau/4}dt/\gamma=\tau\,\mathrm{arsinh}(3/4)$ equals $\tau\ln 2$ because $\mathrm{arsinh}(3/4)=\ln 2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate dp/dt=qE from rest, convert γβ=t/τ into γ and β, then integrate βc for x.
Insert t=3τ/4 into the closed forms and evaluate arsinh(3/4) as ln(3/4+5/4)=ln 2.

milestones.criterion: Derives τ=mc/qE, p=qEt, γ=√(1+(t/τ)²), β=t/√(t²+τ²), x=c(√(t²+τ²)-τ), and proper acceleration qE/m.
Evaluates γ=5/4, β=3/5, x=cτ/4, and proper time τ ln 2 at t=3τ/4.
Rejects Newtonian kinematics and refuses an Abraham–Lorentz runaway or future-boundary substitution.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the relativistic orbit by the Newtonian parabola x=(1/2)(qE/m)t², so γ is not 5/4 at t=3τ/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities γ=√(1+(t/τ)²), x=c(√(t²+τ²)-τ), and the sample values γ=5/4, x=cτ/4 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Lorentz-force hyperbola by the Abraham–Lorentz runaway or a future boundary condition, and denies that the proper time is τ ln 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned initial-value kinematics and the identity τ_p=τ ln 2 are lost, and the six-seed runaway fence is crossed.

hintTree.content: $dp/dt=qE$ and $p(0)=0$ give $p=qEt$. Then $\gamma\beta=t/\tau$ and $\gamma=\sqrt{1+(t/\tau)^2}$.
$dx/dt=\beta c=ct/\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}$ integrates to $x=c(\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}-\tau)$ if $x(0)=0$.
At $t=3\tau/4$ one has $\gamma=5/4$ and $\beta=3/5$. The proper time is $\tau\ln\bigl(3/4+5/4\bigr)=\tau\ln 2$.

GED:010626.canonicalSolution:
The laboratory force is the constant $qE$, so
\[
\frac{dp}{dt}=qE,\qquad p(0)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p=qEt.
\]
The characteristic time $\tau=mc/qE$ converts this to
\[
\gamma\beta=\frac{p}{mc}=\frac{t}{\tau}.
\]
The identity $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ then gives
$\gamma^2-1=(t/\tau)^2$, hence
\[
\gamma=\sqrt{1+\Bigl(\frac{t}{\tau}\Bigr)^2},\qquad
\beta=\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}}.
\]
The laboratory velocity is $dx/dt=\beta c$, so
\[
x=c\int_0^t\frac{s\,ds}{\sqrt{s^2+\tau^2}}
=c\bigl(\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}-\tau\bigr),
\]
using $x(0)=0$. The proper acceleration is the Minkowski
magnitude of the four-acceleration $du^{\mu}/d\tau_{\mathrm{p}}$, which for a pure
electric field on this orbit is the constant
\[
\alpha=\frac{qE}{m}=\frac{c}{\tau}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau=mc/qE,\ p=qEt,\
\gamma=\sqrt{1+(t/\tau)^2},\
\beta=t/\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2},\
x=c(\sqrt{t^2+\tau^2}-\tau),\
\alpha=qE/m}.
\]

Now set $t=3\tau/4$:
\[
\gamma=\sqrt{1+\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr)^2}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{16}}=\frac54,
\]
\[
\beta=\frac{3\tau/4}{\sqrt{(9/16)\tau^2+\tau^2}}
=\frac{3/4}{5/4}=\frac35,
\]
\[
x=c\Bigl(\tau\cdot\frac54-\tau\Bigr)=\frac{c\tau}{4}.
\]
The elapsed proper time is
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{p}}
=\int_0^{3\tau/4}\frac{dt}{\gamma}
=\int_0^{3\tau/4}\frac{dt}{\sqrt{1+(t/\tau)^2}}
=\tau\,\mathrm{arsinh}\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr).
\]
Because
\[
\mathrm{arsinh}\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr)
=\ln\Bigl(\frac34+\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{16}}\Bigr)
=\ln\Bigl(\frac34+\frac54\Bigr)=\ln 2,
\]
one has $\tau_{\mathrm{p}}=\tau\ln 2$.
\[
\boxed{t=3\tau/4:\ \gamma=5/4,\ \beta=3/5,\
x=c\tau/4,\ \tau_{\mathrm{p}}=\tau\ln 2}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the orbit by the Newtonian parabola
$x=\frac12(qE/m)t^2$ and cannot recover $\gamma=5/4$. Sentence
(ii) replaces the Lorentz-force hyperbola by the
Abraham–Lorentz runaway (or a future boundary condition) and
loses $\tau\ln 2$.

The argument never replaces the assigned uniform-field hyperbola
by an Abraham–Lorentz runaway, by a relativistic beaming
radiation integral, by an iris $S$-matrix, by a Rayleigh sphere,
by a Lorentz oscillator, or by a negative-index wave, and it
does not open any of the six existing intake seeds or an
undergraduate Electrodynamics 1 / Electrodynamics 2 substitute.

At $t=3\tau/4$ one has $\gamma=5/4$, $\beta=3/5$, $x=c\tau/4$, and proper time $\tau\ln 2$. This is not an Abraham–Lorentz runaway.

GED:010629.title: Penning modes at ωc=5Ω and ωz=2√2 Ω split as ω+=4Ω and ω−=Ω with product 4Ω²
GED:010629.objective: For a Penning trap with ωc=5Ω and ωz=2√2 Ω, prove the radial discriminant ωc²-2ωz²=9Ω², the normal frequencies ω±=(ωc±√(ωc²-2ωz²))/2 equal to 4Ω and Ω, the sum ω++ω−=5Ω, and the product ω+ω−=4Ω².
GED:010629.statement:
A single charged particle is confined in an ideal Penning trap
with cyclotron frequency $\omega_c=5\Omega$ and axial frequency
$\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$, where $\Omega>0$ is a reference
frequency. The radial normal frequencies are
\[
\omega_\pm=\frac{\omega_c\pm\sqrt{\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2}}{2}.
\]
Do not replace the calculation by an Abraham--Lorentz runaway or
future-boundary radiation-reaction law, a punctured-domain gauge
holonomy, a Green-reciprocity slogan, a relativistic beaming
factor, a cavity-mode completeness argument, or a
Kramers--Kronig half-plane audit. Do not substitute the
undergraduate Electrodynamics~1 cyclotron-only motion
$\omega=\omega_c$ with no magnetron branch.

1. Evaluate the radial discriminant and prove
   \[
   \omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2=9\Omega^2.
   \]
   Confirm the stability inequality $\omega_c^2>2\omega_z^2$.

2. Compute the two radial roots and prove
   \[
   \omega_+=4\Omega,\qquad\omega_-=\Omega.
   \]
   Identify $\omega_+$ as the modified cyclotron frequency and
   $\omega_-$ as the magnetron frequency. The axial frequency
   remains $\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$.

3. Prove the elementary symmetric identities
   \[
   \omega_++\omega_-=\omega_c=5\Omega,\qquad
   \omega_+\omega_-=\frac{\omega_z^2}{2}=4\Omega^2,
   \]
   without recomputing the square root.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the discriminant is
   $\omega_c^2-4\omega_z^2$ or $\omega_c^2-\omega_z^2$, so the
   roots are not $4\Omega$ and $\Omega$”; (ii) “there is only the
   bare cyclotron frequency $\omega_c$, so the magnetron root
   $\Omega$ and the product $4\Omega^2$ do not exist.”
permittedResults: With $\omega_c=5\Omega$ and $\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$ one has $\omega_z^2=8\Omega^2$ and $\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2=25\Omega^2-16\Omega^2=9\Omega^2$.
The roots of $\omega^2-\omega_c\omega+\omega_z^2/2=0$ then satisfy $\omega_+=(5\Omega+3\Omega)/2=4\Omega$, $\omega_-=(5\Omega-3\Omega)/2=\Omega$, and $\omega_+\omega_-=4\Omega^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute omega_c^2-2 omega_z^2 from 25 Omega^2 and 2*(8 Omega^2), then take (5±3)Omega/2.
Read the sum and product from the characteristic polynomial without a second square root.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the discriminant omega_c^2-2 omega_z^2=9 Omega^2 and the split omega_+=4 Omega, omega_-=Omega.
Proves the Vieta identities sum=5 Omega and product=4 Omega^2 from omega_c and omega_z^2/2.
Rejects a corrupted discriminant and refuses a cyclotron-only collapse that erases the magnetron root.

commonErrors.description: Uses the discriminant ωc²-4ωz² or ωc²-ωz² instead of ωc²-2ωz², so the roots are not 4Ω and Ω.
commonErrors.consequence: The required split ω+=4Ω, ω−=Ω and the product 4Ω² fail.

commonErrors.description: Collapses the radial motion to the bare cyclotron frequency ωc and denies the magnetron root Ω and the product 4Ω².
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned two-root Penning ledger is replaced by undergraduate cyclotron-only motion.

hintTree.content: Compute $\omega_z^2=(2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega)^2=8\Omega^2$ and $\omega_c^2=25\Omega^2$. The discriminant is $25\Omega^2-16\Omega^2=9\Omega^2$.
Then $\sqrt{\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2}=3\Omega$, so $\omega_\pm=(5\pm3)\Omega/2$.
Vieta gives $\omega_++\omega_-=\omega_c=5\Omega$ and $\omega_+\omega_-=\omega_z^2/2=4\Omega^2$ without a second square root.

GED:010629.canonicalSolution:
The assigned frequencies are $\omega_c=5\Omega$ and
$\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$, so
\[
\omega_c^2=25\Omega^2,\qquad
\omega_z^2=8\Omega^2,\qquad
2\omega_z^2=16\Omega^2.
\]
The radial discriminant is
\[
\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2=25\Omega^2-16\Omega^2=9\Omega^2>0,
\]
so the trap is radially stable.
\[
\boxed{\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2=9\Omega^2}.
\]

The square root is $3\Omega$. The radial roots are therefore
\[
\omega_+=\frac{5\Omega+3\Omega}{2}=4\Omega,\qquad
\omega_-=\frac{5\Omega-3\Omega}{2}=\Omega.
\]
Thus $\omega_+$ is the modified cyclotron frequency and
$\omega_-$ is the magnetron frequency. The axial frequency is
unchanged: $\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$.
\[
\boxed{\omega_+=4\Omega,\quad\omega_-=\Omega}.
\]

Vieta's formulae on $\omega^2-\omega_c\omega+\omega_z^2/2=0$
give, independently of the square-root evaluation,
\[
\omega_++\omega_-=\omega_c=5\Omega,\qquad
\omega_+\omega_-=\frac{\omega_z^2}{2}=\frac{8\Omega^2}{2}=4\Omega^2.
\]
Both identities are compatible with $4\Omega+\Omega=5\Omega$ and
$4\Omega\cdot\Omega=4\Omega^2$.
\[
\boxed{\omega_++\omega_-=5\Omega,\quad\omega_+\omega_-=4\Omega^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) corrupts the coefficient of $\omega_z^2$ in the
discriminant and cannot recover the split $4\Omega,\Omega$.
Sentence (ii) collapses the radial dynamics to the bare
cyclotron frequency and erases the magnetron root.

The argument never reopens an Abraham--Lorentz runaway, a reserved
seed mechanism, or an Electrodynamics~1 cyclotron-only
undergraduate inventory.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $\omega_c=5\Omega$ and $\omega_z=2\sqrt{2}\,\Omega$ the discriminant is $\omega_c^2-2\omega_z^2=9\Omega^2$. The roots are $\omega_+=4\Omega$ and $\omega_-=\Omega$. Their sum is $5\Omega$ and their product is $4\Omega^2$.
The discriminant is omega_c^2-4 omega_z^2 or omega_c^2-omega_z^2, so the roots are not 4 Omega and Omega. I do not accept the product 4 Omega^2.
There is only the bare cyclotron frequency omega_c. The magnetron root Omega and the product 4 Omega^2 do not exist.

GQM:010117.title: Cyclic e1 on the Jacobi matrix [[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]] has weights 1/4,1/2,1/4 and G11(3)=8/21
GQM:010117.objective: For H=[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]] and cyclic seed e1 prove eigenvalues -sqrt(2),0,sqrt(2), spectral weights 1/4,1/2,1/4, Stieltjes transform G11(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)), G11(3)=8/21, and moments m0..m4=(1,0,1,0,2).
GQM:010117.statement:
Work on $\mathbb{C}^3$ with the standard Hermitian inner product,
linear in the second argument. Let
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
and take the cyclic seed $e_1=(1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$. Do not replace the
spectral-measure ledger by a self-adjoint interval-momentum domain
problem, a singular radial endpoint, or a partial-wave optical
theorem / absorption identity.

1. Prove that the spectrum of $H$ is
   \[
   \sigma(H)=\{-\sqrt{2},\,0,\,\sqrt{2}\},
   \]
   that $e_1$ is cyclic for $H$, and that the spectral weights of
   $e_1$ are
   \[
   w(-\sqrt{2})=\frac14,\qquad
   w(0)=\frac12,\qquad
   w(\sqrt{2})=\frac14.
   \]

2. For the scalar Stieltjes transform
   $G_{11}(z)=\langle e_1|(z-H)^{-1}|e_1\rangle$ prove
   \[
   G_{11}(z)=\frac{z^2-1}{z(z^2-2)}
   \]
   off the spectrum, and evaluate
   \[
   G_{11}(3)=\frac{8}{21}.
   \]

3. Compute the power moments
   $m_n=\langle e_1|H^n|e_1\rangle$ for $n=0,1,2,3,4$ and prove
   \[
   (m_0,m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4)=(1,0,1,0,2).
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the three spectral weights of $e_1$
   are equal, so each is $1/3$ rather than $1/4,1/2,1/4$”; (ii) “the
   Stieltjes transform is $(z^2-2)/(z(z^2-1))$, so $G_{11}(3)=7/24$
   rather than $8/21$.”
permittedResults: $\det(H-\lambda I)=-\lambda(\lambda^2-2)$, so $\sigma(H)=\{-\sqrt{2},0,\sqrt{2}\}$. Normalized eigenvectors for $e_1$ give weights $1/4,1/2,1/4$.
$G_{11}(z)=\frac14/(z+\sqrt{2})+\frac12/z+\frac14/(z-\sqrt{2})=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2))$. At $z=3$ one obtains $8/21$. Direct matrix powers give $(m_0,\dots,m_4)=(1,0,1,0,2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize the 3x3 Jacobi matrix, normalize eigenvectors, and square first components to obtain the atomic spectral measure of e1.
Sum the three simple poles into G11(z), evaluate at z=3, and cross-check moments by direct matrix powers of H.

milestones.criterion: Produces sigma(H)={-sqrt(2),0,sqrt(2)}, cyclic weights 1/4,1/2,1/4, and G11(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)).
Reports G11(3)=8/21 and the moment tuple (1,0,1,0,2).
Rejects equal-weight 1/3 claims or an inverted Stieltjes rational function, and refuses reserved interval-momentum, radial-endpoint, or optical-theorem substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the three spectral weights of e1 are equal and reports each weight as 1/3 instead of 1/4,1/2,1/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The correct atomic measure, the Stieltjes transform (z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)), and the moment ledger (1,0,1,0,2) are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the Stieltjes rational function to (z^2-2)/(z(z^2-1)) and reports G11(3)=7/24 instead of 8/21.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity G11(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)) and the sample value 8/21 are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

hintTree.content: Expand $\det(H-\lambda I)$ along the first row (or use the tridiagonal recurrence). The characteristic polynomial factors as $-\lambda(\lambda^2-2)$.
For $\lambda=\pm\sqrt{2}$ the normalized eigenvectors are $(1,\pm\sqrt{2},1)/2$; for $\lambda=0$ one has $(1,0,-1)/\sqrt{2}$. Square the first components to read the weights.
Combine the three simple poles into a single rational function, or compute $(z-H)^{-1}_{11}$ by Cramer's rule. Moments follow from $H^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,1)$ block form and $H^4=(H^2)^2$.

GQM:010117.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic matrix is
\[
H-\lambda I
=\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&1&0\\1&-\lambda&1\\0&1&-\lambda\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding along the first row gives
\[
\det(H-\lambda I)
=-\lambda\bigl(\lambda^2-1\bigr)-1\cdot(-\lambda)
=-\lambda^3+2\lambda
=-\lambda(\lambda^2-2).
\]
Hence
\[
\sigma(H)=\{-\sqrt{2},\,0,\,\sqrt{2}\}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma(H)=\{-\sqrt{2},0,\sqrt{2}\}}.
\]

For $\lambda=\sqrt{2}$, the eigenvector equation yields
$v\propto(1,\sqrt{2},1)$. Normalizing by $\|v\|=2$ produces
\[
u_+=\Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\tfrac12\Bigr)^{\mathsf T},
\]
so $w(\sqrt{2})=|\langle e_1|u_+\rangle|^2=1/4$. The same computation
with $\lambda=-\sqrt{2}$ produces
$u_-=(1/2,-\sqrt{2}/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T}$ and weight $1/4$. For
$\lambda=0$ one finds $u_0=(1,0,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2}$ and weight
$1/2$. The three eigenvectors are orthonormal and span
$\mathbb{C}^3$, so $e_1$ is cyclic and
\[
\mu_{e_1}
=\frac14\,\delta_{-\sqrt{2}}
+\frac12\,\delta_{0}
+\frac14\,\delta_{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{w(-\sqrt{2})=1/4,\;w(0)=1/2,\;w(\sqrt{2})=1/4}.
\]

The Stieltjes transform is therefore
\begin{align*}
G_{11}(z)
&=\frac{1/4}{z+\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1/2}{z}+\frac{1/4}{z-\sqrt{2}}\\
&=\frac{z}{2(z^2-2)}+\frac{1}{2z}
=\frac{z^2-1}{z(z^2-2)}.
\end{align*}
At the sample point $z=3$,
\[
G_{11}(3)=\frac{9-1}{3(9-2)}=\frac{8}{21}.
\]
\[
\boxed{G_{11}(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)),\;G_{11}(3)=8/21}.
\]

Direct powers give $m_0=\|e_1\|^2=1$ and $m_1=H_{11}=0$. One has
\[
H^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&2&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
so $m_2=(H^2)_{11}=1$. Next
\[
H^3=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&0\\2&0&2\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
hence $m_3=0$, and
\[
H^4=(H^2)^2=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&4&0\\2&0&2\end{pmatrix},
\]
so $m_4=2$. Equivalently,
$m_n=\frac14(-\sqrt{2})^n+\frac12\cdot 0^n+\frac14(\sqrt{2})^n$
reproduces the same five values.
\[
\boxed{(m_0,m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4)=(1,0,1,0,2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces equal weights $1/3$ and destroys both the
Stieltjes transform and the even-moment ledger. Sentence (ii)
inverts the rational function and reports $G_{11}(3)=7/24$ instead
of $8/21$. The construction is a finite Jacobi spectral-measure
audit for a cyclic seed; it is not an interval-momentum domain
problem, a radial endpoint classification, or an optical-theorem
identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The spectrum is $\sigma(H)=\{-\sqrt{2},0,\sqrt{2}\}$ with $e_1$-weights $1/4,1/2,1/4$. The Stieltjes transform is $G_{11}(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2))$, so $G_{11}(3)=8/21$, and the moments are $(m_0,\dots,m_4)=(1,0,1,0,2)$.
The three spectral weights of e1 are equal, so each is 1/3. I do not report the weights 1/4,1/2,1/4 or the measure that produces G11(3)=8/21.
I take G11(z)=(z^2-2)/(z(z^2-1)), so at z=3 I obtain 7/24. I never obtain G11(z)=(z^2-1)/(z(z^2-2)) or G11(3)=8/21.

GQM:010118.title: Riesz projectors of A=[[1,1],[0,2]] are P1=[[1,-1],[0,0]], P2=[[0,1],[0,1]] and exp((ln2)A)=[[2,2],[0,4]]
GQM:010118.objective: For A=[[1,1],[0,2]] prove the Riesz projectors P1=[[1,-1],[0,0]], P2=[[0,1],[0,1]] are idempotent, algebraically orthogonal, sum to I, not self-adjoint, each of operator norm sqrt(2), that exp(tA)=e^t P1+e^{2t} P2, and at t=ln2 the matrix [[2,2],[0,4]].
GQM:010118.statement:
Let
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}
\]
act on $\mathbb{C}^2$ with the standard Hermitian norm. Do not replace
the nonnormal Riesz calculus by a self-adjoint interval-momentum
domain, a ray/Wigner antiunitary symmetry argument, or a
degenerate/non-Abelian adiabatic transport construction.

1. Prove that the spectrum is $\sigma(A)=\{1,2\}$ and that the Riesz
   spectral projections are
   \[
   P_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   P_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Verify $P_j^2=P_j$, $P_1P_2=P_2P_1=0$, $P_1+P_2=I$, and
   $A=1\cdot P_1+2\cdot P_2$.

2. Prove that neither $P_j$ is self-adjoint, and that each has
   operator norm $\|P_j\|=\sqrt{2}$.

3. Using the holomorphic functional calculus, prove
   \[
   e^{tA}=e^{t}P_1+e^{2t}P_2
   \]
   for all real $t$, and evaluate at $t=\ln 2$ to obtain
   \[
   e^{(\ln 2)A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $A$ is upper triangular the
   projectors are the diagonal matrix units
   $E_{11}=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $E_{22}=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$,
   so $P_1$ is not $[[1,-1],[0,0]]$”; (ii) “at $t=\ln 2$ one has
   $e^{tA}=\operatorname{diag}(2,4)$, so the off-diagonal entry is $0$
   rather than $2$.”
permittedResults: $A-I=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $A-2I=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. The algebraic spectral projections are $P_1=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $P_2=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

$\|P_1 v\|=\lvert x-y\rvert$ for $v=(x,y)$, maximized by $\sqrt{2}$ on the unit circle; likewise $\|P_2\|=\sqrt{2}$. At $t=\ln 2$, $e^{tA}=2P_1+4P_2=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\0&4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify the two eigenlines of the upper-triangular matrix and construct the unique complementary Riesz projectors along those lines.
Apply the holomorphic calculus e^{tA}=e^t P1+e^{2t}P2 and insert t=ln2 to obtain 2P1+4P2.

milestones.criterion: Produces P1=[[1,-1],[0,0]], P2=[[0,1],[0,1]] with the algebraic projector and spectral decomposition identities.
Reports non-self-adjointness, norms sqrt(2), the formula exp(tA)=e^t P1+e^{2t}P2, and the sample matrix [[2,2],[0,4]].
Rejects diagonal matrix-unit projectors or a diagonal-only exponential at t=ln2, and refuses reserved domain, Wigner, or adiabatic substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Riesz projectors by the diagonal matrix units diag(1,0) and diag(0,1), denying P1=[[1,-1],[0,0]].
commonErrors.consequence: The correct nonnormal projectors, their off-diagonal structure, and the exponential sample [[2,2],[0,4]] are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims e^{(ln 2)A}=diag(2,4) with vanishing off-diagonal entry, instead of [[2,2],[0,4]].
commonErrors.consequence: The functional-calculus identity e^{tA}=e^t P1+e^{2t}P2 is misapplied and the assigned sample matrix is wrong.

hintTree.content: The characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)$. Solve $(A-\lambda)v=0$ to identify eigenlines, then build the unique complementary projectors along those lines.
Check the four algebraic projector identities by direct $2\times 2$ multiplication; do not assume $P_j^\dagger=P_j$.
The functional calculus is $e^{tA}=e^t P_1+e^{2t}P_2$. Insert $e^{t}=2$ and $e^{2t}=4$ when $t=\ln 2$.

GQM:010118.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic polynomial is
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda),
\]
so $\sigma(A)=\{1,2\}$. The eigenline for $\lambda=1$ is
$\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\}$ and for $\lambda=2$ is
$\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\}$. The unique complementary
idempotents along these lines are
\[
P_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
P_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Direct multiplication yields
\[
P_1^2=P_1,\quad P_2^2=P_2,\quad
P_1P_2=P_2P_1=0,\quad P_1+P_2=I,
\]
and
\[
1\cdot P_1+2\cdot P_2
=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\0&2\end{pmatrix}
=A.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_1=[[1,-1],[0,0]],\;P_2=[[0,1],[0,1]]}.
\]

Neither projector is self-adjoint:
\[
P_1^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\neq P_1,\qquad
P_2^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\neq P_2.
\]
For $v=(x,y)^{\mathsf T}$ one has $P_1v=(x-y,0)^{\mathsf T}$, so
\[
\|P_1v\|=\lvert x-y\rvert
\le\sqrt{2}\,\|v\|
\]
with equality at $v=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2}$. The same estimate
gives $\|P_2\|=\sqrt{2}$.
\[
\boxed{\|P_1\|=\|P_2\|=\sqrt{2},\ \text{not self-adjoint}}.
\]

Because $A=\lambda_1 P_1+\lambda_2 P_2$ with annihilating idempotents,
the holomorphic functional calculus yields
\[
e^{tA}=e^{t}P_1+e^{2t}P_2.
\]
At $t=\ln 2$ one has $e^{t}=2$ and $e^{2t}=4$, so
\[
e^{(\ln 2)A}
=2P_1+4P_2
=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\0&4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{e^{(\ln 2)A}=[[2,2],[0,4]]}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the true Riesz projectors by diagonal matrix
units and loses the off-diagonal structure of $P_1$. Sentence (ii)
drops that off-diagonal contribution in the exponential and reports
$\operatorname{diag}(2,4)$ instead of $[[2,2],[0,4]]$. The
construction is a nonnormal Riesz/functional-calculus audit; it is
not an interval-momentum domain problem, a Wigner antiunitary
symmetry argument, or an adiabatic transport construction.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Riesz projectors are $P_1=[[1,-1],[0,0]]$ and $P_2=[[0,1],[0,1]]$, idempotent, algebraically orthogonal, summing to $I$, not self-adjoint, each of norm $\sqrt{2}$. The calculus gives $e^{tA}=e^t P_1+e^{2t}P_2$, so at $t=\ln 2$ one has $[[2,2],[0,4]]$.
Because A is upper triangular the projectors are the diagonal matrix units diag(1,0) and diag(0,1). I do not report P1=[[1,-1],[0,0]].
At t=ln2 I take e^{tA}=diag(2,4), so the off-diagonal entry is 0. I never obtain [[2,2],[0,4]].

GQM:010119.title: H=diag(-1,0,1)+2vv^dagger with v=(1,0,1)/sqrt(2) has spectrum 1-sqrt(2),0,1+sqrt(2) and v-weights 1/2∓1/(2sqrt(2))
GQM:010119.objective: For A0=diag(-1,0,1), v=(1,0,1)/sqrt(2), and H=A0+2vv^dagger=[[0,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,2]] prove spectrum 1-sqrt(2),0,1+sqrt(2), trace 2, tr(H^2)=6, positive rank-one interlacing against A0, and v-weights 1/2∓1/(2sqrt(2)) on the lower/upper eigenvalues.
GQM:010119.statement:
Let
\[
A_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,1),\qquad
v=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,0,1)^{\mathsf T},
\]
and define the positive rank-one update
\[
H=A_0+2\,vv^\dagger
=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Do not replace the interlacing ledger by a coupled-spin fermion
exchange calculation, a singular radial endpoint, or a
degenerate/non-Abelian adiabatic transport argument.

1. Prove that
   \[
   \sigma(H)=\{1-\sqrt{2},\,0,\,1+\sqrt{2}\},
   \]
   that $\operatorname{tr} H=2$, and that $\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=6$.

2. State the positive rank-one interlacing relations between
   $\sigma(A_0)=\{-1,0,1\}$ and $\sigma(H)$, and verify them
   numerically for the three eigenvalues.

3. For the spectral measure of the unit vector $v$ relative to $H$,
   prove that the weights on the lower and upper eigenvalues are
   \[
   w(1-\sqrt{2})
   =\frac12-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\qquad
   w(1+\sqrt{2})
   =\frac12+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},
   \]
   with vanishing middle weight $w(0)=0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the spectrum of $H$ is still
   $\{-1,0,1\}$, because a rank-one update cannot move every
   eigenvalue”; (ii) “the lower and upper $v$-weights are swapped,
   so $w(1-\sqrt{2})=1/2+1/(2\sqrt{2})$ rather than
   $1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})$.”
permittedResults: $\det(H-\lambda I)=-\lambda(\lambda^2-2\lambda-1)$, so $\sigma(H)=\{0,1\pm\sqrt{2}\}$. Trace identities give $\operatorname{tr} H=2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=6$.

Eigenvectors for $\lambda_\pm=1\pm\sqrt{2}$ are proportional to $(1,0,\lambda_\pm)$; the resulting $v$-weights are $(2\pm\sqrt{2})/4=1/2\pm 1/(2\sqrt{2})$. The middle eigenvector $(0,1,0)$ is orthogonal to $v$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the characteristic polynomial of the explicit 3x3 matrix H and read tr H and tr(H^2) from the matrix entries.
Normalize the eigenvectors (1,0,lambda_pm), square the overlaps with v, and compare ordered spectra of A0 and H for interlacing.

milestones.criterion: Produces spectrum {1-sqrt(2),0,1+sqrt(2)}, tr H=2, tr(H^2)=6, and the positive rank-one interlacing chain against A0.
Reports v-weights 1/2-1/(2sqrt(2)) and 1/2+1/(2sqrt(2)) on the lower and upper eigenvalues, with w(0)=0.
Rejects an unmoved spectrum or swapped v-weights, and refuses reserved exchange, radial-endpoint, or adiabatic substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the spectrum of H remains {-1,0,1}, denying the shifted eigenvalues 1-sqrt(2) and 1+sqrt(2).
commonErrors.consequence: The required spectrum, the trace identity tr H=2, and the interlacing ledger against A0 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the lower and upper v-weights, reporting w(1-sqrt(2))=1/2+1/(2sqrt(2)) instead of 1/2-1/(2sqrt(2)).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned spectral weights of v on the outer eigenvalues are reversed and no longer match the secular formula.

hintTree.content: Expand $\det(H-\lambda I)$ along the middle row. The factor $-\lambda$ isolates the protected middle eigenvalue $0$.
Compare ordered spectra $-1\le 1-\sqrt{2}\le 0\le 0\le 1\le 1+\sqrt{2}$ to read the interlacing chain.
Normalize $(1,0,\lambda_\pm)$ and compute $|\langle v|u_\pm\rangle|^2=(1+\lambda_\pm)^2/(2(1+\lambda_\pm^2))$, which simplifies to $(2\pm\sqrt{2})/4$.

GQM:010119.canonicalSolution:
First verify the matrix form of the update:
\[
vv^\dagger
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
2vv^\dagger
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
so
\[
H=A_0+2vv^\dagger
=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding $\det(H-\lambda I)$ along the middle row yields
\[
\det(H-\lambda I)
=-\lambda\bigl((-\lambda)(2-\lambda)-1\bigr)
=-\lambda(\lambda^2-2\lambda-1).
\]
The roots are $\lambda=0$ and $\lambda=1\pm\sqrt{2}$, hence
\[
\sigma(H)=\{1-\sqrt{2},\,0,\,1+\sqrt{2}\}.
\]
The diagonal sum is $\operatorname{tr} H=2$. Direct multiplication
gives
\[
H^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&0&0\\2&0&5\end{pmatrix},
\]
so $\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=6$.
\[
\boxed{\sigma(H)=\{1-\sqrt{2},0,1+\sqrt{2}\},\;\operatorname{tr} H=2,\;\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=6}.
\]

Writing $\lambda_1=-1\le\lambda_2=0\le\lambda_3=1$ for $A_0$ and
$\mu_1=1-\sqrt{2}\le\mu_2=0\le\mu_3=1+\sqrt{2}$ for $H$, the positive
rank-one interlacing relations
\[
\lambda_1\le\mu_1\le\lambda_2\le\mu_2\le\lambda_3\le\mu_3
\]
hold because
\[
-1\le 1-\sqrt{2}\le 0\le 0\le 1\le 1+\sqrt{2}.
\]
(The middle eigenvalue is fixed because $v\perp e_2$.)
\[
\boxed{\text{positive rank-one interlacing holds}}.
\]

For $\lambda_\pm=1\pm\sqrt{2}$ the eigenvector equation forces the
middle component to vanish and yields $u_\pm\propto(1,0,\lambda_\pm)$.
Normalizing and pairing with $v=(1,0,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2}$ produces
\[
w(\lambda_\pm)
=\frac{(1+\lambda_\pm)^2}{2(1+\lambda_\pm^2)}
=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{2}}{4}
=\frac12\pm\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.
\]
The middle eigenvector $(0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ is orthogonal to $v$, so
$w(0)=0$. In particular the lower/upper weights are
\[
w(1-\sqrt{2})=\frac12-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\qquad
w(1+\sqrt{2})=\frac12+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{w(1-\sqrt{2})=1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2}),\;w(1+\sqrt{2})=1/2+1/(2\sqrt{2})}.
\]

Sentence (i) freezes the spectrum at $\{-1,0,1\}$ and contradicts
both the characteristic polynomial and the trace identity
$\operatorname{tr} H=2$. Sentence (ii) swaps the lower and upper
$v$-weights. The construction is a positive rank-one interlacing
audit; it is not a coupled-spin exchange problem, a radial endpoint
classification, or an adiabatic transport argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: The matrix is $H=[[0,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,2]]$ with spectrum $1-\sqrt{2},0,1+\sqrt{2}$, $\operatorname{tr} H=2$, and $\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=6$. Positive rank-one interlacing holds against $A_0$, and the $v$-weights are $1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})$ and $1/2+1/(2\sqrt{2})$ on the lower and upper eigenvalues.
The spectrum of H is still {-1,0,1}, because a rank-one update cannot move every eigenvalue. I do not report 1-sqrt(2) or 1+sqrt(2).
The lower and upper v-weights are swapped, so w(1-sqrt(2))=1/2+1/(2sqrt(2)). I never obtain w(1-sqrt(2))=1/2-1/(2sqrt(2)).

GQM:010220.title: On Schwartz space the Weyl pair T(pi/2),B(1) has group-commutator phase -i and TBpsi=e^{i(x-pi/2)}psi(x-pi/2)
GQM:010220.objective: For T(a)=e^{-iaP/hbar} and B(b)=e^{ibX/hbar} on Schwartz space prove TB=e^{-iab/hbar}BT, and at hbar=1,a=pi/2,b=1 obtain the phase -i together with the explicit action TBpsi(x)=e^{i(x-pi/2)}psi(x-pi/2).
GQM:010220.statement:
Work on the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ with the usual
self-adjoint position and momentum operators $X$ and $P$
($\hbar>0$). Define the Weyl translation and boost unitaries
\[
T(a)=e^{-iaP/\hbar},\qquad
B(b)=e^{ibX/\hbar},\qquad a,b\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Do not replace the group-commutator phase by a ray/Wigner
antiunitary symmetry classification, a coupled-spin fermion
exchange, or a partial-wave optical theorem / absorption identity.

1. Prove the Weyl relation
   \[
   T(a)B(b)=e^{-iab/\hbar}\,B(b)T(a)
   \]
   as an identity of operators on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$, and
   identify the group-commutator phase
   $T(a)B(b)T(a)^{-1}B(b)^{-1}=e^{-iab/\hbar}$.

2. Specialize to $\hbar=1$, $a=\pi/2$, $b=1$ and prove that the phase
   equals $-i$.

3. For the same sample parameters, prove the explicit pointwise
   formula
   \[
   \bigl(T(\pi/2)B(1)\psi\bigr)(x)
   =e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\,\psi\bigl(x-\pi/2\bigr)
   \]
   for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the group-commutator phase is
   $e^{+iab/\hbar}$, so at the sample one obtains $+i$ rather than
   $-i$”; (ii) “the composed action is
   $e^{ix}\psi(x-\pi/2)$ with no shift of the phase factor, so the
   formula is not $e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\psi(x-\pi/2)$.”
permittedResults: $(B(b)\psi)(x)=e^{ibx/\hbar}\psi(x)$ and $(T(a)\phi)(x)=\phi(x-a)$ imply $(T(a)B(b)\psi)(x)=e^{ib(x-a)/\hbar}\psi(x-a)$ while $(B(b)T(a)\psi)(x)=e^{ibx/\hbar}\psi(x-a)$.
At $\hbar=1$, $a=\pi/2$, $b=1$ the phase factor is $e^{-i\pi/2}=-i$, and $T(\pi/2)B(1)\psi(x)=e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\psi(x-\pi/2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute T(a)B(b) and B(b)T(a) pointwise on Schwartz functions and read off the central phase e^{-iab/hbar}.
Specialize to hbar=1, a=pi/2, b=1 to obtain the phase -i and the shifted phase factor e^{i(x-pi/2)}.

milestones.criterion: Produces the Weyl relation T(a)B(b)=e^{-iab/hbar}B(b)T(a) and identifies the group-commutator phase e^{-iab/hbar}.
Reports the sample phase -i and the pointwise action e^{i(x-pi/2)}psi(x-pi/2).
Rejects a flipped phase +i or an unshifted phase factor e^{ix}, and refuses reserved Wigner, exchange, or optical-theorem substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Flips the Weyl phase to e^{+iab/hbar} and reports the sample phase +i instead of -i.
commonErrors.consequence: The required group-commutator identity T(a)B(b)=e^{-iab/hbar}B(b)T(a) and the sample phase -i are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims (TB psi)(x)=e^{ix}psi(x-pi/2) with an unshifted phase factor, instead of e^{i(x-pi/2)}psi(x-pi/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The pointwise action of T(a)B(b) is wrong and no longer matches the Weyl relation at the sample parameters.

hintTree.content: Apply $B(b)$ first, then translate the resulting function by $a$. The phase factor is evaluated at the shifted point $x-a$.
Compare with $B(b)T(a)$, which multiplies by $e^{ibx/\hbar}$ after the translation. The ratio of the two phase factors is $e^{-iab/\hbar}$.
Insert $\hbar=1$, $a=\pi/2$, $b=1$ into both the abstract phase and the pointwise formula.

GQM:010220.canonicalSolution:
On Schwartz space the unitary groups act by
\[
\bigl(B(b)\psi\bigr)(x)=e^{ibx/\hbar}\psi(x),\qquad
\bigl(T(a)\phi\bigr)(x)=\phi(x-a).
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\bigl(T(a)B(b)\psi\bigr)(x)
&=e^{ib(x-a)/\hbar}\psi(x-a),\\
\bigl(B(b)T(a)\psi\bigr)(x)
&=e^{ibx/\hbar}\psi(x-a).
\end{align*}
Comparing the two formulas yields
\[
T(a)B(b)
=e^{-iab/\hbar}\,B(b)T(a).
\]
Multiplying on the right by $T(a)^{-1}B(b)^{-1}$ produces the group
commutator identity
\[
T(a)B(b)T(a)^{-1}B(b)^{-1}=e^{-iab/\hbar}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T(a)B(b)=e^{-iab/\hbar}B(b)T(a)}.
\]

At $\hbar=1$, $a=\pi/2$, $b=1$ the phase is
\[
e^{-iab/\hbar}=e^{-i\pi/2}=-i.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{sample phase }=-i}.
\]

The same specialization gives the pointwise action
\[
\bigl(T(\pi/2)B(1)\psi\bigr)(x)
=e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\psi\bigl(x-\pi/2\bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{TB\psi=e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\psi(x-\pi/2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the sign of the Weyl phase and reports $+i$ at
the sample. Sentence (ii) multiplies by $e^{ix}$ after translation
instead of by the correctly shifted factor $e^{i(x-\pi/2)}$. The
construction is a Weyl group-commutator phase audit on Schwartz
space; it is not a Wigner antiunitary classification, a fermion
exchange problem, or an optical-theorem identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Weyl relation is $T(a)B(b)=e^{-iab/\hbar}B(b)T(a)$. At $\hbar=1$, $a=\pi/2$, $b=1$ the phase equals $-i$ and $(TB\psi)(x)=e^{i(x-\pi/2)}\psi(x-\pi/2)$.
The group-commutator phase is e^{+iab/hbar}, so at the sample I obtain +i. I do not report the phase -i.
The composed action is e^{ix}psi(x-pi/2) with no shift of the phase factor. I never obtain e^{i(x-pi/2)}psi(x-pi/2).

GQM:010221.title: In hbar=1 units, dilation of the Gaussian at s=ln2 yields psi_s=2^{-1/2}pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8} with VarX=2, VarP=1/8, product 1/4
GQM:010221.objective: For D=(XP+PX)/2 prove [D,X]=-ihbar X, [D,P]=ihbar P, the action (U(s)psi)(x)=e^{-s/2}psi(e^{-s}x) of U=e^{-isD/hbar}, the conjugations U^dagger X U=e^s X and U^dagger P U=e^{-s}P, and then set hbar=1 to show that the Gaussian pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2} at s=ln2 becomes 2^{-1/2}pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8} with VarX=2, VarP=1/8, variance product 1/4, std product 1/2, and <P^2/2>=1/16.
GQM:010221.statement:
Work on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ with $\hbar>0$ and the dilation
generator
\[
D=\frac{XP+PX}{2}.
\]
Write $U(s)=e^{-isD/\hbar}$ for $s\in\mathbb{R}$. Do not replace the
dilation ledger by a self-adjoint interval-momentum domain, a
ray/Wigner antiunitary symmetry argument, or a degenerate/non-Abelian
adiabatic transport construction.

1. Prove the commutation relations
   \[
   [D,X]=-i\hbar X,\qquad [D,P]=i\hbar P.
   \]

2. Prove that $U(s)$ acts by
   \[
   \bigl(U(s)\psi\bigr)(x)
   =e^{-s/2}\,\psi\bigl(e^{-s}x\bigr),
   \]
   and deduce the conjugations
   \[
   U(s)^\dagger XU(s)=e^{s}X,\qquad
   U(s)^\dagger PU(s)=e^{-s}P.
   \]

3. For this numerical Gaussian ledger, now set $\hbar=1$. Start from
   the normalized Gaussian
   \[
   \psi(x)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}
   \]
   and set $s=\ln 2$. Prove that the dilated state is
   \[
   \psi_s(x)
   =2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8},
   \]
   and evaluate
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}_\psi_s(X)=2,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}_\psi_s(P)=\frac18,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(P)=\frac14,
   \]
   together with the standard-deviation product $1/2$ and the kinetic
   expectation $\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the dilation multiplies position by
   $e^{-s}$ in Heisenberg picture, so
   $U^\dagger XU=e^{-s}X$ rather than $e^{s}X$”; (ii) “at $s=\ln 2$
   one has $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(P)=1/2$
   still, so the variance product is not $1/4$ with
   $\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16$.”
permittedResults: From $[X,P]=i\hbar$ one obtains $[XP+PX,X]=-2i\hbar X$ and $[XP+PX,P]=2i\hbar P$, hence $[D,X]=-i\hbar X$ and $[D,P]=i\hbar P$.

After setting $\hbar=1$ for the numerical ledger, at $s=\ln 2$ the Gaussian $\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$ dilates to $2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8}$ with $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(P)=1/8$, product $1/4$, and $\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the commutators of D with X and P from [X,P]=ihbar, then integrate the Heisenberg equations to obtain the exponential rescalings.
Apply the coordinate formula of U(s) to the seed Gaussian at s=ln2 and rescale the known variances 1/2 by e^{±2s}.

milestones.criterion: Produces [D,X]=-ihbar X, [D,P]=ihbar P, the coordinate action of U(s), and the conjugations e^s X and e^{-s}P.
Reports psi_s=2^{-1/2}pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8} with VarX=2, VarP=1/8, product 1/4, std product 1/2, and <P^2/2>=1/16.
Rejects flipped Heisenberg scaling of X or frozen undilated variances, and refuses reserved domain, Wigner, or adiabatic substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims U^dagger X U=e^{-s}X instead of e^{s}X, flipping the Heisenberg-picture dilation of position.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conjugations, the dilated variance VarX=2, and the consistent VarP=1/8 ledger are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that at s=ln2 both variances remain 1/2, denying VarX=2, VarP=1/8, product 1/4, and <P^2/2>=1/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned dilated Gaussian variance ledger is replaced by the undilated seed values.

hintTree.content: Expand $[XP,X]=X[P,X]=-i\hbar X$ and $[PX,X]=[P,X]X=-i\hbar X$, then divide by $2$. The momentum commutator is analogous.
Differentiate $\psi_s(x)=e^{-s/2}\psi(e^{-s}x)$ in $s$ at $s=0$ and recognize $-iD/\hbar$. Alternatively integrate the Heisenberg equations $\dot X=X$, $\dot P=-P$.
With $\hbar=1$, the seed Gaussian has $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(P)=1/2$. Multiply by $e^{2s}=4$ and $e^{-2s}=1/4$ respectively at $s=\ln 2$.

GQM:010221.canonicalSolution:
Using $[X,P]=i\hbar$ one computes
\begin{align*}
[XP,X]&=X[P,X]=-i\hbar X,\\
[PX,X]&=[P,X]X=-i\hbar X,
\end{align*}
so $[XP+PX,X]=-2i\hbar X$ and therefore
\[
[D,X]=-i\hbar X.
\]
The same algebra with $P$ yields
\[
[XP,P]=[X,P]P=i\hbar P,\qquad
[PX,P]=P[X,P]=i\hbar P,
\]
hence $[D,P]=i\hbar P$.
\[
\boxed{[D,X]=-i\hbar X,\;[D,P]=i\hbar P}.
\]

Define $(\mathcal{U}(s)\psi)(x)=e^{-s/2}\psi(e^{-s}x)$. This is a
strongly continuous unitary group on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, and
differentiating at $s=0$ recovers the generator $-iD/\hbar$.
Consequently $U(s)=\mathcal{U}(s)$. Heisenberg evolution of the
quadratures follows by differentiating
$X(s):=U(s)^\dagger XU(s)$ and $P(s):=U(s)^\dagger PU(s)$:
\[
\frac{d}{ds}X(s)=X(s),\qquad
\frac{d}{ds}P(s)=-P(s),
\]
with solutions $X(s)=e^{s}X$ and $P(s)=e^{-s}P$.
\[
\boxed{U^\dagger XU=e^{s}X,\;U^\dagger PU=e^{-s}P}.
\]

For the numerical ledger now set $\hbar=1$, take
$\psi(x)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$, and set $s=\ln 2$. Then
$e^{-s/2}=2^{-1/2}$ and $e^{-s}=1/2$, so
\[
\psi_s(x)
=2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}
\exp\bigl(-(x/2)^2/2\bigr)
=2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8}.
\]
The seed Gaussian is centered with
$\operatorname{Var}_\psi(X)=\operatorname{Var}_\psi(P)=1/2$. Under the
dilation the variances rescale by $e^{2s}=4$ and $e^{-2s}=1/4$:
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{\psi_s}(X)=2,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\psi_s}(P)=\frac18.
\]
The product is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(P)=\frac14,
\]
the standard-deviation product is $1/2$, and because $\langle P\rangle=0$,
\[
\Bigl\langle\frac{P^2}{2}\Bigr\rangle
=\frac12\operatorname{Var}(P)=\frac{1}{16}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\psi_s=2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8},\;
\operatorname{Var}X=2,\;
\operatorname{Var}P=1/8,\;
\text{product }1/4,\;
\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the Heisenberg rescaling of $X$ to $e^{-s}X$.
Sentence (ii) freezes both variances at the undilated values $1/2$
and never produces the product $1/4$ or $\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16$.
The construction is a dilation-generator audit on a Gaussian; it is
not an interval-momentum domain problem, a Wigner antiunitary
argument, or an adiabatic transport construction.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $[D,X]=-i\hbar X$, $[D,P]=i\hbar P$, $(U(s)\psi)(x)=e^{-s/2}\psi(e^{-s}x)$, $U^\dagger XU=e^{s}X$, and $U^\dagger PU=e^{-s}P$. After setting $\hbar=1$ for the numerical ledger, at $s=\ln 2$ the dilated Gaussian is $2^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/8}$ with $\operatorname{Var}X=2$, $\operatorname{Var}P=1/8$, product $1/4$, std product $1/2$, and $\langle P^2/2\rangle=1/16$.
The dilation multiplies position by e^{-s} in Heisenberg picture, so U^dagger X U=e^{-s}X. I do not report U^dagger X U=e^{s}X.
At s=ln2 one has Var(X)=1/2 and Var(P)=1/2 still. I never obtain VarX=2, VarP=1/8, product 1/4, or <P^2/2>=1/16.

GQM:010231.title: The SU(3) fundamental Casimir is sum Ta^2=4I/3, and exp(i alpha T8) with alpha=4pi/sqrt(3) equals e^{2pi i/3} I
GQM:010231.objective: For Ta=lambda_a/2 prove Tr(Ta Tb)=delta_ab/2 and sum_a Ta^2=4I/3, report the Cartan weights (1/2,1/(2 sqrt 3)), (-1/2,1/(2 sqrt 3)), (0,-1/sqrt 3) with sum 0 and each norm^2=1/3, and show that alpha=4pi/sqrt(3) yields exp(i alpha T8)=e^{2pi i/3} I of determinant 1 and trace 3 e^{2pi i/3}. Distinguish Ta from the Gell-Mann lambda normalization.
GQM:010231.statement:
Let $\lambda_a$ ($a=1,\ldots,8$) be the Gell-Mann matrices, and
define the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ generators in the fundamental
representation by
\[
T_a=\frac{\lambda_a}{2}.
\]
Do not replace the calculation by a ray-symmetry / Wigner
antiunitary argument, a coupled-spin fermion-exchange integral, or
a degenerate / non-Abelian adiabatic holonomy.

1. Using $\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_a\lambda_b)=2\delta_{ab}$, prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}(T_a T_b)=\frac12\delta_{ab}
   \]
   and the quadratic Casimir
   \[
   \sum_{a=1}^8 T_a^2=\frac43 I.
   \]
   Distinguish this normalization from the Gell-Mann matrices
   themselves: $\sum_a\lambda_a^2=16I/3$ is not the assigned
   Casimir.

2. In the ordered Cartan pair $(T_3,T_8)$, prove that the three
   fundamental weights are
   \[
   \Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\Bigr),
   \quad
   \Bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\Bigr),
   \quad
   \Bigl(0,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Bigr).
   \]
   Verify that they sum to $0$ and that each has Euclidean norm
   squared $1/3$.

3. Set $\alpha=4\pi/\sqrt{3}$ and prove
   \[
   \exp(i\alpha T_8)
   =e^{2\pi i/3}\,I,
   \]
   with $\det=1$ and trace $3e^{2\pi i/3}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Casimir is computed with
   $\lambda_a$ rather than $T_a=\lambda_a/2$, so
   $\sum_a T_a^2=16I/3$ or $8I/3$”; (ii) “the clock angle is
   $\alpha=2\pi/\sqrt{3}$, so $\exp(i\alpha T_8)$ is not the
   scalar $e^{2\pi i/3}I$.”
permittedResults: For $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ the fundamental Casimir is $(N^2-1)/(2N)$. At $N=3$ this is $4/3$. Equivalently $\sum_a\lambda_a^2=16I/3$ implies $\sum_a T_a^2=4I/3$.
Each listed weight has norm squared $1/4+1/12=1/3$. The third Cartan value of $T_8$ is $-1/\sqrt{3}$, and $e^{-4\pi i/3}=e^{2\pi i/3}$, so $\exp(i\alpha T_8)$ is scalar.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pass from Tr(lambda_a lambda_b)=2 delta_ab to the T_a=lambda_a/2 generators, then invoke C2=(N^2-1)/(2N) at N=3.
Read the weights from the diagonal of (T3,T8) and reduce exp(i alpha T8) by e^{-4pi i/3}=e^{2pi i/3}.

milestones.criterion: Produces Tr(Ta Tb)=delta_ab/2 and the Casimir sum Ta^2=4I/3, distinguishing Ta from lambda_a.
Reports the three Cartan weights with sum 0 and each norm^2=1/3, and the clock identity exp(i alpha T8)=e^{2pi i/3} I at alpha=4pi/sqrt(3).
Rejects a Gell-Mann-normalized Casimir or a halved clock angle, and refuses reserved Wigner, exchange, or adiabatic substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Computes the Casimir with lambda_a rather than Ta=lambda_a/2 and reports sum Ta^2=16I/3 or 8I/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity sum Ta^2=4I/3 is lost, and the Ta versus lambda distinction is not made.

commonErrors.description: Uses the halved angle alpha=2pi/sqrt(3), so exp(i alpha T8) is not the scalar e^{2pi i/3} I.

hintTree.content: Halve the Gell-Mann matrices before forming the Killing-type trace or the Casimir sum. A leftover factor of $2$ or $4$ is the standard normalization trap.
Read the three diagonal pairs from $T_3=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)/2$ and $T_8=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2)/(2\sqrt{3})$.
Compute $\alpha T_8=(2\pi/3)\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2)$. The third entry $e^{-4\pi i/3}$ equals $e^{2\pi i/3}$.

GQM:010231.canonicalSolution:
The Gell-Mann orthogonality $\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_a\lambda_b)=2\delta_{ab}$
and the definition $T_a=\lambda_a/2$ immediately give
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(T_a T_b)
=\frac14\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_a\lambda_b)
=\frac12\delta_{ab}.
\]
The quadratic Casimir of the defining representation of
$\mathrm{SU}(N)$ is $(N^2-1)/(2N)$. For $N=3$ this is $4/3$, so
\[
\sum_{a=1}^8 T_a^2=\frac43 I.
\]
Equivalently, the matrix identity $\sum_a\lambda_a^2=16I/3$
together with $T_a=\lambda_a/2$ yields the same scalar $4/3$.
The Gell-Mann matrices themselves are not the generators: using
$\lambda_a$ in place of $T_a$ produces $16I/3$, and using a mixed
normalization produces $8I/3$. Neither is the assigned Casimir.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Tr}(T_a T_b)=\delta_{ab}/2,\quad \sum_a T_a^2=4I/3}.
\]

The Cartan generators in the fundamental representation are
\[
T_3
=\frac12\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0),
\qquad
T_8
=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2).
\]
Their joint eigenvalues on the ordered basis are the weights
\[
\Bigl(\frac12,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\Bigr),
\quad
\Bigl(-\frac12,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\Bigr),
\quad
\Bigl(0,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Bigr).
\]
The vector sum is
\[
\Bigl(\frac12-\frac12+0,\;
\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Bigr)
=(0,0).
\]
Each Euclidean norm squared equals $1/3$:
\[
\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\Bigr)^2
=\frac14+\frac{1}{12}
=\frac13,
\]
and
\[
0+\Bigl(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Bigr)^2
=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{weights }(1/2,1/(2\sqrt{3})),\ (-1/2,1/(2\sqrt{3})),\ (0,-1/\sqrt{3});\ \text{sum }0,\ \text{each }\|w\|^2=1/3}.
\]

Now set $\alpha=4\pi/\sqrt{3}$. Then
\[
\alpha T_8
=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2)
=\frac{2\pi}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2).
\]
The exponential is diagonal with entries
\[
e^{2\pi i/3},\qquad
e^{2\pi i/3},\qquad
e^{-4\pi i/3}.
\]
The third phase reduces as $e^{-4\pi i/3}=e^{2\pi i/3}$, hence
\[
\exp(i\alpha T_8)
=e^{2\pi i/3}\,I.
\]
The determinant is $(e^{2\pi i/3})^3=e^{2\pi i}=1$, and the trace
is $3e^{2\pi i/3}$.
\[
\boxed{\alpha=4\pi/\sqrt{3}:\ \exp(i\alpha T_8)=e^{2\pi i/3}I,\ \det=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}=3e^{2\pi i/3}}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses $T_a$ with $\lambda_a$ and reports $16I/3$
or $8I/3$. Sentence (ii) halves the clock angle and never obtains
the scalar matrix $e^{2\pi i/3}I$. The construction is a
fundamental $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Casimir and Cartan-weight audit; it
is not a Wigner antiunitary argument, not a fermion-exchange
integral, and not a degenerate / non-Abelian adiabatic holonomy.

graderFixtures.proofText: The generators $T_a=\lambda_a/2$ satisfy $\operatorname{Tr}(T_a T_b)=\delta_{ab}/2$ and $\sum_a T_a^2=4I/3$. The Cartan weights are $(1/2,1/(2\sqrt{3}))$, $(-1/2,1/(2\sqrt{3}))$, and $(0,-1/\sqrt{3})$, summing to $0$, each of norm squared $1/3$. At $\alpha=4\pi/\sqrt{3}$ one has $\exp(i\alpha T_8)=e^{2\pi i/3}I$ with determinant $1$ and trace $3e^{2\pi i/3}$.
The Casimir is computed with lambda_a rather than Ta=lambda_a/2, so sum Ta^2=16I/3 or 8I/3. I do not report sum Ta^2=4I/3.
The clock angle is alpha=2pi/sqrt(3), so exp(i alpha T8) is not the scalar e^{2pi i/3} I. I never accept det=1 with trace 3 e^{2pi i/3} at alpha=4pi/sqrt(3).

GQM:010322.title: The j=1 Wigner d-matrix at pi/2 maps |1> to amplitudes (1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2) with <Jx>=hbar, <Jy>=0, and Var Jz=hbar^2/2
GQM:010322.objective: For j=1 prove d^1(pi/2)=(1/2)[[1,-sqrt(2),1],[sqrt(2),0,-sqrt(2)],[1,sqrt(2),1]], that this matrix is unitary of determinant 1, and that the image of |1> has amplitudes (1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2), probabilities (1/4, 1/2, 1/4), <Jz>=0, Var Jz=hbar^2/2, <Jx>=hbar, and <Jy>=0.
GQM:010322.statement:
Work in the standard $j=1$ angular-momentum basis ordered
$\{|1\rangle,|0\rangle,|-1\rangle\}$, with $J_z|m\rangle=m\hbar|m\rangle$
and $J_{\pm}|m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm 1)}\,|m\pm 1\rangle$.
The active rotation about $\hat y$ is represented by the real Wigner
$d$-matrix $d^{1}(\beta)$ whose rows and columns are labelled in the
same $m=1,0,-1$ order. Do not replace the calculation by a ray-symmetry
or Wigner antiunitary argument, and do not recast the problem as a
self-adjoint momentum domain on a finite interval.

1. Evaluate $d^{1}(\pi/2)$ from the elementary formulae
   \[
   d^{1}_{11}=\frac{1+\cos\beta}{2},\quad
   d^{1}_{10}=-\frac{\sin\beta}{\sqrt{2}},\quad
   d^{1}_{1,-1}=\frac{1-\cos\beta}{2},\quad
   d^{1}_{00}=\cos\beta
   \]
   (and the remaining entries by $d^{j}_{m'm}(\beta)=(-1)^{m'-m}d^{j}_{mm'}(\beta)=d^{j}_{-m,-m'}(\beta)$)
   and prove
   \[
   d^{1}(\pi/2)
   =\frac12
   \begin{pmatrix}
   1&-\sqrt{2}&1\\
   \sqrt{2}&0&-\sqrt{2}\\
   1&\sqrt{2}&1
   \end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Show that this real matrix is unitary and that $\det d^{1}(\pi/2)=1$.

2. Apply the matrix to the highest-weight ket $|1\rangle$ and prove that
   the rotated amplitudes in the ordered basis are
   \[
   \Bigl(\tfrac12,\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\;\tfrac12\Bigr)
   \]
   with occupation probabilities $\bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14\bigr)$.

3. On that same rotated state prove
   \[
   \langle J_z\rangle=0,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var} J_z=\frac{\hbar^2}{2},\qquad
   \langle J_x\rangle=\hbar,\qquad
   \langle J_y\rangle=0.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the physical rotation is $d^{1}(-\pi/2)$,
   so the amplitudes are $(1/2,-1/\sqrt{2},1/2)$ and $\langle J_x\rangle=-\hbar$”;
   (ii) “the $m=\pm 1$ probabilities each contribute $\hbar^2/4$ already
   as a variance, so $\operatorname{Var} J_z=\hbar^2/4$ rather than
   $\hbar^2/2$.”
permittedResults: On $|\psi\rangle=(1/2)|1\rangle+(1/\sqrt{2})|0\rangle+(1/2)|-1\rangle$ one has $\langle J_+\rangle=\langle J_-\rangle=\hbar$, hence $\langle J_x\rangle=\hbar$ and $\langle J_y\rangle=0$, while $\langle J_z^2\rangle=\hbar^2/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Specialize the four independent j=1 d-entries at beta=pi/2, complete the matrix by the standard sign identities, and read the image of |1> from the first column.
Convert amplitudes to probabilities for the Jz moments, then evaluate <J+> and <J-> on the j=1 ladder to obtain <Jx>=hbar and <Jy>=0.

milestones.criterion: Produces d^1(pi/2)=(1/2)[[1,-sqrt(2),1],[sqrt(2),0,-sqrt(2)],[1,sqrt(2),1]], verifies unitarity and det=1, and reads the first-column amplitudes (1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2) with probabilities (1/4, 1/2, 1/4).
Reports <Jz>=0, Var Jz=hbar^2/2, <Jx>=hbar, and <Jy>=0 on the rotated state.
Rejects a negative-angle / transposed d-matrix or a variance hbar^2/4, and refuses reserved ray-symmetry / antiunitary or interval-momentum substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces d^1(pi/2) by d^1(-pi/2) or by its transpose and reports amplitudes (1/2, -1/sqrt(2), 1/2) with <Jx>=-hbar.
commonErrors.consequence: The required first-column amplitudes (1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2) and the moment <Jx>=hbar are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats a single m=±1 channel as the full second moment and reports Var Jz=hbar^2/4 instead of hbar^2/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required variance hbar^2/2 is replaced by half of the correct second moment.

hintTree.content: Substitute $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ and $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ into the four independent $d^{1}$ entries, then fill the remaining five by the standard sign/reflection identities.
The image of $|1\rangle$ is the first column. Probabilities are the squared moduli; they are $(1/4,1/2,1/4)$, not the amplitudes themselves.
Compute $\langle J_{\pm}\rangle$ with $J_{\pm}|m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{2}\,|m\pm 1\rangle$ on the $j=1$ ladder. Variance uses $\langle J_z^2\rangle=\hbar^2(p_1+p_{-1})=\hbar^2/2$.

GQM:010322.canonicalSolution:
The four independent $j=1$ reduced matrix elements at $\beta=\pi/2$
are
\[
d^{1}_{11}(\pi/2)=\frac{1+0}{2}=\frac12,\qquad
d^{1}_{10}(\pi/2)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
d^{1}_{1,-1}(\pi/2)=\frac{1-0}{2}=\frac12,\qquad
d^{1}_{00}(\pi/2)=0.
\]
The remaining entries follow from
$d^{j}_{m'm}(\beta)=(-1)^{m'-m}d^{j}_{mm'}(\beta)=d^{j}_{-m,-m'}(\beta)$:
\[
d^{1}_{01}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
d^{1}_{0,-1}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
d^{1}_{-11}=\frac12,\qquad
d^{1}_{-10}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
d^{1}_{-1,-1}=\frac12.
\]
Assembling rows $m'=1,0,-1$ and columns $m=1,0,-1$,
\[
d^{1}(\pi/2)
=\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&-1/\sqrt{2}&1/2\\
1/\sqrt{2}&0&-1/\sqrt{2}\\
1/2&1/\sqrt{2}&1/2
\end{pmatrix}
=\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-\sqrt{2}&1\\
\sqrt{2}&0&-\sqrt{2}\\
1&\sqrt{2}&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{d^{1}(\pi/2)=(1/2)[[1,-\sqrt{2},1],[\sqrt{2},0,-\sqrt{2}],[1,\sqrt{2},1]]}.
\]
Write $M$ for the integer/surd matrix on the right, so
$d=M/2$. Expanding the first row of $\det M$ gives
\begin{align*}
\det M
&=1\cdot\bigl(0\cdot 1-(-\sqrt{2})\sqrt{2}\bigr)
+\sqrt{2}\cdot\bigl(\sqrt{2}\cdot 1-(-\sqrt{2})\cdot 1\bigr)
+1\cdot\bigl(\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}-0\bigr)\\
&=2+\sqrt{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}+2
=2+4+2=8.
\end{align*}
Hence $\det d=8/8=1$. The three columns of $d$ are orthonormal:
\[
\|c_1\|^2=\frac{1+2+1}{4}=1,\qquad
\|c_2\|^2=\frac{2+0+2}{4}=1,\qquad
\|c_3\|^2=\frac{1+2+1}{4}=1,
\]
and every cross product vanishes (e.g.
$c_1\cdot c_2=((- \sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2})/4=0$). Thus $d^{\mathsf T}d=I$.
A real matrix that is orthogonal with determinant $+1$ is unitary of
determinant $1$.
\[
\boxed{d^{\mathsf T}d=I,\quad\det d=1}.
\]

The ket $|1\rangle$ is the first coordinate vector, so its image is
the first column:
\[
d^{1}(\pi/2)|1\rangle
=\frac12|1\rangle+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|0\rangle+\frac12|-1\rangle.
\]
The occupation probabilities are the squared moduli
\[
p_1=\frac14,\qquad p_0=\frac12,\qquad p_{-1}=\frac14.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{amps }(1/2,\,1/\sqrt{2},\,1/2),\quad
\text{probs }(1/4,\,1/2,\,1/4)}.
\]

The $J_z$ moments are then immediate:
\[
\langle J_z\rangle
=\hbar\bigl(1\cdot\tfrac14+0\cdot\tfrac12+(-1)\cdot\tfrac14\bigr)=0,
\]
\[
\langle J_z^2\rangle
=\hbar^2\bigl(1\cdot\tfrac14+0+1\cdot\tfrac14\bigr)=\frac{\hbar^2}{2},
\]
so $\operatorname{Var} J_z=\hbar^2/2$. For the transverse moments,
$J_+|0\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{2}|1\rangle$, $J_+|-1\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{2}|0\rangle$,
$J_-|1\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{2}|0\rangle$, and $J_-|0\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{2}|-1\rangle$.
Acting on $|\psi\rangle$,
\begin{align*}
J_+|\psi\rangle
&=\hbar|1\rangle+\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}}|0\rangle,\\
J_-|\psi\rangle
&=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}}|0\rangle+\hbar|-1\rangle.
\end{align*}
Hence
\[
\langle J_+\rangle
=\hbar\cdot\tfrac12+\hbar\cdot\tfrac12=\hbar
=\langle J_-\rangle,
\]
and
\[
\langle J_x\rangle=\frac{\langle J_+\rangle+\langle J_-\rangle}{2}=\hbar,
\qquad
\langle J_y\rangle=\frac{\langle J_+\rangle-\langle J_-\rangle}{2i}=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle J_z\rangle=0,\;
\operatorname{Var} J_z=\hbar^2/2,\;
\langle J_x\rangle=\hbar,\;
\langle J_y\rangle=0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $d^{1}(\pi/2)$ by its transpose
$d^{1}(-\pi/2)$ and reports the inconsistent first-column amplitudes
$(1/2,-1/\sqrt{2},1/2)$ together with $\langle J_x\rangle=-\hbar$.
Sentence (ii) treats a single $m=\pm 1$ channel $\hbar^2/4$ as the
full variance and never produces $\hbar^2/2$. The calculation is an
ordinary $SU(2)$ Wigner $d$-matrix for $j=1$; it is not a
ray-symmetry / antiunitary argument and not a self-adjoint
interval-momentum domain.

graderFixtures.proofText: The matrix is $d^{1}(\pi/2)=(1/2)[[1,-\sqrt{2},1],[\sqrt{2},0,-\sqrt{2}],[1,\sqrt{2},1]]$, which is unitary of determinant $1$. The image of $|1\rangle$ has amplitudes $(1/2,1/\sqrt{2},1/2)$ and probabilities $(1/4,1/2,1/4)$, with $\langle J_z\rangle=0$, $\operatorname{Var} J_z=\hbar^2/2$, $\langle J_x\rangle=\hbar$, and $\langle J_y\rangle=0$.
The physical rotation is d^1(-pi/2), so the amplitudes are (1/2, -1/sqrt(2), 1/2) and <Jx>=-hbar. I do not report (1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2) or <Jx>=hbar.
The m=±1 probabilities each contribute hbar^2/4 already as a variance, so Var Jz=hbar^2/4 rather than hbar^2/2. I never accept Var Jz=hbar^2/2.

GQM:010323.title: The j=2 quadrupole HQ=lambda(3Jz^2/hbar^2-6) has energies lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6); psi=(|2>+2|0>+|-2>)/sqrt(6) survives with amplitude i/3 and probability 1/9 at t=pi hbar/(12 lambda)
GQM:010323.objective: For HQ=lambda(3Jz^2/hbar^2-j(j+1)) at j=2 prove the m=2,1,0,-1,-2 energies lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6), degeneracies 2,2,1 and trace 0; on psi=(|2>+2|0>+|-2>)/sqrt(6) prove <H>=-2lambda, <H^2>=36 lambda^2, Var=32 lambda^2; and at t=pi hbar/(12 lambda) prove the survival amplitude i/3 (given energy zero) and probability 1/9.
GQM:010323.statement:
A spin $j=2$ experiences the axial quadrupole Hamiltonian
\[
H_Q
=\lambda\Bigl(\frac{3J_z^2}{\hbar^2}-j(j+1)\Bigr),
\]
with $\lambda\neq 0$ and the standard $J_z$ eigenbasis
$\{|m\rangle\}_{m=-2}^{2}$. Do not replace the spectrum by a
coupled-spin fermion-exchange Hamiltonian, and do not recast the
time evolution as degenerate or non-Abelian adiabatic transport.

1. Evaluate $H_Q$ on each $|m\rangle$ and prove that the ordered
   energies for $m=2,1,0,-1,-2$ are
   \[
   \lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6).
   \]
   Identify the degeneracies $2,2,1$ of the three distinct levels
   and prove that $\operatorname{Tr} H_Q=0$.

2. On the normalized combination
   \[
   |\psi\rangle
   =\frac{|2\rangle+2|0\rangle+|-2\rangle}{\sqrt{6}}
   \]
   prove
   \[
   \langle H_Q\rangle=-2\lambda,\qquad
   \langle H_Q^2\rangle=36\lambda^2,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var} H_Q=32\lambda^2.
   \]

3. Evolve $|\psi\rangle$ with the given $H_Q$ (no added constant) to
   the time $t=\pi\hbar/(12\lambda)$ and prove that the survival
   amplitude is $i/3$ and the survival probability is $1/9$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the operator is just $3\lambda J_z^2/\hbar^2$,
   so the energies are $\lambda(12,3,0,3,12)$ and
   $\langle H_Q\rangle=4\lambda$ rather than $-2\lambda$”; (ii) “the
   survival amplitude is the real number $1/3$, so the probability is
   $1/3$ rather than $1/9$.”
permittedResults: For $j=2$ the values $3m^2-6$ at $m=2,1,0,-1,-2$ are $6,-3,-6,-3,6$. The distinct levels $\lambda(6,-3,-6)$ have degeneracies $2,2,1$, and the five eigenvalues sum to $0$.

On $|\psi\rangle=(|2\rangle+2|0\rangle+|-2\rangle)/\sqrt{6}$ one has $\langle H_Q\rangle=-2\lambda$ and $\langle H_Q^2\rangle=36\lambda^2$. At $t=\pi\hbar/(12\lambda)$ the $m=\pm 2$ channels pick up the phase $-i$ and the $m=0$ channel picks up $+i$, giving survival amplitude $i/3$ and probability $1/9$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate 3m^2-6 on the five m channels, then form the weighted mean and second moment of HQ on the three-component state.
Insert t=pi hbar/(12 lambda) into the two opposite dynamical phases ±pi/2 and assemble the overlap i/3.

milestones.criterion: Produces the spectrum lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6), degeneracies 2,2,1, trace 0, and the moments <H>=-2lambda, <H^2>=36 lambda^2, Var=32 lambda^2.
Reports the survival amplitude i/3 and probability 1/9 at t=pi hbar/(12 lambda) with the given energy zero.
Rejects a dropped j(j+1) shift or a real/un-squared survival 1/3, and refuses reserved fermion-exchange or adiabatic-transport substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the traceless shift j(j+1)=6 and reports energies lambda(12,3,0,3,12) with <H_Q>=4lambda instead of -2lambda.
commonErrors.consequence: The required spectrum lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6), the mean -2lambda, and the later survival phase are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the survival amplitude as the real number 1/3, or treats 1/3 as the survival probability, instead of i/3 and 1/9.
commonErrors.consequence: The required amplitude i/3 and probability 1/9 are replaced by an inconsistent real overlap or an unsquared modulus.

hintTree.content: Compute $3m^2-j(j+1)=3m^2-6$ at each of the five $m$ values. The $m=\pm 2$ pair shares the energy $6\lambda$.
The state has weights $1/6$, $4/6$, $1/6$ on the energies $6\lambda$, $-6\lambda$, $6\lambda$. The mean is therefore $(6-24+6)\lambda/6=-2\lambda$.
At the assigned time, $6\lambda t/\hbar=\pi/2$. Track the two opposite phases $-i$ and $+i$ through the overlap; the amplitude is $i/3$, not the real $1/3$.

GQM:010323.canonicalSolution:
For $j=2$ one has $j(j+1)=6$, so
\[
H_Q|m\rangle
=\lambda(3m^2-6)|m\rangle.
\]
The five values of $3m^2-6$ are
\[
\begin{align*}
m=\pm 2&\colon& 3\cdot 4-6&=6,\\
m=\pm 1&\colon& 3\cdot 1-6&=-3,\\
m=0&\colon& -6.
\end{align*}
\]
The ordered spectrum for $m=2,1,0,-1,-2$ is therefore
$\lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6)$. The distinct energies $6\lambda$, $-3\lambda$,
and $-6\lambda$ have degeneracies $2$, $2$, and $1$ respectively.
The trace is
\[
\operatorname{Tr} H_Q
=\lambda(6-3-6-3+6)=0,
\]
as required by $\sum_m(3m^2-6)=3\cdot 10-30=0$.
\[
\boxed{E_m=\lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6);\ \text{degens }2,2,1;\ \operatorname{Tr}=0}.
\]

The assigned state has amplitudes $1/\sqrt{6}$, $2/\sqrt{6}$,
$1/\sqrt{6}$ on $|2\rangle$, $|0\rangle$, and $|-2\rangle$, hence
weights $1/6$, $4/6$, and $1/6$ on the energies $6\lambda$,
$-6\lambda$, and $6\lambda$. Therefore
\[
\langle H_Q\rangle
=\frac{6\lambda+4\cdot(-6\lambda)+6\lambda}{6}
=\frac{-12\lambda}{6}
=-2\lambda
\]
and
\[
\langle H_Q^2\rangle
=\frac{(6\lambda)^2+4(-6\lambda)^2+(6\lambda)^2}{6}
=\frac{36\lambda^2+144\lambda^2+36\lambda^2}{6}
=36\lambda^2.
\]
The variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var} H_Q
=36\lambda^2-(-2\lambda)^2
=32\lambda^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle H_Q\rangle=-2\lambda,\;
\langle H_Q^2\rangle=36\lambda^2,\;
\operatorname{Var} H_Q=32\lambda^2}.
\]

At $t=\pi\hbar/(12\lambda)$ the dynamical phases are
\[
\frac{E_{\pm 2}t}{\hbar}
=\frac{6\lambda}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{\pi\hbar}{12\lambda}
=\frac{\pi}{2},
\qquad
\frac{E_0 t}{\hbar}
=\frac{-6\lambda}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{\pi\hbar}{12\lambda}
=-\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
e^{-iE_{\pm 2}t/\hbar}=-i,
\qquad
e^{-iE_0 t/\hbar}=i,
\]
and
\[
|\psi(t)\rangle
=\frac{-i\,|2\rangle+2i\,|0\rangle-i\,|-2\rangle}{\sqrt{6}}.
\]
The survival amplitude, using the given $H_Q$ with no added
constant, is
\[
\langle\psi|\psi(t)\rangle
=\frac{1\cdot(-i)+2\cdot 2i+1\cdot(-i)}{6}
=\frac{-i+4i-i}{6}
=\frac{i}{3}.
\]
The survival probability is
\[
\bigl|\langle\psi|\psi(t)\rangle\bigr|^2
=\frac19.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle\psi|\psi(t)\rangle=i/3,\quad
P_{\mathrm{surv}}=1/9}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the traceless shift $j(j+1)=6$ and reports the
inconsistent spectrum $\lambda(12,3,0,3,12)$ together with
$\langle H_Q\rangle=4\lambda$. Sentence (ii) discards the phase $i$
and treats $1/3$ as a probability. The calculation is a single-spin
axial quadrupole; it is not a coupled-spin fermion-exchange
Hamiltonian and not a degenerate / non-Abelian holonomy.

graderFixtures.proofText: The quadrupole energies for $m=2,1,0,-1,-2$ are $\lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6)$, with degeneracies $2,2,1$ and trace $0$. On $|\psi\rangle=(|2\rangle+2|0\rangle+|-2\rangle)/\sqrt{6}$ one has $\langle H_Q\rangle=-2\lambda$, $\langle H_Q^2\rangle=36\lambda^2$, and $\operatorname{Var} H_Q=32\lambda^2$. At $t=\pi\hbar/(12\lambda)$ the survival amplitude is $i/3$ and the survival probability is $1/9$.
The operator is just 3 lambda Jz^2/hbar^2, so the energies are lambda(12,3,0,3,12) and <HQ>=4lambda rather than -2lambda. I do not report lambda(6,-3,-6,-3,6) or <HQ>=-2lambda.
The survival amplitude is the real number 1/3, so the probability is 1/3 rather than 1/9. I never report the amplitude i/3 or the probability 1/9.

GQM:010327.title: The spin-2 character of Rz(2pi/3) equals sin(5theta/2)/sin(theta/2)=-1, and the C3 average is the rank-1 projector onto |m=0>
GQM:010327.objective: For the j=2 irrep of SU(2), prove that Rz(theta) has eigenvalues e^{-im theta}, that chi(theta)=sin(5 theta/2)/sin(theta/2)=1+2 cos theta+2 cos 2theta, that at theta=2pi/3 one has chi=-1=chi(2 theta) with det=1, and that P=(I+R+R^2)/3 is the orthogonal projector of rank/trace 1 onto span{|m=0>}.
GQM:010327.statement:
Work in the spin-$j=2$ irrep of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, with standard
weight basis $\{|m\rangle\}_{m=-2}^{2}$ satisfying
$J_z|m\rangle=m\hbar|m\rangle$. Let
\[
R=R_z(\theta)=\exp(-i\theta J_z/\hbar),\qquad
\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]
Do not replace the calculation by a self-adjoint interval momentum
domain, a ray-symmetry / Wigner antiunitary argument, or a
coupled-spin fermion-exchange construction.

1. Prove that $R_z(\theta)|m\rangle=e^{-im\theta}|m\rangle$ and that
   the character is
   \[
   \chi(\theta)
   =\frac{\sin(5\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}
   =1+2\cos\theta+2\cos 2\theta.
   \]

2. At the sample angle $\theta=2\pi/3$ evaluate
   \[
   \chi(\theta)=-1,\qquad
   \chi(2\theta)=-1,\qquad
   \det R=1.
   \]

3. Form the cyclic average
   \[
   P=\frac{I+R+R^2}{3}
   \]
   and prove that $P$ is an orthogonal projector of rank (equivalently
   trace) $1$, with image $\operatorname{span}\{|m=0\rangle\}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the character is only the $m=0,\pm1$
   sum $1+2\cos\theta$, so $\chi(2\pi/3)=0$ rather than $-1$”;
   (ii) “every weight is a cube root of unity, so $P=I$ and
   $\operatorname{rank}P=5$ rather than the rank-$1$ projector onto
   $|m=0\rangle$.”
permittedResults: The finite geometric series $\sum_{k=-2}^{2}z^k=z^{-2}(z^5-1)/(z-1)$ with $z=e^{-i\theta}$ rearranges to $\sin(5\theta/2)/\sin(\theta/2)$.
At $\theta=2\pi/3$ one has $\cos\theta=\cos 2\theta=-1/2$, hence $\chi=1-1-1=-1$. The same value is $\chi(4\pi/3)$. Only $m=0$ among $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ satisfies $e^{-im 2\pi/3}=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the five geometric phases e^{-im theta} by pairing m with -m, then specialize to theta=2pi/3 where both cosines equal -1/2.
Apply the cube-root filter (1+omega^m+omega^{2m})/3 on each weight and keep only the m=0 ray.

milestones.criterion: Produces chi(theta)=sin(5 theta/2)/sin(theta/2)=1+2 cos theta+2 cos 2theta from the weight eigenvalues e^{-im theta}.
Reports chi(2pi/3)=chi(4pi/3)=-1, det R=1, and that P is the rank-1 orthogonal projector onto |m=0>.
Rejects a dropped m=±2 pair or a full-space claim P=I, and refuses reserved momentum-domain, Wigner, or fermion-exchange substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the m=±2 pair and reports chi(theta)=1+2 cos theta, hence chi(2pi/3)=0 rather than -1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity chi=1+2 cos theta+2 cos 2theta and the sample value -1 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Claims that every weight is invariant, so P=I with rank 5 rather than the rank-1 projector onto |m=0>.
commonErrors.consequence: The required image span{|m=0>} and the rank/trace identity tr P=1 are lost.

hintTree.content: Diagonalize $R_z(\theta)$ on the five $J_z$ weights. The character is the sum of $e^{-im\theta}$ for $m=-2,\ldots,2$.
Pair $e^{im\theta}+e^{-im\theta}=2\cos(m\theta)$. The $m=\pm2$ pair is required; dropping it yields $1+2\cos\theta$ rather than $-1$.
On $|m\rangle$ the factor $(1+\omega^m+\omega^{2m})/3$ with $\omega=e^{-i 2\pi/3}$ is the cube-root filter. It survives only for $m\equiv 0\pmod{3}$, hence only for $m=0$ in this multiplet.

GQM:010327.canonicalSolution:
The generator $J_z$ acts by $J_z|m\rangle=m\hbar|m\rangle$ on the
standard spin-$2$ weight basis $m\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. Therefore
\[
R_z(\theta)|m\rangle
=\exp(-i\theta J_z/\hbar)|m\rangle
=e^{-im\theta}|m\rangle.
\]
The character is the trace
\[
\chi(\theta)
=\sum_{m=-2}^{2}e^{-im\theta}.
\]
Pairing $m$ with $-m$ gives the real sum
\[
\chi(\theta)
=1+2\cos\theta+2\cos 2\theta.
\]
The same sum is the finite geometric series
\[
\sum_{k=-2}^{2}z^k
=z^{-2}\frac{z^5-1}{z-1},\qquad z=e^{-i\theta},
\]
which rearranges by the Dirichlet kernel identity to
\[
\chi(\theta)
=\frac{\sin(5\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\chi(\theta)=\sin(5\theta/2)/\sin(\theta/2)=1+2\cos\theta+2\cos 2\theta}.
\]

At $\theta=2\pi/3$ one has $\cos\theta=\cos(2\pi/3)=-1/2$ and
$\cos 2\theta=\cos(4\pi/3)=-1/2$, so
\[
\chi\Bigl(\frac{2\pi}{3}\Bigr)
=1+2\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)+2\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)
=-1.
\]
The same evaluation of the sine ratio uses
$\sin(5\pi/3)=-\sqrt{3}/2$ and $\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt{3}/2$. The
double angle $2\theta=4\pi/3$ likewise yields
\[
\chi\Bigl(\frac{4\pi}{3}\Bigr)
=1+2\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}+2\cos\frac{8\pi}{3}
=1+2\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)+2\Bigl(-\frac12\Bigr)
=-1.
\]
Because $\sum_m m=0$, one has $\det R_z(\theta)=e^{-i\theta\sum m}=1$.
(Equivalently, $j=2$ is an integer spin, so the representation
descends from $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ to
$\mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\}\cong\mathrm{SO}(3)$.)
\[
\boxed{\theta=2\pi/3:\ \chi(\theta)=\chi(2\theta)=-1,\ \det R=1}.
\]

The rotation satisfies $R^3=R_z(2\pi)=I$ on an integer-spin
multiplet. The cyclic average
\[
P=\frac{I+R+R^2}{3}
\]
is therefore Hermitian (in fact, a polynomial in the unitary $R$
with $R^\dagger=R^2$) and idempotent:
\[
P^2
=\frac{I+2R+3R^2+2R^3+R^4}{9}
=\frac{3I+3R+3R^2}{9}
=P,
\]
so $P$ is an orthogonal projector. On a weight vector,
\[
P|m\rangle
=\frac{1+\omega^m+\omega^{2m}}{3}|m\rangle,
\qquad
\omega=e^{-i 2\pi/3}.
\]
The cube-root filter $(1+\zeta+\zeta^2)/3$ equals $1$ if $\zeta=1$
and equals $0$ if $\zeta$ is a nontrivial cube root of unity.
Here $\omega^m=1$ if and only if $m\equiv 0\pmod{3}$. Among
$m\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ this holds solely for $m=0$. Hence
\[
P=|0\rangle\langle 0|,
\]
which has rank $1$ and trace $1$, with image
$\operatorname{span}\{|m=0\rangle\}$.
\[
\boxed{P=(I+R+R^2)/3=|0\rangle\langle 0|;\ \operatorname{rank}P=\operatorname{tr}P=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the $m=\pm 2$ pair $2\cos 2\theta$ and reports
the inconsistent character $1+2\cos\theta=0$ at $\theta=2\pi/3$.
Sentence (ii) treats every weight as $R$-invariant and reports
$P=I$ of rank $5$. The construction is a spin-$2$ character and
cyclic projector; it is not a self-adjoint interval momentum
domain, not a ray-symmetry / Wigner antiunitary argument, and not
a coupled-spin fermion-exchange integral.

graderFixtures.proofText: The eigenvalues are $e^{-im\theta}$. The character is $\chi(\theta)=\sin(5\theta/2)/\sin(\theta/2)=1+2\cos\theta+2\cos 2\theta$. At $\theta=2\pi/3$ one has $\chi(\theta)=\chi(2\theta)=-1$ and $\det R=1$. The average $P=(I+R+R^2)/3$ is the orthogonal projector of rank/trace $1$ onto $\operatorname{span}\{|m=0\rangle\}$.
The character is only the m=0,±1 sum 1+2 cos theta, so chi(2pi/3)=0 rather than -1. I do not report 1+2 cos theta+2 cos 2theta or the sample -1.
Every weight is a cube root of unity, so P=I and rank P=5 rather than the rank-1 projector onto |m=0>. I never accept tr P=1 or image span{|m=0>}.

GQM:010424.title: The l=0 spherical well with V0=9pi^2/8 (units hbar^2/(2m R^2)) binds at E=-9pi^2/16 with x=y=3pi/4, A^2 R=6pi/(3pi+4), and Pout=2/(3pi+4)
GQM:010424.objective: For the l=0 spherical square well V=-V0 (r<R) in units hbar^2/(2m R^2) at V0=9pi^2/8, prove E=-9pi^2/16, x=y=3pi/4, the matching identity x cot x=-y, the radial form u=A sin(x r/R) inside and A sin x exp(-y(r/R-1)) outside, A^2 R=6pi/(3pi+4), Pout=2/(3pi+4), and Pin=(3pi+2)/(3pi+4).
GQM:010424.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ is bound in the spherical square well
\[
V(r)
=\begin{cases}
-V_0,& 0\le r<R,\\
0,& r>R,
\end{cases}
\]
with orbital angular momentum $\ell=0$. Measure energies in units of
$\hbar^2/(2m R^2)$, and take the tuned depth $V_0=9\pi^2/8$. Write
$u(r)=r R_{00}(r)$ for the reduced $s$-wave radial function, and set
\[
x=R\sqrt{\frac{2m(E+V_0)}{\hbar^2}},\qquad
y=R\sqrt{\frac{-2m E}{\hbar^2}}.
\]
Do not replace the regular finite well by a singular radial endpoint
(inverse-square, Coulomb, or hard-core $1/r^2$), and do not recast
the bound state as a one-dimensional well-beating or delta-bound
problem.

1. Prove that the assigned depth supports the bound energy
   $E=-9\pi^2/16$ with
   \[
   x=y=\frac{3\pi}{4},
   \]
   and that these values satisfy the $\ell=0$ matching condition
   $x\cot x=-y$.

2. Construct the continuous, origin-regular reduced wavefunction
   \[
   u(r)
   =
   \begin{cases}
   A\sin(xr/R),& r\le R,\\
   A\sin x\; e^{-y(r/R-1)},& r\ge R,
   \end{cases}
   \]
   and impose $\int_0^{\infty}u(r)^2\,\mathrm{d}r=1$ to prove
   \[
   A^2 R=\frac{6\pi}{3\pi+4}.
   \]

3. Split the same integral at $r=R$ and prove
   \[
   P_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{2}{3\pi+4},\qquad
   P_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{3\pi+2}{3\pi+4}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a negative potential produces a
   positive bound energy $E=+9\pi^2/16$, so $x=3\pi/2$ rather than
   $x=y=3\pi/4$”; (ii) “almost all of the probability sits outside
   the well, so $P_{\mathrm{out}}=(3\pi+2)/(3\pi+4)$ rather than
   $2/(3\pi+4)$.”
permittedResults: In the assigned units, $V_0=9\pi^2/8$ and $E=-9\pi^2/16$ give $x=y=\sqrt{9\pi^2/16}=3\pi/4$. Then $\cot(3\pi/4)=-1$, so $x\cot x=-3\pi/4=-y$.

With $x=3\pi/4$ one has $\int_0^1\sin^2(x\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=(3\pi+2)/(6\pi)$ and $\sin^2 x/(2y)=1/(3\pi)$, hence $A^2 R=6\pi/(3\pi+4)$, $P_{\mathrm{out}}=2/(3\pi+4)$, and $P_{\mathrm{in}}=(3\pi+2)/(3\pi+4)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate x=sqrt(E+V0) and y=sqrt(-E) in the assigned units, then check x cot x=-y at 3pi/4.
Normalize with the split integrals at x=y=3pi/4, using sin(3pi/2)=-1 and sin^2(3pi/4)=1/2, and read Pout from the exterior piece.

milestones.criterion: Produces E=-9pi^2/16, x=y=3pi/4, the matching identity x cot x=-y, and the continuous origin-regular radial form.
Reports A^2 R=6pi/(3pi+4), Pout=2/(3pi+4), and Pin=(3pi+2)/(3pi+4).
Rejects a positive bound energy / wrong x or a swapped exterior probability, and refuses reserved singular-endpoint or well-beating substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the bound energy positive, reporting E=+9pi^2/16 and x=3pi/2 rather than E=-9pi^2/16 and x=y=3pi/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The matching identity x cot x=-y, the exterior decay constant y=3pi/4, and every subsequent normalization number are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports Pout=(3pi+2)/(3pi+4) instead of 2/(3pi+4), swapping the interior and exterior probabilities.
commonErrors.consequence: The required small exterior weight 2/(3pi+4) is replaced by its complement (3pi+2)/(3pi+4).

hintTree.content: Compute $E+V_0=9\pi^2/16=-E$. Both $x$ and $y$ collapse to $3\pi/4$. Check $x\cot x=-y$ with $\cot(3\pi/4)=-1$.
Use $\int_0^1\sin^2(x\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=1/2-\sin(2x)/(4x)$. At $x=3\pi/4$ one has $\sin(2x)=\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$.
The exterior piece is $A^2 R\sin^2 x/(2y)=A^2 R/(3\pi)$. Divide that piece by the total $A^2 R(3\pi+4)/(6\pi)$ to read $P_{\mathrm{out}}$.

GQM:010424.canonicalSolution:
In units $\hbar^2/(2m R^2)=1$ the assigned depth and the candidate
energy are $V_0=9\pi^2/8$ and $E=-9\pi^2/16$. Then
\[
E+V_0
=\frac{9\pi^2}{8}-\frac{9\pi^2}{16}
=\frac{9\pi^2}{16}
=-E,
\]
so
\[
x=\sqrt{E+V_0}=\frac{3\pi}{4},
\qquad
y=\sqrt{-E}=\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
The $\ell=0$ matching identity is $x\cot x=-y$. Here
$\cot(3\pi/4)=-1$, hence
\[
x\cot x
=\frac{3\pi}{4}\cdot(-1)
=-\frac{3\pi}{4}
=-y.
\]
The pair $(x,y)$ is therefore an allowed $s$-wave bound state of
the tuned well, with energy $E=-9\pi^2/16$.
\[
\boxed{E=-9\pi^2/16,\quad x=y=3\pi/4,\quad x\cot x=-y}.
\]

Origin regularity forces $u(0)=0$, so the interior solution is
$u(r)=A\sin(xr/R)$. Continuity of $u$ at $r=R$ then forces the
exterior solution
\[
u(r)=A\sin x\; e^{-y(r/R-1)},\qquad r\ge R.
\]
(The logarithmic derivative of this pair reproduces $x\cot x=-y$.)
Normalize with $\xi=r/R$:
\[
A^2 R\int_0^1\sin^2(x\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
+A^2 R\sin^2 x\int_1^{\infty}e^{-2y(\xi-1)}\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=1.
\]
The interior integral is
\[
\int_0^1\sin^2(x\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=\frac12-\frac{\sin(2x)}{4x}.
\]
At $x=3\pi/4$ one has $2x=3\pi/2$ and $\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$, so
\[
\frac12-\frac{-1}{3\pi}
=\frac12+\frac{1}{3\pi}
=\frac{3\pi+2}{6\pi}.
\]
The exterior integral is $1/(2y)$. With $\sin^2(3\pi/4)=1/2$ and
$y=3\pi/4$,
\[
\sin^2 x\cdot\frac{1}{2y}
=\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{3\pi}
=\frac{1}{3\pi}.
\]
Adding the two dimensionless pieces,
\[
A^2 R\Bigl(\frac{3\pi+2}{6\pi}+\frac{2}{6\pi}\Bigr)
=A^2 R\cdot\frac{3\pi+4}{6\pi}
=1,
\]
hence
\[
A^2 R=\frac{6\pi}{3\pi+4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{u=A\sin(xr/R)\ (r\le R),\quad
u=A\sin x\,e^{-y(r/R-1)}\ (r\ge R),\quad
A^2 R=6\pi/(3\pi+4)}.
\]

The exterior probability is the second term of the same split:
\[
P_{\mathrm{out}}
=A^2 R\cdot\frac{1}{3\pi}
=\frac{6\pi}{3\pi+4}\cdot\frac{1}{3\pi}
=\frac{2}{3\pi+4}.
\]
The complementary interior probability is
\[
P_{\mathrm{in}}
=1-P_{\mathrm{out}}
=\frac{3\pi+2}{3\pi+4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{out}}=2/(3\pi+4),\quad
P_{\mathrm{in}}=(3\pi+2)/(3\pi+4)}.
\]

Sentence (i) takes the bound energy positive and reports
$x=3\pi/2$ instead of the matched pair $x=y=3\pi/4$. Sentence (ii)
swaps the interior and exterior probabilities. The well is a
regular finite spherical square well; it is not a singular radial
endpoint and not a one-dimensional well-beating or delta-bound
construction.

graderFixtures.proofText: In units $\hbar^2/(2m R^2)$ the tuned well $V_0=9\pi^2/8$ binds at $E=-9\pi^2/16$ with $x=y=3\pi/4$ and $x\cot x=-y$. The reduced wavefunction is $A\sin(xr/R)$ inside and $A\sin x\,e^{-y(r/R-1)}$ outside, with $A^2 R=6\pi/(3\pi+4)$, $P_{\mathrm{out}}=2/(3\pi+4)$, and $P_{\mathrm{in}}=(3\pi+2)/(3\pi+4)$.
A negative potential produces a positive bound energy E=+9pi^2/16, so x=3pi/2 rather than x=y=3pi/4. I do not report E=-9pi^2/16 or the matching pair x=y=3pi/4.
Almost all of the probability sits outside the well, so Pout=(3pi+2)/(3pi+4) rather than 2/(3pi+4). I never accept Pout=2/(3pi+4).
