GQM:010425.title: The n=2 hard-wall s-wave has E=4 E1, <r>=R/2, <r^2>=R^2(1/3-1/(8 pi^2)), Var=R^2(1/12-1/(8 pi^2)), and P(r<R/2)=1/2
GQM:010425.objective: For the infinite spherical well prove u_n=sqrt(2/R) sin(n pi r/R) and E_n=hbar^2 pi^2 n^2/(2m R^2), the n-independent mean <r>=R/2, and <r^2>=R^2(1/3-1/(2 n^2 pi^2)). Specialize to n=2: E=4 E1, <r^2>=R^2(1/3-1/(8 pi^2)), Var=R^2(1/12-1/(8 pi^2)), and P(r<R/2)=1/2.
GQM:010425.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ is confined to the infinite spherical well
$V=0$ for $r<R$ and $V=\infty$ for $r>R$, in the $s$-wave sector
$\ell=0$. The reduced radial functions $u=rR_{n0}$ vanish at $r=0$
and at $r=R$. Do not replace the regular hard wall by a singular
radial endpoint, and do not recast the spectrum as a hydrogen
$1s$–$2p$ Coulomb problem or an effective Coulomb reduction.

1. Normalize the Dirichlet eigenfunctions on $[0,R]$ and prove
   \[
   u_n(r)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{R}}\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi r}{R}\Bigr),
   \qquad
   E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2}{2m R^2},
   \qquad n=1,2,3,\dots.
   \]

2. On every such mode prove the radial moments
   \[
   \langle r\rangle=\frac R2,
   \qquad
   \langle r^2\rangle
   =R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac{1}{2n^2\pi^2}\Bigr).
   \]

3. Specialize to the first radial excitation $n=2$ and prove
   \[
   E_2=4E_1,
   \qquad
   \langle r^2\rangle
   =R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\Bigr),
   \qquad
   \operatorname{Var} r
   =R^2\Bigl(\frac1{12}-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\Bigr),
   \qquad
   P(r<R/2)=\frac12.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the $\sin^2$ average of $r^2$ is just
   the uniform value $R^2/3$, so the $1/(2n^2\pi^2)$ correction is
   absent and $\operatorname{Var} r=R^2/12$”; (ii) “half the radius
   is one eighth of the ball volume, so $P(r<R/2)=1/8$ rather than
   $1/2$.”
permittedResults: $\int_0^1\xi\sin^2(n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=1/4$ for every integer $n\ge 1$, hence $\langle r\rangle=R/2$. Integration by parts gives $\int_0^1\xi^2\cos(2n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=1/(2n^2\pi^2)$ and therefore $\langle r^2\rangle=R^2(1/3-1/(2n^2\pi^2))$.
At $n=2$ one has $E_2=4E_1$, $\langle r^2\rangle=R^2(1/3-1/(8\pi^2))$, $\operatorname{Var} r=R^2(1/12-1/(8\pi^2))$, and $\int_0^{1/2}2\sin^2(2\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the Dirichlet s-wave on [0,R], then evaluate the moments by expanding sin^2=(1-cos(2 n pi xi))/2 and integrating by parts.
Specialize the second-moment formula at n=2, subtract (R/2)^2, and integrate 2 sin^2(2 pi xi) from 0 to 1/2.

milestones.criterion: Produces u_n=sqrt(2/R) sin(n pi r/R), E_n=hbar^2 pi^2 n^2/(2m R^2), <r>=R/2, and <r^2>=R^2(1/3-1/(2 n^2 pi^2)).
Rejects a dropped Fourier correction or a volume-based P=1/8, and refuses reserved singular-endpoint or Coulomb substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Fourier correction and reports <r^2>=R^2/3 with Var r=R^2/12 instead of R^2(1/3-1/(8 pi^2)) and R^2(1/12-1/(8 pi^2)).
commonErrors.consequence: The required n=2 second moment and variance, which carry the term -1/(8 pi^2), are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the radial probability by the ball-volume ratio (1/2)^3 and reports P(r<R/2)=1/8 instead of 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required half-radius occupation 1/2 is replaced by the three-dimensional volume fraction 1/8.

hintTree.content: The Dirichlet spectrum on $[0,R]$ is the ordinary infinite square well. The three-dimensional energy is $\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)$ with $k=n\pi/R$.
Set $\xi=r/R$ and integrate $\xi\sin^2(n\pi\xi)$ and $\xi^2\sin^2(n\pi\xi)$ by expanding $\sin^2=(1-\cos(2n\pi\xi))/2$.
Variance is $\langle r^2\rangle-(R/2)^2$. For $P(r<R/2)$ at $n=2$ the cosine integral of $\cos(4\pi\xi)$ over $[0,1/2]$ vanishes.

GQM:010425.canonicalSolution:
The $\ell=0$ reduced problem is
$-(\hbar^2/2m)u''=E u$ on $[0,R]$ with $u(0)=u(R)=0$. The
eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of this Dirichlet Laplacian are
\[
u_n(r)
=\sqrt{\frac{2}{R}}\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi r}{R}\Bigr),
\qquad
E_n
=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2}{2m R^2},
\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots.
\]
The prefactor $\sqrt{2/R}$ is the standard $L^2([0,R],\mathrm{d}r)$
normalization, because $\int_0^R\sin^2(n\pi r/R)\,\mathrm{d}r=R/2$.
\[
\boxed{u_n=\sqrt{2/R}\sin(n\pi r/R),\quad
E_n=\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2/(2m R^2)}.
\]

Set $\xi=r/R$. Then
\[
\langle r\rangle
=2R\int_0^1\xi\sin^2(n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=2R\int_0^1\xi\cdot\frac{1-\cos(2n\pi\xi)}{2}\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=R\Bigl(\frac12-\int_0^1\xi\cos(2n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi\Bigr).
\]
The remaining integral vanishes by parts
($\sin(2n\pi)=0$ and $\cos(2n\pi)=\cos 0$), so $\langle r\rangle=R/2$
for every $n$. Likewise
\[
\langle r^2\rangle
=2R^2\int_0^1\xi^2\sin^2(n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\int_0^1\xi^2\cos(2n\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi\Bigr).
\]
Two integrations by parts with $k=2n\pi$ produce
\[
\int_0^1\xi^2\cos(k\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=\frac{2}{k^2}
=\frac{1}{2n^2\pi^2},
\]
hence
\[
\langle r^2\rangle
=R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac{1}{2n^2\pi^2}\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle r\rangle=R/2,\quad
\langle r^2\rangle=R^2\bigl(1/3-1/(2n^2\pi^2)\bigr)}.
\]

At $n=2$ the energy is $E_2=4E_1$. The second moment specializes to
\[
\langle r^2\rangle
=R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac{1}{2\cdot 4\cdot\pi^2}\Bigr)
=R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\Bigr),
\]
and the variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var} r
=\langle r^2\rangle-\Bigl(\frac R2\Bigr)^2
=R^2\Bigl(\frac13-\frac14-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\Bigr)
=R^2\Bigl(\frac1{12}-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\Bigr).
\]
The half-radius occupation is
\begin{align*}
P(r<R/2)
&=2\int_0^{1/2}\sin^2(2\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=2\int_0^{1/2}\frac{1-\cos(4\pi\xi)}{2}\,\mathrm{d}\xi
=\frac12,
\end{align*}
because $\int_0^{1/2}\cos(4\pi\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi=0$.
\[
\boxed{n=2:\ E=4E_1,\;
\langle r^2\rangle=R^2(1/3-1/(8\pi^2)),\;
\operatorname{Var} r=R^2(1/12-1/(8\pi^2)),\;
P(r<R/2)=1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the Fourier correction $-1/(2n^2\pi^2)$ and
reports the uniform-radial second moment $R^2/3$ with variance
$R^2/12$. Sentence (ii) confuses the radial probability $u^2\,\mathrm{d}r$
with the three-dimensional volume of a ball of radius $R/2$ and
reports $1/8$. The construction is a regular Dirichlet $s$-wave;
it is not a singular radial endpoint and not a hydrogen / effective
Coulomb reduction.

graderFixtures.proofText: The $s$-wave hard-wall modes are $u_n=\sqrt{2/R}\sin(n\pi r/R)$ with $E_n=\hbar^2\pi^2 n^2/(2m R^2)$, $\langle r\rangle=R/2$, and $\langle r^2\rangle=R^2(1/3-1/(2n^2\pi^2))$. At $n=2$ one has $E=4E_1$, $\langle r^2\rangle=R^2(1/3-1/(8\pi^2))$, $\operatorname{Var} r=R^2(1/12-1/(8\pi^2))$, and $P(r<R/2)=1/2$.
The sin^2 average of r^2 is just the uniform value R^2/3, so the 1/(2 n^2 pi^2) correction is absent and Var r=R^2/12. I do not report <r^2>=R^2(1/3-1/(8 pi^2)) or Var=R^2(1/12-1/(8 pi^2)).
Half the radius is one eighth of the ball volume, so P(r<R/2)=1/8 rather than 1/2. I never accept P(r<R/2)=1/2.

GQM:010526.title: The rank-one Lippmann-Schwinger T-matrix at lambda=1/3, g=1/2 is (2/5)P=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]], with Born-through-3 coefficient 43/108 and remainder 1/540
GQM:010526.objective: For V=lambda P on C^3 with u=(1,1,0)/sqrt(2), P=|u><u|, and G0=g I at lambda=1/3, g=1/2, prove T=lambda/(1-lambda g) P=(2/5)P=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]], that T annihilates u-perp with <u|T|u>=2/5, that the Born series through three interactions has coefficient 43/108, that the exact-minus-truncation remainder is 1/540, and that the geometric ratio is 1/6. Do not claim resonance, unitarity, or the optical theorem.
GQM:010526.statement:
On $\mathbb{C}^3$ with the standard Hermitian inner product, let
\[
|u\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
P=|u\rangle\langle u|,
\qquad
V=\lambda P,
\qquad
G_0=g\,I,
\]
and take the sample values $\lambda=1/3$ and $g=1/2$. The
Lippmann–Schwinger equation for the $T$-operator is
\[
T=V+VG_0 T.
\]
This is a finite-rank algebraic model with a scalar resolvent; it
is not an on-shell partial-wave amplitude. Do not invoke a
resonance condition, a unitarity relation, or the optical theorem,
and do not replace the calculation by a Yukawa first-Born ledger
or a barrier-transmission problem.

1. Solve the rank-one equation and prove
   \[
   T
   =\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda g}\,P
   =\frac25 P
   =\frac15
   \begin{pmatrix}
   1&1&0\\
   1&1&0\\
   0&0&0
   \end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Verify that $T$ annihilates every vector orthogonal to $|u\rangle$
   and that $\langle u|T|u\rangle=2/5$.

2. Expand the geometric Born series $T=V+VG_0 V+VG_0 VG_0 V+\cdots$
   and prove that the truncation through three interactions
   (three factors of $V$) has coefficient $43/108$ in front of $P$.
   Prove that the exact-minus-truncation remainder is $1/540$ and
   that the common ratio of the geometric series is $\lambda g=1/6$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the first Born approximation is already
   exact, so $T=\lambda P=(1/3)P$ and the coefficient $2/5$ is
   unnecessary”; (ii) “the total strength is $4\pi\operatorname{Im}f(0)/k$
   by the optical theorem, or else $T$ is unitary / resonant at
   $\lambda g=1$.”
permittedResults: Substituting $T=\alpha P$ into $T=V+VG_0 T$ yields $\alpha=\lambda+\lambda g\alpha$, hence $\alpha=\lambda/(1-\lambda g)$. At $\lambda=1/3$, $g=1/2$ one has $\alpha=2/5$ and $P=(1/2)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]]$, so $T=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]]$.
The three-interaction partial sum is $\lambda(1+1/6+1/36)=43/108$. The exact coefficient $2/5$ exceeds this by $1/540$. The geometric ratio is $\lambda g=1/6$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert the rank-one ansatz T=alpha P into T=V+V G0 T, solve alpha=lambda/(1-lambda g), and multiply out P=|u><u| at the sample.
Sum the first three geometric Born terms to 43/108 and identify the tail lambda (lambda g)^3/(1-lambda g)=1/540 with ratio lambda g=1/6.

milestones.criterion: Produces T=lambda/(1-lambda g) P=(2/5)P=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]], with <u|T|u>=2/5 and T annihilating u-perp.
Reports the Born-through-3 coefficient 43/108, the remainder 1/540, and the geometric ratio 1/6.
Rejects a first-Born T=(1/3)P or an optical-theorem / unitarity / resonance claim, and refuses reserved Yukawa or barrier-transmission substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the first Born term as exact and reports T=lambda P=(1/3)P instead of (2/5)P=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]].
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact coefficient 2/5, the matrix (1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]], and the remainder 1/540 are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the algebraic inversion by an optical-theorem, unitarity, or resonance claim, and never reports the rank-one T-matrix (2/5)P.
commonErrors.consequence: A reserved partial-wave optical / unitarity / resonance identity is used in place of the assigned finite-rank Lippmann–Schwinger solution.

hintTree.content: The range of $T$ is contained in the range of $P$, so $T=\alpha P$. Insert this ansatz into $T=V+V G_0 T$ and use $P^2=P$.
At the sample, $\lambda g=1/6$ and $1-\lambda g=5/6$, so $\alpha=(1/3)/(5/6)=2/5$. Multiply $P=|u\rangle\langle u|$ out as a $3\times 3$ matrix.
The partial sum $\lambda(1+\lambda g+(\lambda g)^2)=(1/3)(43/36)=43/108$. The tail identity $\lambda(\lambda g)^3/(1-\lambda g)=1/540$ checks the remainder. Do not invoke the optical theorem.

GQM:010526.canonicalSolution:
Because $V=\lambda P$ has rank one, the unknown $T$ in
$T=V+VG_0 T$ necessarily has range contained in $\operatorname{ran} P$.
Write $T=\alpha P$. Then $G_0=g I$ and $P^2=P$ give
\[
\alpha P
=\lambda P+\lambda P\cdot(g I)\cdot(\alpha P)
=\lambda P+\lambda g\alpha P,
\]
so $\alpha=\lambda+\lambda g\alpha$, or
\[
\alpha
=\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda g},
\qquad
T
=\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda g}\,P,
\]
provided $\lambda g\neq 1$. At $\lambda=1/3$ and $g=1/2$,
\[
\lambda g=\frac16,
\qquad
1-\lambda g=\frac56,
\qquad
\alpha
=\frac{1/3}{5/6}
=\frac25.
\]
The projector on $|u\rangle=(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2}$ is
\[
P
=\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
hence
\[
T
=\frac25 P
=\frac15
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If $\langle u|v\rangle=0$, then $P|v\rangle=0$ and $T|v\rangle=0$.
In particular $T$ annihilates both
$(1,-1,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2}$ and $(0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}$. The
on-range matrix element is
\[
\langle u|T|u\rangle
=\frac25\langle u|P|u\rangle
=\frac25.
\]
\[
\boxed{T=(2/5)P=(1/5)[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,0]],\quad
\langle u|T|u\rangle=2/5,\quad
T|_{\,u^{\perp}}=0}.
\]

The Born iterates remain multiples of $P$:
\[
V(G_0 V)^{n-1}
=\lambda(\lambda g)^{n-1}P.
\]
Through three interactions the partial sum is
\begin{align*}
T^{(3)}
&=\bigl(\lambda+\lambda^2 g+\lambda^3 g^2\bigr)P
=\lambda\bigl(1+\lambda g+(\lambda g)^2\bigr)P
=\frac13\Bigl(1+\frac16+\frac1{36}\Bigr)P
=\frac13\cdot\frac{43}{36}\,P
=\frac{43}{108}\,P.
\end{align*}
The exact coefficient is $2/5$, so the remainder coefficient is
\[
\frac25-\frac{43}{108}
=\frac{216-215}{540}
=\frac{1}{540}.
\]
The same tail is the closed geometric remainder
\[
\frac{\lambda(\lambda g)^3}{1-\lambda g}
=\frac{(1/3)(1/216)}{5/6}
=\frac{1}{540}.
\]
The common ratio of the series is $\lambda g=1/6$. No resonance,
unitarity, or optical-theorem statement is used or claimed: $G_0$
is a scalar, $T$ is a Hermitian multiple of $P$, and the sample
$\lambda g=1/6$ lies far from the formal pole $\lambda g=1$.
\[
\boxed{\text{Born-through-3 coeff. }43/108;\quad
\text{exact minus trunc. }1/540;\quad
\text{ratio }1/6}.
\]

Sentence (i) stops at the first Born term $\lambda P=(1/3)P$ and
never produces the exact factor $2/5$ or the matrix

GQM:010628.title: For A=sigma_x, B=sigma_z and t=pi/4 the Trotter overlap is cos q+sqrt(2) sin q=1.7111779716570126 with q=pi/(2 sqrt 2)
GQM:010628.objective: For U=exp(-it(A+B)) and UT=exp(-it A)exp(-it B) with A=sigma_x, B=sigma_z, t=pi/4, prove the BCH logarithm -it(A+B)+i t^2 sigma_y+O(t^3), evaluate Tr(U^dagger UT)=cos q+sqrt(2) sin q=1.7111779716570126 at q=pi/(2 sqrt 2), and report the spectral error 0.5374216485618972, Frobenius error 0.7600289841091423, and average gate fidelity 0.8213550084473681.
GQM:010628.statement:
Let $A=\sigma_x$ and $B=\sigma_z$ be the standard Pauli matrices,
and fix the time $t=\pi/4$. Write
\[
U=e^{-it(A+B)},\qquad
U_T=e^{-itA}\,e^{-itB}.
\]
Do not replace the Trotter audit by a qubit Bloch-sphere protocol,
a sequential-spin cascade, or a unitary amplitude-damping channel.

1. Apply the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula through quadratic
   order and prove
   \[
   \log U_T
   =-it(A+B)+it^2\sigma_y+O(t^3).
   \]

2. Set $q=\pi/(2\sqrt{2})$ and prove that the (real) overlap trace
   is
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)
   =\cos q+\sqrt{2}\,\sin q
   =1.7111779716570126.
   \]

3. From that single real trace evaluate the spectral (operator-norm)
   error, the Frobenius error, and the one-qubit average gate
   fidelity:
   \[
   \|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{op}}
   =\sqrt{2-\operatorname{Tr}}
   =0.5374216485618972,
   \]
   \[
   \|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{F}}
   =\sqrt{4-2\operatorname{Tr}}
   =0.7600289841091423,
   \]
   \[
   F_{\mathrm{avg}}
   =\frac{\operatorname{Tr}^2+2}{6}
   =0.8213550084473681.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the commutator $[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]$
   vanishes through $O(t^2)$, so $\log U_T=-it(A+B)$ with no
   $it^2\sigma_y$ term”; (ii) “the average gate fidelity is the
   normalized overlap $\operatorname{Tr}/2$, or else the Frobenius
   error is already $\sqrt{2-\operatorname{Tr}}$.”
permittedResults: $(A+B)^2=2I$, so $U=\cos(t\sqrt{2})I-i\sin(t\sqrt{2})(A+B)/\sqrt{2}$. At $t=\pi/4$ the angle is $q=\pi/(2\sqrt{2})$.
Direct expansion of $U^{\dagger}U_T$ yields $\operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)=\cos q+\sqrt{2}\sin q$. The three sample distances/fidelity are then algebraic in that single real number.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate [X,Y]/2 from [sigma_x,sigma_z]=-2i sigma_y, then expand U and UT at t=pi/4 and take the identity part of the product.
Convert the single real overlap tau into sqrt(2-tau), sqrt(4-2 tau), and (tau^2+2)/6.

milestones.criterion: Produces the BCH logarithm -it(A+B)+i t^2 sigma_y+O(t^3) and the overlap identity Tr=cos q+sqrt(2) sin q with q=pi/(2 sqrt 2).
Rejects a dropped quadratic BCH term or a Tr/2-as-fidelity / swapped-distance claim, and refuses reserved Bloch, sequential-spin, or amplitude-damping substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Assumes [sigma_x,sigma_z] does not contribute at O(t^2) and writes log UT=-it(A+B) with no it^2 sigma_y term.
commonErrors.consequence: The required quadratic BCH correction it^2 sigma_y is never produced.

commonErrors.description: Reports the average gate fidelity as Tr/2, or else treats the Frobenius error as already equal to sqrt(2-Tr).
commonErrors.consequence: The required F_avg=0.8213550084473681 and/or the distinct distances 0.5374216485618972 and 0.7600289841091423 are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

hintTree.content: Compute $[X,Y]=(-it)^2[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]=-t^2(-2i\sigma_y)=2it^2\sigma_y$, then divide by $2$.
The spectrum of $A+B$ is $\{\pm\sqrt{2}\}$. The exact propagator is therefore a rotation by angle $t\sqrt{2}=q$.
Once the overlap trace $\tau$ is known and real, the three assigned numbers are $\sqrt{2-\tau}$, $\sqrt{4-2\tau}$, and $(\tau^2+2)/6$. Do not replace the last by $\tau/2$.

GQM:010628.canonicalSolution:
Set $X=-itA=-it\sigma_x$ and $Y=-itB=-it\sigma_z$. The
Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula through quadratic order is
\[
\log(e^X e^Y)
=X+Y+\frac12[X,Y]+O(t^3).
\]
The Pauli commutator is $[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]=-2i\sigma_y$, so
\[
[X,Y]
=(-it)^2[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]
=-t^2(-2i\sigma_y)
=2it^2\sigma_y
\]
and $[X,Y]/2=it^2\sigma_y$. Adding the linear piece
$X+Y=-it(A+B)$ produces
\[
\log U_T
=-it(A+B)+it^2\sigma_y+O(t^3).
\]
\[
\boxed{\log U_T=-it(A+B)+it^2\sigma_y+O(t^3)}.
\]

The combination $A+B=\sigma_x+\sigma_z$ satisfies
$(A+B)^2=2I$, hence $\operatorname{spec}(A+B)=\{\pm\sqrt{2}\}$ and
\[
U
=\cos(t\sqrt{2})\,I
-\frac{i\sin(t\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{2}}\,(A+B).
\]
At $t=\pi/4$ the rotation angle is
\[
q:=t\sqrt{2}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}.
\]
The first-order Trotter factor expands as
\[
U_T
=\bigl(\cos t\,I-i\sin t\,\sigma_x\bigr)
\bigl(\cos t\,I-i\sin t\,\sigma_z\bigr).
\]
At $t=\pi/4$ one has $\cos t=\sin t=1/\sqrt{2}$, so
\[
U_T
=\frac12\bigl(I-i(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)+i\sigma_y\bigr).
\]
The product $U^{\dagger}U_T$ is a $2\times 2$ unitary. Taking the
trace, only the identity channel survives, and one obtains the
real overlap
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)
=\cos q+\sqrt{2}\,\sin q
=1.7111779716570126.
\]
\[
\boxed{q=\pi/(2\sqrt{2}),\ \operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)=\cos q+\sqrt{2}\sin q=1.7111779716570126}.
\]

Write $\tau$ for that real trace. The eigenvalues of
$U^{\dagger}U_T$ are $e^{\pm i\phi}$ with $2\cos\phi=\tau$, so
\[
\|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=\bigl|1-e^{i\phi}\bigr|
=\sqrt{2-\tau}
=0.5374216485618972.
\]
The Frobenius identity on $2\times 2$ unitaries is
\[
\|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
=4-2\operatorname{Re}\tau
=4-2\tau,
\]
hence
\[
\|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{F}}
=\sqrt{4-2\tau}
=0.7600289841091423.
\]
The one-qubit average gate fidelity ($d=2$) is
\[
F_{\mathrm{avg}}
=\frac{\lvert\operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)\rvert^2/2+1}{3}
=\frac{\tau^2+2}{6}
=0.8213550084473681.
\]
\[
\boxed{\|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=0.5374216485618972,\quad
\|U-U_T\|_{\mathrm{F}}=0.7600289841091423,\quad
F_{\mathrm{avg}}=0.8213550084473681}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the quadratic BCH commutator and never produces
$it^2\sigma_y$. Sentence (ii) confuses $F_{\mathrm{avg}}$ with the
raw overlap $\tau/2$, or confuses the Frobenius and operator-norm
formulae. The construction is a static two-generator Trotter
audit; it is not a Bloch-sphere protocol, not a sequential-spin
cascade, and not an amplitude-damping channel.

graderFixtures.proofText: The BCH logarithm is $\log U_T=-it(A+B)+it^2\sigma_y+O(t^3)$. With $q=\pi/(2\sqrt{2})$ one has $\operatorname{Tr}(U^{\dagger}U_T)=\cos q+\sqrt{2}\sin q=1.7111779716570126$. The spectral error is $0.5374216485618972$, the Frobenius error is $0.7600289841091423$, and the average gate fidelity is $0.8213550084473681$.
The commutator [sigma_x,sigma_z] vanishes through O(t^2), so log UT=-it(A+B) with no it^2 sigma_y term. I do not report the assigned quadratic BCH correction.

The average gate fidelity is the normalized overlap Tr/2, or else the Frobenius error is already sqrt(2-Tr). I never accept F_avg=(Tr^2+2)/6=0.8213550084473681 together with the two distinct distances.

GQM:010629.title: Magnus terms Omega1=-i(sigma_x+sigma_z) and Omega2=-i sigma_y/3 give radii sqrt(2), sqrt(19)/3 and P2=0.5190422230065088
GQM:010629.objective: For H(t)=a sigma_x+b t sigma_z on [0,T] with hbar=1, prove Omega1=-i(a T sigma_x+b T^2 sigma_z/2) and Omega2=-i a b T^3 sigma_y/6. At a=1, b=2, T=1 report Omega1=-i(sigma_x+sigma_z), Omega2=-i sigma_y/3, radii sqrt(2) and sqrt(19)/3, traces 0.31188738953074874 and 0.23511508915961155, and from |0> the probabilities 0.4878407820314619 and 0.5190422230065088. Do not use Berry or adiabatic framing.
GQM:010629.statement:
Work with $\hbar=1$ and the linearly driven two-level Hamiltonian
\[
H(t)=a\,\sigma_x+bt\,\sigma_z
\]
on the finite interval $[0,T]$. Use the Magnus expansion of the
time-ordered exponential through second order. Do not recast the
drive as a Berry-phase or adiabatic parallel-transport problem, and
do not replace it by a degenerate / non-Abelian holonomy.

1. Prove the first two Magnus generators
   \[
   \Omega_1
   =-i\Bigl(aT\,\sigma_x+\frac{bT^2}{2}\sigma_z\Bigr),
   \]
   \[
   \Omega_2
   =-i\frac{abT^3}{6}\sigma_y.
   \]

2. At the sample $a=1$, $b=2$, $T=1$ obtain
   \[
   \Omega_1=-i(\sigma_x+\sigma_z),\qquad
   \Omega_2=-i\frac{\sigma_y}{3}.
   \]
   Prove that the operator-norm radii are
   \[
   \|\Omega_1\|=\sqrt{2},\qquad
   \|\Omega_1+\Omega_2\|=\frac{\sqrt{19}}{3}.
   \]

3. The corresponding unitaries are rotations, with traces
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}e^{\Omega_1}
   =2\cos\sqrt{2}
   =0.31188738953074874,
   \]
   \[
   \operatorname{Tr}e^{\Omega_1+\Omega_2}
   =2\cos\bigl(\sqrt{19}/3\bigr)
   =0.23511508915961155.
   \]
   Starting from $|0\rangle$ (the $+z$ eigenstate), prove that the
   excitation probabilities are
   \[
   P_1
   =\frac12\sin^2\sqrt{2}
   =0.4878407820314619,
   \]
   \[
   P_2
   =\frac{10}{19}\sin^2\bigl(\sqrt{19}/3\bigr)
   =0.5190422230065088.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “second order is unnecessary, so the
   assigned second-order probability is already $P_1=0.4878407820314619$”;
   (ii) “the second-order radius is $\|\Omega_2\|=1/3$ rather than
   $\|\Omega_1+\Omega_2\|=\sqrt{19}/3$, so the second-order trace is
   $2\cos(1/3)$.”
permittedResults: $[H(t_1),H(t_2)]=2iab(t_1-t_2)\sigma_y$. Integrating the triangle $0\le t_2\le t_1\le T$ produces the coefficient $ab T^3/6$ in $\Omega_2$.

At $a=1$, $b=2$, $T=1$ one has $\mathbf n_1=(1,0,1)$ and $\mathbf n_1+\mathbf n_2=(1,1/3,1)$, hence radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{19}/3$. The $|0\rangle\to|1\rangle$ weights are $\sin^2\sqrt{2}/2$ and $(10/19)\sin^2(\sqrt{19}/3)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate H(t) for Omega1 and evaluate the nested Pauli commutator on the triangle 0<=t2<=t1<=T for Omega2.
Read radii as Euclidean lengths of (1,0,1) and (1,1/3,1), then compute the |0> to |1> weights from the corresponding Pauli rotations.

milestones.criterion: Produces Omega1=-i(a T sigma_x+b T^2 sigma_z/2) and Omega2=-i a b T^3 sigma_y/6, specialized to -i(sigma_x+sigma_z) and -i sigma_y/3.
Rejects a first-order-only probability or a ||Omega2||=1/3 radius, and refuses reserved Berry / adiabatic substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Stops at first order and reports the assigned second-order probability as already P1=0.4878407820314619.
commonErrors.consequence: The required second-order value P2=(10/19) sin^2(sqrt(19)/3)=0.5190422230065088 is never produced.

commonErrors.description: Takes the second-order radius to be ||Omega2||=1/3 rather than ||Omega1+Omega2||=sqrt(19)/3, and reports the trace 2 cos(1/3).
commonErrors.consequence: The required radius sqrt(19)/3 and the sample trace 0.23511508915961155 are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

hintTree.content: Integrate the coefficients of $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_z$ separately to obtain $\Omega_1$. The $\sigma_y$ term arises only from the nested commutator.
The Euclidean length of $(1,0,1)$ is $\sqrt{2}$. Adding $(0,1/3,0)$ produces $(1,1/3,1)$ of length $\sqrt{19}/3$.
On $|0\rangle$ one has $\sigma_x|0\rangle=|1\rangle$, $\sigma_y|0\rangle=i|1\rangle$, and $\sigma_z|0\rangle=|0\rangle$. The first-order amplitude is $-i\sin(\sqrt{2})/\sqrt{2}$.

GQM:010629.canonicalSolution:
The first Magnus generator is the integrated Hamiltonian,
\[
\Omega_1
=-i\int_0^T H(t)\,dt
=-i\int_0^T\bigl(a\sigma_x+bt\sigma_z\bigr)\,dt
=-i\Bigl(aT\sigma_x+\frac{bT^2}{2}\sigma_z\Bigr).
\]
The second generator uses
\[
[H(t_1),H(t_2)]
=[a\sigma_x+bt_1\sigma_z,\,a\sigma_x+bt_2\sigma_z]
=ab(t_2-t_1)[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]
=-2iab(t_2-t_1)\sigma_y.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
\Omega_2
&=\frac{(-i)^2}{2}\int_0^T\mathrm{d}t_1\int_0^{t_1}\mathrm{d}t_2\,
[H(t_1),H(t_2)]\\
&=-\frac12\int_0^T\mathrm{d}t_1\int_0^{t_1}\mathrm{d}t_2\,
\bigl(-2iab(t_2-t_1)\sigma_y\bigr)
=-i\frac{abT^3}{6}\sigma_y.
\end{align*}
(The inner integral is $\int_0^{t_1}(t_2-t_1)\,dt_2=-t_1^2/2$, and
$\int_0^T t_1^2\,dt_1=T^3/3$.)
\[
\boxed{\Omega_1=-i(aT\sigma_x+bT^2\sigma_z/2),\quad
\Omega_2=-i ab T^3\sigma_y/6}.
\]

At $a=1$, $b=2$, $T=1$ these collapse to
\[
\Omega_1=-i(\sigma_x+\sigma_z),\qquad
\Omega_2=-i\frac{\sigma_y}{3}.
\]
The first-order vector is $\mathbf n_1=(1,0,1)$, of Euclidean
length $\sqrt{2}$. Adding the second-order piece gives
$\mathbf n_1+\mathbf n_2=(1,1/3,1)$, of length
\[
\sqrt{1+\frac19+1}=\frac{\sqrt{19}}{3}.
\]
Those lengths are the operator-norm radii of $\Omega_1$ and of
$\Omega_1+\Omega_2$.
\[
\boxed{\Omega_1=-i(\sigma_x+\sigma_z),\ \Omega_2=-i\sigma_y/3;\quad
\|\Omega_1\|=\sqrt{2},\ \|\Omega_1+\Omega_2\|=\sqrt{19}/3}.
\]

A generator $\Omega=-i\,\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ produces the
rotation $e^{\Omega}=\cos r\,I-i\sin r\,\hat n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ with
$r=\lvert\mathbf n\rvert$, hence $\operatorname{Tr}e^{\Omega}=2\cos r$.
The two assigned traces are therefore
\[
\operatorname{Tr}e^{\Omega_1}
=2\cos\sqrt{2}
=0.31188738953074874,
\]
\[
\operatorname{Tr}e^{\Omega_1+\Omega_2}
=2\cos\bigl(\sqrt{19}/3\bigr)
=0.23511508915961155.
\]

Start from $|0\rangle$. The first-order unitary acts by
\[
e^{\Omega_1}|0\rangle
=\cos\sqrt{2}\,|0\rangle
-\frac{i\sin\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)|0\rangle.
\]
Since $(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)|0\rangle=|1\rangle+|0\rangle$, the
excited amplitude is $-i\sin\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{2}$ and
\[
P_1
=\frac12\sin^2\sqrt{2}
=0.4878407820314619.
\]
Through second order, $\hat n=(3,1,3)/\sqrt{19}$ and
\[
\hat n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\,|0\rangle
=\hat n_z|0\rangle+(\hat n_x+i\hat n_y)|1\rangle,
\]
so
\[
P_2
=\sin^2 r\cdot\frac{9+1}{19}
=\frac{10}{19}\sin^2\bigl(\sqrt{19}/3\bigr)
=0.5190422230065088.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_1=0.4878407820314619,\ P_2=0.5190422230065088}.
\]

Sentence (i) stops at first order and reports $P_1$ as if it were
the assigned second-order probability. Sentence (ii) uses the
isolated second-order radius $\|\Omega_2\|=1/3$ rather than
$\|\Omega_1+\Omega_2\|=\sqrt{19}/3$. The calculation is a
finite-interval Magnus truncation of a linear drive; it is not a
Berry-phase argument and not a degenerate / non-Abelian adiabatic
transport.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Magnus generators are $\Omega_1=-i(aT\sigma_x+bT^2\sigma_z/2)$ and $\Omega_2=-i ab T^3\sigma_y/6$. At $a=1$, $b=2$, $T=1$ one has $\Omega_1=-i(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)$, $\Omega_2=-i\sigma_y/3$, radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{19}/3$, traces $2\cos\sqrt{2}=0.31188738953074874$ and $2\cos(\sqrt{19}/3)=0.23511508915961155$, and from $|0\rangle$ the probabilities $P_1=0.4878407820314619$ and $P_2=0.5190422230065088$.
Second order is unnecessary, so the assigned second-order probability is already P1=0.4878407820314619. I do not report P2=0.5190422230065088.
The second-order radius is ||Omega2||=1/3 rather than ||Omega1+Omega2||=sqrt(19)/3, so the second-order trace is 2 cos(1/3). I never accept 2 cos(sqrt(19)/3)=0.23511508915961155.

GQM:010630.title: The Gaussian variational energy of p^2/2+|x| is 3 alpha*/4=0.8128891052089335 at alpha*=(4/pi)^{1/3}
GQM:010630.objective: For H=p^2/2+|x| and the trial psi_alpha=(alpha/pi)^{1/4} exp(-alpha x^2/2), prove E(alpha)=alpha/4+1/sqrt(pi alpha), the stationarity alpha*=(4/pi)^{1/3}=1.0838521402785781, the expectations <T>=0.2709630350696445, <V>=0.5419260701392891, E_var=0.8128891052089335, the virial 2T=V, and the moments <x^2>=0.4613175371610070 and <p^2>=alpha*/2.
GQM:010630.statement:
Work in units $\hbar=m=1$ with the Hamiltonian
\[
H=\frac{p^2}{2}+|x|
\]
on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Use the normalized Gaussian family
\[
\psi_{\alpha}(x)
=\Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\Bigr)^{1/4}e^{-\alpha x^2/2},\qquad
\alpha>0.
\]
Do not replace the variational estimate by a quantum-bouncer WKB
integral, a singular radial endpoint analysis, or a delta-function
bound-state construction.

1. Prove the energy functional
   \[
   E(\alpha)
   =\frac{\alpha}{4}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi\alpha}}.
   \]

2. Minimize and obtain
   \[
   \alpha^{*}
   =\Bigl(\frac{4}{\pi}\Bigr)^{1/3}
   =1.0838521402785781.
   \]
   Evaluate
   \[
   \langle T\rangle=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{4}=0.2709630350696445,
   \]
   \[
   \langle V\rangle=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{2}=0.5419260701392891,
   \]
   \[
   E_{\mathrm{var}}
   =\frac{3\alpha^{*}}{4}
   =0.8128891052089335,
   \]
   and verify the virial relation $2\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$.

3. At the same stationary width report the moments
   \[
   \langle x^2\rangle
   =\frac{1}{2\alpha^{*}}
   =0.4613175371610070,
   \qquad
   \langle p^2\rangle
   =\frac{\alpha^{*}}{2}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the variational energy is the kinetic
   piece $\alpha^{*}/4$, or else only the potential $\alpha^{*}/2$,
   rather than $3\alpha^{*}/4$”; (ii) “stationarity inverts the
   coupling, so $\alpha^{*}=(\pi/4)^{1/3}$ rather than
   $(4/\pi)^{1/3}$.”
permittedResults: $\int_0^{\infty}x e^{-\alpha x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=1/(2\alpha)$ converts the even density $(\alpha/\pi)^{1/2}e^{-\alpha x^2}$ into $\langle|x|\rangle=1/\sqrt{\pi\alpha}$.
Differentiating $E(\alpha)$ gives $1/4=1/(2\alpha\sqrt{\pi\alpha})$, hence $\pi\alpha^3=4$. Substituting back produces $E=3\alpha^{*}/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate Gaussian moments <p^2>=alpha/2 and < |x| >=1/sqrt(pi alpha), then differentiate the energy functional.
Use stationarity 1/sqrt(pi alpha*)=alpha*/2 to read off 2T=V and E=3 alpha*/4 together with the two second moments.

milestones.criterion: Produces E(alpha)=alpha/4+1/sqrt(pi alpha) and the stationary width alpha*=(4/pi)^{1/3}.
Rejects a kinetic-only or potential-only energy or an inverted (pi/4)^{1/3} width, and refuses reserved WKB, radial-endpoint, or delta-bound substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the variational energy as the kinetic piece alpha*/4 or the potential piece alpha*/2 rather than 3 alpha*/4.
Inverts the stationarity relation and reports alpha*=(pi/4)^{1/3} rather than (4/pi)^{1/3}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required width 1.0838521402785781 and every derived sample number are lost.

hintTree.content: The Gaussian kinetic energy is the same as that of the unit-oscillator ground state of frequency $\alpha$, namely $\alpha/4$.
Compute $\langle|x|\rangle$ from twice the half-line integral $\int_0^{\infty}x(\alpha/\pi)^{1/2}e^{-\alpha x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x$.
Set $E'(\alpha)=0$. The inverted root $(\pi/4)^{1/3}$ is not stationary, and neither $\alpha^{*}/4$ nor $\alpha^{*}/2$ is the full variational energy.

GQM:010630.canonicalSolution:
The trial family is normalized because
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\lvert\psi_{\alpha}\rvert^2\,\mathrm{d}x
=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\pi}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\alpha x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x
=1.
\]
The second moment of a centered Gaussian of variance $1/(2\alpha)$ is
\[
\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2\alpha}.
\]
With $\hbar=1$, the Fourier transform of $\psi_{\alpha}$ is a
Gaussian of variance $\alpha/2$, so $\langle p^2\rangle=\alpha/2$
and
\[
\langle T\rangle
=\frac{\langle p^2\rangle}{2}
=\frac{\alpha}{4}.
\]
The potential expectation is even:
\[
\langle|x|\rangle
=2\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\pi}}\int_0^{\infty}x\,e^{-\alpha x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x
=2\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\pi}}\cdot\frac{1}{2\alpha}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi\alpha}}.
\]
Adding the two pieces,
\[
E(\alpha)
=\frac{\alpha}{4}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi\alpha}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E(\alpha)=\alpha/4+1/\sqrt{\pi\alpha}}.
\]

Differentiate:
\[
E'(\alpha)
=\frac14-\frac{1}{2\alpha\sqrt{\pi\alpha}}.
\]
The unique positive critical point satisfies
\[
2\alpha\sqrt{\pi\alpha}=4
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\pi\alpha^3=4
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\alpha^{*}
=\Bigl(\frac{4}{\pi}\Bigr)^{1/3}
=1.0838521402785781.
\]
(The second derivative $E''(\alpha^{*})>0$, so the critical point
is a minimum.) Substituting the stationarity relation
$1/\sqrt{\pi\alpha^{*}}=\alpha^{*}/2$ into the energy functional
gives
\[
\langle T\rangle
=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{4}
=0.2709630350696445,
\qquad
\langle V\rangle
=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{2}
=0.5419260701392891,
\]
\[
E_{\mathrm{var}}
=\frac{3\alpha^{*}}{4}
=0.8128891052089335.
\]
In particular $2\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$, which is the
virial identity for $V=|x|$.
\[
\boxed{\alpha^{*}=(4/\pi)^{1/3}=1.0838521402785781;\quad
\langle T\rangle=0.2709630350696445,\quad
\langle V\rangle=0.5419260701392891,\quad
E_{\mathrm{var}}=0.8128891052089335;\quad
2\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle}.
\]

The same stationary width produces the moments
\[
\langle x^2\rangle
=\frac{1}{2\alpha^{*}}
=0.4613175371610070,
\qquad
\langle p^2\rangle
=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=0.4613175371610070,\ \langle p^2\rangle=\alpha^{*}/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) reports only $\langle T\rangle$ or only $\langle V\rangle$
as the variational energy, missing the factor $3/4$. Sentence (ii)
inverts the coupling and uses $(\pi/4)^{1/3}$. The calculation is
a one-parameter Gaussian variational bound for $p^2/2+|x|$; it is
not a quantum-bouncer WKB integral, not a singular radial endpoint
problem, and not a delta-function bound state.

graderFixtures.proofText: The energy functional is $E(\alpha)=\alpha/4+1/\sqrt{\pi\alpha}$, minimized at $\alpha^{*}=(4/\pi)^{1/3}=1.0838521402785781$. Then $\langle T\rangle=0.2709630350696445$, $\langle V\rangle=0.5419260701392891$, $E_{\mathrm{var}}=0.8128891052089335$, $2\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$, $\langle x^2\rangle=0.4613175371610070$, and $\langle p^2\rangle=\alpha^{*}/2$.
The variational energy is the kinetic piece alpha*/4, or else only the potential alpha*/2, rather than 3 alpha*/4. I do not report E_var=0.8128891052089335.
Stationarity inverts the coupling, so alpha*=(pi/4)^{1/3} rather than (4/pi)^{1/3}. I never accept alpha*=1.0838521402785781.

GQM:020117.title: Hahn echo FPF=P returns |+x> with Mx=1 for every static delta; Gaussian ensemble without pulse is exp(-1/2) at sigma tau=1/2
GQM:020117.objective: For F=exp(-i delta tau sigma_z/2) and P=-i sigma_x prove FPF=P, that initial |+x> returns with Mx=1 for every static delta, that without the pulse Mx=cos(2 delta tau), and that a N(0,sigma^2) ensemble has Mx=exp(-2 sigma^2 tau^2) so sigma tau=1/2 gives exp(-1/2). State that the echo refocuses static/quasistatic detuning only, not arbitrary time-dependent noise or T1/T2.
GQM:020117.statement:
Work with a spin-$1/2$ in a static detuning $\delta$ (units
$\hbar=1$). Write the free propagator across a waiting time $\tau$
and the $\pi$-pulse
\[
F=\exp\bigl(-i\delta\tau\,\sigma_z/2\bigr),\qquad
P=-i\sigma_x.
\]
Do not replace the static-detuning echo ledger by a claim that the
same sequence refocuses arbitrary time-dependent noise, $T_1$, or
$T_2$, and do not replace it by a first-Born / Yukawa scattering
exercise.

1. Prove the operator identity $FPF=P$.

2. Start from the $+1$ eigenstate $|+x\rangle$ of $\sigma_x$. Prove
   that the echoed state $FPF|+x\rangle$ is $|+x\rangle$ up to a
   global phase, and that the transverse magnetization is
   \[
   M_x:=\langle\sigma_x\rangle=1
   \]
   for every static $\delta$.

3. Without the pulse, the evolution on the same total time $2\tau$
   is $F^2$. Prove $M_x=\cos(2\delta\tau)$. If
   $\delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, prove that the ensemble
   average is
   \[
   \overline{M_x}=\exp(-2\sigma^2\tau^2),
   \]
   and therefore that $\sigma\tau=1/2$ yields $\exp(-1/2)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $F$ does not cancel, the
   echoed magnetization remains $M_x=\cos(2\delta\tau)$ rather than
   $M_x=1$”; (ii) “the Gaussian average without the pulse is
   $\exp(-\sigma^2\tau^2)$, so $\sigma\tau=1/2$ gives $\exp(-1/4)$
   rather than $\exp(-1/2)$.” State sharply that the identity
   $FPF=P$ refocuses static or quasistatic detuning only.
permittedResults: $\sigma_x$ anticommutes with $\sigma_z$, so $\sigma_x\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)=\exp(+i\theta\sigma_z/2)\sigma_x$. Therefore $FPF=-i\sigma_x=P$.
Without the pulse, $M_x=\cos(2\delta\tau)$. The $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ average is $\exp(-2\sigma^2\tau^2)$, hence $\sigma\tau=1/2$ gives $\exp(-1/2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pass sigma_x through the free exponential using the Pauli anticommutator to obtain FPF=P, then apply the product to |+x>.
Read the unechoed cosine as the real part of a z-rotation and evaluate the N(0,sigma^2) characteristic function at frequency 2 tau.

milestones.criterion: Produces the identity FPF=P and the echoed magnetization Mx=1 for every static detuning.
Reports unechoed Mx=cos(2 delta tau), ensemble exp(-2 sigma^2 tau^2), and the sample exp(-1/2) at sigma tau=1/2.
Rejects an unechoed cosine after the pulse or a halved Gaussian exponent, and states that the echo does not invert arbitrary time-dependent noise or T1/T2.

commonErrors.description: Claims that after FPF the magnetization remains Mx=cos(2 delta tau) instead of Mx=1 for every static delta.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity FPF=P and the static-detuning refocusing ledger are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the Gaussian ensemble without the pulse is exp(-sigma^2 tau^2), so sigma tau=1/2 gives exp(-1/4) instead of exp(-1/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The characteristic-function identity E[cos(2 delta tau)]=exp(-2 sigma^2 tau^2) and the assigned sample exp(-1/2) are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

hintTree.content: Use $\{\sigma_x,\sigma_z\}=0$ to pass $\sigma_x$ through the second exponential, flipping the sign of the $\sigma_z$ generator.
Because $FPF=P$ and $P|+x\rangle=-i|+x\rangle$, the echoed Bloch vector is still $+x$ for every static $\delta$.
The Gaussian integral $\int\cos(2\delta\tau)\,(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-\delta^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,d\delta$ is the real part of the characteristic function at frequency $2\tau$.

GQM:020117.canonicalSolution:
Write $\theta=\delta\tau$. Then
$F=\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)$. Because $\sigma_x\sigma_z=-\sigma_z\sigma_x$,
\[
\sigma_x\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)=\exp(+i\theta\sigma_z/2)\sigma_x.
\]
Hence
\begin{align*}
FPF
&=\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)\,(-i\sigma_x)\,\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)\\
&=-i\exp(-i\theta\sigma_z/2)\exp(+i\theta\sigma_z/2)\,\sigma_x
=-i\sigma_x
=P.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{FPF=P}.
\]

The state $|+x\rangle$ is the $+1$ eigenvector of $\sigma_x$, so
$P|+x\rangle=-i|+x\rangle$. The echo therefore returns
\[
FPF|+x\rangle=P|+x\rangle=-i|+x\rangle,
\]
a global phase times the initial state, for every static $\delta$.
The transverse magnetization is
\[
M_x=\langle+x|\sigma_x|+x\rangle=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{M_x^{\mathrm{echo}}=1\text{ for every static }\delta}.
\]

Without the pulse the evolution on total time $2\tau$ is
$F^2=\exp(-i\delta\tau\sigma_z)$, a $z$-rotation by angle $2\delta\tau$.
Starting from $|+x\rangle$ one has $M_x=\cos(2\delta\tau)$. If
$\delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, the characteristic function
$\mathbb{E}[e^{it\delta}]=\exp(-\sigma^2 t^2/2)$ at $t=2\tau$ yields
\[
\overline{M_x}=\exp(-2\sigma^2\tau^2).
\]
The sample $\sigma\tau=1/2$ therefore gives
\[
\overline{M_x}=\exp\bigl(-2\cdot\tfrac14\bigr)=\exp(-1/2).
\]
\[
\boxed{\overline{M_x}=e^{-2\sigma^2\tau^2},\;\sigma\tau=1/2\Rightarrow e^{-1/2}}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies $FPF=P$ and reports the unechoed cosine after
the pulse. Sentence (ii) halves the Gaussian exponent and reports
$e^{-1/4}$ at $\sigma\tau=1/2$. The identity refocuses static or
quasistatic detuning only: a genuinely time-dependent $\delta(t)$
need not satisfy $F[\delta]\,P\,F[\delta]=P$, and neither $T_1$
amplitude damping nor a dynamical $T_2$ bath is inverted by this
single $\pi$-pulse.

graderFixtures.proofText: The identity $FPF=P$ returns $|+x\rangle$ with $M_x=1$ for every static $\delta$. Without the pulse $M_x=\cos(2\delta\tau)$, and a $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ ensemble has $\overline{M_x}=\exp(-2\sigma^2\tau^2)$, hence $\sigma\tau=1/2$ gives $\exp(-1/2)$. The sequence refocuses static or quasistatic detuning only, not arbitrary time-dependent noise or $T_1/T_2$.
Because F does not cancel, the echoed magnetization remains Mx=cos(2 delta tau). I do not report Mx=1 after FPF.
The Gaussian average without the pulse is exp(-sigma^2 tau^2), so sigma tau=1/2 gives exp(-1/4). I never obtain exp(-2 sigma^2 tau^2) or the sample exp(-1/2).

GQM:020218.title: Gaussian eikonal through eta^2 at k=a=1, eta=1/2, q=0 equals -1/4+i/32
GQM:020218.objective: For V=V0 exp(-r^2/a^2) with eikonal phase chi(b)=-eta exp(-b^2/a^2) and eta=sqrt(pi) V0 a/(hbar v), expand f(q) through order eta^2 and evaluate f=-1/4+i/32 at k=a=1, eta=1/2, q=0. Keep the second-order term so the exercise is not a first-Born/Yukawa retread, and do not invoke the optical theorem outside approximation control.
GQM:020218.statement:
Consider the Gaussian potential
\[
V(r)=V_0\exp(-r^2/a^2)
\]
in the eikonal approximation at incident wave number $k$ and speed
$v$. Write
\[
\eta=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,V_0 a}{\hbar v},\qquad
\chi(b)=-\eta\exp(-b^2/a^2).
\]
The eikonal amplitude is
\[
f(\mathbf q)=\frac{k}{2\pi i}\int d^2b\,
e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf b}\bigl(e^{i\chi(b)}-1\bigr).
\]
Do not replace the second-order Gaussian eikonal ledger by a
first-Born / Yukawa amplitude, and do not invoke the optical
theorem as an exact identity outside the control of the eikonal
approximation.

1. Expand $e^{i\chi}-1$ in powers of $\eta$ and evaluate the
   two-dimensional Fourier transforms to prove
   \[
   f(q)=\frac{ka^2}{2i}\sum_{n\ge 1}
   \frac{(-i\eta)^n}{n\,n!}\,
   \exp\bigl[-q^2 a^2/(4n)\bigr].
   \]

2. Retain terms through $\eta^2$ and prove
   \[
   f(q)
   =-\frac{ka^2\eta}{2}\exp(-q^2 a^2/4)
   +i\frac{ka^2\eta^2}{8}\exp(-q^2 a^2/8).
   \]

3. Specialize to $k=a=1$, $\eta=1/2$, $q=0$ and prove
   \[
   f=-1/4+i/32.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “only the first-order (Born-like)
   term is needed, so $f=-1/4$ with vanishing imaginary part”;
   (ii) “the optical theorem fixes $|f|^2$ exactly at this
   kinematics, independently of the eikonal truncation.”
permittedResults: $\int d^2b\,e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot b}e^{-n b^2/a^2}=(\pi a^2/n)\exp(-q^2 a^2/(4n))$. Combined with $e^{i\chi}-1=\sum_{n\ge 1}(-i\eta)^n/n!\,e^{-n b^2/a^2}$ this yields the stated series for $f(q)$.
Truncation through $n=2$ gives $f=-(ka^2\eta/2)e^{-q^2 a^2/4}+i(ka^2\eta^2/8)e^{-q^2 a^2/8}$. At $k=a=1$, $\eta=1/2$, $q=0$ one obtains $-1/4+i/32$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand exp(i chi)-1 in powers of eta and Fourier-transform each Gaussian in the impact-parameter plane.
Keep the n=2 term explicitly and insert the sample (k,a,eta,q)=(1,1,1/2,0).

milestones.criterion: Produces the eikonal series for the Gaussian potential and the explicit truncation through eta^2.
Reports the sample amplitude -1/4+i/32 at k=a=1, eta=1/2, q=0.
Rejects a first-Born/Yukawa (first-order-only) retread or an optical-theorem identity used outside eikonal approximation control.

commonErrors.description: Drops the second-order eikonal term and reports f=-1/4 with vanishing imaginary part, instead of -1/4+i/32.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned second-order sample is replaced by a first-Born-like real value and the eta^2 correction is lost.

commonErrors.description: Invokes the optical theorem as an exact identity at this kinematics, independently of the eikonal truncation.
commonErrors.consequence: An on-shell unitarity identity is asserted outside the control of the eikonal approximation, which this packet does not grant.

hintTree.content: Write $e^{i\chi}-1=\sum_{n\ge 1}(-i\eta)^n/n!\,\exp(-n b^2/a^2)$ and Fourier-transform each Gaussian in the impact-parameter plane.
The $n=1$ coefficient is $(ka^2/(2i))(-i\eta)=-(ka^2\eta/2)$. The $n=2$ coefficient uses $(-i\eta)^2=-\eta^2$ and $2\cdot 2!=4$.
At $q=0$ every exponential equals $1$. Insert $k=a=1$ and $\eta=1/2$ into the two retained terms.

GQM:020218.canonicalSolution:
Expand the eikonal profile,
\[
e^{i\chi(b)}-1
=\sum_{n\ge 1}\frac{(-i\eta)^n}{n!}
\exp(-n b^2/a^2).
\]
The two-dimensional Fourier transform of a Gaussian is
\[
\int d^2b\,e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot b}e^{-n b^2/a^2}
=\frac{\pi a^2}{n}\exp\bigl(-q^2 a^2/(4n)\bigr).
\]
Inserting the prefactor $k/(2\pi i)$ produces
\[
f(q)
=\frac{ka^2}{2i}\sum_{n\ge 1}
\frac{(-i\eta)^n}{n\,n!}
\exp\bigl[-q^2 a^2/(4n)\bigr].
\]
\[
\boxed{f(q)=(ka^2/(2i))\sum_{n\ge 1}(-i\eta)^n/(n\,n!)\,e^{-q^2 a^2/(4n)}}.
\]

The $n=1$ term is
\[
\frac{ka^2}{2i}(-i\eta)\exp(-q^2 a^2/4)
=-\frac{ka^2\eta}{2}\exp(-q^2 a^2/4).
\]
The $n=2$ term uses $(-i\eta)^2=-\eta^2$ and $2\cdot 2!=4$,
\[
\frac{ka^2}{2i}\cdot\frac{-\eta^2}{4}\exp(-q^2 a^2/8)
=i\frac{ka^2\eta^2}{8}\exp(-q^2 a^2/8).
\]
Through order $\eta^2$,
\[
f(q)
=-\frac{ka^2\eta}{2}e^{-q^2 a^2/4}
+i\frac{ka^2\eta^2}{8}e^{-q^2 a^2/8}.
\]
\[
\boxed{f=-(ka^2\eta/2)e^{-q^2 a^2/4}+i(ka^2\eta^2/8)e^{-q^2 a^2/8}}.
\]

At $k=a=1$, $\eta=1/2$, $q=0$ every exponential equals $1$, and
\[
f
=-\frac{1\cdot(1/2)}{2}
+i\frac{1\cdot(1/4)}{8}
=-\frac14+\frac{i}{32}.
\]
\[
\boxed{f=-1/4+i/32}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the $n=2$ term and reports a purely real
first-order value $-1/4$, which is a first-Born / Yukawa-style
retread of the same Gaussian rather than the assigned second-order
eikonal sample. Sentence (ii) treats the optical theorem as an
exact constraint at this kinematics; the eikonal truncation does
not furnish an on-shell $S$-matrix identity, so the optical
theorem is not available outside approximation control. The
construction is a second-order Gaussian eikonal audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The eikonal series is $f(q)=(ka^2/(2i))\sum_{n\ge 1}(-i\eta)^n/(n\,n!)\exp[-q^2 a^2/(4n)]$. Through $\eta^2$ one has $f=-(ka^2\eta/2)e^{-q^2 a^2/4}+i(ka^2\eta^2/8)e^{-q^2 a^2/8}$, and at $k=a=1$, $\eta=1/2$, $q=0$ this equals $-1/4+i/32$. The optical theorem is not invoked outside eikonal control.
Only the first-order Born-like term is needed, so f=-1/4 with vanishing imaginary part. I do not report -1/4+i/32.
The optical theorem fixes |f|^2 exactly at this kinematics, independently of the eikonal truncation. I do not stay inside eikonal approximation control.

GQM:020319.title: Single-pair BCS at xi=3/4, Delta=1 has E=5/4, ground=-1/2, u^2=4/5, v^2=1/5, uv=2/5
GQM:020319.objective: For H=xi(n_up+n_down)-Delta(c_up^dag c_down^dag+c_down c_up) on the even basis |0>,|up down> prove the matrix [[0,-Delta],[-Delta,2 xi]], E=sqrt(xi^2+Delta^2), ground energy xi-E, u^2=(1+xi/E)/2, v^2=(1-xi/E)/2, uv=Delta/(2E), and at xi=3/4, Delta=1 obtain E=5/4, ground=-1/2, u^2=4/5, v^2=1/5, uv=2/5, odd energies=3/4, even excited=2. Require u^2+v^2=1 and a sign-convention audit.
GQM:020319.statement:
Consider a single fermionic pair orbital with Hamiltonian
\[
H=\xi(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)
-\Delta\bigl(c_\uparrow^\dagger c_\downarrow^\dagger+c_\downarrow c_\uparrow\bigr),
\]
where $\Delta>0$ is real. Work in the Fock space
$\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle,|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle\}$.
Do not replace the even-sector BCS/Bogoliubov ledger by a
many-mode thermodynamic BCS gap equation, and do not drop the
fermionic normalization $u^2+v^2=1$.

1. In the even-parity basis $\bigl(|0\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle\bigr)$
   prove that $H$ is represented by the real symmetric matrix
   \[
   \begin{pmatrix}0&-\Delta\\-\Delta&2\xi\end{pmatrix}.
   \]
   Diagonalize it and prove that the even eigenvalues are
   $\xi\pm E$ with $E=\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$, so the even ground
   energy is $\xi-E$ and the even excited energy is $\xi+E$.

2. For the ground eigenvector written $u|0\rangle+v|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$
   with the sign convention $uv=\Delta/(2E)>0$, prove
   \[
   u^2=\frac{1+\xi/E}{2},\qquad
   v^2=\frac{1-\xi/E}{2},\qquad
   u^2+v^2=1.
   \]

3. Specialize to $\xi=3/4$, $\Delta=1$ and prove
   \[
   E=\frac54,\qquad
   \xi-E=-\frac12,\qquad
   u^2=\frac45,\qquad
   v^2=\frac15,\qquad
   uv=\frac25,
   \]
   that both odd states $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$ have
   energy $3/4$, and that the even excited level equals $2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the ground energy is $-E=-5/4$
   rather than $\xi-E=-1/2$”; (ii) “the coherence factors are
   swapped, so $u^2=1/5$ and $v^2=4/5$, or else $u^2+v^2\neq 1$.”
permittedResults: $H|0\rangle=-\Delta|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$ and $H|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle=2\xi|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-\Delta|0\rangle$, so the even matrix is $[[0,-\Delta],[-\Delta,2\xi]]$ with eigenvalues $\xi\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$.
At $\xi=3/4$, $\Delta=1$ one has $E=5/4$, ground $\xi-E=-1/2$, $u^2=4/5$, $v^2=1/5$, $uv=2/5$, odd energies $3/4$, and even excited energy $2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate H on the even Fock basis to obtain the 2x2 pairing matrix and read eigenvalues xi pm E.
Impose u^2+v^2=1 with uv=Delta/(2E)>0 and insert xi=3/4, Delta=1.

milestones.criterion: Produces the even-sector matrix [[0,-Delta],[-Delta,2 xi]], E=sqrt(xi^2+Delta^2), and ground energy xi-E.
Reports E=5/4, ground=-1/2, u^2=4/5, v^2=1/5, uv=2/5, odd energies 3/4, even excited 2, and u^2+v^2=1.
Rejects a ground energy -E=-5/4 or swapped coherence factors, and audits the positive-Delta sign convention uv=Delta/(2E).

commonErrors.description: Claims the even ground energy is -E=-5/4 instead of xi-E=-1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required even-sector eigenvalue xi-E and the sample ground energy -1/2 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the coherence factors, reporting u^2=1/5 and v^2=4/5 instead of u^2=4/5 and v^2=1/5, or else violates u^2+v^2=1.
commonErrors.consequence: The positive-Delta convention uv=2/5 and the fermionic normalization u^2+v^2=1 are destroyed.

hintTree.content: Evaluate $H$ on $|0\rangle$ and $|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$ with the CAR. The pairing term is the only off-diagonal even-sector matrix element.
The characteristic polynomial of $[[0,-\Delta],[-\Delta,2\xi]]$ is $\lambda^2-2\xi\lambda-\Delta^2=0$, hence $\lambda=\xi\pm E$.
Insert $\xi/E=(3/4)/(5/4)=3/5$ into $u^2=(1+\xi/E)/2$ and $v^2=(1-\xi/E)/2$, and check $uv=\Delta/(2E)=2/5$.

GQM:020319.canonicalSolution:
The pairing operator sends $|0\rangle$ to $|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$ and
back:
\[
H|0\rangle=-\Delta|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle,\qquad
H|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle=2\xi|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-\Delta|0\rangle.
\]
In the ordered even basis $\bigl(|0\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle\bigr)$
this is the real symmetric matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}0&-\Delta\\-\Delta&2\xi\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2-2\xi\lambda-\Delta^2=0$, so
\[
\lambda=\xi\pm E,\qquad E=\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}.
\]
The even ground energy is therefore $\xi-E$ and the even excited
energy is $\xi+E$.
\[
\boxed{\text{even matrix }[[0,-\Delta],[-\Delta,2\xi]],\;
E=\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2},\;
E_{\mathrm{gs}}=\xi-E}.
\]

For $\lambda=\xi-E$ the eigenvector equation
$(E-\xi)u-\Delta v=0$ together with $u^2+v^2=1$ and the sign
convention $uv=\Delta/(2E)>0$ produces
\[
u^2=\frac{1+\xi/E}{2},\qquad
v^2=\frac{1-\xi/E}{2}.
\]
These sum to $1$ identically. The product is
\[
uv=\frac{\Delta}{2E}.
\]
\[
\boxed{u^2=(1+\xi/E)/2,\;v^2=(1-\xi/E)/2,\;uv=\Delta/(2E),\;u^2+v^2=1}.
\]

Now set $\xi=3/4$ and $\Delta=1$. Then
\[
E=\sqrt{(3/4)^2+1}=\sqrt{25/16}=5/4,
\]
the even ground energy is
\[
\xi-E=3/4-5/4=-1/2,
\]
and the even excited energy is $\xi+E=2$. The ratio $\xi/E=3/5$
gives
\[
u^2=\frac{1+3/5}{2}=\frac45,\qquad
v^2=\frac{1-3/5}{2}=\frac15,\qquad
uv=\frac{1}{2\cdot 5/4}=\frac25.
\]
On the odd subspace the pairing terms annihilate, so
$H|\uparrow\rangle=\xi|\uparrow\rangle$ and
$H|\downarrow\rangle=\xi|\downarrow\rangle$: both odd energies equal
$3/4$.
\[
\boxed{E=5/4,\;E_{\mathrm{gs}}=-1/2,\;u^2=4/5,\;v^2=1/5,\;uv=2/5,\;
E_{\mathrm{odd}}=3/4,\;E_{\mathrm{exc}}=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the shift $\xi$ and reports ground energy
$-E=-5/4$. Sentence (ii) swaps $u^2$ with $v^2$ or violates
$u^2+v^2=1$, destroying the positive-$\Delta$ sign convention
$uv=+2/5$. The construction is a single-orbital fermionic
BCS/Bogoliubov audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The even matrix is $[[0,-\Delta],[-\Delta,2\xi]]$ with $E=\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$ and ground energy $\xi-E$. At $\xi=3/4$, $\Delta=1$ one has $E=5/4$, ground $-1/2$, $u^2=4/5$, $v^2=1/5$, $uv=2/5$, $u^2+v^2=1$, odd energies $3/4$, and even excited energy $2$.
The ground energy is -E=-5/4 rather than xi-E=-1/2. I do not report the even ground energy -1/2.
The coherence factors are swapped, so u^2=1/5 and v^2=4/5. I never obtain u^2=4/5, v^2=1/5, and uv=2/5 with u^2+v^2=1.

GQM:020320.title: Two-mode fermionic Gaussian C=[[3/4,1/4],[1/4,1/2]] has Wick <n1 n2>=5/16, Cov=-1/16, Var(N)=5/16
GQM:020320.objective: For a gauge-invariant fermionic Gaussian CAR state with C=<c_i^dag c_j>=[[3/4,1/4],[1/4,1/2]] prove the eigenvalues (5 pm sqrt(5))/8 lie in [0,1], and that Wick gives <n1 n2>=C11 C22-|C12|^2=5/16, Cov=-1/16, and Var(N)=Tr C(1-C)=5/16. State the Gaussian-state assumption explicitly; do not apply Wick to arbitrary states.
GQM:020320.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a gauge-invariant fermionic Gaussian state for two
canonical anticommuting modes, uniquely determined by the
correlation matrix
\[
C_{ij}=\langle c_i^\dagger c_j\rangle
=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Do not apply Wick's theorem to an arbitrary (non-Gaussian) state,
and do not replace the two-mode CAR ledger by a bosonic covariance
calculation.

1. Prove that the eigenvalues of $C$ are
   \[
   \lambda_\pm=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{5}}{8}
   \]
   and that both lie in the physical interval $[0,1]$.

2. Under the fermionic Gaussian (Wick) assumption, prove
   \[
   \langle n_1 n_2\rangle
   =C_{11}C_{22}-\lvert C_{12}\rvert^2
   =\frac{5}{16},
   \]
   and therefore
   \[
   \operatorname{Cov}(n_1,n_2)
   =\langle n_1 n_2\rangle-\langle n_1\rangle\langle n_2\rangle
   =-\frac{1}{16}.
   \]

3. For $N=n_1+n_2$ prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}(N)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(C(1-C)\bigr)=\frac{5}{16}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Wick's theorem applies to every
   two-mode fermion state, Gaussian or not, so the same
   contractions hold without the Gaussian assumption”; (ii)
   “$\langle n_1 n_2\rangle=C_{11}C_{22}=3/8$ with no subtracted
   coherence, so neither $\langle n_1 n_2\rangle$ nor
   $\operatorname{Var}(N)$ equals $5/16$.”
permittedResults: $\det(C-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(5/4)\lambda+5/16$, so $\lambda_\pm=(5\pm\sqrt{5})/8\in[0,1]$.
Wick gives $\langle n_1 n_2\rangle=(3/4)(1/2)-(1/4)^2=5/16$, $\operatorname{Cov}=-1/16$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(C-C^2)=5/4-15/16=5/16$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the characteristic polynomial of C and check that both roots lie in [0,1].
Apply the fermionic Gaussian Wick identity <n1 n2>=C11 C22-|C12|^2 and evaluate Tr C(1-C).

milestones.criterion: Produces eigenvalues (5 pm sqrt(5))/8 in [0,1] and states the gauge-invariant Gaussian assumption before applying Wick.
Reports <n1 n2>=5/16, Cov=-1/16, and Var(N)=Tr C(1-C)=5/16.
Rejects Wick contractions on arbitrary states or an unsubtracted product C11 C22=3/8.

commonErrors.description: Applies Wick's theorem to an arbitrary two-mode fermion state, omitting the Gaussian-state assumption.
commonErrors.consequence: The number correlators are asserted for states that need not satisfy Wick, so the 5/16 ledger is no longer justified.

commonErrors.description: Reports <n1 n2>=C11 C22=3/8 with no subtracted coherence, denying both <n1 n2>=5/16 and Var(N)=5/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned Wick ledger 5/16 and the covariance -1/16 are replaced by the disconnected product.

hintTree.content: Compute $\operatorname{tr} C=5/4$ and $\det C=3/8-1/16=5/16$. The quadratic $\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr} C)\lambda+\det C=0$ yields $(5\pm\sqrt{5})/8$.
The fermionic Gaussian contraction of $\langle c_1^\dagger c_1 c_2^\dagger c_2\rangle$ subtracts $\lvert C_{12}\rvert^2$ from the disconnected product $C_{11}C_{22}$.
Evaluate $C^2$ and form $\operatorname{Tr}(C-C^2)$, or add $\operatorname{Var}(n_1)+\operatorname{Var}(n_2)+2\operatorname{Cov}(n_1,n_2)$.

GQM:020320.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic polynomial of $C$ is
\begin{align*}
\det(C-\lambda I)
&=\bigl(\tfrac34-\lambda\bigr)\bigl(\tfrac12-\lambda\bigr)-\tfrac1{16}
=\lambda^2-\tfrac54\lambda+\tfrac5{16}.
\end{align*}
The discriminant is $25/16-20/16=5/16$, so
\[
\lambda_\pm=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{5}}{8}.
\]
Numerically $\lambda_+\approx 0.904$ and $\lambda_-\approx 0.345$,
both in $(0,1)$. Equivalently $0<(5-\sqrt{5})/8<(5+\sqrt{5})/8<1$
because $1<\sqrt{5}<5$ and $5+\sqrt{5}<8$.
\[
\boxed{\lambda_\pm=(5\pm\sqrt{5})/8\in[0,1]}.
\]

Because $\rho$ is assumed gauge-invariant and fermionic Gaussian,
Wick's theorem supplies
\[
\langle n_1 n_2\rangle
=C_{11}C_{22}-\lvert C_{12}\rvert^2
=\frac34\cdot\frac12-\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^2
=\frac38-\frac1{16}
=\frac{5}{16}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(n_1,n_2)
=\frac{5}{16}-\frac34\cdot\frac12
=\frac{5}{16}-\frac{6}{16}
=-\frac{1}{16}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle n_1 n_2\rangle=5/16,\;\operatorname{Cov}=-1/16}.
\]

Directly,
\[
C^2
=\begin{pmatrix}5/8&5/16\\5/16&5/16\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr} C=\frac54,\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}(C^2)=\frac{15}{16},
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(N)
=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(C(1-C)\bigr)
=\frac54-\frac{15}{16}
=\frac{5}{16}.
\]
The same value is $\operatorname{Var}(n_1)+\operatorname{Var}(n_2)+2\operatorname{Cov}$:
$\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=C_{ii}(1-C_{ii})$ gives
$(3/4)(1/4)+(1/2)(1/2)+2(-1/16)=3/16+4/16-2/16=5/16$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(N)=\operatorname{Tr}(C(1-C))=5/16}.
\]

Sentence (i) applies Wick contractions to an arbitrary two-mode
fermion state. The identities used here require the Gaussian-state
assumption and are false for a generic state sharing only the
matrix $C$. Sentence (ii) drops the subtracted coherence
$\lvert C_{12}\rvert^2$ and never obtains $5/16$. The construction
is a two-mode fermionic Gaussian Wick audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The state is gauge-invariant fermionic Gaussian with $C=[[3/4,1/4],[1/4,1/2]]$. The eigenvalues are $(5\pm\sqrt{5})/8\in[0,1]$. Wick gives $\langle n_1 n_2\rangle=5/16$, $\operatorname{Cov}=-1/16$, and $\operatorname{Var}(N)=\operatorname{Tr}(C(1-C))=5/16$. Wick is not applied to a non-Gaussian state.
Wick's theorem applies to every two-mode fermion state, Gaussian or not, so the same contractions hold without the Gaussian assumption. I do not restrict Wick to Gaussian states.
I take <n1 n2>=C11 C22=3/8 with no subtracted coherence. I never obtain <n1 n2>=5/16 or Var(N)=5/16.

GQM:020322.title: Jordan-Wigner strings give adjacent σ_j^- σ_{j+1}^+=c_j^dag c_{j+1} and σ_1^- σ_3^+=c_1^dag(1-2n_2)c_3, so physical <100|O|001>=<110|O|011>=+1 while bare c_1^dag c_3 gives +1 then -1
GQM:020322.objective: Declare empty=σ^z +, c_j=(product_{l<j} σ_l^z) σ_j^+, and n_j=(1-σ_j^z)/2. Prove the CAR and P=product σ^z=(-1)^N. Prove the adjacent identity σ_j^- σ_{j+1}^+=c_j^dag c_{j+1} and the three-site identity σ_1^- σ_3^+=c_1^dag(1-2n_2)c_3. Evaluate the physical matrix elements <100|O|001>=<110|O|011>=+1 and contrast them with the bare values +1 then -1 of c_1^dag c_3.
GQM:020322.statement:
Work on a three-site spin chain with the Jordan–Wigner convention
that an empty site is the $+1$ eigenstate of $\sigma^z$ and an
occupied site is the $-1$ eigenstate. The on-site number and the
fermion operators are
\[
n_j=\frac{1-\sigma_j^z}{2},\qquad
c_j=\Bigl(\prod_{l<j}\sigma_l^z\Bigr)\sigma_j^+,\qquad
c_j^{\dagger}=\Bigl(\prod_{l<j}\sigma_l^z\Bigr)\sigma_j^-,
\]
with $\sigma^{\pm}=(\sigma^x\pm i\sigma^y)/2$. Write
$P=\prod_j\sigma_j^z$ and $N=\sum_j n_j$. Occupation kets are
labelled $|n_1 n_2 n_3\rangle$. Do not replace the calculation by
an exchange, Hubbard, or BCS dynamical Hamiltonian, and do not
compute a spectrum.

1. Prove the canonical anticommutation relations
   $\{c_j,c_k^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{jk}$ and $\{c_j,c_k\}=0$, and
   prove the parity identity $P=(-1)^N$.

2. Prove the adjacent string cancellation
   \[
   \sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+=c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}.
   \]
   Across three sites prove
   \[
   \sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+=c_1^{\dagger}(1-2n_2)c_3.
   \]

3. Let $O=\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+$. Evaluate the physical matrix
   elements
   \[
   \langle 100|O|001\rangle=\langle 110|O|011\rangle=+1
   \]
   and contrast them with the bare fermion matrix elements
   \[
   \langle 100|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|001\rangle=+1,\qquad
   \langle 110|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|011\rangle=-1.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the interior string is irrelevant, so
   $O=c_1^{\dagger}c_3$ and $\langle 110|O|011\rangle=-1$ rather
   than $+1$”; (ii) “the adjacent Jordan–Wigner strings do not
   cancel, so $\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+\neq c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}$.”
permittedResults: On a single site, $\sigma^+\sigma^-+\sigma^-\sigma^+=1$ and $(\sigma^{\pm})^2=0$. Off site, $\sigma_j^+$ anticommutes with the factor $\sigma_j^z$ that sits inside $K_k$ whenever $j<k$, which supplies the CAR minus sign. The global parity is $P=\prod_j(1-2n_j)=(-1)^N$.

The adjacent identity is $c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}=\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+$ because $K_{j+1}=K_j\sigma_j^z$ and $\sigma_j^-\sigma_j^z=\sigma_j^-$. Across three sites, $c_1^{\dagger}(1-2n_2)c_3=\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+$. Hence $\langle 100|O|001\rangle=\langle 110|O|011\rangle=+1$, while the bare matrix elements of $c_1^{\dagger}c_3$ are $+1$ and $-1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor every fermion operator as a Hermitian string times an on-site Pauli raising or lowering matrix, then use σ^+ σ^z=-σ^z σ^+ off site and σ^- σ^z=σ^- on site.
Evaluate O=σ_1^- σ_3^+ directly on the occupation kets, then repeat with c_3=σ_1^z σ_2^z σ_3^+ to expose the extra minus when n_2=1.

milestones.criterion: Produces the CAR, the parity identity P=(-1)^N, the adjacent cancellation σ_j^- σ_{j+1}^+=c_j^dag c_{j+1}, and the three-site identity σ_1^- σ_3^+=c_1^dag(1-2n_2)c_3.
Reports the physical matrix elements <100|O|001>=<110|O|011>=+1 and the contrasting bare values +1 then -1 of c_1^dag c_3.
Rejects a dropped interior parity or an uncancelled adjacent string, and refuses reserved exchange / Hubbard / BCS dynamical substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Identifies O=σ_1^- σ_3^+ with the bare bilinear c_1^dag c_3 and reports <110|O|011>=-1 instead of +1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required physical matrix elements +1,+1 are replaced by the bare fermion values +1,-1.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the adjacent Jordan-Wigner strings do not cancel, so σ_j^- σ_{j+1}^+ is not equal to c_j^dag c_{j+1}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required adjacent identity is lost and the three-site string bookkeeping cannot start from a consistent cancellation.

hintTree.content: Write $c_j=K_j\sigma_j^+$ with $K_j^2=1$. On site the CAR reduce to $\sigma^+\sigma^-+\sigma^-\sigma^+=1$. Off site, pass $\sigma_j^+$ through the factor $\sigma_j^z$ inside $K_k$.
For adjacent sites expand $c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}=K_j\sigma_j^-K_j\sigma_j^z\sigma_{j+1}^+$ and use $\sigma_j^-\sigma_j^z=\sigma_j^-$. The three-site case inserts one extra $\sigma_2^z=1-2n_2$.

Act with $O=\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+$ on $|001\rangle$ and $|011\rangle$ directly in the occupation basis. Then repeat with $c_3= \sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z\sigma_3^+$ to see the extra minus when site $2$ is occupied.

GQM:020322.canonicalSolution:
Write $K_j=\prod_{l<j}\sigma_l^z$, so $K_j^{\dagger}=K_j$ and
$K_j^2=1$, and set $c_j=K_j\sigma_j^+$ and
$c_j^{\dagger}=K_j\sigma_j^-$. On a single site the Pauli algebra
gives
\[
\sigma^+\sigma^-+\sigma^-\sigma^+=1,\qquad
(\sigma^{\pm})^2=0,
\]
and $K_j$ commutes with $\sigma_j^{\pm}$. Therefore
\[
\{c_j,c_j^{\dagger}\}
=K_j\sigma_j^+K_j\sigma_j^-+K_j\sigma_j^-K_j\sigma_j^+
=\sigma_j^+\sigma_j^-+\sigma_j^-\sigma_j^+
=1
\]
and $\{c_j,c_j\}=2(\sigma_j^+)^2=0$. If $j<k$, then
$K_k=K_j\sigma_j^z M$ with $M=\prod_{j<l<k}\sigma_l^z$ commuting
with site $j$, and
\[
c_jc_k
=K_j\sigma_j^+\,K_j\sigma_j^z M\sigma_k^+
=\sigma_j^+\sigma_j^z M\sigma_k^+,
\]
\[
c_kc_j
=K_j\sigma_j^z M\sigma_k^+\,K_j\sigma_j^+
=\sigma_j^z\sigma_j^+ M\sigma_k^+.
\]
The on-site identity $\sigma^+\sigma^z=-\sigma^z\sigma^+$ then
yields $c_jc_k=-c_kc_j$. The mixed relation
$\{c_j,c_k^{\dagger}\}=0$ is the same computation with
$\sigma_k^-$ in place of $\sigma_k^+$. This is the CAR.
\[
\boxed{\{c_j,c_k^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{jk},\quad\{c_j,c_k\}=0}.
\]
Because $\sigma_j^z=1-2n_j=(-1)^{n_j}$,
\[
P=\prod_j\sigma_j^z=\prod_j(-1)^{n_j}=(-1)^N.
\]
\[
\boxed{P=\prod_j\sigma_j^z=(-1)^N}.
\]

For adjacent sites, $K_{j+1}=K_j\sigma_j^z$, so
\[
c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}
=K_j\sigma_j^-\,K_j\sigma_j^z\sigma_{j+1}^+
=\sigma_j^-\sigma_j^z\sigma_{j+1}^+.
\]
The lowering matrix $\sigma^-=|\downarrow\rangle\langle\uparrow|$
obeys $\sigma^-\sigma^z=\sigma^-$, and the strings have cancelled,
hence
\[
c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}=\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+=c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}}.
\]
Across three sites one has $c_1^{\dagger}=\sigma_1^-$ and
$c_3=\sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z\sigma_3^+$. Inserting
$1-2n_2=\sigma_2^z$ therefore gives
\begin{align*}
c_1^{\dagger}(1-2n_2)c_3
&=\sigma_1^-\sigma_2^z\,(\sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z\sigma_3^+)
=\sigma_1^-\sigma_1^z(\sigma_2^z)^2\sigma_3^+
=\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+,
\end{align*}
which is the three-site identity.
\[
\boxed{\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+=c_1^{\dagger}(1-2n_2)c_3}.
\]

Let $O=\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+$. Then
$O|001\rangle=\sigma_1^-|000\rangle=|100\rangle$ and
$O|011\rangle=\sigma_1^-|010\rangle=|110\rangle$, so
\[
\langle 100|O|001\rangle=\langle 110|O|011\rangle=+1.
\]
The bare fermion bilinear keeps the interior string:
$c_3|001\rangle=\sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z|000\rangle=+|000\rangle$
because both unoccupied sites have $\sigma^z=+1$, hence
$\langle 100|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|001\rangle=+1$. On the other hand
$c_3|011\rangle=\sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z|010\rangle=-|010\rangle$
because the occupied interior site has $\sigma_2^z=-1$, hence
$\langle 110|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|011\rangle=-1$. The factor
$1-2n_2$ converts the second bare matrix element $-1$ into the
physical value $+1$.
\[
\boxed{\langle 100|O|001\rangle=\langle 110|O|011\rangle=+1,\quad
\langle 100|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|001\rangle=+1,\;
\langle 110|c_1^{\dagger}c_3|011\rangle=-1}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the interior parity and reports the inconsistent
physical matrix element $\langle 110|O|011\rangle=-1$. Sentence
(ii) refuses the adjacent cancellation. The calculation is strictly
CAR / string / parity algebra; it is not an exchange, Hubbard, or
BCS dynamical spectrum.

graderFixtures.proofText: The operators $c_j=(\prod_{l<j}\sigma_l^z)\sigma_j^+$ obey the CAR and $P=\prod\sigma^z=(-1)^N$. Adjacent strings cancel, $\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+=c_j^{\dagger}c_{j+1}$, while across three sites $\sigma_1^-\sigma_3^+=c_1^{\dagger}(1-2n_2)c_3$. The physical matrix elements are $\langle 100|O|001\rangle=\langle 110|O|011\rangle=+1$, whereas bare $c_1^{\dagger}c_3$ gives $+1$ then $-1$.
The interior string is irrelevant, so O=c_1^dag c_3 and <110|O|011>=-1 rather than +1. I do not report <110|O|011>=+1 or the factor (1-2n_2).
The adjacent Jordan-Wigner strings do not cancel, so σ_j^- σ_{j+1}^+ is not equal to c_j^dag c_{j+1}. I never accept the adjacent cancellation.

GQM:020421.title: Euclidean free kernel at m=hbar=1, tau=2, xi=0, xf=1 is e^{-1/4}/(2 sqrt(pi)) with variance 2
GQM:020421.objective: For the Euclidean free-particle kernel K_E=sqrt[m/(2 pi hbar tau)] exp[-m(xf-xi)^2/(2 hbar tau)] prove xf-normalization and semigroup composition, identify the displacement variance hbar tau/m, and evaluate K=e^{-1/4}/(2 sqrt(pi)) with variance 2 at m=hbar=1, tau=2, xi=0, xf=1. Distinguish the Euclidean heat semigroup / Wick rotation from real-time caustics and Maslov phases.
GQM:020421.statement:
The Euclidean free-particle heat kernel on the line is
\[
K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau)
=\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar\tau}}
\exp\Bigl[-\frac{m(x_f-x_i)^2}{2\hbar\tau}\Bigr],
\qquad\tau>0.
\]
Do not identify $K_E$ with the real-time van Vleck propagator, and
do not introduce caustics or Maslov phases.

1. Prove the normalization identity
   \[
   \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau)\,dx_f=1
   \]
   for every $x_i$ and every $\tau>0$.

2. Prove the semigroup (Chapman–Kolmogorov) composition
   \[
   \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
   K_E(x_f,y;\tau_1)\,K_E(y,x_i;\tau_2)\,dy
   =K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau_1+\tau_2).
   \]

3. Identify the displacement $x_f-x_i$ as a centered Gaussian of
   variance $\hbar\tau/m$. Then set $m=\hbar=1$, $\tau=2$,
   $x_i=0$, $x_f=1$ and prove
   \[
   K_E=\frac{e^{-1/4}}{2\sqrt{\pi}},\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(x_f-x_i)=2.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$K_E$ is the real-time propagator,
   so a Maslov/caustic phase must be inserted by hand”; (ii) “at
   the sample one has $K_E=e^{-1/2}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ or variance $1$,
   rather than $e^{-1/4}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ and variance $2$.”
permittedResults: $\int\sqrt{\alpha/\pi}\,e^{-\alpha x^2}\,dx=1$ with $\alpha=m/(2\hbar\tau)$ gives $\int K_E\,dx_f=1$. Composition of centered Gaussians adds the variances $\hbar\tau_1/m+\hbar\tau_2/m$.
At $m=\hbar=1$, $\tau=2$, $x_i=0$, $x_f=1$ one has $K_E=e^{-1/4}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ and displacement variance $2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Recognize K_E as a normalized Gaussian heat kernel and add variances to obtain the semigroup.
Match the quadratic exponent to a Gaussian variance hbar tau/m and insert (m,hbar,tau,xi,xf)=(1,1,2,0,1).

milestones.criterion: Produces xf-normalization of K_E and the semigroup composition K_E(tau1) circ K_E(tau2)=K_E(tau1+tau2).
Reports variance hbar tau/m and the sample e^{-1/4}/(2 sqrt(pi)) with variance 2.
Rejects a real-time caustic/Maslov identification of K_E or a wrong sample kernel/variance.

commonErrors.description: Identifies K_E with the real-time van Vleck propagator and inserts a Maslov/caustic phase.
commonErrors.consequence: The Euclidean heat semigroup / Wick-rotation object is replaced by an oscillatory real-time construction this packet does not ask for.

commonErrors.description: Reports K_E=e^{-1/2}/(2 sqrt(pi)) or displacement variance 1, instead of e^{-1/4}/(2 sqrt(pi)) and variance 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned Euclidean sample kernel and the variance hbar tau/m=2 are both lost.

hintTree.content: Complete the Gaussian integral in $x_f$ with width parameter $m/(2\hbar\tau)$. The prefactor is exactly the $L^1$-normalizing constant.
The product of two heat kernels is a Gaussian in the intermediate point $y$. Completing the square reproduces $K_E(\,\cdot\,;\tau_1+\tau_2)$.
Read $\exp[-m(\Delta x)^2/(2\hbar\tau)]$ as $\exp[-(\Delta x)^2/(2\sigma^2)]$ to obtain $\sigma^2=\hbar\tau/m$. Then insert the sample numbers.

GQM:020421.canonicalSolution:
Write $\alpha=m/(2\hbar\tau)>0$. Then
\[
K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau)
=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\pi}}
\exp\bigl(-\alpha(x_f-x_i)^2\bigr).
\]
The elementary Gaussian integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\alpha x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi/\alpha}$
yields
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau)\,dx_f=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\int K_E\,dx_f=1}.
\]

For the semigroup, the integrand is a product of centered Gaussians
in $(x_f-y)$ and $(y-x_i)$ with inverse variances
$m/(\hbar\tau_1)$ and $m/(\hbar\tau_2)$ in the usual
$\exp[-(\Delta x)^2/(2\sigma^2)]$ parametrization
$\sigma_j^2=\hbar\tau_j/m$. Completing the square in $y$ produces
a Gaussian of variance $\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2=\hbar(\tau_1+\tau_2)/m$
in the total displacement $x_f-x_i$, with prefactor
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi\hbar(\tau_1+\tau_2))}$. This is
$K_E(x_f,x_i;\tau_1+\tau_2)$.
\[
\boxed{K_E(\tau_1)\circ K_E(\tau_2)=K_E(\tau_1+\tau_2)}.
\]

Matching $\exp[-m(\Delta x)^2/(2\hbar\tau)]$ to
$\exp[-(\Delta x)^2/(2\sigma^2)]$ gives the displacement variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}(x_f-x_i)=\frac{\hbar\tau}{m}.
\]
Now set $m=\hbar=1$, $\tau=2$, $x_i=0$, $x_f=1$:
\[
K_E
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4\pi}}
\exp\bigl[-1/(4)\bigr]
=\frac{e^{-1/4}}{2\sqrt{\pi}},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(x_f-x_i)=2.
\]
\[
\boxed{K_E=e^{-1/4}/(2\sqrt{\pi}),\;\operatorname{Var}=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses the Euclidean heat semigroup (Wick rotation
of the free Schrödinger evolution) with the oscillatory real-time
propagator and imports caustics / Maslov phases that $K_E$ does
not carry. Sentence (ii) mis-evaluates the sample, replacing
$e^{-1/4}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ or the variance $2$ by
$e^{-1/2}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ or variance $1$. The construction is a
Euclidean free-particle heat-kernel audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The kernel $K_E$ is $L^1$-normalized in $x_f$ and satisfies the heat semigroup. The displacement variance is $\hbar\tau/m$. At $m=\hbar=1$, $\tau=2$, $x_i=0$, $x_f=1$ one has $K_E=e^{-1/4}/(2\sqrt{\pi})$ and variance $2$. This is the Euclidean heat semigroup (Wick rotation), not a real-time van Vleck / Maslov / caustic propagator.
K_E is the real-time propagator, so a Maslov/caustic phase must be inserted by hand. I do not treat K_E as a Euclidean heat semigroup.
At the sample I take K_E=e^{-1/2}/(2 sqrt(pi)) and variance 1. I never obtain e^{-1/4}/(2 sqrt(pi)) or variance 2.
