GQM:020423.title: The cubic bounce of V=½mω²x²-gx³/3 has xb=mω²/g, xt=3mω²/(2g), xB=xt sech²[ω(τ-τ0)/2], and SB=6m³ω⁵/(5g²); at m=ω=hbar=1, g=1/2 one has xb=2, xt=3, ΔV=2/3, SB=24/5
GQM:020423.objective: For V=½mω²x²-gx³/3 prove xb=mω²/g, ΔV=m³ω⁶/(6g²), the zero-energy turning point xt=3mω²/(2g), the bounce xB=xt sech²[ω(τ-τ0)/2], and SB=6m³ω⁵/(5g²). At m=ω=hbar=1, g=1/2 prove xb=2, xt=3, ΔV=2/3, xB=3 sech²(τ/2), SB=24/5, and the leading decay exponent e^{-24/5} only. Do not supply or claim a determinant prefactor.
GQM:020423.statement:
A one-dimensional particle of mass $m$ has the cubic-unstable
potential
\[
V(x)=\frac12 m\omega^2 x^2-\frac g3 x^3,\qquad g>0,
\]
which is metastable at $x=0$. The Euclidean action is
\[
S_E[x]=\int\mathrm{d}\tau\Bigl(\frac m2\dot x^2+V(x)\Bigr).
\]
Do not replace the bounce by a symmetric double-well kink, a
Duffing instanton, or a Van Vleck determinant, and do not claim
any fluctuation prefactor.

1. Locate the barrier top $x_b$ and prove that the barrier height
   is $\Delta V=m^3\omega^6/(6g^2)$. Find the nonzero root $x_t$
   of $V(x)=0$ (the zero-energy turning point).

2. Show that the zero-energy Euclidean bounce
   \[
   x_B(\tau)=x_t\,\mathrm{sech}^2\bigl[\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2\bigr]
   \]
   satisfies $\frac m2\dot x_B^2=V(x_B)$, and evaluate the bounce
   action
   \[
   S_B=\frac{6m^3\omega^5}{5g^2}.
   \]

3. Specialize to $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and $g=1/2$ and prove
   \[
   x_b=2,\qquad x_t=3,\qquad \Delta V=\frac23,\qquad
   x_B(\tau)=3\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\tau/2),\qquad
   S_B=\frac{24}5.
   \]
   The leading decay exponent is $e^{-S_B/\hbar}=e^{-24/5}$ only.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the bounce turns at the barrier top,
   so $x_t=x_b=2$, $x_B=2\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\tau/2)$, and
   $S_B\neq 24/5$”; (ii) “the decay rate also includes an explicit
   Van Vleck / fluctuation-determinant prefactor, or else the
   trajectory is a symmetric double-well kink.”
permittedResults: Critical points of $V$ are $x=0$ and $x_b=m\omega^2/g$, with $V(x_b)=m^3\omega^6/(6g^2)$. The other root of $V=0$ is $x_t=3m\omega^2/(2g)$.
The profile $x_t\mathrm{sech}^2[\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2]$ obeys $\tfrac m2\dot x^2=V$. The action integral is $S_B=8m\omega x_t^2/15=6m^3\omega^5/(5g^2)$. At the sample this is $24/5$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read xb and xt from V'=0 and V=0, then verify the sech² profile by energy conservation (m/2)ẋ²=V.
Reduce SB to 2∫√(2mV) dx, evaluate the beta-function integral 4/15, and specialize to g=1/2 without a prefactor.

milestones.criterion: Produces xb=mω²/g, ΔV=m³ω⁶/(6g²), xt=3mω²/(2g), the sech² bounce, and SB=6m³ω⁵/(5g²).
At m=ω=hbar=1, g=1/2 reports xb=2, xt=3, ΔV=2/3, xB=3 sech²(τ/2), SB=24/5, and the leading exponent e^{-24/5} only.
Rejects identifying the turning point with the barrier top or attaching a determinant prefactor, and refuses reserved kink / Duffing / Van Vleck substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the zero-energy turning point with the barrier top, reporting xt=xb=2, xB=2 sech²(τ/2), and an action other than 24/5.
commonErrors.consequence: The required turning point xt=3, profile 3 sech²(τ/2), and action SB=24/5 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Attaches a Van Vleck / fluctuation-determinant prefactor to the decay rate, or replaces the cubic bounce by a symmetric double-well kink or Duffing instanton.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned leading exponent e^{-24/5} is replaced by a reserved prefactor or by a different instanton family.

hintTree.content: Compute $V'(x)=x(m\omega^2-gx)$. The barrier value is $V(m\omega^2/g)$. Factor $V(x)=\tfrac12 m\omega^2 x^2(1-x/x_t)$ to read $x_t$.
Differentiate $x_t\mathrm{sech}^2 u$ with $u=\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2$ and compare $\tfrac m2\dot x^2$ to $V(x)$.
Evaluate $S_B=2\int_0^{x_t}\sqrt{2m V}\,\mathrm{d}x$ by the substitution $y=x/x_t$, using $\int_0^1 y\sqrt{1-y}\,\mathrm{d}y=4/15$. Do not attach a determinant.

GQM:020423.canonicalSolution:
The force is $V'(x)=m\omega^2 x-gx^2=x(m\omega^2-gx)$, so the
critical points are the metastable minimum $x=0$ and the barrier
top $x_b=m\omega^2/g$. Substituting the barrier location,
\begin{align*}
V(x_b)
&=\frac12 m\omega^2\Bigl(\frac{m\omega^2}{g}\Bigr)^2
-\frac g3\Bigl(\frac{m\omega^2}{g}\Bigr)^3
=\frac{m^3\omega^6}{2g^2}-\frac{m^3\omega^6}{3g^2}
=\frac{m^3\omega^6}{6g^2}.
\end{align*}
The nonzero root of $V(x)=0$ is
\[
\frac12 m\omega^2=\frac g3\,x_t\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x_t=\frac{3m\omega^2}{2g}.
\]
Equivalently $V(x)=\tfrac12 m\omega^2 x^2\bigl(1-x/x_t\bigr)$.
\[
\boxed{x_b=m\omega^2/g,\quad
\Delta V=m^3\omega^6/(6g^2),\quad
x_t=3m\omega^2/(2g)}.
\]

Set $u=\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2$ and $x_B=x_t\mathrm{sech}^2 u$. Then
\[
\dot x_B=-x_t\omega\,\mathrm{sech}^2 u\,\tanh u,
\]
so
\[
\frac m2\dot x_B^2
=\frac m2\omega^2 x_B^2\tanh^2 u
=\frac m2\omega^2 x_B^2\Bigl(1-\frac{x_B}{x_t}\Bigr)
=V(x_B).
\]
The assigned profile is therefore the zero-energy bounce. Its
action is
\[
S_B
=2\int_0^{x_t}\sqrt{2m V(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x
=2\int_0^{x_t}m\omega x\sqrt{1-x/x_t}\,\mathrm{d}x.
\]
The substitution $y=x/x_t$ and the elementary integral
$\int_0^1 y\sqrt{1-y}\,\mathrm{d}y=4/15$ produce
\[
S_B=\frac{8m\omega x_t^2}{15}.
\]
Inserting $x_t=3m\omega^2/(2g)$ gives
$x_t^2=9m^2\omega^4/(4g^2)$ and
\[
S_B=\frac{8m\omega}{15}\cdot\frac{9m^2\omega^4}{4g^2}
=\frac{6m^3\omega^5}{5g^2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{x_B=x_t\mathrm{sech}^2[\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2],\quad
S_B=6m^3\omega^5/(5g^2)}.
\]

At $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and $g=1/2$,
\[
x_b=\frac{1}{1/2}=2,\qquad
x_t=\frac{3}{2\cdot(1/2)}=3,\qquad
\Delta V=\frac{1}{6\cdot(1/4)}=\frac23,\qquad
S_B=\frac{6}{5\cdot(1/4)}=\frac{24}5,
\]
and with $\tau_0=0$ the profile is $x_B(\tau)=3\mathrm{sech}^2(\tau/2)$.
The leading decay exponent is $e^{-S_B/\hbar}=e^{-24/5}$. No
fluctuation determinant is evaluated or claimed.
\[
\boxed{x_b=2,\;x_t=3,\;\Delta V=2/3,\;
x_B=3\mathrm{sech}^2(\tau/2),\;
S_B=24/5,\;e^{-24/5}}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses the turning point with the barrier top and
loses $x_t=3$ and $S_B=24/5$. Sentence (ii) imports a Van Vleck /
determinant prefactor or replaces the cubic bounce by a symmetric
double-well kink. The calculation is a metastable cubic bounce
only.

graderFixtures.proofText: The cubic potential has $x_b=m\omega^2/g$, $\Delta V=m^3\omega^6/(6g^2)$, $x_t=3m\omega^2/(2g)$, bounce $x_B=x_t\mathrm{sech}^2[\omega(\tau-\tau_0)/2]$, and $S_B=6m^3\omega^5/(5g^2)$. At $m=\omega=\hbar=1$, $g=1/2$ one has $x_b=2$, $x_t=3$, $\Delta V=2/3$, $x_B=3\mathrm{sech}^2(\tau/2)$, $S_B=24/5$, and leading decay exponent $e^{-24/5}$ only. No determinant prefactor is claimed.
The bounce turns at the barrier top, so xt=xb=2, xB=2 sech^2(τ/2), and SB is not 24/5. I do not report xt=3 or SB=24/5.
The decay rate also includes an explicit Van Vleck / fluctuation-determinant prefactor, or else the trajectory is a symmetric double-well kink. I never accept the leading exponent e^{-24/5} alone.

GQM:020424.title: Two Euclidean delta sources at separation ln 2 give G(0)=1/2, G(ln 2)=1/4, JGJ=3/2, Z[J]/Z0=e^{3/4}, means 3/4 at both sources, connected cross 1/4, and full cross 13/16
GQM:020424.objective: For S_E=∫[m(ẋ²+ω²x²)/2-Jx] dτ with G(τ)=e^{-ω|τ|}/(2mω), prove Z[J]/Z0=exp[(JGJ)/(2ħ)], <x>=GJ, and connected <xx>=ħG. At m=ω=ħ=1 and J=δ(τ)+δ(τ-ln 2) prove G(0)=1/2, G_T=1/4, JGJ=3/2, the ratio e^{3/4}, means 3/4 at both sources, connected cross 1/4, and full cross 13/16.
GQM:020424.statement:
The Euclidean oscillator with a linear source has action
\[
S_E[x;J]
=\int\mathrm{d}\tau\Bigl(\frac m2\bigl(\dot x^2+\omega^2 x^2\bigr)-J(\tau)x(\tau)\Bigr)
\]
and translation-invariant Green function
\[
G(\tau)=\frac{e^{-\omega|\tau|}}{2m\omega},
\]
normalized so that $(-m\partial_\tau^2+m\omega^2)G=\delta$. Write
$(JGJ)=\int\mathrm{d}\tau\int\mathrm{d}\tau'\,J(\tau)G(\tau-\tau')J(\tau')$.
Do not replace the sourced generating functional by the free heat
kernel or by an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, and do not omit the
source.

1. Complete the square in $S_E$ and prove
   \[
   \frac{Z[J]}{Z[0]}
   =\exp\Bigl(\frac{JGJ}{2\hbar}\Bigr),\qquad
   \langle x\rangle=GJ,\qquad
   \langle x(\tau)x(\tau')\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=\hbar\,G(\tau-\tau').
   \]

2. Specialize to $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and
   $J(\tau)=\delta(\tau)+\delta(\tau-\ln 2)$. Prove
   \[
   G(0)=\frac12,\qquad
   G(\ln 2)=\frac14,\qquad
   JGJ=\frac32,\qquad
   \frac{Z[J]}{Z[0]}=e^{3/4}.
   \]

3. On the same sample prove that the mean is $3/4$ at both source
   points, that the connected cross correlator is $1/4$, and that
   the full cross correlator is $13/16$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the exponent is $JGJ/\hbar$ rather
   than $JGJ/(2\hbar)$, so the ratio is $e^{3/2}$”; (ii) “the full
   cross correlator is just the connected piece $1/4$, with no
   disconnected $9/16$.”
permittedResults: The Green function $G(\tau)=e^{-\omega|\tau|}/(2m\omega)$ obeys $(-m\partial_\tau^2+m\omega^2)G=\delta$. Completing the square yields $Z[J]/Z[0]=\exp((JGJ)/(2\hbar))$, $\langle x\rangle=GJ$, and $\langle xx\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=\hbar G$.
At $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and separation $\ln 2$ one has $G(0)=1/2$, $G(\ln 2)=1/4$, $JGJ=3/2$, $Z[J]/Z[0]=e^{3/4}$, means $3/4$, connected cross $1/4$, and full cross $13/16$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Complete the square with x=GJ+ξ to read the classical action -(JGJ)/2 and the connected fluctuation ħG.
Evaluate the four pairings of two unit deltas at separation ln 2, then add (3/4)^2 to ħG(ln 2).

milestones.criterion: Produces Z[J]/Z0=exp((JGJ)/(2ħ)), <x>=GJ, connected <xx>=ħG, and the sample values G(0)=1/2, G(ln 2)=1/4, JGJ=3/2.
Reports the ratio e^{3/4}, means 3/4 at both sources, connected cross 1/4, and full cross 13/16.
Rejects an exponent missing the factor 1/2 or a full correlator that omits the disconnected 9/16, and refuses reserved free-kernel / OU substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Writes Z[J]/Z0=exp(JGJ/ħ) instead of exp(JGJ/(2ħ)) and reports the sample ratio e^{3/2} instead of e^{3/4}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required generating-functional ratio e^{3/4} is replaced by its square e^{3/2}.

commonErrors.description: Reports the full cross correlator as the connected piece 1/4, omitting the disconnected product (3/4)^2=9/16 that produces 13/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The required full cross 13/16 is never produced.

hintTree.content: Shift $x=GJ+\xi$. The linear term cancels and the classical action is $-(JGJ)/2$. The fluctuation integral is $Z[0]$.
With two unit deltas, $JGJ=2G(0)+2G(T)$. At $T=\ln 2$ and $m=\omega=1$ this is $1+1/2=3/2$. Divide by $2\hbar=2$.
The mean at each source is $G(0)+G(T)=3/4$. Add the disconnected product $(3/4)^2$ to the connected piece $\hbar G(T)=1/4$.

GQM:020424.canonicalSolution:
Write $K=-m\partial_\tau^2+m\omega^2$ for the positive Euclidean
kinetic operator, so $KG=\delta$ and
$S_E=\frac12\langle x,Kx\rangle-\langle J,x\rangle$ in units where
the $L^2$ pairing includes the implicit $\tau$ integral. Completing
the square,
\[
S_E[x;J]
=\frac12\bigl\langle x-GJ,\,K(x-GJ)\bigr\rangle-\frac12\,JGJ.
\]
The fluctuation integral is independent of $J$ and equals $Z[0]$,
hence
\[
\frac{Z[J]}{Z[0]}
=\exp\Bigl(\frac{JGJ}{2\hbar}\Bigr).
\]
Differentiating once with respect to $J$ produces the mean
$\langle x\rangle=GJ$. Differentiating twice and subtracting the
disconnected product produces the connected correlator
$\langle x(\tau)x(\tau')\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=\hbar G(\tau-\tau')$.
\[
\boxed{Z[J]/Z[0]=\exp((JGJ)/(2\hbar)),\quad
\langle x\rangle=GJ,\quad
\langle xx\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=\hbar G}.
\]

Now take $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and
$J=\delta(\tau)+\delta(\tau-\ln 2)$. Then
\[
G(\tau)=\frac{e^{-|\tau|}}{2},\qquad
G(0)=\frac12,\qquad
G(\ln 2)=\frac{e^{-\ln 2}}{2}=\frac14.
\]
The quadratic source form expands into four pairings,
\[
JGJ=G(0)+G(0)+G(\ln 2)+G(-\ln 2)=\frac12+\frac12+\frac14+\frac14=\frac32,
\]
so
\[
\frac{Z[J]}{Z[0]}
=\exp\Bigl(\frac{3/2}{2}\Bigr)=e^{3/4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{G(0)=1/2,\;G(\ln 2)=1/4,\;JGJ=3/2,\;Z[J]/Z[0]=e^{3/4}}.
\]

The mean is
\[
\langle x(\tau)\rangle=G(\tau)+G(\tau-\ln 2),
\]
hence at the two source points
\[
\langle x(0)\rangle=G(0)+G(-\ln 2)=\frac12+\frac14=\frac34,
\qquad
\langle x(\ln 2)\rangle=G(\ln 2)+G(0)=\frac34.
\]
The connected cross correlator is
\[
\langle x(0)x(\ln 2)\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}
=\hbar G(\ln 2)=\frac14,
\]
and the full correlator adds the disconnected product of means:
\[
\langle x(0)x(\ln 2)\rangle
=\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac34\Bigr)+\frac14
=\frac{9}{16}+\frac{4}{16}
=\frac{13}{16}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle x\rangle_{\mathrm{src}}=3/4,\;
\langle xx\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=1/4,\;
\langle xx\rangle=13/16}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $1/2$ in the exponent and reports
$e^{3/2}$. Sentence (ii) discards the disconnected product and
reports the full cross correlator as $1/4$. The calculation is a
sourced Euclidean Gaussian generating functional; it is not the
free kernel and not an unsourced Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.

graderFixtures.proofText: The sourced Euclidean Gaussian gives $Z[J]/Z[0]=\exp((JGJ)/(2\hbar))$, $\langle x\rangle=GJ$, and $\langle xx\rangle_{\mathrm{c}}=\hbar G$. At $m=\omega=\hbar=1$ and $J=\delta(\tau)+\delta(\tau-\ln 2)$ one has $G(0)=1/2$, $G(\ln 2)=1/4$, $JGJ=3/2$, ratio $e^{3/4}$, means $3/4$ at both sources, connected cross $1/4$, and full cross $13/16$.
The exponent is JGJ/hbar rather than JGJ/(2 hbar), so the ratio is e^{3/2}. I do not report Z[J]/Z0=e^{3/4}.
The full cross correlator is just the connected piece 1/4, with no disconnected 9/16. I never accept the full cross 13/16.

GQM:020525.title: The Klein-Gordon Noether current of φ=(1/2)e^{-ip·x} at p=(5,3,0,0), m=4 is j=(5/2,3/2,0,0) with j²=4; the conjugate mode flips the sign and a real field has j=0
GQM:020525.objective: In metric +---, from L=∂φ*∂φ-m²φ*φ, prove that j^μ=i(φ*∂^μφ-φ∂^μφ*) is conserved. For φ=Ae^{-ip·x} prove j=2p|A|². At p=(5,3,0,0), m=4, A=1/2 prove j=(5/2,3/2,0,0) and j²=4. Show that the conjugate negative-frequency mode gives -j, that a real field has j=0, and that the density is not a positive-definite probability.
GQM:020525.statement:
Work in Minkowski space with metric signature $(+,-,-,-)$. A
complex Klein–Gordon field has Lagrangian density
\[
\mathcal L=\partial_\mu\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-m^2\phi^*\phi
\]
and the $U(1)$ Noether current
\[
j^\mu=i\bigl(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi^*\bigr).
\]
Do not replace the current by a Dirac–Pauli spinor current, a
Yukawa optical theorem, a resonance pole, or a cutoff dispersion
relation.

1. From the Klein–Gordon equation $(\square+m^2)\phi=0$ and its
   conjugate, prove $\partial_\mu j^\mu=0$.

2. For a positive-frequency plane wave $\phi=A e^{-ip\cdot x}$
   on the mass shell $p^2=m^2$, prove $j^\mu=2p^\mu|A|^2$.

3. Specialize to $p^\mu=(5,3,0,0)$, $m=4$, and $A=1/2$, and prove
   \[
   j^\mu=\Bigl(\frac52,\frac32,0,0\Bigr),\qquad j^2=4.
   \]
   Show that the conjugate negative-frequency wave $A e^{+ip\cdot x}$
   produces $-j^\mu$, that a real field has $j^\mu=0$, and that
   $j^0$ is not a positive-definite probability density.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the current is just $p^\mu|A|^2$, so
   $j=(5/4,3/4,0,0)$ and $j^2=1$ rather than $j=(5/2,3/2,0,0)$ and
   $j^2=4$”; (ii) “$j^0$ is an ordinary positive probability
   density, so the Klein–Gordon field has a one-particle
   probabilistic interpretation.”
permittedResults: If $(\square+m^2)\phi=0$ and $(\square+m^2)\phi^*=0$, then $\partial_\mu j^\mu=i(\phi^*\square\phi-\phi\,\square\phi^*)=0$.
For $\phi=Ae^{-ip\cdot x}$ one has $j=2p|A|^2$. At $p=(5,3,0,0)$, $m=4$, $A=1/2$ the mass shell $p^2=16=m^2$ holds and $j=(5/2,3/2,0,0)$ with $j^2=4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand ∂_μ j^μ and insert the Klein–Gordon equation to obtain conservation, then evaluate the two derivative terms on Ae^{-ip·x}.
Check p²=m²=16, multiply 2p|A|²=p/2, and form the Minkowski square (5/2)²-(3/2)².

milestones.criterion: Produces conservation of j^μ and the plane-wave evaluation j=2p|A|², together with the mass-shell check p²=16.
Reports j=(5/2,3/2,0,0) and j²=4, the sign flip on the conjugate mode, j=0 for a real field, and that j^0 is not a positive-definite probability.
Rejects a missing factor of 2 or a probabilistic reading of j^0, and refuses reserved Dirac–Pauli / Yukawa / resonance / cutoff substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor 2 and reports j=p|A|²=(5/4,3/4,0,0) with j²=1 instead of j=(5/2,3/2,0,0) and j²=4.
commonErrors.consequence: The required current (5/2,3/2,0,0) and invariant square 4 are replaced by half-current values.

commonErrors.description: Treats j^0 as an ordinary positive-definite one-particle probability density.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conclusion that the Klein-Gordon density is not a probability is lost.

hintTree.content: Expand $\partial_\mu j^\mu$ and cancel the first-derivative pairings, leaving $i(\phi^*\square\phi-\phi\,\square\phi^*)$. Insert $\square\phi=-m^2\phi$.
On $\phi=Ae^{-ip\cdot x}$ one has $\partial^\mu\phi=-ip^\mu\phi$ and $\partial^\mu\phi^*=+ip^\mu\phi^*$. The two terms in $j^\mu$ add.
Check $p^2=25-9=16=m^2$. Then $j=2p\cdot(1/4)=p/2$. The Minkowski square is $(5/2)^2-(3/2)^2=4$.

GQM:020525.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the current:
\begin{align*}
\partial_\mu j^\mu
&=i\bigl(\partial_\mu\phi^*\,\partial^\mu\phi+\phi^*\square\phi
-\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi^*-\phi\,\square\phi^*\bigr)\\
&=i\bigl(\phi^*\square\phi-\phi\,\square\phi^*\bigr).
\end{align*}
The Klein–Gordon equation $\square\phi=-m^2\phi$ and its conjugate
then give
\[
\partial_\mu j^\mu
=i\bigl(\phi^*(-m^2\phi)-\phi(-m^2\phi^*)\bigr)=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\partial_\mu j^\mu=0}.
\]

On the positive-frequency wave $\phi=A e^{-ip\cdot x}$ one has
$\partial^\mu\phi=-ip^\mu\phi$ and $\partial^\mu\phi^*=+ip^\mu\phi^*$,
hence
\begin{align*}
j^\mu
&=i\bigl(\phi^*(-ip^\mu\phi)-\phi(ip^\mu\phi^*)\bigr)
=i(-ip^\mu-ip^\mu)|A|^2
=2p^\mu|A|^2.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{j^\mu=2p^\mu|A|^2}.
\]
The assigned momentum satisfies the mass shell in signature
$(+,-,-,-)$,
\[
p^2=5^2-3^2=16=m^2.
\]
With $A=1/2$ one has $|A|^2=1/4$, so
\[
j^\mu=2\cdot p^\mu\cdot\frac14=\frac{p^\mu}2
=\Bigl(\frac52,\frac32,0,0\Bigr)
\]
and
\[
j^2=j_\mu j^\mu=\Bigl(\frac52\Bigr)^2-\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2
=\frac{25}{4}-\frac94=4.
\]
\[
\boxed{j=(5/2,3/2,0,0),\quad j^2=4}.
\]
The conjugate negative-frequency wave $\phi=A e^{+ip\cdot x}$
has $\partial^\mu\phi=+ip^\mu\phi$ and therefore produces
$j^\mu=-2p^\mu|A|^2$. If instead $\phi$ is real, then
$\phi^*=\phi$ and the two terms in $j^\mu$ cancel identically,
so $j^\mu=0$. In particular $j^0=2p^0|A|^2$ changes sign with
$p^0$ and is not a positive-definite probability density: the
Klein–Gordon field does not furnish a one-particle probabilistic
interpretation.

Sentence (i) drops the factor $2$ and reports the inconsistent
current $(5/4,3/4,0,0)$ with square $1$. Sentence (ii) treats
$j^0$ as an ordinary probability. The calculation is the complex
KG Noether current; it is not a Dirac–Pauli spinor current, not a
Yukawa optical theorem, not a resonance pole, and not a cutoff
dispersion relation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The current $j^\mu=i(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi^*)$ is conserved. On $\phi=Ae^{-ip\cdot x}$ one has $j=2p|A|^2$. At $p=(5,3,0,0)$, $m=4$, $A=1/2$ this is $j=(5/2,3/2,0,0)$ with $j^2=4$. The conjugate negative-frequency mode produces $-j$, a real field has $j=0$, and $j^0$ is not a positive-definite probability density.
The current is just p|A|^2, so j=(5/4,3/4,0,0) and j^2=1 rather than j=(5/2,3/2,0,0) and j^2=4. I do not report j=(5/2,3/2,0,0).
j^0 is an ordinary positive probability density, so the Klein-Gordon field has a one-particle probabilistic interpretation. I never accept that the density fails to be a probability.

GQM:020526.title: The supercritical KG step m=12, E=13, qV=33 has kL=5, pR=-16, r=-21/11, t=-10/11 and charge-current ratios R=441/121, T=-320/121 with R+T=1
GQM:020526.objective: From [∂x²+(E-qV)²-m²]ψ=0 at m=12, E=13, qV0=33, prove kL=5, right kinetic energy -20, |kR|=16, and that right-going group velocity requires pR=-16. Match e^{i5x}+r e^{-i5x} to t e^{-i16x} and prove r=-21/11, t=-10/11 and the charge-current ratios R=441/121, T=-320/121, R+T=1. Interpret the negative transmitted charge current as Klein-zone superradiance, never as ordinary one-particle probability.
GQM:020526.statement:
A charged Klein–Gordon wave of energy $E$ is incident from the
left on the electrostatic step $qV(x)=0$ for $x<0$ and
$qV(x)=qV_0$ for $x>0$. The stationary equation is
\[
\bigl[\partial_x^2+(E-qV)^2-m^2\bigr]\psi=0.
\]
Take the supercritical sample $m=12$, $E=13$, $qV_0=33$. Do not
replace the problem by a cutoff dispersion, a Dirac–Pauli step, a
Yukawa optical theorem, or a resonance pole, and do not interpret
the transmission as an ordinary one-particle probability.

1. Compute the left wave number $k_L$ and the right local kinetic
   energy $E-qV_0$. Prove that $|k_R|=16$ and that a right-going
   group velocity on the right requires $p_R=-16$.

2. Match
   \[
   \psi_L(x)=e^{i5x}+r e^{-i5x},\qquad
   \psi_R(x)=t e^{-i16x}
   \]
   at $x=0$ and prove $r=-21/11$, $t=-10/11$.

3. Form the Klein–Gordon charge-current ratios
   \[
   R=|r|^2=\frac{441}{121},\qquad
   T=\frac{p_R}{k_L}|t|^2=-\frac{320}{121},
   \]
   and prove $R+T=1$. Interpret the negative transmitted charge
   current as Klein-zone superradiance, not as a one-particle
   probability.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “right-going means $p_R=+16$, so
   $r=-11/21$ and $t=10/21$”; (ii) “$R$ and $T$ are ordinary
   probabilities, so $T=|t|^2=100/121$ is positive and there is
   no Klein-zone superradiance.”
permittedResults: At $m=12$, $E=13$, $qV_0=33$ one has $k_L=\sqrt{169-144}=5$, $E-qV_0=-20$, and $|k_R|=\sqrt{400-144}=16$. Because $E-qV_0<0$, right-going group velocity forces $p_R=-16$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the two local mass-shell wave numbers, then choose the sign of pR so that v_g=p/(E-qV) is positive on the right.
Solve 1+r=t and 5(1-r)=-16t, then form R=|r|^2 and T=(pR/kL)|t|^2 and check R+T=1.

milestones.criterion: Produces kL=5, right kinetic energy -20, |kR|=16, pR=-16 from the right-going group-velocity condition, and the match r=-21/11, t=-10/11.
Reports the charge-current ratios R=441/121, T=-320/121, R+T=1, and interprets T<0 as Klein-zone superradiance.
Rejects pR=+16 or an ordinary-probability T=|t|^2, and refuses reserved cutoff / Dirac–Pauli / Yukawa / resonance substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes the right-going branch as pR=+16 and reports the inconsistent match r=-11/21, t=10/21.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pR=-16, r=-21/11, t=-10/11, and negative T=-320/121 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats R and T as ordinary one-particle probabilities and reports T=|t|^2=100/121>0, denying Klein-zone superradiance.
commonErrors.consequence: The required charge-current ratio T=-320/121 and its Klein-zone interpretation are replaced by a Schrödinger probability.

hintTree.content: Compute $E^2-m^2=25$ on the left and $(E-qV_0)^2-m^2=256$ on the right. The group velocity $v_g=p/(E-qV)$ is positive on the right only if $p$ is negative.
Match value and derivative at $x=0$: $1+r=t$ and $i5(1-r)=-i16 t$. Solve the linear system.
Form $R=r^2$ and $T=(p_R/k_L)t^2$ with $p_R=-16$. Check $R+T=1$. Do not treat $T$ as $|t|^2$.

GQM:020526.canonicalSolution:
On the left, $qV=0$, so
\[
k_L^2=E^2-m^2=13^2-12^2=169-144=25,\qquad k_L=5.
\]
On the right the local kinetic energy is
\[
E-qV_0=13-33=-20,
\]
and
\[
k_R^2=(E-qV_0)^2-m^2=400-144=256,\qquad |k_R|=16.
\]
The group velocity follows by differentiating the local mass-shell
relation $p^2=(E-qV)^2-m^2$:
\[
v_g=\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}p}=\frac{p}{E-qV}.
\]
On the right $E-qV_0=-20<0$, so $v_g>0$ forces $p<0$. The
right-going branch is therefore $p_R=-16$, not $+16$.
\[
\boxed{k_L=5,\quad E-qV_0=-20,\quad |k_R|=16,\quad p_R=-16}.
\]

Continuity of $\psi$ and $\psi'$ at $x=0$ for
$\psi_L=e^{i5x}+r e^{-i5x}$ and $\psi_R=t e^{-i16x}$ is
\[
1+r=t,\qquad 5(1-r)=-16t.
\]
Substitute $t=1+r$ into the second equation:
\[
5-5r=-16-16r\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 21=-11r\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
r=-\frac{21}{11},
\]
\[
t=1-\frac{21}{11}=-\frac{10}{11}.
\]
\[
\boxed{r=-21/11,\quad t=-10/11}.
\]

The incident Klein–Gordon charge current is proportional to $k_L$,
the reflected current to $-k_L|r|^2$, and the transmitted current
to $p_R|t|^2$. The charge-current ratios are therefore
\[
R=|r|^2=\frac{441}{121},
\qquad
T=\frac{p_R}{k_L}|t|^2
=\frac{-16}{5}\cdot\frac{100}{121}
=-\frac{320}{121}.
\]
Their sum is
\[
R+T=\frac{441-320}{121}=1.
\]
The negative transmitted charge current is Klein-zone
superradiance: the supercritical step lies in the Klein region
and the conserved charge current, not a one-particle probability,
is what adds to one. In particular $T$ is not $|t|^2=100/121$
and is not an ordinary transmission probability.
\[
\boxed{R=441/121,\;T=-320/121,\;R+T=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) chooses the positive right momentum $p_R=+16$ and
reports the inconsistent match $r=-11/21$, $t=10/21$. Sentence
(ii) treats $R$ and $T$ as ordinary probabilities. The
calculation is a supercritical Klein–Gordon step; it is not a
cutoff dispersion, a Dirac–Pauli step, a Yukawa optical theorem,
or a resonance pole.

graderFixtures.proofText: The supercritical step has $k_L=5$, right kinetic energy $-20$, $|k_R|=16$, and right-going momentum $p_R=-16$. Matching gives $r=-21/11$ and $t=-10/11$. The charge-current ratios are $R=441/121$ and $T=-320/121$ with $R+T=1$. The negative transmitted charge current is Klein-zone superradiance, not an ordinary one-particle probability.
Right-going means pR=+16, so r=-11/21 and t=10/21. I do not report pR=-16, r=-21/11, or t=-10/11.
R and T are ordinary probabilities, so T=|t|^2=100/121 is positive and there is no Klein-zone superradiance. I never accept T=-320/121.

GQM:020627.title: Natural-log D(|0><0||(I+(3/5)X)/2)=ln(5/2); Z-dephasing drops it by ln(5/4), the reverse is infinite, and Pinsker holds at 17/25
GQM:020627.objective: For rho=|0><0| and sigma=(I+(3/5)X)/2, prove the eigenvalues of sigma are 4/5 and 1/5, that the Umegaki relative entropy is D(rho||sigma)=ln(5/2), that complete Z-dephasing yields D(Delta rho||Delta sigma)=ln 2 with DPI drop ln(5/4)>0, that D(sigma||rho)=infinity by support, and that the trace distance is sqrt(34)/10 so Pinsker gives D>=17/25.
GQM:020627.statement:
Work with the qubit states
\[
\rho=|0\rangle\langle 0|,\qquad
\sigma=\frac{I+(3/5)X}{2}
=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&3/10\\3/10&1/2\end{pmatrix},
\]
and with the natural logarithm in the Umegaki relative entropy
$D(\alpha\|\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha\log\alpha-\alpha\log\beta)$.
Do not replace the calculation by a classical or path-space
Kullback–Leibler divergence, and do not reduce it to a
purity-only identity that never evaluates $D(\rho\|\sigma)$.

1. Prove that $\sigma$ has eigenvalues $4/5$ and $1/5$. Compute
   \[
   D(\rho\|\sigma)=\ln\frac52.
   \]

2. Let $\Delta$ be complete dephasing in the computational $Z$
   basis. Prove
   \[
   \Delta\rho=\rho,\qquad
   \Delta\sigma=\frac I2,\qquad
   D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)=\ln 2,
   \]
   and that the data-processing inequality is strict, with drop
   \[
   D(\rho\|\sigma)-D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)=\ln\frac54>0.
   \]

3. Prove $D(\sigma\|\rho)=+\infty$ by the support condition, and
   that the trace distance before the channel is
   \[
   T(\rho,\sigma)=\frac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1=\frac{\sqrt{34}}{10}.
   \]
   Check Pinsker's inequality in nats,
   $D(\rho\|\sigma)\ge 2T(\rho,\sigma)^2=17/25$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the states commute, so $D$ is the
   classical KL of the eigenvalue lists $\{1,0\}$ and $\{4/5,1/5\}$,
   and the reverse $D(\sigma\|\rho)$ is the finite number
   $\frac45\ln\frac45+\frac15\ln\frac15$”; (ii) “dephasing does not
   decrease $D$, so the assigned drop is $0$, or else Pinsker is
   already $D\ge T$ rather than $D\ge 17/25$.”
permittedResults: A qubit with Bloch vector $\mathbf r$ has eigenvalues $(1\pm|\mathbf r|)/2$. Here $\sigma$ has $\mathbf r=(3/5,0,0)$, so the spectrum is $\{4/5,1/5\}$. The eigenstates of $X$ give $\langle 0|\log\sigma|0\rangle=\frac12\ln(4/25)=\ln(2/5)$.

Bloch vectors $(0,0,1)$ and $(3/5,0,0)$ have Euclidean distance $\sqrt{34}/5$, hence $T=\sqrt{34}/10$ and $2T^2=17/25$. After $\Delta$, the second Bloch vector is $0$, so $D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)=\ln 2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize sigma in the X basis, average -ln lambda against the two equal |0> overlaps, then apply Delta in the Z basis.
Read the reverse divergence from the support condition and convert the Bloch distance into T=sqrt(34)/10 and 2T^2=17/25.

Reports Delta rho=rho, Delta sigma=I/2, D=ln 2, drop ln(5/4)>0, reverse +infinity, T=sqrt(34)/10, and Pinsker 17/25.

hintTree.content: Diagonalize $\sigma$ in the $X$ basis. The computational state $|0\rangle$ is an equal superposition of $|+\rangle$ and $|-\rangle$, so $-\langle 0|\log\sigma|0\rangle$ is the average of $-\ln(4/5)$ and $-\ln(1/5)$.
Complete $Z$-dephasing kills the off-diagonal $3/10$ entries of $\sigma$ and leaves $\rho$ fixed. The resulting $D$ is the binary relative entropy of a point mass versus the fair coin.
The reverse relative entropy is infinite because $\sigma$ charges $|1\rangle$ while $\rho$ does not. For Pinsker, convert the Bloch distance into $2T^2=17/25$ and compare with $\ln(5/2)$.

GQM:020627.canonicalSolution:
The operator $\sigma=(I+(3/5)X)/2$ is a qubit state whose Bloch
vector is $\mathbf r=(3/5,0,0)$. Its eigenvalues are therefore
\[
\frac{1\pm 3/5}{2}=\frac45,\ \frac15.
\]
The corresponding eigenstates are the $X$ eigenvectors
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$. In particular
\[
\log\sigma
=\ln\frac45\,|+\rangle\langle +|
+\ln\frac15\,|-\rangle\langle -|.
\]
Because $\lvert\langle 0|\pm\rangle\rvert^2=1/2$ and $\rho$ is
pure,
\[
D(\rho\|\sigma)
=-\langle 0|\log\sigma|0\rangle
=-\frac12\ln\frac45-\frac12\ln\frac15
=-\frac12\ln\frac{4}{25}
=\ln\frac52.
\]
The states do not commute: $\rho$ is diagonal in the $Z$ basis
while $\sigma$ is diagonal in the $X$ basis. The number
$\ln(5/2)$ is therefore a genuinely quantum relative entropy, not
a classical KL of a shared eigenbasis.
\[
\boxed{D(\rho\|\sigma)=\ln(5/2);\ \operatorname{spec}(\sigma)=\{4/5,1/5\}}.
\]

Complete $Z$-dephasing fixes every computational projector, so
$\Delta\rho=\rho$. It kills the off-diagonal entries of $\sigma$,
leaving
\[
\Delta\sigma=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\Bigr)=\frac I2.
\]
Hence
\[
D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)
=-\langle 0|\log(I/2)|0\rangle
=\ln 2.
\]
Data processing supplies $D(\rho\|\sigma)\ge D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)$.
The drop is strict:
\[
\ln\frac52-\ln 2=\ln\frac54>0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta\rho=\rho,\ \Delta\sigma=I/2,\ D(\Delta\rho\|\Delta\sigma)=\ln 2,\ \text{drop }\ln(5/4)>0}.
\]

The support of $\sigma$ is the full qubit, while
$\operatorname{supp}\rho=\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle\}$. In the
reverse order one has $\operatorname{supp}\sigma\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\rho$,
so
\[
D(\sigma\|\rho)=+\infty.
\]
(The would-be classical reverse KL of the spectra is finite and is
not the assigned quantity.) The Bloch vectors of $\rho$ and
$\sigma$ are $(0,0,1)$ and $(3/5,0,0)$, of Euclidean distance
\[
\bigl\lvert\mathbf r_\rho-\mathbf r_\sigma\bigr\rvert
=\sqrt{\Bigl(\frac35\Bigr)^2+1}
=\frac{\sqrt{34}}{5}.
\]
The trace distance is half of that length,
\[
T(\rho,\sigma)=\frac{\sqrt{34}}{10}.
\]
Pinsker's inequality in nats then reads
\[
D(\rho\|\sigma)
\ge 2T(\rho,\sigma)^2
=2\cdot\frac{34}{100}
=\frac{17}{25}.
\]
The numerical comparison $\ln(5/2)>\frac{17}{25}$ is consistent
and is not itself a substitute for the identity $2T^2=17/25$.
\[
\boxed{D(\sigma\|\rho)=+\infty,\ T(\rho,\sigma)=\sqrt{34}/10,\ D\ge 17/25}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the noncommuting Umegaki quantity by a
classical KL and reports a finite reverse. Sentence (ii) denies
the strict DPI drop or replaces Pinsker's $2T^2=17/25$ by the
weaker comparison $D\ge T$. The construction is a quantum
relative-entropy and dephasing-DPI audit; it is not a classical
or path-space KL and not a purity-only qubit identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The eigenvalues of $\sigma$ are $4/5$ and $1/5$, and $D(\rho\|\sigma)=\ln(5/2)$. Complete $Z$-dephasing gives $\Delta\rho=\rho$, $\Delta\sigma=I/2$, $D=\ln 2$, and drop $\ln(5/4)>0$. The reverse is $+\infty$ by support. The trace distance is $\sqrt{34}/10$ and Pinsker reads $D\ge 17/25$.

The states commute, so D is the classical KL of the eigenvalue lists {1,0} and {4/5,1/5}, and the reverse D(sigma||rho) is the finite number (4/5)ln(4/5)+(1/5)ln(1/5). I do not report ln(5/2) as a noncommuting Umegaki value or an infinite reverse.
Dephasing does not decrease D, so the assigned drop is 0, or else Pinsker is already D>=T rather than D>=17/25. I never accept drop=ln(5/4)>0 together with 2T^2=17/25.

GQM:020628.title: Product |+>^4 has QFI 4 under G=(1/2)sum Z_j while GHZ4 has QFI 16, and the GHZ-parity measurement saturates the bound
GQM:020628.objective: For |psi_theta>=e^{-i theta G}|psi_0> with G=(1/2)sum_{j=1}^4 Z_j and pure-state F_Q=4 Var G, prove that the product |+>^4 has Var G=1 and F_Q=4 with standard-deviation CRB 1/(2 sqrt nu), that GHZ4 has G-eigenvalues +-2, Var G=4, F_Q=16 and bound 1/(4 sqrt nu), and that the GHZ +- measurement with p+=cos^2(2 theta), p-=sin^2(2 theta) has classical FI 16 (e.g. at theta=pi/8) and locally saturates the QCRB.
GQM:020628.statement:
Encode a real parameter $\theta$ by the pure-state family
\[
|\psi_\theta\rangle=e^{-i\theta G}|\psi_0\rangle,\qquad
G=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^4 Z_j
\]
on four qubits. Use the pure-state quantum Fisher information
$F_Q=4\operatorname{Var}_{\psi_0}(G)$ and the quantum Cramér–Rao
bound $\Delta\theta\ge 1/\sqrt{\nu F_Q}$ on the standard deviation
of an unbiased estimator from $\nu$ independent copies. Do not
recast the family as a Berry-phase holonomy, a Rabi or
Landau–Zener two-level sweep, or a Magnus expansion.

1. For the product probe $|\psi_0\rangle=|+\rangle^{\otimes 4}$,
   prove
   \[
   \operatorname{Var} G=1,\qquad
   F_Q=4,\qquad
   \Delta\theta\ge\frac1{2\sqrt{\nu}}.
   \]

2. For the GHZ probe
   $|\mathrm{GHZ}_4\rangle=(|0000\rangle+|1111\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$,
   prove that $G$ has eigenvalues $\pm 2$ on the two computational
   branches, and that
   \[
   \operatorname{Var} G=4,\qquad
   F_Q=16,\qquad
   \Delta\theta\ge\frac1{4\sqrt{\nu}}.
   \]

3. Measure the evolved GHZ family in the parity basis
   $|\pm\rangle=(|0000\rangle\pm|1111\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$. Prove
   \[
   p_+=\cos^2(2\theta),\qquad
   p_-=\sin^2(2\theta),
   \]
   and that the classical Fisher information of this binary
   experiment equals $16$ wherever it is defined (evaluate
   explicitly at $\theta=\pi/8$). Conclude that the measurement
   locally saturates $F_Q$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$G$ is $\sum Z_j$ rather than
   $\frac12\sum Z_j$, so the product already has $\operatorname{Var}G=4$
   and $F_Q=16$”; (ii) “the GHZ $\pm$ probabilities are
   $\cos^2\theta$ and $\sin^2\theta$, so the classical FI is $4$
   rather than $16$ and does not saturate.”
permittedResults: On $|+\rangle^{\otimes 4}$ the four Pauli $Z_j$ are independent, mean-zero, and of variance $1$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(\sum Z_j)=4$ and $\operatorname{Var} G=1$, so $F_Q=4$.

The evolved GHZ state is $\bigl(e^{-2i\theta}|0000\rangle+e^{2i\theta}|1111\rangle\bigr)/\sqrt{2}$. Expanding in the $\pm$ basis produces $p_+=\cos^2(2\theta)$. The binary FI collapses identically to $16$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute Var G from independent single-qubit Z variances on the product, and from the two extreme eigenvalues on GHZ.
Expand the evolved GHZ state in the parity basis and evaluate the binary classical Fisher information, including the sample angle pi/8.

milestones.criterion: Produces product Var G=1 with F_Q=4 and the GHZ eigenvalues +-2 with Var G=4 and F_Q=16, together with the two CRB prefactors.
Reports p+=cos^2(2 theta), p-=sin^2(2 theta), classical FI=16 (e.g. at theta=pi/8), and local saturation of F_Q.
Rejects dropping the 1/2 in G or using unsaturated FI=4, and refuses reserved Berry, Rabi, Landau-Zener, or Magnus substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor 1/2 in G and reports that the product already has Var G=4 and F_Q=16.
commonErrors.consequence: The required product values Var G=1 and F_Q=4, and the distinction from GHZ4, are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses p+=cos^2 theta and p-=sin^2 theta, and reports classical FI=4 rather than 16, denying saturation.
commonErrors.consequence: The required probabilities cos^2(2 theta), sin^2(2 theta) and the saturating value F_c=16 are never produced.

hintTree.content: Keep the factor $1/2$ in $G$. The product variance of $\sum Z_j$ is $4$, but the assigned generator is half of that sum.
On GHZ the two computational branches are $G$-eigenstates with eigenvalues $+2$ and $-2$. The mean vanishes and the second moment is $4$.
Differentiate $p_+=\cos^2(2\theta)$ to obtain $\partial_\theta p_+=-2\sin(4\theta)$. The binary FI identity then yields $16$ at every interior angle, including $\theta=\pi/8$.

GQM:020628.canonicalSolution:
On a product computational eigenstate the operator
$G=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^4 Z_j$ multiplies by
$\frac12(n_0-n_1)$. In particular it is not $\sum Z_j$.

For the product probe $|+\rangle^{\otimes 4}$ each factor satisfies
$\langle Z_j\rangle=0$ and $\langle Z_j^2\rangle=1$, and the four
qubits are independent, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^4 Z_j\Bigr)=4,\qquad
\operatorname{Var} G=\frac14\cdot 4=1.
\]
The pure-state formula therefore gives
\[
F_Q=4\operatorname{Var} G=4.
\]
The quantum Cramér–Rao bound on the standard deviation from $\nu$
copies is
\[
\Delta\theta\ge\frac1{\sqrt{\nu F_Q}}=\frac1{2\sqrt{\nu}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{product: }\operatorname{Var} G=1,\ F_Q=4,\ \Delta\theta\ge 1/(2\sqrt{\nu})}.
\]

The GHZ probe is the equal superposition of the two extreme
computational strings. Those strings are $G$-eigenstates:
\[
G|0000\rangle=2|0000\rangle,\qquad
G|1111\rangle=-2|1111\rangle.
\]
Hence $\langle G\rangle=0$ and $\langle G^2\rangle=4$, so
$\operatorname{Var} G=4$ and
\[
F_Q=4\cdot 4=16,\qquad
\Delta\theta\ge\frac1{4\sqrt{\nu}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{GHZ$_4$: eigenvalues }\pm 2,\ \operatorname{Var} G=4,\ F_Q=16,\ \Delta\theta\ge 1/(4\sqrt{\nu})}.
\]

The evolved state is
\[
|\psi_\theta\rangle
=\frac{e^{-2i\theta}|0000\rangle+e^{2i\theta}|1111\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
Writing $|0000\rangle=(|+\rangle+|-\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ and
$|1111\rangle=(|+\rangle-|-\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ produces
\[
|\psi_\theta\rangle
=\cos(2\theta)\,|+\rangle-i\sin(2\theta)\,|-\rangle,
\]
so the parity measurement has
\[
p_+=\cos^2(2\theta),\qquad
p_-=\sin^2(2\theta).
\]
The binary classical Fisher information is
\[
F_c
=\frac{(\partial_\theta p_+)^2}{p_+}
+\frac{(\partial_\theta p_-)^2}{p_-}.
\]
One has $\partial_\theta p_+=-2\sin(4\theta)$ and
$\partial_\theta p_-=2\sin(4\theta)$, and the trigonometric
identity $\sin(4\theta)=2\sin(2\theta)\cos(2\theta)$ collapses
the sum to the constant $16$ at every angle where
$p_\pm\in(0,1)$. At the sample point $\theta=\pi/8$ one has
$p_+=p_-=1/2$ and still $F_c=16$. Because $F_c=F_Q$, the
measurement locally saturates the quantum Cramér–Rao bound.
\[
\boxed{p_+=\cos^2(2\theta),\ p_-=\sin^2(2\theta),\ F_c=16\text{ (e.g.\ }\theta=\pi/8\text{); saturates }F_Q}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $1/2$ in $G$ and reports the GHZ
figures already for the product. Sentence (ii) uses the single-angle
probabilities $\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta$ and the unsaturated value
$F_c=4$. The construction is a pure-state QFI comparison of a
product probe with GHZ$_4$; it is not a Berry-phase argument, not
a Rabi or Landau–Zener sweep, and not a Magnus expansion.

graderFixtures.proofText: The product $|+\rangle^{\otimes 4}$ has $\operatorname{Var} G=1$, $F_Q=4$, and CRB $1/(2\sqrt{\nu})$. GHZ$_4$ has $G$-eigenvalues $\pm 2$, $\operatorname{Var} G=4$, $F_Q=16$, and CRB $1/(4\sqrt{\nu})$. The parity measurement has $p_+=\cos^2(2\theta)$, $p_-=\sin^2(2\theta)$, classical FI $16$ (e.g.\ at $\theta=\pi/8$), and locally saturates $F_Q$.
G is sum Z_j rather than (1/2)sum Z_j, so the product already has Var G=4 and F_Q=16. I do not report the assigned product values Var G=1 and F_Q=4.
The GHZ +- probabilities are cos^2 theta and sin^2 theta, so the classical FI is 4 rather than 16 and does not saturate. I never accept F_c=16 at theta=pi/8.

GQM:020629.title: Haar average purity of a 2x2 bipartite reduction is 4/5 by the swap trick, with E|r|^2=3/5 and E det rho_A=1/10
GQM:020629.objective: For a Haar-random pure state on C^{dA} ⊗ C^{dB}, use E[rho_psi^{⊗2}]=(I+F)/(D(D+1)) and the swap trick to prove E Tr rho_A^2=(dA+dB)/(dA dB+1). Specialize to dA=dB=2 to obtain 4/5, mean linear entropy 1/5, and for qubit A the Bloch and determinant averages E|r|^2=3/5 and E det rho_A=1/10. Do not claim a Page entropy.
GQM:020629.statement:
Let $|\psi\rangle$ be a Haar-random pure state on
$\mathbb{C}^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d_B}$, write
$D=d_A d_B$ and $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$,
and let $F$ be the swap on two copies of the full space. Use the
symmetric-subspace average
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\rho_\psi^{\otimes 2}\bigr]
=\frac{I+F}{D(D+1)}
\]
together with the swap trick. Do not replace the calculation by a
Werner-state twirl, a Schmidt-coefficient average, or a
tight-binding impurity ensemble, and do not claim a Page entropy.

1. Prove the reduced-purity identity
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2
   =\frac{d_A+d_B}{d_A d_B+1}.
   \]

2. Specialize to $d_A=d_B=2$ and obtain
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=\frac45,\qquad
   \mathbb{E}\,S_L(\rho_A)=\frac15,
   \]
   where $S_L(\rho)=1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ is the linear
   entropy.

3. Viewing $A$ as a qubit with Bloch vector $\mathbf r$, prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2=\frac35,\qquad
   \mathbb{E}\det\rho_A=\frac1{10}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the Haar average of
   $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2$ is already the maximally mixed value
   $1/2$, so $\mathbb{E}\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2=0$”; (ii) “the same
   average is the Page entropy of a $2\times 2$ bipartition, or else
   it is a Werner / Schmidt impurity calculation rather than the
   swap-trick purity.”
permittedResults: $\operatorname{Tr}(S_A)=d_A$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(S_B)=d_B$. Contracting $(S_A\otimes I_{B_1 B_2})$ against $I$ and against $F=S_A\otimes S_B$ produces the two terms $d_A d_B^2$ and $d_A^2 d_B$.
Dividing by $D(D+1)=d_A d_B(d_A d_B+1)$ collapses the sum to $(d_A+d_B)/(d_A d_B+1)$. At $d_A=d_B=2$ this is $4/5$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Contract (S_A ⊗ I ⊗ I) against I and against F=S_A ⊗ S_B, then divide by D(D+1).
Specialise to dA=dB=2 and invert the qubit identities Tr rho^2=(1+|r|^2)/2 and det rho=(1-|r|^2)/4.

milestones.criterion: Produces E Tr rho_A^2=(dA+dB)/(dA dB+1) from the Haar second moment and the swap trick.
Reports the 2x2 specialisation 4/5, mean linear entropy 1/5, E|r|^2=3/5, and E det rho_A=1/10.
Rejects a 1/2-purity or Page-entropy claim, and refuses reserved Werner, Schmidt, or tight-binding substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the Haar average of Tr rho_A^2 as the maximally mixed value 1/2, hence E|r|^2=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required values 4/5, E|r|^2=3/5, and E det=1/10 are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

commonErrors.description: Claims the same average is a Page entropy, or replaces the swap trick by a Werner, Schmidt, or tight-binding impurity calculation.
commonErrors.consequence: The required swap-trick purity identity is never produced, and a reserved Page / Werner / Schmidt claim is introduced.

hintTree.content: Write $\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2$ as a single full-space trace of $(S_A\otimes I\otimes I)(I+F)/(D(D+1))$.
Use $S_A^2=I$ to convert the $F$ contraction into $\operatorname{Tr}(I_A\otimes S_B)=d_A^2 d_B$.
For the qubit specialisation, invert $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=(1+\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2)/2$ and $\det\rho=(1-\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2)/4$. Do not invoke Page's von Neumann formula.

GQM:020629.canonicalSolution:
Let $D=d_A d_B$ and write $S_A$ (resp.\ $S_B$) for the swap on
the two copies of $A$ (resp.\ $B$). The swap trick and the Haar
second moment give
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2
=\frac1{D(D+1)}
\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((S_A\otimes I_{B_1 B_2})(I+F)\bigr),
\]
where $F=S_A\otimes S_B$. The first contraction is
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(S_A\otimes I_{B_1}\otimes I_{B_2})
=\operatorname{Tr}(S_A)\,d_B^2
=d_A d_B^2,
\]
because $\operatorname{Tr}(S_A)=\sum_{i,j}\langle ij|ji\rangle=d_A$.
The second contraction uses $S_A^2=I$:
\[
\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((S_A\otimes I_{B_1 B_2})(S_A\otimes S_B)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Tr}(I_{A_1 A_2}\otimes S_B)
=d_A^2 d_B.
\]
Adding and dividing by $D(D+1)=d_A d_B(d_A d_B+1)$ produces
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2
=\frac{d_A d_B^2+d_A^2 d_B}{d_A d_B(d_A d_B+1)}
=\frac{d_A+d_B}{d_A d_B+1}.
\]
This is a purity identity obtained from the swap trick. It is not
a Page formula for $\mathbb{E}\,S(\rho_A)$, not a Werner twirl,
and not a Schmidt-coefficient average.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=(d_A+d_B)/(d_A d_B+1)}.
\]

At $d_A=d_B=2$ one has $D=4$ and
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2
=\frac{2+2}{4+1}
=\frac45.
\]
The mean linear entropy is therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}\,S_L(\rho_A)
=1-\frac45
=\frac15.
\]
\[
\boxed{d_A=d_B=2:\ \mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=4/5,\ \mathbb{E}\,S_L=1/5}.
\]

A qubit reduction has
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=(1+\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2)/2$, so
\[
\frac{1+\mathbb{E}\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2}{2}
=\frac45
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbb{E}\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2
=\frac35.
\]
The determinant identity $\det\rho_A=(1-\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2)/4$
then yields
\[
\mathbb{E}\det\rho_A
=\frac{1-3/5}{4}
=\frac1{10}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}\lvert\mathbf r\rvert^2=3/5,\ \mathbb{E}\det\rho_A=1/10}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the Haar purity $4/5$ by the maximally mixed
value $1/2$. Sentence (ii) relabels the same number as a Page
entropy or as a Werner / Schmidt / impurity calculation. The
construction is a Haar bipartite purity evaluation by the swap
trick; it does not claim a Page entropy.

The same average is the Page entropy of a 2x2 bipartition, or else it is a Werner / Schmidt impurity calculation rather than the swap-trick purity. I never accept E Tr rho_A^2=(dA+dB)/(dA dB+1) as a purity identity.

GQM:020630.title: The Peres-Mermin square has row products +I,+I,+I and column products +I,+I,-I, so no noncontextual +-1 assignment exists
GQM:020630.objective: For the nine-Pauli square with rows [XI,IX,XX], [IY,YI,YY], [XY,YX,ZZ], prove that each row and each column is a commuting context, that the three row products are +I,+I,+I and the three column products are +I,+I,-I, and that any noncontextual +-1 assignment would force the product of the six context products to be +1, contradicting the quantum value -1. The obstruction is state-independent and is not a CHSH or Bell nonlocality argument.
GQM:020630.statement:
Consider the Peres–Mermin square of two-qubit Pauli observables
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
XI & IX & XX \\
IY & YI & YY \\
XY & YX & ZZ
\end{array}
\]
Each row and each column is to be read as a measurement context.
Do not recast the square as a CHSH inequality, a Bell nonlocality
test, or a spatially separated correlation experiment.

1. Prove that the three observables in every row and in every
   column pairwise commute, so each of the six lines is a valid
   context.

2. Prove the operator identities
   \[
   (XI)(IX)(XX)=+I,\quad
   (IY)(YI)(YY)=+I,\quad
   (XY)(YX)(ZZ)=+I
   \]
   for the rows and
   \[
   (XI)(IY)(XY)=+I,\quad
   (IX)(YI)(YX)=+I,\quad
   (XX)(YY)(ZZ)=-I
   \]
   for the columns.

3. Deduce that the product of the six context products equals
   $-I$. Show that any noncontextual assignment of values
   $\pm 1$ to the nine observables makes each observable appear
   twice in that product, hence forces the scalar $+1$, a
   contradiction. Conclude that the obstruction is
   state-independent.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the third-column product
   $(XX)(YY)(ZZ)$ equals $+I$, so all six products are $+I$ and
   there is no contextuality”; (ii) “the same obstruction is a
   CHSH or Bell nonlocality inequality for a bipartite singlet,
   rather than a state-independent contextuality argument.”
permittedResults: Each row multiplies to $+I$: $(XI)(IX)=XX$ and $XX\cdot XX=I$; likewise $(IY)(YI)=YY$; and $(XY)(YX)=ZZ$, so $(XY)(YX)(ZZ)=I$.
The first two columns likewise multiply to $+I$. The third column is $(XX)(YY)(ZZ)=-(ZZ)(ZZ)=-I$. The product of the six identities is therefore $-I$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply each row and each column factorwise, isolating the single minus sign in (XX)(YY).
Count the occurrence of each observable in the product of the six lines and compare the resulting sign with the operator identity -I.

milestones.criterion: Produces commuting contexts and the six operator products +I,+I,+I and +I,+I,-I.
Reports the quantum product -1 versus the noncontextual +1, and states that the obstruction is state-independent.
Rejects a third-column product +I or a CHSH/Bell recasting, and refuses reserved nonlocality substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims (XX)(YY)(ZZ)=+I, so that all six context products are +I and there is no contextuality.
commonErrors.consequence: The required column product -I and the quantum-versus-noncontextual sign contradiction are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Recasts the obstruction as a CHSH or Bell nonlocality inequality for a bipartite singlet.
commonErrors.consequence: The required state-independent contextuality argument is replaced by a reserved nonlocality claim.

hintTree.content: Pairwise commutation in a row or column follows because each pair multiplies to the remaining Pauli of that line, up to a sign that squares away.
The only minus sign in the six products comes from $(X\otimes X)(Y\otimes Y)=-Z\otimes Z$.
In the product of all six context products, each of the nine observables appears once as a row factor and once as a column factor.

GQM:020630.canonicalSolution:
Each line of the square is a triple of two-qubit Paulis whose
pairwise products (up to a phase) recover the third element of
the line. In particular every pair in a row or in a column
commutes, so each of the six lines is a jointly measurable
context.

The row products are
\begin{align*}
(XI)(IX)(XX)
&=(X\otimes X)(X\otimes X)
=I,\\
(IY)(YI)(YY)
&=(Y\otimes Y)(Y\otimes Y)
=I,\\
(XY)(YX)(ZZ)
&=(X\otimes Y)(Y\otimes X)(Z\otimes Z).
\end{align*}
The first two factors of the third row give
$(XY)\otimes(YX)=(iZ)\otimes(-iZ)=Z\otimes Z$, and then
$(Z\otimes Z)(Z\otimes Z)=I$. Thus every row product is $+I$.
\[
\boxed{\text{row products }+I,+I,+I}.
\]

The first two column products are likewise
\[
(XI)(IY)(XY)=(X\otimes Y)(X\otimes Y)=I,
\]
\[
(IX)(YI)(YX)=(Y\otimes X)(Y\otimes X)=I.
\]
The third column is the only source of a minus sign:
\[
(XX)(YY)
=(XY)\otimes(XY)
=(iZ)\otimes(iZ)
=-ZZ,
\]
and $(-ZZ)(ZZ)=-I$. Therefore the column products are
$+I$, $+I$, and $-I$.
\[
\boxed{\text{column products }+I,+I,-I}.
\]

The product of the six context products is the operator
$(+I)^5(-I)=-I$. On the other hand, each of the nine observables
appears in exactly one row and exactly one column, hence twice in
that product. Any assignment of numbers $\pm 1$ to the nine
observables therefore contributes a square, and the product of the
six assigned context products is $+1$. This contradicts the
quantum value $-1$. The identities used are operator equalities,
so the obstruction holds in every state: the contextuality is
state-independent. It is not a CHSH correlator and not a Bell
nonlocality argument.
\[
\boxed{\text{quantum product }-1\text{ vs noncontextual }+1;\ \text{state-independent, not CHSH}}.
\]

Sentence (i) misses the minus sign in $(XX)(YY)(ZZ)$ and reports
no contextuality. Sentence (ii) recasts the square as CHSH or Bell
nonlocality. The construction is a Peres–Mermin
state-independent contextuality audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: Each row and each column is a commuting context. The row products are $+I,+I,+I$ and the column products are $+I,+I,-I$. The product of the six lines is $-I$, while any noncontextual $\pm 1$ assignment yields $+1$ because each observable occurs twice. The obstruction is state-independent and is not CHSH or Bell nonlocality.

The third-column product (XX)(YY)(ZZ) equals +I, so all six products are +I and there is no contextuality. I do not report the assigned column product -I or a quantum-versus-noncontextual contradiction.
The same obstruction is a CHSH or Bell nonlocality inequality for a bipartite singlet, rather than a state-independent contextuality argument. I never accept a Peres-Mermin contextuality reading.

GQM:020631.title: Independent bit-flip p=0.1 on the three-qubit code has logical error 0.028 after syndrome recovery, strictly below p for 0<p<1/2
GQM:020631.objective: For the three-qubit bit-flip code |0L>=|000>, |1L>=|111> with stabilizers S1=Z1Z2 and S2=Z2Z3, identify the syndromes I(++), X1(-+), X2(--), X3(+-), prove that conditional X recovery corrects every single flip, and for independent bit-flip probability p obtain pL=3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3 and success 1-3p^2+2p^3. At p=0.1 report pL=0.028 and minimum pure-state and entanglement fidelity/success 0.972, and prove pL
GQM:020631.statement:
Encode one logical qubit in the three-qubit bit-flip code
\[
|0_L\rangle=|000\rangle,\qquad
|1_L\rangle=|111\rangle,
\]
with stabilizer generators $S_1=Z_1Z_2$ and $S_2=Z_2Z_3$. The
noise is independent bit-flip $X$ of probability $p$ on each
physical qubit; there is no claim about depolarizing noise,
amplitude damping, or a Lindblad generator beyond this single-$X$
model. Do not replace the code by those reserved channels.

1. Compute the syndrome pair
   $\bigl(\langle S_1\rangle,\langle S_2\rangle\bigr)\in\{\pm\}^2$
   on the four Pauli operators $\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}$, and prove the
   table
   \[
   I\mapsto(++),\quad
   X_1\mapsto(-+),\quad
   X_2\mapsto(--),\quad
   X_3\mapsto(+-).
   \]
   Show that applying the matching $X$ recovery corrects every
   single bit flip.

2. For independent flips of probability $p$, prove that the
   residual logical-error probability after this decoder is
   \[
   p_L
   =3p^2(1-p)+p^3
   =3p^2-2p^3,
   \]
   with success probability
   \[
   1-p_L=1-3p^2+2p^3.
   \]

3. At the sample $p=0.1$ evaluate
   \[
   p_L=0.028,\qquad
   1-p_L=0.972.
   \]
   Identify $1-p_L$ with both the minimum pure-state fidelity and
   the entanglement fidelity of the encoded logical qubit under
   this decoder. Prove $p_L<p$ for every $0<p<1/2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a single flip already causes a
   logical error, so $p_L=3p(1-p)^2$ or even $p_L=p$, and the
   sample value is not $0.028$”; (ii) “the same $p_L$ is the
   logical error of a depolarizing, amplitude-damping, or Lindblad
   model, rather than of independent $X$ noise with single-flip
   recovery.”
permittedResults: $X_1$ anticommutes with $S_1$ and commutes with $S_2$; $X_3$ commutes with $S_1$ and anticommutes with $S_2$; $X_2$ anticommutes with both. These are the four listed syndromes.
The polynomial identity $p_L-p=-p(1-p)(1-2p)$ is strictly negative on $(0,1/2)$. At $p=1/10$ one has $p_L=3/100-2/1000=28/1000$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read each single-X syndrome from the commutation relations with Z1Z2 and Z2Z3, then count the four failing strings under independent noise.
Evaluate the cubic at p=1/10 and factor pL-p=-p(1-p)(1-2p) for the open interval (0,1/2).

milestones.criterion: Produces the four syndromes I(++), X1(-+), X2(--), X3(+-) and the identity pL=3p^2-2p^3 with success 1-3p^2+2p^3.
Reports pL=0.028 and fidelity/success 0.972 at p=0.1, and the strict comparison pL
Rejects a linear-in-p logical error or a reserved Lindblad / depolarizing / amplitude-damping model, and stays inside single-X correction.

hintTree.content: Evaluate $S_1$ and $S_2$ on $X_j|000\rangle$. The two-bit syndrome uniquely labels $I,X_1,X_2,X_3$.
Weight-two errors are decoded as the complementary single flip and leave a logical $X$. The triple flip has trivial syndrome and is also logical $X$.
Factor $p_L-p=-p(1-p)(1-2p)$ to see the open interval $(0,1/2)$. Do not pass to a depolarizing or amplitude-damping generator.

GQM:020631.canonicalSolution:
The stabilizer generators act on computational strings by
comparing bits. In particular, on the four operators of weight at
most one they produce the syndromes
\[
\begin{align*}
I&\mapsto (++),\\
X_1&\mapsto (-+),\\
X_2&\mapsto (--),\\
X_3&\mapsto (+-),
\end{align*}
\]
because $X_1$ anticommutes only with $S_1$, $X_3$ anticommutes
only with $S_2$, and $X_2$ anticommutes with both. These four
syndromes are distinct, so the lookup that applies the matching
$X$ returns every single-flip coset to the code space. Every
single $X$ error is therefore corrected. No claim is made about
any other Pauli, about a depolarizing channel, or about a Lindblad
generator.
\[
\boxed{I(++),\ X_1(-+),\ X_2(--),\ X_3(+-);\ \text{single $X$ corrected}}.
\]

Under independent bit-flip noise of probability $p$, the decoder
succeeds on the identity and on the three weight-one strings, and
fails on the three weight-two strings and on the triple flip
(each of those four strings is equivalent to logical $X$ after
the lookup). Hence
\[
p_L
=3p^2(1-p)+p^3
=3p^2-2p^3,
\]
and the success probability is
\[
1-p_L=1-3p^2+2p^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{p_L=3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3,\quad 1-p_L=1-3p^2+2p^3}.
\]

At the sample $p=1/10$,
\[
p_L
=3\Bigl(\frac1{10}\Bigr)^2-2\Bigl(\frac1{10}\Bigr)^3
=\frac{3}{100}-\frac{2}{1000}
=0.028,
\]
so $1-p_L=0.972$. After decoding, the logical channel on the code
space is the mixture
$(1-p_L)\,\mathcal{I}+p_L\,\operatorname{Ad}_{X_L}$. On a pure
logical input $|\psi\rangle$, its fidelity with the channel output is
\[
F_\psi=1-p_L+p_L|\langle\psi|X_L|\psi\rangle|^2.
\]
The minimum over pure inputs is therefore $1-p_L$, attained when
$\langle\psi|X_L|\psi\rangle=0$. The entanglement fidelity with a
maximally entangled reference is also $1-p_L$ because the logical
$X_L$ Kraus branch has zero trace. Thus the minimum pure-state
fidelity, the entanglement fidelity, and the success probability
are all $0.972$ at $p=0.1$.

Finally,
\[
p_L-p
=3p^2-2p^3-p
=-p(1-p)(1-2p).
\]
For $0<p<1/2$ each factor $p$, $1-p$, and $1-2p$ is positive, so
$p_L<p$ strictly.
\[
\boxed{p=0.1:\ p_L=0.028,\ \text{fidelity/success }=0.972;\ p_L<p\text{ on }(0,1/2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats a single flip as already logical and never
produces $0.028$. Sentence (ii) replaces the independent-$X$
model by a reserved depolarizing, amplitude-damping, or Lindblad
channel. The construction is a single-$X$ three-qubit bit-flip
audit; it makes no claim beyond that decoder.

graderFixtures.proofText: The syndromes are $I(++)$, $X_1(-+)$, $X_2(--)$, $X_3(+-)$, and conditional $X$ recovery corrects every single flip. Independent probability $p$ gives $p_L=3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3$ and success $1-3p^2+2p^3$. At $p=0.1$ one has $p_L=0.028$ and minimum pure-state / entanglement fidelity / success $0.972$, with $p_L<p$ on $(0,1/2)$. No claim is made beyond single-$X$ correction.
A single flip already causes a logical error, so pL=3p(1-p)^2 or even pL=p, and the sample value is not 0.028. I do not report pL=3p^2-2p^3=0.028.
The same pL is the logical error of a depolarizing, amplitude-damping, or Lindblad model, rather than of independent X noise with single-flip recovery. I never accept the assigned single-X cubic.

GRA:010117.title: On the finite-cofinite algebra of N, geometric atoms 2^{-n} extend uniquely with mu(odd)=2/3, mu(3N)=1/7, mu(n>=5)=1/16
GRA:010117.objective: On N={1,2,...} with the finite/cofinite algebra and atom weights 2^{-n}, prove the unique extension satisfies mu(E)=sum_{n in E} 2^{-n}, and evaluate mu(odd)=2/3, mu(3N)=1/7, mu({n>=5})=1/16.
GRA:010117.statement:
Let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and let $\mathcal{A}$ be the
algebra of finite and cofinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. Assign to
each singleton the geometric atom weight $2^{-n}$, and let
$\mu_0$ be the unique finitely additive set function on
$\mathcal{A}$ with $\mu_0(\{n\})=2^{-n}$. Do not replace this
extension ledger by a Carathéodory splitting construction of Borel
measure, an Egorov failure on an infinite-measure runway, or a
pair of disagreeing iterated integrals on a $\sigma$-finite
product.

1. Prove that $\mu_0$ is a $\sigma$-finite premeasure on
   $\mathcal{A}$, that $\sigma(\mathcal{A})=2^{\mathbb{N}}$, and
   that there is a unique measure $\mu$ on $2^{\mathbb{N}}$
   extending $\mu_0$. Identify
   \[
   \mu(E)=\sum_{n\in E}2^{-n}
   \]
   for every $E\subseteq\mathbb{N}$.

2. Evaluate the three sample sets
   \[
   \mu(\{n\text{ odd}\})=\frac23,\qquad
   \mu(3\mathbb{N})=\frac17,\qquad
   \mu(\{n\ge 5\})=\frac1{16}.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the odd integers have counting
   density $1/2$, so $\mu(\text{odd})=1/2$ rather than $2/3$”;
   (ii) “the tail $\{n\ge 5\}$ is the geometric series starting at
   $2^{-4}$, so $\mu(\{n\ge 5\})=1/8$ rather than $1/16$.”
permittedResults: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}=1$. Odd atoms form the geometric series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-(2k+1)}=(1/2)/(1-1/4)=2/3$. Multiples of $3$ form $\sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^{-3k}=(1/8)/(1-1/8)=1/7$.
The tail starting at $n=5$ is $\sum_{n=5}^\infty 2^{-n}=2^{-5}/(1-1/2)=1/16$. Uniqueness of the extension follows from $\sigma$-finiteness of $\mu_0$ on the algebra $\mathcal{A}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify the finite/cofinite algebra, verify that the geometric atoms define a sigma-finite premeasure, and invoke Hahn–Kolmogorov uniqueness on the power set.
Evaluate the three sample sets by summing the corresponding geometric series of atom weights 2^{-n}.

milestones.criterion: Produces the unique extension mu(E)=sum_{n in E} 2^{-n} of the finite/cofinite geometric premeasure on N={1,2,...}.
Reports mu(odd)=2/3, mu(3N)=1/7, and mu({n>=5})=1/16.
Rejects counting-density mu(odd)=1/2 or a tail value 1/8, and refuses reserved Carathéodory-splitting, Egorov-runway, or iterated-integral substitutions.

commonErrors.consequence: The required identity mu(odd)=2/3 and the geometric-atom extension ledger are lost.

commonErrors.consequence: The assigned tail value 1/16 is replaced by the off-by-one geometric sum 1/8.

hintTree.content: Countable unions of singletons generate every subset of $\mathbb{N}$, so $\sigma(\mathcal{A})$ is the power set. Finite additivity on atoms plus $\sigma$-finiteness gives uniqueness.
Sum the odd indices as a geometric series with first term $1/2$ and ratio $1/4$. Sum the multiples of $3$ with first term $1/8$ and ratio $1/8$.
The tail $\{n\ge 5\}$ starts at the atom $2^{-5}$, not at $2^{-4}$. Its sum is $2^{-4}=1/16$.

GRA:010117.canonicalSolution:
The collection $\mathcal{A}$ of finite and cofinite subsets of
$\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\dots\}$ is an algebra. The assignment
$\mu_0(\{n\})=2^{-n}$ extends uniquely by finite additivity to
every finite set. Because
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}=1,
\]
every cofinite set $E$ satisfies
$\mu_0(E)=1-\mu_0(E^c)$. To verify countable additivity, let
$(E_j)$ be pairwise disjoint sets in $\mathcal{A}$ whose union
$E$ also lies in $\mathcal{A}$. If some $E_j$ is cofinite, then all
the other $E_k$ lie in its finite complement, so only finitely many
of them are nonempty and finite additivity applies. If every $E_j$
is finite and $E$ is finite, the same conclusion holds. In the
remaining case every $E_j$ is finite and $E$ is cofinite; since the
atom weights are nonnegative, we may rearrange their sum to obtain
\[
\sum_j\mu_0(E_j)
=\sum_j\sum_{n\in E_j}2^{-n}
=\sum_{n\in E}2^{-n}
=1-\sum_{n\in E^c}2^{-n}
=\mu_0(E).
\]
Thus $\mu_0$ is a finite, hence $\sigma$-finite, premeasure on
$\mathcal{A}$.

Every singleton belongs to $\mathcal{A}$, so
$\sigma(\mathcal{A})=2^{\mathbb{N}}$. Hahn–Kolmogorov therefore
supplies a unique measure $\mu$ on the power set extending
$\mu_0$, necessarily the atomic measure
\[
\mu(E)=\sum_{n\in E}2^{-n}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mu(E)=\sum_{n\in E}2^{-n}}.
\]

The odd integers are $\{1,3,5,\dots\}$, so
\[
\mu(\text{odd})
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-(2k+1)}
=\frac{1/2}{1-1/4}
=\frac{2}{3}.
\]
The multiples of $3$ are $\{3,6,9,\dots\}$, so
\[
\mu(3\mathbb{N})
=\sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^{-3k}
=\frac{1/8}{1-1/8}
=\frac{1}{7}.
\]
The tail starting at $n=5$ is
\[
\mu(\{n\ge 5\})
=\sum_{n=5}^\infty 2^{-n}
=\frac{2^{-5}}{1-1/2}

GRA:010122.title: Counting tails E_n={n,n+1,...} stay infinite while rho(E_n)=2^{1-n} and rho(E_4)=1/8
GRA:010122.objective: On (N,2^N) contrast counting measure of the nested tails E_n={n,n+1,...} (each infinite, intersection empty) with the geometric sample rho({k})=2^{-k} for which rho(E_n)=2^{1-n}->0 and rho(E_4)=1/8, and isolate the finite-first-set hypothesis in continuity from above.
GRA:010122.statement:
Let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ and work on the measurable space
$(\mathbb{N},2^{\mathbb{N}})$. Write
\[
E_n=\{n,n+1,n+2,\ldots\}\qquad(n\ge 1)
\]
for the nested tails. Do not replace this continuity-from-above
ledger by a Carathéodory splitting construction of Borel measure,
an Egorov failure on an infinite-measure runway, or a missing
dominator at a sharp concentration threshold.

   that $\bigcap_{n\ge 1}E_n=\emptyset$, and that $\mu(E_n)=\infty$

   \[
   \mu(E_n)\not\to\mu\Bigl(\bigcap_{n\ge 1}E_n\Bigr).
   \]

2. Let $\rho$ be the unique measure with $\rho(\{k\})=2^{-k}$ for
   each $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Prove
   \[
   \rho(E_n)=2^{1-n}\to 0=\rho(\emptyset),
   \]
   and evaluate the sample
   \[
   \rho(E_4)=\frac18.

   the finite-first-set hypothesis $\mu(E_1)<\infty$, and explain
   precisely why the counting-measure ledger fails that hypothesis

   nested sequence, so the counting tails satisfy $\mu(E_n)\to 0$”;
   (ii) “the geometric tail is $\rho(E_n)=2^{-n}$, so
   $\rho(E_4)=1/16$ rather than $1/8$.”

The sets $E_n=\{n,n+1,\ldots\}$ are nested decreasing because
$E_{n+1}$ is obtained from $E_n$ by deleting the single point $n$.
If $m\in\mathbb{N}$ is fixed, then $m\notin E_n$ whenever $n>m$, so
\[
\bigcap_{n\ge 1}E_n=\emptyset.
\]
Counting measure records cardinality, and each tail is infinite, so
$\mu(E_n)=\infty$ for every $n$. Therefore
\[
\mu(E_n)=\infty\not\to 0=\mu(\emptyset)
=\mu\Bigl(\bigcap_{n\ge 1}E_n\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mu(E_n)=\infty\not\to\mu(\bigcap E_n)=0}.
\]

The geometric sample has
\[
\rho(E_n)
=\sum_{k=n}^\infty 2^{-k}
=2^{-n}\sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{-j}
=2^{-n}\cdot 2
=2^{1-n}.
\]
Hence $\rho(E_n)\to 0=\rho(\emptyset)$. The assigned sample is
\[
\rho(E_4)=2^{1-4}=2^{-3}=\frac18.
\]
\[
\boxed{\rho(E_n)=2^{1-n},\;\rho(E_4)=1/8}.
\]

$\nu(F_1)<\infty$, then $\nu(F_n)\to\nu(F)$. The finite-first-set
hypothesis is essential. In the counting ledger one has
$\mu(E_1)=\infty$, so the theorem does not apply and the numerical
failure $\infty\not\to 0$ is permitted. In the geometric ledger one
has $\rho(E_1)=2^{1-1}=1<\infty$, so the theorem applies and forces
$\rho(E_n)\to\rho(\emptyset)=0$, matching the explicit sum.
\[
\boxed{\text{finite-first-set hypothesis is necessary}}.
\]

concludes that the counting tails tend to $0$. Sentence (ii)
under-sums the geometric tail as $2^{-n}$ and reports
$\rho(E_4)=1/16$ instead of $1/8$. The construction is a
continuity-from-above audit isolating a finite first set; it is not

failure on an infinite-measure runway, or a missing-dominator

GRA:010218.title: Dyadic floor s_n=2^{-n} floor(2^n x) on [0,1] has integral 1/2-2^{-n-1} and at n=3 the ledger 7/16, 1/16, 1/8
GRA:010218.objective: For s_n=2^{-n} floor(2^n x) on [0,1] prove measurability, monotonicity s_n ↑ x, and 0<=x-s_n<2^{-n} a.e.; evaluate integral=1/2-2^{-n-1}, L1 gap 2^{-n-1}, ess-L^∞ gap 2^{-n}; at n=3 obtain 7/16, 1/16, 1/8.
GRA:010218.statement:
On the unit interval $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure, define the
dyadic floor approximants
\[
s_n(x)=2^{-n}\bigl\lfloor 2^n x\bigr\rfloor,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
Do not replace this approximation ledger by an Egorov failure on
an infinite-measure runway, a missing-dominator concentration
threshold, or an undergraduate sequence-of-functions continuity
exercise.

1. Prove that each $s_n$ is Borel measurable, that
   $0\le s_n\le s_{n+1}\le x$ pointwise, and that
   \[
   0\le x-s_n(x)<2^{-n}
   \]
   for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in[0,1]$ (in fact, for every
   $x\in[0,1)$).

2. Prove the integral identity
   \[
   \int_{[0,1]}s_n=\frac12-2^{-n-1},
   \]
   the $L^1$ gap
   \[
   \|x-s_n\|_{L^1([0,1])}=2^{-n-1},
   \]
   and the essential $L^\infty$ gap
   \[
   \|x-s_n\|_{L^\infty([0,1])}=2^{-n}.
   \]

3. Specialize to $n=3$ and obtain the numerical ledger
   \[
   \int s_3=\frac7{16},\qquad
   \|x-s_3\|_1=\frac1{16},\qquad
   \|x-s_3\|_\infty=\frac18.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$s_n$ is the identity in the mean,
   so $\int s_n=1/2$ rather than $1/2-2^{-n-1}$ (and at $n=3$ one
   does not obtain $7/16$)”; (ii) “the essential $L^\infty$ gap
   equals the $L^1$ gap, so at $n=3$ one has
   $\|x-s_3\|_\infty=1/16$ rather than $1/8$.”

Sum $\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1} k$ as $(2^n-1)2^n/2$ and divide by $2^{2n}$ to obtain $1/2-2^{-n-1}$.
The pointwise gap is strictly less than $2^{-n}$ but attains values arbitrarily close to $2^{-n}$, so the essential supremum is $2^{-n}$ rather than the $L^1$ mean $2^{-n-1}$.

GRA:010218.canonicalSolution:
On each half-open dyadic interval
$[k/2^n,(k+1)/2^n)$ one has $\lfloor 2^n x\rfloor=k$, so
$s_n=k/2^n$ there, while $s_n(1)=1$. Thus $s_n$ is a nonnegative
simple Borel function, hence measurable.

If $x\in[k/2^n,(k+1)/2^n)$, the two children of this interval in
the $(n+1)$-mesh have values $2k/2^{n+1}=k/2^n$ and
$(2k+1)/2^{n+1}$, both at least $s_n(x)$. At $x=1$ one has
$s_n(1)=s_{n+1}(1)=1$. Combined with the elementary bound
$0\le x-\lfloor 2^n x\rfloor/2^n<2^{-n}$ on $[0,1)$, one obtains
\[
0\le s_n\le s_{n+1}\le x
\]
pointwise and
\[
0\le x-s_n(x)<2^{-n}
\]
almost everywhere (in fact everywhere on $[0,1)$).
\[
\boxed{s_n\text{ measurable, }s_n\uparrow x,\;0\le x-s_n<2^{-n}\ \text{a.e.}}.
\]

The integral is the finite sum
\begin{align*}
\int_{[0,1]}s_n
&=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}\frac{k}{2^n}\cdot 2^{-n}
=2^{-2n}\cdot\frac{(2^n-1)2^n}{2}
=\frac{2^n-1}{2^{n+1}}
=\frac12-2^{-n-1}.
\end{align*}
Since $\int_{[0,1]}x=1/2$, the $L^1$ gap is
\[
\|x-s_n\|_1
=\frac12-\Bigl(\frac12-2^{-n-1}\Bigr)
=2^{-n-1}.
\]
The pointwise gap is strictly less than $2^{-n}$ yet comes
arbitrarily close to $2^{-n}$ on a set of positive measure, so
\[
\|x-s_n\|_\infty=2^{-n}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\int s_n=1/2-2^{-n-1},\;\|x-s_n\|_1=2^{-n-1},\;\|x-s_n\|_\infty=2^{-n}}.
\]

At $n=3$ these identities become
\[
\int s_3=\frac12-2^{-4}=\frac7{16},\qquad
\|x-s_3\|_1=\frac1{16},\qquad
\|x-s_3\|_\infty=\frac18.
\]
\[
\boxed{n=3\text{ ledger }7/16,\;1/16,\;1/8}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the missing half-bin and reports $\int s_n=1/2$
instead of $7/16$ at $n=3$. Sentence (ii) confuses the essential
$L^\infty$ gap with the $L^1$ gap and reports $1/16$ instead of
$1/8$. The construction is a dyadic-floor approximation audit; it
is not an Egorov runway, a missing-dominator threshold, or an
undergraduate continuity exercise.

s_n is the identity in the mean, so int s_n=1/2. I do not report int s_3=7/16.
The essential L^infty gap equals the L1 gap, so at n=3 one has ||x-s_3||_infty=1/16. I never obtain ||x-s_3||_infty=1/8.

GRA:010223.title: Rational sign f_n=nx/(1+n|x|) has L1 gap 2ln(1+n)/n, L2^2=2/(n+1), and n=3 values 4ln2/3 and 1/2
GRA:010223.objective: On [-1,1] for f_n=nx/(1+n|x|) prove the pointwise limit g=sgn with g(0)=0, the gap 0 at x=0 and (1+n|x|)^{-1} for x!=0 (hence a.e.), L1=2ln(1+n)/n, L2^2=2/(n+1), ess L^infty=1, level measure 2 min(1,(eps^{-1}-1)/n), and the n=3 samples 4ln2/3 and 1/2.
GRA:010223.statement:
Work on the interval $[-1,1]$ with Lebesgue measure. Define
\[
f_n(x)=\frac{nx}{1+n\lvert x\rvert},\qquad n\ge 1,
\]
and write $g=\operatorname{sgn}$ with the convention $g(0)=0$. Do
not replace this rational-sign $L^p$ ledger by an Egorov failure on
an infinite-measure runway, $L^p$ completeness from a summable
telescoping subsequence, or a signed-density Jordan decomposition.

1. Prove that $f_n\to g$ pointwise, and that the gap is
   \[
   \lvert g(x)-f_n(x)\rvert
   =
   \begin{cases}
   0,&x=0,\\
   (1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1},&x\ne0.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   In particular the rational formula holds almost everywhere.

2. Compute the $L^p$ ledger
   \[
   \|g-f_n\|_1=\frac{2\ln(1+n)}{n},\qquad
   \|g-f_n\|_2^2=\frac{2}{n+1},\qquad
   \|g-f_n\|_\infty=1.
   \]

3. For $\varepsilon>0$ prove that the superlevel measure is
   \[
   m\bigl(\{\lvert g-f_n\rvert\ge\varepsilon\}\bigr)
   =2\min\bigl(1,(\varepsilon^{-1}-1)/n\bigr)
   \]
   (interpreting the formula as $0$ when $\varepsilon>1$). Then set
   $n=3$ and evaluate
   \[
   \|g-f_3\|_1=\frac{4\ln 2}{3},\qquad
   \|g-f_3\|_2^2=\frac12.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the $L^1$ gap is $2\ln(1+n)$ with no
   division by $n$, so at $n=3$ one obtains $4\ln 2$ rather than
   $4\ln 2/3$”; (ii) “the squared $L^2$ gap is $2/n$, so at $n=3$
   one obtains $2/3$ rather than $1/2$.”

Thus the absolute gap is $(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1}$ away from the origin (and hence almost everywhere), with the exceptional point value $0$.
$\int_{-1}^1(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1}\,dx=2\ln(1+n)/n$ and $\int_{-1}^1(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-2}\,dx=2/(n+1)$. At $n=3$ these become $4\ln 2/3$ and $1/2$.

Rearrange the superlevel inequality 1/(1+n|x|)>=eps and clip the resulting interval against [-1,1].

milestones.criterion: Produces the pointwise sign limit, the exceptional gap 0 at the origin and a.e. gap (1+n|x|)^{-1}, L1=2ln(1+n)/n, L2^2=2/(n+1), and ess-sup 1.
Reports the superlevel measure 2 min(1,(eps^{-1}-1)/n) and the n=3 samples 4ln2/3 and 1/2.
Rejects an undivided L1 sample 4ln2 or a squared-L2 sample 2/3, and refuses reserved Egorov, telescoping-completeness, or Jordan substitutions.

commonErrors.consequence: The assigned L1 ledger 2ln(1+n)/n and the sample value 4ln2/3 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the squared L2 gap 2/(n+1) by 2/n and reports 2/3 at n=3 instead of 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned identity ||g-f_n||_2^2=2/(n+1) and the sample value 1/2 are replaced by inconsistent numbers.

hintTree.content: Factor $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ from the difference $g-f_n$ on $\{x\neq 0\}$. The remaining scalar is $1-n\lvert x\rvert/(1+n\lvert x\rvert)=(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1}$.
The integrands are even. Compute $\int_0^1(1+nx)^{-1}\,dx=\ln(1+n)/n$ and $\int_0^1(1+nx)^{-2}\,dx=1/(n(n+1))$.

Away from the origin, the inequality $1/(1+n\lvert x\rvert)\ge\varepsilon$ rearranges to $\lvert x\rvert\le(\varepsilon^{-1}-1)/n$ when $0<\varepsilon<1$; clip against $[-1,1]$. Removing the exceptional point $x=0$ does not change the measure, and the level set is empty when $\varepsilon=1$.

GRA:010223.canonicalSolution:
For $x=0$ one has $f_n(0)=0=g(0)$. For $x\neq 0$,
\[
f_n(x)
=\frac{x}{n^{-1}+\lvert x\rvert}
\to\frac{x}{\lvert x\rvert}
=\operatorname{sgn}(x).
\]
The same algebra gives the exact gap:
\begin{align*}
g(x)-f_n(x)
&=\operatorname{sgn}(x)\Bigl(1-\frac{n\lvert x\rvert}{1+n\lvert x\rvert}\Bigr)
=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(x)}{1+n\lvert x\rvert},
\end{align*}
while at the origin $g(0)-f_n(0)=0$. Therefore
\[
\lvert g(x)-f_n(x)\rvert
=
\begin{cases}
0,&x=0,\\
(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1},&x\ne0,
\end{cases}
\]
so the rational gap formula holds almost everywhere.
\[
\boxed{\lvert g-f_n\rvert=(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1}\text{ a.e., with gap }0\text{ at }x=0}.
\]

Evenness reduces the $L^1$ integral to
\[
\|g-f_n\|_1
=2\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+nx}
=\frac{2}{n}\ln(1+n).
\]
The squared $L^2$ norm is
\[
\|g-f_n\|_2^2
=2\int_0^1(1+nx)^{-2}\,dx
=\frac{2}{n}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{1+n}\Bigr)
=\frac{2}{n+1}.
\]
The gap is strictly less than $1$ at every nonzero point and is $0$ at
the origin, but it approaches $1$ as $x\to0$ through nonzero points.
Its essential supremum is therefore $1$, although it is not attained.
\[
\boxed{\|g-f_n\|_1=2\ln(1+n)/n,\;\|g-f_n\|_2^2=2/(n+1),\;\|g-f_n\|_\infty=1}.
\]

If $\varepsilon>1$ then the superlevel set is empty. If
$0<\varepsilon<1$ then, away from the exceptional origin,
\[
\frac{1}{1+n\lvert x\rvert}\ge\varepsilon
\iff
\lvert x\rvert\le\frac{\varepsilon^{-1}-1}{n},
\]
and removing $x=0$ does not change that measure. When $\varepsilon=1$
the actual superlevel set is empty, in agreement with the value $0$
of the same formula. Thus in every case the measure is
$2\min\bigl(1,(\varepsilon^{-1}-1)/n\bigr)$, interpreted as $0$ for
$\varepsilon>1$. At the sample $n=3$,
\[
\|g-f_3\|_1
=\frac{2\ln 4}{3}
=\frac{4\ln 2}{3},\qquad
\|g-f_3\|_2^2
=\frac{2}{4}
=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{n=3:\ L^1=4\ln 2/3,\ L^2\text{-squared}=1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $1/n$ in the $L^1$ antiderivative and
reports $4\ln 2$ at $n=3$. Sentence (ii) replaces $2/(n+1)$ by
$2/n$ and reports $2/3$ instead of $1/2$. The construction is a
rational-sign $L^p$ gap audit on a finite interval; it is not an
Egorov failure on an infinite-measure runway, an $L^p$ completeness
argument from a telescoping subsequence, or a signed-density Jordan
decomposition.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $f_n\to\operatorname{sgn}$ with $g(0)=0$. The gap is $0$ at $x=0$ and $(1+n\lvert x\rvert)^{-1}$ for $x\ne0$, hence the latter formula holds almost everywhere. The norms are $\|g-f_n\|_1=2\ln(1+n)/n$, $\|g-f_n\|_2^2=2/(n+1)$, and $\|g-f_n\|_\infty=1$. Superlevel measure is $2\min(1,(\varepsilon^{-1}-1)/n)$. At $n=3$ one obtains $4\ln 2/3$ and $1/2$.
The L1 gap is 2ln(1+n) with no division by n, so at n=3 I obtain 4ln2. I do not report 2ln(1+n)/n or 4ln2/3.
The squared L2 gap is 2/n, so at n=3 I obtain 2/3. I never obtain 2/(n+1) or the sample 1/2.
