GRA:020221.title: The Hilbert transform of an interval indicator is logarithmic, odd, and still L2
GRA:020221.objective: For Hf=pi^{-1} p.v. int f(y)/(x-y) dy and f=1_[-1,1], prove Hf=pi^{-1} log|(x+1)/(x-1)| a.e., evaluate Hf(0)=0 and Hf(2)=log(3)/pi, and prove that Hf is odd with ||Hf||_2^2=2. Audit the sign convention, the principal value inside (-1,1), and the endpoint logarithms.
GRA:020221.statement:
Adopt the Hilbert transform
\[
Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\,\mathrm{p.v.}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{f(y)}{x-y}\,dy
\]
and let $f=1_{[-1,1]}$.

1. Prove that, almost everywhere,
   \[
   Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{x+1}{x-1}\Bigr\rvert.
   \]
   Evaluate $Hf(0)=0$ and $Hf(2)=\log 3/\pi$.

2. Prove that $Hf$ is odd, and that $\lVert Hf\rVert_2^2=2$.

3. Audit three sentences: (i) “the opposite kernel $1/(y-x)$ is intended, so $Hf$ is the negative logarithm”; (ii) “the principal value may be dropped inside $(-1,1)$, or the integral is ordinary at every $x$”; (iii) “the logarithmic blow-up at $x=\pm 1$ ejects $Hf$ from $L^2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a distributional jump packet, by a diagonal singular kernel, or by any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ the assigned Hilbert transform is an isometry: $\widehat{Hf}(\xi)=-i\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)\hat f(\xi)$, hence $\lVert Hf\rVert_2=\lVert f\rVert_2$. Here $\lVert f\rVert_2^2=2$.
A logarithm is square-integrable near a finite endpoint: $\int_0^{1/2}\lvert\log t\rvert^2\,dt<\infty$. Thus the singularities of $Hf$ at $\pm 1$ do not eject $Hf$ from $L^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the p.v. logarithmic antiderivative from -1 to 1, then specialize at x=0 and x=2.
Use the Fourier multiplier -i sgn(xi) for the L2 isometry, and check square-integrability of log near the endpoints as a spatial audit.

milestones.criterion: Derives Hf=pi^{-1} log|(x+1)/(x-1)| with the assigned kernel and evaluates Hf(0)=0 and Hf(2)=log(3)/pi.
Proves oddness and the L2 identity ||Hf||_2^2=2.
Rejects a sign-flipped kernel, a dropped principal value, and an L2-ejection claim at the endpoints.

commonErrors.description: Uses the opposite kernel 1/(y-x) and reports Hf as the negative logarithm -pi^{-1} log|(x+1)/(x-1)|.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned values Hf(0)=0 still hold, but Hf(2)=log(3)/pi and the oddness orientation relative to the assigned kernel fail.

commonErrors.description: Drops the principal value inside (-1,1), or claims the logarithmic singularities at x=+/-1 eject Hf from L2, or reports ||Hf||_2^2 other than 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The a.e. formula is no longer justified inside the interval, or the isometry ||Hf||_2^2=2 is lost.

hintTree.content: The $y$-antiderivative of $1/(x-y)$ is $-\log\lvert x-y\rvert$. The boundary evaluation is $\log\lvert(x+1)/(x-1)\rvert$, divided by $\pi$.
At $x=0$ the argument of the logarithm is $1$. At $x=2$ it is $3$. Oddness follows from $( -x+1)/(-x-1)=(x-1)/(x+1)$.
The multiplier $-i\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)$ has modulus $1$, so $\lVert Hf\rVert_2^2=\lVert f\rVert_2^2=2$. The log singularities remain square-integrable.

GRA:020221.canonicalSolution:
For $x\notin\{-1,1\}$,
\[
\mathrm{p.v.}\int_{-1}^1\frac{dy}{x-y}
=\mathrm{p.v.}\Bigl[-\log\lvert x-y\rvert\Bigr]_{y=-1}^{y=1}
=\log\lvert x+1\rvert-\log\lvert x-1\rvert
=\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{x+1}{x-1}\Bigr\rvert.
\]
Inside $(-1,1)$ the two improper pieces must be taken as a principal value; the symmetric cancellation of $\log\varepsilon$ terms is what makes the limit finite. Outside $[-1,1]$ the integral is ordinary. Dividing by $\pi$ gives
\[
Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{x+1}{x-1}\Bigr\rvert
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x.
\]
\[
\boxed{Hf=\pi^{-1}\log\lvert(x+1)/(x-1)\rvert}.
\]

In particular
\[
Hf(0)=\frac1\pi\log 1=0,\qquad
Hf(2)=\frac1\pi\log 3.
\]
\[
\boxed{Hf(0)=0,\ Hf(2)=\log 3/\pi}.
\]

Replacing $x$ by $-x$ yields
\[
Hf(-x)=\frac1\pi\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{-x+1}{-x-1}\Bigr\rvert
=\frac1\pi\log\Bigl\lvert\frac{x-1}{x+1}\Bigr\rvert
=-Hf(x),
\]
so $Hf$ is odd. (Equivalently: $f$ is even and the kernel $1/(x-y)$ is odd in $(x,y)$ jointly in the usual way.)

The assigned Hilbert transform acts on the Fourier side by the unimodular multiplier $-i\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)$, hence is an $L^2$ isometry:
\[
\lVert Hf\rVert_2^2=\lVert f\rVert_2^2=\int_{-1}^1 1\,dx=2.
\]
The same conclusion follows from the local integrability $\int_0^{1/2}\lvert\log t\rvert^2\,dt<\infty$ of the endpoint logarithms, together with the decay $Hf(x)\sim 2/(\pi x)$ as $\lvert x\rvert\to\infty$.
\[
\boxed{Hf\text{ odd, }\lVert Hf\rVert_2^2=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) uses the opposite kernel $1/(y-x)$ and produces the negative logarithm. Sentence (ii) drops the principal value inside $(-1,1)$, where the integrand is not Lebesgue integrable. Sentence (iii) treats the logarithmic blow-up at $\pm 1$ as an $L^2$ obstruction, which it is not.

The argument never replaces the interval Hilbert transform by a distributional jump packet or by a diagonal singular kernel, and it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

The multiplier $-i\operatorname{sgn}$ gives $\lVert Hf\rVert_2^2=\lVert f\rVert_2^2=2$, and the endpoint logarithms remain square-integrable.
I use the opposite kernel 1/(y-x) and report Hf=-pi^{-1} log|(x+1)/(x-1)|, so Hf(2) is not log(3)/pi.
I drop the principal value inside (-1,1) and treat the integral as ordinary at every x, or I claim the log blow-up at x=+/-1 ejects Hf from L2 so that ||Hf||_2^2 is infinite rather than 2.

GRA:020322.title: A symmetric box average rounds the absolute-value cusp by exactly epsilon over two
GRA:020322.objective: For the symmetric box kernel rho_e=(2e)^{-1} 1_{[-e,e]} and u=|x|, prove that the convolution v=rho_e*u equals |x| for |x|>=e and (x^2+e^2)/(2e) for |x|<e, that sup(v-u)=e/2 is attained only at the origin, that v'=sign(x) outside and x/e inside, and that v is C^1 but not C^2 at +/-e. Distinguish this rounding of a cusp from seed-style step-function smoothing.
GRA:020322.statement:
Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and let
\[
\rho_\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\,1_{[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]},\qquad
u(x)=\lvert x\rvert,\qquad
v=\rho_\varepsilon*u.
\]
Thus
\[
v(x)=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\int_{x-\varepsilon}^{x+\varepsilon}\lvert t\rvert\,dt.
\]

1. Prove the piecewise formula
   \[
   v(x)=\begin{cases}
   \lvert x\rvert & \text{if }\lvert x\rvert\ge\varepsilon,\\
   \dfrac{x^2+\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon} & \text{if }\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon.
   \end{cases}
   \]

2. Prove $v\ge u$ everywhere, that
   \[
   \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl(v(x)-u(x)\bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
   \]
   and that the supremum is attained only at $x=0$.

3. Prove that $v$ is continuously differentiable,
   \[
   v'(x)=\begin{cases}
   \operatorname{sign}(x) & \text{if }\lvert x\rvert>\varepsilon,\\
   x/\varepsilon & \text{if }\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon,
   \end{cases}
   \]
   with matching one-sided derivatives $v'(\pm\varepsilon)=\pm 1$, yet
   $v''$ jumps from $0$ to $1/\varepsilon$ at $\pm\varepsilon$, so
   $v\in C^1(\mathbb{R})\setminus C^2(\mathbb{R})$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “box averaging a jump produces a
   linear ramp that is only Lipschitz, so $v$ fails to be $C^1$”;
   (ii) “the interior formula is $(\varepsilon^2-x^2)/(2\varepsilon)$
   or the overshoot is $\varepsilon$ rather than $\varepsilon/2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by seed-style Heaviside/step
smoothing, by an approximate-identity $L^\infty$ edge argument,
by the sibling $L^2$ tail truncation of this shard, or by a
weak-limit packet. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the
six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: If $x\ge\varepsilon$ then $[x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon]\subset[0,\infty)$, so $v(x)=(2\varepsilon)^{-1}\int_{x-\varepsilon}^{x+\varepsilon}t\,dt=x$. The case $x\le-\varepsilon$ is symmetric.

On $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ the fundamental theorem gives $v'(x)=(2\varepsilon)^{-1}\bigl(\lvert x+\varepsilon\rvert-\lvert x-\varepsilon\rvert\bigr)=x/\varepsilon$. Matching at the endpoints yields $C^1$ regularity; the second derivative then jumps.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the moving-average integral at the origin when the window meets both signs, and keep a single sign when it does not.
Differentiate the piecewise formula, match one-sided derivatives at +/-e, and read the second-derivative jump 1/e.

milestones.criterion: Derives v=|x| outside |x|>=e and v=(x^2+e^2)/(2e) inside, with sup(v-u)=e/2 only at the origin.
Proves v'=sign(x) outside and x/e inside, matching at +/-e, hence C^1 but not C^2.
Rejects seed-style step/Heaviside smoothing and refuses a wrong interior parabola or overshoot e.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the absolute-value cusp by a Heaviside jump and reports a Lipschitz ramp that fails to be C^1, as in seed-style step smoothing.
commonErrors.consequence: The required C^1 parabola (x^2+e^2)/(2e), the overshoot e/2, and the derivative x/e inside the window are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes the interior average as (e^2-x^2)/(2e) or claims the rounding height is e rather than e/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities v=(x^2+e^2)/(2e) and sup(v-u)=e/2 fail, and the matching derivative x/e is lost.

hintTree.content: Split the integral at the origin when $\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon$, and keep a single sign when $\lvert x\rvert\ge\varepsilon$.
On $[0,\varepsilon]$ the gap $v-u=(x^2+\varepsilon^2)/(2\varepsilon)-x$ has derivative $(x-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\le 0$, so the maximum is the value $\varepsilon/2$ at $x=0$.
Differentiate under the integral, or differentiate the piecewise formula and check the one-sided derivatives at $\pm\varepsilon$. The second derivative is $0$ outside and $1/\varepsilon$ inside.

GRA:020322.canonicalSolution:
Write
\[
v(x)=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\int_{x-\varepsilon}^{x+\varepsilon}\lvert t\rvert\,dt.
\]
If $x\ge\varepsilon$ then $x-\varepsilon\ge 0$, so the integrand is $t$ and
\[
v(x)=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\cdot\frac12\Bigl[(x+\varepsilon)^2-(x-\varepsilon)^2\Bigr]
=\frac{1}{4\varepsilon}\cdot 4x\varepsilon=x=\lvert x\rvert.
\]
If $x\le-\varepsilon$ then $x+\varepsilon\le 0$, so the integrand is $-t$ and
\[
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4\varepsilon}\Bigl[(x+\varepsilon)^2-(x-\varepsilon)^2\Bigr]=-x=\lvert x\rvert.
\]
If $\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon$ the window straddles the origin:
\[
v(x)=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\Biggl(\int_{x-\varepsilon}^{0}(-t)\,dt+\int_{0}^{x+\varepsilon}t\,dt\Biggr)
=\frac{1}{4\varepsilon}\Bigl[(x-\varepsilon)^2+(x+\varepsilon)^2\Bigr]
=\frac{x^2+\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon}.
\]
\[
\boxed{v=\lvert x\rvert\text{ for }\lvert x\rvert\ge\varepsilon,\quad
v=(x^2+\varepsilon^2)/(2\varepsilon)\text{ for }\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon}.
\]

Outside $\lvert x\rvert\ge\varepsilon$ one has $v-u=0$. Inside,
for $x\in[0,\varepsilon]$,
\[
f(x)=\frac{x^2+\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon}-x,\qquad
f'(x)=\frac{x}{\varepsilon}-1=\frac{x-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\le 0,
\]
so $f$ decreases from $f(0)=\varepsilon/2$ to $f(\varepsilon)=0$.
The even case $x\in[-\varepsilon,0]$ is identical. Thus $v\ge u$,
the supremum of $v-u$ is $\varepsilon/2$, and it is attained only
at the origin.
\[
\boxed{\sup(v-u)=\varepsilon/2\text{ at }x=0}.
\]

Differentiating the exterior formula gives $v'=\operatorname{sign}(x)$
for $\lvert x\rvert>\varepsilon$. Differentiating the interior formula
gives $v'=x/\varepsilon$ for $\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon$. The
one-sided derivatives at the interfaces are
\[
v'(\varepsilon-)=1=v'(\varepsilon+),\qquad
v'(-\varepsilon+)=-1=v'(-\varepsilon-),
\]
so $v\in C^1(\mathbb{R})$. The second derivative equals $0$ for
$\lvert x\rvert>\varepsilon$ and equals $1/\varepsilon$ for
$\lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon$, hence jumps at $\pm\varepsilon$.
Therefore $v\notin C^2(\mathbb{R})$.
\[
\boxed{v'=\operatorname{sign}(x)\text{ outside, }x/\varepsilon\text{ inside; }C^1\setminus C^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses the cusp $u=\lvert x\rvert$ with a jump
discontinuity. Box averaging a Heaviside step yields a Lipschitz
ramp that is not $C^1$; the present $u$ is already continuous, and
the average is $C^1$. Sentence (ii) replaces the interior
parabola by $(\varepsilon^2-x^2)/(2\varepsilon)$ or inflates the
overshoot from $\varepsilon/2$ to $\varepsilon$.

The argument never substitutes seed-style step smoothing, an
approximate-identity $L^\infty$ edge, the sibling $L^2$ tail
truncation, or a weak-limit packet, and it does not open any of
the six existing intake seeds.

Then $v-u$ has supremum $\varepsilon/2$ only at the origin, $v'=\operatorname{sign}(x)$ outside and $x/\varepsilon$ inside, and $v$ is $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at $\pm\varepsilon$. This is not Heaviside-step smoothing.
I treat u as a jump and report a Lipschitz ramp that is not C^1, as in seed-style step smoothing. I do not obtain the C^1 parabola (x^2+e^2)/(2e) or the overshoot e/2.
The interior formula is (e^2-x^2)/(2e) and the rounding height is e rather than e/2, so I do not accept v=(x^2+e^2)/(2e) or sup(v-u)=e/2.

GRA:020325.title: Compact truncation reaches an L2 tail at an exact rate while the same function never enters L1
GRA:020325.objective: For f=(1+x)^{-1} 1_{[0,infty)} and f_R=f 1_{[0,R]}, prove the total L2 square equals 1, the tail L2 square equals 1/(R+1), and the tail L2 norm at R=3 equals 1/2. Prove f is not in L1(0,infty). Record that truncation is only the first density step toward C_c^infty.
GRA:020325.statement:
On the half-line define
\[
f(x)=(1+x)^{-1}1_{[0,\infty)}(x),\qquad
f_R:=f\,1_{[0,R]},\qquad R>0.
\]

1. Prove the total $L^2$ square
   \[
   \lVert f\rVert_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2=\int_0^\infty(1+x)^{-2}\,dx=1.
   \]

2. Prove the exact tail rate
   \[
   \lVert f-f_R\rVert_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2=\int_R^\infty(1+x)^{-2}\,dx=\frac{1}{R+1}.
   \]
   In particular, at $R=3$ one has tail square $1/4$ and tail norm
   $1/2$.

3. Prove that $f\notin L^1(0,\infty)$, even though $f\in L^2(0,\infty)$.
   Thus compact truncation produces $L^2$ approximants that remain
   outside $L^1$ in the limit, and $L^2$ membership does not grant
   $L^1$ membership on an infinite interval.

4. Record that $f_R$ is compactly supported and bounded, but that
   truncation is only the first density step: reaching $C_c^\infty$
   still requires a subsequent mollification (not performed here).

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$f$ decays, or $f$ lies in $L^2$, so
   $f$ lies in $L^1(0,\infty)$”; (ii) “the tail $L^2$ square is
   $e^{-R}$ or $1/R^2$, so at $R=3$ the tail norm is not $1/2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a finite-versus-infinite-domain
$L^p$ inclusion lecture, by logarithmic moments, by monotone
truncation of a different profile, by the sibling box-mollified
cusp, or by a tightness/moment-bound packet. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The antiderivative of $(1+x)^{-2}$ is $-(1+x)^{-1}$. Evaluating from $0$ to $\infty$ gives total square $1$; evaluating from $R$ to $\infty$ gives tail square $1/(R+1)$.
The integral $\int_0^\infty(1+x)^{-1}\,dx$ diverges logarithmically, so $f\notin L^1(0,\infty)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the antiderivative -(1+x)^{-1} on [0,infty) and on [R,infty), then specialize R=3.
Contrast the logarithmic divergence of the L1 integral with the convergent p=2 integral.

milestones.criterion: Computes total L2 square 1 and the exact tail square 1/(R+1), hence tail norm 1/2 at R=3.
Proves f is not in L1(0,infty) and records that truncation is only the first density step.
Rejects an L1 membership claim and refuses a wrong tail rate e^{-R} or 1/R^2.

commonErrors.description: Claims f lies in L1(0,infty) because it lies in L2 or because it decays, importing a finite-measure inclusion onto the half-line.
commonErrors.consequence: The required witness f in L2\L1 and the diverging truncation norms log(1+R) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the tail L2 square 1/(R+1) by e^{-R} or 1/R^2, or misses the total square 1, so the R=3 tail norm is not 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required rate 1/(R+1) and the sample value 1/2 at R=3 fail.

hintTree.content: Compute $\int(1+x)^{-2}\,dx=-(1+x)^{-1}$ and evaluate the two limits.
At $R=3$ the tail square is $1/4$, so the tail $L^2$ norm is $1/2$.
Compare $\int_1^X x^{-1}\,dx=\log X\to\infty$ with the convergent $p=2$ integral. Truncation alone does not produce a test function.

GRA:020325.canonicalSolution:
The integrand $(1+x)^{-2}$ has antiderivative $-(1+x)^{-1}$, so
\[
\lVert f\rVert_{L^2(0,\infty)}^2
=\lim_{B\to\infty}\Bigl[-(1+x)^{-1}\Bigr]_0^B
=\lim_{B\to\infty}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{1+B}\Bigr)=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}^2=1}.
\]
The tail is supported on $[R,\infty)$:
\[
\lVert f-f_R\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\int_R^\infty(1+x)^{-2}\,dx
=\lim_{B\to\infty}\Bigl(\frac{1}{R+1}-\frac{1}{B+1}\Bigr)
=\frac{1}{R+1}.
\]
At $R=3$ the tail square is $1/4$ and the tail norm is $1/2$.
\[
\boxed{\lVert f-f_R\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/(R+1),\quad
\lVert f-f_3\rVert_{L^2}=1/2}.
\]

On the other hand
\[
\int_0^B(1+x)^{-1}\,dx=\log(1+B)\to\infty,
\]
so $f\notin L^1(0,\infty)$. Membership in $L^2$ on an infinite
interval does not imply membership in $L^1$. Each truncation
$f_R$ does lie in $L^1$, but the $L^1$ norms
$\lVert f_R\rVert_{L^1}=\log(1+R)$ diverge, so the $L^2$ limit
cannot be upgraded to an $L^1$ limit.
\[
\boxed{f\notin L^1(0,\infty)}.
\]

The functions $f_R$ are bounded and compactly supported, hence
lie in $L^2$. This is only the first density step toward
$C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$: a further cutoff near the origin and a
mollification are still required. Those later steps are not
performed here.

Sentence (i) imports the finite-measure inclusion $L^2\subset L^1$
onto the half-line, or treats decay of order $x^{-1}$ as integrable.
Sentence (ii) invents an exponential or $1/R^2$ tail and cannot
recover the sample value $1/2$ at $R=3$.

The argument never replaces the assigned tail ledger by a
finite-versus-infinite-domain $L^p$ lecture, by logarithmic
moments, by monotone truncation of another profile, by the
sibling box-mollified cusp, or by a tightness/moment packet, and
it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The profile $f=(1+x)^{-1}1_{[0,\infty)}$ has $\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}^2=1$ and tail $\lVert f-f_R\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/(R+1)$, hence tail norm $1/2$ at $R=3$. The same $f$ is not in $L^1(0,\infty)$. Truncation is only the first density step.
Because f lies in L2 and decays, I conclude that f lies in L1(0,infty). I import a finite-measure inclusion onto the half-line.
I take the tail L2 square to be e^{-R} or 1/R^2, so at R=3 the tail norm is not 1/2 and I do not accept the rate 1/(R+1).

GRA:020423.title: Weak convergence does not commute with squaring: sqrt(2) sin(2 pi n x) vanishes while its energy tends to one
GRA:020423.objective: On (0,1), set u_n=sqrt(2) sin(2 pi n x). Prove ||u_n||_L2=1 and u_n weak-L2 to 0, expand u_n^2=1-cos(4 pi n x), prove that u_n^2 converges weakly in L1 to the constant 1 against every L^infty test, and record integral u_n^2=1. Make no pointwise claim.
GRA:020423.statement:
On the unit interval $(0,1)$ define
\[
u_n(x)=\sqrt{2}\,\sin(2\pi n x),\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}.
\]

1. Prove $\lVert u_n\rVert_{L^2(0,1)}=1$. In particular
   $\int_0^1 u_n^2=1$ for every $n$.

2. Prove that $u_n\rightharpoonup 0$ weakly in $L^2(0,1)$: for every
   $v\in L^2(0,1)$,
   \[
   \int_0^1 u_n v\to 0.
   \]
   Do not claim that $u_n(x)\to 0$ at any particular $x$.

3. Expand
   \[
   u_n(x)^2=1-\cos(4\pi n x).
   \]
   Prove that $u_n^2\rightharpoonup 1$ weakly in $L^1(0,1)$ against
   every test $\varphi\in L^\infty(0,1)$:
   \[
   \int_0^1 u_n^2\varphi\to\int_0^1\varphi.
   \]
   Conclude that weak convergence does not commute with the map
   $w\mapsto w^2$, since the square of the weak $L^2$ limit is $0$
   while the weak $L^1$ limit of the squares is $1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$u_n(x)\to 0$ at every $x$, so the
   squares vanish pointwise and therefore weakly”; (ii) “because
   $u_n\rightharpoonup 0$ in $L^2$, one has $u_n^2\rightharpoonup 0$
   in $L^1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by Hilbert-space weak-versus-norm
convergence without a square, by a pushforward of squares, by
oscillatory signed variation, or by the sibling $x^n$ weak-star
packet. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.
permittedResults: The double-angle identity $2\sin^2\theta=1-\cos(2\theta)$ with $\theta=2\pi n x$ yields $u_n^2=1-\cos(4\pi n x)$ and $\int_0^1 u_n^2=1$.
Riemann–Lebesgue: if $g\in L^1(0,1)$ then $\int_0^1 g(x)\cos(4\pi n x)\,dx\to 0$. Taking $g=\varphi\in L^\infty\subset L^1$ on a finite interval gives the weak $L^1$ limit $1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand 2 sin^2 via the double-angle identity, then apply Riemann-Lebesgue to both the sine pairing and the cosine pairing.
Compare the square of the weak L2 limit (the zero function) with the weak L1 limit of the squares (the constant 1).

milestones.criterion: Proves ||u_n||_L2=1, expands u_n^2=1-cos(4 pi n x), and records integral u_n^2=1.
Proves u_n weak-L2 to 0 with no pointwise claim, and u_n^2 weak-L1 to 1 against L^infty tests.
Rejects a pointwise vanishing claim and refuses the assertion that squaring commutes with the weak limit.

commonErrors.description: Claims u_n(x) tends to 0 at every x, or uses a pointwise limit to pass the square inside, contrary to the no-pointwise-claim constraint.
commonErrors.consequence: The required weak-only argument is lost, and the squares are incorrectly declared to vanish.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that u_n weak-L2 to 0 implies u_n^2 weak-L1 to 0, so squaring is treated as weakly continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: The required weak L1 limit 1 and the identity integral u_n^2=1 are replaced by a false null limit.

hintTree.content: Expand $u_n^2=2\sin^2(2\pi n x)=1-\cos(4\pi n x)$ and integrate term by term on $(0,1)$.
Weak $L^2$ vanishing follows from Riemann–Lebesgue, or from orthonormality of $\{\sqrt{2}\sin(2\pi n x)\}$ against a fixed $L^2$ test.
Pair $u_n^2-1=-\cos(4\pi n x)$ against an $L^\infty$ test and apply Riemann–Lebesgue. The square of the weak limit is $0$, not $1$.

GRA:020423.canonicalSolution:
The double-angle identity gives
\[
u_n(x)^2=2\sin^2(2\pi n x)=1-\cos(4\pi n x).
\]
Integrating on $(0,1)$,
\[
\int_0^1 u_n^2=\int_0^1 1\,dx-\int_0^1\cos(4\pi n x)\,dx=1,
\]
so $\lVert u_n\rVert_{L^2(0,1)}=1$.
\[
\boxed{\lVert u_n\rVert_{L^2}=1,\qquad\int u_n^2=1}.
\]

Let $v\in L^2(0,1)$. Then $v\in L^1(0,1)$ on a finite interval, and
Riemann–Lebesgue yields
\[
\int_0^1 u_n v=\sqrt{2}\int_0^1 v(x)\sin(2\pi n x)\,dx\to 0.
\]
Thus $u_n\rightharpoonup 0$ in $L^2(0,1)$. No pointwise statement
is used: at $x=1/4$ one has $u_n(1/4)=\sqrt{2}\sin(n\pi/2)$, which
does not tend to $0$.
\[
\boxed{u_n\rightharpoonup 0\text{ in }L^2(0,1);\text{ no pointwise claim}}.
\]

Now fix $\varphi\in L^\infty(0,1)\subset L^1(0,1)$. Then
\[
\int_0^1 u_n^2\varphi=\int_0^1\varphi-\int_0^1\varphi(x)\cos(4\pi n x)\,dx.
\]
Riemann–Lebesgue sends the cosine integral to $0$, so
\[
u_n^2\rightharpoonup 1\quad\text{weakly in }L^1(0,1)
\]
against every $L^\infty$ test. The square of the weak $L^2$ limit
is $0^2=0$, which is not the weak $L^1$ limit of the squares.
\[
\boxed{u_n^2=1-\cos(4\pi n x)\rightharpoonup 1\text{ in }L^1;\text{ squaring does not commute}}.
\]

Sentence (i) invents a pointwise limit that the sequence does not
possess on a positive-measure set of phases, and then illegally
passes the square through that nonexistent limit. Sentence (ii)
assumes that $w\mapsto w^2$ is weakly continuous on $L^2$, which
the identity $\int u_n^2=1$ already forbids.

The argument never replaces the assigned oscillatory square by
Hilbert-space weak-versus-norm convergence without a square, by a
pushforward of squares, by oscillatory signed variation, or by
the sibling $x^n$ packet, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $(0,1)$, $u_n=\sqrt{2}\sin(2\pi n x)$ has $L^2$ norm $1$ and converges weakly in $L^2$ to $0$, with no pointwise claim. Then $u_n^2=1-\cos(4\pi n x)$ converges weakly in $L^1$ to $1$ against every $L^\infty$ test, and $\int u_n^2=1$. Squaring does not commute with the weak limit.
I claim u_n(x) tends to 0 at every x, so the squares vanish pointwise and therefore weakly. I make a pointwise claim that the problem forbids.
Because u_n converges weakly in L2 to 0, I conclude that u_n^2 converges weakly in L1 to 0. I treat squaring as commuting with the weak limit.

GRA:020426.title: The powers x^n are weak-star null in L-infinity while their supremum norm never moves
GRA:020426.objective: On [0,1], prove x^n converges weak-star to 0 in L^infty=(L1)* by dominated convergence, that ||x^n||_infty=1 for every n, that ||x^n||_p=(np+1)^{-1/p} tends to 0 for each finite p, and that the sample n=4, p=2 equals 1/3. Audit the point x=1 and the weak-star versus norm topologies.
GRA:020426.statement:
On the unit interval $[0,1]$ consider the sequence $u_n(x)=x^n$
for $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

1. View $L^\infty(0,1)$ as the dual of $L^1(0,1)$. Prove that
   $u_n\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}0$ in $L^\infty$: for every
   $g\in L^1(0,1)$,
   \[
   \int_0^1 x^n g(x)\,dx\to 0.
   \]
   Use dominated convergence with the integrable dominant $\lvert g\rvert$,
   together with the almost-everywhere limit $x^n\to 0$ on $[0,1)$.

2. Prove $\lVert u_n\rVert_{L^\infty(0,1)}=1$ for every $n$, so
   $u_n$ does not converge to $0$ in the $L^\infty$ norm. Record
   that the value $u_n(1)=1$ is a single point and does not
   obstruct the almost-everywhere or integral statements.

3. For each finite $p\in[1,\infty)$ prove
   \[
   \lVert u_n\rVert_{L^p(0,1)}=(np+1)^{-1/p}\to 0.
   \]
   Evaluate the sample $n=4$, $p=2$:
   \[
   \lVert x^4\rVert_{L^2(0,1)}=\frac13.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “because $u_n\to 0$ almost everywhere
   or weak-star, one has $\lVert u_n\rVert_\infty\to 0$”; (ii)
   “the persistent value $1$ at $x=1$ blocks weak-star nullity, or
   the $L^p$ formula is wrong so $n=4$, $p=2$ is not $1/3$.”

Do not replace the calculation by Hilbert-space weak-versus-norm
convergence, by the sibling oscillatory-square packet, by a
finite-versus-infinite-domain $L^p$ inclusion, or by a tightness
packet. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.
permittedResults: Dominated convergence: $x^n g(x)\to 0$ for almost every $x\in[0,1]$ and $\lvert x^n g(x)\rvert\le\lvert g(x)\rvert\in L^1$, so the integrals vanish.
The elementary integral $\int_0^1 x^{np}\,dx=1/(np+1)$ yields $\lVert x^n\rVert_p=(np+1)^{-1/p}$. At $n=4$, $p=2$ this is $9^{-1/2}=1/3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply dominated convergence to x^n g with dominant |g|, using x^n->0 almost everywhere on [0,1).
Evaluate int_0^1 x^{np}=1/(np+1) and specialize n=4, p=2 to lock 1/3, while reading the essential supremum from neighborhoods of 1.

milestones.criterion: Proves x^n weak-star to 0 in L^infty by dominated convergence, and ||x^n||_infty=1.
Computes ||x^n||_p=(np+1)^{-1/p} and the sample n=4, p=2 equal to 1/3, auditing x=1 as a null set.
Rejects confusing weak-star or a.e. convergence with the L^infty norm, and refuses a wrong Lp sample.

commonErrors.description: Claims ||x^n||_infty tends to 0 because of almost-everywhere or weak-star convergence, or claims the value 1 at x=1 blocks weak-star nullity.
commonErrors.consequence: The required split between weak-star nullity and a frozen supremum norm 1 is lost, or the null set {1} is misused.

commonErrors.description: Miscomputes ||x^n||_p, so the sample n=4, p=2 is not 1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity (np+1)^{-1/p} and the sample value 1/3 fail.

hintTree.content: On $[0,1)$ one has $x^n\to 0$. The endpoint $x=1$ is a null set. Dominate by $\lvert g\rvert$.
The essential supremum of $x^n$ on $[0,1]$ is $1$ for every $n$, attained on every left neighborhood of $1$.
Integrate $x^{np}$ to lock $(np+1)^{-1/p}$. The sample $n=4$, $p=2$ is $1/\sqrt{9}=1/3$.

GRA:020426.canonicalSolution:
Fix $g\in L^1(0,1)$. Pointwise, $x^n\to 0$ for every $x\in[0,1)$,
while the single point $x=1$ is a null set, so $x^n\to 0$
almost everywhere on $[0,1]$. Moreover
\[
\bigl\lvert x^n g(x)\bigr\rvert\le\lvert g(x)\rvert\in L^1(0,1).
\]
Dominated convergence therefore yields
\[
\int_0^1 x^n g(x)\,dx\to 0.
\]
Thus $u_n\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}0$ in $L^\infty(0,1)$.
\[
\boxed{x^n\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}0\text{ in }L^\infty=(L^1)^*}.
\]

On the other hand $0\le x^n\le 1$ and $x^n\ge 1/2$ on the interval
$[2^{-1/n},1]$ of positive measure, so
\[
\lVert u_n\rVert_{L^\infty(0,1)}=1
\]
for every $n$. In particular $u_n$ does not tend to $0$ in the
$L^\infty$ norm. The point value $u_n(1)=1$ is consistent with
this essential supremum, but as a single point it does not affect
the almost-everywhere limit or the dual pairing.
\[
\boxed{\lVert x^n\rVert_\infty=1;\text{ audit }x=1\text{ as a null set}}.
\]

For finite $p\in[1,\infty)$,
\[
\lVert x^n\rVert_{L^p}^p=\int_0^1 x^{np}\,dx=\frac{1}{np+1},
\]
hence
\[
\lVert x^n\rVert_{L^p}=(np+1)^{-1/p}\to 0.
\]
The sample $n=4$, $p=2$ is
\[
\lVert x^4\rVert_{L^2}=(8+1)^{-1/2}=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lVert x^n\rVert_p=(np+1)^{-1/p},\quad
\lVert x^4\rVert_{L^2}=1/3}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses the weak-star topology (and almost-everywhere
convergence) with the $L^\infty$ norm topology. Sentence (ii)
either treats the null set $\{1\}$ as an obstruction to weak-star
nullity, or miscomputes the $L^p$ integral so that $n=4$, $p=2$
fails to be $1/3$.

The argument never replaces the assigned $x^n$ ledger by
Hilbert-space weak-versus-norm convergence, by the sibling
oscillatory-square packet, by a finite-versus-infinite-domain
$L^p$ inclusion, or by a tightness packet, and it does not open
any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $[0,1]$, $x^n$ converges weak-star to $0$ in $L^\infty=(L^1)^*$ by dominated convergence, while $\lVert x^n\rVert_\infty=1$ for every $n$. The $L^p$ norm is $(np+1)^{-1/p}$, and at $n=4$, $p=2$ this is $1/3$. The point $x=1$ is a null set and does not block weak-star nullity.
Because x^n tends to 0 almost everywhere or weak-star, I conclude that ||x^n||_infty tends to 0. Alternatively I claim the value 1 at x=1 blocks weak-star nullity.
I miscompute the Lp norm of x^n, so at n=4, p=2 I do not obtain 1/3 and I do not accept (np+1)^{-1/p}.

GRA:020524.title: The polynomial x(1-x) passes the sharp Dirichlet Poincare inequality with quotient one tenth
GRA:020524.objective: For u=x(1-x) on (0,1), prove u belongs to H0^1, compute ||u||_L2^2=1/30 and ||u'||_L2^2=1/3, deduce the Rayleigh quotient 1/10, compare it with the sharp constant 1/pi^2, record max u=1/4, and prove that u is not an equality-case eigenfunction.
GRA:020524.statement:
Let $u(x)=x(1-x)$ on the unit interval $(0,1)$.

1. Record the boundary values $u(0)=u(1)=0$ and conclude that
   the absolutely continuous representative places $u$ in
   $H_0^1(0,1)$. Compute $u'=1-2x$.

2. Evaluate the two energies
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{L^2(0,1)}^2=\frac{1}{30},\qquad
   \lVert u'\rVert_{L^2(0,1)}^2=\frac13,
   \]
   and the Rayleigh quotient
   \[
   \frac{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2}{\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2}=\frac{1}{10}.
   \]

3. Recall that the sharp Dirichlet–Poincaré constant on $(0,1)$ is
   $1/\pi^2$, coming from the first eigenfunction $\sin(\pi x)$ of
   $-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$ with zero boundary values. Prove
   \[
   \frac{1}{10}<\frac{1}{\pi^2}
   \]
   and conclude that $u$ satisfies the sharp inequality strictly.
   Prove that $u$ is not a scalar multiple of $\sin(\pi x)$, hence
   not an equality-case eigenfunction.

4. Record $\max_{[0,1]}u=1/4$, attained at $x=1/2$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the quotient equals the sharp
   constant $1/\pi^2$, so $u$ is a first eigenfunction”; (ii)
   “$\int u^2=1/12$ or $\int(u')^2=1/2$, so the quotient is not
   $1/10$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a distributional jump detector,
by a weak-limit packet of this shard, or by a mollified-cusp
packet. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing
intake seeds.
permittedResults: Expand $u^2=x^2-2x^3+x^4$. Termwise integration yields $1/3-1/2+1/5=1/30$. Expand $(u')^2=(1-2x)^2=1-4x+4x^2$, which integrates to $1-2+4/3=1/3$.
Because $\pi^2<10$, one has $1/10<1/\pi^2$. A quadratic vanishing at $0$ and $1$ cannot be a multiple of $\sin(\pi x)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand u^2=x^2-2x^3+x^4 and (u')^2=1-4x+4x^2 and integrate term by term.
Compare the numerical quotient 1/10 with 1/pi^2 by the elementary bound pi^2<10, then rule out a sine profile.

milestones.criterion: Places u in H0^1 and computes ||u||_L2^2=1/30, ||u'||_L2^2=1/3, and quotient 1/10.
Compares 1/10<1/pi^2, records max u=1/4, and proves u is not an equality-case eigenfunction.
Rejects an equality-case or eigenfunction claim and refuses the wrong integrals 1/12 or 1/2.

commonErrors.description: Claims the Rayleigh quotient equals the sharp constant 1/pi^2, or identifies u with a multiple of sin(pi x).
commonErrors.consequence: The required strict inequality 1/10<1/pi^2 and the non-eigenfunction conclusion are lost.

commonErrors.description: Computes ||u||_L2^2 as 1/12 or ||u'||_L2^2 as 1/2, so the Rayleigh quotient is not 1/10.
commonErrors.consequence: The required ledger 1/30, 1/3, 1/10 is replaced by an incorrect quotient.

hintTree.content: Write $u=x-x^2$ and $u'=1-2x$. The endpoint values are visibly zero.
Integrate $x^2-2x^3+x^4$ and $1-4x+4x^2$ term by term to lock $1/30$ and $1/3$.
Compare $1/10$ with $1/\pi^2$ by checking $\pi^2<10$. The maximizer of $u$ is the vertex $x=1/2$.

GRA:020524.canonicalSolution:
The polynomial $u(x)=x-x^2$ is smooth on $[0,1]$ and satisfies
$u(0)=u(1)=0$, so its absolutely continuous representative lies in
$H_0^1(0,1)$. Differentiation gives $u'=1-2x$.

Now
\[
u(x)^2=x^2(1-x)^2=x^2-2x^3+x^4,
\]
\[
\int_0^1 u^2=\Bigl[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{2}+\frac{x^5}{5}\Bigr]_0^1
=\frac13-\frac12+\frac15=\frac{10-15+6}{30}=\frac{1}{30}.
\]
Next
\[
(u')^2=(1-2x)^2=1-4x+4x^2,
\]
\[
\int_0^1(u')^2=\Bigl[x-2x^2+\frac{4x^3}{3}\Bigr]_0^1=1-2+\frac43=\frac13.
\]
The Rayleigh quotient is therefore
\[
\frac{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2}{\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2}
=\frac{1/30}{1/3}=\frac{1}{10}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/30,\quad\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/3,\quad
\text{quotient }=1/10}.
\]

The first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$ on $(0,1)$ is
$\pi^2$, so the sharp Poincaré constant is $1/\pi^2$. Because
$\pi^2<10$, one has $1/10<1/\pi^2$. Thus $u$ satisfies
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\frac{1}{10}\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2
<\frac{1}{\pi^2}\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2
\]
strictly. Equality in the sharp inequality holds only on the span
of $\sin(\pi x)$. The function $u$ is a quadratic, hence not a
scalar multiple of $\sin(\pi x)$, and is not an equality-case
eigenfunction.
\[
\boxed{1/10<1/\pi^2;\ u\text{ is not an eigenfunction}}.
\]

Finally $u'(x)=0$ only at $x=1/2$, and $u(1/2)=1/4$, which is the
maximum on $[0,1]$.
\[
\boxed{\max u=1/4\text{ at }x=1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) inflates the quotient from $1/10$ to the sharp
constant and misidentifies a quadratic as $\sin(\pi x)$. Sentence
(ii) replaces $1/30$ by $1/12$ or $1/3$ by $1/2$ and loses the
quotient $1/10$.

The argument never replaces the assigned Poincaré ledger by a
distributional jump detector, by a weak-limit packet, or by the
sibling mollified-cusp packet, and it does not open any of the
six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The polynomial $u=x(1-x)$ lies in $H_0^1(0,1)$ with $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/30$ and $\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/3$, hence Rayleigh quotient $1/10$. Then $1/10<1/\pi^2$, $\max u=1/4$, and $u$ is not an equality-case eigenfunction.
I take the quotient to be the sharp constant 1/pi^2 and identify u with a multiple of sin(pi x), so I treat u as an equality-case eigenfunction.
I compute ||u||_L2^2=1/12 or ||u'||_L2^2=1/2, so the Rayleigh quotient is not 1/10.

GRA:020527.title: A translated delta derivative carries a testing minus sign, a Fourier multiplier, and a phase
GRA:020527.objective: For T=delta'_2-3 delta_{-1}, prove <T,phi>=-phi'(2)-3 phi(-1), compute the Fourier transform 2 pi i xi e^{-4 pi i xi}-3 e^{2 pi i xi} in the convention hat mu(xi)=<mu,e^{-2 pi i xi x}>, and evaluate hat T(0)=-3 and hat T(1/2)=3+pi i.
GRA:020527.statement:
Let $T=\delta'_2-3\delta_{-1}$ as a compactly supported distribution
on $\mathbb{R}$. Adopt the Fourier convention
\[
\widehat{\mu}(\xi)=\bigl\langle\mu,\,x\mapsto e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\bigr\rangle
\]
for compactly supported $\mu$, equivalently
$\widehat{f}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,dx$ on the
Schwartz class, so that $\widehat{\delta_a}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i a\xi}$ and
differentiation becomes the multiplier $2\pi i\xi$.

1. Prove the testing identity
   \[
   \langle T,\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)
   \]
   for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$.

2. Compute the Fourier transform as the continuous function
   \[
   \widehat{T}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi\,e^{-4\pi i\xi}-3e^{2\pi i\xi}.
   \]

3. Evaluate the two sample values
   \[
   \widehat{T}(0)=-3,\qquad \widehat{T}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)=3+\pi i.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the distributional derivative drops
   the testing minus sign, so $\langle T,\varphi\rangle=\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)$”;
   (ii) “the Fourier transform of $\delta'_2$ is $2\pi i\xi$ with
   no phase, or else carries the inverted phase $e^{+4\pi i\xi}$,
   so $\widehat{T}(1/2)$ is not $3+\pi i$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling fractional Sobolev
indicator, by the lacunary Fourier tail, or by either Wasserstein
packet of this shard. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the
six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Linearity of the distributional pairing gives $\langle\delta'_2-3\delta_{-1},\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)$ with no extra boundary terms.
The same convention yields $\widehat{T}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi e^{-2\pi i\cdot 2\cdot\xi}-3e^{-2\pi i\cdot(-1)\cdot\xi}=2\pi i\xi e^{-4\pi i\xi}-3e^{2\pi i\xi}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pair T against a test function first, then apply the convention hat delta_a=e^{-2 pi i a xi} and the multiplier 2 pi i xi termwise.
Evaluate the closed form at xi=0 and xi=1/2 by reducing the phases e^{-2 pi i}=1 and e^{pi i}=-1.

milestones.criterion: Derives the testing identity <T,phi>=-phi'(2)-3 phi(-1) from the distributional derivative of a translated Dirac mass.
Computes hat T(xi)=2 pi i xi e^{-4 pi i xi}-3 e^{2 pi i xi} and evaluates hat T(0)=-3 and hat T(1/2)=3+pi i.
Rejects a dropped testing minus sign and refuses a missing or inverted Fourier phase.

commonErrors.description: Drops the distributional minus sign and reports <T,phi>=phi'(2)-3 phi(-1) instead of -phi'(2)-3 phi(-1).
commonErrors.consequence: The pairing is wrong on every odd test function about x=2, and the later Fourier multiplier is then attached to the wrong signed source.

commonErrors.description: Computes the Fourier transform of delta'_2 as 2 pi i xi with no phase, or with the inverted phase e^{+4 pi i xi}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity hat T(1/2)=3+pi i fails, and hat T is not 2 pi i xi e^{-4 pi i xi}-3 e^{2 pi i xi}.

hintTree.content: Write $\langle\delta'_2,\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2)$ and $\langle\delta_{-1},\varphi\rangle=\varphi(-1)$. The coefficient $-3$ stays outside.
Apply $\widehat{\delta_a}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i a\xi}$ and the multiplier $2\pi i\xi$ to the two summands separately.
At $\xi=0$ the multiplier vanishes and the second term is $-3$. At $\xi=1/2$ one has $e^{-2\pi i}=1$ and $e^{\pi i}=-1$.

GRA:020527.canonicalSolution:
By definition of the distributional derivative and of a translated
Dirac mass,
\[
\langle\delta'_2,\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2),\qquad
\langle\delta_{-1},\varphi\rangle=\varphi(-1).
\]
Linearity therefore gives
\[
\langle T,\varphi\rangle=\langle\delta'_2,\varphi\rangle-3\langle\delta_{-1},\varphi\rangle
=-\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1).
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle T,\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)}.
\]

Under the assigned convention $\widehat{\delta_a}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i a\xi}$
and $\widehat{\partial_x\mu}=2\pi i\xi\,\widehat{\mu}$, one has
\[
\widehat{\delta'_2}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi\,e^{-2\pi i\cdot 2\cdot\xi}
=2\pi i\xi\,e^{-4\pi i\xi}
\]
and
\[
\widehat{\delta_{-1}}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i\cdot(-1)\cdot\xi}=e^{2\pi i\xi}.
\]
Subtracting three copies of the second identity produces
\[
\widehat{T}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi\,e^{-4\pi i\xi}-3e^{2\pi i\xi}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\widehat{T}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi e^{-4\pi i\xi}-3e^{2\pi i\xi}}.
\]

At $\xi=0$ the first summand vanishes and $e^{0}=1$, so
$\widehat{T}(0)=-3$. At $\xi=1/2$,
\[
2\pi i\cdot\tfrac12\cdot e^{-4\pi i\cdot(1/2)}-3e^{2\pi i\cdot(1/2)}
=\pi i\,e^{-2\pi i}-3e^{\pi i}.
\]
Since $e^{-2\pi i}=1$ and $e^{\pi i}=-1$, this equals
$\pi i-3(-1)=3+\pi i$.
\[
\boxed{\widehat{T}(0)=-3,\quad\widehat{T}(1/2)=3+\pi i}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the testing minus sign and reports
$\langle T,\varphi\rangle=\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)$. Sentence (ii)
either omits the phase $e^{-4\pi i\xi}$ or inverts it, and cannot
recover $\widehat{T}(1/2)=3+\pi i$.

The argument never replaces the assigned translated delta
derivative by the sibling fractional Sobolev indicator, by the
lacunary Fourier tail, or by a Wasserstein packet, and it does not
open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The pairing is $\langle T,\varphi\rangle=-\varphi'(2)-3\varphi(-1)$. Under $\widehat{\delta_a}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i a\xi}$ one has $\widehat{T}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi e^{-4\pi i\xi}-3e^{2\pi i\xi}$, hence $\widehat{T}(0)=-3$ and $\widehat{T}(1/2)=3+\pi i$. The testing minus sign is not dropped.
I drop the testing minus sign and take <T,phi>=phi'(2)-3 phi(-1). I do not report <T,phi>=-phi'(2)-3 phi(-1).
The Fourier transform of delta'_2 is 2 pi i xi with no phase, or else 2 pi i xi e^{+4 pi i xi}, so hat T(1/2) is not 3+pi i.

GRA:020528.title: An interval indicator belongs to fractional H^s exactly below one half, with a computable Gagliardo blow-up
GRA:020528.objective: For f=1_{(0,1)}, prove ||f||_{L^2}^2=1, evaluate the Gagliardo double-integral seminorm as 2/(s(1-2s)) for 0<s<1/2 (hence 16 at s=1/4), prove divergence for s>=1/2, and audit the symmetric factor together with the irrelevance of endpoint values.
GRA:020528.statement:
Let $f=1_{(0,1)}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Write
\[
[f]_{H^s(\mathbb{R})}^2
=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2}\frac{\lvert f(x)-f(y)\rvert^2}{\lvert x-y\rvert^{1+2s}}\,dx\,dy
\]
for $s\in(0,1)$, and $H^s(\mathbb{R})=L^2(\mathbb{R})\cap\dot H^s(\mathbb{R})$.

1. Prove $\lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2=1$.

2. For $0<s<1/2$, evaluate the Gagliardo integral exactly:
   \[
   [f]_{H^s(\mathbb{R})}^2=\frac{2}{s(1-2s)}.
   \]
   In particular the value at $s=1/4$ is $16$.

3. Prove that the same double integral diverges for every
   $s\ge 1/2$, so $f\in H^s(\mathbb{R})$ if and only if $s<1/2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the integrand is supported only on
   $x\in(0,1)$ and $y\notin(0,1)$, so the symmetric copy with
   $x$ and $y$ swapped may be dropped and the seminorm is
   $1/(s(1-2s))$”; (ii) “changing the values of $f$ at the two
   endpoints $0$ and $1$ changes the $L^2$ class or the Gagliardo
   integral, or else $f$ still belongs to $H^{1/2}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling translated delta
Fourier packet, by the lacunary Fourier tail, or by either
Wasserstein packet of this shard. Do not reopen, import, or
execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: For $x\in(0,1)$ one has $\int_{y\notin(0,1)}\lvert x-y\rvert^{-1-2s}\,dy=(2s)^{-1}\bigl(x^{-2s}+(1-x)^{-2s}\bigr)$ whenever $s>0$.
The elementary integral $\int_0^1 x^{-2s}\,dx$ converges if and only if $s<1/2$, and equals $(1-2s)^{-1}$ in that range.

acceptableStrategies.description: Exploit symmetry, integrate the inner tails at fixed x in (0,1), then evaluate int_0^1 x^{-2s} dx.
Read the critical exponent from the local integrability of x^{-2s} near a single jump, then specialise s=1/4.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates ||f||_L2^2=1 and the Gagliardo identity [f]_{H^s}^2=2/(s(1-2s)) for 0<s<1/2, including the value 16 at s=1/4.
Proves divergence for every s>=1/2, hence H^s membership if and only if s<1/2.
Rejects a dropped symmetric factor and refuses endpoint-value or H^{1/2} membership claims.

commonErrors.description: Drops the symmetric copy of the (x in, y out) region and reports the seminorm 1/(s(1-2s)) instead of 2/(s(1-2s)).
commonErrors.consequence: The required sample value 16 at s=1/4 is replaced by 8, and the exact identity is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that changing f at 0 and 1 alters the L2 or Gagliardo class, or claims that f still belongs to H^{1/2}.
commonErrors.consequence: Point values are treated as if they were L2-relevant, and the sharp threshold s<1/2 is lost.

hintTree.content: The $L^2$ square is the length of $(0,1)$. Endpoint modifications are invisible in Lebesgue integrals.
The integrand is symmetric. Compute $2\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus(0,1)}\lvert x-y\rvert^{-1-2s}\,dy\,dx$ and integrate the inner tails first.
After the inner integral one is left with $s^{-1}\int_0^1\bigl(x^{-2s}+(1-x)^{-2s}\bigr)\,dx=2/(s(1-2s))$ for $s<1/2$. At $s=1/4$ this is $16$.

GRA:020528.canonicalSolution:
The function $f$ equals $1$ on a set of measure $1$ and equals $0$
almost everywhere off that set, so
\[
\lVert f\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2=\int_0^1 1\,dx=1.
\]
Changing $f$ at the two endpoints $0$ and $1$ does not change the
Lebesgue class, nor any of the integrals below.
\[
\boxed{\lVert f\rVert_{L^2}^2=1}.
\]

The difference $\lvert f(x)-f(y)\rvert$ equals $1$ precisely when
exactly one of $x,y$ lies in $(0,1)$, and equals $0$ otherwise.
The double integral is therefore twice the contribution with
$x\in(0,1)$ and $y\notin(0,1)$:
\[
[f]_{H^s}^2
=2\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus(0,1)}\lvert x-y\rvert^{-1-2s}\,dy\,dx.
\]
For fixed $x\in(0,1)$ the inner integral splits into a left tail
and a right tail. The substitutions $u=x-y$ on $(-\infty,0)$ and
$v=y-x$ on $(1,\infty)$ give
\[
\int_{-\infty}^0(x-y)^{-1-2s}\,dy=\frac{x^{-2s}}{2s},\qquad
\int_1^\infty(y-x)^{-1-2s}\,dy=\frac{(1-x)^{-2s}}{2s},
\]
hence
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus(0,1)}\lvert x-y\rvert^{-1-2s}\,dy
=\frac{1}{2s}\bigl(x^{-2s}+(1-x)^{-2s}\bigr).
\]
The outer integral becomes
\[
[f]_{H^s}^2
=2\cdot\frac{1}{2s}\int_0^1\bigl(x^{-2s}+(1-x)^{-2s}\bigr)\,dx
=\frac{1}{s}\cdot 2\int_0^1 x^{-2s}\,dx.
\]
The remaining one-dimensional integral converges if and only if
$-2s>-1$, i.e. $s<1/2$, and then equals $(1-2s)^{-1}$. Therefore,
for $0<s<1/2$,
\[
[f]_{H^s(\mathbb{R})}^2=\frac{2}{s(1-2s)}.
\]
At $s=1/4$ one has $s(1-2s)=(1/4)(1/2)=1/8$, so the value is $16$.
\[
\boxed{[f]_{H^s}^2=2/(s(1-2s))\ \bigl(=16\text{ at }s=1/4\bigr)}.
\]

If $s\ge 1/2$ then $\int_0^1 x^{-2s}\,dx$ diverges at $0$ (and
the symmetric copy diverges at $1$). The Gagliardo integral is
therefore infinite, so $f\notin H^s(\mathbb{R})$ for $s\ge 1/2$.
Combined with the $L^2$ membership already established,
$f\in H^s(\mathbb{R})$ if and only if $0<s<1/2$ (and, for the
endpoint $s=0$, in the $L^2$ interpretation).
\[
\boxed{f\in H^s(\mathbb{R})\iff s<1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the symmetric factor $2$ and reports the false
value $1/(s(1-2s))$ (which would be $8$ rather than $16$ at
$s=1/4$). Sentence (ii) treats null endpoint values as if they
altered the $L^2$ or Gagliardo class, or else claims membership
at the critical index $s=1/2$.

The argument never replaces the assigned indicator by the sibling
translated-delta Fourier packet, by the lacunary Fourier tail, or
by a Wasserstein packet, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The $L^2$ square is $1$. Symmetry and the tail integrals give $[f]_{H^s}^2=2/(s(1-2s))$ for $0<s<1/2$, hence $16$ at $s=1/4$. The integral diverges for $s\ge 1/2$. Endpoint values of $f$ are irrelevant.
I drop the symmetric factor and take the Gagliardo seminorm to be 1/(s(1-2s)), so at s=1/4 I report 8 rather than 16.
Changing f at the endpoints 0 and 1 changes the L2 class, and f still belongs to H^{1/2}.

GRA:020529.title: A lacunary Fourier tail has unit L2 mass and dies at the H one-half endpoint
GRA:020529.objective: On T, for the complex series with only uhat(2^j)=2^{-j/2} for j>=1, prove the L2 square is 1, prove the H^s square sum_j (1+4 pi^2 4^j)^s 2^{-j} is finite iff s<1/2 with endpoint terms not tending to 0, and record that partial sums are smooth with L2 tail square 2^{-N}. Do not add negative frequencies.
GRA:020529.statement:
Let $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. Define a complex Fourier
series $u$ on $\mathbb{T}$ by declaring that the only nonzero
coefficients are
\[
\widehat{u}(2^j)=2^{-j/2},\qquad j=1,2,3,\dots
\]
viewed as complex numbers $2^{-j/2}+0i$, and $\widehat{u}(k)=0$
for every other $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Do not add the negative
frequencies $-2^j$. Adopt Plancherel
$\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{T})}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\lvert\widehat{u}(k)\rvert^2$
and the Sobolev square
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2
=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\bigl(1+4\pi^2 k^2\bigr)^s\lvert\widehat{u}(k)\rvert^2.
\]

1. Prove $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{T})}^2=1$.

2. Prove
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2
   =\sum_{j=1}^\infty\bigl(1+4\pi^2 4^j\bigr)^s 2^{-j},
   \]
   and that this sum is finite if and only if $s<1/2$. At the
   endpoint $s=1/2$, show that the general term does not tend to
   $0$ (its limit is $2\pi$).

3. Let $S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\widehat{u}(2^j)\,e^{2\pi i 2^j x}$. Prove
   that each $S_N$ is $C^\infty$ and that the $L^2$ tail satisfies
   \[
   \lVert u-S_N\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{T})}^2=2^{-N}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “reality of $u$ forces the conjugate
   frequencies $\widehat{u}(-2^j)=\overline{\widehat{u}(2^j)}$,
   which doubles the $L^2$ square to $2$”; (ii) “at $s=1/2$ the
   general term tends to $0$, or the multiplier is only
   $(1+k^2)^s$ without the factor $4\pi^2$, so $u\in H^{1/2}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling translated delta
Fourier packet, by the fractional Sobolev indicator, or by either
Wasserstein packet of this shard. Do not reopen, import, or
execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: Plancherel reduces both the $L^2$ square and every $H^s$ square to a numerical series over $j\ge 1$ with terms $2^{-j}$ and $(1+4\pi^2 4^j)^s 2^{-j}$ respectively.
The general term at regularity $s$ is asymptotic to $(4\pi^2)^s 2^{j(2s-1)}$. This is summable if and only if $2s-1<0$, and at $s=1/2$ the terms tend to $2\pi\neq 0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce both norms to geometric series on the positive dyadic frequencies and compare 2^{j(2s-1)} to 1.
Rewrite the s=1/2 term as sqrt(4^{-j}+4 pi^2) to see the limit 2 pi, then read the L2 tail as the leftover geometric sum.

milestones.criterion: Computes the L2 square 1 and the Hs square sum_j (1+4 pi^2 4^j)^s 2^{-j}, finite if and only if s<1/2.
Shows that s=1/2 terms tend to 2 pi rather than 0, and that ||u-S_N||_L2^2=2^{-N} with S_N smooth.
Rejects inserted negative frequencies and refuses H^{1/2} membership or a stripped multiplier.

commonErrors.description: Inserts the conjugate modes uhat(-2^j)=conjugate uhat(2^j) to force a real function, doubling the L2 square to 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned complex series is replaced by a different real series, and the unit L2 mass is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the s=1/2 general term tends to 0, or uses the stripped multiplier (1+k^2)^s, and concludes u lies in H^{1/2}.
commonErrors.consequence: The sharp threshold s<1/2 is lost, and the required identity with 4 pi^2 4^j is not obtained.

hintTree.content: Only the frequencies $k=2^j$ contribute. Each contributes $\lvert\widehat{u}(2^j)\rvert^2=2^{-j}$, and $\sum_{j\ge 1}2^{-j}=1$.
Replace $k^2$ by $4^j$. Compare the general term to $2^{j(2s-1)}$. At $s=1/2$ rewrite the term as $\sqrt{4^{-j}+4\pi^2}$.
Each $S_N$ is a trigonometric polynomial. The tail square is the remaining geometric series $\sum_{j>N}2^{-j}=2^{-N}$.

GRA:020529.canonicalSolution:
The only nonzero Plancherel atoms are $\lvert\widehat{u}(2^j)\rvert^2=2^{-j}$
for $j\ge 1$. The geometric series $\sum_{j=1}^\infty 2^{-j}=1$ therefore
gives
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{T})}^2=1.
\]
No negative frequency is present, and none is added.
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1}.
\]

The Sobolev square collapses to the same support:
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2
=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\bigl(1+4\pi^2(2^j)^2\bigr)^s 2^{-j}
=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\bigl(1+4\pi^2 4^j\bigr)^s 2^{-j}.
\]
For large $j$ one has $1+4\pi^2 4^j\sim 4\pi^2 4^j$, hence
\[
\bigl(1+4\pi^2 4^j\bigr)^s 2^{-j}
\sim(4\pi^2)^s 4^{js}2^{-j}
=(4\pi^2)^s 2^{2js-j}
=(4\pi^2)^s 2^{j(2s-1)}.
\]
The comparison series $\sum 2^{j(2s-1)}$ converges if and only if
$2s-1<0$, i.e. $s<1/2$. Thus $u\in H^s(\mathbb{T})$ if and only if
$s<1/2$.

At the endpoint $s=1/2$ the same rewriting gives
\[
\bigl(1+4\pi^2 4^j\bigr)^{1/2}2^{-j}
=\sqrt{4^{-j}+4\pi^2}\longrightarrow 2\pi\neq 0.
\]
The general term does not tend to $0$, so the $H^{1/2}$ series
diverges for the additional reason that its terms fail the term
test.
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{H^s}^2=\sum_j(1+4\pi^2 4^j)^s 2^{-j}<\infty\iff s<1/2}.
\]

Each partial sum $S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N 2^{-j/2}e^{2\pi i 2^j x}$ is a
trigonometric polynomial, hence $C^\infty(\mathbb{T})$. The $L^2$
tail is the remainder of the same geometric series:
\[
\lVert u-S_N\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\sum_{j=N+1}^\infty 2^{-j}=2^{-N}.
\]
\[
\boxed{S_N\in C^\infty,\quad\lVert u-S_N\rVert_{L^2}^2=2^{-N}}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces a real-valued representative by adding the
negative frequencies and doubles the $L^2$ square. Sentence (ii)
either claims that the $s=1/2$ terms vanish or replaces the
multiplier $1+4\pi^2 k^2$ by $1+k^2$, and then falsely places $u$
in $H^{1/2}$.

The argument never replaces the assigned lacunary tail by the
sibling translated-delta Fourier packet, by the fractional Sobolev
indicator, or by a Wasserstein packet, and it does not open any of
the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: Only the positive coefficients $\widehat{u}(2^j)=2^{-j/2}$ are used, so $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1$ and $\lVert u\rVert_{H^s}^2=\sum_j(1+4\pi^2 4^j)^s 2^{-j}$ is finite iff $s<1/2$. At $s=1/2$ the terms tend to $2\pi\neq 0$. Each $S_N$ is smooth and $\lVert u-S_N\rVert_{L^2}^2=2^{-N}$. Negative frequencies are not added.
I add the negative frequencies uhat(-2^j)=conjugate uhat(2^j) to make u real, so the L2 square becomes 2 rather than 1.
At s=1/2 the general term tends to 0, or the multiplier is only (1+k^2)^s, so u belongs to H^{1/2}.

GRA:020630.title: Vanishing escaping mass converges weakly but stays exactly one unit away in Wasserstein one
GRA:020630.objective: For mu_n=(1-1/n) delta_0+(1/n) delta_n, prove weak convergence to delta_0 with bounded-continuous error at most 2 ||phi||_inf/n, compute first absolute moment 1, W_1(mu_n,delta_0)=1, and second moment n, and show tightness holds while |x| is not uniformly integrable with tail supremum 1.
GRA:020630.statement:
On $\mathbb{R}$ let
\[
\mu_n=\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr)\delta_0+\frac1n\delta_n,\qquad n\ge 1,
\]
and let $\delta_0$ be Dirac mass at the origin.

1. Prove that $\mu_n\to\delta_0$ weakly: for every bounded
   continuous $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$,
   \[
   \biggl\lvert\int\varphi\,d\mu_n-\varphi(0)\biggr\rvert
   \le\frac{2\lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty}{n}.
   \]

2. Compute the first absolute moment, the Wasserstein-$1$ distance
   to $\delta_0$, and the second moment:
   \[
   \int\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=1,\qquad
   W_1(\mu_n,\delta_0)=1,\qquad
   \int x^2\,d\mu_n=n.
   \]

3. Prove that $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ is tight, but that the family
   $\{\lvert x\rvert\}$ is not uniformly integrable for
   $\{\mu_n\}$: the tail supremum equals $1$,
   \[
   \lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\int_{\lvert x\rvert>R}\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=1.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “weak convergence to $\delta_0$
   forces $W_1(\mu_n,\delta_0)\to 0$”; (ii) “the escaping atom
   of mass $1/n$ at position $n$ destroys tightness, or else
   $\lvert x\rvert$ is uniformly integrable because the first
   moments stay equal to $1$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling empirical uniform
Wasserstein rate, or by any distributions-and-Sobolev packet of
this shard. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the six
existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The pairing identity $\int\varphi\,d\mu_n-\varphi(0)=n^{-1}(\varphi(n)-\varphi(0))$ yields the bound $2\lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty/n$ and therefore weak convergence to $\delta_0$.

Prokhorov's theorem on $\mathbb{R}$ makes tightness equivalent to $\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)=0$. Uniform integrability of $\lvert x\rvert$ is a strictly stronger moment condition.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the pairing against a bounded continuous test function, then evaluate moments on the single escaping atom.
Compare the Prokhorov tails mu_n(|x|>R)=1/n with the cost tails int_{|x|>R}|x| d mu_n=1.

milestones.criterion: Proves weak convergence mu_n->delta_0 with the bound 2 ||phi||_inf/n, and computes first moment 1, W_1=1, and second moment n.
Establishes tightness together with the failure of uniform integrability of |x| and the tail supremum 1.
Rejects identifying weak convergence with W_1 convergence and refuses a tightness or UI misdiagnosis.

commonErrors.description: Infers from mu_n -> delta_0 weakly that W_1(mu_n,delta_0) tends to 0.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact identity W_1=1 is lost, and weak convergence is treated as if it controlled first-moment transport.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the escaping atom destroys tightness, or that bounded first moments make |x| uniformly integrable.
commonErrors.consequence: Either a tight sequence is declared non-tight, or the tail supremum 1 is replaced by 0.

hintTree.content: Expand $\int\varphi\,d\mu_n=(1-1/n)\varphi(0)+(1/n)\varphi(n)$ and subtract $\varphi(0)$.
The only contribution to $\int\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n$ and to $W_1(\mu_n,\delta_0)$ is the atom of mass $1/n$ at position $n$. The second moment is $(1/n)n^2=n$.
For tightness, $\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)=1/n$ once $n>R$, which tends to $0$ uniformly in large $n$. For uniform integrability the same tail carries cost $1$.

GRA:020630.canonicalSolution:
For a bounded continuous test function $\varphi$,
\[
\int\varphi\,d\mu_n=\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr)\varphi(0)+\frac1n\varphi(n),
\]
hence
\[
\int\varphi\,d\mu_n-\varphi(0)=\frac1n\bigl(\varphi(n)-\varphi(0)\bigr).
\]
The right-hand side is at most $2\lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty/n$ in
absolute value, and therefore tends to $0$. This is weak
convergence $\mu_n\to\delta_0$.
\[
\boxed{\lvert\int\varphi\,d\mu_n-\varphi(0)\rvert\le 2\lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty/n}.
\]

The first absolute moment is carried entirely by the escaping atom:
\[
\int\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=\frac1n\cdot n=1.
\]
The same computation is the explicit formula for Wasserstein-one
distance to a Dirac mass,
\[
W_1(\mu_n,\delta_0)=\int\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=1.
\]
The second moment is
\[
\int x^2\,d\mu_n=\frac1n\cdot n^2=n.
\]
\[
\boxed{\int\lvert x\rvert=1,\quad W_1=1,\quad\int x^2=n}.
\]

For tightness, fix $R>0$. If $n\le R$ then the support of $\mu_n$
is contained in $[0,R]$, so $\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)=0$. If $n>R$
then $\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)=1/n$. In all cases
$\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)\le 1/\lfloor R\rfloor$ for $R\ge 1$, hence
\[
\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mu_n(\lvert x\rvert>R)=0.
\]
The sequence is tight. Nevertheless $\lvert x\rvert$ is not
uniformly integrable: for any $R>0$ and any integer $n>R$,
\[
\int_{\lvert x\rvert>R}\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=\frac1n\cdot n=1,
\]
so
\[
\sup_n\int_{\lvert x\rvert>R}\lvert x\rvert\,d\mu_n=1
\]
and the limit as $R\to\infty$ remains $1$.
\[
\boxed{\text{tight, but }\lvert x\rvert\text{ not UI; tail supremum }=1}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses weak convergence with $W_1$ convergence and
would force the false limit $W_1\to 0$. Sentence (ii) either
denies tightness or infers uniform integrability from the mere
boundedness of first moments.

The argument never replaces the assigned escaping-mass sequence by
the sibling empirical uniform packet or by a
distributions-and-Sobolev packet, and it does not open any of the
six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The pairing error is at most $2\lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty/n$, so $\mu_n\to\delta_0$ weakly. The escaping atom gives $\int\lvert x\rvert=1$, $W_1(\mu_n,\delta_0)=1$, and $\int x^2=n$. The sequence is tight, but $\lvert x\rvert$ is not uniformly integrable and the tail supremum equals $1$. Weak convergence does not force $W_1\to 0$.
Because mu_n converges weakly to delta_0, I conclude W_1(mu_n,delta_0) tends to 0 rather than remaining equal to 1.
The atom of mass 1/n at position n destroys tightness, or else |x| is uniformly integrable because the first moments stay equal to 1.

GRA:020631.title: Right-endpoint empirical mass approximates the uniform law at exact Wasserstein rate one over two n
GRA:020631.objective: For nu_n=n^{-1} sum_{k=1}^n delta_{k/n}, prove W_1(nu_n,Unif[0,1])=1/(2n), compute the mean (n+1)/(2n), certify the gap by the Lipschitz test function x, evaluate the n=4 value 1/8, deduce weak convergence, and audit a right-endpoint off-by-one.
GRA:020631.statement:
Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, viewed as the
uniform law $\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$. For each integer $n\ge 1$ define
the right-endpoint empirical grid
\[
\nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\delta_{k/n}.
\]
The atoms are $1/n,2/n,\dots,1$; the left endpoint $0$ is not an
atom.

1. Prove the exact Wasserstein-one identity
   \[
   W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)=\frac{1}{2n}.
   \]

2. Compute the mean
   \[
   \int x\,d\nu_n=\frac{n+1}{2n}
   \]
   and observe that the $1$-Lipschitz test function $\varphi(x)=x$
   certifies
   \[
   W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)
   \ge\biggl\lvert\int x\,d\nu_n-\int x\,d\lambda\biggr\rvert
   =\frac{1}{2n},
   \]
   hence is optimal. Evaluate the sample $n=4$ as $W_1=1/8$.

3. Deduce that $\nu_n\to\lambda$ weakly.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the grid is the left-endpoint
   selection $\{0,1/n,\dots,(n-1)/n\}$, or else the off-by-one
   selection $\{0,1/n,\dots,1\}$ with $n+1$ atoms, so the mean
   is not $(n+1)/(2n)$ and $W_1$ is not $1/(2n)$”; (ii) “the
   mesh size is $1/n$, so $W_1=1/n$ (and the $n=4$ value is
   $1/4$ rather than $1/8$).”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling escaping-mass
weak-versus-$W_1$ packet, or by any distributions-and-Sobolev
packet of this shard. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of
the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual gives $W_1(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\mathrm{Lip}\le 1}\bigl(\int\varphi\,d\mu-\int\varphi\,d\nu\bigr)$. The coordinate function $\varphi(x)=x$ is admissible and produces the mean gap $1/(2n)$.
On each bin $[k/n,(k+1)/n)$ the right-endpoint CDF is the constant $k/n$ (with the convention that the CDF vanishes on $[0,1/n)$), and each bin contributes $1/(2n^2)$ to the $L^1$ gap.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate |G_n-x| bin by bin on the n right-endpoint intervals, each contributing 1/(2n^2).
Compute the mean gap 1/(2n) first and invoke Kantorovich–Rubinstein with phi(x)=x to see that the rate is already optimal.

milestones.criterion: Identifies the right-endpoint grid and proves W_1=1/(2n) together with the mean (n+1)/(2n).
Certifies the gap by the Lipschitz test x, evaluates the n=4 value 1/8, and deduces weak convergence.
Rejects a right-endpoint off-by-one and refuses the mesh-size claim W_1=1/n.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the assigned atoms {1/n,...,1} by the left-endpoint grid {0,...,(n-1)/n} or by the n+1-atomic grid {0,1/n,...,1}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required mean (n+1)/(2n) is lost, and the measure is no longer the assigned right-endpoint empirical law.

commonErrors.description: Reports W_1 as the mesh size 1/n rather than 1/(2n), so the n=4 value becomes 1/4 instead of 1/8.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact rate 1/(2n) and the matching Lipschitz certificate are both lost.

hintTree.content: The mean is $n^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^n k=(n+1)/(2n)$. Subtract the uniform mean $1/2$ to obtain $1/(2n)$.
Integrate $\lvert F_{\nu_n}(x)-x\rvert$ bin by bin: on $[0,1/n)$ the CDF is $0$, and on $[k/n,(k+1)/n)$ it equals $k/n\le x$. Each of the $n$ bins contributes $1/(2n^2)$.
The Lipschitz test $x$ matches the integral computation, so the rate $1/(2n)$ is exact. At $n=4$ this is $1/8$.

GRA:020631.canonicalSolution:
The mean of the right-endpoint grid is
\[
\int x\,d\nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\frac kn=\frac1{n^2}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
=\frac{n+1}{2n}.
\]
The uniform mean is $1/2$, so
\[
\biggl\lvert\int x\,d\nu_n-\int x\,d\lambda\biggr\rvert
=\biggl\lvert\frac{n+1}{2n}-\frac12\biggr\rvert=\frac{1}{2n}.
\]
The test function $\varphi(x)=x$ is $1$-Lipschitz, therefore
\[
W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)\ge\frac{1}{2n}.
\]

For the matching upper bound, write $F$ for the uniform CDF
$F(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ and $G_n$ for the CDF of $\nu_n$. Then
$G_n(x)=0$ on $[0,1/n)$ and $G_n(x)=k/n$ on
$[k/n,(k+1)/n)$ for $k=1,\dots,n-1$, with $G_n(1)=1$. On
$[0,1/n)$ one has $\lvert G_n-x\rvert=x$ and
\[
\int_0^{1/n}x\,dx=\frac{1}{2n^2}.
\]
On each subsequent bin $[k/n,(k+1)/n)$ one has $x\ge k/n=G_n(x)$,
so $\lvert G_n-x\rvert=x-k/n$ and
\[
\int_{k/n}^{(k+1)/n}\bigl(x-k/n\bigr)\,dx=\int_0^{1/n}u\,du=\frac{1}{2n^2}.
\]
There are $n$ such bins in total, hence
\[
W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)=\int_0^1\lvert G_n-x\rvert\,dx=n\cdot\frac{1}{2n^2}=\frac{1}{2n}.
\]
The Lipschitz lower bound is therefore sharp. At $n=4$ the
distance is $1/8$.
\[
\boxed{W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)=1/(2n),\quad\int x\,d\nu_n=(n+1)/(2n),\quad W_1|_{n=4}=1/8}.
\]

Since $W_1(\nu_n,\lambda)\to 0$, one has $\nu_n\to\lambda$ weakly.
\[
\boxed{\nu_n\to\lambda\text{ weakly}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the assigned right-endpoint $n$-atomic grid
by a left-endpoint grid or by an $(n+1)$-atomic off-by-one grid,
and then loses the mean $(n+1)/(2n)$. Sentence (ii) reports the
mesh size $1/n$ as if it were the $W_1$ distance and would give
the false sample $1/4$ at $n=4$.

The argument never replaces the assigned empirical grid by the
sibling escaping-mass packet or by a distributions-and-Sobolev
packet, and it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: The atoms are $k/n$ for $k=1,\dots,n$. Binwise integration of $\lvert G_n-x\rvert$ gives $W_1=1/(2n)$, the mean is $(n+1)/(2n)$, and $\varphi(x)=x$ is optimal. At $n=4$ one has $W_1=1/8$, hence weak convergence to $\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$. This is not a left-endpoint or $(n+1)$-atomic grid.
I take the left-endpoint grid {0,1/n,...,(n-1)/n} or the n+1-atomic grid {0,1/n,...,1}, so the mean is not (n+1)/(2n) and I do not accept the assigned right-endpoint law.
The mesh size is 1/n, so W_1=1/n and the n=4 value is 1/4 rather than 1/8.

GSM:010117.title: Six cells 3A+3B, K=#A in left three: counts[1,9,9,1]/20, mean 3/2, var 9/20, segregation 1/10, DeltaS/kB=ln20, identical control 0
GSM:010117.objective: On six labeled cells holding three A and three B, let K be the number of A in the left three cells. Recover the hypergeometric counts [1,9,9,1]/20, the mean 3/2 and variance 9/20, the perfect-segregation probability 1/10, the mixing increment Delta S/kB=ln 20, and the identical-species control 0.
GSM:010117.statement:
Six distinguishable cells are partitioned into a left block of
three and a right block of three. Three indistinguishable particles
of species $A$ and three of species $B$ occupy the cells with
exactly one particle per cell. Let $K$ be the number of $A$
particles in the left block.

1. Count the microstates by the value of $K\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and
   prove that the un-normalized counts are $[1,9,9,1]$ on a total
   of $20$ equally likely placements, so
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(K=k)
   =\frac{1}{20}\binom{3}{k}\binom{3}{3-k},
   \qquad
   \bigl(\mathbb{P}(K=0),\mathbb{P}(K=1),\mathbb{P}(K=2),\mathbb{P}(K=3)\bigr)
   =\Bigl(\tfrac1{20},\tfrac9{20},\tfrac9{20},\tfrac1{20}\Bigr).
   \]

2. Compute the first two moments and prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[K]=\frac32,\qquad
   \mathrm{Var}(K)=\frac9{20}.
   \]

3. Perfect segregation means every $A$ occupies one block and every
   $B$ the other (either orientation). Prove that this event has
   probability $1/10$. Taking the mixed counting entropy
   $S=k_B\ln 20$ relative to a single reference placement, prove
   \[
   \frac{\Delta S}{k_B}=\ln 20.
   \]
   If the two species are identical, the $20$ colorings collapse to
   one occupancy, and the mixing increment is $0$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “each of the four values of $K$ is
   equally likely, or $K$ is binomial with parameters $3$ and
   $1/2$, so the variance is $3/4$”; (ii) “identical species still
   contribute $\Delta S/k_B=\ln 20$, or this is an
   ensemble-equivalence / convex-entropy-intruder exercise.”

Do not replace the hypergeometric count by a supporting-line
ensemble-equivalence argument, and do not treat $A$ and $B$ as
thermodynamic phases.
permittedResults: $\binom{6}{3}=20$ and $\binom{3}{k}\binom{3}{3-k}$ equals $1,9,9,1$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The first two moments of this law are $\mathbb{E}[K]=3/2$ and $\mathbb{E}[K^2]=27/10$.
Perfect segregation is the event $\{K=0\}\cup\{K=3\}$, of probability $2/20=1/10$. For identical species, $W=1$ and $\Delta S=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Enumerate the 3-subsets by how many chosen cells lie in the left block, then compute the first two moments from the four counts.
Identify perfect segregation with the two extreme counts K=0 and K=3, and collapse W from 20 to 1 when the species labels are erased.

milestones.criterion: Recovers the hypergeometric counts [1,9,9,1] on 20 placements and the moments E[K]=3/2, Var(K)=9/20.
Records the segregation probability 1/10, the increment Delta S/kB=ln 20, and the identical-species control 0.
Refuses a binomial/uniform substitute for K and does not replace the count by an ensemble-equivalence exercise.

commonErrors.description: Treats K as uniform on {0,1,2,3} or as Bin(3,1/2), or reports Var(K)=3/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The hypergeometric counts [1,9,9,1]/20 and the variance 9/20 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that identical species still give Delta S/kB=ln 20, or replaces the increment by an ensemble-equivalence supporting line.
commonErrors.consequence: The identical-species control 0, or the finite coloring interpretation of ln 20, is erased.

hintTree.content: The number of ways to put $k$ of the three $A$'s into the left block is $\binom{3}{k}\binom{3}{3-k}$. Summing $k=0$ to $3$ recovers $\binom{6}{3}=20$.
The two fully segregated colorings are $K=0$ and $K=3$. If $A$ and $B$ are the same species there is only one occupancy.

GSM:010117.canonicalSolution:
The sample space consists of the $\binom{6}{3}=20$ ways to choose
the three cells occupied by $A$. For $K=k$ one must choose $k$ of
the three left cells and the remaining $3-k$ of the three right
cells, which can be done in
\[
\binom{3}{k}\binom{3}{3-k}
\]
ways. Explicitly,
\[
k=0:\ 1,\qquad
k=1:\ 3\cdot 3=9,\qquad
k=2:\ 3\cdot 3=9,\qquad
k=3:\ 1.
\]
The counts are therefore $[1,9,9,1]$ on a total of $20$, and
\[
\mathbb{P}(K=k)
=\frac1{20}\binom{3}{k}\binom{3}{3-k}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{counts }[1,9,9,1]/20}.
\]

The mean is
\[
\mathbb{E}[K]
=\frac{0\cdot1+1\cdot9+2\cdot9+3\cdot1}{20}
=\frac{30}{20}
=\frac32.
\]
The second moment is
\[
\mathbb{E}[K^2]
=\frac{0\cdot1+1\cdot9+4\cdot9+9\cdot1}{20}
=\frac{54}{20}
=\frac{27}{10},
\]
so
\[
\mathrm{Var}(K)
=\frac{27}{10}-\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2
=\frac{54}{20}-\frac{45}{20}
=\frac9{20}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[K]=3/2,\quad\mathrm{Var}(K)=9/20}.
\]

Perfect segregation in either orientation is $\{K=0\}\cup\{K=3\}$,
of probability
\[
\frac{1+1}{20}=\frac1{10}.
\]
The mixed counting entropy relative to one reference placement is
$S=k_B\ln 20$, hence $\Delta S/k_B=\ln 20$. If the species labels
are identical, the twenty colorings are a single occupancy and the
mixing increment is $0$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{segregation})=1/10,\quad\Delta S/k_B=\ln 20,\quad\text{identical control }0}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the hypergeometric law by a uniform law on
four values or by a $\mathrm{Bin}(3,1/2)$ count, both of which
produce the false variance $3/4$ (or $5/4$). Sentence (ii) retains
$\ln 20$ after the species labels are erased, or else replaces the
finite coloring count by an ensemble-equivalence / convex-entropy
supporting-line argument, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a thermodynamic potential, never
draws a supporting line to a convex entropy, and never treats the
two blocks as coexisting phases.

graderFixtures.proofText: Hypergeometric counts $[1,9,9,1]/20$, $\mathbb{E}[K]=3/2$, $\mathrm{Var}(K)=9/20$. Perfect segregation (either orientation) has probability $1/10$. Mixed increment $\Delta S/k_B=\ln 20$; identical-species control $0$.
Each of the four values of K is equally likely, or K is binomial with n=3 and p=1/2, so I report Var(K)=3/4 instead of 9/20.
Even if A and B are identical I keep Delta S/kB=ln 20, or I replace the coloring count by an ensemble-equivalence supporting-line argument.

GSM:010118.title: Three-level maxent E=0,eps,2eps, mean 4eps/7: q=1/2 from 10q^2+3q-4=0, p=(4/7,2/7,1/7), beta eps=ln2, H=ln7-(10/7)ln2
GSM:010118.objective: Maximize Shannon entropy on the three-level spectrum {0,eps,2eps} at mean energy 4eps/7. Prove that the positive Boltzmann factor q=e^{-beta eps} is the positive root of 10q^2+3q-4=0, hence q=1/2, recover p=(4/7,2/7,1/7), beta eps=ln 2, and H=ln7-(10/7)ln2, and invoke strict concavity for uniqueness.
GSM:010118.statement:
A single classical degree of freedom has the three-level spectrum
$\{0,\varepsilon,2\varepsilon\}$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Occupations
$p=(p_0,p_1,p_2)$ are required to satisfy
\[
p_0+p_1+p_2=1,\qquad
\varepsilon p_1+2\varepsilon p_2=\frac{4\varepsilon}{7},
\]
and the Shannon entropy $H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\ln p_i$ is to be
maximized.

1. Write the Boltzmann ansatz $p_i\propto e^{-\beta E_i}$ and set
   $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$. Prove that the mean-energy constraint
   is equivalent to
   \[
   10q^2+3q-4=0,
   \]
   and that the unique root in $(0,1)$ is $q=1/2$.

2. Recover the normalized occupation and the inverse temperature,
   \[
   p=\Bigl(\frac47,\frac27,\frac17\Bigr),\qquad
   \beta\varepsilon=\ln 2.
   \]

3. Evaluate the attained entropy and prove
   \[
   H=\ln 7-\frac{10}{7}\ln 2
   =0.9556998911125342.
   \]
   Using strict concavity of $H$ on the probability simplex, deduce
   that this maximizer is unique.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the quadratic also admits the
   negative root, or one may take a uniform occupation, or
   $p\propto 1/E$”; (ii) “$H=\ln 3$ or $H=\ln 7$ with no
   $(10/7)\ln 2$ correction, or uniqueness fails, or this is a
   two-level Einstein-exchange / fluctuation exercise.”

Do not replace the three-level maxent problem by a two-level
system, and do not invoke ensemble-equivalence supporting lines.
permittedResults: The constraint $(q+2q^2)/(1+q+q^2)=4/7$ rearranges to $10q^2+3q-4=0$. The roots are $q=1/2$ and $q=-4/5$; only $q=1/2$ lies in $(0,1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Impose the mean-energy constraint on (q+2q^2)/(1+q+q^2), solve the quadratic, and normalize (1,q,q^2).
Expand -sum p_i ln p_i in terms of ln 2 and ln 7, then cite strict concavity on the simplex.

milestones.criterion: Derives 10q^2+3q-4=0 and selects the positive root q=1/2, giving p=(4/7,2/7,1/7) and beta eps=ln 2.
Evaluates H=ln7-(10/7)ln2=0.9556998911125342 and invokes strict concavity for uniqueness.
Refuses the negative root and a two-level Einstein-exchange reading.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the negative root q=-4/5, or replaces the Boltzmann law by a uniform occupation or by p proportional to 1/E.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned occupation (4/7,2/7,1/7) and beta eps=ln 2 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports H=ln 3 or H=ln 7 without the (10/7)ln 2 term, or claims the maximizer is not unique.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact entropy ln7-(10/7)ln2 or the strict-concavity uniqueness is erased.

hintTree.content: Clear the constraint $(q+2q^2)/(1+q+q^2)=4/7$ to $7q+14q^2=4+4q+4q^2$, then collect $10q^2+3q-4=0$.
Expand $-\sum p_i\ln p_i$ using $\ln(4/7)=2\ln 2-\ln 7$ and $\ln(2/7)=\ln 2-\ln 7$. Strict concavity gives uniqueness.

GSM:010118.canonicalSolution:
The Boltzmann occupation is
\[
p_0=\frac1Z,\qquad
p_1=\frac qZ,\qquad
p_2=\frac{q^2}Z,\qquad
Z=1+q+q^2,
\]
with $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$. The assigned mean energy is
\[
\frac{q+2q^2}{1+q+q^2}=\frac47.
\]
Cross-multiplying,
\[
7q+14q^2=4+4q+4q^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
10q^2+3q-4=0.
\]
The discriminant is $9+160=169$, so
\[
q=\frac{-3\pm 13}{20}.
\]
The roots are $q=1/2$ and $q=-4/5$. Only $q=1/2$ lies in $(0,1)$.
\[
\boxed{10q^2+3q-4=0,\quad q=1/2}.
\]

Then $Z=1+1/2+1/4=7/4$, and
\[
p
=\frac{(1,1/2,1/4)}{7/4}
=\Bigl(\frac47,\frac27,\frac17\Bigr).
\]
The inverse temperature is $\beta\varepsilon=-\ln q=\ln 2$.
\[
\boxed{p=(4/7,2/7,1/7),\quad\beta\varepsilon=\ln 2}.
\]

The entropy is
\[
H
=-\frac47\ln\frac47-\frac27\ln\frac27-\frac17\ln\frac17
=-\frac47(2\ln 2-\ln 7)-\frac27(\ln 2-\ln 7)-\frac17(-\ln 7)
=-\frac{10}{7}\ln 2+\ln 7.
\]
Numerically,
\[
H=\ln 7-\frac{10}{7}\ln 2=0.9556998911125342.
\]
Shannon entropy is strictly concave on the simplex and the
constraint set is convex, so the maximizer is unique.
\[
\boxed{H=\ln 7-(10/7)\ln 2=0.9556998911125342;\ \text{unique}}.
\]

Sentence (i) retains the negative root $q=-4/5$, or replaces the
Boltzmann law by a uniform occupation or by $p\propto 1/E$.
Sentence (ii) reports $H=\ln 3$ or the uncorrected $H=\ln 7$, or
denies uniqueness, or else replaces the three-level maxent problem
by a two-level Einstein-exchange / fluctuation calculation, which
is not asked.

The argument never reduces the spectrum to two levels, never
invokes an Einstein exchange, and never draws a supporting line
to a convex entropy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Positive root $q=1/2$ of $10q^2+3q-4=0$. Occupation $p=(4/7,2/7,1/7)$ and $\beta\varepsilon=\ln 2$. Entropy $H=\ln 7-(10/7)\ln 2=0.9556998911125342$, unique by strict concavity.
I keep the negative root of 10q^2+3q-4=0, or I replace the Boltzmann law by a uniform occupation or by p proportional to 1/E.
I report H=ln 3 or H=ln 7 with no (10/7)ln 2 correction, and I claim the maximizer is not unique.
