GSM:010219.title: Debye low-T asymptotes with zero-point excluded: U~(3pi^4/5)NkT(T/thetaD)^3, C~(12pi^4/5)Nk(T/thetaD)^3, CT/U tends to 4
GSM:010219.objective: From the Debye density g(w)=9N w^2/wD^3 with zero-point energy excluded, evaluate the extended-cutoff low-T asymptotes using int_0^infty x^3/(e^x-1) dx=pi^4/15, prove CT/U tends to 4, and evaluate those asymptotes at T=thetaD/10.
GSM:010219.statement:
A three-dimensional Debye solid has phonon density of states
\[
g(\omega)=\frac{9N\omega^2}{\omega_D^3},\qquad
0\le\omega\le\omega_D,
\]
and Debye temperature $\theta_D=\hbar\omega_D/k_B$. The thermal
internal energy excludes the zero-point contribution: each mode
contributes $\hbar\omega/(e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1)$ only.

Every formula obtained after replacing the finite upper limit
$\theta_D/T$ by infinity is a low-temperature asymptote, not an exact
finite-cutoff identity. In particular the ratio $CT/U$ approaches 4
as $T/\theta_D\to0$.

1. Change variables to $x=\hbar\omega/k_B T$ and, at low
   temperature $T\ll\theta_D$, extend the upper limit to infinity.
   Using
   \[
   \int_0^\infty\frac{x^3}{e^x-1}\,dx=\frac{\pi^4}{15},
   \]
   prove the low-temperature asymptote
   \[
   U\sim\frac{3\pi^4}{5}\,Nk_B T\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3.
   \]

2. Differentiate with respect to $T$ and prove
   \[
   C\sim\frac{12\pi^4}{5}\,Nk_B\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3,
   \qquad
   \frac{CT}{U}\longrightarrow4.
   \]

3. At the working temperature $T=\theta_D/10$, evaluate the
   low-temperature asymptotes
   \[
   \frac{U}{Nk_B\theta_D}\simeq\frac{3\pi^4}{50000},\qquad
   \frac{C}{Nk_B}\simeq\frac{12\pi^4}{5000}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the zero-point $(9/8)Nk_B\theta_D$
   must be added to $U$, which destroys $CT/U=4$”; (ii) “the
   definite integral is $\pi^4/90$ or $\pi^2/6$, or this is a
   thermodynamic Bose/Fermi occupation / dilute-classical-gas
   exercise.”

Do not include the zero-point energy, and do not replace the Debye
integral by a particle Bose/Fermi occupation formula.
permittedResults: The substitution $x=\hbar\omega/k_B T$ converts $g(\omega)\,d\omega$ into $9N(T/\theta_D)^3 x^2\,dx$, so $U=9Nk_B T(T/\theta_D)^3\int_0^{x_D}x^3/(e^x-1)\,dx$.
$\int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x-1)\,dx=\pi^4/15$ yields the prefactor $9\pi^4/15=3\pi^4/5$. At $T=\theta_D/10$ one has $(T/\theta_D)^4=10^{-4}$ and $(T/\theta_D)^3=10^{-3}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute x=hbar omega / kB T into U=int hbar omega n_B g(omega) d omega, extend the limit to infinity, and insert pi^4/15.
Differentiate the T^4 law to get C=4U/T, then evaluate the two dimensionless ratios at T=thetaD/10.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the extended-cutoff low-T Debye integral to U~(3 pi^4/5) N kB T (T/thetaD)^3 with zero-point excluded.
Obtains C~(12 pi^4/5) N kB (T/thetaD)^3, CT/U tending to 4, and labels the T=thetaD/10 values as asymptotic evaluations.
Refuses to add the zero-point energy and does not replace the phonon integral by a particle Bose/Fermi occupation.

commonErrors.description: Adds the Debye zero-point (9/8) N kB thetaD to the thermal U, or denies the low-temperature limit CT/U -> 4.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned thermal-energy asymptote and the limiting ratio CT/U -> 4 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces int x^3/(e^x-1) dx by pi^4/90 or pi^2/6, or substitutes a thermodynamic Bose/Fermi occupation formula.
commonErrors.consequence: The prefactor 3 pi^4/5, or the Debye (as opposed to particle-gas) interpretation, is erased.

hintTree.content: Write $U=\int_0^{\omega_D}(\hbar\omega)/(e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1)\cdot 9N\omega^2/\omega_D^3\,d\omega$ and set $x=\beta\hbar\omega$.
The extended-cutoff low-$T$ integral $\pi^4/15$ produces $U\sim(3\pi^4/5)Nk_B T(T/\theta_D)^3$. Differentiating the asymptotic $T^4$ law gives $C\sim4U/T$.
At $T=\theta_D/10$, the asymptotes give $U/(Nk_B\theta_D)\simeq(3\pi^4/5)\cdot 10^{-4}=3\pi^4/50000$ and $C/(Nk_B)\simeq(12\pi^4/5)\cdot 10^{-3}=12\pi^4/5000$.

GSM:010219.canonicalSolution:
The thermal energy is
\[
U
=\int_0^{\omega_D}
\frac{\hbar\omega}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1}
\cdot\frac{9N\omega^2}{\omega_D^3}\,d\omega.
\]
Set $x=\hbar\omega/k_B T$, so $d\omega=(k_B T/\hbar)\,dx$ and
$\omega_D=k_B\theta_D/\hbar$. Then
\[
\frac{9N\omega^2\,d\omega}{\omega_D^3}
=9N\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3 x^2\,dx,
\]
and
\[
U
=9Nk_B T\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3
\int_0^{\theta_D/T}\frac{x^3}{e^x-1}\,dx.
\]
At low temperature the upper limit may be sent to infinity to obtain
an asymptotic expression. Using
$\int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x-1)\,dx=\pi^4/15$,
\[
U
\sim9Nk_B T\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{15}
=\frac{3\pi^4}{5}\,Nk_B T\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3.
\]
\[
\boxed{U\sim(3\pi^4/5)\,Nk_B T(T/\theta_D)^3}.
\]

Equivalently $U\sim(3\pi^4/5)Nk_B\theta_D^{-3}T^4$, so
\[
C\sim\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}
=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}\,Nk_B\Bigl(\frac{T}{\theta_D}\Bigr)^3.
\]
The ratio of the two $T^4$ formulae is
\[
\frac{CT}{U}
\longrightarrow\frac{(12\pi^4/5)}{(3\pi^4/5)}
=4.
\]
\[
\boxed{C\sim(12\pi^4/5)\,Nk_B(T/\theta_D)^3,\quad CT/U\to4}.
\]

Evaluating these low-temperature asymptotes at $T=\theta_D/10$,
\[
\frac{U}{Nk_B\theta_D}
\simeq\frac{3\pi^4}{5}\Bigl(\frac1{10}\Bigr)^4
=\frac{3\pi^4}{5}\cdot\frac1{10000}
=\frac{3\pi^4}{50000},
\]
\[
\frac{C}{Nk_B}
\simeq\frac{12\pi^4}{5}\Bigl(\frac1{10}\Bigr)^3
=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}\cdot\frac1{1000}
=\frac{12\pi^4}{5000}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T=\theta_D/10:\ U/(Nk_B\theta_D)\simeq3\pi^4/50000,\ C/(Nk_B)\simeq12\pi^4/5000}.
\]

Sentence (i) adds the Debye zero-point $(9/8)Nk_B\theta_D$ to $U$.
That constant (in $T$) leaves $C$ unchanged but destroys the
identity $CT/U=4$. Sentence (ii) replaces $\pi^4/15$ by $\pi^4/90$
or by $\pi^2/6$, or else replaces the phonon integral by a
thermodynamic Bose/Fermi occupation / dilute-classical-gas
calculation, which is not asked.

The argument never includes $\frac12\hbar\omega$, never uses a
particle fugacity, and never recovers a classical ideal gas.

graderFixtures.proofText: Zero-point excluded. In the extended-cutoff low-$T$ asymptote, $U\sim(3\pi^4/5)Nk_B T(T/\theta_D)^3$, $C\sim(12\pi^4/5)Nk_B(T/\theta_D)^3$, and $CT/U\to4$. At $T=\theta_D/10$, the asymptotic evaluations are $U/(Nk_B\theta_D)\simeq3\pi^4/50000$ and $C/(Nk_B)\simeq12\pi^4/5000$.
I add the Debye zero-point (9/8) N kB thetaD to U, so CT/U is no longer 4.
I replace int x^3/(e^x-1) dx by pi^4/90 or by pi^2/6, or I substitute a thermodynamic Bose/Fermi occupation formula for the phonon integral.

GSM:010220.title: T=0 spin-1/2 Fermi sphere n=1/(3pi^2 a^3): kF=1/a, epsF=hbar^2/(2m a^2), U/N=3epsF/5, P=2n epsF/5, <k^2>=3kF^2/5, |k|<=kF/2 is 1/8, kappaT=3/(2n epsF)
GSM:010220.objective: For a three-dimensional spin-1/2 ideal Fermi gas at T=0 with n=1/(3 pi^2 a^3), recover kF=1/a, epsF=hbar^2/(2m a^2), U/N=3 epsF/5, P=2 n epsF/5, <k^2>=3 kF^2/5, the fraction |k|<=kF/2 equal to 1/8, and kappaT=3/(2 n epsF).
GSM:010220.statement:
A spin-$1/2$ ideal Fermi gas lives in three dimensions at
temperature $T=0$. The number density is prescribed as
\[
n=\frac{1}{3\pi^2 a^3}
\]
for a length $a>0$.

1. From the filled Fermi sphere, including the two spin states,
   prove $n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$ and therefore $k_F=1/a$. Deduce
   \[
   \varepsilon_F=\frac{\hbar^2 k_F^2}{2m}=\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma^2}.
   \]

2. Compute the ground-state energy per particle and the pressure,
   and prove
   \[
   \frac UN=\frac35\varepsilon_F,\qquad
   P=\frac25 n\varepsilon_F.
   \]
   From $\varepsilon=\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)$, deduce
   $\langle k^2\rangle=3k_F^2/5$.

3. The fraction of particles with $\lvert k\rvert\le k_F/2$ is the
   volume ratio of the two spheres. Prove that this fraction equals
   $1/8$. From $P\propto n^{5/3}$ at $T=0$, prove the isothermal
   compressibility
   \[
   \kappa_T=\frac{3}{2n\varepsilon_F}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “spinless fermions have
   $n=k_F^3/(6\pi^2)$, so $k_F=2^{1/3}/a$”; (ii) “$U/N=\varepsilon_F/2$
   or the inner-sphere fraction is $(1/2)^2=1/4$, or this is a
   finite-temperature Bose/Fermi occupation / Kubo-response
   exercise.”

Do not drop the spin degeneracy, and do not replace the $T=0$
sphere by a finite-temperature occupation formula.
permittedResults: If $n=1/(3\pi^2 a^3)$ and $n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$, then $k_F=1/a$ and $\varepsilon_F=\hbar^2/(2ma^2)$.

The ball of radius $k_F/2$ occupies the volume fraction $(1/2)^3=1/8$ of the Fermi ball. Differentiating $P=(2/5)n\varepsilon_F$ with $\varepsilon_F\propto n^{2/3}$ gives $\partial P/\partial n=(2/3)\varepsilon_F$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Count k-states in the ball of radius kF with two spins, match the assigned density, and take the first energy moment.
Read the inner-sphere fraction from the volume ratio (1/2)^3 and differentiate P proportional to n^{5/3}.

milestones.criterion: Recovers n=kF^3/(3 pi^2), kF=1/a, and epsF=hbar^2/(2m a^2) for the spin-1/2 T=0 sphere.
Obtains U/N=3 epsF/5, P=2 n epsF/5, <k^2>=3 kF^2/5, the fraction 1/8, and kappaT=3/(2 n epsF).
Keeps the spin degeneracy and refuses a finite-temperature occupation or Kubo reading.

commonErrors.description: Drops the spin degeneracy and writes n=kF^3/(6 pi^2), or reports kF=2^{1/3}/a.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned wavevector kF=1/a and Fermi energy hbar^2/(2m a^2) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports U/N=epsF/2 or the inner-sphere fraction (1/2)^2=1/4, or replaces the T=0 sphere by a finite-temperature Bose/Fermi occupation.
commonErrors.consequence: The ground-state moments 3/5 and 1/8, or the T=0 interpretation, are erased.

hintTree.content: Two states per $k$-point: $N=2\cdot(V/(2\pi)^3)\cdot(4\pi k_F^3/3)=V k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$.
$\langle\varepsilon\rangle=\bigl(\int_0^{k_F}(\hbar^2 k^2/2m)\,k^2\,dk\bigr)/\bigl(\int_0^{k_F}k^2\,dk\bigr)=(3/5)\varepsilon_F$, and $P=(2/3)(U/V)$.
Volume ratio $(k_F/2)^3/k_F^3=1/8$. Then $\partial P/\partial n=(2/3)\varepsilon_F$ so $\kappa_T=3/(2n\varepsilon_F)$.

GSM:010220.canonicalSolution:
Including the two spin states, the number of filled orbitals is
\[
N
=2\cdot\frac{V}{(2\pi)^3}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}k_F^3
=\frac{V k_F^3}{3\pi^2},
\]
hence $n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$. The assigned density $n=1/(3\pi^2 a^3)$
forces $k_F=1/a$, and
\[
\varepsilon_F
=\frac{\hbar^2 k_F^2}{2m}
=\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma^2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2),\quad k_F=1/a,\quad\varepsilon_F=\hbar^2/(2ma^2)}.
\]

The ground-state energy is the first moment of $\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)$
over the filled ball. With the radial measure $k^2\,dk$,
\[
\frac UN
=\frac{\int_0^{k_F}(\hbar^2 k^2/2m)\,k^2\,dk}
{\int_0^{k_F}k^2\,dk}
=\frac35\varepsilon_F.
\]
The $T=0$ identity $P=(2/3)(U/V)$ then gives
\[
P
=\frac23\cdot n\cdot\frac35\varepsilon_F
=\frac25 n\varepsilon_F.
\]
Because $\varepsilon=\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)$, the same moment is
$\langle k^2\rangle=3k_F^2/5$.
\[
\boxed{U/N=3\varepsilon_F/5,\quad P=2n\varepsilon_F/5,\quad\langle k^2\rangle=3k_F^2/5}.
\]

The set $\{\lvert k\rvert\le k_F/2\}$ is a ball of radius $k_F/2$
inside the Fermi ball, so the particle fraction is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{k_F/2}{k_F}\Bigr)^3=\frac18.
\]
From $P=(2/5)n\varepsilon_F$ and $\varepsilon_F\propto n^{2/3}$ one
has $P\propto n^{5/3}$, hence
\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial n}
=\frac53\cdot\frac{P}{n}
=\frac53\cdot\frac25\varepsilon_F
=\frac23\varepsilon_F.
\]
The isothermal compressibility is
\[
\kappa_T
=\frac1n\Bigl(\frac{\partial n}{\partial P}\Bigr)_T
=\frac{1}{n\cdot(2/3)\varepsilon_F}
=\frac{3}{2n\varepsilon_F}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{fraction }1/8,\quad\kappa_T=3/(2n\varepsilon_F)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the spin degeneracy and writes
$n=k_F^3/(6\pi^2)$, which would give $k_F=2^{1/3}/a$. Sentence
(ii) reports $U/N=\varepsilon_F/2$ or the two-dimensional fraction
$(1/2)^2=1/4$, or else replaces the $T=0$ sphere by a
finite-temperature Bose/Fermi occupation or Kubo-response
calculation, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a fugacity, never writes
$n_F=(z^{-1}e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)^{-1}$, and never forms a
response kernel.

graderFixtures.proofText: Spin-$1/2$, $T=0$: $n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$ and $n=1/(3\pi^2 a^3)$ give $k_F=1/a$, $\varepsilon_F=\hbar^2/(2ma^2)$. Then $U/N=3\varepsilon_F/5$, $P=2n\varepsilon_F/5$, $\langle k^2\rangle=3k_F^2/5$, fraction $\lvert k\rvert\le k_F/2$ equals $1/8$, and $\kappa_T=3/(2n\varepsilon_F)$.
I treat the fermions as spinless, write n=kF^3/(6 pi^2), and report kF=2^{1/3}/a.
I report U/N=epsF/2 or the inner-sphere fraction (1/2)^2=1/4, or I replace the T=0 sphere by a finite-temperature Bose/Fermi occupation formula.

GSM:010221.title: Two spinless particles on {0,eps,2eps}, q=1/2: ZB=35/16, ZF=7/8, UB/eps=34/35, UF/eps=11/7, VarB=1434/1225, VarF=26/49, PB(ground)=16/35, PF(lowest)=4/7
GSM:010221.objective: Enumerate the two-particle Bose and Fermi spectra on the three spinless levels {0,eps,2eps} at q=e^{-beta eps}=1/2. Recover ZB=35/16, ZF=7/8, the mean energies 34/35 and 11/7, the variances 1434/1225 and 26/49, and the ground-pair probabilities 16/35 and 4/7.
GSM:010221.statement:
Two indistinguishable spinless particles occupy the three
single-particle levels $\{0,\varepsilon,2\varepsilon\}$. Write
$q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ and specialize to $q=1/2$. Bosons may
multiply occupy a level; spinless fermions occupy each level at
most once. This is a finite enumeration, not a thermodynamic
occupation-number derivation.

1. List the Bose occupation triples $(n_0,n_1,n_2)$ with
   $n_0+n_1+n_2=2$ and the three allowed Fermi pairs. Prove
   \[
   Z_B=\frac{35}{16},\qquad
   Z_F=\frac78.
   \]

2. Compute the mean energies and prove
   \[
   \frac{U_B}{\varepsilon}=\frac{34}{35},\qquad
   \frac{U_F}{\varepsilon}=\frac{11}{7}.
   \]

3. Compute the energy variances and the occupation probabilities
   of the lowest pair in each statistics, and prove
   \[
   \frac{\mathrm{Var}_B}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{1434}{1225},\qquad
   \frac{\mathrm{Var}_F}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{26}{49},
   \]
   \[
   \mathbb{P}_B(\text{both in the ground level})=\frac{16}{35},\qquad
   \mathbb{P}_F(\text{lowest pair }\{0,\varepsilon\})=\frac47.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the particles are distinguishable, so
   $Z=Z_1^2$, or both species use $Z=Z_1^2/2!$”; (ii) “replace the
   enumeration by the thermodynamic occupations
   $n=(q^{-1}e^{\beta E}\pm 1)^{-1}$ and recover a dilute classical
   gas, or this is a Kubo / fluctuation-relation exercise.”

Do not treat the particles as distinguishable, and do not replace
the two-particle spectrum by a thermodynamic Bose/Fermi occupation
formula.
permittedResults: Direct Bose weights $1+q+q^2+q^2+q^3+q^4=35/16$ give $U_B/\varepsilon=34/35$ and $\langle(E/\varepsilon)^2\rangle_B=74/35$. Fermi weights $q+q^2+q^3=7/8$ give $U_F/\varepsilon=11/7$ and $\langle(E/\varepsilon)^2\rangle_F=3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: List the six Bose triples and three Fermi pairs, sum the Boltzmann weights at q=1/2, and match Z_B=1/2(Z_1^2+Z_1(2 beta)).
Form the first two energy moments from the same weights, then read the two ground-pair probabilities as single-term ratios.

milestones.criterion: Enumerates the two-particle Bose and Fermi spectra and obtains ZB=35/16 and ZF=7/8 at q=1/2.
Computes UB/eps=34/35, UF/eps=11/7, VarB/eps^2=1434/1225, VarF/eps^2=26/49, and the lowest-pair probabilities 16/35 and 4/7.
Refuses a distinguishable or Maxwell-Boltzmann substitute and does not replace the enumeration by thermodynamic occupations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the particles as distinguishable and writes Z=Z1^2, or uses Z=Z1^2/2! for both statistics.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned partition functions ZB=35/16 and ZF=7/8 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the two-particle enumeration by the thermodynamic occupations n=(q^{-1}e^{beta E} +/- 1)^{-1}, or by a Kubo / fluctuation-relation argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite two-particle spectrum and the assigned moments are erased.

GSM:010221.canonicalSolution:
The Bose occupations, energies, and weights at $q=1/2$ are
\[
(2,0,0):\ E=0,\ w=1;
\quad
(1,1,0):\ E=\varepsilon,\ w=q=1/2;
\quad
(1,0,1):\ E=2\varepsilon,\ w=q^2=1/4;
\]
\[
(0,2,0):\ E=2\varepsilon,\ w=q^2=1/4;
\quad
(0,1,1):\ E=3\varepsilon,\ w=q^3=1/8;
\quad
(0,0,2):\ E=4\varepsilon,\ w=q^4=1/16.
\]
The partition function is
\[
Z_B
=1+\frac12+\frac14+\frac14+\frac18+\frac1{16}
=\frac{16+8+4+4+2+1}{16}
=\frac{35}{16}.
\]
(The same value is $\frac12\bigl((7/4)^2+(21/16)\bigr)$.) The
Pauli-allowed Fermi pairs contribute
\[
Z_F
=q+q^2+q^3
=\frac12+\frac14+\frac18
=\frac78.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_B=35/16,\quad Z_F=7/8}.
\]

The Bose mean energy is
\[
\frac{U_B}{\varepsilon}
=\frac{16}{35}\Bigl(
1\cdot\frac12+2\cdot\frac14+2\cdot\frac14+3\cdot\frac18+4\cdot\frac1{16}
\Bigr)
=\frac{16}{35}\Bigl(\frac12+\frac12+\frac12+\frac38+\frac14\Bigr)
=\frac{16}{35}\cdot\frac{17}{8}
=\frac{34}{35}.
\]
The Fermi mean energy is
\[
\frac{U_F}{\varepsilon}
=\frac87\Bigl(1\cdot\frac12+2\cdot\frac14+3\cdot\frac18\Bigr)
=\frac87\Bigl(\frac12+\frac12+\frac38\Bigr)
=\frac87\cdot\frac{11}{8}
=\frac{11}{7}.
\]
\[
\boxed{U_B/\varepsilon=34/35,\quad U_F/\varepsilon=11/7}.
\]

The Bose second moment is
\[
\Bigl\langle\Bigl(\frac{E}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^2\Bigr\rangle_B
=\frac{16}{35}\Bigl(
1\cdot\frac12+4\cdot\frac14+4\cdot\frac14+9\cdot\frac18+16\cdot\frac1{16}
\Bigr)
=\frac{16}{35}\cdot\frac{37}{8}
=\frac{74}{35},
\]
so
\[
\frac{\mathrm{Var}_B}{\varepsilon^2}
=\frac{74}{35}-\Bigl(\frac{34}{35}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{2590}{1225}-\frac{1156}{1225}
=\frac{1434}{1225}.
\]
The Fermi second moment is
\[
\Bigl\langle\Bigl(\frac{E}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^2\Bigr\rangle_F
=\frac87\Bigl(1\cdot\frac12+4\cdot\frac14+9\cdot\frac18\Bigr)
=\frac87\cdot\frac{21}{8}
=3,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\mathrm{Var}_F}{\varepsilon^2}
=3-\Bigl(\frac{11}{7}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{147}{49}-\frac{121}{49}
=\frac{26}{49}.
\]
The Bose ground occupation $(2,0,0)$ has probability
$1/Z_B=16/35$. The lowest Fermi pair $\{0,\varepsilon\}$ has
probability $(1/2)/(7/8)=4/7$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Var}_B/\varepsilon^2=1434/1225,\ \mathrm{Var}_F/\varepsilon^2=26/49,\ \mathbb{P}_B=16/35,\ \mathbb{P}_F=4/7}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats the particles as distinguishable ($Z=Z_1^2$)
or forces both statistics onto the Maxwell--Boltzmann count
$Z_1^2/2!$. Sentence (ii) replaces the two-particle enumeration by
the thermodynamic occupations $n=(q^{-1}e^{\beta E}\pm 1)^{-1}$ and
a dilute-classical-gas limit, or else by a Kubo /
fluctuation-relation argument, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a thermodynamic fugacity, never
writes a grand-canonical occupation formula, and never forms a
response kernel.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $q=1/2$, $Z_B=35/16$ and $Z_F=7/8$. Mean energies $U_B/\varepsilon=34/35$ and $U_F/\varepsilon=11/7$. Variances $1434/1225$ and $26/49$. Ground-pair probabilities $16/35$ (Bose, both in the ground level) and $4/7$ (Fermi, pair $\{0,\varepsilon\}$).
I treat the two particles as distinguishable and write Z=Z1^2, or I use the Maxwell-Boltzmann count Z=Z1^2/2! for both Bose and Fermi.
I replace the two-particle enumeration by the thermodynamic occupations n=(q^{-1} e^{beta E} +/- 1)^{-1} and recover a dilute classical gas, or I treat this as a Kubo / fluctuation-relation exercise.

GSM:010322.title: Tonks hard rods N=4 on L=10a: free length 6a, Qconf=54 a^4, beta P a=2/3, n=2/(5a), Z=5/3, kappa_T=9a/(10 k_B T)
GSM:010322.objective: From the Tonks configurational integral Q_conf=(L-N a)^N/N! at N=4 and L=10a, recover the free length 6a, evaluate Q_conf=54 a^4, and extract beta P a=2/3, n=2/(5a), Z=5/3, and kappa_T=9a/(10 k_B T).
GSM:010322.statement:
N=4 identical hard rods of length $a$ occupy a one-dimensional
interval of length $L=10a$. The rods cannot overlap. After the
standard ordered-to-unordered conversion, the configurational
integral is
\[
Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=\frac{(L-Na)^N}{N!}.
\]
The configurational Helmholtz function is
$F_{\mathrm{conf}}=-k_BT\ln Q_{\mathrm{conf}}$, and the pressure,
number density, compressibility factor, and isothermal
compressibility are
\[
P=-\Bigl(\frac{\partial F_{\mathrm{conf}}}{\partial L}\Bigr)_T,
\qquad
n=\frac{N}{L},
\qquad
Z=\frac{P}{nk_BT},
\qquad
\kappa_T=-\frac1L\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial P}\Bigr)_T.
\]

1. Evaluate the free length $L-Na$ and $Q_{\mathrm{conf}}$. Prove
   \[
   L-Na=6a,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=54\,a^4.
   \]

2. Compute $\partial\ln Q_{\mathrm{conf}}/\partial L$ and prove
   \[
   \beta Pa=\frac23,\qquad n=\frac{2}{5a},\qquad Z=\frac53.
   \]

3. Invert $\beta P=N/(L-Na)$ for $L(P)$ and prove
   \[
   \kappa_T=\frac{9a}{10k_BT}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the rods are point particles, so
   $Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=L^N/N!=(10a)^4/24$ and $Z=1$”; (ii) “this is
   a Mayer-graph cancellation through third order, a virial van der
   Waals expansion, or an ensemble-equivalence supporting-line
   argument.”

Do not replace the Tonks free-volume identities by an ideal-gas
configurational integral, a Mayer cluster expansion, or a
two-dimensional van der Waals construction.
permittedResults: If $Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=(L-Na)^N/N!$, then $\ln Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=N\ln(L-Na)-\ln N!$ and $\partial\ln Q_{\mathrm{conf}}/\partial L=N/(L-Na)$.
From $L=Na+N/(\beta P)$ one has $(\partial L/\partial P)_T=-N/(\beta P^2)$, so $\kappa_T=N/(L\beta P^2)$. At the assigned numbers this equals $9a/(10k_BT)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the ordered rods to a free simplex of length L-Na, insert N=4 and L=10a, then differentiate ln Q_conf.
Read Z as beta P/n and invert L=Na+N/(beta P) to obtain kappa_T=N/(L beta P^2).

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the free length 6a and the configurational integral Q_conf=54 a^4.
Extracts beta P a=2/3, n=2/(5a), Z=5/3, and kappa_T=9a/(10 k_B T).
Refuses the ideal-gas replacement Q_conf=L^N/N! and does not recast the Tonks identities as Mayer graphs or van der Waals loops.

commonErrors.description: Drops the excluded length Na and writes Q_conf=L^N/N!=(10a)^4/24, or reports Z=1 as for point particles.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned values Q_conf=54 a^4 and Z=5/3 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Sets beta P=n so that kappa_T=1/(n k_B T)=5a/(2 k_B T), ignoring the free-volume factor (1-na)^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned isothermal compressibility 9a/(10 k_B T) is replaced by the ideal-gas value.

hintTree.content: $\beta P=4/(6a)=2/(3a)$, hence $\beta Pa=2/3$. Density $n=4/(10a)=2/(5a)$ and $Z=\beta P/n=5/3$.
Equivalently $\kappa_T=(1-na)^2/(n k_BT)$ with $na=2/5$, so $(3/5)^2/(2k_BT/(5a))=9a/(10k_BT)$.

GSM:010322.canonicalSolution:
The assigned free length is
\[
L-Na=10a-4a=6a.
\]
Therefore
\[
Q_{\mathrm{conf}}
=\frac{(6a)^4}{4!}
=\frac{1296\,a^4}{24}
=54\,a^4.
\]
\[
\boxed{L-Na=6a,\quad Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=54\,a^4}.
\]

The logarithmic derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial\ln Q_{\mathrm{conf}}}{\partial L}
=\frac{N}{L-Na}
=\frac{4}{6a}
=\frac{2}{3a},
\]
so
\[
\beta P=\frac{2}{3a},\qquad \beta Pa=\frac23.
\]
The number density is
\[
n=\frac{N}{L}=\frac{4}{10a}=\frac{2}{5a}.
\]
The compressibility factor is the ratio
\[
Z=\frac{\beta P}{n}
=\frac{2/(3a)}{2/(5a)}
=\frac53.
\]
\[
\boxed{\beta Pa=2/3,\quad n=2/(5a),\quad Z=5/3}.
\]

Invert $\beta P=N/(L-Na)$ to
\[
L=Na+\frac{N}{\beta P}.
\]
Differentiating at fixed $T$,
\[
\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial P}\Bigr)_T
=-\frac{N}{\beta P^2},
\]
hence
\[
\kappa_T
=\frac{N}{L\beta P^2}.
\]
With $\beta P=2/(3a)$ one has $\beta P^2=4/(9a^2\beta)$, so
\[
\frac{N}{\beta P^2}
=4\cdot\frac{9a^2\beta}{4}
=9a^2\beta,
\]
and
\[
\kappa_T
=\frac{9a^2\beta}{L}
=\frac{9a^2}{10a\,k_BT}
=\frac{9a}{10k_BT}.
\]
The same value follows from $\kappa_T=(1-na)^2/(nk_BT)$:
$na=2/5$ gives $1-na=3/5$ and
\[
\kappa_T
=\frac{9/25}{2k_BT/(5a)}
=\frac{9a}{10k_BT}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\kappa_T=9a/(10k_BT)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the excluded length $Na$ and treats the rods as
point particles. That produces the ideal configurational integral
$(10a)^4/24$ and forces $Z=1$, contradicting both $Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=54a^4$
and $Z=5/3$. Sentence (ii) replaces the one-dimensional free-volume
calculation by a Mayer-graph cancellation, a virial van der Waals
expansion, or an ensemble-equivalence supporting-line argument,
none of which is asked.

The argument never introduces a Mayer cluster, never writes a
two-dimensional van der Waals loop, and never compares ensembles
by a supporting line of a convex entropy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Free length $L-Na=6a$ and $Q_{\mathrm{conf}}=54\,a^4$. Then $\beta Pa=2/3$, $n=2/(5a)$, $Z=5/3$, and $\kappa_T=9a/(10k_BT)$.
The rods are point particles, so I take Q_conf=L^N/N!=(10a)^4/24 and conclude Z=1.
I set beta P=n and report the isothermal compressibility as the ideal-gas value 1/(n k_B T)=5a/(2 k_B T).

GSM:010323.title: Coupled pair V=k(x1^2+x2^2)/2+g(x1-x2)^2/2 at g=k: Zconf=2pi/(beta k sqrt3), <q+^2>=1/(beta k), rho=1/2, energies 1/(3beta)+2/(3beta)=1/beta
GSM:010323.objective: Diagonalize the assigned two-particle Hookean potential at g=k in the orthonormal modes q_pm=(x1pm x2)/sqrt(2), evaluate Z_conf=2pi/(beta k sqrt(3)), and recover the second moments, the correlation rho=1/2, and the interaction/trap/total mean energies 1/(3beta), 2/(3beta), 1/beta.
GSM:010323.statement:
Two classical coordinates have the potential
\[
V=\frac k2\bigl(x_1^2+x_2^2\bigr)+\frac g2(x_1-x_2)^2,
\]
with $k>0$ and $g=k$. The orthonormal change of variables
\[
q_\pm=\frac{x_1\pm x_2}{\sqrt2}
\]
has Jacobian $1$. The configurational integral is
$Z_{\mathrm{conf}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}e^{-\beta V}\,dx_1\,dx_2$.

1. Rewrite $V$ in the coordinates $(q_+,q_-)$ and prove
   \[
   V=\frac k2\,q_+^2+\frac{3k}2\,q_-^2.
   \]
   Evaluate the Gaussian integral and prove
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{conf}}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta k\sqrt3}.
   \]

2. Compute the modal second moments and invert the transformation
   to prove
   \[
   \langle q_+^2\rangle=\frac1{\beta k},\qquad
   \langle q_-^2\rangle=\frac1{3\beta k},
   \]
   \[
   \langle x_1^2\rangle=\langle x_2^2\rangle=\frac2{3\beta k},\qquad
   \langle x_1 x_2\rangle=\frac1{3\beta k}.
   \]
   Deduce the Pearson correlation $\rho=\langle x_1 x_2\rangle/\langle x_1^2\rangle=1/2$.

3. Evaluate $\langle(x_1-x_2)^2\rangle$ and the three mean energies
   \[
   \Bigl\langle\frac g2(x_1-x_2)^2\Bigr\rangle=\frac1{3\beta},\qquad
   \Bigl\langle\frac k2(x_1^2+x_2^2)\Bigr\rangle=\frac2{3\beta},\qquad
   \langle V\rangle=\frac1\beta.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$(x_1-x_2)^2=q_-^2$, so both modal
   springs equal $k$ and $\langle q_\pm^2\rangle=1/(\beta k)$”;
   (ii) “equipartition assigns $k_BT/2$ to each of the three written
   quadratic monomials, or this is a Bose/Fermi occupation, a
   two-level fluctuation, or a Kubo response calculation.”

Do not replace the classical Gaussian pair by quantum occupations,
and do not treat $x_1^2$, $x_2^2$, and $(x_1-x_2)^2$ as independent
quadratic modes.
permittedResults: Two independent classical quadratic modes contribute $k_BT$ in total. The interaction and trap pieces need not each equal $k_BT/2$ because they mix the same coordinates.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rotate to q_pm, read the two Gaussian widths, then invert the orthogonal map for Cartesian moments.
Compute the interaction as (g/2)<(x1-x2)^2> and the trap as (k/2)(<x1^2>+<x2^2>), and check that they sum to k_B T.

milestones.criterion: Diagonalizes V at g=k to (k/2)q_+^2+(3k/2)q_-^2 and evaluates Z_conf=2pi/(beta k sqrt(3)).
Records the modal and Cartesian second moments, rho=1/2, and the energy split 1/(3beta)+2/(3beta)=1/beta.
Keeps the factor (x1-x2)^2=2 q_-^2 and refuses occupation-number or Kubo replacements.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor 2 in (x1-x2)^2=2 q_-^2, or sets both modal springs equal to k, reporting <q_-^2>=1/(beta k).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned minus-mode moment 1/(3 beta k) and every inverted Cartesian moment are lost.

commonErrors.description: Assigns k_B T/2 to each of the three written monomials, or reports rho=0, or sets the interaction energy to 1/(2 beta).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned correlation 1/2 and the energy split 1/(3 beta)+2/(3 beta) are erased.

hintTree.content: Substitute $(x_1-x_2)^2=2q_-^2$ to get the minus-mode spring $k/2+g=3k/2$.
Each Gaussian $\int e^{-\alpha q^2}\,dq=\sqrt{\pi/\alpha}$ produces $Z_{\mathrm{conf}}=\sqrt{2\pi/(\beta k)}\sqrt{2\pi/(3\beta k)}$.
$x_1 x_2=(q_+^2-q_-^2)/2$, so the connected moment is $(1/(\beta k)-1/(3\beta k))/2=1/(3\beta k)$.

GSM:010323.canonicalSolution:
The inverse map is $x_1=(q_++q_-)/\sqrt2$ and
$x_2=(q_+-q_-)/\sqrt2$. Then
\[
x_1^2+x_2^2=q_+^2+q_-^2,
\qquad
(x_1-x_2)^2=2q_-^2.
\]
The potential becomes
\[
V
=\frac k2\bigl(q_+^2+q_-^2\bigr)+\frac g2\cdot 2q_-^2
=\frac k2\,q_+^2+\Bigl(\frac k2+g\Bigr)q_-^2.
\]
At the assigned coupling $g=k$,
\[
V=\frac k2\,q_+^2+\frac{3k}2\,q_-^2.
\]
The Jacobian is $1$, so
\[
Z_{\mathrm{conf}}
=\int e^{-\beta k q_+^2/2}\,dq_+
\int e^{-\beta(3k/2)q_-^2}\,dq_-
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\beta k}}
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{3\beta k}}
=\frac{2\pi}{\beta k\sqrt3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V=(k/2)q_+^2+(3k/2)q_-^2,\quad Z_{\mathrm{conf}}=2\pi/(\beta k\sqrt3)}.
\]

The plus-mode weight is $e^{-(\beta k/2)q_+^2}$, hence
\[
\langle q_+^2\rangle=\frac1{\beta k}.
\]
The minus-mode weight is $e^{-(3\beta k/2)q_-^2}$, hence
\[
\langle q_-^2\rangle=\frac1{3\beta k}.
\]
Because $\langle q_+ q_-\rangle=0$,
\[
\langle x_1^2\rangle
=\frac12\bigl(\langle q_+^2\rangle+\langle q_-^2\rangle\bigr)
=\frac12\Bigl(\frac1{\beta k}+\frac1{3\beta k}\Bigr)
=\frac2{3\beta k},
\]
and likewise $\langle x_2^2\rangle=2/(3\beta k)$. The cross moment is
\[
\langle x_1 x_2\rangle
=\frac12\bigl(\langle q_+^2\rangle-\langle q_-^2\rangle\bigr)
=\frac12\Bigl(\frac1{\beta k}-\frac1{3\beta k}\Bigr)
=\frac1{3\beta k}.
\]
The Pearson correlation is therefore
\[
\rho
=\frac{\langle x_1 x_2\rangle}{\langle x_1^2\rangle}
=\frac{1/(3\beta k)}{2/(3\beta k)}
=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle q_+^2\rangle=1/(\beta k),\ \langle q_-^2\rangle=1/(3\beta k),\ \langle x_i^2\rangle=2/(3\beta k),\ \langle x_1 x_2\rangle=1/(3\beta k),\ \rho=1/2}.
\]

The relative displacement satisfies $\langle(x_1-x_2)^2\rangle=2\langle q_-^2\rangle=2/(3\beta k)$.
The mean interaction, trap, and total energies are
\[
\Bigl\langle\frac g2(x_1-x_2)^2\Bigr\rangle
=\frac k2\cdot\frac2{3\beta k}
=\frac1{3\beta},
\]
\[
\Bigl\langle\frac k2(x_1^2+x_2^2)\Bigr\rangle
=\frac k2\cdot\frac4{3\beta k}
=\frac2{3\beta},
\]
\[
\langle V\rangle
=\frac1{3\beta}+\frac2{3\beta}
=\frac1\beta.
\]
The last identity is also the equipartition value for two independent
quadratic modes.
\[
\boxed{\langle(x_1-x_2)^2\rangle=2/(3\beta k),\ \text{interaction }1/(3\beta),\ \text{trap }2/(3\beta),\ \text{total }1/\beta}.
\]

Sentence (i) forgets the factor $2$ in $(x_1-x_2)^2=2q_-^2$ and
assigns both modes the spring $k$. That produces
$\langle q_-^2\rangle=1/(\beta k)$ instead of $1/(3\beta k)$ and
destroys every inverted moment. Sentence (ii) treats the three
written monomials $x_1^2$, $x_2^2$, and $(x_1-x_2)^2$ as independent
quadratic energies, or else replaces the classical pair by Bose/Fermi
occupations, a two-level fluctuation, or a Kubo formula, none of
which is asked.

The argument never second-quantizes the modes, never introduces a
Fermi or Bose distribution, and never writes a linear-response
kernel.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $g=k$, $V=(k/2)q_+^2+(3k/2)q_-^2$ and $Z_{\mathrm{conf}}=2\pi/(\beta k\sqrt3)$. Then $\langle q_+^2\rangle=1/(\beta k)$, $\langle q_-^2\rangle=1/(3\beta k)$, $\langle x_i^2\rangle=2/(3\beta k)$, $\langle x_1 x_2\rangle=1/(3\beta k)$, $\rho=1/2$, and the mean energies are $1/(3\beta)$, $2/(3\beta)$, $1/\beta$.
I take (x1-x2)^2=q_-^2 so both modal springs equal k, and I report <q_+^2>=<q_-^2>=1/(beta k).
Equipartition assigns k_B T/2 to each of x1^2, x2^2, and (x1-x2)^2, so I set the interaction energy to 1/(2 beta) and take rho=0.

GSM:010324.title: Square well on ring L=4a, beta eps=ln3: Zrel=6a, labelled 24 a^2 vs ideal 16 a^2 ratio 3/2, bound 1/2, <u>=-eps/2, C/kB=(ln3)^2/4
GSM:010324.objective: On a ring of length L=4a with an attractive relative set of measure a at depth -eps and beta eps=ln 3, evaluate the relative normalization 6a, the labelled ratio 24 a^2 versus 16 a^2, the bound probability 1/2, and the energy moments <u>=-eps/2, var=eps^2/4, C/k_B=(ln 3)^2/4.
GSM:010324.statement:
Two distinguishable classical particles move on a ring of
circumference $L=4a$. Their relative coordinate $s$ is measured
along the ring. The pair potential equals $u=-\varepsilon$ on a
measurable attractive set $A\subset[0,L)$ of Lebesgue measure $a$,
and equals $u=0$ on the complementary set of measure $3a$. The
assigned depth is
\[
\beta\varepsilon=\ln 3,
\]
so $e^{\beta\varepsilon}=3$. The relative configurational
normalization is
\[
Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=\int_0^L e^{-\beta u(s)}\,ds.
\]
The labelled two-particle configurational integral is
$Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=L\,Z_{\mathrm{rel}}$. The corresponding ideal
integral (both particles free on the ring) is $Z_{\mathrm{id}}=L^2$.

1. Evaluate $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lab}}$ and prove
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=6a,\qquad
   Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=24a^2,\qquad
   Z_{\mathrm{id}}=16a^2,\qquad
   \frac{Z_{\mathrm{lab}}}{Z_{\mathrm{id}}}=\frac32.
   \]

2. Let $p_{\mathrm{b}}$ be the Boltzmann probability that $s\in A$.
   Prove $p_{\mathrm{b}}=1/2$, and hence
   \[
   \langle u\rangle=-\frac\varepsilon2,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(u)=\frac{\varepsilon^2}4.
   \]

3. From the energy fluctuation formula $C=\operatorname{Var}(u)/(k_BT^2)$
   prove
   \[
   \frac{C}{k_B}=\frac{(\ln 3)^2}{4}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the relative measure is just the
   circumference $L=4a$, so $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=4a$ and
   $p_{\mathrm{b}}=a/L=1/4$”; (ii) “$C/k_B=\operatorname{Var}(u)/(k_BT)$,
   or this is an Einstein exchange, an effusion problem, or a
   Mayer-graph virial coefficient.”

Do not drop the Boltzmann weight on $A$, and do not replace the
two-particle ring by an exchange, effusion, or cluster-expansion
exercise.
permittedResults: With $L=4a$ and $e^{\beta\varepsilon}=3$, one has $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=(L-a)+a\cdot 3=3a+3a=6a$.
The bound probability is the weighted measure $a\cdot 3$ over $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}$, hence $3a/6a=1/2$. Then $C/k_B=(\ln 3)^2/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the ring into the attractive set of measure a and its complement, weighting the former by 3.
Treat u as a two-point random variable at p=1/2 and convert the variance into C/k_B=(beta eps)^2/4.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates Z_rel=6a, the labelled integral 24 a^2, the ideal integral 16 a^2, and the ratio 3/2.
Records p_b=1/2, <u>=-eps/2, Var(u)=eps^2/4, and C/k_B=(ln 3)^2/4.
Keeps the Boltzmann weight e^{beta eps}=3 on the attractive set and refuses exchange, effusion, or Mayer replacements.

commonErrors.description: Sets Z_rel equal to the bare circumference 4a, or reports the bound probability as the unweighted measure a/L=1/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned normalization 6a, the ratio 3/2, and the bound probability 1/2 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes C=Var(u)/T, or C=Var(u)/T^2 without the required k_B, instead of C=Var(u)/(k_B T^2); or reports C/k_B=(ln 3)^2/2 from <u^2> rather than the variance.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned heat capacity (ln 3)^2/4 is replaced by a wrong fluctuation identity.

hintTree.content: Split $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}$ into the complementary set of measure $3a$ with weight $1$ and the attractive set of measure $a$ with weight $3$.
Labelled $Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=L Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=4a\cdot 6a=24a^2$. Ideal $L^2=16a^2$.
$u$ is a two-point random variable at $p=1/2$, so the variance is $\varepsilon^2/4$ and $C/k_B=(\beta\varepsilon)^2/4$.

GSM:010324.canonicalSolution:
On the complementary set the Boltzmann factor is $1$; on $A$ it is
$e^{\beta\varepsilon}=3$. Therefore
\[
Z_{\mathrm{rel}}
=(L-a)\cdot 1+a\cdot 3
=3a+3a
=6a.
\]
The labelled integral is
\[
Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=L Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=4a\cdot 6a=24a^2,
\]
while the ideal integral is
\[
Z_{\mathrm{id}}=L^2=(4a)^2=16a^2.
\]
Their ratio is $24a^2/16a^2=3/2$.
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=6a,\quad Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=24a^2,\quad Z_{\mathrm{id}}=16a^2,\quad\text{ratio }3/2}.
\]

The bound probability is the attractive contribution over the
relative normalization,
\[
p_{\mathrm{b}}
=\frac{a\cdot 3}{6a}
=\frac12.
\]
Hence
\[
\langle u\rangle
=-\varepsilon\cdot\frac12+0\cdot\frac12
=-\frac\varepsilon2.
\]
The second moment is $\langle u^2\rangle=\varepsilon^2/2$, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u)
=\frac{\varepsilon^2}2-\Bigl(\frac\varepsilon2\Bigr)^2
=\frac{\varepsilon^2}4.
\]
\[
\boxed{p_{\mathrm{b}}=1/2,\quad\langle u\rangle=-\varepsilon/2,\quad\operatorname{Var}(u)=\varepsilon^2/4}.
\]

The configurational heat capacity of the pair is
\[
C=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(u)}{k_BT^2},
\qquad
\frac{C}{k_B}
=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(u)}{(k_BT)^2}
=\frac{(\beta\varepsilon)^2}{4}
=\frac{(\ln 3)^2}{4}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C/k_B=(\ln 3)^2/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the Boltzmann weight on $A$ and reports the bare
relative measure $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=L=4a$. That forces
$p_{\mathrm{b}}=a/L=1/4$ and destroys both energy moments. Sentence
(ii) omits $k_B$ or one power of $T$ from
$C=\operatorname{Var}(u)/(k_BT^2)$,
or else replaces the square-well ring by an Einstein exchange, an
effusion flux, or a Mayer virial coefficient, none of which is asked.

The argument never introduces exchange statistics, never writes a
hole-in-the-wall flux, and never expands a Mayer cluster.

graderFixtures.proofText: $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}=6a$, $Z_{\mathrm{lab}}=24a^2$, $Z_{\mathrm{id}}=16a^2$, ratio $3/2$. Bound probability $1/2$, $\langle u\rangle=-\varepsilon/2$, $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\varepsilon^2/4$, and $C/k_B=(\ln 3)^2/4$.
The relative measure is just the circumference L=4a, so I take Z_rel=4a and p_b=a/L=1/4.
I omit k_B or one power of T from C=Var(u)/(k_B T^2), and I report C/k_B=(ln 3)^2/2 from the second moment rather than the variance.

GSM:010425.title: Curie-Weiss phi at K=ln3: stationary 0 and +/-1/2, phi''(0)=1-ln3<0, phi''(+/-)=4/3-ln3>0, barrier ln2-(5/8)ln3, chi=3/(4-3ln3)
GSM:010425.objective: For the assigned Curie-Weiss functional at K=ln 3, prove that 0 and +/-1/2 are the only stationary points, classify them, and evaluate the barrier and local symmetry-broken branch susceptibility 3/(4-3 ln 3).
GSM:010425.statement:
A scalar magnetization $m\in(-1,1)$ is governed by the Curie-Weiss
functional
\[
\phi(m)
=-\frac K2 m^2
+\frac{1+m}2\ln\frac{1+m}2
+\frac{1-m}2\ln\frac{1-m}2,
\]
with the assigned coupling
\[
K=\ln 3.
\]
At zero field stationary points solve $\phi'(m)=0$. To define the
local response, introduce $\phi_h(m)=\phi(m)-hm$ and follow either
symmetry-broken local-minimum branch as $h\to0^\pm$. Its susceptibility
is $\chi=(dm/dh)_{h\to0^\pm}=1/\phi''(m_\star)$. This is not the
finite-$N$ symmetric zero-field response, whose mean magnetization
vanishes.

1. Compute $\phi'(m)$ and prove that the only stationary points are
   \[
   m=0,\qquad m=\pm\frac12.
   \]

2. Compute $\phi''(m)=-K+1/(1-m^2)$ and prove
   \[
   \phi''(0)=1-\ln 3<0,
   \qquad
   \phi''\Bigl(\pm\frac12\Bigr)=\frac43-\ln 3>0.
   \]
   Conclude that $m=0$ is a local maximum and that $m=\pm 1/2$ are
   local minima.

3. Evaluate the barrier $\phi(0)-\phi(1/2)$ and the local
   symmetry-broken branch susceptibility at either minimum, and prove
   \[
   \phi(0)-\phi\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)
   =\ln 2-\frac58\ln 3
   =0.006514500142376645,
   \]
   \[
   \chi
   =\frac{3}{4-3\ln 3}
   =4.260376403088498.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$m=0$ is the global minimum because
   it is stationary, so the local branch susceptibility is
   $1/|\phi''(0)|$”; (ii) “this is a sixth-order Landau
   coexistence/spinodal analysis, a transfer-matrix free energy, or
   a magnetocaloric cycle.”

Do not replace the exact binary-entropy functional by a truncated
Landau polynomial, and do not read thermodynamics from an Ising
transfer matrix.
permittedResults: For $m>0$, $\phi'(m)=0$ is equivalent to $g(m):=\operatorname{artanh}(m)/m=K$. If $q(m)=m/(1-m^2)-\operatorname{artanh}(m)$, then $q'(m)=2m^2/(1-m^2)^2>0$ and $q(0^+)=0$, so $g'(m)=q(m)/m^2>0$. Thus $g(m)=\ln3$ has at most one positive solution; $m=1/2$ is that solution, and oddness supplies only $-1/2$ besides zero.
$\phi''(m)=-K+1/(1-m^2)$. At $m=\pm 1/2$ this is $4/3-\ln 3$, whose reciprocal is $3/(4-3\ln 3)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce phi'(m)=0 to artanh(m)/m=K for m>0, prove that ratio strictly increases, and then use oddness after checking m=1/2.
Evaluate phi at 0 and at 1/2 from the binary entropy, then invert the well curvature 4/3-ln 3.

milestones.criterion: Uses monotonicity of artanh(m)/m to prove the only stationary points are 0 and +/-1/2, then signs their curvatures.
Evaluates the barrier and the local h->0+/- symmetry-broken branch susceptibility 3/(4-3 ln 3).
Refuses to treat m=0 as a minimum and does not replace the functional by a Landau polynomial or a transfer matrix.

commonErrors.description: Declares m=0 the physical minimum because it is stationary, or reports a susceptibility 1/|phi''(0)|=1/(ln 3-1).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned minima +/-1/2 and the well susceptibility 3/(4-3 ln 3) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the barrier as phi(1/2)-phi(0) with the opposite sign, or replaces the calculation by a sixth-order Landau spinodal analysis.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned positive barrier ln 2-(5/8)ln 3 is lost or the functional is discarded.

hintTree.content: Differentiate to obtain $\phi'(m)=-Km+\operatorname{artanh}(m)$. After checking $m=0,\pm1/2$, prove completeness by showing $\operatorname{artanh}(m)/m$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$.
$\phi(0)=-\ln 2$. At $m=1/2$ the entropy terms are $(3/4)\ln(3/4)+(1/4)\ln(1/4)$.

GSM:010425.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating the assigned functional gives
\[
\phi'(m)
=-Km+\frac12\ln\frac{1+m}{1-m}.
\]
Thus $\phi'(m)=0$ if and only if $m=\tanh(Km)$. The root $m=0$ is
immediate. At $m=1/2$ and $K=\ln 3$,
\[
\tanh\Bigl(\frac K2\Bigr)
=\tanh\Bigl(\frac{\ln 3}2\Bigr)
=\frac{e^{\ln 3}-1}{e^{\ln 3}+1}
=\frac{3-1}{3+1}
=\frac12.
\]
Oddness of $\phi'$ supplies the companion root $m=-1/2$.
To prove there are no further roots, let
$g(m)=\operatorname{artanh}(m)/m$ for $m>0$. Its derivative has the
sign of
\[
q(m)=\frac{m}{1-m^2}-\operatorname{artanh}(m).
\]
Since $q(0^+)=0$ and
\[
q'(m)=\frac{2m^2}{(1-m^2)^2}>0,
\]
$g$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$. Therefore $g(m)=K=\ln3$
has the unique positive solution $m=1/2$. Oddness gives the unique
negative solution $m=-1/2$, in addition to $m=0$.
\[
\boxed{\text{stationary points }m=0,\ \pm 1/2}.
\]

A second differentiation produces
\[
\phi''(m)
=-K+\frac{1}{1-m^2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\phi''(0)=1-\ln 3<0,
\]
because $\ln 3>1$, and
\[
\phi''\Bigl(\pm\frac12\Bigr)
=-\ln 3+\frac{1}{1-1/4}
=\frac43-\ln 3>0.
\]
So $m=0$ is a local maximum and $m=\pm 1/2$ are local minima.
\[
\boxed{\phi''(0)=1-\ln 3<0,\quad\phi''(\pm 1/2)=4/3-\ln 3>0}.
\]

The values of the functional are
\[
\phi(0)=\ln\frac12=-\ln 2
\]
and
\begin{align*}
\phi\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)
&=-\frac K8+\frac34\ln\frac34+\frac14\ln\frac14
=-\frac{\ln 3}8+\frac34\ln 3-\ln 4
=\frac58\ln 3-2\ln 2.
\end{align*}
The barrier is therefore
\[
\phi(0)-\phi\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)
=-\ln 2-\frac58\ln 3+2\ln 2
=\ln 2-\frac58\ln 3
=0.006514500142376645.
\]
The local symmetry-broken branch susceptibility at either minimum is
\[
\chi
=\frac1{\phi''(\pm 1/2)}
=\frac1{4/3-\ln 3}
=\frac{3}{4-3\ln 3}
=4.260376403088498.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{barrier }=\ln 2-(5/8)\ln 3,\quad\chi=3/(4-3\ln 3)}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats the unstable stationary point $m=0$ as the
global minimum and inverts $|\phi''(0)|$ for a susceptibility. That
contradicts $\phi''(0)<0$ and the two lower wells at $\pm 1/2$.
Sentence (ii) replaces the exact binary-entropy functional by a
sixth-order Landau analysis of coexistence and spinodals, by an
Ising transfer-matrix free energy, or by a magnetocaloric cycle,
none of which is asked.

The argument never truncates $\phi$ to a polynomial, never locates
a spinodal of a sixth-order Landau theory, and never writes a
transfer matrix.

graderFixtures.proofText: Monotonicity of $\operatorname{artanh}(m)/m$ proves the only stationary points are $m=0,\pm1/2$. Then $\phi''(0)=1-\ln3<0$ and $\phi''(\pm1/2)=4/3-\ln3>0$. The barrier is $\ln2-(5/8)\ln3=0.006514500142376645$, and the local symmetry-broken branch response as $h\to0^\pm$ is $\chi=3/(4-3\ln3)=4.260376403088498$.
m=0 is the global minimum because it is stationary, so I take the physical susceptibility to be 1/|phi''(0)|=1/(ln 3-1).
I report the barrier as phi(1/2)-phi(0) with the opposite sign, or I replace the functional by a sixth-order Landau coexistence and spinodal analysis.

GSM:010426.title: Degree-3 Bethe bond percolation: u=1-p+p u^2, pc=1/2, at p=2/3 physical u=1/2 and Pinf=7/8, below pc S=1+3p/(1-2p), p=1/3 gives S=4
GSM:010426.objective: From the degree-3 Bethe bond-percolation cavity equation u=1-p+p u^2, recover pc=1/2, evaluate the physical root u=1/2 and P_inf=7/8 at p=2/3, and compute the subcritical mean cluster size S=1+3p/(1-2p), which equals 4 at p=1/3.
GSM:010426.statement:
Bond percolation is placed on the Bethe lattice of degree $z=3$:
each edge is occupied independently with probability $p$. Let $u$
be the probability that a given neighbor of the origin is not
connected to infinity through its outward tree. The cavity
self-consistency equation is
\[
u=1-p+p u^{z-1}=1-p+pu^2.
\]
A vertex belongs to the infinite cluster unless all three of its
neighbors fail to connect outward, so
\[
P_\infty=1-u^3.
\]
Below threshold the mean finite cluster size is
\[
S=1+\frac{zp}{1-(z-1)p}=1+\frac{3p}{1-2p}.
\]

1. Linearize $u=1$ in the self-consistency equation and prove that
   the bond threshold is $p_c=1/2$.

2. At $p=2/3$, solve the quadratic and prove that the physical root
   (the unique root in $[0,1)$ above threshold) is $u=1/2$. Deduce
   \[
   P_\infty=1-u^3=\frac78.
   \]

3. Below threshold evaluate $S$ at $p=1/3$ and prove $S=4$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the cavity power is $z$ rather than
   $z-1$, so $u=1-p+pu^3$, and $P_\infty=1-u$”; (ii) “this is a
   kinetic nucleation problem, a renormalization-group flow, a
   Fokker-Planck first-passage, or a sixth-order Landau spinodal.”

Do not replace the static tree recursion by a dynamical nucleation
or renormalization-group calculation, and do not change the
branching power $z-1=2$.
permittedResults: Writing $u=1-\varepsilon$ in $u=1-p+pu^2$ and linearizing gives $\varepsilon=2p\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$. A nonzero $\varepsilon$ first appears at $p_c=1/2$.
At $p=2/3$ the quadratic $2u^2-3u+1=0$ factors as $(2u-1)(u-1)=0$. The physical root is $u=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Linearize u=1-eps in the cavity equation to read pc=1/(z-1), then solve the quadratic at p=2/3.
Convert the physical cavity value into P_inf=1-u^3 and evaluate the geometric series for S below threshold.

milestones.criterion: Recovers pc=1/2 from the degree-3 cavity equation u=1-p+p u^2.
Evaluates the physical root u=1/2 and P_inf=7/8 at p=2/3, and S=4 at p=1/3 from S=1+3p/(1-2p).
Keeps the branching power z-1=2 and refuses nucleation, renormalization-group, or Fokker-Planck replacements.

commonErrors.description: Writes u=1-p+p u^3 with branching power z instead of z-1, or reports a threshold other than 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned cavity equation and the physical root u=1/2 at p=2/3 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Sets P_inf=1-u=1/2 instead of 1-u^3=7/8, or reports S=1/(1-2p)=3 at p=1/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned infinite-cluster density 7/8 or the mean size S=4 is erased.

hintTree.content: The branching factor is $z-1=2$, so $p_c=1/(z-1)=1/2$.
At $p=2/3$, $u=1/3+(2/3)u^2$ rearranges to $2u^2-3u+1=0$. Discard the unphysical root $u=1$.
Below threshold, $S=1+3p/(1-2p)$. At $p=1/3$ the fraction is $1/(1/3)=3$, so $S=4$.

GSM:010426.canonicalSolution:
Substitute $u=1-\varepsilon$ into $u=1-p+pu^2$:
\[
1-\varepsilon
=1-p+p(1-2\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2))
=1-2p\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2).
\]
Hence $\varepsilon=2p\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$. A nonzero
infinitesimal $\varepsilon$ is possible only when $2p=1$, i.e.
\[
p_c=\frac12.
\]
(The same threshold is $1/(z-1)$ for general degree.)
\[
\boxed{p_c=1/2}.
\]

At $p=2/3$ the self-consistency equation is
\[
u=\frac13+\frac23 u^2
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
2u^2-3u+1=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
(2u-1)(u-1)=0.
\]
The roots are $u=1$ and $u=1/2$. Above threshold the physical cavity
value is the root in $[0,1)$, namely $u=1/2$. The infinite-cluster
density is
\[
P_\infty=1-u^3=1-\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^3=1-\frac18=\frac78.
\]
\[
\boxed{p=2/3:\ u=1/2,\ P_\infty=7/8}.
\]

Below threshold, $u=1$ and
\[
S=1+\frac{3p}{1-2p}.
\]
At $p=1/3$,
\[
S=1+\frac{1}{1-2/3}=1+\frac{1}{1/3}=1+3=4.
\]
\[
\boxed{p=1/3:\ S=4}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the branching power $z-1=2$ by $z=3$, writing
$u=1-p+pu^3$, and identifies $P_\infty$ with the single-cavity
defect $1-u$. That destroys both $u=1/2$ and $P_\infty=7/8$.
Sentence (ii) replaces the static tree recursion by kinetic
nucleation, a renormalization-group flow, a Fokker-Planck
first-passage, or a sixth-order Landau spinodal, none of which is
asked.

The argument never introduces a time-dependent nucleus, never
coarse-grains a block spin, and never writes a Fokker-Planck
operator.

graderFixtures.proofText: Degree $3$ gives $u=1-p+pu^2$ and $p_c=1/2$. At $p=2/3$ the physical root is $u=1/2$ and $P_\infty=1-u^3=7/8$. Below threshold $S=1+3p/(1-2p)$, so $p=1/3$ yields $S=4$.
I take the cavity power to be z rather than z-1 and write u=1-p+p u^3, so I do not obtain pc=1/2 from a branching factor 2.
I set P_inf=1-u=1/2 instead of 1-u^3=7/8, and below threshold I report S=1/(1-2p)=3 at p=1/3.

GSM:010427.title: Finite two-state rounding X=±1, weights exp(±At/2): Zred=2cosh(At/2), mean=tanh(At/2), var=sech²; A=8 gives t=0 mean0 var1 slope4 and mean=1/2 at t=ln3/8 with p+=3/4
GSM:010427.objective: From finite-volume phase-branch free energies derive the two-state weights exp(±At/2), then form the reduced partition function, mean, variance, and slope. At A=8 evaluate the assigned observables and locate the unique positive t with mean 1/2. Keep A finite and analytic.
GSM:010427.statement:
A finite system has two competing phase branches labelled by
$X\in\{+1,-1\}$, with branch free energies
\[
F_X(t)=F_0-X\frac{V\ell t}{2},
\]
where $V$ is the volume and $\ell>0$ is the jump in the conjugate
observable. After dropping the common factor $e^{-\beta F_0}$, derive
the Boltzmann weights using $A:=\beta V\ell$:
\[
w(X=+1)=e^{+At/2},\qquad w(X=-1)=e^{-At/2},
\]
with fixed finite $A>0$ and real control parameter $t$.
The reduced partition function is $Z_{\mathrm{red}}=w(+1)+w(-1)$.

1. Prove
   \[
   Z_{\mathrm{red}}=2\cosh(At/2),\qquad
   \langle X\rangle=\tanh(At/2),\qquad
   \mathrm{Var}(X)=\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2),
   \]
   and
   \[
   \frac{d\langle X\rangle}{dt}
   =\frac{A}{2}\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2).
   \]

2. Now set $A=8$. At $t=0$ prove
   \[
   p_+:=\mathbb{P}(X=+1)=\tfrac12,\qquad
   \langle X\rangle=0,\qquad
   \mathrm{Var}(X)=1,\qquad
   \frac{d\langle X\rangle}{dt}=4.
   \]

3. Solve $\langle X\rangle=1/2$ for the unique positive $t$ and prove
   \[
   t=\frac{\ln 3}{8},\qquad p_+=\frac34.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the weights are $e^{\pm At}$, so
   $Z_{\mathrm{red}}=2\cosh(At)$ and $\langle X\rangle=\tanh(At)$,
   hence $t=\ln3/16$ or $t=\ln3$ when the mean is $1/2$”; (ii) “take

permittedResults: $\sinh u/\cosh u=\tanh u$ and $1-\tanh^2 u=\operatorname{sech}^2 u$. Differentiating $\tanh(At/2)$ produces the factor $A/2$.

Solve tanh(4t)=1/2 from e^{8t}=3 and convert the mean into p+=(1+mean)/2.

milestones.criterion: Derives Zred=2cosh(At/2), mean=tanh(At/2), Var=sech^2(At/2), and dmean/dt=(A/2)sech^2(At/2).

hintTree.content: Add the weights: $e^{u}+e^{-u}=2\cosh u$ with $u=At/2$. The mean is $(e^{u}-e^{-u})/(e^{u}+e^{-u})$.
At $t=0$ one has $\operatorname{sech}0=1$, so the slope is $A/2=4$.
$\tanh u=1/2$ if and only if $e^{2u}=3$. With $u=4t$ this is $t=(\ln 3)/8$.

GSM:010427.canonicalSolution:
The branch Boltzmann factor is
$e^{-\beta F_X}=e^{-\beta F_0}e^{X\beta V\ell t/2}$, so after the
common factor is removed the weights are $e^{\pm At/2}$ with
$A=\beta V\ell$. Write $u=At/2$. The two weights are $e^{u}$ and $e^{-u}$, so
\[
Z_{\mathrm{red}}=e^{u}+e^{-u}=2\cosh u=2\cosh(At/2).
\]
The mean is
\[
\langle X\rangle
=\frac{e^{u}-e^{-u}}{e^{u}+e^{-u}}
=\frac{\sinh u}{\cosh u}
=\tanh(At/2).
\]
Because $X^2=1$ identically,
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X)
=1-\langle X\rangle^2
=1-\tanh^2(At/2)
=\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2).
\]
Differentiating the mean,
\[
\frac{d\langle X\rangle}{dt}
=\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2)\cdot\frac{A}{2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{Z_{\mathrm{red}}=2\cosh(At/2),\;
\langle X\rangle=\tanh(At/2),\;
\mathrm{Var}=\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2),\;
d\langle X\rangle/dt=(A/2)\operatorname{sech}^2(At/2)}.
\]

Now set $A=8$. At $t=0$ one has $u=0$, $\tanh 0=0$,
$\operatorname{sech}0=1$, and
\[
p_+=\frac{e^{0}}{2\cosh 0}=\frac12,\qquad
\frac{d\langle X\rangle}{dt}=\frac{8}{2}\cdot 1=4.
\]
\[
\boxed{A=8,\;t=0:\ p_+=1/2,\;\langle X\rangle=0,\;
\mathrm{Var}=1,\;d\langle X\rangle/dt=4}.
\]

The equation $\tanh(At/2)=1/2$ is $\tanh(4t)=1/2$. Then
\[
e^{8t}=\frac{1+1/2}{1-1/2}=3,
\]
so $t=(\ln 3)/8$. Equivalently
$\operatorname{artanh}(1/2)=\frac12\ln 3$ and $At/2=\frac12\ln 3$.
The plus-state probability is the linear readout
\[
p_+=\frac{1+\langle X\rangle}{2}=\frac{1+1/2}{2}=\frac34.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=(\ln 3)/8,\quad p_+=3/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the assigned weights $e^{\pm At/2}$ by
$e^{\pm At}$. That produces $Z_{\mathrm{red}}=2\cosh(At)$ and
$\langle X\rangle=\tanh(At)$, and then a false location
$t=\ln3/16$ (or $t=\ln 3$) for mean $1/2$. Sentence (ii) sends
$A\to\infty$ and replaces the analytic tanh by a step, or else
substitutes a sixth-order Landau spinodal / ensemble-equivalence
supporting-line argument, which is not asked.

The argument never takes $A=\infty$, never introduces a Landau
polynomial, and never compares ensembles along supporting lines.
The assigned amplitude $A=8$ is kept finite throughout.

GSM:010528.title: Yukawa OZ kernel C=A e^{-r/ξ}/r in R³, A=1/(4πξ²): S(k)=1/(1+k²ξ²); S=1,1/2,1/5 at k=0,1/ξ,2/ξ; ∫C=1, ∫r²C=6ξ², second-moment length ξ
GSM:010528.objective: Evaluate the three-dimensional Fourier transform of the assigned Yukawa two-point correlation kernel, obtain S(k)=1/(1+k²ξ²), record the listed values and moments, and distinguish this assigned transform from the direct Ornstein-Zernike correlation relation.
GSM:010528.statement:
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ an isotropic two-point correlation kernel is prescribed
as the Yukawa field
\[
C(\mathbf{r})
=A\frac{e^{-r/\xi}}{r},\qquad
A=\frac{1}{4\pi\xi^2},\qquad
r=|\mathbf{r}|,\quad\xi>0.
\]
The structure factor is the Fourier transform
\[
S(\mathbf{k})
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}C(\mathbf{r})\,d^3r.
\]

1. Evaluate the integral and prove $S(k)=1/(1+k^2\xi^2)$, where
   $k=|\mathbf{k}|$.

2. Record the three values
   \[
   S(0)=1,\qquad
   S(1/\xi)=\tfrac12,\qquad
   S(2/\xi)=\tfrac15.
   \]

3. Prove
   \[
   \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}C(\mathbf{r})\,d^3r=1,\qquad
   \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}r^2 C(\mathbf{r})\,d^3r=6\xi^2,
   \]
   and deduce that the isotropic second-moment length defined by
   \[
   \xi_2^2
   =\frac{1}{6}\frac{\int r^2 C\,d^3r}{\int C\,d^3r}
   \]
   equals $\xi^2$ (so the length is $\xi$).

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the three-dimensional Fourier transform
   of $e^{-\kappa r}/r$ is $1/(k^2+\kappa^2)$ without the factor
   $4\pi$, so $S=A/(1+k^2\xi^2)$”; (ii) “$\int r^2 C= \xi^2$ or
   $S(1/\xi)=1/e$, or this is a connected-fluctuation response / Kubo
   / ensemble-sign audit.”

Do not replace the Fourier evaluation by a Kubo formula. Here $C$ is
the assigned correlation kernel whose transform is $S$; it is not the
Ornstein--Zernike direct correlation $c$, for which the usual relation
would instead read $S(k)=1/[1-\rho\widetilde c(k)]$.
permittedResults: The radial Fourier integral $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}e^{-\kappa r}/r\,d^3r$ equals $4\pi/(k^2+\kappa^2)$. With $\kappa=1/\xi$ and $A=1/(4\pi\xi^2)$ this collapses to $1/(1+k^2\xi^2)$.
Isotropy gives $S(k)=S(0)-(k^2/6)\int r^2 C\,d^3r+O(k^4)$. Matching $S(k)=1-\xi^2 k^2+O(k^4)$ forces $\int r^2 C=6\xi^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the three-dimensional Fourier integral to the sine transform of e^{-κr} and multiply by A=1/(4πξ²).
Read ∫C from S(0) and match the k² coefficient 1-ξ² k² against the isotropic second-moment identity.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the Yukawa Fourier transform and obtains S(k)=1/(1+k^2 xi^2).
Records S=1,1/2,1/5 at k=0,1/xi,2/xi together with integral C=1, integral r^2 C=6 xi^2, and second-moment length xi.
Keeps the 4pi factor and refuses a Kubo or connected-fluctuation-response reading.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor 4π in the Fourier transform of e^{-κr}/r and reports S=A/(1+k²ξ²) or S=1/(4πξ²(1+k²ξ²)).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned normalization S(0)=1 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports ∫r²C=ξ² (or 2ξ²) instead of 6ξ², or claims S(1/ξ)=1/e.
commonErrors.consequence: The second-moment length ξ or the exact samples 1, 1/2, 1/5 are lost.

hintTree.content: Align $\mathbf{k}$ with the polar axis and integrate $u=\cos\theta$ first: $\int_{-1}^{1}e^{-ikr u}\,du=2\sin(kr)/(kr)$.
The remaining radial integral is $\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(kr)\,dr=k/(k^2+\kappa^2)$. Multiply by $4\pi A$.
Either expand $S(k)=1/(1+k^2\xi^2)$ or compute $4\pi A\int_0^\infty r^3 e^{-r/\xi}\,dr=4\pi A\cdot 6\xi^4=6\xi^2$.

GSM:010528.canonicalSolution:
Write $\kappa=1/\xi$. The Fourier integral of the Yukawa profile is
radial. Align $\mathbf{k}$ with the polar axis:
\[
\int e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\frac{e^{-\kappa r}}{r}\,d^3r
=2\pi\int_0^\infty r\,e^{-\kappa r}\,dr
\int_{-1}^{1}e^{-ikr u}\,du
=\frac{4\pi}{k}\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(kr)\,dr.
\]
The sine transform is $k/(k^2+\kappa^2)$, so
\[
\int e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\frac{e^{-\kappa r}}{r}\,d^3r
=\frac{4\pi}{k^2+\kappa^2}.
\]
Multiplying by the assigned amplitude
$A=1/(4\pi\xi^2)= \kappa^2/(4\pi)$ yields
\[
S(k)
=\frac{1}{4\pi\xi^2}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{k^2+1/\xi^2}
=\frac{1/\xi^2}{k^2+1/\xi^2}
=\frac{1}{1+k^2\xi^2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{S(k)=1/(1+k^2\xi^2)}.
\]

The three requested samples are
\[
S(0)=1,\qquad
S(1/\xi)=\frac{1}{1+1}=\frac12,\qquad
S(2/\xi)=\frac{1}{1+4}=\frac15.
\]
\[
\boxed{S(0)=1,\;S(1/\xi)=1/2,\;S(2/\xi)=1/5}.
\]

The $k=0$ value is the integral of the kernel:
\[
\int C\,d^3r=S(0)=1.
\]
The second moment may be read from the small-$k$ expansion
\[
S(k)=1-\xi^2 k^2+O(k^4)
\]
together with the isotropic identity
\[
S(k)
=\int C-\frac{k^2}{6}\int r^2 C\,d^3r+O(k^4),
\]
which forces $\int r^2 C=6\xi^2$. Directly,
\[
\int r^2 C\,d^3r
=4\pi A\int_0^\infty r^3 e^{-r/\xi}\,dr
=4\pi A\cdot 6\xi^4
=\frac{1}{\xi^2}\cdot 6\xi^4
=6\xi^2.
\]
The second-moment length therefore satisfies $\xi_2^2=\xi^2$.
\[
\boxed{\int C=1,\;\int r^2 C=6\xi^2,\;\xi_2=\xi}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $4\pi$ in the Yukawa Fourier transform
and reports $S=A/(1+k^2\xi^2)$, which is smaller than the assigned
transform by $4\pi\xi^2$. Sentence (ii) replaces $\int r^2 C=6\xi^2$
by $\xi^2$, or reports $S(1/\xi)=1/e$ as if $C$ itself were being
sampled, or else substitutes a connected-fluctuation response / Kubo
/ ensemble-sign audit, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a Kubo formula or an ensemble
susceptibility. It treats $C$ only as the assigned correlation kernel
whose Fourier transform is $S$, not as the Ornstein--Zernike direct
correlation $c$ (which would obey $S=1/[1-\rho\widetilde c]$).

graderFixtures.proofText: The Fourier transform is $S(k)=1/(1+k^2\xi^2)$, so $S(0)=1$, $S(1/\xi)=1/2$, and $S(2/\xi)=1/5$. Then $\int C=1$, $\int r^2 C=6\xi^2$, and the second-moment length is $\xi$.
The Fourier transform of e^{-κr}/r is 1/(k²+κ²) with no 4π, so I report S=A/(1+k²ξ²) and S(0)=A=1/(4πξ²).
I take ∫r²C=ξ² rather than 6ξ², and I report S(1/ξ)=1/e because the real-space kernel decays as e^{-r/ξ}.

GSM:010529.title: N=4 independent circle angles, nonzero integer m, ρ=∑e^{imθ}: Eρ=0, E|ρ|²=4, E|ρ|⁴=28, Var|ρ|²=12; S=|ρ|²/N has mean 1 and variance 3/4
GSM:010529.objective: For four independent uniform angles and a nonzero integer wave number, compute the first four circular moments of the density mode ρ=∑ e^{imθ_j}, then convert |ρ|² into the intensive structure factor S=|ρ|²/N and record its mean and variance.
GSM:010529.statement:
Four distinguishable ideal-gas particles have independent angles
$\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3,\theta_4$ drawn uniformly from
$[0,2\pi)$. Let $m\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and define the
circular density mode
\[
\rho=\sum_{j=1}^{4}e^{im\theta_j}.
\]
Write $S=|\rho|^2/N$ with $N=4$.

1. Prove $\mathbb{E}[\rho]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]=4$.

2. By classifying the index contractions in
   $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=\sum_{j,k,p,q}\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{im(\theta_j-\theta_k+\theta_p-\theta_q)}\bigr]$,
   prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=2N^2-N=28
   \]
   and therefore $\mathrm{Var}(|\rho|^2)=12$.

3. Deduce
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[S]=1,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(S)=\frac34.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the mode is complex-Gaussian, so Wick
   gives $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=2\bigl(\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]\bigr)^2=32$
   and $\mathrm{Var}(|\rho|^2)=16$”; (ii) “$\mathrm{Var}(S)=12$ or
   $3$, or this is an Einstein-exchange / two-level fluctuation /
   connected-response audit.”

Do not replace the circular-moment count by a Gaussian Wick
contraction, and do not treat the four angles as a two-level system.
permittedResults: If $z$ is uniform on the unit circle, then $\mathbb{E}[z^p\bar z^q]=\delta_{p,q}$ for $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$. Cross terms with a nonzero net winding on any distinct index vanish.

The surviving contractions of four circle variables are the $N$ fully diagonal terms and the $2N(N-1)$ pairings $(j=q,k=p)$ and $(j=k,p=q)$ with two distinct indices. Hence $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=2N^2-N$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand |ρ|⁴ as a four-index sum and keep only the index patterns whose net winding vanishes at every particle.
Convert moments of |ρ|² into moments of S=|ρ|²/N by dividing by N and N² respectively.

milestones.criterion: Proves E[ρ]=0 and E[|ρ|²]=4 from vanishing odd circular moments.
Classifies the fourth-moment contractions to obtain E[|ρ|⁴]=28, Var(|ρ|²)=12, E[S]=1, and Var(S)=3/4.
Refuses a Gaussian Wick contraction and does not drop the N² scaling of Var(S).

commonErrors.description: Treats ρ as complex Gaussian and reports E[|ρ|⁴]=2(E[|ρ|²])²=32, hence Var(|ρ|²)=16.
commonErrors.consequence: The circular correction −N is lost and the assigned fourth moment 28 is replaced by 32.

commonErrors.description: Reports Var(S)=12 or Var(S)=3, forgetting to divide Var(|ρ|²) by N²=16.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned intensive variance 3/4 is lost.

hintTree.content: $\mathbb{E}[e^{im\theta_j}]=0$ because $m\not=0$. Off-diagonal $\mathbb{E}[e^{im(\theta_j-\theta_k)}]=0$ for $j\not=k$.
The pairing $z_j^2\bar z_k^2$ with $j\not=k$ has expectation $0$. The pairings $|z_j|^2|z_k|^2$ survive.

GSM:010529.canonicalSolution:
Write $z_j=e^{im\theta_j}$. Independence and $m\not=0$ give
$\mathbb{E}[z_j]=0$, so $\mathbb{E}[\rho]=0$. Next
\[
|\rho|^2=\sum_{j,k}z_j\bar z_k,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]
=\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}[|z_j|^2]
=N=4,
\]
because every off-diagonal factor $\mathbb{E}[z_j\bar z_k]$ vanishes.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\rho]=0,\quad\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]=4}.
\]

For the fourth moment,
\[
\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]
=\sum_{j,k,p,q}\mathbb{E}\bigl[z_j\bar z_k z_p\bar z_q\bigr].
\]
The expectation equals $1$ if and only if the net winding at every
index is zero, and equals $0$ otherwise. The surviving patterns are:

- all four indices equal: $N$ terms, each $1$;
- $j=q$, $k=p$, and $j\not=k$: $N(N-1)$ terms of
  $\mathbb{E}[|z_j|^2|z_k|^2]=1$;
- $j=k$, $p=q$, and $j\not=p$: $N(N-1)$ terms of
  $\mathbb{E}[|z_j|^2|z_p|^2]=1$.

The pairing $j=p$, $k=q$, $j\not=k$ produces
$\mathbb{E}[z_j^2\bar z_k^2]=0$. Every three-distinct-index and
four-distinct-index pattern has a leftover winding and vanishes.
Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]
=N+2N(N-1)
=2N^2-N
=32-4=28.
\]
\[
\mathrm{Var}(|\rho|^2)
=\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]-\bigl(\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]\bigr)^2
=28-16=12.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=28,\quad\mathrm{Var}(|\rho|^2)=12}.
\]

With $S=|\rho|^2/N=|\rho|^2/4$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[S]=\frac{4}{4}=1,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(S)=\frac{12}{16}=\frac34.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[S]=1,\quad\mathrm{Var}(S)=3/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) treats $\rho$ as a circularly symmetric complex Gaussian
and applies Wick's rule
$\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=2\bigl(\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]\bigr)^2=32$.
That overcounts by the diagonal correction $N$ and produces the false
variance $16$. Sentence (ii) forgets to divide by $N^2$ when passing
from $|\rho|^2$ to $S$, reporting $\mathrm{Var}(S)=12$ or $3$, or else
replaces the count by an Einstein-exchange / two-level fluctuation /
connected-response argument, which is not asked.

The argument never invokes a Gaussian Wick theorem, never introduces
an exchange process, and never treats the four angles as a two-level
system.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\mathbb{E}[\rho]=0$, $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^2]=4$, $\mathbb{E}[|\rho|^4]=28$, and $\mathrm{Var}(|\rho|^2)=12$. For $S=|\rho|^2/4$ one has $\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)=3/4$.
ρ is a complex Gaussian mode, so Wick's rule gives E[|ρ|⁴]=2(E[|ρ|²])²=32 and Var(|ρ|²)=16.
I keep Var(|ρ|²)=12 but I report Var(S)=12, or I divide by N rather than N² and report Var(S)=3.

GSM:010630.title: Hard-core lattice gas on C5, independent-set counts (1,5,5), z=2: Ξ=31; P(N=0,1,2)=(1,10,20)/31; ⟨N⟩=50/31, ⟨N²⟩=90/31, Var=290/961, density=10/31
GSM:010630.objective: From the independent-set enumeration of the 5-cycle, form the grand partition function at activity z=2, the occupation law of N, the first two moments, the variance, and the density ⟨N⟩/5.
GSM:010630.statement:
A hard-core lattice gas lives on the cycle graph $C_5$. Occupied
vertices form an independent set: no two occupied sites may be
adjacent. The independent-set counts by occupation number are
\[
\bigl(\#\{N=0\},\;\#\{N=1\},\;\#\{N=2\}\bigr)=(1,5,5),
\]
and $N\le 2$. The grand partition function at activity $z>0$ is
\[
\Xi=\sum_{N=0}^{2}z^N\cdot\#\{N\}.
\]

1. Set $z=2$ and prove $\Xi=31$.

2. Prove that the occupation law is
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(N=0)=\frac{1}{31},\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(N=1)=\frac{10}{31},\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(N=2)=\frac{20}{31}.
   \]

3. Compute the occupation moments and the density $\rho=\langle N\rangle/5$,
   and prove
   \[
   \langle N\rangle=\frac{50}{31},\qquad
   \langle N^2\rangle=\frac{90}{31},\qquad
   \mathrm{Var}(N)=\frac{290}{961},\qquad
   \rho=\frac{10}{31}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$C_5$ has $\binom{5}{2}=10$ pairs, so
   there are $10$ dimers, $\Xi=1+5\cdot 2+10\cdot 4=51$, and the
   hard-core constraint may be ignored”; (ii) “the density is
   $\langle N\rangle=50/31$ rather than $\langle N\rangle/5$, or the
   variance is $290/31$, or this is a Mayer-graph / virial-van der
   Waals calculation.”

Do not replace the $C_5$ enumeration by a Mayer-cluster expansion,
and do not admit adjacent occupations.
permittedResults: On $C_5$ the five adjacent pairs are forbidden, leaving exactly five independent dimers (the distance-$2$ pairs). Thus $\Xi=1+5z+5z^2$.
At $z=2$, $\langle N\rangle=(5z+10z^2)/\Xi=50/31$ and $\langle N^2\rangle=(5z+20z^2)/\Xi=90/31$. The variance numerator is $90\cdot 31-50^2=290$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write Ξ=1+5z+5z², substitute z=2, and read P(N) as the normalized monomials.
Compute ⟨N⟩ and ⟨N²⟩ from the same weighted counts, subtract on the common denominator 961, and divide the mean by 5.

milestones.criterion: Forms Ξ=1+5z+5z²=31 at z=2 from the independent-set counts (1,5,5).
Refuses adjacent dimers and does not replace the count by a Mayer or van der Waals argument.

commonErrors.description: Counts all ten vertex pairs as legal dimers, writing Ξ=1+10+40=51.
commonErrors.consequence: The hard-core constraint on C5 is dropped and every assigned probability is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Reports the density as ⟨N⟩=50/31 instead of ⟨N⟩/5=10/31, or leaves Var(N)=290/31.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned density 10/31 or the reduced variance 290/961 is lost.

hintTree.content: $\Xi=1+5\cdot 2+5\cdot 4=1+10+20=31$. Adjacent pairs are absent from the count $(1,5,5)$.
The $N=2$ weight is $5\cdot 4=20$, so $\mathbb{P}(N=2)=20/31$.

GSM:010630.canonicalSolution:
The assigned independent-set counts give
\[
\Xi=1+5z+5z^2.
\]
At $z=2$,
\[
\Xi=1+10+20=31.
\]
(The five $N=2$ configurations are the distance-$2$ pairs on $C_5$;
the five adjacent pairs are excluded by the hard core.)
\[
\boxed{\Xi=31}.
\]

The occupation probabilities are the normalized weights
\[
\mathbb{P}(N=0)=\frac{1}{31},\qquad
\mathbb{P}(N=1)=\frac{5\cdot 2}{31}=\frac{10}{31},\qquad
\mathbb{P}(N=2)=\frac{5\cdot 4}{31}=\frac{20}{31}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(N=0,1,2)=(1,10,20)/31}.
\]

The moments are
\[
\langle N\rangle
=\frac{1\cdot 10+2\cdot 20}{31}
=\frac{50}{31},
\]
\[
\langle N^2\rangle
=\frac{1\cdot 10+4\cdot 20}{31}
=\frac{90}{31}.
\]
The variance is
\[
\mathrm{Var}(N)
=\frac{90}{31}-\left(\frac{50}{31}\right)^2
=\frac{90\cdot 31-2500}{961}
=\frac{2790-2500}{961}
=\frac{290}{961}.
\]
The density on five sites is
\[
\rho=\frac{\langle N\rangle}{5}=\frac{10}{31}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle N\rangle=50/31,\;
\langle N^2\rangle=90/31,\;
\mathrm{Var}(N)=290/961,\;
\rho=10/31}.
\]

Sentence (i) counts all $\binom{5}{2}=10$ pairs as legal dimers and
produces $\Xi=1+10+40=51$, destroying the hard-core constraint.
Sentence (ii) reports the extensive mean $50/31$ as if it were the
density, or leaves the variance as the unreduced fraction $290/31$,
or else replaces the enumeration by a Mayer-graph cancellation /
virial-van der Waals argument, which is not asked.

The argument never generates a Mayer cluster series, never introduces
a van der Waals loop, and never occupies adjacent vertices of $C_5$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Independent-set weights at $z=2$ give $\Xi=31$ and $\mathbb{P}(N=0,1,2)=(1,10,20)/31$. Then $\langle N\rangle=50/31$, $\langle N^2\rangle=90/31$, $\mathrm{Var}(N)=290/961$, and $\rho=10/31$.
C5 has binom(5,2)=10 pairs, so I count 10 dimers, write Ξ=1+5*2+10*4=51, and ignore the hard-core constraint.
I report the density as ⟨N⟩=50/31 rather than ⟨N⟩/5=10/31, and I leave the variance as 290/31.

GSM:010631.title: q=3 Potts triangle, e^{βJ}=2: classes (all-same 3, B=3), (two-same 18, B=1), (all-different 6, B=0); Z=66, probs 4/11,6/11,1/11; ⟨B⟩=18/11, ⟨B²⟩=42/11, var=138/121, U=-18J/11, C/kB=(138/121)(ln2)²=0.5479546770306759
GSM:010631.objective: Enumerate the three spin classes of the q=3 Potts model on a triangle at e^{βJ}=2, form Z and the class probabilities, then compute the bond-count moments, the energy, and the heat capacity C/k_B.
GSM:010631.statement:
The $q=3$ Potts model on the complete graph $K_3$ (a triangle) has
Hamiltonian
\[
H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\delta_{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=-JB,
\]
where $B$ is the number of agreeing edges and each spin takes values
in $\{1,2,3\}$. The assigned coupling is $e^{\beta J}=2$. The
$3^3=27$ configurations fall into three classes:

- all three spins equal: $3$ configurations, $B=3$;
- exactly two spins equal: $18$ configurations, $B=1$;
- all three spins distinct: $6$ configurations, $B=0$.

1. Form the partition function and prove $Z=66$. Then prove that the
   three class probabilities are $4/11$, $6/11$, and $1/11$
   respectively.

2. Prove
   \[
   \langle B\rangle=\frac{18}{11},\qquad
   \langle B^2\rangle=\frac{42}{11},\qquad
   \mathrm{Var}(B)=\frac{138}{121}.
   \]

3. Deduce the internal energy and the heat capacity,
   \[
   U=\langle H\rangle=-\frac{18J}{11},\qquad
   \frac{C}{k_B}
   =\frac{138}{121}(\ln 2)^2
   =0.5479546770306759.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a two-same configuration still has two
   agreeing edges incident to the majority pair, so $B=2$ on that
   class and $Z=3\cdot 8+18\cdot 4+6=78$”; (ii) “$C/k_B=138/121$ or
   $(\ln 2)\cdot 138/121$, or this is an Ising transfer-matrix /
   absence-of-finite-temperature-order argument.”

Do not replace the triangle enumeration by a transfer matrix, and do
not recode the model as $q=2$ Ising.
permittedResults: The class weights are $3(e^{\beta J})^3$, $18\,e^{\beta J}$, and $6$. At $e^{\beta J}=2$ these are $24$, $36$, and $6$, summing to $Z=66$.
$\langle B\rangle=(3\cdot 24+1\cdot 36)/66=18/11$ and $\langle B^2\rangle=(9\cdot 24+1\cdot 36)/66=42/11$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(B)=(42\cdot 11-18^2)/121=138/121$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Weight each class by (e^{βJ})^B times its configuration count, then normalize by Z=66.
Convert bond-count moments into U=-J⟨B⟩ and C/k_B=(ln 2)^2 Var(B) from e^{βJ}=2.

milestones.criterion: Enumerates the three classes with B=3,1,0 and obtains Z=66 with probabilities 4/11, 6/11, 1/11.
Keeps B=1 on the two-same class and refuses an Ising transfer-matrix reading.

commonErrors.description: Assigns B=2 to the two-same class, writing Z=3·8+18·4+6=78 and destroying every subsequent moment.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned partition function 66 and the moments 18/11, 42/11 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports C/k_B=138/121 or C/k_B=(ln 2)·138/121, dropping or mis-powering the factor (βJ)^2=(ln 2)^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned value (138/121)(ln 2)^2=0.5479546770306759 is lost.

hintTree.content: All-same weight $3\cdot 2^3=24$. Two-same weight $18\cdot 2=36$. All-different weight $6$. Sum $66$.

GSM:010631.canonicalSolution:
The three class weights at $e^{\beta J}=2$ are
\[
3\cdot 2^3=24,\qquad 18\cdot 2=36,\qquad 6\cdot 1=6.
\]
Hence
\[
Z=24+36+6=66.
\]
The class probabilities are
\[
\frac{24}{66}=\frac{4}{11},\qquad
\frac{36}{66}=\frac{6}{11},\qquad
\frac{6}{66}=\frac{1}{11}.
\]
(The configuration counts $3+18+6=27$ exhaust the $3^3$ colourings.)
\[
\boxed{Z=66,\quad
\mathbb{P}(\text{all-same},\;\text{two-same},\;\text{all-different})
=(4/11,\;6/11,\;1/11)}.
\]

Bond-count moments use the class values $B=3,1,0$:
\[
\langle B\rangle
=\frac{3\cdot 24+1\cdot 36+0\cdot 6}{66}
=\frac{108}{66}
=\frac{18}{11},
\]
\[
\langle B^2\rangle
=\frac{9\cdot 24+1\cdot 36}{66}
=\frac{252}{66}
=\frac{42}{11}.
\]
\[
\mathrm{Var}(B)
=\frac{42}{11}-\left(\frac{18}{11}\right)^2
=\frac{462-324}{121}
=\frac{138}{121}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle B\rangle=18/11,\;
\langle B^2\rangle=42/11,\;
\mathrm{Var}(B)=138/121}.
\]

The energy is $U=-J\langle B\rangle=-18J/11$. Because
$e^{\beta J}=2$ one has $\beta J=\ln 2$, so
\[
\frac{C}{k_B}
=\beta^2\mathrm{Var}(H)
=(\beta J)^2\mathrm{Var}(B)
=\frac{138}{121}(\ln 2)^2
=0.5479546770306759.
\]
\[
\boxed{U=-18J/11,\quad
C/k_B=(138/121)(\ln 2)^2=0.5479546770306759}.
\]

Sentence (i) assigns $B=2$ to the two-same class, as if both edges
out of a majority pair agreed with the singleton. That replaces the
two-same weight $18\cdot 2$ by $18\cdot 4$ and produces the false
partition function $78$. Sentence (ii) drops the factor $(\beta J)^2$
or replaces it by $\ln 2$, or else substitutes an Ising
transfer-matrix argument for the absence of finite-temperature order,
which is not asked.

The argument never builds a transfer matrix, never sets $q=2$, and
never claims a finite-temperature ordering transition.

graderFixtures.proofText: A two-same colouring has two agreeing edges, so I set B=2 on that class and obtain Z=3*8+18*4+6=78.
I identify C/k_B with Var(B)=138/121, or I multiply by only one factor of ln 2 instead of (ln 2)^2.
