MMP:010623.title: The triple box convolution B=χ*χ*χ equals 3/4-x^2 on |x|≤1/2 and has variance 1/4
MMP:010623.objective: For χ=1_[-1/2,1/2] and B=χ*χ*χ, prove B=3/4-x^2 on |x|≤1/2, B=(1/2)(3/2-|x|)^2 on 1/2≤|x|≤3/2, B=0 outside, support [-3/2,3/2], B(0)=3/4, B(1)=1/8, mass 1, mean 0, variance 1/4, and that B is C^1 but not C^2 with matching at the breakpoints.
MMP:010623.statement:
Let $\chi=1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ be the unit-mass indicator of the centred
half-interval, and let $B=\chi*\chi*\chi$ be the triple convolution
(the centred quadratic cardinal $B$-spline generated by $\chi$).
Work with ordinary $L^{1}$ convolution on $\mathbb{R}$. Do not replace
$B$ by a point-load pairing, a weak variational jump identity, or a
Dirichlet Green function.

1. Prove the compact piecewise formula
   \[
   B(x)=\begin{cases}
   \dfrac34-x^{2}, & |x|\le \dfrac12,\\[4pt]
   \dfrac12\Bigl(\dfrac32-|x|\Bigr)^{2}, & \dfrac12\le |x|\le \dfrac32,\\[4pt]
   0, & |x|\ge \dfrac32.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   Conclude that $\operatorname{supp}B=[-3/2,3/2]$, $B(0)=3/4$, and
   $B(1)=1/8$.

2. Prove that $B$ has mass $1$, mean $0$, and variance $1/4$.

3. Prove that $B$ is $C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ but not $C^{2}$: the pieces
   and first derivatives match at $x=\pm 1/2$ and $x=\pm 3/2$, while
   the second derivative jumps (from $-2$ to $+1$ at $x=1/2+$ after
   the even reflection).

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$B$ is the single tent $\chi*\chi$, or
   the four-fold cubic spline $\chi^{*4}$”; (ii) “$B$ is $C^{2}$, or
   the variance is the single-box value $1/12$.”

Do not replace the convolution by a point-load distribution or an
exact derivative jump, and do not invoke a Fourier-normalization or
Gaussian-Parseval ledger.
permittedResults: For $|x|\le 1/2$ the integrand $1-|x-t|$ never leaves $[-1,1]$ on $t\in[-1/2,1/2]$, and the split at $t=x$ produces $B(x)=3/4-x^{2}$. For $1/2\le x\le 3/2$ the same integral collapses to $(1/2)(3/2-x)^{2}$.

Independence of summands gives $\operatorname{Var}(B)=3\operatorname{Var}(\chi)=3\cdot(1^{2}/12)=1/4$. Matching $B$ and $B'$ at $x=1/2$ (both equal to $1/2$ and $-1$) with $B''$ jumping from $-2$ to $+1$ shows $C^{1}$ but not $C^{2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Average the tent χ*χ against the remaining box, split at the knots x=1/2 and x=3/2, then read mass/mean/variance from three independent Unif[-1/2,1/2] summands.
Check the special values B(0)=3/4 and B(1)=1/8 first as a consistency filter, then match B and B' at the knots and compare B'' across x=1/2.

milestones.criterion: Reports the piecewise formula, support [-3/2,3/2], B(0)=3/4, and B(1)=1/8.
Reports mass 1, mean 0, variance 1/4, and C^1-not-C^2 matching at the breakpoints.
Rejects a tent/cubic or C^2/variance-1/12 reading, and refuses reserved point-load, derivative-jump, or Fourier-Parseval substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Identifies B with the single tent χ*χ or with the four-fold cubic χ^{*4}, or writes a piecewise formula that is not 3/4-x^2 on |x|<=1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required B(0)=3/4, B(1)=1/8, and support [-3/2,3/2] quadratic pieces are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that B is C^2, or reports the variance as the single-box value 1/12 (or as 1/2) instead of 1/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The required moment triple (mass 1, mean 0, variance 1/4) and the C^1-not-C^2 matching statement are replaced.

hintTree.content: First form the tent $\chi*\chi(x)=(1-|x|)_{+}$ on $[-1,1]$, then average it against $\chi$ on an interval of length $1$.
Evenness reduces the pieces to $x\ge 0$. The breakpoint $x=1/2$ is where the tent knot $x-t=\pm 1$ first meets the integration window.
Variance is faster as a sum of independent Unif$[-1/2,1/2]$ random variables than as an explicit $\int x^{2}B(x)\,dx$, but both give $1/4$.

MMP:010623.canonicalSolution:
The box $\chi=1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ has mass $1$. Its self-convolution is
the tent
\[
\Lambda(x)=(\chi*\chi)(x)=(1-|x|)_{+},
\qquad\operatorname{supp}\Lambda=[-1,1].
\]
The triple convolution is the sliding average
\[
B(x)=(\Lambda*\chi)(x)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\Lambda(x-t)\,dt.
\]
The function $B$ is even. Support addition gives
$\operatorname{supp}B=[-3/2,3/2]$, so $B(x)=0$ for $|x|\ge 3/2$.

On $0\le x\le 1/2$ the window $[x-1/2,x+1/2]$ lies inside $[-1,1]$.
Splitting at the tent peak $t=x$ produces
\begin{align*}
B(x)
&=\int_{-1/2}^{x}\bigl(1-(x-t)\bigr)\,dt
+\int_{x}^{1/2}\bigl(1-(t-x)\bigr)\,dt
=\frac34-x^{2}.
\end{align*}
On $1/2\le x\le 3/2$ the tent is nonzero only for $t\ge x-1$, and
$x-t\ge 0$, so
\[
B(x)=\int_{x-1}^{1/2}\bigl(1-(x-t)\bigr)\,dt
=\frac12\Bigl(\frac32-x\Bigr)^{2}.
\]
Evenness extends the outer piece to $1/2\le |x|\le 3/2$.
\[
\boxed{B=3/4-x^{2}\ (|x|\le 1/2);\quad
B=(1/2)(3/2-|x|)^{2}\ (1/2\le |x|\le 3/2)}.
\]
Special values:
\[
B(0)=\frac34,\qquad
B(1)=\frac12\Bigl(\frac32-1\Bigr)^{2}=\frac18,\qquad
\operatorname{supp}B=\Bigl[-\frac32,\frac32\Bigr].
\]
\[
\boxed{B(0)=3/4,\;B(1)=1/8,\;\operatorname{supp}B=[-3/2,3/2]}.
\]

Mass, mean, and variance follow from convolution of measures (or from
the law of the sum of three independent Unif$[-1/2,1/2]$ random
variables):
\[
\int B=1,\qquad
\int xB(x)\,dx=0,\qquad
\int x^{2}B(x)\,dx=3\cdot\frac{1^{2}}{12}=\frac14.
\]
An explicit check of the mass on the two pieces is
\[
2\int_{0}^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac34-x^{2}\Bigr)dx
+2\int_{1/2}^{3/2}\frac12\Bigl(\frac32-x\Bigr)^{2}dx
=2\Bigl(\frac13+\frac16\Bigr)=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{mass }=1,\;\text{mean }=0,\;\text{variance }=1/4}.
\]

At the inner knot $x=1/2$ both pieces give $B=1/2$. The inner
derivative is $B'=-2x$, hence $B'(1/2-)=-1$; the outer derivative
is $B'=-(3/2-x)$ for $x>1/2$, hence $B'(1/2+)=-1$. At $x=3/2$ both
$B$ and $B'$ vanish. Thus $B\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$. The second
derivative jumps from $B''=-2$ on $(0,1/2)$ to $B''=+1$ on
$(1/2,3/2)$, so $B\notin C^{2}$. The same matching holds at the
negative knots by evenness of $B$ and oddness of $B'$.
\[
\boxed{B\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})\setminus C^{2}(\mathbb{R})
\text{ with breakpoint matching}}.
\]

Sentence (i) stops at the tent $\chi*\chi$ (or continues to the cubic
$\chi^{*4}$) and never produces $B(0)=3/4$. Sentence (ii) claims
$C^{2}$ regularity or reports the single-box variance $1/12$. Neither
recovers the piecewise quadratic and the moment triple $(1,0,1/4)$.

The argument never writes a point-load pairing, a weak derivative
jump, a Dirichlet Green function, or a Fourier/Parseval ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: $B=\chi*\chi*\chi$ equals $3/4-x^{2}$ on $|x|\le 1/2$ and $(1/2)(3/2-|x|)^{2}$ on $1/2\le |x|\le 3/2$, with support $[-3/2,3/2]$, $B(0)=3/4$, and $B(1)=1/8$. Mass $1$, mean $0$, variance $1/4$. The pieces match $C^{1}$ but not $C^{2}$ at $\pm 1/2$ and $\pm 3/2$.
B is the tent χ*χ, or else the cubic four-fold convolution. I do not report B=3/4-x^2 on |x|<=1/2, B(0)=3/4, or B(1)=1/8.
The triple convolution is C^2, and its variance is the single-box value 1/12. I do not accept variance 1/4 or a C^1-not-C^2 matching statement.

MMP:010624.title: PV(1/x) equals D(log|x|), annihilates e^{-x^2}, and pairs x e^{-x^2} to sqrt(pi)
MMP:010624.objective: For T=PV(1/x), prove <T,phi>=int_0^infty[phi(x)-phi(-x)]/x dx, D(log|x|)=T, xT=1, <T,e^{-x^2}>=0, and <T,x e^{-x^2}>=sqrt(pi), using symmetric-cutoff cancellation and distinguishing PV from divergent one-sided integrals.
MMP:010624.statement:
Let $T=\operatorname{PV}(1/x)$ act on Schwartz test functions by the
Cauchy principal-value pairing. Distinguish this finite pairing from
the divergent one-sided integrals $\int_{0}^{1}dx/x$ and
$\int_{0}^{\infty}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$. Do not replace $T$ by a
point-load $\delta$, a weak variational jump, or a Dirichlet Green
derivative.

1. Prove the symmetric-cutoff identity
   \[
   \langle T,\varphi\rangle
   =\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)}{x}\,dx.
   \]

2. Prove the distributional identities
   \[
   D(\log|x|)=T,\qquad xT=1.
   \]
   The derivative identity requires a symmetric cutoff: the boundary
   terms $\log\varepsilon\,(\varphi(\varepsilon)-\varphi(-\varepsilon))$
   vanish as $O(\varepsilon\log\varepsilon)$, whereas a one-sided cutoff
   produces a divergent $\log\varepsilon$ remainder.

3. Evaluate the Gaussian pairings
   \[
   \langle T,e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=0,\qquad
   \langle T,x e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=\sqrt{\pi}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the pairing is the one-sided integral
   $\int_{0}^{\infty}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$, which may be assigned
   $\infty$”; (ii) “$T$ is odd, so both Gaussian pairings vanish, or
   else $D(\log|x|)$ fails to exist.”

Do not replace the PV calculus by a point-load jump identity, and do
not invoke a Fourier-normalization or Laplace-boundary ledger.
permittedResults: The substitution $x\mapsto -x$ on the negative half-line converts the two-sided PV cutoff into $\int_{0}^{\infty}(\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x))/x\,dx$. If $\varphi$ is even the integrand vanishes; if $\varphi$ is odd it doubles.

Integration by parts on $\{|x|\ge\varepsilon\}$ produces the boundary remainder $\log\varepsilon\,(\varphi(\varepsilon)-\varphi(-\varepsilon))=O(\varepsilon\log\varepsilon)\to 0$, hence $D(\log|x|)=T$. The odd pairing $\langle T,x e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}}dx=\sqrt{\pi}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert the two-sided PV cutoff by x=-u on the negative axis, then integrate log|x| by parts with a symmetric epsilon and evaluate the two Gaussians from even/odd reductions.
Obtain xT=1 first and reuse it as <T,x e^{-x^2}>=<1,e^{-x^2}>=sqrt(pi), while checking that the log-derivative boundary term is O(eps log eps).

milestones.criterion: Reports the symmetric pairing <T,phi>=int_0^infty[phi(x)-phi(-x)]/x dx together with D(log|x|)=T and xT=1.
Reports <T,e^{-x^2}>=0 and <T,x e^{-x^2}>=sqrt(pi), citing symmetric-cutoff cancellation versus divergent one-sided integrals.
Rejects a one-sided or parity-reversed reading, and refuses reserved point-load, derivative-jump, or Fourier/Laplace substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the PV pairing by a one-sided integral int_0^infty phi(x)/x dx or int_0^1 dx/x, or omits the odd combination phi(x)-phi(-x).
commonErrors.consequence: The finite pairing, the identity D(log|x|)=T, and the Gaussian values 0 and sqrt(pi) are replaced by a divergent integral.

commonErrors.description: Claims both Gaussian pairings vanish because T is odd, swaps the two values, or asserts that D(log|x|) does not exist as a distribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pairings <T,e^{-x^2}>=0 and <T,x e^{-x^2}>=sqrt(pi), or the identity D(log|x|)=T, are lost.

hintTree.content: On the negative axis set $x=-u$ inside $\int_{|x|\ge\varepsilon}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$. The two halves combine into a single integral from $\varepsilon$ to $\infty$.
The combination $\varphi(\varepsilon)-\varphi(-\varepsilon)$ is $O(\varepsilon)$, which beats $\log\varepsilon$. A one-sided cutoff leaves a bare $\log\varepsilon$ and does not define $D(\log|x|)$.
$e^{-x^{2}}$ is even, so the PV integrand vanishes. For $x e^{-x^{2}}$ the integrand becomes $2e^{-x^{2}}$.

MMP:010624.canonicalSolution:
By definition
\[
\langle T,\varphi\rangle
=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^{+}}
\int_{|x|\ge\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}\,dx.
\]
Split the integral at $\pm\varepsilon$ and substitute $x=-u$ on
$(-\infty,-\varepsilon]$:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}\,dx
=-\int_{\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(-u)}{u}\,du.
\]
Adding the positive half produces
\[
\langle T,\varphi\rangle
=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)}{x}\,dx.
\]
The integrand is $O(1)$ near the origin because
$\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)=2x\varphi'(0)+O(x^{3})$. A one-sided integral
$\int_{0}^{\infty}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ lacks this cancellation and
diverges logarithmically whenever $\varphi(0)\neq 0$.
\[
\boxed{\langle T,\varphi\rangle
=\int_{0}^{\infty}[\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)]/x\,dx}.
\]

For the log-derivative, integrate by parts on the symmetric set
$\{|x|\ge\varepsilon\}$ (test functions vanish at infinity):
\begin{align*}
-\int_{|x|\ge\varepsilon}\log|x|\,\varphi'(x)\,dx
&=\log\varepsilon\bigl(\varphi(\varepsilon)-\varphi(-\varepsilon)\bigr)
+\int_{|x|\ge\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}\,dx.
\end{align*}
Here $\varphi(\varepsilon)-\varphi(-\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon)$, so
the boundary remainder is $O(\varepsilon\log\varepsilon)\to 0$. The
remaining integral tends to $\langle T,\varphi\rangle$. A one-sided
cutoff would leave an uncancelled $\log\varepsilon\,\varphi(\varepsilon)$
and would not define a distribution. Therefore
\[
D(\log|x|)=T.
\]
The product identity uses the same pairing:
\[
\langle xT,\varphi\rangle
=\langle T,x\varphi\rangle
=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x\varphi(x)-(-x)\varphi(-x)}{x}\,dx
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\varphi=\langle 1,\varphi\rangle,
\]
so $xT=1$.
\[
\boxed{D(\log|x|)=T,\qquad xT=1}.
\]

The Gaussian $e^{-x^{2}}$ is even, so $\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)=0$ and
\[
\langle T,e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=0.
\]
The function $x e^{-x^{2}}$ is odd, so
$\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)=2x e^{-x^{2}}$ and
\[
\langle T,x e^{-x^{2}}\rangle
=2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}}\,dx
=\sqrt{\pi}.
\]
(The same evaluation is $\langle 1,e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=\sqrt{\pi}$ via
$xT=1$.) Oddness of $T$ does \emph{not} force the second pairing to
vanish: an odd distribution paired against an odd test function is
the pairing of an even density.
\[
\boxed{\langle T,e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=0,\;
\langle T,x e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=\sqrt{\pi}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the odd combination and treats a divergent
one-sided integral as if it were $T$. Sentence (ii) misreads the
parity of $T$ or denies the existence of $D(\log|x|)$. Neither
recovers both Gaussian values and the identities $D(\log|x|)=T$,
$xT=1$.

The argument never introduces a point-load $\delta$, a variational
derivative jump, a Dirichlet Green function, or a Fourier/Laplace
normalization ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Cauchy pairing is $\langle T,\varphi\rangle=\int_{0}^{\infty}[\varphi(x)-\varphi(-x)]/x\,dx$. Symmetric-cutoff integration by parts gives $D(\log|x|)=T$, and $xT=1$. Then $\langle T,e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=0$ and $\langle T,x e^{-x^{2}}\rangle=\sqrt{\pi}$. One-sided integrals $\int_{0}^{\infty}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ diverge and are not $T$.
I pair T by the one-sided integral int_0^infty phi(x)/x dx, which I allow to diverge. I do not form the odd combination [phi(x)-phi(-x)]/x and I do not accept a finite <T,e^{-x^2}>=0.
T is odd, so both Gaussian pairings vanish, and D(log|x|) does not exist. I do not report <T,x e^{-x^2}>=sqrt(pi) or the identity D(log|x|)=T.

MSTAT:010118.title: Helmert coordinates turn an unknown scale into a $t$-pivot
MSTAT:010118.objective: Use an orthogonal Helmert map to prove that the normal sample mean is independent of the sample variance, identify the Student $t$ pivot, and invert it without plugging $S$ into a $z$-interval.
MSTAT:010118.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ observations, now with both $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$ unknown. Write
$$
\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,
\qquad
S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2.
$$
Construct an orthogonal Helmert transformation $Y=HX$ whose first coordinate is $Y_1=\sqrt n\,\bar X$ and whose remaining coordinates are mean-zero contrasts. Prove that $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n$ are independent normals, that
$$
\sum_{i=2}^n Y_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,
$$
and therefore that $\bar X$ is independent of $S^2$ with
$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$
Deduce the exact law of the Student pivot
$$
T=\frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)}{S}.
$$
Invert $|T|\le t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ to obtain a confidence interval for $\mu$, and explain why replacing $\sigma$ by $S$ inside the known-scale $z$-interval, while still quoting $N(0,1)$ quantiles, is invalid.
permittedResults: An orthogonal image of a spherical normal vector is again independent normal, with the same scale and with mean $H\mathbb E[X]$.
A sum of squares of $\nu$ independent standard normals is $\chi^2_\nu$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply a Helmert orthogonal transformation and read independence and the chi-square residual law from the image covariance.
Use the residual projector I-n^{-1}11^T, identify its rank-n-1 Wishart/chi-square law, and form the t ratio from the independent mean coordinate.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Proves mean-variance independence from an orthogonal normal map and inverts the resulting Student pivot rather than a plugged-in z-pivot.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that the sample mean and sample variance are independent for every iid sample, or skips the orthogonal-normal argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The Student representation is not justified, and the claimed t law may be false.

commonErrors.description: Replaces σ by S in the z-pivot but continues to use N(0,1) critical values.
commonErrors.consequence: The interval is too short and does not have exact coverage 1-α.

hintTree.content: The listed Helmert rows are orthonormal, and every row after the first is orthogonal to $(1,\ldots,1)$.
Independence of the $Y_k$ transfers to independence of $Y_1$ and $\sum_{k\ge2}Y_k^2$, which is the residual sum of squares.
Write $T$ as a standard normal divided by the root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom.

MSTAT:010118.canonicalSolution:
Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^\top$. The stated Helmert matrix $H$ has orthonormal rows: the first row is $n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)$, and the $k$th row is a contrast orthogonal to the all-ones vector. Thus $H$ is orthogonal and $Y=HX$ satisfies
$$
Y_1=\sqrt n\,\bar X,
\qquad
\sum_{i=2}^n Y_i^2=\|Y\|^2-Y_1^2=\|X\|^2-n\bar X^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2.
$$

Because $X\sim N(\mu\mathbf 1,\sigma^2 I_n)$ and $H$ is orthogonal,
$$
Y\sim N(\mu H\mathbf 1,\sigma^2 I_n).
$$
Now $H\mathbf 1=(\sqrt n,0,\ldots,0)^\top$, so
$$
Y_1\sim N(\sqrt n\,\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad
Y_2,\ldots,Y_n\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$
are mutually independent. Therefore $\bar X=Y_1/\sqrt n$ is independent of
$\sum_{i=2}^n Y_i^2=(n-1)S^2$, and
$$
\boxed{
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}
=\sum_{i=2}^n\Bigl(\frac{Y_i}{\sigma}\Bigr)^2
\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
}
$$

The known-scale $z$-pivot is
$Z=\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)$, and $Z$ is a function of $Y_1$ only, hence independent of $S^2$. The Student ratio is
$$
T
=\frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)}{S}
=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}/(n-1)}}.
$$
The definition of the $t$ family therefore gives
$$
\boxed{T\sim t_{n-1}}.
$$
In particular $T$ is a pivot: its law does not depend on $(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

Let $t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ be the upper $\alpha/2$ quantile of $t_{n-1}$. Then
$$
P\bigl(|T|\le t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\bigr)=1-\alpha,
$$
which rearranges, because $S>0$ almost surely, to
$$
\boxed{
\bar X-t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n}
\le\mu\le
\bar X+t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n}.
}
$$
The same algebra as in the known-scale case produces the displayed order of endpoints.

Replacing $\sigma$ by $S$ inside $Z$ and still quoting $z_{\alpha/2}$ would pretend that
$\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)/S$ is standard normal. That random variable is $T$, whose tails are heavier than $N(0,1)$ for every finite $n$. The resulting interval therefore has coverage strictly below $1-\alpha$. Independence of $\bar X$ and $S^2$ is a normal-sample fact used to identify the $t$ law; it is not a license to ignore the extra randomness in $S$.

graderFixtures.proofText: A Helmert map sends the normal sample to independent normals with only the first mean nonzero. The residual sum of squares is (n-1)S^2 and is independent of Xbar, so (n-1)S^2/σ^2 ~ χ^2_{n-1} and T = √n (Xbar-μ)/S ~ t_{n-1}. The inverted interval uses t quantiles, not z quantiles with S plugged in.
For any iid sample with finite variance, Xbar and S^2 are independent, so the t representation holds without using normality or a Helmert map.
Because S estimates σ, the interval Xbar ± z_{α/2} S/√n still has exact coverage 1-α by the ordinary normal tail calculation.

MSTAT:010126.title: A Cauchy mean is another Cauchy, so the average does not settle
MSTAT:010126.objective: Identify the exact law of the Cauchy sample mean from characteristic functions, conclude that it is inconsistent, and contrast it with the regular score equation for the location MLE.
MSTAT:010126.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent Cauchy random variables with location $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and known scale $1$, each having density
$$
f_\theta(x)=\frac1{\pi\bigl(1+(x-\theta)^2\bigr)},
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$
Using characteristic functions, prove that $\bar X$ has exactly the same Cauchy$(\theta,1)$ law for every $n\ge1$. Conclude that $\bar X$ is not consistent for $\theta$ and that the ordinary CLT-plus-WLLN justification for the sample mean does not apply. Explain why a method-of-moments estimator based on $\mathbb E[X_1]$ is not defined.

Write the log-likelihood and the score equation for the MLE of $\theta$. Prove that the one-observation score is bounded and that its expectation is zero, and compute the one-observation Fisher information
$$
I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\bigl[(\partial_\theta\log f_\theta(X))^2\bigr].
$$
(The value is the constant $1/2$.) Contrast this regular score behavior with the inconsistent sample mean. Do not construct a Neyman–Pearson test of $\theta=\theta_0$, and do not replace the model by $N(\theta,1)$.
permittedResults: Independent sums multiply characteristic functions. Equality of characteristic functions determines the law.
The substitution $u=x-\theta$ shows that every location functional of the standard Cauchy score is parameter-free.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply characteristic functions for the mean, then compute the score and information by translation to the standard Cauchy.
Use the stability of the Cauchy family under averages, then differentiate under the integrable Cauchy density to center the score.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Proves the sample mean is exactly Cauchy and inconsistent, while the location score remains regular with information 1/2.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Invokes the WLLN or CLT to claim that Xbar is consistent or asymptotically N(θ,σ^2/n) for the Cauchy sample.
commonErrors.consequence: Moment hypotheses that the Cauchy law fails are assumed, and the exact non-concentrating law is missed.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Cauchy density by a N(θ,1) model and quotes information 1 or the z-pivot for the mean.
commonErrors.consequence: The problem is changed into the ordinary normal-mean packet already treated in the z-family.

hintTree.content: The characteristic function of $\bar X$ is $[\varphi(t/n)]^n$.
The Cauchy density has tails $1/(\pi x^2)$, so $\mathbb E|X|$ diverges.
The score is $2(X-\theta)/(1+(X-\theta)^2)$, whose square integrates to $1/2$ against the Cauchy density.

MSTAT:010126.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic function of each $X_j$ is $e^{it\theta-|t|}$. Independence therefore gives
$$
\mathbb E_\theta[e^{it\bar X}]
=\bigl(e^{i(t/n)\theta-|t|/n}\bigr)^n
=e^{it\theta-|t|}.
$$
Hence $\bar X$ is exactly Cauchy$(\theta,1)$ for every $n$. In particular the law of $\bar X$ does not concentrate: for any $\varepsilon>0$,
$$
P_\theta(|\bar X-\theta|>\varepsilon)
=1-\frac2\pi\arctan(\varepsilon)
$$
is independent of $n$ and is not zero. Therefore $\bar X$ is not consistent. The WLLN and CLT require a finite mean (and, for the CLT, a finite variance). A standard Cauchy random variable has neither: the integral $\int |x|/(\pi(1+x^2))\,dx$ diverges, so a moment estimator based on $\mathbb E[X_1]$ is undefined.

The log-density is $-\log\pi-\log\bigl(1+(x-\theta)^2\bigr)$, so the score is
$$
\boxed{
U(\theta;x)
=\frac{2(x-\theta)}{1+(x-\theta)^2}.
}
$$
The function $u\mapsto 2u/(1+u^2)$ is bounded by $1$ in absolute value. Integrating against the Cauchy density and using oddness of the score about $\theta$ gives
$\mathbb E_\theta[U(\theta;X)]=0$. A direct substitution $u=x-\theta$ yields
$$
I(\theta)
=\int_{-\infty}^\infty
\frac{4u^2}{(1+u^2)^2}\cdot\frac{du}{\pi(1+u^2)}
=\frac4\pi\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{u^2}{(1+u^2)^3}\,du.
$$
The even integrand and the standard evaluation
$\int_0^\infty u^2(1+u^2)^{-3}\,du=\pi/16$ give
$$
\boxed{I(\theta)=\frac12.}
$$
Thus the Cauchy location model is regular at the level of a centered, bounded score with finite information $1/2$, even though the sampling mean is useless. The MLE solves
$\sum_{j=1}^n 2(X_j-\theta)/(1+(X_j-\theta)^2)=0$ and, unlike $\bar X$, is a genuine likelihood estimator for this heavy-tailed location family.

The argument never uses a normal approximation to $\bar X$, never quotes $N(\theta,1)$ information $1$, and never constructs a most-powerful test of a point null.

graderFixtures.proofText: The characteristic function of Xbar is e^{itθ-|t|}, so Xbar is Cauchy(θ,1) for every n and is not consistent. The mean does not exist, so MoM from E[X] is undefined. The score 2(x-θ)/(1+(x-θ)^2) is bounded and centered, with Fisher information 1/2. This is not a normal z-pivot problem.
By the CLT, √n (Xbar-θ) is approximately N(0,σ^2) and Xbar is consistent for the Cauchy location by the law of large numbers.
Cauchy location is just like N(θ,1): the sample mean is N(θ,1/n), the information is 1, and the z-interval Xbar ± z_{α/2}/√n is exact.

MSTAT:010221.title: A complete exponential sum yields the survival UMVUE
MSTAT:010221.objective: Recognize a one-parameter exponential family, invoke completeness of the sum, and compute the Lehmann–Scheffé UMVUE of a nonlinear survival functional by conditioning.
MSTAT:010221.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent exponential random variables with rate $\theta>0$, so that each has density $\theta e^{-\theta x}$ on $(0,\infty)$. Write $T=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. Show that the model is a one-parameter exponential family and that $T$ is a complete sufficient statistic. Identify the law of $T$.

The target is $\tau(\theta)=P_\theta(X_1>1)=e^{-\theta}$. Prove that $\delta=\mathbf 1\{X_1>1\}$ is unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$. Then compute
$$
\delta^*(T)=\mathbb E[\delta\mid T]
$$
explicitly, including the case $T\le1$, and verify that the displayed formula does not contain $\theta$. Conclude that $\delta^*$ is the UMVUE of $e^{-\theta}$. Also give the UMVUE of $1/\theta$.

Do not replace this calculation by a Poisson zero-count Rao–Blackwellization, and do not treat the problem as a Neyman–Pearson test of a point null.
permittedResults: The sum of $n$ independent rate-$\theta$ exponentials is $\operatorname{Gamma}(n,\theta)$ (shape-rate) and is complete in $\theta>0$.
The normalized vector $(X_1/T,\ldots,X_n/T)$ is uniform on the simplex and independent of $T$; equivalently $X_1/T\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,n-1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor the joint exponential density, then compute the conditional probability from the Beta(1,n-1) law of X_1/T.
Use the joint density of (X_1,T) from the independent Gamma decomposition X_1 ~ Exp(θ) and T-X_1 ~ Gamma(n-1,θ), then divide.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Identifies the complete exponential-family sum and conditions the survival indicator to produce a parameter-free UMVUE.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Leaves θ inside the displayed estimator, or reports e^{-1/Xbar} or e^{-θ} itself as the UMVUE of e^{-θ}.
commonErrors.consequence: The object is not an estimator computed from the sample alone, or it is the MLE rather than the UMVUE.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the exponential sample by Poisson counts and quotes ((n-1)/n)^S as the improved estimator.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculation answers a different, already-written Poisson Rao–Blackwell problem.

hintTree.content: The joint density is $\theta^n\exp(-\theta T)$ on the positive orthant.
Conditioning on $T=t$ reduces $X_1>1$ to $X_1/T>1/t$. Use the Beta$(1,n-1)$ law on $(0,1)$.
The sample mean is unbiased for $1/\theta$ and is a function of $T$.

MSTAT:010221.canonicalSolution:
The joint density is
$$
f_\theta(x)
=\theta^n\exp\bigl(-\theta\textstyle\sum_i x_i\bigr)
\mathbf 1\{x_i>0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$
This is a full-rank one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter $-\theta$ and natural statistic $T=\sum_i X_i$. Factorization therefore makes $T$ sufficient, and completeness of a full-rank exponential-family statistic gives completeness of $T$. The sum of $n$ independent rate-$\theta$ exponentials is
$$
\boxed{T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n,\theta)},
$$
with density $\theta^n t^{n-1}e^{-\theta t}/(n-1)!$ on $(0,\infty)$.

The memoryless exponential tail yields
$$
\mathbb E_\theta\delta=P_\theta(X_1>1)=e^{-\theta}=\tau(\theta),
$$
so $\delta$ is unbiased. The normalized coordinates $(X_1/T,\ldots,X_n/T)$ are independent of $T$ and uniformly distributed on the simplex, so
$U=X_1/T\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,n-1)$ with density $(n-1)(1-u)^{n-2}$ on $(0,1)$. Therefore, on the event $\{T=t\}$,
$$
P(X_1>1\mid T=t)
=P(U>1/t).
$$
If $t\le1$, then $1/t\ge1$ and this probability is $0$. If $t>1$, then
$$
P(U>1/t)
=\int_{1/t}^1(n-1)(1-u)^{n-2}\,du
=\bigl(1-1/t\bigr)^{n-1}.
$$
Hence
$$
\boxed{
\delta^*(T)
=\Bigl(1-\frac1T\Bigr)^{n-1}\mathbf 1\{T>1\}.
}
$$
The right-hand side is a function of $T$ only. Lehmann–Scheffé therefore implies that $\delta^*$ is the UMVUE of $e^{-\theta}$.

Finally $\mathbb E_\theta X_1=1/\theta$, so
$$
\boxed{\bar X=T/n\text{ is the UMVUE of }1/\theta}.
$$

The calculation uses the exponential spacings/Beta representation. It is not a Poisson count conditioned on a Poisson total, and it is not a likelihood-ratio test.

graderFixtures.proofText: The joint density θ^n e^{-θ T} is a full-rank exponential family, so T is complete sufficient and Gamma(n,θ). The indicator 1{X_1>1} is unbiased for e^{-θ}, and X_1/T ~ Beta(1,n-1) independent of T, so E[δ|T] = (1-1/T)^{n-1} 1{T>1} is the UMVUE. Xbar is the UMVUE of 1/θ.
The UMVUE of e^{-θ} is e^{-1/Xbar}, or equivalently e^{-θ} after substituting the MLE, so the unknown rate may remain in the displayed formula.
Treat the exponential counts as Poisson and Rao–Blackwellize 1{X_1=0} by conditioning on the Poisson total, obtaining ((n-1)/n)^S.

MSTAT:010323.title: The interval $(\theta,2\theta)$ makes the maximum the MLE
MSTAT:010323.objective: Write the two-sided support likelihood for $\operatorname{Uniform}(\theta,2\theta)$, extract the MLE from the monotone factor, compare it with the method of moments, and explain why both extremes remain sufficient.
MSTAT:010323.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $\operatorname{Uniform}(\theta,2\theta)$ observations with unknown $\theta>0$. Write $X_{(1)}$ and $X_{(n)}$ for the sample minimum and maximum. Derive the joint likelihood as a function of $\theta$, including the exact set of $\theta$ compatible with a sample. Prove by factorization that $(X_{(1)},X_{(n)})$ is sufficient. Maximize the likelihood on that compatible set and obtain the MLE $\hat\theta$.

Compute $\mathbb E_\theta[X_1]$ and the method-of-moments estimator $\tilde\theta$. Prove that both $\hat\theta$ and $\tilde\theta$ are consistent as $n\to\infty$. Explain why the one-dimensional maximum that is sufficient for $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ is not sufficient here, without repeating a $\operatorname{Uniform}(\theta,\theta+1)$ completeness counterexample and without inverting a maximum pivot to a confidence interval for an unknown right endpoint $0$.
permittedResults: A continuous uniform sample on an interval of length $\theta$ has joint density $\theta^{-n}$ on that interval and zero outside.
Almost-sure convergence $X_{(n)}\to 2\theta$ and $X_{(1)}\to\theta$, together with $\bar X\to 3\theta/2$ by the WLLN, yield consistency after continuous mapping.

acceptableStrategies.description: Intersect the n support constraints, then maximize θ^{-n} on the resulting interval and match the first moment separately.
Draw the (min,max) support triangle implied by θ ≤ min ≤ max ≤ 2θ and read the MLE as the smallest feasible θ.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Writes the two-sided compatible interval, maximizes the monotone likelihood at the maximum over two, and compares the moment estimator without collapsing to a one-endpoint uniform.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Treats the sample as Uniform(0,θ) or Uniform(θ,θ+1) and quotes a one-sided maximum likelihood or a length-one completeness example.
commonErrors.consequence: The compatible parameter set and the MLE are those of a different model.

commonErrors.description: Reports Xbar, X_(1), or X_(n) itself as the MLE, ignoring that θ^{-n} is maximized at the left endpoint X_(n)/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The likelihood is not maximized on the compatible set.

hintTree.content: The inequalities $\theta\le X_i\le 2\theta$ for every $i$ collapse to $X_{(n)}/2\le\theta\le X_{(1)}$.
On that interval the likelihood is $\theta^{-n}$, which is decreasing in $\theta$.
The midpoint of $[\theta,2\theta]$ is $3\theta/2$.

MSTAT:010323.canonicalSolution:
Each observation has density $\theta^{-1}$ on $[\theta,2\theta]$. The joint likelihood is therefore
$$
L_x(\theta)
=\theta^{-n}
\mathbf 1\{\theta\le x_i\le 2\theta\text{ for every }i\}
=
\theta^{-n}
\mathbf 1\bigl\{x_{(n)}/2\le\theta\le x_{(1)}\bigr\}.
$$
The compatible parameter set is the interval
$[X_{(n)}/2,\,X_{(1)}]$, which is nonempty almost surely because every $X_i$ lies in $[\theta,2\theta]$ and therefore $X_{(n)}\le 2X_{(1)}$. Factorization with $g_\theta(X_{(1)},X_{(n)})=L_X(\theta)$ and $h\equiv 1$ shows that
$$
\boxed{(X_{(1)},X_{(n)})\text{ is sufficient}.}
$$
The pair cannot be reduced to the maximum alone: two samples with the same maximum but different minima generally have different compatible intervals, hence non-proportional likelihood functions.

On the compatible interval, $\theta^{-n}$ is strictly decreasing, so the maximizer is the left endpoint:
$$
\boxed{\hat\theta=X_{(n)}/2}.
$$

The mean of a uniform point on $[\theta,2\theta]$ is the midpoint $3\theta/2$. The method-of-moments equation $\bar X=3\tilde\theta/2$ therefore yields
$$
\boxed{\tilde\theta=\frac{2}{3}\bar X}.
$$

For consistency: $X_{(n)}\le 2\theta$. If $0<\varepsilon<\theta$, then
$$
P_\theta(X_{(n)}\le 2\theta-\varepsilon)
=\bigl((2\theta-\varepsilon-\theta)/\theta\bigr)^n
=(1-\varepsilon/\theta)^n\to0.
$$
If $\varepsilon\ge\theta$, the same event has probability zero. Hence the
claim holds for every $\varepsilon>0$.
Thus $X_{(n)}\to 2\theta$ in probability and $\hat\theta\to\theta$. The WLLN gives $\bar X\to 3\theta/2$, so $\tilde\theta\to\theta$ as well.

The model $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ has a one-sided moving endpoint, and the maximum is sufficient there. Here both endpoints move with the single parameter $\theta$, so both extremes enter the likelihood indicator. That is a different support geometry from $\operatorname{Uniform}(\theta,\theta+1)$ (fixed length one) and from $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ (left endpoint pinned at zero). No completeness counterexample or one-sided maximum-pivot confidence inversion is required.

graderFixtures.proofText: The likelihood is θ^{-n} on X_(n)/2 ≤ θ ≤ X_(1), so (X_(1),X_(n)) is sufficient and the decreasing factor is maximized at θ̂ = X_(n)/2. The mean 3θ/2 gives the moment estimator 2Xbar/3. Both are consistent. The pair of extremes cannot be reduced to a Uniform(0,θ) maximum.
This is the same as Uniform(0,θ), so the MLE is the sample maximum and the minimum is irrelevant. Completeness can be copied from the Uniform(θ,θ+1) range calculation.
Because the likelihood is flat in the observations, the MLE is the sample mean, or alternatively the sample minimum X_(1).

MSTAT:010324.title: The unbiased sample variance is not the MSE winner
MSTAT:010324.objective: Compare exact mean-squared errors of scalar multiples of the normal residual sum of squares, including the unbiased estimator, the MLE, and the MSE-optimal multiple.
MSTAT:010324.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with both parameters unknown and $n\ge2$. Write
$Q=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2$ and $S^2=Q/(n-1)$. Under squared-error loss for the target $\sigma^2$, compute the exact risk of $S^2$ and of the MLE $\hat\sigma^2=Q/n$. Then, for a constant $a\ge0$, compute the exact risk of $aS^2$ and find the unique $a^*$ minimizing that risk. Identify the corresponding estimator as a multiple of $Q$ and compute its risk.

Prove that
$$
R(\sigma^2,S^2)
>R(\sigma^2,\hat\sigma^2)
>R(\sigma^2,a^*S^2)
$$
for every $\sigma^2>0$. This is a comparison of estimators of a scale parameter. Do not compare linear estimators $aX$ of a normal mean, and do not invoke a decision-theoretic shrinkage argument for $\mu$.
permittedResults: $Q/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$, so $\mathbb E[Q]=(n-1)\sigma^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Q)=2(n-1)\sigma^4$.
Consequently $\operatorname{Var}(S^2)=2\sigma^4/(n-1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use chi-square moments of Q and the bias-variance identity, then differentiate the quadratic in a.
Write every estimator as cQ, use E[Q]=(n-1)σ^2 and E[Q^2]=(n-1)(n+1)σ^4, and minimize the resulting quadratic in c.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Computes the three exact scale risks and minimizes the quadratic in the multiple of S^2, without substituting a mean-shrinkage problem.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Declares S^2 best because it is unbiased, or claims the MLE cannot have smaller risk than an unbiased estimator.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact MSE comparison is replaced by a bias-only ranking.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the target σ^2 by a normal mean and quotes the risk a^2+(1-a)^2 θ^2 of the estimators aX.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculation answers the existing mean-shrinkage packet rather than the variance-MSE problem.

hintTree.content: Unbiasedness of $S^2$ makes its risk equal to its variance.
The MLE is $((n-1)/n)S^2$. Compute its bias $-\sigma^2/n$ and scale the variance by $((n-1)/n)^2$.
Differentiate $a^2\operatorname{Var}(S^2)+(a-1)^2\sigma^4$ with respect to $a$.

MSTAT:010324.canonicalSolution:
The residual law $Q/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$ gives
$\mathbb E[S^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S^2)=2\sigma^4/(n-1)$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{R(\sigma^2,S^2)=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}.}
$$

The MLE is $\hat\sigma^2=((n-1)/n)S^2$, with bias $-\sigma^2/n$ and variance
$((n-1)/n)^2\cdot 2\sigma^4/(n-1)=2(n-1)\sigma^4/n^2$. Adding the squared bias,
$$
R(\sigma^2,\hat\sigma^2)
=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2}+\frac{\sigma^4}{n^2}
=\boxed{\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2}.}
$$

For a general multiple,
$$
R(\sigma^2,aS^2)
=a^2\cdot\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}+(a-1)^2\sigma^4.
$$
Differentiating in $a$ yields
$$
\frac{4a\sigma^4}{n-1}+2(a-1)\sigma^4=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{2a}{n-1}+(a-1)=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
a(n+1)=n-1.
$$
The second derivative $4\sigma^4/(n-1)+2\sigma^4>0$, so
$$
\boxed{a^*=\frac{n-1}{n+1}.}
$$
The minimizer is
$$
a^*S^2=\frac{Q}{n+1}.
$$
Its risk is
$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\sigma^2,a^*S^2)
&=\Bigl(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\Bigr)^2\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}
+\Bigl(\frac{-2}{n+1}\Bigr)^2\sigma^4
=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^4+4\sigma^4}{(n+1)^2}
=\boxed{\frac{2\sigma^4}{n+1}.}
\end{aligned}
$$

The three leading coefficients satisfy
$$
\frac2{n-1}
-\frac{2n-1}{n^2}
=\frac{2n^2-(2n-1)(n-1)}{n^2(n-1)}
=\frac{3n-1}{n^2(n-1)}>0
$$
and
$$
\frac{2n-1}{n^2}-\frac2{n+1}
=\frac{(2n-1)(n+1)-2n^2}{n^2(n+1)}
=\frac{n-1}{n^2(n+1)}>0.
$$
Thus the risk ordering holds for every $\sigma^2>0$. Unbiasedness of $S^2$ does not minimize MSE. The comparison is entirely about estimators of $\sigma^2$; no linear shrinkage of a normal mean is used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Var(S^2)=2σ^4/(n-1) is the risk of S^2. The MLE Q/n has risk (2n-1)σ^4/n^2. Minimizing a^2 Var(S^2)+(a-1)^2 σ^4 gives a*=(n-1)/(n+1), i.e. Q/(n+1), with risk 2σ^4/(n+1). The unbiased estimator is worst of the three. This is not the aX mean-shrinkage comparison.
S^2 is unbiased and the MLE is biased, so S^2 has smaller squared-error risk for every σ^2 and no further variance calculation is needed.
The risk of aS^2 is a^2+(1-a)^2 σ^4, the same formula used for aX estimating a normal mean, so the minimax coefficient is σ^2/(1+σ^2).

MSTAT:010325.title: Invariance moves the MLE but not the UMVUE
MSTAT:010325.objective: Prove the invariance property of maximum-likelihood estimators, apply it to a nonlinear Bernoulli functional, and contrast the result with the unbiased estimator of the same functional.
MSTAT:010325.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ observations, $0\le p\le1$, $n\ge2$, and let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be any function, not necessarily injective. Let $\hat p$ be a maximizer of the Bernoulli likelihood. Prove that $g(\hat p)$ maximizes the induced likelihood for the target $\tau=g(p)$. State the induced-likelihood definition you use so that the claim remains valid when $g$ is not one-to-one.

Take $g(p)=p(1-p)$. Write the MLE of $p(1-p)$ explicitly in terms of $\bar X$. Then compute $\mathbb E_p[\bar X(1-\bar X)]$ and produce an unbiased estimator of $p(1-p)$. Explain why invariance does not force that unbiased estimator to equal the MLE, and why a UMVUE need not be a function $g(\hat p)$ of the MLE of $p$.

Do not treat this as a test of $H_0:p=p_0$, and do not Rao–Blackwellize a Poisson zero count.
permittedResults: On the closed parameter space $[0,1]$, the Bernoulli MLE is $\hat p=\bar X$, including the endpoint samples $\bar X\in\{0,1\}$.
$\mathbb E[\bar X(1-\bar X)]=p(1-p)\,(1-1/n)$, so the unbiased correction multiplies by $n/(n-1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare the original likelihood on each g-fiber, then compute the Bernoulli second-moment correction.
Maximize the binomial likelihood in p and compose with g, then obtain the UMVUE from E[S(n-S)] = n(n-1)p(1-p).

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Proves MLE invariance through the induced likelihood and contrasts Xbar(1-Xbar) with its unbiased multiple.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Claims the invariance theorem applies only when g is one-to-one, or tries to invert g to move the likelihood.
commonErrors.consequence: The induced-likelihood definition is abandoned and the theorem is stated too narrowly.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that the UMVUE of p(1-p) equals Xbar(1-Xbar) because the MLE is invariant, or that unbiasedness is preserved by g.
commonErrors.consequence: The bias factor (1-1/n) is missed and two distinct optimality notions are conflated.

hintTree.content: If $L(\hat\theta)\ge L(\theta)$ for every $\theta$, then the supremum of $L$ over each $g$-fiber is attained at a fiber containing $\hat\theta$.
Expand $\bar X(1-\bar X)=\bar X-\bar X^2$ and use $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=p(1-p)/n$.
Unbiasedness is not preserved by nonlinear maps, whereas the induced-likelihood maximizer is.

MSTAT:010325.canonicalSolution:
Let $L$ be the original likelihood and let
$L^*(\tau)=\sup\{L(\theta):g(\theta)=\tau\}$. If $\hat\theta$ maximizes $L$, then for every $\tau$ in the image of $g$,
$$
L^*(\tau)
=\sup_{g(\theta)=\tau}L(\theta)
\le L(\hat\theta)
=L^*(g(\hat\theta)),
$$
because $\hat\theta$ is a feasible point of the fiber $g^{-1}(g(\hat\theta))$. Thus $g(\hat\theta)$ maximizes $L^*$. This argument never divides by $g'$ and never assumes that $g$ is injective.

For Bernoulli trials, $L(p)=p^S(1-p)^{n-S}$ on $[0,1]$ is maximized at $\hat p=\bar X$, including the all-zero and all-one endpoint samples. Therefore the MLE of $\tau(p)=p(1-p)$ is
$$
\boxed{\widehat\tau=\bar X(1-\bar X).}
$$

Now
$$
\mathbb E_p[\bar X]
=p,
\qquad
\mathbb E_p[\bar X^2]
=\operatorname{Var}_p(\bar X)+p^2
=\frac{p(1-p)}n+p^2,
$$
so
$$
\mathbb E_p[\bar X(1-\bar X)]
=p-\frac{p(1-p)}n-p^2
=p(1-p)\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr).
$$
Hence
$$
\boxed{
\frac n{n-1}\bar X(1-\bar X)
}
$$
is unbiased for $p(1-p)$. It is a function of the complete sufficient statistic $S$, so it is the UMVUE.

The two estimators differ by the factor $n/(n-1)\neq1$. Invariance transports maximizers of $L$; it does not transport unbiasedness. A nonlinear $g$ generally introduces bias, so the UMVUE of $g(p)$ need not be $g$ of the UMVUE (or MLE) of $p$. The present calculation is an estimation identity, not a test of a simple Bernoulli hypothesis and not a Poisson Rao–Blackwell argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: The induced likelihood at τ is the supremum of L over the fiber g^{-1}(τ), so g of an MLE is an induced MLE even when g is not injective. For Bernoulli, that gives Xbar(1-Xbar). Its expectation is (1-1/n)p(1-p), so the UMVUE is n/(n-1) Xbar(1-Xbar). Invariance does not preserve unbiasedness.
Invariance of the MLE requires g to be injective so that one can write L(g^{-1}(τ)). For p(1-p) the map is not one-to-one, so there is no MLE of p(1-p).
Because the MLE is invariant, Xbar(1-Xbar) is automatically unbiased and is therefore the UMVUE of p(1-p).

MSTAT:010422.title: Bernoulli information identities hold, then the bound can vanish
MSTAT:010422.objective: Verify the regular score, variance, and Hessian identities in a fixed-support Bernoulli model, obtain Cramér–Rao bounds, and diagnose the vanishing-derivative degeneracy for $p(1-p)$.
MSTAT:010422.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ observations with $0<p<1$ unknown, and write $S=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. Starting from the joint log-likelihood, derive the score $U_n(p)$. Prove the three regular identities
$$
\mathbb E_p[U_n(p)]=0,
\qquad
I_n(p)=\operatorname{Var}_p(U_n(p))
=-\mathbb E_p[\partial_p U_n(p)],
$$
and compute $I_n(p)$ explicitly. Deduce the Cramér–Rao lower bound for every unbiased estimator of $p$, and show that $\bar X$ attains it.

Now let $\tau(p)=p(1-p)$. Compute $\tau'(p)$ and the Cramér–Rao expression for unbiased estimators of $\tau(p)$. Evaluate that expression at $p=1/2$ and explain why a vanishing bound does not produce a zero-variance estimator of $1/4$. Contrast this regular, fixed-support calculation with a model in which the support moves with the parameter: the identities above need not hold there, but do not re-derive a shifted-exponential example.

Do not construct a most-powerful test of $H_0:p=p_0$.
permittedResults: For a regular fixed-support exponential family, the score is centered and the variance and negative-Hessian formulas for information agree.
$S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$, so $\mathbb E[S]=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=np(1-p)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the binomial log-likelihood and evaluate means and variances from S ~ Binomial(n,p).
Use the one-parameter Bernoulli exponential-family formulas for the mean and variance of the natural statistic, then transform to p.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Verifies the regular Bernoulli information identities and explains the vanishing Cramér–Rao bound for p(1-p) without claiming a zero-variance estimator.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that because the Cramér–Rao expression is zero at p=1/2, there exists an unbiased estimator of 1/4 with variance zero.
commonErrors.consequence: A degenerate first-order bound is misread as an attainable variance.

commonErrors.description: Claims the Bernoulli score has nonzero mean, or replaces the calculation by a moving-support shifted-exponential audit.
commonErrors.consequence: The regular fixed-support identities are denied in the model where they hold, or a different existing problem is copied.

hintTree.content: The log-likelihood is $S\log p+(n-S)\log(1-p)$. Differentiate once and twice.
Replace $S$ by its mean to center the score, then compute $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ to get $I_n(p)$.
At $p=1/2$ one has $\tau'(p)=0$, but $p(1-p)$ is not a constant random variable.

MSTAT:010422.canonicalSolution:
The joint mass function on $\{0,1\}^n$ is
$p^S(1-p)^{n-S}$. The log-likelihood
$$
\ell_n(p)=S\log p+(n-S)\log(1-p)
$$
has score
$$
\boxed{
U_n(p)
=\frac S p-\frac{n-S}{1-p}
=\frac{S-np}{p(1-p)}.
}
$$
Because $\mathbb E_p S=np$,
$$
\mathbb E_p[U_n(p)]=0.
$$
The support $\{0,1\}^n$ does not depend on $p\in(0,1)$, so differentiation under the finite sum is legitimate and the score is centered.

Next $\operatorname{Var}_p(S)=np(1-p)$, hence
$$
I_n(p)
=\operatorname{Var}_p(U_n(p))
=\frac{np(1-p)}{(p(1-p))^2}
=\boxed{\frac n{p(1-p)}}.
$$
The second derivative is
$$
\partial_p U_n(p)
=-\frac S{p^2}-\frac{n-S}{(1-p)^2},
$$
and
$$
-\mathbb E_p[\partial_p U_n(p)]
=\frac{np}{p^2}+\frac{n(1-p)}{(1-p)^2}
=\frac n p+\frac n{1-p}
=\frac n{p(1-p)}.
$$
The variance and negative-Hessian formulas therefore agree.

For unbiased estimation of $p$ itself, $\tau'(p)=1$, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}_p(\delta)\ge\frac{p(1-p)}n.
$$
The estimator $\bar X=S/n$ is unbiased and has variance $p(1-p)/n$, so it attains the bound.

For $\tau(p)=p(1-p)$ one has $\tau'(p)=1-2p$, and the bound becomes
$$
\boxed{
\frac{(1-2p)^2 p(1-p)}n.
}
$$
At $p=1/2$ this expression is $0$. That does not mean an unbiased estimator $\delta$ can have variance zero there. If it did, then $\delta=1/4$ almost surely under $P_{1/2}$. Every binary sample has positive probability when $p=1/2$, so $\delta$ would equal $1/4$ on the entire sample space. Its expectation would then be $1/4$ for every $p\in(0,1)$, contradicting unbiasedness for the nonconstant function $p(1-p)$. Thus the first-order Cramér–Rao bound is merely uninformative at the critical point. For example,
$n(n-1)^{-1}\bar X(1-\bar X)$ is unbiased for $n\ge2$ and is nondegenerate.

The identities used domination of a $p$-independent counting measure on a fixed finite set. In a model whose support moves with the parameter, differentiation under the integral can fail and the score need not be centered. That is a different regularity audit and is not repeated here.

No test of a simple Bernoulli hypothesis is required.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Bernoulli score is (S-np)/(p(1-p)), which is centered. Its variance and the negative expected Hessian both equal n/(p(1-p)). Xbar attains the CR bound p(1-p)/n for p. For p(1-p) the bound is (1-2p)^2 p(1-p)/n, which vanishes at 1/2 without producing a zero-variance estimator. The support does not move, unlike irregular location-endpoint models.
At p=1/2 the Cramér–Rao bound for p(1-p) is zero, so there is an unbiased estimator with variance identically zero and 1/4 is estimated without error.
As in a shifted exponential, the Bernoulli score has mean one rather than zero, so the information identities fail and I_n cannot equal n/(p(1-p)).

MSTAT:010517.title: A known-scale normal mean has a nonrandom interval length
MSTAT:010517.objective: Derive the exact $z$-pivot for a normal mean with known scale, invert it without reversing inequalities, compute the nonrandom length, and keep the frequentist coverage statement pre-data.
MSTAT:010517.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ observations, where $\mu\in\mathbb R$ is unknown and the scale $\sigma>0$ is known. Starting from the joint sampling law, derive the exact distribution of
$$
Z=\frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)}{\sigma}.
$$
For a fixed $\alpha\in(0,1)$, let $z_{\alpha/2}$ denote the upper $\alpha/2$ quantile of $N(0,1)$, so $P(Z>z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$. Invert the event
$$
-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}
$$
to obtain a confidence interval $C(X)$ for $\mu$. Prove that the coverage equals $1-\alpha$ for every $\mu\in\mathbb R$. Compute the length of $C(X)$ and prove that this length is a nonrandom function of $(n,\sigma,\alpha)$ only.

Explain why substituting a realized sample mean $\bar x$ is legitimate when reporting the observed interval, but illegitimate when rederiving the coverage probability by treating the unknown $\mu$ as random. Do not replace $\sigma$ by a sample scale, and do not invoke a posterior for $\mu$.
permittedResults: Independent $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ coordinates have sample mean $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$.
If $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $z_{\alpha/2}$ is its upper $\alpha/2$ quantile, then $P(|Z|\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Standardize the exact normal law of the sample mean and invert the central probability event algebraically.
Complete the square in the joint normal exponent to recover the mean law, then translate the same two-sided bound into an interval for μ.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Inverts the exact known-scale normal pivot with the correct endpoint order, proves coverage for every mean, and identifies the interval length as nonrandom.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the known σ by the sample standard deviation inside the z-pivot or reports a t-interval for this known-scale model.
commonErrors.consequence: The displayed pivot is no longer N(0,1), so the claimed exact coverage is false in the stated model.

commonErrors.description: After observing the sample mean, treats the unknown μ as random and assigns it probability 1-α of lying in the reported interval.
commonErrors.consequence: Frequentist coverage is replaced by an unjustified posterior statement.

hintTree.content: Standardize $\bar X$ using its exact normal law. The scale $\sigma$ is a known constant, so it may appear in the pivot.
The event $|Z|\le z_{\alpha/2}$ is equivalent to $|\bar X-\mu|\le z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$. Solve for $\mu$ without flipping the interval.
The two endpoints differ by a constant. Coverage is a statement about the random interval before the sample is observed.

MSTAT:010517.canonicalSolution:
The joint density is
$$
(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2\Bigr).
$$
Completing the square, or using the reproductive property of independent normals, gives
$$
\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n).
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{Z=\frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)}.
$$
The law of $Z$ does not depend on $\mu$, so $Z$ is a pivot.

The standard normal tail definition yields
$$
P_\mu\bigl(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}\bigr)=1-\alpha
$$
for every $\mu$. Because $\sigma>0$ and $\sqrt n>0$,
$$
-z_{\alpha/2}\le\frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X-\mu)}{\sigma}\le z_{\alpha/2}
$$
is equivalent to
$$
-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\le\bar X-\mu\le z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},
$$
and then to
$$
\boxed{
C(X)
=\Bigl[\bar X-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\;
\bar X+z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Bigr].
}
$$
No inequality is reversed when isolating $\mu$, because one subtracts $\bar X$ and then multiplies by $-1$ twice, or equivalently rearranges a two-sided bound on $\bar X-\mu$. Hence
$$
P_\mu\{\mu\in C(X)\}=1-\alpha
\qquad\text{for every }\mu\in\mathbb R.
$$

The length is
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{length}(C(X))
=2z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
}
$$
The right-hand side does not involve $X$, so the length is nonrandom. It shrinks like $n^{-1/2}$ and grows linearly with the known scale.

After observing $\bar X=\bar x$, one reports the numerical interval
$$
\bigl[\bar x-z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n,\;
\bar x+z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n\bigr].
$$
That substitution is a reporting step. Coverage remains an unconditional repeated-sampling probability for the random set $C(X)$. The parameter $\mu$ is fixed in this model. Conditioning on $\bar X=\bar x$ and declaring that the fixed $\mu$ now has probability $1-\alpha$ of lying in the reported interval is not a derivation of frequentist coverage, and no prior was introduced that would justify a posterior statement.

graderFixtures.proofText: Z = √n (Xbar-μ)/σ is exactly N(0,1). Inverting |Z| ≤ z_{α/2} gives the interval Xbar ± z_{α/2} σ/√n, which covers μ with probability 1-α for every μ. Its length 2 z_{α/2} σ/√n does not depend on the sample. Reporting the observed numbers is fine, but μ is not random after the data are seen.
The pivot should use the sample standard deviation S in place of σ, giving √n (Xbar-μ)/S ~ N(0,1) and the interval Xbar ± z_{α/2} S/√n even though σ is known.
After observing Xbar = xbar, the unknown mean becomes random and has probability 1-α of lying inside the reported numerical interval.

MSTAT:010519.title: Variance intervals reverse when the chi-square pivot is inverted
MSTAT:010519.objective: Invert the exact chi-square pivot for a normal variance, keep the quantile order after the reciprocal, and distinguish equal-tail two-sided sets from one-sided rays.
MSTAT:010519.statement:
Continue with $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ independent $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, both parameters unknown, $n\ge2$, and
$S^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$. Using the residual law
$(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$, form a pivot for $\sigma^2$. Let
$\chi^2_{\nu,\beta}$ denote the lower $\beta$ quantile of $\chi^2_\nu$, so
$P(V\le\chi^2_{\nu,\beta})=\beta$ when $V\sim\chi^2_\nu$.

For $\alpha\in(0,1)$, invert the equal-tail event
$$
\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha/2}
\le\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}
\le\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}
$$
to a confidence interval for $\sigma^2$. Show every inequality reversal caused by taking reciprocals of positive quantities, and prove that the coverage is exactly $1-\alpha$. Also construct the exact one-sided upper interval of the form $(0,cS^2]$ with coverage $1-\alpha$, and the exact one-sided lower interval $[cS^2,\infty)$.

Finally explain why the equal-tail choice is not forced by the pivot: a different pair of chi-square quantiles with the same probability content generally produces a different expected length. Do not estimate $\mu$ by a $z$-interval in this problem, and do not treat $S^2$ as already equal to $\sigma^2$.
permittedResults: For a normal sample, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$ and $S^2>0$ almost surely.
If $0<ale ule b$, then $1/ble 1/ule 1/a$. Reciprocals reverse both inequalities.

acceptableStrategies.description: Start from the residual chi-square law and invert the probability-content event by taking reciprocals of positive terms.
Work with the cdf of (n-1)S^2/σ^2 directly and solve the two inequalities for σ^2, then specialize to equal tails or a single tail.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Inverts the chi-square scale pivot with the reciprocal reversal explicit and constructs both equal-tail and one-sided exact sets.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Reports [(n-1)S^2/χ^2_{n-1,α/2}, (n-1)S^2/χ^2_{n-1,1-α/2}] or otherwise keeps the smaller quantile in the lower endpoint.
commonErrors.consequence: The displayed set is not the inversion of the pivot event and can be empty or badly anticonservative.

commonErrors.description: Sets S^2 equal to σ^2 and claims there is nothing left to invert, or quotes a normal interval for the variance.
commonErrors.consequence: The sampling law of S^2 is discarded and no confidence set is derived.

hintTree.content: The pivot is $V=(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$. The unknown $\sigma^2$ sits in the denominator.
From $a\le c/\sigma^2\le b$ with $c=(n-1)S^2>0$, take reciprocals and then multiply by $c$.
A one-sided upper set for $\sigma^2$ comes from a lower tail bound on $V$.

MSTAT:010519.canonicalSolution:
The residual law already established for normal samples gives the pivot
$$
V=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$
Its distribution does not depend on $(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

Let $a=\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ and $b=\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}$, so $0<a<b<\infty$ and $P(a\le V\le b)=1-\alpha$. Write $c=(n-1)S^2>0$. Then
$$
a\le\frac c{\sigma^2}\le b.
$$
All three quantities are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses both inequalities:
$$
\frac1b\le\frac{\sigma^2}c\le\frac1a.
$$
Multiplying through by $c$ yields
$$
\boxed{
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}}
\le\sigma^2\le
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha/2}}.
}
$$
The larger chi-square quantile therefore appears in the lower endpoint for $\sigma^2$. Coverage equals
$P(a\le V\le b)=1-\alpha$ for every $(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

For a one-sided upper interval, start from $P(V\ge\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha})=1-\alpha$. This is
$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\ge\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\sigma^2\le\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}}.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{
C^+(X)=\Bigl(0,\;\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}}\Bigr]
}
$$
has coverage $1-\alpha$. Likewise,
$P(V\le\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha})=1-\alpha$ inverts to the lower ray
$$
\boxed{
C^-(X)=\Bigl[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha}},\;\infty\Bigr).
}
$$

Equal tails are only one choice of a pair $(a,b)$ with $F_{n-1}(b)-F_{n-1}(a)=1-\alpha$. The resulting length is
$$
(n-1)S^2\Bigl(\frac1a-\frac1b\Bigr),
$$
so any other admissible pair generally changes the expected length. The equal-tail interval is convenient and exact; it is not claimed to be shortest. The present derivation uses the scale pivot only and does not produce an interval for $\mu$.

graderFixtures.proofText: V = (n-1)S^2/σ^2 ~ χ^2_{n-1}. The event a ≤ V ≤ b with equal-tail chi-square quantiles inverts to (n-1)S^2/b ≤ σ^2 ≤ (n-1)S^2/a, so the larger quantile sits in the lower endpoint. One-sided sets are (0, (n-1)S^2/χ^2_{n-1,α}] and [(n-1)S^2/χ^2_{n-1,1-α}, ∞). Equal tails are not a shortest-length claim.
From a ≤ (n-1)S^2/σ^2 ≤ b I keep the order after taking reciprocals, so the interval is [(n-1)S^2/a, (n-1)S^2/b] with a = χ^2_{n-1,α/2} the smaller quantile.
S^2 is already an unbiased estimator of σ^2, so the confidence interval is the singleton {S^2} and no chi-square pivot is required.

MSTAT:010520.title: Pooling is valid only while the two normal scales agree
MSTAT:010520.objective: Derive the two-sample pooled $t$-pivot under a common normal scale, invert it for the mean difference, and show that the same ratio is not a pivot when the scales differ.
MSTAT:010520.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be independent $N(\mu_1,\sigma^2)$ and, independently, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be independent $N(\mu_2,\sigma^2)$, with $m,n\ge2$, unknown means, and a common unknown scale $\sigma>0$. Write $\bar X$, $\bar Y$ for the two sample means and $S_X^2$, $S_Y^2$ for the two unbiased sample variances. Define the pooled variance
$$
S_p^2
=\frac{(m-1)S_X^2+(n-1)S_Y^2}{m+n-2}.
$$
Derive the exact laws of $\bar X-\bar Y$ and of $(m+n-2)S_p^2/\sigma^2$, prove they are independent, and identify the law of
$$
T
=\frac{\bar X-\bar Y-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{S_p\sqrt{1/m+1/n}}.
$$
Invert $|T|\le t_{m+n-2,\alpha/2}$ to a confidence interval for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.

Now drop the equal-scale hypothesis and allow $\sigma_X^2\neq\sigma_Y^2$. Show that the same displayed $T$, still formed with $S_p$, is no longer a pivot: its law depends on the unknown scale ratio. Do not construct a Neyman–Pearson test, and do not claim that a $z$-interval with known $\sigma$ solves the unequal-scale problem.
permittedResults: Independent normals add: $\bar X-\bar Y\sim N(\mu_1-\mu_2,\sigma^2(1/m+1/n))$ when the scales agree.
Independent chi-squares add, and a normal vector is independent of residual sums of squares in each sample.

acceptableStrategies.description: Add the two residual chi-squares, standardize the independent mean difference, and invert the resulting t event.
Write the four-dimensional sufficient statistics, factor the joint normal law, and read the same independence and chi-square addition from the factorization.

milestones.criterion: States the sampling model, parameter space, and any support or regularity hypotheses actually used.
Builds the pooled t-pivot from independent normal means and added residual chi-squares, then shows the same ratio loses its parameter-free law when the scales differ.
Completes every requested exact law, inversion, identity, risk, or consistency check with coherent notation and no unjustified posterior language.

commonErrors.description: Claims that T remains t_{m+n-2} or otherwise parameter-free after the two scales are allowed to differ.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported interval does not have a guaranteed exact coverage in the model actually stated.

commonErrors.description: Replaces S_p by a known σ, or treats the two-sample unknown-scale problem as an ordinary one-sample z-interval.
commonErrors.consequence: The nuisance scale is ignored and the pooled t construction is not carried out.

hintTree.content: Independence of the two samples makes $\bar X-\bar Y$ independent of both residual sums of squares.
Add the two chi-squares to obtain $(m+n-2)S_p^2/\sigma^2$, then form a $t$ ratio.
If the scales differ, $S_p^2$ estimates neither scale, and the variance of $\bar X-\bar Y$ is no longer $\sigma^2(1/m+1/n)$.

MSTAT:010520.canonicalSolution:
Under the common-scale model,
$$
\bar X\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma^2/m),
\qquad
\bar Y\sim N(\mu_2,\sigma^2/n)
$$
are independent, so
$$
\bar X-\bar Y\sim N\bigl(\mu_1-\mu_2,\;\sigma^2(1/m+1/n)\bigr).
$$
Each sample contributes an independent residual law
$$
\frac{(m-1)S_X^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{m-1},
\qquad
\frac{(n-1)S_Y^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1},
$$
and both are independent of $(\bar X,\bar Y)$. Adding chi-squares gives
$$
\frac{(m+n-2)S_p^2}{\sigma^2}
\sim\chi^2_{m+n-2},
$$
still independent of $\bar X-\bar Y$. Standardizing the difference and dividing by the independent root-mean-square residual produces
$$
\boxed{T\sim t_{m+n-2}}.
$$
Thus $T$ is a pivot under equal scales. The event $|T|\le t_{m+n-2,\alpha/2}$ inverts to
$$
\boxed{
\bar X-\bar Y
\pm
t_{m+n-2,\alpha/2}\,
S_p\sqrt{\frac1m+\frac1n}.
}
$$
Coverage is exactly $1-\alpha$ for every $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma^2)$.

Now allow $\sigma_X^2\neq\sigma_Y^2$. Then
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X-\bar Y)
=\frac{\sigma_X^2}m+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}n,
$$
while
$$
\mathbb E[S_p^2]
=\frac{(m-1)\sigma_X^2+(n-1)\sigma_Y^2}{m+n-2}
$$
is a different mixture of the two scales. The ratio
can be made explicit. Put $\nu=m+n-2$, $\rho=\sigma_X^2/\sigma_Y^2$, and
$$
Z=\frac{\bar X-\bar Y-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}
{\sqrt{\sigma_X^2/m+\sigma_Y^2/n}},\quad
U=\frac{(m-1)S_X^2}{\sigma_X^2},\quad
V=\frac{(n-1)S_Y^2}{\sigma_Y^2}.
$$
Then $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $U\sim\chi^2_{m-1}$, and
$V\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$ are independent, and
$$
T=Z\sqrt{
\frac{\nu(\rho/m+1/n)}{(\rho U+V)(1/m+1/n)}
}.
$$
Thus the ratio
$$
\frac{\bar X-\bar Y-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{S_p\sqrt{1/m+1/n}}
$$
has a law depending on the unknown ratio $\rho$ (and on $m,n$). It is not a function of a single chi-square and an independent standard normal with parameter-free coefficients, so it is not $t_{m+n-2}$ and is not a pivot. The equal-scale derivation does not apply. (Finding some other exact set in the unequal-scale model is a different problem and is not asked here.)

This construction is an interval inversion, not a most-powerful test of a simple point null. Size, randomization on a likelihood-ratio boundary, and Neyman–Pearson optimality are not used.

graderFixtures.proofText: Under a common scale, Xbar-Ybar is normal and independent of the pooled chi-square (m+n-2)S_p^2/σ^2, so T ~ t_{m+n-2} and the inverted interval is Xbar-Ybar ± t_{m+n-2,α/2} S_p √(1/m+1/n). If the scales differ, Var(Xbar-Ybar) and E[S_p^2] involve different mixtures, so the same T is not a pivot.
Even if σ_X^2 ≠ σ_Y^2, the pooled statistic T is still exactly t_{m+n-2} because adding the two residual sums of squares always produces a chi-square.
Ignore the sample variances and use the known-scale interval Xbar-Ybar ± z_{α/2} σ √(1/m+1/n). The pooled t construction is unnecessary.

MSTAT:020117.title: Poisson UMP: Xi iid Pois(theta), n=2, S~Pois(2theta); H0 theta<=1 vs >; LR incr in S; reject S>=5; alpha=1-7e^{-2}; power(theta=2)=1-(103/3)e^{-4}
MSTAT:020117.objective: For two i.i.d. Poisson observations, identify the sufficient sum, prove that the one-sided likelihood ratio is increasing in that sum, and construct the UMP level-alpha test of the composite hypothesis theta<=1 versus theta>1 by evaluating size at the boundary. Compute the exact Poisson(2) size of the critical region S>=5 and the exact power at theta=2.
MSTAT:020117.statement:
Let $X_1,X_2$ be i.i.d. $\mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$ with unknown
mean $\theta\ge 0$, and write $S=X_1+X_2$. Consider the composite
one-sided problem
\[
H_0:\theta\le 1\qquad\text{versus}\qquad H_1:\theta>1.
\]

1. Prove that $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta)$ is complete
   sufficient, and that the Neyman-Pearson likelihood ratio for
   any pair $0<\theta'<\theta''$ is a nondecreasing function of
   $S$. Conclude that the family has monotone likelihood ratio in
   $S$.

2. Invoke Karlin-Rubin to produce a UMP test of $H_0$ versus
   $H_1$ among tests that reject for large $S$. Explain why the
   size of any such test equals its type I error at the
   composite boundary $\theta=1$, not at an interior point of
   $H_0$ and not at $\theta=0$.

3. Take the critical region $\{S\ge 5\}$. Prove that the size is
   \[
   \alpha
   =\mathbb{P}_{\theta=1}(S\ge 5)
   =1-7e^{-2}
   =0.0526530173437111,
   \]
   and that the power at $\theta=2$ is
   \[
   \beta(2)
   =\mathbb{P}_{\theta=2}(S\ge 5)
   =1-\frac{103}{3}\,e^{-4}
   =0.3711630648201265.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the size may be computed at any
   convenient point of $H_0$, for instance $\theta=0$, or $S$ is
   $\mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$ rather than $\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta)$,
   giving $\alpha=1-e^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{4}1/k!$”; (ii) “the UMP
   test is two-sided, or rejects for small $S$, or the power at
   $\theta=2$ is the $\mathrm{Poisson}(2)$ tail rather than the
   $\mathrm{Poisson}(4)$ tail.”

Stay inside the one-parameter Poisson family with composite
boundary size and MLR. Do not replace the problem by a
normal-mean $z$-test, and do not treat $H_0$ as the simple
hypothesis $\theta=1$ without justifying the boundary
calculation.
permittedResults: Karlin-Rubin: if a family has MLR in $S$, then for $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$ versus $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$ every test that rejects when $S\ge k$ (and possibly randomizes at $S=k$) is UMP of its size. The size equals $\mathbb{P}_{\theta_0}(S\ge k)$ after randomization.
If $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ then $\mathbb{P}(S\ge 5)=1-e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=0}^{4}\lambda^k/k!$. At $\lambda=2$ the sum is $7$; at $\lambda=4$ the sum is $103/3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor the joint Poisson pmf through S, form L(theta'')/L(theta'), and apply Karlin-Rubin.
Use monotonicity of the power function to place the size at theta=1, then expand the Poisson(2) and Poisson(4) cdfs through k=4.

milestones.criterion: Identifies S~Poisson(2theta), proves the likelihood ratio is increasing in S, and invokes Karlin-Rubin for a one-sided UMP test.
Evaluates composite size at the boundary theta=1 as 1-7e^{-2} and the power at theta=2 as 1-(103/3)e^{-4}.
Refuses an interior-null size calculation and a two-sided or wrong-mean Poisson tail.

commonErrors.description: Computes the size at an interior point of H0 such as theta=0, or treats S as Poisson(theta) rather than Poisson(2theta).
commonErrors.consequence: The UMP size 1-7e^{-2} is replaced by a strictly smaller interior type I error or by a one-observation Poisson tail.

commonErrors.description: Uses a two-sided or lower-tailed critical region, or computes the power at theta=2 under Poisson(2) rather than Poisson(4).
commonErrors.consequence: The one-sided UMP identification or the exact power 1-(103/3)e^{-4} is lost.

hintTree.content: The joint pmf is $e^{-2\theta}\theta^{x_1+x_2}/(x_1!x_2!)$. The ratio at $\theta''>\theta'$ is $(\theta''/\theta')^S\exp(-2(\theta''-\theta'))$, which increases in $S$.

Power $\beta(\theta)=\mathbb{P}_\theta(S\ge 5)$ is nondecreasing in $\theta$ because adding an independent Poisson increment stochastically increases $S$. Hence $\sup_{\theta\le 1}\beta(\theta)=\beta(1)$.
Under $\theta=1$, $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2)$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{4}2^k/k!=7$. Under $\theta=2$, $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(4)$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{4}4^k/k!=103/3$.

MSTAT:020117.canonicalSolution:
The joint pmf of $(X_1,X_2)$ is
\[
e^{-2\theta}\frac{\theta^{X_1+X_2}}{X_1!X_2!}.
\]
By the Poisson addition formula, or by recognizing a one-parameter
exponential family, $S=X_1+X_2$ is complete sufficient and
$S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta)$. For $0<\theta'<\theta''$ the
likelihood ratio is
\[
\frac{L(\theta'')}{L(\theta')}
=\Bigl(\frac{\theta''}{\theta'}\Bigr)^{S}
\exp\bigl(-2(\theta''-\theta')\bigr),
\]
which is strictly increasing in $S$. Thus the family has MLR in
$S$.
\[
\boxed{S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta);\ \text{MLR in }S}.
\]

Karlin-Rubin therefore asserts that every test rejecting for large
$S$ is UMP of its size for $H_0:\theta\le 1$ versus $H_1:\theta>1$.
The power function $\beta(\theta)=\mathbb{P}_\theta(S\ge 5)$ is
nondecreasing (the family has MLR, or equivalently
$S_{\theta+\delta}\stackrel{d}{=}S_\theta+W$ with $W\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\delta)$
independent of $S_\theta$). The size of the composite null is
therefore attained at the boundary:
\[
\alpha
=\sup_{\theta\le 1}\beta(\theta)
=\beta(1)
=\mathbb{P}_{\theta=1}(S\ge 5).
\]
Evaluating the type I error at $\theta=0$ or at a strict interior
point of $H_0$ understates the size.
\[
\boxed{\text{size}=\beta(1),\text{ not an interior }H_0\text{ value}}.
\]

Under $\theta=1$ one has $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2)$, so
\[
\mathbb{P}(S\le 4)
=e^{-2}\Bigl(1+2+\frac{4}{2}+\frac{8}{6}+\frac{16}{24}\Bigr)
=e^{-2}\bigl(1+2+2+\tfrac43+\tfrac23\bigr)
=7e^{-2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\alpha=1-7e^{-2}=0.0526530173437111.
\]
Under $\theta=2$ one has $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(4)$, so
\[
\mathbb{P}(S\le 4)
=e^{-4}\Bigl(1+4+8+\frac{64}{6}+\frac{256}{24}\Bigr)
=e^{-4}\bigl(13+\tfrac{64}{3}\bigr)
=\frac{103}{3}\,e^{-4}.
\]
Hence
\[
\beta(2)=1-\frac{103}{3}\,e^{-4}=0.3711630648201265.
\]
\[
\boxed{\alpha=1-7e^{-2},\quad\beta(2)=1-(103/3)e^{-4}}.
\]

Sentence (i) either evaluates size inside $H_0$ rather than at the
boundary, or replaces $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta)$ by
$\mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$. Sentence (ii) replaces the one-sided
MLR test by a two-sided or lower-tailed critical region, or
computes the power at $\theta=2$ under the null Poisson$(2)$ law.
None of those substitutions is asked.

The argument never Gaussianizes $S$, never treats $H_0$ as
two-sided, and never omits the factor $2$ in the Poisson mean of
the sum.

graderFixtures.proofText: The family has MLR in $S\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(2\theta)$. Karlin-Rubin yields the UMP test rejecting for large $S$. Composite size equals the boundary value $\mathbb{P}_{\theta=1}(S\ge 5)=1-7e^{-2}$. Power at $\theta=2$ is $\mathbb{P}(S\ge 5)$ under $\mathrm{Poisson}(4)$, equal to $1-(103/3)e^{-4}$.
I compute the size at theta=0, or I treat S as Poisson(theta) rather than Poisson(2theta), so I do not obtain alpha=1-7e^{-2} at the composite boundary.
I use a two-sided or lower-tailed rejection region, or I compute the power at theta=2 from the Poisson(2) tail instead of the Poisson(4) tail.
