MSTAT:020118.title: Holm step-down alpha=.05, sorted p=(.004,.018,.020,.20); thresholds=(.0125,.0166667,.025,.05); reject H1 only and STOP; adj p=(.016,.054,.054,.20)
MSTAT:020118.objective: Carry out the Holm step-down procedure at level 0.05 on four sorted p-values, form Holm adjusted p-values by cumulative maxima of the raw multiples, and prove familywise-error control under arbitrary dependence by a first-true-null plus union-bound argument.
MSTAT:020118.statement:
Four null hypotheses $H_1,H_2,H_3,H_4$ are tested at familywise
level $\alpha=0.05$. The ordered $p$-values are
\[
p_{(1)}=0.004,\quad
p_{(2)}=0.018,\quad
p_{(3)}=0.020,\quad
p_{(4)}=0.20,
\]
with corresponding ordered hypotheses $H_{(1)},\ldots,H_{(4)}$.
No independence among the $p$-values is assumed; each true-null
$p$-value is only required to be superuniform,
$\mathbb{P}(p_j\le u)\le u$ for $u\in[0,1]$.

1. Write the Holm thresholds $\alpha/(m-i+1)$ for $m=4$ and
   $i=1,2,3,4$, namely
   \[
   (0.0125,\ 0.0166667,\ 0.025,\ 0.05),
   \]
   using the display $0.05/3=1/60\approx 0.0166667$. Carry out the
   step-down comparison and prove that $H_{(1)}$ is rejected,
   that $H_{(2)}$ is not rejected, and that the procedure then
   stops, so $H_{(3)}$ and $H_{(4)}$ are not rejected even though
   $p_{(3)}=0.020<0.025$.

2. Form the raw Holm multiples
   \[
   4p_{(1)}=0.016,\quad
   3p_{(2)}=0.054,\quad
   2p_{(3)}=0.040,\quad
   p_{(4)}=0.20,
   \]
   and prove that the Holm adjusted $p$-values are the cumulative
   maxima
   \[
   (0.016,\ 0.054,\ 0.054,\ 0.20).
   \]
   Confirm that these adjusted values reproduce the same
   reject/retain decisions at $\alpha=0.05$.

3. Prove that Holm controls the familywise error rate at level
   $\alpha$ under arbitrary dependence. Let $I_0$ be the (unknown)
   set of true nulls and let $H_{(k)}$ be the first true null in
   the ordered list. Bound the threshold at that step by
   $\alpha/|I_0|$ and apply a union bound to
   $\min_{j\in I_0}p_j$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “Holm uses the common Bonferroni
   cutoff $0.0125$ at every step (which happens to reject only
   $H_{(1)}$ for these data), or after failing $H_{(2)}$ one still
   tests and rejects $H_{(3)}$ because $0.020<0.025$”; (ii)
   “adjusted $p$-values are the raw multiples
   $(0.016,0.054,0.040,0.20)$ without cumulative maxima, or FWER
   control requires independence of the $p$-values.”

Stay inside Holm step-down FWER. Do not replace the procedure by
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control, and do not assume independence.
permittedResults: Holm at $m=4$, $\alpha=0.05$ uses thresholds $0.05/4$, $0.05/3$, $0.05/2$, $0.05$. The path $0.004<0.0125$ and $0.018>0.05/3$ rejects only $H_{(1)}$ and then stops.

If $I_0$ is the true-null set and $H_{(k)}$ is the first true null, then $m-k+1\ge|I_0|$, so a false rejection implies $\min_{j\in I_0}p_j\le\alpha/|I_0|$. The union bound yields FWER $\le\alpha$ with no independence hypothesis.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare the ordered p-values to alpha/(m-i+1) and stop at the first failure.
Take cumulative maxima of (m-i+1)p_{(i)}, then bound the first true null by alpha/m0 and union-bound.

milestones.criterion: Carries out the Holm path: reject H(1), fail H(2), stop, and leave H(3) and H(4) unrejected.
Forms adjusted p=(0.016, 0.054, 0.054, 0.20) and proves FWER<=alpha under arbitrary dependence by the first true null plus a union bound.
Refuses a Bonferroni-every-step rule, a post-stop comparison of H(3), and an independence assumption.

commonErrors.description: Uses the common cutoff 0.0125 at every step, or continues after failing H(2) and rejects H(3) because 0.020<0.025.
commonErrors.consequence: The Holm rule is replaced by a different procedure, or its stop is lost and H(3) is incorrectly rejected; the common cutoff happens to give the same rejection set only for these data.

commonErrors.description: Reports adjusted p=(0.016, 0.054, 0.040, 0.20) without cumulative maxima, or claims FWER control requires independent p-values.
commonErrors.consequence: The monotone adjusted vector (0.016, 0.054, 0.054, 0.20) or the arbitrary-dependence union-bound proof is erased.

hintTree.content: Compare $0.004$ with $0.05/4=0.0125$, then $0.018$ with $0.05/3=1/60$. Stop at the first failure.
The raw multiples are $4\cdot 0.004$, $3\cdot 0.018$, $2\cdot 0.020$, and $0.20$. Replace the third entry by the running maximum $0.054$.
At the first true null at least $|I_0|$ hypotheses remain, so the cutoff is at most $\alpha/|I_0|$. Union-bound the minimum true-null $p$-value.

MSTAT:020118.canonicalSolution:
The Holm cutoffs for $m=4$ and $\alpha=0.05$ are
\[
\frac{0.05}{4}=0.0125,\qquad
\frac{0.05}{3}=\frac{1}{60}\approx 0.0166667,\qquad
\frac{0.05}{2}=0.025,\qquad
0.05.
\]
Step $1$: $p_{(1)}=0.004\le 0.0125$, so reject $H_{(1)}$.
Step $2$: $p_{(2)}=0.018>1/60$, so fail to reject $H_{(2)}$ and
stop. The remaining hypotheses $H_{(3)}$ and $H_{(4)}$ are not
rejected. In particular $p_{(3)}=0.020<0.025$ is irrelevant
after a stop: Holm is not a step-up or unadjusted comparison.
\[
\boxed{\text{reject }H_{(1)}\text{ only; stop at }H_{(2)}}.
\]

The raw multiples are
\[
4p_{(1)}=0.016,\quad
3p_{(2)}=0.054,\quad
2p_{(3)}=0.040,\quad
p_{(4)}=0.20.
\]
Cumulative maxima produce the Holm adjusted $p$-values
\[
\tilde p_{(1)}=0.016,\qquad
\tilde p_{(2)}=\max(0.016,0.054)=0.054,
\]
\[
\tilde p_{(3)}=\max(0.054,0.040)=0.054,\qquad
\tilde p_{(4)}=\max(0.054,0.20)=0.20.
\]
Comparing with $\alpha=0.05$ again rejects only the first
hypothesis, because $0.016\le 0.05$ while $0.054>0.05$.
\[
\boxed{\text{adjusted }p=(0.016,0.054,0.054,0.20)}.
\]

For FWER, let $I_0$ be the true-null index set and $m_0=|I_0|$.
If $m_0=0$ then FWER $=0$. Otherwise let $H_{(k)}$ be the first
true null in the ordered list. At least $m_0$ hypotheses remain
at that step, so the Holm threshold satisfies
$\alpha/(m-k+1)\le\alpha/m_0$. A familywise error occurs only if
this first true null is rejected, which forces
\[
\min_{j\in I_0}p_j
\le p_{(k)}
\le\frac{\alpha}{m-k+1}
\le\frac{\alpha}{m_0}.
\]
Superuniformity and the union bound, valid under arbitrary
dependence, give
\[
\mathrm{FWER}
=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\min_{j\in I_0}p_j\le\frac{\alpha}{m_0}\Bigr)
\le\sum_{j\in I_0}\mathbb{P}\Bigl(p_j\le\frac{\alpha}{m_0}\Bigr)
\le m_0\cdot\frac{\alpha}{m_0}
=\alpha.
\]
Independence is not used.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{FWER}\le\alpha\text{ under arbitrary dependence}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces Holm by a common Bonferroni cutoff, which
coincidentally gives the same rejection set for these data but is
not the Holm step-down rule, or continues after the first failure
and incorrectly rejects $H_{(3)}$. Sentence (ii) omits the
cumulative-maximum step in the
adjusted $p$-values or claims that FWER control needs
independence. Neither substitution is asked.

The argument never invokes Benjamini-Hochberg $q$-values, never
assumes independence or positive regression dependence, and never
restarts after a stop.

graderFixtures.proofText: Holm thresholds $(0.0125,0.05/3,0.025,0.05)$. Reject $H_{(1)}$ only and stop at $H_{(2)}$; $H_{(3)}$ is not rejected. Adjusted $p$-values are the cumulative maxima $(0.016,0.054,0.054,0.20)$. FWER $\le\alpha$ follows from the first true null and a union bound, with no independence assumption.

I use the common Bonferroni cutoff 0.0125 at every step and call that Holm, even though it only coincidentally gives the same rejection set here; or I continue after failing H(2) and reject H(3) because 0.020<0.025.
I report adjusted p-values as the raw multiples (0.016, 0.054, 0.040, 0.20) without cumulative maxima, or I claim that FWER control requires independent p-values.

MSTAT:020219.title: Exp(rate 2): mu=.5, var=.25; CLT sqrt(n)(xbar-.5)->N(0,.25); S_n->.5; T->N01; n=100, xbar=.58, s=.50 => T=1.6; 95% CI(.482,.678) includes .5
MSTAT:020219.objective: For i.i.d. exponential observations with rate 2, record the mean and variance, pass from the CLT through Slutsky to a studentized N(0,1) limit, and evaluate the Wald statistic and 95 percent normal interval at n=100, xbar=0.58, s=0.50.
MSTAT:020219.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. exponential random variables with
known rate parameterization
\[
f(x)=2e^{-2x}\qquad(x>0),
\]
so the mean and variance are those of $\mathrm{Exp}(\mathrm{rate}=2)$.
Write $\bar X_n$ for the sample mean and $S_n$ for the sample
standard deviation (the positive square root of the usual
$n-1$ or $n$ second-moment estimator; only the in-probability
limit of $S_n$ will matter). The scope is first-order
asymptotic inference as $n\to\infty$; the numerical evaluation
uses $n=100$ and the conventional normal quantile $z_{0.975}=1.96$.
Do not replace the limit by an exact $t_{n-1}$ statement.

1. Prove that $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=1/2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=1/4$.
   Apply the CLT to obtain
   \[
   \sqrt{n}\bigl(\bar X_n-\tfrac12\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\tfrac14).
   \]
   Prove $S_n\to 1/2$ in probability, and conclude by Slutsky that
   the studentized mean satisfies
   \[
   T_n
   =\frac{\sqrt{n}\bigl(\bar X_n-\tfrac12\bigr)}{S_n}
   \Rightarrow N(0,1).
   \]

2. Specialize to $n=100$, $\bar X_n=0.58$, and $S_n=0.50$. Prove
   \[
   T_n=1.6.
   \]

3. Form the Wald $95\%$ interval
   \[
   \bar X_n\pm 1.96\,\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}
   \]
   and prove that it equals $(0.482,0.678)$. Confirm that this
   interval includes the exponential mean $1/2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “rate $2$ means the mean is $2$ and
   the variance is $4$, or $T_n$ is formed with $S_n=\bar X_n$
   rather than the given $S_n=0.50$, producing $T_n=1.6/1.16$ or
   $T_n=0.8$”; (ii) “the $95\%$ interval uses $z=1.645$ or omits
   $\sqrt{n}$, or is an exact $t_{99}$ interval that excludes
   $1/2$.”

Stay inside the rate-$2$ exponential model and first-order Wald
studentization. Do not switch to a scale parameterization that
sets the mean equal to $2$, and do not claim an exact finite-sample
normal or $t$ law.
permittedResults: The CLT gives $\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n-1/2)\Rightarrow N(0,1/4)$. Consistency of the sample standard deviation gives $S_n\to 1/2$. Slutsky produces the $N(0,1)$ studentized limit.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read moments from the rate parameterization, apply the CLT, and studentize by Slutsky.
Insert n=100, xbar=0.58, s=0.50 into T_n and into xbar +/- 1.96 s/sqrt(n).

milestones.criterion: Records mu=1/2, var=1/4, the CLT N(0,1/4) limit, S_n->1/2, and T_n=>N(0,1).
Evaluates T=1.6 and the Wald interval (0.482, 0.678), and notes that 0.5 is inside the interval.
Refuses a rate/scale swap and a non-Wald critical value or missing sqrt(n).

commonErrors.description: Takes the exponential mean to be 2, or forms T_n with S_n=xbar rather than the assigned s=0.50.
commonErrors.consequence: The CLT centering 1/2 or the value T=1.6 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses z=1.645, omits sqrt(n) from the standard error, or treats the interval as exact t_{99} and claims it excludes 1/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The Wald interval (0.482, 0.678) and the inclusion of 1/2 are erased.

hintTree.content: Integrate $x\cdot 2e^{-2x}$ and $x^2\cdot 2e^{-2x}$, or use $\mathbb{E}[X]=1/\lambda$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2$ at $\lambda=2$.
Divide the CLT limit by $S_n\to 1/2$. The given numerical $S_n$ is $0.50$, not $\bar X_n$.
The half-width is $1.96\cdot 0.05=0.098$. Check that $0.5$ lies between $0.58-0.098$ and $0.58+0.098$.

MSTAT:020219.canonicalSolution:
With rate $\lambda=2$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_i]=\frac1\lambda=\frac12,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\frac1{\lambda^2}=\frac14.
\]
The Lindeberg CLT therefore yields
\[
\sqrt{n}\Bigl(\bar X_n-\frac12\Bigr)\Rightarrow N\Bigl(0,\frac14\Bigr).
\]
The sample second moment is consistent for $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)$, so
$S_n\to\sigma=1/2$ in probability. Slutsky's lemma divides the
CLT limit by this consistent scale and produces
\[
T_n
=\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n-1/2)}{S_n}
\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\]
The limit is first-order and does not require an exact gamma or
$t$ law.
\[
\boxed{\mu=1/2,\ \sigma^2=1/4,\ T_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)}.
\]

Now $n=100$, $\bar X_n=0.58$, $S_n=0.50$:
\[
T_n
=\frac{10\cdot(0.58-0.50)}{0.50}
=\frac{0.80}{0.50}
=1.6.
\]
\[
\boxed{T_n=1.6}.
\]

The Wald $95\%$ interval uses $z_{0.975}=1.96$:
\[
\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{0.50}{10}=0.05,\qquad
1.96\cdot 0.05=0.098,
\]
so
\[
\bar X_n\pm 1.96\,\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}
=0.58\pm 0.098
=(0.482,\ 0.678).
\]
The exponential mean $1/2=0.5$ lies in $(0.482,0.678)$.
\[
\boxed{95\%\ \mathrm{CI}=(0.482,0.678),\ \text{includes }1/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses rate with scale, or studentizes with
$\bar X_n$ rather than the assigned $S_n=0.50$. Sentence (ii)
replaces $1.96$ by $1.645$, drops the $\sqrt{n}$ in the standard
error, or pretends the interval is an exact $t_{99}$ statement
that excludes $1/2$. None of those substitutions is asked.

The argument never sets $\mu=2$, never claims a finite-sample
normal pivot, and never uses a $t$ critical value.

graderFixtures.proofText: $\mathrm{Exp}(\mathrm{rate}=2)$ has mean $1/2$ and variance $1/4$. Then $\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n-1/2)\Rightarrow N(0,1/4)$, $S_n\to 1/2$, and $T_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. For $n=100$, $\bar X_n=0.58$, $S_n=0.50$ one has $T_n=1.6$ and Wald $95\%$ interval $(0.482,0.678)$, which includes $1/2$.
I treat rate 2 as meaning the mean is 2, or I studentize with S_n=xbar rather than the given s=0.50, so I do not obtain T=1.6.
I form the 95% interval with z=1.645 or without sqrt(n), or I treat it as an exact t_99 interval that excludes 1/2.

MSTAT:020220.title: Laplace(0,b=2), f(0)=1/4: sqrt(n) median->N(0,4); n=100 SE=.2, med=.30 => z=1.5; 95% CI(-.092,.692); mean AV=8/n, median AV=4/n, ARE=2
MSTAT:020220.objective: For the Laplace location family with scale 2, derive the sample-median asymptotic variance from f(0)=1/4, evaluate the n=100 standard error, z-statistic and 95 percent interval at observed median 0.30, and compute the asymptotic relative efficiency of the median versus the mean.
MSTAT:020220.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. Laplace (double exponential) with
location $0$ and scale $b=2$,
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{2b}\exp\bigl(-|x|/b\bigr)
=\frac14\exp\bigl(-|x|/2\bigr).
\]
Write $m_n$ for the sample median. The scope is first-order
asymptotic inference for a unique median at which $f$ is positive
and continuous. Use $z_{0.975}=1.96$ for the numerical interval.

1. Record $f(0)=1/4$. Prove the sample-median CLT
   \[
   \sqrt{n}\,m_n\Rightarrow N\Bigl(0,\frac{1}{4f(0)^2}\Bigr)
   =N(0,4).
   \]
   At $n=100$ the asymptotic standard error is therefore $0.2$.

2. An observed sample median is $m_n=0.30$. Prove that the
   studentized value is $z=1.5$, and that the Wald $95\%$ interval
   \[
   m_n\pm 1.96\cdot 0.2
   \]
   equals $(-0.092,0.692)$.

3. The Laplace$(0,2)$ mean is $0$ and its variance is $2b^2=8$,
   so $\sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n\Rightarrow N(0,8)$. Compare asymptotic
   variances $8/n$ for the mean and $4/n$ for the median, and
   prove that the asymptotic relative efficiency of the median
   relative to the mean is
   \[
   \mathrm{ARE}(m_n,\bar X_n)
   =\frac{8}{4}
   =2.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the median variance is
   $1/(4nf(0))$ rather than $1/(4nf(0)^2)$, so
   $\sqrt{n}\,m_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)$ and the $n=100$ SE is
   $0.1$”; (ii) “ARE is $\mathrm{AV}(\mathrm{median})/\mathrm{AV}(\mathrm{mean})=1/2$,
   or the mean has the Gaussian variance $1/n$ or $4/n$, or this
   is a Hodges super-efficiency exercise.”

Stay inside the Laplace$(0,2)$ location model and first-order
median asymptotics. Do not replace $f(0)=1/4$ by a Gaussian
density, and do not invert the ARE ratio.
permittedResults: For a unique median $m$ with $f(m)>0$ continuous, $\sqrt{n}(m_n-m)\Rightarrow N(0,1/(4f(m)^2))$. At $f(0)=1/4$ the asymptotic variance is $4$.
Laplace scale $b$ has variance $2b^2$. For $b=2$ this is $8$. Therefore $\mathrm{ARE}(m_n,\bar X_n)=8/4=2$, and at $n=100$ the median SE is $2/10=0.2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert f(0)=1/4 into 1/(4 f(0)^2), then form SE=2/sqrt(n) and the Wald interval.
Compare Laplace mean variance 2 b^2=8 to median variance 4 and take the ratio 8/4.

milestones.criterion: Derives sqrt(n) m_n => N(0,4) from f(0)=1/4 and records the n=100 SE 0.2.
Evaluates z=1.5, the interval (-0.092, 0.692), AV_mean=8/n, AV_median=4/n, and ARE=2.
Refuses an unsquared density in the median variance and an inverted ARE.

commonErrors.description: Uses 1/(4 n f(0)) instead of 1/(4 n f(0)^2), producing asymptotic variance 1 and n=100 SE 0.1.
commonErrors.consequence: The N(0,4) median limit, the SE 0.2, and the z=1.5 interval are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports ARE=1/2 by inverting the variance ratio, or assigns the mean the Gaussian variance 1/n or 4/n.
commonErrors.consequence: The identification ARE(median, mean)=2 from 8/n versus 4/n is erased.

hintTree.content: Compute $1/(4f(0)^2)=1/(4\cdot 1/16)=4$. Then $\mathrm{SE}=2/\sqrt{n}$.
Laplace variance is $2b^2=8$. ARE of the median relative to the mean is $(\,8/n\,)/(\,4/n\,)=2$.

MSTAT:020220.canonicalSolution:
The assigned density has
\[
f(0)=\frac{1}{2\cdot 2}=\frac14.
\]
The sample-median CLT at a unique median with positive continuous
density reads
\[
\sqrt{n}\,m_n
\Rightarrow N\Bigl(0,\frac{1}{4f(0)^2}\Bigr)
=N\Bigl(0,\frac{1}{4\cdot(1/16)}\Bigr)
=N(0,4).
\]
At $n=100$ the asymptotic standard error is
\[
\sqrt{\frac{4}{100}}=\frac{2}{10}=0.2.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sqrt{n}\,m_n\Rightarrow N(0,4),\quad\mathrm{SE}=0.2}.
\]

With observed $m_n=0.30$,
\[
z=\frac{0.30}{0.2}=1.5.
\]
The Wald $95\%$ interval is
\[
0.30\pm 1.96\cdot 0.2
=0.30\pm 0.392
=(-0.092,\ 0.692).
\]
\[
\boxed{z=1.5,\quad 95\%\ \mathrm{CI}=(-0.092,0.692)}.
\]

A Laplace random variable with scale $b$ has variance $2b^2$. For
$b=2$ this is $8$, so
\[
\sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n\Rightarrow N(0,8).
\]
The asymptotic variances of the mean and median are therefore
$8/n$ and $4/n$. The ARE of the median relative to the mean is
the inverted ratio of those variances:
\[
\mathrm{ARE}(m_n,\bar X_n)
=\frac{8/n}{4/n}
=2.
\]
Thus, in this Laplace model, the sample median is first-order
more efficient than the sample mean.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{AV}(\bar X_n)=8/n,\ \mathrm{AV}(m_n)=4/n,\ \mathrm{ARE}=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the square on $f(0)$ and reports asymptotic
variance $1$ with SE $0.1$. Sentence (ii) inverts the ARE, or
replaces the Laplace mean variance $8$ by a Gaussian $1$ or $4$,
or else replaces the efficiency comparison by a Hodges
super-efficiency construction, which is not asked.

The argument never uses a Gaussian density at $0$, never inverts
the ARE ratio, and never treats $m_n$ as a Hodges estimator.

graderFixtures.proofText: Laplace$(0,2)$ has $f(0)=1/4$, so $\sqrt{n}\,m_n\Rightarrow N(0,4)$. At $n=100$ the SE is $0.2$. For $m_n=0.30$, $z=1.5$ and the $95\%$ interval is $(-0.092,0.692)$. Mean AV $=8/n$, median AV $=4/n$, and $\mathrm{ARE}(m_n,\bar X_n)=2$.
I use the median variance 1/(4 n f(0)) without squaring f(0), so I report sqrt(n) m_n => N(0,1) and SE=0.1 at n=100.
I invert the ARE and report 1/2, or I assign the mean a Gaussian variance 1/n or 4/n instead of the Laplace variance 8/n.

MSTAT:020221.title: Hodges: 0 if |xbar|<=n^{-1/4} else xbar; pointwise N01 for theta!=0, degenerate at 0; n=1e4 thresh=.1; along theta_n=.5 n^{-1/4}, set 0 w.p.->1 but sqrt(n)(tilde-theta_n)-> -inf
MSTAT:020221.objective: For i.i.d. N(theta,1) observations, define the Hodges estimator that shrinks the sample mean to 0 inside the n^{-1/4} neighborhood, establish the pointwise limits at theta!=0 and at 0, evaluate the n=10^4 threshold on two observed means, and exhibit nonuniformity along theta_n=0.5 n^{-1/4}.
MSTAT:020221.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. $N(\theta,1)$ and write
$\bar X_n$ for the sample mean. Define the Hodges estimator
\[
\tilde\theta_n
=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if }|\bar X_n|\le n^{-1/4},\\
\bar X_n & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The scope is pointwise asymptotic distribution theory versus
uniformity in $\theta$, including one local sequence
$\theta_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}$.

1. For each fixed $\theta\neq 0$, prove
   \[
   \sqrt{n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,1).
   \]
   At the single point $\theta=0$, prove that
   $\mathbb{P}(\tilde\theta_n=0)\to 1$, so
   $\sqrt{n}\,\tilde\theta_n\to 0$ in probability (super-efficiency).

2. Specialize to $n=10^4$. Prove that the threshold is
   $n^{-1/4}=0.1$. Then $\bar X_n=0.08$ is mapped to $0$, while
   $\bar X_n=0.12$ is left at $0.12$.

3. Along the local sequence $\theta_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}$, prove
   \[
   \mathbb{P}_{\theta_n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n=0\bigr)\to 1,
   \]
   while on that event
   \[
   \sqrt{n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n\bigr)
   =-\tfrac12 n^{1/4}\to-\infty.
   \]
   Conclude that the $N(0,1)$ limit is not uniform in $\theta$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the $N(0,1)$ limit holds uniformly,
   including at $\theta=0$, so $\sqrt{n}\,\tilde\theta_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)$
   at the origin as well”; (ii) “along $\theta_n$ one still has
   $\sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$ or
   $\to 0$, or the threshold is $n^{-1/2}$ rather than
   $n^{-1/4}$, or this is a Laplace-median efficiency
   exercise.”

Stay inside the Hodges shrinkage of the normal mean. Do not
replace the threshold $n^{-1/4}$ by $n^{-1/2}$, and do not claim
a uniform limiting experiment.
permittedResults: For fixed $\theta\neq 0$, $\bar X_n\to\theta$ almost surely while $n^{-1/4}\to 0$, so eventually $\tilde\theta_n=\bar X_n$ and the usual CLT applies. At $\theta=0$, $\mathbb{P}(|\sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n|\le n^{1/4})\to 1$.

Along $\theta_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}$, $\bar X_n=\theta_n+Z_n/\sqrt{n}$ with $Z_n\sim N(0,1)$ yields $\mathbb{P}(|\tfrac12+n^{-1/4}Z_n|\le 1)\to 1$. On $\{\tilde\theta_n=0\}$ one has $\sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n)=-\tfrac12 n^{1/4}\to-\infty$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare the vanishing threshold n^{-1/4} with a fixed nonzero mean, and compare n^{1/4} with an N(0,1) tail at 0.
Center Xbar at theta_n=0.5 n^{-1/4}, divide the shrinkage event by n^{-1/4}, and evaluate sqrt(n)(0-theta_n).

milestones.criterion: Establishes the pointwise limits: N(0,1) for each fixed theta!=0 and degeneration to 0 at theta=0.
Evaluates the n=10^4 threshold 0.1 on 0.08 and 0.12, and shows that along theta_n the normalized error tends to -infty.
Refuses a uniform N(0,1) claim and a wrong threshold or tight local limit.

commonErrors.description: Claims that sqrt(n)(tilde-theta)=>N(0,1) uniformly in theta, or that the limit at theta=0 is still N(0,1).
commonErrors.consequence: Super-efficiency at the origin and the failure of uniformity are erased.

commonErrors.description: Along theta_n reports a N(0,1) or degenerate-0 limit for sqrt(n)(tilde-theta_n), or uses the threshold n^{-1/2}.
commonErrors.consequence: The divergence -0.5 n^{1/4}->-infty, or the assigned n^{-1/4} neighborhood, is lost.

hintTree.content: For fixed $\theta\neq 0$, compare $|\theta|$ with the vanishing threshold $n^{-1/4}$. At $\theta=0$, $n^{1/4}\to\infty$ exceeds any $N(0,1)$ quantile.
Write $\bar X_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}+n^{-1/2}Z_n$ and divide the event $|\bar X_n|\le n^{-1/4}$ by $n^{-1/4}$. The centered statistic on $\{\tilde\theta_n=0\}$ is $-\tfrac12 n^{1/4}$.

MSTAT:020221.canonicalSolution:
Fix $\theta\neq 0$. Then $\bar X_n\to\theta$ almost surely, while
the threshold $n^{-1/4}\to 0$. Hence
$\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n|\le n^{-1/4})\to 0$, so
$\tilde\theta_n=\bar X_n$ with probability tending to $1$. The
ordinary normal-mean CLT therefore remains in force:
\[
\sqrt{n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\]
At $\theta=0$, $\sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n\sim N(0,1)$ and
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n=0\bigr)
=\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\sqrt{n}\,\bar X_n|\le n^{1/4}\bigr)
\to 1,
\]
because $n^{1/4}\to\infty$. Thus $\tilde\theta_n=0$ with
probability tending to $1$, which is a fortiori
$\sqrt{n}\,\tilde\theta_n\to 0$ in probability: the estimator is
super-efficient at the origin.
\[
\boxed{\theta\neq 0:\ N(0,1);\quad\theta=0:\ \sqrt{n}\,\tilde\theta_n\to 0}.
\]

For $n=10^4$,
\[
n^{-1/4}=(10^4)^{-1/4}=10^{-1}=0.1.
\]
If $\bar X_n=0.08$ then $|0.08|\le 0.1$, so $\tilde\theta_n=0$.
If $\bar X_n=0.12$ then $|0.12|>0.1$, so $\tilde\theta_n=0.12$.
\[
\boxed{n=10^4:\ \text{threshold }0.1;\ 0.08\mapsto 0,\ 0.12\mapsto 0.12}.
\]

Now set $\theta_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}$. Write
$\bar X_n=\theta_n+Z_n/\sqrt{n}$ with $Z_n\sim N(0,1)$. The
shrinkage event becomes
\[
\bigl|\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}+n^{-1/2}Z_n\bigr|\le n^{-1/4},
\]
or equivalently
\[
\bigl|\tfrac12+n^{-1/4}Z_n\bigr|\le 1.
\]
Since $n^{-1/4}Z_n\to 0$ in probability,
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\theta_n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n=0\bigr)\to\mathbb{P}(\tfrac12\le 1)=1.
\]
On that event,
\[
\sqrt{n}\bigl(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n\bigr)
=\sqrt{n}\bigl(0-\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}\bigr)
=-\tfrac12 n^{1/4}
\to-\infty.
\]
Therefore $\sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta)$ cannot converge to
$N(0,1)$ uniformly in $\theta$: a local sequence already sends
the normalized error to $-\infty$ in probability.
\[
\boxed{\text{along }\theta_n:\ \tilde\theta_n=0\text{ w.p.}\to 1,\ \sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n)\to-\infty}.
\]

Sentence (i) promotes the pointwise $N(0,1)$ limit to a uniform
limit, including at $\theta=0$. Sentence (ii) claims a tight
$N(0,1)$ or degenerate-$0$ limit along $\theta_n$, or replaces
the threshold $n^{-1/4}$ by $n^{-1/2}$, or else replaces Hodges
shrinkage by a Laplace-median ARE calculation, which is not
asked.

The argument never claims a uniform limiting experiment, never
uses the threshold $n^{-1/2}$, and never identifies
$\tilde\theta_n$ with a sample median.

graderFixtures.proofText: For each fixed $\theta\neq 0$, $\sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. At $\theta=0$, $\tilde\theta_n=0$ with probability $\to 1$. For $n=10^4$ the threshold is $0.1$, so $0.08\mapsto 0$ and $0.12\mapsto 0.12$. Along $\theta_n=\tfrac12 n^{-1/4}$ one has $\mathbb{P}(\tilde\theta_n=0)\to 1$ and $\sqrt{n}(\tilde\theta_n-\theta_n)=-\tfrac12 n^{1/4}\to-\infty$.
I claim the N(0,1) limit holds uniformly in theta, including at theta=0, so I write sqrt(n) tilde => N(0,1) at the origin as well.
Along theta_n I report sqrt(n)(tilde-theta_n)=>N(0,1) or ->0, or I replace the threshold n^{-1/4} by n^{-1/2}.

MSTAT:020322.title: Beta-binomial BF10: n=10,x=8,H0 p=1/2,H1 p~Beta(1,1); m0=45/1024,m1=1/11,BF10=1024/495,P(H1|x)=1024/1519; post Beta(9,3) mean 3/4
MSTAT:020322.objective: With equal model odds, compute both binomial-coefficient-inclusive marginals, the Bayes factor BF10, the posterior model probability of H1, and the H1-conditional Beta(9,3) mean / one-step predictive success probability.
MSTAT:020322.statement:
A binary sample records $x=8$ successes in $n=10$ independent
Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability $p\in(0,1)$.
Two models are compared with equal prior model odds
$\mathbb{P}(H_0)=\mathbb{P}(H_1)=1/2$:
\[
H_0:\ p=\tfrac12,
\qquad
H_1:\ p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)
\]
(the $H_1$ prior is the uniform density on $(0,1)$). The
observation model under either hypothesis is binomial,
\[
f(x\mid p)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}.
\]
The binomial coefficient is part of the probability mass and must
be retained in every marginal.

1. Prove that the $H_0$ marginal mass is
   \[
   m_0
   :=f(x\mid H_0)
   =\binom{10}{8}\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)^{10}
   =\frac{45}{1024}.
   \]

2. Prove that the $H_1$ marginal mass is
   \[
   m_1
   :=f(x\mid H_1)
   =\binom{10}{8}B(9,3)
   =\frac{1}{11},
   \]
   where $B(\alpha,\beta)=\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)$.
   (Thus $B(9,3)=1/495$ and the combinatorial prefactor is required
   to reach $m_1=1/11$.)

3. The Bayes factor for $H_1$ against $H_0$ is $BF_{10}=m_1/m_0$.
   Prove
   \[
   BF_{10}=\frac{1024}{495}=2.06868686868687
   \]
   and, with the assigned equal model odds,
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
   =\frac{BF_{10}}{1+BF_{10}}
   =\frac{1024}{1519}=0.67412771560237.
   \]

4. Conditionally on $H_1$ and the data, prove that
   $p\mid x,H_1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(9,3)$, so the posterior mean and
   the one-step posterior-predictive success probability are both
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[p\mid x,H_1]
   =\mathbb{P}(X_{\mathrm{new}}=1\mid x,H_1)
   =\frac34.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the binomial coefficient cancels or
   may be dropped, so $m_0=1/1024$ and $m_1=B(9,3)=1/495$, or
   $m_1=45\cdot B(8,2)$”; (ii) “$BF_{01}=1024/495$, or
   $\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=m_1$, or the $H_1$-conditional posterior
   is $\mathrm{Beta}(8,2)$ with mean $4/5$, or this is a
   normal-normal / ridge exercise.”

Stay inside the discrete two-model comparison with a
$\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$ parameter prior under $H_1$. Do not replace
the binomial likelihood by a normal approximation, and do not
drop the combinatorial factor from only one of the two
marginals.
permittedResults: $BF_{10}=(1/11)/(45/1024)=1024/495$. Equal model odds convert this into $\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=1024/1519$. Conjugacy produces $\mathrm{Beta}(9,3)$ with mean $9/12=3/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the point-null binomial pmf and the beta-binomial integral with the same C(10,8) prefactor.
Form BF10=m1/m0, convert equal odds into a posterior model probability, then update Beta(1,1) to Beta(9,3).

milestones.criterion: Computes both combinatorial-inclusive marginals m0=45/1024 and m1=1/11, and the Bayes factor BF10=1024/495.
Converts equal model odds into P(H1|x)=1024/1519 and records the H1-conditional Beta(9,3) mean / predictive success 3/4.
Refuses dropping the binomial coefficient from a marginal and an inverted Bayes factor or Beta(8,2) update.

commonErrors.description: Drops C(10,8) from one or both marginals, reporting m0=1/1024 or m1=B(9,3)=1/495, or uses B(8,2) in place of B(9,3).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned masses m0=45/1024 and m1=1/11 are lost, even if a cancelled ratio accidentally recovers BF10.

commonErrors.description: Reports BF01=1024/495, or P(H1|x)=m1, or the H1-conditional posterior Beta(8,2) with mean 4/5.
commonErrors.consequence: The equal-odds posterior 1024/1519 or the conjugate mean 3/4 is erased.

hintTree.content: Keep $\binom{10}{8}=45$ in both marginals. Under $H_0$ only the factor $(1/2)^{10}$ remains.

MSTAT:020322.canonicalSolution:
The $H_0$ sampling model is a point binomial. With $n=10$ and
$x=8$,
\[
m_0
=\binom{10}{8}\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{10}
=45\cdot\frac{1}{1024}
=\frac{45}{1024}.
\]
\[
\boxed{m_0=45/1024}.
\]

Under $H_1$ the prior density of $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$ is identically
$1$, so
\[
m_1
=\int_0^1\binom{10}{8}p^8(1-p)^2\,dp
=\binom{10}{8}B(9,3).
\]
The beta function evaluates as
\[
B(9,3)
=\frac{\Gamma(9)\Gamma(3)}{\Gamma(12)}
=\frac{8!\,2!}{11!}
=\frac{2}{11\cdot10\cdot9}
=\frac{1}{495},
\]
and therefore
\[
m_1
=45\cdot\frac{1}{495}
=\frac{1}{11}.
\]
The same combinatorial factor appears in $m_0$ and in $m_1$; it is
not cancelled before the masses are reported.
\[
\boxed{m_1=\binom{10}{8}B(9,3)=1/11}.
\]

The Bayes factor for $H_1$ against $H_0$ is the ratio of these
masses:
\[
BF_{10}
=\frac{m_1}{m_0}
=\frac{1/11}{45/1024}
=\frac{1024}{11\cdot45}
=\frac{1024}{495}.
\]
The decimal expansion is the repeating value
$1024/495=2.06868686868687$. Equal prior model odds convert the
Bayes factor into posterior model odds, so
\[
\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)
=\frac{BF_{10}}{1+BF_{10}}
=\frac{1024/495}{1519/495}
=\frac{1024}{1519}=0.67412771560237.
\]
Equivalently,
$\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=m_1/(m_0+m_1)$ yields the same fraction
because the prior odds are one.
\[
\boxed{BF_{10}=1024/495,\quad\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=1024/1519}.
\]

Conditionally on $H_1$, the $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$ prior updates by
the binomial sufficient statistic $(x,n-x)=(8,2)$ to
\[
p\mid x,H_1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(9,3).
\]
The posterior mean is $9/(9+3)=3/4$. The one-step posterior
predictive success probability equals that same mean,
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_{\mathrm{new}}=1\mid x,H_1)=\frac34.
\]
\[
\boxed{p\mid x,H_1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(9,3),\ \mathbb{E}[p\mid x,H_1]=3/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $\binom{10}{8}$ from one or both marginals, or
uses the wrong beta arguments $B(8,2)$, destroying the assigned
pair $m_0=45/1024$, $m_1=1/11$. Sentence (ii) inverts the Bayes
factor, confuses a marginal likelihood with a posterior model
probability, or reports the likelihood-only update
$\mathrm{Beta}(8,2)$ with mean $4/5$, or else replaces the
two-model binomial comparison by a normal-normal or ridge
calculation, which is not asked.

The argument never approximates the binomial by a normal, never
places a continuous prior on $p$ under $H_0$, and never omits the
combinatorial factor from only one marginal.

graderFixtures.proofText: Retain $\binom{10}{8}$ in both masses: $m_0=45/1024$ and $m_1=\binom{10}{8}B(9,3)=1/11$. Then $BF_{10}=1024/495$ and, with equal model odds, $\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid x)=1024/1519$. Conditionally on $H_1$, $p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(9,3)$ with mean and one-step predictive success $3/4$.
The binomial coefficient cancels, so I report m0=1/1024 and m1=B(9,3)=1/495, or I write m1=45 B(8,2).
I report BF01=1024/495, or I set P(H1|x)=m1, or I take the H1-conditional posterior to be Beta(8,2) with mean 4/5.

MSTAT:020323.title: Normal-normal: theta~N(10,4), Xi~N(theta,9), n=4, xbar=14; post prec 25/36, mean 314/25, 95% (10.208,14.912); pred N(314/25,261/25)
MSTAT:020323.objective: Update the normal-normal conjugate pair by adding precisions, distinguish the posterior variance of theta from the posterior-predictive variance of a new observation, and evaluate both 95 percent intervals at z=1.96.
MSTAT:020323.statement:
A scalar mean $\theta$ has the conjugate prior
\[
\theta\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)
=\mathcal N(10,4).
\]
Independent observations satisfy $X_i\mid\theta\sim\mathcal N(\theta,9)$
for $i=1,\ldots,n$ with $n=4$ and sample mean $\bar x=14$. Sampling
variances are known; the $95\%$ intervals below use the standard
normal quantile $z_{0.975}=1.96$ (not a $t$ critical value).

1. The prior precision is $1/\tau_0^2=1/4$ and the likelihood
   precision is $n/\sigma^2=4/9$. Prove that the posterior
   precision, variance, mean, and standard deviation are
   \[
   \frac{1}{\tau_n^2}=\frac{25}{36},
   \qquad
   \tau_n^2=\frac{36}{25},
   \qquad
   \mu_n=\frac{314}{25}=12.56,
   \qquad
   \tau_n=\frac65.
   \]
   Hence the $95\%$ posterior interval for $\theta$ is
   \[
   \bigl(10.208,\ 14.912\bigr).
   \]

2. A new independent observation $X^\ast\mid\theta\sim\mathcal N(\theta,9)$
   has posterior-predictive law
   \[
   X^\ast\mid\text{data}
   \sim\mathcal N\Bigl(\mu_n,\ \sigma^2+\tau_n^2\Bigr)
   =\mathcal N\Bigl(\frac{314}{25},\ \frac{261}{25}\Bigr).
   \]
   Prove that the predictive standard deviation is
   $\sqrt{261}/5=3.2310988843$ and that the $95\%$ posterior-predictive
   interval is
   \[
   \bigl(6.22704619,\ 18.89295381\bigr).
   \]

3. Record explicitly that $\tau_n^2=36/25$ is a variance for
   $\theta$, while $261/25=9+36/25$ is a variance for $X^\ast$.
   These two numbers are not interchangeable.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “precisions add as variances, so the
   posterior variance is $4+9/4$ and $\mu_n$ is the unweighted
   average $12$”; (ii) “the predictive variance is $36/25$, or the
   $\theta$ interval uses $261/25$, or $z=1.645$, or this is a
   beta-binomial / ridge exercise.”

Stay inside the known-variance normal-normal model. Do not replace
$z=1.96$ by a $t_{n-1}$ quantile, and do not assign the posterior
variance of $\theta$ to a new observation.
permittedResults: Prior precision $1/4$ plus likelihood precision $4/9$ is $25/36$. Then $\mu_n=(36/25)\bigl(10/4+56/9\bigr)=314/25$ and $\tau_n=6/5$. The $95\%$ $\theta$ interval is $12.56\pm1.96\cdot6/5=(10.208,14.912)$.
Predictive variance $9+36/25=261/25$ has standard deviation $\sqrt{261}/5$. Then $12.56\pm1.96\cdot\sqrt{261}/5=(6.22704619,18.89295381)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Add prior precision 1/4 to likelihood precision 4/9, then form the precision-weighted mean.
Add the sampling variance 9 to tau_n^2 for a new X*, and expand both intervals with z=1.96.

milestones.criterion: Derives posterior precision 25/36, variance 36/25, mean 314/25, and the 95 percent theta interval (10.208,14.912).
Distinguishes the predictive law N(314/25,261/25) and records the 95 percent predictive interval (6.22704619,18.89295381).
Refuses adding variances at the posterior step and swapping the theta variance 36/25 with the predictive variance 261/25.

commonErrors.description: Adds the prior variance 4 to a sampling variance instead of adding precisions 1/4 and 4/9, or reports the unweighted mean 12 in place of 314/25.
commonErrors.consequence: The posterior precision 25/36 and the mean 314/25 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the posterior variance 36/25 to a new observation, or uses 261/25 as the variance of theta, or replaces z=1.96 by 1.645.
commonErrors.consequence: The distinct intervals (10.208,14.912) and (6.22704619,18.89295381) are erased.

hintTree.content: Add precisions, not variances: $1/4+4/9=9/36+16/36=25/36$.
A new $X^\ast$ adds the sampling variance $9$ to $36/25$. Do not reuse $36/25$ as a predictive variance.

MSTAT:020323.canonicalSolution:
The prior precision is $1/4$ and the likelihood precision is
$n/\sigma^2=4/9$. Adding precisions,
\[
\frac{1}{\tau_n^2}
=\frac14+\frac49
=\frac{9}{36}+\frac{16}{36}
=\frac{25}{36},
\qquad
\tau_n^2=\frac{36}{25},
\qquad
\tau_n=\frac65.
\]
The posterior mean is the corresponding precision-weighted
average:
\[
\mu_n
=\frac{36}{25}\Biggl(\frac{10}{4}+\frac{4\cdot14}{9}\Biggr)
=\frac{36}{25}\Biggl(\frac52+\frac{56}{9}\Biggr)
=\frac{36}{25}\cdot\frac{157}{18}
=\frac{314}{25}
=12.56.
\]
The $95\%$ posterior interval for $\theta$ uses $z=1.96$:
\[
12.56\pm1.96\cdot\frac65
=12.56\pm2.352
=(10.208,\ 14.912).
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau_n^{-2}=25/36,\ \tau_n^2=36/25,\ \mu_n=314/25,\ 95\%\ \theta=(10.208,14.912)}.
\]

A new independent observation has sampling variance $9$ about
$\theta$. Integrating out the posterior of $\theta$ therefore
adds the two variances:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X^\ast\mid\text{data})
=9+\frac{36}{25}
=\frac{225}{25}+\frac{36}{25}
=\frac{261}{25}.
\]
The predictive law is $\mathcal N(314/25,261/25)$, with
\[
\mathrm{sd}(X^\ast\mid\text{data})
=\frac{\sqrt{261}}{5}=3.2310988843.
\]
The $95\%$ posterior-predictive interval is
\[
12.56\pm1.96\cdot\frac{\sqrt{261}}{5}
=(6.22704619,\ 18.89295381).
\]
The number $36/25$ is a variance for $\theta$. The number
$261/25$ is a variance for $X^\ast$. They are not interchangeable.
\[
\boxed{X^\ast\mid\mathrm{data}\sim\mathcal N(314/25,261/25),\ 95\%=(6.22704619,18.89295381)}.
\]

Sentence (i) adds prior and sampling variances instead of
precisions, or replaces the precision-weighted mean by the
unweighted average $12$. Sentence (ii) assigns $\tau_n^2$ to a
new observation or $261/25$ to $\theta$, or swaps $z=1.96$ for
$1.645$, or else replaces the conjugate normal calculation by a
beta-binomial or ridge exercise, which is not asked.

The argument never uses a $t$ critical value, never treats
$\sigma^2$ as unknown, and never reports a single variance for
both $\theta$ and $X^\ast$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Posterior precision $1/4+4/9=25/36$, variance $36/25$, mean $314/25$, SD $6/5$. The $95\%$ interval for $\theta$ is $(10.208,14.912)$. Predictive law $\mathcal N(314/25,261/25)$ with SD $\sqrt{261}/5=3.2310988843$ and $95\%$ interval $(6.22704619,18.89295381)$. The two variances are not interchangeable.
I add the prior variance 4 to a sampling variance instead of adding precisions, or I report the unweighted mean 12 rather than 314/25.
I use 36/25 as the predictive variance of a new X*, or I use 261/25 as the variance of theta, or I replace z=1.96 by 1.645.

MSTAT:020424.title: WLS ledger: X rows (1,0),(1,1),(1,2), W=diag(1,2,1), y=(1,2,2); beta=(5/4,1/2), fitted (5/4,7/4,9/4), wSSE=1/4, Cov=sigma^2 (X'WX)^{-1}
MSTAT:020424.objective: Form the three-row WLS ledger X'WX, its inverse, X'Wy, the coefficient vector, fitted values, residuals, the normal-equation identity X'Wr=0, the weighted SSE, and the GLS covariance convention.
MSTAT:020424.statement:
A two-parameter linear model is observed on three design rows
\[
X
=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
1&1\\
1&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
y=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix},
\]
with the positive-definite weight matrix $W=\mathrm{diag}(1,2,1)$.
The WLS criterion is
\[
S(b)=(y-Xb)^{\mathsf T}W(y-Xb).
\]
This is Gauss-Markov / GLS for the second-moment assumption
$\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W^{-1}$. It is not ordinary
least squares, and it is not the convention $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W$.

1. Prove
   \[
   X^{\mathsf T}WX
   =\begin{pmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad
   (X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}
   =\begin{pmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad
   X^{\mathsf T}Wy
   =\begin{pmatrix}7\\8\end{pmatrix}.
   \]

2. Hence
   \[
   \hat\beta
   =(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}Wy
   =\Bigl(\frac54,\ \frac12\Bigr),
   \]
   with fitted vector $\hat y=X\hat\beta=(5/4,7/4,9/4)$ and residual
   $r=y-\hat y=(-1/4,1/4,-1/4)$.

3. Verify the weighted normal equations $X^{\mathsf T}Wr=0$ and
   the weighted residual sum of squares
   \[
   r^{\mathsf T}Wr=\frac14.
   \]

4. Under $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W^{-1}$, record the
   exact finite-sample covariance
   \[
   \mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “ignore $W$ and run OLS, so
   $X^{\mathsf T}X=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
   and $\hat\beta=(1,1/2)$ or $(2/3,1/2)$”; (ii) “$X^{\mathsf T}Wr$
   need not vanish, or $r^{\mathsf T}Wr=3/16$, or
   $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}$, or
   $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W$, or this is an
   omitted-variable / ridge exercise.”

Stay inside three-row WLS with the assigned $W$. Do not replace
the ledger by OLS, and do not invert the role of $W$ in the
sampling covariance.
permittedResults: $WX$ has rows $(1,0)$, $(2,2)$, $(1,2)$, so $X^{\mathsf T}WX=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with inverse $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Then $X^{\mathsf T}Wy=(7,8)$ and $\hat\beta=(5/4,1/2)$.

Fitted values $(5/4,7/4,9/4)$ produce $r=(-1/4,1/4,-1/4)$, $X^{\mathsf T}Wr=0$, and $r^{\mathsf T}Wr=1/4$. Under $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W^{-1}$ one has $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build X'WX and X'Wy from Wy=(1,4,2), invert the 2x2 Gram matrix, and multiply.
Check the weighted normal equations and r'Wr, then quote Cov from the GLS assumption Var(eps)=sigma^2 W^{-1}.

milestones.criterion: Forms X'WX, its inverse, X'Wy, and the WLS coefficient (5/4,1/2) with fitted values and residuals.
Verifies X'Wr=0, weighted SSE=1/4, and the GLS covariance sigma^2 (X'WX)^{-1} under Var(eps)=sigma^2 W^{-1}.
Refuses an OLS substitution and the inverted covariance convention Cov=sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1} or Var(eps)=sigma^2 W.

commonErrors.description: Ignores W and solves the OLS equations, reporting X'X=[[3,3],[3,5]] or a coefficient other than (5/4,1/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned WLS ledger X'WX, inverse, and beta=(5/4,1/2) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports Cov(beta)=sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1}, or assumes Var(eps)=sigma^2 W, or claims X'Wr need not vanish or r'Wr=3/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The GLS identity Cov=sigma^2 (X'WX)^{-1} or the ledger checks X'Wr=0 and r'Wr=1/4 are erased.

hintTree.content: Compute $Wy=(1,4,2)$ and $X^{\mathsf T}Wy=(7,8)$. The Gram matrix is $X^{\mathsf T}WX=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
The inverse is $(1/8)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}6&-4\\-4&4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Multiply by $(7,8)$.
Weighted SSE is $(1/16)\cdot1+(1/16)\cdot2+(1/16)\cdot1=1/4$. Covariance uses $(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}$, not $(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}$.

MSTAT:020424.canonicalSolution:
The weighted design is
\[
WX
=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
2&2\\
1&2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore
\[
X^{\mathsf T}WX
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&2\\1&2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is $24-16=8$, so
\[
(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}
=\frac18\begin{pmatrix}6&-4\\-4&4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The weighted response is $Wy=(1,4,2)$, and
\[
X^{\mathsf T}Wy
=\begin{pmatrix}1+4+2\\0+4+4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}7\\8\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
\boxed{X^{\mathsf T}WX=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{smallmatrix}\bigr),\ (X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr),\ X^{\mathsf T}Wy=(7,8)}.
\]

The WLS estimator is
\[
\hat\beta
=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}7\\8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}21/4-4\\-7/2+4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}5/4\\1/2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Fitted values and residuals are
\[
\hat y
=X\hat\beta
=\Bigl(\frac54,\ \frac74,\ \frac94\Bigr),
\qquad
r
=y-\hat y
=\Bigl(-\frac14,\ \frac14,-\frac14\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta=(5/4,1/2),\ \hat y=(5/4,7/4,9/4),\ r=(-1/4,1/4,-1/4)}.
\]

The weighted residual is $Wr=(-1/4,1/2,-1/4)$, so
\[
X^{\mathsf T}Wr
=\begin{pmatrix}-1/4+1/2-1/4\\0+1/2-1/2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The weighted residual sum of squares is
\[
r^{\mathsf T}Wr
=\frac{1}{16}\cdot1+\frac{1}{16}\cdot2+\frac{1}{16}\cdot1
=\frac14.
\]
Under the GLS second-moment assumption
$\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W^{-1}$,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{X^{\mathsf T}Wr=0,\ r^{\mathsf T}Wr=1/4,\ \mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $W$ and solves the OLS normal equations, which
do not produce $\hat\beta=(5/4,1/2)$. Sentence (ii) denies the
weighted normal equations, miscomputes $r^{\mathsf T}Wr$, or
quotes the OLS covariance $\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}$ / the
inverted second-moment law $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W$,
or else replaces the ledger by an omitted-variable or ridge
calculation, which is not asked.

The argument never sets $W=I$, never treats the middle row as
having weight $1$, and never reports $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)$
from $(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}$.

graderFixtures.proofText: $X^{\mathsf T}WX=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&4\\4&6\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with inverse $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3/4&-1/2\\-1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $X^{\mathsf T}Wy=(7,8)$. Then $\hat\beta=(5/4,1/2)$, $\hat y=(5/4,7/4,9/4)$, $r=(-1/4,1/4,-1/4)$, $X^{\mathsf T}Wr=0$, and $r^{\mathsf T}Wr=1/4$. Under $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 W^{-1}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^{\mathsf T}WX)^{-1}$.
I ignore W and run OLS, so I use X'X=[[3,3],[3,5]] and I report a coefficient other than (5/4,1/2).
I write Cov(beta)=sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1} or Var(eps)=sigma^2 W, or I claim X'Wr need not vanish, or I report r'Wr=3/16.

MSTAT:020425.title: OVB: centered y=beta1 x+beta2 z+u, E[u|x,z]=0; plim=beta1+beta2 Cov(x,z)/Var x; (2,3,Varx=4,Cov=2)=>7/2; z=.5x+v same; zero iff beta2 or Cov vanishes
MSTAT:020425.objective: Derive the omitted-variable probability limit for a centered simple regression on x, evaluate the assigned moments, recover the same limit from the linear projection z=0.5 x+v, and record the vanishing and sign rules.
MSTAT:020425.statement:
All random variables below are square-integrable and centered:
$\mathbb{E}[x]=\mathbb{E}[z]=\mathbb{E}[y]=0$. The structural
equation is
\[
y=\beta_1 x+\beta_2 z+u,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[u\mid x,z]=0.
\]
A researcher regresses $y$ on $x$ alone and forms the population
(and, by the WLLN, probability-limit) slope
\[
\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1
=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}.
\]

1. Prove the omitted-variable identity
   \[
   \mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1
   =\beta_1+\beta_2\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}.
   \]

2. Specialize to $\beta_1=2$, $\beta_2=3$, $\mathrm{Var}(x)=4$,
   and $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=2$. Prove
   \[
   \mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1
   =\frac72.
   \]

3. The same covariance is realized by the linear projection
   $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(x,v)=0$. Prove that this
   representation reproduces $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=2$ and the same
   probability limit $7/2$.

4. Prove that the bias term vanishes if $\beta_2=0$ or
   $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=0$, and that the sign of the bias equals
   the sign of the product $\beta_2\,\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)$ (for
   $\mathrm{Var}(x)>0$).

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the probability limit is
   $\beta_1+\beta_2\mathrm{Var}(x)/\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)$, or
   $\beta_1+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)$, giving $14$ or $8$”;
   (ii) “bias remains when $\beta_2=0$, or the sign follows
   $\beta_1$ alone, or $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ changes the limit, or
   this is a WLS / ridge exercise.”

Stay inside the centered linear structural equation with
$\mathbb{E}[u\mid x,z]=0$. Do not introduce an intercept
estimation problem, and do not replace the omitted-variable
identity by a ridge shrinkage.
permittedResults: Taking $\mathrm{Cov}(x,\cdot)$ through the structural equation produces $\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)/\mathrm{Var}(x)$. The assigned numbers give $2+3\cdot(2/4)=7/2$.
If $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(x,v)=0$, then $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=\tfrac12\mathrm{Var}(x)=2$, so the same limit $7/2$ is recovered. The bias vanishes iff $\beta_2=0$ or $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take Cov(x,·) through the structural equation and divide by Var(x).
Insert the assigned moments, then read vanishing and sign from the product beta2 Cov(x,z).

milestones.criterion: Derives plim=beta1+beta2 Cov(x,z)/Var(x) and evaluates the assigned moments as 7/2.
Shows that z=0.5 x+v reproduces Cov=2 and the same limit, and records the vanishing and sign rules.
Refuses an inverted covariance-to-variance ratio and a claim that bias survives beta2=0 or follows the sign of beta1 alone.

commonErrors.description: Writes plim=beta1+beta2 Var(x)/Cov(x,z) or beta1+beta2 Cov(x,z), producing 14 or 8 instead of 7/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The omitted-variable identity and the assigned limit 7/2 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the bias remains when beta2=0 or Cov(x,z)=0, or that the sign follows beta1 alone, or that z=0.5 x+v changes the limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The product structure of the bias term and the matching auxiliary representation are erased.

hintTree.content: $\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)=\beta_1\mathrm{Var}(x)+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)$ because $\mathrm{Cov}(x,u)=0$. Divide by $\mathrm{Var}(x)$.
Insert $\beta_1=2$, $\beta_2=3$, $\mathrm{Var}(x)=4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=2$ to obtain $2+3/2=7/2$.
The auxiliary $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ is just a realization of $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=2$. Bias is a product and vanishes with either factor.

MSTAT:020425.canonicalSolution:
The structural assumption $\mathbb{E}[u\mid x,z]=0$ implies
$\mathrm{Cov}(x,u)=0$. Therefore
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)
=\beta_1\mathrm{Var}(x)+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z).
\]
Dividing by $\mathrm{Var}(x)>0$ yields the omitted-variable
identity
\[
\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1
=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}
=\beta_1+\beta_2\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)/\mathrm{Var}(x)}.
\]

With the assigned moments,
\[
\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1
=2+3\cdot\frac{2}{4}
=2+\frac32
=\frac72.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1=7/2}.
\]

The linear projection $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(x,v)=0$
reproduces the same covariance,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)
=\frac12\mathrm{Var}(x)+\mathrm{Cov}(x,v)
=2,
\]
and therefore the same probability limit $7/2$. It is not a
different omitted-variable problem.

The contamination term is the product
$\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)/\mathrm{Var}(x)$. It vanishes if
$\beta_2=0$ (the omitted regressor has no structural role) or if
$\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=0$ (the omitted regressor is uncorrelated with
the included regressor). For $\mathrm{Var}(x)>0$ the sign of the
bias equals the sign of $\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)$.
\[
\boxed{\text{bias }=0\text{ if }\beta_2=0\text{ or }\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=0;\ \mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{bias})=\mathrm{sign}(\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z))}.
\]

Sentence (i) inverts the covariance-to-variance ratio or drops
the denominator, producing $14$ or $8$ instead of $7/2$.
Sentence (ii) claims that the bias survives $\beta_2=0$, or that
the sign follows $\beta_1$ alone, or that $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ is a
different limit, or else replaces the omitted-variable identity
by a WLS ledger or a ridge shrinkage, which is not asked.

The argument never estimates an intercept, never treats $u$ as
correlated with $(x,z)$, and never replaces the probability
limit by a finite-sample expectation under fixed design.

graderFixtures.proofText: Centered OVB: $\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)/\mathrm{Var}(x)$. With $\beta_1=2$, $\beta_2=3$, $\mathrm{Var}(x)=4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=2$ the limit is $7/2$. The representation $z=\tfrac12 x+v$ reproduces the same covariance and the same limit. Bias vanishes if $\beta_2=0$ or $\mathrm{Cov}(x,z)=0$, and $\mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{bias})=\mathrm{sign}(\beta_2\mathrm{Cov}(x,z))$.
I invert the ratio and write plim=beta1+beta2 Var(x)/Cov(x,z), or I drop the denominator and write beta1+beta2 Cov(x,z), so I report 14 or 8.
I claim the bias remains when beta2=0, or that the sign follows beta1 alone, or that z=0.5 x+v changes the probability limit.

MSTAT:020426.title: Ridge: ||y-Xb||^2+lambda||b||^2, X'X=diag(4,1), X'y=(8,3), lambda=1; OLS(2,3), ridge(8/5,3/2), shrink(4/5,1/2), df=13/10, bias=(-2/5,-3/2)
MSTAT:020426.objective: Under the penalized-RSS convention ||y-Xb||^2+lambda||b||^2, compute OLS, ridge, spectral shrinkage factors, effective degrees of freedom, and the bias at the assigned true beta.
MSTAT:020426.statement:
Ridge regression is defined here by the penalized residual sum
of squares
\[
S_\lambda(b)
=\lVert y-Xb\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert b\rVert_2^2,
\qquad\lambda>0.
\]
This is the RSS $+\lambda$ convention: the normal equations are
$(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)b=X^{\mathsf T}y$. It is not the
$(1/n)$ RSS convention, not a $\lambda/2$ Gaussian-prior writing,
and not a $2\lambda$ penalty.

The Gram matrix is already diagonal in the working coordinates,
\[
X^{\mathsf T}X=\mathrm{diag}(4,1),
\qquad
X^{\mathsf T}y=(8,3),
\qquad
\lambda=1.
\]

1. Prove that the OLS estimator is $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{OLS}}=(2,3)$
   and that the ridge estimator is
   \[
   \hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}
   =\Bigl(\frac85,\ \frac32\Bigr).
   \]

2. In these eigen-coordinates the spectral shrinkage factors are
   $\lambda_j/(\lambda_j+\lambda)$, where $\lambda_j$ are the
   diagonal entries of $X^{\mathsf T}X$. Prove
   \[
   \Bigl(\frac{4}{5},\ \frac12\Bigr)
   \]
   and that these factors recover
   $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}_j
   =\bigl(\lambda_j/(\lambda_j+\lambda)\bigr)\hat\beta^{\mathrm{OLS}}_j$.

3. The effective degrees of freedom are
   \[
   \mathrm{df}(\lambda)
   =\mathrm{tr}\bigl(X(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\bigr)
   =\sum_j\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j+\lambda}
   =\frac{13}{10}.
   \]

4. Now take the true coefficient to be $\beta=(2,3)$. Under the
   standard linear model $\mathbb{E}[y\mid X]=X\beta$, prove that
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}\bigr]
   =\Bigl(\frac85,\ \frac32\Bigr)
   \]
   (the same numerical vector as the observed ridge fit) and that
   the bias is
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}\bigr]-\beta
   =\Bigl(-\frac25,\ -\frac32\Bigr).
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the penalty is $\lambda/2$ or $2\lambda$,
   so ridge is $(8/4.5,3/1.5)$ or $(8/6,3/3)$”; (ii) “df equals
   $p=2$ or $4/5$, or the bias is the coordinatewise difference
   of ridge and a different target, or this is a WLS /
   omitted-variable exercise.”

Stay inside the RSS $+\lambda\lVert b\rVert^2$ convention with a
diagonal Gram matrix. Do not recenter the penalty about a
nonzero target, and do not replace ridge by WLS.
permittedResults: OLS is $(8/4,3/1)=(2,3)$. Ridge solves $\mathrm{diag}(5,2)\hat\beta=(8,3)$, hence $(8/5,3/2)$. Shrinkage factors are $4/5$ and $1/2$, and df is $4/5+1/2=13/10$.
For true $\beta=(2,3)$, $\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}]=\mathrm{diag}(4/5,1/2)(2,3)=(8/5,3/2)$, so the bias is $(-2/5,-3/2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the diagonal OLS and ridge normal equations, then read shrinkage as lambda_j/(lambda_j+lambda).
Sum the shrinkage factors for df, and subtract the assigned true beta from the shrunk expectation.

milestones.criterion: Records the RSS+lambda convention, OLS=(2,3), ridge=(8/5,3/2), and the spectral shrinkage (4/5,1/2).
Computes df=13/10 and, at true beta=(2,3), the expectation (8/5,3/2) with bias=(-2/5,-3/2).
Refuses a lambda/2 or 2*lambda rewrite and an effective-df or bias target substitution.

commonErrors.description: Replaces ||y-Xb||^2+lambda||b||^2 by a lambda/2 or 2*lambda penalty, producing ridge coordinates other than (8/5,3/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned ridge vector (8/5,3/2) and the matching shrinkage (4/5,1/2) are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports df=p=2 or df=4/5, or computes bias against a target other than beta=(2,3), missing bias=(-2/5,-3/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The effective-df identity 13/10 or the bias at the assigned true beta is erased.

hintTree.content: OLS divides $X^{\mathsf T}y$ by the diagonal of $X^{\mathsf T}X$. Ridge divides by those entries plus $\lambda=1$.
Shrinkage is $4/(4+1)=4/5$ and $1/(1+1)=1/2$. Their sum is the effective df.
Bias is $\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}]-\beta$, not an informal comparison to a different target. With $\beta=(2,3)$ the expectation equals the observed ridge vector.

MSTAT:020426.canonicalSolution:
The assigned convention is the penalized residual sum of squares
$S_\lambda(b)=\lVert y-Xb\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert b\rVert_2^2$.
Ordinary least squares is the $\lambda=0$ case,
\[
\hat\beta^{\mathrm{OLS}}
=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y
=\Bigl(\frac84,\ \frac31\Bigr)
=(2,3).
\]
Ridge adds $\lambda I=\mathrm{diag}(1,1)$ to the Gram matrix:
\[
(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}
=\mathrm{diag}(5,2)\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}
=(8,3),
\]
so
\[
\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}
=\Bigl(\frac85,\ \frac32\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta^{\mathrm{OLS}}=(2,3),\ \hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}=(8/5,3/2)}.
\]

In these eigen-coordinates the spectral shrinkage factors are
\[
\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda}=\frac{4}{5},
\qquad
\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2+\lambda}=\frac12.
\]
They recover the ridge fit from OLS,
\[
\frac45\cdot2=\frac85,
\qquad
\frac12\cdot3=\frac32.
\]
Effective degrees of freedom sum the same factors:
\[
\mathrm{df}(1)
=\frac45+\frac12
=\frac{8}{10}+\frac{5}{10}
=\frac{13}{10}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{shrink }(4/5,1/2),\ \mathrm{df}=13/10}.
\]

Under $\mathbb{E}[y\mid X]=X\beta$ with the assigned true value
$\beta=(2,3)$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}\bigr]
=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}X\beta
=\mathrm{diag}\Bigl(\frac45,\frac12\Bigr)\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}
=\Bigl(\frac85,\ \frac32\Bigr).
\]
That expectation coincides with the observed ridge vector because
the true $\beta$ equals the OLS target $(2,3)$. The bias is
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}\bigr]-\beta
=\Bigl(\frac85-2,\ \frac32-3\Bigr)
=\Bigl(-\frac25,\ -\frac32\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta^{\mathrm{ridge}}]=(8/5,3/2),\ \mathrm{bias}=(-2/5,-3/2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the RSS $+\lambda$ convention by a
$\lambda/2$ or $2\lambda$ penalty, changing the ridge coordinates.
Sentence (ii) reports $\mathrm{df}=p=2$ or only the first
shrinkage factor, or computes bias against a target other than
the assigned $\beta=(2,3)$, or else replaces ridge by a WLS
ledger or an omitted-variable identity, which is not asked.

The argument never recenters the penalty about a nonzero
$\beta_0$, never scales RSS by $1/n$, and never treats
$\lambda$ as a WLS weight.

graderFixtures.proofText: Convention $\lVert y-Xb\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert b\rVert^2$. OLS $(2,3)$, ridge $(8/5,3/2)$, spectral shrinkage $(4/5,1/2)$, $\mathrm{df}=13/10$. For true $\beta=(2,3)$ the ridge expectation is again $(8/5,3/2)$ and the bias is $(-2/5,-3/2)$.
I take the penalty to be lambda/2 or 2*lambda instead of ||y-Xb||^2+lambda||b||^2, so I report ridge coordinates other than (8/5,3/2).
I report df=p=2 or df=4/5, or I compute bias against a target other than the assigned true beta=(2,3).

MSTAT:020527.title: Exact sign test n=10, B=8: Bin(10,1/2), one-sided p=56/1024=7/128=.0546875; doubled two-sided 7/64=.109375; no reject at 5%; ties dropped
MSTAT:020527.objective: For ten continuous paired differences with no ties and eight positive signs, compute the exact Bin(10,1/2) one-sided and doubled two-sided p-values, decide the 5% tests, and record the discard-ties convention.
MSTAT:020527.statement:
Let $D_1,\dots,D_{10}$ be i.i.d. continuous paired differences
with $P(D_i=0)=0$. Exactly eight of the realized differences are
positive and two are negative; there are no ties. Write
$B=\#\{i:D_i>0\}$. Under the sign-test null
$H_0:P(D_i>0)=1/2$ one has $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$.

1. Prove the exact one-sided $p$-value
   \[
   p_+=P(B\ge 8)
   =\frac{\binom{10}{8}+\binom{10}{9}+\binom{10}{10}}{2^{10}}
   =\frac{56}{1024}
   =\frac{7}{128}
   =0.0546875.
   \]

2. The null is symmetric about $5$. Define the doubled two-sided
   $p$-value by $p_{\mathrm{two}}=2p_+$ and prove
   \[
   p_{\mathrm{two}}=\frac{7}{64}=0.109375.
   \]
   At level $\alpha=0.05$, decide both the one-sided test of
   $H_1:P(D_i>0)>1/2$ and the two-sided test of
   $H_1:P(D_i>0)\ne 1/2$. Record that neither test rejects.

3. State the assigned ties convention: because the $D_i$ are
   continuous, $P(D_i=0)=0$. If a numerical tie is nevertheless
   observed, discard that pair and reduce $n$ by one, then rerun
   the exact binomial sign test on the remaining signs. Do not
   count a tie as a success, a failure, or a half-success.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the one-sided tail is
   $P(B>8)=11/1024$, or a normal approximation with or without
   continuity correction replaces the exact binomial, giving a
   $p$-value below $0.05$ and a rejection”; (ii) “the two-sided
   $p$-value is the one-sided tail $7/128$, or ties are counted
   as successes so $B=10$, or this is a Wilcoxon signed-rank /
   asymptotic $z$ exercise.”

Stay inside the exact $\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$ sign test. Do not
replace $B$ by a signed-rank statistic, and do not invoke a
normal approximation.
permittedResults: Both $7/128>0.05$ and $7/64>0.05$, so neither the one-sided nor the doubled two-sided test rejects at $\alpha=0.05$. The discard-ties rule leaves the present sample untouched because no tie was observed.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the three Bin(10,1/2) atoms at 8, 9, and 10, then double the upper tail by symmetry.
Compare both p-values with 0.05 and record that a continuous model discards any later numerical tie rather than scoring it.

milestones.criterion: Computes the exact one-sided tail P(B>=8)=56/1024=7/128=0.0546875 from Bin(10,1/2).
Records the doubled two-sided p-value 7/64=0.109375, refuses both 5% rejections, and states the discard-ties convention.
Refuses a strict inequality P(B>8), a normal approximation, and a Wilcoxon or ties-as-successes substitution.

commonErrors.description: Uses P(B>8)=11/1024 instead of P(B>=8)=56/1024, or replaces the exact binomial by a normal approximation that rejects at 5%.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact one-sided value 7/128=0.0546875 and the non-rejection at alpha=0.05 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the two-sided p-value as the undoubled tail 7/128, or counts ties as successes, or replaces the sign test by Wilcoxon signed-rank or an asymptotic z-test.
commonErrors.consequence: The doubled value 7/64=0.109375 or the discard-ties convention is erased.

hintTree.content: Under $H_0$, $P(B=k)=\binom{10}{k}/1024$. The one-sided tail is the sum of the $k=8,9,10$ terms.
Symmetry of $\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$ about $5$ makes the assigned two-sided $p$-value exactly twice the upper tail.
Compare $7/128=0.0546875$ and $7/64=0.109375$ with $0.05$. A continuous model forbids treating a hypothetical tie as a positive sign.

MSTAT:020527.canonicalSolution:
Under $H_0:P(D_i>0)=1/2$ and the standing continuity assumption
$P(D_i=0)=0$, the sign count is exactly
\[
B\sim\mathrm{Bin}\bigl(10,\tfrac12\bigr),
\qquad
P(B=k)=\frac{\binom{10}{k}}{2^{10}}=\frac{\binom{10}{k}}{1024}.
\]
The observed count is $b=8$, so the one-sided $p$-value is the
upper tail
\[
p_+
=P(B\ge 8)
=\frac{\binom{10}{8}+\binom{10}{9}+\binom{10}{10}}{1024}
=\frac{45+10+1}{1024}
=\frac{56}{1024}
=\frac{7}{128}
=0.0546875.
\]
\[
\boxed{p_+=56/1024=7/128=0.0546875}.
\]

The $\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$ law is symmetric about $5$. The
assigned two-sided $p$-value is therefore the doubled tail
\[
p_{\mathrm{two}}
=2p_+
=\frac{14}{128}
=\frac{7}{64}
=0.109375.
\]
At $\alpha=0.05$ one has $p_+>0.05$ and $p_{\mathrm{two}}>0.05$,
so neither the one-sided test of $H_1:P(D_i>0)>1/2$ nor the
two-sided test of $H_1:P(D_i>0)\ne 1/2$ rejects.
\[
\boxed{p_{\mathrm{two}}=7/64=0.109375;\ \text{no reject at }5\%}.
\]

Because the $D_i$ are continuous, $P(D_i=0)=0$. The assigned
convention, used only if a numerical tie is nevertheless
observed, is to discard that pair, reduce $n$ by one, and recompute
the exact binomial tail on the remaining signs. A tie is not
scored as a success, a failure, or a half-success. The present
sample has no ties, so $n=10$ is left unchanged.

Sentence (i) replaces $P(B\ge 8)$ by $P(B>8)=11/1024$, or else
substitutes a normal approximation (with or without a continuity
correction) that can push the $p$-value below $0.05$ and force a
false rejection. Sentence (ii) reports the two-sided $p$-value as
the undoubled tail $7/128$, or counts hypothetical ties as
successes, or else replaces the exact sign test by a Wilcoxon
signed-rank statistic or an asymptotic $z$-test, which is not
asked.

The argument never introduces Wilcoxon scores, never uses a
normal tail, and never treats a zero difference as a positive
sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: Under $H_0$, $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$. One-sided $p_+=P(B\ge 8)=56/1024=7/128=0.0546875$. Doubled two-sided $p=7/64=0.109375$. Neither test rejects at $\alpha=0.05$. Ties, if observed, are discarded and $n$ is reduced; the present sample has no ties.
I take the one-sided tail to be P(B>8)=11/1024, or I replace the exact Bin(10,1/2) law by a normal approximation and reject at 5%.
I report the two-sided p-value as the undoubled tail 7/128, or I count ties as successes, or I replace the sign test by a Wilcoxon signed-rank or asymptotic z procedure.

MSTAT:020528.title: Spearman x=(1,2,3,4), y=(1,3,2,4): sum d^2=2, rho=4/5; 4 of 24 have rho>=.8 so one-sided 1/6; 8 have |rho|>=.8 so two-sided 1/3
MSTAT:020528.objective: From the assigned four-point rankings compute sum d^2 and Spearman rho, then obtain the exact one-sided and two-sided permutation p-values among the 24 permutations. Do not use an asymptotic t or a midrank/ties correction.
MSTAT:020528.statement:
Two paired rankings of $n=4$ distinct items are
\[
x=(1,2,3,4),\qquad y=(1,3,2,4).
\]
There are no ties. Spearman's rank correlation is
\[
\rho
=1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)},
\qquad
d_i=x_i-y_i.
\]

1. Compute $\sum d_i^2$ and prove $\rho=4/5$.

2. Under the exact permutation null, $x$ is held fixed and $y$
   is uniformly distributed on the $4!=24$ permutations of
   $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Prove that exactly four permutations satisfy
   $\rho\ge 4/5$, hence the one-sided $p$-value is $4/24=1/6$.

3. Prove that exactly eight permutations satisfy $|\rho|\ge 4/5$,
   hence the two-sided $p$-value is $8/24=1/3$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “using divisor $n-1$ rather than $n$
   in a consistently computed Pearson correlation of the ranks
   changes Spearman's $\rho$, or $\sum d_i^2=1$, giving
   $\rho=9/10$”; (ii) “the one-sided count
   is $1/24$ or the two-sided $p$-value is $1/6$, or the
   asymptotic $t=\rho\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-\rho^2)}$ is used, or ties /
   midranks are introduced, or this is a sign-test exercise.”

Stay inside the exact permutation distribution of $\rho$ on $24$
rankings. Do not replace the enumeration by an asymptotic $t$
tail, and do not introduce ties.
permittedResults: For $x=(1,2,3,4)$ and $y=(1,3,2,4)$ one has $d=(0,-1,1,0)$ and $\sum d_i^2=2$. Then $n(n^2-1)=60$ and $\rho=1-12/60=4/5$. The inequality $\rho\ge 4/5$ is equivalent to $\sum d_i^2\le 2$.

Exactly the four permutations $(1,2,3,4)$, $(2,1,3,4)$, $(1,3,2,4)$, $(1,2,4,3)$ have $\sum d_i^2\le 2$. Exactly four further permutations, the order-reversals of those, have $\sum d_i^2\ge 18$ and $\rho\le-4/5$. Thus the tails are $4/24=1/6$ and $8/24=1/3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate 1-6 sum d^2/(n(n^2-1)) on the assigned ranks, then convert rho>=4/5 into sum d^2<=2.
List the identity and three adjacent transpositions for the upper tail, then add the four reversed rankings for the two-sided tail.

milestones.criterion: Computes sum d^2=2 and rho=4/5 from the assigned rankings.
Enumerates the 4 and 8 permutations giving one-sided p=1/6 and two-sided p=1/3.
Refuses an asymptotic t, a midrank/ties correction, and a one-sided count of 1/24.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a consistently used Pearson divisor n-1 rather than n changes the rank correlation, or reports sum d^2=1 and rho=9/10 instead of sum d^2=2 and rho=4/5.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned identity rho=1-6 sum d^2/(n(n^2-1))=4/5 is lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the asymptotic t=rho sqrt((n-2)/(1-rho^2)), or reports a one-sided count of 1/24 or a two-sided p-value of 1/6, or introduces midranks.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact permutation tails 1/6 and 1/3 are erased.

hintTree.content: The differences are $d=(0,-1,1,0)$, so $\sum d_i^2=2$. Then $6\cdot 2/(4\cdot 15)=1/5$ and $\rho=4/5$.
$\rho\ge 4/5$ iff $\sum d_i^2\le 2$. List the identity and the three adjacent transpositions.
The two-sided event also includes the four reversed rankings with $\sum d_i^2\ge 18$. There are $24$ permutations and no $t$ approximation.

MSTAT:020528.canonicalSolution:
The assigned rank vectors give
\[
d
=x-y
=(0,-1,1,0),
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^4 d_i^2
=0+1+1+0
=2.
\]
With $n=4$ one has $n(n^2-1)=4\cdot 15=60$, so
\[
\rho
=1-\frac{6\cdot 2}{60}
=1-\frac{12}{60}
=1-\frac15
=\frac45.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sum d_i^2=2,\quad\rho=4/5}.
\]

The relation $\rho=1-\sum d_i^2/10$ shows that $\rho\ge 4/5$ if
and only if $\sum d_i^2\le 2$. Holding $x=(1,2,3,4)$ fixed, the
permutations of $y$ that meet this bound are
\[
\begin{align*}
(1,2,3,4)&:\ \sum d_i^2=0,\ \rho=1,\\
(2,1,3,4)&:\ \sum d_i^2=2,\ \rho=4/5,\\
(1,3,2,4)&:\ \sum d_i^2=2,\ \rho=4/5,\\
(1,2,4,3)&:\ \sum d_i^2=2,\ \rho=4/5.
\end{align*}
\]
These are four of the $4!=24$ permutations, so the exact
one-sided $p$-value is
\[
P(\rho\ge 4/5)=\frac{4}{24}=\frac16.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{one-sided }4/24=1/6}.
\]

Likewise $\rho\le-4/5$ if and only if $\sum d_i^2\ge 18$. The
four reversed rankings
\[
(4,3,2,1),\ (3,4,2,1),\ (4,2,3,1),\ (4,3,1,2)
\]
have $\sum d_i^2=20,18,18,18$ respectively. Together with the
four upper-tail permutations this is eight rankings with
$|\rho|\ge 4/5$, so
\[
P\bigl(|\rho|\ge 4/5\bigr)=\frac{8}{24}=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{two-sided }8/24=1/3}.
\]

Sentence (i) falsely claims that the consistently used Pearson
divisor changes a correlation, or miscomputes $\sum d_i^2$ and
produces $\rho=9/10$. Sentence (ii) undercounts the upper tail, reports
the two-sided $p$-value as the one-sided $1/6$, or else replaces
the exact count by the asymptotic
$t=\rho\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-\rho^2)}$ or by a midrank / sign-test
construction, which is not asked.

The argument never introduces a $t_2$ tail, never uses midranks,
and never replaces $\rho$ by a sign count.

graderFixtures.proofText: Assigned ranks give $\sum d_i^2=2$ and $\rho=4/5$. Among $24$ permutations, four have $\rho\ge 4/5$ so the one-sided $p$-value is $1/6$; eight have $|\rho|\ge 4/5$ so the two-sided $p$-value is $1/3$. No asymptotic $t$ and no midranks.
I claim that changing the consistently used Pearson divisor from n to n-1 changes Spearman rho, or I compute sum d^2=1 and report rho=9/10 instead of 4/5.
I use the asymptotic t=rho sqrt((n-2)/(1-rho^2)), or I report a one-sided count of 1/24 or a two-sided p-value of 1/6, or I introduce midranks.

MSTAT:020629.title: Jackknife (1,2,4): thetaHat=xbar^2=49/9; loo squares (9,25/4,9/4), mean 35/6; bias=7/9; corrected=14/3; pseudovalues (-5/3,23/6,71/6); V=553/36
MSTAT:020629.objective: For the delete-one jackknife of the squared sample mean on (1,2,4), compute the full estimate, leave-one-out squares, bias, bias-corrected estimate, pseudovalues, and jackknife variance 553/36.
MSTAT:020629.statement:
The sample is $x=(1,2,4)$ with $n=3$. The functional of interest
is the squared sample mean
\[
\hat\theta=\bar x^2.
\]
Write $\hat\theta_{(i)}$ for the same functional computed after
deleting the $i$th observation, and write
$\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}=n^{-1}\sum_i\hat\theta_{(i)}$ for the
leave-one-out mean.

1. Prove $\bar x=7/3$ and $\hat\theta=49/9$. Compute the three
   leave-one-out values
   \[
   \hat\theta_{(1)}=9,\qquad
   \hat\theta_{(2)}=\frac{25}{4},\qquad
   \hat\theta_{(3)}=\frac94,
   \]
   and their mean $\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}=35/6$.

2. The jackknife bias estimate is
   $(n-1)\bigl(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta\bigr)$. Prove that
   this equals $7/9$, and that the bias-corrected estimator
   $\hat\theta-\widehat{\mathrm{bias}}$ equals $14/3$.

3. The pseudovalues are
   $\tilde\theta_i=n\hat\theta-(n-1)\hat\theta_{(i)}$. Prove
   \[
   \bigl(\tilde\theta_1,\tilde\theta_2,\tilde\theta_3\bigr)
   =\Bigl(-\frac53,\frac{23}{6},\frac{71}{6}\Bigr)
   \]
   and that their average is again $14/3$. The jackknife variance
   is
   \[
   \widehat V
   =\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
   \bigl(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}\bigr)^2
   =\frac{1}{n(n-1)}
   \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\tilde\theta_i-\bar{\tilde\theta}\bigr)^2.
   \]
   Prove $\widehat V=553/36$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the bias factor is $n$ rather than
   $n-1$, or the functional is the unsquared mean, giving bias
   $7/18$ or $0$”; (ii) “the variance uses
   $(n-1)/n$ times the sum of *pseudovalue* squared deviations,
   giving $553/9$, or this is a nonparametric bootstrap of the
   sample maximum.”

Stay inside the delete-one jackknife of $\bar x^2$. Do not
replace the functional by $\bar x$ or by a bootstrap of the
maximum.
permittedResults: Pseudovalues: $49/3-18=-5/3$, $49/3-25/2=23/6$, $49/3-9/2=71/6$. Leave-one-out deviations $19/6$, $5/12$, $-43/12$ have sum of squares $553/24$, and $((n-1)/n)$ times that sum is $553/36$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form the three delete-one means, square them, and apply the factor (n-1) to (loo mean minus full estimate).
Convert to pseudovalues and evaluate ((n-1)/n) sum of squared leave-one-out deviations, equivalently 1/(n(n-1)) on the pseudovalues.

milestones.criterion: Computes thetaHat=49/9, the three leave-one-out squares, their mean 35/6, bias 7/9, and the corrected value 14/3.
Records the three pseudovalues and the jackknife variance 553/36 from ((n-1)/n) times the leave-one-out sum of squares.
Refuses a missing factor n-1 in the bias and a (n-1)/n scaling of the pseudovalue deviations.

commonErrors.description: Uses bias factor n instead of n-1, or jackknifes the unsquared mean, producing bias 7/18 or 0 rather than 7/9.
commonErrors.consequence: The bias 7/9 and the corrected estimator 14/3 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Applies (n-1)/n to the sum of squared *pseudovalue* deviations and reports 553/9, or replaces the jackknife by a nonparametric bootstrap of the sample maximum.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned variance 553/36 is erased.

hintTree.content: $\bar x=7/3$ and $\hat\theta=49/9$. The three leave-one-out means are $3$, $5/2$, and $3/2$.
Bias is $2(35/6-49/9)=7/9$, not $35/6-49/9$ itself. The corrected value is $49/9-7/9=14/3$.
Form $\tilde\theta_i=3\cdot(49/9)-2\hat\theta_{(i)}$. Then $\widehat V=((n-1)/n)\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)})^2=553/36$.

MSTAT:020629.canonicalSolution:
The full-sample mean is $\bar x=(1+2+4)/3=7/3$, so
\[
\hat\theta=\Bigl(\frac73\Bigr)^2=\frac{49}{9}.
\]
Deleting one observation at a time,
\[
\begin{align*}
\hat\theta_{(1)}
&=\Bigl(\frac{2+4}{2}\Bigr)^2=3^2=9,\\
\hat\theta_{(2)}
&=\Bigl(\frac{1+4}{2}\Bigr)^2=\Bigl(\frac52\Bigr)^2=\frac{25}{4},\\
\hat\theta_{(3)}
&=\Bigl(\frac{1+2}{2}\Bigr)^2=\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2=\frac94.
\end{align*}
\]
The leave-one-out mean is
\[
\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}
=\frac{1}{3}\Bigl(9+\frac{25}{4}+\frac94\Bigr)
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{35}{2}
=\frac{35}{6}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\hat\theta=49/9,\quad\hat\theta_{(i)}=(9,25/4,9/4),\quad\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}=35/6}.
\]

The jackknife bias uses the factor $n-1=2$:
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{bias}}
=2\Bigl(\frac{35}{6}-\frac{49}{9}\Bigr)
=2\cdot\frac{105-98}{18}
=2\cdot\frac{7}{18}
=\frac79.
\]
The bias-corrected estimator is
\[
\hat\theta-\widehat{\mathrm{bias}}
=\frac{49}{9}-\frac79
=\frac{42}{9}
=\frac{14}{3},
\]
which is the same as $n\hat\theta-(n-1)\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}$.
\[
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{bias}}=7/9,\quad\hat\theta_{\mathrm{jack}}=14/3}.
\]

The three pseudovalues are
\[
\begin{align*}
\tilde\theta_1
&=3\cdot\frac{49}{9}-2\cdot 9
=\frac{49}{3}-18
=-\frac53,\\
\tilde\theta_2
&=\frac{49}{3}-2\cdot\frac{25}{4}
=\frac{49}{3}-\frac{25}{2}
=\frac{23}{6},\\
\tilde\theta_3
&=\frac{49}{3}-2\cdot\frac94
=\frac{49}{3}-\frac92
=\frac{71}{6}.
\end{align*}
\]
Their average is
\[
\frac{1}{3}\Bigl(-\frac53+\frac{23}{6}+\frac{71}{6}\Bigr)
=\frac{14}{3}.
\]
The leave-one-out deviations from $35/6$ are
\[
9-\frac{35}{6}=\frac{19}{6},\qquad
\frac{25}{4}-\frac{35}{6}=\frac{5}{12},\qquad
\frac94-\frac{35}{6}=-\frac{43}{12}.
\]
Their sum of squares is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{19}{6}\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac{5}{12}\Bigr)^2
+\Bigl(\frac{43}{12}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{361}{36}+\frac{1874}{144}
=\frac{3318}{144}
=\frac{553}{24}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\widehat V
=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{553}{24}
=\frac{553}{36}.
\]
Equivalently, the pseudovalue deviations from $14/3$ have sum of
squares $553/6$, and
$n^{-1}(n-1)^{-1}\cdot(553/6)=553/36$.
\[
\boxed{\tilde\theta=(-5/3,23/6,71/6),\quad\widehat V=553/36}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $n-1$ or unsquares the functional,
producing bias $7/18$ or $0$. Sentence (ii) applies the scale
$(n-1)/n$ to the *pseudovalue* deviations and reports $553/9$,
or else replaces the jackknife of $\bar x^2$ by a nonparametric
bootstrap of the sample maximum, which is not asked.

The argument never resamples with replacement, never jackknifes
$\bar x$ itself, and never treats $553/9$ as the variance.

graderFixtures.proofText: On $(1,2,4)$, $\hat\theta=\bar x^2=49/9$. Leave-one-out squares $(9,25/4,9/4)$ have mean $35/6$. Bias $(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)=7/9$ and the corrected estimator is $14/3$. Pseudovalues $(-5/3,23/6,71/6)$ average to $14/3$. $\widehat V=((n-1)/n)\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(\cdot)})^2=553/36$.
I take the jackknife bias factor to be n rather than n-1, or I jackknife the unsquared mean, and I report bias 7/18 or 0 instead of 7/9.
I apply (n-1)/n to the sum of squared *pseudovalue* deviations and report V=553/9, or I replace the jackknife of xbar^2 by a nonparametric bootstrap of the sample maximum.
