MSTAT:020630.title: Parametric bootstrap Exp rate n=4,sum=10: MLE=2/5; S*~Gamma(4,rate 2/5); E*[4/S*]=8/15, bias=2/15, corrected=4/15, Var*=32/225
MSTAT:020630.objective: For four exponential observations with sum 10, form the rate MLE and the exact parametric-bootstrap mean, bias, bias-corrected estimate, and variance of lambdaHat*=4/S*. Do not replace the Gamma law by a nonparametric bootstrap or by the sample maximum.
MSTAT:020630.statement:
Let $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ be i.i.d. exponential with unknown rate
$\lambda>0$, so $E[X_i]=1/\lambda$ and
$f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x>0$. The observed sum is
$\sum_{i=1}^4 X_i=10$. The maximum-likelihood estimator is
$\hat\lambda=n/\sum X_i$.

1. Prove $\hat\lambda=2/5$. Under the fitted law the parametric
   bootstrap sum $S^*=\sum_{i=1}^4 X_i^*$ is
   \[
   S^*\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\bigl(4,\ \mathrm{rate}=2/5\bigr),
   \]
   and the bootstrap replicate is $\hat\lambda^*=4/S^*$.

2. Using $E[S^{*-1}]=\beta/(\alpha-1)$ for
   $\mathrm{Gamma}(\mathrm{shape}=\alpha,\mathrm{rate}=\beta)$
   with $\alpha>1$, prove
   \[
   E_*[\hat\lambda^*]=\frac{8}{15}.
   \]
   Deduce the parametric-bootstrap bias
   $E_*[\hat\lambda^*]-\hat\lambda=2/15$ and the bias-corrected
   estimate $2\hat\lambda-E_*[\hat\lambda^*]=4/15$.

3. Using $E[S^{*-2}]=\beta^2/((\alpha-1)(\alpha-2))$ for
   $\alpha>2$, prove
   \[
   \mathrm{Var}_*(\hat\lambda^*)=\frac{32}{225}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “this is a nonparametric bootstrap,
   or the statistic is the sample maximum, or the mean
   parameterization $\hat\mu=5/2$ is used in place of the rate”;
   (ii) “Jensen gives $E_*[4/S^*]=4/E_*[S^*]=2/5$ so the bias
   vanishes, or $S^*$ is treated as $\mathrm{Gamma}(4,\mathrm{scale}=2/5)$.”

Stay inside the exact parametric bootstrap of the rate MLE.
Do not resample the four observed points, and do not replace
$\hat\lambda$ by a sample maximum.
permittedResults: $\hat\lambda=4/10=2/5$. With $\alpha=4$ and $\beta=2/5$, $E[S^{*-1}]=(2/5)/3=2/15$, hence $E_*[\hat\lambda^*]=8/15$. Bias $8/15-2/5=2/15$ and the corrected value $4/15$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form the rate MLE n/sum, identify S* as Gamma(n, rate=MLE), and apply E[S^{-1}]=beta/(alpha-1).
Subtract the MLE to obtain the bias, then use E[S^{-2}] to get Var(4/S*).

milestones.criterion: Identifies hat lambda=2/5, the fitted Gamma(4, rate 2/5) law, and E*[4/S*]=8/15.
Records bias 2/15, the corrected value 4/15, and Var*=32/225 from the inverse-Gamma second moment.
Refuses a nonparametric bootstrap or sample-maximum substitution and a Jensen plug-in E*=2/5.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the parametric Gamma(4, rate 2/5) law by a nonparametric resample of the four points, or by a bootstrap of the sample maximum, or switches to the mean parameterization hat mu=5/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact parametric moments E*=8/15 and Var*=32/225 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses E*[4/S*]=4/E*[S*]=2/5 and reports vanishing bias, or treats the Gamma second parameter as a scale 2/5 rather than a rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse-Gamma identities E*=8/15 and bias=2/15 are erased.

hintTree.content: The rate MLE is $n/\sum X_i=4/10=2/5$. The fitted sum is $\mathrm{Gamma}(4,\mathrm{rate}=2/5)$, not scale $2/5$.
$E[1/S^*]=\beta/(\alpha-1)=(2/5)/3=2/15$. Multiply by $4$ to obtain $E_*=8/15$.
Compute $E[1/S^{*2}]=\beta^2/((\alpha-1)(\alpha-2))=2/75$, subtract $(2/15)^2$, and multiply by $16$. Do not replace $E[4/S^*]$ by $4/E[S^*]$.

MSTAT:020630.canonicalSolution:
The rate MLE on a sample of size $n=4$ with sum $10$ is
\[
\hat\lambda=\frac{n}{\sum X_i}=\frac{4}{10}=\frac25.
\]
The parametric bootstrap draws $X_i^*$ i.i.d. from
$\mathrm{Exp}(\mathrm{rate}=2/5)$, so the bootstrap sum is
\[
S^*\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\bigl(\mathrm{shape}=4,\ \mathrm{rate}=2/5\bigr)
\]
and $\hat\lambda^*=4/S^*$.
\[
\boxed{\hat\lambda=2/5,\quad S^*\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(4,\mathrm{rate}=2/5),\quad\hat\lambda^*=4/S^*}.
\]

For $S\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha>1$,
\[
E[S^{-1}]=\frac{\beta}{\alpha-1}.
\]
Here $\alpha=4$ and $\beta=2/5$, so
\[
E_*[S^{*-1}]=\frac{2/5}{3}=\frac{2}{15},
\qquad
E_*[\hat\lambda^*]=4\cdot\frac{2}{15}=\frac{8}{15}.
\]
The parametric-bootstrap bias is
\[
E_*[\hat\lambda^*]-\hat\lambda
=\frac{8}{15}-\frac{2}{5}
=\frac{8}{15}-\frac{6}{15}
=\frac{2}{15},
\]
and the bias-corrected estimate is
\[
2\hat\lambda-E_*[\hat\lambda^*]
=\frac{4}{5}-\frac{8}{15}
=\frac{12}{15}-\frac{8}{15}
=\frac{4}{15}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_*=8/15,\quad\mathrm{bias}=2/15,\quad\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{bc}}=4/15}.
\]

For $\alpha>2$,
\[
E[S^{-2}]=\frac{\beta^2}{(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}
=\frac{4/25}{3\cdot 2}
=\frac{4}{150}
=\frac{2}{75}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathrm{Var}_*(S^{*-1})
=\frac{2}{75}-\Bigl(\frac{2}{15}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{6}{225}-\frac{4}{225}
=\frac{2}{225},
\]
and
\[
\mathrm{Var}_*(\hat\lambda^*)
=16\cdot\frac{2}{225}
=\frac{32}{225}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Var}_*=32/225}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the fitted $\mathrm{Gamma}(4,\mathrm{rate}=2/5)$
law by a nonparametric resample of the four observed points, or
by a bootstrap of the sample maximum, or else switches to the
mean parameterization $\hat\mu=5/2$. Sentence (ii) applies Jensen
and writes $E_*[4/S^*]=4/E_*[S^*]=2/5$, forcing a vanishing bias,
or reads the second Gamma parameter as a scale rather than a
rate, which is not asked.

The argument never resamples the observed $4$-tuple, never uses
$\max X_i$ as the statistic, and never replaces $E[1/S]$ by
$1/E[S]$.

graderFixtures.proofText: Rate MLE $\hat\lambda=2/5$. Parametric bootstrap: $S^*\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(4,\mathrm{rate}=2/5)$ and $\hat\lambda^*=4/S^*$. Exact moments $E_*=8/15$, $\mathrm{bias}=2/15$, bias-corrected $4/15$, $\mathrm{Var}_*=32/225$. Not a nonparametric bootstrap and not a bootstrap of the sample maximum.
I replace the parametric Gamma(4, rate 2/5) law by a nonparametric resample of the four observed points, or by a bootstrap of the sample maximum, or I switch to the mean parameterization hat mu=5/2.

MSTAT:020631.title: Antithetic MC for E[U^2]=1/3 with 2 evals: plain var 2/45; A=(U-1/2)^2+1/4 mean 1/3 var 1/180; Cov=-7/90, corr=-7/8, reduction 8
MSTAT:020631.objective: Compare the two-evaluation crude Monte Carlo estimator of E[U^2] with the antithetic estimator A=[U^2+(1-U)^2]/2. Compute both variances, the covariance and correlation of the pair, and the variance-reduction factor 8. Scope the sign of the covariance.
MSTAT:020631.statement:
Let $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. The target is
$\theta=E[U^2]=1/3$. Both estimators below use exactly two
evaluations of the map $u\mapsto u^2$.

1. The crude two-evaluation estimator is
   $(U_1^2+U_2^2)/2$ with $U_1,U_2$ i.i.d. $\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$.
   Prove $\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=4/45$ and that the crude variance is
   \[
   \mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\frac{U_1^2+U_2^2}{2}\Bigr)=\frac{2}{45}.
   \]

2. The antithetic estimator based on a single $U$ is
   \[
   A=\frac{U^2+(1-U)^2}{2}
   =(U-\tfrac12)^2+\tfrac14.
   \]
   Prove $E[A]=1/3$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A)=1/180$.

3. Prove
   \[
   \mathrm{Cov}\bigl(U^2,(1-U)^2\bigr)
   =\frac{1}{30}-\frac19
   =-\frac{7}{90},
   \]
   hence
   \[
   \mathrm{Corr}\bigl(U^2,(1-U)^2\bigr)=-\frac78
   \]
   and the variance-reduction factor
   $(2/45)/(1/180)=8$. Scope the sign: antithetic pairing
   reduces variance here because that covariance is strictly
   negative. The same pairing can inflate variance for a
   non-monotone integrand whose paired covariance is positive.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the crude variance is
   $\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=4/45$, forgetting the two-evaluation
   average, or $\mathrm{Var}(A)=4/45$”; (ii) “the covariance is
   $+7/90$ with correlation $+7/8$, or the reduction factor is
   $1$, or this is a jackknife / parametric-bootstrap exercise.”

Stay inside the two-evaluation comparison of crude and
antithetic Monte Carlo for $E[U^2]$. Do not replace $U^2$ by a
jackknife functional.
permittedResults: $E[U^2]=1/3$ and $E[U^4]=1/5$, so $\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=4/45$. The crude two-evaluation variance is half of that, $2/45$. Expanding $U^2(1-U)^2$ gives $E[U^2(1-U)^2]=1/30$ and covariance $1/30-1/9=-7/90$.
$A=(U-1/2)^2+1/4$ has mean $1/12+1/4=1/3$. With $W=U-1/2$ one has $E[W^4]=1/80$, hence $\mathrm{Var}(A)=1/80-1/144=1/180$. The correlation is $(-7/90)/(4/45)=-7/8$ and the reduction factor is $8$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate Var(U^2)=1/5-1/9 and halve it for the crude two-evaluation estimator, then rewrite A as (U-1/2)^2+1/4.
Compute E[U^2(1-U)^2]=1/30 to get Cov=-7/90, read off the correlation and the factor 8, and record that the sign of the covariance is the scope.

milestones.criterion: Computes the crude two-evaluation variance 2/45 and the antithetic identity A=(U-1/2)^2+1/4 with mean 1/3 and variance 1/180.
Records Cov=-7/90, Corr=-7/8, the reduction factor 8, and scopes the reduction to the negative covariance.
Refuses a forgotten two-evaluation factor of 1/2 and a sign error on the paired covariance.

commonErrors.description: Reports the crude variance as Var(U^2)=4/45, forgetting the two-evaluation average, or assigns Var(A)=4/45 instead of 1/180.
commonErrors.consequence: The comparable two-evaluation crude variance 2/45 and the antithetic variance 1/180 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports Cov=+7/90 and Corr=+7/8, or a reduction factor of 1, or replaces the comparison by a jackknife or parametric-bootstrap exercise.
commonErrors.consequence: The negative covariance -7/90, the correlation -7/8, and the reduction factor 8 are erased.

hintTree.content: $\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=1/5-1/9=4/45$. Averaging two i.i.d. copies halves this to $2/45$.
Rewrite $A=(U-1/2)^2+1/4$. Then $E[A]=\mathrm{Var}(U)+1/4=1/3$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A)=\mathrm{Var}((U-1/2)^2)$.
$E[U^2(1-U)^2]=1/3-1/2+1/5=1/30$. Subtract $(1/3)^2$ to obtain $\mathrm{Cov}=-7/90$. The sign of this covariance is the scope of the reduction.

MSTAT:020631.canonicalSolution:
For $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$,
\[
E[U^2]=\frac13,\qquad E[U^4]=\frac15,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=\frac15-\frac19=\frac{4}{45}.
\]
The crude two-evaluation estimator therefore has variance
\[
\mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\frac{U_1^2+U_2^2}{2}\Bigr)
=\frac12\cdot\frac{4}{45}
=\frac{2}{45}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=4/45,\quad\text{crude two-eval variance }2/45}.
\]

The antithetic estimator expands as
\[
U^2+(1-U)^2
=2U^2-2U+1,
\qquad
A=U^2-U+\frac12
=(U-\tfrac12)^2+\frac14.
\]
Hence
\[
E[A]
=E\bigl[(U-\tfrac12)^2\bigr]+\frac14
=\mathrm{Var}(U)+\frac14
=\frac{1}{12}+\frac14
=\frac13,
\]
as required. Writing $W=U-1/2\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-1/2,1/2)$,
\[
E[W^4]
=2\int_0^{1/2}w^4\,dw
=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{32}
=\frac{1}{80},
\]
so
\[
\mathrm{Var}(A)
=\mathrm{Var}(W^2)
=\frac{1}{80}-\Bigl(\frac{1}{12}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{1}{80}-\frac{1}{144}
=\frac{1}{180}.
\]
\[
\boxed{A=(U-1/2)^2+1/4,\quad E[A]=1/3,\quad\mathrm{Var}(A)=1/180}.
\]

The paired product moment is
\[
E\bigl[U^2(1-U)^2\bigr]
=E[U^2-2U^3+U^4]
=\frac13-\frac12+\frac15
=\frac{1}{30}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathrm{Cov}\bigl(U^2,(1-U)^2\bigr)
=\frac{1}{30}-\frac19
=\frac{3-10}{90}
=-\frac{7}{90}.
\]
Both coordinates have variance $4/45$, so
\[
\mathrm{Corr}\bigl(U^2,(1-U)^2\bigr)
=\frac{-7/90}{4/45}
=-\frac78.
\]
The variance-reduction factor against the crude two-evaluation
estimator is
\[
\frac{2/45}{1/180}=8.
\]
The covariance is strictly negative; that sign is the assigned
scope of the reduction. For an integrand whose pairing with
$u\mapsto 1-u$ produced a positive covariance, the same
antithetic construction would inflate variance.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Cov}=-7/90,\ \mathrm{Corr}=-7/8,\ \text{reduction }8}.
\]

Sentence (i) reports the crude variance as $\mathrm{Var}(U^2)=4/45$,
forgetting that two evaluations average that variance down to
$2/45$, or assigns $\mathrm{Var}(A)=4/45$. Sentence (ii) flips the
covariance sign to $+7/90$, reports correlation $+7/8$ or a
reduction factor of $1$, or else replaces the Monte Carlo
comparison by a jackknife or parametric-bootstrap calculation,
which is not asked.

The argument never jackknifes $U^2$, never bootstraps an
exponential rate, and never claims that antithetic pairing
reduces variance independently of the covariance sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: Target $E[U^2]=1/3$. Crude two-evaluation variance $2/45$. Antithetic $A=[U^2+(1-U)^2]/2=(U-1/2)^2+1/4$ has mean $1/3$ and variance $1/180$. $\mathrm{Cov}(U^2,(1-U)^2)=1/30-1/9=-7/90$, correlation $-7/8$, reduction factor $8$. The reduction is scoped to that negative covariance.
I report the crude variance as Var(U^2)=4/45, forgetting that two evaluations average it to 2/45, or I assign Var(A)=4/45 instead of 1/180.
I report Cov=+7/90 and Corr=+7/8, or a reduction factor of 1, or I replace the antithetic comparison by a jackknife or parametric-bootstrap exercise.

MTP:010117.title: Mixed law (1/4)δ0+(3/4)Exp(rate 2) has F(0)=1/4, density (3/2)e^{-2x} on (0,∞), E=3/8, Var=15/64, median (1/2)log(3/2)
MTP:010117.objective: For μ=(1/4)δ0+(3/4)Exp(rate 2) prove the Lebesgue decomposition, F(x)=0 for x<0, F(0)=1/4, F(x)=1-(3/4)e^{-2x} for x>0, ac density (3/2)e^{-2x}1_{x>0}, E=3/8, E[X^2]=3/8, Var=15/64, Laplace 1/4+(3/4)2/(2+s), and median (1/2)log(3/2).
MTP:010117.statement:
Let $X$ be a real random variable whose law is the mixed
probability
\[
\mu=\frac14\,\delta_0+\frac34\,\operatorname{Exp}(2),
\]
where $\operatorname{Exp}(2)$ denotes the exponential law of rate $2$
(density $2e^{-2x}$ on $(0,\infty)$). Do not replace this mixed-law
Lebesgue ledger by an inverse-image measurability problem for a
random variable, a Kolmogorov tail $0$–$1$ argument, or a
mode-of-convergence / uniform-integrability repair.

1. Write the Lebesgue decomposition $\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}+\mu_{\mathrm{pp}}$
   relative to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$, identify the
   absolutely continuous density, and prove that the cumulative
   distribution function satisfies
   \[
   F(x)=0\quad(x<0),\qquad
   F(0)=\frac14,\qquad
   F(x)=1-\frac34 e^{-2x}\quad(x>0).
   \]

2. Compute the first two moments and the variance:
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[X]=\frac38,\qquad
   \mathbb{E}[X^2]=\frac38,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{15}{64}.
   \]

3. Prove that the Laplace transform is
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-sX}\bigr]
   =\frac14+\frac34\cdot\frac{2}{2+s}
   \qquad(s>-2),
   \]
   and that the median is
   \[
   m=\frac12\log\frac32.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the atom may be dropped, so $X$ is
   purely $\operatorname{Exp}(2)$, hence $F(0)=0$ and
   $\mathbb{E}[X]=1/2$ rather than $F(0)=1/4$ and $\mathbb{E}[X]=3/8$”;
   (ii) “the median solves $1-e^{-2m}=1/2$, so $m=(1/2)\log 2$ rather
   than $(1/2)\log(3/2)$.”
permittedResults: $\operatorname{Exp}(2)$ has density $2e^{-2x}$ on $(0,\infty)$, mean $1/2$, and second moment $1/2$. Mixing against an atom of mass $1/4$ at $0$ produces density $(3/2)e^{-2x}1_{x>0}$ and $F(0)=1/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the mixture into the atom at 0 and the weighted Exp(2) component, then read the CDF, density, and Laplace transform from the two pieces.
Compute moments by linearity against the mixture weights, and solve F(m)=1/2 on (0,∞) because F(0)=1/4 lies strictly below 1/2.

milestones.criterion: Produces the Lebesgue split, F(0)=1/4, F(x)=1-(3/4)e^{-2x} for x>0, and ac density (3/2)e^{-2x}1_{x>0}.
Reports E=3/8, E[X^2]=3/8, Var=15/64, Laplace 1/4+(3/4)2/(2+s), and median (1/2)log(3/2).
Rejects a pure Exp(2) law or the unmixed median (1/2)log 2, and refuses reserved inverse-image, tail 0-1, or uniform-integrability substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the atom and treats X as purely Exp(2), reporting F(0)=0 and E[X]=1/2 instead of F(0)=1/4 and E[X]=3/8.
commonErrors.consequence: The mixed Lebesgue decomposition, the jump F(0)=1/4, the density (3/2)e^{-2x}, and the moment ledger E=3/8, Var=15/64 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Solves the unmixed equation 1-e^{-2m}=1/2 and reports median (1/2)log 2 instead of (1/2)log(3/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned median of the mixed law is replaced by the median of a pure Exp(2) random variable.

hintTree.content: Split $\mu$ into the point mass $(1/4)\delta_0$ and the weighted exponential $(3/4)\operatorname{Exp}(2)$. The ac density is therefore $(3/4)\cdot 2e^{-2x}=(3/2)e^{-2x}$ on $(0,\infty)$.
For $x>0$ one has $F(x)=1/4+(3/4)(1-e^{-2x})=1-(3/4)e^{-2x}$. Moments follow by linearity against the two mixture components.
The Laplace transform mixes $1$ at the atom with $2/(2+s)$ on the exponential. The median lies in $(0,\infty)$ because $F(0)=1/4<1/2$; solve $1-(3/4)e^{-2m}=1/2$.

MTP:010117.canonicalSolution:
Write $\lambda$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$. The mixture
splits as
\[
\mu_{\mathrm{pp}}=\frac14\,\delta_0,\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}=\frac34\,\operatorname{Exp}(2).
\]
The exponential component is absolutely continuous, with density
$2e^{-2x}$ on $(0,\infty)$, so
\[
\frac{d\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}}{d\lambda}(x)
=\frac34\cdot 2e^{-2x}\,1_{x>0}
=\frac32 e^{-2x}\,1_{x>0}.
\]
The atom is singular to $\lambda$. Thus $\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}+\mu_{\mathrm{pp}}$
is the Lebesgue decomposition.
\[
\boxed{\mu=(3/2)e^{-2x}1_{x>0}\,dx+(1/4)\delta_0}.
\]

The support of $\mu$ lies in $[0,\infty)$, so $F(x)=0$ for $x<0$.
Right-continuity and the atom give
\[
F(0)=\mu((-\infty,0])=\mu(\{0\})=\frac14.
\]
For $x>0$,
\begin{align*}
F(x)
&=\frac14+\frac34\bigl(1-e^{-2x}\bigr)
=1-\frac34 e^{-2x}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{F(x)=0\ (x<0),\ F(0)=1/4,\ F(x)=1-(3/4)e^{-2x}\ (x>0)}.
\]

Let $Z\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)$, independent of a Bernoulli coin that
selects the atom. Then $\mathbb{E}[Z]=1/2$ and
$\mathbb{E}[Z^2]=\operatorname{Var}(Z)+(\mathbb{E}[Z])^2=1/4+1/4=1/2$.
Mixing yields
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac38,\qquad
\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac38,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac38-\Bigl(\frac38\Bigr)^2
=\frac{24}{64}-\frac{9}{64}
=\frac{15}{64}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=3/8,\ \mathbb{E}[X^2]=3/8,\ \operatorname{Var}(X)=15/64}.
\]

The Laplace transform of the atom is $1$. The Laplace transform of
$\operatorname{Exp}(2)$ is $2/(2+s)$ for $s>-2$. Mixing gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-sX}\bigr]
=\frac14+\frac34\cdot\frac{2}{2+s}.
\]
Since $F(0)=1/4<1/2$, any median $m$ is strictly positive and solves
$F(m)=1/2$:
\[
1-\frac34 e^{-2m}=\frac12
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
e^{-2m}=\frac23
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
m=\frac12\log\frac32.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[e^{-sX}]=1/4+(3/4)2/(2+s),\ m=(1/2)\log(3/2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the atom, forces $F(0)=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[X]=1/2$,
and destroys the mixed density $(3/2)e^{-2x}$. Sentence (ii) solves
the unmixed exponential median equation and reports
$(1/2)\log 2$ instead of $(1/2)\log(3/2)$. The construction is a
mixed-law Lebesgue-decomposition audit; it is not an inverse-image
measurability problem, a tail $0$–$1$ argument, or a
uniform-integrability repair.

graderFixtures.proofText: The law is $\mu=(1/4)\delta_0+(3/4)\operatorname{Exp}(2)$ with $F(0)=1/4$, $F(x)=1-(3/4)e^{-2x}$ for $x>0$, and ac density $(3/2)e^{-2x}1_{x>0}$. One has $\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]=3/8$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=15/64$, Laplace transform $1/4+(3/4)2/(2+s)$, and median $(1/2)\log(3/2)$.
The atom may be dropped, so X is purely Exp(2). I report F(0)=0 and E[X]=1/2. I do not report F(0)=1/4 or E[X]=3/8.
The median solves 1-e^{-2m}=1/2, so m=(1/2)log 2. I never obtain m=(1/2)log(3/2).

MTP:010118.title: On {1,2,3,4}, L=(2,1,1,3/4) sends P=(1,2,3,4)/10 to Q=(1/5,1/5,3/10,3/10) with E_Q X=3/5 and TV=1/10
MTP:010118.statement:
Let $\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}$ with
\[
P=\Bigl(\frac1{10},\frac2{10},\frac3{10},\frac4{10}\Bigr)
\]
and likelihood
\[
L=(2,1,1,3/4).
\]
Do not replace this finite Radon–Nikodym ledger by an inverse-image
measurability problem, an $L^2$-orthogonality account of conditional
expectation, or a Gaussian characteristic-function limit.

1. Prove that $Q:=LP$ is the probability
   \[
   Q=\Bigl(\frac15,\frac15,\frac3{10},\frac3{10}\Bigr)
   \]
   and that $\mathbb{E}_P[L]=1$, so $L=dQ/dP$.

2. For the coordinate random variable $X=(1,-1,2,0)$, prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}_Q[X]=\mathbb{E}_P[LX]=\frac35.
   \]

3. Prove the total-variation and Kullback–Leibler identities
   \[
   \|Q-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac1{10},\qquad
   D(Q\|P)=\frac15\ln 2+\frac3{10}\ln\frac34.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “change of measure may be ignored, so
   $\mathbb{E}_Q[X]=\mathbb{E}_P[X]=1/2$ rather than $3/5$”; (ii) “total
   variation is the unhalved $\ell^1$ gap $\sum|Q-P|=1/5$, so
   $\|Q-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is not $1/10$.”
permittedResults: $\mathbb{E}_P[LX]=2\cdot 1\cdot(1/10)+1\cdot(-1)\cdot(2/10)+1\cdot 2\cdot(3/10)=3/5$. The $\ell^1$ gap is $1/5$, so $\mathrm{TV}=1/10$. Only the atoms with $L\neq 1$ contribute to $D(Q\|P)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply L against P atomwise, check that the masses sum to 1, and evaluate E_P[LX] on the four-point space.
Halve the ell^1 gap to obtain TV, and sum Q log L only on the atoms where L differs from 1.

milestones.criterion: Produces Q=(1/5,1/5,3/10,3/10), E_P L=1, and the identity E_Q X=E_P[LX]=3/5.
Rejects the unweighted mean E_P X=1/2 or the unhalved TV=1/5, and refuses reserved inverse-image, L2-projection, or Gaussian-CLT substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Ignores the likelihood and reports E_Q[X]=E_P[X]=1/2 instead of E_P[LX]=3/5.
commonErrors.consequence: The change-of-measure identity E_Q X=E_P[LX] and the assigned value 3/5 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports total variation as the unhalved ell^1 gap sum|Q-P|=1/5 instead of TV=1/10.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity ||Q-P||_TV=1/10 is replaced by an inconsistent ell^1 total.

hintTree.content: Multiply $L$ against $P$ atomwise and check that the four masses sum to $1$. The same four products give $\mathbb{E}_P[L]$.
Evaluate $\sum L(\omega)X(\omega)P(\omega)$. The last atom contributes nothing because $X(4)=0$.
Total variation halves $\sum|Q-P|$. For KL, only atoms $1$ and $4$ have $\log L\neq 0$.

MTP:010118.canonicalSolution:
Atomwise multiplication produces
\[
Q=LP
=\Bigl(2\cdot\frac1{10},\,1\cdot\frac2{10},\,1\cdot\frac3{10},\,\frac34\cdot\frac4{10}\Bigr)
=\Bigl(\frac15,\frac15,\frac3{10},\frac3{10}\Bigr).
\]
The four masses sum to $1$, so $Q$ is a probability. Directly,
\[
\mathbb{E}_P[L]
=2\cdot\frac1{10}+1\cdot\frac2{10}+1\cdot\frac3{10}+\frac34\cdot\frac4{10}
=\frac{2+2+3+3}{10}=1.
\]
Hence $L=dQ/dP$.
\[
\boxed{Q=(1/5,1/5,3/10,3/10),\ \mathbb{E}_P[L]=1}.
\]

For $X=(1,-1,2,0)$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_P[LX]
&=2\cdot 1\cdot\frac1{10}
+1\cdot(-1)\cdot\frac2{10}
+1\cdot 2\cdot\frac3{10}
+\frac34\cdot 0\cdot\frac4{10}
=\frac{2-2+6}{10}
=\frac35.
\end{align*}
The change-of-measure identity $\mathbb{E}_Q[X]=\mathbb{E}_P[LX]$ therefore
gives $\mathbb{E}_Q[X]=3/5$. As a check,
\[
\mathbb{E}_Q[X]
=\frac15\cdot 1+\frac15\cdot(-1)+\frac3{10}\cdot 2+\frac3{10}\cdot 0
=\frac35.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}_Q[X]=\mathbb{E}_P[LX]=3/5}.
\]

The signed gaps are
\[
Q-P
=\Bigl(\frac1{10},0,0,-\frac1{10}\Bigr),
\]
so
\[
\|Q-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
=\frac12\Bigl(\frac1{10}+0+0+\frac1{10}\Bigr)
=\frac1{10}.
\]
Only atoms with $L\neq 1$ contribute to Kullback–Leibler:
\[
D(Q\|P)
=Q(1)\ln 2+Q(4)\ln\frac34
=\frac15\ln 2+\frac3{10}\ln\frac34.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{TV}=1/10,\ D(Q\|P)=(1/5)\ln 2+(3/10)\ln(3/4)}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\mathbb{E}_Q[X]$ by the unweighted mean
$\mathbb{E}_P[X]=1/2$. Sentence (ii) forgets the factor $1/2$ in the
definition of total variation and reports $1/5$. The construction
is a finite Radon–Nikodym change-of-measure audit; it is not an
inverse-image measurability problem, an $L^2$ projection of
conditional expectation, or a Gaussian characteristic-function
limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $Q=LP=(1/5,1/5,3/10,3/10)$ and $\mathbb{E}_P[L]=1$. For $X=(1,-1,2,0)$ the change of measure gives $\mathbb{E}_Q[X]=\mathbb{E}_P[LX]=3/5$, $\|Q-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=1/10$, and $D(Q\|P)=(1/5)\ln 2+(3/10)\ln(3/4)$.

MTP:010219.title: Binary Bayes with P(H=1)=1/3 and likelihoods 3/4,1/4 yields posteriors 3/5 and 1/7, E[Var]=6/35, Bayes error 1/4
MTP:010219.objective: For P(H=1)=1/3, P(+|1)=3/4, P(+|0)=1/4 prove P(+)=5/12, P(-)=7/12, posteriors 3/5 and 1/7, tower 1/3, E[Var(H|Y)]=6/35, Var(E[H|Y])=16/315, sum 2/9, and Bayes error 1/4.
MTP:010219.statement:
Let $H\in\{0,1\}$ be a hidden bit with $\mathbb{P}(H=1)=1/3$, and let
$Y\in\{+,-\}$ be an observation with
\[
\mathbb{P}(+\,|\,H=1)=\frac34,\qquad
\mathbb{P}(+\,|\,H=0)=\frac14.
\]
Do not replace this binary Bayes variance ledger by an
$L^2$-orthogonality account of conditional expectation, an optional
stopping argument, or a Gaussian characteristic-function limit.

1. Prove
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(+)=\frac5{12},\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(-)=\frac7{12},
   \]
   and the posteriors
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(H=1\,|\,+)=\frac35,\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(H=1\,|\,-)=\frac17.
   \]

2. Writing $M=\mathbb{E}[H\mid Y]$, prove the tower identity
   $\mathbb{E}[M]=1/3$ and the variance decomposition
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)\bigr]=\frac6{35},\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(M)=\frac{16}{315},\qquad
   \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)]+\operatorname{Var}(M)=\frac29.
   \]

3. For $0$–$1$ loss, prove that the Bayes classifier decides $H=1$
   on $\{+\}$ and $H=0$ on $\{-\}$, with Bayes error $1/4$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the posteriors are swapped, so
   $\mathbb{P}(H=1\,|\,+)=1/7$ rather than $3/5$”; (ii) “the expected
   conditional variance equals the total variance $2/9$, so
   $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)]$ is not $6/35$.”
permittedResults: Bernoulli variances give $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)]=(5/12)(6/25)+(7/12)(6/49)=6/35$ and $\operatorname{Var}(M)=16/315$. Their sum is $\operatorname{Var}(H)=2/9$. The MAP rule errs with probability $1/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the observation masses by the law of total probability, then apply Bayes' rule at each atom to obtain the two posteriors.
Mix the two Bernoulli conditional variances and the two squared posterior means, then read the Bayes classifier from which posterior exceeds 1/2.

milestones.criterion: Produces P(+)=5/12, P(-)=7/12, posteriors 3/5 and 1/7, and the tower identity E[M]=1/3.
Reports E[Var(H|Y)]=6/35, Var(M)=16/315, sum 2/9, and Bayes error 1/4.
Rejects swapped posteriors or the claim E[Var]=2/9, and refuses reserved L2-orthogonality, optional-stopping, or Gaussian-CLT substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Swaps the two posteriors, reporting P(H=1|+)=1/7 instead of 3/5 (and P(H=1|-)=3/5 instead of 1/7).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned posterior ledger, the tower check, the variance split, and the Bayes classifier are all corrupted.

commonErrors.description: Equates E[Var(H|Y)] with the total variance 2/9 instead of the correct value 6/35.
commonErrors.consequence: The law of total variance is collapsed and the assigned split 6/35 + 16/315 = 2/9 is lost.

hintTree.content: Expand $\mathbb{P}(+)$ by the law of total probability. The complementary mass is $\mathbb{P}(-)=7/12$.
Apply Bayes' rule at each observation. Then compute the two Bernoulli conditional variances $(3/5)(2/5)$ and $(1/7)(6/7)$ and mix them by $\mathbb{P}(\pm)$.
The Bayes classifier follows the posterior across $1/2$. The error probability is $\mathbb{P}(+\,|\,0)\mathbb{P}(H=0)+\mathbb{P}(-\,|\,1)\mathbb{P}(H=1)$.

MTP:010219.canonicalSolution:
The prior is $\mathbb{P}(H=1)=1/3$ and $\mathbb{P}(H=0)=2/3$. The
observation masses are
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(+)
&=\frac34\cdot\frac13+\frac14\cdot\frac23
=\frac14+\frac16
=\frac{5}{12},\\
\mathbb{P}(-)
&=1-\frac5{12}=\frac7{12}.
\end{align*}
Bayes' rule gives
\[
\mathbb{P}(H=1\mid +)
=\frac{(3/4)(1/3)}{5/12}
=\frac{1/4}{5/12}
=\frac35,
\]
\[
\mathbb{P}(H=1\mid -)
=\frac{(1/4)(1/3)}{7/12}
=\frac{1/12}{7/12}
=\frac17.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(+)=5/12,\ \mathbb{P}(-)=7/12,\ \text{posteriors }3/5,\,1/7}.
\]

Write $M=\mathbb{E}[H\mid Y]$. Then $M(+)=3/5$ and $M(-)=1/7$, so
\[
\mathbb{E}[M]
=\frac5{12}\cdot\frac35+\frac7{12}\cdot\frac17
=\frac14+\frac1{12}
=\frac13=\mathbb{E}[H].
\]
The conditional variances of the Bernoulli posteriors are
\[
\operatorname{Var}(H\mid +)=\frac35\cdot\frac25=\frac6{25},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(H\mid -)=\frac17\cdot\frac67=\frac6{49}.
\]
Mixing yields
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)\bigr]
=\frac5{12}\cdot\frac6{25}+\frac7{12}\cdot\frac6{49}
=\frac1{10}+\frac1{14}
=\frac6{35}.
\]
Next
\[
\mathbb{E}[M^2]
=\frac5{12}\cdot\frac9{25}+\frac7{12}\cdot\frac1{49}
=\frac3{20}+\frac1{84}
=\frac{17}{105},
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(M)
=\frac{17}{105}-\frac19
=\frac{51}{315}-\frac{35}{315}
=\frac{16}{315}.
\]
Adding the two pieces recovers the prior variance:
\[
\frac6{35}+\frac{16}{315}
=\frac{54}{315}+\frac{16}{315}
=\frac{70}{315}
=\frac29
=\operatorname{Var}(H).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}]=6/35,\ \operatorname{Var}(M)=16/315,\ \text{sum }2/9}.
\]

The posterior $3/5$ exceeds $1/2$ while $1/7$ does not, so the Bayes
classifier decides $H=1$ on $\{+\}$ and $H=0$ on $\{-\}$. Its error
is
\[
\mathbb{P}(+\,|\,H=0)\mathbb{P}(H=0)
+\mathbb{P}(-\,|\,H=1)\mathbb{P}(H=1)
=\frac14\cdot\frac23+\frac14\cdot\frac13
=\frac14.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{Bayes error }=1/4}.
\]

Sentence (i) swaps the two posteriors and destroys both the tower
check and the variance split. Sentence (ii) equates
$\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)]$ with the total variance
$2/9$ instead of $6/35$. The construction is a binary Bayes
conditional-variance audit; it is not an $L^2$-orthogonality
account of conditional expectation, an optional-stopping argument,
or a Gaussian characteristic-function limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $\mathbb{P}(+)=5/12$, $\mathbb{P}(-)=7/12$, posteriors $3/5$ and $1/7$, and $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[H\mid Y]]=1/3$. The variance split is $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H\mid Y)]=6/35$, $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[H\mid Y])=16/315$, summing to $2/9$, and the Bayes error is $1/4$.
The posteriors are swapped, so P(H=1|+)=1/7 rather than 3/5. I do not report P(H=1|+)=3/5.
The expected conditional variance equals the total variance 2/9. I never obtain E[Var(H|Y)]=6/35.

MTP:010222.title: X,Z iid N(0,1) and Y=X+Z give X|Y=y ~ N(y/2,1/2), E[X|Y]=Y/2, MSE=1/2, and P(X>0|Y=2)=Phi(sqrt(2))
MTP:010222.objective: For X,Z iid N(0,1) and Y=X+Z construct the canonical continuous Gaussian regular conditional kernel X|Y=y ~ N(y/2,1/2), use that selected version at y=2, prove that Y/2 is an a.e. version of E[X|Y], and compute E[Var(X|Y)]=Var(E[X|Y])=MSE=1/2 and P(X>0|Y=2)=Phi(sqrt(2)).
MTP:010222.statement:
Let $X$ and $Z$ be i.i.d. standard normals on a probability space,
and set $Y=X+Z$. Work throughout with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on
$\mathbb{R}$. Construct the continuous Gaussian regression kernel
$\kappa(y,\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)$ as a regular conditional
distribution of $X$ given $Y$, and use this specified version when
conditioning at the null singleton $Y=2$. Do not replace the Gaussian
regression ledger by an abstract
$L^1$-projection / $L^2$-orthogonality characterisation of
conditional expectation, by an inverse-image measurability debate,
or by a characteristic-function central-limit argument.

1. Prove that the pair $(X,Y)$ is centred bivariate Gaussian with
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}(X)=1,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(Y)=2,\qquad
   \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1,
   \]
   and prove that the continuous kernel
   \[
   \mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=y)=\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\frac y2,\frac12\Bigr)
   \]
   is a regular conditional law for every $y\in\mathbb{R}$. Explain
   that an arbitrary regular conditional law need only agree with
   this selected kernel for $P_Y$-almost every $y$.

2. Conclude that $Y/2$ is a version of $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$, and
   that this identity is understood almost surely. Compute
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\bigr]
   =\frac12,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\bigr)
   =\frac12,\qquad
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2\bigr]
   =\frac12.
   \]

3. Evaluate the regular conditional probability
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(X>0\mid Y=2)=\Phi(\sqrt{2}),
   \]
   where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the regression slope is $1$, so
   $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=Y$ and $X\mid Y=y\sim\mathcal{N}(y,1)$
   rather than $\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)$”; (ii) “standardising
   $X\mid Y=2$ against mean $1$ and variance $1/2$ produces
   $\Phi(2)$ rather than $\Phi(\sqrt{2})$.”
permittedResults: If $X,Z$ are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $Y=X+Z$, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$. The conditional-density formula therefore defines the continuous regular conditional kernel $\kappa(y,\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)$ for every $y$.

Law of total variance: $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])$. Here both summands equal $1/2$, and $\mathbb{P}(X>0\mid Y=2)=\Phi(\sqrt{2})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read the bivariate Gaussian moments of (X,Y) from Y=X+Z, use the conditional densities to select the continuous Gaussian kernel for every y, and apply the covariance-ratio formulae.
Standardise the N(1,1/2) law at Y=2 and identify the threshold -sqrt(2), then cross-check MSE by expanding (X-Y/2)=(X-Z)/2.

milestones.criterion: Produces the joint moments Var(X)=1, Var(Y)=2, Cov(X,Y)=1 and the selected continuous regular conditional kernel X|Y=y ~ N(y/2,1/2), including why its y=2 value is well-defined for this version.
Reports the a.s. version E[X|Y]=Y/2, the split E[Var]=Var(E)=MSE=1/2, and P(X>0|Y=2)=Phi(sqrt(2)).
Rejects slope-1 regression or a Phi(2) tail, and refuses reserved L1-projection, inverse-image, or characteristic-function substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the regression slope is 1, so E[X|Y]=Y and X|Y=y ~ N(y,1), instead of E[X|Y]=Y/2 and N(y/2,1/2).
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned conditional mean, conditional variance 1/2, and MSE=1/2 ledger are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports P(X>0|Y=2)=Phi(2) instead of Phi(sqrt(2)), mis-standardising the N(1,1/2) law.
commonErrors.consequence: The required regular conditional tail Phi(sqrt(2)) is replaced by an inconsistent normal probability.

hintTree.content: Compute the three second moments of $(X,Y)$ from $Y=X+Z$ and independence of $X$ and $Z$. The pair is jointly Gaussian because it is a linear image of $(X,Z)$.
Insert $\sigma_{XY}=1$ and $\sigma_Y^2=2$ into the bivariate Gaussian conditioning formulae. The conditional mean slope is $1/2$ and the Schur complement is $1-1/2=1/2$.
Given $Y=2$ one has $X\sim\mathcal{N}(1,1/2)$. Standardise: $(0-1)/\sqrt{1/2}=-\sqrt{2}$, so the upper tail is $\Phi(\sqrt{2})$.

MTP:010222.canonicalSolution:
The vector $(X,Z)$ is standard bivariate normal, and
\[
\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}X\\Z\end{pmatrix}
\]
is therefore centred Gaussian. Independence gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=1,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X+Z)=2,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,X+Z)=1.
\]
The Gaussian regression formula gives the conditional-density
kernel
\[
\mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=y)
=\mathcal{N}\Bigl(
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\,y,\;
\operatorname{Var}(X)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}
\Bigr)
=\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\frac y2,\frac12\Bigr)
\]
Because the $\mathcal{N}(0,2)$ density of $Y$ is strictly positive,
the joint-density factorisation verifies the disintegration identity
for the Borel kernel $\kappa(y,\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)$ defined
at every $y\in\mathbb{R}$. Thus $\kappa$ is our selected continuous
regular conditional version. Any other regular conditional version
needs to agree with it only $P_Y$-almost everywhere.
\[
\boxed{X\mid Y=y\sim\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)}.
\]

Integrating the conditional mean against $\sigma(Y)$ shows that
$Y/2$ is $\sigma(Y)$-measurable and satisfies the defining integral
identities of $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$. Thus $Y/2$ is a version of
$\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$; the equality
\[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=\frac Y2
\]
holds almost surely, not pointwise on every atom of an arbitrary
version. The conditional variance is the deterministic Schur
complement $1/2$, so
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\bigr]=\frac12.
\]
The variance of the conditional mean is
\[
\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\frac Y2\Bigr)
=\frac14\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=\frac12.
\]
These two identities recover $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$ by the law of
total variance. The mean-square error of the regression estimator is
the same as the expected conditional variance:
\[
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Bigl(X-\frac Y2\Bigr)^2\Bigr]
=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)\bigr]
=\frac12.
\]
Directly, $X-Y/2=(X-Z)/2$ and
$\mathbb{E}[(X-Z)^2]/4=(1+1)/4=1/2$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=Y/2\text{ a.s.},\;
\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])=\operatorname{MSE}=1/2}.
\]

For the selected continuous kernel, conditioning at $Y=2$ gives
$X\sim\mathcal{N}(1,1/2)$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(X>0\mid Y=2)
&=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{1/2}}>\frac{0-1}{\sqrt{1/2}}\Bigr)
=\mathbb{P}(Z>-\sqrt{2})
=\Phi(\sqrt{2}),
\end{align*}
where $Z$ denotes a standard normal.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X>0\mid Y=2)=\Phi(\sqrt{2})}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the covariance ratio $1/2$ by slope $1$ and
destroys both the conditional variance $1/2$ and the MSE ledger.
Sentence (ii) standardises with the wrong scale and reports
$\Phi(2)$ instead of $\Phi(\sqrt{2})$. The construction is a
bivariate Gaussian regression audit; it is not an $L^1$-projection
characterisation of conditional expectation, an inverse-image
measurability problem, or a characteristic-function CLT.

graderFixtures.proofText: Choose the continuous Gaussian regular conditional kernel $\kappa(y,\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(y/2,1/2)$ for every $y$; arbitrary versions agree only $P_Y$-a.e., and the value at $y=2$ refers to this selected kernel. Then $Y/2$ is an almost-sure version of $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$, $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])=\operatorname{MSE}=1/2$, and $\mathbb{P}(X>0\mid Y=2)=\Phi(\sqrt{2})$.
The regression slope is 1, so E[X|Y]=Y and X|Y=y is N(y,1). I do not report E[X|Y]=Y/2 or the law N(y/2,1/2).
Standardising X|Y=2 against mean 1 and variance 1/2 produces Phi(2). I never obtain P(X>0|Y=2)=Phi(sqrt(2)).

MTP:010320.title: Independent A_n of probability n^{-α} for n≥2: P(i.o.) vanishes iff α>1, and α=2 totals π²/6−1
MTP:010320.objective: For independent events A_n, n≥2, with P(A_n)=n^{-α}, prove α>1 ⇒ P(A_n i.o.)=0, 0<α≤1 ⇒ P(A_n i.o.)=1, that α=2 has expected total π²/6−1, that α=1 diverges, and that independence is used only in the divergent direction.
MTP:010320.statement:
Let $(A_n)_{n\ge 2}$ be independent events on a probability space
with
\[
\mathbb{P}(A_n)=n^{-\alpha},\qquad \alpha>0.
\]
Do not replace this power-threshold Borel–Cantelli ledger by a
Kolmogorov tail $0$–$1$ argument, a mode-of-convergence /
uniform-integrability repair, or an optional-stopping argument.

1. Prove that
   \[
   \sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-\alpha}<\infty
   \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
   \alpha>1.
   \]
   Deduce from Borel–Cantelli I that $\alpha>1$ implies
   $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$, without using independence.

2. Using independence and Borel–Cantelli II, prove that
   $0<\alpha\le 1$ implies $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$. Record
   explicitly that independence is used only in this divergent
   direction.

3. Evaluate the two sample series
   \[
   \sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}-1
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-1}=\infty.
   \]
   In particular the expected total number of occurrences is
   $\pi^2/6-1$ when $\alpha=2$, and is infinite when $\alpha=1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the threshold is reversed, so
   $\alpha>1$ forces $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$ rather than $0$”;
   (ii) “Borel–Cantelli I also needs independence, so the convergent
   conclusion $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ is unavailable without
   it.”
permittedResults: The $p$-series $\sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-\alpha}$ converges if and only if $\alpha>1$. Borel–Cantelli I therefore yields $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ for $\alpha>1$ with no independence hypothesis.
Independence plus Borel–Cantelli II upgrades divergence $0<\alpha\le 1$ to $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$. The $\alpha=2$ total is $\pi^2/6-1$; the $\alpha=1$ harmonic tail diverges.

acceptableStrategies.description: Identify the p-series threshold, apply Borel–Cantelli I on the convergent side, and invoke independence only through Borel–Cantelli II on the divergent side.
Evaluate the Basel tail at α=2 and the harmonic tail at α=1 as the two sample expected totals.

milestones.criterion: Produces the p-series threshold α>1 for convergence and the implication P(i.o.)=0 from Borel–Cantelli I without independence.
Reports P(i.o.)=1 for 0<α≤1 using independence, expected total π²/6-1 at α=2, and divergence at α=1.
Rejects a reversed threshold or a demand that Borel–Cantelli I use independence, and refuses reserved tail 0-1, uniform-integrability, or optional-stopping substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the threshold and claims that α>1 forces P(A_n i.o.)=1 rather than 0.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned Borel–Cantelli dichotomy and the finite expected total π²/6-1 at α=2 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that Borel–Cantelli I also requires independence, so the convergent conclusion P(i.o.)=0 is unavailable without it.
commonErrors.consequence: The distinction that independence is used only in the divergent direction is erased.

hintTree.content: Compare $\sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-\alpha}$ to the integral $\int_2^\infty x^{-\alpha}\,dx$, or invoke the standard $p$-series test.
Borel–Cantelli I is a first-moment / Borel–Cantelli counting argument and never uses independence. Independence enters only through Borel–Cantelli II.
The Basel sum $\sum_{n\ge 1}n^{-2}=\pi^2/6$ leaves the $n=1$ term $1$ to be subtracted. The harmonic series diverges.

MTP:010320.canonicalSolution:
The $p$-series test (or the integral test
$\int_2^\infty x^{-\alpha}\,dx$) yields
\[
\sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-\alpha}<\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha>1.
\]
Borel–Cantelli I therefore gives, with no independence hypothesis,
\[
\alpha>1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\alpha>1\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0
\text{ (no independence used)}}.
\]

If $0<\alpha\le 1$ the same series diverges. Independence of the
family $(A_n)_{n\ge 2}$ lets Borel–Cantelli II upgrade divergence to
almost-sure infinitude:
\[
0<\alpha\le 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1.
\]
Independence is used only in this divergent direction.
\[
\boxed{0<\alpha\le 1\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1
\text{ (independence used)}}.
\]

The Basel sum $\sum_{n\ge 1}n^{-2}=\pi^2/6$ implies
\[
\sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}-1.
\]
Thus when $\alpha=2$ the expected number of occurrences is
$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\sum_{n\ge 2}1_{A_n}\bigr]=\pi^2/6-1<\infty$,
consistent with $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$. When $\alpha=1$ the
harmonic tail $\sum_{n\ge 2}n^{-1}$ diverges, so the expected total
is infinite, consistent with $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$.
\[
\boxed{\alpha=2:\ \mathbb{E}[N]=\pi^2/6-1;\quad
\alpha=1:\ \mathbb{E}[N]=\infty}.
\]

Sentence (i) reverses the threshold and claims that convergence of
the series forces infinitely many occurrences. Sentence (ii)
incorrectly demands independence for Borel–Cantelli I. The
construction is an independent power-law Borel–Cantelli audit; it
is not a Kolmogorov tail $0$–$1$ argument, a uniform-integrability
repair, or an optional-stopping argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: For independent $A_n$ with $\mathbb{P}(A_n)=n^{-\alpha}$, $n\ge 2$, one has $\mathbb{P}(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ when $\alpha>1$ (no independence used) and $=1$ when $0<\alpha\le 1$ (independence used). The $\alpha=2$ expected total is $\pi^2/6-1$, and the $\alpha=1$ series diverges.
The threshold is reversed, so α>1 forces P(A_n i.o.)=1. I do not report P(A_n i.o.)=0 for α>1.
Borel–Cantelli I also needs independence, so the convergent conclusion P(A_n i.o.)=0 is unavailable without it. I never obtain P(i.o.)=0 from the series test alone.

MTP:010321.title: Fair independent U,V and W=U xor V are pairwise independent with support 000,011,101,110 each 1/4 and joint entropy 2 bits
MTP:010321.objective: For fair independent bits U,V and W=U xor V, prove the four-atom support 000,011,101,110 each of mass 1/4, that every pair is uniform with covariance 0, that P(000)=1/4≠1/8, that U xor V xor W=0 a.s., and that the joint entropy is 2 bits against a marginal sum of 3.
MTP:010321.statement:
Let $U,V$ be independent fair bits in $\{0,1\}$, and set
$W=U\oplus V$ (addition modulo $2$). Do not replace this XOR
pairwise-independence ledger by a Kolmogorov tail $0$–$1$ argument,
an inverse-image measurability problem, or a Gaussian
characteristic-function limit.

1. Prove that the joint law of $(U,V,W)$ is supported on the four
   atoms
   \[
   000,\quad 011,\quad 101,\quad 110,
   \]
   each of mass $1/4$.

2. Prove that every pair $(U,V)$, $(U,W)$, $(V,W)$ is uniformly
   distributed on $\{0,1\}^2$ (in particular each pair is
   independent, and every pairwise covariance vanishes), but that
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(U=V=W=0)=\frac14\neq\frac18
   =\mathbb{P}(U=0)\mathbb{P}(V=0)\mathbb{P}(W=0).
   \]

3. Prove the almost-sure linear dependence $U\oplus V\oplus W=0$
   and the entropy comparison
   \[
   H(U,V,W)=2\text{ bits}
   \qquad\text{versus}\qquad
   H(U)+H(V)+H(W)=3\text{ bits}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “pairwise independence upgrades to
   mutual independence, so $\mathbb{P}(000)=1/8$ rather than $1/4$”;
   (ii) “the joint entropy equals the sum of the three marginal
   entropies, so $H(U,V,W)=3$ bits rather than $2$.”
permittedResults: The map $(U,V)\mapsto(U,V,U\oplus V)$ is a bijection onto the even-parity atoms $000,011,101,110$. Each of $U,V$ is fair, so each image atom has mass $1/4$.
Each pair is a bijection of a fair independent pair, hence uniform on $\{0,1\}^2$. The four-atom joint law has entropy $2$, while three fair bits would contribute $3$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Enumerate the four equally likely pairs (U,V), attach W=U xor V, and read the support and all two-dimensional margins from the table.
Compare the four-atom joint entropy 2 with the three fair-bit marginals, and use P(000)=1/4≠1/8 as the atomic witness that mutual independence fails.

milestones.criterion: Produces the four-atom support 000,011,101,110 each of mass 1/4, pairwise uniformity, and vanishing pairwise covariances.
Reports P(000)=1/4≠1/8, the identity U xor V xor W=0 a.s., joint entropy 2 bits, and marginal sum 3 bits.
Rejects mutual independence with P(000)=1/8 or the claim H(U,V,W)=3, and refuses reserved tail 0-1, inverse-image, or Gaussian-CLT substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Upgrades pairwise independence to mutual independence and reports P(000)=1/8 instead of 1/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned four-atom joint law and the witness P(000)=1/4≠1/8 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Equates the joint entropy with the sum of the three marginal entropies and reports H(U,V,W)=3 bits instead of 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The entropy witness that the triple is not mutually independent is replaced by the independent-bits value.

hintTree.content: Enumerate the four equally likely pairs $(U,V)$ and attach $W=U\oplus V$. The odd-parity triples $001,010,100,111$ never occur.
Independence of $U$ and $W$ follows because $W=U\oplus V$ with $V$ an independent fair bit, which is a one-time pad. The pair $(V,W)$ is symmetric.
Four equal atoms give joint entropy $2$. Each coordinate is a fair bit, so the marginal sum is $3$. The identity $U\oplus V\oplus W=0$ is immediate from $W=U\oplus V$.

MTP:010321.canonicalSolution:
The pair $(U,V)$ is uniform on the four bits $00,01,10,11$.
Attaching $W=U\oplus V$ produces
\begin{align*}
(0,0)&\mapsto 000,\\
(0,1)&\mapsto 011,\\
(1,0)&\mapsto 101,\\
(1,1)&\mapsto 110.
\end{align*}
Each of these four atoms therefore has mass $1/4$, and the odd-parity
triples $001,010,100,111$ are impossible.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{supp}=\{000,011,101,110\},\ \text{each mass }1/4}.
\]

The pair $(U,V)$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}^2$ by hypothesis. Given $U=u$,
the bit $W=u\oplus V$ is a fair independent flip of $V$, so $(U,W)$ is
likewise uniform (a one-time pad). The same argument with the roles
of $U$ and $V$ exchanged shows that $(V,W)$ is uniform. In particular
every pair is independent, every coordinate is a fair bit, and every
pairwise covariance vanishes:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=\operatorname{Cov}(U,W)=\operatorname{Cov}(V,W)=0.
\]
Nevertheless the three bits are not mutually independent:
\[
\mathbb{P}(U=V=W=0)=\frac14
\neq\frac18
=\mathbb{P}(U=0)\mathbb{P}(V=0)\mathbb{P}(W=0).
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{pairs uniform / covariance }0,\ \mathbb{P}(000)=1/4\neq 1/8}.
\]

The defining relation $W=U\oplus V$ rearranges to the almost-sure
identity
\[
U\oplus V\oplus W=0.
\]
The joint law is uniform on four atoms, so
\[
H(U,V,W)=-\,4\cdot\frac14\log_2\frac14=2
\]
bits. Each coordinate is a fair bit, hence $H(U)=H(V)=H(W)=1$ and
the marginal sum is $3$ bits. The strict inequality $2<3$ is another
witness that mutual independence fails.
\[
\boxed{U\oplus V\oplus W=0\text{ a.s.},\ H(U,V,W)=2,\ H(U)+H(V)+H(W)=3}.
\]

Sentence (i) upgrades pairwise independence to mutual independence
and reports $\mathbb{P}(000)=1/8$. Sentence (ii) equates joint entropy
with the sum of the marginals and reports $3$ bits instead of $2$.
The construction is a pairwise-versus-mutual XOR audit; it is not a
Kolmogorov tail $0$–$1$ argument, an inverse-image measurability
problem, or a Gaussian characteristic-function limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The triple $(U,V,W)$ is supported on $000,011,101,110$ each of mass $1/4$. Every pair is uniform with covariance $0$, yet $\mathbb{P}(000)=1/4\neq 1/8$. One has $U\oplus V\oplus W=0$ a.s., joint entropy $2$ bits, and marginal sum $3$ bits.
Pairwise independence upgrades to mutual independence, so P(000)=1/8. I do not report P(000)=1/4.
The joint entropy equals the sum of the three marginal entropies, so H(U,V,W)=3 bits. I never obtain H(U,V,W)=2 bits.

MTP:010329.title: Beta(2,1)–Bernoulli mixture has p=2/3, P11=1/2, Cov=1/18, corr=1/4, and predictive (2+s)/(3+s+f)
MTP:010329.objective: For Theta~Beta(2,1) and Xi|Theta iid Bernoulli(Theta) prove p=2/3, the two-step joints P11=1/2 and P10=P01=P00=1/6, Cov=1/18 and corr=1/4, posterior Beta(2+s,1+f), and one-step predictive (2+s)/(3+s+f).
MTP:010329.statement:
Let $\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,1)$, so that $\Theta$ has
density $f(\theta)=2\theta$ on $(0,1)$. Conditionally on
$\Theta=\theta$, let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d.
$\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta)$. Do not replace the exchangeable
mixture ledger by a Kolmogorov $0$–$1$ tail event, by an
inverse-image measurability argument for a random variable, or by a
conditional-expectation projection identity in $L^1$ versus $L^2$.

1. Prove that the sequence is exchangeable but not independent, and
   evaluate
   \[
   p:=\mathbb{P}(X_i=1)=\frac23.
   \]

2. For the two-step joint law prove
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=1)=\frac12,\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=0)
   =\mathbb{P}(X_1=0,X_2=1)
   =\mathbb{P}(X_1=0,X_2=0)
   =\frac16,
   \]
   and deduce
   \[
   \operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=\frac1{18},\qquad
   \operatorname{Corr}(X_1,X_2)=\frac14.
   \]

3. After observing $s$ successes and $f$ failures, prove that the
   posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(2+s,1+f)$ and that the one-step
   predictive probability is
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(X_{\mathrm{next}}=1\mid\text{data})
   =\frac{2+s}{3+s+f}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the coordinates are i.i.d., so
   $\mathbb{P}(X_1=X_2=1)=(2/3)^2=4/9$ and the covariance vanishes,
   rather than $P_{11}=1/2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}=1/18$”;
   (ii) “the predictive probability is $(2+s)/(2+s+f)$, so the
   prior total $3$ never appears in the denominator.”
permittedResults: $\mathbb{E}[\Theta]=2/3$ and $\mathbb{E}[\Theta^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\Theta)+(\mathbb{E}\Theta)^2=1/18+4/9=1/2$, so $P_{11}=1/2$ and $P_{10}=P_{01}=P_{00}=1/6$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=1/2-(2/3)^2=1/18$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=2/9$, hence the correlation is $1/4$. The posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(2+s,1+f)$ with predictive mean $(2+s)/(3+s+f)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the mixture joints as moments of Theta~Beta(2,1), using E[Theta]=2/3 and Var(Theta)=1/18.
Update the Beta prior by conjugacy and read the predictive probability as the posterior mean (2+s)/(3+s+f).

milestones.criterion: Produces p=2/3, the two-step joints 1/2 and 1/6, Cov=1/18, and corr=1/4.
Reports the posterior Beta(2+s,1+f) and the predictive (2+s)/(3+s+f).
Rejects an i.i.d. P11=4/9 ledger or a predictive that forgets the prior total 3, and refuses reserved tail-event, inverse-image, or projection substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the coordinates are i.i.d., so P11=(2/3)^2=4/9 and Cov=0, instead of P11=1/2 and Cov=1/18.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned exchangeable-mixture joints, covariance 1/18, and correlation 1/4 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the one-step predictive is (2+s)/(2+s+f), dropping the prior total 3 from the denominator.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conjugate predictive (2+s)/(3+s+f) is replaced by a count-only ratio.

hintTree.content: Integrate out the latent success probability: $\mathbb{P}(X_i=1)=\mathbb{E}[\Theta]=2/3$. Exchangeability is immediate from the i.i.d. conditional law.
The two-step joints are the moments $\mathbb{E}[\Theta^2]$, $\mathbb{E}[\Theta(1-\Theta)]$, and $\mathbb{E}[(1-\Theta)^2]$. Use $\operatorname{Var}(\Theta)=1/18$.
Multiply the $\operatorname{Beta}(2,1)$ density by $\theta^s(1-\theta)^f$ and renormalize, or quote conjugacy. The predictive is the posterior mean.

MTP:010329.canonicalSolution:
The $\operatorname{Beta}(2,1)$ mean is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Theta]
=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
=\frac{2}{3},
\]
so
\[
p=\mathbb{P}(X_i=1)=\mathbb{E}[\Theta]=\frac23.
\]
Conditionally on $\Theta$ the coordinates are i.i.d., hence the
unconditional sequence is exchangeable. It is not independent:
$\Theta$ is nondegenerate, so
$\mathbb{P}(X_1=X_2=1)=\mathbb{E}[\Theta^2]>(\mathbb{E}\Theta)^2$.
\[
\boxed{p=2/3,\ \text{exchangeable, not independent}}.
\]

The second moment of $\Theta$ is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\Theta)
=\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}
=\frac{2\cdot 1}{9\cdot 4}
=\frac{1}{18},
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Theta^2]
=\operatorname{Var}(\Theta)+(\mathbb{E}\Theta)^2
=\frac{1}{18}+\frac{4}{9}
=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=1)
&=\mathbb{E}[\Theta^2]=\frac12,\\
\mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=0)
&=\mathbb{E}[\Theta(1-\Theta)]
=\frac23-\frac12
=\frac16,\\
\mathbb{P}(X_1=0,X_2=1)
&=\frac16,\\
\mathbb{P}(X_1=0,X_2=0)
&=\mathbb{E}[(1-\Theta)^2]
=1-\frac43+\frac12
=\frac16.
\end{align*}
The covariance is
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)
=\mathbb{E}[X_1X_2]-p^2
=\frac12-\frac49
=\frac{1}{18},
\]
and since $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=p(1-p)=2/9$,
\[
\operatorname{Corr}(X_1,X_2)
=\frac{1/18}{2/9}
=\frac14.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_{11}=1/2,\;P_{10}=P_{01}=P_{00}=1/6,\;\operatorname{Cov}=1/18,\;\operatorname{Corr}=1/4}.
\]

The $\operatorname{Beta}(2,1)$ density $2\theta$ multiplied by the
Bernoulli likelihood $\theta^s(1-\theta)^f$ is proportional to
$\theta^{(2+s)-1}(1-\theta)^{(1+f)-1}$. The conjugate update is
therefore
\[
\Theta\mid\text{data}
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2+s,1+f).
\]
The one-step predictive success probability is the posterior mean
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_{\mathrm{next}}=1\mid\text{data})
=\frac{2+s}{(2+s)+(1+f)}
=\frac{2+s}{3+s+f}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{posterior }\operatorname{Beta}(2+s,1+f),\ \text{predictive }(2+s)/(3+s+f)}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces independence and reports $P_{11}=4/9$ with
vanishing covariance. Sentence (ii) drops the prior total mass
$\alpha+\beta=3$ from the predictive denominator. The construction
is a Beta–Bernoulli exchangeable-mixture audit; it is not a
Kolmogorov $0$–$1$ tail argument, an inverse-image measurability
problem, or an $L^1$/$L^2$ conditional-expectation projection
identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $p=2/3$, joints $P_{11}=1/2$ and $P_{10}=P_{01}=P_{00}=1/6$, $\operatorname{Cov}=1/18$, and $\operatorname{Corr}=1/4$. The posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(2+s,1+f)$ and the predictive is $(2+s)/(3+s+f)$.
The coordinates are i.i.d., so P(X1=X2=1)=(2/3)^2=4/9 and the covariance vanishes. I do not report P11=1/2 or Cov=1/18.
The predictive probability is (2+s)/(2+s+f). I never obtain (2+s)/(3+s+f).

MTP:010423.title: Rademacher harmonic martingale M_n=sum eps_k/k has mean 0, Var(M_3)=49/36, limiting second moment pi^2/6, and diverging absolute series
MTP:010423.objective: For iid fair Rademacher eps_k and M_n=sum_{k=1}^n eps_k/k prove the martingale property, mean 0, Var(M_n)=sum 1/k^2, Var(M_3)=49/36, L2 bound pi^2/6, tail L2 vanishing, a.s. and L2 convergence, and that the absolute series diverges surely.
MTP:010423.statement:
Let $(\varepsilon_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be i.i.d. Rademacher signs,
$\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon_k=\pm 1)=1/2$, and define
\[
M_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\varepsilon_k}{k},\qquad n\ge 1,
\]
with the natural filtration $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n)$.
Do not replace the Rademacher harmonic ledger by a tail-event
Kolmogorov $0$–$1$ argument, by an abstract comparison of
convergence modes repaired by uniform integrability, or by a
characteristic-function Gaussian limit.

1. Prove that $(M_n)$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-martingale with
   $\mathbb{E}[M_n]=0$ and
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}(M_n)=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{k^2}.
   \]
   Evaluate the sample
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}(M_3)=\frac{49}{36}.
   \]

2. Prove that $(M_n)$ is bounded in $L^2$ with
   \[
   \sup_n\mathbb{E}[M_n^2]=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6},
   \]
   and that the $L^2$ tails vanish:
   \[
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[(M_m-M_n)^2\bigr]
   =\sum_{k=n+1}^m\frac1{k^2}\to 0
   \qquad(n,m\to\infty).
   \]

3. Deduce that $M_n$ converges almost surely and in $L^2$ to an
   integrable square-integrable limit $M_\infty$ with
   $\mathbb{E}[M_\infty^2]=\pi^2/6$. Prove nevertheless that the
   absolute series $\sum_k|\varepsilon_k|/k$ diverges almost surely.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “almost-sure convergence of $M_n$
   forces absolute convergence, so $\sum 1/k<\infty$ on a set of
   probability one”; (ii) “$\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=1+1/4+1/4=3/2$
   rather than $49/36$.”
permittedResults: $M_n$ is a martingale because $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=0$. Independence yields $\operatorname{Var}(M_n)=\sum_{k=1}^n 1/k^2$, so $\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=1+1/4+1/9=49/36$.
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty 1/k^2=\pi^2/6$ bounds $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2]$. Kolmogorov's theorem (or $L^2$ martingale convergence) gives a.s. and $L^2$ convergence, while $\sum 1/k=\infty$ a.s.

acceptableStrategies.description: Check the one-step conditional expectation and expand the independent variance sum through n=3 over denominator 36.
Use the p-series of exponent 2 for the L2 Cauchy criterion, then contrast with the deterministic harmonic series of absolute values.

milestones.criterion: Produces the martingale property, mean 0, Var(M_n)=sum 1/k^2, and the sample Var(M_3)=49/36.
Reports the L2 bound pi^2/6, vanishing L2 tails, a.s. and L2 convergence, and almost-sure divergence of sum 1/k.
Rejects absolute-convergence claims or Var(M_3)=3/2, and refuses reserved tail-event, UI-mode, or characteristic-function substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a.s. convergence of M_n forces absolute convergence, so sum |eps_k|/k converges almost surely.
commonErrors.consequence: The required contrast between L2/a.s. convergence and the divergent harmonic series of absolute values is lost.
The assigned variance sample 49/36 is replaced by an inconsistent partial-sum computation.

hintTree.content: Condition on $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$ to isolate the new term $\varepsilon_n/n$. Fairness of $\varepsilon_n$ gives the martingale increment of mean zero.
Expand $\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=1+1/4+1/9$ over the common denominator $36$. The $L^2$ Cauchy tails are the remaining $p$-series of exponent $2$.
Almost-sure convergence of $\sum\varepsilon_k/k$ does not upgrade to $\sum|\varepsilon_k|/k=\sum 1/k<\infty$. The harmonic series diverges.

MTP:010423.canonicalSolution:
The increment $\varepsilon_n/n$ is integrable and
$\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable, and fairness together with independence
of the future sign gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[M_n\bigm|\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\bigr]
=M_{n-1}+\frac1n\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_n]=M_{n-1}.
\]
Thus $(M_n)$ is a martingale. Taking expectations yields
$\mathbb{E}[M_n]=0$. Independence of the summands produces
\[
\operatorname{Var}(M_n)
=\sum_{k=1}^n\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon_k}{k}\Bigr)
=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{k^2}.
\]
The $n=3$ ledger is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(M_3)
=1+\frac14+\frac19
=\frac{36+9+4}{36}
=\frac{49}{36}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=49/36,\quad\mathbb{E}[M_n]=0}.
\]

Monotone convergence of the partial sums of $1/k^2$ gives
\[
\sup_n\mathbb{E}[M_n^2]
=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{6}<\infty,
\]
so $(M_n)$ is $L^2$-bounded. For $m>n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[(M_m-M_n)^2\bigr]
=\sum_{k=n+1}^m\frac1{k^2},
\]
which tends to $0$ as $n,m\to\infty$. Hence $(M_n)$ is Cauchy in
$L^2$ and converges in $L^2$ to some $M_\infty\in L^2$ with
$\mathbb{E}[M_\infty^2]=\pi^2/6$. An $L^2$-bounded martingale also
converges almost surely, and the same almost-sure conclusion follows
from Kolmogorov's theorem for independent series because
$\sum\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_k/k)<\infty$.
\[
\boxed{M_n\to M_\infty\text{ a.s.\ and in }L^2,\quad
\mathbb{E}[M_\infty^2]=\pi^2/6}.
\]

On the other hand $|\varepsilon_k|=1$ surely, so
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{|\varepsilon_k|}{k}
=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1k=\infty
\]
almost surely. Thus the series converges conditionally almost surely
but is not absolutely convergent.
\[
\boxed{\sum|\varepsilon_k|/k=\infty\text{ a.s.}}.
\]

Sentence (i) upgrades $L^2$/a.s.\ convergence to absolute
convergence and contradicts the divergent harmonic series.
Sentence (ii) replaces $1/9$ by $1/4$ and reports
$\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=3/2$ instead of $49/36$. The construction
is a Rademacher harmonic-series audit; it is not a tail-event
$0$–$1$ law, an abstract mode-arrow / uniform-integrability
comparison, or a characteristic-function CLT.

graderFixtures.proofText: $(M_n)$ is a mean-zero martingale with $\operatorname{Var}(M_n)=\sum 1/k^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(M_3)=49/36$. It is $L^2$-bounded by $\pi^2/6$, the $L^2$ tails vanish, and $M_n$ converges almost surely and in $L^2$, while $\sum|\varepsilon_k|/k$ diverges almost surely.
Almost-sure convergence of M_n forces absolute convergence, so sum 1/k is finite on a set of probability one. I do not report that the absolute series diverges surely.
I take Var(M_3)=1+1/4+1/4=3/2. I never obtain Var(M_3)=49/36.

MTP:010524.title: Fair-walk transform T_n=sum S_{k-1}eps_k satisfies S_n^2=n+2T_n, E[T_4^2]=6, and Var(S_4^2)=24
MTP:010524.objective: For the fair simple random walk S_n and T_n=sum_{k=1}^n S_{k-1}eps_k prove S_n^2=n+2T_n, that T is a martingale, E[T_n^2]=n(n-1)/2 (hence 6 at n=4), Var(S_n^2)=2n(n-1) (hence 24 at n=4), and that the predictable bracket sum S_{k-1}^2 has the same expectation n(n-1)/2.
MTP:010524.statement:
Let $(\varepsilon_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be i.i.d. fair signs and let
$S_0=0$, $S_n=\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_n$ be the simple
symmetric random walk. Define the predictable transform
\[
T_n=\sum_{k=1}^n S_{k-1}\varepsilon_k
\]
and write $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n)$.
Do not replace the discrete transform ledger by optional stopping of
a fair game at a sure win, by an $L^1$-projection characterisation
of conditional expectation, or by a tail-event $0$–$1$ argument.

1. Prove the pathwise identity
   \[
   S_n^2=n+2T_n
   \]
   and deduce that $(T_n)$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-martingale with
   $\mathbb{E}[T_n]=0$.

2. Using orthogonality of martingale differences, prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
   \]
   Evaluate the sample $\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]=6$.

3. Deduce
   \[
   \operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)=2n(n-1),
   \]
   so that $\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)=24$. Identify the predictable
   quadratic variation
   \[
   \langle T\rangle_n=\sum_{k=1}^n S_{k-1}^2
   \]
   and prove $\mathbb{E}[\langle T\rangle_n]=n(n-1)/2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the binomial expansion gives
   $S_n^2=n+T_n$ with no factor $2$”; (ii) “$\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)$
   equals $\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]=6$ rather than $24$.”
permittedResults: $(S_{n-1}+\varepsilon_n)^2=S_{n-1}^2+2S_{n-1}\varepsilon_n+1$ iterates to $S_n^2=n+2T_n$. Predictability of $S_{k-1}$ makes $T$ a martingale.
Orthogonal increments give $\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}[S_{k-1}^2]=n(n-1)/2$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)=4\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=2n(n-1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Iterate the one-step expansion of S_n^2 to isolate the factor 2 in front of the predictable transform.
Sum the orthogonal increment variances E[S_{k-1}^2]=k-1, then multiply by 4 to pass from E[T_n^2] to Var(S_n^2).

milestones.criterion: Produces the identity S_n^2=n+2T_n and the martingale property of the predictable transform T.
Reports E[T_n^2]=n(n-1)/2 (value 6 at n=4), Var(S_n^2)=2n(n-1) (value 24 at n=4), and E[<T>_n]=n(n-1)/2.
Rejects a missing factor 2 or Var(S_4^2)=6, and refuses reserved optional-stopping, projection, or tail-event substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the binomial expansion gives S_n^2=n+T_n with no factor 2, instead of S_n^2=n+2T_n.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned pathwise identity and the factor-of-four passage from E[T_n^2] to Var(S_n^2) are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Confuses Var(S_4^2) with E[T_4^2] and reports Var(S_4^2)=6 instead of 24.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned quadratic ledger Var(S_n^2)=2n(n-1) fails at the sample n=4.

hintTree.content: Expand $S_n^2=(S_{n-1}+\varepsilon_n)^2$ and use $\varepsilon_n^2=1$. Induction on $n$ produces the factor $2$ in front of $T_n$.
Martingale differences $S_{k-1}\varepsilon_k$ are orthogonal in $L^2$. The $k$-th second moment is $\mathbb{E}[S_{k-1}^2]=k-1$.
From $S_n^2=n+2T_n$ one has $\operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)=4\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]$. At $n=4$ this is $4\cdot 6=24$.

MTP:010524.canonicalSolution:
Start from $S_0=0$ and expand
\[
S_n^2
=(S_{n-1}+\varepsilon_n)^2
=S_{n-1}^2+2S_{n-1}\varepsilon_n+\varepsilon_n^2
=S_{n-1}^2+2S_{n-1}\varepsilon_n+1.
\]
Induction yields
\[
S_n^2
=n+2\sum_{k=1}^n S_{k-1}\varepsilon_k
=n+2T_n.
\]
\[
\boxed{S_n^2=n+2T_n}.
\]
The integrand $S_{k-1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{k-1}$-measurable and
square-integrable, while $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_k\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]=0$,
so
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[T_n\bigm|\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\bigr]
=T_{n-1}+S_{n-1}\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_n]=T_{n-1}.
\]
Thus $(T_n)$ is a martingale and $\mathbb{E}[T_n]=0$. (This is
compatible with $\mathbb{E}[S_n^2]=n$.)

The increments $\Delta T_k=S_{k-1}\varepsilon_k$ are orthogonal in
$L^2$, and $\varepsilon_k^2=1$, so
\[
\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]
=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}[S_{k-1}^2]
=\sum_{k=1}^n(k-1)
=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}j
=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]
At $n=4$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]=\frac{4\cdot 3}{2}=6.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=n(n-1)/2,\quad\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]=6}.
\]

Because $S_n^2=n+2T_n$ and $n$ is deterministic,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)
=4\operatorname{Var}(T_n)
=4\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]
=2n(n-1).
\]
At $n=4$ one obtains $\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)=2\cdot 4\cdot 3=24$.
The predictable bracket of $T$ is
\[
\langle T\rangle_n
=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}\bigl[(S_{k-1}\varepsilon_k)^2\bigm|\mathcal{F}_{k-1}\bigr]
=\sum_{k=1}^n S_{k-1}^2,
\]
and taking expectations recovers the same ledger
$\mathbb{E}[\langle T\rangle_n]=n(n-1)/2$.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)=2n(n-1),\;
\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)=24,\;
\mathbb{E}[\langle T\rangle_n]=n(n-1)/2}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $2$ in the binomial expansion.
Sentence (ii) confuses $\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)$ with
$\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]$ and reports $6$ instead of $24$. The
construction is a predictable random-walk transform audit; it is
not optional stopping of a fair game, an $L^1$-projection
characterisation of conditional expectation, or a tail-event
$0$–$1$ law.

graderFixtures.proofText: The identity $S_n^2=n+2T_n$ holds pathwise and $T$ is a martingale. One has $\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=n(n-1)/2$ so $\mathbb{E}[T_4^2]=6$, $\operatorname{Var}(S_n^2)=2n(n-1)$ so $\operatorname{Var}(S_4^2)=24$, and $\mathbb{E}[\langle T\rangle_n]=n(n-1)/2$ with $\langle T\rangle_n=\sum S_{k-1}^2$.
The binomial expansion gives S_n^2=n+T_n with no factor 2. I do not report S_n^2=n+2T_n.
Var(S_4^2) equals E[T_4^2]=6. I never obtain Var(S_4^2)=24.

MTP:010525.title: Bernoulli(1/(k+1)) compensator has A_3=13/12, EN_3=13/12, and bracket/variance 95/144, not the mean
MTP:010525.objective: For independent X_k ~ Bernoulli(1/(k+1)), N=sum X, A=sum 1/(k+1), and M=N-A, prove A_3=13/12, EN_3=13/12, that M is a bounded-increment martingale, and that the predictable bracket expectation equals Var(N_3)=sum p(1-p)=95/144. Never confuse A with the variance.
MTP:010525.statement:
Let $(X_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables
with $\mathbb{P}(X_k=1)=p_k=1/(k+1)$, and define
\[
N_n=\sum_{k=1}^n X_k,\qquad
A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n p_k=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{k+1},\qquad
M_n=N_n-A_n.
\]
Do not replace the compensator ledger by optional stopping of a
fair game at a sure win, by a tail-event $0$–$1$ argument, or by an
abstract $L^1$-projection characterisation of conditional
expectation.

1. Prove that $A$ is the predictable compensator of $N$, that $M$
   is a martingale, and that the increments of $M$ are uniformly
   bounded. Evaluate the sample
   \[
   A_3=\frac{13}{12},\qquad
   \mathbb{E}[N_3]=\frac{13}{12}.
   \]

2. Identify the predictable quadratic variation
   \[
   \langle M\rangle_n=\sum_{k=1}^n p_k(1-p_k)
   \]
   and prove
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_3]
   =\operatorname{Var}(N_3)
   =\operatorname{Var}(M_3)
   =\sum_{k=1}^3 p_k(1-p_k)
   =\frac{95}{144}.
   \]

3. Explain why $A_3=13/12$ must not be confused with the variance
   $95/144$: the compensator tracks the mean, while the bracket
   tracks $\sum p(1-p)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the compensator is the sum of the
   Bernoulli variances, so $A_3=95/144$ rather than $13/12$”;
   (ii) “because $N_3$ is a count, $\operatorname{Var}(N_3)$ equals
   the mean $13/12$ rather than $95/144$.”
permittedResults: $A_3=1/2+1/3+1/4=13/12$ and $\mathbb{E}[N_3]=A_3$. Independence makes $M=N-A$ a martingale with $|\Delta M_k|\le 1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Sum the deterministic means 1/2+1/3+1/4 to obtain the compensator, then subtract it from N to form the martingale.
Evaluate the three Bernoulli variances over denominator 144 and refuse any identification of sum p with sum p(1-p).

milestones.criterion: Produces A_3=13/12, EN_3=13/12, and the bounded-increment martingale M=N-A.
Reports E[<M>_3]=Var(N_3)=sum p(1-p)=95/144 and separates the mean compensator from the bracket.
Rejects A_3=95/144 or Var(N_3)=13/12, and refuses reserved optional-stopping, tail-event, or projection substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the compensator is the sum of the Bernoulli variances, so A_3=95/144 rather than 13/12.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned mean compensator A_3=13/12 is replaced by the bracket and the mean/variance distinction is lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims Var(N_3) equals the mean 13/12 instead of 95/144, imposing a Poisson mean-variance identity.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned bracket/variance ledger 95/144 is replaced by the compensator value.

hintTree.content: Write $A_3=1/2+1/3+1/4$ over the common denominator $12$. Predictability of $A$ is immediate because the $p_k$ are deterministic.
The Bernoulli variance identity $p(1-p)$ at $p=1/2,1/3,1/4$ produces $1/4$, $2/9$, and $3/16$. Clear the denominator $144$.
The compensator $A$ equals the mean of $N$. The bracket equals the variance of $N$. These two sequences agree only if $p_k(1-p_k)=p_k$ for every $k$, which fails here.

MTP:010525.canonicalSolution:
Each $p_k=1/(k+1)$ is deterministic, so $A$ is predictable
(even deterministic) and
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[N_n\bigm|\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\bigr]
=N_{n-1}+p_n
=A_n+M_{n-1}.
\]
Hence $M=N-A$ is a martingale. The increments satisfy
\[
\bigl|\Delta M_k\bigr|
=\lvert X_k-p_k\rvert
\le 1,
\]
so $M$ has uniformly bounded increments. The $n=3$ compensator is
\[
A_3
=\frac12+\frac13+\frac14
=\frac{6+4+3}{12}
=\frac{13}{12}.
\]
Taking expectations of the martingale $M$ yields
$\mathbb{E}[N_3]=\mathbb{E}[A_3]=13/12$.
\[
\boxed{A_3=\mathbb{E}[N_3]=13/12}.
\]

Independence gives
\[
\langle M\rangle_n
=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X_k-p_k)^2\bigm|\mathcal{F}_{k-1}\bigr]
=\sum_{k=1}^n p_k(1-p_k),
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_n]
=\operatorname{Var}(M_n)
=\operatorname{Var}(N_n)
=\sum_{k=1}^n p_k(1-p_k).
\]
The $n=3$ terms are
\begin{align*}
p_1(1-p_1)&=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14=\frac{36}{144},\\
p_2(1-p_2)&=\frac13\cdot\frac23=\frac29=\frac{32}{144},\\
p_3(1-p_3)&=\frac14\cdot\frac34=\frac{3}{16}=\frac{27}{144},
\end{align*}
which sum to $95/144$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_3]=\operatorname{Var}(N_3)=95/144}.
\]

The two numerical ledgers $13/12$ and $95/144$ are distinct:
$A$ is the mean compensator $\sum p_k$, while the bracket is
$\sum p_k(1-p_k)$. Equality would require $p_k=0$ for every $k$
(since $p_k(1-p_k)=p_k$ iff $p_k=0$), which fails for
$p_k=1/(k+1)$. In particular one must not
treat $N$ as if it were Poisson with variance equal to its mean.
\[
\boxed{A\text{ is the mean, not the variance}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the compensator by the bracket and reports
$A_3=95/144$. Sentence (ii) imposes a Poisson mean-variance
identity and reports $\operatorname{Var}(N_3)=13/12$. The
construction is an inhomogeneous Bernoulli compensator audit; it is
not optional stopping of a fair game, a tail-event $0$–$1$ law, or
an $L^1$-projection characterisation of conditional expectation.

graderFixtures.proofText: $A_3=\mathbb{E}[N_3]=13/12$ and $M=N-A$ is a martingale with bounded increments. The predictable bracket satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_3]=\operatorname{Var}(N_3)=\sum p(1-p)=95/144$. The compensator $A$ is not the variance.
The compensator is the sum of the Bernoulli variances, so A_3=95/144. I do not report A_3=13/12.
Because N_3 is a count, Var(N_3) equals the mean 13/12. I never obtain Var(N_3)=95/144.

MTP:010527.title: Fair-walk L_n(ln 2)=2^{S_n}/(5/4)^n is a mean-1 martingale with Q(+)=4/5 and E_P L_n^2=(34/25)^n
MTP:010527.objective: For the fair walk S_n prove L_n(theta)=exp(theta S_n)/(cosh theta)^n is a mean-1 martingale, and at theta=ln 2 obtain cosh=5/4, tilted law Q(+)=4/5, Q(-)=1/5, drift 3/5, and E_P L_n^2=(34/25)^n from cosh(2 theta)=17/8.
MTP:010527.statement:
Let $(X_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be i.i.d. with
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_1=+1)=\mathbb{P}(X_1=-1)=\tfrac12,
\]
and write $S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n$ for the associated fair simple random
walk (with $S_0=0$). For $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$ define
\[
L_n(\theta)
=\frac{e^{\theta S_n}}{(\cosh\theta)^n},\qquad n\ge 0
\]
(with the convention $L_0\equiv 1$). Do not replace the
likelihood-ratio martingale and its exponential change of measure
by optional stopping of a fair game at a sure win, by a
conditional-expectation projection identity in $L^1$ versus $L^2$,
or by inverse-image measurability of a random variable.

1. Prove that $(L_n(\theta))_{n\ge 0}$ is a nonnegative martingale
   with respect to $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, and that
   $\mathbb{E}[L_n(\theta)]=1$ for every $n$.

2. Let $\mathbb{Q}_\theta$ be the probability on $\mathcal{F}_n$ with
   density $L_n(\theta)$ relative to $\mathbb{P}$. Prove that the
   increments remain i.i.d. under $\mathbb{Q}_\theta$, and evaluate
   the one-step law at the sample $\theta=\ln 2$:
   \[
   \cosh(\ln 2)=\frac54,\qquad
   \mathbb{Q}(X_1=+1)=\frac45,\qquad
   \mathbb{Q}(X_1=-1)=\frac15,\qquad
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X_1]=\frac35.
   \]

3. Prove
   \[
   \cosh(2\ln 2)=\frac{17}{8}
   \]
   and deduce the second-moment formula
   \[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\bigl[L_n(\ln 2)^2\bigr]
   =\Bigl(\frac{34}{25}\Bigr)^n.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\cosh(\ln 2)=3/2$, so the tilted
   probabilities are $\mathbb{Q}(+)=2/3$ and $\mathbb{Q}(-)=1/3$
   with drift $1/3$, rather than $5/4$, $4/5$, $1/5$, and
   $3/5$”; (ii) “the second moment is
   $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[L_n^2]=(\cosh 2\theta)^n=(17/8)^n$,
   so it is not $(34/25)^n$.”
permittedResults: $\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta X_1}]=\cosh\theta$, so $\mathbb{E}[L_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=L_n$ and $\mathbb{E}[L_n]=1$. At $\theta=\ln 2$ one has $\cosh\theta=5/4$, $\mathbb{Q}(+)=4/5$, $\mathbb{Q}(-)=1/5$, and drift $3/5$.
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[L_n(\theta)^2]=(\cosh(2\theta)/(\cosh\theta)^2)^n$. At $\theta=\ln 2$ one has $\cosh(2\theta)=17/8$ and $\cosh(2\theta)/(\cosh\theta)^2=34/25$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor L_{n+1}/L_n as the independent mean-one increment e^{theta X}/cosh theta, then read the tilted atoms from E_P[1_{X=+1} L_1].
Identify E_P[L_n^2] with (cosh(2 theta)/(cosh theta)^2)^n and insert theta=ln 2 using cosh(ln 2)=5/4 and cosh(2 ln 2)=17/8.

milestones.criterion: Produces the mean-1 martingale identity for L_n(theta) and the sample tilt cosh(ln 2)=5/4, Q(+)=4/5, Q(-)=1/5, drift 3/5.
Reports cosh(2 ln 2)=17/8 and E_P[L_n(ln 2)^2]=(34/25)^n.
Rejects the 3/2-cosh / 2/3-tilt ledger or the omitted-denominator second moment (17/8)^n, and refuses reserved optional-stopping, projection, or inverse-image substitutions.

commonErrors.consequence: The assigned change-of-measure ledger at theta=ln 2 is replaced by an inconsistent hyperbolic-cosine evaluation.
