hintTree.content: Compute $\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta X_1}]=(e^{\theta}+e^{-\theta})/2=\cosh\theta$. The one-step factor of $L_n$ is then mean-one and independent of $\mathcal{F}_n$.
The tilted atom $\mathbb{Q}(X_1=+1)$ is $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[1_{\{X_1=+1\}}L_1]=(1/2)e^{\theta}/\cosh\theta$. Insert $\theta=\ln 2$.
Write $L_n^2=e^{2\theta S_n}/(\cosh\theta)^{2n}$ and take $\mathbb{P}$-expectation to obtain $(\cosh(2\theta)/(\cosh\theta)^2)^n$. Then use $\cosh(2\ln 2)=17/8$ and $(5/4)^2=25/16$.

MTP:010527.canonicalSolution:
The increment Laplace transform is
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\theta X_1}\bigr]
=\frac12\bigl(e^{\theta}+e^{-\theta}\bigr)
=\cosh\theta.
\]
Independence of the increments therefore yields
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\theta S_n}\bigr]
=(\cosh\theta)^n,
\]
so $\mathbb{E}[L_n(\theta)]=1$. Moreover
\[
L_{n+1}(\theta)
=L_n(\theta)\cdot\frac{e^{\theta X_{n+1}}}{\cosh\theta},
\]
and $e^{\theta X_{n+1}}/\cosh\theta$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_n$
with mean $1$. Hence
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[L_{n+1}(\theta)\mid\mathcal{F}_n\bigr]
=L_n(\theta).
\]
Nonnegativity is obvious. Thus $(L_n(\theta))_{n\ge 0}$ is a
nonnegative mean-one martingale.
\[
\boxed{L_n(\theta)\ \text{is a mean-1 martingale}}.
\]

On $\mathcal{F}_n$ define $\mathbb{Q}_\theta$ by
$d\mathbb{Q}_\theta/d\mathbb{P}=L_n(\theta)$. The increments remain
i.i.d. under $\mathbb{Q}_\theta$ because $L_n$ is a product of
identical one-step factors. The one-step atoms are
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{Q}_\theta(X_1=+1)
&=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\bigl[1_{\{X_1=+1\}}L_1(\theta)\bigr]
=\frac12\cdot\frac{e^{\theta}}{\cosh\theta}
=\frac{e^{\theta}}{e^{\theta}+e^{-\theta}},\\
\mathbb{Q}_\theta(X_1=-1)
&=\frac{e^{-\theta}}{e^{\theta}+e^{-\theta}}.
\end{align*}
At the sample $\theta=\ln 2$ one has $e^{\theta}=2$ and
$e^{-\theta}=1/2$, so
\[
\cosh(\ln 2)
=\frac{2+1/2}{2}
=\frac54.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb{Q}(X_1=+1)
=\frac12\cdot\frac{2}{5/4}
=\frac45,\qquad
\mathbb{Q}(X_1=-1)
=\frac12\cdot\frac{1/2}{5/4}
=\frac15,
\]
and the tilted drift is
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[X_1]
=\frac45\cdot 1+\frac15\cdot(-1)
=\frac35.
\]
\[
\boxed{\cosh(\ln 2)=5/4,\;\mathbb{Q}(+)=4/5,\;\mathbb{Q}(-)=1/5,\;\text{drift }3/5}.
\]

For the second moment write
\[
L_n(\theta)^2
=\frac{e^{2\theta S_n}}{(\cosh\theta)^{2n}}.
\]
Taking $\mathbb{P}$-expectation and using
$\mathbb{E}[e^{2\theta S_n}]=(\cosh(2\theta))^n$ produces
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\bigl[L_n(\theta)^2\bigr]
=\Bigl(\frac{\cosh(2\theta)}{(\cosh\theta)^2}\Bigr)^n.
\]
At $\theta=\ln 2$ one has $2\theta=\ln 4$, so
\[
\cosh(2\ln 2)
=\frac{4+1/4}{2}
=\frac{17}{8}.
\]
The denominator is $(\cosh(\ln 2))^2=(5/4)^2=25/16$, and
\[
\frac{17/8}{25/16}
=\frac{17}{8}\cdot\frac{16}{25}
=\frac{34}{25}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\bigl[L_n(\ln 2)^2\bigr]
=\Bigl(\frac{34}{25}\Bigr)^n.
\]
\[
\boxed{\cosh(2\ln 2)=17/8,\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[L_n^2]=(34/25)^n}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\cosh(\ln 2)=5/4$ by $3/2$ and therefore
destroys the tilted atoms $4/5$, $1/5$ and the drift $3/5$.
Sentence (ii) drops the factor $(\cosh\theta)^{-2n}$ and reports
$(17/8)^n$ instead of $(34/25)^n$. The construction is an
exponential likelihood-ratio / change-of-measure audit for a fair
walk; it is not optional stopping of a fair game at a sure win, a
conditional-expectation projection identity, or an inverse-image
measurability argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: The process $L_n(\theta)=e^{\theta S_n}/(\cosh\theta)^n$ is a mean-one martingale. At $\theta=\ln 2$ one has $\cosh\theta=5/4$, $\mathbb{Q}(+)=4/5$, $\mathbb{Q}(-)=1/5$, drift $3/5$, $\cosh(2\theta)=17/8$, and $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[L_n^2]=(34/25)^n$.
I take cosh(ln 2)=3/2, so the tilted probabilities are Q(+)=2/3 and Q(-)=1/3 with drift 1/3. I do not report cosh=5/4, Q(+)=4/5, Q(-)=1/5, or drift 3/5.
The second moment is E_P[L_n^2]=(cosh 2 theta)^n=(17/8)^n. I never obtain (34/25)^n.

MTP:010530.title: Critical binary branching has offspring PGF (1+s^2)/2, Z_n a mean-1 variance-n martingale, q=1, and Z_2 masses 5/8,1/4,1/8
MTP:010530.objective: For Z_0=1 and critical binary offspring {0,2} each of probability 1/2, prove the offspring PGF is (1+s^2)/2 with mean 1 and variance 1, that Z_n is a martingale with E=1 and Var=n, that extinction is the fixed point q=1, and that Z_2 has masses P0=5/8, P2=1/4, P4=1/8 with mean 1 and variance 2.
MTP:010530.statement:
Let $(Z_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a Galton–Watson process with $Z_0=1$ and
offspring law
\[
\mathbb{P}(\xi=0)=\mathbb{P}(\xi=2)=\tfrac12.
\]
Write $f(s)=\mathbb{E}[s^\xi]$ for the offspring probability
generating function. Do not replace the generation-size martingale
and its extinction fixed point by optional stopping of a fair game
at a sure win, by a Kolmogorov $0$–$1$ tail event, or by a
conditional-expectation projection identity in $L^1$ versus $L^2$.

1. Prove
   \[
   f(s)=\frac{1+s^2}{2},\qquad
   \mathbb{E}[\xi]=1,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(\xi)=1.
   \]

2. Prove that $(Z_n)_{n\ge 0}$ is a martingale with
   $\mathbb{E}[Z_n]=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z_n)=n$ for every
   $n\ge 0$. Identify the extinction probability $q$ as the smallest
   root in $[0,1]$ of $q=f(q)$, and prove $q=1$.

3. Compute the generation-$2$ law
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)=\frac58,\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(Z_2=2)=\frac14,\qquad
   \mathbb{P}(Z_2=4)=\frac18,
   \]
   and verify $\mathbb{E}[Z_2]=1$ together with
   $\operatorname{Var}(Z_2)=2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the extinction probability is the
   spurious interior root $q=1/2$, so extinction is not certain”;
   (ii) “$Z_2=0$ occurs only through $Z_1=0$, so
   $\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)=1/2$ rather than $5/8$.”
permittedResults: $f(s)=(1+s^2)/2$, $f'(s)=s$, $f'(1)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(\xi)=f''(1)+f'(1)-(f'(1))^2=1$. The fixed-point equation $q=(1+q^2)/2$ rearranges to $(q-1)^2=0$, so $q=1$.
The iterate $f_2(s)=f(f(s))=5/8+(1/4)s^2+(1/8)s^4$ yields the masses $5/8$, $1/4$, $1/8$. Then $\mathbb{E}[Z_2]=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z_2)=2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read offspring mean and variance from f'(1) and f''(1), then use the branching property to obtain the martingale and the critical variance formula.
Iterate the PGF once, or condition on Z_1 in {0,2}, to extract the generation-2 masses and check mean 1 and variance 2.

milestones.criterion: Produces f(s)=(1+s^2)/2, offspring mean 1 and variance 1, the martingale identities E[Z_n]=1 and Var(Z_n)=n, and extinction q=1.
Reports the Z_2 masses 5/8, 1/4, 1/8 together with E[Z_2]=1 and Var(Z_2)=2.
Rejects an interior extinction root q=1/2 or the claim P(Z_2=0)=1/2, and refuses reserved optional-stopping, tail-event, or projection substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims the extinction probability is the spurious interior root q=1/2, denying certain extinction q=1.
commonErrors.consequence: The fixed-point identity (q-1)^2=0 and the critical extinction ledger q=1 are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims P(Z_2=0)=1/2 by counting only the path Z_1=0, instead of the full mass 5/8.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned generation-2 law 5/8, 1/4, 1/8 and the variance check Var(Z_2)=2 become inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Write $f(s)=(1/2)+(1/2)s^2$. Differentiate once and twice at $s=1$ to read the offspring mean and variance.
The branching property gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=Z_n\cdot\mathbb{E}[\xi]$. For extinction solve $q=(1+q^2)/2$ on $[0,1]$.
Either iterate the PGF or condition on $Z_1\in\{0,2\}$. The double-death path $Z_1=2$ and both children barren contributes an extra $1/8$ to $\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)$.

MTP:010530.canonicalSolution:
The offspring generating function is
\[
f(s)
=\frac12\cdot s^0+\frac12\cdot s^2
=\frac{1+s^2}{2}.
\]
Differentiating gives $f'(s)=s$ and $f''(s)=1$, so
\[
\mathbb{E}[\xi]=f'(1)=1
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\xi)
=f''(1)+f'(1)-\bigl(f'(1)\bigr)^2
=1+1-1
=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{f(s)=(1+s^2)/2,\;\mathbb{E}\xi=1,\;\operatorname{Var}\xi=1}.
\]

The branching property yields
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]
=Z_n\cdot\mathbb{E}[\xi]
=Z_n,
\]
so $(Z_n)$ is a martingale. In particular $\mathbb{E}[Z_n]=Z_0=1$.
The critical finite-variance formula (or an induction on the
conditional variance decomposition) gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z_n)=n\operatorname{Var}(\xi)=n.
\]
Extinction solves $q=f(q)$:
\[
q=\frac{1+q^2}{2}
\iff
q^2-2q+1=0
\iff
(q-1)^2=0.
\]
The only root in $[0,1]$ is $q=1$. (Criticality with
$\mathbb{P}(\xi=1)=0<1$ independently forces certain extinction.)
\[
\boxed{Z_n\text{ is a martingale, }\mathbb{E}Z_n=1,\;\operatorname{Var}Z_n=n,\;q=1}.
\]

The generation-$2$ PGF is the iterate
\begin{align*}
f_2(s)
&=f\bigl(f(s)\bigr)
=\frac{1+\bigl((1+s^2)/2\bigr)^2}{2}
=\frac58+\frac14 s^2+\frac18 s^4.
\end{align*}
Hence
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)=\frac58,\qquad
\mathbb{P}(Z_2=2)=\frac14,\qquad
\mathbb{P}(Z_2=4)=\frac18.
\]
The same masses arise by conditioning:
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)
=\mathbb{P}(Z_1=0)+\mathbb{P}(Z_1=2)\cdot\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^2
=\tfrac12+\tfrac18
=\tfrac58.
\]
The mean and variance are
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z_2]
=2\cdot\frac14+4\cdot\frac18
=1,
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z_2^2]
=4\cdot\frac14+16\cdot\frac18
=3,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z_2)=3-1=2,
\]
in agreement with $\operatorname{Var}(Z_2)=2\cdot 1$.
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)=5/8,\;\mathbb{P}(Z_2=2)=1/4,\;\mathbb{P}(Z_2=4)=1/8,\;\mathbb{E}Z_2=1,\;\operatorname{Var}Z_2=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) invents an interior extinction root $1/2$ and
contradicts $(q-1)^2=0$. Sentence (ii) forgets the double-death
path through $Z_1=2$ and reports $\mathbb{P}(Z_2=0)=1/2$ instead
of $5/8$. The construction is a critical binary branching
martingale audit; it is not optional stopping of a fair game at a
sure win, a tail-event $0$–$1$ law, or an $L^1$/$L^2$ projection
identity. Certain extinction with $\mathbb{E}[Z_n]=1$ is compatible
because the martingale is not uniformly integrable: at large finite
times its expectation is carried by increasingly rare survival events
on which $Z_n$ is large, even though eternal survival has probability
zero.

graderFixtures.proofText: The offspring PGF is $(1+s^2)/2$ with mean $1$ and variance $1$. The generation sizes form a martingale with $\mathbb{E}[Z_n]=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z_n)=n$, and extinction is $q=1$. The generation-$2$ masses are $5/8$, $1/4$, $1/8$, with mean $1$ and variance $2$.
The extinction probability is the spurious interior root q=1/2, so extinction is not certain. I do not report q=1.
Z_2=0 occurs only through Z_1=0, so P(Z_2=0)=1/2. I never obtain P(Z_2=0)=5/8.

MTP:010626.title: Moving atoms delta_{1/n}->delta_0 pass bounded continuous tests, fail the CDF at 0, and have W_p=1/n
MTP:010626.objective: For mu_n=delta_{1/n} prove weak convergence to delta_0 via bounded continuous functions, CDF convergence at every x!=0 but F_n(0)=0 versus F(0)=1, that {0} and (0,infty) are not continuity sets, the open-set probabilities 1 versus 0, W_p=1/n for all p>=1, and the correct Portmanteau open/closed inequalities.
MTP:010626.statement:
Let $\mu_n=\delta_{1/n}$ and $\mu=\delta_0$ be Dirac measures on
$\mathbb{R}$, and write $F_n$ and $F$ for their distribution
functions (right-continuous, $F_n(x)=1_{\{1/n\le x\}}$,
$F(x)=1_{\{0\le x\}}$). Do not replace the moving-atom Portmanteau
ledger by a characteristic-function central-limit argument, by an
abstract comparison of almost-sure / $L^1$ / $L^2$ modes repaired
by uniform integrability, or by a tail-event $0$–$1$ law.

1. Prove that $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ by showing
   $\int f\,d\mu_n=f(1/n)\to f(0)=\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded
   continuous $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$.

2. Prove that $F_n(x)\to F(x)$ for every $x\neq 0$, while
   $F_n(0)=0$ for all $n$ and $F(0)=1$. Conclude that $\{0\}$ and
   $(0,\infty)$ are not continuity sets of $\mu$, with
   \[
   \mu_n(\{0\})=0\neq 1=\mu(\{0\}),\qquad
   \mu_n\bigl((0,\infty)\bigr)=1\neq 0=\mu\bigl((0,\infty)\bigr).
   \]

3. State the Portmanteau open-set and closed-set inequalities and
   verify them on $G=(0,\infty)$ and $F=\{0\}$:
   \[
   \liminf_n\mu_n(G)=1\ge 0=\mu(G),\qquad
   \limsup_n\mu_n(F)=0\le 1=\mu(F).
   \]
   Prove that the $p$-Wasserstein distance satisfies
   $W_p(\mu_n,\mu)=1/n$ for every $p\ge 1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “distribution functions always
   converge at every $x$, so $F_n(0)\to F(0)$ and the atom
   $\{0\}$ is a continuity set”; (ii) “because $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$,
   one has $\mu_n((0,\infty))\to\mu((0,\infty))$, so the open ray
   is a continuity set and the probabilities $1$ and $0$ agree in
   the limit.”
permittedResults: Bounded continuous tests give $f(1/n)\to f(0)$, so $\delta_{1/n}\Rightarrow\delta_0$. The CDF converges off $\{0\}$, but $F_n(0)=0\neq 1=F(0)$.
$\partial\{0\}=\partial(0,\infty)=\{0\}$, so neither set is a continuity set. Portmanteau still yields $\liminf\mu_n((0,\infty))\ge\mu((0,\infty))$ and $\limsup\mu_n(\{0\})\le\mu(\{0\})$. $W_p=1/n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Test bounded continuous functions at the moving point 1/n, then compare CDFs on (-infty,0), {0}, and (0,infty).
Read continuity sets from whether 0 lies on the topological boundary, and compute W_p as the distance between the two atoms.

milestones.criterion: Produces weak convergence via bounded continuous tests and the CDF ledger F_n(x)->F(x) for x!=0 with F_n(0)=0 versus F(0)=1.
Reports that {0} and (0,infty) are not continuity sets, the Portmanteau inequalities liminf mu_n(G)>=mu(G) and limsup mu_n(F)<=mu(F), and W_p=1/n.
Rejects CDF convergence at 0 or open-ray probability convergence, and refuses reserved CLT, UI-mode, or tail-event substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims distribution functions converge at every x, so F_n(0)->F(0) and {0} is a continuity set.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned discontinuity F_n(0)=0 versus F(0)=1 and the non-continuity of {0} are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims mu_n((0,infty))->mu((0,infty)), treating the open ray as a continuity set and forcing 1 to converge to 0.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned Portmanteau strict inequality on (0,infty) is replaced by an illegal setwise limit.

hintTree.content: A bounded continuous function is continuous at $0$, so $f(1/n)\to f(0)$. This is the definition of weak convergence for these two Diracs.
For $x<0$ both CDFs vanish. For $x>0$ one has $1/n\le x$ for all large $n$. At $x=0$ the moving atom remains strictly positive.
The only coupling of $\delta_{1/n}$ and $\delta_0$ is the product (or any joining of the two points), so $W_p(\mu_n,\mu)=1/n$.

MTP:010626.canonicalSolution:
If $f$ is bounded and continuous, then
\[
\int f\,d\mu_n=f\bigl(\tfrac1n\bigr)\to f(0)=\int f\,d\mu
\]
by continuity at $0$. Thus $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$.
\[
\boxed{\delta_{1/n}\Rightarrow\delta_0\text{ via bounded continuous }f}.
\]

The distribution functions are $F_n(x)=1_{\{1/n\le x\}}$ and
$F(x)=1_{\{0\le x\}}$. If $x<0$ then $F_n(x)=F(x)=0$. If $x>0$ then
$1/n\le x$ for all $n\ge 1/x$, so $F_n(x)=1=F(x)$ eventually. At
the remaining point,
\[
F_n(0)=0\qquad\text{for every }n,\qquad F(0)=1.
\]
The topological boundaries are $\partial\{0\}=\{0\}$ and
$\partial(0,\infty)=\{0\}$, and $\mu(\{0\})=1\neq 0$, so neither
$\{0\}$ nor $(0,\infty)$ is a $\mu$-continuity set. Directly,
\[
\mu_n(\{0\})=0\neq 1=\mu(\{0\}),\qquad
\mu_n\bigl((0,\infty)\bigr)=1\neq 0=\mu\bigl((0,\infty)\bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{F_n(x)\to F(x)\text{ iff }x\neq 0;\ \{0\},(0,\infty)\text{ are not continuity sets}}.
\]

Portmanteau's inequalities nevertheless hold. For the open ray
$G=(0,\infty)$,
\[
\liminf_n\mu_n(G)=1\ge 0=\mu(G),
\]
and for the closed singleton $F=\{0\}$,
\[
\limsup_n\mu_n(F)=0\le 1=\mu(F).
\]
The inequalities are strict; weak convergence does not upgrade them
to equalities on non-continuity sets. Finally, the unique coupling
of two Dirac masses yields
\[
W_p(\mu_n,\mu)
=\bigl(\lvert\tfrac1n-0\rvert^p\bigr)^{1/p}
=\frac1n
\qquad\text{for every }p\ge 1.
\]
\[
\boxed{W_p(\delta_{1/n},\delta_0)=1/n,\quad
\liminf\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G),\ \limsup\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces CDF convergence at the discontinuity point $0$
and treats $\{0\}$ as a continuity set. Sentence (ii) upgrades weak
convergence to convergence of open-ray probabilities and treats
$(0,\infty)$ as a continuity set. The construction is a Portmanteau
moving-atom audit; it is not a characteristic-function CLT, an
abstract mode-arrow / uniform-integrability comparison, or a
tail-event $0$–$1$ law.

graderFixtures.proofText: Bounded continuous tests give $\delta_{1/n}\Rightarrow\delta_0$. The CDFs converge at every $x\neq 0$, but $F_n(0)=0\neq 1=F(0)$. Neither $\{0\}$ nor $(0,\infty)$ is a continuity set. Portmanteau yields $\liminf\mu_n((0,\infty))\ge\mu((0,\infty))$ and $\limsup\mu_n(\{0\})\le\mu(\{0\})$, and $W_p(\mu_n,\mu)=1/n$ for all $p\ge 1$.
Distribution functions always converge at every x, so F_n(0)->F(0) and the atom {0} is a continuity set. I do not report F_n(0)=0 versus F(0)=1.

Because mu_n=>mu, one has mu_n((0,infty))->mu((0,infty)), so the open ray is a continuity set and the probabilities 1 and 0 agree in the limit. I never obtain that (0,infty) fails to be a continuity set.

MTP:010628.title: Bin(n,2/n) has PGF limit exp(2(s-1)), mean 2, variance 2(1-2/n), and second factorial moment 4(1-1/n)
MTP:010628.objective: For X_n~Bin(n,2/n) prove the PGF tends to exp(2(s-1)), each fixed-k mass tends to e^{-2} 2^k/k!, the mean is 2, the variance is 2(1-2/n), and the second factorial moment is 4(1-1/n), and refuse a Gaussian CLT substitution.
MTP:010628.statement:
Let $X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,2/n)$ for integers $n\ge 3$. Do
not replace the rare-event Poisson limit by a Gaussian central
limit theorem whose characteristic function is expanded to second
order and checked for continuity at zero, by a modes-of-convergence
repair via uniform integrability, or by a tail-event $0$–$1$ law.

1. For the probability generating function
   $G_n(s)=\mathbb{E}[s^{X_n}]$ prove
   \[
   G_n(s)
   =\Bigl(1+\frac{2}{n}(s-1)\Bigr)^n
   \longrightarrow\exp\bigl(2(s-1)\bigr)
   \]
   pointwise for every real $s$, and identify the limit as the PGF
   of $\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$.

2. For each fixed integer $k\ge 0$ prove
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(X_n=k)
   \longrightarrow e^{-2}\,\frac{2^k}{k!}.
   \]

3. Compute the exact moment ledger
   \[
   \mathbb{E}[X_n]=2,\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(X_n)=2\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{n}\Bigr),\qquad
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[X_n(X_n-1)\bigr]
   =4\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n}\Bigr).
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “after no further scaling, $X_n$
   converges in law to $\mathcal{N}(2,2)$ by the classical CLT,
   so the limit is Gaussian rather than $\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$”;
   (ii) “the second factorial moment is already the Poisson value
   $4$, so it is not $4(1-1/n)$.”
permittedResults: $G_n(s)=(1+(2/n)(s-1))^n\to\exp(2(s-1))$, the PGF of $\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$. Pointwise PGF convergence yields $\mathbb{P}(X_n=k)\to e^{-2}2^k/k!$.
$\mathbb{E}[X_n]=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=2(1-2/n)$, and $\mathbb{E}[X_n(X_n-1)]=n(n-1)(2/n)^2=4(1-1/n)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pass to the limit in the exact binomial PGF (1+(2/n)(s-1))^n and read Poisson(2) masses from the discrete continuity theorem.
Evaluate the falling-factorial identities n(n-1)...(n-k+1)p^k at p=2/n without taking n to infinity first.

milestones.criterion: Produces G_n(s)->exp(2(s-1)) and the Poisson(2) masses e^{-2} 2^k/k!.
Reports the exact ledger E[X_n]=2, Var=2(1-2/n), and E[X_n(X_n-1)]=4(1-1/n).
Rejects a Gaussian N(2,2) limit or a frozen second factorial moment 4, and refuses reserved CLT-characteristic-function, UI, or tail-event substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that X_n converges in law to N(2,2) by the classical CLT, denying the Poisson(2) rare-event limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned PGF limit exp(2(s-1)) and the Poisson masses e^{-2} 2^k/k! are replaced by a Gaussian CLT that the unscaled rare-event window does not support.

commonErrors.description: Claims the second factorial moment is already the Poisson value 4, instead of the exact binomial value 4(1-1/n).
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity E[X_n(X_n-1)]=4(1-1/n) is lost.

hintTree.content: Write the binomial PGF as $(1-p+ps)^n$ and substitute $p=2/n$. The standard limit $(1+a/n)^n\to e^a$ gives $\exp(2(s-1))$.
Extract the coefficient of $s^k$, or invoke the discrete continuity theorem from PGF convergence. The Poisson$(2)$ masses are $e^{-2}2^k/k!$.
Use $\mathbb{E}[X]=np$ and $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]=n(n-1)p^2$ exactly; do not pass to the $n\to\infty$ Poisson moments prematurely.

MTP:010628.canonicalSolution:
The binomial generating function with success probability $p=2/n$ is
\[
G_n(s)
=\bigl(1-p+ps\bigr)^n
=\Bigl(1+\frac{2}{n}(s-1)\Bigr)^n.
\]
The elementary limit $(1+a/n)^n\to e^a$ with $a=2(s-1)$ therefore
yields
\[
G_n(s)\longrightarrow\exp\bigl(2(s-1)\bigr)
\]
for every real $s$. The function $\exp(2(s-1))$ is the PGF of
$\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$.
\[
\boxed{G_n(s)\to\exp(2(s-1))}.
\]

The discrete continuity theorem (or direct extraction of
coefficients) therefore gives, for each fixed $k\ge 0$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(X_n=k)
&=\binom{n}{k}\Bigl(\frac{2}{n}\Bigr)^k\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{n}\Bigr)^{n-k}\\
&=\frac{2^k}{k!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k}
\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{n}\Bigr)^{n-k}\\
&\longrightarrow
\frac{2^k}{k!}\cdot 1\cdot e^{-2}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X_n=k)\to e^{-2}2^k/k!}.
\]

The exact moments are
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_n]=np=2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=np(1-p)=2\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{n}\Bigr),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[X_n(X_n-1)\bigr]
=n(n-1)p^2
=n(n-1)\cdot\frac{4}{n^2}
=4\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n}\Bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}X_n=2,\;\operatorname{Var}X_n=2(1-2/n),\;\mathbb{E}[X_n(X_n-1)]=4(1-1/n)}.
\]

The variance remains of order $1$, so $X_n$ is tight on the
integers about its mean $2$ and cannot satisfy a nondegenerate
Gaussian CLT on the unscaled line. The limit object is
$\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$, not $\mathcal{N}(2,2)$. Sentence (i)
imports a Gaussian CLT that the rare-event window does not support.
Sentence (ii) freezes the second factorial moment at the Poisson
value $4$ and discards the exact prefactor $1-1/n$. The
construction is a binomial-to-Poisson rare-event audit; it is not
a Gaussian characteristic-function CLT, a uniform-integrability
repair of $L^1$ convergence, or a tail-event $0$–$1$ argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: The PGF of $X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,2/n)$ tends to $\exp(2(s-1))$, each fixed-$k$ mass tends to $e^{-2}2^k/k!$, and the exact ledger is $\mathbb{E}[X_n]=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=2(1-2/n)$, $\mathbb{E}[X_n(X_n-1)]=4(1-1/n)$. The limit is $\operatorname{Poisson}(2)$, not $\mathcal{N}(2,2)$.
After no further scaling, X_n converges in law to N(2,2) by the classical CLT. I do not report a Poisson(2) limit or the PGF exp(2(s-1)).
The second factorial moment is already the Poisson value 4. I never obtain 4(1-1/n).

MTP:010631.title: Exp(1) maxima satisfy P(M_n-log n<=x)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n->exp(-e^{-x}) with F(0)=e^{-1} and median -ln ln 2
MTP:010631.objective: For iid Exp(1) variables and M_n=max prove P(M_n-log n<=x)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n tends to exp(-e^{-x}), evaluate the limit at 0 as e^{-1} and the median as -ln ln 2, and prove the log n centering is necessary for a nondegenerate tight limit.
MTP:010631.statement:
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. standard exponential random
variables, so $\mathbb{P}(X_1>t)=e^{-t}$ for $t>0$, and write
$M_n=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}$. Do not replace the extreme-value
Gumbel ledger by a Gaussian central limit theorem whose
characteristic function is expanded to second order and checked
for continuity at zero, by a modes-of-convergence repair via
uniform integrability, or by inverse-image measurability of a
random variable.

1. For every real $x$ and every $n>e^{-x}$ prove the exact identity
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le x)
   =\Bigl(1-\frac{e^{-x}}{n}\Bigr)^n,
   \]
   and deduce the Gumbel limit
   \[
   \mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le x)
   \longrightarrow\exp\bigl(-e^{-x}\bigr).
   \]

2. Evaluate the limiting distribution function at the origin:
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le 0)
   =e^{-1}.
   \]
   Prove that the median $m$ of the Gumbel law
   $F(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$ is
   \[
   m=-\ln\ln 2.
   \]

3. Prove that the centered family $(M_n-\log n)_{n\ge 1}$ is tight
   on $\mathbb{R}$, while the uncentered family $(M_n)_{n\ge 1}$
   is not tight and admits no nondegenerate weak limit on
   $\mathbb{R}$. In particular $M_n\to+\infty$ in probability.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$M_n$ itself converges weakly to the
   Gumbel law $\exp(-e^{-x})$, so no $\log n$ centering is
   required”; (ii) “the limiting median is $+\ln\ln 2$ rather than
   $-\ln\ln 2$.”
permittedResults: $\mathbb{P}(M_n\le x+\log n)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n\to\exp(-e^{-x})$ for each fixed $x$. At $x=0$ the limit is $e^{-1}$. The Gumbel median solves $\exp(-e^{-m})=1/2$, hence $m=-\ln\ln 2$.

For fixed $y\le 0$, $\mathbb{P}(M_n\le y)=0$; for fixed $y>0$, $\mathbb{P}(M_n\le y)=(1-e^{-y})^n\to 0$. Hence $M_n\to+\infty$ in probability and $(M_n)$ is not tight. The Gumbel limit is a proper cdf, so $(M_n-\log n)$ is tight.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rewrite P(M_n<=x+log n) using the exponential survival function e^{-(x+log n)}=e^{-x}/n and pass to the limit (1+a/n)^n.
Solve exp(-e^{-m})=1/2 for the median, then contrast tightness of the Gumbel limit with P(M_n<=y)->0 for each fixed y.

milestones.criterion: Produces the exact identity (1-e^{-x}/n)^n, the Gumbel limit exp(-e^{-x}), the origin value e^{-1}, and the median -ln ln 2.
Proves tightness of (M_n-log n) and that uncentered M_n tends to +infty in probability with no nondegenerate weak limit on R.
Rejects an uncentered Gumbel limit or a sign-flipped median +ln ln 2, and refuses reserved Gaussian-CLT, UI, or inverse-image substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that M_n itself converges weakly to the Gumbel law exp(-e^{-x}), denying the necessity of log n centering.
commonErrors.consequence: The required centered identity P(M_n-log n<=x)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n and the tightness ledger for the uncentered family are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims the Gumbel median is +ln ln 2 instead of -ln ln 2.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned median identity m=-ln ln 2 is replaced by the opposite sign.

hintTree.content: Write $\mathbb{P}(M_n\le x+\log n)=(1-e^{-(x+\log n)})^n$ and simplify the survival probability to $e^{-x}/n$.
The elementary limit $(1+a/n)^n\to e^a$ with $a=-e^{-x}$ produces the Gumbel cdf. Insert $x=0$ and solve $F(m)=1/2$.
Uncentered tightness fails because $\mathbb{P}(M_n\le y)\to 0$ for every fixed $y$. Centered tightness follows from the proper Gumbel limit (or by a direct $\varepsilon$-compact estimate).

MTP:010631.canonicalSolution:
For $n>e^{-x}$ the threshold $x+\log n$ is positive, and
\[
\mathbb{P}(M_n\le x+\log n)
=\bigl(1-e^{-(x+\log n)}\bigr)^n
=\Bigl(1-\frac{e^{-x}}{n}\Bigr)^n.
\]
The elementary limit $(1+a/n)^n\to e^a$ with $a=-e^{-x}$ therefore
yields
\[
\mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le x)
\longrightarrow\exp\bigl(-e^{-x}\bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le x)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n\to\exp(-e^{-x})}.
\]

At the origin one has $e^{-0}=1$, so the limiting value is
\[
\exp(-1)=e^{-1}.
\]
The Gumbel median $m$ solves
\[
\exp\bigl(-e^{-m}\bigr)=\frac12.
\]
Taking logarithms twice,
\[
-e^{-m}=\ln\tfrac12=-\ln 2
\implies
e^{-m}=\ln 2
\implies
m=-\ln\ln 2.
\]
\[
\boxed{F(0)=e^{-1},\;\text{median }=-\ln\ln 2}.
\]

The limiting cdf $F(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$ is a proper probability
distribution on $\mathbb{R}$: $F(x)\to 0$ as $x\to-\infty$ and
$F(x)\to 1$ as $x\to+\infty$. Weak convergence to a tight limit
implies tightness of $(M_n-\log n)_{n\ge 1}$. Explicitly, given
$\varepsilon>0$ choose $A$ large enough that $F(-A)<\varepsilon/2$
and $1-F(A)<\varepsilon/2$; then for all large $n$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\lvert M_n-\log n\rvert>A\bigr)<\varepsilon,
\]
and the finitely many remaining $n$ are controlled by enlarging $A$.

By contrast, if $y\le 0$ then
$\mathbb{P}(M_n\le y)=0$ because standard exponentials are positive
almost surely. If $y>0$, then
\[
\mathbb{P}(M_n\le y)=(1-e^{-y})^n\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus the probability tends to zero for every fixed real $y$.
Thus $M_n\to+\infty$ in probability, the uncentered family
$(M_n)$ is not tight on $\mathbb{R}$, and $M_n$ admits no
nondegenerate weak limit on $\mathbb{R}$. The $\log n$ centering
is therefore necessary for a nondegenerate tight limit.
\[
\boxed{(M_n-\log n)\ \text{tight};\;M_n\to+\infty\text{ in probability}}.
\]

Sentence (i) claims an uncentered Gumbel limit and contradicts
$M_n\to+\infty$. Sentence (ii) flips the sign of the median.
The construction is an exponential-maxima Gumbel-centering audit;
it is not a Gaussian characteristic-function CLT, a
uniform-integrability repair of $L^1$ convergence, or an
inverse-image measurability argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: One has $\mathbb{P}(M_n-\log n\le x)=(1-e^{-x}/n)^n\to\exp(-e^{-x})$, with origin value $e^{-1}$ and median $-\ln\ln 2$. The centered family is tight, while $M_n\to+\infty$ in probability and admits no nondegenerate uncentered weak limit on $\mathbb{R}$.
M_n itself converges weakly to the Gumbel law exp(-e^{-x}), so no log n centering is required. I do not report the centered identity (1-e^{-x}/n)^n or tightness of M_n-log n.
The limiting median is +ln ln 2. I never obtain -ln ln 2.

MOM:010117.title: Hydrostatic 60 MPa compression stores 13.5 kJ/m3; G is 80 GPa and K is 400/3 GPa
MOM:010117.objective: Convert E and nu into G and K, evaluate the three equal normal strains and the volumetric strain under equal principal stresses, prove that the stress deviator and the von Mises equivalent vanish, and compute the elastic strain-energy density.
MOM:010117.statement:
An isotropic linearly elastic solid has
\[
E=200\ \text{GPa},\qquad \nu=\frac14.
\]
A uniform hydrostatic compression
\[
\sigma_x=\sigma_y=\sigma_z=-60\ \text{MPa}
\]
is applied, with every shear stress equal to zero. There is no temperature change and the response remains linear and isotropic. Work in consistent units (convert $E$ to MPa when it multiplies a stress in MPa).

1. Compute the shear modulus $G$ and the bulk modulus $K$ from the isotropic identities that relate $\{E,\nu\}$ to $\{G,K\}$. Leave $K$ as a rational multiple of $1$ GPa.

2. Write the three normal strains from Hooke's law
   \[
   \varepsilon_x=\frac1E\bigl(\sigma_x-\nu(\sigma_y+\sigma_z)\bigr)
   \]
   and the two cyclic companions. Show that the three strains are equal and evaluate the common value.

3. Form the volumetric strain $\varepsilon_v=\varepsilon_x+\varepsilon_y+\varepsilon_z$. Recover the same number from $\varepsilon_v=\sigma_h/K$ with $\sigma_h=(\sigma_x+\sigma_y+\sigma_z)/3$.

4. Write the stress-deviator components $s_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}-\sigma_h\delta_{ij}$ and the von Mises equivalent
   \[
   \sigma_{\mathrm{vm}}=\sqrt{\tfrac32\,s_{ij}s_{ij}}.
   \]
   Then compute the elastic strain-energy density $U=\tfrac12\sigma_{ij}\varepsilon_{ij}$ and convert it to $\text{kJ}/\text{m}^3$. Confirm $U=\sigma_h^2/(2K)$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “each normal strain is simply $\sigma/E$, so $\varepsilon_x=-3\times10^{-4}$”; (ii) “the stored energy density is $\sigma_{ij}\varepsilon_{ij}$ with no factor $\tfrac12$.”

Do not introduce a bilinear (elastic-plastic) constitutive law, a thermal strain, a Mohr transformation of the already-principal state, or a buckling check.
permittedResults: If $\sigma_x=\sigma_y=\sigma_z=\sigma_h$ and all shears vanish, Hooke's law collapses to $\varepsilon_x=\varepsilon_y=\varepsilon_z=\sigma_h(1-2\nu)/E=\sigma_h/(3K)$.
The von Mises equivalent of a pure hydrostatic stress state is identically zero, because $s_{ij}=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert to G and K first, then evaluate Hooke on one normal strain and triple it for the volumetric strain and the energy.
Stay in the hydrostatic identities epsilon=sigma_h(1-2nu)/E and U=sigma_h^2/(2K) after checking that all three principal stresses are equal.

milestones.criterion: Converts E and nu into G=80 GPa and K=400/3 GPa and evaluates the three equal strains -1.5e-4.
Reports eps_v=-4.5e-4, s_ij=0, von Mises 0, and U=0.0135 MPa=13.5 kJ/m3.
Rejects a Poisson-free uniaxial strain and an energy density written without the factor 1/2.

commonErrors.description: Drops the two Poisson terms and reports each normal strain as sigma/E=-3e-4, hence eps_v=-9e-4.
commonErrors.consequence: The volumetric strain and the stored energy are each too large by a factor of two, and the K-check fails.

commonErrors.description: Writes the strain-energy density as sigma_ij epsilon_ij without the factor 1/2, reporting U=0.027 MPa.
commonErrors.consequence: The stored energy is doubled and no longer equals sigma_h^2/(2K).

hintTree.content: $\varepsilon_x=(1/200000)\bigl[-60-(1/4)(-120)\bigr]=(1/200000)(-30)$. The other two normal strains are the same.
With $s_{ij}=0$ the energy is purely volumetric: $U=\sigma_h^2/(2K)=3600/(2\cdot400000/3)=0.0135$ MPa.

MOM:010117.canonicalSolution:
The isotropic conversions are
\[
G=\frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}=\frac{200}{2\bigl(1+\tfrac14\bigr)}=\frac{200}{2\cdot\tfrac54}=\frac{200}{\tfrac52}=\boxed{80\ \text{GPa}}
\]
and
\[
K=\frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}=\frac{200}{3\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)}=\frac{200}{3\cdot\tfrac12}=\frac{200}{\tfrac32}=\boxed{\frac{400}{3}\ \text{GPa}}.
\]

Hooke's law with $E=2\times10^5$ MPa gives
\[
\varepsilon_x
=\frac1{2\times10^5}\Bigl[-60-\frac14(-60-60)\Bigr]
=\frac1{2\times10^5}\bigl[-60+30\bigr]
=\boxed{-1.5\times10^{-4}}.
\]
The same algebra with the cyclic pairs yields $\varepsilon_y=\varepsilon_z=-1.5\times10^{-4}$. The volumetric strain is therefore
\[
\varepsilon_v=3(-1.5\times10^{-4})=\boxed{-4.5\times10^{-4}}.
\]
The mean stress is $\sigma_h=-60$ MPa and $K=(400/3)\times10^3=4\times10^5/3$ MPa, so
\[
\frac{\sigma_h}{K}
=\frac{-60}{4\times10^5/3}
=-\frac{180}{4\times10^5}
=-4.5\times10^{-4},
\]
which matches $\varepsilon_v$. Equivalently $\varepsilon=\sigma_h(1-2\nu)/E=(-60)(1/2)/2\times10^5=-1.5\times10^{-4}$.

Every normal stress equals $\sigma_h$ and every shear vanishes, so
\[
s_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}-\sigma_h\delta_{ij}=\boxed{0}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sigma_{\mathrm{vm}}=\sqrt{\tfrac32\,s_{ij}s_{ij}}=\boxed{0}.
\]
The strain-energy density is
\[
U
=\frac12\bigl(\sigma_x\varepsilon_x+\sigma_y\varepsilon_y+\sigma_z\varepsilon_z\bigr)
=\frac12\cdot3\cdot(-60)(-1.5\times10^{-4})
=\boxed{0.0135\ \text{MPa}}
=\boxed{13.5\ \text{kJ}/\text{m}^3}.
\]
The hydrostatic identity confirms
\[
\frac{\sigma_h^2}{2K}
=\frac{3600}{2\cdot(4\times10^5/3)}
=\frac{3600\cdot3}{8\times10^5}
=0.0135\ \text{MPa}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: omitting the two Poisson terms reports $\varepsilon=\sigma/E=-3\times10^{-4}$ and $\varepsilon_v=-9\times10^{-4}$. Sentence (ii) is false: dropping the factor $\tfrac12$ doubles the energy to $0.027$ MPa.

The calculation uses a single linear isotropic Hooke law under a hydrostatic stress. It does not introduce a bilinear constitutive response, a thermal eigenstrain, a Mohr rotation of an already principal state, or an Euler column check.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $G=80$ GPa and $K=400/3$ GPa. Hooke's law gives each $\varepsilon=-1.5\times10^{-4}$ and $\varepsilon_v=-4.5\times10^{-4}$. The deviator and the von Mises stress vanish, and $U=0.0135$ MPa $=13.5$ kJ/m$^3$.
Each strain is sigma/E, so epsilon_x=epsilon_y=epsilon_z=-60/200000=-3e-4 and eps_v=-9e-4. Then U=(1/2)*3*(60)*(3e-4)=0.027 MPa.
G=80 GPa, K=400/3 GPa, and each epsilon=-1.5e-4 are correct, but the energy is sigma_ij epsilon_ij=3*(60)*(1.5e-4)=0.027 MPa with no factor 1/2.

MOM:010118.title: Constrained plane stress gives sigma_x=3000/13 MPa and stores 115.385 kJ/m3
MOM:010118.objective: Enforce plane stress together with a vanishing in-plane strain, solve Hooke's law for the two in-plane stresses and the through-thickness strain, and evaluate the elastic strain-energy density.
MOM:010118.statement:
A thin isotropic plate is in a state of plane stress,
\[
\sigma_z=0,
\]
with $E=210$ GPa and $\nu=0.3$. A uniform extension is imposed in the $x$-direction while the plate is prevented from straining in the $y$-direction:
\[
\varepsilon_x=0.001,\qquad \varepsilon_y=0.
\]
Shear strains vanish. The plate remains linearly elastic. Convert $E$ to MPa when combining it with stresses in MPa.

1. Write the three normal statements of Hooke's law under $\sigma_z=0$. From $\varepsilon_y=0$ deduce the exact relation between $\sigma_y$ and $\sigma_x$.

2. Substitute that relation into the $\varepsilon_x$ equation and solve for $\sigma_x$. Then obtain $\sigma_y$. Report both stresses as reduced fractions of $1$ MPa and as decimals to four places.

3. Compute the through-thickness strain $\varepsilon_z$. Leave the exact reduced fraction and a scientific-decimal value.

4. Evaluate the elastic strain-energy density $u=\tfrac12\sigma_{ij}\varepsilon_{ij}$ and convert it to $\text{kJ}/\text{m}^3$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\varepsilon_y=0$ does not constrain the stress, so the loading is uniaxial and $\sigma_x=E\varepsilon_x=210$ MPa”; (ii) “the plate is really in plane strain, so the $x$-stiffness is $E(1-\nu)/((1+\nu)(1-2\nu))$.”

Do not introduce a Mohr rotation, a thermal mismatch, a bilinear constitutive law, or a beam or column model.
permittedResults:
In isotropic plane stress with $\sigma_z=0$, $\varepsilon_x=(1/E)(\sigma_x-
u\sigma_y)$ and $\varepsilon_y=(1/E)(\sigma_y-
u\sigma_x)$. The condition $\varepsilon_y=0$ is therefore $\sigma_y=
u\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_x=E\varepsilon_x/(1-
u^2)$.
The elastic strain-energy density reduces to $u=\tfrac12\sigma_x\varepsilon_x$ when $\varepsilon_y=0$ and $\sigma_z=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the 2-by-2 in-plane Hooke system with eps_y=0, then evaluate eps_z and the single surviving energy product.
Insert the isotropic plane-stress compliance and read sigma_x=E eps_x/(1-nu^2) directly after recognizing sigma_y=nu sigma_x.

milestones.criterion: Enforces plane stress and eps_y=0 to obtain sigma_y=nu sigma_x and sigma_x=3000/13 MPa.
Reports sigma_y=900/13 MPa, eps_z=-3/7000, and u=115.385 kJ/m3.
Rejects a uniaxial reading of the constrained plate and a plane-strain stiffness substitution.

commonErrors.description: Treats the loading as uniaxial plane stress, reporting sigma_x=E eps_x=210 MPa and sigma_y=0.
commonErrors.consequence: The implied lateral strain is -nu eps_x rather than the required zero, and the energy and eps_z are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the plane-stress modulus by the plane-strain stiffness E(1-nu)/((1+nu)(1-2nu)), obtaining sigma_x=282.692 MPa.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonzero sigma_z is tacitly introduced and every subsequent strain and energy value leaves the assigned plane-stress state.

hintTree.content: $\varepsilon_y=0$ and $\sigma_z=0$ give $\sigma_y-\nu\sigma_x=0$, so $\sigma_y=\nu\sigma_x$.
Then $\varepsilon_x=(\sigma_x/E)(1-\nu^2)$, hence $\sigma_x=210000\cdot0.001/0.91=3000/13$ MPa.
$\varepsilon_z=-(\nu/E)(\sigma_x+\sigma_y)$ collapses to $-3/7000$. Energy is $\tfrac12\sigma_x\varepsilon_x$ because the other two products vanish.

MOM:010118.canonicalSolution:
Plane-stress Hooke's law with $\sigma_z=0$ reads
\begin{align*}
\varepsilon_x&=\frac1E(\sigma_x-\nu\sigma_y),\\
\varepsilon_y&=\frac1E(\sigma_y-\nu\sigma_x),\\
\varepsilon_z&=-\frac{\nu}{E}(\sigma_x+\sigma_y).
\end{align*}
The constraint $\varepsilon_y=0$ forces
\[
\boxed{\sigma_y=\nu\sigma_x}.
\]
Substitution into the first equation gives
\[
\varepsilon_x=\frac{\sigma_x}{E}(1-\nu^2)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\sigma_x=\frac{E\varepsilon_x}{1-\nu^2}.
\]
With $E=2.10\times10^5$ MPa, $\varepsilon_x=10^{-3}$, and $1-\nu^2=1-0.09=0.91=91/100$,
\[
\sigma_x
=\frac{210\cdot10^3\cdot10^{-3}}{91/100}
=\frac{210}{0.91}
=\frac{21000}{91}
=\boxed{\frac{3000}{13}\ \text{MPa}}
=230.769\ \text{MPa}.
\]
Then
\[
\sigma_y
=0.3\cdot\frac{3000}{13}
=\boxed{\frac{900}{13}\ \text{MPa}}
=69.2308\ \text{MPa}.
\]
The through-thickness strain is
\[
\varepsilon_z
=-\frac{0.3}{2.10\times10^5}\Bigl(\frac{3000}{13}+\frac{900}{13}\Bigr)
=-\frac{0.3}{2.10\times10^5}\cdot\frac{3900}{13}
=-\frac{0.3\cdot300}{2.10\times10^5}
=-\frac{90}{2.10\times10^5}
=\boxed{-\frac{3}{7000}}
=-4.28571\times10^{-4}.
\]
Because $\varepsilon_y=0$ and $\sigma_z=0$,
\[
u
=\frac12\sigma_x\varepsilon_x
=\frac12\cdot\frac{3000}{13}\cdot10^{-3}
=\frac{1.5}{13}
=0.115385\ \text{MPa}
=\boxed{115.385\ \text{kJ}/\text{m}^3}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: a uniaxial reading $\sigma_x=E\varepsilon_x=210$ MPa with $\sigma_y=0$ violates $\varepsilon_y=0$, since that pair produces $\varepsilon_y=-\nu\varepsilon_x=-3\times10^{-4}$. Sentence (ii) is false: plane strain would set $\varepsilon_z=0$ and activate a nonzero $\sigma_z$. The plane-strain $x$-stiffness
\[
\frac{E(1-\nu)}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}
=\frac{210000\cdot0.7}{1.3\cdot0.4}
\]
gives $\sigma_x=282.692$ MPa, which is not the plane-stress solution.

The model is a single linear isotropic plane-stress state with one kinematic constraint. It does not use Mohr's circle, a thermal eigenstrain, a bilinear constitutive law, or a beam/column reduction.

graderFixtures.proofText: Plane stress with $\varepsilon_y=0$ forces $\sigma_y=\nu\sigma_x$. I obtain $\sigma_x=3000/13=230.769$ MPa, $\sigma_y=900/13=69.2308$ MPa, $\varepsilon_z=-3/7000$, and $u=\tfrac12\sigma_x\varepsilon_x=115.385$ kJ/m$^3$.
The plate is thin so the loading is uniaxial. Then sigma_x=E eps_x=210 MPa, sigma_y=0, eps_z=-nu eps_x=-3e-4, and u=0.5*210*0.001=105 kJ/m3.
I treat the constrained plate as plane strain and use sigma_x=E(1-nu)eps_x/((1+nu)(1-2nu))=282.692 MPa. Then sigma_y=nu sigma_x/(1-nu)=121.154 MPa.

MOM:010219.title: The linearly tapered circular bar extends 0.75/pi mm and stores 11.25/pi J
MOM:010219.objective: Integrate the axial stretch of a linearly tapering circular bar, evaluate the end stresses, and compute the elastic strain energy as P delta/2.
MOM:010219.statement:
A straight circular bar has length $L=1$ m. Its diameter varies linearly from
\[
d_0=0.02\ \text{m}
\]
at the loaded end to
\[
d_1=0.04\ \text{m}
\]
at the supported end. A tensile axial load $P=30$ kN is applied at the small end and is reacted at the large end. The material is linearly elastic with $E=200$ GPa. Self-weight is neglected, and the stress is taken as uniformly distributed on each cross-section.

1. Write the diameter $d(x)$ and the area $A(x)$ if $x$ is measured from the small end. Form the elongation integral
   \[
   \delta=\int_0^L\frac{P}{EA(x)}\,dx
   \]
   and reduce it to the closed form $4PL/(\pi E d_0 d_1)$.

2. Evaluate $\delta$ exactly as a multiple of $1/\pi$ meters, and in millimeters to six significant figures.

3. Compute the axial stress at each end. Identify the maximum stress and give both end values as multiples of $1/\pi$ MPa.

4. Because the bar is statically determinate and linearly elastic, the stored energy is $U=P\delta/2$. Evaluate $U$ as a multiple of $1/\pi$ joules.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “with diameters in the formula the factor $4$ is omitted, so $\delta=PL/(\pi E d_0 d_1)$”; (ii) “the stored energy is the full product $P\delta$.”

Do not introduce thermal eigenstrains, a bilinear constitutive law, torsion, a beam deflection, Castigliano's theorem on a redundant frame, or a buckling check.
permittedResults: The elongation of a linearly tapering circular bar under a constant axial force is $\delta=4PL/(\pi E d_0 d_1)$.
The extreme axial stresses occur at the end sections: $\sigma=4P/(\pi d^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Change variable from x to the local diameter, evaluate int dd/d^2, and read 4PL/(pi E d0 d1).
Keep the integral in x, write A(x)=(pi/4)(d0+(d1-d0)x/L)^2, and antiderive 1/(a+bx)^2.

milestones.criterion: Reduces the taper integral to delta=4PL/(pi E d0 d1)=0.00075/pi m=0.238732 mm.
Reports sigma_max=300/pi MPa at the small end, sigma_large=75/pi MPa, and U=11.25/pi J.
Rejects a missing factor 4 in the diameter formula and an energy written as P delta.

commonErrors.description: Writes delta=PL/(pi E d0 d1), omitting the factor 4 required when end diameters (not radii) appear, and reports 0.0001875/pi m.
commonErrors.consequence: The elongation and the stored energy are each too small by a factor of four.

commonErrors.description: Reports the stored energy as the full product P delta=22.5/pi J instead of P delta/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy is doubled and no longer matches the linear-elastic integral of P^2/(2EA).

hintTree.content: With $d(x)=d_0+(d_1-d_0)x/L$ the integral $\int dx/d(x)^2$ evaluates to $L/(d_0 d_1)$. Multiplying by $4P/(\pi E)$ produces the closed form.
The small-end area is $\pi(0.02)^2/4=10^{-4}\pi$ m$^2$, so $\sigma_{\max}=30000/(10^{-4}\pi)=300/\pi$ MPa. Energy is half of $P\delta$.

MOM:010219.canonicalSolution:
Measure $x$ from the small end. The diameter and area are
\[
d(x)=0.02+0.02\,x,\qquad
A(x)=\frac\pi4\bigl(0.02+0.02\,x\bigr)^2.
\]
In general $d(x)=d_0+(d_1-d_0)x/L$ and
\[
\delta
=\int_0^L\frac{P}{E\cdot\pi[d(x)]^2/4}\,dx
=\frac{4P}{\pi E}\int_0^L\frac{dx}{[d(x)]^2}.
\]
The substitution $d=d_0+(d_1-d_0)x/L$ gives $dx=L\,dd/(d_1-d_0)$ and
\[
\int_0^L\frac{dx}{[d(x)]^2}
=\frac{L}{d_1-d_0}\int_{d_0}^{d_1}\frac{dd}{d^2}
=\frac{L}{d_0 d_1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\delta=\frac{4PL}{\pi E d_0 d_1}.
\]
Inserting the data,
\[
\delta
=\frac{4\cdot30000\cdot1}{\pi\cdot2.00\times10^{11}\cdot0.02\cdot0.04}
=\frac{1.20\times10^5}{\pi\cdot1.60\times10^8}
=\boxed{\frac{0.00075}{\pi}\ \text{m}}
=\boxed{0.238732\ \text{mm}}.
\]

The end areas are
\[
A_0=\frac\pi4(0.02)^2=10^{-4}\pi\ \text{m}^2,
\qquad
A_1=\frac\pi4(0.04)^2=4\times10^{-4}\pi\ \text{m}^2.
\]
The corresponding stresses are
\[
\sigma_0
=\frac{30000}{10^{-4}\pi}
=\boxed{\frac{300}{\pi}\ \text{MPa}}
=95.493\ \text{MPa},
\qquad
\sigma_1
=\frac{30000}{4\times10^{-4}\pi}
=\boxed{\frac{75}{\pi}\ \text{MPa}}
=23.873\ \text{MPa}.
\]
The maximum stress is the small-end value $300/\pi$ MPa.

Linear elasticity on a determinate bar gives
\[
U
=\frac{P\delta}{2}
=\frac{30000}{2}\cdot\frac{0.00075}{\pi}
=\boxed{\frac{11.25}{\pi}\ \text{J}}
=3.58099\ \text{J}.
\]
The same number is recovered from $\int_0^L P^2/(2EA(x))\,dx$.

Sentence (i) is false: omitting the factor $4$ reports $\delta=0.0001875/\pi$ m $=0.059683$ mm, one quarter of the true stretch (that formula would be correct only if $d_0,d_1$ were replaced by the end radii). Sentence (ii) is false: $U=P\delta$ doubles the stored energy to $22.5/\pi$ J.

The calculation is a single determinate axial member with a linear taper. It does not use a thermal constraint, a bilinear constitutive law, torsion, Castigliano on a redundant frame, a triangular beam load, or an Euler check.

graderFixtures.proofText: The taper formula gives $\delta=4PL/(\pi E d_0 d_1)=0.00075/\pi$ m $=0.238732$ mm. Stresses are $300/\pi$ MPa at the small end and $75/\pi$ MPa at the large end, and $U=P\delta/2=11.25/\pi=3.58099$ J.
The elongation 0.00075/pi m is correct, but the stored energy is the work P delta=22.5/pi=7.16197 J with no factor 1/2.

MOM:010220.title: Bredt shear flow is 200000/pi N/m and the closed tube twists 0.05/pi rad
MOM:010220.objective: Apply Bredt's shear-flow formula to a thin circular cell, convert the flow into wall shear, form the thin-wall torsion constant, and evaluate the angle of twist.
MOM:010220.statement:
A thin-walled closed tube of circular mean radius
\[
r=0.05\ \text{m}
\]
and uniform thickness
\[
t=0.002\ \text{m}
\]
has length $L=2$ m and shear modulus $G=80$ GPa. A torque $T=1$ kN$\cdot$m is applied about the tube axis. The wall is thin enough that the shear stress may be taken as uniform through the thickness, and the mean radius is the radius of the midline.

1. Compute the enclosed midline area $A_m$ and the Bredt shear flow $q=T/(2A_m)$. Report $q$ in $\text{N}/\text{m}$ as a multiple of $1/\pi$ and in $\text{N}/\text{mm}$.

2. Convert the flow into the wall shear stress $\tau=q/t$. Report $\tau$ as a multiple of $1/\pi$ MPa.

3. Form the thin-wall torsion constant of the circular cell,
   \[
   J_t=2\pi r^3 t=\frac{4A_m^2 t}{\oint\mathrm{d}s},
   \]
   and evaluate it as a multiple of $\pi$ in $\text{m}^4$.

4. Compute the angle of twist $\theta=TL/(GJ_t)$ in radians as a multiple of $1/\pi$, and in degrees.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the shear flow is $q=T/A_m$, so the factor $2$ in Bredt's formula may be dropped”; (ii) “the tube may be treated as a solid circular shaft of radius $r$, with $J=\pi r^4/2$.”

Do not replace the closed cell by an open thin-walled section, do not introduce a bilinear constitutive response, a thermal twist, a beam deflection, Mohr's circle, or an Euler load.
permittedResults: For a circular cell, $A_m=\pi r^2$ and $q=T/(2\pi r^2)$, so $\tau=T/(2\pi r^2 t)$.
The same circular cell has $J_t=2\pi r^3 t$, and therefore $\theta=TL/(G\cdot2\pi r^3 t)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate Am, then q=T/(2Am) and tau=q/t, then Jt=2 pi r^3 t and theta=TL/(G Jt).
Stay in Bredt variables throughout: tau=T/(2 A_m t) and theta=T L (integral ds)/(4 A_m^2 G t).

milestones.criterion: Computes Am=0.0025pi m2 and the Bredt flow q=200000/pi N/m=63.662 N/mm.
Reports tau=100/pi MPa, Jt=5e-7 pi m4, and theta=0.05/pi rad=0.911891 deg.
Rejects dropping the factor 2 in Bredt's formula and a solid-shaft polar moment.

commonErrors.description: Writes q=T/A_m instead of T/(2A_m), reporting q=400000/pi N/m and tau=200/pi MPa.
commonErrors.consequence: The wall shear is doubled and any subsequent strength check is unconservative in the wrong direction.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the thin-wall J_t by the solid-circle polar moment J=pi r^4/2=3.125e-6 pi m4.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted twist 0.008/pi rad is about six times too small.

graderFixtures.proofText: I take the shear flow as q=T/A_m=1000/(0.0025pi)=400000/pi N/m, so tau=200/pi=63.662 MPa. Jt and theta are left at the thin-wall values.
The shear flow 200000/pi N/m is fine, but I twist the member with the solid-circle J=pi r^4/2=3.125e-6 pi m4, so theta=2000/(80e9*3.125e-6 pi)=0.008/pi rad.

MOM:010221.title: Twist governs: d_theta is 72.655 mm, so a 75 mm solid shaft is selected
MOM:010221.objective: Convert delivered power and spin into torque, size a solid circular shaft independently for allowable shear and allowable twist, and select a stock diameter that satisfies the governing (larger) requirement.
MOM:010221.statement:
A solid circular steel shaft transmits
\[
P=60\ \text{kW}
\]
at
\[
n=300\ \text{rpm}.
\]
The shaft has length $L=2$ m and shear modulus $G=80$ GPa. Design limits are
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}=60\ \text{MPa},\qquad
\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}=1^\circ.
\]
The shaft is to be a single solid circular section of constant diameter $d$.

1. Convert the spin rate into $\omega$ in rad/s and compute the transmitted torque $T=P/\omega$. Leave $T$ as a multiple of $1/\pi$ N$\cdot$m.

2. From $\tau=16T/(\pi d^3)\le\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}$, obtain the minimum diameter $d_\tau$ required by strength. Show that
   \[
   d_\tau=\Bigl(\frac{0.0016}{\pi^2}\Bigr)^{1/3}
   \]
   and evaluate it in millimeters.

3. From $\theta=TL/(GJ)\le\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}$ with $J=\pi d^4/32$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}=\pi/180$ rad, obtain the minimum diameter $d_\theta$ required by twist. Show that
   \[
   d_\theta=\Bigl(\frac{0.000864}{\pi^3}\Bigr)^{1/4}
   \]
   and evaluate it in millimeters.

4. State which limit governs. Select the next convenient stock diameter $d=75$ mm and compute the resulting $\tau$ (MPa) and $\theta$ (degrees).

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$300$ rpm may be used directly as $\omega=300$ rad/s”; (ii) “the smaller of $d_\tau$ and $d_\theta$ is the required diameter, so a $55$ mm shaft is acceptable.”

Do not introduce a hollow section, a bilinear constitutive law, a thermal twist, a beam deflection, Mohr's circle, or an Euler buckling load.
permittedResults: The strength diameter of a solid shaft is $d_\tau=\bigl(16T/(\pi\tau_{\mathrm{allow}})\bigr)^{1/3}$.
The stiffness diameter of a solid shaft is $d_\theta=\bigl(32TL/(G\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}\pi)\bigr)^{1/4}$, with $\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}$ in radians.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute T from P=T omega, isolate d from the two closed-form limits, and keep the larger diameter.
Nondimensionalize the two limits as d_tau^3=16T/(pi tau_allow) and d_theta^4=32 T L/(G theta_allow pi), then compare.

milestones.criterion: Converts power and rpm into omega=10pi rad/s and T=6000/pi N m, and obtains d_tau=54.526 mm.
Obtains d_theta=72.655 mm, selects 75 mm because twist governs, and reports tau=23.056 MPa and theta=0.880682 deg.
Rejects treating rpm as rad/s and rejects selecting the smaller stress-based diameter.

commonErrors.description: Takes omega=300 rad/s instead of 10pi rad/s, producing T=200 N m and diameters far below the true pair.
commonErrors.consequence: The shaft is undersized by about a factor of (10pi/300)^{1/3} in stress and (10pi/300)^{1/4} in twist.

commonErrors.description: Computes both trial diameters correctly but selects a 55 mm shaft near d_tau, claiming the smaller value governs.
commonErrors.consequence: The stock shaft meets the shear limit but twists about three degrees, violating theta_allow=1 deg.

hintTree.content: $\omega=300\cdot2\pi/60=10\pi$ rad/s, so $T=60000/(10\pi)=6000/\pi$ N$\cdot$m.
$d_\tau^3=16\cdot(6000/\pi)/(\pi\cdot60\times10^6)=0.0016/\pi^2$. For twist, convert $1^\circ$ to $\pi/180$ before isolating $d^4$.
Compare $54.526$ mm with $72.655$ mm: twist governs. Then evaluate $\tau$ and $\theta$ at $d=75$ mm.

MOM:010221.canonicalSolution:
The spin in SI units is
\[
\omega=300\cdot\frac{2\pi}{60}=\boxed{10\pi\ \text{rad}/\text{s}}.
\]
The delivered torque is
\[
T
=\frac{P}{\omega}
=\frac{60000}{10\pi}
=\boxed{\frac{6000}{\pi}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}}
=1909.86\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}.
\]

Strength requires $16T/(\pi d^3)\le60\times10^6$, so
\[
d_\tau^3
=\frac{16T}{\pi\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}}
=\frac{16\cdot(6000/\pi)}{\pi\cdot60\times10^6}
=\frac{96000}{60\times10^6\,\pi^2}
=\frac{0.0016}{\pi^2}.
\]
Hence
\[
d_\tau
=\boxed{\Bigl(\frac{0.0016}{\pi^2}\Bigr)^{1/3}}
=0.054526\ \text{m}
=54.526\ \text{mm}.
\]

Twist requires $TL/(GJ)\le\pi/180$ with $J=\pi d^4/32$, so
\[
d_\theta^4
=\frac{32TL}{G\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}\pi}
=\frac{32\cdot(6000/\pi)\cdot2}{80\times10^9\cdot(\pi/180)\cdot\pi}
=\frac{384000\cdot180}{80\times10^9\,\pi^3}
=\frac{0.000864}{\pi^3}.
\]
Hence
\[
d_\theta
=\boxed{\Bigl(\frac{0.000864}{\pi^3}\Bigr)^{1/4}}
=0.072655\ \text{m}
=72.655\ \text{mm}.
\]
Because $d_\theta>d_\tau$, \boxed{twist governs}. A stock diameter $d=75$ mm exceeds $d_\theta$ and is therefore admissible.

At $d=0.075$ m,
\[
\tau
=\frac{16T}{\pi d^3}
=\frac{16\cdot(6000/\pi)}{\pi\cdot(0.075)^3}
=\frac{96000}{\pi^2\cdot4.21875\times10^{-4}}
=\boxed{23.056\ \text{MPa}},
\]
and
\[
\theta
=\frac{TL}{GJ}
=\frac{(6000/\pi)\cdot2}{80\times10^9\cdot\pi(0.075)^4/32}
=\boxed{0.880682^\circ}.
\]
Both values lie below the allowables. Equivalently $\tau=\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}(d_\tau/d)^3$ and $\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}(d_\theta/d)^4$.

Sentence (i) is false: using $\omega=300$ rad/s yields $T=200$ N$\cdot$m, about one tenth of the true torque, and both trial diameters collapse. Sentence (ii) is false: the governing diameter is the larger one. A $55$ mm shaft satisfies strength ($d_\tau=54.526$ mm) but twists by
\[
\theta=(72.655/55)^4\cdot1^\circ\approx3.05^\circ,
\]
which violates $\theta_{\mathrm{allow}}$.

The calculation is a solid circular shaft under steady torsion from a known power. It does not use a hollow section, a bilinear law, a thermal twist, a beam field, Mohr's circle, or Euler buckling.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $\omega=10\pi$ rad/s and $T=6000/\pi=1909.86$ N$\cdot$m. Then $d_\tau=54.526$ mm and $d_\theta=72.655$ mm, so twist governs. At the stock diameter $75$ mm I find $\tau=23.056$ MPa and $\theta=0.880682^\circ$.
I take omega=300 rad/s, so T=60000/300=200 N m. Then d_tau=(16*200/(pi*60e6))^{1/3}=25.73 mm and d_theta is similarly reduced. I never convert rpm to rad/s.
I agree that d_tau=54.526 mm and d_theta=72.655 mm, but the required diameter is the smaller one, so a 55 mm shaft is selected. Strength is satisfied and I ignore the 1 degree cap.

MOM:010322.title: Wood-steel beam: ybar=152.5 mm from the top, I'=177083333.333 mm4, steel bottom 64.9412 MPa
MOM:010322.objective: Form the wood-reference transformed section of a wood rectangle with a bonded bottom steel plate, locate the centroid from the top fiber, compute the transformed moment of inertia, and recover signed wood and steel bending stresses at the extreme fibers and at the interface.
MOM:010322.statement:
A simply supported timber beam of rectangular cross-section $100\,\text{mm}$ wide by $200\,\text{mm}$ deep has a steel plate $100\,\text{mm}$ wide by $10\,\text{mm}$ thick bonded to its entire bottom face. The modular ratio is $n=E_s/E_w=20$. The two materials remain linearly elastic and perfectly bonded. A sagging bending moment $M=10\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$ acts about the strong axis of the composite section. Compression is negative.

Work throughout in millimetres and megapascals, taking the wood as the reference material.

1. Form the wood-reference transformed section. State the transformed steel area $A_s'$ and the total transformed area $A'$.

2. Locate the centroidal axis by its distance $\bar y$ measured downward from the top wood fiber. Then compute the transformed second moment $I'$ about that axis, including both own-axis and parallel-axis contributions of wood and transformed steel.

3. Evaluate the wood bending stress at the top fiber and at the wood–steel interface.

4. Recover the steel bending stress at the same interface and at the bottom steel fiber by multiplying the wood-equivalent fiber stress by $n$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “because the materials share the interface strain, the steel stress equals the wood stress at that fiber”; (ii) “the two transformed areas are equal, so the centroid lies at mid-depth of the wood.”

Do not introduce a bilinear constitutive law, a temperature change, or a Mohr transformation of the bending stresses.
permittedResults: The centroid of a two-area transformed section measured from a datum is $\bar y=(\sum A_i y_i)/(\sum A_i)$.
The parallel-axis theorem gives $I=\sum\bigl(I_{\text{own}}+A d^2\bigr)$ about the common centroid.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the steel to wood first, take moments of area from the top fiber, then recover steel stress by multiplying My/I' by n.
Compute I' from the two parallel-axis contributions about ybar=152.5 mm, then evaluate the four fibers as signed My/I' (wood) and n My/I' (steel).

milestones.criterion: Forms A's=20000 mm2 and locates ybar=152.5 mm from the top with I'=177083333.333 mm4.
Reports wood top -8.61176 MPa, wood interface +2.68235 MPa, steel interface +53.6471 MPa, and steel bottom +64.9412 MPa.
Rejects an untransformed steel area and a wood-equivalent steel stress, and states the modular-ratio recovery.

commonErrors.description: Uses the raw steel area 1000 mm2 instead of n As=20000 mm2 when forming the transformed section.
commonErrors.consequence: The centroid drops to 105 mm from the top and every subsequent inertia and stress is computed on the wrong section.

commonErrors.description: Leaves the steel stresses equal to the wood-equivalent My/I' values, omitting the factor n=20.
commonErrors.consequence: The interface and bottom steel stresses are reported as 2.68235 MPa and 3.24706 MPa, understating the steel by a factor of 20.

hintTree.content: The wood area is $100\times 200=20000\,\text{mm}^2$. The transformed steel area is $n$ times $100\times 10$.
Measure $\bar y$ from the top fiber: wood centroid at $100\,\text{mm}$, steel centroid at $205\,\text{mm}$.
Wood-fiber stresses use $My/I'$ with $M=10\times 10^6\,\text{N}\cdot\text{mm}$. Steel fibers then take the factor $n=20$.

MOM:010322.canonicalSolution:
The wood area is $A_w=100\times 200=20000\,\text{mm}^2$. The steel plate has $A_s=100\times 10=1000\,\text{mm}^2$, so the wood-reference transformed steel area is
\[
A_s'=n A_s=20\times 1000=\boxed{20000\,\text{mm}^2}.
\]
The total transformed area is $A'=A_w+A_s'=40000\,\text{mm}^2$.

Measured downward from the top wood fiber, the wood centroid lies at $100\,\text{mm}$ and the steel centroid at $200+5=205\,\text{mm}$. Hence
\[
\bar y=\frac{20000\cdot 100+20000\cdot 205}{40000}=\frac{6100000}{40000}=\boxed{152.5\,\text{mm}}.
\]
The wood own-axis inertia is $100\cdot 200^3/12=66666666.667\,\text{mm}^4$ and the offset is $152.5-100=52.5\,\text{mm}$, so
\[
I_w'=66666666.667+20000\cdot 52.5^2=121791666.667\,\text{mm}^4.
\]
The transformed steel own-axis inertia is $20\cdot 100\cdot 10^3/12=166666.667\,\text{mm}^4$ and the same offset $205-152.5=52.5\,\text{mm}$ gives
\[
I_s'=166666.667+20000\cdot 52.5^2=55291666.667\,\text{mm}^4.
\]
Adding,
\[
I'=I_w'+I_s'=\boxed{177083333.333\,\text{mm}^4}.
\]

Take $M=10\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}=1.0\times 10^7\,\text{N}\cdot\text{mm}$ sagging. Distances from the neutral axis are $152.5\,\text{mm}$ to the top fiber, $200-152.5=47.5\,\text{mm}$ to the interface, and $210-152.5=57.5\,\text{mm}$ to the bottom steel fiber. The wood stresses are
\[
\sigma_{w,\text{top}}=-\frac{M\cdot 152.5}{I'}=\boxed{-8.61176\,\text{MPa}},
\qquad
\sigma_{w,\text{ifc}}=+\frac{M\cdot 47.5}{I'}=\boxed{+2.68235\,\text{MPa}}.
\]
Steel stresses are $n$ times the wood-equivalent fiber values:
\[
\sigma_{s,\text{ifc}}=20\cdot 2.68235=\boxed{+53.6471\,\text{MPa}},
\qquad
\sigma_{s,\text{bot}}=20\cdot\frac{M\cdot 57.5}{I'}=\boxed{+64.9412\,\text{MPa}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: strain continuity does not imply stress continuity when $E_s=20 E_w$. Omitting $n$ would leave the steel interface at $+2.68235\,\text{MPa}$. Sentence (ii) is false: the transformed areas are equal, but the steel lies farther from the top, so $\bar y=152.5\,\text{mm}$ and not the wood mid-depth $100\,\text{mm}$.

The calculation uses a linearly elastic transformed section in pure bending. It does not use a bilinear constitutive model, a thermal eigenstrain, or a Mohr rotation of the uniaxial bending stresses.

graderFixtures.proofText: Wood-reference $A_s'=20000\,\text{mm}^2$ and $\bar y=152.5\,\text{mm}$ from the top give $I'=177083333.333\,\text{mm}^4$. Wood stresses are $-8.61176\,\text{MPa}$ at the top and $+2.68235\,\text{MPa}$ at the interface; steel stresses are $+53.6471\,\text{MPa}$ at the interface and $+64.9412\,\text{MPa}$ at the bottom.

I take the steel as 1000 mm2 of wood. Then A'=21000 mm2 and ybar=(20000*100+1000*205)/21000=105 mm from the top. I' follows from that centroid. Wood stresses are My/I' and steel stresses are n My/I' on that untransformed section.

I obtain ybar=152.5 mm from the top and I'=177083333.333 mm4. The four fiber stresses from My/I' are therefore wood top -8.61176 MPa, wood interface +2.68235 MPa, steel interface +2.68235 MPa, and steel bottom +3.24706 MPa.

MOM:010323.title: At 45 kN m a 60 by 120 mm rectangle has elastic-core half-depth 30sqrt2 mm
MOM:010323.objective: Compute the elastic and plastic section moduli and moments of a rectangular beam, reject the elastic trial at an intermediate moment, and recover the elastic-core half-depth and yielded face depths from the elastic-perfect moment formula.
MOM:010323.statement:
A rectangular cross-section of width $b=60\,\text{mm}$ and depth $h=120\,\text{mm}$ is of an elastic–perfectly plastic material with yield stress $S_y=250\,\text{MPa}$. Plane sections remain plane. The applied bending moment is $M=45\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$, which lies strictly between first yield and full plastification.

1. Compute the second moment $I$, the elastic section modulus $S=I/(h/2)$, the plastic modulus $Z_p=bh^2/4$, the yield moment $M_y=S_y S$, the plastic moment $M_p=S_y Z_p$, and the shape factor $M_p/M_y$.

2. Form the elastic trial stress $M/S$ at the given moment and explain why it is invalid.

3. Write the elastic–perfect moment in the form
   \[
   M=b S_y\Bigl(a^2-\frac{c^2}{3}\Bigr),
   \]
   where $a=h/2$ is the half-depth and $c$ is the elastic-core half-depth. Solve for $c$ at $M=45\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$.

4. State the yielded depth on each face.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$M=45\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}<M_p$, so the section is fully elastic and $\sigma=M/S=312.5\,\text{MPa}$ is acceptable”; (ii) “the elastic-core half-depth is the yielded face depth $17.5736\,\text{mm}$.”

Do not replace the rectangle by an I-section, do not introduce a bilinear hardening law, and do not compute a shear-flow connector spacing.
permittedResults: For a rectangle, $I=bh^3/12$ and $S=I/(h/2)=bh^2/6$, so $M_y=S_y bh^2/6$.
If $M_y<M<M_p$, the elastic trial $\sigma=M/S$ exceeds $S_y$ and cannot be used.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare M with My and Mp first, discard M/S, then invert M=b Sy(a^2-c^2/3) for c.
Nondimensionalize as M/Mp=1-(c/a)^2/3 with Mp=54 kNm, then convert c back to millimetres.

milestones.criterion: Computes I=8.64e6 mm4, S=144000 mm3, Zp=216000 mm3, My=36 kNm, Mp=54 kNm, and shape factor 1.5.
Rejects the elastic trial 312.5 MPa and solves c=30sqrt(2)=42.4264 mm with yielded faces 17.5736 mm.
Distinguishes the elastic core from the yielded face depth and refuses a fully elastic reading of M=45 kNm.

commonErrors.description: Treats M=45 kNm as fully elastic and reports the extreme-fiber stress as M/S=312.5 MPa.
commonErrors.consequence: A stress above Sy is accepted, the elastic core is never found, and the yielded faces are missed.

commonErrors.description: Solves the moment formula but reports the elastic-core half-depth as the yielded face depth 17.5736 mm.
commonErrors.consequence: The remaining elastic core is understated and the plastic penetration is assigned the wrong length.

hintTree.content: The elastic trial $45\times 10^6/144000=312.5\,\text{MPa}$ exceeds $S_y=250\,\text{MPa}$.
With $a=60\,\text{mm}$, the moment formula becomes $45\times 10^6=60\cdot 250\cdot(3600-c^2/3)$.

MOM:010323.canonicalSolution:
The elastic geometric properties are
\[
I=\frac{60\cdot 120^3}{12}=\boxed{8.64\times 10^6\,\text{mm}^4},
\qquad
S=\frac{I}{60}=\boxed{144000\,\text{mm}^3}.
\]
The plastic modulus is
\[
Z_p=\frac{bh^2}{4}=\frac{60\cdot 14400}{4}=\boxed{216000\,\text{mm}^3}.
\]
Hence
\[
M_y=S_y S=250\cdot 144000=\boxed{36\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}},
\qquad
M_p=S_y Z_p=250\cdot 216000=\boxed{54\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}},
\]
and the shape factor is
\[
\frac{M_p}{M_y}=\boxed{1.5}.
\]
The given moment $45\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$ satisfies $M_y<M<M_p$. The elastic trial
\[
\frac{M}{S}=\frac{45\times 10^6}{144000}=312.5\,\text{MPa}
\]
exceeds $S_y=250\,\text{MPa}$ and is therefore invalid.

With $a=h/2=60\,\text{mm}$ the elastic–perfect moment is
\[
M=b S_y\Bigl(a^2-\frac{c^2}{3}\Bigr).
\]
Substitution of $M=45\times 10^6\,\text{N}\cdot\text{mm}$ gives
\[
45\times 10^6=60\cdot 250\Bigl(3600-\frac{c^2}{3}\Bigr)=15000\Bigl(3600-\frac{c^2}{3}\Bigr),
\]
so $3000=3600-c^2/3$ and $c^2=1800$. Therefore
\[
c=30\sqrt{2}=\boxed{42.4264\,\text{mm}}.
\]
The yielded depth on each face is
\[
a-c=60-42.4264=\boxed{17.5736\,\text{mm}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $M<M_p$ does not imply $M\le M_y$. The elastic trial $312.5\,\text{MPa}$ is not a usable stress. Sentence (ii) is false: $c$ is the elastic-core half-depth, not the yielded face depth.

The model is elastic–perfect bending of a single rectangle. It does not use kinematic hardening, an I-section shear flow, or a transformed composite section.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $I=8.64\times 10^6\,\text{mm}^4$, $S=144000\,\text{mm}^3$, $Z_p=216000\,\text{mm}^3$, $M_y=36\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$, $M_p=54\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$, and shape factor $1.5$. The elastic trial $312.5\,\text{MPa}$ is invalid. The moment formula gives $c=30\sqrt{2}=42.4264\,\text{mm}$ and yielded faces of $17.5736\,\text{mm}$.
My=36 kNm and Mp=54 kNm, so M=45 kNm is below Mp and the section is elastic. The extreme-fiber stress is M/S=312.5 MPa.
I invert M=b Sy(a^2-c^2/3) at 45 kNm and obtain 30sqrt(2) mm. That length is the yielded depth on each face, so the elastic-core half-depth is 17.5736 mm.

MOM:010324.title: Built-up I-beam: q=500.74184 N/mm at the flange joint; smax=79.8815 mm
MOM:010324.objective: Compute the strong-axis inertia of a symmetric built-up I-section, form the flange-joint shear flow from the first moment of one flange, convert a two-row connector capacity into a maximum pitch, and evaluate the web shear stress at the neutral axis.
MOM:010324.statement:
A symmetric built-up I-beam has two flanges, each $200\,\text{mm}$ wide by $20\,\text{mm}$ thick, and a web $20\,\text{mm}$ thick by $160\,\text{mm}$ deep. The three plates are joined along the flange–web contacts. A transverse shear $V=100\,\text{kN}$ acts through the shear centre. The material is linearly elastic.

1. Compute the second moment $I$ of the I-section about its strong centroidal axis.

2. For one flange–web joint, form the first moment $Q$ of the outstanding flange about the neutral axis and the shear flow $q=VQ/I$.

3. Each joint is fastened by two connector rows. Each connector has a design capacity of $20\,\text{kN}$. Determine the maximum longitudinal spacing $s_{\max}$. Then evaluate the force per bolt at $s=75\,\text{mm}$ and state why $s=80\,\text{mm}$ is slightly unsafe.

4. At the neutral axis, recompute $Q$ for the half-section (one flange plus half the web) and the average web shear stress $\tau=VQ/(It)$.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$Q$ at the flange–web joint is the first moment of the entire half-section, $424000\,\text{mm}^3$”; (ii) “a single $20\,\text{kN}$ row is adequate at $s=75\,\text{mm}$ because $q\cdot 75<20\,\text{kN}$.”

Do not treat the web as a thin-walled closed tube, do not introduce plastic penetration, and do not compute a midspan flexural deflection.
permittedResults: For a symmetric I-section, $I$ is the sum of the web own-axis inertia and two flange contributions $I_{\text{own}}+A d^2$ with $d$ the flange-centroid offset from the neutral axis.
The average web shear stress at a fiber is $\tau=VQ/(I t)$, with $t$ the web thickness at that fiber.

acceptableStrategies.description: Cut just inside the flange to isolate Q=A_flange*90 mm, convert q to a two-row pitch, then enlarge Q by the half-web for the web stress.
Assemble I from web plus two flange parallel-axis terms, then evaluate q and tau from the same V and I with the matching Q.

milestones.criterion: Computes I=71893333.333 mm4 and the joint pair Q=360000 mm3, q=500.74184 N/mm.
Obtains smax=79.8815 mm, 18.7778 kN/bolt at 75 mm, Q_NA=424000 mm3, and tau_web=29.4881 MPa.
Rejects using the half-section Q at the flange joint and a single-row 20 kN pitch.

commonErrors.description: Uses the neutral-axis first moment Q=424000 mm3 at the flange–web joint.
commonErrors.consequence: The joint shear flow is overstated and the allowable connector pitch is computed on the wrong cut.

commonErrors.description: Sizes the spacing on one 20 kN fastener instead of the two-row capacity 40 kN.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported smax is about 39.94 mm, and a 75 mm pitch is wrongly declared to overload each bolt.

hintTree.content: Each flange centroid lies $90\,\text{mm}$ from the neutral axis, so one flange has $Ad^2=4000\cdot 90^2$.
At the joint, $Q$ is only the flange first moment $4000\cdot 90$. The half-web is not yet cut off.
Two $20\,\text{kN}$ rows give $40\,\text{kN}$ per pitch. Compare $qs$ at $75\,\text{mm}$ and $80\,\text{mm}$ with that capacity.

MOM:010324.canonicalSolution:
The overall depth is $200\,\text{mm}$ and the neutral axis is at mid-depth. The web contribution is
\[
I_{\text{web}}=\frac{20\cdot 160^3}{12}=6826666.667\,\text{mm}^4.
\]
Each flange has $I_{\text{own}}=200\cdot 20^3/12=133333.333\,\text{mm}^4$ and centroidal offset $90\,\text{mm}$, so
\[
I_{\text{flange}}=133333.333+4000\cdot 90^2=32533333.333\,\text{mm}^4.
\]
Two flanges plus the web give
\[
I=\boxed{71893333.333\,\text{mm}^4}.
\]

At a flange–web joint the area beyond the cut is one flange. Its first moment about the neutral axis is
\[
Q=4000\cdot 90=\boxed{360000\,\text{mm}^3}.
\]
The shear flow is
\[
q=\frac{VQ}{I}=\frac{100000\cdot 360000}{71893333.333}=\boxed{500.74184\,\text{N/mm}}.
\]
Two connector rows of $20\,\text{kN}$ each supply $40\,\text{kN}$ per pitch, so
\[
s_{\max}=\frac{40000}{500.74184}=\boxed{79.8815\,\text{mm}}.
\]
At $s=75\,\text{mm}$ the pair carries $q s=37.5556\,\text{kN}$, or
\[
\boxed{18.7778\,\text{kN}}
\]
per bolt, which is below $20\,\text{kN}$. At $s=80\,\text{mm}$ the pair would have to carry $40.0593\,\text{kN}$, slightly above $40\,\text{kN}$, so $80\,\text{mm}$ is unsafe.

At the neutral axis the half-section first moment adds the half-web $20\times 80$ with centroid $40\,\text{mm}$ from the axis:
\[
Q_{\text{NA}}=360000+1600\cdot 40=\boxed{424000\,\text{mm}^3}.
\]
The web thickness is $20\,\text{mm}$, so
\[
\tau_{\text{web}}=\frac{V Q_{\text{NA}}}{I t}=\frac{100000\cdot 424000}{71893333.333\cdot 20}=\boxed{29.4881\,\text{MPa}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $Q=424000\,\text{mm}^3$ is the neutral-axis value, not the joint value. Using it at the flange would overstate $q$. Sentence (ii) is false: $q\cdot 75=37.5556\,\text{kN}$ already exceeds one $20\,\text{kN}$ fastener; the two-row layout is essential.

The calculation is elastic shear flow in an open built-up I-section. It does not use plastic penetration, a closed thin-walled torque flow, or a Castigliano deflection.

graderFixtures.proofText: I obtain $I=71893333.333\,\text{mm}^4$, joint $Q=360000\,\text{mm}^3$, and $q=500.74184\,\text{N/mm}$. Two $20\,\text{kN}$ rows give $s_{\max}=79.8815\,\text{mm}$; at $75\,\text{mm}$ each bolt carries $18.7778\,\text{kN}$. At the neutral axis $Q=424000\,\text{mm}^3$ and $\tau=29.4881\,\text{MPa}$.
The first moment at the flange–web joint is the half-section value Q=424000 mm3. Then q=VQ/I=589.762 N/mm and the two-row smax is 67.82 mm.
I keep Q=360000 mm3 and q=500.74184 N/mm, but I size the pitch on one 20 kN connector: smax=20000/q=39.9407 mm. A 75 mm spacing would then force 37.5556 kN into that single bolt.
