NUM:010420.title: Matching values and derivatives needs repeated-node divided differences
NUM:010420.objective: Build the two-node Hermite interpolant of a quartic from a repeated-node divided-difference table, confirm it independently in the Hermite basis, and identify the exact remainder with the fourth-derivative formula.
NUM:010420.statement:
Let $f(x)=x^4$. Osculatory (Hermite) interpolation at the nodes $0$ and $1$ seeks the unique polynomial $H$ of degree at most $3$ satisfying
\[
H(0)=f(0),\quad H'(0)=f'(0),\quad H(1)=f(1),\quad H'(1)=f'(1).
\]

1. Form the Newton divided-difference table for the repeated abscissae $z=(0,0,1,1)$, using the rule that a first divided difference on a repeated node equals the derivative. Compute every entry, and write the Newton–Hermite form
   \[
   H(x)=f[z_0]+f[z_0,z_1](x-z_0)+f[z_0,z_1,z_2](x-z_0)(x-z_1)+f[z_0,z_1,z_2,z_3](x-z_0)(x-z_1)(x-z_2).
   \]
   Simplify $H$ to the monomial basis.

2. Independently assemble $H$ in the two-node Hermite basis
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \alpha_0(x)&=(1+2x)(1-x)^2,&
   \beta_0(x)&=x(1-x)^2,\\
   \alpha_1(x)&=(3-2x)x^2,&
   \beta_1(x)&=(x-1)x^2,
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   and verify that the two constructions agree. Check the four interpolation conditions directly on your simplified $H$.

3. State the Hermite remainder theorem for this data: there is $\xi_x$ strictly between the extreme nodes and $x$ (when $x\notin\{0,1\}$) such that
   \[
   f(x)-H(x)=\frac{f^{(4)}(\xi_x)}{4!}\,x^2(x-1)^2.
   \]
   Evaluate both sides exactly at $x=1/2$, and conclude that the remainder identity is an equality of polynomials in this example.

4. Explain why a degree-at-most-$1$ Lagrange interpolant of the values $f(0),f(1)$ alone cannot meet the derivative conditions, and why the nodal factor here is $x^2(x-1)^2$ rather than the degree-$4$ equispaced nodal product of a Runge/Chebyshev value-interpolation comparison.

Do not replace the osculatory table by value interpolation on four distinct nodes, and do not treat this as an equispaced-versus-Chebyshev remainder audit.
permittedResults: The Newton series on the repeated abscissae $(x_0,x_0,x_1,x_1)$ is the unique degree-at-most-$3$ Hermite interpolant of $f$ at those two nodes.
If $f\in C^4$, the two-node Hermite remainder is $f(x)-H(x)=f^{(4)}(\xi_x)(x-x_0)^2(x-x_1)^2/24$; here $x_0=0$ and $x_1=1$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fill the osculatory Newton table, simplify, then audit against the Hermite basis and the constant fourth derivative.
Write H=2x^3-x^2 by undetermined coefficients from the four conditions, then recognize the same coefficients in the divided-difference table and in the remainder factorization.

milestones.criterion: Builds the repeated-node divided-difference table and simplifies the Newton–Hermite form to H(x)=2x^3-x^2.
Confirms H in the Hermite basis and checks all four osculatory conditions.
Identifies the exact remainder x^2(x-1)^2, evaluates the 1/16 identity at x=1/2, and separates the construction from value-only or Runge interpolation.

commonErrors.description: Interpolates only the values f(0) and f(1) by the line x (or by some other value-only formula) and calls the result the Hermite interpolant.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative conditions are ignored, so the polynomial is not osculatory.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Hermite remainder factor x^2(x-1)^2 by an equispaced or Chebyshev nodal product of degree 4, as in a Runge comparison.
commonErrors.consequence: The contact order at the two nodes is lost and the exercise is collapsed into a different interpolation packet.

hintTree.content: The first-layer entries of the table are $f'(0)=0$, $(f(1)-f(0))/(1-0)=1$, and $f'(1)=4$.
The top-edge Newton coefficients are $0$, $0$, $1$, $2$, so $H(x)=x^2+2x^2(x-1)$.
Here $f^{(4)}\equiv 24$, so the remainder formula collapses to $x^2(x-1)^2$. At $x=1/2$ both $H$ and that monomial are immediate.

NUM:010420.canonicalSolution:
The data are $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$, and $f'(1)=4$. The repeated-node table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
0&0\\
&&0\\
0&0&&1\\
&&1&&2\\
1&1&&3\\
&&4\\
1&1
\end{array}
\]
because $f[0,0]=f'(0)=0$, $f[0,1]=1$, $f[1,1]=f'(1)=4$, then
\[
f[0,0,1]=\frac{1-0}{1-0}=1,\qquad
f[0,1,1]=\frac{4-1}{1-0}=3,\qquad
f[0,0,1,1]=\frac{3-1}{1-0}=2.
\]
The Newton–Hermite polynomial is therefore
\[
H(x)=0+0\cdot x+1\cdot x^2+2\cdot x^2(x-1)=x^2+2x^3-2x^2=2x^3-x^2.
\]
\[
\boxed{H(x)=2x^3-x^2}.
\]

In the Hermite basis the same data produce
\[
H(x)=f(0)\alpha_0+f'(0)\beta_0+f(1)\alpha_1+f'(1)\beta_1
=(3-2x)x^2+4(x-1)x^2
=x^2\bigl(3-2x+4x-4\bigr)=2x^3-x^2.
\]
The two constructions agree. Direct checks:
\[
H(0)=0,\qquad
H'(x)=6x^2-2x,\qquad
H'(0)=0,\qquad
H(1)=1,\qquad
H'(1)=4.
\]
All four osculatory conditions hold.

Since $f^{(4)}\equiv 24$, the remainder theorem specializes to
\[
f(x)-H(x)=\frac{24}{24}\,x^2(x-1)^2=x^2(x-1)^2.
\]
The identity can also be read off by polynomial arithmetic:
\[
x^4-(2x^3-x^2)=x^2(x-1)^2.
\]
At $x=1/2$ one has $H(1/2)=2\cdot(1/8)-1/4=0$ and $f(1/2)=1/16$, while
\[
\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^2\bigl(\tfrac12-1\bigr)^2=\tfrac1{16}.
\]
Both sides of the remainder formula equal $1/16$, and $\xi_{1/2}$ may be taken anywhere in $(0,1)$ because the fourth derivative is constant.
\[
\boxed{f(1/2)-H(1/2)=1/16=x^2(x-1)^2\big|_{x=1/2}}.
\]

The value-only Lagrange interpolant of $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$ is the line $x$. Its derivative is $1$, which matches neither $f'(0)=0$ nor $f'(1)=4$. Matching derivatives as well as values raises the contact order at each node, so the remainder nodal factor is the square of $(x-0)(x-1)$ rather than a product over four distinct sample abscissae. In particular this is not the degree-$4$ equispaced nodal polynomial of a Runge example, and Chebyshev nodes are not involved. The construction used only two geometric nodes with prescribed first derivatives.

graderFixtures.proofText: The repeated-node table has Newton coefficients $0$, $0$, $1$, $2$, so $H(x)=x^2+2x^2(x-1)=2x^3-x^2$. The Hermite basis reproduces the same cubic, and $f-H=x^2(x-1)^2$. At $x=1/2$ one has $H=0$ and remainder $1/16$.
Hermite interpolation at 0 and 1 is just Lagrange on the two values. Since f(0)=0 and f(1)=1, H(x)=x. I do not form a repeated-node table or match derivatives.
The remainder must use the monic nodal product over four equispaced nodes on [-1,1], or the scaled Chebyshev polynomial T_4/8, as in the Runge example. I never form x^2(x-1)^2 from repeated nodes.

NUM:010421.title: Natural end conditions make a cubic spline, not the interpolating quadratic
NUM:010421.objective: Set up and solve the natural-moment system for a three-knot cubic spline, write both pieces, evaluate the spline at the two midpoints, and separate the construction from the unique interpolating quadratic and from clamped end conditions.
NUM:010421.statement:
Let the interpolation data be the three knots
\[
(x_0,y_0)=(0,1),\qquad (x_1,y_1)=(1,2),\qquad (x_2,y_2)=(2,0).
\]
A cubic spline $s$ on these knots is $C^2$ on $[0,2]$, coincides with a cubic polynomial $s_i$ on each $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, and interpolates the data. It is natural when $s''(0)=s''(2)=0$. Write $M_i:=s''(x_i)$ for the moments.

1. Record the spacing $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and the natural end conditions $M_0=M_2=0$. Write the interior moment equation at $x_1$,
   \[
   h_0 M_0+2(h_0+h_1)M_1+h_1 M_2
   =6\Bigl(\frac{y_2-y_1}{h_1}-\frac{y_1-y_0}{h_0}\Bigr),
   \]
   and solve it for $M_1$.

2. On each subinterval, use the standard moment form
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   s_i(x)
   &=M_i\frac{(x_{i+1}-x)^3}{6h_i}+M_{i+1}\frac{(x-x_i)^3}{6h_i}\\
   &\quad+\Bigl(y_i-\frac{M_i h_i^2}{6}\Bigr)\frac{x_{i+1}-x}{h_i}
   +\Bigl(y_{i+1}-\frac{M_{i+1}h_i^2}{6}\Bigr)\frac{x-x_i}{h_i}
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   to produce explicit cubics $s_0$ on $[0,1]$ and $s_1$ on $[1,2]$. Expand both in the monomial (or shifted monomial) basis.

3. Evaluate $s(1/2)$ and $s(3/2)$ exactly. Verify interpolation at the three knots, continuity of $s'$ at $x=1$, and the natural conditions $s''(0)=s''(2)=0$.

4. Compute the unique polynomial $p$ of degree at most $2$ that interpolates the same three points, and evaluate $p(1/2)$. Prove that $p$ is not the natural spline. Separately explain why the end conditions $s'(0)=s'(2)=0$ would define a different (clamped) spline.

Do not replace the $C^2$ cubic spline by a single global cubic, by the interpolating quadratic, or by a high-degree equispaced interpolant.
permittedResults: For spacings $h_i$ the unknown moments $M_i=s''(x_i)$ of an interpolating cubic spline satisfy the tridiagonal continuity system $h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_i M_{i+1}=6(\Delta y_i/h_i-\Delta y_{i-1}/h_{i-1})$ at each interior knot.
On each subinterval the cubic with prescribed endpoint values and second derivatives is given by the displayed moment formula. Natural ends close the system by $M_0=M_n=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Close the tridiagonal system by M0=M2=0, solve for M1, write the moment formula on each piece, then evaluate and audit C^2.
Postulate cubics with the interpolation and C^2 matching conditions plus s''(0)=s''(2)=0, solve the linear system, and compare the result with the quadratic interpolant.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the natural moment system and solves it to M0=0, M1=-9/2, M2=0.
Produces both cubic pieces and evaluates s(1/2)=57/32 and s(3/2)=41/32, with C^2 and natural-end checks.
Separates the spline from the interpolating quadratic p(1/2)=15/8 and from clamped first-derivative end conditions.

commonErrors.description: Reports the unique quadratic through the three knots as the cubic spline, or gives s(1/2)=15/8 without solving the moment system.
commonErrors.consequence: The result is C^infty but has constant second derivative -3, so it is not a natural cubic spline.

commonErrors.description: Interprets natural end conditions as s'(0)=s'(2)=0, or as not-a-knot continuity of s''' at the first interior knot.
commonErrors.consequence: The moment system is closed incorrectly and the computed pieces are a different spline.

hintTree.content: Here $h_0=h_1=1$, so the interior equation collapses to $4M_1=6((0-2)-(2-1))$.
With $M_0=M_2=0$ and $M_1=-9/2$ the left piece is $s_0(x)=1+(7/4)x-(3/4)x^3$.
The interpolating quadratic through the same three points is $p(x)=1+(5/2)x-(3/2)x^2$. Its second derivative is the nonzero constant $-3$.

NUM:010421.canonicalSolution:
The spacings are $h_0=h_1=1$. Natural ends force $M_0=M_2=0$. The single interior moment equation is
\[
1\cdot 0+2(1+1)M_1+1\cdot 0
=6\Bigl(\frac{0-2}{1}-\frac{2-1}{1}\Bigr)
=6(-2-1)=-18,
\]
so $4M_1=-18$ and
\[
M_1=-\frac92.
\]
\[
\boxed{M_0=0,\; M_1=-9/2,\; M_2=0}.
\]

On $[0,1]$ the moment formula reduces to
\[
s_0(x)
=M_1\frac{x^3}{6}
+y_0(1-x)
+\Bigl(y_1-\frac{M_1}{6}\Bigr)x
=-\frac34 x^3+(1-x)+\Bigl(2+\frac34\Bigr)x
=1+\frac74 x-\frac34 x^3.
\]
On $[1,2]$,
\[
s_1(x)
=M_1\frac{(2-x)^3}{6}
+\Bigl(y_1-\frac{M_1}{6}\Bigr)(2-x)
=-\frac34(2-x)^3+\frac{11}4(2-x).
\]
\[
\boxed{s_0(x)=1+(7/4)x-(3/4)x^3,\quad
s_1(x)=-(3/4)(2-x)^3+(11/4)(2-x)}.
\]

Interpolation is immediate: $s_0(0)=1$, $s_0(1)=1+7/4-3/4=2$, $s_1(1)=-(3/4)+(11/4)=2$, and $s_1(2)=0$. The midpoints are
\[
s\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
=s_0\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
=1+\frac78-\frac3{32}
=\frac{57}{32},
\qquad
s\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)
=s_1\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)
=-\frac3{32}+\frac{11}8
=\frac{41}{32}.
\]
Differentiating,
\[
s_0'(x)=\frac74-\frac94 x^2,\qquad
s_1'(x)=\frac94(2-x)^2-\frac{11}4,
\]
so $s_0'(1)=-1/2=s_1'(1)$. The second derivatives are
\[
s_0''(x)=-\frac92 x,\qquad
s_1''(x)=-\frac92(2-x),
\]
hence $s_0''(0)=0$, $s_0''(1)=-9/2=s_1''(1)$, and $s_1''(2)=0$. Thus $s$ is $C^2$ and natural.
\[
\boxed{s(1/2)=57/32,\qquad s(3/2)=41/32}.
\]

The unique polynomial of degree at most $2$ through the three knots may be written in Newton form $p(x)=1+x+c\,x(x-1)$. The condition $p(2)=0$ forces $1+2+2c=0$, so $c=-3/2$ and
\[
p(x)=1+\frac52 x-\frac32 x^2.
\]
Then $p(1/2)=1+5/4-3/8=15/8=60/32$, which is not $57/32$. Moreover $p''\equiv -3\ne 0$, so $p$ fails the natural end conditions. Therefore $p$ is not the natural spline. Clamped ends $s'(0)=s'(2)=0$ would replace the two conditions $M_0=M_2=0$ by two conditions on $s'$, producing a different tridiagonal system and a different pair of cubics. A single global cubic has four coefficients and cannot in general match three values together with two natural second-derivative conditions and $C^2$ continuity in the spline sense; the spline is piecewise. High-degree equispaced interpolation is a different construction entirely.

graderFixtures.proofText: Natural moments are $M_0=M_2=0$ and $M_1=-9/2$. The pieces are $s_0(x)=1+(7/4)x-(3/4)x^3$ and $s_1(x)=-(3/4)(2-x)^3+(11/4)(2-x)$, with $s(1/2)=57/32$ and $s(3/2)=41/32$. The interpolating quadratic has $p(1/2)=15/8$ and $p''\equiv-3$, so it is not the natural spline.
Three knots determine a unique quadratic p(x)=1+(5/2)x-(3/2)x^2. I call p the cubic spline and report s(1/2)=15/8. There is no need for a moment system or C^2 matching of two cubics.
Natural means the spline comes in horizontally, so I impose s'(0)=s'(2)=0 instead of s''(0)=s''(2)=0. Equivalently I use not-a-knot and never set the endpoint moments to zero.

NUM:010522.title: Two Gauss nodes integrate cubics exactly and miss a concrete quartic
NUM:010522.objective: Construct the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule from the degree-two Legendre polynomial, prove exactness through degree three, and audit the exact error on a monomial of degree four both on the reference interval and after an affine change of interval.
NUM:010522.statement:
Work throughout with the standard $L^2[-1,1]$ inner product. Let $P_0\equiv 1$, $P_1(x)=x$, and $P_2(x)=(3x^2-1)/2$ denote the first three Legendre polynomials, which are orthogonal on $[-1,1]$.

1. Show that the roots of $P_2$ are $x_\pm=\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$. Determine the unique weights $w_\pm$ that make the interpolatory rule
   \[
   Q_2(f)=w_-f(x_-)+w_+f(x_+)
   \]
   exact for $f(x)=1$ and $f(x)=x$. Equivalently, evaluate the classical weight formula
   \[
   w_i=\frac{2}{(1-x_i^2)\bigl(P_2'(x_i)\bigr)^2}.
   \]
   Record $Q_2$ explicitly.

2. Prove that $Q_2$ is exact for every polynomial of degree at most $3$. You may use either the interpolatory error formula or orthogonality of $P_2$ to $\mathbb P_1$. Give a one-line counterexample showing that exactness can fail at degree $4$.

3. Let $I(f)=\int_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,dx$. Compute $I(x^4)$ and $Q_2(x^4)$ as rational numbers, and record the signed error $I(x^4)-Q_2(x^4)$. Deduce the constant $c$ in the representation $I(p)-Q_2(p)=c\,p^{(4)}$ for every quartic $p$. Then, using the three-point Gauss–Legendre nodes $0,\pm\sqrt{3/5}$ and weights $8/9,\,5/9,\,5/9$, verify that the three-point rule is exact on $x^4$.

4. Transfer $Q_2$ to $[0,2]$ by the affine map $t=x+1$. Write the resulting nodes and weights, evaluate the mapped rule on $t\mapsto t^3$ and on $t\mapsto t^4$, and compare with the exact integrals $\int_0^2 t^3\,dt$ and $\int_0^2 t^4\,dt$. Explain why the cubic is recovered exactly while the quartic error equals the reference error from part 3.

Do not replace Gauss nodes by Chebyshev extrema or by equispaced Newton–Cotes nodes, and do not invoke an adaptive panel-halving estimator.
permittedResults: If a quadrature rule with $n$ nodes is interpolatory and the node polynomial is orthogonal to $\mathbb P_{n-1}$ in $L^2[-1,1]$, then the rule is exact on $\mathbb P_{2n-1}$.
For a rule exact on $\mathbb P_{3}$, the error on a quartic is completely determined by the error on $x^4$, because the remainder is a multiple of the constant fourth derivative.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the even/odd moment system for a symmetric two-node rule, then reduce a general cubic against P2.
Evaluate the classical weight formula at the roots of P2 and obtain the degree-four error by comparing I(x^4) with Q2(x^4) before transferring by an affine map.

milestones.criterion: Constructs the two-point nodes and weights and proves exactness through degree 3 from orthogonality or from the interpolatory error formula.
Computes the rational degree-four error 8/45 on [-1,1], identifies the constant 1/135, and checks that the given three-point rule is exact on x^4.
Transfers the rule to [0,2] by t=x+1 and recovers the exact cubic integral 4 together with the same quartic error 8/45.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule is exact for every smooth integrand, or specifically that it integrates x^4 exactly.
commonErrors.consequence: The exactness degree is 3, not 4; the concrete error 8/45 is lost and the three-point comparison becomes meaningless.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Legendre roots by Chebyshev extrema or by equispaced Newton–Cotes nodes and treats the resulting rule as Gauss–Legendre.
commonErrors.consequence: The orthogonality argument and the exact weights w_i=1 fail, and the exercise collapses into an interpolation-node comparison.

hintTree.content: The even/odd split of the moment system forces $w_+=w_-$ as soon as the nodes are symmetric, and the constant-function moment then gives each weight equal to $1$.
Any cubic may be written $q(x)=P_2(x)\ell(x)+r(x)$ with $\deg\ell\le 1$ and $\deg r\le 1$. Orthogonality kills the first integral, and part 1 already integrates $r$ exactly.
On $[0,2]$ the Jacobian is $1$, so the mapped two-point rule is simply $f(1-1/\sqrt{3})+f(1+1/\sqrt{3})$. Expand the even powers of $1\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$.

NUM:010522.canonicalSolution:
The quadratic $3x^2-1=0$ has roots $x_\pm=\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$. The moment conditions $w_-+w_+=2$ and $w_-x_-+w_+x_+=0$ together with $x_+=-x_-$ force $w_+=w_-=1$. The same weights come from $P_2'(x)=3x$:
\[
(1-x_\pm^2)\bigl(P_2'(x_\pm)\bigr)^2=\Bigl(1-\frac13\Bigr)\cdot 3=2,
\]
so $w_\pm=2/2=1$. Thus
\[
\boxed{Q_2(f)=f\bigl(-1/\sqrt{3}\bigr)+f\bigl(1/\sqrt{3}\bigr)}.
\]

Write a cubic as $q=P_2\ell+r$ with $\deg\ell\le 1$ and $\deg r\le 1$. Then $\int_{-1}^{1}P_2\ell=0$ by orthogonality, while $Q_2(P_2\ell)=0$ because $P_2$ vanishes at the nodes. Part 1 already gives $I(r)=Q_2(r)$. Hence $I(q)=Q_2(q)$ on $\mathbb P_3$. The monomial $x^4$ is a counterexample at degree $4$, as the next paragraph computes.

\[
I(x^4)=\frac{2}{5},\qquad Q_2(x^4)=2\cdot\Bigl(\frac{1}{3}\Bigr)^2=\frac{2}{9},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{I(x^4)-Q_2(x^4)=\frac{8}{45}}.
\]
Every quartic has constant fourth derivative, and $(x^4)^{(4)}=24$, therefore
\[
I(p)-Q_2(p)=\frac{8}{45}\cdot\frac{p^{(4)}}{24}=\frac{1}{135}\,p^{(4)}.
\]
The three-point rule returns
\[
2\cdot\frac59\cdot\Bigl(\frac35\Bigr)^2+\frac89\cdot 0=\frac{2}{5}=I(x^4),
\]
so that rule is exact on this quartic, as predicted by the $2n-1=5$ exactness degree.

On $[0,2]$ one has $t=x+1$ and $dt=dx$. The mapped nodes are $1\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$ with unchanged weights $1$. For the cubic,
\[
\bigl(1-s\bigr)^3+\bigl(1+s\bigr)^3=2+6s^2,\qquad s=1/\sqrt{3},
\]
which equals $2+2=4=\int_0^2 t^3\,dt$. For the quartic,
\[
\bigl(1-s\bigr)^4+\bigl(1+s\bigr)^4=2\bigl(1+6s^2+s^4\bigr)=2\Bigl(3+\frac19\Bigr)=\frac{56}{9},
\]
while $\int_0^2 t^4\,dt=32/5$, so the signed error is again $32/5-56/9=8/45$. The identity $(x+1)^4=x^4+q_3(x)$ with $q_3\in\mathbb P_3$ explains the coincidence: $Q_2$ kills the error on $q_3$, and the Jacobian is $1$.
\[
\boxed{\int_0^2 t^3=4\text{ exactly};\quad \int_0^2 t^4-Q=\frac{8}{45}}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: The roots of $P_2$ are $\pm 1/\sqrt{3}$ with weights $1$, so $Q_2$ is exact on $\mathbb P_3$. Then $I(x^4)=2/5$, $Q_2(x^4)=2/9$, and the error $8/45$ is $p^{(4)}/135$ on quartics. The given three-point rule recovers $2/5$. On $[0,2]$ the mapped rule is exact on $t^3$ (value $4$) and repeats the error $8/45$ on $t^4$.
A two-node interpolatory rule is exact for every polynomial, including x^4. Therefore I(x^4)=Q2(x^4) and the error audit is identically zero.
I take the Chebyshev extrema ±√2/2 as nodes, assign equal weights, and call the result the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule because both families are orthogonal polynomials.

NUM:010523.title: A trapezoid Romberg triangle recovers the integral of a fifth power
NUM:010523.objective: Build a three-row Romberg table from composite trapezoid values for a monomial of degree five, identify the Richardson combinators 4^j, and prove that the $(2,2)$ entry is exact while the first extrapolated column is not.
NUM:010523.statement:
Let $I=\int_0^1 x^5\,dx$. Write $T(h)$ for the composite trapezoid rule on $[0,1]$ with uniform spacing $h$, so
\[
T(h)=\frac h2\bigl(f(0)+f(1)\bigr)+h\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}f(ih),\qquad n=1/h.
\]
Assume the Euler–Maclaurin expansion $T(h)=I+a_2h^2+a_4h^4+a_6h^6+\cdots$ whenever $f$ is smooth.

1. Compute the three values $T(1)$, $T(1/2)$, and $T(1/4)$ as rational numbers.

2. Form the Romberg triangle with $R_{k,0}=T(2^{-k})$ for $k=0,1,2$ and
   \[
   R_{k,j}=\frac{4^j R_{k,j-1}-R_{k-1,j-1}}{4^j-1}\qquad (1\le j\le k\le 2).
   \]
   Record every entry as a rational number. Identify $R_{2,2}$ with $I$.

3. Using only the even expansion of $T(h)$, prove that each column $j$ eliminates the terms through $h^{2j}$. Conclude that $R_{k,2}$ is exact for every polynomial of degree at most $5$. Explain why $R_{1,1}$ and $R_{2,1}$ need not equal $I$ for this integrand, and compute those two errors.

4. A colleague proposes to replace the table by a single pair of Simpson panels on $[0,1]$ together with the factor-$15$ difference estimator, or by a recursive adaptive Simpson walk. Explain why that substitution is a different algorithm, and why it is not an acceptable solution of this problem. Also reject the claim that the combinator $4^j$ may be replaced by $2^j$ because "halving $h$ always doubles the order."

Do not invoke an adaptive tolerance budget, a hidden-sample continuous function that vanishes on a dyadic grid, or a numerical-differentiation roundoff model.
permittedResults: Euler–Maclaurin: if $f$ is smooth, then $T(h)=I+\sum_{m=1}^{M}a_{2m}h^{2m}+O(h^{2M+2})$ with coefficients depending only on odd derivatives of $f$ at the endpoints.
If $S(h)=I+c\,h^{p}+O(h^{q})$ with $q>p>0$, the Richardson combination $\bigl(2^{p}S(h/2)-S(h)\bigr)/(2^{p}-1)$ cancels the $h^{p}$ term.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the three trapezoid sums by enumerating dyadic samples, then apply the two Richardson combinators.
Cancel $a_2$ and $a_4$ symbolically from the Euler–Maclaurin series first, then insert the numerical trapezoid values only to read off the exact $1/6$.

milestones.criterion: Computes the three composite trapezoid values as the stated rationals.
Fills the Romberg triangle with combinators 4 and 16 and identifies R_{2,2}=1/6 with the exact integral.
Explains even-power cancellation, records the column-1 errors 1/48 and 1/768, and refuses both a 2^j combinator and an adaptive Simpson substitution.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the trapezoid Romberg table by a two-panel Simpson difference estimator, an adaptive interval walk, or a hidden-sample dyadic vanishing argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned algorithm and the six trapezoid-based rationals are never produced.

commonErrors.description: Uses the combinator 2^j in place of 4^j, as if the leading trapezoid error were $O(h)$ rather than $O(h^2)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The $h^2$ term is not cancelled and $R_{2,2}$ is no longer equal to $1/6$.

hintTree.content: The interior sample of $T(1/2)$ is $(1/2)^5=1/32$. The three interior samples of $T(1/4)$ are $1/1024$, $1/32$, and $243/1024$.
The first extrapolated column uses the combinator $4$: $R_{k,1}=(4R_{k,0}-R_{k-1,0})/3$. The next column uses $16$.

For a polynomial of degree at most $5$, the endpoint difference $f^{(5)}(1)-f^{(5)}(0)$ vanishes, as do all higher endpoint-derivative differences. Thus the $h^6$ and higher Euler–Maclaurin terms vanish after column $j=2$ cancels the $h^2$ and $h^4$ terms.

NUM:010523.canonicalSolution:
The integrand is $f(x)=x^5$, so $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$. Then
\[
T(1)=\frac12,\qquad
T\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)=\frac14+\frac12\cdot\frac1{32}=\frac{17}{64},
\]
and
\[
T\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)=\frac18+\frac14\Bigl(\frac1{1024}+\frac1{32}+\frac{243}{1024}\Bigr)
=\frac18+\frac{69}{1024}=\frac{197}{1024}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T(1)=\frac12,\; T(1/2)=\frac{17}{64},\; T(1/4)=\frac{197}{1024}}.
\]

The Romberg triangle is
\begin{align*}
R_{0,0}&=\frac12,\\
R_{1,0}&=\frac{17}{64},&
R_{1,1}&=\frac{4\cdot 17/64-1/2}{3}=\frac{3}{16},\\
R_{2,0}&=\frac{197}{1024},&
R_{2,1}&=\frac{4\cdot 197/1024-17/64}{3}=\frac{43}{256},&
R_{2,2}&=\frac{16\cdot 43/256-3/16}{15}=\frac16.
\end{align*}
The exact integral is $I=[x^6/6]_0^1=1/6$, so $R_{2,2}=I$.
\[
\boxed{R_{1,1}=3/16,\; R_{2,1}=43/256,\; R_{2,2}=1/6}.
\]

Write $T(h)=I+a_2h^2+a_4h^4+a_6h^6+\cdots$. The combination $(4T(h/2)-T(h))/3$ cancels $a_2$ and leaves an expansion in $h^4,h^6,\ldots$. Repeating with combinator $16$ cancels $a_4$. In the Euler–Maclaurin formula, $a_6$ is proportional to $f^{(5)}(1)-f^{(5)}(0)$. For a polynomial of degree at most $5$, $f^{(5)}$ is constant and every higher endpoint-derivative difference also vanishes. Thus column $j=2$ is exact. Column $j=1$ still carries an $h^4$ term. Explicitly
\[
R_{1,1}-I=\frac{3}{16}-\frac16=\frac1{48},\qquad
R_{2,1}-I=\frac{43}{256}-\frac16=\frac1{768},
\]
and the second error is the first divided by $16$, as predicted by $h\mapsto h/2$ in an $O(h^4)$ expansion.

A pair of Simpson panels with a factor-$15$ estimator is one Richardson step applied to Simpson, not a trapezoid Romberg table; an adaptive walk further changes the sample set according to a local budget. Neither construction produces the six rational entries demanded above. Replacing $4^j$ by $2^j$ would be the correct combinator only for an odd first error term $O(h)$, which Euler–Maclaurin does not supply for the trapezoid rule.

graderFixtures.proofText: The trapezoid values are $1/2$, $17/64$, and $197/1024$. Richardson with combinators $4$ and $16$ produces $R_{1,1}=3/16$, $R_{2,1}=43/256$, and $R_{2,2}=1/6$. Column $2$ is exact on degree $\le 5$; the column-$1$ errors are $1/48$ and $1/768$. Adaptive Simpson is a different algorithm, and the combinator is $4^j$ not $2^j$.
I compare one Simpson panel with two Simpson panels on [0,1], form the factor-15 estimator, and recursively bisect any interval whose estimator exceeds a local budget. That is the Romberg table.
Halving h always doubles accuracy, so I extrapolate by (2 T(h/2)-T(h))/(2-1) in every column. The resulting bottom-right entry is 53/256, which I report as the value of the integral.

NUM:010531.title: A Monte Carlo mean is unbiased, but Chebyshev still buys the sample size
NUM:010531.objective: Prove that the crude Monte Carlo estimator of an explicit integral is unbiased, compute its variance in closed form, and produce a Chebyshev sample-size certificate that is not a deterministic adaptive-quadrature bound.
NUM:010531.statement:
Let $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$ and let
\[
I=\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx.
\]
Draw $U_1,\ldots,U_N$ i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$ and set
\[
I_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(U_i).
\]

1. Evaluate $I$ exactly. Prove that $I_N$ is unbiased, i.e. $\mathbb E[I_N]=I$, using only linearity of expectation and the integral representation of $\mathbb E[f(U)]$. State the $L^1$ hypothesis that makes the expectation finite.

2. Compute $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(f(U))=\int_0^1 f(x)^2\,dx-I^2$ as an exact rational. Deduce $\operatorname{Var}(I_N)$. Explain why independence of the sample is used, and why the variance decays as $N^{-1}$ rather than as a negative power of a mesh width.

3. Chebyshev's inequality gives
   \[
   \mathbb P\bigl(|I_N-I|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(I_N)}{\varepsilon^2}.
   \]
   Find the smallest integer $N$ that makes the right-hand side at most $\delta=1/15$ when $\varepsilon=1/12$. This $N$ is a distribution-free certificate. Explain why a normal-quantile formula with the same $\varepsilon,\delta$ is a different, non-equivalent claim.

4. As a purely algebraic check of the estimator formula, evaluate $I_4$ on the four deterministic abscissae $1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5$ and report the exact error $I_4-I$. This calculation does not prove the Chebyshev bound and is not a quadrature panel. Do not replace $I_N$ by a Simpson or adaptive Simpson estimator, do not invoke the hidden-sampling bump from the adaptive held exercise, and do not balance a differentiation-roundoff model.
permittedResults: If $U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ and $f\in L^1[0,1]$, then $\mathbb E[f(U)]=\int_0^1 f$. If also $f\in L^2[0,1]$, then $\operatorname{Var}(f(U))=\int f^2-(\int f)^2$ is finite.
Chebyshev: $\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E X|\ge\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/\varepsilon^2$ whenever the variance is finite. For an i.i.d. mean this is $\sigma^2/(N\varepsilon^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the first two moments of x^2 on [0,1] exactly, then invert Chebyshev for N.
Separate three claims: an expectation identity, a variance identity that uses independence, and a distribution-free tail bound.

milestones.criterion: Proves E[I_N]=I=1/3 by linearity and the uniform integral, without assuming independence for unbiasedness.
Computes σ^2=4/45 and Var(I_N)=4/(45N), and produces the Chebyshev sample size N=192 for ε=1/12, δ=1/15.
Keeps the four-point check I_4=3/10 separate from the probability bound and refuses to replace MC by adaptive Simpson.

commonErrors.description: Replaces I_N by a composite Simpson or adaptive Simpson estimator, or analyses the hidden-sampling bump and differentiation-roundoff balance from the adaptive held exercise.
commonErrors.consequence: The unbiased random-mean model is abandoned in favour of a deterministic quadrature packet.

commonErrors.description: Reports Var(I_N)=σ^2, or demands only N≥σ/ε, or treats the four deterministic abscissae as a proof that |I_N-I|<ε with probability 1-δ.
commonErrors.consequence: The 1/N variance law or the Chebyshev certificate is lost.

hintTree.content: Each term has the same expectation $\int_0^1 x^2\,dx=1/3$. Linearity does not need independence; the variance identity does.
Compute $\int_0^1 x^4=1/5$ and subtract $(1/3)^2$. The variance of the mean then divides by $N$.
The threshold is $N\ge(4/45)/((1/12)^2(1/15))$. The $4$ in the numerator is $\sigma^2$ times $45$.

NUM:010531.canonicalSolution:
Directly, $I=\int_0^1 x^2\,dx=1/3$. Each $U_i$ is uniform, so
\[
\mathbb E[f(U_i)]=\int_0^1 x^2\,dx=\frac13,
\]
which is finite because $f\in L^1[0,1]$. Linearity of expectation, which does not use independence, gives
\[
\mathbb E[I_N]=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E[f(U_i)]=I.
\]
\[
\boxed{I=1/3,\quad\mathbb E[I_N]=I}.
\]

The second moment is $\int_0^1 x^4\,dx=1/5$, so
\[
\sigma^2=\frac15-\frac19=\frac4{45}.
\]
Independence (or even pairwise uncorrelation) of the sample eliminates cross terms:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(I_N)=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}N=\frac{4}{45N}.
\]
There is no mesh width $h$ in the estimator: the only refinement parameter is the sample size, and the variance is exactly inversely proportional to $N$.
\[
\boxed{\sigma^2=4/45,\quad\operatorname{Var}(I_N)=4/(45N)}.
\]

Chebyshev requires $4/(45N\varepsilon^2)\le\delta$. With $\varepsilon=1/12$ and $\delta=1/15$,
\[
N\ge\frac{4/45}{(1/12)^2\cdot(1/15)}=\frac{4}{45}\cdot 144\cdot 15=192.
\]
The smallest such integer is $192$. A normal-quantile rule $N\ge z_{1-\delta/2}^2\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2$ assumes an approximately Gaussian mean and produces a strictly smaller $N$; it is not implied by Chebyshev and is not the certificate asked for.
\[
\boxed{N\ge 192}.
\]

On the four listed abscissae,
\[
I_4=\frac14\cdot\frac{1+4+9+16}{25}=\frac{30}{100}=\frac3{10},\qquad
I_4-I=\frac3{10}-\frac13=-\frac1{30}.
\]
This checks the arithmetic of the sample-mean formula. It is not a random sample, not a Simpson panel, and not a proof of the probability bound. Adaptive Simpson with a local error budget, hidden dyadic aliasing, and differentiation-roundoff balance belong to a different held exercise: those procedures are deterministic and governed by truncation and sampling rules rather than Monte Carlo sampling variance, and they refine a mesh rather than an i.i.d. sample.

graderFixtures.proofText: I=1/3 and I_N is unbiased by linearity. σ^2=1/5-1/9=4/45, so Var(I_N)=4/(45N). Chebyshev with ε=1/12 and δ=1/15 forces N≥192. The four abscissae give I_4=3/10 and error -1/30, which checks the formula only. This is not Simpson, not adaptive Simpson, and not a CLT certificate.

Monte Carlo with N=4 is just Simpson or two-panel adaptive Simpson on [0,1]. I reuse the step-doubling estimator (S_2-S_1)/15 and the hidden bump that vanishes on the quarter grid, and I discuss the central-difference roundoff balance.
The variance of I_N is 4/45, independent of N, so I take N≥σ/ε=√(4/45)/(1/12). The four points 1/5,…,4/5 already satisfy |I_4-1/3|=1/30<1/12, which proves the Chebyshev bound for N=4.

NUM:010627.title: One classical RK4 step is fifth-order locally and fourth-order globally
NUM:010627.objective: Execute one classical RK4 step with exact stage arithmetic, match the method to the Taylor flow through order four on a linear test, and separate local O(h^5) error from global O(h^4) error on a fixed interval.
NUM:010627.statement:
Classical four-stage Runge–Kutta (RK4) for $y'=f(t,y)$ advances by
\[
\begin{aligned}
k_1&=f(t_n,y_n),\\
k_2&=f\bigl(t_n+\tfrac h2,\,y_n+\tfrac h2 k_1\bigr),\\
k_3&=f\bigl(t_n+\tfrac h2,\,y_n+\tfrac h2 k_2\bigr),\\
k_4&=f(t_n+h,\,y_n+h k_3),\\
y_{n+1}&=y_n+\frac h6\bigl(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The local error of a one-step map $\Phi$ is
$\delta(t;h)=y(t+h)-\bigl(y(t)+h\Phi(t,y(t);h)\bigr)$,
and the local truncation error is $\tau(t;h)=\delta(t;h)/h$.

1. Take $y'=t-y$ with $y(0)=1$ and a single step of size $h=1/2$. Compute $k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4$ and $y_1$ as exact rationals. Derive the exact solution $y(t)=t-1+2e^{-t}$ from the integrating factor $e^{t}$, evaluate $y(1/2)$, and write the local error as an exact expression in $e^{-1/2}$.

2. Now take the linear test $y'=y$. Prove that one RK4 step multiplies the value by
   \[
   R_4(h)=1+h+\frac{h^2}{2}+\frac{h^3}{6}+\frac{h^4}{24}.
   \]
   Compare $R_4(h)$ with the Taylor series of $e^{h}$ and conclude that the local error is $O(h^5)$ while $\tau=O(h^4)$. Evaluate $R_4(1/2)$ exactly.

3. Let $f$ be Lipschitz in $y$, uniformly for $t$ in a fixed compact interval $[0,T]$, and suppose a one-step method has local error $O(h^{p+1})$. Prove that the global error at $t_n=nh\le T$ is $O(h^{p})$. Identify $p$ for classical RK4. Explain why “the local error is $O(h^5)$, therefore the method is fifth order” is false.

4. Do not replace the order argument by a stability-function audit of $R_4(z)$ for $\operatorname{Re}z\ll 0$, do not switch to explicit Euler or the implicit trapezoidal rule, and do not treat a two-stage Heun step as classical RK4. Stiff absolute stability is a different held exercise.
permittedResults: If $f$ is Lipschitz in $y$ on a strip about the graph of a $C^5$ solution, the RK4 increment matches the Taylor expansion of the flow through order $h^4$, so $\delta=O(h^5)$ and $\tau=O(h^4)$.
Ladywindermere's fan: summing $T/h$ local defects of size $O(h^{p+1})$, each amplified by a Lipschitz factor $e^{LT}$ independent of $h$, produces a global bound $O(h^{p})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the four stages in order with exact fractions, then expand the autonomous linear test to read the Taylor polynomial of e^h.
Compare one RK4 step from the exact value against the closed-form flow to isolate the local defect, then invoke Ladywindermere's fan for the global power.

milestones.criterion: Computes the four classical RK4 stages and the exact rational value y_1=137/192 for y'=t-y, and identifies the local error 2e^{-1/2}-233/192.
Derives R_4(h)=1+h+h^2/2+h^3/6+h^4/24, evaluates R_4(1/2)=211/128, and matches the exponential Taylor series through order four.
Concludes that local O(h^5) yields global O(h^4) on a fixed Lipschitz interval and rejects a fifth-order global claim.

commonErrors.description: Declares classical RK4 to be a fifth-order method because a single step has local error O(h^5), or reports the global order as five on [0,T].
commonErrors.consequence: The T/h accumulation of local defects is ignored, so the standard one-step order theorem is misstated.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the four classical stages by explicit Euler, by Heun's two-stage rule, or by evaluating every stage at the left endpoint, and reports the resulting value as the RK4 step.
commonErrors.consequence: The stage vector and the value 137/192 are lost, and the Taylor match through h^4 is no longer the method being discussed.

hintTree.content: The first stage is $k_1=f(0,1)=-1$. The second argument of $k_2$ is $1+(1/4)k_1=3/4$, not $1+(1/2)k_1$.
For $y'=y$ every stage is a multiple of $y_n$. Collect powers of $h$ in $k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4$ before dividing by $6$.
There are $T/h$ steps on $[0,T]$. An $O(h^5)$ defect per step cannot remain $O(h^5)$ after that many additions unless a miraculous cancellation is proved; Lipschitz only gives $O(h^4)$.

NUM:010627.canonicalSolution:
For $y'=t-y$, $y(0)=1$, and $h=1/2$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
k_1&=0-1=-1,\\
k_2&=f\bigl(\tfrac14,1+\tfrac14(-1)\bigr)=f\bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac34\bigr)=\tfrac14-\tfrac34=-\tfrac12,\\
k_3&=f\bigl(\tfrac14,1+\tfrac14(-\tfrac12)\bigr)=f\bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac78\bigr)=\tfrac14-\tfrac78=-\tfrac58,\\
k_4&=f\bigl(\tfrac12,1+\tfrac12(-\tfrac58)\bigr)=f\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac{11}{16}\bigr)=\tfrac12-\tfrac{11}{16}=-\tfrac{3}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The weighted sum is
\[
k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4=-1-1-\tfrac{10}{8}-\tfrac{3}{16}=-\tfrac{55}{16},
\]
so
\[
y_1=1+\frac{1}{12}\Bigl(-\frac{55}{16}\Bigr)=1-\frac{55}{192}=\frac{137}{192}.
\]
\[
\boxed{k=(-1,-1/2,-5/8,-3/16),\quad y_1=137/192}.
\]
The linear ODE $y'+y=t$ has integrating factor $e^{t}$. Then $(ye^{t})'=te^{t}$, so $ye^{t}=e^{t}(t-1)+C$. The condition $y(0)=1$ forces $C=2$, hence $y(t)=t-1+2e^{-t}$ and
\[
y\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)=-\tfrac12+2e^{-1/2}.
\]
Under the definition in the statement, the local error is the exact value minus the computed step:
\[
\delta=\Bigl(-\frac12+2e^{-1/2}\Bigr)-\frac{137}{192}=2e^{-1/2}-\frac{233}{192}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\delta=2e^{-1/2}-233/192}.
\]

For $y'=y$ the stages collapse:
\[
k_1=y,\quad
k_2=y\bigl(1+\tfrac h2\bigr),\quad
k_3=y\bigl(1+\tfrac h2+\tfrac{h^2}{4}\bigr),\quad
k_4=y\bigl(1+h+\tfrac{h^2}{2}+\tfrac{h^3}{4}\bigr).
\]
Adding $k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4$ produces $y(6+3h+h^2+h^3/4)$, and division by $6$ followed by multiplication by $h$ yields
\[
R_4(h)=1+h+\frac{h^2}{2}+\frac{h^3}{6}+\frac{h^4}{24}.
\]
The exact flow multiplies by $e^{h}=R_4(h)+h^5/120+O(h^6)$. Thus $\delta=O(h^5)$ and $\tau=O(h^4)$. At $h=1/2$,
\[
R_4\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)=1+\tfrac12+\tfrac18+\tfrac1{48}+\tfrac1{384}=\frac{211}{128}.
\]
\[
\boxed{R_4(h)=1+h+h^2/2+h^3/6+h^4/24,\quad R_4(1/2)=211/128}.
\]

On a fixed interval $[0,T]$ a Lipschitz constant $L$ for $f$ in $y$ gives a one-step stability factor $1+O(h)$. Ladywindermere's fan then bounds the accumulated error by a constant times $(T/h)\cdot O(h^{p+1})=O(h^{p})$. Classical RK4 has $p=4$: local $O(h^5)$, global $O(h^4)$. Declaring the method fifth order because a single step has defect $O(h^5)$ forgets the $T/h$ steps. The quantity $R_4(z)$ for $\operatorname{Re}z\ll 0$ is a stability-function question and is not required here; the present $h=1/2$ computation is an order audit, not a stiff-amplification audit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The stages are -1, -1/2, -5/8, -3/16 and y_1=137/192. The exact solution is t-1+2e^{-t}, so the exact-minus-numerical local error is 2e^{-1/2}-233/192. For y'=y the RK4 factor is 1+h+h^2/2+h^3/6+h^4/24, equal to 211/128 at h=1/2, hence local O(h^5) and global O(h^4) on a fixed Lipschitz interval. Heun is not RK4, and a local O(h^5) defect is not a global fifth-order theorem.
Each RK4 step has local error O(h^5), so after any number of steps the global error is still O(h^5). Classical RK4 is therefore a fifth-order method on [0,T].
I take the improved Euler / Heun step k_1=f(0,1)=-1, k_2=f(1/2,1/2)=-1/2, and set y_1=1+(1/4)(-1-1/2)=5/8. This is the classical RK4 value because Heun is a Runge–Kutta method.

NUM:010628.title: An AB2 predictor needs a second value before the AM2 corrector can start
NUM:010628.objective: Derive the two-step Adams–Bashforth predictor and the second-order Adams–Moulton corrector from interpolants, audit how the starting value controls the observed error, and execute one PECE step without solving the implicit trapezoidal equation.
NUM:010628.statement:
Work with the linear multistep pair
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{AB2:}\quad
y_{n+1}&=y_n+\frac h2\bigl(3f_n-f_{n-1}\bigr),\\
\text{AM2:}\quad
y_{n+1}&=y_n+\frac h2\bigl(f_{n+1}+f_n\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
where AM2 is the implicit trapezoidal Adams–Moulton formula of order $2$, not the two-step third-order Adams–Moulton formula. A PECE step predicts with AB2, evaluates $f$ at the predicted value, and corrects once with AM2 using that predicted $f_{n+1}$.

1. Derive AB2 by integrating, from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$, the unique linear interpolant of $f$ through $(t_{n-1},f_{n-1})$ and $(t_n,f_n)$. Derive AM2 by integrating the linear interpolant through $(t_n,f_n)$ and $(t_{n+1},f_{n+1})$. State the orders: local increment error $O(h^3)$ and global order $2$ under the usual Lipschitz and zero-stability hypotheses.

2. Starting-value audit. AB2 requires two values. If $y_1=y(h)+\Theta(h)$, the global order on a fixed interval drops to $1$. If $y_1=y(h)+O(h^2)$, global order $2$ is retained. For the manufactured problem $y'=2t$, $y(0)=0$, $h=1/2$, compute two AB2-ready values and the first AB2 step in each of the following starts: (i) explicit Euler for $y_1$; (ii) Heun / improved Euler for $y_1$. Compare both paths with the exact nodes $y(1/2)=1/4$ and $y(1)=1$.

3. PECE computation. For $y'=y$, $y(0)=1$, $h=1/2$, start with one Heun step, then perform one AB2 predict and one AM2 correct to reach $t=2h$. Report $y_1$, $y_2^{\mathrm P}$, and $y_2^{\mathrm C}$ as exact rationals. Do not replace the corrector by the implicit solve $y_2=(1+h/2)/(1-h/2)\,y_1$.

4. Explain why copying $y_1=y_0$ is not an order-$2$ start for $y'=y$. Do not convert the pair into a stiff absolute-stability comparison of Euler against trapezoidal, and do not use the third-order Adams–Moulton weights $(5,8,-1)/12$ while calling the method AM2.
permittedResults: Integrating a degree-$1$ interpolant of $f$ over an interval of length $h$ incurs an $O(h^3)$ increment error when $f$ is $C^2$, which is local error $O(h^3)$ and, for a zero-stable LMM, global order $2$.
Dahlquist's first barrier and the standard LMM convergence theorem: a zero-stable consistent method of order $p$ converges with order $p$ provided the starting errors are $O(h^{p})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the Newton interpolant of f to get the coefficients, then run the two manufactured starts before the PECE arithmetic.
Obtain y_1 by Heun, predict with the AB2 stencil, and correct once with predicted f; compare against the exact quadratic and against e.

milestones.criterion: Derives AB2 and AM2 by integrating the stated linear interpolants and records local O(h^3) increment error with global order 2.
Produces the y'=2t paths (0, 3/4) from Euler and (1/4, 1) from Heun, and the PECE values 13/8, 83/32, 343/128.
Separates a Theta(h) copied start from an O(h^2) start, and refuses to replace PECE by an implicit stiff trapezoidal solve.

commonErrors.description: Sets y_1=y_0 and claims the AB2/AM2 pair still has global order 2, or treats AB2 as a one-step method that does not need a second value.
commonErrors.consequence: The starting-value hypothesis of the LMM convergence theorem is violated, and the PECE arithmetic is started from the wrong node.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the one-evaluation AM2 corrector by the implicit solve y_{n+1}=(1+h/2)/(1-h/2) y_n, or analyses |R(z)| for large negative z, or inserts the AM3 weights (5,8,-1)/12.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned PECE pair is abandoned in favour of the stiff trapezoidal exercise or a different Adams formula.

hintTree.content: Write the AB2 interpolant as $f_n+((t-t_n)/h)(f_n-f_{n-1})$ and integrate $t-t_n$ from $0$ to $h$. The coefficient of $f_n-f_{n-1}$ is $h/2$.
For $y'=2t$ the slope does not depend on $y$, so Euler's $y_1$ is $0$ while $f_1=1$ still. Heun recovers $y_1=h^2=1/4$.
Heun on $y'=y$ with $h=1/2$ gives $y_1=13/8$. Predict with $(h/2)(3f_1-f_0)$, then correct with $(h/2)(f_2^{\mathrm P}+f_1)$.

NUM:010628.canonicalSolution:
Let $s=t-t_n$. The AB2 interpolant is $p(t)=f_n+(s/h)(f_n-f_{n-1})$. Then
\[
\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}p=\;h f_n+\frac{h}{2}(f_n-f_{n-1})=\frac h2(3f_n-f_{n-1}),
\]
which is AB2. The AM2 interpolant through the new node is the trapezoid, with integral $(h/2)(f_n+f_{n+1})$. A $C^2$ integrand makes the linear interpolant's integral error $O(h^3)$, so both formulas have local increment error $O(h^3)$ and, being zero-stable, global order $2$.
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{AB2}:\ (h/2)(3f_n-f_{n-1});\quad\mathrm{AM2}:\ (h/2)(f_n+f_{n+1})}.
\]

For $y'=2t$, $y(0)=0$, $h=1/2$ one has $f_0=0$ and $f_1=1$ independently of $y_1$. Explicit Euler gives $y_1=0$, then
\[
y_2=0+\frac14(3\cdot 1-0)=\frac34.
\]
Heun uses $k_1=0$, $k_2=1$, so $y_1=(1/4)(0+1)=1/4$, then
\[
y_2=\frac14+\frac14(3\cdot 1-0)=1.
\]
The exact nodes are $y(h)=h^2=1/4$ and $y(2h)=1$. Euler therefore misses both nodes; Heun plus AB2 is exact on this quadratic solution.
\[
\boxed{\text{Euler path }(y_1,y_2)=(0,3/4);\quad\text{Heun path }(1/4,1)}.
\]

For $y'=y$, $y(0)=1$, $h=1/2$, Heun gives
\[
k_1=1,\quad k_2=\tfrac32,\quad y_1=1+\tfrac14\bigl(1+\tfrac32\bigr)=\frac{13}{8}.
\]
Then $f_0=1$, $f_1=13/8$, and AB2 predicts
\[
y_2^{\mathrm P}=\frac{13}{8}+\frac14\Bigl(3\cdot\frac{13}{8}-1\Bigr)=\frac{13}{8}+\frac{31}{32}=\frac{83}{32}.
\]
One AM2 correction with the predicted slope $83/32$ produces
\[
y_2^{\mathrm C}=\frac{13}{8}+\frac14\Bigl(\frac{83}{32}+\frac{13}{8}\Bigr)=\frac{13}{8}+\frac{135}{128}=\frac{343}{128}.
\]
\[
\boxed{y_1=13/8,\quad y_2^{\mathrm P}=83/32,\quad y_2^{\mathrm C}=343/128}.
\]
The implicit trapezoidal amplification $(1+h/2)/(1-h/2)$ is a different computation: it solves for an unknown $f_2$ rather than using the PECE predicted slope, and it is the stiff held exercise when $|h\lambda|$ is large.

Copying $y_1=y_0=1$ on $y'=y$ produces a $\Theta(h)$ start because $e^{h}-1\sim h$. The subsequent PECE values are $y_2^{\mathrm P}=3/2$ and $y_2^{\mathrm C}=13/8$, far from $e$. That start is not $O(h^2)$ and does not retain order $2$. A single explicit Euler step is $O(h^2)$ and therefore theoretically order-preserving for this second-order pair, but the safer matched starter is a second-order one-step method such as Heun.

graderFixtures.proofText: AB2 integrates the linear interpolant through f_{n-1},f_n and AM2 integrates the trapezoid through f_n,f_{n+1}. On y'=2t, Euler then AB2 yields (0, 3/4) while Heun then AB2 yields the exact nodes (1/4, 1). On y'=y, Heun gives 13/8, AB2 predicts 83/32, and one AM2 correction with that predicted slope gives 343/128. Copying y_1=y_0 is a Theta(h) start. The implicit factor (1+h/2)/(1-h/2) is not the PECE corrector.
AB2 only needs the current value, so I set y_1=y_0=1 and proceed. Because AB2 and AM2 are both order 2, this copied start still gives a second-order method on [0,1].
The AM2 corrector is the implicit trapezoidal rule, so I set y_2=(1+h/2)/(1-h/2) y_1=(5/3)(13/8)=65/24 and then discuss |R(-10)|. Equivalently I use the weights (5,8,-1)/12.

NUM:010629.title: Linear shooting hits the far boundary in one sensitivity step
NUM:010629.objective: Reduce a linear two-point boundary problem to two initial-value problems, identify the missing slope by a sensitivity solve that terminates in one step, and evaluate a discrete Heun shooting function on a two-step grid.
NUM:010629.statement:
Consider the linear two-point problem
\[
y''=y-t,\qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y(1)=0.
\]

1. Solve the initial-value problem with $y(0)=0$ and $y'(0)=s$ in closed form. Deduce the unique missing slope $s_*$ for which $y(1;s_*)=0$, and write the exact solution $y(t)$. Equivalently, introduce the pair of IVPs
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   u''&=u-t,& u(0)&=0,& u'(0)&=0,\\
   v''&=v,& v(0)&=0,& v'(0)&=1,
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   and obtain $s_*$ from $u(1)+s_* v(1)=0$.

2. Let $z=\partial y/\partial s$. Derive the sensitivity IVP satisfied by $z$, evaluate $z(1)$, and perform one Newton update
   \[
   s_1=s_0-\frac{y(1;s_0)-0}{z(1;s_0)}
   \]
   from the initial guess $s_0=0$. Prove that $s_1=s_*$ and explain why a linear BVP needs only one such correction.

3. Now discretize the first-order system $y'=v$, $v'=y-t$ by Heun's method (improved Euler) with $h=1/2$, starting from $y_0=0$, $v_0=s$. Compute the discrete map $s\mapsto y_2(s)$ with exact rational arithmetic, and solve $y_2(s)=0$. Confirm that one discrete Newton step from $s_0=0$, using the discrete sensitivity $\partial y_2/\partial s$, recovers the same slope.

4. Do not replace shooting by a centered three-point Poisson stencil, do not treat the far condition as $y'(1)=0$, and do not iterate Newton as if $s\mapsto y(1;s)$ were a genuinely nonlinear scalar map.
permittedResults: Superposition for a linear second-order ODE: the IVP solution is $y=u+s v$ with $u$ absorbing the inhomogeneity and left value, and $v$ the homogeneous response to $v'(a)=1$.
If $\phi(s)=A+Bs$ with $B\neq 0$, Newton's method from any $s_0$ yields the exact root in one iteration, because $\phi'(s)=B$ is constant.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the linear IVP by a particular solution plus sinh, then differentiate in s to get the sensitivity.
Run two exact-arithmetic Heun steps with symbolic initial slope s and solve the resulting affine equation y_2(s)=0.

milestones.criterion: Produces the closed-form shooting solution and the exact missing slope 1-1/sinh(1) from the two-IVP superposition.
Derives the sensitivity IVP, evaluates z(1)=sinh(1), and shows that one Newton step from s=0 is exact.
Computes the two-step Heun map y_2=9s/8-1/8 and the discrete slope 1/9, recovered again by one discrete Newton step.

commonErrors.description: Imposes y'(1)=0 instead of y(1)=0, or reports a guessed slope such as s=1 or s=0 as the BVP solution without matching the far value.
commonErrors.consequence: The shooting function is never zeroed, so the two-point problem is not solved.

commonErrors.description: Iterates Newton repeatedly as if φ were nonlinear, or abandons shooting and writes a centered second-difference Poisson system for the same BVP.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact one-step termination for a linear shooting map is missed, or the method is replaced by the finite-difference packet.

hintTree.content: A particular solution of $y''=y-t$ is $y=t$. The homogeneous solutions are $\sinh$ and $\cosh$, and $y(0)=0$ kills the $\cosh$ coefficient.
Differentiating $y''=y-t$ with respect to $s$ gives $z''=z$ with $z(0)=0$ and $z'(0)=1$, so $z=\sinh$.
Heun on the system uses $k_1=(v,y-t)$ and a full Euler predictor before $k_2$. After two steps the $y$-component is affine: $9s/8-1/8$.

NUM:010629.canonicalSolution:
The function $t$ is a particular solution of $y''=y-t$. The general solution with $y(0)=0$ is therefore
\[
y(t;s)=t+(s-1)\sinh t,
\]
because $y'(t;s)=1+(s-1)\cosh t$ forces $y'(0)=s$. The far condition $y(1;s)=0$ reads $1+(s-1)\sinh 1=0$, so
\[
s_*=1-\frac1{\sinh 1}.
\]
Equivalently, $u(t)=t-\sinh t$ and $v(t)=\sinh t$ give $u(1)+s v(1)=1-\sinh 1+s\sinh 1=0$ and the same $s_*$. The exact solution of the BVP is
\[
y(t)=t-\frac{\sinh t}{\sinh 1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{s_*=1-1/\sinh 1,\quad y(t)=t-\sinh t/\sinh 1}.
\]

Differentiating the IVP in $s$ produces $z''=z$, $z(0)=0$, $z'(0)=1$, hence $z(t)=\sinh t$ and $z(1)=\sinh 1$. From $s_0=0$ one has $y(1;0)=1-\sinh 1$, so
\[
s_1=0-\frac{1-\sinh 1}{\sinh 1}=1-\frac1{\sinh 1}=s_*.
\]
The shooting map is affine, $\phi(s)=1+(s-1)\sinh 1$, so $\phi'$ is the nonzero constant $\sinh 1$ and Newton is exact in one step.

Now Heun with $h=1/2$. From $(y,v)=(0,s)$ at $t=0$,
\[
k_1=(s,0),\qquad
Y_{\mathrm e}=(s/2,s),\qquad
k_2=(s,s/2-1/2),
\]
\[
(y_1,v_1)=\bigl(s/2,\,9s/8-1/8\bigr).
\]
The second step, from $t=1/2$, produces
\[
k_1=\bigl(9s/8-1/8,\,s/2-1/2\bigr),
\]
\[
Y_{\mathrm e}=\bigl(17s/16-1/16,\,11s/8-3/8\bigr),
\]
\[
k_2=\bigl(11s/8-3/8,\,17s/16-17/16\bigr),
\]
and the updated $y$-component is
\[
y_2=\frac s2+\frac14\Bigl(\frac{9s}{8}-\frac18+\frac{11s}{8}-\frac38\Bigr)=\frac{9s}{8}-\frac18.
\]
The discrete far condition $y_2=0$ forces $s_h=1/9$. The discrete sensitivity is the constant $9/8$. From $s_0=0$ one has $y_2(0)=-1/8$, and
\[
s_1=0-\frac{-1/8}{9/8}=\frac19=s_h.
\]
\[
\boxed{y_2(s)=9s/8-1/8,\quad s_h=1/9}.
\]
A centered Poisson stencil on the same two interior nodes is a different discretization (the next packet) and does not compute a missing initial slope.

graderFixtures.proofText: y(t;s)=t+(s-1)sinh t, so s_*=1-1/sinh(1) and y(t)=t-sinh(t)/sinh(1). The sensitivity is z=sinh, and one Newton step from 0 returns s_*. Two Heun steps give y_2=9s/8-1/8, hence s_h=1/9, and the discrete Newton update from 0 is again 1/9. The map is affine, so further Newton iterations are unnecessary. This is not a Poisson stencil.

I shoot with s=0, or with s=1, and I stop without enforcing y(1)=0. Alternatively I replace the far condition by y'(1)=0 because a homogeneous left value should match a homogeneous derivative on the right.

Shooting maps are nonlinear, so I run several Newton or secant updates. Better, I discretize y''=y-t by the three-point stencil on x=1/3,2/3 and solve a 2-by-2 Poisson system instead of integrating IVPs.

NUM:010630.title: A two-node Poisson grid makes truncation visible and quadratics exact
NUM:010630.objective: Derive the O(h^2) truncation of the centered second difference, solve an explicit two-unknown Dirichlet Poisson system by hand, and separate nodal error from truncation by comparing a quartic manufactured solution with an exact quadratic.
NUM:010630.statement:
On $(0,1)$ consider the Dirichlet Poisson problem $-u''=f$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$. The centered scheme on a uniform mesh of width $h=1/(N+1)$ with interior nodes $x_i=ih$ reads
\[
\frac{-U_{i-1}+2U_i-U_{i+1}}{h^2}=f(x_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
with $U_0=U_{N+1}=0$.

1. Expand $u(x\pm h)$ through order $h^4$ and prove that the local truncation
   \[
   \tau_i=\frac{-u(x_{i-1})+2u(x_i)-u(x_{i+1})}{h^2}-f(x_i)
   \]
   equals $-(h^2/12)u^{(4)}(\xi_i)$ whenever $-u''=f$ and $u\in C^4$. Identify the order of the scheme.

2. Take the manufactured solution $u(x)=x^2(1-x)^2$. Compute $u''$, $u^{(4)}$, and $f=-u''$. On the two-unknown mesh $h=1/3$, evaluate $f$ at the interior nodes, write the $2\times 2$ system, and solve it exactly. Compare $U$ with the exact nodal samples of $u$, and evaluate $\tau_i$ both from the Taylor formula and by applying the discrete operator to the exact nodal vector.

3. Repeat the same two-unknown mesh for the quadratic problem $-w''=2$, $w(0)=w(1)=0$. Solve the system and compare with $w(x)=x(1-x)$. Explain the exact nodal recovery using part 1.

4. From $AU=F$ and $Au_{\mathrm{nodal}}=F+\tau$, deduce $A(U-u_{\mathrm{nodal}})=-\tau$. Compute the nodal error vector explicitly for the quartic example, and explain why $\|U-u_{\mathrm{nodal}}\|_\infty$ is not equal to $\|\tau\|_\infty$. Do not replace the stencil by a shooting IVP, and do not claim that exactness on quadratics makes the scheme exact for every smooth $f$.
permittedResults: Taylor's theorem with even remainder: $u(x+h)+u(x-h)-2u(x)=h^2 u''(x)+(h^4/12)u^{(4)}(\xi)$ for some $\xi$ between $x-h$ and $x+h$.

The discrete Dirichlet Laplacian $(1/h^2)\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)$ is symmetric positive definite, hence invertible, and the discrete maximum principle bounds $\|e\|_\infty$ by a mesh-independent multiple of $\|\tau\|_\infty$ on $[0,1]$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the even combination u(x+h)+u(x-h), then assemble and invert the 2-by-2 Dirichlet matrix by hand.
Use a manufactured quartic with constant fourth derivative so that τ is a pure multiple of h^2, and audit the same mesh on a quadratic.

milestones.criterion: Derives the centered truncation τ=-(h^2/12)u^{(4)}(ξ) and identifies second-order consistency.
Solves the h=1/3 quartic system as U=(2/27,2/27), matches τ=-2/9 by both Taylor and the discrete residual, and records e=(2/81,2/81).
Recovers the quadratic nodes exactly and explains that nodal error is A^{-1}(-τ), not τ itself.

commonErrors.description: Discretizes u'' by a one-sided first difference, by (u_{i+1}-u_{i-1})/(2h), or by (u_{i+1}-u_{i-1})/(2h^2), and treats the resulting matrix as the Poisson scheme.
commonErrors.consequence: The stencil is inconsistent for -u'' or drops to first order, and the exact 2-by-2 solve is for the wrong operator.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the nodal error 2/81 with the truncation 2/9, or claims that exact recovery of the quadratic makes the scheme exact for the quartic and for every smooth f.
commonErrors.consequence: Consistency is confused with convergence, and the role of A^{-1} is lost.

hintTree.content: Odd powers cancel in $u(x+h)+u(x-h)$. After dividing by $h^2$ and subtracting $f=-u''$, the first surviving term is $-(h^2/12)u^{(4)}$.
For $u=x^2(1-x)^2$ one has $u^{(4)}=24$ constantly, so $\tau_i=-2h^2$ at every interior node. At $h=1/3$ the load is $f\equiv 2/3$ on both nodes.
The matrix is $9\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its inverse is $(1/27)\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.

NUM:010630.canonicalSolution:
Adding the two Taylor expansions cancels odd powers:
\[
u(x+h)+u(x-h)-2u(x)=h^2 u''(x)+\frac{h^4}{12}u^{(4)}(\xi).
\]
Dividing by $-h^2$ and subtracting $f=-u''$ yields
\[
\tau(x)=-\frac{h^2}{12}u^{(4)}(\xi).
\]
The scheme is therefore consistent of order $2$.
\[
\boxed{\tau=-(h^2/12)u^{(4)}(\xi),\quad\text{order }2}.
\]

For $u(x)=x^2(1-x)^2=x^2-2x^3+x^4$ one computes $u''=2-12x+12x^2$ and $u^{(4)}=24$, hence $f=-2+12x-12x^2$ and $\tau_i=-2h^2$ exactly (the sixth derivative vanishes). On $h=1/3$,
\[
f\bigl(\tfrac13\bigr)=f\bigl(\tfrac23\bigr)=\tfrac23,\qquad \tau_i=-\frac29.
\]
The discrete system is
\[
9\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}U_1\\U_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2/3\\2/3\end{pmatrix},
\]
or $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}U=(2/27,2/27)^{\mathsf T}$. Symmetry forces $U_1=U_2=2/27$. The exact nodal values are
\[
u\bigl(\tfrac13\bigr)=u\bigl(\tfrac23\bigr)=\frac19\cdot\frac49=\frac4{81}.
\]
The nodal error is $2/27-4/81=2/81$. Applying the discrete operator to the exact nodal vector recovers
\[
9\left(2\cdot\frac4{81}-\frac4{81}\right)-\frac23
=\frac49-\frac23=-\frac29=\tau,
\]
which matches the Taylor formula.
\[
\boxed{U=(2/27,2/27),\quad u_{\mathrm{nodal}}=(4/81,4/81),\quad e=(2/81,2/81),\quad\tau=(-2/9,-2/9)}.
\]

For $-w''=2$ the exact solution is $w=x(1-x)$, a quadratic, so $w^{(4)}=0$ and $\tau\equiv 0$. The same matrix with load $(2,2)^{\mathsf T}$ produces $W=(2/9,2/9)$, which equals $w(1/3)=w(2/3)$. The scheme is exact on polynomials of degree at most $3$.

Finally $AU=F$ and $Au_{\mathrm{nodal}}=F+\tau$ give $Ae=-\tau$. Here
\[
A^{-1}=\frac1{27}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
e=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}2/9\\2/9\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2/81\\2/81\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus $\|e\|_\infty=2/81$ while $\|\tau\|_\infty=2/9$. The inverse discrete Laplacian converts a residual into a nodal error; the two vectors are not interchangeable. Exactness on the quadratic does not cancel the nonzero $u^{(4)}=24$ of the quartic.

graderFixtures.proofText: Taylor gives τ=-(h^2/12)u^{(4)}. For u=x^2(1-x)^2 one has u^{(4)}=24, so τ=-2h^2=-2/9 on h=1/3. The system yields U=(2/27,2/27) against exact nodes 4/81, hence e=2/81. The quadratic -w''=2 is recovered exactly as 2/9. Nodal error equals A^{-1}(-τ), not τ, so exactness on P_3 does not make every manufactured solution exact.
I discretize u'' by (U_{i+1}-U_{i-1})/(2h) or by the forward difference (U_{i+1}-U_i)/h^2, and I solve that first-order stencil on the two interior nodes.
The computed U differs from u by 2/81, so the truncation error is 2/81. Since the quadratic problem was exact, the scheme is exact for this quartic as well and for every smooth right-hand side.

PDE:010117.title: The Cauchy problem u_t+2u_x=-3u+6 with u(x,0)=1+e^{-x^2} has explicit profile 2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}
PDE:010117.objective: For u_t+2u_x=-3u+6 on R x (0,infty) with u(x,0)=1+e^{-x^2}, prove u=2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}, evaluate u(2,1)=2 and u(0,1)=2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}, and prove sup_x |u-2|=e^{-3t}.
PDE:010117.statement:
Consider the linear Cauchy problem
\[
u_t+2u_x=-3u+6,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0,
\]
with initial datum $u(x,0)=1+e^{-x^2}$.

1. Integrate along the characteristics $dx/dt=2$ and solve the
   linear ODE $du/dt=-3u+6$ to prove
   \[
   u(x,t)=2+\bigl(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1\bigr)e^{-3t}.
   \]

2. Evaluate the two sample values
   \[
   u(2,1)=2,\qquad u(0,1)=2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}.
   \]

3. Prove that
   \[
   \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\lvert u(x,t)-2\rvert=e^{-3t}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the source and the linear reaction
   may be dropped, so the solution is the pure transport
   $u(x,t)=1+e^{-(x-2t)^2}$”; (ii) “the characteristic foot is
   $\xi=x-t$ or $\xi=x+2t$, so $u(2,1)$ is not $2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling dilating
nonconservative transport of this shard, by a one-dimensional or
radial Sobolev membership audit, or by a Dirichlet Laplacian
manufactured mode. Do not reopen, import, or execute any of the
six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The integrating factor $e^{3t}$ converts $du/dt+3u=6$ into $\frac{d}{dt}(ue^{3t})=6e^{3t}$, hence $u=2+C e^{-3t}$. Matching $t=0$ gives $C=u_0(\xi)-2$.
Because $e^{-\xi^2}\in(0,1]$, one has $e^{-\xi^2}-1\in(-1,0]$ and $\lvert e^{-\xi^2}-1\rvert$ approaches $1$ as $\lvert\xi\rvert\to\infty$, so $\sup_x\lvert u-2\rvert=e^{-3t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate dx/dt=2, convert the PDE to du/dt+3u=6, and match C(xi)=u_0(xi)-2.
Read the equilibrium 2 first, factor e^{-3t} out of u-2, and take the Gaussian limit |xi|->infty.

milestones.criterion: Derives the characteristic foot xi=x-2t and the ODE solution u=2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}.
Rejects a dropped reaction/source and refuses a wrong characteristic speed.

commonErrors.description: Drops the linear reaction and the constant source and reports the pure transport u=1+e^{-(x-2t)^2}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required profile 2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}, the value u(2,1)=2, and the decay e^{-3t} are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wrong foot xi=x-t or xi=x+2t instead of xi=x-2t, so the sample point (2,1) is not the Gaussian peak.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity u(2,1)=2 fails, and u(0,1) is not 2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}.

hintTree.content: The orbits are $x=\xi+2t$. The ODE along each orbit is $du/dt=-3u+6$, with equilibrium $2$.
The initial condition forces $2+C(\xi)=1+e^{-\xi^2}$, hence $C=e^{-\xi^2}-1$ and $\xi=x-2t$.
At $(2,1)$ the foot is $0$, so the exponential correction vanishes. At $(0,1)$ the foot is $-2$ and $(e^{-4}-1)e^{-3}=e^{-7}-e^{-3}$.

PDE:010117.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic speed is the constant $2$, so
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=2\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=\xi+2t,\qquad \xi=x-2t.
\]
Along each such curve the PDE collapses to the linear ODE
\[
\frac{du}{dt}=-3u+6\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{du}{dt}+3u=6.
\]
The integrating factor $e^{3t}$ yields
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(u e^{3t}\bigr)=6e^{3t},
\]
hence $u e^{3t}=2e^{3t}+C(\xi)$ and
\[
u=2+C(\xi)\,e^{-3t}.
\]
The initial datum $u(\xi,0)=1+e^{-\xi^2}$ fixes
\[
2+C(\xi)=1+e^{-\xi^2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C(\xi)=e^{-\xi^2}-1.
\]
Substituting $\xi=x-2t$ gives the explicit solution
\[
u(x,t)=2+\bigl(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1\bigr)e^{-3t}.
\]
\[
\boxed{u=2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}}.
\]

At $(x,t)=(2,1)$ the foot is $\xi=0$, so $e^{-\xi^2}-1=0$ and
$u(2,1)=2$. At $(x,t)=(0,1)$ the foot is $\xi=-2$, so
\[
u(0,1)=2+\bigl(e^{-4}-1\bigr)e^{-3}=2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{u(2,1)=2,\quad u(0,1)=2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}}.
\]

For the uniform deviation from equilibrium, write
\[
u(x,t)-2=\bigl(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1\bigr)e^{-3t}.
\]
The Gaussian factor satisfies $0<e^{-(x-2t)^2}\le 1$, hence
$e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1\in(-1,0]$ and
\[
\bigl\lvert u(x,t)-2\bigr\rvert=\bigl(1-e^{-(x-2t)^2}\bigr)e^{-3t}<e^{-3t},
\]
while $\lvert u-2\rvert\to e^{-3t}$ as $\lvert x-2t\rvert\to\infty$.
Thus the supremum is not attained at any finite $x$, but is approached
as $\lvert x-2t\rvert\to\infty$:
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\lvert u(x,t)-2\rvert=e^{-3t}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\sup_x\lvert u-2\rvert=e^{-3t}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops both the reaction and the source and reports the
pure transport $1+e^{-(x-2t)^2}$, which fails $u(2,1)=2$ and the
factor $e^{-3t}$. Sentence (ii) uses the wrong foot $\xi=x-t$ or
$\xi=x+2t$ and cannot recover $u(2,1)=2$.

The argument never replaces the assigned linear
advection–reaction–source by the sibling dilating transport, by a
Sobolev membership computation, or by a Dirichlet Laplacian mode,
and it does not open any of the six existing intake seeds.

graderFixtures.proofText: Characteristics $x=\xi+2t$ reduce the PDE to $du/dt+3u=6$, hence $u=2+C(\xi)e^{-3t}$. The datum forces $C=e^{-\xi^2}-1$ with $\xi=x-2t$, so $u=2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t}$. Then $u(2,1)=2$, $u(0,1)=2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}$, and $\sup_x\lvert u-2\rvert=e^{-3t}$. This is not pure transport.
I drop the reaction and the source and take the pure transport u=1+e^{-(x-2t)^2}. I do not report u=2+(e^{-(x-2t)^2}-1)e^{-3t} and I do not accept u(2,1)=2.
The characteristic foot is xi=x-t or xi=x+2t, so u(2,1) is not 2 and u(0,1) is not 2+e^{-7}-e^{-3}.

PDE:010118.title: Nonconservative dilation u_t+x u_x=0 stretches the Lorentzian to mass pi e^t and L^2 energy (pi/2) e^t
PDE:010118.objective: For u_t+x u_x=0 with u(x,0)=1/(1+x^2), prove x=xi e^t and u=1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t}), evaluate u(2,ln 2)=1/2, show half-height |x|=e^t, and prove mass M=pi e^t with M'=M and ||u||_L2^2=(pi/2)e^t (hence pi at t=ln 2), contrasting only the conservative form.
PDE:010118.statement:
Consider the nonconservative linear transport
\[
u_t+x u_x=0,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},\ t\in\mathbb{R},
\]
with initial datum $u(x,0)=1/(1+x^2)$.

1. Integrate $dx/dt=x$ to prove $x=\xi e^{t}$ and, since $u$ is
   constant along characteristics,
   \[
   u(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+x^2 e^{-2t}}.
   \]
   Evaluate $u(2,\ln 2)=1/2$.

2. The initial Lorentzian has half-height $1/2$ at $\lvert x\rvert=1$.
   Prove that the half-height locations at time $t$ are
   $\lvert x\rvert=e^{t}$.

3. Let $M(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u(x,t)\,dx$. Prove
   \[
   M(t)=\pi e^{t},\qquad M'(t)=M(t),
   \]
   and
   \[
   \lVert u(\,\cdot\,,t)\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\,e^{t},
   \]
   hence the $L^2$ squared mass equals $\pi$ at $t=\ln 2$. Contrast
   only the conservative form $u_t+(xu)_x=0$, which would force
   $M'\equiv 0$ rather than $M'=M$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the PDE is the conservative
   continuity equation $u_t+(xu)_x=0$, so mass is the constant
   $\pi$ and $M'=0$”; (ii) “the change of variables $x=\xi e^{t}$
   may drop the Jacobian $dx=e^{t}\,d\xi$, so $M=\pi$ and
   $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\pi/2$ with no factor $e^{t}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling linear
advection–reaction–source, by a Sobolev membership audit, or by a
Dirichlet Laplacian manufactured mode. Do not reopen, import, or
execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: If $u$ is constant along $x=\xi e^{t}$, then $u(x,t)=u_0(x e^{-t})$. For $u_0(\xi)=1/(1+\xi^2)$ this is $1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})$.
The identities $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+y^2)^{-1}\,dy=\pi$ and $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+y^2)^{-2}\,dy=\pi/2$ convert the dilated integrals after $x=y e^{t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate dx/dt=x, freeze u along orbits, then insert x=y e^t into both integrals.
Read half-height from 1+x^2 e^{-2t}=2 first, then recover mass growth from the Jacobian against the conservative contrast M'=0.

hintTree.content: $dx/dt=x$ integrates to $x=\xi e^{t}$. Constancy of $u$ gives $u=1/(1+\xi^2)=1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})$. At $(2,\ln 2)$ one has $\xi=1$.
Half-height means $1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})=1/2$, hence $\lvert x\rvert=e^{t}$.
Substitute $x=y e^{t}$ so $dx=e^{t}\,dy$. Then $M=\pi e^{t}$ and $\int u^2=\bigl(\int(1+y^2)^{-2}\,dy\bigr)e^{t}=(\pi/2)e^{t}$.

PDE:010118.canonicalSolution:
The characteristic ODE is $dx/dt=x$, so
\[
x=\xi e^{t},\qquad \xi=x e^{-t}.
\]
The nonconservative transport $u_t+x u_x=0$ means $du/dt=0$ along
these curves, hence $u(x,t)=u_0(\xi)=1/(1+\xi^2)$ and
\[
u(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+x^2 e^{-2t}}.
\]
At $(x,t)=(2,\ln 2)$ the foot is $\xi=2 e^{-\ln 2}=1$, so
$u(2,\ln 2)=1/2$.
\[
\boxed{x=\xi e^{t},\quad u=1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t}),\quad u(2,\ln 2)=1/2}.
\]

The profile equals $1/2$ precisely when $x^2 e^{-2t}=1$, i.e.
\[
\lvert x\rvert=e^{t}.
\]
(The initial half-height $\lvert\xi\rvert=1$ is just the same
identity at $t=0$.)
\[
\boxed{\text{half-height }\lvert x\rvert=e^{t}}.
\]

For the mass, substitute $x=y e^{t}$ (so $dx=e^{t}\,dy$):
\[
M(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dx}{1+x^2 e^{-2t}}
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{t}\,dy}{1+y^2}
=\pi e^{t}.
\]
Differentiating the closed form gives $M'= \pi e^{t}=M$. The
conservative contrast $u_t+(xu)_x=0$ would instead force $M'\equiv 0$
and $M\equiv\pi$; that is a different PDE and is used here only as
a contrast.
\[
\boxed{M=\pi e^{t},\quad M'=M}.
\]

The same substitution on the square yields
\[
\lVert u(\,\cdot\,,t)\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dx}{(1+x^2 e^{-2t})^2}
=e^{t}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dy}{(1+y^2)^2}.
\]
The antiderivative identity
$\int(1+y^2)^{-2}\,dy=\tfrac12\bigl(\arctan y+y/(1+y^2)\bigr)$
gives $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+y^2)^{-2}\,dy=\pi/2$, hence
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\,e^{t}.
\]
At $t=\ln 2$ this equals $\pi$.
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=(\pi/2)e^{t}\ \bigl(=\pi\text{ at }t=\ln 2\bigr)}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the assigned nonconservative PDE by the
conservative continuity equation and reports the false conservation
$M=\pi$. Sentence (ii) drops the Jacobian $e^{t}$ and loses every
growth factor.

The argument never replaces the assigned dilation by the sibling
advection–reaction–source, by a Sobolev membership computation, or
by a Dirichlet Laplacian mode, and it does not open any of the six
existing intake seeds.

PDE:010219.title: The power x^{3/4} on (0,1) lies in H^1 with squared norm 61/40, while x^{1/2} fails logarithmically
PDE:010219.objective: For u=x^{3/4} on (0,1), prove ||u||_L2^2=2/5, u'=(3/4)x^{-1/4}, ||u'||_L2^2=9/8, ||u||_H1^2=61/40, and the traces u(0)=0, u(1)=1. Prove x^alpha is in H^1(0,1) iff alpha=0 or alpha>1/2, with a logarithmic failure at alpha=1/2.
PDE:010219.statement:
Let $I=(0,1)$ and $u(x)=x^{3/4}$. Work throughout with the
standard Sobolev space $H^1(I)=W^{1,2}(I)$.

1. Prove
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{L^2(I)}^2=\frac25,\qquad
   u'=\frac34\,x^{-1/4},\qquad
   \lVert u'\rVert_{L^2(I)}^2=\frac98,
   \]
   and therefore
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{H^1(I)}^2=\frac{61}{40}.
   \]

2. Prove that $u$ extends continuously to $\overline{I}$ with
   traces $u(0)=0$ and $u(1)=1$.

3. For the full family $x\mapsto x^{\alpha}$ on $I$, including the
   constant case $\alpha=0$, prove
   \[
   x^{\alpha}\in H^1(I)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
   \alpha=0\ \text{ or }\ \alpha>\frac12,
   \]
   and that the critical power $\alpha=1/2$ fails by a logarithmic
   divergence of $\int_0^1 x^{-1}\,dx$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$u=x^{3/4}$ is not in $H^1(I)$, or
   else $\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2$ is not $9/8$”; (ii) “the critical
   power $x^{1/2}$ lies in $H^1(I)$, so the nonzero-power threshold
   is not the strict inequality $\alpha>1/2$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling radial Sobolev power
on the disk, by a first-order characteristic Cauchy problem, or by
a Dirichlet Laplacian manufactured mode. Do not reopen, import, or
execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: If $u=x^{\alpha}$ then $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\int_0^1 x^{2\alpha}\,dx$ converges for $\alpha>-1/2$. For $\alpha\ne0$, $\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2=\alpha^2\int_0^1 x^{2\alpha-2}\,dx$ converges precisely for $\alpha>1/2$; the separate case $\alpha=0$ is the constant function $1\in H^1(I)$.
At $\alpha=1/2$ one has $u'=(1/2)x^{-1/2}$ and $\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2=(1/4)\int_0^1 x^{-1}\,dx$, which diverges logarithmically.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the two elementary power integrals on (0,1) and add them to obtain 61/40.
Read the H^1 threshold from convergence of int_0^1 x^{2alpha-2} dx, then exhibit the logarithm at alpha=1/2.

milestones.criterion: Proves x^alpha is in H^1(0,1) iff alpha=0 or alpha>1/2, with a logarithmic failure at alpha=1/2.
Rejects excluding x^{3/4} from H^1 and refuses the claim that x^{1/2} lies in H^1.

commonErrors.consequence: The required nonzero-power threshold alpha>1/2 and the logarithmic failure at alpha=1/2 are lost.

hintTree.content: Handle $\alpha=0$ first: $x^0=1$ has weak derivative $0$. For $\alpha\ne0$, the integral $\int_0^1 x^{2\alpha-2}\,dx$ converges iff $2\alpha-2>-1$, i.e. $\alpha>1/2$. At $\alpha=1/2$ one meets $\int x^{-1}\,dx$.

PDE:010219.canonicalSolution:
On $I=(0,1)$ one has $u^2=x^{3/2}$, so
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(I)}^2=\int_0^1 x^{3/2}\,dx
=\Bigl[\frac{x^{5/2}}{5/2}\Bigr]_0^1=\frac25.
\]
The classical derivative is
\[
u'=\frac34\,x^{-1/4}.
\]
Then
\[
\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2(I)}^2
=\frac{9}{16}\int_0^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx
=\frac{9}{16}\Bigl[2x^{1/2}\Bigr]_0^1
=\frac98.
\]
Adding the two squared norms,
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{H^1(I)}^2=\frac25+\frac98=\frac{16}{40}+\frac{45}{40}=\frac{61}{40}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=2/5,\quad u'=(3/4)x^{-1/4},\quad
\lVert u'\rVert_{L^2}^2=9/8,\quad \lVert u\rVert_{H^1}^2=61/40}.
\]

Since $3/4>0$, the pointwise power extends continuously to
$\overline{I}$ with
\[
u(0)=0,\qquad u(1)=1.
\]
These are the $H^1$ traces.
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{tr}u=(0,1)}.
\]

Now let $v_{\alpha}(x)=x^{\alpha}$. The case $\alpha=0$ is the
constant function $1$, whose weak derivative is zero, so
$v_0\in H^1(I)$. For $\alpha\ne0$,
$\lVert v_{\alpha}\rVert_{L^2}^2=\int_0^1 x^{2\alpha}\,dx$ converges
exactly when $\alpha>-1/2$, while
$v_{\alpha}'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$ satisfies
\[
\lVert v_{\alpha}'\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\alpha^2\int_0^1 x^{2\alpha-2}\,dx,
\]
which is finite if and only if $2\alpha-2>-1$, i.e. $\alpha>1/2$.
Thus $x^{\alpha}\in H^1(I)$ if and only if $\alpha=0$ or
$\alpha>1/2$. At the
critical value $\alpha=1/2$,
\[
\lVert v_{1/2}'\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\frac14\int_0^1 x^{-1}\,dx
=\frac14\bigl[\ln x\bigr]_0^1
\]
diverges logarithmically, so $x^{1/2}\notin H^1(I)$.
\[
\boxed{x^{\alpha}\in H^1(I)\iff \alpha=0\text{ or }\alpha>1/2;\quad
\alpha=1/2\text{ logarithmic fail}}.
\]

Sentence (i) excludes the assigned power from $H^1$ or corrupts
the $9/8$ derivative norm. Sentence (ii) claims the critical
logarithmically divergent power lies in $H^1$.

The argument never replaces the one-dimensional power by the
sibling radial disk computation, by a first-order characteristic
Cauchy problem, or by a Dirichlet Laplacian mode, and it does not
open any of the six existing intake seeds.

For the full family, $x^{\alpha}$ lies in $H^1(0,1)$ if and only if $\alpha=0$ or $\alpha>1/2$; at $\alpha=1/2$ the derivative integral diverges logarithmically.
