PDE:010220.title: The radial power r^{1/2} on the unit disk is in H^1 with squared norm 7pi/6, while r^{-1/2} is only L^2
PDE:010220.objective: For u=r^{1/2} on the unit disk, prove ||u||_L2^2=2pi/3, |grad u|^2=1/(4r), ||grad u||_L2^2=pi/2, and ||u||_H1^2=7pi/6. Prove r^alpha is in H^1 iff alpha>=0, including the constant alpha=0 case, and that r^{-1/2} is in L^2 but not in H^1.
PDE:010220.statement:
Let $D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\lvert x\rvert<1\}$ be the open unit
disk and write $r=\lvert x\rvert$. Let $u(x)=r^{1/2}$.

1. Using the polar Jacobian $dx=r\,dr\,d\theta$, prove
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{L^2(D)}^2=\frac{2\pi}{3},\qquad
   \lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=\frac{1}{4r},\qquad
   \lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2(D)}^2=\frac{\pi}{2},
   \]
   and therefore
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{H^1(D)}^2=\frac{7\pi}{6}.
   \]

2. For the full radial family $r\mapsto r^{\alpha}$, including the
   constant case $\alpha=0$, prove
   \[
   r^{\alpha}\in H^1(D)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \alpha\ge0.
   \]

3. Prove that $r^{-1/2}$ lies in $L^2(D)$ but not in $H^1(D)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the polar Jacobian $r$ may be
   dropped, so $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2$ is not $2\pi/3$”; (ii) “the
   one-dimensional threshold $\alpha>1/2$ applies on the disk, or
   else $r^{-1/2}$ lies in $H^1(D)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by the sibling one-dimensional
power on $(0,1)$, by a first-order characteristic Cauchy problem,
or by a Dirichlet Laplacian manufactured mode. Do not reopen,
import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: $\int_D r^{2\alpha}\,dx=2\pi\int_0^1 r^{2\alpha+1}\,dr$ converges for $\alpha>-1$. For $\alpha\ne0$, the gradient integral $2\pi\alpha^2\int_0^1 r^{2\alpha-1}\,dr$ converges precisely for $\alpha>0$; the separate case $\alpha=0$ is the constant function $1\in H^1(D)$.
The function $r^{-1/2}$ satisfies $\int_D r^{-1}\,dx=2\pi\int_0^1 dr<\infty$, so it is in $L^2(D)$, but $\alpha=-1/2$ lies below the $H^1$ threshold $\alpha>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert dx=r dr d theta into both |u|^2=r and |grad u|^2=1/(4r), then add 2pi/3+pi/2.
Read the H^1 threshold from integrability of r^{2alpha-1} near 0, and test alpha=-1/2 separately in L^2.

milestones.criterion: Computes ||u||_L2^2=2pi/3, |grad u|^2=1/(4r), ||grad u||_L2^2=pi/2, and ||u||_H1^2=7pi/6.
Proves r^alpha is in H^1(D) iff alpha>=0, including the alpha=0 constant, and that r^{-1/2} is in L^2(D) but not H^1(D).
Rejects a dropped polar Jacobian and refuses the one-dimensional threshold or r^{-1/2} in H^1.

commonErrors.description: Drops the polar Jacobian r in the area element, so the L^2 and gradient integrals are not 2pi/3 and pi/2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities ||u||_L2^2=2pi/3, ||grad u||_L2^2=pi/2, and ||u||_H1^2=7pi/6 all fail.

commonErrors.description: Omits the alpha=0 constant exception, imports the one-dimensional threshold alpha>1/2 onto the disk, or claims that r^{-1/2} lies in H^1(D).
commonErrors.consequence: The required nonzero-power criterion alpha>0 and the statement that r^{-1/2} is L^2 but not H^1 are lost.

hintTree.content: $\lvert u\rvert^2=r$, so $\int_D u^2=2\pi\int_0^1 r\cdot r\,dr=2\pi\int_0^1 r^2\,dr=2\pi/3$.
$\partial_r r^{1/2}=(1/2)r^{-1/2}$, hence $\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=1/(4r)$. Times the Jacobian $r$, the integrand is $1/4$ and the integral is $\pi/2$.
Then $2\pi/3+\pi/2=4\pi/6+3\pi/6=7\pi/6$. Handle $\alpha=0$ separately as the constant function; for $\alpha\ne0$, the gradient integrand $r^{2\alpha-1}$ is integrable at $0$ iff $\alpha>0$.

PDE:010220.canonicalSolution:
On the unit disk, $\lvert u\rvert^2=r$ and $dx=r\,dr\,d\theta$, so
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(D)}^2
=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta
=2\pi\int_0^1 r^2\,dr
=\frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]
The only nonzero polar derivative is
$\partial_r u=(1/2)r^{-1/2}$, hence
\[
\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=\frac14 r^{-1}=\frac{1}{4r}.
\]
Inserting the Jacobian,
\[
\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2(D)}^2
=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{4r}\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta
=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 \frac14\,dr\,d\theta
=\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Adding the squared norms,
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{H^1(D)}^2=\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{4\pi}{6}+\frac{3\pi}{6}=\frac{7\pi}{6}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=2\pi/3,\quad
\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=1/(4r),\quad
\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^2=\pi/2,\quad
\lVert u\rVert_{H^1}^2=7\pi/6}.
\]

For $v_{\alpha}=r^{\alpha}$, the case $\alpha=0$ is the constant
function $1$, whose weak gradient is zero, so $v_0\in H^1(D)$.
For $\alpha\ne0$ one has
$\lvert\nabla v_{\alpha}\rvert^2=\alpha^2 r^{2\alpha-2}$, so
\[
\lVert\nabla v_{\alpha}\rVert_{L^2(D)}^2
=2\pi\alpha^2\int_0^1 r^{2\alpha-1}\,dr.
\]
The radial integral converges at the origin if and only if
$2\alpha-1>-1$, i.e. $\alpha>0$. The $L^2$ integral of $v_{\alpha}$
itself converges for every $\alpha>-1$. Combining the nonzero powers
with the constant exception therefore gives
\[
r^{\alpha}\in H^1(D)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \alpha\ge0.
\]
\[
\boxed{r^{\alpha}\in H^1(D)\iff\alpha\ge0}.
\]

For $\alpha=-1/2$, $\lvert v\rvert^2=r^{-1}$ and
\[
\int_D r^{-1}\,dx=2\pi\int_0^1 r^{-1}\cdot r\,dr=2\pi\int_0^1 dr=2\pi<\infty,
\]
so $r^{-1/2}\in L^2(D)$. But $-1/2<0$, so $r^{-1/2}\notin H^1(D)$.
(Explicitly, $\lvert\nabla r^{-1/2}\rvert^2\sim r^{-3}$ produces
$\int_0^1 r^{-2}\,dr$, which diverges.)
\[
\boxed{r^{-1/2}\in L^2(D)\setminus H^1(D)}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the polar Jacobian and cannot recover
$2\pi/3$. Sentence (ii) imports the one-dimensional threshold
$\alpha>1/2$ or claims that $r^{-1/2}$ is in $H^1(D)$.

The argument never replaces the radial disk computation by the
sibling interval power, by a first-order characteristic Cauchy
problem, or by a Dirichlet Laplacian mode, and it does not open
any of the six existing intake seeds.

For the full family, $r^{\alpha}$ lies in $H^1(D)$ if and only if $\alpha\ge0$, including the constant $\alpha=0$ case. The function $r^{-1/2}$ is in $L^2(D)$ but not in $H^1(D)$. The one-dimensional threshold $\alpha>1/2$ does not apply.
I drop the polar Jacobian r, so ||u||_L2^2 is not 2pi/3 and ||grad u||_L2^2 is not pi/2. I do not accept ||u||_H1^2=7pi/6.
I omit the alpha=0 constant exception, apply the one-dimensional threshold alpha>1/2 on the disk, and claim r^{-1/2} lies in H^1(D).

PDE:010321.title: The mode sin(pi x)sin(2 pi y) on the unit square has L^2 mass 1/4 and Dirichlet energy 5 pi^2/4
PDE:010321.objective: For u=sin(pi x)sin(2 pi y) on the unit square with f=5 pi^2 u, prove -Delta u=f, ||u||_L2^2=1/4, the energy identity int |grad u|^2=int f u=5 pi^2/4, and the extrema +1 at (1/2,1/4) and -1 at (1/2,3/4).
PDE:010321.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,1)^2$ and
\[
u(x,y)=\sin(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y),\qquad
f=5\pi^2 u.
\]
The unknown vanishes on $\partial\Omega$.

1. Prove that $-\Delta u=f$ pointwise on $\Omega$, so $u$ is the
   manufactured Dirichlet eigenmode for this right-hand side.

2. Prove
   \[
   \lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\frac14
   \]
   and the energy identity
   \[
   \int_{\Omega}\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2
   =\int_{\Omega} f u
   =\frac{5\pi^2}{4}.
   \]

3. Prove that the maximum of $u$ on $\overline{\Omega}$ is $+1$ at
   $(1/2,1/4)$ and the minimum is $-1$ at $(1/2,3/4)$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$-\Delta u$ is $\pi^2 u$ or
   $4\pi^2 u$ rather than $5\pi^2 u$, so the energy is not
   $5\pi^2/4$”; (ii) “the energy is $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/4$
   with no factor $5\pi^2$, or the extrema $\pm 1$ are attached to
   the wrong points.”

Do not replace the calculation by a first-order characteristic
Cauchy problem or by a Sobolev membership audit of a power. Do not
reopen, import, or execute any of the six existing intake seeds.
permittedResults: The $L^2$ integrals factor: $\int_0^1\sin^2(m\pi x)\,dx=1/2$ for each positive integer $m$, so $\lVert\sin(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)\rVert_{L^2}^2=(1/2)\cdot(1/2)=1/4$.
On $[0,1]$ the function $\sin(\pi x)$ attains $1$ only at $x=1/2$, while $\sin(2\pi y)$ attains $1$ at $y=1/4$ and $-1$ at $y=3/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute u_xx and u_yy to lock the eigenvalue 5 pi^2, then factor the two sine-squared integrals.
Read energy as lambda ||u||_L2^2 and locate extrema from the separate one-dimensional sine maxima.

milestones.criterion: Proves -Delta u=5 pi^2 u=f with zero Dirichlet trace, ||u||_L2^2=1/4, and energy 5 pi^2/4.
Locates the maximum +1 at (1/2,1/4) and the minimum -1 at (1/2,3/4).
Rejects a wrong eigenvalue and refuses energy without the 5 pi^2 factor or misplaced extrema.

commonErrors.description: Takes -Delta u to be pi^2 u or 4 pi^2 u instead of 5 pi^2 u, so the manufactured right-hand side and the energy 5 pi^2/4 fail.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identities f=5 pi^2 u and int f u=5 pi^2/4 are replaced by pi^2/4 or pi^2.

commonErrors.description: Reports the energy as ||u||_L2^2=1/4 with no factor 5 pi^2, or attaches the extrema +/-1 to points other than (1/2,1/4) and (1/2,3/4).
commonErrors.consequence: The required energy 5 pi^2/4 and the sample points (1/2,1/4), (1/2,3/4) are lost.

hintTree.content: $u_{xx}=-\pi^2 u$ and $u_{yy}=-4\pi^2 u$, so $-\Delta u=5\pi^2 u=f$. The boundary sines vanish.
$\int_0^1\sin^2(\pi x)\,dx=1/2$ and $\int_0^1\sin^2(2\pi y)\,dy=1/2$, hence $\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/4$ and $\int f u=5\pi^2/4$.
The product of amplitudes is $\pm 1$ only at $(1/2,1/4)$ and $(1/2,3/4)$.

PDE:010321.canonicalSolution:
Differentiate the manufactured mode:
\[
u_{xx}=-\pi^2\sin(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)=-\pi^2 u,
\]
\[
u_{yy}=-4\pi^2\sin(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)=-4\pi^2 u.
\]
Therefore
\[
-\Delta u=(\pi^2+4\pi^2)u=5\pi^2 u=f.
\]
On each edge of $\partial\Omega$ either $\sin(\pi x)=0$ or
$\sin(2\pi y)=0$, so $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$.
\[
\boxed{-\Delta u=5\pi^2 u=f,\quad u\vert_{\partial\Omega}=0}.
\]

The $L^2$ mass factors by Fubini:
\[
\lVert u\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
=\Bigl(\int_0^1\sin^2(\pi x)\,dx\Bigr)
\Bigl(\int_0^1\sin^2(2\pi y)\,dy\Bigr)
=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14.
\]
Green's identity (or the eigenrelation $f=5\pi^2 u$) gives
\[
\int_{\Omega}\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2
=\int_{\Omega} f u
=5\pi^2\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2
=\frac{5\pi^2}{4}.
\]
The same energy is recovered from
$\nabla u=\bigl(\pi\cos(\pi x)\sin(2\pi y),\,2\pi\sin(\pi x)\cos(2\pi y)\bigr)$
by integrating
$\pi^2\cos^2(\pi x)\sin^2(2\pi y)+4\pi^2\sin^2(\pi x)\cos^2(2\pi y)$.
\[
\boxed{\lVert u\rVert_{L^2}^2=1/4,\quad
\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2=\int f u=5\pi^2/4}.
\]

The factor $\sin(\pi x)$ on $[0,1]$ attains its maximum $1$ only at
$x=1/2$. The factor $\sin(2\pi y)$ attains $1$ at $y=1/4$ and $-1$
at $y=3/4$. Hence
\[
\max_{\overline{\Omega}}u=+1\quad\text{at }\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac14\bigr),
\qquad
\min_{\overline{\Omega}}u=-1\quad\text{at }\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac34\bigr).
\]
\[
\boxed{\max=+1\text{ at }(1/2,1/4),\quad
\min=-1\text{ at }(1/2,3/4)}.
\]

Sentence (i) uses the incomplete eigenvalue $\pi^2$ or $4\pi^2$
and cannot recover the energy $5\pi^2/4$. Sentence (ii) either
drops the factor $5\pi^2$ from the energy or attaches the extrema
$\pm 1$ to the wrong points.

The argument never replaces the manufactured Dirichlet mode by a
first-order characteristic Cauchy problem or by a Sobolev power
membership audit, and it does not open any of the six existing
intake seeds.

I take -Delta u to be pi^2 u or 4 pi^2 u rather than 5 pi^2 u, so the energy is not 5 pi^2/4.
The energy is ||u||_L2^2=1/4 with no factor 5 pi^2, and I attach the extrema +/-1 to points other than (1/2,1/4) and (1/2,3/4).

PDE:010322.title: On the unit square, u=x(1-x)y(1-y) has max 1/16, source 1 at the center, and Dirichlet energy 1/45
PDE:010322.objective: For u=x(1-x)y(1-y) on the unit square with Dirichlet data, prove f=-Delta u=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)], max u=1/16, f(1/2,1/2)=1, int u=1/36, ||u||_2^2=1/900, and the Green energy int |grad u|^2=int f u=1/45.
PDE:010322.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,1)^2$ and
\[
u(x,y)=x(1-x)\,y(1-y).
\]
This vanishing-boundary polynomial is a Dirichlet Poisson state: do
not replace it by an eigenmode, a heat flow, or a Neumann mean.

1. Prove that $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and that the Poisson source
   $f:=-\Delta u$ is
   \[
   f(x,y)=2\bigl(y(1-y)+x(1-x)\bigr).
   \]
   Evaluate $f\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)=1$.

2. Prove that the unique critical point in $\Omega$ is
   $\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)$ and
   \[
   \max_{\overline{\Omega}} u=u\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac1{16}.
   \]

3. Prove the integrals
   \[
   \int_\Omega u=\frac1{36},\qquad
   \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\frac1{900}.
   \]

4. By the first Green identity (or integration by parts with $u=0$
   on $\partial\Omega$), prove the Dirichlet energy identity
   \[
   \int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2=\int_\Omega f u=\frac1{45}.
   \]

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$f=\Delta u$, so the source is
   $-2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)]$ and $f(1/2,1/2)=-1$”; (ii) “the energy is
   $\|u\|_{L^2}^2=1/900$, or else $\max u=1/4$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode,
by a forced or decaying heat flow, or by a Neumann mean/mode
ledger.
permittedResults: If $u(x,y)=X(x)Y(y)$ then $\Delta u=X''Y+XY''$. Here $X(x)=x(1-x)$ gives $X''=-2$ and $Y(y)=y(1-y)$ gives $Y''=-2$, so $\Delta u=-2Y-2X$.
Product integrals separate: $\int_\Omega X^a Y^b=\bigl(\int_0^1 X^a\bigr)\bigl(\int_0^1 Y^b\bigr)$. In particular $\int_0^1 t(1-t)\,dt=1/6$ and $\int_0^1 t^2(1-t)^2\,dt=1/30$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor u=X(x)Y(y), compute Delta from X''=Y''=-2, then separate every integral as a product of one-dimensional Beta values.
Locate the maximum at (1/2,1/2) first, then recover the energy from int f u rather than from a raw expansion of |grad u|^2.

milestones.criterion: Derives f=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)], f(1/2,1/2)=1, and max u=1/16 from the unique interior critical point.
Evaluates int u=1/36, ||u||_2^2=1/900, and the Green energy int |grad u|^2=int f u=1/45.
Rejects the sign error f=Delta u and refuses to replace the energy by the L2 mass or the maximum by 1/4.

commonErrors.description: Sets f=Delta u instead of f=-Delta u, so the source is reported as -2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)] and f(1/2,1/2)=-1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required positive source f=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)], the center value 1, and the energy identity int f u=1/45 all fail.

commonErrors.description: Takes the Dirichlet energy to be ||u||_2^2=1/900, or reports max u=1/4 instead of 1/16.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Green identity int |grad u|^2=1/45, or the sharp maximum 1/16, is lost.

hintTree.content: $u$ vanishes whenever $x\in\{0,1\}$ or $y\in\{0,1\}$. Differentiate the product twice in each variable to read $\Delta u=-2y(1-y)-2x(1-x)$.
The only critical point in the open square is $x=y=1/2$, where $u=(1/2)^4=1/16$. The source there is $2(1/4+1/4)=1$.

PDE:010322.canonicalSolution:
Write $u(x,y)=X(x)Y(y)$ with $X(x)=x(1-x)$ and $Y(y)=y(1-y)$.
Then $X(0)=X(1)=0$ and $Y(0)=Y(1)=0$, so $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.
The second derivatives are $X''=-2$ and $Y''=-2$, hence
\[
\Delta u=X''Y+XY''=-2Y-2X=-2\bigl(y(1-y)+x(1-x)\bigr)
\]
and the Poisson source is
\[
f=-\Delta u=2\bigl(y(1-y)+x(1-x)\bigr).
\]
At the center,
\[
f\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)=2\bigl(\tfrac14+\tfrac14\bigr)=1.
\]
\[
\boxed{f=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)],\;f(1/2,1/2)=1}.
\]

Inside $\Omega$ one has $\partial_x u=(1-2x)Y$ and
$\partial_y u=X(1-2y)$, so the only critical point is
$(1/2,1/2)$. On $\partial\Omega$ one has $u=0$, while
\[
u\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\bigr)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\frac1{16}>0.
\]
Thus $\max_{\overline{\Omega}} u=1/16$.
\[
\boxed{\max u=1/16}.
\]

The integrals separate:
\[
\int_0^1 x(1-x)\,dx=\Bigl[\tfrac12 x^2-\tfrac13 x^3\Bigr]_0^1=\frac16,
\]
\[
\int_0^1 x^2(1-x)^2\,dx=\int_0^1(x^2-2x^3+x^4)\,dx=\frac13-\frac12+\frac15=\frac1{30}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_\Omega u=\Bigl(\frac16\Bigr)^2=\frac1{36},\qquad
\|u\|_{L^2}^2=\Bigl(\frac1{30}\Bigr)^2=\frac1{900}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\int u=1/36,\;\|u\|_2^2=1/900}.
\]

Green's identity with $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ gives
$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2=\int_\Omega f u$. Expanding the integrand,
\begin{align*}
\int_\Omega f u
&=2\int_\Omega\bigl(X Y^2+X^2 Y\bigr)
=2\Bigl(\int X\cdot\int Y^2+\int X^2\cdot\int Y\Bigr)\\
&=2\Bigl(\frac16\cdot\frac1{30}+\frac1{30}\cdot\frac16\Bigr)
=\frac4{180}=\frac1{45}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\int|\nabla u|^2=\int f u=1/45}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the minus in $f=-\Delta u$ and reports the
wrong source sign. Sentence (ii) replaces the Dirichlet energy by
the $L^2$ mass $1/900$, or inflates the maximum to $1/4$.

The argument never treats a rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, a forced
or decaying heat flow, or a Neumann mean/mode ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: On the unit square, $u=x(1-x)y(1-y)$ vanishes on the boundary and $f=-\Delta u=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)]$, so $f(1/2,1/2)=1$. The unique interior critical value is $\max u=1/16$. Separated integrals give $\int u=1/36$ and $\|u\|_2^2=1/900$. Green’s identity then yields $\int|\nabla u|^2=\int f u=1/45$. The source sign is not $\Delta u$, and the energy is not the $L^2$ mass.
I take f=Delta u, so the source is -2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)] and f(1/2,1/2)=-1. I do not accept f=-Delta u=2[y(1-y)+x(1-x)] or the energy identity int f u=1/45.
The energy is the L2 mass ||u||_2^2=1/900, and the maximum is u(1/2,1/2)=1/4. I do not report int |grad u|^2=1/45 or max u=1/16.

PDE:010323.title: The mode sin(2πx)sin(3πy) has eigenvalue 13π², L2 mass 1/4, and six nodal rectangles
PDE:010323.objective: For phi=sin(2πx)sin(3πy) on the unit square with Dirichlet conditions, prove -Delta phi=13π² phi, ||phi||_2^2=1/4, Rayleigh=13π², energy=13π²/4, L2-normalized field 2 phi, and exactly six nodal rectangles.
PDE:010323.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,1)^2$ with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, and let
\[
\phi(x,y)=\sin(2\pi x)\,\sin(3\pi y).
\]
This is one Dirichlet eigenmode of $-\Delta$. Do not replace it by a
polynomial Poisson state or by a heat flow.

1. Prove $\phi=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and
   \[
   -\Delta\phi=13\pi^2\,\phi.
   \]

2. Prove
   \[
   \|\phi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\frac14,\qquad
   R(\phi)=\frac{\int_\Omega|\nabla\phi|^2}{\int_\Omega\phi^2}=13\pi^2,
   \]
   and therefore the Dirichlet energy
   \[
   \int_\Omega|\nabla\phi|^2=\frac{13\pi^2}{4}.
   \]

3. Prove that the $L^2$-normalized eigenfunction is $2\phi$, and that
   the nodal set of $\phi$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ partitions $\Omega$
   into exactly six open rectangles.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the eigenvalue is $2^2+3^2=13$ with no
   factor of $\pi^2$, or else $(2+3)^2\pi^2=25\pi^2$”; (ii) “$\|\phi\|_2^2=1/2$,
   or the nodal partition has five or twelve cells rather than six
   rectangles.”

Do not replace the calculation by a polynomial Poisson/Green energy
audit, by a forced or decaying heat flow, or by a Neumann
mean/mode ledger.
permittedResults: $\partial_{xx}\sin(2\pi x)=-(2\pi)^2\sin(2\pi x)$ and $\partial_{yy}\sin(3\pi y)=-(3\pi)^2\sin(3\pi y)$, so $-\Delta\phi=\bigl((2\pi)^2+(3\pi)^2\bigr)\phi=13\pi^2\phi$.
$\int_0^1\sin^2(k\pi t)\,dt=1/2$ for every integer $k\ge 1$. Products therefore give $\|\phi\|_2^2=(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the product sine twice, add (2π)²+(3π)², then convert the Rayleigh identity into the energy 13π²/4.
Compute ||phi||_2^2 as a product of two 1/2 factors first, then read the nodal partition as 2 columns by 3 rows.

milestones.criterion: Proves -Delta phi=13π² phi, ||phi||_2^2=1/4, Rayleigh=13π², and energy=13π²/4.
Identifies the L2-normalized field 2 phi and the six nodal rectangles from the interior lines x=1/2 and y=1/3,2/3.
Rejects an eigenvalue 13 or 25π² and refuses ||phi||_2^2=1/2 or a wrong nodal-cell count.

commonErrors.description: Reports the eigenvalue as 2^2+3^2=13 with no π², or as (2+3)²π²=25π², instead of 13π².
commonErrors.consequence: The required eigenrelation, Rayleigh quotient 13π², and energy 13π²/4 are all attached to the wrong number.

commonErrors.description: Takes ||phi||_2^2=1/2 instead of 1/4, or counts five or twelve nodal cells instead of six rectangles.
commonErrors.consequence: The required mass 1/4, normalized field 2 phi, and six-rectangle nodal partition fail.

hintTree.content: $\phi$ vanishes on $x\in\{0,1\}$ and on $y\in\{0,1\}$. The second derivatives contribute $4\pi^2$ and $9\pi^2$.
Each one-dimensional $L^2$ factor is $1/2$, so $\|\phi\|_2^2=1/4$ and the energy is $13\pi^2\cdot(1/4)$.
$\|\phi\|_2=1/2$, hence $\phi/\|\phi\|_2=2\phi$. Interior nodes $x=1/2$ and $y=1/3,2/3$ cut the square into six rectangles.

PDE:010323.canonicalSolution:
On $x\in\{0,1\}$ one has $\sin(2\pi x)=0$, and on $y\in\{0,1\}$ one
has $\sin(3\pi y)=0$, so $\phi=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Differentiating,
\begin{align*}
\partial_{xx}\phi&=-(2\pi)^2\sin(2\pi x)\sin(3\pi y)=-(4\pi^2)\phi,\\
\partial_{yy}\phi&=-(3\pi)^2\sin(2\pi x)\sin(3\pi y)=-(9\pi^2)\phi,
\end{align*}
hence $\Delta\phi=-13\pi^2\phi$ and
\[
-\Delta\phi=13\pi^2\phi.
\]
\[
\boxed{-\Delta\phi=13\pi^2\phi}.
\]

Each factor is a standard sine on the unit interval:
\[
\int_0^1\sin^2(2\pi x)\,dx=\frac12,\qquad
\int_0^1\sin^2(3\pi y)\,dy=\frac12,
\]
so
\[
\|\phi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\frac14.
\]
The Rayleigh quotient of an eigenfunction equals the eigenvalue,
\[
R(\phi)=13\pi^2,
\]
and the Dirichlet energy is therefore
\[
\int_\Omega|\nabla\phi|^2=13\pi^2\cdot\frac14=\frac{13\pi^2}{4}.
\]
(Directly: $\nabla\phi=(2\pi\cos(2\pi x)\sin(3\pi y),\,3\pi\sin(2\pi x)\cos(3\pi y))$
integrates to $4\pi^2\cdot\tfrac14+9\pi^2\cdot\tfrac14=13\pi^2/4$.)
\[
\boxed{\|\phi\|_2^2=1/4,\;R(\phi)=13\pi^2,\;\int|\nabla\phi|^2=13\pi^2/4}.
\]

Then $\|\phi\|_2=1/2$, so the $L^2$-normalized mode is
\[
\frac{\phi}{\|\phi\|_2}=2\phi.
\]
The zeros of $\sin(2\pi x)$ in $[0,1]$ are $x=0,1/2,1$, and the zeros
of $\sin(3\pi y)$ are $y=0,1/3,2/3,1$. The interior nodal lines
$x=1/2$ and $y=1/3,2/3$ partition $\Omega$ into $2\times 3=6$ open
rectangles.
\[
\boxed{\text{normalized }2\phi;\;\text{six nodal rectangles}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $\pi^2$ or replaces $m^2+n^2$ by $(m+n)^2$.
Sentence (ii) takes $\|\phi\|_2^2=1/2$ or miscounts the nodal cells.

The argument never treats a polynomial Poisson/Green energy audit, a
forced or decaying heat flow, or a Neumann mean/mode ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: On the unit square, $\phi=\sin(2\pi x)\sin(3\pi y)$ is a Dirichlet eigenmode with $-\Delta\phi=13\pi^2\phi$. Then $\|\phi\|_2^2=1/4$, the Rayleigh quotient is $13\pi^2$, and the energy is $13\pi^2/4$. The $L^2$-normalized field is $2\phi$, and the interior nodes $x=1/2$, $y=1/3,2/3$ cut the square into six rectangles. The eigenvalue is not $13$ or $25\pi^2$.
The eigenvalue is 2^2+3^2=13 with no factor of pi^2, or else (2+3)^2 pi^2=25 pi^2. I do not accept -Delta phi=13 pi^2 phi or energy 13 pi^2/4.
I take ||phi||_2^2=1/2, and I count five or twelve nodal cells rather than six rectangles. I do not accept the mass 1/4 or the normalized field 2 phi.

PDE:010424.title: The forced heat flow ut=uxx+sin x, u0=0, is (1-e^{-t})sin x with t=ln 2 mass π/8
PDE:010424.objective: On (0,π) with Dirichlet conditions, for ut=uxx+sin x and u(·,0)=0, prove u=(1-e^{-t})sin x; at t=ln 2, max=1/2, ||u||_2^2=π/8, ||ux||_2^2=π/8, ||ut||_2^2=π/8; and the steady state is sin x.
PDE:010424.statement:
Consider the forced heat equation on $(0,\pi)$ with Dirichlet
conditions
\[
u_t=u_{xx}+\sin x,\qquad
u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0,\qquad
u(x,0)=0.
\]
This is a single-mode forcing problem. Do not replace it by a
homogeneous two-mode decay or by a Neumann mean.

1. Seek $u(x,t)=a(t)\sin x$ and prove
   \[
   a'+a=1,\qquad a(0)=0,
   \]
   hence
   \[
   u(x,t)=\bigl(1-e^{-t}\bigr)\sin x.
   \]

2. At the instant $t=\ln 2$, prove
   \[
   \max_{x\in[0,\pi]} u(x,\ln 2)=\frac12,\qquad
   \|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2(0,\pi)}^2=\frac\pi8,
   \]
   and the companion identities
   \[
   \|u_x(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2}^2=\frac\pi8,\qquad
   \|u_t(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2}^2=\frac\pi8.
   \]

3. Prove that the steady state is $u_\infty(x)=\sin x$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the problem is homogeneous, so
   $u\equiv 0$, or the amplitude is $e^{-t}$ or $t e^{-t}$ rather than
   $1-e^{-t}$”; (ii) “at $t=\ln 2$ the $L^2$ masses of $u$, $u_x$, and
   $u_t$ are not all $\pi/8$, or the steady state is $0$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a polynomial Poisson/Green audit,
by a rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, by a two-mode Dirichlet decay,
or by a Neumann mean/mode ledger.
permittedResults: $\int_0^\pi\sin^2 x\,dx=\int_0^\pi\cos^2 x\,dx=\pi/2$. Consequently a profile $c\sin x$ has $L^2$ mass $c^2\pi/2$, and $c\cos x$ has the same mass.
The unique bounded steady state of $0=u_{xx}+\sin x$ with Dirichlet conditions is $u_\infty=\sin x$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Stay in the first sine mode, solve a'+a=1 by an integrating factor, then evaluate every L2 mass from ∫sin²=∫cos²=π/2.

hintTree.content: Insert $u=a(t)\sin x$ to get $a'\sin x=-a\sin x+\sin x$, so $a'+a=1$ with $a(0)=0$.
The integrating factor $e^{t}$ produces $a=1-e^{-t}$. At $t=\ln 2$ one has $a=1/2$ and $a'=1/2$.
Then $\max u=1/2$ and each of $\|u\|_2^2$, $\|u_x\|_2^2$, $\|u_t\|_2^2$ equals $(1/4)\cdot(\pi/2)=\pi/8$. The rest point is $\sin x$.

PDE:010424.canonicalSolution:
The forcing $\sin x$ is the first Dirichlet eigenfunction, so the
solution remains in that mode: $u(x,t)=a(t)\sin x$. The PDE becomes
\[
a'(t)\sin x=-a(t)\sin x+\sin x,
\]
hence the scalar ODE $a'+a=1$. The initial condition $u(\cdot,0)=0$
forces $a(0)=0$. The integrating factor $e^{t}$ gives
\[
(ae^{t})'=e^{t},\qquad ae^{t}=e^{t}-1,\qquad a(t)=1-e^{-t}.
\]
Therefore
\[
u(x,t)=\bigl(1-e^{-t}\bigr)\sin x.
\]
\[
\boxed{u=(1-e^{-t})\sin x}.
\]

At $t=\ln 2$ one has $e^{-t}=1/2$, so $a=1/2$ and
\[
u(x,\ln 2)=\frac12\sin x.
\]
The maximum on $[0,\pi]$ is $1/2$, attained at $x=\pi/2$. The $L^2$
mass is
\[
\|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2=\frac14\int_0^\pi\sin^2 x\,dx=\frac14\cdot\frac\pi2=\frac\pi8.
\]
Differentiating in $x$ gives $u_x=(1/2)\cos x$ at this instant, so
\[
\|u_x(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2=\frac14\int_0^\pi\cos^2 x\,dx=\frac\pi8.
\]
Differentiating in $t$ gives $u_t=e^{-t}\sin x$, hence
$u_t(\cdot,\ln 2)=(1/2)\sin x$ and
\[
\|u_t(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2=\frac\pi8.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=\ln 2:\ \max=1/2,\ \|u\|_2^2=\|u_x\|_2^2=\|u_t\|_2^2=\pi/8}.
\]

As $t\to\infty$, $a(t)\to 1$, so the unique Dirichlet steady state is
$u_\infty(x)=\sin x$. Directly, $0=\partial_{xx}u_\infty+\sin x$ with
$u_\infty(0)=u_\infty(\pi)=0$ is solved by $u_\infty=\sin x$.
\[
\boxed{u_\infty=\sin x}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the forcing or uses the wrong variation-of-parameters
amplitude. Sentence (ii) breaks the three equal $\pi/8$ masses or
denies the steady state $\sin x$.

The argument never treats a polynomial Poisson/Green audit, a
rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, a two-mode Dirichlet decay, or a
Neumann mean/mode ledger.

PDE:010425.title: The data 3sin x-2sin 2x decays as 3e^{-t}sin x-2e^{-4t}sin 2x with t=ln 2 mass 145π/128
PDE:010425.objective: On (0,π) with Dirichlet heat flow and u0=3sin x-2sin 2x, prove u=3e^{-t}sin x-2e^{-4t}sin 2x; at t=ln 2 the coefficients are 3/2 and -1/8, u(π/2)=3/2, int u=3, ||u||_2^2=145π/128, and ||ux||_2^2=37π/32.
PDE:010425.statement:
Consider the homogeneous heat equation on $(0,\pi)$ with Dirichlet
conditions
\[
u_t=u_{xx},\qquad
u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0,\qquad
u(x,0)=3\sin x-2\sin 2x.
\]
This is a two-mode decay. Do not replace it by a forced single-mode
problem or by a Neumann cosine expansion.

1. Prove
   \[
   u(x,t)=3e^{-t}\sin x-2e^{-4t}\sin 2x.
   \]

2. At $t=\ln 2$, prove that the sine coefficients are $3/2$ and
   $-1/8$, that
   \[
   u\bigl(\tfrac\pi2,\ln 2\bigr)=\frac32,\qquad
   \int_0^\pi u(x,\ln 2)\,dx=3,
   \]
   and that
   \[
   \|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2}^2=\frac{145\pi}{128},\qquad
   \|u_x(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2}^2=\frac{37\pi}{32}.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the second mode decays as $e^{-2t}$
   rather than $e^{-4t}$, because the rate is the frequency $n$ and
   not $n^2$”; (ii) “at $t=\ln 2$ the coefficients are not $3/2$ and
   $-1/8$, or $\int u\ne 3$, or the $L^2$ masses are not
   $145\pi/128$ and $37\pi/32$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a polynomial Poisson/Green audit,
by a rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, by a forced single-mode heat
flow, or by a Neumann mean/mode ledger.
permittedResults: The family $\{\sin(nx)\}_{n\ge 1}$ is $L^2$-orthogonal on $(0,\pi)$ with $\|\sin(nx)\|_2^2=\pi/2$. Cross terms therefore vanish in every $L^2$ mass.
If $u=\sum a_n\sin(nx)$ then $u_x=\sum n a_n\cos(nx)$ and $\|u_x\|_2^2=\sum n^2 a_n^2\cdot(\pi/2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evolve each sine by e^{-n^2 t}, specialize e^{-t}=1/2 and e^{-4t}=1/16, then use orthogonality of {sin nx} and {cos nx}.
Evaluate u(π/2) first (the second sine vanishes), then convert the two coefficients into the L2 and H1 masses from π/2 norms.

milestones.criterion: Writes u=3e^{-t}sin x-2e^{-4t}sin 2x from the Dirichlet eigenvalues 1 and 4.
At t=ln 2 reports coefficients 3/2 and -1/8, u(π/2)=3/2, int u=3, ||u||_2^2=145π/128, and ||ux||_2^2=37π/32.

hintTree.content: Each sine is an eigenfunction: $\partial_{xx}\sin x=-\sin x$ and $\partial_{xx}\sin 2x=-4\sin 2x$. Evolve the coefficients by $e^{-n^2 t}$.
At $t=\ln 2$, $e^{-t}=1/2$ and $e^{-4t}=1/16$, so the field is $(3/2)\sin x-(1/8)\sin 2x$. Then $u(\pi/2)=3/2$ because $\sin\pi=0$.

PDE:010425.canonicalSolution:
The functions $\sin x$ and $\sin 2x$ are Dirichlet eigenfunctions of
$-\partial_{xx}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $4$. The heat equation
therefore multiplies the coefficients by $e^{-t}$ and $e^{-4t}$:
\[
u(x,t)=3e^{-t}\sin x-2e^{-4t}\sin 2x.
\]
The initial datum is recovered at $t=0$, and the endpoint traces
vanish for all $t$.
\[
\boxed{u=3e^{-t}\sin x-2e^{-4t}\sin 2x}.
\]

At $t=\ln 2$ one has $e^{-t}=1/2$ and $e^{-4t}=(e^{-t})^4=1/16$, so
the coefficients are
\[
3\cdot\frac12=\frac32,\qquad
-2\cdot\frac1{16}=-\frac18,
\]
and
\[
u(x,\ln 2)=\frac32\sin x-\frac18\sin 2x.
\]
At $x=\pi/2$,
\[
u\bigl(\tfrac\pi2,\ln 2\bigr)=\frac32\sin\tfrac\pi2-\frac18\sin\pi=\frac32.
\]
The integral is
\[
\int_0^\pi u(x,\ln 2)\,dx=\frac32\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx-\frac18\int_0^\pi\sin 2x\,dx
=\frac32\cdot 2-0=3.
\]
Orthogonality on $(0,\pi)$ gives
\begin{align*}
\|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2
&=\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2+\Bigl(\frac18\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2
=\frac{9\pi}{8}+\frac\pi{128}
=\frac{145\pi}{128}.
\end{align*}
The spatial derivative is
\[
u_x(x,\ln 2)=\frac32\cos x-\frac14\cos 2x,
\]
and a second orthogonality computation yields
\[
\|u_x(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2
=\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2+\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2
=\frac{9\pi}{8}+\frac\pi{32}
=\frac{37\pi}{32}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=\ln 2:\ \text{coeff }3/2,-1/8;\ u(\pi/2)=3/2;\ \int u=3;\ \|u\|_2^2=145\pi/128;\ \|u_x\|_2^2=37\pi/32}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the quadratic rate $n^2$ by the linear rate $n$.
Sentence (ii) corrupts the $t=\ln 2$ coefficient, trace, mass, or
gradient identities.

The argument never treats a polynomial Poisson/Green audit, a
rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, a forced single-mode heat flow, or a
Neumann mean/mode ledger.

The second mode decays as e^{-2t} rather than e^{-4t}, because I take the rate to be the frequency n and not n^2. I do not accept u=3e^{-t}sin x-2e^{-4t}sin 2x.
At t=ln 2 the coefficients are not 3/2 and -1/8, u(π/2) is not 3/2, the integral is not 3, and I do not accept ||u||_2^2=145π/128 or ||ux||_2^2=37π/32.

PDE:010426.title: The Neumann datum 2+3cos x-cos 2x keeps mean 2 and at t=ln 2 has traces 55/16 and 7/16
PDE:010426.objective: On (0,π) with Neumann heat flow and u0=2+3cos x-cos 2x, prove u=2+3e^{-t}cos x-e^{-4t}cos 2x, mean 2, int=2π; at t=ln 2, u(0)=55/16, u(π)=7/16, ||u||_2^2=2625π/512; and ux vanishes at both ends.
PDE:010426.statement:
Consider the homogeneous heat equation on $(0,\pi)$ with Neumann
conditions
\[
u_t=u_{xx},\qquad
u_x(0,t)=u_x(\pi,t)=0,\qquad
u(x,0)=2+3\cos x-\cos 2x.
\]
This is a Neumann mean-and-mode problem. Do not replace it by a
Dirichlet sine expansion or by a forced single-mode flow.

1. Prove
   \[
   u(x,t)=2+3e^{-t}\cos x-e^{-4t}\cos 2x.
   \]

2. Prove that the spatial mean is constantly $2$ and that
   \[
   \int_0^\pi u(x,t)\,dx=2\pi
   \]
   for every $t\ge 0$. Confirm $u_x(0,t)=u_x(\pi,t)=0$ identically.

3. At $t=\ln 2$, prove
   \[
   u(0,\ln 2)=\frac{55}{16},\qquad
   u(\pi,\ln 2)=\frac{7}{16},\qquad
   \|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_{L^2(0,\pi)}^2=\frac{2625\pi}{512}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the boundary condition is Dirichlet, so
   the conserved mean $2$ is dropped and the expansion is written in
   sines”; (ii) “$u_x$ fails to vanish at the ends, or at $t=\ln 2$
   the traces are not $55/16$ and $7/16$, or the $L^2$ mass is not
   $2625\pi/512$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a polynomial Poisson/Green audit,
by a rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, by a forced single-mode heat
flow, or by a two-mode Dirichlet sine decay.
permittedResults: The family $\{\cos(nx)\}_{n\ge 0}$ is $L^2$-orthogonal on $(0,\pi)$, with $\|\cos(nx)\|_2^2=\pi/2$ for $n\ge 1$ and $\|1\|_2^2=\pi$.
Each $\cos(nx)$ is a Neumann eigenfunction with eigenvalue $n^2$, so the $n$th coefficient is multiplied by $e^{-n^2 t}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Keep the constant mode, evolve the two cosines by e^{-n^2 t}, then read the traces at x=0 and x=π from cos(nπ)=(-1)^n.
Check conservation of int u=2π from vanishing endpoint flux first, then expand the t=ln 2 L2 mass with the Neumann orthogonality constants π and π/2.

milestones.criterion: Writes u=2+3e^{-t}cos x-e^{-4t}cos 2x and proves mean 2, int=2π, and ux(0)=ux(π)=0.
Rejects a Dirichlet sine expansion or dropped mean, and refuses nonzero endpoint flux or wrong t=ln 2 traces.

commonErrors.description: Treats the boundary condition as Dirichlet, drops the conserved mean 2, and writes a sine expansion instead of the Neumann cosine field.
commonErrors.consequence: The required constant mode, the integral 2π, and the cosine traces 55/16 and 7/16 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims ux fails to vanish at the ends, or at t=ln 2 reports traces other than 55/16 and 7/16, or a mass other than 2625π/512.
commonErrors.consequence: The Neumann flux identity and the required t=ln 2 traces and L2 mass fail.

hintTree.content: Keep the constant $2$ and evolve the first two cosines by $e^{-t}$ and $e^{-4t}$. Differentiating in $x$ produces sines, which vanish at $0$ and $\pi$.
The mean of $2+3\cos x-\cos 2x$ is $2$, and $\int_0^\pi 2\,dx=2\pi$ is conserved.

PDE:010426.canonicalSolution:
The functions $1$, $\cos x$, and $\cos 2x$ are Neumann eigenfunctions
of $-\partial_{xx}$ with eigenvalues $0$, $1$, and $4$. The heat
equation therefore leaves the mean untouched and multiplies the
oscillatory coefficients by $e^{-t}$ and $e^{-4t}$:
\[
u(x,t)=2+3e^{-t}\cos x-e^{-4t}\cos 2x.
\]
The initial datum is recovered at $t=0$.
\[
\boxed{u=2+3e^{-t}\cos x-e^{-4t}\cos 2x}.
\]

The spatial integral of each cosine vanishes, so
\[
\int_0^\pi u(x,t)\,dx=\int_0^\pi 2\,dx=2\pi
\]
for every $t\ge 0$, and the mean is $2\pi/\pi=2$. Differentiating,
\[
u_x(x,t)=-3e^{-t}\sin x+2e^{-4t}\sin 2x,
\]
hence $u_x(0,t)=u_x(\pi,t)=0$ identically.
\[
\boxed{\text{mean }2,\;\int u=2\pi,\;u_x(0)=u_x(\pi)=0}.
\]

At $t=\ln 2$ one has $e^{-t}=1/2$ and $e^{-4t}=1/16$, so
\[
u(x,\ln 2)=2+\frac32\cos x-\frac1{16}\cos 2x.
\]
The endpoint traces are
\begin{align*}
u(0,\ln 2)&=2+\frac32-\frac1{16}=\frac{56}{16}-\frac1{16}=\frac{55}{16},\\
u(\pi,\ln 2)&=2-\frac32-\frac1{16}=\frac{8}{16}-\frac1{16}=\frac{7}{16}.
\end{align*}
Orthogonality on $(0,\pi)$ gives
\begin{align*}
\|u(\cdot,\ln 2)\|_2^2
&=4\cdot\pi+\Bigl(\frac32\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2+\Bigl(\frac1{16}\Bigr)^2\cdot\frac\pi2
=4\pi+\frac{9\pi}{8}+\frac\pi{512}
=\frac{2625\pi}{512}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{t=\ln 2:\ u(0)=55/16,\ u(\pi)=7/16,\ \|u\|_2^2=2625\pi/512}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces Neumann cosines by Dirichlet sines and drops
the conserved mean. Sentence (ii) denies the endpoint flux identity
or the $t=\ln 2$ traces and mass.

The argument never treats a polynomial Poisson/Green audit, a
rectangle Dirichlet eigenmode, a forced single-mode heat flow, or a
two-mode Dirichlet sine decay.

At $t=\ln 2$ the traces are $u(0)=55/16$ and $u(\pi)=7/16$, and $\|u\|_2^2=2625\pi/512$. The mean is not dropped, and the expansion is not a Dirichlet sine series.
The boundary condition is Dirichlet, so I drop the conserved mean 2 and write a sine expansion. I do not accept u=2+3e^{-t}cos x-e^{-4t}cos 2x or int u=2π.
ux fails to vanish at the ends. At t=ln 2 I do not accept the traces 55/16 and 7/16 or the mass 2625π/512.

PDE:010527.title: The resonant forced wave u_tt-u_xx=sin(2x)cos(2t) has amplitude (t/4)sin(2t) and energy π(4+π²)/256 at t=π/4
PDE:010527.objective: For u_tt-u_xx=sin(2x)cos(2t) on (0,π) with Dirichlet ends and zero Cauchy data, prove the n=2 amplitude is A=(t/4)sin(2t), that A(π/4)=π/16 and A'(π/4)=1/4, that u=π/16 and u_t=1/4 at (x,t)=(π/4,π/4), and that the Dirichlet energy is π(4+π²)/256.
PDE:010527.statement:
Consider the forced one-dimensional wave problem
\[
u_{tt}-u_{xx}=\sin(2x)\cos(2t),\qquad 0<x<\pi,\quad t>0,
\]
with Dirichlet conditions $u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0$ and zero Cauchy data
$u(x,0)=u_t(x,0)=0$. Expand in the sine eigenbasis of $-\partial_{xx}$
on $(0,\pi)$.

1. Prove that only the $n=2$ mode is forced, that its amplitude $A(t)$
   in $u(x,t)=A(t)\sin(2x)$ solves the resonant oscillator
   \[
   A''+4A=\cos(2t),\qquad A(0)=A'(0)=0,
   \]
   and that the unique solution is the secular profile
   \[
   A(t)=\frac{t}{4}\sin(2t).
   \]

2. Prove
   \[
   A\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac\pi{16},\qquad
   A'\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac14,
   \]
   and therefore at the space-time point $(x,t)=(\pi/4,\pi/4)$
   \[
   u=\frac\pi{16},\qquad u_t=\frac14.
   \]

3. With the Dirichlet energy
   $E(t)=\frac12\int_0^\pi\bigl(u_t^2+u_x^2\bigr)\,dx$, prove
   \[
   E\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac{\pi(4+\pi^2)}{256}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the source is absent, so d'Alembert's
   formula on the line with zero data gives $u\equiv0$”; (ii) “the
   oscillator is non-resonant, so $A=\frac18\sin(2t)$ or
   $A=\frac14 t^2$, and the energy is $\frac12\|u\|_{L^2}^2$ as for
   the heat equation.”

Do not replace the calculation by a homogeneous d'Alembert wave on
the line, by a heat-equation Fourier sine series, by a Laplace
Dirichlet disk / mean-value argument, by constant-coefficient linear
transport, by an inviscid Burgers entropy shock, or by an undamped
homogeneous-wave energy identity with no forcing.
permittedResults: A resonant particular solution of $A''+\omega^2 A=\cos(\omega t)$ is $A_p=(t/(2\omega))\sin(\omega t)$. For $\omega=2$ this is $A_p=(t/4)\sin(2t)$, and it already satisfies $A_p(0)=A_p'(0)=0$.
Differentiating $A=(t/4)\sin(2t)$ gives $A'=\frac14\sin(2t)+\frac t2\cos(2t)$. At $t=\pi/4$ one has $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce to the n=2 oscillator, insert the secular ansatz (t/4)sin(2t), then evaluate A, A', and E at t=π/4.
Check A(0)=A'(0)=0 first so no homogeneous correction appears, then convert (A')²+4A² through the identity E=(π/4)((A')²+4A²).

milestones.criterion: Derives the resonant oscillator A''+4A=cos(2t) and the secular amplitude A=(t/4)sin(2t) with zero Cauchy data.
Evaluates A(π/4)=π/16, A'(π/4)=1/4, the point values u=π/16 and ut=1/4, and the energy π(4+π²)/256.
Rejects a homogeneous d'Alembert or non-resonant/heat-energy substitution.

commonErrors.description: Treats A''+4A=cos(2t) as non-resonant and reports A=(1/8)sin(2t) or a polynomial particular solution, omitting the secular factor t/4.
commonErrors.consequence: The required A=(t/4)sin(2t), the values π/16 and 1/4, and the energy π(4+π²)/256 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Drops the source and quotes homogeneous d'Alembert (hence u≡0), or replaces the Dirichlet wave energy by a heat L2 energy ½∫u².
commonErrors.consequence: The forced resonant profile and the energy π(4+π²)/256 are replaced by a reserved homogeneous-wave or heat identity.

hintTree.content: Insert $u=A(t)\sin(2x)$ to obtain $A''+4A=\cos(2t)$. Resonance rules out a bounded particular solution of the form $C\cos(2t)$.
Try $A=(t/4)\sin(2t)$. Then $A(0)=0$ and $A'(0)=0$, so no homogeneous correction is needed.
At $t=\pi/4$, $A=\pi/16$ and $A'=1/4$. Energy is $(\pi/4)\bigl((A')^2+4A^2\bigr)=\pi(4+\pi^2)/256$, not $\frac12\int u^2$.

PDE:010527.canonicalSolution:
The Dirichlet sine basis on $(0,\pi)$ diagonalizes $-\partial_{xx}$.
The source $\sin(2x)\cos(2t)$ is already a single eigenfunction, so
$u(x,t)=A(t)\sin(2x)$ with
\[
A''+4A=\cos(2t),\qquad A(0)=A'(0)=0.
\]
The homogeneous frequency equals the driving frequency, so every
bounded particular solution of the form $C\cos(2t)$ or $C\sin(2t)$
fails. The secular ansatz $A_p=(t/4)\sin(2t)$ gives
\begin{align*}
A_p'&=\frac14\sin(2t)+\frac t2\cos(2t),\\
A_p''&=\cos(2t)-t\sin(2t),
\end{align*}
hence $A_p''+4A_p=\cos(2t)$. Moreover $A_p(0)=0$ and $A_p'(0)=0$, so
the zero Cauchy data need no homogeneous correction:
\[
A(t)=\frac t4\sin(2t).
\]
\[
\boxed{A=(t/4)\sin(2t)}.
\]

At $t=\pi/4$,
\[
A\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac\pi{16}\sin\Bigl(\frac\pi2\Bigr)=\frac\pi{16},
\]
\[
A'\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac14\sin\Bigl(\frac\pi2\Bigr)
+\frac\pi8\cos\Bigl(\frac\pi2\Bigr)=\frac14.
\]
Then $u(\pi/4,\pi/4)=A(\pi/4)\sin(\pi/2)=\pi/16$ and
$u_t(\pi/4,\pi/4)=A'(\pi/4)=\frac14$.
\[
\boxed{A(\pi/4)=\pi/16,\;A'(\pi/4)=1/4,\;
u=\pi/16,\;u_t=1/4}.
\]

The Dirichlet energy of this mode is
\[
E=\frac12\int_0^\pi\bigl((A')^2\sin^2(2x)+4A^2\cos^2(2x)\bigr)\,dx
=\frac\pi4\bigl((A')^2+4A^2\bigr).
\]
At $t=\pi/4$,
\[
(A')^2+4A^2=\frac1{16}+4\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{256}
=\frac{4+\pi^2}{64},
\]
so
\[
E\Bigl(\frac\pi4\Bigr)=\frac\pi4\cdot\frac{4+\pi^2}{64}
=\frac{\pi(4+\pi^2)}{256}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E(\pi/4)=\pi(4+\pi^2)/256}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the source and quotes the reserved homogeneous
d'Alembert seed. Sentence (ii) uses a non-resonant particular
solution and replaces the wave energy by a heat $L^2$ energy.

The argument never solves a heat Fourier sine series, a Laplace
Dirichlet disk / mean-value problem, a constant-coefficient transport
equation, an inviscid Burgers entropy shock, or an undamped
homogeneous-wave energy identity with no forcing.

This is not a homogeneous d'Alembert problem.
The oscillator is non-resonant, so A=(1/8)sin(2t) or A=t^2/4. I omit the secular factor t/4 and I do not report A=(t/4)sin(2t) or A(pi/4)=pi/16.
The source is absent, so d'Alembert on the line with zero data gives u=0. I take the energy to be (1/2) int u^2 as in the heat equation and I do not report pi(4+pi^2)/256.

PDE:010528.title: The underdamped 2-mode of u_tt+2u_t-u_xx=0 is e^{-t}[cos(√3 t)+(1/√3)sin(√3 t)] with first zero 2π/(3√3)
PDE:010528.objective: For the periodic damped wave u_tt+2u_t-u_xx=0 on [0,2π] with u(x,0)=cos(2x) and u_t(x,0)=0, prove A=e^{-t}[cos(√3 t)+(1/√3)sin(√3 t)], A'=-(4/√3)e^{-t}sin(√3 t), that the first positive zero of A is 2π/(3√3), and that at t=π/√3 one has A=-e^{-π/√3}, A'=0, and energy 2π e^{-2π/√3}, with E'=-2∫u_t².
PDE:010528.statement:
On the circle $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ consider the linearly damped
wave equation
\[
u_{tt}+2u_t-u_{xx}=0,\qquad
u(x,0)=\cos(2x),\qquad
u_t(x,0)=0.
\]
Seek a single-mode solution $u(x,t)=A(t)\cos(2x)$.

1. Prove that $A$ solves $A''+2A'+4A=0$ with $A(0)=1$ and $A'(0)=0$,
   that the roots are $-1\pm i\sqrt3$ (underdamped), and that
   \[
   A(t)=e^{-t}\Bigl(\cos(\sqrt3\,t)+\frac1{\sqrt3}\sin(\sqrt3\,t)\Bigr),
   \]
   \[
   A'(t)=-\frac4{\sqrt3}\,e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3\,t).
   \]

2. Prove that the first positive zero of $A$ occurs at
   $t=2\pi/(3\sqrt3)$, and that at the later time $t=\pi/\sqrt3$
   \[
   A=-e^{-\pi/\sqrt3},\qquad A'=0.
   \]

3. With the energy $E(t)=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(u_t^2+u_x^2)\,dx$, prove
   the dissipation law $E'=-2\int_0^{2\pi}u_t^2\,dx$ and the value
   \[
   E\Bigl(\frac\pi{\sqrt3}\Bigr)=2\pi\,e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the characteristic roots are real
   (overdamped or critically damped), or the damping is dropped and
   $A=\cos(2t)$ as in the reserved undamped energy identity”;
   (ii) “the first positive zero of $A$ is $\pi/\sqrt3$, or
   $E$ is conserved.”

Do not replace the calculation by a homogeneous d'Alembert wave, by a
heat Fourier sine series, by a Laplace Dirichlet disk / mean-value
argument, by constant-coefficient linear transport, or by an inviscid
Burgers entropy shock.
permittedResults: The initial conditions $A(0)=1$ and $A'(0)=0$ force $B=1$ and $C=1/\sqrt3$. Differentiating the resulting $A$ collapses to $A'=-(4/\sqrt3)e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3\,t)$.
On a single cosine mode, $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2(2x)\,dx=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2(2x)\,dx=\pi$, so $E=(\pi/2)\bigl((A')^2+4A^2\bigr)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve r²+2r+4=0, fit A(0)=1 and A'(0)=0, then read the first positive root of tan(√3 t)=-√3.
Differentiate A to the collapsed form A'=-(4/√3)e^{-t}sin(√3 t), then evaluate E=(π/2)((A')²+4A²) at A'=0.

milestones.criterion: Derives the underdamped mode A=e^{-t}[cos(√3 t)+(1/√3)sin(√3 t)] and A'=-(4/√3)e^{-t}sin(√3 t).
Locates the first zero at 2π/(3√3) and evaluates A=-e^{-π/√3}, A'=0, E=2π e^{-2π/√3} with E'=-2∫ut².
Rejects overdamped/undamped roots and refuses a conserved-energy or first-zero substitution.

commonErrors.description: Takes real characteristic roots (overdamped or critical) or drops the damping and reports the reserved undamped profile A=cos(2t).
commonErrors.consequence: The required underdamped envelope e^{-t} and the factor 1/√3 are replaced by a different oscillator.

commonErrors.description: Reports the first positive zero of A as π/√3 (the later A'=0 time) or claims that E is conserved.
commonErrors.consequence: The required first zero 2π/(3√3) and the dissipated value 2π e^{-2π/√3} fail.

hintTree.content: $r^2+2r+4=0$ gives $r=-1\pm i\sqrt3$. Then $A(0)=1$ and $A'(0)=-1+C\sqrt3=0$ force $C=1/\sqrt3$.
$A=0$ when $\tan(\sqrt3\,t)=-\sqrt3$. The first positive root is $\sqrt3\,t=2\pi/3$.
At $t=\pi/\sqrt3$ one has $\sqrt3\,t=\pi$, so $A=-e^{-\pi/\sqrt3}$ and $A'=0$. Then $E=(\pi/2)\cdot4A^2=2\pi e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}$.

PDE:010528.canonicalSolution:
Insert $u=A(t)\cos(2x)$ into $u_{tt}+2u_t-u_{xx}=0$ to obtain
\[
A''+2A'+4A=0,\qquad A(0)=1,\qquad A'(0)=0.
\]
The characteristic polynomial $r^2+2r+4=0$ has roots
$r=-1\pm i\sqrt3$. The mode is therefore underdamped:
\[
A(t)=e^{-t}\bigl(B\cos(\sqrt3\,t)+C\sin(\sqrt3\,t)\bigr).
\]
The condition $A(0)=1$ gives $B=1$. Differentiating,
\[
A'(0)=-B+C\sqrt3=0\implies C=\frac1{\sqrt3}.
\]
Hence
\[
A(t)=e^{-t}\Bigl(\cos(\sqrt3\,t)+\frac1{\sqrt3}\sin(\sqrt3\,t)\Bigr).
\]
A direct differentiation cancels the cosine terms and yields
\[
A'(t)=-\frac4{\sqrt3}\,e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3\,t).
\]
\[
\boxed{A=e^{-t}[\cos(\sqrt3 t)+(1/\sqrt3)\sin(\sqrt3 t)],\;
A'=-(4/\sqrt3)e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3 t)}.
\]

The amplitude vanishes when $\cos\theta+(1/\sqrt3)\sin\theta=0$ with
$\theta=\sqrt3\,t$, i.e. $\tan\theta=-\sqrt3$. The first positive
solution is $\theta=2\pi/3$, so
\[
t=\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3}.
\]
At the later time $t=\pi/\sqrt3$ one has $\theta=\pi$, therefore
\[
A=-e^{-\pi/\sqrt3},\qquad
A'=-\frac4{\sqrt3}e^{-\pi/\sqrt3}\sin\pi=0.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{first zero }2\pi/(3\sqrt3);\;
A(\pi/\sqrt3)=-e^{-\pi/\sqrt3},\;A'=0}.
\]

On the circle,
\[
E'=\int_0^{2\pi}u_t(u_{tt}-u_{xx})\,dx
=-2\int_0^{2\pi}u_t^2\,dx.
\]
The same mode gives
$E=(\pi/2)\bigl((A')^2+4A^2\bigr)$. At $t=\pi/\sqrt3$ one has $A'=0$,
so
\[
E=(\pi/2)\cdot 4 e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}=2\pi\,e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E'=-2\int u_t^2;\;
E(\pi/\sqrt3)=2\pi e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the underdamped roots by a real-root or
undamped reserved identity $A=\cos(2t)$. Sentence (ii) confuses the
first zero of $A$ with the later critical time $\pi/\sqrt3$, or
claims $E$ is conserved.

The argument never quotes a homogeneous d'Alembert formula, a heat
Fourier sine series, a Laplace disk / mean-value identity, a
constant-coefficient transport solution, or an inviscid Burgers
entropy shock.

graderFixtures.proofText: The $n=2$ damped oscillator is underdamped with $A=e^{-t}[\cos(\sqrt3 t)+(1/\sqrt3)\sin(\sqrt3 t)]$ and $A'=-(4/\sqrt3)e^{-t}\sin(\sqrt3 t)$. The first positive zero is $2\pi/(3\sqrt3)$. At $t=\pi/\sqrt3$ one has $A=-e^{-\pi/\sqrt3}$, $A'=0$, and $E=2\pi e^{-2\pi/\sqrt3}$, with $E'=-2\int u_t^2$. Energy is not conserved.
The characteristic roots are real, or I drop the damping and take A=cos(2t) as in the undamped wave. I do not report the underdamped envelope e^{-t} or the coefficient 1/sqrt(3).
The first positive zero of A is t=pi/sqrt(3), and the energy E is conserved. I do not accept first zero 2pi/(3sqrt(3)) or E=2pi e^{-2pi/sqrt(3)}.

PDE:010629.title: Burgers data u_L=-1, u_R=1 open a centered rarefaction whose L1 distance from sign is t
PDE:010629.objective: For inviscid Burgers with left state -1 and right state +1, prove the centered rarefaction u=-1 for ξ<-1, u=ξ for -1≤ξ≤1, u=+1 for ξ>1, that the t=2 edges are x=±2, that the samples x∈{-3,1,3} return {-1,1/2,1}, and that the L1 distance from the sign initial datum equals t (hence 2 at t=2).
PDE:010629.statement:
Consider the inviscid Burgers conservation law
\[
u_t+\Bigl(\frac{u^2}2\Bigr)_x=0
\]
with Riemann data $u_L=-1$ and $u_R=+1$ (so $u_L<u_R$). Write
$\xi=x/t$ for $t>0$.

1. Prove that the entropy solution is the centered rarefaction
   \[
   u(x,t)=\begin{cases}
   -1,&\xi<-1,\\
   \xi,&-1\le\xi\le 1,\\
   +1,&\xi>1.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   In particular there is no shock: the entropy-admissible
   Rankine–Hugoniot jump from $-1$ to $+1$ is not selected.

2. At time $t=2$ prove that the rarefaction edges lie at $x=\pm2$.
   Evaluate the three samples
   \[
   u(-3,2)=-1,\qquad u(1,2)=\frac12,\qquad u(3,2)=+1.
   \]

3. Let $u_0=\operatorname{sign}$ (the same states, with a jump at
   $x=0$). Prove that
   \[
   \bigl\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)-u_0\bigr\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}=t,
   \]
   hence that the distance equals $2$ at $t=2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$u_L<u_R$ still produces the stationary
   entropy shock $u=\operatorname{sign}(x)$, so the reserved Burgers
   Rankine–Hugoniot shock seed applies”; (ii) “inside the fan one has
   $u=t/x$ or $u=1/\xi$ rather than $u=\xi$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a homogeneous d'Alembert wave, by a
heat Fourier sine series, by a Laplace Dirichlet disk / mean-value
argument, by constant-coefficient linear transport, or by an undamped
homogeneous-wave energy identity.
permittedResults: Self-similar entropy solutions of Burgers satisfy $u=\xi$ throughout any rarefaction, because $f'(u)=u$ must equal the ray speed $\xi=x/t$.
At time $t$ the edges of the $[-1,1]$ fan are $x=\pm t$. Sampling at $t=2$ therefore uses $\xi=x/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compare u_L and u_R to select a rarefaction, set u=ξ inside the fan, then sample ξ=x/2 at t=2.
Integrate |ξ-sign| on [-t,t] as two elementary triangles, each of area t/2.

milestones.criterion: Identifies u_L<u_R as a centered rarefaction and writes u=-1, ξ, +1 on the three ξ-regions.
Evaluates the t=2 edges ±2, the samples (-1,1/2,1), and the L1 distance t=2 from the sign datum.
Rejects an entropy-shock substitution and refuses a fan written as t/x or 1/ξ.

commonErrors.description: Installs the reserved Burgers entropy-shock / Rankine–Hugoniot seed and reports the stationary jump u=sign(x) even though u_L<u_R.
commonErrors.consequence: The required centered fan, the interior value 1/2, and the L1 distance t are replaced by a shock of distance 0.

commonErrors.description: Writes the rarefaction as u=t/x or u=1/ξ instead of the characteristic identity u=ξ=x/t.
commonErrors.consequence: The sample at (x,t)=(1,2) is not 1/2, and the L1 computation against sign fails.

hintTree.content: $u_L=-1<1=u_R$, so the solution is a rarefaction, not an entropy shock.
Inside the fan, $u=\xi=x/t$. At $t=2$ the edges are $\pm2$, and $x=1$ gives $\xi=1/2$.
Compare to $\operatorname{sign}$ on $[-t,t]$: each half-interval contributes $t/2$ to the $L^1$ distance.

PDE:010629.canonicalSolution:
The Burgers characteristic speed is $f'(u)=u$. Because $u_L=-1<1=u_R$,
the forward characteristics immediately separate and the entropy
solution is the centered rarefaction
\[
u(x,t)=\begin{cases}
-1,& x/t<-1,\\
x/t,& -1\le x/t\le 1,\\
+1,& x/t>1.
\end{cases}
\]
A stationary jump from $-1$ to $+1$ would have Rankine–Hugoniot speed
$s=(1-1)/2=0$, but it violates the Lax condition $u_L>s>u_R$ and is
not the entropy solution.
\[
\boxed{u=-1\ (\xi<-1);\ \xi\ (-1\le\xi\le1);\ +1\ (\xi>1)}.
\]

At $t=2$ the edges are $x=\pm 2$. The three samples are
\[
\frac{-3}{2}=-\frac32<-1\implies u=-1,
\qquad
\frac{1}{2}\in[-1,1]\implies u=\frac12,
\qquad
\frac{3}{2}>1\implies u=+1.
\]
\[
\boxed{t=2\text{ edges }x=\pm2;\;
(u(-3,2),u(1,2),u(3,2))=(-1,1/2,1)}.
\]

Against $u_0=\operatorname{sign}$, the two functions differ only on
$[-t,t]$:
\[
\int_{-t}^0\Bigl(1+\frac xt\Bigr)\,dx=\frac t2,\qquad
\int_0^t\Bigl(1-\frac xt\Bigr)\,dx=\frac t2.
\]
Hence $\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)-u_0\|_{L^1}=t$, and the value at $t=2$ is $2$.
\[
\boxed{\|u(\cdot,t)-\operatorname{sign}\|_{L^1}=t=2\text{ at }t=2}.
\]

Sentence (i) installs the reserved Burgers entropy-shock seed in a
rarefaction Riemann problem. Sentence (ii) writes the fan as $t/x$
or $1/\xi$ instead of $\xi$.

The argument never quotes a homogeneous d'Alembert formula, a heat
Fourier sine series, a Laplace disk / mean-value identity, a
constant-coefficient transport solution, or an undamped
homogeneous-wave energy identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Because $u_L=-1<1=u_R$, the entropy solution is the centered rarefaction $u=-1$ for $\xi<-1$, $u=\xi$ for $-1\le\xi\le1$, and $u=+1$ for $\xi>1$. At $t=2$ the edges are $x=\pm2$ and the samples $x\in\{-3,1,3\}$ return $-1$, $1/2$, $+1$. The $L^1$ distance from $\operatorname{sign}$ equals $t$, hence $2$ at $t=2$. This is not an entropy shock.
Even though uL<uR I take the stationary entropy shock u=sign(x) by Rankine-Hugoniot. I do not open a rarefaction and I report L1 distance 0.
Inside the fan I set u=t/x or u=1/xi rather than u=xi. At (x,t)=(1,2) I therefore do not report u=1/2.

PDE:010630.title: Conservative dilation u_t+(x u)_x=0 carries the Lorentz profile with mass π and L2²=(π/2)e^{-t}
PDE:010630.objective: For u_t+(x u)_x=0 with u(x,0)=1/(1+x²), prove u=e^{-t}/(1+x² e^{-2t}), that u(2,ln 2)=1/4, that mass equals π for all t, that the spatial supremum is e^{-t}, and that ‖u(·,t)‖_{L²}²=(π/2)e^{-t} (hence π/4 at t=ln 2). This is a conservative companion to course-8 nonconservative dilation only.
PDE:010630.statement:
Consider the conservative dilating transport equation
\[
u_t+(xu)_x=0,\qquad
u(x,0)=\frac1{1+x^2}.
\]
The unknown is a density: the flux divergence includes the extra
zeroth-order term $u$, so the equation is not the nonconservative
field $u_t+x u_x=0$. The present packet is an intentional
conservative-form companion to an existing course-8 nonconservative
dilation seed only; that seed is not reused and is not inspected here.

1. Prove that the solution is
   \[
   u(x,t)=\frac{e^{-t}}{1+x^2 e^{-2t}}.
   \]

2. Evaluate the sample
   \[
   u(2,\ln 2)=\frac14.
   \]
   Prove that the mass $\int_{\mathbb{R}}u(x,t)\,dx=\pi$ is conserved
   for every $t$, and that
   $\sup_x u(x,t)=e^{-t}$.

3. Prove the $L^2$ identity
   \[
   \bigl\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\bigr\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2
   =\frac\pi2\,e^{-t},
   \]
   and therefore that the value at $t=\ln 2$ is $\pi/4$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the equation is the nonconservative
   companion $u_t+x u_x=0$, so $u=1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})$ with no
   prefactor $e^{-t}$”; (ii) “mass is not conserved, or the $L^2$
   norm is conserved and equals $\pi/2$ for all $t$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a homogeneous d'Alembert wave, by a
heat Fourier sine series, by a Laplace Dirichlet disk / mean-value
argument, by constant-coefficient linear transport $u_t+c u_x=0$, by
an inviscid Burgers entropy shock, or by an undamped homogeneous-wave
energy identity.
permittedResults: Characteristics of $\dot x=x$ are $x(t)=x_0 e^{t}$. Combined with $\dot u=-u$ one obtains $u(x,t)=e^{-t}u_0(x e^{-t})$.
The identity $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+y^2)^{-2}\,dy=\pi/2$ follows from $\frac{d}{dy}\bigl(\frac12\bigl(y/(1+y^2)+\arctan y\bigr)\bigr)=(1+y^2)^{-2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate ẋ=x and u̇=-u, then substitute y=x e^{-t} to read mass and L2 from the Lorentz integrals.
Evaluate the sample (2,ln 2) first to lock the prefactor e^{-t}, then compute ∫(1+y²)^{-2}=π/2.

milestones.criterion: Derives the conservative profile u=e^{-t}/(1+x² e^{-2t}) and the sample u(2,ln 2)=1/4.
Proves mass π is conserved, sup=e^{-t}, and L2²=(π/2)e^{-t}=π/4 at t=ln 2.
Rejects the nonconservative companion without e^{-t} and refuses a mass/L2 conservation error.

commonErrors.description: Replaces u_t+(x u)_x=0 by the nonconservative companion u_t+x u_x=0 and omits the decay prefactor e^{-t}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required profile e^{-t}/(1+x² e^{-2t}), the sample 1/4, and the decaying L2 identity are lost.

commonErrors.description: Claims that mass is not conserved, or that the L2 norm is conserved and remains π/2 for all t.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conserved mass π and the value L2²=π/4 at t=ln 2 fail.

hintTree.content: Expand $(xu)_x=x u_x+u$. Along $x=x_0 e^{t}$ the density satisfies $\dot u=-u$.
Set $y=x e^{-t}$ to see that mass is $\pi$ and $\|u\|_{L^2}^2=(\pi/2)e^{-t}$.

PDE:010630.canonicalSolution:
Write $u_t+(xu)_x=u_t+x u_x+u=0$. The characteristic equations are
\[
\dot x=x,\qquad \dot u=-u,
\]
so $x(t)=x_0 e^{t}$ and $u(t)=u_0(x_0)e^{-t}$. Inverting
$x_0=x e^{-t}$ and inserting $u_0(x_0)=1/(1+x_0^2)$ produces
\[
u(x,t)=\frac{e^{-t}}{1+x^2 e^{-2t}}.
\]
(The nonconservative companion $u_t+x u_x=0$ would omit the prefactor
$e^{-t}$ and is a different, already-assigned course-8 seed; it is
not used here.)
\[
\boxed{u=e^{-t}/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})}.
\]

At $(x,t)=(2,\ln 2)$ one has $e^{-t}=1/2$ and $e^{-2t}=1/4$, so
\[
u(2,\ln 2)=\frac{1/2}{1+4\cdot(1/4)}=\frac{1/2}{2}=\frac14.
\]
The change of variables $y=x e^{-t}$ gives $dx=e^{t}\,dy$ and
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}u(x,t)\,dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{-t}}{1+y^2}\,e^{t}\,dy
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=\pi.
\]
Mass is therefore conserved. The spatial maximum occurs at $x=0$ and
equals $e^{-t}$.
\[
\boxed{u(2,\ln 2)=1/4;\;\text{mass }\pi;\;\sup u=e^{-t}}.
\]

The same substitution yields
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}u^2\,dx
=e^{-t}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dy}{(1+y^2)^2}.
\]
The antiderivative $\frac12\bigl(y/(1+y^2)+\arctan y\bigr)$ evaluates
to $\pi/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, hence
\[
\bigl\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\bigr\|_{L^2}^2=\frac\pi2\,e^{-t}.
\]
At $t=\ln 2$ this is $\pi/4$.
\[
\boxed{\|u\|_{L^2}^2=(\pi/2)e^{-t}=\pi/4\text{ at }t=\ln 2}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the conservation law by the reserved
nonconservative course-8 companion. Sentence (ii) denies mass
conservation or treats $\|u\|_{L^2}$ as constant.

The argument never quotes a homogeneous d'Alembert formula, a heat
Fourier sine series, a Laplace disk / mean-value identity, a
constant-speed transport solution $u_t+c u_x=0$, an inviscid Burgers
entropy shock, or an undamped homogeneous-wave energy identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Conservative dilation gives $u=e^{-t}/(1+x^2 e^{-2t})$. The sample $u(2,\ln 2)$ is $1/4$, mass $\int u=\pi$ is conserved, $\sup u=e^{-t}$, and $\|u\|_{L^2}^2=(\pi/2)e^{-t}=\pi/4$ at $t=\ln 2$. This is not the nonconservative field $u_t+x u_x=0$.
I treat the PDE as the nonconservative companion ut + x ux = 0 and write u=1/(1+x^2 e^{-2t}) with no prefactor e^{-t}. I do not report u(2,ln 2)=1/4.
Mass is not conserved, and the L2 norm is conserved and equals pi/2 for every t. I do not accept mass pi or L2^2=(pi/2)e^{-t}=pi/4 at t=ln 2.

PDE:010631.title: Linear acoustics with left state (4,1) and right rest has middle state (3,3/2) between x=±2t
PDE:010631.objective: For p_t+4v_x=0 and v_t+p_x=0 with left state (p,v)=(4,1) and right rest, prove c=2 and Z=2, that p+2v is the right-going invariant and p-2v the left-going invariant, that the middle state is (3,3/2) between x=-2t and x=2t, that both jumps satisfy Rankine–Hugoniot, and that (x,t)=(0,1) is the middle state.
PDE:010631.statement:
Consider one-dimensional linear acoustics
\[
p_t+4v_x=0,\qquad v_t+p_x=0,
\]
with Riemann data $(p,v)=(4,1)$ for $x<0$ and $(p,v)=(0,0)$ for $x>0$.

1. Prove that the sound speed and impedance are $c=2$ and $Z=2$, and
   that the Riemann invariants are the right-going field $p+2v$
   (constant along $dx/dt=+2$) and the left-going field $p-2v$
   (constant along $dx/dt=-2$).

2. Prove that the middle state between the acoustic waves $x=-2t$ and
   $x=2t$ is
   \[
   (p_*,v_*)=\Bigl(3,\frac32\Bigr).
   \]

3. Verify the Rankine–Hugoniot relations for both jumps (the left
   jump of speed $-2$ and the right jump of speed $+2$). Evaluate the
   state at the sample $(x,t)=(0,1)$ and confirm it is the middle
   state.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the wave speed is $c=4$ (confusing $c$
   with $c^2$) or the impedance is $Z=4$, so the invariants are
   $p\pm4v$”; (ii) “the middle state is the arithmetic mean $(2,1/2)$,
   or the invariants are matched from the wrong sides.”

Do not replace the calculation by a homogeneous scalar d'Alembert
wave for a single unknown, by a heat Fourier sine series, by a
Laplace Dirichlet disk / mean-value argument, by scalar
constant-coefficient transport, by an inviscid Burgers entropy
shock, or by an undamped homogeneous-wave energy identity.
permittedResults: The middle state solves $p_*+2v_*=p_L+2v_L=6$ and $p_*-2v_*=p_R-2v_R=0$, hence $(p_*,v_*)=(3,3/2)$.
A jump of speed $s$ satisfies $s[p]=4[v]$ and $s[v]=[p]$. Both acoustic waves $s=\pm2$ obey these identities.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read c from the eigenvalues of the symbol matrix, match p+2v from the left and p-2v from the right, then check s[p]=4[v] on both jumps.
Solve the 2×2 invariant system for (p_*,v_*) first, then confirm that x=0 at t=1 lies inside |x|<2t.

milestones.criterion: Identifies c=2, Z=2 and the invariants p+2v (right) and p-2v (left), and solves the middle state (3,3/2).
Verifies Rankine–Hugoniot on both acoustic jumps and evaluates (p,v)=(3,3/2) at (x,t)=(0,1).
Rejects c=4 or Z=4 and refuses an averaged or wrong-sided middle state.

commonErrors.description: Confuses c or Z with the coefficient 4 and reports c=4 or Z=4, hence the wrong invariants p±4v.
commonErrors.consequence: The required middle state (3,3/2) and the wave locations x=±2t are replaced by an incorrect acoustic scaling.

commonErrors.description: Takes the middle state to be the arithmetic mean (2,1/2), or matches the Riemann invariants from the wrong sides.
commonErrors.consequence: The required (p,v)=(3,3/2) between x=±2t, and the sample at (0,1), fail.

hintTree.content: The symbol matrix has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-4=0$, so $c=2$ and $Z=2$.
Match $p+2v=6$ from the left and $p-2v=0$ from the right to obtain $(3,3/2)$.
Check $s[p]=4[v]$ on $s=\pm2$. The ray $x=0$ at $t=1$ lies strictly between $x=\pm2t$.

PDE:010631.canonicalSolution:
The principal symbol has matrix
$A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&4\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, with
characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-4=0$. The acoustic speeds are
therefore $\pm c$ with $c=2$. Matching the system to
$p_t+\rho c^2 v_x=0$ and $v_t+\rho^{-1}p_x=0$ gives $\rho c^2=4$ and
$\rho^{-1}=1$, hence $\rho=1$ and impedance $Z=\rho c=2$. The
invariants are $p+2v$ (right-going) and $p-2v$ (left-going).
\[
\boxed{c=2,\;Z=2;\;p+2v\text{ right},\;p-2v\text{ left}}.
\]

The middle state inherits $p+2v$ from the left and $p-2v$ from the
right:
\[
p_*+2v_*=4+2\cdot1=6,\qquad p_*-2v_*=0.
\]
Adding and subtracting yields $p_*=3$ and $v_*=3/2$. The left
acoustic wave travels at $-c$, the right wave at $+c$, so the middle
state occupies $-2t<x<2t$.
\[
\boxed{(p_*,v_*)=(3,3/2)\text{ on }-2t<x<2t}.
\]

Left jump, $s=-2$, from $(4,1)$ to $(3,3/2)$:
\[
[p]=-1,\qquad [v]=\frac12,
\qquad s[p]=2=4[v],\qquad s[v]=-1=[p].
\]
Right jump, $s=+2$, from $(3,3/2)$ to $(0,0)$:
\[
[p]=-3,\qquad [v]=-\frac32,
\qquad s[p]=-6=4[v],\qquad s[v]=-3=[p].
\]
Both Rankine–Hugoniot relations hold. The sample $(x,t)=(0,1)$
satisfies $|x|<2t$, hence equals the middle state $(3,3/2)$.
\[
\boxed{\text{RH both jumps};\;(p,v)(0,1)=(3,3/2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses $c$ or $Z$ with the coefficient $4=c^2=\rho c^2$.
Sentence (ii) averages the data or matches the invariants from the
wrong sides.

The argument never reduces the system to a single scalar d'Alembert
unknown, never quotes a heat Fourier sine series, a Laplace disk /
mean-value identity, a scalar constant-speed transport solution, an
inviscid Burgers entropy shock, or an undamped homogeneous-wave
energy identity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The system has $c=2$ and $Z=2$, with right-going invariant $p+2v$ and left-going invariant $p-2v$. Matching $6$ from the left and $0$ from the right gives the middle state $(3,3/2)$ on $-2t<x<2t$. Both jumps satisfy Rankine–Hugoniot, and $(x,t)=(0,1)$ is the middle state. This is not $c=4$ and not the average $(2,1/2)$.
I take the wave speed to be c=4, or the impedance to be Z=4, and I use invariants p±4v. I do not report c=2, Z=2, or waves at x=±2t.
The middle state is the arithmetic mean (2,1/2), or I match the invariants from the wrong sides. I do not accept (p,v)=(3,3/2) at (0,1).

PTOP:010117.title: Cofinite opens force infinite sets dense and kill Hausdorff separation
PTOP:010117.objective: Verify the cofinite topology axioms from first principles, characterize closures and limits, prove every subspace is compact, and show the infinite case is T1 but not Hausdorff.
PTOP:010117.statement:
Let $X$ be an infinite set and let
$$
\tau=\{U\subseteq X:U=\emptyset\text{ or }X\setminus U\text{ is finite}\}.
$$
Prove directly that $\tau$ is a topology on $X$. Characterize the closed sets
exactly, and prove that a set $A\subseteq X$ is closed if and only if $A$ is
finite or $A=X$.

For arbitrary $A\subseteq X$, compute $\overline A$ and $\operatorname{int}A$
with proofs. In particular show that every infinite subset is dense.

Prove that every subset of $X$ is compact in the subspace topology induced by
$\tau$. Your argument must use the cofinite nature of nonempty opens rather
than metric sequential compactness.

Finally prove that $(X,\tau)$ is $T_1$ but not Hausdorff. Exhibit, for any two
distinct points, a concrete obstruction to disjoint open neighborhoods.
Diagnose the false claim that “every compact $T_1$ space is Hausdorff.”
permittedResults: A space is $T_1$ if and only if every singleton is closed.
Compactness is preserved by continuous images and by passing to closed subspaces, but need not imply Hausdorff separation.

acceptableStrategies.description: Work entirely with complements: open means cofinite, closed means finite or whole space.
For compactness, extract one nonempty open and cover the finite leftover by hand.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Classifies closed sets, closures, and interiors correctly, then proves universal compactness and the T1-not-Hausdorff separation audit from the cofinite structure.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Treats finite nonempty sets as open, or confuses the cofinite topology with the cocountable or discrete topology.
commonErrors.consequence: The closed-set lattice, closures, and separation conclusions are those of a different space.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that the space is Hausdorff because it is compact and T1, or because singletons are closed.
commonErrors.consequence: The central separation obstruction of the cofinite topology is erased.

hintTree.content: For finite intersections of nonempty opens, the complement is a finite union of finite sets.
If $A$ is infinite and $x\notin A$, every cofinite neighborhood of $x$ still meets $A$.
From a nonempty open cover of a subset, one open already leaves only finitely many points to cover.

PTOP:010117.canonicalSolution:
The empty set is declared open. The whole space $X$ is open because its
complement is empty, hence finite. An arbitrary union of opens is empty or
contains a nonempty open $U$, so its complement is contained in the finite set
$X\setminus U$ and is therefore finite. If $U_1,\ldots,U_n$ are nonempty opens,
then
$$
X\setminus\bigcap_{i=1}^n U_i
=\bigcup_{i=1}^n(X\setminus U_i)
$$
is a finite union of finite sets, so the intersection is open. Thus $\tau$ is
a topology.

Closed sets are exactly the complements of opens: $\emptyset$, $X$, and all
finite subsets of $X$. Equivalently, $A$ is closed if and only if $A$ is finite
or $A=X$.

If $A$ is finite then $A$ is closed, so $\overline A=A$. If $A$ is infinite,
the only closed set containing $A$ is $X$, so $\overline A=X$. Thus every
infinite subset is dense.

For the interior, a nonempty cofinite open set $U$ can be contained in $A$
only if
$$
X\setminus A\subseteq X\setminus U
$$
is finite. Conversely, if $X\setminus A$ is finite, then $A$ itself is open.
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\operatorname{int}A=
\begin{cases}
A,&X\setminus A\text{ is finite},\\
\emptyset,&X\setminus A\text{ is infinite}.
\end{cases}}
$$
This includes $\operatorname{int}X=X$ and shows, for example, that a proper
cofinite subset can have nonempty interior.

Now let $A\subseteq X$ and let $\{U_i\cap A\}$ be an open cover of $A$ by
subspace opens. The empty set is compact, so suppose $A\neq\emptyset$ and
choose a cover member $U_{i_0}\cap A\neq\emptyset$. Then $U_{i_0}$ is a
nonempty cofinite open and
$X\setminus U_{i_0}$ is finite, so
$$
A\setminus U_{i_0}\subseteq X\setminus U_{i_0}
$$
is finite. Cover those finitely many remaining points by finitely many further
sets from the cover. Hence $A$ is compact.

Singletons are finite, so closed, and the space is $T_1$. If $x\neq y$ and $U,V$
are open with $x\in U$ and $y\in V$, then both complements are finite, so
$$
U\cap V=X\setminus\bigl((X\setminus U)\cup(X\setminus V)\bigr)
$$
is cofinite, hence nonempty. No pair of distinct points has disjoint open
neighborhoods, so the space is not Hausdorff.

The diagnosis is immediate: compactness and $T_1$ do not force Hausdorffness,
because the infinite cofinite space is a compact $T_1$ counterexample.

graderFixtures.proofText: Opens are empty or cofinite, so closed sets are finite or the whole space. Infinite sets are dense, while int(A)=A exactly when A is cofinite and is empty otherwise. Any open cover has a nonempty open leaving only finitely many points, so every subset is compact. Singletons are closed, hence T1, but any two nonempty opens meet, so the space is not Hausdorff.
Finite sets are open because they are the basic building blocks of the topology, and infinite sets are closed. Distinct points can then be separated by taking complementary finite opens.
Every subset is compact and singletons are closed, so the space is a compact T1 space and therefore Hausdorff. Disjoint neighborhoods exist by the usual compact-Hausdorff theorem.

PTOP:010118.title: Dictionary order and the plane subspace topology are incomparable
PTOP:010118.objective: Compare the order and Euclidean-subspace topologies on a dictionary-ordered split ladder, exhibit one open set missing from each topology, describe their local bases, and audit the projection and identity maps.
PTOP:010118.statement:
Let
$$
L=\bigl(\{0\}\times[0,1]\bigr)\cup\bigl((0,1]\times\{0\}\bigr)
\subset\mathbb R^2
$$
and equip $L$ with the dictionary order
$$
(x,y)<(x',y')
\quad\text{iff}\quad
x<x'\ \text{or}\ (x=x'\ \text{and}\ y<y').
$$
Write $\tau_<$ for the order topology on $L$ and $\tau_e$ for the subspace
topology inherited from the Euclidean plane.

Prove that both topologies are Hausdorff. Then prove that $\tau_<$ and $\tau_e$
are incomparable: exhibit a $\tau_e$-open neighborhood of $(0,1)$ that is not
$\tau_<$-open, and a $\tau_<$-open neighborhood of $(0,0)$ that is not
$\tau_e$-open.

Describe countable local bases at $(0,0)$, at a point $(0,y)$ with $0<y<1$,
and at a point $(x,0)$ with $0<x\le1$, in each topology. Use the comparison to
decide whether the restricted projection
$$
\pi_x:L\to[0,1],\qquad \pi_x(x,y)=x
$$
is continuous as a map from $(L,\tau_<)$ and from $(L,\tau_e)$ into the usual
interval.

Also decide continuity of both identity maps between $(L,\tau_<)$ and
$(L,\tau_e)$. Finally diagnose the claim “an order-preserving injection into
$\mathbb R$ always induces the order topology as its subspace topology.”
permittedResults: Continuity is tested by preimages: refining the domain topology can only make continuity easier, while refining the codomain can make it harder.
Subspace opens are intersections of ambient opens with the subset; order opens need not arise this way.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write explicit order rays at the bottom and Euclidean traces at the top, then test each against the other topology.
Check projection preimages directly, and use the two witness opens to audit the identity maps.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Produces both incomparability witnesses and correctly compares continuity of the two identity maps and the projection map.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the order and Euclidean subspace topologies are equal or that one contains the other, usually by checking only one joint.
commonErrors.consequence: One of the two opposite open-set witnesses, and hence one identity discontinuity, is missed.

commonErrors.description: Declares pi_x discontinuous from the order topology merely because the local bases differ from the Euclidean ones.
commonErrors.consequence: The order-open preimages of intervals at zero and at positive coordinates are not checked.

hintTree.content: In the order, $(0,1)$ is followed by horizontal points $(x,0)$ with arbitrarily small $x>0$, whereas Euclidean neighborhoods of $(0,1)$ can avoid the horizontal ray.
At the minimum $(0,0)$, an initial order ray can stay on the vertical segment, whereas every Euclidean ball also meets the horizontal ray.
For continuity of $\pi_x$ at value $0$, identify the preimage of a small relative interval $[0,\varepsilon)$ as an initial order ray containing the whole vertical segment.

PTOP:010118.canonicalSolution:
Both topologies are Hausdorff. The Euclidean claim follows by tracing
disjoint plane neighborhoods on $L$. For the order topology, let $p<q$. If
some $r$ satisfies $p<r<q$, the order rays $(-\infty,r)$ and $(r,\infty)$
separate $p,q$. If no such $r$ exists, the rays $(-\infty,q)$ and
$(p,\infty)$ are disjoint and separate them.

The topologies are not comparable. First set
$$
E=\{0\}\times(1/2,1].
$$
This is Euclidean-subspace open because
$E=L\cap(\mathbb R\times(1/2,3/2))$. It is not order open at $(0,1)$:
that point is not an order endpoint, and every order-basic neighborhood of it
extends above it to some horizontal point $(x,0)$ with $x>0$.

In the other direction, set
$$
O=\{0\}\times[0,1/2).
$$
This is the initial order ray $(-\infty,(0,1/2))$, so it is order open. It is
not a Euclidean-subspace neighborhood of $(0,0)$ because every Euclidean ball
about $(0,0)$ meets the horizontal ray. Thus neither topology contains the
other.

At $(0,0)$, order-local bases are
$\{0\}\times[0,1/n)$, while Euclidean-local bases are
$L\cap B((0,0),1/n)$ and include short portions of both arms. At $(0,y)$ with
$0<y<1$, both topologies have vertical local bases
$\{0\}\times(y-\varepsilon,y+\varepsilon)$. At $(x,0)$ with $0<x<1$, both
have horizontal local bases $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\times\{0\}$ for
$\varepsilon<x$; at $x=1$ use the corresponding left-endpoint intervals.

The map $\pi_x:(L,\tau_e)\to[0,1]$ is continuous as a restricted coordinate
projection. It is also continuous from $(L,\tau_<)$. Away from value $0$, the
preimage of a small interval is a horizontal order-open interval. If a relative
open $G\subseteq[0,1]$ contains $0$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ with
$[0,\varepsilon)\subseteq G$; the preimage of this smaller interval is the
initial order ray consisting of the whole vertical segment followed by the
horizontal points with $0<x<\varepsilon$. The remaining preimage is a union of
horizontal order intervals.

Neither identity map is continuous. The identity from $\tau_<$ to $\tau_e$
fails on the Euclidean-open set $E$, and the identity from $\tau_e$ to $\tau_<$
fails on the order-open set $O$.

Finally, an order-preserving injection need not be an order-topological
embedding. Define $j:[0,2]\to\mathbb R$ by $j(t)=t$ for $t\le1$ and
$j(t)=t+1$ for $t>1$. It is strictly order preserving, but its image is
$[0,1]\cup(2,3]$. The subspace-open set $(1/2,1]$ at $j(1)$ pulls back to
$(1/2,1]$, which is not order open at the interior point $1$ of $[0,2]$.
Additional hypotheses such as convex image or order-topological continuity are
needed.

graderFixtures.proofText: The top vertical ray is Euclidean open but not order open, while a bottom initial vertical ray is order open but not Euclidean open, so the topologies are incomparable. Their local bases differ at the two joints. Both identity maps fail in the corresponding direction, while pi_x is continuous from both domains.
The Euclidean top ray is not order open, so I conclude that the Euclidean topology is strictly finer and do not check the order-open bottom ray.
Because an order neighborhood at the bottom can omit horizontal points, I declare pi_x discontinuous without checking preimages of open intervals in [0,1].
