PTOP:010219.title: The diagonal breaks in the box topology, but addition survives
PTOP:010219.objective: Compare product and box topologies on R^N, prove product-continuity by coordinates, show why the diagonal fails for a shrinking box, and prove coordinatewise addition remains continuous between box-topological sequence spaces.
PTOP:010219.statement:
Let $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ denote the set of real sequences. Write $\tau_{\mathrm{prod}}$
for the product topology and $\tau_{\mathrm{box}}$ for the box topology, both using
the usual topology on each factor.

Prove that $\tau_{\mathrm{prod}}\subsetneq\tau_{\mathrm{box}}$. Give an explicit
box-open set that is not product open.

Define
$$
\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{\mathbb N},
\qquad
\delta(t)=(t,t,t,\ldots)
$$
and
$$
\alpha:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\times\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb R^{\mathbb N},
\qquad
\alpha(x,y)=x+y
$$
coordinatewise. Prove that $\delta$ and $\alpha$ are continuous when every
infinite product is given the product topology. Then give
$\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ the box topology and prove that $\delta$ is not
continuous. In contrast, prove that $\alpha$ remains continuous when both
sequence-space factors and its codomain have the box topology (the two-factor
domain carries the ordinary product of those two box topologies).

Finally diagnose the slogan “componentwise continuity always yields continuity
into an infinite product” by stating the precise product-topology theorem and
the box-topology obstruction.
permittedResults: A map into a product is continuous for the product topology if and only if every coordinate projection of the map is continuous.
The same coordinatewise criterion fails for the box topology because basic box neighborhoods constrain infinitely many coordinates at once.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the finite-support description of product basics and the universal property for maps into products.
Test a shrinking box against the diagonal, then construct coordinate neighborhoods for addition.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Separates product from box topology by the diagonal failure while correctly proving that coordinatewise addition still makes the box product a topological group.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Treats the box and product topologies as equal on countable products of lines.
commonErrors.consequence: The continuity failures disappear and the exercise collapses to ordinary coordinatewise calculus.

commonErrors.description: Applies the product-topology coordinate criterion verbatim to the box topology and declares the diagonal continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: The shrinking box whose diagonal preimage is a singleton is ignored.

hintTree.content: The set $\prod_{n}(-1/n,1/n)$ is box open and not product open.
For product continuity of $\delta$, each coordinate is the identity map on $\mathbb R$.
For box-continuity of addition, start with $\prod W_n$ around $x+y$ and choose coordinate neighborhoods $U_n,V_n$ with $U_n+V_n\subseteq W_n$.

PTOP:010219.canonicalSolution:
Every product-basic open is a box-basic open, so
$\tau_{\mathrm{prod}}\subseteq\tau_{\mathrm{box}}$. The set
$$
B=\prod_{n=1}^\infty\bigl(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n\bigr)
$$
is box open. It is not product open: every product-basic neighborhood of $0$
fixes only finitely many coordinates and is unbounded in the remaining
coordinates, hence not contained in $B$. Thus the inclusion is strict.

For the product topology, a map into $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ is continuous if and
only if each coordinate is continuous. Each coordinate of $\delta$ is
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}$, so $\delta$ is product-continuous. Each coordinate of
$\alpha$ is ordinary addition $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, continuous, so
$\alpha$ is product-continuous on the product of product topologies.

Now equip $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the box topology. The same set $B$ is a box
neighborhood of $\delta(0)=0$. But
$$
\delta^{-1}(B)=\{t\in\mathbb R:|t|<1/n\text{ for every }n\}=\{0\},
$$
which is not open in $\mathbb R$. Hence $\delta$ is not box-continuous.

Addition behaves differently. Fix $(x,y)$ and a basic box neighborhood
$$
W=\prod_{n=1}^\infty W_n
$$
of $x+y$. For every $n$, continuity of ordinary real addition supplies open
neighborhoods $U_n\ni x_n$ and $V_n\ni y_n$ such that
$U_n+V_n\subseteq W_n$. Then $U=\prod U_n$ and $V=\prod V_n$ are box-open and
$$
\alpha(U\times V)\subseteq W.
$$
Thus coordinatewise addition is continuous from the product of the two box
spaces to the box space. In particular, for the shrinking box $B$ at zero one
may take $U_n=V_n=(-1/(2n),1/(2n))$.

The coordinatewise-continuity slogan is exactly the universal property for the
product topology. It is not a general criterion for the box topology, as the
diagonal proves. Addition survives only because its coordinate neighborhoods
can be chosen simultaneously and assembled into box neighborhoods.

graderFixtures.proofText: The shrinking box B=prod(-1/n,1/n) is not product open, so the box topology is strictly finer. Diagonal and addition are product-continuous by coordinates. The diagonal is not box-continuous because its preimage of B is {0}; addition is box-continuous because coordinate neighborhoods can be chosen with U_n+V_n inside each target interval.

On a countable product the box and product topologies coincide because sequences have countably many coordinates and each can be controlled. Therefore continuity questions are the same in both topologies.
Each coordinate of the diagonal is continuous, so the diagonal is continuous into the box topology by the product-topology coordinate criterion.

PTOP:010220.title: Finite closed pasting works; a countable closed cover can fail
PTOP:010220.objective: Prove the finite closed pasting lemma, apply it to a two-piece definition, and produce a countable closed cover where a pointwise-compatible family does not paste continuously.
PTOP:010220.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces.

1. Prove the finite closed pasting lemma: if $X=F_1\cup\cdots\cup F_n$ with each
   $F_i$ closed in $X$, and if $f_i:F_i\to Y$ are continuous maps that agree on
   all overlaps $F_i\cap F_j$, then the pasted map $f:X\to Y$ defined by
   $f|_{F_i}=f_i$ is continuous.

2. On $X=[0,2]$ with the Euclidean topology, define
   $$
   f(x)=\begin{cases}
   x,&0\le x\le1,\\
   2-x,&1\le x\le2.
   \end{cases}
   $$
   Realize $f$ as a paste of two closed-piece maps and conclude continuity from
   part (1), not from piecewise-linear folklore.

3. Let $X=[0,1]$, let $F_0=\{0\}$, and let
   $F_n=[1/(n+1),1/n]$ for $n\ge1$. Each $F_n$ is closed and
   $X=\bigcup_{n\ge0}F_n$. Define $g_0(0)=0$ and let
   $g_n:F_n\to\mathbb R$ be the constant map $1$ for $n\ge1$.
   Verify that the pieces agree on overlaps, so they define a function
   $g:X\to\mathbb R$, and prove that $g$ is discontinuous at $0$.

Explain exactly which hypothesis of the finite pasting lemma fails in part (3).
permittedResults: A map is continuous if and only if preimages of closed sets are closed.
A finite union of closed sets is closed; an infinite union need not be.

acceptableStrategies.description: Prefer the closed-preimage formulation of continuity for pasting proofs.
For the counterexample, force a jump at a limit point approached by infinitely many closed pieces.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Proves finite closed pasting from closed preimages and exhibits a countable closed-cover failure with a concrete discontinuity.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Quotes the open-cover pasting lemma while the pieces are closed, or assumes arbitrary covers paste.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-closed hypothesis is never used and the countable counterexample is unexplained.

commonErrors.description: Claims the countable closed family pastes to a continuous function because each piece is continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: The discontinuity at the accumulation point is missed.

hintTree.content: For closed $C\subseteq Y$, show $f^{-1}(C)=\bigcup_i f_i^{-1}(C)$ is a finite union of closed sets in $X$.
The pieces $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$ are closed in $[0,2]$ and agree at $1$.
In the countable example, $g(0)=0$ but $g(x)=1$ for every $x>0$ in the union of the intervals.

PTOP:010220.canonicalSolution:
Let $C\subseteq Y$ be closed. Then
$$
f^{-1}(C)=\bigcup_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}(C).
$$
Each $f_i^{-1}(C)$ is closed in $F_i$ by continuity of $f_i$, and because $F_i$ is
closed in $X$ it remains closed in $X$. A finite union of closed sets is closed,
so $f^{-1}(C)$ is closed. Hence $f$ is continuous.

For the tent map, set $F_1=[0,1]$, $F_2=[1,2]$, $f_1(x)=x$, and $f_2(x)=2-x$.
Both pieces are closed in $[0,2]$, both maps are continuous, and
$f_1(1)=f_2(1)=1$. Part (1) yields continuity of $f$.

In the countable example every $F_n$ is closed in $[0,1]$. Adjacent positive
pieces overlap only at a common endpoint, where both maps have value $1$, and
$F_0$ is disjoint from every positive piece. Thus the maps agree on all
overlaps and paste to a function satisfying $g(0)=0$ and
$g(x)=1$ for all $x\in(0,1]$. Continuity fails at $0$ because the preimage of
$(-1/2,1/2)$ is $\{0\}$, not open, or because $g(x_k)=1\not\to 0$ along
$x_k=1/k$.

The finite-pasting hypothesis fails because infinitely many closed pieces are
used; the union of the closed sets $g^{-1}(\{1\})=\bigcup_n F_n$ is not a finite
union argument available inside the closed-preimage proof.

graderFixtures.proofText: Finite closed pasting follows because preimages of closed sets are finite unions of closed sets. The tent map is the paste of x on [0,1] and 2-x on [1,2]. For F_n=[1/(n+1),1/n] and {0}, the constants 1 and 0 paste to a function discontinuous at 0, so infinitude of pieces is essential.
Any cover by sets on which continuous pieces agree yields a continuous paste. I apply the open pasting lemma to the closed intervals without change.
Each g_n is continuous on a closed set and the values agree on overlaps, so the countable paste g is continuous on [0,1], including at 0.

PTOP:010321.title: A quotient of a compact Hausdorff space is Hausdorff exactly when the relation is closed
PTOP:010321.objective: Prove that a quotient of a compact Hausdorff space is Hausdorff if and only if the equivalence relation is closed in the product, and apply the criterion to endpoint identification on an interval.
PTOP:010321.statement:
Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space and let $q:X\to Y$ be a quotient map
arising from an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $X$. Identify the relation with
its graph
$$
R=\{(x,x')\in X\times X:x\sim x'\}.
$$

1. Prove that if $Y$ is Hausdorff then $R$ is closed in $X\times X$.

2. Conversely, assume $R$ is closed. Prove that $Y$ is Hausdorff. First prove
   directly that $q$ is closed by showing that the saturation of a closed
   subset of $X$ is compact, and then use the closed-map property to build
   saturated neighborhoods of distinct equivalence classes.

3. Let $X=[0,1]$ with the Euclidean topology and identify only the endpoints
   $0\sim 1$, leaving all other points as singleton classes. Prove that the
   relation is closed, conclude that the quotient is Hausdorff, and prove that
   the quotient is homeomorphic to the circle
   $S^1=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\}$.

4. Diagnose the failure mode if one instead collapses the entire open interval
   $(0,1)$ to a point while leaving the endpoints free: is the resulting
   quotient Hausdorff?
permittedResults: A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.
Closed continuous images of compact spaces are compact; compact subspaces of Hausdorff spaces are closed.
A compact Hausdorff space is normal; the proof separates pairs of points and uses finite subcovers twice to separate disjoint closed sets.

acceptableStrategies.description: Pull back the diagonal to test closedness of R, then separate fibers in the compact Hausdorff domain.
Use the continuous closed-map criterion and compact-to-Hausdorff bijections for the circle identification.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Establishes the closed-relation characterization and applies it to endpoint identification versus an open-interval collapse.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Declares every quotient of a compact Hausdorff space Hausdorff without checking closedness of the relation.
commonErrors.consequence: Non-Hausdorff quotients such as open-interval collapses are incorrectly accepted.

commonErrors.description: Claims the induced circle map is a homeomorphism solely because it is a continuous bijection, without compactness or closedness.
commonErrors.consequence: The compact-to-Hausdorff step that legitimizes the homeomorphism is missing.

hintTree.content: If $Y$ is Hausdorff then the diagonal of $Y\times Y$ is closed; pull it back by $q\times q$.
For closed $C\subseteq X$, its saturation is the projection of $R\cap(C\times X)$; compactness and Hausdorffness make this saturation closed.
The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ coequalizes the endpoints and induces the circle homeomorphism.

PTOP:010321.canonicalSolution:
If $Y$ is Hausdorff then the diagonal $\Delta_Y$ is closed in $Y\times Y$. The
map $q\times q:X\times X\to Y\times Y$ is continuous, so
$$
R=(q\times q)^{-1}(\Delta_Y)
$$
is closed in $X\times X$.

Conversely, assume $R$ is closed. First prove that $q$ is closed without
assuming any separation property of $Y$. If $C\subseteq X$ is closed, then
$C$ is compact and
$$
\operatorname{Sat}(C)=q^{-1}(q(C))
=\pi_2\bigl(R\cap(C\times X)\bigr).
$$
The set inside the projection is closed in the compact space $X\times X$, hence
compact. Its projection is compact and therefore closed in the Hausdorff space
$X$. By the quotient condition, a subset of $Y$ is closed exactly when its
preimage under $q$ is closed. Thus $q(C)$ is closed, so $q$ is a closed map.

Let $y_1\neq y_2$ and put $A=q^{-1}(y_1)$ and $B=q^{-1}(y_2)$. Each class is a
closed section of $R$, so $A$ and $B$ are disjoint closed subsets of the compact
Hausdorff, hence normal, space $X$ (the finite-subcover Hausdorff argument is the
theorem recorded above). Choose disjoint opens $U\supseteq A$ and
$V\supseteq B$. Since $q$ is closed, the sets
$$
O_1=Y\setminus q(X\setminus U),
\qquad
O_2=Y\setminus q(X\setminus V)
$$
are open. The whole fiber $A$ lies in $U$, so $y_1\in O_1$ and
$q^{-1}(O_1)\subseteq U$; similarly $y_2\in O_2$ and
$q^{-1}(O_2)\subseteq V$. Hence $O_1$ and $O_2$ are disjoint open
neighborhoods of $y_1,y_2$, and $Y$ is Hausdorff.

For endpoint identification on $[0,1]$, the relation
$$
R=\Delta_{[0,1]}\cup\{(0,1),(1,0)\}
$$
is closed as a finite union of closed sets. Part (2) yields a Hausdorff quotient
$Y$. The continuous surjection
$$
f:[0,1]\to S^1,
\qquad
f(t)=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)
$$
coequalizes $0$ and $1$, so it descends to a continuous bijection
$\overline f:Y\to S^1$. The domain $Y$ is compact and $S^1$ is Hausdorff, so
$\overline f$ is a homeomorphism.

If instead the entire open interval $(0,1)$ is collapsed to a point while $0$
and $1$ remain free, then
$$
R=\Delta_{[0,1]}\cup\bigl((0,1)\times(0,1)\bigr)
$$
is not closed: $(1/n,1/2)\in R$ converges to $(0,1/2)\notin R$. By the proved
criterion, the quotient is not Hausdorff.

graderFixtures.proofText: Hausdorffness of the quotient pulls the diagonal back to a closed relation. Conversely a closed relation on a compact Hausdorff space yields a Hausdorff quotient. Endpoint identification gives a closed relation and a compact Hausdorff quotient homeomorphic to S^1 via the wrapping map. Collapsing (0,1) produces a nonclosed relation and a non-Hausdorff quotient.
Any quotient of a compact Hausdorff space is compact Hausdorff, so the relation is automatically closed and no product-space check is required.
The induced map from the endpoint quotient to the circle is a continuous bijection, hence a homeomorphism with no further hypotheses.

PTOP:010422.title: Regular plus Lindelöf yields normality by countable shrinking
PTOP:010422.objective: Prove that every regular Lindelöf space is normal by extracting countable open covers and performing a disjoint shrinking, then apply the theorem to a standard example class.
PTOP:010422.statement:
Recall that a space is regular when it is $T_1$ and for every closed $F$ and
point $x\notin F$ there are disjoint opens separating $x$ from $F$. A space is
Lindelöf when every open cover has a countable subcover. A space is normal when
it is $T_1$ and disjoint closed sets have disjoint open neighborhoods.

1. Let $X$ be regular and Lindelöf. Let $A,B\subseteq X$ be disjoint closed sets.
   For each $a\in A$ choose an open neighborhood $U_a$ with
   $\overline U_a\cap B=\emptyset$, and likewise for each $b\in B$ choose $V_b$
   with $\overline V_b\cap A=\emptyset$. Explain why regularity supplies these
   neighborhoods.

2. Extract countable subcovers $\{U_{a_n}\}$ of $A$ and $\{V_{b_n}\}$ of $B$
   from the open cover of $X$ obtained by adding $X\setminus(A\cup B)$.

3. Form the disjointifying unions
   $$
   U=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty\Bigl(U_{a_n}\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^n\overline V_{b_k}\Bigr),
   \qquad
   V=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty\Bigl(V_{b_n}\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^n\overline U_{a_k}\Bigr).
   $$
   Prove that $U$ and $V$ are disjoint opens with $A\subseteq U$ and $B\subseteq V$.

4. Conclude that $X$ is normal. Then explain why the theorem does not claim that
   every regular second-countable space needs a separate proof, and why the
   theorem does not apply to an arbitrary regular space that fails Lindelöf.
permittedResults: In a regular space, a point and a disjoint closed set can be placed in disjoint opens, and the point's neighborhood may be chosen with closure missing the closed set.
Second countability implies the Lindelöf property, so regular second-countable spaces are normal by the same argument.

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate points from the opposite closed set with controlled closures, then countabilize.
Disjointify by subtracting earlier closures and compare minimal indices in the intersection argument.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Carries out the countable shrinking construction that turns regularity plus Lindelöf into normality.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Uses compactness or a finite subcover instead of the Lindelöf countable subcover.
commonErrors.consequence: The theorem is reduced to the compact regular case and the countable shrinking formulas are unjustified.

commonErrors.description: Takes raw unions of the U_a and V_b and claims they are disjoint without subtracting closures.
commonErrors.consequence: The opens may meet, so normality is not proved.

hintTree.content: Regularity at $a\notin B$ yields $U_a$ with $\overline U_a\subseteq X\setminus B$.
The sets $U_a$, $V_b$, and $X\setminus(A\cup B)$ cover $X$, so Lindelöf yields countable subcovers of $A$ and $B$.
If a point lay in both $U$ and $V$, compare the least indices and use the deleted closures.

PTOP:010422.canonicalSolution:
Fix $a\in A$. Then $a\notin B$ and $B$ is closed, so regularity supplies disjoint
opens separating $a$ from $B$. Equivalently, there is an open $U_a\ni a$ with
$\overline U_a\cap B=\emptyset$. The symmetric construction produces the sets
$V_b$. If either $A$ or $B$ is empty, the pair $\emptyset,X$ already separates
them, so assume both are nonempty for the indexed construction below.

The collection
$$
\{U_a:a\in A\}\cup\{V_b:b\in B\}\cup\{X\setminus(A\cup B)\}
$$
is an open cover of $X$. Lindelöfness yields a countable subcover. Retaining only
those $U_{a_n}$ that appear and those $V_{b_n}$ that appear gives countable opens
covering $A$ and $B$ respectively (if only finitely many appear, pad the list by
repetition).

The sets $U$ and $V$ displayed in the statement are open as unions of opens.
If $a\in A$, then $a\in U_{a_n}$ for some $n$, and $a\notin\overline V_{b_k}$ for
every $k$ because each $\overline V_{b_k}$ misses $A$. Hence
$a\in U_{a_n}\setminus\bigcup_{k\le n}\overline V_{b_k}\subseteq U$. Likewise
$B\subseteq V$.

Suppose there exists $x\in U\cap V$. Choose least indices $n,m$ with
$$
x\in U_{a_n}\setminus\bigcup_{k\le n}\overline V_{b_k},
\qquad
x\in V_{b_m}\setminus\bigcup_{k\le m}\overline U_{a_k}.
$$
If $n\le m$ then $x\in U_{a_n}$ forces $x\notin V_{b_m}$ after deleting
$\overline U_{a_n}$ from the $V$-side when $m\ge n$, a contradiction. The case
$m<n$ is symmetric. Thus $U\cap V=\emptyset$.

Therefore disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint opens. Since $X$ is
already $T_1$ by regularity conventions used here, $X$ is normal.

Second countability implies Lindelöf, so the theorem specializes to regular
second-countable spaces without a new idea. Without Lindelöf, the countable
shrinking step is unavailable and the argument stops; there exist regular spaces
that are not normal.

graderFixtures.proofText: Regularity supplies neighborhoods whose closures miss the opposite closed set. Lindelöf countabilizes the covers. The disjointifying unions U and V are open, contain A and B, and are disjoint by minimal-index comparison. Thus regular Lindelöf spaces are normal; second-countable regular spaces are included, but Lindelöf cannot be dropped.
Regularity gives neighborhoods of points of A and B. Compactness of A and B is not assumed, but I still extract finite subcovers and paste them as in the compact regular argument.
After choosing countable covers {U_n} of A and {V_n} of B, the sets U=union U_n and V=union V_n are disjoint because each U_n misses B and each V_n misses A.

PTOP:010523.title: One-point compactification is Hausdorff exactly for locally compact Hausdorff spaces
PTOP:010523.objective: Construct the one-point compactification, prove compactness, characterize when it is Hausdorff, and compare the compactifications of the discrete naturals and the rationals.
PTOP:010523.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space and set $\alpha X=X\cup\{\infty\}$ with
$\infty\notin X$. Declare $U\subseteq\alpha X$ open when either
- $U\subseteq X$ and $U$ is open in $X$, or
- $\infty\in U$ and $X\setminus U$ is compact and closed in $X$.

1. Prove that these sets form a topology on $\alpha X$ and that $X$ sits as an
   open subspace. Prove that $\alpha X$ is compact.

2. Prove that $\alpha X$ is Hausdorff if and only if $X$ is locally compact
   Hausdorff. Identify exactly where local compactness is used to separate a
   point of $X$ from $\infty$.

3. For $X=\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ with the discrete topology, prove that
   $\alpha\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ is
   homeomorphic to $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\}$ as a subspace of
   $\mathbb R$.

4. For $X=\mathbb Q$ with the Euclidean subspace topology, prove that
   $\alpha\mathbb Q$ is not Hausdorff by showing $\mathbb Q$ is not locally
   compact.

Do not invoke a black-box uniqueness theorem without proving the concrete
neighborhood criterion at infinity used above.
permittedResults: In a Hausdorff space, compact subsets are closed, and local compactness is equivalent to the existence of relatively compact open neighborhoods.
A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat neighborhoods of infinity as complements of compact closed sets and reduce compactness to covering that compact residue.
Separate finite points from infinity by compact neighborhoods in the locally compact Hausdorff case.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Builds the one-point compactification and pins Hausdorffness exactly to local compactness of the original Hausdorff space.

commonErrors.description: Allows arbitrary supersets of infinity as open sets, or only requires the complement to be compact without closedness in a non-Hausdorff setting.
commonErrors.consequence: The collection may fail to be a topology or may destroy the Hausdorff characterization.

commonErrors.description: Claims that Q is locally compact because it is metrizable or because bounded closed intervals of rationals are compact.
commonErrors.consequence: The non-Hausdorff nature of alpha Q is lost.

hintTree.content: For unions of neighborhoods of infinity, the complement is an intersection of compact closed sets.
To separate $x\in X$ from $\infty$, take a compact Hausdorff neighborhood of $x$ and use its complement as a neighborhood of $\infty$.
Discrete $\mathbb N$ is locally compact Hausdorff; $\mathbb Q$ has no compact neighborhood of any point.

PTOP:010523.canonicalSolution:
The empty set is an ordinary open, and $\alpha X$ is a neighborhood of infinity
because $X\setminus\alpha X=\emptyset$ is compact and closed. Ordinary opens are
stable under unions and finite intersections. If $\{U_i\}$ are neighborhoods of
infinity, then
$$
X\setminus\bigcup U_i=\bigcap(X\setminus U_i)
$$
is a closed subset of any one compact complement, hence compact and closed, so
the union is a neighborhood of infinity. A union containing both ordinary opens
and a neighborhood of infinity has complement obtained by intersecting that
compact complement with further closed sets, so the same argument applies. A
finite intersection of neighborhoods of
infinity has complement equal to a finite union of compact closed sets, hence
compact and closed. Mixed intersections of ordinary opens with neighborhoods of
infinity reduce to ordinary opens in $X$. Thus one has a topology, and $X$ is
open in $\alpha X$.

To see compactness, let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover of $\alpha X$. Some member
$U_\infty$ contains $\infty$, so $K=X\setminus U_\infty$ is compact. Finitely many
members of $\mathcal U$ cover $K$, and adjoining $U_\infty$ covers $\alpha X$.

If $\alpha X$ is Hausdorff then $X$ is Hausdorff as a subspace. For local
compactness at $x\in X$, separate $x$ from $\infty$ by disjoint opens $U\ni x$
and $V\ni\infty$. Then $X\setminus V$ is compact closed and contains a
neighborhood of $x$, so $x$ has a compact neighborhood.

Conversely, if $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff then $X$ is Hausdorff, so points
of $X$ separate as in $X$. For $x\in X$ and $\infty$, choose a compact
neighborhood $K$ of $x$. Hausdorffness makes $K$ closed. Then
$U=\operatorname{int}K$ (or a smaller open inside $K$) and
$V=\alpha X\setminus K$ are disjoint opens separating $x$ from $\infty$.

Discrete $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ is locally compact Hausdorff, and its compact subsets are
exactly the finite subsets. Hence the neighborhoods of $\infty$ in
$\alpha\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ are exactly the sets containing all but finitely many natural
numbers. The bijection
$$
h(\infty)=0,
\qquad h(n)=1/n
$$
matches those cofinite neighborhoods with the subspace neighborhoods of $0$ in
$\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$; continuity at the isolated points is immediate.
Thus $h$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space,
and therefore a homeomorphism.

Finally fix $q\in\mathbb Q$ and suppose a compact neighborhood $K$ of $q$
existed in $\mathbb Q$. It contains
$\mathbb Q\cap(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$ for some $\varepsilon>0$. Choose
an irrational $a$ in that real interval and rationals $r_n\to a$ still inside
the interval. The inclusion $\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ would send the
compact set $K$ to a compact, hence closed, subset of $\mathbb R$ containing
every $r_n$ but not their limit $a$, a contradiction. Thus $\mathbb Q$ is not
locally compact, so $\alpha\mathbb Q$ is not Hausdorff.

graderFixtures.proofText: Opens in alpha X are ordinary opens or complements of compact closed sets plus infinity. Compactness follows by covering the compact residue of one infinity neighborhood. Hausdorffness holds iff X is locally compact Hausdorff. Discrete N yields a convergent sequence compactification; Q is not locally compact, so alpha Q is not Hausdorff.
Any set containing infinity is declared open in alpha X. Compactness is then immediate because a single such set covers the new point, and no closedness restriction is imposed on complements.
The rationals are a metric space, so closed balls are compact and Q is locally compact. Therefore alpha Q is Hausdorff.

PTOP:010524.title: Compact Hausdorff spaces are normal by closed-neighborhood shrinking
PTOP:010524.objective: Prove that compact Hausdorff spaces are normal using point-closed and then closed-closed separation, and contrast the argument with the regular Lindelöf route.
PTOP:010524.statement:
Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff.

1. Prove that $X$ is regular: for a closed set $F$ and point $x\notin F$,
   produce disjoint opens separating them. Use compactness of $F$ and the
   Hausdorff axiom at pairs $(x,y)$ for $y\in F$.

2. Prove that $X$ is normal: for disjoint closed sets $A,B$, first separate each
   point of $A$ from $B$ by an open neighborhood whose closure misses $B$, cover
   $A$ by finitely many such neighborhoods, and disjointify against $B$.

3. Explain why the same finite-subcover step is unavailable in a general regular
   Lindelöf space and how the earlier countable shrinking repairs it.

4. Give a one-sentence reason that the infinite cofinite topology does not
   contradict the theorem.
permittedResults: In a Hausdorff space, compact subsets are closed.
Finite subcovers exist for open covers of compact sets; this is the engine of compact normality proofs.

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate a point from a compact set by finitely many Hausdorff neighborhood pairs.
Upgrade to closed-closed separation by finitely many regular neighborhoods with controlled closures.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Proves regularity and normality of compact Hausdorff spaces by finite closed-neighborhood shrinking.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Asserts that Hausdorffness already separates closed sets, skipping the compact finite-subcover argument.
commonErrors.consequence: Only points are separated, not arbitrary disjoint closed sets.

commonErrors.description: Claims the infinite cofinite space is a compact Hausdorff non-normal space.
commonErrors.consequence: The missing Hausdorff hypothesis is overlooked.

hintTree.content: For each $y\in F$ choose disjoint opens $U_y\ni x$ and $V_y\ni y$, then take a finite subcover of $F$ from the $V_y$.
The finite intersection of the corresponding $U_y$ separates $x$ from $F$.
Normality repeats the idea with $A$ playing the role of the point, using finite subcovers twice.

PTOP:010524.canonicalSolution:
Fix closed $F$ and $x\notin F$. For each $y\in F$, Hausdorffness yields disjoint
opens $U_y\ni x$ and $V_y\ni y$. The sets $\{V_y\}$ cover the compact set $F$, so
finitely many $V_{y_1},\ldots,V_{y_n}$ cover $F$. Then
$$
U=\bigcap_{i=1}^n U_{y_i},
\qquad
V=\bigcup_{i=1}^n V_{y_i}
$$
are disjoint opens with $x\in U$ and $F\subseteq V$. Thus $X$ is regular (and $T_1$
because Hausdorff).

Now let $A,B$ be disjoint closed sets. For each $a\in A$, regularity supplies an
open $U_a\ni a$ with $\overline U_a\cap B=\emptyset$. The sets $U_a$ cover compact
$A$, so finitely many $U_{a_1},\ldots,U_{a_m}$ cover $A$. Set
$$
U=\bigcup_{i=1}^m U_{a_i},
\qquad
V=X\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m\overline U_{a_i}.
$$
Then $U$ and $V$ are disjoint opens, $A\subseteq U$, and $B\subseteq V$ because
each $\overline U_{a_i}$ misses $B$. Hence $X$ is normal.

In a regular Lindelöf space one cannot reduce to finitely many $U_a$; the
countable disjointifying construction is the replacement for the finite union of
closures used here.

The infinite cofinite topology is compact and $T_1$ but not Hausdorff, so the
hypothesis of the theorem fails and there is no contradiction.

graderFixtures.proofText: Finite Hausdorff pairs and a finite subcover separate points from closed sets, so compact Hausdorff spaces are regular. Finite regular neighborhoods with closures missing B then separate disjoint closed sets, so the space is normal. Lindelöf arguments need countable shrinking instead. The cofinite space is not Hausdorff, so it is not a counterexample.
Hausdorffness means any two disjoint sets, in particular closed sets, have disjoint neighborhoods. Compactness is not required for normality.
The infinite cofinite topology is compact Hausdorff yet fails to be normal, contradicting the theorem unless an extra axiom is added.

PTOP:010525.title: First countability turns compact cluster points into subsequences
PTOP:010525.objective: Prove that compact first-countable spaces are sequentially compact, derive countable compactness from sequential compactness, state the extra countability needed for full compactness, and exhibit a compact non-sequential product.
PTOP:010525.statement:
A space is sequentially compact when every sequence has a convergent
subsequence. A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover.

1. Prove that every compact first-countable space is sequentially compact.
   Given a sequence, if it has no convergent subsequence, build a countable open
   cover with no finite subcover using a countable local base at a limit-point
   candidate, or argue via accumulation points.

2. Prove that every sequentially compact first-countable space is countably
   compact (every countable open cover has a finite subcover). Optional brief
   remark: in first-countable spaces, countable compactness implies compactness
   under additional hypotheses such as second countability; do not claim more
   than you prove.

3. Let $X=\{0,1\}^{[0,1]}$ with the product topology. Outline why Tychonoff's
   theorem makes $X$ compact, and prove that $X$ is not sequentially compact by
   exhibiting a sequence with no convergent subsequence. (Use coordinate
   projections indexed by a sequence of distinct points, or characteristic
   functions of initial segments along a countable set of coordinates.)

4. Diagnose the claim “compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness in
   every topological space.”
permittedResults: In a first-countable space, closure points are sequential limits, and continuity can be tested on sequences.
Tychonoff's theorem: an arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use first countability to turn accumulation points into sequential limits.
Build product-space sequences that oscillate on a coordinate indexed by the subsequence itself.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Separates sequential compactness from open-cover compactness and exhibits an uncountable product failure.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Claims compactness and sequential compactness are equivalent in all topological spaces.
commonErrors.consequence: The uncountable product counterexample is impossible to accommodate.

commonErrors.description: Proves the implications only for metric spaces and never uses a countable local base in a general first-countable space.
commonErrors.consequence: The first-countability hypothesis is not actually used in its proper generality.

hintTree.content: A sequence in a compact space has an accumulation point; first countability promotes it to a sequential limit of a subsequence.
From a countable open cover with no finite subcover, pick points avoiding partial unions to build a sequence with no convergent subsequence.
Inject the set of binary sequences $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ into the coordinate set $[0,1]$, and let the $n$th point read the $n$th bit at every encoded coordinate.

PTOP:010525.canonicalSolution:
Let $X$ be compact and first countable, and let $(x_n)$ be a sequence. The set
of tails has the finite intersection property after closing, so there is an
accumulation point $x$: every neighborhood of $x$ meets infinitely many terms.
Let $\{B_k\}$ be a countable nested local base at $x$. Inductively choose
indices $n_k\uparrow$ with $x_{n_k}\in B_k$. Then $x_{n_k}\to x$. Thus $X$ is
sequentially compact.

Conversely, suppose $X$ is sequentially compact and first countable, and let
$\{U_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be a countable open cover with no finite subcover. Choose
$x_n\notin\bigcup_{k=1}^n U_k$. Sequential compactness yields a convergent
subsequence $x_{n_j}\to x$. Then $x\in U_N$ for some $N$, and eventually all
subsequence terms lie in $U_N$, contradicting the avoidance construction for
indices beyond $N$. Hence every countable open cover has a finite subcover.
This conclusion is countable compactness, not full compactness. If $X$ is also
second countable, then it is Lindelöf, so every open cover has a countable
subcover and the preceding conclusion reduces that subcover to a finite one.

Let $X=\{0,1\}^{[0,1]}$. Each factor is compact, so Tychonoff's theorem makes
$X$ compact in the product topology. Encode every binary sequence as a distinct
coordinate by the injection
$$
\phi:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\longrightarrow[0,1],
\qquad
\phi(\sigma)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2\sigma(k)}{3^k}.
$$
For each $n$, define $x_n\in X$ by
$$
x_n(\phi(\sigma))=\sigma(n)
\quad\text{for every }\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},
$$
and set $x_n(t)=0$ at coordinates outside the image of $\phi$.

Take any subsequence $(x_{n_j})$. Choose a binary sequence $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(n_j)=0$ for even $j$ and $\sigma(n_j)=1$ for odd $j$ (assign arbitrary
values at all other indices). At the single coordinate $\phi(\sigma)$, the
values $x_{n_j}(\phi(\sigma))$ alternate between $0$ and $1$. They do not
converge in the discrete factor, so the subsequence cannot converge in the
product topology. Thus $(x_n)$ has no convergent subsequence, and $X$ is compact
but not sequentially compact.

The claim fails: without first countability or metrizability, compactness does
not imply sequential compactness, as the uncountable product shows.

graderFixtures.proofText: Compact first-countable spaces are sequentially compact via accumulation points and nested countable local bases. Sequential compactness yields countable compactness by an avoidance sequence. An uncountable product such as {0,1}^{[0,1]} is compact by Tychonoff but admits a sequence oscillating on a subsequence-coded coordinate, so sequential compactness fails in general.
In every topological space a sequence argument equals an open-cover argument, so compactness and sequential compactness always coincide.
I prove both directions only using epsilon balls and totally bounded metric arguments, then assert the same for first-countable spaces without countable local bases.

PTOP:010626.title: The topologist's comb is path connected yet not locally connected
PTOP:010626.objective: Construct the topologist's comb in the plane, prove it is a compact path-connected metric space, and show local connectedness fails at a limit point approached by infinitely many teeth.
PTOP:010626.statement:
In $\mathbb R^2$ define the topologist's comb
$$
C=\bigl([0,1]\times\{0\}\bigr)
\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times[0,1]\bigr)
\cup\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl\{\frac1n\Bigr\}\times[0,1]\Bigr).
$$
Equip $C$ with the Euclidean subspace topology.

1. Prove that $C$ is path connected (hence connected). Explicitly build paths
   from a point on a tooth $\{1/n\}\times[0,1]$ to a point on the vertical
   segment $\{0\}\times[0,1]$ using the base.

2. Let $p=(0,1)$. Prove that $C$ is not locally connected at $p$. Your argument
   must produce a neighborhood $W$ of $p$ in $C$ such that no open connected
   neighborhood of $p$ in $C$ is contained in $W$. Identify the connected
   components of $W\cap C$ near $p$.

3. Contrast this failure mode with the closed topologist sine curve phenomenon:
   here path components and connected components may still agree globally while
   local connectedness fails. State that distinction precisely.

4. Diagnose the claim “a path-connected metric continuum is locally connected.”
permittedResults: Path connectedness implies connectedness, but neither implies local connectedness.
Connected open sets in the line are intervals; traces of small balls on comb teeth are separated intervals.

acceptableStrategies.description: Route all long-distance paths through the base.
Cut a small ball about (0,1) to disconnect teeth from one another inside that neighborhood.

milestones.criterion: Sets up the space, topology, and requested definitions with the exact hypotheses needed for the argument.
Proves compactness and path connectedness of the topologist's comb and isolates a local connectedness failure at the top of the limit segment.
Completes every requested comparison, counterexample, or diagnosis with coherent topological language.

commonErrors.description: Claims the comb is locally path connected because it is a union of line segments.
commonErrors.consequence: The missing horizontal connections near (0,1) are ignored.

commonErrors.description: Argues that the comb has two path components or that connectedness fails globally, transplanting sine-curve conclusions.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual global path connectedness and local failure mode are misidentified.

hintTree.content: Travel down a tooth to the base, along the base to $0$, then up the vertical segment.
Intersect $C$ with the open rectangle $(-1/2,1/2)\times(1/2,3/2)$ to isolate the tops of the limit segment and nearby teeth.
Those tooth tops are distinct connected components of the small neighborhood.

PTOP:010626.canonicalSolution:
Write
$$
C=([0,1]\times\{0\})
\cup\Bigl((\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\})\times[0,1]\Bigr).
$$
The set $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ is closed, so $C$ is closed and bounded in
$\mathbb R^2$ and therefore compact.

Take points $a=(1/n,s)$ and $b=(0,t)$. The piecewise path that goes vertically
from $a$ to $(1/n,0)$, horizontally along the base to $(0,0)$, and then
vertically to $b$ lies in $C$. The same routing joins arbitrary points of $C$,
so $C$ is path connected and hence connected.

Let $p=(0,1)$ and use the open subspace neighborhood
$$
W=C\cap\bigl((-1/2,1/2)\times(1/2,3/2)\bigr).
$$
Its connected components are exactly
$$
W_0=\{0\}\times(1/2,1]
\quad\text{and}\quad
W_n=\{1/n\}\times(1/2,1]\quad(n\ge3).
$$
Indeed the $x$-projection of any connected subset of $W$ is connected, while
the set of available $x$-coordinates $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge3\}$ has no
non-singleton connected subsets. Each displayed vertical interval is itself
connected, so the list is exact.

The component $W_0$ containing $p$ is not a neighborhood of $p$ in $C$.
Every Euclidean ball about $p$ meets $W_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, since
the teeth approach the limit segment. Hence every $C$-open neighborhood of $p$
contained in $W$ meets components other than $W_0$ and cannot be connected.
Thus $W$ contains no connected open neighborhood of $p$, proving that $C$ is
not locally connected at $p$.

Globally, $C$ has one path component and therefore one connected component.
This differs from the closed topologist sine curve, which is connected but has
more than one path component. The comb isolates a local-connectedness failure
without any global failure of path connectedness.

The diagnosed claim is false: $C$ is a compact path-connected metric space, or
continuum, that is not locally connected.

graderFixtures.proofText: The comb is closed and bounded, hence compact. Paths travel down teeth to the base and up the vertical segment, so C is path connected. In a small rectangular neighborhood of (0,1), tooth tops are separate connected components with no horizontal connection, so local connectedness fails even though the space has one path component globally.
Every point lies on a segment, and segments are locally path connected, so the whole comb is locally path connected at (0,1).
As with the topologist sine curve, the comb is connected but not path connected; the vertical segment is a separate path component.

PWR:010217.title: A 48 V synchronous buck at D=0.25 has 0.90 A inductor ripple and 11.25 mV ESR-free output ripple
PWR:010217.objective: For a lossless synchronous buck with Vin=48 V, D=0.25, 100 kHz, L=100 uH, C=100 uF (ESR-free), and R=3 Ohm, prove Vo=12 V, Io=4 A, Ts=10 us, P=48 W, DeltaIL=0.90 App with extrema 3.55 A and 4.45 A, DeltaVo=11.25 mVpp, and Iinavg=1 A, remaining in CCM.
PWR:010217.statement:
A lossless synchronous buck (complementary high-side and low-side
switches, no diode reverse recovery) is fed from $V_{\mathrm{in}}=48\,\mathrm{V}$
and switched at $f_s=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ with fixed duty $D=0.25$. The
filter is $L=100\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ and $C=100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ with
negligible capacitor ESR. The load is $R=3\,\Omega$. Assume continuous
conduction and a triangular inductor current.

1. Prove the dc conversion
   \[
   V_o=D V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   I_o=V_o/R=4\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s},\qquad
   P=V_o I_o=48\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]

2. Prove the peak-to-peak inductor current
   \[
   \Delta I_L=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D T_s}{L}=0.90\,\mathrm{A}
   \]
   and the extrema $I_{L,\min}=3.55\,\mathrm{A}$,
   $I_{L,\max}=4.45\,\mathrm{A}$. Confirm CCM by $I_{L,\min}>0$.

3. With ESR-free $C$, the capacitor absorbs the ac triangle of $i_L$.
   Prove
   \[
   \Delta V_o=\frac{\Delta I_L}{8 f_s C}=11.25\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}
   \]
   and that the average input current (high-side average) is
   $I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=D I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the assigned work is a hard-switching
   conduction / transition / recovery loss ledger, so the numbers to
   report are $I^2R$ and $CV^2$ energies rather than $\Delta I_L$ and
   $\Delta V_o$”; (ii) “the ESR-free output ripple is the boost
   formula $I_o D/(f_s C)$, or else $\Delta V_o=\Delta I_L\cdot\mathrm{ESR}$
   with a fabricated ESR.”

Do not replace the calculation by a boost DCM gain or CCM–DCM
boundary, by transformer reset or flux walk, by a PFC harmonic/THD
audit, by three-phase SVPWM sector dwell, or by constant-power
negative-impedance stability.
permittedResults: On the high-side interval the inductor slope is $(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)/L$, so $\Delta I_L=(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D T_s/L$. Then $I_{L,\max}=I_o+\Delta I_L/2$ and $I_{L,\min}=I_o-\Delta I_L/2$.
Lossless power balance gives $I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=P/V_{\mathrm{in}}=D I_o$. CCM holds precisely when $I_{L,\min}>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Close volt-second balance to Vo=D Vin, integrate the 36 V on-slope over D Ts, then convert the inductor triangle through Q=DeltaIL Ts/8.
Read Io=Vo/R and Iin=D Io from lossless power, then obtain DeltaVo from the 8 fs C identity rather than from an ESR or boost formula.

milestones.criterion: Proves Vo=12 V, Io=4 A, Ts=10 us, P=48 W, DeltaIL=0.90 App, and the extrema 3.55 A and 4.45 A with CCM.
Evaluates the ESR-free DeltaVo=11.25 mVpp from DeltaIL/(8 fs C) and Iinavg=1 A.
Rejects a reserved hard-switching loss ledger and refuses boost/ESR ripple substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the CCM ripple audit by a hard-switching conduction, transition, and recovery loss ledger, and never computes DeltaIL or the ESR-free DeltaVo.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 0.90 App inductor ripple, 3.55/4.45 A extrema, and 11.25 mVpp output ripple are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the boost capacitor formula Io D/(fs C) or invents an ESR drop DeltaVo=DeltaIL ESR instead of the ESR-free triangle DeltaIL/(8 fs C).
commonErrors.consequence: The required 11.25 mVpp is replaced by 0.10 V or by an unassigned ESR product.

hintTree.content: $D=1/4$ of $48\,\mathrm{V}$ is $12\,\mathrm{V}$. Then $I_o=12/3=4\,\mathrm{A}$ and $T_s=1/10^5=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$.
The high-side on-interval voltage on $L$ is $36\,\mathrm{V}$ during $D T_s=2.5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so $\Delta I_L=36\cdot 2.5/100=0.90\,\mathrm{A}$.
The ESR-free formula is $\Delta I_L/(8 f_s C)=0.90/(8\cdot 10^5\cdot 10^{-4})=0.90/80=11.25\,\mathrm{mV}$. The input average is $0.25\cdot 4=1\,\mathrm{A}$.

PWR:010217.canonicalSolution:
Volt-second balance on the inductor in CCM is
\[
D(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)=(1-D)V_o,
\]
hence $V_o=D V_{\mathrm{in}}=0.25\cdot 48=12\,\mathrm{V}$. The load
and the period follow at once:
\[
I_o=\frac{12}{3}=4\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
T_s=\frac1{100\times 10^3}=10\,\mu\mathrm{s},\qquad
P=12\cdot 4=48\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_o=12\,\mathrm{V},\;I_o=4\,\mathrm{A},\;
T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s},\;P=48\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

During the high-side on-interval the inductor voltage is
$V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o=36\,\mathrm{V}$ for $D T_s=2.5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so
\[
\Delta I_L=\frac{36\cdot 2.5\times 10^{-6}}{100\times 10^{-6}}=0.90\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The same number is $(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D T_s/L$. The extrema about
the average $I_L=I_o=4\,\mathrm{A}$ are
\[
I_{L,\min}=4-0.45=3.55\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
I_{L,\max}=4+0.45=4.45\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Because $I_{L,\min}>0$ the converter is in CCM.
\[
\boxed{\Delta I_L=0.90\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}},\;
I_{L,\min}=3.55\,\mathrm{A},\;I_{L,\max}=4.45\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

An ESR-free capacitor sees only the ac triangle of $i_L$. The charge
above $I_o$ over a half-period is the area of a triangle of height
$\Delta I_L/2$ and base $T_s/2$,
\[
Q=\frac12\cdot\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}\cdot\frac{T_s}{2}=\frac{\Delta I_L T_s}{8},
\]
hence
\[
\Delta V_o=\frac{Q}{C}=\frac{\Delta I_L}{8 f_s C}
=\frac{0.90}{8\cdot 100\times 10^3\cdot 100\times 10^{-6}}
=\frac{0.90}{80}=11.25\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}.
\]
Lossless power balance (or the high-side duty applied to $I_o$) gives
\[
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}=D I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta V_o=11.25\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}},\;
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=1\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the CCM ripple audit by a reserved hard-switching
conduction / transition / recovery loss ledger; those energies are not
the assigned $\Delta I_L$ or $\Delta V_o$. Sentence (ii) imports either
the boost capacitor formula $I_o D/(f_s C)=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$ or a
fabricated ESR drop, both of which miss $11.25\,\mathrm{mV}$.

The argument never uses a boost DCM gain, a CCM–DCM boundary root,
transformer reset or flux walk, a PFC harmonic/THD ledger, SVPWM
sector dwell, or constant-power negative-impedance stability.

graderFixtures.proofText: Volt-second balance gives $V_o=12\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_o=4\,\mathrm{A}$, $T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, and $P=48\,\mathrm{W}$. The on-slope produces $\Delta I_L=0.90\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}}$ with extrema $3.55\,\mathrm{A}$ and $4.45\,\mathrm{A}$, so the converter is in CCM. The ESR-free capacitor identity $\Delta V_o=\Delta I_L/(8 f_s C)$ yields $11.25\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}$, and $I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=D I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}$. A loss ledger is a different exercise.
The assigned numbers are a hard-switching conduction, transition, and recovery loss ledger. I report I^2R and CV^2 switch energies and I never compute DeltaIL=0.90 A or the ESR-free 11.25 mV ripple.
The output capacitor ripple is the boost formula Io D/(fs C)=0.10 V, or equivalently DeltaVo=DeltaIL times a fabricated ESR. I do not accept DeltaIL/(8 fs C)=11.25 mV.

PWR:010218.title: Two 180° bucks at D=0.5 cancel switching ripple and sum to a constant 8 A
PWR:010218.objective: For two matched 180° interleaved bucks, 24 V to 12 V, D=0.5, 200 kHz per phase, L=50 uH each, and 8 A total load, prove each phase averages 4 A with 0.60 App ripple and extrema 3.70 A and 4.30 A, that opposite equal slopes make the inductor sum identically 8 A, and that each high-side averages 2 A for a 4 A input.
PWR:010218.statement:
Two lossless buck phases share one $24\,\mathrm{V}$ source and one
$12\,\mathrm{V}$ load. The phases are matched: each has $L=50\,\mu\mathrm{H}$,
switches at $f_s=200\,\mathrm{kHz}$, and is phased $180^{\circ}$ from
the other. The common duty is $D=0.5$. The total dc load is
$I_{\mathrm{load}}=8\,\mathrm{A}$, split equally.

1. Prove that each phase carries $I_{L,k}=4\,\mathrm{A}$ on average and
   that each inductor has
   \[
   \Delta I_{L,k}=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D T_s}{L}=0.60\,\mathrm{A},
   \]
   with extrema $3.70\,\mathrm{A}$ and $4.30\,\mathrm{A}$.

2. At $D=1/2$ the two $180^{\circ}$ on-intervals are complementary.
   Prove that the inductor slopes are equal in magnitude and opposite
   in sign, so
   \[
   \frac{d}{dt}(i_{L1}+i_{L2})=0
   \]
   identically and the sum is the constant $8\,\mathrm{A}$. In
   particular the switching-frequency current into the shared output
   capacitor from the inductor pair is zero.

3. Prove that each high-side switch averages $2\,\mathrm{A}$ and that
   the total average input current is $4\,\mathrm{A}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “even at $D=0.5$ with $180^{\circ}$
   interleaving a residual switching-frequency inductor-sum ripple
   remains, equal to one phase’s $0.60\,\mathrm{A}$”; (ii) “the
   dwells are three-phase SVPWM sector times, or the $8\,\mathrm{A}$
   load is not split equally so each phase is not $4\,\mathrm{A}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a hard-switching loss ledger, by a
boost DCM/CCM-boundary root, by transformer reset or flux walk, by a
PFC harmonic/THD audit, or by constant-power negative-impedance
stability.
permittedResults: Each phase is an ordinary CCM buck: $\Delta I_{L,k}=(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D T_s/L$ with $T_s=1/f_s=5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$.
Each high-side average is $D I_{L,k}$. The total input average is $2 D I_{L,k}=D I_{\mathrm{load}}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute one phase as an ordinary CCM buck, then use D=1/2 and 180° to cancel the two slopes in the sum.
Write di1/dt=(Vin-Vo)/L and di2/dt=-Vo/L on the complementary window, observe they are negatives, and recover the input current from D times each phase current.

milestones.criterion: Reports each phase average 4 A, DeltaIL=0.60 App, and extrema 3.70 A and 4.30 A.
Proves opposite equal slopes at D=1/2 make the inductor sum identically 8 A, with each high-side 2 A and total input 4 A.
Rejects residual switching-frequency sum ripple and refuses SVPWM or unequal-share substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims that at D=0.5 with 180° interleaving the inductor sum still carries a 0.60 A switching-frequency ripple, denying complementary slope cancellation.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity iL1+iL2=8 A with zero switching-frequency ripple is lost.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the two-phase bucks by three-phase SVPWM sector dwells, or refuses equal sharing so each phase is not 4 A.
commonErrors.consequence: The 3.70/4.30 A extrema, the 2 A high-side averages, and the 4 A input are attached to the wrong topology or the wrong split.

hintTree.content: Each phase sees $V_o=D V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V}$ and half of $8\,\mathrm{A}$, so $4\,\mathrm{A}$ average. $T_s=5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$.
$(24-12)\cdot 0.5\cdot 5\,\mu\mathrm{s}/50\,\mu\mathrm{H}=0.60\,\mathrm{A}$. At $D=1/2$ one has $(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)/L=V_o/L$.
Complementary slopes cancel in the sum. Each high-side averages $0.5\cdot 4=2\,\mathrm{A}$, for $4\,\mathrm{A}$ at the input.

PWR:010218.canonicalSolution:
Each matched phase is a CCM buck with $V_o=D V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V}$.
Equal current sharing splits the $8\,\mathrm{A}$ load, so each inductor
averages $4\,\mathrm{A}$. The common period is
$T_s=1/(200\times 10^3)=5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, and
\[
\Delta I_{L,k}
=\frac{(24-12)\cdot 0.5\cdot 5\times 10^{-6}}{50\times 10^{-6}}
=0.60\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The extrema about $4\,\mathrm{A}$ are $3.70\,\mathrm{A}$ and
$4.30\,\mathrm{A}$.
\[
\boxed{I_{L,k}=4\,\mathrm{A},\;\Delta I_{L,k}=0.60\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}},\;
3.70\,\mathrm{A}/4.30\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

At $D=1/2$ one has $V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o=V_o=12\,\mathrm{V}$, so the
on-slope and off-slope of each inductor have equal magnitude
$12/(50\times 10^{-6})=2.4\times 10^5\,\mathrm{A/s}$. With a
$180^{\circ}$ shift the on-window of phase 1 is exactly the off-window
of phase 2, hence
\[
\frac{di_{L1}}{dt}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o}{L},\qquad
\frac{di_{L2}}{dt}=-\frac{V_o}{L},
\]
and these are negatives of each other. Therefore
$d(i_{L1}+i_{L2})/dt=0$ at every instant, so the inductor sum is
constant. The constant equals the sum of the averages, $8\,\mathrm{A}$.
The switching-frequency component of $i_{L1}+i_{L2}$ is identically
zero; the shared output capacitor sees no switching-frequency inductor
current from the pair.
\[
\boxed{i_{L1}+i_{L2}\equiv 8\,\mathrm{A}
\text{ (zero switching-frequency ripple)}}.
\]

Each high-side conducts only during its own duty, so its average is
$D\cdot 4=2\,\mathrm{A}$. The two high-sides together draw
$4\,\mathrm{A}$ from the source, which is also $D I_{\mathrm{load}}$.
\[
\boxed{\text{each high-side }2\,\mathrm{A};\;
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=4\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) denies the complementary-slope cancellation and leaves a
spurious $0.60\,\mathrm{A}$ sum ripple. Sentence (ii) either replaces
the two-phase bucks by reserved three-phase SVPWM sector dwells or
refuses equal current sharing.

The argument never builds a hard-switching loss ledger, never solves a
boost DCM gain or CCM-boundary root, never treats a transformer reset
or flux walk, never runs a PFC harmonic/THD audit, and never invokes
constant-power negative-impedance stability.

graderFixtures.proofText: Each matched phase averages $4\,\mathrm{A}$ with $\Delta I_L=0.60\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}}$ and extrema $3.70\,\mathrm{A}$ and $4.30\,\mathrm{A}$. At $D=1/2$ the $180^{\circ}$ windows are complementary and the slopes $\pm V_o/L$ cancel, so $i_{L1}+i_{L2}\equiv 8\,\mathrm{A}$ with zero switching-frequency ripple. Each high-side averages $2\,\mathrm{A}$ and the input averages $4\,\mathrm{A}$.
Even at D=0.5 with 180 degree interleaving the two inductor currents add a residual 0.60 A switching-frequency ripple into the capacitor. I do not accept that the sum is the constant 8 A.
The two dwells are three-phase SVPWM sector times, and I do not split the 8 A load equally, so each phase is not 4 A and each high-side is not 2 A.

PWR:010219.title: A 24-to-48 V boost at 192 W stays CCM with 1 A inductor ripple and 0.20 V capacitor ripple
PWR:010219.objective: For a lossless boost, 24 V to 48 V, 192 W, 100 kHz, L=120 uH, C=100 uF, prove D=0.5, Io=4 A, IL=Iin=8 A, DeltaIL=1 App with extrema 7.5 A and 8.5 A, CCM, capacitor ripple 0.20 Vpp, and switch/diode peak 8.5 A, without taking a DCM gain or CCM-boundary root.
PWR:010219.statement:
A lossless boost converts $V_{\mathrm{in}}=24\,\mathrm{V}$ to
$V_o=48\,\mathrm{V}$ at $P=192\,\mathrm{W}$. The switch frequency is
$f_s=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$, $L=120\,\mu\mathrm{H}$, and the output
capacitor is $C=100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ (ESR-free). Operate in CCM; do
not pass to a DCM conversion ratio or to the CCM–DCM boundary as the
operating point.

1. Prove
   \[
   D=1-\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{V_o}=0.5,\qquad
   I_o=\frac{P}{V_o}=4\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   I_L=I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{I_o}{1-D}=8\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

2. Prove
   \[
   \Delta I_L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s}{L}=1.00\,\mathrm{A}
   \]
   with extrema $7.5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $8.5\,\mathrm{A}$. Confirm CCM
   by $I_{L,\min}=7.5\,\mathrm{A}>0$. Do not replace this check by
   solving the CCM–DCM boundary current as a second operating root.

3. While the switch is on, the diode is off and $C$ supplies $I_o$.
   Prove the ESR-free capacitor ripple
   \[
   \Delta V_o=\frac{I_o D}{f_s C}=0.20\,\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{pp}}
   \]
   and that both the switch and the diode have peak current
   $I_{L,\max}=8.5\,\mathrm{A}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the converter is at the CCM–DCM
   boundary, or the DCM relation is
   $M(M-1)=D^2 R T_s/(2L)$ with $M=V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}$, rather than
   the CCM gain $M=1/(1-D)$”; (ii) “the capacitor ripple is the buck
   identity $\Delta I_L/(8 f_s C)$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a hard-switching loss ledger, by
transformer reset or flux walk, by a PFC harmonic/THD audit, by
three-phase SVPWM sector dwell, or by constant-power negative-impedance
stability.
permittedResults: The on-slope is $V_{\mathrm{in}}/L$, so $\Delta I_L=V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s/L$. Then $I_{L,\max}=I_L+\Delta I_L/2$ and $I_{L,\min}=I_L-\Delta I_L/2$.
CCM holds whenever $I_{L,\min}>0$. The boundary current $I_L=\Delta I_L/2$ is a different (much lighter) load and is not this $192\,\mathrm{W}$ point.

acceptableStrategies.description: Close CCM volt-second balance to D=1/2, integrate Vin on L over D Ts, then charge C by Io D Ts.
Read IL=P/Vin and confirm Imin=7.5 A>0 so the point stays CCM, then assign the same ILmax to both the switch and the diode.

milestones.criterion: Derives D=0.5, Io=4 A, IL=Iin=8 A, DeltaIL=1.00 App, and extrema 7.5 A and 8.5 A with CCM.
Evaluates DeltaVo=0.20 Vpp from Io D/(fs C) and the switch/diode peak 8.5 A.
Rejects a DCM-gain or CCM-boundary operating root and refuses the buck 8 fs C capacitor formula.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the CCM gain 1/(1-D) by a DCM conversion ratio, or treats the CCM–DCM boundary ILmin=0 as this 192 W operating point.
commonErrors.consequence: The required D=0.5, IL=8 A, and CCM extrema 7.5/8.5 A are replaced by the reserved boost DCM/boundary seed.

commonErrors.description: Uses the buck ESR-free identity DeltaVo=DeltaIL/(8 fs C) instead of the boost pulse Io D/(fs C)=0.20 V.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 0.20 Vpp capacitor ripple is replaced by 1.25 mV.

hintTree.content: $T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so $\Delta I_L=24\cdot 0.5\cdot 10/120=1\,\mathrm{A}$ and the extrema are $7.5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $8.5\,\mathrm{A}$.
$\Delta V_o=4\cdot 0.5/(10^5\cdot 10^{-4})=0.20\,\mathrm{V}$. Do not use $\Delta I_L/(8 f_s C)$, and do not move the operating point to $I_{L,\min}=0$.

PWR:010219.canonicalSolution:
CCM volt-second balance is $V_o=V_{\mathrm{in}}/(1-D)$, so
\[
1-D=\frac{24}{48}=\frac12,\qquad D=\frac12.
\]
The load and inductor averages follow from $P=192\,\mathrm{W}$:
\[
I_o=\frac{192}{48}=4\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
I_L=I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{192}{24}=\frac{4}{1-D}=8\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{D=0.5,\;I_o=4\,\mathrm{A},\;I_L=I_{\mathrm{in}}=8\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

With $T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ the on-interval applies $24\,\mathrm{V}$
to $L=120\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ for $5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$:
\[
\Delta I_L=\frac{24\cdot 0.5\cdot 10\times 10^{-6}}{120\times 10^{-6}}
=1.00\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The extrema about $8\,\mathrm{A}$ are $7.5\,\mathrm{A}$ and
$8.5\,\mathrm{A}$. Since $I_{L,\min}=7.5>0$ the converter is in CCM.
(The CCM–DCM boundary would require $I_L=\Delta I_L/2=0.5\,\mathrm{A}$,
i.e. $P=12\,\mathrm{W}$, which is not this operating point and is not
to be solved as a second root.)
\[
\boxed{\Delta I_L=1.00\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}},\;
I_{L,\min}=7.5\,\mathrm{A},\;I_{L,\max}=8.5\,\mathrm{A},\;\mathrm{CCM}}.
\]

During the switch on-interval the diode is reverse-biased, so $C$
supplies $I_o$ for $D T_s$. The ESR-free excursion is
\[
\Delta V_o=\frac{I_o D T_s}{C}=\frac{4\cdot 0.5\cdot 10\times 10^{-6}}{100\times 10^{-6}}
=0.20\,\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{pp}}.
\]
The switch conducts $i_L$ while on and the diode conducts $i_L$ while
off, so both devices have peak $I_{L,\max}=8.5\,\mathrm{A}$.
\[
\boxed{\Delta V_o=0.20\,\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{pp}},\;
I_{\mathrm{sw,pk}}=I_{\mathrm{d,pk}}=8.5\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the CCM gain $1/(1-D)$ by a reserved DCM gain
or treats the CCM–DCM boundary as the operating point. Sentence (ii)
imports the buck capacitor identity $\Delta I_L/(8 f_s C)=1.25\,\mathrm{mV}$,
which is not the boost pulse $0.20\,\mathrm{V}$.

The argument never builds a hard-switching loss ledger, never treats
transformer reset or flux walk, never runs a PFC harmonic/THD audit,
never computes SVPWM sector dwells, and never invokes constant-power
negative-impedance stability.

graderFixtures.proofText: CCM balance gives $D=0.5$, $I_o=4\,\mathrm{A}$, and $I_L=I_{\mathrm{in}}=8\,\mathrm{A}$. Then $\Delta I_L=1.00\,\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{pp}}$ with extrema $7.5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $8.5\,\mathrm{A}$, so the converter remains in CCM. The boost capacitor pulse is $\Delta V_o=I_o D/(f_s C)=0.20\,\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{pp}}$, and both the switch and the diode peak at $8.5\,\mathrm{A}$. This is not a DCM-gain or CCM-boundary exercise.
I take the operating point at the CCM-DCM boundary, or I use the DCM relation M(M-1)=D^2 R Ts/(2L) instead of the CCM gain M=1/(1-D). I do not keep IL=8 A with Imin=7.5 A in CCM.
The output capacitor ripple is the buck formula DeltaIL/(8 fs C)=1.25 mV. I do not accept the boost pulse Io D/(fs C)=0.20 V.

PWR:010220.title: An inverting buck–boost at D=0.4 produces −12 V with ILavg=5/3 A and 36.3636 mV ripple
PWR:010220.objective: For a lossless inverting buck–boost with Vin=18 V, D=0.4, R=12 Ohm, 50 kHz, L=300 uH, and C=220 uF, prove Vo=-12 V, |Io|=1 A, ILavg=5/3 A, DeltaIL=0.48 A with extrema 1.42667 A and 1.90667 A, Iinavg=2/3 A, DeltaVo=36.3636 mVpp, and P=12 W.
PWR:010220.statement:
A lossless inverting (common-ground) buck–boost is driven from
$V_{\mathrm{in}}=18\,\mathrm{V}$ at duty $D=0.4$ and $f_s=50\,\mathrm{kHz}$.
The inductor is $L=300\,\mu\mathrm{H}$, the output capacitor is
$C=220\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ (ESR-free), and the load is $R=12\,\Omega$
from the negative output node to ground. Assume CCM.

1. Prove the dc conversion
   \[
   V_o=-\frac{D}{1-D}V_{\mathrm{in}}=-12\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   |I_o|=\frac{|V_o|}{R}=1\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   P=|V_o|\,|I_o|=12\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]

2. The diode conducts only for $(1-D)T_s$ and then carries the
   inductor current, so $I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=|I_o|/(1-D)$. Prove
   \[
   I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=\frac53\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   \Delta I_L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s}{L}=0.48\,\mathrm{A},
   \]
   and the extrema
   $I_{L,\min}=1.42667\,\mathrm{A}$,
   $I_{L,\max}=1.90667\,\mathrm{A}$
   (equivalently $5/3\pm 0.24$). Confirm CCM.

3. Prove the average input current $I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=D I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=2/3\,\mathrm{A}$
   and the ESR-free output ripple
   \[
   \Delta V_o=\frac{|I_o| D}{f_s C}=\frac{2}{55}\,\mathrm{V}
   =36.3636\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the converter is non-inverting, so
   $V_o=+D V_{\mathrm{in}}$ or $V_o=+D V_{\mathrm{in}}/(1-D)$ and the
   polarity $-12\,\mathrm{V}$ is dropped”; (ii) “the inductor average
   equals the load current, $I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=|I_o|=1\,\mathrm{A}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a hard-switching loss ledger, by a
boost DCM/CCM-boundary root, by transformer reset or flux walk, by a
PFC harmonic/THD audit, by three-phase SVPWM sector dwell, or by

\[
D V_{\mathrm{in}}+(1-D)V_o=0,
\]

\[
V_o=-\frac{D}{1-D}V_{\mathrm{in}}
=-\frac{0.4}{0.6}\cdot 18
=-12\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The load current and the power are
\[
|I_o|=\frac{12}{12}=1\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
P=12\cdot 1=12\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_o=-12\,\mathrm{V},\;|I_o|=1\,\mathrm{A},\;P=12\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

The diode window occupies $(1-D)T_s$ and carries $i_L$, therefore
\[

With $T_s=1/(50\times 10^3)=20\,\mu\mathrm{s}$,
\[
\Delta I_L=\frac{18\cdot 0.4\cdot 20\times 10^{-6}}{300\times 10^{-6}}
=0.48\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The half-ripple is $0.24\,\mathrm{A}$, so
\begin{align*}
I_{L,\min}&=\frac53-0.24=\frac{107}{75}=1.42667\,\mathrm{A},\\
I_{L,\max}&=\frac53+0.24=\frac{143}{75}=1.90667\,\mathrm{A}.
\end{align*}
Both are positive, so the converter is in CCM.
\[
\boxed{I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=5/3\,\mathrm{A},\;
\Delta I_L=0.48\,\mathrm{A},\;
1.42667\,\mathrm{A}/1.90667\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

The source conducts only while the switch is on:
\[
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=D I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=0.4\cdot\frac53=\frac23\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
During that same window the diode is off, so $C$ supplies $|I_o|$:
\[
\Delta V_o=\frac{1\cdot 0.4\cdot 20\times 10^{-6}}{220\times 10^{-6}}
=\frac{8}{220}=\frac{2}{55}\,\mathrm{V}
=36.3636\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=2/3\,\mathrm{A},\;
\Delta V_o=36.3636\,\mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{pp}}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the inversion and reports a buck or non-inverting
buck–boost polarity. Sentence (ii) sets $I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=|I_o|$
and loses both $5/3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_{\mathrm{in}}=2/3\,\mathrm{A}$.

PWR:010221.title: A 12-to-18 V SEPIC at D=0.6 has inductor ripples 0.60 A and 0.40 A and a summed peak of 3.0 A
PWR:010221.objective: For a lossless CCM SEPIC, 12 V to 18 V, D=0.6, R=18 Ohm, 100 kHz, L1=120 uH, L2=180 uH, prove VC=12 V, Io=1 A, Iin=IL1=1.5 A, DeltaIL1=0.60 A with extrema 1.20 A and 1.80 A, DeltaIL2=0.40 A with extrema 0.80 A and 1.20 A, switch/diode peak 3.0 A, and (1-D)(IL1+IL2)=1 A.
PWR:010221.statement:
A lossless uncoupled SEPIC steps $V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V}$ to
$V_o=18\,\mathrm{V}$ at duty $D=0.6$ and $f_s=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$.
The two inductors are $L_1=120\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ (input) and
$L_2=180\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ (output), the coupling capacitor has
negligible ripple, and the load is $R=18\,\Omega$. Assume CCM on
both inductors. The two inductors are not a transformer; do not
treat the problem as isolated reset, flux walk, or core saturation.

1. Prove
   \[
   V_C=V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   I_o=\frac{V_o}{R}=1\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   I_{\mathrm{in}}=I_{L1}=\frac{D}{1-D}I_o=1.5\,\mathrm{A},
   \]
   and $I_{L2}=I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}$.

2. During the switch on-interval both inductors see $V_{\mathrm{in}}$.
   Prove
   \[
   \Delta I_{L1}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s}{L_1}=0.60\,\mathrm{A}
   \]
   with extrema $1.20\,\mathrm{A}$ and $1.80\,\mathrm{A}$, and
   \[
   \Delta I_{L2}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s}{L_2}=0.40\,\mathrm{A}
   \]
   with extrema $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$ and $1.20\,\mathrm{A}$.

3. The switch (on) and the diode (off) each carry $i_{L1}+i_{L2}$.
   Prove that the common peak is
   $I_{L1,\max}+I_{L2,\max}=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$, and that the diode
   window recovers the load by
   \[
   (1-D)(I_{L1}+I_{L2})=1\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$L_1$ and $L_2$ form an isolated
   transformer that must be reset, and the assigned numbers are a
   flux-walk or saturation audit”; (ii) “$I_{L2}\ne I_o$, or the
   switch/diode peak is a single inductor extremum rather than the
   sum $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a hard-switching loss ledger, by a
boost DCM/CCM-boundary root, by a PFC harmonic/THD audit, by
three-phase SVPWM sector dwell, or by constant-power negative-impedance
stability.
permittedResults: On the switch on-interval $v_{L1}=V_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $v_{L2}=V_C=V_{\mathrm{in}}$, so $\Delta I_{Lk}=V_{\mathrm{in}} D T_s/L_k$ for $k=1,2$.
Lossless power gives $I_{\mathrm{in}}=V_o I_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}$. For $V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}=D/(1-D)$ this is $I_{L1}=D I_o/(1-D)$.

hintTree.content: $D/(1-D)=0.6/0.4=1.5$, so $V_o=18\,\mathrm{V}$ is consistent, $I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}$, and $I_{L1}=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$. The coupling capacitor sits at $V_C=12\,\mathrm{V}$.
$T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so $\Delta I_{L1}=12\cdot 0.6\cdot 10/120=0.60\,\mathrm{A}$ and $\Delta I_{L2}=12\cdot 0.6\cdot 10/180=0.40\,\mathrm{A}$.
Peaks add: $1.80+1.20=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$. The diode window is $(1-D)(1.5+1.0)=0.4\cdot 2.5=1$.

PWR:010221.canonicalSolution:
CCM SEPIC conversion is $V_o=D V_{\mathrm{in}}/(1-D)$. The assigned
duty already matches $18=0.6\cdot 12/0.4$. The coupling-capacitor
dc voltage equals the source,
\[
V_C=V_{\mathrm{in}}=12\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The load is $I_o=18/18=1\,\mathrm{A}$. Lossless power (or the SEPIC
current ratio) gives
\[
I_{L1}=I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{D}{1-D}I_o=1.5\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
I_{L2}=I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_C=12\,\mathrm{V},\;I_o=1\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_{L1}=I_{\mathrm{in}}=1.5\,\mathrm{A},\;I_{L2}=1\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

On the switch on-interval both inductor voltages equal $V_{\mathrm{in}}$
(because $V_C=V_{\mathrm{in}}$). With $T_s=10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$,
\begin{align*}
\Delta I_{L1}
&=\frac{12\cdot 0.6\cdot 10\times 10^{-6}}{120\times 10^{-6}}
=0.60\,\mathrm{A},\\
\Delta I_{L2}
&=\frac{12\cdot 0.6\cdot 10\times 10^{-6}}{180\times 10^{-6}}
=0.40\,\mathrm{A}.
\end{align*}
The extrema are therefore
\[
I_{L1}\in[1.20,1.80]\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
I_{L2}\in[0.80,1.20]\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Both minima are positive, so both inductors remain in CCM.
\[
\boxed{\Delta I_{L1}=0.60\,\mathrm{A}\ (1.20/1.80),\;
\Delta I_{L2}=0.40\,\mathrm{A}\ (0.80/1.20)}.
\]

The switch current is $i_{L1}+i_{L2}$ while on, and the diode current
is $i_{L1}+i_{L2}$ while off. The common peak is
\[
I_{L1,\max}+I_{L2,\max}=1.80+1.20=3.0\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Charge balance at the output (the diode window) recovers the load:
\[
(1-D)(I_{L1}+I_{L2})=0.4\cdot(1.5+1.0)=1\,\mathrm{A}=I_o.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{\mathrm{sw,pk}}=I_{\mathrm{d,pk}}=3.0\,\mathrm{A},\;
(1-D)(I_{L1}+I_{L2})=1\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the uncoupled SEPIC pair by a reserved isolated
reset / flux-walk / saturation audit. Sentence (ii) either sets
$I_{L2}\ne I_o$ or reports a single-inductor peak $1.80\,\mathrm{A}$
or $1.20\,\mathrm{A}$ instead of the required sum $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$.

The argument never builds a hard-switching loss ledger, never takes a
boost DCM gain or CCM-boundary root, never runs a PFC harmonic/THD
audit, never computes SVPWM sector dwells, and never invokes
constant-power negative-impedance stability.

graderFixtures.proofText: CCM SEPIC averages give $V_C=12\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_{L1}=I_{\mathrm{in}}=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$, and $I_{L2}=1\,\mathrm{A}$. Both inductors see $V_{\mathrm{in}}$ while the switch is on, so $\Delta I_{L1}=0.60\,\mathrm{A}$ ($1.20/1.80$) and $\Delta I_{L2}=0.40\,\mathrm{A}$ ($0.80/1.20$). The switch and the diode each peak at $1.80+1.20=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$, and $(1-D)(I_{L1}+I_{L2})=1\,\mathrm{A}$. The inductors are not a transformer that must be reset.
L1 and L2 form an isolated transformer that must be reset. I replace the SEPIC ripple numbers by a flux-walk and saturation audit and I do not report VC=12 V or the two CCM triangles.
IL2 is not Io, and the switch/diode peak is the single inductor extremum 1.80 A rather than the sum 3.0 A. I do not accept (1-D)(IL1+IL2)=1 A.
