PWR:010322.title: A 400 V / 200 V DAB at n=2, L=50 uH, 100 kHz transfers 2222.222 W at phi=pi/6 and 4 kW at pi/2
PWR:010322.objective: Evaluate the DAB phase-shift law P=n V1 V2/(omega L) phi(1-|phi|/pi), prove P(pi/6)=2222.222 W primary to secondary, Pmax=4 kW at |phi|=pi/2, and select phi=pi/4 rather than 3pi/4 for P=3 kW.
PWR:010322.statement:
A dual-active-bridge converter joins a primary dc bus
$V_1=400\,\mathrm{V}$ to a secondary dc bus $V_2=200\,\mathrm{V}$
through an ideal transformer of turns ratio $n=N_p/N_s=2$ and a
series inductance $L=50\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ referred to the primary.
Both H-bridges switch at $f_s=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ with fifty-percent
duty. The only control coordinate is the phase $\phi$ (radians) by
which the primary square wave leads the secondary square wave. The
average power from primary to secondary is
\[
P(\phi)=\frac{n V_1 V_2}{\omega L}\,\phi\Bigl(1-\frac{|\phi|}{\pi}\Bigr),
\qquad |\phi|\le\pi,
\]
where $\omega=2\pi f_s$. The rails are voltage-matched:
$n V_2=V_1$.

1. Evaluate the prefactor $n V_1 V_2/(\omega L)$ exactly. Substitute
   $\phi=\pi/6$ and prove
   \[
   P\bigl(\pi/6\bigr)=2222.222\,\mathrm{W}
   \]
   from primary to secondary.

2. On $|\phi|\le\pi$, prove that $|P|$ is maximized at
   $|\phi|=\pi/2$ with
   \[
   P_{\max}=4\,\mathrm{kW}.
   \]

3. Solve $P(\phi)=3\,\mathrm{kW}$ for $\phi\in(0,\pi)$. Prove that
   the two roots are $\pi/4$ and $3\pi/4$, and select $\phi=\pi/4$
   as the operating point of lower circulating current.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “negative $\phi$ still sends
   $2222.222\,\mathrm{W}$ from primary to secondary”; (ii) “the
   $3\,\mathrm{kW}$ roots are interchangeable because circulating
   current depends only on power, not on $\phi$.”

Do not replace the phase-shift power law by a hard-switching
conduction / transition / recovery loss ledger, and do not analyze
transformer reset, flux walk, or core saturation.
permittedResults: The prefactor collapses as $n V_1 V_2/(\omega L)=16000/\pi$. Then $P(\pi/6)=(16000/\pi)(\pi/6)(5/6)=20000/9$.
On $(0,\pi)$ the map $u\mapsto u(1-u)$ with $u=\phi/\pi$ has a unique maximum at $u=1/2$ and the level set $u(1-u)=3/16$ is $\{1/4,3/4\}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Collapse the prefactor to 16000/pi, evaluate the two special phases, then solve u(1-u)=3/16 and compare Ipk proportional to |phi|.
Nondimensionalize P=16000 u(1-u), read the unique maximum at u=1/2 off the parabola, and keep the smaller positive root at 3 kW.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates n V1 V2/(omega L)=16000/pi and reports P(pi/6)=2222.222 W from primary to secondary together with Pmax=4 kW at |phi|=pi/2.
Solves P=3 kW as phi=pi/4 or 3pi/4 and selects pi/4 by a matched-rail circulating-current comparison.
Rejects a reversed-phase same-direction claim and refuses reserved hard-switching-loss or magnetics-reset substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats P as even in phi, so a negative phase at |phi|=pi/6 is still reported as 2222.222 W from primary to secondary.
commonErrors.consequence: The direction of power is lost: negative phi reverses transfer and the signed DAB law is not used.

commonErrors.description: Accepts both 3 kW roots as interchangeable, or prefers 3pi/4, without comparing matched-rail circulating current.
commonErrors.consequence: The required lower-circulating operating point phi=pi/4 is not selected.

hintTree.content: Write $\omega L=2\pi\cdot 10^5\cdot 50\times 10^{-6}=10\pi$. The numerator is $n V_1 V_2=160000$, so the prefactor is $16000/\pi$.
For a positive unknown set $u=\phi/\pi$. The equation $P=3\,\mathrm{kW}$ becomes $u(1-u)=3/16$.
On matched rails $I_{\mathrm{pk}}\propto|\phi|$. Between $\pi/4$ and $3\pi/4$ the smaller phase is the lower-circulating root. Negative $\phi$ reverses $P$.

PWR:010322.canonicalSolution:
The angular frequency is $\omega=2\pi f_s=2\pi\times 10^5$. The
inductive reactance factor in the denominator is
\[
\omega L=2\pi\times 10^5\times 50\times 10^{-6}=10\pi.
\]
The numerator is $n V_1 V_2=2\cdot 400\cdot 200=160000$, so
\[
\frac{n V_1 V_2}{\omega L}=\frac{160000}{10\pi}=\frac{16000}{\pi}.
\]
(The rails are matched: $n V_2=400=V_1$.) At $\phi=\pi/6>0$,
\[
P\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{6}\Bigr)
=\frac{16000}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{6}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{6}\Bigr)
=\frac{16000}{6}\cdot\frac{5}{6}
=\frac{20000}{9}
=2222.222\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
Positive $\phi$ means the primary square wave leads, so this power
leaves the primary bus and enters the secondary bus.
\[
\boxed{P(\pi/6)=2222.222\,\mathrm{W}\text{ (primary $\to$ secondary)}}.
\]

On $(0,\pi)$ write $u=\phi/\pi\in(0,1)$ and
\[
P=\frac{16000}{\pi}\cdot(\pi u)(1-u)=16000\,u(1-u).
\]
The quadratic $u(1-u)$ has derivative $1-2u$ and a unique critical
point at $u=1/2$, i.e. $\phi=\pi/2$, where $u(1-u)=1/4$ and
\[
P_{\max}=16000\cdot\frac14=4000\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
The same value occurs at $\phi=-\pi/2$ with reversed direction. At
the endpoints $\phi=0$ and $\phi=\pm\pi$ one has $P=0$. Thus on
$|\phi|\le\pi$
\[
\boxed{P_{\max}=4\,\mathrm{kW}\text{ at }|\phi|=\pi/2}.
\]

The level $P=3000$ is
\[
16000\,u(1-u)=3000\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad u-u^2=\frac{3}{16}.
\]
Clearing gives $16u^2-16u+3=0$, or
\[
(4u-1)(4u-3)=0,
\]
so $u=1/4$ or $u=3/4$. The positive roots are therefore
\[
\phi=\frac{\pi}{4},\qquad \phi=\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
On matched rails the inductor voltage is $0$ outside the phase
window and $\pm 2V_1$ inside it, so the trapezoidal current has
peak $I_{\mathrm{pk}}=(V_1/(\omega L))|\phi|$. Then
\[
I_{\mathrm{pk}}\bigl(\pi/4\bigr)
=\frac13\,I_{\mathrm{pk}}\bigl(3\pi/4\bigr).
\]
The same active power at $3\pi/4$ therefore carries three times the
peak circulating current. The lower-circulating operating point is
$\phi=\pi/4$.
\[
\boxed{\phi=\pi/4\text{ (reject }3\pi/4\text{)}}.
\]

Sentence (i) ignores the oddness of $P(\phi)$. Negative phase
reverses the inductor volt-second polarity and sends the same watts
from secondary to primary. Sentence (ii) treats the two $3\,\mathrm{kW}$
roots as interchangeable; they share $P$ but not $I_{\mathrm{pk}}$.

The argument never tabulates hard-switching conduction, transition,
or recovery energies, and never inspects magnetizing reset, flux
walk, or saturation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The prefactor is $16000/\pi$, so $P(\pi/6)=20000/9=2222.222\,\mathrm{W}$ from primary to secondary. The unique maximum on $|\phi|\le\pi$ is $4\,\mathrm{kW}$ at $|\phi|=\pi/2$. The $3\,\mathrm{kW}$ roots are $\pi/4$ and $3\pi/4$; matched-rail $I_{\mathrm{pk}}\propto|\phi|$ selects $\phi=\pi/4$. Negative $\phi$ reverses the power.
P depends on |phi| only, so phi=-pi/6 still delivers 2222.222 W from the primary bus to the secondary bus. Direction is not part of the DAB law.
P=3 kW at both pi/4 and 3pi/4. Circulating current is fixed by power alone, so either root is acceptable and 3pi/4 may be used.

PWR:010323.title: A 48 V 4:1 forward at D=0.5 into 3 Ohm and 100 uH has 0.30 A ripple and 0.5375 A primary peak
PWR:010323.objective: For an ideal forward converter Vin=48 V, Np:Ns=4:1, D=0.5, R=3 Ohm, Lo=100 uH, 100 kHz, obtain Vs=12 V, Vo=6 V, Io=2 A, DeltaIo=0.30 A, 1.85/2.15 A, primary peak 0.5375 A, average input 0.25 A, 12 W, and 1 A diode averages, without analyzing reset.
PWR:010323.statement:
An ideal single-ended forward converter is fed from
$V_{\mathrm{in}}=48\,\mathrm{V}$. The transformer ratio is
$N_p:N_s=4:1$, the switch duty is $D=0.5$, the output filter is
$L_o=100\,\mu\mathrm{H}$ into $R=3\,\Omega$, and the switching
frequency is $f_s=100\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Devices are ideal. Continuous
conduction of $L_o$ is to be confirmed from the ripple rather than
assumed as a boost DCM/CCM boundary calculation. The transformer
reset is stipulated to be ideal; reset, magnetizing current, flux
walk, and saturation are not analyzed.

1. During the active interval the secondary winding presents
   $V_s=V_{\mathrm{in}} N_s/N_p$. Prove
   \[
   V_s=12\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   V_o=D V_s=6\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   I_o=V_o/R=2\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

2. Prove that the peak-to-peak inductor current is
   \[
   \Delta I_o=\frac{(V_s-V_o)D}{L_o f_s}=0.30\,\mathrm{A},
   \]
   so $i_L$ swings through $[1.85,2.15]\,\mathrm{A}$, and that this
   swing lies entirely above zero.

3. Neglecting magnetizing current, prove that the primary switch
   peak is $0.5375\,\mathrm{A}$, that the average input current is
   $0.25\,\mathrm{A}$, and that the converter power is $12\,\mathrm{W}$.

4. Prove that the secondary rectifier and the freewheel diode each
   carry a $1\,\mathrm{A}$ average. Audit both sentences: (i) “the
   primary peak must include a reset / flux-walk magnetizing
   contribution, so $0.5375\,\mathrm{A}$ is incomplete”; (ii) “average
   input current uses the $2.15\,\mathrm{A}$ peak rather than $I_o$.”

Do not replace the output-ripple audit by a transformer reset, flux
walk, or saturation study, and do not convert the problem into a
hard-switching loss ledger.
permittedResults: Continuous conduction holds whenever $I_o>\Delta I_o/2$. Here $2>0.15$, so the buck gain $V_o=D V_s$ applies.
Average input current equals $P/V_{\mathrm{in}}=D(N_s/N_p)I_o$ and does not use $i_{L,\max}$. Each output diode average is the duty-weighted inductor average on its interval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the secondary as a buck cell at Vs=12 V, integrate inductor volt-seconds, then reflect only iL,max and average with Io.
Confirm CCM from Io>DeltaIo/2 so Vo=D Vs applies, then split diode averages by D and 1-D.

milestones.criterion: Reports Vs=12 V, Vo=6 V, Io=2 A, DeltaIo=0.30 A, and the 1.85/2.15 A inductor swing with CCM confirmed from the ripple.
Computes primary peak 0.5375 A, average input 0.25 A, power 12 W, and rectifier/freewheel averages of 1 A each.
Keeps reset/flux-walk/saturation out of the audit and refuses reserved hard-switching-loss or boost-boundary substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Inserts a magnetizing, reset, or flux-walk current into the primary switch peak, rejecting 0.5375 A as incomplete.
commonErrors.consequence: The stipulated-ideal reset is violated and the packet is replaced by the reserved magnetics-reset family.

commonErrors.description: Computes average input current from iL,max=2.15 A rather than Io=2 A, producing 0.26875 A instead of 0.25 A.
commonErrors.consequence: Power and average input current leave the required 12 W / 0.25 A pair.

hintTree.content: The secondary voltage is $48/4=12\,\mathrm{V}$. The output is then a buck at $D=0.5$.
Volt-seconds on $L_o$ are $(12-6)\cdot 5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Divide by $100\,\mu\mathrm{H}$.
Reflect only $i_{L,\max}=2.15\,\mathrm{A}$ by $1/4$ for the switch peak. Averages use $I_o=2\,\mathrm{A}$, not the peak.

PWR:010323.canonicalSolution:
During the active interval the ideal transformer imposes
\[
V_s=V_{\mathrm{in}}\frac{N_s}{N_p}=48\cdot\frac14=12\,\mathrm{V}
\]
at the rectifier anode. The output inductor and capacitor average
this chopped voltage exactly as a buck cell. Continuous conduction
will be checked after the ripple is known; the candidate gain is
\[
V_o=D V_s=0.5\cdot 12=6\,\mathrm{V},
\]
and the load current is
\[
I_o=\frac{V_o}{R}=\frac{6}{3}=2\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_s=12\,\mathrm{V},\; V_o=6\,\mathrm{V},\; I_o=2\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

On the active interval $v_L=V_s-V_o=6\,\mathrm{V}$ for
$D/f_s=5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so
\[
\Delta I_o
=\frac{(V_s-V_o)D}{L_o f_s}
=\frac{6\cdot 0.5}{100\times 10^{-6}\cdot 100\times 10^3}
=\frac{3}{10}=0.30\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The inductor current is therefore the interval
\[
\bigl[I_o-\Delta I_o/2,\; I_o+\Delta I_o/2\bigr]
=[1.85,2.15]\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The lower endpoint is strictly positive, so continuous conduction
holds and the buck gain used above is consistent. (This is an
output-ripple check, not a boost DCM/CCM boundary calculation.)
\[
\boxed{\Delta I_o=0.30\,\mathrm{A},\; i_L\in[1.85,2.15]\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Ideal reset is stipulated, so magnetizing current is omitted. The
primary switch conducts only while the rectifier is on and then
sees the secondary current scaled by $N_s/N_p$:
\[
i_{Q,\mathrm{pk}}
=\frac{N_s}{N_p}\,i_{L,\max}
=\frac{2.15}{4}=0.5375\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Average input current follows from power, or equivalently from the
duty-weighted reflected inductor average:
\[
P=V_o I_o=12\,\mathrm{W},
\qquad
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}
=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}
=D\frac{N_s}{N_p}I_o
=0.5\cdot\frac14\cdot 2
=0.25\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Replacing $I_o$ by $i_{L,\max}$ would produce the incorrect
$0.26875\,\mathrm{A}$.
\[
\boxed{i_{Q,\mathrm{pk}}=0.5375\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=0.25\,\mathrm{A},\;
P=12\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

The rectifier conducts for duty $D$ at inductor average $I_o$, and
the freewheel diode conducts for duty $1-D$ at the same average:
\[
I_{\mathrm{rec,avg}}=D I_o=1\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
I_{\mathrm{fw,avg}}=(1-D)I_o=1\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{\mathrm{rec,avg}}=I_{\mathrm{fw,avg}}=1\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) reopens the stipulated-ideal reset and tries to insert
a flux-walk or magnetizing contribution into the switch peak. That
is a different reserved exercise. Sentence (ii) confuses the peak
inductor current with the average used for input current and power.

The argument never constructs a hard-switching conduction /
transition / recovery loss ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: Secondary $V_s=12\,\mathrm{V}$ gives $V_o=6\,\mathrm{V}$ and $I_o=2\,\mathrm{A}$. Inductor volt-seconds produce $\Delta I_o=0.30\,\mathrm{A}$ and $i_L\in[1.85,2.15]\,\mathrm{A}$, which stays positive. Ideal reset omits magnetizing current, so the switch peak is $2.15/4=0.5375\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_{\mathrm{in,avg}}=0.25\,\mathrm{A}$, $P=12\,\mathrm{W}$, and each output diode averages $1\,\mathrm{A}$.
The 0.5375 A primary peak is only the reflected inductor peak. A reset or flux-walk magnetizing current must be added, so the true switch peak is larger than 0.5375 A.
Average input current uses the inductor peak: Iin=D (Ns/Np) 2.15=0.26875 A. The 0.25 A figure understates the input.

PWR:010424.title: A 230 Vrms full-controlled bridge at alpha=60 deg and Id=10 A has Vd=103.5364 V
PWR:010424.objective: For a single-phase full-controlled bridge at 230 Vrms, alpha=60 deg, and continuous Id=10 A, obtain Vm=230 sqrt(2), Vd=(2 Vm/pi) cos alpha=103.5364 V, Pd=1.03536 kW, thyristor averages 5 A and rms 7.0711 A, and source Irms=10 A, without PFC or THD.
PWR:010424.statement:
A single-phase fully controlled thyristor bridge is supplied from
$v_s=V_m\sin(\omega t)$ with $V_{s,\mathrm{rms}}=230\,\mathrm{V}$.
The firing angle is $\alpha=60^{\circ}$. A large dc inductor holds
the load current at the constant value $I_d=10\,\mathrm{A}$
(continuous conduction). Devices are ideal.

1. Identify $V_m=230\sqrt{2}$ and prove that the average dc voltage
   is
   \[
   V_d=\frac{2V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha=103.5364\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

2. Prove that the dc power delivered to the current source is
   \[
   P_d=V_d I_d=1.03536\,\mathrm{kW}.
   \]

3. Each thyristor conducts for one half-cycle per source period.
   Prove that the device averages and the device and source rms
   currents are
   \[
   I_{T,\mathrm{avg}}=5\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   I_{T,\mathrm{rms}}=7.0711\,\mathrm{A},\qquad
   I_{s,\mathrm{rms}}=10\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the bridge is uncontrolled, so
   $V_d=2V_m/\pi$ and $\cos\alpha$ is omitted”; (ii) “this is a PFC
   stage, so the source current must be shaped to a sinusoid and the
   answers are THD and power factor.”

Do not replace the firing-angle average by a PFC reference,
harmonics, THD, or power-factor calculation, and do not convert the
problem into a six-pulse SVPWM sector-dwell exercise.
permittedResults: $\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+\pi}\sin\theta\,d\theta=2\cos\alpha$, hence $V_d=(2V_m/\pi)\cos\alpha$. At $\alpha=\pi/3$ one has $\cos\alpha=1/2$ and $V_d=V_m/\pi=230\sqrt{2}/\pi$.
A rectangular pulse of height $I_d$ and duty $1/2$ has average $I_d/2$ and rms $I_d/\sqrt{2}$. A full-period square wave of amplitude $I_d$ has rms $I_d$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate Vm sin theta from alpha to alpha+pi, insert cos 60=1/2, then read device currents from half-period rectangles.
Collapse Vd to Vm/pi at alpha=60 deg, multiply by Id for power, and keep the source current as a square wave of amplitude Id.

milestones.criterion: Computes Vd=(2 Vm/pi) cos alpha=103.5364 V and Pd=1.03536 kW at Id=10 A.
Reports thyristor average 5 A, thyristor rms 7.0711 A, and source rms 10 A from the rectangular conduction pattern.
Refuses the uncontrolled 2 Vm/pi substitute and refuses reserved PFC/THD/PF or SVPWM substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops cos alpha and reports the diode-bridge average Vd=2 Vm/pi=207.0728 V, with power scaled accordingly.
commonErrors.consequence: The required firing-angle law and Vd=103.5364 V are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats the stage as a PFC rectifier, replaces the square-wave source current by a sinusoid, and answers in THD or power factor.
commonErrors.consequence: Is,rms=10 A and the thyristor rectangular averages/rms are replaced by a reserved PFC family.

hintTree.content: $\cos 60^{\circ}=1/2$, so $V_d$ collapses to $V_m/\pi=230\sqrt{2}/\pi$.
Power is the product $V_d I_d$ because $I_d$ is constant.
Do not replace $\pm I_d$ by a sine of rms $10/\sqrt{2}$. PFC shaping and THD are a different exercise.

PWR:010424.canonicalSolution:
The source crest is
\[
V_m=230\sqrt{2}.
\]
With continuous $I_d$ the dc voltage is the half-period average of
the fired sinusoid:
\[
V_d
=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+\pi}V_m\sin\theta\,d\theta
=\frac{2V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha.
\]
At $\alpha=60^{\circ}=\pi/3$ one has $\cos\alpha=1/2$, so
\[
V_d=\frac{V_m}{\pi}=\frac{230\sqrt{2}}{\pi}=103.5364\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
(The numerical value is $230\sqrt{2}/\pi=103.536376\ldots$, which
rounds to the required four decimals.) An uncontrolled diode bridge
would have omitted $\cos\alpha$ and reported $2V_m/\pi=207.0728\,\mathrm{V}$.
\[
\boxed{V_m=230\sqrt{2},\; V_d=103.5364\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

The load current is constant, so the dc power is
\[
P_d=V_d I_d=103.5364\times 10=1035.364\,\mathrm{W}
=1.03536\,\mathrm{kW}.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_d=1.03536\,\mathrm{kW}}.
\]

Each of the four thyristors conducts for half of each source
period at height $I_d$:
\[
I_{T,\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{I_d}{2}=5\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
I_{T,\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_d}{\sqrt{2}}=7.0711\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
The ac source current is the square wave of amplitude $I_d$
produced by the two conducting pairs, so
\[
I_{s,\mathrm{rms}}=I_d=10\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{T,\mathrm{avg}}=5\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_{T,\mathrm{rms}}=7.0711\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_{s,\mathrm{rms}}=10\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $\cos\alpha$ and reports the diode-bridge
average. Sentence (ii) replaces the rectangular source current by
a PFC sinusoidal reference and asks for THD or power factor; those
are reserved and are not computed here. The source current is
deliberately a square wave of rms $10\,\mathrm{A}$.

The argument never introduces a current-loop reference, a harmonic
table, or an SVPWM dwell.

graderFixtures.proofText: Continuous $I_d$ gives $V_d=(2V_m/\pi)\cos 60^{\circ}=230\sqrt{2}/\pi=103.5364\,\mathrm{V}$ and $P_d=1.03536\,\mathrm{kW}$. Each thyristor is a half-period rectangle, so $I_{T,\mathrm{avg}}=5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_{T,\mathrm{rms}}=7.0711\,\mathrm{A}$. The source is $\pm 10\,\mathrm{A}$ with rms $10\,\mathrm{A}$. This is not a PFC/THD calculation.
A full bridge has Vd=2 Vm/pi regardless of firing. With Vm=230 sqrt(2) one gets Vd=207.0728 V and Pd=2.0707 kW. The cosine of alpha is not used.
The converter is a PFC front end, so the source current is shaped to a 230 V sine. The answers are THD and power factor, not a 10 A square-wave rms.

PWR:010425.title: A 400 Vll six-pulse diode bridge at Id=20 A has Vdc=540.1898 V and 300 Hz ripple
PWR:010425.objective: For an ideal three-phase diode bridge at VLL=400 Vrms, 50 Hz, and continuous Id=20 A, obtain Vdc=3 sqrt(2) VLL/pi=540.1898 V, P=10.8038 kW, diode avg 6.6667 A and rms 11.5470 A, line rms 16.3299 A, and 300 Hz ripple, not SVPWM.
PWR:010425.statement:
An ideal three-phase six-pulse diode bridge is supplied from a
balanced three-phase source with line-to-line rms voltage
$V_{LL}=400\,\mathrm{V}$ at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$. A large dc inductor
holds the load current at the constant value $I_d=20\,\mathrm{A}$.
Commutation overlap is neglected.

1. Prove that the average dc voltage and the dc power are
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{dc}}
   =\frac{3\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}}{\pi}
   =540.1898\,\mathrm{V},
   \qquad
   P=V_{\mathrm{dc}} I_d
   =10.8038\,\mathrm{kW}.
   \]

2. Each diode conducts for $120^{\circ}$ per source period. Prove
   \[
   I_{D,\mathrm{avg}}=6.6667\,\mathrm{A},
   \qquad
   I_{D,\mathrm{rms}}=11.5470\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

3. Each ac line carries $+I_d$ for $120^{\circ}$ and $-I_d$ for
   $120^{\circ}$. Prove that the line rms is $16.3299\,\mathrm{A}$
   and that the dominant dc-voltage ripple frequency is
   $300\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “a three-phase rectifier has
   $V_{\mathrm{dc}}=2\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}/\pi$ as in single phase”;
   (ii) “the ac currents are produced by SVPWM, so the answers are
   sector dwell times rather than diode averages.”

Do not replace the six-pulse average by an SVPWM sector-dwell
calculation, and do not convert the problem into a PFC THD or
single-phase firing-angle exercise.
permittedResults: On a $60^{\circ}$ crest centered at its maximum, $(3/\pi)\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}\cos\theta\,d\theta=3\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}/\pi$.
A pulse of height $I_d$ and duty $1/3$ has average $I_d/3$ and rms $I_d/\sqrt{3}$. Two opposite $120^{\circ}$ pulses give line rms $I_d\sqrt{2/3}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Average the six 60-degree line-to-line crests, then read device and line currents from 120-degree rectangles.
Start from Vdc=3 sqrt(2) VLL/pi, multiply by Id, and obtain rms values from duty 1/3 (diode) and 2/3 (line).

milestones.criterion: Computes Vdc=3 sqrt(2) VLL/pi=540.1898 V and P=10.8038 kW.
Reports diode average 6.6667 A, diode rms 11.5470 A, line rms 16.3299 A, and 300 Hz ripple from 120-degree conduction.
Refuses the single-phase 2/pi average and refuses reserved SVPWM sector-dwell or PFC substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Uses the single-phase identity Vdc=2 sqrt(2) VLL/pi=360.1265 V instead of the six-pulse 3 sqrt(2) VLL/pi.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Vdc=540.1898 V and P=10.8038 kW are not produced.

commonErrors.description: Treats the ac currents as an SVPWM inverter output and answers with sector dwell times rather than diode and line rms values.
commonErrors.consequence: The six-pulse conduction pattern, 300 Hz ripple, and device averages are replaced by a reserved SVPWM family.

hintTree.content: The six-pulse factor is $3\sqrt{2}/\pi$, not the single-phase $2\sqrt{2}/\pi$.
Diode duty is $120^{\circ}/360^{\circ}=1/3$. Line conduction occupies $240^{\circ}$ of each period.
Ripple frequency is $6\times 50\,\mathrm{Hz}$, not the $2f$ of a single-phase bridge and not an SVPWM carrier.

PWR:010425.canonicalSolution:
The line-to-line crest is $\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}$. In an ideal
six-pulse diode bridge the dc voltage is the six-fold average of
that crest over $60^{\circ}$ sectors:
\[
V_{\mathrm{dc}}
=\frac{3}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}\cos\theta\,d\theta
=\frac{3\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}}{\pi}.
\]
Substituting $V_{LL}=400$ gives
\[
V_{\mathrm{dc}}
=\frac{1200\sqrt{2}}{\pi}
=540.1898\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
With constant $I_d=20\,\mathrm{A}$,
\[
P=V_{\mathrm{dc}} I_d
=540.1898\times 20
=10803.8\,\mathrm{W}
=10.8038\,\mathrm{kW}.
\]
The single-phase identity $2\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}/\pi$ would have
produced $360.1265\,\mathrm{V}$ and is the wrong topology.
\[
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{dc}}=540.1898\,\mathrm{V},\;
P=10.8038\,\mathrm{kW}}.
\]

Each diode conducts for $120^{\circ}=1/3$ of a source period at
height $I_d$:
\[
I_{D,\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{I_d}{3}=\frac{20}{3}=6.6667\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
I_{D,\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_d}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{20}{\sqrt{3}}
=11.5470\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{D,\mathrm{avg}}=6.6667\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_{D,\mathrm{rms}}=11.5470\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Each ac line is connected to the positive rail for $120^{\circ}$
and to the negative rail for $120^{\circ}$, so the mean-square
line current is
\[
I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2
=I_d^2\cdot\frac{2}{3},
\qquad
I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}
=I_d\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
=20\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
=16.3299\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Six line-to-line peaks occur in each $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ period, so
the dc-voltage ripple frequency is
\[
f_{\mathrm{ripple}}=6\times 50=300\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}=16.3299\,\mathrm{A},\;
f_{\mathrm{ripple}}=300\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
\]

Sentence (i) imports the single-phase $2/\pi$ factor. Sentence (ii)
replaces the uncontrolled diode commutation pattern by an SVPWM
sector-dwell construction, which is reserved and is not used here.

The argument never introduces a current-shaped PFC reference or a
single-phase firing angle.

graderFixtures.proofText: The six-pulse average is $V_{\mathrm{dc}}=3\sqrt{2}\,V_{LL}/\pi=540.1898\,\mathrm{V}$ and $P=10.8038\,\mathrm{kW}$. Each diode is a $120^{\circ}$ pulse, so $I_{D,\mathrm{avg}}=6.6667\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_{D,\mathrm{rms}}=11.5470\,\mathrm{A}$. Each line has rms $20\sqrt{2/3}=16.3299\,\mathrm{A}$. The dc ripple is $6\times 50=300\,\mathrm{Hz}$. This is not SVPWM.
A three-phase rectifier still uses the single-phase factor: Vdc=2 sqrt(2) VLL/pi=360.1265 V and P=7.2025 kW. The 3/pi identity is not needed.
The ac currents come from a three-phase SVPWM inverter. The answers are sector dwell times in each 60-degree sector, not diode averages or a 300 Hz six-pulse ripple.

PWR:010526.title: A +/-200 V 50 Hz square-wave inverter into 10 Ohm + 20 mH has P1+P3=2403.6965 W
PWR:010526.objective: For a full-bridge +/-200 V 50 Hz square wave into R=10 Ohm and L=20 mH, obtain V1rms=180.0633 V, Z1=10+j6.2832 Ohm, I1=15.2466 A at -32.1419 deg, P1=2324.5732 W, the matching third-harmonic set, and P1+P3=2403.6965 W, not the all-harmonics total.
PWR:010526.statement:
A single-phase full-bridge inverter produces the odd square wave
$v(t)=+200\,\mathrm{V}$ on $(0,10\,\mathrm{ms})$ and
$v(t)=-200\,\mathrm{V}$ on $(10\,\mathrm{ms},20\,\mathrm{ms})$,
repeating at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The load is the series pair
$R=10\,\Omega$, $L=20\,\mathrm{mH}$.

The Fourier cosine-free expansion is
$v(t)=\sum_{n\text{ odd}}(4\cdot 200)/(n\pi)\sin(n\omega t)$
with $\omega=2\pi\cdot 50$. The $n$th rms phasor therefore has
magnitude
\[
V_{n,\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\cdot 200}{n\pi}.
\]

1. For the fundamental, prove
   \[
   V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=180.0633\,\mathrm{V},
   \qquad
   Z_1=10+j6.2832\,\Omega,
   \]
   \[
   I_1=15.2466\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-32.1419^{\circ},
   \qquad
   P_1=2324.5732\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]

2. For the third harmonic, prove
   \[
   V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}=60.0211\,\mathrm{V},
   \qquad
   Z_3=10+j18.8496\,\Omega,
   \]
   \[
   I_3=2.81289\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-62.0533^{\circ},
   \qquad
   P_3=79.1233\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]

3. Prove that the first-plus-third average power is
   \[
   P_1+P_3=2403.6965\,\mathrm{W}.
   \]
   Identify this sum as a two-harmonic partial power, not the
   all-harmonics total $\sum_{n\text{ odd}}P_n$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the inverter is a $200\,\mathrm{V}$
   sine, so $V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=200/\sqrt{2}$ and there is no third
   harmonic”; (ii) “$2403.6965\,\mathrm{W}$ is the complete average
   power of the square wave, because higher odd harmonics may be
   ignored or already included.”

Do not replace the two-harmonic audit by an SVPWM sector-dwell
construction, and do not convert the problem into a PFC THD or
constant-power negative-impedance study.
permittedResults: $V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=400\sqrt{2}/\pi$ and $V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}=V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}/3$. At $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\omega L=2\pi\cdot 50\cdot 0.020=2\pi$.
$P_n=V_{n,\mathrm{rms}}^2 R/|Z_n|^2$ with $|Z_n|^2=R^2+(n\omega L)^2$. The remainder $\sum_{k\ge 5,\,k\text{ odd}}P_k$ is strictly positive, so $P_1+P_3$ is not the total.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert n=1 and n=3 into Vn,rms=2 sqrt(2) V/(n pi) and Zn=R+j n omega L, then form Pn=Vn,rms^2 R/|Zn|^2 and add only those two terms.
Evaluate the exact reactances 2 pi and 6 pi, convert each rms voltage through the corresponding impedance phasor, and keep the tail of the odd series out of the reported power.

milestones.criterion: Computes the fundamental set V1rms=180.0633 V, Z1=10+j6.2832 Ohm, I1=15.2466 A at -32.1419 deg, and P1=2324.5732 W.
Computes the third-harmonic set and the partial sum P1+P3=2403.6965 W, identified as not the all-harmonics total.
Rejects a 200 V sine substitute and refuses reserved SVPWM, PFC/THD, or all-harmonics-total claims.

commonErrors.description: Treats the inverter output as a 200 V sine, so V1rms=200/sqrt(2) and the third harmonic is omitted.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 180.0633 V fundamental, the third-harmonic set, and P1+P3=2403.6965 W are not produced.

commonErrors.description: Reports 2403.6965 W as the complete average power of the square wave, treating higher odd harmonics as already included or as zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The required distinction between the first-plus-third partial power and the all-harmonics total is lost.

hintTree.content: The fundamental rms is $2\sqrt{2}\cdot 200/\pi$, not $200/\sqrt{2}$. The reactance $\omega L$ is exactly $2\pi$.
The third-harmonic voltage is one-third of the fundamental; the third-harmonic reactance is three times $2\pi$.
Add only $P_1$ and $P_3$. Every remaining odd harmonic still dissipates a positive $I_n^2 R$.

PWR:010526.canonicalSolution:
The fundamental rms is
\[
V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}
=\frac{2\sqrt{2}\cdot 200}{\pi}
=\frac{400\sqrt{2}}{\pi}
=180.0633\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The fundamental impedance uses $\omega=100\pi$ and
$L=0.020\,\mathrm{H}$:
\[
\omega L=2\pi=6.283185\ldots,
\qquad
Z_1=10+j6.2832\,\Omega.
\]
Then
\[
|Z_1|=\sqrt{10^2+(2\pi)^2}=\sqrt{100+4\pi^2},
\]
\[
I_{1,\mathrm{rms}}
=\frac{V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}}{|Z_1|}
=15.2466\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
\arg I_1
=-\arctan\bigl(2\pi/10\bigr)
=-32.1419^{\circ}.
\]
Average power at the fundamental is
\[
P_1
=\frac{V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}^2 R}{|Z_1|^2}
=2324.5732\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=180.0633\,\mathrm{V},\;
Z_1=10+j6.2832\,\Omega,\;
I_1=15.2466\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-32.1419^{\circ},\;
P_1=2324.5732\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

The third harmonic is the $n=3$ term of the same series:
\[
V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}
=\frac{V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}}{3}
=60.0211\,\mathrm{V},
\qquad
Z_3=10+j3\cdot 2\pi
=10+j18.8496\,\Omega.
\]
Hence
\[
I_{3,\mathrm{rms}}
=\frac{V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}}{|Z_3|}
=2.81289\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
\arg I_3
=-\arctan(18.8496/10)
=-62.0533^{\circ},
\]
\[
P_3
=\frac{V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}^2 R}{|Z_3|^2}
=79.1233\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}=60.0211\,\mathrm{V},\;
Z_3=10+j18.8496\,\Omega,\;
I_3=2.81289\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-62.0533^{\circ},\;
P_3=79.1233\,\mathrm{W}}.
\]

Adding the two computed powers gives the required partial sum
\[
P_1+P_3
=2324.5732+79.1233
=2403.6965\,\mathrm{W}.
\]
Every remaining odd harmonic $n=5,7,\ldots$ still sees a finite
$|Z_n|$ and a positive $V_{n,\mathrm{rms}}$, so $P_n=I_n^2 R>0$.
The displayed sum is therefore not the all-harmonics total.
\[
\boxed{P_1+P_3=2403.6965\,\mathrm{W}\text{ (not }\sum_{\text{odd}}P_n\text{)}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the square wave by a $200\,\mathrm{V}$ sine.
That model has $V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=141.4214\,\mathrm{V}$ and no
third harmonic, so none of the required phasors appear. Sentence
(ii) promotes the two-term partial sum to a complete power; the
tail $\sum_{n\ge 5}P_n$ is omitted but not zero.

The argument never constructs SVPWM dwell times, a PFC harmonic
table, or a constant-power incremental-impedance criterion.

graderFixtures.proofText: The square-wave fundamental is $V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}=400\sqrt{2}/\pi=180.0633\,\mathrm{V}$ into $Z_1=10+j6.2832\,\Omega$, giving $I_1=15.2466\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-32.1419^{\circ}$ and $P_1=2324.5732\,\mathrm{W}$. The third harmonic is $V_{3,\mathrm{rms}}=60.0211\,\mathrm{V}$ into $Z_3=10+j18.8496\,\Omega$, giving $I_3=2.81289\,\mathrm{A}\,\angle-62.0533^{\circ}$ and $P_3=79.1233\,\mathrm{W}$. The partial sum is $P_1+P_3=2403.6965\,\mathrm{W}$ and is not $\sum_{n\text{ odd}}P_n$.
A +/-200 V bridge is just a 200 V sine at 50 Hz, so V1rms=200/sqrt(2)=141.4214 V. There is no third harmonic and no 180.0633 V fundamental.
P1+P3=2403.6965 W is the complete average power into the RL load. Higher odd harmonics are negligible or already included in that total.

PWR:010527.title: A 300 V bipolar H-bridge returns 4.6 kW at duty 53/60 while the motor generates 20 A
PWR:010527.objective: For a 300 V bipolar H-bridge driving E=240 V, Ra=0.5 Ohm with 20 A from motor to bridge, obtain Va=E-IRa=230 V, d=53/60=0.883333, Pmech=4.8 kW, Pcu=200 W, Pbus=4.6 kW, and Ibus=15.3333 A.
PWR:010527.statement:
A separately excited DC machine is driven from a stiff DC bus
$V_{\mathrm{dc}}=300\,\mathrm{V}$ by a bipolar PWM H-bridge. The
armature back-EMF is $E=240\,\mathrm{V}$ and the armature resistance
is $R_a=0.5\,\Omega$. Armature inductance may be neglected in the
PWM-period average. The machine is generating: a regenerative current
$I=20\,\mathrm{A}$ flows from the motor into the bridge. Switching
loss is neglected, so the bridge is an average power-conserving
voltage transformer from bus to armature.

Bipolar PWM applies $+V_{\mathrm{dc}}$ for duty $d$ of each carrier
period and $-V_{\mathrm{dc}}$ for the complementary interval, so the
average armature voltage is
\[
V_a=(2d-1)V_{\mathrm{dc}}.
\]
With the stated generating current, Kirchhoff's voltage law on the
armature is $E=V_a+I R_a$.

1. Prove $V_a=E-I R_a=230\,\mathrm{V}$. Invert the bipolar map and
   prove
   \[
   d=\frac{53}{60}=0.883333.
   \]

2. Prove the mechanical conversion $E I=4.8\,\mathrm{kW}$, the copper
   loss $I^2 R_a=200\,\mathrm{W}$, and the power returned at the
   armature terminals $V_a I=4.6\,\mathrm{kW}$. Confirm the ledger
   $4.8\,\mathrm{kW}-200\,\mathrm{W}=4.6\,\mathrm{kW}$.

3. Prove that the average current returned into the $300\,\mathrm{V}$
   bus is
   \[
   I_{\mathrm{bus}}=\frac{4.6\,\mathrm{kW}}{300\,\mathrm{V}}
   =15.3333\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “regeneration requires $V_a<0$, hence
   $d<1/2$”; (ii) “the bus current equals the armature current
   $20\,\mathrm{A}$, or else $V_a=E+I R_a=250\,\mathrm{V}$.”

Do not replace the average bipolar map by a hard-switching
conduction / transition / recovery loss ledger, do not invoke
three-phase SVPWM sector dwell, and do not discuss transformer
reset or flux walk.
permittedResults: From $V_a=(2d-1)V_{\mathrm{dc}}$ one recovers $d=(V_a/V_{\mathrm{dc}}+1)/2$. Substituting $V_a=230$ and $V_{\mathrm{dc}}=300$ gives $d=53/60$.

Average bus current into a stiff voltage $V_{\mathrm{dc}}$ is $I_{\mathrm{bus}}=P_{\mathrm{bus}}/V_{\mathrm{dc}}$, not the armature current, because the bridge is a voltage transformer rather than a direct series path.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write generating KVL for Va, invert Va=(2d-1)Vdc, then split EI into copper and terminal return.
Form the three armature powers first to lock 4.6 kW, then divide by the stiff 300 V bus to obtain Ibus.

milestones.criterion: Computes Va=230 V from generating KVL and inverts the bipolar map to d=53/60=0.883333.
Closes the ledger Pmech=4.8 kW, Pcu=200 W, Pbus=4.6 kW and reports Ibus=15.3333 A.
Rejects d<1/2 or Ibus=20 A / Va=250 V, and refuses reserved hard-switching, SVPWM, or flux-walk substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Claims regeneration requires Va<0 and therefore d<1/2, discarding Va=230 V and d=53/60.
commonErrors.consequence: The required positive armature voltage and the duty 53/60 are replaced by a motoring-quadrant myth.

commonErrors.description: Sets Ibus=20 A, or writes Va=E+IRa=250 V (and a matching wrong duty), instead of Ibus=Pbus/Vdc and Va=E-IRa.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 15.3333 A bus return and the 230 V / 4.6 kW ledger fail.

hintTree.content: Generating KVL is $V_a=240-20\cdot 0.5$, not $240+10$. The result is still well above zero.
Return $4.6\,\mathrm{kW}$ to the $300\,\mathrm{V}$ bus; the bus current is $4600/300$, not $20$.

PWR:010527.canonicalSolution:
Generating KVL with $I$ directed from machine to bridge is
\[
V_a=E-I R_a=240-20\cdot 0.5=230\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The bipolar average map then reads
\[
230=(2d-1)\cdot 300\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
2d-1=\frac{23}{30}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
d=\frac{53}{60}=0.883333.
\]
Duty remains above one half because $V_a$ is still positive: the
back-EMF $240\,\mathrm{V}$ exceeds the ohmic drop $10\,\mathrm{V}$.
\[
\boxed{V_a=230\,\mathrm{V},\quad d=53/60=0.883333}.
\]

The three powers on the armature are
\begin{align*}
P_{\mathrm{mech}}&=EI=240\cdot 20=4800\,\mathrm{W}=4.8\,\mathrm{kW},\\
P_{\mathrm{cu}}&=I^2 R_a=400\cdot 0.5=200\,\mathrm{W},\\
P_{\mathrm{term}}&=V_a I=230\cdot 20=4600\,\mathrm{W}=4.6\,\mathrm{kW}.
\end{align*}
They close:
\[
P_{\mathrm{mech}}-P_{\mathrm{cu}}=4.8\,\mathrm{kW}-200\,\mathrm{W}
=4.6\,\mathrm{kW}=P_{\mathrm{term}}.
\]
A lossless average H-bridge delivers the same $4.6\,\mathrm{kW}$ to
the stiff bus, so
\[
I_{\mathrm{bus}}=\frac{4600}{300}=\frac{46}{3}=15.3333\,\mathrm{A}
\]
into the bus. The armature current $20\,\mathrm{A}$ is not the bus
current.
\[
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{mech}}=4.8\,\mathrm{kW},\;
P_{\mathrm{cu}}=200\,\mathrm{W},\;
P_{\mathrm{bus}}=4.6\,\mathrm{kW},\;
I_{\mathrm{bus}}=15.3333\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses power direction with voltage polarity.
Regeneration here is a reversed current at still-positive $V_a$, so
$d=53/60>1/2$. Sentence (ii) either equates bus and armature
currents, destroying $I_{\mathrm{bus}}=15.3333\,\mathrm{A}$, or flips
the ohmic sign to $V_a=250\,\mathrm{V}$ and a different duty.

The argument never inventories hard-switching conduction, overlap, or
recovery loss, never partitions a three-phase SVPWM hexagon, and never
treats transformer volt-second reset or flux walk.

graderFixtures.proofText: Generating KVL gives $V_a=240-10=230\,\mathrm{V}$, so $d=53/60=0.883333$. Then $EI=4.8\,\mathrm{kW}$, $I^2 R_a=200\,\mathrm{W}$, and $V_a I=4.6\,\mathrm{kW}$ return to the bus as $I_{\mathrm{bus}}=15.3333\,\mathrm{A}$. Duty stays above one half; the bus current is not $20\,\mathrm{A}$.
Regeneration means the armature voltage must be negative, so d<1/2. I do not accept Va=230 V or d=53/60.
The 20 A armature current is also the bus current, and generating KVL is Va=E+IRa=250 V. I never form Ibus=4.6 kW/300 V=15.3333 A.

PWR:010628.title: A 400 V 100 Ah pack falls to 53.9583% after a 20 kW discharge then ends at 65.4583%
PWR:010628.objective: For a 400 V 100 Ah battery at 80% SoC, discharge 20 kW to the bus for 30 min at 96% then charge 15 kW from the bus for 20 min at 92%, obtain Pbat=20.8333 kW, 10.4167 kWh, 26.0417 Ah, SoC 53.9583%, then 5 kWh bus / 4.6 kWh stored / 11.5 Ah and end SoC 65.4583%.
PWR:010628.statement:
A battery pack is modeled as a constant terminal voltage
$400\,\mathrm{V}$ with nameplate capacity $100\,\mathrm{Ah}$. The
initial state of charge is $80\%$ (that is, $80\,\mathrm{Ah}$). Two
converter intervals follow. Treat voltage as constant for the energy
and ampere-hour ledger; do not introduce an open-circuit-voltage
curve.

Interval A (discharge toward a DC bus). The bus receives a constant
$20\,\mathrm{kW}$ for $30\,\mathrm{min}$. The conversion efficiency
from battery terminals to bus is $96\%$.

Interval B (charge from the same bus). The bus delivers a constant
$15\,\mathrm{kW}$ into the charger for $20\,\mathrm{min}$. The
conversion efficiency from bus to battery terminals is $92\%$.

1. Prove that the battery must supply $20/0.96=20.8333\,\mathrm{kW}$
   during A, that the extracted energy is $10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}$, and
   that the pack loses
   \[
   \frac{10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}}{400\,\mathrm{V}}=26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}.
   \]
   Conclude that the SoC after A is $53.9583\%$.

2. Prove that interval B inputs $5\,\mathrm{kWh}$ at the bus, stores
   $4.6\,\mathrm{kWh}$ in the battery, and restores $11.5\,\mathrm{Ah}$.

3. Prove that the final SoC is $65.4583\%$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “on discharge the battery supplies only
   $20\times 0.96=19.2\,\mathrm{kW}$”; (ii) “ampere-hours equal
   kilowatt-hours at $400\,\mathrm{V}$ with no $E/V$ conversion, or
   the nameplate is $100\,\mathrm{kWh}$.”

Do not replace the SoC ledger by a PFC reference / harmonics / THD /
power-factor audit, and do not recast the pack as a constant-power
negative-impedance load on a source.
permittedResults: A $30\,\mathrm{min}$ interval is $0.5\,\mathrm{h}$, so $20.8333\,\mathrm{kW}$ extracts $10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Dividing by $0.4\,\mathrm{kV}$ yields $26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}$.
A $20\,\mathrm{min}$ interval is $1/3\,\mathrm{h}$, so $15\,\mathrm{kW}$ inputs $5\,\mathrm{kWh}$ at the bus. At $92\%$ the battery stores $4.6\,\mathrm{kWh}=11.5\,\mathrm{Ah}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert each bus specification through the directed efficiency, then divide energy by 400 V to update ampere-hours.
Track SoC only in ampere-hours on the 100 Ah nameplate, applying 20/0.96 for A and 0.92 for B.

milestones.criterion: Places efficiency in the discharge denominator and reports Pbat=20.8333 kW, 10.4167 kWh, 26.0417 Ah, and SoC 53.9583%.
Stores 4.6 kWh / 11.5 Ah from the 5 kWh bus input and reports end SoC 65.4583%.
Rejects 19.2 kW discharge or a kWh/Ah nameplate mix, and refuses reserved PFC or negative-impedance substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes battery discharge power as 20*0.96=19.2 kW instead of 20/0.96=20.8333 kW.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 10.4167 kWh, 26.0417 Ah, and 53.9583% SoC after interval A are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats kilowatt-hours as ampere-hours without dividing by 400 V, or reads the nameplate as 100 kWh rather than 100 Ah.
commonErrors.consequence: The 26.0417 Ah removal, 11.5 Ah restore, and end SoC 65.4583% cannot appear.

hintTree.content: Discharge efficiency sits in the denominator: the battery, not the bus, pays the $4\%$ converter loss.
$10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}$ at $400\,\mathrm{V}$ is $26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}$. Subtract from the initial $80\,\mathrm{Ah}$.
Charge stores $5\times 0.92=4.6\,\mathrm{kWh}=11.5\,\mathrm{Ah}$. Add that to $53.9583\,\mathrm{Ah}$.

PWR:010628.canonicalSolution:
Interval A specifies $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ at the bus and $\eta=0.96$
from battery to bus, so the battery terminals supply
\[
P_{\mathrm{bat}}=\frac{20}{0.96}=20.8333\,\mathrm{kW}.
\]
Over $30\,\mathrm{min}=0.5\,\mathrm{h}$ the extracted energy is
\[
E_{\mathrm{dis}}=20.8333\times 0.5=10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}.
\]
At the constant $400\,\mathrm{V}$,
\[
\Delta Q_{\mathrm{dis}}
=\frac{10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}}{0.4\,\mathrm{kV}}
=26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}.
\]
The pack started at $80\,\mathrm{Ah}$, so after A
\[
Q_A=80-26.0417=53.9583\,\mathrm{Ah},
\]
i.e. SoC $53.9583\%$.
\[
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{bat}}=20.8333\,\mathrm{kW},\;
E_{\mathrm{dis}}=10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh},\;
\Delta Q=26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah},\;
\mathrm{SoC}_A=53.9583\%}.
\]

Interval B inputs $15\,\mathrm{kW}$ at the bus for
$20\,\mathrm{min}=1/3\,\mathrm{h}$:
\[
E_{\mathrm{bus}}=15\times\frac13=5\,\mathrm{kWh}.
\]
At $\eta=0.92$ from bus to battery,
\[
E_{\mathrm{store}}=5\times 0.92=4.6\,\mathrm{kWh},
\qquad
\Delta Q_{\mathrm{chg}}=\frac{4.6}{0.4}=11.5\,\mathrm{Ah}.
\]
The final charge and SoC are
\[
Q_{\mathrm{end}}=53.9583+11.5=65.4583\,\mathrm{Ah},
\qquad
\mathrm{SoC}_{\mathrm{end}}=65.4583\%.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_{\mathrm{bus}}=5\,\mathrm{kWh},\;
E_{\mathrm{store}}=4.6\,\mathrm{kWh},\;
\Delta Q_{\mathrm{chg}}=11.5\,\mathrm{Ah},\;
\mathrm{SoC}_{\mathrm{end}}=65.4583\%}.
\]

Sentence (i) multiplies instead of dividing on discharge, so the
battery is credited with only $19.2\,\mathrm{kW}$ and the
$26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}$ removal disappears. Sentence (ii) either
treats kilowatt-hours as ampere-hours at $400\,\mathrm{V}$ or
replaces the $100\,\mathrm{Ah}$ nameplate by $100\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

The argument never audits a PFC current reference, harmonics, THD, or
power factor, and never treats the pack as a constant-power
negative-impedance load.

graderFixtures.proofText: Discharge sends $20/0.96=20.8333\,\mathrm{kW}$ from the battery, extracting $10.4167\,\mathrm{kWh}=26.0417\,\mathrm{Ah}$ and leaving $53.9583\%$. Charge inputs $5\,\mathrm{kWh}$ at the bus, stores $4.6\,\mathrm{kWh}=11.5\,\mathrm{Ah}$, and ends at $65.4583\%$.
On discharge the battery only has to supply 20*0.96=19.2 kW. I never divide by 0.96 and I do not accept 20.8333 kW or 26.0417 Ah.
At 400 V the ampere-hour change equals the kilowatt-hour change, and the pack is a 100 kWh nameplate. I never divide by 400 V to obtain 26.0417 Ah or 11.5 Ah.

PWR:010629.title: Adding 1 Ohm on source 1 flips 25.8065 A / 12.9032 A sharing to 15.0943 A / 22.6415 A
PWR:010629.objective: For two 400 V sources with m1=0.5 Ohm, m2=1 Ohm, and a 10 Ohm load, obtain the no-line point V=12000/31=387.0968 V, I1=800/31=25.8065 A, I2=400/31=12.9032 A, P=14.9844 kW, then with a 1 Ohm line on source 1 only V=20000/53=377.3585 V, I1=800/53=15.0943 A, I2=1200/53=22.6415 A.
PWR:010629.statement:
Two ideal $400\,\mathrm{V}$ DC sources share a single resistive load
$R_L=10\,\Omega$ through linear droop (series) resistances
$m_1=0.5\,\Omega$ and $m_2=1\,\Omega$. The common load voltage is $V$,
and
\[
I_1=\frac{400-V}{m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}},\qquad
I_2=\frac{400-V}{m_2},\qquad
I_1+I_2=\frac{V}{R_L}.
\]
There is no constant-power load and no small-signal impedance
criterion in this exercise.

1. With no extra line, $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=m_1=0.5\,\Omega$. Prove
   \[
   V=\frac{12000}{31}=387.0968\,\mathrm{V},\quad
   I_1=\frac{800}{31}=25.8065\,\mathrm{A},\quad
   I_2=\frac{400}{31}=12.9032\,\mathrm{A},
   \]
   and that the load power is $P=V^2/R_L=14.9844\,\mathrm{kW}$.

2. A line resistance $1\,\Omega$ is now inserted in series with source
   $1$ only, so $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=1.5\,\Omega$ while $m_2$ is
   unchanged. Prove
   \[
   V=\frac{20000}{53}=377.3585\,\mathrm{V},\quad
   I_1=\frac{800}{53}=15.0943\,\mathrm{A},\quad
   I_2=\frac{1200}{53}=22.6415\,\mathrm{A}.
   \]

3. Observe that source $1$ carried the larger share before the line
   and the smaller share after it.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the added line is common and must be
   charged to both sources, so both effective droops increase by
   $1\,\Omega$”; (ii) “the current ratio remains $I_1=2 I_2$ after
   the line is added.”

Do not replace the resistive sharing calculation by a constant-power
negative-impedance stability argument, and do not invoke PFC
harmonics or three-phase SVPWM sector dwell.
permittedResults: With $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=1.5$ the same KCL becomes $(400-V)(1/1.5+1)=V/10$, hence $5(400-V)=3V/10$ and $V=20000/53$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write KCL in conductances, clear denominators to 31 and then 53, and read each current as (400-V)/m.
Use I proportional to 1/m at a common V to predict the ranking reversal, then compute the two exact voltages.

milestones.criterion: Solves the no-line KCL and reports V=12000/31=387.0968 V, I1=25.8065 A, I2=12.9032 A, and P=14.9844 kW.
Updates only source 1 to 1.5 Ohm and reports V=20000/53=377.3585 V, I1=15.0943 A, I2=22.6415 A.
Rejects a common-line or frozen-ratio reading, and refuses reserved constant-power-stability or PFC/SVPWM substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Adds the 1 Ohm line to both droops, taking (m1,m2)=(1.5,2) instead of (1.5,1).
commonErrors.consequence: The required V=20000/53 and the currents 800/53, 1200/53 are replaced by a different linear system.

commonErrors.description: Keeps I1=2 I2 after the one-sided line, as if droops were still 0.5 Ohm and 1 Ohm.
commonErrors.consequence: The ranking reversal to I1=15.0943 A < I2=22.6415 A never appears.

hintTree.content: No-line conductances are $2\,\mathrm{S}$ and $1\,\mathrm{S}$. Clear the $1/10$ load term to obtain the denominator $31$.
After the $1\,\Omega$ line, source $1$ has conductance $2/3\,\mathrm{S}$. The cleared denominator is $53$.
Compare $I_1/I_2=2$ before the line with $I_1/I_2=(1)/1.5=2/3$ after it; the ranking reverses.

PWR:010629.canonicalSolution:
With no extra line, $m_1=0.5\,\Omega$ and $m_2=1\,\Omega$, so
\[
(400-V)\Bigl(\frac{1}{0.5}+1\Bigr)=\frac{V}{10}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
3(400-V)=\frac{V}{10}.
\]
Clearing the remaining denominator gives $12000-3V=V/10$, or
$120000=31V$, hence
\[
V=\frac{12000}{31}=387.0968\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The branch currents are
\[
I_1=\frac{400-V}{0.5}=\frac{800}{31}=25.8065\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
I_2=\frac{400-V}{1}=\frac{400}{31}=12.9032\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
(The ratio $I_1=2 I_2$ is exactly the inverse-droop ratio $1/0.5$.)
Load power is
\[
P=\frac{V^2}{10}
=\frac{(12000/31)^2}{10}
=14.9844\,\mathrm{kW}.
\]
\[
\boxed{V=12000/31=387.0968\,\mathrm{V},\;
I_1=25.8065\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_2=12.9032\,\mathrm{A},\;
P=14.9844\,\mathrm{kW}}.
\]

Inserting $1\,\Omega$ on source $1$ only sets $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=1.5\,\Omega$:
\[
(400-V)\Bigl(\frac{1}{1.5}+1\Bigr)=\frac{V}{10}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac53(400-V)=\frac{V}{10}.
\]
Clearing yields $50(400-V)=3V$, or $20000=53V$, hence
\[
V=\frac{20000}{53}=377.3585\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The new currents are
\[
I_1=\frac{400-V}{1.5}=\frac{800}{53}=15.0943\,\mathrm{A},
\qquad
I_2=\frac{400-V}{1}=\frac{1200}{53}=22.6415\,\mathrm{A}.
\]
Source $1$ has dropped from the larger share ($25.8065\,\mathrm{A}$)
to the smaller share ($15.0943\,\mathrm{A}$).
\[
\boxed{V=20000/53=377.3585\,\mathrm{V},\;
I_1=15.0943\,\mathrm{A},\;
I_2=22.6415\,\mathrm{A}}.
\]

Sentence (i) charges the line resistor to both sources, which would
replace $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=1.5$ by the pair $(1.5,2)$ and destroy
both displayed fractions. Sentence (ii) freezes the no-line ratio
$I_1=2 I_2$ after the one-sided line, contradicting $800:1200=2:3$.

The argument never linearizes a constant-power load as a negative
incidental resistance, and never mentions PFC harmonics or SVPWM
sector dwell.

graderFixtures.proofText: No line: $V=12000/31=387.0968\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_1=25.8065\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_2=12.9032\,\mathrm{A}$, $P=14.9844\,\mathrm{kW}$. After $1\,\Omega$ on source $1$ only, $m_{1,\mathrm{eff}}=1.5\,\Omega$, $V=20000/53=377.3585\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_1=15.0943\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_2=22.6415\,\mathrm{A}$. The line is not common and the ratio is no longer $2:1$.
The added 1 Ohm line sits on the common bus, so both sources see it. I take m1=1.5 Ohm and m2=2 Ohm and I do not accept V=20000/53.
Current sharing stays I1=2 I2 after the line is added, because the original droops were 0.5 Ohm and 1 Ohm. I never report I1=15.0943 A < I2=22.6415 A.

PWR:010630.title: The 1 mH / 0.5 mH / 20 uF LCL resonates at 1949.2420 Hz so the stated Rd equals 4.08248 Ohm
PWR:010630.objective: For L1=1 mH, L2=0.5 mH, Cf=20 uF, fsw=10 kHz, obtain omega=12247.4487 rad/s, f=1949.2420 Hz, f/fsw=0.194924, |XC|=4.08248 Ohm, XL1=12.24745 Ohm, XL2=6.12372 Ohm, and under the stated criterion Rd=|XC| choose 4.08248 Ohm with no optimality claim.
PWR:010630.statement:
A grid-tied voltage-source converter uses an LCL filter with converter
inductance $L_1=1\,\mathrm{mH}$, grid inductance $L_2=0.5\,\mathrm{mH}$,
and filter capacitance $C_f=20\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. The PWM carrier is
$f_{\mathrm{sw}}=10\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Resistive parasitics are neglected
when locating the undamped resonance. With both AC sources treated as
short circuits for the small-signal LC loop, the resonant frequency is
\[
\omega_{\mathrm{res}}
=\sqrt{\frac{L_1+L_2}{L_1 L_2 C_f}}.
\]

1. Prove
   \[
   \omega_{\mathrm{res}}=12247.4487\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad
   f_{\mathrm{res}}=1949.2420\,\mathrm{Hz},\qquad
   \frac{f_{\mathrm{res}}}{f_{\mathrm{sw}}}=0.194924.
   \]

2. At this $\omega_{\mathrm{res}}$ prove the reactances
   \[
   |X_C|=\frac{1}{\omega_{\mathrm{res}} C_f}=4.08248\,\Omega,\quad
   X_{L_1}=\omega_{\mathrm{res}} L_1=12.24745\,\Omega,\quad
   X_{L_2}=\omega_{\mathrm{res}} L_2=6.12372\,\Omega.
   \]

3. A passive damping resistor $R_d$ is to be chosen by the
   \emph{explicitly stated} criterion $R_d=|X_C|$ evaluated at
   $\omega_{\mathrm{res}}$. Prove that this criterion selects
   $R_d=4.08248\,\Omega$. Do \emph{not} claim that the pick is
   optimal, unique among design methods, or loss-minimal.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the resonance is the converter-side
   $1/\sqrt{L_1 C_f}$, so $L_2$ may be ignored”; (ii) “$R_d$ should
   be $X_{L_1}+X_{L_2}$, or else $R_d=0$ because parasitics were
   neglected.”

Do not replace the resonance calculation by a three-phase SVPWM
sector-dwell table, and do not convert the filter into a PFC
harmonic / THD / power-factor audit.
permittedResults: Then $f_{\mathrm{res}}=\omega_{\mathrm{res}}/(2\pi)$ and $|X_C|=1/(\omega_{\mathrm{res}} C_f)$. The stated rule copies that $|X_C|$ onto $R_d$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form (L1+L2)/(L1 L2 Cf), take the square root, then evaluate the three reactances and copy |XC| onto Rd.
Compute f_res/f_sw first as a sanity bound near 0.2, then back out omega and |XC| for the stated resistor.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates omega=12247.4487 rad/s, f=1949.2420 Hz, and f/fsw=0.194924 from the two-inductor formula.
Reports |XC|=4.08248 Ohm, XL1=12.24745 Ohm, XL2=6.12372 Ohm, and Rd=4.08248 Ohm as the stated |XC| pick.
Rejects a converter-only LC frequency or Rd=XL1+XL2 / Rd=0, claims no optimum, and refuses reserved SVPWM or PFC substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops L2 and locates the resonance at 1/sqrt(L1 Cf) instead of sqrt((L1+L2)/(L1 L2 Cf)).
commonErrors.consequence: The required 12247.4487 rad/s, 1949.2420 Hz, and 0.194924 carrier ratio are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Sets Rd=XL1+XL2 or Rd=0 instead of the stated criterion Rd=|XC|=4.08248 Ohm.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 4.08248 Ohm damping pick is replaced by a different rule, often with an optimality claim.

hintTree.content: Compute $(L_1+L_2)/(L_1 L_2 C_f)=1.5\times 10^8$ before taking the square root. Do not drop $L_2$.
Divide $\omega_{\mathrm{res}}$ by $2\pi$ for hertz, then by $10\,\mathrm{kHz}$ for the carrier ratio.
$|X_C|=1/(\omega_{\mathrm{res}}\cdot 20\,\mu\mathrm{F})=4.08248\,\Omega$. Copy that value to $R_d$; do not add the inductor reactances.

PWR:010630.canonicalSolution:
Substitute the element values:
\[
L_1 L_2 C_f
=10^{-3}\cdot 5\times 10^{-4}\cdot 2\times 10^{-5}
=10^{-11},
\qquad
L_1+L_2=1.5\times 10^{-3},
\]
so
\[
\frac{L_1+L_2}{L_1 L_2 C_f}=1.5\times 10^8,\qquad
\omega_{\mathrm{res}}=\sqrt{1.5\times 10^8}=12247.4487\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
The cyclic frequency and the carrier ratio are
\[
f_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{res}}}{2\pi}=1949.2420\,\mathrm{Hz},
\qquad
\frac{f_{\mathrm{res}}}{f_{\mathrm{sw}}}=0.194924.
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega_{\mathrm{res}}=12247.4487\,\mathrm{rad/s},\;
f_{\mathrm{res}}=1949.2420\,\mathrm{Hz},\;
f_{\mathrm{res}}/f_{\mathrm{sw}}=0.194924}.
\]

The three reactances at $\omega_{\mathrm{res}}$ are
\begin{align*}
|X_C|&=\frac{1}{12247.4487\cdot 2\times 10^{-5}}=4.08248\,\Omega,\\
X_{L_1}&=12247.4487\cdot 10^{-3}=12.24745\,\Omega,\\
X_{L_2}&=12247.4487\cdot 5\times 10^{-4}=6.12372\,\Omega.
\end{align*}
The stated criterion $R_d=|X_C|$ therefore selects
\[
R_d=4.08248\,\Omega.
\]
This is the value of the given rule, not a claim that the resistor is
optimal, unique, or loss-minimal.
\[
\boxed{|X_C|=4.08248\,\Omega,\;
X_{L_1}=12.24745\,\Omega,\;
X_{L_2}=6.12372\,\Omega,\;
R_d=4.08248\,\Omega}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $L_2$ and reports $1/\sqrt{L_1 C_f}$, which is a
different frequency and a different $|X_C|$. Sentence (ii) replaces
the stated $|X_C|$ rule by $X_{L_1}+X_{L_2}=18.37117\,\Omega$ or by
$R_d=0$.

The argument never fills an SVPWM sector-dwell table and never
converts the LCL current into a PFC harmonic, THD, or power-factor
score.

graderFixtures.proofText: Both inductors enter $\omega_{\mathrm{res}}=\sqrt{(L_1+L_2)/(L_1 L_2 C_f)}=12247.4487\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so $f_{\mathrm{res}}=1949.2420\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\mathrm{res}}/f_{\mathrm{sw}}=0.194924$. At resonance $|X_C|=4.08248\,\Omega$, $X_{L_1}=12.24745\,\Omega$, $X_{L_2}=6.12372\,\Omega$. The stated rule $R_d=|X_C|$ selects $4.08248\,\Omega$ and is not an optimality claim.
The grid inductor is small, so the resonance is 1/sqrt(L1 Cf). I drop L2 and I do not accept 12247.4487 rad/s or 1949.2420 Hz.
Damping should cancel the two inductor reactances, so Rd=XL1+XL2, or else Rd=0 because parasitics were neglected. I do not copy |XC|=4.08248 Ohm onto Rd.

PWR:010631.title: A 5 mF 800 V link falls to 721.1103 V after a 20 kW 15 ms hole so Cmin is 6.49351 mF
PWR:010631.objective: For an 800 V bus, C=5 mF, and a constant 20 kW deficit lasting 15 ms, obtain energy 300 J and Vf=sqrt(800^2-2*300/0.005)=721.1103 V, then for a 740 V floor prove Cmin=600/(800^2-740^2)=6.49351 mF.
PWR:010631.statement:
A voltage-source converter is fed from a DC link whose nominal bus is
$V_i=800\,\mathrm{V}$ and whose capacitance is $C=5\,\mathrm{mF}$. For
$15\,\mathrm{ms}$ the upstream source is lost. During that hole the
converter continues to draw a \emph{constant} $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ from
the capacitor alone (constant-power ride-through, not a constant
current). Switching-loss ledgers are out of scope.

The capacitor energy identity is
\[
\frac12 C\bigl(V_i^2-V_f^2\bigr)=P\,\Delta t.
\]

1. Prove that the extracted energy is $300\,\mathrm{J}$. Invert the
   identity and prove
   \[
   V_f=\sqrt{800^2-\frac{2\cdot 300}{0.005}}=721.1103\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

2. A ride-through specification now requires $V_f\ge 740\,\mathrm{V}$
   at the end of the same $15\,\mathrm{ms}$, $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ hole.
   Show that $C=5\,\mathrm{mF}$ is insufficient, and prove
   \[
   C_{\min}=\frac{600}{800^2-740^2}=6.49351\,\mathrm{mF}.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the draw is a constant current
   $I=20\,\mathrm{kW}/800\,\mathrm{V}$, so $\Delta V=I\Delta t/C$”;
   (ii) “the missing energy is $C V\Delta V$ or
   $\tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2$ rather than
   $\tfrac12 C(V_i^2-V_f^2)$.”

Do not recast the capacitor as a constant-power negative-impedance
stability problem on a regulated source, and do not replace the
energy identity by a hard-switching conduction / transition /
recovery loss ledger.
permittedResults: $20\,\mathrm{kW}\times 15\,\mathrm{ms}=300\,\mathrm{J}$. Then $V_f=\sqrt{V_i^2-2E/C}$ with $C=0.005\,\mathrm{F}$.
For $E=300\,\mathrm{J}$ and $V_{\min}=740\,\mathrm{V}$ one has $C_{\min}=600/(800^2-740^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert P Delta t to 300 J, invert the quadratic energy identity for Vf, then repeat at Vmin=740 V for Cmin.
Compare Vf=721.1103 V with the 740 V floor first, then scale C by 300 / (1/2(Vi^2-Vmin^2)).

milestones.criterion: Computes E=300 J and Vf=721.1103 V from (1/2)C(Vi^2-Vf^2)=P Delta t.
Shows 5 mF misses 740 V and reports Cmin=6.49351 mF.
Rejects a constant-current ramp or a wrong capacitor-energy identity, and refuses reserved negative-impedance or hard-switching substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the 20 kW hole by I=25 A and a linear ramp DeltaV=I t/C, typically reporting Vf=725 V.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Vf=721.1103 V and the quadratic Cmin=6.49351 mF never appear.

commonErrors.description: Writes the missing energy as C V DeltaV or (1/2)C(DeltaV)^2 instead of (1/2)C(Vi^2-Vf^2).
commonErrors.consequence: Both Vf=721.1103 V and Cmin=600/(800^2-740^2) become a different algebraic problem.

hintTree.content: Energy is $20000\times 0.015=300\,\mathrm{J}$, not a current times $800\,\mathrm{V}$.
For a $740\,\mathrm{V}$ floor the same $300\,\mathrm{J}$ forces $C_{\min}=600/(640000-547600)$.

PWR:010631.canonicalSolution:
The hole removes
\[
E=P\Delta t=20000\times 0.015=300\,\mathrm{J}.
\]
With $C=5\,\mathrm{mF}=0.005\,\mathrm{F}$,
\[
\frac12\cdot 0.005\cdot\bigl(800^2-V_f^2\bigr)=300
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
800^2-V_f^2=\frac{600}{0.005}=120000.
\]
Hence
\[
V_f=\sqrt{640000-120000}=\sqrt{520000}=721.1103\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E=300\,\mathrm{J},\quad V_f=721.1103\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]
This already lies below $740\,\mathrm{V}$, so $5\,\mathrm{mF}$ fails
the ride-through floor.

Imposing $V_f=740\,\mathrm{V}$ on the same $300\,\mathrm{J}$ gives
\[
\frac12 C_{\min}\bigl(800^2-740^2\bigr)=300
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
C_{\min}=\frac{600}{640000-547600}
=\frac{600}{92400}
=6.49351\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{F}
=6.49351\,\mathrm{mF}.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_{\min}=6.49351\,\mathrm{mF}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces constant power by the constant current
$I=20000/800=25\,\mathrm{A}$ and a linear voltage ramp
$\Delta V=I\Delta t/C=75\,\mathrm{V}$, predicting $V_f=725\,\mathrm{V}$
rather than $721.1103\,\mathrm{V}$. Sentence (ii) uses $C V\Delta V$
or $\tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2$, which are not the stored-energy
difference $\tfrac12 C(V_i^2-V_f^2)$.

The argument never linearizes the converter as a negative incremental
resistance against a regulated source, and never inventories
hard-switching conduction, overlap, or recovery loss.

graderFixtures.proofText: The hole removes $300\,\mathrm{J}$, so $V_f=\sqrt{800^2-2\cdot 300/0.005}=721.1103\,\mathrm{V}$. That misses the $740\,\mathrm{V}$ floor; the same identity gives $C_{\min}=600/(800^2-740^2)=6.49351\,\mathrm{mF}$. The draw is not a constant $25\,\mathrm{A}$ ramp, and the energy is not $C V\Delta V$.
The converter draws a constant current I=20 kW/800 V=25 A, so DeltaV=I t/C=75 V and Vf=725 V. I do not use (1/2)C(Vi^2-Vf^2)=300 J.
The missing energy is C*800*DeltaV, or else (1/2)C(DeltaV)^2. I never write (1/2)C(Vi^2-Vf^2) and I do not accept Vf=721.1103 V or Cmin=6.49351 mF.

PROB:010517.title: Conditioning changes the interval on a triangular support
PROB:010517.objective: Normalize a joint density on a nonrectangular support, derive both conditional densities with parameter-dependent supports, and diagnose dependence through conditional laws, support geometry, and covariance.
PROB:010517.statement:
A random vector $(X,Y)$ has joint density
$$
f_{X,Y}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
C,&0<x<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Find $C$. Derive the marginal densities $f_X$ and $f_Y$, including their
supports, and then derive $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ and
$f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)$ for conditioning values where the relevant marginal
density is positive. Verify directly that each conditional density integrates
to one over its own support.

Compute
$$
\mathbb P(X<Y/2\mid Y=y),\qquad
\mathbb P\!\left(Y<\frac{1+X}{2}\,\middle|\,X=x\right),
$$
for $0<y<1$ and $0<x<1$. Find
$\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]$ and $\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]$, and verify the tower
identity
$$
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]
$$
by explicit integration.

Finally compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$ and prove that $X$ and $Y$ are
not independent in two distinct ways: once from the support or density
factorization, and once from a conditional law or covariance. Explain why a
joint density being constant on its support does not imply independence.
Values assigned to densities on boundary sets of Lebesgue measure zero are
irrelevant.
permittedResults: Tonelli's theorem permits either integration order for a nonnegative joint density.
If $X$ and $Y$ are integrable, then $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]$; independence implies zero covariance whenever these moments exist.
The tower property gives $\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]$ for integrable $X$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Slice the support vertically and horizontally, derive marginals first, then normalize each conditional law and compute its moments.
View the joint law as a uniform point in a triangle, using slice lengths for conditionals while verifying all results by joint-density integrals.

milestones.criterion: States the joint or hierarchical model and carries its exact support, conditioning domain, and normalization through the setup.

Uses the triangular support consistently in every marginal, conditional, expectation, and dependence calculation, and distinguishes a constant density on a nonproduct support from an independent product density.
Completes every requested density normalization, exact probability, moment, tower, transformation, or dependence check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: Uses the joint density itself as a conditional density without dividing by the positive marginal density.
commonErrors.consequence: The alleged conditional density generally does not integrate to one and all derived conditional probabilities or means are invalid.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a density constant on its triangular support makes the coordinates independent.
commonErrors.consequence: The product-support requirement, conditional dependence, and nonzero covariance are all ignored.

hintTree.content: Draw $0<x<y<1$. For fixed $x$, the allowed $y$-interval is $(x,1)$; for fixed $y$, the allowed $x$-interval is $(0,y)$.
After finding the marginals, divide the joint density by $2y$ or $2(1-x)$ and retain the corresponding moving interval.
For dependence, compare the triangular joint support with the rectangular region on which both marginals are positive, and independently compute $\mathbb E[XY]$.

PROB:010517.canonicalSolution:
The support triangle has area $1/2$, so normalization gives
$$
1=C\int_0^1\int_0^y dx\,dy=\frac C2,
\qquad\boxed{C=2}.
$$

For fixed $x\in(0,1)$, the permitted values are $x<y<1$. Hence
$$
\boxed{
f_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
2(1-x),&0<x<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
For fixed $y\in(0,1)$, the permitted values are $0<x<y$. Hence
$$
\boxed{
f_Y(y)=
\begin{cases}
2y,&0<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$

Therefore, for $0<y<1$,
$$
\boxed{
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=
\begin{cases}
1/y,&0<x<y,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}}
$$
and, for $0<x<1$,
$$
\boxed{
f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=
\begin{cases}
1/(1-x),&x<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Indeed,
$$
\int_0^y\frac{dx}{y}=1,
\qquad
\int_x^1\frac{dy}{1-x}=1.
$$
Thus $X\mid(Y=y)$ is uniform on $(0,y)$ and
$Y\mid(X=x)$ is uniform on $(x,1)$. It follows that
$$
\boxed{\mathbb P(X<Y/2\mid Y=y)=\frac12},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\mathbb P\!\left(Y<\frac{1+X}{2}\,\middle|\,X=x\right)
=\frac{(1+x)/2-x}{1-x}=\frac12}.
$$

The two conditional means are
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]=\frac y2},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=\frac{1+x}{2}}.
$$
Also
$$
\mathbb E[X]
=\int_0^1 x\,2(1-x)\,dx
=\frac13.
$$
Using the marginal density of $Y$,
$$
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]
=\int_0^1\frac y2(2y)\,dy
=\int_0^1y^2\,dy
=\frac13
=\mathbb E[X],
$$
which verifies the tower identity directly.

Similarly,
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\int_0^1y(2y)\,dy=\frac23,
$$
and
$$
\mathbb E[XY]
=\int_0^1\int_0^y 2xy\,dx\,dy
=\int_0^1y^3\,dy
=\frac14.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\frac14-\frac13\frac23
=\frac1{36}>0}.
$$
This nonzero covariance already proves dependence.

The support gives a separate proof. Both marginal densities are positive
throughout $(0,1)$, so $f_X(x)f_Y(y)>0$ throughout the square
$(0,1)^2$. But the joint density is zero on the positive-area region
$0<y<x<1$. Thus $f_{X,Y}\ne f_Xf_Y$ almost everywhere, and independence
fails. Equivalently, $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/y$ on $(0,y)$ changes with
$y$ and is not the marginal density $2(1-x)$. Constancy of the joint density
inside a triangle says nothing about factorization across a rectangular
product support.

graderFixtures.proofText: The triangle has area 1/2, so C=2. Its marginals are f_X(x)=2(1-x) and f_Y(y)=2y. Hence X|Y=y is uniform on (0,y), while Y|X=x is uniform on (x,1). Both requested conditional probabilities are 1/2, E[X|Y=y]=y/2, and integrating against 2y gives E[X]=1/3. Also E[Y]=2/3 and E[XY]=1/4, so Cov(X,Y)=1/36. The joint support is triangular rather than the product of marginal supports, so the variables are dependent.
I correctly obtain C=2, f_X(x)=2(1-x), and f_Y(y)=2y, but then set f_{X|Y}(x|y)=2 on 0<x<y because the joint density is 2; I do not divide by f_Y(y).

The normalized joint density is the constant 2 on its support, so X and Y are independent; a constant joint density always factors, and there is no need to compare the triangular support with the marginal supports.

PROB:010518.title: A weighted triangle is not uniform on its conditional slices
PROB:010518.objective: Normalize a linearly weighted joint density, derive both moving-support conditional laws, and detect the error of treating geometric slices as conditionally uniform.
PROB:010518.statement:
A random vector $(X,Y)$ has joint density
$$
f_{X,Y}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
C(x+y),&0<x<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Find $C$. Derive $f_X(x)$, $f_Y(y)$,
$f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$, and $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)$, stating every support
and the conditioning values for which each conditional density is defined.
Verify directly that both conditional densities integrate to one.

Compute exactly
$$
\mathbb P(X<Y/2\mid Y=y)
$$
for $0<y<1$, and
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(
Y<\frac{1+X}{2}\,\middle|\,X=x
\right)
$$
for $0<x<1$. Explain why neither calculation may assume a uniform
conditional distribution merely because the support slice is an interval.

Find $\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]$ and verify
$\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]$ by explicit integration.
Then compute $\mathbb E[Y]$, $\mathbb E[XY]$, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Use either a conditional law or the covariance,
together with the nonrectangular support, to give two valid dependence
diagnostics. Density values on boundary sets may be chosen arbitrarily.
permittedResults: Marginal densities are obtained by integrating the joint density over the support permitted for the other variable.
For integrable $X$, the tower property gives $\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]$.
A nonzero covariance proves dependence whenever the required second mixed moment exists.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the weighted joint density on vertical and horizontal slices, normalize each slice by its marginal mass, then evaluate conditional probabilities and moments.
Scale a fixed-Y slice by u=x/y for the X-given-Y calculations, while deriving the X marginal separately for the reverse conditional law.

milestones.criterion: States the joint or hierarchical model and carries its exact support, conditioning domain, and normalization through the setup.
Carries both the triangular support and the nonconstant weight x+y through normalization, conditioning, exact probabilities, moments, and dependence conclusions.
Completes every requested density normalization, exact probability, moment, tower, transformation, or dependence check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: Treats either conditional law as uniform merely because its support is an interval.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor x+y is discarded, producing wrong conditional probabilities and moments.

commonErrors.description: For fixed x, integrates y from zero to one instead of from x to one.
commonErrors.consequence: The X marginal, the Y-given-X normalizer, and all calculations based on them are invalid.

hintTree.content: Normalize with $\int_0^1\int_0^y C(x+y)\,dx\,dy$. For fixed $x$, remember that $y$ starts at $x$, not at zero.
The two marginals simplify to $3y^2$ and $(1-x)(1+3x)$. Divide by the appropriate one before integrating a conditional probability.
For the first conditional mean, integrate $x\,2(x+y)/(3y^2)$ over $(0,y)$. Then use $f_Y(y)=3y^2$ for the tower check.

PROB:010518.canonicalSolution:
Normalization over the triangular support gives
$$
1=C\int_0^1\int_0^y(x+y)\,dx\,dy.
$$
The inner integral is
$$
\int_0^y(x+y)\,dx=\frac{y^2}{2}+y^2=\frac{3y^2}{2},
$$
so the double integral is $1/2$. Therefore
$$\boxed{C=2}.$$

For $0<y<1$,
$$
f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2(x+y)\,dx
=\boxed{3y^2},
$$
and $f_Y(y)=0$ otherwise. For $0<x<1$,
$$
f_X(x)=\int_x^1 2(x+y)\,dy
=1+2x-3x^2
=\boxed{(1-x)(1+3x)},
$$
and $f_X(x)=0$ otherwise. Both marginals integrate to one.

For $0<y<1$,
$$
\boxed{
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(x+y)}{3y^2},&0<x<y,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Its integral is
$$
\int_0^y\frac{2(x+y)}{3y^2}\,dx
=\frac{2}{3y^2}\left(\frac{y^2}{2}+y^2\right)=1.
$$
For $0<x<1$,
$$
\boxed{
f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(x+y)}{1+2x-3x^2},&x<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Its numerator integrates over $(x,1)$ to
$1+2x-3x^2$, so it also has total mass one.

For the first requested probability,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(X<Y/2\mid Y=y)
&=\int_0^{y/2}\frac{2(x+y)}{3y^2}\,dx\\
&=\frac{(y/2)^2+2y(y/2)}{3y^2}
=\boxed{\frac5{12}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
For the second, write $b=(1+x)/2$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(Y<b\mid X=x)
&=\frac{\int_x^b2(x+y)\,dy}{1+2x-3x^2}\\
&=\frac{(1-x)(1+7x)/4}{(1-x)(1+3x)}
=\boxed{\frac{1+7x}{4(1+3x)}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The density along either slice is proportional to $x+y$, so it is not
constant. The interval geometry alone therefore cannot justify a uniform
conditional law.

The conditional mean of $X$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]
&=\int_0^y x\frac{2(x+y)}{3y^2}\,dx\\
&=\frac{2}{3y^2}\left(\frac{y^3}{3}+\frac{y^3}{2}\right)
=\boxed{\frac{5y}{9}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The marginal calculation gives
$$
\mathbb E[X]
=\int_0^1x(1+2x-3x^2)\,dx
=\boxed{\frac5{12}}.
$$
Directly applying the conditional mean gives the same value:
$$
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]
=\int_0^1\frac{5y}{9}(3y^2)\,dy
=\frac53\int_0^1y^3\,dy
=\frac5{12}.
$$

Also
$$
\mathbb E[Y]
=\int_0^1y(3y^2)\,dy
=\boxed{\frac34}.
$$
Since $\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=5Y/9$,
$$
\mathbb E[XY]
=\mathbb E\!\left[Y\,\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\right]
=\frac59\mathbb E[Y^2].
$$
But
$$
\mathbb E[Y^2]=\int_0^1y^2(3y^2)\,dy=\frac35,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[XY]=\frac13}.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\frac13-\frac5{12}\frac34
=\frac1{48}>0}.
$$
The nonzero covariance proves dependence. Independently, both marginals are
positive throughout $(0,1)$, while the joint density vanishes on the
positive-area half-square $0<y<x<1$. Hence the joint density cannot equal
$f_Xf_Y$ almost everywhere. The changing, nonuniform conditional density
gives the same conclusion.

graderFixtures.proofText: Normalization gives C=2. The marginals are f_Y(y)=3y^2 and f_X(x)=(1-x)(1+3x). Thus f_{X|Y}=2(x+y)/(3y^2) on 0<x<y and f_{Y|X}=2(x+y)/[(1-x)(1+3x)] on x<y<1. The requested probabilities are 5/12 and (1+7x)/(4(1+3x)). Also E[X|Y=y]=5y/9, E[X]=5/12, E[Y]=3/4, E[XY]=1/3, and Cov(X,Y)=1/48, so the variables are dependent.
After correctly finding C=2 and f_Y(y)=3y^2, I say X given Y=y is uniform on (0,y), so P(X<Y/2|Y=y)=1/2 and E[X|Y=y]=y/2; the interval shape makes the conditional law uniform.
For the X marginal I fix x but integrate 2(x+y) from y=0 to y=1, because y always lies between zero and one; I do not impose the joint-support condition y>x.
