PROB:010519.title: A ratio transform turns a dependent triangle into independent coordinates
PROB:010519.objective: Transform a uniform triangular joint law to ratio-height coordinates, derive the image support and Jacobian exactly, and explain why the transformed variables are independent even though the original variables are not.
PROB:010519.statement:
A random vector $(X,Y)$ has joint density
$$
f_{X,Y}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
2,&0<x<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Define
$$
U=\frac XY,\qquad V=Y.
$$
Determine the support of $(U,V)$ by translating the inequalities
$0<X<Y<1$ in both directions. Find the inverse transformation and the
absolute Jacobian determinant required for the density transformation.
Derive the joint density $f_{U,V}$ and both marginal densities.

Prove that $U$ and $V$ are independent. Derive $f_{U\mid V}(u\mid v)$
and interpret the result in terms of the location of $X$ within the interval
$(0,Y)$. Compute exactly
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(U<\frac13,\ V<\frac12\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb P\!\left(U<\frac13\,\middle|\,V<\frac12\right).
$$

Find $\mathbb E[U]$, $\mathbb E[V]$, $\mathbb E[V^2]$, and use
independence together with $X=UV$ and $Y=V$ to compute
$\mathbb E[X]$, $\mathbb E[Y]$, $\mathbb E[XY]$, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Reconcile the independence of $(U,V)$ with the
dependence of $(X,Y)$ using both support geometry and the inverse
transformation. Explain why independence is not automatically preserved when
two new variables are combined to reconstruct the old ones.
permittedResults: If a joint density factors as $f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_U(u)f_V(v)$ almost everywhere, then $U$ and $V$ are independent.
For independent integrable variables, $\mathbb E[a(U)b(V)]=\mathbb E[a(U)]\mathbb E[b(V)]$ whenever the product is integrable.
Independence of $U$ and $V$ does not imply independence of arbitrary functions that each depend on both variables.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the inverse-map density theorem, then obtain probabilities and moments from the factorized transformed density.
Interpret U as relative position conditional on Y and V as scale, then verify the geometric intuition through the Jacobian and marginal densities.

milestones.criterion: States the joint or hierarchical model and carries its exact support, conditioning domain, and normalization through the setup.

Transforms both density and support with the inverse Jacobian, proves independence only after exact factorization, and correctly distinguishes independent ratio-scale coordinates from the dependent reconstructed coordinates.
Completes every requested density normalization, exact probability, moment, tower, transformation, or dependence check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes x=uv and y=v into the old density but omits the inverse Jacobian factor v or replaces it by 1/v.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed density is not normalized and all resulting marginals, probabilities, and moments are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that X and Y are independent merely because U and V are independent.
commonErrors.consequence: The shared factor V in X=UV and Y=V, the triangular support, and the nonzero covariance are ignored.

hintTree.content: The inverse map is $x=uv$, $y=v$. Translate $0<x<y<1$ after substituting these formulas.
Compute $\left|\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)\right|$ from the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}v&u\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
After factorization, use $X=UV$, $Y=V$, and $XY=UV^2$ to obtain the original moments without returning to a triangular double integral.

PROB:010519.canonicalSolution:
Because $0<X<Y$, division by the positive variable $Y$ gives
$$
0<U=\frac XY<1.
$$
Also $V=Y$ satisfies $0<V<1$. Conversely, if $0<u<1$ and $0<v<1$,
then $x=uv$ and $y=v$ satisfy $0<x<y<1$. Thus the image support is the
open unit square
$$
\boxed{0<u<1,\qquad 0<v<1}.
$$

The inverse transformation is
$$
\boxed{x=uv,\qquad y=v}.
$$
Its derivative matrix and absolute determinant are
$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
v&u\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boxed{\left|\det\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=v}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
f_{U,V}(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
2v,&0<u<1,\ 0<v<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
The Jacobian factor is essential: it accounts for the fact that a fixed
increment in $u$ corresponds to an $x$-increment of size $v$.

Integrating gives
$$
\boxed{
f_U(u)=
\begin{cases}
1,&0<u<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
f_V(v)=
\begin{cases}
2v,&0<v<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
On the unit-square support,
$$
f_{U,V}(u,v)=2v=(1)(2v)=f_U(u)f_V(v),
$$
so
$$\boxed{U\ \text{and}\ V\ \text{are independent}.}
$$
For every $0<v<1$,
$$
\boxed{f_{U\mid V}(u\mid v)=1,\qquad 0<u<1}.
$$
Thus, conditional on $Y=v$, the relative position $X/Y$ is uniform on
$(0,1)$ and does not depend on the scale $v$.

The requested joint probability factors:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P\!\left(U<\frac13,V<\frac12\right)
&=\int_0^{1/3}\int_0^{1/2}2v\,dv\,du\\
&=\frac13\left[\vphantom{\frac12}v^2\right]_0^{1/2}
=\boxed{\frac1{12}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Also
$$
\mathbb P(V<1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}2v\,dv=\frac14,
$$
hence
$$
\boxed{
\mathbb P\!\left(U<\frac13\,\middle|\,V<\frac12\right)
=\frac{1/12}{1/4}
=\frac13}.
$$
This also follows immediately from independence.

The transformed moments are
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[U]=\int_0^1u\,du=\frac12},
$$
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[V]=\int_0^1v(2v)\,dv=\frac23},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[V^2]=\int_0^1v^2(2v)\,dv=\frac12}.
$$
Since $X=UV$ and $U,V$ are independent,
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[X]
=\mathbb E[U]\mathbb E[V]
=\frac12\frac23
=\frac13}.
$$
Because $Y=V$,
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[Y]=\frac23}.
$$
Moreover $XY=UV^2$, so
$$
\boxed{\mathbb E[XY]
=\mathbb E[U]\mathbb E[V^2]
=\frac12\frac12
=\frac14}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\frac14-\frac13\frac23
=\frac1{36}>0}.
$$
The original variables are consequently dependent.

There is no contradiction. The transformed coordinates separate relative
position from scale: $U$ is uniform and independent of $V$. But the inverse
map reconstructs
$$
X=UV,\qquad Y=V,
$$
so both original coordinates contain the same factor $V$. Independence of
$U$ and $V$ does not imply independence of $UV$ and $V$. Geometrically,
$(U,V)$ has a rectangular support, whereas $(X,Y)$ has the nonproduct
triangle $0<x<y<1$.

graderFixtures.proofText: The inverse map is x=uv, y=v, its absolute Jacobian is v, and the image support is the unit square. Thus f_{U,V}=2v, with f_U=1 and f_V=2v, so U and V are independent and U|V=v is uniform. The requested probabilities are 1/12 and 1/3. Also E[U]=1/2, E[V]=2/3, and E[V^2]=1/2, giving E[X]=1/3, E[Y]=2/3, E[XY]=1/4, and Cov(X,Y)=1/36. X and Y remain dependent because X=UV and Y=V share V and have triangular support.
The inverse is x=uv and y=v, so I substitute into the original constant density and obtain f_{U,V}(u,v)=2 on the unit square; no Jacobian factor is needed because the transformation is one-to-one.
Using the correct Jacobian, I obtain f_{U,V}(u,v)=2v=f_U(u)f_V(v), so U and V are independent. Therefore X=UV and Y=V must also be independent because they are functions of independent variables.

PROB:010520.title: Continuous Bayes must reverse a parameter-dependent support
PROB:010520.objective: Derive a predictive density and posterior law in a hierarchical continuous model while preserving the likelihood height, reversing the support correctly, and checking posterior moments against prior and predictive identities.
PROB:010520.statement:
Let
$$
X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1),
$$
and, conditional on $X=x$, let
$$
Y\mid(X=x)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,x).
$$
Write the conditional density $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)$ with its complete
support. Derive the joint density $f_{X,Y}$ and verify that it integrates to
one even though it is unbounded near part of the boundary.

Find the predictive or marginal density $f_Y(y)$, including its support,
and verify that it integrates to one. For an observed value $0<y<1$, use
continuous Bayes' rule to derive $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$. State the posterior
support carefully and verify its normalization directly.

Compute exactly
$$
\mathbb P(X>\sqrt y\mid Y=y),
$$
and interpret $\sqrt y$ as a posterior quantile. Find
$$
\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E[X^2\mid Y=y].
$$
Use the predictive density to verify explicitly that
$$
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X].
$$
Finally compute $\mathbb E[Y]$ in two ways—once from the hierarchy and once
from $f_Y$—and compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Explain why the word
“uniform” in the sampling model does not make the posterior uniform in
$x$.
permittedResults: A conditional uniform law on $(0,x)$ has density $1/x$ on that interval, not density one.
For integrable variables, $\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]$ and $\mathbb E[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb E[Y]$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build the joint density from prior times likelihood, integrate over compatible latent values for the predictive density, then normalize with continuous Bayes.
Draw the triangle 0<y<x<1, use horizontal slices for the posterior, and verify the resulting law through posterior and tower identities.

milestones.criterion: States the joint or hierarchical model and carries its exact support, conditioning domain, and normalization through the setup.
Reverses the parameter-dependent sampling support correctly and carries the nonconstant likelihood height through the joint, predictive, posterior, probability, and moment calculations.
Completes every requested density normalization, exact probability, moment, tower, transformation, or dependence check with coherent notation.

commonErrors.description: After observing y, integrates the latent variable x over all of (0,1) instead of the compatible interval (y,1).
commonErrors.consequence: Impossible values x<y receive posterior mass, and the 1/x normalizer may even diverge.

commonErrors.description: Treats the conditional uniform density on (0,x) as having height one and therefore declares the posterior uniform on (y,1).
commonErrors.consequence: The likelihood factor 1/x is lost, so posterior probabilities, quantiles, and moments are wrong.

hintTree.content: The joint support is $0<y<x<1$. After observing $Y=y$, reverse this inequality to obtain $y<x<1$.
Integrating $1/x$ from $x=y$ to $x=1$ gives the predictive normalizer $\log(1/y)$.
In posterior moments, the factor $x$ or $x^2$ cancels part of the posterior's $1/x$ factor. For the tower check, multiply by $f_Y(y)=\log(1/y)$.

PROB:010520.canonicalSolution:
The prior density is
$$
f_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
1,&0<x<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
For a fixed $x\in(0,1)$, the conditional sampling density is
$$
\boxed{
f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=
\begin{cases}
1/x,&0<y<x,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Consequently,
$$
\boxed{
f_{X,Y}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
1/x,&0<y<x<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Although $1/x$ is unbounded as $x\downarrow0$, the narrowing support makes
the joint density integrable:
$$
\int_0^1\int_0^x\frac1x\,dy\,dx
=\int_0^1 1\,dx
=1.
$$

For a fixed $0<y<1$, the joint-support condition requires $y<x<1$.
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
f_Y(y)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\int_y^1\frac{dx}{x}
=\log(1/y),&0<y<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
This is a probability density because
$$
\int_0^1\log(1/y)\,dy=1.
$$

Continuous Bayes' rule now gives, for $0<y<1$,
$$
\boxed{
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{x\log(1/y)},&y<x<1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}}
$$
Its normalization is
$$
\int_y^1\frac{dx}{x\log(1/y)}
=\frac{\log(1/y)}{\log(1/y)}
=1.
$$
The lower limit $x=y$ is dictated by the sampling support: a latent interval
$(0,x)$ cannot produce an observation larger than $x$.

Since $y<\sqrt y<1$ for $0<y<1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(X>\sqrt y\mid Y=y)
&=\int_{\sqrt y}^1\frac{dx}{x\log(1/y)}\\
&=\frac{\log(1/\sqrt y)}{\log(1/y)}
=\boxed{\frac12}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $\sqrt y$ is a posterior median.

The posterior mean is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]
&=\int_y^1x\frac{dx}{x\log(1/y)}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{1-y}{\log(1/y)}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Similarly,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X^2\mid Y=y]
&=\int_y^1x^2\frac{dx}{x\log(1/y)}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{1-y^2}{2\log(1/y)}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
For example, the posterior variance could be recovered as
$$
\frac{1-y^2}{2\log(1/y)}
-\left(\frac{1-y}{\log(1/y)}\right)^2.
$$

The posterior mean passes the tower check:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]
&=\int_0^1
\frac{1-y}{\log(1/y)}
\log(1/y)\,dy\\
&=\int_0^1(1-y)\,dy
=\frac12
=\mathbb E[X].
\end{aligned}
$$

Conditionally, a uniform variable on $(0,x)$ has mean $x/2$. Hence
$$
\mathbb E[Y]
=\mathbb E[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]
=\mathbb E[X/2]
=\boxed{\frac14}.
$$
The predictive density gives the same answer:
$$
\mathbb E[Y]
=\int_0^1y\log(1/y)\,dy
=\boxed{\frac14}.
$$

Finally,
$$
\mathbb E[XY]
=\mathbb E[X\,\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]
=\mathbb E[X^2/2]
=\frac12\cdot\frac13
=\frac16.
$$
Since $\mathbb E[X]=1/2$ and $\mathbb E[Y]=1/4$,
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=\frac16-\frac12\frac14
=\frac1{24}>0}.
$$
Thus $X$ and $Y$ are dependent.

The sampling density is uniform in $y$ after $x$ is fixed, but its height is
$1/x$ and its support also depends on $x$. Once $y$ is observed, both facts
act as a likelihood for $x$. The posterior is therefore proportional to
$1/x$ on $(y,1)$, not uniform on that interval.

graderFixtures.proofText: The likelihood is 1/x on 0<y<x<1, so the joint density is 1/x there. Integrating over x from y to 1 gives f_Y(y)=log(1/y), and Bayes gives f_{X|Y}(x|y)=1/[x log(1/y)] on y<x<1. It integrates to one, P(X>sqrt(y)|Y=y)=1/2, E[X|Y=y]=(1-y)/log(1/y), and E[X^2|Y=y]=(1-y^2)/(2log(1/y)). Integrating the posterior mean against f_Y recovers E[X]=1/2. Both hierarchical and predictive calculations give E[Y]=1/4, and Cov(X,Y)=1/24.
The likelihood is 1/x, but after observing Y=y I normalize it over every prior value 0<x<1. The prior support does not change when data are observed, so values x<y remain possible.
Because Y given X=x is uniform, its likelihood is constant in x. On the correct posterior support y<x<1 I therefore use f_{X|Y}(x|y)=1/(1-y), making the posterior uniform.

QM:010117.title: A qutrit Born audit of A: eigenvalues (−a, 0, 2a) and collapse of the zero outcome to |2⟩
QM:010117.objective: For |ψ⟩=(|1⟩+2|2⟩+i|3⟩)/√6 and A with A|1⟩=−a|1⟩, A|2⟩=0, A|3⟩=2a|3⟩ prove the Born weights (1/6, 2/3, 1/6), ⟨A⟩=a/6, ⟨A²⟩=5a²/6, Var(A)=29a²/36, and that outcome 0 collapses the state to |2⟩.
QM:010117.statement:
Let $\{|1\rangle,|2\rangle,|3\rangle\}$ be an orthonormal basis of a
qutrit, and let
\[
|\psi\rangle=\frac{|1\rangle+2|2\rangle+i|3\rangle}{\sqrt{6}}.
\]
Let $A$ be the Hermitian observable diagonal in this basis with
\[
A|1\rangle=-a|1\rangle,\qquad
A|2\rangle=0,\qquad
A|3\rangle=2a|3\rangle,
\]
where $a>0$ is a fixed real constant. Do not replace the three-outcome
projective measurement by an uncertainty-domain Gaussian equality case,
an angle-momentum commutator trap, a two-party entangled state, or a
no-signaling argument.

1. Verify that $|\psi\rangle$ is normalized. Compute the Born
   probabilities of the three eigenvalues of $A$ and prove
   \[
   P(-a)=\frac16,\qquad
   P(0)=\frac23,\qquad
   P(2a)=\frac16.
   \]

2. Compute the first two moments and the variance, and prove
   \[
   \langle A\rangle=\frac a6,\qquad
   \langle A^2\rangle=\frac{5a^2}{6},\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(A)=\frac{29a^2}{36}.
   \]

3. State the post-measurement state if the outcome $0$ is obtained.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the coefficient $i$ makes $P(2a)$ vanish,
   or the Born weight of $|2\rangle$ is the amplitude $2/\sqrt{6}$
   rather than its modulus squared”; (ii) “the variance equals
   $\langle A^2\rangle=5a^2/6$, so the subtraction of
   $\langle A\rangle^2$ may be omitted.”
permittedResults: $\langle A\rangle=(-a)(1/6)+(2a)(1/6)=a/6$ and $\langle A^2\rangle=a^2(1/6)+4a^2(1/6)=5a^2/6$. Subtracting $(a/6)^2$ produces $29a^2/36$. Outcome $0$ projects onto $|2\rangle$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read the three expansion coefficients in the eigenbasis of A, square their moduli, and average the spectrum and its square against those weights.
Form Var(A)=⟨A²⟩−⟨A⟩² over the common denominator 36, then name the unique eigenstate belonging to the observed eigenvalue 0.

milestones.criterion: Produces the Born weights (1/6, 2/3, 1/6) and the collapse of outcome 0 onto |2⟩.
Reports ⟨A⟩=a/6, ⟨A²⟩=5a²/6, and Var(A)=29a²/36.
Rejects an amplitude-as-probability reading or a variance that omits ⟨A⟩², and refuses reserved uncertainty, angle-momentum, or entanglement substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the Born weight of |2⟩ as the amplitude 2/√6, or claims that the factor i makes P(2a) vanish, and never reports the triple (1/6, 2/3, 1/6).
commonErrors.consequence: The required probabilities (1/6, 2/3, 1/6) and every subsequent moment are lost.

commonErrors.description: Identifies Var(A) with ⟨A²⟩=5a²/6 and omits the subtraction of ⟨A⟩²=(a/6)².
commonErrors.consequence: The required variance 29a²/36 is replaced by the raw second moment 5a²/6.

hintTree.content: The three computational coefficients already sit in the eigenbasis of $A$. Born weights are moduli squared; $|i|^2=1$.
The eigenvalue attached to $|2\rangle$ is $0$, so that channel contributes to $\langle A^2\rangle$ only through a zero term, but it dominates the probability.
Write $\operatorname{Var}(A)$ over a common denominator $36$: $5a^2/6=30a^2/36$ and $(a/6)^2=a^2/36$.

QM:010117.canonicalSolution:
The squared norm of the un-normalized coefficient triple $(1,2,i)$ is
\[
|1|^2+|2|^2+|i|^2=1+4+1=6,
\]
so $|\psi\rangle$ is already normalized.
\[
\boxed{|\psi\rangle\text{ normalized}}.
\]

The observable $A$ is diagonal in the given basis, so the Born weights
are the moduli of the expansion coefficients:
\begin{align*}
P(-a)&=|c_1|^2=\frac1{6},\\
P(0)&=|c_2|^2=\frac4{6}=\frac23,\\
P(2a)&=|c_3|^2=\Bigl|\frac{i}{\sqrt{6}}\Bigr|^2=\frac1{6}.
\end{align*}
The imaginary unit contributes only a phase.
\[
\boxed{P(-a)=1/6,\;P(0)=2/3,\;P(2a)=1/6}.
\]

The first moment is the eigenvalue average
\[
\langle A\rangle
=(-a)\cdot\frac16+0\cdot\frac23+(2a)\cdot\frac16
=\frac{-a+2a}{6}
=\frac a6.
\]
The second moment uses the squared spectrum $\bigl(a^2,0,4a^2\bigr)$:
\[
\langle A^2\rangle
=a^2\cdot\frac16+4a^2\cdot\frac16
=\frac{5a^2}{6}.
\]
The variance subtracts the squared mean,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(A)
=\frac{5a^2}{6}-\Bigl(\frac a6\Bigr)^2
=\frac{30a^2}{36}-\frac{a^2}{36}
=\frac{29a^2}{36}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle A\rangle=a/6,\;
\langle A^2\rangle=5a^2/6,\;
\operatorname{Var}(A)=29a^2/36}.
\]

The eigenvalue $0$ is nondegenerate and belongs to $|2\rangle$. A
projective measurement with that outcome therefore collapses $|\psi\rangle$
onto $|2\rangle$ (the global phase of $c_2$ may be dropped).
\[
\boxed{\text{outcome }0\;\Rightarrow\;|2\rangle}.
\]

Sentence (i) either discards the third Born weight because of the factor
$i$ or reports an amplitude as if it were a probability; both destroy
the triple $(1/6,2/3,1/6)$. Sentence (ii) identifies the variance with
the raw second moment and never produces $29a^2/36$. The construction
is a single-system three-outcome projective measurement; it is not an
uncertainty-domain Gaussian equality, not an angle-momentum trap, and
not a two-party entanglement or no-signaling argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Born weights are $P(-a)=1/6$, $P(0)=2/3$, $P(2a)=1/6$. The moments are $\langle A\rangle=a/6$ and $\langle A^2\rangle=5a^2/6$, so $\operatorname{Var}(A)=29a^2/36$. Outcome $0$ collapses the state to $|2\rangle$.
The Born weight of |2⟩ is the amplitude 2/√6, or the factor i makes P(2a) vanish. I do not report the probability triple (1/6, 2/3, 1/6).
The variance equals ⟨A²⟩=5a²/6. I omit the subtraction of ⟨A⟩² and I never obtain Var(A)=29a²/36.

QM:010118.title: Postselect the plane spanned by u and v, then name the normalized complement
QM:010118.objective: For ψ=(1,1,1)/√3 and the orthonormal pair u=(1,0,1)/√2, v=(1,−2,−1)/√6 prove P(S)=8/9 with normalized postselected state (1,1,2)/√6, and that the complement has probability 1/9 with normalized state (1,1,−1)/√3.
QM:010118.statement:
Work in $\mathbb{C}^3$ with the computational inner product. Let
\[
|\psi\rangle=\frac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt{3}}
\]
and let $S$ be the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the orthonormal
pair
\[
|u\rangle=\frac{(1,0,1)}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
|v\rangle=\frac{(1,-2,-1)}{\sqrt{6}}.
\]
Let $P_S=|u\rangle\langle u|+|v\rangle\langle v|$ be the orthogonal
projector onto $S$, and let $S^\perp$ be the orthogonal complement.
Do not replace the single-system subspace measurement by a two-party
entangled state, a pair of measurement bases used to send a
faster-than-light message, or a spin-addition Clebsch–Gordan
construction.

1. Verify that $\{|u\rangle,|v\rangle\}$ is orthonormal. Compute the
   subspace detection probability and prove $P(S)=8/9$.

2. Construct the (unnormalized) postselected vector $P_S|\psi\rangle$
   and prove that its normalized form is
   \[
   \frac{P_S|\psi\rangle}{\|P_S|\psi\rangle\|}
   =\frac{(1,1,2)}{\sqrt{6}}.
   \]

3. Compute the complement probability $P(S^\perp)=1/9$ and prove that
   the normalized state in $S^\perp$ compatible with the inner product
   $\langle w|\psi\rangle>0$ is $(1,1,-1)/\sqrt{3}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$S$ is spanned by the single vector
   $|u\rangle$, so $P(S)=|\langle u|\psi\rangle|^2=2/3$ and the
   postselected state is $|u\rangle$”; (ii) “the normalized
   postselected state is $(1,1,2)/3$, or the complement direction is
   not $(1,1,-1)$.”
permittedResults: $\langle u|\psi\rangle=2/\sqrt{6}$ and $\langle v|\psi\rangle=-2/\sqrt{18}$, so $|\langle u|\psi\rangle|^2=2/3$ and $|\langle v|\psi\rangle|^2=2/9$. Their sum is $8/9$.

$P_S|\psi\rangle\parallel(1,1,2)$ with Euclidean length $\sqrt{P(S)}\,\sqrt{6}$ after scaling, hence the unit vector $(1,1,2)/\sqrt{6}$. The cross product $(1,0,1)\times(1,-2,-1)$ is parallel to $(1,1,-1)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the two overlaps against the given orthonormal pair, add the Born weights, and expand P_S|ψ⟩ as a linear combination of u and v.
Read the complement direction from the cross product (1,0,1)×(1,−2,−1), normalize by √3, and check that |⟨w|ψ⟩|²=1/9.

milestones.criterion: Verifies orthonormality of {u, v} and reports P(S)=8/9 together with the normalized postselected state (1,1,2)/√6.
Reports P(S^⊥)=1/9 and the normalized complement (1,1,−1)/√3.
Rejects a single-vector subspace or a /3 renormalization of (1,1,2), and refuses reserved entanglement, no-signaling, or spin-addition substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats S as the span of the single vector |u⟩, reports P(S)=|⟨u|ψ⟩|²=2/3, and takes the postselected state to be |u⟩.
commonErrors.consequence: The required probability 8/9 and the postselected direction (1,1,2) are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes the normalized postselected state as (1,1,2)/3, or names a complement direction other than (1,1,−1)/√3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required unit vector (1,1,2)/√6 and the complement (1,1,−1)/√3 are not produced.

hintTree.content: Check $u\cdot v=(1+0-1)/\sqrt{12}=0$ before computing overlaps. Both vectors are already unit length.
Add the two Born weights $2/3$ and $2/9$; do not square the sum of the inner products.
A vector orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$ is the ordinary cross product of $(1,0,1)$ and $(1,-2,-1)$, which is $2(1,1,-1)$. Normalize by $\sqrt{3}$.

QM:010118.canonicalSolution:
Direct dots give
\[
|u|^2=\frac{1+0+1}{2}=1,\qquad
|v|^2=\frac{1+4+1}{6}=1,\qquad
u\cdot v=\frac{1+0-1}{\sqrt{12}}=0,
\]
so $\{|u\rangle,|v\rangle\}$ is orthonormal and $P_S$ is the orthogonal
projector onto their span.
\[
\boxed{\{u,v\}\text{ orthonormal}}.
\]

The overlaps with $|\psi\rangle$ are
\begin{align*}
\langle u|\psi\rangle
&=\frac{1+0+1}{\sqrt{6}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}},\qquad
|\langle u|\psi\rangle|^2=\frac46=\frac23,\\
\langle v|\psi\rangle
&=\frac{1-2-1}{\sqrt{18}}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}},\qquad
|\langle v|\psi\rangle|^2=\frac{4}{18}=\frac29.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\[
P(S)=\frac23+\frac29=\frac89.
\]
\[
\boxed{P(S)=8/9}.
\]

The unnormalized postselected vector is
\begin{align*}
P_S|\psi\rangle
&=\langle u|\psi\rangle\,|u\rangle+\langle v|\psi\rangle\,|v\rangle
=\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot\frac{(1,0,1)}{\sqrt{2}}
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}\cdot\frac{(1,-2,-1)}{\sqrt{6}}\\
&=\frac{(1,0,1)}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{(1,-2,-1)}{3\sqrt{3}}
=\frac{(2,2,4)}{3\sqrt{3}}
=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}(1,1,2).
\end{align*}
Its Euclidean length is
\[
\Bigl\|\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}(1,1,2)\Bigr\|
=\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3\sqrt{3}}
=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}
=\sqrt{\frac89},
\]
so the normalized postselected state is $(1,1,2)/\sqrt{6}$.
\[
\boxed{\text{postselected }(1,1,2)/\sqrt{6}}.
\]

The complement probability is $1-8/9=1/9$. A Cartesian vector
orthogonal to both generators is
\[
(1,0,1)\times(1,-2,-1)=(2,2,-2)=2(1,1,-1).
\]
The unit vector in $S^\perp$ with positive overlap against $|\psi\rangle$
is therefore
\[
|w\rangle=\frac{(1,1,-1)}{\sqrt{3}},
\qquad
\langle w|\psi\rangle=\frac{1+1-1}{3}=\frac13,
\qquad
\bigl|\langle w|\psi\rangle\bigr|^2=\frac19.
\]
\[
\boxed{P(S^\perp)=1/9,\;
\text{complement }(1,1,-1)/\sqrt{3}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the $v$-channel and reports $P(S)=2/3$ with
postselected state $|u\rangle$. Sentence (ii) renormalizes $(1,1,2)$
by $3$ rather than $\sqrt{6}$, or names a complement direction other
than $(1,1,-1)$. The measurement is a single-system rank-two projector;
it is not a two-party entangled state, not a no-signaling argument,
and not a coupled spin basis.

graderFixtures.proofText: The subspace probability is $P(S)=8/9$ and the normalized postselected state is $(1,1,2)/\sqrt{6}$. The complement has probability $1/9$ and normalized state $(1,1,-1)/\sqrt{3}$.
S is spanned by the single vector |u⟩, so P(S)=|⟨u|ψ⟩|²=2/3 and the postselected state is |u⟩. I do not add the v-channel and I do not accept P(S)=8/9.
The normalized postselected state is (1,1,2)/3, or the complement direction is not (1,1,−1)/√3. I never report (1,1,2)/√6.

QM:010219.title: Two stationary states of the infinite well: energy moments, a midpoint density, and the 3E₁ clock
QM:010219.objective: For the infinite well on 0<x<L with ψ=(√3/2)φ₁+(1/2)φ₂ prove energy weights 3/4 and 1/4, ⟨E⟩=7E₁/4, ΔE=3√3 E₁/4, the interference density (2/L)[3sin²(πx/L)/4+sin²(2πx/L)/4+(√3/2)sin(πx/L)sin(2πx/L)cos(3E₁t/ℏ)], the midpoint value 3/(2L), and recurrence 2πℏ/(3E₁)=4mL²/(3πℏ).
QM:010219.statement:
A particle is confined to the infinite square well $0<x<L$, with
stationary states
\[
\phi_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\Bigl(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Bigr),\qquad
E_n=n^2 E_1,\qquad
E_1=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}.
\]
At $t=0$ the state is the two-mode superposition
\[
\psi(x,0)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\phi_1(x)+\frac12\,\phi_2(x).
\]
Work in the Schrödinger picture with the probability density
$|\psi(x,t)|^2$. Do not replace the density by a Heisenberg-picture
operator time dependence, a driven dilation audit of $\langle x^2\rangle$,
a symmetric finite well, or a Coulomb problem with an inverse-square
core.

1. Read off the energy measurement probabilities and prove
   \[
   P(E_1)=\frac34,\qquad P(E_2)=\frac14,\qquad
   \langle E\rangle=\frac{7E_1}{4},\qquad
   \Delta E=\frac{3\sqrt{3}\,E_1}{4}.
   \]

2. Expand $|\psi(x,t)|^2$ and prove
   \[
   |\psi(x,t)|^2
   =\frac2L\Biggl[
   \frac34\sin^2\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
   +\frac14\sin^2\Bigl(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
   +\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
   \sin\Bigl(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
   \cos\Bigl(\frac{3E_1 t}{\hbar}\Bigr)
   \Biggr].
   \]

3. Evaluate the density at the midpoint $x=L/2$ and prove that it
   equals the time-independent value $3/(2L)$. Identify the
   recurrence time of the density as
   \[
   T=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{3E_1}=\frac{4mL^2}{3\pi\hbar}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the well is linear, so $E_2=2E_1$,
   $\langle E\rangle=5E_1/4$, and the cosine oscillates at $E_1/\hbar$”;
   (ii) “$\phi_2(L/2)$ is nonzero, so the midpoint density is not
   $3/(2L)$, or the recurrence is $2\pi\hbar/E_1$.”

The cross coefficient is $2\cdot(\sqrt{3}/2)\cdot(1/2)=\sqrt{3}/2$. At $x=L/2$ one has $\sin\pi=0$, and $E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$ converts $2\pi\hbar/(3E_1)$ into $4mL^2/(3\pi\hbar)$.

Evaluate the density at the node of φ₂ and convert 2πℏ/(3E₁) with E₁=π² ℏ²/(2m L²).

Produces the interference density with cos(3E₁ t/ℏ), the midpoint value 3/(2L), and the recurrence 2πℏ/(3E₁)=4mL²/(3πℏ).

hintTree.content: The infinite-well spectrum is quadratic: $E_2=4E_1$, not $2E_1$. Square the amplitudes $\sqrt{3}/2$ and $1/2$ first.
The relative phase is $\exp\bigl(-i(E_2-E_1)t/\hbar\bigr)=\exp(-i 3E_1 t/\hbar)$. The real part is a cosine.
At $x=L/2$ the second mode has a node. Only the $\phi_1$ diagonal term survives, giving $(3/4)\cdot(2/L)=3/(2L)$.

QM:010219.canonicalSolution:
The initial state is already expanded in the energy basis, with
real amplitudes $c_1=\sqrt{3}/2$ and $c_2=1/2$. The energy
measurement weights are therefore
\[
P(E_1)=\frac34,\qquad P(E_2)=\frac14.
\]
Because $E_n=n^2 E_1$ one has $E_2=4E_1$, so
\[
\langle E\rangle
=\frac34 E_1+\frac14\cdot 4E_1
=\frac{7E_1}{4}.
\]
The second moment is
\[
\langle E^2\rangle
=\frac34 E_1^2+\frac14\cdot 16E_1^2
=\frac{19E_1^2}{4},
\]
and the variance is
\[
(\Delta E)^2
=\frac{19E_1^2}{4}-\Bigl(\frac{7E_1}{4}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{76E_1^2-49E_1^2}{16}
=\frac{27E_1^2}{16}.
\]
Hence $\Delta E=(3\sqrt{3}\,E_1)/4$.
\[
\boxed{P=(3/4,1/4),\;
\langle E\rangle=7E_1/4,\;
\Delta E=3\sqrt{3}\,E_1/4}.
\]

The time-evolved wavefunction is
\[
\psi(x,t)
=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\phi_1 e^{-iE_1 t/\hbar}
+\frac12\phi_2 e^{-i4E_1 t/\hbar}.
\]
Expanding $|\psi|^2$ produces the two diagonal terms and the
interference
\[
2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\frac12\,
\phi_1\phi_2\cos\Bigl(\frac{(E_2-E_1)t}{\hbar}\Bigr)
=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\phi_1\phi_2\cos\Bigl(\frac{3E_1 t}{\hbar}\Bigr).
\]
Inserting $\phi_n=\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L)$ and factoring $2/L$
yields the stated density
\[
|\psi(x,t)|^2
=\frac2L\Biggl[
\frac34\sin^2\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
+\frac14\sin^2\Bigl(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
\sin\Bigl(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\Bigr)
\cos\Bigl(\frac{3E_1 t}{\hbar}\Bigr)
\Biggr].
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{density with }\cos(3E_1 t/\hbar)}.
\]

At the midpoint $x=L/2$ one has $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\sin\pi=0$, so both the $\phi_2$ diagonal term and the interference
vanish. The density collapses to
\[
|\psi(L/2,t)|^2
=\frac2L\cdot\frac34
=\frac{3}{2L}.
\]
The cosine is $2\pi$-periodic in the argument $3E_1 t/\hbar$, so the
smallest positive recurrence time of the density is
\[
T=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{3E_1}.
\]
Substituting $E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$ gives
\[
T
=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{3}\cdot\frac{2mL^2}{\pi^2\hbar^2}
=\frac{4mL^2}{3\pi\hbar}.
\]
\[
\boxed{|\psi(L/2,t)|^2=3/(2L),\;
T=2\pi\hbar/(3E_1)=4mL^2/(3\pi\hbar)}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the quadratic spectrum by a linear one and
destroys $\langle E\rangle$, $\Delta E$, and the beat frequency.
Sentence (ii) either keeps a spurious $\phi_2$ contribution at the
midpoint or drops the factor $3$ from the recurrence. The argument
is a Schrödinger-picture two-mode density of the infinite well; it
is not a Heisenberg dilation audit, not a symmetric finite well, and
not a Coulomb problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: The energy weights are $3/4$ and $1/4$, with $\langle E\rangle=7E_1/4$ and $\Delta E=3\sqrt{3}\,E_1/4$. The density is the stated $(2/L)$ combination with $\cos(3E_1 t/\hbar)$. At $x=L/2$ the density equals $3/(2L)$, and the recurrence is $2\pi\hbar/(3E_1)=4mL^2/(3\pi\hbar)$.
The well is linear, so E₂=2E₁, ⟨E⟩=5E₁/4, and the cosine oscillates at E₁/ℏ. I do not accept ⟨E⟩=7E₁/4 or the beat 3E₁/ℏ.
φ₂(L/2) is nonzero, so the midpoint density is not 3/(2L), or the recurrence is 2πℏ/E₁. I never report 3/(2L) and 2πℏ/(3E₁)=4mL²/(3πℏ).

QM:010220.title: One bound state of −α δ(x): the derivative jump, the exponential tails, and ⟨|x|⟩
QM:010220.objective: For V=−α δ(x) prove κ=mα/ℏ², the sole bound energy E=−mα²/(2ℏ²), the normalized wavefunction √κ e^{−κ|x|}, the derivative jump −2κ ψ(0), the tail probability P(|x|>a)=e^{−2κa}, and ⟨|x|⟩=1/(2κ).
QM:010220.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves on the line under the attractive delta
potential $V(x)=-\alpha\delta(x)$ with $\alpha>0$. Bound states satisfy
$E<0$. Write $\kappa=\sqrt{-2mE}/\hbar>0$ and work with even decaying
exponentials on each half-line. Do not replace the contact potential
by a symmetric finite well, a pair of wall-avoiding finite-well bound
states, a Coulomb problem, or a repulsive inverse-square core.

1. Integrate the stationary Schrödinger equation across an
   infinitesimal interval about the origin and prove the jump
   \[
   \psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)=-\frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0).
   \]
   Matching an even decaying wavefunction $\psi(x)\propto e^{-\kappa|x|}$
   to this jump, prove that there is a single bound value
   \[
   \kappa=\frac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2},\qquad
   E=-\frac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}.
   \]

2. Normalize the even bound state and prove
   \[
   \psi(x)=\sqrt{\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|}.
   \]
   In particular the jump may be rewritten as
   $\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)=-2\kappa\psi(0)$.

3. Compute the tail probability and the mean absolute displacement:
   \[
   P(|x|>a)=e^{-2\kappa a}\qquad(a>0),\qquad
   \langle|x|\rangle=\frac{1}{2\kappa}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the even bound state is normalized as
   $\sqrt{2\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|}$, the one-sided exponential
   convention”; (ii) “the jump is $-\kappa\psi(0)$, so
   $\kappa=2m\alpha/\hbar^2$ and $E=-2m\alpha^2/\hbar^2$, or the tail
   is $e^{-\kappa a}$.”
permittedResults: The jump $-2\kappa=-(2m\alpha/\hbar^2)$ forces $\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2$ and $E=-\hbar^2\kappa^2/(2m)=-m\alpha^2/(2\hbar^2)$. There is no odd bound state, because an odd wavefunction vanishes at the origin and feels no delta.
With $|\psi|^2=\kappa e^{-2\kappa|x|}$ one has $P(|x|>a)=e^{-2\kappa a}$ and $\langle|x|\rangle=2\kappa\int_0^{\infty}x e^{-2\kappa x}\,\mathrm{d}x=1/(2\kappa)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate Schrödinger's equation across the origin, match the even decaying exponential, and solve 2κ=2mα/ℏ².
Normalize with ∫ e^{−2κ|x|} dx=1/κ, then evaluate the two-sided exponential tail and the Gamma integral for ⟨|x|⟩.

milestones.criterion: Derives the jump −2κ ψ(0), the unique bound value κ=mα/ℏ², and E=−mα²/(2ℏ²).
Normalizes ψ=√κ e^{−κ|x|} and reports P(|x|>a)=e^{−2κa} together with ⟨|x|⟩=1/(2κ).
Rejects a √(2κ) normalization or a halved jump / e^{−κa} tail, and refuses reserved finite-well or Coulomb substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Normalizes the even bound state as √(2κ) e^{−κ|x|}, the one-sided exponential convention, instead of √κ e^{−κ|x|}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required unit wavefunction, the tail probability e^{−2κa}, and ⟨|x|⟩=1/(2κ) are all rescaled.

commonErrors.description: Writes the jump as −κ ψ(0), producing κ=2mα/ℏ² and the wrong energy, or reports the tail as e^{−κa} instead of e^{−2κa}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required κ=mα/ℏ², E=−mα²/(2ℏ²), and P(|x|>a)=e^{−2κa} are replaced by inconsistent scales.

hintTree.content: The odd sector is unbound: $\psi(0)=0$ makes the delta invisible. Only the even channel can bind.
The two-sided integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-2\kappa|x|}\,\mathrm{d}x=1/\kappa$ produces the prefactor $\sqrt{\kappa}$, not $\sqrt{2\kappa}$.
The tail integral is $2\int_a^{\infty}\kappa e^{-2\kappa x}\,\mathrm{d}x=e^{-2\kappa a}$. The extra $2$ in the exponent is the square of the wavefunction.

QM:010220.canonicalSolution:
Away from the origin the potential vanishes, so every bound solution
is a linear combination of $e^{\pm\kappa x}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-2mE}/\hbar$. Square-integrability forces
$\psi(x)=A e^{-\kappa|x|}$ (the odd combination is continuous only if
$A=0$, and an odd wavefunction has $\psi(0)=0$, so it never sees the
delta). Thus there is at most one bound state, and it is even.

Integrate the stationary equation
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi''-\alpha\delta(x)\psi=E\psi
\]
from $-\varepsilon$ to $\varepsilon$ and let $\varepsilon\to 0^+$.
Continuity of $\psi$ together with the locally integrable regular
terms yields the jump
\[
\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)
=-\frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0).
\]
For $\psi(x)=A e^{-\kappa|x|}$ the one-sided derivatives are
$\psi'(0^+)=-\kappa A$ and $\psi'(0^-)=+\kappa A$, so the jump is
$-2\kappa A=-2\kappa\psi(0)$. Matching the two expressions gives
\[
2\kappa=\frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\kappa=\frac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}.
\]
The corresponding energy is
\[
E=-\frac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}
=-\frac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2,\;
E=-m\alpha^2/(2\hbar^2),\;
\text{sole even bound state}}.
\]

The $L^2$ norm is
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|A|^2 e^{-2\kappa|x|}\,\mathrm{d}x
=|A|^2\cdot\frac{1}{\kappa},
\]
so $|A|=\sqrt{\kappa}$. Taking $A>0$,
\[
\psi(x)=\sqrt{\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|},
\]
and the jump is $-2\kappa\psi(0)$ as already used.
\[
\boxed{\psi=\sqrt{\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|},\;
\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)=-2\kappa\psi(0)}.
\]

The probability density is $\kappa e^{-2\kappa|x|}$. The tails are
\[
P(|x|>a)
=2\int_a^{\infty}\kappa e^{-2\kappa x}\,\mathrm{d}x
=e^{-2\kappa a}.
\]
The mean absolute displacement is the Gamma integral
\[
\langle|x|\rangle
=2\kappa\int_0^{\infty}x e^{-2\kappa x}\,\mathrm{d}x
=2\kappa\cdot\frac{1}{(2\kappa)^2}
=\frac{1}{2\kappa}.
\]
\[
\boxed{P(|x|>a)=e^{-2\kappa a},\;
\langle|x|\rangle=1/(2\kappa)}.
\]

Sentence (i) imports the one-sided normalization $\sqrt{2\kappa}$
appropriate to a half-line exponential and wrecks both tail integrals.
Sentence (ii) drops a factor of two from the jump, which doubles
$\kappa$ and quarters the energy scale, or else forgets to square the
exponential in the tail. The potential is a single attractive contact;
it is not a symmetric finite well, not a Coulomb problem, and not a
repulsive inverse-square core.

graderFixtures.proofText: The unique bound state has $\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2$, $E=-m\alpha^2/(2\hbar^2)$, and $\psi=\sqrt{\kappa}\,e^{-\kappa|x|}$. The derivative jump is $-2\kappa\psi(0)$, the tail probability is $P(|x|>a)=e^{-2\kappa a}$, and $\langle|x|\rangle=1/(2\kappa)$.
The even bound state is normalized as √(2κ) e^{−κ|x|}, the one-sided convention. I do not accept ψ=√κ e^{−κ|x|} and I rescale the tail integrals.
The jump is −κ ψ(0), so κ=2mα/ℏ², or the tail is e^{−κa}. I never obtain κ=mα/ℏ², E=−mα²/(2ℏ²), and P(|x|>a)=e^{−2κa}.

QM:010221.title: Rectangular-barrier matching at E=V₀/2 with κa=ln 3 yields T=9/25, not the opaque exponential
QM:010221.objective: For a rectangular barrier of height V₀ and width a=ℏ ln 3/√(m V₀) at energy E=V₀/2, prove κa=ln 3, evaluate the exact matching formula T=[1+V₀² sinh²(κa)/(4E(V₀−E))]^{−1}=9/25 and R=16/25, and distinguish the exact value from the opaque approximations e^{−2κa}=1/9 and 4 e^{−2κa}=4/9.
QM:010221.statement:
A rectangular barrier of height $V_0>0$ and width $a>0$ occupies
$0<x<a$. A particle of mass $m$ is incident from the left at energy
\[
E=\frac{V_0}{2}.
\]
The width is tuned to
\[
a=\frac{\hbar\ln 3}{\sqrt{mV_0}}.
\]
Write $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$ and $k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$. Use
exact matching of $\psi$ and $\psi'$ at both interfaces. Do not replace
the scattering problem by a symmetric finite well, a pair of bound
states, a Coulomb problem, or an opaque / WKB exponential quoted as
if it were exact.

1. Prove $k=\kappa=\sqrt{mV_0}/\hbar$ and $\kappa a=\ln 3$.

2. Recall the exact transmission formula obtained by matching,
   \[
   T=\Biggl[1+\frac{V_0^2\sinh^2(\kappa a)}{4E(V_0-E)}\Biggr]^{-1},
   \]
   or equivalently, at this special energy, $T=\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa a)$.
   Evaluate $\sinh(\ln 3)=4/3$ and prove
   \[
   T=\frac9{25},\qquad R=1-T=\frac{16}{25}.
   \]

3. Compute the two standard opaque estimates
   $e^{-2\kappa a}=1/9$ and
   $16E(V_0-E)e^{-2\kappa a}/V_0^2=4/9$, and record that neither
   equals $9/25$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the barrier is thick, so the exact
   transmission is the opaque exponential $e^{-2\kappa a}=1/9$ (or
   $4e^{-2\kappa a}=4/9$)”; (ii) “inside the barrier one should use
   $\sin(ka)$ rather than $\sinh(\kappa a)$, the above-barrier
   oscillatory formula.”
permittedResults: Hence $T=(3/5)^2=9/25$ and $R=16/25$. The opaque numbers are $e^{-2\ln 3}=1/9$ and $4/9$, neither of which equals $9/25$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute E=V₀/2 to collapse 4E(V₀−E)=V₀², evaluate sinh(ln 3)=4/3, and invert 1+16/9.
At k=κ reduce T to sech²(κa)= (3/5)², then compare with e^{−2 ln 3}=1/9 and 4/9.

milestones.criterion: Proves k=κ and κa=ln 3, and evaluates the exact matching formula to T=9/25.
Reports R=16/25 and records that the opaque estimates 1/9 and 4/9 are not the exact transmission.
Rejects an opaque exponential quoted as exact or an oscillatory sin(ka) substitution, and refuses reserved finite-well or Coulomb substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Replaces exact matching by an opaque / WKB exponential and reports T=e^{−2κa}=1/9 or T=4e^{−2κa}=4/9 as the transmission.
commonErrors.consequence: The required exact value T=9/25 is replaced by an opaque estimate that the problem asks to distinguish.

commonErrors.description: Uses the above-barrier formula with sin(ka) in place of sinh(κa), or evaluates sinh(ln 3) as 3 rather than 4/3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required identity sinh(ln 3)=4/3 and the exact T=9/25 are not produced.

hintTree.content: Substitute $E=V_0/2$ into $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$ first. The given width is built so that $\kappa a=\ln 3$.
The oscillatory formula with $\sin(ka)$ applies only for $E>V_0$. Here $E=V_0/2$ is under the barrier.

QM:010221.canonicalSolution:
At the assigned energy $E=V_0/2$ the two wave numbers coincide:
\[
k=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar}=\frac{\sqrt{mV_0}}{\hbar},\qquad
\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}=\frac{\sqrt{mV_0}}{\hbar}.
\]
The given width therefore produces
\[
\kappa a
=\frac{\sqrt{mV_0}}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{\hbar\ln 3}{\sqrt{mV_0}}
=\ln 3.
\]
\[
\boxed{k=\kappa=\sqrt{mV_0}/\hbar,\;\kappa a=\ln 3}.
\]

Exact matching of $\psi$ and $\psi'$ at $x=0$ and $x=a$ yields the
standard transmission formula
\[
T=\Biggl[1+\frac{V_0^2\sinh^2(\kappa a)}{4E(V_0-E)}\Biggr]^{-1}.
\]
(The companion amplitude identity is
$t^{-1}=e^{ika}\bigl[\cosh(\kappa a)+i(\kappa^2-k^2)\sinh(\kappa a)/(2k\kappa)\bigr]$.)
At $E=V_0/2$ one has $4E(V_0-E)=V_0^2$ and $k=\kappa$, so the
imaginary matching coefficient vanishes and
\[
T^{-1}=1+\sinh^2(\kappa a)=\cosh^2(\kappa a),
\qquad
T=\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa a).
\]
Now
\begin{align*}
\sinh(\ln 3)
&=\frac{e^{\ln 3}-e^{-\ln 3}}{2}
=\frac{3-1/3}{2}
=\frac43,\\
\cosh(\ln 3)
&=\frac{3+1/3}{2}
=\frac53.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\[
T=\Bigl(\frac35\Bigr)^2=\frac9{25},\qquad
\sinh^2(\ln 3)=\frac{16}{9},\qquad
T=\Bigl(1+\frac{16}{9}\Bigr)^{-1}=\frac9{25}.
\]
Probability conservation on a real potential gives
\[
R=1-T=\frac{16}{25}.
\]
\[
\boxed{T=9/25,\;R=16/25}.
\]

The crude opaque estimate is
\[
e^{-2\kappa a}=e^{-2\ln 3}=\frac19,
\]
and the standard prefactor improvement uses
$16E(V_0-E)/V_0^2=4$, hence $4e^{-2\kappa a}=4/9$. Numerically
$9/25=0.36$ while $1/9\approx 0.111$ and $4/9\approx 0.444$. Neither
opaque number equals the exact matching value, as expected for
$\kappa a=\ln 3\approx 1.10$, which is not a thick-barrier regime.
\[
\boxed{\text{opaque }1/9\text{ and }4/9\text{ are not }9/25}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces exact matching by an opaque exponential.
Sentence (ii) imports the above-barrier $\sin(ka)$ formula into an
under-barrier problem. The construction is one-dimensional barrier
scattering; it is not a symmetric finite well and not a Coulomb

graderFixtures.proofText: At $E=V_0/2$ one has $\kappa a=\ln 3$ and $\sinh(\ln 3)=4/3$. Exact matching gives $T=9/25$ and $R=16/25$. The opaque estimates $e^{-2\kappa a}=1/9$ and $4e^{-2\kappa a}=4/9$ are not equal to $9/25$.

QM:010322.title: The oscillator state (|0>+i|1>)/sqrt(2) has <x>(t)=x0 sin(omega t) and Delta x Delta p=hbar/sqrt(2) at t=0
QM:010322.objective:
For |psi>=(|0>+i|1>)/sqrt(2) with x0=sqrt(hbar/(2 m omega)) and p0=sqrt(m hbar omega/2), prove =i/2 initially, (t)=x0 sin(omega t),

(t)=p0 cos(omega t), =hbar/(m omega), =m hbar omega, and at t=0 the variances hbar/(m omega) and m hbar omega/2 with product Delta=hbar/sqrt(2) and =hbar omega.
QM:010322.statement:
A one-dimensional harmonic oscillator has the time-independent
Hamiltonian $H=\hbar\omega\bigl(a^{\dagger}a+\tfrac12\bigr)$ and the
standard ladder identifications
\[
x=x_0\bigl(a+a^{\dagger}\bigr),\qquad
p=ip_0\bigl(a^{\dagger}-a\bigr),
\]
with the given scales
\[
x_0=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}},\qquad
p_0=\sqrt{\frac{m\hbar\omega}{2}}.
\]
The normalized state at $t=0$ is the number-state superposition
\[
\lvert\psi\rangle=\frac{\lvert 0\rangle+i\lvert 1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
Do not replace the state by a Gaussian minimum-uncertainty packet,
and do not introduce an explicitly time-dependent Hamiltonian or a
dilation operator.

1. Compute the initial ladder expectation $\langle a\rangle$ and
   prove $\langle a\rangle=i/2$. Evolve $a(t)=ae^{-i\omega t}$ in
   the Heisenberg picture generated by the given time-independent
   $H$, and prove
   \[
   \langle x\rangle(t)=x_0\sin(\omega t),\qquad
   \langle p\rangle(t)=p_0\cos(\omega t).
   \]

2. Prove the time-independent second moments
   \[
   \langle x^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{m\omega},\qquad
   \langle p^2\rangle=m\hbar\omega.
   \]

3. At $t=0$ compute the variances and the uncertainty product, and
   prove
   \[
   (\Delta x)^2=\frac{\hbar}{m\omega},\qquad
   (\Delta p)^2=\frac{m\hbar\omega}{2},\qquad
   \Delta x\,\Delta p=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}},
   \]
   together with the energy $\langle H\rangle=\hbar\omega$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the relative phase is real, so
   $\langle x\rangle(t)=x_0\cos(\omega t)$ and
   $\langle p\rangle(t)=-p_0\sin(\omega t)$”; (ii) “at $t=0$ one
   may skip $\langle p\rangle^2$ and report
   $\Delta x\,\Delta p=\hbar$ or the Gaussian value $\hbar/2$.”
permittedResults: On $\lvert\psi\rangle=(\lvert 0\rangle+i\lvert 1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ one has $a\lvert\psi\rangle=i\lvert 0\rangle/\sqrt{2}$, hence $\langle a\rangle=i/2$ and $\langle a^{\dagger}\rangle=-i/2$. Then $\langle a(t)\rangle=(i/2)e^{-i\omega t}$.

$\langle N\rangle=1/2$, $\langle aa^{\dagger}\rangle=3/2$, and $\langle a^2\rangle=\langle(a^{\dagger})^2\rangle=0$, so $\langle x^2\rangle=2x_0^2=\hbar/(m\omega)$ and $\langle p^2\rangle=2p_0^2=m\hbar\omega$. At $t=0$, $\langle p\rangle=p_0$ forces $(\Delta p)^2=m\hbar\omega/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate a on the n=1 component, evolve a(t)=a e^{-i omega t}, and expand the resulting complex exponentials into sin and cos.
Use <N>=1/2 to read the second moments from <aa^dagger>+<a^dagger a>, then subtract p0^2 from <p^2> at t=0 before forming Delta x Delta p.

milestones.criterion:
Produces =i/2, the Heisenberg means (t)=x0 sin(omega t) and

(t)=p0 cos(omega t), and the second moments =hbar/(m omega), =m hbar omega.
Reports the t=0 variances hbar/(m omega) and m hbar omega/2, the product Delta=hbar/sqrt(2), and <H>=hbar omega.

Rejects a real-phase sin/cos swap or a product that skips

^2, and refuses reserved Gaussian-packet or time-dependent-dilation substitutions.

commonErrors.description:
Treats the relative phase as real and reports (t)=x0 cos(omega t) and

(t)=-p0 sin(omega t) instead of x0 sin(omega t) and p0 cos(omega t).
commonErrors.consequence: The required Heisenberg means for the given phase i are replaced by the orthogonal real-superposition pair.

commonErrors.description:
At t=0 reports Delta x Delta p=hbar from sqrt() or the Gaussian value hbar/2, without subtracting

^2=p0^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required t=0 product hbar/sqrt(2) and the variance (Delta p)^2=m hbar omega/2 are lost.

hintTree.content: Only the $n=1$ component is annihilated. The inner product $\langle\psi\rvert a\lvert\psi\rangle$ therefore reduces to $(1/\sqrt{2})\cdot(i/\sqrt{2})$.
Write $\langle a(t)\rangle=(i/2)e^{-i\omega t}$ and $\langle a^{\dagger}(t)\rangle=(-i/2)e^{i\omega t}$, then expand $e^{\pm i\omega t}$ into $\cos$ and $\sin$.
At $t=0$ one has $\langle x\rangle=0$ but $\langle p\rangle=p_0\neq 0$. Subtract $p_0^2$ from $\langle p^2\rangle$ before forming the product of standard deviations.

QM:010322.canonicalSolution:
The annihilation operator kills $\lvert 0\rangle$ and sends
$\lvert 1\rangle$ to $\lvert 0\rangle$, so
\[
a\lvert\psi\rangle
=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert 0\rangle.
\]
Therefore
\[
\langle a\rangle
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\langle 0\rvert-i\langle 1\rvert\bigr)
\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert 0\rangle
=\frac{i}{2}.
\]
The adjoint is the complex conjugate $\langle a^{\dagger}\rangle=-i/2$.
\[
\boxed{\langle a\rangle=i/2}.
\]

The Hamiltonian is time-independent, so the Heisenberg ladder is
$a(t)=ae^{-i\omega t}$ and
\[
\langle a(t)\rangle=\frac{i}{2}e^{-i\omega t},\qquad
\langle a^{\dagger}(t)\rangle=-\frac{i}{2}e^{i\omega t}.
\]
The position mean is
\begin{align*}
\langle x\rangle(t)
&=x_0\Bigl(\frac{i}{2}e^{-i\omega t}-\frac{i}{2}e^{i\omega t}\Bigr)
=x_0\cdot\frac{i}{2}\bigl(e^{-i\omega t}-e^{i\omega t}\bigr)
=x_0\sin(\omega t).
\end{align*}
The momentum mean is
\begin{align*}
\langle p\rangle(t)
&=ip_0\Bigl(-\frac{i}{2}e^{i\omega t}-\frac{i}{2}e^{-i\omega t}\Bigr)
=p_0\cos(\omega t).
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{\langle x\rangle(t)=x_0\sin(\omega t),\;
\langle p\rangle(t)=p_0\cos(\omega t)}.
\]

The number mean on the equal-weight superposition is
$\langle N\rangle=1/2$, and $aa^{\dagger}=N+1$ gives
$\langle aa^{\dagger}\rangle=3/2$. Both $\langle a^2\rangle$ and
$\langle(a^{\dagger})^2\rangle$ vanish because $a^2\lvert\psi\rangle=0$
and $(a^{\dagger})^2\lvert\psi\rangle$ is orthogonal to the
$n\in\{0,1\}$ support. Hence
\[
\langle x^2\rangle
=x_0^2\bigl(\langle aa^{\dagger}\rangle+\langle a^{\dagger}a\rangle\bigr)
=2x_0^2
=\frac{\hbar}{m\omega},
\]
\[
\langle p^2\rangle
=p_0^2\bigl(\langle aa^{\dagger}\rangle+\langle a^{\dagger}a\rangle\bigr)
=2p_0^2
=m\hbar\omega.
\]
Both second moments are time-independent because $\langle a^2\rangle$
remains zero after the Heisenberg phase $e^{-2i\omega t}$.
\[
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=\hbar/(m\omega),\;
\langle p^2\rangle=m\hbar\omega}.
\]

At $t=0$ one has $\langle x\rangle=0$ and $\langle p\rangle=p_0$, so
\[
(\Delta x)^2=\frac{\hbar}{m\omega},\qquad
(\Delta p)^2=m\hbar\omega-p_0^2=\frac{m\hbar\omega}{2}.
\]
The product of standard deviations is
\[
\Delta x\,\Delta p
=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega}\cdot\frac{m\hbar\omega}{2}}
=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
The energy is
\[
\langle H\rangle
=\hbar\omega\bigl(\langle N\rangle+\tfrac12\bigr)
=\hbar\omega.
\]
\[
\boxed{(\Delta x)^2=\hbar/(m\omega),\;
(\Delta p)^2=m\hbar\omega/2,\;
\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar/\sqrt{2},\;
\langle H\rangle=\hbar\omega}.
\]

Sentence (i) is the real superposition $\lvert 0\rangle+\lvert 1\rangle$,
not the given relative phase $i$; it replaces the required
$\sin/\cos$ pair. Sentence (ii) either reports
$\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle\langle p^2\rangle}=\hbar$ or quotes the
Gaussian bound $\hbar/2$, both of which skip the subtraction of
$\langle p\rangle^2=p_0^2$ at $t=0$. The construction uses a
time-independent oscillator Hamiltonian on a two-level number-state
superposition; it never introduces a Gaussian packet and never
introduces a time-dependent dilation operator.

graderFixtures.proofText: Initially $\langle a\rangle=i/2$. Heisenberg evolution of the time-independent oscillator gives $\langle x\rangle(t)=x_0\sin(\omega t)$ and $\langle p\rangle(t)=p_0\cos(\omega t)$. The second moments are $\langle x^2\rangle=\hbar/(m\omega)$ and $\langle p^2\rangle=m\hbar\omega$. At $t=0$ the variances are $\hbar/(m\omega)$ and $m\hbar\omega/2$, the product is $\hbar/\sqrt{2}$, and $\langle H\rangle=\hbar\omega$.

The relative phase is real, so I report (t)=x0 cos(omega t) and

(t)=-p0 sin(omega t). I do not obtain x0 sin(omega t) or p0 cos(omega t).

At t=0 I take Delta x Delta p=sqrt()=hbar, or I quote the Gaussian value hbar/2. I never subtract

^2=p0^2 and I do not report hbar/sqrt(2).

QM:010323.title: The ring state (|2>+i|-2>)/sqrt(2) has certain energy 2 hbar^2/I and density [1+sin(4 phi)]/(2 pi)
QM:010323.objective: For H=Lz^2/(2I) on a ring with R|m>=|-m| and psi=(|2>+i|-2>)/sqrt(2), prove [H,R]=0, that E=2 hbar^2/I is certain, that the R± probabilities are each 1/2, that <Lz>=0, <Lz^2>=4 hbar^2 and Delta Lz=2 hbar, and that the azimuthal density is [1+sin(4 phi)]/(2 pi) and is stationary by degeneracy.
QM:010323.statement:
A particle on a ring has Hamiltonian $H=L_z^2/(2I)$ and
eigenstates $\lvert m\rangle$ of $L_z$ with
$L_z\lvert m\rangle=m\hbar\lvert m\rangle$, $m\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Reflection through a diameter acts by $R\lvert m\rangle=\lvert -m\rangle$.
The normalized state is
\[
\lvert\psi\rangle
=\frac{\lvert 2\rangle+i\lvert -2\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
Do not replace the ring by a symmetric finite well, and do not
introduce an explicitly time-dependent operator.

1. Prove $[H,R]=0$. Show that $\lvert\psi\rangle$ is an energy
   eigenstate with the certain value
   \[
   E=\frac{2\hbar^2}{I}.
   \]

2. Let $\lvert R_\pm\rangle=(\lvert 2\rangle\pm\lvert -2\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$
   be the $\pm 1$ eigenstates of $R$. Prove that each outcome of $R$
   has probability $1/2$.

3. Compute $\langle L_z\rangle$, $\langle L_z^2\rangle$, and
   $\Delta L_z$, and prove
   \[
   \langle L_z\rangle=0,\qquad
   \langle L_z^2\rangle=4\hbar^2,\qquad
   \Delta L_z=2\hbar.
   \]

4. In the azimuthal representation
   $\langle\phi\lvert m\rangle=e^{im\phi}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, prove that
   the probability density is
   \[
   \lvert\psi(\phi)\rvert^2=\frac{1+\sin(4\phi)}{2\pi}
   \]
   and that the density is stationary. Audit both sentences:
   (i) “$H=L_z^2/I$, so the certain energy is $4\hbar^2/I$”;
   (ii) “the relative phase $i$ makes the density
   $(1+\cos 4\phi)/(2\pi)$, or the state is non-stationary because
   $m$ and $-m$ are distinct.”
permittedResults: Both $\lvert 2\rangle$ and $\lvert -2\rangle$ have $L_z^2=4\hbar^2$, hence $E=4\hbar^2/(2I)=2\hbar^2/I$. Expanding $\lvert\psi\rangle$ in the $R_\pm$ basis gives amplitudes $(1\pm i)/2$ and probabilities $1/2$.
Equal weights on $m=\pm 2$ force $\langle L_z\rangle=0$ and $\langle L_z^2\rangle=4\hbar^2$. The azimuthal cross term is $i e^{-i4\phi}-i e^{i4\phi}=2\sin(4\phi)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use R Lz R^dagger=-Lz to obtain [H,R]=0, then evaluate H on the common Lz^2 eigenvalue 4 hbar^2.
Expand in the R± basis for the reflection probabilities, then form the azimuthal interference of e^{i2 phi} with i e^{-i2 phi}.

milestones.criterion: Proves [H,R]=0, the certain energy 2 hbar^2/I, and the reflection probabilities P(R±)=1/2.
Reports <Lz>=0, <Lz^2>=4 hbar^2, Delta Lz=2 hbar, the density [1+sin(4 phi)]/(2 pi), and stationarity from the m=±2 degeneracy.
Rejects E=4 hbar^2/I or a cosine / non-stationary density, and refuses reserved finite-well or time-dependent-operator substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes H=Lz^2/I, or otherwise reports the certain energy as 4 hbar^2/I instead of 2 hbar^2/I.
commonErrors.consequence: The required energy eigenvalue 2 hbar^2/I is replaced by twice the rotor value.

commonErrors.description: Reports the azimuthal density (1+cos(4 phi))/(2 pi), or claims the state is non-stationary because m and -m are distinct.
commonErrors.consequence: The required sine interference and the degeneracy argument for stationarity are lost.

hintTree.content: Because $H$ depends only on $L_z^2$, conjugating $L_z\to -L_z$ leaves $H$ invariant, so $R$ commutes with $H$.
Write $\lvert 2\rangle=(\lvert R_+\rangle+\lvert R_-\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ and $\lvert -2\rangle=(\lvert R_+\rangle-\lvert R_-\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$, then collect coefficients of $\lvert R_\pm\rangle$.
The density cross term comes from $e^{i2\phi}\overline{(i e^{-i2\phi})}+\mathrm{c.c.}$. The factor $i$ converts the cosine interference into $\sin(4\phi)$.

QM:010323.canonicalSolution:
Reflection sends $L_z$ to $-L_z$:
\[
RL_z\lvert m\rangle
=m\hbar\lvert -m\rangle
=-L_z R\lvert m\rangle,
\]
so $RL_zR^{\dagger}=-L_z$ and $RL_z^2R^{\dagger}=L_z^2$. Therefore
$RHR^{\dagger}=H$ and $[H,R]=0$.
\[
\boxed{[H,R]=0}.
\]

Both $\lvert 2\rangle$ and $\lvert -2\rangle$ are eigenstates of
$L_z^2$ with eigenvalue $4\hbar^2$, hence eigenstates of $H$ with
\[
E=\frac{4\hbar^2}{2I}=\frac{2\hbar^2}{I}.
\]
The given superposition is therefore itself an energy eigenstate,
and a measurement of $H$ returns $2\hbar^2/I$ with probability $1$.
\[
\boxed{E=2\hbar^2/I\text{ certain}}.
\]

The reflection eigenstates are
$\lvert R_\pm\rangle=(\lvert 2\rangle\pm\lvert -2\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$.
Inverting,
\[
\lvert 2\rangle=\frac{\lvert R_+\rangle+\lvert R_-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}},
\qquad
\lvert -2\rangle=\frac{\lvert R_+\rangle-\lvert R_-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}},
\]
so
\[
\lvert\psi\rangle
=\frac{(1+i)\lvert R_+\rangle+(1-i)\lvert R_-\rangle}{2}.
\]
The probabilities are
\[
P(R_+)=\frac{\lvert 1+i\rvert^2}{4}=\frac12,\qquad
P(R_-)=\frac{\lvert 1-i\rvert^2}{4}=\frac12.
\]
\[
\boxed{P(R_\pm)=1/2}.
\]

Equal weights on $m=\pm 2$ give
\[
\langle L_z\rangle
=\hbar\Bigl(2\cdot\tfrac12+(-2)\cdot\tfrac12\Bigr)=0,
\qquad
\langle L_z^2\rangle=4\hbar^2,
\qquad
\Delta L_z=2\hbar.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle L_z\rangle=0,\;
\langle L_z^2\rangle=4\hbar^2,\;
\Delta L_z=2\hbar}.
\]

The azimuthal wavefunction is
\[
\psi(\phi)
=\frac{e^{i2\phi}+i e^{-i2\phi}}{\sqrt{4\pi}}.
\]
Writing $A=e^{i2\phi}$ and $B=i e^{-i2\phi}$,
\[
\lvert A+B\rvert^2
=2+A\overline{B}+\overline{A}B
=2-ie^{i4\phi}+ie^{-i4\phi}
=2+2\sin(4\phi).
\]
Hence
\[
\lvert\psi(\phi)\rvert^2
=\frac{1+\sin(4\phi)}{2\pi}.
\]
Because $E_2=E_{-2}$, the relative phase $i$ does not evolve under
$H$, so the density is stationary.
\[
\boxed{\lvert\psi(\phi)\rvert^2=[1+\sin(4\phi)]/(2\pi)
\text{ stationary}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the factor $2$ in the denominator of $H$ and
reports $4\hbar^2/I$. Sentence (ii) either replaces $\sin(4\phi)$
by $\cos(4\phi)$ or claims non-stationarity from $m\neq -m$,
ignoring the $L_z^2$ degeneracy. The construction is a rigid rotor
with a spatial reflection; it never matches a symmetric finite well
and never introduces a time-dependent operator.

graderFixtures.proofText: $[H,R]=0$ and $E=2\hbar^2/I$ is certain. Each reflection eigenvalue has probability $1/2$. The moments are $\langle L_z\rangle=0$, $\langle L_z^2\rangle=4\hbar^2$, and $\Delta L_z=2\hbar$. The azimuthal density is $[1+\sin(4\phi)]/(2\pi)$ and is stationary by the $m=\pm 2$ degeneracy.
I take H=Lz^2/I, so the certain energy is 4 hbar^2/I. I do not report E=2 hbar^2/I.
The density is (1+cos(4 phi))/(2 pi), or the state is non-stationary because m=2 and m=-2 are different. I never obtain [1+sin(4 phi)]/(2 pi) as a stationary density.

QM:010424.title: A +x spin measured along n=(3/5,0,4/5) has P+=4/5, then P(z+|n+)=9/10
QM:010424.objective: For a spin-1/2 prepared in |+x> and n=(3/5,0,4/5), prove that Sn has outcomes ±hbar/2 with P+=4/5 and P-=1/5, that <Sn>=3 hbar/10, Var=4 hbar^2/25 and Delta=2 hbar/5, and that after the n+ outcome a subsequent Sz measurement has Pz+=9/10 and Pz-=1/10, in that explicit sequential order.
QM:010424.statement:
A spin-$1/2$ is prepared in the eigenstate $\lvert +x\rangle$ of
$S_x$. Let $\mathbf n=(3/5,0,4/5)$ and write
$S_{\mathbf n}=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf S$. Do not replace the
single-spin sequential measurements by addition of spin $1$ and
spin $1/2$, and do not introduce an entangled two-spin state or a
no-signalling argument.

1. Show that a measurement of $S_{\mathbf n}$ has outcomes
   $\pm\hbar/2$ with
   \[
   P_+=\frac45,\qquad P_-=\frac15.
   \]

2. Compute the first-measurement moments and prove
   \[
   \langle S_{\mathbf n}\rangle=\frac{3\hbar}{10},\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(S_{\mathbf n})=\frac{4\hbar^2}{25},\qquad
   \Delta S_{\mathbf n}=\frac{2\hbar}{5}.
   \]

3. Condition on the outcome $+\hbar/2$ of $S_{\mathbf n}$. Then
   measure $S_z$ on the collapsed state, and prove
   \[
   P(z+\mid n+)=\frac{9}{10},\qquad
   P(z-\mid n+)=\frac{1}{10}.
   \]
   The order is first $S_{\mathbf n}$, then $S_z$. Do not replace
   the second probabilities by the $S_z$ statistics of the original
   $\lvert +x\rangle$ preparation.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$P_+=(1+n_z)/2=9/10$ already at the
   first measurement, because $\mathbf n$ is closer to $z$ than to
   $x$”; (ii) “after obtaining $n+$ one may still use the original
   $\lvert +x\rangle$, so $P(z+)=1/2$, or $S_{\mathbf n}$ and $S_z$
   may be treated as simultaneous.”
permittedResults: $\mathbf n\cdot\hat{\mathbf x}=3/5$, so $P_+=(1+3/5)/2=4/5$ and $P_-=1/5$. Then $\langle S_{\mathbf n}\rangle=(\hbar/2)(3/5)=3\hbar/10$ and $\operatorname{Var}=(\hbar/2)^2-(3\hbar/10)^2=4\hbar^2/25$.
$\mathbf n=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta)$ has $\cos\theta=4/5$. The collapsed ket is $\lvert n+\rangle=\sqrt{9/10}\lvert +z\rangle+\sqrt{1/10}\lvert -z\rangle$, so $P(z+\mid n+)=9/10$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the first Born rule with n·x̂=3/5, then obtain the variance from (hbar/2)^2 minus the squared mean.
Collapse onto |n+> with cos θ=4/5 and read P(z+|n+)=cos^2(θ/2)=(1+4/5)/2=9/10.

milestones.criterion: Produces the Sn outcomes ±hbar/2 with P+=4/5, P-=1/5, and the moments <Sn>=3 hbar/10, Var=4 hbar^2/25, Delta=2 hbar/5.
After the n+ collapse, reports the subsequent Sz probabilities 9/10 and 1/10 in that explicit sequential order.
Rejects a first-shot P+=9/10 or a no-collapse / simultaneous measurement, and refuses reserved spin-addition or entanglement substitutions.

hintTree.content: The first-measurement overlap uses $\mathbf n\cdot\hat{\mathbf x}=3/5$, not $\mathbf n\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=4/5$.
$S_{\mathbf n}^2=(\hbar/2)^2 I$ on a spin-$1/2$, so the variance is $\hbar^2/4$ minus the square of the mean.
After collapse, $\lvert n+\rangle$ has polar angle with $\cos\theta=4/5$, hence $P(z+)=\cos^2(\theta/2)=(1+\cos\theta)/2=9/10$.

QM:010424.canonicalSolution:
The operator $S_{\mathbf n}$ is $(\hbar/2)$ times a Pauli combination
with eigenvalues $\pm 1$, so the outcomes are $\pm\hbar/2$. The
preparation is polarized along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and
\[
\mathbf n\cdot\hat{\mathbf x}=\frac35,
\]
hence
\[
P_+=\frac{1+3/5}{2}=\frac45,\qquad
P_-=\frac{1-3/5}{2}=\frac15.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{outcomes }\pm\hbar/2,\;P_+=4/5,\;P_-=1/5}.
\]

The mean is the same inner product times $\hbar/2$:
\[
\langle S_{\mathbf n}\rangle
=\frac{\hbar}{2}\cdot\frac35
=\frac{3\hbar}{10}.
\]
On a spin-$1/2$ one has $S_{\mathbf n}^2=\hbar^2/4$, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(S_{\mathbf n})
=\frac{\hbar^2}{4}-\Bigl(\frac{3\hbar}{10}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{25\hbar^2-9\hbar^2}{100}
=\frac{4\hbar^2}{25},
\]
and $\Delta S_{\mathbf n}=2\hbar/5$.
\[
\boxed{\langle S_{\mathbf n}\rangle=3\hbar/10,\;
\operatorname{Var}=4\hbar^2/25,\;
\Delta=2\hbar/5}.
\]

The $+$ outcome of $S_{\mathbf n}$ collapses the state onto
$\lvert n+\rangle$. With $\mathbf n=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta)$ one
has $\cos\theta=4/5$ and $\phi=0$, so
\[
\cos\frac{\theta}{2}
=\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}}
=\sqrt{\frac{9}{10}},\qquad
\sin\frac{\theta}{2}
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\lvert n+\rangle
=\sqrt{\frac{9}{10}}\lvert +z\rangle
+\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}}\lvert -z\rangle,
\]
and a subsequent $S_z$ measurement yields
\[
P(z+\mid n+)=\frac{9}{10},\qquad
P(z-\mid n+)=\frac{1}{10}.
\]
The order is first $S_{\mathbf n}$, then $S_z$ on the collapsed
state; the original $\lvert +x\rangle$ is no longer available.
\[
\boxed{P(z+\mid n+)=9/10,\;P(z-\mid n+)=1/10
\text{ after }n+}.
\]

Sentence (i) uses $n_z$ in the first Born rule and reports the
conditional second-measurement value $9/10$ as if it were $P_+$.
Sentence (ii) either ignores collapse, leaving $P(z+)=1/2$ from
the original $\lvert +x\rangle$, or treats the non-commuting pair
$S_{\mathbf n}$ and $S_z$ as simultaneous. The construction is a
single spin-$1/2$ with two sequential projective measurements; it
never adds spin $1$ to spin $1/2$ and never introduces an
entangled pair or a no-signalling ledger.

graderFixtures.proofText: A measurement of $S_{\mathbf n}$ on $\lvert +x\rangle$ has outcomes $\pm\hbar/2$ with $P_+=4/5$ and $P_-=1/5$. The moments are $\langle S_{\mathbf n}\rangle=3\hbar/10$, $\operatorname{Var}=4\hbar^2/25$, and $\Delta=2\hbar/5$. After the $n+$ outcome, a subsequent $S_z$ measurement has $P(z+\mid n+)=9/10$ and $P(z-\mid n+)=1/10$.
I use n·z=4/5 in the first Born rule and report P+=9/10 for Sn. I do not obtain P+=4/5 or <Sn>=3 hbar/10.
After getting n+ I keep the original |+x>, so P(z+)=1/2, or I measure Sn and Sz simultaneously. I never report the sequential values 9/10 and 1/10.

QM:010425.title: The superposition sqrt(2/5) Y_2^1 + i sqrt(3/5) Y_3^{-2} has <L^2>=48 hbar^2/5 and Delta Lz=3 sqrt(6) hbar/5
QM:010425.objective: For psi=sqrt(2/5) Y_2^1 + i sqrt(3/5) Y_3^{-2}, prove that L^2 has outcomes 6 hbar^2 (prob 2/5) and 12 hbar^2 (prob 3/5) with mean 48 hbar^2/5; that Lz has outcomes +hbar (2/5) and -2 hbar (3/5) with mean -4 hbar/5; that <Lz^2>=14 hbar^2/5, Var=54 hbar^2/25 and Delta=3 sqrt(6) hbar/5; and that the conditional quantum numbers are deterministic.
QM:010425.statement:
An orbital angular-momentum state on the sphere is the
normalized superposition of spherical harmonics
\[
\psi
=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}\,Y_2^{1}
+i\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}\,Y_3^{-2}.
\]
Do not replace the single-particle orbital ledger by addition of
spin $1$ and spin $1/2$, and do not introduce an entangled pair.

1. List the possible outcomes of $L^2$ with their probabilities,
   and prove that the mean is
   \[
   \langle L^2\rangle=\frac{48\hbar^2}{5}.
   \]

2. List the possible outcomes of $L_z$ with their probabilities,
   and prove
   \[
   \langle L_z\rangle=-\frac{4\hbar}{5}.
   \]

3. Compute the second $L_z$ moment, the variance, and the standard
   deviation, and prove
   \[
   \langle L_z^2\rangle=\frac{14\hbar^2}{5},\qquad
   \operatorname{Var}(L_z)=\frac{54\hbar^2}{25},\qquad
   \Delta L_z=\frac{3\sqrt{6}\,\hbar}{5}.
   \]

4. Show that a measurement of $L^2$ determines both quantum
   numbers $(\ell,m)$ with certainty, and likewise for a
   measurement of $L_z$. Audit both sentences: (i) “$L^2$ has
   eigenvalues $\ell^2\hbar^2$, so the outcomes are $4\hbar^2$ and
   $9\hbar^2$”; (ii) “the mean of $L_z$ is $+4\hbar/5$, or the
   width is $\sqrt{\langle L_z^2\rangle}$ without subtracting the
   squared mean.”
permittedResults: The $\ell=2$ term has $L^2=6\hbar^2$ and $L_z=+\hbar$ with probability $2/5$. The $\ell=3$ term has $L^2=12\hbar^2$ and $L_z=-2\hbar$ with probability $3/5$.

$\langle L^2\rangle=(2/5)6\hbar^2+(3/5)12\hbar^2=48\hbar^2/5$ and $\langle L_z\rangle=(2/5)\hbar+(3/5)(-2\hbar)=-4\hbar/5$. Then $\langle L_z^2\rangle=14\hbar^2/5$ and $\operatorname{Var}=54\hbar^2/25$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Read ell(ell+1) and m from each Y_lm, square the moduli for the probabilities, and form the two means as weighted sums.
Compute <Lz^2> from the same weights, subtract <Lz>^2=16 hbar^2/25, and note that each observable selects a unique (ell,m) pair.

milestones.criterion: Lists the L^2 outcomes 6 hbar^2 (2/5) and 12 hbar^2 (3/5) with mean 48 hbar^2/5, and the Lz outcomes +hbar (2/5) and -2 hbar (3/5) with mean -4 hbar/5.
Reports <Lz^2>=14 hbar^2/5, Var=54 hbar^2/25, Delta=3 sqrt(6) hbar/5, and the deterministic conditional quantum numbers.
Rejects L^2=ell^2 hbar^2 or a sign / unsubtracted-width error, and refuses reserved spin-addition or entanglement substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes L^2 eigenvalues as ell^2 hbar^2 and reports outcomes 4 hbar^2 and 9 hbar^2 instead of 6 hbar^2 and 12 hbar^2.
commonErrors.consequence: The required L^2 ledger and the mean 48 hbar^2/5 are replaced by the incorrect ell^2 spectrum.

commonErrors.description: Reports <Lz>=+4 hbar/5, or takes Delta Lz=sqrt(<Lz^2>) without subtracting the squared mean.
commonErrors.consequence: The required mean -4 hbar/5 and the width 3 sqrt(6) hbar/5 are lost.

hintTree.content: The $L^2$ eigenvalues are $\ell(\ell+1)\hbar^2$: $2\cdot 3=6$ and $3\cdot 4=12$, not $2^2$ and $3^2$.
The coefficient $i\sqrt{3/5}$ contributes probability $3/5$ to $m=-2$. The sign of that $m$ makes $\langle L_z\rangle$ negative.
Subtract $\langle L_z\rangle^2=16\hbar^2/25$ from $\langle L_z^2\rangle=14\hbar^2/5=70\hbar^2/25$ to obtain the variance $54\hbar^2/25$.

QM:010425.canonicalSolution:
The two spherical harmonics are orthogonal eigenfunctions of
$L^2$. The first has $\ell=2$, so
\[
L^2 Y_2^{1}=2\cdot 3\,\hbar^2\,Y_2^{1}=6\hbar^2\,Y_2^{1},
\]
with probability $\lvert\sqrt{2/5}\rvert^2=2/5$. The second has
$\ell=3$, so
\[
L^2 Y_3^{-2}=3\cdot 4\,\hbar^2\,Y_3^{-2}=12\hbar^2\,Y_3^{-2},
\]
with probability $\lvert i\sqrt{3/5}\rvert^2=3/5$. The mean is
\[
\langle L^2\rangle
=\frac25\cdot 6\hbar^2+\frac35\cdot 12\hbar^2
=\frac{12+36}{5}\hbar^2
=\frac{48\hbar^2}{5}.
\]
\[
\boxed{L^2:\ 6\hbar^2\ (2/5),\ 12\hbar^2\ (3/5);\;
\langle L^2\rangle=48\hbar^2/5}.
\]

The same weights give the $L_z$ ledger: $m=1$ with probability
$2/5$ and $m=-2$ with probability $3/5$. Hence the outcomes are
$+\hbar$ and $-2\hbar$, and
\[
\langle L_z\rangle
=\frac25\hbar+\frac35(-2\hbar)
=\frac{2-6}{5}\hbar
=-\frac{4\hbar}{5}.
\]
\[
\boxed{L_z:\ +\hbar\ (2/5),\ -2\hbar\ (3/5);\;
\langle L_z\rangle=-4\hbar/5}.
\]

The second moment is
\[
\langle L_z^2\rangle
=\frac25\hbar^2+\frac35\cdot 4\hbar^2
=\frac{2+12}{5}\hbar^2
=\frac{14\hbar^2}{5}.
\]
Subtracting the squared mean,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(L_z)
=\frac{14\hbar^2}{5}-\Bigl(-\frac{4\hbar}{5}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{70\hbar^2}{25}-\frac{16\hbar^2}{25}
=\frac{54\hbar^2}{25},
\]
so
\[
\Delta L_z
=\frac{\sqrt{54}}{5}\hbar
=\frac{3\sqrt{6}\,\hbar}{5}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle L_z^2\rangle=14\hbar^2/5,\;
\operatorname{Var}=54\hbar^2/25,\;
\Delta L_z=3\sqrt{6}\,\hbar/5}.
\]

Each term carries a unique $\ell$ and a unique $m$. Conditioning
on $L^2=6\hbar^2$ forces $(\ell,m)=(2,1)$; conditioning on
$L^2=12\hbar^2$ forces $(\ell,m)=(3,-2)$. Conditioning on
$L_z=+\hbar$ forces $(\ell,m)=(2,1)$; conditioning on $L_z=-2\hbar$
forces $(\ell,m)=(3,-2)$. The relative phase $i$ never enters a
probability.

Sentence (i) replaces $\ell(\ell+1)$ by $\ell^2$ and reports
$4\hbar^2$ and $9\hbar^2$. Sentence (ii) either flips the sign of
$\langle L_z\rangle$ or reports $\sqrt{\langle L_z^2\rangle}$ as
the width. The construction is a single orbital wavefunction in
the $Y_\ell^m$ basis; it never adds spin $1$ to spin $1/2$ and
never introduces an entangled pair.

graderFixtures.proofText: $L^2$ has outcomes $6\hbar^2$ with probability $2/5$ and $12\hbar^2$ with probability $3/5$, hence $\langle L^2\rangle=48\hbar^2/5$. $L_z$ has outcomes $+\hbar$ with probability $2/5$ and $-2\hbar$ with probability $3/5$, hence $\langle L_z\rangle=-4\hbar/5$. Then $\langle L_z^2\rangle=14\hbar^2/5$, $\operatorname{Var}=54\hbar^2/25$, and $\Delta L_z=3\sqrt{6}\,\hbar/5$. Each measurement of $L^2$ or $L_z$ determines $(\ell,m)$ with certainty.
L^2 has eigenvalues ell^2 hbar^2, so the outcomes are 4 hbar^2 and 9 hbar^2. I do not report 6 hbar^2, 12 hbar^2, or <L^2>=48 hbar^2/5.
I take <Lz>=+4 hbar/5, or I report Delta Lz=sqrt(<Lz^2>) without subtracting the squared mean. I never obtain -4 hbar/5 or 3 sqrt(6) hbar/5.

QM:010526.title: The hydrogen 1s radial density has mode a0, <r>=3 a0/2, and tail 5 e^{-2} beyond a0
QM:010526.objective: For the hydrogen 1s wavefunction psi=(pi a0^3)^{-1/2} e^{-r/a0}, prove that the radial density is 4 r^2 e^{-2r/a0}/a0^3 with mode a0, that <r>=3 a0/2, <r^2>=3 a0^2 and Delta=sqrt(3) a0/2, that the CDF is 1-e^{-2R/a0}[1+2R/a0+2(R/a0)^2] with tail 5 e^{-2} beyond a0, and that E1=-hbar^2/(2 m a0^2).
QM:010526.statement:
The normalized hydrogen $1s$ spatial wavefunction is
\[
\psi(\mathbf r)
=(\pi a_0^3)^{-1/2}\,e^{-r/a_0}.
\]
Work with the ordinary Coulomb ground state; do not add a repulsive
inverse-square term and do not change the radial boundary condition.

1. Form the radial probability density $P(r)=4\pi r^2\lvert\psi\rvert^2$
   and prove
   \[
   P(r)=\frac{4r^2}{a_0^3}\,e^{-2r/a_0}.
   \]
   Show that $P$ attains its unique maximum at the mode $r=a_0$.

2. Compute the radial moments and prove
   \[
   \langle r\rangle=\frac{3a_0}{2},\qquad
   \langle r^2\rangle=3a_0^2,\qquad
   \Delta r=\frac{\sqrt{3}\,a_0}{2}.
   \]

3. Let $F(R)=\int_0^R P(r)\,\mathrm{d}r$ be the cumulative
   distribution. Prove
   \[
   F(R)
   =1-e^{-2R/a_0}\Bigl(1+\frac{2R}{a_0}+2\Bigl(\frac{R}{a_0}\Bigr)^2\Bigr)
   \]
   and that the tail beyond one Bohr radius is
   \[
   P(r>a_0)=5e^{-2}.
   \]

4. Identify the ground-state energy as
   $E_1=-\hbar^2/(2ma_0^2)$. Audit both sentences: (i) “the radial
   density is $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$, so the mode is $r=0$”;
   (ii) “the tail beyond $a_0$ is the bare exponential $e^{-2}$,
   because the incomplete-gamma polynomial may be omitted.”
permittedResults: $\lvert\psi\rvert^2=e^{-2r/a_0}/(\pi a_0^3)$, so $P(r)=4r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}/a_0^3$. Logarithmic differentiation of $r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}$ vanishes at $r=a_0$.

$\int_0^\infty r^3 e^{-\alpha r}\,\mathrm{d}r=6/\alpha^4$ and $\int_0^\infty r^4 e^{-\alpha r}\,\mathrm{d}r=24/\alpha^5$ at $\alpha=2/a_0$ give $\langle r\rangle=3a_0/2$ and $\langle r^2\rangle=3a_0^2$. The tail polynomial at $R=a_0$ is $1+2+2=5$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert |psi|^2 into the radial density 4 pi r^2 |psi|^2, then locate the mode by differentiating r^2 e^{-2r/a0}.
Evaluate the gamma moments at alpha=2/a0 and integrate the incomplete gamma to read the CDF polynomial and the factor 5 at R=a0.

milestones.criterion: Produces the radial density 4 r^2 e^{-2r/a0}/a0^3 with mode a0, and the moments <r>=3 a0/2, <r^2>=3 a0^2, Delta=sqrt(3) a0/2.
Reports the CDF 1-e^{-2R/a0}[1+2R/a0+2(R/a0)^2], the tail 5 e^{-2} beyond a0, and E1=-hbar^2/(2 m a0^2).
Rejects a |psi|^2 mode at the origin or a bare-exponential tail, and refuses a repulsive inverse-square / altered-boundary substitution.

commonErrors.description: Treats |psi|^2 as the radial density and reports the mode as r=0 instead of the shell maximum at r=a0.
commonErrors.consequence: The required radial density 4 r^2 e^{-2r/a0}/a0^3 and the mode a0 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Omits the incomplete-gamma polynomial and reports the tail beyond a0 as e^{-2} instead of 5 e^{-2}.
commonErrors.consequence: The required CDF polynomial and the tail 5 e^{-2} are replaced by the bare Boltzmann factor.

hintTree.content: Multiply $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$ by the spherical shell $4\pi r^2$. The factor $4\pi/(\pi a_0^3)$ is $4/a_0^3$.
Set the derivative of $r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}$ to zero: $2r-(2/a_0)r^2=0$ forces the positive critical point $r=a_0$.
Integrate by parts twice, or quote $\int\rho^2 e^{-\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\rho=-e^{-\rho}(\rho^2+2\rho+2)$ after $\rho=2r/a_0$. At $R=a_0$ the parenthesis is $5$.

QM:010526.canonicalSolution:
The three-dimensional density is
\[
\lvert\psi\rvert^2
=\frac{e^{-2r/a_0}}{\pi a_0^3}.
\]
The radial density therefore reads
\[
P(r)
=4\pi r^2\lvert\psi\rvert^2
=\frac{4r^2}{a_0^3}\,e^{-2r/a_0}.
\]
Differentiating $f(r)=r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}$ gives
\[
f'(r)
=e^{-2r/a_0}\bigl(2r-\tfrac{2}{a_0}r^2\bigr),
\]
so the only positive critical point is $r=a_0$. The sign of $f'$
changes from $+$ to $-$ there, and $P(0)=P(\infty)=0$, so $r=a_0$
is the unique mode.
\[
\boxed{P(r)=4r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}/a_0^3,\;\text{mode }a_0}.
\]

With $\alpha=2/a_0$ and
$\int_0^\infty r^n e^{-\alpha r}\,\mathrm{d}r=n!/\alpha^{n+1}$,
\[
\langle r\rangle
=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\cdot\frac{6}{\alpha^4}
=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\cdot\frac{6a_0^4}{16}
=\frac{3a_0}{2},
\]
\[
\langle r^2\rangle
=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\cdot\frac{24}{\alpha^5}
=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\cdot\frac{24a_0^5}{32}
=3a_0^2.
\]
The variance is
\[
(\Delta r)^2
=3a_0^2-\Bigl(\frac{3a_0}{2}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{3a_0^2}{4},
\]
hence $\Delta r=\sqrt{3}\,a_0/2$.
\[
\boxed{\langle r\rangle=3a_0/2,\;
\langle r^2\rangle=3a_0^2,\;
\Delta r=\sqrt{3}\,a_0/2}.
\]

Set $\rho=2r/a_0$. Then
\[
P(r)\,\mathrm{d}r
=\frac12\rho^2 e^{-\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\rho,
\]
and
\[
\int\rho^2 e^{-\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\rho
=-e^{-\rho}(\rho^2+2\rho+2).
\]
Integrating from $0$ to $2R/a_0$ produces
\[
F(R)
=1-e^{-2R/a_0}\Bigl(1+\frac{2R}{a_0}+2\Bigl(\frac{R}{a_0}\Bigr)^2\Bigr).
\]
The complementary tail at $R=a_0$ is
\[
P(r>a_0)
=e^{-2}(1+2+2)
=5e^{-2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{F(R)=1-e^{-2R/a_0}[1+2R/a_0+2(R/a_0)^2],\;
P(r>a_0)=5e^{-2}}.
\]

The Bohr radius and the Rydberg energy of the pure Coulomb problem
are related by
\[
E_1=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma_0^2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_1=-\hbar^2/(2ma_0^2)}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$ with the radial density
and reports the origin as the mode. Sentence (ii) drops the
incomplete-gamma polynomial and reports the tail $e^{-2}$ instead
of $5e^{-2}$. The construction is the ordinary hydrogen $1s$
Coulomb ground state; it never adds a repulsive inverse-square
term and never changes the radial boundary condition.

graderFixtures.proofText: The radial density is $P(r)=4r^2 e^{-2r/a_0}/a_0^3$ with mode $a_0$. The moments are $\langle r\rangle=3a_0/2$, $\langle r^2\rangle=3a_0^2$, and $\Delta r=\sqrt{3}\,a_0/2$. The CDF is $1-e^{-2R/a_0}[1+2R/a_0+2(R/a_0)^2]$, the tail beyond $a_0$ is $5e^{-2}$, and $E_1=-\hbar^2/(2ma_0^2)$.
The radial density is |psi|^2, so the mode is r=0. I do not report 4 r^2 e^{-2r/a0}/a0^3 or the mode a0.
The tail beyond a0 is the bare exponential e^{-2}. I omit the polynomial 1+2+2 and I do not report 5 e^{-2}.
