SDP:010322.title: Two high-forward decades at 300 K extract n=1.5, Is=6.92263 pA, and rd=3.87780 kOhm at 10 uA
SDP:010322.objective: From the declared high-forward pair I=10 uA at 0.550000 V and I=100 uA at 0.639289644 V at 300 K, extract VT=25.8520 mV, the decade slope 89.289644 mV/dec, ideality n=1.5, Is=6.92263 pA, and rd=3.87780 kOhm at 10 uA (387.780 Ohm at 100 uA), and refuse a circuit load-line or n=1 substitution.
SDP:010322.statement:
A PN junction is measured at $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$ in the declared
high-forward exponential regime
\[
I=I_S\exp\bigl(V/(n V_T)\bigr),\qquad I\gg I_S,
\]
so the $-1$ in the Shockley factor is dropped. Two consistent points
are
\[
I_1=10\,\mu\mathrm{A}\ \text{at}\ V_1=0.550000\,\mathrm{V},
\qquad
I_2=100\,\mu\mathrm{A}\ \text{at}\ V_2=0.639289644\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
Use $k=1.380649\times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ and
$q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, and take
$V_T=kT/q$. Series resistance is neglected; $n$ and $I_S$ are
constant on this decade.

1. Prove $V_T=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. From the decade $I_2/I_1=10$,
   prove that the forward slope is
   \[
   S=V_2-V_1=89.289644\,\mathrm{mV/dec}
   \]
   and that the ideality is the unique value $n=1.5$.

2. Recover the saturation current from either point and prove
   $I_S=6.92263\,\mathrm{pA}$. Confirm that the second point returns
   the same $I_S$.

3. Linearize the high-forward law about each measured current and
   prove the incremental resistances
   \[
   r_d(10\,\mu\mathrm{A})=3.87780\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,
   \qquad
   r_d(100\,\mu\mathrm{A})=387.780\,\Omega.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “silicon is ideal, so $n=1$ and the
   decade must be $V_T\ln 10=59.526\,\mathrm{mV}$”; (ii) “this is a
   circuit load-line root, or else $r_d=V_T/I$ with $n$ omitted.”

Do not replace the extraction by a Shockley / resistor load-line
Newton solve, and do not invoke asymmetric depletion widths, Fermi
regime screens, or MOS threshold partitions.
permittedResults: At $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, $V_T=kT/q=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. One current decade forces $\Delta V=n V_T\ln 10$, so $n=\Delta V/(V_T\ln 10)$.
Once $n$ is known, $I_S=I\exp(-V/(n V_T))$ is the same at every point on the exponential, and $r_d=n V_T/I$ at each current.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form VT, divide the measured decade voltage by VT ln 10 to lock n, then back-substitute either current for Is and rd=n VT/I.
Check consistency by recovering the same Is from both points, then compare rd=n VT/I against the n=1 and VT/I foils.

milestones.criterion: Extracts VT=25.8520 mV, the decade slope 89.289644 mV/dec, and the unique ideality n=1.5 from the two high-forward points.
Reports Is=6.92263 pA and the incremental resistances 3.87780 kOhm at 10 uA and 387.780 Ohm at 100 uA.
Rejects n=1 and a load-line or n-free rd substitution, and refuses reserved depletion, Fermi-regime, or MOS-threshold replacements.

commonErrors.description: Sets n=1, takes the decade as VT ln 10=59.526 mV, and never extracts n=1.5 from the given 89.289644 mV pair.
commonErrors.consequence: Is and both incremental resistances are computed from the wrong thermal voltage n VT, so 6.92263 pA and 3.87780 kOhm are lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats the exercise as a Shockley / resistor load-line root, or writes rd=VT/I with the extracted ideality omitted.
commonErrors.consequence: The two-point extraction is replaced by a different circuit problem, or rd collapses to 2.58520 kOhm and 258.520 Ohm.

hintTree.content: $V_T=kT/q$ with the given $k,q,T$ is $25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. The decade voltage is just $V_2-V_1$.
$V_T\ln 10=59.526429\,\mathrm{mV}$. Divide the measured $89.289644\,\mathrm{mV}$ by that figure to get $n$.
Then $n V_T=38.778\,\mathrm{mV}$. Exponentiate $V_1/(n V_T)$ to recover $I_S$, and form $r_d=n V_T/I$ at each current.

SDP:010322.canonicalSolution:
The thermal voltage at the stated temperature is
\[
V_T=\frac{kT}{q}
=\frac{1.380649\times 10^{-23}\cdot 300}{1.602176634\times 10^{-19}}
=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}.
\]
The two currents differ by exactly one decade, so the measured slope
is the voltage difference itself:
\[
S=V_2-V_1=0.639289644-0.550000=89.289644\,\mathrm{mV/dec}.
\]
The high-forward law implies $S=n V_T\ln 10$. With
$\ln 10=2.302585093$ one has
\[
V_T\ln 10=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}\cdot 2.302585093=59.526429\,\mathrm{mV},
\]
and therefore
\[
n=\frac{89.289644}{59.526429}=1.5
\]
exactly. Two parameters are being fit to two consistent points, so
this $n$ is unique inside the declared model.
\[
\boxed{V_T=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV},\quad
S=89.289644\,\mathrm{mV/dec},\quad n=1.5}.
\]

The product $n V_T=1.5\cdot 25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}=38.778\,\mathrm{mV}$.
At the first point
\[
\frac{V_1}{n V_T}=\frac{0.550000}{0.038778}=14.183300,
\qquad
I_S=I_1 e^{-V_1/(n V_T)}
=10\,\mu\mathrm{A}\cdot e^{-14.183300}
=6.92263\,\mathrm{pA}.
\]
The second point is one decade higher in current and
$n V_T\ln 10=89.289644\,\mathrm{mV}$ higher in voltage, so it returns
the same $I_S$:
\[
\frac{V_2}{n V_T}=16.485885,\qquad
I_S=100\,\mu\mathrm{A}\cdot e^{-16.485885}=6.92263\,\mathrm{pA}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I_S=6.92263\,\mathrm{pA}}.
\]

High-forward linearization is $r_d=n V_T/I$ (the $I_S$ correction is
already discarded by $I\gg I_S$):
\begin{align*}
r_d(10\,\mu\mathrm{A})
&=\frac{0.038778}{10\times 10^{-6}}
=3.87780\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\\
r_d(100\,\mu\mathrm{A})
&=\frac{0.038778}{100\times 10^{-6}}
=387.780\,\Omega.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{r_d(10\,\mu\mathrm{A})=3.87780\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad
r_d(100\,\mu\mathrm{A})=387.780\,\Omega}.
\]

Sentence (i) forces $n=1$ and a $59.526\,\mathrm{mV}$ decade, which
contradicts the given $89.289644\,\mathrm{mV}$ pair and yields a
wrong $I_S$. Sentence (ii) either replaces the extraction by a
source/resistor load-line root or drops $n$ from $r_d$, producing
$V_T/I=2.58520\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $258.520\,\Omega$ instead of
the required pair.

The argument never solves a Shockley / load-line intersection, never
integrates an asymmetric depletion field, and never audits a Fermi
statistics regime or an MOS oxide partition.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $300\,\mathrm{K}$, $V_T=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. The high-forward decade $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}\to 100\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ spans $89.289644\,\mathrm{mV}$, so $n=89.289644/(V_T\ln 10)=1.5$. Then $I_S=6.92263\,\mathrm{pA}$ from either point and $r_d=n V_T/I$ equals $3.87780\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ at $10\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ and $387.780\,\Omega$ at $100\,\mu\mathrm{A}$. This is a two-parameter extraction, not a load line, and $n=1$ is incompatible with the measured decade.
A silicon PN diode is ideal, so n=1 and the current decade must be VT ln 10=59.526 mV. I do not extract n=1.5 from 89.289644 mV/dec and I do not accept Is=6.92263 pA from n=1.5.
This is a Shockley load-line root against a bias resistor. I never extract n from two currents, and I take rd=VT/I so the resistances are 2.58520 kOhm and 258.520 Ohm.

SDP:010323.title: A 0.8 eV Schottky at 300 K has Js=3.9265873e-7 A/cm2 and a 0.10 eV barrier drop multiplies Js by 47.8549
SDP:010323.objective: For A**=120 A cm^-2 K^-2, T=300 K, barrier potential PhiB=0.8 V (barrier energy q PhiB=0.8 eV), area=1e-4 cm^2, and n=1.1, obtain Js=3.9265873e-7 A/cm2, Is=39.2659 pA, I(0.30 V)=1.49837 uA, and the factor 47.8549 by which lowering the barrier energy 0.10 eV multiplies Js.
SDP:010323.statement:
A metal--semiconductor (Schottky) contact is modeled by thermionic
emission over a uniform barrier. The Richardson--Dushman saturation
current density and the device current are
\[
J_S=A^{**}T^2\exp\bigl(-q\Phi_B/kT\bigr),
\qquad
I=I_S\bigl(e^{V/(n V_T)}-1\bigr),
\qquad
I_S=J_S A,
\]
with $A^{**}=120\,\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}\,K^{-2}}$, $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$,
barrier potential $\Phi_B=0.8\,\mathrm{V}$ (equivalently barrier energy
$q\Phi_B=0.8\,\mathrm{eV}$), area $A=1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$,
and ideality $n=1.1$. Use the same constants as in the companion
extraction: $k=1.380649\times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$,
$q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, so
$V_T=kT/q=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. Image-force lowering is omitted
from the base barrier and is introduced only as the $0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$
comparison in part 3. Area units stay in $\mathrm{cm^2}$ to match
$A^{**}$.

1. Evaluate $J_S$ and prove
   $J_S=3.9265873\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}$. Multiply by the
   area and prove $I_S=39.2659\,\mathrm{pA}$.

2. At $V=0.30\,\mathrm{V}$ include the $-1$ in the Shockley factor
   and prove $I=1.49837\,\mu\mathrm{A}$.

3. Holding $A^{**}$ and $T$ fixed, lower the barrier energy by
   $0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$, equivalently $\Delta\Phi_B=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$.
   Prove that $J_S$ is multiplied by exactly
   $\exp(0.10/V_T)=47.8549$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the $T^2$ prefactor may be dropped, so
   $J_S=A^{**}e^{-\Phi_B/V_T}$”; (ii) “a $0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ barrier
   cut is a $0.10/0.8=12.5\%$ linear change in $J_S$.”

Do not replace the thermionic law by a PN depletion-field integral,
a Fermi-regime screen, or a Shockley / load-line circuit root.
permittedResults: Forward current keeps the $-1$: $I=I_S(e^{V/(n V_T)}-1)$. A barrier drop $\Delta\Phi_B$ multiplies $J_S$ by $e^{\Delta\Phi_B/V_T}$ independently of area and of $n$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Form A** T^2 and PhiB/VT, exponentiate to Js, convert by area, then evaluate I at 0.30 V and the exp(Delta PhiB/VT) ratio.
First lock VT=25.8520 mV so every exponent shares one thermal voltage, then treat the 0.10 eV shift as a pure multiplier of Js.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the Richardson law to Js=3.9265873e-7 A/cm2 and Is=39.2659 pA, keeping the T^2 prefactor and the cm^2 area.
Reports I(0.30 V)=1.49837 uA with n=1.1 and the -1 retained, and the 0.10 eV multiplier 47.8549.
Rejects a T^2-free Js or a linear 12.5% barrier shift, and refuses reserved depletion, Fermi-regime, or load-line replacements.

commonErrors.description: Writes Js=A** exp(-PhiB/VT), discarding the T^2 prefactor 300^2=9e4.
commonErrors.consequence: Js and Is are low by 90000, so 3.9265873e-7 A/cm2, 39.2659 pA, and 1.49837 uA are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats a 0.10 eV barrier reduction as the linear fraction 0.10/0.8=12.5% rather than the thermionic factor exp(0.10/VT)=47.8549.
commonErrors.consequence: The required multiplier 47.8549 is replaced by a 12.5% perturbation that is not the Richardson ratio.

hintTree.content: Compute $A^{**}T^2=1.08\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}$ and $\Phi_B/V_T=0.8/0.0258520$ before exponentiating.
Area $1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ converts $J_S$ into $I_S$ in picoamperes. At $0.30\,\mathrm{V}$ use $n V_T=28.4372\,\mathrm{mV}$.
The $0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ multiplier is $e^{0.10/0.0258520}$, not $0.10/0.8$. The $T^2$ factor does not cancel in $J_S$ itself.

SDP:010323.canonicalSolution:
The thermal voltage is again
$V_T=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$. The Richardson prefactor is
\[
A^{**}T^2=120\cdot 300^2=1.08\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}.
\]
The exponent is the barrier in units of $V_T$:
\[
\frac{q\Phi_B}{kT}=\frac{\Phi_B}{V_T}=\frac{0.8}{0.0258520}=30.945845.
\]
Therefore
\[
J_S=1.08\times 10^{7}\,e^{-30.945845}
=3.9265873\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}.
\]
The contact area converts this to a device saturation current
\[
I_S=J_S A
=3.9265873\times 10^{-7}\cdot 1\times 10^{-4}
=3.9265873\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{A}
=39.2659\,\mathrm{pA}.
\]
\[
\boxed{J_S=3.9265873\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2},\quad
I_S=39.2659\,\mathrm{pA}}.
\]

At $V=0.30\,\mathrm{V}$ the ideality-scaled thermal voltage is
$n V_T=1.1\cdot 25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}=28.4372\,\mathrm{mV}$, so
\[
\frac{V}{n V_T}=\frac{0.30}{0.0284372}=10.549551,
\qquad
e^{V/(n V_T)}=3.81564\times 10^{4}.
\]
Keeping the $-1$,
\[
I=I_S\bigl(e^{V/(n V_T)}-1\bigr)
=39.2659\,\mathrm{pA}\cdot(3.81564\times 10^{4}-1)
=1.49837\,\mu\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{I(0.30\,\mathrm{V})=1.49837\,\mu\mathrm{A}}.
\]

A barrier-potential reduction $\Delta\Phi_B=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$, equivalently
an energy reduction $q\Delta\Phi_B=0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ (same $A^{**}$,
same $T$), multiplies $J_S$ by
\[
\frac{J_S(\Phi_B-0.10)}{J_S(\Phi_B)}
=e^{0.10/V_T}
=e^{0.10/0.0258520}
=e^{3.868173}=47.8549.
\]
The $T^2$ prefactor and the area cancel in the ratio; $n$ never
enters $J_S$.
\[
\boxed{J_S\mapsto 47.8549\,J_S\text{ when }\Phi_B\mapsto\Phi_B-0.10\,\mathrm{eV}}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops $T^2$ and reports a current density
$120\,e^{-30.945845}$ that is $9\times 10^{4}$ too small. Sentence
(ii) replaces the exponential leverage $e^{\Delta\Phi_B/V_T}$ by the
linear fraction $0.10/0.8=12.5\%$.

The argument never integrates a PN depletion field, never screens a
Fermi statistics regime, and never solves a circuit load line.

graderFixtures.proofText: Richardson's law with $A^{**}T^2=1.08\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}$ and $\Phi_B/V_T=30.945845$ gives $J_S=3.9265873\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{A/cm^2}$ and $I_S=39.2659\,\mathrm{pA}$. At $0.30\,\mathrm{V}$ with $n=1.1$, $I=1.49837\,\mu\mathrm{A}$. Lowering the barrier by $0.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ multiplies $J_S$ by $e^{0.10/V_T}=47.8549$, not by $12.5\%$. The $T^2$ prefactor is required.
I take Js=A** exp(-PhiB/VT) and drop T^2. The 90000 K^2 factor is only a weak correction, so I do not report Js=3.9265873e-7 A/cm2.
Cutting the 0.8 eV barrier by 0.10 eV is a 12.5% change, so Js falls or rises by 12.5%. I do not form exp(0.10/VT)=47.8549.

SDP:010324.title: The ideal 35 mA cell has Voc=0.5388857 V, Vmp=0.4536147 V, Imp=32.75959 mA, and FF=0.7878816
SDP:010324.objective: For Iph=35 mA, Is=1 nA, n=1.2, T=300 K, and zero series/shunt resistance, obtain n VT=31.02240 mV, Voc=0.5388857 V, the MPP root (1+x)e^x=1+Iph/Is with x=14.6221677, Vmp=0.4536147 V, Imp=32.75959 mA, Pmp=14.86023 mW, and FF=0.7878816.
SDP:010324.statement:
An illuminated PN junction is modeled by the ideal single-diode law
with photocurrent $I_{\mathrm{ph}}=35\,\mathrm{mA}$, saturation
current $I_S=1\,\mathrm{nA}$, ideality $n=1.2$, and $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$.
Series resistance is zero and shunt resistance is infinite, so
\[
I(V)=I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_S\bigl(e^{V/(n V_T)}-1\bigr)
\]
on $0\le V\le V_{\mathrm{oc}}$, with $V_T=kT/q=25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}$
from the same constants as the companion packets. Superposition is
assumed: $I_{\mathrm{sc}}=I_{\mathrm{ph}}$ at $V=0$. Temperature is
fixed; no other optical or distributed-resistance corrections are
present.

1. Prove $n V_T=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}$. From $I(V_{\mathrm{oc}})=0$
   prove
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{oc}}=n V_T\ln\bigl(1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S\bigr)
   =0.5388857\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

2. Maximize $P=V I(V)$. With $x=V/(n V_T)$, prove that the unique
   interior critical point satisfies
   \[
   (1+x)e^{x}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S
   \]
   and that the physical root is $x=14.6221677$. Conclude
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{mp}}=0.4536147\,\mathrm{V},
   \qquad
   I_{\mathrm{mp}}=32.75959\,\mathrm{mA}.
   \]

3. Prove $P_{\mathrm{mp}}=14.86023\,\mathrm{mW}$ and the fill factor
   \[
   \mathrm{FF}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{mp}}}{V_{\mathrm{oc}} I_{\mathrm{ph}}}
   =0.7878816.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “maximum power occurs at
   $V_{\mathrm{mp}}=V_{\mathrm{oc}}/2$”; (ii) “the fill factor is just
   $V_{\mathrm{mp}}/V_{\mathrm{oc}}$ (or $I_{\mathrm{mp}}/I_{\mathrm{ph}}$)
   alone.”

Do not replace the implicit MPP condition by a depletion-capacitance
calculation, a continuity / quasi-Fermi boundary-value problem, or a
circuit load-line diode root.
permittedResults: Open circuit forces $e^{V_{\mathrm{oc}}/(n V_T)}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S$. Here $I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S=3.5\times 10^{7}$.
Stationarity of $P=VI$ is $I+V\,dI/dV=0$. Substituting $dI/dV=-(I_S/(n V_T))e^{V/(n V_T)}$ produces $(1+x)e^{x}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Lock Voc from I=0, then impose dP/dV=0 to obtain (1+x)e^x=1+Iph/Is and convert x into Vmp, Imp, Pmp, and FF.
Test the candidate x=14.6221677 directly in (1+x)e^x, recover Imp from the diode law, and form FF as the power-rectangle ratio.

milestones.criterion: Computes n VT=31.02240 mV and Voc=0.5388857 V from I(Voc)=0.
Solves (1+x)e^x=1+Iph/Is at x=14.6221677 and reports Vmp=0.4536147 V, Imp=32.75959 mA, Pmp=14.86023 mW, and FF=0.7878816.
Rejects Vmp=Voc/2 and a single-ratio fill factor, and refuses reserved depletion, quasi-Fermi, or load-line replacements.

commonErrors.description: Sets Vmp=Voc/2=0.2694428 V instead of solving (1+x)e^x=1+Iph/Is for x=14.6221677.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Vmp=0.4536147 V, Imp=32.75959 mA, and Pmp=14.86023 mW are all replaced by a half-Voc fiction.

commonErrors.description: Reports FF=Vmp/Voc or FF=Imp/Iph instead of Pmp/(Voc Iph)=0.7878816.
commonErrors.consequence: The fill factor is identified with one utilization ratio and the required 0.7878816 is lost.

hintTree.content: $n V_T=1.2\cdot 25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}$. Then $V_{\mathrm{oc}}=n V_T\ln(1+3.5\times 10^{7})$.
Set $dP/dV=0$ and collect $e^{x}$ to obtain $(1+x)e^{x}=35000001$. The physical root is $x=14.6221677$.
$I_{\mathrm{mp}}=I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_S(e^{x}-1)$. Fill factor uses $V_{\mathrm{oc}} I_{\mathrm{ph}}$, not $V_{\mathrm{mp}}/V_{\mathrm{oc}}$ alone.

SDP:010324.canonicalSolution:
The scaled thermal voltage is
\[
n V_T=1.2\cdot 25.8520\,\mathrm{mV}=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}.
\]
Open circuit sets $I=0$, hence
\[
e^{V_{\mathrm{oc}}/(n V_T)}=1+\frac{I_{\mathrm{ph}}}{I_S}
=1+\frac{0.035}{10^{-9}}=3.5000001\times 10^{7}.
\]
Taking the logarithm,
\[
V_{\mathrm{oc}}
=n V_T\ln(3.5000001\times 10^{7})
=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}\cdot 17.370848
=0.5388857\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{n V_T=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV},\quad V_{\mathrm{oc}}=0.5388857\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Write $x=V/(n V_T)$ and $P=V\bigl(I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_S(e^{x}-1)\bigr)$.
Differentiating and setting $dP/dV=0$ uses
$dI/dV=-(I_S/(n V_T))e^{x}$:
\[
I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_S(e^{x}-1)-x I_S e^{x}=0,
\]
which rearranges to the implicit condition
\[
(1+x)e^{x}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S=3.5000001\times 10^{7}.
\]
The unique positive root of this strictly increasing map is
$x=14.6221677$. (As a check,
$1+x=15.6221677$ and $e^{x}=2.2404148\times 10^{6}$, whose product
is $3.5000001\times 10^{7}$.) Therefore
\[
V_{\mathrm{mp}}=x\cdot n V_T
=14.6221677\cdot 31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}
=0.4536147\,\mathrm{V}
\]
and
\begin{align*}
I_{\mathrm{mp}}
&=I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_S(e^{x}-1)\\
&=35\,\mathrm{mA}-10^{-9}(2.2404148\times 10^{6}-1)\,\mathrm{A}\\
&=32.75959\,\mathrm{mA}.
\end{align*}
\[
\boxed{x=14.6221677,\quad
V_{\mathrm{mp}}=0.4536147\,\mathrm{V},\quad
I_{\mathrm{mp}}=32.75959\,\mathrm{mA}}.
\]

The maximum-power rectangle and the fill factor are
\[
P_{\mathrm{mp}}=V_{\mathrm{mp}} I_{\mathrm{mp}}
=0.4536147\cdot 32.75959\,\mathrm{mA}
=14.86023\,\mathrm{mW},
\]
\[
\mathrm{FF}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{mp}}}{V_{\mathrm{oc}} I_{\mathrm{ph}}}
=\frac{14.86023\,\mathrm{mW}}{0.5388857\cdot 35\,\mathrm{mA}}
=0.7878816.
\]
\[
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{mp}}=14.86023\,\mathrm{mW},\quad \mathrm{FF}=0.7878816}.
\]
The separate utilization ratios
$V_{\mathrm{mp}}/V_{\mathrm{oc}}=0.841764$ and
$I_{\mathrm{mp}}/I_{\mathrm{ph}}=0.935988$ multiply to the same
$\mathrm{FF}$; neither ratio alone is $\mathrm{FF}$.

Sentence (i) sets $V_{\mathrm{mp}}=V_{\mathrm{oc}}/2=0.2694428\,\mathrm{V}$,
which is not a root of $(1+x)e^{x}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S$. Sentence
(ii) reports $\mathrm{FF}=V_{\mathrm{mp}}/V_{\mathrm{oc}}$ (or
$I_{\mathrm{mp}}/I_{\mathrm{ph}}$) and never forms the power
rectangle over $V_{\mathrm{oc}} I_{\mathrm{ph}}$.

The argument never computes a depletion capacitance, never solves a
continuity / quasi-Fermi boundary-value problem, and never treats the
photocell as a dark-diode load-line circuit.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $n V_T=31.02240\,\mathrm{mV}$ the open-circuit voltage is $V_{\mathrm{oc}}=0.5388857\,\mathrm{V}$. Maximum power solves $(1+x)e^{x}=1+I_{\mathrm{ph}}/I_S$ at $x=14.6221677$, hence $V_{\mathrm{mp}}=0.4536147\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_{\mathrm{mp}}=32.75959\,\mathrm{mA}$, $P_{\mathrm{mp}}=14.86023\,\mathrm{mW}$, and $\mathrm{FF}=P_{\mathrm{mp}}/(V_{\mathrm{oc}} I_{\mathrm{ph}})=0.7878816$. Half of $V_{\mathrm{oc}}$ is not the MPP, and $\mathrm{FF}$ is not $V_{\mathrm{mp}}/V_{\mathrm{oc}}$ alone.
Maximum power is at half the open-circuit voltage, so Vmp=Voc/2=0.2694428 V. I do not solve (1+x)e^x=1+Iph/Is and I do not accept x=14.6221677.
The fill factor is the voltage ratio Vmp/Voc=0.841763, or else Imp/Iph. I never form Pmp/(Voc Iph)=0.7878816.

SDP:010325.title: An 850 nm photodiode at 100 uW has R=0.548457 A/W, RSS noise 4.38553 nA, and current SNR=12506.1
SDP:010325.objective: For 850 nm, eta=0.8, P=100 uW, Idark=5 nA, Cd=10 pF, RL=10 kOhm, T=300 K, and rectangular B=1 MHz, obtain R=0.548457 A/W, Iph=54.8457 uA, fc=1.59155 MHz, shot 4.19239 nA rms, thermal 1.28716 nA rms, RSS 4.38553 nA, and current SNR=12506.1.
SDP:010325.statement:
A reverse-biased PN photodiode is illuminated at
$\lambda=850\,\mathrm{nm}$ with optical power $P=100\,\mu\mathrm{W}$
and quantum efficiency $\eta=0.8$. The dark current is
$I_{\mathrm{dark}}=5\,\mathrm{nA}$. The junction plus stray
capacitance is $C_d=10\,\mathrm{pF}$, the load is
$R_L=10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, and the assigned
noise bandwidth is the rectangular value $B=1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ (not
the full single-pole noise bandwidth $(\pi/2)f_c$). Use
$h=6.62607015\times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$,
$c=2.99792458\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$,
$q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, and
$k=1.380649\times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Amplifier noise
and $1/f$ noise are omitted. Shot and thermal contributions are
uncorrelated.

1. Prove the responsivity and photocurrent
   \[
   \mathcal{R}=\frac{\eta q\lambda}{hc}=0.548457\,\mathrm{A/W},
   \qquad
   I_{\mathrm{ph}}=\mathcal{R}P=54.8457\,\mu\mathrm{A}.
   \]

2. Prove the load-pole frequency
   $f_c=1/(2\pi R_L C_d)=1.59155\,\mathrm{MHz}$. Note that
   $B<f_c$, so the rectangular bandwidth $B$ is the assigned noise
   window.

3. With total current $I_{\mathrm{ph}}+I_{\mathrm{dark}}$ in the
   shot formula, prove
   \[
   i_{\mathrm{shot}}=\sqrt{2q(I_{\mathrm{ph}}+I_{\mathrm{dark}})B}
   =4.19239\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}},
   \]
   \[
   i_{\mathrm{th}}=\sqrt{4kTB/R_L}=1.28716\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}},
   \]
   the RSS combination $i_n=4.38553\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}$, and the
   current signal-to-noise ratio
   $I_{\mathrm{ph}}/i_n=12506.1$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “responsivity is the quantum efficiency,
   so $\mathcal{R}=\eta=0.8\,\mathrm{A/W}$”; (ii) “shot noise uses
   only $I_{\mathrm{dark}}$, or SNR is the power ratio
   $(I_{\mathrm{ph}}/i_n)^2$.”

Do not replace the photodiode noise budget by a short-channel
scale-length argument, a MOS threshold partition, or a solar-cell
fill-factor calculation.
permittedResults: Photon energy at $850\,\mathrm{nm}$ is $hc/\lambda=2.3369947\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}=1.45864\,\mathrm{eV}$, so $\mathcal{R}=0.8\,q\lambda/(hc)$.
A current SNR is $I_{\mathrm{ph}}/i_n$. Squaring it produces a power SNR, which is a different figure and is not requested.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert hc/lambda into responsivity, then evaluate the RC pole and the two current-noise densities under rectangular B.
Form Iph first, add Idark only inside the shot formula, RSS-combine with Johnson current, and quote SNR as Iph/in.

milestones.criterion: Computes R=0.548457 A/W, Iph=54.8457 uA, and fc=1.59155 MHz, keeping B as the rectangular 1 MHz window below fc.
Reports shot 4.19239 nA from Iph+Idark, thermal 1.28716 nA, RSS 4.38553 nA, and current SNR=12506.1.
Rejects R=eta or dark-only/power SNR substitutions, and refuses reserved short-channel, MOS-threshold, or fill-factor replacements.

commonErrors.description: Sets R=eta=0.8 A/W and Iph=80 uA, never forming eta q lambda/(h c)=0.548457 A/W.
commonErrors.consequence: The photocurrent, both noise currents that depend on Iph, and SNR=12506.1 are all computed from the wrong optical conversion.

commonErrors.description: Forms shot noise from Idark alone, or reports the power SNR (Iph/in)^2 instead of the current ratio 12506.1.
commonErrors.consequence: The required 4.19239 nA shot term and the current SNR 12506.1 are replaced by a dark-only or squared figure.

hintTree.content: Compute $E_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda$ first, then $\mathcal{R}=\eta q/E_{\mathrm{ph}}$, then $I_{\mathrm{ph}}=\mathcal{R}P$.
$2\pi R_L C_d=2\pi\cdot 10^{4}\cdot 10^{-11}=2\pi\times 10^{-7}$. The pole is the reciprocal.
Shot uses $I_{\mathrm{ph}}+I_{\mathrm{dark}}=54.8507\,\mu\mathrm{A}$, not $5\,\mathrm{nA}$ alone. SNR is the current ratio.

SDP:010325.canonicalSolution:
The photon energy at $850\,\mathrm{nm}$ is
\[
E_{\mathrm{ph}}=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
=\frac{6.62607015\times 10^{-34}\cdot 2.99792458\times 10^{8}}{850\times 10^{-9}}
=2.3369947\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}
=1.45864\,\mathrm{eV}.
\]
Responsivity and photocurrent follow at once:
\[
\mathcal{R}=\frac{\eta q}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}
=\frac{0.8\cdot 1.602176634\times 10^{-19}}{2.3369947\times 10^{-19}}
=0.548457\,\mathrm{A/W},
\]
\[
I_{\mathrm{ph}}=\mathcal{R}P
=0.548457\cdot 100\,\mu\mathrm{W}
=54.8457\,\mu\mathrm{A}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathcal{R}=0.548457\,\mathrm{A/W},\quad
I_{\mathrm{ph}}=54.8457\,\mu\mathrm{A}}.
\]

The $R_L C_d$ pole is
\[
f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi R_L C_d}
=\frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 10^{4}\cdot 10\times 10^{-12}}
=1.59155\,\mathrm{MHz}.
\]
The assigned rectangular bandwidth $B=1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ lies below
this pole, so no $(\pi/2)f_c$ noise-bandwidth substitution is
authorized.
\[
\boxed{f_c=1.59155\,\mathrm{MHz},\quad B=1\,\mathrm{MHz}<f_c}.
\]

Shot noise uses the total current through the junction:
\[
I_{\mathrm{tot}}=I_{\mathrm{ph}}+I_{\mathrm{dark}}
=54.8457\,\mu\mathrm{A}+5\,\mathrm{nA}
=54.8507\,\mu\mathrm{A},
\]
\[
i_{\mathrm{shot}}
=\sqrt{2q I_{\mathrm{tot}} B}
=\sqrt{2\cdot 1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\cdot 54.8507\times 10^{-6}\cdot 10^{6}}
=4.19239\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}.
\]
The load resistor's Johnson current (equivalently
$\sqrt{4kTR_L B}/R_L$) is
\[
i_{\mathrm{th}}
=\sqrt{\frac{4kTB}{R_L}}
=\sqrt{\frac{4\cdot 1.380649\times 10^{-23}\cdot 300\cdot 10^{6}}{10^{4}}}
=1.28716\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}.
\]
Uncorrelated RSS combination and the current SNR are
\[
i_n=\sqrt{i_{\mathrm{shot}}^2+i_{\mathrm{th}}^2}
=\sqrt{4.19239^2+1.28716^2}\,\mathrm{nA}
=4.38553\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}},
\]
\[
\mathrm{SNR}_I=\frac{I_{\mathrm{ph}}}{i_n}
=\frac{54.8457\times 10^{-6}}{4.38553\times 10^{-9}}
=12506.1.
\]
\[
\boxed{i_{\mathrm{shot}}=4.19239\,\mathrm{nA},\quad
i_{\mathrm{th}}=1.28716\,\mathrm{nA},\quad
i_n=4.38553\,\mathrm{nA},\quad
\mathrm{SNR}_I=12506.1}.
\]

Sentence (i) sets $\mathcal{R}=\eta=0.8\,\mathrm{A/W}$ and
$I_{\mathrm{ph}}=80\,\mu\mathrm{A}$, ignoring $hc/\lambda$. Sentence
(ii) either forms shot noise from $I_{\mathrm{dark}}$ alone
($\sqrt{2q I_{\mathrm{dark}} B}=0.0400272\,\mathrm{nA}$) or reports
the power SNR $(I_{\mathrm{ph}}/i_n)^2$ instead of the requested
current ratio.

The argument never invokes a short-channel scale length, an MOS
threshold oxide partition, or a photovoltaic fill factor.

graderFixtures.proofText: At $850\,\mathrm{nm}$, $\mathcal{R}=\eta q\lambda/(hc)=0.548457\,\mathrm{A/W}$ and $I_{\mathrm{ph}}=54.8457\,\mu\mathrm{A}$. The load pole is $f_c=1.59155\,\mathrm{MHz}>B$. Shot noise from $I_{\mathrm{ph}}+I_{\mathrm{dark}}$ is $4.19239\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}$, Johnson current is $1.28716\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}$, RSS is $4.38553\,\mathrm{nA_{rms}}$, and the current SNR is $12506.1$. Responsivity is not $\eta$, and SNR is not the squared power ratio.
Responsivity equals the quantum efficiency, so R=0.8 A/W and Iph=80 uA at 100 uW. I do not divide by the 850 nm photon energy and I do not accept 0.548457 A/W.
Shot noise is set by the dark current alone, so ishot=sqrt(2 q Idark B). I also report SNR as (Iph/in)^2 rather than the current ratio 12506.1.

SDP:010330.title: One-sided Ec=3e5 V/cm toy breaks at W=1.939749 um and VBR=29.09623 V
SDP:010330.objective: For the declared one-sided abrupt toy with ND=1e16 cm^-3, eps_s=11.7 eps0, and Ec=3e5 V/cm, prove W=1.939749 um and VBR=29.09623 V; at half doping prove W=3.879497 um and VBR=58.19246 V. Make no edge, fabricated, or safety claim.
SDP:010330.statement:
A one-sided abrupt $p^{+}n$ junction is given the constant-critical-
field toy
\[
E_{\mathrm{peak}}=E_c=3\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{V/cm}
\]
at breakdown. The lighter doping is $N_D=1\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$
and the semiconductor permittivity is $\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0$
with
$\varepsilon_0=8.854187817\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{F/cm}$. Take
$q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. In this model the
depletion field is a triangle of height $E_c$ and base $W$, Poisson
fixes
\[
W=\frac{\varepsilon_s E_c}{q N_D},
\]
and the breakdown voltage is the triangle area
\[
V_{\mathrm{BR}}=\frac12 E_c W.
\]

1. At $N_D=1\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ prove
   \[
   W=1.939749\,\mu\mathrm{m},\qquad
   V_{\mathrm{BR}}=29.09623\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

2. Repeat at half doping $N_D'=N_D/2$, keeping $E_c$ fixed. Prove
   that both $W$ and $V_{\mathrm{BR}}$ double:
   \[
   W'=3.879497\,\mu\mathrm{m},\qquad
   V_{\mathrm{BR}}'=58.19246\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

3. Confirm the scaling $W\propto 1/N_D$ and $V_{\mathrm{BR}}\propto 1/N_D$
   for this constant-$E_c$ triangle, and note that a full ionization-
   integral model is a different problem.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$V_{\mathrm{BR}}=E_c W$ because the
   field is constant across $W$”; (ii) “$29.09623\,\mathrm{V}$ is a
   fabricated, edge-limited, or safety-rated breakdown voltage.”
   Do not replace the toy by a standard built-in-voltage piecewise
   depletion audit, and do not treat the numbers as a hardware
   rating.

The construction is an analytical critical-field toy. It is not a
measured avalanche voltage and not a clearance or protection limit.
permittedResults: With $\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0$ and $N_D=1\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, $W=\varepsilon_s E_c/(q N_D)$ evaluates to $1.939749\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.
Because $W\propto 1/N_D$ at fixed $E_c$, both $W$ and $V_{\mathrm{BR}}=\tfrac12 E_c W$ double when $N_D$ is halved.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate W=eps_s Ec/(q ND) in centimetres, then take the triangle area (1/2) Ec W.
Use the exact 1/ND scaling of the constant-Ec toy to double both W and VBR at half doping.

milestones.criterion: Computes W=1.939749 um and VBR=29.09623 V from the one-sided triangle at ND=1e16 cm^-3.
Shows that half doping doubles both results to W=3.879497 um and VBR=58.19246 V.
Rejects VBR=Ec W and any fabricated, edge, or safety claim, and refuses reserved PN-depletion substitutions.

commonErrors.consequence: The required triangle voltage 29.09623 V is replaced by its double, and the half-doping comparison is shifted by the same factor.

commonErrors.description: Reports 29.09623 V or 58.19246 V as a fabricated, edge-limited, or safety-rated breakdown voltage.
commonErrors.consequence: An analytical critical-field toy is converted into a hardware or protection claim the packet forbids.

hintTree.content: Keep every quantity in centimetres: $\varepsilon_0=8.854187817\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{F/cm}$ and $E_c=3\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{V/cm}$.
After $W$ is known, $V_{\mathrm{BR}}$ is half of $E_c W$, not the full product. $E_c W=58.19246\,\mathrm{V}$.
Halving $N_D$ doubles $W$ at fixed $E_c$. The same factor doubles $V_{\mathrm{BR}}$. Neither number is a safety limit.

SDP:010330.canonicalSolution:
Insert the declared constants:
\[
\varepsilon_s
=11.7\cdot 8.854187817\times 10^{-14}
=1.0359399746\times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/cm}.
\]
Poisson at peak field $E_c$ gives
\[
W
=\frac{\varepsilon_s E_c}{q N_D}
=\frac{1.0359399746\times 10^{-12}\cdot 3\times 10^{5}}
{1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\cdot 1\times 10^{16}}
=1.939749\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm}
=1.939749\,\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
The triangle area is
\[
V_{\mathrm{BR}}
=\frac12\cdot 3\times 10^{5}\cdot 1.939749\times 10^{-4}
=29.09623\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\[
\boxed{W=1.939749\,\mu\mathrm{m},\;
V_{\mathrm{BR}}=29.09623\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

At $N_D'=5\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ the same $E_c$ doubles
the width and the voltage:
\[
W'=2W=3.879497\,\mu\mathrm{m},\qquad
V_{\mathrm{BR}}'=2V_{\mathrm{BR}}=58.19246\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
Equivalently $W\propto 1/N_D$ and $V_{\mathrm{BR}}\propto 1/N_D$
inside this constant-$E_c$ toy. An ionization-integral
$E_c(N_D)$ would break that exact doubling; that is a different
model.
\[
\boxed{W'=3.879497\,\mu\mathrm{m},\;
V_{\mathrm{BR}}'=58.19246\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the triangle by a rectangle and reports
$E_c W=58.19246\,\mathrm{V}$ at the original doping. Sentence (ii)
promotes $29.09623\,\mathrm{V}$ into a fabricated, edge-limited,
or safety-rated breakdown. The argument never performs a standard
built-in-voltage piecewise depletion audit and never claims a
hardware rating.

The construction remains a held analytical toy. It is not an
edge breakdown, not a measured avalanche voltage, and not a
clearance or protection limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The one-sided triangle with $E_c=3\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{V/cm}$ gives $W=\varepsilon_s E_c/(q N_D)=1.939749\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and $V_{\mathrm{BR}}=\tfrac12 E_c W=29.09623\,\mathrm{V}$. Halving $N_D$ doubles both to $3.879497\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and $58.19246\,\mathrm{V}$. $V_{\mathrm{BR}}$ is not $E_c W$, and neither voltage is a fabricated or safety rating.
The field equals Ec across the whole depletion layer, so VBR=Ec W=58.19246 V at ND=1e16 cm^-3. I do not accept the triangle value 29.09623 V.
29.09623 V is the fabricated breakdown rating of this junction and may be used as an edge-limited safety limit. Half doping is then a 58.19246 V protection specification.

SDP:010427.title: High-frequency MOS C-V on 20 nm oxide reaches Cmin=2.163166 pF and ratio 0.1252872
SDP:010427.objective: For A=1e-4 cm2, tox=20 nm, NA=5e15 cm^-3, ni=1e10 cm^-3 at 300 K, prove phiF=0.3392393 V, Cox'=1.7265666e-7 F/cm2, Cox=17.26567 pF, Wdmax=0.4188998 um, Cdep=2.473002 pF, high-frequency Cmin=2.163166 pF, and Cmin/Cox=0.1252872 in series, refusing threshold and body-effect substitutions.
SDP:010427.statement:
An ideal p-type MOS capacitor has gate area
$A=1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}$, oxide thickness
$t_{\mathrm{ox}}=20\,\mathrm{nm}$, substrate doping
$N_A=5\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, and intrinsic concentration
$n_i=1\times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ at $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$. Take
\[
k=1.380649\times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K},\qquad
q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C},\qquad
\varepsilon_0=8.854187817\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{F/cm},
\]
$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ox}}=3.9\varepsilon_0$, and
$\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0$. The Fermi potential is
$\phi_F=(kT/q)\ln(N_A/n_i)$. Oxide capacitance per unit area is
$C_{\mathrm{ox}}'=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ox}}/t_{\mathrm{ox}}$. At the
onset of strong inversion the maximum depletion width is the
two-Fermi-potential construction
\[
W_{d,\max}=\sqrt{\frac{4\varepsilon_s\phi_F}{q N_A}}.
\]
High-frequency $C$–$V$ treats the inversion sheet as too slow to
follow the probe, so the measured minimum is the series stack of
$C_{\mathrm{ox}}=C_{\mathrm{ox}}'A$ and
$C_{\mathrm{dep}}=A\varepsilon_s/W_{d,\max}$.

1. Prove
   \[
   \phi_F=0.3392393\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   C_{\mathrm{ox}}'=1.7265666\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{F/cm}^{2},\qquad
   C_{\mathrm{ox}}=17.26567\,\mathrm{pF}.
   \]

2. Prove
   \[
   W_{d,\max}=0.4188998\,\mu\mathrm{m},\qquad
   C_{\mathrm{dep}}=2.473002\,\mathrm{pF}.
   \]

3. Form the high-frequency series minimum and the normalized swing
   \[
   C_{\min}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{ox}}C_{\mathrm{dep}}}{C_{\mathrm{ox}}+C_{\mathrm{dep}}}
   =2.163166\,\mathrm{pF},\qquad
   \frac{C_{\min}}{C_{\mathrm{ox}}}=0.1252872.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “at strong inversion the inversion
   charge follows the probe, so $C_{\min}=C_{\mathrm{ox}}$”;
   (ii) “$W_{d,\max}$ uses only one $\phi_F$, or the problem is
   really a threshold/body-effect charge-sheet calculation.” Keep
   the series model. Do not compute a threshold voltage
   $V_{\mathrm{th}}$, introduce a body coefficient, or replace the
   capacitor by a Fermi-level
   neutrality root or a quasi-Fermi continuity profile.

The numbers are a held analytical stack, not a fabricated $C$–$V$
trace and not a process-control limit.
permittedResults: With $kT/q=0.025851999786\,\mathrm{V}$ and $\ln(N_A/n_i)=\ln(5\times 10^{5})=13.1223633774$, one has $\phi_F=0.3392393\,\mathrm{V}$. Then $C_{\mathrm{ox}}'=3.9\varepsilon_0/t_{\mathrm{ox}}$ with $t_{\mathrm{ox}}=2\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Poisson in a uniformly doped depletion layer at band bending $2\phi_F$ gives $W_{d,\max}=\sqrt{4\varepsilon_s\phi_F/(q N_A)}$. Series combination yields $C_{\min}^{-1}=C_{\mathrm{ox}}^{-1}+C_{\mathrm{dep}}^{-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate phiF and Cox' first, convert to Cox with the given area, then form Wdmax from 4 phiF and the series Cmin.
Compute Cdep=A eps_s/Wdmax and immediately take the parallel-reciprocal series combination, checking the ratio Cdep/(Cox+Cdep).

milestones.criterion: Computes phiF=0.3392393 V, Cox'=1.7265666e-7 F/cm2, and Cox=17.26567 pF from the stated constants and geometry.
Evaluates Wdmax=0.4188998 um, Cdep=2.473002 pF, high-frequency Cmin=2.163166 pF, and Cmin/Cox=0.1252872 as a series stack.
Rejects low-frequency Cmin=Cox and threshold/body-effect substitutions, and refuses reserved Fermi-level or quasi-Fermi replacements.

commonErrors.description: Treats inversion charge as able to follow the probe and reports Cmin=Cox=17.26567 pF (ratio 1) instead of the high-frequency series stack.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Cmin=2.163166 pF and ratio 0.1252872 disappear, and Wdmax is never used as a capacitor.

commonErrors.description: Builds Wdmax from only one phiF, or replaces the C-V stack by a MOS threshold/body-effect charge-sheet calculation.
commonErrors.consequence: Wdmax=0.4188998 um and Cdep=2.473002 pF are lost, and the packet is converted into a reserved seed family.

hintTree.content: Convert $t_{\mathrm{ox}}=20\,\mathrm{nm}$ to $2\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$ before dividing $3.9\varepsilon_0$. The area factor $A=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ converts $C_{\mathrm{ox}}'$ into picofarads.
The four, not two, in $W_{d,\max}$ is $2\times(2\phi_F)$. Keep $\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0$ and $N_A=5\times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ in centimetres.
High-frequency $C_{\min}$ is smaller than both $C_{\mathrm{ox}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{dep}}$. The ratio $C_{\min}/C_{\mathrm{ox}}$ is $C_{\mathrm{dep}}/(C_{\mathrm{ox}}+C_{\mathrm{dep}})$, not $1$.

SDP:010427.canonicalSolution:
The thermal voltage at $300\,\mathrm{K}$ is
\[
\frac{kT}{q}
=\frac{1.380649\times 10^{-23}\cdot 300}{1.602176634\times 10^{-19}}
=0.025851999786\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
Then
\[
\phi_F
=\frac{kT}{q}\ln\Bigl(\frac{5\times 10^{15}}{1\times 10^{10}}\Bigr)
=0.025851999786\ln(5\times 10^{5})
=0.3392393\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The oxide thickness is $t_{\mathrm{ox}}=20\,\mathrm{nm}=2\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$, so
\[
C_{\mathrm{ox}}'
=\frac{3.9\cdot 8.854187817\times 10^{-14}}{2\times 10^{-6}}
=1.7265666\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{F/cm}^{2}
\]
and
\[
C_{\mathrm{ox}}
=C_{\mathrm{ox}}'A
=1.7265666\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{F}
=17.26567\,\mathrm{pF}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\phi_F=0.3392393\,\mathrm{V},\;
C_{\mathrm{ox}}'=1.7265666\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{F/cm}^{2},\;
C_{\mathrm{ox}}=17.26567\,\mathrm{pF}}.
\]

With $\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0$,
\[
W_{d,\max}
=\sqrt{\frac{4\cdot 11.7\cdot 8.854187817\times 10^{-14}\cdot 0.3392393}
{1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\cdot 5\times 10^{15}}}
=4.188998\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}
=0.4188998\,\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
The depletion capacitor on area $A$ is
\[
C_{\mathrm{dep}}
=\frac{A\varepsilon_s}{W_{d,\max}}
=2.473002\,\mathrm{pF}.
\]
\[
\boxed{W_{d,\max}=0.4188998\,\mu\mathrm{m},\;
C_{\mathrm{dep}}=2.473002\,\mathrm{pF}}.
\]

High-frequency $C$–$V$ places $C_{\mathrm{ox}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{dep}}$
in series:
\[
C_{\min}
=\frac{17.26567\cdot 2.473002}{17.26567+2.473002}
=2.163166\,\mathrm{pF},
\]
\[
\frac{C_{\min}}{C_{\mathrm{ox}}}=0.1252872.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_{\min}=2.163166\,\mathrm{pF},\;
C_{\min}/C_{\mathrm{ox}}=0.1252872}.
\]

Sentence (i) is the low-frequency inversion model, which returns
$C_{\mathrm{ox}}$ rather than the series minimum. Sentence (ii)
either drops the second $\phi_F$ in $W_{d,\max}$ or replaces the
capacitor by a threshold/body-effect charge sheet. This packet never
computes a threshold voltage $V_{\mathrm{th}}$, introduces a body
factor, or solves a Fermi-level neutrality root or a quasi-Fermi
continuity profile.

The stack is an analytical high-frequency model. It is not a
measured $C$–$V$ curve and not a fabricated-process specification.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $kT/q$ at $300\,\mathrm{K}$, $\phi_F=0.3392393\,\mathrm{V}$, $C_{\mathrm{ox}}'=1.7265666\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{F/cm}^{2}$, and $C_{\mathrm{ox}}=17.26567\,\mathrm{pF}$. Then $W_{d,\max}=\sqrt{4\varepsilon_s\phi_F/(q N_A)}=0.4188998\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and $C_{\mathrm{dep}}=2.473002\,\mathrm{pF}$. High-frequency series combination gives $C_{\min}=2.163166\,\mathrm{pF}$ and $C_{\min}/C_{\mathrm{ox}}=0.1252872$. This is not $C_{\min}=C_{\mathrm{ox}}$ and not a threshold-voltage/body-effect calculation.
In strong inversion the inversion charge follows the AC probe, so Cmin equals Cox=17.26567 pF and the ratio is 1. I never place Cox in series with Cdep.
I take Wdmax=sqrt(2 eps_s phiF/(q NA)) using only one phiF, and I replace the C-V request by a threshold and body-effect charge-sheet calculation of Vth.

SDP:010526.title: A 450 nm 20 mA / 3 V LED at 20 mW optical has EQE=0.3629495, extraction=0.4536868, and wall-plug 1/3
SDP:010526.objective: For a 450 nm LED driven at 20 mA and 3 V with 20 mW extracted optical power and IQE=0.8, obtain E_ph=4.4143241e-19 J=2.7552044 eV, electron rate 1.2483018e17 /s, photon rate 4.5307049e16 /s, EQE=0.3629495, extraction=0.4536868, wall-plug=1/3, and nonoptical 40 mW.
SDP:010526.statement:
A $450\,\mathrm{nm}$ electroluminescent diode (LED) is driven at
$I=20\,\mathrm{mA}$ and $V=3\,\mathrm{V}$. The extracted optical
power in the $450\,\mathrm{nm}$ line is $P_{\mathrm{opt}}=20\,\mathrm{mW}$,
and the internal quantum efficiency is given as $\mathrm{IQE}=0.8$.
Use
$h=6.62607015\times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$,
$c=2.99792458\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and
$q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Treat the optical output
as monochromatic at $450\,\mathrm{nm}$. Electrical input is $IV$.
This is an efficiency audit of a luminescent junction, not a BJT
base-transport or emitter-injection calculation.

1. Prove the photon energy
   \[
   E_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/\lambda
   =4.4143241\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}
   =2.7552044\,\mathrm{eV}.
   \]

2. Convert the drive current and the optical power into rates and
   prove
   \[
   \Gamma_e=I/q=1.2483018\times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},
   \qquad
   \Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}=P_{\mathrm{opt}}/E_{\mathrm{ph}}
   =4.5307049\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}.
   \]
   Conclude that the external quantum efficiency is
   $\mathrm{EQE}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}/\Gamma_e=0.3629495$.

3. Using $\mathrm{EQE}=\mathrm{IQE}\cdot\eta_{\mathrm{ext}}$, prove
   the extraction efficiency $\eta_{\mathrm{ext}}=0.4536868$. Prove
   that the wall-plug efficiency is
   $P_{\mathrm{opt}}/(IV)=1/3$ and that the non-optical power is
   $IV-P_{\mathrm{opt}}=40\,\mathrm{mW}$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “EQE is the wall-plug ratio
   $P_{\mathrm{opt}}/(IV)=1/3$”; (ii) “extraction equals the given
   IQE, or $\mathrm{EQE}=\mathrm{IQE}$ with extraction omitted.”

Do not replace the efficiency split by a finite-base BJT transport
factor, an emitter-injection-efficiency argument, or a short-channel
scale-length limit.
permittedResults: With $hc=1239.84198\,\mathrm{eV\cdot nm}$, a $450\,\mathrm{nm}$ photon has energy $2.7552044\,\mathrm{eV}=4.4143241\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

$\Gamma_e=I/q$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}=P_{\mathrm{opt}}/E_{\mathrm{ph}}$ convert the two measured powers into the EQE ratio. Then $\eta_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathrm{EQE}/\mathrm{IQE}$ and $\eta_{\mathrm{WP}}=P_{\mathrm{opt}}/(IV)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert lambda into E_ph, form the two rates I/q and Popt/E_ph, then split EQE=IQE*eta_ext and Popt/(IV).
First lock wall-plug=20/60=1/3 and the 40 mW remainder, then show EQE is the distinct rate ratio 0.3629495 whose quotient by IQE is extraction.

milestones.criterion: Reports extraction=0.4536868, wall-plug=1/3, and nonoptical power 40 mW.
Rejects identifying EQE with wall-plug or extraction with IQE, and refuses reserved BJT-transport or short-channel replacements.

commonErrors.description: Identifies EQE with the wall-plug ratio Popt/(IV)=1/3 and never forms Gamma_ph/Gamma_e=0.3629495.
commonErrors.consequence: The required EQE=0.3629495 and the extraction 0.4536868 derived from it are replaced by a power-ratio figure.

commonErrors.description: Sets eta_ext=IQE=0.8, or sets EQE=IQE, omitting EQE=IQE*eta_ext.
commonErrors.consequence: The required extraction 0.4536868 and the EQE 0.3629495 split are lost.

hintTree.content: $E_{\mathrm{ph}}=hc/450\,\mathrm{nm}$. Divide by $q$ to report electron-volts, or keep joules for the photon rate.
Electron rate is $20\,\mathrm{mA}/q$. Photon rate is $20\,\mathrm{mW}/E_{\mathrm{ph}}$. EQE is their ratio.
Extraction is $\mathrm{EQE}/0.8$. Wall-plug is $20\,\mathrm{mW}/60\,\mathrm{mW}=1/3$, leaving $40\,\mathrm{mW}$ non-optical.

SDP:010526.canonicalSolution:
The $450\,\mathrm{nm}$ photon energy is
\[
E_{\mathrm{ph}}
=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
=\frac{6.62607015\times 10^{-34}\cdot 2.99792458\times 10^{8}}{450\times 10^{-9}}
=4.4143241\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}.
\]
Dividing by $q$ gives the same energy in electron-volts:
\[
E_{\mathrm{ph}}/q
=\frac{1239.84198\,\mathrm{eV\cdot nm}}{450\,\mathrm{nm}}
=2.7552044\,\mathrm{eV}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_{\mathrm{ph}}=4.4143241\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}
=2.7552044\,\mathrm{eV}}.
\]

Injected electrons and extracted photons per second are
\[
\Gamma_e=\frac{I}{q}
=\frac{20\times 10^{-3}}{1.602176634\times 10^{-19}}
=1.2483018\times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]
\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{opt}}}{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}
=\frac{20\times 10^{-3}}{4.4143241\times 10^{-19}}
=4.5307049\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}.
\]
External quantum efficiency is the ratio of those rates:
\[
\mathrm{EQE}
=\frac{\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}}{\Gamma_e}
=\frac{4.5307049\times 10^{16}}{1.2483018\times 10^{17}}
=0.3629495.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Gamma_e=1.2483018\times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}=4.5307049\times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad
\mathrm{EQE}=0.3629495}.
\]

The given internal quantum efficiency factors as
$\mathrm{EQE}=\mathrm{IQE}\cdot\eta_{\mathrm{ext}}$, so
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{ext}}
=\frac{\mathrm{EQE}}{\mathrm{IQE}}
=\frac{0.3629495}{0.8}
=0.4536868.
\]
Electrical input power is $IV=20\,\mathrm{mA}\cdot 3\,\mathrm{V}=60\,\mathrm{mW}$,
hence
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{WP}}
=\frac{P_{\mathrm{opt}}}{IV}

SDP:010529.title: WB=0.50 um base transit of 50 ps sets fT=1.98944 GHz; half WB raises fT by 1.88235
SDP:010529.objective: For WB=0.50 um, Dn=25 cm2/s, emitter delay 20 ps, and collector delay 10 ps, prove tauB=50 ps, total 80 ps, fT=1.98944 GHz; after half WB prove tauB=12.5 ps, total 42.5 ps, fT=3.74482 GHz, and increase 1.88235, refusing a finite-base gain decomposition.
SDP:010529.statement:
A uniformly doped npn has neutral base width $W_B=0.50\,\mu\mathrm{m}$
and minority-electron diffusivity $D_n=25\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}/\mathrm{s}$.
Charge-control delays outside the base are declared as an emitter
charging time $\tau_E=20\,\mathrm{ps}$ and a collector delay
$\tau_C=10\,\mathrm{ps}$. The low-field uniform-base transit time is
\[
\tau_B=\frac{W_B^{2}}{2 D_n},
\]
the total delay used here is $\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}=\tau_B+\tau_E+\tau_C$,
and the delay-sum unity-gain frequency is
\[
f_T=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}}.
\]

1. Convert $W_B$ to centimetres and prove
   \[
   \tau_B=50\,\mathrm{ps},\qquad
   \tau_{\mathrm{ec}}=80\,\mathrm{ps},\qquad
   f_T=1.98944\,\mathrm{GHz}.
   \]

2. Repeat at half base width $W_B'=W_B/2$, keeping $\tau_E$ and
   $\tau_C$ fixed. Prove
   \[
   \tau_B'=12.5\,\mathrm{ps},\qquad
   \tau_{\mathrm{ec}}'=42.5\,\mathrm{ps},\qquad
   f_T'=3.74482\,\mathrm{GHz}.
   \]

3. Prove that the frequency increase is the delay ratio
   \[
   \frac{f_T'}{f_T}=\frac{80}{42.5}=1.88235.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the factor $2$ in $\tau_B$ may be
   dropped, so $\tau_B=W_B^{2}/D_n$”; (ii) “$f_T$ is $1/\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}$
   rather than $1/(2\pi\tau_{\mathrm{ec}})$.” Do not replace the
   delay sum by a finite-base minority-profile gain decomposition
   ($\alpha$, $\beta$, transport factor), and do not invoke a
   quasi-Fermi continuity profile.

These $f_T$ figures are delay-sum identities for the stated toy.
They are not measured cutoff frequencies of a fabricated BJT.

Halving $W_B$ quarters $\tau_B$. Because $f_T\propto 1/\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}$, the frequency ratio equals $80/42.5$.

Write $W_B=0.50\,\mu\mathrm{m}=5.0\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}$. Then
\[
\tau_B
=\frac{(5.0\times 10^{-5})^{2}}{2\cdot 25}
=\frac{2.5\times 10^{-9}}{50}
=5.0\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{s}
=50\,\mathrm{ps}.
\]
The declared extras give
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}=50+20+10=80\,\mathrm{ps},
\]
so
\[
f_T
=\frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 80\times 10^{-12}}
=1.98944\,\mathrm{GHz}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau_B=50\,\mathrm{ps},\;
\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}=80\,\mathrm{ps},\;
f_T=1.98944\,\mathrm{GHz}}.
\]

At $W_B'=0.25\,\mu\mathrm{m}=2.5\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}$,
\[
\tau_B'
=\frac{(2.5\times 10^{-5})^{2}}{50}
=12.5\,\mathrm{ps}.
\]
Emitter and collector delays are held fixed, so
\[
\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}'=12.5+20+10=42.5\,\mathrm{ps},
\]
\[
f_T'
=\frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 42.5\times 10^{-12}}
=3.74482\,\mathrm{GHz}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\tau_B'=12.5\,\mathrm{ps},\;
\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}'=42.5\,\mathrm{ps},\;
f_T'=3.74482\,\mathrm{GHz}}.
\]

Because $f_T$ is reciprocal in the delay sum,
\[
\frac{f_T'}{f_T}
=\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{ec}}'}
=\frac{80}{42.5}
=1.88235.
\]
The increase is not $4$, because $\tau_E+\tau_C$ does not scale with
$W_B$.
\[
\boxed{f_T'/f_T=1.88235}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $\tau_B=W_B^{2}/(2 D_n)$ by $W_B^{2}/D_n$,
doubling the base delay to $100\,\mathrm{ps}$. Sentence (ii) drops
the $2\pi$ in $f_T$. The argument never constructs a finite-base
minority profile, never reports $\beta$ or a transport factor, and
never solves a quasi-Fermi continuity problem.

The figures are delay-sum identities for the stated widths. They
are not a fabricated $f_T$ measurement.

SDP:010531.title: Qc=0.65 well screen keeps E2=0.2244956 eV under 0.26 eV by 35.5044 meV
SDP:010531.objective: For DeltaEg=0.40 eV, Qc=0.65, well=10 nm, and me=0.067 m0, prove DeltaEc=0.26 eV, DeltaEv=0.14 eV, infinite-well E1=0.0561239 eV, E2=0.2244956 eV, E3=0.5051151 eV, that the first two lie below the barrier with E2 margin 35.5044 meV while E3 is above, and that E2-E1=0.1683717 eV corresponds to 7.36372 um. Treat the result as a screen, not an exact finite-well count.
SDP:010531.statement:
A type-I heterojunction is assigned a gap difference
$\Delta E_g=0.40\,\mathrm{eV}$ and a conduction-band offset ratio
$Q_c=0.65$, so
\[
\Delta E_c=Q_c\Delta E_g,\qquad
\Delta E_v=(1-Q_c)\Delta E_g.
\]
A rectangular well of width $L=10\,\mathrm{nm}$ is to be screened
with the infinite-wall spectrum
\[
E_n=\frac{n^{2}\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}}{2 m_e^{*} L^{2}},\qquad
m_e^{*}=0.067\,m_0,
\]
using
\[
\hbar=1.054571817\times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s},\qquad
m_0=9.1093837\times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg},\qquad
q=1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}.
\]
A level is provisionally inside the electron well when $E_n<\Delta E_c$.
The $1\to 2$ spacing is converted with $hc=1.23984198\,\mathrm{eV\cdot\mu m}$.

1. Prove
   \[
   \Delta E_c=0.26\,\mathrm{eV},\qquad
   \Delta E_v=0.14\,\mathrm{eV}.
   \]

2. Prove the first three infinite-well energies
   \[
   E_1=0.0561239\,\mathrm{eV},\qquad
   E_2=0.2244956\,\mathrm{eV},\qquad
   E_3=0.5051151\,\mathrm{eV}.
   \]

3. Show that $E_1$ and $E_2$ lie below $\Delta E_c$ while $E_3$ lies
   above, that the $E_2$ margin is
   \[
   \Delta E_c-E_2=35.5044\,\mathrm{meV},
   \]
   and that
   \[
   E_2-E_1=0.1683717\,\mathrm{eV}
   \quad\text{corresponds to}\quad
   \lambda=\frac{hc}{E_2-E_1}=7.36372\,\mu\mathrm{m}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the offset is split $50/50$, so
   $\Delta E_c=\Delta E_v=0.20\,\mathrm{eV}$”; (ii) “because two
   infinite-well levels sit below $\Delta E_c$, the finite well
   has exactly two bound states.” This is an explicit screen, not
   an exact finite-barrier eigenvalue count. Do not replace the
   screen by a BJT finite-base gain decomposition.

The wavelengths and margins are analytical screens. They are not a
fabricated quantum-well spectrum.

With the stated $\hbar$, $m_e^{*}$, and $L$, $E_1=\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/(2 m_e^{*} L^{2})=0.0561239\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $E_n=n^{2} E_1$. Then $\lambda=hc/(E_2-E_1)$ uses $hc=1.23984198\,\mathrm{eV\cdot\mu m}$.

Form the optical gap E2-E1=3 E1 and convert with hc=1.23984198 eV um after the below-barrier screen.

Convert $E_1$ from joules to electron-volts with $q$. Then $E_2=4 E_1$ and $E_3=9 E_1$.
Compare each $E_n$ to $0.26\,\mathrm{eV}$. The $E_2$ slack is $35.5044\,\mathrm{meV}$; $E_3$ is already above the barrier. The screen is not a finite-well count.

SDP:010531.canonicalSolution:
The offset split is immediate:
\[
\Delta E_c=0.65\cdot 0.40=0.26\,\mathrm{eV},\qquad
\Delta E_v=0.35\cdot 0.40=0.14\,\mathrm{eV}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta E_c=0.26\,\mathrm{eV},\;
\Delta E_v=0.14\,\mathrm{eV}}.
\]

The infinite-well ground state with $L=10\,\mathrm{nm}$ and
$m_e^{*}=0.067\,m_0$ is
\[
E_1
=\frac{\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}}{2 m_e^{*} L^{2} q}
=0.0561239\,\mathrm{eV}.
\]
Scaling by $n^{2}$ gives
\[
E_2=4 E_1=0.2244956\,\mathrm{eV},\qquad
E_3=9 E_1=0.5051151\,\mathrm{eV}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_1=0.0561239\,\mathrm{eV},\;
E_2=0.2244956\,\mathrm{eV},\;
E_3=0.5051151\,\mathrm{eV}}.
\]

Comparison with the electron barrier:
\[
E_1=0.0561239<0.26,\qquad
E_2=0.2244956<0.26,\qquad
E_3=0.5051151>0.26.
\]
The $E_2$ margin is
\[
\Delta E_c-E_2=0.0355044\,\mathrm{eV}=35.5044\,\mathrm{meV}.
\]
The first optical spacing and its vacuum wavelength are
\[
E_2-E_1=0.1683717\,\mathrm{eV},
\qquad
\lambda
=\frac{1.23984198}{0.1683717}
=7.36372\,\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_1,E_2\text{ below }\Delta E_c;\;
E_2\text{ margin }35.5044\,\mathrm{meV};\;
E_3\text{ above};\;
\lambda=7.36372\,\mu\mathrm{m}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces $Q_c=0.65$ by a $50/50$ split and moves the
barrier to $0.20\,\mathrm{eV}$, which would push $E_2$ above the
well. Sentence (ii) reads the infinite-well screen as an exact
finite-well bound-state count. Finite walls lower every $E_n$ and
can change the number of confined states; this packet does not
solve that eigenvalue problem. The argument never constructs a
BJT finite-base gain decomposition.

The construction is an explicit analytical screen. It is not a
fabricated quantum-well spectrum and not an exact finite-barrier
count.

SDP:010628.title: Declared FN J=1e-6 E^2 exp(-25/E) rises by 2.184331 from 10 to 12 MV/cm
SDP:010628.objective: Using the declared empirical law J=1e-6 E^2 exp(-25/E) A/cm2 with E numeric in MV/cm, A=1e-4 cm2, and tox=5 nm, prove at E=10 that Vox=5 V, J=8.20850 uA/cm2, I=0.820850 nA, and at E=12 that Vox=6 V, J=17.93008 uA/cm2, I=1.793008 nA with ratio 2.184331, refusing any reliability prediction.
SDP:010628.statement:
A thin-oxide current density is declared, for this packet only, by
the empirical Fowler–Nordheim-shaped law
\[
J=1\times 10^{-6}\,E^{2}\exp(-25/E)\qquad(\mathrm{A/cm}^{2}),
\]
where the symbol $E$ is the numeric oxide field in $\mathrm{MV/cm}$
(so $E=10$ means $10\,\mathrm{MV/cm}$, not $10\,\mathrm{V/cm}$). The
oxide thickness is $t_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{nm}$ and the device
area is $A=1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}$. The oxide voltage is
the uniform-field identity $V_{\mathrm{ox}}=E\,t_{\mathrm{ox}}$ with
consistent units, and the terminal current is $I=JA$.

1. At $E=10$ prove
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   J=8.20850\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},\qquad
   I=0.820850\,\mathrm{nA}.
   \]

2. At $E=12$ prove
   \[
   V_{\mathrm{ox}}=6\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
   J=17.93008\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},\qquad
   I=1.793008\,\mathrm{nA}.
   \]

3. Form the current-density ratio
   \[
   \frac{J(12)}{J(10)}=2.184331
   \]
   and confirm that the same ratio holds for the currents.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$E$ must be rewritten in $\mathrm{V/cm}$
   before it enters $E^{2}\exp(-25/E)$”; (ii) “these two currents are
   a TDDB lifetime, a wear-out acceleration, or a fabricated-oxide
   reliability prediction.” Do not replace the calculation by a
   short-channel scale-length or drain-coupling Laplace problem.

The law is a declared numerical toy. It is not a first-principles
barrier integral and not a process-qualification model.

t_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{nm}=5\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{cm}.
\]
A numeric field $E$ in $\mathrm{MV/cm}$ is $E\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{V/cm}$, so
\[
V_{\mathrm{ox}}=(E\times 10^{6})(5\times 10^{-7})=0.5 E\quad(\mathrm{V}).
\]
At $E=10$,
\[
V_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The declared law uses that same numeric $E$:
\[
J(10)
=1\times 10^{-6}\cdot 10^{2}\cdot e^{-25/10}
=1\times 10^{-4}\,e^{-2.5}.
\]
Since $e^{-2.5}=0.08208499862$,
\[
J(10)=8.20850\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{A/cm}^{2}
=8.20850\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},
\]
\[
I(10)=J(10)A=8.20850\times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{A}
=0.820850\,\mathrm{nA}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E=10:\;V_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{V},\;
J=8.20850\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},\;
I=0.820850\,\mathrm{nA}}.
\]

At $E=12$,
\[
V_{\mathrm{ox}}=6\,\mathrm{V},
\]
\[
J(12)
=1\times 10^{-6}\cdot 12^{2}\cdot e^{-25/12}
=1.44\times 10^{-4}\,e^{-2.083\overline{3}}
=17.93008\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},
\]
\[
I(12)=1.793008\,\mathrm{nA}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E=12:\;V_{\mathrm{ox}}=6\,\mathrm{V},\;
J=17.93008\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2},\;
I=1.793008\,\mathrm{nA}}.
\]

The density ratio is
\[
\frac{J(12)}{J(10)}
=\frac{144}{100}\exp\Bigl(2.5-\frac{25}{12}\Bigr)
=1.44\exp(0.416\overline{6})
=2.184331,
\]
and $I(12)/I(10)$ is the same because the area cancels.
\[
\boxed{J(12)/J(10)=I(12)/I(10)=2.184331}.
\]

Sentence (i) inserts $E=1\times 10^{7}$ into a law whose constants
were declared for numeric $\mathrm{MV/cm}$, destroying both currents.
Sentence (ii) promotes two DC evaluations into a reliability,
TDDB, or wear-out prediction, which this packet does not support.
The argument never solves a short-channel scale-length or drain-
coupling Laplace problem.

The law remains a declared empirical toy. It is not a fabricated
oxide specification and not a lifetime model.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $E$ numeric in $\mathrm{MV/cm}$, $E=10$ gives $V_{\mathrm{ox}}=5\,\mathrm{V}$, $J=8.20850\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2}$, $I=0.820850\,\mathrm{nA}$, and $E=12$ gives $V_{\mathrm{ox}}=6\,\mathrm{V}$, $J=17.93008\,\mu\mathrm{A/cm}^{2}$, $I=1.793008\,\mathrm{nA}$. The ratio is $2.184331$. The law is a declared DC toy, not a reliability prediction, and $E$ is not rewritten in $\mathrm{V/cm}$.

SIG:010117.title: The scaled reversed triangle x(2-3t) lives on [1/3,1], has energy 2/9, and is not an LTI test
SIG:010117.objective: Determine the exact support and two linear pieces of y(t)=x(2-3t) for the unit-height triangle of width two, compute Ex=2/3, Ey=2/9 and area 1/3 from the time-scale Jacobian, and reject both an unscaled energy claim and any LTI classification of this pointwise warping.
SIG:010117.statement:
Let $x$ be the continuous-time triangle
\[
x(t)=\begin{cases}
1-|t|,&|t|\le 1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Define the pointwise time-warped signal $y(t)=x(2-3t)$. Energy and area are
the ordinary integrals
\[
E_x=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad
E_y=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad
A_y=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}y(t)\,dt.
\]

1. Prove that $y(t)$ is nonzero if and only if $t\in[1/3,1]$. Identify the
   unique breakpoint inside that interval at which $2-3t$ changes sign, and
   write the two ordinary formulas of $y$ on the resulting subintervals.
   Sketch the sequence of elementary operations (time reversal, compression
   by $3$, and translation) that produces $y$ from $x$, and confirm that the
   same closed support is obtained from the composite.

2. Compute $E_x$ by splitting at the origin. Then compute $E_y$ in two ways:
   directly from the two linear pieces, and by the change of variable
   $\tau=2-3t$. Prove that the Jacobian supplies the factor $1/3$ and that
   $E_y=E_x/3$. Compute the signed area $A_y$ by the same substitution.

3. Evaluate $y$ at the interior peak and check continuity of the two pieces
   at that peak and at the support endpoints.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “time scaling preserves energy, so $E_y=E_x$”
   (or “amplitude scaling by $3$ gives $E_y=E_x/9$”); (ii) “the map $x\mapsto y$
   is an LTI system, so the same calculation classifies memory and
   convolution kernels.”

Do not replace the problem by an exponential-memory operator, and do not
classify a fixed-origin counterexample.
permittedResults: The inequality $|at+b|\le 1$ is equivalent to $t$ lying in a closed interval of length $2/|a|$.
The substitution $\tau=at+b$ gives $\int |x(at+b)|^2\,dt=\int |x(\tau)|^2\,d\tau/|a|$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve |2-3t|<=1 for the support, split at the zero of 2-3t, then evaluate both integrals by substitution.
Factor y(t)=x(-3(t-2/3)), transport the interval [-1,1] through compression, reversal, and a shift by 2/3, then apply Ey=Ex/|a|.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact support [1/3,1] and the two linear pieces 3t-1 then 3-3t from the sign of 2-3t.
Computes Ex=2/3, Ey=2/9, and area 1/3, with the time-scale Jacobian 1/3 made explicit.
Rejects energy invariance and any LTI or memory-system reading of the pointwise warp.

commonErrors.description: Drops reversal or the offset 2 and reports a symmetric support such as [-1/3,1/3] or a right-shift-only interval such as [1,5/3].
commonErrors.consequence: The pieces 3t-1 and 3-3t are attached to the wrong interval, so every subsequent integral is taken over the wrong set.

commonErrors.description: Claims time scaling preserves energy so Ey=Ex=2/3, or treats the factor 3 as an amplitude and reports Ey=Ex/9=2/27.
commonErrors.consequence: The change of variable d tau = -3 dt is omitted, and the required values Ey=2/9 and area 1/3 are lost.

hintTree.content: The condition $|2-3t|\le 1$ rearranges to $1\le 3t\le 3$, hence $t\in[1/3,1]$. The argument $2-3t$ vanishes at $t=2/3$.
The triangle energy is $2\int_0^1(1-t)^2\,dt=2/3$. The change $\tau=2-3t$ divides every integral by $3$.

SIG:010117.canonicalSolution:
The value $y(t)=x(2-3t)$ is nonzero precisely when $|2-3t|\le 1$, that is
\[
-1\le 2-3t\le 1.
\]
The left inequality is $t\le 1$ and the right inequality is $t\ge 1/3$.
Thus the closed support is exactly $[1/3,1]$. The argument $2-3t$ decreases
from $1$ to $-1$ as $t$ runs from $1/3$ to $1$, and it is zero at the unique
interior point $t=2/3$.

On $[1/3,2/3]$ one has $2-3t\ge 0$, so
\[
y(t)=1-(2-3t)=3t-1.
\]
On $[2/3,1]$ one has $2-3t\le 0$, so
\[
y(t)=1-(3t-2)=3-3t.
\]
The same support is recovered by composing elementary maps. Write
$y(t)=x\bigl(-3(t-2/3)\bigr)$. Compression by $3$ sends $\operatorname{supp}x=[-1,1]$
to $[-1/3,1/3]$; reversal leaves that symmetric interval unchanged; a shift
to the right by $2/3$ produces $[1/3,1]$.
\[
\boxed{y(t)=3t-1\text{ on }[1/3,2/3],\quad y(t)=3-3t\text{ on }[2/3,1]}.
\]
Both pieces equal $1$ at $t=2/3$ and equal $0$ at the endpoints $t=1/3$ and
$t=1$, so $y$ is continuous.

The triangle energy splits at the origin:
\[
E_x=2\int_0^1(1-t)^2\,dt=2\Bigl[-\frac{(1-t)^3}{3}\Bigr]_0^1=\frac23.
\]
Directly from the pieces,
\begin{align*}
E_y
&=\int_{1/3}^{2/3}(3t-1)^2\,dt+\int_{2/3}^{1}(3-3t)^2\,dt.
\end{align*}
The first integrand is $(3(t-1/3))^2=9(t-1/3)^2$, and the second is
$9(1-t)^2$. Each integral equals $9\cdot(1/3)^3/3=1/9$, so $E_y=2/9$.
Alternatively, set $\tau=2-3t$. Then $d\tau=-3\,dt$ and as $t$ runs from
$1/3$ to $1$ the variable $\tau$ runs from $1$ down to $-1$, whence
\[
E_y=\int_{1/3}^{1}x(2-3t)^2\,dt=\int_{-1}^{1}x(\tau)^2\frac{d\tau}{3}
=\frac{E_x}{3}=\frac29.
\]
The same Jacobian gives the signed area. The area of $x$ is
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}(1-|t|)\,dt=2\int_0^1(1-t)\,dt=1,
\]
so $A_y=1/3$. Adding the two pieces confirms the value:
\[
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}(3t-1)\,dt+\int_{2/3}^{1}(3-3t)\,dt=\frac16+\frac16=\frac13.
\]
\[
\boxed{E_x=2/3,\quad E_y=2/9,\quad A_y=1/3}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses a time-scale Jacobian with an amplitude gain.
Preserving the graph height while compressing the time axis by $3$ divides
energy by $3$, not by $1$ and not by $9$. Sentence (ii) replaces a
pointwise change of the time argument by an LTI operator. The assignment
$x\mapsto x(2-3t)$ is not a convolution and is not time-invariant (a shift
of $x$ does not become the same shift of $y$). Memory-system language and
impulse-response classification are therefore out of scope.

The argument never introduces an exponential-memory kernel and never tests
a fixed-origin operator.

graderFixtures.proofText: Support is $[1/3,1]$ with breakpoint $t=2/3$. The pieces are $y=3t-1$ then $y=3-3t$. Triangle energy $E_x=2/3$ scales by the Jacobian $1/3$ to $E_y=2/9$ and area $1/3$. Energy is not invariant, and the warp is not an LTI test.

Compressing x(t) by 3 produces support [-1/3,1/3]. Reversal does not change a symmetric interval, and I ignore the constant 2 because it is only a vertical offset. So y lives on [-1/3,1/3] and the pieces are written there.
Time scaling never changes energy, so Ey equals Ex=2/3. If a factor of 3 must appear it is an amplitude, and then Ey=Ex/9=2/27. The area of y is likewise 1.

SIG:010118.title: The everlasting 3 cos(2 pi t) has power 9/2; its [-1,1] window has energy 9; the two-tone sequence has period 12 and power 1
SIG:010118.objective: Classify 3 cos(2 pi t) as a power signal with P=9/2 and infinite energy, classify its compact window on [-1,1] as an energy signal with E=9 and average power 0, and prove that z[n]=cos(pi n/3)+sin(pi n/2) has fundamental period 12, average power 1, and infinite energy.
SIG:010118.statement:
Use the standing conventions
\[
E_x=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad
P_x=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|x(t)|^2\,dt
\]
in continuous time, and
\[
E_z=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|z[n]|^2,\qquad
P_z=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^{N}|z[n]|^2
\]
in discrete time. A periodic discrete-time signal of period $N$ has
$P_z=N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|z[n]|^2$. A signal is an energy signal when
$0<E<\infty$ (then necessarily $P=0$ under these limits) and a power
signal when $0<P<\infty$ (then necessarily $E=\infty$).

1. Let $x(t)=3\cos(2\pi t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$. Prove that $x$ is
   periodic, compute $E_x$ and $P_x$, and classify $x$.

2. Let $w$ be the compact window of $x$ on $[-1,1]$:
   \[
   w(t)=\begin{cases}
   3\cos(2\pi t),&|t|\le 1,\\
   0,&\text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   Compute $E_w$ and $P_w$ and classify $w$. Explain why windowing
   destroys the power-signal classification of $x$.

3. Let
   \[
   z[n]=\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)+\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr).
   \]
   Prove that $z$ is periodic, determine its fundamental period, compute
   $P_z$ from a single fundamental period (including a proof that the
   cross term averages to zero), and classify $z$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “every everlasting sinusoid is an energy
   signal because a cosine is bounded”; (ii) “the fundamental period of
   $z$ is $6$ or $4$, so the power is the sum of the two separate powers
   without an orthogonality check.”

Do not expand $x$ or $z$ as a square-wave Fourier series, and do not
invoke Gibbs or Parseval identities for a discontinuous periodic wave.
permittedResults: The identity $\cos^2\theta=(1+\cos 2\theta)/2$ converts the average power of $A\cos(\omega t)$ into $A^2/2$, provided $\omega\ne 0$.
If $\omega/\pi$ is rational and $\omega\not\equiv 0\pmod{2\pi}$, the sequence $\cos(\omega n)$ (respectively $\sin(\omega n)$) has average power $1/2$ over any common period.

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert every cosine-square by the double-angle identity, then compute the discrete power from the length-12 average after an lcm period argument.
First evaluate the twelve samples of z explicitly to lock power 1 and period 12, then identify the same numbers as averages of the two quadratures.

milestones.criterion: Classifies 3 cos(2 pi t) as a power signal with P=9/2 and infinite energy, and its [-1,1] window as an energy signal with E=9 and P=0.
Proves that z[n] has fundamental period 12, average power 1, and infinite energy, with the cross term shown to average to zero.
Rejects treating a bounded everlasting sinusoid as an energy signal and rejects an understated period that skips the orthogonality check.

commonErrors.description: Calls 3 cos(2 pi t) an energy signal, or reports finite energy, or replaces the power 9/2 by the peak value 9 or by the window energy 9.
commonErrors.consequence: The power-signal classification and the distinction between the everlasting wave and its compact window are lost.

commonErrors.description: Takes 6 or 4 as a fundamental period of z, or adds the two powers without checking that the cross term averages to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: A non-period is treated as fundamental, or the value Pz=1 is no longer justified.

hintTree.content: Over a long interval the average of $\cos^2(2\pi t)$ is $1/2$, so $P_x=9/2$. The same integrand over the finite window $[-1,1]$ produces energy $9$.
The sequence $\cos(\pi n/3)$ has period $6$ and $\sin(\pi n/2)$ has period $4$. Their least common multiple is $12$. Check $z[1]$ against $z[7]$ to see that $6$ fails.
The cross term $2\cos(\pi n/3)\sin(\pi n/2)$ is a sum of two discrete sinusoids whose frequencies are integer numbers of cycles in length $12$, hence average to zero.

SIG:010118.canonicalSolution:
The signal $x(t)=3\cos(2\pi t)$ satisfies $x(t+1)=x(t)$ and is nonconstant,
so it is periodic of fundamental period $1$. Its instantaneous power is
$9\cos^2(2\pi t)=9(1+\cos(4\pi t))/2$. Over $\mathbb R$ the integral of a
nonnegative periodic function with positive mean diverges, so $E_x=\infty$.
The two-sided power limit exists and equals the mean over one period:
\[
P_x=\int_0^1 9\cos^2(2\pi t)\,dt=\frac92.
\]
Thus $x$ is a power signal and not an energy signal.
\[
\boxed{P_x=9/2,\quad E_x=\infty}.
\]

The window $w$ vanishes off $[-1,1]$, so
\[
E_w=\int_{-1}^{1}9\cos^2(2\pi t)\,dt
=9\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1+\cos(4\pi t)}{2}\,dt
=\frac92\bigl[t+\tfrac{\sin(4\pi t)}{4\pi}\bigr]_{-1}^{1}=9.
\]
A compactly supported square-integrable signal has vanishing average power:
for $T>1$ the integral in the definition of $P_w$ is the constant $9$, and
$9/(2T)\to 0$. Hence $w$ is an energy signal with $P_w=0$. Windowing
removes the everlasting tails that produced a positive power mean.

Now $z[n]=\cos(\pi n/3)+\sin(\pi n/2)$. The first summand has
$\frac{\pi}{3}N=2\pi k$ when $N=6k$, so its fundamental period is $6$.
The second has $\frac{\pi}{2}N=2\pi k$ when $N=4k$, so its fundamental
period is $4$. The sum is therefore periodic of period $\operatorname{lcm}(6,4)=12$:
\[
z[n+12]=\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}+4\pi\Bigr)+\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}+6\pi\Bigr)=z[n].
\]
Period $6$ fails: $z[1]=\cos(\pi/3)+\sin(\pi/2)=3/2$ while
$z[7]=\cos(7\pi/3)+\sin(7\pi/2)=1/2-1=-1/2$. Period $4$ fails already on
the cosine term. Thus $12$ is fundamental.

Over one period the average of $\cos^2(\pi n/3)$ is $1/2$ and the average
of $\sin^2(\pi n/2)$ is $1/2$, because neither discrete frequency is an
integer multiple of $\pi$. The cross term is
\[
2\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{3}\Bigr)\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi n}{2}\Bigr)
=\sin\Bigl(\frac{5\pi n}{6}\Bigr)-\sin\Bigl(-\frac{\pi n}{6}\Bigr).
\]
Each sinusoid completes an integer number of cycles in length $12$, so
both averages vanish. Therefore
\[
P_z=\frac12+\frac12=1.
\]
An explicit check sums $|z[n]|^2$ on $\{0,\ldots,11\}$ to $12$, hence
the mean is $1$. Infinite duration then gives $E_z=\infty$, so $z$ is a
discrete-time power signal.
\[
\boxed{\text{fundamental period }12,\quad P_z=1,\quad E_z=\infty}.
\]

Sentence (i) confuses boundedness with square integrability over
$\mathbb R$. Boundedness of $x$ controls neither $E_x$ nor $P_x$.
Sentence (ii) either understates the fundamental period or adds the two
powers without checking orthogonality of the cross term; both mistakes
are available even if the numerical value $1$ is accidentally retained.

The argument never forms a square-wave Fourier series and never cites
Gibbs overshoot or a Parseval identity for a jump discontinuity.

graderFixtures.proofText: The everlasting $3\cos(2\pi t)$ has $P=9/2$ and $E=\infty$. Its window on $[-1,1]$ has energy $9$ and power $0$. The sum $z[n]$ has fundamental period $12$ (since $z[1]\ne z[7]$), average power $1$, and infinite energy. The cross term averages to zero over length $12$.
A cosine is bounded, so it is square integrable and 3 cos(2 pi t) is an energy signal. Its energy equals the window integral 9, and I do not need a separate power calculation.
cos(pi n/3) already has period 6, so that is the fundamental period of z. I add the two powers 1/2+1/2 without looking at the product term, and I do not check z[1] against z[7].

SIG:010219.title: Linear convolution of [1,-2,1] with [1,1,1] is [1,-1,0,-1,1] and deconvolution recovers the input
SIG:010219.objective: Compute the length-5 linear convolution y=[1,-1,0,-1,1], identify the ordinary generating functions X(q)=(1-q)^2 and H(q)=1+q+q^2, factor the FIR cascade, and recover x from y by polynomial division; reject circular wraparound and the seed discrete output [1,1,-1,2].
SIG:010219.statement:
Work in discrete time with ordinary generating functions
\[
X(q)=\sum_{n\ge 0}x[n]q^n.
\]
Let $x$ and $h$ be the causal finite sequences
\[
x[0]=1,\quad x[1]=-2,\quad x[2]=1,
\qquad
h[0]=1,\quad h[1]=1,\quad h[2]=1,
\]
and $x[n]=h[n]=0$ for every other integer $n$. Linear convolution is
\[
y[n]=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}x[k]h[n-k].
\]

1. Compute every nonzero sample of $y$ directly from the sum, state the
   support of $y$, and write the length-5 coefficient list starting at
   $n=0$. Confirm the same list by expanding the product $X(q)H(q)$.

2. Factor $X(q)$ and $H(q)$ over the polynomials. Exhibit $y$ as the
   cascade of two first-difference FIR stages with the length-3 moving-sum
   FIR, and also as the cascade of a first difference with the comb
   $1-q^3$. Explain why these factorizations describe linear, not circular,
   convolution.

3. Recover $x$ from the pair $(y,h)$ by polynomial division of $Y(q)$ by
   $H(q)$, or equivalently by sequential deconvolution
   $x[n]=y[n]-\sum_{k=1}^{2}h[k]x[n-k]$ with $h[0]=1$. Check that the
   recovered sequence is exactly $[1,-2,1]$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “both sequences are length $3$, so the output
   is the length-$3$ circular convolution, or else the seed list
   $[1,1,-1,2]$”; (ii) “because $1+q+q^2$ vanishes at the nonreal cube
   roots of unity, $x$ cannot be recovered from $y$.”

Do not replace the calculation by a continuous-time triangle-rectangle
overlap, and do not invoke a hidden-mode state realization.
permittedResults: The identities $1-2q+q^2=(1-q)^2$ and $(1-q)(1+q+q^2)=1-q^3$ factor the present FIR cascade.
If $H(0)\ne 0$, a finite $h$ may be deconvolved from a finite $y$ by forward substitution, and the result is unique among causal sequences of the expected length.

acceptableStrategies.description: Tabulate the five inner products, then confirm by expanding (1-2q+q^2)(1+q+q^2) and dividing the product back by H.
Factor through (1-q)(1-q^3), implement the cascade, and invert the moving-sum stage by forward substitution.

milestones.criterion: Computes the linear convolution y=[1,-1,0,-1,1] from the sum and from the product of generating functions.
Factors X(q)=(1-q)^2 and H(q)=1+q+q^2 and recovers x by deconvolution or polynomial division.
Rejects circular convolution, the seed list [1,1,-1,2], and the claim that zeros of H block exact recovery.

commonErrors.description: Wraps indices modulo 3 and reports a circular convolution, or substitutes the unrelated seed list [1,1,-1,2] for y.
commonErrors.consequence: The length-5 linear output [1,-1,0,-1,1] is never produced, so the generating-function identity fails.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the zeros of 1+q+q^2 make x unrecoverable, or returns a quotient other than (1-q)^2.
commonErrors.consequence: An exact polynomial division with zero remainder is replaced by a spectral-zero obstruction that the finite data do not have.

hintTree.content: The five possibly nonzero indices are $n=0,1,2,3,4$. Direct expansion gives $1$, $1-2$, $1-2+1$, $-2+1$, and $1$.
Dividing $1-q-q^3+q^4$ by $1+q+q^2$ returns $1-2q+q^2$. Circular wrap of a length-3 buffer is a different sum.

SIG:010219.canonicalSolution:
Support additivity for nonnegative index sets gives
$\operatorname{supp}y\subseteq\{0,1,2,3,4\}$. Evaluating the finite sum
$y[n]=x[0]h[n]+x[1]h[n-1]+x[2]h[n-2]$ produces
\begin{align*}
y[0]&=1,\\
y[1]&=1-2=-1,\\
y[2]&=1-2+1=0,\\
y[3]&=-2+1=-1,\\
y[4]&=1.
\end{align*}
Thus
\[
\boxed{y=[1,-1,0,-1,1]}.
\]
The ordinary generating functions are
\[
X(q)=1-2q+q^2=(1-q)^2,\qquad
H(q)=1+q+q^2.
\]
Their product is
\begin{align*}
Y(q)
&=(1-2q+q^2)(1+q+q^2)\\
&=1+q+q^2-2q-2q^2-2q^3+q^2+q^3+q^4\\
&=1-q-q^3+q^4,
\end{align*}
which is the same coefficient list. Equivalently,
\[
Y(q)=(1-q)^2(1+q+q^2)=(1-q)(1-q^3),
\]
so $y$ is the cascade of two first-difference stages $1-q$ with the
moving-sum $1+q+q^2$, or of one first difference with the comb $1-q^3$.
These are polynomial identities for ordinary (linear) convolution: no
index is reduced modulo $3$ or modulo $5$.

Because $h[0]=1$, forward substitution
\[
x[n]=y[n]-h[1]x[n-1]-h[2]x[n-2]
\]
(with $x[m]=0$ for $m<0$) yields $x[0]=1$, $x[1]=-1-1=-2$,
$x[2]=0-(-2)-1=1$, and then $x[3]=-1-1-(-2)=0$, $x[4]=1-0-1=0$.
Polynomial division of $1-q-q^3+q^4$ by $1+q+q^2$ returns the same
quotient $1-2q+q^2$ with zero remainder. The input is therefore recovered
exactly.
\[
\boxed{X(q)=(1-q)^2,\quad H(q)=1+q+q^2}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces linear convolution by a circular operator on a
length-$3$ buffer, or else imports the unrelated seed list $[1,1,-1,2]$.
Neither list equals $[1,-1,0,-1,1]$. Sentence (ii) notes that $H$ vanishes
at the nonreal cube roots of unity, but $Y$ has the same zeros (because
$Y=(1-q)(1-q^3)$), so the quotient is still the polynomial $X$. Finite
support makes the recovery an exact polynomial division, not an unstable
inversion of a spectral zero.

The calculation never integrates a continuous triangle against a rectangle
and never realizes a hidden mode.

graderFixtures.proofText: Linear convolution is $y=[1,-1,0,-1,1]$. Generating functions are $X(q)=(1-q)^2$ and $H(q)=1+q+q^2$, and $Y=(1-q)(1-q^3)$. Division of $Y$ by $H$ recovers $[1,-2,1]$. Circular wrap and the seed list $[1,1,-1,2]$ are different operators.

Both sequences have length 3, so I compute circular convolution of length 3 and obtain a 3-vector. Alternatively I reuse the discrete output [1,1,-1,2] from the triangle-rectangle seed, which I treat as the same FIR exercise.
H(q)=1+q+q^2 vanishes at the primitive cube roots of unity, so Y/H is undefined and x cannot be recovered from y. I stop at the product Y and do not divide.
