STAT:010324.title: Stage arms 0.60/0.15 and 0.20/0.05 multiply to 16P; the pins are 5P up and 20P down
STAT:010324.objective: On a two-stage first-class compound lever with a tension link, obtain J=4P and Q=16P, evaluate J=1000 N and Q=4000 N at P=250 N, and audit the fulcrum reactions 1250 N up on stage 1 and 5000 N down on stage 2 together with two-force-link equilibrium and the actual Newton-third-law pairs at each pin.
STAT:010324.statement:
A compound lever press consists of two weightless first-class levers joined
by a vertical tension link. Treat each lever as planar and quasistatic.

Stage $1$ has fulcrum pin $F_1$. An operator force $P>0$ acts downward at
$0.60\,\mathrm{m}$ to the left of $F_1$. The tension link attaches
$0.15\,\mathrm{m}$ to the right of $F_1$ and therefore pulls downward on
stage $1$ with force $J>0$.

Stage $2$ has fulcrum pin $F_2$. The same tension link attaches
$0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ to the left of $F_2$ and, because the weightless
two-force link is in equilibrium, pulls upward on stage $2$ with the same
force $J$. A press ram attaches
$0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ to the right of $F_2$. The lever pushes downward on the
ram with force $Q>0$, so the ram pushes upward on the lever with force $Q$.

Do not replace the exercise by a symmetric toggle or by virtual work.

1. From moment equilibrium of each lever, determine $J$ in terms of $P$ and
   $Q$ in terms of $J$ and of $P$. State the two mechanical advantages.
2. From vertical force equilibrium of each lever, determine the force of pin
   $F_1$ on stage $1$ and the force of pin $F_2$ on stage $2$, including
   sense (up or down on that lever).
3. Substitute $P=250\,\mathrm{N}$ and report $J$, $Q$, and both pin forces
   with units and sense.
4. Audit the link and contact forces carefully. Explain why equilibrium of
   the weightless two-force link makes its forces on stages $1$ and $2$
   equal and opposite, while each Newton-third-law pair is between a lever
   and the link at the same pin. Also audit the force of each lever on its
   fulcrum pin versus the force of the pin on the lever, and the ram contact.
   Then audit these claims: (i) each fulcrum reaction
   equals the nearby load $P$ or $J$ alone; (ii) the link pulls both levers
   downward; (iii) $Q=4P$ because each stage was forgotten except one.
   State the first-class, tension-link, and weightless-lever hypotheses.
permittedResults: Moment equilibrium of a first-class lever about its fulcrum equates (force)$\times$(arm) on the two sides. Here $P\cdot 0.60=J\cdot 0.15$ and $J\cdot 0.20=Q\cdot 0.05$.
Vertical equilibrium of a weightless lever equates the fulcrum reaction to the algebraic sum of the two loads that act on that lever.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take moments about each fulcrum to get the two advantages, then sum vertical forces on each lever to get the pins.
Track the tension-link pair first so the stage-2 input is upward, then the ram reaction is upward and the stage-2 pin must act downward.

milestones.criterion: Obtains J=4P from the 0.60/0.15 arms and Q=16P from the 0.20/0.05 arms.
Evaluates J=1000 N, Q=4000 N at P=250 N and the pin forces 1250 N up on stage 1 and 5000 N down on stage 2.
Distinguishes two-force-link equilibrium from the Newton-third-law pairs at each contact, and rejects a one-stage Q=4P, a same-way link, and a pin equal to a single load.

commonErrors.description: Reports Q=4P by keeping only one stage, or sets a fulcrum reaction equal to P or J alone instead of the sum of the two loads on that lever.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Q=4000 N and the pin pair 1250 N up / 5000 N down are lost.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the tension-link force as downward on both stages, violating equilibrium of the weightless two-force link, or mismatches a Newton-third-law pair at a link, fulcrum, or ram contact.
commonErrors.consequence: Stage 2 equilibrium flips and the 5000 N downward pin reaction cannot appear.

hintTree.content: Stage $1$ moments about $F_1$ give $J=P\cdot 0.60/0.15=4P$. Stage $2$ moments about $F_2$ give $Q=J\cdot 0.20/0.05=4J$.
On stage $1$ both $P$ and $J$ act downward, so the pin must push upward with $P+J=5P$. On stage $2$ both $J$ and $Q$ act upward, so the pin must pull downward with $J+Q=20P$.

The link cannot pull both levers downward: equilibrium of the weightless two-force link makes its end forces on the two levers equal and opposite. Pair each of those forces with its reciprocal lever-on-link force at the same pin.

STAT:010324.canonicalSolution:
Stage $1$ moments about $F_1$. The two downward loads sit on opposite
sides of the fulcrum:
\[
P\cdot 0.60=J\cdot 0.15\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{J=4P}.
\]
The first-stage mechanical advantage is $0.60/0.15=4$.

Stage $2$ moments about $F_2$. The upward link force $J$ and the upward
ram reaction $Q$ sit on opposite sides:
\[
J\cdot 0.20=Q\cdot 0.05\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{Q=4J=16P}.
\]
The second-stage mechanical advantage is $0.20/0.05=4$, and the compound
advantage is $16$.

Pin $F_1$ on stage $1$. Both $P$ and $J$ act downward on the lever, so
vertical equilibrium is
\[
F_{1,\mathrm{on}\,1}-P-J=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
F_{1,\mathrm{on}\,1}=P+J=5P
\]
upward on stage $1$.

Pin $F_2$ on stage $2$. Both $J$ and $Q$ act upward on the lever, so
\[
F_{2,\mathrm{on}\,2}+J+Q=0\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
F_{2,\mathrm{on}\,2}=-(J+Q)=-20P,
\]
that is, $20P$ downward on stage $2$.

At $P=250\,\mathrm{N}$,
\[
\boxed{J=1000\,\mathrm{N}},\qquad
\boxed{Q=4000\,\mathrm{N}},
\]
the force of $F_1$ on stage $1$ is
\[
\boxed{1250\,\mathrm{N}\text{ upward}},
\]
and the force of $F_2$ on stage $2$ is
\[
\boxed{5000\,\mathrm{N}\text{ downward}}.
\]

Link/contact audit. Equilibrium of the weightless two-force link makes the
forces it exerts on the levers equal and opposite: it pulls stage $1$
downward with $1000\,\mathrm{N}$ and stage $2$ upward with
$1000\,\mathrm{N}$. The corresponding Newton-third-law partners are the
upward force of stage $1$ on the link at its pin and the downward force of
stage $2$ on the link at its pin.
Stage $1$ pushes $F_1$ downward with $1250\,\mathrm{N}$; the pin pushes
the lever upward with $1250\,\mathrm{N}$. Stage $2$ pulls $F_2$ upward
with $5000\,\mathrm{N}$; the pin pulls the lever downward with
$5000\,\mathrm{N}$. The ram is pushed downward with $4000\,\mathrm{N}$
and therefore pushes the lever upward with $4000\,\mathrm{N}$.

Claim (i) drops a load from the pin sum and would report $250\,\mathrm{N}$
or $1000\,\mathrm{N}$ at $F_1$ instead of $1250\,\mathrm{N}$. Claim (ii)
assigns the same link direction to both levers and violates equilibrium of
the weightless two-force link. Claim (iii) keeps only one stage and reports
$Q=4P=1000\,\mathrm{N}$.
The model uses two first-class levers, a tension-only link, and
weightless members. Each isolated lever is determinate.

graderFixtures.proofText: Stage $1$ gives $J=4P$. Stage $2$ gives $Q=4J=16P$. At $P=250\,\mathrm{N}$ one has $J=1000\,\mathrm{N}$ and $Q=4000\,\mathrm{N}$. Pin $F_1$ pushes stage $1$ upward with $1250\,\mathrm{N}$; pin $F_2$ pulls stage $2$ downward with $5000\,\mathrm{N}$. The link pulls stage $1$ down and stage $2$ up with $1000\,\mathrm{N}$. $Q$ is not $4P$, and neither pin equals a single adjacent load.
Only the 0.60/0.15 pair matters, so Q=4P=1000 N. The pin at F1 equals the operator load P=250 N, and the pin at F2 equals J=1000 N.
The tension link pulls downward on stage 1 and also downward on stage 2, because a cable always pulls down. Then both pins push up and F2 cannot be 5000 N down.

STAT:010337.title: Triangle A(0,0),B(4,0),C(0,3) with three vertical rollers has m+r=2j=6 but support-wrench rank 2 and a horizontal mechanism
STAT:010337.objective: Show that the planar Maxwell count m+r=2j is necessary but not sufficient: three vertical rollers on a rigid triangle leave a rank-2 support wrench and a horizontal rigid-body mechanism.
STAT:010337.statement:
A plane pin-jointed assembly occupies the right triangle with joints
\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(4,0),\qquad C=(0,3)
\]
(meters). The only members are $AB$, $AC$, and $BC$. Each joint rests on a vertical roller: the foundation can exert a purely vertical force at $A$, at $B$, and at $C$, and no horizontal force at any support. Member pins connect the bars to one another; they do not attach the assembly to a wall.

Do not replace any roller by a pin or by a built-in couple, do not cut a section through $BC$, $BE$, and $DE$, do not invoke a zero-force-member rule, and do not convert the triangle into a compound lever or an internal-hinge frame.

1. Count the joints $j$, the members $m$, and the independent support reactions $r$. Evaluate $m+r$ and $2j$.

2. Write the three planar support wrenches about the origin as columns of a $3\times 3$ matrix whose rows are $F_x$, $F_y$, and $M_z$. Compute the rank of that matrix and name the missing wrench component.

3. Exhibit a nonzero infinitesimal rigid displacement of the whole triangle that does no virtual work on any support reaction.

4. Decide whether $m+r=2j$ is sufficient for external immobility of this assembly.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$m+r=2j$, therefore the truss is statically determinate and immobile”; (ii) “each roller is equivalent to a pin, so $r=6$ and the truss is redundant.”

The exercise is a support-rank question. It is not a method-of-sections force reading, not a proof of the zero-force-member rule, and not a rigid-body equilibrium support model for a loaded plate.
permittedResults: The planar wrench of a vertical force $F_y$ acting at $(x,y)$ about the origin is $(0,F_y,x F_y)$. A set of purely vertical forces therefore lies in the $F_y$--$M_z$ plane and has rank at most $2$.

If the support wrench matrix has rank less than $3$, there exists a rigid-body twist (here a horizontal translation) orthogonal to every support wrench; the count $m+r=2j$ is then not sufficient for immobility.

acceptableStrategies.description: Count first, then write the 3x3 support wrench matrix about the origin and read its rank and kernel.
After confirming the triangle is internally rigid, test a horizontal rigid translation against the three vertical reactions.

milestones.criterion: Counts j=3, m=3, r=3 and records m+r=6=2j.
Shows the three vertical support wrenches have rank 2, miss Fx, and admit a horizontal rigid-body mechanism, so the count is not sufficient.
Rejects reading the count as a determinacy proof and rejects treating the rollers as pins.

commonErrors.description: Treats m+r=2j as a sufficient certificate that the truss is statically determinate and immobile, and reports no mechanism.
commonErrors.consequence: The horizontal rigid-body motion is missed even though the support wrench rank is only 2.

commonErrors.description: Replaces each vertical roller by a pin, counts r=6, and declares the assembly redundant or statically indeterminate.
commonErrors.consequence: Three fictitious horizontal reactions are introduced, so both the count and the stability conclusion are wrong.

hintTree.content: There are three joints, three bars, and one reaction component at each roller, so $j=3$, $m=3$, $r=3$ and $m+r=6=2j$.
The support wrenches about the origin are $(0,A_y,0)$, $(0,B_y,4B_y)$, and $(0,C_y,0)$. Their span has dimension $2$ and contains no $F_x$.
A unit horizontal translation of the whole triangle does no work on a vertical reaction. That mechanism survives even though the triangle is internally a rigid simplex.

STAT:010337.canonicalSolution:
The assembly has $j=3$ joints and $m=3$ bars. Each vertical roller supplies one unknown, so $r=3$. The Maxwell count is
\[
m+r=3+3=6=2j.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{j=3,\ m=3,\ r=3,\quad m+r=6=2j}.
\]
Internally the three bars form a triangle, so the bar graph is rigid in the plane ($m=2j-3$). The remaining question is external.

Number the planar wrench as $(F_x,F_y,M_z)$ about the origin. A vertical force at $A=(0,0)$ contributes $(0,A_y,0)$. A vertical force at $B=(4,0)$ contributes $(0,B_y,4B_y)$. A vertical force at $C=(0,3)$ contributes $(0,C_y,0\cdot C_y)=(0,C_y,0)$. The support matrix is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & 4 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose column space is $\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}=2},
\]
and the missing component is
\[
\boxed{F_x}.
\]
(The reactions at $A$ and $C$ are the same wrench; height at $C$ does not create a moment about $O$ when the force is vertical.)

A rigid translation $\delta\mathbf u=(\delta u,0)$ of the whole triangle has virtual work $A_y\cdot 0+B_y\cdot 0+C_y\cdot 0=0$. It is a horizontal rigid-body mechanism. The count equality is
\[
\boxed{\text{necessary but not sufficient}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: $m+r=2j$ does not detect a rank-deficient support span. Sentence (ii) is false: a vertical roller is not a pin; replacing each roller by a pin would invent three nonexistent horizontal reactions and would misclassify the assembly as redundant.

The argument uses only a joint-and-reaction count and the rank of the support wrenches. It does not cut members, does not name a zero-force bar, and does not replace the rollers by an internal hinge.

graderFixtures.proofText: I count $j=3$, $m=3$, $r=3$, so $m+r=6=2j$. The support wrenches $(0,A_y,0)$, $(0,B_y,4B_y)$, $(0,C_y,0)$ have rank $2$ and miss $F_x$. A horizontal rigid translation is a mechanism. The count is necessary but not sufficient.
j=3, m=3, r=3 so m+r=2j. The Maxwell count is satisfied, therefore the truss is statically determinate and immobile. I report no mechanism.
Each support is a joint on the foundation, so each is a pin with two reactions. Then r=6, m+r=9>2j, and the truss is redundant.

STAT:010338.title: Symmetric cable span 8 sag 2 under w=3 kN/m has H=12, support tension 12sqrt2, midspan y=x^2/8, slope 1, midspan tension 12
STAT:010338.objective: From a symmetric cable under uniform load per unit horizontal span, recover the constant thrust, the vertical reactions, the support tension, the midspan parabola, the support slope, and the midspan tension.
STAT:010338.statement:
A flexible inextensible cable hangs symmetrically between two supports at the same height. The horizontal span is $L=8$ m and the sag at midspan is $f=2$ m. The cable carries a uniform downward load of intensity $w=3$ kN/m measured per unit horizontal distance (a deck load). The equilibrium curve is therefore a parabola, not a catenary. Place a Cartesian origin at the lowest point of the cable, with $x$ horizontal and $y$ upward along the sag.

Do not replace the cable by three concurrent ring tensions, do not treat the load as a spatial gravity wrench of discrete wires, do not invoke virtual work on a block tackle, and do not convert the supports into an internal hinge.

1. Compute the constant horizontal thrust from $H=wL^2/(8f)$. State the units.

2. Compute each vertical support reaction from global vertical equilibrium.

3. Compute the cable tension at either support.

4. With $x$ measured from midspan, write the cable equation $y=wx^2/(2H)$ and evaluate the slope magnitude at a support.

5. Report the midspan tension.

6. Audit both sentences: (i) “the eight in the thrust formula is really a two, so $H=wL^2/(2f)=48$ kN”; (ii) “the support tension equals the horizontal thrust $H$.”

The load is uniform in $x$, so the shape is parabolic. This is not a three-cable ring, not a method-of-sections truss, and not a catenary of uniform self-weight along the arc.
permittedResults: A symmetric parabolic cable of span $L$ and sag $f$ under uniform $w$ per unit horizontal length has $H=wL^2/(8f)$. Substituting the support abscissa $x=L/2$ into $y=wx^2/(2H)$ recovers $y=f$.

If the support slope has magnitude $1$, then the vertical and horizontal force components are equal and the support tension is $H\sqrt{2}$. The midspan tension is $H$ itself because the slope vanishes there.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate H from the sag formula, split the total load for the vertical reactions, then reconstruct T, y(x), and the support slope from the midspan free body.
After H is known, write y=wx^2/(2H), differentiate to get the support slope, and assemble T=H/cosθ with |tanθ|=1.

milestones.criterion: Computes H=12 kN from wL^2/(8f) and the vertical reactions 12 kN.
Reports support tension 12sqrt2 kN, y=x^2/8 from midspan, support-slope magnitude 1, and midspan tension 12 kN.
Rejects replacing 8 by 2 in the thrust formula and rejects equating the support tension to H.

commonErrors.description: Replaces H=wL^2/(8f) by H=wL^2/(2f), obtaining H=48 kN and an inconsistent sag.
commonErrors.consequence: Every later slope and tension is computed from the wrong thrust, so the support tension and the midspan law are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets the support tension equal to the horizontal thrust H=12 kN, ignoring the equal vertical component at the 45-degree support.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported support tension is smaller than the true value 12sqrt2 kN by the missing vertical part.

hintTree.content: Insert $w=3$, $L=8$, $f=2$ into $H=wL^2/(8f)$ to obtain $H=12$ kN. Each vertical reaction is $wL/2=12$ kN.
The support tension is $\sqrt{H^2+V^2}=12\sqrt{2}$ kN. From midspan, $y=wx^2/(2H)=x^2/8$.
At $x=4$ the slope is $x/4=1$. Midspan slope is zero, so the midspan tension equals $H=12$ kN.

STAT:010338.canonicalSolution:
The horizontal thrust is
\[
H=\frac{wL^2}{8f}=\frac{3\cdot 8^2}{8\cdot 2}=\frac{192}{16}=\boxed{12\ \text{kN}}.
\]
The total downward load is $wL=24$ kN. Symmetry splits it equally, so each vertical support reaction is
\[
\boxed{V=12\ \text{kN}}.
\]
The support tension is therefore
\[
T_{\text{support}}=\sqrt{H^2+V^2}=\sqrt{144+144}=\boxed{12\sqrt{2}\ \text{kN}}.
\]
Measured from midspan,
\[
y=\frac{wx^2}{2H}=\frac{3x^2}{24}=\boxed{\frac{x^2}{8}}.
\]
At a support $x=\pm 4$ this returns $y=2$ m, which matches the given sag. The slope is
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x}{4},
\]
so the support-slope magnitude is
\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
At midspan the slope vanishes, and the tension reduces to the thrust:
\[
\boxed{T_{\text{mid}}=12\ \text{kN}}.
\]

Sentence (i) is false: dropping the factor $8$ down to $2$ produces $H=48$ kN, which would make the sag $y(4)=3\cdot 16/(2\cdot 48)=1/2$ m instead of $2$ m. Sentence (ii) is false: the support tension is $12\sqrt{2}$ kN, not the midspan value $H=12$ kN.

The calculation uses only the parabolic free-body under a load counted per unit $x$. It is not a concurrent three-cable ring and not a catenary.

graderFixtures.proofText: The thrust is $H=wL^2/(8f)=12$ kN. Each vertical reaction is $12$ kN, the support tension is $12\sqrt{2}$ kN, $y=x^2/8$ from midspan, the support-slope magnitude is $1$, and the midspan tension is $12$ kN.
I take H=wL^2/(2f)=3*64/4=48 kN. Then V=12 kN still, and I keep T_support=sqrt(48^2+12^2).
H=12 kN is fine and V=12 kN. The cable tension at the support is the same constant H, so T_support=12 kN.

STAT:010425.title: The hole subtracts area; y-bar stays on the midline and x-bar is not the hole center
STAT:010425.objective: For a 6-by-4-meter rectangle with a radius-1-meter hole centered at (4,2) meters, compute A=(24-pi) m^2, x-bar=[(72-4pi)/(24-pi)] m approximately 2.8494 m, and y-bar=2 m by signed composite first moments.
STAT:010425.statement:
A homogeneous plate of uniform thickness occupies the rectangle
\[
0\le x\le 6,\qquad 0\le y\le 4
\]
in meters, except that an open circular hole of radius $1\,\mathrm{m}$ is
centered at $(4,2)$. The plate is otherwise complete. Take the area centroid
$(\bar x,\bar y)$ of the remaining material with respect to the given axes.

Do not replace the exercise by a signed transverse line load on a beam, and
do not collapse the plate to a pure couple.

1. Compute the net area $A$ as a signed composite: rectangle minus disk.
2. Compute the first moments of area about the $y$-axis and about the
   $x$-axis. Hence obtain exact expressions for $\bar x$ and $\bar y$.
   Show that $\bar y$ equals the horizontal midline of the rectangle.
   Report area in $\mathrm{m^2}$, first moments in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and
   centroid coordinates in meters.
3. Evaluate $\bar x$ numerically to four digits after the decimal point,
   using a value of $\pi$ accurate enough that the correctly rounded
   four-decimal value is unambiguous.
4. Audit these claims: (i) the hole is added, so $A=24+\pi$ and the hole
   first moment is taken with a plus sign; (ii) the centroid is at the
   hole center $(4,2)$ because that is where material is missing; (iii)
   $\bar y$ follows the hole and is therefore strictly less than $2$, or
   else $\bar x$ may be replaced by the rectangle center $3$ without a
   first-moment calculation. State the uniform-thickness and
   homogeneous-plate hypotheses.
permittedResults: If a body is the signed union of figures with areas $A_i$ and centroids $(\tilde x_i,\tilde y_i)$, then $A=\sum A_i$, $A\bar x=\sum \tilde x_i A_i$, and $A\bar y=\sum \tilde y_i A_i$. A hole is a negative $A_i$.
If a region and a coordinate axis are symmetric across a line $y=c$, then $\bar y=c$. Here both the rectangle and the hole are symmetric across $y=2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Tabulate rectangle and hole areas and centroids, subtract the hole row, and divide first moments by net area.
Invoke y=2 symmetry for y-bar first, then compute only the x first moment.

milestones.criterion: Computes the signed area A=(24-pi) m^2 with the disk subtracted.
Obtains x-bar=[(72-4pi)/(24-pi)] m approximately 2.8494 m and y-bar=2 m from first moments Q_y=(72-4pi) m^3 and Q_x=2(24-pi) m^3.
Rejects adding the hole, identifying the centroid with (4,2) or with 3, and any claim that y-bar leaves the midline.

commonErrors.description: Adds the disk area, writing A=24+pi and x-bar=(72+4pi)/(24+pi), or otherwise treats the hole as extra material.
commonErrors.consequence: The centroid is thrown to the right of x=3 instead of to the left.

commonErrors.description: Sets the centroid at the hole center (4,2), or replaces x-bar by the rectangle center 3, or claims y-bar moves off the midline.
commonErrors.consequence: The required pair x-bar approximately 2.8494 and y-bar=2 is not obtained.

hintTree.content: Rectangle area $6\cdot 4=24$, disk area $\pi\cdot 1^2=\pi$, so $A=24-\pi$. The rectangle centroid is $(3,2)$ and the hole centroid is $(4,2)$.
The $x$ first moment is $3\cdot 24-4\cdot\pi=72-4\pi$. The $y$ first moment is $2\cdot 24-2\cdot\pi=2(24-\pi)$.
Because $24-\pi$ cancels in $\bar y$, the midline $y=2$ survives. The four-decimal value of $(72-4\pi)/(24-\pi)$ is $2.8494$.

STAT:010425.canonicalSolution:
Areas. The intact rectangle has area $A_R=6\cdot 4=24\,\mathrm{m^2}$. The hole has
area $A_H=\pi(1)^2=\pi\,\mathrm{m^2}$. The remaining plate has
\[
\boxed{A=(24-\pi)\,\mathrm{m^2}}.
\]

First moments. The rectangle centroid is $(3,2)$ and the hole centroid is
$(4,2)$. With the hole signed negative,
\[
Q_y=(72-4\pi)\,\mathrm{m^3},
\qquad
Q_x=(48-2\pi)\,\mathrm{m^3}=2(24-\pi)\,\mathrm{m^3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\bar x=\frac{72-4\pi}{24-\pi}\,\mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{\bar y=\frac{2(24-\pi)}{24-\pi}\,\mathrm m=2\,\mathrm m}.
\]
The cancellation in $\bar y$ is the horizontal midline symmetry: both
the rectangle and the hole are symmetric across $y=2$, so the difference
is as well.

Numerical value. Using $\pi=3.141592653589793$,
\[
72-4\pi=59.43362938564083,\qquad
24-\pi=20.858407346410207,
\]
and
\[
\bar x=2.849384825916228\,\mathrm m\approx\boxed{2.8494\,\mathrm m}
\]
after correct four-decimal rounding.

Claim (i) adds the hole and would produce
$(72+4\pi)/(24+\pi)\approx 3.115$, on the wrong side of $x=3$. Claim
(ii) confuses a missing-material location with the centroid of what
remains; removing area to the right of $x=3$ must shift $\bar x$ to the
left. Claim (iii) either breaks the midline symmetry or skips the first
moment. The plate is homogeneous with uniform thickness, so the mass
centroid coincides with the area centroid. The calculation is not a
beam line-load resultant and leaves a nonzero area, so no pure-couple
limit arises.

graderFixtures.proofText: Signed composite: $A=(24-\pi)\,\mathrm{m^2}$, $Q_y=(72-4\pi)\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $Q_x=2(24-\pi)\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Thus $\bar x=[(72-4\pi)/(24-\pi)]\,\mathrm m\approx 2.8494\,\mathrm m$ and $\bar y=2\,\mathrm m$. The hole is subtracted, not added. The centroid is neither $(4,2)$ nor $(3,2)$. Midline symmetry keeps $\bar y=2\,\mathrm m$.
A hole is a region, so I add it: A=24+pi and x-bar=(3*24+4*pi)/(24+pi)=(72+4pi)/(24+pi), which is about 3.12.
Material is missing at (4,2), so that is the centroid. Alternatively the rectangle center (3,2) is good enough and y-bar should drop below 2 because the hole sits on the midline and removes height.

STAT:010426.title: Three orthogonal wires have r_G=(16/25,27/50,8/25); gravity about O is not a wrench pitch
STAT:010426.objective: For orthogonal rods of lengths 4, 3, 2 m and densities 2, 3, 4 kg/m, compute masses 8, 9, 8 kg, total mass 25 kg, r_G=(16/25,27/50,8/25) m, and the gravity moment M_O=(-27g/2,16g,0) N m about O.
STAT:010426.statement:
Three straight, slender, homogeneous rods meet at the origin $O$ of a
right-handed frame and run along the positive coordinate axes:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{rod}&\text{segment}&\lambda\ (\mathrm{kg/m})\\ \hline
1&(0,0,0)\to(4,0,0)&2\\
2&(0,0,0)\to(0,3,0)&3\\
3&(0,0,0)\to(0,0,2)&4.
\end{array}
\]
Lengths are in meters. Gravity is uniform and acts in the $-\mathbf k$
direction with acceleration $g>0$ in $\mathrm{m/s}^2$. The rods are welded
at $O$ and otherwise free of applied couples.

Do not replace the exercise by reducing a general spatial force system to a
wrench, and do not introduce a central-axis pitch.

1. Compute the three masses and the total mass.
2. Locate each rod's mass center and compute the composite mass center
   $\mathbf r_G=(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)$ as an exact triple of meters.
3. Replace the weights by the single resultant $-(mg)_{\mathrm{tot}}\mathbf k$
   acting at $\mathbf r_G$, and compute the moment $\mathbf M_O$ of that
   gravity system about $O$. Keep $g$ symbolic and give units $\mathrm{N\,m}$.
4. Audit these claims: (i) the masses equal the lengths $4,3,2$, or all
   three densities may be ignored; (ii) $\mathbf M_O$ is obtained from
   $\mathbf W\times\mathbf r_G$ rather than $\mathbf r_G\times\mathbf W$;
   (iii) the system should next be reduced to a wrench of nonzero pitch, or
   a central-axis formula $\mathbf r_c=(\mathbf R\times\mathbf M_O)/\|\mathbf R\|^2$
   is required. State the slender-rod and uniform-gravity hypotheses.
permittedResults: Composite mass center: $m_{\mathrm{tot}}\mathbf r_G=\sum m_i\mathbf r_i$ with $m_i=\lambda_i L_i$ and $\mathbf r_i$ the midpoint of rod $i$.

If $\mathbf W=W\mathbf k$, then $\mathbf r\times\mathbf W=(r_yW)\,\mathbf i-(r_xW)\,\mathbf j$. Here the signed scalar is $W=-m_{\mathrm{tot}}g$, producing a negative $i$ component and a positive $j$ component when $r_x,r_y>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Tabulate m_i and midpoints, form the weighted average r_G, then evaluate the single cross product r_G times (0,0,-25g).
Compute the three individual weight moments about O and add them; each rod contributes only the components from its own midpoint.

milestones.criterion: Computes masses 8, 9, 8 kg and total mass 25 kg from density times length.
Rejects length-as-mass, a reversed cross product, and a wrench or central-axis reduction.

commonErrors.description: Takes the masses to be the lengths 4, 3, 2 or otherwise ignores the three densities when forming r_G.
commonErrors.consequence: The required r_G=(16/25,27/50,8/25) is replaced by a length-weighted or unweighted midpoint.

commonErrors.description: Computes W cross r_G and reports (27g/2,-16g,0), or continues into a nonzero-pitch wrench and a central-axis construction.
commonErrors.consequence: The assigned gravity moment (-27g/2,16g,0) is lost or replaced by the seed wrench exercise.

hintTree.content: Masses are $2\cdot 4=8$, $3\cdot 3=9$, and $4\cdot 2=8$, totaling $25\,\mathrm{kg}$. Midpoints are $(2,0,0)$, $(0,3/2,0)$, and $(0,0,1)$.
$\mathbf r_G\times(0,0,-25g)$ has $i$-component $(27/50)(-25g)=-27g/2$ and $j$-component $-(16/25)(-25g)=16g$.

STAT:010426.canonicalSolution:
Masses. Linear density times length gives
\[
m_1=2\cdot 4=8,\qquad m_2=3\cdot 3=9,\qquad m_3=4\cdot 2=8
\]
in kilograms, and
\[
\boxed{m_{\mathrm{tot}}=25\,\mathrm{kg}}.
\]

Mass centers. Homogeneous rods have midpoints
\[
\mathbf r_1=(2,0,0),\qquad
\mathbf r_2=\Bigl(0,\frac32,0\Bigr),\qquad
\mathbf r_3=(0,0,1)
\]
in meters. The composite center is
\[
\mathbf r_G=\frac{1}{25}\bigl(8(2,0,0)+9(0,3/2,0)+8(0,0,1)\bigr),
\]
so
\[
\bar x=\frac{16}{25},\qquad
\bar y=\frac{27}{50},\qquad
\bar z=\frac{8}{25},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\mathbf r_G=\Bigl(\frac{16}{25},\frac{27}{50},\frac{8}{25}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{m}}.
\]

Gravity moment about $O$. The total weight is
\[
\mathbf W=(0,0,-25g)\ \mathrm{N}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbf M_O=\mathbf r_G\times\mathbf W
=\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\
16/25&27/50&8/25\\
0&0&-25g
\end{vmatrix}
=\Bigl(-\frac{27g}{2},\,16g,\,0\Bigr).
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\mathbf M_O=\Bigl(-\frac{27g}{2},\,16g,\,0\Bigr)\ \mathrm{N\,m}}.
\]
As a check, $m_{\mathrm{tot}}g\bar y=(25g)(27/50)=27g/2$ is the magnitude
of the $x$-moment of a downward system whose mass center lies in $y>0$,
and the sign is negative because $\mathbf r_G\times(-g\mathbf k)$ points
toward $-\mathbf i$ when $\bar y>0$. The $y$-moment $m_{\mathrm{tot}}g\bar x=16g$
is positive.

Claim (i) drops the densities and would produce a different $\mathbf r_G$.
Claim (ii) reverses the cross product and would report
$(27g/2,-16g,0)$. Claim (iii) imports a wrench/central-axis reduction
that is not asked: the present system is already a single force through
$G$, so its pitch about that line is zero and no further axis hunt is
required. The model uses slender homogeneous rods and uniform gravity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Masses $8,9,8$ kg total $25$ kg. Midpoints $(2,0,0)$, $(0,3/2,0)$, $(0,0,1)$ give $\mathbf r_G=(16/25,27/50,8/25)$ m. Then $\mathbf r_G\times(0,0,-25g)$ is $\mathbf M_O=(-27g/2,16g,0)$ N m. Densities are not optional. The cross-product order is not $\mathbf W\times\mathbf r_G$. No wrench pitch or central axis is required.
I treat the three rods as unit density, so the masses are the lengths 4, 3, 2 and the total is 9. Then r_G is the length-weighted midpoint (16/9, 1/2, 4/9).
M_O is W cross r_G, which gives (27g/2, -16g, 0). I then compute the pitch p=(R·M_O)/||R||^2 and a central-axis point r_c=(R cross M_O)/||R||^2 as in a spatial wrench reduction.

STAT:010439.title: Vertical gate width 2 height 3 with top at the free surface and gamma=10 has F=90, center of pressure at depth 2, moment about the top 180
STAT:010439.objective: Compute the hydrostatic resultant on a vertical rectangular gate, place that resultant at the center of pressure rather than at the area centroid, and evaluate the moment about the top edge.
STAT:010439.statement:
A plane rectangular gate stands vertically. Its width is $b=2$ m and its height is $h=3$ m. The top edge of the gate lies in the free surface of a liquid of specific weight $\gamma=10$ kN/m$^3$. The pressure is hydrostatic, $p=\gamma z$ at depth $z$, and acts normal to the gate. There is no hole in the plate and the liquid is not replaced by a discrete wire system.

Do not subtract a hole from the area, do not locate a spatial center of gravity of three orthogonal wires, do not collapse the pressure into a signed line load that keeps a couple by inspection, and do not invoke friction or a capstan.

1. Compute the resultant hydrostatic force on the wet face from $F=\gamma b h^2/2$. State the units.

2. Locate the center of pressure: the depth below the free surface at which the single force $F$ is equipollent to the pressure field.

3. Compute the moment of that resultant about the top edge of the gate.

4. Confirm that the area centroid of the rectangle lies at depth $h/2$ and is not the center of pressure.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the resultant acts at the area centroid, so its depth is $h/2=1.5$ m and the top moment is $135$ kN m”; (ii) “the force is $\gamma$ times area times the bottom depth, so $F=\gamma A h=180$ kN.”

The pressure varies linearly with depth on a vertical rectangle whose top is the free surface. This is not a holed-centroid exercise and not a spatial-wire gravity problem.
permittedResults: If $p=\gamma z$ on $0\le z\le h$ and the width is $b$, then $F=\int_0^h \gamma z\,b\,\mathrm{d}z=\gamma b h^2/2$ and the moment about the top is $\int_0^h z\cdot\gamma z\,b\,\mathrm{d}z=\gamma b h^3/3$, hence the center of pressure is at $z_P=(2/3)h$.
The first-moment identity $z_P=I_{\text{free}}/(\bar z A)$ for this rectangle gives $z_P=(bh^3/12+\bar z^2 A)/(\bar z A)=2h/3$, confirming that $z_P$ is not $\bar z$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate p=gamma z across the rectangle to obtain both F and the top moment, then divide to locate z_P.
Use F=gamma zbar A together with the parallel-axis formula z_P=I/(zbar A) for a vertical rectangle with top at the free surface.

milestones.criterion: Computes the hydrostatic resultant F=90 kN from gamma b h^2/2 or equivalently gamma zbar A.
Places the center of pressure at depth 2 m and reports the top-edge moment 180 kN m.
Rejects the area-centroid line of action and rejects using the bottom depth in F=gamma A h.

commonErrors.description: Places the resultant at the area centroid depth h/2=1.5 m and reports the top moment as 135 kN m.
commonErrors.consequence: The force magnitude may be right, but the line of action and every moment about a gate edge are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Computes F=gamma A h=180 kN by using the bottom depth in place of the centroid depth.
commonErrors.consequence: The resultant is doubled, so the subsequent center of pressure and the top moment cannot be correct.

hintTree.content: The resultant is $F=\gamma b h^2/2=10\cdot 2\cdot 9/2=90$ kN. Equivalently $F=\gamma\bar z A$ with $\bar z=3/2$ and $A=6$.
On a vertical rectangle with top at the free surface the center of pressure is at depth $2h/3=2$ m, not at $h/2$.
The moment about the top is $F\cdot(2h/3)=90\cdot 2=180$ kN m, which is also $\gamma b h^3/3$.

STAT:010439.canonicalSolution:
The wet area is $A=bh=6$ m$^2$ and the centroid depth is $\bar z=h/2=3/2$ m. The resultant force is
\[
F=\gamma\bar z A=10\cdot\frac{3}{2}\cdot 6
=\gamma\frac{b h^2}{2}=10\cdot 2\cdot\frac{9}{2}
=\boxed{90\ \text{kN}}.
\]
The first moment of the pressure about the free surface (the top edge) is
\[
\int_0^3 z\cdot(10 z)\cdot 2\,\mathrm{d}z
=20\int_0^3 z^2\,\mathrm{d}z
=20\cdot 9
=180\ \text{kN m}.
\]
The center of pressure therefore sits at
\[
z_P=\frac{180}{90}=\frac{2h}{3}=\boxed{2\ \text{m}}
\]
below the free surface, and the moment about the top is
\[
\boxed{180\ \text{kN m}}.
\]
The area centroid at depth $h/2=1.5$ m is a different point; it is the correct depth for computing $F$, not the line of action of $F$.

Sentence (i) is false: placing $F$ at the centroid gives the wrong moment $90\cdot 1.5=135$ kN m. Sentence (ii) is false: replacing $\bar z$ by the bottom depth $h$ inflates the force to $\gamma A h=180$ kN.

The pressure field is integrated on an intact vertical rectangle. No hole is subtracted and no discrete-wire center of gravity is formed.

graderFixtures.proofText: The resultant is $F=\gamma b h^2/2=90$ kN. The center of pressure is at depth $2h/3=2$ m, not at the centroid $h/2$. The moment about the top is $180$ kN m.
F=90 kN is fine. The pressure resultant acts at the area centroid, depth h/2=1.5 m, so the moment about the top is 90*1.5=135 kN m.
The deepest pressure is gamma*h, so F=gamma*A*h=10*6*3=180 kN. I then take z_P=2h/3=2 m.

STAT:010440.title: T-section web 2x3 on y=0..3 and flange 6x1 on y=3..4 has areas 6 and 6, ybar=5/2, Ix=17, Iy=20, Ixy=0
STAT:010440.objective: Locate the centroid of a symmetric T built from two rectangles, then evaluate both centroidal second moments and the product of inertia, keeping the parallel-axis terms and the vertical symmetry.
STAT:010440.statement:
A plane T-section is the union of two rectangles, with $y$ measured upward from the foot of the web:
- web: width $2$, height $3$, occupying $|x|\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3$;
- flange: width $6$, height $1$, occupying $|x|\le 3$ and $3\le y\le 4$.

All lengths are in meters. The two areas are $A_w=6$ m$^2$ and $A_f=6$ m$^2$. The section is symmetric about the $y$-axis. There is no hole, and the parts are lamina areas, not spatial wires.

Do not subtract a hole, do not move $\bar y$ onto a hole center, do not replace the T by three orthogonal wires, and do not collapse the figure into a signed line load.

1. Compute $\bar y$ from the web foot $y=0$.

2. About the horizontal centroidal axis, compute $I_x$ by the parallel-axis theorem applied to each rectangle.

3. About the vertical centroidal axis (the axis of symmetry), compute $I_y$.

4. Compute the product of inertia $I_{xy}$ about the centroidal pair.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$I_x$ is only the sum of the own-centroid second moments $9/2+1/2=5$, because the parallel-axis terms cancel”; (ii) “$\bar y$ is the web--flange joint, so $\bar y=3$.”

The figure is an intact T. This is not the holed-plate centroid of the prior fence and not a gravity wrench of discrete wires.
permittedResults: If two parts have equal area and centroidal offsets of equal magnitude about the composite $\bar y$, each parallel-axis contribution is $A d^2$ with the same $d$, and those terms add rather than cancel.
A region symmetric with respect to the $y$-axis has vanishing product of inertia $I_{xy}$ about any origin on that axis, including the area centroid.

acceptableStrategies.description: Locate ybar first, then apply bh^3/12 plus Ad^2 to each rectangle about the two centroidal axes, and invoke vertical symmetry for Ixy.
Check the Ix arithmetic as (9/2+6)+(1/2+6) and the Iy arithmetic as 2+18 before concluding Ixy=0.

milestones.criterion: Computes the composite centroid ybar=5/2 from the two equal areas 6 and 6.
Reports Ix=17 with both parallel-axis terms, Iy=20, and Ixy=0.
Rejects omitting Ad^2 from Ix and rejects setting ybar equal to the web-flange joint.

commonErrors.description: Reports Ix as the sum of own-centroid second moments 9/2+1/2=5, claiming the parallel-axis terms cancel.
commonErrors.consequence: Both Ad^2 contributions are dropped, so Ix is 12 too small and any later stress or radius of gyration is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Places the composite centroid at the web-flange interface y=3 instead of at y=5/2.
commonErrors.consequence: Every parallel-axis distance is measured from the wrong axis, so both Ix and the later transfer identities fail.

hintTree.content: The first moment about $y=0$ is $6\cdot(3/2)+6\cdot(7/2)=9+21=30$, so $\bar y=30/12=5/2$.
Web: $2\cdot 3^3/12=9/2$ and $A d^2=6\cdot 1^2=6$. Flange: $6\cdot 1^3/12=1/2$ and $A d^2=6$. Hence $I_x=17$.
About the axis of symmetry, $I_y=3\cdot 2^3/12+1\cdot 6^3/12=2+18=20$. Each part has $x$-centroid $0$, so $I_{xy}=0$.

STAT:010440.canonicalSolution:
The areas are $A_w=2\cdot 3=6$ and $A_f=6\cdot 1=6$. The composite centroid measured from $y=0$ is
\[
\bar y
=\frac{6\cdot(3/2)+6\cdot(7/2)}{12}
=\frac{9+21}{12}
=\boxed{\dfrac{5}{2}}.
\]
About the horizontal axis through $y=5/2$, the web contributes
\[
\frac{2\cdot 3^3}{12}+6\Bigl(\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{9}{2}+6,
\]
and the flange contributes
\[
\frac{6\cdot 1^3}{12}+6\Bigl(\frac{7}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{1}{2}+6.
\]
Therefore
\[
I_x=\Bigl(\frac{9}{2}+6\Bigr)+\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}+6\Bigr)=\boxed{17}.
\]
About the vertical axis of symmetry each rectangle is already centered, so
\[
I_y=\frac{3\cdot 2^3}{12}+\frac{1\cdot 6^3}{12}=2+18=\boxed{20}.
\]
Each part has vanishing own-product $I_{xy}$ and vanishing $x$-centroid, hence
\[
\boxed{I_{xy}=0}
\]
by vertical symmetry.

Sentence (i) is false: the parallel-axis terms are $+6$ and $+6$; they add, giving $17$ rather than $5$. Sentence (ii) is false: the joint $y=3$ is not the area centroid.

No hole is subtracted. The second moments are those of an intact T, not of a plate with a cutout and not of a spatial wire system.

graderFixtures.proofText: Areas $6$ and $6$ give $\bar y=5/2$. Then $I_x=(9/2+6)+(1/2+6)=17$, $I_y=2+18=20$, and $I_{xy}=0$ by vertical symmetry.
ybar=5/2 is fine. Ix is just the local second moments 2*27/12 + 6*1/12 = 9/2+1/2=5. The Ad^2 terms cancel because the offsets are opposite.
The web meets the flange at y=3, so that joint is the centroid, ybar=3. I then transfer Ix using d_web=1.5 and d_flange=0.5.

STAT:010441.title: Linear p=3x+6y on 0<=x<=2, 0<=y<=1 has R=(0,0,-12), M_O=(-7,14,0), vertical resultant through (7/6,7/12)
STAT:010441.objective: Integrate a linearly varying downward pressure on a rectangle to a single force and a moment about the origin, then locate the vertical resultant and confirm that it lies inside the loaded area.
STAT:010441.statement:
A horizontal rectangular patch occupies $0\le x\le 2$, $0\le y\le 1$ (meters). A downward surface pressure
\[
p(x,y)=3x+6y\qquad\text{kN/m}^2
\]
acts on the patch (the force on $\mathrm{d}A$ is $(0,0,-p\,\mathrm{d}A)$ kN). The origin $O$ is the corner $(0,0)$ of the rectangle. The pressure is not hydrostatic, not a T-section self-weight, and not a discrete-wire gravity system.

Do not replace $p$ by a vertical-gate hydrostatic field, do not compute a second-moment of a T, do not subtract a hole, and do not treat gravity about $O$ as a wrench pitch.

1. Compute the force resultant $\mathbf R=\iint (0,0,-p)\,\mathrm{d}A$.

2. Compute the moment about $O$, $\mathbf M_O=\iint \mathbf r\times(0,0,-p)\,\mathrm{d}A$.

3. Locate the point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ in the plane through which the single vertical force $\mathbf R$ is equipollent to the pressure field.

4. Confirm that $(\bar x,\bar y)$ lies in the closed rectangle.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the resultant acts at the area centroid $(1,1/2)$”; (ii) “the resultant acts at the pressure peak $(2,1)$.”

The load is a linearly varying surface pressure on an intact rectangle. It is not a signed line load whose couple must be kept by inspection, and it is not the spatial-wire center of gravity of the prior fence.
permittedResults: On the rectangle $[0,2]\times[0,1]$, $\iint(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}A=12$. The first moments are $\iint x(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}A=14$ and $\iint y(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}A=7$.
If $\mathbf R=(0,0,-12)$ and $\mathbf M_O=(-7,14,0)$, then $\bar y=7/12$ and $\bar x=7/6$. Both coordinates lie in $[0,2]\times[0,1]$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate p, xp, and yp over the rectangle, assemble R and M_O, then solve r×R=M_O for the interior point.
Reduce the linear field to first moments of 3x and 6y separately, add them, and check that (7/6,7/12) lies in [0,2]×[0,1].

milestones.criterion: Integrates p to the force resultant R=(0,0,-12) kN.
Reports M_O=(-7,14,0) kN m and the line of action (7/6,7/12) inside the rectangle.
Rejects the area-centroid placement and rejects the pressure-peak placement.

commonErrors.description: Sends the vertical resultant through the area centroid (1,1/2), obtaining M_O=(-6,12,0).
commonErrors.consequence: The first moments of a non-constant p are replaced by those of a uniform load, so both moment components are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sends the vertical resultant through the pressure-maximum corner (2,1).
commonErrors.consequence: The line of action is forced to a boundary corner that does not reproduce M_O=(-7,14,0).

hintTree.content: Integrate in $x$ first: $\int_0^2(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}x=6+12y$. Then $\int_0^1(6+12y)\,\mathrm{d}y=12$, so $\mathbf R=(0,0,-12)$.
The moment integrands are $-yp$ and $xp$. They evaluate to $M_x=-7$ and $M_y=14$.
A force $(0,0,-12)$ at $(\bar x,\bar y)$ matches $\mathbf M_O$ when $\bar x=7/6$ and $\bar y=7/12$, which is inside the rectangle.

STAT:010441.canonicalSolution:
The downward resultant has magnitude
\[
\iint_\Omega p\,\mathrm{d}A
=\int_0^1\int_0^2(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
=\int_0^1\bigl[ \tfrac32 x^2+6yx\bigr]_0^2\,\mathrm{d}y
=\int_0^1(6+12y)\,\mathrm{d}y
=6+6=12.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbf R=\boxed{(0,0,-12)\ \text{kN}}.
\]
The moment about $O$ uses $\mathbf r\times(0,0,-p)=(-yp,\,xp,\,0)$:
\[
M_x
=-\int_0^1\int_0^2 y(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
=-\int_0^1(6y+12y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y
=-(3+4)
=-7,
\]
\[
M_y
=\int_0^1\int_0^2 x(3x+6y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
=\int_0^1(8+12y)\,\mathrm{d}y
=8+6
=14.
\]
So
\[
\mathbf M_O=\boxed{(-7,14,0)\ \text{kN m}}.
\]
A single vertical force $(0,0,-12)$ at $(\bar x,\bar y)$ produces
\[
\mathbf M_O=(-12\bar y,\ 12\bar x,\ 0).
\]
Matching components gives
\[
\bar y=\frac{7}{12},\qquad
\bar x=\frac{14}{12}=\frac{7}{6},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\Bigl(\bar x,\bar y\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{7}{6},\frac{7}{12}\Bigr)}.
\]
This point satisfies $0\le 7/6\le 2$ and $0\le 7/12\le 1$, so it lies inside the loaded rectangle.

Sentence (i) is false: the area centroid is $(1,1/2)$, which would produce $\mathbf M_O=(-6,12,0)$, not $(-7,14,0)$. Sentence (ii) is false: the pressure peak at $(2,1)$ would produce $\mathbf M_O=(-12,24,0)$.

The integration is over an intact linearly varying field. It does not use a hydrostatic $2h/3$ rule, a T-section second moment, or a spatial-wire center of gravity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Integrating $p=3x+6y$ gives $\mathbf R=(0,0,-12)$ kN and $\mathbf M_O=(-7,14,0)$ kN m. The vertical resultant acts at $(7/6,7/12)$, which lies inside the rectangle.
The force is R=(0,0,-12). A uniform-load shortcut puts that force at the area centroid (1,1/2), so M_O=(-6,12,0).
R=(0,0,-12) is fine. The pressure is largest at (2,1), so the resultant acts there and M_O=(-12,24,0).

STAT:010527.title: A pushed block tips before it exhausts static friction
STAT:010527.objective: Compare sliding and tipping thresholds, locate the subcritical normal resultant, and identify the friction coefficient at which both modes become simultaneous.
STAT:010527.statement:
A uniform rectangular block of weight $W=1000\ \mathrm N$ rests on a rough horizontal floor. Its base width in the push direction is $b=0.60\ \mathrm m$, and its height is $a=0.80\ \mathrm m$. A horizontal force $P$ is applied to the right at the top edge. The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s=0.40$. Treat the contact pressure as a compressive resultant normal force $N\ge0$ whose line of action may shift within the base. For $P>0$, let $F\ge0$ denote the magnitude of the floor friction acting to the left on the block, and let $x_N>0$ denote a rightward shift of the normal resultant from the base center.

1. Assuming full contact, determine the force $P_{slide}$ at which sliding would become impending.
2. Determine the force $P_{tip}$ at which the normal resultant reaches the right edge of the base. Which event occurs first as $P$ grows quasistatically?
3. At $P=300\ \mathrm N$, find $F$, $N$, and the horizontal shift $x_N$ of the normal resultant from the base center. Verify both the friction inequality and $|x_N|<b/2$.
4. Find the value of $\mu_s$ for which sliding and tipping would begin simultaneously. Explain why a calculation beyond the first threshold cannot keep assuming the same full-contact static model.

Take counterclockwise moments as positive. This is a finite-contact block problem, not a ladder-contact problem.
permittedResults: With $F\ge0$ defined as the leftward friction magnitude and $x_N>0$ toward the pushed edge, full-contact equilibrium gives $F=P$, $N=W$, and $x_NW=Pa$.
The two candidate thresholds are $P_{slide}=\mu_sW$ and $P_{tip}=Wb/(2a)$; the smaller admissible value occurs first.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve full-contact force and moment balance, then compare the independent friction and eccentricity limits.
Compute the maximum admissible horizontal force from each failure mode and choose the smaller bound.

milestones.criterion: Derives and evaluates both candidate thresholds and selects tipping as the first event.
Solves the P=300 N equilibrium with 300 N leftward friction, N=1000 N, the 0.240 m rightward normal-resultant shift, and both admissibility checks.
Finds mu_s=0.375 for simultaneous onset and states the post-threshold model boundary.

commonErrors.description: Sets F=mu_s N for every static load or concludes sliding first solely from the friction capacity.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual subcritical friction and the competing tipping threshold are lost.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the normal resultant at the base center while claiming moment equilibrium, or uses the full width rather than half-width at tipping.
commonErrors.consequence: The tipping force and contact admissibility check are wrong.

hintTree.content: Solve force balance without setting friction equal to its maximum until the sliding threshold is requested.
At tipping, set $x_N=b/2$ in the moment equation $x_NW=Pa$.
For simultaneous onset, equate the two candidate threshold forces and solve for mu_s.

STAT:010527.canonicalSolution:
While the block has full static contact, the floor friction acts left with
magnitude $F$, so
\[
F=P,\qquad N=W.
\]
The friction limit would be reached at
\[
\boxed{P_{slide}=\mu_sW=(0.40)(1000)=400\ \mathrm N}.
\]
Moment equilibrium about the base center gives $x_NW=Pa$. At incipient tipping $x_N=b/2$, so
\[
\boxed{P_{tip}=\frac{Wb}{2a}
=\frac{(1000)(0.60)}{2(0.80)}=375\ \mathrm N}.
\]
Thus tipping occurs first. At that force the required friction is only $375\ \mathrm N<400\ \mathrm N$.

For $P=300\ \mathrm N$,
\[
\boxed{F=300\ \mathrm N},\qquad
\boxed{N=1000\ \mathrm N},\qquad
\boxed{x_N=\frac{Pa}{W}=0.240\ \mathrm m}.
\]
Indeed $F=300<\mu_sN=400\ \mathrm N$ and $x_N=0.240<b/2=0.300\ \mathrm m$, so neither failure mode is impending.

Simultaneous onset requires
\[
\mu_sW=\frac{Wb}{2a},
\qquad
\boxed{\mu_s=\frac b{2a}=0.375}.
\]
Once tipping begins, the assumed full-contact pressure distribution no longer applies; once sliding begins, a zero-acceleration static model no longer determines the subsequent motion.

graderFixtures.proofText: $P_{slide}=\mu_sW=400$ N, whereas $P_{tip}=Wb/(2a)=375$ N, so tipping occurs first. At $P=300$ N, friction has leftward magnitude $F=300$ N, $N=1000$ N, and the normal shift is rightward with $x_N=Pa/W=0.240$ m, below both limits. Simultaneous onset requires $\mu_s=b/(2a)=0.375$.
Static friction always equals mu_s N=400 N, so sliding is impending for every value of P and must occur before tipping.
The normal remains at the base center. Tipping starts when Pa=Wb, giving P=750 N, so it cannot compete with sliding.

STAT:010528.title: A half-wrap capstan doubles tension at impending slip
STAT:010528.objective: Derive and apply the capstan tension-ratio inequality, then convert the limiting tension difference into transmitted torque.
STAT:010528.statement:
A flexible belt wraps through angle $\beta$ around a fixed rough circular drum of radius $r$. Let $T_{tight}\ge T_{slack}>0$. The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s$. For a differential belt element subtending $d\theta$, use tangential limiting balance $dT=\mu_s\,dN$ and radial balance $dN=T\,d\theta$ to first order.

1. Derive the limiting capstan relation $T_{tight}/T_{slack}=e^{\mu_s\beta}$ for impending slip, and state the corresponding inequality for a static belt not necessarily at the limit.
2. Let
\[
\beta=\pi,\qquad \mu_s=\frac{\ln2}{\pi},\qquad
T_{slack}=300\ \mathrm N,
\qquad r=0.20\ \mathrm m.
\]
Find the largest admissible tight-side tension.
3. Find the corresponding maximum torque magnitude transmitted to the drum, using $\tau=(T_{tight}-T_{slack})r$.
4. Explain why equality must not be imposed for every static operating tension and why the wrap angle must be in radians.

Assume the belt is light and flexible and the stated coefficient is uniform.
permittedResults: At limiting friction, $dT/T=\mu_s\,d\theta$ integrates across the contact arc.
The belt forces exert opposing moments about the drum axis, leaving torque magnitude $(T_{tight}-T_{slack})r$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the differential limiting-friction balance over the contact angle and then apply the static bound.
Use the known capstan inequality with an explicit impending-slip justification, then take moments of the two end tensions.

milestones.criterion: Derives dT/T=mu_s dtheta and the limiting exponential relation with the proper static inequality.
Computes the limiting ratio 2 and tight-side tension 600 N.
Computes 60.0 N m from the tension difference and explains equality and radian scope.

commonErrors.description: Uses a linear tension law, reverses the ratio, or imposes equality on every static belt state.
commonErrors.consequence: The distributed friction capacity and operating regime are misrepresented.

commonErrors.description: Computes torque from T_tight r alone or adds the two tension moments.
commonErrors.consequence: The opposing slack-side moment is omitted and the torque is wrong.

hintTree.content: Combine dT=mu_s dN with dN=T dtheta before integrating from slack side to tight side.
Here $\mu_s\beta=(\ln2/\pi)\pi=\ln2$.
Use the tension difference, not the tight-side tension alone, in the torque formula.

STAT:010528.canonicalSolution:
At impending slip the differential balances give
\[
dT=\mu_sT\,d\theta,
\qquad
\frac{dT}{T}=\mu_s\,d\theta.
\]
Integrating from the slack side to the tight side yields
\[
\ln\frac{T_{tight}}{T_{slack}}=\mu_s\beta,
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{T_{tight}}{T_{slack}}=e^{\mu_s\beta}}.
\]
For a static belt below impending slip, the correct statement is
\[
\boxed{\frac{T_{tight}}{T_{slack}}\le e^{\mu_s\beta}}.
\]
With the supplied data, $e^{\mu_s\beta}=e^{\ln2}=2$, so
\[
\boxed{T_{tight,max}=2(300)=600\ \mathrm N}.
\]
The limiting transmitted torque magnitude is
\[
\boxed{\tau_{max}=(600-300)(0.20)=60.0\ \mathrm{N\,m}}.
\]
Static friction adjusts below its limiting distribution, so equality marks impending slip rather than all static operation. Radian measure is required because $d\theta$ is dimensionless arc angle in the differential balance.

graderFixtures.proofText: Limiting element equilibrium gives $dT/T=\mu_s d\theta$, so $T_{tight}/T_{slack}\le e^{\mu_s\beta}$, with equality only at impending slip. Here the bound is $e^{\ln2}=2$, hence $T_{tight,max}=600$ N and $\tau_{max}=(600-300)(0.20)=60.0$ N m.
The belt is static, so Ttight/Tslack=1+mu beta=1+ln2 at every operating point; static friction is always maximal.
At the limit Ttight=600 N, so the transmitted torque is Ttight r=120 N m because only the tight side acts on the drum.

STAT:010529.title: A square-thread screw raises easily enough but still self-locks
STAT:010529.objective: Use lead and friction angles to compute raising and lowering torques, establish self-locking, and evaluate ideal raising efficiency.
STAT:010529.statement:
A single-start square-thread power screw supports an axial load $W=2.20\ \mathrm{kN}$. Use the mean thread radius $r=0.0500\ \mathrm m$. Collar friction is negligible. The lead angle $\lambda$ and thread friction angle $\phi$ satisfy
\[
\tan\lambda=\frac14,
\qquad
\tan\phi=\mu=\frac13.
\]
Model one turn of the thread as an inclined plane wrapped around the mean cylinder.

1. Derive or state with justification the raising torque
\[
M_{raise}=Wr\tan(\phi+\lambda)
\]
and calculate it.
2. For controlled lowering, derive the required torque magnitude
\[
M_{lower}=Wr\tan(\phi-\lambda)
\]
when $\phi>\lambda$, and calculate it. State the direction of this applied torque relative to the load's tendency to descend.
3. Decide whether the screw is self-locking and explain the angle criterion.
4. For one ideal turn, define raising efficiency as useful work $W\ell$ divided by input work $2\pi M_{raise}$, where the lead satisfies $\ell=2\pi r\tan\lambda$. Show that $\eta=\tan\lambda/\tan(\phi+\lambda)$ and evaluate it.

Keep raising torque, controlled-lowering torque, and the load's unrestrained torque tendency distinct.
permittedResults: $\tan(\phi\pm\lambda)=(\tan\phi\pm\tan\lambda)/(1\mp\tan\phi\tan\lambda)$.
For a square thread without collar friction, raising uses the effective incline angle $\phi+\lambda$, while controlled lowering of a self-locking load uses $\phi-\lambda$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Unwrap the thread into a rough incline and apply friction-angle addition separately for raising and lowering.
Use the standard square-thread torque formulas, verify them by angle ordering, and derive efficiency from work per turn.

milestones.criterion: Computes both compound-angle tangents and the raising and controlled-lowering torque magnitudes.
Correctly identifies self-locking from phi greater than lambda and explains the lowering torque direction.
Derives the work ratio and evaluates the ideal raising efficiency as 11/28.

commonErrors.description: Uses phi-lambda for raising, phi+lambda for lowering, or reports the controlled-lowering torque as a negative magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The two physical operating cases and their numerical torques are confused.

commonErrors.description: Calls the screw overhauling despite phi>lambda or computes efficiency without the lead-angle work relation.
commonErrors.consequence: The back-drive conclusion or the required efficiency 11/28 is wrong.

hintTree.content: Use $Wr=(2200)(0.0500)=110\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ and cancel $2\pi Wr$ in the efficiency ratio.

STAT:010529.canonicalSolution:
Unwrapping the mean thread gives the standard rough-incline result
\[
M_{raise}=Wr\tan(\phi+\lambda).
\]
The tangent addition formula gives
\[
\tan(\phi+\lambda)
=\frac{1/3+1/4}{1-(1/3)(1/4)}
=\frac7{11}.
\]
Since $Wr=(2200)(0.0500)=110\ \mathrm{N\,m}$,
\[
\boxed{M_{raise}=110\frac7{11}=70.0\ \mathrm{N\,m}}.
\]
For lowering,
\[
\tan(\phi-\lambda)
=\frac{1/3-1/4}{1+(1/3)(1/4)}
=\frac1{13},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{M_{lower}=\frac{110}{13}\ \mathrm{N\,m}
\approx8.46\ \mathrm{N\,m}}.
\]
This torque is applied in the lowering direction to make descent impending; friction otherwise prevents the load from back-driving the screw.

Because $\tan\phi=1/3>1/4=\tan\lambda$ and both angles lie between $0$ and $\pi/2$, $\phi>\lambda$. The screw is therefore self-locking.

For one turn,
\[
\eta=\frac{W(2\pi r\tan\lambda)}{2\pi Wr\tan(\phi+\lambda)}
=\frac{\tan\lambda}{\tan(\phi+\lambda)}
=\frac{1/4}{7/11}
=\boxed{\frac{11}{28}\approx0.3929}.
\]

STAT:010542.title: Horizontal P on a 3-4-5 rough incline with W=100 and mu_s=1/2 admits 200/11<=P<=200; f=+500/11 downslope-impending, f=-100 upslope-impending, and f=0 at 75
STAT:010542.objective: Resolve a horizontal push on a 3-4-5 rough plane into a P-dependent normal and a signed upslope friction, then close the Coulomb inequality to a two-sided rest window with identified impending ends.
STAT:010542.statement:
A block of weight $W=100\,\mathrm{N}$ rests on a fixed rough plane that rises to the right. The plane makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal satisfying
\[
\sin\theta=\frac35,\qquad\cos\theta=\frac45.
\]
The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s=\tfrac12$. A single horizontal force $P$ (newtons), directed toward the rising side of the plane, acts on the block. The block is prevented from tipping, so the only unknown contact actions are the outward normal $N$ and a tangential friction. Take the rightward-horizontal and upward-vertical unit vectors as the laboratory basis, the unit tangent up the plane as $\hat{\mathbf e}_t=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, and the outward unit normal as $\hat{\mathbf e}_n=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$. Write the friction force on the block as $f\,\hat{\mathbf e}_t$, with the sign convention that $f>0$ is upslope.

Do not replace $P$ by a force already parallel to the plane, do not convert the exercise into a tipping-versus-sliding audit, and do not introduce a capstan wrap or a square-thread screw.

1. Write the two scalar equilibrium statements obtained by projecting $\mathbf P-W\mathbf j+N\hat{\mathbf e}_n+f\hat{\mathbf e}_t=\mathbf 0$ onto $\hat{\mathbf e}_n$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_t$. Solve the linear system and show
   \[
   N=80+\frac{3P}{5},\qquad f=60-\frac{4P}{5}.
   \]

2. Impose the Coulomb rest restriction $|f|\le\mu_s N$. Obtain the closed interval of $P$ for which rest is possible. (The algebra produces the endpoints $P=200/11$ and $P=200$.)

3. Evaluate the signed friction at each endpoint. Identify which end is downslope-impending and which end is upslope-impending, and record the two friction values.

4. Find the unique force $P$ at which the friction vanishes.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “$P$ already acts up the plane, so $N=W\cos\theta=80$ and $f=W\sin\theta-P=60-P$”; (ii) “the normal is only the weight projection $N=80$, independent of the horizontal push.”

Do not declare impending slip from $W\sin\theta$ versus $\mu_s W\cos\theta$ alone, do not use a kinetic coefficient, and do not treat the block as a three-force body whose lines must meet.
permittedResults: On the 3-4-5 plane $\hat{\mathbf e}_n=(-3/5,4/5)$, $\hat{\mathbf e}_t=(4/5,3/5)$, the projections of a rightward horizontal $P$ and a downward $W$ are $P\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_n=-3P/5$, $P\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_t=4P/5$, $W\mathbf j\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_n=4W/5$, and $W\mathbf j\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_t=3W/5$.
If $N=80+3P/5$ and $f=60-4P/5$ with $\mu_s=1/2$, then $|60-4P/5|\le 40+3P/10$ rearranges to the closed window $200/11\le P\le 200$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Project the four forces onto the plane normal and tangent, solve the 2-by-2 system for N(P) and f(P), then split the Coulomb inequality.
Write laboratory components, eliminate one unknown at a time to reach N=80+3P/5 and f=60-4P/5, then test both impending senses.

milestones.criterion: Resolves the horizontal push on the 3-4-5 basis and reports N=80+3P/5 together with signed upslope f=60-4P/5.
Closes |f|<=N/2 on 200/11<=P<=200 and identifies f=+500/11 downslope-impending, f=-100 upslope-impending, and f=0 at P=75.
Rejects an already-parallel P and rejects a P-independent normal N=80.

commonErrors.description: Treats the applied P as already acting up the plane, writes N=W cosθ=80 and f=60-P, and reports the window 20<=P<=100.
commonErrors.consequence: Both contact actions miss the normal component of P, so every endpoint, every impending friction, and the zero-friction load are attached to the wrong resolution.

commonErrors.description: Keeps a signed tangent formula involving P but freezes N=W cosθ=80, independent of the horizontal push, and obtains a different rest interval.
commonErrors.consequence: The Coulomb comparison uses an understated normal, so the admissible P-window is wrong at both ends.

hintTree.content: Project onto $\hat{\mathbf e}_n$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_t$. The normal balance is $N-3P/5-80=0$ after $W\cos\theta=80$ is inserted, and the tangent balance is $f-60+4P/5=0$.
Coulomb rest is $\bigl|60-4P/5\bigr|\le\tfrac12\bigl(80+3P/5\bigr)=40+3P/10$. Split into $60-4P/5\le 40+3P/10$ and the opposite inequality.
The lower end $P=200/11$ produces $f=+500/11>0$ (downslope-impending). The upper end $P=200$ produces $f=-100$ (upslope-impending). Setting $f=0$ gives $P=75$.

STAT:010542.canonicalSolution:
The laboratory force balance is
\[
(P,0)+(0,-100)+N\Bigl(-\frac35,\frac45\Bigr)+f\Bigl(\frac45,\frac35\Bigr)=\mathbf 0.
\]
The two scalar statements are
\[
P-\frac35 N+\frac45 f=0,\qquad
-100+\frac45 N+\frac35 f=0,
\]
or, after clearing denominators,
\[
3N-4f=5P,\qquad 4N+3f=500.
\]
Multiplying the second by $4$ and the first by $3$ and adding eliminates $f$:
\[
16N+12f+9N-12f=2000+15P\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 25N=2000+15P,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{N=80+\dfrac{3P}{5}}.
\]
Multiplying the second by $3$ and the first by $4$ and subtracting eliminates $N$:
\[
12N+9f-(12N-16f)=1500-20P\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 25f=1500-20P,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{f=60-\dfrac{4P}{5}}.
\]
(The same pair is recovered by projecting onto $\hat{\mathbf e}_n$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_t$ directly.) Coulomb rest requires
\[
\Bigl|60-\frac{4P}{5}\Bigr|
\le
\frac12\Bigl(80+\frac{3P}{5}\Bigr)
=40+\frac{3P}{10}.
\]
The first half is
\[
60-\frac{4P}{5}\le 40+\frac{3P}{10}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
20\le\frac{11P}{10}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
P\ge\frac{200}{11}.
\]
The second half is
\[
-60+\frac{4P}{5}\le 40+\frac{3P}{10}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{P}{2}\le 100
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
P\le 200.
\]
Hence rest is possible precisely on the closed window
\[
\boxed{\dfrac{200}{11}\le P\le 200}.
\]
At the lower end $P=200/11$,
\[
f=60-\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{200}{11}=60-\frac{160}{11}=\boxed{\dfrac{500}{11}},
\]
and $N=80+3\cdot(200/11)/5=1000/11$, so $|f|=N/2$. The friction is positive, therefore downslope-impending. At the upper end $P=200$,
\[
f=60-\frac{4}{5}\cdot 200=60-160=\boxed{-100},
\]
and $N=80+120=200$, so $|f|=N/2$. The friction is negative, therefore upslope-impending. The friction vanishes when $60-4P/5=0$, i.e.
\[
\boxed{P=75}.
\]
That interior value lies in the window, as $200/11<75<200$.

Sentence (i) is false: a horizontal $P$ is not an upslope load. Replacing it by an already-parallel force produces the different pair $N=80$, $f=60-P$ and the spurious window $20\le P\le 100$. Sentence (ii) is false: the horizontal push has a nonzero projection on $\hat{\mathbf e}_n$, so $N$ grows with $P$. Dropping that projection again freezes $N=80$ and yields the different window $25\le P\le 125$.

The model is a single rigid block on a fixed rough plane with a horizontal load. It is not a tip-versus-slide comparison, not a belt-wrap capstan, and not a square-thread screw.

graderFixtures.proofText: Equilibrium on the 3-4-5 basis gives $N=80+3P/5$ and signed upslope $f=60-4P/5$. Then $|f|\le N/2$ is $200/11\le P\le 200$, with $f=+500/11$ downslope-impending, $f=-100$ upslope-impending, and $f=0$ at $P=75$.
P already acts up the plane, so N=W cosθ=80 and f=60-P. Then |60-P|<=40 gives 20<=P<=100. I never form 80+3P/5.
I keep f=60-4P/5 but take N=W cosθ=80 with no P in the normal. Then |60-4P/5|<=40 and the window is 25<=P<=125.

STAT:010543.title: Drum torque 100 on radius 1/2 needs |F|=200 and N=500 at mu=0.4; lever moments at A=(0.4,0.2) give P=180 versus P=20 according to drum sense
STAT:010543.objective: Convert a held drum torque into a pad friction and its Coulomb companion normal, then take lever moments about the fulcrum to obtain the two direction-dependent efforts.
STAT:010543.statement:
A brake drum of radius $r=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{m}$ is to be held against a constant torque of $100\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$. A rigid lever in the plane has its fulcrum at the origin $O$. The pad contacts the drum at the point $A=(0.4,0.2)\,\mathrm{m}$. The operator applies a downward effort $P$ at $B=(1,0)\,\mathrm{m}$. The force exerted by the pad on the lever is a purely horizontal normal $-N\,\mathbf i$ together with a vertical friction $\pm F\,\mathbf j$ whose sign follows the sense of the impending drum rotation. Take impending slip at the pad with $\mu=0.4$, and assume the drum torque is carried entirely by the pad friction. Lengths are in metres and forces in newtons.

Do not replace the lever by a compound press with staged arms, do not wrap a belt about the drum, and do not treat the contact as a square-thread screw.

1. From the drum moment about its centre, obtain the friction magnitude $|F|$. Then impose impending slip at the pad to obtain the companion normal $N=|F|/\mu$.

2. Take moments of the lever about $O$. With the two admissible friction senses, show that the downward effort satisfies
   \[
   P=0.2\,N\pm 0.4\,F.
   \]

3. Insert the impending pair $(N,|F|)$ and evaluate the two numerical efforts. Identify which drum sense is self-energizing (the smaller $P$).

4. Confirm that reversing the drum rotation reverses the sign in front of the $0.4F$ term and therefore swaps the two efforts.

5. Audit both sentences: (i) “the horizontal normal at $A$ has no moment about $O$, so $P=\pm 0.4F$ only”; (ii) “drum sense cannot change the effort, so $P=0.2N=100$ independently of rotation.”

Do not introduce a capstan exponential, do not resolve the pad as a three-force concurrency on the drum alone, and do not replace $A$ by a hinge that transmits a couple.
permittedResults: A drum of radius $r$ held by a rim friction $F$ against a torque $M$ satisfies $|F|=M/r$. At impending slip with coefficient $\mu$ the companion normal is $N=|F|/\mu$.
The planar moment about the origin is $xF_y-yF_x$. For a force $(-N,\pm F)$ at $(0.4,0.2)$ and a force $(0,-P)$ at $(1,0)$, equilibrium of moments is $P=0.2N\pm 0.4F$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fix |F| and N from the drum and Coulomb, then write the two signed moments of the pad force about O and solve for P.
Compute the moment arms 0.2 m for N and 0.4 m for F directly from A=(0.4,0.2), add the operator arm at B, and evaluate both signs.

milestones.criterion: Obtains |F|=200 and the impending normal N=500 from the drum torque and mu=0.4.
Takes moments about O to P=0.2N±0.4F and reports the two efforts 180 and 20 with drum-sense reversal.
Rejects omitting the normal lever arm at A and rejects a single effort independent of drum sense.

commonErrors.description: Declares that the horizontal normal at A has no moment about O, drops the 0.2N term, and reports P=±0.4F=±80.
commonErrors.consequence: The operator effort is detached from the pad pressure, so neither numerical value 180 nor 20 can appear.

commonErrors.description: Drops the friction moment on the lever and reports the single effort P=0.2N=100, claiming drum rotation cannot change P.
commonErrors.consequence: The self-energizing and self-de-energizing values are collapsed to one incorrect number.

hintTree.content: The drum balance is $|F|\cdot\tfrac12=100$, so $|F|=200$. Impending slip then gives $N=200/0.4=500$.
Moment of $(-N,\pm F)$ about $O$ is $0.4(\pm F)-0.2(-N)=\pm 0.4F+0.2N$. The downward $P$ contributes $-P$.
Hence $P=0.2\cdot 500\pm 0.4\cdot 200=100\pm 80$, so the two efforts are $180$ and $20$. The smaller value is the self-energizing sense.

STAT:010543.canonicalSolution:
The drum is held by the pad friction alone, so
\[
|F|\cdot\frac12=100\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{|F|=200\,\mathrm{N}}.
\]
Impending slip at the pad with $\mu=0.4$ then forces
\[
N=\frac{|F|}{\mu}=\frac{200}{0.4}=\boxed{500\,\mathrm{N}}.
\]
On the lever the pad force is $(-N,\pm F)$ at $A=(0.4,0.2)$ and the operator force is $(0,-P)$ at $B=(1,0)$. The planar moment about the fulcrum $O$ is $xF_y-yF_x$, hence
\[
0.4(\pm F)-0.2(-N)+1\cdot(-P)=0,
\]
which rearranges to
\[
\boxed{P=0.2\,N\pm 0.4\,F}.
\]
Inserting the impending pair gives
\[
P=0.2\cdot 500\pm 0.4\cdot 200=100\pm 80,
\]
so the two admissible efforts are
\[
\boxed{P=180\,\mathrm{N}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boxed{P=20\,\mathrm{N}}.
\]
The smaller value $P=20\,\mathrm{N}$ is the self-energizing drum sense: friction on the lever then acts downward and helps the operator. The larger value $P=180\,\mathrm{N}$ is the self-de-energizing sense: friction on the lever acts upward and opposes the operator. Reversing the drum rotation flips the sign in front of $0.4F$ and therefore swaps the two numbers; the pair $\{20,180\}$ is attached to the two senses and is not a single effort.

Sentence (i) is false: $A$ does not lie on the $x$-axis, so the horizontal normal has lever arm $0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ and contributes the $0.2N$ term. Dropping that arm leaves $P=\pm 80$, which cannot hold the impending pad. Sentence (ii) is false: the friction moment $\pm 0.4F$ changes sign with the drum, so the effort cannot be the single number $0.2N=100$.

The model is a single lever and a single pad on a drum. It is not a staged compound press, not a wrapped capstan, and not a screw.

graderFixtures.proofText: Drum balance gives $|F|=200$ and impending slip gives $N=500$. Lever moments about $O$ are $P=0.2N\pm 0.4F$, hence $P=180$ versus $P=20$, and reversing the drum swaps the two efforts.
N is horizontal so it has no moment about O. Then P=±0.4F=±80. I never form 0.2N and I do not report 180 or 20.
I agree |F|=200 and N=500, but drum sense cannot change the effort. I drop ±0.4F and report the single value P=0.2N=100.

STAT:010630.title: Four supporting cable segments give an ideal four-to-one block tackle
STAT:010630.objective: Differentiate a constant-length cable constraint and use compatible virtual work to determine ideal effort and displacement ratio.
STAT:010630.statement:
An ideal block-and-tackle has one moving block carrying a load $W$. Exactly four straight cable segments change length by the same amount when the moving block rises; all other cable portions have constant length. The cable is massless, the pulleys are frictionless, and the free end is pulled downward by an applied force $P$.

Let $y$ be the upward displacement of the moving block and let $x$ be the downward displacement of the free end. For compatible positive virtual displacements, the cable geometry gives a constant-length relation.

1. Derive $\delta x=4\,\delta y$ from the cable-length constraint, making the signs explicit.
2. Write the virtual work of $P$ and $W$ and derive the equilibrium relation between them.
3. For $W=8.00\ \mathrm{kN}$, compute the ideal effort $P$ and state how far the free end must move to raise the load $0.250\ \mathrm m$.
4. Check the result by equal cable tension and force equilibrium of the moving block. Explain why ideal pulley support reactions do no virtual work in the chosen system.

Do not vary $x$ and $y$ independently; they are coupled by one cable.
permittedResults: If upward block motion shortens four supporting segments by $\delta y$ each, constant cable length requires the pulled free length to increase by $\delta x=4\delta y$.
For compatible virtual motion in equilibrium, the total virtual work of applied loads is zero.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the cable-length constraint and substitute it directly into the virtual-work equation.
Use equal cable tension for a force-balance solution, then verify the reciprocal displacement ratio by work conservation.

milestones.criterion: Derives the four-segment compatible displacement relation with consistent signs.
Uses virtual work to obtain P=W/4 and evaluates P=2.00 kN and x=1.00 m.
Confirms the result from four equal tensions and explains the ideal-reaction work boundary.

commonErrors.description: Varies x and y independently or uses delta y=4 delta x for the stated coordinate directions.
commonErrors.consequence: The cable constraint and mechanical advantage are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Adds the weight work with the wrong sign or concludes P=4W.
commonErrors.consequence: The equilibrium effort contradicts both work balance and the four supporting tensions.

hintTree.content: Write cable length as constant terms plus four variable supporting lengths minus the downward free-end coordinate, then differentiate.
With the selected positive directions, $\delta U=P\delta x-W\delta y$.
For the force check, each of the four supporting segments exerts the same upward tension on the moving assembly.

STAT:010630.canonicalSolution:
When the block rises by $\delta y$, each of the four supporting segments shortens by $\delta y$. Pulling the free end downward supplies an additional length $\delta x$. Constant total length therefore gives
\[
-4\delta y+\delta x=0,
\qquad
\boxed{\delta x=4\delta y}.
\]
The applied force acts along positive $x$, while the weight acts opposite positive $y$, so equilibrium virtual work is
\[
0=P\delta x-W\delta y
=(4P-W)\delta y.
\]
For a nonzero compatible virtual displacement,
\[
\boxed{P=\frac W4}.
\]
Thus for $W=8.00\ \mathrm{kN}$,
\[
\boxed{P=2.00\ \mathrm{kN}}.
\]
Raising the load $0.250\ \mathrm m$ requires
\[
\boxed{x=4(0.250)=1.00\ \mathrm m}
\]
of downward free-end motion.

The ideal cable has uniform tension $T=P$. Four segments support the moving block, so $4T-W=0$, again giving $P=W/4$. Fixed-pulley bearing reactions act at fixed points, and ideal internal cable-pulley contact forces cancel within the selected mechanism, so they contribute no virtual work.

graderFixtures.proofText: Constant cable length gives $-4\delta y+\delta x=0$, so $\delta x=4\delta y$. Virtual work is $P\delta x-W\delta y=0$, hence $P=W/4=2.00$ kN. A 0.250 m lift requires 1.00 m of pull. Four equal tensions give the same result.
The free end and load can be varied independently. Choosing delta x=0 with nonzero delta y shows W must vanish; alternatively delta y=4 delta x.
Both P and W do positive work, so P delta x+W delta y=0. Taking magnitudes gives P=4W=32 kN.
