TRAN:010424.title: Unequal tanks 1 L / 3 L with kA=0.4 L/min meet C1=6, C2=2 at t=(15/8)ln 3 and conserve inventory 12
TRAN:010424.objective: For V1=1 L, V2=3 L, kA=0.4 L/min, C1(0)=12, C2(0)=0, obtain C_inf=3, Delta=12 e^{-8t/15}, C1=3+9 e^{-8t/15}, C2=3-3 e^{-8t/15}; at t=(15/8)ln 3 one has C1=6, C2=2, flux 1.6; initial flux 4.8; half-time (15/8)ln 2. Audit the equal-volume formula and inventory.
TRAN:010424.statement:
Two well-mixed compartments exchange a dilute solute through a
membrane. The volumes are $V_1=1\,\mathrm{L}$ and $V_2=3\,\mathrm{L}$,
the membrane capacity is
$kA=0.4\,\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{min}$, and the initial data are
$C_1(0)=12$ and $C_2(0)=0$ (same concentration units). The molar
flux from 1 into 2 is $kA(C_1-C_2)$. There is no reaction.

1. Prove that the conserved inventory is $V_1 C_1+V_2 C_2=12$ and
   that the equilibrium concentration is $C_\infty=3$. Writing
   $\Delta:=C_1-C_2$, prove
   \[
   \Delta(t)=12\,e^{-8t/15}
   \]
   and therefore
   \[
   C_1=3+9\,e^{-8t/15},\qquad
   C_2=3-3\,e^{-8t/15}.
   \]

2. At the instant $t=(15/8)\ln 3$, prove $C_1=6$, $C_2=2$, and that
   the instantaneous membrane flux is $1.6$ (concentration units
   times $\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{min}$). Confirm that the initial flux
   is $4.8$.

3. Define the half-time by $\Delta(t_{1/2})=\Delta(0)/2$ and prove
   $t_{1/2}=(15/8)\ln 2$.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the tanks may be treated as equal
   volume, so the decay rate is $2kA/V$ with $V=2\,\mathrm{L}$ and
   $C_1,C_2$ are symmetric about $6$”; (ii) “inventory need not be
   conserved, so $C_\infty=0$ or $C_\infty=12$.” Also refuse a CRE
   reaction-inventory reading of the two tanks.

Do not replace the membrane ODE by a ternary Maxwell–Stefan inversion
or by a flux-ledger exact boundary layer.
permittedResults: $\dot\Delta=-kA(1/V_1+1/V_2)\Delta$. Here $kA(1+1/3)=8/15\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}$, so $\Delta(t)=\Delta(0)e^{-8t/15}$.
Inverting $C_1-C_2=\Delta$ against $V_1 C_1+V_2 C_2=12$ yields $C_1=C_\infty+(V_2/(V_1+V_2))\Delta$ and $C_2=C_\infty-(V_1/(V_1+V_2))\Delta$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Conserve V1 C1+V2 C2=12, decay Delta at kA(1/V1+1/V2)=8/15, then invert for C1 and C2.
Check the inventory identity on the proposed C1, C2 first, then evaluate the special time (15/8)ln 3 and the half-time.

milestones.criterion: Derives C_inf=3, Delta=12 e^{-8t/15}, C1=3+9 e^{-8t/15}, and C2=3-3 e^{-8t/15} from the conserved inventory 12.
Evaluates C1=6, C2=2, flux 1.6 at t=(15/8)ln 3, the initial flux 4.8, and t_{1/2}=(15/8)ln 2.
Rejects equal-volume decay and inventory loss, and refuses CRE, Maxwell–Stefan, or flux-ledger substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the tanks as equal volume, uses decay rate 2kA/V, and forces C1 and C2 to be symmetric about 6 rather than about 3.
commonErrors.consequence: The required rate 8/15, the 9:3 split, C1=6 and C2=2 at (15/8)ln 3, and the flux 1.6 are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Drops conservation of V1 C1+V2 C2=12 and reports C_inf=0 or C_inf=12, or lets the two concentrations evolve independently.
commonErrors.consequence: Equilibrium 3, the identities C1=3+9e^{-8t/15} and C2=3-3e^{-8t/15}, and the later numerical checks fail.

hintTree.content: Inventory $1\cdot 12+3\cdot 0=12$ forces $C_\infty=12/4=3$. The difference decays at $0.4(1+1/3)=8/15$.

TRAN:010424.canonicalSolution:
There is no reaction, so
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(V_1 C_1+V_2 C_2)=0.
\]
The initial inventory is $1\cdot 12+3\cdot 0=12$, and this value is
conserved for all later time. Equilibrium equalizes the
concentrations, hence
\[
C_\infty=\frac{12}{V_1+V_2}=3.
\]
The difference $\Delta=C_1-C_2$ obeys
\[
\dot\Delta
=-kA\Bigl(\frac1{V_1}+\frac1{V_2}\Bigr)\Delta
=-0.4\Bigl(1+\frac13\Bigr)\Delta
=-\frac{8}{15}\Delta.
\]
With $\Delta(0)=12$,
\[
\Delta(t)=12\,e^{-8t/15}.
\]
Solving simultaneously with the inventory identity produces
\begin{align*}
C_1
&=C_\infty+\frac{V_2}{V_1+V_2}\Delta
=3+\frac34\cdot 12\,e^{-8t/15}
=3+9\,e^{-8t/15},\\
C_2
&=C_\infty-\frac{V_1}{V_1+V_2}\Delta
=3-\frac14\cdot 12\,e^{-8t/15}
=3-3\,e^{-8t/15}.
\end{align*}
(The check $V_1 C_1+V_2 C_2=3+9e+9-9e=12$ holds identically.)
\[
\boxed{C_\infty=3,\;
\Delta=12e^{-8t/15},\;
C_1=3+9e^{-8t/15},\;
C_2=3-3e^{-8t/15}}.
\]

At $t=(15/8)\ln 3$ one has $e^{-8t/15}=e^{-\ln 3}=1/3$, so
\[
C_1=3+9\cdot\frac13=6,\qquad
C_2=3-3\cdot\frac13=2,
\]
and the membrane flux is
\[
kA(C_1-C_2)=0.4\cdot 4=1.6.
\]
The initial flux is $kA\cdot 12=4.8$.
\[
\boxed{t=(15/8)\ln 3\Rightarrow C_1=6,\;C_2=2,\;\text{flux }1.6;
\quad\text{initial flux }4.8}.
\]

Half-decay of $\Delta$ occurs when $e^{-8t/15}=1/2$, i.e.
\[
t_{1/2}=\frac{15}{8}\ln 2.
\]
\[
\boxed{t_{1/2}=(15/8)\ln 2}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the pair $(V_1,V_2)=(1,3)$ by equal volumes.
Then the rate would be $2kA/V$ and the two concentrations would be
symmetric about $6$, destroying $C_\infty=3$ and the $9:3$ split.
Sentence (ii) drops conservation of the $12$ units of inventory.
The two tanks are not a CRE reaction inventory: $kA$ is a membrane
conductance, not a rate constant times a reacting volume.

The argument never inverts a ternary Maxwell–Stefan matrix and never
appeals to a flux-ledger exact 1D boundary layer.

graderFixtures.proofText: Inventory $V_1 C_1+V_2 C_2=12$ forces $C_\infty=3$ and $\Delta=12e^{-8t/15}$, hence $C_1=3+9e^{-8t/15}$ and $C_2=3-3e^{-8t/15}$. At $t=(15/8)\ln 3$ one has $C_1=6$, $C_2=2$, and flux $1.6$; the initial flux is $4.8$ and $t_{1/2}=(15/8)\ln 2$. Equal-volume $2kA/V$ formulae are false here.
The two tanks may be treated as equal volume V=2 L, so the decay rate is 2 kA/V and C1, C2 are symmetric about 6. I never form the rate 8/15 or C_inf=3.
Inventory need not be conserved, so I take C_inf=0 (or 12) and I let C1 and C2 run independently. I do not accept C1=3+9 e^{-8t/15}.

TRAN:010425.title: Taylor–Aris Deff=3.083333333e-6 turns a unit pulse at t=100 into centroid 1 m, sigma 0.024832774, peak 16.06515163
TRAN:010425.objective: For a=0.001, U=0.01, D=1e-6 obtain Deff=D+U^2 a^2/(48 D)=3.083333333e-6; radial time a^2/D=1 s so t=100 is long-time. For an areal pulse Gamma=1 the mean field is Gamma/sqrt(4 pi Deff t) exp[-(z-U t)^2/(4 Deff t)], with centroid 1 m, variance 2 Deff t=6.166666667e-4, sigma=0.024832774, peak=16.06515163. Audit molecular-D-only and the variance factor 2.
TRAN:010425.statement:
A solute is carried down a straight circular tube of radius
$a=0.001\,\mathrm{m}$ by a fully developed Poiseuille flow of
cross-sectional mean speed $U=0.01\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. The
molecular diffusivity is $D=1\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$.
After a long time the cross-sectionally averaged concentration obeys
a one-dimensional advection–diffusion equation with the Taylor–Aris
dispersivity
\[
D_{\mathrm{eff}}=D+\frac{U^2 a^2}{48 D}.
\]

1. Prove $D_{\mathrm{eff}}=3.083333333\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$.
   The radial diffusion time is $a^2/D$. Prove that this time is
   $1\,\mathrm{s}$ and that the observation instant $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$
   is therefore a long-time station.

2. An areal pulse of strength $\Gamma=1$ (concentration times length)
   is released at $z=0$ when $t=0$. Prove that the mean field is
   \[
   \bar c(z,t)
   =\frac{\Gamma}{\sqrt{4\pi D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}}
   \exp\Bigl(-\frac{(z-Ut)^2}{4 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}\Bigr).
   \]
   At $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ prove that the centroid is at $z=1\,\mathrm{m}$,
   that the axial variance is
   $2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t=6.166666667\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2$,
   that $\sigma=0.024832774\,\mathrm{m}$, and that the peak value is
   $16.06515163$ (same units as $\bar c$).

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “axial spreading uses the molecular $D$
   only, so $D_{\mathrm{eff}}=D$ and the variance is $2Dt$”; (ii)
   “the Gaussian variance is $D_{\mathrm{eff}} t$ rather than
   $2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t$.” Also refuse to treat the mean field as a
   bare Continuum/PDE Laplacian that ignores the Taylor shear
   contribution.

Do not replace the long-time pulse by a Graetz developing-thermal
scaling or by a ternary Maxwell–Stefan inversion.
permittedResults: The radial time $a^2/D$ is the waiting time after which the Taylor–Aris reduction is legitimate. Here $a^2/D=1\,\mathrm{s}$, so $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ is one hundred radial times.
A unit-mass Gaussian $(4\pi\kappa t)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^2/(4\kappa t))$ has variance $2\kappa t$. Substituting $\kappa=D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $x=z-Ut$ gives the displayed moments.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate U^2 a^2/(48 D), add D, then read centroid Ut and variance 2 Deff t from the moving Gaussian.
First confirm t/(a^2/D)=100 so the Taylor–Aris reduction applies, then compute the peak as 1/sqrt(4 pi Deff t).

milestones.criterion: Computes Deff=3.083333333e-6 and identifies t=100 as long-time from a^2/D=1 s.
Writes the moving Gaussian and reports centroid 1 m, variance 6.166666667e-4, sigma=0.024832774, and peak 16.06515163.
Rejects molecular-D-only and a missing variance factor 2, and refuses Graetz, Maxwell–Stefan, or bare-Laplacian substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Sets Deff=D, ignoring U^2 a^2/(48 D), and reports the molecular variance 2 D t=2e-4 together with the corresponding narrower Gaussian.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Deff=3.083333333e-6, variance 6.166666667e-4, sigma=0.024832774, and peak 16.06515163 all fail.

commonErrors.description: Writes the axial variance as Deff t rather than 2 Deff t, so sigma and the peak normalization are inconsistent with the heat kernel.
commonErrors.consequence: The required variance 6.166666667e-4 and sigma=0.024832774 are replaced by figures too small by sqrt(2).

hintTree.content: The centroid is $Ut=1\,\mathrm{m}$. Variance is $2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t$, not $D_{\mathrm{eff}} t$ and not $2 D t$.
The peak is $1/\sqrt{4\pi D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}$. Insert $D_{\mathrm{eff}} t=3.083333333\times 10^{-4}$.

TRAN:010425.canonicalSolution:
The shear contribution is
\[
\frac{U^2 a^2}{48 D}
=\frac{(10^{-2})^2(10^{-3})^2}{48\cdot 10^{-6}}
=\frac{10^{-10}}{4.8\times 10^{-5}}
=2.083333333\times 10^{-6}.
\]
Adding the molecular piece,
\[
D_{\mathrm{eff}}
=10^{-6}+2.083333333\times 10^{-6}
=3.083333333\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}.
\]
The radial time is
\[
\frac{a^2}{D}=\frac{10^{-6}}{10^{-6}}=1\,\mathrm{s},
\]
so $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ is one hundred radial times and lies deep in
the long-time regime.
\[
\boxed{D_{\mathrm{eff}}=3.083333333\times 10^{-6},\quad
a^2/D=1\,\mathrm{s},\;t=100\text{ is long-time}}.
\]

On that regime the mean concentration of an areal pulse $\Gamma$
released at the origin is the moving Gaussian
\[
\bar c(z,t)
=\frac{\Gamma}{\sqrt{4\pi D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}}
\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(z-Ut)^2}{4 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}\Bigr).
\]
With $\Gamma=1$ and $t=100$,
\[
Ut=0.01\cdot 100=1\,\mathrm{m},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z)
=2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t
=2\cdot 3.083333333\times 10^{-6}\cdot 100
=6.166666667\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2,
\]
\[
\sigma=\sqrt{2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}=0.024832774\,\mathrm{m}.
\]
The peak, attained at the centroid, is
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi D_{\mathrm{eff}} t}}
=16.06515163.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{centroid }1\,\mathrm{m},\;
\operatorname{Var}=6.166666667\times 10^{-4},\;
\sigma=0.024832774,\;
\text{peak }16.06515163}.
\]

Sentence (i) drops the shear piece and uses molecular $D$ only,
producing $D_{\mathrm{eff}}=10^{-6}$ and variance $2Dt=2\times 10^{-4}$,
which is not $6.166666667\times 10^{-4}$. Sentence (ii) quotes the
heat-kernel convention that writes a diffusion equation as
$\partial_t=\kappa\partial_{zz}$ but then forgets that the Gaussian
variance is $2\kappa t$, not $\kappa t$. A Continuum/PDE Laplacian
that keeps only $D\partial_{zz}$ makes the same molecular-only
error: it never generates the $U^2 a^2/(48 D)$ term.

The argument never invokes a Graetz developing-thermal scaling and
never inverts a ternary Maxwell–Stefan matrix.

graderFixtures.proofText: Taylor–Aris gives $D_{\mathrm{eff}}=D+U^2 a^2/(48 D)=3.083333333\times 10^{-6}$. The radial time is $1\,\mathrm{s}$, so $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ is long-time. The unit areal pulse is the moving Gaussian with centroid $Ut=1\,\mathrm{m}$, variance $2 D_{\mathrm{eff}} t=6.166666667\times 10^{-4}$, $\sigma=0.024832774\,\mathrm{m}$, and peak $16.06515163$. Molecular $D$ alone, or variance $D_{\mathrm{eff}} t$, is wrong.
Axial spreading uses the molecular D only, so Deff=D=1e-6 and the variance is 2 D t=2e-4. I never add U^2 a^2/(48 D).
The Gaussian variance is Deff t, not 2 Deff t. I report variance 3.083333333e-4 and I do not accept 6.166666667e-4.

TRAN:010426.title: A diffusion-limited sphere with R0=1 mm lasts 2500 s and is at R=0.5 mm at 1875 s
TRAN:010426.objective: For R0=0.001 m, D=2e-5 m^2/s, DeltaC=0.5 mol/m^3, c_l=5e4 mol/m^3, obtain the quasi-steady field C=C_inf+DeltaC R/r, molar rate 4 pi D R DeltaC, d(R^2)/dt=-2 D DeltaC/c_l=-4e-10 m^2/s, lifetime 2500 s, R=0.5 mm at 1875 s, and initial rate 4 pi e-8 mol/s. Audit a frozen radius and a non-moving inventory.
TRAN:010426.statement:
A solid sphere of instantaneous radius $R(t)$ dissolves into an
unbounded stagnant solvent. The far-field concentration is $C_\infty$,
the surface is held at $C_\infty+\Delta C$ with
$\Delta C=0.5\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, the solvent diffusivity is
$D=2\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the solid molar
density is $c_\ell=5\times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and the initial radius is
$R_0=0.001\,\mathrm{m}$. The process is diffusion-limited and
quasi-steady: at each frozen $R$ the exterior concentration solves
Laplace's equation.

1. Prove that the exterior field is
   \[
   C(r)=C_\infty+\Delta C\,\frac{R}{r}\qquad(r\ge R)
   \]
   and that the instantaneous molar dissolution rate (solute leaving
   the sphere) is $4\pi D R\,\Delta C$ in $\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

2. Equating that rate to the loss of solid inventory
   $-\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\tfrac43\pi R^3 c_\ell\bigr)$, prove
   \[
   \frac{d}{dt}(R^2)=-\frac{2 D\Delta C}{c_\ell}=-4\times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}.
   \]
   Conclude that the lifetime (the time at which $R=0$) is
   $2500\,\mathrm{s}$, that $R=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ at $t=1875\,\mathrm{s}$,
   and that the initial rate is
   $4\pi\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the radius may be frozen at $R_0$, so
   the rate remains $4\pi D R_0\Delta C$ forever and there is no
   finite lifetime”; (ii) “the moving inventory may be ignored, or
   the solid volume may be held fixed while only the exterior Laplace
   field is retained.” Also refuse a CRE reaction-limited (constant
   $k$ times area) shrinkage and a Continuum/PDE Laplace field that
   never feeds back onto $R(t)$.

Do not replace the shrinking sphere by a coupled thermodiffusion slab
or by an exact matched-diffusivity analogy.
permittedResults: The general radial harmonic vanishing at infinity is $A/r$. Matching $C(R)=C_\infty+\Delta C$ forces $A=\Delta C\,R$.
From $c_\ell R\,\dot R=-D\Delta C$ one has $R^2(t)=R_0^2-(2 D\Delta C/c_\ell)t$. The lifetime is $R_0^2 c_\ell/(2 D\Delta C)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fit the exterior harmonic to the two Dirichlet data, convert flux to a rate, then close on d(R^3)/dt.
Integrate the R^2 law first to lock 2500 s and 1875 s, then recover the Laplace field and the initial 4 pi e-8 rate.

milestones.criterion: Writes C=C_inf+DeltaC R/r and the instantaneous molar rate 4 pi D R DeltaC with units mol/s.
Derives d(R^2)/dt=-4e-10 m^2/s, lifetime 2500 s, R=0.5 mm at 1875 s, and initial rate 4 pi e-8 mol/s.
Rejects a frozen radius or a non-moving inventory, and refuses CRE, static-Laplace, slab, or analogy substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Freezes R at R0, keeps the rate at the constant 4 pi D R0 DeltaC, and concludes that there is no finite lifetime.
commonErrors.consequence: The R^2 law, the 2500 s lifetime, and the 1875 s half-radius station all disappear.

commonErrors.description: Treats the solid volume as fixed or otherwise refuses to set -d(4/3 pi R^3 c_l)/dt equal to the dissolution rate.
commonErrors.consequence: d(R^2)/dt=-4e-10 is never obtained, so the lifetime 2500 s and the 1875 s checkpoint cannot appear.

hintTree.content: Laplace in spherical symmetry with a far-field constant is $C=C_\infty+A/r$. Fit $A$ at $r=R$.
Rate $4\pi R^2\cdot D\Delta C/R=4\pi D R\Delta C$. Set this equal to $-c_\ell\cdot 4\pi R^2\dot R$.

TRAN:010426.canonicalSolution:
The quasi-steady exterior problem is $\nabla^2 C=0$ for $r>R$,
with $C(R)=C_\infty+\Delta C$ and $C\to C_\infty$ at infinity. The
radial harmonics are constants and $1/r$; boundedness at infinity
keeps
\[
C(r)=C_\infty+\Delta C\,\frac{R}{r}.
\]
The radial derivative is $\partial_r C=-\Delta C\,R/r^2$, so the
outward diffusive flux at $r=R$ is $D\Delta C/R$. Multiplying by
the instantaneous area $4\pi R^2$ produces the molar rate
\[
4\pi D R\,\Delta C.
\]
\[
\boxed{C=C_\infty+\Delta C\,R/r,\quad
\text{rate }4\pi D R\Delta C\;\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}}.
\]

The solid inventory is $\tfrac43\pi R^3 c_\ell$. Its decay equals
the dissolution rate:
\[
-\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(\tfrac43\pi R^3 c_\ell\Bigr)
=4\pi D R\Delta C.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
c_\ell R\dot R=-D\Delta C,
\qquad
\frac{d}{dt}(R^2)=-\frac{2 D\Delta C}{c_\ell}.
\]
Inserting the given numbers,
\[
\frac{2 D\Delta C}{c_\ell}
=\frac{2\cdot 2\times 10^{-5}\cdot 0.5}{5\times 10^{4}}
=4\times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}.
\]
Hence $R^2(t)=R_0^2-4\times 10^{-10}\,t$. The lifetime is the root
$R=0$:
\[
t_\star=\frac{R_0^2}{4\times 10^{-10}}
=\frac{10^{-6}}{4\times 10^{-10}}
=2500\,\mathrm{s}.
\]
The station $R=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}=5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}$ has
$R^2=2.5\times 10^{-7}$, so
\[
t=\frac{10^{-6}-2.5\times 10^{-7}}{4\times 10^{-10}}=1875\,\mathrm{s}.
\]
The initial rate is
\[
4\pi D R_0\Delta C
=4\pi\cdot 2\times 10^{-5}\cdot 10^{-3}\cdot 0.5
=4\pi\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{d(R^2)/dt=-4\times 10^{-10},\;
t_\star=2500\,\mathrm{s},\;
R=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\text{ at }1875\,\mathrm{s},\;
\text{initial rate }4\pi\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}}.
\]

Sentence (i) freezes $R\equiv R_0$, so the rate never falls and no
lifetime exists. Sentence (ii) keeps a Continuum/PDE Laplace field
on a fixed domain, or otherwise refuses to let the solid inventory
move with $R(t)$. A CRE reaction-limited law would replace
$4\pi D R\Delta C$ by a constant $k$ times area and would produce
linear (not $R^2$) shrinkage.

The argument never invokes a coupled thermodiffusion slab and never
imports a matched-diffusivity triple analogy.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $\Delta C=0.5\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ and $c_\ell=5\times10^4\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, the quasi-steady field is $C=C_\infty+\Delta C\,R/r$ with molar rate $4\pi D R\Delta C$. Closing on the moving inventory yields $d(R^2)/dt=-2 D\Delta C/c_\ell=-4\times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$, lifetime $2500\,\mathrm{s}$, $R=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ at $1875\,\mathrm{s}$, and initial rate $4\pi\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{s}$. A frozen radius or a fixed-volume inventory is a different model.
The radius may be frozen at R0, so the rate remains 4 pi D R0 DeltaC forever and there is no finite lifetime. I never form d(R^2)/dt=-4e-10.
The solid volume is held fixed and only the exterior Laplace field is retained. I do not set -d(4/3 pi R^3 c_l)/dt equal to the dissolution rate, so I have no 2500 s lifetime.

TRAN:010527.title: Two-film absorption with kG=0.1, kL=0.2, H=2 has 1/KG=20, N=0.4, and 50/50 resistances
TRAN:010527.objective: From N=kG(pb-pi)=kL(Ci-Cb) and pi=H Ci with kG=0.1 mol/(m^2 s kPa), kL=0.2 m/s, H=2 kPa m^3/mol, pb=10 kPa, Cb=1 mol/m^3, prove 1/KG=1/kG+H/kL=20 m^2 s kPa/mol, KG=0.05 mol/(m^2 s kPa), total drive 8 kPa, N=0.4 mol/(m^2 s), interface (pi,Ci)=(6 kPa,3 mol/m^3), equal 10+10 resistances (50% each), and that omitting either film doubles N.
TRAN:010527.statement:
A dilute gas $A$ is absorbed across a flat gas–liquid interface.
Whitman two-film constitutive laws and a linear Henry interface read
\[
N=k_G(p_b-p_i)=k_L(C_i-C_b),\qquad p_i=H C_i,
\]
with the numerical coefficients and bulk states
\[
k_G=0.1\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{kPa}^{-1},
\qquad k_L=0.2\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1},
\]
\[
H=2\,\mathrm{kPa}\,\mathrm{m}^{3}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1},\qquad
p_b=10\,\mathrm{kPa},\qquad C_b=1\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}
\]
so $N$ is measured in $\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

1. Eliminate the unknown interface state and prove that the overall
   gas-side coefficient defined by $N=K_G(p_b-H C_b)$ satisfies
   \[
   \frac1{K_G}=\frac1{k_G}+\frac{H}{k_L}
   =20\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1},
   \qquad
   K_G=0.05\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{kPa}^{-1}.
   \]
   Identify the overall driving force $p_b-H C_b=8\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and
   conclude $N=0.4\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

2. Recover the interface and prove
   \[
   p_i=6\,\mathrm{kPa},\qquad
   C_i=3\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}.
   \]
   Confirm both film laws reproduce $N=0.4$.

3. Split the overall resistance into the gas-film term $1/k_G$ and the
   liquid-film term $H/k_L$. Prove that the two contributions are
   $10\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$
   and $10\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$,
   hence $50\%$ each.

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the liquid film may be omitted, so
   $N=k_G(p_b-H C_b)=0.8$” (or the symmetric claim that drops the gas
   film); (ii) “Henry’s law is only a bulk constraint, so $p_b=H C_b$
   and there is no interface to solve.” Also show that omitting either
   one of the two resistances doubles $N$.

Do not replace the two-film balance by a local flux-ledger plus an
exact one-dimensional boundary layer, by ternary Maxwell–Stefan
inversion, by Graetz scaling, or by a thermodiffusion slab. Do not
import a Fluid Mechanics pipe closure, a Heat Transfer entry-length
eigenvalue, a Continuum constitutive identity, an abstract PDE
well-posedness argument, or a Chemical Reaction Engineering rate law.
permittedResults: From $p_b-p_i=N/k_G$ and $C_i-C_b=N/k_L$ together with $p_i=H C_i$ one has $p_b-H C_b=N/k_G+H N/k_L$, hence $1/K_G=1/k_G+H/k_L$.
If either resistance is dropped, $K_G$ doubles whenever the two resistances are equal, and therefore $N$ doubles against a fixed overall drive.

acceptableStrategies.description: Add the inverted film jumps with pi=H Ci to lock 1/KG, then back-substitute N to recover (pi,Ci) and the 50/50 split.
Solve the two linear films simultaneously for (pi,Ci), read N from either law, and only afterwards identify KG and the resistance percentages.

milestones.criterion: Derives 1/KG=20, KG=0.05, overall drive 8, and N=0.4 from the two film laws and pi=H Ci.
Recovers the interface (pi,Ci)=(6,3), splits the resistances 10+10 as 50% each, and shows that omitting either film doubles N.
Rejects a one-film N=0.8 or a bulk Henry collapse, and refuses reserved flux-ledger, Graetz, Maxwell-Stefan, thermodiffusion, or sister-course substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the liquid film (or the gas film) and reports N=kG(pb-H Cb)=0.8, or N=kL(pb/H-Cb)=0.8, as the two-film flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The required KG=0.05, N=0.4, and equal 50% resistances are replaced by a single-film value that is exactly twice as large.

commonErrors.description: Treats Henry’s law as a bulk constraint pb=H Cb, concludes that there is no driving force or no interface to compute, or reports a pair other than (pi,Ci)=(6,3).
commonErrors.consequence: The interface (6,3) and the consistent flux N=0.4 disappear, and the resistance split cannot be checked.

hintTree.content: Compute $1/k_G=10$ and $H/k_L=2/0.2=10$ first. Their sum is the overall resistance.
The overall drive is $p_b-H C_b=10-2=8$, so $N=8/20=0.4$. Then $p_b-p_i=N/k_G=4$.
Omitting either $10$ leaves resistance $10$ and $K_G=0.1$, which doubles $N$ against the same drive $8$.

TRAN:010527.canonicalSolution:
Start from the two film laws and Henry’s interface
\[
N=k_G(p_b-p_i)=k_L(C_i-C_b),\qquad p_i=H C_i.
\]
Solve the films for the jumps
\[
p_b-p_i=\frac{N}{k_G},\qquad C_i-C_b=\frac{N}{k_L}.
\]
Multiply the liquid jump by $H$ and add:
\[
p_b-H C_b
=\frac{N}{k_G}+H\frac{N}{k_L}
=N\Bigl(\frac1{k_G}+\frac{H}{k_L}\Bigr).
\]
The overall gas-side coefficient defined by $N=K_G(p_b-H C_b)$ is
therefore
\[
\frac1{K_G}=\frac1{k_G}+\frac{H}{k_L}
=\frac1{0.1}+\frac{2}{0.2}
=10+10=20,
\]
so $K_G=1/20=0.05$. The overall driving force is
\[
p_b-H C_b=10-2\cdot 1=8,
\]
and the flux is
\[
N=K_G\cdot 8=0.05\cdot 8=0.4.
\]
\[
\boxed{1/K_G=20\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{mol},\quad
K_G=0.05\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}),\quad
p_b-H C_b=8\,\mathrm{kPa},\quad
N=0.4\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s})}.
\]

The gas-film jump is $N/k_G=0.4/0.1=4$, hence
\[
p_i=p_b-4=6,\qquad C_i=p_i/H=6/2=3.
\]
The liquid-film law returns the same flux:
\[
k_L(C_i-C_b)=0.2\cdot(3-1)=0.4.
\]
\[
\boxed{p_i=6\,\mathrm{kPa},\quad
C_i=3\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}}.
\]

The two resistances are the addends already computed:
\[
\frac1{k_G}=10\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{mol},
\qquad
\frac{H}{k_L}=10\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{mol}.
\]
Each is $10/20=50\%$ of the overall resistance.

If the liquid film is omitted then $1/K_G=1/k_G=10$ and
$N=0.1\cdot 8=0.8$. If the gas film is omitted then
$1/K_G=H/k_L=10$ and again $N=0.8$. In either case $N$ doubles.
Sentence (i) is exactly that omission. Sentence (ii) replaces the
interface Henry law by a bulk equilibrium $p_b=H C_b$, which would
force $N=0$ and erase the interface $(6,3)$.

The argument never writes a local flux ledger plus an exact
one-dimensional boundary layer, never inverts a ternary Maxwell–Stefan
matrix, never invokes Graetz eigenvalues, and never solves a
thermodiffusion slab. It is not a Fluid Mechanics pipe problem, not a
Heat Transfer entry-length computation, not a Continuum constitutive
exercise, not an abstract PDE, and not a reactor design.

graderFixtures.proofText: The inverted films plus $p_i=H C_i$ give $1/K_G=1/k_G+H/k_L=10+10=20\,\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa}/\mathrm{mol}$, so $K_G=0.05\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{kPa})$. The overall drive is $p_b-H C_b=8\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $N=0.4\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s})$. Then $p_i=6\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $C_i=3\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$. The two resistances are equal ($50\%$ each); omitting either one leaves resistance $10$ and doubles $N$ to $0.8\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s})$.
The liquid film is negligible, so N=kG(pb-H Cb)=0.1*8=0.8. I never form 1/KG=20 and I do not accept N=0.4.
Henry’s law applies to the bulks, so pb=H Cb and there is no interface state to compute. I do not report (pi,Ci)=(6,3).

TRAN:010528.title: Higbie contact tc=4 s averages kL=1.784124116e-5 and uptake 7.136496465e-5
TRAN:010528.objective: For Higbie penetration with tc=4, D=1e-9, DeltaC=1, obtain the instantaneous law N=DeltaC sqrt(D/(pi t)), the contact averages kLavg=2 sqrt(D/(pi tc))=1.784124116e-5 and uptake/area=2 DeltaC sqrt(D tc/pi)=7.136496465e-5, the depth 2 sqrt(D tc)=1.264911064e-4, and audit endpoint averaging versus the factor 2.
TRAN:010528.statement:
A liquid element is exposed to a solute for a single contact time
$t_c=4\,\mathrm{s}$. The diffusivity is $D=1\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$
and the surface–bulk concentration jump is held at
$\Delta C=1\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^3$. Higbie’s penetration model
gives the instantaneous interfacial flux
\[
N(t)=\Delta C\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t}}\qquad(t>0).
\]

1. Define the contact-averaged mass-transfer coefficient by
   \[
   k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}
   :=\frac1{t_c}\int_0^{t_c}\frac{N(t)}{\Delta C}\,dt.
   \]
   Prove the exact identity
   \[
   k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=2\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t_c}}
   =1.784124116\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}.
   \]

2. Prove that the molar uptake per unit area over the contact is
   \[
   \int_0^{t_c}N(t)\,dt
   =2\Delta C\sqrt{\frac{D t_c}{\pi}}
   =7.136496465\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^2.
   \]
   Confirm the consistency check
   $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}\,\Delta C\, t_c$ equals that uptake.

3. Taking the penetration depth as the Gaussian scale
   $\delta=2\sqrt{D t_c}$, prove
   \[
   \delta=1.264911064\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}.
   \]

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “the average coefficient is the
   endpoint value $k_L(t_c)=\sqrt{D/(\pi t_c)}$, so the factor $2$ is
   optional”; (ii) “one may average the endpoints $N(0)$ and $N(t_c)$,
   or replace $\delta$ by $\sqrt{D t_c}$.” Record that $N(t_c)$ is
   exactly half the true time-averaged flux.

Do not replace Higbie averaging by a Whitman two-film resistance
network, by Graetz scaling, by an exact one-dimensional similarity
boundary layer of Blasius type, by a matched-diffusivity
momentum/heat/mass analogy, or by a thermodiffusion slab. Do not
import Fluid, Heat, Continuum, PDE, or CRE substitutions.
permittedResults: $\int_0^{t_c}t^{-1/2}\,dt=2 t_c^{1/2}$, so $\int_0^{t_c}\sqrt{D/(\pi t)}\,dt=2\sqrt{D t_c/\pi}$ and the contact mean is twice the endpoint $k_L(t_c)$.
The Gaussian penetration scale $\delta=2\sqrt{D t_c}$ is $\sqrt{4 D t_c}$, not $\sqrt{D t_c}$. Uptake per area equals $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}\Delta C t_c$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate t^{-1/2} once to lock the factor 2, then evaluate the three numerical targets from D and tc.
Compute the uptake integral first, divide by DeltaC tc to read kLavg, and compare it with twice the endpoint kL(tc).

milestones.criterion: Derives kLavg=2 sqrt(D/(pi tc))=1.784124116e-5 m/s from the integrable t^{-1/2} contact integral.
Reports uptake/area=7.136496465e-5 mol/m2, depth 1.264911064e-4 m, and the consistency check with kLavg DeltaC tc.
Rejects endpoint averaging or dropping the factor 2, and refuses reserved two-film, Graetz, analogy, or sister-course substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes kLavg equal to the endpoint sqrt(D/(pi tc)), or averages N(0) with N(tc), thereby dropping the exact factor 2 from the t^{-1/2} integral.
commonErrors.consequence: kLavg and the uptake are each too small by one half, so the required 1.784124116e-5 and 7.136496465e-5 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Reports the penetration depth as sqrt(D tc) or sqrt(pi D tc) rather than 2 sqrt(D tc)=1.264911064e-4 m, or breaks the uptake identity 2 DeltaC sqrt(D tc/pi).
commonErrors.consequence: The required depth 1.264911064e-4 m and/or the uptake 7.136496465e-5 mol/m2 are replaced by a different scale.

hintTree.content: The antiderivative of $t^{-1/2}$ is $2 t^{1/2}$. The endpoint integrand is therefore half the mean.
Uptake per area is $2\Delta C\sqrt{D t_c/\pi}$. With $\Delta C=1$ and $t_c=4$ this is $2\sqrt{4\times 10^{-9}/\pi}$.
$\sqrt{D t_c}=\sqrt{4\times 10^{-9}}=6.324555320\times 10^{-5}$, so twice that depth is $1.264911064\times 10^{-4}$.

TRAN:010528.canonicalSolution:
The instantaneous law is given:
\[
N(t)=\Delta C\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t}}.
\]
The contact-averaged coefficient is
\begin{align*}
k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}
&=\frac1{t_c}\int_0^{t_c}\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t}}\,dt
=\frac1{t_c}\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi}}\cdot 2 t_c^{1/2}
=2\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t_c}}.
\end{align*}
Substitute $D=10^{-9}$ and $t_c=4$:
\[
k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}
=2\sqrt{\frac{10^{-9}}{4\pi}}
=1.784124116\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}.
\]
(The same digits are $2\sqrt{D/(\pi t_c)}$.) The endpoint value
\[
k_L(t_c)=\sqrt{\frac{D}{\pi t_c}}
=\tfrac12 k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}
\]
is therefore exactly half the average: the factor $2$ is not optional.
\[
\boxed{k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=2\sqrt{D/(\pi t_c)}=1.784124116\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}}.
\]

The molar uptake per unit area is the time integral of $N$:
\[
\int_0^{t_c}N(t)\,dt
=\Delta C\cdot 2\sqrt{\frac{D t_c}{\pi}}
=2\sqrt{\frac{4\times 10^{-9}}{\pi}}
=7.136496465\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^2.
\]
Consistency with the average coefficient is immediate:
\[
k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}\,\Delta C\, t_c
=1.784124116\times 10^{-5}\cdot 1\cdot 4
=7.136496464\times 10^{-5},
\]
which matches the uptake to the reported digits. The instantaneous
endpoint flux is $N(t_c)=k_L(t_c)\Delta C$, hence exactly half the
true mean flux $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}\Delta C$.
\[
\boxed{\text{uptake}/{\text{area}}=7.136496465\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^2}.
\]

The stated penetration depth is
\[
\delta=2\sqrt{D t_c}=2\sqrt{4\times 10^{-9}}
=2\times 6.324555320\times 10^{-5}
=1.264911064\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\delta=1.264911064\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}}.
\]

Sentence (i) replaces the contact mean by the endpoint $k_L(t_c)$ and
drops the factor $2$, underestimating both $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}$ and the
uptake by one half. Sentence (ii) attempts an endpoint average. The
integrand $N(t)$ diverges at $t=0$, so $(N(0)+N(t_c))/2$ is not a
number; any finite substitute still misses the exact $t^{-1/2}$
integral. Replacing $\delta$ by $\sqrt{D t_c}$ loses another factor
$2$.

The argument never builds a two-film $K_G$ network, never solves a
Graetz problem, never invokes a Blasius or flux-ledger boundary layer,
never claims a matched-diffusivity analogy, and never treats a
thermodiffusion slab.

graderFixtures.proofText: Higbie’s $N(t)=\Delta C\sqrt{D/(\pi t)}$ averages to $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}=2\sqrt{D/(\pi t_c)}=1.784124116\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. Uptake per area is $2\Delta C\sqrt{D t_c/\pi}=7.136496465\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^2$, which equals $k_{L,\mathrm{avg}}\Delta C t_c$. The depth is $2\sqrt{D t_c}=1.264911064\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}$. The endpoint $N(t_c)$ is half the mean; endpoint averaging is not the contact integral.
The average coefficient is just the value at the end of the contact, kL=sqrt(D/(pi tc)), so I drop the factor 2 and I also average N(0) with N(tc). I do not accept 1.784124116e-5.
I take the penetration depth to be sqrt(D tc)=6.32e-5 m and I never form 2 sqrt(D tc)=1.264911064e-4 m. The uptake is then inconsistent with 7.136496465e-5.

TRAN:010629.title: Zero-current ambipolar salt flux is 1.2e-4 with junction +0.019709862 V
TRAN:010629.objective: For a 1:1 electrolyte with c+=c-=c, D+=2e-9, D-=1e-9, L=0.001, c0=100, cL=10, T=298, impose N+=N-=Ns, obtain Damb=2 D+ D-/(D++D-)=(4/3)e-9, linear c, Ns=1.2e-4, and phiL-phi0=(RT/F)(D+-D-)/(D++D-) ln(c0/cL)=+0.019709862 V, and audit independent Fick/nonzero current and the log sign/dimension.
TRAN:010629.statement:
A dilute $1{:}1$ electrolyte occupies the slab $0\le x\le L$ with
$L=0.001\,\mathrm{m}$. Electroneutrality is enforced as
$c_+=c_-=c(x)$. The Nernst–Planck diffusivities, end concentrations,
and temperature are
\[
D_+=2\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s},\quad
D_-=1\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s},
\]
\[
c(0)=c_0=100\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^3,\quad
c(L)=c_L=10\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^3,\quad
T=298\,\mathrm{K}.
\]
Use $R=8.314462618\,\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ and
$F=96485.33212\,\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$. The ionic fluxes are
\[
N_\pm=-D_\pm\Bigl(\frac{dc}{dx}\pm\frac{c F}{RT}\frac{d\phi}{dx}\Bigr).
\]
Open-circuit electrodes (or insulating ends) enforce zero current, hence
$N_+=N_-=N_s$.

1. Eliminate the electric field and prove that the salt flux obeys
   Fick’s law with the ambipolar diffusivity
   \[
   D_{\mathrm{amb}}=\frac{2 D_+ D_-}{D_++D_-}
   =\frac43\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}.
   \]
   Conclude that $c(x)$ is linear and that
   \[
   N_s=1.2\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.
   \]

2. Recover the field from the same pair of Nernst–Planck laws and
   integrate to prove
   \[
   \phi(L)-\phi(0)
   =\frac{RT}{F}\frac{D_+-D_-}{D_++D_-}\ln\frac{c_0}{c_L}
   =+0.019709862\,\mathrm{V}.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “each ion may be treated by independent
   Fick’s law, so $N_+\ne N_-$ and a nonzero current is acceptable”;
   (ii) “the junction potential is
   $(RT/F)(D_+-D_-)/(D_++D_-)\ln(c_L/c_0)$, or is the dimensionless
   number $\ln(c_0/c_L)$ with no $RT/F$.” Record the sign: $D_+>D_-$
   and $c_0>c_L$ force $\phi(L)>\phi(0)$.

Do not replace the zero-current pair by a ternary Maxwell–Stefan
inversion, by a coupled thermodiffusion slab, by a matched-diffusivity
analogy, or by Graetz scaling. Do not import Fluid, Heat, Continuum,
PDE, or CRE substitutions.
permittedResults: Adding $N_s/D_+$ and $N_s/D_-$ cancels migration and produces $N_s=-[2 D_+ D_-/(D_++D_-)] dc/dx$. With constant $D_{\mathrm{amb}}$, steady $N_s$ forces $c$ to be linear.
Subtracting the same pair gives $d\phi/dx=-(RT/F)(D_+-D_-)/(D_++D_-)\,(1/c)\,dc/dx$, hence $\phi(L)-\phi(0)=(RT/F)(D_+-D_-)/(D_++D_-)\ln(c_0/c_L)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Add the divided Nernst–Planck laws to kill the field and lock Damb, then subtract to integrate the junction potential.
First impose Ns and linearity to get the salt flux, then restore dφ/dx from either ion law and integrate ln c.

milestones.criterion: Derives Damb=(4/3)e-9, linearity of c, and Ns=1.2e-4 from N+=N-=Ns.
Integrates the leftover field to phiL-phi0=+0.019709862 V with the stated R and F.
Rejects independent Fick/nonzero current and a log-sign or missing-RT/F voltage, and refuses reserved Maxwell-Stefan, thermodiffusion, or sister-course substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two ions by independent Fick laws N±=-D± dc/dx, accepts N+≠N-, and therefore carries a nonzero current.
commonErrors.consequence: The ambipolar coefficient (4/3)e-9 and the required Ns=1.2e-4 are replaced by two unequal fluxes (1.8e-4 and 9e-5).

commonErrors.description: Writes φL-φ0 with ln(cL/c0) instead of ln(c0/cL), or reports the dimensionless ln(c0/cL) (or ln(c0/cL)/3) as the voltage, dropping RT/F.
commonErrors.consequence: The required +0.019709862 V is replaced by a negative value or by a quantity that is not a voltage.

hintTree.content: Write $N_s/D_\pm=-dc/dx\mp(c F/RT)d\phi/dx$ and add. The migration terms cancel.

TRAN:010629.canonicalSolution:
Divide the Nernst–Planck laws by the diffusivities:
\[
\frac{N_s}{D_+}=-\frac{dc}{dx}-\frac{c F}{RT}\frac{d\phi}{dx},\qquad
\frac{N_s}{D_-}=-\frac{dc}{dx}+\frac{c F}{RT}\frac{d\phi}{dx}.
\]
Adding cancels the field and produces
\[
N_s\Bigl(\frac1{D_+}+\frac1{D_-}\Bigr)=-2\frac{dc}{dx},
\]
hence
\[
N_s=-\frac{2 D_+ D_-}{D_++D_-}\frac{dc}{dx}
=-D_{\mathrm{amb}}\frac{dc}{dx}
\]
with
\[
D_{\mathrm{amb}}
=\frac{2\cdot(2\times 10^{-9})\cdot(1\times 10^{-9})}{3\times 10^{-9}}
=\frac43\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}.
\]
A steady, divergence-free salt flux in one dimension is constant, so
$dc/dx$ is constant and $c$ is linear:
\[
\frac{dc}{dx}=\frac{c_L-c_0}{L}=\frac{10-100}{0.001}=-9\times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
N_s=-D_{\mathrm{amb}}\frac{dc}{dx}
=\frac43\times 10^{-9}\cdot 9\times 10^{4}
=1.2\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.
\]
\[
\boxed{D_{\mathrm{amb}}=(4/3)\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s},\quad
c\text{ linear},\quad N_s=1.2\times 10^{-4}}.
\]

Subtracting the divided Nernst–Planck laws isolates the field:
\[
\frac{c F}{RT}\frac{d\phi}{dx}
=\frac{D_--D_+}{D_++D_-}\frac{dc}{dx},
\]
or
\[
\frac{d\phi}{dx}
=-\frac{RT}{F}\frac{D_+-D_-}{D_++D_-}\frac1c\frac{dc}{dx}.
\]
Integrate from $0$ to $L$:
\[
\phi(L)-\phi(0)
=\frac{RT}{F}\frac{D_+-D_-}{D_++D_-}\ln\frac{c_0}{c_L}.
\]
The mobility contrast is $(D_+-D_-)/(D_++D_-)=1/3$ and
$\ln(c_0/c_L)=\ln 10$. With the stated constants
\[
\frac{RT}{F}
=\frac{8.314462618\cdot 298}{96485.33212}
=0.0256796531\,\mathrm{V},
\]
one finds
\[
\phi(L)-\phi(0)
=\frac{0.0256796531}{3}\cdot\ln 10
=+0.019709862157\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
The sign is required: $D_+>D_-$ so the field must retard the faster
cations. With $c$ falling toward $x=L$, that field has $d\phi/dx>0$,
hence $\phi(L)>\phi(0)$.
\[
\boxed{\phi(L)-\phi(0)=+0.019709862157\,\mathrm{V}}.
\]

Independent Fick fluxes would be
$N_+=-D_+ dc/dx=1.8\times 10^{-4}$ and
$N_-=-D_- dc/dx=9\times 10^{-5}$. Those are unequal, so they carry a
nonzero current $F(N_+-N_-)$ and are forbidden by the end condition.
Sentence (i) is that error. Sentence (ii) either flips the logarithm
to $\ln(c_L/c_0)$ (wrong sign) or drops $RT/F$ (wrong dimension: a
pure logarithm is not a voltage).

The argument never inverts a ternary Maxwell–Stefan matrix, never
couples heat and mass through a Soret slab, never assumes equal
transport diffusivities for an analogy, and never solves a Graetz
problem.

graderFixtures.proofText: Zero current forces $N_+=N_-=N_s=-D_{\mathrm{amb}} dc/dx$ with $D_{\mathrm{amb}}=2 D_+ D_-/(D_++D_-)=(4/3)\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$. Then $c$ is linear and $N_s=1.2\times 10^{-4}$. The leftover field integrates to $\phi(L)-\phi(0)=(RT/F)(D_+-D_-)/(D_++D_-)\ln(c_0/c_L)=+0.019709862\,\mathrm{V}$. Independent Fick fluxes would carry current; the logarithm cannot be flipped and cannot shed $RT/F$.
Each ion follows its own Fick law, so N+=1.8e-4 and N-=9e-5. I do not enforce N+=N- and I accept the resulting current.
The junction potential is (RT/F)(D+-D-)/(D++D-) ln(cL/c0), or else just ln(c0/cL) with no RT/F. I do not accept +0.019709862 V.

TRAN:010630.title: Wet-surface balance closes at Ts=20 with N=0.005 and q=200=Lambda N
TRAN:010630.objective: Solve h(Tinf-Ts)=Lambda km(Cs(Ts)-Cinf) for Tinf=30 deg C, h=20 W/(m^2 K), km=0.01 m/s, Cinf=0.1 mol/m^3, Cs(T)=(0.2+0.02 T) mol/m^3 with T numerical in deg C, Lambda=40000 J/mol, obtaining Ts=20 deg C, N=0.005 mol/(m^2 s), q=200 W/m^2=Lambda N, and audit evaluating Cs at Tinf or mishandling latent units.
TRAN:010630.statement:
A wet surface exchanges heat and vapor with a bulk stream. The bulk
temperature and vapor concentration are
$T_\infty=30\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and
$C_\infty=0.1\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The heat- and
mass-transfer coefficients, the interfacial
vapor equilibrium, and the latent heat per mole are
\[
h=20\,\mathrm{W}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1},\qquad
k_m=0.01\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1},
\]
\[
C_s(T)=(0.2+0.02\,T)\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3},\qquad
\Lambda=40000\,\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{mol}^{-1},
\]
where $T$ is inserted into the empirical $C_s$ law as its numerical
value in degrees Celsius.
Steady energy balance at the surface (no net enthalpy storage, no
radiation, no conduction into the solid) equates convective heat
arrival to latent heat departure:
\[
h(T_\infty-T_s)=\Lambda\, k_m\bigl(C_s(T_s)-C_\infty\bigr).
\]
The evaporative molar flux is $N=k_m(C_s(T_s)-C_\infty)$ and the heat
flux toward the surface is $q=h(T_\infty-T_s)$.

1. Solve the balance for the unknown surface temperature and prove
   $T_s=20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

2. Evaluate the interface concentration, the molar flux, and the heat
   flux, and prove
   \[
   C_s(T_s)=0.6\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3},\qquad
   N=0.005\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1},
   \qquad
   q=200\,\mathrm{W}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}=\Lambda N.
   \]

3. Audit both sentences: (i) “the vapor pressure may be frozen at the
   bulk temperature, so $C_s=C_s(T_\infty)=0.8$ and $T_s$ is never
   solved”; (ii) “the energy balance is $h(T_\infty-T_s)=k_m(C_s-C_\infty)$,
   dropping $\Lambda$, or $\Lambda$ is treated as a heat-transfer
   coefficient.” Record that $C_s(T_\infty)$ is the wrong interface
   state, and that $\Lambda$ carries latent energy per mole.

Do not replace the algebraic surface balance by a Graetz problem, by
a matched-diffusivity momentum/heat/mass analogy, by a coupled
thermodiffusion slab, or by Higbie penetration averaging. Do not
import Fluid pipe flow, Continuum constitutive theory, abstract PDE
theory, or a Chemical Reaction Engineering rate.
permittedResults: With the linear law $C_s(T)=0.2+0.02 T$ the energy balance is a linear equation for $T_s$. Substituting the given numbers produces $30-T_s=2+0.4 T_s$, hence $T_s=20$.
Once $T_s$ is known, $N=k_m(C_s(T_s)-C_\infty)$ and $q=h(T_\infty-T_s)$ must coincide with $\Lambda N$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert the linear Cs(T) into h(Tinf-Ts)=Lambda km(Cs-Cinf), solve the scalar equation for Ts, then read N and q.
Assume a trial Ts, enforce q=Lambda N as a consistency check, and adjust until both sides equal 200 at Ts=20.

milestones.criterion: Solves the linear surface balance and reports Ts=20 deg C.
Evaluates Cs(Ts)=0.6 mol/m^3, N=0.005 mol/(m^2 s), and q=200 W/m^2=Lambda N.
Rejects Cs(Tinf) or a latent-unit error, and refuses reserved Graetz, analogy, thermodiffusion, Higbie, or sister-course substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Freezes the interface concentration at Cs(Tinf)=0.8 and never solves for Ts, or reports a surface temperature other than 20.
commonErrors.consequence: The required Ts=20, Cs=0.6, N=0.005, and the closed identity q=Lambda N=200 are lost.

commonErrors.description: Writes the energy balance without Lambda, or treats Lambda=40000 as a heat-transfer coefficient rather than latent energy per mole.
commonErrors.consequence: The identity q=Lambda N=200 fails, and the heat and mass fluxes are no longer in consistent energy units.

hintTree.content: The right-hand side simplifies to $400(0.1+0.02 T_s)$. Divide by $20$ to obtain $30-T_s=2+0.4 T_s$.

TRAN:010630.canonicalSolution:
Substitute the linear equilibrium into the surface balance:
\[
20(30-T_s)
=40000\cdot 0.01\cdot\bigl(0.2+0.02 T_s-0.1\bigr)
=400\bigl(0.1+0.02 T_s\bigr).
\]
Divide by $20$:
\[
30-T_s=20\bigl(0.1+0.02 T_s\bigr)=2+0.4 T_s.
\]
Hence $28=1.4 T_s$ and
\[
T_s=20.
\]
\[
\boxed{T_s=20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}}.
\]
The interface concentration and the two fluxes are then
\begin{align*}
C_s(T_s)&=0.2+0.02\cdot 20=0.6,\\
N&=k_m(C_s-C_\infty)=0.01\cdot(0.6-0.1)=0.005,\\
q&=h(T_\infty-T_s)=20\cdot(30-20)=200.
\end{align*}
The latent identity closes:
\[
\Lambda N=40000\cdot 0.005=200=q.
\]
\[
\boxed{C_s=0.6\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3},\quad
N=0.005\,\mathrm{mol}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1},\quad
q=200\,\mathrm{W}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}=\Lambda N}.
\]

Sentence (i) evaluates $C_s$ at the bulk temperature:
$C_s(T_\infty)=0.2+0.02\cdot 30=0.8$. That is not the interface state.
Using it would produce a mass flux $0.01\cdot 0.7=0.007$ that cannot
satisfy $h(T_\infty-T_s)=\Lambda N$ at any $T_s$ consistent with that
frozen $C_s$. Sentence (ii) drops $\Lambda$ or treats $\Lambda$ as if
it had the units of $h$. Either error destroys $q=\Lambda N=200$.

The argument never solves a Graetz eigenvalue problem, never assumes
equal momentum/heat/mass diffusivities, never treats a Soret
thermodiffusion slab, and never averages a Higbie contact.

graderFixtures.proofText: The surface balance $h(T_\infty-T_s)=\Lambda k_m(C_s(T_s)-C_\infty)$ with $C_s(T)=0.2+0.02 T$ is linear and yields $T_s=20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Then $C_s=0.6\,\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$, $N=0.005\,\mathrm{mol}/(\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{s})$, and $q=200\,\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}=\Lambda N$. The interface state is $C_s(T_s)$, not $C_s(T_\infty)$; $\Lambda$ converts molar flux into energy flux.
I evaluate Cs at the bulk temperature, Cs(Tinf)=0.8, and I never solve for Ts. I do not accept Ts=20 or Cs=0.6.
The energy balance is h(Tinf-Ts)=km(Cs-Cinf) with no Lambda, or else Lambda is just another heat-transfer coefficient. I do not accept q=Lambda N=200.

TRAN:010631.title: Thin-EDL electroosmosis cancels at dp/dx=280 with zero mean and wall shear 0.014 Pa
TRAN:010631.objective: For a thin-EDL capillary a=100 um, epsilon=7e-10, zeta=-50 mV, E=+1e4, mu=1e-3, obtain slip ueo=+3.5e-4, the cancelling dp/dx=+280, the profile u(r)=ueo-(dp/dx)(a^2-r^2)/(4 mu), Ubar=0, center -3.5e-4, wall +3.5e-4, a zero at a/sqrt(2), and wall-shear magnitude 0.014 Pa, and audit sign and that zero mean is not zero local.
TRAN:010631.statement:
A circular capillary of radius $a=100\,\mu\mathrm{m}=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}$
has a thin electric double layer. The electrolyte permittivity,
wall zeta potential, applied axial field, and viscosity are
\[
\varepsilon=7\times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}/\mathrm{m},\quad
\zeta=-50\,\mathrm{mV}=-0.05\,\mathrm{V},
\]
\[
E=+1\times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m},\quad
\mu=1\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa}\cdot\mathrm{s}.
\]
In the thin-EDL (Helmholtz–Smoluchowski) limit the interior sees a
uniform electroosmotic slip
\[
u_{\mathrm{eo}}=-\frac{\varepsilon\zeta E}{\mu}
\]
superposed on a pressure-driven Hagen–Poiseuille field. An imposed
axial pressure gradient $dp/dx$ produces the exact profile
\[
u(r)=u_{\mathrm{eo}}-\frac{dp/dx}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2).
\]
The corresponding mean speed is
\[
\bar U=u_{\mathrm{eo}}-\frac{(dp/dx)\,a^2}{8\mu}.
\]

1. Prove $u_{\mathrm{eo}}=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$.
   Determine the unique adverse gradient that cancels the net flow,
   and prove $dp/dx=+280\,\mathrm{Pa}/\mathrm{m}$.

2. With that gradient, evaluate the centerline and wall velocities
   and prove
   \[
   u(0)=-3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s},\qquad
   u(a)=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}.
   \]
   Show that $u$ vanishes at $r=a/\sqrt{2}$, and that $\bar U=0$.

3. Prove that the wall shear magnitude is
   \[
   \bigl|\tau_w\bigr|=0.014\,\mathrm{Pa}.
   \]
   (The thin-EDL plug carries no interior shear; all shear is the
   parabolic contribution.)

4. Audit both sentences: (i) “$\zeta<0$ makes $u_{\mathrm{eo}}$
   negative, or $E>0$ drives fluid toward decreasing $x$”; (ii)
   “$\bar U=0$ means the fluid is at rest, so $u(r)\equiv 0$ and the
   wall shear vanishes.” Record that a zero mean is not a zero local
   field.

Do not replace the thin-EDL superposition by a pressure-driven
annular logarithm with wall-traction / pipe-slit limits, by a
flux-ledger boundary layer, by Graetz scaling, or by a
matched-diffusivity analogy. Do not import a pure Fluid Mechanics
pipe problem without electroosmosis, a Heat Transfer closure, a
Continuum constitutive derivation, an abstract PDE, or a CRE reactor.
permittedResults: Zero net flow forces $dp/dx=8\mu u_{\mathrm{eo}}/a^2$. The local field is then $u(r)=u_{\mathrm{eo}}\bigl(2(r/a)^2-1\bigr)$, which changes sign at $r=a/\sqrt{2}$.
Interior shear comes only from the parabola: $\tau_{rz}=\mu\,\partial u/\partial r=(dp/dx)\,r/2$, so $|\tau_w|=(dp/dx)a/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the Helmholtz–Smoluchowski slip, cancel the disk-averaged Poiseuille contribution, then read center, wall, node, and shear from the residual parabola.
Nondimensionalize as u/ueo=2(r/a)^2-1 at cancellation, then recover dp/dx from the mean identity and tau_w=(dp/dx)a/2.

milestones.criterion: Computes ueo=+3.5e-4 m/s and the cancelling gradient dp/dx=+280 Pa/m with Ubar=0.
Reports u(0)=-3.5e-4, u(a)=+3.5e-4, the node at a/sqrt(2), and |tau_w|=0.014 Pa.
Rejects a slip-sign error or reading zero mean as zero local, and refuses reserved annular, Graetz, analogy, or sister-course substitutions.

commonErrors.description: Takes ueo negative because zeta is negative, or drives the plug against a positive E, and therefore obtains the wrong sign of dp/dx.
commonErrors.consequence: The required slip +3.5e-4 m/s and adverse gradient +280 Pa/m are replaced by the opposite electroosmotic direction.

commonErrors.description: Interprets Ubar=0 as u(r)≡0, reports a vanishing wall shear, or misses the centerline reversal and the node at a/sqrt(2).
commonErrors.consequence: The local field u(0)=-3.5e-4, u(a)=+3.5e-4, the zero at a/sqrt(2), and |tau_w|=0.014 Pa all disappear.

hintTree.content: Compute $\varepsilon\zeta E/\mu=7\times 10^{-10}\cdot(-0.05)\cdot 10^{4}/10^{-3}=-3.5\times 10^{-4}$. The slip is the negative of that product.
Set $\bar U=0$ to get $dp/dx=8\mu u_{\mathrm{eo}}/a^2=8\cdot 10^{-3}\cdot 3.5\times 10^{-4}/10^{-8}=280$.
At cancellation the parabola’s centerline is $2 u_{\mathrm{eo}}$, so $u(0)=-u_{\mathrm{eo}}$. Shear is $(dp/dx)a/2=0.014$.

TRAN:010631.canonicalSolution:
The Helmholtz–Smoluchowski slip is
\[
u_{\mathrm{eo}}
=-\frac{\varepsilon\zeta E}{\mu}
=-\frac{(7\times 10^{-10})(-0.05)(1\times 10^{4})}{1\times 10^{-3}}.
\]
The product $\varepsilon\zeta E=7\times 10^{-10}\cdot(-0.05)\cdot 10^{4}
=-3.5\times 10^{-7}$, so
\[
u_{\mathrm{eo}}
=-\frac{-3.5\times 10^{-7}}{10^{-3}}
=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}.
\]
Negative $\zeta$ with a positive axial field drives fluid in the
$+x$ direction: cations in the thin double layer drag the interior
plug toward the cathode.
\[
\boxed{u_{\mathrm{eo}}=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}}.
\]

Zero mean speed requires
\[
u_{\mathrm{eo}}=\frac{(dp/dx)\,a^2}{8\mu},
\qquad
\frac{dp}{dx}=\frac{8\mu u_{\mathrm{eo}}}{a^2}
=\frac{8\cdot 10^{-3}\cdot 3.5\times 10^{-4}}{(10^{-4})^2}
=\frac{2.8\times 10^{-6}}{10^{-8}}
=+280\,\mathrm{Pa}/\mathrm{m}.
\]
The gradient is adverse (positive $dp/dx$ against a positive slip).
\[
\boxed{dp/dx=+280\,\mathrm{Pa}/\mathrm{m},\quad \bar U=0}.
\]

Substitute into the local profile. The Poiseuille centerline amplitude
is
\[
\frac{(dp/dx)a^2}{4\mu}
=\frac{280\cdot 10^{-8}}{4\times 10^{-3}}
=7\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s},
\]
so
\begin{align*}
u(0)
&=u_{\mathrm{eo}}-7\times 10^{-4}
=-3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s},\\
u(a)
&=u_{\mathrm{eo}}=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}.
\end{align*}
The zero of $u$ occurs where
\[
u_{\mathrm{eo}}=\frac{dp/dx}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2)
=2 u_{\mathrm{eo}}\bigl(1-(r/a)^2\bigr),
\]
hence $1-(r/a)^2=1/2$ and $r=a/\sqrt{2}$. Equivalently
\[
u(r)=u_{\mathrm{eo}}\bigl(2(r/a)^2-1\bigr).
\]
The mean of this profile over the disk is zero by construction, but
the local velocity is not identically zero: the wall stream still
moves forward at $+3.5\times 10^{-4}$ and the core reverses.
\[
\boxed{u(0)=-3.5\times 10^{-4},\;
u(a)=+3.5\times 10^{-4},\;
u(a/\sqrt{2})=0,\;
\bar U=0}.
\]

Interior shear is purely parabolic. Differentiating gives
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}=\frac{dp/dx}{2\mu}\,r,
\qquad
\tau_{rz}=\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}=\frac{dp}{dx}\frac{r}{2}.
\]
At the wall,
\[
\bigl|\tau_w\bigr|
=\frac{dp}{dx}\frac{a}{2}
=280\cdot\frac{10^{-4}}{2}
=0.014\,\mathrm{Pa}.
\]
(The same magnitude is $\mu|\partial u/\partial r|_{r=a}
=10^{-3}\cdot 14=0.014$.)
\[
\boxed{|\tau_w|=0.014\,\mathrm{Pa}}.
\]

Sentence (i) flips the slip sign, contradicting
$u_{\mathrm{eo}}=-\varepsilon\zeta E/\mu$ with $\zeta<0$ and $E>0$.
Sentence (ii) reads a vanishing mean as a vanishing field, so it
cannot produce the centerline reversal, the node at $a/\sqrt{2}$, or
a nonzero wall shear. Zero mean is not zero local.

The argument never solves an annular logarithm, never computes
pipe/slit traction limits as the primary object, never writes a
flux-ledger boundary layer, and never invokes Graetz or a
matched-diffusivity analogy.

graderFixtures.proofText: Helmholtz–Smoluchowski gives $u_{\mathrm{eo}}=-\varepsilon\zeta E/\mu=+3.5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. Zero net flow forces $dp/dx=+280\,\mathrm{Pa}/\mathrm{m}$ and $\bar U=0$, but $u(0)=-3.5\times 10^{-4}$, $u(a)=+3.5\times 10^{-4}$, and $u$ vanishes at $r=a/\sqrt{2}$. The wall-shear magnitude is $0.014\,\mathrm{Pa}$. A zero mean is not a zero local field.
Because zeta is negative I take ueo=-3.5e-4 m/s and I drive the plug against the positive field. I do not accept ueo=+3.5e-4 or dp/dx=+280.
Ubar=0 means the fluid is at rest, so u(r)=0 everywhere and the wall shear is zero. I do not report a centerline reversal, a node at a/sqrt(2), or 0.014 Pa.

WAVE:010117.title: Recovering an oscillator from its ring-down peaks
WAVE:010117.objective: Derive logarithmic decrement from the underdamped free response, recover physical parameters from measured peaks and period, and distinguish amplitude decay from energy decay.
WAVE:010117.statement:
A mass attached to a linear spring and viscous damper obeys
\[
m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0,
\qquad m,b,k>0.
\]
The motion is underdamped. Two successive positive displacement maxima have
magnitudes \(12.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) and \(8.50\,\mathrm{mm}\), and the elapsed
time between them is \(0.800\,\mathrm{s}\). The mass is
\(m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}\).

Starting from the characteristic roots, derive the decaying sinusoidal
response and prove that the logarithmic decrement between successive
same-sense peaks is \(\delta=\beta T_d\), where
\(\beta=b/(2m)\) and \(T_d=2\pi/\omega_d\). Use the data to determine
\(\beta,\omega_d,\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m},b,k\), and
\(Q=\omega_0/(2\beta)\). Compute the ratio of mechanical energies at the two
peaks and the time required for the peak envelope to fall to two percent of
its initial value.

State why absolute peak magnitudes must be used if alternating maxima are
recorded, identify the underdamping check, and explain which inferred
quantity would be wrong if the measured peak interval were mistakenly treated
as half a damped period.
permittedResults: For \(\beta<\omega_0\), the roots of \(r^2+2\beta r+\omega_0^2=0\) are \(-\beta\pm i\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\beta^2}\).
Successive extrema of one sign in a decaying sinusoid are separated by \(2\pi/\omega_d\), and their envelope ratio is therefore \(e^{\beta T_d}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the characteristic equation, use the exact peak-envelope ratio, and infer the parameters sequentially.
Fit the exponential envelope and damped period first, then translate the fitted beta and omega-d into the physical coefficients.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the same-sense peak decrement and consistently recovers damping rate, damped and natural frequencies, spring and damper constants, quality factor, energy ratio, and settling time.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the energy-decay exponent for displacement amplitude or fails to square the amplitude ratio when computing the energy ratio.
commonErrors.consequence: The inferred damping or energy loss is wrong by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Treats the stated interval between successive positive maxima as one half-period.
commonErrors.consequence: The damped frequency and all stiffness-dependent quantities are incorrect.

hintTree.content: Write the real solution as \(C e^{-\beta t}\cos(\omega_dt-\phi)\); the phase does not affect the ratio of same-sense peak envelopes.
Use \(\delta=\ln(12.0/8.50)\), then \(\beta=\delta/T_d\) and \(\omega_d=2\pi/T_d\).
Recover \(\omega_0\) from \(\omega_d^2=\omega_0^2-\beta^2\); the energy ratio is the square of the amplitude ratio.

WAVE:010117.canonicalSolution:
Dividing by \(m\) gives
\[
\ddot x+2\beta\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0,
\qquad \beta=\frac b{2m},\quad \omega_0^2=\frac km.
\]
Underdamping means \(\beta<\omega_0\), so the characteristic roots are
\(-\beta\pm i\omega_d\), with
\(\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\beta^2}\). Hence
\[
x(t)=C e^{-\beta t}\cos(\omega_dt-\phi).
\]
Extrema of the same sign recur after \(T_d=2\pi/\omega_d\). Although their
phases are shifted slightly from the cosine maxima when damping is present,
the same phase recurs one full damped period later, so their magnitude ratio is
exactly
\[
\frac{|x_n|}{|x_{n+1}|}=e^{\beta T_d},
\qquad \delta=\ln\frac{|x_n|}{|x_{n+1}|}=\beta T_d.
\]

The measurements give
\[
\delta=\ln\!\left(\frac{12.0}{8.50}\right)=0.34484,
\quad \beta=\frac{0.34484}{0.800}=0.43105\ \mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]
and
\[
\omega_d=\frac{2\pi}{0.800}=7.85398\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\omega_0=\sqrt{\omega_d^2+\beta^2}=7.8658\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},
\]
\[
b=2m\beta=0.4311\ \mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-1}},
\qquad k=m\omega_0^2=30.94\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}},
\]
and
\[
Q=\frac{\omega_0}{2\beta}=9.12.
\]
At a displacement extremum the speed is zero, so \(E=kx^2/2\). Thus
\[
\frac{E_{n+1}}{E_n}=\left(\frac{8.50}{12.0}\right)^2=0.5017
=e^{-2\delta}.
\]
The envelope reaches \(0.02\) of its initial value when
\(e^{-\beta t}=0.02\), giving
\[
t_{2\%}=\frac{\ln 50}{\beta}=9.08\ \mathrm{s}.
\]

If adjacent extrema of alternating sign are used, their signed ratio is
negative and their separation is \(T_d/2\); one must use absolute magnitudes
and the correct interval. Calling the stated same-sense interval a half-period
would double \(\omega_d\) and corrupt \(\omega_0\) and \(k\). The recovered
values satisfy \(\beta<\omega_0\), confirming the assumed underdamped regime.

graderFixtures.proofText: The roots are \(-\beta\pm i\omega_d\), so same-sense extrema one \(T_d\) apart have ratio \(e^{\beta T_d}\). Thus \(\beta=0.431\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(\omega_d=7.854\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(\omega_0=7.866\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(b=0.431\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}\), and \(k=30.94\,\mathrm{N/m}\). Energy falls by \((8.50/12.0)^2\).
Because adjacent peaks are half a cycle apart, the damped period is 1.60 s. The energy ratio is 8.50/12.0 because energy follows the same exponential as amplitude.

WAVE:010118.title: When a vibrating base actually isolates a machine
WAVE:010118.objective: Derive absolute-displacement transmissibility for a base-excited damped oscillator, identify the exact isolation threshold, and audit its high-frequency and numerical behavior.
WAVE:010118.statement:
A machine of mass \(m\) is connected to a moving base by a linear spring
\(k\) and viscous damper \(c\). Let \(x(t)\) be the machine's absolute
displacement in an inertial frame and let the base motion be
\(y(t)=Y\cos\omega t\). There is no other applied force.

Derive the equation of motion in terms of the relative spring and damper
deformations. Using phasors with \(e^{i\omega t}\), derive the complex ratio
\(X/Y\) and the absolute-displacement transmissibility
\[
T_x=\frac{|X|}{|Y|}
\]
in terms of \(r=\omega/\omega_n\),
\(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\), and
\(\zeta=c/(2m\omega_n)\). Prove that \(T_x<1\) exactly when
\(r>\sqrt2\), independent of positive \(\zeta\). Determine the low- and
high-frequency limits and explain why adding damping can reduce the resonant
peak yet increase high-frequency absolute motion.

For \(m=20.0\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=8000\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\zeta=0.100\), a base amplitude of \(Y=1.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), and a running
speed of \(600\,\mathrm{rpm}\), compute \(r,T_x\), and the machine's absolute
displacement amplitude. State the linear, steady-state, harmonic-base, and
inertial-frame assumptions, and do not substitute force-excitation
magnification for base-excitation transmissibility.
permittedResults: A spring and damper between moving endpoints depend on relative displacement \(x-y\) and relative velocity \(\dot x-\dot y\).
For a complex ratio, its magnitude is the square root of the ratio of squared real and imaginary parts.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use absolute-coordinate Newtonian dynamics followed by a phasor transfer-function calculation.
Change to relative displacement first, solve the harmonically forced relative equation, and reconstruct the absolute displacement with the same final transfer ratio.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the base-excitation transfer function from relative element motion, proves the isolation threshold, and correctly evaluates limiting and numerical behavior.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the force-excitation magnification factor with numerator one instead of the base-excitation numerator.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted machine motion and high-frequency behavior are for the wrong physical system.

commonErrors.description: Uses 600 directly as radians per second or omits the conversion from revolutions per minute to angular frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerical frequency ratio and transmissibility are invalid.

hintTree.content: Newton's law is \(m\ddot x+c(\dot x-\dot y)+k(x-y)=0\).
After phasor substitution, collect the \(Y\) terms on the right before taking the magnitude.
To test \(T_x<1\), square both sides and cancel the identical damping term from numerator and denominator.

WAVE:010118.canonicalSolution:
The connector forces depend on relative motion, so
\[
m\ddot x+c(\dot x-\dot y)+k(x-y)=0.
\]
With \(x=\operatorname{Re}(Xe^{i\omega t})\) and
\(y=\operatorname{Re}(Ye^{i\omega t})\),
\[
(k-m\omega^2+i c\omega)X=(k+i c\omega)Y.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac XY=\frac{k+i c\omega}{k-m\omega^2+i c\omega}}.
\]
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(k=m\omega_n^2\) gives
\[
\boxed{T_x=
\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}
{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}}.
\]
Since both sides are nonnegative, \(T_x<1\) is equivalent to
\[
1+(2\zeta r)^2<(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2.
\]
Thus \(1<(1-r^2)^2\). For \(r\ge0\), the only solution is
\(r^2>2\), so
\[
\boxed{T_x<1\iff r>\sqrt2}.
\]
At low frequency \(T_x\to1\): the machine follows the slowly moving base.
For nonzero \(\zeta\),
\(T_x\sim 2\zeta/r\) at high frequency; if \(\zeta=0\) exactly, the faster
decay is \(T_x\sim1/r^2\). Damping controls the resonance but also transmits a
velocity-proportional force, explaining the larger high-frequency tail.

Here
\[
\omega_n=\sqrt{8000/20}=20.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
The running speed is \(600\,\mathrm{rpm}=10.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), hence
\(\omega=20\pi=62.832\,\mathrm{rad/s}\) and
\(r=\pi=3.1416\). Then
\[
T_x=\sqrt{\frac{1+(0.2\pi)^2}
{(1-\pi^2)^2+(0.2\pi)^2}}=0.1328.
\]
Thus
\[
|X|=T_xY=0.1328\ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
The result assumes linear elements, prescribed sinusoidal base motion,
constant parameters, one-dimensional motion measured in an inertial frame,
and decay of the homogeneous transient. A force-driven formula has a different
numerator and cannot replace this base-excitation result.

graderFixtures.proofText: Relative spring and damper motion gives \((k-m\omega^2+ic\omega)X=(k+ic\omega)Y\), hence \(T_x^2=[1+(2\zeta r)^2]/[(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2]\). Cancelling the damping terms shows isolation begins at \(r>\sqrt2\). Here \(r=\pi\), \(T_x=0.1328\), and \(|X|=0.1328\,\mathrm{mm}\).
The usual force magnification is one over the square root of the denominator. At 600 rpm I use omega equals 600 radians per second, which gives almost perfect isolation.

WAVE:010119.title: Overshoot and settling after a sudden constant force
WAVE:010119.objective: Derive the underdamped step response from its initial conditions, obtain exact peak overshoot, and distinguish an envelope-based settling guarantee from a rule of thumb.
WAVE:010119.statement:
A mass-spring-damper starts from rest at equilibrium and obeys
\[
m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_0H(t),
\qquad m,c,k,F_0>0,
\]
where \(H\) is the unit step. Define
\(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\),
\(\zeta=c/(2m\omega_n)\), and assume \(0<\zeta<1\).

Derive the complete response for \(t>0\), enforcing both initial conditions.
Find the first peak time and prove that the fractional overshoot above the
static displacement is
\[
M_p=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\right].
\]
Derive a sufficient time after which the absolute error is guaranteed to stay
within two percent of the static displacement by bounding the decaying
oscillatory factor. Compare this exact envelope guarantee with the common
approximation \(t_s\approx4/(\zeta\omega_n)\).

For \(m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(c=8.00\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}\), and \(F_0=100\,\mathrm N\), compute
\(\omega_n,\zeta,\omega_d\), the static displacement, first peak time,
first peak displacement, and the envelope-based two-percent settling bound.
Explain why displacement and velocity are continuous at the force step even
though acceleration jumps.
permittedResults: For \(0<\zeta<1\), the homogeneous roots are \(-\zeta\omega_n\pm i\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\).
The combination \(\cos u+a\sin u\) has absolute value at most \(\sqrt{1+a^2}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Subtract the static equilibrium, solve the homogeneous initial-value problem, and analyze its derivative and envelope.
Use a Laplace transform for the step response, provided the same time-domain constants, peak derivation, and exact envelope bound are supplied.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the exact underdamped step response, peak overshoot and time, and a mathematically sufficient settling envelope before performing the numerical evaluation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Omits the sine term required by the zero initial velocity or uses its coefficient with the wrong sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed response fails the stated initial conditions and gives wrong transient metrics.

commonErrors.description: Defines settling as the first time the oscillation enters the two-percent band without ensuring it remains there.
commonErrors.consequence: A later oscillation can leave the claimed settled region.

hintTree.content: Subtract the static particular solution \(x_s=F_0/k\), then solve the homogeneous initial-value problem for \(x-x_s\).
Differentiate the final response before solving for the first positive zero of velocity; cancellations leave \(\sin(\omega_dt)=0\).
Rewrite the normalized error as \(e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}[\cos\omega_dt+\zeta(1-\zeta^2)^{-1/2}\sin\omega_dt]\) and bound the bracket by \((1-\zeta^2)^{-1/2}\).

WAVE:010119.canonicalSolution:
The static particular solution is \(x_s=F_0/k\). Let
\(z=x-x_s\). For \(t>0\),
\[
\ddot z+2\zeta\omega_n\dot z+\omega_n^2z=0,
\quad z(0)=-x_s,
\quad \dot z(0)=0.
\]
Writing \(\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\) and applying the initial
conditions gives
\[
\boxed{x(t)=x_s\left[1-e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}
\left(\cos\omega_dt+
\frac{\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\sin\omega_dt\right)\right]}.
\]
Differentiation simplifies to a positive constant times
\(e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}\sin\omega_dt\), so the first maximum occurs at
\[
\boxed{t_p=\frac\pi{\omega_d}}.
\]
At that time the sine term vanishes and the cosine is minus one, hence
\[
x(t_p)=x_s\left(1+e^{-\zeta\omega_n\pi/\omega_d}\right),
\]
which proves
\[
\boxed{M_p=e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}}.
\]

The normalized error satisfies
\[
\frac{|x-x_s|}{x_s}
\le \frac{e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}.
\]
Therefore a sufficient two-percent bound is
\[
\boxed{t\ge t_{2\%}^{\mathrm{env}}=
\frac{\ln[1/(0.02\sqrt{1-\zeta^2})]}{\zeta\omega_n}}.
\]
Replacing the logarithm by approximately four and ignoring its weak damping
dependence gives the familiar \(4/(\zeta\omega_n)\) estimate.

For the data,
\[
\omega_n=10.0\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad
\zeta=\frac8{2(2)(10)}=0.200,
\]
\[
\omega_d=9.798\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad x_s=0.500\,\mathrm m.
\]
Thus
\[
t_p=0.3206\,\mathrm s,
\quad M_p=e^{-0.6413}=0.5266,
\quad \boxed{x(t_p)=0.7633\,\mathrm m}.
\]
The guaranteed envelope time is
\[
t_{2\%}^{\mathrm{env}}=
\frac{\ln[1/(0.02\sqrt{0.96})]}2=1.966\,\mathrm s,
\]
close to the rule-of-thumb value \(2.00\,\mathrm s\).

A bounded force step has no impulse. Integrating the equation across an
infinitesimal interval around zero therefore gives no momentum or velocity
jump. A displacement jump would make \(\dot x\) contain a delta and
\(\ddot x\) contain a delta-prime, neither of which can be balanced by the
stated forcing. Position and velocity remain continuous; the finite
right-hand-side change instead produces a jump in acceleration.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(x_s=F_0/k\), the response is \(x_s[1-e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}(\cos\omega_dt+\zeta\sin\omega_dt/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2})]\). Its first peak is at \(\pi/\omega_d\), with overshoot \(e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\). The error envelope is \(x_se^{-\zeta\omega_nt}/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\).
The response is one minus an exponentially damped cosine, with no sine term. Settling occurs at the first zero crossing of the error, because the response has reached its final value there.
