WAVE:010120.title: A viscoelastic oscillator with an internal relaxation mode
WAVE:010120.objective: Model a spring--dashpot Maxwell arm with an internal force, derive the resulting cubic dynamics, prove dissipation and stability, and connect transient roots to complex stiffness.
WAVE:010120.statement:
A mass \(m\) moves horizontally with displacement \(x(t)\). It is attached
to a fixed wall by an elastic spring \(k_0\) in parallel with a Maxwell arm.
The Maxwell arm consists of a spring \(k_1\) in series with a viscous dashpot
of coefficient \(\eta\). Let \(q(t)\) be the common tensile force in that
series arm; take positive \(q\) to oppose positive mass displacement. All
parameters are strictly positive, and all elements are linear.

Starting from strain compatibility in the Maxwell arm, derive the coupled
equations for \(x\) and \(q\). Eliminate \(q\) for free motion and obtain a
third-order equation for \(x\). Derive its characteristic polynomial and use
the cubic Routh--Hurwitz criterion to prove that all three roots have negative
real part for every finite \(0<\eta<\infty\).

Construct the stored mechanical energy using the Maxwell spring deformation,
and show directly that its derivative equals minus the dashpot dissipation.
Explain why the derivative is only negative semidefinite but the equilibrium
is nevertheless asymptotically stable. Discuss carefully the singular limits
\(\eta\to0\) and \(\eta\to\infty\); do not claim the finite-eta decay rate
stays bounded away from zero in either limit.

For a harmonic force \(F_0\cos\omega t\), derive the Maxwell arm's complex
stiffness, its storage and loss parts, and the mass displacement phasor.
Finally take
\[
m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg},\quad k_0=4.00\,\mathrm{N/m},\quad
k_1=5.00\,\mathrm{N/m},\quad \eta=2.50\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}.
\]
Factor the free-motion characteristic polynomial. If
\(x(0)=x_0\), \(\dot x(0)=0\), and the Maxwell arm is initially relaxed
\(q(0)=0\), find the exact displacement for all \(t\ge0\). For
\(x_0=5.00\,\mathrm{cm}\), compute the initial energy. Also compute the
steady displacement amplitude, lag, and mean dissipated power for
\(F_0=1.00\,\mathrm N\) and \(\omega=2.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).
permittedResults: A real cubic with positive coefficients is Hurwitz precisely when the product of its quadratic and linear coefficients exceeds the product of its cubic and constant coefficients.
For a harmonic displacement phasor \(X\), a loss stiffness \(K''>0\) dissipates mean power \(\tfrac12\omega K''|X|^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Keep the Maxwell force as an internal state, eliminate it for the root calculation, and use its spring energy for the Lyapunov balance.

Use Laplace-domain Maxwell compliance and a state-space realization, provided the same cubic, strict stability result, energy law, singular limits, exact release response, and harmonic numbers are recovered.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Derives the Maxwell internal-variable dynamics and cubic, proves finite-parameter stability by Routh and energy, and obtains a convention-consistent complex stiffness, exact transient, and dissipation audit.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Writes the Maxwell arm force as eta times x-dot, ignoring that the spring and dashpot are in series.
commonErrors.consequence: The internal relaxation state, cubic characteristic equation, and frequency-dependent stiffness disappear.

commonErrors.description: Claims the energy law either proves no decay because its derivative can vanish instantaneously, or proves a viscosity-independent exponential rate.
commonErrors.consequence: Invariant-set stability and the two singular viscosity limits are both misinterpreted.

hintTree.content: If the Maxwell spring and dashpot extensions are \(x_s,x_d\), then \(x=x_s+x_d\), \(q=k_1x_s=\eta\dot x_d\).
Try \(E=m\dot x^2/2+k_0x^2/2+q^2/(2k_1)\), then use both coupled equations before simplifying.
With \(a=k_1/\eta\), harmonic compatibility gives \(q/X=k_1i\omega/(a+i\omega)\).

WAVE:010120.canonicalSolution:
Compatibility and the two constitutive laws give
\[
\dot x=\dot x_s+\dot x_d=\frac{\dot q}{k_1}+\frac q\eta,
\]
so, with \(a=k_1/\eta\),
\[
\boxed{m\ddot x+k_0x+q=F(t)},\qquad
\boxed{\dot q+aq=k_1\dot x}.
\]
For free motion, applying \(d/dt+a\) to the mass equation and using the
internal-force equation eliminates \(q\):
\[
\boxed{m x^{(3)}+ma\ddot x+(k_0+k_1)\dot x+ak_0x=0}.
\]
Thus
\[
p(s)=ms^3+mas^2+(k_0+k_1)s+ak_0.
\]
Every coefficient is positive, and the nontrivial cubic Routh condition is
\[
(ma)(k_0+k_1)>m(ak_0),
\]
whose difference is \(mak_1>0\). Hence all three roots are strictly in the
left half-plane for finite positive parameters.

The Maxwell spring extension is \(q/k_1\), so
\[
E=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12k_0x^2+\frac{q^2}{2k_1}.
\]
Using \(m\ddot x=-k_0x-q\) and
\(\dot q/k_1=\dot x-q/\eta\) gives
\[
\boxed{\dot E=-\frac{q^2}{\eta}\le0}.
\]
Equality at an instant need not mean equilibrium. But a trajectory that stays
in \(q=0\) must also have \(\dot q=k_1\dot x=0\); the mass equation then
forces \(x=0\). Thus the only invariant subset of \(\dot E=0\) is the
equilibrium, consistent with the Hurwitz result.

As \(\eta\to0\), \(a\to\infty\): the Maxwell force relaxes on a fast time
scale and the remaining oscillator approaches the undamped \(k_0\) spring.
As \(\eta\to\infty\), \(a\to0\): the dashpot is effectively locked over
finite observation times, the incremental stiffness approaches \(k_0+k_1\),
and a relaxation root approaches zero. Both are singular nondissipative
limits, so finite-eta asymptotic stability does not imply uniform decay there.

For the \(e^{i\omega t}\) convention,
\[
\widehat q=K_M^*(\omega)X,\qquad
\boxed{K_M^*(\omega)=\frac{k_1i\omega}{a+i\omega}
=\frac{k_1\omega^2}{a^2+\omega^2}
+i\frac{k_1a\omega}{a^2+\omega^2}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
K'=\frac{k_1\omega^2}{a^2+\omega^2},\qquad
K''=\frac{k_1a\omega}{a^2+\omega^2},
\]
and the displacement phasor is
\[
\boxed{X=\frac{F_0}{k_0-m\omega^2+K'+iK''}}.
\]

For the numerical data, \(a=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and
\[
p(s)=s^3+2s^2+9s+8=(s+1)(s^2+s+8).
\]
The roots are \(-1\) and \(-1/2\pm i\sqrt{31}/2\). The relaxed-arm condition
sets \(\ddot x(0)=-k_0x_0/m=-4x_0\). Matching \(x,\dot x,\ddot x\) gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{x(t)}{x_0}=\frac12e^{-t}
+e^{-t/2}\left[
\frac12\cos\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{31}}2t\right)
+\frac{3}{2\sqrt{31}}\sin\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{31}}2t\right)
\right]}.
\]
Substitution at zero gives \(x/x_0=1\), \(\dot x=0\), and
\(\ddot x/x_0=-4\), as required. With \(q(0)=\dot x(0)=0\),
\[
\boxed{E(0)=\frac12k_0x_0^2=5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J}.
\]

At \(\omega=a=2.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\(K'=K''=k_1/2=2.50\,\mathrm{N/m}\), while
\(k_0-m\omega^2=0\). Hence
\[
|X|=\frac1{\sqrt{2.50^2+2.50^2}}
=\boxed{0.2828\,\mathrm m},
\qquad \boxed{\text{lag}=45.0^\circ}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{\langle P_{\rm diss}\rangle
=\frac12\omega K''|X|^2=0.200\,\mathrm W},
\]
which also equals \(\langle q^2\rangle/\eta\).

graderFixtures.proofText: Compatibility gives \(\dot q+(k_1/\eta)q=k_1\dot x\). Elimination produces \(ms^3+ma s^2+(k_0+k_1)s+ak_0\), whose cubic Routh gap is \(mak_1>0\). The energy \(m\dot x^2/2+k_0x^2/2+q^2/(2k_1)\) obeys \(\dot E=-q^2/\eta\), and harmonic motion sees \(K_M^*=k_1i\omega/(a+i\omega)\).

Because the dashpot is attached to the mass, I set q equal to eta x-dot and obtain the ordinary quadratic damped oscillator. Since energy derivative can equal zero at one instant, asymptotic stability cannot be decided for any finite eta.

WAVE:010121.title: A sudden stiffness quench injects phase-dependent work
WAVE:010121.objective: Solve a harmonic oscillator across an instantaneous frequency change, derive phase-dependent amplitude and work, and construct an exact two-quench echo.
WAVE:010121.statement:
A mass m executes an undamped oscillation with angular frequency \(\omega_1\).
At \(t=0\), an external controller changes the spring stiffness
instantaneously so that the new frequency is
\(\omega_2>\omega_1>0\). The controller
applies no direct impulse to the mass. Just before the change, write the state
as
\[
x(0^-)=A\cos\phi,\qquad
\dot x(0^-)=-A\omega_1\sin\phi.
\]

Derive the exact motion for \(t>0\), including the new oscillation amplitude
as a function of phase. Compute the mechanical energy immediately before and
after the quench and prove that the controller's work is
\[
W=\frac12m(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2)x(0)^2.
\]
Identify the phases receiving maximum and zero work. Average uniformly over
the initial phase and derive the mean energy ratio. Explain why displacement
and velocity remain continuous while acceleration need not.

Now quench from \(\omega_1\) to \(\omega_2\), wait a duration tau, and
quench back to \(\omega_1\). Write the state-propagation matrix during the
middle interval. Find every positive tau for which every initial state is
restored up to an overall minus sign or exactly restored, and show that the
original \(\omega_1\) energy is then recovered for all phases. Do not use
adiabatic invariance for an instantaneous protocol.

For \(m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\omega_1=4.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\(\omega_2=7.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(A=0.100\,\mathrm m\), and
\(\phi=\pi/3\), compute the switch state, new amplitude, old and new energy,
work, phase-averaged energy ratio, and the shortest positive echo time.
permittedResults: A frequency-omega oscillator propagates \((x,v)^T\) for time t by \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t/\omega\\-\omega\sin\omega t&\cos\omega t\end{pmatrix}\).
An instantaneous change in potential stiffness changes energy through the potential term evaluated at the unchanged position.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match the continuous switch state, compare the two quadratic energies, and use the middle-interval state-transition matrix.
Use complex oscillator quadratures or canonical phase-space rotations, provided the amplitude, phase work, ensemble mean, echo set, numerical values, and nonadiabatic interpretation agree.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the phase-dependent post-quench motion and energy transfer, then proves the exact all-state two-quench echo with the correct propagation matrix.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Introduces a velocity or displacement jump even though the stiffness change carries no direct impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: The post-quench coefficients and work ledger do not follow the stated equation.

commonErrors.description: Uses conservation of E over omega across the instantaneous change.
commonErrors.consequence: The phase-dependent work and exact sudden-quench state matching are replaced by an inapplicable slow-variation approximation.

hintTree.content: Use continuity to set the cosine and sine coefficients of the post-quench solution from the given pre-quench state.
Subtract \(m(v^2+\omega_1^2x^2)/2\) from \(m(v^2+\omega_2^2x^2)/2\) at the same state.
For a state-independent echo, the middle propagator itself must equal plus or minus the identity.

WAVE:010121.canonicalSolution:
Because the stiffness step supplies no delta impulse, integrating the equation
across zero leaves x and v continuous. Therefore
\[
\boxed{x(t)=A\cos\phi\cos\omega_2t
-A\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}\sin\phi\sin\omega_2t},
\qquad t>0.
\]
The new free-oscillation amplitude is
\[
\boxed{B=A\sqrt{\cos^2\phi+
\frac{\omega_1^2}{\omega_2^2}\sin^2\phi}}.
\]
The energies on the two sides are
\[
E_1=\frac12m\omega_1^2A^2,
\]
\[
E_2=\frac12mA^2
(\omega_1^2\sin^2\phi+\omega_2^2\cos^2\phi).
\]
Their difference is
\[
\boxed{W=E_2-E_1=
\frac12m(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2)A^2\cos^2\phi
=\frac12m(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2)x(0)^2}.
\]
For a stiffening quench, work is maximal at displacement extrema
\(\phi=0\pmod\pi\) and zero at equilibrium crossings
\(\phi=\pi/2\pmod\pi\). Acceleration changes because its coefficient
changes, but neither state variable jumps. Uniform phase averaging gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{\langle E_2\rangle_\phi}{E_1}
=\frac12\left[1+\left(\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}\right)^2\right]}.
\]

During the middle interval the unchanged state is propagated by
\[
M_2(\tau)=\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta&\sin\theta/\omega_2\\
-\omega_2\sin\theta&\cos\theta
\end{pmatrix},\qquad \theta=\omega_2\tau.
\]
The return quench also leaves x and v unchanged. State-independent recovery
up to sign requires \(M_2=\pm I\), hence
\[
\boxed{\tau_n=\frac{n\pi}{\omega_2}},\qquad n=1,2,3,\ldots.
\]
Odd n gives the negative of the initial state; even n restores it exactly.
Either way the quadratic \(\omega_1\) energy is identical to its initial
value for every phase. This is a finite-time matrix identity, not an
adiabatic-invariant argument.

For the numerical state,
\[
x(0)=0.100\cos(\pi/3)=\boxed{0.050000\,\mathrm m},
\]
\[
v(0)=-0.100(4)\sin(\pi/3)
=\boxed{-0.346410\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The new amplitude is
\[
B=0.100\sqrt{\frac14+\frac{16}{49}\frac34}
=\boxed{0.070349\,\mathrm m}.
\]
The energies and work are
\[
\boxed{E_1=0.040000\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_2=0.060625\,\mathrm J},
\]
\[
\boxed{W=0.020625\,\mathrm J}.
\]
The phase-averaged ratio is
\[
\boxed{\frac12[1+(7/4)^2]=2.03125},
\]
and the shortest echo time is
\[
\boxed{\tau_1=\pi/7=0.448799\,\mathrm s},
\]
which returns every state with an overall minus sign before the stiffness is
switched back.

graderFixtures.proofText: Continuity gives \(x=A\cos\phi\cos\omega_2t-A(\omega_1/\omega_2)\sin\phi\sin\omega_2t\). The work is \(m(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2)x(0)^2/2\), and the phase mean ratio is \([1+(\omega_2/\omega_1)^2]/2\). A quench back after \(n\pi/\omega_2\) restores every state up to sign.

I conserve E divided by omega through the instantaneous change and add a velocity jump from the stiffness step. I then call one specially chosen phase return a universal echo without checking the state matrix.

WAVE:010122.title: Thermal motion reveals a damped oscillator's susceptibility
WAVE:010122.objective: Derive the displacement spectrum of a Langevin oscillator, connect it to equipartition, and separate exact peak location from high-Q linewidth approximations.
WAVE:010122.statement:
A one-dimensional mechanical mode in equilibrium with a heat bath obeys the
Langevin equation
\[
m\ddot x+\gamma\dot x+kx=\xi(t),
\]
where \(m,\gamma,k>0\). Use the Fourier convention
\(x(t)=\int \tilde x(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,d\omega/(2\pi)\).
The bath force is stationary and has the two-sided angular-frequency spectrum
\[
S_\xi(\omega)=2\gamma k_BT,
\qquad
\langle x^2\rangle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
S_x(\omega)\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}.
\]

Derive the mechanical susceptibility and \(S_x(\omega)\). Find the exact
nonzero frequency at which the displacement spectrum is maximal, state the
condition for that peak to exist, and explain why the often-used linewidth
\(\gamma/m\) is a high-Q approximation rather than a universal exact
full-width formula. Use equilibrium statistical mechanics to state and check
the integrals of the displacement and velocity spectra. Discuss the limit
\(\gamma\to0^+\): the peak height diverges, but the integrated variance must
not.

For \(m=1.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{kg}\),
\(k=0.100\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\gamma=2.00\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{kg/s}\), and
\(T=300\,\mathrm K\), compute \(\omega_0\), the quality factor
\(Q=m\omega_0/\gamma\), the exact spectral-peak frequency,
\(x_{\rm rms}\), \(v_{\rm rms}\), \(S_x(0)\), and
\(S_x(\omega_0)\). Keep the two-sided angular-frequency convention
throughout; do not silently convert to a one-sided per-hertz spectrum.
permittedResults: For a linear filter, \(S_x(\omega)=|\chi(\omega)|^2S_\xi(\omega)\).
Classical equipartition gives \(k\langle x^2\rangle=k_BT\) and \(m\langle\dot x^2\rangle=k_BT\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Fourier-transform the Langevin equation, filter the white force spectrum, and use equipartition for the spectral-area checks.
Use the oscillator Green function and Wiener-Khinchin theorem, provided the same PSD convention, exact peak, numerical values, and finite-area limit are obtained.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the susceptibility and thermal displacement PSD, locates its exact peak with the correct existence condition, and reconciles the narrow-resonance limit with equipartition.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Mixes one-sided per-hertz and two-sided angular-frequency spectra without the required conversion factors.
commonErrors.consequence: The PSD levels and integrated variances are numerically inconsistent.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that thermal variance diverges as damping vanishes because the resonant peak height diverges.
commonErrors.consequence: The conclusion violates equipartition and ignores the simultaneous linewidth collapse.

hintTree.content: Fourier transformation replaces \(\dot x\) by \(-i\omega\tilde x\).
Minimize \((k-m\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2\) to locate the nonzero PSD maximum.
Use \(S_v=\omega^2S_x\) and equipartition to check spectral area without evaluating the quartic integral by residues.

WAVE:010122.canonicalSolution:
Fourier transformation gives
\[
(k-m\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)\tilde x=\tilde\xi,
\qquad
\boxed{\chi(\omega)=\frac1{k-m\omega^2-i\gamma\omega}}.
\]
Therefore the specified two-sided PSD is
\[
\boxed{S_x(\omega)=
\frac{2\gamma k_BT}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2}}.
\]
Differentiating the denominator shows that a nonzero maximum occurs at
\[
\boxed{\omega_{\rm pk}^2=\frac{k}{m}-\frac{\gamma^2}{2m^2}}
\]
when \(\gamma^2<2mk\), equivalently \(Q>1/\sqrt2\). Otherwise the
displacement PSD is largest at zero frequency. Near a narrow resonance,
linearizing \(k-m\omega^2\) about \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) produces an
approximately Lorentzian peak with full width \(\gamma/m\). Away from high Q,
the quartic denominator and the shifted peak make that width statement only an
approximation.

The fluctuation-dissipation normalization is consistent with
\[
\int S_x\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{k_BT}{k},
\qquad
\int \omega^2S_x\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}=\frac{k_BT}{m}.
\]
Thus \(x_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{k_BT/k}\) and
\(v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{k_BT/m}\). As \(\gamma\to0^+\), the two narrow peaks
at \(\pm\omega_0\) become taller and narrower while their combined area
remains \(k_BT/k\); interpreting only the height as total noise is incorrect.

Numerically,
\[
\omega_0=\sqrt{10^5}=\boxed{316.228\,\mathrm{rad/s}},
\qquad Q=\frac{10^{-6}(316.228)}{2\times10^{-5}}
=\boxed{15.811}.
\]
The exact peak is
\[
\omega_{\rm pk}=\sqrt{100000-200}
=\boxed{315.911\,\mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
With \(k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}\),
\[
x_{\rm rms}=\boxed{2.0352\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m},
\qquad
v_{\rm rms}=\boxed{6.4358\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Finally,
\[
S_x(0)=\frac{2\gamma k_BT}{k^2}
=\boxed{1.6568\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{m^2s}},
\]
and because the elastic and inertial terms cancel at \(\omega_0\),
\[
S_x(\omega_0)=\frac{2k_BT}{\gamma\omega_0^2}
=\boxed{4.1419\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{m^2s}}.
\]
The units are per radian per second in the stated angular-frequency
normalization; a per-hertz, one-sided number would require explicit factors.

graderFixtures.proofText: The response is \(\chi=(k-m\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)^{-1}\), so \(S_x=2\gamma k_BT/[(k-m\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2]\). Its nonzero peak has \(\omega_{pk}^2=k/m-\gamma^2/(2m^2)\), while the total areas give \(k_BT/k\) and \(k_BT/m\).

I use a one-sided PSD formula but integrate it over both positive and negative angular frequencies. Since the peak height grows like one over damping, I conclude that the thermal mean-square displacement diverges when damping goes to zero.

WAVE:010123.title: A dry-friction oscillator stops after a finite number of turns
WAVE:010123.objective: Derive an exact half-cycle turning map for a spring-mass oscillator with Coulomb friction, determine its finite arrest point, and close the work-energy ledger.
WAVE:010123.statement:
A block of mass \(m\) slides horizontally while attached to a spring of
stiffness \(k\). While the block is moving, the contact force has constant
magnitude \(F_c>0\) and points opposite the velocity:
\[
m\ddot x+kx+F_c\operatorname{sgn}(\dot x)=0.
\]
When the block is instantaneously at rest, static friction may take any value
with magnitude at most \(F_c\). The block is released from
\(x(0)=A_0>F_c/k\), \(\dot x(0)=0\), and initially moves to the left.

On an arbitrary moving half-cycle, solve the equation exactly about its
shifted equilibrium. Derive a recurrence for successive signed turning
points and show that the magnitude falls by \(2F_c/k\) on an opposite-side
leg that is followed by another leg. Show separately how a terminal leg can
stop on the same side of equilibrium, so its magnitude need not fall by that
amount. State the precise static-arrest test at a turning point; do not
continue the kinetic-friction formula through a point where static friction
can hold the block. Give a floor/ceiling-free algorithm that determines the
first arrest point from \(A_0\), and prove that it terminates in finitely many
steps. Derive the total sliding distance and verify that frictional work
equals the change in spring energy between release and arrest.

For \(m=0.800\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(F_c=0.300\,\mathrm N\), and \(A_0=9.30\,\mathrm{mm}\), list every
turning point, identify the arrest point, compute the stopping time, total
sliding distance, frictional work, and final stored spring energy. Explain why
an exponential envelope and a constant viscous-damping ratio are invalid for
this model, and check both dimensions and energy signs.
permittedResults: On an interval with fixed velocity sign, shifting by the corresponding equilibrium \(\pm F_c/k\) reduces the equation to a simple harmonic oscillator with frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\).
The work of kinetic friction over a monotone segment is minus its magnitude times the distance traveled.

acceptableStrategies.description: Shift the equilibrium separately on each fixed-velocity interval and iterate the resulting signed turning map.
Use energy loss over each monotone leg to derive the same amplitude decrement, while retaining signed positions for the final static-friction test.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and applies the exact signed half-cycle map with the static-arrest condition, then closes the finite-time distance and energy ledger.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Continues the kinetic-friction recurrence from a turning point whose spring force is small enough for static friction to hold.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted later turns and stopping position are physically nonexistent.

commonErrors.description: Models the constant dry-friction force as viscous damping and imposes an exponential amplitude envelope.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite arrest time, constant per-half-cycle decrement, and energy ledger are wrong.

hintTree.content: Set \(a=F_c/k\). On a leftward segment the shifted coordinate is \(x-a\), whereas on a rightward segment it is \(x+a\).
A segment that begins at rest at \(x_n\) reaches its next zero-velocity point after \(\pi/\omega_0\); evaluate the shifted cosine there.
Iterate only while the new turning point fails the static-friction inequality, and telescope the distances between successive turns.

WAVE:010123.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
a=\frac{F_c}{k},\qquad \omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}.
\]
Suppose a half-cycle starts from rest at a positive turning point \(X>a\)
and moves left. Then \(\operatorname{sgn}\dot x=-1\), so
\(m\ddot x+kx-F_c=0\). Therefore
\[
x(t)=a+(X-a)\cos\omega_0t,
\]
and the next zero of velocity occurs at \(t=\pi/\omega_0\), at
\[
x'=2a-X.
\]
Similarly, starting at a negative point \(X<-a\) and moving right gives
\(x(t)=-a+(X+a)\cos\omega_0t\) and \(x'=-2a-X\). Combining the cases,
\[
\boxed{x_{n+1}=-x_n+2a\operatorname{sgn}(x_n)}.
\]
If the new turn lies on the opposite side, then
\(|x_{n+1}|=|x_n|-2a\). If instead \(a<|x_n|<2a\), the terminal turn stays
on the same side and \(|x_{n+1}|=2a-|x_n|<a\). Thus the fixed \(2a\)
decrement applies to every leg that is followed by another leg, but it must
not be extrapolated to the terminal arrested leg.

The exact algorithm is: begin at \(x_0=A_0\). If \(|x_n|\le a\), stop.
Otherwise compute the signed next turn from the boxed map. At that point stop
if \(|x_{n+1}|\le a\); if not, reverse the sliding direction and repeat.
Every continued step reduces the magnitude by \(2a>0\), so after finitely
many steps the newly reached point lies in \([-a,a]\). Static friction then
balances \(-kx_*\). Notice that the final point can have either sign and a
small nonzero displacement.

For the data,
\[
a=\frac{0.300}{200}=1.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m,
\qquad \omega_0=\sqrt{250}=15.8114\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
\]
The signed turns are
\[
x_0=+9.30\ \mathrm{mm},\quad
x_1=3.00-9.30=-6.30\ \mathrm{mm},
\]
\[
x_2=-3.00-(-6.30)=+3.30\ \mathrm{mm},\quad
x_3=3.00-3.30=-0.300\ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
Since \(|x_3|=0.300\,\mathrm{mm}<a=1.50\,\mathrm{mm}\), the third
arriving turn is the arrest point. Three half-periods elapse:
\[
\boxed{t_{\rm stop}=\frac{3\pi}{\omega_0}=0.596075\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The total sliding distance is
\[
D=|9.30-(-6.30)|+|-6.30-3.30|+|3.30-(-0.300)|
=\boxed{28.8\ \mathrm{mm}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{W_f=-F_cD=-0.300(0.0288)=-8.640\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The endpoint spring energies are
\[
E_0=\tfrac12kA_0^2=8.649\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm J,
\qquad
E_f=\tfrac12kx_3^2=\boxed{9.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm J}.
\]
Indeed \(E_f-E_0=-8.640\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J=W_f\). The loss is
negative work, while the heat generated has positive magnitude. Because the
amplitude loses a fixed length per completed half-cycle rather than a fixed
fraction, its envelope is piecewise linear in cycle count, not exponential;
there is no constant viscous damping ratio. Also, \(F_c/k\) has dimensions of
length and \(F_cD\) has dimensions of energy, as required.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(a=F_c/k\), a positive-to-left leg has \(x=a+(X-a)\cos\omega_0t\), so \(x' =2a-X\); the negative case gives the unified map \(x'=-x+2a\operatorname{sgn}x\). Iteration gives \(9.30,-6.30,3.30,-0.300\) mm, where static friction holds. The three-half-period time is \(0.596075\) s and \(-F_cD=-8.640\) mJ equals the spring-energy change.
I replace dry friction by an equivalent viscous coefficient, fit an exponential envelope, and keep iterating past the small final turning point until the displacement is exactly zero.

WAVE:010124.title: Coherent kicks make oscillator energy grow quadratically
WAVE:010124.objective: Construct the exact stroboscopic map of an impulse-driven oscillator and distinguish resonance, antiresonance, and bounded detuned response.
WAVE:010124.statement:
An undamped oscillator satisfies \(m\ddot x+m\omega_0^2x=0\) between
instantaneous impulses. Starting from rest, it receives \(N\) identical
positive impulses of momentum \(J\) at times \(t=0,T,2T,\ldots,(N-1)T\).
Sample the state immediately after each kick. An impulse changes velocity by
\(J/m\) but leaves displacement continuous.

Using the scaled phase-space state \((x,v/\omega_0)\), derive the exact
free-rotation matrix and the affine kick map. Introduce one complex state and
sum the map to obtain a closed formula for the state magnitude and mechanical
energy after \(N\) kicks. Treat \(\theta=\omega_0T\) equal to an integer
multiple of \(2\pi\) by a limit, not by dividing by zero. Prove the
\(N^2\) resonant energy law, describe antiresonance at odd multiples of
\(\pi\), and derive the near-resonant line shape when
\(\theta=2\pi q+\delta\). Explain why adding the individual kick energies
misses interference work \(Jv^-\).

For \(m=0.250\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\omega_0=20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\(J=0.0500\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), \(N=25\), and
\(T=(2\pi+0.0800)/\omega_0\), compute the scaled single-kick increment,
final phase-space radius, and final energy. Compare with exact resonance for
the same \(N\), and state which idealizations become suspect if the resonant
amplitude grows without bound.
permittedResults: Free oscillator evolution through phase \(\theta\) rotates \((x,v/\omega_0)\) by \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the complex phase-space state and a geometric series.
Iterate the two-dimensional affine symplectic map and diagonalize its rotation, retaining the impulse work cross term.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the affine rotation-kick map, sums it exactly, and correctly separates resonant quadratic growth, antiresonance, and finite detuning.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds only J squared over two m per kick and omits the pre-kick velocity cross term.
commonErrors.consequence: Resonant energy is predicted to grow linearly rather than quadratically.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes exact resonance into the geometric quotient and treats its zero denominator as a divergence or undefined state.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite N coherent sum and exact resonant state are lost.

hintTree.content: Let \(z=x+i v/\omega_0\); free evolution multiplies \(z\) by \(e^{-i\theta}\), while a positive kick adds \(ip\) with \(p=J/(m\omega_0)\).
Starting before the first kick, iterate \(z_n=e^{-i\theta}z_{n-1}+ip\) and take the modulus of the geometric sum.
Use \(|1-e^{-iN\theta}|=2|\sin(N\theta/2)|\), then examine \(\theta\to2\pi q\) and \(\theta=(2q+1)\pi\).

WAVE:010124.canonicalSolution:
Write \(u=(x,v/\omega_0)^T\). Between kicks,
\[
u\longmapsto R(\theta)u,
\quad R(\theta)=
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},
\quad \theta=\omega_0T.
\]
A kick adds \((0,p)^T\), where
\[
p=\frac{J}{m\omega_0}.
\]
For \(z=x+i v/\omega_0\), sampling just after successive kicks and taking
\(z_0=0\) immediately before the first one gives
\[
z_n=e^{-i\theta}z_{n-1}+ip,
\qquad
z_N=ip\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{-ij\theta}.
\]
Thus, away from exact resonance,
\[
\boxed{|z_N|=p\left|\frac{\sin(N\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}\right|},
\]
and because \(E=m\omega_0^2|z|^2/2\),
\[
\boxed{E_N=\frac{J^2}{2m}
\frac{\sin^2(N\theta/2)}{\sin^2(\theta/2)}}.
\]

If \(\theta=2\pi q\), every free rotation is the identity. The sum is
then exactly \(N\), or equivalently follows from the displayed ratio's
limit, so
\[
|z_N|=Np,\qquad \boxed{E_N=N^2J^2/(2m)}.
\]
The quadratic law is coherent: the kick work is
\(\Delta E=Jv^-+J^2/(2m)\), so a kick arriving in phase does more than add
its isolated rest-state energy. At \(\theta=(2q+1)\pi\), successive terms
alternate. This antiresonance makes even \(N\) give zero final state, while odd \(N\) leaves one-kick
magnitude. For \(\theta=2\pi q+\delta\),
\[
|z_N|=p\left|\frac{\sin(N\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}\right|,
\]
the exact finite-train near-resonant response.

Numerically,
\[
p=\frac{0.0500}{0.250(20.0)}=\boxed{0.010000\ \mathrm m}.
\]
Here \(\delta=0.0800\), hence
\[
\frac{|\sin(25\delta/2)|}{|\sin(\delta/2)|}
=\frac{\sin1.000}{\sin0.0400}=21.0424\ldots,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{|z_{25}|=0.210424\ \mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{E_{25}=2.21391\ \mathrm J}\quad\text{(rounded)}.
\]
At exact resonance the corresponding values are
\[
|z_{25}|=25p=\boxed{0.2500\ \mathrm m},
\qquad
E_{25}=625\frac{0.0500^2}{2(0.250)}
=\boxed{3.125\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The ideal unbounded law eventually violates assumptions behind a perfectly
linear spring, instantaneous identical impulses, unlimited travel, no loss,
and parameter-independent \(\omega_0\). The phase-space radius has units of
length, while \(J^2/m\) has units of energy.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(z=x+iv/\omega_0\), \(z_n=e^{-i\theta}z_{n-1}+ip\). Therefore \(|z_N|=p|\sin(N\theta/2)/\sin(\theta/2)|\) and \(E_N=J^2|\cdots|^2/(2m)\). The resonance limit is N, while odd-pi spacing cancels pairs. For the detuned data the radius is about 0.2104 m and the energy about 2.214 J.

Each kick contributes J squared over two m independently, so after N kicks the energy is N times that amount. At theta equal to two pi the sine quotient divides by zero, proving the response is undefined.

WAVE:010125.title: A finite force pulse can leave no vibration at all
WAVE:010125.objective: Solve a rectangularly forced oscillator across switch-off, derive its residual vibration and work, and identify pulse lengths that cancel or maximize the free response.
WAVE:010125.statement:
An undamped mass-spring oscillator starts from rest at equilibrium. A constant
force \(F_0\) is applied at \(t=0\), held until \(t=\tau\), and then removed
instantaneously:
\[
m\ddot x+kx=F_0\,[H(t)-H(t-\tau)],\qquad x(0)=\dot x(0)=0.
\]
Displacement and velocity remain continuous when the force switches, although
acceleration need not.

Solve the motion during the pulse without discarding the homogeneous term.
Match the state at switch-off and express the later free motion both as a
sine-cosine combination and as a single residual amplitude with phase. Derive
closed expressions for the residual amplitude and energy in terms of
\(\Theta=\omega_0\tau\), where \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). Independently compute
the work done by the constant force and prove that it equals the mechanical
energy present immediately after removal. Identify every nonzero pulse length
that produces zero residual vibration and every pulse length that maximizes
the residual amplitude. Explain why a static-deflection argument alone gives
the wrong switch-off state.

For \(m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(F_0=50.0\,\mathrm N\), and \(\tau=0.200\,\mathrm s\), calculate
\(\omega_0,\Theta,x(\tau),\dot x(\tau)\), the residual amplitude, residual
energy, and input work. Also give the shortest positive cancellation pulse.
Check continuity, dimensions, and the limiting cases \(\tau\to0\) and
\(\tau\to2\pi/\omega_0\).
permittedResults: For \(y=a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t\), the oscillation amplitude is \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).
A finite jump in force changes acceleration but cannot create an impulse in velocity.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the two constant-coefficient intervals and match the phase-space state at force removal.
Use the impulse response convolution, then reduce the two endpoint contributions as phasors.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Matches the exact forced and free states and reconciles the residual amplitude, cancellation timing, and work-energy result.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses F0 over k as the complete loading motion and omits the transient satisfying the initial state.
commonErrors.consequence: Switch-off displacement, velocity, residual amplitude, and cancellation times are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Allows the finite force step at removal to create an instantaneous velocity jump.
commonErrors.consequence: The matched free state violates the integrated equation of motion.

hintTree.content: During the pulse use the static displacement \(x_s=F_0/k\) only as a particular solution, then enforce both initial conditions.
After switch-off write \(s=t-\tau\) and use \(x=x_\tau\cos\omega_0s+(\dot x_\tau/\omega_0)\sin\omega_0s\).
Reduce \((1-\cos\Theta)^2+\sin^2\Theta\) with a half-angle identity and compare \(F_0x(\tau)\) with \(kA_r^2/2\).

WAVE:010125.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad x_s=\frac{F_0}{k},
\qquad \Theta=\omega_0\tau.
\]
While the force is present, a constant particular solution is \(x_s\).
Enforcing the initial rest state gives
\[
\boxed{x(t)=x_s(1-\cos\omega_0t)},\qquad
\boxed{\dot x(t)=x_s\omega_0\sin\omega_0t}
\quad(0\le t\le\tau).
\]
Thus
\[
x_\tau=x_s(1-\cos\Theta),\qquad
v_\tau=x_s\omega_0\sin\Theta.
\]
There is no impulse at either switching event, so these are also the initial
data for the unforced interval. With \(s=t-\tau\),
\[
\boxed{x(t)=x_\tau\cos\omega_0s+
\frac{v_\tau}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0s}.
\]
Its residual amplitude is
\[
A_r=x_s\sqrt{(1-\cos\Theta)^2+\sin^2\Theta}
=\boxed{2x_s\left|\sin\frac{\Theta}{2}\right|}.
\]
The corresponding free energy is
\[
\boxed{E_r=\frac12kA_r^2
=\frac{F_0^2}{k}(1-\cos\Theta)
=\frac{2F_0^2}{k}\sin^2\frac{\Theta}{2}}.
\]
During loading the applied force does work
\[
W=\int_0^\tau F_0\dot x\,dt=F_0x_\tau
=\frac{F_0^2}{k}(1-\cos\Theta)=E_r.
\]
Removal itself occurs at fixed displacement and has no impulsive mechanical
work; it changes which potential is regarded as external, not the continuous
mass-spring state.

Cancellation requires \(\sin(\Theta/2)=0\), so every
\(\tau=2\pi n/\omega_0\), \(n=1,2,\ldots\), leaves the oscillator exactly at
rest at \(x=0\). Maximal residual amplitude \(2F_0/k\) occurs for
\(\Theta=(2n+1)\pi\). Treating the mass as if it sat at the static displacement
throughout the pulse omits the transient cosine and therefore cannot predict
either cancellation or the correct switch-off velocity.

For the stated data,
\[
\omega_0=\sqrt{200/2}=\boxed{10.0000\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\Theta=2.00000.
\]
Using \(\cos2=-0.4161468\) and \(\sin2=0.9092974\),
\[
\boxed{x_\tau=0.354037\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{v_\tau=2.27324\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The residual values are
\[
\boxed{A_r=0.420735\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{E_r=17.7018\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The work is \(F_0x_\tau=\boxed{17.7018\ \mathrm J}\), in agreement. The
shortest positive cancellation pulse is
\[
\boxed{\tau_c=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=0.628319\ \mathrm s}.
\]
As \(\tau\to0\), both state and energy vanish; at \(\tau_c\), the two switching
transients cancel exactly. The ratios \(F_0/k\) and \(v_\tau/\omega_0\) both
have dimensions of length.

graderFixtures.proofText: During loading \(x=(F_0/k)(1-\cos\omega_0t)\). Matching at tau gives \(A_r=2(F_0/k)|\sin(\omega_0\tau/2)|\) and \(E_r=F_0^2(1-\cos\Theta)/k=F_0x_\tau\). Numerically \(A_r=0.420735\) m and \(E_r=17.7018\) J; the first cancellation is 0.628319 s.
The block immediately reaches F0 over k, and when the force is removed its velocity jumps to zero, so every pulse leaves no residual motion.

WAVE:010126.title: A ramped equilibrium has a sinc-shaped vibration penalty
WAVE:010126.objective: Derive exact tracking and residual vibration for an oscillator whose spring equilibrium is translated at constant speed, including zero-vibration command times.
WAVE:010126.statement:
A mass is attached to a spring whose other end is commanded to position \(y(t)\).
There is no damping:
\[
m\ddot x+k(x-y)=0,\qquad x(0)=\dot x(0)=0.
\]
The command moves from zero to \(d\) at constant speed and then holds:
\[
y(t)=\begin{cases}dt/T,&0\le t\le T,\\ d,&t\ge T.\end{cases}
\]
Assume the command begins and ends with finite velocity jumps but no
displacement jumps.

Solve the mass motion on the ramp and determine its displacement and velocity
relative to the new equilibrium at \(t=T\). Reduce the residual amplitude to
a sinc law in \(\Theta=\omega_0T\). Derive the residual energy and show directly
from the time-dependent spring potential that actuator work equals this energy.
Identify all command times that leave exactly zero vibration. Establish the
fast-command and slow-command limits, and explain why following \(y(t)\)
quasistatically is not valid unless the ramp spans many natural periods.

For \(m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(d=50.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), and \(T=0.400\,\mathrm s\), compute the final
relative displacement, velocity, residual amplitude, and residual energy.
Find the shortest nonzero zero-vibration ramp time and compare it with the
chosen ramp. State the sign convention for actuator work and verify that the
result is independent of an arbitrary absolute origin.
permittedResults: For a potential \(V(x,y)=k(x-y)^2/2\), work delivered through the prescribed coordinate is \(\int(\partial V/\partial y)\,dy=\int k(y-x)\,dy\).
\(\sin^2\Theta+(1-\cos\Theta)^2=4\sin^2(\Theta/2)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the forced equation on the ramp and match the state into the final relative coordinate.
Differentiate the equilibrium command into an impulse-response convolution and integrate its phasor content at the natural frequency.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the exact tracking error and sinc residual, then confirms the same result from generalized actuator work.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets x equal to y throughout a finite-speed ramp despite the required initial acceleration and inertia.
commonErrors.consequence: The tracking error, residual vibration, and actuator work are all erased.

commonErrors.description: Treats x(T) rather than x(T)-d as the later free displacement.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed residual amplitude includes a spurious static offset.

hintTree.content: During the ramp try \(x_p=dt/T\), then add the sine term required to make the initial velocity zero.
At \(T\), form \(q_T=x(T)-d\) and \(v_T/\omega_0\) before taking the Euclidean phase-space radius.
For actuator work integrate \(k(y-x)\dot y\) over the ramp and compare with \(k[q_T^2+(v_T/\omega_0)^2]/2\).

WAVE:010126.canonicalSolution:
Set \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\Theta=\omega_0T\). During the
ramp,
\[
\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=\omega_0^2\frac{dt}{T}.
\]
A particular solution is \(dt/T\). The initial conditions require
\[
\boxed{x(t)=d\left(\frac tT-\frac{\sin\omega_0t}{\omega_0T}\right)},
\qquad
\boxed{\dot x(t)=\frac dT(1-\cos\omega_0t)}.
\]
At the end of the ramp, relative to the final equilibrium,
\[
q_T=x(T)-d=-d\frac{\sin\Theta}{\Theta},
\qquad
v_T=\frac dT(1-\cos\Theta).
\]
For later time \(s=t-T\),
\[
q(s)=q_T\cos\omega_0s+\frac{v_T}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0s.
\]
The residual amplitude is therefore
\[
A_r=d\sqrt{\frac{\sin^2\Theta+(1-\cos\Theta)^2}{\Theta^2}}
=\boxed{d\left|\frac{\sin(\Theta/2)}{\Theta/2}\right|}.
\]
It is the magnitude of a sinc function. The residual energy is
\[
\boxed{E_r=\frac12kA_r^2}.
\]

The actuator force conjugate to y is \(k(y-x)\). Hence the work delivered to
the mass-spring system is
\[
W_a=\int_0^T k(y-x)\dot y\,dt.
\]
Substituting \(y-x=d\sin(\omega_0t)/(\omega_0T)\) and \(\dot y=d/T\),
\[
W_a=\frac{kd^2}{\omega_0T^2}\int_0^T\sin\omega_0t\,dt
=\frac{kd^2}{\Theta^2}(1-\cos\Theta)
=\frac12kd^2\frac{4\sin^2(\Theta/2)}{\Theta^2}=E_r.
\]
Changing the absolute coordinate origin shifts x and y together and leaves
\(x-y\), the work, and the energy unchanged.

Zero residual vibration occurs when \(\Theta=2\pi n\), \(n=1,2,\ldots\).
As \(T\to0\), sinc tends to one, so an almost instantaneous equilibrium step
leaves amplitude d. For long T the envelope is bounded by \(2d/\Theta\);
quasistatic tracking is recovered only when the command is slow compared with
the natural period.

Numerically, \(\omega_0=10.0000\,\mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\Theta=4.00000\).
Thus
\[
\boxed{q_T=+9.46003\ \mathrm{mm}},\qquad
\boxed{v_T=0.206705\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{A_r=22.7324\ \mathrm{mm}},\qquad
\boxed{E_r=0.0258382\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The first zero-vibration duration is
\[
\boxed{T_c=\frac{2\pi}{10}=0.628319\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The selected ramp is shorter, so it leaves a substantial but smaller-than-d
residual. The work convention used above is positive when the actuator gives
energy to the oscillator; the equal positive result confirms the sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: The ramp solution is \(x=d[t/T-\sin(\omega_0t)/(\omega_0T)]\). At T, \(q=-d\sin\Theta/\Theta\) and \(v=d(1-\cos\Theta)/T\), giving \(A_r=d|\sin(\Theta/2)/(\Theta/2)|\). The data give q 9.460 mm, v 0.206705 m/s, amplitude 22.732 mm, and energy 0.025838 J.
The mass follows the support exactly during the ramp. Afterward I use x(T), without subtracting d, as the oscillation amplitude and conclude the actuator did no work.

WAVE:010127.title: A slow chirp deposits a finite resonant oscillation
WAVE:010127.objective: Derive the controlled rotating-wave envelope for a linear oscillator swept through resonance and evaluate its Fresnel amplitude and energy.
WAVE:010127.statement:
An undamped oscillator obeys
\[
m\ddot x+m\omega_0^2x=F\cos\left(\omega_0t+\frac12\alpha t^2\right),
\qquad \alpha>0.
\]
The drive is far below resonance as \(t\to-\infty\), crosses resonance at
\(t=0\), and is far above resonance as \(t\to+\infty\). Interpret the
solution by adiabatically switching the force on in the remote past. Assume
\(\sqrt\alpha/\omega_0\ll1\), so a rotating-wave approximation is permitted,
but do not call that approximation an exact solution of the second-order
equation.

Write \(x=\operatorname{Re}[a(t)e^{i\omega_0t}]\), neglect the counter-rotating
and second-envelope-derivative terms with an explicit scale estimate, and
derive the first-order complex envelope. Express \(a(t)\) with a Fresnel
integral. Evaluate the state at resonance and after the sweep, including the
phase of the deposited free oscillation. Compute the post-sweep mechanical
energy and show its inverse dependence on sweep rate. Explain why substituting
the instantaneous static response near resonance fails and why the limit
\(\alpha\to0\) is nonuniform for an undamped oscillator.

For \(m=1.50\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\omega_0=20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\(F=3.00\,\mathrm N\), and \(\alpha=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}\), compute the
stationary-phase time scale, the final amplitude and energy, and the envelope
amplitude and energy at \(t=0\). Audit the approximation parameter and all
units.
permittedResults: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{i\alpha s^2/2}ds=\sqrt{2\pi/\alpha}\,e^{i\pi/4}\) for \(\alpha>0\).
For a slowly varying complex amplitude, \(\ddot{(ae^{i\omega_0t})}+\omega_0^2ae^{i\omega_0t}\simeq2i\omega_0\dot a e^{i\omega_0t}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a complex carrier envelope and isolate the stationary near-resonant forcing term.
Apply variation of constants to the exact Green integral, then evaluate its resonant stationary-phase contribution.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the slow envelope with its approximation scale and evaluates the complete resonance-passage amplitude, phase, and energy.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the instantaneous steady-state denominator through zero detuning and reports a divergent displacement at the crossing.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-duration phase coherence and Fresnel memory are erased.

commonErrors.description: Presents the first-order envelope as exact without stating or checking the small parameter sqrt alpha over omega zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Counter-rotating and envelope-acceleration errors are hidden.

hintTree.content: Represent the cosine by two complex exponentials and retain the component rotating with \(e^{i\omega_0t}\).
Choose the remote-past condition \(a(-\infty)=0\); the accumulated envelope is a quadratic-phase integral.
The integral from minus infinity to zero is exactly one half of the full Fresnel integral by evenness of the quadratic phase.

WAVE:010127.canonicalSolution:
Put \(x=\operatorname{Re}[ae^{i\omega_0t}]\). The resonant complex
forcing is \(F e^{i(\omega_0t+\alpha t^2/2)}\); the conjugate component rotates
near \(-\omega_0\). Keeping the resonant component and using
\(\ddot a\ll\omega_0\dot a\) gives
\[
2i m\omega_0\dot a=F e^{i\alpha t^2/2},
\qquad
\boxed{\dot a=-i\frac{F}{2m\omega_0}e^{i\alpha t^2/2}}.
\]
Thus, with remote-past rest,
\[
\boxed{a(t)=-i\frac{F}{2m\omega_0}
\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{i\alpha s^2/2}ds}.
\]
The coherent interval has width \(t_{\rm sp}\sim\alpha^{-1/2}\). Over it,
\(|\ddot a|/(\omega_0|\dot a|)\sim\sqrt\alpha/\omega_0\), and the discarded
counter-rotating integral has no stationary point and is smaller by the same
high-carrier ordering.

The full Fresnel integral yields
\[
a(+\infty)=-i\frac{F}{2m\omega_0}
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}}e^{i\pi/4}
=\frac{F}{2m\omega_0}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}}e^{-i\pi/4}.
\]
Therefore the deposited free oscillation is
\[
\boxed{x(t)\sim A_\infty\cos(\omega_0t-\pi/4)},\qquad
\boxed{A_\infty=\frac{F}{2m\omega_0}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}}}.
\]
Its energy is
\[
\boxed{E_\infty=\frac12m\omega_0^2A_\infty^2
=\frac{\pi F^2}{4m\alpha}}.
\]
At \(t=0\), evenness gives half the full integral, so
\(a(0)=a(\infty)/2\). The amplitude is \(A_\infty/2\), and the energy of
that instantaneous envelope state is \(E_\infty/4\).

For the data,
\[
\boxed{t_{\rm sp}=\alpha^{-1/2}=0.500000\ \mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{\sqrt\alpha/\omega_0=0.100000}.
\]
The numerical predictions are
\[
\boxed{A_\infty=0.0626657\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{E_\infty=1.17810\ \mathrm J},
\]
and at crossing
\[
\boxed{|a(0)|=0.0313329\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{E(0)=0.294524\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The inverse-\(\alpha\) energy growth does not permit setting \(\alpha=0\): an
exactly resonant undamped drive acts forever and produces secular growth, so
the slow-sweep limit is nonuniform. Instantaneous static response divides by
the vanishing detuning and misses the finite memory encoded by the Fresnel
integral. The factor \(F/(m\omega_0)\) has velocity units and
\(\alpha^{-1/2}\) has time units, giving a displacement as required.

graderFixtures.proofText: The slow envelope satisfies \(\dot a=-iF e^{i\alpha t^2/2}/(2m\omega_0)\). Fresnel evaluation gives \(A_\infty=F\sqrt{2\pi/\alpha}/(2m\omega_0)\), phase minus pi over four, and \(E_\infty=\pi F^2/(4m\alpha)\). Numerically these are 0.0626657 m and 1.17810 J, with one-half amplitude at resonance.
I insert the instantaneous chirped frequency into the static response, divide by zero at resonance, and call the resulting divergence an exact solution without a rotating-wave error estimate.

WAVE:010128.title: An oscillator loses energy into an infinite string
WAVE:010128.objective: Eliminate a semi-infinite string with an outgoing-wave condition and derive exact radiation damping, motion, and energy flux.
WAVE:010128.statement:
A mass \(m\) attached to a horizontal spring \(k\) moves transversely at the
end \(x=0\) of a taut semi-infinite string \(x>0\). The string has tension
\(T\), linear density \(\mu\), displacement \(y(x,t)\), and wave speed
\(c=\sqrt{T/\mu}\). The attachment is ideal, so \(y(0,t)=q(t)\), where q is
the mass displacement. No wave arrives from \(x=+\infty\).

Use the outgoing-wave condition to eliminate the complete string field and
show that the endpoint force is local and proportional to velocity. Derive
the exact reduced initial-value equation, identify the mechanical radiation
impedance, and solve the underdamped release \(q(0)=q_0,\dot q(0)=0\).
Derive the instantaneous string power flux directly from the wave energy
continuity equation and prove that it equals the loss of mass-spring energy.
Explain why energy conservation is not violated even though the reduced
oscillator equation is damped. State what changes if an incoming wave or a
finite reflecting string is allowed.

For \(m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(T=100\,\mathrm N\), \(\mu=0.0400\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and
\(q_0=50.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute c, radiation impedance, decay rate,
damped frequency, quality factor, initial energy, amplitude e-folding time,
and peak-energy e-folding time. Check the signs and units.
permittedResults: For \(\mu y_{tt}=Ty_{xx}\), energy density \((\mu y_t^2+Ty_x^2)/2\) and rightward flux \(-Ty_ty_x\) obey a local conservation law.
The underdamped equation \(\ddot q+2\gamma\dot q+\omega_0^2q=0\) has \(\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the d'Alembert solution with the no-incoming-wave boundary condition.
Derive the endpoint impedance in the frequency domain, then transform its constant real value back to time.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Eliminates the outgoing string exactly and reconciles the damped endpoint motion with conservative wave-energy transport.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses q of t plus x over c for an outgoing wave on the positive half-line and obtains an antidamping endpoint force.
commonErrors.consequence: The mass gains energy while the claimed wave also carries energy outward.

commonErrors.description: Calls the reduced damping an intrinsic loss and omits the equal string energy flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The conservative full-system energy balance is misrepresented.

hintTree.content: No incoming wave means \(y(x,t)=q(t-x/c)\), so evaluate \(y_x\) at the endpoint.
The string pulls the mass with \(Ty_x(0,t)\); check that this opposes positive endpoint velocity.
For the release from rest, the sine coefficient in the damped solution is \(\gamma/\omega_d\).

WAVE:010128.canonicalSolution:
The no-incoming-wave solution compatible with the endpoint is
\[
\boxed{y(x,t)=q(t-x/c)}.
\]
Therefore \(y_x(0,t)=-\dot q/c\), and the transverse string force on the mass
is
\[
F_s=Ty_x(0,t)=-\frac{T}{c}\dot q=-\sqrt{T\mu}\,\dot q.
\]
Define the real outgoing impedance
\[
\boxed{Z=T/c=\sqrt{T\mu}}.
\]
The exact reduced equation under the stated semi-infinite nondispersive model is
\[
\boxed{m\ddot q+Z\dot q+kq=0}.
\]
Let \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\), \(\gamma=Z/(2m)\), and
\(\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}\). For release from rest,
\[
\boxed{q(t)=q_0e^{-\gamma t}
\left(\cos\omega_dt+\frac{\gamma}{\omega_d}\sin\omega_dt\right)}.
\]

The string energy law follows by multiplying its wave equation by \(y_t\):
\[
\partial_t\left(\frac12\mu y_t^2+\frac12Ty_x^2\right)
+\partial_x(-Ty_ty_x)=0.
\]
For the outgoing field, the rightward endpoint flux is
\[
\boxed{P(0,t)=-Ty_t y_x=\frac{T}{c}\dot q^2=Z\dot q^2\ge0}.
\]
Meanwhile the mass-spring energy satisfies
\[
\frac d{dt}\left(\frac12m\dot q^2+\frac12kq^2\right)
=\dot q(m\ddot q+kq)=-Z\dot q^2=-P(0,t).
\]
Thus the full conservative oscillator-plus-string system merely exports
energy down the string. A finite string later returns reflected waves and
produces memory or delayed feedback; an incoming wave adds a driving term, so
neither case is represented by the homogeneous local damping law alone.

For the data,
\[
\boxed{c=50.0000\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{Z=2.00000\ \mathrm{kg/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\gamma=0.500000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_d=9.98749\ \mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
With \(Q=m\omega_0/Z=\omega_0/(2\gamma)\),
\[
\boxed{Q=10.0000},\qquad
\boxed{E(0)=\tfrac12kq_0^2=0.250000\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The amplitude envelope e-folds in
\(\boxed{\tau_A=1/\gamma=2.00000\ \mathrm s}\), while energy at equivalent
phase points scales as \(e^{-2\gamma t}\) and e-folds in
\(\boxed{\tau_E=1/(2\gamma)=1.00000\ \mathrm s}\). The impedance has units
N divided by m/s, namely kg/s, and positive flux corresponds to decreasing
oscillator energy, fixing the sign.

graderFixtures.proofText: Outgoing displacement is \(y=q(t-x/c)\), so the string contributes \(-Z\dot q\) with \(Z=\sqrt{T\mu}\). The reduced equation is damped but \(-dE_{osc}/dt=Z\dot q^2\) is exactly the outgoing string flux. The data give c 50 m/s, Z 2 kg/s, gamma 0.5 per s, omega d 9.98749 rad/s, and Q 10.
I choose q of t plus x over c as the outgoing field, obtain a force that amplifies the mass, and say the semi-infinite string destroys mechanical energy without carrying any flux.

WAVE:010129.title: A delayed feedback loop destabilizes an oscillator
WAVE:010129.objective: Derive every imaginary-axis crossing of a retarded oscillator and identify the first destabilizing delay from the characteristic root velocity.
WAVE:010129.statement:
A linear oscillator with delayed displacement feedback obeys
\[
\ddot x(t)+2\gamma\dot x(t)+\omega_0^2x(t)=Gx(t-\tau),
\qquad \gamma,\omega_0,G,\tau>0.
\]
Derive its characteristic equation. Put a root on the imaginary axis and
obtain separate real and imaginary Hopf conditions. Eliminate the delay to
find an algebraic equation for every possible crossing frequency. Then
recover all nonnegative delays with a quadrant-aware phase, rather than with
an unqualified inverse tangent.

Implicitly differentiate the characteristic equation and derive
\(d\lambda/d\tau\). Use its real part to determine the direction in which
each root pair crosses. Explain why merely finding a purely imaginary root
does not prove which side is stable, and why a delay equation has infinitely
many roots even though the no-delay equation is quadratic.

For \(\gamma=0.200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\omega_0=2.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), and \(G=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}\),
verify stability at \(\tau=0\). Compute both positive crossing frequencies,
the smallest positive delay belonging to each, and the sign of
\(\operatorname{Re}(d\lambda/d\tau)\). Identify the first loss of stability
as delay grows from zero. Give at least six significant digits and audit the
units.
permittedResults: For a simple root \(D(\lambda,\tau)=0\), implicit differentiation gives \(d\lambda/d\tau=-D_\tau/D_\lambda\).
A real retarded equation has conjugate characteristic roots, so a nonzero imaginary-axis crossing occurs as a pair.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the characteristic quasipolynomial and eliminate the trigonometric phase only after preserving its signs.
Track a simple characteristic root locally by implicit differentiation and combine that direction with no-delay stability.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Finds and classifies the delay-induced imaginary-axis crossings without treating a phase equation or one quadratic root as sufficient.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses a principal arctangent without reconstructing the sine and cosine quadrant, producing the wrong critical delay.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed first crossing is not a root of the characteristic equation.

commonErrors.description: Declares an imaginary root destabilizing without computing a root derivative or another justified stability argument.
commonErrors.consequence: A stabilizing crossing is indistinguishable from a destabilizing one.

hintTree.content: With \(\lambda=i\Omega\), expand \(e^{-i\Omega\tau}\) before separating real and imaginary parts.
Squaring and adding the two Hopf equations gives a quadratic equation in \(y=\Omega^2\).
Use \(\operatorname{atan2}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\) modulo \(2\pi\), then divide \(\theta+2\pi n\) by \(\Omega\).

WAVE:010129.canonicalSolution:
A trial \(x=e^{\lambda t}\) gives
\[
\boxed{D(\lambda,\tau)=\lambda^2+2\gamma\lambda+\omega_0^2
-Ge^{-\lambda\tau}=0}.
\]
At \(\lambda=i\Omega\), \(\Omega>0\), the two Hopf equations are
\[
\boxed{\omega_0^2-\Omega^2-G\cos(\Omega\tau)=0},\qquad
\boxed{2\gamma\Omega+G\sin(\Omega\tau)=0}.
\]
Consequently \(y=\Omega^2\) must satisfy
\[
\boxed{(\omega_0^2-y)^2+4\gamma^2y=G^2}.
\]
For each positive root, define
\[
c_\Omega=\frac{\omega_0^2-\Omega^2}{G},\qquad
s_\Omega=-\frac{2\gamma\Omega}{G},\qquad
\theta_\Omega=\operatorname{atan2}(s_\Omega,c_\Omega)\pmod{2\pi}.
\]
All nonnegative crossing delays are
\[
\boxed{\tau_n=\frac{\theta_\Omega+2\pi n}{\Omega}},\qquad n=0,1,\ldots .
\]

Since
\[
D_\tau=G\lambda e^{-\lambda\tau},\qquad
D_\lambda=2\lambda+2\gamma+G\tau e^{-\lambda\tau},
\]
the simple-root velocity is
\[
\boxed{\frac{d\lambda}{d\tau}
=-\frac{G\lambda e^{-\lambda\tau}}
{2\lambda+2\gamma+G\tau e^{-\lambda\tau}}}.
\]
The sign of its real part must be evaluated at the crossing; the imaginary
root conditions alone contain no stability direction.

For the data, the no-delay polynomial is
\(\lambda^2+0.400\lambda+3.00\), whose roots have negative real part. The
two roots of the frequency equation give
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\Omega\ (\mathrm{rad/s})&\theta\ (\mathrm{rad})&
\tau_0\ (\mathrm s)&\operatorname{Re}(d\lambda/d\tau)\ (\mathrm{s^{-2}})\\ \hline
1.82062906&5.46741805&3.00303789&-0.10029558\\
2.12727756&4.15930978&1.95522665&+0.15467364
\end{array}
\]
Thus the first event encountered from zero delay is
\[
\boxed{\tau_c=1.95522665\ \mathrm s,\qquad
\Omega_c=2.12727756\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\]
and its positive root velocity sends the pair into the unstable half-plane.
The later negative crossing cannot be used to infer the complete global
switching sequence without tracking the other infinitely many
quasipolynomial roots. The gain has units \(\mathrm{s^{-2}}\); hence every
term in \(D\) has units \(\mathrm{s^{-2}}\), and root velocity has units
\(\mathrm{s^{-2}}\).

graderFixtures.proofText: The Hopf equations are \(\omega_0^2-\Omega^2=G\cos\Omega\tau\) and \(2\gamma\Omega=-G\sin\Omega\tau\). Their two frequencies are 1.82062906 and 2.12727756 rad/s. Quadrant-aware phases give delays 3.00303789 and 1.95522665 s, with root-velocity real parts -0.10029558 and +0.15467364 s\(^{-2}\), respectively, so the latter is the first destabilization.
I square the Hopf equations, keep one frequency, use the principal arctangent for its phase, and call the resulting imaginary root unstable without checking a crossing direction.

WAVE:010130.title: Phase diffusion broadens a pure oscillator line
WAVE:010130.objective: Derive the autocorrelation, two-sided spectrum, linewidth, and coherence time of an oscillator with Wiener phase noise.
WAVE:010130.statement:
Let
\[
x(t)=A\cos[\omega_0t+\phi(t)],
\]
where the initial phase is uniform modulo \(2\pi\) and independent of the
increments. The phase increments are Gaussian with
\[
\phi(t+\tau)-\phi(t)\sim N(0,\,2D|\tau|),
\qquad D>0.
\]
Treat \(x\) as a wide-sense stationary real process. Starting from the
Gaussian characteristic function, derive the autocorrelation
\(R_x(\tau)=\mathbb E[x(t+\tau)x(t)]\). With the convention
\[
S_x(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}R_x(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\tau,
\qquad
R_x(0)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_x(\omega)\,d\omega,
\]
derive the complete two-sided power spectral density.

State the full width at half maximum of either isolated Lorentzian component
in angular frequency and ordinary frequency, the \(1/e\) coherence time, and
the corresponding line-quality factor. Verify the total spectral area.
Explain why Brownian phase itself is not stationary while the randomized
cosine can be wide-sense stationary, and do not silently replace a two-sided
real spectrum by a one-sided convention.

For \(A=10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(f_0=10.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), and
\(D=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), compute \(\omega_0\), coherence time, both
linewidth units, quality factor, \(R_x(0)\), and \(S_x(\omega_0)\), including
the small tail from the negative-frequency line. Audit PSD units.
permittedResults: If \(Y\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), then \(\mathbb E[e^{iY}]=e^{-\sigma^2/2}\).
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-D|\tau|}e^{-i\Omega\tau}\,d\tau=2D/(D^2+\Omega^2)\) for \(D>0\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Average the phase factors before applying the Wiener-Khinchin transform.
Represent the damped cosine as a sum of shifted exponential-correlation transforms.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the randomized oscillator's stationary second-order statistics while preserving the real-signal and Fourier normalization conventions.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the increment variance directly in the exponential and obtains an envelope such as exp(-2D times lag) or exp(-D lag over two).
commonErrors.consequence: The coherence time and linewidth are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Reports only the positive-frequency Lorentzian while claiming it is the complete two-sided PSD of a real cosine.
commonErrors.consequence: The spectrum is not even and fails the stated area convention.

hintTree.content: Product-to-sum leaves a phase-difference term; the uniform initial phase kills the phase-sum term.
Write the cosine in the autocorrelation as two exponentials before transforming.
The area of each shifted Lorentzian is \(\pi/D\) before multiplying by its numerator.

WAVE:010130.canonicalSolution:
The phase-difference characteristic function is
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{i(\phi(t+\tau)-\phi(t))}\right]
=e^{-D|\tau|}.
\]
The phase-sum term averages to zero because of the independent uniform
initial phase. Product-to-sum therefore gives
\[
\boxed{R_x(\tau)=\frac{A^2}{2}e^{-D|\tau|}\cos(\omega_0\tau)}.
\]
Transforming its two exponential components yields
\[
\boxed{S_x(\omega)=\frac{A^2D}{2}\left[
\frac1{(\omega-\omega_0)^2+D^2}
+\frac1{(\omega+\omega_0)^2+D^2}\right]}.
\]
This even, nonnegative spectrum is required for a real process.

Each separated component has half-width \(D\), so
\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega_{\rm FWHM}=2D},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta f_{\rm FWHM}=D/\pi},\qquad
\boxed{\tau_{\rm coh}=D^{-1}},\qquad
\boxed{Q=\omega_0/(2D)}.
\]
These linewidths describe an individual Lorentzian; overlap of the two tails
can slightly alter a half-height measured from the sum when
\(\omega_0/D\) is not large. Direct area integration gives
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int S_x\,d\omega=\frac{A^2}{2}=R_x(0).
\]

For the data,
\[
\omega_0=2\pi f_0=\boxed{62.8318531\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\tau_{\rm coh}=2.00000\ \mathrm s},
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega_{\rm FWHM}=1.00000\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta f_{\rm FWHM}=0.159154943\ \mathrm{Hz}},
\]
\[
\boxed{Q=62.8318531},\qquad
\boxed{R_x(0)=5.00000\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2}}.
\]
At the positive carrier,
\[
S_x(\omega_0)=\frac{A^2D}{2}
\left[\frac1{D^2}+\frac1{4\omega_0^2+D^2}\right]
=\boxed{1.00001583\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s}}.
\]
The Wiener phase has a variance tied to the choice of time origin and is not
stationary, but uniformizing the absolute phase removes that origin from the
second-order statistics of the cosine. Since angular frequency has units
\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), the two-sided PSD has units
\(\mathrm{m^2\,s}\), consistent with its area.

graderFixtures.proofText: Uniform absolute phase removes the sum term and Gaussian increments give \(R_x=A^2e^{-D|\tau|}\cos(\omega_0\tau)/2\). Its two-sided PSD is the sum of Lorentzians at plus and minus \(\omega_0\), each of FWHM \(2D\). The data give 2 s coherence, 0.159154943 Hz linewidth, \(Q=62.8318531\), and \(S_x(\omega_0)=1.00001583\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2s}\).
I use exp(-2D times lag), keep only a positive-frequency spectral peak, and integrate it without the one-over-two-pi convention.

WAVE:010131.title: A colored random force drives a finite oscillator variance
WAVE:010131.objective: Connect an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck force spectrum to oscillator response and independently recover the stationary displacement variance from moment equations.
WAVE:010131.statement:
A damped oscillator is driven by a stationary colored force:
\[
m\ddot x+m\Gamma\dot x+m\omega_0^2x=F(t),
\qquad
\dot F=-\frac{F}{\tau_c}+\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau_c}\,\xi(t),
\]
where \(\langle\xi(t)\xi(t')\rangle=\delta(t-t')\), and all parameters are
positive. Use the two-sided angular-frequency convention
\(S_y(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}C_y(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}d\tau\).

Derive the stationary force autocorrelation and spectrum. Find the complex
mechanical susceptibility and the displacement spectrum, including its
low- and high-frequency limits. Then derive \(\langle x^2\rangle\) without
performing a contour integral: write closed equations for the stationary
moments of the Markov state \((x,v,F)\), solve them, and show that the result
has the correct white-force limit as \(\tau_c\to0\) with \(D\) fixed.
Explain why substituting \(F_{\rm rms}^2\) for a flat spectral density would
lose a factor with units of time.

For \(m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\Gamma=0.800\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\omega_0=6.00\,\mathrm{{rad/s}}\), \(\tau_c=0.200\,\mathrm s\), and
\(D=0.0400\,\mathrm{N^2s}\), compute \(\langle F^2\rangle\),
\(S_F(0)\), \(S_x(0)\), \(S_x(\omega_0)\), \(\langle x^2\rangle\), and
the RMS displacement. State the units of every spectrum and variance.
permittedResults: A stable linear filter with transfer function \(\chi(\omega)\) maps an input spectrum to \(S_x(\omega)=|\chi(\omega)|^2S_F(\omega)\).
For a stationary It\^o diffusion, setting the time derivatives of all second moments to zero gives the continuous Lyapunov equations for its covariance.

acceptableStrategies.description: Filter the OU spectrum through the oscillator susceptibility and audit the asymptotic powers of frequency.
Solve the closed stationary covariance equations of the augmented Markov state and compare with the spectral route.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Keeps force variance, force spectral density, and filtered displacement variance dimensionally distinct while deriving the same stationary result from state moments.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses D over tau_c, which is a force variance, as a flat force spectrum.
commonErrors.consequence: The response has incorrect units and loses both the OU rolloff and the white-noise limit.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor omega_0 squared plus Gamma over tau_c plus one over tau_c squared from the stationary moment solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted variance does not solve the Lyapunov equations and diverges in the wrong correlation-time limit.

hintTree.content: The OU variance follows from \(d\langle F^2\rangle/dt=-2\langle F^2\rangle/\tau_c+2D/\tau_c^2\).
At stationarity, first show \(\langle xv\rangle=0\) and \(\langle vF\rangle=\langle xF\rangle/\tau_c\).
Use the \(vF\), \(v^2\), and \(xv\) balances in that order; no spectral integral is needed.

WAVE:010131.canonicalSolution:
The OU moment equation gives
\[
\boxed{\langle F^2\rangle=\frac D{\tau_c}},\qquad
C_F(\tau)=\frac D{\tau_c}e^{-|\tau|/\tau_c}.
\]
Fourier transformation therefore yields
\[
\boxed{S_F(\omega)=\frac{2D}{1+\omega^2\tau_c^2}}.
\]
With the \(e^{-i\omega t}\) phasor convention,
\[
\chi(\omega)=\frac1{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\Gamma\omega)},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{S_x(\omega)=\frac{2D}{m^2(1+\omega^2\tau_c^2)
[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\Gamma^2\omega^2]}}.
\]
Thus \(S_x(0)=2D/(m^2\omega_0^4)\), while
\(S_x\sim2D/(m^2\tau_c^2\omega^6)\) at high frequency. The extra
\(\omega^{-2}\) compared with white forcing comes from the OU rolloff.

Let \(v=\dot x\). Stationarity gives
\[
\langle xv\rangle=0,\qquad
\langle vF\rangle=\frac{\langle xF\rangle}{\tau_c}.
\]
The \(vF\) equation then gives
\[
\langle xF\rangle=
\frac{D/\tau_c}{m(\omega_0^2+\Gamma/\tau_c+1/\tau_c^2)}.
\]
The \(v^2\) and \(xv\) balances give
\(\langle v^2\rangle=\langle xF\rangle/(m\Gamma\tau_c)\) and
\(\langle v^2\rangle-\omega_0^2\langle x^2\rangle+
\langle xF\rangle/m=0\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=
\frac{D(1+\Gamma\tau_c)}
{m^2\Gamma\tau_c^2\omega_0^2
\bigl(\omega_0^2+\Gamma/\tau_c+1/\tau_c^2\bigr)}}.
\]
As \(\tau_c\to0\), this tends to
\(D/(m^2\Gamma\omega_0^2)\), the white-force result for
\(S_F\to2D\).

Numerically,
\[
\langle F^2\rangle=0.200000\ \mathrm{N^2},\quad
S_F(0)=0.0800000\ \mathrm{N^2s},
\]
\[
\boxed{S_x(0)=2.46913580\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2s}},\qquad
\boxed{S_x(\omega_0)=5.69216758\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=2.47863248\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{x_{\rm rms}=4.97858661\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m}.
\]
A variance has units of amplitude squared; a two-sided angular-frequency PSD
has those units times seconds. Replacing a PSD by \(F_{\rm rms}^2\) is
therefore dimensionally invalid.

graderFixtures.proofText: The OU force has \(S_F=2D/(1+\omega^2\tau_c^2)\), so \(S_x=|\chi|^2S_F\). Solving the \((x,v,F)\) moment equations gives the full multiplicative covariance denominator and \(\langle x^2\rangle=2.47863248\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
I set the force spectrum equal to D over tau_c at every frequency and omit the OU-state factor from the displacement covariance.
