WAVE:010132.title: A half-order memory element damps an oscillator
WAVE:010132.objective: Derive the causal harmonic response of a fractionally damped oscillator and use passivity, asymptotics, and absorbed power to audit the complex square-root branch.
WAVE:010132.statement:
A linear oscillator contains a hereditary damping element modeled by a
half derivative:
\[
m\left[\ddot x+\omega_0^2x+\gamma\,{}^{C}D_t^{1/2}x\right]
=F_0\cos(\omega t),
\qquad m,\omega_0,\gamma,F_0,\omega>0.
\]
Assume the drive has acted since the remote past, so all preparation
transients have died away. For the causal steady-state branch and the
\(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention, you may use
\[
{}^{C}D_t^{1/2}e^{-i\omega t}
=(-i\omega)^{1/2}e^{-i\omega t},
\qquad
(-i\omega)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2}}(1-i)
\quad(\omega>0).
\]
First audit the units of \(\gamma\). Derive the complex susceptibility
\(X=\chi(\omega)F_0\), its magnitude, and the displacement lag relative to
the force. Separate the dynamic stiffness into real and loss parts. Derive
the cycle-averaged input power and show directly that the declared causal
branch is passive. Explain what goes wrong if the opposite square-root
branch is inserted while every other convention is left unchanged.

Find the leading low- and high-frequency forms of the real and imaginary
parts of \(\chi\). Compare the high-frequency power law with ordinary
viscous damping without claiming that the fractional model is local in time.

For \(m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\gamma=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-3/2}}\), \(F_0=1.20\,\mathrm N\), and
\(\omega=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), compute both dynamic-stiffness components,
the complex susceptibility, response amplitude, phase lag, and average
absorbed power. Give at least six significant digits.
permittedResults: For real signals written as real parts of \(e^{-i\omega t}\) phasors, \(\langle \operatorname{Re}(Ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(Be^{-i\omega t})\rangle=\operatorname{Re}(AB^*)/2\).
A passive scalar susceptibility in the \(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention has \(\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)\ge0\) for positive frequency.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the steady harmonic eigenvalue of the causal half derivative and invert the resulting complex dynamic stiffness.
Use the average work per cycle to choose the physical square-root branch independently of algebraic manipulation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Keeps the fractional branch, phasor convention, dynamic-stiffness units, phase lag, and positive dissipated power mutually consistent.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses a square-root branch that makes the positive-frequency imaginary part of the susceptibility negative.
commonErrors.consequence: The nominal damping element delivers net energy under a steady drive.

commonErrors.description: Assigns gamma inverse-time units as if it multiplied a first derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The equation and every numerical dynamic-stiffness term are dimensionally inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Write \(m[A(\omega)-iB(\omega)]X=F_0\), with both \(A\) and \(B\) real.
The velocity phasor is \(-i\omega X\); average force times velocity before simplifying.
At high frequency, expand the reciprocal around \(-m\omega^2\) and retain the first imaginary correction.

WAVE:010132.canonicalSolution:
The half derivative has units \(x\,\mathrm{s^{-1/2}}\), so
\[
\boxed{[\gamma]=\mathrm{s^{-3/2}}}.
\]
For \(x(t)=\operatorname{Re}(Xe^{-i\omega t})\), define
\[
A(\omega)=\omega_0^2-\omega^2+\gamma\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2}},
\qquad
B(\omega)=\gamma\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2}}>0.
\]
The phasor equation is
\[
m[A(\omega)-iB(\omega)]X=F_0,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{\chi(\omega)=\frac{1}{m[A-iB]}
=\frac{A+iB}{m(A^2+B^2)}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{|\chi|=\frac1{m\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\phi=\operatorname{atan2}(B,A)}
\]
is the displacement lag: \(x=F_0|\chi|\cos(\omega t-\phi)\).
The real stiffness is \(mA\), while the positive loss stiffness is \(mB\).

The velocity phasor is \(-i\omega X\). Hence the mean input power is
\[
\overline P=\frac12\operatorname{Re}
\left[F_0(i\omega X^*)\right]
=\frac{\omega F_0^2}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi
=\boxed{\frac{\omega F_0^2B}{2m(A^2+B^2)}}>0.
\]
This is a direct passivity check. Choosing
\(( -i\omega)^{1/2}=-\sqrt{\omega/2}(1-i)\), or using the conjugate branch
without changing the Fourier convention, reverses the loss sign over part
or all of the positive-frequency axis and predicts negative absorbed power.
A branch is not an arbitrary algebraic sign once causality is declared.

As \(\omega\to0^+\),
\[
\operatorname{Re}\chi=\frac1{m\omega_0^2}+O(\sqrt\omega),
\qquad
\boxed{\operatorname{Im}\chi\sim
\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt2\,m\omega_0^4}\sqrt\omega}.
\]
As \(\omega\to\infty\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Re}\chi\sim-\frac1{m\omega^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\operatorname{Im}\chi\sim
\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt2\,m\omega^{7/2}}}.
\]
Ordinary viscous damping instead supplies an imaginary correction of order
\(\omega^{-3}\). The different exponent records hereditary rather than
instantaneous friction.

For the supplied frequency,
\[
\sqrt{\omega/2}=\sqrt2,\qquad
\boxed{A=11.8284271\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}},
\qquad
\boxed{B=2.82842712\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}}.
\]
The full force-per-displacement components are
\[
\boxed{mA=5.91421356\ \mathrm{N/m}},\qquad
\boxed{mB=1.41421356\ \mathrm{N/m}}.
\]
The susceptibility and response are
\[
\boxed{\chi=0.159939046+0.0382448089i\ \mathrm{m/N}},
\]
\[
\boxed{|X|=F_0|\chi|=0.197337669\ \mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{\phi=0.234713832\ \mathrm{rad}=13.4481^\circ}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{\overline P=0.110145050\ \mathrm W}.
\]
The real and loss stiffnesses have inverse-time-squared units before
multiplication by mass, \(\chi\) has displacement-per-force units, and the
power expression reduces to joules per second.

graderFixtures.proofText: The causal branch gives \(A=11.8284271\), \(B=2.82842712\) s\(^{-2}\), \(\chi=(A+iB)/[m(A^2+B^2)]\), amplitude 0.197337669 m, lag 0.234713832 rad, and positive mean power 0.110145050 W.
I give gamma viscous inverse-time units and choose the conjugate square-root branch, obtaining a negative imaginary susceptibility and negative absorbed power.

WAVE:010133.title: Noisy feedback cools an oscillator only up to a point
WAVE:010133.objective: Derive the closed-loop response and stationary temperature of a velocity-feedback oscillator, including the measurement noise fed back by the controller.
WAVE:010133.statement:
A mechanical mode of mass \(m\), natural angular frequency \(\omega_0\),
and intrinsic damping rate \(\Gamma_0\) is in a thermal bath at temperature
\(T\). A controller measures
\[
v_m(t)=\dot x(t)+v_n(t)
\]
and applies \(F_{\rm fb}=-m\Gamma_fv_m\), where \(\Gamma_f\ge0\). Use the
two-sided white-noise convention
\[
\langle F_T(t)F_T(t')\rangle=2m\Gamma_0k_BT\,\delta(t-t'),
\qquad
\langle v_n(t)v_n(t')\rangle=S_v\,\delta(t-t'),
\]
with independent noises.

Derive the closed-loop equation and susceptibility to an additional
deterministic force. Find the total force-noise intensity and solve the
stationary second-moment equations for \(\langle v^2\rangle\) and
\(\langle x^2\rangle\). Define \(T_{\rm eff}\) by
\(m\langle v^2\rangle=k_BT_{\rm eff}\). Show that feedback initially cools
the mode but measurement imprecision makes \(T_{\rm eff}\) rise at large
gain. Find the unique nonnegative gain minimizing it and check its units and
stability.

For \(m=0.100\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\omega_0=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\Gamma_0=0.200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(T=300\,\mathrm K\), and
\[
A_n\equiv\frac{mS_v}{2k_B}=1.50\,\mathrm{K\,s},
\]
compute the optimal feedback rate, total damping, minimum effective
temperature, cooling factor \(T/T_{\rm eff}\), and RMS displacement. Use the
exact SI value of \(k_B\).
permittedResults: For \(m\ddot x+m\Gamma\dot x+m\omega_0^2x=F\) with \(\langle F(t)F(t')\rangle=Q\delta(t-t')\), stationarity gives \(\langle v^2\rangle=Q/(2m^2\Gamma)\) and \(\langle x^2\rangle=\langle v^2\rangle/\omega_0^2\).
A differentiable function on \([0,\infty)\) that diverges at infinity and has one positive stationary point attains its unique minimum there.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the Lyapunov moment equations for the state pair x and v, then optimize the resulting effective temperature.
Integrate the closed-loop displacement spectrum and reduce the rational integral to the same stationary variance.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Keeps the deterministic feedback damping and gain-squared measurement-noise heating in the same closed-loop stochastic model.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds feedback damping but omits the measurement noise multiplied by the same controller gain.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted temperature decreases to zero at infinite gain and the requested optimum disappears.

commonErrors.description: Makes the fed-back force-noise intensity proportional to Gamma_f rather than Gamma_f squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The units, stationary covariance, and optimizing quadratic are all wrong.

hintTree.content: Move the noiseless velocity-feedback term to the left but keep \(-m\Gamma_fv_n\) on the force side.
Write \(T_{\rm eff}=(\Gamma_0T+A_n\Gamma_f^2)/(\Gamma_0+\Gamma_f)\) before differentiating.
The positive quadratic root is \(-\Gamma_0+\sqrt{\Gamma_0^2+\Gamma_0T/A_n}\).

WAVE:010133.canonicalSolution:
The controller force separates into damping and injected noise:
\[
m\ddot x+m(\Gamma_0+\Gamma_f)\dot x+m\omega_0^2x
=F_T-m\Gamma_fv_n+F_{\rm ext}.
\]
Thus, with the \(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention,
\[
\boxed{\chi_f(\omega)=
\frac{1}{m[\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i(\Gamma_0+\Gamma_f)\omega]}}.
\]
The two independent force noises add, so
\[
\boxed{Q=2m\Gamma_0k_BT+m^2\Gamma_f^2S_v}.
\]
The feedback-noise contribution is quadratic in gain; treating it as
gain-independent would erase the optimum.

Let \(\Gamma=\Gamma_0+\Gamma_f\). Multiplying the stochastic equation by
\(x\) and \(v=\dot x\), or using the stated moment theorem, gives
\[
\langle xv\rangle=0,\qquad
\langle v^2\rangle=\frac{Q}{2m^2\Gamma},\qquad
\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{Q}{2m^2\Gamma\omega_0^2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{T_{\rm eff}=
\frac{\Gamma_0T+A_n\Gamma_f^2}{\Gamma_0+\Gamma_f}},
\qquad
A_n=\frac{mS_v}{2k_B}.
\]
At zero gain this is \(T\). For large gain it behaves as
\(A_n\Gamma_f\), so arbitrarily strong feedback heats rather than cools.

Differentiation yields
\[
A_n\Gamma_f^2+2A_n\Gamma_0\Gamma_f-\Gamma_0T=0.
\]
Only one root is nonnegative:
\[
\boxed{\Gamma_{f,\rm opt}=
-\Gamma_0+\sqrt{\Gamma_0^2+\frac{\Gamma_0T}{A_n}}}.
\]
All coefficients on the left-hand side remain positive at this gain, so the
closed loop is asymptotically stable. Since \(T/A_n\) has units
\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), the square root has rate units.

For the supplied data,
\[
\boxed{\Gamma_{f,\rm opt}=6.12771681\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\Gamma_{\rm tot}=6.32771681\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{T_{\rm eff,min}=18.3831504\ \mathrm K},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{T}{T_{\rm eff,min}}=16.3192920}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{k_BT_{\rm eff}}{m\omega_0^2}
=6.34516956\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{m^2},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{x_{\rm rms}=2.51896200\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm m}.
\]
The white velocity-noise intensity has units \(\mathrm{m^2/s}\), making
\(A_n\) a kelvin-second and every term in the numerator of \(T_{\rm eff}\)
a kelvin per second.

WAVE:010134.title: Random kicks leave a non-Gaussian oscillator fingerprint
WAVE:010134.objective: Use a damped Green function and Poisson cumulants to distinguish impulsive shot forcing from Gaussian noise with the same power spectrum.
WAVE:010134.statement:
A stable underdamped oscillator is kicked at Poisson arrival times \(t_j\):
\[
m\ddot x+m\Gamma\dot x+m\omega_0^2x
=\sum_jJ_j\delta(t-t_j).
\]
The arrivals have rate \(\lambda\), and the independent impulse amplitudes
\(J_j\) are also independent of the arrival process. Work in the stationary
regime extending from the remote past. Derive the causal displacement
response to one unit impulse and express \(x(t)\) as a shot-noise sum.

For general kick moments, derive the mean, the continuous two-sided force
spectrum after removing any DC mean, and the displacement spectrum. State
and use the compound-Poisson cumulant rule
\[
\kappa_n[x(t)]=\lambda\langle J^n\rangle
\int_0^\infty h(s)^n\,ds.
\]
Evaluate the second and third equal-time cumulants explicitly. Explain why a
Gaussian white force with the same spectrum reproduces the variance but not
the third cumulant.

Take \(m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\Gamma=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(\lambda=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
and let \(J=2J_0\) with probability \(1/3\), while \(J=-J_0\) with
probability \(2/3\), where \(J_0=0.0200\,\mathrm{N\,s}\). Compute
\(\omega_d\), the kick moments through order three, displacement variance,
RMS displacement, third cumulant, standardized skewness, and \(S_x(0)\).
permittedResults: Campbell's theorem gives the nth cumulant of a marked Poisson shot sum as the arrival rate times the nth mark moment times the integral of the nth pulse shape.
\(\int_0^\infty e^{-at}\sin(bt)\,dt=b/(a^2+b^2)\) for \(a>0\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply Campbell's theorem directly to the marked Poisson response sum.
Derive the characteristic functional of the shot process and differentiate its logarithm to obtain cumulants.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the same causal response kernel consistently for spectral density, variance, and the genuinely non-Gaussian third cumulant.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the Poisson kicks by Gaussian white noise and then reports zero skewness as though it answered the stated model.
commonErrors.consequence: The principal non-Gaussian observable and kick-amplitude third moment are lost.

commonErrors.description: Assigns J force units rather than momentum units despite the time delta in the equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The force spectrum, displacement variance, and all reported SI units are inconsistent.

hintTree.content: For one force impulse, \(h(t)=\Theta(t)e^{-\Gamma t/2}\sin(\omega_dt)/(m\omega_d)\).
Use the white continuous spectrum \(S_F=\lambda\langle J^2\rangle\) when the kick mean is zero.
Expand \(\sin^3z=(3\sin z-\sin3z)/4\) before evaluating the third cumulant integral.

WAVE:010134.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\Gamma^2/4}.
\]
Integrating the equation across a unit force impulse makes the velocity jump
by \(1/m\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{h(t)=\Theta(t)\frac{e^{-\Gamma t/2}\sin(\omega_dt)}
{m\omega_d}},
\qquad
x(t)=\sum_{t_j<t}J_jh(t-t_j).
\]
The stationary mean is
\[
\langle x\rangle=\lambda\langle J\rangle\int_0^\infty h(s)ds
=\frac{\lambda\langle J\rangle}{m\omega_0^2}.
\]
After subtracting this mean, the continuous shot-force spectrum is white:
\[
\boxed{S_F(\omega)=\lambda\langle J^2\rangle},
\qquad
\boxed{S_x(\omega)=
\frac{\lambda\langle J^2\rangle}
{m^2[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\Gamma^2\omega^2]}}.
\]

Campbell's cumulant rule gives
\[
\kappa_2=\lambda\langle J^2\rangle\int_0^\infty h^2dt
=\boxed{\frac{\lambda\langle J^2\rangle}
{2m^2\Gamma\omega_0^2}}.
\]
For the third order set \(a=3\Gamma/2\). The sine-cube identity gives
\[
\int_0^\infty h^3dt
=\frac{3}{4m^3\omega_d^2}
\left[
\frac1{a^2+\omega_d^2}
-\frac1{a^2+9\omega_d^2}
\right],
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{\kappa_3=\lambda\langle J^3\rangle
\frac{3}{4m^3\omega_d^2}
\left[
\frac1{a^2+\omega_d^2}
-\frac1{a^2+9\omega_d^2}
\right]}.
\]
A Gaussian process is fixed by its first two cumulants and has
\(\kappa_3=0\). Matching \(S_F\) therefore cannot reproduce this asymmetric
one-point distribution.

For the stated kick law,
\[
\langle J\rangle=0,\qquad
\boxed{\langle J^2\rangle=2J_0^2=8.00000\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N^2s^2}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\langle J^3\rangle=2J_0^3
=1.60000\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N^3s^3}}.
\]
Also
\[
\boxed{\omega_d=4.97493719\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\kappa_2=2.56000\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{x_{\rm rms}=0.0160000\ \mathrm m}.
\]
The cubic response integral is
\(7.90123457\times10^{-3}\) in its corresponding SI units, giving
\[
\boxed{\kappa_3=5.05679012\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^3}},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\kappa_3}{\kappa_2^{3/2}}=0.123456790}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{S_x(0)=
\frac{\lambda\langle J^2\rangle}{m^2\omega_0^4}
=2.04800\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2s}}.
\]
The delta impulse makes \(J\) a momentum, not a force; this unit distinction
is required for every spectrum and cumulant above.

graderFixtures.proofText: The marked Poisson sum uses \(h=e^{-\Gamma t/2}\sin(\omega_dt)/(m\omega_d)\). Its spectrum is \(\lambda\langle J^2\rangle|\chi|^2\), while Campbell's cubic integral gives \(\kappa_3=5.05679012\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m^3}\) and skewness \(0.123456790\).
I replace the kick train by Gaussian white noise immediately, call J a force, and conclude that the stationary displacement must have zero third cumulant.

WAVE:010135.title: A structural loss factor describes a narrow band, not all frequencies
WAVE:010135.objective: Derive the response, cycle loss, and linewidth of a structurally damped oscillator while keeping the constant-loss-factor model inside its physical range of validity.
WAVE:010135.statement:
A single mechanical coordinate has mass \(m\), elastic stiffness \(k\), and a
small structural loss factor \(\eta>0\). In a narrow frequency band an engineer
models its harmonic constitutive law by the complex stiffness
\(k^\ast=k(1+i\eta)\). Use real fields with the \(e^{i\omega t}\) phasor
convention and a force \(F(t)=\operatorname{Re}(F_0e^{i\omega t})\), where
\(F_0>0\).

Derive the displacement phasor, amplitude, and phase. Obtain the average
input power and energy dissipated per cycle without treating \(i\eta kx\) as
an ordinary real time-domain force. Show that the loss factor gives
\(Q^{-1}=\eta\) when stored energy is based on the elastic spring. Locate the
amplitude maximum and the two conventional half-power (half-amplitude-squared)
frequencies exactly, and compare
their bandwidth with \(\eta\omega_0\), where \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\).

For \(m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=800\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\eta=0.0400\), and \(F_0=1.00\,\mathrm N\), calculate the resonant
amplitude, average resonant power, loss per cycle, stored energy, both
half-power angular frequencies, and the exact bandwidth. Finally explain why
a frequency-independent positive loss factor cannot be asserted from zero to
infinite frequency as a causal material law, even though it is useful in the
stated narrow band.
permittedResults: For phasors with \(e^{i\omega t}\), \(\langle Fv\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(F_0V^\ast)\).
A passive causal response has linked real and imaginary parts; a constant-sign imaginary stiffness at every signed frequency is not a complete causal constitutive law.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the displacement and velocity phasors, then evaluate complex power and the response denominator.
Use the force-displacement hysteresis ellipse for cycle loss and recover the same linewidth from the squared amplitude.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the complex stiffness consistently in harmonic response while explicitly refusing to promote the narrow-band loss model to an all-frequency causal time-domain law.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wrong phasor conjugation and obtains negative average power for a passive positive loss factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed damping injects energy and the cycle-loss and quality-factor conclusions fail.

commonErrors.description: Treats a constant positive imaginary stiffness as an exact causal material law at every frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Reality symmetry and the causal relation between storage and loss are ignored.

hintTree.content: Write \(X=F_0/[k-m\omega^2+i\eta k]\) and use \(V=i\omega X\).
At fixed \(F_0\), half resonant amplitude squared means \((k-m\omega^2)^2=(\eta k)^2\).
Compute cycle loss as average power times \(2\pi/\omega\), then compare it with \(2\pi\) times the maximum elastic energy.

WAVE:010135.canonicalSolution:
The phasor balance is
\[
[k-m\omega^2+i\eta k]X=F_0,\qquad
\boxed{X=\frac{F_0}{k-m\omega^2+i\eta k}}.
\]
Hence
\[
|X|=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+\eta^2k^2}},\qquad
\arg X=-\tan^{-1}_{2}(\eta k,k-m\omega^2).
\]
With \(V=i\omega X\), cycle averaging gives
\[
\boxed{\overline P=\frac{\omega F_0^2\eta k}
{2[(k-m\omega^2)^2+\eta^2k^2]}}.
\]
Equivalently, for displacement amplitude \(A=|X|\),
\[
\boxed{\Delta E=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\overline P
=\pi\eta kA^2}.
\]
The maximum elastic energy is \(E_s=kA^2/2\), so
\(\Delta E/(2\pi E_s)=\eta\), or \(\boxed{Q=1/\eta}\) under this
engineering definition.

The amplitude denominator is smallest at \(k-m\omega^2=0\); therefore the
peak remains at \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). The frequencies where the squared
amplitude is one half of its resonant value obey
\[
(k-m\omega_\pm^2)^2=\eta^2k^2,\qquad
\boxed{\omega_-=\omega_0\sqrt{1-\eta},\quad
\omega_+=\omega_0\sqrt{1+\eta}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\Delta\omega=\omega_0(\sqrt{1+\eta}-\sqrt{1-\eta})
=\eta\omega_0+O(\eta^3).
\]
These are conventionally called half-power points because the cycle loss at
fixed frequency is proportional to amplitude squared; the extra factor of
\(\omega\) in average power means literal average power is not exactly
halved at both frequencies for this frequency-domain structural-loss model.

Numerically, \(\omega_0=20.0000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). At resonance,
\[
\boxed{A_0=\frac{1}{0.04(800)}=0.0312500\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{\overline P_0=0.312500\ \mathrm W}.
\]
The period is \(2\pi/20\), giving
\[
\boxed{\Delta E_0=0.0981748\ \mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_s=0.390625\ \mathrm J},\qquad Q=25.0000.
\]
The exact half-amplitude-squared values are
\[
\boxed{\omega_-=19.5959179\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=20.3960781\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
and \(\boxed{\Delta\omega=0.8001602\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}\), close to
\(\eta\omega_0=0.8000000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

The factor \(i\eta k\) is a frequency-domain approximation, not a real
constant-coefficient force law. Extending the same positive imaginary part
to all signed frequencies violates the conjugate symmetry required of a real
impulse response and is incompatible with causal dispersion relations.
Thus the stiffness phase is \(\delta=\arctan\eta\), while
\(\eta=\tan\delta\) is the loss factor used throughout. Therefore the
calculated band response is useful, but an all-frequency
causality claim would not be.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(e^{i\omega t}\), \(X=F_0/(k-m\omega^2+i\eta k)\), \(\Delta E=\pi\eta k|X|^2\), and \(\omega_\pm=\omega_0\sqrt{1\pm\eta}\). Eta is the loss factor and the phase angle is \(\arctan\eta\); the constant factor is only a narrow-band engineering model.
I insert the imaginary stiffness as a real force, get negative dissipated power, and say the same constant loss factor is causal from zero to infinite frequency.

WAVE:010136.title: A growing auxiliary mode closes a damped oscillator Hamiltonian
WAVE:010136.objective: Derive the Bateman doubled oscillator and explain exactly how an antidamped auxiliary coordinate restores a time-independent Hamiltonian and zero total phase-volume divergence.
WAVE:010136.statement:
A physical coordinate \(x(t)\) is linearly damped. Bateman's doubled
description introduces an auxiliary coordinate \(y(t)\) and the
time-independent Lagrangian
\[
L=m\dot x\dot y+\frac{\gamma}{2}(x\dot y-\dot x y)-kxy,
\]
where \(m,k,\gamma>0\). Treat \(x\) and \(y\) as independent generalized
coordinates; the auxiliary variable is a mathematical partner, not a second
passive copy of the physical oscillator.

Derive both Euler--Lagrange equations, paying attention to which coordinate
variation produces which equation. Find the two canonical momenta, invert
for the velocities, and perform the Legendre transform. Express the
Hamiltonian in canonical variables and also in velocity variables. Prove
directly that it is conserved. Determine whether it is positive definite and
explain why conservation of this doubled quantity does not mean that the
mechanical energy of \(x\) is conserved.

Write each second-order equation as a planar first-order flow. Compute the
phase-volume divergence of the physical \((x,\dot x)\) subsystem, the
auxiliary \((y,\dot y)\) subsystem, and their four-dimensional product.
Reconcile contraction of the damped subsystem with Liouville preservation
of the complete canonical system.

In the underdamped regime solve both initial-value problems in closed form.
For \(m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\gamma=4.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}\),
\(k=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(x(0)=0.100\,\mathrm m\),
\(\dot x(0)=0\), \(y(0)=0.200\,\mathrm m\), and \(\dot y(0)=0\),
calculate the decay/growth rate, damped angular frequency, initial canonical
momenta, and conserved Hamiltonian. Evaluate \(x,y,\dot x,\dot y\), both
momenta, and the Hamiltonian again at \(t=0.500\,\mathrm s\). Finally state
why the growing auxiliary sector is not a microscopic model of an ordinary
passive heat bath.
permittedResults: An autonomous regular Lagrangian has a conserved Legendre energy \(H=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L\).
For a first-order flow \(\dot z=F(z)\), local phase-volume expansion is the divergence \(\nabla_z\mathbin{\cdot}F\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Vary the cross-coupled Lagrangian, perform the full Legendre transform, and then audit conservation in velocity variables.
Solve the damped and antidamped initial-value equations first, then reconstruct momenta, Hamiltonian, and compensating phase-volume divergences.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Shows that autonomous Hamiltonian closure of the damped equation is obtained only by an expanding auxiliary sector and keeps that formal conservation distinct from physical subsystem energy.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Gives the auxiliary coordinate the same damping sign as the physical coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: The Euler--Lagrange system, autonomous conservation law, and zero total divergence all fail.

commonErrors.description: Calls the bilinear Hamiltonian a positive physical energy or interprets the growing partner as an ordinary passive reservoir mode.
commonErrors.consequence: The indefinite signature and the formal scope of the doubled construction are erased.

hintTree.content: Variation with respect to y produces the damped equation for x; variation with respect to x produces the sign-reversed damping equation for y.
The momenta are \(p_x=m\dot y-\gamma y/2\) and \(p_y=m\dot x+\gamma x/2\).
Set \(\Gamma=\gamma/(2m)\) and \(\Omega=\sqrt{k/m-\Gamma^2}\); the two envelopes are \(e^{-\Gamma t}\) and \(e^{+\Gamma t}\).

WAVE:010136.canonicalSolution:
The y variation gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left(m\dot x+\frac\gamma2x\right)
-\left(-\frac\gamma2\dot x-kx\right)=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{m\ddot x+\gamma\dot x+kx=0}.
\]
The x variation similarly yields
\[
\boxed{m\ddot y-\gamma\dot y+ky=0}.
\]
Thus the partner has the time-reversed damping sign.

The canonical momenta are
\[
\boxed{p_x=m\dot y-\frac\gamma2y},\qquad
\boxed{p_y=m\dot x+\frac\gamma2x}.
\]
Hence
\[
\dot x=\frac{p_y-\gamma x/2}{m},\qquad
\dot y=\frac{p_x+\gamma y/2}{m}.
\]
The Legendre transform gives
\[
\boxed{H=\frac{p_xp_y}{m}
+\frac{\gamma}{2m}(yp_y-xp_x)
+\left(k-\frac{\gamma^2}{4m}\right)xy}.
\]
Substituting the velocities simplifies it to
\[
\boxed{H=m\dot x\dot y+kxy}.
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\dot H=m(\ddot x\dot y+\dot x\ddot y)
+k(\dot x y+x\dot y)=0
\]
after using both equations. This bilinear form is indefinite: for zero
velocities, choosing \(x=y\) or \(x=-y\) makes the potential term have
opposite signs and unbounded magnitude. It is therefore not the positive
mechanical energy of the x oscillator.

The physical flow is
\[
(\dot x,\dot v_x)=(v_x,-\gamma v_x/m-kx/m),
\]
whose divergence is \(\boxed{-\gamma/m}\). The auxiliary flow has
\[
(\dot y,\dot v_y)=(v_y,+\gamma v_y/m-ky/m)
\]
and divergence \(\boxed{+\gamma/m}\). Their four-dimensional divergence
is exactly zero. The contracting physical projection is balanced by
expansion of the auxiliary projection, so it does not contradict Liouville
preservation of the complete Hamiltonian flow.

Let
\[
\Gamma=\frac\gamma{2m},\qquad
\Omega=\sqrt{\frac km-\Gamma^2}.
\]
For \(k/m>\Gamma^2\), the initial-value solutions are
\[
\boxed{x(t)=e^{-\Gamma t}\left[
x_0\cos\Omega t+\frac{v_{x0}+\Gamma x_0}{\Omega}\sin\Omega t
\right]},
\]
\[
\boxed{y(t)=e^{+\Gamma t}\left[
y_0\cos\Omega t+\frac{v_{y0}-\Gamma y_0}{\Omega}\sin\Omega t
\right]}.
\]
They display reciprocal envelope rates but the same damped angular
frequency.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\Gamma=1.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=3.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
Initially,
\[
\boxed{p_x(0)=-0.400000\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{p_y(0)=0.200000\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{H(0)=m(0)(0)+k(0.1)(0.2)=0.400000\ \mathrm J}.
\]
At \(t=0.500\,\mathrm s\), direct evaluation gives
\[
\boxed{x=0.0244574712\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{y=-0.0863142277\ \mathrm m},
\]
\[
\boxed{\dot x=-0.201670431\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\dot y=-1.09639413\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{p_x=-2.02015981\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{p_y=-0.354425919\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}}.
\]
Both the velocity expression and the canonical expression reproduce
\[
\boxed{H(0.500\,\mathrm s)=0.400000\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The auxiliary exponential represents the degree of freedom required by this
autonomous mathematical embedding. A passive thermal environment instead
has many modes, fluctuations, and a positive total energy; the single
antidamped coordinate should not be promoted to that microscopic claim.

graderFixtures.proofText: Variation gives \(m\ddot x+\gamma\dot x+kx=0\) and \(m\ddot y-\gamma\dot y+ky=0\). The conserved but indefinite quantity is \(H=m\dot x\dot y+kxy\), while subsystem divergences \(-\gamma/m\) and \(+\gamma/m\) cancel.
I give x and y the same damping sign, set both canonical momenta equal to ordinary mechanical momenta, and call a positive sum of their mechanical energies the conserved passive-bath Hamiltonian.

WAVE:010137.title: Random resets bias an otherwise conservative oscillator
WAVE:010137.objective: Use renewal age statistics to derive the stationary sampled moments of a harmonic oscillator returned to one fixed state at Poisson times.
WAVE:010137.statement:
A mass $m$ evolves without damping according to
$\ddot x+\omega^2x=0$. At event times of an independent Poisson process of
rate $r>0$, an ideal controller instantaneously resets the complete state to
$x=A,\ \dot x=0$. Between events the motion is conservative. Assume the
resetting process has operated from the remote past, and observe the oscillator
at a time selected independently of the reset clock.

Derive the density of the age $\tau$, the elapsed time since the latest
reset. Use it to calculate
$\langle x\rangle,\langle\dot x\rangle,\langle x^2\rangle,
\langle\dot x^2\rangle$, and $\langle x\dot x\rangle$ exactly. Explain why
the stationary phase is not uniform. Determine the mean mechanical energy and
decide whether this particular complete-state reset changes it. Obtain the
limits $r/\omega\to0$ and $r/\omega\to\infty$, without replacing the
random age by its mean before averaging.

For $m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}$, $A=0.0400\,\mathrm m$,
$\omega=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $r=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, report all
five moments and the energy. State what fails if a reset changes only position
while retaining velocity. The external controller is ideal; make no thermal
equilibrium claim.
permittedResults: For a stationary Poisson process, $p_\tau(s)=re^{-rs}$ for $s\ge0$.
The exponential averages of $\cos(as)$ and $\sin(as)$ are $r^2/(r^2+a^2)$ and $ra/(r^2+a^2)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the age-conditioned state directly against the exponential density.
Use the exponential characteristic function and double-angle identities.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Conditions the harmonic trajectory on Poisson age and averages before making stationarity or energy claims.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Evaluates the oscillator only at the mean reset age instead of averaging its distribution.
commonErrors.consequence: Every stationary moment and limiting case is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims energy loss for the complete reset or treats a position-only reset as equivalent.
commonErrors.consequence: Controller work and the conditional trajectory are misidentified.

hintTree.content: Conditioned on age $\tau$, use $x=A\cos\omega\tau$ and $\dot x=-A\omega\sin\omega\tau$.
Reduce quadratic moments with double-angle identities before integration.
Evaluate $m(\dot x^2+\omega^2x^2)/2$ on each free arc.

WAVE:010137.canonicalSolution:
The memoryless stationary Poisson clock gives
$$
\boxed{p_\tau(s)=re^{-rs}H(s)}.
$$
After an age $s$, $x=A\cos\omega s$ and
$v=-A\omega\sin\omega s$. Laplace integration gives
$$
\boxed{\langle x\rangle=A\frac{r^2}{r^2+\omega^2}},\qquad
\boxed{\langle v\rangle=-A\frac{r\omega^2}{r^2+\omega^2}}.
$$
Double-angle identities similarly give
$$
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{A^2}{2}
\left(1+\frac{r^2}{r^2+4\omega^2}\right)},
$$
$$
\boxed{\langle v^2\rangle=\frac{A^2\omega^2}{2}
\left(1-\frac{r^2}{r^2+4\omega^2}\right)},\qquad
\boxed{\langle xv\rangle=-\frac{A^2r\omega^2}{r^2+4\omega^2}}.
$$
The nonzero means and covariance show that exponentially distributed ages
overweight phases just after reset. Substituting the mean age $1/r$ into a
cosine would not reproduce these renewal averages.

Every free arc has
$$
E=\frac m2(v^2+\omega^2x^2)=\frac12m\omega^2A^2.
$$
The pre-reset state and $(A,0)$ lie on the same energy ellipse, so this
special reset rearranges phase without changing energy:
$\boxed{\langle E\rangle=m\omega^2A^2/2}$. A position-only reset would retain
an unrelated velocity, generally change energy, and invalidate the one-age
conditional trajectory.

As $r/\omega\to0$, both means vanish,
$\langle x^2\rangle\to A^2/2$,
$\langle v^2\rangle\to A^2\omega^2/2$, and
$\langle xv\rangle\to0$. As $r/\omega\to\infty$, observations concentrate
at $(A,0)$.

Numerically,
$$
\boxed{\langle x\rangle=5.51724\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m},\quad
\boxed{\langle v\rangle=-6.89655\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=8.30769\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}},\quad
\boxed{\langle v^2\rangle=1.92308\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\langle xv\rangle=-7.69231\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\langle E\rangle=1.00000\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm J}.
$$
This stationary renewal experiment is neither damping nor thermalization.

graderFixtures.proofText: The age is exponential. Hence $\langle x\rangle=Ar^2/(r^2+\omega^2)$, $\langle v\rangle=-Ar\omega^2/(r^2+\omega^2)$, quadratic moments use $r^2+4\omega^2$, and $E=m\omega^2A^2/2$.
I substitute the mean age, call the phase uniform, and treat a position-only reset as the same energy-preserving operation.

WAVE:010138.title: Off-period samples make a regular oscillator look statistical
WAVE:010138.objective: Classify rational and irrational sampling of a harmonic oscillator and derive its exact empirical distribution and correlations.
WAVE:010138.statement:
An undamped oscillator follows
$x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$. An instrument records only
$x_n=x(nT_s)$, where its periodic clock does not perturb the motion. Let
$\theta=\omega T_s$ modulo $2\pi$.

Represent sampled phase as a circle rotation. If
$\theta/(2\pi)=p/q$ in lowest terms, prove the phase record has period
$q$ and explain how the coordinate record can show repeated values. If the
ratio is irrational, use equidistribution to derive the long-record density
of $x_n$, its mean, variance, and lag-$\ell$ empirical correlation.
Explain why the resulting histogram is not evidence of noise or
thermalization. Derive the family of continuous frequencies producing
identical samples and distinguish aliasing from irrational phase coverage.

For a rational example take $\phi=0$ and $T_s=\pi/(2\omega)$, and list
one sample period. For an irrational example use
$A=0.0600\,\mathrm m$, $\omega=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$T_s=\pi\sqrt2/40\,\mathrm s$. Calculate $\theta/(2\pi)$, limiting
root-mean-square displacement, and normalized lag-three correlation. State
which results are finite identities and which are infinite-record limits.
permittedResults: An irrational rotation $n\theta+\phi\pmod{2\pi}$ is equidistributed on the circle.
Uniform phase pushed through $x=A\cos\psi$ has density $1/[\pi\sqrt{A^2-x^2}]$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Analyze the unit-circle rotation and push its phase measure through cosine.
Use trigonometric sums and equidistribution to derive moments and correlations.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Separates rational periodicity, irrational equidistribution, and aliasing while deriving statistics from phase rather than noise.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assumes uniform phase produces uniform displacement.
commonErrors.consequence: Endpoint weighting and variance are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Treats irrational sampling as noise or says samples determine a unique continuous frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Deterministic coverage and exact aliases are confused.

hintTree.content: Write $z_{n+1}=e^{i\theta}z_n$, where $z_n=e^{i(\phi+n\theta)}$.
Replace irrational long-run averages by uniform phase integrals.
Use $2\cos u\cos(u+\ell\theta)=\cos\ell\theta+\cos(2u+\ell\theta)$.

WAVE:010138.canonicalSolution:
With $z_n=e^{i(\phi+n\theta)}$, the exact sample map is
$$
\boxed{z_{n+1}=e^{i\theta}z_n},\qquad x_n=A\operatorname{Re}z_n.
$$
If $\theta/(2\pi)=p/q$, with $\gcd(p,q)=1$, then
$z_{n+q}=z_n$, and no smaller positive power returns every phase. The
coordinate record can repeat values within that phase period because cosine
is not one-to-one, but the phase orbit has $q$ points.

For irrational ratio, equidistribution pushes uniform phase through cosine:
$$
\boxed{\rho(x)=\frac1{\pi\sqrt{A^2-x^2}}},\qquad -A<x<A.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{\overline x=0},\qquad
\boxed{\overline{x^2}=A^2/2},\qquad
\boxed{x_{\rm rms}=A/\sqrt2}.
$$
At integer lag $\ell$, the product identity gives
$$
\boxed{\overline{x_nx_{n+\ell}}=\frac{A^2}{2}\cos(\ell\theta)},\qquad
\boxed{C_\ell/C_0=\cos(\ell\theta)}.
$$
These deterministic infinite-record limits do not add physical noise.

At every sample time, the replacement
$$
\boxed{\omega'=\omega+\frac{2\pi k}{T_s}},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,
$$
leaves complex phases unchanged. Real cosines also allow reflected-frequency
aliases with a corresponding phase choice. Aliasing is this nonuniqueness;
it is separate from whether the phase orbit is rational or irrational.

For $T_s=\pi/(2\omega)$, $\theta=\pi/2$, so one exact coordinate period is
$$
\boxed{A,\ 0,\ -A,\ 0}.
$$
For the second clock,
$$
\theta=\frac{\pi\sqrt2}{5},\qquad
\boxed{\theta/(2\pi)=\sqrt2/10},
$$
which is irrational. Thus
$$
\boxed{x_{\rm rms}=0.0424264\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{C_3/C_0=\cos(3\pi\sqrt2/5)=-0.888898}.
$$
The four samples form a finite identity; the arcsine law and correlations are
limits as sample count tends to infinity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Irrational phase gives $\rho(x)=1/[\pi\sqrt{A^2-x^2}]$ and $C_\ell=(A^2/2)\cos(\ell\theta)$, while $\omega+2\pi k/T_s$ produces identical samples.
I call the record noisy, use a uniform density on [-A,A], and assert that its samples determine one unique angular frequency.

WAVE:010139.title: A stale feedback sample destabilizes a perfect oscillator
WAVE:010139.objective: Derive the exact zero-order-hold map of an oscillator driven by its last position sample and diagnose its discrete-time stability.
WAVE:010139.statement:
A unit-mass oscillator has natural angular frequency
$\omega_0$. At times $t_n=nh$, a digital controller measures $x_n=x(t_n)$.
During the entire next interval it holds the force at the stale value
$F(t)=-\kappa x_n$, so
$$
\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=-\kappa x_n,\qquad t_n\le t<t_{n+1}.
$$
The measurement and force update are instantaneous, and there is no viscous
damping. Define $y_n=v_n/\omega_0$, $\theta=\omega_0h$, and
$\alpha=\kappa/\omega_0^2>0$.

Solve one held-force interval exactly and construct the two-by-two map taking
$(x_n,y_n)$ to $(x_{n+1},y_{n+1})$. Calculate its trace and determinant.
Apply the complete Jury conditions to the characteristic polynomial rather
than importing the continuous-time intuition that negative position feedback
must stabilize. Prove what happens for $0<\theta<2\pi$ and identify the
exceptional sampling phases. Interpret the determinant as phase-area change
caused by the external sample-and-hold controller.

For $\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $h=0.160\,\mathrm s$, and
$\kappa=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, report the map, trace, determinant,
eigenvalue modulus, and amplitude multiplication after 100 samples when the
eigenvalues are complex. Do not replace the held force by the continuously
updated force $-\kappa x(t)$.
permittedResults: For $\lambda^2-T\lambda+D$, the strict Jury conditions are $1-T+D>0$, $1+T+D>0$, and $1-D>0$.
A two-dimensional linear map multiplies oriented phase area by its determinant.

acceptableStrategies.description: Propagate about the held-force equilibrium and analyze the resulting matrix.
Construct the exact state transition plus constant-input convolution, then apply Jury.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Builds the exact stale-sample map and uses its determinant and Jury inequalities to prove nontrivial positive-gain sampling is not Schur stable.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the measured sample by the continuously changing coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: The controller and its stability problem become a different system.

commonErrors.description: Sets the determinant to one or omits the failing Jury inequality.
commonErrors.consequence: The controller-induced phase-area growth and instability are missed.

hintTree.content: Shift to the interval equilibrium $x_{\rm eq}=-\alpha x_n$.
Differentiate the exact interval solution before setting $t-t_n=h$.
Inspect $1-D$ before doing any eigenvalue algebra.

WAVE:010139.canonicalSolution:
On one interval the forcing is a constant determined
by the initial sample. With $u=t-t_n$,
$$
x(u)=(1+\alpha)x_n\cos(\omega_0u)
+y_n\sin(\omega_0u)-\alpha x_n.
$$
Differentiation and evaluation at $u=h$ give the exact map
$$
\binom{x_{n+1}}{y_{n+1}}=
\boxed{M\binom{x_n}{y_n}},\qquad
M=\begin{pmatrix}
(1+\alpha)c-\alpha&s\\
-(1+\alpha)s&c
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $c=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sin\theta$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{T=\operatorname{tr}M=(2+\alpha)c-\alpha},\qquad
\boxed{D=\det M=1+\alpha(1-c)}.
$$
The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-T\lambda+D$. For positive
$\alpha$ and $0<\theta<2\pi$, except at the endpoint-equivalent phase
$\theta=2\pi$, one has $c<1$ and hence
$$
1-D=-\alpha(1-c)<0.
$$
Thus one necessary Jury inequality fails: the map is not Schur stable. This
is not a paradox. The force is based on an old coordinate, so the controller
can do net work. It is not the autonomous oscillator with stiffness
$\omega_0^2+\kappa$. At $\theta=2\pi j$, $M=I$ and sampling produces the
identity map; these marginal cases are not asymptotically stable. The result
$D>1$ also says that each nontrivial update expands phase area.

For the data, $\theta=0.800000$ and $\alpha=0.200000$. Thus
$$
\boxed{M=\begin{pmatrix}
0.636048&0.717356\\
-0.860827&0.696707
\end{pmatrix}},
$$
$$
\boxed{T=1.332755},\qquad \boxed{D=1.060659}.
$$
The discriminant is negative, so the conjugate eigenvalues each have modulus
$$
\boxed{|\lambda|=\sqrt D=1.029883}.
$$
Consequently their modal envelope is multiplied after 100 updates by
$$
\boxed{|\lambda|^{100}=19.0012\ \text{(approximately)}}.
$$
This multiplier describes the complex eigencoordinates; an arbitrary real
state also has a bounded phase-dependent prefactor. The exact instability
diagnosis comes from the sampled map, not from substituting $x(t)$ for $x_n$.

WAVE:010140.title: A sudden stiffness quench makes a stationary cloud breathe
WAVE:010140.objective: Propagate a thermal oscillator ensemble through an instantaneous frequency change and separate covariance breathing from thermalization.
WAVE:010140.statement:
For $t<0$, a classical oscillator of mass $m$ and
frequency $\omega_i$ is sampled from a canonical ensemble at temperature
$T$: $\langle x_0\rangle=\langle v_0\rangle=0$,
$\langle x_0^2\rangle=k_BT/(m\omega_i^2)$,
$\langle v_0^2\rangle=k_BT/m$, and $\langle x_0v_0\rangle=0$.
At $t=0$ its stiffness is changed instantaneously without changing $x_0$ or
$v_0$, giving a new frequency $\omega_f$. It then evolves in isolation.

Propagate the covariance matrix exactly. Find $\langle x^2(t)\rangle$,
$\langle v^2(t)\rangle$, and $\langle x(t)v(t)\rangle$. Determine the
constant mean post-quench energy and the mean and variance of the impulsive
work $W=E_f(0^+)-E_i(0^-)$. At a quarter of the new period, identify which
quadrature variance is squeezed relative to its initial value. Explain why
the breathing covariance is not a sequence of equilibrium states and why
Liouville area is preserved.

Use $m=0.250\,\mathrm{kg}$, $T=300\,\mathrm K$,
$\omega_i=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$\omega_f=40.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Report all results in units of $k_BT$
or normalized by the initial variances; no numerical value of Boltzmann's
constant is needed. Distinguish work done at the quench from heat.
permittedResults: A centered Gaussian propagated by a linear map $S$ has covariance $S\Sigma S^{\mathsf T}$.
For a centered Gaussian $x$, $\operatorname{var}(x^2)=2\langle x^2\rangle^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Propagate initial moments directly using the exact sine-cosine solution.
Use a symplectic covariance matrix and Gaussian quadratic-form moments.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Propagates the initial Gaussian covariance under the post-quench symplectic map and derives the work statistics from the unchanged quench coordinates.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the post-quench covariance by a new canonical covariance.
commonErrors.consequence: The deterministic covariance breathing and injected work disappear.

commonErrors.description: Labels the isolated parameter impulse as heat or changes phase coordinates during it.
commonErrors.consequence: The first-law accounting and work distribution are wrong.

hintTree.content: Use $x=x_0\cos\omega_ft+(v_0/\omega_f)\sin\omega_ft$.
The quench work depends only on $x_0^2$.
Check the covariance determinant rather than each diagonal entry for phase-area preservation.

WAVE:010140.canonicalSolution:
Write $c=\cos\omega_ft$ and $s=\sin\omega_ft$.
The post-quench trajectory is
$$
x=cx_0+\frac{s}{\omega_f}v_0,\qquad
v=-\omega_fsx_0+cv_0.
$$
Using the independent initial quadratures gives
$$
\boxed{\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{k_BT}{m}
\left(\frac{c^2}{\omega_i^2}+\frac{s^2}{\omega_f^2}\right)},
$$
$$
\boxed{\langle v^2\rangle=\frac{k_BT}{m}
\left(\frac{\omega_f^2}{\omega_i^2}s^2+c^2\right)},
$$
$$
\boxed{\langle xv\rangle=\frac{k_BT}{m}cs
\left(\frac1{\omega_f}-\frac{\omega_f}{\omega_i^2}\right)}.
$$
The new Hamiltonian is conserved after the switch. Its ensemble mean is
$$
\boxed{\langle E_f\rangle=\frac{k_BT}{2}
\left(1+\frac{\omega_f^2}{\omega_i^2}\right)}.
$$
During the instantaneous change,
$$
W=\frac m2(\omega_f^2-\omega_i^2)x_0^2.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\langle W\rangle=\frac{k_BT}{2}
\left(\frac{\omega_f^2}{\omega_i^2}-1\right)},
$$
and Gaussian fourth moments give
$$
\boxed{\operatorname{var}W=\frac{(k_BT)^2}{2}
\left(\frac{\omega_f^2}{\omega_i^2}-1\right)^2}.
$$
This is parameter work, not heat exchange.

At $t=\pi/(2\omega_f)$, the normalized variances are
$$
\frac{\langle x^2\rangle}{\langle x_0^2\rangle}
=\frac{\omega_i^2}{\omega_f^2},\qquad
\frac{\langle v^2\rangle}{\langle v_0^2\rangle}
=\frac{\omega_f^2}{\omega_i^2}.
$$
Thus a stiffening quench squeezes coordinate spread and expands velocity
spread. The symplectic trajectory matrix has determinant one, so
$\det\Sigma(t)=\det\Sigma(0)$ even though its entries breathe. A true
canonical covariance at the new frequency would be time independent and
would require an energy distribution set by a bath.

Here $\omega_f/\omega_i=2$. Hence
$$
\boxed{\langle E_f\rangle=2.50000\,k_BT},\qquad
\boxed{\langle W\rangle=1.50000\,k_BT},
$$
$$
\boxed{\operatorname{var}W=4.50000\,(k_BT)^2}.
$$
At the first quarter-period, $t=\pi/80=0.0392699\,\mathrm s$,
$\langle x^2\rangle$ is $0.250000$ of its initial value and
$\langle v^2\rangle$ is $4.00000$ times its initial value, while the
cross covariance is zero at that instant.

WAVE:010141.title: A relaxing spring gives an oscillator two different loss peaks
WAVE:010141.objective: Derive the complex stiffness of a standard linear solid and distinguish loss-modulus, loss-tangent, and oscillator-response landmarks.
WAVE:010141.statement:
A mass $m$ is attached to a standard linear solid whose
force $F$ and extension $x$ obey
$$
F+\tau\dot F=K_Rx+\tau K_U\dot x,
$$
where $K_U>K_R>0$ and $\tau>0$. Use the convention
$x(t)=\operatorname{Re}(Xe^{i\omega t})$ and define $F(t)$ similarly.

Locate both the maximum of $K''$ and the maximum of the loss tangent

frequencies. Then include the inertia of the mass: find the dynamic stiffness

For $K_R=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $K_U=400\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$\tau=0.0500\,\mathrm s$, and $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, report the two loss-peak

WAVE:010141.canonicalSolution:
Substitution of the harmonic amplitudes in the
constitutive law gives
$$
(1+iq)F=(K_R+iqK_U)X,
$$
where $q=\omega\tau$. Thus, with $\Delta K=K_U-K_R$,
$$
\boxed{K^*=K_R+\Delta K\frac{iq}{1+iq}},
$$
and rationalization yields
$$
\boxed{K'=K_R+\Delta K\frac{q^2}{1+q^2}},\qquad
\boxed{K''=\Delta K\frac{q}{1+q^2}}.
$$
For positive frequency $K''>0$, as passivity requires in this convention.
The derivative of $q/(1+q^2)$ vanishes at $q=1$, so
$$
\omega_{K''}=\frac1\tau,\qquad K''_{\max}=\frac{\Delta K}{2}.
$$
By contrast,
$$
\tan\delta=\frac{\Delta Kq}{K_R+K_Uq^2}.
$$
Its derivative vanishes at $q^2=K_R/K_U$, giving
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\tan\delta}=\frac1\tau\sqrt{\frac{K_R}{K_U}}},\qquad
\boxed{(\tan\delta)_{\max}=\frac{\Delta K}{2\sqrt{K_RK_U}}}.
$$
The two peaks agree only in a degenerate no-relaxation limit.

Including inertia, force balance gives
$$
\boxed{Z(\omega)=K^*(\omega)-m\omega^2},\qquad
\boxed{H(\omega)=\frac1{Z(\omega)}}.
$$
The equation $\operatorname{Re}Z=K'-m\omega^2=0$ marks a quadrature or
phase-crossover condition: there $H=1/(iK'')=-i/K''$. An amplitude maximum
instead minimizes $|Z|^2=(K'-m\omega^2)^2+(K'')^2$; because both moduli vary
with frequency, its derivative need not vanish at the phase crossover.

For the numerical values, $\Delta K=300\,\mathrm{N/m}$. The loss-modulus
peak is
$$
\boxed{\omega_{K''}=20.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad
K''_{\max}=150.000\,\mathrm{N/m}}.
$$
The loss-tangent peak has $q=1/2$ and hence
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\tan\delta}=10.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad
(\tan\delta)_{\max}=0.750000}.
$$
Writing $\omega=20q$ in $K'=m\omega^2$ reduces the nonzero solution to
$q^2=1/2$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\omega=14.1421\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
K''=141.421\,\mathrm{N/m},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{|H|=7.07107\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m/N}},\qquad
\boxed{\arg H=-\pi/2}.
$$

Finally, $K^*\to K_R$ as $q\to0$ and $K^*\to K_U$ as $q\to\infty$.
The cycle-average absorbed power is
$\tfrac12\omega K''|X|^2>0$. For a held step $x=x_0$, the differential
equation becomes $F+\tau\dot F=K_Rx_0$ after the impulse at application, so
$F$ relaxes from $K_Ux_0$ to $K_Rx_0$ with time constant $\tau$. These
limits connect the frequency-domain result to the material's time response.

WAVE:010142.title: Dry friction turns exponential decay into a finite stopping map
WAVE:010142.objective: Derive an exact turning-point recurrence for combined Coulomb and viscous damping and apply the correct static-friction stopping condition.
WAVE:010142.statement:
A mass obeys
$$
m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx+F_c\operatorname{sgn}(\dot x)=0
$$
while it is sliding, where $m,k,F_c>0$, $c\ge0$, and the system is
underdamped. At rest, the friction force may take any value with magnitude at
most $F_c$. The mass is released from rest at a positive turning point $A$.

Solve one negative-going half-cycle exactly. Define a decay factor and derive
the signed next turning position. From it, give both the magnitude recurrence
for a half-cycle that crosses the origin and the precise condition for another
crossing. Distinguish failure to cross from the final static-friction hold;
do not continue a kinetic-friction formula after sticking. Prove the
mechanical-energy balance during sliding and explain why a single exponential
envelope is inadequate.

For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$c=2.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $F_c=1.00\,\mathrm N$, and $A_0=0.100\,\mathrm m$,
calculate the damped frequency, half-cycle decay factor, crossing threshold,
successive turning positions, number of completed sliding half-cycles, and
stopping time. Verify that the final coordinate can be supported by static
friction.
permittedResults: For $\ddot z+2a\dot z+\omega_0^2z=0$ with $a<\omega_0$, $\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-a^2}$.
On a sliding segment, multiplying the equation by $\dot x$ gives the exact mechanical-energy rate.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve each constant-sign sliding segment about its shifted equilibrium.
Track turning magnitudes with an affine recurrence and test static admissibility after every segment.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Constructs the exact piecewise turning map, separates origin-crossing from continued-sliding thresholds, and applies static friction rather than extrapolating kinetic motion.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses only a viscous exponential envelope for the mixed-damping motion.
commonErrors.consequence: Finite stopping and the affine amplitude decrement disappear.

commonErrors.description: Continues the kinetic-friction solution after a rest point can be held statically.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted later oscillations are not solutions of the friction law.

hintTree.content: On the first half-cycle friction points right, so shift by $x_c=F_c/k$.
At $t=\pi/\omega_d$, the sine term vanishes and the velocity is again zero.
A new crossing requires more than merely landing outside $|x|\le x_c$.

WAVE:010142.canonicalSolution:
Set
$$
\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m},\qquad a=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad
\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-a^2},\qquad x_c=\frac{F_c}{k}.
$$
Immediately after release the velocity is negative, so kinetic friction points
in the positive direction. The equation is
$m\ddot x+c\dot x+k(x-x_c)=0$. With $x(0)=A$ and $\dot x(0)=0$,
$$
x(t)=x_c+(A-x_c)e^{-at}
\left[\cos(\omega_dt)+\frac{a}{\omega_d}\sin(\omega_dt)\right].
$$
The next zero of velocity occurs at $t_h=\pi/\omega_d$. Define
$$
r=e^{-a\pi/\omega_d}.
$$
The signed next turning coordinate is therefore
$$
\boxed{x_1=(1+r)x_c-rA}.
$$
The mass starts sliding only when $A>x_c$. This segment crosses the origin
exactly when
$$
\boxed{A>A_{\rm cross}=\left(1+\frac1r\right)x_c},
$$
because this is equivalent to $x_1<0$. For a segment that crosses, symmetry
gives the opposite-side turning magnitude map
$$
\boxed{A_{n+1}=rA_n-(1+r)x_c}
$$
with $A_{n+1}=|x_1|$. The landing point lies beyond the opposite static band
and therefore reverses into another sliding segment only if
$A_{n+1}>x_c$, which is the stronger condition
$$
\boxed{A_n>A_{\rm continue}=\left(1+\frac{2}{r}\right)x_c}.
$$
If $x_c<A\le A_{\rm cross}$, sliding begins but stops on the original side
before crossing. If $A_{\rm cross}<A\le A_{\rm continue}$, it crosses once
but lands inside the opposite static band. In either case the final turning
point satisfies $|x_1|\le x_c$. The physical static-friction force then
supplies $+kx_1$, balancing the spring force $-kx_1$, and the mass remains
there. A later segment crosses back only when its own starting
magnitude satisfies $A_{n+1}>A_{\rm cross}$. These separate tests prevent the
kinetic formula from being continued after sticking.

For $E=\tfrac12m\dot x^2+\tfrac12kx^2$, multiplication by $\dot x$ gives
$$
\boxed{\dot E=-c\dot x^2-F_c|\dot x|\le0}
$$
during sliding. Viscous loss is speed-dependent while Coulomb loss is
proportional to distance traveled. Their combination produces an affine
turning map, not a single exponential envelope.

Numerically,
$$
\omega_d=\sqrt{99}=9.94987\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\qquad
\boxed{r=0.729248},\qquad x_c=0.010000\,\mathrm m.
$$
The crossing and continuation thresholds are
$$
\boxed{A_{\rm cross}=(1+1/r)x_c=0.0237128\,\mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{(1+2/r)x_c=0.0374255\,\mathrm m}.
$$
Starting at $+0.100000\,\mathrm m$, the first two complete crossings give
$$
+0.100000\ \longrightarrow\ -0.0556323
\ \longrightarrow\ +0.0232772\ \mathrm m.
$$
The magnitude $0.0232772\,\mathrm m$ exceeds $x_c$, so a third sliding
segment starts, but it is below $A_{\rm cross}=0.0237128\,\mathrm m$ and
therefore does not reach the negative side. Its zero-velocity endpoint is
$$
\boxed{x_f=(1+r)x_c-r(0.0232772)=+0.000317608\,\mathrm m}.
$$
Thus three sliding half-cycle time intervals elapse, but only the first two
cross the origin. The stopping time is
$$
\boxed{t_s=3\pi/\omega_d=0.947226\,\mathrm s}.
$$
Finally $|kx_f|=0.0317608\,\mathrm N<F_c=1.00\,\mathrm N$, so static
friction can support the final coordinate.

WAVE:010143.title: A half-sine base shock can leave a resonator perfectly still
WAVE:010143.objective: Derive the exact residual vibration after a finite half-sine base-acceleration shock and identify its cancellation durations and removable resonant limit.
WAVE:010143.statement:
An undamped mass--spring oscillator has natural angular
frequency $\omega_0$. Its support displacement is $y(t)$ and the relative
coordinate is $q=x-y$. Initially the mass and support are at rest. During
$0<t<T$ the support acceleration is
$$
\ddot y(t)=a_0\sin(\Omega t),\qquad \Omega=\frac{\pi}{T},
$$
and it is zero afterwards. Treat the acceleration endpoints as ideal and use
the relative equation, rather than replacing the base motion by a force with
an unexplained sign.

Solve for $q(t)$ during the shock. Find $q(T)$ and $\dot q(T)$, then express
the free-vibration amplitude $R$ after the shock in terms of
$r=\omega_0T$. Locate every nontrivial duration that gives $R=0$. The
formula appears singular at $r=\pi$; evaluate that limit and explain why it
is not a cancellation. Give the residual mechanical energy for mass $m$ and
audit the impulsive and adiabatic limits.

For $m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\omega_0=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$a_0=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $T=0.400\,\mathrm s$, calculate $\Omega$,
$q(T)$, $\dot q(T)$, $R$, the static-deflection ratio
$R/(a_0/\omega_0^2)$, and the residual energy. State why damping during the
pulse or a discontinuous velocity input would require a different formula.
permittedResults: For free motion after $T$, $R^2=q(T)^2+[\dot q(T)/\omega_0]^2$.
A base acceleration enters the relative equation as $-\ddot y$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the forced relative equation and carry both endpoint coordinates into the free response.
Evaluate the acceleration convolution at the oscillator frequency and interpret its complex magnitude.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Propagates the complete endpoint state of the base-excited oscillator and distinguishes genuine residual cancellation from the removable resonant singularity.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+ddot y$ in the relative equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The endpoint state has the wrong physical phase and sign.

commonErrors.description: Calls $omega_0T=pi$ a cancellation by substituting only into the numerator.
commonErrors.consequence: A removable $0/0$ point is mistaken for zero vibration.

hintTree.content: Solve $\ddot q+\omega_0^2q=-a_0\sin(\Omega t)$ with zero initial data.
At $t=T$, use $\sin\Omega T=0$ and $\cos\Omega T=-1$.
Reduce $\sin^2r+(1+\cos r)^2$ before taking the limit $r\to\pi$.

WAVE:010143.canonicalSolution:
The absolute equation is
$m\ddot x+k(x-y)=0$. Since $q=x-y$ and $\omega_0^2=k/m$,
$$
\boxed{\ddot q+\omega_0^2q=-\ddot y}.
$$
For $0<t<T$ and $\Omega\ne\omega_0$, the zero-data solution is
$$
\boxed{q(t)=\frac{a_0}{\omega_0^2-\Omega^2}
\left[\frac{\Omega}{\omega_0}\sin(\omega_0t)-\sin(\Omega t)\right]}.
$$
This expression has both $q(0)=0$ and $\dot q(0)=0$; the minus sign on the
base acceleration is therefore fixed rather than guessed.

At the end of the pulse,
$$
q_T=\frac{a_0\Omega}{\omega_0(\omega_0^2-\Omega^2)}\sin r,
\qquad
v_T=\frac{a_0\Omega}{\omega_0^2-\Omega^2}(1+\cos r),
$$
where $r=\omega_0T$. Hence
$$
R=\sqrt{q_T^2+(v_T/\omega_0)^2}
=\frac{2a_0\Omega}{\omega_0|\omega_0^2-\Omega^2|}
\left|\cos\frac r2\right|.
$$
Using $\Omega=\pi\omega_0/r$ gives the shock-response spectrum
$$
\boxed{\frac{R}{a_0/\omega_0^2}=
\frac{2\pi r|\cos(r/2)|}{|r^2-\pi^2|}}.
$$
Its zeros occur at $r=(2n+1)\pi$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$, namely
$T=(2n+1)\pi/\omega_0$. The apparent first zero $r=\pi$ is also where the
denominator vanishes. Expanding about $r=\pi$ or applying l'Hopital gives
$$
\boxed{\lim_{r\to\pi}\frac{R}{a_0/\omega_0^2}=\frac\pi2},
$$
so a pulse resonant with the oscillator leaves a finite, nonzero response.
The post-pulse energy is
$$
\boxed{E_R=\frac12m\omega_0^2R^2}.
$$

Numerically, $\Omega=\pi/T=7.85398\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $r=4.00000$.
Direct substitution gives
$$
\boxed{q_T=-3.10266\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{v_T=1.41995\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{R=3.41215\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{R/(a_0/\omega_0^2)=1.70607},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{E_R=2.91069\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J}.
$$
For $r\to0$, the short pulse has vanishing impulse because its duration
shrinks at fixed $a_0$, and the response ratio is asymptotic to $2r/\pi$.
For $r\to\infty$, the support acceleration is slow and the ratio decays as
$O(1/r)$ apart from its cancellation zeros. Damping would change both the
Green function and phase-plane norm. A support-velocity jump would add an
impulsive term and a jump in the relative velocity, neither of which is in
the stated smooth half-sine acceleration model.

=\frac{2a_0\Omega}{\omega_0|\omega_0^2-\Omega^2|}
\left|\cos\frac r2\right|.
$$
Using $\Omega=\pi\omega_0/r$ gives the shock-response spectrum
$$
\boxed{\frac{R}{a_0/\omega_0^2}=
\frac{2\pi r|\cos(r/2)|}{|r^2-\pi^2|}}.
$$
Its zeros occur at $r=(2n+1)\pi$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$, namely
$T=(2n+1)\pi/\omega_0$. The apparent first zero $r=\pi$ is also where the
denominator vanishes. Expanding about $r=\pi$ or applying l'Hopital gives
$$
\boxed{\lim_{r\to\pi}\frac{R}{a_0/\omega_0^2}=\frac\pi2},
$$
so a pulse resonant with the oscillator leaves a finite, nonzero response.
The post-pulse energy is
$$
\boxed{E_R=\frac12m\omega_0^2R^2}.
$$

Numerically, $\Omega=\pi/T=7.85398\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $r=4.00000$.
Direct substitution gives
$$
\boxed{q_T=-3.10266\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{v_T=1.41995\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{R=3.41215\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{R/(a_0/\omega_0^2)=1.70607},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{E_R=2.91069\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J}.
$$
For $r\to0$, the short pulse has vanishing impulse because its duration
shrinks at fixed $a_0$, and the response ratio is asymptotic to $2r/\pi$.
For $r\to\infty$, the support acceleration is slow and the ratio decays as
$O(1/r)$ apart from its cancellation zeros. Damping would change both the
Green function and phase-plane norm. A support-velocity jump would add an
impulsive term and a jump in the relative velocity, neither of which is in
the stated smooth half-sine acceleration model.
I use $ddot q+omega_0^2q=+ddot y$ and set every odd multiple, including $omega_0T=pi$, equal to zero without taking the removable limit or carrying the endpoint velocity.

WAVE:010144.title: The best energy-harvesting damper is not always the internal damper
WAVE:010144.objective: Optimize power delivered to a tunable viscous load on a driven oscillator and reconcile the optimum with the full steady-state power balance.
WAVE:010144.statement:
A mass is driven by $F(t)=F_0\cos\omega t$ and obeys
$$
m\ddot x+(c_0+c_h)\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t,
$$
where $c_0>0$ is unavoidable internal damping and $c_h\ge0$ is a tunable
energy-harvesting load. In the steady state use
$x(t)=\operatorname{Re}(Xe^{i\omega t})$ and state the displacement phase
relative to the force.

Derive the average power $P_h$ absorbed by the load. At a fixed drive
frequency, optimize $P_h$ over $c_h$ without assuming resonance. Show how
the optimum reduces on resonance, find the resonant maximum, and explain why
the condition is an impedance-magnitude balance rather than simply
$c_h=c_0$ off resonance. Prove the average input-power ledger and audit the
limits $c_h\to0$ and $c_h\to\infty$.

For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$c_0=2.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $F_0=10.0\,\mathrm N$, and
$\omega=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, calculate the optimum $c_h$, response
amplitude, phase lag, harvested power, internal dissipation, and input power.
State why this linear optimum does not include stroke limits, force limits,
rectifier losses, or changes of the mechanical coefficients with amplitude.
permittedResults: For $v(t)=\operatorname{Re}(Ve^{i\omega t})$, $\langle c v^2\rangle=c|V|^2/2$.
The maximum of $u/(a^2+(b+u)^2)$ for $u\ge0$ occurs at $u=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate harvested power after reducing the response to one dynamic-stiffness magnitude.
Use mechanical impedance and maximum-power geometry, then verify by direct differentiation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Optimizes the passive load against both resistive and reactive mechanical impedance and verifies the optimum with a complete cycle-average power balance.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets $c_h=c_0$ at every drive frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Reactive detuning is omitted and the off-resonance optimum is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Equates input power to harvested power while ignoring internal damping.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed steady state violates energy conservation.

hintTree.content: Write the dynamic stiffness as $\Delta+i\omega(c_0+c_h)$.
Divide the squared detuning by $\omega^2$ before differentiating with respect to $c_h$.
Input power equals total viscous loss, not the harvesting term alone.

WAVE:010144.canonicalSolution:
The complex amplitude is
$$
X=\frac{F_0}{\Delta+i\omega(c_0+c_h)},\qquad
\Delta=k-m\omega^2.
$$
Thus
$$
|X|=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{\Delta^2+\omega^2(c_0+c_h)^2}},
$$
and the displacement lags the force by
$$
\phi=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\omega(c_0+c_h),\Delta\right).
$$
The average harvested power is
$$
\boxed{P_h=\frac12c_h\omega^2|X|^2
=\frac{F_0^2}{2}\frac{c_h}{(\Delta/\omega)^2+(c_0+c_h)^2}}.
$$
Set $a=|\Delta|/\omega$. Differentiation gives a numerator proportional to
$a^2+c_0^2-c_h^2$, so the unique positive optimum is
$$
\boxed{c_h^*=\sqrt{c_0^2+\left(\frac{k-m\omega^2}{\omega}\right)^2}}.
$$
Off resonance the load must balance the magnitude of the pre-existing
mechanical impedance: both internal resistance and reactive detuning matter.
At resonance $\Delta=0$, this reduces to $c_h^*=c_0$, with
$$
\boxed{P_{h,\mathrm{res}}^{\max}=\frac{F_0^2}{8c_0}}.
$$

The mean input power is
$$
P_{\rm in}=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(F_0V^*)
=\frac12F_0\omega|X|\sin\phi.
$$
Using the phasor equation shows
$$
\boxed{P_{\rm in}=\frac12(c_0+c_h)\omega^2|X|^2
=P_0+P_h},
$$
where $P_0=c_0\omega^2|X|^2/2$. The spring and mass exchange energy but
have zero cycle-average power. Both $c_h\to0$ and $c_h\to\infty$ give
$P_h\to0$: the first removes the load, while the second immobilizes the
response faster than it increases the damping coefficient.

For the stated values, $\Delta=36.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and
$|\Delta|/\omega=4.50\,\mathrm{kg/s}$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{c_h^*=4.92443\,\mathrm{kg/s}}.
$$
At this load,
$$
\boxed{|X|=0.151365\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{\phi=0.994510\,\mathrm{rad}=56.9812^\circ}.
$$
The three powers are
$$
\boxed{P_h=3.61041\,\mathrm W},\qquad
\boxed{P_0=1.46632\,\mathrm W},\qquad
\boxed{P_{\rm in}=5.07673\,\mathrm W},
$$
which independently close the power ledger. This is a steady linear optimum
at one prescribed frequency. A real harvester can be limited by displacement,
force, nonlinear stiffness, electrical conversion, or a frequency-dependent
load, and any of those changes the optimization problem.

WAVE:010145.title: A dying force leaves an undamped oscillator ringing forever
WAVE:010145.objective: Solve a causal exponentially decaying drive exactly, isolate its surviving free oscillation, and reconcile its energy with impulse and slow-decay limits.
WAVE:010145.statement:
An undamped oscillator is at rest before $t=0$ and obeys
$$
m\ddot x+m\omega_0^2x=F_0e^{-t/\tau},\qquad t\ge0,
$$
with $F_0>0$ and $\tau>0$. The force is switched on abruptly at $t=0$ and
then decays; it is not a force pulse with a finite shutoff time.

Derive $x(t)$ with both initial conditions enforced. Separate the part that
vanishes as $t\to\infty$ from the surviving sinusoid, and give the latter's
amplitude and phase. Find the asymptotic mechanical energy and explain why it
equals the total work delivered by the force even though the oscillator has
no damping. Audit the limits $\tau\to0$ and $\tau\to\infty$, including the
impulse interpretation of the first and the noncommuting long-time issue in
the second.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$F_0=10.0\,\mathrm N$, and $\tau=0.200\,\mathrm s$, calculate the decay
rate, the coefficient of the transient, the surviving amplitude and phase,
and the asymptotic energy. Also calculate $x$ and $\dot x$ at
$t=0.400\,\mathrm s$. State what would change if viscous damping were
present or if the turn-on were smoothed over a specified rise time.
permittedResults: For an undamped oscillator, $d[m\dot x^2/2+m\omega_0^2x^2/2]/dt=F(t)\dot x$.
A short force history with impulse $J$ produces velocity jump $J/m$ when displacement changes negligibly during the impulse.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use an exponential particular solution and enforce both initial data.
Evaluate the causal convolution and read the late-time sine and cosine transform components of the force.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Separates the decaying particular motion from the complete surviving phase-plane state and derives its energy without treating the forcing transient as dissipation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only $C(e^{-at}-\cos\omega_0t)$ and therefore violates $\dot x(0)=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The late-time amplitude, phase, and energy are all incomplete.

commonErrors.description: Claims the $\tau\to\infty$ response vanishes by adiabatic following while retaining the abrupt force jump at $t=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonzero excitation caused by the turn-on is discarded.

hintTree.content: Put $a=1/\tau$ and try a particular solution proportional to $e^{-at}$.
Use both zero-data conditions to determine the cosine and sine coefficients.
Write $-\cos\omega_0t+(a/\omega_0)\sin\omega_0t$ as one shifted sine.

WAVE:010145.canonicalSolution:
Write $a=1/\tau$ and $f_0=F_0/m$. A particular
solution is $Ce^{-at}$ with
$$
C=\frac{f_0}{\omega_0^2+a^2}.
$$
Adding the homogeneous motion and imposing $x(0)=\dot x(0)=0$ gives
$$
\boxed{x(t)=C\left[e^{-at}-\cos(\omega_0t)
+\frac{a}{\omega_0}\sin(\omega_0t)\right]}.
$$
Direct differentiation verifies both initial data; omitting the sine term
would violate the initial velocity.

The first term vanishes. Define
$\alpha=\tan^{-1}(\omega_0/a)$, with $0<\alpha<\pi/2$. The surviving part is
$$
x_{\rm free}(t)=A_\infty\sin(\omega_0t-\alpha),
\qquad
\boxed{A_\infty=\frac{F_0}{m\omega_0
\sqrt{\omega_0^2+a^2}}}.
$$
Indeed $-C=-A_\infty\sin\alpha$ and
$Ca/\omega_0=A_\infty\cos\alpha$. Its mechanical energy is
$$
\boxed{E_\infty=\frac12m\omega_0^2A_\infty^2
=\frac{F_0^2}{2m(\omega_0^2+a^2)}}.
$$
The exact energy identity $\dot E=F\dot x$, integrated from zero to infinity,
shows that this is also $\int_0^\infty F\dot x\,dt$. No energy is dissipated:
the transient force does work and the resulting energy remains in the free
mode after the force has become negligible.

As $\tau\to0$, $a\to\infty$ and
$A_\infty\sim F_0\tau/(m\omega_0)$. This is precisely the amplitude from the
small impulse $J=\int_0^\infty Fdt=F_0\tau$. As $\tau\to\infty$ after taking
the long-time limit, $A_\infty\to F_0/(m\omega_0^2)$ and
$E_\infty\to F_0^2/(2m\omega_0^2)$. This is not adiabatic turn-on: the force
still jumps from zero to $F_0$ at $t=0$. Taking $\tau\to\infty$ first instead
produces a permanent step force, so the phrase “after the force dies” then
has no finite-time meaning.

Numerically $a=5.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and
$C=0.100000\,\mathrm m$. Thus
$$
\boxed{A_\infty=0.141421\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\pi/4=0.785398\,\mathrm{rad}},
$$
and $\boxed{E_\infty=0.500000\,\mathrm J}$. At $t=0.400\,\mathrm s$,
$$
\boxed{x=0.146078\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{\dot x=0.178908\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
Viscous damping would make the final sinusoid decay and would add dissipated
heat to the work ledger. A specified smooth rise would alter the high-frequency
content and hence the residual amplitude; it cannot be inferred from the
abrupt-turn-on solution without supplying that rise history.

I use $x=C(e^{-at}-\cos\omega_0t)$, which has $\dot x(0)=-aC$ rather than zero, and I then call the large-$\tau$ limit adiabatic despite leaving the instantaneous jump from zero to $F_0$ in place.
