WAVE:010225.title: A magnetic field splits a planar oscillator into circular modes
WAVE:010225.objective: Diagonalize a velocity-coupled isotropic oscillator in circular coordinates and reconstruct its real initial-value motion without assigning work to the magnetic force.
WAVE:010225.statement:
A particle of mass \(m\) and positive charge \(q\) moves in the xy plane in
an isotropic harmonic trap of stiffness \(k\). A uniform magnetic field
\(B\hat z\) is present. Use the sign convention
\[
m\ddot x+kx=qB\dot y,\qquad
m\ddot y+ky=-qB\dot x.
\]
Define \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\omega_c=qB/m>0\).

Combine the equations using \(z=x+iy\). Derive the two positive circular-mode
frequencies and prove their product is \(\omega_0^2\) while their difference is
\(\omega_c\). Determine which complex exponential rotates in each direction.
For initial data \(x(0)=A\), \(y(0)=0\), and zero velocity, find the exact
coefficients of both circular modes and write real formulas for x and y.
Identify the relative-phase recurrence time. Prove directly that the Lorentz
force does no work and that the ordinary kinetic-plus-trap energy is conserved.
Explain why treating the coupling as an added spring gives an incorrect
spectrum.

For \(m=0.200\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\omega_c=6.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and \(A=40.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute
both frequencies, both circular amplitudes, the first relative-phase
recurrence time, and the conserved energy. Verify the zero-field limit and
the strong-field asymptotics.
permittedResults: The magnetic power is \(q(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf v=0\).
The roots of \(\omega^2\mp\omega_c\omega-\omega_0^2=0\) can be organized as two positive frequencies about \(\sqrt{\omega_0^2+\omega_c^2/4}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the complex planar coordinate to diagonalize handed rotations.
Insert circular polarization vectors into the real matrix equation, then solve the initial modal coefficients.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and reconstructs the circular modes while preserving the exact magnetic no-work energy law.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the velocity-dependent Lorentz terms by an added coordinate stiffness.
commonErrors.consequence: The circular handedness, frequency product, and energy interpretation are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Assigns equal circular amplitudes when the split frequencies differ.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed solution has nonzero initial velocity.

hintTree.content: Show that z obeys \(\ddot z+i\omega_c\dot z+\omega_0^2z=0\).
Use \(z=C_+e^{-i\omega_+t}+C_-e^{+i\omega_-t}\) and solve the two linear equations at t=0.
Relative phase repeats when \((\omega_++\omega_-)t\) is \(2\pi\), not when the frequency difference alone completes a cycle.

WAVE:010225.canonicalSolution:
With \(z=x+iy\), the two real equations combine to
\[
\boxed{\ddot z+i\omega_c\dot z+\omega_0^2z=0}.
\]
Let
\[
\Omega=\sqrt{\omega_0^2+\frac{\omega_c^2}{4}}.
\]
Substitution of the two rotation senses gives
\[
\boxed{\omega_+=\Omega+\frac{\omega_c}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_-=\Omega-\frac{\omega_c}{2}}.
\]
Both are positive. They satisfy
\[
\omega_+-\omega_-=\omega_c,\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+\omega_-=\omega_0^2}.
\]
The general complex motion can be written
\[
z(t)=C_+e^{-i\omega_+t}+C_-e^{+i\omega_-t}.
\]
The first term rotates clockwise in the complex plane and the second
counterclockwise for the adopted axes.

The initial conditions require
\[
C_++C_-=A,\qquad -\omega_+C_++\omega_-C_-=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{C_+=\frac{A\omega_-}{\omega_++\omega_-}},\qquad
\boxed{C_-=\frac{A\omega_+}{\omega_++\omega_-}}.
\]
They are real for the chosen initial direction, and
\[
x=C_+\cos\omega_+t+C_-\cos\omega_-t,
\]
\[
y=-C_+\sin\omega_+t+C_-\sin\omega_-t.
\]
The phase difference between the counterrotating contributions grows at
\(\omega_++\omega_-=2\Omega\), so the first recurrence of their relative
orientation is
\[
\boxed{t_r=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_++\omega_-}=\frac{\pi}{\Omega}}.
\]

Multiplying the x and y equations by their respective velocities and adding
causes the magnetic terms to cancel:
\[
\frac d{dt}\left[\frac m2(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)
+\frac k2(x^2+y^2)\right]
=qB(\dot x\dot y-\dot y\dot x)=0.
\]
Thus the field changes direction of velocity but supplies no energy. Calling
it an additional spring would incorrectly create a coordinate-dependent
potential and miss the handed frequency splitting.

For the data, \(\omega_0=10.0000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and
\(\Omega=\sqrt{109}=10.4403\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\omega_+=13.4403\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_-=7.44031\ \mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
The circular amplitudes are
\[
\boxed{C_+=14.2530\ \mathrm{mm}},\qquad
\boxed{C_-=25.7470\ \mathrm{mm}}.
\]
Also
\[
\boxed{t_r=0.300910\ \mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{E=\tfrac12kA^2=0.0160000\ \mathrm J}.
\]
As \(B\to0\), both frequencies approach \(\omega_0\) and the decomposition
recombines into a line oscillation. For \(\omega_c\gg\omega_0\),
\(\omega_+\sim\omega_c\) while
\(\omega_-\sim\omega_0^2/\omega_c\), consistent with their fixed product.

graderFixtures.proofText: For \(z=x+iy\), \(\ddot z+i\omega_c\dot z+\omega_0^2z=0\). The frequencies are \(\Omega\pm\omega_c/2\), with product \(\omega_0^2\). Zero initial velocity gives \(C_+=A\omega_-/(\omega_++\omega_-)\) and \(C_-=A\omega_+/(\omega_++\omega_-)\). Numerically they are 13.4403 and 7.44031 rad/s with amplitudes 14.253 and 25.747 mm.
I model qB as an extra spring constant and split the initial displacement equally between the two unequal-frequency modes, while claiming the field adds potential energy.

WAVE:010226.title: A free support reorganizes two pendulum modes
WAVE:010226.objective: Derive all generalized modes of two pendula mounted on a freely translating support, including the rigid-translation zero mode, and solve a localized release by mass-metric projection.
WAVE:010226.statement:
A cart of mass \(M\) moves without horizontal friction. Two identical simple
pendula, each with bob mass \(m\) and length \(\ell\), hang from the same
point on the cart. Let X be the cart displacement and let \(\theta_1,\theta_2\)
be small angles from the downward vertical. There is no spring connecting the
cart to ground.

Starting from the bob positions, derive the quadratic kinetic and potential
energies without discarding the cart-angle velocity cross terms. Write the
linear equations as
\[
\mathsf M\ddot{\mathbf q}+\mathsf K\mathbf q=0,
\qquad \mathbf q=(X,\theta_1,\theta_2)^T,
\]
and prove that the mass matrix is positive definite. Identify the conserved
horizontal momentum and explain why translational invariance requires a
zero-frequency mode.

Find the rigid-translation, antisymmetric, and symmetric modes. Derive the two
nonzero frequencies and show that the three displayed mode vectors are
mutually orthogonal in the mass metric. For the localized release
\[
X(0)=0,\quad \theta_1(0)=\theta_0,\quad \theta_2(0)=0,
\qquad \dot X(0)=\dot\theta_1(0)=\dot\theta_2(0)=0,
\]
perform the full modal decomposition, including the static zero-mode
coefficient. Give exact formulas for all three coordinates and verify that
the horizontal center of mass remains fixed.

For \(M=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}\),
\(\ell=0.500\,\mathrm m\), \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and
\(\theta_0=0.0800\,\mathrm{rad}\), compute both nonzero frequencies, the
zero-mode cart offset, the maximum cart excursion, and the quadratic energy.
Check the heavy-cart limit and explain why deleting the zero mode violates
the initial displacement or center-of-mass constraint.
permittedResults: A cyclic coordinate gives a conserved conjugate momentum; here \(P_X=\partial T/\partial\dot X\).
For \(\mathsf K v_j=\omega_j^2\mathsf Mv_j\) with symmetric matrices, modes having distinct squared frequencies satisfy \(v_i^T\mathsf Mv_j=0\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use symmetric and antisymmetric angular coordinates while retaining the cyclic support coordinate.
Solve the full generalized eigenproblem and project the initial vector using the mass inner product.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Builds the free-support generalized eigenproblem, binds the zero mode to momentum conservation, and reconstructs the localized release by mass-metric projection.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats each bob velocity as only ell theta dot and drops its shared cart velocity and cross term.
commonErrors.consequence: The mass matrix, symmetric frequency, support recoil, and momentum law are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Expands the localized release in only the two angular oscillatory modes and discards rigid translation.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed initial cart coordinate or fixed center-of-mass condition fails.

hintTree.content: To quadratic order each bob's horizontal velocity is \(\dot X+\ell\dot\theta_j\).
The antisymmetric mode has \(X=0\) and \(\theta_1=-\theta_2\); the symmetric mode must recoil the support so total horizontal momentum vanishes.
Decompose the localized release into one translation vector plus equal symmetric and antisymmetric angular amplitudes.

WAVE:010226.canonicalSolution:
To quadratic order the bob velocities give
\[
T=\frac12(M+2m)\dot X^2
+m\ell\dot X(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)
+\frac12m\ell^2(\dot\theta_1^2+\dot\theta_2^2),
\qquad
V=\frac12mg\ell(\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2).
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathsf M=\begin{pmatrix}
M+2m&m\ell&m\ell\\m\ell&m\ell^2&0\\m\ell&0&m\ell^2
\end{pmatrix}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathsf K=\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&0\\0&mg\ell&0\\0&0&mg\ell
\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
The Schur complement of the angular block in \(\mathsf M\) is M, so
\(\det\mathsf M=M m^2\ell^4>0\); the angular block is positive and therefore
\(\mathsf M\) is positive definite. The cyclic coordinate gives
\[
\boxed{P_X=(M+2m)\dot X+m\ell(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)},
\]
which is conserved.

Convenient mode vectors are
\[
v_0=(1,0,0)^T,\qquad v_a=(0,1,-1)^T,
\]
\[
v_s=\left(-\frac{2m\ell}{M+2m},1,1\right)^T.
\]
Direct substitution gives
\[
\boxed{\omega_0=0},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_a^2=\frac g\ell},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_s^2=\frac g\ell\frac{M+2m}{M}}.
\]
The mass norms are
\[
v_0^T\mathsf Mv_0=M+2m,\quad
v_a^T\mathsf Mv_a=2m\ell^2,\quad
v_s^T\mathsf Mv_s=\frac{2mM\ell^2}{M+2m},
\]
and all three cross products \(v_i^T\mathsf Mv_j\) vanish. In particular,
the support component of \(v_s\) is precisely the recoil needed for zero
horizontal momentum.

The initial vector decomposes as
\[
\mathbf q(0)=\frac{m\ell\theta_0}{M+2m}v_0
+\frac{\theta_0}{2}v_a+\frac{\theta_0}{2}v_s.
\]
Zero initial velocity removes all sine terms, so
\[
\boxed{X(t)=\frac{m\ell\theta_0}{M+2m}
[1-\cos(\omega_st)]},
\]
\[
\boxed{\theta_1(t)=\frac{\theta_0}{2}
[\cos(\omega_at)+\cos(\omega_st)]},
\]
\[
\boxed{\theta_2(t)=\frac{\theta_0}{2}
[-\cos(\omega_at)+\cos(\omega_st)]}.
\]
Consequently
\[
(M+2m)X+m\ell(\theta_1+\theta_2)=m\ell\theta_0
\]
is constant: the horizontal center of mass does not move.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\omega_a=4.42945\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_s=5.42494\ \mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
The zero-mode offset is
\[
\boxed{X_0=\frac{m\ell\theta_0}{M+2m}=6.66667\ \mathrm{mm}},
\]
and X ranges from zero to
\(\boxed{X_{\max}=2X_0=13.3333\ \mathrm{mm}}\). The release energy is
\[
\boxed{E=\frac12mg\ell\theta_0^2=0.0156960\ \mathrm J}.
\]
As \(M\to\infty\), support recoil vanishes and both angular frequencies tend
to \(\sqrt{g/\ell}\), as for two independent pendula on a fixed support.
Omitting \(v_0\) would force the wrong initial X or move the horizontal center
of mass, even though the zero mode carries no oscillatory energy.

graderFixtures.proofText: The modes are \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,-1)\), and \((-2m\ell/(M+2m),1,1)\), with frequencies zero, \(\sqrt{g/\ell}\), and \(\sqrt{(g/\ell)(M+2m)/M}\). The release includes static coefficient \(m\ell\theta_0/(M+2m)\), giving frequencies 4.42945 and 5.42494 rad/s and maximum cart travel 13.3333 mm.
I omit cart-angle kinetic cross terms, use only symmetric and antisymmetric oscillations, and set the translation coefficient to zero even though the reconstructed cart starts displaced.

WAVE:010227.title: An odd SSH chain has an exact edge mode
WAVE:010227.objective: Derive the complete finite spectrum and exact sublattice-polarized zero mode of a five-site dimerized coupled-mode chain.
WAVE:010227.statement:
Five lossless resonant modes have complex amplitudes ordered as
\((A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2,A_3)\). In a common rotating frame they obey
\(i\dot{\mathbf a}=H\mathbf a\), with zero on-site detuning and real positive
nearest-neighbor couplings \(v,w,v,w\). Thus v connects each \(A_n\) to
\(B_n\), while w connects \(B_n\) to \(A_{n+1}\).

Write H explicitly and prove its chiral anticommutation relation. Use that
symmetry and the sublattice imbalance to construct an exact zero-frequency
mode without evaluating a fifth-degree determinant. Normalize it, find its
localization length in unit cells, and explain which edge is selected when
v/w is reversed. Derive all four nonzero eigenvalues by reducing the problem
to the two-by-two matrix \(Q^TQ\), and show their plus-minus pairing.
Compute the fraction of norm on the first site and the inverse participation
ratio. State precisely what is protected by chiral symmetry and why arbitrary
on-site detuning can move the zero eigenvalue even if the state remains
spatially localized.

For \(v=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and \(w=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), compute
the complete spectrum, normalized zero-mode vector, first-site weight,
inverse participation ratio, and localization length. Verify norm
conservation and the uniform-coupling boundary (v=w).
permittedResults: A rectangular bipartite coupling matrix with more rows than columns has a nontrivial null vector on the larger sublattice.
The nonzero eigenvalues of \(\begin{pmatrix}0&Q\\Q^T&0\end{pmatrix}\) are plus and minus the singular values of Q.

acceptableStrategies.description: Construct the zero mode by sublattice recursion and obtain the rest from singular values.
Evaluate the characteristic polynomial using chiral block form and factor out the sublattice-imbalance zero.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses bipartite structure to obtain the exact finite spectrum and quantitatively characterize the unpaired edge mode.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assigns nonzero B amplitudes to the unpaired zero state without satisfying the A-site equations.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed vector is not in the kernel of the chiral coupling matrix.

commonErrors.description: Claims arbitrary diagonal detuning preserves exact zero frequency merely because the vector is edge localized.
commonErrors.consequence: The required chiral anticommutation and spectral pairing are lost.

hintTree.content: Set both B amplitudes to zero; the B-site equations give \(vA_n+wA_{n+1}=0\).
In the ordering with all A sites first, use \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}v&0\\w&v\\0&w\end{pmatrix}\).
Normalize the geometric vector \((1,-v/w,(v/w)^2)\) before computing site weights or the IPR.

WAVE:010227.canonicalSolution:
In the stated site order,
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}
0&v&0&0&0\\v&0&w&0&0\\0&w&0&v&0\\
0&0&v&0&w\\0&0&0&w&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
With \(\Gamma=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1,1)\), every nonzero matrix
element connects opposite signs, so
\[
\boxed{\Gamma H\Gamma=-H},\qquad \{\Gamma,H\}=0.
\]
Hence nonzero eigenvalues occur in plus-minus pairs. Because the A sublattice
has one extra site, a zero vector can live entirely on A. The B equations give
\[
vA_1+wA_2=0,\qquad vA_2+wA_3=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{a_0=\mathcal N(1,0,-r,0,r^2)^T},\qquad
r=v/w,\qquad \mathcal N=(1+r^2+r^4)^{-1/2}.
\]
For \(r<1\) it is localized on the left; for \(r>1\), rewriting relative to
the last site shows right localization. The amplitude falls as
\(e^{-(n-1)/\xi}\), so
\[
\boxed{\xi=1/|\ln|w/v||}
\]
in unit cells.

Reorder sites as all A followed by all B. Then
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q\\Q^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
Q=\begin{pmatrix}v&0\\w&v\\0&w\end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\[
Q^TQ=\begin{pmatrix}v^2+w^2&vw\\vw&v^2+w^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(v^2+w^2\pm vw\). Therefore the complete spectrum is
\[
\boxed{0,\quad\pm\sqrt{v^2+w^2-vw},\quad
\pm\sqrt{v^2+w^2+vw}}.
\]

For \(v=1,w=2\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{spec}H=\{0,\pm\sqrt3,\pm\sqrt7\}}
=\{0,\pm1.73205,\pm2.64575\}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
\]
The normalized zero mode is
\[
\boxed{a_0=(0.872872,0,-0.436436,0,0.218218)^T}.
\]
Its first-site norm fraction and IPR are
\[
\boxed{|A_1|^2=0.761905},\qquad
\boxed{\sum_j|a_{0j}|^4=0.619048},
\]
and \(\boxed{\xi=1/\ln2=1.44270}\) cells. Hermiticity gives
\(d(\mathbf a^\dagger\mathbf a)/dt=0\). At \(v=w\), the zero vector is
alternating with equal A magnitudes rather than exponentially localized.
Chiral-preserving coupling disorder cannot remove the unpaired zero state
while the sublattice count and connectivity persist. On-site detuning breaks
the anticommutation, so zero frequency is no longer pinned; localization by
itself is not the protecting symmetry.

graderFixtures.proofText: Chiral symmetry leaves an A-only zero vector proportional to \((1,0,-v/w,0,(v/w)^2)\). The other eigenvalues are plus or minus square roots of \(v^2+w^2\pm vw\). For v=1,w=2 the normalized edge vector is (0.872872,0,-0.436436,0,0.218218), with first-site weight 0.761905 and IPR 0.619048.
I put equal amplitudes on every site, call it the zero mode without multiplying by H, and say any on-site disorder preserves zero because the vector remains near an edge.

WAVE:010228.title: Nonreciprocal coupling piles every open-chain mode at one edge
WAVE:010228.objective: Solve the open Hatano-Nelson chain by a nonunitary similarity transform and contrast its real spectrum and skin modes with periodic boundaries.
WAVE:010228.statement:
An active N-site coupled-mode chain obeys \(i\dot{\mathbf a}=H\mathbf a\).
For open boundaries, \(H_{n,n+1}=t_R>0\), \(H_{n+1,n}=t_L>0\), and all
other entries vanish. The matrix is non-Hermitian when \(t_R\ne t_L\).

Construct a diagonal nonunitary similarity transform that maps the open chain
to a symmetric nearest-neighbor chain. Derive every eigenvalue and both right
and left eigenvectors, including a biorthogonal normalization. Show explicitly
why the eigenvalues remain real although ordinary norm need not be conserved,
and quantify the common exponential skin factor of the right eigenvectors.
Explain why a similarity transform does not make H Hermitian in the original
Euclidean inner product.

Close the chain periodically and derive the Bloch dispersion. Show that it is
an ellipse in the complex plane when the hoppings differ, so the periodic and
open spectra differ macroscopically. State the role of boundary conditions and
why one cannot infer the open spectrum by inserting real Bloch wave number.

For \(N=4,t_R=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},t_L=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), compute
the open spectrum, decay ratio, localization length, normalized right
eigenvector for \(j=1\), its first-site weight and IPR, and the periodic
ellipse semiaxes. Keep right, left, Euclidean, and biorthogonal normalizations
distinct.
permittedResults: Similarity transformations preserve eigenvalues but not Euclidean inner products or normality.
The symmetric open chain with hopping g has eigenvectors \(\sin(nj\pi/(N+1))\) and eigenvalues \(2g\cos(j\pi/(N+1))\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Gauge the hopping asymmetry into a diagonal similarity transform and solve the reciprocal partner.
Use the open-chain recurrence with a generalized complex wave number and construct dual left solutions.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Solves the open nonreciprocal chain exactly and explains the boundary-sensitive spectral and eigenvector geometry.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Calls the diagonal rescaling unitary and concludes ordinary right eigenvectors are orthogonal and norm is conserved.
commonErrors.consequence: The non-Hermitian metric, skin envelope, and active norm balance are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the real-k periodic Bloch ellipse as the eigenvalue set of the open finite chain.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact real open spectrum and boundary sensitivity are contradicted.

hintTree.content: Try \(S_{nn}=r^{n-1}\) and require both off-diagonal entries of \(S^{-1}HS\) to equal \(\sqrt{t_Rt_L}\).
Right modes are S times sine modes; left row modes contain the reciprocal powers of r.
For periodic boundaries insert \(a_n=e^{ikn}\) before imposing any open-chain similarity transform.

WAVE:010228.canonicalSolution:
Let
\[
g=\sqrt{t_Rt_L},\qquad r=\sqrt{t_L/t_R},\qquad
S=\operatorname{diag}(1,r,r^2,\ldots,r^{N-1}).
\]
Then the upper entry of \(S^{-1}HS\) is \(t_Rr=g\), and the lower entry is
\(t_L/r=g\). Hence
\[
\boxed{S^{-1}HS=H_0},
\]
where \(H_0\) is the real symmetric open chain with hopping g. Its modes give
\[
\boxed{E_j=2g\cos\frac{j\pi}{N+1}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.
\]
If \(\varphi_j(n)=\sqrt{2/(N+1)}\sin[nj\pi/(N+1)]\), right and left modes are
\[
\boxed{R_j(n)=r^{n-1}\varphi_j(n)},\qquad
\boxed{L_j(n)=r^{-(n-1)}\varphi_j(n)}.
\]
They satisfy \(\sum_nL_i(n)R_j(n)=\delta_{ij}\). This normalization is
biorthogonal; a separately Euclidean-normalized right mode requires another
j-dependent scalar. When \(r<1\), every right mode has a left-edge envelope
\(r^{n-1}=e^{-(n-1)/\xi}\), with
\[
\boxed{\xi=1/|\ln r|}.
\]
The real spectrum follows from similarity to \(H_0\), not from Hermiticity of
H. Since \(H\ne H^\dagger\), ordinary \(\sum_n|a_n|^2\) is generally not
conserved by the active evolution.

With periodic boundaries, a Bloch vector gives
\[
\boxed{E(k)=t_Re^{ik}+t_Le^{-ik}
=(t_R+t_L)\cos k+i(t_R-t_L)\sin k}.
\]
This is an ellipse with real and imaginary semiaxes \(t_R+t_L\) and
\(|t_R-t_L|\). Its complex loop cannot be continuously identified with the
real open segment using real k; the boundary-sensitive nonunitary gauge is
obstructed when it must close around the ring.

For the data, \(g=2\), \(r=1/2\), and
\[
\boxed{E_j=4\cos(j\pi/5)
=\{3.23607,1.23607,-1.23607,-3.23607\}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
The localization length is
\(\boxed{\xi=1/\ln2=1.44270}\) sites. Euclidean normalization of the \(j=1\)
right vector gives
\[
\boxed{R_1=(0.738463,0.597429,0.298715,0.0923079)^T}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{|R_1(1)|^2=0.545327},\qquad
\boxed{\mathrm{IPR}=0.432810}.
\]
The periodic spectral ellipse has semiaxes
\(\boxed{5.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}\) and
\(\boxed{3.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}\). At \(t_R=t_L\), r is one, the
similarity becomes unitary-trivial, the skin envelope disappears, and both
boundary spectra reduce to the familiar reciprocal chain samples.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(r=\sqrt{t_L/t_R}\), \(S^{-1}HS\) is a symmetric chain of hopping \(g=\sqrt{t_Rt_L}\). Open eigenvalues are \(2g\cos[j\pi/(N+1)]\), while right modes carry \(r^{n-1}\) and left modes its reciprocal. For 4 and 1 hopping, the spectrum is plus or minus 3.23607 and 1.23607, whereas the periodic ellipse has semiaxes 5 and 3.
I call S unitary, normalize the left vector identically to the right, and use the periodic complex ellipse as the four open-chain eigenvalues.

WAVE:010229.title: A finite Bragg grating opens a reflection stop band
WAVE:010229.objective: Exponentiate counterpropagating coupled-mode equations to derive finite-length reflection, transmission, flux conservation, and the stop-band continuation.
WAVE:010229.statement:
A uniform, lossless Bragg grating couples slowly varying forward and backward
wave envelopes \(A(z)\) and \(B(z)\) over \(0\le z\le L\):
\[
\frac{dA}{dz}=i\delta A+i\kappa B,\qquad
\frac{dB}{dz}=-i\delta B-i\kappa A,
\qquad \kappa>0.
\]
Here \(\delta\) is detuning from the Bragg condition, and \(\kappa\) and
\(\delta\) have inverse-length units. Normalize the incident forward wave by
\(A(0)=1\), impose no wave incident from the far side with \(B(L)=0\), and
define \(r=B(0)\), \(t=A(L)\).

Write the system as a constant two-by-two spatial generator. Show that its
square is proportional to the identity, and exponentiate it without first
diagonalizing. For \(|\delta|<\kappa\), derive the complete transfer matrix,
the complex amplitudes \(r,t\), and the power reflectance and transmittance
\(R=|r|^2\), \(T=|t|^2\). Derive the conserved counterpropagating flux and
use it to audit \(R+T\).

Identify the stop-band edges. Take the band-edge limit rather than inserting
zero into a quotient. Continue the result to \(|\delta|>\kappa\), where the
spatial exponent becomes imaginary, and identify the perfect-transmission
conditions. Explain physically why a lossless grating can have exponential
spatial dependence inside its stop band without dissipating energy.

For \(\kappa=1.50\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), \(L=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}\), and
\(\delta=1.20\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), compute the stop-band exponent, \(r\),
\(t\), \(R\), and \(T\). Also compute the on-Bragg reflectance and the
reflectance exactly at either band edge. Give at least six significant
digits and audit every dimensionless combination.
permittedResults: If a constant matrix satisfies \(M^2=q^2I\), then \(e^{ML}=I\cosh(qL)+(M/q)\sinh(qL)\), with the zero-q value taken by continuity.
For \(q=i\beta\), analytic continuation gives \(\cosh(qL)=\cos(\beta L)\) and \(\sinh(qL)/q=\sin(\beta L)/\beta\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Exponentiate the two-by-two generator through its quadratic minimal polynomial and impose the one-sided scattering boundary data.
Derive reflection from a transfer matrix, then independently audit it with the counterpropagating flux invariant and analytic continuation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives finite-grating reflection from the spatial coupled-mode generator while preserving the stop-band continuation and signed flux conservation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the sum of forward and backward intensities as the conserved through-flux.
commonErrors.consequence: The scattering amplitudes no longer satisfy the lossless relation R plus T equals one.

commonErrors.description: Uses a real square root of delta squared minus kappa squared inside the stop band and applies sine-cosine evolution there.
commonErrors.consequence: Strong Bragg reflection is replaced by spurious periodic pass-through points.

hintTree.content: Use \(M=\begin{pmatrix}i\delta&i\kappa\\-i\kappa&-i\delta\end{pmatrix}\) and multiply it by itself before solving for eigenvectors.
Apply \(B(L)=0\) to the second row of the transfer relation; the transmitted amplitude then follows from the unit determinant.
Differentiate \(|A|^2-|B|^2\), not the sum, because B transports energy toward decreasing z.

WAVE:010229.canonicalSolution:
With \(\Psi=(A,B)^T\), the spatial system is \(\Psi'=M\Psi\), where
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}i\delta&i\kappa\\-i\kappa&-i\delta\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boxed{M^2=(\kappa^2-\delta^2)I}.
\]
Inside the stop band define \(q=\sqrt{\kappa^2-\delta^2}>0\). Then
\[
e^{ML}=\begin{pmatrix}
C+i\delta S/q&i\kappa S/q\\
-i\kappa S/q&C-i\delta S/q
\end{pmatrix},qquad
C=\cosh(qL),\quad S=\sinh(qL).
\]
The condition \(B(L)=0\), applied to
\(\Psi(L)=e^{ML}(1,r)^T\), gives
\[
\boxed{r=\frac{i\kappa S}{qC-i\delta S}},\qquad
\boxed{t=\frac{q}{qC-i\delta S}}.
\]
The expression for t also follows because \(\operatorname{tr}M=0\), so the
transfer matrix has determinant one. Therefore
\[
\boxed{R=\frac{\kappa^2\sinh^2(qL)}
{q^2+\kappa^2\sinh^2(qL)}},\qquad
\boxed{T=\frac{q^2}{q^2+\kappa^2\sinh^2(qL)}}.
\]

Directly from the coupled equations,
\[
\frac d{dz}\left(|A|^2-|B|^2\right)=0.
\]
At the two ends this states \(1-|r|^2=|t|^2\), confirming
\(\boxed{R+T=1}\). Hyperbolic envelope evolution represents coherent
conversion between counterpropagating channels, not absorption; the net
signed flux remains constant.

The stop band is \(|\delta|<\kappa\), with edges at
\(|\delta|=\kappa\). Letting \(q\to0\) and using
\(\sinh(qL)\sim qL\) gives
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm edge}=\frac{\kappa^2L^2}{1+\kappa^2L^2}}.
\]
On Bragg resonance,
\[
\boxed{R(0)=\tanh^2(\kappa L)}.
\]
Outside the stop band set \(\beta=\sqrt{\delta^2-\kappa^2}\). Analytic
continuation yields
\[
\boxed{R=\frac{\kappa^2\sin^2(\beta L)}
{\beta^2+\kappa^2\sin^2(\beta L)}}.
\]
Thus \(\beta L=n\pi\), with positive integer n, gives perfect transmission.

For the supplied stop-band point,
\[
\boxed{q=0.900000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{qL=1.80000},
\]
\[
\boxed{r=-0.768058168+0.608407233i},\qquad
\boxed{t=0.124072983+0.156630728i},
\]
\[
\boxed{R=0.960072710},\qquad
\boxed{T=0.0399272900}.
\]
At exact Bragg resonance and at either edge,
\[
\boxed{R(0)=0.990133963},\qquad
\boxed{R_{\rm edge}=0.900000}.
\]
The products \(qL\), \(\kappa L\), and \(\beta L\) are dimensionless;
reflection and transmission amplitudes and powers are dimensionless in the
stated flux normalization.

graderFixtures.proofText: The generator obeys \(M^2=(\kappa^2-\delta^2)I\). For \(q>0\), \(r=i\kappa\sinh(qL)/[q\cosh(qL)-i\delta\sinh(qL)]\), and \(|A|^2-|B|^2\) proves \(R+T=1\). The data give \(q=0.900000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), \(R=0.960072710\), and \(T=0.0399272900\).

I conserve the sum of forward and backward intensities. At delta below kappa I call square root of delta squared minus kappa squared real, use sine-cosine evolution, and predict periodic perfect transmission inside the stop band.

WAVE:010230.title: Rapid detuning can switch off mode tunneling
WAVE:010230.objective: Derive the leading high-frequency Floquet coupling of a periodically detuned dimer and state the approximation boundary at a Bessel zero.
WAVE:010230.statement:
Consider the normalized two-mode system
\[
i\dot\psi(t)=\left[\frac{A}{2}\cos(\Omega t)\,\sigma_z
+g\sigma_x\right]\psi(t),
\qquad g>0,\quad\Omega>0,
\]
where \(A,g,\Omega\) have angular-frequency units. Apply a periodic diagonal
unitary transformation that removes the explicit detuning term. Show that
the off-diagonal coupling then acquires opposite phase factors containing
\(\sin\Omega t\). Use the Jacobi-Anger expansion to obtain the leading
high-frequency, zero-Fourier-harmonic effective Hamiltonian.

Derive the effective coupling \(g_{\rm eff}\), the corresponding leading
transition probability from mode 1 to mode 2, and the first complete-transfer
time when \(g_{\rm eff}\ne0\). Identify the first positive modulation ratio
that suppresses this leading coupling. Clearly distinguish “zero leading
Floquet coupling” from an exact finite-frequency theorem: state the
high-frequency assumption and the scale of omitted virtual-harmonic effects.

For \(g=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and
\(\Omega=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), use
\(j_{0,1}=2.4048255577\). Compute the required \(A\) at the first
suppression point. For comparison, at \(A/\Omega=2.00000\), use
\(J_0(2)=0.2238907791\) to compute \(g_{\rm eff}\) and the leading first
complete-transfer time. Audit the dimensionless Bessel argument.
permittedResults: The Jacobi-Anger identity is \(e^{iz\sin\theta}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(z)e^{in\theta}\).
For \(H=g_{\rm eff}\sigma_x\), a state initially in mode 1 has transition probability \(\sin^2(|g_{\rm eff}|t)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Remove the longitudinal drive with a periodic diagonal unitary and Fourier-expand the residual transverse coupling.
Check the leading effective model by solving its constant two-state evolution and then estimate omitted harmonic scales.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the Bessel-renormalized leading coupling and preserves the distinction between a controlled Floquet approximation and exact dynamics.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses (J_0(A/(2Omega))) after forgetting that the relative off-diagonal phase is twice the single-state gauge phase.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted suppression amplitude is wrong by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Claims a Bessel zero eliminates all tunneling exactly for arbitrary finite drive frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: Virtual higher harmonics and the approximation regime are erased.

hintTree.content: Try \(U(t)=\exp[-i(A/2\Omega)\sin(\Omega t)\sigma_z]\) and keep track of whether \(\psi=U\chi\) or its inverse.
The relative phase of the two off-diagonal matrix elements is twice the exponent used on either basis state.
Only the \(n=0\) Fourier harmonic survives the leading period average.

WAVE:010230.canonicalSolution:
Set
\[
U(t)=\exp\!\left[-i\frac{A}{2\Omega}\sin(\Omega t)\sigma_z\right],
\qquad \psi=U\chi.
\]
The term \(-iU^\dagger\dot U\) cancels the diagonal modulation. The transformed
Hamiltonian is
\[
H'(t)=g\begin{pmatrix}
0&e^{i(A/\Omega)\sin\Omega t}\\
e^{-i(A/\Omega)\sin\Omega t}&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Jacobi-Anger series shows that its zero harmonic is
\[
\boxed{H_{\rm eff}^{(0)}=gJ_0(A/\Omega)\sigma_x},\qquad
\boxed{g_{\rm eff}=gJ_0(A/\Omega)}.
\]
Thus, to this order,
\[
\boxed{P_{1\to2}(t)=\sin^2(|g_{\rm eff}|t)},\qquad
\boxed{t_{\pi/2}=\frac{\pi}{2|g_{\rm eff}|}}.
\]

At \(A/\Omega=j_{0,1}\), \(J_0\) vanishes and the leading averaged tunneling
is suppressed. This statement assumes \(\Omega\gg g\) while the ratio
\(A/\Omega\) may remain order one. Nonzero harmonics mediate corrections
whose generator scale begins beyond the period average, typically of order
\(g^2/\Omega\) before symmetry-specific cancellations; hence exact freezing
at finite \(\Omega\) has not been proved.

For the supplied frequency,
\[
\boxed{A=j_{0,1}\Omega=48.0965112\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
At ratio two,
\[
\boxed{g_{\rm eff}=0.223890779\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{t_{\pi/2}=7.01590451\ \mathrm s}.
\]
Here \(\Omega/g=20\), so the averaging hierarchy is explicit. A Bessel
function requires a dimensionless argument: \(A/\Omega\) is dimensionless
because both quantities are angular frequencies.

graderFixtures.proofText: The detuning-removing unitary gives off-diagonal phases \(e^{\pm i(A/\Omega)\sin\Omega t}\). Period averaging therefore yields \(g_{\rm eff}=gJ_0(A/\Omega)\). The first leading suppression point needs \(A=48.0965112\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\); at ratio two, \(g_{\rm eff}=0.223890779\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and \(t_{\pi/2}=7.01590451\) s, subject to \(\Omega\gg g\).
I average the single-state phase, get J zero of A over two Omega, and assert exact tunneling suppression at every drive frequency.

WAVE:010231.title: All-to-all coupling leaves one bright mode and many dark modes
WAVE:010231.objective: Use projectors to solve a complete graph of identical oscillators and separate localized motion from the response to a uniform drive.
WAVE:010231.statement:
Five identical unit-mass oscillators have on-site angular frequency \(\omega_0\),
and every unordered pair is joined by a spring whose stiffness per unit mass
is \(\kappa\). More generally, for \(N\) sites,
\[
\ddot x_i+\omega_0^2x_i+\kappa\sum_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)=f_i(t).
\]
Write the dynamical matrix using the normalized uniform vector and its
orthogonal projector. Find the complete spectrum, including multiplicities,
and construct the exact matrix propagator without choosing an arbitrary
basis inside the degenerate subspace.

For initial data \(x_1(0)=A\), all other displacements zero, and all
velocities zero, derive \(x_1(t)\) and every \(x_{j\ne1}(t)\). State the
center-of-mass motion and verify the initial condition. Separately, apply a
uniform harmonic force \(f_i(t)=F\cos\Omega t\) and explain why the
degenerate modes are dark even if the drive frequency equals their natural
frequency. Then state how a small site-dependent frequency disorder changes,
but does not instantly erase, the bright/dark picture.

For \(N=5\), \(\omega_0=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\(\kappa=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}\), and \(A=10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute both
distinct modal frequencies, the uniform-mode and dark-subspace weights in
the localized initial displacement, \(x_1\) and the other-site displacement
at the first time when the two cosines have opposite extrema if such a time
is exactly available, and otherwise give the algebraic extremal bounds.
permittedResults: For the normalized uniform vector \(u\), the projectors \(P=uu^T\) and \(Q=I-P\) satisfy \(P^2=P\), \(Q^2=Q\), and \(PQ=0\).
A complete-graph Laplacian is \(NQ\): it vanishes on the uniform vector and equals \(N\) on its orthogonal complement.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize the complete-graph Laplacian abstractly with its uniform and orthogonal projectors.
Sum the component equations to obtain center-of-mass motion and subtract it to solve the relative coordinates.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses symmetry projectors to preserve the entire degenerate dark subspace and distinguishes frequency coincidence from drive overlap.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses N minus one rather than N as the nonzero complete-graph Laplacian eigenvalue.
commonErrors.consequence: Every dark-mode frequency and localized-motion coefficient is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a spatially uniform force excites the orthogonal dark subspace merely because its frequency matches.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact symmetry selection rule Q f equals zero is violated.

hintTree.content: Rewrite \(\sum_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)=Nx_i-\sum_jx_j\).
Decompose the localized vector \(e_1\) as \(Pe_1+Qe_1\) before evolving it.
A uniform force is proportional to \(u\), so project the forced equation with \(Q\).

WAVE:010231.canonicalSolution:
Let \(u=N^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T\), \(P=uu^T\), and
\(Q=I-P\). The complete-graph Laplacian is \(NQ\), so the dynamical matrix is
\[
\boxed{K=\omega_0^2P+(\omega_0^2+N\kappa)Q}.
\]
There is one uniform frequency \(\omega_b=\omega_0\) and an
\((N-1)\)-fold frequency
\[
\boxed{\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2+N\kappa}}.
\]
The zero-velocity propagator is basis-free:
\[
\cos(\sqrt Kt)=P\cos\omega_bt+Q\cos\omega_dt.
\]
Since \(Pe_1=N^{-1}{\bf1}\), localized displacement evolves as
\[
\boxed{x_1(t)=A\left[\frac1N\cos\omega_bt+
\left(1-\frac1N\right)\cos\omega_dt\right]},
\]
\[
\boxed{x_{j\ne1}(t)=\frac A N
(\cos\omega_bt-\cos\omega_dt)}.
\]
The center of mass is \(N^{-1}\sum_ix_i=A\cos\omega_bt/N\), and evaluating
at zero recovers \(x_1=A\), \(x_{j\ne1}=0\). The squared Euclidean weights
of the initial vector are \(\|Pe_1\|^2=1/N\) and
\(\|Qe_1\|^2=1-1/N\).

For a uniform force, \(Qf=0\). Therefore only the bright coordinate obeys
the forced scalar oscillator equation. Tuning \(\Omega=\omega_d\) does not
excite a dark mode because the forcing numerator is exactly zero; resonance
requires overlap as well as frequency matching. Weak disorder makes \(P\)
and \(Q\) only approximate invariant subspaces, giving small dark-mode
oscillator strengths proportional to the induced mixing.

For the data,
\[
\boxed{\omega_b=2.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_d=\sqrt{19}=4.35889894\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
The squared weights are \(0.200000\) and \(0.800000\). Because
\(\omega_d/\omega_b=\sqrt{19}/2\) is irrational, the two cosines never
reach exactly opposite extrema at a common finite time. The two
opposite-extremum combinations would give \(x_1=\pm0.600000A\) and
\(|x_{j\ne1}|=0.400000A\); irrational phase flow approaches those
combinations arbitrarily closely. The full algebraic bounds are
\[
-A\le x_1\le A,
\qquad |x_{j\ne1}|\le\frac{2A}{5}.
\]
Thus \(|x_1|\le10.0000\,\mathrm{mm}\) and
\(|x_{j\ne1}|\le4.00000\,\mathrm{mm}\).

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(P=uu^T\), the matrix is \(\omega_0^2P+(\omega_0^2+N\kappa)Q\). The data give frequencies 2 and \(\sqrt{19}\) s\(^{-1}\), squared weights 0.2 and 0.8, and a uniform drive has exactly zero dark projection.
I use N minus one as the Laplacian eigenvalue and say a uniform drive resonates with every dark mode when its frequency is square root of nineteen.

WAVE:010232.title: A side resonator cuts a notch into a lossless waveguide
WAVE:010232.objective: Solve a two-port temporal coupled-mode scattering problem and audit its resonant interference, linewidth, stored energy, and unitarity.
WAVE:010232.statement:
A mirror-symmetric, lossless side resonator couples equally to the two directions
of an otherwise transparent single-mode waveguide. In a rotating-wave
normalization where \(|a|^2\) is stored energy and \(|s|^2\) is power,
\[
\dot a=(i\omega_0-\gamma)a+\sqrt\gamma\,(s_{1+}+s_{2+}),
\]
\[
s_{1-}=s_{2+}-\sqrt\gamma\,a,\qquad
s_{2-}=s_{1+}-\sqrt\gamma\,a.
\]
Here \(\gamma>0\) is the total amplitude decay rate into the two ports. Send
a monochromatic wave \(s_{1+}=s_0e^{-i\omega t}\) from port 1 and set
\(s_{2+}=0\). Derive the steady resonator amplitude and the complex
reflection and transmission coefficients. Prove power conservation for
every detuning and explain the destructive interference that makes the
through amplitude vanish on resonance even though the device has no loss.

Find the reflected-power full width at half maximum, the stored-energy
residence ratio \(|a|^2/|s_0|^2\), and its on-resonance value. Identify what
would cease to hold if an unmodeled intrinsic loss rate were inserted only
in the resonator equation without the associated dissipative power channel.

For \(\gamma=1.00\times10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and
\(\Delta=\omega-\omega_0=0.750\times10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), compute the
complex \(r,t\), reflected and transmitted powers, relative scattering
phase, and residence ratio.
permittedResults: For a passive lossless scattering system, its frequency-domain scattering matrix is unitary on the real-frequency axis.
A Lorentzian \(\gamma^2/(\gamma^2+\Delta^2)\) falls to half its peak at \(|\Delta|=\gamma\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the temporal coupled-mode equation in steady state, then substitute into both port relations.
Change to even and odd port combinations, noting that only the even channel couples to the resonator.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.

commonErrors.description: Sets the transmitted wave equal only to resonator reradiation and omits the direct unit-amplitude waveguide path.
commonErrors.consequence: The resonance becomes a transmission peak and the scattering matrix is not the stated device.

commonErrors.description: Calls the zero resonant transmission absorbed power even though no intrinsic loss channel exists.
commonErrors.consequence: Power conservation and the unit reflected amplitude are contradicted.

hintTree.content: Insert \(a(t)=a_0e^{-i\omega t}\) and keep \(\Delta=\omega-\omega_0\) signed.
The reflected wave has no direct term, while the transmitted wave has both the unit direct term and resonant reradiation.
Check \(|r|^2+|t|^2\) over a common denominator before interpreting the resonance.

WAVE:010232.canonicalSolution:
With \(a=a_0e^{-i\omega t}\), the resonator equation gives
\[
(\gamma-i\Delta)a_0=\sqrt\gamma\,s_0,
\qquad
\boxed{a_0=\frac{\sqrt\gamma}{\gamma-i\Delta}s_0}.
\]
The output relations yield
\[
\boxed{r=\frac{s_{1-}}{s_0}=-\frac\gamma{\gamma-i\Delta}},
\qquad
\boxed{t=\frac{s_{2-}}{s_0}=1-\frac\gamma{\gamma-i\Delta}
=\frac{-i\Delta}{\gamma-i\Delta}}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{R=|r|^2=\frac{\gamma^2}{\gamma^2+\Delta^2}},\qquad
\boxed{T=|t|^2=\frac{\Delta^2}{\gamma^2+\Delta^2}},
\]
and \(R+T=1\). At resonance, the resonator reradiates a through-port field
equal and opposite to the direct field, so \(t=0\) and \(r=-1\). Energy is
returned to the incident port rather than absorbed.

The reflection is half its peak at \(|\Delta|=\gamma\), hence
\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega_{\rm FWHM}=2\gamma}.
\]
The energy-to-power ratio is
\[
\boxed{\frac{|a_0|^2}{|s_0|^2}=
\frac\gamma{\gamma^2+\Delta^2}},
\]
which has units of seconds and equals \(1/\gamma\) on resonance. If an
intrinsic decay were added, \(R+T<1\); the deficit is physical absorption
and must be included rather than still claiming a unitary two-port matrix.

For \(\Delta/\gamma=0.75\),
\[
\boxed{r=-0.640000-0.480000i},\qquad
\boxed{t=0.360000-0.480000i}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{R=0.640000},\qquad \boxed{T=0.360000}.
\]
Their ratio is \(r/t=-4i/3\), so the reflected amplitude lags the
transmitted amplitude by \(\pi/2\) modulo \(2\pi\). Finally,
\[
\boxed{\frac{|a_0|^2}{|s_0|^2}=6.40000\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The amplitudes \(r,t\) and powers \(R,T\) are dimensionless; the resonator
amplitude itself has square-root-energy units.

graderFixtures.proofText: The solution is \(a_0=\sqrt\gamma s_0/(\gamma-i\Delta)\), \(r=-\gamma/(\gamma-i\Delta)\), and \(t=-i\Delta/(\gamma-i\Delta)\). At the specified detuning, \(R=0.64\), \(T=0.36\), and the residence ratio is \(6.4\times10^{-7}\) s.
I omit the direct term from transmission and say the missing on-resonance power is absorbed even though the model has no intrinsic loss.

WAVE:010233.title: A frequency gradient makes a coupled array return home
WAVE:010233.objective: Derive the Wannier--Stark ladder and exact Bloch revival of a linearly detuned coupled-resonator chain.
WAVE:010233.statement:
An infinite array of lossless single-mode resonators has complex amplitudes
\(a_n(t)\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\), normalized by
\(\sum_n|a_n|^2=1\). In a rotating frame the coupled-mode equations are
\[
i\dot a_n=n\Delta a_n-J(a_{n+1}+a_{n-1}),
\qquad J>0,\quad\Delta>0,
\]
where \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are angular-frequency rates.

Find all normal-mode eigenvalues and show that they form an equally spaced
Wannier--Stark ladder even though the array is infinite. Construct normalized
eigenvectors using the Bessel recurrence, and explain why each ladder mode is
localized in site index. Then solve the initial-value problem
\(a_n(0)=\delta_{n0}\). Derive the exact Bessel propagator, prove complete
revival after one Bloch period, and compute the time-dependent second moment
\(\sum_n n^2|a_n|^2\). Distinguish spreading width from center-of-mass motion:
the chosen localized initial condition remains centered by symmetry.

For \(J=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
compute the ladder spacing, Bloch period, half-period time, largest Bessel
argument, maximum RMS site index, and the argument controlling the stationary
eigenmode centered at \(m=0\). Check the zero-gradient limit without replacing
the exact ladder by a finite-band dispersion at nonzero \(\Delta\).
permittedResults: \(\ell J_\ell(z)=\frac z2[J_{\ell-1}(z)+J_{\ell+1}(z)]\) and \(\sum_{\ell=-\infty}^{\infty}J_\ell(z)^2=1\).
\(\sum_{\ell=-\infty}^{\infty}\ell^2J_\ell(z)^2=z^2/2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the stationary recurrence first and re-sum the ladder eigenmode expansion.
Gauge away the linear onsite ramp and integrate the time-dependent hopping phase directly.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects the Bessel-localized eigenbasis, equally spaced eigenvalues, exact propagator, and finite Bloch revival without mixing their two different Bessel arguments.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the untilted cosine band as the exact spectrum while Delta is nonzero.
commonErrors.consequence: The equally spaced ladder and exact common revival period disappear.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the symmetric second moment of a single-site launch as center-of-mass displacement.
commonErrors.consequence: A state with identically zero mean site index is assigned spurious directed transport.

hintTree.content: Try an eigenvalue \(E_m=m\Delta\) and a profile depending only on \(n-m\).
Gauge away \(n\Delta\) first; the hopping phases then integrate to a sine over half a Bloch period.
At \(t=2\pi/\Delta\), the Bessel argument vanishes and only \(J_0(0)\) survives.

WAVE:010233.canonicalSolution:
For \(a_n(t)=u_n^{(m)}e^{-iE_mt}\), choose
\[
E_m=m\Delta,\qquad
\boxed{u_n^{(m)}=J_{n-m}\left(\frac{2J}{\Delta}\right)}.
\]
Writing \(\ell=n-m\), the eigenvalue equation becomes
\[
\ell\Delta J_\ell(2J/\Delta)
=J[J_{\ell-1}(2J/\Delta)+J_{\ell+1}(2J/\Delta)],
\]
which is exactly the Bessel recurrence. The sum-of-squares identity normalizes
each mode. Therefore
\[
\boxed{E_m=m\Delta},\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.
\]
For fixed argument, \(J_\ell\) decays rapidly when \(|\ell|\) exceeds that
argument, so every eigenvector is localized about its ladder index \(m\).

A gauge transformation followed by a generating-function expansion gives,
for the single-site initial condition,
\[
\boxed{
a_n(t)=i^n e^{-in\Delta t/2}
J_n\left[\frac{4J}{\Delta}\sin\left(\frac{\Delta t}{2}\right)\right]
}.
\]
The small-time result \(a_{\pm1}\sim iJt\) checks the hopping sign. Define
\[
z(t)=\frac{4J}{\Delta}\sin\left(\frac{\Delta t}{2}\right).
\]
Then \(|a_n|^2=J_n(z)^2\), so symmetry gives
\[
\langle n\rangle=0,\qquad
\boxed{\langle n^2\rangle=\frac{z(t)^2}{2}
=\frac{8J^2}{\Delta^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta t}{2}\right)}.
\]
At
\[
\boxed{T_B=\frac{2\pi}{\Delta}},
\]
\(z=0\), all off-center amplitudes vanish, and \(a_0=1\): the state revives
exactly. This is ladder rephasing, not irreversible spreading.

For the numerical array,
\[
\boxed{\Delta E=\Delta=2.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{T_B=\pi=3.14159265\ \mathrm s},
\]
\[
\boxed{T_B/2=1.57079633\ \mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{z_{\max}=\frac{4J}{\Delta}=6.00000}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{n_{\rm rms,max}=\frac{z_{\max}}{\sqrt2}
=4.24264069},
\]
while each stationary ladder eigenmode uses the smaller Bessel argument
\[
\boxed{\frac{2J}{\Delta}=3.00000}.
\]
As \(\Delta\to0\), both the period and localization extent diverge and the
usual translation-invariant band is recovered only in that singular limit.

graderFixtures.proofText: The exact eigenpairs are \(E_m=m\Delta\) and \(J_{n-m}(2J/\Delta)\). A site-zero launch has amplitudes \(i^ne^{-in\Delta t/2}J_n[(4J/\Delta)\sin(\Delta t/2)]\), giving period \(3.14159265\) s and maximum RMS width \(4.24264069\) sites.
I keep the translation-invariant cosine band despite the onsite gradient and interpret the symmetric Bessel spreading as a nonzero center-of-mass trajectory.

WAVE:010234.title: A quasiperiodic chain reaches a self-dual transition
WAVE:010234.objective: Derive Aubry--Andre Fourier duality, locate the global transition, and state precisely when the supercritical Lyapunov exponent yields spectral localization.
WAVE:010234.statement:
Consider the infinite coupled-mode eigenproblem
\[
E\psi_n=J(\psi_{n+1}+\psi_{n-1})
+V\cos(2\pi\alpha n+\phi)\psi_n,
\]
where \(J>0\), \(V\ge0\), \(\alpha\) is a Diophantine irrational, and
\(\phi\) belongs to the full-measure nonresonant phase set in the
supercritical almost-Mathieu localization theorem. This deterministic
quasiperiodic modulation is not random disorder.

Apply the Fourier-series transform
\[
\psi_n=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\widetilde\psi_m
e^{im(2\pi\alpha n+\phi)}
\]
and derive the exact dual recurrence. Identify which coefficients exchange
roles, find the self-dual ratio, and state the extended, critical, and
exponentially localized regimes under the stated arithmetic and phase
hypotheses. In the supercritical regime use the exact Lyapunov exponent to
obtain the localization length, and explain why positivity of that exponent
alone is not a theorem of pure-point localization for every irrational
frequency and every phase. Explain why this ideal model has no
energy-dependent mobility edge within the covered regime: the spectral
energies cross the transition together. Define the inverse participation
ratio and state its scaling for normalized extended and localized states.

For the Diophantine frequency \(\alpha=(\sqrt5-1)/2\), take \(\phi\) from
the stated full-measure nonresonant set, \(J=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and
\(V=3.20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Compute the dimensionless
modulation ratio, Lyapunov exponent, localization length in sites, the
asymptotic amplitude ratio between neighboring sites, and the amplitude
suppression eight sites from a localization center. Also give the dual
model's hopping and modulation coefficients.
permittedResults: For irrational \(\alpha\), the almost-Mathieu Lyapunov exponent on the supercritical spectrum is \(\gamma_L=\ln[V/(2J)]>0\); positivity alone does not determine spectral type for every frequency and phase.
For Diophantine \(\alpha\) and Lebesgue-almost every phase, the supercritical almost-Mathieu operator has pure-point spectrum with exponentially localized eigenfunctions.
A normalized state spread uniformly over \(N\) sites has inverse participation ratio \(1/N\), while an exponentially localized state has a nonzero large-\(N\) limit.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the infinite recurrence term by term and read the self-dual parameter exchange.
Use rational Fibonacci approximants to observe IPR scaling, then identify the exact irrational-limit transition from duality.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Performs the quasiperiodic Fourier transform explicitly, keeps duality and localization length consistent, and limits pure-point exponential localization to the declared Diophantine and nonresonant-phase regime.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the deterministic cosine sequence as independent random onsite disorder and invokes one-dimensional Anderson localization at every nonzero V.
commonErrors.consequence: The extended phase and exact self-dual transition are erased.

commonErrors.description: Misses the one-half from decomposing the cosine and places the transition at V equals J.
commonErrors.consequence: The dual recurrence, critical ratio, and localization length are all incorrect.

hintTree.content: With the declared phase-inclusive Fourier basis, hopping becomes multiplication by \(2J\cos(2\pi\alpha m)\) in the dual index.
The cosine modulation shifts the dual index by one with coefficient \(V/2\).
Write \(g=V/(2J)\); duality sends \(g\) to \(1/g\).

WAVE:010234.canonicalSolution:
Insert the Fourier series into the recurrence. Translating \(n\) by one
multiplies the \(m\)th Fourier component by
\(e^{\pm i2\pi\alpha m}\), while multiplying by the cosine shifts \(m\) by
one. The declared Fourier basis absorbs the phase origin, giving
\[
\boxed{
E\widetilde\psi_m
=2J\cos(2\pi\alpha m)\widetilde\psi_m
+\frac V2(\widetilde\psi_{m+1}+\widetilde\psi_{m-1})
}.
\]
The original hopping \(J\) becomes dual modulation amplitude \(2J\), and
the original modulation amplitude \(V\) becomes dual hopping \(V/2\).
Consequently \(g=V/(2J)\) maps to \(1/g\), and
\[
\boxed{V_c=2J}
\]
is self-dual.

Duality fixes the transition ratio, and for irrational \(\alpha\) the
supercritical Lyapunov exponent on the spectrum is positive. Positivity of a
Lyapunov exponent alone, however, does not imply pure-point exponentially
localized eigenstates for every irrational frequency and every phase.

Under the declared Diophantine-frequency and full-measure nonresonant-phase
hypotheses, the almost-Mathieu spectral classification is
\[
V<2J:\ \text{extended (absolutely continuous)},\qquad
V=2J:\ \text{critical},
\]
\[
V>2J:\ \text{pure point with exponentially localized eigenfunctions}.
\]
Exceptional arithmetic frequencies or resonant phases require separate
spectral analysis and are not covered by the last claim. Within the stated
regime there is no energy-dependent mobility edge; introducing one would
require an altered hopping law or onsite modulation. In the supercritical
regime,
\[
\boxed{\gamma_L=\ln\left(\frac V{2J}\right)},\qquad
\boxed{\xi=\gamma_L^{-1}},
\]
so a typical envelope scales as
\(|\psi_{n+\ell}|/|\psi_n|\sim e^{-|\ell|/\xi}\).
For a normalized state
\[
\operatorname{IPR}=\sum_n|\psi_n|^4.
\]
It scales as \(1/N\) for an extended state on an \(N\)-site rational
approximant, but approaches a nonzero value when the localization length
stays finite.

For the supplied values,
\[
\boxed{g=\frac{V}{2J}=1.600000},
\qquad
\boxed{\gamma_L=\ln1.6=0.470003629},
\]
\[
\boxed{\xi=2.12764315\ \text{sites}}.
\]
The asymptotic neighboring-site envelope ratio is
\[
\boxed{e^{-1/\xi}=\frac{2J}{V}=0.625000},
\]
and eight sites away it is
\[
\boxed{e^{-8/\xi}=0.625^8=0.0232830644}.
\]
The dual recurrence has hopping
\[
\boxed{J_{\rm dual}=V/2=1.60000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}
\]
and modulation amplitude
\[
\boxed{V_{\rm dual}=2J=2.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
The irrational frequency controls quasiperiodicity. With the stated
transform, \(\phi\) is carried by the Fourier basis rather than the dual
onsite cosine; the critical ratio and Lyapunov exponent do not depend on
that phase origin.

graderFixtures.proofText: Fourier duality maps hopping \(J\) to modulation \(2J\) and modulation \(V\) to hopping \(V/2\), so \(V_c=2J\). For the declared Diophantine frequency and nonresonant full-measure phase set, the supercritical spectrum is pure point with exponentially localized eigenfunctions; exceptional frequencies or resonant phases are not covered. At \(V=3.2J\), \(\gamma_L=\ln1.6\), \(\xi=2.12764315\) sites, and the eight-site envelope ratio is \(0.0232830644\).
I model the quasiperiodic onsite terms as independent random numbers and miss the cosine factor of one half, placing the transition at V equals J.

WAVE:010235.title: Nonproportional damping needs complex modes
WAVE:010235.objective: Formulate and normalize the quadratic eigenproblem of a damped two-degree system, prove its bilinear orthogonality relation, and audit stability from energy.
WAVE:010235.statement:
A real two-degree mechanical system satisfies
\[
M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=0,
\]
where \(M,K\) are symmetric positive definite and \(C\) is symmetric
positive definite, but \(M^{-1}C\) and \(M^{-1}K\) do not commute. Do not
assume that the undamped normal modes diagonalize the damping.

Derive the quadratic eigenproblem for a motion \(q=u e^{\lambda t}\) and its
equivalent first-order state matrix. For two distinct roots \(\lambda_i\) and
\(\lambda_j\), prove the symmetric-polynomial bilinear relation
\[
u_j^T[(\lambda_i+\lambda_j)M+C]u_i=0.
\]
Explain why this is not ordinary Euclidean orthogonality and why conjugate
pairs are needed for a real response. Prove asymptotic stability using the
mechanical energy rather than numerical roots alone.

For
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.3\\0.3&0.4\end{pmatrix},\quad
K=\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix},
\]
derive the scalar characteristic polynomial and calculate all four roots to
at least six significant digits. Report the two decay rates and damped
angular frequencies, and verify that neither \(C\) nor \(K\) has been silently
replaced by a proportional-damping approximation.
permittedResults: For symmetric \(M,C,K\), transpose of \(Q(\lambda_j)u_j=0\) may be multiplied by another right eigenvector without complex conjugation.
If \(E=\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q+\tfrac12q^TKq\), then \(\dot E=-\dot q^TC\dot q\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Work directly with the symmetric quadratic matrix polynomial and use energy for the stability proof.
Linearize to first-order state space, compute conjugate eigenpairs, and recover the quadratic bilinear identity afterward.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Treats nonproportional damping as a genuine quadratic eigenproblem and uses its correct bilinear mode relation instead of importing undamped orthogonality.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Projects onto undamped modes and assumes the damping matrix becomes diagonal without a proportionality or commutation check.
commonErrors.consequence: The computed decay rates and mode shapes solve a different system.

commonErrors.description: Uses ordinary conjugate Euclidean orthogonality for complex quadratic modes.
commonErrors.consequence: Modal coefficients and reconstruction are not justified by the actual matrix polynomial.

hintTree.content: Subtract \(u_j^TQ(\lambda_j)u_i=0\) from \(u_j^TQ(\lambda_i)u_i=0\), then factor \(\lambda_i-\lambda_j\).
Use the state \(z=(q,\dot q)\) and lower block rows \(-M^{-1}K,-M^{-1}C\).
The determinant expands to \(2\lambda^4+1.3\lambda^3+14.11\lambda^2+5.6\lambda+20\).

WAVE:010235.canonicalSolution:
Substitution of \(q=u e^{\lambda t}\) gives
\[
\boxed{Q(\lambda)u=(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K)u=0}.
\]
With \(z=(q,\dot q)^T\), the equivalent state equation is
\[
\dot z=Az,\qquad
\boxed{A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-M^{-1}K&-M^{-1}C\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
This first-order matrix supplies four eigenvalues and state eigenvectors
\((u,\lambda u)^T\).

Because the quadratic coefficients are symmetric,
\(u_j^TQ(\lambda_j)=0\). Therefore
\[
0=u_j^T[Q(\lambda_i)-Q(\lambda_j)]u_i
=(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)
u_j^T[(\lambda_i+\lambda_j)M+C]u_i.
\]
For distinct roots,
\[
\boxed{u_j^T[(\lambda_i+\lambda_j)M+C]u_i=0}.
\]
The bilinear form depends on both eigenvalues and uses transpose, not a
fixed Euclidean inner product. It therefore does not license the usual
orthogonal modal projection. Since all matrices are real, nonreal roots and
vectors occur in conjugate pairs; conjugate coefficients must be combined
to produce real \(q(t)\).

For the stated matrices,
\[
\det(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K)
=\boxed{2\lambda^4+1.3\lambda^3+14.11\lambda^2+5.6\lambda+20}.
\]
Its roots are
\[
\boxed{\lambda=-0.252286544\pm1.39596947\,i},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda=-0.0727134563\pm2.22799349\,i}.
\]
Thus the decay rates are \(0.252286544\) and \(0.0727134563\)
\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), while the damped angular frequencies are
\(1.39596947\) and \(2.22799349\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

Stability does not rest on rounded roots. The matrices \(M\) and \(K\) are
positive definite. Also \(C_{11}>0\) and
\(\det C=0.5(0.4)-0.3^2=0.11>0\), so \(C\) is positive definite. Hence
\[
E=\frac12\dot q^TM\dot q+\frac12q^TKq>0,\qquad
\dot E=-\dot q^TC\dot q\le0.
\]
The only invariant set with \(\dot E=0\) has \(\dot q=0\); the equation then
forces \(Kq=0\), hence \(q=0\). LaSalle's argument gives asymptotic
stability.

Finally, direct multiplication shows
\([M^{-1}K,M^{-1}C]\ne0\) (for example its upper-right entry is nonzero).
Thus the undamped modes do not diagonalize \(C\), and the complex quadratic
mode calculation cannot be replaced by two independent scalar damped
oscillators.

graderFixtures.proofText: The modes solve \((\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K)u=0\). Symmetry gives \(u_j^T[(\lambda_i+\lambda_j)M+C]u_i=0\), and the roots are \(-0.252286544\pm1.39596947i\) and \(-0.0727134563\pm2.22799349i\).
I diagonalize K in the mass metric, assume C is diagonal in the same basis, and use ordinary Hermitian orthogonality without checking the nonzero commutator.

WAVE:010236.title: Circulatory coupling turns two stable oscillators into flutter
WAVE:010236.objective: Analyze a genuinely nonconservative two-coordinate coupling through right and left modes, orientation-dependent loop work, and the exact transition from bounded oscillation to flutter.
WAVE:010236.statement:
A two-coordinate undamped device is modeled by
\[
m\ddot q+(K+N)q=0,\qquad
K=\begin{pmatrix}k_x&0\\0&k_y\end{pmatrix},\qquad
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&n\\-n&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(m,k_x,k_y>0\), \(k_x\ne k_y\), and \(n\) has stiffness units.
The symmetric part \(K\) stores elastic energy. The skew positional term is
a circulatory follower-force idealization; it is not viscous damping and it
does not derive from a scalar potential.

Use \(q=u e^{\lambda t}\) to derive the characteristic polynomial and the
exact threshold in \(|n|\) separating two real squared frequencies from a
complex-conjugate pair of squared frequencies. In the bounded regime find
both frequencies and convenient right and left mode vectors. Prove the
appropriate left-right biorthogonality and show why ordinary Euclidean
orthogonality is unavailable. At threshold determine whether the repeated
mode is generically diagonalizable. Above threshold express the four
exponents as a complex quartet and identify the positive growth rate.

Let \(E=m\dot q^T\dot q/2+q^TKq/2\). Derive \(\dot E\), and calculate the
work done by the circulatory force around the counterclockwise circle
\(q=A(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^T\). Reconcile this nonzero loop work with
the algebraic identity \(q^TNq=0\).

For \(m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k_x=9.00\,\mathrm{N/m}\), and
\(k_y=25.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), calculate the threshold. At
\(n=6.00\,\mathrm{N/m}\), compute both frequencies and right-mode
component ratios. At \(n=10.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), compute the flutter growth
and oscillation rates. Check the \(n\to0\) limit and state the idealization
behind the positional follower force.
permittedResults: Distinct eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix have left and right eigenvectors satisfying \(\ell_i^Tr_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\).
If \(z=-a+ib\) with \(a>0\), then its square roots have real magnitude \(\sqrt{(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a)/2}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Analyze the nonsymmetric stiffness eigenvalues first, then take square roots of the lambda-squared branches and construct left-right modes.
Use the closed-loop work to diagnose nonconservativity, and independently confirm the same transition from the quartic characteristic polynomial.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects nonsymmetric positional coupling to biorthogonal modes and proves that its oriented loop work is the mechanism behind the exact flutter threshold.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the skew off-diagonal pair by equal signs or obtains a minus n-squared determinant.
commonErrors.consequence: The threshold, modes, and flutter quartet belong to a different reciprocal system.

commonErrors.description: Uses q transpose N q equals zero to assert zero power and a conserved positive mechanical energy.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores the velocity-position bilinear power and the nonzero work around a closed loop.

hintTree.content: The determinant is \((m\lambda^2+k_x)(m\lambda^2+k_y)+n^2\); the plus sign follows from the opposite off-diagonal signs.
For a stable squared frequency, set a right vector to \((1,(m\omega^2-k_x)/n)^T\) and solve the transposed problem for its left partner.
The identity \(q^TNq=0\) uses position twice; power contains \(\dot q^TNq\), with two generally different vectors.

WAVE:010236.canonicalSolution:
The exponential ansatz gives
\[
\left[m\lambda^2I+K+N\right]u=0,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{(m\lambda^2+k_x)(m\lambda^2+k_y)+n^2=0}.
\]
For a bounded harmonic mode \(\lambda=i\omega\), the roots are
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pm^2=\frac{k_x+k_y\pm
\sqrt{(k_x-k_y)^2-4n^2}}{2m}}.
\]
They remain distinct, positive, and real precisely when
\[
\boxed{|n|<n_c=\frac{|k_y-k_x|}{2}}.
\]
Their positive sum and product establish positivity in this regime. At
equality the matrix \(K+N\) has one repeated eigenvalue but, for
\(n\ne0\), only one eigenvector; the collision is defective rather than
an ordinary crossing.

For either stable root, convenient right and left vectors are
\[
r_j=\begin{pmatrix}1\\\dfrac{m\omega_j^2-k_x}{n}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\ell_j=\begin{pmatrix}1\\\dfrac{k_x-m\omega_j^2}{n}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
They solve \((K+N)r_j=m\omega_j^2r_j\) and
\(\ell_j^T(K+N)=m\omega_j^2\ell_j^T\). Subtracting the two eigenvalue
relations gives
\[
(\omega_j^2-\omega_i^2)\ell_i^Tr_j=0,
\]
so \(\boxed{\ell_i^Tr_j=0}\) for distinct modes. The right vectors are
not mutually Euclidean-orthogonal because the positional operator is not
symmetric.

Above threshold, put
\[
a=\frac{k_x+k_y}{2m},\qquad
b=\frac{\sqrt{4n^2-(k_x-k_y)^2}}{2m},\qquad R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.
\]
Then \(\lambda^2=-a\pm ib\), and the four exponents form the quartet
\[
\boxed{\lambda=\pm(\sigma+i\Omega),\quad
\lambda=\pm(\sigma-i\Omega)},
\]
where
\[
\boxed{\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{R-a}{2}}},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=\sqrt{\frac{R+a}{2}}}.
\]
The members with real part \(+\sigma\) flutter.

Multiplying the equation by \(\dot q^T\) gives
\[
\boxed{\dot E=-\dot q^TNq},
\]
which has no fixed sign. The nonconservative force is
\(-Nq=(-ny,nx)^T\). On the counterclockwise circle,
\[
(-Nq)\mathbin{\cdot}dq=nA^2\,d\theta,\qquad
\boxed{W_{\rm ccw}=2\pi nA^2}.
\]
Reversing the path reverses the work. Although \(q^TNq=0\) for a skew
matrix, power contains the distinct vectors \(\dot q\) and \(q\); the
zero quadratic form does not make the force conservative.

For the data, \(n_c=8.00000\,\mathrm{N/m}\). At \(n=6\),
\[
\omega_-^2=17-\sqrt{28},\qquad \omega_+^2=17+\sqrt{28},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\omega_-=3.42176817\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=4.72138779\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
With first component one, the right-mode second components are
\[
\boxed{r_{-,2}=0.451416230},\qquad
\boxed{r_{+,2}=2.21525044}.
\]
Their product is one, so their ordinary dot product is two, while each left
mode has the negative second component and annihilates the other right mode.

At \(n=10\), \(\lambda^2=-17\pm6i\), giving
\[
\boxed{\sigma=0.716852976\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=4.18495856\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
As \(n\to0\), the squared frequencies return to \(k_x/m\) and \(k_y/m\).
The skew stiffness is an ideal linearization of a maintained follower-force
mechanism; its actuator can supply the loop work, so this is not a closed
passive spring system.

graderFixtures.proofText: The determinant is \((m\lambda^2+k_x)(m\lambda^2+k_y)+n^2\), so \(n_c=|k_y-k_x|/2\). Right modes require left partners for biorthogonality, and \(\dot E=-\dot q^TNq\); the counterclockwise circular work is \(2\pi nA^2\).
I change both off-diagonal entries to plus n, obtain a minus n-squared determinant, use ordinary orthogonal modes, and say q transpose N q equals zero proves the force does no loop work.
