WAVE:010237.title: A connector duct splits the pressure modes of two acoustic cavities
WAVE:010237.objective: Derive the symmetric and antisymmetric pressure modes of two vented cavities joined by an acoustic inertance and audit the connector flow and conserved energy.
WAVE:010237.statement:
Two identical, rigid acoustic cavities are modeled as
lumped compliances $C=V/(\rho c^2)$. Each cavity vents to a large pressure
reservoir through an identical lossless neck of acoustic inertance $L$. A
third narrow duct of inertance $L_c$ joins the two cavities. Let $p_1,p_2$ be
gauge pressures, let $q_1,q_2$ be volume velocities directed outward through
the external necks, and let $q_c$ be positive from cavity 1 to cavity 2. The
linear element laws are $L\dot q_j=p_j$ and
$L_c\dot q_c=p_1-p_2$.

Use volume continuity to close the five first-order equations. Eliminate the
flows and derive the two pressure normal modes and their frequencies. Identify
which mode leaves the connector duct motionless and explain the result without
calling it an absence of pressure. Derive a conserved quadratic acoustic
energy, including every neck. Starting from
$p_1(0)=P_0$, $p_2(0)=0$, and all three initial volume velocities zero, obtain
$p_1(t)$, $p_2(t)$, and $q_c(t)$. Check both the sealed-connector limit
$L_c\to\infty$ and the dimensional units of the model.

For air with $\rho=1.20\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and
$c=343\,\mathrm{m/s}$, take each cavity volume to be
$V=2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Each exterior neck has effective length
$\ell=8.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m$ and area
$S=4.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$; the connector has
$\ell_c=0.120\,\mathrm m$ and $S_c=8.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
Using $L=\rho\ell/S$ and $L_c=\rho\ell_c/S_c$, calculate both frequencies
in radians per second and hertz. For $P_0=100\,\mathrm{Pa}$, calculate the
initial stored energy and the peak connector volume velocity. State explicitly
why the acoustic wavelength must be much larger than every cavity dimension,
so that pressure is approximately spatially uniform in each cavity, and give
the remaining small-amplitude assumptions needed for a lossless lumped
description.
permittedResults: An exchange-symmetric two-coordinate system diagonalizes into the subspaces $p_1=p_2$ and $p_1=-p_2$.
For lossless compliance and inertance elements, stored energy is quadratic in pressure and volume velocity.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the five first-order pressure-flow equations and diagonalize their second-order pressure reduction.
Use symmetric and antisymmetric pressure coordinates from the start, then reconstruct physical pressures and connector flow.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Diagonalizes the signed acoustic network, verifies its connector behavior through a complete energy ledger, and explicitly states that the acoustic wavelength is much larger than every cavity dimension and pressure is approximately spatially uniform in each cavity.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same connector-flow sign in both continuity equations or drives it with equal cavity pressures.
commonErrors.consequence: The mode ordering and connector response are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Omits connector inertance energy or treats an inertance as a compliance.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed conservation and dimensions fail.

hintTree.content: With the stated directions, continuity is $C\dot p_1=-q_1-q_c$ and $C\dot p_2=-q_2+q_c$.
Add and subtract the two second-order pressure equations before solving the initial-value problem.
Differentiate the proposed energy and use the five first-order element equations; every pressure-flow power term should cancel.

WAVE:010237.canonicalSolution:
The signed continuity and inertance equations are
$$
C\dot p_1=-q_1-q_c,\qquad C\dot p_2=-q_2+q_c,
$$
$$
L\dot q_1=p_1,\qquad L\dot q_2=p_2,\qquad
L_c\dot q_c=p_1-p_2.
$$
Differentiating continuity gives
$$
C\ddot p_1=-\frac{p_1}{L}-\frac{p_1-p_2}{L_c},\qquad
C\ddot p_2=-\frac{p_2}{L}+\frac{p_1-p_2}{L_c}.
$$
The symmetric vector $(1,1)$ therefore has
$$
\boxed{\omega_s^2=\frac{1}{LC}},
$$
whereas the antisymmetric vector $(1,-1)$ has
$$
\boxed{\omega_a^2=\frac{1/L+2/L_c}{C}}.
$$
Equal pressures produce no connector pressure drop, so $q_c=0$ in the
symmetric mode even though both cavity pressures and both exterior-neck flows
may be nonzero. Opposite pressures drive the connector and raise the
antisymmetric frequency.

The complete stored energy is
$$
\boxed{\mathcal E=\frac C2(p_1^2+p_2^2)
+\frac L2(q_1^2+q_2^2)+\frac{L_c}{2}q_c^2}.
$$
Its derivative is
$$
p_1(-q_1-q_c)+p_2(-q_2+q_c)+q_1p_1+q_2p_2
+q_c(p_1-p_2)=0,
$$
so no neck energy may be omitted.

The initial pressure vector is half symmetric plus half antisymmetric. Thus
$$
\boxed{p_1(t)=\frac{P_0}{2}
[\cos(\omega_st)+\cos(\omega_at)]},
$$
$$
\boxed{p_2(t)=\frac{P_0}{2}
[\cos(\omega_st)-\cos(\omega_at)]}.
$$
Because $p_1-p_2=P_0\cos(\omega_at)$ and $q_c(0)=0$,
$$
\boxed{q_c(t)=\frac{P_0}{L_c\omega_a}\sin(\omega_at)}.
$$
When $L_c\to\infty$, the connector flow vanishes and
$\omega_a\to\omega_s$: the two uncoupled identical cavity frequencies become
degenerate. Units also close because $LC$ has units of seconds squared and
$Lq^2$ has units of joules.

For the stated geometry,
$$
C=\frac{0.0200}{1.20(343)^2}
=1.41664\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^5/N},
$$
$$
L=240\ \mathrm{kg/m^4},\qquad L_c=180\ \mathrm{kg/m^4}.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{\omega_s=171.500\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{f_s=27.2951\ \mathrm{Hz}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\omega_a=328.397\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{f_a=52.2661\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
$$
At release, only cavity 1 stores energy, so
$$
\boxed{\mathcal E(0)=CP_0^2/2
=7.08322\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm J}.
$$
The connector amplitude is
$$
\boxed{q_{c,\max}=\frac{P_0}{L_c\omega_a}
=1.69172\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}}.
$$
The single-compliance approximation requires the acoustic wavelength to be
much larger than every cavity dimension, not merely larger than each neck.
This makes pressure approximately spatially uniform in each cavity. Each neck
must also be short compared with the wavelength so its flow can be lumped.
The remaining assumptions are small pressure perturbations, plane plug-like
neck flow, end corrections already included in effective lengths, and
negligible viscosity, thermal loss, and radiation.

graderFixtures.proofText: Continuity gives $C\dot p_1=-q_1-q_c$ and $C\dot p_2=-q_2+q_c$. Hence $\omega_s^2=1/(LC)$, $\omega_a^2=(1/L+2/L_c)/C$, and $q_c=P_0\sin(\omega_at)/(L_c\omega_a)$ for the stated release. The acoustic wavelength must be much larger than every cavity dimension so pressure is approximately spatially uniform in each cavity.
I send the connector flow out of both cavities, make equal pressures drive it, and omit the connector inertance from the energy.

WAVE:010238.title: A resistive shunt turns piezoelectric coupling into damping
WAVE:010238.objective: Eliminate an electrical relaxation coordinate and optimize the resulting frequency-dependent damping and resistor power.
WAVE:010238.statement:
A piezoelectric mechanical mode is modeled by
$$
m\ddot x+c_m\dot x+kx-\theta v=F(t),\qquad
C_p\dot v+\frac vR+\theta\dot x=0.
$$
Here $v$ is electrode voltage, $C_p>0$ is clamped capacitance, and $R>0$
is a shunt resistor. Use the $e^{i\omega t}$ phasor convention.

Eliminate voltage and derive the mechanical dynamic stiffness. Separate the
electrical contribution into a real stiffness increment and effective
viscous coefficient $c_e(\omega,R)$. Prove passivity by equating average
mechanical power removed by $c_e$ to resistor Joule power. Find the
resistance maximizing $c_e$ at prescribed frequency. Derive short- and
open-circuit natural frequencies, and explain why optimization at one
frequency is not frequency-independent damping.

Take $m=0.0500\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=500\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$c_m=0.200\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}$, $\theta=0.0200\,\mathrm{N/V}$,
$C_p=2.00\,\mu\mathrm F$, $F_0=1.00\,\mathrm N$, and
$\omega=100\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Calculate limiting natural frequencies,
optimal resistance, maximum electrical damping, displacement and voltage
amplitudes, and average resistor power. Do not use peak voltage in an RMS
power formula.
permittedResults: For peak phasors, resistor power is $|V|^2/(2R)$.
For positive $a$, $R/(1+a^2R^2)$ is maximal at $R=1/a$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute the voltage phasor into mechanical impedance and optimize its imaginary part.
Compute resistor power and identify the equivalent mechanical damping.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Eliminates the electrical coordinate and verifies optimized damping with an exact power balance.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Obtains negative damping from a positive resistor.
commonErrors.consequence: A passive shunt becomes an energy source.

commonErrors.description: Reverses open and short stiffness or omits the one-half peak-phasor factor.
commonErrors.consequence: Limiting frequencies or energy balance fails.

hintTree.content: The electrical equation gives $V=-i\omega\theta X/(R^{-1}+i\omega C_p)$.
Rationalize $i\omega\theta^2/(R^{-1}+i\omega C_p)$.
At $\omega RC_p=1$, $k_e=\theta^2/(2C_p)$ and $c_e=\theta^2/(2\omega C_p)$.

WAVE:010238.canonicalSolution:
Electrical balance gives
$$
\boxed{V=-\frac{i\omega\theta}{R^{-1}+i\omega C_p}X}.
$$
Substitution yields
$$
\left[k-m\omega^2+i\omega c_m+
\frac{i\omega\theta^2}{R^{-1}+i\omega C_p}\right]X=F_0.
$$
Writing $G=1/R$,
$$
\frac{i\omega\theta^2}{G+i\omega C_p}
=\frac{\omega^2\theta^2C_p}{G^2+\omega^2C_p^2}
+i\omega\frac{\theta^2G}{G^2+\omega^2C_p^2}.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{k_e=\frac{\omega^2\theta^2C_p}{G^2+\omega^2C_p^2}},\qquad
\boxed{c_e=\frac{\theta^2R}{1+(\omega RC_p)^2}}.
$$
Both are nonnegative. Moreover
$$
\frac{|V|^2}{2R}
=\frac{\omega^2\theta^2|X|^2G}{2(G^2+\omega^2C_p^2)}
=\boxed{\frac12c_e\omega^2|X|^2},
$$
so resistor and mechanical loss agree exactly.

Optimization gives
$$
\boxed{R_{\rm opt}=\frac1{\omega C_p}},\qquad
\boxed{c_{e,\max}=\frac{\theta^2}{2\omega C_p}}.
$$
The short circuit has
$\omega_{\rm sc}=\sqrt{k/m}$. Open circuit contributes
$\theta^2/C_p$, so
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\rm oc}=\sqrt{(k+\theta^2/C_p)/m}}.
$$

Numerically,
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\rm sc}=100.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\quad
\boxed{\omega_{\rm oc}=118.322\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{R_{\rm opt}=5.00000\,\mathrm{k\Omega}},\quad
\boxed{c_{e,\max}=1.00000\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}}.
$$
At the optimum, $k_e=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and the dynamic-stiffness magnitude
is $\sqrt{100^2+120^2}=156.205\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Hence
$$
\boxed{|X|=6.40184\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{|V|=45.2679\,\mathrm V},
$$
$$
\boxed{\overline P_R=|V|^2/(2R)=0.204918\,\mathrm W}.
$$
Because the optimum is tied to $\omega RC_p=1$, one fixed resistor cannot
maximize or imitate constant damping at all frequencies.

graderFixtures.proofText: Elimination gives $k_e=\omega^2\theta^2C_p/(G^2+\omega^2C_p^2)$, $c_e=\theta^2G/(G^2+\omega^2C_p^2)$, optimum $R=1/(\omega C_p)$, and $|V|^2/(2R)=c_e\omega^2|X|^2/2$.
I obtain negative damping from R>0, say short circuit is stiffer, and compute power as peak voltage squared divided by R.

WAVE:010239.title: A gyroscopic coupling splits modes without doing work
WAVE:010239.objective: Find the normal frequencies and phase-quadrature polarizations of an anisotropic gyroscopic oscillator and audit its conserved energy.
WAVE:010239.statement:
Two unit-mass coordinates obey
$$
\ddot x-2\Omega\dot y+\omega_x^2x=0,
\qquad
\ddot y+2\Omega\dot x+\omega_y^2y=0,
$$
with $\omega_x,\omega_y>0$ and real $\Omega$. This is a skew, velocity-based
coupling; it is not a symmetric spring coupling and it is not damping.

Insert $(x,y)=\operatorname{Re}[(X,Y)e^{-i\sigma t}]$ and derive the
frequency equation. Solve explicitly for both values of $\sigma^2$ and prove
they remain positive. Obtain $Y/X$ for each mode, including its complex phase,
and interpret the coordinate motion as an ellipse with a definite sense of
rotation. Derive a conserved quadratic energy directly from the differential
equations and explain why the gyroscopic force contributes zero instantaneous
power even though it changes both frequencies.

For $\omega_x=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$\omega_y=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$\Omega=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute both positive normal frequencies
and both ratios $Y/X$ when $X$ is chosen real and positive. Verify the product
of the two squared frequencies. State what becomes singular in the displayed
polarization formula as $\Omega\to0$ and how the uncoupled limit should instead
be read.
permittedResults: The roots of $z^2-Bz+C=0$ are positive when $B>0$, $C>0$, and the discriminant is nonnegative with $B$ exceeding its square root.
A skew matrix $G$ satisfies $u^{\mathsf T}Gu=0$ for every real vector $u$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use a complex harmonic ansatz and solve the quadratic in squared frequency.
Diagonalize the first-order Hamiltonian system and recover coordinate polarizations.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Solves the skew velocity-coupled eigenproblem, retains complex polarization phase, and proves the coupling performs zero power.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the velocity coupling as an ordinary symmetric spring.
commonErrors.consequence: Both the frequency polynomial and polarization are incorrect.

commonErrors.description: Calls the skew coupling damping or omits its power cancellation.
commonErrors.consequence: The conserved energy and physical mechanism are misidentified.

hintTree.content: The determinant is $(\omega_x^2-\sigma^2)(\omega_y^2-\sigma^2)-4\Omega^2\sigma^2$.
Choose real $X$ and solve the first row for the generally imaginary $Y$.
Multiply the two equations by $\dot x$ and $\dot y$ and add.

WAVE:010239.canonicalSolution:
The complex-amplitude equations are
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\omega_x^2-\sigma^2&2i\Omega\sigma\\
-2i\Omega\sigma&\omega_y^2-\sigma^2
\end{pmatrix}\binom X Y=0.
$$
Thus, with $z=\sigma^2$,
$$
z^2-(\omega_x^2+\omega_y^2+4\Omega^2)z
+\omega_x^2\omega_y^2=0.
$$
Writing $B=\omega_x^2+\omega_y^2+4\Omega^2$, the two roots are
$$
\boxed{\sigma_\pm^2=\frac{B\pm
\sqrt{B^2-4\omega_x^2\omega_y^2}}2}.
$$
Their sum and product are positive, and
$B>2\omega_x\omega_y$, so both roots are strictly positive.

The first row gives
$$
\boxed{\frac YX=i\frac{\omega_x^2-\sigma^2}{2\Omega\sigma}}.
$$
For real $X$, $Y$ is purely imaginary: the coordinates are one quarter-cycle
out of phase. The sign of its imaginary coefficient fixes the traversal sense
of the polarization ellipse and reverses between the two branches.

Multiplication by velocities and addition yields
$$
\frac d{dt}\left[\frac12(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)
+\frac12(\omega_x^2x^2+\omega_y^2y^2)\right]=0,
$$
because $(-2\Omega\dot y)\dot x+(2\Omega\dot x)\dot y=0$. Hence
$$
\boxed{E=\frac12(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\omega_x^2x^2+\omega_y^2y^2)}
$$
is conserved although the mode spectrum changes.

For the data, $B=38$ and the discriminant is $544$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\sigma_-=2.70889\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_+=5.53732\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The polarizations are
$$
\boxed{(Y/X)_-=0.306750i},\qquad
\boxed{(Y/X)_+=-1.95599i}.
$$
The numerical squared-frequency product is
$7.33810\times30.6619=225.000=\omega_x^2\omega_y^2$.
As $\Omega\to0$, the quotient formula is a zero-over-zero representation on
the branch approaching $\omega_x$ and a divergent normalization on the branch
approaching $\omega_y$. The physical limit is simply the two Cartesian
uncoupled modes; one should return to the matrix equations rather than divide
by a vanishing coupling.

The complex-amplitude equations are
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\omega_x^2-\sigma^2&2i\Omega\sigma\\
-2i\Omega\sigma&\omega_y^2-\sigma^2
\end{pmatrix}\binom X Y=0.
$$
Thus, with $z=\sigma^2$,
$$
z^2-(\omega_x^2+\omega_y^2+4\Omega^2)z
+\omega_x^2\omega_y^2=0.
$$
Writing $B=\omega_x^2+\omega_y^2+4\Omega^2$, the two roots are
$$
\boxed{\sigma_\pm^2=\frac{B\pm
\sqrt{B^2-4\omega_x^2\omega_y^2}}2}.
$$
Their sum and product are positive, and
$B>2\omega_x\omega_y$, so both roots are strictly positive.

The first row gives
$$
\boxed{\frac YX=i\frac{\omega_x^2-\sigma^2}{2\Omega\sigma}}.
$$
For real $X$, $Y$ is purely imaginary: the coordinates are one quarter-cycle
out of phase. The sign of its imaginary coefficient fixes the traversal sense
of the polarization ellipse and reverses between the two branches.

Multiplication by velocities and addition yields
$$
\frac d{dt}\left[\frac12(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)
+\frac12(\omega_x^2x^2+\omega_y^2y^2)\right]=0,
$$
because $(-2\Omega\dot y)\dot x+(2\Omega\dot x)\dot y=0$. Hence
$$
\boxed{E=\frac12(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\omega_x^2x^2+\omega_y^2y^2)}
$$
is conserved although the mode spectrum changes.

For the data, $B=38$ and the discriminant is $544$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\sigma_-=2.70889\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_+=5.53732\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The polarizations are
$$
\boxed{(Y/X)_-=0.306750i},\qquad
\boxed{(Y/X)_+=-1.95599i}.
$$
The numerical squared-frequency product is
$7.33810\times30.6619=225.000=\omega_x^2\omega_y^2$.

the branch approaching $\omega_x$ and a divergent normalization on the branch
approaching $\omega_y$. The physical limit is simply the two Cartesian
uncoupled modes; one should return to the matrix equations rather than divide
by a vanishing coupling.
I replace the velocity terms by a symmetric spring, take both mode vectors real, and interpret the frequency split as energy loss.

WAVE:010240.title: An internal dark mode pins a driven carrier
WAVE:010240.objective: Separate rigid, bright, and dark motions of two resonators on a free carrier and derive the carrier antiresonance.
WAVE:010240.statement:
A free carrier of mass $M$ translates with coordinate
$X$. Two identical internal masses $m$ have absolute coordinates $x_1,x_2$;
each is attached to the carrier by a spring $k$. There is no attachment to
ground and no damping. A harmonic force $F(t)=\operatorname{Re}(F_0e^{-i\omega t})$
acts only on the carrier.

Introduce symmetric and antisymmetric internal coordinates. Find all free
normal frequencies, including the rigid-translation zero mode, and identify
which finite-frequency mode is dark to a carrier force. Eliminate the internal
coordinates in the forced symmetric sector to derive the exact carrier
receptance $X/F_0$. Locate its poles and its finite-frequency zero. Explain why
that zero is an antiresonance rather than a normal-mode pole and why the
undamped steady-state formula is not valid exactly at a pole. Track the phase
sign of $X/F_0$ on either side of the antiresonance.

For $M=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, and
$k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$, give the dark frequency, bright frequency, and the
carrier displacement per unit force at $\omega=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
At the antiresonance state the carrier is fixed; state how the two internal
mass amplitudes must relate for the free dark mode.
permittedResults: Exchange symmetry splits identical internal coordinates into invariant symmetric and antisymmetric sectors.
Poles and zeros of a receptance depend on both system modes and the chosen drive-observation pair.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use exchange-symmetry coordinates before solving either free or forced motion.
Form the dynamic-stiffness matrix and calculate the carrier cofactor over determinant.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Separates dark and bright symmetry sectors, derives the carrier transfer-function zero at the dark internal frequency, and gives the three correct receptance-sign intervals around that zero and the bright pole.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses an in-phase internal vector for the carrier-dark mode.
commonErrors.consequence: The wrong sector and wrong frequency are identified as dark.

commonErrors.description: Calls the receptance zero a resonant pole or cancels it away.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested antiresonance mechanism is lost.

hintTree.content: In the symmetric forced sector, $q=kX/(k-m\omega^2)$.
Keep the numerator when combining the carrier dynamic stiffness.

WAVE:010240.canonicalSolution:
The equations are
$$
m\ddot x_j+k(x_j-X)=0,\qquad
M\ddot X+k(2X-x_1-x_2)=F.
$$
With $q=(x_1+x_2)/2$ and $d=(x_1-x_2)/2$, the antisymmetric coordinate obeys
$$
m\ddot d+kd=0.
$$
It has the dark frequency
$$
\boxed{\omega_d=\sqrt{k/m}},
$$
with $X=q=0$ and $x_1=-x_2$. The symmetric sector contains rigid translation
$x_1=x_2=X$ at zero frequency and a bright internal mode at
$$
\boxed{\omega_b^2=k\left(\frac1m+\frac2M\right)}.
$$

For harmonic response away from poles,
$(k-m\omega^2)q=kX$. Substitution into the carrier equation gives
$$
\frac XF=\frac1{-M\omega^2+2k-2k^2/(k-m\omega^2)}
=\boxed{\frac{k-m\omega^2}
{\omega^2[Mm\omega^2-k(M+2m)]}}.
$$
The denominator displays the rigid pole at zero and the bright pole at
$\omega_b$. The numerator vanishes at
$$
\boxed{\omega_a=\sqrt{k/m}=\omega_d}.
$$
This zero is the carrier antiresonance. Internal antisymmetric motion can exist
there, but the symmetric carrier drive has zero overlap with that free dark
mode; in the forced limit the internal spring forces cancel the applied
carrier response. Exactly at an undamped pole no finite steady harmonic state
exists without specifying transients or damping. For positive frequency, the
real receptance has the explicit sign pattern
$$
\boxed{X/F_0<0\quad(0<\omega<10.0000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})},
$$
$$
\boxed{X/F_0>0\quad(10.0000<\omega<12.2474\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{X/F_0<0\quad(\omega>12.2474\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})}.
$$
The endpoints are, respectively, the rigid pole at zero, the antiresonance
zero, and the bright pole. This interval statement is more precise than merely
saying that a sign changes whenever a numerator or denominator factor is
crossed.

Numerically,
$$
\boxed{\omega_d=\omega_a=10.0000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_b=12.2474\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
At $\omega=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{\frac XF=\frac{36}{64(256-600)}
=-1.63517\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m/N}}.
$$
The negative sign means the carrier displacement is opposite the force phasor
under the adopted $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention. The free dark state requires
equal and opposite internal amplitudes, not two equal in-phase amplitudes.

WAVE:010241.title: A square oscillator ring splits into four symmetry sectors
WAVE:010241.objective: Diagonalize a square-symmetric four-oscillator network and interpret degeneracy, diagonal coupling, and forcing selection by symmetry.
WAVE:010241.statement:
Four identical scalar oscillators sit at the vertices
of a square and are labeled $j=0,1,2,3$ cyclically. Each mass $m$ has an
on-site spring $K$. Neighboring vertices are coupled by edge springs $k$, and
opposite vertices by diagonal springs $\kappa$. Their small scalar coordinates
$q_j$ obey
$$
m\ddot q_j+Kq_j+k(2q_j-q_{j-1}-q_{j+1})
+\kappa(q_j-q_{j+2})=0,
$$
with indices modulo four.

Use the four irreducible Fourier sectors of the cyclic square symmetry to
find every normal frequency. Give a real basis for the degenerate sector and
explain how its complex combinations represent a circulating phase pattern,
not literal rigid rotation of the masses. State exactly which sectors are
shifted by the diagonal springs and why. For a harmonic drive with spatial
pattern $(1,0,-1,0)$, identify the accessible modes using projection rather
than frequency guessing.

For $K=4.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $k=3.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$\kappa=1.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, list the frequencies
in nondecreasing order with degeneracies. Normalize the complex eigenvectors
to unit Euclidean norm and state the modal mass in that convention. Audit the
limits $k=\kappa=0$ and $\kappa=0$.
permittedResults: The vectors $v_j^{(\ell)}=2^{-1}e^{i\ell\pi j/2}$ diagonalize a four-by-four circulant matrix.
A drive excites only modes with nonzero mass-weighted projection onto its spatial force vector.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize the circulant stiffness matrix with discrete Fourier vectors.
Use real symmetry-adapted coordinates and then pair the degenerate odd modes.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the $C_4$ Fourier sectors to obtain all four mode frequencies and correctly connects symmetry to degeneracy, bond extension, and forcing selection.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds diagonal stiffness to every symmetry sector.
commonErrors.consequence: Modes with equal opposite-vertex motion are assigned stretched diagonal springs.

commonErrors.description: Interprets a complex scalar eigenvector as literal rigid rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: The mathematical phase convention is confused with absent vector mechanics.

hintTree.content: Insert $q_j=Ae^{i(\ell\pi j/2-\omega t)}$.
For the opposite vertex, the phase factor is $e^{i\ell\pi}=(-1)^\ell$.
Expand $(1,0,-1,0)$ in the two real vectors of the odd sector.

WAVE:010241.canonicalSolution:
Take the normalized cyclic eigenvectors
$$
v_j^{(\ell)}=\frac12e^{i\ell\pi j/2},\qquad \ell=0,1,2,3.
$$
Substitution gives the eigenvalue formula
$$
\boxed{\omega_\ell^2=\frac{K+2k[1-\cos(\ell\pi/2)]
+\kappa[1-(-1)^\ell]}{m}}.
$$
The four sectors are therefore
$$
\omega_0^2=\frac Km,
$$
$$
\omega_1^2=\omega_3^2=\frac{K+2k+2\kappa}{m},
$$
and
$$
\omega_2^2=\frac{K+4k}{m}.
$$
The odd sectors are a conjugate degenerate pair. A real basis is proportional
to
$$
(1,0,-1,0),\qquad (0,1,0,-1).
$$
Their combinations with relative phase $\pm\pi/2$ reproduce $v^{(1)}$ and
$v^{(3)}$, so the scalar pattern advances around the square in phase. That is
a circulating phase pattern in coordinate space; the model does not assign
two-dimensional rigid-body motion to each mass.

Opposite vertices move equally in the $\ell=0$ and $\ell=2$ sectors because
$(-1)^\ell=1$, so diagonal springs are unextended there. They move oppositely
for odd $\ell$, and the diagonal contribution is $2\kappa$. The drive
$(1,0,-1,0)$ is exactly one real vector in the odd two-dimensional eigenspace.
It has zero projection on the uniform and checkerboard sectors and excites
only the degenerate odd frequency.

For the given values,
$$
\boxed{\omega_0=\sqrt2=1.41421\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\omega_1=\omega_3=\sqrt6=2.44949\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}
\quad\text{(double)},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{\omega_2=\sqrt8=2.82843\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The factor $1/2$ makes $\sum_j|v_j^{(\ell)}|^2=1$. Consequently the kinetic
energy of a modal amplitude $Q_\ell$ is
$\tfrac12m|\dot Q_\ell|^2$. The modal mass in this convention is
$\boxed{m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}}$. Complex amplitudes are a convenient
representation; real motion combines conjugate sectors.

If $k=\kappa=0$, all four independent on-site oscillators have frequency
$\sqrt{K/m}$. If only $\kappa=0$, the usual four-site ring spectrum remains:
the odd pair stays degenerate at $(K+2k)/m$, while uniform and checkerboard
sectors lie at $K/m$ and $(K+4k)/m$. These checks also confirm which bonds are
extended in each symmetry pattern.

WAVE:010242.title: Rotating the stiffness axes creates beating without an impulse
WAVE:010242.objective: Project initial data through a sudden rotation of anisotropic normal axes and audit modal energy, quench work, and beating.
WAVE:010242.statement:
A two-dimensional oscillator of mass $m$ initially
has laboratory-axis frequencies $\omega_x<\omega_y$. It is at
$\mathbf r(0^-)=(A,0)$ with $\dot{\mathbf r}(0^-)=0$. At $t=0$ the principal
axes of the stiffness tensor are rotated counterclockwise through an angle
$\beta$, while its two eigenvalues remain $m\omega_x^2$ and
$m\omega_y^2$. The parameter change is instantaneous but applies no momentum
impulse, so position and velocity are continuous.

Resolve the post-quench motion along the new principal axes and transform it
back to the laboratory coordinates. Calculate each modal energy, the total
post-quench energy, and the work done by the sudden parameter change. Show
the beating form when $\beta=\pi/4$. State which quantities are continuous or
conserved at the quench, and explain why angular momentum need not be
conserved afterward.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $A=0.100\,\mathrm m$,
$\omega_x=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\omega_y=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$\beta=\pi/4$, report the initial energy, both post-quench modal energies,
total work, explicit $x(t)$ and $y(t)$, and the state at $t=\pi$ and
$t=2\pi$. Audit $\beta=0$, $\omega_x=\omega_y$, and a quasistatic rotation
as distinct limits.
permittedResults: For an instantaneous stiffness change at fixed position, the work is the change in potential energy.
The identities $\cos a\pm\cos b=2\cos[(a+b)/2]\cos[(a-b)/2]$ or its sine counterpart expose beats.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize the post-quench stiffness tensor and project the unchanged initial state.
Use the rotated stiffness matrix directly, then rewrite its solution in principal coordinates.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Projects the continuous state onto suddenly rotated stiffness axes and correctly accounts for modal energy, actuator work, and laboratory-frame beating.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Conserves mechanical energy through the instantaneous stiffness rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: The actuator work at fixed nonzero displacement is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Rotates the physical position vector along with the apparatus at the quench.
commonErrors.consequence: Continuity of the mass coordinate is violated.

hintTree.content: Use $\mathbf e_1=(\cos\beta,\sin\beta)$ and $\mathbf e_2=(-\sin\beta,\cos\beta)$.
Project $(A,0)$ onto both new axes before evolving them.
At $\beta=\pi/4$, convert sums and differences of cosines.

WAVE:010242.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$
\mathbf e_1=(\cos\beta,\sin\beta),\qquad
\mathbf e_2=(-\sin\beta,\cos\beta).
$$
The continuous initial coordinate has projections
$q_1(0)=A\cos\beta$ and $q_2(0)=-A\sin\beta$, with both modal velocities zero.
Thus
$$
q_1=A\cos\beta\cos(\omega_xt),\qquad
q_2=-A\sin\beta\cos(\omega_yt).
$$
Transforming back gives
$$
\boxed{x(t)=A[\cos^2\beta\cos(\omega_xt)+
\sin^2\beta\cos(\omega_yt)]},
$$
$$
\boxed{y(t)=A\sin\beta\cos\beta[
\cos(\omega_xt)-\cos(\omega_yt)]}.
$$
The conserved post-quench modal energies are
$$
\boxed{E_1=\tfrac12m\omega_x^2A^2\cos^2\beta},\qquad
\boxed{E_2=\tfrac12m\omega_y^2A^2\sin^2\beta}.
$$
Before the change $E_i=\tfrac12m\omega_x^2A^2$. Hence the external actuator
does work
$$
\boxed{W=E_1+E_2-E_i
=\tfrac12mA^2(\omega_y^2-\omega_x^2)\sin^2\beta}.
$$
Position and velocity are continuous, but energy is not conserved across the
parameter change. Afterward the new time-independent Hamiltonian conserves
$E_1+E_2$. The anisotropic stiffness generally exerts torque about the origin,
so angular momentum is not a post-quench invariant.

For the data,
$$
\boxed{E_i=0.0900\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_1=0.0450\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_2=0.1250\,\mathrm J},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{E_f=0.1700\,\mathrm J},\qquad \boxed{W=0.0800\,\mathrm J}.
$$
At $\beta=\pi/4$,
$$
x(t)=0.0500[\cos(3t)+\cos(5t)]
=\boxed{0.100\cos(4t)\cos t\ \mathrm m},
$$
$$
y(t)=0.0500[\cos(3t)-\cos(5t)]
=\boxed{0.100\sin(4t)\sin t\ \mathrm m}.
$$
Consequently $\mathbf r(\pi)=(-0.100,0)\,\mathrm m$ and
$\mathbf r(2\pi)=(+0.100,0)\,\mathrm m$, with zero velocity at both times.

When $\beta=0$, only the original $\omega_x$ mode is occupied and $W=0$.
When $\omega_x=\omega_y$, the stiffness is isotropic, rotating its axes
changes no physical tensor, and again $W=0$. A quasistatic rotation is a
different protocol: the state can evolve throughout the change and need not
receive the sudden-quench energy partition above.

Position and velocity are continuous, but energy is not conserved across the
parameter change. Afterward the new time-independent Hamiltonian conserves
$E_1+E_2$. The anisotropic stiffness generally exerts torque about the origin,
so angular momentum is not a post-quench invariant.

For the data,
$$
\boxed{E_i=0.0900\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_1=0.0450\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_2=0.1250\,\mathrm J},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{E_f=0.1700\,\mathrm J},\qquad \boxed{W=0.0800\,\mathrm J}.
$$
At $\beta=\pi/4$,
$$
x(t)=0.0500[\cos(3t)+\cos(5t)]
=\boxed{0.100\cos(4t)\cos t\ \mathrm m},
$$
$$
y(t)=0.0500[\cos(3t)-\cos(5t)]
=\boxed{0.100\sin(4t)\sin t\ \mathrm m}.
$$
Consequently $\mathbf r(\pi)=(-0.100,0)\,\mathrm m$ and
$\mathbf r(2\pi)=(+0.100,0)\,\mathrm m$, with zero velocity at both times.

When $\beta=0$, only the original $\omega_x$ mode is occupied and $W=0$.
When $\omega_x=\omega_y$, the stiffness is isotropic, rotating its axes
changes no physical tensor, and again $W=0$. A quasistatic rotation is a
different protocol: the state can evolve throughout the change and need not
receive the sudden-quench energy partition above.
I rotate the mass position with the spring axes and conserve its old energy across the instantaneous parameter change.

WAVE:010243.title: A stable neighbor can rescue one negative-stiffness coordinate
WAVE:010243.objective: Derive when conservative coupling stabilizes a negative-stiffness coordinate and connect the soft normal mode to divergent static compliance at threshold.
WAVE:010243.statement:
Two equal masses $m$ have coordinates $x,y$ and potential
$$
U=\frac12(-k)x^2+\frac12k_s y^2+\frac12K(x-y)^2,
$$
where $k,k_s,K>0$. The isolated $x$ coordinate is unstable; the $y$
coordinate is stable. No gyroscopic force, damping, active feedback, or
time-periodic switching is present.

Construct the stiffness matrix and find necessary and sufficient conditions
for linear stability. Assuming $k_s>k$, derive the exact critical coupling
$K_c$. Obtain both stiffness eigenvalues, angular frequencies, and mode-shape
ratios $y/x$. Identify the zero-mode shape at threshold. Apply a static force
$F$ to $x$, derive the compliance $x/F$, and show how it diverges on the
stable side of the threshold. Explain why a large coupling cannot stabilize
the pair when $k_s\le k$.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$k_s=80.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $K=30.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, calculate $K_c$,
both frequencies, both $y/x$ ratios, and $x/F$. Repeat only the unstable
eigenvalue calculation for $K=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and report its exponential
growth rate. Distinguish this conservative stiffness problem from a
first-order two-level conversion or detuned Rabi-oscillation model.
permittedResults: A real symmetric $2\times2$ stiffness matrix is positive definite exactly when its first principal minor and determinant are positive.
Static compliance is an entry of the inverse stiffness matrix and diverges when a loaded soft mode makes the determinant vanish.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply Sylvester's criterion before solving the normal modes.
Diagonalize the stiffness matrix and then interpret its inverse spectrally near the soft mode.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses positive-definite stiffness, rather than coupling magnitude alone, to derive stabilization and connects the vanishing eigenvalue to static susceptibility.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Claims any positive coupling stabilizes the negative coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: The determinant can remain negative and one mode still grows.

commonErrors.description: Recasts the task as detuned two-state conversion with a Rabi frequency and transfer probability.
commonErrors.consequence: A second-order stiffness stability problem is replaced by a materially different first-order model.

hintTree.content: The matrix entries are $K-k,-K,-K,K+k_s$.
Its determinant simplifies to $K(k_s-k)-kk_s$.
Use the lower eigenvalue to convert negative squared frequency into a real growth rate.

WAVE:010243.canonicalSolution:
The equations are $m\ddot{\mathbf q}+A\mathbf q=0$ with
$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}K-k&-K\\-K&K+k_s\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Its determinant and trace are
$$
\det A=K(k_s-k)-kk_s,
\qquad \operatorname{tr}A=2K+k_s-k.
$$
If $k_s>k$, positivity of the determinant implies $K>k$, so the first
principal minor is then positive automatically. Thus stability is equivalent
to
$$
\boxed{K>K_c=\frac{kk_s}{k_s-k}}.
$$
If $k_s\le k$, the determinant is negative for every $K>0$ (or equals
$-kk_s$ when $k_s=k$), so one unstable direction always remains. Coupling
cannot create net positive curvature when the stable coordinate is not stiff
enough to carry the negative one.

The two stiffness eigenvalues are
$$
\boxed{\lambda_\pm=\frac{2K+k_s-k
\pm\sqrt{(k+k_s)^2+4K^2}}{2}},
\qquad \omega_\pm=\sqrt{\lambda_\pm/m}.
$$
For either eigenvalue a convenient mode ratio is
$$
\boxed{\frac{y}{x}=\frac{K-k-\lambda}{K}}.
$$
At $K=K_c$, the zero mode satisfies
$$
\boxed{(x,y)\propto(1,k/k_s)}.
$$
The coordinates move together enough that the stable spring supplies the
curvature missing from $x$.

Under a static force $(F,0)^T$, inversion gives
$$
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{F}{K(k_s-k)-kk_s}
\begin{pmatrix}K+k_s\\K\end{pmatrix},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\frac{x}{F}=\frac{K+k_s}{K(k_s-k)-kk_s}}.
$$
It diverges like $(K-K_c)^{-1}$ as the stable side approaches the soft-mode
threshold. This is a zero-frequency susceptibility, not a population-transfer
probability or a beat maximum.

Numerically, $K_c=26.6667\,\mathrm{N/m}$. For $K=30.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$$
\lambda_-=1.69048\,\mathrm{N/m},\qquad
\lambda_+=118.310\,\mathrm{N/m},
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{\omega_-=0.919370\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=7.69121\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The corresponding ratios are
$$
\boxed{(y/x)_-=0.276984},\qquad
\boxed{(y/x)_+=-3.61032},
$$
and the static compliance is
$$
\boxed{x/F=0.550000\,\mathrm{m/N}}.
$$
For $K=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, the lower stiffness eigenvalue is
$\lambda_-=-3.85165\,\mathrm{N/m}$. The unstable modal coordinate grows as
$e^{\sigma t}$ with
$$
\boxed{\sigma=\sqrt{-\lambda_-/m}=1.38774\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
All results come from a second-order conservative stiffness matrix; no
Hermitian two-state detuning, Rabi frequency, conversion ceiling, or first
transfer maximum is part of this exercise.

WAVE:010244.title: One shared radiation channel leaves half an excitation dark
WAVE:010244.objective: Diagonalize collective radiation damping and track how destructive interference traps a dark-mode energy fraction.
WAVE:010244.statement:
Two identical weakly excited resonators radiate into the same
single far-field channel. After removing their common carrier oscillation,
their complex envelopes obey
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix}
=-\frac\gamma2
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma>0.
$$
Use the normalization $E=|a_1|^2+|a_2|^2$ and take the radiated field
amplitude proportional to $a_1+a_2$.

Find orthonormal bright and dark coordinates, their amplitude decay rates,
and the radiated-power law required by the energy balance. Starting from
$a_1(0)=A$, $a_2(0)=0$, derive $a_1(t)$, $a_2(t)$, stored energy, cumulative
radiated energy, and long-time state. Explain why one resonator's late
amplitude can have the opposite sign even though the damping is passive.
Also analyze a purely antisymmetric initial state.

For real $A=1.00$, $\gamma=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $t=0.300\,\mathrm s$,
report both amplitudes, stored and radiated energy fractions, and instantaneous
radiated power in the stated normalization. State what changes if the two
resonators have unequal frequencies, independent loss, or more than one
radiation channel.
permittedResults: The matrix of all ones has eigenvalues $2$ and $0$ on the symmetric and antisymmetric vectors.
With the stated energy normalization, radiated power is $-dE/dt$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the eigenvectors of the all-ones damping matrix.
Infer the dark component by projecting the initial state, then close the result with the radiation-energy integral.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Diagonalizes the rank-one dissipative coupling and uses coherent interference plus energy conservation to identify the radiative and protected subspaces.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Lets each resonator decay independently at the same rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The common-channel interference and dark subspace disappear.

commonErrors.description: Uses the amplitude decay rate as the bright energy decay rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The radiated-power and cumulative-energy ledger are wrong by a factor of two.

hintTree.content: Set $b=(a_1+a_2)/\sqrt2$ and $d=(a_1-a_2)/\sqrt2$.
Only $b$ decays; transform the two coordinates back after solving.
Integrate $2\gamma|b|^2$ to audit the cumulative radiation.

WAVE:010244.canonicalSolution:
Define
$$
b=\frac{a_1+a_2}{\sqrt2},\qquad
d=\frac{a_1-a_2}{\sqrt2}.
$$
The transformation is unitary, so $E=|b|^2+|d|^2$. The equations become
$$
\boxed{\dot b=-\gamma b},\qquad \boxed{\dot d=0}.
$$
Thus the bright amplitude has decay rate $\gamma$ and its energy has decay
rate $2\gamma$, while the ideal dark amplitude is constant. Differentiating
the energy gives
$$
\boxed{P_{\rm rad}=-\dot E=2\gamma|b|^2
=\gamma|a_1+a_2|^2},
$$
which has the required dependence on the coherent far-field sum.

For $a_1(0)=A,a_2(0)=0$, one has $b(0)=d(0)=A/\sqrt2$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{a_1(t)=\frac A2(1+e^{-\gamma t})},\qquad
\boxed{a_2(t)=\frac A2(e^{-\gamma t}-1)}.
$$
The minus sign in $a_2$ is a relative phase: the surviving part is the
antisymmetric dark state, not energy generation. The stored energy and
cumulative radiation are
$$
\boxed{E(t)=\frac{|A|^2}{2}(1+e^{-2\gamma t})},
$$
$$
\boxed{E_{\rm rad}(t)=|A|^2-E(t)
=\frac{|A|^2}{2}(1-e^{-2\gamma t})}.
$$
At late time the state is $(A/2,-A/2)$, with half of the initial energy
trapped in the ideal dark coordinate. If instead the initial state is
$(A/\sqrt2,-A/\sqrt2)$, then $b=0$ from the start, $P_{\rm rad}=0$, and the
state is exactly constant in this envelope model.

For $A=1$, $\gamma t=1.2$ and $e^{-1.2}=0.301194$. Hence
$$
\boxed{a_1=0.650597},\qquad \boxed{a_2=-0.349403},
$$
$$
\boxed{E=0.545359},\qquad
\boxed{E_{\rm rad}=0.454641},
$$
and
$$
\boxed{P_{\rm rad}=\gamma e^{-2\gamma t}=0.362872\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}
$$
in energy-fraction units. The sum of stored and radiated energy is exactly
one. Frequency mismatch mixes bright and dark coordinates and permits slow
leakage. Independent loss damps both physical resonators even when the common
channel cancels. Additional independent radiation channels generally raise
the damping matrix rank and can eliminate the exact nullspace.

WAVE:010245.title: A free two-mass molecule translates and vibrates at once
WAVE:010245.objective: Separate the rigid zero mode from internal stretch using center-of-mass and reduced-mass coordinates, then reconstruct an impulsive response and energy partition.
WAVE:010245.statement:
Two point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ move without external
supports on a frictionless line and are joined by a spring of stiffness $k$
and unstretched separation already removed from the coordinates. Their small
displacements are $x_1,x_2$. At $t=0$ both displacements and velocities are
zero, after which an ideal impulse $J$ is delivered to mass 1 in the positive
direction.

Starting from the kinetic and spring energies, introduce a center coordinate
and a relative coordinate that diagonalize both energies. Identify the rigid
zero mode, the internal frequency, and the reduced mass. Solve exactly for
$x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ after the impulse. Verify total momentum and split the
initial kinetic energy into translational and internal pieces, showing that
they sum to the impulse energy. Explain why simply deleting the zero mode is
not allowed for this initial condition.

For $m_1=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$,
$k=12.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $J=2.00\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, calculate the total
and reduced masses, internal angular frequency, both energy pieces, and both
positions and velocities at $t=\pi/8\,\mathrm s$. State how a weak external
grounding spring would alter the zero mode.
permittedResults: With $R=(m_1x_1+m_2x_2)/M$ and $r=x_2-x_1$, the kinetic energy is $M\dot R^2/2+\mu\dot r^2/2$.
An external impulse equals the jump in total momentum.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize with center-of-mass and separation coordinates before applying the impulse.
Use the two mass-weighted eigenvectors, including the zero eigenvalue, and project the velocity jump onto both.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Retains both the translational zero mode and reduced-mass internal mode when reconstructing an initial condition with nonzero net impulse.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets the center of mass to rest after a nonzero external impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: Total momentum and both reconstructed initial velocities are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses $m_1+m_2$ rather than $m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ as the inertia of $r=x_2-x_1$.
commonErrors.consequence: The stretch frequency and internal energy are wrong.

hintTree.content: Invert the coordinates as $x_1=R-(m_2/M)r$ and $x_2=R+(m_1/M)r$.
The impulse sets $\dot x_1(0^+)=J/m_1$ but leaves $\dot x_2(0^+)=0$.
Do not force the center coordinate to remain at zero after a nonzero net impulse.

WAVE:010245.canonicalSolution:
Let
$$
M=m_1+m_2,\qquad \mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\qquad
R=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\qquad r=x_2-x_1.
$$
The inverse relations are
$x_1=R-(m_2/M)r$ and $x_2=R+(m_1/M)r$. Substitution gives
$$
\mathcal T=\frac12M\dot R^2+\frac12\mu\dot r^2,\qquad
\mathcal V=\frac12kr^2.
$$
Thus $R$ is the rigid zero mode, $\ddot R=0$, while
$$
\ddot r+\omega_s^2r=0,\qquad
\boxed{\omega_s=\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}
=\sqrt{k\left(\frac1{m_1}+\frac1{m_2}\right)}}.
$$

The impulse produces $\dot x_1(0^+)=J/m_1$ and
$\dot x_2(0^+)=0$. Hence
$$
\dot R(0^+)=\frac JM,\qquad \dot r(0^+)=-\frac J{m_1}.
$$
With zero initial positions,
$$
R(t)=\frac{Jt}{M},\qquad
r(t)=-\frac{J}{m_1\omega_s}\sin\omega_st.
$$
Reconstruction yields the exact motion
$$
\boxed{x_1(t)=\frac{Jt}{M}
+\frac{m_2J}{Mm_1\omega_s}\sin\omega_st},
$$
$$
\boxed{x_2(t)=\frac{Jt}{M}
-\frac{J}{M\omega_s}\sin\omega_st}.
$$
The total momentum is $M\dot R=J$ at every time. The impulse energy
$J^2/(2m_1)$ divides into
$$
\boxed{E_{\rm trans}=\frac{J^2}{2M}},\qquad
\boxed{E_{\rm int}=\frac12\mu\left(\frac J{m_1}\right)^2
=\frac{J^2m_2}{2m_1M}}.
$$
Their sum is $J^2/(2m_1)$ exactly. Deleting the zero mode would set the total
momentum to zero and fail to reconstruct either initial velocity.

For the stated values,
$$
\boxed{M=4.00000\,\mathrm{kg}},\qquad
\boxed{\mu=0.750000\,\mathrm{kg}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_s=4.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The translational and internal energies are respectively
$\boxed{0.500000\,\mathrm J}$ and $\boxed{1.50000\,\mathrm J}$, summing to
$2.00000\,\mathrm J$. At $t=\pi/8\,\mathrm s$, $\omega_st=\pi/2$ and
$$
\boxed{x_1=0.571350\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{x_2=0.0713495\,\mathrm m},
$$
while $\boxed{\dot x_1=\dot x_2=0.500000\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. At that instant
the internal energy is entirely spring potential. A weak grounding spring
would break translation invariance and lift the zero frequency to a small
nonzero normal-mode frequency; the exact uniform-drift term would then be
replaced by slow bounded motion.

Let

$$
R(t)=\frac{Jt}{M},\qquad
r(t)=-\frac{J}{m_1\omega_s}\sin\omega_st.
$$
Reconstruction yields the exact motion
$$
\boxed{x_1(t)=\frac{Jt}{M}
+\frac{m_2J}{Mm_1\omega_s}\sin\omega_st},
$$
$$
\boxed{x_2(t)=\frac{Jt}{M}
-\frac{J}{M\omega_s}\sin\omega_st}.
$$
The total momentum is $M\dot R=J$ at every time. The impulse energy
$J^2/(2m_1)$ divides into
$$
\boxed{E_{\rm trans}=\frac{J^2}{2M}},\qquad
\boxed{E_{\rm int}=\frac12\mu\left(\frac J{m_1}\right)^2
=\frac{J^2m_2}{2m_1M}}.
$$
Their sum is $J^2/(2m_1)$ exactly. Deleting the zero mode would set the total
momentum to zero and fail to reconstruct either initial velocity.

For the stated values,
$$
\boxed{M=4.00000\,\mathrm{kg}},\qquad
\boxed{\mu=0.750000\,\mathrm{kg}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_s=4.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The translational and internal energies are respectively
$\boxed{0.500000\,\mathrm J}$ and $\boxed{1.50000\,\mathrm J}$, summing to
$2.00000\,\mathrm J$. At $t=\pi/8\,\mathrm s$, $\omega_st=\pi/2$ and
$$
\boxed{x_1=0.571350\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{x_2=0.0713495\,\mathrm m},
$$
while $\boxed{\dot x_1=\dot x_2=0.500000\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. At that instant
the internal energy is entirely spring potential. A weak grounding spring
would break translation invariance and lift the zero frequency to a small
nonzero normal-mode frequency; the exact uniform-drift term would then be
replaced by slow bounded motion.
I discard the rigid zero mode and impose $R=0$ even though the impulse gives total momentum $J$. I also assign the relative coordinate the mass $m_1+m_2$, obtaining $\omega_s=\sqrt{k/(m_1+m_2)}$.

WAVE:010246.title: A base jolt excites both modes of a two-story shear frame
WAVE:010246.objective: Derive the golden-ratio modes of a two-story shear model and project a uniform base-velocity impulse into exact modal participation and energy fractions.
WAVE:010246.statement:
An ideal two-story shear frame has two equal floor
masses $m$. Each story has lateral stiffness $k$: the first spring connects
the base to floor 1 and the second connects floor 1 to floor 2. With floor
displacements measured relative to base motion $y(t)$, let
$q=(q_1,q_2)^T$. The undamped equations are
$$
m\ddot q+Kq=-m\mathbf 1\,\ddot y,
\qquad
K=k\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Find both Euclidean-orthonormal mode shapes and natural frequencies. At $t=0$ the
base receives an ideal positive velocity step $\Delta\dot y=V$ and thereafter
moves at constant velocity; the floors cannot acquire finite absolute
velocity through finite springs during the impulse. Derive the resulting
relative initial conditions, modal participation factors, exact free response,
and modal energy fractions. Prove the fractions sum to the initial relative
kinetic energy and explain why the higher mode is weakly but not exactly dark.
Give an explicit upper bound on the roof relative displacement obtained by
summing its two modal amplitudes.

For $m=1000\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=2.00\times10^6\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and
$V=0.100\,\mathrm{m/s}$, calculate both angular and ordinary frequencies,
both participation factors, both modal energies, and the two signed roof
amplitudes and their absolute-sum bound. State how damping, a finite-duration
base pulse, or unequal floor masses would change the result.
permittedResults: For equal masses, Euclidean-unit stiffness eigenvectors are also mass-orthogonal, and modal energy is $m(\dot z_j^2+\omega_j^2z_j^2)/2$.
Across an ideal base velocity jump, absolute floor velocities remain continuous when spring forces have no impulse.

acceptableStrategies.description: Diagonalize the shear stiffness matrix and project the impulsive relative velocity into modal coordinates.
Integrate the matrix impulse response against the base acceleration and use spectral projectors of the two stiffness eigenvalues.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Projects the uniform base impulse onto a complete orthonormal mode set and preserves both the weak high-mode contribution and the exact kinetic-energy ledger.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\dot q(0^+)=+V\mathbf1$ for a positive base velocity jump while absolute floor velocities remain continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: Every modal phase and signed floor response is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Declares uniform base motion orthogonal to the higher mode and deletes it.
commonErrors.consequence: The unequal components of the high mode leave a nonzero participation factor and energy.

hintTree.content: The dimensionless stiffness eigenvalues are $(3\mp\sqrt5)/2$.
Integrate $\ddot q=-\mathbf1\ddot y+O(1)$ across the base impulse.
Project $\dot q(0^+)=-V\mathbf1$ onto each orthonormal mode.

WAVE:010246.canonicalSolution:
Let $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. The dimensionless
stiffness eigenvalues are
$$
\lambda_- =\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2},\qquad
\lambda_+ =\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\omega_\pm=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\lambda_\pm}}.
$$
A convenient Euclidean-orthonormal eigenbasis is
$$
\boxed{v_- =\frac{(1,\varphi)^T}{\sqrt{1+\varphi^2}}},\qquad
\boxed{v_+ =\frac{(1,-1/\varphi)^T}{\sqrt{1+1/\varphi^2}}}.
$$
Direct multiplication verifies the eigenvalue pairing and $v_-^Tv_+=0$.

Integrating the relative equation through the base impulse gives
$$
\boxed{q(0^+)=0},\qquad
\boxed{\dot q(0^+)=-V\mathbf1}.
$$
This also follows because absolute velocities $\dot x=\dot y\mathbf1+\dot q$
remain zero across finite spring forces. Define
$$
\Gamma_j=v_j^T\mathbf1.
$$
Then modal coordinates $z_j=v_j^Tq$ have
$z_j(0)=0$, $\dot z_j(0)=-V\Gamma_j$, and hence
$$
\boxed{q(t)=-V\sum_{j=\pm}\frac{\Gamma_j}{\omega_j}
\sin(\omega_jt)v_j}.
$$
Here
$$
\boxed{\Gamma_- =\frac{1+\varphi}{\sqrt{1+\varphi^2}}},\qquad
\boxed{\Gamma_+ =\frac{1-1/\varphi}{\sqrt{1+1/\varphi^2}}}.
$$
The high-mode factor is small but nonzero because its opposite-sign floor
components do not have equal magnitudes.

Each modal energy is constant:
$$
\boxed{E_j=\frac12mV^2\Gamma_j^2}.
$$
Completeness gives $\Gamma_-^2+\Gamma_+^2=\|\mathbf1\|^2=2$, so
$E_-+E_+=mV^2$, exactly the initial relative kinetic energy
$m(V^2+V^2)/2$. The roof response is
$$
q_2(t)=B_-\sin\omega_-t+B_+\sin\omega_+t,
$$
where
$$
B_j=-\frac{V\Gamma_j(v_j)_2}{\omega_j},
\qquad
\boxed{|q_2(t)|\le |B_-|+|B_+|}.
$$

Numerically
$$
\boxed{\omega_-=27.6393\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad f_-=4.39893\,\mathrm{Hz}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\omega_+=72.3607\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\quad f_+=11.5166\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
$$
The participation factors are
$$
\boxed{\Gamma_-=1.37638},\qquad \boxed{\Gamma_+=0.324920}.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{E_-=9.47214\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E_+=0.527864\,\mathrm J},
$$
which sum to $10.0000\,\mathrm J$. The signed roof amplitudes are
$$
\boxed{B_-=-4.23607\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{B_+=+2.36068\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm m},
$$
so $\boxed{|q_2|\le4.47214\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m}$. Damping would make
modal energies decay and, if nonproportional, would also spoil this real
orthogonal decoupling. A finite pulse replaces the velocity-jump projection
by each mode's convolution with the acceleration history. Unequal masses
require mass-normalized eigenvectors and the mass inner product rather than
the Euclidean formulas used here.

WAVE:010317.title: A string whose boundary has inertia
WAVE:010317.objective: Derive the frequency-dependent boundary condition created by an endpoint mass, obtain its transcendental spectrum, and prove the correct mass-augmented mode orthogonality.
WAVE:010317.statement:
A taut uniform string occupies \(0\le x\le L\), has tension \(T\) and
linear density \(\mu\), and undergoes small transverse motion \(y(x,t)\).
The left end is fixed. The right end is attached to a point mass \(M\) that
moves transversely with the string; there is no other restoring force or
damping at that endpoint.

Derive the wave equation and the exact dynamic boundary condition at
\(x=L\), including its sign. For a separated normal mode, derive the
transcendental equation for \(z=kL\). Show that its roots approach the
fixed-free spectrum as \(M\to0\). Show that the \(M\to\infty\) limit is
singular: the lowest positive root becomes a soft mode with
\(z_{\mathrm{soft}}\sim\sqrt{\mu L/M}\) and
\(\omega_{\mathrm{soft}}\sim\sqrt{T/(ML)}\), while the higher branches
approach the fixed-fixed spectrum.

Prove that distinct modes are orthogonal not under the string integral alone,
but under
\[
\langle\phi_m,\phi_n\rangle
=\int_0^L\mu\phi_m\phi_n\,dx
+M\phi_m(L)\phi_n(L).
\]
For \(L=1.00\,\mathrm m\), \(T=40.0\,\mathrm N\),
\(\mu=0.100\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and \(M=0.100\,\mathrm{kg}\), compute the
first two positive normal frequencies using the roots
\(z_1\approx0.860334\) and \(z_2\approx3.42562\), and check their units.
permittedResults: For small transverse slope, a taut string satisfies \(\mu y_{tt}=T y_{xx}\) and transmits transverse endpoint force equal to tension times signed slope.
Subtracting two Sturm-Liouville mode equations and integrating by parts exposes both bulk and boundary contributions to orthogonality.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply Newton's law to a string element and endpoint mass, then use separation of variables and an integration-by-parts orthogonality proof.
Derive the same spectrum from a variational energy formulation, provided the endpoint kinetic energy and resulting boundary term are shown explicitly.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the inertial endpoint boundary condition and transcendental spectrum, proves the boundary-mass orthogonality relation, and checks limiting and numerical frequencies.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wrong endpoint-force sign and obtains a tangent equation with the wrong sign or reciprocal.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted eigenfrequencies do not belong to the stated string-mass system.

commonErrors.description: Claims distinct modes are orthogonal under the string integral while omitting the endpoint mass contribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The kinetic-energy inner product and modal projection are incomplete.

hintTree.content: The force exerted by the string on the right mass is \(-T y_x(L,t)\).
With \(\phi=A\sin kx\) and \(\omega=ck\), the boundary relation reduces to \(\tan(kL)=\mu/(Mk)\).
For orthogonality, integrate \(\phi_m''\phi_n-\phi_n''\phi_m\) and then replace endpoint derivatives using each mode's dynamic boundary condition.

WAVE:010317.canonicalSolution:
Small-slope force balance on the string gives
\[
\mu y_{tt}=T y_{xx},\qquad c=\sqrt{T/\mu}.
\]
The fixed end gives \(y(0,t)=0\). At the right endpoint, the string pulls the
mass with transverse force \(-T y_x(L,t)\), so Newton's law is
\[
M y_{tt}(L,t)=-T y_x(L,t).
\]
For \(y=\phi(x)\cos\omega t\), this becomes
\[
T\phi'(L)=M\omega^2\phi(L).
\]
The fixed-end spatial solution is \(\phi=A\sin kx\), with \(\omega=ck\).
Therefore
\[
Tk\cos(kL)=M\frac{T}{\mu}k^2\sin(kL),
\]
or
\[
\boxed{\tan(kL)=\frac{\mu}{Mk}}.
\]
Writing \(z=kL\) and \(\eta=M/(\mu L)\) gives
\(\tan z=1/(\eta z)\). As \(M\to0\), the original boundary condition tends
to \(\phi'(L)=0\), so the roots tend
\(z=(n+\tfrac12)\pi\).

The \(M\to\infty\) limit has two scales. For the lowest root, \(z\to0\), so
\(\tan z\sim z\) gives
\[
z_{\mathrm{soft}}\sim\eta^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu L}{M}},
\qquad
\omega_{\mathrm{soft}}=\frac cLz_{\mathrm{soft}}
\sim\sqrt{\frac{T}{ML}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For every higher branch, write \(z_n=n\pi+\varepsilon_n\), \(n\ge1\).
Then \(\varepsilon_n\sim1/(\eta n\pi)\), so
\(z_n\to n\pi\), the fixed-fixed values. Simply imposing
\(\phi(L)=0\) captures those finite-frequency branches but loses the soft
mode, which is why the infinite-mass limit is singular.

For two modes,
\(\phi_n''+k_n^2\phi_n=0\). Multiply crosswise, subtract, and integrate:
\[
(k_n^2-k_m^2)\int_0^L\phi_m\phi_n\,dx
=\left[\phi_m'\phi_n-\phi_n'\phi_m\right]_0^L.
\]
The left endpoint term vanishes. Using
\(T\phi_n'(L)=M\omega_n^2\phi_n(L)=M(T/\mu)k_n^2\phi_n(L)\),
the right side equals
\((M/\mu)(k_m^2-k_n^2)\phi_m(L)\phi_n(L)\). Hence, for distinct
eigenvalues,
\[
\boxed{\int_0^L\mu\phi_m\phi_n\,dx
+M\phi_m(L)\phi_n(L)=0}.
\]

For the data, \(M=\mu L\) and
\(c=\sqrt{40.0/0.100}=20.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Since
\(\omega_n=ck_n=cz_n/L\),
\[
\boxed{\omega_1=17.21\,\mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_2=68.51\,\mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
The radian is dimensionless, and \(c/L\) supplies \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

graderFixtures.proofText: Newton's law at the mass is \(My_{tt}=-Ty_x\), so a mode satisfies \(T\phi'=M\omega^2\phi\). With \(\phi=\sin kx\), \(\tan(kL)=\mu/(Mk)\). Integration by parts gives orthogonality under \(\int\mu\phi_m\phi_n dx+M\phi_m(L)\phi_n(L)\). For large \(M\), the lowest root is soft, \(z\sim\sqrt{\mu L/M}\), while higher roots tend \(n\pi\).
The endpoint is effectively free for every mass, so cos(kL)=0. Ordinary string orthogonality under the integral is unchanged because a point mass has zero length.

WAVE:010318.title: A state rotating inside a square membrane's degenerate eigenspace
WAVE:010318.objective: Derive and normalize the fixed-boundary modes of a rectangular membrane, analyze symmetry degeneracy on a square, and solve an initial-value problem that rotates within a two-dimensional eigenspace while conserving energy.
WAVE:010318.statement:
A membrane with uniform areal mass density \(\sigma\) and isotropic tension
per unit length \(\mathcal T\) occupies \(0<x<a\), \(0<y<b\). Its small
transverse displacement satisfies
\[
\sigma u_{tt}=\mathcal T(u_{xx}+u_{yy}),
\qquad c=\sqrt{\mathcal T/\sigma},
\]
and all four edges are fixed.

Use separation of variables to derive every spatial mode and angular
frequency. Normalize the modes under the area-averaged inner product
\[
\langle f,g\rangle_A=\frac1{ab}\int_0^a\!\int_0^b f(x,y)g(x,y)\,dy\,dx,
\]
and prove their orthogonality. Specialize to a square \(a=b=L\). Explain why
the \((m,n)\) and \((n,m)\) modes are degenerate when \(m\ne n\), and why
every fixed linear combination in their span is another mode.

Let \(\phi_{mn}\) denote your dimensionless area-normalized square modes and
let \(\omega=\omega_{12}=\omega_{21}\). Impose
\[
u(x,y,0)=A\phi_{12}(x,y),
\qquad
u_t(x,y,0)=A\omega\phi_{21}(x,y).
\]
Find the exact motion. Show that after one quarter period the displacement is
\(A\phi_{21}\), so the state has rotated through the degenerate modal plane,
and prove conservation of the full kinetic-plus-membrane energy.

For \(L=0.800\,\mathrm m\), \(c=120\,\mathrm{m/s}\),
\(\sigma=0.0500\,\mathrm{kg/m^2}\), and \(A=2.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute
\(\omega\), the ordinary frequency, the quarter-period time, and the total
energy. Finally explain how a slight rectangular distortion \(a\ne b\)
splits the two frequencies and replaces uniform eigenspace rotation by a beat
between distinct modes.
permittedResults: For positive integers \(m,p\), \(\int_0^a\sin(m\pi x/a)\sin(p\pi x/a)\,dx=(a/2)\delta_{mp}\).
For a Dirichlet Laplacian eigenmode \(-\nabla^2\phi=(\omega^2/c^2)\phi\), integration by parts gives \(\int|\nabla\phi|^2=(\omega^2/c^2)\int|\phi|^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate the Dirichlet membrane equation, normalize the sine-product modes, and project the initial data in the degenerate eigenspace.
Use the self-adjoint Dirichlet Laplacian spectral theorem, provided the explicit modes, normalization, frequency, modal motion, and energy calculation are all retained.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and normalizes the rectangular membrane modes, identifies the square's degenerate eigenspace, and solves and energetically verifies the phase-quadrature modal rotation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds coordinate wavenumbers linearly rather than adding their squares in the membrane eigenvalue.
commonErrors.consequence: The eigenfrequencies and the claimed degeneracy are mathematically wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims the exchanged-index modes remain degenerate for an arbitrary rectangle with unequal side lengths.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact eigenspace rotation is applied after the symmetry that supports it has been broken.

hintTree.content: The fixed boundaries require sine factors in both coordinates, and the separation eigenvalue is the sum of two squared wavenumbers.
Under the declared area-averaged inner product, multiply the sine product by two rather than by \(2/\sqrt{ab}\).
On the square, the two requested modes have one common oscillator frequency, so the displacement and velocity data become cosine and sine quadratures.

WAVE:010318.canonicalSolution:
Set \(u=X(x)Y(y)Q(t)\). The four fixed edges require
\[
X_m(x)=\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a},
\qquad
Y_n(y)=\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b},
\qquad m,n=1,2,\ldots
\]
and the time equation is harmonic with
\[
\boxed{\omega_{mn}=c\pi
\sqrt{\frac{m^2}{a^2}+\frac{n^2}{b^2}}}.
\]
Since each sine factor has mean square one half on its interval, the
dimensionless area-normalized modes are
\[
\boxed{\phi_{mn}(x,y)=2
\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}}.
\]
The product of the two one-dimensional orthogonality integrals gives
\[
\langle\phi_{mn},\phi_{pq}\rangle_A=\delta_{mp}\delta_{nq}.
\]

On a square,
\[
\omega_{mn}=\frac{c\pi}{L}\sqrt{m^2+n^2},
\]
which is invariant under exchanging \(m\) and \(n\). The independent modes
\(\phi_{12}\) and \(\phi_{21}\) therefore span a two-dimensional eigenspace;
linearity makes every fixed combination another eigenmode at their common
frequency
\[
\omega=\frac{c\pi\sqrt5}{L}.
\]
Projection of the initial data yields
\[
\boxed{u(x,y,t)=A\phi_{12}(x,y)\cos\omega t
+A\phi_{21}(x,y)\sin\omega t}.
\]
At \(t=\pi/(2\omega)\), the cosine vanishes and the sine is one, so the
displacement is exactly \(A\phi_{21}\). The coefficients
\(q_1=A\cos\omega t\) and \(q_2=A\sin\omega t\) trace a circle in the
degenerate modal plane.

The physical energy is
\[
E=\frac12\int_0^L\!\int_0^L
\left[\sigma u_t^2+\mathcal T|\nabla u|^2\right]dy\,dx.
\]
Orthogonality, \(\int\phi_j^2=L^2\), and
\(\mathcal T\int|\nabla\phi_j|^2=\sigma\omega^2L^2\) give
\[
E=\frac{\sigma L^2}{2}
\sum_{j=1}^2(\dot q_j^2+\omega^2q_j^2)
=\boxed{\sigma L^2A^2\omega^2},
\]
which is constant.

Numerically,
\[
\omega=\frac{120\pi\sqrt5}{0.800}
=1053.72\,\mathrm{rad/s},
\qquad
f=\frac\omega{2\pi}=167.7\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]
The quarter-period time is
\[
\frac\pi{2\omega}=1.491\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s,
\]
and
\[
E=(0.0500)(0.800)^2(0.00200)^2(1053.72)^2
=\boxed{0.1421\,\mathrm J}.
\]
If \(a\ne b\), then
\(\omega_{12}=c\pi\sqrt{a^{-2}+4b^{-2}}\) and
\(\omega_{21}=c\pi\sqrt{4a^{-2}+b^{-2}}\) differ. The two coefficients
then accumulate different phases, producing a beat rather than uniform
rotation within a single eigenspace.

graderFixtures.proofText: Fixed boundaries give \(\phi_{mn}=2\sin(m\pi x/a)\sin(n\pi y/b)\) under area-averaged normalization and \(\omega_{mn}=c\pi\sqrt{m^2/a^2+n^2/b^2}\). On a square, modes 12 and 21 share one frequency, so the data give \(u=A\phi_{12}\cos\omega t+A\phi_{21}\sin\omega t\), which becomes \(A\phi_{21}\) after a quarter period while total energy stays constant.
The frequency is c pi times m over a plus n over b. Exchanging m and n always gives the same frequency even on a nonsquare rectangle, so the quarter-period rotation is universal.

WAVE:010319.title: Bessel modes of a freely hanging chain
WAVE:010319.objective: Derive the variable-tension wave equation for a hanging chain, obtain and normalize its Bessel spectrum, expand a simple initial shape, and reconcile modal energy with the continuum energy.
WAVE:010319.statement:
A uniform flexible chain of length \(L\) and linear density \(\mu\)
hangs vertically under gravity. Let \(x\) measure distance upward from its free
lower end, so the static tension is \(T(x)=\mu g x\). Its upper end at \(x=L\)
is fixed. Let \(y(x,t)\) be a small horizontal displacement.

Derive the transverse wave equation directly from force balance. Separate
variables and show that regularity at the tensionless lower end selects Bessel
functions. Find every normal-mode frequency and mode shape in terms of the
positive zeros \(j_{0,n}\) of \(J_0\). State the natural lower-end boundary
condition, prove orthogonality, and evaluate the squared norm of each
unnormalized mode.

The chain is released from rest with the straight initial shape
\[
y(x,0)=h\left(1-\frac{x}{L}\right),\qquad y_t(x,0)=0.
\]
Find its exact normal-mode expansion, including a closed formula for every
coefficient. Verify the expansion's total energy both directly and mode by
mode; you may use \(\sum_{n\ge1}j_{0,n}^{-4}=1/32\).

For \(L=2.00\,\mathrm m\), \(\mu=0.0500\,\mathrm{kg/m}\),
\(h=1.00\,\mathrm{cm}\), and \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), use
\(j_{0,1}=2.40483\), \(j_{0,2}=5.52008\),
\(J_1(j_{0,1})=0.519147\), and \(J_1(j_{0,2})=-0.340265\) to compute
the first two frequencies and displacement coefficients, the fundamental
period, the interior node of the second mode, and the total energy.
permittedResults: If \(j_{0,n}\) is a zero of \(J_0\), then \(\int_0^1 rJ_0(j_{0,m}r)J_0(j_{0,n}r)\,dr=\tfrac12J_1(j_{0,n})^2\delta_{mn}\).
The identities \(\frac{d}{dr}[rJ_1(jr)]=jrJ_0(jr)\) and \(\frac{d}{dr}[r^2J_2(jr)]=jr^2J_1(jr)\) evaluate the needed projection integral.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the separated variable-coefficient equation to Bessel order zero, then use its weighted radial orthogonality after x equals L r squared.
Treat the spatial equation directly as a singular Sturm--Liouville problem, provided the Bessel spectrum, endpoint condition, projection integral, and energy identity are all made explicit.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the hanging-chain Bessel spectrum from force balance, proves the correct orthogonality and norm, projects the released straight shape, and closes the continuum and modal energy calculations.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the hanging chain by a constant-tension string and uses sine modes.
commonErrors.consequence: The variable-coefficient equation, Bessel spectrum, and free lower-end behavior are all lost.

commonErrors.description: Retains the Y-zero Bessel solution or imposes a fixed-displacement condition at the free lower end.
commonErrors.consequence: The mode is singular or the physical endpoint condition is wrong, changing the spectrum.

hintTree.content: The separated spatial equation is \(xX''+X'+(\omega^2/g)X=0\). Try the variable \(z=2\omega\sqrt{x/g}\).
In \(r=\sqrt{x/L}\), the mode is \(J_0(j_{0,n}r)\) and \(dx=2Lr\,dr\).
At a zero j of \(J_0\), the projection integral reduces to \(\int_0^1 2r(1-r^2)J_0(jr)\,dr=8J_1(j)/j^3\).

WAVE:010319.canonicalSolution:
A slice has transverse force difference
\(\partial_x(Ty_x)\,dx\) and mass \(\mu\,dx\), so
\[
\boxed{y_{tt}=g(xy_x)_x}.
\]
With \(y=X(x)\cos\omega t\),
\[
xX''+X'+\frac{\omega^2}{g}X=0.
\]
Writing \(z=2\omega\sqrt{x/g}\) gives Bessel's equation of order zero.
The \(Y_0(z)\) solution diverges at \(x=0\), whereas \(J_0(z)\) is regular
and satisfies the natural condition \(\lim_{x\downarrow0}xX'(x)=0\).
The fixed top requires
\[
J_0\!\left(2\omega\sqrt{L/g}\right)=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\omega_n=\frac{j_{0,n}}2\sqrt{\frac gL}},\qquad
\boxed{X_n(x)=J_0\!\left(j_{0,n}\sqrt{\frac xL}\right)}.
\]

The equation is the self-adjoint problem
\(-(xX')'=\lambda X\) with unit weight. Integration by parts, using
\(X(L)=0\) and the vanishing lower flux, proves orthogonality. With
\(r=\sqrt{x/L}\),
\[
\boxed{\int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx
=LJ_1(j_{0,n})^2\delta_{mn}}.
\]

Write \(y(x,t)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nX_n(x)\cos\omega_nt\). Projection gives
\[
a_n=\frac{h\int_0^L(1-x/L)X_n(x)\,dx}
{LJ_1(j_{0,n})^2}.
\]
The stated Bessel identities and \(J_0(j_{0,n})=0\) yield
\[
\int_0^L(1-x/L)X_n\,dx
=\frac{8LJ_1(j_{0,n})}{j_{0,n}^3},
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{a_n=\frac{8h}{j_{0,n}^3J_1(j_{0,n})}},\qquad
\boxed{y(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac{8hJ_0(j_{0,n}\sqrt{x/L})}{j_{0,n}^3J_1(j_{0,n})}
\cos\!\left(\frac{j_{0,n}}2\sqrt{g/L}\,t\right)}.
\]

Directly at release,
\[
E=\frac12\int_0^L\mu gx\,y_x^2\,dx
=\boxed{\frac{\mu gh^2}{4}}.
\]
For one mode, the Sturm--Liouville equation gives
\(\int_0^LxX_n'^2dx=(j_{0,n}^2/4)J_1(j_{0,n})^2\), so
\[
E_n=\frac12\mu g a_n^2\int_0^LxX_n'^2dx
=\frac{8\mu gh^2}{j_{0,n}^4}.
\]
Thus \(\sum E_n=8\mu gh^2(1/32)=\mu gh^2/4\), agreeing exactly.

Numerically,
\[
\omega_1=2.663\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad
\omega_2=6.113\,\mathrm{rad/s},
\]
\[
a_1=1.108\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m,\qquad
a_2=-1.398\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m,
\qquad T_1=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_1}=2.360\,\mathrm s.
\]
The second mode's interior node occurs when
\(j_{0,2}\sqrt{x/L}=j_{0,1}\), so
\[
\boxed{x=L(j_{0,1}/j_{0,2})^2=0.3796\,\mathrm m}
\]
above the free end. Finally,
\[
\boxed{E=\mu gh^2/4=1.226\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: Force balance gives \(y_{tt}=g(xy_x)_x\). Regular separated modes are \(J_0(j_{0,n}\sqrt{x/L})\), with \(\omega_n=(j_{0,n}/2)\sqrt{g/L}\) and norm squared \(LJ_1(j_{0,n})^2\). Projection of \(h(1-x/L)\) gives \(a_n=8h/[j_{0,n}^3J_1(j_{0,n})]\), and the modal energies sum to \(\mu gh^2/4\).
The chain has tension mu g L everywhere, so its modes are sine waves with frequencies n pi times square root g over L. The free lower end must have zero displacement.
