WAVE:010320.title: The exact modal spectrum of an off-center plucked string
WAVE:010320.objective: Expand a triangular pluck in fixed-string modes, solve the wave initial-value problem, and reconcile kink convergence and total energy with modal coefficients.
WAVE:010320.statement:
A string of length \(L\), tension \(T\), and linear density \(\mu\) is
fixed at both ends. It is pulled to height \(h\) at \(x=a\), with
\(0<a<L\), so its initial displacement is the continuous triangular function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
hx/a,&0\le x\le a,\\
h(L-x)/(L-a),&a\le x\le L,
\end{cases}
\]
and it is released from rest.

Derive the sine-series coefficients without quoting a centered-pluck formula,
then write the complete displacement. Show the \(1/n^2\) coefficient decay
and explain how it is consistent with continuity of displacement but a jump in
slope at the pluck point. Compute the initial elastic energy directly and show
how modal orthogonality expresses the same energy as a convergent series.

For \(L=1.00\,\mathrm m\), \(a=0.400\,\mathrm m\),
\(h=1.00\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(T=100\,\mathrm N\), and
\(\mu=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), compute the wave speed, fundamental
frequency, first sine coefficient, and total initial energy. Explain why an
ideal point pluck does not imply an infinite energy even though the slope is
discontinuous, and what kind of displacement discontinuity would change the
coefficient decay and energy conclusion.
permittedResults: For \(f(0)=f(L)=0\), the sine coefficient is \(B_n=(2/L)\int_0^Lf(x)\sin(n\pi x/L)dx\).
Piecewise integration by parts makes derivative jumps appear in the high-mode coefficient asymptotics.

acceptableStrategies.description: Project the two linear pieces directly onto sine modes and use orthogonality for time evolution and energy.
Integrate by parts in a distribution-aware way using the slope jump, provided the exact coefficient and direct physical-energy check are recovered.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the off-center triangular-pluck coefficients, constructs the fixed-string solution, and reconciles coefficient decay and the direct and modal energy calculations.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the centered-pluck odd-harmonic coefficients despite the stated off-center location.
commonErrors.consequence: The initial shape and spectrum are not those of the problem.

commonErrors.description: Claims a finite jump in slope makes the ideal string energy infinite.
commonErrors.consequence: The integrability of the piecewise-constant slope and the convergent modal energy are misread.

hintTree.content: Split the projection integral at x equals a and integrate the two linear pieces by parts; endpoint terms cancel.
The result is proportional to \(\sin(n\pi a/L)/n^2\).
At release, kinetic energy vanishes and elastic energy is \((T/2)\int_0^L[f'(x)]^2dx\).

WAVE:010320.canonicalSolution:
The string wave speed is \(c=\sqrt{T/\mu}\), and the fixed-end modes are
\(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with \(\omega_n=n\pi c/L\). Projection gives
\[
B_n=\frac2L\left[
\int_0^a\frac{hx}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx
+\int_a^L\frac{h(L-x)}{L-a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx
\right].
\]
Integrating the two linear pieces and simplifying yields
\[
\boxed{B_n=\frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2n^2a(L-a)}
\sin\frac{n\pi a}{L}}.
\]
Zero initial velocity eliminates sine-in-time terms, so
\[
\boxed{u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n
\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\cos\frac{n\pi ct}{L}}.
\]
The coefficients are \(O(n^{-2})\), with additional zeros when the pluck
location makes the sine factor vanish. A continuous function with a finite
jump in its first derivative has precisely this faster decay than a function
with a displacement jump, whose coefficients are generally only \(O(n^{-1})\).

At release,
\[
E=\frac T2\int_0^L[f'(x)]^2dx
=\frac{Th^2}{2}\left(\frac1a+\frac1{L-a}\right).
\]
Modal orthogonality gives the equivalent expression
\[
E=\frac{TL}{4}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2B_n^2.
\]
Because \(B_n=O(n^{-2})\), this energy series behaves like
\(\sum n^{-2}\) and converges.

Numerically,
\[
c=\sqrt{100/0.0100}=100\,\mathrm{m/s},
\qquad f_1=\frac{c}{2L}=50.0\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]
The first coefficient is
\[
B_1=\frac{2(0.0100)}{\pi^2(0.400)(0.600)}\sin(0.4\pi)
=8.03\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m.
\]
The total initial energy is
\[
\boxed{E=\frac{100(0.0100)^2}{2}
\left(\frac1{0.400}+\frac1{0.600}\right)
=2.083\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J}.
\]
The ideal kink has finite piecewise-constant slope, so its squared slope is
integrable. A literal displacement jump would introduce a distributional
derivative in the ideal model, slow the modal decay, and make the classical
string elastic energy divergent.

graderFixtures.proofText: Projection of the two linear pieces gives \(B_n=2hL^2\sin(n\pi a/L)/[\pi^2n^2a(L-a)]\), and release from rest gives cosine time factors. Direct energy is \(Th^2[1/a+1/(L-a)]/2\), finite because the kink has a bounded slope on either side and B-n decays as n to minus two.
Every triangular pluck has only odd coefficients eight h over pi squared n squared, regardless of where it is plucked. The slope discontinuity is a delta function, so the elastic energy is infinite.

WAVE:010321.title: A moving string carries its two wave families at unequal laboratory speeds
WAVE:010321.objective: Derive the convected wave equation of an axially transported string, solve its characteristic initial-value problem, and reconcile signed laboratory transport with exact energy conservation.
WAVE:010321.statement:
An effectively infinite string is transported through an ideal apparatus at
constant axial speed \(U>0\). Let x be the laboratory coordinate and
\(y(x,t)\) the small transverse displacement. The string has constant mass
per length \(\mu\) and constant tension T. The axial drive maintains U, and
bending stiffness, gravity, damping, and endpoint effects are neglected. A
material point on the string therefore has transverse velocity
\[
v_m=(\partial_t+U\partial_x)y.
\]

Derive the transverse equation of motion from force balance on a moving
material slice. Expand and factor the differential operator, and show that
the material coordinate \(X=x-Ut\) reduces the equation to the ordinary wave
equation. For a plane wave \(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\), derive the two dispersion
branches and their laboratory phase and group velocities. Explain what
happens to the two characteristic directions when \(0<U<c\), \(U=c\), and
\(U>c\), where \(c=\sqrt{T/\mu}\). Do not infer instability merely because
both branches travel downstream in the last case.

Write the general solution as two arbitrary characteristic profiles. If
\(y(x,0)=f(x)\) and \(v_m(x,0)=g(x)\), derive equations determining both
profiles. Then take
\[
f(x)=A e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad g(x)=0,
\]
and obtain the exact two-pulse solution, including each pulse's amplitude,
center, and energy.

Derive a local conservation law using the physical perturbation energy
\[
e=\frac12\mu v_m^2+\frac12T y_x^2.
\]
Identify the laboratory energy flux, including its advective term, and prove
that a pure wave family carries energy at its own signed characteristic
speed. Explain the zero and sign change of the slow-family flux at \(U=c\)
without replacing material velocity by \(y_t\).

For \(T=100\,\mathrm N\), \(\mu=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg/m}\),
\(U=30.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(A=2.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), and
\(\sigma=0.200\,\mathrm m\), find c, both characteristic-component centers and peak amplitudes
at \(t=5.00\,\mathrm{ms}\), the energy of each pulse, and the total energy.
Finally, at laboratory frequency \(50.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), compute the signed
wavenumber and positive wavelength on each branch.
permittedResults: For constant U, the change of variables \(X=x-Ut\) turns \(\partial_t+U\partial_x\) into differentiation at fixed X.
Multiplying a lossless field equation by its material velocity exposes the energy density and the complete laboratory flux, including advection.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform to the material coordinate, use d'Alembert's solution, and transform both the initial material velocity and energy flux back to the laboratory.
Factor the laboratory PDE directly and use characteristic variables, provided the plane-wave signs, Gaussian split, conserved energy, branch fluxes, and numerical values all agree.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the convected string equation and its characteristic Cauchy solution, then proves the complete laboratory energy law and signed transport of both wave families.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses y-tt equals c squared y-xx and ignores the material derivative of the translating string.
commonErrors.consequence: Both laboratory characteristic speeds, the initial-velocity decomposition, and the transport interpretation are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses only minus T times y-t times y-x as the laboratory flux or replaces material velocity by the partial time derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed energy direction fails at U equals c and does not obey the derived local conservation law.

hintTree.content: A material string slice experiences transverse acceleration \((\partial_t+U\partial_x)^2y\), not merely \(y_{tt}\).
For \(y=F(x-(U+c)t)+G(x-(U-c)t)\), compute \(v_m\) before applying the initial conditions.
In the energy identity, rewrite \((\partial_t+U\partial_x)e\) as a laboratory time derivative plus a spatial flux.

WAVE:010321.canonicalSolution:
A material interval has mass \(\mu\,dx\). To first order, the transverse
tension resultant is \(T y_{xx}\,dx\), while its transverse acceleration is
the second material derivative. Hence
\[
\boxed{\mu(\partial_t+U\partial_x)^2y=T y_{xx}},
\qquad c=\sqrt{T/\mu}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
y_{tt}+2Uy_{xt}+(U^2-c^2)y_{xx}=0
\]
and the operator factors as
\[
\boxed{[\partial_t+(U+c)\partial_x]
[\partial_t+(U-c)\partial_x]y=0}.
\]
With \(X=x-Ut\) and \(Y(X,t)=y(x,t)\), the material derivative becomes
\(Y_t\) and \(y_x=Y_X\), so \(Y_{tt}=c^2Y_{XX}\).

For a plane wave,
\[
\boxed{(\omega-Uk)^2=c^2k^2},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_\pm=(U\pm c)k}.
\]
Both phase and group velocities on a specified branch are \(U\pm c\). If
\(0<U<c\), the plus family travels downstream and the minus family upstream.
At \(U=c\), the minus-family profile is stationary in the laboratory. If
\(U>c\), both families travel downstream. The intrinsic frequencies remain
real, so this direction change is not by itself a temporal instability.

The exact characteristic solution is
\[
\boxed{y(x,t)=F(x-(U+c)t)+G(x-(U-c)t)}.
\]
At t equals zero,
\[
f'=F'+G',\qquad g=c(G'-F'),
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{F'=\frac12\left(f'-\frac gc\right)},\qquad
\boxed{G'=\frac12\left(f'+\frac gc\right)}.
\]
Additive constants are fixed by a chosen far-field displacement. For the
localized Gaussian with \(g=0\), take \(F=G=f/2\), obtaining
\[
\boxed{y=\frac A2 e^{-[x-(U+c)t]^2/(2\sigma^2)}
+\frac A2 e^{-[x-(U-c)t]^2/(2\sigma^2)}}.
\]
Each pulse has peak amplitude \(A/2\), and its center moves at the
corresponding signed characteristic speed.

Let \(v_m=(\partial_t+U\partial_x)y\). Multiplication of
\(\mu(\partial_t+U\partial_x)v_m=T y_{xx}\) by \(v_m\), together with
\((\partial_t+U\partial_x)y_x=(v_m)_x\), gives
\[
(\partial_t+U\partial_x)e=\partial_x(Tv_m y_x).
\]
Thus the laboratory conservation law is
\[
\boxed{\partial_t e+\partial_xJ=0},\qquad
\boxed{J=Ue-Tv_m y_x}.
\]
For the F family, \(v_m=-cF'\), while for the G family
\(v_m=cG'\). In a general superposition the cross terms cancel exactly:
\[
e=T[(F')^2+(G')^2],
\]
\[
\boxed{J=(U+c)T(F')^2+(U-c)T(G')^2}.
\]
Therefore each pure family carries its energy density at speed \(U+c\) or
\(U-c\). The slow-family flux is negative for \(U<c\), zero for \(U=c\),
and positive for \(U>c\). Its zero at the critical speed is a cancellation
between advection and tension work, not zero material motion or zero energy.

For the Gaussian,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(f')^2dx
=\frac{A^2\sqrt\pi}{2\sigma}.
\]
Since each profile is f over two,
\[
\boxed{E_+=E_-=\frac{TA^2\sqrt\pi}{8\sigma}},\qquad
\boxed{E_{\rm total}=\frac{TA^2\sqrt\pi}{4\sigma}}.
\]

Numerically, \(c=\sqrt{100/0.0100}=\boxed{100\,\mathrm{m/s}}\). At
5.00 ms the pulse centers are
\[
\boxed{x_+=0.650\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{x_-=-0.350\,\mathrm m},
\]
and both characteristic-component peak amplitudes are
\(\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm{mm}}\). Their energies
are
\[
\boxed{E_+=E_-=4.43113\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J},
\qquad
\boxed{E_{\rm total}=8.86227\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J}.
\]
At \(f_{\rm lab}=50.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(\omega=100\pi\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).
Consequently
\[
\boxed{k_+=\frac{100\pi}{130}=2.41661\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\qquad \boxed{\lambda_+=2.600\,\mathrm m},
\]
whereas the upstream branch has
\[
\boxed{k_-=\frac{100\pi}{-70}=-4.48799\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\qquad \boxed{\lambda_-=1.400\,\mathrm m}.
\]
The negative k is the required direction marker for a positive laboratory
frequency on the upstream branch; replacing it by its magnitude inside the
dispersion relation would reverse the wave.

graderFixtures.proofText: Force balance gives \(\mu(\partial_t+U\partial_x)^2y=Ty_{xx}\), with families \(F(x-(U+c)t)\) and \(G(x-(U-c)t)\). Material initial velocity gives \(F'=(f'-g/c)/2\) and \(G'=(f'+g/c)/2\). The conserved flux is \(J=Ue-Tv_m y_x=(U+c)T(F')^2+(U-c)T(G')^2\).

I use the ordinary laboratory wave equation, so the pulses travel at plus or minus c regardless of U. I compute flux as minus T times y-t times y-x and conclude that the slow family always carries energy upstream.

WAVE:010322.title: Internal viscosity damps short string waves first
WAVE:010322.objective: Reduce a Kelvin--Voigt string PDE to damped modes, derive the mode-dependent underdamped threshold, and prove energy dissipation from the continuum equation.
WAVE:010322.statement:
A string of length \(L\) and linear density \(\mu\) is fixed at both ends.
Its incremental transverse force is modeled by the Kelvin--Voigt law
\[
N=T u_x+\eta u_{xt},
\]
where \(T>0\) is the elastic tension and \(\eta>0\) has units of force times
time. Force balance gives \(\mu u_{tt}=N_x\).

Derive the PDE and expand it in the fixed-end sine modes. For mode \(n\),
derive its undamped frequency, amplitude-decay rate, and damped frequency when
underdamped. Find the exact wavenumber threshold separating underdamped and
overdamped modes. Explain why this constitutive model damps higher spatial
frequencies more strongly and why its high-wavenumber behavior should not be
extrapolated beyond the continuum model's range.

Construct the sum of kinetic and elastic string energy and prove directly
from the PDE that its derivative is negative, including the boundary term.
For an initially displaced single mode with zero velocity, write the full
underdamped modal response; do not omit the sine-in-time term required by the
zero-velocity condition.

Take \(L=1.00\,\mathrm m\), \(T=100\,\mathrm N\),
\(\mu=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and \(\eta=0.200\,\mathrm{N,s}\).
Determine which positive integer modes are underdamped. Compute the decay
rate and damped frequency for modes 1 and 3, and show numerically that mode 4
is overdamped.
permittedResults: Fixed-end eigenfunctions are \(\sin(k_nx)\) with \(k_n=n\pi/L\).
Integration by parts converts the internal-force work into a boundary power term minus a nonnegative bulk dissipation integral.

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate variables in the fixed-end sine basis and analyze each damped temporal oscillator.
Use an operator eigenfunction expansion or weak-energy formulation, provided the same modal coefficients, threshold, initialized response, energy identity, and numerical classifications result.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the damped modal equations and underdamped threshold from the Kelvin--Voigt PDE, proves continuum energy loss, and correctly evaluates the mode-dependent numerical regime.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats Kelvin--Voigt internal viscosity as a mode-independent drag coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The k-squared damping rate and underdamped cutoff are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses only an exponentially damped cosine for a mode released from rest.
commonErrors.consequence: Its derivative at time zero is nonzero and violates the initial data.

hintTree.content: Substitution of one sine mode gives \(\mu\ddot q_n+\eta k_n^2\dot q_n+Tk_n^2q_n=0\).
Compare \(\beta_n=\eta k_n^2/(2\mu)\) with \(\omega_{0n}=\sqrt{T/\mu}\,k_n\).
Multiply the PDE by \(u_t\), integrate, and use \(u_t=0\) at both fixed endpoints.

WAVE:010322.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating the constitutive force gives
\[
\boxed{\mu u_{tt}=Tu_{xx}+\eta u_{xxt}},\qquad u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0.
\]
With \(u=\sum q_n(t)\sin(k_nx)\), \(k_n=n\pi/L\), orthogonality gives
\[
\mu\ddot q_n+\eta k_n^2\dot q_n+Tk_n^2q_n=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\omega_{0n}=ck_n,\quad c=\sqrt{T/\mu},\qquad
\boxed{\beta_n=\frac{\eta k_n^2}{2\mu}},
\]
and, when \(\beta_n<\omega_{0n}\),
\[
\boxed{\omega_{dn}=\sqrt{c^2k_n^2-\beta_n^2}}.
\]
The underdamped condition is
\[
\boxed{k_n<k_c=\frac{2\sqrt{\mu T}}{\eta}}.
\]
Because \(\beta_n\) grows as \(k_n^2\) while \(\omega_{0n}\) grows only as
\(k_n\), sufficiently short waves are overdamped in this idealized model.
At molecular or microstructural scales, constant \(T,\eta,\mu\) and a
one-dimensional continuum cease to be reliable, so the formal large-k trend
is not a universal material prediction.

The mechanical energy is
\[
E=\frac12\int_0^L(\mu u_t^2+Tu_x^2)\,dx.
\]
Using the PDE and integrating the elastic and viscous terms by parts gives
\[
\dot E=[u_t(Tu_x+\eta u_{xt})]_0^L
-\eta\int_0^L u_{xt}^2\,dx.
\]
Fixed displacement implies \(u_t=0\) at both endpoints, so
\[
\boxed{\dot E=-\eta\int_0^L u_{xt}^2\,dx\le0}.
\]
For \(q_n(0)=A\), \(\dot q_n(0)=0\), an underdamped mode is
\[
\boxed{q_n(t)=Ae^{-\beta_nt}
\left[\cos\omega_{dn}t+\frac{\beta_n}{\omega_{dn}}
\sin\omega_{dn}t\right]}.
\]

Numerically \(c=100.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and
\(k_c=2\sqrt{1}/0.2=10.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\). Since
\(k_n=n\pi\), the underdamped integers are exactly
\(\boxed{n=1,2,3}\).

For mode 1,
\[
\beta_1=\frac{0.2\pi^2}{0.02}
=\boxed{98.696\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\omega_{d1}=\sqrt{(100\pi)^2-\beta_1^2}
=\boxed{298.253\,\mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
For mode 3,
\[
\beta_3=9\beta_1=\boxed{888.264\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\omega_{d3}=\sqrt{(300\pi)^2-\beta_3^2}
=\boxed{315.041\,\mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
For mode 4,
\[
\beta_4=16\beta_1=1579.14\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}
>\omega_{04}=400\pi=1256.64\,\mathrm{rad/s},
\]
so its temporal roots are real and it is overdamped.

graderFixtures.proofText: Mode n satisfies \(\mu q_n''+\eta k_n^2q_n'+Tk_n^2q_n=0\), so \(\beta_n=\eta k_n^2/(2\mu)\) and underdamping requires \(k_n<2\sqrt{\mu T}/\eta\). The energy obeys \(\dot E=-\eta\int u_{xt}^2dx\), and zero initial velocity adds \((\beta_n/\omega_{dn})\sin\omega_{dn}t\).
I replace internal viscosity by the same dashpot coefficient for every mode. I then use only an exponentially damped cosine for release from rest, even though its initial derivative is not zero.

WAVE:010323.title: A bead at a string's midpoint moves only half the normal modes
WAVE:010323.objective: Derive parity-separated eigenfrequencies for a fixed string carrying an interior point mass and audit the massless and heavy-bead limits.
WAVE:010323.statement:
A uniform string of length \(L\), tension \(T\), and linear density
\(\mu\) is fixed at \(x=0,L\). A point mass \(M\) is attached to the
string at \(x=L/2\) and must share the string's transverse displacement
there. Small transverse motion obeys the ordinary string wave equation away
from the mass. Slopes may jump at the attachment, but displacement is
continuous.

Starting from transverse force balance on the bead, derive the derivative
jump condition with its sign. Classify modes by reflection parity about the
midpoint. Show that antisymmetric modes leave the bead stationary and give
their exact wave numbers. For symmetric modes, derive the transcendental
equation in \(z=kL/2\), and explain how its roots interlace with the
antisymmetric family. Recover the complete fixed-string spectrum as
\(M\to0\), and derive the leading heavy-mass frequency of the lowest
symmetric mode as \(M\to\infty\). Interpret that limit using the static
transverse stiffness of two half-strings.

For \(L=1.20\,\mathrm m\), \(T=120\,\mathrm N\),
\(\mu=0.0300\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and \(M=0.120\,\mathrm{kg}\), solve the
lowest symmetric root to at least five significant figures, compute its
angular frequency, and compare with the first antisymmetric frequency and the
heavy-mass approximation. State the small-slope, perfectly flexible,
point-mass, and lossless assumptions.
permittedResults: For harmonic motion with \(\omega=ck\) and \(c=\sqrt{T/\mu}\), each uniform segment solves \(Y''+k^2Y=0\).
For small \(z\), \(\tan z=z+O(z^3)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve each half-string and enforce continuity, force jump, and midpoint parity.
Use a distributional mass density with a midpoint delta term, then exploit reflection symmetry and derive the same matching equation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the bead force jump, separates parity families, obtains the correct transcendental equation, and verifies its limiting and numerical spectra.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Forces the spatial derivative to remain continuous even though the bead has nonzero transverse acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The bead inertia has no spectral effect and the symmetric eigenvalue equation is lost.

commonErrors.description: Applies the symmetric jump equation to antisymmetric modes whose midpoint displacement is zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact bead-node family is incorrectly moved with M.

hintTree.content: The bead equation is \(-M\omega^2Y(L/2)=T[Y'(L/2^+)-Y'(L/2^-)]\).
For a symmetric mode use \(Y=A\sin kx\) on the left and \(Y=A\sin k(L-x)\) on the right.
After setting \(z=kL/2\), track the factor of two in the force jump and the factor of two in \(k=2z/L\); they cancel in the final dimensionless coefficient.

WAVE:010323.canonicalSolution:
Away from the bead,
\[
\mu y_{tt}=Ty_{xx},\qquad c=\sqrt{T/\mu},\qquad \omega=ck.
\]
The upward components of tension on a short bead control volume give
\[
\boxed{-M\omega^2Y(L/2)=T\{Y'(L/2^+)-Y'(L/2^-)\}}.
\]
Displacement itself is continuous.

An antisymmetric mode has \(Y(L/2)=0\). Each half is then fixed at both
ends, and
\[
\boxed{k_{a,n}=\frac{2n\pi}{L}},\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.
\]
The two slopes agree across the midpoint for the globally smooth
antisymmetric sine, so the zero right side also satisfies the bead equation.

For a symmetric mode take
\[
Y=A\sin kx\quad(0<x<L/2),\qquad
Y=A\sin k(L-x)\quad(L/2<x<L).
\]
At the bead, \(Y=A\sin(kL/2)\), while the slope jump is
\(-2Ak\cos(kL/2)\). Thus
\[
M c^2 k^2\sin(kL/2)=2Tk\cos(kL/2).
\]
Using \(T=\mu c^2\) and \(z=kL/2\),
\[
\boxed{\tan z=\frac{\mu L}{Mz}}.
\]
There is one positive symmetric root in each interval where the two sides
have the same sign, interlacing with the bead-node family. When \(M\to0\),
the right side diverges and symmetric roots approach
\(z=(n+1/2)\pi\), or \(k=(2n+1)\pi/L\). Together with the antisymmetric
even multiples, these recover every fixed-string value \(k_j=j\pi/L\).

For a heavy bead, the lowest root is small. Then
\[
z^2\sim\frac{\mu L}{M},
\quad k\sim2\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{ML}},
\quad
\boxed{\omega\sim\sqrt{\frac{4T}{ML}}}.
\]
Each nearly straight half-string supplies transverse stiffness \(2T/L\),
so the two halves in parallel give \(4T/L\), exactly matching this limit.

For the numerical data, \(c=\sqrt{4000}=63.2456\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and
\(\mu L/M=0.300000\). Solving
\(\tan z=0.3/z\) gives
\[
\boxed{z_1=0.521791\ldots},\qquad
k_1=\frac{2z_1}{L}=0.869652\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega_{s,1}=55.0016\ \mathrm{rad/s}}\quad\text{(rounded)}.
\]
The first bead-node mode is
\[
\boxed{\omega_{a,1}=c\frac{2\pi}{L}=331.153\ \mathrm{rad/s}}.
\]
The leading heavy-bead estimate is
\[
\sqrt{\frac{4(120)}{0.120(1.20)}}=57.735\ \mathrm{rad/s},
\]
reasonably close but high because \(M/(\mu L)=3.33\) is finite rather than
asymptotically infinite. The derivation assumes small slopes, constant
tension, a perfectly flexible massless-bending string, an ideal point bead,
and no loss.

graderFixtures.proofText: The bead balance is \(-M\omega^2Y=T(Y'_+-Y'_-)\). Antisymmetric modes have \(k=2n\pi/L\). Symmetric segment sines give \(\tan z=\mu L/(Mz)\), \(z=kL/2\). It recovers odd fixed-string modes as M tends to zero and gives \(\omega\sim\sqrt{4T/(ML)}\) for a heavy bead. For the data, z is about 0.52179 and omega about 55.0 rad/s.
The string slope must be continuous at every interior point, so the bead cannot affect any eigenfrequency. I shift the antisymmetric node modes by the same equation anyway.

WAVE:010324.title: A spinning radial string hides a Legendre spectrum
WAVE:010324.objective: Derive the centrifugal equilibrium tension of a rotating radial string and solve its variable-coefficient transverse spectrum exactly as odd Legendre modes.
WAVE:010324.statement:
A uniform flexible string of length \(L\) and linear density \(\mu\) rotates
steadily in a horizontal plane with prescribed angular speed \(\Omega\).
Its inner end is fixed at the rotation axis, and its outer end is free. In the
steady configuration the string is straight and radial. Let \(r\) measure
distance from the axis and let \(y(r,t)\) be a small displacement perpendicular
to the plane of rotation. Ignore gravity, bending stiffness, and drag.

First isolate a section of the unperturbed string and derive its tension
\(T(r)\) from the centripetal force required by all material farther out.
Then derive the linear transverse equation
\(\mu y_{tt}=\partial_r(Ty_r)\). State the hub condition and the correct
regularity or finite-energy condition at the free tip, where the tension
vanishes; do not impose an extra zero-slope condition there.

For a normal mode, nondimensionalize with \(x=r/L\) and show that the spatial
equation is Legendre's equation. Prove that regularity at \(x=1\) discards the
second-kind solution and that the fixed hub selects odd polynomial degrees.
Derive all eigenfrequencies and mode shapes. Establish orthogonality using the
Sturm-Liouville form, normalize each mode to unit generalized mass, and verify
the spectrum independently from a Rayleigh quotient.

For \(L=1.50\,\mathrm m\), \(\mu=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and
\(\Omega=12.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), compute the hub tension and the first three
angular frequencies. Write the first three unnormalized mode polynomials and
locate the interior node of the second mode. Explain why replacing T by its
hub value gives the wrong boundary behavior and spectrum.
permittedResults: Legendre's equation \([(1-x^2)Y']'+\lambda Y=0\) has a solution regular at \(x=1\); the second independent solution is logarithmically singular there.
The polynomial solutions satisfy \(\int_{-1}^{1}P_\ell P_j\,dx=2\delta_{\ell j}/(2\ell+1)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the equilibrium load first, reduce the separated equation to Legendre form, and apply singular-endpoint regularity plus the fixed hub.
Use the Rayleigh quotient and Sturm-Liouville boundary form to infer orthogonality and confirm the explicit polynomial spectrum.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the centrifugal tension and variable-coefficient wave equation, selects the regular odd Legendre spectrum, and verifies its normalization and numerical modes.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the centrifugal profile by its hub value throughout the string.
commonErrors.consequence: The free-tip degeneracy and Legendre spectrum are replaced by an unrelated constant-coefficient string problem.

commonErrors.description: Imposes Y prime of L equals zero in addition to regularity even though the endpoint tension already vanishes.
commonErrors.consequence: The valid odd Legendre modes are incorrectly rejected or the spectrum is overconstrained.

hintTree.content: For a cut at r, integrate the outward centripetal load \(\mu\Omega^2s\,ds\) over the portion beyond the cut.
After substituting \(y=Y(r)e^{-i\omega t}\), multiply the spatial equation by \(2/\Omega^2\) and set \(x=r/L\).
The hub condition is \(Y(0)=0\). Use the value of \(P_\nu(0)\), or parity of polynomial solutions, to determine the allowed degrees.

WAVE:010324.canonicalSolution:
The portion outside a cut at r requires inward force
\[
T(r)=\int_r^L\mu\Omega^2s\,ds
=\boxed{\frac12\mu\Omega^2(L^2-r^2)}.
\]
It falls from \(T(0)=\mu\Omega^2L^2/2\) to zero at the free tip. For a
small out-of-plane slope, the difference of transverse tension components on
an element gives
\[
\boxed{\mu y_{tt}=\frac\partial{\partial r}\left(T(r)y_r\right)}.
\]
The hub is fixed, so \(y(0,t)=0\). At r=L the physical requirement is that
y remain finite and have finite energy
\(\int_0^LT|y_r|^2dr\); because T itself vanishes, \(y_r(L,t)=0\) is not
an additional boundary condition.

Put \(y=Y(r)e^{-i\omega t}\) and \(x=r/L\). Cancellation of \(\mu\)
and L gives
\[
\boxed{\frac d{dx}\left[(1-x^2)\frac{dY}{dx}\right]
+\lambda Y=0},\qquad \lambda=\frac{2\omega^2}{\Omega^2}.
\]
This is Legendre's equation. The second-kind solution diverges logarithmically
at x=1 and has infinite endpoint energy, so \(Y\) is proportional to
\(P_\nu(x)\), with \(\lambda=\nu(\nu+1)\). The identity
\[
P_\nu(0)=\frac{\sqrt\pi}
{\Gamma((1-\nu)/2)\Gamma(1+\nu/2)}
\]
vanishes for the nonnegative degrees \(\nu=1,3,5,\ldots\). Thus
\[
\boxed{Y_n(r)=P_{2n+1}(r/L)},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_n=\Omega\sqrt{\frac{(2n+1)(2n+2)}2}},
\quad n=0,1,2,\ldots
\]

The spatial operator is self-adjoint. Its boundary term
\([(1-x^2)(Y_jY_\ell'-Y_\ell Y_j')]_0^1\) vanishes at the hub because
both modes vanish there and at the tip because \(1-x^2\) vanishes while the
regular modes remain finite. Hence distinct modes are orthogonal. Since odd
Legendre polynomials have even products,
\[
\int_0^1P_\ell P_j\,dx=\frac{\delta_{\ell j}}{2\ell+1}
\quad(\ell,j\text{ odd}),
\]
so the unit-generalized-mass mode is
\[
\boxed{\widehat Y_\ell(r)=
\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{\mu L}}P_\ell(r/L)}.
\]
Multiplication of the eigen-equation by Y and integration gives
\[
\frac{\int_0^LT(Y')^2dr}{\int_0^L\mu Y^2dr}
=\frac{\Omega^2}{2}
\frac{\int_0^1(1-x^2)(Y_x)^2dx}{\int_0^1Y^2dx}
=\frac{\Omega^2}2\ell(\ell+1)=\omega_\ell^2,
\]
which independently verifies the spectrum.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{T(0)=\tfrac12(0.0200)(12.0)^2(1.50)^2=3.240\ \mathrm N}.
\]
For \(\ell=1,3,5\),
\[
\boxed{\omega_1=12.0000},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_3=29.3939},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_5=46.4758}\quad\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
The corresponding unnormalized shapes are
\[
P_1=x,\qquad P_3=\frac{5x^3-3x}{2},\qquad
P_5=\frac{63x^5-70x^3+15x}{8}.
\]
Besides the hub, the second mode has a node at
\[
\boxed{r=L\sqrt{3/5}=1.16190\ \mathrm m}.
\]
A constant-hub-tension model would retain nonzero tension at the free tip and
would demand an ordinary Neumann condition, producing trigonometric rather
than Legendre modes. It erases the singular endpoint that controls this
spectrum.

graderFixtures.proofText: The equilibrium tension is \(\mu\Omega^2(L^2-r^2)/2\). Separation gives \([(1-x^2)Y']'+(2\omega^2/\Omega^2)Y=0\). Tip regularity selects P, and Y(0)=0 selects degrees 1,3,5,..., so \(\omega_\ell=\Omega\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\). The data give hub tension 3.240 N and the first frequencies 12.0000, 29.3939, and 46.4758 rad/s.
I use the hub tension at every radius and impose zero slope at the free tip. That produces ordinary sine and cosine modes and discards the singular-endpoint physics.

WAVE:010325.title: A center strike selects only axisymmetric membrane modes
WAVE:010325.objective: Separate the circular membrane wave equation, derive its Bessel spectrum and degeneracy, and project an axisymmetric displacement onto the fundamental mode.
WAVE:010325.statement:
A uniform circular membrane of radius a has tension \(T\) per unit length and
surface mass density \(\sigma\). Its transverse displacement satisfies
\[
u_{tt}=c^2\nabla^2u,\qquad c=\sqrt{T/\sigma},
\]
with fixed edge \(u(a,\theta,t)=0\) and regularity at the center.

Separate variables in polar coordinates. Show why regularity excludes the
Neumann \(Y_m\) solution and why single-valuedness forces integer angular
order m. Derive the eigenfunctions, frequencies, and the twofold angular
degeneracy for \(m>0\). Explain which modes an ideal centered point impulse
can excite and why. For the axisymmetric initial displacement
\[
u(r,0)=U_0\left(1-\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right),\qquad u_t(r,0)=0,
\]
derive the coefficient of each \(J_0(j_{0n}r/a)\) mode using weighted radial
orthogonality. Reduce the numerator at a zero of \(J_0\) and give a closed
coefficient formula.

For \(a=0.300\,\mathrm m\), \(T=120\,\mathrm{N/m}\), and
\(\sigma=0.0750\,\mathrm{kg/m^2}\), compute c and the frequencies associated
with \(j_{01}=2.40482556\), \(j_{11}=3.83170597\), and
\(j_{21}=5.13562230\). Using \(J_1(j_{01})=0.519147497\), calculate the
fundamental axisymmetric coefficient relative to \(U_0\). Distinguish a
degenerate pair from two different radial eigenvalues and check units.
permittedResults:
\( rac d{dho}[ho^
u J_
u(jho)]=jho^
u J_{
u-1}(jho)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate the polar wave equation and use Sturm-Liouville orthogonality with weight r.
Use the membrane Green-function eigenbasis and evaluate the axisymmetric overlaps via Bessel recurrences.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the Bessel spectrum and center-selection rule, then evaluates the nontrivial weighted projection coefficient.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the Y_m radial solution at the membrane center.
commonErrors.consequence: The displacement is singular and violates the physical regularity condition.

commonErrors.description: Projects modes with dr instead of the polar area weight r dr.
commonErrors.consequence: The modal coefficients and normalization are incorrect.

hintTree.content: The radial equation is Bessel's equation after setting \(\lambda=\omega/c\); impose \(J_m(\lambda a)=0\).
At r=0, \(J_m(0)=0\) for positive m, so a centered point coupling has no overlap with those angular modes.
For the parabolic profile evaluate \(\int_0^1\rho(1-\rho^2)J_0(j\rho)d\rho\) by two Bessel derivative identities.

WAVE:010325.canonicalSolution:
With \(u=R(r)\Theta(\theta)Q(t)\), angular periodicity gives
\[
\Theta''+m^2\Theta=0,\qquad m=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
The radial equation is
\[
r^2R''+rR'+[(\lambda r)^2-m^2]R=0.
\]
Its solutions are \(J_m(\lambda r)\) and \(Y_m(\lambda r)\), but \(Y_m\)
is singular at the center and is excluded. The fixed edge requires
\[
J_m(\lambda a)=0,\qquad \lambda_{mn}=\frac{j_{mn}}a.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\omega_{mn}=c\frac{j_{mn}}a},
\]
with eigenfunctions
\[
J_m(j_{mn}r/a)\cos m\theta,\qquad
J_m(j_{mn}r/a)\sin m\theta
\]
for \(m>0\). These two orientations form one degenerate pair; different n
or different Bessel zeros are different eigenvalues unless an accidental
equality occurs. Since \(J_m(0)=0\) for \(m>0\), an ideal centered point
impulse couples only to \(m=0\).

For the axisymmetric release, write
\[
u(r,0)=\sum_{n\ge1}A_nJ_0(j_{0n}r/a).
\]
Radial orthogonality yields
\[
\frac{A_n}{U_0}=
\frac{\int_0^1\rho(1-\rho^2)J_0(j\rho)d\rho}
{\int_0^1\rho J_0(j\rho)^2d\rho},\qquad j=j_{0n}.
\]
Now
\[
\int_0^1\rho J_0(j\rho)d\rho=\frac{J_1(j)}j,
\]
and integration by parts with
\(d[\rho^2J_2(j\rho)]/d\rho=j\rho^2J_1(j\rho)\) gives
\[
\int_0^1\rho^3J_0(j\rho)d\rho
=\frac{J_1(j)}j-\frac{2J_2(j)}{j^2}.
\]
Their difference is \(2J_2(j)/j^2\). At a zero of \(J_0\), the recurrence
gives \(J_2(j)=2J_1(j)/j\), so
\[
\boxed{\frac{A_n}{U_0}=\frac{8}{j_{0n}^3J_1(j_{0n})}}.
\]

For the data,
\[
\boxed{c=\sqrt{120/0.0750}=40.0000\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The three frequencies in hertz are
\[
\boxed{f_{01}=51.0320\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_{11}=81.3113\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_{21}=108.981\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
The first axisymmetric projection is
\[
\boxed{\frac{A_1}{U_0}
=\frac8{(2.40482556)^3(0.519147497)}=1.10802}.
\]
A modal coefficient may exceed the peak displacement because other modes
interfere to reproduce the initial shape; it is not a pointwise probability.
The ratio \(T/\sigma\) has units of speed squared, and \(cj/a\) has units of
angular frequency.

graderFixtures.proofText: Regular fixed-edge modes are \(J_m(j_{mn}r/a)\) with \(\omega=cj_{mn}/a\); m positive has sine/cosine degeneracy, while a center impulse selects m=0. The parabolic axisymmetric profile has \(A_n/U_0=8/[j_{0n}^3J_1(j_{0n})]\). Numerically f01 is 51.0320 Hz and A1/U0 is 1.10802.
I include Y_m at the center and project the initial displacement using an unweighted dr integral, then insist every modal coefficient must be below one.

WAVE:010326.title: A graded string accumulates phase and reshapes its modes
WAVE:010326.objective: Apply WKB analysis to a fixed string with smoothly graded density, deriving phase quantization, flux-controlled amplitude, and a quantitative validity test.
WAVE:010326.statement:
A string of length L is held at constant tension \(T\), but its linear density
varies smoothly:
\[
\mu(x)=\mu_0\left(1+\epsilon\frac xL\right)^2,\qquad
0\le x\le L,\quad \epsilon>0.
\]
Small transverse motion satisfies
\[
\mu(x)u_{tt}=Tu_{xx},\qquad u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0.
\]
Consider a mode \(u=\operatorname{Re}\{\psi(x)e^{-i\omega t}\}\).

Derive the local wave number and leading WKB traveling-wave amplitudes.
Use constant time-averaged energy flux to confirm the amplitude transport
law independently. Combine counterpropagating waves to satisfy the fixed
ends and obtain the leading quantization rule. Evaluate the phase integral
exactly for the stated density and derive the approximate spectrum. Give a
dimensionless WKB validity measure and explain why low modes can fail it even
when density is smooth. Distinguish phase travel time from geometric length
divided by an arithmetic-average speed.

For \(L=2.00\,\mathrm m\), \(T=100\,\mathrm N\),
\(\mu_0=0.0400\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), \(\epsilon=0.500\), and mode \(n=5\),
compute the reference speed, one-way phase travel time, frequency, endpoint
wave numbers, endpoint amplitude ratio, and worst endpoint value of
\(|k'|/k^2\). State what is controlled and what remains only asymptotic.
permittedResults: For \(\psi''+k(x)^2\psi=0\), leading WKB waves are \(k^{-1/2}\exp[\pm i\int k\,dx]\).
The leading mean flux of a local harmonic string wave is proportional to \(T\omega k|A|^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply Liouville-Green WKB directly to the variable-coefficient modal equation.
Derive local phase from travel time and amplitude from conserved flux, then enforce the two fixed-end phases.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the graded-string WKB phase and amplitude, quantizes the phase integral, and audits the approximation quantitatively.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the integral of slowness by length divided by an arithmetic-average wave speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The modal phase and spectrum are quantitatively wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims the leading WKB eigenvalue is exact and omits the adiabatic error test.
commonErrors.consequence: Low-mode approximation error and derivative corrections are hidden.

hintTree.content: Here \(c(x)=\sqrt{T/\mu(x)}=c_0/(1+\epsilon x/L)\), so slowness is linear.
Fixed endpoints require the accumulated phase \(\int_0^Lk(x)dx\) to equal \(n\pi\).
Because k is proportional to \(1+\epsilon x/L\), the largest \(|k'|/k^2\) occurs at x=0.

WAVE:010326.canonicalSolution:
The modal equation is
\[
\psi''+\frac{\omega^2\mu(x)}T\psi=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{k(x)=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu(x)}T}
=\frac{\omega}{c_0}\left(1+\epsilon\frac xL\right)},
\qquad c_0=\sqrt{\frac T{\mu_0}}.
\]
The leading traveling WKB waves are
\[
\psi_\pm(x)\simeq\frac{C_\pm}{\sqrt{k(x)}}
\exp\left(\pm i\int_0^xk(s)\,ds\right).
\]
Therefore amplitude scales as \(k^{-1/2}\), equivalently
\[
\boxed{A(x)\propto\mu(x)^{-1/4}}.
\]
The same result follows from mean energy flux:
\(\langle P\rangle\propto T\omega kA^2\); conservation of flux makes
\(kA^2\) constant.

A standing combination that vanishes at x=0 is proportional to
\[
\frac1{\sqrt{k(x)}}\sin\left(\int_0^xk(s)\,ds\right).
\]
The second fixed end gives
\[
\int_0^Lk(x)\,dx=n\pi.
\]
Because
\[
\tau_{\rm ph}=\int_0^L\frac{dx}{c(x)}
=\frac{L}{c_0}\left(1+\frac\epsilon2\right),
\]
the leading spectrum is
\[
\boxed{\omega_n\simeq
\frac{n\pi c_0}{L(1+\epsilon/2)}}.
\]
This uses integrated slowness exactly within leading WKB; substituting an
arithmetic-average speed would not produce the same phase.

The adiabatic measure is
\[
\boxed{\eta(x)=\frac{|k'(x)|}{k(x)^2}},\qquad
k'=\frac{\omega\epsilon}{c_0L}.
\]
The approximation requires eta much less than one. At fixed profile,
\(\eta\) scales as \(1/n\), so smoothness alone does not guarantee accuracy
for the fundamental mode.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{c_0=50.0000\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\tau_{\rm ph}=0.0500000\ \mathrm s}.
\]
For \(n=5\),
\[
\boxed{\omega_5=314.159\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{f_5=50.0000\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
The endpoint wave numbers are
\[
\boxed{k(0)=6.28319\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{k(L)=9.42478\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
The transported amplitude ratio is
\[
\boxed{\frac{A(L)}{A(0)}=(1+\epsilon)^{-1/2}
=0.816497}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{\eta_{\max}=\eta(0)=0.0397887},
\]
small enough for a useful fifth-mode leading approximation. The phase
integral, transport law, and error parameter are controlled; the displayed
frequency is not claimed as an exact eigenvalue of the variable-coefficient
boundary problem. Dimensional checks give k in inverse length and tau in time.

graderFixtures.proofText: The local wave number is \(k=(\omega/c_0)(1+\epsilon x/L)\), amplitude scales as \(k^{-1/2}=\mu^{-1/4}\), and fixed ends require \(\omega\int dx/c=n\pi\). For the fifth mode, f is 50.0 Hz, k runs from 6.28319 to 9.42478 per m, the amplitude ratio is 0.816497, and max \(|k'|/k^2\) is 0.0397887.
I average the local speed arithmetically, keep a constant WKB amplitude, and call the resulting fundamental spectrum exact without checking k prime over k squared.

WAVE:010327.title: An exponential horn creates an acoustic cutoff
WAVE:010327.objective: Transform Webster's variable-area wave equation to a constant-coefficient dispersive equation and derive horn cutoff and velocity relations.
WAVE:010327.statement:
A lossless slowly varying acoustic horn has cross-sectional area
\(S(x)=S_0e^{2\alpha x}\), \(x\ge0\), with \(\alpha>0\). Its velocity
potential satisfies Webster's equation
\[
\frac1S\frac\partial{\partial x}\left(S\phi_x\right)
-\frac1{c^2}\phi_{tt}=0.
\]
Pressure and volume velocity are \(p=-\rho\phi_t\) and \(U=S\phi_x\).

Find a dependent-variable transformation that removes the first spatial
derivative. Derive the propagating dispersion relation, cutoff frequency,
phase velocity, and group velocity, and prove the phase-group product. Give
the evanescent solutions below cutoff and distinguish geometric amplitude
scaling from dissipative attenuation. For a traveling wave above cutoff,
show how the \(e^{-\alpha x}\) potential amplitude combines with expanding
area so the mean power is independent of x. State the slow-horn assumptions
behind Webster's one-dimensional model.

For \(c=340\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(\alpha=0.200\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), and
\(f=50.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), compute cutoff frequency, wave number, phase and
group velocities, their product, and the potential-amplitude e-folding
distance. Explain the limits at cutoff and far above cutoff, with dimensions.
permittedResults: For \(\omega^2=c^2(k^2+\alpha^2)\), \(v_p=\omega/k\), \(v_g=c^2k/\omega\), and \(v_pv_g=c^2\).
The cycle-averaged acoustic power in a lossless duct is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(pU^*)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Remove the first derivative by a Liouville transformation and solve the resulting constant-coefficient equation.
Use harmonic pressure and volume velocity directly in Webster's equation and identify the conserved Wronskian power flux.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Transforms the variable-area continuum model and reconciles its cutoff dispersion with lossless power transport.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Interprets the factor e to the minus alpha x as dissipated power without including the exponentially growing area.
commonErrors.consequence: The lossless mean-power conservation law is contradicted.

commonErrors.description: Uses k squared equal omega squared over c squared plus alpha squared and predicts propagation at every frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The exponential-horn cutoff and its limiting velocities disappear.

hintTree.content: Set \(\phi=e^{-\alpha x}\psi\) after expanding Webster's operator.
Below cutoff write k as i times a positive decay constant and keep both transformed and physical exponential factors distinct.
For a monochromatic traveling potential, p scales as \(e^{-\alpha x}\) while U contains S times the same potential.

WAVE:010327.canonicalSolution:
Expanding the area derivative gives
\[
\phi_{xx}+2\alpha\phi_x-c^{-2}\phi_{tt}=0.
\]
Set \(\phi=e^{-\alpha x}\psi\). Then
\[
\boxed{\psi_{xx}-c^{-2}\psi_{tt}-\alpha^2\psi=0}.
\]
For \(\psi=\Psi e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\),
\[
\boxed{\omega^2=c^2(k^2+\alpha^2)},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_c=\alpha c}.
\]
Above cutoff,
\[
\boxed{k=\sqrt{\omega^2/c^2-\alpha^2}},\quad
\boxed{v_p=\omega/k},\quad
\boxed{v_g=c^2k/\omega},\quad
\boxed{v_pv_g=c^2}.
\]
Below cutoff, \(k=i\kappa\) with
\(\kappa=\sqrt{\alpha^2-\omega^2/c^2}\), so transformed fields vary as
\(e^{\pm\kappa x}\), while the physical potential has the additional
\(e^{-\alpha x}\) factor. Boundary conditions choose the admissible
combination; no propagating mean power follows from a single real evanescent
solution.

For the right-going above-cutoff field
\(\phi=Ae^{-\alpha x}e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\), complex amplitudes are
\[
p=i\rho\omega\phi,\qquad
U=S(-\alpha+ik)\phi.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac12\operatorname{Re}(pU^*)
=\frac12\rho\omega k S|\phi|^2.
\]
Because \(S|\phi|^2=S_0e^{2\alpha x}|A|^2e^{-2\alpha x}\), this power is
constant. The decreasing potential and pressure amplitude is geometric
spreading, not loss. Webster theory additionally assumes transverse
equilibration, wavelengths and area-variation scales large compared with
duct dimensions, and no higher transverse modes, viscosity, or radiation
loading outside the declared horn.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{f_c=\frac{\alpha c}{2\pi}=10.8225\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
At 50 Hz,
\[
\boxed{k=0.902093\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{v_p=348.256\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{v_g=331.940\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{v_pv_g=115600\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}=c^2}.
\]
The physical potential's geometric e-folding distance is
\(\boxed{1/\alpha=5.00000\ \mathrm m}\). As cutoff is approached from
above, \(k,v_g\to0\) while \(v_p\to\infty\); no energy travels at the
diverging phase speed. Far above cutoff, both velocities approach c.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(\phi=e^{-\alpha x}\psi\), the transformed equation gives \(\omega^2=c^2(k^2+\alpha^2)\), cutoff \(\alpha c\), and \(v_pv_g=c^2\). Although potential amplitude falls as \(e^{-\alpha x}\), area grows as \(e^{2\alpha x}\), so mean power is constant. The data give fc 10.8225 Hz, k 0.902093 per m, vp 348.256 and vg 331.940 m/s.
I keep the first derivative, change its sign into gain, claim there is no cutoff, and interpret the pressure amplitude decrease as irreversible energy loss despite the expanding area.

WAVE:010328.title: A star junction splits a wave with a unitary scattering matrix
WAVE:010328.objective: Derive N-port scattering at a massless junction of identical strings and prove flux conservation from the junction conditions.
WAVE:010328.statement:
N identical semi-infinite strings meet at a massless junction. Each branch has
outward coordinate \(x_j\ge0\), tension T, density \(\mu\), and wave speed c.
The junction displacement is continuous, and the sum of outward transverse
forces vanishes. A unit-amplitude monochromatic wave is incident toward the
junction on branch 1; there are no other incoming waves.

Choose an explicit \(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention and write the incident,
reflected, and transmitted fields with the correct signs of wave number.
Derive the reflection and every transmission amplitude for general N. Prove
energy-flux conservation without assuming it, and build the full N-by-N
scattering matrix. Diagonalize that matrix into its symmetric and
antisymmetric junction channels and prove it is both real symmetric and
unitary. Interpret the phase reversals and the N=2 boundary.

For N=4, \(T=80.0\,\mathrm N\), \(\mu=0.0500\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), incident
displacement amplitude \(A=3.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), and \(f=25.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\),
compute c, k, reflection and transmission amplitudes, all power fractions,
and the incident mean power. Explain why summing displacement amplitudes
instead of quadratic fluxes gives the wrong conservation test.
permittedResults: A traveling string wave of displacement amplitude A carries mean power \(T\omega k|A|^2/2\) in its propagation direction.
The all-ones matrix J has eigenvalue N on the uniform vector and zero on its orthogonal complement.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match one incident wave to all outgoing waves using continuity and force balance.
Decompose incoming data into the uniform junction channel and its zero-sum orthogonal complement.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the complete star-junction scattering operator and verifies its channel structure and flux unitarity.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the outgoing exponential for the wave incident toward decreasing outward coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative force balance and reflection phase are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Tests conservation by adding signed displacement amplitudes rather than directed quadratic energy fluxes.
commonErrors.consequence: A unitary junction can be falsely labeled lossy or amplifying.

hintTree.content: With outward x and time factor \(e^{-i\omega t}\), the incoming branch-1 wave is \(e^{-ikx}\), while every outgoing wave is proportional to \(e^{ikx}\).
Continuity gives \(1+R=\tau\); outward force balance gives \(R-1+(N-1)\tau=0\).
Write the multiport answer as \(S=(2/N)J-I\) and square it using \(J^2=NJ\).

WAVE:010328.canonicalSolution:
Suppress the common time factor. On branch 1 write
\[
y_1=A(e^{-ikx}+Re^{ikx}),
\]
and on every other branch write \(y_j=A\tau e^{ikx}\). Continuity at zero
gives \(1+R=\tau\). Since all coordinates point outward, massless force
balance is \(\sum_jTy_{j,x}(0)=0\), hence
\[
R-1+(N-1)\tau=0.
\]
Solving,
\[
\boxed{R=\frac2N-1},\qquad \boxed{\tau=\frac2N}.
\]
The strings have equal impedance, so flux fractions are squared amplitude
magnitudes. Directly,
\[
|R|^2+(N-1)|\tau|^2
=\left(1-\frac2N\right)^2+(N-1)\frac4{N^2}=1.
\]

For arbitrary incoming ports the scattering matrix is
\[
\boxed{S=\frac2N J-I}.
\]
The uniform channel has \(J\mathbf1=N\mathbf1\), so S has eigenvalue +1
there. Every vector whose components sum to zero has J eigenvalue zero and S
eigenvalue -1. Therefore
\[
S^T=S,\qquad S^2=I,
\]
so S is reciprocal and unitary. The symmetric channel passes the junction
without a phase reversal, while all (N-1) antisymmetric channels acquire
phase pi. At N=2, \(R=0\) and \(\tau=1\): two identical half-strings are simply
one uniform string.

For N=4,
\[
\boxed{c=\sqrt{T/\mu}=40.0000\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{k=2\pi f/c=3.92699\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
The amplitudes are
\[
\boxed{R=-0.500000},\qquad \boxed{\tau=0.500000}.
\]
Reflected power is 0.25 of incident power, and each of three transmitted
branches carries 0.25, for total one. The incident mean power is
\[
\boxed{\overline P_{in}=\frac12T\omega kA^2
=0.222066\ \mathrm W}.
\]
Thus 0.0555165 W is reflected and the same amount enters each outgoing other
branch. Linear amplitudes can have signs and interfere at the junction;
energy flux is quadratic, so adding \(R+3\tau=1\) is not the conservation
law. The force and power signs follow from the declared outward coordinates.

graderFixtures.proofText: Continuity and outward force balance give \(R=2/N-1\), \(\tau=2/N\), and \(|R|^2+(N-1)|\tau|^2=1\). The full matrix is \(2J/N-I\), with eigenvalue plus one on the uniform channel and minus one on all zero-sum channels. For N=4 every outgoing power fraction is one quarter and incident mean power is 0.222066 W.
I use e to the plus ikx for the incident wave, add R and three transmission amplitudes as if they were powers, and obtain a scattering matrix that does not square to identity.

WAVE:010329.title: A pulsating sphere radiates an acoustic wave
WAVE:010329.objective: Solve the outgoing spherical Helmholtz field and derive its finite-size radiation impedance, far pressure, and power.
WAVE:010329.statement:
A sphere of radius \(a\) in an inviscid fluid has a prescribed small,
uniform radial surface velocity
\[
u_r(a,t)=\operatorname{Re}[U_0e^{-i\omega t}].
\]
The fluid has equilibrium density \(\rho\), sound speed \(c\), and no incoming
wave. Introduce a velocity potential with \(\mathbf u=\nabla\phi\) and
acoustic pressure \(p=-\rho\,\partial_t\phi\). Use the outgoing spherical
ansatz
\[
\phi(r,t)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\frac{C e^{ikr}}{r}e^{-i\omega t}\right],
\qquad k=\omega/c.
\]

Determine \(C\) from the velocity boundary condition. Derive the specific
surface radiation impedance \(Z_s=p(a)/U_0\), displaying its resistive and
reactive parts. Compute the time-averaged total radiated power in two ways:
from the surface impedance and from the far-field intensity. Derive the
far-field pressure amplitude at radius \(r\), and discuss the small-\(ka\)
and large-\(ka\) limits. Keep the stated \(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention so the
reactance sign is unambiguous.

For air with \(\rho=1.20\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\),
\(c=343\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(a=0.0500\,\mathrm m\),
\(f=1.00\,\mathrm{kHz}\), and \(|U_0|=0.0100\,\mathrm{m/s}\), compute
\(ka\), both parts of \(Z_s\), total average power, and the far-field
pressure amplitude at \(r=1.00\,\mathrm m\). Audit all units.
permittedResults: For peak phasors, the time-averaged surface power density is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(pU^*)\).
An outgoing spherical wave has far-field intensity \(|p|^2/(2\rho c)\) and area \(4\pi r^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the radial Helmholtz boundary-value problem directly in velocity-potential form.
Use surface work and far-field intensity as independent audits of amplitude and normalization.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the spherical radiation field from its boundary velocity and reconciles impedance power with far-field flux.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets the surface impedance equal to rho c without retaining its ka-dependent resistance and reactance.
commonErrors.consequence: Near-field storage and low-frequency radiation efficiency are lost.

commonErrors.description: Mixes peak phasors with an RMS power formula and loses or doubles the factor one half.
commonErrors.consequence: Surface and far-field powers fail to agree.

hintTree.content: Differentiate \(e^{ikr}/r\) before imposing \(u_r(a)=U_0\).
Write \(x=ka\) and rationalize \(i\rho cx/(ix-1)\).
In the far field, pressure and velocity are locally in phase; multiply intensity by the spherical area.

WAVE:010329.canonicalSolution:
The radial phasor velocity is
\[
u_r(r)=C e^{ikr}\frac{ikr-1}{r^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{C=\frac{U_0a^2e^{-ika}}{ika-1}}.
\]
Because the pressure phasor is \(p=i\rho\omega C e^{ikr}/r\), the surface
specific impedance, with \(x=ka\), is
\[
Z_s=\frac{i\rho\omega a}{ix-1}
=\boxed{\rho c\left[\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}
-i\frac{x}{1+x^2}\right]}.
\]
The negative reactance follows from the chosen \(e^{-i\omega t}\) convention.

Using peak amplitudes, the sphere emits
\[
\boxed{\overline P
=\frac12(4\pi a^2)\operatorname{Re}Z_s\,|U_0|^2
=2\pi a^2\rho c|U_0|^2\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}}.
\]
Far from the sphere,
\[
\boxed{|p(r)|=\frac{\rho\omega |U_0|a^2}
{r\sqrt{1+x^2}}}.
\]
Substitution into \(4\pi r^2|p|^2/(2\rho c)\) reproduces the same power,
since \(\omega=cx/a\). For \(x\ll1\), resistance is proportional to
\(x^2\), reactance is proportional to \(-x\), and radiation is inefficient.
For \(x\gg1\), \(Z_s\to\rho c\) and the surface is locally plane-wave-like.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{ka=0.915916226},
\]
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Re}Z_s=187.770845\ \mathrm{Pa\,s/m}},\qquad
\boxed{\operatorname{Im}Z_s=-205.008755\ \mathrm{Pa\,s/m}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\overline P=2.94949754\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm W},\qquad
\boxed{|p(1\,\mathrm m)|=0.139002230\ \mathrm{Pa}}.
\]
Pressure divided by velocity has units \(\mathrm{Pa\,s/m}\); multiplying its
real part by area and velocity squared gives watts, as required.

graderFixtures.proofText: The boundary derivative gives \(C=U_0a^2e^{-ika}/(ika-1)\) and \(Z_s=\rho c[(ka)^2-i(ka)]/[1+(ka)^2]\). The data give \(ka=0.915916226\), \(Z_s=(187.770845-i205.008755)\ \mathrm{Pa\,s/m}\), power \(2.94949754\times10^{-4}\) W, and far pressure 0.139002230 Pa.
I use the plane-wave impedance rho c at the sphere, ignore the radial derivative term, and combine peak pressure with RMS power.

WAVE:010330.title: A closed basin rings in seiche modes
WAVE:010330.objective: Derive closed-basin shallow-water modes and reconstruct a two-mode free-surface initial-value problem with its velocity field.
WAVE:010330.statement:
A long rectangular basin has uniform undisturbed depth \(h\), length \(L\),
and rigid vertical end walls at \(x=0,L\). In the inviscid linear
shallow-water approximation, the free-surface displacement \(\eta(x,t)\)
and depth-averaged horizontal velocity \(u(x,t)\) obey
\[
\eta_t+h u_x=0,\qquad u_t+g\eta_x=0.
\]
The walls impose \(u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0\).

Eliminate either field to obtain the wave equation and derive the admissible
free-surface eigenfunctions, wavenumbers, frequencies, and periods. Explain
why the wall condition becomes a Neumann condition on every nonzero-frequency
\(\eta\) mode, and identify the special zero mode. Reconstruct both
\(\eta\) and \(u\) for
\[
\eta(x,0)=\eta_0\cos(\pi x/L)
+\frac{\eta_0}{2}\cos(2\pi x/L),\qquad u(x,0)=0.
\]
Verify both first-order equations rather than checking only the derived wave
equation, and state a nondispersive phase relation between the surface and
velocity amplitudes.

For \(L=1.00\,\mathrm{km}\), \(h=25.0\,\mathrm m\),
\(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and \(\eta_0=0.200\,\mathrm m\), compute the
wave speed and the first two modal periods. At one quarter of the fundamental
period, compute \(\eta\) and \(u\) at \(x=L/3\). Check the shallow-water
parameters \(k_1h\) and \(k_2h\).

For the linear shallow-water equations, the nondispersive speed is \(c=\sqrt{gh}\).

hintTree.content: Differentiate continuity in time and momentum in space before eliminating \(u_{xt}\).
For a cosine surface mode, choose a sine velocity mode so that the wall velocity vanishes.
At \(t=T_1/4\), the first temporal cosine vanishes while the second equals minus one.

WAVE:010330.canonicalSolution:
Elimination gives
\[
\boxed{\eta_{tt}-gh\,\eta_{xx}=0},\qquad
\boxed{u_{tt}-gh\,u_{xx}=0},\qquad c=\sqrt{gh}.
\]
For a nonzero-frequency harmonic, \(u=0\) at a wall for all time and
\(u_t=-g\eta_x\), so \(\eta_x=0\) there. Hence
\[
\boxed{k_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}},\qquad
\boxed{\eta_n\propto\cos(k_nx)},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_n=ck_n},\qquad
\boxed{T_n=\frac{2L}{nc}}\quad(n\ge1).
\]
The \(n=0\) mode is a spatially uniform, volume-changing offset with zero
frequency; volume conservation fixes it rather than making it an
oscillatory seiche.

For the stated release,
\[
\boxed{\eta=\eta_0\cos(k_1x)\cos(\omega_1t)
+\frac{\eta_0}{2}\cos(k_2x)\cos(\omega_2t)}
\]
and momentum determines
\[
\boxed{u=\frac{c\eta_0}{h}\sin(k_1x)\sin(\omega_1t)
+\frac{c\eta_0}{2h}\sin(k_2x)\sin(\omega_2t)}.
\]
Direct differentiation verifies both \(\eta_t+hu_x=0\) and
\(u_t+g\eta_x=0\), using \(c^2=gh\). Each traveling-wave component has
velocity-to-surface amplitude ratio \(c/h=g/c\).

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{c=15.6604598\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{T_1=127.710\ \mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{T_2=63.8548\ \mathrm s}.
\]
At \(t=T_1/4\) and \(x=L/3\), the first surface term vanishes, the second
temporal cosine is \(-1\), and both second-mode velocity factors vanish:
\[
\boxed{\eta=0.0500000\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{u=0.108499\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{k_1h=0.0785398},\qquad
\boxed{k_2h=0.157080},
\]
so both retained modes are reasonably within the long-wave ordering, with
the second less asymptotic than the first.

WAVE:010331.title: A membrane annulus has two Bessel boundaries
WAVE:010331.objective: Derive the axisymmetric spectrum of a fixed annular membrane, retain both Bessel branches, and connect the roots to disk and thin-strip limits.
WAVE:010331.statement:
A membrane occupies the annulus \(b\le r\le a\), has uniform
surface density \(\mu\), isotropic tension \(T\), and wave speed
\(c=\sqrt{T/\mu}\). Both circular edges are fixed:
\[
u(b,t)=u(a,t)=0.
\]
Restrict attention to axisymmetric motion. Starting from the polar wave
equation, derive the radial eigenfunctions without imposing regularity at the
excluded point \(r=0\). With
\[
\eta=\frac ba,\qquad q=ka,
\]
obtain a dimensionless determinant whose positive zeros \(q_n\) give the
frequencies. Prove orthogonality of distinct modes with the correct radial
weight and write the conserved mechanical energy.

Analyze two geometric limits: \(\eta\to0\), where the hole closes, and
\(\eta\to1^-\), where the annulus becomes a narrow strip. State the limiting
root conditions, including the leading thin-annulus estimate.

For \(\eta=0.500\), you may use the first three determinant zeros
\[
q_1=6.246061839,\qquad q_2=12.54687143,\qquad q_3=18.83641508.
\]
If \(a=0.400\,\mathrm m\) and \(c=120\,\mathrm{m/s}\), compute the first three
ordinary frequencies. Compare \(q_1\) with the thin-strip estimate and report
its percentage overestimate.
permittedResults: Solutions of \(R''+R'/r+k^2R=0\) on an interval bounded away from zero are linear combinations of \(J_0(kr)\) and \(Y_0(kr)\).
For two separated radial eigenfunctions, Green's identity makes \((k_m^2-k_n^2)\int_b^a rR_mR_n\,dr\) equal to a boundary Wronskian.

acceptableStrategies.description: Build an inner-edge-vanishing Bessel combination and impose the outer edge as one scalar determinant.
Start with the general two-coefficient Bessel solution and set the determinant of the two boundary equations to zero.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Treats the annulus as a two-boundary radial Sturm--Liouville system and verifies its determinant through orthogonality and geometric limits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Discards the Y0 solution by imposing regularity at r equals zero even though the membrane begins at positive b.
commonErrors.consequence: The two fixed edges are generally incompatible and the resulting spectrum is that of a disk, not an annulus.

commonErrors.description: Uses an unweighted radial inner product for the separated modes.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed orthogonality and modal projection do not follow from the polar wave operator.

hintTree.content: Choose a linear combination that vanishes at \(r=b\) before imposing the outer condition.
In the small-hole limit, the divergent coefficient \(Y_0(\eta q)\) makes the finite-root condition approach \(J_0(q)=0\).
For a narrow annulus, unwrap the radial interval of width \(a-b\) and compare with a string fixed at both ends.

WAVE:010331.canonicalSolution:
Axisymmetry gives
\[
u_{tt}=c^2\left(u_{rr}+\frac1r u_r\right).
\]
For a separated mode \(u=R(r)\cos(\omega t)\), \(k=\omega/c\), and
\[
R(r)=A J_0(kr)+B Y_0(kr).
\]
The \(Y_0\) term is allowed because \(r\ge b>0\). A convenient shape that
already vanishes at the inner edge is
\[
\Phi_q(r)=Y_0(\eta q)J_0\left(\frac{qr}{a}\right)
-J_0(\eta q)Y_0\left(\frac{qr}{a}\right).
\]
The outer edge therefore requires
\[
\boxed{D_\eta(q)=Y_0(\eta q)J_0(q)
-J_0(\eta q)Y_0(q)=0},
\qquad
\boxed{\omega_n=\frac{cq_n}{a}}.
\]

Multiplying the radial equations for \(\Phi_m,\Phi_n\) crosswise and
subtracting gives
\[
(k_m^2-k_n^2)\int_b^a r\Phi_m(r)\Phi_n(r)\,dr
=\left[r(\Phi_n\Phi_m'-\Phi_m\Phi_n')\right]_b^a=0.
\]
Thus distinct modes are orthogonal with weight \(r\), not with weight one.
The conserved energy is
\[
\boxed{\mathcal E=\pi\int_b^a
\left[\mu r u_t^2+T r u_r^2\right]dr}.
\]
The factor \(\pi\) results from the angular integral and the usual one-half
in kinetic and elastic energy.

As \(\eta\to0\), finite positive roots satisfy
\[
\boxed{J_0(q_n)=0},
\]
recovering regular disk modes. When \(1-\eta\ll1\), curvature varies little
across the width \(a-b\), so fixed--fixed strip modes give
\[
\boxed{q_n\sim\frac{n\pi}{1-\eta}}\qquad(n=1,2,\ldots).
\]
This is a geometric asymptotic statement, not an exact determinant identity.

For the supplied roots,
\[
\boxed{f_1=298.227485\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_2=599.068982\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_3=899.372571\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
At \(\eta=0.5\), the strip estimate is \(q_1^{\rm strip}=2\pi\), which
overestimates the exact first root by
\[
\boxed{100\left(\frac{2\pi}{q_1}-1\right)=0.594350\%}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: An inner-edge-vanishing mode is \(Y_0(\eta q)J_0(qr/a)-J_0(\eta q)Y_0(qr/a)\). The outer edge gives \(D_\eta(q)=0\), the weight is \(r\), and the first frequency is \(298.227485\) Hz.
I throw out Y zero because it diverges at the origin, use disk zeros J zero of q, and project the modes with dr rather than r dr.

WAVE:010332.title: A tapered shaft turns torsional modes into Bessel modes
WAVE:010332.objective: Transform the variable-coefficient torsional-wave equation of a linearly tapered shaft and derive its fixed-free frequency determinant.
WAVE:010332.statement:
A circular elastic shaft occupies \(0\le x\le L\) and has radius
\[
R(x)=R_0\left(1+\alpha\frac{x}{L}\right),\qquad \alpha>0.
\]
Its shear modulus \(G\) and density \(\rho\) are uniform. For a circular
section the polar second moment is \(J_p(x)=\pi R(x)^4/2\). The twist angle
\(\theta(x,t)\) is fixed at \(x=0\), while the end \(x=L\) is torque-free.

Derive the variable-coefficient torsional wave equation from angular-momentum
balance and separate variables. Introduce
\[
s=1+\alpha x/L,\qquad
c_t=\sqrt{G/\rho},\qquad
\lambda=\frac{\omega L}{\alpha c_t}.
\]
Show that the spatial equation reduces to a Bessel equation after a power
substitution. Derive a determinant involving half-integer Bessel functions
whose positive roots determine the fixed-free spectrum. State the modal
orthogonality weight and the conserved energy.

Explain why \(R_0\) cancels from every natural frequency even though the
shaft stiffness changes with radius. Recover the uniform-shaft spectrum in
the singular limit \(\alpha\to0\) by keeping \(q=\alpha\lambda=\omega L/c_t\)
finite.

For \(\alpha=1.00\), use
\[
\lambda_1=0.824971200,\qquad
\lambda_2=4.600454229,\qquad
\lambda_3=7.789096696.
\]
With \(G=26.0\,\mathrm{GPa}\), \(\rho=2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and
\(L=1.20\,\mathrm m\), compute the first three ordinary frequencies and
compare the fundamental with that of a uniform fixed-free shaft.
permittedResults: The equation \(X_{ss}+4X_s/s+\lambda^2X=0\) has basis \(s^{-3/2}J_{3/2}(\lambda s)\), \(s^{-3/2}Y_{3/2}(\lambda s)\).

\( rac{d}{ds}[s^{-
u}J_
u(\lambda s)]=-\lambda s^{-
u}J_{
u+1}(\lambda s)\), with the analogous identity for \(Y_
u\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the divergence-form eigenproblem using the dimensionless radius s and then remove the first-derivative coefficient by a power substitution.
Express the half-integer Bessel basis as elementary sine and cosine functions and impose the same fixed-free determinant.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Carries the linear radius taper through the torsional field equation, boundary determinant, modal weight, and uniform-limit audit.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the varying polar second moment by a constant before deriving the spectrum.
commonErrors.consequence: The half-order Bessel equation and all taper dependence disappear.

commonErrors.description: Imposes zero twist instead of zero torque at the free end.
commonErrors.consequence: The determinant uses order three-halves at both ends and produces a fixed-fixed spectrum.

hintTree.content: Apply angular-momentum balance to an element whose torque is \(GJ_p\theta_x\).
After changing to \(s\), divide \((s^4X_s)_s+\lambda^2s^4X=0\) by \(s^4\).
Use the fixed condition to form one row with order \(3/2\), and the free derivative condition to form a second row with order \(5/2\).

WAVE:010332.canonicalSolution:
Angular-momentum balance gives
\[
\boxed{\rho J_p(x)\theta_{tt}
=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(GJ_p(x)\theta_x\right)}.
\]
For \(\theta=X(x)\cos(\omega t)\), the spatial equation is
\[
(GJ_pX')'+\rho J_p\omega^2X=0.
\]
Because \(J_p=J_0s^4\), where \(J_0=\pi R_0^4/2\), the change of variable
specified in the question produces
\[
(s^4X_s)_s+\lambda^2s^4X=0,
\qquad
X_{ss}+\frac4sX_s+\lambda^2X=0.
\]
Writing \(X=s^{-3/2}Z(\lambda s)\) gives Bessel's equation of order \(3/2\),
so
\[
X(s)=s^{-3/2}\left[A J_{3/2}(\lambda s)
+B Y_{3/2}(\lambda s)\right].
\]

The fixed condition at \(s=1\) and the free condition at
\(s_1=1+\alpha\) are
\[
A J_{3/2}(\lambda)+B Y_{3/2}(\lambda)=0,
\]
\[
A J_{5/2}(\lambda s_1)+B Y_{5/2}(\lambda s_1)=0.
\]
A nonzero pair \(A,B\) therefore requires
\[
\boxed{
J_{3/2}(\lambda)Y_{5/2}(\lambda(1+\alpha))
-Y_{3/2}(\lambda)J_{5/2}(\lambda(1+\alpha))=0
}.
\]
Each root gives
\[
\boxed{\omega_n=\frac{\alpha c_t}{L}\lambda_n}.
\]

Self-adjointness of \((GJ_pX')'\) gives orthogonality
\[
\boxed{\int_0^L J_p(x)X_m(x)X_n(x)\,dx=0\quad(m\ne n)},
\]
with the constant density optionally included in the weight. The energy is
\[
\boxed{\mathcal E=\frac12\int_0^L
\left[\rho J_p\theta_t^2+GJ_p\theta_x^2\right]dx}.
\]
Both inertia and rigidity contain the same multiplicative factor
\(J_0\propto R_0^4\), so it cancels from the eigenvalue equation. The taper
ratio still matters through \(s^4\).

As \(\alpha\to0\), \(\lambda\) diverges while
\(q=\alpha\lambda=\omega L/c_t\) stays finite. The problem approaches a
uniform fixed-free shaft, hence
\[
\boxed{q_n\longrightarrow\left(n+\frac12\right)\pi},
\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]

For the stated material,
\[
\boxed{c_t=3103.16445\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Using \(f_n=\alpha c_t\lambda_n/(2\pi L)\) gives
\[
\boxed{f_1=339.533371\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_2=1893.40880\ \mathrm{Hz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_3=3205.75828\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
A uniform fixed-free shaft has
\[
f_1^{(0)}=\frac{c_t}{4L}=646.492595\ \mathrm{Hz},
\]
so this widening taper lowers the fundamental to
\[
\boxed{f_1/f_1^{(0)}=0.525193}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(s=1+\alpha x/L\), the mode is \(s^{-3/2}[AJ_{3/2}(\lambda s)+BY_{3/2}(\lambda s)]\). Fixed and free conditions produce the \(3/2\)-\(5/2\) determinant, and \(f_1=339.533371\) Hz.
I freeze J p at its root value, solve a constant-coefficient sine problem, and impose zero angle at the endpoint described as torque-free.
