WAVE:010417.title: What a sharp rectangular pulse costs in wavenumber space
WAVE:010417.objective: Transform a compact rectangular pulse under an explicit convention, verify Parseval normalization, and diagnose why its root-mean-square spectral width diverges.
WAVE:010417.statement:
Use the Fourier-transform convention
\[
F(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx,
\qquad
f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(k)e^{ikx}\,dk.
\]
Let \(f(x)=A\) for \(|x|<a\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(|x|>a\), where
\(A\) is real and nonzero. Values at \(x=\pm a\) may be chosen arbitrarily.

Derive \(F(k)\), including its continuous value at \(k=0\), and locate its
first zeros and central-lobe width. Verify Parseval's identity for this pair
and thereby derive
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\sin u}{u}\right)^2du=\pi.
\]
Then determine whether the spectral second moment
\(\int k^2|F(k)|^2dk\) is finite. Explain precisely why compact support does
not imply finite root-mean-square bandwidth here, how the jump discontinuities
control the high-\(|k|\) tail, and why changing the pulse's two endpoint values
does not change its transform as an \(L^1\) function.
permittedResults: Under the stated convention, Parseval's identity is \(\int|f|^2dx=(2\pi)^{-1}\int|F|^2dk\).
Changing an integrable function on a set of measure zero does not change its Fourier integral.

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the pulse directly, use Parseval with a dimensionless substitution, and test the second-moment tail.
Obtain the transform from step-function differences, provided the same convention, removable limit, zeros, and convergence analysis are explicit.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Computes the sinc spectrum and normalization, derives the Parseval integral identity, and correctly proves divergence of the spectral second moment from the jump-controlled tail.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses a Parseval factor inconsistent with the declared transform and inverse conventions.
commonErrors.consequence: The spectral-energy identity and sinc integral have the wrong constant.

commonErrors.description: Claims the compact pulse has finite RMS bandwidth without testing the second spectral moment.
commonErrors.consequence: The conclusion contradicts the nonintegrable high-wavenumber moment.

hintTree.content: Integrate \(Ae^{-ikx}\) from \(-a\) to \(a\), then take the \(k\to0\) limit rather than substituting into a quotient.
For Parseval, substitute \(u=ka\) after writing \(|F(k)|^2\).
Multiply the large-\(|k|\) form of \(|F|^2\) by \(k^2\); the remaining oscillatory factor does not have a convergent integral.

WAVE:010417.canonicalSolution:
Direct integration gives, for \(k\ne0\),
\[
F(k)=A\frac{e^{-ika}-e^{ika}}{-ik}
=\frac{2A\sin(ka)}k
=2Aa\,\operatorname{sinc}(ka),
\]
where \(\operatorname{sinc}u=\sin u/u\). The removable limit is
\[
\boxed{F(0)=2Aa},
\]
equal to the pulse area. The nearest zeros occur at
\(k=\pm\pi/a\), so the central-lobe zero-to-zero width is
\[
\boxed{2\pi/a}.
\]

The spatial norm is
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(x)|^2dx=2aA^2.
\]
Parseval's right side is
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
4A^2a^2\left(\frac{\sin(ka)}{ka}\right)^2dk
=\frac{2A^2a}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\sin u}{u}\right)^2du.
\]
Since \(A\ne0\) and \(a>0\), equating this with \(2aA^2\) and cancelling
the nonzero factor \(2aA^2\) gives
\[
\boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\sin u/u)^2du=\pi}.
\]

However,
\[
k^2|F(k)|^2=4A^2\sin^2(ka).
\]
Its integral over the real line diverges: each successive interval contains a
fixed positive average contribution. Thus the RMS spectral width is infinite,
even though the pulse occupies only a finite spatial interval. The jumps make
\(F(k)=O(1/k)\), so \(|F|^2=O(1/k^2)\), enough for total spectral power but
not for its second moment. Smoothing the edges can produce faster decay.
Finally, endpoint values affect only two points, a measure-zero set, and hence
do not alter the Fourier integral or any \(L^p\) equivalence class.

graderFixtures.proofText: The transform is \(F(k)=2A\sin(ka)/k\) with \(F(0)=2Aa\) and first zeros \(\pm\pi/a\). Parseval gives the sinc-squared integral \(\pi\). But \(k^2|F|^2=4A^2\sin^2(ka)\), whose nonnegative integral diverges, so RMS bandwidth is not finite.
Because the pulse has finite support, every spectral moment is finite. I use Parseval without a two-pi factor and obtain an integral of two-pi for sinc squared.

WAVE:010418.title: Spectral leakage from a finite carrier burst
WAVE:010418.objective: Use the Fourier modulation property to derive the spectrum of a finite wave train, quantify main-lobe resolution, and relate real and complex carrier representations.
WAVE:010418.statement:
Use the same convention
\(F(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx\). Define the complex finite wave train
\[
g(x)=
\begin{cases}
A e^{ik_0x},&|x|<L/2,\\
0,&|x|>L/2,
\end{cases}
\qquad L>0,\quad k_0>0.
\]
Derive \(G(k)\), locate its peak and first zeros, and give the zero-to-zero
main-lobe width. Explain quantitatively how increasing the number of carrier
cycles in the window improves wavenumber resolution while retaining sinc
sidelobes.

Now take the real burst \(f(x)=A\cos(k_0x)\) on the same interval and zero
outside. Derive its transform as the sum of two shifted sinc functions. State
why a real signal must have conjugate-symmetric spectral content. If
\(k_0L=2\pi N\) for a positive integer \(N\), use Parseval to verify
\(\int|f|^2dx=A^2L/2\). Give a defensible separation condition for treating
the positive- and negative-wavenumber main lobes as distinct, and distinguish
finite-window spectral leakage from physical dispersion.
permittedResults: Multiplication by \(e^{ik_0x}\) shifts a Fourier transform from \(k\) to \(k-k_0\).
For real \(f\), the transform satisfies \(F(-k)=F(k)^*\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the rectangular window once and apply modulation shifts for complex and real carriers.
Integrate each exponential carrier directly, then identify the same shifted sinc lobes and verify Parseval.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses modulation and window transforms to derive both complex and real burst spectra, quantifies resolution, and verifies energy under the declared normalization.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assigns a real cosine burst only the positive-wavenumber sinc lobe.
commonErrors.consequence: The spectrum violates the conjugate symmetry required for a real signal.

commonErrors.description: Places the first zeros at one over L without the two-pi factor or reports half the zero-to-zero width.
commonErrors.consequence: The resolution and lobe-separation conclusions are quantitatively wrong.

hintTree.content: Integrate \(e^{-i(k-k_0)x}\) over the symmetric interval and express the result with \(\operatorname{sinc}\).
Write \(\cos(k_0x)=(e^{ik_0x}+e^{-ik_0x})/2\).
Each shifted sinc has first zeros \(2\pi/L\) from its center; compare this with the center separation \(2k_0\).

WAVE:010418.canonicalSolution:
For the complex burst,
\[
G(k)=A\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}e^{-i(k-k_0)x}dx
=\boxed{AL\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{(k-k_0)L}{2}\right)}.
\]
Its peak is \(AL\) at \(k=k_0\), and its first zeros are
\[
k=k_0\pm\frac{2\pi}{L}.
\]
Thus the main-lobe zero-to-zero width is \(4\pi/L\). If the window contains
\(N=k_0L/(2\pi)\) cycles, increasing \(N\) at fixed \(k_0\) increases \(L\)
and narrows the main lobe like \(1/L\). Abrupt rectangular edges leave the
sinc sidelobes rather than producing a compact spectral line.

For the real burst,
\[
\boxed{F(k)=\frac{AL}{2}\left[
\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{(k-k_0)L}{2}\right)
+\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{(k+k_0)L}{2}\right)
\right]}.
\]
The two terms are centered at \(\pm k_0\). Here the spectrum is real and even;
more generally real time- or space-domain data require conjugate symmetry.

When \(k_0L=2\pi N\),
\[
\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}A^2\cos^2(k_0x)dx
=\frac{A^2L}{2}
+\frac{A^2}{2}\left[\frac{\sin(2k_0x)}{2k_0}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2}
=\boxed{\frac{A^2L}{2}}.
\]
Parseval then gives
\((2\pi)^{-1}\int|F(k)|^2dk=A^2L/2\), including the cross terms between
the shifted lobes. A simple zero-to-zero separation criterion is that the
right edge of the negative main lobe lie below the left edge of the positive
one:
\[
-k_0+\frac{2\pi}{L}<k_0-\frac{2\pi}{L},
\quad\text{or}\quad k_0L>2\pi.
\]
Stronger practical resolution criteria may be chosen, but must be stated.
These sidelobes arise from finite observation or truncation; dispersion instead
means that the medium has a nonlinear \(\omega(k)\) relation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The complex burst gives \(G=AL\operatorname{sinc}[(k-k_0)L/2]\), with first zeros \(k_0\pm2\pi/L\). A real cosine is half the sum of positive and negative carriers, so its transform has sinc lobes at both \(\pm k_0\). For an integer number of cycles, direct integration and Parseval give energy \(A^2L/2\).
A real cosine has only a spectral peak at positive k because k-zero is positive. The first zeros are k-zero plus or minus one over L, so the main lobe has width two over L.

WAVE:010419.title: The Lorentzian-squared spectrum of a cusped wave packet
WAVE:010419.objective: Transform a two-sided exponential packet, verify Parseval and derivative-energy identities, and connect its cusp to algebraic spectral decay without misclassifying a weak derivative.
WAVE:010419.statement:
Use the Fourier convention
\[
F(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx,
\qquad
f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(k)e^{ikx}\,dk.
\]
Let \(f(x)=A e^{-|x|/a}\), where \(a>0\) and \(A\ne0\) is real.

Derive \(F(k)\) by splitting the integral at the cusp. Locate the half-power
points of \(|F(k)|^2\), compute its full width at half maximum, and determine
the root-mean-square wavenumber using \(|F|^2\) as the spectral weight.
Verify Parseval's identity and the derivative identity
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f'(x)|^2dx
=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}k^2|F(k)|^2dk.
\]
Explain why the cusp at \(x=0\) does not add a delta function to the first
weak derivative, why the RMS wavenumber is finite, and why the second spatial
derivative does contain a singular contribution.

For \(a=0.250\,\mathrm m\) and \(A=3.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute
\(F(0)\), the spectral-power FWHM, the RMS wavenumber, and both sides of
Parseval's identity with units.
permittedResults: Under the declared convention, \(\int|f|^2dx=(2\pi)^{-1}\int|F|^2dk\), and if the weak derivative is square integrable then its transform is \(ikF(k)\).
The integrals \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(1+u^2)^{-2}du\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u^2(1+u^2)^{-2}du\) both equal \(\pi/2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Split the transform into two elementary exponential integrals, then evaluate moments by dimensionless rational integrals.
Use the known transform of a two-sided exponential, provided its normalization is derived and both weak-derivative and numerical audits are explicit.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the packet spectrum and quantitative widths, verifies both Parseval identities, and correctly connects continuity, the slope cusp, weak derivatives, and spectral-moment convergence.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds a delta function to the first derivative merely because the ordinary derivative jumps at the cusp.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative Parseval identity and spectral-tail interpretation are corrupted.

commonErrors.description: Finds half-amplitude points while calling them half-power points, or omits the square on the spectral amplitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported FWHM has the wrong numerical factor.

hintTree.content: Evenness reduces the transform to twice a cosine transform on the positive half-line.
Half power means \((1+a^2k^2)^2=2\), not \(1+a^2k^2=2\).
For the RMS ratio, substitute \(u=ak\) in numerator and denominator; the two dimensionless integrals are equal.

WAVE:010419.canonicalSolution:
Evenness gives
\[
F(k)=2A\int_0^\infty e^{-x/a}\cos(kx)\,dx
=\boxed{\frac{2Aa}{1+a^2k^2}}.
\]
Thus \(|F|^2=4A^2a^2(1+a^2k^2)^{-2}\). At half power,
\((1+a^2k^2)^2=2\), so the two points are
\[
k_\pm=\pm\frac{\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}}a,
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\Delta k_{\mathrm{FWHM}}
=\frac{2\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}}a}.
\]

The spectrum is even, so its mean wavenumber is zero. Its second moment is
\[
\langle k^2\rangle=
\frac{\int k^2(1+a^2k^2)^{-2}dk}
{\int(1+a^2k^2)^{-2}dk}
=\frac1{a^2}
\frac{\int u^2(1+u^2)^{-2}du}
{\int(1+u^2)^{-2}du}
=\frac1{a^2}.
\]
Hence \(k_{\mathrm{rms}}=1/a\).

Directly,
\[
\int|f|^2dx=2A^2\int_0^\infty e^{-2x/a}dx=A^2a.
\]
The spectral side is
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int|F|^2dk
=\frac{4A^2a}{2\pi}\int\frac{du}{(1+u^2)^2}
=A^2a.
\]
For \(x\ne0\), \(|f'|^2=A^2a^{-2}e^{-2|x|/a}\), so
\[
\int|f'|^2dx=\frac{A^2}{a}.
\]
The spectral derivative side equals the Parseval norm times
\(\langle k^2\rangle\), also \(A^2/a\).

The function itself is continuous at zero, so its distributional first
derivative has no delta. Its ordinary slopes jump from \(A/a\) to \(-A/a\),
but that bounded piecewise derivative is square integrable. Differentiating
the slope jump produces a \(-2A/a\) delta contribution in \(f''\), consistent
with \(F(k)\sim k^{-2}\) and finite \(k^2\)- but not \(k^4\)-weighted
spectral norm.

Numerically,
\[
F(0)=2Aa=1.50\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2},
\]
\[
\Delta k_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=
\frac{2(0.643594)}{0.250}=5.149\,\mathrm{m^{-1}},
\qquad k_{\mathrm{rms}}=4.000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}.
\]
Both Parseval sides equal
\[
A^2a=(0.00300)^2(0.250)
=\boxed{2.25\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3}}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: Splitting at zero gives \(F=2Aa/(1+a^2k^2)\). Half spectral power occurs at \(|k|=\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}/a\), and the ratio of the two rational moment integrals gives \(k_{\rm rms}=1/a\). Both Parseval norms equal \(A^2a\), while derivative Parseval gives \(A^2/a\); continuity of f prevents a delta in its first weak derivative.
The cusp means the first derivative contains a delta, so its squared norm is infinite. Half power occurs when the Lorentzian amplitude is one half, giving points at k equals plus or minus one over a.

WAVE:010420.title: Bessel sidebands from a sinusoidally phase-modulated carrier
WAVE:010420.objective: Expand a pure phase modulation into discrete Fourier sidebands, use Parseval to conserve power, and distinguish bounded local wavenumber from infinite spectral support.
WAVE:010420.statement:
Consider the complex spatial carrier
\[
\psi(x)=A\exp\!\left[i k_0x+i\eta\sin(Kx)\right],
\]
where \(A\ne0\), \(K>0\), and \(\eta\) is a real dimensionless modulation
index. You may use the Jacobi-Anger identity
\[
e^{i\eta\sin\theta}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\eta)e^{in\theta},
\qquad J_{-n}(\eta)=(-1)^nJ_n(\eta).
\]

Derive the complete sideband spectrum and identify the complex amplitude and
power fraction of each line. Prove
\(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\eta)^2=1\) from Parseval rather than quoting
it. Obtain the sideband amplitudes through second order in small \(|\eta|\),
and verify power conservation to the first nontrivial order.

Differentiate the phase to obtain the local wavenumber. Explain why its
bounded range \(k_0-|\eta|K\le k_{\rm local}\le k_0+|\eta|K\) does not mean
the exact Fourier spectrum has finite support. For \(\eta=0.600\), use
\[
J_0=0.912005,\quad J_1=0.286701,
\quad J_2=0.0436651,
\]
to compute the carrier power fraction and the combined powers in the first
and second sideband pairs. Quantify the unlisted higher-order remainder.
permittedResults: Parseval for a unit-modulus periodic factor equates its mean squared magnitude with the sum of squared Fourier-series coefficients.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the supplied Jacobi-Anger identity and Fourier-series Parseval over one modulation period.
Derive the Bessel coefficients from their Fourier integrals, provided the full line locations, signs, normalization, asymptotics, and local-wavenumber interpretation remain explicit.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses Jacobi-Anger and periodic Parseval to derive and normalize the sidebands, performs the small-index and numerical audits, and correctly separates local phase slope from global Fourier support.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats signed Bessel amplitudes themselves as power fractions or allows an odd negative sideband to carry negative power.
commonErrors.consequence: The power normalization and numerical distribution are invalid.

commonErrors.description: Claims the bounded instantaneous wavenumber implies that sufficiently distant Bessel sidebands vanish exactly.
commonErrors.consequence: A local phase derivative is incorrectly equated with compact Fourier support.

hintTree.content: Apply Jacobi-Anger with \(\theta=Kx\); every term then has wavenumber \(k_0+nK\).
The periodic modulation factor has magnitude one at every x, so its period-averaged squared magnitude is one.
Power in the pair n and minus n is \(2J_n^2\), even though their amplitudes differ by a sign for odd n.

WAVE:010420.canonicalSolution:
Jacobi-Anger gives
\[
\boxed{\psi(x)=A\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}
J_n(\eta)e^{i(k_0+nK)x}}.
\]
Thus line \(n\) has complex amplitude \(AJ_n(\eta)\) and power fraction
\(J_n(\eta)^2\) relative to \(|A|^2\). Over one modulation period, the
factor \(e^{i\eta\sin Kx}\) has magnitude one. Fourier-series Parseval
therefore gives
\[
1=\frac{K}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi/K}
|e^{i\eta\sin Kx}|^2dx
=\boxed{\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\eta)^2}.
\]

Through second order,
\[
J_0=1-\frac{\eta^2}{4}+O(\eta^4),
\quad J_{+1}=\frac\eta2+O(\eta^3),
\quad J_{-1}=-\frac\eta2+O(\eta^3),
\]
\[
J_{+2}=J_{-2}=\frac{\eta^2}{8}+O(\eta^4).
\]
At order \(\eta^2\), the carrier power is
\(J_0^2=1-\eta^2/2+O(\eta^4)\), and the first pair contributes
\(2J_1^2=\eta^2/2+O(\eta^4)\); their sum is one through that order. The
second pair first contributes at order \(\eta^4\).

The phase is \(\Phi=k_0x+\eta\sin Kx\), so
\[
\boxed{k_{\rm local}=\Phi'(x)=k_0+\eta K\cos Kx}.
\]
This derivative is pointwise bounded, but the nonlinear exponential of the
sinusoid has nonzero Bessel coefficients at arbitrarily large integer order.
Local phase slope and global Fourier support are different descriptions; the
exact spectral lines extend to all \(k_0+nK\), with rapidly decreasing weight.

For \(\eta=0.600\),
\[
P_0=J_0^2=0.831753,
\]
\[
P_{|n|=1}=2J_1^2=0.164395,
\qquad
P_{|n|=2}=2J_2^2=0.00381330.
\]
These listed fractions sum to \(0.999961\), so all sidebands with
\(|n|\ge3\) together carry
\[
\boxed{3.9\times10^{-5}}
\]
of the power, with the small difference depending on rounding of the supplied
Bessel values.

graderFixtures.proofText: Jacobi-Anger gives lines at \(k_0+nK\) with amplitudes \(AJ_n(\eta)\) and powers \(J_n^2\). Periodic Parseval of the unit-modulus phase factor proves \(\sum J_n^2=1\). At small eta the carrier loses eta-squared over two power, which the first pair gains; the exact local slope is bounded although infinitely many Bessel lines remain.

The negative first sideband has negative power because J minus one is negative. Since the local wavenumber stays between k-zero plus or minus eta K, every Fourier line outside that interval is exactly zero.

WAVE:010421.title: An odd Gaussian pulse removes DC and creates twin spectral peaks
WAVE:010421.objective: Transform a derivative-shaped Gaussian packet, locate its spectral lobes, verify Parseval normalization, and compute energy-weighted spatial and spectral widths.
WAVE:010421.statement:
Use the Fourier-transform convention
\[
\widetilde f(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx,
\qquad
f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\widetilde f(k)e^{ikx}\,dk.
\]
Consider the real odd pulse
\[
f(x)=A\frac{x}{\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
\qquad A,\sigma>0.
\]

Derive its transform from the transform of a Gaussian rather than evaluating
a new integral from scratch. Explain why the zero-wavenumber component
vanishes, locate the two maxima of the spectral intensity
\(|\widetilde f(k)|^2\), and calculate both the real-space energy norm and
the corresponding spectral integral to verify Parseval's identity.

Define RMS widths using the normalized densities \(|f|^2\) and
\(|\widetilde f|^2\). Compute \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta k\), and their
product. Explain why this packet does not attain the Gaussian minimum-width
product even though it is built from a Gaussian envelope. For
\(A=4.00\,\mathrm{mm}\) and \(\sigma=0.250\,\mathrm m\), compute the
spectral-peak wavenumbers, the real-space norm, the magnitude of the transform
at either peak, and both RMS widths. Keep the transform normalization fixed
through the entire calculation.
permittedResults: For this convention, \(\int e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-ikx}dx=\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\).
Parseval's identity is \(\int|f|^2dx=(2\pi)^{-1}\int|\widetilde f|^2dk\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the known Gaussian transform and evaluate Gaussian moment ratios.
Integrate directly and use Hermite--Gaussian identities, provided the transform phase, Parseval factors, peak locations, RMS widths, and numerical values match.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the odd packet's transform and twin peaks, verifies Parseval with consistent normalization, and obtains the correct energy-weighted width product.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the odd pulse like an ordinary Gaussian and places its spectral maximum at zero wavenumber.
commonErrors.consequence: The transform ignores the factor of k and violates the pulse's zero signed area.

commonErrors.description: Computes moments from f or the transform amplitude rather than from normalized squared magnitudes.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported RMS widths and uncertainty product do not describe packet energy.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the Gaussian transform with respect to k and use \(\partial_k\widetilde g=-i\int xg(x)e^{-ikx}dx\).
Maximize \(k^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}\) as a function of \(|k|\).
The needed Gaussian moments reduce to integrals of \(x^2e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}\) and \(x^4e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}\).

WAVE:010421.canonicalSolution:
Let \(g(x)=e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), so
\(\widetilde g=\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\). Since
\(\partial_k\widetilde g=-i\int xg(x)e^{-ikx}dx\),
\[
\boxed{\widetilde f(k)=-iA\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma^2k
e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}}.
\]
Oddness makes \(\widetilde f(0)=0\): the two signed lobes of \(f\) have
zero net area. The spectral intensity is
\[
|\widetilde f|^2=2\pi A^2\sigma^4k^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}.
\]
Differentiation with respect to \(|k|\) gives maxima at
\[
\boxed{k=\pm\sigma^{-1}}.
\]

The real-space norm is
\[
\int|f|^2dx=\frac{A^2}{\sigma^2}
\int x^2e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}dx
=\boxed{\frac{A^2\sqrt\pi\sigma}{2}}.
\]
On the transform side,
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int|\widetilde f|^2dk
=A^2\sigma^4\int k^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}dk
=\frac{A^2\sqrt\pi\sigma}{2},
\]
which verifies Parseval with the stated convention.

Both squared-magnitude densities are even, so their means vanish. Gaussian
moment ratios give
\[
\boxed{\Delta x=\sqrt{\frac32}\,\sigma},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta k=\sqrt{\frac32}\,\frac1\sigma},
\qquad
\boxed{\Delta x\Delta k=\frac32}.
\]
The differentiation inserts factors of \(x\) and \(k\), producing an odd
first-excited Hermite--Gaussian rather than the nodeless minimum-width
Gaussian; a Gaussian envelope alone does not guarantee the minimum product.

For \(A=0.00400\,\mathrm m\) and \(\sigma=0.250\,\mathrm m\),
\[
\boxed{k_{\rm pk}=\pm4.000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\int|f|^2dx=\boxed{3.5449\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3}}.
\]
At either peak,
\[
|\widetilde f|=A\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-1/2}
=\boxed{1.52035\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{\Delta x=0.30619\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta k=4.89898\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
Their numerical product is 1.50000, consistent with the analytic result.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differentiating the Gaussian transform gives \(\widetilde f=-iA\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma^2k e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\). Thus the intensity vanishes at zero, peaks at \(|k|=1/\sigma\), satisfies Parseval with norm \(A^2\sqrt\pi\sigma/2\), and has \(\Delta x\Delta k=3/2\).
Because the envelope is Gaussian, I use another Gaussian transform centered at zero and call zero the spectral peak. I calculate widths from the signed amplitude rather than its squared magnitude.

WAVE:010422.title: Two separated packets encode their phase in spectral fringes
WAVE:010422.objective: Use Fourier shifts to derive the interference spectrum of two coherent Gaussian packets, connect fringe phase to separation, and verify the overlap-dependent norm.
WAVE:010422.statement:
With the same Fourier convention
\(\widetilde f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx\), consider
\[
f(x)=A\left[
e^{-(x-d/2)^2/(2\sigma^2)}
+e^{i\phi}e^{-(x+d/2)^2/(2\sigma^2)}
\right],
\]
where \(A,\sigma,d>0\) and \(\phi\) is a controlled relative phase.

Derive the transform using the shift theorem. Obtain its spectral intensity
as a Gaussian envelope times an interference factor. Find the fringe spacing
and all spectral zeros, and show how changing \(\phi\) translates the fringes
without changing the envelope. Compute \(\int|f|^2dx\), including the
finite-overlap interference term, and verify that integrating the spectrum
gives the same result. Explain why widely separated packets can have strong
spectral fringes even when their real-space overlap contribution to total
energy is exponentially small; coherence and local overlap are not the same
claim.

For \(A=1.00\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(\sigma=0.500\,\mathrm m\),
\(d=3.00\,\mathrm m\), and \(\phi=\pi/2\), compute the fringe spacing,
the nearest positive spectral zero, the real-space norm, and the central
spectral intensity. State why the intensity need not be even in k when the
spatial field is complex.
permittedResults: If \(g(x-x_0)\) transforms to \(e^{-ikx_0}\widetilde g(k)\), spatial separation becomes phase variation in k.
The product of the two displaced Gaussian envelopes integrates to \(\sqrt\pi\sigma e^{-d^2/(4\sigma^2)}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the Fourier shift theorem to the two Gaussian components and expand squared magnitudes in both domains.
Use center-of-mass and separation coordinates in direct Gaussian integrals, provided the same transform phases, zeros, overlap factor, numerical results, and symmetry explanation emerge.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the coherent two-packet spectrum and fringe locations, verifies the overlap-sensitive Parseval norm, and correctly separates coherence from real-space overlap.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two spectral intensities incoherently and drops the phase-dependent cross term.
commonErrors.consequence: All spectral fringes and their phase translation disappear.

commonErrors.description: Assumes separated Gaussian packets are exactly orthogonal at finite d and omits their overlap contribution to the norm.
commonErrors.consequence: The real-space and spectral Parseval calculations disagree for general phase.

hintTree.content: Factor out \(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\) from both shifted transforms.
The bracket magnitude squared is \(2+2\cos(\phi+kd)\).
In real space, expand \(|f|^2\); only the cross term depends on \(\phi\).

WAVE:010422.canonicalSolution:
Applying the two shifts gives
\[
\boxed{\widetilde f(k)=A\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}
\left(e^{-ikd/2}+e^{i\phi}e^{ikd/2}\right)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{|\widetilde f(k)|^2=
2\pi A^2\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}
[2+2\cos(\phi+kd)]}.
\]
The interference factor repeats when \(kd\) changes by \(2\pi\), so
\[
\boxed{\Delta k_{\rm fringe}=\frac{2\pi}{d}}.
\]
Zeros occur at
\[
\boxed{k_n=\frac{(2n+1)\pi-\phi}{d}},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Changing relative phase translates these positions but leaves the Gaussian
factor unchanged.

Expanding the real-space squared magnitude gives two equal self terms and a
cross term. Its integral is
\[
\boxed{\int|f|^2dx=
2A^2\sqrt\pi\sigma
\left[1+e^{-d^2/(4\sigma^2)}\cos\phi\right]}.
\]
Integrating the spectral formula and dividing by \(2\pi\) gives the same
answer: the cosine transform of \(e^{-\sigma^2k^2}\) produces the overlap
factor. When \(d\gg\sigma\), that contribution to the integrated energy is
tiny, but the two transform amplitudes still arrive at every k with a stable
phase difference \(\phi+kd\), so the interference factor can reach both zero
and four. This is spectral coherence, not large pointwise spatial overlap.

For the numerical values,
\[
\boxed{\Delta k_{\rm fringe}=2.09440\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
With \(\phi=\pi/2\), the nearest positive zero uses \(n=0\):
\[
\boxed{k_0=\frac{\pi}{6}=0.523599\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
Because \(\cos\phi=0\),
\[
\int|f|^2dx=2(0.0100)^2\sqrt\pi(0.500)
=\boxed{1.77245\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}}.
\]
At k equals zero the bracket is two, hence
\[
\boxed{|\widetilde f(0)|^2=4\pi A^2\sigma^2
=3.14159\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^4}}.
\]
For a complex spatial field \(f\), Hermitian symmetry
\(\widetilde f(-k)=\widetilde f(k)^*\) is not required, so a nonzero phase
can shift the intensity pattern away from even symmetry.

graderFixtures.proofText: The transform is proportional to \(e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}[e^{-ikd/2}+e^{i\phi}e^{ikd/2}]\), giving intensity factor \(2+2\cos(\phi+kd)\), spacing \(2\pi/d\), and zeros \(((2n+1)\pi-\phi)/d\). The norm contains \(e^{-d^2/(4\sigma^2)}\cos\phi\).
Because the packets are separated, I add their spectral intensities and discard every cross term. I also set their real-space overlap exactly to zero for finite separation.

WAVE:010423.title: A chirp broadens a Gaussian spectrum without changing its envelope
WAVE:010423.objective: Transform a linearly chirped Gaussian exactly, derive its time-frequency covariance and uncertainty product, and verify Parseval normalization.
WAVE:010423.statement:
Use the Fourier convention
\[
\widetilde\psi(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\psi(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt,
\qquad
\psi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\widetilde\psi(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}
\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}.
\]
Consider the analytic wave packet
\[
\psi(t)=A\exp\!\left[-\frac{t^2}{2\tau^2}\right]
\exp\!\left[-i\omega_ct-i\frac{C t^2}{2\tau^2}\right],
\]
where \(A,\tau>0\), \(C\) is real, and \(\omega_c>0\).

Evaluate the complex Gaussian integral with a branch choice continuous from
\(C=0\), and derive \(\widetilde\psi(\omega)\) including its complex phase.
From the intensity distributions \(|\psi|^2\) and
\(|\widetilde\psi|^2\), compute their means and variances
\(\Delta t^2,\Delta\omega^2\), and prove
\(\Delta t\Delta\omega=\sqrt{1+C^2}/2\). Relate the sign of C to the
instantaneous frequency sweep and calculate the covariance
\(\langle t(\omega_{\rm inst}-\omega_c)\rangle\) under the normalized time
intensity. Verify Parseval's theorem explicitly. Explain why spectral
intensity alone determines \(|C|\) but not its sign.

For \(A=2.00\), \(\tau=0.400\,\mathrm s\), \(C=3.00\), and
\(\omega_c=50.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), compute \(\Delta t\),
\(\Delta\omega\), their product, the packet energy
\(\int|\psi|^2dt\), and \(|\widetilde\psi(\omega_c)|\). Keep angular
frequency distinct from cycles per second.
permittedResults: If \(\operatorname{Re}a>0\), then \(\int e^{-at^2+bt}dt=\sqrt{\pi/a}\,e^{b^2/(4a)}\), with the square-root branch continued from positive real a.
For this Fourier pair, \(\int|\psi|^2dt=\int|\widetilde\psi|^2d\omega/(2\pi)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Complete the complex Gaussian square and read second moments from the time and frequency intensities.
Propagate the Gaussian covariance matrix through a Fourier rotation, while independently fixing the transform amplitude and phase by direct integration.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Evaluates the full complex transform, derives the correct intensity moments and covariance, and closes the Parseval and numerical normalization checks.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses tau directly as the RMS width of the squared temporal envelope or drops the corresponding square-root-of-two factor in frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The uncertainty product and all numerical widths are incorrect.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the measured spectral intensity distinguishes positive from negative chirp.
commonErrors.consequence: Phase information absent from the modulus is invented.

hintTree.content: Combine the quadratic terms with \(a=(1+iC)/(2\tau^2)\) and the linear term with \(b=i(\omega-\omega_c)\).
The squared spectral modulus is a real Gaussian proportional to \(\exp[-\tau^2(\omega-\omega_c)^2/(1+C^2)]\).
Write the field phase as \(-\Phi(t)\); then \(\omega_{\rm inst}=d\Phi/dt\).

WAVE:010423.canonicalSolution:
Combining exponents gives
\[
\widetilde\psi(\omega)=A\int
\exp\left[-\frac{1+iC}{2\tau^2}t^2
+i(\omega-\omega_c)t\right]dt.
\]
Using the square root that equals one when \(C=0\),
\[
\boxed{\widetilde\psi(\omega)=
\frac{A\tau\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{1+iC}}
\exp\left[-\frac{\tau^2(\omega-\omega_c)^2}{2(1+iC)}\right]}.
\]
Its modulus is
\[
|\widetilde\psi|^2=
\frac{2\pi A^2\tau^2}{\sqrt{1+C^2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{\tau^2(\omega-\omega_c)^2}{1+C^2}\right].
\]
Meanwhile \(|\psi|^2=A^2e^{-t^2/\tau^2}\). Both distributions are
centered at zero offset from their respective means, so
\[
\langle t\rangle=0,\quad \langle\omega\rangle=\omega_c,
\quad
\boxed{\Delta t^2=\frac{\tau^2}{2}},
\quad
\boxed{\Delta\omega^2=\frac{1+C^2}{2\tau^2}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\Delta t\Delta\omega=\frac12\sqrt{1+C^2}}.
\]
Only the unchirped packet saturates the one-dimensional Fourier Gaussian
bound.

The phase is \(-\Phi(t)\), where
\(\Phi=\omega_ct+Ct^2/(2\tau^2)\). Hence
\[
\omega_{\rm inst}=\omega_c+\frac{C}{\tau^2}t,
\]
and the normalized time-intensity covariance is
\[
\boxed{\langle t(\omega_{\rm inst}-\omega_c)\rangle
=\frac{C}{\tau^2}\langle t^2\rangle=\frac C2}.
\]
This signed covariance changes under \(C\to-C\), while the spectral
intensity contains only \(C^2\); phase-sensitive information is required to
recover chirp sign.

The time-domain energy is
\[
\int|\psi|^2dt=A^2\tau\sqrt\pi.
\]
Integrating the spectral Gaussian gives
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\frac{2\pi A^2\tau^2}{\sqrt{1+C^2}}
\frac{\sqrt{\pi(1+C^2)}}{\tau}
=A^2\tau\sqrt\pi,
\]
which proves Parseval with the declared convention.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\Delta t=\tau/\sqrt2=0.282843\ \mathrm s},
\]
\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt2(0.400)}
=5.59017\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\quad
\boxed{\Delta t\Delta\omega=\sqrt{10}/2=1.58114}.
\]
The energy is
\[
\boxed{A^2\tau\sqrt\pi=2.83593},
\]
in the units carried by \(|A|^2\) times seconds. At line center,
\[
\boxed{|\widetilde\psi(\omega_c)|=
\frac{A\tau\sqrt{2\pi}}{(1+C^2)^{1/4}}=1.12766},
\]
with units of A times seconds. Converting \(\Delta\omega\) to hertz would
require division by \(2\pi\), which is not part of this angular-frequency
calculation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The transform is \(A\tau\sqrt{2\pi}(1+iC)^{-1/2}\exp[-\tau^2(\omega-\omega_c)^2/(2(1+iC))]\). Thus \(\Delta t=\tau/\sqrt2\), \(\Delta\omega=\sqrt{1+C^2}/(\sqrt2\tau)\), covariance C/2, and Parseval energy \(A^2\tau\sqrt\pi\). The numerical widths are 0.282843 s and 5.59017 rad/s.
The temporal RMS width equals tau, and the spectrum determines whether C is positive or negative because its width changes sign. I omit the two-pi factor in Parseval.

WAVE:010424.title: A one-sided Cauchy wavelet separates positive-frequency energy
WAVE:010424.objective: Construct an analytic Cauchy wavelet from its one-sided spectrum, prove its exact admissibility and energy identity, and derive its scale-selective response to complex and real tones.
WAVE:010424.statement:
Use the angular-frequency Fourier pair
\[
\Psi(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi(t)e^{-i\omega t}\,dt,
\qquad
\psi(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\Psi(\omega)e^{i\omega t}\,d\omega.
\]
Let m be a positive integer and prescribe the mother wavelet in frequency by
\[
\Psi_m(\omega)=B_m\omega^m e^{-\omega}H(\omega),
\]
where \(H(\omega)=1\) for positive omega and zero for negative omega. The
mother coordinate and its omega are dimensionless.

Choose \(B_m>0\) so that \(\|\psi_m\|_2=1\), and invert the transform to
obtain psi in closed form. Prove directly that it has zero mean and algebraic,
not Gaussian, time decay. Evaluate exactly the admissibility constant
\[
\mathcal C_\psi=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{|\Psi(\omega)|^2}{|\omega|}\,d\omega<\infty,
\]
and show why m=0 would fail. Explain why one-sided frequency support makes
this a complex analytic wavelet rather than a real wavelet.

For \(s>0\) and real b, define
\(\psi_{s,b}(t)=s^{-1/2}\psi((t-b)/s)\). Derive its Fourier transform,
prove preservation of norm, and obtain its positive-frequency support.
For the continuous-wavelet coefficient
\(W_f(s,b)=\int f(t)\psi_{s,b}^*(t)dt\), derive the response to a constant
and to \(f(t)=e^{i\Omega t}\). Show that a negative-frequency complex tone
is rejected exactly. For a fixed
positive tone, maximize coefficient magnitude over s and distinguish this
optimal CWT scale from the scale that merely aligns the peak of
\(|\Psi_m|\) with the tone.

For square-integrable f, derive the scale-space energy identity. Prove that
the corresponding synthesis integral reconstructs the positive-frequency
projection \(f_+\), not an arbitrary two-sided signal. State how a real
zero-mean signal is recovered from that projection.

Take \(m=3\), \(\Omega=10.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), and
\(b=0.3000\,\mathrm s\). Compute \(B_m\), the time-domain prefactor, the
admissibility constant, the optimal tone scale, the wavelet-spectrum peak
frequency at that scale, and the positive-tone coefficient in polar form.
Also give the coefficient for \(e^{-i\Omega t}\) and for
\(\cos\Omega t\). Track the square-root-time units of coefficients after
physical scaling.
permittedResults: For \(\operatorname{Re}z>0\), \(\int_0^\infty \omega^n e^{-z\omega}d\omega=\Gamma(n+1)/z^{n+1}\).
Parseval's identity for the stated pair is \(\int|\psi|^2dt=(2\pi)^{-1}\int|\Psi|^2d\omega\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Start from the one-sided spectrum, use Gamma integrals for normalization, inverse transform, and admissibility, then derive scale response.
Use Parseval in translation and integrate over scale to prove the energy identity and positive-frequency reconstruction before evaluating tones.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Constructs and normalizes the analytic Cauchy wavelet, proves its exact admissibility and positive-frequency isometry, and derives correct scale-selective tone responses.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Allows m equal to zero and asserts that exponential high-frequency decay alone guarantees admissibility.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse-frequency integrand behaves as one over omega at zero and diverges logarithmically.

commonErrors.description: Claims the analytic wavelet reconstructs negative frequencies, or maximizes tone response after dropping square root s.
commonErrors.consequence: The synthesis target or optimal scale is wrong, and the negative-frequency rejection is lost.

hintTree.content: Use Parseval and \(\int_0^\infty\omega^{2m}e^{-2\omega}d\omega=\Gamma(2m+1)/2^{2m+1}\) to normalize.
Invert only over positive omega and recognize a Gamma integral with \(z=1-it\).
For the positive tone set \(x=s\Omega\); apart from a constant, coefficient magnitude is \(x^{m+1/2}e^{-x}\).

WAVE:010424.canonicalSolution:
Parseval normalization gives
\[
1=\frac{B_m^2}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty
\omega^{2m}e^{-2\omega}d\omega
=\frac{B_m^2}{2\pi}\frac{(2m)!}{2^{2m+1}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{B_m=2^{m+1}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{(2m)!}}}.
\]
Inverting only the positive-frequency half-line and using the Gamma integral,
\[
\psi_m(t)=\frac{B_m}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty
\omega^m e^{-(1-it)\omega}d\omega
=\boxed{\frac{B_m m!}{2\pi}(1-it)^{-(m+1)}}.
\]
Hence \(|\psi_m(t)|=O(|t|^{-(m+1)})\): the wavelet is algebraically
localized in time. For m at least one it is integrable, and
\[
\int\psi_m(t)dt=\Psi_m(0)=0.
\]
It cannot be real, because a real time signal would require
\(\Psi(-\omega)=\Psi(\omega)^*\), whereas this spectrum vanishes on the
entire negative half-line but not the positive one.

The admissibility constant is exact:
\[
\mathcal C_\psi=B_m^2\int_0^\infty
\omega^{2m-1}e^{-2\omega}d\omega
=B_m^2\frac{(2m-1)!}{2^{2m}}
=\boxed{\frac{2\pi}{m}}.
\]
Near zero the integrand is proportional to \(\omega^{2m-1}\), which is
integrable precisely for positive m. If m=0 it behaves as \(1/\omega\)
and diverges logarithmically; the zero-mean condition and admissibility fail
together.

Changing variables in the scaled wavelet gives
\[
\boxed{\Psi_{s,b}(\omega)=\sqrt{s}\,e^{-i\omega b}\Psi_m(s\omega)}.
\]
It remains supported only at positive frequency, and
\(\|\psi_{s,b}\|_2=1\). A constant has zero coefficient. For a positive
complex tone,
\[
\boxed{W_{e^{i\Omega t}}(s,b)=
\sqrt{s}\,e^{i\Omega b}\Psi_m(s\Omega)^*}
=\sqrt{s}\,B_m(s\Omega)^m e^{-s\Omega}e^{i\Omega b}.
\]
For \(e^{-i\Omega t}\) with positive Omega, the coefficient is exactly zero
because \(\Psi_m(-s\Omega)=0\). Consequently a real cosine has one half of
the positive-tone coefficient.

Let \(x=s\Omega\). Apart from \(B_m/\sqrt\Omega\), the positive-tone
magnitude is
\[
x^{m+1/2}e^{-x}.
\]
Its log derivative vanishes at
\[
\boxed{x_*=m+\tfrac12},\qquad
\boxed{s_*=\frac{m+1/2}{\Omega}}.
\]
By contrast, the mother spectrum \(\omega^me^{-\omega}\) itself peaks at
omega=m, so simple peak alignment would choose \(s=m/\Omega\). The extra
half comes from the square-root-s normalization in the CWT coefficient.

For completeness, write F for the Fourier transform of an L2 signal and
\(f_+\) for its positive-frequency projection. Parseval in b gives
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|W_f(s,b)|^2db
=\frac{s}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty
|F(\omega)|^2|\Psi_m(s\omega)|^2d\omega.
\]
Integration over scale and the substitution \(u=s\omega\) produce the exact
isometry
\[
\boxed{\int_0^\infty\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
|W_f(s,b)|^2\,db\,\frac{ds}{s^2}
=\mathcal C_\psi\|f_+\|_2^2}.
\]
Likewise the synthesis operator
\[
\boxed{\frac1{\mathcal C_\psi}\int_0^\infty
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}W_f(s,b)\psi_{s,b}(t)
\,db\,\frac{ds}{s^2}=f_+(t)}
\]
holds in L2. Negative frequencies are absent, so this does not reconstruct a
general two-sided f. For a real zero-mean signal,
\(f_-=\overline{f_+}\) and \(\boxed{f=2\operatorname{Re}f_+}\); an
isolated DC value is irrelevant in L2 but cannot be recovered by a zero-mean
wavelet.

For m=3,
\[
\boxed{B_3=16\sqrt{\frac\pi{720}}=1.0568873},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{B_3 3!}{2\pi}=1.0092530},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\mathcal C_\psi=\frac{2\pi}{3}=2.0943951}.
\]
At \(\Omega=10.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\[
\boxed{s_*=0.350000\ \mathrm s},\qquad x_*=3.5.
\]
The scaled wavelet spectrum itself peaks at
\[
\boxed{\omega_{\rm peak}=m/s_*=8.57143\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\]
which illustrates the distinction from coefficient-optimal scale. With
\(\Omega b=3\),
\[
\boxed{W_{e^{i\Omega t}}(s_*,b)
=0.8095359\,e^{i3.00000}\ \sqrt{\mathrm s}}.
\]
The negative-frequency tone gives zero, and
\[
\boxed{W_{\cos\Omega t}(s_*,b)
=0.4047680\,e^{i3.00000}\ \sqrt{\mathrm s}}.
\]
The square-root-time units follow because an L2-normalized physical wavelet
has units \(\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}\) and the coefficient integrates over time.

graderFixtures.proofText: Normalization gives \(B_m=2^{m+1}\sqrt{\pi/(2m)!}\), inversion gives \(\psi_m=B_mm!/[2\pi(1-it)^{m+1}]\), and admissibility is \(\mathcal C_\psi=2\pi/m\). Scaling yields \(\Psi_{s,b}=\sqrt{s}e^{-i\omega b}\Psi(s\omega)\). Parseval over translation and scale gives \(\int_0^\infty\!\int_{-\infty}^\infty|W_f|^2db\,ds/s^2=\mathcal C_\psi\|f_+\|_2^2\); synthesis divided by \(\mathcal C_\psi\) equals \(f_+\), and a real zero-mean signal is \(f=2\operatorname{Re}f_+\). A positive tone is maximal at \(s=(m+1/2)/\Omega\); negative tones vanish. For m=3 the optimal scale is 0.35 s and the coefficient is \(0.809536e^{i3}\sqrt{\mathrm s}\).
I allow m equal to zero because the high-frequency tail decays. I drop square root s, choose s=m/Omega, and claim the one-sided wavelet reconstructs negative frequencies too.

WAVE:010425.title: A Gaussian pulse train becomes a weighted frequency comb
WAVE:010425.objective: Derive the exact Fourier-series comb of a periodic Gaussian train and the finite-train Dirichlet line shape without confusing spectral weights and line widths.
WAVE:010425.statement:
Let
\[
g_p(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}
\exp\left[-\frac{(t-nT)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad \sigma>0.
\]
Use the transform convention
\[
G(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(t)e^{-i\omega t}\,dt,
\qquad
g(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}G(\omega)e^{i\omega t}\,d\omega.
\]

Prove that the train is T-periodic and compute every Fourier-series
coefficient by unfolding one period to the real line. State the equivalent
Poisson-summation representation and identify the comb spacing and Gaussian
line weights. Use Parseval to write the exact mean-square value as a convergent
series. Then replace the infinite train by
\[
g_J(t)=\sum_{n=-J}^{J}
\exp[-(t-nT)^2/(2\sigma^2)]
\]
with \(N=2J+1\), and derive its continuous transform and Dirichlet factor.
Find the nearest zeros around each comb line and explain why a finite train
has narrow lobes rather than delta functions. Prove the symmetric-window
limit in tempered distributions, including the exact delta-line masses.

For \(T=1.000\,\mathrm{ms}\), \(\sigma=50.0\,\mu\mathrm s\), and \(J=10\),
compute the comb spacing in hertz, \(c_0,c_1,c_5\), the fifth-line weight
relative to dc, and the nearest-zero offset around a comb line. Distinguish
the coefficient amplitude from its power. State separately what happens as
\(J\to\infty\) at fixed \(\sigma/T\), and as \(\sigma/T\to0\) with either
unit pulse height or unit pulse area.
permittedResults: \(\int e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-i\omega t}dt=\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}\).
For \(g_p=\sum_m c_me^{im\Omega t}\), \(T^{-1}\int_0^T|g_p|^2dt=\sum_m|c_m|^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Unfold the Fourier-series coefficient into the transform of one Gaussian.
Transform a finite translated sum and evaluate its geometric phase series.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives both the periodic Poisson comb and finite coherent line shape with correct normalization, weights, and zeros.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the spectrum of a finite pulse train as exact delta functions.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite Dirichlet linewidth and nearest zeros disappear.

commonErrors.description: Confuses complex coefficient amplitude with spectral power and squares or unsquares the Gaussian weight incorrectly.
commonErrors.consequence: Reported harmonic ratios and Parseval power are inconsistent.

hintTree.content: For \(c_m=T^{-1}\int_0^Tg_p(t)e^{-im\Omega t}dt\), shift each pulse interval and combine them into one real-line integral.
The symmetric finite train transform is the single-pulse Gaussian transform times \(\sum_{n=-J}^{J}e^{-i\omega nT}\).
Near \(\omega=m\Omega\), the first numerator zeros occur when \((\omega-m\Omega)NT/2=\pm\pi\).

WAVE:010425.canonicalSolution:
Periodicity follows by shifting the summation index:
\(g_p(t+T)=g_p(t)\). Let \(\Omega=2\pi/T\). Its coefficient is
\[
c_m=\frac1T\int_0^Tg_p(t)e^{-im\Omega t}dt.
\]
For the nth translated Gaussian, set \(s=t-nT\). Since
\(e^{-im\Omega nT}=e^{-i2\pi mn}=1\), the translated intervals tile the
real line, giving
\[
\boxed{c_m=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}{T}
\exp\left[-\frac12\sigma^2m^2\Omega^2\right]}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{g_p(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}{T}
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\sigma^2m^2\Omega^2/2}e^{im\Omega t}},
\]
the Poisson-summation form. The lines are spaced by \(\Omega\) in angular
frequency, or \(1/T\) in hertz. Parseval gives
\[
\boxed{\frac1T\int_0^T|g_p|^2dt
=\frac{2\pi\sigma^2}{T^2}
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\sigma^2m^2\Omega^2}}.
\]

For the symmetric finite train, the single-pulse transform is
\(G_0=\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}\), and
\[
\sum_{n=-J}^{J}e^{-i\omega nT}
=\frac{\sin(N\omega T/2)}{\sin(\omega T/2)},
\qquad N=2J+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{G_N(\omega)=\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}
\frac{\sin(N\omega T/2)}{\sin(\omega T/2)}}.
\]
At a comb line the removable quotient has magnitude N. Its nearest zeros
satisfy
\[
\boxed{\omega-m\Omega=\pm\frac{2\pi}{NT}},
\]
or frequency offset \(\pm1/(NT)\). Only the infinite periodic distribution
has delta lines; each finite window is an ordinary continuous function with
lobes of width proportional to \(1/(NT)\).

The limiting claim is precise for this symmetric nested sequence. Pairing
the translated Gaussians with any Schwartz test function gives an absolutely
convergent series, so \(g_J\to g_p\) in \(\mathcal S'\). Continuity of the
Fourier transform on \(\mathcal S'\) gives
\[
\boxed{G_J\longrightarrow G_p
=\frac{2\pi}{T}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}G_0(m\Omega)
\delta(\omega-m\Omega)
=2\pi\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}c_m\delta(\omega-m\Omega)}.
\]
Thus each delta mass is \(2\pi c_m\), not the height N of a finite lobe.

For the data, the spacing is
\[
\boxed{\Delta f=1/T=1000.00\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
The coefficients are
\[
\boxed{c_0=0.125331},\qquad
\boxed{c_1=0.119297},\qquad
\boxed{c_5=0.0364981}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{c_5/c_0=0.291213},
\]
while the corresponding power ratio is its square, \(0.0848050\), not the
same number. The nearest zero is
\[
\boxed{\Delta f_{\rm zero}=47.6190\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
At fixed \(\sigma/T\), taking \(J\to\infty\) produces the distributional
comb above. Now hold T fixed and let \(\sigma\to0\). At fixed unit pulse
height, \(c_m\) scales as \(\sigma/T\), and the whole train tends to zero
distributionally, even though roughly \(T/\sigma\) harmonics remain
appreciable. If instead each pulse is normalized to unit area by dividing by
\(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma\), then \(c_m\to1/T\) for every fixed m and the time
signal tends to the unit Dirac comb. These two normalizations must not be
conflated.

graderFixtures.proofText: The periodic coefficients are \(c_m=(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/T)e^{-\sigma^2m^2\Omega^2/2}\). The symmetric 21-pulse transform multiplies the Gaussian by the sine quotient and converges in tempered distributions to \(2\pi\sum c_m\delta(\omega-m\Omega)\). Here spacing is 1000 Hz, c0 is 0.125331, c5/c0 is 0.291213, and nearest zeros lie 47.6190 Hz from a line.
I call the twenty-one-pulse transform a set of delta functions, omit the delta masses in the limiting distribution, and use c5 over c0 directly as its power ratio without squaring.

WAVE:010426.title: A triangular spectrum produces a sinc-squared pulse
WAVE:010426.objective: Invert a compact triangular spectrum, verify its energy and sampling threshold, and track a concrete aliased frequency.
WAVE:010426.statement:
Use the Fourier convention
\[
F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)e^{-i\omega t}dt,\qquad
f(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\omega)e^{i\omega t}d\omega.
\]
Consider the real even triangular spectrum
\[
F(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
A(1-|\omega|/\Omega),&|\omega|\le\Omega,\\
0,&|\omega|>\Omega.
\end{cases}
\]

Compute the inverse transform, including its removable value at t=0, and
express it as a squared sinc. Determine the first zeros and the asymptotic
time-domain decay. Use Parseval to calculate the total signal energy directly
from the spectral triangle and verify it from the time-domain scaling.
Derive the Nyquist bound on uniform sample spacing and state an exact ideal
interpolation formula. Explain why compact spectral support does not imply
compact time support.

For \(A=1.000\,\mathrm s\), \(\Omega=2\pi(200\,\mathrm{Hz})\), and
\(T_s=2.000\,\mathrm{ms}\), compute f(0), f(Ts), the sample rate, and the
critical sample spacing. Confirm that this sampling is alias-free. If instead
\(T_s=3.000\,\mathrm{ms}\), determine where a \(+190\,\mathrm{Hz}\)
component appears in the principal sampled-frequency interval. Keep angular
frequency and ordinary frequency factors explicit.
permittedResults: \(\int|f|^2dt=(2\pi)^{-1}\int|F|^2d\omega\) for the stated convention.
A signal supported in \(|\omega|\le\Omega\) is recoverable from uniform samples when \(\pi/T_s\ge\Omega\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the even triangular spectrum directly and then apply Parseval.
Recognize the triangle as a convolution of rectangles, so its inverse is a product of sinc functions.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects the triangular spectral support to its exact pulse, energy, ideal reconstruction, and concrete alias map.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses Omega directly as a hertz bandwidth or omits a factor of two pi in the sampling bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed sample rate and alias-free conclusion are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims compact spectral support makes the sinc-squared pulse vanish outside a finite time window.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact inverse transform and its algebraic tails are contradicted.

hintTree.content: Exploit evenness to integrate \(2\int_0^\Omega(1-\omega/\Omega)\cos\omega t\,d\omega\).
Factor \(1-\cos\Omega t=2\sin^2(\Omega t/2)\) to expose the squared sinc.
For the undersampled case subtract one sample rate from 190 Hz to place it inside the principal interval.

WAVE:010426.canonicalSolution:
Evenness gives
\[
f(t)=\frac A\pi\int_0^\Omega
\left(1-\frac\omega\Omega\right)\cos\omega t\,d\omega.
\]
Direct integration yields
\[
\boxed{f(t)=\frac{A(1-\cos\Omega t)}{\pi\Omega t^2}}
=\boxed{\frac{A\Omega}{2\pi}
\left[\frac{\sin(\Omega t/2)}{\Omega t/2}\right]^2}.
\]
The removable central value is
\[
\boxed{f(0)=\frac{A\Omega}{2\pi}}.
\]
The first nonzero zeros occur at \(t=\pm2\pi/\Omega\), and the envelope
decays as \(t^{-2}\). Compact frequency support therefore produces an
infinite-duration analytic tail rather than compact time support.

Parseval gives
\[
\int|f|^2dt=\frac1{2\pi}
2A^2\int_0^\Omega(1-\omega/\Omega)^2d\omega
=\boxed{\frac{A^2\Omega}{3\pi}}.
\]
The time-domain check is exact, not only dimensional. Put
\(s=\Omega t/2\), so \(dt=2\,ds/\Omega\). Then
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(t)|^2dt
=\frac{A^2\Omega}{2\pi^2}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\sin s}{s}\right)^4ds.
\]
To evaluate the remaining integral, integrate by parts twice on the positive
half-line. Since
\[
\frac{d^2}{ds^2}\sin^4s=2(\cos2s-\cos4s),
\]
and \(\int_0^\infty(1-\cos as)s^{-2}ds=\pi a/2\) for \(a>0\),
\[
\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin^4s}{s^4}ds
=\frac16\int_0^\infty\frac{2(\cos2s-\cos4s)}{s^2}ds
=\frac\pi3.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\sin s/s)^4ds=\frac{2\pi}{3}},
\]
and substitution recovers exactly
\(A^2\Omega/(3\pi)\), matching spectral Parseval.

The sampling condition is
\[
\boxed{T_s\le\frac{\pi}{\Omega}},
\]
equivalently \(f_s\ge2B\) for \(B=\Omega/(2\pi)\). With ideal sampling,
one valid reconstruction is
\[
\boxed{f(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f(nT_s)
\operatorname{sinc}\left[\pi\left(\frac t{T_s}-n\right)\right]},
\]
when the ideal interpolation passband includes the entire support and no
replicas overlap.

Numerically, \(B=200\,\mathrm{Hz}\), so
\[
\boxed{f(0)=200.000},\qquad
\boxed{T_{s,\rm crit}=2.50000\ \mathrm{ms}}.
\]
At \(T_s=2.000\,\mathrm{ms}\),
\[
\frac{\Omega T_s}{2}=0.4\pi,\qquad
\boxed{f(T_s)=114.557}.
\]
The sample rate is \(\boxed{500.000\,\mathrm{Hz}}\), above the
\(400\,\mathrm{Hz}\) Nyquist rate. For \(T_s=3.000\,\mathrm{ms}\),
\(f_s=333.333\,\mathrm{Hz}\), and
\[
190-333.333=\boxed{-143.333\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
Thus the positive 190-Hz component aliases to a negative principal-interval
frequency. Using omega directly in the hertz subtraction would introduce an
incorrect factor of \(2\pi\).

graderFixtures.proofText: The inverse is \(A\Omega/(2\pi)\operatorname{sinc}^2(\Omega t/2)\), with energy \(A^2\Omega/(3\pi)\). Nyquist requires \(T_s\le\pi/\Omega\). For 200 Hz bandwidth and 2 ms samples, f0 is 200, f(Ts) is 114.557, and 500 Hz is safe; at 3 ms, +190 Hz aliases to -143.333 Hz.
I treat Omega as 200 hertz without dividing by two pi, conclude the pulse is time limited, and place the undersampled 190-hertz tone at a positive 190 hertz.

WAVE:010427.title: Two Gaussian packets make a negative Wigner fringe
WAVE:010427.objective: Derive the normalized Wigner distribution of two overlapping Gaussian packets and verify its interference term, marginals, and a concrete negative value.
WAVE:010427.statement:
For \(\sigma>0\) and \(a>0\), define the normalized real packets
\[
g_{\pm}(t)=(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(t\mp a)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad
S=\langle g_+,g_-\rangle,
\]
and the coherent even superposition
\[
\psi(t)=\frac{g_+(t)+g_-(t)}{\sqrt{2(1+S)}}.
\]
Use the angular-frequency convention
\[
\widehat\psi(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi(t)e^{-i\omega t}\,dt,
\qquad
W(t,\omega)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\psi^*(t-\tau/2)\psi(t+\tau/2)e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\tau.
\]

Compute \(S\), derive \(W\) in closed form, and identify the two direct
Gaussian terms and the oscillatory interference term. Verify both marginal
identities with every normalization factor:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}W(t,\omega)\,d\omega=|\psi(t)|^2,
\qquad
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}W(t,\omega)\,dt=\frac{|\widehat\psi(\omega)|^2}{2\pi}.
\]
Use them to prove \(\iint W\,dt\,d\omega=1\). At
\(\omega_*=\pi/(2a)\), evaluate \(W(0,\omega_*)\) and prove that it is
negative for every \(a>0\). Explain why this does not contradict either
marginal being nonnegative.

For \(\sigma=0.200\,\mathrm s\) and \(a=0.400\,\mathrm s\), compute
\(S\), the superposition normalization factor \([2(1+S)]^{-1/2}\),
\(\omega_*\), and \(W(0,\omega_*)\). State the units of the Wigner
distribution under the given convention.
permittedResults: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-A\tau^2-iB\tau}\,d\tau=\sqrt{\pi/A}\,e^{-B^2/(4A)}\) for \(A>0\).
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\omega=2\pi\delta(\tau)\) in the tempered-distribution sense.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate all four bilinear Gaussian terms separately, then collect the conjugate pair into a cosine.
Use the defining integral and a change of variables to audit the marginals independently of the closed form.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the complete normalized Wigner distribution and verifies its marginals and explicit negativity without treating it as an ordinary probability density.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the interference term by the packet overlap S, eliminating the strong central fringes of well-separated coherent packets.
commonErrors.consequence: The derived quasidistribution and its marginals are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims the angular-frequency marginal equals the transform intensity rather than that intensity divided by two pi.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated transform convention and total normalization are inconsistent.

hintTree.content: First compute \(S\) by completing the square in \(g_+g_-\).
Expand the bilinear Wigner integral into two direct terms and two conjugate cross terms.
At \(t=0\), the direct terms carry the overlap factor \(S\), whereas the cross term contains \(\cos(2a\omega)\).

WAVE:010427.canonicalSolution:
The overlap is
\[
S=(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
e^{-[(t-a)^2+(t+a)^2]/(2\sigma^2)}\,dt
=\boxed{e^{-a^2/\sigma^2}}.
\]
For one centered normalized Gaussian, direct evaluation gives
\[
W_0(t,\omega)=\frac1\pi e^{-t^2/\sigma^2-\sigma^2\omega^2}.
\]
Translation produces \(W_0(t\mp a,\omega)\). The two cross integrals sum
to
\[
\frac{2}{\pi}e^{-t^2/\sigma^2-\sigma^2\omega^2}\cos(2a\omega).
\]
Dividing the full bilinear expansion by \(2(1+S)\) therefore yields
\[
\boxed{
W(t,\omega)=\frac{e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2}}{2\pi(1+S)}
\left[e^{-(t-a)^2/\sigma^2}+e^{-(t+a)^2/\sigma^2}
+2e^{-t^2/\sigma^2}\cos(2a\omega)\right]}.
\]

Integrating the defining formula over \(\omega\) produces
\(2\pi\delta(\tau)\), canceled by the prefactor, and hence
\[
\boxed{\int W(t,\omega)\,d\omega=|\psi(t)|^2}.
\]
For the other marginal, put \(u=t-\tau/2\), \(v=t+\tau/2\). The Jacobian
of \((t,\tau)\mapsto(u,v)\) has magnitude one, so
\[
\int W(t,\omega)\,dt
=\frac1{2\pi}\iint\psi^*(u)\psi(v)e^{-i\omega(v-u)}\,du\,dv
=\boxed{\frac{|\widehat\psi(\omega)|^2}{2\pi}}.
\]
Either marginal followed by its normalized integral gives
\(\boxed{\iint W\,dt\,d\omega=1}\).

At \(t=0\), the two direct terms are each \(S\), while
\(\cos(2a\omega_*)=\cos\pi=-1\). Thus
\[
\boxed{W(0,\omega_*)=
\frac{e^{-\sigma^2\omega_*^2}}{\pi(1+S)}(S-1)<0}
\]
because \(0<S<1\) for \(a>0\). A quasidistribution may be negative locally;
the oscillations integrate with the direct terms to give the nonnegative
marginals.

For the supplied values,
\[
\boxed{S=e^{-4}=0.0183156},\qquad
\boxed{[2(1+S)]^{-1/2}=0.700719},
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega_*=3.92699\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{W(0,\omega_*)=-0.165594}.
\]
Since \(\int W\,d\omega\) has units \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) for a
unit-normalized time wavefunction and \(d\omega\) has units
\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(W\) itself is dimensionless under
this angular-frequency convention.

graderFixtures.proofText: The overlap is \(S=e^{-a^2/\sigma^2}\). Expanding the bilinear integral gives two displaced direct Gaussians plus \(2e^{-t^2/\sigma^2}\cos(2a\omega)\), all divided by \(2\pi(1+S)\) with the common spectral Gaussian. Both marginals have the required convention factors, and the central value at \(\pi/(2a)\) is negative.
I damp the interference term by the overlap, omit the one-over-two-pi factor from the frequency marginal, and conclude that the Wigner function cannot be negative because both marginals are positive.

WAVE:010428.title: A linear chirp has a tilted ambiguity ridge
WAVE:010428.objective: Derive the exact delay-Doppler ambiguity function of a rectangular linear chirp and verify its ridge, zeros, and Moyal normalization.
WAVE:010428.statement:
Let the unit-energy rectangular linear-frequency-modulated pulse be
\[
s(t)=\begin{cases}
T^{-1/2}e^{i\pi\mu t^2},&|t|\le T/2,\\
0,&|t|>T/2,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\mu\) is the chirp rate in \(\mathrm{Hz/s}\). Define the symmetric
delay-Doppler ambiguity function using ordinary Doppler frequency \(\nu\):
\[
\chi(\tau,\nu)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
s(t+\tau/2)s^*(t-\tau/2)e^{-i2\pi\nu t}\,dt.
\]
Use \(\operatorname{sinc}x=\sin x/x\), with
\(\operatorname{sinc}0=1\).

Determine the exact overlap interval and derive \(\chi\) for all real
\(\tau,\nu\), including the boundary \(|\tau|=T\). Find the ridge of
maximum magnitude, the nearest Doppler zeros at fixed delay, and the
zero-Doppler response. Explain delay-Doppler coupling and distinguish the
ridge width from the full swept bandwidth \(B=|\mu|T\). Then verify the
Moyal identity directly from your closed form:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
|\chi(\tau,\nu)|^2\,d\nu\,d\tau=1.
\]

For \(T=20.0\,\mu\mathrm s\), \(B=5.00\,\mathrm{MHz}\), and positive
chirp, compute \(\mu\). At \(\tau=4.00\,\mu\mathrm s\), compute the overlap
length, ridge Doppler, and nearest-zero offset from the ridge. Evaluate
\(|\chi(4.00\,\mu\mathrm s,0)|\), and state the peak ridge magnitude at
that delay.
permittedResults: \(\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}e^{-i2\pi f t}\,dt=L\,\operatorname{sinc}(\pi Lf)\).
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sinc}^2(\pi Lx)\,dx=1/L\) for \(L>0\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Intersect the two shifted supports before simplifying the quadratic phase.
Use Parseval in Doppler at each fixed delay as an independent check of the Moyal integral.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the exact finite-pulse ambiguity function and distinguishes its tilted ridge, overlap-controlled width, and normalization.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Places the ridge at nu equals minus mu tau despite the stated conjugation and Doppler convention.
commonErrors.consequence: The delay-Doppler coupling is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses T rather than the overlap length T minus absolute tau in the sinc width and amplitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-support geometry, boundary behavior, and normalization all fail.

hintTree.content: The two rectangular supports overlap on a centered interval of length \(L=T-|\tau|\) when \(|\tau|<T\).
Expand \((t+\tau/2)^2-(t-\tau/2)^2\); only a term linear in t remains.
For the Moyal check, integrate the squared sinc over Doppler before integrating over delay.

WAVE:010428.canonicalSolution:
The support conditions are
\(|t+\tau/2|\le T/2\) and \(|t-\tau/2|\le T/2\). For
\(|\tau|<T\), their intersection is the centered interval
\([-L/2,L/2]\), where
\[
\boxed{L=T-|\tau|}.
\]
For \(|\tau|\ge T\) the overlap has zero measure. In the overlap,
\[
(t+\tau/2)^2-(t-\tau/2)^2=2t\tau,
\]
so the phase is \(e^{-i2\pi(\nu-\mu\tau)t}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
\chi(\tau,\nu)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{L}{T}\operatorname{sinc}[\pi L(\nu-\mu\tau)],&|\tau|<T,\\
0,&|\tau|\ge T.
\end{cases}}
\]
The value at \(|\tau|=T\) is zero because the supports meet only at one
point.

The magnitude ridge is
\[
\boxed{\nu=\mu\tau},\qquad
\boxed{|\chi(\tau,\mu\tau)|=1-|\tau|/T}.
\]
At fixed \(\tau\), the first zeros around the ridge are
\[
\boxed{\nu=\mu\tau\pm\frac1L}.
\]
At zero Doppler,
\[
\boxed{\chi(\tau,0)=\frac LT
\operatorname{sinc}(\pi L\mu\tau)}.
\]
The Doppler main-lobe zero offset \(1/L\) is set by the surviving overlap;
the full sweep bandwidth \(B=|\mu|T\) instead sets the slope and total
frequency excursion. They are not interchangeable.

For the normalization audit, at every \(|\tau|<T\), translation in \(\nu\)
does not change the integral and
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\chi|^2d\nu
=\frac{L^2}{T^2}\frac1L=\frac{L}{T^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{T-|\tau|}{T^2}\,d\tau
=\frac2{T^2}\int_0^T(T-\tau)\,d\tau
=\boxed{1},
\]
which is the requested Moyal identity for this unit-energy pulse.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\mu=B/T=2.50\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz/s}}.
\]
At \(\tau=4.00\,\mu\mathrm s\),
\[
\boxed{L=16.0\,\mu\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{\nu_{\rm ridge}=1.00\,\mathrm{MHz}},
\]
and the nearest-zero offset is
\[
\boxed{1/L=62.5\,\mathrm{kHz}}.
\]
Because \(\pi L\mu\tau=16\pi\),
\[
\boxed{|\chi(4.00\,\mu\mathrm s,0)|=0},
\qquad
\boxed{|\chi|_{\rm ridge}=L/T=0.800}.
\]

graderFixtures.proofText: The shifted rectangles overlap for \(|\tau|<T\) with \(L=T-|\tau|\). Their quadratic-phase difference is \(2t\tau\), so \(\chi=(L/T)\operatorname{sinc}[\pi L(\nu-\mu\tau)]\). The ridge is \(\nu=\mu\tau\), its nearest zeros are one over L away, and integrating the squared sinc gives total Moyal mass one.
I use the full pulse duration at every delay, put the ridge at minus mu tau, and assert Moyal normalization without integrating the overlap-dependent sinc.

WAVE:010429.title: A sinc operator finds the most concentrated packet
WAVE:010429.objective: Derive the Slepian time-band concentration eigenproblem, prove its spectral bounds, and interpret the time-bandwidth trace without calling it an exact rank.
WAVE:010429.statement:
Use the angular-frequency transform pair
\[
G(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(t)e^{-i\omega t}\,dt,\qquad
g(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}G(\omega)e^{i\omega t}\,d\omega.
\]
Restrict attention to signals bandlimited to \(|\omega|\le\Omega\), and define
their fraction of energy in the time window \(I=[-T/2,T/2]\) by
\[
\Lambda[g]=\frac{\int_I|g(t)|^2dt}
{\int_{\mathbb R}|g(t)|^2dt}.
\]
Starting from the orthogonal bandlimiting projection, derive the sinc kernel
\[
K(t,s)=\frac{\sin[\Omega(t-s)]}{\pi(t-s)}
\]
with its diagonal value defined by continuity. Show that maximizing
concentration leads to an eigenproblem for \(K\) on \(I\), and explain why
its eigenvalue equals the concentration of the associated bandlimited
packet.

Prove that the operator is self-adjoint and positive, that every eigenvalue
lies in \([0,1]\), and that
\(\sum_n\lambda_n=\operatorname{tr}K=\Omega T/\pi\). State carefully what
this “Shannon number” does and does not mean. Use the normalized constant
trial function on \(I\) to derive a lower bound on the largest eigenvalue in
terms of the sine integral
\(\operatorname{Si}(x)=\int_0^x\sin u/u\,du\).

For \(\Omega T=6\pi\), compute the trace, the constant-trial lower bound
using \(\operatorname{Si}(6\pi)=1.51803396147\), and the strongest integer
upper bound obtainable from the trace on the number of eigenvalues at least
\(0.900\). Do not claim that this count is attained.
permittedResults: A self-adjoint positive contraction has spectrum in \([0,1]\), and its largest eigenvalue is the supremum of its Rayleigh quotient.
For a positive trace-class operator, \(\operatorname{tr}K=\int_I K(t,t)\,dt=\sum_n\lambda_n\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Factor the concentration problem into time- and band-projection operators and use their norms.
Audit the spectral result with both a trace calculation and an explicit constant-function Rayleigh quotient.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects the time-band variational problem to the sinc operator and interprets its trace quantitatively without turning an effective dimension into an exact rank.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: States that Omega T over pi is the exact number of nonzero or perfectly concentrated eigenfunctions.
commonErrors.consequence: A trace of fractional eigenvalues is misinterpreted as an algebraic rank.

commonErrors.description: Uses a bandwidth or sinc normalization inconsistent with the stated angular-frequency transform.
commonErrors.consequence: The kernel diagonal, trace, and numerical Shannon number disagree.

hintTree.content: Insert the inverse transform restricted to \([-\Omega,\Omega]\) to obtain the bandlimiting projection in time.
If \(h\) is supported on \(I\) and \(Kh=\lambda h\), compare the total and in-window norms of \(g=Bh\).
For the constant trial, change variables from \(t,s\) to the difference \(u=t-s\) and use the triangular overlap length \(T-|u|\).

WAVE:010429.canonicalSolution:
The orthogonal projection \(B\) onto the band is
\[
(Bf)(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\sin[\Omega(t-s)]}{\pi(t-s)}f(s)\,ds.
\]
Let \(P\) restrict to \(I\). On functions supported in \(I\),
\(K=PBP\) has the stated kernel. It is self-adjoint because the kernel is
real and symmetric, and
\[
\langle h,Kh\rangle=\langle h,Bh\rangle=\|Bh\|^2\ge0.
\]
Since \(B\) and \(P\) are orthogonal projections,
\(\langle h,Kh\rangle\le\|h\|^2\); hence \(0\le\lambda_n\le1\).

If \(Kh=\lambda h\) and \(g=Bh\), then
\[
\|g\|^2=\langle h,Bh\rangle=\lambda\|h\|^2,\qquad
\|Pg\|^2=\|Kh\|^2=\lambda^2\|h\|^2.
\]
Therefore \(\Lambda[g]=\lambda\). Extremizing the Rayleigh quotient of \(K\)
thus produces the optimally concentrated bandlimited packets.

On the diagonal, \(K(t,t)=\Omega/\pi\), so
\[
\boxed{\sum_n\lambda_n=\operatorname{tr}K=\frac{\Omega T}{\pi}}.
\]
This is an effective dimension, not an integer rank and not a proof that
exactly that many eigenvalues equal one.

For \(h(t)=T^{-1/2}\) on \(I\), the triangular-overlap reduction gives
\[
\frac{\langle h,Kh\rangle}{\langle h,h\rangle}
=\frac{2}{\pi T}\left[
T\operatorname{Si}(\Omega T)-\frac{1-\cos(\Omega T)}{\Omega}\right].
\]
Thus this expression is a rigorous lower bound on \(\lambda_0\). At
\(\Omega T=6\pi\), the cosine term vanishes and
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{tr}K=6},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_0\ge\frac2\pi\operatorname{Si}(6\pi)
=0.966410435}.
\]
If \(M\) eigenvalues are at least \(0.900\), positivity and the trace give
\(0.900M\le6\), hence
\[
\boxed{M\le6}.
\]
The integer floor is essential, and the trace alone supplies no matching
lower bound on \(M\).

graderFixtures.proofText: The time-limited band projection has kernel \(\sin[\Omega(t-s)]/[\pi(t-s)]\), positive contraction eigenvalues equal to packet concentrations, and trace \(\Omega T/\pi\). At \(6\pi\), the trace is 6, the constant trial proves \(\lambda_0\ge0.966410435\), and at most six eigenvalues can be at least 0.900.
I use an ordinary-frequency sinc with the angular-frequency transform, call the trace an exact rank of six, and infer that six eigenvalues exceed 0.9.
