WAVE:010445.title: A Lorentzian pulse has an exact analytic signal
WAVE:010445.objective: Construct an analytic signal from an exact Hilbert-transform pair and distinguish its one-sided spectrum, envelope, phase, and instantaneous frequency.
WAVE:010445.statement:
Use the Fourier convention
$$G(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(t)e^{-i\omega t}dt$$
and the Hilbert-transform convention
$$
(\mathcal Hg)(t)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{g(\tau)}{t-\tau}\,d\tau,
$$
whose Fourier multiplier is $-i\operatorname{sgn}\omega$. Let
$$g(t)=\frac{a}{\pi(t^2+a^2)},\qquad a>0.$$

Find $G(\omega)$ and $\mathcal Hg$ exactly. Form the analytic signal
$z=g+i\mathcal Hg$, derive its spectrum including the positive-frequency
factor of two, and find its envelope, unwrapped phase, and instantaneous
angular frequency. Audit the sign of the frequency and the behavior as
$t\to\pm\infty$. Compare the energy in $g$ with the energy in $z$, and
explain why the analytic envelope does not have a finite second temporal
moment even though $g^2$ does.

For $a=0.250\,\mathrm s$, calculate $g(0)$, $\mathcal Hg(a)$,
$|z(a)|$, the instantaneous frequencies at $t=0$ and $t=a$, the real-signal
energy, and the analytic spectrum at $\omega=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
State how reversing the Hilbert-transform kernel convention would affect
the reported signs.
permittedResults: The transform of $a/[\pi(t^2+a^2)]$ is $e^{-a|\omega|}$.
Multiplication by $t$ in time corresponds to $i\,d/d\omega$ in this Fourier convention.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the known Lorentzian transform and the Hilbert Fourier multiplier.
Recognize the real and imaginary parts as the boundary values of a simple pole in one half-plane.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses one Fourier/Hilbert convention consistently enough that quadrature sign, one-sided support, phase direction, and instantaneous frequency all agree.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $-t/[\pi(t^2+a^2)]$ while retaining the multiplier $-i\operatorname{sgn}\omega$.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed quadrature and frequency half-axis contradict the stated convention.

commonErrors.description: Sets $Z(\omega)=e^{-a\omega}$ for $\omega>0$ after deleting the negative-frequency half.
commonErrors.consequence: The real part of the inverse transform is only half of $g$.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $e^{-a|\omega|}$ to identify the transform of $t/[\pi(t^2+a^2)]$.
Use $1+\operatorname{sgn}\omega$ when transforming $g+i\mathcal Hg$.
Write $z=1/[\pi(a-it)]$ before reading its magnitude and phase.

WAVE:010445.canonicalSolution:
The standard contour transform gives
$$
\boxed{G(\omega)=e^{-a|\omega|}}.
$$
Since the Hilbert multiplier is $-i\operatorname{sgn}\omega$ and
$$
\mathcal F\left\{\frac{t}{\pi(t^2+a^2)}\right\}
=-i\operatorname{sgn}\omega\,e^{-a|\omega|},
$$
the exact Hilbert pair is
$$
\boxed{(\mathcal Hg)(t)=\frac{t}{\pi(t^2+a^2)}}.
$$
The analytic signal simplifies to
$$
\boxed{z(t)=\frac{a+it}{\pi(t^2+a^2)}
=\frac1{\pi(a-it)}}.
$$
Its spectrum, apart from the immaterial convention at the single point
$\omega=0$, is
$$
\boxed{Z(\omega)=\begin{cases}2e^{-a\omega},&\omega>0,\\0,&\omega<0.
\end{cases}}
$$
The factor two is required because removing the negative-frequency half must
preserve the real part $g$.

Magnitude and unwrapped phase are
$$
\boxed{|z(t)|=\frac1{\pi\sqrt{a^2+t^2}}},\qquad
\boxed{\phi(t)=\tan^{-1}(t/a)}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\rm inst}(t)=\phi'(t)=\frac{a}{a^2+t^2}>0}.
$$
The phase rises continuously from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$, while the frequency
tends to zero at both tails and reaches $1/a$ at the center. A negative
frequency here would signal a Hilbert-sign convention mismatch.

Direct integration or Parseval gives
$$
\boxed{\int g^2dt=\frac1{2\pi a}},\qquad
\boxed{\int|z|^2dt=\frac1{\pi a}}.
$$
Thus analytic-signal energy is twice real-signal energy. Although
$\int t^2g(t)^2dt$ is finite, $t^2|z|^2$ approaches a nonzero constant, so
the analytic envelope intensity has divergent second temporal moment. Tail
decay, not visual central width, decides that moment.

For $a=0.250\,\mathrm s$,
$$
\boxed{g(0)=1.27324\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{(\mathcal Hg)(a)=0.636620\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{|z(a)|=0.900316\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The instantaneous frequencies are
$\boxed{\omega_{\rm inst}(0)=4.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ and
$\boxed{\omega_{\rm inst}(a)=2.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. The real-signal
energy is $\boxed{0.636620\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ in the corresponding squared
signal units, and
$$
\boxed{Z(8.00)=2e^{-2}=0.270671}.
$$
If the Hilbert kernel were defined with the opposite denominator, its
multiplier, quadrature sign, supported frequency half-axis, phase, and
instantaneous-frequency sign would all reverse together; mixing conventions
rather than changing them consistently is the error.

WAVE:010446.title: A matched filter turns a buried Gaussian into a sharp correlation peak
WAVE:010446.objective: Derive the delay response and output signal-to-noise ratio of a Gaussian matched filter, including the exact white-noise normalization and width conventions.
WAVE:010446.statement:
A known real pulse
$$s(t)=A\exp[-t^2/(2\tau^2)]$$
arrives with unknown delay $t_0$ in data $r(t)=s(t-t_0)+n(t)$. The additive
noise is zero-mean white noise with two-sided power spectral density $N_0/2$,
so $\mathbb E[n(t)n(t')]=(N_0/2)\delta(t-t')$. Define the correlation
output
$$C(b)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}r(t)s(t-b)dt.$$

Derive the signal-only output as a function of trial delay $b$ and show where
it peaks. Calculate the pulse energy, output-noise variance, peak amplitude
signal-to-noise ratio, and peak power signal-to-noise ratio. Derive the
Fourier transform of the template, its energy-spectrum RMS angular bandwidth,
the RMS width of the correlation amplitude as a function of delay, and the
RMS width of its squared magnitude. Keep those two width conventions distinct.
Explain why correlation is the white-noise matched filter and what weighting
would change for colored noise.

For $A=2.00$, $\tau=0.100\,\mathrm s$, $N_0=0.0400$ in consistent
two-sided units, and $t_0=0.370\,\mathrm s$, calculate the peak location and
mean, noise standard deviation, both peak SNRs, spectral RMS bandwidth, and
both delay widths. State why a finite observation window or an unknown pulse
amplitude changes estimation details but not the ideal peak shape derived here.
permittedResults: For white noise and deterministic $h$, the variance of $\int n(t)h(t)dt$ is $(N_0/2)\int|h(t)|^2dt$.
The matched filter maximizes output SNR by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.

acceptableStrategies.description: Complete the square directly in time and propagate delta-correlated noise through the template integral.
Use the frequency-domain Cauchy--Schwarz matched-filter derivation and inverse-transform the Gaussian output spectrum.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Propagates one explicit two-sided noise convention through the matched-filter mean, variance, SNR, bandwidth, and delay-width calculations without mixing amplitude and intensity profiles.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses noise variance $N_0E_s$ despite the stated two-sided PSD $N_0/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Every reported output SNR has the wrong factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Calls $\tau$ the RMS width of the correlation amplitude rather than of $|C_s|^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Amplitude and squared-magnitude Gaussian widths are conflated.

hintTree.content: Complete the square in the product of the received and trial Gaussians.
At the correct delay, the signal mean equals $E_s=\int s^2dt$.
Specify whether an RMS width belongs to correlation amplitude or its squared magnitude.

WAVE:010446.canonicalSolution:
The pulse energy is
$$
\boxed{E_s=\int s^2dt=A^2\sqrt\pi\,\tau}.
$$
Completing the square in the correlation integral gives
$$
\boxed{C_s(b)=E_s\exp\left[-\frac{(b-t_0)^2}{4\tau^2}\right]}.
$$
It has its unique maximum $E_s$ at $b=t_0$. The noise part is a linear
functional of white noise, so its variance is independent of $b$ and equals
$$
\boxed{\sigma_C^2=\frac{N_0}{2}E_s}.
$$
Consequently the peak mean-to-standard-deviation ratio and its square are
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm amp}=\sqrt{\frac{2E_s}{N_0}}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm power}=\frac{2E_s}{N_0}}.
$$
The factor $1/2$ follows from the explicitly two-sided PSD; silently using a
one-sided convention doubles the variance or halves the stated SNR.

With the stated Fourier convention,
$$
\boxed{S(\omega)=A\tau\sqrt{2\pi}\,
e^{-\tau^2\omega^2/2}}.
$$
Since $|S|^2\propto e^{-\tau^2\omega^2}$, its RMS angular bandwidth is
$$
\boxed{\sigma_\omega=\frac1{\sqrt2\tau}}.
$$
As a function of delay, the correlation amplitude has Gaussian RMS width
$\boxed{\sqrt2\tau}$ because its exponent is
$-(b-t_0)^2/(4\tau^2)$. Its squared magnitude has exponent
$-(b-t_0)^2/(2\tau^2)$ and RMS width $\boxed{\tau}$. These are not
contradictory widths; they refer to different nonnegative profiles.

Correlation is convolution with the time-reversed template. In white noise,
all spectral components have equal noise weight, so this filter saturates the
Cauchy--Schwarz SNR bound. For colored noise the optimum spectrum is instead
proportional to $S^*(\omega)/\Phi_n(\omega)$, subject to the chosen delay
phase and regularity assumptions.

Numerically
$$
\boxed{E_s=0.708982},\qquad \boxed{b_{\rm peak}=0.370000\,\mathrm s}.
$$
The peak mean is $0.708982$, while
$$
\boxed{\sigma_C=0.119078}.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm amp}=5.95391},\qquad
\boxed{\mathrm{SNR}_{\rm power}=35.4491}.
$$
The spectral RMS bandwidth is
$\boxed{7.07107\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$; the correlation-amplitude and
correlation-intensity RMS delay widths are respectively
$\boxed{0.141421\,\mathrm s}$ and $\boxed{0.100000\,\mathrm s}$. A finite
window truncates the integrals and can make the noise variance delay
dependent near its edges. If the amplitude is unknown, one normally
normalizes or jointly estimates it, but the ideal untruncated correlation
peak shape remains the Gaussian derived above.

WAVE:010517.title: The capillary-gravity speed minimum on deep water
WAVE:010517.objective: Analyze capillary-gravity dispersion, derive phase and group velocities and their crossover, and compute the characteristic wavelength and minimum speed for water.
WAVE:010517.statement:
For small-amplitude waves on deep water, take the dispersion relation
\[
\omega^2=gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3,
\qquad k>0,
\]
where \(\rho\) is density and \(\gamma\) is surface tension. Treat the fluid
as inviscid, incompressible, irrotational, and deep compared with the
wavelength.

Derive the phase velocity \(c_p\) and group velocity \(c_g\). Find the
wavenumber at which \(c_p\) is minimal, prove that \(c_g=c_p\) there, and
derive the exact minimum speed. Determine the gravity-dominated and
capillary-dominated limits of \(c_g/c_p\).

For \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\),
\(\gamma=0.0720\,\mathrm{N/m}\), and
\(\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), compute the crossover wavenumber,
wavelength, and minimum phase speed. Explain why the group velocity is not
automatically a signal front velocity and identify which assumptions become
suspect for very short capillary waves.
permittedResults: For a narrow packet governed by differentiable \(\omega(k)\), \(c_g=d\omega/dk\), while \(c_p=\omega/k\).
At a stationary point of \(c_p=\omega/k\), the identity \(d(\omega/k)/dk=0\) implies \(d\omega/dk=\omega/k\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Minimize the squared phase speed and independently differentiate the dispersion relation for group speed.
Use logarithmic differentiation and the general stationary-phase-speed identity, provided the exact crossover and numerical scale are shown.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives phase and group speeds from the same dispersion relation, locates and interprets the exact crossover minimum, and computes the physical scale with valid asymptotic limits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Claims group and phase velocity are equal for every wavenumber rather than only at the phase-speed minimum.
commonErrors.consequence: The central physical effect of dispersion is erased.

commonErrors.description: Balances the terms with the wrong power of k or uses wavelength equal to one over k.
commonErrors.consequence: The characteristic length scale and minimum speed are incorrect.

hintTree.content: Let \(\alpha=\gamma/\rho\); then \(c_p^2=g/k+\alpha k\).
Differentiate \(\omega=(gk+\alpha k^3)^{1/2}\) without first taking a limiting approximation.
At the minimum, \(\alpha k^2=g\), so the gravity and capillary terms are equal.

WAVE:010517.canonicalSolution:
Let \(\alpha=\gamma/\rho\). Then
\[
\boxed{c_p=\frac\omega k=\sqrt{\frac gk+\alpha k}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{c_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}
=\frac{g+3\alpha k^2}{2\sqrt{gk+\alpha k^3}}
=\frac{c_p}{2}\frac{g+3\alpha k^2}{g+\alpha k^2}}.
\]
Minimizing \(c_p^2\) gives
\[
-\frac g{k^2}+\alpha=0,
\qquad
\boxed{k_*=\sqrt{\frac g\alpha}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho g}{\gamma}}}.
\]
At this point \(\alpha k_*^2=g\), so the group-to-phase ratio is
\(\tfrac12(4g)/(2g)=1\). Equivalently, any stationary point of
\(\omega/k\) obeys \(d\omega/dk=\omega/k\). The minimum speed is
\[
\boxed{c_{p,\min}=\left(\frac{4g\gamma}{\rho}\right)^{1/4}}.
\]
For \(k\ll k_*\), gravity dominates and \(c_g/c_p\to1/2\). For
\(k\gg k_*\), capillarity dominates and \(c_g/c_p\to3/2\).

Numerically,
\[
k_*=\sqrt{\frac{1000(9.81)}{0.0720}}
=369.1\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},
\]
\[
\lambda_*=\frac{2\pi}{k_*}=1.702\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m
=1.70\ \mathrm{cm},
\]
and
\[
c_{p,\min}=\left(\frac{4(9.81)(0.0720)}{1000}\right)^{1/4}
=0.2306\ \mathrm{m/s}.
\]
Group velocity describes a narrowband envelope within the stated model; a
causal front depends on the full dispersive and dissipative response. At very
short wavelengths, viscosity, contamination-dependent surface tension,
molecular-scale effects, and failure of the ideal small-amplitude continuum
model can matter.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(\alpha=\gamma/\rho\), \(c_p^2=g/k+\alpha k\) and \(c_g=(g+3\alpha k^2)/(2\omega)\). The minimum has \(k_*^2=g/\alpha\), where \(c_g=c_p\), and \(c_{p,\min}=(4g\gamma/\rho)^{1/4}\). For water, \(k_*=369.1\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\) and \(\lambda_*=1.70\,\mathrm{cm}\).
Phase and group speeds are always identical because both describe the same wave. I balance g k with alpha k squared and call one over k the wavelength.

WAVE:010518.title: Superluminal phase without superluminal transport
WAVE:010518.objective: Analyze a cutoff dispersion relation, prove the phase-group velocity product, and distinguish propagating and evanescent regimes without assigning a signal speed to phase velocity.
WAVE:010518.statement:
A lossless guided mode has longitudinal dispersion relation
\[
\omega^2=\omega_c^2+c^2k^2,
\]
where \(\omega_c>0\) is the cutoff angular frequency and \(c\) is the
underlying bulk wave speed. For \(\omega>\omega_c\), take \(k>0\).

Derive the phase and group velocities and prove their product is \(c^2\).
Show which is greater than \(c\), which is less, and find both limits as
\(\omega\downarrow\omega_c\) and \(\omega\to\infty\). Evaluate
\(k c/\omega_c\), \(v_p/c\), and \(v_g/c\) at
\(\omega=1.25\omega_c\).

For \(0<\omega<\omega_c\), derive the positive attenuation constant
\(\kappa\) when \(k=i\kappa\), and explain why this is an evanescent rather
than a propagating mode in an infinitely long ideal guide. Explain why
\(v_p>c\) above cutoff does not imply superluminal energy or information
transport and state the narrowband assumption behind identifying
\(v_g\) with envelope transport.
permittedResults: Implicit differentiation of \(\omega^2=\omega_c^2+c^2k^2\) gives the group velocity without solving for \(k(\omega)\) first.
A phase crest need not represent a localized causal signal or energy packet.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the dispersion relation explicitly for k and differentiate omega with respect to k.
Use implicit differentiation for group speed and algebraic substitution for the evanescent regime.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and interprets phase, group, cutoff, and evanescent behavior consistently, including the exact product, limiting cases, and dimensionless numerical evaluation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the super-c phase velocity as the energy or information velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical interpretation of a dispersive guided mode is incorrect.

commonErrors.description: Treats the below-cutoff longitudinal wavenumber as real and assigns it an ordinary propagating wavelength.
commonErrors.consequence: An evanescent field is misclassified as a traveling mode.

hintTree.content: Use \(v_p=\omega/k\) and \(2\omega\,d\omega/dk=2c^2k\).
Below cutoff, substitute \(k=i\kappa\) and choose \(\kappa>0\) for decay in the positive longitudinal direction.

WAVE:010518.canonicalSolution:
For propagation above cutoff,
\[
v_p=\frac\omega k
=\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-(\omega_c/\omega)^2}}>c.
\]
Implicit differentiation gives
\[
2\omega\frac{d\omega}{dk}=2c^2k,
\qquad
v_g=\frac{c^2k}{\omega}
=c\sqrt{1-(\omega_c/\omega)^2}<c.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{v_pv_g=c^2}.
\]
As \(\omega\downarrow\omega_c\), \(k\to0\),
\(v_p\to\infty\), and \(v_g\to0\). As \(\omega\to\infty\), both speeds
approach \(c\), from above and below respectively.

At \(\omega=1.25\omega_c\),
\[
\frac{ck}{\omega_c}=\sqrt{1.25^2-1}=0.75,
\quad
\boxed{\frac{v_p}{c}=\frac{1.25}{0.75}=\frac53},
\quad
\boxed{\frac{v_g}{c}=\frac{0.75}{1.25}=\frac35}.
\]

Below cutoff, put \(k=i\kappa\). Then
\[
\omega^2=\omega_c^2-c^2\kappa^2,
\qquad
\boxed{\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{\omega_c^2-\omega^2}}c}.
\]
A factor \(e^{ikz}\) becomes \(e^{-\kappa z}\), so the field decays rather
than accumulating a real propagation phase. In a finite structure, evanescent
coupling can still matter, but it is not a freely propagating ideal-guide mode.
The superluminal phase speed tracks constant-phase surfaces, not a localized
message or energy centroid. Group velocity describes a slowly modulated,
narrowband packet when the dispersion relation is smooth over its bandwidth;
causal front behavior requires the full response.

graderFixtures.proofText: Above cutoff, \(v_p=\omega/k>c\) and \(v_g=c^2k/\omega<c\), so \(v_pv_g=c^2\). At \(1.25\omega_c\), \(ck/\omega_c=0.75\), \(v_p/c=5/3\), and \(v_g/c=3/5\). Below cutoff, \(k=i\sqrt{\omega_c^2-\omega^2}/c\), giving exponential decay.
Since phase velocity is larger than c, this guide sends information faster than c. Below cutoff the wavenumber is the real square root of omega-c squared minus omega squared divided by c.

WAVE:010519.title: From nondispersive shallow water to dispersive deep water
WAVE:010519.objective: Derive phase and group speeds from finite-depth gravity-wave dispersion, obtain controlled shallow- and deep-water limits, and classify a numerical wave by its dimensionless depth.
WAVE:010519.statement:
Small-amplitude inviscid surface waves of wavenumber \(k>0\) on water of
uniform depth \(h\) obey
\[
\omega^2=gk\tanh(kh).
\]
Assume incompressible, irrotational flow, negligible surface tension and
viscosity, and a flat impermeable bottom.

Derive the phase velocity and show that the group-to-phase ratio is
\[
\frac{c_g}{c_p}=\frac12
\left(1+\frac{2kh}{\sinh(2kh)}\right).
\]
Obtain the first dispersive corrections to \(c_p\) and \(c_g\) for
\(kh\ll1\). Derive the \(kh\gg1\) limits, and explain why the shallow-water
limit is nondispersive to leading order while the deep-water group speed is
half the phase speed.

For \(h=4.00\,\mathrm m\) and wavelength \(\lambda=10.0\,\mathrm m\),
compute \(kh,\omega,c_p,c_g\), and the travel-time separation after the phase
crests and a narrow envelope have covered a horizontal distance of
\(100\,\mathrm m\). State why neither a single crest nor a group velocity
outside its narrowband regime should automatically be called the causal signal
front.
permittedResults: For small \(q\), \(\tanh q=q-q^3/3+O(q^5)\), and \((1+\epsilon)^{1/2}=1+\epsilon/2+O(\epsilon^2)\).
For a differentiable narrowband dispersion relation, \(c_p=\omega/k\) and \(c_g=d\omega/dk\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the exact dispersion relation and then expand the resulting phase and group speeds in kh.
Use logarithmic differentiation for the exact ratio and an independent small-k expansion for the shallow-water correction.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the exact finite-depth phase/group relation, obtains controlled shallow and deep asymptotics, and correctly classifies and evaluates the intermediate-depth numerical wave.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Classifies depth using h or wavelength alone instead of the dimensionless product kh, or uses k equal to one over wavelength.
commonErrors.consequence: The asymptotic regime and all numerical speeds are misidentified.

commonErrors.description: Claims group and phase speed remain equal beyond leading shallow-water order or in deep water.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-depth dispersion requested by the problem is erased.

hintTree.content: Logarithmically differentiate \(\omega=[gk\tanh(kh)]^{1/2}\) and use \(d\ln\tanh(kh)/d\ln k=2kh/\sinh(2kh)\).
In shallow water, expand omega before dividing by k or differentiating.
Use k equals two pi over lambda in the numerical case; compare 100 over c-p with 100 over c-g.

WAVE:010519.canonicalSolution:
The phase speed is
\[
\boxed{c_p=\frac\omega k
=\sqrt{\frac gk\tanh(kh)}}.
\]
Logarithmic differentiation gives
\[
\frac{k}{\omega}\frac{d\omega}{dk}
=\frac12\left[1+
\frac{kh\,\operatorname{sech}^2(kh)}{\tanh(kh)}\right]
=\frac12\left(1+\frac{2kh}{\sinh(2kh)}\right).
\]
Since the left side is \(c_g/c_p\), this proves the stated result.

Let \(q=kh\ll1\). Then
\[
\omega=\sqrt{gh}\,k
\left(1-\frac{q^2}{6}+O(q^4)\right),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{c_p=\sqrt{gh}
\left(1-\frac{q^2}{6}+O(q^4)\right)},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_g=\sqrt{gh}
\left(1-\frac{q^2}{2}+O(q^4)\right)}.
\]
Both approach \(\sqrt{gh}\), independent of k at leading order. For
\(q\gg1\), \(\tanh q\to1\) and \(2q/\sinh2q\to0\), giving
\[
c_p\sim\sqrt{g/k},\qquad c_g\sim\frac12\sqrt{g/k}=\frac12c_p.
\]

Numerically,
\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{10.0}=0.628319\,\mathrm{m^{-1}},
\qquad q=kh=2.51327.
\]
Using \(\tanh q=0.98696\),
\[
\omega=\sqrt{(9.81)(0.628319)(0.98696)}
=2.4665\,\mathrm{rad/s},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_p=\omega/k=3.926\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The ratio is
\[
\frac{c_g}{c_p}=\frac12
\left(1+\frac{5.02655}{\sinh5.02655}\right)
=0.5330,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{c_g=2.092\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The crest and narrow-envelope travel times over \(100\,\mathrm m\) are
\(25.47\,\mathrm s\) and \(47.80\,\mathrm s\), respectively, a separation
of approximately
\[
\boxed{22.3\,\mathrm s}.
\]
A phase crest is not a localized message. Group speed tracks an envelope only
when the spectrum is narrow enough that a first-order expansion of
\(\omega(k)\) is accurate; the causal front depends on the full physical
response and neglected dissipation or capillarity.

graderFixtures.proofText: Differentiation gives \(c_g/c_p=[1+2kh/\sinh(2kh)]/2\). For small kh, \(c_p=\sqrt{gh}[1-(kh)^2/6+\cdots]\) and \(c_g=\sqrt{gh}[1-(kh)^2/2+\cdots]\); deep water gives one-half. For the data, kh is 2.513, c-p is about 3.926 m/s, and c-g about 2.092 m/s.
Depth is four meters and wavelength is ten meters, so h is less than lambda and the wave is exactly shallow. I use k equals one over lambda and set group speed equal to phase speed at every depth.

WAVE:010520.title: A flexural-wave envelope outruns its phase crests
WAVE:010520.objective: Derive Euler-Bernoulli flexural-wave dispersion, recover phase and group speeds, and use an exact two-wave beat to distinguish envelope and carrier motion within the beam model.
WAVE:010520.statement:
A uniform slender Euler-Bernoulli beam has Young modulus \(E\), second area
moment \(I\), density \(\rho\), cross-sectional area \(S\), and transverse
displacement \(y(x,t)\). Neglect rotary inertia, shear deformation, damping,
axial tension, and boundaries, so the beam is effectively infinite.

Starting from force and moment balance or from the stated model assumptions,
derive
\[
\rho S y_{tt}+EIy_{xxxx}=0.
\]
Insert a harmonic traveling wave to find \(\omega(k)\), and derive phase and
group velocities with their units. Superpose two equal-amplitude waves with
wavenumbers \(k_1\) and \(k_2\). Use trigonometric identities to show that
the exact beat-envelope speed equals the group velocity evaluated at the mean
wavenumber, not merely its small-separation limit.

For \(E=70.0\,\mathrm{GPa}\), \(\rho=2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), a rectangular
cross-section of width \(20.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) and thickness
\(2.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), and \(k_1=10.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\),
\(k_2=12.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), compute \(I,S\), the dispersion coefficient,
both angular frequencies, the phase speed evaluated at \(\bar k\), the exact
two-wave carrier speed \(\bar\omega/\bar k\), and the envelope velocity.
Explain why \(v_g>v_p\) here does not violate relativity and identify when the
Euler-Bernoulli approximation becomes unreliable.
permittedResults: For a rectangular cross-section bent about the axis parallel to its width, \(I=bt^3/12\) and \(S=bt\).
The sum of two cosines is \(2\cos[(\Delta k\,x-\Delta\omega\,t)/2]\cos[(\bar kx-\bar\omega t)]\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the Euler-Bernoulli PDE from moment and shear balance and then analyze plane waves and a two-cosine superposition.
Start from the accepted Euler-Bernoulli PDE under the stated assumptions, provided the dispersion, exact beat identity, section calculation, and validity limits are fully derived.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the beam wave equation and quadratic dispersion, proves the exact two-wave envelope speed, and performs the geometric, dimensional, numerical, and model-validity audits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats flexural dispersion as omega proportional to k or takes alpha equal to EI over rho S without the square root.
commonErrors.consequence: Phase, group, units, and all numerical speeds are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the cosine carrier speed to the beat envelope or omits the difference-frequency over difference-wavenumber calculation.
commonErrors.consequence: The central manifestation of quadratic dispersion is misidentified.

hintTree.content: A wave \(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) turns the fourth spatial derivative into \(k^4\) and the second time derivative into minus omega squared.
Define \(\alpha=\sqrt{EI/(\rho S)}\), so the positive branch is \(\omega=\alpha k^2\).
The beat-envelope speed is \(\Delta\omega/\Delta k=\alpha(k_2+k_1)=2\alpha\bar k\).

WAVE:010520.canonicalSolution:
Euler-Bernoulli curvature gives bending moment \(M=-EIy_{xx}\).
Differentiating the moment to obtain shear and then transverse force density,
with a consistent sign convention, gives
\[
\boxed{\rho S y_{tt}+EIy_{xxxx}=0}.
\]
For \(y=e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\),
\[
-\rho S\omega^2+EIk^4=0.
\]
On the positive-frequency branch,
\[
\boxed{\omega=\alpha k^2},
\qquad
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho S}}.
\]
The coefficient \(\alpha\) has units \(\mathrm{m^2/s}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{v_p=\omega/k=\alpha k},
\qquad
\boxed{v_g=d\omega/dk=2\alpha k=2v_p}.
\]

For two waves, the cosine-sum identity yields a carrier at
\((\bar k,\bar\omega)\) multiplied by an envelope
\(\cos[(\Delta kx-\Delta\omega t)/2]\). Thus
\[
v_{\rm env}=\frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta k}
=\alpha\frac{k_2^2-k_1^2}{k_2-k_1}
=\alpha(k_1+k_2)=2\alpha\bar k
=v_g(\bar k).
\]
Because the dispersion is exactly quadratic, this equality holds for any two
distinct positive wavenumbers, not only infinitesimally close ones.
The carrier factor itself has phase speed
\[
\boxed{v_{\rm carrier}=\frac{\bar\omega}{\bar k}
=\alpha\frac{k_1^2+k_2^2}{k_1+k_2}},
\]
which generally differs from the single-mode phase speed
\(v_p(\bar k)=\alpha\bar k\). The difference is second order in the
wavenumber separation and vanishes only as the two waves coalesce.

For the rectangular section,
\[
S=bt=(0.0200)(0.00200)=4.00\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2},
\]
\[
I=\frac{bt^3}{12}=1.3333\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{(70.0\times10^9)(1.3333\times10^{-11})}
{(2700)(4.00\times10^{-5})}}
=2.940\,\mathrm{m^2/s}.
\]
The frequencies are
\[
\omega_1=\alpha(10.0)^2=294.0\,\mathrm{rad/s},
\qquad
\omega_2=\alpha(12.0)^2=423.3\,\mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
At \(\bar k=11.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\),
\[
\boxed{v_p(\bar k)=32.34\,\mathrm{m/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{v_{\rm carrier}=32.60\,\mathrm{m/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{v_{\rm env}=v_g(\bar k)=64.68\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The nonrelativistic Euler-Bernoulli continuum model omits high-frequency
rotary inertia, shear deformation, microstructure, and ultimately relativistic
causality. Its formal unbounded group speed at large k signals breakdown of
the approximation, not superluminal information. It is reliable only for
wavelengths long compared with cross-sectional dimensions and frequencies
where those neglected effects remain small.

graderFixtures.proofText: Plane waves in \(\rho S y_{tt}+EIy_{xxxx}=0\) give \(\omega=\alpha k^2\), alpha equal to the square root of EI over rho S. For two waves, delta omega over delta k equals alpha times k-one plus k-two, exactly v-g at their mean. The carrier factor travels at bar-omega over bar-k, while the single-mode phase speed evaluated at bar-k is alpha bar-k.
The fourth derivative contributes k squared, so omega equals EI over rho S times k. The envelope moves at the same speed as the mean phase crest because both are visible parts of one waveform.

WAVE:010521.title: Rossby-wave crests move west while energy can move east
WAVE:010521.objective: Derive the anisotropic Rossby-wave dispersion relation and group velocity, identify when zonal phase and group velocities oppose, and evaluate a deformation-radius example.
WAVE:010521.statement:
On a beta plane, the linear barotropic quasigeostrophic streamfunction obeys
\[
\partial_t\left(\nabla^2\psi-\frac{\psi}{L_D^2}\right)
+\beta\,\partial_x\psi=0,
\]
where \(\beta>0\) and \(L_D>0\). Use a plane wave
\(\psi=\Re\{\Psi e^{i(kx+\ell y-\omega t)}\}\).

Derive \(\omega(k,\ell)\), the zonal phase velocity \(\omega/k\), and both
components of group velocity. Determine the exact condition under which the
zonal group velocity is eastward even though the zonal phase velocity is
westward. Explain physically and mathematically why the group-velocity vector
need not be parallel to the wavevector. Discuss the limits of very large total
wavenumber and very small wavenumber when \(L_D\) is finite.

Take \(\beta=2.00\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}s^{-1}}\),
\(L_D=1000\,\mathrm{km}\), zonal wavelength \(4000\,\mathrm{km}\), and
meridional wavelength \(6000\,\mathrm{km}\), with positive k and ell.
Compute the angular frequency, period in days, zonal phase speed, and both
group-velocity components. State the propagation directions from their signs;
do not replace the gradient of omega by the scalar derivative with respect to
the magnitude of the wavevector.
permittedResults: For a multidimensional packet, \(\mathbf c_g=\nabla_{(k,\ell)}\omega\).
The sign of a phase speed tracks crest propagation, whereas group velocity tracks the local envelope only within the narrow-packet linear model.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute the plane wave into the potential-vorticity equation and differentiate omega with respect to both wavevector components.
Use Fourier-symbol analysis of the linear PDE, provided the same signs, anisotropic derivatives, limits, directional interpretation, and numerical results are obtained.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the anisotropic Rossby dispersion and vector group velocity, identifies opposing zonal phase and group directions, and evaluates the finite-deformation-radius example correctly.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Drops the minus sign in the Rossby dispersion relation for positive beta and k.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted crest direction is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Treats omega as a function only of total wavenumber and forces group velocity parallel to the wavevector.
commonErrors.consequence: The anisotropic zonal and meridional energy-propagation components are wrong.

hintTree.content: The plane-wave potential-vorticity factor is \(-(k^2+\ell^2+L_D^{-2})\Psi\).
Differentiate \(-\beta k/D\) with \(D=k^2+\ell^2+L_D^{-2}\) using the quotient rule.
Eastward zonal group motion requires the numerator \(k^2-\ell^2-L_D^{-2}\) to be positive.

WAVE:010521.canonicalSolution:
Let \(D=k^2+\ell^2+L_D^{-2}\). Substitution into the PDE gives
\(i\omega D\Psi+i\beta k\Psi=0\), hence
\[
\boxed{\omega=-\frac{\beta k}{D}}.
\]
For positive k, the zonal phase velocity is always westward:
\[
\boxed{c_{px}=\frac\omega k=-\frac\beta D<0}.
\]
Taking the two-dimensional gradient yields
\[
\boxed{c_{gx}=\frac{\beta(k^2-\ell^2-L_D^{-2})}{D^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{c_{gy}=\frac{2\beta k\ell}{D^2}}.
\]
Thus zonal group motion is eastward precisely when
\[
\boxed{k^2>\ell^2+L_D^{-2}}.
\]
The dispersion depends separately on the signed zonal component k and on the
total denominator, so its gradient is generally not radial; anisotropy makes
group velocity nonparallel to the wavevector.

At very large wavenumber, \(|\omega|\sim\beta|k|/(k^2+\ell^2)\) and the
frequency tends toward zero along fixed directions. As k and ell both tend
to zero with finite \(L_D\), \(\omega\sim-\beta L_D^2k\), so the zonal
phase and group speeds both approach \(-\beta L_D^2\); retaining the
deformation term changes the long-wave limit.

For the given wavelengths,
\[
k=1.57080\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}},\qquad
\ell=1.04720\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}},
\]
and
\[
D=4.56402\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\omega=-6.88338\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{P=\frac{2\pi}{|\omega|}=10.5649\,\mathrm{days}}.
\]
The zonal phase speed is
\[
\boxed{c_{px}=-4.38210\,\mathrm{m/s}},
\]
while the group components are
\[
\boxed{c_{gx}=+0.355999\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{c_{gy}=+3.15873\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Thus crests propagate west, while this packet's group velocity points east
and north. This is a statement about the linear narrowband envelope, not a
claim that every disturbance or information front moves at that vector.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(D=k^2+\ell^2+L_D^{-2}\), \(\omega=-\beta k/D\). Hence \(c_{gx}=\beta(k^2-\ell^2-L_D^{-2})/D^2\) and \(c_{gy}=2\beta k\ell/D^2\), so positive k has westward phase but eastward zonal group motion when \(k^2>\ell^2+L_D^{-2}\).
I make omega positive for positive beta and k, then differentiate only with respect to the wavevector magnitude and force the group velocity to be parallel to the wavevector.

WAVE:010522.title: A whistler packet has a fastest group but a saturating frequency
WAVE:010522.objective: Analyze a bounded whistler-type dispersion law, derive its phase and group speeds and curvature turnover, and interpret the asymptotic limits without extending group speed into a front-speed claim.
WAVE:010522.statement:
A reduced model for a parallel whistler branch is
\[
\omega(k)=\Omega\frac{k^2d^2}{1+k^2d^2},
\qquad k>0,
\]
where \(\Omega>0\) is a characteristic angular frequency and \(d>0\) is
an inertial length. Treat this dispersion law as given; conclusions apply only
inside the reduced model's physical regime.

Derive phase and group velocities and their ratio. Determine where they are
equal. Find the wavenumber at which group velocity is maximal and calculate
that maximum exactly. Compute the second derivative of omega, showing that the
same dimensionless wavenumber marks zero group-velocity dispersion. Analyze
both \(kd\ll1\) and \(kd\gg1\), explaining how frequency saturation and
vanishing group velocity coexist at large k.

For \(\Omega=2\pi(1000)\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(d=20.0\,\mathrm m\), and
\(k=0.0400\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), compute \(kd\), frequency in hertz, phase
speed, group speed, and the sign and value of the curvature. Also compute the
wavenumber and speed at the group-velocity maximum. Explain why none of these
group velocities alone establishes a signal-front speed outside the stated
model.
permittedResults: For a narrow one-dimensional packet, \(v_g=d\omega/dk\) and quadratic spreading is controlled locally by \(d^2\omega/dk^2\).
A stationary point of group velocity occurs where the dispersion curvature vanishes, though endpoints and validity bounds still require inspection.

acceptableStrategies.description: Nondimensionalize with q equals k d, differentiate analytically, and optimize the resulting rational group-speed function.
Use quotient-rule derivatives directly in k, provided the crossing, maximum, curvature, asymptotic limits, numerical values, and validity caveat all agree.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and optimizes the bounded dispersion's phase and group velocities, connects the curvature turnover to the maximum, and evaluates the numerical branch without overclaiming front speed.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assumes group velocity is maximal where phase and group velocities are equal at k d equals one.
commonErrors.consequence: The maximizing wavenumber and maximum speed are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Declares the reduced-branch group velocity to be a universal causal signal-front speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The interpretation exceeds both the narrow-packet calculation and the model's validity.

hintTree.content: Introduce \(q=kd\) before differentiating or optimizing.
Up to the constant \(2\Omega d\), group speed is \(q/(1+q^2)^2\).
Differentiate once more to obtain a numerator proportional to \(1-3q^2\).

WAVE:010522.canonicalSolution:
Let \(q=kd\). The phase and group velocities are
\[
\boxed{v_p=\frac\omega k=\Omega d\frac{q}{1+q^2}},
\]
\[
\boxed{v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}
=2\Omega d\frac{q}{(1+q^2)^2}}.
\]
Their ratio is
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_g}{v_p}=\frac{2}{1+q^2}},
\]
so they are equal at \(q=1\). Optimizing \(q/(1+q^2)^2\) gives
\(1-3q^2=0\), hence
\[
\boxed{k_{g,\max}=\frac1{\sqrt3d}},\qquad
\boxed{v_{g,\max}=\frac{9}{8\sqrt3}\Omega d}.
\]
The curvature is
\[
\boxed{\frac{d^2\omega}{dk^2}=
2\Omega d^2\frac{1-3q^2}{(1+q^2)^3}},
\]
so it changes sign at the group-speed maximum.

For \(q\ll1\), \(\omega\sim\Omega d^2k^2\),
\(v_g\sim2v_p\), and the curvature is positive. For \(q\gg1\),
\(\omega\to\Omega\), while \(v_p\sim\Omega/k\) and
\(v_g\sim2\Omega/(d^2k^3)\) both vanish. A nearly horizontal dispersion
curve therefore has a finite frequency but little change of frequency with
wavenumber.

For the data, \(q=kd=\boxed{0.8000}\) and
\[
f=\frac\omega{2\pi}=1000\frac{0.64}{1.64}
=\boxed{390.244\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
The two speeds are
\[
\boxed{v_p=6.12994\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{v_g=7.47553\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The curvature is already negative:
\[
\boxed{\omega''=-1.04840\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^2/s}}.
\]
The maximum occurs at
\[
\boxed{k_{g,\max}=0.0288675\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\]
with
\[
\boxed{v_{g,\max}=8.16210\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Group velocity describes the center of a sufficiently narrow packet within
this branch. A causal front depends on the complete high-frequency medium and
model validity, so it cannot be inferred from this reduced formula alone.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(q=kd\), \(v_p=\Omega d q/(1+q^2)\), \(v_g=2\Omega d q/(1+q^2)^2\), and \(\omega''=2\Omega d^2(1-3q^2)/(1+q^2)^3\). Thus the group maximum is at \(q=1/\sqrt3\), while phase and group speeds cross at q equals one.
I put the group-speed maximum at k d equals one because that is where phase and group speeds are equal. I then identify that group speed with the universal causal front speed.

WAVE:010523.title: Internal-wave phase crests and energy rays travel at right angles
WAVE:010523.objective: Derive the anisotropic dispersion, polarization, phase velocity, group velocity, and energy-flux direction of a two-dimensional Boussinesq internal gravity wave.
WAVE:010523.statement:
A uniformly stratified, inviscid Boussinesq fluid in the x-z plane obeys
\[
u_t=-p_x/\rho_0,\qquad
w_t=-p_z/\rho_0+b,
\]
\[
b_t+N^2w=0,\qquad u_x+w_z=0,
\]
where b is upward buoyancy acceleration and \(N>0\) is constant. Consider a
plane wave proportional to \(e^{i(kx+mz-\omega t)}\), with \(k>0\), and
take the positive-frequency branch.

Eliminate the amplitudes to derive the internal-gravity-wave dispersion.
Find the velocity, pressure, and buoyancy polarization ratios relative to a
chosen vertical-velocity amplitude W. Derive the phase-velocity vector and
the two components of group velocity. Prove that the group-velocity vector is
orthogonal to the wave vector, and interpret this geometry: phase propagates
normal to the crests while a localized energy packet travels along a crest.

Using the quadratic perturbation-energy balance, or direct time averaging,
show that the mean pressure-work flux
\(\langle p(u,w)\rangle\) is parallel to group velocity. Keep the signs of
m, vertical flux, and vertical group velocity consistent. Explain why the
limit \(m\to0\) has nonzero frequency but zero group velocity, and state the
Boussinesq, inviscid, and linear-amplitude restrictions behind the model.

Take \(N=0.0200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), horizontal wavelength
\(\lambda_x=1000\,\mathrm m\), vertical wavelength
\(\lambda_z=500\,\mathrm m\), \(m>0\), \(\rho_0=1025\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\),
and real \(W=0.0100\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Compute the frequency and period,
phase-velocity and group-velocity vectors, U, the complex buoyancy amplitude,
the pressure amplitude, and both components of the mean pressure-work flux.
permittedResults: For a dispersion \(\omega(\mathbf k)\), a narrow packet travels with \(\mathbf c_g=\nabla_{\mathbf k}\omega\).
For real harmonic amplitudes U, W, and P under the stated convention, \(\langle p\mathbf u\rangle=\tfrac12P(U,W)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate pressure and buoyancy from the plane-wave amplitude equations, then differentiate the resulting two-dimensional dispersion.
Use incompressibility for polarization and compare time-averaged pressure-work flux directly with the group-velocity vector.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives internal-wave dispersion and polarization, proves phase-group orthogonality, and verifies that pressure-work energy flux follows the group ray.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the scalar derivative with respect to k as the whole group velocity and makes the energy ray normal to the crests.
commonErrors.consequence: The vertical group component and the defining phase-group orthogonality are lost.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor of i in the buoyancy equation and makes B real when W is real.
commonErrors.consequence: The polarization phase, vertical momentum balance, and energy accounting become inconsistent.

hintTree.content: Incompressibility gives \(kU+mW=0\), and the buoyancy equation makes B one quarter-cycle out of phase with W.
For k positive, differentiate \(\omega=Nk/(k^2+m^2)^{1/2}\) with respect to k and m separately.
Compare the component ratio of pressure-work flux with the component ratio of group velocity before evaluating numbers.

WAVE:010523.canonicalSolution:
Let U, W, P, and B be the complex amplitudes. The four
plane-wave equations are
\[
-i\omega U=-ikP/\rho_0,\quad
-i\omega W=-imP/\rho_0+B,
\]
\[
-i\omega B+N^2W=0,\quad kU+mW=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{U=-\frac mkW},\qquad
\boxed{B=-i\frac{N^2}{\omega}W},\qquad
\boxed{P=-\rho_0\frac{\omega m}{k^2}W}.
\]
Substitution in vertical momentum yields
\[
\boxed{\omega^2=N^2\frac{k^2}{k^2+m^2}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega=\frac{Nk}{K}},\quad K=\sqrt{k^2+m^2},
\]
for k positive. Frequency is below N unless m=0.

The phase-velocity vector is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf c_p=\frac{\omega}{K^2}(k,m)}.
\]
Differentiating the positive branch gives
\[
\boxed{\mathbf c_g=
\left(\frac{Nm^2}{K^3},-\frac{Nkm}{K^3}\right)}.
\]
Consequently
\[
(k,m)\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf c_g=0.
\]
The group velocity, and hence a narrow energy packet, lies along a constant
phase line; the phase velocity is normal to that line. Reversing the sign of
m reverses both vertical phase and group directions while preserving this
orthogonality.

For real W, U and P are real under this convention. The mean pressure-work
flux is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf F=\langle p(u,w)\rangle
=\frac12P(U,W)}.
\]
Its component ratio is
\[
\frac{F_z}{F_x}=\frac WU=-\frac{k}{m}
=\frac{c_{gz}}{c_{gx}},
\]
so it is parallel, not antiparallel, to \(\mathbf c_g\); for m positive,
both \(P\) and U are negative relative to positive W, making \(F_x>0\)
and \(F_z<0\). At m=0, \(\omega=N\) is independent of wave vector to
first order and group velocity is zero: a uniform vertical structure does
not define a propagating internal-wave energy ray in this model.

Numerically,
\[
k=6.28319\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\quad
m=1.25664\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\quad K=\sqrt5\,k.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\omega=N/\sqrt5=8.94427\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad \boxed{\mathcal P=2\pi/\omega=702.481\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The velocity vectors are
\[
\boxed{\mathbf c_p=(0.284705,\ 0.569410)\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbf c_g=(1.13882,\ -0.569410)\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
For \(W=0.0100\,\mathrm{m/s}\),
\[
\boxed{U=-0.0200\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\quad \boxed{B=-i(4.47214\times10^{-4})\ \mathrm{m/s^2}},
\quad \boxed{P=-29.1823\ \mathrm{Pa}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\mathbf F=(0.291823,\ -0.145911)\ \mathrm{W/m^2}},
\]
again parallel to the group vector. The Boussinesq description requires
density variations to be small except in buoyancy, wavelengths long compared
with molecular scales, and amplitudes small enough to neglect advection and
overturning; uniform N and no rotation or viscosity are additional idealizations.

graderFixtures.proofText: Elimination gives \(\omega^2=N^2k^2/(k^2+m^2)\), \(U=-mW/k\), \(B=-iN^2W/\omega\), and \(P=-\rho_0\omega mW/k^2\). The group vector \((Nm^2,-Nkm)/(k^2+m^2)^{3/2}\) is orthogonal to (k,m) and parallel to mean pressure-work flux. Numerically omega is 0.00894427 per second and cg is (1.13882,-0.569410) m/s.
I differentiate only with respect to horizontal k and point the energy ray normal to the crests. I also take buoyancy in phase with vertical velocity, omitting its factor of minus i.

WAVE:010524.title: A point impulse unfolds into an Airy dispersive wake
WAVE:010524.objective: Derive the Airy Green function of a third-order dispersive evolution, its similarity scaling and conservation laws, and the stationary-phase rays of its oscillatory wake.
WAVE:010524.statement:
On the whole real line, a scalar field satisfies
\[
u_t-\beta u_{xxx}=0,\qquad \beta>0.
\]
Use the Fourier convention
\(u(x,t)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int\widehat u(k,t)e^{ikx}\,dk\).

Derive the plane-wave dispersion, phase velocity, and group velocity. Starting
from the impulsive initial condition \(u(x,0)=\delta(x)\), evaluate the
Fourier integral exactly in terms of the Airy function, using
\[
\operatorname{Ai}(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
e^{i(q^3/3+zq)}\,dq
\]
in its oscillatory sense. Verify the distributional initial condition and unit
integral. Identify the amplitude and width similarity exponents. For smooth,
rapidly decaying initial data, prove conservation of \(\int u\,dx\) and
\(\int u^2\,dx\), and explain why the delta Green function itself is not an
L2 initial datum.

Apply stationary phase to the Green integral. Determine where real stationary
wave numbers exist, relate their ray x/t to group velocity, and explain the
oscillatory wake on one side and exponential Airy tail on the other. Reconcile
the nonnegative group velocity of every real Fourier component with the
nonzero tail at negative x; this third-order asymptotic model has no finite
front speed.

For \(\beta=2.00\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\) and \(t=4.00\,\mathrm s\), compute the
similarity length and \(G(0,t)\), using
\(\operatorname{Ai}(0)=0.3550280539\). On the ray x=6.00 m, compute both
stationary wave numbers, their angular frequencies, phase velocities, and
group velocities, and verify x/t equals the group speed.
permittedResults: The delta distribution has Fourier transform 1 under the stated convention.
Integration by parts on the whole line produces no boundary terms for smooth rapidly decaying data.

acceptableStrategies.description: Fourier-transform the third-order PDE, rescale its cubic phase into the defining Airy integral, and verify normalization in transform space.
Use similarity balance plus stationary phase, then audit conservation separately for smooth rapidly decaying solutions.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the Airy impulse response with correct sign and scaling, proves its regular-data invariants, and connects stationary wave numbers to dispersive rays.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the Airy argument plus x over a for the stated PDE and Fourier convention.
commonErrors.consequence: The oscillatory and exponentially small sides are interchanged, contradicting the stationary-phase condition.

commonErrors.description: Applies the finite L2 conservation value directly to the delta initial condition.
commonErrors.consequence: A distribution with infinite initial L2 norm is assigned a nonexistent finite conserved energy.

hintTree.content: In the Green integral set \(q=-(3\beta t)^{1/3}k\) and compare term by term with the defining Airy integral.
Differentiate the phase \(kx-\beta tk^3\); real stationary points require \(x/(3\beta t)\ge0\).
Separate conservation for regular data from normalization of the distributional Green function.

WAVE:010524.canonicalSolution:
For \(u=e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\), the PDE gives
\[
\boxed{\omega(k)=\beta k^3},\qquad
\boxed{v_p=\beta k^2},\qquad
\boxed{v_g=3\beta k^2\ge0}.
\]
The transformed impulse evolves as
\(\widehat G(k,t)=e^{-i\beta k^3t}\), hence
\[
G(x,t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
e^{i(kx-\beta tk^3)}\,dk.
\]
Let \(a=(3\beta t)^{1/3}\) and q=-ak. Reversing the transformed limits
gives
\[
\boxed{G(x,t)=\frac1a\operatorname{Ai}\left(-\frac xa\right)}.
\]
As t tends to zero from above its Fourier transform tends pointwise to 1,
so G tends to delta in the tempered-distribution sense. Equivalently, for a
Schwartz test function, convolution with G tends to that function. Also
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}G(x,t)\,dx=\widehat G(0,t)=1.
\]
The solution has amplitude scale \(t^{-1/3}\) and width scale \(t^{1/3}\),
so their product preserves the unit integral.

For smooth decaying u, the PDE is \(u_t=\beta u_{xxx}\), and
\[
\frac d{dt}\int u\,dx=\beta\int u_{xxx}\,dx=0.
\]
Likewise,
\[
\frac12\frac d{dt}\int u^2dx
=\beta\int uu_{xxx}dx
=-\frac\beta2\int\frac d{dx}(u_x^2)dx=0.
\]
The impulse has infinite L2 norm at t=0, so this second identity applies to
regular initial data, not as a finite-energy claim about delta itself.

The Fourier phase \(\Phi(k)=kx-\beta tk^3\) obeys
\[
\Phi'(k)=x-3\beta tk^2.
\]
For x positive there are two real stationary wave numbers
\[
\boxed{k_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\frac{x}{3\beta t}}},
\]
and their ray condition is exactly
\[
\frac xt=3\beta k_\pm^2=v_g(k_\pm).
\]
This produces the oscillatory Airy wake because \(\operatorname{Ai}(-x/a)\)
has negative argument. For x negative there is no real stationary point and
the positive-argument Airy tail is exponentially small. It is nevertheless
nonzero: the third-order evolution is dispersive rather than a finite-speed
hyperbolic propagation law. Nonnegative real-k group velocities describe
stationary packet rays, not compact causal support of its Green function.

For the numbers,
\[
\boxed{a=(3(2.00)(4.00))^{1/3}=2.88450\ \mathrm m},
\]
\[
\boxed{G(0,4)=\frac{0.3550280539}{2.884499}=0.123081\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
On x=6.00 m,
\[
\boxed{k_\pm=\pm0.500000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\omega_+=+0.250000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_-=-0.250000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
while both phase velocities are
\(\boxed{v_p=0.500000\ \mathrm{m/s}}\) and both group velocities are
\(\boxed{v_g=1.50000\ \mathrm{m/s}}\). Finally
\(x/t=6/4=1.50000\,\mathrm{m/s}\), confirming the ray condition. The
coefficient beta has dimensions length cubed per time, making both sides of
the PDE dimensions of u per time.

graderFixtures.proofText: The dispersion is \(\omega=\beta k^3\). With \(a=(3\beta t)^{1/3}\), the impulse response is \(a^{-1}\operatorname{Ai}(-x/a)\), with unit integral, t to the minus one third amplitude, and t to the one third width. Real stationary points occur for positive x at \(k=\pm\sqrt{x/(3\beta t)}\). For the data a is 2.88450 m and the x=6 m ray uses k plus or minus 0.5 per m and group speed 1.5 m/s.
I flip the Airy argument so the oscillatory wake lies where stationary phase has no real roots. I also assign the delta impulse a finite conserved L2 norm.

WAVE:010525.title: Rotation turns shallow-water waves into Poincare waves
WAVE:010525.objective: Derive inertia-gravity dispersion and polarization from the rotating shallow-water system and quantify phase-group separation near the deformation scale.
WAVE:010525.statement:
On an f-plane, linear shallow-water perturbations about depth H satisfy
\[
u_t-fv=-g\eta_x,\qquad
v_t+fu=-g\eta_y,\qquad
\eta_t+H(u_x+v_y)=0.
\]
Take plane waves proportional to
\(e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\), with
\(K=|\mathbf k|>0\) and \(f>0\).

Compute the determinant of the three-field system and identify both the
zero-frequency geostrophic branch and the two propagating Poincare branches.
For positive frequency, derive phase and group speeds, show that their product
is \(gH\), and prove group velocity is parallel to the wave vector. Choose the
x axis along k and derive the velocity polarization, including the quadrature
and magnitude ratio of transverse to longitudinal motion. Define the Rossby
deformation radius and interpret the limits \(KR_d\gg1\) and \(KR_d\ll1\).
Do not describe the zero branch using formulas that divided by omega.

For \(H=4000\,\mathrm m\), \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\),
\(f=1.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and wavelength
\(\lambda=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m\), compute c, K, omega, period in
hours, phase speed, group speed, \(R_d\), \(KR_d\), and the transverse-to-
longitudinal velocity amplitude ratio. Check the nonrotating and long-wave
limits.
permittedResults: For isotropic \(\omega(K)\), \(\mathbf c_g=(d\omega/dK)\hat{\mathbf k}\).
The determinant factorizes as \(\omega[\omega^2-f^2-gHK^2]\) for the linear f-plane system.

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the plane-wave determinant, then differentiate the isotropic positive branch.
Eliminate velocity to a scalar height equation and recover polarization afterward from momentum and continuity.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives all rotating shallow-water branches and quantitatively connects dispersion, velocity polarization, and deformation scale.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Divides the determinant by omega and reports only the two propagating branches.
commonErrors.consequence: The balanced zero-frequency mode is incorrectly removed from the system.

commonErrors.description: Sets phase and group speeds both equal to square root gH at finite rotation.
commonErrors.consequence: The deformation-scale dispersion and numerical energy propagation speed are lost.

hintTree.content: Rotate coordinates so \(\mathbf k=(K,0)\) only after deriving the invariant dispersion relation.
For the propagating branch, continuity gives \(u=\omega\eta/(HK)\), and the transverse momentum equation fixes v in quadrature.
Write \(\omega=f\sqrt{1+(KR_d)^2}\) to expose both asymptotic regimes.

WAVE:010525.canonicalSolution:
Substitution of the plane wave turns the system into a homogeneous
three-by-three algebraic problem. Its determinant is
\[
\boxed{\omega\left(\omega^2-f^2-gHK^2\right)=0}.
\]
The root \(\omega=0\) is the steady geostrophic branch, for which pressure
gradient balances Coriolis acceleration and the velocity is nondivergent.
The propagating roots are
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pm=\pm\sqrt{f^2+c^2K^2}},\qquad c=\sqrt{gH}.
\]
For the positive branch,
\[
\boxed{v_p=\frac{\omega}{K}},\qquad
\boxed{v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dK}=\frac{c^2K}{\omega}},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{v_pv_g=c^2=gH}.
\]
Because the dispersion depends only on K, the group-velocity vector is
parallel to k.

Choose \(\mathbf k=(K,0)\). Continuity and transverse momentum give
\[
u=\frac{\omega}{HK}\eta,\qquad
v=-i\frac f\omega u.
\]
Thus transverse velocity is one quarter-cycle out of phase and
\[
\boxed{\frac{|v|}{|u|}=\frac f\omega}.
\]
The deformation radius \(R_d=c/f\) gives
\[
\omega=f\sqrt{1+(KR_d)^2}.
\]
For \(KR_d\gg1\), rotation is weak and \(\omega\simeq cK\). For
\(KR_d\ll1\), frequency approaches f, phase speed grows like \(f/K\), and
group speed tends to zero. These divided-by-omega polarization formulas do
not define the separate geostrophic root.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{c=198.091\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{K=6.28319\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\omega=1.59660\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
The period is
\[
\boxed{\mathcal P=10.9315\ \mathrm h}.
\]
The speeds are
\[
\boxed{v_p=254.107\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{v_g=154.423\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
whose product is \(39240.0\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}=gH\). Also
\[
\boxed{R_d=1.98091\times10^6\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{KR_d=1.24464},
\]
\[
\boxed{|v|/|u|=0.626331}.
\]
As f tends to zero, transverse motion vanishes and both speeds approach c.
At very long wavelength the propagating frequency tends to f rather than
zero.

graderFixtures.proofText: The determinant is \(\omega(\omega^2-f^2-gHK^2)\). For positive omega, \(v_p=\omega/K\), \(v_g=c^2K/\omega\), and their product is c squared. With k along x, \(v=-ifu/\omega\). The data give period 10.9315 h, phase speed 254.107 m/s, group speed 154.423 m/s, and polarization ratio 0.626331.
I divide by omega and lose the balanced branch, then set both phase and group speed equal to square root gH even though rotation is finite.

WAVE:010526.title: A slow elastic layer traps dispersive Love waves
WAVE:010526.objective: Derive the Love-wave dispersion equation from stress matching, identify its allowed phase-speed interval and higher-mode cutoffs, and solve one mode numerically.
WAVE:010526.statement:
An elastic layer occupies \(0\le z\le h\), over a half-space \(z\ge h\).
Horizontally polarized shear displacement is
\(u_y(x,z,t)=U(z)e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\). The layer has density
\(\rho_1\), shear speed \(\beta_1\), and modulus
\(\mu_1=\rho_1\beta_1^2\); the half-space has
\(\rho_2,\beta_2,\mu_2\), with \(\beta_2>\beta_1\). The surface z=0 is
stress free, displacement and shear stress are continuous at z=h, and the
mode must decay as \(z\to\infty\).

Derive the vertical equations and show that a trapped mode requires phase
speed \(c_p=\omega/k\) strictly between the two shear speeds. Define the real
layer wave number q and half-space decay constant p. Apply all boundary
conditions with a consistent z direction to obtain the Love-wave dispersion
equation. Explain the branch intervals of tangent and derive the cutoff
frequencies of higher modes from the limit \(c_p\to\beta_2\). Show why the
fundamental has no nonzero cutoff.

For \(\rho_1=2500\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\beta_1=2000\,\mathrm{m/s}\),
\(\rho_2=3000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\beta_2=3500\,\mathrm{m/s}\),
\(h=1000\,\mathrm m\), and \(f=0.500\,\mathrm{Hz}\), solve the fundamental
dispersion root for phase speed. Compute k, q, p, wavelength, penetration
depth, \(qh\), and interface-to-surface displacement ratio. Compute the first
higher-mode cutoff and state how many modes exist at the chosen frequency.
permittedResults: In each uniform medium, \(U''+(\omega^2/\beta^2-k^2)U=0\).
At a free SH surface, shear stress \(\mu\,dU/dz\) vanishes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Match oscillatory layer and evanescent substrate solutions through displacement and shear stress.
Form the SH transfer matrix across the layer and impose free-surface and radiation conditions.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Builds the trapped layered mode from all boundary conditions and connects its tangent branches to cutoffs and a verified numerical root.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Matches displacement derivatives directly instead of shear stresses weighted by the two moduli.
commonErrors.consequence: The dispersion equation and numerical phase speed are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Chooses phase speed above beta2 and uses an oscillatory half-space field for a trapped mode.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy radiates into the substrate, so the claimed Love mode is not guided.

hintTree.content: Use \(U_1=A\cos qz\) in the layer and \(U_2=C e^{-p(z-h)}\) in the half-space.
Continuity at h gives C=A cos(qh); stress continuity then produces a tangent after division by cosine.
At higher-mode cutoff p tends to zero, so tan(qh) tends to zero with \(qh=n\pi\).

WAVE:010526.canonicalSolution:
The SH equation in either medium is
\[
U''+\left(\frac{\omega^2}{\beta^2}-k^2\right)U=0.
\]
A trapped oscillatory layer and evanescent substrate require
\[
\beta_1<c_p=\frac\omega k<\beta_2.
\]
Define
\[
\boxed{q=\sqrt{\frac{\omega^2}{\beta_1^2}-k^2}},\qquad
\boxed{p=\sqrt{k^2-\frac{\omega^2}{\beta_2^2}}}.
\]
The free surface selects
\[
U_1=A\cos(qz),
\]
and decay selects
\[
U_2=C e^{-p(z-h)}.
\]
At z=h, displacement continuity gives \(C=A\cos(qh)\). Stress continuity,
\(\mu_1U_1'=\mu_2U_2'\), then gives
\[
-\mu_1Aq\sin(qh)=-\mu_2Cp.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\mu_1q\tan(qh)=\mu_2p}.
\]
Because \(\mu_1q>0\) and \(\mu_2p>0\), a physical root must have positive
tangent. The branch intervals are therefore exactly
\[
\boxed{n\pi<qh<n\pi+\frac\pi2},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
The interval \(0<qh<\pi/2\) is the fundamental branch; \(n\ge1\) labels the
higher branches. Intervals with negative tangent cannot satisfy the matching
equation and poles of tangent are not eigenvalues.

At cutoff into the half-space, \(c_p\to\beta_2\) and \(p\to0\). Higher
branches approach \(qh=n\pi\), \(n=1,2,\ldots\), so
\[
\boxed{\omega_{c,n}=
\frac{n\pi}{h\sqrt{\beta_1^{-2}-\beta_2^{-2}}}}.
\]
The n=0 fundamental condition has zero cutoff and persists to arbitrarily
low frequency, approaching the substrate speed as frequency vanishes.

For the data, numerical solution on the fundamental branch gives
\[
\boxed{c_p=2858.22\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
With \(\omega=\pi\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
\[
\boxed{k=1.09914\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{q=1.12218\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{p=6.34374\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\lambda=5716.45\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{1/p=1576.36\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{qh=1.12218}.
\]
Because \(C/A=\cos(qh)\),
\[
\boxed{C/A=0.433719}.
\]
The first higher cutoff is
\[
\boxed{f_{c,1}=1.21854\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
Since 0.500 Hz is below it, only the fundamental Love mode exists. The
phase speed lies between 2000 and 3500 m/s as required; selecting a root
outside that interval would make either q or p imaginary in the wrong region.

graderFixtures.proofText: With \(U_1=A\cos qz\) and \(U_2=Ce^{-p(z-h)}\), matching gives \(\mu_1q\tan(qh)=\mu_2p\), with roots on \(n\pi<qh<n\pi+\pi/2\) and n=0 fundamental. The data give c 2858.22 m/s, qh 1.12218, penetration 1576.36 m, and only the fundamental below the 1.21854 Hz first cutoff.
I match unweighted slopes at the interface and choose a phase speed above the faster half-space speed while still calling the substrate field evanescent.

WAVE:010527.title: An elastic cover selects a minimum wave speed
WAVE:010527.objective: Analyze the deep-water flexural-gravity dispersion relation, locate its phase-speed minimum, and compare phase and group velocities across the gravity and flexural regimes.
WAVE:010527.statement:
An inviscid incompressible liquid of density \(\rho\) occupies deep water
and is covered by a thin massless elastic plate of flexural rigidity \(D\).
For a plane wave proportional to \(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\), with \(k>0\),
linear theory gives
\[
\omega^2=gk+\frac{D}{\rho}k^5.
\]

Derive the phase velocity \(c_p\) and group velocity \(c_g\). Find the
unique positive wavenumber \(k_*\) at which \(c_p\) is minimized, and prove
that \(c_g=c_p\) there. Express \(k_*\), the minimum phase speed, and the
corresponding angular frequency in terms of \(D,\rho,g\). Give the
gravity-dominated and flexural-dominated power laws for \(\omega,c_p,c_g\),
including the limiting ratios \(c_g/c_p\).

Define \(k_c\) as the wavenumber at which the gravity and flexural terms in
\(\omega^2\) are equal. Compare \(k_c\) with \(k_*\), and compute
\(c_p,c_g\) and their ratio at \(k_c\).

For \(D=5.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{N\,m}\),
\(\rho=1025\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), compute
\(k_*\), \(\omega_*\), \(f_*\), and the common speed at the minimum.
Also compute \(k_c,\omega_c,f_c,c_p(k_c)\), and \(c_g(k_c)\). Audit the
dimensions of \(D/\rho\) and state the assumptions under which the supplied
dispersion relation is applicable.
permittedResults: At an interior extremum of \(c_p=\omega/k\), \(dc_p/dk=0\) implies \(d\omega/dk=\omega/k\), hence \(c_g=c_p\).
If \(\omega\propto k^n\), then \(c_g=n c_p\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the squared phase speed, then use the extremum condition to simplify all requested values.
Nondimensionalize wavenumber by the gravity-flexural crossover and inspect the low- and high-wavenumber limits.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Finds and interprets the flexural-gravity phase-speed minimum while keeping it distinct from the restoring-force crossover.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets the gravity and flexural terms equal and identifies that point as the phase-speed minimum.
commonErrors.consequence: The required factor of three in the extremum condition and all minimum values are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Treats the bending-dominated omega proportional to k to the five-halves law as nondispersive or assigns group speed equal to phase speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The flexural asymptotic transport behavior is misidentified.

hintTree.content: Minimize \(c_p^2=g/k+(D/\rho)k^3\) rather than differentiating a square root.
At the minimum, the flexural contribution to \(c_p^2\) is one third of the gravity contribution.
At \(k_c\), use \((D/\rho)k_c^4=g\) before evaluating the group velocity.

WAVE:010527.canonicalSolution:
Write \(\beta=D/\rho\). Then
\[
\boxed{c_p=\frac\omega k=\sqrt{\frac gk+\beta k^3}},
\qquad
\boxed{c_g=\frac{g+5\beta k^4}{2\sqrt{gk+\beta k^5}}}.
\]
Because
\[
\frac d{dk}c_p^2=-\frac g{k^2}+3\beta k^2,
\]
the unique positive stationary point satisfies
\[
\boxed{k_*^4=\frac{g}{3\beta}=\frac{\rho g}{3D}},
\qquad
\boxed{k_*=\left(\frac{\rho g}{3D}\right)^{1/4}}.
\]
The derivative is negative below this point and positive above it, so the
point is the global minimum. At any interior phase-speed extremum,
\(d(\omega/k)/dk=0\) gives \(c_g=c_p\). Using
\(\beta k_*^4=g/3\),
\[
\boxed{c_{p,\min}=c_g(k_*)=
\sqrt{\frac{4g}{3k_*}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\omega_*=k_*c_{p,\min}=\sqrt{\frac{4gk_*}{3}}}.
\]

For \(k\ll k_c\), gravity dominates:
\[
\omega\sim\sqrt{gk},\qquad c_p\sim\sqrt{g/k},\qquad
c_g\sim\frac12c_p.
\]
For \(k\gg k_c\), bending dominates:
\[
\omega\sim\sqrt\beta\,k^{5/2},\qquad
c_p\sim\sqrt\beta\,k^{3/2},\qquad c_g\sim\frac52c_p.
\]
Equality of the two terms in \(\omega^2\) gives
\[
\boxed{k_c=(g/\beta)^{1/4}=3^{1/4}k_*}.
\]
At \(k_c\), \(\omega_c^2=2gk_c\) and
\[
\boxed{c_p(k_c)=\sqrt{\frac{2g}{k_c}}},
\qquad
\boxed{c_g(k_c)=\frac32c_p(k_c)}.
\]

For the numerical data,
\[
\boxed{k_*=0.0508833\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\quad
\boxed{\omega_*=0.815815\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\quad
\boxed{f_*=0.129841\ \mathrm{Hz}},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_{p,\min}=c_g(k_*)=16.0331\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The equal-term crossover values are
\[
\boxed{k_c=0.0669662\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\quad
\boxed{\omega_c=1.14624\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\quad
\boxed{f_c=0.182431\ \mathrm{Hz}},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_p(k_c)=17.1168\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{c_g(k_c)=25.6751\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Since \([D]=\mathrm{N\,m}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^2}\),
\([D/\rho]=\mathrm{m^5/s^2}\), so both terms in \(\omega^2\) have units
\(\mathrm{s^{-2}}\). The model assumes linear small-amplitude motion,
deep water, an inviscid incompressible fluid, a thin massless plate, and no
surface tension or plate inertia.

graderFixtures.proofText: Minimizing \(c_p^2=g/k+(D/\rho)k^3\) gives \(k_*^4=\rho g/(3D)\). There \(c_g=c_p=\sqrt{4g/(3k_*)}\). Equal restoring terms instead occur at \(k_c=3^{1/4}k_*\), where \(c_g/c_p=3/2\).
I call the equal-restoring-term wavenumber the speed minimum, omit the factor of three, and claim the high-wavenumber flexural waves are nondispersive.

WAVE:010528.title: A Rayleigh wave is trapped near an elastic surface
WAVE:010528.objective: Reduce the Rayleigh surface-wave condition to its physical speed root and calculate the distinct compressional and shear evanescence depths.
WAVE:010528.statement:
An isotropic homogeneous elastic half-space has compressional speed \(c_P\)
and shear speed \(c_S<c_P\). A traction-free Rayleigh wave travels along
the surface with angular frequency \(\omega\), wavenumber \(k>0\), and
phase speed \(c_R=\omega/k<c_S\). Define
\[
\xi=\frac{c_R}{c_S},
\qquad
\kappa=\frac{c_S^2}{c_P^2},
\qquad 0<\kappa<1.
\]
The traction-free boundary determinant reduces to
\[
(2-\xi^2)^2=4\sqrt{1-\xi^2}\sqrt{1-\kappa\xi^2}.
\]

Square and simplify this equation to obtain the standard cubic polynomial in
\(\xi^2\), carefully removing the zero factor introduced before division.
Explain why every polynomial root must be checked in the unsquared radical
equation and why a Rayleigh root must lie in \(0<\xi<1\).

For Poisson ratio \(\nu=1/4\), use the isotropic identity
\[
\frac{c_P^2}{c_S^2}=\frac{2(1-\nu)}{1-2\nu}
\]
to determine \(\kappa\), and find the physical Rayleigh root numerically.
For \(c_S=3.00\,\mathrm{km/s}\) and \(f=10.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\), compute
\(c_R\), wavelength, and wavenumber.

The scalar compressional and shear potentials decay with depth \(z>0\) as
\[
e^{-pkz},\qquad e^{-qkz},
\qquad
p=\sqrt{1-\kappa\xi^2},\quad q=\sqrt{1-\xi^2}.
\]
Compute \(p,q\) and the two one-over-e amplitude depths. Identify which
potential penetrates farther. Explain why the mode is nondispersive in this
ideal continuum even though its displacement is depth dependent.
permittedResults: Squaring an equation is not reversible unless candidate roots are substituted into the original equation to reject sign-induced extraneous roots.
In a scale-free homogeneous elastic half-space, the Rayleigh secular equation depends only on speed ratios, not on frequency.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use y equals xi squared to solve the cubic, then filter all numerical candidates with the original radical determinant.
Build the surface wave from decaying compressional and shear potentials and enforce both traction-free conditions.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Obtains the physical Rayleigh speed from the unsquared secular condition and computes both wavelength-scaled evanescence depths.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Accepts a root of the squared polynomial without checking the original radical equation and the subsonic interval.
commonErrors.consequence: An extraneous or nondecaying candidate can be mislabeled as the surface mode.

commonErrors.description: Reports one over p and one over q as dimensional penetration depths without dividing by k.
commonErrors.consequence: The wavelength scaling and units of the evanescence depth are lost.

hintTree.content: After expansion, both sides have the same constant term; factor out \(\xi^2\) before writing the cubic in \(\xi^2\).
For \(\nu=1/4\), the speed ratio satisfies \(c_P^2/c_S^2=3\).
The depth factors multiply k, so the amplitude depths are \(1/(pk)\) and \(1/(qk)\), not simply \(1/p\) and \(1/q\).

WAVE:010528.canonicalSolution:
Squaring the radical equation gives
\[
(2-\xi^2)^4=16(1-\xi^2)(1-\kappa\xi^2).
\]
Expansion and cancellation of the constant terms produces
\[
\xi^2\left[\xi^6-8\xi^4+(24-16\kappa)\xi^2
-16(1-\kappa)\right]=0.
\]
The factor \(\xi^2=0\) is not a propagating Rayleigh wave and was introduced
before dividing to obtain the standard equation
\[
\boxed{\xi^6-8\xi^4+(24-16\kappa)\xi^2-16(1-\kappa)=0}.
\]
Because the radical equation was squared, a polynomial zero is only a
candidate. It must satisfy the unsquared equation with real positive decay
factors. The trapped subsonic mode requires \(0<\xi<1\), which also keeps
both square roots real.

At \(\nu=1/4\),
\[
\frac{c_P^2}{c_S^2}=3,
\qquad
\boxed{\kappa=\frac13}.
\]
Solving the polynomial in \(0<\xi<1\) and checking the radical equation gives
\[
\boxed{\xi=0.919402}.
\]
Thus, for \(c_S=3000\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(f=10.0\,\mathrm{Hz}\),
\[
\boxed{c_R=2758.21\,\mathrm{m/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_R=c_R/f=275.821\,\mathrm m},
\]
\[
\boxed{k=2\pi/\lambda_R=0.0227800\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
The decay factors are
\[
\boxed{p=\sqrt{1-\kappa\xi^2}=0.847487},
\qquad
\boxed{q=\sqrt{1-\xi^2}=0.393320}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{d_P=\frac1{pk}=51.7981\,\mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{d_S=\frac1{qk}=111.609\,\mathrm m}.
\]
The shear potential penetrates farther because \(q<p\). The secular
equation fixes a frequency-independent speed ratio in the ideal homogeneous
half-space, so \(\omega=c_Rk\) is linear and the wave is nondispersive.
The factors \(pk\) and \(qk\) still make the depth profile scale with the
wavelength; depth dependence by itself is not frequency dispersion.

graderFixtures.proofText: After squaring and removing the zero factor, the equation is \(\xi^6-8\xi^4+(24-16\kappa)\xi^2-16(1-\kappa)=0\). For \(\kappa=1/3\), the radical-checked root is 0.919402. The compressional and shear depths are \(1/(pk)\) and \(1/(qk)\), about 51.8 m and 111.6 m at 10 Hz.
I accept every root of the squared polynomial, include xi equals zero as a wave, and call one over p and one over q the penetration depths without the wavenumber.
