WAVE:010529.title: A condensate wave crosses from sound to particles
WAVE:010529.objective: Linearize a dispersive nonlinear matter-wave equation and derive the Bogoliubov spectrum, crossover, phase speed, and group speed.
WAVE:010529.statement:
A one-dimensional weakly interacting condensate is modeled by
\[
i\hbar\psi_t=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi_{xx}
+g|\psi|^2\psi,\qquad g>0.
\]
Its uniform state is
\(\psi_0=\sqrt{n_0}e^{-i\mu t/\hbar}\), with
\(\mu=gn_0\). Perturb it using
\[
\psi=e^{-i\mu t/\hbar}\left[\sqrt{n_0}
+u e^{i(kx-\omega t)}+v^*e^{-i(kx-\omega t)}\right].
\]
Linearize in \(u,v\), display the two-by-two Bogoliubov system, and derive
the positive-frequency dispersion. Define
\[
c_s=\sqrt{\frac{gn_0}{m}},\qquad
\xi=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt2\,mc_s}.
\]
Rewrite the dispersion in terms of \(c_s,\xi\). Derive phase and group
velocities, identify where the acoustic and quartic contributions to
\(\omega^2\) are equal, and obtain both long- and short-wavelength limits.
Explain why the group speed approaches twice the phase speed in the
particle-like limit without violating relativity in this nonrelativistic
model.

For \(c_s=2.00\,\mathrm{mm/s}\) and \(\xi=0.300\,\mu\mathrm m\), evaluate
\(\omega\), phase speed, and group speed at \(k\xi=1\). Compute the crossover
wavenumber and wavelength. Audit dimensions and keep angular frequency
distinct from cycles per second.
permittedResults: A nontrivial homogeneous two-by-two system exists when its determinant vanishes.
For a packet on a smooth positive branch, \(c_p=\omega/k\) and \(c_g=d\omega/dk\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Retain both conjugate perturbation amplitudes and solve the resulting Bogoliubov determinant.
Rewrite with the healing length before differentiating and checking asymptotic velocity ratios.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the collective-mode spectrum from the nonlinear background and quantifies its sound-to-particle dispersive crossover.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Linearizes with only the u component and omits coupling to the conjugate v amplitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The collective acoustic branch is not recovered.

commonErrors.description: Assumes group and phase velocities remain equal after the quartic term becomes important.
commonErrors.consequence: The particle-like limit and numerical group speed are wrong.

hintTree.content: Let \(\epsilon_k=\hbar^2k^2/(2m)\); the diagonal linearized energy is \(\epsilon_k+gn_0\) and the pairing magnitude is \(gn_0\).
The determinant simplifies to \((\hbar\omega)^2=\epsilon_k(\epsilon_k+2gn_0)\).
Differentiate \(\omega=c_sk\sqrt{1+(k\xi)^2/2}\) before inserting numbers.

WAVE:010529.canonicalSolution:
Writing \(\epsilon_k=\hbar^2k^2/(2m)\), linearization gives
\[
\hbar\omega\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
\epsilon_k+gn_0&gn_0\\
-gn_0&-(\epsilon_k+gn_0)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The determinant condition is
\[
(\hbar\omega)^2=(\epsilon_k+gn_0)^2-(gn_0)^2
=\epsilon_k(\epsilon_k+2gn_0).
\]
Thus the positive branch is
\[
\boxed{\omega^2=c_s^2k^2+\frac{\hbar^2k^4}{4m^2}
=c_s^2k^2\left[1+\frac{(k\xi)^2}{2}\right]}.
\]
For \(q=k\xi\),
\[
\boxed{c_p=c_s\sqrt{1+\frac{q^2}{2}}},\qquad
\boxed{c_g=c_s\frac{1+q^2}{\sqrt{1+q^2/2}}}.
\]
The two terms in \(\omega^2\) are equal at
\[
\boxed{k_c=\frac{\sqrt2}{\xi}}.
\]
For \(q\ll1\), \(\omega\simeq c_sk\) and both velocities approach sound
speed. For \(q\gg1\), \(\omega\simeq\hbar k^2/(2m)\),
\(c_p\simeq\hbar k/(2m)\), and \(c_g\simeq\hbar k/m=2c_p\). This is the
group velocity of a nonrelativistic effective equation, whose domain does
not include relativistic momenta.

At \(q=1\), \(k=1/\xi=3.33333333\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), so
\[
\boxed{\omega=8.16496581\times10^3\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_p=2.44948974\ \mathrm{mm/s}},\qquad
\boxed{c_g=3.26598632\ \mathrm{mm/s}}.
\]
The crossover values are
\[
\boxed{k_c=4.71404521\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_c=\frac{2\pi}{k_c}=1.33286488\ \mu\mathrm m}.
\]
The product \(c_sk\) has angular-frequency units, while \(k\xi\) is
dimensionless.

graderFixtures.proofText: The determinant gives \(\omega^2=c_s^2k^2[1+(k\xi)^2/2]\), so \(c_p=c_s\sqrt{1+q^2/2}\) and \(c_g=c_s(1+q^2)/\sqrt{1+q^2/2}\). At \(q=1\), the values are 8164.96581 s\(^{-1}\), 2.44948974 mm/s, and 3.26598632 mm/s.
I discard the conjugate perturbation, keep only a free-particle frequency, and set group velocity equal to phase velocity at every k.

WAVE:010530.title: Shear and rotation split a beam into two branches
WAVE:010530.objective: Derive the two Timoshenko-beam dispersion branches and connect their cutoff and asymptotes to Euler-Bernoulli and bulk wave speeds.
WAVE:010530.statement:
A uniform Timoshenko beam has transverse displacement \(w(x,t)\) and
cross-section rotation \(\varphi(x,t)\). Let
\[
S=\kappa GA,
\]
where \(S\) is the shear rigidity, \(EI\) the bending rigidity,
\(\rho A\) the mass per length, and \(\rho I\) the rotary inertia per length.
Use the equations
\[
\rho A\,w_{tt}=S(w_{xx}-\varphi_x),\qquad
\rho I\,\varphi_{tt}=EI\varphi_{xx}+S(w_x-\varphi).
\]
Insert plane waves \(w=W e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\),
\(\varphi=\Phi e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\). Derive the amplitude matrix and the
quadratic equation for \(y=\omega^2\). Give both nonnegative branches in
closed form.

Analyze \(k=0\), showing one zero-frequency translation and one rotational
cutoff. Derive the leading small-\(k\) acoustic branch and show that it
recovers Euler-Bernoulli bending. Find both large-\(k\) limiting phase speeds.
Explain why setting \(\varphi=w_x\) at the beginning destroys a branch and
is only an asymptotic constraint in the appropriate regime.

For \(\rho A=2.00\,\mathrm{kg/m}\),
\(\rho I=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\),
\(EI=8.00\,\mathrm{N\,m^2}\), \(S=200\,\mathrm N\), and
\(k=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), compute both positive angular frequencies,
the zero-wavenumber cutoff, and the Euler-Bernoulli estimate of the lower
frequency at that \(k\). Audit units.
permittedResults: For \(ay^2-by+c=0\), the roots are \([b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}]/(2a)\).
Euler-Bernoulli bending has \(\omega^2=(EI/\rho A)k^4\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Form the coupled plane-wave matrix and solve its determinant as a quadratic in squared frequency.
Check the exact roots against zero-, small-, and large-wavenumber limits before numerical evaluation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Preserves both beam degrees of freedom through the dispersion calculation and verifies their cutoff and asymptotic physical limits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wrong product sign for the imaginary off-diagonal couplings and changes the constant term of the dispersion polynomial.
commonErrors.consequence: The low-frequency branch no longer recovers bending correctly.

commonErrors.description: Sets cross-section rotation equal to centerline slope before solving the two-field system.
commonErrors.consequence: The shear-rotary branch and its cutoff are deleted by assumption.

hintTree.content: After substitution, the off-diagonal entries are \(iSk\) and \(-iSk\); their product has positive sign in the determinant subtraction.
Expand the product of the two diagonal factors before collecting powers of \(y=\omega^2\).
At large k, retain the highest powers and factor the resulting equation into the shear and rotational wave speeds.

WAVE:010530.canonicalSolution:
Plane-wave substitution gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
Sk^2-\rho A\omega^2&iSk\\
-iSk&EI k^2+S-\rho I\omega^2
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}W\\\Phi\end{pmatrix}=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\rho A\rho I\,y^2-By+SEI\,k^4=0},
\]
where
\[
\boxed{B=S\rho I k^2+\rho A(EI k^2+S)}.
\]
The two branches are
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pm^2=\frac{B\pm
\sqrt{B^2-4\rho A\rho I\,SEI\,k^4}}
{2\rho A\rho I}}.
\]

At \(k=0\), \(\omega_-=0\) and
\[
\boxed{\omega_+(0)=\sqrt{S/(\rho I)}}.
\]
Expanding the lower root for small k gives
\[
\boxed{\omega_-^2=\frac{EI}{\rho A}k^4+O(k^6)},
\]
the Euler-Bernoulli bending law. At large k, the two phase speeds approach,
up to ordering,
\[
\boxed{\sqrt{S/(\rho A)}}\quad\text{and}\quad
\boxed{\sqrt{EI/(\rho I)}}.
\]
Enforcing \(\varphi=w_x\) identically removes shear deformation and its
independent inertia, collapsing the two-field model before these limits can
be assessed.

For the data at \(k=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\),
\[
B=480.000,\qquad SEI\,k^4=25600.0
\]
in the consistent determinant units, and
\[
\boxed{\omega_-=7.31932381\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=109.299714\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
The cutoff is
\[
\boxed{\omega_+(0)=100.000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
while Euler-Bernoulli gives
\[
\boxed{\omega_{\rm EB}=\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)}\,k^2
=8.00000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
Here \(\rho I\) has units \(\mathrm{kg\,m}\), so
\(S/(\rho I)\) has units \(\mathrm{s^{-2}}\), and both reported roots are
angular frequencies.

graderFixtures.proofText: The determinant yields \(\rho A\rho I y^2-By+SEI k^4=0\), with \(B=S\rho I k^2+\rho A(EIk^2+S)\). The data give frequencies 7.31932381 and 109.299714 s\(^{-1}\), cutoff 100 s\(^{-1}\), and Euler-Bernoulli estimate 8 s\(^{-1}\).

Before collapsing the fields I give both off-diagonal matrix entries the same plus i S k sign, so their product changes the dispersion constant term. I then set phi equal to w sub x, reduce to one equation, and report only the Euler-Bernoulli branch.

WAVE:010531.title: A Lorentz dielectric splits light into two polariton branches
WAVE:010531.objective: Solve a lossless Lorentz-medium dispersion relation and connect its branch limits to the negative-permittivity reststrahlen interval.
WAVE:010531.statement:
A lossless polar dielectric has relative permittivity
\[
\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon_\infty
\frac{\omega_L^2-\omega^2}{\omega_T^2-\omega^2},
\qquad 0<\omega_T<\omega_L,
\]
and transverse electromagnetic plane waves satisfy
\(c^2k^2=\omega^2\varepsilon(\omega)\). Derive the two positive-frequency
polariton branches explicitly as functions of \(k\) by solving a quadratic
in \(y=\omega^2\). Find their limits at \(k=0\) and large \(k\), and
identify which branch approaches the transverse resonance.

Use the sign of \(\varepsilon\) to identify every propagating and
evanescent frequency interval. Inside the reststrahlen interval, write the
decay constant for a real imposed frequency. Explain why multiplying across
the pole can produce formal algebraic roots that still require a sign and
branch audit before being called propagating waves.

Take \(\varepsilon_\infty=4.00\), \(f_T=5.00\,\mathrm{THz}\), and
\(f_L=6.00\,\mathrm{THz}\). At a wavenumber satisfying
\(ck=\omega_T\), compute both branch frequencies. At
\(f=5.50\,\mathrm{THz}\), compute \(\varepsilon\), the evanescent decay
constant, and the one-over-e penetration depth using
\(c=299792458\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
permittedResults: A real isotropic medium supports a real transverse wavenumber only when \(\omega^2\varepsilon(\omega)\ge0\).
If \(k=i\kappa\) with \(\kappa>0\), a field proportional to \(e^{ikz}\) decays as \(e^{-\kappa z}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the transverse Maxwell dispersion as a quadratic in squared frequency and analyze its root sum and product.
Analyze the dielectric sign first, then use numerical branch roots only in the permitted propagating intervals.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects the algebraic polariton roots back to the original constitutive pole, permittivity sign, and physical propagation condition.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Calls the interval between omega_T and omega_L a real-k propagating bulk band despite negative permittivity.
commonErrors.consequence: An evanescent field is assigned a real phase velocity.

commonErrors.description: Sends the lower branch to omega_L or the upper k-zero branch to omega_T.
commonErrors.consequence: The quadratic roots no longer satisfy their zero-wavenumber product and sum.

hintTree.content: Multiply by \(\omega_T^2-y\) and collect a quadratic with leading coefficient \(\varepsilon_\infty\).
At large k, balance one root near \(\omega_T\) and use the sum of roots for the other.
Inside the negative-permittivity interval, set \(k=i(\omega/c)\sqrt{-\varepsilon}\).

WAVE:010531.canonicalSolution:
Writing \(y=\omega^2\), the dispersion relation becomes
\[
\varepsilon_\infty y^2-
(\varepsilon_\infty\omega_L^2+c^2k^2)y
+c^2k^2\omega_T^2=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pm^2(k)=\frac{\varepsilon_\infty\omega_L^2+c^2k^2
\pm\sqrt{(\varepsilon_\infty\omega_L^2+c^2k^2)^2
-4\varepsilon_\infty c^2k^2\omega_T^2}}
{2\varepsilon_\infty}}.
\]
At \(k=0\), \(\omega_-=0\) and \(\omega_+=\omega_L\). As
\(k\to\infty\), the lower branch approaches \(\omega_T\) from below,
while the upper branch grows as \(ck/\sqrt{\varepsilon_\infty}\).

The permittivity is positive for \(0<\omega<\omega_T\), negative for
\(\omega_T<\omega<\omega_L\), and positive again above \(\omega_L\).
Thus the middle interval has
\[
\boxed{k=i\kappa,\qquad
\kappa=\frac\omega c\sqrt{-\varepsilon(\omega)}}.
\]
The pole at \(\omega_T\) was removed when forming the quadratic; the
original constitutive relation and the sign of \(k^2\) remain part of the
physical solution test.

Measure angular frequencies in the common unit \(2\pi\,\mathrm{THz}\).
At \(ck=\omega_T\), the quadratic roots are
\[
\omega_-^2=4.09515487,\qquad \omega_+^2=38.1548451,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{f_-=2.02364890\ \mathrm{THz}},\qquad
\boxed{f_+=6.17696083\ \mathrm{THz}}.
\]
At 5.50 THz,
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon=4\frac{6^2-5.5^2}{5^2-5.5^2}
=-4.38095238}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{\kappa=2.41271554\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\kappa^{-1}=4.14470742\ \mathrm{\mu m}}.
\]
The dielectric function and branch-frequency ratios are dimensionless;
\(k\) and \(\kappa\) have inverse-length units.

graderFixtures.proofText: The squared branches solve the Lorentz quadratic; at k zero they are zero and \(\omega_L^2\), and the lower branch approaches \(\omega_T\). Between \(\omega_T\) and \(\omega_L\), epsilon is negative. At 5.5 THz, the depth is 4.14470742 micrometers.
I call the negative-permittivity interval a propagating band and swap the transverse and longitudinal limits of the two polariton branches.

WAVE:010532.title: A metal interface traps a surface-plasmon wave
WAVE:010532.objective: Derive the transverse-magnetic surface-mode dispersion at a dielectric--Drude interface and audit its existence and penetration scales.
WAVE:010532.statement:
The plane \(z=0\) separates a nondispersive dielectric
\(\varepsilon_d>0\) for \(z>0\) from a lossless Drude metal
\[
\varepsilon_m(\omega)=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}
\]
for \(z<0\). Seek a transverse-magnetic surface wave proportional to
\(e^{ikx-i\omega t}\), decaying away from the interface as
\(e^{-\alpha_dz}\) above and \(e^{+\alpha_mz}\) below. Derive the relations
\(\alpha_j^2=k^2-\varepsilon_j\omega^2/c^2\) and impose Maxwell boundary
conditions to obtain the TM dispersion relation.

Solve for \(k(\omega)\). Derive the frequency interval in which both decay
constants are real and positive, the low-frequency light-line limit, and
the large-k surface-plasmon asymptote. Explain why a TE surface mode does not
exist here when both magnetic permeabilities are positive. Keep the signs of
the two normal derivatives distinct.

For \(\varepsilon_d=2.25\), \(\omega_p=1.50\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\),
and \(\omega=0.500\,\omega_{sp}\), compute \(\omega_{sp}\),
\(\varepsilon_m\), \(k/(\omega/c)\), \(k\), and both one-over-e
penetration depths using \(c=299792458\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
permittedResults: Continuity of tangential electric and magnetic fields for a source-free interface yields \(\alpha_d/\varepsilon_d+\alpha_m/\varepsilon_m=0\) for a TM bound mode.
For positive permeabilities, the analogous TE condition is a sum of positive decay constants and cannot vanish.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write the evanescent TM fields on both sides and eliminate their amplitudes with tangential boundary continuity.
Start from the proposed closed dispersion, reconstruct both decay constants, and verify the signed boundary condition and asymptotes.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives a genuinely bound interface branch by matching both Maxwell polarization conditions and positive decay constants on opposite sides.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same normal exponential derivative sign above and below the interface.
commonErrors.consequence: The TM boundary condition loses the permittivity sign contrast that binds the mode.

commonErrors.description: Allows the mode whenever the metal permittivity is merely negative rather than less than minus epsilon_d.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed in-plane wavenumber or dielectric decay constant becomes nonreal.

hintTree.content: Use opposite signs for \(\partial_z\) above and below before applying tangential-field continuity.
Eliminate \(\alpha_d,\alpha_m\) between the TM boundary condition and their bulk dispersion relations.
The large-k limit requires \(\varepsilon_m+\varepsilon_d\to0^-\).

WAVE:010532.canonicalSolution:
The evanescent bulk relations are
\[
\alpha_d^2=k^2-\varepsilon_d\frac{\omega^2}{c^2},\qquad
\alpha_m^2=k^2-\varepsilon_m\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}.
\]
Tangential-field continuity for TM polarization gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{\alpha_d}{\varepsilon_d}+
\frac{\alpha_m}{\varepsilon_m}=0}.
\]
Eliminating the decay constants produces
\[
\boxed{k=\frac\omega c
\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_d\varepsilon_m}
{\varepsilon_d+\varepsilon_m}}}.
\]
A bound lossless mode requires \(\varepsilon_m<-\varepsilon_d\), or
\[
\boxed{0<\omega<\omega_{sp}=
\frac{\omega_p}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon_d}}}.
\]
At low frequency \(\varepsilon_m\to-\infty\), so
\(k\to\sqrt{\varepsilon_d}\,\omega/c\) from above. As
\(k\to\infty\), the frequency approaches \(\omega_{sp}\) from below.
For TE polarization, positive permeabilities make the required sum of
positive normal decay constants impossible, so no analogous bound mode
exists in this model.

For \(\varepsilon_d=2.25\),
\[
\boxed{\omega_{sp}=8.32050294\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
At half this frequency, \(\omega_p^2/\omega^2=13\), hence
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon_m=-12.0000},\qquad
\boxed{\frac{k}{\omega/c}=\sqrt{\frac{2.25(-12)}{2.25-12}}
=1.66410059}.
\]
With \(\omega/c=1.38771052\times10^7\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\),
\[
\boxed{k=2.30928989\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
The decay constants give
\[
\boxed{\alpha_d^{-1}=1.00004815\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m
=100.005\ \mathrm{nm}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\alpha_m^{-1}=1.87509028\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm m
=18.7509\ \mathrm{nm}}.
\]
Both positive depths verify confinement; the metal-side field is more
tightly localized for these parameters.

graderFixtures.proofText: TM matching gives \(\alpha_d/\varepsilon_d+\alpha_m/\varepsilon_m=0\) and \(k=(\omega/c)\sqrt{\varepsilon_d\varepsilon_m/(\varepsilon_d+\varepsilon_m)}\). At half omega_sp, epsilon_m is -12 and the depths are 100.005 nm and 18.7509 nm.
I give both half-space exponentials the same normal derivative and claim any negative metal permittivity supports the bound branch.

WAVE:010533.title: An indefinite crystal sends phase and energy to opposite sides
WAVE:010533.objective: Derive extraordinary-wave dispersion in a hyperbolic medium and distinguish wavevector refraction from group-velocity refraction.
WAVE:010533.statement:
At one fixed frequency, model a lossless local uniaxial medium by
\[
\boldsymbol\varepsilon=
\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel),
\qquad
\varepsilon_\perp>0,\quad\varepsilon_\parallel<0,
\]
with optic axis \(z\) and scalar permeability \(\mu_r=1\). Consider an
extraordinary plane wave with \(\mathbf k=(k_x,0,k_z)\).

Derive its dispersion relation from Maxwell's equations and show that the
isofrequency curve is open. Find the direction normal to that curve and use
it as the group-velocity direction within this ideal frequency-slice model.
A planar interface is at \(z=0\), vacuum is at \(z<0\), and the hyperbolic
medium is at \(z>0\). Use tangential-wavevector conservation to select the
root carrying energy into the medium. Explain how the tangential components
of phase and group velocity can have opposite signs and why arbitrarily
large local-model wavenumbers are not a claim of a physical infinite
bandwidth.

For \(\varepsilon_\perp=2.25\), \(\varepsilon_\parallel=-4.00\), and a
vacuum incident angle \(30.0^\circ\), compute \(k_x/k_0\), \(k_z/k_0\),
the phase-wavevector angle, \(v_{gx}/v_{gz}\), and the group-refraction
angle. Here \(k_0=\omega/c\), and all angles are measured from the positive
interface normal, with their tangential sign retained.
permittedResults: For a uniaxial extraordinary wave in the x-z plane, \(k_x^2/\varepsilon_\parallel+k_z^2/\varepsilon_\perp=k_0^2\).
At a translation-invariant planar interface, tangential frequency and tangential wavevector are conserved.

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the two-component extraordinary Maxwell determinant and differentiate its isofrequency equation.
Use the known uniaxial dispersion, then audit its signs through boundary matching and the group-normal construction.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Keeps tensor signs, interface-root selection, phase direction, group direction, and the effective-medium cutoff caveat mutually consistent.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the group velocity is parallel to k as in an isotropic positive-index medium.
commonErrors.consequence: The tangential energy-flow sign and negative-refraction result are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the transmitted root solely by positive phase k_z without checking the normal group velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: In a general indefinite orientation the selected solution can carry energy toward the interface.

hintTree.content: Eliminate the magnetic field from \(\mathbf k\times(\mathbf k\times\mathbf E)+k_0^2\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mathbf E=0\).
Differentiate the dispersion function with respect to \(k_x\) and \(k_z\) to get the group-direction ratio.
Choose \(k_z>0\) here because \(v_{gz}\) is proportional to \(k_z/\varepsilon_\perp\).

WAVE:010533.canonicalSolution:
The extraordinary electric field lies in the x-z plane. Eliminating its two
components from the anisotropic Maxwell system gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{k_x^2}{\varepsilon_\parallel}
+\frac{k_z^2}{\varepsilon_\perp}=k_0^2}.
\]
Because \(\varepsilon_\parallel<0\) and \(\varepsilon_\perp>0\), this is
\[
\frac{k_z^2}{\varepsilon_\perp}
-\frac{k_x^2}{|\varepsilon_\parallel|}=k_0^2,
\]
an open hyperbola. Solving for the normal component,
\[
\boxed{k_z^2=\varepsilon_\perp k_0^2
\left(1+\frac{k_x^2}{|\varepsilon_\parallel|k_0^2}\right)},
\]
so the local model has real \(k_z\) for every tangential \(k_x\).

The normal to the isofrequency curve is proportional to
\[
\left(\frac{k_x}{\varepsilon_\parallel},
\frac{k_z}{\varepsilon_\perp}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{gx}}{v_{gz}}=
\frac{k_x/\varepsilon_\parallel}{k_z/\varepsilon_\perp}}.
\]
Tangential phase matching preserves the sign of \(k_x\). Energy into
\(z>0\) requires \(v_{gz}>0\), so with positive \(\varepsilon_\perp\) we
choose \(k_z>0\). Yet \(v_{gx}\) has the sign opposite \(k_x\) because
\(\varepsilon_\parallel<0\). Phase and energy therefore refract to opposite
tangential sides.

For incidence at \(30^\circ\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{k_x}{k_0}=\sin30^\circ=0.500000}.
\]
The positive-energy root is
\[
\boxed{\frac{k_z}{k_0}
=\sqrt{2.25\left(1+\frac{0.5^2}{4}\right)}
=1.54616461}.
\]
The wavevector angle is
\[
\boxed{\theta_k=\tan^{-1}(k_x/k_z)=17.9202131^\circ},
\]
whereas
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{gx}}{v_{gz}}=-0.181901719},
\qquad
\boxed{\theta_g=-10.3094796^\circ}.
\]
The opposite signs are the negative group-refraction result.

A passive realization with a negative permittivity component must be
frequency dispersive and generally lossy. Unit-cell scale, spatial
dispersion, and loss cut off the formal large-\(k\) states. The open
hyperbola is therefore a local effective-medium prediction, not permission
to transmit unbounded spatial frequency with no cost.

graderFixtures.proofText: The dispersion is \(k_x^2/\varepsilon_\parallel+k_z^2/\varepsilon_\perp=k_0^2\), and the group normal is proportional to \((k_x/\varepsilon_\parallel,k_z/\varepsilon_\perp)\). The data give \(k_z/k_0=1.54616461\) and group angle \(-10.3094796^\circ\).
I draw group velocity parallel to the positive transmitted wavevector and select roots by phase direction alone, so both refraction angles have the same sign.

WAVE:010534.title: A free elastic plate splits into symmetric and antisymmetric waves
WAVE:010534.objective: Derive the Rayleigh--Lamb branch equations and recover their low-frequency extensional and flexural limits.
WAVE:010534.statement:
An isotropic elastic plate occupies \(-h\le z\le h\), is infinite in \(x\),
and has traction-free faces at \(z=\pm h\). Its density is \(\rho\), Lamé
parameters are \(\lambda,\mu\), and
\[
c_L=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda+2\mu}{\rho}},\qquad
c_T=\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\rho}}.
\]
For plane-strain waves proportional to \(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\), introduce
longitudinal and shear potentials and impose both zero normal stress and zero
shear stress at each face.

Derive the symmetric and antisymmetric Rayleigh--Lamb equations in terms of
\[
p^2=\frac{\omega^2}{c_L^2}-k^2,\qquad
q^2=\frac{\omega^2}{c_T^2}-k^2.
\]
State how the equations continue when \(p\) or \(q\) is imaginary. Identify
the low-frequency \(S_0\) extensional branch and \(A_0\) flexural branch,
deriving their leading dispersions using the full thickness \(d=2h\).
Explain why neither branch is obtained by simply setting
\(\omega=c_Lk\) or \(\omega=c_Tk\).

For \(E=70.0\,\mathrm{GPa}\), \(\nu=0.330\),
\(\rho=2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(d=4.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), and
\(k=25.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), compute \(c_L,c_T\), the plane-stress
extensional speed \(c_E\), the bending rigidity \(D\), \(kh\), and the
leading \(S_0\) and \(A_0\) ordinary frequencies.
permittedResults: Plane-strain displacement may be written \(u_x=\Phi_x-\Psi_z\), \(u_z=\Phi_z+\Psi_x\), where \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) satisfy longitudinal and shear Helmholtz equations.
A thin traction-free plate has \(S_0:\omega\sim c_Ek\) and \(A_0:\omega\sim k^2\sqrt{D/(\rho d)}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Choose midplane parity first and evaluate the two face tractions as a two-by-two determinant.
Start from the standard potential determinant and independently recover each low-frequency limit from extensional and bending plate energies.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Carries longitudinal and shear potentials through parity, two traction conditions, branch determinants, and dimensionally correct thin-plate limits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses only a longitudinal or only a shear bulk potential for a nontrivial plate branch.
commonErrors.consequence: Normal and shear traction cannot both vanish at the two free faces.

commonErrors.description: Uses full thickness d inside tan of p h and q h while also defining the faces at plus or minus h.
commonErrors.consequence: Every determinant phase and numerical branch location is shifted by a factor of two.

hintTree.content: Choose sine or cosine parity for each potential before applying stress conditions at one face.
Keep h, the half-thickness, inside the tangent functions; use d equals 2h only in the thin-plate constants.
When p is imaginary, replace \(\tan(iph)\) by \(i\tanh(|p|h)\) rather than discarding the branch.

WAVE:010534.canonicalSolution:
With
\[
u_x=\Phi_x-\Psi_z,\qquad u_z=\Phi_z+\Psi_x,
\]
the potentials satisfy
\[
(\partial_z^2+p^2)\Phi=0,\qquad
(\partial_z^2+q^2)\Psi=0.
\]
Choosing opposite parities of the two potentials and imposing
\(\sigma_{zz}=\sigma_{xz}=0\) at \(z=h\) gives the Rayleigh--Lamb equations
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\tan(qh)}{\tan(ph)}
=-\frac{4k^2pq}{(q^2-k^2)^2}
}\qquad(S),
\]
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\tan(qh)}{\tan(ph)}
=-\frac{(q^2-k^2)^2}{4k^2pq}
}\qquad(A).
\]
Cross-multiplied determinant forms should be used at apparent tangent poles.
If \(p=i\alpha\) or \(q=i\beta\), analytic continuation
\(\tan(ix)=i\tanh x\) keeps the equations real in the appropriate
subsonic intervals.

At \(kd\ll1\), the lowest symmetric branch is an extensional plate wave:
\[
\boxed{\omega_{S_0}\sim c_Ek},\qquad
\boxed{c_E=\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho(1-\nu^2)}}}.
\]
The lowest antisymmetric branch is bending dominated:
\[
\boxed{\omega_{A_0}\sim k^2\sqrt{\frac{D}{\rho d}}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\frac{Ed^3}{12(1-\nu^2)}}.
\]
Thus \(S_0\) is linear while \(A_0\) is quadratic and strongly dispersive.
Both combine longitudinal and shear potentials to satisfy two traction
conditions, so neither is a pure bulk L or T wave.

For the specified material,
\[
\mu=\frac{E}{2(1+\nu)},\qquad
\lambda=\frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}.
\]
Numerically,
\[
\boxed{c_L=6197.82430\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{c_T=3121.95271\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{c_E=5393.91274\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=418.957842\ \mathrm{N\,m}}.
\]
Here
\[
\boxed{kh=k(d/2)=0.0500000},
\]
so the leading thin-plate estimates are appropriate:
\[
\boxed{f_{S_0}\sim\frac{c_Ek}{2\pi}
=21461.6969\ \mathrm{Hz}},
\]
\[
\boxed{f_{A_0}\sim\frac{k^2}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{D}{\rho d}}
=619.545823\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
These are asymptotic branch values, not claimed exact roots at finite
thickness. Using \(d\) instead of \(h\) inside the tangent equations doubles
every thickness phase and does not represent the stated faces.

graderFixtures.proofText: The symmetric ratio is \(\tan(qh)/\tan(ph)=-4k^2pq/(q^2-k^2)^2\), with the reciprocal expression for antisymmetric modes. The thin limits give \(f_{S_0}=21461.6969\) Hz and \(f_{A_0}=619.545823\) Hz at \(kh=0.05\).
I keep only a longitudinal potential and put the full thickness inside both tangent arguments, then call omega equals c L k the S zero branch.

WAVE:010535.title: Pressure stabilizes short waves but not long gravitational modes
WAVE:010535.objective: Derive Jeans dispersion from the coupled fluid and Poisson fields, separate oscillatory and growing regimes, and determine exactly which mean-zero modes fit in a periodic box.
WAVE:010535.statement:
Use the ideal Jeans model for a uniform, inviscid, barotropic medium of
background density \(\rho_0\) and constant sound speed \(c_s\). The
unperturbed gravitational field of the infinite uniform background is
subtracted; only perturbations source \(\Phi_1\). This local homogeneous
model is an idealization, not a claim that a static infinite gravitating
medium is a complete global equilibrium.

Linear perturbations obey
\[
\partial_t\rho_1+\rho_0\nabla\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf u=0,
\qquad
\partial_t\mathbf u=-\frac{c_s^2}{\rho_0}\nabla\rho_1-\nabla\Phi_1,
\qquad
\nabla^2\Phi_1=4\pi G\rho_1.
\]
Insert a plane wave proportional to
\(e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\), eliminate velocity and
potential, and derive the dispersion relation with its sign. Find the Jeans
wavenumber and wavelength. For the stable branch calculate phase and group
speeds and prove their product is \(c_s^2\). Explain why the group speed
diverges as the cutoff is approached from above without making the signal
front propagate infinitely fast. For the unstable branch derive the
exponential growth rate.

Now impose a one-dimensional periodic box of length \(L\), require zero
mean density perturbation, and use \(k_n=2\pi n/L\). State exactly which
nonzero Fourier indices are unstable when \(L=3\lambda_J\), including the
neutral boundary indices.

Take \(G=6.67430\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}\),
\(\rho_0=3.00\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and
\(c_s=200\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Compute \(k_J\), \(\lambda_J\) in meters
and parsecs, and the box length. For a perturbation of wavelength
\(2\lambda_J\), compute its growth rate and e-folding time. For wavelength
\(\lambda_J/2\), compute angular frequency, period, phase speed, and group
speed. State the limitations of neglecting expansion, boundaries, magnetic
fields, viscosity, and nonlinear collapse.
permittedResults: For a Fourier mode, Poisson's equation gives \(-k^2\Phi_1=4\pi G\rho_1\).
A constant-coefficient hyperbolic fluid system has high-wavenumber characteristic speed \(c_s\); a divergent narrow-band group derivative at a cutoff does not set the front speed.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate potential with Fourier Poisson inversion, then eliminate longitudinal velocity with continuity and classify the sign of omega squared.
Combine continuity and momentum into a density wave equation first, insert Poisson's equation, and only then impose continuous or periodic Fourier spectra.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses Poisson-coupled compressible dynamics to derive the pressure-gravity cutoff and carries it consistently into growth, propagation, and discrete finite-domain mode counting.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses plus four pi G rho zero in omega squared or otherwise makes perturbation self-gravity a restoring contribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The Jeans cutoff and long-wave growth disappear or occur in the wrong regime.

commonErrors.description: Calls the divergent near-cutoff group derivative an infinite signal speed or counts the excluded uniform density mode as a box instability.
commonErrors.consequence: The propagation interpretation or finite-domain spectrum violates the stated model.

hintTree.content: Take the component of the momentum equation along k and use continuity to replace \(\mathbf k\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf u\).
Write \(\omega^2=c_s^2(k^2-k_J^2)\), then use a real omega above cutoff and \(\omega=i\sigma\) below it.
In the box, instability is the strict inequality \(0<|n|<L/\lambda_J\); the mean mode is excluded by the stated zero-mean condition.

WAVE:010535.canonicalSolution:
Fourier transformation gives
\[
-i\omega\rho_1+i\rho_0\mathbf k\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf u=0,
\]
\[
-i\omega\mathbf u=-i\mathbf k
\left(\frac{c_s^2\rho_1}{\rho_0}+\Phi_1\right),\qquad
-k^2\Phi_1=4\pi G\rho_1.
\]
Taking the longitudinal component of momentum and using continuity yields
\[
\boxed{\omega^2=c_s^2k^2-4\pi G\rho_0}.
\]
The negative gravitational term follows from the minus sign in Fourier
Poisson inversion; reversing it would incorrectly make self-gravity
restoring.

Define
\[
\boxed{k_J=\frac{\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}}{c_s}},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_J=\frac{2\pi}{k_J}
=c_s\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{G\rho_0}}}.
\]
For \(k>k_J\), choose the positive-frequency branch
\[
\omega=c_s\sqrt{k^2-k_J^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{v_p=\frac\omega k
=c_s\sqrt{1-\frac{k_J^2}{k^2}}},
\qquad
\boxed{v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}
=\frac{c_s}{\sqrt{1-k_J^2/k^2}}},
\]
and \(\boxed{v_pv_g=c_s^2}\). The derivative diverges as
\(k\downarrow k_J\), where a narrow packet samples very strong dispersion
and its carrier frequency tends to zero. The front is controlled by the
large-k asymptote \(\omega\sim c_sk\), so the model's characteristic
front speed remains \(c_s\).

For \(0<k<k_J\), write \(\omega=i\sigma\). The growing solution has
\[
\boxed{\sigma(k)=\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0-c_s^2k^2}}.
\]
In a periodic box, \(k_n=2\pi n/L\). With zero mean, \(n=0\) is absent.
At \(L=3\lambda_J\),
\[
0<|n|<3
\]
is unstable. Thus \(n=\pm1,\pm2\) are the four unstable complex Fourier
indices, or two unstable real sine-cosine pairs. The indices \(n=\pm3\)
are neutral, and all larger magnitudes oscillate.

For the numerical data,
\[
\boxed{k_J=2.50806291\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\lambda_J=2.50519446\times10^{16}\ \mathrm m
=0.811878233\ \mathrm{pc}},
\]
using \(1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.08567758\times10^{16}\,\mathrm m\). Hence
\[
\boxed{L=7.51558338\times10^{16}\ \mathrm m
=2.43563470\ \mathrm{pc}}.
\]
At wavelength \(2\lambda_J\), \(k=k_J/2\), so
\[
\boxed{\sigma=4.34409239\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma^{-1}=2.30197683\times10^{13}\ \mathrm s
=7.29452\times10^5\ \mathrm{yr}}.
\]
At wavelength \(\lambda_J/2\), \(k=2k_J\), giving
\[
\boxed{\omega=8.68818477\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{T=7.23187348\times10^{13}\ \mathrm s
=2.29164\times10^6\ \mathrm{yr}},
\]
\[
\boxed{v_p=173.205081\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{v_g=230.940108\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The linear model predicts only initial growth or oscillation. Cosmological
expansion, finite boundaries, magnetic stress, viscosity, temperature
evolution, and nonlinear collapse can change the spectrum or terminate the
linear regime; none is represented here.

graderFixtures.proofText: Elimination gives \(\omega^2=c_s^2k^2-4\pi G\rho_0\), so \(k_J=\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}/c_s\). In a zero-mean box of length \(3\lambda_J\), only \(n=\pm1,\pm2\) grow and \(n=\pm3\) are neutral; the front speed remains \(c_s\).
I use a plus gravitational term so every mode oscillates, then include n equals zero as the fastest box mode and interpret the near-cutoff group derivative as infinite signal propagation.

WAVE:010536.title: Gravity and surface tension bound a shear instability
WAVE:010536.objective: Derive the gravity-capillary Kelvin--Helmholtz dispersion relation and compute its threshold, finite unstable band, and fastest growth rate.
WAVE:010536.statement:
Two deep, inviscid, incompressible fluids meet at the horizontal plane
\(z=0\). Fluid 1 of density \(\rho_1\) occupies \(z>0\) and moves at
uniform speed \(U_1\hat{\mathbf x}\); fluid 2 of density \(\rho_2>\rho_1\)
occupies \(z<0\) and moves at \(U_2\hat{\mathbf x}\). Gravity is downward
with magnitude g, and the interface has surface tension gamma. Neglect
viscosity and take a perturbation proportional to
\(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) with \(k>0\).

Use decaying velocity potentials in the two half-spaces and the linearized
kinematic and dynamic interface conditions to derive the two branches of
the dispersion relation. Identify the density-weighted advection frequency
and determine precisely when the square root becomes imaginary. Minimize
the required shear over k to find the critical velocity difference. For a
supercritical shear, derive both endpoints of the finite unstable wavenumber
band. Also derive the wavenumber that maximizes the temporal growth rate and
the corresponding growth-rate formula.

Take \(\rho_1=1.20\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\),
\(\rho_2=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\),
\(\gamma=0.0720\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\),
\(U_1=7.00\,\mathrm{m/s}\), and \(U_2=0\). Compute the critical shear,
unstable wavenumber and wavelength intervals, fastest-growing wavenumber and
wavelength, maximum growth rate, e-folding time, and density-weighted phase
advection speed. State why omitting either gravity or surface tension would
destroy one edge of the finite band.
permittedResults: Deep-water potential perturbations decay as \(e^{-kz}\) above and \(e^{kz}\) below the interface.
A quadratic \(\gamma k^2-Ck+G\) is negative only between two positive roots when \(C^2>4\gamma G\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate the two decaying potential amplitudes with the kinematic conditions, then analyze the dynamic-condition discriminant as a quadratic in k.
Begin from the standard two-fluid gravity-capillary dispersion and independently verify its threshold by minimizing the shear required at each wavenumber.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the interfacial radical with correct density factors and carries its sign analysis through threshold, finite band, fastest growth, and units.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses one-fluid free-surface density factors and omits the product rho one rho two in the shear term.
commonErrors.consequence: The threshold and numerical band are dimensionally or quantitatively wrong.

commonErrors.description: Drops gravity or surface tension while claiming to have found the stated finite instability interval.
commonErrors.consequence: One stabilizing edge of the band cannot exist in the resulting model.

hintTree.content: Keep the Doppler factors \(\omega-kU_j\) separate until the two dynamic pressures are combined.
After extracting one positive k, test the sign of \(G+\gamma k^2-Ck\), where \(G=(\rho_2-\rho_1)g\).
Maximize growth-rate squared; differentiating it avoids differentiating a square root.

WAVE:010536.canonicalSolution:
The decaying perturbation potentials have the forms
\(\phi_1'\propto e^{-kz}e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) and
\(\phi_2'\propto e^{kz}e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\). Applying the kinematic
condition to each and balancing linearized Bernoulli pressure with gravity
and the capillary pressure jump gives
\[
\boxed{
\omega=k\bar U\pm
\sqrt{
\frac{(\rho_2-\rho_1)gk+\gamma k^3}{\rho_1+\rho_2}
-\frac{\rho_1\rho_2}{(\rho_1+\rho_2)^2}
(U_1-U_2)^2k^2}},
\]
where
\[
\boxed{\bar U=\frac{\rho_1U_1+\rho_2U_2}{\rho_1+\rho_2}}.
\]

Let \(S=\rho_1+\rho_2\), \(G=(\rho_2-\rho_1)g\),
\(\Delta U=U_1-U_2\), and
\[
C=\frac{\rho_1\rho_2}{S}(\Delta U)^2.
\]
For positive k, the radical is negative exactly when
\[
\gamma k^2-Ck+G<0.
\]
The shear needed at fixed k is minimized when
\(k=\sqrt{G/\gamma}\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{(\Delta U_c)^2=
\frac{2S\sqrt{\gamma G}}{\rho_1\rho_2}}.
\]
When \(|\Delta U|>\Delta U_c\), the unstable band is
\[
\boxed{k_-<k<k_+},\qquad
\boxed{k_\pm=\frac{C\pm\sqrt{C^2-4\gamma G}}{2\gamma}}.
\]

Inside that band, writing the growing root as
\(\omega=k\bar U+i\sigma\) gives
\[
\sigma^2=ak^2-bk-ck^3,
\quad
a=\frac{\rho_1\rho_2(\Delta U)^2}{S^2},\quad
b=\frac GS,\quad c=\frac\gamma S.
\]
The interior maximum is the larger stationary root,
\[
\boxed{k_{\rm max}=\frac{a+\sqrt{a^2-3bc}}{3c}},
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_{\rm max}=\sqrt{ak_{\rm max}^2-bk_{\rm max}-ck_{\rm max}^3}}.
\]

For the numerical values,
\[
\boxed{\Delta U_c=6.65740234\ \mathrm{m/s}},
\]
so the specified shear is supercritical. The endpoints are
\[
\boxed{k_-=233.918179\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{k_+=581.769662\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
\]
Since wavelength decreases as k increases, this is equivalently
\[
\boxed{10.8001254\ \mathrm{mm}<\lambda<26.8606114\ \mathrm{mm}}.
\]
The fastest mode has
\[
\boxed{k_{\rm max}=440.908489\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_{\rm max}=14.2505428\ \mathrm{mm}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{\rm max}=30.4053996\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_{\rm max}^{-1}=0.0328888951\ \mathrm s}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{\bar U=0.00838993208\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
Gravity stabilizes the low-k edge and surface tension stabilizes the high-k
edge. Omitting gravity lets the formal unstable range extend toward zero k;
omitting surface tension removes the high-k cutoff in this inviscid model.

graderFixtures.proofText: The radical becomes negative when \(\gamma k^2-Ck+G<0\). Here the critical shear is 6.65740234 meters per second, the unstable band is 233.918179 to 581.769662 inverse meters, and maximum growth is 30.4053996 per second.
I use the air density alone in the restoring terms, omit surface tension, and declare every wavenumber above one gravity cutoff unstable.

WAVE:010537.title: Deep-water dispersion fixes a ship wake's cusp angle
WAVE:010537.objective: Derive the Kelvin wake wedge from the steady-source condition and the envelope of relative group-velocity rays.
WAVE:010537.statement:
An ideal point disturbance moves at speed $U$ in
the positive $x$ direction over inviscid, infinitely deep water. Ignore
surface tension. Linear gravity waves obey $\omega^2=gk$, and a packet
carries energy at $c_g\widehat{\boldsymbol k}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle
between $\boldsymbol k$ and the ship track.

In the ship frame, derive the stationarity condition and selected wavenumber.
Form the group-velocity ray relative to the source. If $\alpha$ is its
downstream angle measured from the negative $x$ axis, derive
$\tan\alpha(\theta)$. Locate the ray envelope or cusp and the classical wake
half-angle. At the cusp calculate wavenumber, wavelength, laboratory group
speed, and both relative-ray components. Explain why wavevector, crest,
group-ray, and envelope angles are not interchangeable.

For $U=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, report all cusp
quantities. State the idealizations behind the speed-independent angle and
why finite depth, capillarity, hull spectrum, or nonlinearity can alter the
visible wake. Do not identify this stationary pattern with a universal signal
front.
permittedResults: For deep-water gravity waves, $c_g=d\omega/dk=\tfrac12\sqrt{g/k}$.
A one-parameter ray envelope occurs at a stationary observation angle.

acceptableStrategies.description: Parameterize stationary components by wavevector angle and maximize the relative ray angle.
Construct the downstream ray family and locate its caustic.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Builds the wake envelope from phase matching and relative group velocity rather than one crest direction.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses phase velocity or wavevector angle as the energy ray.
commonErrors.consequence: The relative rays and cusp are not derived.

commonErrors.description: Claims arbitrary depth, capillarity, source spectra, and signal fronts retain the angle.
commonErrors.consequence: A model-specific stationary result is overgeneralized.

hintTree.content: Stationarity gives $\sqrt{gk}=Uk\cos\theta$.
Use $\boldsymbol v_{\rm rel}=c_g(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)-U(1,0)$.
Maximize $u(1-u)/(1+u)^2$, where $u=\sin^2\theta$.

WAVE:010537.canonicalSolution:
Steadiness requires
$$
\omega-\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol U=0.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{k(\theta)=\frac{g}{U^2\cos^2\theta}}.
$$
The group speed becomes $c_g=U\cos\theta/2$, and the ray relative to the
ship is
$$
\boldsymbol v_{\rm rel}=U\left(\frac{\cos^2\theta}{2}-1,
\frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2}\right).
$$
It points downstream. Measured from the negative track,
$$
\boxed{\tan\alpha=
\frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2-\cos^2\theta}
=\frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}}.
$$
With $u=\sin^2\theta$, its square is
$u(1-u)/(1+u)^2$, whose derivative vanishes at $u=1/3$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\theta_c=\arcsin(1/\sqrt3)=35.2644^\circ},
$$
$$
\boxed{\alpha_K=\arcsin(1/3)=19.4712^\circ},\qquad
\tan\alpha_K=\frac1{2\sqrt2}.
$$
At the cusp,
$$
\boxed{k_c=\frac{3g}{2U^2}},\quad
\boxed{\lambda_c=\frac{4\pi U^2}{3g}},\quad
\boxed{c_{g,c}=\frac{U}{\sqrt6}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_x=-2U/3},\qquad \boxed{v_y=U\sqrt2/6}.
$$

For $U=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$$
\boxed{k_c=0.147150\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\quad
\boxed{\lambda_c=42.6992\,\mathrm m},\quad
\boxed{c_{g,c}=4.08248\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{(v_x,v_y)=(-6.66667,\ 2.35702)\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
Wavevector is normal to crests, group velocity sets energy rays, subtraction
of source velocity changes their direction, and the wake boundary is an
envelope of many rays. None of these angles may be substituted for another.

The angle follows from isotropic deep-water $\omega\propto k^{1/2}$, a
steady point source, and linear stationary phase. Finite depth, surface
tension, hull weighting, dissipation, and nonlinearity change dispersion or
visibility. The steady ray construction is not a universal front-speed
argument.

graderFixtures.proofText: Stationarity gives $k=g/(U^2\cos^2\theta)$. Relative rays obey $\tan\alpha=\sin\theta\cos\theta/(1+\sin^2\theta)$, whose cusp has $\sin^2\theta=1/3$ and $\alpha=\arcsin(1/3)$.
I set the wake direction equal to wavevector angle, use phase velocity for energy, and call it a universal signal front.

WAVE:010538.title: A relaxing gas changes sound speed across one molecular clock
WAVE:010538.objective: Derive complex acoustic dispersion from a relaxing bulk modulus and distinguish attenuation per length from loss per wavelength.
WAVE:010538.statement:
A homogeneous gas of density $\rho_0$ has
$$
K(\omega)=K_\infty-\frac{K_\infty-K_0}{1-i\omega\tau},\qquad
0<K_0<K_\infty,\quad\tau>0.
$$
Use fields proportional to $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$; the sign convention is
chosen so the passive branch attenuates with $x$.

Starting from linear continuity and momentum balance with
$p'=K(\omega)\rho'/\rho_0$, derive complex dispersion and choose the
physical square-root branch. Obtain low- and high-frequency sound speeds.
For weak relaxation
$\varepsilon=(K_\infty-K_0)/K_\infty\ll1$, expand $k$ to first order.
Derive attenuation per length and
$2\,\operatorname{Im}k/\operatorname{Re}k$. Explain why the latter peaks
near $\omega\tau=1$, while attenuation per metre tends to a constant in
this ideal model. Do not claim every attenuation measure has one maximum.

For $\rho_0=1.20\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $c_0=330\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$c_\infty=340\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\tau=1.00\,\mathrm{ms}$, and
$\omega=1000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, set $K_j=\rho_0c_j^2$. Calculate
complex modulus, wavenumber, phase speed, attenuation length, and exact
dimensionless loss. State the local scalar-model assumptions.
permittedResults: For $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$, the passive branch has $\operatorname{Re}k>0$ and $\operatorname{Im}k>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate acoustic fields, choose the complex square root, and expand weak relaxation.
Separate modulus storage and loss, then verify limits and dimensionless attenuation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Carries one passive constitutive convention through dispersion, asymptotics, and numerical branch selection.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Chooses negative imaginary wavenumber for the stated convention.
commonErrors.consequence: A passive gas amplifies with distance.

commonErrors.description: Claims attenuation per metre and per wavelength have the same peak.
commonErrors.consequence: Different observables are conflated.

hintTree.content: Eliminate density and velocity to obtain $k^2=\rho_0\omega^2/K(\omega)$.
Write $K/K_\infty=1-\varepsilon/(1-i\omega\tau)$.
Compare $x/(1+x^2)$ with $x^2/(1+x^2)$.

WAVE:010538.canonicalSolution:
Continuity and momentum are
$$
-i\omega\rho'+ik\rho_0u=0,\qquad
-i\omega\rho_0u=-ikp'.
$$
Elimination gives
$$
\boxed{k^2(\omega)=\frac{\rho_0\omega^2}{K(\omega)}}.
$$
Choose $\operatorname{Re}k>0,\operatorname{Im}k>0$, so $e^{ikx}$
decays. Since $K(0)=K_0$ and $K(\infty)=K_\infty$,
$$
\boxed{c(0)=c_0=\sqrt{K_0/\rho_0}},\qquad
\boxed{c(\infty)=c_\infty=\sqrt{K_\infty/\rho_0}}.
$$

Let $x=\omega\tau$. Then
$$
\frac{K}{K_\infty}=1-\frac{\varepsilon}{1-ix},
$$
$$
k=\frac{\omega}{c_\infty}
\left[1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1-ix)}\right]+O(\varepsilon^2).
$$
Thus
$$
\operatorname{Re}k\simeq\frac{\omega}{c_\infty}
\left[1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+x^2)}\right],
$$
$$
\boxed{\alpha=\operatorname{Im}k\simeq
\frac{\varepsilon\omega^2\tau}{2c_\infty(1+\omega^2\tau^2)}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\frac{2\operatorname{Im}k}{\operatorname{Re}k}
\simeq\frac{\varepsilon x}{1+x^2}}.
$$
The last function peaks at $x=1$. By contrast, $\alpha$ contains
$x^2/(1+x^2)$ after extracting $1/\tau$ and tends to
$\varepsilon/(2c_\infty\tau)$. The observables answer different questions.

Numerically,
$$
K_0=130680\,\mathrm{Pa},\quad K_\infty=138720\,\mathrm{Pa},\quad
\boxed{K=134700-4020i\,\mathrm{Pa}}.
$$
The passive square root is
$$
\boxed{k=(2.98375+0.0445137i)\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{c_{\rm ph}=335.149\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\ell_\alpha=1/\operatorname{Im}k=22.4650\,\mathrm m},
$$
$$
\boxed{2\operatorname{Im}k/\operatorname{Re}k=0.0298375}.
$$
This assumes linear perturbations, homogeneity, one Debye relaxation, no
shear response, and wavelengths long relative to microscopic nonlocal scales.
Viscosity, heat conduction, boundaries, or more relaxation channels alter
attenuation.

graderFixtures.proofText: The passive root of $k^2=\rho_0\omega^2/K$ has positive real and imaginary parts. Weak relaxation gives $2k_i/k_r\simeq\varepsilon\omega\tau/(1+\omega^2\tau^2)$, while attenuation per metre tends to a constant.
I choose the spatially growing root and say attenuation per metre and per wavelength share the same maximum.

WAVE:010539.title: An opposing current blocks a deep-water wave train
WAVE:010539.objective: Locate the group-velocity horizon of deep-water gravity waves on a uniform current and classify the wavenumber roots at fixed laboratory frequency.
WAVE:010539.statement:
One-dimensional small-amplitude gravity waves travel
on deep water with a uniform current $U<0$ opposing propagation in the
positive $x$ direction. For positive wavenumber $k$, the laboratory-frame
dispersion branch is
$$
\omega(k)=Uk+\sqrt{gk}.
$$

Derive the intrinsic frequency and distinguish intrinsic phase/group speeds
from their laboratory values. Find the positive wavenumber $k_b$ at which the
laboratory group velocity vanishes and the corresponding maximum laboratory
frequency $\omega_b$. Show directly that solving the fixed-frequency
dispersion gives two, one, or zero positive roots according as
$0<\omega<\omega_b$, $\omega=\omega_b$, or $\omega>\omega_b$.
Interpret root coalescence as blocking, not as dissipation. Determine the two
roots explicitly by setting $q=\sqrt{k}$ and identify which branch has
upstream laboratory group velocity.

For $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $U=-2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, calculate
$k_b$, wavelength $\lambda_b$, $\omega_b$, and $f_b$. At
$\omega=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, calculate both positive wavenumbers and
the sign of their laboratory group velocities. State the deep-water and
linear-amplitude assumptions that limit this model.
permittedResults: For a uniform current, $\omega_{\rm lab}=Uk+\omega_{\rm intrinsic}$.
A double root occurs when a dispersion equation and its derivative with respect to wavenumber vanish together.

acceptableStrategies.description: Maximize the laboratory dispersion curve and then solve it as a quadratic in square-root wavenumber.
Solve the double-root equations for the Doppler-shifted intrinsic dispersion.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.

Distinguishes intrinsic from laboratory phase and group speeds, then uses the laboratory dispersion derivative and fixed-frequency discriminant to identify the blocking double root and its two neighboring propagation branches.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses intrinsic group speed as the laboratory group speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The blocking condition and branch directions are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Attributes the missing real root to damping in this inviscid model.
commonErrors.consequence: Root coalescence is replaced by an absent mechanism.

hintTree.content: Set $d\omega/dk=U+\sqrt g/(2\sqrt k)$ to zero.
With $q=\sqrt k$, the fixed-frequency equation is $|U|q^2-\sqrt gq+\omega=0$.
The sign of group velocity changes at $q_b=\sqrt g/(2|U|)$.

WAVE:010539.canonicalSolution:
The intrinsic frequency is
$\Omega=\omega-Uk=\sqrt{gk}$. Thus intrinsic phase and group speeds are
$\sqrt{g/k}$ and $\tfrac12\sqrt{g/k}$. The laboratory phase and group speeds
are, respectively,
$$
\boxed{v_{p,\mathrm{lab}}=\frac{\omega}{k}=U+\sqrt{\frac gk}},
\qquad
\boxed{v_{g,\mathrm{lab}}=\frac{d\omega}{dk}
=U+\frac12\sqrt{\frac gk}}.
$$
Setting it to zero gives
$$
\boxed{k_b=\frac{g}{4U^2}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_b=\omega(k_b)=\frac{g}{4|U|}}.
$$
This is the maximum of the positive-$k$ branch.

At fixed $\omega$, let $q=\sqrt k$ and write $V=|U|$. Then
$$
Vq^2-\sqrt gq+\omega=0,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{q_\pm=\frac{\sqrt g\pm\sqrt{g-4V\omega}}{2V}},
\qquad \boxed{k_\pm=q_\pm^2}.
$$
The discriminant is positive, zero, or negative precisely below, at, or above
$\omega_b=g/(4V)$. The smaller root has $v_g>0$ and can carry a packet
upstream against the current; the larger root has $v_g<0$. At the double root
the packet stalls. No attenuation or viscosity was included.

For $U=-2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$$
\boxed{k_b=0.613125\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_b=10.2478\,\mathrm m},
$$
$$
\boxed{\omega_b=1.22625\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{f_b=0.195164\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
$$
At $\omega=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{k_-=0.0325530\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{k_+=1.91995\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
$$
The corresponding group velocities are positive and negative, respectively.
The model assumes wavelength short compared with water depth, small steepness,
irrotational perturbations, a prescribed uniform current, and negligible
surface tension and viscosity.

WAVE:010540.title: Next-neighbor springs create a backward lattice branch
WAVE:010540.objective: Derive how positive next-neighbor coupling creates an interior dispersion maximum and a negative-group-velocity interval in a stable chain.
WAVE:010540.statement:
An infinite chain has equal masses $m$ at spacing
$a$. Nearest neighbors are connected by springs $K_1>0$, and next-nearest
neighbors by springs $K_2>0$. Longitudinal displacements satisfy
$$
m\ddot u_n=K_1(u_{n+1}-2u_n+u_{n-1})
+K_2(u_{n+2}-2u_n+u_{n-2}).
$$

Derive the dispersion relation over $0\le q=ka\le\pi$ and prove stability.
Find every stationary point inside the Brillouin half-zone. Show that an
interior maximum exists exactly when $K_2>K_1/4$, and find its location.
Determine the sign of group velocity beyond it, compare its frequency with the
zone-edge frequency, and explain how two positive wavenumbers can share one
frequency without there being a second polarization or a dissipative mode.
Check the long-wavelength sound speed.

For $m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}$, $K_1=20.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$K_2=10.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $a=0.100\,\mathrm m$, compute the interior
$q_*$, its angular frequency, the zone-edge angular frequency, and the
long-wave sound speed. State whether energy and group velocity have the same
sign on the descending branch.
permittedResults: A plane wave $u_n=Ue^{i(nq-\omega t)}$ converts a symmetric lattice difference into a sine-squared factor.
For a positive-frequency branch, the sign of group velocity equals the sign of $d(\omega^2)/dk$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute a lattice plane wave and analyze the derivative of squared frequency.
Construct the harmonic energy in Fourier space and inspect its positive dispersion symbol.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Differentiates the stable extended-chain dispersion to locate the coupling threshold, interior maximum, and conservative negative-group interval.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats a two-site spring as another nearest-neighbor term.
commonErrors.consequence: The dispersion, sound speed, and threshold are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Equates negative group velocity with negative squared frequency or damping.
commonErrors.consequence: A stable conservative branch is misclassified.

hintTree.content: Obtain $\omega^2=(4/m)[K_1\sin^2(q/2)+K_2\sin^2q]$.
Differentiate the bracket to get $\sin q(K_1/2+2K_2\cos q)$.
At small $q$, retain both the $q^2/4$ and $q^2$ contributions.

WAVE:010540.canonicalSolution:
The plane-wave substitution gives
$$
\boxed{\omega^2(q)=\frac4m\left[K_1\sin^2\frac q2
+K_2\sin^2q\right]}.
$$
Both terms are nonnegative, so the branch is stable. Differentiating the
bracket gives
$$
\sin q\left(\frac{K_1}{2}+2K_2\cos q\right).
$$
Besides $q=0,\pi$, an interior stationary point satisfies
$$
\boxed{\cos q_*=-\frac{K_1}{4K_2}}.
$$
It exists precisely when $K_2>K_1/4$. The derivative changes from positive to
negative there, so it is a maximum. Between $q_*$ and $\pi$, $d\omega/dk<0$:
the energy transported by a localized packet has negative velocity even
though $k$ and $\omega$ are positive. Frequencies between the zone-edge value
and the maximum occur at two distinct positive wavenumbers on the same single
polarization branch.

At small $q$,
$$
\omega^2\sim\frac{a^2k^2}{m}(K_1+4K_2),
$$
so
$$
\boxed{c_s=a\sqrt{(K_1+4K_2)/m}}.
$$
For the data, $K_2=K_1/2$ and
$$
\boxed{q_*=\arccos(-1/2)=2\pi/3=2.09440}.
$$
At this point the dimensionless spring bracket is
$20(3/4)+10(3/4)=22.5\,\mathrm{N/m}$, giving
$$
\boxed{\omega_*=\sqrt{4(22.5)/0.5}=13.4164\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
At $q=\pi$, only nearest neighbors contribute:
$$
\boxed{\omega_{\rm edge}=2\sqrt{K_1/m}=12.6491\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
Finally,
$$
\boxed{c_s=0.100\sqrt{60/0.500}=1.09545\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The descending branch is conservative; negative group velocity is an energy
transport direction, not negative energy or attenuation.

WAVE:010541.title: Two cold counterstreams turn a real dispersion branch into growth
WAVE:010541.objective: Derive the equal-beam cold two-stream dispersion relation, its complete branches, instability band, and fastest growth with explicit conventions.
WAVE:010541.statement:
A one-dimensional, collisionless, cold electron
plasma consists of two beams of equal density $n_0/2$ moving at equilibrium
velocities $+U$ and $-U$. Immobile ions supply a uniform neutralizing
background. Define the plasma frequency from the total electron density by
$\omega_p^2=n_0e^2/(m\epsilon_0)$. Consider longitudinal electrostatic
perturbations proportional to $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$.

Linearize the cold continuity and momentum equations for both beams and
Poisson's equation to derive the dielectric dispersion relation. Reduce it to
a quadratic equation for $x=\omega^2$ and give both $x_\pm(k)$. Enumerate the
frequency branches, determine exactly when the lower branch is unstable, and
choose the growing sign consistently with $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$. Maximize the
growth rate over $k$ and report both the fastest wavenumber and growth rate.
Discuss $k=0$, the instability boundary, and the stable large-$k$ regime.

For $\omega_p=1.00\times10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and
$U=2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, report the unstable $k$ interval,
$k_{\max}$, and $\gamma_{\max}$. At $k=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, compute the
growing rate and the positive upper-branch frequency. State the physical
assumptions that would fail for warm, collisional, electromagnetic, or
unequal-beam plasmas rather than applying this formula beyond its model.
permittedResults: The cold beam susceptibility is $-\omega_{pb}^2/(\omega-kU_b)^2$.
A negative root $x=\omega^2$ produces the pair $\omega=\pm i\sqrt{-x}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Linearize both cold beams and combine their Doppler-shifted susceptibilities.
Start from the dielectric function, reduce to a quadratic in $omega^2$, and analyze its lower root.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the correctly normalized symmetric cold two-stream dielectric and obtains its full branch structure, finite instability band, and fastest growing mode.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the total $omega_p^2$ contribution to each half-density beam.
commonErrors.consequence: The band, frequencies, and growth maximum are all mis-scaled.

commonErrors.description: Chooses $omega=-igamma$ as the growing branch under $e^{i(kx-omega t)}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated growing solution actually decays.

commonErrors.description: Applies the cold electrostatic result unchanged to warm or unequal beams.
commonErrors.consequence: Physical effects excluded from the dielectric function are silently ignored.

hintTree.content: Each beam has plasma-frequency square $\omega_p^2/2$.
Combine the two shifted denominators before setting $x=\omega^2$ and $a=k^2U^2$.
Differentiate $\gamma^2$ with respect to $a$, not $k$.

WAVE:010541.canonicalSolution:
For beam $s=\pm$, the linearized continuity and
momentum equations give a density response proportional to
$(\omega-skU)^{-2}$. Poisson's equation therefore gives
$$
\boxed{\epsilon(\omega,k)=1-\frac{\omega_p^2/2}{(\omega-kU)^2}
-\frac{\omega_p^2/2}{(\omega+kU)^2}=0}.
$$
Let $x=\omega^2$ and $a=k^2U^2$. Combining fractions yields
$$
(x-a)^2-\omega_p^2(x+a)=0,
$$
or
$$
x^2-(2a+\omega_p^2)x+a(a-\omega_p^2)=0.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{x_\pm=a+\frac{\omega_p^2}{2}
\pm\frac{\omega_p}{2}\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}}.
$$
The upper root is positive. The lower root is negative exactly when
$0<a<\omega_p^2$, equivalently
$$
\boxed{0<|k|U<\omega_p}.
$$
The branches are $\omega=\pm\sqrt{x_+}$ and, when $x_->0$,
$\omega=\pm\sqrt{x_-}$. In the unstable band the lower pair is
$\omega=\pm i\gamma$ with
$$
\gamma^2=\frac{\omega_p}{2}\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}
-a-\frac{\omega_p^2}{2}.
$$
The growing sign is $\omega=+i\gamma$, because
$e^{-i(i\gamma)t}=e^{\gamma t}$.

Differentiating with respect to $a$ gives
$d\gamma^2/da=2\omega_p/\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}-1$. The maximum occurs at
$$
\boxed{a_{\max}=3\omega_p^2/8},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{|k_{\max}|U=\sqrt{3/8}\,\omega_p},\qquad
\boxed{\gamma_{\max}=\frac{\omega_p}{2\sqrt2}}.
$$
At $k=0$, the polynomial branches limit to $x_+=\omega_p^2$ and $x_-=0$.
The susceptibility formula itself divided by $\omega^2$ and is singular at
that zero root; in the full cold-fluid equations it is the limiting neutral,
charge-canceling beam-density rearrangement, not strict exponential growth.
At $|k|U=\omega_p$, the lower
root again reaches zero. Beyond it both roots are positive and all four cold
fluid frequencies are real.

For the numerical values the unstable interval is
$$
\boxed{0<|k|<5.00000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
$$
The fastest values are
$$
\boxed{|k_{\max}|=3.06186\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\gamma_{\max}=3.53553\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
At $k=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $kU=4.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The lower root is $x_-=-9.49834\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ and the
upper is $x_+=1.41498\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, giving
$$
\boxed{\gamma=3.08194\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=1.18953\times10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

This derivation assumes one spatial dimension, cold pressureless fluids,
equal beam densities and speeds, immobile neutralizing ions, no collisions,
and longitudinal electrostatic perturbations. Thermal velocity spread changes
the susceptibilities and introduces kinetic effects such as Landau response;
collisions, electromagnetic fields, or unequal beams require different
dispersion relations.

graderFixtures.proofText:
For beam $s=\pm$, the linearized continuity and
momentum equations give a density response proportional to
$(\omega-skU)^{-2}$. Poisson's equation therefore gives
$$
\boxed{\epsilon(\omega,k)=1-\frac{\omega_p^2/2}{(\omega-kU)^2}
-\frac{\omega_p^2/2}{(\omega+kU)^2}=0}.
$$
Let $x=\omega^2$ and $a=k^2U^2$. Combining fractions yields
$$
(x-a)^2-\omega_p^2(x+a)=0,
$$
or
$$
x^2-(2a+\omega_p^2)x+a(a-\omega_p^2)=0.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{x_\pm=a+\frac{\omega_p^2}{2}
\pm\frac{\omega_p}{2}\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}}.
$$
The upper root is positive. The lower root is negative exactly when
$0<a<\omega_p^2$, equivalently
$$
\boxed{0<|k|U<\omega_p}.
$$
The branches are $\omega=\pm\sqrt{x_+}$ and, when $x_->0$,
$\omega=\pm\sqrt{x_-}$. In the unstable band the lower pair is
$\omega=\pm i\gamma$ with
$$
\gamma^2=\frac{\omega_p}{2}\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}
-a-\frac{\omega_p^2}{2}.
$$
The growing sign is $\omega=+i\gamma$, because
$e^{-i(i\gamma)t}=e^{\gamma t}$.

Differentiating with respect to $a$ gives
$d\gamma^2/da=2\omega_p/\sqrt{\omega_p^2+8a}-1$. The maximum occurs at
$$
\boxed{a_{\max}=3\omega_p^2/8},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{|k_{\max}|U=\sqrt{3/8}\,\omega_p},\qquad
\boxed{\gamma_{\max}=\frac{\omega_p}{2\sqrt2}}.
$$
At $k=0$, the polynomial branches limit to $x_+=\omega_p^2$ and $x_-=0$.
The susceptibility formula itself divided by $\omega^2$ and is singular at
that zero root; in the full cold-fluid equations it is the limiting neutral,
charge-canceling beam-density rearrangement, not strict exponential growth.
At $|k|U=\omega_p$, the lower
root again reaches zero. Beyond it both roots are positive and all four cold
fluid frequencies are real.

For the numerical values the unstable interval is
$$
\boxed{0<|k|<5.00000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.
$$
The fastest values are
$$
\boxed{|k_{\max}|=3.06186\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\gamma_{\max}=3.53553\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
At $k=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $kU=4.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The lower root is $x_-=-9.49834\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ and the
upper is $x_+=1.41498\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, giving
$$
\boxed{\gamma=3.08194\times10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_+=1.18953\times10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

This derivation assumes one spatial dimension, cold pressureless fluids,
equal beam densities and speeds, immobile neutralizing ions, no collisions,
and longitudinal electrostatic perturbations. Thermal velocity spread changes
the susceptibilities and introduces kinetic effects such as Landau response;
collisions, electromagnetic fields, or unequal beams require different
dispersion relations.
I use $omega_p^2$ for each beam, select $-igamma$ as growth, and claim the same band holds unchanged with thermal spread and collisions.
