WAVE:010542.title: Oblique magnetic sound sends its slow-wave energy along the field
WAVE:010542.objective: Derive the Alfvén and fast/slow magnetosonic branches of uniform ideal MHD and distinguish wave-normal phase speed from anisotropic group transport.
WAVE:010542.statement:
A uniform, stationary ideal-MHD plasma has density
$\rho_0$, adiabatic sound speed $c_s$, and magnetic field
$\mathbf B_0=B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Define
$$
v_A=\frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_0}}.
$$
Neglect gravity, resistivity, viscosity, Hall terms, and equilibrium gradients.
For linear perturbations proportional to
$e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r-\omega t)}$, take
$\mathbf k=(k_x,0,k_z)=k(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta)$ with
$k>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$, and use $p_1=c_s^2\rho_1$.

Starting from continuity, momentum, and ideal induction, eliminate the density,
pressure, and magnetic perturbations. Isolate the shear Alfvén polarization and
construct the two-by-two compressional matrix for $(v_x,v_z)$. Derive all three
positive-frequency dispersion branches. For each magnetosonic branch, give
$v_z/v_x$ and identify whether the numerical components are in phase or in
opposite phase.

Although every ideal branch is homogeneous of degree one in $k$, the phase
speed depends on direction. Derive the full group-velocity vector of the fast
and slow branches, not just $\omega/k$, and derive the Alfvén group velocity
for $k_z>0$. For $c_s=6.00\,\mathrm{km/s}$,
$v_A=10.0\,\mathrm{km/s}$, $\theta=60.0^\circ$, and
$k=2.00\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, report phase speeds, angular
frequencies, polarization ratios, group-velocity components, and ray angles
measured from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ toward $+\hat{\mathbf x}$. Audit the limits
$\theta\to0$, $\theta\to\pi/2$, $v_A\to0$, and $c_s\to0$, and state the
scale restrictions under which ideal MHD is valid.
permittedResults: The ideal induction equation linearized about a uniform field is $\partial_t\mathbf b=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B_0)$.
If $\omega=k c(\theta)$ in the $x$-$z$ plane, then $\mathbf v_g=c\hat{\mathbf k}+c'(\theta)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ with $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=(\cos\theta,0,-\sin\theta)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Eliminate thermodynamic and magnetic perturbations, separate the shear polarization, and diagonalize the compressional matrix.
Project momentum parallel and perpendicular to the background field, then differentiate the resulting angular phase speeds.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives all three oblique ideal-MHD wave branches and correctly converts angular phase-speed anisotropy into branch-dependent group rays and polarizations.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Adds or subtracts $v_A$ and $c_s$ directly instead of solving the angular quadratic for squared speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The fast and slow branches, their degeneracies, and their oblique limits are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets group velocity equal to $c_pmhat{mathbf k}$ despite angular phase-speed dependence.
commonErrors.consequence: The transverse angular derivative and the field-guided slow-wave energy ray are lost.

commonErrors.description: Mixes the $y$-polarized Alfvén branch into the compressional eigenvector or omits it.
commonErrors.consequence: The three-branch ideal-MHD spectrum and polarization structure are incomplete.

hintTree.content: The $y$ momentum equation decouples and gives the shear Alfvén branch.
Use $k_x=k\sin\theta$ and $k_z=k\cos\theta$ only after taking the compressional determinant.
Differentiate $c_\pm^2(\theta)$ first; radial differentiation alone misses the angular component of group velocity.

WAVE:010542.canonicalSolution:
The linearized continuity and adiabatic closure give
$$
\rho_1=\frac{\rho_0}{\omega}(k_xv_x+k_zv_z),
\qquad p_1=c_s^2\rho_1.
$$
The induction equation gives
$$
\boxed{\mathbf b=\frac{B_0}{\omega}
(-k_zv_x,-k_zv_y,k_xv_x)},
$$
which automatically satisfies $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf b=0$. Substitution in
the linearized momentum equation separates the $y$ polarization:
$$
\boxed{\omega_A^2=v_A^2k_z^2},\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf v_A\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}}.
$$
For $k_z>0$ and the positive-frequency branch,
$\omega_A=v_Ak_z$.

The compressional components obey
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\omega^2-v_A^2k^2-c_s^2k_x^2&-c_s^2k_xk_z\\
-c_s^2k_xk_z&\omega^2-c_s^2k_z^2
\end{pmatrix}
\binom{v_x}{v_z}=0.
$$
Its determinant is
$$
\omega^4-k^2(v_A^2+c_s^2)\omega^2
+v_A^2c_s^2k^2k_z^2=0.
$$
Define
$$
D(\theta)=\sqrt{(v_A^2+c_s^2)^2
-4v_A^2c_s^2\cos^2\theta}.
$$
The fast $(+)$ and slow $(-)$ phase speeds and positive-frequency branches are
$$
\boxed{c_\pm^2(\theta)=\frac12[v_A^2+c_s^2\pm D(\theta)]},
\qquad
\boxed{\omega_\pm=kc_\pm}.
$$
The second row of the matrix gives the branch polarization
$$
\boxed{\frac{v_z}{v_x}=
\frac{c_s^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}
{c_\pm^2-c_s^2\cos^2\theta}}.
$$
This ratio is to be evaluated by a limiting eigenvector at special degeneracies
where both numerator and denominator vanish.

The medium is uniform but anisotropic. Differentiating the angular phase speed
gives
$$
\boxed{c_\pm'(\theta)=\pm
\frac{v_A^2c_s^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{c_\pm D}}.
$$
Since $\hat{\mathbf k}=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta)$ and
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=(\cos\theta,0,-\sin\theta)$,
$$
\boxed{v_{gx,\pm}=c_\pm\sin\theta+c_\pm'\cos\theta},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_{gz,\pm}=c_\pm\cos\theta-c_\pm'\sin\theta}.
$$
Thus degree-one dispersion does not force $\mathbf v_g$ to be parallel to
$\mathbf k$ when $c$ depends on direction. For the positive-$k_z$ Alfvén
branch, $\omega_A=v_Ak_z$, so
$$
\boxed{\mathbf v_{g,A}=v_A\hat{\mathbf z}},
$$
even though its wave normal can be oblique.

For the stated values,
$$
D=122.049\,(\mathrm{km/s})^2,
$$
and
$$
\boxed{c_+=11.3589\,\mathrm{km/s}},\qquad
\boxed{c_-=2.64110\,\mathrm{km/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_A/k=5.00000\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
At $k=2.00\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{\omega_+=0.227178\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_-=0.0528220\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_A=0.100000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The polarization ratios are
$$
\boxed{(v_z/v_x)_+=0.129877},\qquad
\boxed{(v_z/v_x)_-=-7.69958}.
$$
The fast compressional components are in phase, whereas the slow branch has
opposite-sign $x$ and $z$ velocity components in this eigenvector convention.
The angular derivatives are
$c_+'=1.12443\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and
$c_-'=-4.83597\,\mathrm{km/s}$ per radian. Therefore
$$
\boxed{\mathbf v_{g,+}=(10.3993,0,4.70567)\,\mathrm{km/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\mathbf v_{g,-}=(-0.130723,0,5.50862)\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
Their ray angles from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ toward $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ are
$$
\boxed{\theta_{g,+}=65.6533^\circ},\qquad
\boxed{\theta_{g,-}=-1.35941^\circ}.
$$
The slow-wave energy ray is nearly field-aligned and is slightly on the
negative-$x$ side even though the wave normal has positive $k_x$. The Alfvén
ray is exactly field-aligned with
$\mathbf v_{g,A}=(0,0,10.0000)\,\mathrm{km/s}$.

For parallel propagation, the magnetosonic phase speeds reduce to
$\max(v_A,c_s)$ and $\min(v_A,c_s)$, while the shear Alfvén speed is $v_A$;
the labels meet degeneracies according to the ordering of $v_A$ and $c_s$.
For perpendicular propagation, $c_+=\sqrt{v_A^2+c_s^2}$ and both the ideal
slow and shear-Alfvén frequencies vanish. As $v_A\to0$, the fast branch becomes
ordinary sound and the other restoring magnetic branches collapse to zero.
As $c_s\to0$, the fast speed becomes $v_A$, the slow speed collapses, and the
shear branch remains $v_A|\cos\theta|$.

The model requires linear amplitudes, a uniform equilibrium, wavelengths long
compared with kinetic scales such as gyroradii and inertial lengths, frequencies
well below relevant cyclotron frequencies, an adiabatic fluid closure, and
negligible resistive and viscous damping. Outside those conditions Hall,
finite-Larmor-radius, kinetic, dissipative, or inhomogeneous-plasma corrections
change the dispersion and polarization.

WAVE:010543.title: A lattice band edge stops packets and piles up states
WAVE:010543.objective: Derive a monoatomic lattice density of states and relate its band-edge singularity to vanishing group speed and Gaussian packet spreading.
WAVE:010543.statement:
An infinite monoatomic chain has mass $m$, spacing $a$, and
nearest-neighbor spring stiffness $K$:
$$
m\ddot u_n=K(u_{n+1}-2u_n+u_{n-1}).
$$
Use real $k$ in the first Brillouin zone and the positive-frequency branch.

Derive the dispersion relation and group velocity. Counting both signs of
$k$, derive the density of positive-frequency modes per unit length per unit
angular frequency. Verify its integral over the band gives one mode per
lattice site and obtain both the acoustic low-frequency limit and the
band-edge singularity. Explain physically why the density diverges where the
group speed vanishes.

For a narrow Gaussian packet centered at $k_0>0$, let its initial intensity
RMS width be $\sigma_{x0}$ and assume the quadratic expansion of
$\omega(k)$ is valid. Derive its center motion and RMS width versus time.
For $m=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg}$, $K=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$a=0.0500\,\mathrm m$, $k_0a=\pi/2$, $\sigma_{x0}=0.200\,\mathrm m$, and
$t=2.00\,\mathrm s$, compute the band edge, carrier frequency, group speed,
$\omega''(k_0)$, center displacement, final RMS width, and density of states
at the carrier. State the narrowband and infinite-chain assumptions.
permittedResults: In one dimension, each periodic-box wave number occupies $2\pi/L$ and $g(\omega)=\pi^{-1}|dk/d\omega|$ after counting $\pm k$.
A minimum-uncertainty Gaussian with initial intensity width $\sigma_{x0}$ broadens under quadratic dispersion to $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_{x0}^2+[\omega''t/(2\sigma_{x0})]^2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Invert the positive dispersion branch and count both wave-number signs in a long periodic box.
Use $gpropto1/|v_g|$ for the state density, then expand the phase to second order for the packet.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the one-dimensional mode density from the same dispersion derivatives that govern packet transport and spreading.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Counts only positive wave numbers while claiming the full one-dimensional density.
commonErrors.consequence: The density integrates to half a mode per site.

commonErrors.description: Uses group velocity alone and claims the finite-width packet never broadens.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonzero dispersion curvature is omitted.

hintTree.content: Insert $u_n=Ue^{i(kna-\omega t)}$ and keep the positive square root.
Invert $\omega=2\sqrt{K/m}\sin(ka/2)$ for $0<k<\pi/a$.
The packet center uses $\omega'$ while its broadening uses $\omega''$.

WAVE:010543.canonicalSolution:
The Bloch substitution gives
$$
m\omega^2=4K\sin^2\frac{ka}{2}.
$$
Writing $\omega_s=\sqrt{K/m}$, the positive branch is
$$
\boxed{\omega(k)=2\omega_s\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|}.
$$
For $0<k<\pi/a$,
$$
\boxed{v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}=a\omega_s\cos\frac{ka}{2}},
$$
and the upper band edge is $2\omega_s$.

Both $+k$ and $-k$ contribute. Since
$$
k(\omega)=\frac2a\arcsin\frac{\omega}{2\omega_s},
$$
the density per length is
$$
\boxed{g(\omega)=\frac{1}{\pi a\omega_s
\sqrt{1-(\omega/2\omega_s)^2}}},\qquad 0<\omega<2\omega_s.
$$
Its normalization is
$$
\int_0^{2\omega_s}g(\omega)d\omega=\frac1a,
$$
one mode per site per unit length. At low frequency,
$g\to1/(\pi a\omega_s)=1/(\pi c)$ with acoustic speed
$c=a\omega_s$. Near the upper edge the square root in the denominator
vanishes, producing the one-dimensional inverse-square-root Van Hove
singularity. Equivalently $g\propto1/|v_g|$: many wave numbers are squeezed
into a small frequency interval when the group speed approaches zero.

For a narrow unchirped Gaussian packet, the quadratic dispersion expansion
gives
$$
\boxed{x_c(t)=x_c(0)+v_g(k_0)t},
$$
$$
\boxed{\sigma_x(t)=\sigma_{x0}
\sqrt{1+\left[\frac{\omega''(k_0)t}{2\sigma_{x0}^2}\right]^2}},
$$
where
$$
\omega''(k_0)=-\frac{a^2\omega_s}{2}\sin\frac{k_0a}{2}.
$$

Numerically, $\omega_s=100.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and the band edge is
$\boxed{200.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. At $k_0a=\pi/2$,
$$
\boxed{k_0=31.4159\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_0=141.421\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_g=3.53553\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega''=-8.83883\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}}.
$$
After $2.00\,\mathrm s$, the center has advanced
$\boxed{7.07107\,\mathrm m}$ and
$$
\boxed{\sigma_x=0.485090\,\mathrm m}.
$$
At the carrier,
$$
\boxed{g(\omega_0)=9.00316\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s/m}}.
$$
The packet formula assumes its wave-number spread is small enough that cubic
and higher dispersion are negligible and small enough not to sample the
Brillouin-zone edge. The state count assumes an effectively infinite or very
long periodic chain; a finite chain replaces the singular continuum by
discrete modes.

\int_0^{2\omega_s}g(\omega)d\omega=\frac1a,
$$
one mode per site per unit length. At low frequency,
$g\to1/(\pi a\omega_s)=1/(\pi c)$ with acoustic speed
$c=a\omega_s$. Near the upper edge the square root in the denominator
vanishes, producing the one-dimensional inverse-square-root Van Hove
singularity. Equivalently $g\propto1/|v_g|$: many wave numbers are squeezed
into a small frequency interval when the group speed approaches zero.

For a narrow unchirped Gaussian packet, the quadratic dispersion expansion
gives
$$
\boxed{x_c(t)=x_c(0)+v_g(k_0)t},
$$
$$
\boxed{\sigma_x(t)=\sigma_{x0}
\sqrt{1+\left[\frac{\omega''(k_0)t}{2\sigma_{x0}^2}\right]^2}},
$$
where
$$
\omega''(k_0)=-\frac{a^2\omega_s}{2}\sin\frac{k_0a}{2}.
$$

Numerically, $\omega_s=100.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and the band edge is
$\boxed{200.000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. At $k_0a=\pi/2$,
$$
\boxed{k_0=31.4159\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_0=141.421\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_g=3.53553\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\omega''=-8.83883\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}}.
$$
After $2.00\,\mathrm s$, the center has advanced
$\boxed{7.07107\,\mathrm m}$ and
$$
\boxed{\sigma_x=0.485090\,\mathrm m}.
$$
At the carrier,
$$
\boxed{g(\omega_0)=9.00316\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s/m}}.
$$
The packet formula assumes its wave-number spread is small enough that cubic
and higher dispersion are negligible and small enough not to sample the
Brillouin-zone edge. The state count assumes an effectively infinite or very
long periodic chain; a finite chain replaces the singular continuum by
discrete modes.
I count only $k>0$ but call it the full density, so the integral gives $1/(2a)$. I then translate every packet rigidly with $v_g$ and ignore $omega''$.

WAVE:010544.title: Quadratic dispersion can first compress a chirped Gaussian and then broaden it
WAVE:010544.objective: Propagate a chirped Gaussian through quadratic dispersion and solve for its compression distance, minimum width, residual chirp, and peak scaling.
WAVE:010544.statement:
Use
$$
\widetilde A(\Omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}A(t)e^{i\Omega t}dt,
\qquad
A(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int\widetilde A(\Omega)e^{-i\Omega t}d\Omega.
$$
At $z=0$ let
$$
A(t,0)=A_0\exp\left[-\frac{(1+iC)t^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right],
$$
with real $C$. Propagation through a lossless quadratic-dispersion section
multiplies the spectrum by $\exp(i\beta_2z\Omega^2/2)$, where the sign of
$\beta_2$ is part of this convention.

Evaluate the propagated Gaussian exactly up to its overall complex phase.
Derive the output chirp, intensity RMS width, compression condition and
distance, minimum width, and the conserved-energy implications for peak
intensity and peak amplitude. State the sign condition for a positive
compression distance and show that the pulse re-broadens after its transform
limit. Contrast this propagation/design calculation with merely transforming
the initial chirped Gaussian or rotating it by a fractional Fourier transform.

For $\tau_0=2.00\,\mathrm{ps}$, $C=3.00$, and
$\beta_2=-20.0\,\mathrm{ps^2/km}$, calculate the compression distance,
initial and minimum RMS widths, peak intensity and amplitude factors. At
$z=0.100\,\mathrm{km}$ calculate the residual chirp, RMS width, and peak
intensity factor. State the second-order, lossless, infinite-bandwidth model
limits.
permittedResults: A Gaussian with spectral quadratic coefficient $Q$ transforms back with temporal coefficient $Q^{-1}$.
A unit-modulus spectral phase preserves $\int|A|^2dt$ by Parseval.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the initial Gaussian, add the propagation phase, and invert the combined complex quadratic coefficient.
Track the temporal covariance under the dispersion shear and minimize its time variance over distance.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the evolving spectral quadratic phase to solve a physical compression design problem while preserving energy and tracking the chirp sign.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive compression length when $C\beta_2>0$ under the stated phase convention.
commonErrors.consequence: The device increases the initial chirp instead of cancelling it.

commonErrors.description: Lets width shrink without increasing peak intensity at fixed energy, or equates intensity and amplitude factors.
commonErrors.consequence: The lossless Parseval ledger and field scaling are violated.

hintTree.content: The effective spectral coefficient is $(1+iC)^{-1}\tau_0^2-i\beta_2z$.
Define $B=\beta_2z/\tau_0^2$ and $s=C+(1+C^2)B$.
At fixed energy, peak intensity is inversely proportional to the Gaussian width parameter.

WAVE:010544.canonicalSolution:
The input temporal quadratic coefficient is
$q_0=(1+iC)/\tau_0^2$. Its spectrum is proportional to
$$
q_0^{-1/2}\exp\left[-\frac{\Omega^2}{2q_0}\right].
$$
After propagation, the spectral quadratic coefficient is
$q_0^{-1}-i\beta_2z$, so the output temporal coefficient is
$$
q(z)=\frac1{q_0^{-1}-i\beta_2z}.
$$
Let
$$
B=\frac{\beta_2z}{\tau_0^2},\qquad
s=C+(1+C^2)B.
$$
Algebra gives
$$
\boxed{q(z)=\frac{1+C^2}{\tau_0^2}
\frac{1+is}{1+s^2}}.
$$
Thus, apart from normalization and overall phase, the pulse can be written
with output width parameter
$$
\tau(z)=\tau_0\sqrt{\frac{1+s^2}{1+C^2}}
$$
and output chirp
$$
\boxed{C_{\rm out}=s=C+(1+C^2)\frac{\beta_2z}{\tau_0^2}}.
$$
Since intensity is proportional to $e^{-t^2/\tau(z)^2}$, its RMS width is
$$
\boxed{\sigma_t(z)=\frac{\tau_0}{\sqrt{2(1+C^2)}}\sqrt{1+s^2}}.
$$

Compression reaches its minimum when $s=0$:
$$
\boxed{z_*=-\frac{C\tau_0^2}{\beta_2(1+C^2)}}.
$$
A positive device length therefore requires $C\beta_2<0$. The minimum is
$$
\boxed{\sigma_{\min}=\frac{\tau_0}{\sqrt{2(1+C^2)}}},
$$
while $\sigma_0=\tau_0/\sqrt2$. The spectrum magnitude and total energy are
unchanged. Hence the peak-intensity ratio is
$$
\boxed{\frac{I_{\rm pk}(z)}{I_{\rm pk}(0)}
=\frac{\sqrt{1+C^2}}{\sqrt{1+s^2}}},
$$
and the field-amplitude ratio is its square root. At the minimum these factors
are $\sqrt{1+C^2}$ and $(1+C^2)^{1/4}$. For $z$ beyond $z_*$, $s$ changes
sign and grows in magnitude, so the pulse acquires opposite chirp and
re-broadens.

Numerically,
$$
\boxed{z_*=0.0600000\,\mathrm{km}=60.0000\,\mathrm m}.
$$
The initial and minimum RMS widths are
$$
\boxed{\sigma_0=1.41421\,\mathrm{ps}},\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_{\min}=0.447214\,\mathrm{ps}}.
$$
At the minimum the peak-intensity factor is
$\boxed{\sqrt{10}=3.16228}$ and the peak-amplitude factor is
$\boxed{10^{1/4}=1.77828}$.

At $z=0.100\,\mathrm{km}$, $B=-0.500000$ and
$$
\boxed{C_{\rm out}=s=-2.00000}.
$$
The RMS width is
$$
\boxed{\sigma_t=1.00000\,\mathrm{ps}},
$$
and the peak-intensity factor relative to input is
$\boxed{\sqrt{10/5}=1.41421}$. This task uses the already declared spectral
phase to determine physical propagation length and compression. It does not
redo the initial time--frequency covariance calculation or a fractional
Fourier phase-space rotation. Higher dispersion, loss, nonlinear phase,
finite bandwidth, and non-Gaussian structure can all change the optimum and
are excluded here.

WAVE:010545.title: Above a waveguide cutoff, phase outruns the signal
WAVE:010545.objective: Derive Klein--Gordon cutoff dispersion, relate phase and group speeds, and separate evanescent penetration and phase speed from causal front propagation.
WAVE:010545.statement:
A scalar field satisfies the one-dimensional
Klein--Gordon wave equation
$$u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}+\omega_c^2u=0,$$
where $c>0$ and $\omega_c>0$. This equation also models one ideal waveguide
mode above its transverse cutoff.

Derive the real traveling-wave dispersion relation and compute phase velocity,
group velocity, their product, and the curvature $d^2\omega/dk^2$. Audit the
limits $k\to0$ and $|k|\to\infty$. For a boundary driven at a prescribed
positive frequency $\Omega<\omega_c$, derive the evanescent decay constant
and penetration length. Explain why a phase velocity larger than $c$ does
not transmit information faster than $c$, and why a single decaying
evanescent exponential should not be assigned the real-wave group velocity.

For $c=200\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\omega_c=100\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$k=0.750\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, calculate $\omega$, phase and group velocities,
their product, and dispersion curvature. For a drive
$\Omega=80.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, calculate the evanescent decay constant and
penetration length. State how loss or a finite below-cutoff section would
extend the ideal model.
permittedResults: For a narrow real-$k$ packet, $v_g=d\omega/dk$ governs its leading envelope motion when higher dispersion is weak.
The principal part $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}$ has characteristic speed $c$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the plane-wave spectrum and analytically continue wavenumber below cutoff.
Use the waveguide-mode energy picture to obtain group speed, then verify it by differentiating the Klein--Gordon branch.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the same dispersion relation on real and imaginary wavenumber branches without turning superluminal phase or evanescent decay into superluminal information transport.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Derives $\omega^2=c^2k^2-\omega_c^2$ from the stated PDE.
commonErrors.consequence: The cutoff, velocities, and evanescent branch are all reversed.

commonErrors.description: Identifies $v_p>c$ as the causal signal or front speed.
commonErrors.consequence: A crest velocity is confused with transport of newly introduced information.

hintTree.content: Substitute $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ and retain the sign of the $\omega_c^2$ term.
Differentiate the positive branch $\omega=(\omega_c^2+c^2k^2)^{1/2}$.
Below cutoff set $k=i\kappa$ with $\kappa>0$ for decay into $x>0$.

WAVE:010545.canonicalSolution:
A plane-wave substitution gives
$$
\boxed{\omega^2=\omega_c^2+c^2k^2}.
$$
On the positive-frequency branch and for $k>0$,
$$
\boxed{v_p=\frac\omega k},\qquad
\boxed{v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}=\frac{c^2k}{\omega}},\qquad
\boxed{v_pv_g=c^2}.
$$
Thus $v_p>c$ and $0<v_g<c$. Differentiating once more yields
$$
\boxed{\omega''(k)=\frac{c^2\omega_c^2}{\omega^3}}>0.
$$
As $k\to0^+$, $\omega\to\omega_c$, $v_g\to0$, and $v_p\to\infty$.
As $k\to\infty$, both velocities approach $c$ from below and above,
respectively, while the curvature vanishes.

For a prescribed frequency below cutoff, solve the same dispersion relation
for wavenumber:
$$
k^2=\frac{\Omega^2-\omega_c^2}{c^2}=-\kappa^2,\qquad
\boxed{\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{\omega_c^2-\Omega^2}}{c}},
$$
so a field entering $x>0$ has factor $e^{-\kappa x}$ and penetration length
$$
\boxed{\ell_{\rm ev}=\kappa^{-1}}.
$$
This isolated exponential has imaginary $k$, not a narrow packet on the real
dispersion branch; assigning it the above real-$k$ group velocity has no
meaning. A finite barrier can transmit through interference of both boundary
solutions, but that is a separate scattering calculation.

The super-$c$ phase speed tracks constant-phase crests, which carry no
independently switchable new information. The PDE's principal wave operator
has characteristics $dx/dt=\pm c$, so a causal front cannot outrun $c$ in
this ideal model. The high-frequency limit also approaches that same front
speed.

Numerically
$$
\boxed{\omega=180.278\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{v_p=240.370\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_g=166.410\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{v_pv_g=4.00000\times10^4\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}}.
$$
The curvature is
$\boxed{\omega''=68.2708\,\mathrm{m^2/s}}$. At
$\Omega=80.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{\kappa=0.300000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\ell_{\rm ev}=3.33333\,\mathrm m}.
$$
Material loss makes $k$ complex even above cutoff and changes energy velocity.
A finite below-cutoff section needs both exponentials and interface matching,
producing nonzero tunneling rather than the semi-infinite decay considered
here.

WAVE:010546.title: Long waves in a telegraph medium stop oscillating before they stop evolving
WAVE:010546.objective: Analyze temporal and spatial dispersion of the damped wave equation without confusing overdamped modes, complex wavenumbers, group slopes, or causal fronts.
WAVE:010546.statement:
A real field on a uniform medium satisfies the
telegraph equation
$$
u_{tt}+2\gamma u_t-c^2u_{xx}=0,
$$
with $c>0$ and $\gamma>0$. Treat first an unbounded or periodic medium so
that boundary power terms vanish.

For a real spatial Fourier wavenumber $k$, derive both complex temporal
frequencies using $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$. Classify the underdamped and
overdamped ranges and find the critical wavenumber. In the overdamped range,
write the two real time exponents and explain why “nonpropagating” does not
mean “static.” In the underdamped range, derive the phase velocity and the
derivative of the real oscillation frequency. Explain why that derivative
can exceed $c$ near threshold without becoming a causal front speed.

Next prescribe a real drive frequency $\Omega>0$ into a semi-infinite medium
and derive the complex wavenumber with the sign chosen for decay into $x>0$.
Give phase and attenuation constants and penetration length. Derive the
energy-decay identity for free motion and audit the high-wavenumber and
zero-damping limits.

For $c=100\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\gamma=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, calculate the
critical wavenumber and the complex frequency, phase velocity, and real-branch
slope at $k=0.500\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. At $k=0.100\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, calculate
both decay exponents. For a real drive $\Omega=30.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
calculate complex wavenumber, phase velocity, and attenuation length. State
how boundary reflections or frequency-dependent damping would extend this
constant-coefficient model.
permittedResults: The principal part $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}$ has finite characteristic speed $c$ even when lower-order damping is present.
Multiplying the PDE by $u_t$ gives a mechanical energy identity after integration by parts.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the temporal quadratic for each real Fourier mode, then solve the same algebraic dispersion relation for complex wavenumber under real drive.
Remove the uniform temporal envelope in the underdamped regime and use energy estimates to audit damping and front propagation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Keeps real-wavenumber temporal decay, real-frequency spatial attenuation, dispersive slopes, and the causal front as distinct consequences of one damped PDE.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets all $|k|<\gamma/c$ modes to zero or static instead of retaining their two real decay exponents.
commonErrors.consequence: The long-wavelength initial-value dynamics are deleted.

commonErrors.description: Calls $d\Omega_k/dk>c$ near threshold the causal front speed.
commonErrors.consequence: A singular, strongly distorted packet slope is confused with the finite domain-of-dependence speed.

hintTree.content: The temporal quadratic is $\omega^2+2i\gamma\omega-c^2k^2=0$.
For overdamped modes it is cleaner to write $u_k\propto e^{st}$ and solve for real $s$.
For a real drive, choose the square-root branch of $k^2=(\Omega^2+2i\gamma\Omega)/c^2$ with positive imaginary part.

WAVE:010546.canonicalSolution:
Substitution of $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ gives
$$
\omega^2+2i\gamma\omega-c^2k^2=0,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{\omega_\pm=-i\gamma\pm\sqrt{c^2k^2-\gamma^2}}.
$$
The critical wavenumber is
$$
\boxed{k_c=\gamma/c}.
$$
For $|k|>k_c$, a mode oscillates at
$\Omega_k=\sqrt{c^2k^2-\gamma^2}$ under the envelope $e^{-\gamma t}$.
For $|k|<k_c$, the mode is overdamped; writing the time dependence as $e^{st}$ gives two real rates
$$
\boxed{s_\pm=-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-c^2k^2}}.
$$
Both are negative for nonzero $k$: a long Fourier component relaxes through
slow and fast exponentials rather than remaining static. At $k=0$, the
constant displacement mode has $s_+=0$ while its velocity transient decays.

On the positive underdamped branch,
$$
\boxed{v_p=\frac{\Omega_k}{k}},\qquad
\boxed{\frac{d\Omega_k}{dk}=\frac{c^2k}{\Omega_k}},
$$
and their product is $c^2$. Near $k_c$ the derivative diverges, but a narrow
packet there is strongly attenuated and highly distorted, so this slope is
not a front velocity. The PDE principal part still confines the earliest
causal disturbance to speed $c$. At large $|k|$, both real-branch velocities
approach $c$ and damping becomes a small fractional correction.

For a real drive $u\propto e^{i(kx-\Omega t)}$,
$$
\boxed{k^2=\frac{\Omega^2+2i\gamma\Omega}{c^2}}.
$$
Choose $k=\beta+i\alpha$ with $\alpha>0$ for decay $e^{-\alpha x}$ into
$x>0$. If $R=\sqrt{\Omega^4+4\gamma^2\Omega^2}$, then
$$
\boxed{\beta=\frac1c\sqrt{\frac{R+\Omega^2}{2}}},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\frac1c\sqrt{\frac{R-\Omega^2}{2}}},
$$
with driven phase velocity $\Omega/\beta$ and attenuation length $1/\alpha$.
Temporal and spatial formulations answer different experimental questions
and their imaginary parts must not be interchanged.

Define
$$
E=\frac12\int\left(u_t^2+c^2u_x^2\right)dx.
$$
Multiplying the PDE by $u_t$ and discarding boundary flux gives
$$
\boxed{\frac{dE}{dt}=-2\gamma\int u_t^2dx\le0}.
$$
When $\gamma\to0$, temporal frequencies become $\pm c|k|$, the driven
wavenumber becomes $\Omega/c$, and energy is conserved.

Numerically $\boxed{k_c=0.200000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}$. At
$k=0.500\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{\omega_+=45.8258-20.0000i\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_p=91.6515\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{d\Omega_k/dk=109.109\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The super-$c$ slope is not the front speed. At $k=0.100\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{s_+=-2.67949\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{s_-=-37.3205\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

$$
\boxed{k=0.346410+0.173205i\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_{p,\rm drive}=86.6025\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\ell_{\rm att}=5.77350\,\mathrm m}.
$$
Boundaries combine forward and reflected complex waves into resonances.
Frequency-dependent or memory damping replaces the constant $2\gamma$ by a
complex response kernel and requires a new causal dispersion relation.

Substitution of $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ gives
$$
\omega^2+2i\gamma\omega-c^2k^2=0,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{\omega_\pm=-i\gamma\pm\sqrt{c^2k^2-\gamma^2}}.
$$
The critical wavenumber is
$$
\boxed{k_c=\gamma/c}.
$$
For $|k|>k_c$, a mode oscillates at
$\Omega_k=\sqrt{c^2k^2-\gamma^2}$ under the envelope $e^{-\gamma t}$.
For $|k|<k_c$, the mode is overdamped; writing the time dependence as $e^{st}$ gives two real rates
$$
\boxed{s_\pm=-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-c^2k^2}}.
$$
Both are negative for nonzero $k$: a long Fourier component relaxes through
slow and fast exponentials rather than remaining static. At $k=0$, the
constant displacement mode has $s_+=0$ while its velocity transient decays.

On the positive underdamped branch,
$$
\boxed{v_p=\frac{\Omega_k}{k}},\qquad
\boxed{\frac{d\Omega_k}{dk}=\frac{c^2k}{\Omega_k}},
$$
and their product is $c^2$. Near $k_c$ the derivative diverges, but a narrow
packet there is strongly attenuated and highly distorted, so this slope is
not a front velocity. The PDE principal part still confines the earliest
causal disturbance to speed $c$. At large $|k|$, both real-branch velocities
approach $c$ and damping becomes a small fractional correction.

For a real drive $u\propto e^{i(kx-\Omega t)}$,
$$
\boxed{k^2=\frac{\Omega^2+2i\gamma\Omega}{c^2}}.
$$
Choose $k=\beta+i\alpha$ with $\alpha>0$ for decay $e^{-\alpha x}$ into
$x>0$. If $R=\sqrt{\Omega^4+4\gamma^2\Omega^2}$, then
$$
\boxed{\beta=\frac1c\sqrt{\frac{R+\Omega^2}{2}}},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\frac1c\sqrt{\frac{R-\Omega^2}{2}}},
$$
with driven phase velocity $\Omega/\beta$ and attenuation length $1/\alpha$.
Temporal and spatial formulations answer different experimental questions
and their imaginary parts must not be interchanged.

Define
$$
E=\frac12\int\left(u_t^2+c^2u_x^2\right)dx.

\boxed{s_+=-2.67949\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{s_-=-37.3205\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

$$
\boxed{k=0.346410+0.173205i\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_{p,\rm drive}=86.6025\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\ell_{\rm att}=5.77350\,\mathrm m}.

I discard every $|k|<\gamma/c$ component as static rather than solving its two decay rates. Since $d\Omega_k/dk$ exceeds $c$ just above threshold, I also claim the PDE sends a causal front faster than $c$.

WAVE:010617.title: Duffing response branches and the limits of harmonic balance
WAVE:010617.objective: Derive the one-harmonic Duffing amplitude equation, locate its fold condition, and separate approximate multivalued response from a complete nonlinear stability claim.
WAVE:010617.statement:
Consider the driven Duffing oscillator
\[
\ddot x+2\beta\dot x+\omega_0^2x+\alpha x^3
=f\cos\omega t,
\]
with \(\beta>0\). Assume a periodic response dominated by its fundamental,
\(x(t)\approx A\cos(\omega t-\delta)\), and use
\(\cos^3\theta=(3\cos\theta+\cos3\theta)/4\).

Perform one-harmonic balance to derive the implicit amplitude equation and
phase relation. Recover the undamped, unforced backbone relation and explain
how the sign of \(\alpha\) determines hardening or softening. Let
\(y=A^2\), \(\Delta=\omega_0^2-\omega^2\),
\(q=3\alpha/4\), and \(d=2\beta\omega\). Derive the condition for folds of
the algebraic response curve at fixed \(\omega\), and show that the candidate
fold values satisfy
\[
q y=\frac{-2\Delta\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2-3d^2}}3.
\]
State the existence and positivity conditions.

For \(\omega_0=1\), \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=0.05\), and
\(\omega=1.20\), compute the two fold amplitudes and the corresponding force
levels. Explain what three algebraic amplitudes between the force folds do and
do not establish about dynamical stability, and identify the approximation
discarded by one-harmonic balance.
permittedResults: Keeping only the fundamental of \(A^3\cos^3\theta\) replaces the cubic term by \((3/4)\alpha A^3\cos\theta\).
A multiple-valued harmonic-balance equation is an algebraic approximation; stability requires perturbation, averaging, Floquet, or direct dynamical analysis.

acceptableStrategies.description: Balance cosine and sine components, square and add, then differentiate the squared-force function with respect to squared amplitude.
Use a complex-amplitude or averaging derivation, provided it yields the same one-harmonic coefficients and explicitly states the discarded harmonics and stability limitation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Carries out consistent one-harmonic balance, derives the response-fold equation and numerical folds, and clearly limits the approximation and stability claims.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the cubic fundamental by alpha A cubed without the factor three quarters.
commonErrors.consequence: The backbone, amplitude response, and fold locations are all wrong.

commonErrors.description: Claims every positive root of the harmonic-balance amplitude equation is necessarily a stable periodic motion.
commonErrors.consequence: An approximate algebraic response count is promoted to an unsupported dynamical stability result.

hintTree.content: Balance in-phase and quadrature components relative to \(\cos(\omega t-\delta)\), then square and add.
Write \(f^2=G(y)=y[(\Delta+qy)^2+d^2]\); folds obey \(G'(y)=0\).
After differentiating, set \(z=qy\) and solve \(3z^2+4\Delta z+\Delta^2+d^2=0\).

WAVE:010617.canonicalSolution:
Discarding the third harmonic from \(x^3\), the fundamental balance is
equivalent to a linear phasor equation with amplitude-dependent stiffness.
Its in-phase and quadrature components give
\[
f\cos\delta=A\left(\omega_0^2-\omega^2+\frac34\alpha A^2\right),
\qquad
f\sin\delta=2\beta\omega A.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A^2\left[
\left(\omega_0^2-\omega^2+\frac34\alpha A^2\right)^2
+(2\beta\omega)^2\right]=f^2}
\]
and a quadrant-aware phase is
\[
\boxed{\delta=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(2\beta\omega,\omega_0^2-\omega^2+\frac34\alpha A^2\right)}.
\]
In the conservative unforced limit, a nonzero fundamental satisfies
\[
\boxed{\omega^2\approx\omega_0^2+\frac34\alpha A^2}.
\]
Thus \(\alpha>0\) bends the backbone to higher frequency and
\(\alpha<0\) to lower frequency.

With the stated abbreviations,
\[
G(y)=y[(\Delta+qy)^2+d^2].
\]
A fold obeys
\[
G'(y)=(\Delta+qy)(\Delta+3qy)+d^2=0.
\]
Putting \(z=qy\) gives
\(3z^2+4\Delta z+\Delta^2+d^2=0\), hence
\[
\boxed{qy=\frac{-2\Delta\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2-3d^2}}3}.
\]
Real folds require \(\Delta^2\ge3d^2\), and a physical fold also requires
\(y>0\), so the numerator must have the same sign as \(q\).

For the numerical case,
\[
\Delta=1-1.2^2=-0.44,\quad q=0.75,\quad d=0.12.
\]
The two values of \(z=qy\) are approximately \(0.1641\) and \(0.4226\),
so
\[
\boxed{A_{f,1}=0.468},\qquad \boxed{A_{f,2}=0.751}.
\]
Substitution into \(f=\sqrt{G(y)}\) gives approximately
\[
\boxed{f_{f,1}=0.141},\qquad \boxed{f_{f,2}=0.0910}.
\]
For forcing between these two levels, the cubic amplitude equation can have
three positive solutions. That predicts multiple one-harmonic response
branches, not that all three periodic motions are dynamically stable; the
middle branch is commonly unstable, but that conclusion requires a stability
analysis. Harmonic balance has discarded the generated \(3\omega\) component
and all higher corrections, so it is controlled only when the response is
sufficiently fundamental-dominated.

graderFixtures.proofText: One-harmonic balance gives \(A^2[(\Delta+3\alpha A^2/4)^2+(2\beta\omega)^2]=f^2\). With \(y=A^2\), differentiating \(G(y)\) yields \((\Delta+qy)(\Delta+3qy)+d^2=0\). The numerical folds are near \(A=0.468,0.751\), but algebraic branches alone do not prove stability.
Since cosine cubed is just cosine at the fundamental, I use alpha A cubed with coefficient one. Every positive root is a stable solution because it satisfies the amplitude equation.

WAVE:010618.title: The nonlinear pendulum period beyond the small-angle limit
WAVE:010618.objective: Derive the exact finite-amplitude pendulum period as an elliptic integral, obtain its small-amplitude expansion, and interpret the separatrix divergence.
WAVE:010618.statement:
A point mass on a massless rigid rod of length \(\ell\) moves without
friction in a uniform gravitational field. Its angular displacement obeys
\[
\ddot\theta+\frac g\ell\sin\theta=0.
\]
It is released from rest at \(\theta(0)=\theta_0\), where
\(0<\theta_0<\pi\).

Use energy conservation to derive the exact period in the form
\[
T=4\sqrt{\frac\ell g}\,K(k),
\qquad k=\sin(\theta_0/2),
\]
where
\(K(k)=\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-k^2\sin^2\phi)^{-1/2}d\phi\).
Show the substitution that converts the quarter-period integral into this
form. Starting with the series for the integrand or for \(K\), derive
\[
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac\ell g}
\left(1+\frac{\theta_0^2}{16}
+\frac{11\theta_0^4}{3072}+O(\theta_0^6)\right).
\]

For \(\theta_0=60^\circ\), compute the exact ratio
\(T/T_0=2K(1/2)/\pi\) using \(K(1/2)\approx1.68575\), compare it with the
fourth-order approximation, and explain why the period diverges as
\(\theta_0\to\pi^-\). State why inserting degrees directly into the power
series is invalid.
permittedResults: Energy conservation gives \(\tfrac12\ell^2\dot\theta^2+g\ell(1-\cos\theta)=g\ell(1-\cos\theta_0)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the energy integral and half-angle substitution, then expand the complete elliptic integral and the modulus consistently.
Apply a Lindstedt expansion for the small-amplitude series only if the exact energy-to-elliptic-integral derivation and separatrix interpretation are also supplied.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the elliptic-integral period from energy, obtains the correct theta-amplitude expansion through fourth order, and interprets the numerical correction and separatrix limit.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Omits the factor of four when converting the bottom-to-turning-point time into a full period.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact and small-angle periods have the wrong normalization.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the numerical degree measure into a Taylor expansion derived for dimensionless radians.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-amplitude correction is meaningless and extremely large.

hintTree.content: Use \(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0=2[\sin^2(\theta_0/2)-\sin^2(\theta/2)]\).
Set \(\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin\phi\); the turning point maps to \(\phi=\pi/2\).
Expand \(k^2=\sin^2(\theta_0/2)=\theta_0^2/4-\theta_0^4/48+O(\theta_0^6)\) before collecting fourth-order terms.

WAVE:010618.canonicalSolution:
Taking potential energy zero at the bottom, conservation from the release
point gives
\[
\frac12\ell^2\dot\theta^2+g\ell(1-\cos\theta)
=g\ell(1-\cos\theta_0).
\]
During a quarter cycle from \(0\) to \(\theta_0\),
\[
dt=\sqrt{\frac\ell{2g}}
\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0}}.
\]
Let \(k=\sin(\theta_0/2)\) and set
\(\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin\phi\). Using
\(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0=2k^2\cos^2\phi\) and differentiating the
substitution yields
\[
dt=\sqrt{\frac\ell g}
\frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\phi}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{T=4\sqrt{\frac\ell g}K(k)}.
\]

Using
\[
K(k)=\frac\pi2\left(1+\frac{k^2}{4}
+\frac{9k^4}{64}+O(k^6)\right),
\]
together with
\[
k^2=\frac{\theta_0^2}{4}-\frac{\theta_0^4}{48}+O(\theta_0^6),
\qquad k^4=\frac{\theta_0^4}{16}+O(\theta_0^6),
\]
gives
\[
\boxed{T=T_0\left(1+\frac{\theta_0^2}{16}
+\frac{11\theta_0^4}{3072}+O(\theta_0^6)\right)},
\qquad T_0=2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}.
\]

At \(60^\circ\), \(\theta_0=\pi/3\) radians and \(k=1/2\). Therefore
\[
\frac T{T_0}=\frac{2K(1/2)}\pi
=\frac{2(1.68575)}\pi=1.07318.
\]
The fourth-order series gives
\[
1+\frac{(\pi/3)^2}{16}
+\frac{11(\pi/3)^4}{3072}=1.07285,
\]
an error of about \(3.3\times10^{-4}\) in the ratio. As
\(\theta_0\to\pi^-\), \(k\to1^-\) and the elliptic integrand becomes
nonintegrably large near \(\phi=\pi/2\) in the limiting sense; physically the
pendulum approaches the unstable top with vanishing speed and takes infinite
time. Taylor-series angles are dimensionless radian measures, so substituting
60 as though degrees were the expansion variable is invalid.

graderFixtures.proofText: Energy gives \(dt=\sqrt{\ell/(2g)}d\theta/\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0}\). With \(\sin(\theta/2)=k\sin\phi\), the full period is \(4\sqrt{\ell/g}K(k)\). Expanding both K and \(k=\sin(\theta_0/2)\) gives coefficients \(1/16\) and \(11/3072\).
The integral from zero to the maximum is already the complete period, so T equals square root ell over g times K. For sixty degrees I substitute theta-zero equals sixty into the series.

WAVE:010619.title: How nonlinear damping selects the Van der Pol amplitude
WAVE:010619.objective: Derive the weakly nonlinear Van der Pol amplitude equation from averaged energy balance, solve its slow flow, and separate leading-order limit-cycle selection from an exact waveform claim.
WAVE:010619.statement:
Consider the dimensionless Van der Pol oscillator
\[
\ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+x=0,
\qquad 0<\mu\ll1.
\]
Define the harmonic energy \(E=(\dot x^2+x^2)/2\). Derive its exact time
derivative. On one fast cycle, assume
\(x\approx r(t)\cos(t+\phi)\), with \(r\) and \(\phi\) varying only on the
slow time scale. Average the energy balance to derive the leading amplitude
equation
\[
\dot r=\frac\mu2r\left(1-\frac{r^2}{4}\right).
\]
Classify its nonnegative fixed points and explain physically why small
oscillations grow while sufficiently large oscillations shrink.

Solve the averaged initial-value problem explicitly for \(r(t)\) in terms of
\(r_0>0\). For \(\mu=0.100\) and \(r_0=1.00\), estimate the slow-flow time
to reach \(r=1.98\). State what this calculation establishes about the
leading limit-cycle amplitude and what it does not establish about the exact
Van der Pol waveform, frequency, transient phase, or behavior when \(\mu\) is
not small.
permittedResults: Over one cycle, \(\langle\sin^2\theta\rangle=1/2\) and \(\langle\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta\rangle=1/8\).
A one-dimensional fixed point is locally attracting when the derivative of its flow function is negative and repelling when that derivative is positive.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use harmonic energy balance and cycle averages, then solve the squared-amplitude logistic equation.
Use first-order multiple scales or averaging directly on amplitude and phase, provided the same slow flow, stability, solution, and scope limitations are derived.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the averaged amplitude equation from exact energy balance, classifies and solves its flow, and keeps every limit-cycle and timing claim within the weakly nonlinear approximation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Factorizes the average of x squared times x-dot squared or uses one quarter instead of one eighth for its cycle average.
commonErrors.consequence: The selected amplitude and amplitude-flow coefficients are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Declares the sinusoidal amplitude-two waveform and computed transient time exact for arbitrary mu.
commonErrors.consequence: A leading weak-nonlinearity approximation is promoted beyond its regime of validity.

hintTree.content: Multiply the differential equation by x-dot to obtain \(\dot E\).
Use \(E\approx r^2/2\), \(\dot x\approx-r\sin(t+\phi)\), and average only after forming the full nonlinear power.
Set \(y=r^2\); then \(\dot y=\mu y(1-y/4)\) is logistic.

WAVE:010619.canonicalSolution:
Rearranging the equation gives
\(\ddot x+x=\mu(1-x^2)\dot x\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\dot E=\dot x(\ddot x+x)
=\mu(1-x^2)\dot x^2}.
\]
For \(x\approx r\cos\theta\), \(\dot x\approx-r\sin\theta\) on one fast
cycle. Hence
\[
\langle\dot E\rangle
=\mu\left[r^2\langle\sin^2\theta\rangle
-r^4\langle\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta\rangle\right]
=\mu\left(\frac{r^2}{2}-\frac{r^4}{8}\right).
\]
Since \(E\approx r^2/2\), its slow derivative is \(r\dot r\). For
\(r>0\),
\[
\boxed{\dot r=\frac\mu2r\left(1-\frac{r^2}{4}\right)}.
\]
Continuity extends this to \(r=0\).

The fixed points are \(r=0\) and \(r=2\). Near zero, \(\dot r\approx
\mu r/2>0\), so zero is repelling. Differentiating the slow-flow right side
shows a negative derivative at \(r=2\), so the positive amplitude is
attracting. The nonlinear damping injects energy when \(|x|<1\) and removes
it when \(|x|>1\); the cycle average balances at amplitude two.

Let \(y=r^2\). Then
\[
\dot y=\mu y\left(1-\frac y4\right),
\]
so for \(y_0=r_0^2>0\),
\[
\boxed{r(t)=\frac{2}{
\sqrt{1+(4/r_0^2-1)e^{-\mu t}}}}.
\]
For \(r_0=1\), the constant is three. Solving for \(r=1.98\) gives
\[
e^{-\mu t}=\frac{4/(1.98)^2-1}{3}=0.006768,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{t=\frac{-\ln(0.006768)}{0.100}=49.96}
\]
in the dimensionless time units.

This establishes the leading weak-nonlinearity envelope attraction to
amplitude two on the slow scale. It does not say the exact periodic orbit is a
pure sinusoid of amplitude exactly two for finite \(\mu\), nor does it compute
the higher-order frequency shift, waveform harmonics, transient phase, or the
relaxation-oscillation regime at large \(\mu\). Those require higher-order
averaging, numerical integration, or a different asymptotic analysis.

graderFixtures.proofText: Exact energy balance is \(\dot E=\mu(1-x^2)\dot x^2\). Harmonic averaging gives \(\mu(r^2/2-r^4/8)\); since E is approximately r-squared over two, \(\dot r=\mu r(1-r^2/4)/2\). The origin repels, r equals two attracts, and squared amplitude follows a logistic law.

I multiply the separate averages of x squared and x-dot squared, obtaining one quarter for their product. The resulting sinusoid of amplitude two is the exact Van der Pol solution for every positive mu.

WAVE:010620.title: Amplitude, speed, and width of a KdV soliton
WAVE:010620.objective: Reduce the Korteweg-de Vries equation to a traveling-wave orbit, derive its localized sech-squared soliton, and verify the amplitude-speed-width relation and two conserved integrals.
WAVE:010620.statement:
Consider the dimensionless Korteweg-de Vries equation
\[
u_t+6uu_x+u_{xxx}=0
\]
on the real line. Seek a smooth traveling wave
\(u(x,t)=U(\xi)\), \(\xi=x-ct\), with
\(U,U',U''\to0\) as \(|\xi|\to\infty\).

Reduce the PDE to a second-order autonomous equation, keeping the integration
constant and using the decay conditions to determine it. Derive—not merely
quote—the positive localized solution in the form
\[
U(\xi)=A\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa\xi),
\]
and find the exact relations among \(A,\kappa,c\). Verify the solution by
substitution.

Compute the conserved mass-like and squared-amplitude integrals
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}U\,d\xi\) and
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}U^2d\xi\), and derive the full width at half maximum.
For \(A=0.500\), compute \(c,\kappa\), both integrals, and the FWHM.
Explain how nonlinearity and dispersion balance, why taller positive solitons
are narrower and faster in this normalization, and why this exact result does
not by itself establish stability under arbitrary perturbations.
permittedResults: If \(s(\xi)=\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa\xi)\), then \(s''=4\kappa^2s-6\kappa^2s^2\).
The integrals \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}^2z\,dz=2\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}^4z\,dz=4/3\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the traveling-wave ODE and match coefficients after inserting the sech-squared identity.
Use the first integral of the traveling-wave phase portrait to solve the homoclinic orbit, provided the same explicit profile, constants, invariants, FWHM, and scope statement are obtained.

hintTree.content: Substitution gives \(-cU'+6UU'+U'''=0\); integrate once before choosing a profile.
Multiply \(U''=cU-3U^2\) by U-prime and use decay to derive \((U')^2=U^2(c-2U)\) before separating variables.
Half maximum means \(\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa\xi)=1/2\), hence \(\cosh(\kappa|\xi|)=\sqrt2\).

WAVE:010620.canonicalSolution:
The traveling-wave substitution gives
\[
-cU'+6UU'+U'''=0.
\]
Integrating once,
\[
-cU+3U^2+U''=C.
\]
The decay of \(U\) and \(U''\) at infinity forces \(C=0\), so
\[
\boxed{U''=cU-3U^2}.
\]

Multiply the reduced equation by \(U'\) and integrate again:
\[
\frac12(U')^2=\frac c2U^2-U^3+C_2.
\]
Decay forces \(C_2=0\), hence
\[
\boxed{(U')^2=U^2(c-2U)}.
\]
At the positive crest \(U=A\), symmetry gives \(U'=0\), so
\(A=c/2\). On either monotone half of the pulse, separation gives
\[
\frac{dU}{U\sqrt{c-2U}}=\pm d\xi.
\]
Integrating and choosing the crest at \(\xi=0\) yields
\[
\boxed{U(\xi)=\frac c2
\operatorname{sech}^2\!\left(\frac{\sqrt c}{2}\xi\right)}.
\]
Thus \(U=As\), where \(s=\operatorname{sech}^2(\kappa\xi)\), with
\(A=c/2\) and \(\kappa=\sqrt c/2\). As an independent substitution check,
\[
U''=4\kappa^2U-\frac{6\kappa^2}{A}U^2.
\]
Comparison with \(cU-3U^2\) gives
\[
\boxed{c=4\kappa^2},
\qquad
\boxed{A=2\kappa^2},
\]
or equivalently
\[
\boxed{c=2A},
\qquad
\boxed{\kappa=\sqrt{A/2}}.
\]
These coefficient equalities verify both the derived profile in the reduced
equation and the original PDE.

Changing variables \(z=\kappa\xi\),
\[
\boxed{\int U\,d\xi=\frac{2A}{\kappa}=2\sqrt{2A}},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\int U^2d\xi=\frac{4A^2}{3\kappa}
=\frac{4\sqrt2}{3}A^{3/2}}.
\]
At half maximum,
\(\cosh(\kappa|\xi|)=\sqrt2\), so
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{FWHM}=\frac{2\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2}{\kappa}}.
\]

For \(A=0.500\),
\[
c=1.000,\qquad \kappa=0.500,
\]
\[
\int U\,d\xi=2.000,
\qquad
\int U^2d\xi=\frac23=0.6667,
\]
and, using \(\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2=0.881374\),
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{FWHM}=3.5255}.
\]
The nonlinear steepening term and third-derivative dispersion have matched
coefficients in the traveling orbit. Increasing A raises c and kappa, making
the positive pulse faster and narrower. This proves an exact coherent
solution and its integral values; orbital stability, perturbation evolution,
and multi-soliton collisions require separate spectral, inverse-scattering,
or energy analysis.

graderFixtures.proofText: One integration gives \(-cU+3U^2+U''=0\); multiplying by U-prime and using decay gives \((U')^2=U^2(c-2U)\). The crest has \(A=c/2\), and separation yields \(U=(c/2)\operatorname{sech}^2(\sqrt c\,\xi/2)\). Substitution then confirms c equals four kappa squared and A equals two kappa squared; the integrals and FWHM follow by z equals kappa xi.

The standard KdV soliton always has speed equal to its amplitude, so I use c equals A without checking normalization. Because the profile is exact, it is automatically stable under every perturbation.

WAVE:010621.title: A sine--Gordon kink carries topology and relativistic energy
WAVE:010621.objective: Derive the moving sine--Gordon kink from a first integral, compute its topological charge, energy, momentum, and contracted width, and separate exact existence from stability claims.
WAVE:010621.statement:
Consider the dimensionless sine--Gordon equation
\[
u_{tt}-u_{xx}+\sin u=0
\]
on the whole line. Seek a right-moving finite-energy kink satisfying
\(u(-\infty,t)=0\) and \(u(+\infty,t)=2\pi\), with speed \(0<v<1\).

Use the Lorentz-scaled coordinate
\(\xi=(x-vt-x_0)/\sqrt{1-v^2}\). Reduce the PDE to an ODE, derive its first
integral using both boundary conditions, and solve it to obtain the explicit
kink. Verify the solution by differentiating an identity rather than merely
quoting a standard formula. Compute its topological charge
\([u(+\infty)-u(-\infty)]/(2\pi)\).

For the energy density
\(\mathcal E=(u_t^2+u_x^2)/2+1-\cos u\), compute the total energy and
canonical momentum \(P=-\int u_tu_x\,dx\). Find the physical distance over
which u rises from \(\pi/2\) to \(3\pi/2\), and show its contraction with
speed. For \(v=0.600\), compute energy, momentum, and this width. State why
constructing an exact kink does not by itself prove nonlinear orbital
stability or describe kink collisions.
permittedResults: The identity \(1-\cos U=2\sin^2(U/2)\) turns the kink first integral into a separable first-order equation.
For \(U=4\arctan e^\xi\), \(U'=2\operatorname{sech}\xi\) and \(1-\cos U=2\operatorname{sech}^2\xi\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Integrate the traveling profile once, separate the increasing branch, and evaluate conserved-density integrals.

Apply a Lorentz boost to a separately derived static kink, provided the first integral, boundary constant, topology, energy, momentum, width, numerical values, and stability scope are all demonstrated.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives and verifies the kink from its first integral, computes topology and conserved energy-momentum, and obtains the speed-contracted transition width without claiming unproved stability.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Retains a nonzero first-integral constant or does not use the finite-energy asymptotic vacua.
commonErrors.consequence: The profile fails to approach the required equilibria with zero derivative.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the physical kink width by the Lorentz gamma factor instead of contracting it.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated level-set positions contradict the explicit moving solution.

hintTree.content: The scaled coordinate makes \(u_{tt}-u_{xx}=-U''\), so the profile equation is \(U''=\sin U\).
Multiply by \(U'\) and use the zero derivative and zero potential at either spatial infinity to remove the integration constant.
For the width endpoints, use \(\tan(\pi/8)=\sqrt2-1\) and \(\tan(3\pi/8)=\sqrt2+1\).

WAVE:010621.canonicalSolution:
With \(u=U(\xi)\), the scaled derivatives give
\(u_{tt}-u_{xx}=-U''\), hence
\[
\boxed{U''=\sin U}.
\]
Multiplication by \(U'\) and integration yields
\[
\frac12(U')^2=1-\cos U+C.
\]
At either asymptotic vacuum, both \(U'\) and \(1-\cos U\) vanish, so
\(C=0\). For the increasing kink,
\[
U'=2\sin(U/2).
\]
Separation gives \(\log\tan(U/4)=\xi\) after absorbing a translation into
\(x_0\), and therefore
\[
\boxed{u(x,t)=4\arctan\exp\!\left(
\frac{x-vt-x_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}\right)}.
\]
Differentiating gives \(U'=2\operatorname{sech}\xi\); another derivative
equals \(\sin U\), verifying the profile ODE. Its charge is
\[
\boxed{Q_{\rm top}=\frac{2\pi-0}{2\pi}=1}.
\]

For the rest kink, the first integral makes gradient and potential
contributions equal, and direct integration gives rest energy 8. The moving
derivatives and \(dx=\sqrt{1-v^2}\,d\xi\) give
\[
\boxed{E=\frac8{\sqrt{1-v^2}}},\qquad
\boxed{P=\frac{8v}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}}.
\]
The signs follow the stated positive-v convention and
\(P=-\int u_tu_xdx\). The two level values correspond to
\(\xi=\mp\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2\), so the physical transition width is
\[
\boxed{W_{1/2}=2\sqrt{1-v^2}\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2}.
\]
It contracts by the factor \(\sqrt{1-v^2}\) relative to the rest kink.

At \(v=0.600\), \(\sqrt{1-v^2}=0.800\), hence
\[
\boxed{E=10.000},\qquad \boxed{P=6.000}.
\]
Using \(\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2=0.881374\),
\[
\boxed{W_{1/2}=1.41020}.
\]
This calculation proves an exact finite-energy traveling solution and its
conserved quantities. Stability under perturbations and multi-kink collision
dynamics require additional spectral, variational, or integrability analysis;
they do not follow from substitution of one profile.

graderFixtures.proofText: The scaled profile satisfies \(U''=\sin U\) and \((U')^2/2=1-\cos U\), giving \(U=4\arctan e^\xi\). Its charge is one, \(E=8/\sqrt{1-v^2}\), \(P=8v/\sqrt{1-v^2}\), and its pi-over-two to three-pi-over-two width is \(2\sqrt{1-v^2}\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2\).
I keep an arbitrary nonzero integration constant despite the vacuum boundary conditions. I also make the moving kink wider by multiplying its rest width by the Lorentz gamma factor.

WAVE:010622.title: Focusing nonlinearity amplifies sidebands and supports a bright envelope
WAVE:010622.objective: Linearize focusing nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics about a plane wave, derive the modulational-instability band, and independently verify a bright-soliton family and its invariants.
WAVE:010622.statement:
Consider the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation
\[
i\psi_t+\psi_{xx}+2|\psi|^2\psi=0
\]
on the real line. First verify the constant-amplitude carrier
\(\psi_0=Ae^{2iA^2t}\), where \(A>0\). Set
\(\psi=e^{2iA^2t}(A+u+iv)\) with real small u and v. Derive the coupled
linearized equations and use a perturbation proportional to
\(e^{iKx+\lambda t}\) to find the exact growth-rate relation. Identify the
unstable band, fastest sideband, and maximum growth rate. Distinguish a real
growth rate from an oscillatory stable sideband outside the band.

Separately verify the bright-soliton family
\[
\psi=\eta\,\operatorname{sech}[\eta(x-2\xi t-x_0)]
e^{i[\xi x+(\eta^2-\xi^2)t+\phi_0]}.
\]
Compute its norm \(N=\int|\psi|^2dx\), Hamiltonian
\(H=\int(|\psi_x|^2-|\psi|^4)dx\), velocity, and intensity FWHM. Explain
why modulational instability of a nonzero background and existence of a
localized zero-background soliton are related consequences of focusing
nonlinearity but are not the same proof.

For \(A=0.500\), evaluate the unstable interval, fastest wavenumber, and
maximum growth rate; also find the growth rate at \(K=0.600\). For a soliton
with \(\eta=0.800\) and \(\xi=0.300\), compute norm, velocity, Hamiltonian,
and intensity FWHM.
permittedResults: The integrals \(\int\operatorname{sech}^2y\,dy=2\), \(\int\operatorname{sech}^4y\,dy=4/3\), and \(\int\operatorname{sech}^2y\tanh^2y\,dy=2/3\) hold over the real line.
A positive lambda squared gives exponential modes, while a negative lambda squared gives purely oscillatory linearized modes.

acceptableStrategies.description: Linearize in real amplitude and phase quadratures, then verify the sech solution and integrate its invariants.

Use paired Fourier sidebands in complex form and direct traveling-envelope substitution, provided the same instability polynomial, band, soliton parameters, integrals, numerical values, and logical separation result.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the focusing-NLS sideband growth law and fastest mode, then independently verifies the bright-soliton invariants and clearly separates the two claims.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses the defocusing sign or omits the amplitude-phase coupling, producing the wrong sideband band or no instability.
commonErrors.consequence: The growth rate fails the linearized focusing NLS equations.

commonErrors.description: Omits the phase-gradient contribution from a moving soliton's Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: The invariant is wrong whenever xi is nonzero.

hintTree.content: After removing the carrier phase, the linearized real equations are \(-v_t+u_{xx}+4A^2u=0\) and \(u_t+v_{xx}=0\).
Eliminate the sideband amplitudes to obtain \(\lambda^2=K^2(4A^2-K^2)\).
For the soliton Hamiltonian, separate the amplitude derivative from the constant phase gradient xi.

WAVE:010622.canonicalSolution:
Substitution immediately verifies
\(i\partial_t(Ae^{2iA^2t})+2A^3e^{2iA^2t}=0\). Keeping terms linear in
real u and v after removing the carrier phase gives
\[
\boxed{-v_t+u_{xx}+4A^2u=0},\qquad
\boxed{u_t+v_{xx}=0}.
\]
For \((u,v)=(U,V)e^{iKx+\lambda t}\),
\[
-\lambda V+(4A^2-K^2)U=0,
\qquad \lambda U-K^2V=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\lambda^2=K^2(4A^2-K^2)}.
\]
The carrier is modulationally unstable for
\[
\boxed{0<|K|<2A}.
\]
Maximizing \(K^2(4A^2-K^2)\) gives
\[
\boxed{|K|_{\max}=\sqrt2A},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_{\max}=2A^2}.
\]
For \(|K|>2A\), lambda is imaginary and the linear sideband oscillates
rather than grows exponentially.

For the stated bright envelope, differentiating the sech profile and phase
and substituting verifies the NLS equation. With
\(y=\eta(x-2\xi t-x_0)\),
\[
\boxed{N=\int|\psi|^2dx=2\eta},\qquad
\boxed{v_{\rm sol}=2\xi}.
\]
The amplitude-gradient contribution is \(2\eta^3/3\), the phase-gradient
contribution is \(2\eta\xi^2\), and the quartic integral is
\(4\eta^3/3\). Hence
\[
\boxed{H=2\eta\xi^2-\frac23\eta^3}.
\]
Half maximum intensity requires \(\operatorname{sech}^2y=1/2\), so
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{FWHM}=\frac{2\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2}{\eta}}.
\]

For \(A=0.500\), the unstable interval is
\(\boxed{0<|K|<1.000}\), with
\[
\boxed{|K|_{\max}=0.707107},\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_{\max}=0.5000}.
\]
At \(K=0.600\),
\[
\boxed{\lambda=0.600\sqrt{1-0.600^2}=0.4800}.
\]
For \(\eta=0.800\) and \(\xi=0.300\),
\[
\boxed{N=1.600},\qquad \boxed{v_{\rm sol}=0.600},
\]
\[
\boxed{H=2(0.8)(0.3)^2-\frac23(0.8)^3=-0.197333},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{FWHM}=2.20343}.
\]
The instability calculation concerns perturbations of a nonzero plane-wave
background. The soliton calculation concerns an exact localized orbit that
decays to zero. Focusing nonlinearity enables both, but deriving one does not
logically establish the other or prove nonlinear stability.

graderFixtures.proofText: Linearization gives \(-v_t+u_{xx}+4A^2u=0\), \(u_t+v_{xx}=0\), hence \(\lambda^2=K^2(4A^2-K^2)\). The sech soliton has \(N=2\eta\), velocity \(2\xi\), \(H=2\eta\xi^2-2\eta^3/3\), and intensity FWHM \(2\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt2/\eta\).
I use the defocusing sideband sign and obtain no unstable band. For the moving soliton I compute the Hamiltonian from the amplitude alone and drop the constant phase-gradient term.

WAVE:010623.title: A quadratic spring nonlinearity shifts the mean before the frequency
WAVE:010623.objective: Use Poincare-Lindstedt perturbation theory to derive the static offset, second harmonic, turning-point asymmetry, and leading frequency shift of an oscillator with quadratic restoring nonlinearity.
WAVE:010623.statement:
A mass obeys
\[
m\ddot x+kx+\gamma x^2=0,
\qquad m,k>0,
\]
with \(\gamma>0\). It is released from \(x(0)=A>0\), \(\dot x(0)=0\).
Define \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) and the small dimensionless amplitude
\(\epsilon=\gamma A/k\ll1\).

Introduce \(y=x/A\), strained time \(\tau=\Omega t\), and expansions
\[
y=y_0+\epsilon y_1+\epsilon^2y_2+\cdots,
\qquad
\frac\Omega{\omega_0}=1+\epsilon\nu_1+\epsilon^2\nu_2+\cdots.
\]
Enforce the initial conditions order by order. Derive the complete first-order
waveform, including its mean, fundamental correction, and second harmonic.
Show by eliminating secular terms that \(\nu_1=0\): a quadratic nonlinearity
changes waveform symmetry before it shifts frequency. Continue only far enough
at second order to find \(\nu_2\).

Derive the potential energy and use exact energy conservation to find the
opposite turning point through first order in epsilon. Show that it agrees with
the perturbative waveform at \(\tau=\pi\). Locate the additional equilibrium,
classify it, and state the energy-barrier condition needed for bounded motion
in the local well; the cubic potential is not globally confining.

For \(m=1.50\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=150\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\gamma=300\,\mathrm{N/m^2}\), and \(A=0.0200\,\mathrm m\), compute
epsilon, the mean offset, second-harmonic amplitude, first-order negative
turning point, leading corrected frequency and period, and initial energy.
Solve the exact turning-point energy equation numerically and compare it with
the first-order prediction.
permittedResults: A resonant forcing proportional to \(\cos\tau\) in \(z''+z=f(\tau)\) generates a secular term unless its coefficient is removed.
For a conservative one-dimensional oscillator, turning points have zero kinetic energy and therefore equal potential energy.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use strained time, remove resonant terms order by order, and enforce release conditions on each waveform correction.
Use energy to obtain the opposite turning point independently, then use only the resonant second-order forcing to find frequency.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Carries Poincare-Lindstedt expansion through the first nonzero frequency correction and reconciles waveform and energy predictions for asymmetric turns.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only a particular first-order solution and omits the cosine needed to make y1 of zero vanish.
commonErrors.consequence: The perturbative waveform no longer satisfies the prescribed release amplitude and disagrees with the energy turn.

commonErrors.description: Assigns a nonzero order-epsilon frequency correction even though quadratic forcing has no fundamental harmonic at first order.
commonErrors.consequence: A secular-cancellation condition is invented and the leading minus five epsilon squared over twelve shift is missed.

hintTree.content: At first order use \(y_0^2=(1+\cos2\tau)/2\), then add the homogeneous term required by \(y_1(0)=y_1'(0)=0\).
At second order, only the coefficient of \(\cos\tau\) is needed to determine \(\nu_2\); the full y2 waveform is unnecessary.
Write the negative turn as \(-A+\Delta\), expand its potential through first order in gamma, and compare with the value at +A.

WAVE:010623.canonicalSolution:
The dimensionless strained-time equation is
\[
\frac{\Omega^2}{\omega_0^2}y''+y+\epsilon y^2=0,
\qquad y(0)=1,\quad y'(0)=0.
\]
At leading order, \(y_0=\cos\tau\). At first order,
\[
y_1''+y_1=2\nu_1\cos\tau-\frac12(1+\cos2\tau).
\]
Eliminating resonant forcing gives \(\boxed{\nu_1=0}\). A particular
solution plus the homogeneous term required by the initial data gives
\[
\boxed{y_1=\frac13\cos\tau+\frac16\cos2\tau-\frac12}.
\]
Therefore the complete first-order motion is
\[
\boxed{x(t)=A\left[\cos\tau+\epsilon\left(
\frac13\cos\tau+\frac16\cos2\tau-\frac12\right)\right]
+O(\epsilon^2A)}.
\]
Its mean is \(-\epsilon A/2\), its generated second-harmonic amplitude is
\(\epsilon A/6\), and the \(\epsilon A/3\) fundamental correction ensures
the prescribed positive turning point remains exactly A at this order.

Because \(\nu_1=0\), the second-order equation has resonant forcing
\[
y_2''+y_2=\left(2\nu_2+\frac56\right)\cos\tau
-\frac13-\frac13\cos2\tau-\frac16\cos3\tau.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\nu_2=-\frac5{12}},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=\omega_0\left(1-\frac5{12}\epsilon^2
+O(\epsilon^3)\right)}.
\]
The leading frequency change is quadratic in epsilon even though waveform
asymmetry appears linearly.

The exact potential is
\[
\boxed{V(x)=\frac12kx^2+\frac13\gamma x^3}.
\]
Writing the negative turn as \(x_-=-A+\Delta\), equating \(V(x_-)\) with
\(V(A)\), and retaining first order in gamma gives
\[
-kA\Delta-\frac13\gamma A^3=\frac13\gamma A^3,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{x_-=-A-\frac{2\gamma A^2}{3k}+O(\epsilon^2A)
=-A\left(1+\frac23\epsilon\right)+O(\epsilon^2A)}.
\]
Putting \(\tau=\pi\) in the waveform gives the same result. Besides the
stable equilibrium x=0, there is an unstable equilibrium
\(x_b=-k/\gamma\), where \(V''=-k\). Its barrier energy is
\[
\boxed{V_b=\frac{k^3}{6\gamma^2}}.
\]
Motion launched in the local well is bounded only when its energy is below
this barrier; toward negative infinity the cubic potential is unbounded.

For the data,
\[
\boxed{\omega_0=10.0000\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\epsilon=\gamma A/k=0.0400000}.
\]
The mean and second harmonic are
\[
\boxed{\overline x=-0.400000\ \mathrm{mm}},\qquad
\boxed{A_2=0.133333\ \mathrm{mm}}.
\]
The first-order opposite turn is
\[
\boxed{x_-^{(1)}=-20.5333\ \mathrm{mm}}.
\]
The leading corrected frequency and period are
\[
\boxed{\Omega=9.99333\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathcal P=0.628738\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The initial energy is
\[
\boxed{E_0=\tfrac12(150)(0.0200)^2
+\tfrac13(300)(0.0200)^3=0.0308000\ \mathrm J},
\]
far below \(V_b=6.25\,\mathrm J\). Numerical solution of
\(V(x_-)=E_0\) on the negative side gives
\[
\boxed{x_-=-20.5484\ \mathrm{mm}},
\]
only 0.0151 mm beyond the first-order prediction, a discrepancy of the
expected second order.

graderFixtures.proofText: The first correction is \(y_1=\cos\tau/3+\cos2\tau/6-1/2\), so the mean is negative epsilon A over two, the second harmonic is epsilon A over six, and nu1 is zero. Second-order resonance removal gives \(\nu_2=-5/12\). Energy gives \(x_-=-A(1+2\epsilon/3)+O(\epsilon^2A)\). Numerically epsilon is 0.04, the mean is -0.400 mm, and the corrected frequency is 9.99333 rad/s.
I omit the homogeneous cosine from y1, so the expansion misses the release amplitude, and I force an order-epsilon frequency shift even though no resonant cosine appears there.
