WAVE:010624.title: Quadratic drag gives an algebraic, not exponential, ring-down
WAVE:010624.objective: Average the exact energy loss of a weak quadratically damped oscillator and derive its amplitude envelope, energy law, and amplitude-dependent quality factor.
WAVE:010624.statement:
A spring-mass oscillator moves in a fluid whose drag force is quadratic in
speed:
\[
m\ddot x+kx+b|\dot x|\dot x=0,
\qquad m,k,b>0.
\]
Assume damping is weak enough that during one cycle
\(x(t)\simeq A(t)\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)\), with
\(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\) and A varying slowly. Start from the exact
mechanical-energy equation rather than replacing the nonlinear drag by an
unjustified constant viscous coefficient.

Average the dissipated power over a cycle, evaluating the required absolute
sine integral. Derive the slow amplitude equation and solve it for A(t).
Obtain the corresponding energy envelope and show that the time to reduce
amplitude by a fixed factor depends inversely on initial amplitude. Derive the
leading energy lost per cycle and the amplitude-dependent quality factor
\(Q(A)=2\pi E/|\Delta E_{\rm cycle}|\). Give a quantitative weak-damping
criterion and explain why the approximation eventually improves as the
amplitude decays.

For \(m=1.20\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=108\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(b=0.800\,\mathrm{kg/m}\), and \(A_0=0.0800\,\mathrm m\), compute
\(\omega_0\), the envelope coefficient, the half-amplitude time, A and
energy ratio after 10.0 s, and Q initially and after 10.0 s. Compare the
qualitative envelope with linear viscous damping and check the units of b and
the decay coefficient.
permittedResults: Over one period, \((2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin\theta|^3d\theta=4/(3\pi)\).
For a weakly perturbed harmonic oscillator, \(E\simeq kA^2/2\) and \(dE/dt\simeq kA\dot A\) on the slow time scale.

acceptableStrategies.description: Average exact dissipated power over a slowly changing harmonic orbit and convert energy loss to amplitude loss.
Apply the method of averaging to amplitude and phase equations, then verify the amplitude equation independently from the cycle energy integral.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the nonlinear energy ledger and cycle averaging to derive algebraic amplitude and energy decay with a consistent amplitude-dependent quality factor.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces b absolute-v v by a constant linear viscous coefficient and reports exponential decay with constant Q.
commonErrors.consequence: The amplitude dependence and algebraic ring-down law are erased.

commonErrors.description: Uses v cubed rather than absolute-v cubed in the averaged dissipated power, causing cancellation over a cycle.
commonErrors.consequence: The model falsely predicts zero net energy loss.

hintTree.content: Multiply the exact equation by \(\dot x\) to get \(\dot E=-b|\dot x|^3\).
Substitute \(|\dot x|\simeq A\omega_0|\sin(\omega_0t+\phi)|\) before averaging.
The equation \(\dot A=-\alpha A^2\) integrates by differentiating \(1/A\).

WAVE:010624.canonicalSolution:
The exact mechanical energy
\[
E=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2
\]
satisfies
\[
\boxed{\dot E=-b|\dot x|^3\le0}.
\]
Using the slowly modulated sinusoid,
\[
\langle|\dot x|^3\rangle
=A^3\omega_0^3\frac{4}{3\pi}.
\]
Since \(E\simeq kA^2/2\), the averaged balance is
\[
kA\dot A=-\frac{4b}{3\pi}A^3\omega_0^3.
\]
With \(k=m\omega_0^2\),
\[
\boxed{\dot A=-\alpha A^2},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{4b\omega_0}{3\pi m}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A(t)=\frac{A_0}{1+\alpha A_0t}},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{E(t)}{E_0}=\frac{1}{(1+\alpha A_0t)^2}}.
\]
The time to reach \(A_0/r\) is \((r-1)/(\alpha A_0)\), explicitly
depending on initial amplitude rather than only a constant damping time.

During one nearly harmonic cycle,
\[
|\Delta E|\simeq bA^3\omega_0^3
\frac1{\omega_0}\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin\theta|^3d\theta
=\frac83bA^3\omega_0^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{Q(A)=\frac{2\pi(kA^2/2)}{(8/3)bA^3\omega_0^2}
=\frac{3\pi m}{8bA}}.
\]
A useful weak-loss condition is \(|\Delta E|/E=2\pi/Q\ll1\), or
\(bA/m\ll1\) up to the displayed numerical factor. Since A decreases,
Q increases and the averaging becomes more accurate at late times.

Numerically,
\[
\boxed{\omega_0=\sqrt{108/1.2}=9.48683\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{4(0.8)(9.48683)}{3\pi(1.2)}
=2.68422\ \mathrm{m^{-1}s^{-1}}}.
\]
The half-amplitude time is
\[
\boxed{t_{1/2}=\frac1{\alpha A_0}=4.657\ \mathrm s}.
\]
At 10.0 s,
\[
1+\alpha A_0t=3.14738,
\qquad
\boxed{A(10)=0.0254180\ \mathrm m},
\]
\[
\boxed{E(10)/E_0=0.10095}.
\]
The quality factors are
\[
\boxed{Q_0=\frac{3\pi(1.2)}{8(0.8)(0.0800)}=22.089},
\]
\[
\boxed{Q(10)=\frac{3\pi(1.2)}{8(0.8)(0.0254180)}=69.5235}.
\]
Unlike linear viscous damping's exponential amplitude with constant Q, this
weak quadratic-drag envelope has an inverse-linear amplitude and a Q that
grows as amplitude falls. Because \(b|v|v\) is a force, b has units
\(\mathrm{kg/m}\); consequently alpha has units
\(\mathrm{m^{-1}s^{-1}}\), making \(\alpha A_0t\) dimensionless.

graderFixtures.proofText: Multiplying by v gives \(\dot E=-b|v|^3\). Averaging with \(\langle|\sin|^3\rangle=4/(3\pi)\) yields \(\dot A=-[4b\omega_0/(3\pi m)]A^2\), so A is inverse-linear and energy is inverse-square. The data give alpha 2.68422, half-time 4.657 s, A(10) about 0.02542 m, and Q rising from 22.09 to about 69.5.
I average v cubed without an absolute value, obtain zero, and then replace the drag by a constant viscous coefficient to claim an exponential envelope and constant Q.

WAVE:010625.title: The phi-four kink carries an internal shape mode
WAVE:010625.objective: Derive the topological phi-four kink, its sharp energy bound, and the complete discrete spectrum of small oscillations around it.
WAVE:010625.statement:
Consider the dimensionless real scalar field on the line with Lagrangian density
\[
\mathcal L=\frac12\phi_t^2-\frac12\phi_x^2
-\frac12(1-\phi^2)^2.
\]
Finite-energy configurations in the kink sector satisfy
\(\phi(-\infty)=-1\) and \(\phi(+\infty)=+1\).

Derive the field equation. Complete the square in the static energy to prove
a sharp lower bound in this sector, solve the first-order equation that
saturates it, and compute the kink energy and topological charge. Explain the
translation parameter and obtain the uniformly moving kink by a Lorentz
boost.

Next put \(\phi=\phi_K+\varepsilon\eta(x)e^{-i\omega t}\) and derive the
one-dimensional Schrödinger operator governing linear perturbations. Find and
normalize every square-integrable eigenmode: the translational zero mode and
the nonzero internal shape mode. State the continuum threshold, factor the
operator to prove nonnegative squared frequencies, and distinguish linear
spectral stability from nonlinear orbital or asymptotic stability.

Compute the rest-frame shape frequency and continuum threshold. For a kink
moving at \(v=0.600\) in units where the limiting wave speed is one, compute
the Lorentz factor, total energy, and spatial width relative to the resting
kink. Explain why the internal bound mode is a feature not inferred merely
from the existence of a topological kink.
permittedResults: If a static energy can be written as a nonnegative square plus a boundary term, the boundary term gives a sharp sector-dependent lower bound.
For \(H=A^\dagger A\), every spectral value of H is nonnegative; a normalizable solution of \(A\eta=0\) is a zero mode.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use square completion for the kink and direct substitution into the resulting Poschl-Teller operator.
Factor the linearized operator, then use its asymptotic constant and explicit bound eigenfunctions to classify the spectrum.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the sharp kink energy and complete localized perturbation spectrum while separating topology, spectral stability, and nonlinear evolution.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses a field equation whose nonlinear sign is inconsistent with the stated double-well energy or with tanh as a static solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed kink, energy bound, and perturbation operator cannot all solve the same model.

commonErrors.description: Omits the translational zero mode or places the nonzero shape mode in the radiation continuum.
commonErrors.consequence: The discrete spectral count and stability conclusion are wrong.

hintTree.content: For the increasing kink, set \(\phi_x=1-\phi^2\) after completing the static energy square.
The perturbation potential is \(V''(\phi_K)=6\phi_K^2-2=4-6\operatorname{sech}^2x\).
Test functions proportional to \(\operatorname{sech}^2x\) and \(\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x\), then normalize by substituting \(u=\tanh x\).

WAVE:010625.canonicalSolution:
The Euler-Lagrange equation is
\[
\boxed{\phi_{tt}-\phi_{xx}+2\phi(\phi^2-1)=0}.
\]
For a static field in the increasing kink sector,
\[
E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\left[\frac12\phi_x^2+\frac12(1-\phi^2)^2\right]dx
\]
\[
=\frac12\int[\phi_x-(1-\phi^2)]^2dx
+\int\phi_x(1-\phi^2)dx.
\]
The boundary term is
\[
\left[\phi-\frac{\phi^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\frac43,
\]
so \(E\ge4/3\). Equality requires
\[
\phi_x=1-\phi^2.
\]
Integration gives the one-parameter family
\[
\boxed{\phi_K(x)=\tanh(x-X_0)},\qquad \boxed{E_K=\frac43}.
\]
Its charge is
\[
\boxed{Q=\frac{\phi(+\infty)-\phi(-\infty)}2=1}.
\]
The free parameter \(X_0\) is the broken-translation coordinate. Lorentz
invariance supplies
\[
\boxed{\phi_v(x,t)=\tanh\{\gamma[x-vt-X_0]\}},\qquad
\gamma=(1-v^2)^{-1/2},
\]
with energy \(E_v=\gamma E_K\).

Set \(X_0=0\) for the spectral calculation. At first order in epsilon,
\[
\boxed{H\eta=\omega^2\eta},\qquad
\boxed{H=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+4-6\operatorname{sech}^2x}.
\]
The discrete eigenfunctions and eigenvalues are
\[
\boxed{\eta_0(x)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\operatorname{sech}^2x},
\qquad \boxed{\omega_0^2=0},
\]
\[
\boxed{\eta_1(x)=\sqrt{\frac32}\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x},
\qquad \boxed{\omega_1^2=3}.
\]
Indeed, \(\int\operatorname{sech}^4x\,dx=4/3\) and, with
\(u=\tanh x\),
\[
\int\operatorname{sech}^2x\tanh^2x\,dx
=\int_{-1}^{1}u^2du=\frac23,
\]
which proves the normalizations. The zero eigenfunction is proportional to
\(d\phi_K/dx\), as translation symmetry requires. Since the potential tends
to four at both infinities, scattering states begin at
\(\boxed{\omega^2=4}\), or \(|\omega|=2\). Thus the shape mode at
\(\omega=\sqrt3\) is genuinely localized below the radiation band.

Nonnegativity follows without guessing the spectrum because
\[
H=A^\dagger A,\qquad
A=\frac d{dx}+2\tanh x,\qquad
A^\dagger=-\frac d{dx}+2\tanh x.
\]
Therefore there is no negative \(\omega^2\) mode: the kink is linearly
spectrally stable. Completeness of the discrete list follows from the partner
chain
\[
AA^\dagger=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+4-2\operatorname{sech}^2x
=B^\dagger B+3,
\qquad B=\frac d{dx}+\tanh x,
\]
while
\[
BB^\dagger+3=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+4.
\]
The free final partner has no square-integrable state below four. Hence the
intermediate partner has only its \(B\)-kernel at eigenvalue three, and H has
only that inherited state plus its \(A\)-kernel at zero. There are no omitted
bound modes. This spectral statement alone does not prove nonlinear
asymptotic stability or quantify radiation damping of a finite shape
oscillation.

The rest-frame shape frequency and continuum threshold are
\[
\boxed{\omega_{\rm shape}=\sqrt3=1.73205},\qquad
\boxed{\omega_{\rm cont}=2.00000}.
\]
At \(v=0.600\),
\[
\boxed{\gamma=1.25000},\qquad
\boxed{E_v=\frac53=1.66667},\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\text{moving width}}{\text{rest width}}=\frac1\gamma=0.800000}.
\]
The topological boundary conditions guarantee a kink sector, but the
localized shape eigenmode follows from the specific phi-four linearized
operator; topology by itself does not determine that spectrum.

graderFixtures.proofText: Square completion gives \(E\ge4/3\), saturated by \(\phi_K=\tanh(x-X_0)\). Linearization gives \(H=-d^2/dx^2+4-6\operatorname{sech}^2x\), with normalized modes \((\sqrt3/2)\operatorname{sech}^2x\) at zero and \(\sqrt{3/2}\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x\) at \(\omega^2=3\); the continuum starts at four.
I reverse the double-well force sign but keep tanh as the kink, then omit the translation mode and call the shape frequency part of the continuum.

WAVE:010626.title: The FPU beta lattice has an exact nonlinear pi mode
WAVE:010626.objective: Reduce an alternating FPU-beta lattice motion to one Duffing coordinate, derive its energy and frequency shift, and separate invariance from stability.
WAVE:010626.statement:
An even periodic chain of N equal masses has displacements \(x_n\), with
\(x_{n+N}=x_n\). Neighboring extension
\(r_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\) has potential
\[
V(r)=\frac K2r^2+\frac\beta4r^4,\qquad K,\beta>0.
\]
The equations are
\[
m\ddot x_n=K(x_{n+1}-2x_n+x_{n-1})
+\beta[(x_{n+1}-x_n)^3-(x_n-x_{n-1})^3].
\]

Show that the alternating ansatz \(x_n=(-1)^nQ(t)\) is an exact invariant
nonlinear normal mode, not merely a linear approximation. Derive the scalar
Duffing equation with every numerical factor. Derive the exact conserved
energy of the full N-particle state and its value at turning amplitude A.
Using a first-order Poincare-Lindstedt or harmonic-balance calculation,
obtain the leading amplitude-dependent frequency. Explain why the exact
invariant subspace does not by itself prove stability to perturbations in
other lattice modes, and identify the small dimensionless nonlinearity.

For \(N=16\), \(m=0.100\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(K=40.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\),
\(\beta=2000\,\mathrm{N/m^3}\), and \(A=10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), compute the
linear pi-mode frequency, nonlinearity parameter, leading corrected
frequency and period, energy per mass, and total energy. Check the units and
compare the nonlinear shift with the linear bandwidth scale without claiming
stability.
permittedResults: For \(\ddot Q+\omega_0^2Q+\alpha Q^3=0\) at small amplitude A, \(\Omega=\omega_0[1+3\alpha A^2/(8\omega_0^2)+O(A^4)]\).
An invariant solution can still be transversely unstable; invariance and Lyapunov or Floquet stability are different claims.

acceptableStrategies.description: Substitute the alternating invariant ansatz directly into every bond force and energy.
Use symmetry to identify the pi-mode invariant subspace, then apply Poincare-Lindstedt within that subspace.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Reduces the full nonlinear lattice exactly, closes its energy, and derives the small hardening shift while preserving the stability boundary.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Misses the factor sixteen from the two cubed bond extensions.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced equation, energy, and amplitude-frequency shift are inconsistent with the lattice.

commonErrors.description: Claims the exact alternating solution is stable against all other lattice perturbations without a Floquet analysis.
commonErrors.consequence: A separate transverse-instability question is falsely declared solved.

hintTree.content: Under the alternating ansatz, each bond extension is \(-2(-1)^nQ\); cube it before subtracting adjacent bond forces.
There are N bonds in the periodic chain, and every mass has speed magnitude \(|\dot Q|\).
Put \(\omega_\pi^2=4K/m\) and \(\alpha=16\beta/m\) into the standard Duffing frequency formula.

WAVE:010626.canonicalSolution:
For \(x_n=(-1)^nQ\),
\[
x_{n+1}-2x_n+x_{n-1}=-4(-1)^nQ.
\]
Also
\[
x_{n+1}-x_n=-2(-1)^nQ,\qquad
x_n-x_{n-1}=2(-1)^nQ.
\]
The difference of their cubes is \(-16(-1)^nQ^3\). Cancelling the common
alternating factor gives the exact scalar equation
\[
\boxed{m\ddot Q+4KQ+16\beta Q^3=0}.
\]
No neglected harmonic appears in another lattice coordinate, so this is an
exact invariant subspace.

The full energy is
\[
E=\sum_{n=1}^N\left[
\frac m2\dot x_n^2+\frac K2r_n^2+\frac\beta4r_n^4\right].
\]
Every bond has \(r_n^2=4Q^2\) and \(r_n^4=16Q^4\), hence
\[
\boxed{E=N\left(\frac m2\dot Q^2+2KQ^2+4\beta Q^4\right)}.
\]
At \(Q=A,\dot Q=0\),
\[
\boxed{\frac EN=2KA^2+4\beta A^4}.
\]

The linear pi frequency is
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pi=2\sqrt{\frac Km}}.
\]
Dividing the scalar equation by m gives cubic coefficient
\(\alpha=16\beta/m\). Therefore
\[
\Omega=\omega_\pi\left[
1+\frac{3(16\beta/m)A^2}{8(4K/m)}+O(A^4)\right]
=\boxed{\omega_\pi\left(1+\frac{3\beta A^2}{2K}
+O\left((\beta A^2/K)^2\right)\right)}.
\]
The natural small parameter is
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon=\frac{\beta A^2}{K}}.
\]
The hardening nonlinearity raises the frequency. This frequency calculation
describes motion within the invariant pi subspace only; perturbations at
other wave numbers require a separate Floquet stability analysis and can
grow even though the exact pi trajectory exists.

For the data,
\[
\boxed{\omega_\pi=40.0000\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\varepsilon=0.00500000}.
\]
The leading correction gives
\[
\boxed{\Omega=40.3000\ \mathrm{rad/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathcal P=0.155910\ \mathrm s}.
\]
Energy per particle and total energy are
\[
\boxed{E/N=0.00808000\ \mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{E=0.129280\ \mathrm J}.
\]
The relative frequency shift is only \(0.75\%\), consistent with the small
parameter. Since beta times A squared has the same units as K, epsilon is
dimensionless. The linear nearest-neighbor band spans zero to
\(2\sqrt{K/m}=40\,\mathrm{rad/s}\); being slightly above the linear band edge
is a nonlinear frequency statement, not proof against sideband instability.

graderFixtures.proofText: The alternating ansatz gives \(m\ddot Q+4KQ+16\beta Q^3=0\) exactly and \(E/N=m\dot Q^2/2+2KQ^2+4\beta Q^4\). The small-amplitude frequency is \(\omega_\pi[1+3\beta A^2/(2K)]\). Numerically it is 40.3000 rad/s with 0.008080 J per mass, but stability remains unclaimed.
I use only one bond cube and obtain a factor eight, then say the existence of the alternating orbit proves every perturbation is stable.

WAVE:010627.title: The Adler phase locks or slips
WAVE:010627.objective: Classify locking in the Adler phase equation, compute the tilted-potential barrier and relaxation rate, and derive the mean unlocked phase-slip frequency.
WAVE:010627.statement:
The phase difference \(\phi(t)\) between a weakly forced oscillator and its
drive is modeled by the Adler equation
\[
\dot\phi=\Delta-K\sin\phi,
\qquad K>0,
\]
where \(\Delta\) and \(K\) have units of angular frequency. Treat \(\phi\)
as an unwrapped phase when discussing slips.

Determine the complete locking condition. For \(|\Delta|<K\), list the
stable and unstable fixed points modulo \(2\pi\), derive the linear
relaxation rate about the stable point, and write the dynamics as overdamped
motion \(\dot\phi=-dU/d\phi\) in a tilted periodic potential. For
\(0<\Delta<K\), compute the forward barrier from the stable point to the
next unstable point in the direction of positive phase. Show that the barrier
vanishes at the positive locking boundary.

For \(\Delta>K\), integrate one full slip to derive its period and mean
unwrapped slip rate. Explain the bottleneck as \(\Delta\downarrow K\), and
state the corresponding result for \(\Delta<-K\).

First take \(K=5.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\Delta=3.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).
Compute the stable and forward unstable phases in \([0,2\pi)\), the
relaxation rate and time, and the forward potential barrier. Then keep the
same K but take \(\Delta=6.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\); compute the mean slip rate
and slip period. Distinguish angular slip rate from cycles per second.
permittedResults: For \(a>|b|\), \(\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi/(a-b\sin\phi)=2\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}\).
A one-dimensional fixed point is linearly stable when the derivative of its vector field is negative.

acceptableStrategies.description: Analyze the phase-line fixed points and then integrate the monotone vector field over one period outside the locking interval.
Use the tilted washboard potential to distinguish local stability, forward escape barrier, and saddle-node loss of locking.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Classifies locked and slipping Adler dynamics and derives both local relaxation and global slip behavior from the same phase equation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Labels the fixed point with negative cosine as stable or fails to distinguish the two arcsine branches.
commonErrors.consequence: The relaxation sign and barrier orientation are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Averages Delta minus K sine phi uniformly over phase and reports mean slip rate Delta.
commonErrors.consequence: The long bottleneck near the locking boundary and the exact square-root rate are missed.

hintTree.content: At a fixed point, \(\sin\phi=\Delta/K\); use the sign of \(-K\cos\phi\) for stability.
Choose \(U(\phi)=-\Delta\phi-K\cos\phi\). For positive detuning, the forward unstable point is \(\pi-\phi_s\).
In the unlocked regime, the time for one slip is the integral of \(d\phi/(\Delta-K\sin\phi)\) over any interval of length \(2\pi\).

WAVE:010627.canonicalSolution:
Fixed points require \(|\Delta|\le K\). Away from the equality case, let
\[
\phi_s=\arcsin(\Delta/K)
\]
on the branch with \(\cos\phi_s>0\). Then modulo \(2\pi\),
\[
\boxed{\phi_s\ \text{is stable}},
\qquad
\boxed{\phi_u=\pi-\phi_s\ \text{is unstable}}.
\]
Indeed, the vector-field derivative is \(-K\cos\phi\). A perturbation
\(\eta\) about the stable point obeys
\[
\dot\eta=-K\cos\phi_s\,\eta,
\]
so the relaxation rate and time are
\[
\boxed{\lambda=K\cos\phi_s=\sqrt{K^2-\Delta^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\tau_{\rm relax}=1/\lambda}.
\]
At \(|\Delta|=K\), the stable and unstable points coalesce in a nonhyperbolic
saddle-node; this is the locking boundary, not exponentially stable locking.

With
\[
\boxed{U(\phi)=-\Delta\phi-K\cos\phi},
\]
the equation is \(\dot\phi=-U'(\phi)\). For \(0<\Delta<K\), the forward
barrier is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta U_+&=U(\phi_u)-U(\phi_s)\\
&=2K\cos\phi_s-\Delta(\pi-2\phi_s),
\end{aligned}
\]
or
\[
\boxed{\Delta U_+=2\sqrt{K^2-\Delta^2}
-\Delta\left[\pi-2\arcsin(\Delta/K)\right]}.
\]
Both terms combine continuously to zero as \(\Delta\uparrow K\).

For \(\Delta>K\), the phase increases monotonically. One slip takes
\[
T_{\rm slip}=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\phi}{\Delta-K\sin\phi}
=\boxed{\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\Delta^2-K^2}}},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\langle\dot\phi\rangle=\sqrt{\Delta^2-K^2}}.
\]
The rate tends to zero as a square root at the boundary because the motion
spends most of each cycle near the annihilated fixed points. For
\(\Delta<-K\), slips run backward and
\[
\boxed{\langle\dot\phi\rangle=-\sqrt{\Delta^2-K^2}}.
\]

For \(K=5.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\Delta=3.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\[
\boxed{\phi_s=0.643501\ \mathrm{rad}},
\qquad
\boxed{\phi_u=2.49809\ \mathrm{rad}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\lambda=4.00000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\tau_{\rm relax}=0.250000\,\mathrm s},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\Delta U_+=2.43623\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
Because phase is dimensionless, \(U=-\Delta\phi-K\cos\phi\) and its barrier
have inverse-time units; radians may be written conventionally in the
frequency labels but do not supply an additional physical dimension. Only
differences in U matter.

For \(\Delta=6.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}\),
\[
\boxed{\langle\dot\phi\rangle=\sqrt{11}=3.31662\,\mathrm{rad/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{T_{\rm slip}=1.89445\,\mathrm s}.
\]
The slip frequency in cycles per second is
\(\langle\dot\phi\rangle/(2\pi)=0.527857\,\mathrm{Hz}\), not
\(3.31662\,\mathrm{Hz}\).

graderFixtures.proofText: For \(|\Delta|<K\), the stable phase is the arcsine branch with positive cosine and the relaxation rate is \(\sqrt{K^2-\Delta^2}\). The forward barrier follows from \(U=-\Delta\phi-K\cos\phi\). Outside locking, integrating one period gives signed mean slip rate \(\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta)\sqrt{\Delta^2-K^2}\).
I choose the negative-cosine branch as stable and average the sinusoidal term uniformly to claim that the unlocked mean phase speed is simply the detuning.

WAVE:010628.title: A nonlinear dimer can trap its population imbalance
WAVE:010628.objective: Use the reduced Hamiltonian of a discrete nonlinear Schrödinger dimer to derive the self-trapping threshold, turning imbalance, and symmetry-broken fixed points.
WAVE:010628.statement:
A conservative symmetric discrete nonlinear Schrödinger dimer has complex
site amplitudes with fixed total norm. In standard dimensionless time, define
the normalized population imbalance \(-1<z<1\), relative phase \(\phi\),
and positive interaction parameter \(\Lambda\). Their reduced Hamiltonian is
\[
H(z,\phi)=\frac{\Lambda}{2}z^2-\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\phi,
\]
with canonical equations
\[
\dot z=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial\phi},
\qquad
\dot\phi=\frac{\partial H}{\partial z}.
\]

Write the equations explicitly and prove that H is conserved. Locate the
zero-imbalance fixed point at \((0,\pi)\), determine when it is a saddle,
and identify its \(H=1\) contour as the self-trapping separatrix in that
regime. Show that any orbit with \(H>1\) can never cross \(z=0\). For initial data
\(z(0)=z_0>0\), \(\phi(0)=0\), derive the critical \(\Lambda_c(z_0)\) at
which the orbit reaches the separatrix. State carefully what the energy
criterion proves and why \(H\le1\) alone does not force every trajectory to
cross zero.

For \(z_0=0.800\) and \(\Lambda=6.00\), compute \(\Lambda_c\), the conserved
energy, and the smallest positive imbalance reached on the orbit. Derive the
nonzero fixed points at \(\phi=\pi\), and compute their imbalance for
\(\Lambda=6.00\). Linearize about either such fixed point and find the small
oscillation frequency in the stated dimensionless time. Explain how that
frequency would be converted back to physical units if the dimensionless time
were defined by \(\tau=2Jt/\hbar\).
permittedResults: For canonical Hamiltonian flow, \(dH/dt=H_z\dot z+H_\phi\dot\phi=0\).
At \(z=0\), this Hamiltonian has the restricted range \(-1\le H(0,\phi)\le1\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use conservation and the restricted energy range at zero imbalance before solving any time-dependent equations.
Locate fixed points from the canonical equations and linearize through the Hamiltonian Hessian.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the dimer phase portrait and separatrix energy to establish self-trapping and quantify the bounded nonlinear orbit.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Derives a threshold from imbalance alone while omitting the initial relative-phase contribution to the Hamiltonian.
commonErrors.consequence: The separatrix criterion is applied to the wrong energy contour.

commonErrors.description: Claims that every orbit with H less than or equal to one must cross zero imbalance.
commonErrors.consequence: A sufficient obstruction is incorrectly promoted to a complete dynamical classification.

hintTree.content: The relevant saddle is \((z,\phi)=(0,\pi)\), where \(H=1\).
For the smallest positive turning point of the numerical orbit, use \(\phi=\pi\), set \(y=\sqrt{1-z^2}\), and solve a quadratic in y.
At a nonzero pi-phase fixed point, \(\sqrt{1-z_*^2}=1/\Lambda\).

WAVE:010628.canonicalSolution:
Hamilton's equations are
\[
\boxed{\dot z=-\sqrt{1-z^2}\sin\phi},
\qquad
\boxed{\dot\phi=\Lambda z+\frac{z}{\sqrt{1-z^2}}\cos\phi}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\dot H=H_z(-H_\phi)+H_\phi H_z=\boxed{0}.
\]
The point \((0,\pi)\) has \(H=1\). Its Hessian entries are
\(H_{zz}=\Lambda-1\) and \(H_{\phi\phi}=-1\), so it is a saddle when
\(\Lambda>1\), becomes nonhyperbolic at \(\Lambda=1\), and is not a saddle
for \(0<\Lambda<1\). In the self-trapping regime its \(H=1\) contour is the
separatrix. If an orbit with H greater than one
crossed \(z=0\), it would have to satisfy
\[
H(0,\phi)=-\cos\phi\le1,
\]
a contradiction. Thus
\[
\boxed{H>1\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the sign of z is trapped}}.
\]
The converse is not automatic from energy alone: contours with \(H\le1\)
may have different initial phases and topology, so that inequality by itself
does not prove a zero crossing.

For \(z(0)=z_0>0\), \(\phi(0)=0\),
\[
H_0=\frac{\Lambda}{2}z_0^2-\sqrt{1-z_0^2}.
\]
Setting \(H_0=1\) gives the separatrix threshold
\[
\boxed{\Lambda_c(z_0)=
\frac{2[1+\sqrt{1-z_0^2}]}{z_0^2}}.
\]
For \(z_0=0.800\),
\[
\boxed{\Lambda_c=5.00000}.
\]
At \(\Lambda=6.00\),
\[
\boxed{H_0=3(0.8)^2-0.6=1.32000>1},
\]
so the orbit is self-trapped.

At the other imbalance turning point \(\phi=\pi\). Put
\(y=\sqrt{1-z^2}\); conservation gives
\[
3(1-y^2)+y=1.32,
\]
or \(3y^2-y-1.68=0\). The physical root is \(y=14/15\), hence
\[
\boxed{z_{\min}=\sqrt{1-(14/15)^2}=0.359011}.
\]

For a nonzero fixed point, \(\sin\phi=0\). On the \(\phi=\pi\) branch,
\[
0=\dot\phi=z\left(\Lambda-\frac1{\sqrt{1-z^2}}\right),
\]
so these symmetry-broken points exist for \(\Lambda>1\) at
\[
\boxed{z_*=\pm\sqrt{1-\Lambda^{-2}}}.
\]
For \(\Lambda=6\), \(\boxed{|z_*|=0.986013}\).

At either point, the mixed Hessian entry vanishes,
\(H_{\phi\phi}=-1/\Lambda\), and
\(H_{zz}=\Lambda-\Lambda^3\). Linearized Hamilton equations therefore give
\[
\delta\ddot z+(\Lambda^2-1)\delta z=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\Omega_{\rm small}=\sqrt{\Lambda^2-1}=\sqrt{35}=5.91608}
\]
in dimensionless inverse-time units. If \(\tau=2Jt/\hbar\), then the
physical angular frequency is
\(\boxed{\omega_{\rm physical}=(2J/\hbar)\Omega_{\rm small}}\).

graderFixtures.proofText: At \(z=0\), \(H=-\cos\phi\le1\), so \(H>1\) forbids an imbalance sign change. For phase-zero initial data, the separatrix condition gives \(\Lambda_c=2[1+\sqrt{1-z_0^2}]/z_0^2\). At \(z_0=0.8,\Lambda=6\), H is 1.32 and the positive turning point is 0.359011.
I ignore the initial phase in the energy, assert the converse of the H greater than one obstruction, and derive the symmetry-broken fixed points on the zero-phase branch.

WAVE:010629.title: A second harmonic depletes its fundamental
WAVE:010629.objective: Solve a phase-matched quadratic frequency-conversion model exactly and verify its Manley-Rowe invariant and asymptotic depletion.
WAVE:010629.statement:
In a lossless, exactly phase-matched quadratic medium, choose phases so the
relevant normalized envelopes \(A_1(z),A_2(z)\) are real and obey
\[
\frac{dA_1}{dz}=-\kappa A_1A_2,\qquad
\frac{dA_2}{dz}=\frac{\kappa}{2}A_1^2,
\qquad
A_1(0)=A_0>0,\quad A_2(0)=0.
\]
The normalization is chosen so that \(A_1^2+2A_2^2\) is proportional to
the conserved fundamental-frequency photon flux.

Derive the invariant directly from the coupled equations. Use it to solve
the depleted-pump problem exactly, giving both envelopes in hyperbolic
functions. Verify the solution by substitution, not only by invoking the
invariant. Determine the converted fraction
\(2A_2^2/A_0^2\), its small-distance behavior, and its limiting value.
Explain why the undepleted-pump approximation predicts \(A_2\) correctly
only at short distance and eventually violates conservation.

For normalized \(A_0=1.000\) and
\(\kappa A_0=0.800\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), evaluate both amplitudes and the
converted fraction at \(z=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}\). Compute the distance at which
half the invariant is in the second harmonic. State the dimensions of the
combination \(\kappa A_0z\).
permittedResults: The initial-value equation \(u'=a(1-u^2)\), \(u(0)=0\), has solution \(u=\tanh(az)\).
\(1-\tanh^2x=\operatorname{sech}^2x\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the weighted quadratic invariant before reducing the system to one separable amplitude.
Check the exact hyperbolic solution against both differential equations and its short-distance expansion.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Uses the Manley-Rowe invariant to solve and verify finite pump depletion with the correct normalization and conversion fraction.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses (A_1^2+A_2^2) as the invariant and loses the factor two associated with the harmonic normalization.
commonErrors.consequence: The solution scale and conversion fraction are inconsistent with the equations.

commonErrors.description: Holds (A_1=A_0) at every distance and reports unbounded linear growth of (A_2) as the exact solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The lossless conservation law is violated.

hintTree.content: Differentiate \(A_1^2+2A_2^2\) and use both coupled equations.
Set \(u=\sqrt2A_2/A_0\), then eliminate \(A_1^2\) with the invariant.
Half conversion means \(\tanh^2\zeta=1/2\), not \(\tanh\zeta=1/2\).

WAVE:010629.canonicalSolution:
Direct differentiation gives
\[
\frac d{dz}(A_1^2+2A_2^2)
=-2\kappa A_1^2A_2+2\kappa A_1^2A_2=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{A_1^2+2A_2^2=A_0^2}.
\]
Let \(u=\sqrt2A_2/A_0\). Then
\[
u'=\frac{\kappa A_0}{\sqrt2}(1-u^2),\qquad u(0)=0.
\]
With \(\zeta=\kappa A_0z/\sqrt2\),
\[
\boxed{A_1(z)=A_0\operatorname{sech}\zeta},\qquad
\boxed{A_2(z)=\frac{A_0}{\sqrt2}\tanh\zeta}.
\]
Differentiating both expressions reproduces the two original equations, so
the phase-locked solution satisfies more than the invariant alone.

The converted fraction is
\[
\boxed{\eta_2=\frac{2A_2^2}{A_0^2}=\tanh^2\zeta}.
\]
For short distance, \(\eta_2\simeq(\kappa A_0z)^2/2\) and
\(A_2\simeq\kappa A_0^2z/2\), the undepleted result. Extending that linear
growth indefinitely would make the generated weighted flux exceed
\(A_0^2\); depletion instead makes \(\eta_2\to1\) asymptotically.

At \(z=2.00\) cm, \(\zeta=1.13137085\), giving
\[
\boxed{A_1=0.584369207},\qquad
\boxed{A_2=0.573808605},\qquad
\boxed{\eta_2=0.658512630}.
\]
Half conversion requires
\[
\zeta=\operatorname{artanh}(1/\sqrt2)=0.881373587,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{z_{50}=\frac{\sqrt2\,\operatorname{artanh}(1/\sqrt2)}
{\kappa A_0}=1.55806\ \mathrm{cm}}.
\]
The product \(\kappa A_0\) has inverse-length units in this amplitude
normalization, making \(\kappa A_0z\) dimensionless.

graderFixtures.proofText: The invariant is \(A_1^2+2A_2^2=A_0^2\). With \(\zeta=\kappa A_0z/\sqrt2\), \(A_1=A_0\operatorname{sech}\zeta\), \(A_2=A_0\tanh\zeta/\sqrt2\), and conversion is \(\tanh^2\zeta\). At 2 cm the values are 0.584369207, 0.573808605, and 0.658512630.
I conserve A one squared plus A two squared, freeze the pump at A zero, and let the harmonic grow linearly without bound.

WAVE:010630.title: A Kerr medium chirps a Gaussian pulse
WAVE:010630.objective: Solve dispersionless self-phase modulation and quantify its instantaneous-frequency excursion and exact RMS spectral broadening by Parseval.
WAVE:010630.statement:
A slowly varying pulse envelope propagates through a lossless Kerr medium in
the dispersionless model
\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial z}=i\gamma |A|^2A,\qquad
A(0,t)=\sqrt{P_0}\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2T_0^2}\right),
\]
where \(\gamma P_0z\) is dimensionless. Solve the propagation equation
exactly at every retarded time. Show that intensity is unchanged while a
time-dependent nonlinear phase develops.

Define the instantaneous angular-frequency shift relative to the carrier by
\(\delta\omega(t)=-\partial_t\phi_{\rm NL}(t)\). Derive its extrema and
sign on the leading and trailing sides of the pulse. Then use the transform
\(\widehat A(\omega)=\int A(t)e^{-i\omega t}dt\) and Parseval to derive the
zero-mean RMS spectral width
\[
\sigma_\omega^2=
\frac{\int|\partial_tA|^2dt}{\int|A|^2dt}.
\]
Evaluate both the transform-limited contribution and the nonlinear chirp
contribution exactly. Explain why unchanged temporal intensity does not imply
an unchanged spectrum, and why this no-dispersion solution should not be
extrapolated through a medium where accumulated group-velocity dispersion is
large.

For \(T_0=1.00\,\mathrm{ps}\) and nonlinear phase
\(B=\gamma P_0L=3.00\), compute the maximum magnitude of the frequency
shift, the input and output RMS angular-frequency widths, and the broadening
factor. Give angular-frequency results in \(\mathrm{rad/s}\).
permittedResults: Parseval gives \((2\pi)^{-1}\int\omega^2|\widehat A|^2d\omega=\int|A_t|^2dt\).
For Gaussian weight \(e^{-at^2}\), \(\int t^2e^{-at^2}dt=\sqrt\pi/(2a^{3/2})\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Use conservation of pointwise intensity to integrate the nonlinear phase exactly.
Compute RMS bandwidth in time through Parseval, separating amplitude and phase derivatives.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects an exact Kerr phase solution to both local chirp and globally normalized spectral broadening without confusing time intensity with spectral intensity.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Defines the shift with the wrong sign or differentiates the Gaussian phase without its factor two.
commonErrors.consequence: The chirp direction and maximum excursion are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Adds a spurious cross term between the real amplitude slope and imaginary phase slope, or omits the Gaussian intensity weighting.
commonErrors.consequence: The RMS broadening law has the wrong dependence on nonlinear phase.

hintTree.content: Differentiate \(|A|^2\) with respect to z before solving the remaining phase equation.
The largest value of \(|t|e^{-t^2/T_0^2}\) occurs at \(|t|=T_0/\sqrt2\).
In \(|A_t|^2\), the real Gaussian-slope term and imaginary phase-slope term have no cross contribution.

WAVE:010630.canonicalSolution:
The propagation equation gives
\[
\partial_z|A|^2=A^*\partial_zA+A\partial_zA^*=0.
\]
Thus the input intensity is fixed along z, and direct integration yields
\[
\boxed{A(z,t)=\sqrt{P_0}e^{-t^2/(2T_0^2)}
\exp\!\left[i\gamma P_0z\,e^{-t^2/T_0^2}\right]}.
\]
At \(z=L\), write \(B=\gamma P_0L\). The nonlinear phase and frequency
shift are
\[
\phi_{\rm NL}=Be^{-t^2/T_0^2},\qquad
\boxed{\delta\omega(t)=\frac{2Bt}{T_0^2}e^{-t^2/T_0^2}}.
\]
The shift is negative on the leading side and positive on the trailing side
for \(B>0\), with
\[
\boxed{|\delta\omega|_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac2e}\frac{|B|}{T_0}}
\quad\text{at}\quad |t|=\frac{T_0}{\sqrt2}.
\]

Differentiating the exact envelope gives a real amplitude-slope term
\(-t/T_0^2\) and an imaginary phase-slope term. Their squared magnitudes
add. Gaussian integration produces
\[
\frac{\int (t^2/T_0^4)|A|^2dt}{\int|A|^2dt}
=\frac1{2T_0^2},
\]
and
\[
\frac{\int (\partial_t\phi_{\rm NL})^2|A|^2dt}
{\int|A|^2dt}
=\frac{2B^2}{3\sqrt3\,T_0^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\sigma_\omega^2=\frac1{T_0^2}
\left(\frac12+\frac{2B^2}{3\sqrt3}\right)},\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\sigma_\omega}{\sigma_{\omega,0}}
=\sqrt{1+\frac{4B^2}{3\sqrt3}}}.
\]

For \(T_0=10^{-12}\) s and \(B=3\),
\[
\boxed{|\delta\omega|_{\max}=2.57329165\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_{\omega,0}=7.07106781\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_\omega=1.99100518\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{rad/s}},
\]
\[
\boxed{\sigma_\omega/\sigma_{\omega,0}=2.81570652}.
\]
Temporal magnitude can remain fixed while phase curvature changes the Fourier
spectrum. If dispersion accumulates appreciably, that phase and the
intensity profile interact and the local-in-time solution no longer applies.

graderFixtures.proofText: The pulse keeps its Gaussian intensity and acquires phase \(Be^{-t^2/T_0^2}\). Hence \(\delta\omega=2Bt e^{-t^2/T_0^2}/T_0^2\), and Parseval gives \(\sigma_\omega^2=T_0^{-2}[1/2+2B^2/(3\sqrt3)]\). At B=3 the maximum shift is \(2.57329165\times10^{12}\) rad/s and the broadening factor is 2.81570652.

I define the frequency shift with the opposite sign and differentiate the Gaussian phase without its factor two. In the RMS calculation I add a cross term between the real amplitude slope and imaginary phase slope and drop the Gaussian intensity weighting.

WAVE:010631.title: A Melnikov integral predicts homoclinic tangling
WAVE:010631.objective: Evaluate the Melnikov function for a weakly perturbed double-well Duffing oscillator and interpret its simple-zero threshold cautiously.
WAVE:010631.statement:
Consider the weakly perturbed Duffing equation
\[
\ddot x-x+x^3=\epsilon[-\delta\dot x+\gamma\cos(\omega t)],
\qquad 0<\epsilon\ll1,
\]
with \(\delta,\gamma,\omega>0\). For \(\epsilon=0\), verify that one
homoclinic orbit of the saddle at the origin is
\[
x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,
\qquad
v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t.
\]
Construct the Melnikov function measuring first-order separation of the
stable and unstable manifolds as a function of forcing phase \(t_0\).
Evaluate both required integrals, using the Fourier transform of sech if
helpful, and derive the threshold for simple zeros.

Explain what a simple zero proves for sufficiently small epsilon and what it
does not prove about a finite-parameter experimental time series. Distinguish
the strict transverse-intersection threshold from equality, where the
first-order zero is tangent.

For \(\delta=0.0500\), \(\omega=1.20\), compute the critical \(\gamma_c\).
For \(\gamma=0.0600\), compute the dissipative offset, forcing amplitude in
the Melnikov function, their ratio, and the two root phases modulo \(2\pi\).
permittedResults: A simple zero of the Melnikov function implies a transverse homoclinic intersection for sufficiently small nonzero perturbation under the method's regularity assumptions.
\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\,e^{i\omega t}dt=\pi/\cosh(\pi\omega/2)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Insert the explicit homoclinic orbit into the planar determinant form of the Melnikov integral and use parity.
Transform the homoclinic coordinate first, obtain its velocity transform by differentiation, and reconstruct the phase dependence.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Evaluates the signed manifold-separation integral exactly and distinguishes a first-order transverse-intersection criterion from a blanket numerical claim of chaos.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor omega or the hyperbolic-cosine denominator in the forcing integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted threshold has the wrong frequency dependence.

commonErrors.description: Calls equality at the threshold a simple zero and guaranteed transverse intersection.
commonErrors.consequence: A tangent first-order contact is misclassified as a homoclinic tangle.

hintTree.content: Use \(M(t_0)=\int v_h(t)[-\delta v_h(t)+\gamma\cos(\omega(t+t_0))]dt\).
The cosine part vanishes by parity; integrate the sine part by recognizing \(v_h=x_h'\).
Simple roots exist only when the sinusoidal amplitude is strictly larger than the constant damping offset.

WAVE:010631.canonicalSolution:
Substitution verifies \(\ddot x_h-x_h+x_h^3=0\), and the orbit tends
to the saddle as \(t\to\pm\infty\). The planar Melnikov function is
\[
M(t_0)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)
[-\delta v_h(t)+\gamma\cos(\omega(t+t_0))]dt.
\]
With \(u=\tanh t\),
\[
\int v_h^2dt=2\int_{-1}^1u^2du=\frac43.
\]
Parity removes the cosine transform. Integration by parts and the sech
transform give
\[
\int v_h(t)\sin(\omega t)dt
=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi\omega}{\cosh(\pi\omega/2)}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{M(t_0)=-\frac{4\delta}{3}+
\frac{\sqrt2\pi\gamma\omega}{\cosh(\pi\omega/2)}
\sin(\omega t_0)}.
\]
Simple zeros exist precisely when
\[
\boxed{\gamma>\gamma_c=
\frac{4\delta}{3}\frac{\cosh(\pi\omega/2)}
{\sqrt2\pi\omega}}.
\]
Equality gives a double tangency of this first-order function, not the
transverse result. Above threshold, Melnikov theory implies a transverse
homoclinic intersection and horseshoe dynamics for sufficiently small
\(\epsilon\). It does not say that every trajectory looks irregular, nor
does it provide a quantitatively exact finite-epsilon onset.

For \(\delta=0.05\), \(\omega=1.2\),
\[
\boxed{\gamma_c=0.0421267}.
\]
At \(\gamma=0.06\), the constant offset magnitude and sinusoidal amplitude
are
\[
\boxed{B=4\delta/3=0.0666667},\qquad
\boxed{A=0.0949517},\qquad \boxed{A/B=1.42428}.
\]
The phase equation is \(\sin(\omega t_0)=B/A\). Thus, modulo \(2\pi\),
\[
\boxed{\omega t_0=0.778358\quad\text{or}\quad2.363235}.
\]
All variables were nondimensionalized in the stated Duffing equation;
restoring physical scales must be done before assigning laboratory units to
\(\delta,\gamma\), or the Melnikov integral.

graderFixtures.proofText: The Melnikov function is \(-4\delta/3+[\sqrt2\pi\gamma\omega/\cosh(\pi\omega/2)]\sin(\omega t_0)\). Simple zeros require strict gamma above 0.0421267; at gamma 0.06 the phase roots are 0.778358 and 2.363235.
I omit the frequency factor from the sech transform and call equality at the threshold a guaranteed transverse chaotic intersection.

WAVE:010632.title: A Morse oscillator softens on the way to dissociation
WAVE:010632.objective: Derive turning points, action, frequency, and period of a classical Morse oscillator and connect the small-energy and dissociation limits.
WAVE:010632.statement:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves in the Morse potential
\[
V(x)=D\left(1-e^{-ax}\right)^2,
\qquad D>0,\quad a>0.
\]
For a bound orbit with \(0<E<D\), find both turning points and show their
asymmetry about the potential minimum. Evaluate the classical action
\[
J(E)=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dx
\]
and use \(\Omega(E)=dE/dJ\) to obtain the nonlinear frequency and period.
You may change variables to \(y=e^{-ax}\), but must preserve which turning
point corresponds to compression and which to extension.

Check the small-amplitude curvature frequency, the limit \(E\to0\), and the
dissociation limit \(E\to D^-\). Explain why the period diverges even though
the compressed turning point remains finite. Invert \(J(E)\) to exhibit the
quadratic dependence of energy on action and identify its allowed action
range.

For \(m=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(D=0.500\,\mathrm J\),
\(a=4.00\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), and \(E=0.320\,\mathrm J\), compute both
turning points, the small-amplitude frequency, nonlinear frequency, period,
and action.
permittedResults: For a one-degree-of-freedom integrable oscillator, \(dJ/dE=T/(2\pi)\) and \(\Omega=dE/dJ\).
The curvature of \(D(1-e^{-ax})^2\) at zero is \(2Da^2\), so \(\omega_0=a\sqrt{2D/m}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Evaluate the phase-space area after the exponential coordinate change, then differentiate the action.
Compute the period directly from the energy integral and integrate dJ/dE equals T over two pi with J of zero equal to zero.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Connects the asymmetric orbit geometry to an exact action-energy relation and its physical softening limits.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Swaps one plus square root e and one minus square root e in the logarithmic turning points.
commonErrors.consequence: The compressed side is predicted to diverge while the dissociating outer side remains finite.

commonErrors.description: Uses omega_0 divided by square root of one minus E over D instead of multiplying by it.
commonErrors.consequence: The frequency diverges rather than vanishing at dissociation.

hintTree.content: At a turning point, \(1-e^{-ax}=\pm\sqrt{E/D}\).
After substituting \(y=e^{-ax}\), the action integral is elementary after centering y at one.
Differentiate the proposed action with respect to E and compare with the period before inverting it.

WAVE:010632.canonicalSolution:
Let \(e=E/D\). The turning-point equation gives
\(e^{-ax}=1\pm\sqrt e\). Thus
\[
\boxed{x_-= -\frac1a\ln(1+\sqrt e)},\qquad
\boxed{x_+= -\frac1a\ln(1-\sqrt e)}.
\]
The negative point is compressed and remains finite as \(e\to1\); the
positive point moves to infinity.

Evaluating \(J=(1/\pi)\int_{x_-}^{x_+}\sqrt{2m(E-V)}dx\) after
\(y=e^{-ax}\) gives
\[
\boxed{J(E)=\frac{\sqrt{2mD}}a
\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac ED}\right)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\Omega(E)=\left(\frac{dJ}{dE}\right)^{-1}
=a\sqrt{\frac{2(D-E)}m}
=\omega_0\sqrt{1-\frac ED}},
\]
\[
\boxed{T(E)=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega(E)}}.
\]
At small energy, \(\Omega\to\omega_0=a\sqrt{2D/m}\), matching the
curvature of the potential. At dissociation, the outer turning point and
period diverge while \(\Omega\to0\): the particle spends arbitrarily long in
the flat outer tail.

Solving for energy gives
\[
\boxed{E(J)=\omega_0J-\frac{a^2}{2m}J^2},
\qquad
0\le J<\frac{\sqrt{2mD}}a.
\]
The negative quadratic term is the exact classical softening, not a
low-amplitude truncation.

For \(e=0.64\),
\[
\boxed{x_-=-0.146947\ \mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{x_+=0.402359\ \mathrm m}.
\]
The frequencies and period are
\[
\boxed{\omega_0=28.2843\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=16.9706\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{T=0.370240\ \mathrm s}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\boxed{J=1.41421\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J\,s}}.
\]
The action has angular-momentum units, and differentiating energy with
respect to it produces radians per second.

graderFixtures.proofText: The turning points are \(-a^{-1}\ln(1+\sqrt{E/D})\) and \(-a^{-1}\ln(1-\sqrt{E/D})\). The action gives \(\Omega=\omega_0\sqrt{1-E/D}\). The data yield period 0.370240 s and action 0.0141421 J s.
I swap the two logarithmic turning-point branches and make the Morse frequency grow as one over square root of one minus E over D.

WAVE:010633.title: An uncompressed bead chain has solitary pulses but no sound speed
WAVE:010633.objective: Derive the preload-dependent acoustic speed of a Hertz chain and the force scaling of strongly nonlinear pulses in its sonic-vacuum limit.
WAVE:010633.statement:
Identical beads of mass \(m\) and equilibrium center spacing \(a\) interact
only while in compression. If \(\delta_n\) is the overlap at contact \(n\),
\[
F_n=A[\delta_n]_+^{3/2},\qquad [y]_+=\max(y,0).
\]
With a static overlap \(\delta_0\ge0\), write
\(\delta_n=\delta_0+u_{n-1}-u_n\) and derive the exact discrete equations.

For \(\delta_0>0\), linearize about equilibrium, find the acoustic
dispersion relation, and obtain the long-wavelength sound speed. Then take
the limit \(\delta_0\to0\) correctly and explain the term sonic vacuum:
finite-amplitude compression pulses may propagate, but infinitesimal sound
has zero speed. By balancing inertia with the Hertz force, derive the
strongly nonlinear scaling
\[
V\propto a\sqrt{A/m}\,\delta_m^{1/4}
\]
and rewrite it in terms of peak force \(F_m\). Derive the peak contact-energy
scaling and state which dimensionless profile constant cannot be obtained
from scaling alone.

For \(A=1.00\times10^9\,\mathrm{N/m^{3/2}}\),
\(m=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(a=0.0100\,\mathrm m\), and
\(\delta_0=10.0\,\mu\mathrm m\), compute the tangent stiffness, preload
force, and linear sound speed. If one strongly nonlinear pulse has 64 times
the peak force of another in the uncompressed chain, compute their peak
overlap, speed, contact-energy, and duration ratios under the same
dimensionless pulse shape.
permittedResults: Linearizing \(A\delta^{3/2}\) about positive \(\delta_0\) gives tangent stiffness \(K_{\rm lin}=(3/2)A\delta_0^{1/2}\).
The potential stored by one Hertz contact is \(U(\delta)=\int_0^\delta A s^{3/2}ds=(2/5)A\delta^{5/2}\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Linearize the exact discrete Hertz equations at positive preload, then perform a separate finite-amplitude balance at zero preload.
Use contact time and energy scales to derive the same strong-pulse exponents independently.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Separates preloaded linear acoustics from the zero-preload strongly nonlinear scaling and keeps overlap, force, speed, energy, and duration exponents consistent.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Linearizes the uncompressed contact as a spring with nonzero stiffness.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining zero sound speed and preload dependence are lost.

commonErrors.description: Uses the overlap exponent one-fourth directly as the peak-force exponent.
commonErrors.consequence: The required conversion through (F=Adelta^{3/2}) is missed and every ratio is wrong.

hintTree.content: The bead equation is the left contact force minus the right contact force.
For a linearized plane wave, use \(u_n\propto e^{i(kna-\omega t)}\).
Use \(\delta_m=(F_m/A)^{2/3}\) before converting the speed and energy exponents to force exponents.

WAVE:010633.canonicalSolution:
The overlap on the left of bead n is
\(\delta_0+u_{n-1}-u_n\), and that on its right is
\(\delta_0+u_n-u_{n+1}\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
m\ddot u_n=A[\delta_0+u_{n-1}-u_n]_+^{3/2}
-A[\delta_0+u_n-u_{n+1}]_+^{3/2}
}.
\]
For positive preload the tangent stiffness is
\[
\boxed{K_{\rm lin}=\frac32A\sqrt{\delta_0}}.
\]
Linearization gives
\[
m\ddot u_n=K_{\rm lin}(u_{n-1}-2u_n+u_{n+1}),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\omega^2(k)=\frac{4K_{\rm lin}}m
\sin^2\left(\frac{ka}{2}\right)}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{c_0=a\sqrt{\frac{K_{\rm lin}}m}
=a\sqrt{\frac{3A}{2m}}\,\delta_0^{1/4}}.
\]
At zero preload, \(K_{\rm lin}=0\) and \(c_0=0\). Replacing the Hertz law by
a nonzero linear spring at \(\delta_0=0\) would destroy the sonic-vacuum
limit.

For a finite pulse with peak overlap \(\delta_m\), the characteristic
contact acceleration scale is \(A\delta_m^{3/2}/m\). Balancing it over one
bead spacing gives
\[
\boxed{V=C_Va\sqrt{\frac Am}\,\delta_m^{1/4}},
\]
where the dimensionless \(C_V\) depends on the discrete or chosen continuum
pulse profile and cannot be fixed by dimensional scaling alone. Since
\(F_m=A\delta_m^{3/2}\),
\[
\boxed{V\propto aA^{1/3}m^{-1/2}F_m^{1/6}}.
\]
The peak contact energy obeys
\[
\boxed{U_m=\frac25A\delta_m^{5/2}
\propto A^{-2/3}F_m^{5/3}}.
\]
For comparable profile widths measured in bead counts, duration scales as
\(V^{-1}\propto F_m^{-1/6}\).

For the specified preload,
\[
\boxed{K_{\rm lin}=4.74341649\times10^6\ \mathrm{N/m}},
\]
\[
\boxed{F_0=A\delta_0^{3/2}=31.6227766\ \mathrm N},
\qquad
\boxed{c_0=217.793859\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
If \(F_{m,2}/F_{m,1}=64=2^6\), then
\[
\boxed{\frac{\delta_{m,2}}{\delta_{m,1}}=64^{2/3}=16},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{V_2}{V_1}=64^{1/6}=2},
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{U_{m,2}}{U_{m,1}}=64^{5/3}=1024},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\tau_2}{\tau_1}=\frac12}.
\]
The speed ratio is universal for the shared profile assumption; an absolute
speed still requires \(C_V\), which the scaling argument deliberately does
not invent.

graderFixtures.proofText: At positive preload \(K_{\rm lin}=(3/2)A\sqrt{\delta_0}\) and \(c_0=a\sqrt{K_{\rm lin}/m}\); at zero preload both vanish. Finite pulses scale as \(V\propto F_m^{1/6}\), so a force ratio 64 gives speed ratio 2 and energy ratio 1024.
I assign the uncompressed chain a finite linear spring speed and use peak force to the one-fourth power for solitary-pulse speed.

WAVE:010634.title: An empty cavity collapses in finite time
WAVE:010634.objective: Integrate the nonlinear Rayleigh collapse equation exactly and distinguish empty-cavity collapse from small gas-bubble oscillations.
WAVE:010634.statement:
An empty spherical cavity of initial radius \(R_0\) is at rest in an
infinite incompressible, inviscid liquid of density \(\rho\). At \(t=0\), a
constant excess far-field pressure \(\Delta p>0\) is applied. Neglect vapor
pressure, surface tension, viscosity, gravity, and liquid compressibility.
The Rayleigh equation is
\[
R\ddot R+\frac32\dot R^2=-\frac{\Delta p}{\rho},
\qquad R(0)=R_0,\quad\dot R(0)=0.
\]

Derive a first integral either from this ODE or from the kinetic energy of
the radial liquid flow. Select the collapsing velocity branch and integrate
to obtain the finite collapse time in beta-function form. Evaluate its
dimensionless constant and identify why the model becomes singular as
\(R\to0\).

Then add a gas pressure
\(p_g(R)=p_\infty(R_0/R)^{3\kappa}\) with equilibrium
\(p_g(R_0)=p_\infty\), still omitting surface tension. Linearize about \(R_0\)
and derive the small-amplitude Minnaert frequency. Explain why this harmonic
frequency must not be inserted into the empty-cavity collapse problem.

For \(R_0=1.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and
\(\Delta p=100\,\mathrm{kPa}\), compute the collapse time. For a gas bubble
with the same radius, \(p_\infty=100\,\mathrm{kPa}\), and
\(\kappa=1.40\), compute its linear angular and ordinary frequencies.
permittedResults: The incompressible radial velocity outside a sphere is \(v(r,t)=R^2\dot R/r^2\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the radius equation to a first-order equation for squared speed and evaluate the scaled collapse integral.
Compute radial-flow kinetic energy and pressure work, then integrate the resulting speed-radius relation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the finite-time nonlinear collapse from energy and cleanly separates it from the harmonic gas-bubble restoring mechanism.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the radius equation as constant acceleration by dropping the R-dependent inertial and velocity-squared terms.
commonErrors.consequence: The first integral, collapse coefficient, and singular velocity scaling are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses the gas-bubble Minnaert frequency to estimate the empty-cavity collapse time.
commonErrors.consequence: A restoring gas pressure absent from the stated collapse model is silently introduced.

hintTree.content: Set \(y(R)=\dot R^2\), so \(\ddot R=\frac12dy/dR\).
After scaling \(x=R/R_0\), write \(x^{-3}-1=(1-x^3)/x^3\).
For the gas bubble, put \(R=R_0(1+\epsilon)\) and expand \((1+\epsilon)^{-3\kappa}\).

WAVE:010634.canonicalSolution:
Let \(y(R)=\dot R^2\). Then
\(\ddot R=\frac12y'(R)\), and the Rayleigh equation becomes
\[
Ry'+3y=-\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}.
\]
Multiplication by \(R^2\) and integration with \(y(R_0)=0\) gives
\[
\boxed{\dot R^2=\frac{2\Delta p}{3\rho}
\left[\left(\frac{R_0}{R}\right)^3-1\right]}.
\]
The collapsing solution takes the negative square root. The same integral
follows from the liquid kinetic energy
\[
K=2\pi\rho R^3\dot R^2
\]
and pressure work
\((4\pi\Delta p/3)(R_0^3-R^3)\).

The time to reach zero radius is
\[
t_c=R_0\sqrt{\frac{3\rho}{2\Delta p}}
\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{-3}-1}}.
\]
Using the beta integral,
\[
\boxed{
t_c=R_0\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\Delta p}}\,
\sqrt{\frac32}\,\frac13B\left(\frac56,\frac12\right)
}
\]
or
\[
\boxed{t_c=0.914681357\,R_0\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\Delta p}}}.
\]
As \(R\to0\), the predicted speed diverges as \(R^{-3/2}\). Liquid
compressibility, viscosity, gas, vapor, and ultimately other physics cannot
remain negligible near that singular endpoint.

For a gas bubble, the inviscid radius equation near equilibrium has
right-hand side
\[
\frac{p_g(R)-p_\infty}{\rho}
\approx-\frac{3\kappa p_\infty}{\rho}\epsilon,
\qquad R=R_0(1+\epsilon).
\]
To first order the left side is \(R_0^2\ddot\epsilon\), so
\[
\boxed{\omega_M^2=\frac{3\kappa p_\infty}{\rho R_0^2}}.
\]
This restoring pressure is absent for the empty cavity; its finite collapse
is not one quarter of a Minnaert period.

For the collapse data,
\[
\boxed{t_c=9.14681357\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm s
=91.4681357\ \mathrm{\mu s}}.
\]
For the gas bubble,
\[
\boxed{\omega_M=2.04939015\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},
\]
\[
\boxed{f_M=\frac{\omega_M}{2\pi}=3261.70573\ \mathrm{Hz}}.
\]
The collapse scaling contains \(\sqrt{\rho/\Delta p}\), while the gas
frequency contains \(\sqrt{p_\infty/\rho}/R_0\); their inverse-looking
dimensions reflect two different initial-value problems, not competing
formulas for one motion.

graderFixtures.proofText: The first integral is \(\dot R^2=[2\Delta p/(3\rho)][(R_0/R)^3-1]\), with the negative root during collapse. It gives \(t_c=0.914681357R_0\sqrt{\rho/\Delta p}=91.4681357\) microseconds; the separate gas bubble has \(f_M=3261.70573\) Hz.
I drop the velocity-squared term, use constant radial acceleration, and then estimate the empty-cavity collapse as one quarter of a Minnaert period.

WAVE:010635.title: An exponential lattice carries an exact compression soliton
WAVE:010635.objective: Verify the exact Toda one-soliton, extract its bond compression, force, width, and amplitude-dependent speed, and restore physical units.
WAVE:010635.statement:
Let \(q_n(t)\) be the longitudinal displacement of site n in an infinite
lattice of spacing a and mass m. Neighboring displacement differences
\(r_n=q_{n+1}-q_n\) have Toda potential
\[
V(r)=\frac{K}{b^2}\left(e^{-br}+br-1\right),
\]
where \(K>0\) has units \(\mathrm{N/m}\) and \(b>0\) has units
\(\mathrm{m^{-1}}\). Derive the discrete equations of motion and scale them
using \(y_n=bq_n\) and \(\tau=\sqrt{K/m}\,t\).

For \(\kappa>0\), define
\[
\tau_n=1+\exp(2\kappa n-2\sinh\kappa\,\tau+\delta),
\qquad
y_n=\log\frac{\tau_{n-1}}{\tau_n}.
\]
Verify that this is an exact one-soliton solution, either by direct
substitution or a tau-function identity. Derive a closed expression for
\(e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}\), and from it find the center speed, characteristic
width in sites, maximum bond shortening, and maximum excess compressive
force. State the small-kappa speed limit and explain why the solution is a
localized strain pulse even though the displacement has different constants
as \(n\to\pm\infty\).

For \(m=0.0500\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(a=0.0250\,\mathrm m\),
\(K=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(b=40.0\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), and
\(\kappa=0.800\), compute the physical soliton speed, inverse-kappa width
scale in sites, maximum bond shortening, and peak excess compressive force.
permittedResults: For \(\tau_n=1+e^{2\zeta_n}\), the identity \(\tau_{n+1}\tau_{n-1}/\tau_n^2=1+\sinh^2\kappa\,\operatorname{sech}^2\zeta_n\) holds when \(\zeta_{n+1}-\zeta_n=\kappa\).
The dimensionless Toda equation is \(y_n''=e^{-(y_n-y_{n-1})}-e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}\), with primes denoting tau derivatives.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the tau ratio to reduce both the acceleration and exponential bond terms to rational functions of one traveling exponential.
First prove the closed bond-force identity, then difference it across adjacent bonds to audit the logarithmic displacement acceleration.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Verifies the discrete one-soliton exactly and consistently converts its dimensionless center, strain, force, and speed back to physical variables.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes a continuum sech-squared ansatz but never verifies the discrete lattice shifts.
commonErrors.consequence: An approximation is mislabeled as the exact Toda one-soliton.

commonErrors.description: Uses the acoustic speed for every kappa and drops the factor sinh kappa over kappa.
commonErrors.consequence: The soliton's amplitude-dependent speed and numerical result are wrong.

hintTree.content: Differentiate V carefully: the constant linear term makes the equilibrium force zero but cancels out of the site equation.
Write \(e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}=\tau_{n+1}\tau_{n-1}/\tau_n^2\) and set the exponential in tau n equal to a single variable.
The pulse center is where \(\kappa n-\sinh\kappa\,\tau+\delta/2=0\).

WAVE:010635.canonicalSolution:
With \(r_n=q_{n+1}-q_n\), force balance gives
\[
\boxed{m\ddot q_n=\frac Kb
\left[e^{-b(q_n-q_{n-1})}-e^{-b(q_{n+1}-q_n)}\right]}.
\]
Under \(y_n=bq_n\) and \(\tau=\sqrt{K/m}\,t\), this becomes
\[
\boxed{y_n''=e^{-(y_n-y_{n-1})}-e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}}.
\]

Let
\[
\zeta_n=\kappa n-\sinh\kappa\,\tau+\delta/2,
\qquad \tau_n=1+e^{2\zeta_n}.
\]
The proposed displacement implies
\[
e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}
=\frac{\tau_{n+1}\tau_{n-1}}{\tau_n^2}.
\]
Putting \(z=e^{2\zeta_n}\) and expanding the numerator gives
\[
\frac{(1+e^{2\kappa}z)(1+e^{-2\kappa}z)}{(1+z)^2}
=1+\frac{4\sinh^2\kappa\,z}{(1+z)^2}.
\]
Since \(4z/(1+z)^2=\operatorname{sech}^2\zeta_n\),
\[
\boxed{e^{-(y_{n+1}-y_n)}
=1+\sinh^2\kappa\,\operatorname{sech}^2\zeta_n}.
\]
Twice differentiating the logarithmic tau ratio and using this identity at
n and n minus one verifies the Toda equation exactly; the coefficient
\(2\sinh\kappa\) in time is required by that identity.

The center condition gives the dimensionless site speed
\(dn/d\tau=\sinh\kappa/\kappa\), hence
\[
\boxed{v=a\sqrt{K/m}\,\frac{\sinh\kappa}{\kappa}}.
\]
The sech-squared argument gives a characteristic width \(1/\kappa\) sites.
At the center,
\[
b r_{\min}=-\log(1+\sinh^2\kappa)
=-2\log\cosh\kappa,
\]
so the maximum positive shortening and excess compressive force are
\[
\boxed{\Delta_{\max}=\frac{2\log\cosh\kappa}{b}},
\qquad
\boxed{F_{\max}=\frac Kb\sinh^2\kappa}.
\]
As \(\kappa\to0\), \(\sinh\kappa/\kappa\to1\), giving the acoustic speed
\(a\sqrt{K/m}\). Meanwhile \(y_n\to0\) at one spatial infinity and
\(y_n\to-2\kappa\) at the other. Their difference is a displacement step,
but the bond strain is the localized sech-squared-related pulse above.

For the stated parameters,
\[
\sqrt{K/m}=63.2455532\ \mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{v=1.75527357\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The requested width scale is
\[
\boxed{1/\kappa=1.25000\ \text{sites}}.
\]
The center shortening and force are
\[
\boxed{\Delta_{\max}=0.0145376780\ \mathrm m},
\qquad
\boxed{F_{\max}=3.94366118\ \mathrm N}.
\]
Replacing sinh kappa by kappa would retain only the small-amplitude speed
and erase the exact amplitude-speed relation that makes the pulse nonlinear.

graderFixtures.proofText: The exact bond factor is \(1+\sinh^2\kappa\,\operatorname{sech}^2\zeta_n\), and the center moves at \(a\sqrt{K/m}\sinh\kappa/\kappa\). The data give 1.75527357 meters per second and peak shortening 0.0145376780 meter.
I insert a continuum sech profile, call it exact without checking lattice shifts, and use the small-amplitude acoustic speed at kappa zero point eight.

WAVE:010636.title: A rigid stop turns smooth oscillation into a nonsmooth map
WAVE:010636.objective: Construct an exact impact-to-impact map for a harmonic oscillator and expose the restitution decay and square-root singularity at grazing.
WAVE:010636.statement:
A unit-mass coordinate obeys \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=0\) whenever
\(x<d\), with a rigid unilateral stop at \(x=d>0\). At an impact,
position is continuous and Newton restitution gives
\[
\dot x^+=-e\dot x^-,\qquad 0<e<1,
\]
for an incoming velocity \(\dot x^->0\). There is no forcing or damping
between impacts. A hypothetical free orbit of amplitude A approaches the
stop; it impacts only when \(A>d\).

Find the first preimpact speed in terms of A. Starting immediately after an
impact with outgoing speed magnitude u, solve the harmonic flight exactly
and find the smallest positive return time to the stop and the next incoming
speed. Use these results to construct a scalar impact map for the sequence
of incoming speed magnitudes \(v_j\), including its flight-time sequence.
Determine the kinetic-energy loss at each collision and decide whether the
impacts accumulate in finite time. Then analyze \(A\downarrow d\): show the
square-root onset of collision speed, the divergent derivative with respect
to A, and explain why this grazing singularity is present even though the
impact-to-impact velocity map itself is linear.

For \(\omega_0=20.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(d=0.100\,\mathrm m\),
\(A=0.105\,\mathrm m\), and \(e=0.600\), compute the first incoming and
outgoing velocities, angular distance from the free positive turning point
to impact, the first two postimpact flight times, the natural period, energy
loss per unit mass at the first collision, and \(dv_0/dA\).
permittedResults: A free harmonic trajectory starting at \(x=d\) with velocity \(-u\) is \(x(t)=d\cos\omega_0t-(u/\omega_0)\sin\omega_0t\).
Near grazing, \(A^2-d^2=(A-d)(A+d)\sim2d(A-d)\).

acceptableStrategies.description: Build the Poincare map by solving one exact postimpact harmonic flight and composing it with the restitution law.
Use energy to obtain collision speeds and half-angle identities to determine which return-time root is physically next.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Separates conservative flight, instantaneous restitution, and amplitude-to-event grazing geometry while keeping event signs, times, and energy losses consistent.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Chooses a return angle in zero to pi for a trajectory leaving the positive stop with negative velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated event occurs before the oscillator has completed the physically required inward excursion.

commonErrors.description: Extends the impact velocity as a differentiable linear function through A equals d or ignores the no-impact side.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining square-root event singularity at grazing is removed.

hintTree.content: Use conservation of harmonic energy before the first impact to obtain its velocity.
Set x of t equal to d and use half-angle identities; the next nonzero root has angle between pi and two pi.
Distinguish the smooth restitution map in collision speed from the map that first converts free amplitude into collision speed.

WAVE:010636.canonicalSolution:
The free-orbit energy per unit mass is
\(\frac12\omega_0^2A^2\). At \(x=d\), conservation gives the first
incoming speed
\[
\boxed{v_0=\omega_0\sqrt{A^2-d^2}},\qquad A>d.
\]
The first outgoing velocity is \(-ev_0\).

More generally, start a flight at \(x(0)=d\), \(\dot x(0)=-u\), where
u is positive. Then
\[
x(t)=d\cos\theta-\frac{u}{\omega_0}\sin\theta,
\qquad \theta=\omega_0t.
\]
Setting x equal to d and excluding the root theta zero gives
\[
-2d\sin^2(\theta/2)
=2\frac{u}{\omega_0}\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2).
\]
The smallest positive nonzero root lies in \((\pi,2\pi)\):
\[
\boxed{t_f(u)=\frac{2\pi-2\arctan[u/(\omega_0d)]}{\omega_0}}.
\]
Differentiating the flight solution at this root gives incoming velocity
plus u, as required also by conservation at the same position.

Let \(v_j>0\) be the incoming speed at collision j. Restitution makes the
outgoing speed magnitude \(u_j=ev_j\); the next conservative return has that
same incoming magnitude. Hence the exact event map and flight time are
\[
\boxed{v_{j+1}=ev_j},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta t_j=\frac{2\pi-2\arctan[ev_j/(\omega_0d)]}{\omega_0}}.
\]
Thus \(v_j=e^jv_0\), and the energy lost per unit mass at collision j is
\[
\boxed{\Delta E_j/m=\frac12(1-e^2)v_j^2}.
\]
As j grows, \(\Delta t_j\to2\pi/\omega_0>0\), so event times diverge rather
than accumulating: this single-stop oscillator has no finite-time chatter.

At grazing, A equals d and
\[
v_0=\omega_0\sqrt{(A-d)(A+d)}
\sim\omega_0\sqrt{2d(A-d)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac{dv_0}{dA}=\frac{\omega_0A}{\sqrt{A^2-d^2}}\to\infty}
\]
as A decreases to d from above. The collision-to-collision rule has slope e,
but the creation or loss of the collision event is a square-root map from
the smooth free-orbit amplitude. That event geometry is the grazing
nonsmoothness.

For the specified parameters,
\[
\boxed{v_0=0.640312424\ \mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{\dot x_0^+=-0.384187454\ \mathrm{m/s}}.
\]
The angular distance from the free positive turning point is
\[
\boxed{\arccos(d/A)=0.309844640\ \mathrm{rad}}.
\]
The first postimpact flight uses \(u_0=ev_0\), while the second uses
\(u_1=e^2v_0\), giving
\[
\boxed{\Delta t_0=0.295181071\ \mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{\Delta t_1=0.302684274\ \mathrm s}.
\]
For comparison,
\[
\boxed{T_0=2\pi/\omega_0=0.314159265\ \mathrm s}.
\]
The first energy loss per unit mass and amplitude sensitivity are
\[
\boxed{\Delta E_0/m=0.131200000\ \mathrm{J/kg}},
\qquad
\boxed{dv_0/dA=65.5929800\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
\]
Applying restitution to position, or choosing the short algebraic root of
the half-angle equation outside the physical return interval, would break
this event map.

graderFixtures.proofText: The map is \(v_{j+1}=ev_j\) with flight time \([2\pi-2\arctan(ev_j/(\omega_0d))]/\omega_0\). Here \(v_0=0.640312424\) meters per second and \(\Delta t_0=0.295181071\) second; near grazing \(v_0\) scales as square root of A minus d.
I take the short return root before pi, make collision speed linear through A equals d, and claim the geometrically shrinking velocities force finite-time chatter.
