WAVE:010637.title: A sine coordinate solves an oscillator between tangent walls
WAVE:010637.objective: Use energy and a bounded coordinate transform to derive the exact amplitude-dependent period of a tangent-wall oscillator.
WAVE:010637.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in the interval
$|x|<\pi a/2$ under the conservative potential
$$
V(x)=\frac12m\omega_0^2a^2\tan^2(x/a),
$$
where $a>0$ and $\omega_0>0$. It is released from rest at the positive
turning point $x=A$, with $0<A<\pi a/2$.

Write the exact energy equation and introduce $u=\sin(x/a)$. Show from the
energy identity, with a continuity argument at turning points, that $u$ obeys
a linear oscillator. Derive its angular frequency, the exact physical
trajectory $x(t)$, and the period as functions of $A$. Explain carefully why
the transformed coordinate is sinusoidal but $x$ is not. Recover the
small-amplitude limit and describe what happens as the turning point approaches
either infinite potential wall. Find the maximum speed and the acceleration
magnitude at release, checking their dimensions.

For $m=0.400\,\mathrm{kg}$, $a=0.250\,\mathrm m$,
$\omega_0=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $A=\pi a/3$, calculate the energy,
exact nonlinear angular frequency and period, small-amplitude period, maximum
speed, wall location, and release acceleration. State why the hardening
frequency is an energy effect rather than a linear superposition of
different-amplitude motions. Do not extend the principal inverse sine through
the singular walls.
permittedResults: For $|x|<\pi a/2$, $u=\sin(x/a)$ is one-to-one and $\tan^2(x/a)=u^2/(1-u^2)$.
A continuous periodic coordinate mapped through a one-to-one continuous inverse has the same fundamental period.

acceptableStrategies.description: Transform the first integral to a quadratic energy in the sine coordinate, then recover the physical orbit.
Use the turning-point energy to derive the frequency before checking limits and dimensional quantities.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Linearizes the bounded sine coordinate while preserving the physical inverse map, energy dependence, and singular-wall domain.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Claims the physical coordinate x is the sinusoidal transformed coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-amplitude trajectory and acceleration are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Makes the period grow with amplitude or continues motion through an infinite wall.
commonErrors.consequence: Both the exact frequency law and the physical domain are violated.

hintTree.content: Set $q=x/a$ and $\varepsilon=2E/(ma^2)$ before multiplying the energy equation by $1-u^2$.
At release, $\varepsilon=\omega_0^2\tan^2(A/a)$, so $\omega_0^2+\varepsilon$ simplifies to a secant squared.
Use $x=a\arcsin u$ only on the physical principal branch between the two walls.

WAVE:010637.canonicalSolution:
Let $q=x/a$ and define
$$
\varepsilon=\frac{2E}{ma^2}.
$$
The energy equation is
$$
\varepsilon=\dot q^2+\omega_0^2\tan^2q.
$$
For $u=\sin q$, one has
$\dot q=\dot u/\sqrt{1-u^2}$ and
$\tan^2q=u^2/(1-u^2)$. Multiplication by $1-u^2$ gives
$$
\boxed{\dot u^2+(\omega_0^2+\varepsilon)u^2=\varepsilon}.
$$
Differentiating away from a turning point yields
$$
\ddot u+(\omega_0^2+\varepsilon)u=0.
$$
Both sides are continuous, so the equation also holds at the isolated turning
points. At $x=A$ the energy and transformed amplitude are
$$
\varepsilon=\omega_0^2\tan^2(A/a),\qquad
u_{\max}=\sin(A/a).
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\Omega(A)=\sqrt{\omega_0^2+\varepsilon}
=\omega_0\sec(A/a)}
$$
and, choosing release at $t=0$,
$$
\boxed{u(t)=\sin(A/a)\cos[\Omega(A)t]}.
$$
The physical orbit is
$$
\boxed{x(t)=a\arcsin\!\left(\sin(A/a)
\cos[\Omega(A)t]\right)},
$$
with the principal inverse sine. The inverse is one-to-one on the allowed
interval, so
$$
\boxed{T(A)=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega(A)}
=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}\cos(A/a)}.
$$
The arcsine makes $x(t)$ nonsinusoidal at finite amplitude; only $u(t)$ obeys
superposition at a fixed value of its energy-dependent coefficient.

As $A/a\to0$, $\Omega\to\omega_0$ and
$T\to2\pi/\omega_0$, consistent with
$V(x)\sim m\omega_0^2x^2/2$. As
$A\to\pi a/2$, energy and frequency diverge while the period tends to zero.
No finite-energy trajectory reaches or crosses a wall. Energy at the center is
purely kinetic, so
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=\sqrt{2E/m}=a\omega_0\tan(A/a)}.
$$
The equation of motion gives the release acceleration magnitude
$$
\boxed{|\ddot x(0)|=a\omega_0^2\tan(A/a)\sec^2(A/a)}.
$$

For $A/a=\pi/3$,
$$
A=0.261799\ \mathrm m,\qquad
E=\frac12m\omega_0^2a^2\tan^2(\pi/3)
=\boxed{2.40000\ \mathrm J}.
$$
Since $\sec(\pi/3)=2$,
$$
\boxed{\Omega=16.0000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{T=0.392699\ \mathrm s}.
$$
The small-amplitude period is
$\boxed{T_0=2\pi/8=0.785398\ \mathrm s}$. Also,
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=3.46410\ \mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{|\ddot x(0)|=110.851\ \mathrm{m/s^2}},\qquad
\boxed{x_{\rm wall}=\pi a/2=0.392699\ \mathrm m}.
$$
The harder response follows because a larger turning point selects a larger
conserved energy and hence a larger coefficient $\Omega^2$ in the transformed
equation. Adding two solutions with different energies would not solve one
common physical equation for $x$.

graderFixtures.proofText: With $u=\sin(x/a)$, energy gives $\dot u^2+(\omega_0^2+\varepsilon)u^2=\varepsilon$. Hence $\Omega=\omega_0\sec(A/a)$ and $x=a\arcsin[\sin(A/a)\cos(\Omega t)]$ on the principal branch.
I set x itself equal to A cosine omega-zero t, say the period grows near the wall, and continue the orbit across the tangent singularity.

WAVE:010638.title: A nonlinear inertial metric still permits an exact sinusoid
WAVE:010638.objective: Derive the Mathews--Lakshmanan oscillator and its exact amplitude-dependent sinusoidal family.
WAVE:010638.statement:
Consider
$$
L=\frac{m}{2}\frac{\dot x^2-\omega_0^2x^2}{1+\lambda x^2}
$$
on a connected domain where $1+\lambda x^2>0$. The parameter $\lambda$
has inverse-length-squared units and may have either sign in that domain.

Derive the Euler--Lagrange equation and conserved energy. Prove by direct
substitution that every admissible amplitude $A$ supports an exact
$x=A\cos(\Omega t+\phi)$, and determine $\Omega(A)$, period, and
turning-point energy. Explain how a nonlinear equation can have a sinusoidal
orbit without superposition. Classify softening for $\lambda>0$, hardening
and the amplitude boundary for $\lambda<0$, and the $\lambda\to0$ limit.
Check the solution in both equation and energy.

For $m=0.750\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\omega_0=6.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$\lambda=0.500\,\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, and $A=1.20\,\mathrm m$, calculate
$\Omega$, period, energy, and maximum speed. Do not call $\omega_0$ the
observed finite-amplitude frequency or extrapolate across a zero of
$1+\lambda x^2$.
permittedResults: For a time-independent Lagrangian, $E=\dot x\,\partial L/\partial\dot x-L$ is conserved.
A sinusoidal trajectory family is not linear when its frequency depends on amplitude.

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the equation, substitute a sinusoid, and solve the consistency relation.
Use energy at the turning point and center to recover and check the frequency.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Verifies the amplitude-frequency family in both equation and energy while respecting the kinetic metric domain.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Sets finite-amplitude frequency to omega zero or infers superposition.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining nonlinear amplitude dependence is lost.

commonErrors.description: Drops the energy denominator or crosses a zero of one plus lambda x squared.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy and kinetic positivity fail.

hintTree.content: Multiply Euler--Lagrange by $(1+\lambda x^2)^2/m$.
For $x=A\cos\Omega t$, use $\dot x^2=\Omega^2(A^2-x^2)$.
Compare energy at a turning point and at $x=0$.

WAVE:010638.canonicalSolution:
The momentum is
$p=m\dot x/(1+\lambda x^2)$. Euler--Lagrange simplifies to
$$
\boxed{(1+\lambda x^2)\ddot x-\lambda x\dot x^2+\omega_0^2x=0}.
$$
Time-translation invariance gives
$$
\boxed{E=\frac{m}{2}\frac{\dot x^2+\omega_0^2x^2}{1+\lambda x^2}}.
$$

For $x=A\cos(\Omega t+\phi)$,
$\ddot x=-\Omega^2x$ and
$\dot x^2=\Omega^2(A^2-x^2)$. The equation becomes
$$
x[\omega_0^2-\Omega^2(1+\lambda A^2)]=0.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{\Omega(A)=\frac{\omega_0}{\sqrt{1+\lambda A^2}}},\qquad
\boxed{T(A)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}\sqrt{1+\lambda A^2}}.
$$
At a turning point,
$$
\boxed{E(A)=\frac{m\omega_0^2A^2}{2(1+\lambda A^2)}}.
$$
At $x=0$, energy is $mA^2\Omega^2/2$, identical after using the frequency
relation. This independently checks conservation.

For $\lambda>0$, frequency falls with amplitude: softening. For
$\lambda<0$, admissible amplitudes satisfy
$A<1/\sqrt{-\lambda}$; frequency rises toward the boundary. Crossing that
zero is outside the positive-metric model. At $\lambda=0$, ordinary
harmonic motion and quadratic energy return. Although each orbit is
sinusoidal, different amplitudes generally have different frequencies, so
their sum is not a solution.

Numerically, $1+\lambda A^2=1.72$, so
$$
\boxed{\Omega=4.57496\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{T=1.37339\,\mathrm s},
$$
$$
\boxed{E=11.3023\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{v_{\max}=A\Omega=5.48995\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The parameter $\omega_0$ is the zero-amplitude limit, not the observed
finite-amplitude frequency.

graderFixtures.proofText: Euler--Lagrange gives $(1+\lambda x^2)\ddot x-\lambda x\dot x^2+\omega_0^2x=0$. Exact motion has $\Omega=\omega_0/\sqrt{1+\lambda A^2}$ and $E=m\omega_0^2A^2/[2(1+\lambda A^2)]$.
I call the equation linear, set Omega to omega zero for every amplitude, drop the energy denominator, and cross the metric singularity.

WAVE:010639.title: A relativistic speed limit softens a harmonic oscillator
WAVE:010639.objective: Derive the exact amplitude-dependent period of a one-dimensional relativistic particle in a quadratic potential and recover both speed regimes.
WAVE:010639.statement:
A particle of rest mass $m$ moves in one dimension in
the prescribed harmonic potential $V(x)=kx^2/2$. Its special-relativistic
Hamiltonian is
$$
H(x,p)=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}+\frac12kx^2,
$$
where $c$ is the limiting speed. There is no radiation, damping, or retardation
of the imposed potential. The particle is released from rest at $x=A>0$ and
executes a symmetric bound orbit.

Use energy conservation to express the Lorentz factor, velocity, and momentum
as functions of $x$. Introduce
$$
\epsilon=\frac{kA^2}{2mc^2}
$$
and reduce the full period to a dimensionless quarter-cycle quadrature. Show
that its endpoint singularity is integrable. Calculate the maximum speed and
momentum at the origin. Derive the weakly relativistic period through first
order in $\epsilon$, including the sign of the correction. Then obtain the
ultrarelativistic large-amplitude limit and explain its relation to the minimum
travel time imposed by $|v|<c$.

For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$c=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $A=1.00\,\mathrm m$, compute $\epsilon$, total
energy including rest energy, origin speed and momentum, and the period by
numerical quadrature. Compare it with the nonrelativistic harmonic period and
with $4A/c$. Audit units and state why substituting $p^2/(2m)$ would erase the
amplitude dependence being tested.
permittedResults: For a time-independent Hamiltonian, $H$ is conserved along the trajectory.
If $\gamma\ge1$, then $v/c=\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}}$ and $p/(mc)=\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the Hamiltonian energy shell for velocity, nondimensionalize position, and evaluate the quarter-cycle time.
Express the motion through the Lorentz factor, then use matched small- and large-energy limits of the time integral.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Inverts the conserved relativistic energy to an exact period quadrature and derives both the positive weak-relativity correction and the speed-limited large-amplitude asymptote.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the square-root kinetic energy by $p^2/(2m)$ and reports an amplitude-independent period.
commonErrors.consequence: The relativistic speed bound, nonlinear quadrature, and both requested limits disappear.

commonErrors.description: Calls the square-root turning endpoint nonintegrable or gives a large-amplitude period below $4A/c$.
commonErrors.consequence: The bound orbit time and its causal ultrarelativistic limit are misclassified.

hintTree.content: At release, $H=mc^2+kA^2/2$; subtract $kx^2/2$ and divide by $mc^2$.
Set $y=x/A$ before expanding the reciprocal velocity for small $\epsilon$.
For numerical work, $y=\sin\theta$ removes the visible square-root endpoint singularity.

WAVE:010639.canonicalSolution:
At release the conserved total energy, including rest
energy, is
$$
\boxed{E=mc^2+\frac12kA^2=mc^2(1+\epsilon)}.
$$
At a general position the relativistic kinetic-plus-rest energy is
$E-kx^2/2=\gamma mc^2$. With $y=x/A$, this gives
$$
\boxed{\gamma(y)=1+\epsilon(1-y^2)}.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{v(y)=c\sqrt{1-\gamma(y)^{-2}}},\qquad
\boxed{p(y)=mc\sqrt{\gamma(y)^2-1}},
$$
with the sign of each chosen to match the direction of travel. At the origin,
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=c\sqrt{1-(1+\epsilon)^{-2}}},\qquad
\boxed{p_{\max}=mc\sqrt{\epsilon(2+\epsilon)}}.
$$

Fourfold symmetry converts the travel time from zero to $A$ into
$$
\boxed{T=\frac{4A}{c}\int_0^1
\frac{1+\epsilon(1-y^2)}
{\sqrt{[1+\epsilon(1-y^2)]^2-1}}\,dy}.
$$
Near $y=1$, the denominator is proportional to $\sqrt{1-y}$ while the
numerator tends to one, so the singularity is integrable. Equivalently,
$y=\sin\theta$ makes the transformed integrand finite at
$\theta=\pi/2$, with limiting value $1/\sqrt{2\epsilon}$.

For $\epsilon\ll1$, put $\delta=\epsilon(1-y^2)$. Expanding the reciprocal
speed gives
$$
\frac{c}{v}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\delta}}
\left(1+\frac34\delta+O(\delta^2)\right).
$$
Using
$\int_0^1(1-y^2)^{-1/2}dy=\pi/2$ and
$\int_0^1\sqrt{1-y^2}\,dy=\pi/4$ yields
$$
\boxed{T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}
\left(1+\frac38\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2)\right)}.
$$
The positive correction is relativistic softening: the speed limit lengthens
the period. In the opposite limit $\epsilon\to\infty$, the particle moves at
nearly $c$ except in shrinking turning layers, so the dimensionless integral
tends to one and
$$
\boxed{T\sim\frac{4A}{c}}.
$$
For every finite amplitude, $|v|<c$ makes $T>4A/c$; the asymptote saturates
that causal travel-time bound rather than crossing it.

For the stated data, $mc^2=100.000\,\mathrm J$ and $kA^2/2=100.000\,\mathrm J$,
so
$$
\boxed{\epsilon=1.00000},\qquad \boxed{E=200.000\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The origin values are
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=8.66025\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{p_{\max}=17.3205\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}.
$$
Numerically, the dimensionless integral is $1.4763013158$, giving
$$
\boxed{T=0.590521\,\mathrm s}.
$$
By comparison,
$2\pi\sqrt{m/k}=0.444288\,\mathrm s$ and $4A/c=0.400000\,\mathrm s$.
The exact period is larger than both, as expected. The parameter $\epsilon$ is
dimensionless because both $kA^2$ and $mc^2$ are energies; $A/c$ has units of
time. Replacing the kinetic term by $p^2/(2m)$ would restore an exactly
amplitude-independent sinusoid and remove both the speed bound and the tested
relativistic correction.

At release the conserved total energy, including rest
energy, is
$$
\boxed{E=mc^2+\frac12kA^2=mc^2(1+\epsilon)}.
$$
At a general position the relativistic kinetic-plus-rest energy is
$E-kx^2/2=\gamma mc^2$. With $y=x/A$, this gives
$$
\boxed{\gamma(y)=1+\epsilon(1-y^2)}.
$$
Consequently
$$
\boxed{v(y)=c\sqrt{1-\gamma(y)^{-2}}},\qquad
\boxed{p(y)=mc\sqrt{\gamma(y)^2-1}},
$$
with the sign of each chosen to match the direction of travel. At the origin,
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=c\sqrt{1-(1+\epsilon)^{-2}}},\qquad
\boxed{p_{\max}=mc\sqrt{\epsilon(2+\epsilon)}}.
$$

Fourfold symmetry converts the travel time from zero to $A$ into
$$
\boxed{T=\frac{4A}{c}\int_0^1
\frac{1+\epsilon(1-y^2)}
{\sqrt{[1+\epsilon(1-y^2)]^2-1}}\,dy}.
$$
Near $y=1$, the denominator is proportional to $\sqrt{1-y}$ while the
numerator tends to one, so the singularity is integrable. Equivalently,
$y=\sin\theta$ makes the transformed integrand finite at
$\theta=\pi/2$, with limiting value $1/\sqrt{2\epsilon}$.

For $\epsilon\ll1$, put $\delta=\epsilon(1-y^2)$. Expanding the reciprocal
speed gives
$$
\frac{c}{v}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\delta}}
\left(1+\frac34\delta+O(\delta^2)\right).
$$
Using
$\int_0^1(1-y^2)^{-1/2}dy=\pi/2$ and
$\int_0^1\sqrt{1-y^2}\,dy=\pi/4$ yields
$$
\boxed{T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}
\left(1+\frac38\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2)\right)}.
$$
The positive correction is relativistic softening: the speed limit lengthens
the period. In the opposite limit $\epsilon\to\infty$, the particle moves at
nearly $c$ except in shrinking turning layers, so the dimensionless integral
tends to one and
$$
\boxed{T\sim\frac{4A}{c}}.
$$
For every finite amplitude, $|v|<c$ makes $T>4A/c$; the asymptote saturates
that causal travel-time bound rather than crossing it.

For the stated data, $mc^2=100.000\,\mathrm J$ and $kA^2/2=100.000\,\mathrm J$,
so
$$
\boxed{\epsilon=1.00000},\qquad \boxed{E=200.000\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The origin values are
$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=8.66025\,\mathrm{m/s}},\qquad
\boxed{p_{\max}=17.3205\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}.
$$
Numerically, the dimensionless integral is $1.4763013158$, giving
$$
\boxed{T=0.590521\,\mathrm s}.
$$
By comparison,
$2\pi\sqrt{m/k}=0.444288\,\mathrm s$ and $4A/c=0.400000\,\mathrm s$.
The exact period is larger than both, as expected. The parameter $\epsilon$ is
dimensionless because both $kA^2$ and $mc^2$ are energies; $A/c$ has units of
time. Replacing the kinetic term by $p^2/(2m)$ would restore an exactly
amplitude-independent sinusoid and remove both the speed bound and the tested
relativistic correction.

I substitute the nonrelativistic kinetic energy, keep the period equal to $2pisqrt{m/k}$ at every amplitude, call the turning-point square root divergent, and let the large-amplitude period fall below $4A/c$.

WAVE:010640.title: Two half-cycle stiffnesses make an asymmetric but isochronous orbit
WAVE:010640.objective: Assemble the exact orbit of a conservative bilinear oscillator and derive its energy-independent period, dwell fractions, and nonzero mean.
WAVE:010640.statement:
A mass $m$ moves in the continuous piecewise-quadratic
potential
$$
V(x)=\begin{cases}
\tfrac12k_+x^2,&x\ge0,\\
\tfrac12k_-x^2,&x<0,
\end{cases}
$$
where $k_+,k_->0$ and $k_+\ne k_-$. There is no damping or forcing. At
$x=0$ the force is continuous, but its slope changes.

For a fixed energy $E>0$, find both turning points and assemble one full orbit
from the two harmonic half-cycles, matching position and velocity at the
origin. Derive the exact period and fundamental angular frequency. Prove that
the period is independent of $E$ even though the orbit is not one sinusoid.
Calculate the fractions of a period spent on each side and the time-averaged
displacement. Verify the virial split between average kinetic and potential
energy. Determine the highest derivative of $x(t)$ that must remain continuous
at an origin crossing, and connect the first derivative jump above that order
to the stiffness change.

For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k_+=16.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$k_-=4.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $E=0.500\,\mathrm J$, report both turning
points, origin-crossing speed, period, fundamental frequency, side dwell
fractions, mean displacement, and mean kinetic and potential energies. Do not
replace the two stiffnesses by their arithmetic average.
permittedResults: A harmonic excursion from an origin crossing back to the origin takes one half-period $\pi/\omega$.
For a degree-two potential, including a continuous piecewise degree-two potential, the periodic virial identity gives $\langle K\rangle=\langle V\rangle$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Assemble positive and negative half-sine excursions from energy and crossing continuity.
Evaluate the period and observables from piecewise energy quadratures.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Matches the two harmonic half-orbits at equal energy and derives exact global timing and averages without homogenizing the stiffness jump.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the two restoring slopes by one averaged spring constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Asymmetry, dwell times, mean displacement, and exact period are lost.

commonErrors.description: Allows energy or velocity magnitude to jump at the origin in the conservative model.
commonErrors.consequence: The two half-orbits do not form a physical periodic trajectory.

hintTree.content: Set $A_+=\sqrt{2E/k_+}$, $A_-=\sqrt{2E/k_-}$, and $\omega_\pm=\sqrt{k_\pm/m}$.
Integrate $A_+\sin(\omega_+t)$ and $-A_-\sin(\omega_-t)$ over their separate half-cycles.
At $x=0$, compare $x''=-\omega_\pm^2x$ and then differentiate once more.

WAVE:010640.canonicalSolution:
Energy conservation gives the positive and negative
turning displacements
$$
\boxed{x_+=A_+=\sqrt{2E/k_+}},\qquad
\boxed{x_-=-A_-=-\sqrt{2E/k_-}}.
$$
At every origin crossing the speed magnitude is
$\boxed{v_0=\sqrt{2E/m}}$. Starting at the origin with positive velocity, the
positive excursion is $x=A_+\sin(\omega_+t)$ for
$0\le t\le\pi/\omega_+$, where $\omega_+=\sqrt{k_+/m}$. The negative
excursion is a shifted $-A_-\sin(\omega_-s)$ over
$0\le s\le\pi/\omega_-$. Positions and velocities match at the crossing.

The full period and fundamental frequency are therefore
$$
\boxed{T=\pi\left(\frac1{\omega_+}+\frac1{\omega_-}\right)},
\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=\frac{2}{1/\omega_++1/\omega_-}}.
$$
Neither depends on $E$: each half is harmonic, but with a different clock.
The positive and negative dwell fractions are
$$
\boxed{f_+=\frac{1/\omega_+}{1/\omega_++1/\omega_-}},\qquad
\boxed{f_-=1-f_+}.
$$
Integrating the two half-sines gives
$$
\boxed{\langle x\rangle=\frac{2(A_+-A_-)}{\pi}}.
$$
The longer, softer excursion biases the mean toward its side.

On each half-cycle, harmonic averaging gives equal kinetic and potential
contributions. Weighting the halves therefore preserves
$$
\boxed{\langle K\rangle=\langle V\rangle=E/2}.
$$
At the crossing, $x$ and $\dot x$ match by construction, and
$\ddot x=-\omega_\pm^2x=0$ from both sides. But
$x'''=-\omega_\pm^2\dot x$ jumps when the nonzero crossing velocity meets the
new stiffness. Thus the orbit is necessarily twice continuously
differentiable but generally not three times continuously differentiable.

Numerically, $\omega_+=4$ and $\omega_-=2\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Hence
$$
\boxed{x_+=0.250000\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{x_-=-0.500000\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{v_0=1.00000\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
Also
$$
\boxed{T=3\pi/4=2.35619\,\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega=8/3=2.66667\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
$$
\boxed{f_+=1/3},\qquad \boxed{f_-=2/3},\qquad
\boxed{\langle x\rangle=-1/(2\pi)=-0.159155\,\mathrm m},
$$
and $\boxed{\langle K\rangle=\langle V\rangle=0.250000\,\mathrm J}$.
An arithmetic-average stiffness would yield one symmetric sinusoid, the wrong
period, equal dwell fractions, and zero mean.

WAVE:010641.title: Cubic softening and quintic hardening compete in the period
WAVE:010641.objective: Obtain the amplitude-dependent frequency and period of a cubic-quintic conservative oscillator through fourth order and test the expansion numerically.
WAVE:010641.statement:
A conservative oscillator satisfies
$$
\ddot x+\omega_0^2x+\alpha x^3+\beta x^5=0,
$$
and is released from rest at the positive turning point $x=A$. Treat $A$ as
the physical turning amplitude, not the coefficient of an uncorrected trial
cosine.

Write the conserved energy and its exact period quadrature. By a
Poincare-Lindstedt calculation or a controlled expansion of the quadrature,
find the angular frequency $\Omega(A)$ through order $A^4$, including the
second-order cubic correction and the first quintic correction. Invert it to
obtain the period $T(A)$ through the same order. Identify hardening and
softening contributions and state the smallness conditions on the two
dimensionless nonlinear parameters.

For $\omega_0=10.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$\alpha=-200\,\mathrm{s^{-2}m^{-2}}$, $\beta=1.00\times10^4\,
\mathrm{s^{-2}m^{-4}}$, and $A=0.200\,\mathrm m$, calculate both
dimensionless parameters, the fourth-order $\Omega$ and $T$, and compare with
an exact numerical evaluation of the energy quadrature. Explain why dropping
the $\alpha^2A^4$ term is inconsistent, and audit local oscillation when a
negative nonlinear coefficient makes the global potential nonconfining.
permittedResults: For a one-dimensional conservative orbit, $T=4\int_0^A dx/\sqrt{2[E-V(x)]}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use Poincare-Lindstedt with amplitude normalization at the turning point.
Expand the exact energy quadrature after the substitution $x=Asin	heta$.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Maintains physical turning amplitude and asymptotic order while deriving the competing cubic-quintic frequency and period corrections through $A^4$.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the quintic $A^4$ term but drops the second-order cubic contribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The claimed fourth-order expansion is incomplete.

commonErrors.description: Uses the frequency coefficients unchanged for the period.
commonErrors.consequence: Series inversion and its squared lower-order term are omitted.

hintTree.content: Use $E=V(A)$ with $V=\omega_0^2x^2/2+\alpha x^4/4+\beta x^6/6$.
The pure Duffing fourth-order frequency coefficient is $-21/256$ in the physical-amplitude convention.
When inverting the frequency series, retain the square of the $A^2$ coefficient.

WAVE:010641.canonicalSolution:
The potential and turning-point energy are
$$
V(x)=\frac12\omega_0^2x^2+\frac\alpha4x^4+\frac\beta6x^6,
\qquad
\boxed{E=V(A)}.
$$
The exact period is
$$
\boxed{T=4\int_0^A\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2[E-V(x)]}}}.
$$
A Poincare-Lindstedt expansion with the turning amplitude held fixed gives
$$
\boxed{\Omega=\omega_0\left[1+\frac{3\alpha A^2}{8\omega_0^2}
+\left(\frac{5\beta}{16\omega_0^2}
-\frac{21\alpha^2}{256\omega_0^4}\right)A^4+O(A^6)\right]}.
$$
The cubic term contributes at order $A^2$ and also feeds back at order $A^4$.
The quintic term first appears at order $A^4$. Series inversion yields
$$
\boxed{T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}\left[1-\frac{3\alpha A^2}{8\omega_0^2}
+\left(\frac{57\alpha^2}{256\omega_0^4}
-\frac{5\beta}{16\omega_0^2}\right)A^4+O(A^6)\right]}.
$$
Positive $\alpha$ and $\beta$ give leading hardening contributions to
frequency; negative values give softening at their respective orders. The
expansion requires
$|\alpha|A^2/\omega_0^2\ll1$ and
$|\beta|A^4/\omega_0^2\ll1$, with a real bounded orbit over $[-A,A]$.

For the data define
$$
p=\alpha A^2/\omega_0^2=-0.0800000,\qquad
q=\beta A^4/\omega_0^2=0.160000.
$$
The cubic term softens while the quintic term hardens more strongly at this
amplitude. The frequency factor is
$$
1+3p/8+5q/16-21p^2/256=1.019475,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\Omega_{(4)}=10.19475\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The period factor is
$$
1-3p/8+57p^2/256-5q/16=0.981425,
$$
giving
$$
\boxed{T_{(4)}=0.616648\,\mathrm s}.
$$
For stable numerical quadrature put $x=A\sin\theta$; cancellation of the
endpoint cosine gives
$$
T=4\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\omega_0^2+
(\alpha A^2/2)(1+\sin^2\theta)+
(\beta A^4/3)(1+\sin^2\theta+\sin^4\theta)}}.
$$
Numerical evaluation gives
$$
\boxed{T_{\rm exact}=0.616240\,\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{\Omega_{\rm exact}=10.1960\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
which is close despite the only moderately small $q=0.16$. Omitting the
$\alpha^2A^4$ term while retaining the quintic $A^4$ term mixes asymptotic
orders and changes both coefficients.

Here $\beta>0$ makes the potential globally confining despite $\alpha<0$.
If instead the highest retained coefficient were negative, the polynomial
potential could be unbounded at large $|x|$; the period formula would still
describe a local bounded orbit only when $E-V(x)>0$ inside the chosen turning
interval and the orbit lies below any escape barrier.

WAVE:010642.title: A resonant spring pump amplifies one quadrature and suppresses the other
WAVE:010642.objective: Derive below-threshold phase-sensitive quadrature gain for a degenerate parametric oscillator and connect it to pump energy flow.
WAVE:010642.statement:
A weakly damped oscillator is pumped by a small
spring modulation at twice its natural frequency:
$$
\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2[1+h\cos(2\omega_0t)]x
=f_c\cos(\omega_0t)+f_s\sin(\omega_0t).
$$
Assume $h\ll1$, $\gamma/\omega_0\ll1$, exact pump and signal resonance, and
slow quadratures
$$
x=X(t)\cos(\omega_0t)+Y(t)\sin(\omega_0t).
$$

Average over the carrier to derive the coupled equations for $X$ and $Y$,
including the drive signs. Diagonalize them with
$Q_+=(X+Y)/\sqrt2$ and $Q_-=(X-Y)/\sqrt2$. Identify the two decay rates, the
below-threshold condition, and the spring-modulation threshold. For a drive
phase that selects one eigenquadrature at a time, find the steady amplitude
gain relative to the same drive with the pump off. Explain which quadrature
is amplified, which is deamplified, and how the pump's phase-sensitive energy
flow is consistent with passive damping.

For $\omega_0=1000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\gamma=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$h=0.0120$, calculate the coupling $g$, decay rates, both amplitude gains,
and threshold $h_{\rm th}$. With drive acceleration magnitude
$f_0=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ phased to select each eigenquadrature, report the
two steady amplitudes. State the rotating-wave assumptions and what changes
at or above threshold.
permittedResults: Only carrier-frequency terms survive first-order rotating-wave averaging; terms at $3\omega_0$ average away.
A real symmetric two-by-two matrix with equal diagonals is diagonalized by sum and difference coordinates.

acceptableStrategies.description: Average the carrier ansatz and diagonalize the resulting symmetric quadrature matrix.
Use a complex envelope coupled to its conjugate, then rotate to real pump-phase eigenquadratures.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the phase-sensitive averaged quadratures and shows that a below-threshold pump suppresses one response while amplifying the orthogonal one with a finite threshold.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Assigns both quadratures the same decay rate or reverses which phase is amplified for the stated pump phase.
commonErrors.consequence: Phase-sensitive amplification disappears or is attached to the wrong drive projection.

commonErrors.description: Uses $homega_0/2$ instead of $homega_0/4$ for the averaged coupling.
commonErrors.consequence: The gain and threshold are wrong by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Extends the finite linear steady-state gain formula above threshold.
commonErrors.consequence: An unstable unsaturated model is presented as a bounded amplifier.

hintTree.content: Retain the resonant halves of $\cos2\omega_0t\cos\omega_0t$ and $\cos2\omega_0t\sin\omega_0t$.
Define $g=h\omega_0/4$ after dividing the resonant equations by $2\omega_0$.
Compare $1/(\gamma\pm g)$ with the pump-off response $1/\gamma$ for the same projected drive.

WAVE:010642.canonicalSolution:
Substitute the slow-quadrature ansatz and neglect
second derivatives of $X,Y$, products of $\gamma$ with slow derivatives, and
the nonresonant $3\omega_0$ terms. Matching carrier cosine and sine terms gives
$$
\boxed{\dot X=-\gamma X-gY-\frac{f_s}{2\omega_0}},
$$
$$
\boxed{\dot Y=-gX-\gamma Y+\frac{f_c}{2\omega_0}},
\qquad
\boxed{g=\frac{h\omega_0}{4}}.
$$
With $Q_+=(X+Y)/\sqrt2$ and $Q_-=(X-Y)/\sqrt2$, these become
$$
\dot Q_+=-(\gamma+g)Q_++b_+,
\qquad
\dot Q_-=-(\gamma-g)Q_-+b_-,
$$
where
$$
b_+=\frac{f_c-f_s}{2\sqrt2\omega_0},\qquad
b_-=-\frac{f_c+f_s}{2\sqrt2\omega_0}.
$$
Thus $Q_+$ decays at $\gamma+g$, while $Q_-$ decays at $\gamma-g$. The
linear below-threshold condition is
$$
\boxed{g<\gamma},
$$
or
$$
\boxed{h<h_{\rm th}=4\gamma/\omega_0}.
$$

A phase choice $f_c=-f_s=f_0/\sqrt2$ selects $Q_+$ with
$b_+=f_0/(2\omega_0)$. A phase choice $f_c=f_s=f_0/\sqrt2$ selects $Q_-$
with $|b_-|=f_0/(2\omega_0)$. The steady magnitudes are
$$
|Q_+|=\frac{f_0}{2\omega_0(\gamma+g)},\qquad
|Q_-|=\frac{f_0}{2\omega_0(\gamma-g)}.
$$
Relative to the pump-off magnitude $f_0/(2\omega_0\gamma)$, the amplitude
gains are
$$
\boxed{G_+=\frac\gamma{\gamma+g}<1},\qquad
\boxed{G_-=\frac\gamma{\gamma-g}>1}.
$$
These are amplitude gains; power gains would be their squares.

$R^2=X^2+Y^2=Q_+^2+Q_-^2$,
$$
\frac{dR^2}{dt}=-2(\gamma+g)Q_+^2-2(\gamma-g)Q_-^2.
$$
Below threshold both terms are negative, but the pump increases the effective
loss of one phase and offsets part of the damping of the orthogonal phase.
The enhanced driven response is powered by the external spring modulation;
it does not imply negative mechanical damping in every phase.

Numerically,
$$
\boxed{g=h\omega_0/4=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The decay rates are
$$
\boxed{\gamma+g=8.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{\gamma-g=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
and the gains are
$$
\boxed{G_+=0.625},\qquad \boxed{G_-=2.50}.
$$
The threshold is
$$
\boxed{h_{\rm th}=0.0200}.
$$
For $f_0=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, the selected steady amplitudes are
$$
\boxed{|Q_+|=6.25\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{|Q_-|=2.50\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm m}.
$$

parametrically unstable; nonlinearities, detuning, or pump depletion must

continued.

WAVE:010643.title: Cubic velocity damping produces an algebraic ring-down
WAVE:010643.objective: Use energy averaging to derive the amplitude and energy envelopes of a weak cubic-velocity damper and audit its first-order phase behavior.
WAVE:010643.statement:
A weakly damped oscillator obeys
$$
m\ddot x+kx+\beta\dot x^3=0,
$$
where $m,k,\beta>0$. Let $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$ and assume the initial
motion is $x(0)=A_0$, $\dot x(0)=0$. The damping is weak on one carrier
period.

Derive the exact mechanical-energy loss law. Insert a slowly varying harmonic
ansatz and average over one cycle to obtain the leading amplitude equation.
Solve it for $A(t)$, derive the energy envelope, and find the half-energy and
half-amplitude times. Calculate the mean dissipated power and show why the
first-order frequency shift vanishes even though a third harmonic is
generated. State the dimensionless weak-damping condition and explain why the
envelope cannot be extrapolated to amplitudes for which it fails.

For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$,
$\beta=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg\,s/m^2}$, and $A_0=0.100\,\mathrm m$, compute
the weak parameter, characteristic time, half-energy and half-amplitude
times, initial energy and averaged loss power. At $t=100\,\mathrm s$, report
the amplitude, energy, and averaged power. Distinguish this dissipative
slow-envelope task from an inverse-square-plus-quadratic turning-point
problem.
permittedResults: For harmonic motion, $\langle\sin^4\theta\rangle=3/8$.
A damping term in carrier quadrature changes amplitude at first order; an in-phase projection would change phase and frequency.

acceptableStrategies.description: Average the exact mechanical-energy loss over a slowly varying harmonic orbit.
Project the nonlinear damping onto carrier sine and cosine quadratures, then integrate the amplitude equation.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the algebraic ring-down coefficient from the exact energy ledger and correct fourth-moment average, while separating first-order amplitude and phase effects.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $langlesin^4angle=1/2$ or otherwise misses the $3/8$ coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The entire decay timescale and power law are quantitatively wrong.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the damping task by an inverse-square-plus-quadratic equilibrium and turning-point problem.
commonErrors.consequence: The required dissipative energy envelope is never derived.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $E=m\dot x^2/2+kx^2/2$.
Use $\langle\dot x^4\rangle=3\omega_0^4A^4/8$ and $E=m\omega_0^2A^2/2$.
Integrate the equation for $A^{-2}$ rather than for $A$.

WAVE:010643.canonicalSolution:
Multiplying the equation by $\dot x$ gives the exact law
$$
\boxed{\dot E=-\beta\dot x^4\le0},\qquad
E=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2.
$$
For weak damping take $x=A(t)\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)$ over one cycle. To leading
order,
$$
\langle\dot x^4\rangle=\frac38\omega_0^4A^4,
\qquad E=\frac12m\omega_0^2A^2.
$$
Therefore $m\omega_0^2AA'=-3\beta\omega_0^4A^4/8$, or
$$
\boxed{A'=-\frac{3\beta\omega_0^2}{8m}A^3}.
$$
Integrating gives
$$
\boxed{A(t)=\frac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+t/t_0}}},\qquad
\boxed{t_0=\frac{4m}{3\beta\omega_0^2A_0^2}}.
$$
The averaged energy is
$$
\boxed{E(t)=\frac{E_0}{1+t/t_0}},\qquad
E_0=\frac12m\omega_0^2A_0^2.
$$
Thus energy halves at $t=t_0$, while amplitude halves only at
$t=3t_0$. The average dissipated power is
$$
\boxed{\overline P=\frac{3\beta\omega_0^4A^4}{8}}
=\frac{E_0/t_0}{(1+t/t_0)^2}.
$$

Because $\dot x^3\propto-\sin^3\theta=-(3\sin\theta-\sin3\theta)/4$, its
fundamental is in the velocity quadrature. It changes amplitude but has no
first-order in-phase projection that would shift the carrier frequency.
Hence $\phi'=0$ at this order; a third harmonic and higher-order corrections
remain. The required small parameter is
$$
\boxed{\epsilon=\frac{\beta\omega_0A_0^2}{m}\ll1},
$$
which is dimensionless because $[\beta]=\mathrm{kg\,s/m^2}$.

Numerically $\omega_0=10.0000\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and
$\epsilon=0.00200000$. The characteristic and landmark times are
$$
\boxed{t_0=66.6667\,\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{t_{E/2}=66.6667\,\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{t_{A/2}=200.000\,\mathrm s}.
$$
The initial energy and average loss are
$$
\boxed{E_0=0.500000\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{\overline P(0)=7.50000\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm W}.
$$
At $t=100\,\mathrm s$, $1+t/t_0=2.5$, giving
$$
\boxed{A=0.0632456\,\mathrm m},\qquad
\boxed{E=0.200000\,\mathrm J},\qquad
\boxed{\overline P=1.20000\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm W}.
$$
This is a dissipative averaged ring-down. It contains no inverse-square
barrier, shifted equilibrium, $x^2$ coordinate linearization, or conservative
turning-point construction. If $\epsilon$ is not small, the waveform ceases
to be nearly harmonic and the one-cycle averages used above must be replaced
by the full nonlinear motion.

WAVE:010644.title: A constant torque erases a pendulum well at a saddle-node threshold
WAVE:010644.objective: Analyze stable and unstable equilibria, escape barrier, and critical softening of a pendulum tilted by constant torque.
WAVE:010644.statement:
A pendulum bob of mass $m$ and length $\ell$ is subject to
a constant applied torque $\tau>0$ about its pivot. With angle increasing in
the torque direction, its conservative equation is
$$
m\ell^2\ddot\theta+mg\ell\sin\theta=\tau.
$$
Treat the torque as an ideal conservative generalized force over the angular
range considered, so
$U(\theta)=mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)-\tau\theta$.

Define $\eta=\tau/(mg\ell)$. For $0\le\eta<1$, find and classify the stable
and unstable equilibria in each tilted well. Derive the small-oscillation
frequency and the forward escape barrier. Determine the critical torque and
describe the saddle-node at $\eta=1$. With $\delta=1-\eta\downarrow0$, derive
the leading scaling of both the small frequency and forward barrier. Explain
why the potential is not periodic even though its sinusoidal part is.

For $m=0.500\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=1.00\,\mathrm m$,
$g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\tau=3.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, calculate
$\eta$, stable and forward-saddle angles in one cell, small frequency, and
forward barrier. State how dissipation, time-dependent drive, or rotations
over many cells would change the model.
permittedResults: A stable equilibrium has $U''>0$ and small frequency $\sqrt{U''/(m\ell^2)}$.
Near a generic saddle-node, curvature softens as $\delta^{1/2}$ and the barrier as $\delta^{3/2}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Classify the two inverse-sine equilibrium branches and compare their potential values.
Expand the tilted potential locally about the critical inflection point to obtain the saddle-node normal form.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the metastable well, soft frequency, and escape barrier from the same tilted potential and resolves their distinct saddle-node scalings.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Treats the full tilted potential as periodic and assigns identical absolute energy to every cell.
commonErrors.consequence: The constant torque's work and forward barrier are misrepresented.

commonErrors.description: Claims the small frequency and barrier vanish with the same power of $1-eta$.
commonErrors.consequence: Curvature softening and barrier collapse are conflated.

hintTree.content: Solve $\sin\theta=\eta$ and classify with $\cos\theta$.
Evaluate $U(\pi-\arcsin\eta)-U(\arcsin\eta)$.
Use $\arcsin(1-\delta)=\pi/2-\sqrt{2\delta}[1+\delta/12+\cdots]$.

WAVE:010644.canonicalSolution:
Let $\omega_0=\sqrt{g/\ell}$. Equilibrium requires
$$
\sin\theta=\eta,\qquad \eta=\frac{\tau}{mg\ell}.
$$
For $0\le\eta<1$, write $a=\arcsin\eta$. In each cell,
$$
\boxed{\theta_s=a+2\pi n},\qquad
\boxed{\theta_u=\pi-a+2\pi n}.
$$
Since $U''=mg\ell\cos\theta$, the first is stable and the second is the
forward unstable saddle. The small frequency is
$$
\boxed{\omega_s=\omega_0\sqrt{\cos a}
=\omega_0(1-\eta^2)^{1/4}}.
$$

With $c=\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$, the forward barrier is
$$
\Delta U_+=U(\pi-a)-U(a)
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{\Delta U_+=mg\ell
\left[2c-\eta(\pi-2a)\right]}.
$$
At $\eta=1$, the stable point and forward saddle merge at
$\theta=\pi/2+2\pi n$ and $U''=0$. For $\eta>1$ there is no stationary
point: the constant torque exceeds the largest gravitational restoring
torque. Hence
$$
\boxed{\tau_c=mg\ell}.
$$

Let $\eta=1-\delta$ with $0<\delta\ll1$. Then
$c\sim\sqrt{2\delta}$ and
$$
\boxed{\omega_s\sim\omega_0(2\delta)^{1/4}}.
$$
Using the next term in the arcsine expansion in the barrier formula gives
$$
\boxed{\Delta U_+\sim mg\ell\frac{4\sqrt2}{3}\delta^{3/2}}.
$$
The linear term $-\tau\theta$ makes $U(\theta+2\pi)=U(\theta)-2\pi\tau$;
the tilted potential is therefore not periodic even though the gravitational
substrate is.

Numerically $mg\ell=4.905\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ and
$$
\boxed{\eta=0.611621}.
$$
In the chosen cell,
$$
\boxed{\theta_s=0.658108\,\mathrm{rad}},\qquad
\boxed{\theta_u=2.48349\,\mathrm{rad}}.
$$
Since $\cos\theta_s=0.791151$ and $\omega_0=3.13209\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$,
$$
\boxed{\omega_s=2.78589\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
The forward barrier is
$$
\boxed{\Delta U_+=2.28506\,\mathrm J}.
$$
Dissipation makes barrier crossing history-dependent and destroys exact
energy conservation. A time-dependent torque creates a driven nonlinear
problem rather than a static tilt. Once the pendulum rotates through many
cells, the ideal constant torque continually lowers the energy reference;
the local metastable-well analysis remains useful, but global motion and the
torque source's work must be tracked explicitly.

WAVE:010645.title: Geometric stretching hardens a string's fundamental mode
WAVE:010645.objective: Reduce a globally stretched string to a Duffing modal coordinate and derive its amplitude-dependent frequency from a consistent nonlinear energy.
WAVE:010645.statement:
A string of length $L$, linear density $\mu$,
baseline tension $T_0$, cross-sectional area $A_s$, and Young modulus $E_Y$
is fixed at both ends. Its ends cannot move axially. In a single-mode small-
slope approximation let
$$y(x,t)=q(t)\sin(\pi x/L).$$
The transverse slope lengthens the string, creating an additional uniform
tension. Retain the leading geometric elongation but neglect bending stiffness,
longitudinal inertia, and all other transverse modes.

Derive the elongation, additional tension, effective modal kinetic and
potential energies, and the resulting Duffing equation for $q$. Obtain the
leading amplitude-dependent angular frequency for peak modal amplitude $Q$.
State separate smallness conditions for slope and for the perturbative
frequency shift. Compute the turning-point energy and explain why inserting
$Q$ as a constant tension before deriving the equation does not reproduce
the instantaneous cubic force.

For $L=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\mu=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg/m}$,
$T_0=100\,\mathrm N$, $E_YA_s=1.00\times10^5\,\mathrm N$, and
$Q=2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$, calculate the linear frequency, peak tension increase,
fractional leading frequency shift, shifted ordinary frequency, and total
turning-point energy. State when axial dynamics or multimode coupling would
invalidate this reduction.
permittedResults: For $\ddot q+\omega_0^2q+\alpha q^3=0$ with weak hardening, $\Omega=\omega_0[1+3\alpha Q^2/(8\omega_0^2)]+O(Q^4)$.
At small slope, arc-length increase is $\Delta L=\tfrac12\int_0^L y_x^2dx+O(y_x^4)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Reduce the kinetic and elastic energy on the fundamental sine shape and apply Lagrange's equation.
Project the constant-in-space, amplitude-dependent tension wave equation onto the fundamental and verify its potential by integration.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Derives the instantaneous cubic restoring force and amplitude shift from one consistent geometric energy instead of inserting a peak-amplitude tension into a linear equation.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\Delta L=\int y_x^2dx$ and loses the factor $1/2$ from the arc-length expansion.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonlinear tension, cubic coefficient, and frequency shift are doubled.

commonErrors.description: Replaces instantaneous $q^2(t)$ by $Q^2$ before deriving the equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The Duffing force and its correct averaged frequency coefficient are not obtained.

hintTree.content: For the sine mode, $\int_0^L\cos^2(\pi x/L)dx=L/2$.
The stretching energy is $(E_YA_s/2L)(\Delta L)^2$.
Differentiate the reduced potential with respect to the instantaneous coordinate, not its peak value.

WAVE:010645.canonicalSolution:
For the assumed shape,
$$
\Delta L=\frac12\int_0^Ly_x^2dx
=\boxed{\frac{\pi^2q^2}{4L}}.
$$
The additional uniform tension is therefore
$$
\boxed{\Delta T=\frac{E_YA_s}{L}\Delta L
=\frac{E_YA_s\pi^2q^2}{4L^2}}.
$$
The reduced kinetic energy, baseline tension energy, and stretching energy are
$$
\mathcal T=\frac{\mu L}{4}\dot q^2,
$$
$$
\mathcal V=\frac{T_0\pi^2}{4L}q^2
+\frac{E_YA_s\pi^4}{32L^3}q^4.
$$
Thus the effective modal mass is $\mu L/2$, and Lagrange's equation gives
$$
\boxed{\ddot q+\omega_0^2q+\alpha q^3=0},
$$
$$
\boxed{\omega_0^2=\frac{T_0\pi^2}{\mu L^2}},\qquad
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{E_YA_s\pi^4}{4\mu L^4}}.
$$
The positive cubic coefficient means hardening. For peak amplitude $Q$,
harmonic balance or averaging gives
$$
\boxed{\Omega\simeq\omega_0\left[1+
\frac{3E_YA_s\pi^2Q^2}{32T_0L^2}\right]}.
$$
The geometric expansion needs $\pi Q/L\ll1$, while the perturbative
frequency formula additionally needs
$E_YA_s\pi^2Q^2/(T_0L^2)\ll1$. These conditions test different approximations.

At a turning point, all modal energy is potential:
$$
\boxed{E_{\rm turn}=\frac{T_0\pi^2Q^2}{4L}
+\frac{E_YA_s\pi^4Q^4}{32L^3}}.
$$
Replacing $q^2(t)$ by $Q^2$ in the tension before variation creates a linear
oscillator with a guessed constant tension. It loses the instantaneous cubic
force, the correct energy, waveform distortion, and the coefficient $3/8$
that comes from averaging $q^3$ at the fundamental.

Numerically
$$
\boxed{\omega_0=314.159\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},\qquad
\boxed{f_0=50.0000\,\mathrm{Hz}}.
$$
The peak tension increase is
$\boxed{\Delta T_{\max}=0.986960\,\mathrm N}$. The leading fractional shift is
$$
\boxed{\frac{\Omega-\omega_0}{\omega_0}=0.00370110},
$$
so $\boxed{f\simeq50.1851\,\mathrm{Hz}}$. The turning-point energy is
$$
\boxed{E_{\rm turn}=9.91831\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J}.
$$
If longitudinal travel times are not short compared with the transverse
period, the added tension is not spatially instantaneous. Larger amplitudes
also excite other transverse modes and internal resonances, requiring a
multimode field model rather than this conservative one-coordinate reduction.

WAVE:010646.title: A smooth sinusoid overturns into a shock in finite time
WAVE:010646.objective: Use characteristics to locate the first gradient catastrophe of an inviscid nonlinear wave and mark the precise boundary between classical and entropy solutions.
WAVE:010646.statement:
On a periodic line, consider inviscid Burgers flow
$$u_t+u\,u_x=0,
\qquad u(x,0)=U\sin(kx),$$
with $U>0$ and $k>0$. Treat $u$ as a wave speed perturbation with units of
velocity; do not add viscosity unless explicitly discussing the post-breaking
extension.

Label characteristics by their initial position $\xi$. Derive the parametric
solution, the characteristic-map Jacobian, and the exact spatial gradient
before breaking. Find the first catastrophe time, every equivalent location
in the periodic domain, and the sign of the diverging slope. Explain why the
crest is not the first breaking location. Prove the solution remains a unique
classical field before that time and state what fails afterwards. Give the
implicit pre-shock form and audit conservation of the period mean and
quadratic integral while the solution is smooth. Explain what an entropy
solution and small positive viscosity change after shock formation.

For $U=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $k=\pi\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, calculate wavelength,
breaking time and location in one period, and the gradient at that location
at $t=0.100\,\mathrm s$. State the post-shock speed implied by symmetry at
the central descending zero crossing, without pretending that the pre-shock
parametric map remains single valued.
permittedResults: For $u_t+u u_x=0$, $u$ is constant along $dx/dt=u$.
The first breaking time for smooth data is $t_s=-1/\min_x u_0'(x)$ when that minimum is negative.

acceptableStrategies.description: Follow constant values along characteristics and monitor the map Jacobian.
Solve the differentiated PDE for the slope along characteristics and identify its Riccati blow-up from the minimum initial derivative.

milestones.criterion: States the physical model, transform or phase convention, variables, and controlling assumptions before applying formulas.
Locates breaking from loss of invertibility of the characteristic map and stops using the classical solution exactly when it becomes multivalued.
Completes the requested limiting, dimensional, numerical, or conservation checks and connects them to the mathematical result.
Uses coherent notation, reports units and signs where applicable, and distinguishes exact results from approximations or modeling interpretations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $x=\xi-U\sin(k\xi)t$ for the equation $u_t+u u_x=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The compression side, breaking location, and gradient sign are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Continues the overlapping characteristic map after its Jacobian vanishes and calls the multivalued result the solution.
commonErrors.consequence: No single-valued weak or entropy solution is supplied after breaking.

hintTree.content: Write $x=\xi+U\sin(k\xi)t$ and differentiate with respect to $\xi$.
The most negative initial slope occurs where $\cos(k\xi)=-1$.
Use change of variables from the current coordinate back to the characteristic label before the Jacobian vanishes.

WAVE:010646.canonicalSolution:
Along a characteristic, $du/dt=u_t+u u_x=0$.
Thus the characteristic launched at $\xi$ carries
$u=U\sin(k\xi)$ and follows
$$
\boxed{x(\xi,t)=\xi+U\sin(k\xi)t},\qquad
\boxed{u(x(\xi,t),t)=U\sin(k\xi)}.
$$
The map Jacobian and gradient are
$$
\boxed{x_\xi=1+Uk\cos(k\xi)t},
$$
$$
\boxed{u_x=\frac{Uk\cos(k\xi)}
{1+Uk\cos(k\xi)t}}.
$$
The first zero of the Jacobian occurs at the most negative initial slope,
$\cos(k\xi)=-1$. Hence
$$
\boxed{t_s=\frac1{Uk}},\qquad
\boxed{\xi_s=x_s=\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{k}},\quad j\in\mathbb Z.
$$
Since the sine vanishes there, the breaking characteristic remains at that
location. As $t\uparrow t_s$, its slope tends to $-\infty$. The crests have
$u_x=0$ initially; breaking occurs instead at the descending zero crossings,
where faster positive values behind catch slower or negative values ahead.

For $0\le t<t_s$, $x_\xi>0$ for every label, so the characteristic map is
one-to-one and defines a unique smooth solution. Eliminating the label gives
the implicit pre-shock relation
$$
\boxed{u(x,t)=U\sin[k(x-u(x,t)t)]}.
$$
After $t_s$, labels overlap, this relation has multiple branches, and the
classical construction is no longer a physical single-valued field.

For a smooth periodic solution, integration by parts gives
$d\int u\,dx/dt=0$ and $d\int u^2/2\,dx/dt=0$. Once shocks form, a weak
conservation law still preserves mean, but the entropy solution dissipates
the quadratic entropy. Adding small positive viscosity smooths the shock over
a thin layer and selects that entropy solution in the vanishing-viscosity
limit.

Numerically the wavelength is
$\boxed{\lambda=2\pi/k=2.00000\,\mathrm m}$ and
$$
\boxed{t_s=\frac1{2\pi}=0.159155\,\mathrm s},\qquad
\boxed{x_s=1.00000\,\mathrm m\pmod{2.00000\,\mathrm m}}.
$$
At that location and $t=0.100\,\mathrm s$,
$$
\boxed{u_x=\frac{-2\pi}{1-0.2\pi}
=-16.9048\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
For the symmetric periodic sine wave, the entropy shock emerging from the
descending zero crossing has equal and opposite left and right states, so
the Rankine--Hugoniot speed $(u_L+u_R)/2$ is $\boxed{0}$ and the central shock
remains at $x=1\,\mathrm m$ modulo a period. This post-shock statement uses
weak-solution symmetry, not a continuation of the now multivalued classical
map.
